en: The Nectar-Treasury of the Established Principles of Grammar.
Om! Salutations to the self-luminous one, the source of the attainment of fully kindled bliss.
Salutations to the pure Self of Consciousness, the cause of the cosmic manifestations.
To the one in whom the objects dwelling in the world are woven together with his own existence.
Salutations to the Brahman of speech, whose secrets are difficult to fathom. || 1.1.2 ||
With thousands of great rays of light arising from the great [sun], the kinsman of the day-lotuses, together with the winds.
Victorious is the triad of the great sages, like the three eyes of the moon-crested Lord Śiva.
Victorious is the splendor of the well-born Pārijāta tree of speech among those born as they were born.
[He is] a particle of the pollen from the lotus feet of the wise Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, who is an ornament of the learned. || 1.1.4 ||
One of small intellect is not at all able to find the way within the domain of the Lord of Serpents.
The streams of grace from the Lord of the Gods, moreover, begin to bring about assistance from afar. || 1.1.5 ||

Powerfully dispelling the doubt of one who desires thorough understanding and is affectionate toward the essence, and effortlessly intensifying the curiosity of the assembly of the most excellent wise men.

Having realized that state, Viśveśvara spreads forth this treasury of nectar— the Siddhānta— according to the scripture of the son of Dakṣī (Śaṅkarācārya), for the benefit of all who behold it through these many words.

In this regard, since the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), qualified by its own object, is the cause for engaging in action, the Bhāṣya—which aims to demonstrate that grammar is the means for knowing words—introduces itself when those persons who possess the aforementioned knowledge of correct words (*sādhuśabda*) have a desire for the means of knowing those words.

Now, regarding the phrase "atha śabdānuśāsanam" (now, the instruction of words): here, by virtue of the connection with the prefix (*upasarga*), the word *anuśāsana*—which inherently signifies that which brings about an understanding preceded by a distinction relative to its own class—assumes, through the force of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *śabda* ending in the genitive case, the sense of being directed toward valid knowledge (*pramā*) preceded by a distinction relative to corrupt words (*apaśabda*). Furthermore, since the suffix *lyuṭ* has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), and since the genitive in *śabdānām* functions as the denotation of the object of qualification (*viśeṣyatva*), and since the word *atha* signifies "commencement," [the meaning is established].

The meaning is that the treatise is commenced as the instrument for producing a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose qualifier is the difference (*bheda*), which has as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) that which is delimited by the state of being an incorrect word (*apaśabdatva*), and whose qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is a correct word (*sādhuśabda*). Consequently, even if some correct word were known through other means merely in its own form (*svarūpamātra*), the treatise would not be rendered useless; for it lacks the status of having the aforementioned difference as its qualifier. Nor should it be argued that such a status could indeed occur in some instances through the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) and so forth; for since words are infinite, that [status] is impossible in all cases.

And so it was said by the Blessed One: "Bṛhaspati taught Indra for a thousand celestial years the complete study of words (*śabdapārāyaṇa*) consisting of words formulated word-by-word, yet he did not reach the end. Nor should it be argued that even through grammar there is an impossibility of attaining a cognition whose qualificandum is delimited by each respective individuality and whose qualifier is the aforementioned difference, on the grounds that words are infinite; for while grammar provides knowledge of as many correct word-forms as it covers, it is impossible to know that same number of forms by any other means.

When there is knowledge of the word, it is impossible for that [knowledge] to have the aforementioned distinction as its qualifier in any other way. Furthermore, for a person who has not yet had the presentation of specific instances of correct words, the knowledge of the means for a cognition that has the aforementioned distinction as its qualifier—where the qualificandum is delimited by the nature of those specific instances—remains intact. Nor is it possible to grasp the distinctness from corrupt words merely through the apprehension of the co-occurrence of the universal "word-ness" (*śabdatva*) with an authoritative statement and so forth.

Because, in the absence of a specific qualification regarding the [speaker's] intent, there is no apprehension of that person's reliability; for it is only such a cognition as being unassailed by a knowledge of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*) that is intended [as the object]. Here, in the word *śabdānām*, the genitive case is governed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), and not by the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66). This is because the rule *karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.14) prohibits the formation of a compound with a term ending in a genitive case that is prescribed by the rule *ubhayaprāptau*. Some maintain that this is a "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, the word *atha* expresses the commencement [of the subject matter].

The word *atha* is employed here in the sense of "introducing a new topic" (*adhikāra*), according to the statement of the Blessed One [Śaṅkara]. However, its purpose is merely auspiciousness (*maṅgala*); it is not the primary denoted meaning, because it does not connect with the meaning of the sentence. This is clear from the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* and other works. By this, it is understood that: "At the beginning of creation, before the world, the syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha* emerged from Brahmā’s throat; therefore, both are auspicious."

Thus the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) has been explained. As for the claim that the word *atha* indicates the beginning but does not denote it—because it is a particle (*nipāta*), like a prefix (*upasarga*)—that is not correct. For the reason [given] lacks pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). Furthermore, being a prefix (*upasargatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor can it be argued that [the reason] is non-pervasive with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*) in cases such as *śa*, because it is pervasive with respect to the probandum as delimited by the property of being a particle (*nipātatva*). Nor should it be said that the probandum is simply the absence of denotative power (*vācakatvābhāva*), for [the reason] would then be non-pervasive with respect to the probandum in cases like *hi*, which serve merely to fill out a verse-line (*pādapūraṇa*) and thus constitute a locus of the probandum as delimited by the reason.

This is because the absence of a means of proving [the existence of] expressive power (*śakti*) serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of particles that resemble case-endings. However, the Miśras say: "If particles (*nipāta*) were merely denoters (*vācaka*), they would already be established by the rule *arthavad...* [Pāṇini 1.2.45]; thus, the Vārttika stating 'a particle that is meaningless receives the designation of a nominal stem' (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would be redundant. Conversely, if particles were indicators (*dyotaka*), then since there would be nothing to exclude from the scope of the rule, the qualifying portion 'that which is meaningless' (*anarthakasya*) would be superfluous. Therefore, words such as *ca* and so forth are denoters, whereas words such as *pra* and so forth are indicators."

As for the claim that the conclusion [of the *vārttika*] is not as stated because it is possible to reach a conclusion through the opposite interpretation as well—that is incorrect. For it is more reasonable to assume that a *vārttika* has a narrower scope than the *sūtra*.

As the learned scholars who know the *vārttikas* say: "That wherein an investigation (*cintā*) proceeds regarding what has been stated, what has not been stated, or what has been stated twice, they call that a *vārttika*."

This is because of that statement. Nor should it be argued that one could simply say, "In this way, the prefix [itself] would receive the designation of *prātipadika*"; for that objection applies equally to you as well regarding particles (*cādi*) and so forth. Furthermore, although the Vārttika stated in the rule *adhi-parī anarthakau* was refuted in the Bhāṣya, [the following argument remains]: in examples such as *kuto 'dhyāgacchati* and *kutaḥ paryāgacchati*, the designation of *karmapravacanīya* would be redundant, as it would supersede the designation of *gati* (which is intended to prevent the application of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *gati-gatau*). This is because, since the two terms are meaningless (*anarthaka*), there is an absence of connection with an action, and thus the status of being a *gati* does not arise at all.

Having raised the objection that since the status of [the words *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*] as prepositions (*upapada*) is already established by the rule "pañcamyā apāṅparibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.10), the present rule is unnecessary, it is stated in response: "The formulation of this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is for the purpose of making it known that even these [words], though devoid of meaning [in isolation], perform their function as if they possessed meaning. Furthermore, the non-employment of the aforementioned Vārttika is its specific purpose. Therefore, the interpretation based on that [objection] is indeed not to be trusted. That too is incorrect; for even by that much, it is established that the aforementioned meaning is the intended scope of the Vārttika.

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya himself introduced the two sūtras *jātyākhyāyām* and *sarūpāṇām*, even though they were to be rejected, as indicators (*jñāpaka*) for the two positions regarding universals (*jāti*) and individuals (*vyakti*). Alternatively, it is because the subsequent Bhāṣya states that these two [sūtras] are not purposeless, thereby asserting the necessity of prescribing those technical designations (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, this is supported by Kaiyaṭa’s statement that the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the prefixes *adhi* and *pari* possess a simultaneous denotative power (*sahābhidhāyitva*).

This is because the authority of this [specific] commentary leads one to infer that even the commentary on the sūtra *arthavat* lacks the intention to refute those vārttikas. Furthermore, Śākaṭāyana holds that "prepositions (upasarga), when fixed [in composition], express meaning through their own sense. Gārgya, however, maintains that "they serve to illuminate the connection with the action for nouns (nāman) and verbs (ākhyāta), and thus various word-meanings arise"; as it is said: "Whatever meaning these [prepositions] convey, they effect a modification of the meaning of the noun and the verb," and so forth.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the second chapter [of the *Nirukta*], it is stated: "Now, particles (*nipātas*) fall upon various meanings," and so forth; and because it is said that the function of prefixes (*upasargas*) is to modify the meaning of nouns and verbs, making them convey a different sense through their connection with those two, it is clear that particles (*nipātas*) function in the opposite manner.

As for the claim that in expressions such as *gurur upāsyate* ("the teacher is worshipped"), since the verbal root lacks the sense of a transitive action (*sakarmaka-kriyā*), the use of the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in the passive/objective sense would otherwise be untenable; therefore, just like prefixes (*upasarga*), particles (*nipāta*) must also possess a "manifestative" (*dyotaka*) function—this being necessitated by instances such as *sākṣātkriyate* ("is directly perceived") and *alaṅkriyate* ("is adorned")—that is not correct. For even if that were the case in specific instances, there is no evidence to justify such a postulation universally. This is because the tendency of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apply to general cases is necessarily governed by the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

As for the claim that the Vārttika was composed for the sake of cases where even the indicated meaning (*dyotya-artha*) is not intended to be expressed—citing Amara’s “*tu hi ca sma ha vai* [are used] for filling the verse-line" and the *Nirukta*’s "‘kaṃ īm id’ are for the purpose of filling the verse-line"—that too is incorrect, because other particles are established as being meaningful. As for the argument that it [the suffix] functions solely through the indicated meaning, that is not so; for the connection with the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*), which has become a qualifier (*prakārībhūta*) in the word, cannot be taken as referring to both meanings simultaneously by virtue of being the very nature of its function (*vṛtti-svarūpa*), following the pattern of words such as *rāma*.

Because there is no evidence for such a recurrence (*āvṛtti*). As for the claim that "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*) consists merely in being the object of a cognition that generates the comprehension of meaning—and not in possessing either direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—and that this [quality] is common to both expressive elements (*dyotaka*) and denoters (*vācaka*), that too is incorrect. For in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ*, the case-ending would result even from each individual phoneme. It might be argued: "Because the rules concerning the suffixes beginning with *su* (*svādi*) and the rules concerning number (*saṅkhyā*) form a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatva*), each individual [phoneme] does not denote number; therefore, [the objection] does not apply. To this effect is the *Bhāṣya* on the *Hayavaraṭ* sūtra:

[The opponent argues: "Because the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) has a single referent, there is no occurrence of *sup* [suffixes] after a phoneme. Or else, by the logic of reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana*), the case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises from the aggregate itself. Or else, by the logic of that which falls within [the whole] (*tanmadhyapatita-nyāya*), because each subsequent case-ending is a constituent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is elision (*luk*) according to the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*. Alternatively, the word *rāma* is a single unit ending in a compound-suffix (*samāsānta*); in that case, there is elision as in *rājapuruṣa* and similar forms. Regarding these, the first [position] is not correct. Since even particles (*nipāta*) do not denote number, the production of *sup* suffixes is unestablished.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the principle that "the singular number is the general rule," [the word *tad*] does not denote number even though it is used; for this would apply equally to each individual phoneme. Nor is the second alternative tenable, because the very basis for this [view] is that the parts are benefited by the operation of the whole, and because the case-ending following the whole belongs to each individual phoneme as a word (*pada*). Nor is the third alternative valid, because [the suffix] is not a part of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); for Kaiyaṭa has stated that the maxim regarding "that which falls within" applies only when a specific composite form of a word is being introduced.

Because the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), it is impossible for a mere collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) to be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable; for there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) in *dhanaṃ* and *vanaṃ*, the augment *ṅamuṭ* in *hastī* (due to *jaśtva*), the substitution of *ḍha* in *hastī*, the substitution of *gha* in *deha*, the substitution of *ṣ* in *parimṛjaḥ*, *yājakaḥ*, *rājā*, and *chāyā*, and the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) in *panthānau*.

However, if one were to argue that the absence of those respective grammatical operations is due to specific rules such as *dhanagaṇaṃ labdhā*, *vanagiryoḥ*, *ahastyādibhyaḥ*, *parimṛjāpanudoḥ*, *yājakādibhiśca*, *rājāhaḥ sakhibhyaḥ*, *chāyā bāhulye*, and *bhṛśādibhyaḥ*; and furthermore, that there is no compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) because the rule *ito 'tsarvanāmasthāne* prescribes the substitution of *āt* for the vowel of the word *pathin*. [The answer follows: This is not so. For the rule *dhanagaṇaṃ labdhā* is intended to apply to the word *dhana* when it is a separate item [not part of a compound]; the mention of *vana* and *giri* in *vanagiryoḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the application of the suffix *ka* [which would otherwise apply by *prāgvateṣṭhañ*] to the compounds *vanaka* and *girika*; the mention of *ahasti* in *ahastyādibhyaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṭhak* [which would otherwise apply by *tena krītam*] from the word *hastin* when preceded by *nañ*; the mention of *parimṛja* and *apanuda* in *parimṛjāpanudoḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *kha* [which would otherwise apply by *saṃpṛcānurudhādyam*] from the words *parimārjaka* and *apanodaka*; the mention of *yājaka* and others in *yājakādibhiśca* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṭac* [which would otherwise apply by *saptamī*] from the word *yājaka* when preceded by *nañ*; the mention of *rāja* and *ahan* in *rājāhaḥ sakhibhyaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṭac* [which would otherwise apply by *saptamī*] from the words *rājan* and *ahan* when preceded by *nañ*; the mention of *chāyā* in *chāyā bāhulye* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṅīp* [which would otherwise apply by *puṃyogādākhyāyām*] from the word *chāyā* when it denotes abundance; and the mention of *bhṛśa* and others in *bhṛśādibhyaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *kyaṅ* [which would otherwise apply by *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*] from the word *bhṛśa* when it denotes intensity. Thus, these rules do not serve to exclude the operations in question here. Moreover, since the rule *ito 'tsarvanāmasthāne* prescribes the substitution of *āt* for the final *i* of *pathin* only when followed by a non-*sarvanāmasthāna* case ending, this does not prevent the application of the compound-ending suffix. Therefore, the form *pathika* is established.

Otherwise, since the dual and plural numbers would already be established by that [rule], it would follow that the rule for *at* (the substitution of *a*) would apply only to *su* and *am*; such considerations lead to prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, because the rule for *at* must necessarily be prescribed for all *sarvanāmasthāna* endings in accordance with words like *mathin*, it would be prolix to prescribe it separately for *su* and *am* in the word *pathin*. Now, by the force of the inclusion of the term "end of a word" (*padānta*), those respective grammatical operations apply only when the designation "word" (*pada*) is applied to the entire aggregate.

If it is considered that, otherwise, because the designation *pada* would apply universally to every member occurring within a compound under this view, the inclusion of that [term "meaningful"] would be redundant, then in cases such as *rājapuruṣa*, the elision of the *n* (in *rājan*) would not occur; for that elision occurs precisely by virtue of the *pada*-designation applying to the preceding member which is a constituent of the compound. In fact, however, the authors of the Bhāṣya themselves have stated that the mention of "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is intended to exclude declensional endings from individual phonemes.

Even though meaningfulness is established through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the purpose [of the prohibition] is the exclusion of that which possesses similarity based on being prompted by another property; for if one intended the meaningfulness as you have stated it, that [meaningfulness] would be established even without that [exclusion]. Furthermore, this would result in the undesired consequence (the *iṣṭāpādana*) of what was stated by Kaiyaṭa and others: that if an "unmeaningful" element were to receive the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) according to the rule *arthavad...* etc., then since there would be no meaning to be manifested, the undesirable contingency would arise of producing case-endings for every individual phoneme, just as for a whole aggregate.

Therefore, by using the term *arthavat-pada* (meaning-bearing word) specifically to exclude phonemes (*varṇa*), the bringing forth of case-endings from them imitates the logic of the emergence of a *vetāla* (vampire) during a rite for peace (*śāntikarman*). As for the claim that case-endings follow from particles (*nipāta*) precisely as the counter-correlates of elision according to the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*, that is not correct; for it is accepted that the application of a word-meaning occurs through restatement (*anuvāda*) when there is no other means of obtaining it, and because such [elision] is possible due to the presence of vowels and so forth. Furthermore, as for the claim that case-endings follow from a meaningless particle according to the rule *nipātasyānarthakasya*, [that too is incorrect].

That too is incorrect; for by that very [argument], expressiveness (*vācakatva*) is not established on the basis of its coreferentiality with the nature of being a particle (*nipātatva*). As for the argument that, because the rule "the particles *adhi* and *pari* are meaningless" (*adhiparī anarthakau*) shows—by virtue of the qualifier—that even the meaningless words *adhi* and *pari* take a dual ending, one must therefore rely on the principle that the knowledge of case-endings following a meaningless particle depends on a general [rule], and thus a case-ending follows a particle even when it is meaningless—that too is incorrect.

Because the words *adhi* and *pari* possess meaning through their conformity with the form of the word (*śabda*) and its referent (*artha*); for the statement regarding their "meaninglessness" was intended precisely to convey that there is no meaning beyond the sense of the verbal root (*dhātu*), which resides in the object being imitated (*anukārya*). As for the claim that this is established by the particle *ca* in the rule *kṛt-taddhita-*, that too is incorrect.

The mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes [in Pāṇini’s rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that only a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in these suffixes receives the designation of *prātipadika*, and no other; and the mention of *samāsa* (compound) is also for the purpose of restriction, meaning that among meaningful aggregates (*arthavat-samudāya*), only the compound receives the designation of *prātipadika*. This is because the *Bhāṣya* and other works state that this rule serves as a restrictive one. Furthermore, if the particle *ca* were intended to introduce a new injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), it would contradict its co-occurrence [with the restrictive sense]. Even if one were to gather those [meanings] together out of necessity in some instances, it would be inappropriate to do so arbitrarily. By this [it is shown that]: "That [word] is either expressive (*vācaka*) of particulars because they are possible, or else it is indicative (*dyotaka*)."

Thus, the *Vākyapadīya* has been explained as having the sense of an option that is restricted (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). Furthermore, distinctions that are possible in certain instances but not indicated by the verbal roots alone are manifested through their connection with prefixes such as *pra*, *parā*, and so forth.

Thus, because the discussion began with *upasargas*, it must be stated that the word *tat* refers exclusively to those [prefixes]. This is because it would be untenable for even your own accepted view—that it is merely a particle (*nipāta*)—to possess both forms [of being a prefix and a particle]; whereas if it were intended to refer merely to the particle introduced previously, there would be no contradiction even in the aforementioned [explanation]. By this, the claim that there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in "a jar and so forth" (*ghaṭaśca*) regarding the conjoined jar is also refuted, because that would contradict the rule that a *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of *ca*. Nor does it follow that it would be used independently, since it is identical [in function] to suffixes and the like. And thus says the *Vākyapadīya*: "Even though it is expressive, a suffix is not used in isolation."

"Even when there is an expression of conjunction (*samuccaya*), no distinction (*vyatireka*) exists. Nor should it be said that for these [particles], there is no grammatical instruction regarding their subordinacy (*paratva*) as in the case of suffixes (*pratyaya*); for conjunction and the like, which constitute their meaning, do not appear without something related to them. And thus says the *Vākyapadīya*:

Even when expressing a collective sense, words are connected with their respective qualifiers by virtue of denoting a specific meaning; however, particles such as *ca* and others are dependent on those [qualifiers].

Thus [it is said]. For when only the particle *ca* is uttered, there is the intended understanding of mere conjunction (*samuccaya*). Precisely for this reason, there arises an expectancy for a specific counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) in that case. Precisely for this reason, since the verbal cognition of an absence unmixed with a counter-correlate arises from expressions such as "not" (*na*), the very nature of the perceptibility of an absence is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the causal efficacy of the knowledge of the counter-correlate. Precisely for this reason, it is shown in the Bhāṣya that when "nanu" is uttered, the meaning is "there is no absence. This is because it is stated that even by means of a particle (*nipāta*), a case-role (*kāraka*) can be denoted.

Furthermore, because we observe the suffix *tumun* (infinitive) based on its connection with a verbal action in such passages as "it is not even appropriate for you to avoid [it]," and because the *bhūvādi* sūtra commentary states "not at all," and because the fact that the particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) is established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and in the section on conjunction (*samuccayādhikaraṇa*), and because all tantric authorities employ the term "exclusion by negation" (*paryudāsa*) regarding the negative particle (*nañ*).

Nor should it be argued that the qualifier is connected with the sense of *ca* (and) even in the case of "a beautiful conjunction" (*śobhanaḥ samuccayaḥ*), and that there would likewise be a genitive case—as in "the conjunction of the pot and the cloth. This is because such an understanding would contradict the fact that the object presented by an indeclinable (*nipāta*) cannot function as the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) when its qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) is delimited by a relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*). Furthermore, the referent of a noun is connected to the sense of *ca* by way of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*). For this very reason, in the expression "the pot is not" (*ghaṭo na*), the cognition has counter-correlativity as its relation.

In the expression "the absence of a jar" (*ghaṭasyābhāvaḥ*), [the relation] has the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) as its qualifier; for it is impossible for the meaning of a noun—other than an indeclinable (*nipāta*)—to enter into a relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*). As for the verse:
"As one would uproot the northern mountains with sharp arrows, as if they were grass... [this is explained as follows].

In such instances as "with arrows resembling rays" (*usrasadṛśaiḥ śaraiḥ*), the view that [particles like *iva*] are merely indicators (*dyotaka*) is possible; however, that is incorrect. For in that case, similarity itself is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to the arrows by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas of poetry, which holds that when words such as *iva* are employed, the simile is verbal (*śrautī*), whereas when words such as *sadṛśa* are used, it is figurative (*ārthī*). Furthermore, the case-ending following the word *usra* serves only for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Let this suffice. It might be argued: "Even prefixes (*upasarga*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) alone."

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as *na ca tatra prajayati* ("he does not excel there"), the meaning of the prefix (*pra-*)—namely, excellence (*prakarṣa*)—could not be construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) by way of being its locus; for if there were no such construction of difference between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of such a relation in cases like *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"). This objection is invalid because "noun" (*nāman*) is qualified by the condition of being distinct from a particle (*nipātātirikta*). Furthermore, in the view of the Guru (Prabhākara), regarding the sentence *na kalañjaṃ bhakṣayet* ("one should not eat *kalañja*"), the verbal root-meaning functions as a qualifier of the absence (*abhāva*) through its status as the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*), such that the meaning is: "there is an obligation (*kārya*) whose object is the absence of eating *kalañja*."

In the Nyāya system, the eating of *kalañja* [is understood] as the absence of the non-existence of the state of not producing sin; furthermore, because it is a qualifier, it functions as a mode (*prakāra*) within the meaning of the verbal root. Moreover, in cases such as "he does not see the sky," since a visual perception possessing ordinary objective reference (*laukika-viṣayatā*) directed toward the sky is unestablished, there arises the cognition of the absence of having the sky as its object within the act of seeing. Furthermore, in your own view as well, there would result the undesirable consequence of cognizing an excellence of staying (*sthitiprakarṣa*) through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "pratiṣṭhate" (he stands).

This is because the claim that "the property of being a cognition qualified by the mode 'going-ness' (*gamanatva-prakāraka-bodhatva*) is the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*)" is equally applicable to the stated co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*). Furthermore, by accepting that the prefix *pra-* has the sense of negation (*abhāva*), when it is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—namely, the absence of going—as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there arises the cognition of the absence of the absence of going. Thus, as in the case of "the pot is not" (*ghaṭo na*), there is no deficiency even in the absence of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth.

The authors of the *Kandalī* and others maintain that in cases such as *upāsyate*, although the prefix (*upasarga*) functions as a dyotaka (indicator) due to the force of the otherwise inexplicability of the respective meanings, there is no logical flaw. Regarding this, they argue as follows: Since it is simpler to assume that the power of the verbal root (*dhātu*), which is already established with respect to the substantive element (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), also extends to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the prefix serves merely to delimit that power rather than being itself endowed with a power; for otherwise, one would incur the fault of having to postulate a separate power. However, this is not the case according to the aforementioned view, because it is precisely the presence of mutually exclusive multiple grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) that necessitates the postulation of distinct powers.

However, since the state of being "superior victory" (*prakṛṣṭajayatva*) is pervaded by the state of being "victory" (*jayatva*), if it is considered—on the grounds of parsimony—that there is a difference in denotative power (*śakti*) merely due to a difference in the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), then let there be only indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of "superior victory. But how can there be indication in the case of "qualified victory" (*viśiṣṭajaya*), given that the qualified is not a different entity? For a relation defined by itself cannot exist in itself. On this point, Miśra and others hold: the relation of identity (*abheda*) is here the delimitor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence that the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) would also have indication with respect to a jar.

For that [prefix] is accepted solely for the purpose of conveying a cognition characterized by a specific quality (*viśeṣaprakāraka*). Likewise, in the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, there would be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between the meaning of the prefix and the meaning of the suffix, because it would not be the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). Nor can it be argued that "absence of motion" is the meaning of the prefix *pra* while "absence" is the meaning of the root; for this would entail the fallacies of abandoning what has been done (*kṛtahāna*) and acquiring what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Nor can it be argued that "motion" and "absence" are two distinct meanings of the root, such that "motion" connects with the meaning of the prefix (absence), and that absence connects with the meaning of the root (absence).

Because the connection of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) with the action (*gati*) is more immediate due to being governed by the same grammatical word (*samānaśruti*), and because a cognition characterized by the mode "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) is not established [otherwise], such is the direction of the argument. Let us return to the subject at hand. Now, an objection may be raised: "If *śabdatva* (the property of being a word) alone were the delimitor of what is to be defined (*vyutpādyatāvacchedaka*), then it would be common to both correct words (*sādhū*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*s). This is not so, because it is *sādhutva* (correctness) that possesses this status. And that will be defined later. Furthermore, there is no other purpose in defining the suffixes *ḍa*, *ap*, *sup*, substitutes (*ādeśa*), and so forth, since they are useful for the comprehension of words such as "cow" (*gauḥ*).

Nor should it be argued that [the definition] lacks unique utility because it is applicable even in cases such as "Rāma" (where the *sup* suffix is present), nor that it lacks utility in cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) because it does not apply to the delimitor of the state of being derivable (*vyutpādyatāvacchedaka*). This is because it is precisely the lack of utility with respect to the delimitor of the state of being definable (*nirūpaṇīyatāvacchedaka*) that leads to the fallacy of a different meaning (*arthāntara*). For if utility were established merely through co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the delimitor of the state of being derivable, there would be no room for such a fallacy.

Although the relationship of denoted and denoter exists between [the word] and categories such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), these have been examined elsewhere and are not useful for the comprehension of the nature of the word itself. Words are of two kinds: worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*). Worldliness consists in being fit for use by persons possessing generated knowledge. Vedic-ness, however, consists in being employed exclusively in the Vedas. Furthermore, the term "Veda" refers solely to that which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), provided it has as its object a thing that is not the content of a valid cognition produced by any means of knowledge other than the word and the means of knowledge dependent upon that word.

Therefore, there is no harm even if Vedic words are employed in the *Smṛtis* and other such texts. These [examples] are: "śannodevīrabhiṣṭaye," "iṣetvorjetvā," "agnimīḍepurohitam," and "agnaāyāhivītaye"—so says the commentary (*bhāṣya*). The citation of the first example is for the purpose of establishing that all Vedic words are derivable [through grammar], and to indicate its distinction from the *Prātiśākhyas*, which derive only a portion of the Veda. The word "devīḥ" (goddesses), being in the nominative plural, is mentioned first because it is a Vedic form.

In the phrase *iṣetva*, the form *śreṣṭhatamāya* [is used] because the suffix *tamap* is elided; the absence of elision in *īśate* and the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇa-dīrgha* in *bahvīḥ* are both due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). Nor should it be argued that, even so, *śanno devīḥ* must have its primacy after *agnim īḷe* rather than after *iṣe*, since there is no reason for violating the sequence when Vedic usage applies to both cases. This is because a disparity exists: in one case the word indicating Vedic usage (*chāndasa*) occurs within the very mantra-portion (*pratīka*), whereas in the other it occurs subsequent to it.

It might be argued as follows: Even the meanings of Vedic words are purely worldly, for even when words such as *ghṛtācī* are used in the Veda for things like the night, there is no difference in the referent (*vācya*). Furthermore, there is no evidence that word and meaning are absolutely distinct from one another, since in common usage such as "this is a cow," it is precisely their non-difference (*abheda*) that is apprehended. For instance, even in your own view, in the process of verbal cognition, the word appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to its meaning through the relation of *śakti* (denotative power), just as a universal (*jāti*) appears in relation to an individual through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). As it is said: "The capacity to be grasped (*grāhyatva*) and the capacity to grasp (*grāhakatva*) are two powers of the word, just as [heat and light are] of fire."
In the same way, these [phonemes] exist separately from all words.

Because it has been said thus. Furthermore, even in mere cognition, there is the manifestation of words. As it has been stated: "There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words;
every cognition appears as if permeated by words."
For it is possible to recall a word from its meaning, just as one recalls a meaning from a word whose relationship has been grasped. As it has been said:
"The recollection of the name that occurs therein does not itself have another cause;
for it is the individual object (piṇḍa) alone, when perceived, that is capable of causing the name to be remembered."

Although there is no agreement with the statement cited from Vācaspati and others—since they explain that "not caused by anything else" means "not caused by identity with the individual"—there is nevertheless agreement regarding the aspect of establishing the rule for the presentation of meaning through words. This is the formal argument: The meaning is non-different from the word, because it is not the object of a cognition that does not have the word as its object. Whatever is not the object of a cognition that does not have X as its object is non-different from X; for example, a cow itself is not the object of a cognition that does not have the cow as its object, and thus it is non-different from itself.

For this restriction does not apply when there is absolute difference; otherwise, it would follow that a horse and a buffalo must necessarily never be the objects of a cognition that takes the other as its object. Thus, since there is no difference in meaning, even the distinction between Vedic and worldly words is untenable; so how can they be described as falling into two groups? It is with this very intention that the *Bhāṣya* asks: "In the case of 'cow,' what is the word?"

Nor should it be argued that the Bhāṣya’s suspicion regarding the non-difference of the word [from its meaning] is unjustified, on the grounds that while the substance (*dravya*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) are indeed objects of the cognition "this is a cow," qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) are not so; for, having raised the objection as to how difference and non-difference—which are contradictory—can coexist, the example is provided precisely to address this. Furthermore, proponents of both difference and non-difference accept non-difference even in those cases. Nor should it be asked: "Even if qualities and actions are not [non-different from the word], how can there still be such a suspicion of their non-difference from the word? [The answer is: Because the Bhāṣya intends to show that the relationship between the word and its meaning is one of identity, and that this identity is not restricted solely to substances and universals. Thus, by citing qualities and actions as examples, it demonstrates that the same principle applies to them as well. Therefore, the Bhāṣya is entirely consistent.

It should not be argued that because the word is non-different from the substance, its non-difference from the word is also established; nor that in that case there is non-difference through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), whereas in the present case, since they are the objects of a single cognition, one does not admit such a notion as "the word 'jar' is the jar. For this reason, the means of proof (*sādhana*) for the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would not be identical. This is incorrect, because when the aforementioned proof is stated, another proof has already been mentioned.

It is precisely because we observe the linguistic usage of non-difference between word and object in cases such as "this is a cow" that the *Śaṅkābhāṣya* (the section on doubt) is introduced here. However, some explain the refutation passage as follows, with the intention that even for the word "cow," the relation in the case of the cow might simply be identity (*tādātmya*). They argue that in this way, since what is non-different from that which is non-different from [a substance] is itself non-different from it, there could be a suspicion of non-difference between the word and substances, qualities, and universals; having thus explained the doubt regarding non-difference, they interpret the refutation text accordingly.

[Objection: Even though both the difference from a conventional cloth and the identity with an illusory cloth exist in a jar, difference and identity of equal ontological status (*samasattāka*) are indeed contradictory. Otherwise, since there would be no difference between existence, quality-ness, and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence that pleasure, pain, heaven, hell, and the like would also be non-different; consequently, there would be no distinction between engagement and withdrawal based on the apprehension of difference, nor would there be the cessation of error through the apprehension of difference. [Response: This is to be considered. For in cases such as "the jar is blue," those who maintain that [position] admit only difference and identity of equal ontological status.

This has been stated in the *Vācaspatya*: "Our conviction that something is contradictory arises only when it lacks authoritative evidence; however, in the cognition of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), both difference and non-difference appear. Consequently, although there is no co-referentiality between a counter-positive and its absence elsewhere, such co-referentiality is accepted in the case of conjunction and its absence in accordance with experience. Furthermore, even though pleasure, pain, and so forth are non-different from existence (*sattā*) and the like, the restriction of activity and other functions is established precisely because they possess difference by virtue of their own specific attributes (*prātisvikadharma*).

[Objection: Since the state of having contradictory objects (*virodhiviṣayakatva*) alone is the essential factor (*tantra*) for sublation (*bādhakatva*), error is removed by the apprehension of difference; furthermore, if the restriction [of the relation] arises by taking the power-relation (*śaktisaṃbandha*) as the mode (*prakāratā*), then a subsequent suspicion that identity (*tādātmya*) is the relation cannot arise. [Reply: It is said: There is no non-difference (*abheda*) between two word-meanings (*padārtha*), because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—since we accept the difference between a substance (*dravya*) and a universal (*sāmānya*), even though they have objects necessarily determined by a single cognition. Nor should it be argued that in an inference such as "it possesses cowness" (*gotvavān*), the cow and so forth do not function as the object (*viṣayatva*).

Since "cowness" (*gotvatva*) appears as the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), the individual cow (*go*) is also an object of cognition by virtue of being a constituent part of that [cowness]. Thus, by the statement "that which is called substance is that which is called generality," an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is stated regarding the reason under discussion. Furthermore, the division [of the definition] is stated such that the example is unestablished (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) due to the exclusion of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*). To explain: in the case of "the pot is blue," does the grammatical coreferentiality (*śābda-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) establish non-difference, or is it the factual coreferentiality (*ārtha*)? It is not the first, because it would be contradictory, as it establishes only difference.

Not the latter; for, since it is established in both ways, it is incapable of proving that [the word is the object], so say the teachers beginning with Udayana. A detailed discussion is found in the *Tarkakautūhala*. It might be argued as follows: there is no evidence for the assumption that verbal cognition has the word as its object, because such a natural experience is lacking. Nor should it be said that the assumption of the word "cow" (*gopada*) as the qualifier is not excessive, given that the qualifierhood of "cowness" (*gotva*) is universally established, because by means of a specific conventional relation (*saṅketaviśeṣasambandha*), the word "cow" itself is of the nature of cowness.

This is because it would involve the unnecessary postulation of a modehood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the wordhood of "cow" (*gopadatva*), since one already accepts that the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) itself constitutes the mode; and because it would entail accepting that "cowness" is a mode by way of inherence (*samavāya*); and because it would result in the impossibility of [the object] being verbal (*śābda*), as the word itself is not the object of its own function (*vṛtti*); and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that even ether (*ākāśa*) and other things—which are presented from the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) as being related by inherence—would also be verbal objects. Nor should it be argued that the state of being the object of a function consists simply in possessing a function through either the relation of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) or the relation of being a determiner (*nirūpakatva*).

Because there is no evidence for [the word] being the locus (āśraya). As for the argument that in cases such as "utter the word *gā-ve*," the syntactic connection would otherwise be untenable—since it is impossible to utter a meaning and since there is the burden of assuming a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of the word—it is not so; for us, however, since the word is present as a qualifier, its connection with the act of utterance is logically established.

Nor should it be argued that there is no *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the sake of making the individual the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because the property of being a cognition having the word as the qualifier and the individual as the qualificand (*padaprakārakavyaktiviśeṣyakabodhatva*) alone constitutes the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), just as in cases such as "the jar is eternal. For in those cases, such a status [of the word as qualifier] exists precisely to conform to a cognition whose qualifier is "jar-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*); furthermore, otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence of a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition regarding the aspect of "jar-ness. In the present case, however, since the specific phonetic sequence (*ānupūrvīviśeṣa*) also appears as the delimiter of the word, that consequence does not arise; moreover, if the individual as the qualificand were not to appear, the primacy of the word would be established by implication.

Alternatively, it might be argued that the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) of the cognition of word-potency (*śaktijñāna*) is not "being a cognition having a word as its qualifier" (*padaprakārakabodhatva*), but rather "being a cognition having cowness as its qualifier" (*gotvaprakārakabodhatva*) alone, because this is what is presented first; and by the force of the general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*), the word appears as a qualifier, since the rule that [a universal] must be a qualifier in a perceptual cognition following an indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpakottarapratyakṣa*)—just as with a genus—is thus established. This too is incorrect, because that which is presented as the delimiting factor of an individual cannot be construed with something else.

For it is precisely for the sake of independent presentation (*svatantra-upasthiti*) that the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is employed there with respect to "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). For this very reason, the *Darpaṇa*, the *Cintāmaṇi*, and other works maintain that the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") has indication with respect to the water-lily (*kumuda*). This is the essential point here: when a word presents its meaning under a certain form (*rūpa*), if it is possible for that meaning to connect with the meanings of other words in that same form, there is no indication. As in the case of "The cow is impermanent" (*gaur anityaḥ*). For "cow-ness" (*gotva*), which is presented as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), is fit to connect with impermanence as a delimiting factor.

In the case of "The cow is eternal" (*gauḥ nityaḥ*), however, because that [cow] which is presented as a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) is unfit for the connection with eternality as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), [the word "cow"] is not [the cause]. This is because a presentation produced by a word is the cause for a cognition in which the word-meaning is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and [something else] is the qualificand. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as the object (*karmatva*) in sentences such as "See the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ paśya*); furthermore, there would be no harm even if a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of pot-ness were to arise.

Furthermore, if the condition for the causality of the knowledge of the word *go*’s power (śakti) toward a cognition that has the word as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and the individual object as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) were either "having the same object" (*samānaviṣayakatva*) or "having the same qualifier" (*samānaprakārakatva*), then the recollection of the word *go* without it being the qualificand would be impossible. Nor should it be argued that there must simply be a recollection where the word *go* is the qualificand and the word *go* is the qualifier related by the relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*); for identity is not included in the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the effect of the knowledge of the power.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of even a cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and "pot-ness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*) [occurring]. Furthermore, if mere mental presence (*upasthiti*) were the regulator for something being an object of verbal cognition (*śābdaviṣayatva*), it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For it is not the case that something appears in verbal cognition simply because it is mentally present; this is evident from the statement of the author of the *Dīdhiti*. Moreover, the existence of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends its substrate (*dharmigrāhakamāna*) in that very way [as devoid of qualifiers]. Therefore, there is no evidence for the appearance of the word itself in verbal cognition; and if it appeared in any cognition at all, it would be even more so [absurdly] in the case of mere cognition.

For you yourself admit that the cognition of an individual (vyakti) serves as a reminder of the word, since it is stated that "only when the individual object is perceived does [the word] act as a stimulus," for it is impossible for that which is unknown to be a stimulator. Thus, it must be said that the initial cognition of the individual is indeed devoid of the word as its object, because at that time the word is not present. Consequently, the deviation (vyabhicāra) is quite evident; for there is no such after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) as "I know the cow by means of the word 'cow'," in the way that one has "I know the cow by means of cowness" (gotva). To this, the following is said in reply: [The opponent's position: It is established that the initial cognition of the individual is devoid of the word, because the word is not present at that time. Therefore, the deviation is clear, as there is no after-cognition such as "I know the cow through the word 'cow'," in contrast to "I know the cow through cowness. Since it is necessary to postulate that cognition in general has words as its objects in accordance with experience, the rule is postulated that the causal complex for cognition in general (*jñānasāmānyasāmagrī*) brings about the understanding of an object precisely as qualified by a word. Therefore, there is no deficiency even in the absence of the contact of a *vṛtti* (mental modification) and so forth. For this very reason, the Naiyāyikas maintain that the fact that desire and the like have the "I" portion (*mad-aṃśa*) and so forth as their objects is not determined by [external] causes. Furthermore:

It is an established fact of experience that for one who has not grasped the word-potency (*pada-śakti*) regarding the word "pot," even when there is a visual contact (*cakṣuḥ-sannikarṣa*) with a pot, a visual cognition having "potness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and the "pot" as its substantive (*viśeṣya*) does not arise. This restrictive rule (*niyama*) is caused solely by the absence of the causal complex for a cognition qualified by a word through the relation of potency; since other causes are present, the absence [of the effect] must have the absence of that [causal complex] as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, the verbal component (*śabda-bhāga*) must be admitted as the factor whose absence acts as the cause of that absence. However, this is the distinction:

Sometimes a certain property (*kiñcitpadatva*) serves as the delimiting factor of the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedaka*), and sometimes it is *ghaṭatva*, *paṭatva*, and so forth. This should be understood even in other philosophical systems, because the experience [of such cognition] cannot be denied. For this very reason, in the *Bhāmatī* commentary on the established conclusion of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-sūtra* (1.3.13), "Because [the Imperishable] supports everything up to the ether," it is admitted that even in mere knowledge there is the status of having a word as its object. However, a name (*saṃjñā*)—due to the force of extreme repetition by those who have grasped the relationship [between word and object]—is remembered as having entered into the individual object (*piṇḍa*) itself, arriving through the occasion of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). As it is said:
"In that case, there is the recollection of the name," and so forth.
For even when it is being remembered, a name does not sublate the perceptual nature [of its object];
for that name stands apart from the named thing and is incapable of obscuring its form.

Thus [it is said]: by those who have grasped the relationship and possess knowledge of the signified and the signifier, the [word] does not reside in the individual [object], as it has not attained identity with the particular. Since the name being remembered is remote (*parokṣa*), the object qualified by it would not be perceptible; therefore, [the sūtra says] "accompanied by the name" (*saṃjñā-hī*). Even though the name is being remembered, it does not obstruct the perceptibility of the named object (*saṃjñin*). For that [name] stands apart and is not inherent in the object; therefore, it is incapable of obscuring the true nature of the object.

The meaning is that because two cognitions—consisting of apprehension (*grahaṇa*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*)—are admitted, a perception of the designatum (*saṃjñin*) as qualified by the name (*saṃjñā*) is not admitted. Thus, it is stated in the *Līlāvatī*: "Nor is the word the object of a perception of relation; therefore, only the relation to the universal (*jāti*) appears therein. However, the word, understood at the time of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), is recollected here, but no relation whatsoever appears," and so forth.

And thus, the distinction in the view of the Grammarians (Śābdika) is simply that even the word (*śabda*) appears as a qualifier of the individual (*vyakti*). This is the direction [of the argument]. Now, one might object: "Even so, how can the word be a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the individual through the relation of *śakti* (denotative power), since in this system it is the *sphoṭa* alone that possesses denotative capacity? Otherwise, there would be no evidence for the existence of the *sphoṭa* itself. This is true; however, such a statement is made by taking up a denotative capacity that is merely superimposed (*āropita*). Now, there is a dispute regarding the *varṇasphoṭa*: namely, whether suffixes such as *tip* and so forth are denotative or not.

If the expressive power (*bodhakatva*) of the *l*-class suffixes and so forth belongs to those [suffixes] as remembered by the Tibetans and others, then it falls under the negative alternative (*niṣedhakoṭi*); but if it belongs only to those that are actually heard, then it falls under the positive alternative (*vidhi*). Others, however, state a dispute concerning the substituendum (*sthānin*), asking whether the phonemes not included within the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the word being employed are expressive or not. In the first case, the positive alternative belongs to the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and the negative alternative to the Logicians (*naiyāyika*) and others; in the second case, however, the situation is reversed.

Now, in the first case, by taking the suffix *ktip* and so forth, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) if it is a positive injunction (*vidhi*), and sublation (*bādha*) if it is a negation (*niṣedha*). In the second case as well, by taking the phonemes contained within expressions such as *yajasi* that are not included within the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of expressions such as *pacasi*, the same fallacies of *siddhasādhana* and *bādha* arise. Nor can it be argued that being a substitute (*ādeśatva*) is the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) in the first case, while being a substituendum (*sthānitva*) is so in the second; for even so, those two [cases] would still not be excluded because they possess the capacity to denote singularity and so forth.

Even in the second [interpretation], in instances such as the substitution of *bhū*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of those two [the suffixes] being denotative of the verb *as* (to be) and so forth, since they are not included within the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words like *abhūt*. True; however, because the state of being the denotator of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth constitutes the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*). This is well-known: that [denotative power] exists in words such as *pacati* (he cooks), while its absence exists in words such as *ghaṭa* (pot). Furthermore, "not being included within the co-occurrence with *pacati* and so forth" is a qualifier for *ti*-suffixes and the like. And in the case of the second [interpretation], in such instances, the only recourse is to restrict the scope of the subject (*pakṣasaṅkoca*).

And this position is accepted in the *sthānivadbhāva* sūtra within the *bhāṣya* passage beginning with "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words," by relying on the fact that the word *pada* refers to the meaning—based on the etymology "that by which the meaning is known"—and by such passages as: "the meaning of *erur* is *testuḥ*, because the relationship between the original (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) rests only upon that which possesses meaning. Regarding this, they say: the *lakāra* alone is the expressive element, and not the *asti*, *si*, and so forth occurring within the actual usage, because that would entail the postulation of multiple expressive powers (*śakti*).

This is also because of the grammatical rule, "laḥ karmaṇi," and so forth. Nor can it be argued that for those who lack the cognition of the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), understanding would be impossible; for such understanding is possible through a misconception (*bhrama*) regarding their expressive power (*śakti*). Furthermore, one should not say that there would be no disparity in understanding between [the suffixes] *śatṛ* and others and the *lakāra*, since the expressive *lakāra* is one and the same; for according to the rule "kṛt [suffixes denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), and because of the coreferential relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and its referent, those [suffixes like *śatṛ*] have the agent and so forth as their primary denotatum.

As for the point that—regarding forms such as *rāma*, the followers of Pāṇini prescribe the suffix *sup*, while the followers of Kumāra prescribe *sim*, others prescribe the suffix *rup*, and in the case of *tāvān*, according to the method of the Sūtra, they prescribe *vat*; furthermore, according to the method stated in the Vārttika of the former teachers—"the substitution of *ā* occurs for a pronoun" (*ā sarvanāmnaḥ*)—they prescribe *ḍāvat* because of the distinction in meaning—one might ask: what is there to be remembered here? Nor can it be said that one should remember the specific forms found in the grammar one has studied oneself, since there is no criterion for deciding which among those who have studied all grammars is correct. That is not so.

This is because a systematic arrangement is possible according to the respective indicators (*udbodhaka*), and because when there is a convergence [of multiple indicators], there is no redundancy (*vaiyarthya*) in either one. Nor should it be argued that, since the substituends (*sthānin*) are also numerous according to the aforementioned method, the assumption of multiple powers (*śakti*) is equal [in both cases], and that the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) determines the power only with respect to the substitutes (*ādeśa*). This is because the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) serves to determine the power. Nor should it be argued that its purpose lies solely in the instruction of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva-anuśāsana*) and not in the determination of power. For it is said: "The apprehension of power [is obtained] from grammar, comparison, lexicons, the speech of reliable persons, and usage."
The elders declare that [the meaning] is established through the remainder of the sentence, through explicit exposition, and through the proximity of a word whose meaning is already known.

Thus, in the first stage [of analysis], the assumption of that [additional power] is untenable; for it is also untenable on the basis of supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) and so forth. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would contradict the *trivṛccaru* and other such authoritative sections (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, common usage (*vyavahāra*) itself does not intend to convey such a [separate] power, since the grounds for inferring it are equally applicable [to both sides]. Moreover, you yourself have admitted that the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) cited is the very authority for the existence of the agent’s power (*kartṛśakti*), and because you accept an additional power in cases such as the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24).

Nor does it follow that [the word] *bhū* alone is the cause of cognition, because it is equivalent to *bhūti*. This is because both are equally the objects of the application of other rules, such as those concerning the suffix *śap*, and because they are likewise equally incomplete. Furthermore, the knowledge that a form is ungrammatical (*asādhutva*) is an obstacle to verbal cognition. Nor should it be argued that the meaning "the letters are the denoters" follows from the lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamakābhāva*)—namely, whether it is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words like *bhavati* or the letters themselves that are the denoters.

For co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) is sometimes of the nature of a preceding or succeeding element, as in the case of a stem and suffix in "ghaṭam" and so forth; and sometimes it is of the nature of intention (*tātparya*), as in "The king’s son comes; let the man be removed. Even when such co-utterance exists [in the latter example], there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the king and the man because of the absence of intention. Furthermore, its status as a denotative factor (*vācakatā*) has never been stated anywhere, since its function as an auxiliary consists solely in the specific syntactic relation among the meanings presented by the words.

Even granting your position, we say: you yourself must admit that the letter *l* possesses denotative power (*vācakatva*). If the letter *l* were the denoter, there would be a discrepancy between it and suffixes such as *tiP* and *śatṛ*. Nor can this be resolved by the rule "kṛt [suffixes] denote the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), because that rule does not apply to *śatṛ* and others, since they are already satisfied by the meaning of the substituendum (*sthānin*) itself; whereas *ṇvul* and other such suffixes, not being substitutes, do require a meaning and thus the rule applies to them. This is established by the maxim that "the prescription of what is required is superior."

In that case, if the letter *l* (the *lakāra*) does not denote any meaning whatsoever, how could there be a cessation of the expectancy for meaning regarding the suffixes *śatṛ* and so on through its meaning? And how, by means of that [letter], could there be the suffix *śānac* in the sense of a state (*bhāva*) in examples such as "he was going" (*ayaṃ gataḥ*), or in the sense of an object (*karman*) in examples such as "the pot is being made" (*ghaṭaḥ kriyamāṇaḥ*)?

If it is argued that—according to our own view, since suffixes such as *śānac* and others are likewise substitutes for *l*, one may simply superimpose the denotative power residing in them onto the *l*-suffix and thereby accept the statement regarding its meaning—let this matter rest for now; however, the claim that the Mīmāṃsakas hold the view of the Naiyāyikas (Tārkikas) that the *l*-suffix alone is the denoter is unproven. This is because the Ācārya [Udayana] stated in the *Kusumāñjali* that the *tiṅ*-suffix has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the operation (*vyāpāra*), and the Upādhyāya [Śrīdhara] held that the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) is merely the number, such as singularity.

Even in the *Ākhyāta-dīdhiti*, although some have explained that "verbal suffix-ness" (*ākhyātatva*) is simply the property of being a *la*-suffix (*latva*), which is common to all ten tenses (*lakāras*), it has nevertheless been explained as follows: verbal suffix-ness is not a universal (*jāti*), because it would lead to a logical confusion (*saṅkara*) with properties such as "cowness" (*gotva*), and because there is no evidence for its existence. Rather, it is the possession of the word-form "verbal suffix" (*ākhyātapadatva*) by virtue of a specific convention established by experts. However, the delimiting factor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is specifically the property of being *ti* (*tip-tva*) and so forth, because no verbal cognition arises when one is in a state of ignorance regarding that form. Thus it has been explained.

Even according to others, by virtue of being included within a single utterance, the property of *tip*-ness (*tiptva*) and so forth alone serves as the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for both the effort of the agent and the state of being present, just as in the case of the term *puṣpavant* (the sun and moon). For this very reason, in cases such as *pacati*, there is no usage when there is an absence of the intention (*tātparya*) to convey the effort of the agent through the suffix *at* (the *tip* portion), just as in the expression "the hot *puṣpavant*" (where one intends to refer only to the sun). Thus, the absolute assumption that in the Nyāya system the *l*-suffix alone is the denoter is merely a result of negligence. If it is asked: "In that case, how is it that [the grammarians] say 'there is a power [of the suffix] in the sense of oneness by virtue of being a *su*' (the nominative singular ending)? and so forth?

Not so; for there is no restrictive rule that [the expressive power] belongs only to the substituend (*sthānin*) or only to the substitute (*ādeśa*). Indeed, even in your own view, there is no restriction that the expressive power belongs only to the substitute; otherwise, cognition would not arise from forms such as *bhyām*. Nor can it be argued that in the case of *rāmabhyām*, the form *rāmābhyām* is a substitute [for *rāmabhyām*] by way of the lengthening [prescribed] in the rule *supi ca*; for the theory of the phoneme-sphoṭa (*varṇa-sphoṭa*) is distinct from the word-sphoṭa (*pada-sphoṭa*) theory, since the status of being expressive rests solely upon the authority of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Even though there exist grammatical rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi*, that [agency] belongs only to their substitutes (*ādeśas*), because those [original *l*-suffixes] are restricted by the absence of usage; for the letter *l* is mentioned therein merely for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). Furthermore, you yourself have accepted this very point. Nor should it be argued that the rule *tiṅkarmaṇica* etc. alone should suffice for that [purpose], because there would be complexity (*gaurava*) if the property of being a *tiṅ*—defined as being any one of *tiṅ*, *si*, etc.—were taken as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the predicate.

Nor should it be argued that there is brevity (lāghava) due to the non-composition of the rule *laṭ* and the subsequent rules such as *laṭ*. For even if the case-endings (*sub-vibhakti*) were prescribed independently because their meanings are uniform, the formation of the *tiṅ*-endings cannot be accounted for otherwise; this is because they exhibit a variety of internal operations triggered by their respective specific times, which necessitates that the rule be established precisely according to the distinction between the substituends (*sthānin*).

Let us return to the subject at hand. By specifying the forms of the case-endings through rules such as *supāṃ ca svaujas-*, and by subsequently providing specific semantic indications therein—such as "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one [objects]" respectively—it follows that *sutva* (the property of being a *su*-ending) and so forth alone constitute the delimitors of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). For this very reason, the expressive power for [conveying] singularity and so on resides in *ti* and other suffixes alone. Even in your view, if the property of being a *visarga* were the delimitor of expressive power in cases like *rāmaḥ*, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases like *pacati*; furthermore, *sutva* is simpler than the property of being a *visarga* standing in the place of *su*.

However, in cases such as *gaurī* where the suffix begins with *ṭ*, since that [suffix] is also capable of being used in its own form, it is necessary to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for it. Otherwise, if one were to postulate such powers for the substitutes *in* and so on as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate three distinct powers: (1) for the suffix *ṭāp* alone in all feminine bases ending in consonants and in masculine-neuter bases—as in *rāmeṇa* and the like; (2) for the substitute *in* in places where the technical name *ghisamjñā* applies—as in *hariṇā*; and (3) for the substitute *nā*—as in *hariṇā*. Furthermore, there is no evidence to sublate the denotative power residing in the original element (*sthānin*), nor is there any evidence to establish a denotative power in the substitutes *in* and so forth.

This is because [the meaning] is possible through recollection for those who are proficient, and through a misconception regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) for others. For this very reason, the Naiyāyikas maintain that the expressive power resides in the phoneme *ṭ* (as in *pacati*), as well as in its oneness and its instrumentality. Furthermore, even for suffixes such as *ti*, the expressive power lies only in the meaning common to all verbal endings (*lakāra*). However, with respect to their respective specific meanings, the power of suffixes such as *laṭ* resides in that particular form alone; otherwise, the distinctness of the resulting cognition would be inexplicable. Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*), however, hold that the power of *laṭ* and other suffixes resides in [meanings such as] present time and so forth.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that in verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*), the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by virtue of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*), whereas the incitement (*pravartanā*) is expressed by virtue of being a verbal suffix in general (*tiṅtva*). As they say:

"The optative and other such suffixes express one thing alone, namely the denotative productive urge (*abhidhā-bhāvanā*); the productive urge consisting of the object (*arthātmabhāvanā*), however, is the domain of all verbal suffixes."

Thus, this is established: when there is no usage of that which is free from substitutes (*ādeśa*), the expressive power belongs to the substitutes alone; but when both [substitute and original] are used, the expressive power belongs to the originals (*sthānin*) alone. However, where even though the substitutes are present, the specific meaning is presented through the original—as in the case of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others—there, regarding the meaning common to all, the status belongs to the substitutes, while regarding the specific meaning, it belongs to the originals. And thus, in the second point of contention, the position of non-existence is sublated, and much more of this sort should be understood.

If it is argued that the *sphoṭa* is established only in those cases where the expressive power (*vācakatva*) of the substitutes (*ādeśa*) is admitted, we say: not so. If you claim that the *sphoṭa* is simply the expressive power of the suffixes such as *tiP* and others, then we have no objection (*iṣṭāpatti*). However, if you claim that the expressive power belongs to each individual phoneme—such as the letter *t* or the vowel *i*—that is not correct. Why? Because that would contradict your own established doctrine (*asiddhānta*), and because it would render untenable the explanation of the commentators who state that the rule *erur* means *testuḥ*.

Even if the vowel *i* were meaningful, there would be no violation of the rule that the relationship between a substituend (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) must exist only between two meaningful units; for even when *i* is replaced by *u*, the substitute remains meaningful. If it is objected: "In that case, in examples such as *caitraḥ pacatu*, the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (P. 8.1.28) prescribing the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) for a finite verb followed by another finite verb would not apply, because the mere vowel *i* in *pacatu* lacks the status of being a finite verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)," we reply: what does that matter? For we do not establish a fixed rule that the substitution of *u* for *i* applies only to the vowel *i*. Rather, there is no contradiction with our established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*) in the fact that the mere vowel *i* possesses denotative power (*vācakatva*).

Otherwise, one might as well say that the meaning is "of the suffix *ti*" in accordance with the rule for elision (*nighāta*), rather than in accordance with the logic already stated; thus, this [objection] is of no consequence. By this, the claim that "if the substitutes (*ādeśa*) are accepted as denotative, then the word-sphoṭa and sentence-sphoṭa would also be established in cases such as *ghaṭena*, *dadhi*, *idam*, *hare ava*, *viṣṇo ave*, etc. is refuted. For comprehension is possible even through the recollection of forms such as *ava*; furthermore, there is no harm even if the elision of the vowel *a* is accepted in instances of the *pūrvarūpa* sandhi.

Even when there is confusion regarding the division between base and suffix in forms such as *vasnas* and others, understanding still occurs because one remembers the substituends (*sthānin*) such as *yuṣmākam*. Otherwise, since those [substituends] are common to the genitive, dative, and accusative cases, it would be difficult to grasp their specific meaning. Furthermore, it is not accepted that substitutes (*ādeśa*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), for such a status exists only when there is evidence to establish the expressive power of the substitute. But is it not said: "For Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī, all words are substitutes for all words;
for if there were modification of even a single part, its eternity (*nityatva*) would not be tenable"?

If it is argued that, according to this principle, in place of *hare ava*, the substitution *hare'va* itself is prescribed by means of the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute for two homogeneous vowels), let it be so prescribed, since the means for understanding the meaning has already been stated.
