Nor should it be asked how such a substitute possesses meaning; for you too would face the same challenge as to how the original element (*sthānin*) possesses meaning. According to the logic already stated, the meaningfulness of the original element is established just as it is for the substitute.
If it is argued that the original element possesses meaning only because the substitute does, then it is equally true that the substitute possesses meaning only because the original element does.

Regarding the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*), however, this is also investigated: there is no evidence for the view that the knowledge of the power of a specific sentence is the cause of the cognition of the specific sentence-meaning. To explain: does the proponent of sentence-power (*vākyaśaktivādin*) accept that words possess power and that the knowledge thereof is the cause of verbal cognition, or not? Not the first, because if the cognition of the sentence-meaning can be accounted for by that alone, there is no occasion to postulate sentence-power. Nor the second, because if there were an absence of knowledge of word-power, it would follow that cognition would arise from the knowledge of sentence-power alone.

Furthermore, even when the knowledge of word-potency (*pada-śakti*) is present, no absence of verbal cognition is observed in the absence of the knowledge of sentence-potency (*vākya-śakti*). As for the argument that the respective effects delimited by the conditions of "verbal cognition of word-meaning" and "verbal cognition of sentence-meaning" belong to the knowledge of word-potency and sentence-potency respectively—thereby avoiding the redundancy of either—it is not so. Is the verbal cognition of word-meaning the intended object of the speaker’s purport independently, or in some other manner? Not the first, because there would be no purpose [for it].

This is because it would follow that the cognition of the word-meanings and the sentence-meaning would be a single unified apprehension (*samūhālambana*). Furthermore, at the time of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, a fragmented cognition of the word-meanings is not supported by valid evidence. Nor is the second alternative tenable, as there exists no mode of operation other than the utility of the word-meanings for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; for you yourself have stated that the recollection of the word-meanings serves as the mediating instrument (*dvāra*) when the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is to be produced by the knowledge of the word-potencies.

Furthermore, since the cognition of the act of bringing the pot is established solely through the knowledge of the sentence’s power (*vākyaśakti*), it is impossible for the cognitions of the pot and so forth produced by each individual word to be of utility therein. [Objection: But surely, the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the knowledge of the power of words such as "pot" is precisely the state of being a verbal cognition (*śābdatva*) where the pot is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and potness (*ghaṭatva*) is the qualifier (*prakāra*). How, then, can the knowledge of the sentence-meaning be accounted for by that? Therefore, one must necessarily postulate the power of the sentence itself as the delimiting factor, in its capacity as an object, within the cognition that serves as its cause.

If it is argued: "Whatever effect is of a different class from another effect is produced by causes that are of a different class from the causes of that other effect—just as a cloth, which is of a different class from a jar, is so produced; therefore, by this logic, the state of being the cognition of the meaning of the sentence 'Bring the jar' is the delimitor of an effectness that stands in the relation of effectness to a causeness not delimited by a nature that delimits the causeness standing in the relation of causeness to the effectness delimited by the cognition of the meaning of each individual word, because it possesses a property that delimits an effectness distinct from the effectness delimited by those [word-meaning] properties," we say: No.

This is because, through the cognitions of individual word-potencies, there is the possibility of producing a cognition delimited by a specific composite property (viśiṣṭadharma), due to the assistance provided by factors such as expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) and others, which produce effects delimited by their respective delimiters of effect-ness (svasvakāryatāvacchedaka). As for the objection that, rather than accepting the cognition of word-potencies as the cause, one should instead accept the cognition of sentence-potency (*vākyaśakti*) itself as the cause—this is not tenable. For does that [sentence-potency] generate the cognition of the sentence-meaning independently, or while depending on something else? Not the first, because [if it were independent], a cognition would result even from "The pot," "Objectness," "Bringing," and "Effort" [when uttered separately].

Not the latter [alternative], because the requirement is simply the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth. Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "the jar is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), verbal cognition indeed occurs when there is a grasp of the word-potency (*śakti*); for if that were so, one would fail to account for the observed difference in cases such as "The buffalo is grazing on the bank of the river whose water is pure" (*vimalaṃ jalaṃ nadyāḥ kacche mahiṣaścaratīti*), where the meaning of "river" is sometimes perceived as connected with "water" and sometimes as connected with "bank," since the knowledge of the potency for both sentence-meanings would be equally present. Nor can it be argued that the determination [of the specific connection] is made by the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), as is the case with words having multiple meanings (*nānārtha*).

[Otherwise] it would follow that the knowledge of *tātparya* (speaker's intention) is a cause [of verbal comprehension]. Nor should it be argued that even so, in a case where there is knowledge of *ākāṅkṣā* (syntactic expectancy), there would be knowledge of the sentence's power (*vākya-śakti*). For then the two expressions "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*) and "jar, objecthood" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) would be on an equal footing, resulting in their being used interchangeably. Nor can it be said that for one who has acquired a contrary linguistic habit (*viparīta-vyutpanna*), comprehension arises from the second expression alone; for there is no evidence that such a person possesses a contrary linguistic habit. Furthermore, it is difficult to state any seed of that [comprehension] other than the presence of syntactic expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*).

Furthermore, because sentences such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), "bring the jar" (*ānaya ghaṭam*), and "the jar is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) are distinct, it would follow that three separate causes must be postulated for the cognition of "bringing the jar as the object. Moreover, the specific sequence (*ānupūrvī*) of each word would have to be included within the definition of the effect-determining property (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, you yourself cannot coherently define "sentence-ness" (*vākyatva*) as something other than that. Nor should it be said that a sentence is merely a collection of words possessing mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*); for the status of the knowledge of expectancy itself as a cause [of verbal comprehension] remains unestablished.

Furthermore, in cases such as "he sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*), the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) is impossible because the sentence-meaning—in the form of sprinkling where fire is the instrument—is not established. This is because, in my view, there is a rule that the individual word-meanings must each be established. As for the argument that "the qualified [meaning] is not something additional, but rather those very same word-meanings, and they are indeed well-established," that is trivial; for you too must accept the power residing in the word-meanings, making it redundant to accept a power residing in the sentence-meaning.

Taking up that very same distinction by which you maintain the non-difference between the meaning of a word and the meaning of a sentence, [we reply] that for that very reason, because it is unestablished, it cannot be the denotable meaning (*vācya*). Otherwise, there would be no such thing as "incompatibility" (*ayogyatva*) in cases such as "stones float," nor would there be "unestablished substratum" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and so forth in cases such as "the mountain is made of gold. Furthermore, this is because the qualified object (*viśiṣṭapadārtha*) is precisely the objective state (*viṣayatā*) residing in that [object] by way of the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*). By this, the inferred view—that in the case of "the yellow conch does not exist," the cognition is that of the existence of a superimposed yellow conch—is refuted.

Even in that case, the existence of a yellow conch is not established. As for the claim that the counter-positive is established through a mental construction (*āhārya*), since "non-constructedness" (*anāhāryatva*) is not included [in the definition of the cause] because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) when the cognition of the counter-positive is the cause of the cognition of absence—that is incorrect. For such [establishment] must come either from the word itself or from something else. It cannot be the first, because indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is necessarily non-constructed, and because that [knowledge] is impossible without the apprehension of linguistic capacity (*śaktigraha*). Nor can it be the latter, because what is the object of another cognition cannot logically enter into a verbal relation (*śābdānvaya*).

This is because there would be the consequence of a lack of concomitance with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) by virtue of its being superimposed. By this, the position that the causality of the knowledge of the counter-positive is identical to the causality of the knowledge of the qualifier-determining attribute (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāraka-jñāna*) is also refuted; for even in that case, from a purely voluntary (*āhārya*) cognition, there could arise a cognition of a qualified object characterized by a superimposed property (*āhārya-viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-bodha*). Even with that much, the aforementioned defect remains unremoved according to the stated reasoning. Moreover, this has been stated for the sake of convenience; in reality, however, since the meaning of a sentence is always something not previously known (*apūrva*), the apprehension of a linguistic convention (*śakti-graha*) is impossible in every such case.

As for the objection that—whether one holds the sentence-meaning to be secondary (lakṣya) or maintains that the word-potency resides in the related (anvita)—it is impossible to grasp the potency (vṛttigraha) prior to the presentation of that [sentence-meaning], and thus how can their position be sustained?—this may perhaps be consistent when addressed to the Bhaṭṭas and others; however, against the Naiyāyikas and others, this answer is by no means tenable.

For even they accept that the apprehension of potency takes the form "the word 'jar' has potency with respect to a jar related to something else," and they do not admit that it takes the form "it has potency with respect to a jar related to the objecthood (karmatva)."

As for the objection that, according to those for whom the sentence-meaning is secondary (lakṣya) or for whom the word-potency resides in the related (anvita), how can their position be sustained since the potency cannot be grasped prior to the non-appearance of that [sentence-meaning], and so forth—this may perhaps be consistent for the sake of Bhaṭṭas and others; however, as far as Naiyāyikas and others are concerned, this answer is by no means tenable.

This is because even they accept the grasp of potency only in the form "the word 'jar' has potency with respect to a jar related to another," and they do not admit that it has potency with respect to a jar related to the objective case (karmatva).

As for the claim that "the word-potency (*pada-śakti*) is required as something known with respect to the word-meaning (*padārtha*), but as something existing in its own right (*svarūpa-sat*) with respect to the relation (*anvaya*); thus, just as in the theory of 'crooked potency' (*kubja-śakti-vāda*), let it be that for us too the word-potency is required as something known, while the sentence-potency (*vākya-śakti*) is required as something unknown," that too is incorrect. For the utility of sentence-potency must consist either in the cognition of word-meanings or in the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). It cannot be the first, because that is already established by word-potency alone. Nor can it be the latter.

Since the power of the word (*padaśakti*) is established for both [the denotation and the relation], and since the power that is useful for the aspect of syntactic connection (*anvaya*)—though unknown—is also to be postulated in the words themselves; furthermore, if the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) were useful when unknown, then in cases such as "the jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*) and "objectness" (*karmatvam*), where the knowledge of the sentence-power exists, verbal cognition (*śābda*) would indeed occur, whereas otherwise it would not occur due to the absence of that [sentence-power], which would contradict what was stated previously.

And here is the summary of the Naiyāyika position: although words possess a power (*śakti*) with respect to the generation of the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*), because that which lacks power does not produce [the effect], and because the cognition of the relation arises from the word due to the existence of God’s will; nevertheless, that power functions as something merely existent in its own nature (*svarūpasatī*) regarding the cognition of the relation, and not as something known, since the cognition of the relation of a jar is established simply from what is known as having the power to produce the cognition of a jar.

Furthermore, when a means of knowledge (*karaṇa*) is being cognized, there is a rule that it must convey a relation whose counter-correlate is the object, provided that its connection is useful for the cognition. This is because the cognition of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) related to fire, as well as the cognition of a pervasion related to that [fire], is not a constituent factor for the inference of fire. Nor is it the case that the property of being a "cognition of a jar" exists even in a cognition of a jar conjoined with something else; therefore, by that form, the utility of the known power (*śakti*) would apply even to a cognition of a jar conjoined with something else.

Because the relational component (*anvayāṃśa*) is cumbersome and obtainable through other means, it is accepted that the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is simply "the cognition of a jar" (*ghaṭajñānatva*), and not "the cognition of a related jar" (*anvitaghaṭajñānatva*). For this very reason, in both systems, the cognition of the word that presents the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the relation with the jar and so forth is the delimitor of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). However, the difference lies in the fact that the delimitor of the resultant capacity (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is, according to the Bhaṭṭa school, "the verbal nature of the cognition of a related jar," whereas according to the Nyāya school, it is simply "the verbal nature of the cognition of a jar."

Therefore, in the view of Bhaṭṭa, just as in the case of a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), there is only one power (*śakti*) with respect to the individual (*vyakti*); this power, while existing by its own nature (*svarūpasatī*), operates with respect to the factor of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) when it is known, and with respect to the word-meaning (*padārtha*) when it is known. It should not be argued that this is not so because the genus and the individual are cognized in a single cognition (*samānasaṃvitsaṃvedyatva*), whereas for the cognition of a jar (*ghaṭajñāna*), there is no rule that it must have syntactic connection as its object, since there is deviation in the case of memory. For the specific jar-experience and the syntactic connection of the jar are both cognized in a single cognition.

Furthermore, because the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) functions as a cause [of recollection] by virtue of being known as related [to its meaning] during the act of recollection, therefore the cognition of the word is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recollection of the word-meaning is the operation (*vyāpāra*), and the experience of the connection between the recalled meanings—by force of auxiliary factors such as expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth—is the result (*phala*). And since the recollection of the word-meaning is an operation, it does not constitute an intervention. Thus, there is no evidence for the existence of *vākyaśakti* (sentence-potency), given that the word-meaning lacks the status of being a delimiting property (*avacchedakatva*) by way of being an object of a cognition that is the counter-positive of the absence which causes the lack of comprehension of the connection.

However, there is a disparity because one and the same word-power (*padaśakti*) is postulated as being useful for the aspect of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) when it is not [otherwise] known. In cases such as "the hamlet is on the Haridrā river" (*haridrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), since it is possible to have a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is improper; therefore, because the word *haridrā* shares the same referent as the word *nadī* (river) which has its conventional meaning established, one postulates that *haridrā* denotes a specific river. Following the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the poor woman (*daridrā*) and the river, the word *nadī* then possesses a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the bank.

As for the claim that—even though the meaning of the sentence is presented from that very [word] through the assistance of the presentation of word-meanings, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and so forth—that cognition is not verbal (*śābda*) and therefore the postulation of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is necessary in between; and that, by analogy, the postulation of *śakti* (denotative power) is likewise required here—that is not correct. For "verbal-ness" (*śābdatva*) is certainly not "being produced by the power of a word," since that would remain unestablished even when *lakṣaṇā* is postulated. Nor is it "being produced by a function of a word," since this is already established according to the principles of Nyāya itself. Nor is it "being produced by a knowledge of a function whose object is the object of the [cognition] itself."

If *anvaya* (syntactic relation) were a word-meaning (*padārtha*), then, just as in the case of those [other meanings], it too would result in being an object of the relation (*saṃsarga*), leading to a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) therein; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For this very reason, if *anvaya* were the primary denotation (*śakya*) and, like other word-meanings, were to function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it would follow that the relation of the relation (*saṃsarga-saṃsarga*) would also appear [in cognition]. Thus, the intention is that *anvaya* is not the denotation, because it cannot be sustained by a primary expressive power (*śakti*). Nor should it be argued that the relation of the relation is verbal (*śābda*) even without a linguistic function (*vṛtti*).

For such a conceptualization is appropriate only when there is a relation between word-meanings; furthermore, there is no reason to maintain that even for a word-meaning, its own relation does not appear [in cognition]. Even in the Bhaṭṭa school, since metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted by words as applying to the general relation itself—just as they apply to their own expressive power (*śakti*)—the prior requirement of the presentation of a specific relation is unnecessary. This is because the establishment of a specific relation is admitted to occur through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors.

As for the claim that, although there is initially a mental apprehension of the relation, because that is common to doubt as well, one relies on verbal testimony (*śābda*) for the sake of a definitive ascertainment (*nirṇaya*); and that in reality, the grasp of the power of the word regarding the element of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs at that very moment by taking into account the presentation consisting of the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-jñāna*)—that is incorrect. For while that may be possible in the case of worldly sentences, it is impossible in the case of Vedic ones. This is because the meaning of the Veda cannot be known through any other means of knowledge, and because such [intention] does not produce cognition initially. Furthermore, the knowledge of intention is not accepted as a cause for that which is delimited by being a verbal cognition. By this, the certainty regarding the statement being uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) is also explained away.
However, the fact that a statement was uttered by a reliable person (āptoktatā) is not useful [as a means of proof] unless it is already known to be pregnant with the meaning of the sentence;
for since the meanings of sentences are unprecedented, a connection [of the probans] arises even when there is doubt [regarding reliability].

Because it has been stated thus; and because the intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the meaning of a sentence consists in the fact that, for example, the word "pot" is directed toward a cognition whose qualifier is its own referent and whose qualificandum is the objecthood (*karmatva*), since [the sentence-meaning] is composed of the word-meanings as its constituent parts in this manner—this is the general direction. Furthermore, you yourself must admit, in accordance with experience, that there is an intermediate cognition similar to the cognition of word-meanings, and that this serves as the cause for the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the cognition of the great sentence-meaning occurring at the very time one determines the inapplicability (*ayogyatva*) of the intermediate sentence-meanings.

Because it is impossible for cognition to function as an obstructive factor (pratibandhaka) unless it either fails to apprehend the absence of the object to be grasped or disrupts the cognition that produces [that apprehension], it is necessary that the knowledge of the mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between the words *ghaṭa* and *ampada* is a cause for the understanding in which "pot" is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and "objectness" (*karmatva*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Nor can this be established through the knowledge of the word-potency (*pada-śakti*) alone in expressions such as *ghaṭam*, because the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākya-sphoṭa*) is distinct from the word-sphoṭa (*pada-sphoṭa*), according to your own admission that "word-meanings are understood by means of words, while the sentence-meaning is understood by means of the sentence."

In this context, the word *pada* refers to each individual base (*prakṛti*) and so forth. For this very reason, the texts of the traditional grammarians state: "The mention of 'compound' (*samāsa*) is for the sake of restriction; it serves to exclude the designation of 'nominal stem' (*prātipadika*) from a sentence (*vākya*). Otherwise, since the aggregate such as *ghaṭam* would not be excluded by that restriction, and because it possesses meaning, it would incur the status of a nominal stem by virtue of the rule "that which has meaning" (*arthavat*) and so on. Nor can the term *pada* be taken as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that [aggregate].

Even under the view that the word is a *pada-sphoṭa*, [the suffix] is not delimited by the property that serves as the counter-correlate for determining its status as a meaningful aggregate; for the aggregate "ghaṭam" possesses a difference of suffixes. Furthermore, there is no evidence for the exclusion of suffixes other than those at the end [of the word]. Moreover, even you must maintain that the cognition of the absence of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) acts as an inhibitor according to the analogy of the jewel and the mantra; whereas in your own system, the absence of the cognition of the absence of expectancy is the cause [of the comprehension of meaning].

For me, however, there is simplicity regarding the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). [In your view,] since "lack of expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) consists both in the absence of expectancy and in being distinct from that which possesses expectancy, it would follow that there must be causal efficacy for both the opposition between these two and the absence of both. Nor can these be subsumed under the property of being a cognition opposed to expectancy, because opposition differs according to the difference in the delimiters of opposition (*virodhitāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, if the cognition of lack of expectancy were a subverting factor (*pratibandhaka*), one would have to state that the absence of the ascertainment of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-niścaya*) is its delimiting condition.

In view of that, it is logical that the absence of the cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñānābhāva*) alone serves as the determinant (*avacchedaka*) for the cause of the determination of expectancy. This is due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I am cognizing the relation verbally" occurs because the understanding of the sentence-meaning is produced by the word. Nor does this imply that the word-meanings themselves are non-verbal; for there is a disparity [between them] due to the absence of any other cause [for their cognition]. As stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda:
"When these [word-meanings] have been fully grasped through those [words], the [sentence-meaning] is understood from the word-meanings.
Although the sentence-meaning is not verbal [in itself], there is no lack of verbal status in the word-meanings."
These [words] have no possibility of having other causes for their meaning than the sentence-meaning itself;

nor is the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (śakti) based on linguistic usage directed toward the sentence-meaning alone. For at the time of postulating the word’s power through the process of insertion and deletion (āvāpodvāpa), the apprehension of that [sentence-meaning] would be erroneous due to the faults of prolixity (gaurava) and being obtainable by other means (anyalabhyatva), just like the apprehension of the moon as small.

There is a disagreement regarding the indivisible *sphoṭa*. In the *Līlāvatī*, the author of the *Upāya* [Śrīdhara] poses the question: "Does the property of being a word (*śabdatva*) reside in the material cause of sound or not? The affirmative position belongs to the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*), while the negative position belongs to the Logicians (*Naiyāyikas*) and others. The "material cause of sound" is ether (*ākāśa*); its residence therein is well-established in its specific quality (*viśeṣa*) or its dimension (*parimāṇa*). Its absence, however, is found in things such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Nor does there arise the fault of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratva*) by virtue of its residing in ether even in the subject (*pakṣa*).

Because the cognition of the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)—namely, "being inherent in all sounds while not being inherent in what is other than sound"—acts as a sublater (*bādhaka*). This is because, without the subsistence [of the probandum] in the *k* and other phonemes which have the *sphoṭa*-natured sound as their material cause, the probandum cannot be subsumed. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa and others hold that, since the communication of meaning by a word would otherwise be inexplicable, one postulates a partless (*akhaṇḍa*) word distinct from the phonemes, and likewise a sentence distinct from the words. For a cognition of meaning does not arise from a single phoneme alone; this is because it contradicts experience and because other phonemes would otherwise be rendered useless.

Nor can it be by means of the aggregate [of letters], because there is no simultaneous conjunction (*melaka*) of them. This is because, whether the letters are eternal or their manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is non-eternal, it is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the letters themselves that possesses sequence. Furthermore, it cannot be maintained through a cognition whose object is the whole (*samūhālambana*), aided by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding letter; for in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, or *nadī* and *dīnaḥ*, or *jāraḥ* and *rājā*, the comprehension of specific meanings would be impossible, since the nature of the letters is identical in these instances. Therefore, the word or sentence, which is manifested by the letters and so forth, consists of an indivisible *sphoṭa* and is the conveyor of meaning.
As it has been said:

Because each individual phoneme lacks the capacity [to convey meaning] and because their combination is impossible, there is a single cognition; due to its similarity to the perception of a river or a sound, that is the *sphoṭa*, and it is of two kinds.

On this point, they say: Is the *sphoṭa* manifested by the cognition of each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), or by the cognition of their collection? Not the first, because the remaining [phonemes] would be useless. Not the second, because a combination [of the phonemes] is impossible; for it is impossible to perceive that which is to be manifested in the absence of its manifestor. As it has been said: "The partless *sphoṭa*, which is manifested by the cognitions of the phonemes..."
Even he is not liberated from this by means of such an inquiry.

This very point has also been stated in the *Sāṅkhyasūtra*: "Sound is not of the nature of a *sphoṭa*, because of [the possibility of its] perception and non-perception. The meaning is that if the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a word is admitted, the comprehension of the object occurs by that very [perception]; and in the absence of that [perception], there is an absence of the manifestor. As for the claim that the direct perception of a word is untenable—that is incorrect. The "succession" (*ānupūrvī*) of the phonemes *gha* and *ṭa* consists in their being objects of a cognition immediately following the cognition of *gha*. This is in accordance with the silence of the poet (in the *mauniśloka*). And that succession is grasped by the mind alone, just as in the case of the cognitions of a jar and a cloth.

And that which is presented by the mental organ (*mānasa*) appears to the auditory organ, as in the case of [the cognition] "fragrant sandalwood" and the like; for it is accepted that even that which is unsuitable for an external sense organ may be grasped when presented by the mental organ. Objection: If this were so, there could be no ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*) having the letter *ṭ* as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) and a specific sequence as its qualifier, with the object being the letter *ṭ* which follows the cognition of the letter *gh*. This is because by the time one has the production of the letter *ṭ*, the cognition thereof, and the grasping of its immediate succession to the cognition of *gh*, the letter *ṭ* would have already perished, resulting in the absence of the qualificand.
Response: It is said:

According to the analogy of waves and ripples, various instances of the letter *ṭa* arise through the delimitation of the auditory organ (*śrotra*). In this regard, despite the difference between those individual instances, because the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) is one and the same, when the first *ṭa* is inherent in the auditory organ, the universal *ṭatva* inherent in it is apprehended through inherence-in-the-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), resulting in a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception. It is accepted that in the case of the second *ṭa*, the previously known sequence appears as a qualifier by means of a relation constituted by the preceding *ṭa*.

And thus, there is the production of the letter *ṭ*, the cognition of that [letter], and immediately after that cognition, the apprehension of the immediate succession (*gha-jñānānantarya*) therein. That sequence (*ānupūrvī*), even when the preceding *ṭ* has perished, appears as a qualifier in the auditory perception of a subsequent *ṭ*. Alternatively, according to the aforementioned order, the sequence itself—though grasped at a different time—is remembered at the moment of the *ṭ*'s production; consequently, it appears as a qualifier precisely at the moment of the *ṭ*'s duration. Otherwise, as has been stated, your own position would likewise be untenable.

As for the claim that "the word (*pada*) and the sentence (*vākya*) are indeed indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*), and not a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*); for there is no evidence for the postulation of infinite phonemes; and because, given that the conjunctions of air intended as either the producers (*janaka*) or the manifesters (*vyañjaka*) of those [phonemes] must necessarily possess distinct universals (*vaijātya*) delimiting both [producer and manifester], it is in my view more appropriate to admit that properties such as *katva* (the universal of *ka*, etc. reside in the conjunctions of air themselves. And it is not the case that this would result in the conjunctions of air alone being the denoters (*vācaka*). For it is more fitting that the phonemes *ka* and so forth, which are established by perception, are the denoters.

And thus, since denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) cannot otherwise be accounted for, the indivisible *sphoṭa* is established by such cognitions as "this is a word" or "this is a sentence. Furthermore, properties such as *ka*-ness and so forth are superimposed upon it—just as high pitch (*tāratva*) and the like are superimposed on the letter *ka* in the Bhaṭṭa school's view. Therefore, it is the conjunctions of air alone that manifest the *sphoṭa*. Nor does the dilemma of whether they act individually or collectively arise here; for it is accepted that all of them are manifestors through their distinct modes, such as being a *ga*, an *au*, or a *visarga*.

Nor is it the case that if the manifestation occurs by means of one [letter], the others would be useless; for clarity of cognition is precisely what is to be accomplished by such manifestation. Nor should it be argued that the letters themselves may likewise serve as the means for the cognition of meaning; for we admit the appearance of clarity or lack of clarity only in the case of cognitions consisting of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the cognition of meaning does not consist of direct perception. As it has been said: "But its manifestation occurs in its entirety at the very end, like the true nature of a gem."

Thus, for this very reason, there is no admission of phonemes (*varṇa*) distinct from those [already mentioned]. This is because the difference in the cognition of /ka/ and so forth is accounted for solely by the superimposition of properties such as being the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) upon the *sphoṭa*. By this, the argument that "there is no *sphoṭa* distinct from the phonemes /ga/, /au/, and the visarga" is refuted; for those very [phonemes] are not admitted to be distinct from the *sphoṭa*, since it is precisely the cognition of them that has the *sphoṭa* as its object. For this very reason, Vācaspatimiśra stated in the *Tattvabindu*: "In reality, because there is no phoneme /ga/ whose form exceeds that of the phoneme /ka/," thus expressing the view of the proponents of the *sphoṭa*. It was also stated by Hari:
In a word, phonemes do not exist; nor do parts exist within phonemes.
There is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and the sentence.

Thus: just as in the case of the vowel *ṛ* and others, there is an appearance of a single part having the same form as the letter *r*, so too is there the cognition of letters within an indivisible word (*akhaṇḍapada*); this is the second quarter [of the verse] taken up as an illustration. This is clear in the reading "like parts" (*avayavā iva*).

On this point, the following must be said: superimposition (*āropa*) is defined as the cognition of certain properties appearing as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in a substratum (*dharmin*) that has been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). However, in this case, the aforementioned *sphoṭa* is not established by any other means of valid cognition. Nor is there any subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the fact that the perceived qualities such as *katva* (the property of being *ka*) reside in the phoneme *ka*, nor any proof for their residing in the conjunctions with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*). For it would follow [absurdly] that they would reside in the factors that produce those conjunctions with air as well.

Furthermore, the letter *a* is distinct from the letter *au*, because there is a cognition of difference between the qualificandum of a cognition having "being *ga*" (*gatva*) as its qualifier and the qualificandum of a cognition having "being *au*" (*autva*) as its qualifier; and because manifestors are useful only by virtue of their grasping specific properties residing in the manifested. As for the argument that the *sphoṭa* must be something distinct from the letters, because of the cognition "the word is in the series of letters"—otherwise, it would follow that a jar could not be established as distinct from its shards—that is not correct. For the object of this cognition is either the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), or the relation of manifester and manifested (*abhivyañjaka-abhivyaṅgya-bhāva*).

Not the first [alternative], because that would entail a deviation from your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), as you do not admit that the *sphoṭa* depends on them for its production or its persistence. Nor the last, because even when a jar is manifested by light, the cognition "the jar is in the light" does not arise; such is the general direction [of the argument].

To this it is replied: the establishment of the indivisible *sphoṭa* follows simply from the force of the universally established cognition that "one word is one sentence. For this very reason, in the *Līlāvatyupāya*, when presenting the view of the *sphoṭa*-proponents, that aforementioned cognition itself was stated as the proof, and not the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the comprehension of meaning. The cognition "this is one word" is established by the experience of everyone; it cannot have the individual phonemes as its object, because phonemes are many. Nor can it be based on the phonemes themselves under the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of producing the cognition of a single meaning.

Because [the cognition of meaning] arises even when there is no consideration of the *upādhi* (limiting adjunct), that which is its object is precisely the *sphoṭa*. For here there is no room for the maxim "that which is the cause of that" (*taddhetu*). This is because it is impossible to say, in the absence of accepting the *sphoṭa*, that "let the cognition of meaning arise from the very cause of the *sphoṭa*," nor does it mean "from what you consider to be the cause of that"; for otherwise, all conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) would result in being abolished.

Therefore, since the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) is necessarily a cause of qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), it is the very principle that this alone is the cause of purposeful action (*pravṛtti*); thus, this logic does not serve as a sublation (*bādhaka*) for the postulation of a false qualified cognition. For the causality of the non-apprehension of difference with respect to error must be postulated only after the error itself has been postulated; consequently, at the time of apprehending its status as a cause of action, there is no presentation (*upasthiti*) of it [as being the cause of error]. The Naiyāyikas maintain that since the time of the operation of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the "result-oriented complexity" (*phalamukhagaurava*)—which is refuted by whether [the alternative] is established or not—is not a defect.

Nor does this result in the annihilation of the aforementioned logical principle, because that principle finds its scope only when the subject (*dharmin*), which is its cause, is established by another means of valid cognition (*māna*). This is because Miśra and others have stated that it is the contact between the sense organ and the subject (*dharmīndriyasannikarṣa*), which is necessarily required as the cause for the cognition of the subject, that serves as the cause of doubt, and not the cognition of the subject itself. If it is argued that here too, once the clarity [of the object] is established through the aforementioned cognition, the aforementioned principle should apply, [we reply: [This objection is rejected by the following: ... [The text continues with the refutation of the opponent's view regarding the necessity of a second perception. ... Therefore, since the cognition of the subject is already established by the first perception, there is no room for the application of the principle that a second perception is required for the ascertainment of the object. Thus, the conclusion stands.

In that case, it is established that the dispute concerns only the *sphoṭa*’s status as the signifier (*vācaka*), not its essential nature (*svarūpa*), since you yourself accept it. Nor should it be said that its status as a signifier, as intended by you, is not proven; for its status as a signifier is easily established by the cognition, "From this sentence, this meaning was understood. It might be argued: "There is no evidence that the cognition 'this is a word' (*padam*) and so forth has an object distinct [from the phonemes]. For it was stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*:
As for the cognition that "this word 'gauḥ' is one," it is merely figurative, based on the delimitation of a single meaning across many phonemes, just like the cognitions of a forest or an army.
On this point, Vācaspatimiśra has also stated:

"Therefore, in the memory-cognition—which arises from a collection of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) produced by the experience of each individual phoneme and which encompasses all the phonemes—the phonemes appearing therein possess a figurative unity, either by virtue of being the objects of a single cognition of that [unified] form, or by virtue of being the cause of a single cognition of a single meaning."
Therefore they say:
"Even that cognition which is unitary is shown to be merely adventitious by a more powerful subverting cognition; therefore, the sphoṭa does not possess the status of a valid object."

This is not so; for even in the absence of the aforementioned recollection of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there arises a cognition of identity. Furthermore, this is because there is a disparity with the cognitions of an "army" or a "forest," which do not arise without the cognition of their respective adjuncts. Moreover, the mere fact of being the object of a single cognition does not produce a perception of identity in the case of jars, cloths, and so forth, when they are presented together in a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*). Finally, the property of being the cause of a single cognition regarding an object is something that can only be postulated after the denotative capacity of the letters has been established.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition of unity arises solely by virtue of being delimited by a single *su*-affix and a single *tiṅ*-affix; otherwise, there would be no distinction between a *sphoṭa* consisting of a word and a *sphoṭa* consisting of a sentence. Thus, the qualification (*upādhi*) stated in the *Līlāvatī* is correct. This is because, in reality, that [qualification] itself serves as the regulator, rendering the [cognition of] knowledge superfluous. Having accepted this very point, Kaiyaṭa has stated: "The Grammarians maintain that the expressive capacity belongs to a word or a sentence distinct from the individual phonemes."

Now, the position regarding the universal-sphoṭa (*jātisphoṭa*). To explain: first of all, the denial of phonemes (*varṇa*) established by perception is not tenable, for reasons already stated. Furthermore, if one were to accept a sphoṭa as something distinct [from phonemes] while also accepting universals such as "g-ness" (*gatva*), it would involve the conceptualization of a sphoṭa over and above that, which is cumbersome (*gaurava*), since on the view of the permanence of phonemes, the nature of the letter *ga* and so forth could very well be the universal "g-ness" itself. Moreover, if one does not accept such universals, it contradicts experience. Nor should it be argued that "g-ness" and so forth are accepted in the conjunction of air or in the sound (*dhvani*), and that this is then superimposed upon the letter *ga* and so forth.

Since it is improper to assume that a cognition is erroneous in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), and since it is possible for the conjunction with air itself to have the nature of the letter *ga*, and because—just as in the case of *gatva* (the universal "ga-ness") residing therein—it is also possible to assume that this [conjunction] is not perceptible by the sense of hearing; therefore, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed distinct entities. However, due to the principle of prolixity (*gaurava*), they are not the denoters (*vācaka*). For, according to the logic of the section on generic forms (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*), it is more appropriate to accept that both the state of being the denoted (*vācyatā*) and the state of being the denoter (*vācakatā*) reside in the universal (*jāti*) alone.

A specific universal (jāti) is established because it serves as the delimiting factor of the generative capacity (janakatā) that is itself delimited by the status of being produced by the "presence of Hari" (haryupasthititvāvacchinna), and because of the cognition "this is the word *hari*. Furthermore, if the delimitation of that cognition were explained solely through the sequence of phonemes (varṇānupūrvī), it would follow that even universals such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and "cloth-ness" (paṭatva) would be otherwise accounted for (anyathāsiddhi) by means of specific conjunctions with clay, shapes, and so forth. Therefore, the expressive power (vācakatva) belongs to the universal alone, and its status as a delimiting factor [of the word] is by way of identity (tādātmya).

Furthermore, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that manifests the specific class (*jāti*) is the nature of a particular sequence (*ānupūrvī*). By means of this, the difference in the cognition of meaning in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*—despite the identity of the phonemes—is logically accounted for. And it has been stated by Vopadeva: "Let the simplicity of the universal (*jāti*) be observed in its capacity to be denoted (*śakyatva*) as well as in its capacity to denote (*śaktatva*);
or let there be a distinction among the phonemes based on limiting adjuncts, like the distinction between high and low pitches."

The word *vā* has the same meaning as the word *tu*. The phrase "the example of phonemes (*varṇānām*)" serves as an illustration for the fact that a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the cause of the differentiation of cognitions; this is to be understood as being in the view of Bhaṭṭa. It is also stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "The universal (*jāti*) manifested by many individuals (*vyakti*) is known as *sphoṭa*; by some, the individuals themselves have been conceived as the *dhvani*s."

Thus [ends the citation]. The meaning of this is as follows: although in the theory of *sphoṭa* there exists the defect that the cognition of specific meanings in cases such as *saraḥ* (lake) and *rasaḥ* (taste) would be impossible, nevertheless, this is not the case in the theories of *pada-sphoṭa* (word-*sphoṭa*) and *vākya-sphoṭa* (sentence-*sphoṭa*). This is because, in those cases, the fact that the universal (*jāti*) resides distributively across multiple instances is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehend the subject itself. Nor does it follow that, because the universal is eternal, there would be a constant cognition of word-meanings; for it is only when that universal is known that it produces its effect, and because the manifestation of the phonemes (*varṇa*) serves as the manifestor of that [universal].

He states another view previously mentioned, namely that it is the very *dhvanis* (articulatory sounds), which are intended to manifest the phonemes (*varṇas*), that appear as *ka*-ness and so forth. This is indicated by the words "by some. The meaning is: by those who do not admit the existence of phonemes as distinct entities. As it was stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:

The learned grammarians have designated as *dhvani* that sound which manifests the *sphoṭa*, which is the primary entity. Furthermore, the universal (*jāti*) is either ignorance (*avidyā*) as qualified by those respective individual instances (*vyakti*), or a specific attribute belonging to it. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa maintains that even universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) are impermanent within the perspective of Brahman, because of the scriptural teaching that "all this is indeed the Self" (*ātmaivedaṃ sarvam*). However, in reality, the Vedāntic conclusion is that Brahman itself, as qualified by those respective individual instances, is the universal such as "cowness. As it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
Existence itself, when differentiated according to its various correlates in cows and other things, is called a "universal" (jāti); all words are established in that [existence].
They declare that [Bhāva] to be the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root;
it is eternal, it is the Great Self, and it is what the suffixes -tva, -tal, and so forth, express.

In the case of the relatives—the specific individuals intended as the locus of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth—existence (*sattā*), which is of the nature of being (*sad-rūpa*), becomes differentiated by becoming the object of specific cognitions whose content is cowness and the like. To the extent that there are individual cows and other such entities, cowness and the like are simply of the nature of being, through a relation of identity (*tādātmya*) residing in any one of them. Nor is there a lack of uniformity regarding the relation; for it is accepted that in cases such as causality, the use of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) is not a defect, and because [the relation] is unified by way of being "any one of these" (*anyatamatva*).

Even though there is an infinity of such identities (*tādātmya*), [the cause] is introduced by its very nature as one or another of those individual instances; for it would otherwise be superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*) if another pervasive form were present. For this very reason, in cases such as the causality of absence (*abhāva*) through the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), the state of being "one or another of those natures" is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) precisely by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), because otherwise it would be difficult to explain causality and so forth through non-pervasive relations.

Therefore, where for others the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is an additional limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*), for us that very same thing exists as the nature of Being (*sadrūpa*) through the aforementioned relation. Nor should it be argued: "Since causality can be established by taking any one of the individual cows (*govyakti*) as the limiting factor, why should the universal of Being (*sattāsāmānya*) alone be the limiting adjunct? For even if one accepts an additional cowness and so forth, both parties must admit that such a factor is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) by that form, due to the absence of any such decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*). Thus say the modern Vedāntins.

Let us return to the subject at hand. "Established in that" means they are denoters of it. We shall demonstrate that the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the rule concerning the prohibition [of the feminine suffix]. And we shall demonstrate its status as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in the *bhūvādi* sūtra. "Eternal" (*nitya*) means that, because its nature is Brahman, it does not possess the property of being a counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva*). Otherwise, since the form of eternality consisting in not being a counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) could also exist in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*), he says precisely this: "That is the Great Self."

If, however, it were of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), then—given the accepted view that ignorance is to be destroyed by the direct realization of Brahman—that [realization] would not occur. In the phrase "that" (*tām*), the meaning of the accusative case is the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), because suffixes such as *tv* and *tal* convey that [state] as the qualificand; for [otherwise], even words like "pot" (*ghaṭa*) would convey it as a qualifier (*prakāra*). By this, the two interpretations found in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary—the one stating that Brahman itself, delimited by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of non-existence, is the denotation of the word, and the other stating that the very reality of Brahman appears in the form of the word—are explained. The statement that "the state of being a foot of Hari" (*haripadatva*) and so forth is a *jāti* (universal) follows the *Bhūṣaṇā*. However, the authors of the *Kaustubha* maintain that it is rather the property of being a *ṭa*-suffix following a *ghu*-suffix (*ghottara-ṭatva*) and the like that is the expressive [denotative] element, and that this is indeed of the nature of an *upādhi* (limiting adjunct). They further argue that an *upādhi* is simply a *jāti* related through a mediated connection (*paramparā-sambaddhā*). This is because even in cases such as "fire-possessiveness" (*vahnimattva*), although fire and other factors are manifold, the logicians themselves accept that the generality (*sāmānyatva*) belongs precisely to the *jāti* of "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) and the like, by way of the relation of conjunction with its own inherent substratum (*svasamavāyi-saṃyoga*). The rest is as before. And this is correct.

There is no evidence for accepting universals such as "being a *pada*" (a word), because even you must necessarily accept that such a universal is not manifested at a time when there is no cognition having "the quality of being a *ṭa* following a *gha*" (*ghottara-ṭatva*) as its qualifier; otherwise, the impossibility of understanding specific meanings in cases such as *saro* and *raso* would remain as it was. By this, the counter-argument regarding universals such as "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) is also refuted, since a cognition qualified by "potness" arises even for those who lack knowledge of the specific conjunctions [of phonemes] and so forth. Let this suffice.

Now, if it is asked what prompts one to engage in the study of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the Bhāṣya on this point states: "What, then, are its purposes? Preservation (*rakṣā*), comprehension (*ūha*), tradition (*āgama*), brevity (*laghu*), and absence of doubt (*asaṃdeha*) are the purposes. Here, the word *prayojana* (purpose) occurs once in the masculine gender, referring to the impelling injunction (*pravarttaka-vidhi*). The suffix *-lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of the rule allowing for diversity (*bāhulaka*), or in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). The second instance, however, is neuter, referring to the result (*phala*). Since there are two instances of the word, the neuter singular remainder (*napuṃsakaikaśeṣa*) applies according to the rule *pum-napumsakayoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.69], resulting in an optional singular collective form.

Therefore, there is the plural number in the question and the singular in the answer. In this context, scripture (*āgama*) is the instigator, while the other four are the results. An example of the first is as follows: "The Veda, with its six auxiliary limbs, should be studied and known by a Brahmin as a duty without motive" (*niṣkāraṇo dharmaḥ*). Here, "without motive" (*niṣkāraṇa*) means independent of visible motives (*dṛṣṭakāraṇa*). This is because the word *kāraṇa* (motive) is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, whereby it denotes the result that generates activity through the relation of being the object of the desire that produces such activity.

By this, it is stated that "perpetuity" (*nityatva*) consists in being the counter-positive of an absence that serves as the means for incurring sin (*pratyavāya*). Consequently, one engages in this practice just as one does in the case of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other such rites. Nor is there a contradiction with the "intermediation by the fruit" (*phalasandaṃśa*); for there is no conflict between the fruit and its status as a perpetual duty. Regarding this scripture, the Grammarians (*śābdika*) maintain that the term *āgama* is a conventional designation (*rūḍhi*) for the Veda, whereas the Mīmāṃsakas hold it to be a traditional text (*smṛti*).

For this very reason, anticipating that those [authorities] might intend for the *āgama* itself to be the result—since it is impossible for grammar to have the *āgama* as its result in its own form—they might argue that grammar has *dharma* as its purpose by way of explaining words which are useful for the knowledge of *dharma* consisting of the meaning of Vedic sentences; thus, they might figuratively (through *lakṣaṇā*) speak of the *āgama* as the result. Anticipating this, [the author] states with the word "and" (*ca*) that since both the study and the knowledge of the six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Veda are understood to be enjoined as being useful for the performance of sacrifices (*kratvanuṣṭhāna*), there is no [need for] the knowledge of *dharma* here.

The cognition that [the study of the Vedas] has as its fruit the study of the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is not a fault of "splitting the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) based on the multiplicity of things to be enjoined; for it has been stated that, being of human origin, such a statement is not defective. Furthermore, their status as "auxiliaries" (*aṅga*) is due to the superimposition [of that term] upon them because they assist [the Veda]. Thus, it is said in the *Śikṣā*:
"Grammar is its mouth, and astrology is called its eye;
Etymology is designated as its head, and the investigation of meters is its feet."

Śikṣā is said to be the nose of the Veda, while the Kalpasūtras are its hands. Vyākaraṇa (Grammar) is useful for determining the meaning of words through accents and other means; Jyotiṣa (Astronomy/Calendar) for knowing the specific times required for study and performance; Nirukta (Etymology) for explaining elision, augmentation, and modification; Chandoviciti (Metrics) for determining the meaning of injunctions such as "one sacrifices with a Gāyatrī" by defining the characteristics of the Gāyatrī and other meters; and Śikṣā for the method of pronouncing phonemes. Furthermore, the Kalpasūtras are useful for knowing the full extent of ritual application through the synthesis of those rites obtained through logic and those subsidiary elements found in other recensions.
Even there, grammar is primary, because the determination of words and word-meanings—which are useful for the knowledge of sentence-meaning—is derived from that alone.

Now, it might be argued that preservation is not its fruit; for that [preservation] must pertain either to worldly words or to Vedic words. It cannot be the former, because [worldly words] are established through common usage itself. Nor can it be the latter, because the preservation of words, just like sentences, is possible through the very tradition of the students. This is not so.

Although the mere form of the word (*pada*) is not useful for its indirect preservation, the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is necessarily required, and since that [knowledge] is rooted in the apprehension of word-meanings (*padārtha*), and because the apprehension of meaning from words such as *ātmanā* and others is untenable through common usage (*loka*), they are useful by way of being explained through elision (*lopa*) and other operations. For example, elision (*lopa*) is seen in: *tmanā deveṣu vividima tad druhaḥ*. In mantras, there is elision of the initial vowel of *ātman-* according to the rule *āṅyāderātmanaḥ*. For example, an augment (*āgama*) is seen in: *devāsaḥ*, *brāhmaṇāsaḥ*. Here, the suffix *-as-* is added according to the rule *ājjaseḥ*. For example, both [elision and augment] are seen in: [the forms *devāsaḥ* and *brāhmaṇāsaḥ*].

The gods milked; the meaning is "they milked. In the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *duh*, there is the substitution of *ad* for the *jha* ending. The elision of *ta* occurs by the rule "lopast ātmanepadeṣu. The augment *ruṭ* is added because of the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. By this, the form *nāśiraṃ duhe*—which ends in *laṭ* (present)—is also explained. The meaning is: "They do not milk the *āśira* (the mixture of milk and soma) for the purpose of preparing the *soma*. As for the modification (*vikāra*): *gṛbhṇāmi te mahate saubhagāya*. [The change is] "h" for "hr" and "grah" in the Veda; it should be stated that this applies to the letter *ha*. Thus, there is the substitution of *bha* for *ha*. As for the suffix (*pratyaya*): [Example follows].

Regarding the phrase *udgrābhaṃ ca nigrābhaṃ ca*: in the rule *udgrābhanigrābhau ca chandasi srugudyamananipātanayoḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *grah* even when preceded by the prefix *ni*, according to the Vārttika; the substitution of *ā* for *i* (the *bhādeśa*) is as previously stated. Although the word *sruk* here refers generally to sacrificial vessels characterized by their specific arrangement, in this context it refers specifically to the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, because of the scriptural injunction: "With *udgrābham*, he lifts up the *juhū*; with *nigrābham*, he lowers the *upabhṛt*."

If it is argued that the nature of *ūha* (modification) is indeed rooted in the logic taught in Mīmāṃsā, whereas the nature of the specific words being modified is established from common worldly usage alone, we say no. This is because, in cases requiring modification, it is impossible to distinguish the original form (*prakṛti*) and so forth without grammar. To explain: that in which the full collection of constituent parts is taught is the *prakṛti* (archetype), such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. That in which they are not taught is the *vikṛti* (ectype).

For example: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya; one desiring long life should offer a *caru* oblation in ghee to Prajāpati," and so forth. Furthermore, extension (*atideśa*) is threefold: by direct statement (*pratyakṣavacana*), as in "In the *iṣṭi* sacrifice lasting one day, the rest is the same as the Śyena"; by name (*nāmadheya*), as in "At the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, one performs the Agnihotra for a month"; and by inferential statement (*ānumānikavacana*), as in "The Saurya [oblation]," and so forth. If it is argued that there is no extension of ritual properties (*dharma*) here because of a lack of evidence, we say no.

In the sentence-meaning "one should bring about *brahmavarcasa* (Vedic luster) by means of sacrifice," there is a rule that the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) requires three constituent parts: "what" (*kim*), "by what" (*kena*), and "how" (*katham*). Although the "what" part is fulfilled by the mention of the result (*bhāvya*) and the "by what" part by the mention of the sacrifice (*yāga*), the "how" part—the constituent of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—is not yet fulfilled; therefore, because of this expectancy, the application of extended injunction (*atideśa*) is necessary.

Nor should it be argued that since the Vedic procedure for the *darśa* and other sacrifices is restricted solely to those specific rites and cannot be extended elsewhere, whereas the worldly procedure for the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* and others is common to many due to its recurrence, the latter alone should be adopted; for if the instrument (*karaṇa*) is Vedic, then only a Vedic procedure is required for it. Nor should it be argued that this [worldly] procedure is also indeed Vedic because it is based on a Veda that serves as the source for the Smṛti.

Because the "how-to" (kathaṃbhāva) of the Darśa and other sacrifices is rooted in direct Vedic perception (*pratyakṣa-veda*), they possess a distinction [from the Saurya sacrifice] based on that. Furthermore, the primary Saurya sacrifice would have to proceed in the *vaitānika* fire, whereas the worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would proceed according to custom (*ācāra*) in the Smārta fire; thus, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*) occupying different locations. Moreover, the relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) is easily understood through such factors as having the same deity. For instance, the Saurya is an ectype of the Āgneya because it shares the status of being the locus for the fulfillment of a single deity, and because its substance is plants (*oṣadhi*).

The injunction "one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu" is a sacrifice that, because it has two deities, is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *aindrāgna* sacrifice; and the injunction "in the afternoon one should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with clarified butter (*ājya*)" is a modification of the *upāṃśuyāja*, because its substance is clarified butter, and so forth.

Since modification (*ūha*) is also a form of partial sublation (*bādha*), the manner in which sublation operates is now demonstrated. This was investigated in the tenth [book]: "Is everything archetypal (*prākṛta*) to be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*), or is that for which the archetypal purpose has been lost not to be performed?

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The collection of archetypal subsidiaries, even if its purpose is no longer required, is extended to the ectype by its mere essential nature alone. Therefore, even when the purpose such as dehusking (*vaituṣya*) is impossible—as in the case of *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces—acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) must still be performed in accordance with the authority that prescribes them, by postulating an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: [...]
The extension [of properties] to things is based on dependence, existence, and fitness;
because these are absent, no extension of properties to categories is postulated.

Regarding the statement "one should effect [the result] by means of sacrifice"—that is, when it is said that one should act in such a way that the sacrifice becomes a means to the result—the specific operation (*vyāpāra*) by which the sacrifice becomes the generator of the result is precisely what is required, not merely the essential nature of the ritual object itself. Proximity (*sannidhi*) also pertains only to the assistance [rendered]. This is because, due to the similarity with injunctions such as *nirvapet* (he should offer), the modified sentence brings to mind the sentences concerning the archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛtāṅga*).

And because that [injunction] brings about a meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) endowed with three factors, and because the modified (vaikṛta) sentence specifically mentions both the goal (sādhya) and the means (sādhana), those two are disregarded; rather, it grasps only the factor of "how" (kathaṃbhāva), which consists in the accomplishment of the assistance produced by the subsidiaries.

The capacity to fulfill the requirement [of the sacrifice] belongs to the ritual procedure (*vyāpāra*) itself, not to its constituent parts. Therefore, it is the auxiliary benefits (*upakāra*) as qualified by their respective word-meanings that are extended (*atideśa*), not the mere essential forms of those word-meanings. Consequently, when the original function is impossible in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no extension of that constituent part at all. Thus, in the case of "one threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the removal of husks (*vaituṣya*) is established as the benefit of threshing; since that [benefit] is impossible in the case of *kṛṣṇala* seeds, there is indeed a sublation (*bādha*).

However, as for the cooking in ghee, it occurs because of the direct scriptural statement, "he cooks in ghee"; thus there is a disparity [between the two cases]. Furthermore, the status of mantras as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) is mediated by their illumination of the meaning to be performed. In that regard, when everything denoted by the mantra is absent in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the entire mantra is excluded. For example, the mantra for threshing, "Drive away the Rakṣas from heaven, slay the rival," is excluded in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces.

However, when only a portion of the meaning is absent, there is the removal of only that part of the word which expresses a meaning that is the counter-correlative of the absence of the modified function (*vikṛti-vṛtti*). For example, in the mantra *agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*, the word *agni* [is removed] because the word *sūrya* is used in its place; and by implication, the vowel *e* is also removed, since in the original form ending in *a*, the *ya*-sound alone is grammatically correct for the dative case. Therefore, in place of *agnaye*, which has the middle accent (*madhyodātta*), one should substitute *sūryāya*, which has the initial accent (*ādyudātta*).

An example of [modification] according to the gender (*liṅga*) is as follows: for the mantra "O divine waters, you are pure" (*devīr āpaḥ śuddhā stha*), which is applied to water, there is the modification "O divine clarified butter, you are pure" (*devājya śuddham asi*). An example of [modification] of the verbal suffix alone (*pratyaya-mātra*) is as follows: regarding the mantra for the cutting of portions (*avadāna-mantra*) used for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), "Do not fear, do not tremble" (*mā bher mā saṃvikthāḥ*), Haradatta and others hold that for parched grains (*dhānāḥ*), it becomes "Do not fear, do not tremble" (*mā bhaiṣṭa mā saṃvijidhvam*). The ritualists (*yājñikāḥ*), however, say "do not tremble" (*mā saṃvigdhvam*). Their intention is that, because the root *vij* (meaning "to separate") is not used in its undesirable form (*aniṭ*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), this is an instance of its usage [with the vowel lengthened].

The intention of the predecessors is as follows: the author of the commentary on that mantra stated that between the two meanings of the root *ovijī*—namely, "fear" and "trembling"—since fear is already prohibited by the word *mā bhaiḥ* ("do not fear"), the word *mā saṃvikthāḥ* ("do not tremble") prohibits trembling. This is because, in a mantra intended for the purpose of the *avadāna* (cutting of portions), it is inappropriate to prohibit the state of being separate. Thus, although the augment *iṭ* is absent there due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatva*), since the *ūha* (modification) lacks the status of being Veda, it is proper that the *iṭ* augment be applied when the modification is being made.

[Objection: But surely simplicity (*lāghava*) is not the goal; for since the recitation of the *sūtras* and so forth is composed of technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) that are non-worldly, and since the *Bhāṣya*, *Vārttika*, and other works are extremely complex, the opposite—namely, complexity (*gaurava*)—would result. [Reply: This is not so. Because words are infinite, it is impossible to provide a word-for-word recitation (*pratipadapāṭha*). Therefore, the method of explaining them by means of grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*) consisting of general principles (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*) is indeed simpler. Furthermore, the formulation of these rules is based on either the theory of the class (*jāti*) or the individual (*vyakti*).

We shall demonstrate in the section on the rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedha-sūtra*) that conformity with the linguistic data (*lakṣya-anurodha*) is the determining factor in choosing between these two positions.

"Absence of doubt" (*asaṃdehaḥ*) is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvaḥ*) of doubt, not its destruction (*dhvaṃsaḥ*). Kaiyaṭa states that this is because doubt does not arise for a grammarian. Nor is it the case that, because [the absence of doubt] is beginningless (*anādi*), it cannot be considered a result (*phalam*); for when doubt does not arise, one accepts that its status as an achievable goal (*sādhyatvam*)—common to both [types of results] such as security (*kṣema*)—consists precisely in the persistence of its prior non-existence in the subsequent moment. For this very reason, there is no possibility of [forming] an *avyayībhāva* compound [with *na*]. This is because it will be explained later that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvaḥ*), and thus denotes the absence of that [doubt].

Regarding the injunction "One should sacrifice a speckled ox (sthūlapṛṣatīmanaḍvāhīm)," there arises a doubt: does the term *sthūlapṛṣatī* function as a *karmadhāraya* compound, wherein "thickness" (*sthūlatva*) qualifies the cow, since the word *pṛṣatī* indicates "possessing spots" through *matvarthalakṣaṇā*? Or does it function as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, wherein [the quality] resides in the spots (*pṛṣatsu*)? In this regard, observing that the final syllable of the first member is accented, one determines it to be a *bahuvrīhi* by means of the accentuation of the original form of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).

If it is objected that, in this way, even in the case of the mantra "I partake, having been invited, of what was drunk by Indra" (*upahūta indrapītasya bhakṣayāmi*), a determination that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound would be possible simply from the fact that the word *indra* is read with an acute accent on the first syllable—and thus the section concerning "what was drunk by Indra" (*indrapītādhikaraṇa*) would become redundant—[the authors] reply: "That [redundancy] applies only to those who are not grammarians, or else it is a case of the principle of 'deliberation as if it were established' (*kṛtvācintānyāya*)."

It might be argued as follows: by the rule *tṛtīyā-karmaṇi*, which prescribes that when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix with an active sense follows, the preceding member ending in the third case retains its original accent (*prakṛti-svara*), the word *indra* ending in the third case would retain its original accent even when compounded with the word *pīta* ending in a *kṛt* suffix denoting the object. Consequently, since this rule already establishes the accent, it would be improper for the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) to serve as a decisive authority; therefore, the section is purposeful. To this they reply: in this context, it is necessary to understand the word *pīta* as referring to the act of giving.

Because a deity, being insentient, cannot drink, and because of the observation of textual passages such as "given to Indra" (*indrāya dattasya*), it follows that when a gift is made with reference to Indra, it is impossible for him to be either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, since the dative ending must be used [to express the recipient], this is not the scope of the aforementioned sūtra. Nor can the third case ending be used to express the sense of cause (*hetu*).

Because the case-ending denoting the *kāraka* (the agent or object of action) is stronger than the case-ending used for a secondary word (*upapada-vibhakti*), there is no impossibility of forming a *caturthī-samāsa* (compound with the dative case), even though such compounds are generally restricted to cases involving the relationship between a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). This is because rules such as "Pāṇini 2.1.30: *tṛtīyā-tat-kṛtārthena*" do not apply here, and thus a *tṛtīyā-samāsa* (compound with the instrumental case) is also impossible. Furthermore, since the rule for the dative compound (*caturthī*) can be applied by means of a syntactic split (*yogavibhāga*) of the sūtra itself, one must conclude that the *caturthī-samāsa* or the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) is to be accepted on the grounds of Vedic usage (*chāndasatva*).

Moreover, since a difference in accentuation (*svara-bheda*) is necessary here, it is indeed appropriate to determine the correct form based on the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*).

On this point, the Neo-Mīmāṃsakas maintain: here there is no application of the rule for *bahuvrīhi* compounds, because that rule is prescribed only for those [compounds] consisting of co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) members. The formation of [compounds] such as *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* is established solely by the force of the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau*. In the case of a *tatpuruṣa*, however, there is application of the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*; and by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), the formation of a compound with a dative [member] is also justified.

Nor does the redundancy of the present section remain even if the determination of the *bahuvrīhi* compound were possible through accent alone. Even though the determination of the *bahuvrīhi* is possible, the redundancy of the section persists because, despite the presence of an accent that indicates a *bahuvrīhi*, there is a definitive determination of it as a *tatpuruṣa* in order to favor its own primary meaning; thus, according to the maxim of "the conflict between the subordinate and the quality" (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*), the accent, which is a property of the word, must be explained as being overridden.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be no determination by accent even in the case of *sthūlapṛṣatīm*, and that if such a consequence were accepted, it would contradict the *Mahābhāṣya*; for in that case, there is a difference because a coordinate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) bahuvrīhi is possible.
