Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the operations of elision (*lopa*) and the like would apply only to the word *ṭīti* itself and not to the final vowel or other phoneme [of the original term]; for they reply that this is accepted through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereby the word refers to that [original phoneme].

Ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*), however, is simply being different from that [grammatical form], and not a distinct genus (*jāti*), because there is a lack of evidence for such a category. Furthermore, the experience of that [ungrammatical word] is experienced as not having the absence of grammaticality as its object; moreover, it is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*). Grammaticality (*sādhutva*), on the other hand, is apprehended by the sense of hearing aided by the mental processing (*saṃskāra*) of grammar. As it has been said: "It is manifested through grammatical analysis (*prakriyā*). And likewise: "In that regard, the true nature [of the word] arises from diligent application (*abhiyoga*). Similarly: "And those who are experts therein, whose purpose is fixed upon it..."
And they are considered authorized in the knowledge of the virtues and faults pertaining thereto.

Furthermore, if it were said that the practice of correct instruction (*sādhvanuśāsana*) produces mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding incorrect forms (*asādhu*), there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, in the case of technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*), this is the distinction: "As for these technical terms created by one's own will, such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, *bhū*, and so on—how could they possibly possess correctness? They are certainly not considered to be correct."
Because they possess a non-corrupt form, these [expressions] are not ungrammatical;
just as hand gestures are used in the world, so too have these been established by convention.
In their application, there may be either spiritual merit or even demerit;
however, they are employed solely for the sake of understanding the meaning with brevity.
Thus, there is exclusion from both [categories].
For the sake of linguistic convention, the application of a name to its bearer is restricted in certain cases;
however, the relationship is indeed eternal, as in the case of "Dittha" and so forth, just like "cow" and so forth.
Furthermore, in this treatise, the relationship between [the terms] such as *vṛddhi* and so on is natural, characterized by the delimitation of their capacities,
just like that between a qualifier and a qualified.

According to this reasoning, if one holds the position that even these [names] are beginningless, then they are indeed correct (*sādhutva*). However, regarding the act of naming, correctness belongs only to those names that conform to the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, according to the rule: "One should employ a primary derivative (*kṛt*), not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). This is because the Vedic injunction, "On the twelfth day, the father shall give a name," is more authoritative than a Smṛti rule concerning a specific case. As for names following local dialects (*deśabhāṣā*), they do not possess that status. Thus, it is said in the *Śabdakaṇṭakoddhāra*: "If correctness consists in being beginningless, what is the status of proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*)? It is replied:
because there is a restrictive scriptural injunction (*niyamaśruti*) in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* regarding the act of naming."
For us, there is no application of names according to one's own whim;
therefore, even regarding names, beginninglessness is not established.

However, those designations (*saṃjñā*) which exist through the local dialects of that region do not possess correctness (*sādhutva*). For this very reason, because they lack a basis in *nyāya* (logical necessity), it is stated in the third *vārttika*—namely, "the correctness of words that have no beginning" (*anādiśabdānām sādhutvam*)—that there is a conceptual construction (*kalpana*) regarding designations and the like. It should be noted, however, that the mention of "third" refers to a reverse counting. This *vārttika* is explicit in the *ṛlṛk-sūtra*. Therefore, it is established that correct words (*sādhuśabda*) are here derived through the conceptual construction of the division between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus ends the investigation into correctness (*sādhutvavicāra*).

Now, if this were the case, the instruction on phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*) would be purposeless, because through [the sūtra] *aiuṇ* and so forth, one would not understand the correctness (*sādhutva*) of any particular sound. Nor can its purpose be the cognition of the nature of phonemes as being free from defects, since that is already established through common worldly usage (*loka*). Otherwise, it would follow that there should also be an instruction for [phonetic features] such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so on. As it has been said:

"If it is argued that the instruction is for the sake of producing the desired cognition, then there would also have to be an instruction for the acute, grave, circumflex, nasalized, long, and protracted [vowels]."

The word "should be performed" (*kartavyaḥ*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. When the Sūtra is recited with the three accents (*traisvaryeṇa*), although the performance of both [the acute and grave] is established by the single utterance of one [accent], the recitation of all three—acute and so forth—is brought about with the intention of reciting them in monotone (*ekaśruti*). Nor can it be argued that the mention [of the acute accent] refers to the genus (*jāti*) and thus includes the acute and others; for then there would be the unwanted consequence of including even the "closed" (*saṃvṛta*) vowel-quality and so on, since they too are delimited by their respective genera. As it has been said:
"If it is argued that [the rule] is established because the instruction is given in terms of the form (*ākṛti*), then there must be a prohibition regarding the 'closed' vowels and the like."

The ellipsis is "one should be compliant. Although the short vowel *a* is closed (*saṃvṛta*), the closure of the other vowels is a defect. The Commentary states the items included by the word "etcetera":

the closed, the hoarse, the blown, the eṇī-made, the half-vowel, the swallowed, the ejected, the sung, the accompanied song, the nasalized, the hairy, the hanging, the struck out, the bitten, and the scattered.
Another says:
Seized, rejected, supported, expelled, nasalized, blown, shaken, bitten, made like a doe's call, half-uttered, hurried, and scattered— these are the conceptualizations of defects in vocal tone.

And Kaiyaṭa has explained [the terms as follows]: *kala* is produced in another place and is well known as *kākalī*. *Dhmāta* is that which, due to being full of breath, appears long even though it is short. *Eṇīkṛta* is undistinguished, where there is doubt as to whether it is the vowel *o* or *au*. *Ambūkṛta* is that which, though distinct, is heard as if turned inward. *Arddhaka* is that which, though long, is like short. *Grasta* is held at the root of the tongue; others say it is indistinct. *Nirasta* is harsh.

*Pragīta* is uttered like a *sāman* chant. *Upagīta* is embellished by a song of another vowel nearby. *Kṣviṇṇa* is as if trembling. *Romaśa* is deep. *Avalambita* is mixed with another vowel. *Nirhata* is harsh. *Saṃdaṣṭa* is as if increased. *Vikīrṇa* is spread across another vowel; others say it is when even a single [vowel] appears as many. The "cultivations of defects of tone" (*svaradoṣabhāvanā*) are the lineages of defects of tone. For the defects are infinite, being produced by incapacity and negligence.

Nor does the mention of even those [sounds] qualified by defects (doṣa) entail the application of such [defective sounds] themselves; for at the end of the treatise, all individual phonemes (*varṇavyakti*) are to be recited in their pure form. Just as in the final view (*siddhānta*), despite the proposition that all individual phonemes are "open" (*vivṛta*), they are treated as "contracted" (*saṃvṛta*) by the rule *aa* (Pāṇini 1.1.9); so too, by being recited at the end of the treatise, the status of being "not established" (*asiddha*) is obtained everywhere. Thus, there is brevity due to the abandonment of the designation *it* for the *anubandhas* and the subsequent elision (*lopa*). To explain:

In the root *śī*, only the vowel *ī* is to be recited as the *kala*. The *ātmanepada* suffixes follow from the *kala*. After a root ending in *dhmā*, they apply when the action benefits the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*). Expressions such as "the beginning and end are the *kala* and *dhmā*" should be recited in their respective places. The *iḍānugā* and others, as well as the *kaladhmātā*, are to be recited in their proper sequence. In the case of *ḍukṛñ*, "kṛ" is to be recited with two defects (the *ḍu* and the *ñ*). However, the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are to be discarded everywhere. In the rule *ādirantyena sahetā*, it should be stated that the initial letter is together with the final *kala*.

If, however, the reading were *kalena*, then according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), just as the final *ṇ* and so forth [do not receive a technical name], here too the final phoneme would not receive its designation. In rules such as *ḍhralopaḥ*, the term *aṇaḥ* would have to be replaced by *aoḥ*. [The absence of sandhi] is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. It is thus established, yet it becomes un-Pāṇinian. On this point, there is a Siddhānta-vārttika:

"Augments (*āgama*) and modifications (*vikāra*), along with suffixes (*pratyaya*), are uttered together with verbal roots (*dhātu*). Therefore, these [technical names] such as *kala* and the rest do not apply to them."

The meaning is that even in a treatise where the enumeration is by class (*jātiparanirdeśa*), the removal of defects occurs through the specific recitation of *āgama* suffixes and so forth. Nor is there a defect regarding nominal bases (*prātipadika*) that are not recited, because you too must necessarily resort to a word-for-word recitation (*pratipadapāṭha*). Otherwise, in cases such as *śaśaḥ*, *mañcakaḥ*, and *palāśaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of forms such as *ṣaṣaḥ*, *mañcakaḥ*, and *palāṣaḥ*.

[Objection: "Surely, for the sake of determining vowels and so forth, let there also be the removal of defects from the *pratipadapāṭha* [recitation of every word], and let there be the authorization of grammatical correctness through the *uṇādi* or *pṛṣodarādi* classes; as for the specific determination [of meaning], let that be done by means of lexicons and the like. If this is argued, then let the removal of defects also result from the *śikṣā* and other such works. [Reply: True. However, since the removal of defects is merely incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*), the primary purpose is indeed the accomplishment of the *pratyāhāras*.

And these [terms] are beginningless (*anādi*). This is because of the etymological derivation: "that in which letters (*varṇa*) are extended (*pratatāḥ*) and condensed (*saṃkṣipyante*). Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since even though several items are presented by the letters *a* and so forth in the introductory statement (*grahaṇaka-vākya*), conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) itself serves as the regulator. Furthermore, the usage found in the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* provides evidence for this. Nor is there an absence of a delimiter for the conventional meaning; for just as "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*) is the delimiter in the word *paṅkaja*, here too, "the status of being a technical term (*saṃjñātva*)"—as prescribed by the sūtra *ādir antyena* (P. 1.1.71)—serves as that delimiter. Consequently, it applies commonly to *sup*, *tiṅ*, and so forth.

If, however, there is a rule that the delimitor of the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is precisely the mode of the cognition produced by that word—since the text states that "the adjunct of denotative power (*śakti-upādhi*) is necessarily the object of verbal cognition"—then let the aforementioned property be merely an adjunct of usage (*prayoga-upādhi*). This is because it possesses the quality of being the counter-positive of the absence that is incompatible with the knowledge of the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) produced by its usage. Alternatively, being a technical name (*saṃjñā*) as described above is itself the state of being a *pratyāhāra*;
for we observe that names established by the rule *ādirantyena...* (Pāṇini 1.1.71) are designated by the term *pratyāhāra*. Thus, all is auspicious.
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the Siddhāntasudhānidhi composed by the preceptor Viśveśvara, the sovereign of the illustrious Kūrmācala.
*aiuṇ* 1.

By virtue of the technical convention of the sūtra to be stated later, *ādirantyena*, there are fourteen sūtras intended to present the sequence of phonemes to be included under the technical designations such as *aṇ* and so forth. For the sake of clear understanding, there is an absence of *guṇa* and other such modifications [in these initial vowels].

As for the objection that in the word *a*, because the elision (*lopa*) [of the case-ending] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *ik* for *ik* by the rule *iko'savarṇe* does not apply; and because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṛtyaka* when there is an *ṛ* sound, the substitutions *ay* and *āy* for *e* and *ai* would be unavoidable—this is not correct. For the *prakṛtibhāva* applies specifically to the end of a word (*padānta*). Furthermore, rather than assuming the elision of the case-ending on the grounds of Vedic usage (*chāndasatva*), it is more appropriate to assume the absence of sandhi (*asandhi*).

Kaiyaṭa, however, maintains that there is no *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) because the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *aj* and so forth have not yet been established at the time of the instruction of the phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*). His intention is as follows: "Because they are not established" means that due to the deficiency of the specific form required for the application of the rule whose own cause [the designation] is yet to be produced; that is to say, because they do not fall under the delimitor of the objecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) which excludes the context of the instruction of phonemes. This is because only correct words (*sādhuśabda*) are to be derived [by grammar], and these [phonemes] are not included among either worldly or Vedic words. Furthermore, there is no evidence for regarding the [phonetic symbols] such as *aiuṇ* as being words that possess technical designations (*saṃjñāśabda*).

By this [it is shown that] the sequence of textual recitation (*pāṭhapaurvāparya*) is not the governing factor in the operation of the treatise (*śāstrapravṛtti*). For it is frequently observed in the earlier sūtras that operations prompted by subsequent sūtras are indicated; otherwise, such an indication would be untenable. Furthermore, in rules such as *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (P. 1.1.9), there would result the non-application of rules like the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), which depend upon technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *savarṇa* that are themselves enjoined therein. This is because the application of an operation toward that which is delimited by a property (*dharma*) grasped as the delimiting condition of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) in an injunctive rule (*vidhisūtra*) is necessarily required.

For this very reason, it is consistent that statements such as "there is nothing manifold here" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*) convey the falsity of themselves as well, by way of being delimited by properties such as "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*), which serve as the delimiters of the negandum. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the rule of "taking hold" (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) would also apply to itself, resulting in the collapse of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that long vowels do not include their homogeneous counterparts because they are not short (*anaṇ*).

In this regard, the objection that "because the long vowels are not present prior to the application of that rule (*tacchāstra*)—since [the rule] does not bring about the presence of the long vowels for *a* and so forth, and thus there is no apprehension of them as being the objects of the rule (*uddeśya*)"—should be understood as irrelevant. This is because the rule applies there precisely because the words *tulyāsyaprayatnam* and so on are grammatically correct (*sādhutvena*). Furthermore, in the comprehension of the meaning of that sentence, it is only the presence of the meanings of the words *tulyāsyaprayatnam* etc. that is required; a cognition characterized by the property of "long vowel substitution" (*savarṇadīrghatva*) is not required. As for the claim that the operation does not occur due to the absence of *saṃhitā* (euphonic junction)—it is said:
"The *saṃhitā* is obligatory within a single word, and obligatory between a verbal root and a prefix."
It is constant in a compound, but in a sentence it depends upon the speaker's intention.

Regarding the statement that this is because *saṃhitā* is not mandatory (*anityatva*) within a sentence (*vākya*), that is to be considered. For vowels such as *a* and *i* do not constitute a sentence, as they do not present meanings that serve as correlates for the mutual connection of meanings. Nor should it be argued that since the vowels *a* and others mentioned in this sūtra do serve as correlates for connection in rules such as *aṇudit savarṇasya ca*, they therefore constitute a sentence; for even if that [other rule] were a sentence, this [present case] would still not be established as one. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

However, some argue that because words such as *ca* are listed among the indeclinables (*nipāta*), they possess the designation of *pragṛhya* by the rule "an indeclinable consisting of a single vowel [is *pragṛhya*]," and thus undergo *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of their original form). It should not be argued that, if this were so, rules such as "from *at*, *iñ*" would fail to apply in cases like *dākṣi*; for the inclusion of the *t* in *tapara* (e.g., *at*) serves to restrict the reference to the vowel *a* belonging specifically to the traditional alphabet (*akṣarasamāmnāyika*). Since there is no possibility of another *a* being included as a *sarvaṇa* (homogeneous) sound, the *tapara* marker would be useless for the purpose of excluding such other vowels. This objection is invalid.

They say: "Since it is impossible to specify every individual instance, and since some specification of instances is inevitable, even if one specifies only those instances that are *nipātas* for the sake of clear comprehension—given the absence of *saṃhitā*-operations—the goal is achieved because all instances of every form are presented through similarity. This too is incorrect; for if one intends similarity by means of a property subsumed under *varṇatva* (phonemic-ness) that resides in the [individual] itself, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of including long vowels as well. Nor is this fault avoided even when specifying instances other than *nipātas*.

This is because we accept the designation of the mere individual instance (*vyakti*) alone, without intending to express any internal properties (*antara-dharma*). Nor should it be argued that the mere individual instance of a vowel (*avarṇa-vyakti*)—which lacks both the property of being a particle (*nipātatva*) and the property of being different from that—is unreal; for what has been stated is merely the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding those two properties. Furthermore, the property of being a particle must necessarily be intended for the sake of the designation *pragṛhya*. As for the suffix *-kāra*, however, it does not apply here, because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the sūtra "rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvulbahulam," since the mention of "optionally" (*bahula*) applies to that specific prescription.

It might be argued as follows: According to the *śikṣā* statement that "the vowel *a* is closed" (*saṃvṛta*), the short *a* produced with a closed articulatory effort (*saṃvṛta-prayatna*) lacks homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the long and protracted *ā*s produced with open articulatory efforts (*vivṛta-prayatna*). Consequently, how can there be a reference to the long vowel in rules such as "asya ccau"? For the rule "aṇudit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.69) specifies that only homogeneous sounds are included [by a term], and there is no homogeneity between sounds produced with different articulatory efforts.

If it is argued that in this case, in the word *agnidatta*, there should not be a long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrgha*) with the protracted *ā* according to the rule *guroranṛtaḥ*, that is true; for this very reason, the vowel *a* here is taught as being strictly open (*vivṛta*). As the Vārttika states:
"The teaching of the vowel *a* as open is for the sake of including [it within] the vowel *ā*."

And here, at the end of the treatise, the *pratyāpatti-sūtra* "a a" serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). For in that rule, having pronounced the vowel *a* characterized by openness (*vivṛtatva*) and the vowel *a* characterized by closure (*saṃvṛtatva*), the closed form of the vowel *a* is prescribed with reference to the open one. By the maxim "when there is a qualified [subject]," the status of being the thing to be prescribed (*vidheya*) ultimately falls upon closure itself. Furthermore, if the closure of the vowel *a* were already accepted during the stage of the technical grammatical process (*śāstrīyaprakriyā*), it would result in the redundancy of the rule prescribing closure.

Therefore, since it is accepted that the vowel *a* is "open" (*vivṛta*) even prior [to the application of specific rules], there is no fault either in the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*) or in the stage of actual usage (*prayoga-daśā*). This is because the quality of being "closed" (*saṃvṛta*), which is prescribed at the end of the treatise, is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the entire treatise. Furthermore, the openness of the vowel *ā* is stated in the *Pāṇinīya-śikṣā*: "The production (*karaṇa*) of the vowels and the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is traditionally held to be open.
Among those, *e* and *o* are more open than them, and likewise *ai* and *au*."

The term *svarapada* (the vowel-position) refers to that which is other than [the vowels] *e* and *ai*, and the term *bhinnapara* (other than the distinct) refers to that which is other than the short forms of the [vowels] *ā*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ*. This is because another *śikṣā* states, "the vowel *a* is closed" (*saṃvṛta*). Thus, while the short forms of the vowels other than *ā*—namely the sounds *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ*—are open (*vivṛta*), there is a greater degree of openness in *e* and *o* than in those, and a still greater degree in *ai* and *au*. However, some maintain that the word *vivṛta* appearing in the aforementioned *vārttika* means "more open" (*vivṛtatara*). This is because the long form of the vowel *ā* is more open than the short one; therefore, its homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the others cannot be established by mere openness alone. Accordingly, another *śikṣā* states:
The vowels are [produced with] open articulation (*vivṛta-karaṇa*); among them, *e* and *o* are more open (*vivṛtatara*), *ai* and *au* are more open than those, and *ā* is even more open than those.

It should not be argued that since there is a rule that what is delimited by a pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*) is necessarily delimited by its pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*), and thus the quality of being open (*vivṛtatva*) does not depart from that which is more open (*vivṛtatara*), the term *vivṛta* found in the Vārttika may be taken exactly as it is heard (i.e., as "open") because homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) can be established on that basis alone. This is because homogeneity must be stated precisely by means of the pervaded property.

For this very reason, relying on the fact that the *uṣman* sounds possess a slight opening (*vivṛtatva*), the authors of the *Bhāṣya* will refute—via the rule *nāj-jhalau*—the notion that they share the same phonetic character (*sāvarṇya*) with vowels such as *i*, which possess a full opening (*vivṛta-prayatna*). Alternatively, they say that by virtue of the overall capacity [of the definition], even those that are more open (*vivṛtatara*) possess the quality of being open (*vivṛtatva*) in its mere sense; otherwise, the formal declaration of their openness would be purposeless.

Others, however, maintain that there is indeed *sāvarṇya* even between what is more open and what is merely open, because the author of the *Sūtras* composed the rule *nāj-jhalau*. It is for this very reason that—
"The four internal efforts (ābhyantara-prayatna) are relied upon in the definition of homogeneous sounds (savarṇa-saṃjñā)," so says the Vṛtti.

But surely, in this way, there would be homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *ai* and *au* on the one hand and *e* and *o* on the other, because even though the former are more opened (*vivṛtatara*), they do not lose their quality of being opened (*vivṛtatva*). Nor is this a desirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for it would lead to errors such as the substitution of *ā* by the rule "auto'mśasoḥ" in *nāvam* and *nāvaḥ*; the status of being a *pragṛhya* by the rule "edait" in *karavāvahai* and *atre*; and the formation of the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) in *kasmai*, *adāt*, *viṣṇau*, and *asti*. Not so. Because of the force of their separate mention here, or due to the force of the two indicatory markers (*anubandha*), homogeneity does not apply in those cases.

Otherwise, one would have to employ grammatical operations using only a single *anubandha*, or one would not have specified *ai* and *au* [as separate]. For they say that [the distinction] is established by the very rule of technical inclusion (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*). Here, this must be considered: in the rule "eco 'yavāyāvaḥ," the separate instruction of the vowels *ai* and *au* is for the purpose of regulating the substitutes; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion among the substitutes.

Alternatively, the solution in that case can be achieved by the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* (the rule of closest similarity) alone. Since the diphthongs (*ec*) consist of semivowels (*saṃvṛta*), for the palatal *e* which has a semivocalized *a*, there is the corresponding *ay*; for the labial *o* which has a semivocalized *a*, there is the corresponding *av*. Furthermore, since it will be stated later that the latter element of *ai* and *au* is predominant, and because the *a* sound possesses half a mora while the *i* and *u* sounds possess one and a half morae respectively, the following arrangement is possible: for the palatal *ai* which has a wide-open (*vivṛta*) *a*, there is the corresponding *āy*; and for the labial *au* which has a wide-open *a*, there is the corresponding *āv*. Thus, the systematic application is established.

Not so; for it is declared that the vowel *a* is "open" (*vivṛta*) during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). As for the argument regarding the separate *anubandhas*, that is incorrect. Both *anubandhas* are necessary for the purpose of restricting the application of the technical terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* to their respective designated objects (*saṃjñin*). Nor can the matter be settled by referring to the *saṃjñins* in their own form (*svarūpeṇa*) alone; for if that were the case, there would be the heaviness (*gaurava*) of eight morae (*mātrā*) involved. But according to our system, each of the two terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* consists of one and a half morae, and the phonetic inventory (*varṇasamāmnāya*) consists of half a mora; thus, there are only five and a half morae in total, which is more economical (*lāghava*).

It should not be argued that in the case of the technical term *guṇa*, the bearer of the name (*saṃjñin*) is indicated by its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), whereas in the case of the term *vṛddhi*, it is indicated only by means of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Even so, there is an increase of one *mātrā* because, when combined, four *mātrās* are involved in the *guṇa* designation and two and a half *mātrās* in the *vṛddhi* designation, resulting in a total of six and a half *mātrās*. [Objection: But surely, in rules such as "eṅaḥ padāntād... (Pāṇini 6.1.109), since the mention of the word *eṅ* is made instead of *ec*, there can be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to *ai* and *au* simply by the force of that specific mention.

If it is argued that the phrase "the non-application of *sāvarṇya*" means "the non-application of operations caused by it," this is not correct; for even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in rules such as "auto'mśasoḥ. Indeed, it is not the case that because a vowel (*aṇ*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhakatva*) in instances where it is marked with a *t*-stop (*tapara*), the same should apply in other instances as well; such is the direction of the argument.

And here, by means of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from a group of similar items), there is the inclusion of all six short vowels; the elision of the case-ending is due to the fact that this is a sūtra. The same applies to the subsequent rule as well. For this very reason, the statement that "long vowels are not *aṇ*" is also consistent. Thus, in cases such as the reference (*anuvāda*) "asyacvau," and in prescriptive rules (*vidhi*) such as "tyadādīnāmaḥ," where short vowels are specified, the short vowels everywhere indeed possess the status of *aṇ*. Consequently, the composition of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule defining the scope of *aṇ*) is undertaken for the sake of achieving the desired result: namely, that in a reference (*anuvāda*) long vowels and others are included, but in a prescription (*vidhi*) they are not.

For without that [distinction], the establishment of the categories of "existent" (sat) would be untenable. Thus, in the view that there are an equal number of eternal, uniform individual instances (*vyakti*) for each contradictory property, this Sūtra does not apply at all. Since there exist in the world only six individual instances of the short form of the letter *a*, if one were to assert their distinctness, then because the *a*s situated in verbal roots, nominal stems, suffixes, and particles would not constitute the aggregate of distinct individual instances of the six *a*s specified by the *pratyāhāra* [AṬ], the respective functions of those vowels would be accomplished without effort.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the Bhāṣya on the *hayavaraṭ* sūtra—which states that "all the phonemes (*varṇas*) are taught simultaneously"—because you yourself accept the mention of six instances of the letter *a*. For the meaning of that [Bhāṣya] is simply that they are to be pronounced with the same effort (*prayatna*). This is evident from the Bhāṣya's statement: "He names the phonemes to be pronounced, saying, 'These phonemes have been taught'. If it is objected that no scholar of the system (*tāntrika*) holds the view that there are eighteen distinct and eternal *a*-sounds, that is true; however, this position must be accepted because it withstands logical reasoning (*yuktisahatva*). To explain: ... [text continues] ... Thus, [the conclusion is reached].

In the view of Bhaṭṭa, each individual manifestation of the phoneme *a* and so forth is indeed eternal, because of the recognition that "this is that very same *a*. Nor can it be said that this [recognition] apprehends merely the belonging to the same class (*tajjātīyatva*), for it is only on the strength of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*)—as in the case of the recognition of a flame—that such recognition is said to have as its object a member of the same class; and in the present case, no such subverting factor exists. Furthermore, cognitions of production and destruction, such as "the phoneme *ga* has arisen" or "it has perished," are not [valid proofs of non-eternality] in this way, because the production and destruction belong to the manifesting sound (*dhvani*) and are superimposed upon the phoneme.

Nor should it be argued that since origination—defined as the relation to a time-point that is not the locus of the destruction of the moment that is its own locus—is constituted by the property of "selfhood" (*svatva*) and is thus distinct for each different substratum (*dharmin*), how could the origination of one thing be superimposed upon another? For when the constituent elements of origination are presented individually—in the manner of "in the locus of 'a'," "in that moment," "in the destruction of that," "in the locus of that," and so forth—it is possible to have a delusion of a composite origination.

For this very reason, even though the "unbroken pervasion" (*akhaṇḍavyāpti*)—which consists of fire co-occurring with that which is delimited by firehood (fireness) that is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence co-occurring with fuel—is unestablished (because firehood lacks the status of being a non-delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence co-occurring with fuel), there is nonetheless an illusion of pervasion (*vyāptibhrama*) precisely because the constituent elements of that [definition] are taken as the objects of their mutual connection. Nor should it be argued that the recognition itself is an error, on the grounds of conforming to the cognition [of pervasion].

Nevertheless, this is not the case because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary], and because the conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) involved in postulating an infinite number of sounds, their destructions, antecedent non-existences (*prāgabhāva*), and so forth, favors the position of their permanence. Nor should it be argued that the difference between sounds is due to distinctions such as intensity (*tāratva*) and dullness (*mandatva*), since contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single substratum at the same time; for intensity and the like are properties of the air (*vāyu*), just as the darkening of a face is a property of the mirror.

Otherwise, the relationship of pervader and pervaded between the universals such as *gatva* (the universal of being the letter *ga*), which are held to reside in the phoneme (*varṇa*), would be untenable. For *gatva* is not pervaded by *tāratva* (high pitch), since it exists even in a low-pitched *ga*. Nor is *tāratva* pervaded by *gatva*, since it exists even in the case of the letter *ka* and others. Furthermore, there would be a confusion (*sāṃkarya*) of the two in the case of a high-pitched *ga*.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, qualities such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*) would not be perceivable by the auditory organ; for while the auditory organ lacks the capacity to grasp air itself, it likewise lacks the capacity to grasp the attributes of air. This is because there is no sublation [of the claim] that some attributes of air are indeed grasped by it, just as we accept that odors, tastes, and sounds are grasped by the nose, tongue, and ear, even though earth, water, and ether are not grasped by those respective organs.

Alternatively, since the Naiyāyikas accept that the air-currents (*vāyu*) which produce high (*tāra*) or low (*manda*) pitches possess tactile qualities (*sparśa*) arising from their intensity or lack thereof, it is possible for qualities such as pitch (*tāratva*)—which are perceived by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*) when delimited by the ear-cavity—to be grasped by the auditory organ (*śrotra*). For this very reason, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that sequence (*ānupūrvī*), which consists in being the object of a cognition immediately following [the cognition of] a *gha* sound and so forth, is grasped by the auditory organ itself when it is presented (*upanīta*) to the mind in the case of the letter *ṭa* and others.

For this very reason, the cognition "he utters the letter *ga* ten times" refers exclusively to the repetition [of the utterance], and does not involve the apprehension of a difference between individual instances, as in the thought "he produces ten distinct *ga*s. As it has been said: "Therefore, whatever is sought from the universal (*jāti*) will be obtained from the phoneme itself; however, that which is obtainable from the individuals is obtained from the sounds (*nāda*). Thus, the notion of 'the property of being *ga*' (*gatva*) and so forth is redundant."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that the justification for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) lies in the identity of the phonemes (*varṇa*), while the possession of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmavattā*) resides in the sounds (*dhvani*). And here, the justification for the Sūtra is as follows: because all *a*-phonemes situated in verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth are identical, they all possess the status of *aṇ*; consequently, the application of the "comprehensive rule" (*grahaṇakaśāstra*) occurs for the *a* in forms such as *asyacvau*. In *śāmyati* and similar forms, the long vowel is applied by the rule "śamāmaṣṭānām. In *dṛṣad*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the final *a* of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established by a Phiṭ-sūtra.

That which is situated at the beginning [of a word] (*ādi*) has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). In forms such as *avanamati*, the acute accent is applied by the rule "prefixes (*upasarga*) [are acute], except for *abhi*. Otherwise, if the *a*-sounds were distinct, then even if the *a* in the phonetic inventory (*varṇopadeśa*) is postulated to be wide-open (*vivṛta*), those *a*s occurring elsewhere would lack that wide-open quality; consequently, the grammatical operations prescribed for such sounds would fail to apply. This is because properties such as shortness (*hrasvatva*) and acute accent (*udāttatva*) belong to the single entity *ac* (vowel), and only that which is included within the traditional list of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*) possesses the status of being a vowel (*actva*).

Furthermore, since no grammatical operation is prescribed with reference merely to the individual phonemes taught in the *varṇasamāmnāya*, one would have to assume that such operations proceed solely by the force of the aforementioned statement;

however, it should not be argued that in this way the operations of the suffix *aṇ* would apply to the suffix *ka*, and the operations of the suffix *ka* to the suffix *aṇ*, because that would result in a confusion of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*).

Because the restriction of the grammatical operations resulting from those respective suffixes is established by the very capacity of their fixed connection (*niyatānubandha*) through the presentation of those specific markers (*tattaddeśa*), even in common worldly practice, when there is an instruction of multiple attributes in such a manner as "be shaven-headed here," "be matted-haired here," or "be naked here," we observe that the application of each attribute is restricted only to where the person is instructed as being delimited by that particular attribute. Similarly, in rules such as *karmaṇyaṇ*, the marker *ṇ* is restricted to that [suffix] alone; and in rules such as *careṣṭaḥ*, the marker *ṭ* is restricted to that [suffix] alone.

In the case of *gāpoṣṭak*, there is the status of being *kit* and *ṭit*. For this very reason, the purpose of the repeated application of the *ṇit* designation in rules such as *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* and *ṭhasivādibhyo’ṇ* is rendered meaningful.

But even so, [one might object that] in the case of *ghaṭika* (one who crosses by means of a jar), the suffix *ṭhan* prescribed by the rule *naudvyacaṣṭhan* would not apply; nor would the suffix *yat* prescribed under the heading *tasya nimittaṃ saṃyogotpātau* by the rule *godvyaco'saṃkhyāparimāṇāśvāderyat* in the case of *dhanya* (a conjunction or portent caused by wealth) apply, because since the vowel *a* is single, there is no "dvyac" (two-vowel) status. Yet, the sūtra does indeed apply in cases such as *bāhuka* (one who crosses with arms), where there are two dissimilar vowels (*a* and *u*).

If it is argued that there is scope [for the application of the rule] there, we say no; for by way of repetition (*āvṛtti*), the word *ghaṭa* and others also possess two vowels (*dvyactva*). Nor does the maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) apply here. This is because in the rule *godvyacaḥ*, by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words such as *aśva*—which are not numbers, measures, or horses—the absence of those qualities is also indicated. Otherwise, since the word *aśva* lacks the status of being a primary *dvyac*, the suffix *yat* would not apply, rendering the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) useless. For this very reason, in forms such as *kiriṇā* and *giriṇā*, the acute accent (*udātatva*) of the case-ending according to the rule *sāvekācaḥ* does not occur.

Because even by means of the secondary designation as "having two vowels" (*dvyañ*), the designation as "having one vowel" (*ekāj*) is sublated. Following this very line of reasoning, it should be noted that even in the Vedānta system, the existence of *prakṛti* (primordial matter) is established, wherein there is only a single individual instance of the phoneme 'a' and others, produced at the time of creation and persisting until its dissolution. However, this is incorrect; for if qualities such as high pitch (*tāratva*) were properties of air (*vāyu*), then qualities such as 'k'-ness (*katva*) would also necessarily be so. For it has been stated by the teacher Udayana in the *Tātparyaśuddhi*:

Even if one were to postulate that the phoneme (*varṇa*) is eternal, it must be postulated as a single entity, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and because there is a lack of evidence for its diversity. As for properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*), they appear therein as adventitious (*aupādhika*). Thus, let qualities such as "k-ness" (*katva*) also be adventitious to it, just like intensity (*tīvratva*) and so forth; enough with this web of numerous, unauthoritative postulations. Furthermore, since the adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) are many, one would have to postulate a universal of unity residing in them—this is the dawn breaking upon the very wall where one was working.

Now, if—out of fear of the aforementioned defects—it is accepted that intensity and so forth are indeed inherent [in the phonemes], then, in that case, just as with the *dhvani*s, the same would apply to the *ka*-sounds and others; thus, the universal of *katva* (the property of being *ka*) would have to recur [infinitely].

Nor should the cognitions of production and destruction be considered erroneous, as there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) [to the contrary]. Furthermore, the postulation of non-existence prior to destruction (*prāgabhāva*), destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), and so forth, is merely for the sake of the final result (*phalamukha*). Moreover, in that [opponent’s] view, the property of being produced by the impact of the throat, palate, and so forth (*kaṇṭhatālvādyabhighāta-janya*) is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the direct perception of *ka*, whereas in my view, it is simply the property of being *ka* (*katva*) itself; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). Nor should it be argued that even in that view, the property of being *ka* (*katva*) alone—qualified by the relation of ordinary objecthood (*laukika-viṣayitā*)—is the delimiting factor for the effect, because "ordinariness" (*laukikatva*) is not a uniform or recurring property (*ananugata*).

Furthermore, the perception of a "tumult" (kolāhala) is untenable because there is no cognition of [individual properties] such as *katva* (the quality of being *ka*) therein. Even if these were perceived, they would lack the status of being objects of ordinary experience (*laukika-viṣayatva*) as *katva* and so forth. This is because the referent of the term "tumult" consists of various sounds characterized by a genus (*jāti*) that pervades the state of not being grasped as specific words like *ka*. Nor should it be argued that *katva* and the like do not exist at all in that case; for it is established by the experience of everyone that when there is a desire to know, one hears *katva* and other such qualities. Furthermore, identity cannot be established merely through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as "this very same *gurjarī*," it would follow that even phonemes (*dhvani*) are eternal. Furthermore, the recognition "this is that very same letter *ga*" is erroneous only if its object is the non-difference of the individual instances (*vyakti*). However, if it is intended to mean the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the universal *gatva* (the property of being the letter *ga*), then it is indeed a valid cognition (*pramā*). Nor should it be argued that the recognition of a universal always takes the form "this belongs to that class" (*tajjātīyo 'yam*); for in cases such as "this very same medicine, which was taken by many, is now being taken by me too," we do not observe that form of recognition even though it concerns the non-difference of things belonging to the same class.

However, this is the distinction: when the universal (*jāti*) also appears upon the perception [of the individual], then [the cognition is] "this belongs to that class" (*tajjātīyo 'yam*); but in the absence of that [appearance of the universal], it is the very nature of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), namely "this is that" (*so 'yam*). Therefore, phonemes (*varṇas*) are indeed infinite, being produced by their respective individual natures (*svarūpa*). If it is argued: "In that case, a word would not be capable of conveying meaning, because that specific word upon which the apprehension of its expressive power (*śakti*) occurred has perished," we say: not so.

Just as when a jar or similar object that was the locus of the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) is destroyed, another jar is still understood from the word "jar," so too, even upon the destruction of a word known to possess potency, understanding from another word of the same class is logically established. As for the objection that if the individuals were identical, the universal (*sāmānya*) would not exist at all—and how then could there be understanding from another word—that is not correct, because the difference between individuals has also been proven. Thus say the Naiyāyikas.

In this case as well, the recognition of the identity of the individual phoneme (*vyakti*) is indeed an error. Thus, if one follows this view here, because there is a difference between phonemes at each utterance, the vowel *a* in rules such as "asya cvau" would lack the status of being an *aṇ* (a short vowel), and consequently, it would not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Therefore, in that context, there exists a genus (*jāti*)—subsumed under the genus delimited by the production [of sounds] from the throat and other places—which resides in all short vowels. That very genus is taught in the *varṇasamāmnāya* (the traditional list of phonemes) as being characterized by openness (*vivṛtatva*). For this very reason, all short vowels possess the status of *aṇ*, and thus there is no inconsistency anywhere.

In this regard, the following must also be considered: there is no evidence for a universal (*jāti*) that subsists solely in short vowels (*hrasva*). Nor can its existence be established merely on the basis of a recurring cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*) among short vowels that excludes long ones and so forth; for such a cognition is adequately accounted for by the property of shortness itself. Nor should it be argued that shortness itself is that universal and not something distinct from it; for in that case, it would be impossible for it to be subsumed under [the universals] *atva* (the state of being *a*, etc. and so forth. Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*saṅkara*) of the overlap between *atva* and shortness within a long vowel form (*dīrghākāra*). Finally, one cannot argue that shortness is not a single entity but rather manifold, in order to avoid being subsumed under *atva* and the like.

Because a continuous cognition (anugata-pratyaya) is untenable regarding short *a*, *i*, and so forth; and because shortness (*hrasvatva*) lacks the status of a universal (*jāti*), as stated in the rule "A vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *ū* is short, long, or protracted"; and because shortness, being essentially dependent on pronunciation, is merely an adventitious property (*upādhi*). Therefore, there are exactly eighteen individual instances (*vyakti*) of the letter *a*, all of which are eternal. Thus, the distinction from the two other views is that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is accepted as valid knowledge, and the imposition (*āropa*) of contradictory properties is not admitted. Furthermore, by accepting a commonality such as "a-ness" (*atva*) that persists through these individuals, the perception of a tumultuous noise (*kolāhala*) is rendered possible.

Nor should it be argued that, if the property of being a *ka*-sound (*katva*) and so forth were the delimitors of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) by virtue of the relation of being an object of the worldly [cognition], how could there be a perception of a "tumultuous noise" (*kolāhala*), since *ka*-ness and the like are not apprehended therein? For even so, the relation that serves as the delimitor of effectness is simply the objective state (*viṣayatā*) residing in its own substratum; and this is beyond dispute, given that the *k*-sounds and other phonemes which are the substrata of *ka*-ness and the like possess objective status in the perception of a tumultuous noise.

Just as, according to that [opponent's] view, the conjunction with a heterogeneous wind (*vijātīyapavanasaṃyoga*) is the cause for [producing] the letter *a* and so on by way of the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā*), and inherence (*samavāya*) is the delimitator of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), so too here, in the direct perception of that [sound], the auditory organ (*śravaṇa*)—which possesses the conjunction with wind—is the locus where the auditory perception of sound arises by way of delimitation; and in the perception of "a-ness" (*atva*) and so on, auditory inherence (*śrāvaṇasamavāya*) is the regulating factor. This is because "a-ness" inheres in the auditory *a*. Furthermore, in the auditory perception of the absence of "ka-ness" (*katva*) residing in the letter *a*, auditory qualification (*śrāvaṇaviśeṣaṇatā*) is the regulating factor. This is because, in this position, [the opponent's claims of] auditory inherence and so forth are not accepted.

Now, in the case of the auditory conjunction (*śrāvaṇa-samavāya-sannikarṣa*), is "auditory" (*śrāvaṇa*) a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)? It cannot be the first, because even during the state of non-manifestation, the letter *a* would be characterized as auditory; consequently, the perception of its shortness (*atva*) would occur even then. Nor can it be the second, because at that time, without the production of an auditory [quality] in the letter *a*, it is impossible for it to be qualified by audibility. This would entail the acceptance of the perception of the mere phoneme (*avarṇa*) prior to the production of the perception of its shortness. And this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

If it is argued that because the relation of being a worldly object-possessor (*laukika-viṣayitā*) residing in its own locus serves as the delimiting factor for the effect [of perception], the direct perception of the mere word is impossible—since a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) worldly object-possessor is not admitted—then this is not so. For we have previously accepted the very existence of a direct perception whose qualifier is "word-ness" (*śabdatva*) and so forth. If it is further asked: "In this case too, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) which apprehends the identity between the form of the acute accent (*udātta*) and the form of the grave accent (*anudātta*) is nothing but an error," the answer is: True. Nevertheless, one should infer [the following]: that many such [cognitions] must be protected from being classified as valid cognitions (*pramā*), and so on.

Furthermore, this position—that individual instances of phonemes such as *ga* and others, though differentiated by properties such as high or low pitch, must be eternal—is virtually a suspicion already raised in the Nyāya treatises as a partial view of Bhaṭṭa regarding the doctrine of the non-eternality of phonemes; it is also presented here in the *Śabdakaustubha*, where it states that there are eighteen distinct individual phonemes. And this has been followed by the venerable authors of the *Vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya*.

For instance, in the rule *aa*, there is a twofold resolution of the following concern: since the preceding vowel *ā*—which serves as the subject (*anuvādya*)—brings about the presence of the long vowels and others by virtue of the introductory grammatical rule (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*), it might be suspected that these [long vowels] would also be prescribed as being "closed" (*saṃvṛta*) during their actual usage. Therefore, it has been resolved in two ways.

The [desired] result is established either by the mention of *ta* as a limit (*tapara-nirdeśāt*) or by the mention through *ekaśeṣa*; thus, for the Blessed Pāṇini, [the rule] is established for vowels that differ in accent and nasality. The reading should be *at* (with a short *a*), and consequently, because of the rule "that which has *ta* as its limit [denotes] only its own duration," there is no inclusion of long vowels and so forth—this is the first solution. Dissatisfied with this because it lacks the natural elegance of the Sūtra, the second [solution] is that the mention *a* is made by means of *ekaśeṣa* of all six short vowels; and by virtue of that [mention], the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* does not operate.

Therefore, since the intended meaning is that there are exactly six individual instances of the short vowel *a*, it follows by implication that there is permanence (*nityatva*) through the acquisition of that many long and protracted instances as well. Furthermore, without the use of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for the six, there would be no inclusion of all short *a*-sounds; and since the existence of a genus (*jāti*)—which is not pervaded by the mere occurrence in short vowels—is established by its very nature as referring to those [six], the mention of *ekaśeṣa* as a restatement would be untenable, resulting in the conclusion that [the genus] is permanent.

If it is argued that, in this way, since the formation of grammatical operations could be accomplished everywhere in cases where there is no mention of *savarṇagrahaṇa* (the inclusion of homogeneous sounds) by means of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of two identical words) alone, the rule *taparas tatkālasya* would be redundant—this is not so. For, although *ekaśeṣa* may be accepted here based on the natural force of the wording of the rule, it is more cumbersome than relying on the presence of *taparatva* (the addition of *t* as a marker). Furthermore, in rules such as *upasargād ṛti dhātau*, it is impossible to establish the inclusion of the *ḷ*-vowel by means of the *ṛ*-vowel through *ekaśeṣa*.

In that context, since the status of having *t* as a marker (*taparatva*) is necessary for the purpose of excluding the apprehension of the long vowel, it is also more appropriate in other instances; by this, the recourse to an interpretative indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the sake of accomplishing the grammatical operation even in secondary (*gauṇa*) cases—such as in *ghaṭena tarati*—is refuted, because the operation is accomplished through the primary sense alone. This is because, in the case of a two-syllable word, when one syllable is acute (*udātta*), the other is necessarily grave (*anudātta*) due to the rule of "the rest being unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*), and thus a distinction exists.

Thus, in the opinion of Bhaṭṭa, in forms such as *kiriṇā* and so on, the acute accent would apply by the rule *sāvekācastṛtīyādirvibhaktiḥ*, which means that when there is a monosyllabic (*ekāc*) word ending in the nominative plural suffix *sU*, the third-case and subsequent case endings following it would be acute. This is because in *kiriṣu*, there exists the status of being a monosyllable (*ekāctva*). As for the claim made by the author of the *Avṛtti* that the designation of being a disyllable (*dvyajvyapadeśa*) removes the inherent monosyllabic status of the base itself—that is incorrect. For just as the status of being a boy is not removed by the secondary (*gauṇa*) status of being a fire, the status of being a monosyllable is not removed by the secondary status of being a disyllable. Furthermore, the absence of the designation "having two sons" in one who has three sons is due to the fact that even the state of having three sons is not superimposed [upon him].

The expression "having two sons" (*dviputra*) is not a valid means of knowledge with respect to that person only when it intends to convey the state of being a person who lacks the causal capacity defined by being produced by a person who is not the locus of the complete possession (*paryāpti*) of a number that is either duality or another number residing distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*). However, it is a valid means of knowledge when there is the intention to express possibility (*saṃbhava*), because even the state of having three sons is untenable without the state of having two sons.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Dravyopāya* and other works: "Nor does the exclusion of other numbers constitute the meaning of the statement 'there are exactly nine substances,' because the state of being nine is impossible without the prior production of that preceding number. For this same reason, there are such usages as "the first three categories possess generality" (*sāmānyavat*). Even when it is said that the exclusion of horses and so forth serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) dependent upon a generality, the justification lies solely in the application of the grammatical operation (*kāryapravṛtti*) to the secondary sense (*gauṇa*), and not in the exclusion of the primary sense (*mukhya*), since the expressive power (*sāmarthya*) is exhausted by that alone.

If it is argued: "In the rule *rājñaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168) and others, the word *sā* was stated in order to prevent the acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending; however, if one accepts that [the base] possesses its own inherent status as a monosyllable (*ekāctva*), then since the status of being a monosyllable exists even in *rājasu*, the prevention [of the accent] would not occur there either. Therefore, in this context, the word *sā* itself is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the removal of the inherent status of being a monosyllable. This is not so. For that [word *sā*] can have purpose through the prevention [of the accent] in cases such as *bāhunā*. Nor is there an exclusion of that [base] by the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.59), because even in the singular locative [ending], that [base] also possesses the status of being a monosyllable.

This is because the author of the Bhāṣya stated in the seventh [chapter] that "the substitution of *au* must be marked with the *ḍit* designation. Furthermore, one should not intend for the status of being a single vowel (*ekāctva*) to apply to all case-endings (*vibhakti*) indiscriminately; otherwise, the mention of *sā-* [in the rule *sāvekācastṛtīyādivibhaktau*] would be redundant.

Moreover, it is established in both the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya on the rule *padādiṣu niśantāni prayojayanti* that, by the continued application of the term *ekāj* from the rule *ūḍidampadādyappuṃraidyubhyaḥ*, the words beginning with *pad* mentioned in the rule *paddannomās* are understood as ending with *niś*, because the subsequent words such as *asat* and others consist of more than one vowel (*anekāctva*).

If it is argued that, because the secondary status of having two syllables (*dvyactva*) would not preclude the primary status of being a single-syllable (*ekāctva*) of its own substratum, then words such as *asan*, *yakan*, *śakan*, and *āsan* would also be included as having more than one syllable (*anekāctva*), and thus their contradiction [with the rule] would be unavoidable; therefore, the Vārttika and other such texts must be taken as indicators (*jñāpaka*) for the preclusion of that [contradiction]—this is true. However, rather than resorting to such a difficult construction, the aforementioned method itself is more appropriate; for all the aforementioned works are consistent only when interpreted according to the view that there is a distinction between individual instances of the letter 'a' (*akāravyaktibheda*). This is the general direction of the argument.

According to the view of the *Vārttika*, however, the mention [of the vowel] is intended to denote the genus (*jāti*) such as shortness (*atva*) and so forth. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that long vowels would also include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*); for that is precluded by the force of the actual utterance of the long vowel. If all [homogeneous sounds] were intended to be included, it would follow that only the short vowel should have been mentioned for the sake of brevity. Furthermore, one should not argue that even under this view, a long vowel would still include a protracted (*pluta*) vowel; for since the mention of a protracted vowel would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), its exclusion is established, and thus the utterance of the long vowel lacks the capacity (*sāmarthya*) to include it.

Because there is no common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) that distinguishes [the short vowel] from its counterparts, the mention of *aṇ* need not be made in the *grahaṇaka-śāstra*. As it has been said:
"The mention of *aṇ* with respect to a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) is not a general rule (*aparibhāṣya*), because the class-form (*ākṛti*) is what is grasped.

However, the rule *tapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) serves only to exclude the reference to the genus (*jāti*) in specific instances. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the rule would also apply to long vowels and others in prescriptive contexts (*vidheya-sthala*), resulting in the prescription of long vowels and so forth in rules such as *tyadādīnām aḥ* and *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ*; for in those cases, singularity—just like the singularity of an animal—is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*) by virtue of being a qualifier of the thing to be prescribed (*vidheya-viśeṣaṇatayā*).

Nor should it be argued that since the prescription [of the vowel] as delimited by the property of being *tathā* (such) is already fulfilled by the long vowel (*dīrgha*), the long vowel alone should be the prescribed element; for, rather than postulating an unestablished long vowel, it is the established short vowel (*hrasva*) itself that must be the object of the prescription. Nor should it be argued that the state of being short (*hrasvatva*) is not established as a referential category (*padārtha*); for the short vowel is uttered in its own form (*svarūpa*). However, in cases such as "asya cvau," because it serves as a qualifier of the subject of reference (*anuvādya*), there is no intention to express that [shortness], just as with the singularity [of a noun]; thus, it refers to all [short vowels].

As for the claim that, according to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), there is no fixed rule regarding whether qualifiers of what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) or what is being restated (*anuvādya*) are intended (*vivakṣita*) or unintended (*avivakṣita*): this is because we observe a difference in intention even when the status as a qualifier of what is enjoined is identical—as in the case of *upeyivān*, *anāśvān*, and *anūcānaḥ*, where the elements *upa-* and so on, as well as the negative particle *nañ* and so on, are equally qualifiers of what is enjoined; and also because in the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ*, the quality of beginning with a *val* letter (*valāditva*), though a qualifier of what is being restated, is nonetheless intended. For this very reason, the mention of the word "one" (*eka*) in the sūtra *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is [justified].

"Otherwise, since the rule *ād guṇaḥ* is already justified by the intention to express singularity alone [in the case of *ad-eguṇaḥ*], [the mention of *eka* is redundant]. This is trivial; for even among the Mīmāṃsakas and others, there is no such thing as a "family custom" regarding non-intention (*avivakṣā*) and so forth. Even though the intention to express the meaning conveyed by the word is constant, that intention is abandoned on the strength of logic (*nyāya*) due to the impossibility of its connection with the injunction (*vidhi*). When there is a conflict between logic and the explicit statement, logic is ineffective; thus, even a qualifier of something being restated (*anuvādya*) may sometimes be intended to be expressed. Precisely for this reason:
"The followers of the Taittirīya school should perform the Śrāvaṇī rite at the *parvan* occurring at sunrise."

In this context, if one were to enjoin a restriction on the agent—namely, that only the Taittirīyakas [should perform] the Upākarma characterized by the lunar day (parvan) and qualified by its occurrence at sunrise (audayikatva)—this would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda) dependent on the intentionality of qualifying the subject. Consequently, the word "Taittirīyaka" is treated as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all followers of the Yajurveda (*yājuṣa*). Thus, there is an injunction of mere "occurrence at sunrise" with respect to the Upākarma qualified by the lunar day. This is because it is accepted that if even the lunar day were not intended to be significant, the statement "The Bahvṛcas should perform it during the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra]" would become redundant.

For this very reason, in the case of the text, "If both sacrificial offerings (*havis*) of one should suffer damage," since mere damage—unqualified by any specific counter-correlate—is constant and thus cannot function as a *nimitta* (occasioning condition), the qualification "sacrificial offering" (*havis*) itself is indeed intended. As it has been said: "We tolerate the qualification by 'sacrificial offering,' for a qualification of that which has already reached its final determination would cause a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the qualification "bothness" (*ubhayatva*) is not intended.

In reality, since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) here is used in a residual sense (*śaiṣika*), a connection with a verbal action is not strictly necessary; and because the qualification [of the root] as being "before an *ardhadhātuka* suffix" is possible even prior [to the application of the rule], there is no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), as in the case of the expression *aśvābhidhānīm*. Furthermore, since forms such as *īyivāṃsam* and *atistriyam* are observed in usage—both when the prefix is absent and when preceded by other prefixes—the element *upa-* is not intended to be significant. Moreover, because the *Manoramā* and *Kaustubha* state that for the sake of expressing singular number (*ekatva*), a single substitution of *u* occurs in place of the two *u*s, and because the mention of "one" (*eka*) was rejected by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa has stated therein: [The relevant passage from Kaiyaṭa: ...because the singular number is intended, a single *u* is substituted in place of the two *u*s. Thus, the mention of "one" (*eka*) was rejected by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. And so it was said there by Kaiyaṭa: (Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence regarding Kaiyaṭa's commentary; the translation reflects the available portion.)

Thus, the requirement of singular number has been rejected; for in rules such as "ād guṇaḥ," the number expressed by the word is intended to be significant. However, where the number is not intended to be significant, the very fact that the desired result (lakṣya) is established serves as the reason for its non-significance.

The term *saṃkhyā* (number) refers to what is under discussion [in the preceding context], and it is also an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other qualifiers of the predicate. Furthermore, even granting this, we say: even if one were to formulate the rule as *tapara-pratyayau tatkālasya*, there would be no need for the mention of *aṇ* in the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*, because the prevention of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in rules such as *tyadādīnām aḥ* could be achieved quite clearly by that very means. Moreover, in cases other than those involving *aṇ*, it must necessarily be stated that the reference to a phoneme (*varṇa-nirdeśa*) intends the genus (*jāti*).

Otherwise, in the case of *avāt stām*, between the two *t* sounds of the suffix *sicaḥ*, only one would possess the status of being a *jhal* (a consonant other than a semivowel or nasal), but not both; for neither of the two is specified in the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the traditional list of phonemes). Consequently, the elision of *sic* by the rule *jhalo jhali* would not occur. Nor can the force of the specific grammatical statement (*vacana*) serve as a solution, because that rule finds its scope of application in cases like *abhitthāḥ*, where a dissimilar sound follows. Thus, even under the view that effort (*prayatna*) is the defining criterion for similarity, the rule *nāj-jhalau* need not be formulated, which is a matter of parsimony (*lāghava*).

For the non-apprehension of *ha*-sounds and so forth by means of *a*-sounds and so forth is established precisely by the absence of a single genus (*jāti*) common to both. Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *daṇḍahastaḥ*, the prevention of *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution) would be difficult to justify without a prohibition of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity). This is because that [substitution] is possible simply through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *aci* in that rule; for even in the view that the Sūtra is actually formulated, the continued application of *aci* is necessary to avoid the fault in examples such as *kumārī śete*. This is because the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the prohibition "vowels and consonants are not homogeneous" (*nāj-jhalau*) applies only to those [sounds] which have not yet been apprehended as homogeneous. Such is the direction of the argument.

As for the claim that the letter *a* and others taught in the *pratyāhāra* sūtras, by virtue of a relationship of similarity (*sādṛśya*), bring to mind six individual instances similar to themselves—and that there is no impossibility of their syntactic connection (*śābdānvaya*) in a sentence because they are not brought to mind through a specific function (*vṛtti*), since this is possible according to the opinion of Guru—that is to be considered. For if the intention were to express similarity based on shortness (*hrasvatva*), it would follow that the letter *i* and others would also be brought to mind. However, if the intention were to express similarity based on both "being *at*" (*atva*) and shortness, then one could intend similarity based on *atva* alone, whereby the bringing to mind of all eighteen individual instances is indeed possible.

Furthermore, disregarding the intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding the universal of *a*-ness (*atva-jāti*) which appears as the form of *pra* above the letter *a*, it would be subject to the fallacy of "being swallowed by the possibility of non-utterance" (*anukti-sambhava-grasta*) to postulate the presentation of another *a* by means of a more cumbersome property (*dharma*) composed of that [universal].
[The sūtra] *ṛlṛk* (2).

[Objection: Surely, in the rules prescribing [the application of] grammatical operations (*vidhipradeśa*), since it is possible for the twelve varieties of the phoneme *ḷ* to be included by the phoneme *ṛ*—just as the eighteen varieties [of *ṛ*] are included—is the teaching of *ḷ* here redundant? Nor should it be argued that because of the difference in their points of articulation (*sthāna*)—namely, the palate (*mūrdhan*) and the teeth (*danta*)—there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), and thus the rule of inclusion (*grahaṇakaśāstra*) cannot apply. This is because homogeneity is established through an explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika-sāvarṇya*): "The mutual homogeneity of the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* must be stated. Nor should it be argued that that very [rule] need not be commenced.

Because of the rule *upasargād ṛti dhātau*, the term *ṛti* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule *vā supy āpiśaleḥ*; therefore, that [term] is necessary for the purpose of applying the optional *vṛddhi* substitution in forms such as *prālkārīyati*.

Alternatively, this is what must be explained: according to the principle stated in the *Bahvṛca-Prātiśākhya*, "The sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*, as well as the sixth *ūṣman* (the *jihvāmūlīya*), [are homogeneous]," their homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) is established by the very rule because they share the same place of articulation (*tulyasthānatvāt*). For this very reason, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *klṛp-* in the rule "after *ṛ* or a root ending in *uṣadha*, except for *klṛp* and *cṛ*" is consistent. Furthermore, in the case of *klṛp*, the *ḷ* is merely an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the *ḷ* sound; for there is no *ḷ* distinct from that [imitated sound] existing independently in either common usage (*loka*) or the Veda.

Since the substitution of *l* for *ṛ* (the *latva* rule) is considered *asiddha* with respect to vowel-related operations (*svarakārya*), the form remains that of *ṛ* during such operations; thus, the derivation of forms involving *vṛddhi* and other rules is established. Consequently, the formal instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* (*lṛkāropadeśa*) and the *sāvarṇya-vārttika* [which establishes its homogeneity with *ṛ*] are entirely redundant.

Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *ḷ* for *r* prescribed by the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* is itself *asiddha*, but not the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that [substituted form] occurring in such expressions as *lṛkārīyati*; for by the extended application (*atideśa*) "an imitation is like its prototype" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), that [imitation] is also *asiddha*. Otherwise, in the example *dviḥ pacantv ity āha*, the elision (*nighāta*) of the accent of the word *pacantu* according to the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would not occur; because, although it is an imitation of a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), it lacks the status of being a verbal suffix in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*).

Nor should it be argued that because the *taittirīya* recension reads the word with an initial udātta accent, a *nighāta* (anudātta) accent is simply not desired there; for by the force of the examples cited in the *Bhāṣya*, one can infer that even in other recensions (*śākhāntara*), a reading with *nighāta* exists. Likewise, in cases such as *agnī ity āha*, the designation of *pragṛhya*—by the rule "īdūded dvivacanam"—would not apply. Furthermore, it should not be argued that if an operation proceeds on the basis of the cognition of the vowel *ṛ*, then only *raparatva* (substitution of *ra*) would apply to its substitute *guṇa*, and not *laparatva* (substitution of *la*).

In the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, the inclusion of the pratyāhāra [ṛ] would otherwise result in redundancy, as it serves no purpose anywhere in the original formulation (*prakṛti*). Nor can it be argued that its utility in the original formulation lies in cases such as *klṛpe* (where the reduplicated syllable undergoes *atva*), because since *halādiśeṣaḥ* is mandatory there, there is no defect even if the *rapara* substitute were applied. Furthermore, it is not useful in forms like *klṛptaḥ* or *āklṛptaḥ*; for when the *vṛddhi* substitution is applied by the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*, the *latva* (substitution of *l*) is considered *asiddha*, so that *vṛddhi* applies to the *ṛ*-vowel itself, and the desired form is established by the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* alone once the *rapara* status is reached.

Nor should it be argued: "Since that *r* (in *klṛp*) is independent and not included within the *ṛ*-vowel, how can there be the substitution of *l* (*latva*) for it? For this must be established by the two subsequent rules that even the *r* belonging to the root *kṛp* undergoes the substitution of *l*. Nor should it be argued: "Even so, how is the case handled when there is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the *ḷ*-vowel found in roots such as *gamlṛ* (meaning 'to go'), since the rules regarding *asiddha* (non-application) and extension (*atideśa*) do not apply there? This is because the status of that *ḷ* as an *ac* (vowel) is established through the evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the application of the *yaṇ* substitute before the *ḷ*-vowel in the rule *puṣādidyutādyḷditaḥ*, as well as through the restatement of its *itsaṃjñā* (the designation of an *it*).

In reality, although it is possible for the statement to conclude by merely indicating that the designation *itsaṃjñā* (the technical name *it*) results in the application of rules concerning consonants (*hal-kārya*), the mention of *yaṇ* itself is the actual indicator.

As for the objection that, since there exist restatements such as *idito num* and indicative marks (*jñāpaka*) such as *ṛtyakaḥ*, the vowels beginning with *ikāra* (i, u, ṛ, ḷ) should likewise not be explicitly mentioned [in the *pratyāhāra*], that is not so. Without their explicit mention, it would be difficult to grasp even the status of being a vowel-function (*acakāryatva*) and so forth. Furthermore, because the scope of the letter *ḷ* is extremely limited, its mention follows the restatements merely to avoid the inconsistency in the aforementioned instances. To the question, "For what purpose is the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the letter *ḷ*? the following is stated:
The instruction of the letter *ḷ* is for the sake of onomatopoeia (*yadṛcchā*), imitation of inability (*aśaktijānukaraṇa*), prolation (*pluti*), and so forth.

The word *dadhyalṛtakāya* is an instance of a word produced by chance (*yadṛcchāśabda*). When the pronunciation of the vowel *ṛ* was intended, due to a lack of vocal facility, one said *lṛju*; thus, *kumārīlṛju āha* is an imitation arising from incapacity (*aśaktijānukaraṇa*). The terms *pluta*, *dvirvacana*, and *svarita* refer to protracted vowels (*pluti*) and so forth.
