In the example *klṛptaśikhaḥ*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs according to the rule: "According to the Easterners, [the final syllable] of a heavy (*guru*) vowel that is not followed by *ṛ*, even if it is not final, receives the protracted accent for each individual [syllable]. Otherwise, there would be the prohibition "not when followed by *ṛ*" (*anṛtaḥ*). In *klṛpta*, doubling (*dvitva*) occurs according to the rule: "Also before a non-consonant (*anaci*)" (*anaci ca*).

In the word *praklṛpta*, which ends in the *kta* suffix with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) not included, the rule "a preceding prefix [is unaccented] when followed by a word ending in the *kta* suffix denoting the object" (*gatiranantaraḥ*) applies; this prescribes that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is maintained when followed immediately by a word ending in the *kta* suffix used in the objective sense. Consequently, the prefix *pra-* is acute (*udātta*). By the principle of the remaining syllables being grave (*śeṣanighāta*), the vowel *ṛ* of the suffix and the vowel *a* are both grave (*anudātta*). Thereafter, by the rule "of a grave [vowel] following an acute," the vowel *ṛ* becomes circumflex (*svarita*).

For this cannot be established on the grounds of being *asiddha* (not yet established). This is because the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* precedes this [rule], and that which precedes is not *asiddha* with respect to what follows. Nor should one suspect that the grave accent (*anudātta*) occurring before a circumflex (*svarita*) is also a motive [for the rule], since that too is a property of vowels (*ajmātra*) alone; for the residual grave accent (*śeṣanighāta*), being a rule of the sixth book (*ṣāṣṭha*), is *asiddha* with respect to the former, and thus [the substitution] proceeds by virtue of the vowel being an *ṛ*-sound itself. Regarding this, the first motive is refuted by the Vārttika: "In the case of technical names (*saṃjñā*) and the like, there is no assumption [of a substitute] because of the absence of logical necessity."

The meaning is as follows: From the root *ṛti* specified in the rule *ṛter īyaṅ*, by means of the *uṇādi* sūtra "kvun śilpisaṃjñayor apūrvasyāpi," which conveys that the suffix *kvun* occurs after a root—whether with or without a prefix—when a craftsman is to be denoted or when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed, the suffix *kvun* is applied. Since the word *ṛtaka* is thus derived as a name and conforms to the grammatical system, and because it accords with the *Gṛhya-smṛti* injunction "one should use a primary derivative (*kṛt*), not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*"), the correct name is *ṛtaka* alone, and not *lṛtaka*.

This is because the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*) is not admitted. By this, the incorrectness of names such as *kūcī* and *mañcī*, which are formed according to regional dialects and do not conform to the treatises (*śāstra*), is also explained. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is indicated that even in the case of imitations (*anukaraṇa*), one observes adherence to the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Furthermore, the imitation of a long *ḷ*-vowel is likewise incorrect when performed by transgressing the established rule that there are no long forms of the *ḷ*-vowel.

Although the long *ḷ* vowel is well-known in the context of the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* and other such practices within the mantra scriptures, it is absent elsewhere; for this very reason, even the imitation [of speech] in the form "He said: 'Give curd to *ḷtaka*" is indeed ungrammatical. Nor should it be argued that because the word *ṛtaka* conforms to the grammatical treatises, while the word *ḷtaka*—though not a technical name (*saṃjñā*)—is unavoidable as a proper name (*yadṛcchāśabda*) according to the rule "ḷphiḍa-ḷphiḍḍa," since there too, the forms *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa* (ending in the *uṇādi* suffixes *phiḍa* and *phiḍḍa* added to the root *ṛ*) serve as the basis for those derivatives.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated: "Explanations [of grammatical correctness] can also be provided by other alternative views. By this, even words used by chance (yadṛcchāśabda) possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Nor is there any contradiction with the *Gṛhya-smṛti*, because the grammatical correctness of these words is established just as it is for names such as *aupagava* and the like. In that regard, the transgression incurred by the name-giver arises solely from violating the aforementioned scriptural injunctions, and not from the use of ungrammatical forms. For this very reason, the status of *saṃjñā* (proper names) for words such as *kātyāyana* and others is beyond dispute. As for the Vārttika—"An imitation [is correct] when [the original speaker] is neither a learned authority (*śiṣṭa*) nor a non-authority (*aśiṣṭa*), nor is [the act] prohibited"—which was intended to refute the second purpose [of the rule]: [The translation of the provided text is: In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated: "Explanations [of grammatical correctness] can also be provided by other alternative views. By this, even words used by chance (*yadṛcchāśabda*) possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Nor is there any contradiction with the *Gṛhya-smṛti*, because the grammatical correctness of these words is established just as it is for names such as *aupagava* and the like. In that regard, the transgression incurred by the name-giver arises solely from violating the aforementioned scriptural injunctions, and not from the use of ungrammatical forms. For this very reason, the status of *saṃjñā* (proper names) for words such as *kātyāyana* and others is beyond dispute. As for the Vārttika—"An imitation [is correct] when [the original speaker] is neither a learned authority (*śiṣṭa*) nor a non-authority (*aśiṣṭa*), nor is [the act] prohibited"—which was intended to refute the second purpose [of the rule]:

The meaning of this is as follows: the imitation of that which is prescribed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), or that which is neither prescribed nor prohibited by them, or that which is other than both prescribed and prohibited, is correct (*sādhu*). Consequently, since the use of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) is prohibited, even the imitation thereof is indeed incorrect (*asādhu*).

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, supports that purpose [of the rule]. For ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*) does not arise merely from being the denotator of an *apaśabda* (corrupt word). Otherwise, even the word *apaśabda* itself would incur ungrammaticality because it denotes corrupt forms such as *gāvī* and the like. Precisely for this reason, the grammatical correctness of onomatopoeic expressions such as "those Asuras, saying 'helayo helayaḥ'" is established by all.

Nor can there be an extension of ungrammaticality under the principle "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), because since an *apaśabda* is not taught [in the grammar], it lacks the status of a technical "original" (*prakṛti*) within the system; furthermore, ungrammaticality itself is not a result produced by the grammatical rules.

Furthermore, regarding the Vārttika intended to refute the third objection— which states that "due to the non-difference of that which is modified in one part, [operations such as] *pluti* apply"— it is as follows:

This is its meaning as well: according to the method to be explained, when the *repha* (the letter *r*)—which is a constituent part of the vowel *ṛ*—is changed into *l*, then due to the principle that "that which is modified in one part remains identical [to the original]," operations such as *pluti* apply. Nor does there arise the contingency of the prohibition of *pluti* by the rule *anṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.127), because one should read *aravataḥ* instead of *anṛtaḥ*. Just as a dog whose tail has been cut off does not lose its status as a dog, yet operations conditioned by having a tail do not apply; likewise, even though the *repha* has departed from the *ṛ*-vowel, prohibitions conditioned by the presence of a *repha* do not apply.

Nor should it be argued that, by this same reasoning, there would result the prohibition of *pluta* (protracted) length even for long vowels such as in *hotṛ3kāra*, on the grounds that they possess the letter *r*. For it must be stated [in the rule] that "there is no [prohibition] for a short vowel that possesses *r*" (*hrasvasya ravato na*). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya says: "This teaching of the vowel *lṛ* through a separate sūtra—which was intended for the sake of *pluta* and other purposes—is now rejected; it is like pulling a small creeper from a great bamboo thicket. The meaning of this is as follows:

To reject the single vowel *lṛ*, one might rely on a more cumbersome formulation of the rule *anṛtaḥ*—namely, *laghoḥ sthāne hrasvasya ravato na*—which results in the very opposite of parsimony, namely, increased complexity (*gaurava*).

The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *laṭvā* may refer to a species of *karañja*, to a fruit, to something blameworthy, or to a particular bird. This might be argued: Let the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* ("for the *ṛ* of *kṛp*, there is *l*") be placed before the rule *ai au ca* ("*ai* and *au* are *praśliṣṭa* vowels"). Then, because [the substitution of *l*] would be considered *asiddha* (not yet established) [relative to the subsequent rules], cases such as *pluti* (protracted vowel) and others will be successfully accomplished; thus, let the rule remain exactly as it is, namely *anṛta*. To this, they reply: If that were the case, for the purpose of carrying forward (*anuvṛtti*) the phrase *ro laḥ* from that rule, it would follow that the rule *gro yaṅi* ("*gṛ* becomes *gl* before the suffix *yaṅ*") must also be read in that very same place. Consequently, in the form *nijegilyate*, since the substitution of *l* would be *asiddha*, the root would still end in *r*; and as a result, the long vowel [of the penultimate syllable] would occur by the rule *halica* ("a short vowel is lengthened before a consonant ending in *h* or *l*"). Thus, the undesired form would be *nijegīryate* instead of *nijegilyate*.

Furthermore, this point must be noted here: let the reading "guroranṛtaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.89) be taken as having a long vowel, with the analysis being *an-ṛ-lṛ-taḥ*. Since the letter *t* follows the compound, by virtue of its grammatical capacity (*sāmarthya*), it also connects with the letter *ṛ*. Because a long *ḷ* vowel is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), it cannot be excluded [from the prohibition]. Moreover, in the rule for protracted (*pluta*) vowels, the reference (*anuvāda*) to the protracted vowel would be untenable if the *t* were not present; thus, the status of being followed by *t* (*taparatva*) is utilized only for the letter *ṛ*. Consequently, there is no possibility of a prohibition of the protracted form of the long *ṛ* vowel.

In the case of the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel-lengthening) of *ṛ* and *ṝ*, there is the long *ṛ*. Furthermore, the term *anṛtaḥ* is a qualifier of *guror* (of a heavy syllable). The meaning of the sūtra is that a protracted (*pluta*) vowel occurs for a heavy *lṛ* that is distinct from a short *ṛ*. It should not be argued that the protraction would apply only to the vowel *lṛ* and not to other vowels, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *lṛ*; for if that were so, the qualifier "distinct from a short *ṛ*" would become redundant. Nor does it follow that here too the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *lṛ* would result from the presence of the term *anṛtaḥ*.

This is because of the specific force of the inclusion of the *ḷ* vowel. Nor does it follow that there would be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of only the long *ṝ* vowel; for, by virtue of the commentary, the determination of homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) applies to both *ṛ* and *ḷ*. Furthermore, one should not argue that even so, there is no economy (*lāghava*) in teaching the phonemes with a single-mora increase (*ekamātrāvṛddhi*) when compared to the recitation of the *ḷ* vowel; for the effort required to establish the mere *pluta* (protracted) vowel is more appropriately applied to its own specific rule.

Furthermore, regarding the rule *rvor upadhāyā dīrghaḥ*, one may explain that due to the doubling of the letter *r* (*praśleṣa*), the lengthening occurs only when the *upadhā* itself is an *r*-sound, and not even when the *r* is one produced by the rules of *asiddha* status. Having thus explained this, since it is possible to prevent the lengthening in *nijegilyate* by the rule *hali ca*, the attainment of *pluti* and other such effects is secured even by placing the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* at the very end of the treatise.

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as *pipaṭhīḥ*, the long vowel would likewise not occur because the substitution of *ru* for *s* would take effect since the change to *ṣ* is considered *asiddha*; for in that case, the status of being *asiddha* depends solely upon the presence of *t* (the dental), and thus the substitution of *ru* occurs after that [substitution of *ṣ*]. This is the general direction [of the argument]. *eoṅ* 3; *aiauc* 4.

But surely, in this context, the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) must be stated in rules such as *et ot ṅ* and so forth; otherwise, when prescribing short vowels for *ec*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that only the short *e* and *o* are substituted due to positional proximity (*sthānata āntaratamya*). However, if the *tapara* is present, then by the rule *acaśca*, only those [vowels] consisting of two morae (*mātrā*) are presented [for substitution], and since the short vowels—consisting of only one mora—lack the designation of "short" (*hrasva*), that [substitution] does not occur. Nor can it be argued that the undesired consequence is invalid because of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that short vowels do not exist; for in the *Chāndogya* [Upaniṣad], among the followers of Sātyamugri and Rāṇāyanīya, we find: *sujāteeśvasūnṛteadhvaryoodribhiḥ sutam*.

[The opponent argues: "This is not so, because *śukraṃ te anyat* is well-known as an instance of *e* and *o* having one mātrā; and because that Prātiśākhya prescribes those short *e* and *o* for [syllables] situated within a *pāda* that are not followed by *y* or *v*. Nor can it be said that this [objection] is refuted by the very commencement of the rule *eca igghrasvādeśe*, since that would result in the very same burden of complexity (gaurava) that prompted the formulation of that rule."

Now, although that may be the case there due to the influence of the meter (*gīti*), such a convention is not established for the short *e* and *o* elsewhere, either in the Veda or in common usage. This is because, in the absence of a purpose, even those two [long vowels] mentioned there are not intended here. Otherwise, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), just like the letter *a* and so on, only those two [short vowels] would have been taught here; for the inclusion of the long and protracted (*pluta*) vowels would already be accomplished by the rule concerning the "comprehension" (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*). Nor is it the case that the teaching of the two measures (*dvimātra*) here is for the purpose of obtaining the designation of "two measures" for the technical term "guṇa."

In that regard, since a long designation is possible by its own nature alone, [the rule] states: "The *guṇa* [substitution occurs] for *a* and *e*. For according to the other arrangement, in the instruction of the phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*), there are four *mātrās*; and in the technical name *guṇa*, since *eṅ* consists of one and a half *mātrās* each, there are two such units, making six and a half *mātrās* in both cases. However, according to the stated method, there are two *mātrās* in the instruction of the phonemes and four in the technical name *guṇa*, totaling exactly six. Furthermore, the inclusion of the phoneme *ṅ* as an *anubandha* in the instruction of the phonemes is common to both positions.

The rule *eca igghrasvādeśe* is not intended for the exclusion of the short vowels *e* and *o*; rather, it is solely for the purpose of excluding them because, since there is no short vowel most similar to both [the long vowels] *ai* and *au*—which are produced at the throat and palate (*kaṇṭhya-tālavya*) and the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhya-oṣṭhya*) respectively—the substitution of *a* would apply by virtue of its being the closest in terms of the throat location (due to similarity with the first part) for all four [long vowels], and the substitution of *u* would apply for *o* and *au* by virtue of their lip location. Thus, the rule is meant to prevent even the optional application of *a* and *u*.

For this very reason, the ancient teachers designated the *ec* vowels as "sandhyakṣara" (euphonic combinations), because they possess constituent parts similar to the two phonemes being joined. It is with this intention that it is said:
"From the union of the phonemes *a* and *i*, the phoneme *e* arises."

Such is the conventional usage in the *Mantraśāstra*. As for the claim that this sūtra will be rejected on the grounds that these [sounds] are pure palatals (*tālavya*) or pure labials (*oṣṭhya*), that is another matter altogether. Therefore, if one asks: "For what purpose is the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel)?"—do not say so. Even then, in cases such as *gaṅgodakam*, *rameśaḥ*, *khaṭvailakā*, and *khaṭvaudanaḥ*, because the preceding and following sounds combined would have a duration of three or four morae (*mātrā*), there would arise the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of substitutes having exactly that same duration by virtue of being the closest in measure (*pramāṇata āntaratamyena*).

Nor is the four-mora [vowel] unestablished, for it is established in the *Chāndogya* and because of the *Bhāṣya*: "A *pluta* [vowel] is indeed accepted as having four morae. However, if the vowel is followed by *t* (as in *at*), then by the rule "that which is followed by *t* denotes its own duration," the three-mora vowels and others would not be included; yet there is no fault, as they lack designations such as *guṇa* and so forth. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the statement "and the *pluta* is prescribed in its specific scope" applies only when there is a possibility of both *pluta* and non-*pluta* vowels occurring.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because, in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, one could split the yoga by taking *dīrghaḥ* separately and explain it as: "That which is prescribed under the governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* becomes long. For this would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *pūrvarūpa* (in *ami pūrvaḥ* and *samprasāraṇācca*) and the *pararūpa* (in *ato guṇe*) both becoming long vowels.

Now, since the rule *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one) is under the governing jurisdiction (*adhikāra*) of the sūtra *prathamayoḥ*, and because the phrase *pūrvaparayoḥ* (of the preceding and the following) is brought into play, the mention of *pūrva* (preceding) serves to explain that the resulting form is exactly like the preceding vowel and not different from it; thus, in forms such as *gaurīm*, a long vowel occurs, while in forms such as *pathum*, a short vowel occurs.

In the rule *samprasāraṇācca* as well, because that same word *pūrva* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*), and because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) consisting in the prescription of lengthening for a *samprasāraṇa* followed by a consonant in the rule *halaḥ*, there is no lengthening in the case of *viddham*. Furthermore, in the rule *ato guṇe*, since the desired result would already be established by the mention of the subsequent element (*para*) alone, the explicit mention of the term *rūpa* (form) serves as an indicator that the substitute must be of the same class (*sajātīya*) as the original.

In reality, however, if an *a* follows, the long vowel would be established by the rule for homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*), and if an *eṅ* follows, it would be established by the rule for *vṛddhi*; thus, the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) would be entirely redundant. Nor can it be argued that even without *vṛddhi*, the prescription of the form *eṅ* for the *a* ensures the application of the long-vowel rule, and that the rule [6.1.97] is intended solely to prohibit *vṛddhi*. For even so, since there would be no result when an *a* follows, the rule would have to be formulated as *ata eṅi* alone; furthermore, this being the case, it is simpler by one syllable.

And for this reason, because of the very power of the rule prescribing *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent form) when followed by a short *a*, there is no fault in the case of *pacanti*. Therefore, it is concluded that the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is indeed faultless. Nevertheless, in cases such as *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ* and *tavalkāraḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution would not occur; for since a long vowel is prescribed for the letter *a*, and since there is no closest proximity (*āntaratamya*) with the *eṅ* vowels, the *guṇa* is precluded. Furthermore, the prescription of *guṇa* finds its scope of application when *i* or *u* follows. Moreover, the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* serves its purpose in the domain of *vṛddhi* substitution. Consequently, in these instances, one would hear the original vowels (*ik* and *uk*) in their separated forms.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, by virtue of the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* prescribing the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), such [substitution] does not occur? Nor can its purposefulness be established as being for the sake of preventing *yaṇ*-substitution and the like; for if the rule could be maintained simply by stating *ikaḥ*, the inclusion of *akaḥ* (the letter *a*) would result in redundancy. [Response: True. Nevertheless, since the letter *a* shares partial positional similarity (*sthānasāmya*) with *e* and *o*, there would still be the undesirable consequence of applying [the substitution] to them alone. Furthermore, following the indications of rules such as *kartari carṣidevatayoḥ* would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Therefore, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is indeed defective, and the use of the *t*-marker (*taparatva*) is necessary to exclude cases involving three morae (*trimātra*) and so forth—this being the position reached.

It is said: because the designation of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* applies specifically to the long vowels (*dīrgha*) among the *ec* sounds by virtue of their being followed by *tā* (the augment), there is no fault; for the protracted vowel (*pluta*) lacks the designations of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. This is because the inclusion of the term "vowel" (*varṇa*) in the rule "sahivahorodavarṇasya" indicates that [the substitute] also grasps those of the same duration as that which follows *tā*.

Nor should it be argued that, although the terms *aiC* and *auC* bring about the presence of long vowels (*dīrgha*) by virtue of having *t* as their final element (*taparatva*), those long vowels—being unpronounced (*anuccārita*)—lack *taparatva* and would therefore necessarily bring about the presence of their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). This is because *taparatva* is not utilized for the sake of a technical name (*saṃjñā*); rather, by implication (*sāmarthya*), its purpose is to determine the duration of the named entities (*sañjñin*) brought forth by those terms.

Nor should it be argued that because the vowel *a* lacks the capacity to include its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), the *t* in that rule [P. 1.1.70]—despite having the power to include *ai* and *au* which share its duration—is not so [inclusive] regarding the technical name *guṇa*; for there is no pointlessness [in the rule], as that [mention of *a*] is utilized precisely to prohibit the inclusion of *a* itself in the definition of *guṇa*. This is because both cases are resolved simply by explaining that in the rule "aṇ-udit savarṇasya" (P. 1.1.69), following the recurrence from the rule "svaṃ rūpam" (P. 1.1.68) of the phrase "not when it is a technical name" (*aśabda-sañjñā*), an *aṇ* does not include its homogeneous sounds when it is being used to establish a technical designation.

This is because the purpose of the *tapara* designation (the addition of *t* to indicate length) is solely to ensure a clearer comprehension of the actual form of the element being named (*sañjñin*). If it were stated simply as "aiṅ guṇaḥ," even though the absence of the letter *ṛ* after *aikāra* would lead to the determination that the vowel *a* is to be elided (*praśleṣa*), there would still remain doubt regarding whether it is short or long; furthermore, in the case of *ej*, there would be doubt as to whether the vowel *ā* is to be elided.

In the case of *mālāprastha*, there is the rule *mālādīnāṃ ca* which prescribes an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) once again; this necessitates the assumption of a *praśleṣa* (elision/merging) of the vowel *ā* in the rule *prasthe'vṛddhamakarkyādīnām*. This is because otherwise, the technical designation *vṛddhi*—which constitutes the delimiter (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the distinction (*bheda*) in that rule—would be untenable with respect to the vowel *ā*. Furthermore, such an assumption would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

In reality, even with the reading "eṅad guṇaḥ," it is possible for the letter *a* alone to denote its own duration; therefore, the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the mention of the letter *t* in the middle of the rule "adeṅ guṇa" remains entirely intact. Nor is there an excess of one mātrā, since the reading "guṇa eṅad" is also possible. Just as in the case of "vṛddhirādaic" and other such rules, the determination of the technical term (*saṃjñā*) and the bearer of the term (*saṃjñin*) is established through interpretation (*vyākhyāna*).

If the short vowel (*hrasva*) brought forward by the *ac* word in the *ūkāla-sūtra* were to denote its own class of phonemes (*varṇagrāhaka*), then the letter *a* would possess three technical designations (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, although the *Bhāṣya* states that in the case of a technical name for a word (*śabda-saṃjñā*), an *aṇ* does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhaka*), that statement is merely an incidental argument (*abhyuccayamātra*). Now, one might object: "If a letter also denotes its own duration when followed by *t*, then the suffix *ap* prescribed by the rule *ṛdorap* would apply only in cases such as *yavaḥ* and *stavaḥ*, but not in cases like *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ*. To this, the *Bhāṣya* replies: "This is not the letter *t*; rather, the letter *d* is used either to avoid ambiguity or for ease of pronunciation."

Now, regarding the substitution of *u* in the rule *diva uṭ*, in order to prevent the *svarita* accent for forms such as *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* by the rule *titsvaritam*, it is established that this [substitute] is indeed the letter *d* (as in *dyu*) and not the letter *t*. Having raised the objection that—just as in the rule *adaso'serdādu do maḥ*—there might be a perception of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrāhakatva*) even for a vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) such as *u*, the *Ṣaṣṭhabhāṣya* resolves this by stating that since the letter *d* is also indicated in the rule *tapara* through the process of *carv* (substitution) when the text is read in *saṃhitā*, the letter *d* likewise causes the perception of its own duration (*tatkāla*).

If it is asked: "How can it be said here that, because of the mention of the letter *d* in the rule *ṛdorap*, there is no grasping of [sounds] of its own duration? To this they reply: The *d* intended here is that which is produced by the substitution of *jaś* (voiced unaspirated) in place of either *th* or *dh*. However, the natural *d* is cited there as an example for grasping sounds of its own duration; thus, there is no contradiction.

Some, however, say that this portion of the Bhāṣya follows the opinion of the Vārttikakāra—who, by stating "the mention of the suffix must be made when *ti* follows," did not accept that the letter *d* grasps sounds of its own duration.

Others, however, maintain that because the desired forms such as *dyubhiḥ* are established by the very *paribhāṣā*—"when there is a choice between a substitute and its original, the substitute alone is to be understood"—no difficulty whatsoever needs to be pursued.

As for Haradatta’s remark that this effort [of ours] was undertaken by the great masters because this *paribhāṣā* is not seen here in the *Bhāṣya* or the *Vārttika*, that is to be questioned; for in the *Bhāṣya*, when refuting the rule *aṅgasya*, this very *paribhāṣā* is explicitly introduced.

Furthermore, although in cases such as *śri-arthaṃ* and *bhū-arthaṃ*, the application of *iyaṅ*, *uvaṅ*, and so on, is prevented by the two paribhāṣās—the one concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) and the one concerning the mention of a meaningful element (*arthavat*)—nevertheless, in forms like *nirutaṃ* and *durutaṃ*, a long vowel would result for the *saṃprasāraṇa* following a consonant (*hal*). Since this cannot be prevented by those two paribhāṣās, the necessity of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*) is established; consequently, the uselessness of the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix is precisely what is accepted in the Bhāṣya. For this very reason, the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix is [invoked] under the rule *titsvaritam*.

It should not be said that this is the intention of Haradatta, based on Kaiyaṭa’s statement that [the *t*-marker] is never relied upon by either the author of the Bhāṣya or the author of the Vārttika; for even so, in cases such as "diva ut," there is simply no possibility of the occurrence of svaritatva. This is because the aforementioned forced interpretation (*kusṛṣṭi*) alone is unacceptable. Furthermore, since the word "ud" is an imitation of the vowel *u* which is being prescribed, although this [word "ud"] possesses the *t*-marker, the prescribed vowel *u* lacks it. Moreover, even though the technical name (*saṃjñā*) ends in *t*, it lacks the status of being a *ti*.

This is because the status of having a *t* as its subsequent element (*taparatva*) required by the rule *taparas tatkālasya* is established even without the designation *it*; thus, there is no evidence that the letter *t* must indeed receive the designation *it*.

Nor should one say that Kaiyaṭa’s statement is correct—that just as in the rule *aco yat*, by virtue of the property of being a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *yat* which is to be prescribed undergoes the operation of a *t*-suffix because of its *ti*-ness, so too here, by means of the technical name, the designated element (*saṃjñin*) would undergo the operation of a *t*-suffix; for in that case, the letter *t* serves no other purpose, whereas here, since the vowel *u* being prescribed is seen to function as a *grāhaka* (a term that includes others), there is no functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) for [the designation] to exclude it.

Nor should it be argued that this [principle] might also apply because we observe that suffixes (anubandhas) have multiple functions; for although that may be the case in instances where it is desired, here it is impossible to assume both functions and thereby postulate a *ṭ* as a means to exclude them. Therefore, the Bhāṣya and other texts on that point are merely *abhyupetyavāda* (arguments made for the sake of argument). However, the Bhāṣya on this point is correct exactly as it stands, since there is no purpose in assuming that the letter *d* denotes its own time-period (*tatkāla*). Thus they say.

In this regard, the following must be considered: if a distinct entity—different from the *takāra*-ending [base] being pronounced and devoid of the status of having *t* as its limit (*taparatva*)—were to be prescribed as the technical name (*saṃjñin*), then how could the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of suffixes (*apratyaya*) apply in rules such as "tyadādīnām aḥ"? Since this [technical name] would lack the status of being that which is to be prescribed (*vidheya*), the distinction of being a prescribed element would not exist, and consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of its including all homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrāhakatva*).

Now, if it is assumed—on the basis of contextual capacity—that the word conveying the thing to be prescribed (*vidheya*) alone is construed there as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the difference, then what follows? Since the meaning of the rule *tapara* is the absence of being a grasper (*grāhakatva*) precisely for that which was previously liable to be a grasper of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), [the svarita accent] would result as residing only in the word conveying the thing to be prescribed, because the thing to be prescribed itself lacks the state of having *t* as its final element (*taparatva*). Thus, the svarita accent would necessarily apply [only] to the word conveying the thing to be prescribed.

Nor should it be argued that the operation prompted by such an *anubandha* applies only to that which is enjoined when the *anubandha* serves no other purpose; for this would apply equally in the case of *diva ut*. This is because, in the view that [the *anubandha*] designates a phoneme (*varṇasaṃjñāpakṣa*), its purpose is fulfilled by excluding the lengthening (*dīrgha*) that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *halaḥ* (P. 6.4.2) in forms like *dyubhyām*, and by the rule *saṃprasāraṇasya ca* (P. 6.3.139) in forms like *dyuloka*; this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources.

In the rule *adaso'seḥ*, one could have formed a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) of the short and long *u*-sounds, resulting in the single designation *u*; thus, there would have been no need for the specific instruction that even a vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhaka*). By this, the view that—due to a lack of necessity—the quality of *t* inherent in a technical name (*saṃjñā*) does not trigger grammatical operations in the named element (*saṃjñin*) is refuted. This is because, since there is no underlying inconsistency (*anupapatti*), the necessity (*sāmarthya*) of such an instruction is absent; yet, even in the absence of such necessity, there is no harm. Furthermore, the necessity (*sāmarthya*) can be preserved in the manner already explained.

Nor should it be argued: "If its purpose is for accent (*svara*), why is its prohibition stated by another method? For, if its prohibition were stated in the manner described [without this qualification], then the fact that *dittva* has accent as its purpose would be understood; however, the intended meaning [of *dittva*] is precisely subverted by the aforementioned reasoning. Otherwise, the occurrence of the circumflex (*svarita*) would be unavoidable. Thus, since the contingency of the circumflex has been resolved by relying on *daparatva*, and since there is no further purpose for *dittva* to denote that specific time, the present Bhāṣya is beautiful exactly as it stands.

However, since the accentuation prescribed by that [rule] is unavoidable even when the word has a different meaning, and since the *Ṣaṣṭhabhāṣya* and the commentary on this very point—which were composed to provide a solution for that meaning through an alternative method—must resolve the contradiction by intending to refer to the letter *da* belonging to another location, the aforementioned labor is rendered futile.

Now, if this were so, then in rules such as *aut* and *iṭo't*, there would also be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the svarita accent. Nor can this be accepted as the intended result (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it is not observed in examples such as *stīrṇe barhiṣi samidhāne agnau*. Furthermore, in the case of *laviṣīya*, the fact that the final syllable is udātta is stated in the Bhāṣya itself under the rule *ādyudāttaśca*. If you argue thus, we say: do not speak so. For in that context, the designation *it* is prohibited by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*; such is the direction of the argument.

It might be argued as follows: In the perception of a phoneme (*varṇa*), do the portions within that phoneme which resemble other phonemes trigger the grammatical operation, or not? It cannot be the first case. For if they did, there would result the application of the *savarṇadīrgha* rule in *agne indra*, the *pūrvarūpa* rule "eṅaḥ padāntāt" in *agne ehi*, the *tugāgama* rule "hrasvasya piti kṛti" in *ālūya*, and the rule "ato bhisa ais" in *mālābhiḥ*.

[Objection: The first alternative is not tenable because of the similarity between the *iu* vowels and the upper portion [of the *ṛ* vowel]. Nor is the second, because the upper portion of *ā* and the other long vowels is similar to its own short counterpart. Furthermore, the latter alternative is untenable: if the *r* sound contained within the *ṛ* vowel were not treated as an independent element, then the addition of the augment *nuṭ* in the rule "tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ" would be impossible; likewise, the rule "kṛpo ro laḥ" would be untenable, since there is no *r* sound in that context other than the one included within the *ṛ* vowel. Moreover, in forms such as *gṛṇāti*, the substitution of *ṇ* caused by the *r* sound would be impossible. [Reply: Not so. There is no fault in either of the two positions.

In this regard, one position is that [the *nuṭ* augment] does not apply. This is because, like the case of *nṛsiṃha*, there is no evidence for the application of grammatical operations conditioned by those specific phonemes (*varṇa*) when they constitute a distinct phoneme within a different word. Furthermore, this is supported by the force of the separate mention of the words *go* and *nau* in the rules *godvyacaḥ* and *naudvyacaḥ*. Otherwise, since both would possess two vowels (*dvyac*) by taking their preceding and following parts, those rules would become redundant. However, specific counter-arguments must be formulated regarding the rule for the *nuṭ* augment, the substitution of *la* (for *lu*), and the change of *m* to *n*.

According to the statement in the *Prātiśākhya*, "The substitution of a retroflex (*mūrddhanya*) for a dental (*dantya*) is termed *nati*," the word *vināma* in the present context refers to the change of *na* to *ṇa*. Regarding the rule for the augment *nuṭ*, one should formulate the sūtra simply as "tasmānnuṭ" (the augment *nuṭ* follows that [long vowel]), instead of using "dvihalaḥ. Its meaning is that *nuṭ* occurs after a long vowel from the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *āṭa* or *āṭatuḥ*.

Regarding the rule *aśnoteśca*, according to the standard arrangement, since this serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for that which was previously an injunctive rule (*vidhyartha*), its purpose is to restrict the addition of the augment *nuṭ* to *aśnoti* alone among those roots whose penultimate vowel is *a*. This is because the prohibition of that [augment] alone would already be established by the rule *nāśnaḥ*. Furthermore, in the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*, the analysis is *kṛpaḥ uḥ raḥ laḥ*. The mention of *kṛpa* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). The vowel *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Regarding the rule *kṛpeḥ yo rephaḥ tasya laḥ*: this means that for the *repha* which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the *ṛ*-vowel of the root *kṛp*, that is to say, for the *repha* resembling [the sound of] *ṛ*, there is the substitution of *la*. Consequently, in forms such as *calīklṛpyate*, the substitution of *la* is established even for the *repha* of the augment *rīg* by the rule *rīgṛtvataḥ*. For this very reason, the reading *kṛpe ro laḥ* should be disregarded due to its contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*.

In reality, by relying on the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to denote a general relationship, and because both the *repha* that is an immediate constituent and the *repha* that is an indirect constituent are included under "of *kṛp-*," there is no fault even in that case; for the *Bhāṣya* is merely intended as an illustration of the solution. Furthermore, since it will be stated later by the author himself that "the class [of phonemes] occurring as independent or non-independent [is not what is meant]," one must reflect upon the point: how could the substitution of *la* prescribed for the *repha* apply to a portion of the *ḷ*-phoneme? Thus, the phrase "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) should be considered.

As for the argument that in the rule *ro raḥ*, a genus (*jāti*) common to both independent and dependent phonemes should be understood as the referent in both the subject (*anuvādya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), and that therefore the substitution of *lṛ* for the *ṛ*-vowel is what is prescribed here—since it is impossible to separate a single part [of a phoneme]—that is not correct. For there is no evidence for such a genus. Furthermore, the formulation of rules such as *luṭi ca klṛpaḥ* serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) in this regard.

Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in forms such as *gṛṇāti*, the word *ṛt* is separated from the rule *chandasyṛdavagrahāt*; thus, the *ṇatva* of a *n* following an *ṛ* is prescribed. Following that, there is another rule: *chandasyavagrahāt*. By the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ṛtaḥ* [from the previous rule], the *ṇatva* occurs in the *padapāṭha* form of *pitṛyāṇaṃ dyumat*. Nor should it be argued that, because of the specific mention of the short vowel *ṛ* (*taparatva*), the *ṇatva* would not apply in cases such as *mātṝṇām*.

In the rule *raṣābhyām* as well, since the inclusion of both the letter *r* and its similar portion (*bhāga*) is common to both, the result is established from that very fact. Nor is there a lack of evidence for including the similar portion of *r* there; for this is precisely how the reading of the word *tṛpnoti* and the word *nṛnamana* is treated in the list of *kṣubhnādi* words.

It should not be argued that the reading of the word *nṛnamana* in the rule *nṛnamanasyāpatyaṃ nārnamaniḥ* is purposeful because it prevents the application of the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) caused by an independent *r*, and therefore how could it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For this is already established by the principle itself: "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*). Thus, although the alternative involving the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is mentioned later, the intention of the Bhāṣya does not lie there; rather, it lies precisely here for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). This is how it should be understood.

Nor should it be argued that the rule *raṣābhyām* cannot apply because the letter *ṛ* is separated from the preceding *r* by the vowel portion (*ajbhāga*) that follows it; for there is a separate rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating *vyavāye 'pi* ("even when there is an intervention"). Furthermore, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to cases such as *kṛtena*, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi*. The meaning of that [separate rule] is: if the operation occurs when there is an intervention by letters belonging to the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the alphabet) or those included therein, then it occurs only through these [specific letters].

In fact, according to this view, based on the aforementioned *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) and the mention of *praśāstṝṇām* and so forth, it is more parsimonious (*lāghavāt*) to understand that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs specifically for a letter following an *ṛ*-vowel. This is because the *Bhāṣya* records the rule by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) precisely after introducing the position that "parts of a phoneme are included under the designation of the whole phoneme."

If it is asked, "How can the previously mentioned defects be avoided in that view? it is replied: Because these [vowels] possess two parts (*bhāga*) that are more open (*vivṛtataratva*), there is no occurrence of *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel by homogeneous merger) in cases such as *agne indra*. This is because the independent *i* and *u* lack homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) due to a difference in effort (*prayatna-bheda*) caused by their being more open. For this very reason, in *agne ehi*, there is no occurrence of *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute for a preceding *a* and following *e*). This is because, due to the lack of homogeneity with the vowel *a* in the rule "*eṅaḥ padāntādati*," the portion of the preceding *a* belonging to the *ec* vowels is not brought forward.

Since the rule could have been established by a single yoga as "dīrghāt padāntādvā," the fact that the *tuk* augment is prescribed separately after a long vowel (*dīrghāt*) and then the optionality is prescribed separately as "padāntādvā" indicates that a rule dependent on a short vowel does not apply when a long vowel is present. Indeed, there is a separate rule in that context for the purpose of establishing the distinction: that *tuk* is obligatory after a long vowel at the end of a word, and optional when at the end of a word.

If, however, the *tuka* augment prescribed for a short vowel by the rule *che ca* were to apply even to a long vowel, then since that same rule would already account for the *tuka* after a long vowel at the end of a word (*apadānta*), it would only need to prescribe an option for the long vowel at the end of a word (*padānta*). For this very reason, there is an absence of *tuka* in *alūya* and *pramāya* according to the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*. Furthermore, in cases such as *khaṭvābhiḥ* and *mālābhiḥ*, the substitution of *ais* (for *i* and *u*) does not occur either. This is due to the force of the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *hrasvat*); otherwise, he would have simply said *asya*.

In examples such as *yātā vātā*, the elision of the *at* (*ato lopa*) does not occur either. This is because the rule *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8) contains a *kit* marker (*kittvena*), which indicates that the elision of the *at* does not apply when there is a long *ā*. Otherwise, if the *a* belonging to the latter part of the long *ā* were elided, and the *a* belonging to the former part were replaced by the subsequent affixal *ā* via the *pararūpa* rule, forms such as *sāmagaḥ* and *surāpaḥ* would be established; in that case, the *kit* marker would be redundant for the purpose of triggering the elision of *ā* by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*. This is the general direction of the argument.

Now, one might argue that in cases such as *sayyantā*, *sarvvatsaraḥ*, and *sallokaḥ*, even a single phoneme like *y* (in *sayyantā*) is grasped through its homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the two *y*s taught by the rule *aṇ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), which consists of multiple phonemes; thus, let there be the designation *hal*. But how can this apply to instances such as *kukkuṭaḥ*, *pippalī*, and *pittam*, since *k*, *pp*, and *tt* are indivisible units and therefore consist of only a single phoneme? Otherwise, since a consonant has a duration of half a mora (*ardhamātra*), it would be impossible for *kak* and so forth to have the duration of one full mora (*mātrākāla*).

If it is argued that, because that [syllable] and its two constituent parts are not included within the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated list), and because they are not grasped by those [sounds] that are recited [in the *pratyāhāra*], they lack the designation *hal*; consequently, in the absence of the designation *saṃyoga*, the rule "a vowel is heavy before a *saṃyoga*" would not apply; and thus, since the preceding syllable beginning with *u* would not be heavy, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) prescribed by the rule "after a heavy syllable, except for *ṛ*" would not occur.

On this point, they say: "In this case, there are indeed two instances each of the letters *ka*, *pa*, and *ta*, each having the duration of one *mātrā*. However, because they are uttered with an identical mode of articulation and are pronounced so rapidly, there arises the delusion that the two are one; such is the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭa-sampradāya*). In ultimate reality, however, since phonemes are partless, this investigation pertains only to the stage of grammatical analysis (*prakriyā-daśā*)."

*Hayavaraṭ* (5). Here, the instruction of the letter *ha* is for the purpose of including it in the categories of *aṭ*, *aś*, *haś*, and *iṇ*. Consequently, in the example *mahān hi*, the substitution of *ru* for the nasal *n* occurs by depending on the letter *ha* as an *aṭ* according to the rule *dīrghādaṭi samānapāde*; the nasalization (*anunāsika*) occurs by the rule *āto'ṭi nityam*; and the elision (*lopa*) of the *y* that stands in the place of *ru* (by the rule *bho-bhago-*) occurs by the rule *hali sarveṣām*. This is because the term *aśi* is also understood to apply there. In the example *brāhmaṇo hasati*, the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *haśi ca*.

In the forms *lilihidhve* and *lilihidhve*, there is an optional substitution of *ḍha* by the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*. This is because the word *iṇaḥ* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) from the sūtra *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*; thus, that sūtra prescribes the optional cerebral (*mūrddhanya*) substitute for the *ṣ* following an *iṭ* that itself follows an *iṇ*.

The instruction regarding those [letters] in the final sūtra is for the purpose of including them within the pratyāhāras *val*, *ral*, *jhal*, and *śal*. Consequently, in forms such as *rudihi* and *svapihi*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "after roots beginning with *rud*, before a sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with *val*" (*rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*). Furthermore, in forms such as *snihitvā* / *snehitvā* and *sisnihiṣati* / *sisnehiṣati*, there is an optionality regarding the *kit* status [of the suffixes], according to the rule "the suffixes *ktvā* and *san* are optionally *kit* after a root ending in *ra* or *la*, having *u* or *i* as its penultimate letter, and beginning with a consonant" (*ralo vyupadhāddhalādeḥ saṃśca*), whereby the suffixes *ktvā* and *san* following a root ending in *ra* or *la* with either *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter may optionally be treated as *kit*.

In *adāgdhām* and *adāgdham*, because the substitution of *gh* for the initial *d* of a root (by the rule *dāder dhātor ghaḥ*) is considered *asiddha*, the *s* of the suffix *sic* following the *jhāl* sound *h* is elided by the rule *jhalo jhali*. In *aruksat* and *alikṣat*, the substitution of *ks* for *sic* is triggered by the fact that the root ends in a *śal* sound (by the rule *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*). Therefore, Dīkṣita maintains that the mention of both [groups] in each of the four *pratyāhāras* is for the purpose of including them individually.

The modern grammarians (*navya*), however, maintain that the inclusion [of *am*] in the *am*-pratyāhāra is also a purpose for the first instruction (*upadeśa*). This is because the restriction to four purposes is not stated in the *Bhāṣya*. In the case of an imitation of the consonants *k* and *h*, such as in the compound *puṃsaḥ khau*, the substitution of *r* (ru-tva) by the rule "pumaḥ khayyampare" is the purpose.

As for the claim that because the suffix *kāra* is mandatory, the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between these two [the *saṃyoga* and the *k*] is impossible—that is not correct. For it has been stated in the *Kaustubha* and other works that "that rule is applied extensively (*bahulam*). By this, the argument that the absence of that [suffix] in rules such as "skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ" is merely Vedic (*chāndasa*), just as the suffix *kāra* occurs even after a word in cases like "uccaistarāṃ vā vaṣaṭkāraḥ," is refuted. This is because, rather than resorting to the status of being Vedic, it is more appropriate to assume the extensive application (*bāhulaka*) in the form of optional occurrence.

Furthermore, in the rule defining *savarṇa* (Pāṇini 1.1.9), the usage of *caśayoḥ* and *kaṅayoḥ*, as well as the examples from the *Kaustubha* such as *śaṣasavisarjanīya*, cannot be justified as being Vedic (*chāndasa*)—given the numerous usages by both ancient and modern authors in their commentaries on those respective rules—and because the employment of *kāra* after a solitary consonant is nowhere observed among learned authorities.

Furthermore, one might argue that because the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) for *jhal* sounds at the end of a word (*jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*) is unavoidable, the letter *ha* cannot be followed by a *khay* sound (an unvoiced stop). Nor can it be argued that since this rule applies only to actual word-finales, it does not apply here—where *ha* is at the end of a "designative" word-final (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*)—because otherwise the second mention of "end" (*anta*) in the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca* would be redundant, as the word "end" could simply have been carried over from that previous rule. This argument is invalid, because the mention of "end" (*anta*) serves its purpose through the exclusion of the condition *jhalī* and the inclusion of the condition *padasya*.

That too is incorrect; for the cessation of the requirement "in a *jh* consonant" (*jhali*) is established by the very force of the separate mention of the word *jhal*, which serves to introduce the locus [of the rule]. Otherwise, immediately after the rule "from a *jh* consonant, before a *jh* consonant" (*jhalo jhali*), the rule would simply have been "at the end, [before] a *jaś* sound" (*jaśante*). This is because the separate mention of the word "end" (*anta*) in the rule "of *s* and *k*" (*skoḥ*) itself justifies the non-continuation of that [word *jhal*] in the two intermediate rules.

Nor should it be argued that even so, the term *lopa* would not carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into those two rules; for since *jaś* lacks the *svarita* accent, it does not carry over, and thus it is logical that *lopa* is obtained as the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*). Nor should it be argued that because the word *jhalaḥ* in the rule *jhalo jhali*—which prescribes the elision of a *s* following a *jhala*—is in the ablative case, the word *jaś* in the rule *jaś-ante* could not be in the genitive case; this is because we rely on the principle of the governing power of the word (*śabdādhikāra*). Nor is there the consequence that the word *saḥ* (from *sasajuṣoḥ*) would also have to carry over.

For that [term *jhala*], which is carried over from the previous rule, must be either in the ablative case or the genitive case. It cannot be the first [the ablative]. If the meaning were "jaś-substitution occurs for *s* following *jhala*," then since *jhali* and *ante* would both function as causes independently, there would be a contradiction with the rule "jhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26), which prescribes the elision [of *s*] when *jhala* follows. Nor can there be a conjunction [of the two conditions], because there is no particle such as *ca* (and) and because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory. By this, the alternative [of taking them as optional] is also refuted.

The first [alternative] is untenable because it is impossible for that [condition] to apply to both what is already established (*klṛpta*) and what is to be established (*kalpya*), and because there would be no further questioning (*niranuyogatvāt*). Nor is the latter [alternative] correct, because the substitute (*sthānin*) lacks expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, *jhal* cannot qualify the letter *s* non-differently (i.e., as a general term), because there is no deviation (*avyabhicārāt*). Nor can there be a qualifier-qualified relationship in the reverse order, because the portion serving as the qualified would be redundant.

In reality, however, after the rule *iṭa īṭi*, one should formulate the rule *jhalo jhali* and then the rule *jaś ante*. In this way, the status of the letter *s* as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of elision (*lopa*) within the two rules *hrasvādaṅgāt* and *iṭa īṭi* is established without obstruction. The non-continuation (*ananuvṛtti*) of the letter *s* and so forth remains as before. The rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyośca* should be recited; for, by the inclusion of the word *anta* in the rule *jaś ante* and by the particle *ca*, the application of the term *jhali* is logically obtained.

If, however, you maintain the stubborn insistence that the particle *ca* serves to include the *jaś*-rule even here, then let the rule "skoḥ" remain exactly as it is heard [in the text]. Furthermore, by the force of the repeated mention of the word *anta*, there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of anything specified in the rule "jaś-antaḥ".

This being established, since the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* is applied with an intervening [element], the cessation of the application of *jhalī* is already accomplished by the very force of the re-mention of *jhalām*; therefore, because the inclusion of *anta-* must necessarily be for the purpose of grasping the primary end (*mukhyānta*), a resolution based on *jaś*-substitution here is not superior. For this very reason, there are usages such as *cit*, *pit*, *kit*, and *dit*.

Regarding the rule *ādaij* (Pāṇini 1.1.1), the two points stated in the Kaustubha are consistent: first, the objection that the inclusion of *t* (the *tapara*) is for the sake of subsequent rules, which would lead to the contingency that *jaś*-substitution does not apply because the vowels would lack the status of being word-final (*padānta*); and second, the resolution that this is a supplement to the preceding rule (*pūrvaśeṣa*) intended to prevent ambiguity.

As for what was also stated: in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "ñamaṅaṇanam," it will be said that the *jhakāra* and *bhakāra* do not exist as word-final elements (*padānta*) in order to reject the *makāra* as an *anubandha*. According to the aforementioned reasoning, in cases such as *pumkjh* (he says) and *pumkbh* (he says), where *kjh* and *kbh* are used as phonetic imitations (*anukaraṇa*) of the *añ* and *ṅañ* pratyāhāras respectively, there would also be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the *yañ* pratyāhāra; thus, there would be a contradiction with that *Bhāṣya*. In my view, however, there is no over-extension due to the application of *jaś*-substitution. Nor is that [substitution] considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), because it is prior even with respect to the three [operations].

Therefore, on the strength of the Bhāṣya which establishes the absence of the letters *ja* and *bha* at the end of a word, one must necessarily either accept non-utterance (*anabhidhāna*) of *jaś*-substitution and so forth in such instances, or else [accept the following]. Otherwise, in cases such as *kaś h ity āha*, there would be the contingency of the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), which would necessitate the rule *saṅi*; this would contradict the Bhāṣya contained within the rule *pareś ca ghāṅkayoḥ*, which refutes that very point. That too is incorrect; for even if non-utterance is accepted by the force of that [Bhāṣya] in cases of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), there is no such subverting reason (*bādhaka*) in the present case.

For there is no possibility here of the elision of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) and so forth; because the *saṃyoga* is not followed by a *jhal* sound, and because it does not occur at the end of a word (*padānta*). Nor does the internal case-ending (*antarvartinī vibhakti*) render the element *h* at the end of a word in the present context, because of the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of rules based on what follows) by the rule "when it is the second member of a compound, the treatment of the preceding as the beginning of a word is suspended" (*uttarapadatve cāpadādividhau*). Furthermore, there is a purpose for the inclusion of forms such as *pum* and *t* in the phonetic imitation (*anukaraṇa*) when followed by *am*.

Regarding the form *tacchlo*, some maintain that there is a purpose [for the rule] by means of the statement "the substitution of *c* occurs before *am*. That is questionable; for, according to the literal reading, this is already subsumed by the mention of *aṭ* as the purpose. Therefore, the direction is that the purpose [of the rule] with respect to *am* is unavoidable.

It might be argued as follows: Since the letter *r* (repha) is included within the *ya*-pratyāhāra, its grammatical operations would follow as well. For instance, in the case of *madrahradaḥ* or *bhadrahradaḥ*, there would result a doubling (*dvitva*) of the *yar* [consonant] following the *r* and *h* by the rule *aco rahābhyām* ("doubling of a *yar* following *r* or *h* after a vowel"). Nor can this be avoided by the elision (*lopa*) of *r* according to *ro ri*; for that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the doubling. Furthermore, since the elision of *yam* [consonants] following *yam* [consonants] according to *halo yamāṃ yami* is optional, there would arise the undesirable consequence of hearing two *r*s in one alternative case.

In the cases *kuṇḍaṃ rathena* and *vanaṃ rathena*, the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* would apply. Nor can it be argued that there is no fault because the *repha* (the sound *r*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*) lack homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*); for even in the absence of such homogeneous sounds, the substitution of the *repha* itself would result. Furthermore, in examples such as *prātarnayati*, the rule *yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* would cause the optional substitution of the nasal *ṇakāra* by virtue of the similarity of place of articulation (*sthānasāmya*).

Nor should it be argued that in the word *harayavaṭ*, the letter *r* must be specified before the letters *y* and *v*; for in the case of *devitvā* and *dideviṣati*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix being *kit* under the rule *ralo vyupadhāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.26), since the letter *v* is also included within the term *ral* according to the method already stated. Nor can it be argued that there is no fault regarding words ending in *v* because one could interpret the rule as *avyupadhāt* by omitting the *i* and *u* (from *iy-uv-upadhāt*), and then, by *praśleṣa* (splitting and joining), explain it as "after a word ending in *v* which has neither *v* nor *u* as its penultimate letter."

Nevertheless, in cases such as *gaudhera*, when the suffix *ḍhrak* is applied by the rule "godhāyā ḍhrak," the *ḍha* is replaced by *ey*, the initial vowel undergoes *vṛddhi*, and the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule "yasyeti ca," the elision of the letter *ya*—prescribed by the rule "lopo vyorvali"—would be impossible because the letter *ra* is not included among the *val* sounds. Furthermore, in the case of *paceran*, after the addition of *sīyuṭ* and the elision of *sa*, resulting in *paca īy ran*, that [elision of *ya*] would also be unestablished, since the letter *ra* is not included within the *val* sounds.

Nor should it be argued that one should simply state *vali* there [in the rule]; for then the elision of the letter *ya* would also undesirably follow in forms such as *hayyāditya* (from *haya-gatau*). Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because, by splitting the word *sarepha* from the original formulation as *r-vali*, the rule prescribes elision when a *repha* (*r*) or a *val* follows; for even so, one would have to formulate the rule as *raṇi* in every instance where *yaṇ* applies. Furthermore, by the *yathāsaṃkhya-paribhāṣā* (the maxim of corresponding order), this would result in the substitution of *repha*, *yakāra*, and *vakāra* in place of the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* respectively.

Nor can the matter be resolved by the *paribhāṣā* "sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ" (when a substitute is to be made in place [of something], that which is most similar [to the original] occurs), because they argue that due to its superior status, the rule of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) would instead apply.

In reality, however, since we observe the substitution of *yakāra* and *vakāra* in place of *ikāra* and *ukāra* in the rule "vyupadhāt," and the substitution of *repha* in place of *ṛkāra* in the rule "arvaṇastrasau," it is precisely the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* that operates here.

Alternatively, the *nyāsa* (substitution) should also be made for the preceding [rules] as "aṛiṇ" and "ulṛk. In the rules (*pradeśa*), one should employ the term "ṛk" in place of "ik" and "ṛṇ" in place of "iṇ," because even in the final system (*siddhānta*), all occurrences of the term "iṇ" must be expressed by means of the second nasal "ṇ. Likewise, in the case of the *ic*-pratyāhāra, the word "ṛc" itself should be used. Even in the rule "isusuktāntāt," the word "ṛk" should be substituted for "uk. Nor does this result in the inclusion of an extra "i" sound; for such an inclusion is indeed desired.

By applying the elision of the *i*-vowel and the substitution of *i* according to the rule "yasyeti ca," the form is established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) exactly as it is; the same applies to the substitution of *ka*. However, the mere non-application of the rule "yasyeti ca" does not constitute a fault. Even in the rule "śryukaḥ kiti," although the inclusion of the word *ṛk* serves to encompass the additional *i*-vowel, the mention of *śri* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

In reality, this is for the purpose of indicating that the letter *i* is not included anywhere within the *ṛk-pratyāhāra*. Consequently, there is no fault in rules such as "ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne" and "ugitaśca. Furthermore, in the case of the word *hāstikaṃ* (a collection of female elephants), when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, the absence of the substitution of *i* ensures that the designation *bha* does not apply; thus, the rule "bhasyāḍhe taddhite" preventing the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) remains unassailable, and there is no fault. However, regarding the rule "aṇudit savarṇasya," there is no distinction whatsoever.

In that case, [the fault arises] because of the inclusion [of the vowel *u*] by the subsequent *aṇ*-pratyāhāra. However, since elsewhere the *aṇ*-pratyāhāra is to be understood as being formed by the preceding [vowel], there would be the defect that the vowel *u* would be excluded from it while the vowel *ṛ* would be included within it. But in all such instances, one should instead specify "vy" (i.e., *v* + *y*). This is because *u*, *i*, and *a* are all subsumed therein. Furthermore, by virtue of the interpretive explanation (*vyākhyāna*), the letters beginning with *v* are not included.

Even in the Siddhānta, since the commentary itself must be respected for the sake of determining whether the *pratyāhāra* is formed with the preceding or the following *ṇakāra*, the *ṇakāra* as an *anubandha* in the former case must be discarded. Nor is it the case that there is a lack of evidence for the maxim "the specific [meaning] is understood from the commentary" (*vyākhyānato viśeṣapratipattiḥ*), because other evidence is possible.

In reality, however, the placement (*nyāsa*) should be made as *aṇ* and *lṛk*. Consequently, the letter *u* is not excluded. What remains is the contingency that the additional letter *ṛ* would be included; this too must be resolved as follows: by the mention of "the third" [vowel], it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that *ṛ* is not included in the references to *aṇ*. For instance, it will be established in the *laṇ* rule that there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *aṇ* in the rule *halaḥ*. Nevertheless, even that is only from the perspective of the final established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

In this view, however, the term *aṇ* must indeed be carried over (*anuvartate*) even there; for it is clear in the Bhāṣya itself that even in the rule "ikaḥ kāśe," the resolution is achieved by carrying that [term] over and interpreting it as a non-differentiation (*abhedānvaya*) with the sense of *aṇ* whose form is *ik*.

Furthermore, if the vowel *ṛ* were also included by the mention of *aṇ* in the rule *ḍhralope*, then the same would apply to the rule *halaḥ* as well; consequently, in the word *tṛtīyā*, after the substitution of the semivowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the *r* in the suffix *tīya* resulting in *ṛ*, the *ṛ* would also incur lengthening, and thus the form *tṛtīyā* would become untenable. Therefore, in accordance with the desired results, it is established that in instances where *aṇ* is mentioned, the vowel *ṛ* is not included therein, thereby ensuring the success of all intended outcomes.

This might be argued: according to the view that maintains the original arrangement [of the *Śivasūtra*], when the *aṇ*-pratyāhāra is formed with the preceding [vowel], the letter *ṛ* is excluded from it; therefore, the inclusion of *aṇ* with the preceding [vowel] in that rule (*tṛtīyā*) is accepted for the purpose of excluding it. However, under the proposed arrangement, even if *aṇ* were included with the preceding [vowel], it would be impossible for *ṛ* to be excluded from it. Furthermore, since the aforementioned over-extension could be prevented by the very mention of "the third case" (*tṛtīyā*), there is no evidence that *aṇ* must be included with the preceding [vowel] in that rule.

If it is argued that even when *aṇ* is included by another [rule], the acceptance that the vowel *ṛ* is excluded from the category of *aṇ* would result in the impossibility of its inclusion in the rule "aṇudit savarṇasya," [we reply: True. However, because of the force of the introduction of the mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ*, its status as a grasper (*grāhakatva*) is established. Nor should it be said that this [homogeneity] has its utility in the application of rules for long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) and so forth.

Nevertheless, in the rule *ṛdupadhāccālkṛpicṛteḥ*, since the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *kṛp* is required as a counter-positive to the distinction [of other roots], there must be the application of an operation conditioned by having *ṛ* as a penultimate vowel; for if the vowel *ṛ* did not include *lṛ*, the general rule would have no occasion to apply to that domain, and consequently, the exclusion of *kṛp*—which aims at precluding that very domain—would result in being purposeless.

In reality, since the length of the *hal* vowels is sublated and there is no distinction between the *ec* vowels [in that regard], the subsequent mention of the term *aṇ* would be redundant there. Thus, the intention of the venerable Bhāṣyakāra is that the matter is resolved by the *yathāsaṅkhya-paribhāṣā* (the rule of corresponding order) alone. Furthermore, by the explanation "before a *rvat*" (*rvati*), after establishing forms such as *paceyuḥ* and *godhera*, and because no further defects are raised, his agreement with that solution is determined as the remedy for those defects.

For this very reason, in the statement, "Or rather, let there be instruction by another," the removal of the *repha* is mentioned as a means of rectifying the fault in the original formulation (*yathānyāsa*) on an equal footing [with the alternative]. For example, in the case of the injunction, "Let the Brāhmaṇas be fed; let Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya serve the food," the feeding which is generally applicable is set aside by the specific instruction of serving. Similarly, here, the status of being the correlate of the operation (*kāryapratiyogitva*) is sublated by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding the cause of the doubling (*dvitvanimittatva*), which consists in the state of being prior (*pūrvatva*) as determined by posteriority residing in the correlates of the operation. This is my view.

In such cases, there is no doubling (dvitva). This is because, until the general rule reaches its specific application, the very other operation explicitly heard in the scripture presents itself first, and thus the [doubling] applies to that specific instance. This is what has been stated: "These two, *ra* and *ha*, are not the subjects of the doubling; rather, they are the cause (nimitta) [of it]."

Just as there is no doubling (*dvitva*) for the letter *ha* when it is external to the group *yar*, so too there is none for the letter *ra* when it is included within that same group. This is because, given the equality of the deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces the effect, mere inclusion [within the group] is irrelevant. This is because, in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the property of being *yar* (*yartva*) is absent; whereas in the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*), [the *ra*] is the counter-positive of the difference that constitutes the delimitor of the scope of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). For, by the force of logic, it is precisely the property of being *yar* distinct from *ra* (*repha-bhinna-yartva*) that serves as the delimitor of the scope of the subject in the rule prescribing doubling.

Thus, by the rule *anaci ca*, there is no doubling of the letter *r* even in cases such as *haryanubhava*. This is because, under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of meaning, the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* applies there as well, since [the *r*] is followed by something other than *r*. If it is argued that, in this way, rules such as *iko yaṇ aci* would not apply in instances like *dadhyudakam*, because the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) for the *ik* vowels would be sublated by the specifically heard status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*), Kaiyaṭa states on this point: "The aforementioned principle does not operate there, because of the specific indications such as *tasmād ity uttarasya*."

As for what is stated in the *Kaustubha*: "In the view that [the word] denotes the individual (*vyaktipakṣa*), since the rule must apply repeatedly to each instance of the object of the rule (*pratilakṣyam*), that very [view] must be adopted there. Or rather, there is a simultaneous enunciation (*tantra*) of all the distinct rules for each instance of the object, such as 'iko yaṇ aci'. And thus, when the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed for all individual instances of the vowel *i*, the *yaṇ* is established even when followed by a vowel other than *i*; otherwise, because all instances of *i* would be followed by a consonant other than *i*, the restrictive condition would be absent, and the purpose of the injunction would not be fulfilled."

Nor is there an over-extension [of the rule], because by considering the context of the exception (*apavāda*) and the injunction (*vidhi*), one does not assume such an intention (*tātparya*) regarding that specific individual instance (*tadvyakti*). This is to be reflected upon; for even on the view that words denote individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), once it is established—by the force of logic—that the word *ac* which provides the cause [for the application of the rule] refers to the class (*jāti*) distinct from the individual, there is no evidence that the individual instance of *ic* occurring prior to the form *ac* is the intended object (*uddeśyatva*). Consequently, its application in cases such as *dadhy-udaka* would be difficult to justify.

In a sentence being heard, other sentences of the same form operate by logical parity (nyāyasāmya) only upon those individuals delimited by those properties which are ascertained through their status as delimiters of the object-to-be-indicated (uddeśyatāvacchedaka) and the property-to-be-prescribed (vidheyatāvacchedaka). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the application of *yaṇ* and other rules even when followed by a consonant (*hal*). Nor can the force of the employment of the term *ac* [be invoked as a justification], because there is no other means to include everything except *ig*. For if it were simply stated *ecī*, there would be an excess of such [elements] and the vowel *a* would not be included; this is the general direction (*dig*). On this point, the Vārttika says:

In the eight [consonants], there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *ayogavāha*s; among the *śar*s, there is the substitution of *jaś* and *ṣatva*; and without distinction, there are the designations of *saṃyoga* and *upadhā*, as well as the prohibitions regarding the final vowel (*alo'ntyatva*) and the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

For those whose inclusion within specific pratyāhāras is desired only by virtue of particular purposes, their inclusion in other pratyāhāras would result in their not being taught in the *varṇasamāmnāya*; therefore, it is established that their inclusion in these specific pratyāhāras serves a purpose.

The *ayoga* [consonant clusters] are those which, either by their own form or by their mode of articulation, are not included within *pratyāhāra* [abbreviations], yet are heard in actual usage; and these consist of the *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, *anusvāra*, and *yama*, according to the *Bhāṣya*.

Although the slightly contacted (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) sounds *ṛ* and *lṛ*—which will be mentioned in the sixth [chapter] as "before *ṛ*, *ṛ* optionally" and "before *lṛ*, *lṛ* optionally"—are not explicitly stated here, they should nevertheless be understood as included here. This is because we see in the commentary on the *Tulyāsyaprayatna* sūtra that their status as vowels (*ac*) will be explained. Their inclusion among the eight [vowels] must be effected; for instance, in the derivation of *uraḥkāyaḥ* (chest-protector) and *uraḥpātaḥ* (chest-fall), the suffix *kap* is applied. In forms such as *uraḥkeṇa* and *uraḥpeṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* (*ṇatva*) must occur. Otherwise, if they lacked the status of *aṭ*, the rule *aḍvyavāye 'pi* would not apply.

Furthermore, the instruction [of the *śar* substitute] must be provided. In the case of the root *ubj* (meaning "to straighten"), which has the upadhmānīya as its penultimate letter, the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* would otherwise apply the *jaś*-substitution; however, by virtue of the closest phonetic proximity (*āntaratamya*), the substitution of *ba* occurs in place of the upadhmānīya, resulting in forms such as *ubjitā*. This is because once the status of being a *śar* is established, the status of being a *jhal* is necessarily established as well. Furthermore, this is necessary so that in forms such as *sarpiḥṣu* and *dhanuḥṣu*, the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vyavāye 'pi* may apply to produce the *ṣatva* substitution.

Nor can it be argued that the desired result is achieved there simply by the separate mention of the *visarjanīya*; for that very *visarjanīya* is to be rejected according to the reasoning already stated.

The meaning is: by means of the personification of *pratyāhāra* (phoneme-grouping) employed for the five purposes without distinction. By this, in the case of *u3bjaka*, the status of being a *hal* (consonant) serves as the cause for the designation of *saṃyoga* (conjunction), which in turn triggers the designation of *guru* (heavy) for the protracted (*pluta*) vowel *ū* in *u3*.
