In the case of *niṣkṛtaṃ duṣkṛtam*, the status of being the final member (*antyatva*)—which is the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the property of being immediately preceded (*avyavahitapūrvatvanirūpaka*) by a phoneme residing in the qualified (*viśeṣyabhūta*) [the *duṣ-*]—serves as the cause for the designation of *upadhā* (penultimate), which is employed for the application of the rule "idudupadhasya" (*Pāṇini 8.3.41*) to effect the substitution of *ṣ*. In the case of *vṛkṣastarati*, [the same applies] to that which ends in a *visarjanīya*.

The meaning of the Vārttika is as follows: in the view that *sa* (the substitute) is a whole-word replacement (*sarvādeśa*), *altva* (the property of being an *al*) serves as the delimiting factor for the status of the original locus (*sthānitāvacchedaka*) prescribed by the rule *alo'ntyasūtra*, in order to prevent such a status [for the whole word]. Furthermore, in the case of *vyūḍhoraskena*, where the substitution of *ṇa* would otherwise apply by the rule *aḍvyavāya* due to the status of the original locus (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the letter *s*, *altva* serves as the delimiting factor for the counter-correlate of the difference (*bhedapratiyogitāvacchedaka*) within the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed by the rule *analvidhau*. Additionally, in cases such as *uraḥkaḥ* and *uraḥpaḥ*, *artva* (the property of being an *ar*) serves as the delimiting factor for the counter-correlate of doubling (*dvitvapratiyogitāvacchedaka*) according to the rule *anaci ca*; thus, the *visarga* and other such forms are established.

Herein lies the distinction: the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) is not the intended purpose [of the rule]. This is because there is no evidence for the presence of the *upadhmānīya* as an initial element in the root *ubj*, and furthermore, it would result in the failure to derive the form *ubjijiṣati*. To explain: if the entire cluster including the *ba* were subject to reduplication, then by the rule "the first consonant remains" (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*), the *ja* would be eliminated, and only the *ba* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable. Nor should it be argued that the reduplication of the *ba*-cluster does not occur because the *jaś*-substitution is considered "not yet established" (*asiddha*); for it is stated that "that which is treated as not yet established applies only to what precedes, but not to reduplication."

Now, regarding the form *prāṇiṇiṣati*, the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* for both *n*s in the reduplicated stem (*ubhau sābhyāsasya*) indicates that the aforementioned paribhāṣā is not universally obligatory. Otherwise, if the reduplication were applied only to the form already characterized by *ṇ*, the *ṇ* would be established in the reduplicative syllable automatically, rendering the rule superfluous. For this very reason, it is accepted that in the form *aujaḍhat*, the letter *j* is established in the reduplicative syllable. Nevertheless, even so, the desired result is not achieved.

Kaiyaṭa and others argue that if the result of the reduplication were to consist of only the *upadhmānīya*, then by the rule "in the reduplication, [the first consonant is] *car*" (*abhyāse carc*), the *bakāra* itself would have to be heard due to the application of the *jaś* rule; since the resulting form would be identical to *ubibjiṣati*, there would be no difference in the fault.

As for the established conclusion that, according to the maxim *prakṛticaraṃ prakṛticaraḥ*, there would necessarily be the hearing of the *upadhmānīya* alone during reduplication—that is to be reconsidered. For, by virtue of the statement regarding inclusion within specific pratyāhāras (phonetic groupings) based on their restricted domains, the status of being a *cartva* (retroflex) is not established [for the *upadhmānīya*]. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the designation *jhala* would also fail to apply; for there is a disparity [between the two cases], since the designation *jhala* is implied by the mention of *jaśtva* as its purpose, thereby forming a single syntactical unit with it.

For it cannot be said that only *jaś*-substitution (as prescribed by *jhalāñ jaś jhaś*) is intended there, because there is no supporting evidence (*bījābhāvāt*); such is the opinion of the elders (*vṛddha*). Therefore, the failure to establish the form *ubjijiṣati* remains as it was.

In this way, from the very same [root], by applying the suffix *ghañ*, the substitution of *ga* for *ja* occurs via the rule "cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ," and the substitution of *ba* for the *upadhmānīya* occurs via the *jaś*-rule. Once the forms *abhyudga* and *samudga* have thus resulted, one must apply the rule "so'padādau" (Pāṇini 8.3.34) under its governing heading, and then by another Vārttika, "upadhmānīyasya ca," substitute *sa* for the *upadhmānīya* when followed by a *ka*-class consonant (*kavarga*). Then, in that position, one must further substitute *da* for *sa* because of the common dental place of articulation (*danta-sthāna-sāmyāt*) via the *jaś*-rule. Thus, the forms *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ* are to be established.
Even if one were to begin a separate rule to prescribe this *satva* (the change to *sa*), there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).

If, however, one relies on the view of the Vṛtti that this [root] has *ba* as its penultimate letter (*bakāropadha*), even then there would be the very same complexity of having to infer two separate rules to establish both the prohibition of doubling for the *ni* with *ba* and the change of *ba* to *da* in forms such as *abhyudga*. Therefore, this [root] has *da* as its penultimate letter (*dakāropadha*) alone; for forms such as *abhyudga* are established naturally [by this view]. Nor should it be asked how, in that case, forms such as *ubjitā* are accounted for.

In the rule *bhujanyubjau*, the pronunciation of the letter *ba* is for the purpose of establishing the absence of the *kutva* substitution; from this, one infers a statement such as *bha udjeḥ* or *ba udjeḥ*. This means that in cases where *kutva* does not apply, the *da* of the root *udj* may become either *bha* or *ba*. Furthermore, because this [rule] is formulated after the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*, the *da* present in the *tavarga* (dental class) is obtained as the substitute.

And thus, because of the prohibition of doubling for the letter *d* by the rule "consonant clusters beginning with *n* or *d* [are not doubled]" (*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*), when the word *ji* alone undergoes doubling and the letter *d* is converted to *b* by the aforementioned rule, the form *ubjijiṣati* is also established. Nor does there arise the contingency of the conversion to *b* occurring first—due to its being a subsequent rule—prior to the doubling; for according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), "where a preceding operation is considered non-existent [for the purpose of a subsequent one], there is no conflict (of rules). Nor does it occur due to its being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, precisely because it is non-existent [in the eyes of the subsequent rule]. Nor is there a prohibition of that [doubling] by the rule "that which is non-existent regarding a preceding operation does not apply when doubling is to occur," because that rule applies only when doubling is being prescribed. And in this case, there is a disparity because of the prohibition of doubling.

In this regard, the following should be noted: In the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*, the letter *ba* is also included by *praśleṣa* (elision) before either the *da* or the *ra* via the elision rule *lopo vyor vali*. Consequently, according to both the view of the Vārttika and the view of the Bhāṣya, there is no need to follow another statement for the purpose of prohibiting the doubling (*dvitva*) of the *ba* in the root *ubj*. This is because, even in the Vārttika view, the prohibition of the doubling of *ba* is established by relying on the principle that "what is not established in what precedes [is not subject to] reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane*). Therefore, in the Bhāṣya view, there is no room for the claim of parsimony (*lāghava*).

The assumption of an additional singular number, however, is common to all three [positions]. This much, then, is the distinction: according to the Vārttika view, a rule prescribing the substitution of *s* for the *upadhmānīya* must be assumed; according to the Bhāṣya view, a rule prescribing the substitution of *b* for *d* must be assumed; but according to the Vṛtti view, a rule prescribing the substitution of *d* for *b* must be assumed.

If, however, it is assumed that according to the Bhāṣya’s view there is brevity because the substitution of *ba* for *da* occurs solely by virtue of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) "bhujanyubjau," and thus the aforementioned rule need not be inferred, then the doubling of the letter *ba* itself would result. This is because [the substitution] is not considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*). Even if one were to assume—on the strength of the mention of the stem ending in *da* (*dakāropadha*)—that the doubling of *da* occurs immediately after the doubling of the syllable *ji*, this would still lead to the same undesirable consequence in forms such as *abhyudga*.

Even if one assumes that the substitution of *ba* for *da* is prescribed (*nipātana*) only in cases where *ku*-substitution (*kutva*) does not apply, the teaching of the letter *da* would still serve its purpose as a means of being heard in cases where *ku*-substitution does apply; therefore, the substitution of *ba* would not occur immediately after the doubling (*dvitva*).

Alternatively, having accepted the prescription of *ba* without distinction, it is maintained that no suffix such as *ghañ* occurs after the root *ubj* when preceded by another prefix or when used alone, because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). As for forms such as *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ*, they are explained as being derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍa* following two prefixes.

Therefore, even according to the views of the Vārttika and the Vṛtti, since forms such as *abhyudga* can be established by the very method already stated, there is no need to postulate a rule prescribing *satva* for the *upadhmānīya* nor a rule prescribing *datva* for the letter *ba*; thus, how could there be any complexity (*gaurava*) in that case either?

However, in the case of the *upadhmānīya*, one must assume an additional instruction (*upadeśa*) for *ś* and *ṛ*, which is cumbersome. In the view of the *vṛtti* author, however, the cumbersomeness resulting from the inclusion of the letter *ba* (as a *praśleṣa*) should be understood as common to the *vārttika* as well. Furthermore, according to the views of both the *bhāṣya* and the *vṛtti*, no further effort need be made to establish the technical name (*saṃjñā*) of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). But in the view of the *vārttika* author, such an effort is necessary according to the previously mentioned method; thus, there is cumbersomeness.

If it is argued that the teaching of *śar* must necessarily be included for the sake of establishing the substitution of *ṣ*, and therefore its inclusion does not constitute a redundancy—this is not so. For that purpose, there is no need to include the *visarga* within *śar*. In fact, even that [inclusion] is unnecessary; since the term *visarjanīya* exists in the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vaḥ saṃyogāder āto dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.58), the establishment of *ṣ* when there is an intervention by those [sounds] is unimpeded. Nor should it be said that the term *visarjanīya* should simply not be used there, because once the established rule has been rejected, to postulate a different effort would be utterly futile.

As for the argument that by the teaching of *śar* as a term, just as *jhalatva* is established, so too are *haltva*, *artva*, and *khar-tva* established; and that the result of *khar-tva* is the substitution of *visarga* by the rule "kupvoḥ ḥkaḥpau ca"; therefore, since the teaching of *śar* is necessary, if the desired result can be achieved through that alone, the mention of *visarjanīya* in the sūtra should not be made at all—this is to be considered doubtful. For, although *jhalatva* is established by the statement that it serves as the purpose (*prayojana*) for *jaś-tva*, the properties of *haltva* and the others are not implied by that [teaching of *śar*].

This is because *haltva*, *yartva*, and so forth are prescribed in their own specific forms, and because the status of *visarga* is established precisely by its being a *sautra* (technical) term. Even if it were desired in common usage (*loka*), it would have been appropriate to include it under the term "without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa*). Alternatively, let it be that by that very indicator (*jñāpaka*) the status of *khartva* is also established independently; however, this does not imply that *haltva*, *yartva*, and the like are implied by *śartva*, as there is no evidence for such a claim.

Or, let it be granted that even for those [sounds] implied by the term *śar*, there is a restriction based on specific functions. The Vārttika beginning with "without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa*) implies that in every respect, these [sounds] are not included in any *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated technical term) other than those mentioned as having such functions. For this very reason, in the rule "kupvoḥ ḥkaḥpau," the substitute is the *visarga* itself according to the rule "kharpare śari"; otherwise, the alternative "vā śari" would apply, which is refuted here.

For this very reason, the following views have been refuted: first, the view that although other designations could be established by teaching the *aṭ* [pratyāhāra] as the body (*śarīra*), the *vārttika* author nevertheless arranged the syllables of the *vārttika* by setting forth specific *pratyāhāras* separately, with the intention that one means of expression does not invalidate another; and second, the view that the arrangement of the *vārttika* syllables was made in the stated manner solely for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This is because it is more appropriate to compose the *vārttika* in the stated manner precisely for the sake of restriction.

By this [explanation], even the laborious effort of following the rule that the *visarga* and *anusvāra* are non-existent (*asiddha*) in order to prevent the *yaṇ* substitution in such cases as "hariḥ karoti" and "hariṃ paśya" is discarded. By this very same [reasoning], the objection that the instruction regarding the *aṭ* augment must be applied only immediately after the vowel *a*—lest, by being included within the *iṇ*-pratyāhāra, the rule for the change of *s* to *ṣ* (ṣatva) would undesirably apply to the *s* following the *anusvāra* in "saṃskarttā"—is likewise discarded.

This has been indicated by Kaiyaṭa himself when he stated that there is doubling of the *s* following the vowel after the *anusvāra* in the word *saṃskarttā*, and when, according to the aforementioned method, he produced the letter *b* in the reduplication of *ubibjiṣati*. This is the direction [of the argument]. Therefore, it is established that *jaś*-ness and *ṣatva*-ness have no purpose here.

This is also necessary for the author of the Bhāṣya; otherwise, since the teaching of *śar* would be required for the sake of *ṣatva*, and since *jaśtva* would be established by that very fact through its being a *jhal*, even according to the view of the Vārttika, the teaching of *śar* would not incur the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), because the author of the Bhāṣya would have to assume an additional intention for the irregularity (*nipātana*) "bhujanyubjau" regarding the portion concerning *batva*. Furthermore, any other complexity has already been avoided.

Furthermore, in the view of the *Vārttika*, there is no burden resulting from the necessity of an effort to establish the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). In the rule *bhujanyubjau* (Pāṇini 6.1.172), by the force of the heavy articulation [of the vowel *u*], one assumes that the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*) does not apply to the substitution of *jaś* sounds; thus, the designation is accomplished by taking the letter *ba* itself. Moreover, the statement regarding the purpose of the designation of a "conjunction" refers strictly to the literal wording [of the rule].

Therefore, based on the authority of the Bhāṣya which rejects the necessity of the rule for *jaś*-substitution, one may infer its agreement even with the rejection of the necessity of *ṣatva*-substitution in the present context. As for the establishment of the visarga when followed by a jihvāmūlīya, that occurs precisely through the force of the nipātana rule "kupvoḥ ḥkaḥpau ca. Consequently, there is no inconsistency in rules such as "khayāṃ yamāḥ khayaḥ ḥkaḥpau"; this should be understood with subtlety.

The designation *upadhā* (penultimate) is also not required; for this is established by explaining [the rule] as "the *visarga* that has *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* as its *upadhā*," or because the mention of *upadhā* is rejected once the rule is already established by [interpreting it as] "of the *visarga* following *i* or *u*. Furthermore, the rule regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyavidhi*) is also not required; for this is established simply by explaining [the rule] as "the *sakāra* [substitutes] that *visarjanīya* which belongs to a word (*pada*)."

Furthermore, the prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) is not a purpose [for the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*]. This is because it is already established by the principle: "In regard to what is *asiddha* in what precedes it, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*. Nor is that principle restricted solely to the domain of the rule *acaḥ parasmin*; for its application to the *sthānivadbhāva* is based on the general logic (*nyāyamūlaka*) that what resides in the final three chapters (*tripādī*) is *asiddha* with respect to the *sthānivadbhāva*, and thus it pertains to the *sthānivadbhāva* in general. Therefore, the two purposes alone are established: the substitution of *ṇa* for *ṭ* in the case of *aṭsu*, and the doubling [of a consonant] according to the rule *anaci ca*. [The letter] *laṇ* is the sixth.

Although the letter *a* at the beginning of the word *hakāra* serves merely the purpose of ease of pronunciation, it nevertheless receives the technical designation *it* here because it is nasalized (*ānunāsika*), according to the established principle that "the followers of Pāṇini [assert] that nasality is inherent [in certain sounds]. Consequently, when the vowel *a* is pronounced together with the letter *r*, both the letter *r* and the letter *l* are included within the pratyāhāra *rapara* in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*. Furthermore, the statement in the Vārttika that there is "homogeneity" (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ* serves as the authority for this point.

Now, one might object: "In rules such as *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ*, does the mention of the term *aṇ* refer to the preceding *ṇ* or the following *ṇ*? Thus, a doubt arises. If this is asked, the answer is no; for that doubt is removed by the authority of the interpretation that, according to the *paribhāṣā* (metarule) on technical definitions (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*), the term refers to the following [letter] in those specific cases, but elsewhere it refers to the preceding one. To explain:

Since the rule would be established by the word *aca* alone, because there is no distinction regarding the lengthening of *ec* vowels; or since it would be established by *aka* alone, because lengthening is a property belonging solely to vowels (*aj*), and thus impossible for *ha*-sounds and the like; and since it would be established even without the mention of *aj*, the mention of *aṇ* [in the rule *ḍhralope*] must, by its very force, be understood as referring to the preceding *aṇ*.

Furthermore, from the root *vṛh* in the present participle (*vṛhan*), by virtue of its being marked with *ū*, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* according to the rule *svaratisūti*. Then, the *ṛ* undergoes *guṇa*; *b* becomes *ḍh* by *ho ḍhaḥ*; the *t* of the suffix becomes *dh* by *jhaṣastathordho 'dhaḥ*; *ḍh* becomes *ḍ* by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*; the preceding *ḍh* is elided by *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ*. Since the elision of *ḍh* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of the preceding rule, the *ṛ* that precedes it receives the designation of *upadhā* (penultimate vowel). Consequently, by *upadhāyāśca*, the *ṛ* becomes *i*, followed by the substitution of *ra* (*rapara*). Finally, the *i* undergoes *guṇa* as a light *upadhā* vowel.

Nor should it be argued that the subsequent mention of *aṇ* is for the sake of including the form *verdheta*; for that would contradict the *paribhāṣā* "acaśca" (P. 1.1.51), as a long vowel cannot occur for the letter *r*. Nor can the force (*sāmarthya*) of the subsequent mention of *aṇ* be invoked, because that would lead to a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, this is contradicted by the *bhāṣya*, which demonstrates the force of the mention of *aṇ*; and finally, the point is established even by the inclusion of *ṭ* together with *ṭ* in the *pratyāhāra* "aṭ".

As for the argument that because of the mention of the third [term] (*tṛtīya*), the *aṇ* here must be the one from the preceding rule [Pāṇini 6.1.72], otherwise, since the *aṇ* from this very rule would also carry over into the rule "halaḥ" (6.4.2), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of lengthening even the *ṛ*-vowel that takes the place of the *repha* when the *tri* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*—that is to be considered. For the meaning of that [rule] is simply: "there shall be lengthening of the *aṅga* which ends in that *saṃprasāraṇa* which follows a *hal* that is a constituent part of the *aṅga*. Furthermore, there is no evidence for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *aṇ*, which has been interrupted in rules such as "ikaḥ kāśe" (6.3.125).
And so, in that Bhāṣya, after first providing a solution by carrying forward the mention of *aṇ* from the preceding sūtra, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):

"Or rather, both [the mention of *aṇ* and the word *dvitīya*] have been withdrawn; why then does [the form] 'tṛtīya' not occur? This is established by the specific grammatical citation (*nipātana*) of 'dvitīya' and 'tṛtīya'. Therefore, it is the consensus of the Bhāṣya that the very mention of *aṇ* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

As for the counter-example given by the Easterners (*prācām*)—"kiṃ dṛḍhaḥ?"—that is to be considered [with suspicion]. In the rule "dṛḍhaḥ sthūlabalayoḥ," the absence of *iṭ*, the elision of the letters *n* and *h*, and the substitution of *ḍha* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix are treated as *nipātana*s (irregularities). It is not the case that the operations such as the substitution of *ḍha* found in the section on what is "not established" (*asiddhakāṇḍa*) apply here.

Many scholars maintain this because it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other works that otherwise, in the form *paridraḍhayya*, the substitution of *ay* by the rule "lyapi laghupūrvāt" would result in an impossibility, and in forms such as *pāridṛḍhīkā*, there would arise the impossibility of the absence of *yaṅ* due to the lack of a heavy penultimate syllable (*gurūpottama*).

The author of the *Prasāda*, however, by stating that there is an elision (*lopa*) and an irregular insertion (*nipātana*) of the letter *na*, maintains that this is indeed an irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the root *dṛṃh* itself; thus, he asserts that it is entirely appropriate for it to serve as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to the root *vṛh* (meaning "to grow"). And this is correct, because of the natural force (*svārasya*) of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the forms *ādṛḍhaḥ* and *āvṛḍhaḥ*. For this very reason, even the assumption that the rule "gha is substituted for the initial *dh* of a root" (*dāderdhātorghaḥ*) does not apply and that there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* is not faulty, since it is supported by powerful evidence.

By this, the statement in the *Kāśikā* that this [substitution] is also a *nipātana* (irregularity) for the root *dṛh* is refuted; for such a hypothesis is undermined by its contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the stated rule. By this same reasoning, the attempt to derive the absence of the *āyādeśa* in *pāridṛḍhī* from *paridraḍhayya*—by assuming the suffix *yaṅ*—is merely an argumentum ad absurdum (*iṣṭāpādana*), since there is no obstacle to accepting a difference in form, and because the proof has already been shown. By this, the assumption of the reading *tṛḍha* in the grammatical analysis (*prakriyā*) is also refuted. Furthermore, the rule *ke'ṇaḥ* is also governed by the preceding [rule].

In the *Kaustubha*, it is stated that in examples such as *gokā* and *naukā*, as well as *upānatkā* and *catuṣkam*, although there is the possibility of subsequent vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*), the rule "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*)—which is present due to the application of the rule for shortening—is followed, because the substitution of *dha* and *visarjanīya* is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*).

However, in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, it is explained that in the rule *na mu ne*, by means of a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) using the word "not" (*na*), the non-existence of *dha* and other such substitutions does not apply; thus, there is simply no possibility of *ha*-sounds and so forth occurring before the suffix *kap*. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases like *gokā*, because that would result in the necessity of stating the rule simply as "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*).

In the rule *aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*, although there is indeed the possibility of the existence of *ṛ*-sounds and others in their own forms when using the subsequent *pratyāhāra*—since *ya*, *va*, and *la* are each twofold, distinguished as nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*ananunāsika*), as seen in examples such as *karttṛ*, *agne*, *vāyo*, *pacai*, *māla* (from *mālāmācakṣāṇaḥ*), and *vṛkṣav* (from the verb root *vṛkṣavati* with the suffix *ap*)—nevertheless, by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed in the term *apragṛhyasya*, [only the non-nasalized forms are intended].

By the force of grammatical usage (*vyutpatti*), there arises the cognition of only that *anuyogin* which is delimited by a property that is the immediate pervader (*sākṣād-vyāpaka*) of the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of a difference residing in the counter-correlate of the difference (*bhedapratiyogivṛtti-bhedapratiyogitāvacchedaka*). Since it is thus established that only the vowel *a* is presented as being distinct from *pra* and *gṛhya*, the inclusion of the term *aṇ* [in the rule] indicates that the *pratyāhāra* must be formed with the preceding [vowel] alone.

The word *vṛkṣavaḥ* has been explained by Kaiyaṭa as follows: from the root *vṛśc* (to cut), one forms *vṛkṣavṛścam* [meaning "one who cuts trees"] using the suffix *kvip*. Then, by applying the causative suffix *ṇic*, and subsequently the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya*, there is elision (*ṭilopa*) of the *ṛ*, *ś*, and *c* sounds. Thus, the form *vṛkṣavayati* is established, after which the suffix *vic* is added. It is not, however, formed with *kvip*, because that would entail vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) due to the *kit* designation; furthermore, it would result in the application of the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), which prescribes the substitution of *ūṭ* for the *v* sound, thereby subverting the intended elision of *v*. Nor can the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇilopa*) be considered subject to the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Because of the prohibition—"that which is elided by *kvip* is not like the original" (*kvau luptaṃ na sthānivat*)—and specifically "not like the original with respect to an operation caused by *kvip*" (*kvau vidhiṃ prati na sthānivat*), there is no elision of the *val* sounds (consonants) due to their being treated as the original when *vic* is applied; thus the derivation is maintained. Nor should it be argued that, even so, the elision prescribed by the rule "before a consonant, for all [grammarians]" (*hali sarveṣām*) would apply [to the *u* of *ūḍh*]. This is because, regarding what is considered "not established" (*asiddha*) in the preceding context, the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply. Furthermore, in that rule (*hali sarveṣām*), the term *aśi* is understood to carry over from the previous rule "for *bho*, *bhago*, etc. (*bhobhago*). Nor can it be claimed that there is the contingency of applying *ūṭh* by relying solely on the *kvip* suffix that precedes the *ṇic*.

Because the elision of the suffix *ṭi* (ṭilopa) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the external causative affix (*ṇic*), since it depends on that which is external, while the internal operation [of the *kvip* suffix] must take place first by virtue of its being based on the internal *kvip*.

As for the argument in the *Kaustubha* that, because a partially modified form is not distinct from the original, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "vraśca" would be unavoidable; nor can the status of the *ṇi*-affix elision (*ṇilopa*) be treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), because of the prohibition "not in the case of a rule concerning the end of a word," and because that [prohibition] does not apply when a preceding operation is *asiddha*. Therefore, one who seeks a tree is *vṛkṣavīḥ*, and one who blows [wind] upon a tree is *vṛkṣavāḥ*. From the causative form (*ṇyanta*) meaning "he describes one who seeks trees" or "one who blows upon trees," the suffix *vic* is applied. Nor is there the contingency of the elision of *v* and *y* by the rule "lopo vyoḥ," because the elision of the *ṇi*-affix is treated as *sthānivadbhāva*.

[The opponent argues: "Because a deletion (*lopa*) is not a constituent part (*anavayavatva*), the prohibition 'not at the end of a word' (*na padānta*)—which means that [a rule] does not apply if it is prescribed for the end of a word—does not take effect. This is to be considered. For, in the rule *vraścādi* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), regarding the sequence *icchaśām*, two *c* sounds are elided before the *ch*; by this, one *c* indicates its own inherent form, while the other indicates a *c* substituted for *j*. Thus, the rule prescribes *ṣatva* specifically for the *c* and *j* of roots such as *vraśc*. Furthermore, one expedient (*upāya*) does not invalidate another expedient.

This may be so. In the Bhāṣya, after deliberating whether or not the mention of *kit* is to be understood as carrying over (*anuvartate*) from the rule "cchvoḥ," it is stated: "If the mention of *kit* is carried over, it must be stated that there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *ch*."

The meaning of this is as follows: in the absence of its (the *cha*-sound’s) recurrence [from the previous rule], since the substitution of *ś* for *cha* by the rule *icchvoḥ* and the subsequent prescription of *ṣ* for that *ś* would already suffice, there would be no need to include *cha* in the rule *vraśca-*. Thus, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), if the intention of the Bhāṣya were simply to omit *cha* here, why was the *praśleṣa* (the inclusion of both *cha* and *ja*) stated? True; nevertheless, because the rule for *ṣ*-substitution would apply only to the *ca* and *ja* sounds by the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning the final letter), the *ṣ*-substitution would not have occurred for the *va* sound.
This is because, within the scope of the *vraśca-* rule, the *ṣ*-substitution serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ku*-substitution (*kutva*).

Haradatta, however, has established in the commentary on the sūtra *hali sarveṣām* that the usage *vṛkṣav karoti* does not exist at all; for, based on the statement in the Bhāṣya—"there are no hal consonants at the end of a word that are not aṇ"—it is certain that such a form is unexpressed (*anabhidhāna*).

On this point, Kaustubha-kāra states: In the *Laṇ-sūtra-bhāṣya*, the reading is indeed "na padāntāḥ pare’ṇaḥ santi. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with Kaiyaṭa, who maintains that because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of non-*pragṛhya* vowels, only vowels are subject to grammatical operations (*kāryabhāk*), and thus no other [consonants] exist as such subjects. This, however, is questionable. For although the *bhāṣya*—which aims to demonstrate the existence of [sounds] such as *kartṛ*—shows the presence of vowels, there is no evidence for the existence of consonants (*hal*). Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa’s statement as it stands is contrary to reason.

Since the *aṇ* vowels, beginning with *ṛ*, exist in their own form (*svarūpeṇa*), there is no contradiction in negating them [as such]. However, with the intention that the absence of the qualified (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) would reside in *ṛ*-vowels and the rest by means of the very absence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāva*), thereby applying universally to all consonants (*hal*), you have introduced an interpretation according to your stated method, namely that "there are no objects of operation (*kāryin*). But this is not correct; because the mention of *aṇ* was established in conjunction with the preceding rule, it is not yet proven that *ṛ*-vowels and the rest can serve as the locus for an absence of the qualified based on the absence of the qualifier.

Otherwise, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself would not even arise; furthermore, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "But surely this agent exists" would be untenable. For, when there is a doubt as to whether the vowel *ṛ* and so forth participate in grammatical operations, the statement that they exist merely in their own form (*svarūpa*) is irrelevant as a reason.

Therefore, when there is a doubt regarding the non-existence of *ṛ*-sounds and others at the end of words (*padānta*) by virtue of their own form (*svarūpeṇa*), the existence of the *ṛ*-sound is stated as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the subsequent vowels (*aj*). Once its existence is thus established, the statement "there are no *aṇ* sounds after word-final [consonants]"—which conveys the absence of word-final *ṛ*-sounds and so on—is determined to be non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇya*) with respect to the vowel portion (*ajaṃśe*). However, since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding its capacity to convey the absence of *ha*-sounds and others, its authority is ultimately established in that respect. This is the essential meaning derived from the fact that the statement "there are no *hal* [consonants] after *aṇ* sounds" has been cited by the Miśras.

Nor should it be argued that, since the mention of the vowel *ṛ* is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), the consonants (*hal*) should also be understood as being illustrated; for there is no evidence for this. This is because the rules such as "guṇa of a short vowel" (*hrasvasya guṇaḥ*), "ai for e and o" (*eta ai*), and "au for ā before ṇal" (*āta au ṇalaḥ*) serve as indicators of the intention (*tātparya*) that the portion referring to vowels (*aj-aṃśa*) is indeed illustrative. Furthermore, one might argue that regarding the portion concerning consonants (*hal-aṃśa*), the Bhāṣya on the rule "hali sarveṣām" (*hali sarveṣām*)—which states, "so that [the substitution] occurs in the case of *hal* but not here, as in *vṛkṣav* from the verb *vṛkṣavati*, when the suffix *apratyaya* follows, as in *vṛkṣav karoti*"—serves as an indicator of the intended meaning. However, this argument is not valid.

This is because that [other] commentary is a *prauḍhivāda* (an assertion made for the sake of argument) due to its contradiction with this [present] commentary. Nor can the reverse be maintained; for primacy itself is the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*), and because an alternative (*vikalpa*) is impossible regarding a real entity (*vastu*). As the authorities have said: "Indeed, it is the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) that is subject to option, not the thing itself.

Nor should it be argued that the intention of the earlier commentary cannot be so determined because it contradicts the clear meaning of the commentary stating "he makes a tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ karoti*); for that too is otherwise inexplicable.

Nor should it be argued that there is no harm even if the entire portion [of the rule] is invalid due to its being part of the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*), because—just as in the case of the portion that conveys the absence of *aja*—there exists a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) that renders the stated objection invalid even in the portion that conveys the absence of *hal*. For this meaning is understood even from the subsequent Bhāṣya, which states "this exists," thereby excluding the absolute impossibility of negation. This is because no letter such as *ha*, etc., is admitted by both parties to be the final member of a word.

This is because the partial negation of those who hold a mistaken view is approved by the Bhāṣya; otherwise, the [application of] the previous rule would not be established due to the non-inclusion of *aṇ*. To explain: since the term "non-*pragṛhya*" (apragṛhyasya) implies vowels (*ac*) by virtue of its etymological derivation, and since consonant clusters such as *hay* cannot be the objects of the operation, it is established that the rule concerns only vowels (*aj*). Consequently, one cannot claim that the previous rule applies by the force of the word *aṇ*, for once the status of *ha*, etc., as the objects of the operation is established through the force of the word *aṇ*, the general principle (*nyāya*) becomes irrelevant.

Because that maxim is not universally applicable, as evidenced by the inclusion of the term *arthavat* ("meaningful") in the rule *arthavadadhāturapratyayaḥ*, and by the explicit mention of "case-endings" (*vibhakti*) in rules such as *oṣadheśca vibhaktāvaprathamāyām*. Furthermore, in the rule *avarṇastrasāvanañaḥ*, when a difference is perceived where the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) resides in a property that directly pervades the delimitor of the locus (*anuyogitā*), it is precisely the status of being a case-ending (*vibhaktitva*) that serves as that [delimitor]; since the rule would otherwise fail to apply to *aṇ* and other suffixes not delimited by that [status], there would be the undesirable consequence of the unestablishment of forms such as *ārvatam*.

Furthermore, if a prohibition were accepted, there would be a contradiction with such examples as "vāhairalupyata sahasradṛgarvagarvaḥ" (the pride of the thousand-eyed Indra was shattered by the horses). Moreover, if one intends to express similarity based merely on a property residing in a counter-correlate other than that which delimits the counter-correlativity of the difference, then—just as *pratyayatva* (being an affix) serves as such a property in that case—here too *altva* (being an *al*-phoneme) would serve as such; consequently, it would be impossible to exclude *v* and the others, which are delimited by that [property]. By this, the argument that the inclusion of *aṇ* is justified even by the preceding rule and thus subverts the maxim of "that which is connected with a negative particle" (*nañivayukta-nyāya*) is also refuted.

Since both [interpretations] are otherwise possible, it is more logical to restrict the rule (*nyāyasaṅkoca*) itself. However, there is a difference [in the case of *ke'ṇaḥ* etc.], because in such instances, the vowel (*ac*) is brought to mind by the very mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*), and thus the rule must conform to that. But according to the method stated above, since the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) is dependent upon all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible for the *hal* (consonants) to be included as *aṇ* at the end of a word; therefore, the inclusion of them cannot be achieved through the force of the mention of *aṇ*. Consequently, by abandoning the term *ac* and relying solely on the force of the mention of *aṇ*, the inclusion of *aṇ* by the preceding rule is established.

Therefore, the meaning stated by Haradatta alone is appropriate for the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this point, because Kaiyaṭa’s intention also lies precisely here. To explain: having raised the objection that there would be a contradiction with the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* commentary as it stands—since he will later state that the purpose of the recurrence of the word *apada* [in P. 8.4.2] is [to exclude consonants from being *apṛkta*]—the resolution provided, namely that "other than those excluded by the aforementioned prohibition, no [consonants] possess grammatical operations," has its primary intent (*tātparya*) precisely in the statement: "there are no consonants other than those at the end of a word which are not *aṇ*. Since vowels such as *ṛ* exist in their own right, the qualification "possessing grammatical operations" [is necessary to exclude them].

And that qualified absence is non-distinct [in both cases]: it is non-distinct from the absence of the qualifier in the case of *ṛ*-sounds and the like, and from the absence of the qualificand in the case of *ha*-sounds and the like; for in both instances, if the purpose were merely the absence of the qualifier, the portion consisting of the qualificand would be redundant.

Although this [reasoning] is initially unestablished—because at that time the rule for nasalization (*anunāsika*) does not apply to *ṛ*-vowels and the like, and thus remains unestablished even then—nevertheless, by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "except when *pragṛhya*," only vowels (*ac*) can be subject to nasalization, and not consonants (*hal*). This is the sense of the argument (*phakkikā*), with the understood remainder being "provided that consonants are impossible as *aṇ*" (i.e., *aṇ* sounds). Otherwise, if the principle did not apply according to the stated method, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of nasalization occurring for *v* and other consonants as well; and it has already been effectively stated that there are no consonants at the end of a word that are *aṇ*.
Thus, the intention is that the eighth-century *Bhāṣya* passage is merely a display of boldness (*prauḍhimātra*).

He states the meaning of the phrase "not at the end of a word" as: "the meaning is 'those which undergo a grammatical operation'. Thus, by revealing the intended meaning of the aforementioned specific absence, he shows that this is indeed the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) and not a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*); such is the sense.

The other [author], however, states a refutation based on the literal meaning [of the rule]. In the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "But surely this...", the Teacher reveals his own intended position which was previously challenged: "If that is so... The point is that since it is impossible for *hal* (consonants) to be *aṇ* (vowels) at the end of a word, and since the inclusion of vowels alone is established through the method of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the force of the explicit mention of *aṇ* implies that [the rule applies] only by means of the preceding [definition of *aṇ*]. For this very reason, it is stated as a supporting argument that only vowels become *pragṛhya*.

Furthermore, according to the reasoning already stated, since *hal* consonants exist as *aṇ* sounds at the end of words, that [argument] is simply not a proof. Thus, Kaiyaṭa’s intent is that both the Bhāṣya passage stating "in every way there are no *pare'ṇaḥ* (subsequent *aṇ*s) at the end of words" and the Bhāṣya passage itself represent the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). This is because if either were merely a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), both of these two texts would become irrelevant. Moreover, in the case of *vṛkṣav hasati*, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) cannot be avoided even by carrying forward the word *aś* from the previous rule; therefore, you too must necessarily resort to the doctrine of non-occurrence (*anabhidhāna*) in that instance.
Furthermore, since non-denotation consists in being subsumed under a specific word, it results merely in the absence of the usage "vṛkṣav"; let this suffice for the detailed discussion.

The rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* also applies with the preceding [sūtra], because there is no purpose for it with the following one. Nor should it be argued that the following [sūtra] would be necessary for the sake of *raparatva* (the substitution of *r*) in cases such as *hotṝkāraḥ* and *mātṝṇām*, where the long vowel resulting from the *savarṇadīrgha* (homogeneous lengthening) or the *dīrgha* by the rule *nāmi* would require *raparatva*. This is because the inclusion of the term *dhātu-* (root) in the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For if the rule were to prescribe the substitution of *i* for every instance of final *ṛ*, then *itva* would undesirably apply even in cases like *mātṝṇām*; thus, the mention of *dhātu-* is intended to prevent such over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Even in that case, if *rapara* were applied, the form would end in *r* rather than ending in *ṛ*; since the rule [for the substitution of *i* for *ṛ*] would not apply due to the absence of an *ṛ*-ending, what would be the use of that [dhātu-grahaṇa]? Nor should it be argued that the mention of *dhātu* in the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca" is solely for the sake of subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*), on the grounds that just as in forms like *cikīrṣati*—where the *ṛ* is lengthened by "ajjhanagamāṃ sani" and becomes *rapara*, resulting in the substitution of *i* for the *ṛ* by the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca"—the same would occur in forms like *mātṝṇām* once *rapara* is applied. [This argument is invalid because: In *cikīrṣati*, the substitution of *i* for the *ṛ* occurs because the *ṛ* is followed by a consonant (*jhal*) and the suffix *san* is a *kit*. However, in *mātṝṇām*, the *ṛ* is followed by a vowel (*n*), so the condition for the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca" is not met. Therefore, the mention of *dhātu* is necessary to ensure the rule applies only when the *ṛ* belongs to a verbal root (*dhātu*). Thus, the purpose of *dhātu-grahaṇa* is indeed to restrict the scope of the rule.

Nevertheless, because that very [term] would result in its being the material cause (*upādāna*) for that [substitution], the mention of it in the preceding rule is intended to be informative (*jñāpanārtha*). Furthermore, it is possible for the mention of *aṇ* itself to serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Otherwise, one would simply have said "uraḥ raparaḥ. For in those various instances, since the substitutes (*ādeśa*) corresponding to the vowel *ṛ*—namely, the acute, grave, circumflex, nasalized, and long forms—would already be established as having *ra* as their subsequent element (*raparatva*), the purpose could have been accomplished by that alone.

Now, regarding the rule *kartr-artham* and others, the mention of *aṇ* [in Pāṇini’s sūtra *uraṇ raparaḥ*] is for the purpose of establishing that the substitution of *repha* (*r*) for the vowel *ṛ* by means of the *yaṇ*-substitution is followed by *r*. If it is argued: "Since the elision of the non-*r* *repha* is mandatory by the rule *halo yamāṃ yami*, the status of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) is redundant there," we say no. This is because it has been stated that the optionality from the rule *jhayo ho'nyatarasyām* is understood to carry over there. [To this objection, we reply: No, because the elision by the rule *rori* would be unavoidable. Nor is that [elision by *rori*] restricted solely to the domain of word-final [rephas].

Otherwise, the formation of *ajarghāt* and similar forms would result in an impossibility. For, from the root *gṛdh* in the sense of "desire," when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), after doubling, applying the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uradattva*), and applying the substitution of the *jaś* sounds, and after adding the augment *ruk* to the reduplicated syllable by the rule "ru-g-ri-k-au ca luki," then in the *laṅ* tense, with the addition of *aṭ*, the elision of *śap*, the application of *guṇa*, the replacement of *ṛ* by *ra* (*raparatva*), the elision of *si*, the change of *g* to *gh* by the rule *bhaṣ-bhāva*, the change of *dh* to *d* by *jaś-tva*, the change of *d* to *r* (*rutva*), the elision of the *ra* following the *gh* by the rule "ḍh-ra-lopa," the lengthening of the vowel following the *gh* by "ḍh-ra-lopaḥ," and finally the visarga for the *r* by "kha-ra-vasānayoḥ"—the form is thus established. And all this is a statement made on the basis of a hypothetical admission (*abhyupagamyavāda*).

In reality, however, when the substitution of *ra* for *aṇ*s in place of *ṛ* is to be prescribed, both *ṛ* and *lṛ* appear as the substituends (*sthānin*), while the *r* and *l* appear as the substituents (*ādeśa*). By the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the term *aṇ*, which introduces the substituents, is restricted to those *aṇ*s that are distinct from the substituends—that is, those distinct from *r* and *l*. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *mātṝṇām*, nor does the occurrence of two *r*s arise in cases such as *kartṛ-artham*.

And thus, the meaning of the Bhāṣya—that there would be the consequence of futility (*vaiyarthyāpatti*) if it were grasped by another [term], due to the force of the mention of *aṇ*—is as follows: for if taken literally, the fault stated in the Kaustubha would arise, since in the case of *lākṛtiḥ*, the result could possibly belong to the substitution of *l* alone. Nor is there deliverance through the mention of *dhātu*, because that [mention] may also be intended for what follows.

As for the argument that *nuṭ* should be explicitly stated for the sake of subsequent rules, and that its mention here is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) according to the maxim of *trapu*, that is not correct. For in the rule *nāmi*, it has been established that the inclusion of *nuṭ*-qualified forms serves exclusively for the sake of subsequent rules; thus, there is no such restriction. Nor does an explicit statement override the *takrakauṇḍinya* maxim (the principle of the curd-milk exclusion), since the purpose is already served by the preceding rule. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of overriding even the elision prescribed by *ro ri* in cases such as *artthārtham*.

Furthermore, the subversion of logical reasoning (*nyāyabādha*) is not preferable to the subversion of the expressive power of a statement (*vacanasāmarthya*). In that context, if the elision of the letter *r* (*rephalopa*) were accepted, the rule regarding *r* being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) would become redundant; for the subversion of the statement teaching that [rule] would apply equally there as well. Moreover, since the purpose [of the rule] cannot be fulfilled by mere application if its sound is not heard anywhere, otherwise the Bhāṣya and other texts—which serve both to indicate the optional recurrence (*vikalpānuvṛtti*) of the rule "śaro'ci" and to refute it—would be inexplicable. This is the general direction of the argument.

However, in the rule *aṇudit savarṇasya ca*, [the term *aṇ*] refers only to the subsequent [vowel]. This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule *urṛt*. For that [rule] is intended to prescribe the short *ṛ* in place of the long *ṛ* in forms such as *acīkṛtat*—derived from the root *kṝ* (meaning "to sound") belonging to the curādigaṇa, followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, and then the aorist (*luṅ*) with the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli* according to the rule *ṇiśri*—in order to provide the short *ṛ* in place of the long *ṛ*. In that context, the addition of the *t* (as in *urṛt*) is for the purpose of ensuring that even in the place of a long vowel, only the short *ṛ* is substituted.

In the *Grahaṇaka-śāstra*, if the term *aṇ* were understood according to the former [interpretation], then since there would be no possibility for the long vowel (*dīrgha*) to be either the substitute (*ādeśa*) or the original locus (*sthānin*) of the *ṛ*-vowel, the rule would be purposeless. However, if that term is understood according to the latter [interpretation], then by the inclusion of the homogeneous *ṛ*-vowel within the term *ṛ* in the rule *ur ṛt*, there arises the possibility of that [long *ṛ*] being the original locus.

Nor is the purpose of the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) redundant even when [the vowel] is apprehended by another [element], because here, due to the impossibility of being a grasper (*grāhaka*) simply by virtue of being enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*), it results merely in the exclusion of modification (*vikāra*). Thus says the Vṛttikāra: "And this *aṇ* is not something to be produced (*bhāvyamāna*), but rather its own form is authorized for the sake of excluding other substitutes. However, it is a different matter that through the force of the *tapara*, the status of being something to be produced is also obtained in the place of a long vowel.

However, the *iṇ*-pratyāhāra everywhere includes only the subsequent [sounds]. This is because in the rule *aci śnu*, the letters *y* and *v* are specified by their own form (*svarūpeṇa*) as *ikāra* and *ukāra*; otherwise, he would have simply said *iṇaḥ*. In the *saṃhitā* reading according to this arrangement, there are two half-mātrās for *hal* and two mātrās for *aukāra*, totaling three mātrās; but if *iṇaḥ* were stated, there would be only one and a half mātrās.

Even in the analysis of the words (*padaccheda*), there is a sequence of three and a half *mātrās* (three half-*mātrās* and two *mātrās*) and three *mātrās*, which is more concise. Regarding the rule *ralo vyupadhāt*, the author of the *Nyāsa* maintains that the explicit mention of the letters *u* and *i* in their own forms serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this.

Therefore, it is established that the secondary marker (anubandha) *Ṇ* is attached again for the purpose of making known the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "The specific [application] is understood from the explanation; for a rule is not rendered invalid by doubt. Furthermore, there is no restriction that doubt must always concern only the formal nature (*svarūpa*) of an element. For instance, in the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite*, the phrase *agner ḍhak* is connected as the counter-correlate (*bhedapratiyogin*) of the distinction [implied by *aḍhe*], based on the explanation, and not the phrase *strībhyaḥ ḍhak*, because such is seen in authoritative texts. However, by this rule, even doubts concerning the specific base (*prakṛti*) prescribed by a particular rule and so forth are to be removed; thus, everything is clear.

*Ñamaṅaṇanaṃ* (7), *jhabhañ* (8). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states that the letter *m* should not be included as an *anubandha* here. This is because the three *pratyāhāras*—*yam*, *ṅam*, and *am*—can be accounted for by the letter *ñ* alone. To illustrate: the rule should be formulated as *halo yañāṃ yañi lopaḥ*. There is no possibility of the elision of the letters *jha* and *bha* situated between them, because there is no occurrence anywhere of a *jha* or *bha* following another *jha* or *bha*. Furthermore, the rule should be read as *pumaḥ khayyañpare*; and there is no risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Because those two [substitutions] are impossible in the case of *khay* and *parau*. Likewise, it should be stated: "After a short vowel, *ṅañ* is always replaced by *ṅañuṇ* when followed by a vowel. Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because *jha* and *bha* are not established at the end of a word (*padānte*). As for *ujjhi*, its form is simply *ud* due to the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). However, in the case of *labh* and others, the substitution of *jaś* is necessary. The rest has already been explained.

[Objection: Even so, in the *Uṇādi* section, [the rule] "from roots ending in *ñ* or *m*, the suffix *ḍa*" (*ñamantāḍ ḍaḥ*) is necessary; otherwise, the suffix *ḍa* would undesirably apply even to roots ending in *jh* or *bh*. [Response: True. Even there, the reading should indeed be "from those ending in *ñ* or *ñ*" (*ña-ñantāt*). Some say that since no suffix *ḍa* arises from all roots ending in *ñ* or *m*, one must necessarily resort to the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*), and by that alone, the prevention of the suffix for roots ending in *jh* or *bh* is possible. However, in reality, since roots ending in the letters *ñ* or *ṅ* are not well-known, the intention of the *Bhāṣya* is that the sūtra should simply be formulated as "maṇanāḍ ḍaḥ."

*gha-ḍha-dha-ṣ* 9; *ja-ba-ḍa-da-ś* 10; *kha-pha-cha-ṭha-tha-ca-ṭa-ta-v* 11; *ka-pa-y* 12; *śa-ṣa-s-ar* 13; *hal* 14. These are the *pratyāhāra*-sūtras of Maheśvara. Regarding this, the ancients say: "From one [consonant], *ṅ*, *ña*, *ṇ*, *va*, and *ṭ* [are formed]; from two, *ṣ*; and from three, *ka*, *ṇ*, and *ma*."
The letters *jña*, *ya*, and *ca* are to be known as arising from four [consonants]; *ra* from five; and *śa* and *la* from six.

On this point, they say: this is a compendium of the *pratyāhāras* employed in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, which were formed by the vowels (*its*) and consonants (*hal*s) found in the fourteen initial *sūtras*. Therefore, there is no fault even if there is an addition of the *rapratyāhāra* (used for *suptiṅādi*), the *ñampratyāhāra* (employed in the *Uṇādisūtra* and the *Kārikā* of Vyāghrabhūti in the rules "ñamantāḍḍaḥ" and "yamirñamanteṣu"), and the *caypratyāhāra* (employed by the author of the *Vārttika* in the rule "cayo dvitīyā").

The meaning of this is as follows: the letter *ṅ* should be understood as occurring only after a single [vowel]. This is according to the rule "eṅi pararūpam. However, in rules such as "ṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ," the term *aṅ* is not a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation). This is because the phrase "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) is understood to carry over from the *grahaṇaka-sūtra* "ādirantyena. Nor does this lead to an inconsistency in rules such as "iko yaṇaci," for in those cases, there is the association with a *pratyāhāra*.

Alternatively, [the mention of *guṇa*] would be redundant in the *Bhidādi* group, because if *rekhā*, *lekhā*, and so forth were *ni-pātita* (irregularly formed) as *guṇa*-less, the status of being *ṅit* would be meaningless. Furthermore, in the rule "śāsa idaṅ-haloḥ," if the meaning were "before an affix beginning with *aṅ* and before one beginning with a consonant (*hal*)," the qualification [*aṅ-haloḥ*] would be useless. For if one were to explain it as "before an affix beginning with *aṅ* and before one beginning with *hal*," then the expression "*aṅ-haloḥ*" would be superfluous, since there are no *ṅit* affixes other than those beginning with *aṅ* or *hal*. One would simply have said "*ṅiti*" [without the qualification]. Moreover, in the Parasmaipada, there are no *ṅit* affixes beginning with *a* or *j*.

However, in the case of *karmavyatihāra* (reciprocal action), in the form *vyatiśāse*, there is no substitution of a single element (*ekādeśa*) together with the augment *āṭ*, because [the root] lacks the *ṅit* designation; furthermore, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, it would still not be treated as beginning with *aṅ*. In the rule *ṛdṛśo'ṅi* as well, the term is not a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference), because in the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām*, *guṇa* is prescribed for roots ending in the vowel *ṛ*. Similarly, in *sani ca* and *iṅaśca*, these are also not *pratyāhāras*. As for *sani ca*, this is because of the force of the separate prescription of the substitute *gami* for the root *iṇ*. Nor should it be argued that the separate mention [of *iṇ*] is for the purpose of excluding *iṇ* from the substitute *gami* when the meaning is "to understand" (*bodhana*).

This is because such a formulation alone is sufficient: "iṅo gāṅ liṭi," "vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ," "ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ," "sani gamiḥ," "iṇo'bodhane," and "ṇau ca gā luṅi. This is because it lacks the complexity found in alternative formulations such as "iṇo gā luṅi," "ṇau gamirabodhane," "sani ca," and "iṅaśca. Furthermore, rather than prescribing the substitute *gami* with reference to both the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the desiderative suffix (*san*), the rule prescribing it with reference to the causative suffix alone—and the subsequent exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by restating the desiderative and the causative—is more parsimonious.

Some maintain that this is because, in view of the requirement for the connection (*anusaṃdhāna*) with three sūtras, it is simpler [to assume the substitute] in two sūtras; and because, due to the prescription of *kit* status by the rule *iko jhal* and the prescription of lengthening by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani*, the aforementioned two sūtras would become devoid of scope if the substitute *gami* were applied to roots ending in *iṅ*. Similarly, the prescription of *iṭ* after the four roots ending in *ṛ* (beginning with *kṝ*) when followed by *san*—as in the rule *kiraśca pañcabhyaḥ*—should also be understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), since *iṭ* is established for those ending in *iṅ* simply through the substitute *gami*. Furthermore, the rules *parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ* and *iṅaśca* are not of that nature [i.e., they do not indicate the same].

Because [roots] ending in *ik*, *uk*, and *ṛ* are already blocked by being followed by suffixes (*pratyaya*), and because roots ending in *ej* have already undergone the substitution of *āt* (*attva*) previously, [the rule] would apply only to those ending in *ṛ*. Furthermore, if it were intended only for those ending in *ṛ*, there would be the consequence of mentioning them in their own form alone; and since the *ghañ* suffix would be established by the general rule itself, the present rule would result in being redundant. If, on the other hand, it were intended as an option (*vikalpa*) for *ghañ* together with the suffixes *ac* and *ap*, then it would follow that the mention of *vā* (or) should have occurred in the very rules "ṛdorap" and "erac. Moreover, the expression "krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau" is not a *pratyāhāra* (a contraction).

Since the substitution of *āt* for the roots ending in *e* is already established by another rule, the term *ikaḥ* alone would have sufficed; furthermore, the separate mention of *krī* and *jyā* would otherwise be inexplicable. By this, even the suspicion that the rule is intended as a restrictive one—meaning "only these two [among the roots ending in *i*]"—is dispelled.

Nor should it be argued that the prescription of *ā* in the case of the root *iṅ* (in the sense of studying) is intended to prevent the general application of *ā* that would otherwise occur for roots ending in *e* when followed by the causal suffix *ṇic*; for even so, this is precluded by the force of the rule "oḥ puyaṇjyapare," which prescribes *it* for the reduplicated syllable. Furthermore, the rule "iṅdhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi" does not apply here either, because of the association with the root *dhṛ*, which is a verbal root (*dhātu*) in its own form.

In reality, because of the force of its separate mention from *dhāri*, the *ṅ* in *eṅ* constitutes a single *pratyāhāra*. Likewise, the *ñ* also [constitutes a single *pratyāhāra*] from only one [letter], as in the rule "ato dīrgho yañi," where *yañ* is formed as *añ*, *iñ*, and *yañ* among the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*). If it is asked why it is not so in this case, it is because the word "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) is understood to follow from the rule "the first [consonant] with the last [vowel]" (*ādirantyena*). The initial *ṇ* also constitutes a single [pratyāhāra] from only one [letter], as in the various occurrences of the term *aṇ* that fall outside the scope of the "comprehensive rule" (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*). The *v* in the rule "gaś chavy apraśān" [constitutes a single *pratyāhāra*].

The letter *ṭ* [is used in a pratyāhāra], as in "aṭ-kupvāṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.2). However, "iṭa īṭi" (Pāṇini 8.2.28) is not a pratyāhāra; for it is impossible for a vowel other than the letter *i* to precede the letter *s* when followed by *īṭ*.

Furthermore, there is no established usage for [the augment] *ay* in forms such as *ayāsīt*, because even in the view that accepts the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference), it is excluded from that set; because the substitution of *ā* is prescribed only for those ending in *ej* at the very time of their original enunciation (*upadeśa*); because it is impossible for denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*) to be *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment); because for roots ending in *h* that are *aniṭ*, the substitute *ks* is prescribed, and thus only *īṭ* is established; because for those with the *iṭ* augment, the vowel *i* alone is necessary; because roots ending in *ṣ* or *ṇ* that are *aniṭ* are not established; and because for roots ending in consonants (*hal*), even in the *pratyāhāra* view, [the augment] does not apply.

Furthermore, because the substitution of *vṛddhi* is mandatory for roots ending in *ik* that lack the augment *iṭ*, the term *iṭ* in this rule [Pāṇini 1.1.5] cannot be a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation). This is because the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the *ṭit* designation indicate a relationship between a part and a whole. The letter *ṣ* occurs three times: in "ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya," in "akaḥ savarṇe," and in "iko yaṇ. The second occurrence of the letter *ṇ* also occurs three times: in "aṇudit savarṇasya" (where *aṇ* refers to a single vowel), in "iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam," and in "iko yaṇ. The letter *m* also occurs three times.

For example: *am*, *yam*, *ṅam*; the letter *c* [is substituted] for four [sounds]: "iko yaṇaci", "ica ekāco'm", "eco'yavāyāvaḥ", and "vṛddhirādaic". The letter *y* likewise [is substituted] for four: "anusvārasya yayi", "maya uñaḥ", "jhayo haḥ", and "pumaḥ khayi". The letter *r* [is substituted] for five: "yaro'nunāsike", "jharo jhari", "kharica", "abhyāse carca", and "vā śari". The letter *ś* [is substituted] for six.

"yo'śi," "haśi ca," "neḍ vaśi," "jhalāñ jaś jhaśi," and "ekāco baśo"—thus [the rules concerning] *la*. "alo'ntyasya," "hali sarveṣām," "lopo vyor vali," "ralo vyupadhāt," "jhalāñ jaś," and "śala igupadhāt. The sequential arrangement of these six numbers, beginning with one, is for the sake of the variety of expression.

It might be argued as follows: Since the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are included within the *pratyāhāras*, there would arise a confusion (*sāṅkarya*) regarding those beginning with *a* and so forth. For *ṇa*, *ā*, and others, because they are taught in both [the *aṇ* and *hal*] groups, they would possess both designations (*saṃjñā*). The same would apply to the letter *a*, since it is stated that the *it-saṃjñā* (the designation of being an indicatory letter) applies to the *a* situated in the *la* group. And thus, in forms such as *dadhi-ṇakārīyati*, there would occur *yaṇ*-substitution and so on; and in forms such as *rucīnām*, there would occur *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) by the rule "even when separated by an *aṭ*" (*aḍ-vyavāye’pi*), and so forth. This being the position reached, there is a *vārttika* on the *sūtra* *hayavaraṭ*: "How is it that in the *pratyāhāra* [lists], the *anubandhas* are not [included] in the mentions of *ac*? Because of usage, because they are subordinate, and because elision (*lopa*) is more powerful. [Translation of the *vārttika*: How is it that in the *pratyāhāra* lists, the *anubandhas* are not included in the mentions of *ac*? [The answer is:
Because of established usage (*ācāra*), because they are subordinate (*apradhānatva*), and because elision (*lopa*) is more powerful (*balavattara*).

Regarding the suffixes beginning with *ṇ*, such as *ṇakāra* and so on, how is it that [the rule] does not apply? Here, the connection is precisely with their being grasped as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the absence that is to be negated. The term *ac-pada* refers to the entire pratyāhāra (phonetic shorthand).

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is as follows: according to the rule *ādirantyena*, if an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) possessing some phoneme were to be designated by its mere specific occurrence as a constituent of that particular collection of phonemes situated between [the first and last letters] through the relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) of not including even the vowels such as *a* and so on; therefore, since a designation is necessary even for the specific phonemes that serve as the *upasthāpaka* (the signifiers), it is unavoidable that *anubandhas* occurring in the middle and those *anubandhas* that constitute the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of the signified] would also be included. This is the doubt [raised].

He provides the resolution, stating: "On account of usage (*ācārāt*)," that is, on account of the application by the Teacher (*ācāryaprayoga*). This is because in rules such as *uṇādayaḥ*, *tṛṣimṛṣikṛṣeḥ*, and *ṅasiṅasośca*, the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) lack the capacity to trigger operations necessitated by their inclusion within those respective *pratyāhāras*. Since the grammarians agree that these [indicatory letters] are not denotable by terms like *aj-ādi* (because they are the counter-correlates of the absence which causes the absence of operations), there is no evidence for the convention "the first [letter] together with the last" to apply to them as well.

When there is a difference in the *anubandhas* (indicatory markers) of words such as *ajādi*, the property of being a phoneme (*varṇatva*) that constitutes a member of that collection [of phonemes] serves as the delimiting condition (*viṣayatāvacchedaka*) of the scope. By the phrase "being existent" (*satyantena*), even those elements that constitute a technical name (*saṃjñā*) containing an *anubandha* situated in the middle are excluded.

However, some maintain that even the mention of *anunāsika* (nasalized vowel) in the rule is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For the sūtra *pratyayasthāc ca* operates, without objection, with respect to both *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes by virtue of the force of the commencement of the prohibition. In that case, according to the maxim *anantarasya* (the operation applies to what is immediately preceding), only the elision taught by *yasyeti ca* would be barred; thus, the application of *iko yaṇ aci* would be unavoidable in the case of the word *nāsikā*, which is derived from the root *nas* with the suffix *kvun*.

If one accepts that, by the principle of "non-attainment" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), only the *yaṇ* substitution is sublated, then the elision of *i* (*yasyeti lopa*) would be unavoidable after the word *asā* when the suffix *ka* is applied; for, since the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are included within the pratyāhāras, the suffix *ka* is a taddhita beginning with a vowel (*ajādita*), and thus the preceding element would receive the designation *bha*. Nor can it be argued that both [the *yaṇ* and the elision] are sublated by the force of the specific rule (*vacana-sāmarthya*); rather, it is more appropriate to understand that this [rule] merely teaches that the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* are not included in the pratyāhāras. This [position] is to be considered.

This is because it can be inferred that the designation *bha* does not apply when the suffix *kap* follows, due to the force of the rule prescribing the short vowel in *ke’ṇaḥ*; for if the elision of *ya* (by *yasyeti ca*) were necessary for both the vowels *a* and *i*, then the prescription would have applied to the vowel *u* alone.
In reality, however, even there, since the substitution of *guṇa* for *o* would result, there is no distinction [between the two cases].

He states another solution: "Because [the indicatory letters] are subordinate" (*apradhānatvāt*). Since the inclusion of the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) is solely for the purpose of establishing that they constitute the very form of the technical name (*saṃjñā*), the things named (*saṃjñin*) themselves possess primacy and are thus what is grasped, according to the maxim: "Between the primary and the subordinate, the primary is understood. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the letter *a* and others would also be included; for by the continued application of the rule *svaṃ rūpam* ("its own form"), these too are indeed the things named. Furthermore, one should not argue that the *anubandhas* should also be grasped by the word *sva*; for by the instrumental case in *itā* ("by means of it"), the subordination of the *it* is obtained, and because pronouns generally refer to that which is primary.

This, however, is merely an exaggeration. If being a "named object" (*saṃjñitva*) were the primary factor [for denotation], then there would be a circular dependency (*parasparāśraya*). If, on the other hand, the primary factor is being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) in the cognition produced by the science [of grammar] which grasps the convention (*saṃketa*), that is not the case; for that [qualificandum-ness] is irrelevant. Furthermore, because the grasp of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs even with respect to the qualifier in such cases as "a pot qualified by pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) is the denotable object (*vācya*) of the word 'pot'. Moreover, according to the Mīmāṃsakas' maxim "the qualifier is not grasped unless it is itself grasped," the grasp of the power occurs precisely with respect to the qualifier. Finally, even by the method already stated, the inclusion of the intermediate indicatory letters (*anubandha*) remains unavoidable.

He states another solution: "and there is elision" (*lopaśca*). The suffix *-tarap* in *balavattaraḥ* is used in its own sense (i.e., as an intensifier). Once the designation *it* has been applied, both the designation *ac* and the elision of the *ṇakāra* and others would apply; however, because the rule for elision is stronger, elision occurs first. Since they do not exist at the time the designation [of the *ādi*] is to take effect once elision has occurred, the designation does not apply to them. This is because, by the principle of "having previously existed" (*bhūtapūrva-nyāya*), the designation could only apply to that which begins with the final letter [of the original base]. Otherwise, the statement [of the rule] would be purposeless. Yet even this is not real, because the existence [of the letters] at the time the designation takes effect is of no use in the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa says in the commentary on the *Vṛddhi* sūtra:
Whether a conceptual object (*saṃjñin*) exists or not, once it has been made an object of cognition and previously indicated by means of a word, the name (*saṃjñā*) functions [with respect to it].

For this very reason, in the rule *halantyam*, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The designation *it* applies to the final consonant of a *la*-ending suffix. Therefore, the intended meaning is precisely as stated above; such is the direction of the argument.

Thus ends the second Āhnika of the first Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi. *Vṛddhir ādaic*. The vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* shall bear the technical designation *vṛddhi*, whether they function as substitutes (*ādeśa*) or non-substitutes (*anādeśa*). The rules (*pradeśa*) where this term is employed include, for instance, *vṛddhireci* (P. 6.1.88) and others in the context of original injunctions (*vidhi*), whereas in the context of restatements (*anuvāda*), there are rules such as *vṛddhir yasyācām* (P. 1.1.73). Here, because of the extended application (*atideśa*) that "the Sūtras are like Vedic [in their formation]," the designation *bha* applies by the rule *ayasmayādīni cchandasi* (P. 1.4.20), resulting in the absence of the change of *k* to *g* (*kutva*) which would otherwise be triggered by the condition of being at the end of a word (*padānta*).

However, since the designation *pada* (word) is indeed applicable for the purpose of *jaś*-substitution, *jaś*-substitution certainly occurs when the rule "vṛddhir ādaic," "adeṅ guṇaḥ" is recited in *saṃhitā* (continuous) form. As the *Bhāṣya* states regarding the example: "sasuṣṭubhā sa ṛkvatā gaṇena. The distinction here is that while in the cited example the *pada*-designation is applicable for the purpose of *kutva*-substitution, it is not applicable for the purpose of *jaś*-substitution. In this context, the mention of the short *a* (taparatva) is for the sake of excluding [long vowels]; therefore, as stated previously, the designation does not apply to those [vowels] consisting of three morae (*mātrā*) or more.

Nor should it be argued that, because there is thus an absence of being at the end of a word (*padāntatva*), the substitution of *d* would not occur; for it is possible that [the rule] may also serve as a supplement to what precedes, in order to avoid ambiguity. Furthermore, it was established previously that the letter *d* functions as a marker (*grāhaka*) for its own time-period. It might be argued: based on the natural sense of the *Bhāṣya*, which states "the correctness of these two has been established," the expression *ādaic* is indeed a single compound. This is because the meaning of that passage is "of these two words. Even though in the *Paspaśā* section it was stated that *vṛddhiḥ*, *āt*, and *aij* are separate words, even so, that is merely an incidental elaboration (*abhyuccaya*). For otherwise, one would have to interpret it as referring to "these two portions of the *sūtra*."

Furthermore, this contradicts the Bhāṣya, which states: "The root *vṛdh* is taught in the list of verbal roots (*prakṛtipāṭha*) without qualification; therefore, the suffix *ktin* applies to form the feminine. Also, the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are taught in the traditional recitation of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*). It also entails the undesirable consequence of having to supply the word *ca* ("and"). Thus, if it were a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the suffix for a compound ending would apply according to the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in *c*, *ṣ*, or *h*"; whereas if it were a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*), a dual ending would result. This is true; however, because the rule for compound suffixes is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), the collective *dvandva* alone is free from fault.

In this regard, the evidence is the inclusion of the word *rājan* in the *aṃśvādi* group within the rule *prater aṃśvādayas tatpuruṣe*. The meaning of that rule is that words such as *aṃśu* following *prati* are oxytone (*antodātta*). If, however, the suffix *ṭac* were obligatory by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaḥ*, the oxytoneness would already be established simply by its being a *cit* suffix (i.e., having a *c* marker). Similarly, while the phrase *apācca* is still in force, the mention of the word *adhvan* in the rule prescribing oxytoneness—*sphigapūtavīṇāñjodhvakukṣisīranāmanāma ca*—is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*). For if the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) prescribed by *upasargād adhvanaḥ* were obligatory, the desired form would already be established by that very rule.
