However, some maintain that the mention of *mūrdhan* without the suffix *samāsānta* (Pāṇini 5.4.115: *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrddhasu bahuvrīhau*) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this [rule]. For that [mention] is intended to provide an option regarding the final acute accent (*anta-udātta*) in cases such as *dvimūrdhā* and *trimūrdhā*. If the suffix *ṣ* prescribed by the rule *dvitribhyāṃ ṣa mūrdhnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.115) were mandatory, then a bahuvrīhi compound ending in *-ān*—such as *dvimūrdhan*—would be entirely non-existent; for *dvimūrdha* and similar forms would end in *-a*, since the *samāsānta* suffixes constitute part of the whole compound.

Furthermore, since it is established in the Bhāṣya that the status of being a *samāsānta* (compound-ending suffix) occurs by virtue of its being a constituent part of the end of the final member of a compound, it is indeed possible for the word *mūrdhan*, even when qualified by the suffix *ṣa*, to be included [by the rule]. Thus, one might argue that in *dvimūrdhaḥ* and *trimūrdhaḥ*, the suffix applies only optionally to the neuter *akārānta* (*mūrdha*) within the *bahuvrīhi*. However, this must be rejected because that position is merely a secondary view (*abhyuccaya-mātra*), and because the author of the Sūtras—having abandoned the form *mūrddheṣu*—undertook the more cumbersome formulation containing the *bahuvrīhi* as its core, which indicates his lack of approval for such a view.

It should not be argued that [the mention of *bahuvrīhi*] is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) because the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is necessary to exclude the *tatpuruṣa*—as in "he has two feet" (*dvipāt*) or "see the elephant with two tusks" (*dvidantaḥ*)—and thus the very formulation (*nyāsa*) using the word *mūrdhneṣu* would involve greater complexity. For, by virtue of the co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) with the word *mūrdhan* as qualified by a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), it is possible to understand that only the words *pād* and *dat*, when they are constituents of a *bahuvrīhi*, are intended; therefore, the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is not strictly necessary.

By this, the claim made in the *Kaustubha*—that the mention of *bahuvrīhi* in the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pāddan* (Pāṇini 5.4.138) is itself the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned paribhāṣā; otherwise, the rule would have been stated simply as *pāddanmūrddheṣu*; and furthermore, because the context concerns words that have already undergone the application of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), and that anything other than a *bahuvrīhi* will be excluded precisely by the absence of such a suffix—is refuted.

Even according to the alternative arrangement (*yathānyāsa*), since it has been stated that the aforementioned sūtra does not apply to forms ending in the suffix *ṣa*, the inclusion of the term "bahuvrīhi" must be accepted as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for that very fact; for it would otherwise be illogical to claim its status as an indicator by asserting a distinction between the subject matter (*lakṣya*) of the rule. To claim its status as an indicator while accepting such a distinction between subjects is contrary to traditional doctrine (*asāmpradāyika*).

Regarding the question of how the substitution of *d* for *t* occurs in the word *dvitaḥ* (from *dvi-tas*) in the phrase "paśya dvitaḥ," one might raise the objection that this is impossible because the rule *paddannomās-* does not admit of an extension (*tadantavidhi*) to include words ending in those stems. To this, it is stated there [in the commentary] that the desired result is achieved through two principles: first, by the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the rule concerning the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the suffix *ṣyaṅ*; and second, by the logic of the eighth-lecture (*aṣṭamika*) Bhāṣya and Vārttika which states, "But it is established because the part is not different [from the whole]. However, even that is to be reconsidered; for since the rules prescribe the substitutes *pad-* and so on for the preceding elements *pād-* and so on when followed by case-endings such as *śas*, the aforementioned objection and its resolution are irrelevant.

By this, even the prescription of the suffix *ṣa*—in place of the suffix *ṣac* prescribed by the rule "dvitribhyāṃ ṣa mūrdhnaḥ"—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For that [prescription of *ṣa*] serves the purpose of ensuring that the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*), which is obtainable through the capacity of the *cit* designation of *ṣac*, does not subvert the optional final acute accent prescribed by the rule "dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrdhasu"; this is possible only if there is some scope for the optionality [of the former rule], just as in the case of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound governed by the rule "bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā."

Furthermore, the possibility [of applying the rule] is obtained only on the basis of the non-constancy (*anityatva*) of the suffixes added at the end of compounds; thus, even the example "trimūrdhānaṃ saptaraśmiṃ gṛṇīṣe" is refuted.

In examples such as *dvimūrddha*, since it has been stated that the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.173] does not apply once the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) has been added, there is no possibility of suspecting that the oxytone accent (*antodāttatva*) obtained through the force of the *cit* designation would sublate that optional rule (*vikalpa*). Alternatively, even if one were to grant that the optional rule applies there, it still cannot serve as the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because the accent prescribed by the *cit* designation finds its application in cases falling under the preceding rule, "In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the second member is oxytone] after *sakthi* and *akṣi*" (Pāṇini 6.2.117)—as in *phalakasakthaḥ* and *viśālākṣaḥ*—and thus it cannot logically be considered a sublater of the optional rule.

Nor should it be argued that the *kit*-status of the suffix *ṣac* (in the rule *dvitribhyām*) is indeed purposeless; for [the *kit*-status] of the suffix from the preceding rule alone is what is carried over here. Otherwise, the statement in the Bhāṣya regarding the section on pratyāhāras—"the *kit*-status of the suffix *kap* in the rule *āta* [is not a *jñāpaka*] because the elision of the *at* which is a portion of the vowel *ā* does not occur"—would be untenable, since that status would already have its purpose fulfilled in the subsequent rule, *tundaśokayoḥ parimṛjāpanudoḥ*.

Nor should it be argued that the prescription of the suffix *ṣa* would thus be rendered useless; for it has been established that the aforementioned optional rule regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*) applies only in the case where there is no compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). Furthermore, even in the rule "dvitribhyām," since the final acute accent obtained by virtue of the *cit* designation in the prescription of the suffix *ṣa* would be without exception, forms such as *dvimūrdha* would result in that very accent. However, when the suffix *ṣa* is applied, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails; thus, they say, its utility is secured through this distinction.

In this regard, the following must be considered: the claim that the aforementioned option regarding the final acute accent applies only to the alternative where the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is absent is contrary to the authoritative grammatical treatises (*ākara*). For if the suffix *ṣac* were present here, there would necessarily be a final acute accent. However, the optional final acute accent prescribed by the rule "dvitribhyām" finds its scope of application precisely when, due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rule for compound-endings, the suffix *dvimūrdha* lacks such an ending. Thus, [the option] remains valid in that specific instance.

For it has been stated in the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on that point that when the suffix *ṣa* is present, even under the view that it is a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), there is optionally an udātta accent on the final syllable, while under the other view there is an udātta on the first syllable by the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), thus resulting in two possible accents; therefore, the aforementioned hypothesis is to be rejected precisely because it lacks a foundation. Furthermore, the fact that the mention of *mūrddhasu* serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for what was stated is clear from the Bhāṣya and other sources themselves.

For this very reason, the argument that the rule *mūrddhaṣu* (Pāṇini 5.4.115) indicates that the author of the Sūtras does not favor the view that the members [of a compound] following the first member (*uttarapada*) are themselves the basis for the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), is refuted. This is because even under the view that there is no compound-final suffix, the abandonment of such a placement [of the word *mūrddhaṣu*] is justified as being intended to trigger an optional application (*vikalpa*). For the same reason, the claim that the prescription of the suffix *ṣa* (in *mūrddhaṣu*) also shows that the Sūtrakāra does not favor that view is discarded; for even under the view that the compound-final suffix applies, that placement serves the purpose of triggering an option regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*).

As for what was also stated: although in the *bhāṣya* on the rule "samāsāntāḥ" the position that suffixes called *samāsānta* are themselves directly *samāsāntas* has been established—and although in examples such as *dvidhurī* and *tridhurī*, the position that the *samāsānta* suffix is applied after the final member (*uttarapada*) of the compound (in accordance with the *vārttika*: "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in *a* is used in the feminine") has been recorded—nevertheless, in the rule "samāsāntāḥ," there exists a reading of the *vārttika* as "from a *dvigu* ending in *a*," which lacks the word *uttarapada*.

Since forms such as *dvidhura* have already been established under the view that they are directly samāsānta suffixes, it is more appropriate to adopt the position that they are directly samāsānta suffixes—rather than relying on the view that samāsānta suffixes are parts of the final member (*uttarapada*) based solely on the word "final member" (*uttarapada*) found in the Vārttika—and thereby assume that the optional application of the final-acute accent (*antodātta*) does not occur in cases like *dvimūrdha* once the samāsānta suffix has been applied. In this way alone, according to the stated method, the purposefulness of both the formulation of the heavy rule (*guru-sūtra*) and the specific injunction (*vidhāna*) is maintained.

That too is incorrect; for even when the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied by resorting to that position, the great effort [of the commentators] is rendered meaningful precisely through the operation of the alternative analysis (*vikalpa*), as stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other works. Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa has stated that the view that "the compound-endings are the finals of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadāntāḥ samāsāntāḥ*) is also approved by the *Bhāṣya* regarding the rule *sarūpāṇām*. Moreover, in the rule *gostrīyoḥ*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* explicitly recorded that very position in order to refute the *Vārttika* which proposes a prohibition regarding the suffix *kap*.

Furthermore, by examining the commentary on the sūtra *dvitribhyāṃ pāddan*, it is quite clear that that particular position—and the example *dvimūrddha*—are not intended by the Bhāṣya. For instance, if there were a mention of a stem ending in *a*, there would be a need for an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding stems ending in *n*; conversely, if there were a mention of a stem ending in *n*, there would be a need for an addition regarding stems ending in *a*.

Regarding the second alternative, it has been stated that when the final member (*uttarapada*) is the locus of the operation, once the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) has been applied, the acute accent (*udātta*) prescribed for the final syllable of the *uttarapada* cannot apply to the suffix because it is not situated within a suffix (*pratyaya*). Consequently, when the *uttarapada* is acutely accented on its final syllable, the suffix becomes unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule of "remaining low tone" (*śeṣanighāta*). Then, upon the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*), the suffix receives the acute accent by the rule of "the accentuation of what remains after the removal of an acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). Nor should it be argued that the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*) occurs earlier—prior to the application of the acute accent on the final syllable of the *uttarapada*—on the grounds that it is a subsequent rule (*paratva*). For the application of the acute accent on the final syllable occurs prior to the application of the compound-final suffix, precisely because it is the subsequent rule in that specific context.

And at that time, since there is no possibility for the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel of the first member), the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not apply first on the grounds of being "obligatory" (*nitya*)—as it would apply regardless of whether [the *ṭi*-elision] has already occurred or not. This is because the same logic applies even to a word that is otherwise oxytone (*antodātta*). Nor should it be argued that once the compound-ending suffix has been applied, the oxytonic accent of the second member (*uttarapada*) would not obtain, because it is superseded by the *ṭi*-elision due to its higher status; for although the cause [for the accent] is destroyed by the elision, the compound-ending suffix itself is not destroyed by it. This is because it is accepted that a rule is not considered non-obligatory (*anitya*) merely when its cause is destroyed by another grammatical rule.

That too must be considered. Is it intended here that the position—that *samāsānta* suffixes apply to the end of the *uttarapada*—does not exist? Or is it that the aforementioned alternative does not apply in cases such as *dvimūrdha*? Not the first, because Kaiyaṭa himself has stated that this deliberation applies when the position is that the *samāsānta* suffix is applied after the compound has been formed; however, when the position is that the *samāsānta* suffix is applied from the *uttarapada* which conveys the meaning of the compound, then no such deliberation exists at all. Nor the second, for Kaiyaṭa has explained [the rule] immediately following that very point:

If the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) were obligatory, then it would have been explicitly stated—either to exclude ambiguity regarding the specific grammatical operation (*kāryi*) or to maintain consistency with the introductory rule. However, because it is not so stated, the non-obligatory nature of the compound-final suffix is indicated. In that regard, when the compound-final suffix is absent, there is no distinction whether the entire compound or the final member (*uttarapada*) is the locus of the grammatical operation. But when the compound-final suffix is applied, if the entire compound is the locus of the operation, then the accentuation applies to the compound-final suffix itself.

Even when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is the element undergoing the grammatical operation, then, since the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) applies by virtue of its being the subsequent rule, the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is added. In that case, even if the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the desired result is established by the accent of the disappearance of an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*). Now, one might object: "The accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) ought to apply to the compound-final suffix. This is not so; for that [suffix-accent] is superseded by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. And this [accentuation of the *bahuvrīhi*] is also superseded by the present rule. By this [rule], the status of being an optional example is also secured for cases such as *dvirmūrdha*.
For this very reason, the hypothesis that in the case of the suffix *ṣa*, there is only the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) is also refuted.

As for what was also stated—that although the heavy designation (*gurunirdeśa*) in the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *mūrdhan*" may somehow be meaningful by relying on the aforementioned position, the prescription of the suffix *ṣa* is impossible therein—this is because the suffix *ṣac*, which is already fulfilled in its purpose within the scope of the preceding rule by yielding an oxytone accent through the power of its own *cittva* (as in *dvimūrdha*), can be sublated in cases such as *dvimūrdha* by the subsequent optional rule regarding oxytonicity.

Furthermore, there is no determining factor to suggest that the acute accent on the final syllable (*āntodāttatva*) conditioned by *cittva* subverts only the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) and not the aforementioned alternative; for its establishment follows the maxim stated in the Bhāṣya—"A higher stage (*kakṣā*) must be measured against a lower stage"—the meaning of which is that what is obtained at a later stage subverts what was obtained at an earlier stage. For this very reason, when *yaṇ*-substitution and *guṇa*-substitution are both applicable in the first stage, the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel lengthening) applies; and this is further subverted by the *pararūpa* (single-substitute rule) applicable in the third stage, as prescribed by the rule "ato guṇe."

In the present case as well, there are two subverting factors (*bādhaka*) located in the third stage: first, in the initial stage, the rule "of a compound" (*samāsasya*) [prescribes] an udātta accent on the final syllable; second, in the second stage, the rule for the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), which possesses an udātta on the final syllable by virtue of the force of the term *cita* in the rule for *ṣat*, along with the aforementioned optional alternative. Among these, according to the principle of conflict between exceptions (*apavāda-vipratiṣedha*), because the subsequent rule prevails, only the optional alternative for the final-udātta will occur; thus, the matter is established by the very rule concerning *ṣat* under discussion.

That too must be considered. For if the rule (*ṣac*) were prescribed and it were mandatory (*nitya*), there could be no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because there would be no scope for an alternative (*vikalpa*) once the subject matter is excluded from the *citsvara*. If it is argued that the alternative finds its scope in the case where the compound suffix (*samāsānta*) is absent, that is untenable; for there is no evidence that the alternative pertains specifically to the case of the presence of the compound suffix, and thus, due to a lack of common subject matter, such a conflict is impossible. Furthermore, a mandatory rule cannot apply to a domain governed by an optional rule.

And thus, since the option is established precisely because [the other rule] has no scope (*niravakāśatvāt*), the prescription of the suffix *ṣa* implies that the option does have scope; by being the motivator (*prayojaka*) of that, it indicates that the rule for compound endings (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not mandatory (*anityatva*). This is the general direction. Now, one might object: "But in this case, there is no possibility of the substitution of *ku*-hood (*kutva*) at all, because only worldly and Vedic words are to be derived. To this, they say:

Because a word possessing multiple powers is applied to its designated object by delimiting those powers, and because all designations are eternal and worldly, there is an application of the rule from the Śāstra—whether the word *ādaic* is an imitative word (*anukaraṇaśabda*) or a generic class-word (*jātiśabda*).

The connection is that because the word *ādi* is worldly (*laukika*), its application according to the technical treatise (*śāstra*) exists. In this regard, "because of its eternality" is the reason; for the word *ādi* possesses a conventional power (*sāṅketika-śakti*) with respect to both vowels beginning with *ā* and those distinct from them. [Objection: But if this were so, the formulation of the technical name would be redundant. Therefore, it is said: "by means of the delimitation of power. And that contraction of power consists in being the qualificandum of a specific intention whose mode is the capacity to convey a specific individual, namely: "May this word convey this meaning. This is what is meant.

Because [the word] is applied to the cognition—which serves as the qualifier by way of the relation of being the qualificandum—when the desire to speak regarding the named object has been expressed; and because it is established that [the word] generates a verbal cognition having that [cognition] as its object through the cooperation of the knowledge of the aforementioned convention. And it has been said:
"The restriction of a name to a named object is for the sake of linguistic usage in certain cases;
however, the relation is indeed eternal, as in the case of 'Dittha' and so forth, just like 'cow' and so forth."
Furthermore, in this treatise, the relationship between [the terms] such as *vṛddhi* and so forth is innate, characterized by the delimitation of their expressive power,
just like that between a qualifier and a qualified.

Thus, in this treatise, the meaning is that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for the purpose of establishing the rule that only *a*, *ai*, and *au* are to be understood by the term "vṛddhi. He establishes this through the word "due to its eternality" (*nityatvāt*), explaining: "because it possesses multiple powers" (*anekaśakteḥ*). This means that it has multiple powers with respect to many [objects], being capable of conveying any particular individual (*vyakti*) that is the object of the speaker’s intention, without depending on any specific ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) residing in the meaning. Nor does the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) apply here, as in the rule "not for that which has *ka* as its penultimate letter" (*na kopadhāyāḥ*).

This is because the inclusion of the term *taddhita* will be stated there [in the following rule]. As for the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇavākya*), "that which has a power (*śakti*) whose object (*viṣaya*) is manifold," its intended meaning is that "object-ness" (*viṣayatva*) is the sense of the locative case. According to the first view, there is only one power (*śakti*) despite the difference in delimiters (*avacchedaka*), because the difference based on limiting conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*) results merely in the difference of those conditions. According to the second view, there is a plurality of powers (*śakti*). [Objection: But how can this be so, given that it is established in the *Vārttika* on the *ṛlṛk* sūtra that "there are no arbitrary words" (*yadṛcchā-śabda*)?

Therefore, it is said: "because it is a word denoting a universal" (*jātiśabdatvāt*). Now, if one intends to express the non-difference between the original (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*), then since no case-ending (*sup*) would be produced, there would be no *pada*-status; consequently, the substitution of *ku* (for *t*) would not apply. On the other hand, if one intends to express their difference, then since the word *ai*—which is employed in another location—is what is perceived here, the vowels *ā* and so on would not be included [in the imitation], and thus it would be impossible for them to function as the designatum (*saṃjñin*). To this, the answer is: because it is a word denoting a universal. Since the cognition of "being *ai*" (*aic-tva*) follows through the two individual instances of the vowel *ai*, this is a specific general property (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) that pervades the two respective universals residing in the individual instances of *ai* and *au*.

[The opponent argues: "Even if this [universal] is accepted, there is no subverting argument (bādhaka), just as in the case of substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth. [Response: That is not correct. Because it would result in a confusion (sāṅkarya) with specific universals that serve as the inferential grounds for [properties] such as "belonging to Devadatta. Furthermore, the claim that "there is no such fault regarding universals residing in qualities" is baseless. Moreover, the inclusive cognition [of a universal] does not have an objective referent beyond the adjunct of a technical name (saṃjñā) prescribed by the rule *ādirantyena* [Pāṇini 1.1.71]. As for the view in the Siddhānta that a universal is simply "existence" (sattā) as qualified by a particular individual, let that be the case here as well. And the particular individuals are those whose own essential existence (svarūpasattā) is rendered inclusive through non-difference from that [existence].

"All words are established in that [universal] as its substratum," according to the statement of Hari; this too is exactly so. For even in his view, one must follow the arguments that refute [the existence of] universals (*jāti*), and because a conceptualizer (*kalpaka*) must be postulated. Indeed, this is not the exclusive family tradition of the logicians (*tārkika*), as it is accepted by the Buddhists (*saugata*) as well. As it has been stated in the *Kusumāñjali*:

For two universals, or for two exclusions (*tadvyāvṛtti*) that are co-inherent, there exists only a relationship of higher and lower [universality]. Nor should it be argued that, on the view which accepts the plurality of inferential universals, there is no possibility of confusion (*saṅkara*); because even so, there is no evidence for postulating additional universals beyond those already established. Therefore, the status of being a "universal-word" (*jātiśabda*) is based solely upon universals such as *ai*-ness (*aitva*) residing in the objects to be denoted. This is precisely the intended meaning of the *Vivaraṇa* when it states, "the universal *ai*-ness and so forth exists."

Even in the word *kutva*, since the word *ku* is conventionally assigned (saṃketita) to any phoneme belonging to that [velar] class (*tadvargīya*), the denotatum (*vācya*) of the cognition of its being subsequent to that [word *ku*] is the pentad of universals (*jāti*) such as *katva* and so forth; for the qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha-prakāra*) is the meaning of the suffix *tva*.

And so, in the present case, when *katva* (the property of being *ka*) is presented as having the form of "being inherent in all *ka*s while not being inherent in anything other than *ka*," it is impossible to impose the universal *katva* upon the letter *ca* due to the force of a contradiction (*bādha*). Since the imposition must ultimately conclude by way of its own substratum (the individual *ka*), the meaning of the Bhāṣya is: why does the substitution of *ka* for *ca* not occur? This should be understood everywhere in this manner. It might be argued: "In verbal cognition, it is universally established that what is mentioned first is the subject (*uddeśya*) and what is mentioned later is the predicate (*vidheya*).
The characteristics of the subject are its connection with the relative pronoun *yat*, its being mentioned first, and so forth."
The connection with that word [tac-], its posteriority, its being the probandum, and its status as the predicate (vidheya).

Thus says the statement of the learned (Abhiyukta). If it is asked, "How then is the designation *vṛddhi* prescribed here by means of the mention of *ā*, *ai*, and *au*?"—it is replied: because the word *ādaic* is not employed in the *pradeśas* (rules of application), its meaning is already established; whereas, due to the opposite nature of the word *vṛddhi*, it is impossible for it to be the subject of the rule (*uddeśya*). Therefore, once it is determined that *vṛddhi* alone is the name (*saṃjñā*), the prescription of the name *vṛddhi* is effected by assuming a reversed order [of the letters]. Nor does this result in a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) on the grounds of its being human-made (*pauruṣeya*).

Because being the intended object of the treatise (*śāstra*) alone is the determinant of that [validity]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that sentences such as "he takes up the horse's halter" (*aśvābhidhānīm ādatte*) would not possess validity in their exclusion of the donkey's halter and so forth. Furthermore, in rules such as "after *ḍ*, before *si*, there is *dhuṭ*" (*ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*), when both [the ablative and locative] are mentioned, the ablative mention is stronger; thus, there would follow the same undesirable consequence for the status of the genitive ending [in *dhuṭaḥ*] when it is construed with the word *si* (which ends in the locative). And finally, the word *vṛddhi* is placed first here for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).

Nor should it be asked, "For what purpose [is this]? since the teacher, by virtue of being devoid of the latent impressions of false knowledge, is entirely free from general demerit (*durita*), and thus lacks even the possibility of doubt regarding obstacles that are its particular instances.

Nevertheless, out of supreme compassion and on the grounds that [the author] is the sole authority for all perfected sages (*siddhas*) and refined scholars (*śiṣṭas*), he establishes—by means of inference—the necessity of performing auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) at the commencement of the desired actions of his disciples. This is achieved through the power of his own scholarship, rooted in the successful completion of his own work, which serves as the basis for the incidental attainment of auspiciousness for those very disciples. Furthermore, according to the previously mentioned method, this is for the sake of the sacrificer’s attainment of numerous visible and invisible fruits produced by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) during their eligibility for various rituals, as well as for those performed without desire (*niṣkāma*).
For it is possible that those very same actions lead to the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*), the supreme human goal, by means of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

As for the position that "the restriction is for the sake of linguistic usage," and that in this treatise the vowels *a*, *ai*, and *au* alone are to be understood by the term *vṛddhi*—taking the literal sense as correct—that is not so. Because even in a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the requirement of the same sequential order (*sāmānānupūrvīkatva*) as the original injunction (*vidhi*) is necessary. The distinction there lies merely in the fact that, since the meaning is already established, the intention is the exclusion of anything other than that. Otherwise, in rules such as "adeṅguṇaḥ," one would have to assume a reversed sequence.
Even in cases such as *vrīhīnavahanti* ("one threshes rice"), threshing is enjoined precisely with reference to the rice (*vrīhi*).

Furthermore, even under the view that "these technical names (*saṃjñās*) are created according to one's own will," by resorting to the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) theory, the meaning is that "the *vṛddhi* [substitutes] *ā*, *ai*, and *au* take the place of *mṛj*"—thus, the literal reading itself is correct. In that context, the use of the *t*-marker (*taparatva*) is indeed unnecessary, because since the substitute is being prescribed (*bhāvyamāna*), there is no possibility of its including homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrāhakatva*).

Just as the words *jyotiṣṭoma*, *rājasūya*, and so forth are understood to be names because they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) specifically with the injunction of a sacrifice—and not through another sentence—so too is it in this view regarding the words *vṛddhi* and the rest. The rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (P. 1.1.1), however, serves merely to present the word-forms, just like the rule "iko guṇavṛddhī" (P. 1.1.3). Its designation as a "definition-sūtra" (*saṃjñāsūtra*) is based on the fact that what is presented [by the former] is the name-bearer (*saṃjñin*). Nor should it be argued that in cases of restatement (*anuvāda*), such as "vṛddhir yasyācām" (P. 1.1.73), the letters *ā*, *ai*, and *au* would then include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*).

Because there is no such object to be characterized; because it would entail the postulation of multiple powers; and because, since injunctive sentences are primary, one must accept the meaning determined therein for other instances as well, and so forth.

That too must be considered. For otherwise, there would be the contingency of three substitutes in place of the vowel *ṛ*, and thus the purpose of the rule would not be fulfilled. It is for this very reason that Kaiyaṭa states: "Because they are yet to be produced (*bhāvyamānatvāt*), the diphthongs (*ai* and *au*) will not be perceivers [of the substitution]; this is not so, for here in the formulation of the technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), the diphthongs are not being produced. The author of the *Vivaraṇa* says: "The objection is based on the view that the rule applies at the time of its operation (*kāryakāla-pakṣa*), while the resolution is based on the view that it applies according to its original enunciation (*yathoddeśa-pakṣa*). Therefore, in this case, only the *yathoddeśa* view should be accepted.

In this regard, the following should be noted: the word *vṛddhi* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote that which is expressed by the word *vṛddhi*. Nor is there an initial non-apprehension of that [meaning], because when one has the knowledge that the word *vṛddhi* denotes some object, there is a general apprehension of it in the form "there exists some object denoted by the word *vṛddhi*. Its relation is identity (*abheda*). Thus, the cognition is: "The *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are non-different from that which is denoted by the word *vṛddhi*. Consequently, in this cognition, that in which denotability (*vācyatva*) is the qualifier is the named entity (*saṃjñin*).

That which is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the denotable object (*vācya*) is the name (*saṃjñā*). This same principle applies even in cases such as "Indra," "Marutvān," and "Maghavān. For the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) of a single word necessarily requires this alternative method; otherwise, one who lacks the knowledge of the power residing merely in its synonyms would not grasp that power even from sources such as a lexicon (*kośa*).

As for the claim that *ā* and the other vowels are qualifiers (*viśeṣya*) in relation to *vṛddhi* through a relation of non-difference (*abheda-saṃsarga*), that is not correct. For what is the meaning of the phrase "in relation to *vṛddhi*"? Does it mean "in relation to the word *vṛddhi*" or "in relation to the referent of the word *vṛddhi*"? It cannot be the first, because that would not be obtained without resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, this contradicts the subsequent passage which states that the explanation is possible even without metaphorical indication.

It should not be argued that since nothing exists that is denotable by the word *vṛddhi*, the word is obtained through its presence as a qualifier in the cognition [of the rule], and thus there is no need for *lakṣaṇā* (indication); for that [indication] is necessary for its independent presentation. Even granting this, we say: if the word *vṛddhi* functions as a qualifier and non-difference (*abheda*) is the relation (*saṃsarga*), the resulting cognition would be "the *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are non-different from the word *vṛddhi*. But this is not an acceptable conclusion, because it is logically untenable (*ayogyatva*). Nor can denotability (*vācyatva*) be the relation.

Because a difference-relation (*bhedānvaya*) is impossible between two things presented by words that have the same case-role (*samavibhaktika*), for this very reason the second [alternative] is not tenable. Nor should it be argued that since the state of being denotable by the word *vṛddhi* is also present through the aforementioned manner of presentation, let that alone be the qualifier in a relation of non-difference; for that too has become a qualifier with respect to a specific object.

In reality, even according to the Grammarians (Śābdika), since it is admitted that the *pada* itself possesses the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) and since denotability (*vācyatva*) functions as a relation (*saṃsarga*), the cognition produced by the word "vṛddhi" based on the apprehension of its general denotative power (*sāmānya-śakti-graha*) has denotability as its very relation. Consequently, when there is a presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the word "vṛddhi," how can words such as "ākāra" be construed with denotability—which has attained the status of a relation? This is because denotability is not an object of the presentation produced by the word. Otherwise, one could even say, "The mountain possesses fire; [it is] a quality," because a non-difference relation (*abheda-anvaya*) would be possible for "quality" with respect to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) when the latter has attained the status of a relation.

If it is argued that the intention of the aforementioned text is that the term *vṛddhi* denotes *ā*, *ai*, and *au* because its denotative capacity is manifold according to the maxim "the existence of multiple capacities [is accepted]," and therefore—just as in the case of "the pot is blue"—the meaning of that [term] itself connects with *ā* and *ai* through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), we say: not so. For if that were the case, there would be a lack of syntactic expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) due to the resulting identity between the delimiting factor of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), making the sentence like "the pot is a pot. It is for this very reason that it was stated in the *Upāyādi* and other works that in sentences such as "space is the substratum of sound," the word "space" refers to what is denoted by that [word "space"], since such a sentence would be useless for one who is already proficient in the linguistic convention.

As for what was also stated—that having raised the objection regarding the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication of possessiveness) under the view that [the word] is an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), it was established that terms such as *udbhid* are names (*nāmadheya*) because even if they were names, the indirect indication would be equally present—that too is weak. For, in the case of the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), since the aspect of the quality and its associated gender, number, and grammatical relation (*kāraka*) are not known through any other means of knowledge, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to postulate separate injunctions for those qualifiers in order to establish them. This necessitates the assumption of *matvarthalakṣaṇā*. However, in the case of a name, since the meaning is already known from usage, no such further injunction is required. Thus, the two cases are not equal. Therefore, the objection is refuted.

However, since a name that has merely presented itself to the ear lacks the status of being the meaning of a name, it cannot be connected with the root-meaning—the sacrifice—by way of the relation of denotability; thus, in this view, there is no room for the doubt regarding the postulation of an injunction in that respect.

Even in the view that [the word] is a name (*nāman*), although the word *udbhid* would have to be accepted as denoting the meaning of the third case-ending, and even if one were to postulate its connection with the sacrifice which is the meaning of the verbal root, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) because it lacks the capacity to necessitate a separate injunction for a qualifier. Otherwise, in your own position, even in cases such as "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), the status of being a name would be established without any figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), simply by avoiding the indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). Consequently, words such as "soma" would also be nothing but names, resulting in the total destruction of the category of injunctions regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*). Enough of this prolixity.

The delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka) for the knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word *vṛddhi* is the state of being a cognition whose qualifier is either of those respective properties residing in this triad [of meanings]. It is not, however, the state of being a cognition whose qualifier is one of those [properties] while not residing in that which lacks the qualifier of either of them—just as, in the case of the word *puṣpavant*, it is the state of being a cognition whose qualifier is "moon-ness" while not residing in that which lacks the qualifier of "sun-ness. Regarding that:
"By a single expression, the two Puṣpavants—the maker of day and the maker of night [are denoted]."

Thus, because [the required condition] exists in the case of the *pramāṇa* (measure) and because it is absent here; on the contrary, in rules such as *vṛddhireci*, since only one element (*ekaḥ*)—namely, that which follows from *pūrvaparayoḥ*—is understood to be the object of prescription, and because of [the rule] *vṛddhiryasyācāmādiḥ*. Indeed, those three aforementioned vowels do not occur at the beginning of any word without being separated [by others]. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the rule *mālādīnāṃ ca*. Otherwise, since they would not be "non-vṛddha," the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) would be established by the preceding rule alone. The same applies to subsequent cases as well.

This very principle is expressed as "the completion of the sentence with each [word] individually. However, where the authority for the operation resides in the capacity of the entire collection—as in the rule "both [are called *abhyasta*]"—there the denotation does not belong to the individual parts alone. Rather, the delimitor of the status of being the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is simply the state of being a cognition that does not have a single phoneme as its object, while having as its object another phoneme that does not occur in isolation. For this very reason, the term "both" (*ubhe*) is employed there; otherwise, by virtue of the general rule, the designation would undesirably apply to both [phonemes] even when they are mutually independent.

Therefore, it is established that the completion of the sentence (*vākya-parisamāpti*) occurs only when there exists another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Let us return to the subject at hand. Now, is the designation *vṛddhi* applied to the forms of *āT*, *aiC*, and so on by their own nature, or only to those [sounds] prescribed by the word *vṛddhi* through one of the methods such as *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*? It cannot be the first alternative; for in examples such as *sarvabhāsaḥ*, the rule "when the final syllable of the second member is *vṛddhi*, *sarva-* [is also acute]" would result in the acute accent on the end of the first member, thereby preventing the desired acute accent on the end of the compound.

Furthermore, in cases such as *tāvatī bhāryā asya* ("his wife is so-many") or *tāvadbhāryaḥ*, there would result the undesired prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "and [the feminine suffix is not replaced] when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) occasioning *vṛddhi* follows. This is because the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the pronoun (by the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*) would serve as the occasioning cause for the suffix *-vat*. Nor is the second alternative [correct], because in forms such as *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*, the suffix *-cha* prescribed by the rule "from a word with *vṛddhi* in the first syllable" (*vṛddhāt*) would be unestablished. Moreover, in forms such as *āmramayam* and *śālamayam*, the suffix *-mayaṭ* prescribed by the rule "the suffix *-mayaṭ* always [occurs] after words with *vṛddhi* and after *śara*, etc. (*nityaṃ vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ*) would be untenable.

Furthermore, in the case of *āmraguptāyaniḥ* and *śālaguptāyaniḥ*, the suffix *phiñ*—which is conditioned by the term *vṛddha* according to the rule "udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt"—would not apply. Even though the desired form could be established by the suffix *phin* according to the rule "prācāmavṛddhāt phin bahulam," there would be no difference in accentuation under the rule "ñnityādirnityam. Moreover, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in the compound *āmraguptāyanībhārya* by the previously mentioned sūtra is not strictly necessary; for the form is also established by the rule "jāteśca," since [the name] is a "jāti" (generic class) as defined by the technical rule "gotraṃ ca caraṇaiḥ saha."

Regarding the students of Āmraguptāyana, when the suffix *cha* is intended after a word ending in *vṛddhi*, there is an option for elision (*luk*) by the rule "phak-phiñor anyatarasyām. Consequently, the two forms *āmraguptīyāḥ* and *āmraguptāyanīyāḥ* would result; however, even in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), this dual formality is not desired. This is because the term *yūni* (referring to a youth) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule "phak-phiñoḥ."

From the word *Yāska*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ* (as in *Śivādibhyaḥ*), the suffix *phiñ* is applied by the rule *aṇo dvyacaḥ*. Thus, the descendant of Yāska in the younger generation is *Yāskāyaniḥ*; his students are *Yāskīyāḥ* or *Yāskāyanīyāḥ*, as that is how it is illustrated there. Consequently, there is no distinction regarding the suffix *phiñ*. Nevertheless, this would result in a violation of the natural consistency (*svārasya*) of the sūtra, which contains the qualification of specific teachers: *prācām udīcām*.

Furthermore, since the *Bhāṣya* states that when an alternative solution is provided for the sūtra *ṛto bhāradvājasya*, "this Bhāradvāja would be made to deviate from his own view," deviation from one's own view is also considered a fault.

Furthermore, in the case of the *phiñ* suffix, regarding the sense "the contemptible offspring of Āmraguptāyani," if the *cha* and *ṭhak* suffixes—prescribed by the rule *pheścha ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.148) in the sense of "offspring from a *sauvīra* gotra when contempt is implied"—were not to apply, the two forms *āmraguptāyanīyaḥ* and *āmraguptāyanikaḥ* would not exist; for under the governing heading *vṛddhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.147), only the *phiñ* suffix is specifically mentioned therein. [As it is said:
"Yamunda, Suṣāman, and Vārṣyāyaṇi are recorded as having the *phiñ* suffix."

This is because such an enumeration is of human origin; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the writing of the text "taikāyaniḥ" as a counter-example for the *sauvīra* gotra and *tapada* suffix. Furthermore, among the three mentioned [in that context], the word "taikāyani" is not included therein.

Furthermore, consider the descendant of Āmraguptāyani, a youth. According to the rule *prāg dīvyato’ṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañito yūni lugaṇiñoḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of both *aṇ* and *iñ* when forming the junior descendant. Consequently, the father would be called Āmraguptāyani and the son would also be called Āmraguptāyani—this dual form would not be possible through the suffix *phin*. This is because, due to the absence of the marker *ñit*, the aforementioned elision (*luk*) does not apply. Moreover, since the extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the suffix for the junior descendant applies only to non-Brāhmaṇa lineages (*gotra*), it does not operate within a Brāhmaṇa lineage. Thus, on this view, the rule *mālādīnāṃ ca* would be rendered useless.

Since the term "not increased" (*avṛddha*) would suffice [to exclude the case of *vṛddhi*], even if one resorts to the methods of *tantra* (simultaneous application) and so forth regarding the word *vṛddhi*, there is still prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, to avoid mutual dependence—where the designation (*saṃjñā*) is established by the rule and the rule is established by the designated—the designation must be understood as "future" (*bhāvin*), like the expression "the cloth made of thread" (*sūtra-śāṭaka*); yet even in this case, there is prolixity. To this, it is replied:

The designation *vṛddhi* applies without distinction to the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*. This is because the aforementioned defects do not apply here; for in the rule "sarvaṃ ca [in the case of] the *vṛddhi* of the second member" (*Pāṇini 7.3.20*), only that *vṛddhi* which is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the second member" (*uttarapada*) is to be understood. Consequently, there is no defect in forms such as *sarvabhāsa*. Otherwise, in examples such as *sarvaḥ kārakaḥ* (i.e., *sarvakārakaḥ*), since the second member would possess that *vṛddhi* which is enjoined by the term *vṛddhi*, the aforementioned accentuation would result. Furthermore, the very mention of "the second member" (*uttarapada*) serves as the indicator (*liṅga*) that the *vṛddhi* to be understood is specifically that which is prescribed under that governing heading.

Otherwise, since the mere vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* would lack the status of being a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*), it would follow that the rule is redundant once a subsequent member containing a *vṛddhi*-vowel is obtained through the very force of the context. Therefore, its application occurs only in cases such as *sarvapāñcāla*, where there is a *vṛddhi* vowel [by the rule] "after *su*, *sarva*, and *ardha*, the [first vowel] of a country name [is *vṛddhi*]. Thus, there is no over-extension even to the case of *tāvadbhārya*.

Since there is no possibility of non-differentiation (abhedānvaya) due to the absence of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) whose nature is "vṛddhi," even if the meaning "the cause of *vṛddhi*" were obtained through the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) "vṛddhes taddhitaḥ" by the mere expression "vṛddhitaddhitasya," one must nevertheless resort to a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) bahuvrīhi—"that in which the cause of *vṛddhi* exists"—by virtue of the force of employing the word "nimitta. Thus, in the case of secondary derivatives such as *aṇ*, *añ*, and *phak*, where the cause of *vṛddhi* exists in relation to the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) consisting of the letters *ñ*, *ṇ*, *k*, *k*, and *r*, it is precisely that secondary derivative which [is intended].

In that regard, because of the interpretation that there is a prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment), and because even though the vowel *ā* is prescribed in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*), the suffix *vatup* lacks the stated cause for *vṛddhi*.

Nor should it be argued that, in the case of the word *arśasā* in the expression *na cārśasā bhāryā asya*, because the feminine suffix *ṭāp* follows the possessive suffix *matUP*, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for both the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) and the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is treated as the beginning of the subsequent element; and since it is thus included by the mention of "secondary suffix" (*taddhita*), a secondary suffix consisting of a vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*) is indeed possible there—therefore, how can the force of employing the word "cause" (*nimitta*) be effective? Even so, due to the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not colored" (*arakta*), the suspicion of a *karmadhāraya* compound is untenable.
This is because a suffix meaning "coloring" or "modification" (*vikāra*) does not consist of a vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*), and thus there is no possibility of its application in that context.

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of the rule is: "that which is the cause of the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the word *vṛddhi*. This is because the word *vṛddhi* is used as a technical term (*tantra*) and so forth. And such a *vṛddhi* is every *vṛddhi* whatsoever caused by a suffix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*. Nor should it be argued that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *vaiyākaraṇabhāryaḥ* ("the wife of a grammarian") or *sauvaśvabhāryaḥ* ("the wife of a descendant of Suvaśva"), because the *aṇ* [in these cases] is not the cause of the aforementioned *vṛddhi*. For the meaning of the word "cause" (*nimitta*) here is "being the basis for the application of the result," and in those cases, *vṛddhi* is prohibited by the rule "na yvābhyām" (Pāṇini 1.1.3).

They say that even here, there is no contribution toward the result (*phalopadhāna*) by taking [the *aij* vowels] as a single unit (*eka*), because those two are prescribed in their own forms (*svarūpeṇa*).

Others, however, maintain that a *taddhita* suffix which possesses some result while being capable of generating *vṛddhi* must be intended by the term "cause" (*nimitta*). In cases such as *vaiyākaraṇabhārya*, however, there is no contribution toward the result for the *aṇ* suffix by means of the *aij* vowels; for there is no evidence that those two—being taught in conjunction with the prohibition of *vṛddhi*—are caused by the *aṇ* suffix. Furthermore, even if they were caused by the *vṛddhi* that is the counter-positive of the prohibition, the *aṇ* suffix cannot serve as the cause for the introduction of the *aij* augment. This is what they say.

Both of these [definitions] must be examined. For "fitness" (*yogyatva*) is simply the possession of a form that delimits fitness (*yogyatāvacchedaka-rūpa*). And in this context, since it is cognizable solely through the treatise (*śāstra*), that form consists precisely in the properties of *ñit*, *ṇit*, and *kit*. The actual production of the result (*phalopadhāna*) must also be stated in that very same form, because there is a rule that the apprehension of fitness is necessarily determined by a property that does not admit of any other way of being established (*anyathāsiddhi*) residing in that which is qualified by the result. Under such circumstances, how could there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of the term *vaiyākaraṇabhārya*?

Because the suffix *aṇ* is *ṇit*, it brings about the result of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in another base (*prakṛti*). Nor should it be argued that what is intended is the presence of that result in whatever specific instance of *aṇ* etc. is employed after a particular base; for this would lead to the consequence that the capacity to produce *vṛddhi* in all instances would be impossible to ascertain.

For, when one intends to express the contribution toward the result (*phalopadhāna*) by means of that specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*)—prioritizing its own base (*svaprakṛti*)—in the case of the manifestation of suffixes such as *iñ* in [words like] *dākṣi*, it is impossible to apprehend the suitability of that very form (*tatsvarūpa-yogyatva*) in the *vṛddhi* contained within words such as *aupagava*. This is because bases other than those ending in *-a* lack the status of being its base (*tatprakṛtitva*). Furthermore, it is impossible to assert that there is suitability through one property while the contribution toward the result occurs through another property. For this very reason, the referent portion (*viśeṣya-bhāga*) would be redundant.

In some cases, because there is an absence of even the capacity for the result to be produced, that [result] would not occur; and thus, in certain instances, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply. This is because among the three suffixes beginning with *ñit*, there is no rule requiring that they all necessarily have the same base (*prakṛti*). For this very reason, the previously mentioned view—that [the suffix] is the cause of the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the word "vṛddhi"—is also refuted, since the capacity for the production of the result is necessarily delimited by a property that qualifies it, and thus the aforementioned fault arises in that case as well.

Therefore, the essential point here is this: the state of being a cause for *vṛddhi* consists in being capable of undergoing *vṛddhi*, provided that it is not of a nature where *vṛddhi* is already prohibited. By means of the qualified portion (*viśeṣya*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to [the word] *bhāryā*; and by means of the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no over-extension to [the compound] *vaiyākaraṇabhāryā*. Furthermore, in accordance with this qualifying aspect, this definition applies generally to all such secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) following a specific base; such is the direction of the argument.

This also should be noted here: according to the view that "the individual form (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning and the qualities (*guṇa*) are the differentiators," the utterance of a [phoneme] qualified by certain qualities serves as the name for those possessing other qualities. Now, this [use of] *tapara* (a letter followed by *t*) is for the sake of naming even those joined with other qualities; this is the opinion of the Vārttika. In this view, the rule *taparaḥ* (P. 1.1.70) has the purpose of an extended injunction (*atideśavidhi*), because it causes the inclusion of even non-*aṇ* vowels.

For in the Veda, when an acute accent (*udātta*) is to be applied, the observation of faults—both seen and unseen—is found in the utterance of an acute instead of an unaccented one (*anudātta*); thus, the qualities necessarily function as differentiators.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated: "This one self called 'water' becomes different due to the difference in its qualities; this [quality] is cold, and this [other quality] is hot. In that context, oneness is not intended with reference to the universal (jāti) of water-ness (*jalatva*), because if difference could be established simply from the difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), it would be illogical to cite the difference caused by the difference in qualities as an example. For when it is said, "the pot is different," what is understood is a difference whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is another specific pot.

Kaiyaṭa explains that the meaning is this: although [the substance] is one, because it resides in a single vessel, there is a linguistic usage of distinction (*bhedavyavahāra*) due to the connection with different qualities (*guṇa*) delimited by their respective adjuncts (*upādhi*).

In some cases, however, these qualities do not cause distinction; for instance, when a theft is committed while one is bald, even during the state of having matted hair (*kuntalita*), the linguistic usage "this man is a thief" persists. Regarding what is logical within this grammatical system, the author of the Bhāṣya states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Qualities are indeed non-distinctive."

For this very reason, the rule *anaṅ udāttaḥ* and others are consistent. Since it is impossible to pronounce that which is devoid of its phonetic qualities (*guṇa*), even though a quality is pronounced as an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*), it is not intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*) without a specific effort. Otherwise, one would simply pronounce the acute accent (*udātta*) itself; thus, some maintain that the meaning of the particle *eva* in the sūtra is that one should not have included the mention of "acute" (*udāttagrahaṇa*).

Others, however, maintain that the recitation of the Sūtra is in a single tone (*ekaśruti*). Furthermore, a quality (*guṇa*), even if it exists in its mere essential form (*svarūpa-mātra*) when not adopted as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), does not effect differentiation. There is no dispute that such a quality serves as a delimiting factor only in cases such as "one buys with a red [cow]" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*), and not when merely stated as "one should give a cow" (*gāṃ dadyāt*).

Furthermore, regarding the particle *eva* in the Bhāṣya, its intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies in the remainder of the statement: "But one should not make the mention of the acute accent (*udātta-grahaṇa*) after pronouncing [the word] with a single [monotonic] intonation. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "One should not make the mention of the acute accent for the sake of clarity. Moreover, since the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* would apply to the substitute *vadhi* by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like its original) due to being unaccented, the author would have prescribed the acute accent for the substitute *vadhyādeśa*. This is because it would otherwise contradict the Bhāṣya’s remark that "the mention of 'single-vowel' (*ekāj*) in the rule *ekāca upadeśe* need not be made," and it would also contradict the Bhāṣya’s statement that "the initial acute accent will be prescribed for *catasṛ*."

By this, Kaiyaṭa’s hypothesis—that because of the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*, the accent that would otherwise apply to the substitute should have been pronounced instead, and that the actual pronunciation of the acute (udātta) is for the sake of specific intention (*vivakṣā*) due to the greater effort required—is refuted. This is because, whether the word *catur* is treated as un-derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*) or derived (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*) by the rule *traḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ*, it is acutely accented on the first syllable in both cases, the latter by virtue of being formed with the suffix *uran* under the rule *ñ-nity-ādir nityam*.

Furthermore, since *asthi* and other such words are also acute-accented on the first syllable, the remaining syllables would be unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule of *śeṣanighāta*; consequently, the substitute *anaṅ* would also necessarily be unaccented. Thus, the explicit mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) would have to serve the purpose of indicating that it is intended to be uttered as such, which would render the mention of *udātta* redundant. On the contrary, even with this additional effort, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being understood as indicating non-intention (*avivakṣā*). However, if the Sūtra were recited in the *ekaśruti* (monotone) manner, then the specific adoption of an accent would indeed serve the purpose of indicating intention, and thus there would be no fault.

As for what is stated in the *Kaustubha*—namely, that the mention of "acute" (*udātta*) implies that a quality not explicitly mentioned by its own term does not serve as a differentiator, whether because it is inherently so or due to the absence of a specific effort (*yatna*)—the first alternative is not tenable, because it would result in the accentuation of a *nipātana* being intended as significant. Nor is the second alternative correct; for while a specific effort exists precisely as the cause for intending the utterance of the acute accent, the probans (*jñāpaka*) cannot be established through such a weakening of the root principle (*mūlaśaithilya*), since the very fact that necessitates the redundancy of its own mention is what must be made known [by the rule]. Furthermore, it is well-established in common experience that qualities which are explicitly mentioned do indeed function as differentiators.

This is because it has been stated exactly so in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, the inclusion here is twofold: by way of its own form (*svarūpeṇa*) and by way of being delimited by specific words such as "acute" (*udātta*) and so forth.

By this [explanation], having accepted optional monotonous intonation (*ekaśrutya*), it was said that "by the maxim 'remedies are also possible through other alternatives,' the introduction of the acute accent (*ādyudāttanipātana*) will be applied there. However, in this case, relying on the recitation of the Sūtras according to their threefold nature (*traiśvaryeṇa*), it was stated that the mention of "acute" (*udāttagrahaṇa*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding a quality that is included by its own form due to its inseparability (*nāntarīyakatva*).

Therefore, the objection that there is no contradiction between the earlier and later commentaries (bhāṣyas) is refuted, because the differentiating power of phonetic qualities (guṇas) must necessarily be accepted. Furthermore, the current commentary should be interpreted according to the recitation of the sūtras in a single tone (ekaśrutya). For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *aṇ* in the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* is justified in order to include the *y*, *v*, and *l* sounds which are distinct by virtue of their phonetic qualities. It is for this same reason that the nasalization (*anunāsika*) does not occur in the case of the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan*, nor in the substitution of *at* for *idam* and other words of the *tyadādi* class. All of this was implied by Kaiyaṭa himself when he subsequently presented the view of reciting [the sūtras] in a single tone; let there be no further elaboration. *adeṅ guṇaḥ* (1.1.2).

The sounds *a*, *e*, and *o* shall, without distinction, bear the technical designation *guṇa*. The specific rules (*pradeśa*) are those such as "ādguṇaḥ" (P. 6.1.87) and others which enjoin [the substitution], and those such as "ato guṇe" (P. 6.1.97) and others which refer back to them (*anuvāda*). The rest is to be inferred as before. Regarding the rule "iko guṇavṛddhī" (P. 1.1.3): wherever the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* function as the providers of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), one should understand that the word *ikaḥ*—ending in the genitive case—is present as the provider of the locus (*sthānin*) whenever no specific locus is explicitly mentioned.

And although the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are already under discussion (*prakṛta*), their mention again here allows for the understanding [of the rule] by resorting to the operation of the word itself; otherwise, one would have simply said *ikaḥ*. As for the objection that even so one should say *ikastau*, and that in reality one should say only *ikaḥ*: this is because of the interpretation that, having carried over the entire preceding pair of sūtras, the genitive case-ending word *ikaḥ* applies wherever *āT-aiC* are prescribed as *vṛddhi* and *adeṄ* are prescribed as *guṇa*. And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this in the inclusion of the term *id-* in the rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne*.

The argument that "even if the letter *a* is enjoined in its own form, the mention of the word *it* would be redundant when [the substitute] is presented by the word *ik*"—this is to be considered. For it is impossible for the word *tat* (in *tadguṇavṛddhi*) to refer to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* as subordinate elements, since pronouns generally refer to the principal element; moreover, this follows necessarily from the standard rule of interpretation (*autsargika-vyutpatti*), which need not be assumed. Furthermore, the aforementioned indicative mark (*liṅga*) is otherwise established, as it serves to exclude the *ṛ* and *u* sounds contained within the word *ṛbhukṣin*.

Furthermore, when that [word] continues into the sentence, it is directed toward a distinct and qualified meaning, and thus its connection with the subject matter at hand is untenable. Nor can this be resolved by appealing to the governing rule of "words" (*śabdādhikāra*). For that rule is accepted only for individual words; moreover, since the meaning of a sentence is the primary object of the speaker's ultimate intention (*paramatātparya*), it would be improper to violate that intention. On the other hand, the meaning of a word, being independent and not itself the primary object of that intention, does not violate the intention even when connected with another sentence. Furthermore, if one were to assume that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of these [words] acts as an obstacle to the cognition of that sentence-meaning, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, there is the principle of *gaurava* (excessive complexity) in postulating additional cognitions of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, as determined by various distinct word-meanings (*padārtha*).

As for the Bhāṣya and other texts asking "What is the purpose of including [the term] *idam*?", that is intended to raise an objection against the entire Sūtra by way of its constituent parts; for when the principal element is objected to, the objection to its subordinate elements follows as a matter of course. For this very reason, regarding the statement "The compound begins before *kaḍāra*," Kaiyaṭa explains on the Bhāṣya's question "What is the purpose of the word *prāk*? that by means of an objection directed at the indicator of the limit (*avadhi*), this is also an objection against the limit itself. This is also evident from the natural inclination (*svarasa*) of the Bhāṣya and other works, which state that it is due to the force of the repeated mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* within the section governing *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

By thus explaining the aforementioned passage as being intent on the force of the recurrence of the entire pair of sūtras, the objection raised against the previously stated interpretation—namely, that it does not conform to the natural sense of the words—is refuted; for the natural sense [of the words] points in the opposite direction. This is the general direction [of the argument].

Furthermore, this sūtra is not injunctive (*vidhi*) in nature, because the separate mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would otherwise be redundant. Nor is it a governing heading (*adhikāra*), for if it were so, it would follow that the negative particle (*nañ*) should also be read right here. There is no reason for such an asymmetry—whereby *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, which serve as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), are mentioned here, while their negation is mentioned later. If the purpose were to ensure the presentation of the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* in place of *ik* for application in subsequent rules, then it would be more appropriate to take the entire complex (the whole sūtra) as the governing heading, just as in the case of "sarvasya dve" and other such rules.

In passages such as *pratyayaḥ* and *paraśca*, the separate recitation is justified by the difference in what is to be prescribed (*vidheya*). By the former, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is prescribed; by the latter, however, its status as "following" (*paratva*) in relation to the base (*prakṛti*) is established. Therefore, this is indeed a *paribhāṣā* (metarule). Furthermore, the indicator (*liṅga*) for the application of this rule is the prescription of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* by means of those specific terms, characterized by the absence of any mention of other substituends (*sthānin*), and not merely the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* themselves. We shall demonstrate later that [if it were otherwise], there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in rules such as *aco ñṇiti*.

The examples are *cetā*, *stotā*, *karttā*, *acaiṣīt*, *astauṣīt*, and *ahārṣīt*. However, the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) are *yātā*, *glāyati*, and *umbhitā*; here, let there not be a *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ā* with *a*, for *ai* with *e*, or for *m* with *o* due to similarity of place of articulation. As the Vārttika states:
"The mention of *iK* is for the purpose of excluding *āT*, diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), and consonants."

This might be the case: in forms such as *pacati*, even if the vowel of the root (*dhātu*) undergoes *guṇa* by depending on the affix *śap* according to the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya*, and the vowel of the suffix (*pratyaya*) undergoes *guṇa* by depending on the *tip* ending according to the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*, there would still be no difference [in the result]. Nor does the problem arise that when *cikīrṣa-aka-* is in the state of being established, the vowel *a* would be subject to *vṛddhi*. This is because the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) takes precedence over *vṛddhi* by virtue of the statement in the Vārttika: "The elision of *at* prevails by prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over *ṇi*-affixation, *al*-elision, *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening."

Even in the Siddhānta (the established doctrine), since the rule *aco ñṇiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.115] specifies the locus (*sthāna*) for the *vṛddhi* substitution, the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* does not apply; therefore, the matter must be resolved in the manner already stated. Furthermore, in forms such as *ayāsīt*, there is no fault even if the *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule *saci vṛddhiḥ* [Vārttika on Pāṇini 7.2.3], because some maintain that this is superseded by *sag* and *iṭ* due to their higher status according to the rule *yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.73]. Others hold that it is superseded because it is an exception (*apavāda*) by virtue of the principle of "that which applies when another does not" (*yenanāprāptinyāya*).

In examples such as *yātā* (from the root *yā*), the *guṇa* substitution is indeed refuted by the very fact that the suffix *ṭak* in *gāpoṣṭak* is marked with *k*, according to the principle stated in the introduction to the section on phonemes—that parts of a phoneme are not grasped by the mention of the whole phoneme. Otherwise, since the form would be established simply by the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule between the two *a*s, the *k*-marking intended for the application of *āto lopaḥ* would become redundant. Therefore, the desired result cannot be achieved there through elision (*lopa*).

This is because, by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *upadeśa* from the rule "anudāttopadeśa," the elision is prescribed only for that which ends in /a/ at the time of its introduction as an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix. However, since the root *gā* ends in /ā/ at the moment the suffix *ṭa* arises, [the elision does not apply]. Otherwise, in forms such as *gataḥ*, once the elision of the *m* is performed, the elision of the final vowel would undesirably follow due to the presence of /a/. Now, if one were to rely on the fact that the elision of *m* and so forth is "unestablished" (*asiddha*) here because it belongs to the *ābhīya* group (i.e., it occurs within a single word), even then the forms *at*, *pat*, and *it*—which are accepted by Mādhava and others as derived from the roots *aya* and *paya* with the suffix *kvip*—would not be established. This is because the rule "lopo vyoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.66) is not considered *ābhīya*.

And it should not be argued that, in the case of the roots *dhivi* (in the sense of pleasing) and *kṛvi* (in the senses of harming and doing), because they are marked with the *it*-sign, the augment *num* is inserted; and when the substitution of *a* for the *v* occurs by the rule "dhinvikṛṇvyora ca" and the suffix *u* is added, the elision of the *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) would not take place, since at the time of the production of the suffix *u*, the word lacks the status of ending in *a*. Some maintain that this objection is invalid because, precisely at the time of the production of the suffix *u*, this [elision] also presents itself to the mind as being taught in grammatical connection (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*) with it.

Others maintain that even if there were simultaneity, the status of having a final *a* (adantatva) does not exist at the very moment the suffix *u* is prescribed; thus, out of dissatisfaction with this view, they argue that based on the order of instruction, first the suffix *at* is applied, and then the suffix *u* is drawn in by the word *ca*.
Therefore, this sūtra need not be commenced for the purpose of removing the long vowel *ā*.

Nor is it for the purpose of excluding *ai*. For that is already prevented by the very efficacy of the prescription of *ai* (in *aij*). Otherwise, one would have pronounced only *e*. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the substitution of *āy* (*āy-ādeśa*) would also not occur; for there is a difference: the prescription of *ai* is a sublater (*bādhaka*) with respect to the *guṇa* substitution because its own prescription would otherwise be rendered useless (*vaiyarthyāpatti*), whereas in the case of the *āy* substitution, the sound *ai* itself is the cause (*nimitta*). As they say: "That rule for which the prescription [of a substitute] is useless is sublated; but that rule which is the very cause of another rule is not sublated."

Furthermore, it is not possible to simply read [the root] as *glai*, because in forms such as *tvayā glāyate*, there would be the undesirable consequence of two *yak* suffixes; and if it lacked a long final vowel (*ādantatva*), forms such as *jaglau* would remain unestablished. [Objection: But in that case, even the substitution of *āt* (by the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*) would be sublated, since the presence of *āt* is possible even when [the root] is taught with a final *eṅ* vowel, and thus the teaching of *aij* cannot be the cause for that [substitution].

When the suffix begins with *śit*, since both the substitution of *guṇa* and the substitution of *ātva* are equally obstructed by the presence of *aij* (the diphthongs *ai* and *au*) when the suffix is not *śit*, it would be impossible to determine that only *guṇa* is set aside by the teaching of *aij* and not *ātva*. Furthermore, in the case of roots ending in *eṅ* such as *dhēṭ* ("to drink"), the rule for *ātva* also finds its scope of application. Moreover, the mention of *aij* in the rule for *ātva* is intended for subsequent purposes, namely the rule "mīnāti-minoti-dīṅāṃ lyapi ca. This is because, according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, the prescription of *ātva* for roots ending in *eṅ* such as *dīṅ* will be stated in the section on the technical designation *ghu*.

On this point, Kaiyaṭa and others state: "In the rule *na dhyākhyā*, the very mention of the root *dhyai* (to think), which has already undergone the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*), serves as the deciding factor that the *ātva* is not barred [from applying]. As for the claim that the *ātva* occurs by virtue of the force of the mention of *ej* (the vowel *e* and *o*), that cannot be suspected of being for the sake of subsequent rules; for according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the rule *mīnāti* prescribes the *ātva* precisely at the stage of the original form (*upadeśāvasthā*) when a suffix that causes *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* is intended to be applied, and not after *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* have already taken effect—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)."

Otherwise, in the case of *dāya*, because it would end in the vowel *i*, the suffix *ghañ* would be superseded by *ac*; in *īṣadavadāna* and similar forms, the suffix *yuc* (prescribed by the rule "āto yuc") would not apply; and in *avadāya*, the suffix *ṇa*—characterized by the presence of a final *ā* according to the rule "śyādvyadha"—would also not apply. Furthermore, this [result] is established even by the prescription of *ā*-substitution for roots such as *dīṅ* when there is the intention to express a suffix conditioned by *eṅ*.
