It should not be argued that because affixes marked with *ṇ* (ṇit) and those marked with *ñ* (ñit) are causes for *vṛddhi*, they cannot be causes for the substitution of *eṅ*; otherwise, when one intends to use the *ghañ* or *ṇij* affixes, the substitution of *āt* would not occur. This is because, even though *vṛddhi* subverts *guṇa*, these affixes do not lose their inherent capacity (*svarūpayogyatva*) toward *guṇa*. Furthermore, since the substitution of *āt* is accepted [by the rule] even before the occasion for *ej* arises, it would be impossible to intend the actual production of the result (*phalopadhāna*). That is not correct. Since a general rule (*utsarga*) operates only by avoiding the domain of its exception (*apavāda*), there is no evidence that the *ṇij* affix and others lack the capacity toward *ej*. Therefore, it is established that the diphthongs (*aic*) are not *guṇa*.

Nor is it for the purpose of excluding the consonant; for by making the suffix *ḍ* in the rule "the suffix *ḍa* is added after the root *jan* when preceded by a word ending in the locative case" (*saptamyāṃ janerḍaḥ*) a *ḍit*, it is indicated that no *guṇa* substitution occurs for the consonant. Otherwise, if the vowel *a* were substituted as the *guṇa* in place of the half-mātrā consonant, the form would be established through the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule, rendering that [marking of *ḍ*] useless. Nor should it be argued that the *guṇa* substitute for the letter *n* would necessarily be the nasalized vowel *ā*; for since the result would already be established by the word "following" (*para*) alone, the inclusion of the term "form" (*rūpa*) has the purpose of ensuring that the following form remains exactly as it is, characterized by whatever *guṇa* may apply. On this point, the Bhāṣya states:

The inclusion of the marker *ḍ* is not an indicator [of the rule's intended meaning]. This is because, by the Vārttika taught within the section beginning with "gamaśca" and "antātyantādhvadūrapāra"—namely, "it is also seen after other [roots]" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*)—the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed for the root *gam* as well. Furthermore, if *guṇa* were admitted there, since the *m* [in *gam*] shares the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) as the lips, the *guṇa* would result in the vowel *o*, leading to the failure of forms such as *nagaḥ* and *agaḥ*.

Although this suffix *ḍa* occurs elsewhere than in the section governed by the rule "saptamyāṃ janerḍaḥ," nevertheless, within the section "janerḍaḥ," the meaning [of the suffix] was stated by the Vārttika as being already contained within the word *api* in the sūtra "anyeṣvapi dṛśyate," and not as something new.
Alternatively, some maintain that the intention of the Bhāṣya is that this very Vārttika is indeed superfluous.

If it is argued that the prescription of the suffix *ḍoṣ* in the rule "gamerḍoḥ" is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *guṇa* substitution of *o* for the *m* does not occur—since otherwise the form *go* would be established by applying *guṇa* to the suffix *vic* alone—or alternatively, that this very rule indicates the absence of *guṇa* for a consonant, we say: not so. For the prescription of the suffix *ḍoṣ* serves a purpose: to exclude the nasalized vowel *a* (ṅ) in place of the *m*.

Nevertheless, the fact that the suffix *ḍau* is prescribed by the rule "tanoter ḍauḥ sanvacca" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a vowel does not undergo *guṇa* substitution when followed by a consonant. Otherwise, since the result could have been established through the *guṇa* of the letter *n* together with the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) of the suffixal vowel *ā*, the prescription of *ḍit* would be purposeless.

Furthermore, since the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* find their application in cases such as *cetā* and *acaiṣīt*—where there is proximity (*āntaratamya*) by both place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*)—they will not apply to consonants and the like based solely on proximity of place. Nor should it be argued that, because these rules find their application in cases such as *netā* and *anaiṣīt* through proximity determined by all three factors—place, quality (*guṇa*), and measure (*pramāṇa*)—they would consequently fail to apply to short vowels.

This is because the addition of the *k* marker in the rule *sṛghasyadaḥ kmarac* indicates that, by way of authoritative evidence, phonetic proximity (*āntarya*) is not intended [as the sole criterion for substitution]. Nor should it be argued that in the forms *īhitā* and *īśitā*, the *a* and *e* sounds would respectively replace the guttural *ha* and palatal *śa* due to their proximity in terms of place of articulation and quality (*sthāna-guṇa*), since both *ha* and *śa* are open (*vivṛta*). This is because it will be stated later that the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are only slightly open (*īṣadvivṛta*). Furthermore, while vowels such as *i* are indeed open, and although other *śikṣā* texts state that vowels such as *e* are more open (*vivṛtatara*), this is not accepted in the *Sūtra*, the *Bhāṣya*, and other authoritative works.

Alternatively, because the occurrence of *guṇa* is inferred in vowels beginning with *i* by virtue of their being stated [in the rule] as having *kṛt* status; therefore, since the absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*) is established by the aforementioned method alone, this sūtra is useless—this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that this [paribhāṣā] is intended to ensure that the *vṛddhi* which is to be prohibited in the rule *ṅkiti ca* possesses the character of being "conditioned by an *ik*" (*iglakṣaṇatva*). For without this paribhāṣā, the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* conditioned by an *ik* would not be possible, because the delimiting property of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) would remain unestablished. When this [paribhāṣā] exists, however, the character of being conditioned by an *ik*—defined as being prescribed by employing the word *ik*—becomes established. This is because the meaning of that word is obtained through the particle *ca* in that rule, which signifies the word *iti*.

Nor should it be argued that the prohibition applies to those two [suffixes] precisely when they are not specified; for if that were so, there would result the undesirable consequence of prohibiting even the *guṇa* substitution of *o* (in the rule *orguṇaḥ*) in the formation of *laigavāyana* from the base *laigū*, by means of the suffix *phak* prescribed after bases beginning with *naḍ*. Nor can it be said that the rule has its own inherent power (*vidhānasāmarthya*) to prevent this, because that power is already fulfilled in cases such as *aupagava*. Furthermore, in cases like *paurohitya*, where the suffix *yak* follows, the initial *vṛddhi* will certainly occur by the rule *kiti ca*; for while the rule prescribing [the *guṇa*] has its scope elsewhere, the prohibition finds its application in *kit* suffixes other than *taddhita*.

For this very reason, there is no resolution even by means of prohibiting the *guṇa* that has *ik* as its locus (*ik-sthānika*), because the aforementioned *guṇa* possesses the status of having the vowel *u* as its locus (*ukāra-sthāniyatā*). Therefore, this [sūtra] is intended to establish the fact of being characterized by *ik* (*ig-lakṣaṇatva*), which serves as the delimiting factor (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) for the negation. As for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, however, they everywhere ultimately result in being replacements for *ik*, even when occurring apart from those specific rules.

For instance: in the rules *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* and *jusi ca*, the substitution of *guṇa* would—by the maxim *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* (which applies to the final letter)—apply to the final phoneme; however, by virtue of the previously mentioned *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), these substitutions rest only upon the [initial] *ik* vowels. In rules such as *miderguṇaḥ* and *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*, however, the *sthānin* (the element to be replaced) is also explicitly specified: *mida* refers to the root *mid*; its *guṇa* is the substitute. *Puganta* means "that which ends in *pu*" (*puki antaḥ*). In the term *puki*, the locative case indicates the condition (*viṣayasaptamī*); the meaning is: "when *pu* is intended to be expressed, that which is the end."

Thus, it is concluded that [the augment] *puK* occurs when the preceding element is separated by *puk*. Furthermore, *laghvī* (light) and *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) form a *karmadhāraya* compound. Then, in the *samāhāra-dvandva* "that which ends in *puk* and has a light penultimate vowel," the neuter gender is applied. In forms such as *vāpayati*, however, because the *puK* augment—produced by the proximity (*sannipāta*) of the suffix beginning with *ā*—does not trigger the *guṇa* substitution which would otherwise destroy that very *puK*.

In the rule "*ṛcchatyṝtām*" as well, there is a *dvandva* between the words *ṛ* and *ṛccha*; having formed a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound of the word *ṛcchati* with the vowel *ṛ*, one obtains a *dvandva* within the latter member of a *tatpuruṣa* compound contained within the former member.

Alternatively, according to the aforementioned method, there is a three-membered *dvandva* compound consisting of the first member (which contains a *tatpuruṣa*), the syllable *ṛ*, and the word *ṛccha*. By this, the status of being the substitute for the vowel *ṛ* of the root *ṛcchati* is obtained. For the sake of establishing the *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *ārivān*, a fourth *ṛ* should also be elided (*praśleṣya*) in the middle [of the rule] in order to include the root *ṛdh*. Otherwise, due to the force of the *kit* designation of the suffix *kvasu*, the *guṇa* would not occur. However, when there is an elision (*praśleṣa*), the *guṇa* is established by the force of the specific injunction.

In the rule *ṛdṛśo'ṅi*, there is a separate rule: *uraṅi guṇaḥ*, followed by *dṛśaḥ*. By the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *uḥ* and through a non-co-referential genitive (*vyadhikaraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the meaning is that there is a *guṇa* substitution for the *ṛ*-vowel belonging to the root *dṛś*. In the rule *sthūladūrayuvahrasvakṣiprakṣudrāṇāṃ yaṇādiparaṃ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ*, there is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). One rule is: *sthūladūrayuvahrasvānāṃ yaṇādiparam*; the second is: *kṣiprakṣudrayoḥ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ*.

When *l*, *r*, and *v* ending in a youth-forming suffix (*yuvan*) are elided along with the following vowel *a*, the substitution of *guṇa* for the *u* by the rule "orguṇaḥ" and the subsequent substitution of *ava* result in forms such as *sthavīyān* and *davīyān*. The compound *yaṇādiḥ* means "that which has a *yaṇ* at its beginning"; the meaning is that after the *yaṇ* (the *p* and *d*) preceded by *r* in the words *kṣipra* and *kṣudra*, there is the elision of the following *ra*, and the *guṇa* substitution of the *i* and *l* vowels preceding those two [consonants].

In this way, the term *guṇamātra* (merely a *guṇa*) is restricted to the case of *ikṣu*. However, in the rule *mṛjervṛddhiḥ*, the word *acaḥ* is drawn down [from the previous rule], so that there shall be *vṛddhi* of the vowel (*ac*) belonging to the root *mṛj*. Then follows the rule *ñṇiti*. By the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *acaḥ*, the meaning of this rule is exactly as it is in the established order (*yathānyāsa*). Thus, in forms such as *amārṭ*, there is no *vṛddhi* of the augment *aṭ*; for in the view where *aṭ* is applied after the substitutes for *l* (the *l*-affixes), *vṛddhi* would apply first because it is subsequent, since a grammatical operation (*śāstra*) fulfills its purpose only once (*sakṛt*).

However, one might argue that since the augment *āṭ* occurs precisely in the state of the suffix *lā*, and because when *adhyaiyātām* is analyzed as *adhi-ā-i-ātām*, the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82) would apply—thereby substituting *yaṇ* for the *i* of *adhi* by overriding *iyaṅ* (via *aci śnudhātubhruvām*)—since *āṭ* is part of the beginning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and thus the root becomes *anekāc*. This objection is not tenable, for the following solution is adopted: the rule *eranekācaḥ* is split apart; the word *iṇaḥ* is carried over from the previous rule *iṇo yaṇ* (Pāṇini 6.4.79), and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is established: "If *yaṇ* is to be substituted for an *anekāc* [element], then it must be for the vowel *i* of the root *iṇ* [only]. By this restriction, the application of *yaṇ* is prevented. Consequently, when the suffix *liṅ* follows, the prohibition stated in *ṅkiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5) applies.

Since the state of the vowel *l* (the substitute for *la*) is difficult to obtain at the stage of *vṛddhi*, the augment *aṭ* arises first due to its being *antaraṅga*; thus, even though *vṛddhi* would apply to that [augment], the solution is possible through the paribhāṣā: "When there is a conflict with respect to the final element, [the rule applies] to that which is proximate to the final."

However, according to the view that [the *ṭi*] is rejected (*pratyākhyāna*), because the suffix (*pratyaya*) implied by the rule (*aṅga*) qualifies the vowel (*aj*), and because that [vowel] is prescribed when a suffix follows, the *vṛddhi* substitution applies only to the *ṛ*-vowel and not to the *aṭ* augment. This is because, in the absence of an immediately preceding suffix, even if there is an intervention of a single phoneme, the *vṛddhi* occurs for the *ṛ*-vowel alone; for there is no authority for its application when there is an intervention of multiple phonemes. This follows from the maxim: "That by which there is no intervention [is considered present] even when there is an intervention, on the strength of the explicit statement."

Even in the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, this sūtra is not intended for the purpose of prohibiting the *vṛddhi* substitution of the vowel *a* in forms such as *acakīrṣīt*; for it has already been stated that the elision (*alopa*) possesses greater force by virtue of the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The same solution applies even regarding the long vowel *ā*. Furthermore, there is no verbal root ending in *ej* at all; since the substitution of *āt* occurs prior [to any other operation], it is independent of external conditions (*anaimittika*). As for the words *rai*, *nao*, and *glau* when followed by the *kvip* suffix denoting habitual action (*ācāra-kvip*), there is no difference whether the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place or not.

Nor does there arise the contingency of *vṛddhi* in the case of *udaboḍhām*, where the *ḍha* is first elided; for since that [elision] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the preceding operation, the *vṛddhi* characterized by the rule for word-final consonants (*hal-anta-lakṣaṇā*) occurs first, followed by the elision of *ḍha*. Thus, because of the principle "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is *asiddha* with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)," the condition of being vowel-final (*od-antatva*) does not exist, which serves as the resolution. Furthermore, this is not intended for the purpose of prohibiting *vṛddhi* in the form *agavīt*, derived from the word *go* with the suffix *kvip*.

In the *Kaustubha*, it is explained that because the word *dhātu* (root) is supplied from the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* and thus qualifies the root implied by the suffix *sic* through identity, the term refers only to that which is a root and not to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in any sense whatsoever.
Mādhava, however, maintains that for the words *kavi*, *vidhu*, and *pitṛ*, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, the forms in the *luṅ* tense are *akavāyīt*, *avidhāvīt*, and *apitārīt*.

His intention is as follows: What is the meaning of the phrase "only a verbal root" (*dhātureva*)? Does it mean that [the element] is designated as a verbal root even when followed by another suffix, or that it lacks the status of being a base for a suffix whose application is not based on its being a verbal root? Not the first. For in that case, would one posit a property that is directly subsumed by "suffix-ness" (*pratyayatva*) as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of difference, or a property that is somehow subsumed by "suffix-ness"? Not the first; because even in the case of *kṛt* suffixes and the like—which possess a difference delimited by *tiṅ*-ness and so forth—the form ending in *kvip* would still have the status of a verbal root. Nor the second.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because even in *ta* and other such suffixes—which are distinct from those delimited by *tiP*—there is no exclusion of that [property], since they too possess the status of verbal roots (*dhātu*). Nor is the second [alternative] correct; for in the case of forms ending in *kvip*, such as *harati* and *karoti*, there would result an over-extension of the exclusion, since these are bases for *su*-case endings (*svādi-prakṛti*). Nor can it be argued that only those [bases] qualified by the augment *tuK* are bases for *su*-case endings; for even with that much, the difference between the substrata (*dharmibheda*) is not established. Furthermore, this would lead to the non-occurrence of *vṛddhi* in forms like *alāvīt*, where pure roots such as *lū* (which share the same phonetic form as roots ending in *kvip*) would be treated as bases for *su*-case endings.

Nor should it be said that because they are nominal stems (*prātipadika*), they do not receive the designation of verbal root (*dhātu*); for this is evident from the statement in the grammatical treatises: "The designation of verbal root occurs only after the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) have been elided in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). Furthermore, since *hṛ* and other such forms receive the designation of verbal root immediately after being established as meaningful while being distinct from nominal stems and suffixes, the presence or absence of the indicatory letters is irrelevant.

Even if it is argued—following Kaiyaṭa’s statement that the second mention of the term *dhātu* is for the purpose of including verbal roots taught as such [in the Dhātupāṭha], thereby excluding nominal stems (*nāman*)—nevertheless, it is not appropriate to exclude *vṛddhi* in the case of a root ending in an *ik* vowel followed by *kvip* when *sic* follows; for since that [vṛddhi] is desired when the *ig-upadeśa* paribhāṣā is operative, it remains so even when that paribhāṣā is not commenced. Since such a meaning must be established through some other means, it is settled that one must instead strive to exclude roots ending in *o*. Regarding this, some say as follows:

Just as in the case of the rule *dhātoḥ*, one might argue that by carrying forward [the term] *otaḥ* from the previous rule, the interpretation should be: "If a vowel *vṛddhi* substitution occurs for a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in *o*, then it must be for a verbal root alone, and not for a nominalized root (*nāmadhātu*). This, however, is questionable. For there is no established instance of a verbal root other than a nominalized root that ends in *o*. Furthermore, since the substitution of *ā* (i.e., *ātva*) applies to those [nominalized roots] even earlier, and because it has already been stated that there is no distinction whether *vṛddhi* occurs or not when what is characterized by ending in *o* is in the state of ending in *ā*.

Therefore, in the rule *neṭi*, one should separate the connection with *na* and carry forward the term *otaḥ* from the preceding rule; thus, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* for that which ends in the vowel *o*. Alternatively, by carrying forward the mention of *bahulam* (diversely), the absence of *vṛddhi* for that which ends in *od* is to be established through *bāhulaka*; this much indeed appears most reasonable. In this way, there is no possibility of *vṛddhi* occurring for roots ending in consonants (*hal*) after the suffix *sic*, because by the maxim *yenanāprāpte*, the *vṛddhi* conditioned by a final consonant can indeed be sublated [by the prohibition].

Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *akopīt* and *amoṣīt*, the rule "the vowel of a root ending in *vat*, *vraj*, or a consonant [undergoes] vṛddhi before *sic*" would result in the vṛddhi of the consonant (hal), because the prohibition "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*) is without exception (*nirapavāda*). This is because we accept that the prohibition "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*) applies to vṛddhi in general. Therefore, it is established that this Paribhāṣā is intended to secure for the prohibition "before *kṅit*" (*kṅiti ca*) the status of being a qualifier of the vṛddhi by means of the condition of being characterized by an *ik* vowel (*iglakṣaṇatva*).

Now, even so, in examples such as *kṛtam* and *chinnam*, let there be the mention of *guṇa* alone for the purpose of prohibiting the *guṇa* prescribed by the rules *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* and *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*; there is no need for the mention of *vṛddhi*. Nor should it be argued that the mention of *vṛddhi* is necessary to establish its status as being characterized by an *ik* vowel (*iglakṣaṇatā*) in order to prohibit *vṛddhi* in forms such as *mṛṣṭaḥ*.

If it is argued that, according to the statement in the Bhāṣya—"In the case of *mṛj*, they optionally initiate the [application of] *vṛddhi* when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel"—the rule "optionally before an affix beginning with a vowel that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter" (*ajādau kṅiti vā*) must necessarily follow the rule "vṛddhi for *mṛj*" (*mṛjervṛddhiḥ*); and that in this context, the rule "before an affix beginning with a vowel that has *ṅ* or *k* as an indicatory letter" (*adājau ṅkiti*) is split, so that by the restrictive rule "if it applies before an affix having *ṅ* or *k* as an indicatory letter, it applies only when that affix begins with a vowel," the application of that [vṛddhi] is established even when the affix does not begin with a vowel—then, on this point, they say: [The response follows: ... [as per the original Sanskrit commentary].

Regarding the forms *anuvīt* and *adhuvīt*, which are desired as the *luṅ* (aorist) forms of the roots *ṇu* (in the sense of praise) and *dhū* (in the sense of shaking)—both of which are listed in the *kuṭādi* group—the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* applies. Because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the *ṅit*-property [to these roots], the prohibition of *vṛddhi* for the *sic* augment by the rule *ṅkiti ca* would otherwise apply; therefore, the mention of *vṛddhi* [in the rule] is intended to establish that this [prohibition] pertains specifically to *vṛddhi* characterized by an *ik* vowel.

It might be argued as follows: Since the substitution of *uvaṅ* depends only on the inclusion of the suffix *siC*, it is *antaraṅga* (internal) compared to the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), which depends on both the suffix *siC* and the *parasmaipada* (active voice). Thus, because *uvaṅ* applies prior to *vṛddhi*, the word remains *halanta* (ending in a consonant), and consequently, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "neṭi" is already established. Nor should it be said that this is not so because of the established doctrine that "there is no *antaraṅga* operation in the presence of *siC*"; for that doctrine lacks logical justification.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *na caivamacaiṣīt*, because it is *antaraṅga*, the *guṇa* substitution would occur instead of the *vṛddhi* in the *sic* suffix; for since *vṛddhi* is indeed possible in that very case, the desired result (*iṣṭāpatti*) follows. This is because, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no restriction regarding *vṛddhi* being the substitute for the short *i* vowel, and because the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* was introduced precisely for the purpose of not including the mention of *vṛddhi*.

One might argue: "In cases such as *nanvastauṣīt*, there is no possibility of *vṛddhi* for the *guṇa* [element], because it has been established that *vṛddhi* is prohibited after a stem ending in *o*. And if you say that even in the previously mentioned case, the same applies under the view that *vṛddhi* does not occur for a stem ending in *i* by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), we reply: 'Not so. For some maintain that there is no fault in this, because the rule 'after a verbal root ending in *o*' refers only to a verbal root (*dhātu*) and not to a nominalized root (*nāmadhātu*)."

That is to be considered; for that [position] has been refuted. Nor should it be argued that the status of ending in *o* (odanta) is well-established only here as a distinct verbal root (*dhātu*) other than a nominal stem (*nāman*), specifically in the state of *vṛddhi*. For at the time of the production of the suffix, what is required is the status of ending in *o*, not merely being so at some point; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition applying even in cases such as *avidhat* and *avidhat* (from the root *vidh*), since those too end in *o* in forms like *vidhavati*. Furthermore, if the internal (*antaraṅga*) operation is accepted, the status of ending in *o* exists precisely there [in the form *vidhavati*]. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it is beset by the aforementioned defects. Otherwise, even the lack of contradiction between Kaiyaṭa and Mādhava regarding that point would be untenable.

Therefore, it must be explained as follows: by dividing the rule *sici* and carrying forward both *otaḥ* and *bahulam*, and by relying on the principle of restricted optionality (*vyavasthita-bāhulaka*), there would be *vṛddhi* for a root ending in *o* before the suffix *sic*; and because of this restricted optionality, it does not occur in the case of denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*). Thus, the presentation of two forms—*akavayīt* and *akavāyīt*—in the *Siddhāntakaumudī* based on these two views is entirely without justification.

For in that portion [of the rule], unanimity (*aikamatya*) between both [grammarians] has indeed been established. Nor should it be argued that, in this view, the inconsistency of the form *avidhīt* remains as before; for even there, the substitution of *guṇa* must be admitted first. This is because the negation is accepted as applying only to that which naturally ends in *u*. In forms such as *akārṣīt*, once *guṇa* has been applied, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by the rule "vadavrajahalantasya."

Nor should it be argued that in examples such as *atārīt*, once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, the prohibition of the *vṛddhi* characterized by a final consonant (*hal*)—by the rule *neṭi*—would result in the optional *vṛddhi* prescribed by *ato halāder laghoḥ*. This is because the obligatory *vṛddhi* of *ato lrāntasya* is possible as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [optional rule]. Nor should it be argued that even so, the same contingency of an optional application would arise in the case of *alāvīt*.

In the rule *irāntasya*, by incorporating (*praśliṣya*) the letter *va* from the rule *lopo vyoḥ*, it must be stated that a compulsory (*nitya*) *vṛddhi* substitution is prescribed even for that which ends in [the root] *vī*. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, a compulsory *vṛddhi* would undesirably apply even in cases such as *mā bhavānavīd* and *mā bhavānamavīt*; for the prohibition is established by inserting *avi* and *mavi* in place of the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* in the sūtra *hrmyantakṣaṇa*.

Regarding this position, one might argue that in forms such as *aunayīt* and *aśvayīt*, since the internal operations (*antaraṅga*) of *guṇa* and *āy-ādeśa* would have already taken effect, the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] would apply simply because the root ends in *yā*; thus, the desired optional alternative (*vikalpa*) would not be established there. However, this must be addressed as follows: by the inclusion of *avi* and *mavi* [into the rule], there is a prohibition specifically against the obligatory *vṛddhi* resulting from the *praśleṣa* (insertion) of the letter *v*. This is because the optional [vṛddhi] prescribed by the rule "ato halādeḥ" is possible for *mavi*, according to the maxim: "Exceptions (*apavāda*) set aside preceding rules, but not subsequent ones."

Nor should it be argued that the same undesirable contingency of optionality (*vikalpāpatti*) arises here for *ajāgarīt* as well, because since both rules are contained within a single sūtra, it would be impossible for "ato halādeḥ" to subvert [the application of] the other even in that portion. For in that case, by considering the subversion in its general form (*bādhyasāmānyacintayā*), there is a subversion of all *vṛddhi* that falls within its own scope. Since there is no other way out, such an inequality must be tolerated. Alternatively, let the prohibition apply only to the *vṛddhi* prescribed by "ato lrāntasya. And in this way, the contingency of "ato halādeḥ" applying to both *ajāgarīt* and *amavīt* does not arise.

Even when there is a prohibition of the increase (*vṛddhi*) that would otherwise occur by way of an exception (*apavāda*), the operation of the general rule (*utsarga*)—which consists of an option (*vikalpa*)—remains active in the case of *mavati*, but not in the case of *jāgartti*. Therefore, if the letter *v* were included by *praśleṣa* (elision) within the rule *lṛntasya*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of obligatory *vṛddhi* even for the root *śava*. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this, because both the author of the *Bhāṣya* and the author of the *Nirukta* have stated: "The root *śavati*, meaning 'to go,' is used among the Kambojas; the Āryas speak of it as *vikāra*. Nor should it be argued that the reading *avi-mavi-vat* should also be inserted there [into the rule], because it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to omit the two roots *ṇi* and *śvi* and insert three instead. This is the general direction of the argument.

In this regard, the following should be understood: on the basis of this [argument], it is not logical to accept the principle that "there is no internal operation (*antaraṅga*) which is superseded by another internal operation," because the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *v* is not admitted. Nor does there arise the contingency of an optional alternative (*vikalpa*) in the case of *ālāvīt*, since in the rule *vadavraja* (Pāṇini 7.2.3), one can explain the prescription of *vṛddhi* for the substitute *ava* by reading the sūtra as *vada-ava-vraja*. Furthermore, it should not be argued that, due to association with verbal roots (*dhātu-sāhacarya*), the term *acaḥ* would refer only to vowels belonging to verbal roots.

This is because the inclusion of the term *kṛtvo'rtha* (meaning "times") in the rule *dvistricatur* indicates that association (*sāhacarya*) is not a restrictive factor in all cases; furthermore, it is universally established that the prohibition in the rule *neṭi* applies specifically to the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by a final consonant. By this reasoning, even in cases such as *avidhau* and *īd*, the contradiction with the views expressed in the aforementioned texts can be refuted by means of the obligatory *vṛddhi*. Consequently, in the rule *hrasvyantakṣaṇa*, the mention of the roots *ṇi* and *śvi* need not be made at all.

It is all the more appropriate to insert [the prohibition] for *avimavyoḥ* in that very place; it should have been done even earlier than for *śavateḥ*, because there is no purpose [for doing so later]. Once the *guṇa* substitution has taken effect, the prohibition of *ṇi* and *śvi* is already established simply by virtue of their ending in *y*. Furthermore, since the insertion of *av-ādi* is based solely on preventing over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) caused by the inclusion of the letter *v*, once that [insertion] is abandoned, the matter is resolved by the very destruction of its root. And thus, the discrepancy regarding the recourse to the consideration of general versus specific sublation through a division of parts in that context does not arise.

Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa and others [argue as follows]: The roots *ciri* and *jiri* are recited in the *svādi* class in the sense of "injury. From these two, with the suffix *sic*, forms such as *acirāyīt* and *ajirāyīt* are desired. Similarly, from the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive without *yaṅ*) of *cinoti* and *nayati*, with *sic*, forms such as *acecāyīt* and *anenanāyīt* are desired. However, if the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā* were applied in the domain of *sic*, then due to the occurrence of *guṇa* and *āyādeśa*, the stems would end in *y*; consequently, by the prohibition of *vṛddhi* in the rule "hmyantakṣaṇa," forms such as *acirayīt* would result instead. Therefore, it is necessary that the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not operate in the domain of *sic*.

That too must be considered. Since it is possible to assume that, by virtue of the co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) with the letters *ha* and *ma*, the letter *ya* is also understood as being only that which is original (*aupadeśika*), the prohibition does not apply when the substitution of *ay* has taken place. Furthermore, the mention of the roots *ṇi* and *śvi* is indeed maintained in that very rule (*Pāṇini 1.1.5*). That itself is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition applies only to that which ends in *ya* as something original. Otherwise, since the prohibition would be established simply by the fact of ending in *ya* once the *guṇa* and *ay* substitutions have been made, its inclusion would result in redundancy.

Thus, even such frivolous objections as that the restrictive nature of concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is not universal find no footing. Furthermore, the presentation of the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule "there is no internal operation (*antaraṅga*) in the case of *sic*" is also untenable; for even according to our own view, there is no pointlessness (*vaiyarthyābhāva*) in that [mention].

By this very support of the aforementioned indicative mark (*liṅga*), and relying on the maxim that "even when coexistence is possible, there is sublation," the internal (*antaraṅga*) [element] is sublated by *vṛddhi*. Otherwise, curd would not be sublated by buttermilk, and the suffixes *śap* and *kap* and others would not be sublated by *śram*, *kaj*, and so forth; for according to the rule "the augment *mit* follows after the final vowel of the [root]," *śram* occurs after the final vowel of the root, while *śap* occurs after the mere constituent of the base.

Because there is a difference of location (deśabheda) due to *akac* being situated between *a* and *ṭi*, while the suffix *kap* is situated outside of that; nor should it be argued that, by the maxim of "an exception [applies] in the middle," only *uvaṅ* would be sublated by the *vṛddhi* rule and not the *guṇa*, since the latter is recited later—because, according to the view concerning the general sublation (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), everything other than the specific exception that falls within its own scope is admitted to be sublated.

Otherwise, the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* would subvert the substitution of *r* for the *ṛ* in *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, as well as the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* and the *utva* [substitutions] in the first two cases, but it would not subvert the *guṇa* prescribed by *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ*, because that rule is read later. Furthermore, the consideration of whether a general rule is subverted by a specific one is settled according to the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*); such arguments are also refuted, because in the present case the grounds for such an assumption have been explained otherwise, and because an assumption is subject to the "subversion" characterized by the destruction of its very root. As for what was stated by the venerable Bhāṣyakāra:

And as for the inclusion of the term *akāra* (the letter *a*) in the rule "laghoriti kṛte'pi," this is its intended meaning: in the rule "ato halāderlaghoḥ," the mention of *at* is not for the purpose of excluding the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), since that is already established by the word *laghoḥ* itself. What remains to be excluded are the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*, as in examples such as *acetīt*, *amoṣīt*, and *anartīt*.

If, however, *sici* were internal (*antaraṅga*), then since the *guṇa* would be established by its very internality, the mention of "after *at*" (*ataḥ*) in the rule would be redundant for the purpose of preventing *vṛddhi* there; for by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it would be established that the rule applies only to the vowel *a*. Even so, this must be considered: in forms such as *akuṭīt* and *apuṭīt*, because the *guṇa* does not apply due to the *ṅit*-designation in the rule "gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ," the mention of *at* (*ad-grahaṇa*) is indeed meaningful, so that *vṛddhi* may not occur there.

Nor should it be argued that even the substitution of *vṛddhi* will not occur there simply because [the suffix] is marked with *ṅit*; for since the rule "laghoḥ" (P. 7.4.94) specifies a particular locus (*nirdiṣṭasthānika*), it does not apply here because [the *vṛddhi*] is not characterized by an *ik* vowel.

As for the argument that, when a *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] has been superseded by an *antaraṅga* *guṇa*, even though the *guṇa* itself is subsequently superseded by the *ṅit*-designation, the *vṛddhi* does not nevertheless take effect—on the grounds of the maxim "when the killer of Devadatta is killed, Devadatta does not return to life"—that is incorrect. If one is insistent on the meaningfulness of the vowel *a*, then let it be accepted that the original rule (*utsarga*) applies again once the exception (*apavāda*) has been negated. Otherwise, however, there is no harm even in abandoning that maxim.

For this very reason, in our view, even the additional inclusion of the letter *va* in the rule *vadavraja* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) does not constitute a fault; for there is economy (*lāghava*) by abandoning the mention of *vṛddhi*. However, regarding the rule *nāntaḥpādam* (Pāṇini 6.1.115), it was stated that when the *pūrvarūpa* [sandhi] is prohibited, the rules concerning *ay-ādi* substitutions do not apply, in order to establish forms such as *sujātīśvasūnṛte*. In the present case, however, there is a discrepancy because results such as *acirāyīt* are established in a different manner. Furthermore, it is improper to state that some meaning is being conveyed merely for the sake of the word's meaningfulness, even in the absence of a specific result. Enough of this digression.

Therefore, it is established that the mention of *vṛddhi* (the term "vṛddhi") here is indeed unnecessary. This [conclusion], however, is based on the commonality with the mention of *guṇa*. In reality, let it be as it may according to the final view (*siddhānta*). But in the alternative where the mention of *vṛddhi* is not included in the *ik-paribhāṣā*, since a *vṛddhi* characterized by an *ik* vowel would be unestablished, the purpose of the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.102) is precisely to prevent *vṛddhi* in forms such as *akuṭīt* and the like; for in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), only *vṛddhi* in general is to be prohibited, and the rule *halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) finds its scope in instances other than those beginning with *kuṭ* etc. Enough of this digression.

This, however, must be stated by way of the commonality of the apprehension of the quality (*guṇa*). Even though, according to the method described, the status of *i* as the locus of substitution for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is established through the assumption of various artificial constructions, it is more appropriate to rely on the rule "iko guṇavṛddhī" (P. 1.1.3) rather than that [assumption]. This is because of the similarity of the maxim: "This [small] creeper is dragged out from the great pillar of the bamboo"—such is the intention of the author of the Sūtras and others.

Let us return to the main subject. Why is there recourse to the operation of words? [It is so that] in examples such as *dyoḥ panthāḥ* and *imam*, the rules "diva aut," "pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt," and "tyadādīnāmaḥ"—which prescribe the substitution of *aut*, *āt*, and *at* respectively—should apply to the final letter alone according to the maxim of the final phoneme (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*). Thus, *aut* is applied to the end of *div-* to form *dyoḥ*, *āt* to the end of *pathin-* to form *panthāḥ*, and *at* to the end of *idam-* to form *imam*.

As for the fact that *sa imam* was cited in the Bhāṣya, some say that the portion *sa* has entered there by chance as part of the Brāhmaṇa sentence, "He recited this mantra (*sa imaṃ mantram apaṭhat*)," and thus it was not intended to be included in the formal example; for since the vowel *ik* cannot occur in the word *tat*, no suspicion of the application of the restrictive rule could arise. Others, however, maintain that when the term *ikaḥ* is supplied from the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ*, the substitution of *a* would apply to the words *dvi* and *idam* but not to others; since the mention of the specific list [of pronouns] can serve as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) for the subsequent rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau*, they conclude that *sa* is indeed a valid example.

In reality, if that were the case, the rule *idamo maḥ* would be redundant; for its purpose is merely to block the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement of the initial vowel by *a*) in place of the letter *m*. Furthermore, according to the reasoning stated above, there is no possibility of *atva* applying to the letter *m*. Similarly, the rule *ido'y puṃsi* would also be redundant; since the letter *i* belongs to the *tyadādi* group, its substitution by *a* is already established by the very injunction *do 'y puṃsi*. If, however, its purpose were restricted solely to the word *dvi*, its function would be accomplished simply by the *paribhāṣā* regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*).

In this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), the positions of "that which remains" (*taccheṣa*) and "its exception" (*tadapavāda*) are considered as prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas the position of "proximity of the word" (*padopasthiti*) is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Regarding the first [view], for example, in the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*, by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the terms *aṅga* and *guṇa*, the genitive indication *aṅgasya* serves as a formal indicator (*liṅga*) that the maxim "the substitution occurs at the end of the element" (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*) applies; furthermore, from the word *guṇa*, the maxim concerning the vowel *ik* (*ikparibhāṣā*) also presents itself. In that context, the term *ik* is a qualifier of *aṅga*, meaning that the *guṇa* substitution occurs for an *aṅga* ending in an *ik* vowel.
And that [operation] being [prescribed] by the rule *alo'ntyasya*, it applies to the final [element]; thus, in that case, the *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* is supplementary (*śeṣa*) to this [rule].

Alternatively, if the genitive case in *aṅgasya* is established by the *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* upon the final vowel (*ali*), such that [the meaning is] "guṇa is for the final element of the *aṅga*," and subsequently the final element is further specified as "guṇa shall be for the *ik* which is the final element of the *aṅga*," then this [rule] alone is supplementary to that [paribhāṣā]. This is the position known as *taccheṣapakṣa*.

The phrase "that word" (*tatpadam*) encompasses both positions—that it refers to the penultimate rule (*antyaparibhāṣā*) and that it refers to the subsequent rule—because it is common to both the Bahuvrīhi and Tatpuruṣa interpretations. It should be understood that being "subsidiary to that" (*taccheṣatvam*) consists in having a scope of application that occurs subsequent to the application of that [rule], which is common to both cases.

By this, the following [objections] are refuted: (1) that if the meaning of the word *taccheṣa* were the state of being in syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the two previously mentioned *paribhāṣās*, then in forms such as *rājakīya*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) of the non-application of the *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*; and (2) that it is impossible for two rules located in different places, which are mutually independent yet assist in the application of a primary injunction (*vidhi*), to form a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*). This is because, when the application of both is possible within a single injunction, what is intended is their status as "refiners" (*pariṣkāraka*) of the injunction refined by the other.

Now, in the rules prescribing *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the term "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) is not a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), but rather a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to "the *ik*" (*ikaḥ*), meaning "of the *ik* that is a part of the *aṅga*. In that case, because there is no indicative mark (liṅga) in the form of a genitive of location, the paribhāṣā "of the final [element]" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*) does not apply. Consequently, since *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occur for the *ik* situated anywhere within a part of the *aṅga*, this constitutes the position of the counter-exception (*apavāda-pakṣa*).

For, in reality, there is no possibility of sublation (*bādha*) of that which has already been established by a scriptural rule; rather, it is understood that the scriptural rule intended to be the sublater lacks application to its own domain within the scriptural rule intended to be sublated—thinking, "If this [latter] did not exist, the former would apply here as well. It is a universally accepted tenet that "sublation" consists precisely in the conceptualization that the general rule (*utsarga*) does not have its own domain as its object.

However, a combination (of both meanings) is not possible, because by virtue of the authority of both paribhāṣās, there would be guna for both the final [element] and the *ik* vowel; thus, in the rule "miderguṇaḥ," there would be guna for both the final [element] and the *ik*. This is because it is impossible for a single occurrence of the genitive case in the word "aṅgasya" to convey two distinct meanings—namely, connection with a substitute (*sthāne-yoga*) and connection with a part (*avayava-yoga*). Furthermore, since there is no evidence (*liṅga*) for anything other than connection with a substitute, the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyasya" (P. 1.1.52) would apply. Moreover, there is no proof for [the assumption of] repetition (*āvṛtti*) or any such device.

For this very reason, with the intention that even the option (vikalpa) regarding the substitution of a *guṇa* for the final *ik* of the root *mid* is untenable, these two [paribhāṣās] were not even considered as a possibility in the Bhāṣya. In that regard, there is a fault in the first [paribhāṣā] in rules such as "miderguṇaḥ," because the final letter is not an *ik*, and the *ik* is not the final letter. Consequently, since both paribhāṣās have their scope in forms like *bhavati*, and there is no deciding factor (*vinigamaka*) here to choose between them, if both were abandoned, it would follow that the *guṇa* substitution applies to the whole of the stem. As the Vārttika states:

If it is argued that [the rule] "vṛddhi and guṇa are substitutes for the final [element]" applies here, then the term *ig* must be explicitly mentioned in the rules concerning *mid*, *mṛj*, roots ending in *puk*, those with a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), *ṛcchi*, *dṛśi*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of these substitutions applying to the entire stem (*sarvādeśa*) in cases where the suffix does not begin with a vowel (*aniganta*).

Because the particle *ca* has the sense of providing a reason (*hetvarthaka*), the term *ig* must be mentioned in each of those specific instances to prevent the application of the substitution to the whole stem in the aforementioned cases.

If, however, following the aforementioned improper interpretation (*kukalpanā*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) were to be restricted exclusively to *ik* everywhere, then there would be extreme heaviness (*gaurava*) in comprehension; furthermore, in cases such as *bhinna*, since it lacks the characteristic of being an *ik*, the prohibition of *guṇa* would fail to apply.

If, however, it is assumed that because *kn* is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the prohibition of the rule based on a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha-lakṣaṇa*), but not of *guṇa* in general—and therefore no prohibition of *guṇa* applies in cases such as *laigavāyana*—then, rather than that assumption, the position that the word itself is present (*padopasthiti-pakṣa*) should be accepted for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, even under that view of an exception (*apavāda-pakṣa*), just as in *ajuhavuḥ*, there would be *guṇa* by the rule "jusi ca" in forms such as *anenijuḥ* and *paryaveviṣuḥ*.

Just as in the case of *bhavati* and so forth, in *īhitam* and so forth as well, there would be the *guṇa* substitution [of *i* for *ī*] by the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*. Just as in *agne*, in *agnicit* and so forth as well, there would be the *guṇa* of the vocative [substituting *e* for *i*] by the rule *hrasvasya guṇaḥ*. Just as in *agnayaḥ*, in *agnicitaḥ* and so forth as well, there would be the *guṇa* [substituting *e* for *i*] by the rule *jasi ca*. Just as in *kartari*, in *sukṛti* and so forth as well, there would be the *guṇa* [substituting *ar* for *ṛ*] by the rule *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ*. Just as in *agnaye*, in *agnicite* and so forth as well, there would be the *guṇa* [substituting *e* for *i*] by the rule *gherṅiti*.
In cases such as *bābhravya* and *vatsauśruta*, there would also be the application of the *guṇa* substitution by the rule "orguṇaḥ. Accordingly, the Vārttika states:

"If [the objection] is raised that [the rule applies] to every *iṅ*, then there must be a prohibition against the final [element] regarding the *guṇa* substitutions for *jus*, *sārvadhātuka*, *ārdhadhātuka*, and those beginning with a short vowel (*hrasva*).

It should not be argued that because the two initial vowels (*ā* and *i*) are qualified by "short" (*hrasva*), the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is difficult to obtain here—since that rule exists for the purpose of providing a restriction where there would otherwise be no restriction—and furthermore, that even if a *guṇa* were to apply to the vowel *a*, there would be no harm as no other phoneme would be substituted. For if "short" were a qualifier of the base (*aṅga*), and that [base] were in turn a qualifier of *ig* through the relationship of part and whole, then the meaning of the sūtra would have to be: "A *guṇa* should occur in place of an *ik* which is a part of that base which ends in a short vowel."

Furthermore, because [the word] *agnicit* and others do not end in a short vowel, there would be no over-extension; yet, even in the absence of such an over-extension, a *guṇa* substitution would occur for the *u* sound and so forth in words such as *upagoḥ*.

Alternatively, in order to avoid the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between the two short vowels, and to prevent the genitive case following the word *aṅga* from being interpreted as a "substitution for" (*sthāneyoga*), so that the quality (*guṇa*) may be established even for a non-final vowel, the paribhāṣā "ik" would have to be brought into operation. In that case, both "the base" (*aṅgam*) and "short" (*hrasvam*) would qualify only "ik. The distinction is that for the former, the relation is that of being a constituent part (*avayavatvam*), while for the latter, it is identity (*abheda*) as the mode of connection. Consequently, the meaning is: "There shall be *guṇa* substitution for an *ik* that is non-different from a short vowel which is a constituent part of the base."

And likewise, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of both [rules], "of the short vowel" (*hrasvasya*) and "also before *jas*" (*jasi ca*), is easily established. Similarly, in the rule "ṛto ṅi," the meaning is "of that which is a non-different from *ṛ* belonging to a member of a stem (*aṅgāvayava*). In the rule "orguṇaḥ," the meaning is "of an *ik* vowel belonging to a member of a stem that is a non-different from the letter *u*. However, in cases such as *agnicite*, if one holds the view that the designation *ghi* resides solely in the phoneme (*varṇaniṣṭhā*) and not in the word (*padaniṣṭhā*), then there would be an over-extension of the rule "gherṅiti."

If it is argued that, under the view that *guṇa* applies to the *ik* vowels that are parts of a verbal root (*dhātu*), forms such as *bhettā* would already have *guṇa* established even without the rule "the *puk*-ending [roots] and those with a light penultimate vowel" (*pugantalaghūpadhasya*), and thus that rule serves merely as a restriction (*niyamārtha*)—so that there is no fault in cases like *īhita* and the like—here they say:

if the restriction were "only for a light penultimate vowel before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes," then there would indeed be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the rules "guṇa for a short vowel" (*hrasvasya guṇaḥ*) and "guṇa for *o*" (*orguṇaḥ*). For in those instances, the *guṇa* is not caused by *sārvadhātuka* or other such suffixes.

If it is argued that [the rule] "guṇa occurs only before sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka suffixes when the penultimate vowel is light" applies, then there would indeed be a fault in forms such as *īhitā*. For in this case, the guṇa substitution does not apply to a light penultimate vowel. Nor can one find a solution through the two restrictive rules (*niyama*), because those two cannot be obtained within a single sentence.

Even if one resorts to the interpretation of non-recurrence (*āvṛtti*) and so forth, there would still be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *anenejuḥ*, because a stem (*aṅga*) with a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) and a sārvadhātuka suffix exist there. Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa states that in cases such as *he buddhe*, *buddhayaḥ*, *picavya*, and *buddhaye*, since there is no light penultimate vowel, an over-extension is absolutely unavoidable. Therefore, it is established that the position [of the rule] as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule] is indeed defective.
On this point, they say: since the stem itself is qualified by the affix implied by the term "stem," the aforementioned defect does not apply.

If, however, the *ik* is qualified by the suffix (*pratyaya*) being heard and by the *jus* etc., such that—according to the literal statement—the *guṇa* would apply to an *ik* followed by a suffix or followed by *jus* etc., and likewise [the rule] "of an *ik* belonging to a stem ending in *ṛ*, which is a constituent of a stem followed by the suffixes *ṅi* or a *sarvanāmasthāna*" and so forth were intended, then there would be no fault; yet this must be considered. For the stem (*aṅga*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) possess a mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) toward one another.

Nor should it be argued that, because the *aṅga* has attained the status of being a qualifier of the *ik*, it is more appropriate for the suffix (*pratyaya*) to be construed with the qualified object—the *ik*—rather than with the *aṅga*. This is because the construction follows the principle of "the qualification of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭasya vaiśiṣṭyam*), meaning: "that *aṅga* which ends in *ṛt* and is followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix], the *ik* that is a constituent part of it [is strengthened]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of qualities such as redness (*raktatva*) not being construed with the staff (*daṇḍa*) and so forth, but rather being construed only with the person (*puruṣa*) through the conjunction with that in which they inhere (*svasamavāyisaṃyoga*).

Now, if one were to postulate a syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in accordance with the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*) and thereby construct the connection [of the suffix], even then, when considering the relative weight (*tāratamya*) of the two positions—namely, the position that the word-meaning is presented through the word (*padopasthiti*) versus the other—the presence of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) is unavoidable. This is because a mere possibility of some kind of justification is of no consequence; rather, it is only the relative simplicity (*lāghava*) in comparison to the opposing view that determines the establishment of a particular position. By this, the argument for the validity of the "remainder" (*taccheṣa*) position, based on the intention to postulate forms such as *mid-i* from *mid*, is also refuted.

Now, let it be that this *ik-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning the substitution of *iK*) sublates the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* (the rule concerning the substitution of the final letter) by means of the principle of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*); this is the position accepted by the teacher Kroṣṭrīya. It should not be argued that a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between two rules occurs only when both have found their scope elsewhere, whereas the *ik-paribhāṣā* has no scope at all because there is no subject matter for it apart from the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*. For such a conflict is indeed possible.

Regarding the argument that in *rāmebhyaḥ* there is a possibility of two substitutes for one original (*sthānin*), whereas in *medyate* there is no possibility of even a single substitute for two originals—and thus "impossibility" alone constitutes the meaning of the term *vipratiṣedha* (conflict)—that is not correct. For, by means of the two paribhāṣās, the *ikāra* and the *dakāra* apply with respect to distinct domains; and since there is indeed a possibility that both might occur simultaneously, this case does not differ from the position [of the Paribhāṣā] concerning the remainder (*taccheṣa*).

However, on the view that there is indeed sublation (*bādhana*) even when [two rules] are simultaneously applicable, if this paribhāṣā were not commenced, then by the rule *alo 'ntyasya*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply to the letter *d* alone. Therefore, by the maxim *yenāprāpte*, it is precisely an exception (*apavāda*) to that; and since a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception is impossible, it is improper to postulate a meaning for the term "conflict" that is not well-established.
Consequently, the position involving the presence of the word (*padopasthitipakṣa*) alone is superior.

They say that when the word *ika* occurs in rules such as "jusi ca," its connection [with the rule] is *antaraṅga* because of the unity of the sentence (*padaikyavākyatā*). However, the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyasya" (P. 1.1.52) is connected there through the unity of the larger sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*) only after the understanding of the intermediate sentential meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*) regarding the injunction has occurred; thus, its connection is *bahiraṅga*. This is because, without the understanding of the intermediate sentential meaning, there can be no determination that the genitive case denotes a "place" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).

That is questionable; for if there were no comprehension of the intermediate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*) in injunctive sentences, the application of the *ik-paribhāṣā* would also be difficult to establish. If the mere words "guṇa" and so forth were to trigger its application, it would follow that it would apply even in cases where a specific substitute (*sthānin*) is indicated. Its application occurs only when, through the comprehension of the intermediate sentence-meaning "the *guṇa* of the *aṅga* should take place," the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*)—namely, between the *aṅga* and the *guṇa*—is understood. Nor does this render the aforementioned defect unavoidable.

This is because a specific locus (*sthānin*) is indicated. Nor does this lead to the untenability of the application of the *ik-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the substitution of *ik* vowels) in cases such as *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*, where there is a mention of the locus as "of the *aṅga*. This is because what is intended is the absence of a mention of a locus that does not give rise to a desire to know another locus. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the statement, "In this way, the *ik-paribhāṣā* is brought to mind by the word 'guṇa'," for that [statement] intends only a qualified [locus].
For this very reason, they have explained: "Wherever *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are enjoined by means of the words 'guṇa' and 'vṛddhi'..."

By this, the following view is refuted: that since a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) does not apply to a restatement (*anuvāda*), the term *ik* cannot possibly apply to a restatement such as "vṛddhir yasya," and therefore that [mention of *ik*] is merely a statement of the resultant meaning. This is because the aforementioned absence—which is implied by the fact of being a thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*)—enters into the scope of the indicator (*liṅga*) as its delimiting property (*liṅgatā-avacchedakatā*). Therefore, first there is the cognition of the meaning of the subordinate sentence; then follows the application of the *ik-paribhāṣā*; and finally, through syntactic unity with the word *ik*, there arises the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*).

In that case, first there is the comprehension of the meaning of the injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*). Then, by means of the genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), the *paribhāṣā* rule "of the final [element]" (*alo 'ntyasya*) is brought to mind. Subsequently, there is the application of this *paribhāṣā* to the final vowel (*al*) within the scope of the genitive of locus heard in the injunctive sentence. However, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) at the level of the words themselves. Thus, the comprehension of the intermediate sentence-meanings (*avāntara-vākyārtha*) serves as the basis for both.

[Objection: But in this way, in rules such as "mider guṇaḥ," since the *ik-paribhāṣā* itself would result in being *bahiraṅga*, only the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* would be applicable. [Response: True. However, since the status of being a *sthāna* (original locus) is defined in relation to a substitute (*ādeśa*), it is necessary that the specific nature of the enjoined element be included within the indicator (*liṅga*) even there; for a cognition of *sthānatva* that does not apprehend a specific substitute is untenable, and furthermore, such a cognition would be useless for the operation of that *paribhāṣā*.

Nor should it be argued that even so, there is no regulating factor for the application of the *ik-paribhāṣā* alone in that instance; for, although there is an absence of the relationship between *antaraṅga* and *bahiraṅga* according to the aforementioned reasoning, the *ik-paribhāṣā* must still be stated as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*. Since the operation of the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* occurs only after first avoiding its exceptions, and since knowledge of the avoidance of its domain is impossible without certainty regarding the operation of those exceptions, the determination of the operation of the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* is dependent upon that [certainty]. Consequently, the status of the *ik-paribhāṣā* as *bahiraṅga* remains unaltered.

By this, the argument that there is parity between the two positions even in the case of the rule *alo'ntyasya*—provided that one accepts the position of the word (*pada*) being present—is refuted; for that position is not supported by the Bhāṣya and other authoritative sources.

However, some maintain that in the context of that [view], in the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, the term *alpa* would not have its meaning as the primary referent (*arthaparatva*). Consequently, the mention of the non-compound form (*asamāsanirdeśa*) would be redundant; furthermore, in the case of *dvīpam*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *ī*-substitution for the initial vowel of the compound word *āp*. This is because even in the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, only the view that the word (*pada*) is present [in the cognition] is expressed by it, and thus the meaning of *alpa* being the primary referent is of no use. Even so, they say that since the connection between two words must be expressed, the status of being "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*) is not removed.

In this regard, because a coreferential (sāmānādhikaraṇya) connection between "of the *aṅga*" and "of the *ik*" is more logical, when the referent of the word *ik* functions as a qualifier of the *aṅga*, the resulting sentence-meaning is "of the *aṅga* ending in an *ik*. Consequently, since the condition for the genitive case in the sense of "in place of" (*sthāne-yoga*) remains intact, the paribhāṣā "an operation concerning an *al* applies to the final [al]" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*) indeed presents itself.

In cases such as *miderguṇaḥ*, however, because the stem ends in a consonant (*halanta*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the rule *iko yaṇaci* is impossible. Consequently, the word *ikaḥ* must be construed in a non-coreferential manner (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) as "the *ik* which is a constituent of *mid*. Since there is no evidence in the form of a genitive of place (*sthāneyoga-ṣaṣṭhī*), the paribhāṣā "the substitute takes the place of the final letter" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*) does not apply; thus, the *guṇa* substitution is established for the non-final vowel. Nor should it be argued that here too the paribhāṣā "the substitute takes the place of the final letter" would be triggered by the genitive of place (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) contained in the word *ikaḥ*.

In this regard, immediately after the application of the term *ikaḥ*, when the paribhāṣā "the substitute is in place of the final [element]" (*alo 'ntyaparibhāṣā*) presents itself, the meanings of both "of the final *ik*" and "of the final member of the *ig*" are sublated. This is because the final element of *mid* lacks the status of being an *ik*, and because it is impossible for the final letter *d* to be a member of an *ig*. Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with what is presupposed (*upajīvya-virodha*) if one were to understand *ikaḥ* as denoting the substituendum independently while simultaneously prescribing a guna for the final element.

However, in cases such as *aṅgasya*, because the status of the original element (*sthānitva*) of the *aṅga* is established by way of its constituent parts, there is no contradiction with what is presupposed; thus, there is a difference [between these two cases]. Therefore, it is established that the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is indeed the indicator (*liṅga*) for the paribhāṣā "of the vowel at the end" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*), provided it does not contradict the status of the original element.
Thus ends the third Āhnika of the first Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi.

Na dhātulopa ārddhadhātuke 4: When an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is the cause for the elision of a portion of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions for *ik*-vowels do not take place. Examples: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*. [These are derived] from the roots *lolū*, etc., with the *yaṅ* affix, followed by the *ac* affix (of the *pacādi* class). By the rule "yaṅo'ci ca," there is the elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ*.

In this context, because the rule "sanādyantā dhātavaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.32) assigns the technical designation *dhātu* (verbal root) to a form ending in *yaṅ*, the guna substitution prescribed by the rule "sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84)—which is occasioned by the elision of the *yak* that is a constituent part of that [verbal base]—would otherwise apply by taking the *ac*-affix as its cause. That [guna] is prohibited by this present statement. Here, "oneness" (*aikyam*) refers only to the individual instance (*vyakti*) that serves as the cause, and not even to the property-limiting factor (*nimittatāvacchedaka*). Otherwise, since the elision of the verbal-base constituent would have *actva* (the property of being an *ac*) as its limiting factor, while the guna substitution would have *ārddhadhātukatva* (the property of being an *ārddhadhātuka*) as the limiting factor for the *ac*-affix, it would follow that the prohibition could not take effect.

In this context, the term *dhātu* (verbal root) is used figuratively to refer to its constituent parts. Although in the word *dūram*—derived from the prefix *duḥ* and the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *rak* according to the rule "durīṇo lopaśca," wherein the root undergoes elision and the final *r* of the prefix is dropped by "ro ri," followed by lengthening by "ḍhralope"—there is indeed an elision of the entire verbal root, nevertheless, such an elision is redundant because there is no possibility of the application of *guṇa* or other such modifications that would need to be prohibited.

Regarding the term *dhātulopa* (in the context of Pāṇini 1.1.4), under the view that it is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, three interpretations are possible: that the mention of *ārddhadhātuka* is a qualifier of the elision (*lopa*), a qualifier of the prohibited element (*niṣedhya*), or a qualifier of both. Among these, in the first case, the meaning is that when there is an elision of a portion of the verbal root caused by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur.

In that case, since there would be the undesirable consequence of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* even when they are caused by other factors, the *guṇa* substitution in *pra iddhaḥ*—formed from the root *indh* with the prefix *pra* and the suffix *kta*, where the elision of the nasal (*n*) is triggered by the rule *aniditām*—would not occur. This is because the elision of the nasal is conditioned by the *ardhadhātuka* suffix *kta*, and although that elision has both [the vowel and the nasal] as its substituends, it does not lose its status as having the vowel *i* as a substituend. Nor can one argue that the prohibition does not apply because the rule was not formulated by explicitly pronouncing the word *ik*; for while that might be the case elsewhere due to the force of the word *ca* (and), here there is no evidence that the rule intends to refer to the specific phonetic form of the word *ik*.
This is because the word "ika" refers solely to its meaning; otherwise, the refutation belonging to the third position should be applied.

Now, in this matter, regarding the view that "first the verbal root is joined with its suffix, and afterwards with the prefix," the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)—which depends on the suffix *kta* presented first—is indeed *antaraṅga*; whereas in the view that "first with the prefix, and afterwards with the suffix," the *guṇa* substitution is likewise [the *antaraṅga*]. In either case, the *guṇa* is without exception; for by the maxim "that which is *bahiraṅga* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*," the *guṇa* cannot be subject to prohibition because it is *asiddha*, and since the prohibition itself is *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga*, the *guṇa* remains without exception.

True; this fault does not indeed apply to the present case. However, followers of Kaiyaṭa maintain that the very same refutation which will be stated later regarding the third alternative—beginning with "but it is divided" (bhedyate)—should be understood here as well.

However, the followers of Haradatta maintain that because of the prohibition, "When there is no immediate sequence with a vowel (*ajānantarya*), the designation as external (*bahiṣṭva*) is not established," the rule "An external operation is as if unestablished" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*) does not apply here. This is because the meaning of that [prohibition] is that when one of two [operations] depends upon immediate sequence with a vowel, the rule "as if unestablished" does not operate. And in this case, since the sequence [of sounds] in the formation of *ādguṇa* (the single substitute for *ā* + *i*) does not involve a vowel, it depends upon immediate sequence with a vowel; therefore, they say that even the non-establishment of *preddham* is a flaw in this context.
We shall examine this further under the sūtra "A substitute for a vowel is like the original when followed by something else" (*acaḥ parasmin*).

If, however, *ārddhadhātuka* were a qualifier of that which is to be prohibited (*niṣedhya*), then the rule would mean: "When there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātulopa*) caused by any cause whatsoever, guna and vṛddhi [substitutions] caused by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix do not occur. Consequently, from the root *knūyī* (meaning "to sound") with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the augment *puk*, and the elision of *y* according to the rule "lopo vyoḥ," the guna substitution characterized by the suffix ending in *puk* would also not take place. If one were to avoid this prohibition by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) such as the rule "cele knopeḥ," it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), as well as the fault about to be mentioned. If, on the other hand, both [the elided element and the suffix] are qualified by the same principle through methods such as *tantra*, that very same complexity remains.

Even if the meaning "when there is elision of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix as its cause, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur" is established, the prohibition would still apply even in cases where two distinct individual instances—one bearing the technical designation *ārdhadhātuka*—are both the cause for the elision and the cause for the *guṇa* substitution, respectively.

Furthermore, from the root *bhid* with the causative suffix (*ṇi*), when the suffix *yak* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*)—resulting in the form *bhidiya*—the elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*) would occur by the rule "ṇeraniṭi" because it is mandatory. Once that elision has occurred, even the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would not take effect, as it is performed by relying on the causative marker (*ṇic*) which has been elided, yet its presence is still required by the principle of "designation based on what has been [previously] present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, the form *bhidyate* would not be possible; this is because both the causative marker (*ṇi*) and the suffix *yak* are considered *ārddhadhātuka*.

Nor should it be argued that, because a *guṇa* substitution—which depends merely on a condition (*pratyaya*)—is *antaraṅga* (internal) relative to the elision of the *ṇi*-affix which depends on a specific condition, namely an *ardhadhātuka* suffix, the *guṇa* would necessarily occur first. This is because the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* prevents its application; for since the elision of the *ṇi* is yet to come into being, the *ardhadhātuka* suffix that serves as the cause for the *guṇa* is itself on the verge of destruction. Furthermore, this follows from the maxim: "An *utsarga* (general rule), even when its cause has already arisen, is set aside by an *apavāda* (exception), even when the latter's cause is yet to arise. Once the *ṇi* is elided, the elision of a portion of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is accomplished, and thus this prohibition [of *guṇa*] will indeed take effect.

However, some say that even the principle already stated is included within the "principle of non-completed arrangement" (*akṛtavyūha*), because the absence of an exception's scope also enters into the category of causes.

Therefore, the meaning is simply this: when there is a *lopa* (elision) of a verbal root in a particular *ardhadhātuka* suffix, guna and vṛddhi do not occur on account of that [suffix]. Since it is established that the elision and the guna, etc., share the same individual *ardhadhātuka* suffix as their cause, the desired conclusion is proven.

In this regard, although the meaning of the sūtra might appear to be that—inasmuch as the word-meaning [of *ik*] has already been presented by the preceding sentence as the object of negation (*pratiyogin*)—only that [word-meaning] would be construed when there is an expectancy for the correlate of the negation, and thus the word *ik* would not be presented in the aforementioned instance; and consequently, the prohibition of *guṇa* would not apply to forms such as *loluva*, whereas on the contrary, in cases like *bhedyate*, *guṇa* would undesirably result for the consonant (*vyañjana*). Nevertheless, if the sūtra *dīdhīvevīṭām* were to prohibit the presentation of the word *ik* in those instances, then [conflict would arise] between the *ik-paribhāṣā* and the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*.

Since there would be no distinction in the result, the prohibition of word-based presentation (*padopasthiti*) would be rendered meaningless; therefore, even here, word-based presentation is not what is prohibited. Rather, when the general rule (*utsarga*) that [the suffix] *bhavati* occurs presents itself, the meaning of the sentence is that "guṇa and vṛddhi do not occur. Why is it stated "*dhātulope*" (when there is elision of a verbal root)? It is so that, because [the suffix] is both prescribed and prohibited only for the *ārddhadhātuka* context, there may be no unintended option (*vikalpa*) due to a lack of other recourse. Why is it stated "*ārddhadhātuke*" (in an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix)?

In examples such as *totorti* and *momorti*, when the technical designation *sārvadhātuka* applies to the suffix *tip*, the rule "rāllopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.21) effects the elision of the consonants *ch* and *v*. In that case, this example is intended to ensure that the prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), which would otherwise depend on the suffix *tip*, does not take effect. The meaning of the rule is: "There shall be elision of the consonants *ch* and *v* following a *repha* (the letter *r*) when a suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound, or one that is nasalized (*anunāsika*), follows. This is the illustrative example for that interpretation. However, when the meaning is "when a suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound or one that is nasalized follows," this is the illustrative example for that [other] interpretation.

However, when the view is that *kṅiti* is a qualifier for *jhalādau* in that context, then [the forms] such as *totormī* arise; for in those cases, the rule applies because of the subsequent suffixes beginning with a nasal (*anunāsika*). What is the purpose of specifying the substitute (*sthānin*) as *ika*? [It is so that] in the case of *abhāji rāgaḥ*, where the suffixes *ciṇ* and *ghañ* have been applied to the roots *bhañj* and *rañj*, and the *nakāra* has been elided by the rules "bhañjeśca ciṇi" and "ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ," the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" should not take effect.
