However, this must be noted: from the root *pac* with the *yaṅ* suffix, namely *pāpacya*, when the suffix *ṇvul* is added, the rule "yasya halaḥ" prescribes the elision of *ya* following a consonant (*hal*). By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "ādeḥ parasya"—which means that whatever is prescribed for what follows [something] should be understood as applying to its initial element—the elision of the mere consonant (*vyañjana*) occurs. Subsequently, by the rule "ato lopaḥ," the vowel *a* is elided separately. Then, by the rule "acaḥ parasmin," the elision of the *a* is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), which obstructs the status of the radical *a* as a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Consequently, due to the absence of this penultimate vowel, the *vṛddhi* strengthening does not take place.

The form *pāpacaka* is derived as follows: when there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix, since the elision of the entire complex is accepted, the substitute *ajjhal* does not possess the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*); consequently, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) indeed occurs, resulting in *pāpācaka*. This is because the prohibition under discussion does not apply there, as it pertains only to that which is characterized by an *ik* vowel (i.e., the substitution of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* for an *ik*). It is just as in the case of *nonau* [in the expression] *na nau*.

On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya says: This sūtra is indeed unnecessary. Even in the case of the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅ-luk*), by accepting a separate elision of *al*, the absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is established simply because the *aṅga* no longer ends in an *ik* vowel due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor should it be argued that the rule "yaṅo'ci ca" (Pāṇini 2.4.74) would, by the principle of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenanāprāpti-nyāya*), act as an exception (*bādhaka*) to the elision of *at*.

In the rule *yasya halaḥ*, by dividing the connection as *yasya* and continuing the term *ato lopaḥ* from the previous rule, the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* of the word *ya* is prescribed. Since the elision of the consonant alone is governed by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca*, there is no absence of the maxim *yenanāprāpte* (the maxim of non-application where [a rule] would otherwise apply) due to the difference in scope—namely, that there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *a* and the elision (*luk*) of the *y*. Thus, since the result is achieved through the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), this sūtra is indeed redundant.

It should not be argued that, in this way, there would be no *vṛddhi* in the word *nonāva* in the phrase *na caivaṃ kṛṣṇo nonāva vṛṣabham*, nor would there be [the form] *pāpācaka*; for [it might be claimed] that this is due to the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as being *sthānivat*. This is because we accept that only an elision (*luk*) caused by a vowel (*ajnimittaka*) can have a consonant alone as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*).

Because of the word *ca* in the rule, by virtue of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely), there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix even in cases other than those involving an *ac* suffix; however, because this is not invariably required (*anaimittikatvāt*), it operates prior to the very production of the suffix. This is due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal) compared to the *bahiraṅga* (external) operations such as the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*), which depend on the presence of the suffix for their application. Moreover, that elision is indeed relative to the entire complex (*samudāya-pratiyogika*). And for that [elision], there is no status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), because it is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for both vowels (*aj*) and consonants (*hal*). For the rule regarding *sthānivadbhāva* is prescribed only for a substitute whose original locus (*sthānin*) consists solely of vowels.

Now, if this were the case, then *uvaṅ* and other such substitutes would not occur either; for if the *a* were treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, there would be no immediate succession (*avyavahita-paratva*) of an *ac*-affix [to the *a*]. To this, Kaiyaṭa and others reply: *uvaṅ* and the rest occur there by relying on the *a* itself which has become *sthānivadbhūta*, and not by taking the *ac*-affix (such as the *ac* of *pac-ādi*) as the cause. This is due to the reasoning already stated. Nor should it be argued that the mere *a* which is a part of the *yaṅ* suffix lacks the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*); for after the elision of the *y*, even that [remaining *a*] possesses the status of an affix.

Nor should it be argued: "Since the vowel *a* lacks the status of being an affix (*pratyaya*) at the time the consonant *y* is present, and since it has already been elided prior to the *y*, the status of being an affix cannot apply even after the elision of *y*; for a property that is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the original element (*sthānin*) cannot be obtained even through extended application (*atideśa*). This is because extended application is accepted on the basis of mere possibility.

If, after the elision of the *yakāra*, the elision of the [subsequent] *yakāra* were not to occur, then that [subsequent *yakāra*] would indeed possess the status of an affix (*pratyayatva*). Therefore, since there is no obstacle to the extension (*atideśa*) of the possible status of being an affix even when it has been elided—by virtue of its grammatical fitness—the prohibition regarding the *vare* (the *vara*-suffix) serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) here. For instance, in the case of *yāti* derived from the *yaṅ*-stem with the suffix *varaC*, once the elision of *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) and the elision of *y* and *v* (*lopo vyor vali*) have taken place, the elision of the *ā* [of *yā*] by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" would apply, triggered by the *a* through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). To prevent this elision of the *ā*, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* is initiated in that context. Thus, the prohibition regarding the *vare* is the evidence for this.

If, however, there were an extension (*atideśa*) only of what is seen in the original locus (*sthānin*), then even though the letter *a* would possess the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would lack the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*). Consequently, it would all the more lack the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka*. Furthermore, since the suffix *varaP* would not begin with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) and would be separated from the preceding element by the letter *a*, the elision of the long *ā* (*āto lopaḥ*) would simply not apply; thus, that [rule] would result in being redundant.

On this point, Haradatta and others argue as follows: when *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* have been applied to words ending in short or long vowels, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would be unavoidable. Nor should it be argued that the status of the vowel *u* as a penultimate (*upadhātva*) is precluded by the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of the substitute being like the original) of the elision of *a* (*allopasya*); for the vowel *u* does not precede any vowel (*acaḥ*) that has not already undergone a grammatical operation (*anādiṣṭāt*). This is because *uvaṅ* applies immediately after the elision of *a*. Furthermore, in the word *jaṅgama*, there would be the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) according to the rule "gamahana... (*Pāṇini 6.4.98*).

If, however, there were a prohibition by the term *anaṅ*, then in the case of *darīdṛśaḥ*, the guṇa substitution [of *ar* for *ṛ*] prescribed by the rule "ṛdṛśo'ṅi" would occur; in *dedyaḥ*, the augment *yuṭ* prescribed by "dīṅo yuḍaci" would occur; and in *sanīsraṃsaḥ* and *danīdhvaṃsaḥ*, the elision [of the nasal] prescribed by "aniditām" would occur; and in *yāyāḥ*, *vāvāḥ*, and so forth, the elision of the vowel *ā* prescribed by "āto lopa" would occur. Therefore, since the acceptance of the elision of the entire cluster is necessary, the sūtra must be commenced for the sake of establishing forms such as *loluva*.

As for the argument that there is no possibility of *guṇa* substitution because of the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule—since there exists a state of being prior to an unspecified vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) by way of the original locus (*sthānin*)—that is not correct. For although the *uvaṅ* substitute may possess the state of being prior to an unspecified vowel by way of its original locus (*sthānin*), the letter *u* itself does not. Even though the state of being prior to the vowel *a*, which was observed in the *u* at the stage of *lolūya*, could potentially apply to the *uvaṅ*, no rule whatsoever is applicable to it here. Furthermore, since the letter *u* alone is not the substratum sufficient to constitute the status of being an *ādeśa*, it is impossible to extend (*atideśa*) the state of being prior to an unspecified vowel—which resides in the letter *ū*—to that [substitute *uvaṅ*].

As for what was also stated—namely, that by the maxim "all substitutes are in place of all words," the relationship between the original (sthānin) and the substitute (ādeśa) rests only upon meaningful elements; thus, by way of *uvaṅ*, the substitute *loluv* takes the place of *lolū*, and since this [substitute] is prior to the vowel (*ac*) before which no rule has yet been applied (*anādiṣṭāt*), it is correct that when the substitution of *lolov* is to be effected via *guṇa*, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is indeed *sthānivat*—that too is incorrect.

That being the case, in place of *lolūya*, through the elision of *y* (yalopa) and subsequently the elision of *u* (allopa), the substitute *lolū* results; since this specific form alone enters the scope of the substituendum (*sthānin*), even "precedence" (*pūrvatva*)—even by way of the substituendum—is difficult to establish with respect to the vowel *a*.

In fact, we shall explain right there that the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule would be baseless if one were to rely on a "precedence" from a non-prescribed vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) via the substituendum.

As for what they say—that by the *paribhāṣā* "there is no rule [for application] when there is a further operation on that which has already undergone an operation on its parts," once *uvaṅ* has been applied, the *guṇa* substitution does not take effect—that too is incorrect; for even so, forms such as *cekṣiyaḥ* and *toṣṭuvaḥ* would remain unestablished. To explain: by the maxim "even those operations that are *antaraṅga* [are superseded]," the *yaṅ*-suffix is elided (*luk*), thereby overriding the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ."

Then, one might raise the objection that even if the elision (*allopa*) is treated as *sthānivat*, in the sequence *cekṣi a a toṣṭu a a*, the penultimate vowel of the stem would become light (*laghūpadha*) once the final *a* of the original element has been made the substitute; thus, since an *ac*-affix follows, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) should occur. Anticipating this, it was stated by the author himself that the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions take effect because they are *antaraṅga* (internal). Furthermore, the meaning of the stated *paribhāṣā* is: "When another stem-operation would apply only when a certain stem-operation has already taken place, that [subsequent] operation does not occur once the former has been performed. In this case, the *guṇa* for a light penultimate vowel does not apply only when the *uvaṅ* has occurred, because that [guṇa] would have applied even prior to it.

As for the claim that in the word *jaṅgama*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) need not be applied—on the grounds that by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not in [a stem ending in] *aṅ*," the rule is prescribed for a similar form (*aṅ-sadṛśa*) beginning with a visible vowel (*śrūyamāṇa-aj-ādi*)—that is not correct. For in that case, a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is indeed necessary; moreover, it has been explained by the author himself that the phrase "not in *aṅ*" (*na tv aṅi*) constitutes such a negation.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting that even "being heard" (*śrūyamāṇatva*) and "meaninglessness" (*anarthakatva*) possess the status of being the delimitors of the substratum of difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by that [property]. Consequently, in forms such as *jagmuḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) would not occur even in the second-person plural ending and the like. Furthermore, since "naturalness" (*svābhāvikatva*) and "beginning with a vowel" (*ajāditva*) would also result in having that same status, the elision would likewise fail to occur in forms such as *jagmuṣaḥ*.

This is because there is no restrictive rule to determine that among the properties residing in the counter-correlate of the difference—properties other than the delimiters of that counter-correlativity—it is specifically "being heard" that serves as the delimitor of the substratum of the difference.
As for what was also stated— that because of the mention of the *anubandha* in the rule "dīṅaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.1.45] in the context of the form *dedya*, the *yuṭ* augment does not apply— it has been said:
"That which is indicated by a *śtip*, a *śap*, an *anubandha*, or a *gaṇa*,
as well as where there is the mention of a single vowel (*ekāj*), these five cases do not occur in the *yaṅluk*."

This too is incorrect. Here, because *yah* is specified as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the elision (*lopa*), the meaning understood is that the operation does not apply to anything other than that. Furthermore, that which has entered the category of the cause (*nimitta*) is not connected with the effect (*kārya*). Whether this entry is direct or otherwise is a separate matter. For this very reason, in the rule *suptiṅantam*, if the inclusion of the suffix *tadanta* (ending in that) were absent in the phrase *kṛttaddhita*, then only the primary *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes themselves would incur the designation [of "word"], and consequently, designations would not apply to forms such as *bhid*. This is because of the prohibition "not a verbal root" (*adhātu*), which would prevent the application of the rule "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat-sūtra*).

Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa has stated immediately after [the passage] "nor [is it applicable] to *kvip* and the like, because they are not heard": "Nor does it apply by virtue of the rule for the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), for that which is prescribed as an operation for another on account of an affix occurs when the affix is elided; however, even that which is an operation belonging to the affix itself does not occur [in such a case], because that which is non-existent cannot be made the locus of an operation even by a hundred statements."

In this regard, the only distinction is that here there is a prohibition where previously there was a rule; for even the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) such as [the mention of] *śtip* pertains to matters other than the *yaṅ* [intensive] operation. And that—whether it be the mention of the single term *ekācaḥ* or the specific reference to each respective part—is another matter altogether.

By this, the objection raised against Haradatta’s statement in that [other] context—that the mention of the *anubandha* "dīṅaḥ" is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ-luk*—is also refuted. This is because in that context, its purpose was stated to be the prevention of the augment *yuṭ* associated with other suffixes; whereas here, there is no contradiction in applying that [augment] by relying on the letter "a" which is a constituent part of the *yaṅ*.

If it is argued: "Even so, the occurrence of *yuṭ* based on the *yaṅ*-suffix would still be improper, because *yuṭ* is prescribed for an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel (other than *a*) following *dīṅ*, and since this [suffix] remains a *yaṅ*-operation, [the substitution] does not lose its status; furthermore, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* in a rule concerning itself," we reply: True, but this leaves the impropriety of your own citation of the rule "śtipā śapā... and so forth exactly as it was.

The intention of the *Miśra* authors, however, is as follows: there is no evidence for the rule that the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) occurs immediately after the elision of *a* (*allopa*). This is because they accept that *luk* (complete elision) is stronger than all other types of elision. For this very reason, in forms such as *gomatpriya*, the elision of the case-ending *s* (*su*) is governed by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, and not by the elision of *hal* and *ṅi* endings (*halṅyādinimitta-lopa*). This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because [otherwise], due to the application of the rule regarding the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the insertion of *num* and so forth.

Nor should it be asked how [the elision] can occur when the *ac*-suffix is separated from the *yaṅ* by the letter *a*; for there exists a non-intervention relative to that which is delimited by the property of being *yaṅ*, which serves as the delimiting factor (*nirdeśyatāvacchedaka*) for the designation. However, due to the force of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the elision of *y* results in its application to all consonants (*vyañjana*)—this is another matter. But if one were to adopt a non-intervention only relative to that where the operation actually finds its rest in reality, it would contradict the passage in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *kṅiti ca*.

Because there is an intervention by the *akāra* which has become a *sthānivadbhūta*, how could [the rule apply] even afterwards? Furthermore, the situation remains the same. If it is argued that "only the non-intervention established by direct audition (*śruti*) is relied upon due to the authority of the grammatical statement," then from what is the fact that the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) has a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*) determined? For the locative case in *aci* can be justified as a locative absolute (*satisaptamī*). However, there is a discrepancy: whereas the elision of *y* is accepted as having a subsequent cause for the sake of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of *a*.

There is no evidence for accepting a locative case in the sense of "with reference to" (*parasaptamī*) even in the absence of a purpose; for even in cases such as *lolūyate*, the mere existence of the vowel (*ac*) is accepted in order to prevent the elision of the suffix *yak*. Nor should it be argued that, even so, the application of the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding the specific mention of a letter) is unavoidable; for in the sūtra *śnānnalopaḥ*, if one follows the view that the term *kṅiti* is carried over from a previous rule, the elision of *n* would not occur in *hinasti*, and thus the Bhāṣya provides a solution by adopting the locative in the sense of "when [the suffix] exists" (*satisaptamī*).

Is this not merely a description of the opponent's (pūrvapakṣin’s) position? For even in cases where the locative case (*saptamī*) is intended to signify posteriority (*paratva*), the locative still functions as a condition for the occurrence of an operation (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*); there is no specific rule for a locative signifying posteriority. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* would fail to apply even in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*. True. Nevertheless, because it is accepted that the locative here denotes the "domain" (*viṣaya-saptamī*), its non-application in those instances is established by the final doctrine (*siddhānta*). Thus, the application of *yuṭ* would indeed occur at the very moment the [suffix] is heard.

Nor should it be argued that, in view of that [subsequent rule], the elision (*lop*) itself must apply first; for the augment *yuṭ*, prescribed by reference to a marker with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*), is stronger due to its being without any other scope (*anavakāśatā*). This is because, after the root *dīṅ*, it is difficult to find any other *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) that bears the *ṅ*-sign. Nor should it be argued that the portion "bearing the *ṅ*-sign" (*ṅit*) is intended solely for what follows; for when it is possible, it is difficult to maintain that a rule serves only a subsequent purpose. For this very reason, the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the non-application of a rule once a grammatical operation has taken place) does not apply here either, since the cause [of the operation] is not itself the subject of the operation (*kāryin*).

If it is argued: "In that case, why not apply the *guṇa* substitution in *īkṣiya* and similar forms at the very stage when it is heard [in the rule], rather than by resorting to the *m* that has become a *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original) to effect that application? True. However, there is a disparity: the *guṇa* prescribed by rules such as *sārvadhātuka-ārdhadhātukayoḥ* is prohibited by the rule *kṅiti ca*; furthermore, the *guṇa* of a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha-guṇa*) cannot be applied while depending on that [substituted *m*], because the status of being a light penultimate vowel is only achieved by taking that [original *m*] itself. Moreover, since these two [rules] have their scope elsewhere, the elision (*lopa*) takes precedence there. Thus, the cases are dissimilar.

Let us return to the subject at hand. As for what they say—"In the rule *yasya halaḥ*, you yourself have accepted that the elision (*lopa*) has as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) merely a constituent part (*avayava*)."—in that regard, although it might not be worth raising the objection that the suffix *yuṭ* would occur in *dedīyaka* (since the elision of *y* would be impossible due to the absence of a *hal* [consonant] following it, and the form *dedīyaka* is therefore accepted), nor is the elision of *n* in *sanīsrasaka* and similar forms to be raised as an objection because it is universally agreed upon; nor is the elision of the vowel (*ā*) in *yāyāyakaḥ*, *vāvāyakaḥ*, and so forth to be raised as an objection.

Because of the absence of the elision of *y* (yalopa), there is an absence of the condition of being followed by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix that is marked with *k* or *ṅ* (ajādi-ṅit-ārdhadhātukaparatva); nevertheless, just as in the case of *jaṅgamakaḥ*—derived from the root *gam* with *yaṅ* and the suffix *ṇvul*—there is an absence of *vṛddhi* due to the status of the elision of *a* (*allopa*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, so too would there be an elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*). If, however, there is a prohibition here by the rule "not when *aṅ* follows" (*anaṅi*), then in the case of *tarīdṛśakaḥ*, there would be *guṇa* substitution by the rule "there is *guṇa* for *ṛ* and *dṛś* before *aṅ*" (*ṛdṛśo'ṅi*).

If, however, the resolution here is sought through the *paribhāṣā* regarding the function of constituent elements (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*) or by the rule "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not universally valid" (*saṃjñāpūrvako vidhir anityaḥ*), then one should not fear the elision of *n* in *sanīsrasaḥ* (in the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ) or the elision of the long *ā* in forms such as *yāyā*, *vāvā*, etc.; for the same resolution applies to both cases.

That too must be considered. Even if there is elision by the rule *yasya halaḥ*, one must still accept that the elision has the entire complex (*saṅghāta*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Nor should it be argued that the elision of *ya* following a consonant (*hal*) before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix—established as applying to the consonant alone by the maxim *ādeḥ parasya*—could not result in the elision of the whole complex.

According to the principle of non-attainment (*yenānāprāptinyāya*), since the elision [of *ya*] by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* is an exception to the elision of *at*, for you too, how could there be an elision of a constituent part (*avayavalopa*) in that case? This is equally applicable. Nor can the solution be found through the aforementioned splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). For here too, it has been stated as a resolution that by carrying over *ataḥ* from the rule *ato lopaḥ* and explaining it as "of that which ends in *a*, namely *yaṅ*," the rule *ādeḥ parasya* does not apply due to the force of the qualification.

This is because one can easily argue that, having formed a collective *dvandva* compound of *vyañjana* (consonant) and *ākāra* (the vowel *ā*), the application of the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.54] is precluded by the very force of prescribing the elision of both; furthermore, this is supported by Vāmana’s statement in his commentary that the term *yasya* refers to a cluster (*saṅghāta*). It is also supported by the natural sense of ancient manuscripts which cite *bebhiditā* and *marīmṛjitā* as examples under this sūtra. Moreover, since it has been stated that in the present prohibition, due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *ika*, this prohibition does not apply to the case of *pāpācaka* where the augment *vṛddhi* occurs according to the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116).

Furthermore, without the elision (*ya-lopa*) being correlative to a *saṅghāta* (a composite), it would be difficult to justify the occurrence of the aforementioned *vṛddhi* in that context. As for the explanation of Vāmana’s statement—that the elision applies only to the *yakāra* situated within the aggregate of *yakāra* and *akāra*, and not to the solitary *yakāra* in forms such as *aharyīd* or *amavyīd*—that is questionable. For even though such a status [of being part of an aggregate] is intended to be excluded from the grammatical description (*nirdeśa*), it actually exists there; moreover, at the time the elision is to take effect, such a status is absent even in what is to be included under the rule. This is because, according to that very view, the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) must be admitted to occur prior to this.

Furthermore, Haradatta’s interpretation is merely a restatement of another's commentary and lacks his own independent approval. For this very reason, the authors of the *Prakāśa*, after not extending the faults mentioned by Haradatta to the view that the elision (*lopa*) in the term *yasya* is an elision of a constituent part—thereby adopting the position that it is an elision of a part of the *yaṅ-luk*—concluded their discussion. Therefore, those who set out to establish the rule must accept that even in the case of elision (*lopa*), just as in the case of elision (*luk*), there is the cessation of the entire aggregate. This is because they proceeded specifically to refute the works of Haradatta and others, while supporting themselves with the aforementioned arguments and the statement of Vāmana.

For their intention is as follows: regarding the portion concerning Haradatta, "subversion of the text" (*granthopamarda*) refers to the interpretation that there is no intended meaning for the elision of the *yasya* [in the rule] to be an elision of a constituent part (*avayavalopa*); however, in both cases, for those who maintain that it is an elision of a constituent part, "subversion" indeed means a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).

By this, the objection that the *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening] in the word *pāpācaka*—derived from the root *pac* with the suffix *yaṅ* followed by the suffix *ṇvul*—is contrary to the *Bhāṣya* is refuted. For, when this sūtra is rejected, there is no intention (*tātparya*) in the *Bhāṣya* to prevent the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (P. 7.2.116), because the condition for the application of that rule is met: the elision of the entire cluster [of *yaṅ*] by the rule "yasya" (P. 6.4.148) does not qualify as a *sthānivadbhāva* substitute for an *aj* vowel (since the elided portion consists of both *a* and *y*), and thus the *upadhā-vṛddhi* remains valid. Furthermore, it has been stated that the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] under P. 1.1.5 does not apply here, because the elision is not conditioned by an *ik* vowel.

Furthermore, regarding the sūtra *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the Bhāṣya will state that under the view that "the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) applies when the original [element] is not being resorted to," the inclusion of *dvirvacana*, *vareya*, and *lopa* must be made in the sūtra *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58). For under the view that "the original is being resorted to," in the case of *dvirvacana*, by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *anaci*, only a consonant (*hal*) similar to that [original vowel] is resorted to, and not a vowel (*ac*). However, in the case of *vara*—when the elision of the vowel *ā* is prescribed—the original [vowel] is indeed resorted to by the rule *aci kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.65). Anticipating the objection, "How then can the mention of the word *vara* be necessitated?", Kaiyaṭa has stated:

Furthermore, since the status of being a suffix (pratyayatva) belongs to the aggregate as a whole and not to its constituent part, the vowel *ā*, there is no possibility [of its application] here at all, because the elision of *ā* is prescribed when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows. Thus, the intention of the authors of the Bhāṣya and others regarding how the substitution *uvaṅ* could depend on that [vowel], or how an extended application (*atideśa*) could apply even to what is merely possible, is as follows: [they intend to show that such an objection is invalid].

Furthermore, in examples such as *jaṅgama*, the introduction of operations like elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) which depend upon the *ṅit*-character would be untenable for both [the *yaṅ* suffix and the *kṅit* suffixes]. This is because the letter *ṅ* is an *anubandha* (indicatory marker) of the entire complex (*samudāya*) in the case of *yaṅ*. Even if the mere letter *a* were to undergo *sthānivadbhāva* (treatment as the original), its status as being of the nature of *yaṅ* would be difficult to establish. For this very reason, in forms such as *ramāyai*, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by the rule "vṛddhireci" alone and not by "āṭaśca"—as has been stated by the venerable Dīkṣitas; thus, one should reflect upon what has not been explicitly prescribed. This is the general direction [of the argument]. *kṅiti ca* 5.1.5.

In this definition, when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are dependent upon a suffix (*pratyaya*), they do not occur if that suffix possesses the markers *g*, *k*, or *ṅ*. This is because, by means of the rule of *carv-ādeśa*, the letter *ga* is also included as being prefixed before the letter *ka*.

As for the interpretation that those [persons] who obtain [the title] by relying on the status of being a *kīdā* (one who has studied) and so forth as the cause (*nimitta*), that is to be considered doubtful. This is because there is a rule of cognition that a property appearing as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the understanding generated by a word construed with words such as "cause" (*nimitta*) must be perceived as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that causality and so forth. This is evident from the cognition that in cases such as "the staff is the cause," the property of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) is the delimiting factor of causality, and in cases such as "the jar is the effect," the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) is the delimiting factor of effectness.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that causal agency (*kāraṇatva*) and so forth could not be apprehended from such a word. Consequently, if the status of being an effect—defined by a causal power delimited by *kittva* (the property of having the *kit* suffix)—were to reside in the vowels *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* as objects of the word, it would follow that the rule (*vṛtti*) [of Pāṇini] would lack authority. Furthermore, if the scripture (*śāstra*) were intended to apply there, an option (*vikalpa*) would result, similar to the case of taking up or not taking up the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; let this matter rest for now.

*Git*: *jiṣṇuḥ*. [The suffix] *gsnu* is applied by the rule "glājisthaśca. It is *kit*. [Examples: *stutaḥ*, *stutavān*. *ṅit*: *cinutaḥ*, *sunutaḥ*. The status of being *ṅit* is established by the rule "sārvadhātukamapit. Why specify "characterized by an *iK vowel" (*iglakṣaṇe*)? Consider *laigavāyanaḥ*. Because the rule "orguṇaḥ" specifies a particular locus (the *u* of *lau*), the term *iK* does not apply there; thus, even though the suffix *phak* is *kit*, the *guṇa* substitution caused by it still takes place.

For this very reason, in the case of *kāmayate*, although the suffix *ṇiṅ* has the marker *ṅit*, the vowel *vṛddhi* substitution for the radical *a* still occurs by virtue of that [marker], according to the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ. Why say "by virtue of"? [So that] in cases such as *chinnaṃ* and *bhinnaṃ*, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) likewise does not occur.

In this context, the words *ikaḥ* and *guṇavṛddhī* are understood from the preceding rules. Therein, when *ik* is qualified by the term *kṅiti*, the meaning becomes "when a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix follows, [a substitution occurs] for that *ik*. Upon the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when [something] is specified by a word ending in the locative case, the operation applies to what precedes it," the word *nirdiṣṭa* (specified) signifies that which is uttered immediately [before]. Consequently, in forms such as *citam* and *stutam*, the prohibition of *guṇa* would apply only to that *ik* which is situated immediately before the *kit* suffix and so on, but not in cases such as *bhinnim*. This is because [the *ik*] is separated [from the suffix] by the letter *d*.

Therefore, *kṅiti* is indeed a qualifier of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Consequently, this is not a locative of position (*parasaptamī*), because *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are not prescribed when *kṅit* follows; otherwise, there would result an undesirable optionality. Rather, it expresses mere causality (*nimittatāmātra*). And that [causality] is understood according to what is applicable: as being immediate in the case of a stem ending in *iK*, and as being mediate in the case of a light penultimate vowel. This is because a restatement (*anuvāda*) is restricted to referring to what has already been established by other rules. Furthermore, the status of being a cause is determined by specific properties such as being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, as heard in their respective individual rules.

This is because of the force of the prohibition regarding [affixes] beginning with *k* and *ṅ*, and because such [affixes] are not mentioned in the prescriptive rules themselves. Although the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) as the meaning of the locative case is not explicitly stated, nevertheless, when the connection is made—"those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which would otherwise occur when a *kit* or *ṅit* [affix] follows"—it is said that, by implication, the status of being a cause belongs to that affix. The evidence for this is the extension of the *kit*-status in rules such as *ralo vyupadhāt*. Otherwise, if the prohibition of *guṇa* did not apply due to the intervention [of the augment], the *kit*-status intended for that purpose would result in being redundant.

In reality, regarding the requirement for a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the rule *kṅiti*, although the term *ārdhadhātuka* from the preceding sūtra could provide that [qualificand] in the form of being a suffix mentioned under the heading of roots (*dhātu*), provided it is distinct from *tiṅ* and *śit*, if one were to accept such a qualified entity as the qualificand here, then rules such as *sārvadhātukam apit* would become redundant. Therefore, setting aside the "provided that" (*satyanta*) portion, the status of being a suffix mentioned under the heading of roots alone serves as the delimiting property of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*), because words expressing a qualified entity [denote the qualifier] only when there is a subverting reason (*bādhaka*).

This is because the status of referring to the mere qualificand (*viśeṣyamātra*) is accepted even without resorting to *lakṣaṇā*; for instance, in the rule "He should be heard from the Vedic texts" (*śrotavyaḥ śrutivākyebhyaḥ*), the word *śruti* is accepted as referring to all words that serve as means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, since the suffix brings the stem (*aṅga*) to mind, and because there is no intervention between the light-penultimate (*laghūpadha*) and the stem, the prohibition is established in both cases as well. This is because only an absence of intervention relative to the stem is accepted. And this is made clear right here by Kaiyaṭa.

In this regard, other grammarians introduce an optional *vṛddhi* for the root *mṛj* before an affix beginning with a vowel that is marked by *k* or *ṅ* (*kṅit*), according to the commentary on the preceding sūtra: *vā kṅiti aci*. Here, "affix" (*saṃkrama*) refers to a *kṅit* affix which serves as the cause for the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, based on the convention of the ancient teachers. The meaning of that [sūtra] is that when a *kṅit* affix beginning with a vowel follows, *vṛddhi* optionally occurs for *mṛj*: thus we have both *mṛjanti* and *mārjanti*.

Regarding this, Haradatta states: "Since the rule is already established by the paribhāṣā *'yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe'* (when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to a specific sound, it applies to that sound and what precedes it), the explicit mention of 'beginning with a vowel' (*ajādau*) is for the purpose of including the primary [vowel] beginning. Consequently, by virtue of the principle *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as identical to that which it designates), the operation does not apply to those cases where [the suffix] merely begins with a vowel [by virtue of being part of a larger form]. For example: *yūyam amṛja* and *tvayā amṛje*."

On this point, some [object]: even so, the dilemma regarding *mamṛja* remains unavoidable. For the substitution of the vowel *a* prescribed in place of the suffix *tha* (the middle-person plural ending) of the *liṭ* [perfect tense] would apply to the final [sound]. Nor should it be argued that such a rule is redundant, because the vowel following the letter *th* already exists there by its very nature.

Anticipating the objection that [the rule] is purposeful because it ensures the correct application of *ṇal* and other suffixes according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhya*), [the author replies]: This substitute consists of two *a*-sounds; because it has more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it replaces the whole [of the original]. Alternatively, since the governing context (*adhikāra*) is "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*), when an *a* is prescribed for the *tha* following a root, the *a* applies specifically to the letter *th* by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of the first of the subsequent" (*ādeḥ parasya*). In either case, the resulting form is the single substitute (*pararūpa*) according to the rule "for *at* before a guṇa-vowel" (*ato guṇe*); this is clear from the *Bhāṣya*. By virtue of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it indeed possesses the primary quality of beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*).

Others, however, say: "This [objection] is not sound, because it can be argued that just as the status of being a *jāti* (genus) based on the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as identical with its designator) is secondary (*gauṇa*), so too can the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original) be said to be secondary. Furthermore, the phrase 'in a vowel beginning with *a*' (*ajādau*) is not the body of an injunctive rule (*vidhi-vākya*) such that it would make known the aforementioned meaning; rather, it is precisely what is read later in the Bhāṣya under the rule *kṅityaci vā*. The word *ajādi* occurring in the earlier part of the Bhāṣya is merely a restatement of the meaning established by the *paribhāṣā* rule *yasmin* (P. 1.1.72) applied to the term *aci*."

Therefore, what was stated by Haradatta is not correct. For this very reason, Ātreya maintains that in the form *mamṛja*, there is an absence of *vṛddhi* precisely because of its inclusion in the *gaṇa*-list; likewise, in the *dhātuvṛttis*, the forms *yūyam mamṛja* and *mamārja* have been cited as examples.

This other point should also be noted: since the option (*vikalpa*) begins only with *kṅit* suffixes, it was stated here that this option does not apply to the suffix *ac*, which is the cause for the prohibition of *vṛddhi* due to its being the occasion for the elision of a portion of the root (*dhātvaṃśa*). However, in the context of the refutation (*pratyākhyāna*) of that rule, it was stated that by resorting to the status of the elided *at* as *sthānivadbhāva*, the option regarding *vṛddhi* certainly occurs according to the authority of the successive sages; that [latter view] is to be considered.

Since the intention of the Bhāṣya must necessarily be applied there—just as it is in the case of accepting the formulation of the Sūtra, so too it is in the case of its rejection—the point is established here by the very intention stated by Haradatta; such is the direction of the argument.

But [one might object]: in cases such as *nanvacinot* and *amārṭ*, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the suffixes *tiP* and so on would possess the property of being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅittva*), which would result in the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Nor can one argue that this is prohibited by the rule *analvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), because that rule does not apply to operations concerning *anubandhas*. And this is correct: since *anubandhas* are designated by the technical term *it*, they are elided even before the substitution occurs, and thus do not coexist with the original element (*sthānin*). This is because the status of being a *sthānin* belongs only to that which is the counter-positive of the cessation brought about by the substitute.

Furthermore, since the introduction or removal of *lakāra*-markers (*anubandhas*) is governed by the presence or absence of substitutes (*ādeśas*), and because, under the view that "markers are non-finite" (*anekāntā anubandhāḥ*), their inclusion within the category of substituenda is far-fetched; and because there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) here in the prohibition of *ītvam* in the rule "na lyapi," for if the *kittvam* of *ktvā* did not apply to *lyap* by virtue of being a substitute, then *ītvam* would not even arise due to the absence of *kittvam*, making that prohibition redundant—if this is argued, the Vārttika states:

"If it is argued that because the *lakāra* has a *ṅit* marker, there is the contingency of [its properties] applying to its substitutes by the principle of 'behaving like the original' (*sthānivadbhāva*), [the answer is] that it is established by the fact that *yāsuṭ* has two *ṅit* markers."

Otherwise, since the substitutes for [the affixes] would possess the *ṅit* property by virtue of the *liṅvad-bhāva* (the treatment as if being the original *liṅ*), the *yāsuṭ* which is a part thereof would also possess that property; consequently, the explicit statement in the rule "yāsuṭ is udātta and *ṅit* in the *parasmaipada*" would be redundant.

One might argue: "Let the designation *ṅit* be prescribed in rules such as *na ca stuyāt* for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *vṛddhi* by the rule *uto vṛddhir luki hali*—since that *vṛddhi* is not characterized by *it* because its locus (*sthānin*) is specified as *uta*—and for the purpose of prohibiting the *guṇa* substitution by the rule *jusi ca*, which is an exception to the prohibition *kṅiti ca* in forms like *cinuyuḥ*. For otherwise, without the force of the *ṅit* designation itself, the prohibition would be untenable based merely on the *ṅit*-ness resulting from *sthānivadbhāva*. How, then, can this [the *ṅit* designation] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? [Response: This should not be said. For the *ṅit* designation is indeed intended for the sake of the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions; however, since the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions in question are not characterized by *it* (*aniglakṣaṇa*), they are already prohibited even without the *ṅit* designation. Therefore, the *ṅit* designation is not required for that purpose. Consequently, it cannot be an indicator. Furthermore, in the case of *cinuyuḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution is not applicable because the suffix *jus* is treated as having the *ṅit* property by the rule *jusi ca*, which is an exception to the prohibition *kṅiti ca*; thus, there is no need for a further *ṅit* designation. Hence, the *ṅit* designation does not serve as an indicator.

Moreover, since the desired result would already be established by the rule *uta au* alone, the explicit mention of *vṛddhi* serves to establish the prohibition of *vṛddhi* on the basis of the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory. Alternatively, because the rule *ksasyāci* continues the word *aci*, the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for *jus* when it begins with a vowel; thus, once *yāsuṭ* is applied, *jus* becomes characterized by having a consonant as its initial element. Or else, in the *saṃhitā* reading of the rule *miderguṇo jusi ca*, one may divide it as *ajusi*, thereby prescribing the *guṇa* substitution for *us* when it begins with a vowel.

As for the objection that this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *cakruḥ* and *jahuḥ*, that is not so; because there is no deviation from the status of beginning with *a* (ajāditva) in those cases, the qualifier would be rendered redundant, and by virtue of that [qualifier], the rule necessarily applies only to the *jus* suffix.

In reality, however, *accāsāv us* is not a *karmadhāraya* compound; for the distinction of being an *ac* (vowel) is sublated within the aggregate consisting of the phonemes *u* and *s*. Nor is the word *ac* figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) when applied to the beginning of an *aj-ādi* (vowel-initial) element, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, there is no resolution here by means of the paribhāṣā: "When a rule is stated with reference to something [X], it applies to that which begins with X. This is because that paribhāṣā operates only when the genitive ending *alaḥ* follows an item cited in the locative case (*yasmin*), as indicated by the locative suffix in *yasmin*. And in this case, since the word is construed with the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the application of the paribhāṣā occurs only if this [word *ac*] itself ends in the locative case.

Furthermore, because the connection with the qualified [word] occurs through the fulfillment of grammatical fitness (*yogyatā*) by virtue of being followed by *aj* and so on, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). By this, the analysis as *uj-si* is also refuted. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya in the seventh [chapter] established the view that the word *aci* from the previous rule is to be understood as ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*); such is the direction of the argument.

Nor does this render the relevant *vārttika*—which states that there is no prohibition of *yāsuṭ* when there is *guṇa* in *jusi*—meaningless; for its intended purpose has been explained therein according to the aforementioned method. Furthermore, one should not argue that even so, in the case of *brūtāt*, the augment *iṭ* would undesirably apply by the rule "bruva īṭ," because the substitute *tātaṅ* is treated as *sthānivat* and thus possesses the property of being *pit*; for this is avoided by the principle that "the teaching regarding augments is not eternal."

According to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, in the rule *sārvadhātukamapit*, the term *apid* is divided into a separate *yoga*, and *ṅit* is carried over [from the previous rule]. By treating the negative particle *nañ* as having an exclusionary (*paryudāsa*) function and separating it, two sentences are postulated through repetition: "a suffix marked with *ṅ* is not *pit*" and "[a suffix] that is not *pit* [is *ṅit*]. Thus, when it is established that the properties of being *ṅit* and *pit* are mutually pervaded by absolute non-existence, it follows by implication that an original (*aupadeśika*) property subverts a derivative (*ātideśika*) one. Consequently, in the form *brūtāt*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur.

Because the *ṅit*-ness (*ṅittva*) taught by the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.4] sublates the *vit*-ness (*vit-tva*) that is extended [to it] by extension (*atideśa*). However, in cases such as *acinot*, because the *pit*-ness is taught directly by the rule [Pāṇini 3.4.78], the opposite occurs, and thus the prevention of *guṇa* and so forth is established. Here, the prescription of *ṅit*-ness for *yāsuṭ* is precisely for the purpose of re-establishing *ṅit*-ness, since the *ṅit*-ness derived from the *liṅ* suffix through extension is sublated by the *pit*-ness derived from the *tiP* and other affixes.

Consequently, when both are taught directly, the rule of "the sublation of the limited by the unlimited" (*sāvakāśa-niravakāśa-nyāya*) applies; thus, in cases like *cinoti*, the *pit*-ness, which has scope elsewhere, is sublated by the *ṅit*-ness, which has no other scope.

In the case of the items preceding the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—which are distinct from the *prāyaṇīya* and others—the rule "whatever is prior to the *agnīṣomīya*, one should perform with low voice" (*yatkiñcit prācīnam agnīṣomīyāt tenoṣāṃśu caranti*) has scope. However, it is set aside by the following rules which have no other scope: "One should recite for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* in such a tone as one desires; softly for the *prāyaṇīyā*; more softly for the *ātithyā*; in a low voice for the *upasad*s; and loudly for the *agnīṣomīya*. Therefore, in the word *stuyāt*, the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed after a *pit* (the suffix *yāt*) followed by a consonant does not apply. As for the word *cinuyuḥ*, the solution has already been stated.

[Objection: In that case, there would be the status of being *ṅit* (indicating the absence of guṇa/avṛddhi) in [the suffix] *bhaviṣīṣṭa*, because there is no rule to block the *ṅit*-status transferred [from the original suffix]. Similarly, in [the form] *kariṣyamāṇā*, since the substitute *śānac* of the *lṛṭ* [tense] possesses the status of being *ugit* and *ṭit* by transfer, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the suffix *ṅīp*. To this, they say: In the rule "halaḥ śnaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.83), the fact that *śānac* is marked with *ś* indicates that even in certain operations dependent on an indicatory letter (*anubandha-kārya*), the prohibition "not when a rule is prescribed for a non-suffix element" (*analvidhau*) applies. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not arise. Consequently, even according to the view of the Vārttika, there is no possibility of the augment *īṭ* in [the form] *brūtāt*.
[This concludes the discussion of] "dīdhīvevīṭām" (Pāṇini 1.1.6).

In the case of the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, as well as for the augment *iṭ*, neither *guṇa* nor *vṛddhi* substitutions occur. Thus: *ādīdhyanam*, *ādīdhyakaḥ*; *āvevyanam*, *āvevyakaḥ*. [Regarding the forms] *akaṇiṣam*, *araṇiṣam*, *kaṇitā śvaḥ*, and *raṇitā śvaḥ*: when the term "base" (*aṅga*) is used, by the rule of including what begins with that base, the base ending in the suffix *sij* (as in *akaṇiṣam*) is relative to the substitute *mip*, and the base *kaṇit* is relative to the substitute *ḍā* (the first person singular ending). In those cases, this is a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution—which would otherwise apply because of the light penultimate vowel—triggered by the two aforementioned substitutes which are sārvadhātuka endings.

In the case of forms ending in *tṛc* and the like, since the augment *iṭ* is a constituent part of the suffix (*pratyaya*), there is no other suffix following it; and because it is not included within the *aṅga* (the stem), the application of *guṇa* is impossible. Therefore, the word "tomorrow" (*śva*) was mentioned to indicate that the form ends in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. This is because, with respect to the substitution of *ḍā*, the entire form ending in *tās* constitutes the *aṅga*, and thus the *guṇa* of the *iṭ*—which is a constituent part of that *tās*—is possible.

Nor should it be argued that only *dīṅ* (in the sense of decay), *dhīṅ* (in the sense of disrespect), *veñ* (in the sense of weaving), and *vī* (in the sense of motion, etc. are intended to be included here. This is because of the maxim: "The conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the etymological meaning of its parts. Furthermore, this is due to the power of the specific sequence [of phonemes] which serves as the indicator for the intended meaning of that [root] alone. Moreover, *iṭ* is simply an augment (*āgama*), and not the root *iṭ* (meaning "to go"). This is because the rule that restricts the application of association (*sāhacarya*) by means of the mention of the term *kṛtvas* has been shown to be non-binding.

On this point, they say: *dīdhyakaḥ* and *vevyakaḥ* are the forms of the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* in their pure (non-causative) state, and not those of the causative (*ṇic*) forms; for in that context, only the forms *ādīdhakaḥ* and *āvevakaḥ* are accepted.

As for what Haradatta has stated—that by the force of the mention of the *varṇa* (phoneme), the elision (*lopa*) occurs only when the *ivarṇa* is actually being heard and not when it has already been elided; therefore, in the case of *ṇvul* after the two roots with *ṇic*, although the elision of *ṇi* would be subject to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* for a preceding operation, because the [elided sound] is not being heard, there is no elision, and once the *yaṇ* substitution is made, the forms *dīdhyakaḥ* and *vevyakaḥ* result in a form identical in shape to the original—this is to be considered doubtful, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *nāglopi*.

Regarding this, one might suspect that the mention of the *varṇa* (the phoneme) is for the purpose of ensuring the rule applies even when the *ivarṇa* has been elided; however, this suspicion is unfounded because the result is established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, and because the mention of the *varṇa* has been rejected on the grounds that the elision by the rule "yīvarṇayoḥ" is established prior to the elision of *ṇi* due to its being an *antaraṅga* operation. Furthermore, the correctness [of the form] is accepted in accordance with the author of the Bhāṣya.

However, this sūtra has been rejected in both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika. This is because *dīdhī* and *vevī* are Vedic (*chāndasa*), and thus unfit for use in common worldly speech; furthermore, since the presence of the *guṇa* [vowel strengthening] is observed in the Veda. For instance: "Prajāpati indeed meditated (*adīdhet*) upon whatever he conceived in his mind," "Having been chosen for the office of the Hotṛ-priest, he meditated with compassion," and "They meditated (*adīdhayuḥ*) for the sake of the Dāsa king," and so forth. Moreover, rather than requiring an explanation based on their being Vedic, it is more appropriate to establish the absence of the *guṇa*—which is actually heard in certain instances—precisely by that [Vedic status].

For this reason as well, the inclusion [of *iṭ*] is redundant. In the rule prescribing *iṭ*, by carrying forward the mention of *iṭ* from the sūtra "neḍvaśi kṛti," one interpretation of the single term *iṭ* is that it refers to that which is devoid of modification; thus, by explaining it as "that which is indeed devoid of modification," the absence of *guṇa* is already established.

Nor should it be argued that, in such forms as *pipaṭhīḥ*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule "rvor upadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ" would likewise not occur; for that [rule] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the present restrictive rule (*niyama*). Alternatively, since the restrictive rule falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "aṅga" (the stem), the restriction excludes only those modifications occurring therein; thus, the two aforementioned instances of lengthening remain unimpeded—so says the author of the Bhāṣya.

In the case of *apāṭhīt* as well, the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution) occurs by virtue of the metarule: "The elision of *siC* is to be stated as established (*siddha*) when there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). Nor does the prohibition [of *guṇa*] apply here on the grounds that the rule *graho liṭi* is also a subordinate element (*aṅga*), for Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this is due to the force of its specific formulation. In reality, however, the term *vikāra* refers to a genus (*jāti*) residing in the letter *i* which serves as the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) of difference; thus, the prohibition applies only to such modifications as *e* and so forth, and not to the long vowel (*dīrgha*). The secret of this is that even the long vowel is delimited by the property of being *it* (the short *i*).

This might be argued: in the case of *pipaṭhīṃṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule "sānta-mahataḥ saṃyogasya" would not occur. This is because [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] is already established, because it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), because it has its utility elsewhere, and because it is not delimited by a specific class (*vaijātya*).

On this point, they say: the aforementioned usage is indeed incorrect. Because of the status of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) regarding the elision of the letter *a*, the suffix *jhal* is absent; consequently, the *num* augment characterized by that [suffix] is difficult to obtain. Nor should it be argued that *num* would then occur simply because the stem ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). For the *num* required by the property of ending in a vowel would necessarily follow after the letter *s*. Since there is no *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) beginning with *s*, the *sthānivadbhāva* cannot apply to it. Furthermore, in the case of *pipaṭhiṣa*—which ends in a vowel—at the stage prior to the elision, there is no "precedence" (*pūrvatva*) relative to the letter *a*; for that which is qualified by the letter *a* cannot be prior to the letter *a*. This is because such a relation is precluded.

Nor should it be argued that, because of the rule "what is elided by *kku* is not like the original" (*kkau luptaṃ na sthānivat*), the elision of the vowel *a* would lack the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), and thus the augment *num*—characterized by the condition of being after a consonant (*jhal*)—would necessarily occur. This is because the specific meaning of the rule "not like the original with respect to an operation [governed] by *kku*" has been established as follows: when the word *lava* (meaning "one who expresses cutting," derived from the root *lū* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by the *kvip* suffix) undergoes the elision of the *ṇic* by the rule "the *ṇic* is elided before a non-iṭ suffix" (*ṇeraniṭi*), this ensures that the elision of the vowel *a* caused by the *ṇic* does not behave as "like the original" when the substitution of *ūṭh* for the *vakāra* is to be performed.

Even if one were to rely on the principle that "what is elided by *kvip* is as if non-existent" (*kvau luptam*)—in order to prevent the substitution of *yaṇ* (by P. 6.1.77) from occurring when the elision of *a* and the elision of *y* have been performed after the roots *sukhīyati* and *sutīyati*—this would not be effective here. This is because, as will be stated in the *napadānta* sūtra, that principle is not universally applicable. Furthermore, in the present case, since the *num* augment is not caused by *kvip*, the rule *kvau vidhiḥ* does not apply.
[Now, the definition of a cluster: "Consonants that are without an interval between them are called a *saṃyoga* (cluster). (P. 1.1.7)

Consonants (*hal*) that are not separated by vowels shall be designated as *saṃyoga* (conjunctions). The rules [that apply] to these are such as "there is elision of what ends in a *saṃyoga*" (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*), and so forth. Why specify "consonants"? Consider the word *titaupade*; let there not be elision of a final *saṃyoga*. Nor should it be argued that the absence of such elision is established simply by the force of the vocalization of the letter *u* in the rule "from the root *tan*, [the suffix] *ḍauḥ* is added, and it is treated like *san*" (*tanoterḍauḥ sanvacca*), because that [vocalization] is purposeful in cases where the designation *bha* applies, since in those instances there is no possibility for the elision of a final *saṃyoga* to occur.

Now, is this a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *antara* meaning "accompanied by," or is it with the word *antarā*? In the first case, since the word *antara* denotes that which is contained within, even when there is an avagraha (pause) in the designation of a consonant-group (*saṃyoga*) that is devoid of any dissimilar phoneme (*vijātīyavarṇa*) relative to the following consonant, the designation of *saṃyoga* is established. For in that regard, there are two views: one holds that another phoneme is uttered with an interval of one *mātrā*, while the other holds that it is with an interval of half a *mātrā*; in both cases, despite the temporal interval, there is an absence of an interval caused by another [dissimilar] phoneme.

If it is argued that in the second definition, however, because the prohibition of temporal intervention (*kāla-vyavadhāna*) applies even to the substratum (*ādhāra*), the designation of *saṃyoga* would not apply to a hiatus (*avagraha*), since the property of being the counter-positive of an utterance occurring at a time that is not a locus for the destruction of a time which is itself a locus for the destruction of the time of the utterance of the consonant (*hal*) is absent both when there is no vowel-intervention (*aj-avyavadhāna*) and when there is temporal intervention; thus, because this specific condition exists— [The response follows: ...no, because the term "immediate succession" (*anantaritatva*) is intended to exclude only the intervention of a vowel (*aj-antara*). Otherwise, since the interval between two *saṃyoga* clusters such as *kakkha* and *gaggha* would also involve the intervention of a consonant (*hal-antara*), the designation of *saṃyoga* would fail to apply there as well. Therefore, the exclusion of vowel-intervention is established by the very fact that the term "immediate succession" is employed. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the qualification "occurring at a time that is not a locus for the destruction of a time which is itself a locus for the destruction of the time of the utterance of the consonant" is included to prevent the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the designation to cases such as *kakuda*, where the first *k* is separated from the second *k* by the intervening *u*. This is because, in that case, the first *k* is indeed the counter-positive of an utterance occurring at a time that is a locus for the destruction of a time which is a locus for the destruction of the time of the utterance of the consonant *u*. Hence, the definition is faultless. As for the objection regarding the *avagraha*, it is resolved by the fact that the *avagraha* mark is merely a conventional sign (*saṅketa*) indicating a pause, and not a phoneme (*varṇa*) in its own right. Consequently, since there is no actual phonemic utterance between the two parts of the *avagraha*, the designation of *saṃyoga* does not apply. Thus, all objections are set aside. Finally, the inclusion of the phrase "occurring at a time that is not a locus for the destruction of a time which is a locus for the destruction of the time of the utterance of the consonant" serves to exclude the application of the designation to the *saṃyoga* in *kakuda* mentioned above. Regarding this, the commentators [state]: "There is neither a fault nor a purpose. The meaning of this is that both positions are flawless. Nor should it be asked: "In examples such as *na cāpsu*, since there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.86], a prolated vowel (*pluta*) occurs because of the weight [of the syllable], but not otherwise; so how can there be an absence of both [fault and purpose]? For in that case, the [consonant] functions as a locus (*adhikaraṇavṛtti*) and thus lacks a connection with what is distant (*dūraddhūta*). However, in cases such as *vicāryamāṇānām*, since the prolation is prescribed for the *ṭi* (the final vowel) of the sentence itself, the designation of "heavy" (*guru*) is not required.

Nor should it be argued that because the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of "born in" (*apsavya*)—due to its inclusion in the *digādi* group—and because there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending according to the rule "there is no elision of the locative ending before *ap-* when followed by *yoni*, *yāt*, or *matup*," there would consequently arise a difference in the phonetic result (*phala-bheda*) due to the connection with the vocative form "O *apsavya*" when called from a distance; for in such cases, the makers of the *padapāṭha* do not apply the *avagraha* (separation), as is established by tradition. Nor should it be argued that there would be a distinction in the case of the expression "a horse born in water" (*apsu yonir vāśvaḥ*);

for Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that since the tradition of the *padakāras* is that the end of a compound word is what is separated (*avagṛhyate*), there is likewise no *avagraha* prior to the word *su-* even in that instance.

Furthermore, this designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to a composite whole (*samudāya*) and not merely to its individual components, because it is understood as a term based on its etymological meaning: "in this composite whole the phonemes (*varṇa*) are conjoined. Otherwise, in forms such as *niryāyāt*, since the designation "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) would apply to each [phoneme] individually—namely to the *repha* (the sound *r*) and the *yakāra* (the sound *y*)—the *yakāra* would also be preceded by a conjunction. Consequently, by the rule "alternatively for another [consonant] beginning a conjunction" (*vā'nyasya saṃyogādeḥ*), the substitution of *e* would occur, just as in *gleyāt* and similar forms. Nor should it be argued that even in the established system (*siddhānta*), the aforementioned fault would still arise because the doubling of the *yakāra* by the rule "after *ac*, [doubling occurs] after *ra* and *ha*" (*aco rahābhyām*) results in two *yakāra*s. For that [doubling] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [for the purposes of the preceding rule], and thus the designation "conjunction" is not yet established.

Furthermore, if the view were that each vowel is a separate *saṃjñā*, then in the case of *saṃhṛṣīṣṭa*, the augment *iṭ* would apply by the rule "ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ," and in the case of *saṃhriyate*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply by the rule "guṇo 'rttisaṃyogādyoḥ. This is because the final consonant constitutes the *saṃyoga*, thereby ensuring that the vowels *ṛ* and *ṛi* possess the status of being the first member of a *saṃyoga*. Consequently, in the case of *dṛṣat karoti*, there would be the elision (*lopa*) of the *k* which is at the end of the *saṃyoga*, since the *d* would constitute the *saṃyoga* and the condition of being "at the end thereof" (*tadantatva*) would be satisfied.

In the case of *śaktā* and *vastā*, there would be the elision of the initial *s* and *k* of the cluster according to the rule *skoḥ*; this is because the *t* follows a *jhal* sound. Furthermore, in forms such as *niryātaḥ*, there would be the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā* [suffix] according to the rule *saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ*.

However, if in the rule *vā'nyasya saṃyogādeḥ*, by the mere mention of *saṃyogāt*—meaning that the substitution of *et* occurs for a stem whose final vowel is preceded by a single *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster)—one were to disregard the restriction that in a compound (*vṛtti*), due to the force of the inclusion of the word *ādi* ("beginning with"), only the singular number of non-difference appears, and instead understand from the sense of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) that there is a perception of duality as in *saṃyogau ādī yasya*, then the meaning of the sūtra would result in the substitution of *et* occurring only after two *saṃyogas* and so forth; thus, there would be no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in this case.

In this same manner, the rules "ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ" and "guṇo'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ" are also to be explained. Furthermore, regarding the rule "saṃyogāntasya," since the elision is prescribed for that which ends in a pair of *saṃyogas* according to the previous reasoning, there is no occurrence of the fault in the case of *dṛṣatkaroti*.

Even in the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, although the expression "of the two conjuncts" (*saṃyogayoḥ*) would suffice by reference to the duality of the *s* and *k*, the inclusion of the word "initial" (*ādi*) serves to establish that the elision applies to the *k* and *s* which are the initial—that is, the immediate neighbors—of a conjunct that occurs before a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word. Consequently, there is no over-extension of the rule to forms such as *śaktāḥ* and *vastāḥ*.

Even in the rule *saṃyogāderātaḥ*, it could be established by the meaning: "there is substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following a root ending in an *ā* that is preceded by a *saṃyoga*"; thus, because the inclusion of the word *ādi-* (beginning) allows for the acquisition of the sense of "two or more *saṃyogas*," one might argue that the aforementioned fault does not apply in the case of *niryāta*. Nevertheless, it should be noted that this involves excessive complexity in comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*), and that the acceptance of the designation *saṃyoga* for each individual [consonant] is useless, as it serves no purpose anywhere.

In the rule *halaḥ*, the plural number (*bahutva*) is not intended to be significant; otherwise, in cases such as *śikṣā*, the suffix *ap* prescribed by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* would be untenable. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that even a single consonant (*hal*) not separated by a vowel would receive the designation *saṃyoga*; for, in accordance with the meaning of the constituent parts of the term, two [consonants] must necessarily be expected. However, where there is no separation between many consonants, the designation applies without distinction to both pairs and groups of many.

Furthermore, the logic of the single-vowel (*ekāc*) rule does not apply here, because the accomplishment of the grammatical operation for the parts is based precisely on the operation of the whole; for when *nij* is reduplicated, the reduplication of all the single-vowels contained within it is thereby effected. In this case, however, there is a disparity: while many [vowels] receive the designation [*ekāc*], the operation of that designation cannot be established for only two of them. To illustrate: in the form *saṃsvaryata*, the rule "guṇo 'rti" would not apply.

In the case of *gomān karoti*, when it is established as *gomān t karoti*, there would be no elision (*lopa*) of the final *t* by the rule for the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). In *maṅktā*, when the augment *num* is applied by the rule "for the roots *masji* and *naś* before a *jhal*-ending," resulting in *man s j*, there would be no elision of the *s* by the rule "elision of *sk* and *v*" (*skoḥ*), because the *s* is not the first member of a conjunct. In cases such as *nirgleiyāt*, since the conjunct containing the *repha* (r) does not belong to the beginning of the stem (*aṅga*), and since the collection of *g* and *l* at the beginning of the stem does not possess the designation of a "conjunct" (*saṃyoga*), the substitution of *e* (etvam) would not occur. Likewise, in *nirglāna*, the substitution of *ṇ* (natvam) would not occur.

Now, if it is argued that *indidrīyiṣati* is thus not established—on the grounds that there are two conjuncts (*saṃyoga*) therein, one consisting of the letters *na* and *ka*, and another consisting of *da* and *ra*—and that since, according to the aforementioned rule, the letter *da* like the letter *na* is the first member of a conjunct, the prohibition of doubling by the rule "the *na*, *ndra*, and [nasals] at the beginning of a conjunct are not doubled" applies, then upon doubling only the syllable *rī*, the form would be *indrirīyiṣati*—this is true.

For in that context, the word *ajādeḥ* (beginning with a vowel other than 'a'), ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyantam*), follows from the rule *ajāder dvitīyasya*. The meaning of the rule is: "Consonants (*saṃyoga*) beginning with a letter other than *na* or *da*, which follow the initial vowel, are not reduplicated. Consequently, although the letter *da* is the first member of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), because it does not follow the initial vowel, the prohibition [of reduplication] does not apply; thus, when the word *drī* is reduplicated, after the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* and the shortening of the abhyāsa (*abhyāsasya hrasvaḥ*), the desired form is established.

And thus, since being the second [occurrence] is pervaded by being the single-vowel (*ekāc*) following the initial vowel (*ādi*), the word "second" (*dvitīya*) need not even be included in that sūtra; this is the conclusion.
A sound articulated through both the mouth and the nose is *anunāsika* (nasalized). 8.

A phoneme (*varṇa*) pronounced through both the mouth and the nose shall be designated as *anunāsika* (nasalized). As in *abhra āṃ apaḥ*, the *ā* becomes nasalized by the rule *āṅo 'nunāsikaś chandasi*. The compound *nāsikavacana* is formed by resorting to a *madhyamapadalopa-samāsa* (elision of the middle term) in order to avoid the undesirable consequence that, because the nose is a limb of a living being, the *dvandva* compound would be neuter (*klība*) and thus result in the form *nāsikam-vacana*. If, however, the form is accepted as correct exactly as heard due to *nipātana* (irregularity), then *mukhanāsikavacana* would be incorrect. Yet, according to the view that "irregularities do not constitute exceptions [to grammatical rules]," even that form is correct.

Alternatively, by treating *mukha-nāsika* as a compound with the particle *nañ* in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*), it forms a compound with the word *vacana*, preceded by the suffix *tādṛś* (meaning "of such a kind"). The quality of being "slight" arises because one part is uttered by the mouth and another part by the nose. This occurs when, between two parts—the preceding and the following—one part is uttered by the mouth while the second is uttered by the nose. In that case, due to the influence of the nasalized portion, the portion uttered by the mouth also appears as if it were uttered by the nose.

This was stated based on the view that in examples such as *saṃyantā*, due to the coloring [of the vowel] by a nasalized *y* and so forth, there is also the perception of the vowel *a* as being nasalized.

But when this very intermediate space situated between the mouth and the nose is the cause for the pronunciation [of the sound], then the compound is "the nose conjoined with the mouth" (*mukhopasaṃhitā nāsikā*), because both words indicate by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the location in the interval between their own respective objects. This is like the case of "he digs half within the altar (*antarvedi*) and half outside the altar (*bahirvedi*)," which refers to that interval. In that regard, according to the first position, the principle of "those who live in the palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*) applies: just as by the term "those who live in the palace," those who live on the ground are not included, whereas by the term "those who live there," only the inhabitants of the house itself are grasped.

However, those residing in both [the upper and lower stories] are included by the mention of "those residing in the palace" and the mention of "those residing on the ground," because they are delimited by both of the two properties that serve as the delimiters of the grasping subject (*grāhakatāvacchedaka-dharma*). It is quite clear, moreover, that this [objection] does not apply to the latter two views.

Now, according to the view that word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*) occurs first, the word *vacana* ends in the instrumental *lyuṭ* suffix; having been derived as "that by which one speaks" (*ucyate 'nena*), it is subsequently connected with the word *mukhanāsikā*. Since the formation of the word (*pada-saṃskāra*) has already taken place due to its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), it is not sublated by the femininity perceived at the stage of syntactic connection with another word—which is an external factor (*bahiraṅga*). Thus, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not occur. However, if the intention to express femininity were present from the very beginning, then the form *mukhanāsikāvacanīka* would also be unobjectionable.

Thus, according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya, the compound is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that whose speech is through the mouth and nose" (*mukha-nāsikā-vacanam*) or "that whose speech is by means of the mouth and nose" (*mukha-nāsika-avacanam*).

Some, however, accept the suffix *lyu* in the sense of the object (*karman*) by virtue of its irregular application (*bāhulaka*), as in the expression "rice for the king's eating" (*rāja-bhojanāḥ śālayaḥ*), and maintain that this is a compound with a genitive of object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* asks: "What is the purpose of including the mention of 'mouth' (*mukha*)? It is so that [the term 'nasal'] may not apply only to the *yamas* and *anusvāras*. The meaning of this is as follows: according to the view of the Madhyamakas, by the term "articulated by the nose" (*nāsikāvacana*), a sound whose place of articulation is both [oral and nasal] would not be included; rather, only the *yamas* and *anusvāras* would be. This is because, in their specific opinion, these alone have the nose as their sole place of articulation. Thus, the *Taittirīya-Prātiśākhya* states: "The *nāsikyas* have the nose as their place of articulation, or they are articulated by both mouth and nose."
