And thus, in prescriptive rules such as *āṅo’nunāsikaḥ*, those very [nasals] would be prescribed; however, in descriptive (anuvāda) rules such as *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*, since there is a rule that a description must concern a subject matter already established, and because a suffix such as *viṭ* followed by a *yama* or *anusvāra* is not established [as having a nasal], there would be no comprehension [of the rule's application]. Therefore, in that view, the word *mukha* is meaningful.

In the first view, however, since it is possible to include even those sounds articulated by the mouth by means of the very term "articulated by the nose" (*mukhanāsikāvacana*)—according to the maxim of the "dweller in the palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*)—that [separate mention] would be entirely redundant. Nor is there the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with respect to the *yama*s and the *anusvāra*. This is because *yama*s and *anusvāra*s cannot occur in a restatement (*anuvāda*), and in a rule of prescription (*vidhi*), since the substituend (*sthānin*) is articulated by both the mouth and the nose, the substitute (*ādeśa*) must be that which is most similar to it; thus, only that which is articulated by both the mouth and the nose can be the substitute. Consequently, since *yama*s and the like—which are articulated solely by the nose—lack such similarity (*āntaratamya*), the possibility of over-extension is naturally averted.
As the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated: "There is neither a fault nor a purpose [for the separate mention]."

And thus, since there is no fault in the application of the designation even for those [letters], it is established that the word *mukha* (the beginning) need not be supplied at all. However, if the word *nāsikā* (the nose) were omitted, then [the designation] would apply to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* as well. Consequently, there would be elision of the *k* in *śaktaḥ*, the *c* in *pakvaḥ*, and the *p* in *taptam*. Furthermore, in cases such as *odanapag*, there would also be the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ."

Regarding this, they say: In the *vargas*, after the first four [consonants] when followed by a fifth, another sound (*varṇāntara*)—which has the same form as the preceding letter—is prescribed in the *Prātiśākhya* as an *āgama* (augment) under the technical name *yama*. Because a similarity is generally observed between the two born as twins (*yamala-jāti*), this is a secondary (*gauṇī*) designation, "twin" (*yama*) being used for what is "like a twin. For example, in *pilikknī*, *cakhvnatuḥ*, *agnniḥ*, and *aghghan*, there is an augment similar to each respective [preceding consonant] following *k*, *kh*, *g*, and *gh*.

However, this notion that the production of the *yama* occurs only within an indivisible word (*akhaṇḍapada*) must be disregarded due to a lack of evidence; for the root text itself, by stating "in the subsequent part" (*parabhāge*), establishes that it possesses the status of being a prior constituent (*pūrvāvayavatva*). For this very reason, the sūtra of the teacher named Audavraji, the author of the *Chāndogyalakṣaṇa*, states: "In the conjunction of non-final and final [consonants], there is a *yama* in the middle, which is an auxiliary (*guṇa*) of the preceding [sound]. Here, "non-final" refers to the first four [classes of consonants], and "final" refers to the *ṅ*-class and so forth. "Auxiliary" (*guṇa*) means it is a subordinate part of the preceding [sound]; that is to say, it is a constituent (*avayava*) of it.

As for what the author of the *Vivaraṇa* stated—that the letters beginning with *ya*, when joined with the fifth letter of their respective vargas, are called *yamas*—that is questionable. It contradicts the *Bhāṣya* on the *hayavaraṭ* sūtra, which establishes that they are *ayogavāha* (consonants not occurring in conjunction), and it also contradicts the *Bhāṣya* cited by others regarding their being produced solely from the nasal cavity (*nāsikā*).

In this regard, the following must be considered: Since the four [consonants *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*] at the beginning [of their respective groups] are distinct by virtue of having the quality of nasality (*anunāsika*), even though they belong to the same class (*jāti*), they are not included among the *aṇ* sounds taught in the grammatical rules (*sūtra*) because they possess nasality—just like the nasalized *yakāra* and others. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that they are *ayogavāha* (consonants occurring only in conjunction with vowels). For the unaspirated *ka*-series and so forth are not recited within the *aṇ* category; were they so recited, their inclusion would have been established by the "comprehensive rule" (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) itself, which would contradict the demonstration of their status as *ayogavāha*.

Therefore, the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya and other works is simply that the letters beginning with *ka* are of two kinds—namely, distinguished as nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*)—and not that they possess the absence of a genus directly pervaded by "phoneme-ness" (*varṇatva*) residing in the *ka*-series. This is because there is no evidence for such a claim.

For this very reason, the textual passages concerning the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth—namely *kuṃ*, *khuṃ*, *guṃ*, and *ghuṃ*—are consistent. This is because *kuṃ* refers to the first letter of each respective consonant class (*varga*), while *khuṃ* and the others refer to the second letters of those classes. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the second point, as the nasal quality (*nāsikya*) is merely an additional feature of the vowel *am* and its like.

Even though the *yama*s and the *anusvāra* are articulated through both the mouth and the nose (*mukhanāsikya*), they also possess nasality (*ānunāsikatva*) according to the principle of "dwelling in a palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*); it is not merely that portion [of their articulation] which is so. This is because you yourself have stated that this [nasality] is a subsequent property (*paratva*). By this, the claim that the four [consonants] at the beginning [of the *yama* group] cannot possibly possess that [nasality] is refuted, since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) as long as there is evidence (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued: "Since qualities (*guṇa*) do not cause differentiation, it is possible for them to be included within other *pratyāhāra*s; therefore, there is indeed a contradiction with the Bhāṣya and Vārttika passages concerning the teaching of the *ayogavāha*s as *aṭ*," we say: not so.

Although they are included under the term *ayogavāha*, since the purpose for teaching only the *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and *anusvāra* therein has been stated, whereas the purpose for the *yamās* has not been mentioned anywhere there; nevertheless, because that [inclusion] serves to establish a restrictive rule specifically by means of certain *pratyāhāras*, and because it is determined that there is no intention to teach the *yamās* therein, there is no contradiction.

As for what was stated—that there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya which says "neither a fault nor a purpose," because in your view a fault is prominent in examples such as *yad ghnanti* due to the application of the rule *yaro 'nunāsike*—that too is incorrect. This is because, while the status of being a *yar* (a consonant other than semivowels and nasals) is restricted to those [consonants] by virtue of being part of the same syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) as the rule for doubling (*dvirvacana*), we nevertheless accept the sublation of the status of being a *yar* that is part of the same syntactical unit as the rules for nasality (*anunāsika*) and so forth, even though the *yam*s (nasals) are included within the category of *yars*.

And thus, because of the rule that *yama*s must be followed by a consonant (*vyañjana-paratva-niyama*), the rule *anaci ca* never applies there; consequently, it is established that, as a result, in the case of the *yama*s, there is simply a sublation of their being *yaṇ*-substitutes and so forth. This is because even though *guṇas* do not cause differentiation, the *yama*s do not trigger those respective grammatical operations.

Therefore, the intent of the Bhāṣya—which establishes that [the sounds] *yam* are not *yogavāha*—is precisely to ordain their non-inclusion within those respective *pratyāhāra*s, under the guise of not citing examples of operations necessitated by such inclusion. Otherwise, if there were no operation necessitated by inclusion, the prescription [of their non-inclusion] would be purposeless; furthermore, a prohibition cannot apply to what is not possible (*aprasakta*). And the possibility [of inclusion] is untenable under the view that they are distinct phonemes (*varṇāntara*), because they are not taught within the midst of the *varṇasamāmnāya*.

The inclusion [of the letters *kh*, *ph*, *ch*, *ṭh*, etc. within the very middle of the *kakāra* group is accepted. For if that were the case, since the *guṇas* (the secondary vowels) would not be distinct [from the *mūrdhanya* class], it would follow that they are already included by the mention of *kh*, *ph*, *ch*, *ṭh*, and so on; thus, the prohibition [of their being called *mūrdhanya*] becomes logically consistent. Therefore, having taken the aforementioned passage from the Bhāṣya—which cannot be explained otherwise—as the foundation, any attempt to interpret the subsequent statements as intending them to be distinct phonemes (*varṇāntara*) is to be rejected. Taking up the single weapon of Brahman, the wise hero never counts anything else; for him, there is no defeat in the playful battles of combat.

This is according to the established rule. For instance, in the *Prātiśākhya*, it is stated: "The *yamāḥ* are the nasalized (*anunāsika*) stops (*sparśa*) when followed by non-nasalized stops of their own class. Since the term "their own" (*svāt*) refers to the four initial letters of the respective consonant classes (*varga*), the meaning is clearly that when non-nasalized stops of those classes follow, the first [letters] of those classes—namely the stops characterized by nasality—are designated as *yamāḥ*. Furthermore, given this definition of *sparśa* (stop), what purpose would there be in intending them to be distinct phonemes?

By this, the claim that the letter *cha* and others are distinct phonemes (*varṇāntara*)—based on the observation of the word *parastāt* in the rule “*sparśasyoṣmaprakṛteḥ parastādyamāpattiḥ*,” which was formulated to prevent the occurrence of *yam* for the substitute *cha* and others in place of the sibilants (*uṣman*) such as *śa* in the rule "*pradodhruvacchvaśuṣu*"—is refuted. For although the word *parastāt* may yield the status of being an augment (*āgama*), there is no possibility of stating that it yields the status of being a distinct phoneme.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Nāradīyaśikṣā*:
"If [a sound] occurs before the final [consonant], it would indeed be [the *yam*] of the final; if it occurs after the final..."
In that case, he who stands in the middle [of two castes] shall have the same caste as the two preceding castes.

"Savarṇa" means similar (*sadṛśa*). It is intended that even the duality [of the phoneme] is significant. Regarding the claim of its commentators—that although there are two *ja*-phonemes in examples such as *yajña*, there are no two *ja*-phonemes in examples such as *jmayā atra vasavo rantidevāḥ*—that too is of no consequence. This is because, in the context of an augment (*āgama*), one does not understand from that [similarity] a "difference of phoneme" (*varṇāntaratva*) consisting in the absence of a genus subsumed under the property of being a phoneme (*varṇatva-vyāpya-jāti*) that resides in the augmented element; for similarity (*sāvarṇya*) is established precisely through the difference in quality (*guṇabheda*). Furthermore, in the *Audavraji-sūtra* as well, only the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) is obtained.

The meaning of the *Gautamaśikṣā* passage, "They call the *yama* bodiless," has been stated by those very [authorities] as follows: "Bodiless" means devoid of a specific written character that manifests it, such as a *svarabhakti*. Since the determination of its specific location is possible solely through its phonetic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the teachers who established the tradition of writing did not devise a manifesting script for the *yama*, just as they did not for the *svarabhakti*. This is because it is well-known from the *Śikṣā* and other sources that "a *svarabhakti* occurs between [the consonants] *r* and *l* when a sibilant (*ūṣman*) follows."

However, where it is not possible to determine the status [of a sound] by such a definition, another script has been introduced as a last resort, as in the case of the *visarga* and so forth. Yet, this much does not establish that it is a different phoneme (*varṇāntara*). For while there is a presence [of the property] in the positive instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*) even if it were a different phoneme, there is an absence of it in the negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). Otherwise, by not mentioning it, there would be the consequence of a deficiency in the classification [of phonemes] in the *Śikṣā* and other texts.
As it is said in the *Pāṇinīya-śikṣā*:
"The phonemes are considered to be sixty-three or sixty-four in number."
They were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One himself, both in the Prakrit and in the Sanskrit languages.
The vowels are twenty-one, and the sparśas (stops) are twenty-five;
the letters beginning with ya are remembered as eight, and the yamas are remembered as four.

The anusvāra, the visarga, the letter ḥ (jihvāmūlīya), the letter kaḥ (upadhmānīya), the two r-sounds [ṛ and ḷ], and the indistinct sound— these should be known as such, as well as the protracted *ḷ* vowel.

In that regard, there are twelve varieties of the vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* due to the distinctions of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*). The vowel *ḷ* has only the short form. There are eight varieties of the diphthongs (*ec*) due to the distinctions of long and protracted. Thus, there are twenty-one vowels (*ac*). The "contact" consonants (*sparśa*) are those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*. There are eight [semivowels and sibilants]: *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*. There are four *yamas*, distinguished by the limiting conditions of being first, second, third, or fourth [in their respective groups]. The four beginning with *anusvāra* are clear. The *duḥspṛṣṭa* (difficult contact) is well-known in the *Bāhvṛcya* [tradition]. Thus, there are sixty-three; including the possibility of the protracted form of *ḷ*, there are sixty-four.

Regarding the claim that the *yamas* are clearly distinct phonemes (*varṇāntara*) because they are enumerated separately here, that too is incorrect. For it is not necessarily the case that another number to be counted must lack the universal (*jāti*) subsumed under "phoneme-ness" (*varṇatva*) that resides in a single countable entity; this is because such universals as "a-ness" (*atva*) exist in short *a* and so forth. Thus, since we observe enumeration here based on a difference in universals in some cases and a difference in qualities (*guṇa*) in others, it is impossible to assert that there is scriptural authority for the absence of the universal residing in *ka* and the rest even in the portion consisting of the *yamas*.

Nor should it be argued that there is no justification for the number eight regarding *ya* and the others, because *ya*, *va*, and *la* are of two kinds due to the difference in their qualities (*guṇa*). For in that case, it is precisely the genus common to both [the voiced and unvoiced] that is intended as the differentiator. Furthermore, the Great Sage, being independent in his will, cannot be subjected to censure or questioning; moreover, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) has been refuted by the manner already stated. Therefore, one should observe closely that the view of the *Vivaraṇa* alone is the most excellent. "Those produced in the same place and with the same effort are homogeneous (*savarṇa*). (Pāṇini 1.1.9)

The designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) shall apply between two phonemes that share both the same place of articulation (*sthāna*), such as the palate, and the same internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*). The rules [where this applies] are "a long vowel replaces a short *ak*-vowel before a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) and so forth. Regarding the compound here, there are four possible positions: a *dvandva* within the second member, a *tatpuruṣa* within the second member, a *tatpuruṣa* within the first member, or a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*. Among these, the first has already been explained.

The term *āsyaprayatna* refers to the mouth (*āsya*) and the effort (*prayatna*). It is stated that these two are equal for this [sound]. Alternatively, *āsyaprayatna* means the effort in the mouth. Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence of the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case according to the rule "from a word denoting a body part other than 'head' or 'crown,' when not meaning 'desire'" (Pāṇini 6.3.12), because the word *āsya*, being a derivative (*taddhita*), does not denote a mere body part. The second [interpretation] is: that which has such [an effort] as its equal (*tulya*) is "equal-mouthed" (*tulyāsya*). This is grammatically correct because it belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*. The third [interpretation] is: that which has such an effort as its equal.

The fourth [type] is that in which the effort (*prayatna*) is equal in the mouth (*āsya*). This is because, by the force of employing multiple words, a *bahuvrīhi* compound consisting of even three words is accepted. Furthermore, although the word *tulya* is etymologically derived as "that which is measured by a scale" (*tulayā saṃmita*), it has a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of "mere similarity," just like the word *pravīṇa* and others.

Regarding the word *āsya*, there are various etymological derivations (*vyutpatti*). It is called *āsya* because "by means of this, syllables (*varṇa*) are cast forth (*asyante*) or uttered"; the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of the rule for "diversity" (*bāhulaka*). Alternatively, it is *āsya* because "food, having reached it, flows forth (*āsyandate*) or becomes liquefied"; the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule "also in other cases. Or else, it is *āsya* because "it is made to flow (*dravīkriyate*) by food"; here the suffix *ḍa* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), with the causative force (*ṇyartha*) being internally contained.

It might be argued as follows: By this Bhāṣya, which aims to demonstrate that the meaning of the components [of the compound *āsya*] is not fixed in this way, the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *āsya* in the sense of "mouth" is intended. And since conventional usage is more powerful, it is not possible to grasp the palate and other [articulatory organs] by means of the etymological meaning alone; for the Bhāṣya states: "The common mouth extends from the lips up to the *kākalaka*. If this were so, the inclusion of that [term *āsya*] would be useless, because all phonemes are produced within the mouth alone. Nor is there any deviation [from this rule] in the case of the nasalized sounds (*nāsikya*).

For the nose is not the cause for the production of a phoneme (*varṇa*), because there is no contact with the tip of the tongue or other such organs there; rather, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is a stretched membrane within the mouth, and the line connected to it is the "nose" (*nāsikā*); the production of the phoneme occurs therein due to the impact of air. Even though some accept the chest (*uras*) as the place of articulation (*sthāna*) for the visarga, there is no fault even if it lacks homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) [with other sounds]. Furthermore, if one intends to mean similarity merely in terms of the articulatory effort (*prayatna*), then *ja*, *ba*, *ga*, *ḍa*, and *da* would result in being homogeneous due to their similarity in the effort of complete contact (*spṛṣṭa*).

The inclusion of the letter *ś* in the Bhāṣya is merely incidental (*saṃpātāyātam*), because there is a difference in effort (*prayatna*) due to its being a wide-open articulation (*vivṛta*). Consequently, in forms such as *ūrgja*, the elision prescribed by the rule "a *jh* sound is dropped before a homogeneous *jh* sound" (*jharo jhari savarṇe*) would occur. [Example: *ūrg annam*. Here, the suffix *ḍa* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in the fifth case, when not denoting a genus" (*pañcamyām ajātau*). When this situation arises, the author of the Vārttika states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) through a different formulation (*nyāsa-bheda*): "A *savarṇa* [sound] is that which has the same place and effort within the mouth."

The meaning of this is as follows: those whose *āsya* (oral cavity) and *prayatna* (articulatory effort) have the same location (*deśa*) receive the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous). In the case mentioned [in the previous example], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because of the difference in location. The term *āsya* is intended as a qualifier for *prayatna*; by this, external articulatory efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*) are excluded. Thus, although it is redundant with respect to the aspect of location, there is no harm. Furthermore, the eight external articulatory efforts—beginning with *vivāra* (opening) and ending with *mahāprāṇa* (great breath)—are explicitly stated in the *Bhāṣya*.

[Objection: Even so, the letter *a* would not receive the designation "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), because some authorities maintain that the place of articulation for the vowel *a* is below the larynx (*kākalaka*), and because that [place] is excluded from what is called "the mouth" (*āsya*). [Reply: Not so. For it is accepted that the entire mouth is involved in the production of the vowel *a*. Nor is there an equal difficulty regarding the aforementioned logical inconsistency—namely, that its place is the mouth itself, rather than being a part within the mouth. This is established by applying the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

This is because the word *āsya* refers to the mouth as characterized by its state in all instances, whereas the word *deśa* refers to that [mouth] as characterized by the state that is the cause for the production of the sound *a*.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, say: *āsyam* means "that which exists in the mouth" (*āsye bhavam*), derived from the word for body-part (*śarīrāvayava*) with the suffix *yat*. The elision of *y* occurs by the rule "halo yamām" (Pāṇini 8.4.64). Nor does the elision of *a* (in *āsyam*) possess the status of being a *sthānivat* substitute, because that prohibition applies specifically to the elision of *y*. Thus, since the location [of the articulation] is obtained from the word *āsya* itself, it is not proper to break up the sūtra [by interpreting it as *āsyaprayatnasamānāḥ*]. Furthermore, there is no failure to achieve homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) due to a difference in external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*), because such a distinction is excluded precisely by the etymological derivation of *prayatna* as "the commencement of an effort. This is because it will be explained later that external efforts occur subsequent to the production of the phoneme.

Or let the term "effort" (*prayatna*) remain exactly as it is heard [in the sūtra]. For even when there is external difference, homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) is established through internal similarity. This is because there is no purpose in intending a similarity of all efforts; for when the place of articulation (*sthāna*) is identical, the mere similarity of some effort is sufficient to avoid over-extension (*anatiprasakti*). Nor should it be argued that even so, this would result in homogeneity between the vowel *a* and the diphthongs *e* and *o*, because in those cases the distinction between their constituent parts (*bhāga-viveka*) is well-established.

Because the *avarṇa* [the short *a*] is more open (*vivṛtatara*), and because the *eṅs* and *aic*s differ in their points of articulation (*sthāna*), the undesired consequence does not arise. This was stated in that very [work] regarding the sūtra "eoṅ": "due to the force of the separate indicatory letters (*anubandha*) and because the *aic*s are mentioned separately. By this, the *aic*s are also explained, as they likewise differ in their points of articulation. Nor should it be argued that even so, there would be no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the udātta and anudātta accents due to the difference in effort (*prayatna*), for we accept that qualities existing merely as inherent forms do not cause differentiation.

As for the claim that this is merely a display of boldness (*prauḍhi*) on the part of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), it is as follows: Is the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the vowel *a* brought about by means of the *e*-portion, or by means of the *ai* and *au* vowels themselves? Not the first, because it would result in the elision [of the final *i*] by the rule "yasyeti ca" in forms such as *gavyaṃ* and *nāvyam*, which contradicts the texts of Kaiyaṭa’s *Vivaraṇa* and others; furthermore, because there is an intervention by the latter portion [of the diphthong]. Moreover, the Commentator himself has stated a separate rule (*yogavibhāga*)—"even when there is an intervention"—for the sake of applying the substitution of *ṇ* in forms such as *kartṝṇām*.

Nor should it be said that only the latter part [of the vowel] is similar to the [preceding] phoneme (*avarṇa*); for this would contradict the fact that the formation of *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute rule) in cases such as *agni ehi* has been established by the Bhāṣya itself, and because it is precisely the status of being a distinct class (*jātyantara*) that is established there as the final conclusion. Nor is the second alternative [correct], because reasons such as "the two phonemes are fused" (*praśliṣṭa*) would be untenable; rather, a different reason must be stated. For this very reason, it is said: "There is no mutual similarity (*sāvarṇya*) between *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels, nor between them and diphthongs (*ec*)."

In this regard, the following must be stated: the very doubt as to what constitutes the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) of a constituent part finds no place here. This is because it is explicitly stated in the *Bhāṣya* that the designation of "homogeneous" (*savarṇasaṃjñā*) would apply to the vowel *a* and to the diphthongs (*eṅ*). If it is argued that Kaiyaṭa’s introductory remark—that the designation of "homogeneous" applies to the diphthongs because the first portion of them resembles the vowel *a*—suggests such a view, we say no.

Since it has already been reconciled within that very explanation of the *ādyudātta* rule that there is similarity of the vowel *a* even through its door [of the *y*], and because the objection that the *yasyeti lopa* would apply to the word *nāvyam* would arise [if the *a* were not considered similar], Kaiyaṭa’s introductory premise—that the *a* follows the vowel *a*—cannot even be suspected, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya’s demonstration that the objection regarding the application of *yasyeti lopa* raised by Kaiyaṭa and others is merely a display of boldness (*prauḍhivāda*).

Regarding the phrase "the two conjoined vowels" (*praśliṣṭāvarṇau*), the reason [given for their non-inclusion] is untenable, because regarding the *eṅ* portion, another reason has already been stated: that these two consist of more-open (*vivṛtatara*) vowel-sounds. The first [reason—that they are not included because they are not perceived as separate parts] is not tenable; for the reason remains sound in that case, since there is no perception of the constituent parts separately. However, it is established in both the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the *Pratyāhārāhnika* that in the case of *ai* and *au*, the letter *a* is clearly manifested. By this, the possibility of phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) even for the *a* that is a constituent part is refuted. It should be understood that the same applies to *i* and *u* as well. And thus, the *Bhāṣya* on that point says:

"That vowel (*avarṇa*) which is more open (*vivṛtatara*) than another vowel—namely, the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels that are more open than other *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels—is [not included] by those other *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels.

Kaiyaṭa has also stated: "Thus, because the constituent part situated in [the diphthongs] beginning with *ā* is not perceived as distinct, there is non-inclusion; however, because that which is situated in the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) lacks similarity (*asāvarṇya*), it is excluded; whereas that which is situated in *ṛ* is perceived as distinct and is therefore included. Thus, the application of the augment *nuṭ* and so forth is established. In this context, the word "beginning with *ā*" (*ākārādi*) refers to *ai* and *au*. The word "diphthong" (*sandhyakṣara*) refers to *ai* and *au*. The meaning is that [the *ṛ* sound] is included by the mention of the letter *r*.

If it is argued that even if the occurrence of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) for the composite form is thus avoided, the failure to state a solution regarding the occurrence of such homogeneity for the *eC* vowels remains as it was, we say: not so. In that case, one might simply say that there is no occurrence of homogeneity for the *eC* vowels with the vowel *a*; what is the use of pointing out the failure to state a solution? If it is argued that their homogeneity occurs by means of the homogeneity of their constituent parts, then their avoidance of that [homogeneity] is well-established by means of the avoidance of that [homogeneity of the parts].
Thus, the interpretation based on a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva* has been explained.

Now, one might object: in the latter three positions, since there is no grammatical connection (*samanvaya*) between the word *tulya* and the word *āsya*, there would be homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) even for sounds produced in different places, provided their effort (*prayatna*) is the same. This is not so. By virtue of the inclusion of the word *āsya* as a *taddhita*-derived term (meaning "belonging to the mouth"), the singular number is intended; thus, the meaning obtained is that two sounds have the same effort at the very same place.

Otherwise, since it is a rule that places of articulation reside within the mouth, all places would already be obtained by the word *āsya* alone, and the point that "even when the places differ, the effort is the same" would be established [without need for the singular].

[Objection: Even so, there would be *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between one sound and another that shares the same place and effort with a third sound, because no specific counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) has been specified. To prevent this, the word "of that" (*tasya*) must be stated; for by obtaining the meaning "that which has the same place and effort as *this* is homogeneous to *this*," the aforementioned over-extension is avoided. [Response: Not so. For if that were the case, the rule prescribing the technical term *savarṇa* would be rendered useless. Furthermore, since everything would then stand in a relationship of homogeneity with everything else, there would be nothing left to exclude.

Nor can [the rule] be meaningful as a restriction for the sake of excluding [the application of *sthānivadbhāva*] on the grounds that no similarity (*sāvarṇya*) has been established between the letter *r* and the sibilants (*ūṣman*); for even in those cases, similarity determined by itself is admitted. This is because the traditional dictum that "there are no similar sounds for the letter *r* and the sibilants" intends to mean only that there are no similar sounds of a different class.

In reality, however, the stated meaning is established precisely because the word *tulya* (equal) is inherently relational. In expressions such as "the father must be served," one obtains the status of being a server for that very fatherhood which has been defined [in relation to the son]. For this very reason, in cases such as "a girl should be given to an equal," the recipient is understood to be equal [to the giver] by way of that same caste (*jāti*) which defines the girlhood [of the bride].

Why is the mention of *sthāna* (place of articulation) included? It is so that [the rule] does not apply to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*; for their effort (*prayatna*) is identical. Otherwise, in the case of *tartṛ* [from *tṛ-tṛ-ti*], there would be elision of the *p* sound by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe*. Why is the mention of *prayatna* (effort) included? It is so that [the rule] does not apply to the letter *ca* and the letter *śa*; for their place of articulation (*sthāna*) is identical. However, because of the difference between the efforts of *spṛṣṭa* (contact) and *vivṛta* (open), there is no over-extension [of the rule]. Otherwise, in the case of *vāk ścyotati*, there would be elision of the *ś* sound by the preceding rule.

For this very reason, the qualification "internal" (*abhyantara*) is also meaningful; otherwise, since there would be a similarity with the three external efforts known as breath (*śvāsa*), non-voiced (*aghoṣa*), and open (*vivāra*), the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would remain as it was. If one intended to imply a similarity in all efforts, that [qualification] could not be adopted, because even in the case of *ka* and *ṅa*, there is a difference in external effort, which would result in the absence of *parasavarṇa* (substitution by the homogeneous following letter) in examples such as *aṅkita*. This is because the difference between the external efforts of the *ca*-class and the *śa*-class—consisting of "weak breath" (*alpaprāṇa*) and "strong breath" (*mahāprāṇa*)—is irrelevant [to the internal classification].

Furthermore, if only "jharo jhari" were stated, then—just as in the case of "halo yamāṃ yami"—a sequential correspondence (yathāsaṃkhya) would apply, and consequently, the elision of the letter *ḍ* in forms such as *śiṇḍhi* would not occur; therefore, the term "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) was included there [in the rule]. However, if one intends to include all similarity of effort, then even between *ḍ* and *ḍh*, since their efforts differ in being "unaspired" (*alpa-prāṇa*) and "aspirated" (*mahā-prāṇa*) respectively, homogeneity would be impossible, and the elision of *ḍ* would remain unestablished; thus, the word "homogeneous" would be redundant.

In reality, however, in cases such as *abhitthā*, the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) remains meaningful for the purpose of effecting the elision of the *sakāra*; this is because there is also a similarity between the *sakāra* and the *thakāra* by virtue of both being "great breaths" (*mahāprāṇa*). Nevertheless, it should be understood that [the rule] would also result in elision in cases such as *niśchajham*, *niṣṭhuram*, *nissthānam*, *madhuliṭ*, and *sthānam*.

Now, one might argue that even so, since both the place (*sthāna*) and the effort (*prayatna*) can be obtained through the force of the word *āsya* (oral cavity) ending in a *taddhita* suffix, the inclusion of the term *prayatna* is redundant; for like the palate and other locations, the effort also resides within the oral cavity. If this is said, we reply: no. Both are mentioned for the purpose of excluding the operation of each individually. Therefore, similarity of phonetic quality (*sāvarṇya*) exists only when there is equality in both [place and effort], and not even when there is equality in only one of the two; thus, there is no fault.

Now, the distinction between the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the efforts (*prayatna*): the throat (*kaṇṭha*) is the place for *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and *visarjanīya*; the palate (*tālu*) for *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa*; the head (*mūrdhan*) for *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa*; the teeth (*danta*) for *lṛ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa*; the lips (*oṣṭha*) for *u*, *pu*, and the *upadhmānīya*; the throat and palate (*kaṇṭhatālu*) for *e* and *ai*; the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭha*) for *o* and *au*; the teeth and lips (*dantoṣṭha*) for *va*; the root of the tongue (*jihvāmūla*) for the *jihvāmūlīya*; and the nose (*nāsikā*) for the *anusvāra*.

Some, however, say that for the fifth letters of each class (*varga*), the nose is an additional place of articulation with respect to their respective classes. Others, however, maintain: "The nose is held to be the place of articulation for the *anusvāra* and the *yamas*."
Thus, because the nose is not mentioned as the place of articulation for the five [nasal consonants] in the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā, some say that it is not so; this shall be examined further below.

Effort (*yatna*) is twofold: internal (*ābhyantara*) and external (*bāhya*). The former is fourfold, based on the distinctions of *spṛṣṭa* (contact), *īṣatspṛṣṭa* (slight contact), *vivṛta* (open), and *saṃvṛta* (contracted). Contact is the effort of the stops (*sparśa*). Slight contact is that of the semivowels (*antasthā*). Openness belongs to the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels (*svara*). It was stated previously that the vowel *a* is contracted (*saṃvṛta*) in its state of actual usage (*prayoga*), but is declared to be open (*vivṛta*) in its state of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). And these [efforts] are "internal" because they precede the production of the phonemes.

For instance: the vital air (prāṇavāyu), impelled by effort from the region of the navel, moves upward; when it is restrained by effort at any one of the locations beginning with the chest, it strikes that location, and from that arises either the phoneme (varṇa) or the manifesting sound (dhvani).

In that regard, prior to the production of a phoneme (*varṇa*), when there is a complete contact between the tip, middle, and root of the tongue and their respective places of articulation, such as the palate and so forth, that is "contact" (*spṛṣṭatva*). When the contact is slight, it is "slight contact" (*īṣatspṛṣṭatva*). When there is mere proximity, it is "contracted" (*saṃvṛtatva*); but when there is distance, it is "open" (*vivṛtatva*). And here is the essential point: there are eight places of articulation for phonemes—the chest, the throat, the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate.

"By reflecting on such scriptural passages as 'the wind, having been impelled and struck at the head, reaches the mouth and produces the phonemes,' it is understood that the status of being a *sthāna* (articulatory place) consists in being the cause of a phoneme by way of the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), with respect to [that phoneme] through the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā*). And this delimitation is a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) that governs the cognition of experts, such as 'the letter *a* is in the throat' (*kaṇṭhe akāraḥ*), similar to [the expression] 'sound is in the drum' (*bheryāṃ śabdaḥ*). For one cannot posit a relation distinct from that [essential relation] based on the etymological derivation 'it is a *sthāna* because [the air] stays in it' (*tiṣṭhanty asmin sthānam*)."

On the theory of production (*utpatti-pakṣa*), phonemes are inherent in space (*ākāśa-samavetatva*); and on the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti-pakṣa*), because they are all-pervading (*vibhutva*), they do not reside [in a specific location]. By this, the *Vārttika* passage containing the word "location" (*deśa*)—which indicates the locus in the rule "that which has the same location and effort in the mouth" (*āsye tulyadeśaprayatnam*)—is also explained.

Furthermore, regarding the term *karaṇapada* (the word for instrument), Kaiyaṭa has explained it—based on the *Bhāṣya* which asks, "What indeed is the place (*sthāna*) and what is the instrument (*karaṇa*) within the mouth?"—as being the tip, middle, and root of the tongue. Among these, the first [explanation], beginning with "the effort of contact" (*spṛṣṭaprayatna*), etc., is intended for conventional usage and is not ontological. For instance, the status of an instrument cannot logically belong to the contact between the palate and so forth—which is the counter-correlative of the tip of the tongue and so forth—as that contact is understood from words such as "contact" (*spṛṣṭa*); this is because it is devoid of activity (*vyāpāra*).

For phonemes are not produced by generating something else through the aforementioned conjunction; this is because there is no evidence for such a claim. By this, the sound (*dhvani*) that manifests them is also explained [as not being a cause]. However, it is entirely appropriate for the tip of the tongue and other organs to function as instruments (*karaṇa*) by relying on the operation of the aforementioned conjunction, since it is well-established that the self functions as the instrument for cognition through its conjunction with the mind, and that the eyes and other senses function as the instruments for visual perception and so forth through their conjunction with jars and other objects.

For this very reason, the technical experts proclaim that the delimiting property (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) of the production of the sound *ka*—whether it be the quality of being *ka* or the direct perception of *ka*—is the impact upon the throat and other articulatory sites. In this context, the relation of "delimitation" (*avacchedakatā*) is the relation that delimits the effect, whereas "inherence" (*samavāya*) is the relation that delimits the cause. And by way of delimitation, the contact of the tip of the tongue and so forth resides in the palate and other sites which possess the phoneme, through the relation of inherence.

Thus, by way of a relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandha*), the tip of the tongue and so forth possess the status of being causes. Nor does this result in the undesirable consequence of the identity of the instruments (*karaṇa*). For, in the production of a particular phoneme, that which serves as the limiting locus (*avacchedaka*) is the point of articulation; since the conjunction with the tip of the tongue and so forth—conjoined with that specific locus—is the operative function (*vyāpāra*) therein, the instruments are distinct according to the distinction of those loci.

And thus, if it were the case that the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*) should not be made because that [articulatory effort] also resides in the mouth (*āsya*), this would indeed be true; however, both are mentioned in order to exclude [the application of the rule] to each individual [factor]. Therefore, the formulation of the text—"the designation *savarṇa* occurs when there is equality between the two"—is also consistent. For the aforementioned conjunction (*saṃyoga*) does not reside in the mouth; rather, since its nature consists in being the locus of inherence (*samavāya*) within the mouth, it can only exist in the parts of the mouth such as the palate (*tālu*). The aforementioned conjunction, however, inheres precisely in the parts of the mouth.

Although the tips of the tongue and so forth do not directly possess the status of being the relatum (*nirūpaka*) of inherence (*samavāya*) residing in the mouth—since they stand in a part-whole relationship (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) with the tongue alone—nevertheless, the property of being the relatum of an inherence as defined by the mouth must be stated as common to both. That is to say, the state of being the substrate (*anuyogitva*) of the inherence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the mouth exists in the palate and other such locations; whereas the state of being the substrate of an inherence whose counter-correlate is the tongue—and which itself has as its substrate that [palate]—exists in the tip of the tongue and so forth. This, however, does not apply to the previously mentioned conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Because there can be no inclusion [of that contact] without providing an additional contact whose counter-correlative is the tip of the tongue. If, however, it is considered that this is not included because teeth are not parts of the body (*śarīra*), then in the phrase "having the mouth as its counter-correlative" (*āsyapratiyogika*), one must say "direct relation" (*sākṣātsambandha*) instead of "inherence" (*samavāya*), since it is only conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence that possess such a status. Furthermore, this must be stated in the same way even in the alternative view.

Therefore, the meaning of the objection is that the state of being produced in the mouth (*āsyabhavatva*) as defined above is the delimiting factor for the denotable object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *āsya* ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

Since it is necessary to include the term "distinct effort" (*pṛthak-prayatna*) in order to exclude homogeneity (*savarṇatva*) when there is only partial similarity, the aforementioned definition cannot be the delimiting property of the denotable object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) for the word *āsya*; for there is no evidence for such a claim. Rather, it is common to all places of articulation (*sthāna*) alone, because the acceptance of a function (*vṛtti*) follows only from the requirements of what is to be included.

In reality, however, the relation delimiting the status of being the locus of the definition (lakṣyatāvacchedaka-sambandha) is the state of being the determiner of inherence in the mouth. The delimitor of the status of being the locus of the definition, moreover, is precisely the possession of a causality that has as its counter-correlative the effect-ness residing in the phonemes, as delimited by the relation of "delimitor-ness" (avacchedakatā). Otherwise, [the definition] would be over-extended to the form of the mouth and so forth, as well as to other parts thereof.

Let us return to our subject. There are eleven external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*): opening (*vivāra*), closing (*saṃvāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), resonance (*nāda*), voiced (*ghoṣa*), voiceless (*aghoṣa*), weak aspiration (*alpaprāṇa*), strong aspiration (*mahāprāṇa*), acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*). These are called "external" because they arise after the production of the phoneme, once the vital air (*prāṇa*) has turned back from its impact at the palate. When the air strikes the throat, the opening of the glottis results in *vivāra*; its contraction results in *saṃvāra*.

For this very reason, there is a distinction between these two based on their being situated at a distance or nearby, and being either internal (*ābhyantara*) or open (*vivṛta*) versus closed (*saṃvṛta*). Regarding the nature of the others, the author of the *Nyāsa* says: "In a closed glottis, the indistinct sound is *nāda*; in an open one, it is *śvāsa*. Some declare that *śvāsa* and *nāda*, which exist above [the glottis], are the *anupradāna* (after-gift). It is called *anupradāna* because it is bestowed (*pradīyate*) after (*anu*) the production of the phoneme."

Others, however, say: *anupradāna* is *anusvāra*. In the sound produced by the impact of the articulatory site (*sthāna*), which resembles the resonance of a bell, *nāda* (tone) is perceived; through the conjunction of that *nāda* with the sound, *ghoṣa* (voicedness) arises. When *śvāsa* (breath) is emitted as the secondary impulse, then through the conjunction of that *śvāsa* with the sound, *aghoṣa* (unvoicedness) arises. When the air is great, it is *mahāprāṇa* (aspirated); when the air is small, it is *alpaprāṇa* (unaspirated).

When the effort (*prayatna*) is intense and pervades all the limbs, then there is a contraction of the body, a narrowing of the opening of the throat (*kaṇṭhavivara*), and a harshness of the tone (*svara*) due to the rapid movement of the breath; this they call *udātta* (high-pitched). When, however, the effort is weak, then there is a relaxation of the body, a widening of the throat-opening, and a smoothness of the tone due to the slow movement of the breath; this they call *anudātta* (low-pitched).
From the proximity of the *udātta* and *anudātta*, the quality of *svarita* arises.

And although these [consonants] have no utility in the definition of *savarṇa* (homogeneity), they are nonetheless taught in this treatise because they are presented as things to be excluded by the qualification "internal" (*ābhyantara*), and because they are useful for the investigation of "nearness" (*āntaratamya*). Thus, there is no fault. This is the summary:
The hard consonants (*khara*), *ka*, *pa*, and *visarga* are characterized by breath, lack of voicing (*aghoṣa*), and openness (*vivāra*).
The soft consonants (*ha*, *anusvāra*, the *jhaś* class, and the semivowels) possess voicing (*ghoṣavat*), resonance (*nāda*), and closure (*saṃvṛta*).
The *jaś* sounds (*j, b, g, d, d*) have few breaths (*alpaprāṇa*), while all the others (*cay*, *kh, ph, ch, ṭh, th, t, k, p*) have great breaths (*mahāprāṇa*).
The fifth letters (*ñ, ṇ, n, m, ṅ*) are like the *jaś* sounds, with the addition of nasality (*anunāsikatā*).

This is the meaning: the first and second letters of the classes (*varga*), as well as *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *ha*—along with the *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and *visarga*—possess the articulatory efforts (*prayatna*) of aspiration (*śvāsa*), lack of voicing (*aghoṣa*), and openness (*vivāra*). The letter *ha*, the *anusvāra*, the third and fourth letters of the classes, and *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* possess the articulatory efforts of voicing (*ghoṣa*), resonance (*nāda*), and closure (*saṃvāra*). Among these, the third and first letters of the classes, as well as *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*, are "weakly aspirated" (*alpaprāṇa*). All others are "strongly aspirated" (*mahāprāṇa*). The fifth letters of the classes, however, have articulatory efforts identical to those of the third letters of their respective classes; the only additional quality they possess is nasality (*anunāsikatva*).

It might be argued as follows: How can the three [properties], namely the acute (*udātta*) and the rest, be considered external (*bāhya*)? For in that context, only eight [properties], beginning with openness (*vivāra*), are enumerated in the Bhāṣya; and because the objection—that the acute and the rest cannot attain *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity)—was refuted on the grounds that qualities do not cause differentiation, it is impossible to establish the absence of *sāvarṇya* for the acute and the rest by claiming they are external, since they lack similarity with those [eight]. Furthermore, this would render the adoption of the position that qualities do not differentiate superfluous. If this is said, we reply: No.

Although it has been stated that the udātta and other accents are external (*bāhya*), the commentators themselves have remarked that this is said while provisionally accepting the possibility of their being internal (*abhyantara*). Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa states: "The eleven efforts [of articulation] are vivāra and so forth. This is the general direction of the argument.

On this point, some [object]: even granting that [the effort] is internal, the subsequent Bhāṣya—which raises the doubt regarding the absence of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*)—is indeed untenable. For even though there is a difference in the articulatory efforts (*prayatna*) consisting of the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth, homogeneity is established because of the identity of the "open" (*vivṛta*) form. Furthermore, if one intends to require identity in all efforts, then the inclusion of the term "internal" (*ābhyantara*) would be for the purpose of ensuring that homogeneity does not occur when there is equality of external effort despite a difference in internal effort; thus, [the objection] contradicts the original source (*ākara*).

Because it is untenable [to apply the rule] to the locus of the fault (*āpatti-sthala*) due to the absence of a single effort (*prayatna-ekya*), and because the prefix *pra-* would be redundant for that purpose, as established by the force of the Bhāṣya and other authorities on the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50).

Furthermore, since the second and fourth letters of each class (varga) are also perceived as *ūṣman*—just like the letter *śa* and others—the inclusion of those [second and fourth letters] would be unavoidable even in the statement *vivṛtam ūṣmaṇām*. Consequently, because the second and fourth letters of each class possess both the effort (*prayatna*) of being *vivṛta* and that of being *sparśa*, they would lack homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with respect to the first and third letters of each class—which possess only the *sparśa* effort—due to their greater number of efforts. As a result, their inclusion in rules such as *coḥ kuḥ* would be untenable.

Because, in comparison with the letter *ka* and others, the letters *ṅa* and others possess an additional nasal cavity (*nāsikā*) as their place of articulation, they would fail to achieve homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*). Furthermore, it would follow that one must intend to include the full extent of the places of articulation (*sthāna*), just as one does for the efforts (*prayatna*), since there is no reason for such an asymmetry. In our view, however, there is no evidence for intending to include the full extent [of the places]; thus, by the similarity of the nasal cavity as their place of articulation, *ña*, *ma*, *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na* are mutually homogeneous. Consequently, in forms such as *tvannayasi*, the rule "vā padāntasya" (P. 8.4.59) applies optionally in some cases, resulting in the occurrence of *ña* and the other letters.

In this regard, the following must be stated: for this is the intended meaning of the source [text]. If one intends to express equality of effort (*prayatna*) without including internal effort (*ābhyantara*), the result is that a phoneme which possesses both the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and the same effort as another phoneme is its *savarṇa* (homogeneous).

In that regard, is the intended scope [of the definition] limited to the effort (*prayatna*) or not? Not the first, because it would result in the impossibility of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the first and third [letters] on one hand, and the second and fourth on the other, due to their difference in being "weak-voiced" (*alpaprāṇa*) and "strong-voiced" (*mahāprāṇa*). Nor the latter, because it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of homogeneity between *kha* and *ha*, since both are produced in the throat (*kaṇṭhya*) and are strong-voiced. The same should be applied elsewhere as well.

If, however, similarity of internal effort were also to be included, then, since there would be no over-extension by that alone, the inclusion of similarity of external effort would be both useless and productive of non-application. Thus, because the exclusion of external [efforts] is absent merely by virtue of being "not produced" (*asambhava*), it is necessary to employ the word *yatna* qualified by the prefix *pra-* in order to obtain only the internal [effort].

The term *āsya-pada* (mouth-word) refers merely to the location [of articulation], because there would be no purpose in taking it to mean "effort" (*prayatna*). Thus, for the author of the *Ākara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*), who refutes the alternative view that homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) is caused by the similarity of external effort, there is no intention to imply either a restriction on the number of efforts or their absence; for if accents such as the acute (*udātta*) were internal, then the doubt regarding the lack of homogeneity due to their differences would contradict that [position].

Now, even so, although in the Siddhānta only the internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) is relevant for the application of the technical term *savarṇa* (homogeneous), what is the purpose of specifying "as many as there are" (*yāvat-tva-vivakṣaṇa*) therein, such that a doubt might arise regarding the lack of homogeneity among vowels like the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*), given that there is no other vowel to be excluded when [the condition] "having the same place of articulation as that letter" and "possessing the same internal effort as that letter" is satisfied? For it is indeed desired that the acute, grave, and other accents be homogeneous.

If it is argued that this is not so because there is no phoneme to be excluded [by the rule], and because it is impossible for vowels such as *udātta* and *anudātta* to be excluded since their mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) is accepted—[we reply: No. In expressions such as "Devadatta and Yajñadatta have equal wealth," in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), one understands that the wealth and so forth are neither less nor more; thus, this [equality] is the general rule (*autsargika*) and does not depend on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). However, in cases such as "the king’s two ministers are equal," perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge act as subverting factors. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya:

"Given that there is a difference, [the author] says 'given that' (*sati*). For it is only when there is a difference that the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) can apply. Why is this so? Because the designation *savarṇa* is based upon difference. For if it were to apply where everything is identical, the prescription of the *savarṇa* designation would be purposeless."

For this is its meaning: if, by including external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*) within the term "mouth" (*āsya*), it were understood that the cause for the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is the equality of all internal and external efforts, then a phoneme would be homogeneous only with itself and not with other phonemes; thus, the designation would be rendered useless. To avoid this, one must abandon the general meaning [of the rule] on the strength of its specific formulation (*vidhānasāmarthyāt*).

For this very reason, there would be the apprehension that [the rule] might apply even when there is only slight similarity if the restriction were not present; thus, the following textual passage is consistent: "If, then, the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) were to occur on the grounds that something is similar despite the existence of difference, then the designation *savarṇa* would result for the *śa*-class and *cha*-class sounds, the *ṣa*-class and *ṭha*-class sounds, and the *sa*-class and *tha*-class sounds, for all of these are identical in every respect except for their *karaṇa* (articulatory effort)."

This is because there is equality regarding the four external efforts—namely, aspiration (*śvāsa*), voicelessness (*aghoṣa*), openness (*vivāra*), and the great breath-force (*mahāprāṇa*)—as well as the commonality of the articulatory locations such as the palate. However, the distinction lies in the internal effort: for the sibilants (*śar*), it is openness (*vivṛtatva*), whereas for the stops beginning with *ca* (*chādīnām*), it is contact (*spṛṣṭatva*).

And thus, if the word *prayatna* (effort) were used to include only internal effort, and the word *sthāna* (place) were used to include only the location [of articulation], then the aforementioned fault would not arise. However, according to the general rule (*autsargika-rīti*), it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the word *prāt* refers to everything up to internal effort, because no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) can be easily stated. Therefore, the intention of the objection is: "In that case, the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would not apply to the acute accent (*udātta*) and the others."

Therefore, since the purpose is served simply by the non-differentiating nature of the *guṇas*, it is not proper to override the general rule (*autsargika-artha*) by assuming that they are intended for some specific effort; such is the justification for the rebuttal. By this, the argument that the view of their differentiating nature alone is correct—just as in the case of rules such as *anudāttāder añ*—is refuted, because it contradicts all the texts situated within the *vṛddhi* and other sūtras, and because it contradicts sūtras such as *ām udāttaḥ*.

In rules such as *anudāttādeḥ*, however, there is an intention to specify those [classes] because they serve to characterize individual instances that have an anudātta accent as their initial element; for otherwise, since it is impossible to specifically point out each of those numerous instances, the mention of the term *anudātta* would result in being redundant.

As for the statement beginning with "sthāne 'ntaratame," that is not correct. For in the rule *vivṛtam ūṣmaṇām*, does the openness (*vivṛtatva*) enjoin the openness of the second and fourth letters of the classes by setting aside their contact (*spṛṣṭatva*)—according to the maxim of the general and the particular—just as the rule "one offers in the Āhavanīya fire" sets aside the rule "one offers in the vessel" by being more specific? Or rather, is the openness enjoined for the second and fourth letters according to the maxim of the non-conflicting and the conflicting, since the rule "the effort of the *sparśa* [consonants] is contact" (*spṛṣṭam prayatnam sparśānām*) already finds its scope in the first and other [letters]? As for that voice...

[The opponent might argue: "One should recite for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] for that long," and so forth; or similarly, "Whatever is prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, one performs that in a low voice (*upāṃśu*)," and so on. [Response: The first [alternative] is not tenable. For the relationship between the general and the particular does not apply to the portion of the injunction (*vidheya*), because there is a contradiction between the qualities of being a "contacted" (*spṛṣṭa*) articulation and being "open" (*vivṛta*). Nor does it apply to the portion of the restatement (*anuvāda*), because in the case of the sibilants (*ś*, *ṣ*, *s*) and the first and third consonants of each class, the properties of being a "contacted" articulation (*sparśatva*) and being a "breath-sound" (*ūṣmatva*) are co-located with their respective absolute non-existences (*atyantābhāva*). The second [alternative] is also not tenable.

Because the rule for *vivṛtatva* (open articulation) also finds scope among the sibilants (*ūṣman*), just as the rule for *spṛṣṭatva* (contact) applies to the odd-numbered consonants within each class; nor should it be said that the second and fourth [consonants] of each class lack the quality of being *sparśas*, for that would contradict the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and other texts which state, "Among the *sparśas*, the sixteenth and the twenty-first," and it would also contradict the *Śikṣā* which states, "The *sparśas* are twenty-five," and furthermore, it would result in the first, third, and fifth [consonants] of each class not sharing the same phonetic character (*sāvarṇya*) with them.

Nor should it be argued that openness (*vivṛtatva*) is enjoined without setting aside the state of being touched (*spṛṣṭatva*); for since these two are contradictory, they cannot be combined. This is because of the maxim: "Even scripture does not cause one to understand a matter that has been sublated. Therefore, this [objection] amounts to nothing.

As for what was said—that there would be no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *kaṅ* and so on—on this point some say: "The nose is not the place of articulation (*sthāna*) for the fifth letters of the vargas, because the Śikṣā mentions that as such only for the *yamas* and *anusvāras*; rather, it is the organ of articulation (*karaṇa*), since they are produced by its operation. If being a place of articulation were based merely on that [nasal resonance], then vowels such as *a* would also have to be considered nasalized places of articulation; furthermore, this would result in an omission [in the Śikṣā] by failing to mention them."

As for the argument that—even though the nose is indeed an organ (*karaṇa*)—its inclusion by the word *āsya* (mouth) as ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) makes homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) untenable when there is a difference between them; and that there is no reason to restrict the scope of the word *āsya* to the mere location (*sthāna*) alone—this is not correct. For there is no evidence that the word *āsya* refers specifically to the organ. Furthermore, such restriction is far-fetched, because "restriction" (*saṃkoca*) consists precisely in the absence of an intention to refer to any particular individual instance as delimited by the property that serves as the delimitor of the scope of the word's function (*vṛtti*).

By this, the objection that there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya—namely, "What then [is meant by] 'occurring in the mouth' (āsye bhavaḥ)? which asks whether it is the location (*sthāna*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*)—is also refuted. For we do not say that the instrument is not "occurring in the mouth"; rather, we maintain that in the present context, the very nature of being a location (*sthānatva*) is what delimits the meaning of the term "mouth" (*āsyapada*).

As for what was also stated—that by this [argument], the restriction of the word *āsya* (oral cavity), which arises later, is more logical than the restriction of the word *tulya* (similar)—that too is refuted. For, since a sub-distinction within the place of articulation (*sthāna*) and so forth is necessary to account for the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the sounds *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa*, etc., even under the view that the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) applies when there is similarity in all respects, a restriction of the word *tulya* is likewise indispensable. That too is incorrect; the restriction of the word *āsya* is merely the establishment of its status as the delimiting factor (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) for the target, excluding the organs of articulation (*karaṇa*).

And that [interpretation] is logical, because there is no evidence for its being common to both. Furthermore, restricting the word "equal" (*tulya*) to mean "any [place]" would be illogical, as it is not stated by the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities. Moreover, [the rule regarding] *ka-kha*, etc., would be entirely redundant; for if one intends to express similarity of place by means of the form that delimits the status of being a place (*sthānatāvacchedaka-rūpa*), then even though a subordinate distinction exists in reality, there is no fault, since that distinction does not delimit the status of being a place. Additionally, in your view, there is a disparity because a restriction applies in both cases.

As for what was also stated—that if the word *tulya* (equal) were intended to mean "neither less nor more," then since there would be no identity between the two as long as they are distinct, the rule would not apply, resulting in the futility of including the term *prayatna* (effort)—by this, the view that the organ consisting of the nose is not included by the word *āsya* (mouth) ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) because *prayatna* is mentioned separately, is also refuted.

"Since it is possible to assert equality in both cases, and since it would lead to the unwarranted assumption of an inferential statement (*ānumānika-vacana-kalpanā*)—and because restriction (*saṃkoca*) is improper due to the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-viraha*) for its application everywhere—it is proper to explain the word *prayatna* as that which indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*) in all instances. This too is incorrect. Is this fault incurred if the word *āsya* refers merely to the "place" (*sthāna*), or if it refers to "that which originates in the mouth" (*āsya-bhava*)? Not the first, because it would not result in the word *prayatna* being redundant. Nor the second, because we do not accept that [the word *āsya*] has that [meaning] as its referent.

Nor should it be argued that, by depending on the inclusion of another word, it is correct to take the word *āsya* as referring to both [place and instrument]. For, since the term *prayatna* must necessarily be meaningful in order to prevent the application of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) when there is similarity in each individual case, the assumption that the word *āsya* refers to both is itself more cumbersome. Furthermore, it is difficult to state a delimiting property (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) that is common to both the place (*sthāna*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).

As for the claim that [the rule] "yattu tvannayasi" and so forth also applies to the *ṅ* sounds and others, that is mere recklessness; for it is not accepted by any grammarians (*śābdika*). For this very reason, even in the *Kaustubha*, it is stated that if one intends to include similarity based on the entire place of articulation (*sthāna*), then the *ñ*, *m*, *ṅ*, *ṇ*, and *n* would fail to be homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*) with their respective class members (*svavargya*). Otherwise, it would follow that they would also lack mutual homogeneity among themselves.

In short, even by those who maintain that the nose is a [vocal] place of articulation (*sthāna*), it is accepted that—as long as one intends only the similarity of place—the nose itself is not applicable for the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneous). And thus is the meaning of that text:

Objection: Is not the prohibition of *ścutva* for the retroflex *ta*-group (*tavarga*) following the letter *ś* in the rule *śād* (Pāṇini 8.4.44) redundant? For in the rule *stoḥ* (8.4.39), the letter *na* is not included by the word *tu*; and because it possesses an additional place of articulation—the nose—it lacks *savarṇatva* (homogeneity) with the other members of its class, and thus does not fall within the scope of the application of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule Pāṇini 1.1.69). Reply: Not so. This very point serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the equality of the nasal place of articulation is not taken into account in the technical definition of *savarṇa*.

Nor should it be argued that any mere similarity of position (*sthāna*) is sufficient to trigger *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity), and thus that [the restriction] is not purposeless; for if that were the case, then in forms such as *tvā nayasi*, the rule for *ṅ* and the others would result in applying simultaneously by way of mutual option (*paryāya*).

Others, however, maintain that "having the same place of articulation" (*tulyasthānatvam*) means simply "not having fewer places of articulation. Although the five [consonants of a class] share the same nasal cavity as their place of articulation, they do not share the same place of articulation such as the palate (*tālu*). Nevertheless, with respect to their own class members, even though there may be an excess of places of articulation, there is no deficiency; thus, they possess homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*). By this, the derivation of *ṅ* and other letters in forms such as *tvaṅkaroṣi* is established. Nor should it be argued that the homogeneity of the first [consonants of a class] with the fifth is likewise unestablished; for, due to the absence of any purpose, such a consequence is accepted.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *gauri ehi*, there would result a long vowel by rule of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*), and that the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would not occur; for we accept a difference in effort (*prayatna-bheda*) by relying on the fact that the phoneme *e* is more opened (*vivṛtatara*). Nor should it be argued that in the rule *tor li*, because the letter *l* possesses the property of being an *aṇ*, it would cause the substitution of the letter *v* [for *t*], leading to the undesirable result that in forms such as *tadvastu*, the dental *d* would become *v*; for by the elision (*praśleṣa*) of a second *k*, the rule specifically adopts the actual form of the letter *l* itself.

Nor does there arise the contingency of optional *kittva* (the status of having a *k*-marker) in forms such as *devitvā* and *dideviṣati* under the rule *ralo vyupadhāt*, even if the letter *v* were included within the *ra* and *la* of that rule by means of the letter *l*. This is because, according to the method stated in the *Bhāṣya* during the discussion on the transposition of the *repha* before the *ya* in the *hayavaraṭ* sūtra, a solution is possible by resolving the compound as *ava-kārāt* ("from the letter *v*").

Alternatively, *sthānatva* (the status of being a place of articulation) consists in being the locus of the complete pervasion (*paryāpti*) that delimits the status of being a place of articulation. In the case of the statement "the *vakāra* [is articulated] at the teeth and lips" (*dantoṣṭham*), the delimiter of the status of being a place of articulation is the state of being both (*ubhayatva*), due to the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*); and since this [state of being both] does not reside in each [individual member], there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the *vakāra* and the *lakāra*. In the rule *lugvā duhaḥ* and in the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, only the property of being produced in the teeth (*dantyatva*) and the property of being produced in the lips (*oṣṭhyatva*)—that is, merely the fact of occurring in the teeth and so forth—are introduced, but not the status of being a place of articulation (*tat-sthānatva*).

In this regard, because the *Grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule for the inclusion of sounds) applies to both [the homogeneous sounds] by virtue of their etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) alone, phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) need not be taken into account. Consequently, just as in *adugdhām* and so forth, the elision of *ks* occurs in *aduḥ-vahī* and so forth; and just as in *pupūrṣati* and so forth, the substitution of *u* (*utva*) occurs in *susvūrṣati* and so forth. Therefore, they say that even the possibility of a nasalized *v* arising from the *parasavarṇa* of the *anusvāra* in *yallom̐kam* and so forth is not to be considered. Let us return to our subject: in every respect, it is established that there is no mutual phonetic similarity among the fifth letters of the classes.

As for what was also stated—"In the production of phonemes (*varṇa*), the nose functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*), like wood [in cooking] or like a pot"—this is not the first case. For that would contradict the *vārttika* containing the word "place" (*deśa*)—which indicates the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—along with its commentary (*bhāṣya*), which states: "Those [sounds] produced in the same place and with the same effort in the mouth are homogeneous (*savarṇa*). Furthermore, the *bhāṣya* establishes the status of the mouth and nose as loci by means of the maxim of "the dweller in the palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*), which illustrates the nature of a locus. Nor is it the second case.

As for the claim that "even if it were an instrument (*karaṇa*), its status as a location (*sthāna*) would be unavoidable," that too is incorrect. Since the throat and so forth are themselves the locations of the phonemes *ṅ* and so on, there is no contradiction with that [rule]. For by that [rule], the nose is not taught to be the location of *ṅ* and so on either, because there is a lack of both a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and a purpose (*prayojana*). This is because the nose is of no use in the technical designation of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇasaṃjñā*).

Even when the first position—that every single phoneme (*varṇa*) is pronounced by both [the mouth and the nose] according to the principle of "dwelling in a palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*)—is introduced, in the two subsequent positions, there is no room for that [simultaneous pronunciation]. This is because, in one case, one part is pronounced by the mouth while the second is pronounced by the nose; or else, in the other case, it is held that another location situated between those two is the very cause for its pronunciation. This is also clear in the *Kaustubha*. As it has been said:
"Just as the odd-numbered letters of the classes, the *yama*s, and the *yaṇ* sounds are recorded as having little vitality (*alpāsava*)."

In this context, because the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), there is the inclusion of the *aja*-class consonants. This is established by the authority of the *Bhāṣya* and other works on the sūtra *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), from which the quality of having low breath-force (*alpaprāṇatva*) is perceived for these sounds. Alternatively, as in the case of the sūtra *kvinpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.62), by the authority of Kaiyaṭa and others, the fourth letters of the vargas also possess low breath-force, while the labio-dental *va* possesses great breath-force (*mahāprāṇatā*). Likewise, in the aforementioned *Śikṣā*, the inclusion of the *ña*-class consonants and the vowels beginning with *a* by means of the particle *ca* is to be explained in the same manner.

"Therefore, the fact that the letters beginning with *ña* have the nose as their place of articulation (*sthāna*) is stated directly in the *Kaustubha*. This too is incorrect, because there is a disparity due to the absence of a supporting authority (*kalpaka*) in the present case, and because even the mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) of *ña* and the others is not accepted by the *Kaustubha*. Such is the direction [of the argument].

In reality, if those [letters] were to be homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*), one should have recited any one of *ña*, *ma*, *ṅa*, *ṇa*, or *na* with an attached *m* (i.e., *ṇam*) before the *laṇ* sūtra; for by that alone, the inclusion of the others would be established. Nor should it be argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of including even the letters of its own class (*svavargya*), because their separate recitation possesses the force of exclusion. Furthermore, it should not be said that in this case, the substitution of *cha* (in *tacchlokena*) would not occur, on the grounds that *la* would fall outside the scope of *am*; for it must be stated that *chatva* applies to *aṇ*, and since nothing more than *am* is included, there is no such unintended inclusion.

Because, outside of the *Grahana-ka-śāstra*, the rule "the [suffix] aṇ is understood from what precedes" is taken in its literal sense; nor is there any fault in the case of *yaṇ*, since the arrangement is justified by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), and because it is accepted by you as well. By this, the pratyāhāra *rap* is also explained.

Nor does the inclusion of *iṇ* within this [definition] lead to the undesirable consequence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in cases such as *suhinsu*; for even according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the rule "num-visarjanīya" would otherwise entail *ṣatva* there, the mention of *num* must be interpreted as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the anusvāra that occupies its place.
