Since no other reason for this interpretation can be stated, and because that interpretation is untenable without the certainty that *ṣatva* does not apply to an *s* immediately following a *num*, the restriction is justified here by that very principle.

Homage is paid directly to the material cause (upādāna); however, there is a restriction [of its scope] through the indication (lakṣaṇā) of that [cause] as a substitute (ādeśa). But when it is included within another pratyāhāra, it refers to what is distinct from that; this is another matter.

Alternatively—immediately after "laṇ" in the instruction on the phonemes (varṇopadeśa), one of the letters beginning with *ñ* should be recited without an indicatory marker (*mānubaddha*). In the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*, however, let there simply be "am" in place of the term "aṇ," because of its greater brevity (*lāghava*). Nor is there the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms like *mid* and so on in rules such as "aco ñṇiti" or "ñnityādirnityam," due to the force of employing both [terms]. This should be applied similarly in the rule "ṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk śari. Nor does this apply to the rule "kṅiti ca."

Otherwise, the designation *ṇit* for the purpose of [triggering] *vṛddhi* in *ṇal* and other such suffixes would result in being redundant; nor could it be argued that [the *ṇit* designation is necessary] because of the rule "midaco'ntyātparaḥ" (P. 1.1.47) [which applies to *ṇal* etc.], since the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (P. 7.2.116) would otherwise be rendered redundant.

[Objection: But surely there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the rule *midaco 'ntyāt paraḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.47]; likewise, [the rule] *mo 'nusvāraḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.23] would apply before words beginning with a *ṇa*, [the rule] *ṇo naḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.1] before words beginning with a *na*, [the rule] *nodāttopadeśasya māntasyānācameḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.9] before words beginning with a *na*, and by [the rule] *raṣābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.4.1], the substitution of *ṇa* for *ma* and others would also occur. Thus, one might argue that these consequences should be applied as appropriate. [Response: True. However, because only the letter *ṅa* is to be recited [in the *pratyāhāra*], there is no possibility of *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, or *ma* being included as *savarṇa*-graspers (i.e., including their homogeneous sounds).

Now, one might argue that even so, by the rule *grahijyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), there would be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) in forms such as *jagrāha* and *grāhyam*, because the letter *ṅ* in the term *ṅiti* includes the letter *ṇ* as well. This is not so; for in the rule *bhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.47), the letter *ṅ* is understood through phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*) and elision (*praśleṣa*), such that only the letter *ṅ* in its own form is grasped. Nor should it be said that, even if this were the case, there would be a lack of correspondence in the rule *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.64) regarding the portion beginning with *ñ*; for since there is no possibility of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in that instance, there is no harm.

Nor should it be argued that there is the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *ṅamuṭ* even in the rule "ṅamo hrasvād aci ṅamuṇ nityam," because *ṅa-ṇa-na* must be recited in their own forms (*svarūpeṇa*). In the rule for *ṅamuṭ*, one should simply read "dve" (two).

Alternatively, in the instruction on the phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*), one should not read "ṅam. By this, it is established that the phoneme *ṅ* and the phoneme *m* are not mutual apprehenders (*grāhaka*). Consequently, there is no fault in the rule "ṅamo hrasvād" (Pāṇini 8.3.32). Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the rule "midaco'ntyāt" (Pāṇini 1.1.47) to suffixes such as *aṇ*, *phin*, and *phiñ*. This is because the status of being *ṅit* is accepted as applying only in cases where *ṅit*-ness serves no other purpose; whereas *nit*-ness and so forth are already exhausted by their function in effecting accent (*svara*) and vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*), and since they are suffixes, their status as "subsequent" (*para*) is logically established.

Nor does the application [of the rule] follow the logic of *tātaṅ* (the substitution of *tāt* for *hi*), because in that case the letter *ṅ* is actually heard [in the form *tāt*], whereas in the present context there is no evidence for assuming an exception (*apavāda*) after having accepted the inclusion of homogeneous letters (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). This is because, compared to the alternative formulation, there is a greater degree of parsimony (*lāghava*). In the instance of the pratyāhāra *may*, one should simply read *ṅi*. In the rule "*tubhyamahyau ṅayi*" (*Pāṇini 7.2.95*), there is no over-extension (*anatiprasaṅga*) because of the sublation of suffixes such as *ghañ* derived from those [stems], and because this occurs within the section on case-endings (*vibhaktiprakaraṇa*).

In cases such as *vahnūñji*, since doubling (*dvitva*) by the rule *aco rahābhyām* is desired even according to the final established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no fault even if the rule *yaṇo mayaḥ* were to apply.

Nor does this entail the inclusion of the letter *ñ*, which would be redundant; for since the letter *ñ* is not established at the end of a word (*padānte*), there is likewise no fault in the rule *maya uñaḥ*. Therefore, it is established that there is no mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) among *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, and *m*. Otherwise, if such homogeneity were to exist, it would result in those [nasalized] *y*, *v*, *l*, and *m* also being mutually homogeneous, leading to their optional appearance in rotation across the three positions in examples such as *sayyam̐ntāḥ*.

Furthermore, according to the view of the author of the *Vivaraṇa*, since the voiced stops (yamas) such as the nasalized *ka* (*k̆*) and others are also considered *yamas*, there arises the undesirable consequence that they would share the same phonetic class (*sāvarṇya*). Consequently, in forms such as *tvannayasi*, the *yama* substitutes for the letter *ka* and others would also incur the status of being substitutes (*ādeśatva*). Even if one attempts to resolve this by assuming that these [nasalized *yamas*] have the nose alone as their place of articulation—on the premise that *sāvarṇya* is accepted only when there is equality of place of articulation—the difficulty remains unavoidable because they would still possess both mouth and nose as their places of articulation. This is because, according to the rule "The *nāsikya*s are those whose place of articulation is the nose, or those whose place of articulation is both mouth and nose," the term "mouth" (*mukha*) must be understood as referring specifically to the place of articulation belonging to its respective class.

Even under the view that [the *yama*] is a different phoneme (*varṇāntara*), since no other place of articulation (*sthāna*) is mentioned, what must be expressed is precisely the state of having the same place of articulation and effort as the phoneme that serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the similarity residing in itself. And in that case, even such rules as "when a fifth [consonant] follows, there is the production of a *yama*" would become confused.

If it is argued that even so, the status of the nose as a *sthāna* (articulatory place) is established by the aforementioned statement, [we reply: true. However, this is because the word *sthāna* here refers merely to being articulated from that location. In the sentence "those produced by the mouth and nose" (*mukhanāsikya*), the status of the throat and other parts of the mouth as *sthānas* is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In the expression "articulated by the mouth and nose" (*mukhanāsikāvacana*), due to the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word *vacana*, what is understood is precisely the state of being articulated by the mouth and nose.

For this very reason, following the mention of external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*), the *Bhāṣya*—stating, "As are the third [consonants], so are the fifth, with the exception of nasality (*ānunāsikya*); nasality is their additional quality"—is consistent. Otherwise, in the context of discussing the equality of external effort, it would be inappropriate to mention a difference in place of articulation (*sthānavaiṣamya*). However, according to the aforementioned method, such a statement is appropriate because it serves the purpose of examining mere internal similarity (*āntaratamya*).

Nor should it be argued that nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) cannot be a quality because it is not perceived apart from the letter *ṅa* and others; for if that were so, it would follow that color and other properties of water-atoms could not be qualities. Furthermore, being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in that [substratum] is not useful as a definition of a quality. This is because such definitions as "that which enters into existence and departs from it," and so forth, will be explained in a different manner.

Furthermore, it is established in all treatises that, according to the definition of *anunāsika* (nasalized), the mouth and the nose function as the *karaṇa* (articulatory organs) in its production. And "place" (*sthāna*) is defined as being the relatum (*anuyogin*) of a conjunction whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the *karaṇa*. In this context, the property of being the counter-correlate of the *karaṇa* may be either an incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) or a defining attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*). It cannot be the first [option], because it would result in the tongue-tip and other such parts also being considered places of articulation. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, for by taking that similarity into account, there would follow the undesirable result of phonetic homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between sounds produced with identical effort.

In your view, only some degree of similarity of place (*sthāna*) would need to be required; thus, the second alternative [of total identity] is not tenable. This is because one does not admit that the property of being the locus (*anuyogitva*) of a conjunction qualified by having itself as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*) resides in itself; consequently, the nose could not be established as a place of articulation due to its immobility. Let this digression suffice. We shall now return to the subject at hand. Since the designation of homogeneity (*savarṇasaṃjñā*) does not apply to the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* due to their difference in place of articulation, the following Vārttika is commenced to establish it:
"The mutual homogeneity of the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* must be stated."

Regarding this, they explain as follows: the analysis of the compound is *ā ca ā ca ralau*, and those two are the two phonemes (*varṇau*); or alternatively, it is *uśca ul ca ṛlostayoḥ*. This is because of the established grammatical principle that the analysis may be performed using either a word ending in the nominative case or one whose case-ending is already fixed.

In that case, when *ṛ*, *lṛ*, and *au* remain, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*. Then, by the rule *ṛto ṅi*, there is a *guṇa* substitution for the *lṛ*-vowel, followed by a *yaṇ* substitute for the *ṛ*-vowel. Nor is the preservation of the original form untenable on the grounds of the maxim of "not performing what has not yet been performed" (*akṛtavyūhanyāya*), because even when the *guṇa* occurs, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* is possible, as there is no destruction of the cause [for the subsequent operation]. Furthermore, it is not the case that the *yaṇ* substitution would likewise be difficult to obtain.

In the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*, the term *aci* is carried over from the preceding rule *plutapragṛhyā aci*; since this refers specifically to an operation concerning the vowel *ṛ*, that [operation] alone is excluded. However, the substitution of *yaṇ* depends upon the general category of vowels (*acsāmānya*), and therefore its exclusion is not established.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that even an absence (*abhāva*) is extended [by analogy] by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, the absence of *yaṇ* (semivowel) coextensive with the duration of the vowel *ṛ* is also extended to the case of *guṇa*. This is because such an extension is prohibited by the rule *na padānta...*. Since the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) possesses the designation *pada* due to being a *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix) by virtue of the intermediate case-suffix (*antarvartin-vibhakti*), [the prohibition applies]. In the second alternative (*dvitīya*), however, since *guṇa* is difficult to obtain before the suffix *osi*, one must accept the presence of an *a* following the [original] *a* for the sake of pronunciation, as well as the *yaṇ* substitution caused by that [subsequent *a*], and then apply the rule accordingly.

Regarding the reading *ṛloḥ* as an alternative, the following should be understood here: being caused by a cause in the form of the phoneme *ṛ* does not mean having a cause delimited by the property of being *ṛ*. For if that were the case, there would be no way to exclude the cases of *savarṇadīrgha*, *yaṇ*, and *ay-ādi* [substitutions], because in those instances there is an absence of causality by virtue of being *ṛ*. Furthermore, this would lead to a total contradiction of established principles, such as the fact that the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) in the rule *upasargād ṛti dhātau* would have to be interpreted as intended to prevent the optional application of *prakṛtibhāva* (non-substitution) in some cases, whereas it actually functions to ensure its application in certain instances.
Nor can it mean having a cause that culminates specifically in the phoneme *ṛ*, because that would apply equally to the *yaṇ* substitution.

If it is argued that "the very absence of an operation—which is caused by the absence of the condition of being followed by *ṛ* in a particular target instance—is what is excluded by the rule of *prakṛtibhāva*," this is not correct. For, prior to the application of *guṇa*, the substitution of *yaṇ* would also result in such an [absence], leading to its unintended application. This is because, since the absence of being followed by *ṛ* is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*) in that particular instance, the "causality" (*prayuktatva*) must be stated in the form: "if there were no following of *ṛ* in this case, then the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur."

Furthermore, since in cases such as *dadhyatra*, the absence of the *yaṇ* substitution is not observed even though there is no subsequent *ṛ*-vowel, it is impossible for [the presence of an *ā*] to be the cause [of that absence]. Similarly, one should apply the argument that in cases such as *brahma-ṛṣiḥ*, the occurrence of *guṇa* before a vowel (*aci*) is unavoidable. Thus, in the present case, the absence of the *yaṇ* substitution is not caused by the exclusion of a subsequent *ṛ*-vowel following the *guṇa*; rather, it is established even by the presence of a subsequent *ā*. Therefore, even a slight suspicion [of such a rule being applicable] finds no room.

Even in cases where there is an absence of an *ādeśa*, although the long vowel by *savarṇa-dīrgha* is excluded, it follows that other *ādeśas* would unavoidably apply according to their respective requirements. Therefore, even if the term *aci* is continued [from the previous rule], since it is difficult to state a specific delimiter (*nivartyatāvacchedaka*) for the exclusion of the *yaṇ*-substitution, its role is merely as a distinguishing adjunct (*uparañjaka*); it does not possess functional utility (*upayuktatva*). Thus, this [objection] amounts to nothing.

As for what was also stated—that under the view where the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) does not apply, the rule "an operation pertaining to a suffix (*āṅga*) is stronger than one pertaining to a phoneme (*vārṇa*)" would allow for the easy application of the *yaṇ*-substitution once the *guṇa* has been performed—that too is incorrect. For it is clear from the *Kaustubha* and other works that this maxim applies only when two operations occur simultaneously and possess identical causes. By this, the claim that there is no evidence for such a state of affairs is refuted.

Even if one accepts the application of that [rule] on the grounds of following the specific instances (*lakṣya*) when there is a basis for it being dependent on different substrates (*vyāśrayatva*), in the present case, since there is no certainty regarding the specific instance, it is more appropriate to accept its non-application by relying on the general rule (*autsargikī*) that it applies to identical substrates (*samānāśraya*). This is similar to the principles such as "what is elided before *kvip* is not like the original" (*kvau luptaṃ na sthānivat*) or "a rule before *kvip* is not like the original. Therefore, in the view where the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) applies, the forms are *ṛalau* and *ṛlor*; in its absence, however, they are *rau* and *ror*, respectively. Thus, the forms should be understood according to the context; enough with further elaboration.

The purpose of [specifying] "homogeneity" (*sāvarṇya*), however, is so that when *hotṛ* and *lṛkāra* are established, the long vowel by way of "lengthening with a homogeneous vowel" (*savarṇadīrgha*) may occur, resulting in *hotṝkāraḥ*. Since a long vowel most similar to both—namely, one most similar to *lṛkāra*—is impossible, the long vowel most similar to *ṛkāra* (i.e., *ṛkāra*) is substituted.

Now, in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe*, the following is recited: *ṛti ṛ vā* and *lṛti lṛ vā*. When a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) follows a short *ak* vowel (*akaḥ*), this substitute *ṛ* may optionally take the place of both the preceding and the following sounds when an *ṛ* follows. This [substitute] is slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) and has two morae (*dvimātra*). There are two *r*-sounds in the middle, one of which constitutes one mora; the second mora consists of the vowel-quality (*aj-bhakta*) on both sides. The same should be understood for the substitute *lṛ*, which is prescribed by the second statement; the distinction there is that there are two *l*-sounds in the middle. Since the efforts (*prayatna*) of both [substitutes] differ, they are not included among the *ṛ* and *lṛ* phonemes, and thus, because they lack the status of being vowels (*actva*), they are prescribed here even though they were not otherwise applicable.

In this regard, one might argue: "Let us accept that the particle *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and let the long vowel be prescribed even where it is not otherwise obtained; what is the use of [the requirement of] homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*)? Nor should it be said that if the word *savarṇa* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the second [vārttika], its technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would also be necessary, whereas if it were not carried over, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *dadhy-ṛkāra*. For in the first vārttika, having removed *ṛti*, one should read *ṛtaḥ* (in the ablative case). Nor is there an over-extension in cases such as *dhātraṃśaḥ*, because the word *savarṇe* is carried over. [Response: This is not so. Otherwise, there would be merely the prescription of those two [sounds], but not the designation of the protracted (*pluta*), because the latter depends solely upon vowel-operations (*ajmātrakārya*). However, when vowelhood exists, since the three-mora sounds are also included by virtue of their being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*) with those two, the designation of *pluta* applies, and thus the protracted vowel is established.

Thus, both desired outcomes—the *vivṛta* and the *īṣatspṛṣṭa*—are established. Furthermore, this does not entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the substitute in place of the *ḷ*-vowel would also be followed by *ra* (*raparatva*) under the view that *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) is prescribed.

Although they have the same place and effort (*tulyasthānaprayatna*), *a* and *jhals* are not designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to one another. Otherwise, in the rule *yasyeti ca*, there would be the undesirable consequence that the *hakāra* and *śakāra* would also be included by the *grahaṇaka-sūtra* (the rule for the inclusion of sounds) along with the short vowels *a* and *i*, just as the long vowels and others are included. Up to and including the rule "ā kaḍārāt," there is only one designation [for each grammatical element].

From here onwards, until the rule *kaḍārādekā karmadhāraye*, there shall be only one designation for each [term]. The distinction is this: when both [rules] have their own scope of application (*sāvakāśatva*), the subsequent one prevails due to conflict (*vipratiṣedha*); however, when they lack such scope (*niravakāśatva*), that very [subsequent one] alone applies. It should not be argued that the subsequent [designation] is already established by the rule *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (in case of conflict, the subsequent operation takes effect), and that the one lacking scope is established simply because it is specifically prescribed according to the logic of the *takrakauṇḍinya* (the maxim of the yogurt and Kauṇḍinya). This is because we observe the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of designations, which leaves no room for a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

Furthermore, the absence of a difference in result is rooted in the principle of the *takrakauṇḍinya* rule (the exclusion of Kauṇḍinya from receiving curd). This is because one observes a difference in results in cases such as "it must be done" (*kartavyam*), where there is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛtya* applied to the suffix by Pāṇini’s rule, the designation of *aṅga* for the verbal root, the designation of *pratipadika* (noun) for the base, and the prescription of the operation for the object by the rule "of those two [roots and suffixes] alone. Thus, a difference in result is evident.

Nor should it be argued that "let there simply be the rule *ā dvandvād ekā saṃjñā* (from here up to *dvandva*, there is one designation)," because after the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ*, this [proposed rule] would have no utility. For if the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇi-* were to serve as the limit by virtue of the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*), it would be impossible for the designations *saṃbuddhi* and *āmantrita* to coexist. Precisely for this reason, in the reading *ā kaḍārāt*, the rule *prākkaḍārātsamāsaḥ* does not function as the limit. In this context, there is also a reading: *prākkaḍārātparaṃ kāryam*. The relative superiority between these two readings was deliberated upon in the Bhāṣya.

For instance: in the reading "ekā saṃjñā" (one technical name), there is prolixity due to the inclusion of the word *saṃjñā*. In the reading "paraṃ kāryam" (the subsequent operation [prevails]), there is brevity because one could have simply formulated the rule later as "vipratiṣedhe ca" (and in case of conflict), thereby dispensing with the phrase "paraṃ kāryam" found therein. Furthermore, in this present sūtra, the word *kārya* (operation) refers exclusively to a technical name (*saṃjñā*), owing to the context.

When the application of a subsequent technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would result in the sublation of a preceding one that lacks an occasion for application, that subsequent designation is set aside by this [rule]. Thus, this is for the purpose of a general injunction (*vidhi*), not for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Furthermore, this very prescription of subsequent designations serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the relationship between the sublated and the sublater among designations within this section. In that regard, when there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between two designations that both have occasions for application, the preceding one is sublated by the subsequent one.

Furthermore, it need not be stated by me that the rule should have been formulated as *ā kaḍārādekā*. Since this occurs within the section on technical designations (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*), the feminine designation of the word *ekā* is not contradictory even when the technical term itself is not explicitly uttered. Moreover, after this rule, the section beginning with *sarūpāṇām śeṣa ekavibhaktau* should be composed. In that case, because the word *eka* here would be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) by virtue of its *svarita* accent, it could be connected through a change of gender (*liṅga-vipariṇāma*). Thus, the word *eka* need not be mentioned again, which constitutes economy (*lāghava*); so it should be argued.

Nevertheless, there would be the undesirable consequence of the designation *aṅga* being sublated by the designations *bha* and *pada*. Consequently, in forms such as *sārpiṣkaḥ* and *yājuṣkaḥ*, the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) prescribed for the *aṅga* would not take place. For the designation *aṅga* indeed finds its scope in forms such as *karttavyam*, because in the case of roots and suffixes, the designations *bha* and *pada* do not apply to what precedes them.

Nor should it be argued that there is a simultaneous application (samāveśa) [of the two designations] due to the force of the rule prescribing *vṛddhi* for the *aṅga* in "taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ" and "kiti ca"; for by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*), there would be *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel even for what is not an *aṅga*, provided it is subject to *vṛddhi*. This is just as, in the case of *ḍit* suffixes, although they belong to the *bha* category, the elision of the *ṭi* occurs in forms such as *kumudvān* due to the force of the inclusion of the *ḍ* as an *anubandha*. However, under the view that "the subsequent operation takes precedence," since the designations *bha* and *pada* apply first and the designation *aṅga* applies later, there is no fault.

This is because we rely on the following rules: *yasmātpratyayavidhistadādi suptiṅantaṃ padam* (P. 1.4.13–14), *naḥkye siti ca* (P. 1.4.15–16), and *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne yaci bham* (P. 1.4.17–18), which state that [the sequence] beginning with that from which a suffix is prescribed up to the suffix itself is a *pada*, a *bha*, and an *aṅga* respectively. Thus, by the force of their very formulation (*ārambhasāmarthya*), the designations *bha* and *pada* coexist, and because they are operations applied to what follows (*parakāryatva*), the designation *aṅga* also coexists; hence, the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of these designations is established.

Nor should it be argued that there is a coexistence [of the two designations] based on the explanation that "in the reading *na caikā saṃjñā*, a base (*aṅga*) becomes designated by the term *sadbhapada*"; for, because of the statement "only one designation," since the designation *aṅga* would otherwise be subject to permanent sublation (*nitye bādhe*), the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*) would have to serve the purpose of providing an option (*paryāya*). This is because there is no permanent sublation [of the *aṅga*-designation], and because the subsequent application must be purposeful.

On this point, they say: because there is no other purpose for the continued application of the designation *aṅga*, the term "alternatively" (*paryāya*) is stated here; however, the purpose for the continued application of the designation *pada* within the context of the *bha*-designation is so that the *bha*-designation may function as a *pada*-operation. Consequently, due to the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *na padānta...*, the *bha*-designation applies to [the suffix] by the rule *tasau matvarthe*, and since the status of being a *pada* is absent, the form *vetasvān* is established.

For in the rule prescribing the technical term *bha*, the word "pada" is understood by virtue of its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*); thus, once the designation *pada* has first been applied, it is established that the operation of the *bha*-designation is a *pada*-operation. However, once the *bha*-designation has taken effect, the *pada*-designation is sublated by it, according to the restrictive rule that "only one designation [applies at a time]."

Furthermore, regarding the position that "there is only one designation" (*ekā saṃjñā*): if the designation *karmadhāraya* is applied either under the heading of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*) or elsewhere, then the mention of *tatpuruṣa* must be made. In the first case, it is for the purpose of allowing the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of designations; in the second, it is for the purpose of precluding the *karmadhāraya* designation from other types of compounds. However, according to the position that "the subsequent operation prevails" (*paraṃ kāryam*), the *karmadhāraya* designation is applied within this very section, and since the coexistence of designations is thereby established, the mention of *tatpuruṣa* need not be made—this constitutes parsimony (*lāghava*).

The words *pūrva*, *kāla*, *eka*, *sarva*, *jara*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* form a *karmadhāraya* compound when joined with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), based on the formulation in the Nyāsa: "In that case, [a word] such as *śrita* following [the first member] forms a *tatpuruṣa*. In this instance, the designation *karmadhāraya* applies by virtue of the rule's initial formulation, while the designation *tatpuruṣa* applies because it is a subsequent operation. Nor should it be asked how a word in apposition can have the designation *tatpuruṣa*; for the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). Thus, one should first apply the designation *tatpuruṣa*—as in the rule "the second [case-ending] with *śrita*"—and only thereafter [apply the designation *karmadhāraya*].

In the rule for *tatpuruṣa*, since the technical designation *tatpuruṣa* is prescribed by continuing the application of the rules beginning with *pūrvakāla-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49), [one might object]: "Under the view that there is only one designation (*ekasaṃjñā*), after prescribing the *tatpuruṣa* designation for those [compounds] with different coreferential bases (*vyadhikaraṇa*), and then—by the continued application of the *tatpuruṣa* designation—to prescribe the *karmadhāraya* designation preceded by the *tatpuruṣa* designation for those with identical coreferential bases (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there would result only an option (*paryāya*).

Likewise, under the view of 'only one designation,' the inclusion of the word *ca* ('and') in the rule *dviguśca* (Pāṇini 2.1.52) must be made. [Objection: But surely the entire sūtra itself ought to be formulated; why is only the word *ca* being questioned?

Regarding this, they say: "The rule *diviguśca* need not be formulated for either of the two positions. In the position where there is only one designation (*ekasaṃjñāpakṣa*), the word *ca* in the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvodviguśca* must be used for the purpose of inclusive conjunction (*samāveśārtha*), but it need not be used in the other position; such is the intention of the Vārttika. The Bhāṣya should also be explained in this way: 'In the rule *taddhitārtha-*, it was stated that a compound preceded by a numeral is both a *tatpuruṣa* and a *dvigu*. That is to say, it receives two designations. It is for this purpose that the word *ca* must be employed.'"

In the view that this is a mandatory rule (*paraṃ kāryam*), however, the following must be explained as before: "A *dvigu* compound is one preceded by a numeral, when there is the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a subsequent member, or a collective (*samāhāra*); in such a case, words like *śrita* etc. form a *tatpuruṣa* compound at its end. Furthermore, in the rules "prepositions (*upasarga*) [are so called] when connected with a verb" and "and *gatis* [are so called]," the word "and" (*ca*) must be included; otherwise, the designation *upasarga* would have no scope and would subvert the designation *gati*, which finds its scope in words like *ūry-ādi*.

In reality, the designation *gati* is prescribed here by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "prepositions" (*prādayaḥ*) from the previous rule; and since an option would otherwise be obtained by the force of the statement itself, the recurrence of the designation *upasarga* is for the purpose of co-occurrence (*samāveśa*), which is why the word *ca* ("and") is included. Even under the view that there is only one designation, this inclusion is not necessary. Furthermore, the purposes of this co-occurrence are seen in examples such as *praṇītam* and *abhiṣiktam*, where it serves both to provide the accent of a *gati* and to trigger the substitution of *ṇ* and *ṣ*.

Thus, in the rule *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* ("the most effective instrument is called *karaṇa*"), the word *ca* ("and") should be added to the rule *divaḥ karma ca* ("and [the object] of the root *div*"). Otherwise, the designation *karaṇa* would be sublated by the designation *karman*. However, according to the view that "the subsequent operation prevails," that which is the most effective instrument of the root *div* becomes both the *karman* and the *karaṇa*. Consequently, the phrase "the most effective instrument of *div*" is removed [from the formulation]. And thus there is a co-occurrence [of designations], as in: *akṣair devayate devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta plays with dice by means of Yajñadatta").

By the rule "gati-buddhi-pratyavasāna-artha-... (Pāṇini 1.4.52), the designation *karman* (object) is removed from the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*). Furthermore, by the rule "aṇau akarmakāc... (Pāṇini 1.3.88), the *parasmaipada* (active voice) suffix is excluded. It should not be argued that, in this case, the accusative case in "akṣān dīvyati" (he plays with dice) would not occur because it would be superseded by the instrumental case due to its higher status; for the designation *karman* serves the purpose of precluding the technical term *akarmaka* (intransitive). Nor should it be argued that the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) applies here—as in "devanā akṣāḥ" (dice as the instrument of play)—because the suffix *lyuṭ* [which forms the word *devana*] has that meaning. This is because we adopt the position that "technical designations and rules of interpretation apply at the time they are to be used" (*kāryakālaṃ saṃjñā-paribhāṣam*).

In the rule "the second case-affix [is used] for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), the application of the technical designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) is without scope; thus, the second case-affix would be impossible. In examples such as *akṣāṇāṃ devitā* ("one who plays with dice"), the second case-affix is superseded because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the sixth case-affix used in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. However, the third case-affix applies by virtue of its higher priority. Furthermore, in the rule "that which prompts [an action] is both the agent and the cause" (*tatprayojako hetuśca*), the particle *ca* ("and") must also be supplied; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the designation "agent" (*kartṛsaṃjñā*) being superseded. And the co-occurrence [of these designations] is necessary for the purpose of using the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in the sense of the agent when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, as in *kārayati*.

In this way, there would be an annulment of the designations *guru* (heavy) and *laghu* (light) by the designations *nadī* (feminine noun ending in /ī/ or /ū/) and *ghu*. This fault occurs if the designations *ghu* and *nadī* apply to the phoneme (*varṇa*) alone; however, when they apply to that which ends in such a phoneme, their coexistence is established because they have different domains of application. The purpose of this is as follows: in the case of *vātsībandhuḥ*, the rule *nadībandhuni* prescribes the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of the preceding word; whereas in the case of *vātsībandho*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) prescribed by *guroranṛtaḥ* is dependent upon the designation *guru*.

Regarding the application of the technical designations *ghu* and *laghu*, in the case of *vica* and *na* [forming] *vinarau*, there is a prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) conditioned by the suffix *ghi*. From the state of *vinu* [is derived] *vainnam* by the rule "after a stem ending in *iK* that has a *laghu* vowel as its penultimate, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Now, if it is considered that this is not so because of the potential application of the suffix *vuñ* by the rule "after *dvandva* and *manojña* etc.," then [the derivation is as follows]: from *vinara* one says *vinayati* (he disciplines), using the causative suffix (*ṇic*) by the rule "one performs that, or one expresses that. Due to the extension [of properties] by the rule "in the presence of *ṇi*, as if the state [of the base] were already established," there is the elision of the *i* (*ṭilopa*). From *vivinayya* [is derived the gerund], where the substitution of *ay* occurs by the rule "after a stem with a *laghu* penultimate vowel, when *lyap* follows."

Nor should it be argued that, because the rule *acaḥ parasmin* prescribes the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) even for an operation prescribed by what precedes [the original], the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) would likewise be subject to the status of being a substitute; for that [rule] is non-permanent (*anitya*), or else because the compound with the fifth case (*pañcamīsamāsa*) is resorted to.

Furthermore, the designation *parasmaipada* would subvert the designation *puruṣa*; consequently, in forms such as *krāmati*, the lengthening [of the vowel] would not occur. Nor can it be argued that there is a co-occurrence [of the two designations] based on the *jñāpaka* rule "there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] for *sic* in *parasmaipada*s," because even if alternation were established, co-occurrence would still not be proven. Thus, the *vṛddhi* substitution would only be optional. However, if one were to rely on the force of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *parasmaipada* from the rule "the three [designations] following *tiṅ*" [to this rule], [then the desired result follows].

However, if the reading is *paraṃ kāryam*, the word *ṛtviya* is not established. [The rule] *ṛtoraṇaśchandasighas* [prescribes the suffix *ghas* after *ṛtu*]; thus: *ayaṃ te yonirṛtviyaḥ* ("This is your seasonal womb") and *prajāṃ viṃdāma ṛtviyaḥ* ("May we find offspring according to the season"). In these cases, by the rule *siti ca*, only the designation *pada* (word) is desired. Because of the statement *paraṃ kāryam*, the designation *bha* would also apply; and consequently, the *guṇa* substitution of *o* [in *ṛtviya*] would result. Furthermore, the *pada* designation would serve the purpose of *avagraha* (word division).

In the case of roots such as *gati* (motion), *buddhi* (cognition), etc., when followed by a causative (*ṇi*) suffix, the object [of the action] would incur both the designations *karman* (object) and *kartṛ* (agent).

For instance, within the section on the designation of "object" (karmasaṃjñā) under the heading of "single designation" (ekasaṃjñā), once the designation of object is established, the rule concerning motion (gati) and so forth serves as a restrictive injunction (niyamārtha).

For instance, since the one being prompted (*prayojya*) is independent in its own operation but is brought about by the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka*), there arises the contingency of two designations [simultaneously]. Given the rule that only one designation applies when there is a conflict between designations, it must be governed by whichever designation pertains to the primary element. In this case, because the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is predominant, the designation must be applied precisely as prompted by that [suffix]; for when both a subordinate and a predominant factor are present, the predominant factor can function as the prompter, whereas it is logically impossible for subordinate factors to act as prompters of their own contrary effects.

Therefore, once the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) has been established for the agent of the base verb, a restriction is made that only the agent of roots meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*) and so forth, when in their non-causative (*aṇyantā*) state, receives the designation "object" in their causative (*ṇyantā*) state, and not others. Consequently, in the sentence *pācayaty odanaṃ devadatto yajñadattena*, the designation "object" does not apply; rather, because there is no sublater [of the agent designation], the very designation "agent" prevails, based on the primary action.

However, if the reading were *paraṃ kāryam* (the operation is subsequent), then since there would be no contradiction, both designations would apply everywhere; and even though the designation of "object" (*karma*) would be excluded for things prompted by other causative roots through the restrictive rule that it applies only to those beginning with "gati-artha" (verbs meaning motion), the two designations would still apply to that which is prompted by verbs beginning with "gati-artha."

If, however, it is assumed that the mention of *anyatarasyām* in the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.53) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) does not apply when the designation of "object" (*karman-saṃjñā*) is in force—on the grounds that if the prompted agent (*prayojya*) of verbs meaning "to go" and so forth were to possess both designations simultaneously, the rule would have been formulated as simply *hṛkroḥ*—then there is no fault. Likewise, in the case of the designation *dhi*, the mention of *śeṣa* need not be made for the purpose of excluding the designation *nadī*. Otherwise, after the suffix *ṅe* is added to the word *śakaṭi*, if the designation *nadī* were applied, the augment *āṭ* would be inserted; and because that [augment] is part of a suffix marked with *ṅ*, the substitution of *guṇa* would occur by the rule *gherṅiti*.

In reality, if the designation *ghisamjñā* were to apply here, then by virtue of its being *antaraṅga*, it would have applied previously. However, the designation *nadīsamjñā*—which depends on a *ṅit* affix according to the rule "ṅiti hrasvaśca"—is *bahiraṅga*. Once the *guṇa* substitution characterized by *ghisamjñā* had taken effect, the short vowel (*hrasva*) would no longer exist; furthermore, because it would not be a substitute for a vowel (*alvidhi*), the status of being a *sthānin* would not apply, and thus the *nadīsamjñā* could never have occurred. Consequently, the prescription of the *nadīsamjñā* would be entirely redundant. Therefore, one must understand that by the very force of the prescription of the *nadīsamjñā*, the *ghisamjñā* does not apply in this instance.

Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the substitution of *yaṇ* would also not occur; for according to the maxim: "That rule whose prescription becomes purposeless with respect to a particular operation is sublated, but that which is merely the cause for another rule is not sublated.

Furthermore, the mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder) in the rule *śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ* must be made. This is for the purpose of preventing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designation *bahuvrīhi* with the designation *avyayībhāva* in cases such as *unmattagaṅgam*, where the latter applies because the compound has another word as its predominant meaning.

Otherwise, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member would be optional, and the compound-ending suffix *kap* would also occur optionally. In the case of *śastrīśyāmā*, when the word *śyāmā* refers only to the object of comparison (*upamāna*), namely the knife, while the object being compared (*upameya*) is expressed by the compound itself, then—since it would function as a meaning other than the constituent members—the designation of a *bahuvrīhi* would apply, and consequently, the suffix *kap* would occur optionally. Regarding the accent, however, there is no difference here, because the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its] original accent when it has the sense of 'equal to,' or is a third-case, seventh-case, comparative, indeclinable, second-case, or gerundive" prescribes the preservation of the original accent of the first member.

In the view that the word *samāhāra* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), in the case of *pañcagavam*, because it is a *dvigu* compound where the meaning of the external member (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, there would be the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*). Nor can it be argued that the suffix *kap* does not apply here because the whole is not "entire" (*aśeṣatvāt*). Furthermore, one should not say that the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* will not occur because of the *cit* marker on the suffix *ṭac*; for *pañcapātram* is precisely the example that should be cited.

Thus, in the case of *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *nivārāṇasiḥ*, if the meaning of the word *krānta* (passed beyond) were expressed by the compound itself, then, given that it would have the designation of a *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *kap*—which is conditioned by the rule for [compounds ending in] river names (*nadī*)—would apply. However, if the meaning of "passed beyond" and so forth belongs solely to the first member (*pūrvapada*), then it would be an *avyayībhāva*. Even if the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) were included [in the definition], a *bahuvrīhi* would not apply in the case of *dvīrāvatīko deśaḥ*.

Furthermore, because there would be the undesirable consequence of [the term] *nadībhiḥ* being an *avyayībhāva*, if the meaning of that which is being compounded were to be expressed by it, then since an occasion for it exists in cases such as *pañcanadam*, the *bahuvrīhi* would not apply even in instances such as *vīrapuruṣakaḥ grāmaḥ* (a village with brave men) or *abrahmaṇakoha deśaḥ* (a region without Brahmins), as these have already been utilized in the rules *tatpuruṣaḥ samānādhikaraṇaḥ* and *avyayaṃ vibhakti*.

In the view that there is only one designation (*ekasaṃjñā*), however, the mention of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is not made, because the sublation of the *bahuvrīhi* designation by the *avyayībhāva* and other designations—which have no other scope—is already established. In cases such as *dvīrāvatīka*, the *bahuvrīhi* will occur due to its higher status. Likewise, in the sense of "one from whom leaves have fallen" (*prapatitaparṇa*), the *bahuvrīhi* form *praparṇa* would not occur; for, as in the case of *niḥkauśāmbi*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *tatpuruṣa* designation applying. And thus, in the view where there is only one designation, the *tatpuruṣa* designation applies where the meaning of the suffix *-kta* constitutes the meaning of the compound.

In the case of *praparṇa*, however, since the meaning of the suffix *-ta* (*ktārtha*) is an adjective qualifying *parṇa*, while the meaning of the compound is something entirely different, the *bahuvrīhi* is established. Therefore, regarding the reading "there is only one designation" (*ekā saṃjñā*), there is no fault, because the *ca*s (conjunctions) have been placed within the very sūtras where the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of those designations is desired. However, regarding the reading "the subsequent operation" (*paraṃ kāryam*), it is established that there is a fault in the aforementioned instances. Now, the purposes (*prayojana*) are stated; the distinction here is that for those second [designations] which are recited in this or another section and whose co-occurrence is not desired, there is an "addition" (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

In the rule *ūkālo’j* (Pāṇini 1.2.27), the designation of "short" (*hrasva*) is prescribed for that which has the duration of *u*, *ū*, or *u3*. Since this [designation] includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhaka*) by virtue of being a vowel (*aṇ*), the designation of "short" would also apply to long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels; however, that [application] is superseded by the designations of "long" and "protracted. And that supersession has been examined in that very [context].

Thus, by the designation *ārdhadhātuka* applied to the *liṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes, the designation *sārvadhātuka*—which would otherwise apply because they are *tiṅ*s—is sublated. Otherwise, if both designations were to apply simultaneously, the *śap* augment and other such elements as well as *iṭ* would have to be inserted. Nor can the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), which prescribes both designations for Vedic usage, be taken as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of their co-occurrence; for that rule is logically consistent even if it intends the *ārdhadhātuka* designation for *tiṅ*s and the *sārvadhātuka* designation for everything else.

The designation *yuvan* (youth) subverts the designations *apatya* (descendant) and *vṛddha* (senior). For if there were co-occurrence (*samāveśa*), then in the case of "the students of Śālanki and Paila who are youths," the optional elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *phakphiñoranyatarasyām* would—due to its immediate proximity—subvert only the elision prescribed by *yūni luk*, and thus would not subvert the elision prescribed by *pailādibhyaśca*. The designation *nadī* (river/feminine name ending in long ī or ū) subverts the designation *ghi*. Consequently, in the form *śakaṭyai*, there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution. The designation *guru* (heavy syllable, defined as a consonant cluster or a vowel followed by a consonant cluster) subverts the designation *laghu* (light syllable). Consequently, in forms such as *atatakṣat*, there is no application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule.

"Subsequent *kāraka* designations supersede the designation of *apādāna*. Therefore, in the case of *dhanuṣā vidhyati* ('he pierces with a bow'), since there is no intention to express departure (*apāya*), the bow lacks the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*); thus, when both designations would otherwise apply, the designation of *karaṇa* (instrument) prevails due to its higher priority. In *kāṃsyapātryāṃ bhuṅkte* ('he eats from a bronze vessel'), the designation is *adhikaraṇa* (locus); in *gāṃ dogdhi* ('he milks the cow'), the designation is *karman* (object); and in *dhanurvidhyati* ('he pierces with a bow'), the designation is *kartṛ* (agent)."

When the roots *krudh* (to be angry) and *duh* (to milk) are preceded by a prefix (*upasṛṣṭa*), the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) is superseded by the designation of "object" (*karman*). Later designations supersede the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*); therefore, in examples such as *dhanur vidhyati* ("he pierces with a bow"), the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) applies. The designation of "location" (*adhikaraṇa*) is superseded by the designation of "object," as in *gehaṃ praviśati* ("he enters the house"). The designation of "agent" supersedes that of "location," as in *sthālī pacati* ("the pot cooks"). When preceded by the prefix *adhi*, the root *vas* takes the designation of "location" for its object, as in *gṛham adhivasati* ("he dwells in the house").

The technical designations *gati* (motion) and *upasarga* (preverb) are superseded by the designation *karmapravacanīya* (governing particle). Consequently, in examples such as *susiktam*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] does not occur; furthermore, the final acute accent [prescribed] for a word having the designation *gati*—by the rule *sūpamānāt ktaḥ*—does not apply to the word *su*, and thus only the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) remains.

The designation *parasmaipada* (active voice) is superseded by the designation *ātmanepada* (middle voice). Consequently, in examples such as *acyoṣṭa* and *ākramata*, there is an absence of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) and other such operations.

Whichever technical designations for compound types are subsequent and without scope, they supersede those which are prior and possess scope. Consequently, in *lohitagaṅgam*, it is an *avyayībhāva* compound; whereas in *dvīrāvatīkaḥ*, it is exclusively a *bahuvrīhi*.

It should be stated that a meaningful nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which expresses a quality (*guṇavacana*) receives the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of compound (*samāsa*), primary derivative (*kṛt*), secondary derivative (*taddhita*), indeclinable (*avyaya*), and pronoun (*sarvanāma*). Because they share the same domain and because of the use of the word "and" (*ca*), there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations "quality-expressing" and "nominal stem. As for the designation "nominal stem," its co-occurrence [with others] follows from its recurrence in the subsequent designations. However, the designation "quality-expressing" is superseded by those other designations ending in "-saṃjñā. The purpose of the designation "quality-expressing," however, is the application of the suffix *ṣyañ*.

In the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*, the inclusion of the term *brāhmaṇādi* (the "brāhmaṇa-group") is for the purpose of including words that serve as the basis for technical designations such as compounds (*samāsa*) and the like; for the purpose of overriding the suffixes prescribed by the rules concerning living beings (*prāṇabhṛt*) and *jāti*; and for the purpose of ensuring the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the *yuvan*-group. It should also be stated that *jāti* is that which does not possess all genders. Furthermore, there is no intention to define *jāti* based on its participation in all genders. The designation *dru* and the designation *saṃkhyā* should also be stated. The term *dru* is an ancient usage for the designation *ṣaṭ* ("six").

It should also be stated that a *saṃjñā* (name) is applied to a single substance (*ekadravyopaniveśinī*). This means that for arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*) such as *ḍittha*, there is the designation "name" (*saṃjñāsaṃjñā*). Because designations such as *samāsa* (compound) and others supersede the designation *guṇavacana* (quality-word), the suffix *ṣyañ* does not occur in cases such as *citragutva*, *kārakatva*, *auṣagavatva*, *uccaistva*, *sarvatva*, *gotva*, *bahutva*, *pañcatva*, and *ḍitthatva*. However, in cases such as *aikya* and *rājapauruṣya*, the suffix *ṣyañ* does occur because they belong to the *brāhmaṇādi* group. Pāṇini 1.1.11: A dual ending containing *i*, *u*, or *e* is *pragṛhya* (retains its original form).

A dual ending (dvivacana) that ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e* shall be designated as *pragṛhya*. The rules [governing such cases] are "pluta-pragṛhyāḥ" and so forth. Examples: *harī etau* (these two Hari-s), *viṣṇū imau* (these two Viṣṇu-s), *gaṅge amū* (those two Gaṅgā-s). Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) here? In the view that [phonemes] denote individual instances (*vyaktipakṣa*), since *ī* and *ū* are long vowels, they are not *aṇ* sounds; consequently, they lack the capacity to include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhakatva*). Therefore, it would seem impossible for the *tapara* to serve the purpose of including those [vowels] of the same duration. Nor can it be argued that it is for the sake of including long *ī* and *ū* vowels endowed with the qualities of acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), or circumflex (*svarita*) accents.

If it is argued that this is established simply because qualities (*guṇa*) do not differentiate [the phoneme], and that even in the view where the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, the exclusion of the short vowel is achieved by the force of the long pronunciation itself, and furthermore, the exclusion of the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is undesired even in the final Siddhānta—then here is the Bhāṣya:

"In the view that the individual (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning and qualities are the differentiators, the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) is for the purpose of including long vowels endowed with qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*)."

Nor should it be said that the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) is for the purpose of preventing the inclusion of the protracted (*pluta*) vowel by the rule of apprehension (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*), on the grounds that the single *e* sound is an *aṇ* (a simple vowel) only when it refers to the individual phoneme (*vyakti*). This is because, in the *tapara-sūtra*, the term *aṇ* is understood as being carried over (*anuvṛtti*), and it will be explained later that the same applies to its meaning (*artha*) as well.

Regarding this, they say: even so, since the inclusion of the long vowel *ū*—which possesses a different quality (*guṇa*)—is established for *u* precisely by virtue of its having a fixed limit (*taparatva*), and since the inclusion of the long vowel *ai* is established for *e* simply by virtue of its being an *aṇ*, the presence of the fixed limit (*taparatva*) in both cases serves merely to eliminate doubt. It would be better, however, to adopt the position that "qualities do not differentiate" (*guṇānām abhedakatva*) and hold that the fixed limit in the case of *i* is for the sake of eliminating doubt. With this intention, the authors of the *Vṛtti* maintain that the fixed limit is everywhere for the purpose of eliminating doubt.

In reality, however, it is easy to maintain that the *ū* vowel has the *tapara* designation because there is no evidence for a fifth-case compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) that would cause the subsequent [vowel] to be grasped as belonging to that same time; whereas the *e* vowel is indeed specified without the *tapara* designation.

To claim that the *e* vowel is used alone contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, which asks: "For what purpose is the *pragṛhya* designation applied to the *īt* vowels etc., which already have the *tapara* designation? For by that [statement], it is understood that all three [vowels] are specified with the *tapara* designation.

Objection: Since the *pluta* vowel is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the *tapara* [vowel], the *pragṛhya* designation applies only to that which has two morae (*dvimātra*). Therefore, there is no harm even if the *pluta* is not included in the definition of *pragṛhya*. Nor should it be argued that this fault is unavoidable because, in the section on vowel sandhi (*svarasandhi*), the rule "plutapragṛhyā aci" indicates that the *pluta* is established (*siddha*) by virtue of its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). This is because the word *pluta* can, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), refer to its substituendum (*sthānin*), and thus it cannot serve as a *jñāpaka* (an indicator) for the establishment of the *pluta*.

This is because, compared to the assumption of another sentence based on presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) derived from what has been heard, it is more appropriate to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Even though the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) conditioned by prolation (*plutatva*) is established by making known that the prolated vowel is already accomplished, [the original form] conditioned by the status of being a *pragṛhya* would remain unestablished [for the prolated vowel]. Do not say so. For if the prolated vowel were unestablished (*asiddha*), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "of that which is not a *pragṛhya*" (*apragṛhyasya*) would not apply, and consequently, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) prescribed by the rule "a non-*pragṛhya* *aṇ* becomes nasalized" (*aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*) would be unavoidable.

Now, although *aikāra* here is an *aṇ* (a short vowel) and thus capable of including its own class (*pluta*), how can it include *ī* and *ū*, since long vowels are not *aṇ* and therefore lack the capacity to include their homogeneous counterparts? Nor is the reference [to *aikāra*] intended to denote the genus (*jāti*), for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the short vowels as well. If it is argued that the genus inherent specifically in the long individual instances is what is intended, we say no; for that would still leave the inclusion of the *pluta* (protracted) vowels unresolved. And this is not an acceptable conclusion.

In cases such as *agnī 3 iti*, although the substitution of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) for the non-protracted (*apluta*) by the rule *aplutavad upasthite*—when followed by the common (laukika) word *iti*—prohibits the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) caused by protraction, the *prakṛtibhāva* based on the status of being a *pragṛhya* is nonetheless desired. Accordingly, there is a Vārttika in the sixth [chapter]:

"The mention of 'like' (*vat*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the grammatical effects of the protracted vowel; for if there were a prohibition of the protracted vowel itself, there would follow the undesirable consequence of prohibiting the protracted *pragṛhya* vowels, since that [prohibition] is ordained by another [rule]."

The meaning of the objection is this: since the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) must necessarily prevent the euphonic combination (*svarasandhi*) of a protracted vowel (*pluta*), the protracted vowel itself should simply be prohibited; what is the point of a rule that serves as a mere extension (*atideśa*)? The meaning of the resolution is this: although the prohibition caused by the protracted vowel would apply because the preservation of the original form is triggered by both [the *pragṛhya* status and the protraction], the preservation of the original form caused by the *pragṛhya* status still exists, thereby ensuring the hearing of the protracted vowel; however, if the protracted vowel were prohibited outright, its hearing would not occur.

Nor should it be argued that the rule *aplutavat* would thus become redundant, because the mere prohibition of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) caused by a protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not establish any specific distinction [for this rule]. This is because the rule finds its purposeful application (*caritārthatva*) in cases where the designation *pragṛhya* does not exist, such as in *suślokā3 iti* → *suśloketi*. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states:

In the view that technical designations (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) follow the order of their enunciation (*yathoddeśa*), the designation *pragṛhya* is established because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the *pragṛhya* designation; thus, the perception of its having two morae (*dvimātra*) remains unimpeded. However, in the view that they function according to the time of their application (*kāryakāla*), the *pragṛhya* designation shares the same domain as the rule "aṇo 'pragṛhyasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.57); consequently, since the protracted vowel would not be non-existent with respect to that designation, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) would occur.

If it is argued that since technical names (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) exist for the sake of specific operations, the view that they apply at the time of the operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*) alone is logical, the following is said in response: "Even when no specific purpose is perceived, the view that they apply according to their original enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*) is established by the mere knowledge that they possess some general utility."

Just as—in injunctions where no specific result is heard—by taking a general desired object (*iṣṭasāmānya*) as the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), one establishes the threefold character of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), and subsequently determines a specific desired object based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) or through postulation (*kalpanā*); likewise, by reflecting upon the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), the "time-of-operation" view (*kāryakālapakṣa*) is established.

Regarding this, Haradatta states: although the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), it is not so with respect to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*). Consequently, that two-mora (*dvimātra*) vowel for which the designation was made by this rule is not the substitute (*sthānin*) in the rule prescribing the nasalized vowel; rather, it is the three-mora (*trimātra*) vowel. Nor does the three-mora vowel acquire the status of a *pragṛhya* through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), because such a treatment is precluded in rules concerning vowels (*al-vidhi*). This is because the *pragṛhya* designation of the dual ending of an *ī*-stem depends on the specific form beginning with the vowel *ī*, thereby requiring the presence of an *al* (vowel) as a qualifier.

Furthermore, one must necessarily rely on the rule "siddhaḥ plutaḥ svarasaṃdhiṣu" so that, in cases such as *daṇaaḍa āḍhakam*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) may be replaced by a long vowel (*dīrgha*). For this very reason, in the case of *suślokā 3* [becoming] *suśloketi*, the resulting *guṇa* vowel replaces the protracted vowel itself and not its original substrate (*sthānin*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the protracted vowel in the substitute (*ādeśa*). How, then, is the desired result achieved even under the *yathoddeśa* view? On this point, Kaiyaṭa says:

"And because one relies on the fact that [the rule] is not established by the technical treatise (śāstra), when the status of being a *pragṛhya* is prescribed in the absence of the cognition of a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, the cognition proceeds with reference to a duration of two morae (*dvimātra*)."

The meaning is as follows: even when a two-mora [vowel] is replaced by a three-mora [vowel], because the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (P. 8.2.1) indicates that the former is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the latter, the designation *pragṛhya* is applied to the three-mora [vowel] itself through the cognition of it as being a two-mora [vowel]. We do not, however, extend (*atideśa*) the *pragṛhya* designation already established for a two-mora [vowel] to the three-mora [vowel]; for if we did, there would be a suspicion of its absence due to the rule being one where the substitute is a long vowel (*alvidhi*). Thus, the application of the *pragṛhya* designation occurs only in the case of the three-mora [vowel].

Even though the application of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) proceeds on the basis of the cognition of it as having two morae (*dvimātra*), in reality, because the substratum (*dharmin*) consists of three moraes, the operation comes to rest in that very [substratum], just as an activity triggered by the error of [perceiving] silver has as its object the mother-of-pearl. Nor can it be asked how the scripture (*śāstra*) functions through a superimposition (*āropa*) that is forced (*āhārya*); for the scripture itself states that such [superimposition] is the cause for the application of the scripture, since it is impossible for the scripture to be non-existent in reality. By this, the objection that the *pluta* substitute would be heard in cases such as "suśloke" is also refuted.

Since the cessation of the prolated vowel (*pluta*)—which is the qualificandum of that cognition—is established by the very fact that the modification (*guṇa*) is produced by a cognition of two measures (*dvimātra*), the point is made; such is the direction [of the argument].

In this regard, four possible interpretations arise. The first is: *īd* and so forth are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) and the term "dual" (*dvivacana*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); the meaning is that those forms beginning with *ī* and so forth which bear the technical designation "dual" are *pragṛhya*. The second is: by the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix, the word "dual" refers to that which ends in a dual suffix; since "dual" qualifies *ī* and so forth, there is an extension of the rule to include what ends in them (*tadantavidhi*). Thus, the meaning is "that which ends in a dual suffix and begins with *ī* and so forth. The third is: "that which is a dual ending in *ī* and so forth, and which [further] ends in [a dual suffix]."

The fourth [interpretation] is that the dual number alone is the technical term (*saṃjñin*), because of the reasoning to be stated later; thus, the meaning of the sentence is that a dual ending beginning with *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is designated as *pragṛhya*.

In that regard, in the first case (the view that *dvivacana* refers to the grammatical number), there would be no application of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) in examples such as *pace-te*, because although the single vowel *e* is a constituent part of a dual ending, it lacks the status of being a dual ending itself. Nor can it be argued that the term applies to the secondary sense (*gauṇa*) on the grounds that the primary sense is impossible and the treatise must be given life; for in cases like *gaṅge*, the term finds its scope through the application of the rule "as if the end were the beginning" (*antādivat*), whereby the single *e* is treated as a primary dual ending. In the second case (where *dvivacana* refers to the word-form), there is the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the rule to forms such as *kumāry-agāram* (the house of two maidens) and *vadhv-agāram* (the house of two wives).

This is because [the word *śuklī*] ends in a dual suffix according to its derivative characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), and it also ends in *ī* or *ū* by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Regarding the third case as well, in the example *aśukle śukle samapadyetāṃ śuklyāstāṃ vastrē*, the dual nominative ending (*prathamādvivacana*) undergoes the substitution *śī* by the rule "napuṃsakācca. After the suffix *cvī* has been applied and the case-ending (*sup*) elided by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ," the final vowel *a* of the word *śukla* is changed to *ī* by the rule "asyacvau. Since the resulting form ends in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), the case-ending that arises is indeclinable (*avyaya*) and is subsequently elided; thus, the word *śī* remains ending in the vowel *ī*.

There would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because, by the rule for the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the dual ending would still constitute a *pada*, and that which ends in it [would also be subject to the rule].

Now, one might argue that there is no fault in either of the two positions; for even though the word "locative" (*saptamī*) alone was used in the rule "īdūtau ca saptamyarthe," the designation of *pragṛhya* could have been established in the case of "somogaurī adhiśrita" through the presence of the suffix. Therefore, by the inclusion of the word "in the sense of" (*arthagrahaṇa*), it can be made known that within the section on *pragṛhya* designations, the presence of a suffix does not apply.

If it is argued that in the case of *śuklāḥ* (in the phrase *śuklāḥ stām*), by the maxim "an external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules," the elision of the vowel *au* alone occurs, thereby preventing the application of the *śī* substitution; and since there is no fault even if the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule [of treating the suffix as present] were to apply—because the status of having *ī* etc. as the final element is not obtained merely by that much—the answer is: not so. For even then, both positions are defective precisely because the inclusion of the word "ending in" (*tadanta*) remains difficult to secure.

"In the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no application of the rule for 'that which ends with it' (*tadantavidhi*)," because this was made known by the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) in the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam*. Therefore, it is more appropriate to say that the name applies to a dual number ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *e*. For, by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*), it is understood that the dual number itself is the object of the designation (*saṃjñin*).

Nor should it be argued that, in the examples cited above, the quality of "ending in that" (*tadantatva*) does not exist in the forms *ī* and so on; for such a status is possible through the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).
Regarding this, the author of the *Vṛtti* reads: "A prohibition must be stated for words such as *maṇi*, etc.," and provides examples such as *maṇīva*, *rodasīva*, and *dampatīva*.

However, Keyaṭa and others maintain that this is not authoritative because it was not read by either the author of the *Bhāṣya* or the author of the *Vārttika*. They argue that the usage *maṇīvoṣṭrasya* (like two jewels on a camel) employs the particle *vā* in the sense of comparison (*upamāna*), whereas usages such as *rodasīva* are Vedic (*chāndasa*).

And thus, by parity of reasoning, this same principle applies to those rules not mentioned by the three sages but stated solely by the author of the Vṛtti, such as: *turīyasyeṣṭiḥ*, *śaṃsiduhiguhibhyo vā*, and *knameke chandasi bhāṣāyāṃ ca*. Now, consider this:
Like a pair of bees upon two blossoming blue lotuses, two drops of collyrium—dark as jewels, trembling like sapphires—fell upon her heart in the guise of bud-like curls and shone brightly.

If it is argued that such is the fate of the Nala [verse], because the word *vā* is inappropriate here and because [the verse] is of human (pauruṣeya) origin, to this they reply: this is an employment of the word *vā* in the sense of *iva*. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this; for the *Viśvaprakāśa* states: "One should know that *vam* and that indeclinable [word *vā*] are used in the sense of *iva*. Furthermore, there is the usage: "The lotuses, as if (*va*) their petals were torn by kādamba birds," and so forth. Moreover, in the commentary on Amara’s lexicon on the rule "va, vā, yathā, tathā, eva, evam," the commentators have cited the usage by Kālidāsa: "They drank the fame of the enemy (*śātravam va papuryaśaḥ*)."

As for the claim that the reading *ayam* alone is correct in the *Amara-kośa*, and not *vadvā* as stated by Kṣīrasvāmī—on the grounds that in the context of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *vat* is inappropriate, and because suffixes such as *aṇ*, *phañ*, and *vuñ* are not mentioned among the synonyms for "offspring" (*apatya*) or "collection" (*samūha*)—that is questionable. For if there were a contradiction with the context merely on account of being a *taddhita* suffix, it would follow that even [the examples] beginning with *yathā* should not have been included. However, if the contradiction lies in the specific base (*prakṛti*) being excluded, then the fixed nature of the specific base serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Because suffixes such as *aṇ* and others are prescribed only after specific bases (*prakṛti*), whereas for the suffix *vat*, that [specific basis] is absent. For this very reason, the argument beginning with "of *aṇ* and others" is rejected; for those [suffixes] lack a unique form that is not shared with other specific meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) or "collection" (*samūha*). Moreover, since they are shown many times in their respective sections through their inclusion of specific bases—as in "the suffix *iṇ* [is added] after *garbhin*"—and because the suffix *vat* is prescribed only in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), [the rule] "after *adas*, [the suffix] *māt*" [is established].

The *parādi* (beginning with the subsequent sound) and *adūtau* (the sounds *a* and *u*) are *pragṛhya* when following *māt* (an *m* sound). Examples: *amī īśāḥ*; *rāmakṛṣṇāvamū āsāte*. Why "following *m*" (*māt*)? Consider: *amuke'tra*. One should not argue that there is no over-extension here simply because the sound *e* does not recur [in the rule]; for the non-recurrence of *e* is obtained precisely through the force of including *māt*. This is because it is impossible for that [sound *e*] to occur immediately after an *m* belonging to the word *adas*. Nor should one argue that in the example *amū āsāte*, the result is already established by the preceding rule alone.

Because of the non-application (*asiddhatva*) of the *mutva* [substitution of *m* for *n*] in that context, the form ends in the diphthong *au*. Nor is there a failure of resolution even by this [rule], because the very fact of its formulation implies that *mutva* is not considered non-applicable here. As the Vārttika states: "Non-application [of a rule] due to its basis, as in the case of *ror utve*."

Furthermore, in the case of the dual number for feminine and neuter nouns, even though the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered *asiddha*, the status of being a *pragṛhya* is established by the preceding rule (*aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*) on the basis of their ending in the vowel *e*. For that very reason, both the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) and the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsika-paryudāsa*) are also established. However, under the view that the time of application is determined by the effect (*kāryakāla-pakṣa*), when the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is being applied by the rule "aṇo 'pragṛhyasya," the substitution of *m* is already established; thus, in the dual of all three genders, the exclusion of nasalization is established by the preceding rule alone.
The distinction is that this sūtra is for the sake of the plural meaning and for the sake of preserving the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the masculine dual. *Śe* 13.

This [verse] is to be recited with *pragṛhya* status: *asme indrābṛhaspatī* and *na yuṣme vājabandhavaḥ*. In the first instance, in place of the fourth case plural, and in the second, in place of the second case plural, the substitute *śe* is applied by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (*Pāṇini 7.1.39*). Because it is marked with the *śit* indicator, it replaces the entire form. By the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (*Pāṇini 7.2.90*), the final *ṭi* (the vowel *e*) is elided. Nor is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) useless; for it serves a purpose when the word *iti* is employed during the recitation of the *padapāṭha*. In the same way, examples such as *asme dhatta vasavo vasūni* should also be understood.

In cases such as *kāśe*, *kuśe*, and *vaṃśe*, there is no fault because of the suffix *śa* [added] due to their inclusion in the *lomādi* group; likewise, in cases such as *hariśe* and *babhruśe*, there is no fault by virtue of the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by a specific rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*). 14. *nipāta ekājanāṅ*: A monosyllabic (*ekāc*) indeclinable (*nipāta*) that is not *āṅ* is designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *a* (in the sense of reproach or rejection); *i* (in the sense of wonder); *u* (in the sense of disgust, etc.). Here, the term *ekāc* is a *karmadhāraya* compound for the sake of brevity, and this is supported by the usage in the rule "the deer utters [the sound] *mṛga*" (*vyāharati mṛgaḥ*). Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *predam brahma*.
