[Objection: In that case, the mention of *eka* (single) is redundant; for the designation [of *pragṛhya*] is already established by the fact that the particle (*nipāta*) begins with a vowel (*ac*). Nor should it be said that this is for the purpose of excluding the meaning "a particle ending in a vowel" (*ajanta*), because that would result in the qualifier being superfluous. This is because there is no harm even if a particle ending in a consonant (*halanta*) were to possess the *pragṛhya* designation. Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *puro 'sti*, if the initial state (*prakṛtibhāva*) applied to the word ending in *s*, the substitution of *u* for *r* (*ror utvam*) would not occur; for with respect to the designation, the substitution of *u* for *r* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

Nor can it be argued that by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the designation [of *sarvanāmasthāna*] would undesirably apply to that which ends in *r*; for even with respect to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), the substitution of *ru* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). Furthermore, there is no possibility of such a designation applying to that which ends in *s*, since it follows from operations belonging to the section on established rules (*siddhakāṇḍa*). Nor should it be said that the qualification is intended to convey the meaning that the designation applies only to what ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) and not to every vowel (*ajmātra*); for according to the rule "in a single element, as if it were both beginning and end" (*ādyantavad ekasmin*), even a mere vowel (*ajmātra*) possesses the status of ending in a vowel (*ajantatva*).

Nor can the force of the qualifier justify abandoning the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as identical with what it designates). For that principle remains valid even by abandoning the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to that which ends in such), since its purpose can still be fulfilled. Nor is there a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamaka*), because the very term "anāṅ" itself serves that purpose. Indeed, if only *vyapadeśivadbhāva* were sublated, the term would be redundant; for since *āṅ* consists solely of a vowel, there is no possibility of its occurrence [in the first place]. However, if "vowel" (*ac*) is the object qualified (*viśeṣya*), then there is not even a suspicion of *tadantavidhi*; so why [use] a single word? Such being the position reached, the author of the Bhāṣya says:

By employing the term *eka* (single) to dispel the suspicion that a collection [of phonemes] might be intended, the Teacher makes it known: in the mention of phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*), the number of individual instances is not intended to be significant; rather, only the genus (*jāti*) is being indicated.
Therefore, regarding the rule *halantācca*, the Vārttikakāra will state:
"The [prohibition of the elision of the final *t*] is established because the mention of *hal* in the root *dambh* denotes the genus."

That is indeed subsumed by the sūtra itself. For its meaning is that [the *kittva*] is established for the root *dambh-*; this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). The word "kit-tvam" (the status of being *kit*) is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). The reason for this is that the mention of *hal* (consonants) denotes the genus (*jāti*). From the root *dambh-* with the suffix *san*: by the rule "sanīvanta... and so forth, there is an option regarding the absence of *iṭ*. By the rule "dambha icca," there is the substitution of *i* (and optionally *ī*). When [the form] *dinbhsati* or *dīn‌bhsati* is established, the *kittva* of the suffix *san* is desired by the rule "halantācca."

The meaning of that [rule] is: "An *ik* [vowel] which is immediately followed by a *hal* [consonant] shall be *kit*. In the present case, however, the *ik* is followed by the letter *n*, but it is not followed by a *hal* that stands immediately after it, because of the intervention of the letter *bh*. Furthermore, while the letter *n* follows the word *bha*, the word *bha* itself is not followed by an *ik*, because of the intervention of the letter *n*; thus, the status of being *kit* would not apply. However, if the term refers to the class (*jāti*), then since the letters *n* and *bh* are both delimited by the single property of being a *hal*, the desired result is established. Consequently, due to its *kit* status, there is the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).

By the substitution of *d* for *da* through the rule *bhaṣū-bhāvena*, and the substitution of *p* for *b* through the rule *ca-rtvena*, the forms *dhīpsati* and *dhīpsati* are established. Now, one might object: "The term 'single word' (*ekapadam*) should exist solely for the purpose of excluding a collection of vowels (*ac-samudāya*). For in the case of *aiu apehi*, the designation [of *eṅ*] would apply only to the entire collection, and not to the preceding two [sounds]; consequently, *guṇa* and other operations would apply there. To this they reply: Since the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is that which is to be enjoined, it possesses primacy, whereas the named entity (*saṃjñin*) is subordinate. Thus, just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the exclusion of the collection occurs precisely because the singularity is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*).

Although the principle that the accomplishment of the function of the parts by means of the function of the whole is the basis for the rule regarding the doubling of a single vowel (*ekāco dvirvacanam*), this is not the case here; because the status of the parts as *prakṛti* (original forms) cannot be established by the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the whole, that principle does not apply here. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the inclusion of the word "single" (*eka-*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), made precisely to dispel the doubt that the term refers to the whole. What is the purpose of the word "particle" (*nipāta*)? [Consider the example: *cakārātra*. Let there not be the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) for the vowel *a* of the suffix *ṇal*. Nor can the matter be resolved by the maxim of "mentioning that which possesses meaning" (*arthavadgrahaṇanyāya*).

Because the suffix (*pratyaya*) also possesses meaning through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and because the fact that neither the particle (*nipāta*) nor the suffix alone is ever used is equally applicable to both cases. Thus, in the case of the root *ata* in the sense of "continuous motion," the suffix *ḍa* is applied by the rule "also after other roots," followed by the elision of the *ṭi*-portion; "a āgaccha" is also a counter-example. Although, by the principle of "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva*" (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*), only a particle distinct from *āṅ* would be understood, there is no fault here because that principle is subject to exceptions.

The inclusion of the letter *ṅ* as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) of the distinction is for the purpose that the designation *pragṛhya* should apply to those [particles] marked with *ṅ*. The distinction between them is stated in the Bhāṣya:

"One should know that particle which occurs in the sense of 'slight' (*īṣadartha*), in connection with a verb (*kriyāyoga*), and in the senses of 'limit exclusive' (*maryādā*) and 'limit inclusive* (*abhividhi*) as being *ṅit*; that which occurs in the senses of 'sentence' (*vākya*) and 'recollection' (*smaraṇa*) is *aṅit*."

*Ā-uṣṇam*, *oṣṇam*. The particle *āṅ* is indicated as having the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*) by the inclusion of the marker *ṅ*. *Ā-itaḥ*, *etaḥ*. [The particle] *pra* and others are listed as having the marker *ṅ*. *Ā-udakāntāt*, *audakāntāt*; *ā-ahicchatrāt*, *āhicchatrāt*. Regarding the rule "the particle *āṅ* [expresses] limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*"): "limit" (*maryādā*) means "without that" (*vinā tena*); "inclusion" (*abhividhi*) means "together with that" (*saha tena*). Both cases occur when the boundary is not included within what is delimited, and when it is included.

Likewise, it should be understood that when a word co-occurring with a term signifying a limit (avadhi) is intended to exclude what follows its own referent, it is a *maryādā* (exclusive limit); whereas when it is intended to exclude only what follows its own referent, it is an *abhividhi* (inclusive limit). Here, because of the *ṅit* designation, there is no *prakṛtibhāva*.

As for *aṅit* (the unaccented *ā*): *ā* [is used] as in *ā evaṃ nu manyase* ("Is this indeed how you think?"). The particle *ā* serves to indicate that the meaning of the sentence previously introduced has been altered. The sense is: "Previously you thought thus, but now you think otherwise. Others say that *ā* indicates the commencement of a sentence, as in *ā evaṃ kila tat* ("Indeed, it is thus"). The particle *ā* is an indicator of recollection; by means of it, the object remembered is pointed out. And here, the intent lies solely in the recollection of the sentence.

Therefore, although [the particle *ā*] is not included within the four categories beginning with "expressing a slight degree" (*īṣadartha*), it possesses the property of being *ṅit* when it differs from both [of those sets]. Consequently, the author of the treatise maintains that in the example *abhra ām̐ apaḥ*, even for the vowel *ā* functioning in the sense of the locative case, the rule "āṅo’nunāsikaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.96) is established. For this very reason, since this word refers back to the four meanings mentioned in the first half-verse, and because it lacks the status of referring back to the subject of a prescription regarding the *ṅit* property, it does not possess the character of an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference); thus, its absence of the *enā* substitute is logically consistent.
This is because, according to the fourth quarter [of the verse], the *ṅit* property is established by implication only in the sense that differs from both [sets].

Some, however, say that because this word was not previously mentioned by means of the pronoun *etad*, it does not possess the status of an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference). That is not correct; for the author of the Bhāṣya will state later that the status of an *anvādeśa* occurs even when [the antecedent] is expressed by another word. Therefore, the term *vṛtti* (function) is not something to be prescribed as occurring in the sense of "slightly" (*īṣadartha*) and so on, but rather it is employed merely as a defining characteristic (*paricāyaka*). Thus, it is not [a case of] *vṛtti* in that sense—so says Dīkṣita; the details are elsewhere.

On this point, they say: "It is not appropriate for *anāṅ* to be a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion). For instance, the word *a-* has the meaning of Vāsudeva; [the form] *āṅ* is a *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *āṅ maryādā'bhividhyoḥ*; [then] *ā* + *āt* becomes *ā* with the shortening prescribed by *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*. If one were to rely on the inherent difference of *a-* from *āṅ* and the status of being a particle (*nipātatva*) produced by the *sthānivadbhāva* [substitution], then the designation *pragṛhya* would undesirably apply in cases such as *a itaḥ* and *etaḥ*. [Therefore,] it is a compound, like *āsamudrakṣitīśānām*."

Furthermore, the designation of being distinct from *āṅ* does not cease even when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the status of *āṅ*. This is because, just as in the rule "one should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher," the status of being a teacher is not extended [to the son] by means of the extension of the status of being a teacher; so too, here, the status of being *āṅ* is not extended by the extension of the status of *āṅ*. Alternatively, even if there were an extension, there would be no contradiction in the cognition "this is distinct from *āṅ*" arising from the superimposed cognition (*āhāryabuddhi*) that "the letter *a* here is *āṅ*. Moreover, extensions do not cause the cessation of their own substratum, just as in the rule "one should behave toward this Kṣatriya as toward a Brāhmaṇa," there is no cessation of the designation of being a Kṣatriya.

Or rather, even in the case of a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), one may rely on the fact that it is distinct from the *aṅga* by means of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule itself; for Kaiyaṭa and others also rely on the fact that the single substitute is distinct from the *aṅga* by means of the *parādivadbhāva* rule. Therefore, a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) alone is appropriate, since resorting to a split sentence (*vākyabheda*) and an ungrammatical compound (*asamarthasamāsa*) is not a fault when dictated by the requirements of the operation, as in the cases of the rules *anaci* and *aśiti*. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya statement—"This [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of prohibiting what was previously established"—is consistent.

However, this must be noted: although the status of being a particle (*nipāta*) could be obtained even under the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the force of the maxim "the negative particle *nañ* is like *iva*" (*nañivayuktanyāya*), the explicit mention of the term "particle" (*nipātapada*) serves the purpose of ensuring that only that which is itself a particle is *pragṛhya*, and not something that merely acquires the status of a particle through the principle of substitution (*sthānivadbhāva*). Consequently, the aforementioned fault does not arise; for in that case, the status of being a particle is brought about solely by the process of extension (*atideśa*).

Furthermore, although the inclusion of the term *nipāta* (particle) is for the sake of what follows, its inclusion here cannot be discarded, as a purpose is possible according to the maxim: "When even a small amount [is useful], it should be accepted. Likewise, since there is no purpose for the inclusion of the word *eka* (one) here in the manner previously stated, the word *eka* should be explained in its primary sense alone, according to Amara’s statement: "The words *eka*, *mukhya*, *anya*, and *kevala* [are synonyms]. And in this context, that [primary sense] is to be understood as the state of being directly taught (*aupadeśikatva*).

Therefore, since primacy (*mukhyatva*) is obtained through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and thus the status of being a particle (*nipātatva*) is established, there is no aforementioned defect by relying on the extended application (*ātideśika*) of that particle-status. Nor does this render the indicator (*jñāpaka*)—namely, the rule "in the mention of a phoneme, there is the inclusion of the genus (*jāti*)"—untenable; for even the mention of the word "single" (*eka*) in the rule defining the technical term *apṛkta* is stated in the Bhāṣya itself to be an indicator of that very point. By this, the further objection—that since [the desired result] is already established from that [Bhāṣya], the mention of "single" here is redundant—is also refuted, as there is no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) [to prefer one over the other]. Kaiyaṭa will state exactly that in that context.

One might argue that even so, the contradiction with the Bhāṣya statement “for the purpose of excluding what is prohibited” remains unavoidable. However, this objection is invalid; for the aforementioned passage [of the Bhāṣya] is merely a *prauḍhivāda* (an assertion made for the sake of argument), since the proposed solution—namely, the application of the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* to resolve the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *ado’bhavat*—is untenable. Nor should it be said that only the subsequent passage is a *prauḍhivāda*, on the grounds that the *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* does not apply when letters (*varṇa*) are specifically mentioned.

Nevertheless, [the rule] is unnecessary because over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and other such faults do not arise in cases like *go'bhavat*. Furthermore, in the case of *anāṅ* (P. 1.1.14), if one adopts the view that it is a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there would result the undesirable consequence of having to resort to a split sentence (*vākyabheda*) and an ungrammatical compound (*asamarthasamāsa*). Moreover, even if the designation "different from that" (*tadbhinnatva*) is removed by the extension (*atideśa*) of the absence of *āṅ*, the operations (*kārya*) dependent upon that [designation] are nonetheless excluded. This is because, although the designation "different from a guru" exists in the case of a teacher (*guru*), the operations conditioned by being a "guru" still take effect; for even a superimposed cognition (*āhāryabuddhi*) can determine grammatical operations by virtue of the authority of the treatise (*śāstra*), since this is established as the very principle in the case of what is "not yet established" (*asiddha*). *Ot* (P. 1.1.15) 15.

A particle ending in the vowel *o* is *pragṛhya*. For example: *āho* and *utāho*. Why specify "a particle"? [To exclude cases such as: "niyutvān vāyavāyāhi" and "viṣṇor urugāyasya te somaḥ," etc., where the rule should not apply.
However, the author of the Vṛtti also provides the counter-example: "gavity ayam āha."

Regarding this, they say: "Even if the designation *pragṛhya* were present there, there would be no harm; for in the rule prescribing the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), the non-application [of sandhi] follows precisely from the governing heading (*adhikāra*) 'at the end of a word' (*padānta*). Furthermore, in the case of *gavityayamāha*, because there is no hearing of an inflection (*vibhakti*), and because the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is absent due to the lack of meaningfulness—since one intends to express the non-difference between the original form and its imitation—the inflection is not produced, and thus there is no 'end of a word. Moreover, the injunction 'one should not employ what is not a word' (*apadaṃ na prayuñjīta*) serves to prohibit the use of forms that have not been fully established."

And in the present case, since the very form *go* is already established as final, for this reason the rule "lopaḥ śākalyasya" does not apply here. Nor should it be asked how, in the expression "he'layo he'laya iti kurvantaḥ," the rules for *rutva*, *yatva*, and *yalopa* can apply; for in that instance, having applied the *sup* suffix with the intention of expressing distinction (*bhedavivakṣayā*), the status of being a word-final (*padāntatva*) arises either through the elision of the case-ending by the rule "halṅyābbhyaḥ" or by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the principle "an imitation is like the original."

"Therefore, the commentary (*vṛtti*) should be interpreted with the intention that there is no recurrence of the mention of 'end of a word' (*padānta*) in the rule prescribing the *prakṛtibhāva*. Now, one might object: "Expressions such as *āho*, etc., are collections of particles, such as *āha u āho*, *uta āha u*, *utāho*, and so forth; therefore, their designation is already established by the preceding rule [P. 1.1.14] through the principle of *ādivadbhāva* (treating the beginning as the whole). Nor is there the possibility of applying the rule *uña ūm̐* [P. 1.1.17] to cases like *āho iti*, because in that context only the particle *uñ* bearing the indicatory letter *ñ* is intended to be grasped. Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for the existence of the vowel *u* without an indicatory letter (*niranubandha*)."

Because this will be explained in that very same commentary (*bhāṣya*). Nor should it be argued that when *ā* and *u* undergo a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting in *o*, the rule "not [after] *āṅ*" (*anāṅ*) would apply—due to the treatment of the substitute as the end of the preceding element (*antavadbhāva*)—and thus the prohibition would block the designation of *pragṛhya*; therefore, this [sūtra] is intended to remove that objection. Otherwise, in cases such as "oṣu yātaṃ marutaḥ," "oṣu yātaṃ bṛhatī śakvarī ca," and "ocitsakhāyaṃ sakhyāvavṛtyām," the designation of *pragṛhya* would not apply. Nor should it be said that even if that designation were present, there would be no difference because of the absence of a vowel (*ac*) following it; for [the sūtra is necessary].

In a certain recensional branch (*śākhā*), the reading is *o ayātam*, and since a specific [application] is possible there, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) itself serves as the authority for the view that this rule is commenced for the purpose of prohibition. Nor should it be argued that this was not intended by the author of the commentary, because the possibility of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ado 'bhavat* is raised later on; for if the purpose were merely prohibitive, there would be no possibility of such an over-extension occurring there at all. This is because it has been resolved that even if the rule serves both purposes (prohibition and injunction), there is no contradiction, since its status as an injunction and its priority allow it to override the prohibition "anāṅ" (Pāṇini 6.1.95).

Or, let it be that *anāṅ* is indeed a *paryudāsa* (exclusion); even so, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *āṅ* and *anāṅ* is treated as being like the first member (*ādivadbhāva*), it would be included by the mention of *anāṅ*. If one asks, "For what purpose, then, is this rule?"—the *Bhāṣya* on this point states: "These are single indeclinables (*ekanipātāḥ*). They are indeed indivisible units, not merely collections of indeclinables. Therefore, this is simply an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). For this very reason, in examples such as *oṣu yātaṃ marutaḥ*, they are recited as a single word (*aikapadyena*) during the *padapāṭha*. Similarly, in the case of *ām āho devadatta iti*, there is also the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *āma ekāntaramāmantritam*.

Now, even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *ado'bhavat* (it became edible), derived from the word *anada-* with the suffix *cvipratyaya*, where *gati-saṃjñā* is applied by the rule "ūryādicviḍācaśca," followed by the compound formation by "kugatiprādayaḥ. This is because words ending in the suffix *cvipratyaya* are *nipātas* due to their inclusion within the governing heading "prāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ" which governs the definition of *gati*. Nor can this be resolved by the paribhāṣā regarding "the [application of] a technical term to that which is stated by its specific definition (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*"), since that paribhāṣā does not apply to the inclusion of individual phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*).

Otherwise, in examples such as *haraye*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-application of the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*; yet that rule is purposefully applied in cases such as *cakre idam*. Furthermore, even so, defects remain unavoidable in instances like *agaur gaur abhavat* or *go 'bhavat*, because the vowel *o* in the suffix *ḍoḥ* (in the derivation of *go*) is taught as a specific form (*pratipadokta*) by its direct pronunciation. To this, the Bhāṣya states: "Between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the operation applies to the primary."

For example: "A bull is to be bound for sacrifice; a goat is for Agni-Soma. In this case, a Vāhīka (a person from a specific region) is not bound. This is the meaning: since the inclusion of "meaning" (*artha*) was indicated by the mention of "form" (*rūpa*) in the rule *svaṃ rūpam*, an operation must apply to that which possesses meaning. Meaning is twofold: primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*). The former is the domain of the word's primary denotative power (*śakti*); the secondary, however, is the domain of usage based on similarity.

Because, just as in the case of a word, there is the natural use of a secondary (gauṇa) term even with respect to the object by virtue of its being related to a function based on qualities, the primary meaning alone is grasped therein due to its priority; for it is only upon the sublation of that [primary meaning] that another mode of signification (vṛtti) manifests. This is because the appearance of the denoted meaning (śakyārtha) is also admitted there, and because [secondary signification] is preceded by that; furthermore, it is admitted that the state of being a cognition whose qualifier is a quality inherent in the denoted meaning is precisely the delimitor of the effect-ness of the knowledge of the function, which consists in the possession of a quality inherent in one's own denoted meaning.

Consequently, in the case of *go'bhavat* ("he became a cow"), agency belongs to the material cause (*prakṛti*) alone; for this is because the grammatical regulation regarding number is established from that very source in examples such as *saṅghībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ* ("the Brahmins form a group") and *paṭībhavanti tantavaḥ* ("the threads become a cloth"), and the regulation regarding person is established from that same source in examples such as *tvadbhavati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta becomes like you"), *madbhavasi tvam* ("you become like me"), and *tvadbhavāmyaham* ("I become like you").

In this context, "being the primary nature" (*prakṛtitva*) should be understood as being the object of superimposition (*āropaviṣayatva*). And in that regard, [the term] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth is merely superimposed, not primary. Nor should it be argued: "Since even in figurative usage (*gauṇa*) it is accepted that only qualities (*guṇa*) serve as the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), how can there be a superimposition of cowness upon a *vāhīka* (a barbarian) and the like? For that statement was made according to the view that "figurative usage consists in being the object of a superimposition arising from one's own imagination," because in this case, a word does not apply elsewhere merely through a connection with qualities in the absence of its own primary denotation.

Superimposition (āropa) consists precisely in the superimposition of the property that serves as the delimiting factor (viṣayitāvacchedaka-dharma) upon the object of superimposition. Nor is this untenable on account of [the object's] distinctness; for just as there is the superimposition of silver-ness and so forth upon mother-of-pearl and the like due to similarity such as glittering, and just as in the Pañcāgnividyā there is the superimposition of fire-ness upon a woman due to her similarity to being the locus of the oblation consisting of the casting of semen, and just as there is the superimposition of cow-ness or lion-ness upon a Vāhīka or a young boy due to similarity such as dullness or cruelty—let this incidental discussion suffice.

Therefore, the designation *pragṛhya* does not apply to secondary (gauna) [meanings]. If it is objected that, in this case, even rules such as *vṛddhi* and *ātva* would not apply to secondary meanings in examples like *gauḥ tiṣṭhati* ("the cow stands") or *gām ānaya* ("bring the cow"), Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others reply here: "This principle applies to operations concerning words (*pada*), but not to operations concerning nominal stems (*prātipadika*). To explain: when a case-ending is produced from a nominal stem used in its primary sense, and the grammatical operations have been performed, the status of being secondary is understood through the proximity of another word. However, in the case of *go'bhavat*, the suffix *cvī* itself would be impossible without the status of being secondary; thus there is a difference [between the two cases].

Furthermore, the connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and an action (*kriyā*) is directly expressed by the word (*śrauta*), as in "one should sacrifice a white goat" (*śvetaṃ chāgamālabheta*). However, according to the principle of syntactical connection (*vākyīya nyāya*), when there is a mutual requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*)—the quality "white" requiring a substrate and the "goat" requiring a quality—the "goat" is determined through the principle of the denotation of the individual (*vyaktivacana-nyāya*), while the "white" is determined through the goat's requirement for a quality; thus, their mutual delimitation (*parasparāvaccheda*) occurs subsequently (*pārṣṭhika*). But the established doctrine of the Bhaṭṭas is that the verbal connection (*śābdānvaya*) pertains only to the action.

Thus, in the case of the command "bring the Gāṃvāhīka," once the case-ending has been produced based on the prior requirement for a connection with an action, the figurative meaning subsequently emerges due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). This very point was stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya:
"That which depends upon a word occurs in the mere word; and [the operations of] *vṛddhi* and *ātva* depend upon the word."

As for the claim that, under the view that sentence refinement (*vākya-saṃskāra*) occurs first, the primary meaning is understood even before the application of *vṛddhi* and *ātva*, and therefore the first [position] is incorrect—that is unsound. For the mere comprehension of the secondary meaning is irrelevant; it is of no use in the actual operation of the grammatical rule. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that rules such as *vṛddhi* could not apply to the primary sense in an injunction like "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*).

As for the claim that "the statement beginning with 'kiñca' is incorrect, because one must resort to figurative usage (gauṇatā) precisely for the sake of connecting [the word] with actions such as 'brūte' (he speaks) or 'pāṭhaya' (he causes to read)," that too is false. For even in cases such as "He buys Soma with a red, one-year-old, yellow-eyed cow," since it would be impossible for the quality alone to be the means of purchase in the sentence "He buys with the red one," that quality would necessarily have to connect with the purchase beforehand through its relation to the substance that serves as the means of purchase; this would result in the subversion of that established doctrinal conclusion (siddhānta).

Since the cognition of unfitness acts as an obstacle to verbal comprehension, its absence—in the form of mere existence (*svarūpasattā*)—is required for the connection of redness (*āruṇya*) with the efficient-force of purchase (*krayabhāvanā*) to be understood. Only after this connection is known does the requirement for fitness (*yogyatākāṅkṣā*) arise; at that point, although redness is directly unfit due to its incorporeality (*amūrtatva*), its fitness as an instrument is determined through the mediation of the function of delimiting the substance. This is because it has been established there [in the *Tantravārttika*] that, initially, the connection of redness with the efficient-force is just like that of other factors of action (*kāraka*). In the present case as well, according to that same principle, there is no reason to assume a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) prior to the primary connection.

As for what was said—that although the statement "the mat is also the object, as are Bhīṣma and the others" is possible under one view, yet because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the second case ending applies to Bhīṣma and so on; thus, in the alternative view stated in the Bhāṣya, there is no application of the logic you have presented—that too is incorrect. For that [statement] is established precisely by intending the state of mutual exclusion (*parasparāvaccheda*) occurring subsequently, and thus the prior cognition of figurative status (*gauṇatva*) is not necessary. This is because, in this view, grammatical coreferentiality itself is not admitted at the outset.

As for what they say—that in examples such as *mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ*, the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ānmahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.46) is correctly restricted from applying in a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense because it is performed by reference to a specific form—here, however, why should the designation *pragṛhya*, which is prescribed by reference to the phoneme *o* in the rule *od* (Pāṇini 1.1.15), not apply to that which functions in a secondary sense? For its designation as a particle (*nipāta*), on the other hand, remains primary even in that case. Precisely for this reason, in the word *śvāśuriḥ*—meaning the offspring of someone whose name is *śvaśura*—the suffix *iñ* applies by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), because [the application of the suffix] depends upon the phoneme *a*.

But it is not the case that the suffix *yat* applies by the rule "from *rājan*, *śvaśura*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.137), because of the specific mention of the particular forms [in the rule]. Otherwise, there would be an equal status (*tulyayogakṣematā*) between *iñ* and *yat*. Furthermore, even though the *vṛddhi* and *ātva* substitutions occur in the word *go*, they occur precisely because they depend on the phoneme (*varṇāśrayatvāt*), and not because they are operations pertaining to the nominal stem (*prātipadikakāryatvāt*). As for the argument that the *ta*-marker in the rule "gotaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.139) is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words ending in the vowel *o*, that too is to be considered with suspicion (*cintyam*).

This is because there would be a contradiction with the passages in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts on the *aiuṇ* sūtra—which address the concern that if the letters beginning with *a* were considered identical [to their respective phonemes], then rules such as *naudvyacaḥ*, which find their application in examples like *bāhuka*, would fail to apply in cases such as *ghaṭika*; and furthermore, because this would contradict the *Bhāṣya* on the present sūtra itself.

As for the rule beginning with "rājaśvaśurāt," that is incorrect. For in the case of the word *śvaśura*, when it denotes the father of either the wife or the husband, masculinity (*pumstva*) is the delimiting factor of its denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); however, in the case of the proper name *Śvaśura*, the individual form itself is the denoted meaning (*śakya*), and the phonetic form of the word is the delimiting factor of its denotative power. The distinction is that the former is more rapidly presented to the mind due to its conventional renown, whereas the latter is not.

In a case where the word *śvaśura* is employed in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), the grammatical rule [teaching the suffix *aṇ*] has fulfilled its purpose by providing for the swift presentation [of the meaning]; thus, it does not operate in the second instance [where the compound *śvaśurya* occurs]. However, in the rule "ata iñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.95), since the technical name (*saṃjñā*) *śvaśura* exists as ending in the vowel *a*, why would the suffix *iñ* not apply? Upon the presentation of that [suffix], the understanding of the meaning of the first word *śvaśura* is not required; therefore, there is no lack of the word's being presented first.

In the present case, however, there is a discrepancy: since the prescription of the *pragṛhya* designation for the indeclinable ending in *-o* is conditioned by its being an indeclinable qualified by having *-o* as its final vowel, when the word *go* ending in the suffix *cv-* is presented, the knowledge that the word *go* ending in *cv-* has a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning must—by the rule that the knowledge of a primary (*śakya*) meaning necessarily precedes [the knowledge of a secondary one]—be apprehended even before [the application of the designation]. [Objection: Even so, because the character defining the scope of the designation (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-rūpa*) remains unchanged, the application of the designation is unavoidable. [Reply: This is not so.

For in this context, the status of being a particle (*nipātatva*) is the delimitor of the property to be designated (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), whereas ending in the vowel *o* (*odantatva*) is the delimitor of that delimiting property (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*). If the relationship constituting that [delimitor] were merely co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇyamātra*), then in the case of "athopayantrā sadṛśena yuktām," because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would be included as the prior limit (*pūrvāntatvena*), both the quality of ending in *o* and the status of being a particle would exist; consequently, even in cases such as "athāto brahmajijñāsā," the designation *pragṛhya* would apply to the word *atha*.

And thus, it must be stated that the application of the aforementioned rule occurs in that individual instance where the properties of ending in "o" (odantatva) and being a particle (nipātatva) are co-extensive (samaniyata). In the word *go*, since it possesses the property of ending in "o" even when it lacks the status of being a particle, the rule does not apply. In cases such as *aho*, both properties are present, so there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti). By this, the view that the designation of "particle" (*nipātasaṃjñā*) applies to it in its primary sense is refuted; for, according to the reasoning stated, the defining characteristic of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is deficient. Moreover, a mere designation is of no consequence [in determining the scope of a grammatical operation].

By this, the *Bhāṣya* statement "between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*)" is explained; the meaning is that here [in this rule] that which never lacks the status of being a particle (*nipāta*) when ending in *o* is what is intended. **Sūtra 16:** *sambuddhau śākalyasyetāv anārṣe* The term *ṛṣi* refers to the Veda, as seen in such expressions as "it was said by the *ṛṣi*" (*tad uktam ṛṣiṇā*), and also from the lexicographical definition: "*Ṛṣi* [is used] for the Veda and for [sages] such as Vasiṣṭha. When the non-Vedic (*anārṣa*) particle *iti* follows, the vowel *o* caused by the vocative case may optionally be *pragṛhya*. Examples: *viṣṇo iti* / *viṣṇav iti*. Why "non-Vedic" (*anārṣe*)? [Counter-example: *brahmabandhav ity abravīt* ("He said, 'O wretched Brahmin'"). Why "particle" (*itau*)? [Counter-example: *viṣṇo atra* ("O Viṣṇu, here").

*uña ūm̐* (Pāṇini 1.1.17). Here, a threefold form is intended: *ūm̐*, *u*, and *v*. When there is an option for the substitute (*ādeśa-vikalpa*) and an option for the *pragṛhya* designation (*pragṛhyatva-vikalpa*), [the forms are] *ūm̐*, *u*, and *v*. In the case where both are absent, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. However, this is not established by a single sūtra. For if *uñaḥ* were connected with the substitute as it is heard [in the sūtra], then while there would be an option for the substitute by the continued application of the word *śākalya*, in the absence of that [substitute], the *pragṛhya* designation would apply by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14), resulting necessarily in only two forms. Therefore, the sūtra must be explained by means of a formal division (*yogavibhāga*).

The words *uñaḥ* and *śākalyasya* from the previous rule, as well as *iti pragṛhyam*, carry over here. Thus, when followed by the word *iti*, the substitute *uñ* optionally receives the designation *pragṛhya*. Examples: *u iti* and *v iti*. Then follows the second rule: *ūm̐*. Here, if both *pragṛhyasya* and *śākalyasya* do not carry over, then when the *pragṛhya* substitute *uñ* is replaced by *ūm̐*, the resulting form *ūm̐ iti* is desired; this is because, since the substitution depends on the entire group (*uñ*) rather than a single letter (*al*), it does not lose its status as a *pragṛhya* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*.

If *ūm* were substituted for that which is not a *pragṛhya*, and *yaṇ* were applied, then by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), there would result a second form containing an anusvāra along with a nasalized *v*; however, this form is undesirable.

If, on the other hand, the term *pragṛhya* from the rule *uñaḥ* were to continue to apply here, then, since the substitution would be prescribed as mandatory for the *pragṛhya* *uñ*, only two forms would result: *ūm* and *vit*.

If, however, the mere mention of Śākalya were to follow, then, given the optionality of the substitute for both *pragṛhya* and *apragṛhya* vowels, there would be two forms for the *pragṛhya*: namely, *ūm̐* and *u*. Furthermore, in the case where it is not *pragṛhya*, there would be two forms: one with the nasalized *v* when the substitute undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution, and another with the non-nasalized *v* when the pure vowel undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution. Thus, among the four resulting forms combined, the form containing the nasalized *v* would be undesirable.

Therefore, because both [the *pragṛhya* designation and the substitution] apply concurrently, when there is an option regarding the substitute for the *pragṛhya*, the three desired forms are established. Thus, the meaning is that for the *pragṛhya* vowel *ūṃ*, the substitute *ūṃ* may optionally occur. If it is objected: "The *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) occurs only according to the opinion of Śākalya, and the substitute *ūṃ* occurs only in that same view. Consequently, the form *u iti* would not be possible, because there is no authority for the *pragṛhya* designation in the absence of a substitute," we say: not so. This is because the word "Śākalya" has as its sole purport the indication of an option (*vikalpa*).

It is for this very reason that recourse is taken to a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule). For this same reason, the *Bhāṣya*—"In the opinion of the teacher Śākalya, *ūm̐* is optionally this substitute"—is explained as demonstrating, by means of the mention of the word *vā*, that the result belongs specifically to the *Śākalya-śruti*.

However, some say that even if the mention of Śākalya were taken literally, since the status of *pragṛhya* would already be established by the rule "A single vowel that is a particle [is *pragṛhya*]," the sūtra "uñaḥ" is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*); its meaning is that in the opinion of anyone other than Śākalya, the *pragṛhya* status of *uñ* does not apply. Furthermore, in the sūtra "ūm," although Śākalya is obtained simply by the words "of the *pragṛhya* *uñ*," the fact that Śākalya is mentioned again implies that according to the opinions of others as well, there is an optional *pragṛhya* status. Therefore, they claim that the form "u iti" is established; but this is to be considered.

Because an inference that contradicts the rules of Śruti is defeated by the destruction of its very foundation; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of evidence even if it were to persist in contradiction with them.

As for what they say: "In the rule *ūṃ*, because of the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of Śākalya and because of resorting to the governing topic of words (*śabdādhikāra*), a Śākalya other than the one continued from the previous rule is understood. For there is no obstacle to the existence of two descendants of the sage Śakala. Nor should it be argued that, since the designation *pragṛhya* is not mentioned in the opinion of the second Śākalya, the substitute would not possess the status of being *pragṛhya*; for that [status] is obtained precisely by the force of the restatement (*anuvāda*) when the substitute for *uṃ* is prescribed as *pragṛhya*.

Regarding the statement that in rules such as *ḍhralope* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), the attainment of the word-meaning is accepted even by the force of restatement (*anuvāda*) due to lack of other recourse—that too is to be reconsidered; for when [the meaning] is obtained through direct statement (*śruti*) itself, it is improper to pursue [the interpretation] up to that extent. Haradatta maintains that in the imitation [of the Vedic text] "yadetadūnūm," the substitution of a nasal (*anunāsika*) occurs according to the rule *yaro 'nunāsike*.
Also, [the rule] *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe* (Pāṇini 1.1.18).

There is the exclusion of the word *vikalpa* (option) and the word *iti*. A word-form ending in *ī* or *ū* that occurs in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*) shall be designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *adhyasyāṃ māmakītanū* ("upon this my body"). In both cases, there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* [Pāṇini 7.1.39]. Its status as an example is due to the employment of the word *iti* after it at the time of the *padapāṭha*. Another example: *somogaurī adhiśritaḥ* ("Soma is placed upon the cow-hide"). It is also an example in the *saṃhitā* text. Why specify "ending in *ī* or *ū*" (*īdūtau*)? Consider: *priyaḥ sūrye priyo agnā bhavāti* ("He shall be dear to Sūrya, dear to Agni"). Here, *sūrye* and *agnā* are not *pragṛhya* because they do not end in *ī* or *ū*.

From the word *agni*, there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the locative case-ending (*saptamī*). To illustrate what [is meant by] "in the sense of the locative": *dhītī*, *matī*, *suṣṭutī*. Here, the long *ī* is the *pūrvasavarṇa* (homogeneous with the preceding vowel) of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*). Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:
"By the rule 'īdūt-au [are substituted] for the locative,' [the desired forms] would occur even when [the case-ending] is elided, because the meaning [of the case] is taken [as the basis].
However, if that [substitution] were to apply to the preceding [vowel], then the augment *āṭ* and the substitution of *ām* would undesirably follow."
If the word *sarasī* were to occur even in those cases where lengthening occurs by virtue of a [subsequent] word,
it would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that the final element belongs to the compound, or else let it be [an indication] regarding the preceding member.

This is the meaning: let the rule simply be "īdūt-au [are pragṛhya] when [a word ending in] ī or ū is in the locative case"; for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *artha*? The question is: since the intended meaning would be that "whatever ends in ī or ū is co-occurrent with the locative case," or "that which stands before the locative case is designated as pragṛhya"—then in examples such as *somogaurī adhiśritaḥ*, where the locative suffix is elided, the status of being pragṛhya would already be established by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating the form as if the suffix were present). Thus is the objection.

In the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it (*tadantagrahaṇa*). Without the mention of its meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*), the locative case itself would be the named entity (*saṃjñin*); furthermore, since a grammatical operation (*kārya*) cannot apply to a suffix that has been elided, the rule for *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating an elided suffix as present) teaches a grammatical operation for something else by taking the suffix as the cause, and because such a suffix is absent in its own operation, the designation of *pragṛhya* would not apply in the case of *gaurī*. Therefore, the meaning must be mentioned. And because the name is based on the meaning, it does not depend on the actual hearing of the suffix; thus, even when the locative case is elided, the intention is that the name "original form" (*prakṛtibhāva*) applies—this is the point of the reply, "when [the suffix] is elided."

One might object: "In the case of *gaurī*, there is no elision of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*); rather, as in the examples *dhītī*, *matī*, and *suṣṭutī*, there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe*. And because that substitute is treated as if it were the first element (*ādivadbhāva*), the vowel *ī* indeed remains a locative case-ending; therefore, this [example] is not a valid purpose [for the rule]. To this he replies with the words *pūrvasya ced* etc. He refutes this by stating *āṅām-bhāvaḥ*: the augment *āṭ* would apply, since it is both subsequent and part of the stem (*āṅga*). Furthermore, the substitution of *ām* for the locative case-ending by the rule *ṅerām nadyāmnībhyaḥ* would also occur, thereby overriding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). This is the meaning.

One might object: "Since there is no [ending] *ī* or *ū* at the end [of the word] without the elision of the locative case (*saptamī*), and since there is no other purpose for the technical name (*saṃjñā*) elsewhere, and because such elision of the locative is universal in these instances, the name would become useless if it did not apply there; therefore, by the very force of that [name], the name will certainly apply even when the locative has been elided. To this, he says: "By virtue of the explicit statement (*vacanāt*)."

Since the designation [of *sarvanāman*] would find its purpose only where the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) undergoes the substitution of *ī* by virtue of Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) is exhausted; consequently, the designation would not apply at all in instances where the seventh case-ending is elided. Thus he says: "where there is lengthening. For example, in the passage "dṛtiṃ na śuṣkaṃ sarasī śayānam," the singular locative case-ending following the word *saras-* is replaced by *ī* according to the rule "iyāḍiyā jīkārāṇām upasaṃkhyānam.
In that instance, because the seventh case-ending is actually heard (*śrūyamāṇatvena*), the prescription of the designation finds its application.

One might object: even there, the substitution of *ī* for the locative case-ending does not occur, because there is no purpose for it; rather, there is simply the elision (*lopa*) of the locative ending following the word *sarasī*. Thus, the capacity of the rule for technical designation (*saṃjñā-vidhi*) indeed exists. To this he says: "Even there... This is a doubt where there is no doubt, as in the expression, "If the scriptures were authoritative... (from the *Śabdārṇava*). According to the *Śabdārṇava*: "A *sarasī* is a great lake (*mahāsaraḥ*)," and "In the Deccan, great lakes are called *mahāsaraḥ*."

For it is stated by the Blessed One: "In the southern region, great lakes are called *sarasī*"; and because we see such usage as in: "They bear a similarity of speech to a great lake (*mahāsarasya*)," and so forth. Now, one might object: "Even so, what is the proof that this is a usage of the word *sarasī* itself with its locative case-ending elided, and not of the word *saraḥ*? For the inclusion of the word 'meaning' (*artha*) for that purpose alone would contradict the context. To this, they reply: [The verse continues: "By the power of the Lord, the ocean of milk, which is the abode of Lakṣmī, Is surpassed by the nectar of the words of the son of Śūra, Which is like a great lake (*mahāsarasīva*). Here, the word *mahāsarasīva* is used with the elision of the case-ending; otherwise, the form *mahāsara iva* would be required. Therefore, it is established that the word *sarasī* exists independently. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that the word *sarasī* is feminine, since it is derived from the root *sṛ* (to flow) with the suffix *ī*, just as the word *nadī* is. Moreover, the word *sarasī* is well-known in the world as denoting a large lake, as seen in such expressions as "the *sarasī* of the Yamunā," "the *sarasī* of the Gaṅgā," and "the *sarasī* of the Sarasvatī. Thus, the meaning of the word *sarasī* is clearly established. Consequently, the word *sarasī* is indeed a distinct term, and the word *saraḥ* is not merely a synonym for it. This is the conclusion. As for the objection that the word *sarasī* is not attested in the lexicons, we reply that it is attested in the *Amarakośa*: "A large lake is called *sarasī*. And as for the claim that the word *sarasī* is not attested in the *Śabdakalpadruma*, that is incorrect; for the *Śabdakalpadruma* states: "The word *sarasī* is found in the *Amara* [Kośa] and other works. Furthermore, the word *sarasī* is attested in the *Vaijayantī* lexicon as well: "A large lake is called *sarasī*. Therefore, the existence of the word *sarasī* is beyond doubt. Thus ends the discussion. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having established the existence of the word *sarasī*, the author now proceeds to explain the meaning of the verse. Regarding the phrase "by the power of the Lord" (*prabhāvāt prabhoḥ*), the word *prabhu* refers to Viṣṇu, who is the Lord of the world. The word *prabhāva* means power or majesty. The compound *prabhuprabhāva* is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound meaning "the power of the Lord. The word *payorāśiḥ* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which has water as its receptacle," i.e., the ocean. The word *lakṣmīgṛham* is a tatpuruṣa compound meaning "the abode of Lakṣmī. The word *parājitaḥ* means "conquered" or "surpassed. The word *sudhāyāḥ* is a genitive singular of *sudhā*, meaning "of nectar. The word *rasaḥ* means "essence" or "flavor. In the case of *sarasīśayānam*, the fact that it is read with the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) is itself the proof. This is because, among the words listed in the *gaurādi* group, there is the rule "and *pippalyādayaḥ*," by virtue of which the word *sarasi*—ending in the suffix *ṅīṣ* and falling under that category—is specifically acute-accented on the final syllable. Otherwise, if the word were derived from the root *sṛ* with the suffix *asun*, it would result in being acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) due to the *nit-svara* rule. Therefore, it is established that there is no need for the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*).

He says, "It might be an indicator," in order to show that within the section on the *pragṛhya* designation, the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations by virtue of a suffix) does not apply; the phrase "of the stated meaning" is to be supplied as the remainder. He states its purpose: "in the case of being that-final. The meaning is that under the rule *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, both the interpretation "a dual ending [consisting of] *ī*, *ū*, or *e*" and the alternative interpretation "that which ends in a dual [suffix] consisting of *ī*, *ū*, or *e*" become established.

[Objection: But surely those two positions have already been refuted simply by the absence of the rule regarding the inclusion of the final element (*tadanta-vidhi*) in that context; therefore, the purpose of making this point known is indeed useless. To this, he says: "Mā bhūt" (lest it be so). Regarding the phrase "of the preceding member": in the compounds *vāpy-aśvaḥ* ("a horse in a pond") and *nady-ātiḥ* ("one who has gone beyond a river"), where the words *vāpī* and *nadī* have lost their locative case endings, there might otherwise be the status of a *pragṛhya* vowel for them because they would be considered as ending in the locative by means of the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is meaningful precisely for the sake of preventing this.

[Objection: But even when the word *artha* (meaning) is included, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there remains unavoidable, because the meaning of the locative case (*saptamy-artha*) is being cognized [in that instance]. [Reply: Not so. In the view that the compound functions by abandoning its own original meanings (*jahatsvārthavṛtti*), since a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) is accepted for the compound as a whole, the prior member is devoid of meaning. Even in the view that the compound functions without abandoning its own meanings (*ajahatsvārthavṛtti*), there is merely a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the locative meaning in the prior member. However, by including the word *artha*, one obtains the condition of "having an expectancy (*upasthiti*) produced by the word 'locative' through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*). It should be understood that the exclusion of the locative meaning (such as the substratum) cognized within the compound is achieved precisely because it lacks that status [of being produced by the word 'locative'].

In this regard, the following should be noted: this *yoga* (rule) is strictly Vedic (*chāndasa*). Therefore, even though the words *yayī*, *papī*, and *vātapramī* end in the vowel *ī* in the locative singular, they do not receive the designation of *pragṛhya*. Otherwise, since these very words could potentially end in *ī* when appearing in the locative case, the pursuit of the argument extending up to the verse "tatrāpi sarasī yadi" would result in being rendered purposeless. By this, the claim that [the rule follows the Vedic usage] because such a form ending in *ū* is impossible in the common language (*bhāṣā*) is also refuted. *Ihadatta* also holds this view. For this very reason, the author of the *Prasāda* has introduced this *sūtra* only within the section on Vedic grammar (*vaidikaprakriyā*).

*dā-dhā-ghvadāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20). Roots having the form *dā* and roots having the form *dhā*, with the exception of *dāp* and *daip*, shall be designated as *ghu*. The rules [where this designation applies] are such as *nergadanadapatapada...* (Pāṇini 8.4.17) and others. There are four roots having the form *dā*: *ḍudāñ* (to give), *dāṇ* (to give), *do* (to cut), and *deṅ* (to protect). There are two roots having the form *dhā*: *ḍudhāñ* (to hold/sustain) and *dheṭ* (to drink). Those ending in *e* possess the form *dā* through the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ādeca upadeśe...* (Pāṇini 6.1.45). This is because the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) holds that the substitution of *ā* is not dependent on any external cause (*anaimittika*), yet there is a prohibition when a *śit* affix follows.

Nor should it be said that an imitation (anukaraṇa) lacks the status of a verbal root (dhātu), for that is possible through the extended application (atideśa) rule: "An imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*). Nor should it be argued that the imitations of those roots which already possess the *āt* augment in their original forms may suffice, making the extended application unnecessary; for in cases where the *āt* augment is absent—such as in *praṇidyati* and *praṇidayate*—the designation *ghu* would not apply. Consequently, there is a *dvandva* compound following the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the four roots ending in *dā* and the two roots ending in *dhā*.

Because the designation *prātipadika* does not apply here due to the non-application of the rule of extension (*atideśa*), [the word] ends in a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*). Furthermore, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "when there is a mention of a form without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), that which possesses an indicatory letter is not included" does not apply here, because all [forms] are specifically mentioned. What is the purpose of [specifying] *adāb*? [Consider] *dāp* in the sense of cutting: *dātaṃ barhiḥ*, meaning "the sacrificial grass is cut. Here, there is no substitution of *dad* by the rule *do dad ghoḥ*. [Also consider] *daip* in the sense of purification: *avadātaṃ mukham*, "a bright face."

Because the *ghu* designation does not apply [to *dā*], the rule "aca upasargāt taḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.47) does not operate. This statement is intended to dispel the suspicion that even these two (*dā* and *dhā*) might be considered mere phonetic imitations (*anukaraṇa*) within the word *dā*, which serves as the designatum (*uddeśya*). Therefore, there is no harm even if these two are not treated as imitations. Nor should it be argued: "Why is *dīṅ* also not included here, since it too ends in /ā/ according to the rule 'mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca' (Pāṇini 6.1.50)? For in the case of an imitation of its actual form (*svarūpa*), the substitution of /ā/ is untenable. According to the view of the Vārttika, the substitution of /ā/ is prescribed after the application of *guṇa*. However, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, it occurs when a suffix conditioned by *guṇa* and the like follows.

In both cases, there is an absence of application [of the rule] because it is a conditional (*naimittika*) operation; however, the substitution of *ā* in the rule "ādecaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.45) applies even to the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) because it is non-conditional (*anaimittika*), and thus there is a difference.

The author of the *Vārttika*, however, maintains that because there is no evidence for these being imitations (*anukaraṇa*) of roots ending in *e* (as in *ej*), and because such an interpretation would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), this reference by means of *ekaśeṣa* refers only to those forms ending in *ā* that are actually used in usage. Alternatively, the term *dādhā* may be a separate word serving as a general imitation (*sāmānyānukaraṇa*). If it is objected: "In that case, in forms such as *praṇidyati* and *praṇidayate*, the designation *ghu* would not apply, and thus the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would not occur; for you accept the *ghu* designation only for those roots that have already undergone the substitution of *ā* (i.e., after the prohibition of *āt* before a *śit* affix has been applied)," [the reply is: True. This is to be resolved by a specific rule (*vacana*). And so says the *Kātyāyana-vārttika*:
"In the rule for the designation *ghu*, the mention of the 'original form' (*prakṛti*) is for the sake of the *śit* suffixes.

However, the followers of Bhāradvāja read: "The mention of the original form is for the sake of the modified forms (*vikṛta*). This is the meaning: the rule should be formulated as "the roots *dā* and *dhā*, along with their original forms, are designated as *ghu*. By the portion "dādhā," the designation *ghu* applies to those ending in long *ā* when they are actually used in speech. And because the term "original form" (*prakṛti*) occurs in close proximity, it refers specifically to the original forms of *dā* and *dhā*. Consequently, even in cases where the long *ā* is absent, those roots for which the substitution of long *ā* has been prescribed anywhere else are also designated as *ghu*.

Even when there is no immediate placement [of the augment], the status of being its original form—that is, possessing the property that serves as the delimiting characteristic of the substituendum for the *āt* replacement—is present. By this, forms such as *praṇidyati* are established.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: "In the rule *nergada*, in the case of *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the word *prakṛti* must necessarily be read immediately after the word *ghu*, as in *ghuprakṛtim eti*. Otherwise, the substitution of *ṇ* would be untenable in *praṇimayate*, because the root *meṅ* cannot be included by the word *mā* due to its being *lākṣaṇika* [derived through a secondary derivation]. But when *prakṛti* is included, since the word *prakṛti* is in close proximity, the inclusion of *meṅ* is established by virtue of its having the root *mā* as its *prakṛti*."

Nor does this [rule] apply to the roots *mīnāti* and *minoti*, such that by the prescription of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) in certain instances via the rule "mīnātiminoti... etc., these two would also incur the substitution of *ṇatva* because they have *mā* as their base; for the root *māṅ* is also recited with the indicatory letter *ṅ*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of including *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*) as well. Thus, one should abandon the reading "ghumāṅprakṛti" and instead read "ghuprakṛtimāṅ," and so forth.

In the *dvandva* compound *ghuśca prakṛtiśca māṅ ca*, the term *prakṛti*—due to its proximity—refers to both the preceding and the following *prakṛtis*. Thus, when it is said "the *ghu-prakṛtis," since the forms beginning with *dā* (such as *dadāti*) are brought to mind by the word *ghu*, one obtains the nature of a verbal root (*dhātu*) by virtue of being their *prakṛti*; consequently, in forms such as *praṇidyati* and *praṇidayate*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is established even without the technical designation *ghu*. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *prakṛti* in the definition of the *ghu* designation is redundant.

As for what was stated by the followers of Bhāradvāja—that [the term *ghu*] refers to a modified form (*vikṛtārtha*)—that too is not correct. By the paribhāṣā, "In the case of the mention of *ga*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction," the designation *ghu* is established even for a form like *dā* that is derived through a secondary derivation (*lākṣaṇika*). And in this regard, the fact that the root *daip* (to purify) is marked with the indicator *p* is itself the evidence. For that [indicator *p*] serves the purpose of including *daip* within the scope of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule *adāp*.

If, however, by the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a rule applies only to what is explicitly stated by its own definition and not to what is arrived at through a grammatical operation), the inclusion of the root *dā* were not to apply, then because the *ā*-vowel substitution in *daip* is itself the result of a grammatical operation (*lākṣaṇika*), it would remain excluded from being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Consequently, the [intended] purpose [of the rule] would be rendered futile. [Objection: Even so, the designation *ghu* would not apply to the root *dheṭ*. And this cannot be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because even if the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* were established by the word "root" (*prakṛti*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that other operations conditioned by the *ghu* designation would not be established. [Reply: True.

In the rule *do dad ghoḥ*, the mention of *da*—intended to exclude the root *dhēṭ*—also serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *dhēṭ* possesses the designation *ghu*. For, in the absence of *ghu*-status, the application of that [designation] would not even arise because the root would not be subsumed under the defining property of the substituendum (*sthānitāvacchedaka*); thus, an effort to exclude it would be inappropriate. Nor is the mention of *da* meaningful for the purpose of excluding *dadhāti*, since the rule *dadhāter hiḥ* prescribes the substitute *hi* for it; by the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*), the word *ghu* can be understood as referring to everything other than *dadhāti*.

Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *dārayati* and *dhārayati*—derived from the roots *dṛ* and *dhṛ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—because these possess the form *dā-dhā*, since the vowels *ā* are substituted by *vṛddhi* [from *ṛ*], and because the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (raparatva) occurs only subsequently; thus, being part of that [subsequent] process, it does not cause the application of the rule to anything other than those [original roots]. This is what must be said.

However, according to the *Vārttika* rule, "But [the substitution] is established in the case of *prasaṅga* because of the status of being followed by *r*," the substitute *ār* itself is prescribed as the *vṛddhi*. Consequently, since only *dār* and *dhār* possess meaning (*arthavat*), the components *dā* and *dhā* are not included here; this is due to the maxim: "When there is a mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included. In forms such as *dāpayati* and *dhāpayati*, however, the designation *ghu* applies even before the augment *pu*; thus, the form qualified by *pu* is also included by the mention of *ghu*.

Even granting this, we say: although the components *dā* and *dhā* of the words *pradāra* and *pradhāra* possess the designation *ghu*, there is no risk of the substitution of *ṇ* in forms such as *praṇidārayati*. This is because the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* prescribes it for the prefix *ni* when it follows that which has the status of a prefix (*upasarga*) as defined by the *ghu* designation. In that context, however, the status of being a prefix belongs only to that which is qualified by the letter *r*, and not to what precedes it when divested of that [letter]. This is due to the restrictive rule: "The prefixes *pra* and so forth have the designations 'gati' and 'upasarga' only with respect to that action (*kriyā*) with which they are connected."

If it is argued that, in this case, the same [application of the rule] would not apply to the roots *dāpayati* and *dhāpayati*, we say no. For even when an augment (*āgama*) is added, the previously established designation remains as it was. However, when the prefix (*upasarga*) functions to qualify the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*), then because the form beginning with *ā* lacks the status of a prefix, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur at all; rather, by the rule "optionally in the remainder" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*), it is merely optional. Thus, three views have been concluded.

The view of the author of the *Sūtras* is that the three previously mentioned roots ending in /a/ and the three ending in /eṅ/ are specifically designated as *ghu*; the view of the author of the *Vārttikas* is that in actual usage (*prayoga*), the designation applies to those ending in /ā/ that have the form of *dā*, *dhā*, and their primitives; and the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya* is that the designation applies only to those ending in /ā/ in actual usage, whereas for their primitives, by virtue of the inclusion of "the primitive" (*prakṛtigrahaṇa*) in the rule prescribing the substitution of /ṇ/, there is only the substitution of /ṇ/, but not the *ghu* designation.

This being the case, one might argue: in the form *upadidīṣate*, when the suffix *san* follows the root *dīṅ*, the substitution of *is* would occur by the rule "In *san*, [the roots] *mī*, *mā*, *ghu*, *rabh*, etc. This is because, according to the Vārttika view, *dīṅ* has *dā* as its base form due to the prescription of *ā*-substitution in the rule "In *lyap* and [before *san*], there is *ā* for *mīnāti*, *minoti*, and *dīṅ*," which results in *dīṅ* being designated as a *ghu* root. If the prescription of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) were intended for the root *dīṅ* ending in *ī* alone, then this fault would arise; however, that is not the case. Rather, once the *guṇa* (vocalization) has been applied, *ātva* is prescribed for that which ends in *e*. Consequently, the status of being the base (*prakṛti*) of *dā* belongs only to *de*, and not to *dī*. Furthermore, in the form *upadidīṣate*, because it lacks the suffix *ejanta* (ending in *e*), it does not possess the status of being the base of *dā*; thus, due to the absence of the designation *ghu*, the *sthānitva* (status as a substitute) defined by the state of *dā*—which consists in being the counter-correlative of the cessation induced by that [base]—rests solely upon that which ends in *e*.

Nor is there a failure to establish the suffix *yuc* and others caused by the fact that [the root] ends in an *ā*; for the author of the Vārttika has specifically prescribed that rule by stating, "The prescription of a suffix is conditioned by the fact that [the root] ends in the vowel *ā*. If it is argued: "Even so, according to the views of both the author of the Vārttika and the Bhāṣyakāra, in the form *upādāsta*, the substitution of *it* (short *i*) would apply by the rule *sthāghvoricca*; for in actual usage, the quality of ending in an *ā* exists here, and thus even in the Bhāṣya's view, the technical designation *ghu* applies," we reply: regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "There is a prohibition of *dīṅ* in the case of the *it* substitution for *sthā* and *dhū*.
Thus, its absence is established solely by explicit statement (*vācanika*).

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, has resolved this by means of the principle of *saṃnipātalakṣaṇa* (an operation conditioned by the immediate proximity of phonemes). For instance: if one were to accept the prescription of *ātva* for roots ending in *ej* according to the previously mentioned method, there would be the disadvantage of having to compose another Vārttika to ensure the formation of suffixes such as *yuc*; therefore, *ātva* is prescribed specifically in the domain of *ej*. That is to say, it applies when a suffix that causes *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* is intended to be expressed. Consequently, since roots such as *dīṅ* already possess the form ending in *ā* prior to the arising of the suffix, the suffix characterized by that form is established; thus, there is economy (*lāghava*).

This being the case, the state of not having *kittva* (*akittva*) is the cause for the substitution of *ā* [for the *s* of *siC*]. For if *kittva* were present, the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would render the application of *ejviṣaya* impossible. Consequently, the substitution of *ā*, which is produced by the condition of *akittva*, does not trigger the designation *ghu* for *siC*, which is the cause for *kittva*. This is because, if *kittva* were applied, it would remove the scope of *ejviṣaya*, resulting in the destruction of the cause for the *ā*-substitution that serves as the basis for the *ghu* designation.

This might be the case: according to the view of the Sūtra, in forms such as *praṇidātā*, once the substitution of *ā* for *dīṅ* has been applied, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur because the designation *ghu* is absent. However, according to the views of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṇ*-substitution, because in actual usage the root ends in long *ā*, and since it is the base form of *dā*, the designation *ghu* exists; thus, there is a contradiction between these two views and the author of the Sūtra. Similarly, in forms such as *praṇidīyate* and *praṇidīna*, according to the Bhāṣya view, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs invariably by the rule *nergada* (Pāṇini 8.4.17), because in that context the inclusion of the "base form" (*prakṛti*) is not required for the application of the *ghu* designation.

However, according to the view of the Vārttika, it is optional by the rule "śeṣe vibhāṣā. If it is argued that there is an unavoidable mutual contradiction between these two views—since only those ending in *ej* (i, u, ṛ) are accepted as having *dā* as their base, whereas that which ends in *ī* is not accepted as such—the following is said in response:

Since, according to the *Bhāṣya*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *d* in the root *dīṅ* is mandatory (*nitya*) in all instances, even under the view of the Sūtra and Vārttika, one must accept the mandatory substitution of *ṇ* by relying on the fact that the rule "optionally in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*) applies as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) specifically to the root *dīṅ*. This is because of the established principle (*siddhānta*) that "the authority of the sages increases in successive order. If it is objected: "The term 'adādi' (beginning with *a*) in the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) should refer only to the root *dāp* 'to cut,' and not to *daiṣ* [the desiderative form], because a vowel (*ā*) cannot follow a letter marked with *p*," we say: do not speak thus.

In the view that the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are non-exclusive (*anekānta*), the letter *p* is not an integral part of the base; therefore, the fact that the verbal root ends in *e* remains unchanged. Even in the view that they are exclusive (*ekānta*), the rule "udīcāṃ māṅo vyatīhāre" (Pāṇini 1.2.15)—which provides a reference to *meṅ* after its vowel has been changed to *ā*—indicates the principle that "the status of not ending in *e* is not affected by an indicatory letter. Thus, in either case, there is no obstacle to the application of the change to *ā*. Nor should it be argued that this [reference to *māṅ*] must refer only to the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*).

This is because the root *vṛt* occurs [in the sense of] exchange (*vyatīhāra*) only when there is an intention to express an exchange of actions; whereas the root *meṅ* occurs in that sense by its very nature. Furthermore, it is precisely from this [root *meṅ*] that the suffix *tkā* is prescribed for the sense of exchange by this rule. Moreover, since the words *praṇidāna* and *vyatīhāra* have the same meaning, and by the authority of the Bhāṣya, it is determined that the suffix *tkā*—which signifies an action occurring at a prior time—is not applicable to the root *māṅ*. Thus, while "meṅ" should be read [in the sūtra], the fact that "māṅ" is read therein serves as an unimpeded indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In reality, however, the fact that the root *daip* is marked with the indicator *pittva* is itself the evidence here. For that [indicator] is indeed for the purpose of including *daip* in the exclusion (*paryudāsa*). If the *ātva* substitution were not applied, there would be no basis for that exclusion, which would result in the indicator being rendered useless. If it is argued that the indicator serves its purpose merely by indicating the non-application of the maxim regarding "the expressed form versus the one defined by a rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), we say no; because as long as the subject of the rule remains unestablished, such a mere indication would be pointless.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says that this [root] is only *dai* (to give), and there is no *dai* (to play). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the form *dāyati* would not be possible; for since it is listed among the *div*-class roots, its occurrence is possible through the addition of the *śyan* suffix. Indeed, there is no difference in accent here, because in forms such as *dāyati*, the word is acute on the first syllable in both cases. This is because, by the rule *tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttamaṅghyoḥ*, the *tib* and other affixes following *śap* and *śyan*—which are taught with a short *a* (*adupadeśa*)—are prescribed to be unaccented.

Nor should it be argued that there would be a difference in accentuation between *dāyamāna* (formed with the suffix *cānaś*) and other forms, because *cānaś* lacks the status of a *sārvadhātuka* substitute for *l* (the verbal suffix), and thus lacks the *anudātta* accent; whereas in the case of *śyan*, the root has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by the *nit-svara* rule, while in the case of *śap*, it is *anudātta* due to being marked as *pit*, and in the case of *cānaś*, it would have its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) by the *cit-svara* rule. For even though the accent of *śyan* is *satiśiṣṭa* (later applied), the *antodātta* accent still applies there as well, by virtue of the exclusion rule: "except for the *vikaraṇa*s."

"Even though the accent of the *vikaraṇa* remains, it does not subvert the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*, since this [rule] teaches that what follows *tās* (the affix *liṭ*) is unaccented (*anudātta*). One might argue that this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only for the *lasārvadhātuka* itself; but no, he says, 'the indicator applies without distinction. This is because we see such a view in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ātmamāne khaś ca*. Consequently, they say that just as in that case the accent of *śyan* is subverted by the accent of *khaś*, so too here the accent of *cānaś* subverts [the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*]. This is how the meaning is understood.

Even so, there is no risk of this [rule] being excluded by the prohibition [of *ghu* for *dā*].
