This is because, according to the *yathoddeśa* (definition-based) view, the designation *ghu* applies prior to the augment *puK*, owing to its being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation. If it is argued: "But on the *kāryakāla* (operation-based) view, since the substitution of *ṇatva* and the designation *ghu* occupy the same location, they are both considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the augment *puK*. Consequently, the maxim 'between the internal and the external' does not apply, and thus *puK* would occur first; thereafter, the designation *ghu* would not apply," the *Bhāṣya* states: "I shall state that *dā* and *dhā* are *ghu* except when followed by *ap*."

And thus, since the property of being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of difference (*bhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) does not exist in the case of *p* in the word *dāpayati*, there is no fault.

Alternatively, the aforementioned verbal roots end in *b*; the sūtra also ends in *b*. However, the sound *p* is heard due to the rule of *car*-substitution. Therefore, there is no fault. [Pāṇini 1.1.21:
"In a single entity, [the properties of] the beginning and the end [apply]."

Even in the case of that which is without a companion (*asahāya*), the operation [of the suffix] should be like that at the beginning and at the end; for in the phrase "in one" (*ekasmin*), the locative case is seen in the object of comparison, and thus the suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the locative case according to the rule "like the beginning and the end" (*ādyantavat*). This is observed in such instances as "the wall in Pāṭaliputra is like that in Mathurā. Furthermore, the word *eka* here denotes "without a companion," and not "number one"; for since oneness exists in every entity whatsoever, it would lack the capacity to serve as a differentiator.

In this context, "being without a companion" (*asahāyatvam*) should be understood as being singular in nature, while simultaneously being the locus of the complete inherence (*paryāpti*) of the property that delimits the scope of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-dharma*). Furthermore, the phrase "not denoting number" (*na saṃkhyāvācī*) intends to exclude the denotability of number when it is divested of the aforementioned qualifying portion. For instance, in the rule prescribing the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*), the vowel *a* in forms such as *aupagavaḥ* is the locus of the complete inherence of the property of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*), which serves as the delimiting property of the objective. However, in the case of suffixes like *tavyat*, this is excluded by the qualifying member (*viśeṣyadala*) "consisting of so many phonemes" (*tāvad-varṇāḥ*).

In that regard, the purposes for treating [the suffix] as if it were the first element (*ādivattva*) are as follows: 1. To ensure that the accent falls on the beginning of the affix, so that in cases such as *aupagava* (as well as *taittirīya*), the same rule applies as in those cases. By the rule "A word beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always acute," the accent would apply not only in cases like *āhicumbakāyaniḥ* and *āgniveśya*, but also in cases like *gārgyaḥ* and *kṛtiḥ*. 2. To ensure that the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule "The augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārddhadhātuka* affix beginning with a consonant other than *y*," so that it occurs not only in cases like *kariṣyati*, but also in cases like *joṣiṣat*.

According to the rule "In a mention of a vowel, the operation applies to that which begins with it," the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions prescribed for vowels beginning with *a*—such as in *śriyaḥ* and *bhruvaḥ*—would also apply in cases like *śriyau* and *bhruvau*. Similarly, the *āṭ* augment prescribed for roots beginning with *a*—as in *aikṣiṣṭa*—would also apply in cases such as *adhyaiṣṭa*.

Now, the purposes for [the vowels] having an end (antavat-tva) are as follows: 1. By the rule "īdūded dvivacanam," the status of being a *pragṛhya* (non-sandhi vowel) should apply to words like *khaṭve* just as it does to *pacete*. 2. By the rule "napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ," the *num* augment should appear at the end of words like *yāni* just as it does in *kuṇḍāni*, according to the rule "midaco'ntyātparaḥ. 3. By the technical designation "aco'ntyādi ṭi," the substitution of *e* for the final *i* of *ātmanepada* endings ending in *ṭi* should apply to forms like *kurve* just as it does to *kurvāte*, according to the rule "ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere."

By the rule *supi ca*, the lengthening of a final vowel of a stem (*aṅga*)—as in *ghaṭābhyām* and so forth—should apply even in cases such as *ābhyām*. By the rule *yena vidhiḥ*, that which is prescribed for a stem ending in *ya*—as in *yat* and *jeyam* and so forth—should apply even in cases such as *adhyeyam*.

For instance, there is a well-established linguistic usage: "That which does not exist before another when that other exists is the first (ādi)," and "That which does not exist after another when that other exists is the last (anya). Following this principle, when the firstness and lastness of phonemes (varṇas) are defined, firstness consists in being a temporal occurrence that possesses a property residing in itself, while having as its locus a time that is the substratum of the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the locus of that property, and yet is not a locus of the destruction (dhvaṃsa) of that locus of the property.

The definition of "finality" (antatva) results in: existing at a time that is the locus of the destruction of the substratum of its own resident property (*svavṛttidharma*), while simultaneously existing at a time that is not the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the substratum of that same property. The term "self" (*sva*) refers to each specific individual intended to be defined. Furthermore, the property residing therein (*tadvṛttidharma*) should be understood as that which serves as the delimiting condition of the objective referent (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) in the corresponding rule. And the substratum of that property (*taddharmāśraya*) must be understood as being included within the specific instances of those respective suffixes; otherwise, the definition would fail to apply due to the impossibility of such a substratum being established.

The qualifier is applied in both instances to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to that which stands in the middle. This [qualifier] exists in *iy-* and so forth, but not in the letter *a* alone. Therefore, the rule, having fulfilled its purpose regarding the primary [meaning], would not apply to the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense—namely, to that which merely possesses the nature of being "first" or "last"—if it were not for the fact that [the term *ādi*] signifies "that which has no predecessor" (*anuttara*) and "that which has no successor" (*apūrvarūpa*). Hence, this sūtra [is formulated]. As for the Vārttika: "Because they are characterized by having nothing before them and nothing after them, the status of being first and last is established even in a single instance."

"Being unprecedented (*apūrvatva*) is itself being the beginning (*āditva*); being unsurpassed (*anuttaratva*) is itself being the end (*antatva*). Since [the status of] being primary is thus established everywhere, this sūtra is redundant. To this, the Bhāṣya states:
"Gonardīya, however, says: 'This is true; but [it applies] when there is something else.'"

And thus, because it conforms to natural intuition (*svārasikapratīti*), the aforementioned specific property alone is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for the words "beginning" and "end"; this is the meaning of the statement that the cited Vārttika is incorrect. [Question: What is the purpose of the word "in one" (*ekasmin*)? [Answer: Consider the term *sābhāsaṃnayanaḥ*, meaning "that which occurs at the *abhisaṃnayana* sacrifice. Here, by relying on the vowel *ā* following the sound *bha*, the designation "vṛddha" (per the rule *vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ*) should not apply.

Now, if it is argued that there is no fault here because of the word *ādi* (beginning) itself in the technical definition rule for *vṛddha*, namely "vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ," we say no; for the word *ādi* in that context does not intend the primary sense of "beginning. Otherwise, in cases such as *jñā* (derived from *jānāti*) meaning "a Brāhmaṇī woman," the word *jñā* would not be considered *vṛddha*, and consequently, the suffix *cha* would not apply to form *jñīya*. However, when the word *eka* (one/only) is included here [in the definition], the word *ādi* in that rule becomes meaningful as a means of excluding those vowels situated in the middle or at the end, since they lack the status of being a "beginning" by extension. Thus, the inclusion of *eka* serves to restrict the scope of *ādi* to the primary beginning alone.

On this point, the author of the *Nyāsa* states: If the term *eka* (‘one’) were absent from the rule of extension (*atideśasūtra*), then the mention of the word *ādi* (‘beginning with’) in the rule defining the technical term *vṛddha* would serve to exclude the application of that term to those [sounds] not subject to the extension; consequently, it would preclude the *vṛddha* designation for *jña* and others when they are not accompanied by other sounds. However, in the case of *sabhāsannayana*, the designation would indeed apply, because there the non-extended status of being the ‘first’ exists in relation to the four vowels that follow it.

Regarding this, they say: "In the absence of the mention of 'the first' (*ekagrahaṇa*) here, everything where there is no primary status of being 'first' would become a subject for extended application (*atideśa*). Consequently, just as *jña* and others do not possess the quality of being 'old' (*vṛddha*), so too the act of bringing [someone] to the assembly (*sabhāsannayana*) would not [be included]. Since, like one who is not accompanied, even when situated in the middle, the conventional usage of 'primary status of being first' is absent, how then can the aforementioned discrepancy be explained? However, the intention of the author of the *Nyāsa* is as follows: "The formulation of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) is made in accordance with linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). As it has been said by the Teachers: 'Indeed, those who investigate [grammar] should merely follow what is already established (*siddha*)."
There is no negation of that which is established for the entire world by means of its defining characteristic.

Thus, when it is said that "this is the beginning," there is necessarily an expectancy for what follows it as the "end," and when it is said that "this is the end," there is an expectancy for what precedes it; however, it is established by all authorities that this is not an expectancy for the absence of what precedes or the absence of what follows. This is because the properties of being "prior" and being "final" are defined solely in relation to what follows and what precedes respectively, and because occasional expectancy does not determine the inherent power (*śakti*) of words.

And this has been stated quite clearly even in the *Nyāsa*: "The words 'beginning' (*ādi*) and 'end' (*anta*) function by depending on a companion such as the second [member] and so forth. For instance, in common usage, when there is another companion, one designates the preceding member as the 'beginning,'" and so on. For this very reason, the author of the *Dīdhiti* and others maintain that "spatial priority and posteriority depend upon a third [factor], whereas temporal priority and posteriority depend upon mutual dependence."

For Bharata is not prior to Lakṣmaṇa, nor is Lakṣmaṇa younger than Bharata; thus, these two [terms] possess a figurative (gauṇa) status. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even the middle term would possess an initial udātta accent. This is because the cognition of a suffix and so forth—delimited by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as "suffix-hood"—occurs precisely through the co-utterance (samabhivyāhāra) with words such as "suffix"; just as in the expression "the first son of Daśaratha," there is a cognition of that [son] in relation to those sons of his who are delimited by being other than him. Let this incidental discussion suffice.

Is it not rather more appropriate [to state the rule] as "vyapadeśivadekasmin"? This is so that in forms such as *iyāya* and *āre*, doubling may occur for the *i*-vowel and the *ṛ*-vowel by relying on their being parts of a verbal root (*dhātu*), their being initial, and their being single-voweled (*ekāc*). For the term "ekācaḥ" is indeed a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Likewise, in forms such as "sa devānyakṣat," where the fifth lakāra (the optative) follows the root *yaj*, there may be the insertion of *sip* by the rule "sibbahulaṃ leṭi" and its subsequent change to *ṣ*.

Because the rule for changing *s* to *ṣ* applies to that *s* which is a member (*avayava*) of the suffix (*pratyaya*), and because even though operations conditioned by being "the beginning" or "the end" are established by the statement "it is as if it were the beginning or the end," the specific operations [of the present rule] are not established [for the whole]. "Designation" (*vyapadeśa*) refers to primary usage; that which possesses such usage due to some cause is "possessing the designation" (*vyapadeśin*). However, that which behaves as if it possessed that [designation] with respect to an operation, even in the absence of a cause for such a designation, is "like one possessing the designation" (*vyapadeśivat*). Thus, if it is argued that the meaning of the statement is that the operation should apply to even a single element as if it were primary, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* reply here:
"It is established through worldly understanding, as there is no [need for an explicit] statement."

Since this is established through worldly usage independent of specific grammatical rules, both the principles "like the beginning and the end" (*ādyantavat*) and "like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivat*) need not be formulated. For the root *i* (to go) assumes many forms due to variations in usage, such as *eti*, *itaḥ*, and *yanti*. In the form *iyāya*, the vowel *i* appears as if it were a constituent part of that [root].

Alternatively, this single vowel (*ac*) is a mere phonetic form (*varṇarūpa*) belonging to a meaningful verbal root (*dhātu*); thus, it is designated as distinct by virtue of two properties: that which delimits its status as denoting an action (*kriyāvācakatāvacchedaka*), and that which is other than it. Similarly, in forms such as *joṣiṣat*, the suffix *sip* is accompanied by the augment *iṭ*, whereas in forms such as *vakṣat*, it is alone; thus, one says, "this *s* belongs to the suffix. Even in common worldly usage, although a man has many sons, regarding a single son one says, "this is my eldest son," "this is the middle one," or "this is the youngest. Likewise, even when a woman has not yet given birth or will not give birth, people say of her first pregnancy, "she has been struck down by her first conception."

[Objection: Surely these are secondary (gauṇa) usages; for the first [usage] has the intention of excluding other sons, and the second means "by a fetus that is not contemporaneous with the destruction of that [previous] fetus. Furthermore, since the scripture has fulfilled its purpose regarding the primary meaning, how could it apply to a secondary one? [Reply: This is not so, because through established usage (*nirūḍha*), it stands on an equal footing with the primary meaning. Moreover, by the rule "ṛdorap," [the suffix *ap*] is marked with *pit* to indicate that it is *anudātta*; otherwise, since the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) would not even arise, the rule intended to prohibit it would be rendered useless. Thus, it is both primary and secondary.

This is also because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule *iṭa īṭi*. Otherwise, since the *s-* of *sic* would consist solely of the letter *s*, it would lack the status of being *val-ādi* (beginning with a consonant), and thus the addition of *iṭ* would be untenable.

**ghaḥ 21**: These two (*tarap* and *tamap*) are designated as *gha*. [Example: *racayati ruciḥ śoṇīmetāṃ kumāritarā raveḥ* ("The light of the sun creates this red glow, more youthful than before"). By the term *gharūpa*, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) that would have been obtained by the rule *tasilādiṣu* is set aside, and a short vowel is substituted. However, this does not apply in the case of *nadītaraḥ* from *nadyāstaraḥ*, because of the association with the suffix *tamap*. Furthermore, even though the word *tama* itself can be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the presence of the indicatory letter *p* (in *tamap*) serves as the determining factor.

In reality, however, even if the designation *ghasaṃjñā* were present, there would be no harm; for the rule prescribing the short vowel applies only when a feminine word in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) follows. And this coreferentiality belongs only to the suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*), not to forms such as *tarā* derived from the root *tṛ* ("to cross").

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated: "When that very river is being crossed by that very person, then [the suffix] would apply. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa raises the objection that if the suffix *ktin* were applied in the feminine to express the abstract action (*bhāva*), the form should be *tīrṇiḥ*; he resolves this by stating: "The word is first derived in its general sense as 'that which is crossed' (*tīryate*) or 'crossing' (*tara*), and is subsequently qualified by the word 'river' (*nadī*). The resolution there is: "That [form] applies only in cases such as *gā* and others which are feminine," because the word *tara* itself lacks femininity.

Otherwise, in the case of *mahiṣīva rūpam* (a form like a buffalo), there would also result in the shortening of the vowel [to *mahiṣirūpam*]. The compound is formed according to the rule *sup supā*. The meaning is: "this form is like a buffalo. Regarding this, they say: by departing from the context of the superlative suffixes (*ātiśāyanika*) and abandoning that specific section, the introduction of the aforementioned rule—setting aside the rules *tādī ghaḥ* and *pitau ghaḥ*—is for the purpose of indicating that the suffix *tarap* exists even when used in its own sense (*svārthika*). By means of this, forms such as *alpāctaram* are established.

However, some, relying on an indicator that depends upon a general category, maintain that the suffix *īyasun* also has a svārthika (intensive) function; thus, they say that forms such as "aho mahīyastava sāhasikyam" ("Oh, how great is your audacity! are established.

Vāmana, however, in his *Kāvyālaṅkāra*, within the section on the purity of words, states that the superlative suffixes (*ātiśāyanika*) are used even when there is a requirement for a correlate of greatness.

The meaning is that [the suffixes] occur by virtue of the mere fact that the excellence (*atiśaya*) is understood—even when that [word expressing the standard of comparison] is not employed—relative to whatever excellence is being conveyed. This is consistent with the *Bhāṣya* on the passage, "May the god Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent work" (*devo vaḥ savitā prārpayatu śreṣṭhatamāya karmaṇe*), which states, "The superlative suffix *tamap* is Vedic. Otherwise, its formation would be justified simply as being pleonastic (*svārthika*).
[The rule] "The words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vatu*, and *ḍati* are numerals" (Pāṇini 1.1.23) [is now discussed].

These shall be known as numerical designations (*saṃkhyā-saṃjñā*). *bahukṛtvaḥ*: The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is added to a numeral when counting the repetition of an action. *bahudhā*: The suffix *dhā* is added to a numeral in the sense of manner (*vidhārtha*). *bahukaḥ*: [The meaning is] "bought for many. The suffix *kan* is added to a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śat*. *bahuśaḥ*: By the rule "after a numeral and a singular term, when expressing distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), the suffix *śas* is added," the suffix *śas* is applied. The same applies to the subsequent examples. *yāvatkṛtvaḥ*, etc.: By the rule "from *yat*, *tat*, and *etad*, the suffix *vatup* is added in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*)," and by the rule "the vowel *ā* replaces the final of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*"), the substitution of *ā* occurs. *katikṛtvaḥ*, etc.: By the rule "after *kim*, the suffix *ḍati* is added in the sense of numerical measure," the suffix *ḍati* is added.

But surely, this designation should also be prescribed for words such as *eka* and so on; otherwise, in specific rules (*pradeśa*), by the maxim "between the technical and the non-technical, the application of the operation is understood to belong to the technical one," only the technical number would be grasped, and not that which is established in common usage. This is because when a word capable of conveying all meanings is restricted to a specific meaning for the sake of linguistic practice, it becomes intent upon that alone. Otherwise, the prescription of the designation would result in being purposeless.

Nor does this lead to the same undesirable consequence in the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇībhyaḥ*; for, by the force of employing the words *paurṇamāsī* and so forth, an artificial river is not intended there. This is not so; because this sūtra is for the purpose of extending the grammatical operations pertaining to number (*saṃkhyākārya*) and lacks the status of being a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhāyaka*). This is evident from the fact that its meaning is frequently understood even without the suffix *vat*.

Or rather—because even here there is no such restrictive rule. This is because of counter-examples (*vyabhicāra*) in rules such as "kartari karmavyatihāre" (Pāṇini 1.3.14) and "śabdavairakalahābhrakaṇvameghebhyaḥ karaṇe" (Pāṇini 3.1.17). Nor can it be argued that the required status arises from the force of the context (*sāmarthya*) in those instances; for here too, a specific effort is present. This is because, in the rule "saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan" (Pāṇini 5.1.22), by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of numbers ending in *ti* and *śat*, it is indicated (*jñāpyatva*) that conventional numbers (*laukika-saṃkhyā*) are to be understood.

This is because terms such as *viṃśati* and *triṃśat* are not technical (*pāribhāṣika*) [in this context]; for that technical number [defined by Pāṇini] lacks the property of ending in those suffixes. Nor should it be argued that the word *kati* itself is a technical number ending in the suffix *ti*; for, according to the paribhāṣā "that which possesses meaning is included," the word *ti*—which is merely a portion of the suffix *ḍati*—is not taken here as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the difference. As it has been said: "In this science, both types of understanding apply."

Thus, the words *bahu* and *gaṇa*, which signify "extensiveness" (*vaipulya*) and "multitude" (*saṅgha*), are not intended here; rather, they are taken only in the sense of "number. And this [restriction] is for the purpose of limitation: among those that do not denote an indefinite plurality, only these two receive the technical designation of "number," but not words such as *bhūri* and the like. Consequently, there is no exclusion of the words *eka* and *dvi*, which lack the capacity to denote plurality, nor of the words *tri* and so forth, which denote a definite plurality.

This is because, through their respective roles as qualificand and qualifier, they do not fall within the scope of the delimitors of the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the selection [of those denoting number].

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: "By the rules 'bahupūgagaṇasaṅghasya tithuk', 'vatorithuk', and 'ṣaṭkatikatipayacaturāṃ thuk', which prescribe augments when the suffix *ḍaṭ* follows, the fact that these [words] possess the nature of numerals (*saṃkhyātva*) is made known. Otherwise, in the absence of the nature of being a numeral, the suffix *ḍaṭ* itself would be untenable. Thus, this rule must indeed be formulated."

Nor should it be argued that, in this case, even for words such as *pūga* (a multitude), suffixes like *kṛtvasuc* and others—indicating numerical operations—would apply; for while the status of being a number (*saṃkhyātva*) is signaled for the words *bahu* and *gaṇa* in terms of their general function, for *pūga* and the rest, it depends strictly upon specific [categorical] requirements. There is no evidence for such a discrepancy, because that [distinction] is accepted in accordance with the observed usage (*lakṣya*). The author of the *Kaustubha* maintains that, following this very principle, the present sūtra is necessary.
Regarding this, there are Vārttikas intended to establish specific numerical operations even for other words.

The inclusion of the term *adhyardha* is for the purpose of prescribing a specific type of compound (*samāsa*). *Adhyardha* means "exceeding by half. Since the word *ardha*, when used in the sense of a part, forms a compound with the prefix *adhi*, it conveys a derivative meaning; because it lacks a numerical suffix—unlike words such as *tribhāga* and others—it does not denote a number. Therefore, this [rule] is intended as a prescription. In the expression *adhyardhaśūrpa* ("bought for one and a half winnowing-baskets"), the analysis is as follows: when the governing rule *dīk-saṃkhye* (Pāṇini 2.1.50) is in effect, the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51) applies. Thus, when there is the intention to express a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the sense of "bought," a compound is formed with the word *śūrpa*. Consequently, that which is bought for one and a half *śūrpa*s is called *adhyardhaśūrpa*.

Then, by the rule *śūrpādañ-itarasyām*, either *añ* or *ṭhañ* [is applied]. By the rule *adhyardhapūrva*, there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. That which is bought for one and a half [measures] is *adhyarddhakam*. [The suffix] *kan* is applied by the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśantāyāḥ*. The phrase "for the purpose of prescribing a compound" means that the genitive case is used in the sense of a general relationship; thus, the meaning is: when a compound or an operation conditioned by a compound is to be prescribed. By this, even the elision (*luk*) conditioned by a *dvigu* compound is established.

And thus, in the rule *adhyardhapūrvācca dvigoḥ*, the mention of *adhyardha* may be rejected; for [the desired form] is established by the fact of being a *dvigu* compound itself. As it has been said: "In the case of elision (*luk*), there is no mention [of *adhyardha*].
Others, however, say that the word *adhyardha* also signifies a number, because one observes its use in common parlance in such enumerations as "one and a half," "two and a half," and so forth.

According to that principle, the Vārttika *adhyardha* is for the purpose of restricting the status of being a number (*saṃkhyātva*) to words such as *sārddha* and others; it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Furthermore, by means of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), there is a second restriction: the status of being a number applies only to those two aforementioned operations and not to other grammatical operations. Consequently, Kaiyaṭa states that suffixes such as *kṛtvasuc* do not apply.
Moreover, a word preceded by *ardha-* is one that ends in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyayānta*).

The phrase "for the purpose of prescribing compounds and *kan* suffixes" continues [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that when a word ending in a *pūraṇa* (ordinal) suffix is the second member (*uttarapada*), or when the word *ardha* is the first member (*pūrvapada*), such a compound—provided its first member is then compounded with another word and the *kan* suffix is to be applied—is designated as a "number" (*saṃkhyā*). For example: *ardhapañcamaśūrpa* ("bought for four and a half winnowing-baskets"), and *ardhapañcamaka* ("bought for four and a half [units]"), where the compounding and so forth proceed as before.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "additional" (*adhika*) is for the sake of causing the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the second member of the compound when there is no *luk* elision.

Even though the word *adhika* functions as a qualifier of a number, because it lacks the nature of a number (*saṃkhyātva*), this [rule] is also an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). For example: *adhikaṣāṣṭikaḥ* (bought for more than sixty) and *adhikasāptatikaḥ* (bought for more than seventy). This is a compound according to the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51). The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "prāgvateṣṭhañ" (Pāṇini 5.1.18). Because of the statement "alukī" (non-elision), when elision (*luk*) is to be applied, the designation of "number" (*saṃkhyā-saṃjñā*) does not exist; therefore, by the rule "saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.52), the designation of "dvigu" does not apply. Consequently, by the rule "adhyardhapūrva" (Pāṇini 5.1.28), there is no elision of the suffix *ṭhañ*.

The vowel lengthening of the final syllable of the second member [of the compound] occurs by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca*. Otherwise, since the word *ṣaṣṭi* would not denote a number, that rule would not apply. If it is argued that the separate mention of that [word *ṣaṣṭi*] is redundant because the non-elision (*aluk*) can be inferred from the very fact that the vowel lengthening of the second member is required, they say here: since the vowel lengthening of the second member finds its scope only in those suffixes following words in the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*), and thus there is no possibility of elision (*luk*) for those suffixes, it is impossible to infer the non-elision (*aluk*) based on that alone. [The sūtra: "Those ending in *ṣ* or *n* are called *ṣaṭ*" (Pāṇini 1.1.24). 23.

A number that ends in *ṣ* or *n* shall be designated as *ṣaṭ* (six). Examples: *ṣaṭ tiṣṭhanti* ("six stand"), *ṣaṭ paśya* ("see six"), *pañca*, *sapta*, and so forth. By the rule "elision after *ṣaṣ*," there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings *jas* and *śas*. Why is it specified as "a number"? [Consider] *vipruṣaḥ* ("drops") and *pāmānaḥ* ("scabs"). One might object: "In these cases, there is no word for 'number,' nor does the term [from the previous rule] carry over [to this one], because that [previous term] is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) and thus lacks the capacity to denote worldly numbers. It is replied: [The definition applies even to non-numerical words ending in *ṣ* or *n* when they function as the subject of a grammatical operation. For example: *ṣaṇṇām gavām* ("of six cows"), *ṣaṇṇām puruṣāṇām* ("of six men"), *ṣaṭsu goṣu* ("in six cows"), *ṣaṭsu puruṣeṣu* ("in six men"). Here, although the word *ṣaṣ* is not a number, the genitive plural ending *ām* is applied by the rule "the suffix *ām* is used after words ending in *ṣaṣ* and those ending in *n*" (*ṣaṣṭhī-āmantrita-nidhāta-yoḥ*). Similarly, in *ṣaṇṇām gavām*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule "the substitute *ṇ* is applied in place of *n* at the end of a word, before a suffix beginning with *s* or *r*" (*na-lopaḥ prātipadika-anta-sya*). Furthermore, in *ṣaṇṇavatiḥ* ("ninety-six"), the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule "the substitute *ṣ* is applied in place of *s* at the end of a word, before a suffix beginning with *t* or *th*" (*ṣ-ṭ-ṭh-āṃ saḥ*). Thus, the designation *ṣaṭ* is established based on the presence of the phonemes *ṣ* and *n*, regardless of whether the word denotes a number. Therefore, the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) in the rule is intended to exclude cases such as *vipruṣaḥ* and *pāmānaḥ*, where the phonemes *ṣ* and *n* do not belong to a word denoting a number. However, since the word *ṣaṣ* itself is included in the category of numbers, the designation *ṣaṭ* applies to it as well, and the aforementioned operations are correctly derived. Consequently, the mention of "number" in the rule is indeed necessary. Thus, the definition of *ṣaṭ* is established.

In the view that this is an extension (*atideśa*), the recurrence of the word *saṃkhyā* (number) is well-established. Even in the view that it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), since a feminine substantive is required in the rule *ṣṇāntā*, the word *saṃkhyā*—despite not being marked with an indicatory vowel (*svarita*)—is understood to recur here; thus, by virtue of the governing context of words (*śabdādhikāra*), its intended meaning is established. This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the preceding sūtra.

One might object: "In this context, one should say 'upon the instruction' (*upadeśe*), which means 'at the time of the production of the suffix. Otherwise, in cases such as *śatāni* and *sahasrāṇi*, since *num* would be a preceding constituent, the number would acquire the property of ending in *n* (*nāntatva*); consequently, the designation *ṣaṭ* would apply, leading to the undesirable result of the elision (*luk*) of the case endings *jas* and so forth. If this is argued, we reply: No. It is impossible for *num*, which is produced through the conjunction with a *sarvanāmasthāna* (a strong case ending), to serve as a cause for the designation *ṣaṭ*, which in turn triggers the elision of the case ending *ta*. This is because a factor produced by the very presence of another factor cannot itself be the cause for the operation that destroys that same factor.

Now, one might argue that even so, when the form *aṣṭan* remains, the substitution of *ā* by the rule "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.2.84) would apply because it is both subsequent and obligatory; consequently, since the word would no longer end in *n*, the designation *ṣaṭ* would be impossible, and thus the augment *nuṭ* prescribed by "ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca" (Pāṇini 7.1.55) would not occur. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *upadeśa* (in the definition of *ṣaṭ*) is necessary for that very purpose. If this is argued, we say no. According to the *yathoddeśa* (definition-based) view, the designation *ṣaṭ* applies prior to the arising of the case-endings due to its being an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation. Thus, by means of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original), the designation *ṣaṭ* is easily established even for a stem ending in *ā*.

Now, if it is argued that under the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) view, even the designation *ṣaṭ*—which has entered into a single syntactical unit with the rule for the augment *nuṭ*—lacks *antaraṅga* status because it depends upon a case-ending (*vibhakti*), and thus the substitution of *āt* occurs first, leaving the defect as it was; or if it is argued that even under the *yathoddeśa* (time-of-enunciation) view, since the letter *n* is required as a basis for the designation *ṣaṭ*, and since it is not a rule concerning a letter (*al-vidhi*), an extended application (*atideśa*) would be difficult to obtain—this is true. However, by the inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) in the accent-rule "aṣṭano dīrghāt," it is made known that the designation *ṣaṭ* applies even to that which has undergone the substitution of *āt*.

For instance: although the word *aṣṭan* would otherwise have its first syllable acute according to the rule "traḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ," it has its final syllable acute due to its inclusion in the *ghṛtādi* group. Thus, two forms are desired for it: *aṣṭabhiḥ* with the middle syllable acute, and *aṣṭābhiḥ* with the final syllable acute.

In that case, by the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) on the initial syllable of the case-ending would have been obtained; however, setting that aside, by the rule *jhalyupottamam*, a middle acute accent is obtained. The meaning of that [latter] rule is: when a case-ending beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows the words *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, or *catur*, the penultimate syllable of the word ending in that suffix becomes acute. To set aside that [rule], there is the sūtra *aṣṭano dīrghāt*.

The meaning of that [rule] is that a case-ending (*vibhakti*) other than a *sarvanāmasthāna* following the word *aṣṭan* when its final vowel is long should be acute (*udātta*). The mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is for the purpose of preventing the application of that rule in the alternative where the substitution of *ā* (in *aṣṭā-*) does not occur. For if, in the alternative where the substitution of *ā* occurs, the designation *ṣaṭ* were not applicable, then the rule "of *aṣṭan*" would find its scope of application precisely there; consequently, in the alternative where the substitution of *ā* does not occur, the acute accent of the case-ending would be correctly barred by the subsequent rule "the penultimate syllable is acute before a consonant ending in *jhal*" (*jhalyupottamam*), rendering the mention of "long" (*dīrghāt*) redundant.

Even in the alternative where *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) occurs, if the designation *ṣaṭ* were applied, then because the rule "the penultimate syllable is acute when followed by a consonant (*jhali*)" would have no remaining scope once the accent on the case-ending has been removed, it would—by the maxim of "that which applies where the other does not" (*yenāprāpte*)—serve as an exception to that [accent on the ending] and thus result in the sublation of the middle-acute even in the alternative where *ātva* is absent. Therefore, the word "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) was stated. Consequently, in the case of *aṣṭabhiḥ*, since there is no application of the accent on the case-ending, the middle-acute is established by the rule "the penultimate syllable is acute when followed by a consonant."

Nor should it be argued that the rule for the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) in the case of *aṣṭau* has no scope, because there—due to the absence of an affix beginning with a *jhal* sound—the occurrence of a middle acute accent (*madhyodātta*) would not otherwise be possible. This is because the matter is already settled by the rule "An *ekādeśa* [substitute] is acute when the preceding element is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*). Furthermore, since it has been stated that the word *aṣṭan* is acutely accented on the final syllable, and because the inclusion of the term "final-accented" (*antodātta*) from the previous rule "after *aṣṭan*" (*aṣṭanaḥ*) into this sūtra is accepted as the authoritative tradition (*ākarasaṃmata*).

By this, the objection—"Since *kadoṣṭan* is acute on the first syllable by the rule of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of an indeclinable as the prior member, the rule prescribing the acute for the case-ending (*vibhaktyudāttatva*) in *kadoṣṭān* (in the *śas* case) has its scope" —is also refuted. This is because, in that instance, there is an absence of the final acute, and thus the application of the rule "aṣṭanaḥ" [which prescribes the acute for the case-ending] is untenable.

Although it has been stated in the *Manoramā* and other works that the term "antodātta" (final acute) does not carry over to the rule "aṣṭano dīrghāt," since its carry-over can be justified in the subsequent rule by means of "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), nevertheless, that should be understood as merely a concessionary argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).

By this, it is also refuted [by the opponent] that—on account of parsimony (*lāghava*)—the very status of being subject to the *ṣaṭ-svara* (the accentuation of the word *ṣaṣ*) should be made known for the form *aṣṭan* when its vowel has been changed to *a*, because the indicator (*jñāpaka*) resides within the section on accents (*svaraprakaraṇa*), and because the designation *ṣaṭ-saṃjñā* is not present there; and because, even if that designation were present as the cause for the subverting *ṣaṭ-svara*, the *ṣaṭ-svara* itself would be the first to be presented. This is because it is a general rule that presumption (*arthāpatti*) concerns that which directly accounts for the anomaly. For that alone is to be inferred through presumption for whose absence the anomaly is perceived. As it has been said: [The original Sanskrit verse follows here: *arthāpatter hi sākṣādupapādakaviṣayatvam autsargikam* || *yadvyatirekeṇānupapattipratisandhānaṃ tasyaivārthāpattyā kalpyatvāt* || (Translation of the verse: "For it is a general rule that presumption concerns that which directly accounts for the anomaly; because that alone is to be inferred through presumption for whose absence the anomaly is perceived."
"There is no logical inconsistency for that which is not subject to restriction, nor is there a restrictor that brings about [an effect] for what is not restricted.

Thus, in the view that the *āt* substitution applies, if the designation *ṣaṭ* were not present, then the rule "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) would be rendered meaningless; this is precisely how the justification is established. Nor should it be argued that "the absence of the accentuation of *ṣaṭ*" (*ṣaṭ-svara*) should be the very basis for the objection (*upapādaka*). This is because the absence of the accentuation caused by the designation *ṣaṭ* is necessarily preceded by the absence of the designation *ṣaṭ* itself, and thus the designation *ṣaṭ* is the first thing to be presented in the mind. If the absence of the *ṣaṭ*-accent were the basis for the objection, then the absence of that very accent would have to be the probandum (*sādhya*), otherwise the argument would result in a logical reversal (*viparyaya-paryavasāna*).

This is because *tarka* functions as an auxiliary only to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose probandum is established through the exclusion of the pervader (*āpādaka-vyatireka-sādhya*). And whether that means of valid cognition is inference (*anumāna*) or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is another matter.

And thus, if the six-vowel accent (*ṣaṭ-svara*) itself were the object of the presumption (*arthāpatti*), then the rule "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) would be entirely redundant; for in the alternative case of the *ātva* substitution, a middle-udātta form of the six-vowel accent is undesired. Even if it were desired, it would result in the total redundancy of the entire rule "of *aṣṭan*" (*aṣṭanaḥ*). Therefore, it is the designation "six" (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñā*) alone that is being indicated. This is because the application of the accent based on that designation is already accounted for by that very [designation] in the context of the rule "of *aṣṭan*."

Because there is no pointlessness [of the rule] due to its serving as the instigator of the *nuṭ* augment, everything is thus resolved. For this very reason, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "When the substitution of *āt* has been made, the designation *ṣaṭ* [is established]. And for this same reason, it was stated in the preceding sūtra: "The augments prescribed when *ḍaṭ* follows indicate that the status of being a number (*saṃkhyātva*) is the basis for the application of *ḍaṭ*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of indicating the status of being a number for *ḍaṭ* itself. Furthermore, there is no purpose in indicating the existence of the *ṣaṭ*-accent for a word ending in long *ā*.

In examples such as *aṣṭābhiḥ*, the rule *aṣṭanaḥ* applies specifically because it prescribes an udātta accent for the case-ending. Furthermore, in cases like *priyāṣṭābhiḥ*, the accent of the number-word *ṣaṣ* (six) is not applicable because the word is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatvāt*). This is because the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyaḥ* employs the plural form; otherwise, the author would have simply stated the singular after forming a collective dvandva compound. Moreover, even in the rule *jhalyupottamam*, it is appropriate that the application occurs only when the meaning of "six" is predominant, due to the governing context of the meaning.

For this very reason, the authors of the Bhāṣya stated regarding the rule *caturaḥ śasi*: "Since the elision (*lopa*) of *jaś* and *śas* following the word *ṣaṣ* is prescribed [by *ṣaḍbhyo luk*], and since other plural endings are restricted to beginning with a consonant (*hal*), there is no utility for the term 'beginning with a consonant' (*halādi*) as it occurs in the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyaḥ* for that purpose. This would be inconsistent if the rule were to apply even to secondary (*gauṇa*) usage, because in that case, it would be possible for the term to serve the purpose of excluding other words beginning with vowels (*ajādi*).

Even in cases such as *paramāṣṭābhiḥ*, [the rule P. 6.1.172] does not apply because it is not prescribed after [stems ending in] six (*ṣaṣ*) and so on. For Haradatta has stated in the commentary on "ṣaṭtricaturbhyaḥ" that the word "prescribed" (*vihita*) is an adjective [qualifying the stem], and this has been stated by [the author of the Vṛtti] himself. In reality, however, if one accepts the view that the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the rule indicates the existence of the accent for the number six (*ṣaṣ*) in instances where the substitution of *ā* has occurred, then forms such as *priyāṣṭābhiḥ* would indeed be the purpose [of the rule]. This is because, when the accent indicated by this [indication] is applied, there is no requirement for the predominance of the meaning of "six" and so forth; for the requirement for that [predominance] exists only when the accent is being prescribed by the rule "jhalyupottamam" (P. 6.1.180).

If it is argued that the designation *ṣaṭ* itself is being made known by this [sūtra], and that consequently the application of the accent is suspected to occur solely by virtue of the rule "jhalyupottamam," then our desired conclusion is established. Therefore, it should be understood that by the reasoning already stated, the application of the accent for the word *ṣaṭ* is not what is being made known.

As for the argument that, even under the view that *āt* is substituted, the rule "dīrghāt" (Pāṇini 8.2.86) is meaningful because it indicates the absence of the six accents (*ṣaṭ-svara*) when that substitution is absent—and thus, due to the lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), there would be the undesirable consequence of indicating both [the presence and absence of the accent]—that is questionable. For, just as in the case of the rule "svaratisūtisūyati" (Pāṇini 1.2.17), where it is established that between a root with a *luk*-suffix and one without a *luk*-suffix, only the one without the *luk*-suffix is taken, so too here, the indication that "only the one with the *luk*-suffix is taken" would follow; by that alone, the redundancy of specifying both [possibilities] would be removed.

For the claim that "only a desired object is made known" is common to both positions; since even those who make everything known could be considered purposeful by making known some particular object, and because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of eliminating the fact that indicators everywhere have as their objects specific, particular meanings.

As for what was also stated—that the purposefulness [of the rule] lies in its being a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) for the sake of [the form] *dīrghāt*: in that context, *dīrgha* is a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) with its case-ending elided, while *āt* ends in the first case (*prathamā*). Thus, *dīrghāt*, which is carried over (*anuvṛtta*), serves as a qualifier of *aṣṭan*. For this very reason, the rule was not formulated as *dīrghādaṣṭanaḥ*; otherwise, there would arise a separation between the qualifier (*dīrgha*) and the qualified (*aṣṭan*) due to the intervention of *āt*, which is a first-case ending. Furthermore, it would be impossible for *aṣṭan* to be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) to the rule *dīrghāt*.

The meaning is that after the word *aṣṭan* ending in a long vowel, the vowel of a case-ending other than the *asarvanāmasthāna* endings becomes udātta. And this [rule] is for the sake of making the final syllable of *aṣṭānām* udātta; however, that is entirely incorrect.

For this [objection] applies here in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* under the view that *halīti* is to be elided, or even in its absence. It is not the first case; for it is impossible for the *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*)—which destroys the *nāntatva* (the state of ending in *n*)—to serve as a cause for the *nuṭ* augment, which was produced by that very *nāntatva*. Nor can it be argued that there is no fault because that [rule] is non-eternal (*anitya*), since the *nuṭ* would be difficult to obtain by the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that what is about to be destroyed does not cause an operation). This is because the cause [of the *nuṭ*] is already facing destruction due to the impending *ātva*.

Because the form *aṣṭānām* is established by the rule *nopadhāyāḥ* through the lengthening of the vowel and the elision of the nasal *n*, just as in the case of *pañcānām* and others, it would be redundant to accept that the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* (the principle of non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship) does not apply here; therefore, that [interpretation] is to be rejected. By this, the aforementioned split of the *yoga* (division of the rule) is also refuted, since the acute accent (*udātta*) on the vowel of the case-ending is already established by the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ*.

As for the claim that, by the rule *yad uktaṃ yogavibhāgāt*, the substitution of *ā* in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* refers to [the form] taught directly (*pratipadokta*), and not to [the form resulting from] the rule *nopadhāyāḥ* because that involves a delayed cognition (*vilambitapratītika*), and that such a distinction is difficult to establish once the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* has begun to operate—therefore the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* does not apply here—that is incorrect.

Regarding the question of whether the principle of *sannipāta* (the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship) should be set aside in favor of the requirement for *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) in the case of *aṣṭanaḥ*, or whether its lack of established status (*asiddhatvam*) should be set aside so that the rule *nopadhāyāḥ* (P. 6.4.7) may apply even when a long vowel occurs—there is no deciding factor (*vinigamakābhāvāt*) between these two options. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of setting aside both the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding forms specified by their technical definitions) and the principle of *asiddhatvam*; for in your own view as well, there must be a setting aside of both the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* and the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.

As for what was also stated—that because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the numeral *aṣṭan* lacks a long final vowel, and thus the application of the aforementioned rule does not occur even in the alternative case where the penultimate vowel is lengthened by the rule "nopadhāyāḥ"—that too is incorrect. This is because of the restriction established by the rule "nalopaḥ supsvara... and so forth. Nor should it be argued that this is merely a rule concerning accent (*svaravidhi*). For such a status is accepted only when an accent is to be prescribed for a word ending in *n*; this is observed in cases such as *pañcārmam*, and because other grammatical operations (*kāryāntara*) therein also involve the relationship of being dependent on the stem (*aṅga*).

And here, the second [alternative] is also not tenable; for in that case, by the rule "nopadhāyāḥ," only a long vowel would be prescribed, making it difficult to obtain the short *ā* vowel as explicitly stated [in the sūtra]. Furthermore, there is no justification for arbitrarily splitting the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*) or assuming it to be Vedic (*chāndasa*). Nor is there any evidence for treating the two words *asarvanāmasthāna* and *vibhakti*, which appear in the nominative case, as if they were in the genitive.

And this was stated as a concession; for regarding the word *aṣṭānām*, since its vowel-accentuation (*ākāra-udātta*) is established by the very method already mentioned, there is no basis for the previously cited *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules). Consequently, any investigation into its application is without scope.

As for the claim that the purpose of this [rule] is to indicate the non-application of the designation *ṣaṭ* to the word *āmparāṣṭan*, on the basis that even in the alternative where *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) does not occur, there would be an absence of the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*), that is incorrect. For a grammatical construction (*kalpanā*) is not prompted by the pursuit of results that lack authoritative support (*aprāmāṇika*). Otherwise, one could arbitrarily perform a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) and thereby indicate numerous other results. Therefore, it is established that what is indicated is the very designation *ṣaṭ* for that which has undergone *ātva*.

[Objection: But in this way, the indication of the optionality of *āt* (the substitution of *ā*) by means of the mention of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) would be untenable, because [the rule] would already have achieved its purpose according to the manner stated above. [Reply: Not so. For that which makes its own [mention] redundant—namely, the counter-positive of the absence (*vyatirekapratiyogin*)—whether it be one or many, is what is to be indicated. Without the indication of both, the redundancy of the mention of the long vowel cannot be removed; for the purpose of the mention of the long vowel—to ensure that there be no sublation of the mid-tone accent (*madhyodātta*) in the alternative where *āt* is absent—remains as redundant as ever without the alternative of the absence of *āt*. This is the general direction of the argument.

Alternatively, it should be understood here that there is also an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā*. The meaning is: that which has the letter *ṣ*, the letter *n*, and the vowel *ā* at its end. [Objection: But if this were so, in cases such as *dvābhyām*, since the rule *jhalyupottamam* would not apply to a word with two vowels (*dvyaci*), the final syllable would become udātta by the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyaḥ* [which prescribes udātta for the case endings]. This is not an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because in passages such as *ā dvābhyāṃ haribhyāmindra yāhi*, the initial syllable is indeed recited as udātta. [Response: Do not say so.

This is because, in the technical definition (*saṃjñā*), only the vowel *ā* that occurs in place of *na* is taken up [as the referent]. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this here, since proximity (*sannidhāna*) itself serves as the basis for such determination. For this very reason, in the rule defining the term *ghu*, regarding the expression "nergada," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that when the reading is "ghuprakṛtimāṅ," the word "prakṛti" refers to both the preceding and the following prakṛtis.

In reality, however, by splitting the second *nakāra* in the rule *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ*, the vowel *ā* should be explained here as the substitute for *na*. The Bhāṣya passage which introduces the aforementioned fault regarding accent (*svara*) is merely a concession (*abhyupetyavāda*). By this, the subsequent text concerning the doubt of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is also explained.

Alternatively, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) should be made at the seventh [sūtra]. The meaning of the rule "ṣaḍbhyo luk" (P. 7.1.22) is that "whatever has been prescribed after the word 'ṣaṣ', that also applies to 'aṣṭan' when it ends in the form 'kṛtākāra' (i.e., with the vowel 'a' added). By this, the augment *nuṭ* is established. Nor can it be argued that there is no evidence for the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the phrase "yaduktaṃ" (whatever has been prescribed), because the *Bhāṣya* itself serves as the authority. Furthermore, one should not say that, if this were the case, the elision (*luk*) of the case endings *jas* and *śas* would also be extended [to *aṣṭan*], for that would result in the rule prescribing the substitution *auś* (P. 7.1.21) becoming redundant.

By this, the following is refuted: the claim that, rather than postulating an inferential statement (*anumānika-vacana*), it is more logical to postulate the absence of the six designations (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñā*) at the end of the stem-form ending in *ākāra*. This is because it must be postulated that the extension (*atideśa*) does not apply to the domain of elision (*luk*). Furthermore, even in your own view, the functional force of the rule (*vidhi-sāmarthya*) must necessarily be admitted in order to prevent elision precisely when the stem ends in *n* (i.e., in the state where it is *n-anta*). Nor can there be a contrary implication (*viparītārthāpatti*) that "whatever was stated for *aṣṭan* should also apply to the six [numbers]"; for there is a fixed principle that the separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) is intended solely for the sake of establishing a desired result. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the very purpose of separating rules.

Alternatively, immediately after the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, one should divide the sūtra into a separate rule *rāyaḥ* and explain *hali* as applying to both [the preceding and the following]. Thus, since the substitution of *ā* is prescribed only when a case-ending beginning with a consonant (*hal*) follows, the augment *nuṭ* indeed comes first. Nor should it be argued that in this way the substitution of *ā* would not occur for the case-endings *jas* and *śas*; for by the specific mention of the form *aṣṭābhyaḥ*—which is characterized by the substitution of *ā*—that substitution is inferred there. Otherwise, he would have said either *aṣṭā* or *aṣṭa*.

Nor is there any inconsistency in such forms as *prayāṣṭau* or *priyāṣṭāḥ*; for the very forms *priyāṣṭānau* and *priyāṣṭānaḥ*, etc., are what are accepted as correct (*sādhutva*). As the Bhāṣya states:
"According to the grammatical rule, [the form is used] when not employed [in common usage].
Kaiyaṭa explains that the meaning here is: "Let there be no substitution of *āt* (i.e., *ā*) in this case."

Some, however, say that the meaning of the Bhāṣya is that *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) certainly occurs here; but that is to be considered. For the doubt concerns the alternative view (*apakarṣapakṣa*), and thus it is more appropriate to provide the resolution right there. Furthermore, since the condition of beginning with a consonant (*halāditva*) is absent there, there is no possibility of *ātvam* applying, and thus Kaiyaṭa’s explanation alone is correct. This, then, is the resulting meaning: first, according to the *yathoddeśa* view, five resolutions for the word *aṣṭan* arise from the long vowel *ā* and the two divisions [of the rule]. And this is the distinction here:
in the case of the forms ending in *auṅ*, *aṣṭābhiḥ*, and *aṣṭāsu*, there is no *ātvam* in the final opinion regarding the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense.
However, in that case, the substitution of ātva does indeed occur in the first four alternatives.

For instance, according to the view that the substitution of *āt* is prescribed for case-endings beginning with *ha*, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *priyāṣṭā*, the substitution of *āt* would not apply from the ending *auṅ* up to *ṭā*, nor in the cases *ām*, *ṅe*, *ṅasi*, *ṅas*, *ṅi*, and the two instances of *os*, because these endings do not begin with a vowel (*aj*). Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of the application of *āt* here at all due to the prohibition of *tadantavidhi* (the rule applying to what ends with the stem) by the principle "by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a specific designation [for a grammatical operation], [the operation applies only to] that which ends with it"; for this prohibition is overridden by the rule "in the governing context of a word (*pada*) or a stem (*aṅga*), [the operation applies] to that [stem] and to its following member."

Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of the *luṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes, the substitution of *ātva* (*ā*) also does not apply when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). This is because there is a disparity: in the rule prescribing those [suffixes], the use of the plural number results in the attainment of the primary meaning of the object, whereas in the rule prescribing *ātva*, the use of the singular number prevents this. If it is asked, "What then is the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya in this matter?"—do not say so. Because the singular number is used in the rule prescribing *ātva*, there is a reference to the phonetic form itself (*svarūpa*) and not to the meaning; therefore, *ātva* occurs even when [the stem] *aṣṭan* is used as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).

For Haradatta, by stating, "In that case as well, because it is subject to optionality, one also has *priyāṣṭā*, *priyāṣṭānau*, and *priyāṣṭānaḥ*," has made it perfectly clear that the intention of the Bhāṣya is not to apply the rule *halī* (Pāṇini 6.1.69) [as a restrictive restriction].

As for the argument that the statement by Haradatta—that the rule "from eight" (*aṣṭābhyaḥ*) refers to forms ending in that word, and thus, having cited *paramāṣṭau*, the substitution of *au* does not occur in *priyāṣṭānaḥ* because the replacement by *āt* is absent—contradicts the Vṛtti commentary (which states that *au* occurs), and furthermore contradicts the passage by Haradatta himself which says, "Just as the replacement by *āt* does not occur when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*), so too will it be explained in the very rule prescribing that [substitution]," and therefore that passage by Haradatta is incorrect—that is to be considered. For in the phrase "it will be explained," it is intended that the author of the Vṛtti is meant.

Furthermore, the extraction of the word *hal* (from the rule *hali*) as the cause for the absence of *ātva* is quite clear there [in the Bhāṣya], because the literal reading of the Vṛtti text is untenable. This is because, by indicating the predominance of the meaning in the form "aṣṭābhyaḥ," it is made explicit that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the very fact of being secondary (*gauṇatva*) is the cause for the absence of *auś*, and not the absence of *ātva*; for the absence of *ātva* is not the cause for the absence of *auś*. If it is asked: "Even so, how is it established that the intention of the Bhāṣya is not that *hal* is to be extracted [from the rule]? It is said in reply:

For it is precisely the understanding of all four positions that serves as the reason in this case; since it is impossible for the intended meaning (*tātparya*), which is understood by many, to be sublated by one [position]. Moreover, even those who are inferior are to be favored when they are in the majority, and this is all the more so when they are of equal status. Indeed, there is no rule that what is stated last must necessarily be stronger.

Even though the statement "the elision of *s* occurs only in the case of *apsaras*, as in *payasyate*" is presented later in the commentary on the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.11), Kaiyaṭa has stated that "this is not the established position. Furthermore, the intention of the authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) is settled in cases such as the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 11.1.38–42) to favor parsimony (*lāghava*). Moreover, in the view that *halīti* is to be drawn down [from a previous rule], the sublation of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* and other rules is clear according to the method already described.

And in the view that the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) indicates that the designation *ṣaṭ* applies to that which has undergone the substitution of *ātva*, there is no occurrence of that [substitution].

As for the claim that there is an absence of result (*phalābhāva*) regarding the designation *ṣaṭ* when the stem ends in long *ā*, and that the augment *nuṭ* alone is not the result—because by the withdrawal of the rule *halī* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the substitution of *ā* (for *auṅ*) does not apply before *nuṭ*, and because that [withdrawal] is necessary for the sake of forms such as *priyāṣṭnaḥ*—that is incorrect. For it is impossible to put forward the aforementioned reasoning against one who objects to the withdrawal of *halī*. Otherwise, since the designation *ṣaṭ* would already be established for a stem ending in long *ā*, the claim that there is an absence of result in the withdrawal of *halī* would be unavoidable; furthermore, the form *priyāṣṭnaḥ* is justifiable even under the alternative view where the substitution of *ā* does not occur.

In reality, if the intention were to express that *hali* is a remainder for both [the preceding and following rules], one would have composed a single rule: *rāyaṣṭanorā hali vibhaktau*. Furthermore, if the Bhāṣya were fully committed to this position, it would have stated that the formulation should be made exactly in that manner.

As for the objection that, under the view that "the word *rai* is Vedic," the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* would also occur only in the Veda—that is not so. For there is no evidence that a grammatical operation applies only in the Veda simply because it occurs alongside another word that is Vedic. Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that the prohibition of the elision of *n* in the vocative (*sambuddhi*) would likewise apply only in the Veda. Moreover, Kaiyaṭa has stated: "The word *rai* ending in *kyac* is itself Vedic."

As for the claim that there would also be the undesirable consequence of an optional application of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) even for the word *rai*, that too is incorrect. This is because there is no word in the rule that indicates such an option. Furthermore, since the optional *ātva* is made known through the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) and so on, there is a rule of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the indicator (*liṅga*) and that which is indicated (*liṅgin*). Moreover, this [substitution] pertains exclusively to the word *aṣṭan*. Even though the optional application of the *ṅīṣ* suffix after words ending in *pitṛ* is made known by the inclusion of the word *mātāmaha* in the *gaura*-group, it is not accepted that the *ṅīṣ* of the *gaura*-group functions in the same way.

This [objection] is refuted: in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, if the term *hali* were included, its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) would not apply in the case of *rāyaḥ*; for by the inclusion of *aci* in the rule *yo'ci*, it is indicated that the word *hal* does not recur in the subsequent rules. Furthermore, the argument that the inclusion of *hali* is for the purpose of making the substitution of *ā* (in *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*) applicable to case-endings beginning with consonants is also rejected; because if the two rules were treated as a single compound injunction (*ekayoga*), the aforementioned fault would not arise.

In reality, since the general rule (*utsarga*) is that [the substitution of] *āt* occurs for the final phoneme, and the exception (*apavāda*) is that this applies when followed by a consonant (*hal*), the author of the Bhāṣya—by rejecting the inclusion of the term *ac* (vowel) in that context—intends to indicate that the term *hal* (consonant) is indeed carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule "yuṣmadasmadoḥ. This is how it should be understood.

As for what they say—that even Haradatta’s statement that the form *priyāṣṭṇa* occurs when the substitution of *ā* is absent, provided that *al*-lopa and *ṣṭu*-tva apply—this too is questionable. For, due to the status of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding *al*-lopa in a rule concerning what precedes it, there is an intervention by the vowel *a*, making *ṣṭu*-tva difficult to obtain. Nor can it be argued that "in a rule concerning what precedes, [the *sthānivadbhāva*] does not apply," because of the prohibition: "there is a fault in this [rule] regarding the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), *latva*, and *ṇatva*. Since this prohibition applies, the [*sthānivadbhāva*] does not operate in the prescription of *ṇatva*.

Nor should it be argued that in that context, only the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) explicitly prescribed by the rule "raṣābhyām" is understood, because the *ṇatva* obtainable through the rule for *ṣṭutva* involves a delayed cognition. This is because the inclusion of *ṇ* in that [rule] has been rejected in the Bhāṣya by virtue of the continued application of the mention of the retroflex (*mūrddhanya*). Furthermore, it should not be claimed that this would lead to the impossibility of *ṇatva* in forms such as *pūṣṇaḥ*, since *ṇatva* is established there by the rule "aṭ-kupvāṅ-num-vyavāye'pi. That [objection] is to be considered carefully.

Even so, because the status of being "pratipadokta" (stated in its own specific form) is easily established by virtue of the fact that the delimiting factor of the predicate (*vidheya*) rests solely upon the quality of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*), and because that very *ṇatva* for which there is the employment of the word *ṇa* in the rule is indeed *pratipadokta*, even when the letter *ṇ* itself is rejected; furthermore, the employment [of the term] qualified by the absence of rejection is not the determining factor, as its utility lies merely in indicating a specific statement.

Even for words that have been rejected [by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*], their presentation by the commentators (*bhāṣyakāra*) as indicators (*jñāpaka*) makes it all the more appropriate to accept their status as *upalakṣaṇa* (indicators) without regard for a restrictive rule of existence (*sattvaniyama*). This is because it is universally accepted that the word *seṭi* in the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*, although rejected by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, serves as an indicator that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution of the original element) does not apply in a rule concerning what precedes. Furthermore, this is supported by the association with substitutes whose original elements (*sthānin*) are not at the end of a word (*apadānta*);
for even if the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) depends on being at the end of a word, its counterpart—the elision (*lopa*)—and its correlates, the *s* and *k* sounds, are not at the end of a word.

Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *la* (in *na ca nilayate*) applies even when [the *ya*] stands at the end of a word; for in that case, neither the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* nor its prohibition would apply. If it is argued that the restrictive force of *sāhacarya* (association) is not absolute, then the same would hold for the *pañcamī-samāsa* (genitive compound), as the situation is identical. Furthermore, the principle that "application is the default" (*pravṛtter autsargikatvam*) applies equally to both cases.

Furthermore, since you yourself have rejected both the analysis of *pūrvavidhau* as a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) and the inclusion of the term *ṇatva* in the rule *tasya doṣaḥ*, [your objection is invalid]. Nor should it be argued that, because the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is "unestablished" (*asiddha*) with respect to the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) by the principle "that which is external is unestablished with respect to the internal," there is still no substitution of *ṣṭu* [for *ṣṭu*]. This is because, according to the *yathoddeśa* view, that principle does not apply during the prescription of *ṣṭutva*; for *ṣṭutva* is itself unestablished with respect to that [principle].

As for the claim that, for the sake of achieving a single result (*phalaikya*), the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that a rule operates at the time the effect is to be produced) alone is logical here—that is not correct. For the unity of result would have to be established either through the inclusion and subsequent rejection of the mention of *ṇa* in the rule *raṣābhyām*, or through the inclusion and subsequent rejection of the mention of *ṇatva* in the rule *tasya doṣaḥ*, or through the acceptance and subsequent rejection of the *pañcamī-samāsa* (genitive compound) interpretation in the rule *acaḥ parasmin*. It is not the first case.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because by the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding what is taught by rule versus what is taught as a word-form), and in its absence by the rejection of the *ṇatva* (nasalization) on the grounds that "it is a fault," the occurrence of *ṣṭutva* is easily established. Nor is the second; for when *ṇatva* is mentioned, by the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*, and in its absence due to the lack of any subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the occurrence of *ṣṭutva* is certain. Nor is the third; for under the view of the genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*), by the principle of the *pratipadokta-nyāya*, and in its absence for the very same reason, the occurrence of *ṣṭutva* is proven. Therefore, since it serves to bring about their identity, the *yathoddeśa-pakṣa* (the view that grammatical operations apply to the original form) alone is appropriate here.

In reality, however, this will be stated in the *sūtra* "na padānta" by both the *vārttika* and the *bhāṣya*: "The rules concerning doubling (*dvirvacana*) and so forth [are not applied] except in cases of elision of *vṛddhi* (*vareya-lopa*) and accent (*svara*). Thus, even where a property common to *ṇakāra* and others serves as the delimiting factor for what is to be prescribed (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*), if that were included under the term "ṇatva" in the rule "tasya doṣaḥ," then because it would apply even in forms like *śiṇḍhi*, the application of the rule "pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat" would become untenable; therefore, the rejection of the mention of "homogeneous letters" (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) based on that [rule] is not [justified].

It might be argued: according to your view, in the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*, since the letter *ṇ* is also prescribed as that which is to be substituted (*vidheya*), there would be an injunction for *ṇ*-hood (*ṇatva*). Consequently, only that where the status of being a substitute (*ādeśatva*) is restricted solely to the individual instance delimited by *ṇ*-hood is what is grasped by the term *ṇatva*. And this is exactly the same whether one accepts the inclusion of the letter *ṇ* in the rule *raṣābhyām* or the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "cerebral" (*mūrdhanya*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. (24) A numeral ending in *ḍati* shall be designated as *ṣaṭ* ("six"). Examples: *kati santi* ("how many are there?"); *katy adrākṣīḥ* ("how many did you see?"). By the rule *ṣaḍbhyaḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings *jas* and *śas*. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states:

The rule should be formulated as follows: "vahugaṇavatu-saṃkhyā," "ḍati ca," and "ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ. This is because, according to the alternative formulation, there would be unnecessary complexity due to the inclusion of the term *ḍati* in both rules. In the rule "ḍati ca," the word *saṃkhyā* (numeral) is understood from the previous rule. However, in the rule "ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ," both *saṃkhyā* and *ḍati* are understood. It should not be argued that, if this were the case, the Uṇādi derivative *ḍati* in "pāterḍatiḥ" would also be subject to the designation *saṃkhyā*, leading to the elision of the case-ending (*luk*) in forms such as *patayaḥ*.

This is because, by association with the term *saṃkhyā*, only the *ḍati* suffix belonging to the secondary nominal derivation (*taddhita*) is intended to be included. This same reasoning applies even to the alternative formulation.

25. *Kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*. These two have the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *niṣṭhā*. Examples: *kṛtaḥ*, *kṛtavān*. The term "*niṣṭhā*" is prescribed for both [suffixes]. As for the mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—where the designation applies to those that are prescribed, and the prescription applies to those that possess the designation—we shall resolve that very point later. Why is there the mention of the suffixes with their indicatory letters (*sānubandha*)? [It is] so that [the designation does not apply] to forms such as *lotaḥ* (imperative) or *gartaḥ* (a hole).

It might be argued as follows: the inclusion of *anubandhas* (phonetic markers) is for the sake of the grammatical operation (*kārya*), but they do not constitute an integral part of the application (*prayogasamavāya*). Consequently, when an *anubandha* has been elided, in cases where the remaining portion possesses absolute similarity [to another form], there would be no regulation of the operations triggered by that [original] form. Nor should it be said that this case is like Devadatta’s house, where even after the crow has flown away, the cognition of its distinction from other houses persists; for in that case, there is a specific configuration [of the house] as the basis, whereas here there is no other property (*rūpāntara*) to serve as the delimiting factor (*upalakṣyatāvacchedaka*) for what is to be characterized.
For an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is precisely that which causes the cognition of exclusion by means of presenting another property whose occurrence is excluded [from the subject]. As it has been said:
"In the case of the technical designation *niṣṭhā*, there is a prohibition of the application of the same term."

Not so. Here, specific meanings such as time (*kāla*) and grammatical relations (*kāraka*) themselves occupy the place of specific configurations (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*) and the like. Upon seeing these, when there is a recollection of their respective *anubandhas*, the correctness (*sādhutva*) of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) conditioned by those respective *anubandhas* is understood. For instance, when "the rice was reaped by Devadatta" (*devadattena lūnaḥ śāliḥ*) is uttered, one who knows the technical definitions understands that this is the suffix *kta* because of the comprehension of the object (*karman*) and the past tense (*bhūtakāla*). But when "one should sacrifice a *lota*" (*lotam ālabheta*) is said, the word *lota* is understood to denote a ram.

This is because of the *uṇādi* sūtra: "The suffix *tan* is applied after the roots *has*, *mṛ*, *ṛ*, *ṇī*, *vā*, *mi*, *da*, *mil*, *ū*, *pū*, *dhū*, and *vṛ*. Now, by the *uṇādi* rule "The suffix *kta* is applied after the roots *añj*, *ghṛ*, and *si*," the same designation (*saṃjñā*) would also apply to the *kta* prescribed in the examples *aktaṃ*, *ghṛtaṃ*, and *sitam*. This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would result in those words being *udātta* (accented on the first syllable) according to the rule "A *niṣṭhā* [suffix] ending in two vowels is *udātta* when used as a name (*saṃjñā*), provided that the vowel *ā* does not occur at the beginning. The meaning of that rule is that a name consisting of two syllables ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix has its first syllable accented, unless the vowel *ā* is the initial one. 26. *Sarvādīni sarvanāmāni* (The words beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns). Words whose forms begin with *sarva* shall receive the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). The specific rules (*pradeśa*) are those such as "for a pronoun, [the ending] *smai*" and so forth.
