[Objection: But the word *sarva* itself should not receive this designation, because the word *sarva* is not recited at the beginning [of the list]. [Response: True. The term *sarvādīni* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those which have *sarva* at their beginning. Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound: *sarva* and that which is the beginning (*ādi*) is *sarvādi*. Although the word *ādi* has no functional purpose here, it is employed merely for the sake of achieving formal symmetry.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, whereas in a *karmadhāraya*, there is the udātta accent on the final syllable. According to the rule "among those differing in accent, that which follows remains," when a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is formed between a *bahuvrīhi* and a *tatpuruṣa*, the *tatpuruṣa* is eliminated.

However, in reality, this is established because the *bahuvrīhi* possesses that quality. For this very reason, in the Sūtra "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]," the venerable Śaṅkarācārya and others state that "even birth is a defining characteristic of Brahman. We shall discuss this further under the Sūtra concerning the technical name (*saṃjñā*) of the *bahuvrīhi*.

For here, the meaning of the compound (*samāsa*) is a collection (*samudāya*) whose constituent parts (*avayava*) are manifest. Since such a collection cannot be employed [as a word] simultaneously [in its entirety], the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), which is pervaded by the purpose of serving as a name for an effect, is applied to its constituents. Because there is no distinction [between them], it is applied even to the word *sarva*. For this very reason, the plural form in the rule "*sarvādīni*" is consistent; for if the collection were the named entity (*saṃjñin*), a singular number would have resulted. The use of a "great designation" (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the sake of understanding its etymological significance (*anvarthatva*). By this, words that are themselves designations (*saṃjñā*) or subordinate members (*upasarjana*) are excluded, because they denote merely a specific property (*dharma*) of a substratum (*dharmī*).

Now, what is this "being a pronoun" (*sarvanāmatva*)? It is not simply the capacity to convey a complete meaning, because words such as *pūrva* (eastern) do not denote jars and the like. Nor should it be argued that they possess that status because they generate the cognition of an object in the form of "easterness" and so on, since what is intended here is the capacity to generate the cognition of every possible meaning in some form or other; for all-pervading substances (*vibhudravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are not cognized even in the form of "easterness. Furthermore, there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of the words *sva*, *yuṣmad*, and *asmat* when applied to oneself and others.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the Bhāṣya passage “the names of all,” stated: “The status of being a pronoun (sarvanāmatva) is relative to its own specific object, just as universals such as ‘cowness’ are all-pervasive (sarvagata) relative to their own objects. Nor does it consist in denoting multiple objects; for even the word *sarva* when used as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) possesses that same quality [of being a pronoun], since the individuals denoted by it differ according to their various states. Nor does it consist in denoting multiple things of different classes, because that would result in the definition being under-extended (*avyāpti*) to words such as *sva* and others, since those are of the same class (*sājātya*) by virtue of being the self (*ātman*).

If it is argued that because the term *sarva* in *priyasarvau* and *caitramaitrau* functions as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and therefore it is difficult to state a defining characteristic (*avayavārthatāvacchedaka*) for the term that excludes both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members—this is true. However, it is not the intention of the Bhāṣya that the exclusion of both is achieved solely by the etymological name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). Rather, its role there is merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhakatvamātra*); the actual exclusion follows precisely from the statement of the Vārttika: "The prohibition [applies] to technical names and subordinate members. Nor does the aforementioned objection apply even in that case.

A modern convention (*saṃjñā*) is [the term] *vṛtti-praveśa* (entry into a compound), because both [schools] agree that this constitutes being a subordinate element (*upasarjanatva*). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa will state later on:
"The prohibition regarding the subordinate element belongs to the author of the Vārttika, not to the author of the Sūtra; for [the rule] 'not in a Bahuvrīhi' has been introduced."

His intention is that there is also an exclusion [of the suffix] by resorting to the fact that the term *saṃjñā* (name) is based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthatva*). Now, one might object: in the word *sarvanāma*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] would occur by the rule "after a preceding member, when a name is formed" (*pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*). If an irregular formation (*nipātana*) were accepted, it would result in the incorrectness of the form without *ṇ*. Nor can it be argued that both forms are correct because both authorities [the general rule and the specific exception] are valid; for in a case where there is a prohibition, this would lead to an option (*vikalpa*), since the restriction of a general rule by a specific rule is equal [in force]. True. The form with *ṇ* is indeed incorrect, according to the reasoning already stated.

Nor does the rule "in the sense of continuity of action" (kriyāsātatye) result in the sublation of the word *santata*; for, by way of partial approval (*ekadeśānumati*), it serves merely to indicate the ancient preceptor’s verse: "one should drop [the 't' of] *avaśyam* before a gerundive suffix" (*lumpedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye*). Nor does the non-occurrence of the augment *nuṭ* in the rule "in words proclaimed as ancient" (*purāṇaprokteṣu*) result in the ungrammaticality of the word *purātana*, since some maintain that this is indeed desired. Kaiyaṭa, however, maintains that it is because the word is included among the items listed in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

The authors of the *Kaustubha*, however, state that by the mention of the word "purāṇa," it is merely indicated that the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables when followed by a *bha*-affix" (*avyayānāṃ bhamātre ṭilopaḥ*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By this, forms such as "purātanaṃ tvāṃ puruṣaṃ purāvidaḥ" are established. Regarding the method of prohibiting [the application of] technical names (*saṃjñā*) to those that are themselves technical names (*saṃjñā*) or secondary members (*upasarjana*), the author of the *Vārttika* says: "Exclusion is based on the recitation; for those items that have been recited, a technical name is assigned."

The meaning is this: since those words that have technical names (*saṃjñā*) as their subordinate members (*upasarjana*) are not included among the *sarvādi* group, this statement is commenced. Having excluded them from the list, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be prescribed for those [words] that are actually recited. Alternatively, this is not a rule defining a technical name (*saṃjñā-sūtra*), but rather its sole purpose is to purify the list (*gaṇa-śuddhi*). For example, in the rule "tiṅo gotrādīni kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ," only those forms of the words *gotra* and so forth that function in the sense of contempt or frequency are recited in the *gotrādi* group, and not others of a different nature.

Therefore, in the rules "canacidīvagotrāditaddhitāmreḍiteṣvagateḥ" and "kutsane ca supyagotrādau," only those [words] of that specific nature are understood, and not those occurring with different meanings. Likewise here as well, only those which denote the members of the *sarvādi* group are listed in the *sarvādi* list, and not those that have become technical names (*saṃjñā*) or secondary adjuncts (*upasarjana*). This is because those function as specific designations. Likewise here as well, only those which denote the members of the *sarvādi* group are listed in the *sarvādi* list, and not those that have become technical names or secondary adjuncts.

Because they function as specific [terms], and thus, precisely because they are not included in the *gaṇa*-list, there is no possibility of their being designated by that technical name (*saṃjñā*). Nor does this result in the failure of grammatical operations conditioned by that designation; for in rules such as *sarvanāmnaḥ*, only the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) is intended to be grasped.

In reality, however, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *sakala* and *kṛtsna*. Therefore, in the rule *sarvādīni*, there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) in both senses: those which are names of all [things] are themselves the "beginning with *sarva*" (*sarvādīni*), forming a single sentence for the purpose of purifying the *gaṇa*.
The author of the Vārttika previously established the purification of the *gaṇa* by means of another statement.

The distinction, however, is that the Commentator [Patañjali] says "in this very manner. Since the rule states "those which are *sarva* etc. are designated as *sarvanāman*," the second mention is for the purpose of providing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), and thus there is no fault whatsoever. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, because there is an absence of simultaneous intention to express (*sahavivakṣā*), the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) would be untenable; for the two meanings are construed by reversing the relationship between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheyabhāva*). This is because, even in the absence of simultaneous intention to express during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), the rule prescribing *ekaśeṣa* is accepted as being applicable, despite the fact that the *sarūpa-sūtra* itself has been rejected under the theory of universals (*jāti-pakṣa*).

For those who do not accept the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) [for words like *eka*, *ubha*, etc.], the solution established in the Bhāṣya—which will be stated in the fourth [chapter]—must also be applied here: namely, that in the rule "not in a Bahuvrīhi" (*na bahuvrīhau*), the prohibition of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be explained by means of a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) using the word "not" (*na*).

Furthermore, according to the Vārttika view, since the technical name "pronoun" (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) is sublated by the technical name "technical name" (*saṃjñā-saṃjñā*)—as per the principle to be stated under the heading "one technical name" (*ekasaṃjñā-adhikāra*)—the matter regarding the technical name itself is to be resolved in that manner. This is the general direction.

Therefore, for those [words], there is no operation based on their technical name (*saṃjñā*) nor any internal-group operation (*antargaṇakārya*). An operation based on a technical name is as follows: *sarva* is the name of someone; for him, *sarvāya*. *Atisarva* means one who has surpassed everything; for him, *atisarvāya*. An internal-group operation is as follows: *tat* is the name of someone; by the rule "for *tyad* and so forth, *a*" (*tyadādīnām aḥ*), the substitution of *a* does not occur. One who has surpassed him is *atitat*; by the rule "the substitute *adḍ* for *ḍatarādi*," the substitute *adḍ* does not occur. Nor is the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) redundant because the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) alone would prevent [the application of the rules] to a name. Haradatta and others maintain that this is because such an outcome is desired.

Kaiyaṭa says that this [rule] has as its object only those operations (*padakārya*) that pertain to the word-form itself. However, rules such as *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso’ś* apply even in cases like *atitvam*, because they depend solely on the phonetic form of the word and thus do not require its inclusion in a *gaṇa* list. Nor does this lead to an over-extension in rules such as *yuṣmadyupapade*; for, according to the maxim *abhivyaktapadārthā ye*, such rules operate only when the word refers to its conventional meaning, whereas in the present case, the rule depends on the word-form itself. On this point, the Bhāṣya states:

The prohibition of *saṃjñā* (technical name) would be redundant, because in the rule *pūrvaparāvareṣu...* the word *asaṃjñāyām* has been separated as a distinct *yoga*, which is then explained as being supplementary (*śeṣa*) to both what precedes and what follows it.

Thus, since even the rule *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 1.4.13) has been rejected as superfluous for the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), there is no purpose for its governing authority (*adhikāra*). We shall explain that very point in its proper place. However, that [rule] must be interpreted differently: the term *anupasarjana* here ends in the genitive case (*anupasarjanasya*), and the elision of the suffix *-s* occurs due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*). The meaning is that the substitutions *ā* and *at* apply to the non-subordinate element. Nor does this lead to the failure of the form *atiyuṣmad*.

By joining the vowel *a* (akāra) [from the rule *ataḥ*] with the following [rule], the two previously mentioned substitutes (*ad* and *adḍ*) are qualified by it. This is because of the interpretation that "the vowels *a* and *kāra* which follow an *a*"—thus, the substitution of *at* for *tyad*-type pronouns and the substitute *adḍ* are prescribed as occurring after an *a*, and therefore the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) applies there. However, this does not apply to the substitution of *ad* in the case of *atiyuṣmad*, because the rule "the *at* of the fifth case" prescribes the substitution of *ad* for the *ṅasi* and other endings that follow *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; and since those two [words] do not end in the vowel *a*.

But surely, in this way, when there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *priyadvir* (meaning "one who has two beloveds"), the substitution of *yatva* for the pronouns *tyad* and so on would apply to the form *priyau dvau asya*. This is because the *ā* that replaces the *i* is situated after the *v*, and since it is not prescribed immediately after the *a*, the aforementioned paribhāṣā does not apply. Similarly, the substitution of *s* by the rule "tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ" would also occur even when [the word] is subordinate (*upasarjana*). This is because the letter *s* is not mentioned in the aforementioned paribhāṣā. Not so.

Since the inclusion of non-adjunct (*anupasarjana*) forms is already established by the paribhāṣā stated under the rule *tyadādīnāmaḥ*, the word *dvi* is taken here as being of that same nature due to association (*sāhacarya*). Furthermore, even in the rule prescribing the substitution of *sa* (satva), only such [non-adjunct] forms of the *tyadādi* group are to be understood, because of the governing context of meaning (*arthādhikāra*).
Alternatively, in the sections concerning *aṅga* (bases), a qualification based on meaning must be resorted to. As it has been said:
"In the *aṅga*-sections, that which is stated applies to the base as it appears with its case-ending."

If the meaning were "the case-ending (*vibhakti*) prescribed for that which is being grasped [as the referent]," then in examples such as *paramapañca*, there would be no elision (*luk*). Consequently, the meaning would be: "for the *ṅe* ending expressing number and grammatical relation (*kāraka*) residing in the sense of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), *smai* should be substituted," and so forth. However, in cases such as *priyaviśvāya*, number and the rest are expressed by the case-ending precisely as they reside in the meaning of the external member (*anyapadārtha*), and not as they reside in the meaning of the word *sarva*; thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, in cases such as *paramasarva*, these [number and relation] reside precisely in the meaning of the word *sarva*; therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

[Objection: But surely, by the *jñāpaka* rule "dvandve ca," there is *tadantavidhi* (the application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element) regarding the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Thus, since compounds such as *priyaviśva* would also possess the status of a pronoun, the capacity of the case-ending to express number and so forth—which functions upon the meaning of a pronoun—would remain intact. [Response: True. However, the status of being a pronoun is introduced here as existing only when [the word] is listed in the *sarvādi* group. Although the designation [of "pronoun"] may apply to a compound ending in such a word, that [group membership] is absent in the compound itself. Nor should it be argued that this is established simply by treating the specific rule as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*); for one expedient does not preclude another expedient.
Others, however, say that the adoption of this etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) is due to dissatisfaction with the previous view;

for in reality, under the etymological view, it is difficult to state a meaning for the constituent parts that excludes the *upasarjana*. The Bhāṣya does not intend that [meaning]. As for the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) implied by the sūtra "dvandve ca," it applies only where the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is predominant, in accordance with the observed examples (*lakṣya*) and in accordance with the evidence that establishes the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*). Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *atisarva*.

As for the sūtra "na bahuvrīhau," however, it is a separate matter whether it should be rejected as being intended to prohibit technical designations (*saṃjñā*) in the non-grammatical sentence (*alaukikavākya*).

The over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from the application of the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the element]" (*tadantavidhi*), which is obtained through the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the *aṅga* (stem), will be avoided in that very instance by means of a qualification of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). Otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid it even by that [qualification]. For in that case, the avoidance of that defect by means of a qualification of what is prescribed is accepted by all; otherwise, since the statement would be justified simply as a prohibition of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the constituent parts, it could not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule of extension to that which ends with [the element]. This is precisely Kaiyaṭa’s intention as well.

However, in cases such as *atisarvāya*, the non-avoidance of the general grammatical operation remains; for the fault was recorded by [the author] precisely while proceeding with the previously mentioned position, namely, the rule *anupasarjanāt*. This is because, under the view that the specific case-ending is qualified by the meaning (*arthadvāraka*), he accepted the absence of that fault. The phrase "general grammatical operation" means that which is occasioned by the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). Therefore, the intention of the Bhāṣya lies solely in the view that the specific case-ending is qualified by the meaning.

If it is argued that in the case of *pañcakāḥ śakunayaḥ* ("five birds"), because the suffix is used in its own sense (*svārthika*) and the meaning of the number six is predominant, there should be elision (*luk*) by the rule *ṣaḍbhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.22], we say no. This is because the word qualified by the suffix is a distinct word (*śabdāntara*), and since it lacks the final phoneme *n*, it is devoid of the technical designation *ṣaṭ*. If it is further argued that rules such as *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso'ś* [Pāṇini 7.1.27] would also not apply when [the pronoun] is subordinate (*upasarjana*), because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) therein does not denote the number and other properties residing in the meaning of *yuṣmad* and so on, we say no.

In that context, because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is to be qualified merely by its being subsequent to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* through the medium of the meaning of the stem (*aṅga*), the meaning is as follows: "The forms *aś* and so forth occur in place of the case-endings such as *ṅasi*, etc., which follow *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when these denote a number residing in the stem. However, in the rule "ad-ḍ ḍatarādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.25), since there is no governing heading (*adhikāra*) for "stem" (*aṅga*), one must resort to an interpretation based on the meaning: "that which is prescribed after those beginning with *ḍatara*."

Therefore, there is neither under-extension (*avyāpti*) nor over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *paramakatarat* and *atikatarat*. However, in rules such as "asthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanuṅ udāttaḥ" and "tyadādīnām aḥ," because the genitive case "aṅgasya" is also present, both interpretations are possible: either the case-ending is qualified by the member (*aṅga*)—namely, *asthi* and so on—or the member is qualified by the case-ending. Thus, in the rule for *asthi* and so on, the meaning of the sentence is: "when a case-ending follows a member, *anaṅ* shall replace *asthi* and the others. Consequently, there is no under-extension in forms such as *priyasakthnā*.

In this context, the word *sakthi* denotes a part of a cart; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*ṣaṭ-prasaṅga*) of the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the substitution of *ṣat* occurs] for *sakthi* and *akṣan*" applying here. However, in rules such as "for *tyad* etc., [the substitute] *aḥ*," the words *tyad* etc. qualify the case-ending (*vibhakti*), while [the word] *aṅgasya* qualifies the vowel *a*. The meaning is: when a case-ending expresses number and so forth residing in the referent of *tyad* etc., the vowel *a* shall be the final substitute for the stem (*aṅga*). Consequently, in forms such as *atisa* and *atitad*, there is neither under-extension (*avyāpti*) nor over-extension (*ativyāpti*), since the application of the grammatical explanation proceeds solely in accordance with the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*). Let this suffice.

The word *ubha* denotes that which is qualified by duality through the sense of pervasion (*paryāpti*). For this very reason, it always ends in the dual number. [Objection: If this is so, its inclusion in the list of *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) is useless; for we observe specific grammatical operations conditioned by the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) only in the singular and plural numbers. Furthermore, forms such as *ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām* ("by both causes") in the instrumental case would be established even without depending on the *sarvanāma-saṃjñā* mentioned in the Vārttika on the rule *nimittakāraṇahetuṣu sarvāsāṃ prāyadarśanam*, since there is no difference between the suffixes *ka* and *kak*. [Response: True. Its inclusion here is for the sake of the suffix *akac*, as in the form *ubhakau*.

For this [form] is not established by means of the *kap* suffix, because it would result in the form *ubhaya* (by the rule *ubhād-ayac ca*). This is because there is a restrictive rule that the suffix *ayac* is produced from the word *ubha* only in instances other than the dual number. To explain: in the rule "ubhādudātto nityam," the portion "ubhāt" is separated as a distinct *yoga*. From the word *ubha*, which denotes a number and functions to express parts (*avayava-vṛtti*), the suffix *ayac* occurs in the sense of the whole (*avayavin*): *ubhayo maṇiḥ* (a gem consisting of two parts). The meaning is that it is composed of two portions, black and red. Then follows "nityam": after the word *ubha*, the suffix *ayac* occurs invariably; since no specific meaning is indicated, it occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*).

"One who has both sons" is *ubhayaputraḥ*. Nor is there any inconsistency in such forms as *dvidaṇḍi* and others regarding the impossibility of the form *ubhāhasta*; for that is established there by the optional substitution of the suffix *aṇ* for *yañ*. As stated by the author of the Vārttika:
"The absence of *anya* [is indicated] because [the term *ubhaya*] is the domain of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, as in 'ubhaya elsewhere'."

The meaning is: "except when followed by a dual ending. Thus, because of the intervention of the *kap* suffix, there is no following of a dual ending, and consequently *ayac* would apply. However, in the case of *akac*, since it is inserted in the middle, the word *ubha* is indeed followed by a dual ending; therefore, that [application of *ayac*] does not occur.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: because it is *svārthika* (denoting its own inherent meaning) and because it has the same meaning as the word *ubha*, it indeed possesses the status of being a dual ending (*dvivacana*) for that form; this must necessarily be stated. And thus, since the suffix *kap*—which has a base denoting duality—is also a dual ending by virtue of being a suffix that expresses duality, there is no application of the rule *ayac* when that suffix follows. This is because the technical term "dual ending" (*dvivacana*) alone is not what is intended in the aforementioned Vārttika.

For this very reason, in the rule *ṇeraṇau*, the word *karman* (object) is understood to mean *kriyā* (action). Therefore, the word *ubhaya* (both) should not be read here at all. Consequently, it should be understood that the insertion of the phrase *vṛttimātre* (in every case of verbal activity) into the explanation of the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) as *nityam* is without foundation.

As for the argument that—in cases such as *ubhayataḥ* and *ubhayatra*—the suffix *añ* is likewise untenable; and that one should not say that because *tas* is prescribed after a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*), it expresses an additional meaning (the case-meaning) and thus does not denote mere duality; and furthermore, because the suffix *kap* also conveys meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) etc., and because it expresses an additional meaning under the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors (*pañcaka*)—that [argument] is to be considered. For denoting mere duality is not the same as being a dual ending (*dvivacana*), since even the objecthood (*karmatva*) and other factors are understood from it.

Now, if it is argued that "denoting duality alone" means not denoting anything other than duality by way of a form that delimits the denotative capacity for duality, [we reply: in that case, there is denotation of *karmatva* (objecthood) and so forth by means of the suffix *-tā* and the like, while there is denotation of duality by means of *-aut* and the like; however, this is equivalent because the *kap* suffix also denotes duality since its stem has duality as its meaning, yet it also denotes meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) because it is prescribed for those specific meanings. Thus, the two cases are equal.

In reality, however, because *trataḥ* and *soḥ* are indeclinables (*avyaya*), they lack the capacity to denote duality; thus, according to Kaiyaṭa’s statement, these two do not function as dual endings. Even if they were considered suffixes added for their own sake (*svārthika*), it would be impossible for them to express a meaning that contradicts their own inherent nature. Furthermore, there is no evidence to suggest that the cognition of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) depends on their being *svārthika* suffixes, nor does the relevant Bhāṣya passage serve as such a refutation. As for the word *ubhaya*, it has already been explained; it refers to a whole (*avayavin*) composed of two parts. An example is: "Those who are friends and those who are enemies, and those kings who are both."

The meaning is that [the objects] are delimited by the properties of being a friend and being an enemy. Furthermore, the distinction is that these two properties appear as co-occurrent with the difference between individuals delimited by their respective qualifiers (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*), but not in mutual co-occurrence with one another. However, in expressions such as "The wise speak of both," the word "both" is intended to refer to the collection of the two parts, namely Indra and Daśaratha, by taking those two forms as its constituents.

However, when it is intended to express two such gems together after having derived the form *ubhaya* as meaning "both gems," then the dual number—which would otherwise result through the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of identical forms)—must be prevented due to non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). This is because Kaiyaṭa states regarding the sūtra "taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ" that the word *ubhaya* is "not used with all case-endings" (*asarvavibhakti*) precisely because the dual number does not arise for it. Thus, the purpose [of the rule] is that a specific enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made to exclude its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Haradatta, however, stated that because the capacity for enumeration is exhausted by its function as an exclusion of forms such as *pacatikalpam*, the dual number indeed occurs after the word *ubhaya*. If it is objected: "Since *ayac* is a substitute for the *tayap* suffix, the designation 'pronoun' (*sarvanāma*) would apply when the suffix *jas* follows, by virtue of the rule *prathamacaramatayālpārdhakati...etc.*," [the reply is: "Not so. Some say that in this case the designation is obligatory, either due to a restricted option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) or through the application of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Others hold that the optional designation is superseded by the obligatory one, because the latter is internal (*antaraṅga*) as it does not depend on a case-ending, whereas the former is external (*bahiraṅga*) as it does depend on a case-ending.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: this suffix *ayaC* is indeed independent (*svatantra*). There is no evidence for the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *tayap* in its rule formulation. Nor should it be argued that, in the case of *ubhayī*, the suffix *ṅīp*—which is triggered by the presence of a word ending in *tayap* according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*—would not apply. For, in the word *mātrac* found therein [in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*], if one takes a pratyāhāra (abbreviated reference) starting from the word *mātra* up to the letter *c* in *ayaC*, then because *ayaC* is included within that, the suffix *ṅīp* is established even for *ayaC* independently. And thus, the mention of *tayap* there [in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*] need not be made; for the desired result is established simply through inclusion in the aforementioned pratyāhāra.

Alternatively, *dvayasaj* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term), and therefore there is no need to include the inclusion of *daghnañ* and *mātrac* as well. However, if the rule were read as *pramāṇe mātraj-dvayasaj-daghnacaḥ*, then *mātraj* alone would be the pratyāhāra. Nor should it be argued that this would lead to the undesired application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* in cases such as *kati striyaḥ*, because *ḍati* is also included within that [pratyāhāra]; for there is a prohibition by the rule *na ṣaṭ-svasrādibhyaḥ*, and furthermore, because the word *ataḥ* (from *at*) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule *ṭiḍ-ḍhāṇañ-...*.

Nor should it be argued that even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *tailamātra* and the like, because in the view of *pratyāhāra*, the letter *ca* is not a qualifier with respect to the word *mātra*; and because, since there is no evidence for the inclusion of the word *mātra* ending in *ca*, there would follow the inclusion of even the word *tran* ending in the suffix *tran* (as in *huyāmāśruvasibhasibhyastran*). This is not to be said, because even a similar form is not included within a *pratyāhāra*. Furthermore, the word *mātra* is understood only when it occurs as the object of knowledge (*prameya-vṛtti*), being prescribed after a word denoting the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because the word *mātra* functions as a mere imitation of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it lacks the status of referring to the aforementioned nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

If it is asked, "How then is there the designation 'pronoun' (*sarvanāman*) in the phrase *vyathāṃ dvayeṣām api medinībhṛtām*?", the answer is: True; some maintain that the reference is intended to convey the meaning "both" (*ubhaya*).

Others maintain that this [interpretation] is not tenable due to contradictions such as *gurudvayāya* and *guruṇoḥ*; rather, it should be resolved in some way as *dvayeṣām*, meaning "of those who go (*iṣanti*) toward duality (*dvayam*)," i.e., toward the two-fold state. Still others hold that because the word *dvaya* is accepted as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) even in the *Cākravarmaṇa-vyākaraṇa*, it refers to "that" (*tat*). And this alone is correct, because of the natural sense of the *Mahābhāṣya* regarding the sūtras "the sixth case is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows" and "after a root preceded by a motion-word, a kāraka, or an upapada," wherein suffixes are indeed prescribed after a root in two ways. For this very reason—
Are words such as "yava" (barley) polysemous or not, given the agreement between Aryans and Mlecchas? In both cases, meanings such as long-awned barley and *priyaṅgu* are posited as alternatives.

Thus is the application by Mādhavācārya in the section concerning *yava* and *varāha*. Nor can its formation be established by the rule *prathamacarama* (Pāṇini 1.1.33) on the grounds that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*), because the established conclusion of the Bhāṣya is that *ayac* is indeed a distinct suffix (*pratyaya*). *Ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are suffixes; therefore, words ending in them are to be understood [as the referents]. Even though there is no rule for inclusion of what ends in something (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the prescription of the name for the two suffixes alone would otherwise be purposeless.

The word *anya* signifies that which possesses mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). Because the object denoted by a co-occurring term, such as a jar, is construed with one part of that [meaning], there arises the cognition "other than a jar" in expressions such as *ghaṭād anyaḥ* ("other than a jar"). Regarding the words *anyatara* and *anyatama*, Kaiyaṭa states in the *Paspaśā* [section of the Mahābhāṣya] that they are un-derived (irregular) and, by their very nature, function to denote a selection from among two or many [respectively]. In that regard, because the second [of these two words, i.e., *anyatama*] lacks the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), its specific grammatical operations do not apply. It is for this very reason that we find usages such as: "Darkness is certainly not 'one of several' (*anyatama*) among the categories beginning with generality (*sāmānya*)."

Śākaṭāyana explains that although those two [words] are derived as being formed with the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*, because the inclusion of the word *anyatara* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*), the word *anyatama* lacks the grammatical operations [such as accentuation] associated with the *gaṇa*. Amara states: "The word *itara* [is used] in the senses of 'other' and 'low'. If one asks, "How then [do you explain] the Naiyāyikas' statement in the *Upādhivāda*: 'And because of over-extension to the other side of the subject (*pakṣetara*)'?"—this is true; the ancient scholars there maintain that the word *itara* is a *kṛdanta* (a derivative) meaning "that which goes beyond the subject (*pakṣam itarayati*)."

Others hold that in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *pakṣa itaraḥ*, [the word *itara*] lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). The *miśra* teachers maintain that the term *pakṣetara* is technical (*pāribhāṣika*), referring to "that which is other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*); therefore, like the modern designation *itara*, this too lacks the status of a pronoun.
By this, expressions such as *vanyetarā jānapadopadābhiḥ* are explained.

Both *tva* and *tvam* end in the vowel *a* and are synonyms for "other. Some say that in the passage *etaṃ tvamanye daśayantramutsam*, the form *tvam* is udātta, whereas in *uta tvaḥ paśyan* and similar instances, it is anudātta.

The first [instance] ends in *t*. Regarding the mantra, "tarīruta tvadbhavati sūta uta tvad," the Vedabhāṣya states: "In the word *tvat*, which is listed among the pronouns (*sarvanāman*), it is unaccented and signifies 'another' (*anya*). Furthermore, there is the usage by Jayadeva: "pibantam tvadadharamadhuramadhūni" (drinking the sweet honey of your lower lip). This is because its meaning is simply "the lower lip of another than you. Others, however, argue that this is not the correct analysis (*vigraha*)—namely, "your lower lip" (*tavādharas tvadadharaḥ*)—because of the consideration of the preceding sentence: "paśyati diśi diśi rahasi bhavantam" (he sees you in secret in every direction). In that context, the former interpretation is more appropriate.

Thus, although these [two forms] are equally authoritative, the determination that *tad* is a sarvādi (a pronoun belonging to the class beginning with *sarva*) is made because we observe forms such as *smāt* following the form *uta u tvasmai tanvaṃ visasre*, which is unaccented (*anudātta*).

However, if the reading here were either an accented form ending in *-ā* or one ending in *-t*, there would be doubt. Having observed the occurrence of forms like *smāt* for the former and forms like *akañ* for the latter in certain recensions (*śākhā*), the matter must be determined.

In reality, since it is possible to read two forms ending in *-ā*—even though they have different accents—simultaneously through *ekaśruti* (monotone) by means of *tantra* (a single application), some maintain that on the strength of both readings being present, it is more logical that the first form ends in *-t*.

The meaning of the word *nema* is "half. This is seen from the passage: "In him, O Soma, [the world] was seen" (*pranemasmin dadṛśe soma*). The words *sama* and *sima* are synonyms for "all. This is seen from such passages as "Do not harm us at all" (*mā naḥ samasya drvyah*) and "Protect us from every one who intends evil" (*uruṣyāṇo aghāyataḥ samasmāt*). It is also seen from the passage: "Night spreads her garment for everyone" (*ādrātrīvāsastanute simasmai*). Although anudātta (low-pitched) accent would have been expected according to the *Phaṭ-sūtra*—"The words *tva*, *tvas*, *asama*, and *sima* are anudātta"—the word *sima* receives the udātta (high-pitched) accent by virtue of the specific rule: "*Sima* is udātta in the Atharvaṇa. This is because the term "Atharvaṇa" has been explained as being used figuratively to indicate any Vedic text.

However, the term *tulyaparyāyasama* (synonym for "equal") is not a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). This is because of the indicative rule (*jñāpaka*): "The sequential assignment of equal [terms] follows their respective order.

Furthermore, the following are not designations (*saṃjñā*) when used in their restricted senses (*vyavasthāyām*): *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara*; *sva* when it does not denote "kinsman" or "wealth"; and *antara* when it denotes "connection with the outside" (*bahiryoga*) or "inclusion" (*upasaṃvyāna*).

The five [terms] beginning with *pūrva* (east) apply to space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*), as well as to that which is delimited by them; for example: "in the eastern direction," "in the eastern pond," "at the earlier time," or "in the elder teacher," and so forth. The words *dakṣiṇā* (south) and *adhara* (lower) apply to the direction and to that which is delimited by it; for instance: "be the consort of the southern direction. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this restriction of meaning, because the very term *vyavasthāyām* (in the sense of fixed determination) serves as the proof. For "fixed determination" (*vyavasthā*) is indeed the restriction of a limit relative to its own denotation.

Furthermore, because the meanings already expressed by words such as *pūrva* (east) necessarily require a point of reference (*avadhi*), when "east" and so forth are mentioned, the expectation arises: "from what? Even in the case of *dakṣiṇasyāḥ* (of the south), there is indeed a point of reference in reality; however, due to conventional usage, it is not explicitly employed. Nor does the prohibition "not in the case of a technical name" (*saṃjñā*) apply here. For commentators explain in the fifth [chapter] that a "technical name" (*saṃjñā*) is merely a modern convention, and such a convention does not exist regarding the directions. What is the purpose of the condition "in the sense of a fixed direction" (*vyavasthāyām*)? Consider: *dakṣiṇā gāthakāḥ* ("skilled singers"). Here it means "expert. *adhare tāmbūlarāgaḥ* ("the betel-stain on the lower lip"). Here it means "on the lip. *uttare śaktaḥ* ("capable in reply"). Here it means "in response," and so forth.

Now, if it is asked how Kalidasa and others can use the expression “*tathā pareṣāṃ yudhi ca*,” the answer is: true. The word *para*, which primarily refers to a specific relational state (such as being an enemy), is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇayā*) for enmity and the like. Yet, this does not constitute subordination (*upasarjanatā*). For subordination consists precisely in the word’s being directed toward another meaning qualified by its own primary sense; and here, although there is a cognition characterized by enmity and so forth through metaphorical indication, the primary sense (*śakyārtha*) does not enter into the relation within that [metaphorical] context.

For this very reason, regarding the term *itarat* in the expression *pakṣetara*, the commentators on the *Dīdhiti* maintain that although the word *itara* primarily denotes a state (*bhāvapradhāna*), because the grammatical operations of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) would otherwise apply, one must first form a *bahuvrīhi* compound and only then resort to the primary denotation of the state.

As for the claim that in cases such as "therefore, [it] possesses fire," the function of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*) occurs even under the view that the cognition is produced through *jñāna-lakṣaṇā* (indication by means of a cognition), that is questionable. For even if one accepts indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "smoke" within the causal phrase "due to smoke" (*dhūmāt*), there is no evidence for indication in the pronoun "therefore" (*tasmāt*), since the cognition of smoke can be conveyed by that pronoun through its primary denotative power (*śakti*) alone. In the case of "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), there is no contradiction, because the Naiyāyikas maintain that the pronoun "That" refers precisely to the Self previously introduced, and thus indicates something similar to it.

As for the claim that a cognition characterized by the mode "enmity" (*śatrutva*) and so forth is purely mental (*mānasa*), whereas verbal cognition (*śābda*) is characterized only by modes such as "residing in another location," that is to be reconsidered; for there is no rule governing the mental causal complex (*sāmagrī*) subsequent to that [verbal cognition]. What is the purpose of the prohibition regarding names (*asaṃjñāyām*)? Consider: *uttarāḥ kuravaḥ* ("the Northern Kurus"). Even though the word *uttara* ("northern") applies to the Kurus with Mount Sumeru as its limit, it does not possess the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) because it is a name (*saṃjñā*). Nor is there any lack of evidence for the claim that there is no naming (*saṃjñā*) regarding the directions but there is naming regarding the Kurus; for the authority rests precisely on the words of commentators whose tradition is based on an unbroken lineage of prosperity.

"Self" (*svo*) [is used] in the sense of kinsmen and self; "self" (*svaḥ*) in three genders [is used] in the sense of one's own; "self" (*svam*) in the neuter is used in the sense of wealth. (Amara-kośa). The word *ātmani* (in the sense of self) is construed with a masculine noun. Because [the term] is prohibited from being a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) when applied to kinsmen or wealth, it functions as a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) when expressing either "self" or "one's own. By the force of the inclusion of the word "designation" (*ākhyā*) [in the rule], it remains a pronoun even when the intention is to convey kinsmen or wealth as "one's own," provided they are not understood as specific designations. For example: *sve putrāḥ* ("one's own sons") and *sve gāvaḥ* ("one's own cows"). This prohibition applies only where there is a cognition produced by the word *sva* regarding kinsmen or wealth through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*).

As for the statement used by some, "nirākṛtaḥ svasyāṃ satatamitarasyāṃ praṇayavān" (disregarded by his own [wife], yet always full of affection for another), that too must somehow be explained as having the sense of "one's own" (*ātmīya*), by supplying a feminine substantive such as *tanu* (body/wife) as the headword. Some, however, say that one should simply read the rule as "svam ātmātmīyayoḥ. They argue that there is no risk of failing to include the meaning of "lordship" (*aiśvarya*)—as in the rule "svāminnaiśvarye"—because that [meaning of lordship] pertains exclusively to that [context], and without the possessive suffix *-in* (forming *svāmin*), the word is unfit for usage in that sense.
The word *antara* is used in the senses of interval, space, limit, clothing, division,
purpose, hole, one's own, absence, exterior, opportunity, middle, and the inner self.

It has two meanings. In this context, "outside" (bahiḥ) refers to an uncovered space; conjunction with that constitutes being "external. "Inside" (antara) or "within" (antarā) refers to houses. The meaning is houses outside the city, such as those of the Caṇḍālas and others. However, if the word *bahiḥ* is taken to mean residing in that [specific] place, then because of the connection of the interior with what exists outside, the meaning is houses within the city. Both meanings are accepted here. The word *upasaṃvyāna* also denotes the upper garment (*uttarīya*) through an instrumental derivation, but the lower garment (*antarīya*) through an accusative derivation.

It should be stated that [the word *apuri*] means "in a non-city. In the case of *antarāyāṃ puri*, because it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the grammatical operation [of substitution] does not apply. Alternatively, there might be an application here due to the inclusion of the single substitute as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*) by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*. Nor should it be argued that this Vārttika is merely a supplement to the rule regarding the optional [substitution] in the *jas* case-ending, since it is recited only in that context; for even in the absence of the final vowel *a*, the substitution of *śī* for *jas* after a feminine stem ending in *ṭāp* would not be applicable.

Because it is performed again due to the distinction between the inner and outer parts of the garment, both [interpretations] are tenable. The mention of the "undergarment" (*upasaṃvyāna*) is redundant because its outer connection has already been established. If the term refers to the upper garment (*uttarīya*), it takes the first meaning of the word "outer connection" (*bahiryoga*). However, if it refers to the undergarment (*antarīya*), it is established by taking the second meaning; this is the sense. Alternatively, it is not for the purpose of [referring to] a pair of garments and so forth.

The intention of the Vārttika is that when a pair of garments of equal measure has not been put on, because there is no understanding of which is the upper garment (*uttarīya*) and which is the inner garment (*antarīya*), and because it cannot function as such through external connection while in the state of not being worn, the term *upasaṃvyāna* (lower garment) is included [in the definition].

However, the authors of the Bhāṣya say that even the status of being an *upasaṃvyāna* does not exist in the state of not being worn; since mental determination is equally applicable even to what is externally connected, the inclusion of the term *upasaṃvyāna* is redundant.

However, some maintain that for a body in contact with three garments, there is no conjunction with the third external garment through its own conjunction with that which is conjoined [to it]. Nor can this be established by means of conjunction with the middle garment, because even the middle one is external in relation to that [third] garment. For "externality" is understood in relation to whatever aggregate is present in the mind. Likewise, there is no conjunction of the external garment with the internal one conjoined to the body; for the middle garment lacks internality according to the reasoning already stated.

This should be applied similarly to the fourfold case as well. They say that by including the word "ādi" (and so forth) in the phrase "for the sake of a pair of garments, etc.," the intended meaning of the *Vārttika* is thus obtained.

However, the intention of the *Bhāṣya* is as follows: because the term "bahir-yoge" (in connection with the external) is marked with the *svarita* accent, it includes even a figurative sense; thus, by taking recourse to an indirect relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*), the connection between the external and internal is established there as well, and consequently, the term *antara* possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) in both of its two senses.

*Tyat* and *tat* are these two [pronouns] used for referring back to what has been previously mentioned (*pūrvaparāmarśaka*). Some maintain that the first (*tyad*) is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*), because it appears in Vedic usage such as "eṣasya vāji" but is not seen in common worldly usage. Others hold that by the force of the inclusion of the word "Veda" (*chandas*) in the rule "syaśchandasi," it is used in worldly usage as well. The word *yat* expresses the subject (*uddeśya*). *Etad* and *idam* refer to what is perceptually present. *Adas* refers to what is remote. The word *eka* is used in the sense of "other," "principal," "first," and "alone."
It is employed in the sense of "common," "equal," and "number."

In the phrase "One protects the subjects, one [protects] strength," it has the sense of "another. In "the sole hero" (*ekavīraḥ*) and so forth, it has the sense of "principal. In "some have little life-force" (*eke 'lpaprāṇāḥ*) and so forth, it has the sense of "first. In "in the middle of a single consonant" (*ata ekahalmadhye*) and so forth, it has the sense of "unaccompanied" or "exclusive" (*kevala*). In "these two share a single wealth" (*etāvekadhanau dvau*) and so forth, it has the sense of "common. In "in the same direction as that" (*tenaikadik*) and so forth, it has the sense of "identical. In "one, two" (*eko dvau*) and so forth, it has the sense of "number."

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*, three meanings of this word [“eka”] are stated: number, solitude, and otherness. In Amara’s lexicon, it is also stated that “*eka* means principal, other, and absolute. Its usage elsewhere [in the sense of “one of many”] is by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because there is no evidence for it in its primary power (*śakti*). For this very reason, in the *Advaitacandrikā*, while commenting on the passage “Brahman is one only, without a second,” the possibility of its denoting meanings such as “equal” was rejected.

In the sutra *tenaikadik*, the term "secondary" (*gauṇa*) is employed because of their commonality as being of the same kind. *Saudāmanī* means "in the same direction as Sudāman," that is, the direction associated with the mountain named Sudāman; in other words, it is the direction associated with a similar location. Similarly, in the expression *caitramaitrāvekadhanau*, [the word *ekadhana* is used] because of the similarity consisting in being fit for disposal at will; that is to say, Caitra is one who may dispose at will of the wealth that Maitra is fit to dispose of at will. This is because it has been so stated.

The referent of *yuṣmad* is the object of address; the referent of the word *asmad*, however, is the speaker. The absence of gender (*aliṅgatvam*) is common to both. Furthermore, the quality of being a speaker (*uccārakatvam*) applies only where the sentence has no intention (*tātparya*) other than that of a single speaker. Therefore, in such cases as "That king must be addressed by you according to my words," there is no fault even though the word *mama* (my) does not refer to Kālidāsa, because that statement was uttered with Sītā in mind. For this very reason, it is said in the *Kusumāñjali*:

In passages such as "Then he thought: 'May I become many,'" the Supreme Person (uttamapuruṣa) is necessarily coreferential with the sense of the first-person pronoun "we" (asmad). By implying that [the agent], and using the reason that the word "we" (asmad-śabda) here has no other intended meaning than "I may become many," one establishes that the passage refers to a speaker, thereby proving the existence of God. It is clear from the works of Vardhamāna and others that the inclusion of the condition "having no other intended meaning" is for the purpose of avoiding a fallacy in cases such as "I grasp your hand for the sake of good fortune."

The word *bhavat* has the same meaning as the word *yuṣmad*, but it is characterized by gender (*liṅga*). Its distinction lies in the fact that it is not restricted to the vocative case in compounds such as *atrabhavat*. It is derived according to the rule "from the root *bhā*, the suffix *ḍvatu*. Now, one might object: since this word ends in a consonant (*halanta*), the forms *smāy* and so forth do not apply; furthermore, the third case ending is already accounted for by the rule "nimittakāraṇahetupu... (Pāṇini 2.3.23). To this they reply: "The priority of the suffixes *phiñ*, *añ*, and *mayaṭ*; likewise *ṭhak*, *cha*, and *s*; the absence of *ātva*, *śeṣaṣyañ*, and *viraha*; and *akac*—these are the fruits [of using] *bhavataḥ*. [Examples: *āpiśalapāṇinīyam* (formed with *phiñ*), *kāpaṭavam* (formed with *añ*), *aurṇamāyikam* (formed with *mayaṭ*), *kāraṇam* (formed with *ṭhak*), *kāraṇīyam* (formed with *cha*), *kāraṇam* (formed with *s*), *bhavadīyaḥ* (formed with *śeṣaṣyañ*), *bhavadīyaḥ* (formed with *viraha*), and *abhavadīyaḥ* (formed with *akac*)."

In this regard, the formation of a single substitute (*ekaśeṣa*) for non-initial vowels (*akac*) has been explicitly stated in the Bhāṣya; others are included by way of illustration. From *vata* comes *bhāvatāyaniḥ*: since it belongs to the *tyadādi* group, it receives the designation *vṛddha*, and thus the suffix *phiñ* is applied according to the rule "udīcāṃ vṛddhāt. From *bhavantam añcati* comes *bhavadyaṅ*: by the word *ca* in the rule "viṣvag-devayoś ca ṭer adryañcatāv apratyaye," the term *sarvanāman* is understood, resulting in the substitution of *adri* for the final syllable (*ṭi*). In *bhavanmaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to the rule "nityaṃ vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ."

*Bhavanmitraḥ*: The prior placement [of *bhavat*] is according to the rule "sarvanāmasaṃkhyayoḥ. This is because, in the rule "bhavataṣṭhakchasau," the term *vṛddhāt* is understood as a governing word (*anuvṛtti*) to exclude the word *bhavat* ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*. However, it should be understood that this is not an absolute rule, since the form can also be accounted for by reading it as *bhavatoḥ*. *Bhavādṛk*: "He is seen like you. The substitution of *ā* (ātvam) occurs according to the rule "ā sarvanāmnaḥ. *Devadattaś ca bhavām̐ś ca bhavantau*: "Devadatta and you two. The single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) is formed according to the rule "tyadādīni sarvaiḥ."

In the case of *bhavataḥ bhāvaḥ* (the state of being yours), because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) subordinates the designation of "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*), the suffix *ṣyañ* does not apply; this is because the author of the Vārttika has stated under the heading of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*) that "the designation of quality-word subordinates the designation of pronominal. In the case of *bhavakān*, the suffix *akac* is applied by the rule "of indeclinables and pronouns. If the suffix *kap* were used, the form would be *bhavatka* alone. Furthermore, according to the statement in the Bhāṣya, "in all simple formations of a pronoun," the result is also the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), as in Śrīharṣa’s verse: *bhavanmayo dhyāyati nāvanīpatiḥ* ("The lord of the earth, consisting of you, meditates").

The word *kim* is used in the sense of both inquiry (*praśna*) and censure (*ākṣepa*). Inquiry is of two kinds: that rooted in a desire to know (*jijñāsāmūlaka*) and that rooted in contradiction (*vipratipattimūlaka*). An example of the former is: "What is the one deity in the world, or what is the one ultimate refuge? An example of the latter is: "What is the proof for the existence of God? This very [inquiry] is the cause for the commencement of discourse, because the first kind finds its rest in the mere instruction [of the answer], once the desire to know has been satisfied. Censure is, for example: "What indeed is this rising of the sun? This is a censure of two deities, as seen in such expressions as "the censure of a bedpost" (*khaṭvā-ākṣepa*).

Regarding the objection, "What is the proof?"—having introduced this, a fourfold alternative was stated: "Does this word 'what' (kiṃ) have the sense of an objection, or the sense of contempt, or the sense of deliberation, or the sense of a question? These were explained in sequence as having the purpose of establishing non-existence, the purpose of establishing defectiveness, the purpose of expressing doubt, and the purpose of indicating that it is an object of inquiry.

It should be understood that the intended meaning is derived from the following conclusions: in the first case, "there is no proof for the existence of God"; in the second, "the proof is defective"; in the third, "the proof is something else"; and in the fourth, "proof is an object of inquiry. The term *vṛt* belongs to the *sarvādi* group; its meaning here is "completed" or "finished," because the word *vṛt* is conventionally defined as signifying completion within the list of gaṇas.

As for the fact that the functions of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) are observed even for words such as *avama* in passages like "O Indra and Agni, who are on the lowest earth, on the middle one, and on the highest," Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this is due solely to its being Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). However, in cases such as *itaretarasmāt* and *anyo'nyeṣām*, [the desired form] is established by the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*), according to the view that "doubling" (*dvirvacana*) consists in the double employment [of the word]. This is because the extension to what ends in that is accepted regarding the technical designation of pronouns (*sarvanāmasaṃjñā*) by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "dvandve ca."

In the view that [the doubling] occurs in place of the original (*sthāne-dvirvacana-pakṣe*), however, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) is maintained through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original). This is because, by the rule of "taught as co-occurring" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭatva*), the doubling—even though it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*)—is superseded; for, according to the maxim "even internal operations [are superseded]," the elision (*luk*) conditioned by the status of being a compound (*samāsatva*) applies first via the rule "and optionally like a compound" (*samāsavacca bahulam*). Otherwise, if there were doubling of the inflected word (*subanta*), since the original would lack the status of being a pronoun, that status could not be attributed to its substitute either. Nor does this lead to an impossibility of doubling under the heading of "word-status" (*padatva*), as there would be no word-status [in that case].

This is because it conforms to the definition of a suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). Since it does not fall under the jurisdiction of the section on *aṅga* (bases), the prohibition by the rule "na lumatā" (Pāṇini 1.1.63) does not apply. In the case of *anyo'nyeṣām*, however, even though it lacks the status of a compound (*samāsa*), the distinction between base and suffix is established by the force of the statement: "The first singular ending belongs to the preceding word (*pūrvapada*), while the second [dual] and so forth belong to the following word (*parapada*)."

In this regard, the following should be further considered: the denotative power (*śakti*) of pronouns and similar words consists in their having the state of being present in the mind (*buddhisthatva*) as their meaning. It should not be argued that, if this were so, the resulting cognition would have "being present in the mind" as its qualifier (*prakāra*), rather than "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), because there is a rule that verbal cognition must have the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier. For in this case, that [state of being present in the mind] is abandoned. This is because the function of a word depends upon the result [of the cognition]. For this very reason, there is the traditional saying that there is no metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of pronouns; for the ancients maintain that the cognition having that [specific property] as its qualifier arises through denotative power alone.

Others, however, maintain that properties such as *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and the like are themselves the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), since it is accepted that words can have multiple meanings. Nor should it be argued that in cases where there is verbal cognition having a heavy property co-extensive with a light one as its qualifier, this would entail *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication), thereby contradicting the aforementioned doctrine; for *kambugrīvādimattva* (the state of possessing a neck and so forth) is heavier than *ghaṭatva*, and thus cannot be its own delimiter of denotability. Furthermore, it should not be claimed that if one accepts a cognition of the individual devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka*) from that word, it would contradict the rule that words do not produce indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognitions.

They say that [the view] is established within the very position that accepts non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), because it enters [into the discussion] there; furthermore, even if that [non-conceptual cognition] is rejected, there is no loss [to their position]. The Miśras, however, maintain that since there is no evidence for multiple meanings—as in the case of the word *hari*—being-present-in-the-mind (*buddhisthatva*) serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) that unifies the various delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). This is because the apprehension of the word’s power (*śakti*) occurs in the form: "The denotable object of these [words] is that which is delimited by the delimiter of being an object of cognition."

And thus, when the property of being the delimitor of the objectness of a person’s cognition with respect to a particular property is apprehended at a particular time, then—due to the awakening of that portion of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the aforementioned apprehension of power—the recollection of word-meanings and the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) have that very property as their qualifier. In this way, there is a unification (*anugama*) of the qualifier-positions residing in potness and so forth, because of the identity of the delimitor of the qualifier-position, which consists in being the object of cognition.

However, if one were to specifically accept that potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like are the delimiters of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) due to the infinity of the modes (*prakāratā*) residing therein. For they say that, just as the unity of the delimiter of the denotative capacity brings about the unity of the power (*śakti*), so too does the delimiter of the delimiter of the denotative capacity bring about the unity of the power.

Others, however, argue that even in this way, in order to account for the fact that at one time there is a cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and at another time a cognition having "cloth-ness" as its qualifier, one must state that the cause of a cognition having pot-ness as its qualifier is the knowledge of the word's expressive power (*śakti*) qualified by pot-ness as delimited by "being present in the mind" (*buddhisthatva*). This applies similarly in other cases as well. They maintain that introducing the qualification of "being delimited by being present in the mind" within the scope of the stated causal relation involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); rather, it is more appropriate to accept polysemy (*nānārthatva*) itself and to postulate that "being present in the mind" is merely a contextual adjunct (*prayogopādhi*) to usage.

If it is argued that even so, all pronouns would be synonyms, we say no; for that [synonymy] does not exist due to the distinction of cognition (*buddhi-viśeṣa*). When the word *sarva* has the property of being the delimitor of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatva*), its denotative power (*śakti*) resides in as many modes as are objects of cognition. Nor is the term "subject" (*uddeśya*) redundant, because the things to be predicated (*vidheya*) do not have that [subjecthood] as their purpose. And even so, there is no consequence of its being a synonym for the word *yat*.

In that context, this is because the intended meaning is a subordinate sentence’s subject-cognition which stands in expectancy for a sentence containing that [correlative] pronoun (*tatpada*); or else, because there is a distinction due to the multiplicity of the mode (*prakāra*) [of the cognition]. For instance, in such cases as "That which is ether is the substratum of sound," there is a deviation from the multiplicity of the mode produced by the cognition generated by the word *yat*. By this, the objection regarding the commonality of the *tatpada* is also refuted. Furthermore, in this case, there is no requirement for co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words;
for we observe in "all Brāhmaṇas" that the word refers to those delimited by *brāhmaṇa*-hood, while in "all [things]" and so forth, it refers to those delimited by knowability (*prameyatva*).

The denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *kim* (what) resides in that which is delimited by the object of a question and a private cognition (*pratyekabuddhi*). If it is objected: "How can there be a question? For desire does not arise regarding what is unknown, and curiosity (*jijñāsā*) does not arise regarding what is already known," we reply: No. In such cases as "What is the one deity in the world? (*kimekaṃ daivataṃ loke*), although the property delimiting the object-sphere (*viṣayatāvacchedakadharma*) is the same in both the knowledge that generates the question and the knowledge produced by the answer, the meaning of the interrogative sentence is: "A cognition whose qualifier is a property subsumed under 'being a single deity' is the object of my desire."

In this case, the modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in Viṣṇu-ness is delimited by the property of being a single deity; however, in the expression "Viṣṇu is the deity," it is undelimited (*anavacchinna*). Thus, there is no fault, because the interrogative sentence arises from a desire for knowledge whose modehood regarding that attribute is undelimited, whereas the answer is produced by a knowledge whose modehood regarding that same attribute is delimited by something. Although the aforementioned [definition] is over-exclusive (*avyāpta*) in the case of expressing doubt—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—and in the case of an inquiry such as "Who is this?", nevertheless, a separate denotative power (*śakti*) must be postulated for those instances.

The denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *yat* resides in that which is delimited by the qualifier being the object of a cognition that is the subject of a subordinate sentence requiring the sentence containing *tat*; and the power of the word *tat* resides in the object of a cognition that is the subject of a subordinate sentence requiring the sentence containing *yat*. Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "He who has gone, he has returned," because what is intended here is a word having the same meaning as the word *tat*.

However, this is the distinction: the word *tat*, when signifying a topic already introduced (*prakrānta*), a well-known thing (*prasiddha*), or something previously experienced (*anubhūta*), does not require the word *yat*. Examples in order: "Policy alone is cowardice; valor is the behavior of a beast."
Therefore, he sought success through the union of both.
The king known as Atithi has departed from here;
now two things have become objects of pity because of their longing for union with the Skull-bearer (Śiva).
And you are that radiant digit of the moon, the moonlight for the eyes of this world.
Here, the digit of the moon is well known.
Your eyes, trembling and casting their garments askance due to fear, are darting restlessly in every direction.
You were suddenly consumed by a cruel fire, fierce and filled with smoke, and were not even looked upon.

"Sāgarikā’s eyes were previously experienced by the King of Vatsa"—thus it is stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*. Furthermore, a relative pronoun (*yacchabda*) contained within a subsequent sentence does not necessarily require the employment of a correlative pronoun (*tacchabda*) in the preceding sentence.
For example, in such passages as "That wonder arose there upon the surface of the earth, which was contemplated by the rows [of gods]," even though the correlative pronoun is present—

"In the verse beginning 'Excellent is what has been done by the lotuses toward the moon, which is superior in loveliness,' [the pronoun *tat*] is absent. Regarding this, some say that even in the aforementioned instance, the word *tat* is implied.

Others, however, maintain that there is a distinct power (*śakti*) here. The Miśras have stated: "The word *tat* refers to the object denoted by the subject of the subordinate clause (*avāntaravākya-uddeśya*). In the verse "Excellent is what has been done by the lotuses toward the moon," when the subject is understood through the word *yat*, the comprehension of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) arises immediately after the comprehension produced by the first quarter-verse. This is because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to assume a comprehension produced by the first quarter-verse again by means of the implication of the word *tat*. Thus—

Even in such passages as "The birth of the moon is seen to be fruitless indeed by him who has not [seen] the night-lotus blooming," there would be the consequence of tautology if the word *tat* were supplied, because the object presented would already be qualified by its nature as the moon (*indutva*). Nor can there be a cognition from the word *tat* as being qualified by the absence of the sight of the blooming lotus; for the referent of the word *yat* alone serves as the qualifier of the sight. Furthermore, since the word *yat* itself expresses the *mīlita* (the closed state) in the phrase "that which is closed" (*yanmīlitam*), there is no redundancy between the two words in this case of conjunction (*sambheda*), as neither would be superfluous. And yet, the word *yat* is not redundant.
They say that because of the rule, "The connection with the word *yat* [indicates] primacy," this serves to establish [the milk] as the object of reference (*uddeśya*).

The denotative power (*śakti*) of the words *idam* and *etad* resides in that which is proximate and delimited by the property that serves as the delimitor of perceptual objecthood (*pratyakṣa-viṣayatāvacchedaka*). For this very reason, Vardhamānopādhyāya states: "There is a repetition of the sentence for every handful (*añjali*), because it would be impossible to point out with *idam* the milk that is yet to be taken up. Others hold that the power resides in that which is delimited by a property capable of such perception; thus, since the author of the *Nibandhana* states that there is a reference by *etad* even to the handfuls that are being taken up, they maintain that there is only a single sentence.

Others, however, maintain that even in the case of an object of mental perception—such as when one uses the word "this" (*idam*) with respect to time, as in "the jar is now"—it is indeed possible to designate the milk that is about to be taken up by means of the pronoun "this. Nevertheless, at that moment, the destruction of ownership does not occur there because of the abandonment [of the milk]. This is because ownership has not arisen there prior to the act of taking up, and it is impossible for that which has not arisen to undergo destruction.

The word *adas* has its denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward that which is currently out of sight, delimited by the delimitor of the objecthood of perception (*pratyakṣaviṣayatāvacchedaka*). "Separation" (*vyavadhāna*), however, occurs through space and time; for the word is employed with respect to what is remote from that which is made known by *idam* and the like, and because it is employed as *ayam* with respect to the object of the first perception, and as *asau* with respect to the object of the second perception. Some maintain that in both cases, "being first" and "being second" are qualifiers of the perception itself, as appropriate.

The denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *yuṣmad* resides in that which is delimited by the property in respect of which there is the cognition of being the object of address; and the denotative power of the word *asmad* resides in that which is delimited by the property in respect of which there is the cognition of being the utterer of a particular sentence. Being the object of address (*sambodhyatva*) consists in being the object of a specific cognition conducive to making [someone] face [the speaker]. Utterance (*uccāraṇa*) is the mental coordination (*anusandhāna*) of a particular word following another particular word. Being the utterer (*uccārayitṛtva*) consists in possessing the activity conducive to that [utterance]. This is because [the definition] applies even to a silent sage (*mauni*). Furthermore, it has already been stated that utterance includes the condition of not having any other primary intention (*ananyatātparyakatva*).

If it is argued that, in this case, the use of the word *tvat* (your) would not occur in poetry and the like with respect to insentient objects, nor in such expressions as "thus we go," then the answer is: true. This is because what is intended is the possession of a property that delimits the scope of the intention (*tātparya*) of the speaker regarding the act of utterance; for even in those cases, the superimposition (*āropa*) of being a speaker is possible.

Others, however, hold that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* resides in that which is delimited by the property of being the person addressed (*sambodhyatāvacchedaka*) and that which is delimited by the property of being the speaker (*uccārayitṛtāvacchedaka*). This state of being a delimiter consists in being the self (*ātmatva*) as delimited by the body of Caitra and so forth. As for the verbal cognition arising from [the use of these pronouns] when the person addressed is not actually present, due to an error regarding that [delimitor], it must be explained as resulting from an error regarding the denotative power itself. For this very reason, such [cognition] lacks epistemic validity (*aprāmāṇya*).
[Example: "Who are you, sir? "Tell me, know me to be a wretched man, a *śākhoṭaka* tree."

In such cases as these, since error is impossible, there is *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), because the connection with the primary meaning is untenable. The same applies in cases such as "I know that everyone is virtuous," for the cognition of being the person addressed or the speaker serves as the purpose (*prayojana*) according to the circumstances. Regarding expressions such as "We are going," they say that it is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an irregular singular remainder) as stated by Mahārṇava.

But surely, if [the self] were understood by way of Caitra-ness and so forth, there would be a contradiction with the text stating, "These two have their power restricted solely to the Self. This is because the terms are used for the Self alone in the Śruti and Smṛti passages such as "That thou art" and "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa"; because Caitra-ness and the like are classes residing in the body; because the injunction for naming—"one performs the naming ceremony for one who is born"—prescribes the naming of the body itself; and because expressions such as "Caitra is learned" are only figurative. For this very reason, even a deceased person is designated by terms such as "Caitra."

This is because the aforementioned method is necessary for the purpose of establishing the lineage (*gotra*). True; for it is possible for "Caitra-ness" (*caitratva*) and so forth to reside in the self through a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*) constituted by the body. This is the direction [of the argument]. The explanation of the *sarvādi* group is complete.
*Vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.28).

In this case, the designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal) may optionally apply. The intermediate space between the northern and eastern directions is called *uttarapūrvā*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule "names of directions [form a compound] when referring to an intermediate space. For that [direction], one says *uttarapūrvasyai* or *uttarapūrvāyai*. Because the rule specifies the inclusion of only those compounds of directions explicitly taught [by the sūtra], it does not apply here: that which is east is north for one who is confused; he is *uttarapūrva*. To him, give: *uttarapūrvāya dehi*.

As for the argument that the analysis *yasya yottarā sā pūrvā* (that which is its northern [side] is its eastern [side]) is the proper one—otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of reversing the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*)—that is not correct. In reality, in the phrase "that which is actually eastern is the object of a cognition whose qualifier is 'northernness'," the word *uttarā* (northern) itself is the qualifier.
