However, when one does not intend to express an error where the qualificandum is the "northern" and the qualifier is "easternness," the form *pūrvottarā* is also desired. Thus, the rule *bahuvrīhau* need not be applied; for the prohibition regarding the compound *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām* is already secured by the very paribhāṣā concerning the prohibition of a *dvandva*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that this [prohibition] is for the purpose of ensuring that the restriction applies only to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* by its own nature, as stated in the subsequent sūtra, and not to a *bahuvrīhi* that is extended [by analogy]? Otherwise, in cases such as *ekaikasmai dehi*, where there is a doubling according to the rules "the word *eka* is like a *bahuvrīhi*" and "also in the sense of intensity," there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition applying even there. [Reply: Not so. Since the term "compound" (*samāsa*) is understood by virtue of its recurrence [from the previous rule], the meaning obtained is "only that which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Thus, the prohibition does not apply to a *bahuvrīhi* [formed by doubling]. (Pāṇini 6.1.28)

The aforementioned designation [of *sarvanāman*] would not apply to a word that has become the locus for the application of the technical name *bahuvrīhi*. Nor, however, is it the case that such a word lacks the status of being the referent of a *bahuvrīhi*, for the term "it" (*tat*) is applicable because the word serves that purpose. Furthermore, this does not result in an undesired prohibition even in the case of a colloquial analytical statement (*laukika-vigraha*), because although that statement is intended to demonstrate the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi*, it does not itself serve that purpose. This is according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that a formal derivation (*vṛtti*) occurs only when there is semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*), whereas in the state of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), there is only a sentence (*vākya*). Moreover, it is accepted that the application of compound formation (*samāsa*) occurs only in the supra-colloquial sentence (*alaukika-vākya*). Thus, Kaiyaṭa has stated:

This prohibition applies to that syntactical construction (*prakriyāvākya*) which is inherent in the process of grammatical derivation (*aprayogasamavāyin*), and not to a worldly sentence (*laukikavākya*) fit for actual usage, because such a sentence is employed separately [from its derived form].

But surely, in this case, the prohibition would be useless even in the case of an *alaukika-vigraha* (non-grammatical analytical statement), because there is no possibility of its application simply due to its being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Nor should it be argued that since such a word does not generate a cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*), how can it be considered a subordinate member; for we observe its status as a subordinate member within a compound, and thus infer it there as well. Otherwise, as will be stated later, the application of the compound rule would be untenable due to the absence of semantic expectancy (*sāmarthya*).

It should not be argued that only *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) is inferred there by the force of scriptural restatements such as “*anekam anyapadārthe*,” and not *upasarjanatva* (subordinacy) as well, because the latter is not the object of *arthāpatti* (presumption) since it is of no utility for the operation of the compound formation. This is true, for it is difficult to define a *sāmarthya* distinct from *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning). Furthermore, subordinacy is established through implication precisely by the implication of that [unification]. Indeed, once the compound has been formed, there is no purpose in postulating a separate *sāmarthya*.

Since a compound cannot otherwise be accounted for, it is inferred that even in an extra-ordinary sentence (*alaukika-vākya*), the capacity (*sāmarthya*) resides in the aggregate alone, and not in the individual words, because neither of those two [individual capacities] can be conceived as having a separate purpose. Thus, since a mere constituent part would not be a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*), the application of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would follow; therefore, the prohibition [of that designation] is logically established.

The position that this prohibition applies specifically to the primary *bahuvrīhi* compound was also presented first in the *Bhāṣya*. For example: *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* ("one whose father is you") and *matkapitṛkaḥ* ("one whose father is me"). In these cases, if the designation of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) were applied, the suffix *akac* would be added before the final vowel according to the rule "the suffix *akac* is added after indeclinables and pronouns, prior to the final *ṭi*" (*avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*). This is because *akac* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kap*. Similarly, one may cite as an example: *dvikaputraḥ* ("one who has two sons").

Kaiyaṭa states that the Bhāṣya’s mention of "a specific rule for the crow [substitution] at the end of consonants" indicates that the condition of being distinct from those ending in *a* is implied there. Consequently, since forms such as *tvakatpitṛkaḥ*, *makatpitṛkaḥ*, and *dvakiputraḥ* would otherwise result, this prohibition is formulated.

But even so, does this not lead to the undesirable consequence (*akaṭ-prasaṅga*)? For that [suffix *ka*] is *antaraṅga* because it is conditioned by a name (*saṃjñā*), whereas the *bahuvrīhi* compound—occurring when there is the proximity of another word and when one intends to express a meaning other than the specific meanings of the constituent words—is *bahiraṅga*. And thus, since *aka* has already applied prior to the formation of the compound, it cannot be sublated by the aforementioned prohibition, which applies only after the compound has been formed.

Nor should it be argued that, just as by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, the elision (*luk*) based on a compound—though extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*)—is an obstructer even of intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) operations, so too by the force of the aforementioned prohibition, the compound itself would operate by obstructing *akac*. For this [prohibition] is also justified for the sake of forms such as *priyaviśvāya* (dative singular), where by the rule *vā priyasya*, the word *priya* is optionally placed first. Similarly, one has *dvyanyāya* and *tryanyāya*.

This is because it will be stated [later] that "in the case of a collision between a pronominal (sarvanāman) and a numeral, the numeral takes the prior position due to its higher status. For here, under the view that the time of application is determined by the rule itself (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the designation of pronominal (*sarvanāmasaṃjñā*) is in syntactic unity with the rules for the substitution of *smāi* and so forth; thus, based on the pronominal designation of the word *viśva*, the designation would apply to the word *priyaviśva* by means of the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*). To prevent this from occurring, the designation is prohibited specifically for the word *viśva*.

In this case, since the stated rule has its purpose fulfilled by prohibiting the application of a technical designation that would otherwise have occurred after the designation *bahuvrīhi* has been assigned, it is untenable for it to indicate the aforementioned meaning. This is not so; for even by means of the prohibition regarding the *upasarjana*, this much alone is established, and thus the indication of the stated meaning remains well-founded. It is precisely relying upon this position that the ancients explained [the matter].

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) would not apply to words beginning with *sarva*. For example, in *priyasarvāya*. According to the view of the author of the Sūtras (*sūtrakāra*), there is no pronoun-status in a *bahuvrīhi*; according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya (*bhāṣyakāra*), this applies whenever there is even a degree of secondary usage (*gauṇatva*). Regarding forms such as *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ*, since the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are components of the compound, they would possess pronoun-status; consequently, because this is not a primary grammatical operation (*anaṅgakāryatva*), the suffix *akac* would have to be applied. To prevent this and ensure that only the suffix *kap* is applied, the author of the Nyāsa holds that this sūtra exists for that purpose. Here, what is intended is the prohibition of the designation [of pronoun-status] for the component part.

Therefore, the alternative view—that this is a prohibition of the entire collection—is rejected; for, with reference to the text stating that "the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) does not apply to *sarva* and the others," no such doubt arises.

But how could the designation [of *samāsa*] apply even to a constituent part (*avayava*), given that the author of the Vārttika stated that there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) because subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) are explicitly listed? True; however, this is because the author of the Sūtras does not accept that [exclusion]. Thus he says: "according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras. And here, the very commencement of this Sūtra serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Even under the view that a compound expression denotes its own meaning (*jahatsvārthavṛtti*), the capacity to denote its own meaning—which is useful for the technical designation—remains present even within the compound formation (*vṛtti*).

By this, the *Prasāda* commentary on the explanation of the term *tvatkapitṛka*—which states, "because the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, falling within the compound, denote all meanings"—and the *Nyāsa* commentary—which states, "for while the whole [compound] refers to a specific [individual], the first member (*pūrvapada*) does not lose its quality of denoting all meanings"—are both explained. By this, the view that "the exclusion of the *upasarjana* is obtained from the very syllables of the sūtra by the force of the definition being literal (*anvarthasaṃjñā*)" is also refuted.

One might object: "Since the application of a term according to its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) already effects the exclusion of the technical name [of the whole], *akac* will not occur here, because [the rule] pertains specifically to that [whole]. Anticipating this objection, the author states, "This is not so; for the whole... and so forth, introducing the subsequent passage. His intention is that, according to the reasoning already stated, there is no exclusion of the parts. To explain: what is this "pertaining specifically to that"? It cannot mean "not being productive of a cognition whose qualifiers are all the properties that delimit the capacity [of the word]," because even in cases such as *tvakaṃ pitā yasya* ("one whose father is you"), that would still apply.

This is because there is no simultaneous cognition possessing all those specific modes (*prakāra*). Furthermore, a cognition possessing some property as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the objecthood (*viṣayatā*) of the intellect arises in both cases alike. For this very reason, one should not even suspect that [the word] fails to produce a cognition of all individuals delimited by any particular property that serves as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); for such a failure occurs in cases like "all jars have been brought," according to the maxim: "The quality of being 'all' is based on the context. Nor does it possess a denotability delimited by a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*).

This is because all pronouns possess that very nature [of being relative]. Nor is it [the definition] "that which has a denotatum not delimited by any other property," because this would apply commonly to the individual parts [of a compound]. Nor is it "being distinct from both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*)," because this would result in the term becoming merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*), thereby failing to establish its status as a meaningful name (*anvartha-saṃjñā*).

If it is asked, "But how can this be so, given that in a *vṛtti* consisting of a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), no internal division of words is admitted?"—do not say so. This is because it is accepted that the operations of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) take place only during the stage of analysis (*prakriyā-daśā*), and do not apply to the final, established form (*pariniṣṭhita-pada*). Otherwise, the status of being a "final form" would be contradicted. For that [status] consists in not being subsumed under a property that serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka-dharma*) for the object of an eternal rule (*nitya-vidhi*) that has not yet applied. The word "not applied" (*apravṛtta*) is used to avoid the over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) that would otherwise occur in cases such as finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) where [the rule] has already applied.

This is because it has been stated by [the author] himself that the word "nitya" (invariable) is used to prevent the over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) of the rule to forms such as *seddha*, which fall within the scope of the delimitors (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of optional (*vaikalpika*) augmentations (*āgama*). For this very reason, the Vārttika—"In the case of *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, there is a statement regarding their being invariably compoundable when followed by a subsequent member"—is consistent. Otherwise, since the intermediate *tatpuruṣa* would be optional by virtue of the *mahāvibhāṣā* rule, that Vārttika would be inconsistent. We shall refute the claim that, regarding that portion, the Vārttika is merely a restatement of a meaning already established by reasoning (*nyāyasiddha*), at that very place.

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "In the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) type of compound, the individual meanings of the constituent members do not exist at all; even in the *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) type, their status as subordinate (*upasarjana*) is evident, since they function toward another meaning qualified by their own meaning. This is refuted because the meaning useful for the analytical derivation (*prakriyā*) exists even in the *jahatsvārthā* type; for this has been established as the settled doctrine (*siddhānta*) by the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities in the case of *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and so forth. Otherwise, the rule "dvandve ca" would be untenable.

Since that which is included within a compound (vṛttyantargata) lacks meaning, it cannot be a pronoun; thus, by the rule of extension to what ends with such a term (tadantavidhi), the occurrence of its status as a pronoun within a compound is difficult to establish. Furthermore, it is hard to maintain that this [rule] refers to the non-locus-classical analysis (alaukikavigraha), because the established doctrine (siddhānta) holds that this prohibition applies to the whole compound. Moreover, how could there be the status of a pronoun in cases such as *paramasarva*? There is no reason for the disparity that while the constituent members of a *dvandva* or *karmadhāraya* possess meaning, those of a *bahuvrīhi* and so forth do not.

This is because the operation (*vṛtti*) is common to both cases; furthermore, it has already been stated by [the author] himself that the distinction between being a preceding or a following member (*pūrvottarapadatva*) is irrelevant. Likewise, this is precisely the intended meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which states: "Thus, even when *etad* has *tyad* and so forth as its predominant element, this is established. Otherwise, he would have simply said that since it is meaningless (*anarthaka*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply here, and consequently, there is no possibility of the suffix *akac*.

However, this is the meaning of the word *api*: since the purpose of this prohibition [of *akac*] is fulfilled in cases such as *priyaviśvāya*, how can there be an exclusion of *akac* in instances like *tvatkapitṛka*, given that it would apply even prior to the formation of the compound due to its being *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned), as has already been stated?

If, however, for the sake of preserving the principle that "even before [the application of] *akac*, there is no operation [of *akac*] due to the force of the prohibition," one resorts to the prohibition of the *upasarjana* (subordinate element) in the case of *priyaviśvāya*, then in the case of *tvatkapitṛka*, *akac* would likewise not occur by that very same [prohibition], rendering the stated prohibition useless. But if one accepts that the commencement [of the rule] is for the purpose of prohibiting *akac* only in the non-orthodox sentence (*alaukikavākya*), then the conclusion remains with the second position alone.

Regarding the passage beginning with "even in the case of *ajahatsvārthā*," one must also ask: is it intended that subordination (*upasarjanatva*) arises because the word's own meaning has become a qualifier of another, or because its own [primary] meaning is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to another object? It cannot be the first, for then [subordination] would undesirably follow even in cases such as *sarvasmai*, since [the stem *sarva-*] there becomes a qualifier of the meaning of the case-ending. Nor can it be the second, for there is a contradiction with the texts of both ourselves and others in asserting that being figurative constitutes subordination; furthermore, under the view that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound only the prior member is figurative with respect to the meaning of the other members, this [definition] would have no application to the present topic.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Now, one might object that if the exclusion of *upasarjana* (subordinate term) is not accepted, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *atisarvāya*; to this, he says: "by the author of the Bhāṣya. The point is this: although the entry into a compound (*vṛtti-praveśa*) is the same, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply where the meaning of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), but it certainly applies where it functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), as in examples like *paramasarve*.

Consequently, since the example *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* would otherwise be untenable, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that this sūtra is intended as a prohibition regarding the non-grammatical analytical construction (*alaukika-vigraha*); such is the view of the ancient commentators.

The author of the *Nyāsa*, however, says: "The example *priyaviśvāya* is not valid, because the entire compound (*samudāya*) is not a pronominal (*asarvanāmatvāt*). Furthermore, the extension of the rule to that which ends in [a pronominal] (*tadantavidhi*), which is obtained through an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the context of technical names (*saṃjñā*), pertains to cases where the meaning of the pronominal is primary. And since the components of that compound, such as *viśva* and so on, pertain to cases where the meaning of the pronominal is not primary, there is no possibility of applying the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to pronouns to those components. This is because the suffixes beginning with *smai* fall under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'stem' (*aṅga*)."

Nor can that [undesired] application be avoided by relying on the status of being subsequent to an *aṅga* ending in a pronoun, based on the established rule (*siddhānta*) stating, "In the context of *aṅga*, [the substitution applies] to that [pronoun] and to its following word. This is because the rule must be understood as having a qualification regarding what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*). The meaning is: "The substitution applies to the case endings beginning with *ṅe* when they are prescribed after a pronoun which itself follows an *aṅga*. In this regard, the usage in the Bhāṣya—namely, *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām* under the rule *dvandve ca*—serves as the authority, since a single syntactic unit (*ekavākya*) operates everywhere in a uniform manner.

Nor does the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) persist by virtue of the implication that [the suffix applies] after a stem ending in a pronominal; for that would render the qualification "prescribed" (vihita) redundant. This is because it is accepted that the pronominal itself is the qualified object in the rule "after a pronominal which is a stem" (aṅgāt sarvanāmnaḥ), and by that, the rule of extension to what ends in that (tadantavidhi) does not apply. For this very reason, the authors of the *Prakāśa* stated:
"Even though the mere constituent part possesses the status of a pronominal, there is no fault."

And thus, since the prohibition "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*na bahuvrīhau*) is not required in the case of *priyaviśvāya*, by the force of that [prohibition], even the *antaranga* suffix *akac* does not apply prior to the compound; therefore, the example *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and others are perfectly established. It is thus proven that this sūtra is intended solely for the purpose of prohibiting the designation of the members [of the compound] once the *bahuvrīhi* has been formed. He presents this very point with the words beginning with *tvatkapitṛkaḥ*.

And thus, by the statement "according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras," it is said that this sūtra was composed because he did not accept the prohibition regarding upasarjana [compounds]. However, according to the Vārttika school, the matter is already established simply by the prohibition of upasarjana; such is the meaning. But when there is a desire to know the specific scope, according to the Bhāṣya school, this prohibition applies to the non-ordinary (alaukika) analytical statement (vigraha).

In the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa, however, the distinction is stated as "of the members in a *bahuvrīhi*. Nor should it be asked: "Since this [distinction] is also written first in the Bhāṣya, how can it be attributed to the author of the Nyāsa? For in the first [case], the impossibility of forms such as *priyaviśvāya* was explained by means of the prohibition regarding the *upasarjana*; whereas in the second, having accepted the technical name (*saṃjñā*), it was explained by a different method. Thus, when the Sūtra has been explained in this way, the author of the Bhāṣya speaks with the intention of rejecting [the distinction], saying: "But Gonardīya says: 'The accentuation of the particle *akac* must be applied to each member without doubt.'"

It must be *tvakat-pitṛkaḥ* or *makat-pitṛkaḥ*. Regarding the accent, by the rule "svāṅga-śiṭām-adantām," there is an udātta on the first syllable. According to the increasing authority of the sages and following the Bhāṣya, the determination of correctness is established precisely in this manner. [This concerns] the third-case compound (29).

The designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) would not apply [in the following case]: *māsapūrvāya dehi* ("Give to one preceded by a month"). Furthermore, the repetition of the term *samāsa* (compound) is for the purpose of obtaining the prohibition even in a sentence that has the sense of a compound, through a division of the rule (*vākyabheda*). Example: *māsena pūrvāya*. Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) in cases such as *tvayakā kṛtam* or *tvakatkṛtam*, because the term refers specifically to the compound taught by its own technical rule (*pratipadokta*), namely the compound formed by the rule "pūrvasadṛśa... (Pāṇini 2.1.31).

Alternatively, "in a non-compound" (*asamāse*) is a separate rule (*yoga*). By way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), this refers to worldly sentences (*laukika-vākya*) that resemble compounds. Nor should it be argued that, as in the previous rule, this too should refer only to unformed (*alaukika*) sentences; for in the case of words ending in *at*, there would be no distinction between the suffixes *kā* and *aca*, and in the case of words ending in *t*, there would be the consequence of redundancy, since there is no third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) explicitly prescribed (*pratipadokta*) for them. And [the rule applies] in a *dvandva* compound. (30)

The designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal) would not apply [to the words] *pūrva*, *apara*, and *adhara*. This prohibition concerns the whole (*samudāya*) and not its individual parts (*avayava*). Nor is there an absence of the possibility for the designation to apply to the whole, because that is inferred precisely from the stated prohibition; furthermore, this is supported by the *vārttika*: "The purpose [of this rule] is [to ensure the application of] the designations *sarvanāman* and *avyaya*."

If it is asked, "Why should this not be a prohibition of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the individual members [of a compound] alone?", do not say so. This is because there would be no purpose [for such a prohibition]. Since the forms preceding *tyad* and the others end in *-a*, there is no distinction between the suffixes *kā* and *ka*. Furthermore, since *tyad* and the others are formed by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), a *dvandva* compound is not even established in their case. Moreover, as will be stated later, *ekaśeṣa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *dvandva*. Finally, in the example *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is intended.

In the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre* ("in all formations [of a compound], [the name] sarvanāman [is applied]"), because that which has the designation *sarvanāman* anywhere at all is what is referred to, the [application of the] designation would be unavoidable even by means of its prohibition. Nor should it be argued that, on the view that the word *tvad* ends in *t*, the prohibition is intended solely for the purpose of excluding *akac* in that case; for this would result in the rule having too narrow a scope (*alpaviṣayakatva*). [Objection: Even so, if one does not accept the prohibition of the designation for the constituent part (*avayava*), then in the aforementioned instance, *suṭ* would apply by means of the *tadantavidhi* (the rule that a grammatical operation applies to that which ends with the element specified) under the heading of *aṅga*.

Nor is the prohibition (niṣedha) purposeless, because it serves a meaningful purpose by excluding suffixes such as *tratas* and *til* which fall outside the scope of the governing rule (*aṅgādhikāra*). Regarding this, they say:
"There is no fault, because the specific qualification is prescribed for operations concerning *aṅga*s.
31. *vibhāṣā jasi*.

When the substitution of *śī* is to be applied [to the case-ending] *jas*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) previously stated for a *dvandva* compound may optionally apply. For example: *varṇāśrametare* or *varṇāśrametarāḥ*. The term "in *jas*" (*jasi*) denotes a locative sense (*ādhāratva*) with respect to the operation [of the rule]. Although there can be no relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) between two things occurring at different times because the original *jas* is removed by its substitute, nevertheless, that relationship should be understood in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*), consisting in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the contingency (*prasaṅga*) that triggers the application of the substitute.

Some, however, say that *jas-ir* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). They maintain that the locative ending in *jasi* is an archaic elision (*sautra-lopa*), and that the long vowel *ī* is obtained through the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule for including sounds).

Others, however, maintain that under the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that the technical name applies at the time the operation is to be performed), this designation (*saṃjñā*) is present specifically in the rule *jasaḥ śī*; all of this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. In any case, the option applies only with respect to the substitution of *śī*; elsewhere, there is only the prohibition by the preceding rule. Consequently, in forms such as *varṇāśrametarakāḥ*, the suffix *akac* does not occur, but rather the suffix *kap* alone. If *akac* were applied, then by the principle of inclusion within a compound (*tanmadhyapatitanyāya*), *śī* would optionally replace *jas* in some instances. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "The operation of *jas* is optional, for *akac* does not occur."

The words *prathama*, *carama*, *alpa*, *ardha*, *katipaya*, and *nema* [are optionally called *sarvanāman*] when the feminine suffix *śī* is to be applied. This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*): it applies to *nema* where [the designation] has already been established, but to the others where it has not yet been established.
As Bhavabhūti says: "Of those beings who existed in the first age, the ancient ones, he is the bearer of their burden."
"They were not like you in the past, nor will they be in the future;
we see them with our own ears and hear them when they are uttered, yet we are too limited to describe them.
Our hands possess the skill to fashion decorative leaf-designs upon the breasts of Vaidehī."
And Murāri says: "A few rays of the moon [are those] whose function is the vow of dissolution. The rest is easy to understand. [The rule:

*pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara* [take the feminine suffix *ṅīp*] when used in the sense of relative position (*vyavasthā*) and not as proper names (*asaṃjñā*). 33.

34. *Sva* [is used] when not meaning "one's own" or "wealth. 35. *Antara* [is used] when meaning "that which is inside" or "that which is worn as an outer garment. These three sūtras have already been explained in the commentary on the *gaṇa* [of pronouns], because they are of the same form. This present rule is commenced for the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*) in the case of the *jas* ending, regarding that very same sense for which the designation was previously prescribed as compulsory (*nitya*). Examples include *pūrve*, *pūrvāḥ*, and so forth. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:
Furthermore, the inclusion of *avara* and the others in the recitation of the sūtra would be redundant, since they are already listed in the [gaṇapāṭha] list.

The meaning of this is as follows: because the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "of *avara* etc. has the sense of "type" (*prakāra*), there is also the inclusion of *pūrva* and *para*. Thus, since *pūrva* and the others are listed in the gaṇa specifically for the purpose of establishing their technical designation (*saṃjñā*) based on the aforementioned specific meanings, the sūtra should have been formulated simply as "the nine beginning with *pūrva*" (*pūrvādīni nava*). This is because it is precisely those [nine] that are recognized here.

In that very context, the mention of the meaning serves as a qualification of the recitation; for instance, in the rule "tiṅo gotrādīni kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ," the inclusion of the terms *kutsanā* (censure) and *abhīkṣṇya* (frequency) indicates that the recitation of the *gotra*-class words is intended for the purpose of specifying this particular meaning. By this, the view that there is a separate recitation for each [meaning] here is also refuted.

Regarding the statement, "The nine beginning with *pūrva*," the rule (*sūtra*) in this context will be one where the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies according to the circumstances. Now, there is no evidence for the claim that the recitation of the rules (*sūtrapāṭha*) follows the recitation of the lists (*gaṇapāṭha*) arranged in a fixed order. Furthermore, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the expression "*sarvādīni*" can also have the sense of "type" (*prakāra*). It is for the purpose of demonstrating this that the learned recite the lists; for instance, we see such statements as "the group beginning with *śreṇi* is recited" and "the group beginning with *kṛt* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class-based group)."

Furthermore, since the authors of the commentaries (*vṛttikāra*) have cited *kṛta* and so forth for the sake of illustration, and since forms such as *madhyamasyām* and *avamasyām* are also observed in the Veda, [one might argue that these belong to the *sarvanāman* class]. This is not so; because by the inclusion of the word "nine" in the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā*, the fact that the list in the *gaṇapāṭha* is exhaustive is made known. Otherwise, the inclusion of the word "nine" would be useless, as its purpose is to exclude words like *tyad* (the pronominal series). Therefore, in the rule *sarvādīni*, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to establish a fixed limit. Otherwise, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *sakala*. Moreover, forms such as *madhyamasyām* are Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Now, after the recitation of *tyad* and so forth, some recite *pūrva* and the others. In that case, a prohibition of suffixes such as *tratasil* would apply to *pūrva* and the rest, because under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from *kim*, pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and *bahuvrīhi*," there is the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not from *dvi* and so forth"; thus, those suffixes are prescribed only for pronouns other than *dvi* and the like. Therefore, this specific enumeration (*pratipadapāṭha*) is for the purpose of re-establishing the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" for these words. By its very force (*sāmarthya*), the exclusion is thereby set aside.

For example: by the re-enactment of the rule "anurlakṣaṇe," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed to express the sense of cause (*hetu*). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) would not be obtained in the *jas* case-ending; for that too is prescribed through a split in the rules (*vākya-bheda*). If you argue that—as in the cases of "ami pūrvaḥ" and "saṃprasāraṇācca"—the connection with the phrase "vā chandasi" (optionally in the Vedic) occurs through a split in the rules, resulting in an option regarding the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*) in the Vedic language, then do not say so.

Since it can be understood from the very usage of the *sūtra* and *vārttika*, "If it is argued that [the rule] is not established with respect to the preceding because of the occurrence of *jaś*, then there would be the undesirable consequence of an exception (*apavāda*) due to its absence in the subsequent," that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "from *dvi* and so on" does not apply to *pūrva* and the others, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) once the objection—that the explicit recitation (*pratipadapāṭha*) of *pūrva* and the others qualified by specific meanings—is redundant:
"I shall state an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the *jas* ending."

The meaning of this is as follows: if the rule were formulated here simply as *pūrvādīni nava* ("the nine beginning with *pūrva*"), then, since the mention of meanings in the list of words (*gaṇapāṭha*) would serve only for the prescription of permanent technical names (*nityasaṃjñā*), there would be no authority for [the rule] to qualify the specific recitation [of those words]. Consequently, this would be an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding meanings other than those [already mentioned], where *pūrva* and the others have not [otherwise] been established. Nor can it be argued that even so, let this remain an optional rule where [the name] is already established; for that would entail the fault of restating what has already been stated (*uktānuvādadoṣa*), whereas an optional rule applies only where [the name] has not yet been established (*aprāptivibhāṣā*). Thus, it is a prescription of something previously unestablished.

For instance: if the mention of the meaning were not a qualification of the *pāṭha* (the list of words), then words such as *pūrva* and others would be listed at the beginning of the *sarvādi* group without being delimited by any specific meaning. The mention of the meaning, however, is employed only for the sake of the optional designation (*vibhāṣā*) in the case of the permanent designation (*nityasaṃjñā*). Thus, in cases such as "fixed order" (*vyavasthā*), the designation is permanent. But when considering whether the optional designation in the *jas* case applies to those *pūrva* and other words occurring in the sense of "fixed order" and so forth, or to those occurring in other meanings, in the former case there is the fault of "reiteration" (*anuvādadoṣa*), because the designation is already established even for the *jas* case.

In the second case, however, since the designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed precisely as something not previously established, it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor can it be argued that here too there is a restatement regarding the negative alternative (*abhāvakoṭi*) and a prescription regarding the positive alternative (*bhāvakoṭi*), whereas in the case of an option based on what is already established (*prāptavibhāṣā*), there is a restatement regarding the positive alternative and a prescription regarding the negative alternative; for only when the interpretation as referring to a positive state is untenable does one, out of necessity, assume the intention (*tātparya*) of the rule to lie in a prohibition. This is because it would be inappropriate to apply [the rule] to other meanings when it is possible to prescribe a designation for something not yet established.

Therefore, even in the *Vibhāṣā*, the recitation of "east" (*pūrva*) and the other directions is preceded by a specific distinction of meaning. And by virtue of that, it constitutes an optional rule (*vibhāṣā-prāpta*) because it is prescribed with reference to a specific meaning; for it would be illogical for an option to apply to a different meaning when it has been enjoined with reference to a specific one.

Regarding this, they say: immediately after the aforementioned *trimūtryaḥ* in the *Gaṇapāṭha*, one should read "vibhāṣā jasi. This is because the option (*vikalpa*) is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of *pūrva* and the others as qualified by their specific meanings. Nor does it follow that *sarva* and the rest would also be carried over; for the option regarding *jasi* is initiated specifically for *nema*. And it should not be argued that even though the non-continued application (*ananuvṛtti*) of everything up to *nema* has been indicated by that [reading], the continued application of *sama* and *sima* remains unavoidable; for the purpose can be accomplished by reading the list as *samasimanemāḥ*.

Alternatively, the following entries should be made in the seventh [chapter] of the *Nyāsa*: "For the case endings *jas*, *ṅasi*, and *ṅi*, [the substitutes] *śī*, *smāt*, and *smin* [are applied respectively]"; "Optionally [so] for the nine beginning with *pūrva*"; "For *auṅ* [following] a stem ending in *āp*, [the substitute] *śī*"; and "Also after a neuter [stem]. This is because, in view of the provision for optional technical designations (*saṃjñā*), even though the word *śī* is introduced in two forms, there is greater brevity compared to the alternative arrangement.

Alternatively—the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā* may be explained by carrying it over (*anuvṛtti*) to the rule *jasaḥ śī* and interpreting it through a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*): "After these nine [words], there shall optionally be the substitution of *śī* for *jas*. Therefore, the two aforementioned sūtras need not be recited in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. In this regard, the following must be considered: if the optional application of the technical name (*saṃjñā-vikalpa*) were not commenced under the rule for *jas*, then in forms such as *pūrvāḥ*, even in the alternative where the substitution of *śī* does not occur, the technical name "pronoun" (*sarvanāma*) would still be present, resulting in the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the word being acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādy-udātta*). However, according to the established system (*yathānyāsa*), in that case the word is acute-accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*). Thus, there is a difference in the result (*phala-vaiṣamya*).
In the *Vibhāṣā-prakaraṇa*, there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the suffix *tīya* when it is marked with the *ṅit* designation:

*dvitīyasmai*, *dvitīyāyai*, and so forth. In this way, the rule "optionally [the substitution of *ām* occurs] after *dvitīya* and *tṛtīya*" need not be commenced. For the rule is already established even in the feminine gender, either by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a word denotes also its form qualified by gender) through the inclusion of the single substitute as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*), or else because the feminine is explicitly mentioned. There is no lack of a determining factor (*vinigamakābhāva*), since by the mention of the feminine gender, the operation is not established for the masculine and neuter. [The suffix] *cha* occurs after a word ending in *jāti* when it expresses a "relative" (*bandhu*). Example: *brāhmaṇajātīyāya*. [The suffix] *jātīyar* occurs in the sense of expressing a "kind" (*prakāra*). Example: *paṭujātīyāya*.

From the two words *mukha* and *pārśva*, the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule for the *gaha*-class (Pāṇini 4.2.138), resulting in *mukhatīya* and *pārśvatīya*. In these cases, there is no status as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), because they are derivative forms (*lākṣaṇika*) and because they lack independent meaning (*anarthaka*). Furthermore, when the suffix *an* is applied by the rule "after a ordinal number ending in *tīya*, the suffix *an* is used to denote a portion" (Pāṇini 5.3.48), and the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "and that which is designated as *it*" (Pāṇini 6.4.148)—as in the case of *tṛtīyāya bhāgāya*—there too the status of a pronoun does not apply, because the form is derivative. Nor does the maxim of "substitution of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) apply here, because the form ending in *an* is distinct [from the original ordinal] and because the suffix *an* is not a modification (*vikāra*) of the preceding element. Thus ends the section on the technical designation of pronouns (*sarvanāma*). Now, the rule: "Indeclinables (*avyaya*) consist of those beginning with *svara* and the particles (*nipāta*). (Pāṇini 1.1.37)

The *svarādi* group and the *nipātas* (particles) shall be designated as indeclinables (*avyaya*). The term *dvandva* here denotes a collective compound. The *nipātas* will be explained under the governing rule beginning with "prior to *rīśvara*" and extending up to "the word *adhi* when meaning 'lord'. Objection: One might argue that instead of listing *svarādi* etc., one could have simply included them within the *cādi* group; then, in the rules concerning indeclinables, one could have merely employed the term *nipāta* itself to establish their designation as indeclinables, and thus not have begun a separate section for them. Reply: This is not so. For the designation *nipāta* applies specifically to those *cādi* items that denote non-substantial entities (*asattvavācin*).

In the case of the verse "They lead the *lodha*, considering it an animal," the word *paśu* would apply only in its sense of "correctly" (*samyag-artha*), and not in instances such as "He created those animals" (*paśūṃstāṃścakre*), where it denotes a living being (*sattva*). However, for words like *svaḥ*, even when they denote a living being, the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) applies, as seen in examples such as "Look at the sky! (*svaḥ paśya*); thus, there is a distinction [between these two cases].

Now, if it is argued that even so, the *Nyāsa* should be formulated as: "Those before *rīśvara* are particles (*nipāta*)," "The *svarādi* group," and "The *ca*-group when not denoting a substance (*asattve*)," we say no. This is because the designation of *pragṛhya*—namely, "A particle consisting of a single vowel, except for *aṅ*"—would then undesirably apply to those *svarādi* items that consist of a single vowel. Furthermore, this would include the *at* suffix in *kimo't*, the *āc* suffix in *dakṣiṇādāc*, and other *taddhita* suffixes, as well as *kṛt* formations such as *ken*, all of which consist of a single vowel and are included among the *svarādi* items. Nor can it be said that one should simply read the rule as "The *ca*-group, consisting of a single vowel, except for *aṅ*."

If there were no qualification that *ca* and so forth denote non-substances (*asattvavācin*), then since the word *i*, which denotes desire, is also used in the vocative (as in *i evam*), it would undesirably result in its being a *pragṛhya* by the rule *eco 'pragṛhyasyāyavāyāvaḥ*. However, when it is stated that they are "particles" (*nipāta*), the designation applies only to those *ca*-type words that denote non-substances; thus, there is no over-extension. Furthermore, because the technical name "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) is understood as an etymological designation—meaning that which does not undergo various modifications (*vikāra*), that is to say, it does not assume the properties of substance such as gender, number, or case-role—the designation does not apply to secondary elements (*upasarjana*). [The term *avyaya*] signifies that which does not go through diverse transformations.

Therefore, in the case of *atyuccais-au* and *atyuccais-a*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the nominal suffix (*sup*) because they lack the designation of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*). This is because [the compound] assumes the properties of a substantive (*sattva-dharma*) by virtue of the predominance of that which has been transcended (*atikrānta-prādhānya*). Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility whatsoever for this designation [of "indeclinable"] to apply here; for even the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadanta-vidhi*) is indicated precisely by the etymological nature of the designation itself. Otherwise, since there would be no possibility of its application to a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the purpose of excluding it [from being called an indeclinable] would be untenable. However, in cases such as *paramasvara*, where the meaning of the final member is predominant, the elision does indeed occur. Furthermore, the Vedic scripture cited in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) regarding the *Praṇava-vidyā* in the *Ātharvaṇa* also serves as authority for this point.
That which remains the same across the three genders, all case endings,
and all numbers, and does not change— that is called indeclinable (avyaya).

And there is no similarity [of indeclinables] with respect to the expression of specific gender, because they lack the capacity for that. However, some say that even in the absence of a connection to specific gender, indeclinables do indeed possess a connection to gender in general. That is not correct; Kaiyaṭa states that there is no evidence for gender in general [in the case of indeclinables]. [This applies] to case-endings (*vibhakti*) and grammatical relations (*kāraka*). Because indeclinables, which have the means of action (*sādhana*) as their primary element, do not admit the entry of other powers (*śakti*), and because those whose primary element is the action (*kriyā*) lack a connection to such powers. [This also applies] to numbers (*vacana*), such as singular and plural.

However, although an *avyayībhāva* compound may be joined with gender and number, it retains its indeclinability by virtue of an explicit rule, just as the term *karmapravacanīya* applies to words such as *su* and others.

Now, the particles beginning with *svar*. *Svar* is used for heaven and the other world. For heaven: "fearing battle with those born in *svas* and *rasātala*. For the other world: "those friends who have gone to *svaḥ*, equal to life itself, have suddenly become equal [to me]. *Antar* means in the middle: "the interior (*antar*) of the *hemaketaka* petals, dusty, where beauty is difficult to attain even in a valley (*droṇī*). *Prātar* means at dawn: "Look, friend, in the morning (*prātaḥ*), the lotus has become like a poor man—its seal [of closed petals] broken open. The word *svaḥ* is *svarita*-accented.

According to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* rule, "The words *nyaḥ* and *svarau* are *svarita*," and because of the usage "the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*) and then the heaven (*svar*"), these two [words] have their final syllables accented (*antodātta*). This is seen in such instances as "In the morning we invoke Agni; in the morning Indra. The word *punaḥ* is used in the senses of "not being first" and "distinction. In the sense of "not being first": "Abandon our practice of reciting hymns that are redundant due to repeated experience. In the sense of "distinction": "What more need be said regarding the ninth [day]? This [word *punaḥ*] has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). The word *sanutaḥ* means "in concealment": "The thief goes away in secret."

*Uccais* means "loudly" or "greatly," as in: "Just as this sound rises loudly, piercing the path of the ears. *Nīcais* means "softly" or "slightly," as in: "Speak softly, for surely my lord of life resides within my heart. *Śanais* indicates slowness of action, as in: "O wielder of the stone, [drive away] the enemies slowly. *Ṛdhak* signifies "separately" or "distinctly. *Hyas* refers to the day immediately preceding. *Śvas* refers to the day immediately following.

"In the hope of attaining her tomorrow" (*śvas-tasyāḥ priyam-āptum-uddhura-dhiyaḥ*); "streams from the flow" (*dhārāḥ sr̥jantyā rayāt*). "By day" (*divā*) means during the daytime; "it is not good that you sleep by day. "At night" (*rātrau*) means at night; "with tears shed, distressed by the sound of clouds sluggish with heavy rain at night. "In the evening" (*sāyam*) means at the onset of night; "the evening bath was performed, and the body was anointed with sandalwood paste. "For a long time" (*ciram*) means for a great duration; "who was long accustomed to touches cool as nectar according to his own will. "Slightly" (*manāk*) is used in the sense of "a little."

"By the slightly wafting fragrance, he was drawn away from the ghee-rich food. *Īṣat* means "slightly" (*alpe*). "The pair of breasts of that deer-eyed woman was slightly spread apart. *Joṣam* means both "happiness" (*sukhe*) and "silence" (*maune*). Regarding happiness: "The one who has conquered his senses remains in joy (*joṣam āste*). Regarding silence: "He remained in silence, in silence, indeed in silence (*joṣaṃ joṣaṃ joṣam evāvatasthe*). *Tūṣṇīm* means silence (*maune*). "He became silent, not causing harm to others (*babhūva tūṣṇīm ahita-apakārakaḥ*). *Bahiḥ* and *avas* mean "outside" (*bāhye*). "Outside the city, there was one possessing the prowess of Indra (*bahiḥ puras abhūt puruhūta-pauruṣaḥ*)."

*Samayā* means near or in the middle; *nikaṣā* means in the vicinity—as in, "Having bypassed Laṅkā, he will slay [the enemy] *nikaṣā*. *Svayam* means by oneself—as in, "These, having been abandoned of their own accord (*svayam*), bestow infinite bliss of tranquility. *Vṛthā* means in vain—as in, "To joke in vain is audacity. *Naktam* means at night—as in: "At night, this mountain is remembered for the clamor of crows gathering with the brilliance of its jewel-like rays, and for its cave-dwellings being inhabited by terrified owls."

*Nañ* signifies negation. "The wise do not value even nectar (*sudhā*) in that way. *Hetau* means for the sake of a cause or motive. *Iddha* denotes brilliance or manifestation. *Addhā* signifies clarity and certainty; some say it denotes reality and excellence. Amara states: "In the sense of reality, *addhā* and *añjasā* [are used] for both. Example: "Behold here his cutting off of hands, which is truly (*addhā*) inspiring faith (*śraddhākara*). *Sāmi* signifies proximity and what is loathed. Example: "Previously, the Mandākinī was partially (*sāmi*) joined and then released by the son of Gādhi."

According to the *Kāśikā*, the twenty-two words beginning with *hyas* and ending with *sāmi* have the udātta accent on the final syllable; however, according to the *Kaustubha*, forms such as *vṛthā sṛjat pathibhiḥ* and *naktaṃ dadṛśre kuhacid dive yuḥ* are used with the udātta accent on the first syllable.

The suffix *vat* [is mentioned here]. A word ending in the suffix *vat* is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). The inclusion of *vat* refers to that which is prescribed in the sense of equality (*tulyārtha*) and in the sense of similarity (*ivārtha*), because there is no distinction made; it does not, however, refer to that which is prescribed by the rule "after a preposition, in the Veda, in the sense of the verbal root" (*upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe*), because that has a substantive meaning (*sattvārthaka*). For example: *yad udvato nivataḥ*, meaning "from those that have gone up and those that have gone down. *Sanā*, *sanat*, and *sanāt*—these denote eternity. Examples include *sanātanaḥ* (eternal) and *sanatkumāraḥ* (Sanatkumāra).

For this very reason, the venerable Nārāyaṇasarvajña, in his commentary on the Sanatsujātīya, states: "The word *sanat* has the sense of 'eternal,' as such is seen in Vedic usage in the phrase *sanadvāja-sanam*; [the name] *Sujāta* (Well-born) is due to his body having manifested through his own dharma. This refers to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Nārada approached Sanatkumāra, saying, 'Teach me, O Blessed One!'"

In the mantra, "imā gira ādityebhyo ghṛtasnūḥ sanādrājabhyo juhvā juhomi," the author of the *Nirukta* has also stated that the word *cira* (long) is the meaning of *ciram*, as in "I offer for a long time with the ladle (*juhvā*) and for a long time to the kings. The term *tiras* is used in the sense of disappearance (*antarddhi*) and in the sense of across or obliquely (*tiryag*). Regarding disappearance: "whose bodily lines were eclipsed by the spreading of her loveliness"; and in such passages as "he was surpassed by his [rival] who outshone people," it is used figuratively (*upacārāt*) in the sense of being overcome. According to the *Kāśikā*, these words are udātta on the first syllable.

In the *Kaustubha*, it is stated that the two words *sanāti* and *araḥ* are seen in the Veda with the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable (*antodātta*). The words *antarā* and *antareṇa* signify "in the middle" (*madhye*) and "without" (*vinā*), respectively, and they have the acute accent on the final syllable. Regarding the sense of "in the middle": — "The son of Gadhi [Viśvāmitra] was situated between heaven and the earth" (*dyāmantarā vasumatīmapi gādhijanmā*). — "The Lord stood between the two waving chowries, which were as pure as lotus fibers" (*mṛṇālasūtrāmalamantareṇa sthitaścalaccāmarayordvayasaḥ*). Regarding the sense of "without": — "O lotus-eyed one, without you... (*tvāmantarā tāmarasāyatākṣi*). — "O crow, plunge yourself into the sound that pierces the ear without [any other cause]" (*karṇāruntudamantareṇa raṇitaṃ gāhasva kāka svayam*).

The particle *jyok* is used in the sense of a long duration of time (*kāla-bhūyastva*) in its first occurrence, and in the senses of "quickly" (*śīghra*) and "presently" (*saṃprati*). As stated in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "He attains a full lifespan, he lives *jyok*, he becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. The particle *kam* is used in the senses of water (*vāri*), head (*mūrdhan*), censure (*nindā*), and happiness (*sukha*). In order, examples are as follows: *kañjam* (a lotus); *kañjāḥ* (hair); *kandarpaḥ* (the god of love); *kaṃyuḥ*. The suffix *yu* is added in the sense of possession according to the rule "after *kam* and *śam*, the suffix *yu* [is added]. *Śam* signifies happiness; thus, *śaṃyuḥ*. The particle *sahasā* is used in the senses of "suddenly" (*ākasmika*) and "without reflection" (*avimarśa*).

"The fire in the inner apartments suddenly rose up like women distressed by a conflagration"; "she was suddenly burnt by the cruel one because of his ferocity. *Svadhā* is used for offerings to the ancestors; "that which was made as *svadhā* for the ancestors by their sons. *Alam* is used for ornamentation, sufficiency, capability, warding off, and prohibition; "having adorned [himself], he mounted the swift horse."

"While they were reciting, she heard Nala and became so thrilled that her hair stood on end. "To explain [the meaning] after having studied the texts—this is sufficient even for those of dull intellect. "By this much alone is it sufficient for men to destroy their sins. "Do not delay; for the time is indeed pressing. *Vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *śrauṣaṭ*—these are used in the offering of oblations. "In the Vaitāna sacrifices, at the fires born of wood, they utter *vaṣaṭ* over the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)."

"The two breasts from which the gods subsist are the *svāhākāra* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. *Vinā* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). For example: "This form of yours is without her. *Nānā* has the senses of "many" and "without. For example: "the charming fickleness of Śrī wandering through various places"; "fruitless is the worldly journey without a woman"; and in the phrase "here there is nothing diverse (*nānā*) whatsoever," the word *nānā* has the meaning of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), as it is synonymous with the negative particle *nañ*.

Regarding the word *nānā*: because it is derived from the negative particle *na* with the addition of the suffix *nāñ* (by the rule *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau nasaha*), and because that suffix is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*), the followers of the Upaniṣads maintain that since it refers to the substratum (*dharmiparatayā*), the meaning is "there is no difference. *Svasti* is used for auspiciousness, as in: "May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being (*svasti na indro vṛddhaśravāḥ*"). *Anyat* is used in the sense of "other," as in: "Devadatta has arrived, and Yajñadatta is another (*anyat*). *Asti* denotes existence, as in: "There is love for you, there is curiosity (*asti vāmyabharamasti kautukam*"). *Upāṃśu* refers to both silent, unmanifest utterance and a secret.

"The Ṛgveda is recited loudly, the Yajurveda in a low voice, and the Sāmaveda in a whisper"—such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). *Kṣamā* is used in the sense of patience, as in "May your lordship be patient. *Vihāyas* is used in the sense of the sky, as in "The beautiful [city] shines from here by way of the sky. *Doṣā* is used for night, as in "Even at night, this one is surely the sun, it is said. *Mṛṣā* and *mithyā* both mean falsehood; as in "Is the moonlight or nectar false? and "O messenger who speaks falsely, you who do not perceive the arrival of suffering for your kinsmen. *Mudhā* means in vain.

"For fools indeed serve [the wicked], while the wise, alas, serve from womb to womb. The *gaṇasūtras*—"after *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun*," "those ending in *kun*, *makāra*, and diphthongs," and "also the *avyayībhāva* compound"—have the same meaning as the three *sūtras* found in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. Their meaning will be explained in that very place. The word *purā* may denote a continuous sequence, the distant past, or the near future.

Thus says Amara: "upādhyāyena purā'dhīyate" (the teacher studied previously). This means he studied incessantly. In phrases such as "smareṇa mukteṣu purā purārau" (formerly released by Smara upon the Enemy of Pura), it has the sense of past time. "purā vikurute māyām" (he will soon transform his illusion); this means he will transform it immediately thereafter. *Mithas* and *mithaḥ* signify secrecy and companionship. "kathāprabandheṣu mithaḥ sakhīmukhāt" (in the compositions of stories, [heard] secretly from the mouth of a friend). The sense of companionship (*sahārtha*) implies mutualness (*anyo'nyārtha*). Amara states: "mitho'nyo'nyaṃ rahasyapi" (mutual, each other, and also in secret). *Prāyas* signifies abundance; that is, an abundance of concomitance characterized by occasional deviation.

"Lions and kings generally languish in misery. The word *muhuḥ* signifies "again" (*punararthe*). As in: "by repeatedly fanning with fans and by the application of abundant sandalwood [paste]. *Prāhuḥkam* means "simultaneously" (*samakāle*) and "upwards" (*ūrdhvārthe*). Some say it means *pravāhikā*. *Āryahalam* means "by force" (*balātkāre*). Śākaṭāyana states: "*Ārya* is used in the sense of restraint (*pratibandhe*), while *halam* is used in the senses of prohibition and dispute (*pratiṣedha-vivādayoḥ*). *Abhīkṣṇam* signifies "repetition" (*paunaḥpunye*). As in: "even though [it was] hot, for him who was already hot, [it was applied] repeatedly. *Sākam* and *sārddham* both signify "together" (*sahārthe*).
"It was raised together with the horripilation of Sauśika, and lowered along with the faces [of the kings].
"It was struck together with the doubting minds of the kings and Janaka.
*Namaḥ* means "in bowing," as in "Salutation to you, O Rudra, for your wrath. *Hiruk* means "in exclusion."
"That which resembles the moon is far removed from it. The word *dhik* is used for censure and reproach: "Fie upon this wretched display! That this moon, though risen, has been swallowed by darkness!

"Fie upon that Brahminhood, and fie upon the lineage of Aṅgiras, even though it is dear [to me]! The suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with *edhāc*, as well as *śas*, *tas*, *kṛtvasuc*, *suc*, *āsthālau*, and those used in the sense of *cvy-artha*, are the rules of the *gaṇa-sūtra*.

This is the meaning: words ending in those secondary suffixes (taddhita) prescribed by the sūtras beginning with "pañcamyāstasil" and ending with "edhācca" should be understood as belonging to the *svarādi* group. The suffix *śas* is prescribed [after words] expressing "much" or "little" (*bahvalpārthāt*). The suffix *tasi* occurs in connection with *prati*. The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is prescribed after a numeral when counting the repetition of an action (*saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc*). The suffix *suc* occurs after the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*. The suffix *āsi* is prescribed by the *uṇādi* sūtra "iṇa āsiḥ"; its form is *ayā*.

The suffix *thāl* is prescribed by the rule *pratnapūrvaviśvemātthāl chandasi*. An example is: *taṃ pratnathā pūrvathā viśvathemathā*. Those ending in *cvī*, *sāti*, *trā*, and *ḍāc*—as in the rules *sampadyakartari cvī*, *vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye*, *deye trā ca*, and *anidau ḍāc*—are also to be understood as included. The suffix *ām* is prescribed by the rule *amu ca chandasi*. *Ām* is used in the sense of assent (*aṅgīkāre*). Example:

*āṃ jānīmo gamanasamaye hanta kāntārasīmāny ekākinyāḥ kuvalayadṛśo luṇṭhitā locanaśrīḥ*. (Yes, we know that at the time of her departure, alas, the beauty of the eyes of that lotus-eyed woman was plundered on the borders of the forest while she was alone.)

Others maintain that [the suffix] *ām* is also prescribed by the rules "kimettiṅavyayādām" (Pāṇini 5.4.11) and "kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi" (Pāṇini 3.1.35). *Pratām* is used in the sense of exhaustion (*glāni*). *Praśān* is used in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), as in: *praśān devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta is like Yajñadatta"). *Pratān* is used in the sense of expansion (*vistāra*). *Mā* is used in prohibition (*niṣedha*), as in: *mā jānīta vidarbhajām aviduṣīm kīrtir mudaḥ śreyasī* ("Do not consider the daughter of Vidarbha to be ignorant; fame is better than joy"). *Māṅ* is used in prohibition and apprehension (*niṣedhāśaṅkayoḥ*), as in: *mā te malīmasavikāraghanā matir bhūt* ("Let your mind not become thick with dark transformations"). Because it is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, other words beginning with vowels are also included. *Kāmam* is used in the sense of willfulness (*svācchandya*) and lack of insistence (*anāsthā*).
"Granted, let them be; I am Rāma, firm, hard-hearted, and all-enduring.

*Prakāmāḥ* means "excessively"; *nikāmam* signifies intensity, as in: "The slender-limbed woman was exceedingly beautiful like the core of a fresh plantain tree. *Bhūyaḥ* has the sense of "again," as in: "Once more, indeed, the pride [born] of the similarity to her lower lip. *Sāmpratam* means "properly" or "rightly."

Regarding the phrase *rāmāllabdhasamastahetiguruṇo vīryasya yatsāmpratam*: the word *param* is used here in the sense of *kiṃtu* (but/however), as in the expression *vaktuṃ viśeṣaḥ paramasti viśeṣaḥ*. The word *sākṣāt* means "before the eyes" (*pratyakṣe*), as in *tadeva sākṣādamṛtāṃśumānanam*; it refers to being devoid of any intervening obstruction (*vyavadhānarahitatve’pi*), such as in the term *sākṣātkāraṇam*. The word *sāci* means "obliquely" (*tiryagarthe*), as in *kākuvyākulavāci sācihasitasphūrjatkapolaśriyā*.

*Satyam* is used in the sense of partial acceptance (*ardhāṅgīkāre*), as in: "It is true that women are enchanting; it is true that riches are delightful. *Maṅkṣu* and *āśu* both denote swiftness (*śaighrye*). *Saṃvat* denotes a year (*varṣe*). *Avaśyam* denotes certainty (*niścaye*), as in: "Objects of the senses must inevitably depart, even after having been enjoyed for a very long time. *Sapadi* denotes swiftness (*śaighrye*), as in: "May they bring you to my presence immediately.
*Balavat* denotes intensity (*atiśaye*), as in: "It seems to me as if my heart is being forcibly drawn toward that which is fleeing away. *Prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* denote manifestation (*prākāśye*).
"From the manifestation of his form, this was inferred regarding his previous birth:
'Like cātaka birds, they resort to those whose faces are bright with manifest affection.'"

*Aniśam*, *nityadā*, *sadā*, *ajasram*, and *satatam*—these [words] signify continuity (*sātatye*). For example: "The water of the great ocean is always salty" (*lavaṇamambu sadaiva mahodadheḥ*); "with one who has constantly approached his presence" (*ajasramabhyāśamupeyuṣā samam*). *Uṣā* means at night. *Rodasī* refers to heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). *Oṃ* signifies both the Absolute (*brahman*) and assent. For example: "Oṃ! Salutation to all beings" (*oṃ namaḥ sarvabhūtāni*); and "Then, having uttered the word 'Oṃ' by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, [the arrow entered] the sky" (*oṃmityuktavato'tha śārṅgiṇa iti vyāhṛtya vācaṃ nabhaḥ*). *Bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ* refer to the worlds of the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven, respectively.

"To behold that abode of yours after so long—the triad of the worlds *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*—these two arms of mine, wearying greatly, long for that medicine which heals the wound in the vitals of the heart. *Jhaṭiti*, *jhagiti*, and *tarasā* signify speed; for example: "Who is this seen so suddenly (*jhaṭiti*) that he acts as a nectar-ointment for the eyes? "I quickly (*jhagiti*) offer a rosary of black beads to the Lord Bhairava. *Srāk*, *jhaṭiti*, *añjasā*, *ahnāya*, *drāk*, *maṅkṣu*, *sapadi*, and *drute* all mean "instantly" or "swiftly."

Thus says Amara: "suṣṭhu" is used in the sense of praise; as in, "those who exist in your heart are truly (suṣṭhu) worthy of connection. "ku" is used in the senses of contempt and slight; as in, "Fie (dhik) upon the poetry of that dull-witted bad poet (kukavi)," or "Immediately by the stroke of this dagger, his head was severed with a 'ṭhaṇ' sound and rolled away. "Añjasā" is used in the senses of reality and speed. "a" is used in the sense of negation. "Mithunam" means "two."

*Mithunam* means a pair. *Viṣvak* means on all sides; as in: "The appearance of a vast mass of smoke, spread and whirled about on every side by the force of the wind. *Bhājak* denotes speed; as in: "He cooks quickly. *Anvak* denotes conformity; as in: "Following after.
Words such as *cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, and *cirasyāt* express the sense of "long ago" or "for a long time";
the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to *ciraṃ*, *cireṇa*, *cirāt*, and so forth.
"For a long time, O destroyer of nights, you have been observing the circle of heroes as a master of the science of archery.
Having heard that he had been initiated for a long period, Yudhiṣṭhira—

"Through the ripening of good conduct, a long-awaited reunion has been attained. "Obtained after a long time through many desires. "After a long duration, beautiful with its rising utterance. *Asta* means destruction, as in "the kingdom whose lord has set" (*astamiteśvara*). *Ānuṣak* denotes succession, as in "the bard said he entered in succession" (*ānuṣak praviśati*). Some say this [word] ends in *d*. Śākaṭāyana says it begins with a short vowel and is used in inference. *Amnaḥ* means "quickly" or "immediately," as in "just now" (*amnareva*). *Sthāne* means "properly" or "fittingly."

"For his sake, a battle between Garuḍa and the Lord of the Immortals (Indra) occurred; this was appropriate, as their status was equal. The word *varam* is used in the sense of slight superiority: "Even being subject to reproach is better than the folded hands of servitude. The word *duṣṭa* is used in the sense of something extracted or set apart. The word *balāt* is used in the sense of force: "It spreads forth by force, having broken through. The particle *śu* is used in the sense of worship or praise: "Śunāsīra," "May the Śutudrī and Paruṣṇī attend our hymn of praise.
Words such as *arvāk* (hitherward), *sudi* (the bright fortnight), and *vadi* (the dark fortnight) are to be understood according to their usage.
A secondary derivative (*taddhita*) that does not take all case-endings [is indeclinable]. 37.

Since three numbers (vacana) do not arise [from it], but rather only the singular number, that word ending in a *taddhita* suffix shall be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). In this regard: *tatra*, *tataḥ*. Why specify "ending in a *taddhita* suffix"? [Consider: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*. Because these have a fixed number, the three numbers do not arise from them. Why specify "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*)? [Consider: *aupagavaḥ*. Here, if for the production of a certain *taddhita* suffix the entire set of case-endings (*sarvavibhakti*) is not the cause, but rather its production occurs only by taking a specific case-ending into account, that [suffix] receives the designation of an indeclinable.

For instance, according to the rule *sarva-eka-anya-kim-yad-tado dā* [Pāṇini 5.3.15], which states that the suffix *dā* arises only when the locative case (*saptamī*) is the cause of its production, there would be an under-extension (*avyāpti*); the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) would not apply to words such as *vinā* and *nānā*, because no case-ending whatsoever is required for their production. Furthermore, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *dākṣi*, since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is relied upon as the cause by the rule *tasyāpatyam* [Pāṇini 4.1.92]. Likewise, the status of *avyaya* would not apply to suffixes such as *tral*.

Nor should it be said that for those [suffixes], only a single case-ending—namely the fifth (ablative) for *tasil* and the seventh (locative) for *tral*—is the cause [for their application]. For they are prescribed even after other case-endings by the rule "they are seen after others as well" (*itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante*). If, on the other hand, an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is defined as a word whose case-endings are not heard, then there is no over-extension to words like *dadhi* or *madhu*, because other case-endings are indeed heard there. But in that case, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): the loss of the case-ending occurs because of its being an indeclinable, and its being an indeclinable occurs when that [loss of the case-ending] has taken place.

If, however, it is argued that "indeclinability" (*avyayatva*) consists in being devoid of gender and number, and that there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) here—because the non-connection with gender and number depends on the inherent nature of the word (*śabdasvābhāvyādhīnatva*) and is not something established by rule (*avācanikatva*)—then this is indeed correct; such is the view of the Bhāṣya. The Vārttikakāra, however, states: "It is established by recitation (*pāṭha*): *tasil* and so forth [up to] *pāśap*; *śas* and so forth up to the end of the *samāsānta* suffixes; the *m*-ending [suffixes] having the sense of 'times' (*kṛtvas-artha*); *tas* and *vat*; and *nānā* and *añ*."

Furthermore, there is no exclusion of the suffix *thāl* prescribed by the rule beginning with "pratnapūrva," because that rule prescribes *thāl* specifically in the sense of expressing a manner (*prakāra*). Others maintain that it is included by virtue of its recitation in the list beginning with *svar*. Regarding the term "ending in *m*": this means *am* and *ām*. By the word *tasi*, both suffixes prescribed by the rules "pañcamyāstasi" (P. 5.4.44), "tenaikadik" (P. 4.3.112), and "tasiśca" (P. 4.3.113) are understood. "The sense of *kṛtvas*" refers to the suffixes *kṛtvasuc* and *suc*.

This might be argued: since the rules for *kārakas* (grammatical relations) and the rules for *vacanas* (numbers) form a single syntactic unit with the rules for *svādi* suffixes, it is difficult to establish the application of *svādi* suffixes to indeclinables (*avyaya*) at all. This is because, in the absence of [grammatical relations such as] objecthood (*karmatva*) or singularity (*ekatva*), the specific rules prescribing those respective case-endings do not apply to indeclinables. True—

Four positions regarding this matter are observed in the treatises. The first is that from indeclinables (*avyaya*), all seven case-endings (*vibhakti*) occur in all three numbers (*vacana*). The second is that from them, only the singular occurs for all seven cases. The third is that only the nominative occurs in all three numbers. The fourth is that only the singular occurs. Among these, the first three are merely supplementary views; the last, however, is the actual truth.

And as for these [rules], they are either a restriction on meaning (*arthaniyama*), such as: "if the object is expressed, the second case alone [is used]"; "if [the number] one is expressed, the singular alone [is used]," and so forth; or they are a restriction on grammatical suffixes (*vibhaktiniyama*) relative to the intended meaning, such as: "the second case is used only for the object," and so forth. Regarding this, there is a well-known rule: "The meanings of *sup* suffixes are the object and so forth, as well as number; likewise for *tiṅ* suffixes.
In that regard, there is a restriction [of meaning], or a restriction among those [meanings] already under discussion."

Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya. Here, the first restriction is stated by the third quarter [of the verse], and the second restriction is stated by the final quarter. Then, because of the rule for elision—"avyayād āpsupaḥ"—which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the suffix *sum* alone is established without distinction.

However, if the rule *dvibahordvivacanabahuvacane* ("the dual and plural endings occur for two and many") were formulated, and instead of *ekasmin* ("in one"), the rule *ekavacanam* ("the singular ending occurs") were stated as a separate rule, then it would follow that the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs only with respect to the object (*karman*) and not with respect to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so on; likewise, the dual and plural endings would occur only for duality and plurality and not for singularity. Such a restriction would be relative to its own kind (*sajātīyāpekṣa*). In that case, all case-endings would apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*), because there is no other meaning [for them] to exclude from the stated restriction.

Because there is no obstacle to the production of those respective case endings, the rule *tatraikavacanam* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), meaning that when both the singular and the dual (and so forth) would otherwise apply, only the singular occurs.

Alternatively—by relying on the general restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "the second case suffix occurs only when there is an object" (*karmaṇy eva dvitīyā*), such that the second case suffix would not apply in the absence of objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth, the sūtra "ekavacanam" [Pāṇini 1.4.22] serves solely as an injunction (*vidhi*). And since this sūtra forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the sūtra for feminine suffixes in *-ī* and *-ā* (*ṅyāp-sūtra*), the singular number is already established for the feminine suffixes *-ī* and *-ā* in the sense of object and so forth; thus, by the force of the sūtra, its establishment occurs only from indeclinables (*avyaya*). Furthermore, its status as a single syntactic unit with the *ṅyāp-sūtra* is intended to prevent its production after verbal endings (*tiṅanta*).
Its reading in another location [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī] constitutes the second alternative (*pakṣa*).

Now, the second [alternative] is that the restriction of suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*) is general, beginning with the rule "only in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇy eva*), etc. And since the restriction "the first case-suffix (*prathamā*) is used only in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)" prohibits it only in cases where there is an addition of the object and so forth, the first case-suffix alone occurs after indeclinables (*avyaya*). As for the rule "in the singular and dual" (*dvyekayoḥ*), however, it remains exactly as stated. This is the third alternative: the restriction of suffixes is relative to its own class (*sajātīyāpekṣa*), meaning that the singular number is used only when there is singularity, and not in the case of duality and so forth; this applies because indeclinables lack number.

Because, although the three numbers of the nominative case arise for those [words], there is no contradiction with the restrictive rule (*niyama*), since that [nominative] does not arise when the number differs from the respective inherent number of its own referent.

However, if—according to the second position—there is the application of the singular number for all case-endings, and the nominative singular alone is applied because it is the first to present itself due to the desire to express singularity (*ekatva-vivakṣā*), then that is the fourth [position].

However, in the first three positions, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *pacatirūpam*; for in that instance, only the nominative singular is intended, due to the requirement of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words like *devadatta* ending in the nominative case. Furthermore, according to that logic, other case-endings would also follow; moreover, in cases such as *pacatirūpam* and *pacantirūpam*, there is no purpose for the production of dual endings and so forth, since the cognition of duality and the rest is already present through the verb (*ākhyāta*) itself. Therefore, the final position alone is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [Pāṇini 1.1.39] *kṛnmejantaḥ*.

A *kṛt*-derived suffix that ends in *m* or *e* shall be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). [Examples: *svāduṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it sweet); *vakṣe rāyaḥ* (may he speak wealth). [The rule] "after the root *svādū*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied" [is used]. By the rule "after the root *vac*, the suffix *se* is applied in the sense of *lum*," the suffix *se* is added to the root *vac*.
