In this context, if the term *kṛt* is qualified by that which ends in *mej* (*mejanta*), then it is the aforementioned position (the first alternative). However, if one applies the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) to *kṛt* and then qualifies "that which ends in a *kṛt*" (*kṛdanta*) by that which ends in *mej*, then the position is as follows: "That which ends in a *kṛt* suffix and ends in *mej* shall be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Even though there is no explicit mention of extension (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix is mentioned in a rule for assigning a technical designation (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), such an extension occurs here either because of the statement, "The purpose [of mentioning a suffix] lies in the designations of pronouns and indeclinables," or by virtue of the etymological force of the designation itself.

Since it is impossible for a mere suffix (*pratyaya*) that is unfit for usage to undergo various operations such as having diverse forms like the plural number, and since its prohibition [as a *kṛt*] would be illogical, [the objection is raised]: "In the first alternative, the designation *kṛt* would not apply to the form ending in *ām*, as in *kārayāñcakāra*; for although it might have the *kṛt* designation by the rule *kṛdatiṅ*, it lacks the final *m*, and the suffix *ām* itself lacks the *kṛt* designation. True. However, the form is established by the inclusion of "ām" among the items in the *svarādi* list.

Now, if in that context the term *ām* refers specifically to the *taddhita* suffix *ām*, then even when the case endings (*svādi*) are produced after a *kṛt* suffix, the elision (*luk*) is established by the rule "āmaḥ. Nor is there any carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *leḥ* (from the previous rule) in that instance, because it would serve no purpose. Furthermore, there is no undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of elision occurring for suffixes such as *tarap* and so on.

Because the meaning [of the suffix] is incomplete—due to its nature as having an expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) regarding objects such as number and grammatical relations (kāraka)—suffixes like *tarap* do not arise [from the base alone]. Therefore, since an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*) is necessary for that purpose, the excellence inherent in the meaning of the suffix *ām* is perceived precisely through the *tarap* and other suffixes produced after the auxiliary verb being employed. For this very reason, it will be stated under the rule "kṛñ cānuprayujyate" that [the mention of the verb root] is intended to exclude those that are separated [by an intervention].

Alternatively, according to the established doctrine (siddhānta) stated in the preceding sūtra, Dīkṣita maintains that only the case-ending *su* arises, and then there is the elision of that [case-ending] by the rule *hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*.

Now, if it is argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *pratāmau* and *pratāmaḥ* because, by the rule for the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), they end in a *kṛt*-suffix, and yet they also end in *m* by their own form, we say: no. For, by the inclusion of the word *praśām* among the *svarādi* (indeclinables), it is indicated (*jñāpita*) that the designation of indeclinable does not apply here, as one cannot rely on the status of being a *kṛdanta* derived through the characteristics of suffixes. Nor should it be said that this [form] ends in *m* once the substitution of *n* for *m* has occurred according to the rule "the *m* of a root is replaced by *n*" (*mo no dhātoḥ*), because that substitution of *n* (*natva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

It should not be argued that the designation *saṃjñā* would likewise not apply to the form ending in *ām*, such as *kārayāñcakāra*, because it would be a *kṛdanta* by virtue of the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). For the restriction [of the rule] applies only to the verbal root (*dhātu*) by depending on its own class (*sajātīya*), whereas there is no obstacle to the form ending in *ām* being considered a *kṛdanta* through the rule regarding suffixes.

Nor should it be argued that the word *praśān* is included in the list of words beginning with vowels (svarādi) as a form derived from the root *śāna* (meaning "to sharpen") belonging to the *curādi* class—since there is no rule restricting it to the *saṇ* suffix (*sannanta*)—and thus how could it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because, based on the authority of the Bhāṣya which presents this very point as an indicator, it is determined that the *kvip* suffix does not apply to it due to lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). Furthermore, one should not argue that words such as *gauḥ*, *glauḥ*, and *nauḥ* would also acquire the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*), for the *uṇādi* suffixes are considered non-etymological (*avyutpanna*).

Even under the view that [the term] is derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), the *uṇādi* sūtra "cviravyayam" restricts the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) status only to those forms ending in the suffix *cvi* which end in the suffix *ḍoḍau*. If it is objected that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of indeclinability for forms such as *ādhaye*, *cikīrṣave*, and *cikīrṣoḥ*, the Vārttika provides the solution: "It should be stated that [the suffix *cvi*] has *i* and *u* as its original base (*prakṛti*). In the aforementioned cases, however, there is no fault because they have *i* and *u* as their original bases. If, even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *kumbhakārebhyaḥ* and *nagarakārebhyaḥ*, then it must be stated that [the suffix *cvi*] has no other original base (*ananyaprakṛti*). By this, forms that are merely substitutes (*ādeśa*) are excluded.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: "A rule conditioned by a specific grammatical combination (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) is not the cause for the destruction of that very combination. Because this *paribhāṣā* is necessary, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. This is because the status of ending in *ej* (e, o, au), which is produced by the combination with a *sup* suffix, cannot be the cause for the application of the technical term *avyaya*, which destroys that very combination. For if that term were applied, the elision of the *sup* suffix would result, thereby destroying the condition of ending in *ej*.

The meaning is this: a rule (*vidhi*) whose occasion (*nimitta*) is a "conjunction" (*sannipāta*), that is, a relationship (*saṃbandha*), does not become the occasion for an operation (*kārya*) that destroys it—that is, an operation which destroys the relationship that constitutes its own occasion.

This is established by logic (*nyāya*): for that which depends [on another] (*upajīvaka*) operates only in a manner that does not contradict that upon which it depends (*upajīvya*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, fire and the like would not possess the power to destroy grass and such; for the aforementioned principle is a matter of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), whereas in other cases, things are established exactly according to the available evidence (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, if experience (*anubhava*) were the cause of memory (*smṛti*), the status of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as its cause would not be established.

Because experience lacks the state of being an immediately preceding antecedent to its own result (recollection), its causality toward recollection cannot be established; therefore, for the sake of establishing that [causality], one must postulate a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), since the causality of experience depends upon that [impression]. For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* is set aside with respect to the short vowel portion by the rule *kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*. However, as for rules such as *kṛnmejantaḥ*, because they find scope in cases where the suffix naturally ends in *ej*, they do not have the power to set aside the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* in the case under discussion.

This, however, must be noted: where the property that serves as the delimiting condition (*upajīvyatāvacchedaka-dharma*) does not change even when there is a transformation into another form, the aforementioned rule (*nyāya*) does not apply. For example, in the case of *kariṣyasi*, the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix characterized by having a *val* sound (i.e., *s*) is the basis (*upajīvya*) for the augment *iṭ*; therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* following the root vowel *i* indeed occurs. Even when the *ṣ*-substitution has been effected, the character of having a *val* sound remains unimpaired. The same applies in cases such as *sarveṣām*.

Even though the letter *s* serves as the cause for the change of *e*, once the substitution of *ṣ* has been applied because it follows the letter *e*, the status of being preceded by a *jhal* sound remains unaltered. As for the common assertion that the rule "hali sarveṣām" (Pāṇini 8.3.22) indicates that the principle of *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-destruction of a cause-effect relationship) does not apply here, this should be understood as a concession made for the sake of argument. This is because the proposed solution—based on assuming the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the rule by postulating that "there is no destruction even of that specific individual instance in which the causality of a particular form is ultimately established"—contradicts the context of the discussion.

In this context, other purposes of this [rule] are also presented as a digression. In the word *amunā*, although there is the status of ending in the vowel *a* due to the substitution of *mu* for *na*, the long vowel in the case ending *supi* (as prescribed by *supi ca*) does not occur, because the rule depends upon the presence of the *nā*-substitution which serves as the cause for the designation *ghi*. This is because otherwise, the designation *ghi* would be subverted. As for the interpretation that in the rule *na mu ne*, the substitution of *mu* is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) both when the *nā*-substitution is about to be applied and when it has already been applied, that is merely a theoretical possibility; for the matter is well-established by the method already stated.

When the substitution of *au* for the genitive singular ending (*ṅi*) occurs after words such as *śakaṭi-paddhati*, and by virtue of that same rule (*tatsanniyogena*) the substitution of *a* for the vowel *i* is performed, the suffix *ṭāp*—which would otherwise apply because the stem ends in *a*—does not take place. This is because the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) between the two operations would be disrupted. If it is argued: "Even though the substitution of *au* is conditioned by immediate sequence, there is no evidence that the same applies to the substitution of *a* prescribed in conjunction with it," this is true. However, precisely because of this lack of satisfaction, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated in the seventh book: "The substitution of *au* should be marked with the *ḍit* designation. Thus, there is no fault;
for by virtue of being *ḍit*, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final syllable) occurs, and since the stem then ends in a consonant (*hal*), the suffix *ṭāp* does not even arise.

Thus, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ijādeśca gurumataḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.36), having raised the objection that *ām* would apply even in forms such as *iyeṣa*, the Vārttika *upadeśavacanāt siddham* is refuted by stating that the *guṇa* produced by the presence of the *liṭ* suffix cannot be the cause for the *ām* which destroys that very presence of the *liṭ*. This is because [if it were], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* by the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81).

Thus, regarding the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), in the view that does not accept the analysis as a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*), consider the word *māthitikaḥ*, derived from the sense "this has *mathitam* as its merchandise" (*tadasya paṇyam*). When the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *tadasya paṇyam*, the substitution of *ik* for *ṭhak* occurs, followed by the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. In this case, because the stem ends in *t* (i.e., it is *tānta*), the substitution of *ka* for *ṭhak* does not take place. For the status of being *tānta* is the cause (*nimitta*) for that [substitution of *ka*], and in that context, the suffix *ik* is present; since the elision of the vowel *a* arises when that [suffix *ik*] follows, if the substitution of *ka* were to occur, it would result in the destruction (*vighāta*) of that very cause. Other similar cases should be inferred in the same way.

In examples such as *dākṣi*, the fact that the suffix *iñ* depends upon the elision of the vowel *a* as its cause is due precisely to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the aforementioned Paribhāṣā; the proof for this has already been stated previously. Furthermore, the rule *na yāsayoḥ* is also an authority in this regard. Otherwise, since the feminine suffix *ṭāp*—which is produced by the presence of the vowel *a*—could not logically serve as a cause for the elision of *i* (which destroys that very presence), the prohibition of *i* would be redundant.

This might be the case: even in the *agni* word, if derived from the root *aj* (to drive) according to the *phiṭ-sūtra* accentuation, it would be oxytone; however, if derived from the root *añj* (to anoint), it would be oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). From that, the suffix *matup* is added. Because that [suffix] is oxytone, the rule "hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup" (Pāṇini 6.1.175)—which prescribes that the *matup* following a short vowel or the augment *nuṭ* is itself oxytone—would apply and render the *matup* oxytone. Consequently, by the rule "anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam" (Pāṇini 6.1.158), which dictates that all syllables in a word except one are unaccented (*anudātta*), the remaining portion of the base (*prakṛti*) would not be unaccented.

This is because its own final udātta accent depends upon the udātta accent of the *matup* suffix; for in the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup*, the term *antodāttāt* (from a word having an udātta on the final syllable) is understood by way of anuvṛtti from the preceding rule *antodāttād uttarapadāt*. It is replied: there is no fault here precisely because [the rule] is non-obligatory (*anitya*).

For this very reason, in the case of *paramavācā*, the udātta accent prescribed for the case-ending following a word with an udātta on the final syllable by the rule *antodāttād uttarapadād anyatarasyām anityasamāse* indeed serves as the cause for the *śeṣanighāta* (the subsequent loss of accent) of the base portion.

As for the claim that the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* does not apply in rules concerning accentuation (*svaravidhi*), that is questionable, as there is a lack of evidence. To explain: in the word *gopāyatam*, the root *gup* is acutely accented on the final syllable by its own root-accent. The suffix *āya* is acutely accented on its first syllable. Then, by the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots," it receives the designation of a root once again; thus, by virtue of being acutely accented on the final syllable, the vowel *a* of the suffix *yak* becomes acute, and not the *u* or the *ā*. This is according to the maxim: "An accent established later is stronger. Following that comes the suffix *śap*.

By the rule *anudāttau suppitau*, [the suffix] is anudātta. By the rule *ato guṇe*, there is the substitution of the single substitute (pararūpa). By the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, the vowel *a* is udātta. That substitute is anudātta by virtue of the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*. By the rule *udāttādanudāttasya*, it becomes svarita. Depending on that [svarita], the *śeṣanighāta* (the anudātta accent for the remaining syllables) would apply to the preceding [syllable]. However, it does not occur due to the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* (the metarule concerning the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship), because a svarita which depends upon an udātta cannot trigger the *nighāta* (anudātta) which destroys that very [udātta] upon which it depends.

As for what they say—that according to the *yathoddeśa* (definition-based) view, the paribhāṣā regarding the non-accentuation of the remainder (*śeṣanighāta*) does not apply within the Tripādī; therefore, when the non-accentuation of the remainder is being effected, because the circumflex (*svarita*) is [regarded as] unestablished (*asiddha*), there is no non-accentuation of the remainder, and thus the paribhāṣā concerning the destruction of a cause (*sannipātaparibhāṣā*) has no purpose there—and that there is no evidence for its application only under the *yathoddeśa* view: this is incorrect, for the addition of the *t* in the rule "tavyattavyānīyaraḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.96) serves as proof [of its application].

For instance: even if the suffix *tavya* alone were to have its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), and the remaining syllables were made grave (*anudātta*) by the rule of "grave for the rest" (*śeṣanighāta*), there would be no distinction from the circumflex (*svarita*) produced by the rule "the grave following an acute" (*udāttādanudāttasya*). Furthermore, since the maxim of "grave for the rest" (*śeṣanighātaparibhāṣā*) applies even at the time of the operation (*kāryakāla*), that circumflex—being in the same domain as the rule "the grave following an acute"—would not be considered non-existent with respect to the subsequent application of "grave for the rest. Thus, once the grave accent has been applied, the two cases would be identical in their tone; consequently, the designation of *tavya* as *ti* (for the purposes of the substitution of *liṭ* for *luṅ*, etc. would be rendered useless.

If its application were indeed according to the order of enunciation (*yathoddeśam*), then because the rule *udāttāt* (P. 8.4.66) would be non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the subsequent elision of the remaining syllables (*śeṣanighāta*) regarding the circumflex (*svarita*), the elision of the remaining syllables would not occur in the case of the suffix *tavya*. However, in the case of the suffix *tavyat*, since the rule *titsvaritam* (P. 6.1.185) belongs to the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādhyāya*), it is not non-existent with respect to that elision; thus, the elision of the remaining syllables does indeed occur. Therefore, the status of having the letter *t* as an indicatory mark (*tittva*) is indeed meaningful.

That too must be considered. Because, by the principle of *saṃnipāta* (the non-disturbance of a cause by its own effect), a *svarita* accent—which depends upon an *udātta* accent—cannot trigger the *śeṣanighāta* (the subsequent loss of accent) which would destroy that very [condition]; thus, the *śeṣanighāta* does not apply to the *tavya* suffix. However, since the rule "titsvaritam" (P. 6.1.185) lacks dependence on an *udātta*, its status as a cause for *śeṣanighāta* remains unimpeded. Consequently, because the difference in result is clear and the employment of the marker *ti* is not redundant, the proposed indicator (*jñāpaka*) is untenable. Furthermore, the establishment of the non-application of the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* to accent rules would lead to a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

By this, the role of the sūtra *yato 'nāvaḥ* as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that the paribhāṣā regarding the enclitic accentuation (*śeṣanighāta*) operates according to its *yathoddeśa* (spatial) application is established. For the meaning of that [sūtra] is: "In a word ending in the suffix *yat*, provided it is not the word *nau* and consists of two syllables, the first syllable is acute. Otherwise, since the suffix *yat* is svarita by virtue of being *tittva*, the enclitic accentuation (*śeṣanighāta*) of the preceding syllable—relying on that svarita—would occur even without the stated sūtra.

Even if the initial syllable were made udātta, once the subsequent syllables had become anudātta by the rule of *śeṣanighāta* (the enunciation of the remaining syllables as anudātta), and once the following syllable had become svarita by the rule *udāttādanudāttasya*, the preceding syllable would remain anudātta due to *śeṣanighāta*; thus, since there would be no difference [in the result], the sūtra *yato 'nāvaḥ* would be entirely useless. Furthermore, the argument that the sūtra is meaningful because the *paribhāṣā* of *śeṣanighāta* operates only *yathoddeśam* (by its original enunciation)—whereby *śeṣanighāta* does not apply to the operation *udāttādanudāttasya* because the latter is *asiddha* with respect to the former—is also refuted.

Because a *svarita* accent belonging to the third case (the *traipādika*) depends upon an *udātta*, it does not trigger the *śeṣanighāta* (the neutralization of other accents) which would subvert that *udātta*; thus, there is a difference in the resulting effect (*phalabheda*) when the rule is initiated. Furthermore, since the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "except for *āvaḥ*" is logically untenable without something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the purposefulness of the rule is established precisely for that purpose.

Therefore, since all desired results are established simply by the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, the assumption of a restrictive rule—that the *śeṣanighāta-paribhāṣā* operates only according to its formal enunciation (*yathoddeśa*)—is entirely without authority. For this very reason, even in the *Śabdakaustubha* under this very sūtra, it is stated regarding the word *agnimān* that the *śeṣanighāta* occurs precisely because the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* is non-eternal. Thus, the works such as the *Manoramā* cited above are indeed devoid of justification; this is the direction of the argument. [Pāṇini 6.1.159: *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca*. *katvātoḥ saṅkasu-naḥ* 39.

Up to this point, the term *avyaya* (indeclinable) applies. Having performed [the action], [one says] *purā sūryasyodetoḥ* ("before the rising of the sun") or *purā vatsānām apākartoḥ* ("before driving away the calves"). The meaning is "prior to sunrise" and "prior to the driving away. [The suffix] *tosun* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *iṇ*, *kṛ*, *vadi*, *car*, *hṛ*, *mi*, *jan* when there is a characteristic of an action (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*). Examples include: *purā krūrasya visṛpo virapśin* ("O mighty one, before the creeping of the cruel one") and *purā jatrubhya ātṛdaḥ* ("before piercing the collarbones"). The suffix *kasun* is used after the roots *sṛp* and *tṛd*; these two are Vedic (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, the *avyayībhāva* compound (40) shall be designated as *avyaya*. An exhaustive enumeration must be made.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of elision (*luk*) and in the cessation of the accent on the first syllable (*mukhasvara-upacāra*)," the examples are as follows: In the case of *luk*: *upāgni*, *pratyagni*. Here, by the rule "after an indeclinable, there is *luk* of the case-endings *āp* and *sup*" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*), there is *luk* of the *sup* ending. In the case of the cessation of the accent on the first syllable: *upāgnimukhaḥ*, *pratyagnimukhaḥ*. Although the rule "the first syllable of a word denoting a limb of one's own body is acute" (*mukhaṃ svāṅgam*) would have required the initial syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) to be acutely accented, this is prohibited by the rule: "there is no [acute accent] after an indeclinable, a directional word (*dik-śabda*), *go*, *mahat*, *sthūla*, *muṣṭi*, *pṛthu*, or *vatsa*" (*nāvyaya-dik-śabda-gomahat-sthūla-muṣṭi-pṛthu-vatsabhyaḥ*).

Furthermore, in the case of *upāgnimukha*—meaning "one whose face is near the fire"—the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails according to the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member retains its own accent]. And because it is a compound, that [first member] is oxytone (*antodātta*). Regarding the substitution of *visarga* for the letter *s*, the name *upacāra* was used by the ancient grammarians. To illustrate its non-application: *upapayaḥkāraḥ* (one who makes milk) and *upapayaḥkāmaḥ* (one who desires milk). Although the substitution of *s* would have applied here by the rule "after *at*, [before *kṛ*, *ka*, *mi*, etc.]," there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "not of an indeclinable. Why is there an enumeration? Consider *upagnyadhīyāna* (studying near the fire).

By virtue of the treatment as a *parāṅgavat* (as if it were part of the subsequent member), the sixth [rule], namely the acute accent on the initial syllable according to *āmantritasya ca*, applies; otherwise, because there is a prohibition against the *parāṅgavat* treatment for indeclinables (*avyaya*), that accent would not occur. In examples such as *upāgnikam*, the suffix *akac* does not apply by the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām*. In *upakumbhammanyaḥ*, the suffix *mum* applies by the rule *arurdviṣad-*. Otherwise, there would be a prohibition by the rule *anavyayasya*. In *upakumbhībhūtaḥ*, the prohibition regarding the addition of indeclinables to the rule *asya cvau* does not apply.

This should be noted: the elision (*luk*) is established precisely by the specific prohibition in the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt*. In the rule *ataḥ kṛkami*, the term *anuttarapadasthasya* ("not standing in a subsequent member") is understood by way of *anuvṛtti* (carrying over), so that the substitution of *s* does not occur. Therefore, the only purpose [of the prohibition] is the avoidance of the accent on the first syllable (*mukhasvara*).

Regarding this, some say: the accent on the first syllable is indeed desired. If this were the sole purpose, he would have stated it right there as *nāvyayād avyayībhāvācca*, according to the natural sense of the *Bhāṣya*.

Others, however, maintain that because the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) is understood according to its etymological meaning—as that which does not undergo change (*na vyeti*)—the cessation of the [Vedic] *mukha-svara* will occur automatically; thus, this rule (*sūtra*) is unnecessary in every respect. The same applies to the four rules beginning with "taddhitaśca. For, by the rule "taddhitaśca," the meaning of the rule "kṛnmejantaḥ" is subsumed—excluding the *uṇādi* suffixes up to *āsi*—by specifying that the *taddhita* suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with *edhāc* [are indeclinables], provided they do not occur at the beginning of a word (*svarādau*). 41. *śi sarvanāmasthānam*. [The suffix *śi* is called *sarvanāmasthāna*.]

The substitute *śī* for *jas* and *śas* is designated by the technical term [saṃjñā] stated [in the rule]. [Thus we get] *vārīṇi*. [The lengthening of the vowel occurs] by the rule "and in a sarvanāmasthāna [suffix], except in the vocative singular. If, however, it were stated as *śi-suṭoḥ* in the specific rules (*pradeśeṣu*) themselves, it would apply even in the neuter. Nor can the mention of *śi* be considered purposeful (i.e., sufficient), because its function is exhausted by the meaning of *śas*. Therefore, the formulation of this technical designation is necessary. Its greatness, however, stems from the tradition of the ancient masters. *Sūtra 42*: *suḍanapuṃsakasya* ("*suṭ* [is applied] to that which is not neuter").

The five case-endings beginning with *su* (the nominative singular through the locative plural) that do not belong to the neuter gender receive the aforementioned designation (*saṃjñā*). *rājā* (king), *rājānau* (two kings), *rājānaḥ* (kings); *rājānam* (the king), *rājānau* (two kings). [In the formation of the accusative plural,] there is lengthening as before. Why "not neuter"? Consider *sāmanī* (two Sāmans). Since the elision (*allop*) of the *i* is absent by the rule "optionally in the *ṅi* and *śi* cases," there is no application of the designation; thus, there is no lengthening. Why is this a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion)? It is so that the designation obtained by the previous rule may apply to the neuter, since for the neuter there is neither a positive injunction nor a prohibition [regarding this specific rule]. By this, forms such as *vanāni* (forests) are established. Nor is the rule's formulation purposeless, because it serves its function in the substitution of *śas*.

Alternatively, this is indeed a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Nor is the aforementioned fault applicable here, because the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes" does not hold in this case. Otherwise, for the sake of brevity in comprehension, he would have stated "suṭ strīpuṃsayoḥ" [Pāṇini 8.3.45]. By the statement "of that which is not neuter" (*anapuṃsakasya*), the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of certain negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) is indicated even when they lack semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). By this, forms such as *aśrāddhabhojī* ("one who does not eat at a funeral feast") are established. As for the objection regarding the heaviness [of the formulation]—namely, that it involves either an incompetent compound (*asamarthasamāsa*) or a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*)—it is not a fault, because it is "aimed at the result" (*phalamukhatvāt*). 43. *na veti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.44). "The option 'or not' (*na vā*) is called *vibhāṣā*. This is a technical term (*paribhāṣā*) for the two options: the application of a rule and its non-application. It is taught by the Vārttika: "The word *vibhāṣā* is a name for the two options: the application and the non-application of a rule. Its purpose is to avoid the repetition of the word "option" (*vibhāṣā*) in subsequent rules. For example, in the rule "the augment *ṇiṭ* is optional after roots ending in long *ṛ*" (*ṛdhaḥ ṇiṭ ca*), the word "optional" need not be repeated, as it is understood from the previous rule. Furthermore, it serves to indicate that the negation (*nañ*) in such cases is a restrictive negation (*paryudāsa*), meaning "that which is other than the neuter," rather than an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Thus, the form *anaḍvān* ("ox") is established. If it were an absolute negation, the form would be *an-aḍvān*. Moreover, it indicates that the neuter gender is excluded from the scope of the rule. Therefore, the forms *atvasantasya ca dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14) and *diva aut* (Pāṇini 7.1.84) apply only to non-neuter stems. Otherwise, the form *dyubhyām* would be incorrect. However, in the case of *nañ-samāsa*, the neuter is included, as in *an-ṛkārānta* ("not ending in ṛ"). This is because the negative particle (*nañ*) in a compound denotes exclusion (*anyapadārtha*), whereas in a sentence it denotes absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Consequently, the forms *an-ṛkāra* and *an-ṛkārānta* are both valid. Furthermore, the word *vibhāṣā* is used in the sense of "optionality" (*vikalpa*) in the sense of "being divided" (*vibhajyate*). Or, it may mean "that which is divided" (*vibhajyate*). That is, it is divided into two parts: the application and the non-application. The designation *vibhāṣā* (optionality) shall apply to both negation (*niṣedha*) and alternative (*vikalpa*), because the word *iti* is connected with both. Furthermore, that [word *iti*] effects a reversal of the referent of the word (*padārtha*). For in common usage, words such as "cow" (*go*) are directed toward the object; however, when used with the particle *iti*, as in "he says 'cow'" (*gaurityāha*), they are directed toward the word itself. In grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), however, the general rule (*utsarga*) is that a word refers to its own form (*svarūpa*), according to the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) "the word's own form [is the term]. The distinction is that by means of the particle *iti*, the word is made to refer to the object. Therefore, in this context, the object alone is both the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*).

Nor does the word *na vā* incur the status of being a technical term (*saṃjñin*) for the mere negation that constitutes the meaning of the indeclinable particle *na*; this is because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "vibhāṣā diksamāse. Otherwise, since the result would already be established by the rule "na bahuvrīhau," such an indication would be unnecessary. However, in the absence of the word *iti*, in rules such as "vibhāṣā śveḥ," the word *na vā iti* itself would have to be the substitute. Since it is the meaning that serves as the technical term, the removal of the resulting inconsistency in cases such as "anyatarasyām" can be explained according to the method that will be stated later.

For instance, its utility lies only in both instances of *vibhāṣā* (optionality) and not elsewhere. In the case of the optionality obtained by the rule "vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne," since the *ātmanepada* is invariably required by rules such as "svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale," this [rule] merely prescribes the suspension of that [mandatory application] in one alternative; thus, the phrase "it occurs optionally" (*pakṣe bhavati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Similarly, in the case of "vibhāṣorṇoḥ," because the *ṅit*-status is accepted as mandatory, the absence of that [ṅit-status] is already established in forms such as *praurṇavitā*; therefore, this rule merely prescribes the positive aspect [of the ṅit-status] in that alternative.

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ*, if it were to apply as an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both ways [positive and negative], then if it operated by way of a positive injunction (*vidhimukhena*), the option would apply only to those suffixes marked with *p* (pit), whereas for those marked with *k* (kit), the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) would occur invariably due to the rule *yajādi-tvāt*. Conversely, if it were to operate by way of a prohibition (*niṣedhamukhena*), the option would apply only to those marked with *k*, but not to those marked with *p*, because there would be no possibility of its application [to the latter] in that case. However, if it were to operate in both ways simultaneously, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by dissimilarity (*vairūpya*).

However, since the application of the prohibition "na" occurs first among the *kit* suffixes by virtue of the sequence of their mention in the *Śikṣā*, and thereafter—when all *liṭ* suffixes, whether *kit* or *akit*, have attained a uniform state—the option proceeds by way of a positive injunction (*vidhi-mukha*) alone, meaning that [the substitution] occurs optionally; thus there is no lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*). This rule functions through the single application of the grammatical operation (*lakṣaṇa*) to the class (*ākṛti*), which is the referent of the term and constitutes a collective whole.

But in the view that the individual word is the unit of meaning (*vyaktipakṣa*), since rules such as *vibhāṣā śveḥ* differ according to each specific instance (*pratilakṣyam*), their application occurs sometimes by way of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*) and sometimes by way of negation (*niṣedhamukhena*). Since there is no lack of uniformity (*vairūpyābhāva*) due to the distinction between these grammatical markers (*lakṣaṇabheda*), [the rule] need not be commenced. Thus says the Vārttika:
"Or rather, it need not be taught, because it is already known."

Regarding this, they say: even in the view that [the term] refers to the *ākṛti* (form), the rule beginning with "na vā śveḥ" should be recited only in the specific rules (*pradeśa*). Otherwise, a technical name (*saṃjñā*) initiated for one purpose might apply even in a different context, such as in the rule "vibhāṣorṇoḥ," because prohibitions are stronger [than general rules]. Consequently, in the form *praurṇuvīti*, there would first be a prohibition of the *ṅit*-characteristic, and subsequently the optionality would apply. However, in reality, the word "vibhāṣā" itself should be recited in those specific rules. Even in the view that it is a technical name, since the prohibition applies first and the optionality follows, there exists a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by repetition (*āvṛtti*).

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya has included the rules "gro yaṅi" and "aci vibhāṣā" among the *aprāptavibhāṣā* (optional rules where [the application] was not otherwise established). Against this, some object: since the discussion begins with the phrase "those involving three doubts," and since only those optional rules (*vibhāṣā*) that constitute objects of doubt—namely, whether the rule applies, does not apply, or both—are to be explained here, there is no possibility of mentioning all three alternatives in this context. To illustrate: in the form *nijegilyate*, the substitution of *l* is obligatory; there is no occasion for an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) to apply, and thus no room for an *aprāptavibhāṣā*.

Nor should it be argued that its occurrence is possible because of the rule *yaṅi* being carried over [from a previous sūtra], and because of the interpretation that the substitution of *la* for the *repha* caused by *yaṅ* occurs when a vowel (*ac*) follows. For when the form *nijegir ya ac* is established, at the time when the application of the rule *gro yaṅi* is due, there is no possibility of the optional (*vibhāṣā*) application, since the condition of being followed by a vowel (*acparatva*) is absent. Nor can it be assumed that, by the force of the introduction of the optional rule, the rule *gro yaṅi* does not apply prior to the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*). Even so, the status of being an optional rule (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣātva*) would remain difficult to establish in both cases.

In the *Vibhāṣā*, because [the rule] finds its application in cases such as *girati* and *gilati*, the rule *gro yaṅi* operates even before the elision (*luṅ*) of the *yaṅ* affix; thus, the two [operations] do not occur simultaneously. Nor should it be argued that, because the substitution of *la* for *ra* is unestablished (*asiddha*) and therefore weak, the elision (*luṅ*) must occur prior to it. This is because, with respect to the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitution of *la*, which depends on the *yaṅ* contained within the root, the elision (*luṅ*)—which depends on an external (*bahirbhūta*) affix—is unestablished. Since the former does not exist at that time, the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (what is unestablished in what precedes is treated as non-existent) does not apply.

On this point, they say: [The rule] is indeed an *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an optional rule where the operation has not otherwise been established) according to the manner already stated. However, its status as an *aprāptavibhāṣā* is as follows: by the maxim "even internal operations [are superseded]," the elision (*luk*) occurs prior to the substitution of *l* for *r*. Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *l* must occur even before the elision caused by the suffix *ac*, because the elision is *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule) due to its being external (*bahiraṅga*), since it depends upon the meaning of the agent; and furthermore, since the principle of "being non-existent in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) does not apply when the subsequent operation is absent. This is because the mention of the rule for *tuka* in the context of *kṛt* suffixes indicates that the *paribhāṣā* regarding external operations is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

Furthermore, by means of the cognition that apprehends the substratum (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), just as in the case of elision (*luk*), the superior force of compounds, suffixes, and so forth—which depend upon that [elision]—is also established.

[Objection: Even so, in the case of *nijegirya* (from *gir*), the substitution of *l* for *r* is difficult to obtain, because there is no subsequent element (*para*) that is a *yaṅ* affix, and because the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule is prohibited by the rule *na lumatā*. Nor should it be argued that the rule does not apply here because the substitution of *l* falls outside the jurisdiction of the heading on *aṅga* (the stem); for the meaning of that rule is that whatever operation would otherwise accrue to an *aṅga*, whether it actually falls within or without the jurisdiction of the *aṅga*-heading, does not take place. Therefore, how is the possibility of the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) applicable in both cases? [Reply: This is not so.

Because the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) is possible by virtue of the rule "acaḥ parasmin" (P. 1.1.57), which relies on a separate elision (*allopa*). This is because the prohibition "there is no *sthānivadbhāva* when what precedes is *asiddha*" (P. 1.1.58) is specifically barred by the statement: "That [prohibition] is an exception in the case of the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga*, and in the cases of *latva* and *ṇatva*. Nor should it be argued that even so, the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) in both instances remains untenable; for with respect to the rule "groyaṅi" (P. 6.1.43), the rule "aci vibhāṣā" (P. 6.1.44) is *asiddha*, and thus there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). This is established by the analytical division (*yogavibhāga*) of the word "na" in the rule "na mu ne" (P. 8.2.3).

Alternatively, a *yoga* (rule) is not unestablished (*asiddha*) merely because of another *yoga*; rather, this is due to the adoption of the principle that "within a context, [the subsequent rule within] that context [prevails]. However, in the view that there is elision of the entire aggregate (*samudāyalopa*), it should be understood that *latva* (the substitution of *l* for *r*) is obligatory because it is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned) with respect to the vowel (*ac*). This is merely an argument to justify the possibility of such a statement. In the final established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, *latva* is obligatory precisely because the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*).
Thus ends the sixth lesson in the first quarter of the first chapter of the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*. P. 1.1.45:
*ig yaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* ("The *ig* vowels [i, u, ṛ, ḷ] are termed *saṃprasāraṇa* when they replace *yaṇ* [y, v, r, l]").

The meaning of the sentence—"an *ig* [vowel] occurs in place of a *yaṇ*"—as well as the phoneme in the form of an *ig* which has a *yaṇ* as its substitute, both are designated by the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa*. In rules such as "the *saṃprasāraṇa* of *ṣyaṅ*," the meaning of the sentence is taken; however, in cases of restatement (*anuvāda*) such as "and after a *saṃprasāraṇa*," it is the phoneme that is taken. This distinction arises from the recurrence of the word *iti*; thus, when it recurs, the meaning of the sentence is the thing to be named (*saṃjñin*), whereas in its absence, the sentence itself is the name (*saṃjñā*). Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence that the sentence itself would become the object of prescription (*vidheya*).

In the rule *vāha ūṭh*, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is the meaning of that very [term] which is to be enjoined. Furthermore, in rules such as *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, one must assume that the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) refers to the general case. Nor should it be argued: "Let the designation apply to the sentence or its meaning within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), but how could it apply to a phoneme? For one may resort to any one of the methods of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this;
for the formulation of the sūtra, by means of the case endings that provide the enjoinable and the referent, is of such a nature. As it has been said:
The specific mention of the case-ending is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that both designations apply.
This was also stated by Hari:
"In the definition of *saṃprasāraṇa*, [the dual number] serves as the indicative mark for both the individual phoneme and the sentence."
Likewise, a detailed classification arises within a single sutra itself.

Likewise, in the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, the use of the singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*)—characterized by the methods of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, and so forth—is indeed supported in the Bhāṣya itself. *Tantra* is twofold: *śabdatantra* (phonetic extension) and *arthatantra* (semantic extension). The former applies when there is a difference in words due to a difference in meaning; the latter applies when there is identity of word.
Alternatively, the sentence-meaning itself is the technical term (*saṃjñin*), while in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the phoneme produced thereby.

Or else, as the Bhāṣya states: "The phoneme itself is the technical term; at the point of application of the rule, one must resort to a future designation, like the expression 'the cloth-thread' (*sūtra-śāṭaka*)."

Now, regarding the form *aduhitarām*: here, in place of the letter *l*, there is the first person singular ending (*iṭ*). Since this [ending] is a substitute for a semi-vowel (*yaṇ-sthānika*), it receives the designation *saṃprasāraṇa*; consequently, by the rule *halaḥ*, a long vowel is substituted [for the preceding short vowel], because the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is the *aṅga* relative to the suffix *tarap*. On this point, some say:
"By resorting to the principle of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*), the designation *saṃprasāraṇa* applies only to that *ikāra* which is the substitute for the letter *yakāra*."

For instance, in the view that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the named entity (*saṃjñin*), since that [sentence-meaning] consists of a relation between the subject and the predicate, the intermediate sentence-meaning arises when the rule of "correspondence" (*yathāsaṃkhya-paribhāṣā*) is applied: "In place of *yaṇ*, *iK* shall occur in correspondence. The great sentence-meaning (*mahāvākyārtha*) is: "That [intermediate meaning] shall be designated as *saṃprasāraṇa*. Nor does this lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of applying the term to forms such as *yāti* or *vāti* by grasping the intermediate sentence-meaning; for the intention there lies solely in the connection with the technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Otherwise, rules such as *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* would be rendered meaningless, and forms such as *aduhīt* would not possess that [status]. Even in the view that both [names] apply, because the [term] is already present, the designation applies only to the phoneme (*varṇa*) according to its respective order. Furthermore, this form [of the word *sthāna*] occurs either in the sense of a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*) or as a pure agent (*kartṛ*). However, in the view where it is a designation for a phoneme (*varṇasaṃjñā*), there is no application according to order, because a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply to a restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the connection with a substitute (*sthāniyoga*) would also not occur; for in the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*, this [word *sthāne*] must be understood as being carried over (*anuvartamāna*) and thus explained. As it has been said:
But [the desired result] is established by the explicit statement (*vacana*) within the section on the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyadhikāra*).

Alternatively, by the maxim of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokita*), the mention of *sthāna* (place/substratum) may be drawn back to this very rule; for in the rule *saṃprasāraṇasya*, there is a reference to that which is to become [the semivowel] through the use of *tantra* and other such devices.

Or else, according to the view that the time of operation is determined by the rule itself (*kāryakālapakṣa*), since the meaning of the sentence is "the *yaṇ* becomes an *ik* called *saṃprasāraṇa*," it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). When the paribhāṣā regarding correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is present, the phoneme that actually undergoes the operation is the one designated as the technical term (*saṃjñin*); that same phoneme is what presents itself in rules such as *saṃprasāraṇasya*.

Alternatively, it may be said that even in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), a connection established by worldly convention through the order of positions is easily available; thus, in the word *dyubhyām*, the lengthening [prescribed] by the rule *halaḥ* does not apply. This is because of the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*u*) in the rule *diva ut*. Similarly, in the word *dyuloka*, the lengthening [prescribed] by the rule *saṃprasāraṇasya* does not apply. Nor should it be argued: "Since the *tapara* marker has already served its purpose by preventing the application of lengthening, how can it function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that 'even when being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), the vowel *u* includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhaka*)'?"

This is because [the rule] is stated under the view that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the named entity (*saṃjñin*), or else because in the rule "of the *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*saṃprasāraṇasya*), there is the inclusion of that which has been transformed into it (*tadbhāvita*).

In the alternative view, however, the rule *ṛta ud* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence that in forms such as *akṣadyuvau* and *akṣadyuvaḥ*, once the *ūṭh* substitute has received the designation of *saṃprasāraṇa*, the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* would cause the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) for the diphthong *au* and so on. This is because of the statement in the Vārttika: "When [the result of] *saṃprasāraṇa* is to be preceded by [the original vowel], the term 'stem' (*aṅga*) must be understood as referring to the same constituent element. For the designation of 'stem' (*aṅga*) defined with respect to the *kvin* suffix applies only to the verbal root, whereas the designation defined with respect to the case-ending finds its rest in the entire composite form (the compound). Furthermore, a rule pertaining to the phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one pertaining to the stem (*āṅga*).

However, in the view that the *vākyārtha* (the sentence-meaning) is the name-bearer (*saṃjñin*), there is simply no possibility of the occurrence of the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute form of the preceding vowel). In cases such as *hūtaḥ* and *jīnaḥ*, however, by the force of the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), the lengthening occurs even when the substitute has been produced from the *saṃprasāraṇa*.

This is because, even in the view that the individual phoneme (*varṇa*) is the name-bearer, since the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is impossible in an operation concerning a phoneme (*alvidhi*), it must be stated that the application of the grammatical operation takes place in the substitute for the *saṃprasāraṇa* due to the very power of the rule's formulation.
[Pāṇini 1.1.46: "The markers *ṭ* and *k* are respectively at the beginning and at the end."

The *ṭ* and *k* which are prescribed belong respectively to the initial and final portions of that [element] to which they are attached. For example: *bhavitā* and *pāyayati*. Nor should it be argued that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this rule to cases such as "careṣṭaḥ," "gāpoṣṭak," and "vrīhiśālyorḍhak. This is because, by the maxim of the prior exception (*purastādapavādanyāya*), this exception regarding the specific locus (*sthāneyoga*) is superseded by the subsequent rules "pratyayaḥ" and "paraśca. This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical metarule), because of its association with the subsequent section on *paribhāṣās*; or rather, according to the *Bhāṣya*, it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) itself.

For instance—the compound *ṭakitau* is a *karmadhāraya*. The letters *ṭ* and *k*, bearing the technical designation *it*, serve as markers (*saṃjñā*) for the beginning and the end [of a grammatical element]. Consequently, in the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ*, there occurs the presentation of the word *ikādi* (beginning with *i*). In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *ikārādiḥ*, the analysis is: "that of which *ikāra* is the beginning. By the paribhāṣā regarding the closest substitute (*sthāne 'ntaratama*), the substitution of *itavya* for *tavya* is established. Thus they say:

It is said that for those [sounds] which do not have a specific location, there are designations (*ādeśa*) that do have a location. Thus, in the case of *yāpayati*, there is the designation *yāp* for the element *yā*. One should not object, saying: "Let it simply be that 'the *ṭ* and *k* are at the beginning and end' (P. 1.1.46); since a technical name (*saṃjñā*) functions merely by making known the named object (*saṃjñin*), it does not itself participate in the grammatical operation. For if this were so, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in rules such as "the suffixes *āl* and *aṭac*" and "for *ṭha*, substitute *ika*" (P. 7.3.50). Rather, the designation *it* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a specific location. Therefore, the letters *ṭ* and *k* are the names when they reside in that very location which belongs to the sound marked with the *it* designation.

There is no fault here, for the *ikādeśa* (the substitution of *i*) and the *kakāra* (the letter *k*) in *āṭ-acaṣṭakāraḥ* are not like that. Nor should it be argued that in the case of the augment *aṭ*, there would be an *ādeśa* of *bhū* as *abhū*, and by the rule *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*, the final syllable of the *aṅga* (stem) would become udātta; for this is explained by means of a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound—*a-ṭ-udāttaśca yasya*—meaning that the *ādeśa* *abhū* begins with an udātta vowel *ā*. Even though the word *udātta* functions as an adjective, its placement at the end [of the compound] is a Vedic (*sautra*) irregularity.

Nor should it be argued that even so, there is a fault in the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 3.1.36), because even if the word *udātta* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], the augment *āṭ*—being heard together with that [word *udātta*]—cannot form a *bahuvrīhi* compound [with it]. This is because that sūtra has been rejected (*pratyākhyāna*). And the author of the Vārttika will state:

"The [vowel-raising] for *ajādīnām* is accomplished by means of *āṭ*, etc. [Vārttika 5 on Pāṇini 3.1.36]. *Midaco'ntyātparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.47). [An augment denoted by the technical term *mit* is placed after the final vowel among the consonants.]

Among these vowels (*ac*), that which is *mit* (marked with the *m*-sign) occurs after the final vowel. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules regarding the place of substitution (*sthāneyoga*) and to the rule "and what follows" (*paraśca*). [Examples: *vanāni*, *yaśāṃsi*. [The suffix] *śnam* [is applied] "after roots beginning with *rudh*" (*rudhādibhyaḥ śanam*); as in *ruṇaddhi*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that this [rule for *śnam*] would fail to supersede the rule "and what follows" (*paraśca*), as was the case previously. For it is accepted that, when considering the general scope of what is to be superseded, everything applicable within its own domain is superseded; otherwise, the *mit*-designation of *śnam* would be purposeless.

Because the mention of *tṛṇahaḥ* [in Pāṇini 6.4.103] would otherwise be impossible for the sake of hearing the sound *m*, the genitive case in *acaḥ* is used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇe*). It is in the singular number because it refers to the class [of vowels]. Nor should it be argued that *acaḥ* is actually in the ablative case, on the grounds of its coreferentiality with the ablative *antyāt*; for if this were so, in rules such as *śe mucādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.59), since a final vowel is impossible [in roots like *muc*], this rule would not apply, and consequently the general maxim *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* would take effect, rendering the designation *mit* (as in *muc*) redundant.
Thus, the commentary of the ancients, which states that "the *mit* should follow the final vowel," is also to be explained in exactly this way.

Others, however, argue that since the word *acaḥ* occurs there, let it be the ablative (*pañcamī*) itself. If this is so, is it intended that the augment *num* would not occur at all, or that it would not occur in its desired location? Not the first, because that would render the rule meaningless. Not the second, because even if the final vowel is set aside, it is still possible for [the *num*] to follow a vowel (*ac*); and since it is more appropriate to assume the setting aside of a subordinate element (*guṇa*) rather than a principal one (*pradhāna*), the desired result is achieved. By this, the claim that the rule would apply even when a portion of the vowel (*ac*) is missing is also refuted; for since the vowel is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the application [of the rule] does not occur when it is deficient. Thus they say.

Because the term *antagrahaṇa* (the mention of the "end") from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) here as well, [the suffix] *mat* has its final letter [as the marker]. If it were not a non-suffix (*abhakta*), then in examples such as *tā tā piṇḍānām*, the elision of *śi* by the rule *śeś chandasi bahulam* would not result in the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*), because it would not be at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, in the case of *vahaṃlihaḥ*, the *anusvāra* of the letter *m* in the augment *mum* would not occur, because it would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*).

If one were to explain [the rule] as *parādiḥ* (beginning with the subsequent element) by following the recurrence of the term *ādi* ("and so forth"), then in forms such as *vāriṇe*, the guṇa substitution prescribed by the rule *gher ṅiti* would occur; furthermore, in *vahaṃlihaḥ*, the anusvāra would not appear. Also, in the case of *atisakhīni brāhmaṇakulāni* (Brāhmaṇa families whose friends are preeminent), the rule *sakhyurasambuddhau* would cause vṛddhi due to the *ṇit*-designation [of the suffix]; nor could its absence be argued on the grounds of the word being secondary (*gauṇa*), because that rule applies even when the word is secondary, as in the case of *asthidadhi* and so forth.

In this way, in forms such as *trapūṇi*, because the stem (*aṅga*) lacks the property of ending in *n* (*nāntitva*), the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* would not apply to produce the long vowel. Therefore, the view that the augment is a *pūrvānta* (anterior element) is correct. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "The augment *m* should be placed before the final letter [of the root] for the sake of the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* and the initial member of the *saṃyoga* in the case of the root *masj*."

*Magnaḥ* means one who has immersed himself. By the rule *oditaśca*, the *niṣṭhā* suffix [ta] becomes *na*; however, because that [substitution] is not yet established (*asiddha*), the *kutva* change [of *s* to *ṣ*] occurs. By the rule *masjinaśorjhali*, the augment *num* is added; if this were placed immediately after the final vowel, then by the rule *aniditām*, there would be no elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the penultimate *n*). *Anuṣaṅga* is the technical term used by the Eastern grammarians for the penultimate *n*. Nor should it be argued that the elision of the *n* occurs because it becomes the penultimate (*upadhā*) once the *s* is dropped by the rule *skoḥ* [saṃyogādyoḥ...]; for with respect to that [elision of *n*], the elision of the *s* is considered *asiddha*.

Furthermore, according to the view that the designation *saṃyoga* applies only to a collection (*samudāya*) when many [consonants] are in conjunction, the letter *s* lacks the status of being the beginning of a *saṃyoga*. In this way, forms such as *maṅktā* and *maṅktavyam* should be understood. Regarding the rule *“bharjimarcyośca”* (and in the case of *bharji* and *marci*), the phrase “the augment *miṭ* occurs before the final [letter]” is understood to carry over. The root *bhṛjī* means ‘to roast’; when the *uṇādi* suffix *ac* is applied, the augment *um* is added, resulting in *bharujā*. The root *marca* belongs to the *curādi* class and means ‘sound’; it takes the *uṇādi* suffix *i*, with the augment *īm*, resulting in *marīciḥ*. This is established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

This is a rejection of the Vārttika that was stated. This is because the word *bharuja* is listed among *aṅguli* and others, while the word *marīci* is listed among *bāhu* and others. As for the statement "from the roots *mṛ* and *kaṇi*, [the suffix] *īci*: *marīci*," that is merely another method (*upāyāntara*). [Now follows:
"In place of *ec*, there is *ig* when a short vowel is substituted. (Pāṇini 1.1.47)

*Ādeśa* means "that which is prescribed. [The compound] *hrasva* is a *karmadhāraya*. The locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The singular number is used for the sake of denoting the class (*jāti*). Among the short vowels that are being prescribed, *ec* (the diphthongs) shall be replaced by *ic* (the simple vowels) alone. For example: *atihi kulam* (having surpassed the word *he*), *citraguḥ*, *atiri*, *atinu*. This rule is intended to exclude the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels—which might otherwise apply due to partial similarity—since there exists no short vowel most similar to the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*). However, the author of the *Vārttika* says: "It is already established because *eṅ* shares the same place of articulation [with *i* and *u*], and because the latter part of *aic* is predominant."

The meaning is this: due to the *paravipratiṣedha* (the rule that in a conflict, the subsequent [operation prevails]), the *i* and *u* vowels alone are the most similar (*antaratama*) to the subsequent portion of *eṅ*. Thus, Kaiyaṭa states in the sixth [chapter]: "The restriction that 'in a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails' does not mean that in a conflict between two grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*), the subsequent one occurs; rather, even when two operations are prescribed by a single rule, in the event of a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails because it falls under the scope of the word 'subsequent' (*para*). This is also the sense adopted here.
Alternatively, it is established according to the view that the vowel *e* is purely palatal (*tālavya*) and the vowel *o* is purely labial (*auṣṭhya*). Thus, the *Bahvṛca-prātiśākhya* states:
"The vowels *e* and *ai*, the *ca*-group, the vowels *i* and *ī*, the letter *y*, and the letter *ś* are palatal; the remainder is produced by the lips."

The collection of phonemes (*varṇarāśi*) distinct from those previously mentioned is to be established by means of the two lips (*oṣṭha*). The author of the *Vṛtti* states: "The phoneme *u*, the labial class (*pavarga*), *au* and *aut*, and the *upadhmānīya*—these are labials (*oṣṭhya*). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that, the reading is: "The remaining [phonemes] are labials, with the exception of the apavāda. This means excluding those that will be mentioned in the subsequent sūtra. This is for the sake of clarity. Furthermore, the author of the *Vārttika* states another solution regarding the diphthongs (*aic*): "And of *ai* and *au*... The syntactical connection is: "and because of the greater number of [labial elements] in the latter."

In the view that the vowel *a* has half a *mātrā* while the vowels *i* and *u* have one and a half *mātrās*, the substitutes *iK* and *uK* would be designated by their greater duration—just as in the case of "Mallagrāma" and similar names; thus, the present sūtra would not need to be commenced. Furthermore, the position that the division [of the *mātrās*] is equal is established in the eighth [chapter], where the same two solutions previously mentioned apply.
[The sūtra: "The genitive [case ending] is used in the sense of 'in place of' (sthāne). (P. 1.1.49)

The suffix *ac* is applied [to the word *yoga*] by virtue of its inclusion in the *arśa-ādi* group, in the sense of abundance (*bhūma-artha*), meaning "that which is characterized by many possible relations. Alternatively, if the word is analyzed as *ayo-ga*, it should be understood as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) whose specific relation is not determined, referring instead to a relation occasioned by position (*sthāna*). "Position" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*), as in the example: "In place of *darbha* grasses, one should spread *śara* grass. In the doubt—"Is *bhū-* near to or immediately following *as-*?"—the meaning "it should be pronounced in its place" implies the exclusion of mere proximity and so forth. Why [is the word] *yoga* used? [To exclude cases where there is no such connection.]

[This rule] is intended so that [the substitution of *ū* for the penultimate vowel] does not occur in cases such as *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ* ("for the root *guh*, the penultimate vowel is replaced by *ū*") and *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* ("for *śās*, *i* is substituted before *aṅ* and *hal*"). Otherwise, in place of the roots *guh* and *śās*, the substitutions *ū* and *i* would apply to the penultimate vowel of any verbal root whatsoever.

Alternatively, *sthāneyoga* is a single compound word. It is a *bahuvrīhi* with either a locative or an instrumental case-ending in the first member; or, by virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is elision of the case-ending and the substitution of the suffix *tva*. Nor does this lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in rules such as *gohaḥ* or *śāsaḥ*, because a *paribhāṣā* operates specifically for the purpose of restriction when there would otherwise be a lack of restriction. Furthermore, due to the proximity of the term *upadhā*, it is determined that the genitive denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), thereby eliminating any further expectancy. This is analogous to how, when asking for directions, even if one points out the way by taking the left or right, the instruction applies only at a point where the path bifurcates.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: because of the conformity with the examples (*lakṣyānurodhāt*), because of its being *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned), and because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, it is possible to explain that the application of the substitute occurs by position (*sthāneyoga*) only in those desired instances; therefore, this is not the meaning of the sentence. Rather, it is simply this: only that which is actually uttered with a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is joined with the position (*sthānena yujyeta*), and not that which is merely understood (*pratīyamāna*). Thus it is said: "Substitutes apply to that which is specifically pointed out (*nirdiśyamānasya*).

Consequently, in rules such as *jarāyā jaras*, the substitution of *jaras* applies to the word *jarā* which is a constituent part of the stem (*aṅga*) ending in *jarā*, but it does not apply to the [genitive suffix] *-niḥ* either.

As for the fact that the genitive case following the word *jarā* conveys the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) residing only in the word *jarā*, which constitutes its own base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), and not in words such as *nirjarā*; this is because [the latter] lacks the status of being the base-meaning. Nor should it be argued that even that [word *nirjarā*] is the base-meaning by virtue of the *tadanta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding "ending in that"). For that rule operates based on the understanding that the substitution occurs "in place of the stem (*aṅga*) consisting of the word *jarā*"; thus, without contradicting that [rule], the status of being a substitute for words like *nirjarā* must be understood precisely through their constituent parts.

For this very reason, in rules such as *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, the term *oṣṭhya* and so forth serve as qualifiers for the *ṛ*-vowels and others, which constitute a single portion of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśa*). For this same reason, there is no substitution for that which includes the augment (*sāgamaka*). This is because, during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), the statement "those without augments undergo substitution by those with augments" would be inappropriate. However, under the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original), since the operation proceeds precisely through the cognition of the original (*sthānin*), there is no sublation of the maxim regarding "that which is being pointed out" (*nirdiśyamāna*).

Or, let there be the explicit (vācanikī) *paribhāṣā* "of that which is being pointed out" (*nirdiśyamānasya*), derived from the aforementioned sūtra according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya. And let it be argued that this [paribhāṣā] sublates [rules such as] "in the context of a bahiraṅga word or an aṅga. This is to be considered. Even if the status of being the substitute (*sthānitva*) is understood for that which ends in [the element], the sublation of the status of being the substitute for the *aṅga* whose form is *jaras* is necessary; for the contradiction with what is presupposed (*upajīvya*) is unavoidable. Furthermore, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the view of the Vārttika, the status of being the substitute belongs only to the *aṇga* ending in the word *jaras*, while the substitution is established for the simple word *jaras* itself by means of the principle of "designation as if possessing the whole" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

Thus, although the word *jarā* within the compound *nirjarā* lacks the status of being a grammatical *aṅga*, there is no contradiction with the rule that serves as its basis (*upajīvya*), because one can easily argue that the rule applies by taking the portion consisting of its *sthānin* (the original element). However, in rules such as "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya," the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the designation of the final letter (*tadantavidhi*) occurs only after the connection with the qualifier has been established. As for the two rules "alo'ntyasya" and "ādeḥ parasya," they are set aside by the present rule due to the force of their specific formulation. Yet, since there is no conflict with the rule "anekāl śit sarvasya," they are to be combined with it.
In this way, even the meaning previously stated should be understood through methods such as *tantra* for the sake of clear comprehension.

Regarding this, they say: "Let this rule (*yoga*) function as a bringer of the word (*padopasthāpaka*), just like the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*. In this grammar, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), when its specific relation is not determined, is joined with the word *sthāne*; thus the word *sthāne*, ending in the locative case, is brought into proximity there. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: 'that which has a connection with *sthāna* (substitution) is [the genitive]'. This applies likewise in cases such as *alo'ntyasya* and *ṅicca*. *Sthāne'ntaratamaḥ* (1.1.50): Among those [elements] that are applicable, the substitute shall be the one most similar."

If this were an independent injunction (*vidhi*), then, because no specific thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) as a substitute has been specified, the word *dadhi* would itself have to be its own substitute. For that [substitute] too, there would be yet another, and that the same again; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, since there would be no regulating factor for an operation proceeding without a specific purpose, it would apply only once. Consequently, as every word would be prone to cessation, there would be no usage of words for the sake of conveying meaning.

Thus, in cases such as *bisaṃ* and *musalam*, even though the substitute (*ādeśa*) applies to the whole (*samudāya*) in place of the whole, the letter *s* would incur the fault of becoming *ṣ* when *s* is substituted for *s*, because that [specific letter] alone has not been substituted. Therefore, the *Bhāṣya* states that this is a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule) due to the context. And that [substitution] is fourfold: among these, by position (*sthāna*), as in *suddhyupāsyaḥ*, *madhvariḥ*, *dhātraṃśaḥ*, and *lākṛtiḥ*. For the letters *y* and so on have the same position as the letters *i* and so on; this rule operates even under the view of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṅkhya*) because there is no contradiction. Examples such as *daityāriḥ* and *śrīśaḥ* should also be cited.

An example based on meaning is *vātaṇḍyayuvatiḥ* ("the young woman who is a descendant of Vataṇḍa"). [The derivation is as follows: From the word *vataṇḍa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule "vataṇḍācca" to denote a descendant (*apatya*). Then, by the rule "luk striyām," the suffix is elided in the feminine. Because the word belongs to the *śārṅgarava*-class, the feminine suffix *ṅīn* is added. In the analysis (*vigraha*)—"she is both a *vataṇḍī* and a young woman"—a compound is formed by the rule "poṭāyuvati," etc. By the rule "puṃvat karmadhāraye," there is an extension of the masculine form; thus, in place of the word *vataṇḍī*, which denotes a female descendant, the word *vātaṇḍya*—which denotes a male descendant—is substituted.

According to quality (*guṇataḥ*), as in *pākaḥ* (cooking) and *tyāgaḥ* (renunciation): by the rule "of *ca* and *ja*" (*cajoḥ*), when the *k*-substitution (*kutva*) occurs, the unaspirated, voiceless *c* and the voiced, sonant, aspirated *j* are respectively replaced by the corresponding *k* and *g*.

Regarding [substitution] by measure (*pramāṇataḥ*): as in *amum*, *amū*, *amūn*. By the rule *adaso'seḥ*, the vowel *u* is prescribed; that is, a short vowel is replaced by a short *u*, and a long vowel by a long *u*. Furthermore, because of the repeated mention of the term "place" (*sthāna*), there is another meaning of the sentence: namely, that which is the most similar (*antaratama*) in terms of its place of articulation—meaning that which possesses a proximity induced by that place. It should be understood as being among those that are otherwise applicable. As it has been said: "Where there is a manifold kind of similarity (*āntarya*), there similarity based on place (*sthānataḥ*) is stronger.
Therefore, in forms such as *cetā* and *stotā*, even though the vowel *a* is closer in terms of measure (*pramāṇataḥ*), it is not the substitute.

Because the mention of *tam* (that) serves as a means of proof for avoiding ambiguity in the sentence. If one intended to express a similarity based solely on position (*sthāna*), there would be no possibility of any other kind of similarity; thus, the mention of *tam* for the purpose of excluding such [other similarities] would be useless. Therefore, in cases such as *vāgghariḥ*, where the second letters—those with aspiration (*soṣman*)—are applicable under the rule "aspirates [replace aspirates]," and the third letters—those possessing resonance (*nādatva*)—are applicable under the rule "those possessing resonance [replace those possessing resonance]," it is because of the mention of *tam* that those possessing both qualities become the fourth letters.

According to the statement in the *Bahvṛca-Prātiśākhya*—"In each class (*varga*), the first and third are voiced (*ghoṣa*), the second and fourth are aspirates (*soṣman*), and the last is nasal"—they [the second letters] possess aspiration (*soṣmatva*). Another *Śikṣā* states: "The sibilants (*ūṣman*) beginning with *ś* are the counterparts (*sasthāna*) of the second [consonants] by position, and the fourth [consonants] are the counterparts of *ha*. The instrumental case here is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūta-lakṣaṇa*). The letters *ha*, *ś*, *ṣ*, and *sa* are the counterparts of the second letters of the *kha*, *cha*, and other classes respectively. The meaning is that just as those [sibilants] are aspirates (*ūṣman*), so too are the second [consonants]. There is no aspirate (*ūṣman*) that is the counterpart of the letter *pha*.

Therefore, its status as a *ūṣman* (aspirate/fricative) must be stated specifically. Haradatta explains that by the phrase "the fourth [consonants] with *ha*," the meaning is that just as *ha* is an *ūṣman*, so too are those [fourth consonants]. Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as *iṣṭaḥ* and *uptaḥ*, by virtue of similarity (*āntarya*), a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) consisting of half a mora (*ardhamātra*) would be replaced by an *ik* vowel of the same duration. This is because an *ik* vowel consisting of half a mora is not established [in the grammatical system]. By this, the doubt that in examples such as *dadhy atra* and *sudhy upāsyaḥ*, a *yaṇ* of the same duration as either a single-mora (*mātṛka*) or double-mora (*dvimātṛka*) vowel would arise, is also refuted; for such a result is unestablished in both common usage and the Veda.

It might be argued as follows: In the recitation of the *saṃhitā*, let the word *antaratame* be taken as ending in the locative case. The term *ṣaṣṭhī* (the genitive) is understood from the previous context. Thus, the meaning of the rule is that the genitive case is to be applied to the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute-base (*sthānin*). By this, in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe*, the desired result is established through the application of the genitive to the most similar substitute-base of the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*). This is because the word *sthāna* (base/place) is inherently relational, and thus the quality of being "most similar" is obtained only in relation to the element to be prescribed.

However, in the view that [the word *ecaḥ*] ends in the nominative case (*prathamāntacchedapakṣe*), one would have to specify the substituends (*sthāninirdeśa*) as "of *o* and *au*" in the rule *vānto yi*; for if *ecaḥ* were merely continued [from the previous rule], the substitute *vānta* would apply to every *ec*. But since the most similar (*antaratama*) substituend is established through the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the phrase *ecaḥ*, the result is achieved by restricting the *vānta* substitute to its most similar substituends, namely the forms *o* and *au*. On this point, the Bhāṣya says:

This being the case, if the meaning were that "the substitute which is the closest in terms of place of articulation (*sthāna*) should be taken," then *yaṇ* would apply only to short vowels and not to long ones; for in the rule *ikaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.3), the genitive case is restricted to those [vowels] whose closest counterpart is of exactly one morae (*mātrā*), as the half-mora vowel has a counterpart of exactly one mora. However, if one follows the indicative force (*jñāpaka*) of rules such as *lvādibhyaḥ* and *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*, there is the drawback of excessive complexity in understanding (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

Regarding the rules "iko guṇavṛddhī" and "aco ñṇiti," even though these two genitive-case rules [specify the substitutes], if they were restricted (upasaṃhāra) only to the *ik* vowels and *ac* vowels that are most similar (*antaratama*) to the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* to be prescribed, then the application of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* via the rules "sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ" and "aco ñṇiti" would occur only in cases ending in long vowels, such as *netā*, *lavitā*, *nāyakaḥ*, and *lāvakaḥ*. It would not occur in cases such as *cetā*, *stotā*, *cāyakaḥ*, and *stāvakaḥ*. This is because the two prescribed [substitutes] consist of two morae (*dvimātra*), and thus there is no similarity (*antaratamya*) between them and a short vowel.
