However, there is no fault in the view that the substitution is the most similar (*antaratama*) according to the specific instruction (*ādeśataḥ*), because the genitive case denoting the substituendum (*sthāni-ṣaṣṭhī*) is unrestricted. Nor does it follow that *ej* alone would undergo the substitution of *vānt* (the sounds *v* and *au*). This is because, in the rule *eco'yavāyāvaḥ*, both the rule of corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) and the maxim of the most similar (*antaratama-paribhāṣā*) operate; and by relying on the governing topic (*adhikāra*), the meaning of the sūtra is that the same kind of *vānt* substitution previously observed occurs when followed by an affix beginning with *y*. And such [substitutions] are *av* in place of *o* and *āv* in place of *au*.

Alternatively—"vānta" means that which is to be abandoned. By dividing the rule *kṣyyajayyau* and explaining it as a restriction—that if [the suffix] occurs after a root beginning with a guttural (*kaṇ*), a labial (*ṭa*), or a palatal (*tālavya*), it must be *kṣi* or *ji*—the substitution of *ay* (in forms such as *ceya*) is prevented. The second rule, *kṣijyoḥ śakyārthe eva*, restricts these two roots to the sense of possibility; therefore, even for those two, there is no substitution of *ay* in senses such as "deserving. As for the form *raiyati* in the sense "he desires wealth," the word *rāyi* is Vedic, for the Bhāṣya states that in the Veda one follows whatever is observed. Some maintain that the word *rai* ending in *kyac* is indeed Vedic, whereas other forms of it exist even in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
However, [the form] *kyac* does not exist because of the rule stating "not after a word ending in a letter identical to that of *go*.
Others, however, say that the word *rai* is never used in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*); thus says Kaiyaṭa.

But even so, in the case of the word *nara* [in the rule] *nṛnarayośca*, the vṛddhi prescribed in conjunction with the suffix *ṅīn* would apply to the final letter by the rule *alo’ntyasya*. Furthermore, once the elision of *ya* (*yasyeti lopa*) has taken place, the prescription of vṛddhi would be rendered useless. If its purpose were merely for the sake of the stem *nṛ*, one would have to resort to the formulation *nurvṛddhiśca*. Nor can it be argued that, because the elision of *ya* takes precedence, the vṛddhi applies to the initial *a*; for vṛddhi is an *antaranga* (internal) operation, being prescribed in conjunction with the suffix.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because, by the maxim of "conflict between a subordinate and a quality" (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*), the internal rule (*antaraṅgaparibhāṣā*) is set aside; and since the *yasyeti* elision (*lopa*) applies later, it occurs first, after which the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) takes place—on the grounds that the *vṛddhi* would set aside the elision by virtue of its own specific statement, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of subverting the substratum (*dharmibādha*). Even so, the analysis [of the word] as ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) is indispensable. For in that case, since the substitution of the most similar (*antaratama*) element occurs for the original locus (*sthānin*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is restricted to the locus that is most similar to the *vṛddhi*, whereby the *vṛddhi* replaces the vowel *a*.

However, under the view that the word is cut off [before] the first case-ending (*prathamāntacchedapakṣa*), since the substitution is determined by the closest possible element (*antaratama*) according to the original form (*prakṛti*), even though the substitution of the non-closest element is excluded, there would still be a substitution for the *repha* (the letter *r*) due to the absence of a rule restricting the locus (*sthānin*), as per the maxim "of the vowel, the last" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*). Regarding this, they say: the rejection of the reading of the word *nara* is indeed the consensus of the author, as evidenced by the Bhāṣya which refutes the interpretation of the word-break as ending in the locative case (*saptamyantaccheda*). Nor does it follow that the form *narī* would result from the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* applied to *nara* on the basis of its being a genus (*jāti*), because such a form is actually desired; for we see forms such as *kinnarīṇām* and *narīṇām*.

Alternatively—the word *nara* has a fixed masculine gender (*niyata-puṃliṅga*). As for the usage *narī*, it occurs by means of the suffix *ṅīṣ* under the rule for [denoting] connection with a male (*puṃyoga-lakṣaṇe*). For even according to the other grammatical arrangement (*yathānyāsa*), that [usage] is unavoidable. Alternatively—in the rule *nṛnarayoḥ*, the term *ataḥ* (of *at*) is carried over from the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*. This is because the intention of this very *gaṇa*-sūtra has been brought forward by the phrase *śārṅgaravādyañ* etc. That [term *ataḥ*], having been modified into the genitive case, is connected with the word *nara* in a non-co-referential manner (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*): namely, "there is vṛddhi of the *at* which belongs to the word *nara*. Therefore, the paribhāṣā concerning the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*) does not apply.

Alternatively, *nara* is an imitation of a word ending in *ra* with its vowel *a* elided; [the form] *naraḥ* is derived from that, and by adding *vṛddhi*, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied according to the rule *cād gaṇapāṭhāt*.

As for the fact that Haradatta established the form *nārī* by relying on the principle that the substitution must be the most similar (*antaratama*) to the original element (*sthānin*), there is no contradiction, as that relies on the maxim: "The means are for the sake of attaining the goal."

In the Bhāṣya, however, this very sūtra is rejected. For when it is said, "Let [them] sit in the assembly," the learned, the poets, and the warriors sit together only with their own peers—the learned and so forth—not in a mixed fashion. Likewise, even among animals, one sees such things as "the herd of cows runs" or "the horse [runs] of horses. Therefore, the attainment of the meaning of the first sentence is not the purpose of this [sūtra]. Furthermore, the fact that proximity (*sthāna*) possesses greater force [in determining similarity] is established from common worldly usage.

Furthermore, when two cows or two horses that are accustomed to moving together are joined with others of their own kind, even though they possess similar qualities such as leanness or paleness, it is observed that they look toward one another solely on account of the similarity of their position. Thus, this is established by common worldly experience.
*Uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50).

The *aṇ* substitute in place of an *ṛ*-vowel should be followed by *r* (*rapara*) only in the state of its actual occurrence (*prasaṅgāvasthā*). Here, *ra* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation), and *ṛ* is the designation for thirty sounds. Due to internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), the rule is established that the substitute in place of the vowel *ṛ* is followed by *r*, while the substitute in place of the vowel *ḷ* is followed by *l*. Examples are *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ* and *tavalkāraḥ*. However, the ancient teachers (*prāñcaḥ*) explained it as: "the *aṇ* substitute in place of both *ṛ* and *ḷ* [is followed by *r*]."

As for the argument that—given the analyses *ā ca ā ca* and *ralau*, or *uśca ul ca* and *ṛlau*—a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is difficult to justify because the rule for *ekaśeṣa* applies even to dissimilar forms provided they have the same meaning—that is incorrect. For in the sentence intended to demonstrate that the word *ṛ* in the Sūtra refers to both [ṛ and ḷ], it is not intended that the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ* are mutual substitutes for one another; thus, they do not possess the same meaning. This is because the Sūtra refers merely to the phonetic forms themselves.

This is because the Vārttika, "Because there is a distinction between a collection (*samāhāra*) and an aggregate (*samūha*)," has been explained by all [commentators] in exactly that way; otherwise, the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would undesirably apply even in cases such as "mihira-aruṇa-pūṣaṇaḥ."

In this context, four possible interpretations of the sentence-meaning are possible: The first is that *aṇ* qualified by the property of having *r* as its subsequent element (*rapara*) is prescribed in place of *ṛ*. The second is that there is a restriction (*niyama*) stating that when both *aṇ*s and non-*aṇ*s are applicable, only an *aṇ* occurs; furthermore, through a split in the sentence-structure (*vākya-bheda*), the property of having *r* as its subsequent element is prescribed for that [restricted *aṇ*]. The third is that, having referred back (*anūdya*) an *aṇ* that occupies the position of *ṛ*, the property of having *r* as its subsequent element is prescribed for it. The fourth is that the property of having *r* as its subsequent element is prescribed precisely at the stage of the occasion for application (*prasaṅga-avasthā*).

In that regard, the analysis of the statement in the first case is as follows: if the substitute *aṇ* were to apply to whatever is merely indicated by the genitive case, then it would be the closest (*antaratama*) [substitute] for the *ṛ*-vowel according to the rule *ṛvarṇasya tvaṇ raparaḥ*. Consequently, since this *aṇ* is prescribed when the udātta and other accents have not yet taken effect, it would subvert those accents. And thus, in the word *kṛtiḥ*, the initial vowel would not be udātta according to the rule *ñnityādir nityam*.

In the case of *prakṛtaṃ prahṛtam*, because of the rule "the immediately preceding *gati* [is acute]" (*gatiranantaraḥ*), the word *pra-* would be acute; consequently, the subsequent syllables would be subject to the *śeṣanighāta* (the remaining syllables are unaccented) and the rule "after an acute, an unaccented [syllable becomes] circumflex" (*udāttādanudāttasya*) would not apply [to produce the circumflex]. Furthermore, in *nṝn pāhi*, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) would not occur, because in all such cases there would be the application of an *aṇ* vowel followed by *r* (*rapara*) as qualified by those respective qualities; however, the vowel *ṛ* does not possess the property of being an *aṇ*. Nor should it be asked: "Why was it not stated that even the long vowel [of *nṝn*] would not occur? For that [long vowel] is established by the specific grammatical instruction *nṝn pe*.

Furthermore, in the case of the forms *karttā* and *kāraka*, the suffix *aṇ* prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.1.137] to supersede *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* might occasionally become *i* or *u*, because there would be no restrictive rule stating that it must be *a* alone. Moreover, in the case of the specifically stated rules for *it* and *ut* substitutions—namely, "ṛta iddhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100) and "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya" (Pāṇini 7.1.102)—the substitution of *r* as the subsequent element (*raparatva*) would not occur, because those rules would be superseded by the [general rule for *aṇ*].

Now, let the second position be accepted: since there is a restriction that "in the event of a conflict between *aṇ* and non-*aṇ*, only *aṇ* applies," there is no fault regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* in examples such as *kartṛ* and *kāraka*. [Objection: But surely, for the short *ṛ*-vowel, every *vṛddhi* is equally proximate (*anantaratama*), because all *vṛddhi* is of two morae (*dvimātra*); however, for the long [vowels], every [substitute] is equally proximate in terms of measure (*pramāṇataḥ*). Thus, since there is no distinction, when all *vṛddhi*s would apply in both cases, let the restriction "only *aṇ*" hold.

In the domain of *guṇa* substitution, however, in cases such as *kartā*, since the short *ṛ*-vowel consists of one mora (*mātrika*), the *a*-vowel alone is the most similar (*antaratama*). In cases such as *taritā*, since the long *ṛ*-vowel consists of two moras (*dvimātrika*), the *eṅ* diphthongs alone are the most similar. Thus, because the application of both [the *a* and *eṅ*] is restricted by this specific determination (*vyavasthā*) in both instances, there is no possibility for either to apply in both cases; consequently, in the absence of the operation of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the *guṇa* prescribed for the long *ṛ*-vowel would be only *eṅ*. But for the short [ṛ], even if it were to become *a*, it would not be followed by *r* (i.e., it would not be *rapara*).

If it is argued that when both *aṇ* and *aṇan* are applicable, the rule restricts [the substitution] to *aṇ* alone, and since the second [rule] prescribes that this very *aṇ* is followed by *r*, the fault regarding the *guṇa* [substitution] remains unavoidable—this is true. However, the scope of the maxim *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (P. 1.1.50) is exemplified by rules such as *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (P. 7.3.52), whereas the scope of this present rule is the prescription of *vṛddhi*. Since both would apply in the case of a *guṇa*, this very rule prevails due to its posteriority; thus, there is no fault. This is true, yet the fault remains as it was in the case of [the substitution of] acute (*udātta*) accents and other specifically prescribed (*pratipadokta*) elements.

Now, let the third position be accepted: since the rules for [the substitution of] udātta and other accents—refined by the *antaratama* (most similar) paribhāṣā—prescribe that very *ṛ*-vowel as delimited by its respective quality (*guṇa*), and since that [substitute] lacks the status of being an *aṇ*, there is no possibility of its being replaced by *ra*. Furthermore, there is no fault even regarding the *it* (indicatory *i*) and other such substitutes prescribed by specific rule (*pratipadokta*), because the status of being an *aṇ* belonging to the locus of the *ṛ*-vowel exists there as well; thus, the replacement by *ra* is established in cases such as *kirati*. Not so! For the fault remains in the case of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions.

In the case of *kartṛ*, although there is no fault—since the short *ṛ* (mātrika) is replaced by *a* through *guṇa*, and then *ra* is substituted for it due to its being a single mora (*mātrikatva*)—in forms such as *tarita*, there would be the undesirable consequence of replacing the two-mora long vowel (*dīrgha*) with an *eṅ* of the same duration. Furthermore, in the case of *vṛddhi*, according to the previously mentioned reasoning, since there is no proximity (*antaratamya*) between a short vowel and the *vṛddhi* vowel, and because of the proximity between long vowels, both types of *vṛddhi* would apply in all three ways. Even though forms like *kāraḥ* and *tāraḥ* would be established, there would also be the undesirable consequence of *ai* and *au* appearing in certain instances, resulting in forms such as *kāyaḥ*, *kāvaḥ*, *tāyaḥ*, and *tāvaḥ*.

It might be argued as follows: This position is indeed faultless, because the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika have stated in the previous sūtra that "the non-intervening nature of these two is itself their intervention," or that there is a "conjunction like that of a lost horse and a burnt chariot. For instance, one [sound] has no most similar *prakṛti* (original form), and for the other, there is no most similar substitute (*ādeśa*). Therefore, the status of being "most similar" (*antaratama*) is established precisely through the property of lacking a corresponding correlate. Indeed, there is no restrictive rule that intervention must be of only four kinds, as this is not stated by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali).

On the contrary, since the *Bhāṣya* and other works accept that "the sibilants [replace] sibilants," the meaning of the passage beginning with "samprayoga" is as follows: even in the view that rejects the rule "the most similar [substitute takes the place] of the original," the relationship between the original (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is based on mutual dependence, because both lack a corresponding counterpart. This is what is stated.

Even though the original element (*sthānin*) delimited by the class *ṛ* lacks the closest similarity with the substitute (*ādeśa*) delimited by the class *at*, this fault is prominent when examining similarity based on individual phonetic instances (*vyakti*). For a one-mora (*mātrika*) *ṛ*-vowel, such an *a*-sound is the closest similar counterpart; however, for a two-mora (*dvimātra*) vowel, the *e*- and *o*-sounds are the closest counterparts, as suitable correlates are thus easily available. Furthermore, because of the grammatical rule "the independent [agent] is the *kartṛ*," there is no reciprocal exchange [of roles].

Furthermore, because the discussion begins with the *Acivibhāṣā* ("or not"), there is no optionality (*vikalpa*); for even if one were to assume such optionality, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, the fourth [interpretation] is faultless. As it has been said:
"But it is established by the fact that [the substitution] occurs in the context of the contingency (*prasaṅga*) due to being followed by *r*" (*raparatvāt*).
This means that at the very time of prescribing the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the injunctive rule, the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* (*aṇo raparatvam*) takes place.

Now, an objection might be raised: since the word *sthāne* is understood here as meaning "in the state of expectancy" (*prasaṅgāvasthāyām*), the genitive case in *ṛkārasya* would not have "substitution" (*sthāna*) as its meaning. For *aṇ* is prescribed by another rule, and not by this one; thus, the paribhāṣā "The sixth [case-ending denotes] connection with substitution" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*) does not apply at all. This is because of the maxim: "A paribhāṣā applies to a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), but not to a restatement (*anuvāda*). It is for this very reason that the term *sthāne* is explicitly mentioned in the rule "In the place of the short *ā*, according to the Northern grammarians, when preceded by *ya* or *ka*" (*udīcām ātaḥ sthāne yakapūrvāyāḥ*).

And thus, if it were argued that the *aṇ* substitute for *ṛ* would be followed by *r* (*rapara*) only in the state of contingency (*prasaṅgāvasthā*), then even an *aṇ* adjacent to *ṛ* would have to be *rapara*; this is not so, because the word "in place of" (*sthāne*) is understood from the second [sūtra] as well. Consequently, while the connection with the "place" (*sthāna*) is established by the first [mention], the second establishes the specific time, namely that it occurs only in the state of contingency.

In the rule *sthāne'ntaratamaḥ*, although the word *sthāna* was previously explained as referring to the articulatory organs such as the palate (*tālu*), here, within this section on phonemes (*śabdādhikāra*), it is explained as referring to the occasion for substitution (*prasaṅga*). Thus, according to the paribhāṣā *sthāne'ntaratamaḥ*, in forms such as *kṛtiḥ*, only the *ṛ*-vowel replaces the *ṛ*-vowel; consequently, there is no occasion at all for the application of the suffix *aṇ*.

Since the substitution of *ra* for the final element of *aṇ* would apply precisely at the stage when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are about to take effect, the substitutes *ar* and *ār*—being the most similar (*antaratama*) according to the interpretive rule (*vyākhyāna*)—become the replacements for the vowel *ṛ*, rather than *eṅ* and *aiC* which are the most similar in terms of phonetic measure (*pramāṇa*). Thus, there is no fault. If it is objected that, because the substitute consists of more than one letter (*anekāl*), it should therefore be a replacement for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*), we say no. This is because the status of being a whole-word replacement cannot occur, as it contradicts the condition of *raparatva* (the suffix *ra* following the vowel), which depends upon the original position of *ṛ*. Accordingly, there is a Vārttika on the preceding sūtra:

There is the contingency of all substitutions [occurring] because [the substitute] consists of multiple phonemes; or rather, there is no obstruction to the substitution of the vowel *a* because the property of consisting of multiple phonemes depends upon that [substitution].

What is the purpose of including the mention of *ṛ*? It is so that *akaṅ*, *lopa*, *ānaṅ*, *anaṅ*, *rīṅ*, and *riṅ* do not undergo the substitution of *ra* for the final element (*raparatva*). In the word *saudhātakiḥ*, the substitute *akaṅ* takes the place of the vowel *ṛ* because the suffix is marked with *ṅ* (indicating it is *ṅit*), according to the rule "sudhāturakaṅ ca. In the word *paitṛṣvaseyaḥ*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *ṛ* according to the rule "ḍhaki lopaḥ. In the word *hotāpotārau*, the substitute *ānaṅ* takes the place of the vowel *ṛ* in a *dvandva* compound, according to the rule "ānaṅ ṛto dvandve. In the word *karttā*, the substitute *anaṅ* takes the place of the vowel *ṛ* according to the rule "ṛduśanaḥ. In the word *mātrīyati*, the substitute *rīṅ* takes the place of the vowel *ṛ* according to the rule "rīṅ ṛtaḥ."

In the word *kriyate*, the substitution *riṅ* applies by the rule *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*. Nor should it be argued that the rule for the elision of the *ṛ*-vowel (*ṛkāralopa*) is redundant because the form would be established even by *yaṇ* substitution once the *ḍhak* suffix has been elided and the *rapara* (substitution of *r*) has taken effect; for, by virtue of the specific capacity [of the rule], the general rule of substitution for the final letter (*alo'ntyavidhi*) is set aside, resulting in the elision of the entire vowel. Nor should it be argued that there is no harm even if *rapara* were applied in the case of *hotāpotārāḥ*, since the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) could occur there; for Kaiyaṭa states that such elision is untenable because that [elision of the *ḍhak*] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of the subsequent operation.

As for the two positions—"there is a prohibition of the *yaṇ* [substitution] when there is elision of a final conjunct" (*saṃyogāntalope yaṇaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ*) and "or rather, not so, because of the elision of the *jhal* [consonant]" (*na vā jhalo lopāt*)—in both cases, there is simply no possibility of the elision of the *repha*. Furthermore, regarding the position "nor because it is characterized as external" (*nāpi bahiraṅgalakṣaṇatvāt*), some say that the intent of the Bhāṣya is precisely this fault: that since the *anaṅ* (the substitution of *an* for *nakāra*) is caused by the subsequent word (*uttarapada*), it would be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when the internal rule of elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is to be applied; thus, the *nakāra* and *repha* would be heard. This is not correct, however, because the elision of a final conjunct depends upon the designation of both members of the conjunct (*saṃyoga*).

Nor should it be argued that, in view of the requirement for a subsequent word (*uttarapada*), the *pada* designation must also be required for the element *aṅ*; for that [element] is required merely as a constituent of the compound (*samāsāvayava*). This is because the *pada* designation is not accepted anywhere for the final portion of a compound when followed by a *sup* suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). This has been determined in exactly the same way in the *Kaustubha*. Thus, by this logic, even the long *ṛ*-sounds (*ṛkāra*) that are originally acute (*udātta*) and so forth would undergo substitution by *ra* (*raparatva*); such is the direction of the argument.

This might be argued: in cases such as *khaṭvarśyaḥ*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*) would not occur, because [the substitute] does not have the mere vowel *ṛ* as its locus (*sthānin*). This is because, in that context, the entire aggregate (*samudāya*) is accepted as the locus. Nor should it be said that, by the rule "one [substitute] in place of the preceding and following" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*), the aggregate—whose internal distinctions of parts are manifested—is designated; and since the two parts are mutually dependent, they constitute the aggregate, so that the status of the vowel *ṛ* as the locus remains intact. For if this were so, the same *raparatva* would undesirably apply to *ānaṅ* as well, because even there, the constituent part is an *aṇ* (a vowel).

For it would be impossible to prevent the substitution of *ra* for *a* (raparatva) even in the case of an *aṇ* substitute—whether its nature be *aṇ* or non-*aṇ*—if that *aṇ* occupies the same position as both the letter *ṛ* and anything else.
As it has been said: "If it is argued that [the rule applies] because of the mention of a constituent part, then there must be a prohibition regarding a substitute ending in *r*."

Nor should it be argued that because the term *ur* is used to denote the vowel *ṛ*, and because when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned [in a rule] it includes that which ends with it, the substitution of *rapara* (with *r* as the final element) applies to an *aṇ* in place of that which ends in *ṛ*, but not here [in the case of *kartṛ*]. For that would be unestablished in cases such as *kartṛ*; since the genitive in *aṅgasya* restricts [the operation] to the final phoneme of the stem (*aṅga*), and since the rule prescribes *guṇa* substitution for the *ṛ*-vowel itself, whereas that [stem *kartṛ*] does not end in *ṛ*. Nor can there be the treatment of a thing as if it were what it designates (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), because it lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*).

Therefore, it must be stated as an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) that [the substitution of *u*] applies to a single portion [of the compound], and that there is a prohibition of the rule "ṛta ud" in cases such as *mātuḥ*. If this is argued, we say no; for since the two constituent parts themselves possess the status of the substituend (*sthānin*) in the case of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), the status of having *ṛ* as the substituend remains intact. For this very reason, the mention of the singular (*eka*) in that rule was made so that the difference in the substituends does not result in a difference in the substitutes. It is for this same reason that in common usage, Devadatta’s son is designated by both [terms]: "Devadatta’s son" and "Devadatta’s [female] son. Furthermore, in the case of *mātuḥ*, there is no fault even if the substitution of *r* (*raparatva*) were applied.

In the case of *rātsasya*, since the form is established by the elision of the *s* and the substitution of the *visarjanīya* for the *repha*, there is no occurrence of the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) leading to the substitution of *ṣ* in the example *mātuḥ karoti*. This is because the inclusion of the word *bhrātuṣputra* in the *kaskādi* list (Pāṇini 8.3.48) indicates that the *ṣ* substitution does not occur for a *visarjanīya* that follows a substitute resulting from a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule.

This point also should be noted here: when "at the end" (anta) is carried over from the preceding sūtra, this [repha] is a prior-element (pūrvānta); when "at the beginning" (ādi) is carried over, it is a posterior-element (parādi); but when both are carried over, it is possible for it to be non-separable (abhakta). Although in the rule *rapara* the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, nevertheless, because the repha is predominant as the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it should be understood that the quality of being "at the end" is an attribute of that very repha.

Nor should it be argued that since the substitution of *apṛkta* [for *aṇ*] is prescribed specifically for what is *prasajyamāna* (occurring as a suffix), how can there be a suspicion of three alternatives regarding the mere *repha*? This is because this [objection] is resolved by relying on the third alternative. With reference to the last [alternative], the Vārttika states: "When [the augment] is not attached, there is a prohibition of the lengthening, the status of being a *lat*, the *yaṇ*-substitution, the *abhyasta-svara*, the elision of the initial consonant, and the *visarjanīya*; furthermore, there would be a lack of fixed determination regarding the suffix."

In the case of *gīḥ pūḥ*, the long vowel would not occur because the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not end in *r*. [If one were to argue that] the rule applies to a word (*pada*) ending in *r* or *v*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *agniḥ* and *vāyuḥ*. Nor can it be argued that the meaning is "the single substitute for a word ending in *r* or *v* which is a verbal root," because this would lead to an over-extension in cases such as *priyagrāmaṇiḥ* and *priyasenāniḥ*. Furthermore, in the form *nijegilyate*, the substitution of *l* by the rule *gro yaṅi* would not occur, because the term *graḥ* ends in a genitive expressing a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Nor is this a genitive of immediate sequence (*ānantarya-ṣaṣṭhī*).

For [otherwise] the same fault would arise even in the case of *svar-jegilyate*. If, however, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is qualified by the *yaṅ* affix, or if it is stated that the word *graḥ* is in the ablative case (fifth case), then there is no fault. In the case of *gīryate* and *pūryate* [in the sense of] "it swallows itself" or "it fills itself," the accent prescribed by the rule *acaḥ kartṛyaki* would not apply because of the intervention of the letter *r*. This objection is not valid, as in the formulation of accent rules, a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent.

By this, the accentuation in the phrase *mā hi sma te piparuḥ*—whereby the initial syllable of reduplicated forms (*abhyasta*) becomes acute (*udātta*) before a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel—is also explained. Furthermore, in forms such as *vavṛte*, the elision of the *repha* (the *r*) by the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* would not occur, because that rule is prescribed for the first consonant of the reduplicated portion. Moreover, in cases such as *nārkuṭaḥ* and *nārpatyaḥ*, since the word ending in *repha* would be treated as a *pada* (ending in a case-suffix), the *visarga* would arise according to the rules governing case endings (*sup*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Likewise, forms such as *kirataḥ* and *girataḥ* would not be possible.

In the singular form *kirati*, the *vikaraṇa* (the suffix *śap*) must necessarily apply first because it is obligatory; however, the augment *āṅt* is not obligatory, for if the *vikaraṇa* has not yet been applied, the *guṇa* substitution would apply, whereas if it has been applied, the substitution of *it* applies. But in the dual form, since both are obligatory, the *it* substitution takes precedence due to its higher status. Because the *repha* (*r*) is not a part of the suffix (*abhakta*), it does not constitute a constituent of the verbal root (*dhātu*); therefore, the *vikaraṇa* would not apply, as that [suffix] is prescribed only when it follows a verbal root. Nor is the *repha* subsequent to the *vikaraṇa*; even so, it is impossible for it to follow an *aṇ* vowel that stands in the place of the *ṛ*-vowel.

Moreover, being "subsequent" (*paratva*) is not common to [the cases of] intervention (*vyavahita*), because that would leave the desired result unestablished. However, if it were considered "prior" (*pūrvāditva*), then the restriction "in *sup*" (*roḥ supi*) would have to be formulated as: "only for *ru* when followed by *sup*, and not for anything else. This is so that the rule might apply in examples such as *sarpiḥṣu* and *dhanuḥṣu*, but not in examples such as *gīrṣu* and *pūrṣu*. This same fault applies even if [the *ru*] is not part of the suffix (*abhakta*). For, according to the principle of "beginning with that" (*tadādivacanāt*), the portion preceding the suffix—even if the suffix itself is included—would still be considered the end of a word (*padānta*). On the other hand, under the view that it is "subsequent" (*parāditva*), it is not the end of a word because it is part of the case-ending (*subbhakta*); however, in this case, there would be the undesirable consequence of a visarga in *nārkalpiḥ*. As it has been stated in the Bhāṣya:

This [word *nṛkalpa*] is considered a part of a collection of words (*padasaṃghāta*) and is thus unable to set aside the status of its constituent member as being "at the end of a word" (*padāntatā*). Consequently, in the formation of *nṛkalpa* with the suffix *iñ*, there is *vṛddhi*. However, the letter *r* is a constituent of the entire suffix *kalpi*, and not a constituent of the element *kalpa* alone. Thus, when the technical term *pada* is prescribed for what precedes the word *kalpa*, that designation applies to the syllable ending in *r* because of the rule concerning "that which begins with it" (*tadādivacana*); hence, the *visarga* would occur. This is because the *Bhāṣya* explains that the term *pada* refers to the suffix, based on the etymological derivation: "that by which meaning is reached (*padyate*) is a *pada*."

Even when the word *kalpa* follows, although the *repha* (the letter *r*) is situated [therein], it lacks the status of being a constituent part (*avayava*) of that [word]; because of the existence of a temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) between those two, it is illogical for that which is a constituent part of the [word] itself to obstruct its status as a "word-final" (*padānta*). However, if the reading is *kalpapadasaṃghāta*, it should be explained as follows: "that which belongs to the word *kalpa*" refers to the word *nārkalpi*; the "constituent part" of that word is the suffix-cluster *kalpi*, and [the *repha*] is "subordinate to" (*bhakta*) that [cluster]. Therefore, this aforementioned rule must also be commenced for this purpose.

Regarding the word *gīryate*, the accentuation [of the vowel] is unimpeded by the rule "the vowel [is udātta] before a *yak* when it denotes the agent," because it is explained that the root ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) in its original form (*upadeśa*). However, the author of the Vārttika states the defects in the view that the augment (*āT*) is initial (*parādi*): "If it were initial, there would be the elision of the vowel *a*, the substitution of *au*, the prohibition of the *puk* augment, the shortening of the penultimate vowel in the *caṅ* reduplication, uncertainty regarding the augment *iṭ*, the elision of the reduplicated syllable, the designation as 'repeated' (*abhyasta*), and the lengthening of the vowel."

For instance: in the case of *kartā* and *hartā*, there would be the elision of the *akāra* [by P. 6.4.64]. Nor can there be an extension of the term *upadeśa* [from P. 6.4.7 to P. 6.4.64]. Even if the elision of *akāra* did not occur in the singular form *dhinoti*—where [the form] is established either by *ād-guṇaḥ* (P. 6.1.87) or by the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) through the *guṇa* of the vowel *u*—[the forms] *dhinutaḥ* and *kṛṇutaḥ* would still be untenable. However, if the meaning is "that which ends in *akāra* in the *upadeśa* of the *ārddhadhātuka*," then there is no fault. But in the cases of *cakāra* and *jahāra*, the substitution of *aut* [for the final vowel] would occur in the suffix *ṇal*. This fault does not apply because of the principle: "Substitutions apply only to that which is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*)."

Nor does the substitution of *au* for the *repha* (the /r/) follow from the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), because by the word "of the *ṇal*" (*ṇalaḥ*), the application of the substitute is intended to occur after a stem ending in *ā* that is followed by a specific instance of the vowel *a* occurring in actual usage (*prayogasamavāyin*). However, there is no substitute for the *repha*, which is merely inferred;

for in the Bhāṣya, it is stated that "that which is indicated by the genitive" refers to the identity between the signified and the signifier, and thus [the substitute applies] to the mere vowel *a*, which is separated from the *repha*.

If, however, it were stated as "of the affix" (pratyayasya) or "in the case of the *liṭ* suffix," then an undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) would arise: in the form *kārayati*, the augment *puk* would occur because the root ends in a long vowel; and in the form *acīkarat*, the shortening prescribed by the rule "ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ" would not take place, because the letter *r* is treated as following [the root], making it impossible for the vowel *ā* to be designated as the penultimate (*upadhā*).

In forms such as *āstarita*, because the substitution of *guṇa* and the subsequent substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* are obligatory (*nitya*), the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "neḍvaśi kṛti" would apply; or, if *iṭ* were to apply, it would have to precede the *repha*. Thus, the desired grammatical status would be difficult to establish, since both [the *guṇa* and the *ra-ādeśa*] are initial elements [of the suffix]. Furthermore, in forms such as *vavṛte*, the rule "halādiḥ śeṣaḥ" (retention of the first consonant) would not apply, because [the *ra*] would not be a constituent part of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). In the example "mā hi sma te piparuḥ," since the *us* of the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffix begins with a *repha*, it would not be vowel-initial (*aj-ādi*); consequently, the acute accent on the first syllable of the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta-ādyudātta*) would not occur.

In examples such as *prakartā* and *prakartum*, the accent prescribed by the rule "tādau ca niti" would not apply. This fault does not arise, however, because the interpretation is that the rule applies when the *kṛt*-suffix begins with the letter *t* in its original instruction (*upadeśe*). In cases like *gīḥ* and *pūḥ*, if one were to accept that the *repha* (the sound *r*) is a constituent of the *sub* (case-ending) due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*), then after the elision of the suffix by the rule "rātsasya," the lengthening (*dīrgha*) would not occur because that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Therefore, the position of the *pūrvānta* (the suffix being part of the preceding element) alone remains valid; for since the restriction "roḥ supi" has already been introduced, it cannot be the subject of this objection. [The rule] "of the final [al-phoneme]" (Pāṇini 1.1.52).

That which is designated by a genitive of position (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) should be understood as applying to the final [element] of that [which is designated]. [For example: *tyadādīnām aḥ* (the substitute *a* replaces the final element of *tyad* etc.); thus we have *saḥ* (he) and *yaḥ* (who). The term "genitive of position" is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*. Now, one might object: let us explain *al* as being in the nominative plural and take it as a qualifier of the substitute (*ādeśa*). In this way, the meaning would be that a substitute consisting of one or more phonemes (*al-ātmaka*) applies to the final [element], and consequently, the mention of *anekāl* ("consisting of more than one phoneme") in the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya* would not need to be made, resulting in simplicity (*lāghava*).

Not so; for even under the view that the final *viśeṣaṇa* (specifier) is not included [in the definition of *aṅga*], the possibility of rejecting that [final specifier] remains by relying on the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that only that which is *ṅit*—and not that which is *aṅit*—becomes the substitute for the final element of a multi-syllabic stem. Otherwise, in cases such as *virajīkaroti*, the substitution of elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule "arurmanaścakṣuścetorahorajasām" would result in being a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), because it would not be *an-antya* (not non-final). This should be understood to apply similarly to the rules "pādaśatasya" and "ḍhe lopaḥ". Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitute applying to the very end of a word (*pada*).

Furthermore, the substitution of *d* prescribed by the rule *vasusraṃsu-dhvaṃsv-an-ta-raṭ-nuḍ-vāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.72), which is formulated under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *padasya*, would apply to the entire word *anuḍuh* in the form *paramānaḍudbhyām*. Moreover, the inclusion of the term *anekāl* ("having more than one letter") is necessary in both views; otherwise, when there is a reference to the ablative case as in *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), even a substitute with more than one letter would affect only the first letter of the original element, according to the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54).

Nor should one argue that the fault [of over-extension] regarding *ais* is avoided by interpreting the rule *ādeḥ parasya* as follows: by carrying forward the word *al* from the previous rule as a nominative (*prathamānta*), one explains that the *al* prescribed for what follows shall belong to the beginning; thus, since *ais* does not consist of vowels (*analtvāt*), the fault is precluded. This cannot be said, because in the derivation of *bhūmā* (the state of being much) from *bahu* with the suffix *imanic*, the elision of the vowel *i* would be untenable. Furthermore, if that [interpretation] were present, the substitution of the whole (*sarvādeśa*) would be established by its priority over the prohibition of the exception (*apavāda-pratiṣedha*).
And this is the meaning here: the genitive case, which has been determined as having the sense of "in place of" (*sthāneyoga*), is extended by this [rule] to the final vowel (*antye’li*).

Alternatively: "That which is a determined (niścita) substitute (ādeśa) occurs in place of the final *al*. For if there were merely a reference to the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [without the restriction of "determined"], then even those suffixes marked with the markers *ṭ*, *k*, or *m* would result in being considered final constituents (*antyāvayava*). Consequently, the augment *iṭ* prescribed by the rule "ārddhadhātukasya" would precede the *ṛ* of the suffix *tṛc*, and the *puK* augment in forms such as *dāpayati* would become a final constituent of the vowel *ā*. In that case, the principle "an augment (*āgama*) belongs only to that which possesses meaning" would be contradicted. Therefore, this [sūtra] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the rule "the genitive denotes the relation of 'in place of' (*sthāneyoga*)."

In this context, the reading [of the rule] beginning with "ṅicca" is for the purpose of establishing a connection. Furthermore, one should not raise the objection that the meaning is: "Whatever genitive case occurs in the treatise refers to the final phoneme, and that [genitive] is connected only to the *sthāna* (the locus of substitution)," because if one were to accept such a retrospective application (*anusaṃhāra*) after the knowledge that it is a *sthāneyoga*, there would be an excessive burden on the cognition (*pratipattigaurava*). This is because the same defect would persist in the case of suffixes marked with the markers *ṭ*, *k*, and *m*.

For instance: by the two rules "ādyantau ṭakitau" (P. 1.1.46) and "midaco'ntyātparaḥ" (P. 1.1.47), the relation of *sthāneyoga* (substitution for a specific position) alone would be sublated; this is because, due to their homogeneous nature, it is specifically that [particular] relationship which is sublated. However, the actual form of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) remains established with respect to the final phoneme (*al*). As for the subsequent application (*anusaṃhāra*), there is no fault, as it is sublated by other subsequent applications such as "ādeḥ parasya" (P. 1.1.54) and "anekālśit sarvasya" (P. 1.1.55). [Rule 1.1.53: "And [a substitute] marked with Ṅ replaces the final [phoneme]. (Ṅicca 52)

Even when it consists of more than one letter, a substitute marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter (*ṅit*) shall replace only the final letter [of the original]. For example, in *dadhnā*, the substitution of *anaṅ* for the entire stem occurs according to the rule *asthidadhi...* [Pāṇini 7.1.75], yet this applies only to the final vowel *i*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that *tātaṅ* (the substitute for *ta*) would also replace only the final letter; for while *anaṅ* and others serve their purpose through having a *ṅ* indicatory letter for no other reason, this rule [regarding *ṅit* substitutes] is superseded by the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.55] because *tātaṅ* is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. And one should not ask how there can be a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) in this case;

for since the *ṅ* indicatory letter is justified as being for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [as in the case of *anaṅ*], it is uncertain whether this [present rule regarding *ṅit* substitutes] would apply there [to *tātaṅ*].

Nor should it be argued that, since there is no status as a suffix (*pratyaya*) without being a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatva*), the purpose of [the marker *ṅ*] being the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would be difficult to establish, and thus there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). This is because, immediately after the rule "eruḥ," when the substitution of *tād-* is to be applied, the fact that the application of the marker *ṅ* serves the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is determined.
[Pāṇini 1.1.54: "ādeḥ parasya. (The substitute takes the place of the initial element of that which follows.)

That which is prescribed by a rule stated in the ablative case (pañcamī-nirdeśa) should be understood as applying to the vowel following that [ablative element]. In the rule *īdāsaḥ* ("ī for *ās*"), the phrase *tasmādityuttarasya* ("from that, of what follows") is supplied. By this, the vowel *i* replaces the vowel *ā*. Thus: *āsīnaḥ*. In the word *dvīpam*—meaning "that in which water has gone twice"—the suffix *ap* is added as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*. The substitution of *ī* for the word *āp* following *dvi*, *antar*, or a preposition (*upasarga*), as prescribed by the rule *dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ*, is thus established for the initial vowel *ā*.

It might be argued as follows: since there would be the disadvantage of having to include both the word *uttara* from the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* and the word *para* from the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, let the formulation simply be *tasmādityuttarasyādeḥ*. In that case, *ādeḥ* would be a separate sentence; the word *uttarasya* would be carried over (*anuvartate*) from the previous rule, and that genitive case would be used in the sense of "in place of" (*sthāneyoga*). This is because, even though the subsequent technical term (*paribhāṣā*) [stating that a genitive denotes the "place of"] does not apply here due to the context of a restatement (*anuvāda*), its meaning is obtained either through the continued application of the word *sthāne* from elsewhere, or because there is no other result [for it].

And thus, by the mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*), the meaning—understood through the unification of both [rules]—is that whatever operation is prescribed by such a mention pertains to what follows, and being ordained in place of what follows, it should be understood as applying to the initial element (*ādi*). Furthermore, due to the force of the syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), in rules such as *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ*, the first sentence-meaning alone operates even when the second part is deficient. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this syntactical split; for the evidence is the non-compounded mention *uttarasyādeḥ*. Otherwise, he would have simply said *uttarādeḥ*.

Nor should it be argued that, if the second part were to function independently—just as the first part was deficient—then in the rule *nityaṃ ṅitaḥ* ("there is always elision of the final letter of a ṅit ending"), the elision would apply to the entire ṅit ending in the first person plural (the suffixes *vas* and *mas*, which end in *s*), resulting in forms such as *bhaveva*, *bhavema*, *bhūyāstva*, and *bhūyāsma* where the initial *i*, *u*, and so on, of the first person endings would be elided rather than the final *s* according to the *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the elision of the final letter).

Because at the time of understanding the meaning of the second sentence, the understanding of the first sentence has already arisen, and there is no evidence for its abandonment, it is impossible for an operation to occur that is deficient in its initial portion. Furthermore, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only the substitute (*ādeśa*) introduced by the preceding rule can be accepted. Thus, in the very sūtra "tasmādityuttarasya," the word *ādeḥ* (of the beginning) should be read as an addition, and the sūtra "ādeḥ parasya" should be discarded; this is the meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the previously mentioned placement [of the rule] should occur before the sūtra *anekāl-śit sarvasya*; for in that case, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *nirdiṣṭa* would not be established. However, according to the stated method, its recurrence is secured from the sūtra *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya*, which constitutes a difference [between the two cases]. Nor should it be argued that that sūtra (*tasminniti...*) should also be brought down (*apakarṣa*) to this very point.

Nevertheless, because of the association with rules such as "ṅicca," there arises the implication that when a grammatical operation is prescribed by means of a locative or ablative case ending, it must be understood to apply in place of both the preceding and the following elements indicated by a genitive case ending. Furthermore, this fault is particularly prominent in rules such as "sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ" and "gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ.

Others, however, argue that if that were the case, the rule "tasmādityuttarasya" would be sublated by the rule "anekāl-śit sarvasya" due to its superior status (paratva); consequently, in the example "brāhmaṇā aṣṭau," there would result the undesirable application of the substitution of "auś" for the preceding *jaś* and *śas* endings after the word "aṣṭan."

Others, however, maintain that this is not correct; for since the base (*prakṛti*) is implied by the [suffixes] *jaś* and *śas*, and the *aṅga* is also in close proximity, only the word *aṣṭan* is understood. Even though the rule "of all" (*sarvasya*) applies, there remains the necessity of doubt as to whether it refers to the preceding or the following element; thus, there is no obstacle to the application of the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "from that [element], the subsequent [element is affected]."

By the term "of all" (*sarvasya*), the status of having only a single substitute as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*) is excluded; and by the rule "thereafter, of the subsequent" (*tasmād uttarasya*), the status of having the preceding element as its counter-correlative is excluded. Thus, there is no contradiction because their scopes (*viṣaya*) differ. Furthermore, since the rule "of all" would otherwise have no scope for application, it would lack its intended purpose (*caritārthatva*) in rules such as "in that" (*tasmin*) and "thereafter" (*tasmāt*).

They say that this is because the rule "in that" (*tasmin*) applies in cases such as *jarāyā jaras* ("jarā becomes *jaras*"), while the rule "thereafter" (*tasmāt*) applies in cases such as *parasmaipadānāṃ ṇalatusus* ("for the parasmaipada endings, *ṇal*, *atus*, etc.").

In this regard, the following must be considered: In the rule *aṣṭābhya auś*, if the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* ("from that [which is mentioned in the ablative], the subsequent [element]") were not present, then given the sentence-meaning "after *aṣṭan*, for both the preceding and the following [elements] beginning with *jas*, there is *auś*," the substitution would apply to both. Since there would be no doubt regarding the status of both as substituends (*sthānin*), the application of the rule *tasmād* would be difficult to establish. Furthermore, a distinction of scope (*viṣayabheda*) is also untenable.

For here, since the portion *ādeḥ* has a scope of application, when it operates, there is indeed a conflict between it and the [rule] *sarvasya*. This is because we do not admit the operation of *ādeḥ* when deprived of its first part; thus, a separate conflict between *sarvasya* and the first part need not be considered. Nor should it be argued that even if the first part—which forms a single syntactical unit with [the rule for] *sarvasya*—is sublated by *sarvasya* due to a specific contradiction, it would nevertheless operate again independently.

In rules such as *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ*, since there is no scope for the second part [of the rule], that [rule] has already fulfilled its purpose by operating therein; therefore, there is no evidence for its independent operation after having sublated the second part with which it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). By this, the objection that the rule *sarvasya* lacks a field of application (*cāritārthya*) outside the scope of those two sūtras is also refuted; for its utility is clearly established in instances excluded from the second part forming a single unit with it, such as *asterbhūḥ*.

Since there is no harm even if the rule "tasmād ity uttarasya" (P. 1.1.67) were to be subsumed under the term "sarvasya" (P. 1.1.55) alone—because the intended fault is avoided simply by applying the rule to a domain that excludes the second part qualified by that [first part]—one might argue that there is no defect even in the formulation "tasmād ity uttarasyādeḥ. To this, it is replied:

If this were the case, the portion [of the rule] beginning with *satyādeḥ* would sublate the portion *sarvasya*, because it is subsequent. Consequently, the substitute *auś* would apply to the letter *a* alone. This is because the rule *sarvasya* finds its scope of application in examples such as *jarāyā jaras*, while the present rule (*anekāl-śit sarvasya*) finds its scope in examples such as *bahoḥ lopaḥ*.
*anekāl-śit sarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55).

An *ādeśa* (substitute) consisting of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) is marked with the indicator *ś* (*śit*), and thus, according to one view, it would replace the whole [of the original]. For example: *aster bhūḥ* [becomes] *bhavitā*; *idama iś* [becomes] *itaḥ*. Here, by the rule *halantyam*, the *it*-designation is established because the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*) is not required; consequently, since the status of being *śit* is established even without the status of being a total replacement (*sarvādeśatva*), the mention of *anekāl* was stated previously for the purpose of prohibiting exceptions (*apavāda*).

As for the example given for the *śit* [suffix] in the rule "jaśśasoḥ śiḥ," that is questionable. For the status of being *śit* cannot be established except through its being a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*). Indeed, if it were a universal substitute, then by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the technical designation of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) would apply [to the substitute]; however, since a single part of a suffix cannot be considered a suffix, it is illogical for its substitute to be a suffix. Consequently, the designation *it* would apply via the rule "laśakvataddhite," and subsequently there would be elision (*lopa*), because the letter *ś* has already served its purpose in effecting the status of being a multi-alphabetic element (*anekāl*).

Therefore, even though [the substitute] consists of a single phoneme (*ekāl*), there is no loss of its status as a *sarvādeśa* (total replacement), because that would contradict what it depends upon (*upajīvya*). Consequently, in this case, it is precisely because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) that it is a total replacement. Nor does this render the mention of *śit* (having *ś* as an indicatory letter) redundant in rules such as *śi* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), since its purpose is to indicate the principle: "The status of having more than one phoneme is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). By virtue of this, in cases such as *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131) and *arvaṇas tṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.127), there is no total replacement.

However, if one holds the position that the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are non-exclusive (*anekānta*), then the aforementioned indication is not purposeful. The inclusion of the letter *ś* [in the term *śit*] is for the sake of ensuring that the *lopa* (elision) in the rule "ghvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca" is a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), by interpreting the *śit*-ness—which was applied to the technical name (*saṃjñā*)—as being useful for the named entity (*saṃjñin*) itself, since it is of no use there; this is analogous to the *ṭit*-ness of the augment *ṅamuṭ*.

According to the view of the *Vārttika*, however, the rule is established simply by the principle: "In the case of a meaningless element, the operation [prescribed] for the final letter does not apply. Nor is there an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the phrase "not a modification of the reduplicated form," because in rules such as "for the roots *bhṛ* etc., *i*" (*bhṛñām it*), only a modification in the form of a positive addition (*bhāva-rūpa*) is mentioned; whereas elision (*lopa*) is not of that nature. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* in the *Paspaśā* section is consistent when it states: "Elision is a modification of the phoneme. Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the *Pṛṣodarādi* rule, states: "And there are two others: modification and destruction of the phoneme."

As for the argument that even under the view of absolute unity (*ekāntapakṣa*), the designation (*saṃjñā*) occurs precisely at the stage of instruction because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), and that—according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—only those suffixes (*anubandhas*) which are remembered as perishing immediately upon being uttered can effect the grammatical operation; and thus, since a substitute such as *tṛ-au-t* would not be subject to the contingency of becoming a "total replacement" (*sarvādeśa*) due to its having a single phoneme (*ekāl*) at the time of its application, the previously mentioned indication (*jñāpana*) is redundant, and all the more so the mention of *śit*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that substitutes like *iś* and *īś* would also fail to be total replacements.

In that case, since elision (*lopa*) has not yet occurred at the outset, the pronunciation of the letter *ś* possesses the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) [to prevent elision]. Nor does the objection raised by Haradatta—that even if the universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) were applied, there would be no occasion for the *ś* to receive the technical designation *it* due to a lack of purpose—apply here; for elision itself serves as the purpose. Furthermore, the pronunciation is not redundant, as it serves a purpose by effecting the status of being a universal substitute. Therefore, the intention of both the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Bhāṣya in this matter must be considered. But that [objection] is to be reconsidered; for just as other grammatical operations are triggered by the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) as they are remembered, so too the property of having "more than one *al*" (*anekāl*) would be unavoidable.

As for the argument that, having read the rule *nānekāl śit* and continuing with the phrase *antyasyādeḥ*, one could omit the word *sarvasya* in the prohibition of the two subsequent applications (*anusaṃhāra*), that too must be considered carefully; for the resulting heaviness of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*) is unavoidable. To explain: by the mention of the genitive case of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), an operation being prescribed is established as applying to the whole [of the substitute] precisely because there is no restrictive factor (*vinigamaka*). That [application to the whole] is then set aside by the rule *alo’ntyasya*, which prescribes the operation for the final [element].

Regarding that [substitute], there are two exceptions: "ādeḥ parasya" and "anekāl". The established fact is that "ṅicca" is an exception to "anekāl". According to the method of formulation mentioned above, if a substitute consisting of more than one phoneme (anekāl) and one ending in ṅ (ṅit) were not to replace both the initial and the final [of the element for which they are prescribed], then even though the negation of being related to only a part of the whole is stated as the meaning of the sentence, it is nevertheless necessary to keep in mind the relation to the whole (sarvapratiyogikatva) established by logic. Therefore, for the sake of brevity, it is more appropriate to simply state "sarvasya" (of the whole).
Thus ends the seventh Āhnika of the first Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the Śrī Siddhāntasudhānidhi.

*Sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56): An *ādeśa* (substitute) functions like the *sthānin* (original element), except in operations concerning vowels (*al-vidhi*). This means that it itself undergoes its own grammatical operation and also causes the operation belonging to the original element to take effect; this is because similarity is based on the capacity to undergo grammatical operations. This capacity to undergo operations consists of two forms: being the object of that operation and being the cause of it. For instance, in *kena*, *kābhyām*, and so on, the substitute *kā-* for *kim* undergoes the operation pertaining to the *aṅga* (stem). However, in *vṛkṣāya* and so on, the substitute *yā-* for *ṅe* causes the lengthening of the *aṅga* to take effect; such is the distinction.

The meaning is that if a property is the counter-positive of an absence which serves as the cause for the non-occurrence of the application of an *upadeśa* (original form), and if that property is not unique to the *sthānin* (the element undergoing substitution) and the *al* (the substitute), [then the rule does not apply].

[Objection: One might argue that in the case of *vṛkṣāya*, since the substituendum (*sthānin*) is the single phoneme *e* (ekāra), which is not an *al*, the property of being like the substituendum (*sthānivadbhāva*) should not apply. [Response: This is not so. For here, the non-application of the rule *supi ca* is caused by the fact that the substitute (*yādeśa*) lacks the status of being a *sup* (case-ending). It is for this purpose that the extension (*atideśa*) is followed. And although the status of being a *sup* resides in the *al* consisting of the single phoneme *e*, nevertheless, it is not exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) to that *al*. This is because in forms such as *bhyām*, the status of being a *sup* resides only in the entire aggregate (*samudāya*), and thus it does not reside in the *al* alone.

[Objection: Even so, the property of "not occurring in any letter other than an *al*" remains unimpaired; however, such letters are not established [as a class]. [Reply: This is not so. For its meaning is: "the state of having a locus for the distribution (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatā*) of itself, which is pervaded by the locus for the distribution of *altva*. Indeed, where there is a locus for the distribution of *suptva* (the state of being a word) in a collection such as *abhyām*, there is no locus for the distribution of *altva*; because *altva* is pervaded by each individual [letter].

[Objection: But surely, in the case of [the substitution of] *dīrgha* (long vowel) when a suffix beginning with *yañ* follows, because the rule depends on an *al* (vowel), the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) should still not apply; [Response: Not so. For this very reason, the *al* is qualified by its relationship to the *sthānin*. Indeed, in this case, there is no absence of the application of the original instruction (*upadeśa*) for the substitute *yā* that is caused by the absence of the property of beginning with *yañ* in the original. This is because that [substitute] is inherently one that begins with *yañ*. By this, the augment *iṭ* in forms such as *aruditām* and *aruditam*—by the rule "after roots beginning with *rud*, before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"—is also explained.

This is because the property of being a *sārvadhātuka*—which is the counter-positive of the absence that serves as the cause for the non-application of the *upadeśa* (original form)—does not reside solely in the aforementioned *al* (vowels); furthermore, the property of beginning with a *val* (consonant) exists naturally in the substitutes such as *tām* and others. Nor should it be argued that if one were to resort to an *al* belonging to the substitute without distinction, the aforementioned prohibition would apply; for a prohibition that has entered into a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with a rule of extended application (*atideśa*) operates only with respect to that which is obtained through such extension.

Therefore, in the extended injunction (atideśa), "One should behave toward the son of the guru as toward the guru himself, except for eating his leftovers and clasping his feet," the prohibition of eating leftovers and so forth—which was already established by the extension itself—applies specifically to the eating of leftovers and such acts, but not to those acts [of eating leftovers] that were established by the original injunction (upadeśa). This is because, even though the status of being a "guru" exists in the case of the guru's son, the eating of his leftovers and so forth would proceed based on that [status of being a guru].

Nor should it be argued that while there is not even a partial requirement for extension (*atideśa*) in that case, here, however, such dependence is necessary for the application of the augment *iṭ* due to the absence of the status of being a *sārvadhātuka*. For the relationship of the dependent and the supported (*upajīvya-upajīvaka-bhāva*) does not serve as a determinant in every respect. In forms such as *pradīvyet*, however, because the substitute *lyap* itself lacks the property of beginning with a *val* consonant, the non-application [of the rule] caused by that [property] would also follow; thus, the prohibition applies in accordance with the extension even for the sake of [preserving] the status of beginning with a *val* consonant.

Even if one resorts to [the suffix] as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*), its application will be explained later. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the *kit* status would also not be obtained; for under the view that the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are non-exclusive (*anekāntapakṣa*), they lack the status of being *al*-segments belonging to the substituend (*sthānin*). Even under the view that they are exclusive (*ekāntapakṣa*), because of their *antaranga* nature, they are elided even earlier; thus, at the time of the substitution, there is no connection with them. For this very reason, the prohibition "not before *ya*" (*nalyapi*) is consistent; otherwise, since *it* would not apply due to the absence of *kit* status, that prohibition would be redundant.

This very point serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) even for the extension of a specific rule (*viśeṣātideśa*). Otherwise, since a specific rule would not be extended when there is an extension of a general rule (*sāmānyātideśa*), the extension of *kittva* (the status of having the marker *k*) would not occur in forms such as *pradīvya*, because *kittva* is not a property common to all *ktvā* suffixes; for its prohibition occurs in certain instances by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" ("*ktvā* with the augment *iṭ* is not [treated as having *k*]"). For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the rule "āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca" ("in the sense of expectation, like the past") is an extension only of the *luṅ* (aorist) tense—since that is prescribed in the general category of the past—and not of the *luṅ* and *liṭ* (perfect), which are prescribed for specific types of the past. However, the ancients (*prāñcaḥ*) say that the very prohibition "analvidhau" ("not in the prescription of an operation concerning a letter") is the indicator for the extension of a specific rule.

As for the claim that in examples such as *vyūḍhoraskeṇa* and *ka iṣṭaḥ*, the prohibition [contained in the rule] *analvidhau* (P. 1.1.56) has its purpose fulfilled by prohibiting *aṭtva* and *haśtva*, which are the pervaders (*vyāpaka*) of *visargatva* and *yatva* respectively; that is to be considered doubtful. For, in comparison with *visargatva* and *yatva*, *aṭtva* and *haśtva* are specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*), and thus their occurrence would be impossible without a specific extension (*viśeṣātideśa*).

If it is argued that *aṭ*-ness (*aṭ-tva*) and *haś*-ness (*haś-tva*) are general properties (*sāmānya-dharma*), because while residing in all individual phonemes delimited by *visarga*-ness and *yakāra*-ness, they also reside in those beyond them; whereas *visarga*-ness and *yakāra*-ness are particular properties (*viśeṣa-dharma*), because they are counter-correlatives of absolute non-existence residing in those phonemes other than *visarga* and *yakāra* which are delimited by *aṭ*-ness and *haś*-ness—then this is not so.

For in this context, neither "universality"—defined as the state of not being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in some individual delimited by that form—nor "particularity"—defined as the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in some individual delimited by that form—is intended; for there is a lack of evidence [for such definitions].

However, in an extended application rule (*atideśavākya*), is it the state of being a general property (*sāmānyatva*) that constitutes the delimitor of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedakatva*) of the suffix *-vat*? For in such cases as "one should behave toward this Kṣatriya as toward a Brāhmaṇa," the understanding occurs precisely in that manner. And thus, in the resulting extended application rule, "the *sakāra* is like the *visarga*," since it is the status of being a *visarga* (*visargatva*) and so forth that possesses that character, there is no extended application of the status of being an *aṭ* (*aṭtva*) and the like. Even though individual instances are subsumed under the categories of "original element" (*sthānitva*) and "substitute" (*ādeśatva*) within the sūtra, the extended application rules themselves differ according to the distinction between the original element and its substitute.

As for the claim that the *kit* status is not a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) of *ktvā*, that is incorrect. By the rule "na ktvā seṭ," although the operation of being *kit* is prohibited, the *it*-designation of the letter *k* is not prohibited. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the sound of *k* in that instance. Nor can it be argued that because only the letter *k* is to be extended (*atideśya*), it functions as the cause for the application of the *kit* operation and thus is not a general property of *ktvā*; for such an objection would leave the flaw as it was.

Even for those duties (*dharma*) that proceed on the basis of being a Brāhmaṇa, there is no rule that they must apply specifically as delimited by the property of being a Brāhmaṇa, because they are absent in cases such as a fallen (*patita*) Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, this is equally applicable even when the result is not produced due to an obstruction, since the state of being delimited by the specific form that serves as the cause for those respective effects certainly exists therein. Therefore, it is established that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) indeed occurs in instances such as *vṛkṣāya*.

Although, according to the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) view, when a substitute (*yādeśa*) is applied, only the technical designation *sup* is extended by atideśa—since that too is based on a formal rule (*śāstrīya*), and thus there is no possibility of suspecting it to be an *al-vidhi* (an operation dependent on a phoneme)—the lengthening is established by the very instruction "supi ca. Nevertheless, this was stated with reference to the *yathoddeśa* (time-of-enunciation) view.

Furthermore, the suffix *vati* would be redundant; for even without *vati*, the meaning of that [suffix] is understood when another word is employed in place of another, as seen in rules such as "the *liṭ* [affix] is *kit* after a root ending in a non-conjunct consonant," in common usage such as "the face is the moon," and in other systems such as "he performs the *Agnihotra* for a month. Nor does the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the term for the substitute (*ādeśa*) and the term for the original (*sthānin*) entail that the substitute takes on the nature of the original, for that would render the rule prescribing the substitute useless. Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) based on the authority of two statements.

Otherwise, the rule *vā liṭi* would be redundant. Nor can it be argued that this rule is for the purpose of restriction—meaning that the substitution of *khyāñ* for *cakṣiṅ* occurs only in the *liṭ* (perfect)—because the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) in rules such as *vibhāṣā luṅ-lṛṅoḥ* would then be redundant; for since this is an option where [the substitution] was not otherwise established, the desired result is achieved simply by the prescription of the *khyāñ* substitution itself. Furthermore, once the two forms are established through *asti* and *bhū*, the rule *asterbhūḥ* and others would likewise be rendered redundant.

On this point, they say: if that were the case, the original element (*sthānin*) would become the name (*saṃjñā*) for the substitute (*ādeśa*), because the present context concerns rules defining names. Consequently, in the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would apply only to the root *vadhi* and not to *han*. Nor can it be argued that the actual form (*svarūpa*) itself is also included, because of the prohibition: "not when it is a grammatical technical term" (*aśabdasaṃjñā*). Furthermore, one should not claim that such being the case, the substitute would incur the fault of being mentioned first [as the named], since it is the object to be designated; for according to the view that "the restriction is for the sake of linguistic usage," it is the name itself that is the object to be designated.

Nor should it be said that one should use only the root *vadhi* [in this context], for then there would be the undesirable consequence of including the root *vadha* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* (meaning "to injure"). Even if the meaning were "the designation of the substitute belongs to the original base (*sthānin*)," then in the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ*, the word *khyāti* would necessarily include only the root *cakṣiṅ*; consequently, *aṅ* would apply in *samacakṣiṣṭa*, but would not apply in *akhyata*, which is an unacceptable result that cannot be avoided.

If it is argued that one should simply say *cakṣiṅ* because the mention of the suffix (*anubandha*) excludes the *yaṅ*-luṅ form, that is true; nevertheless, in the rule *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ...* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), in order to capture the vowel *iṅ*, one must refer to the mere substituendum (*sthānin*), and thus it should have been stated as *iṅ*. However, in the rule *gameḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.58), there would be the inclusion of only these three: *iṇ* (to go), *iṅ* (to study), and *ik* (to remember).

Because there are many original elements (*sthānin*), the apprehension of the substitute (*ādeśa*) as being identical in form to the root *gam* would result in an erroneous sense of weightiness (i.e., it would be understood as the specific root *gam* rather than a general substitute), and thus it could not serve as the basis for the designation [of the term "substitute"]. Nor should it be argued that this rule should instead be formulated in a separate section, on the grounds of the economy resulting from abandoning the use of the suffix *-vat*; for if that were the case, since the mention of the word "substitute" (*ādeśa*) would be mandatory, its purpose of including inferential substitutes (*anumānika-ādeśa*) would be untenable.
Furthermore, even if one were to grant that the suffix *-vat* is extended to both the existent and the non-existent—as will be stated later—that too would be impossible without the suffix *-vat*.

It might be argued: "If this is so, how is an extended application (*atideśa*) obtained elsewhere in the section on technical names (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*) without the suffix -vatī, as in the case of *kit-ṅit* and so forth? This is not correct. For by the prohibition "not [before] *tkā* or a root with the augment *iṭ*" (*na tkā seṭ*), it is established that *kit*-ness does not possess the status of a technical name (*saṃjñātva*). Since that [term *kit*] has not attained the status of a technical name, it cannot be the object of a prohibition. Nor can it be said that the prohibition applies to what was already applicable by rules such as "mṛḍamṛda," and that an option (*vikalpa*) should be allowed based on the authority of both statements.

In examples such as *mṛḍa*, that [result] is possible by the very mention of the option (*vāvacana*) alone; furthermore, rules such as *niṣṭhā śīṅ* would otherwise be rendered useless, because no one could apply the designation *kit* there. For this very reason, the designation *ṅit* is also an extended application (*atideśa*), due to its association with *kit*. If it were a technical name (*saṃjñā*), then in the rule *grahijyādi*, only this [present case] would have to be included; consequently, since *samprasāraṇa* would not apply in *vāvaśyate*, the prohibition *na vaśaḥ* would result in being redundant.

In the rule *kṅiti ca*, since the terms *kit* and *ṅit* must necessarily be understood as referring to the technical definitions (*saṃjñā*), the actual forms of those definitions are not uttered there; therefore, the aforementioned technical names are not grasped in that context. Furthermore, in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ*, the inclusion of the term *kuṭādi* would otherwise be redundant. However, in the rule *bahugaṇa*, an extension (*atideśa*) applies because of the employment of a major technical name (*mahāsaṃjñā*). In rules such as *kikinau liṭ ca*, however, no such extension applies because they do not occur within the section dealing with technical names (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*); this is the general direction of the argument.

Is not the inclusion of the term *ādeśa* (substitute) redundant? For since the word *sthānin* (original) is inherently relational, the meaning is obtained by the expression *sthānivat* alone—just as when one says "he studies like his father," it is understood that he studies "like his son. True. However, if that were the case, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* would apply only to an overt substitute such as *bhū* [for] *as*, and not to an inferred substitute such as *tu* [for] *ti*. It is precisely by the force of including the term *ādeśa* that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* applies in both instances.

And thus, there is the economy [of effort] that a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for "that which is modified in one part" is unnecessary.
