For instance, in the rule *eruḥ*, by means of the vowels *i* and *u*—which serve as both the substituends (*sthānin*) and the substitutes (*ādeśa*)—those [elements] ending in them are inferred. Consequently, the resulting meaning is *testuḥ*. Nor should it be argued that even if only the vowel *i* were changed to *u*, the designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) would still apply because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]; for the relation between substituend and substitute rests only upon that which possesses meaning.

The position [of the opponent] takes the form of an objection (*prasaṅga*), because it is untenable if [the substitution] were meaningless; for a linguistic application (*prayoga*) intended for communication is possible only when it possesses meaning. This is because, in rules such as *cleḥ sic*, even in the absence of that [meaningful element], its presence is possible, and thus its abandonment would be improper. As it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika:
"All substitutions are replacements of entire words for Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī; for if there were a modification of only a single part, permanence (*nityatva*) would not be tenable."

The word *pada* is meaningful in this context. Thus, in reality, there is no modification (*vikāra*) at all; rather, the sense is that in such a usage, one [form] should be employed in place of another, and according to the meaning of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), this consists merely of the mental cognition of the disappearance of the original element (*sthānin*) and the appearance of the substitute (*ādeśa*).
Or, as the Vārttika states: "Or, because of the transformation of the effect" (*kāryavipariṇāmāt*).

Here, the term *kārya* (effect) refers to cognition. Consequently, the resulting meaning is that the status of being an original element (*sthānitva*) consists in being the counter-positive of an absence conditioned by that rule, while the status of being a substitute (*ādeśatva*) consists in being the object of a rule that causes the absence of that [original element].

Now, one might argue that even when there is an exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*) would still apply; for since the prescription of something else occurs in the context of another, the status of being a substitute (*sthānin*) exists there as well. Consequently, even from a word ending in the suffix *kap*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would arise by virtue of its being considered to end in *aṇ*, and so it would be in other cases too. To this, the Vārttika states:
"But [the desired result] is established by the statement that what is designated by the genitive case [as the element to be replaced] is treated like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*)."

The meaning is that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is carried over from the rule "ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā" (Pāṇini 1.1.49). Furthermore, because an exception (*apavāda*) does not apply to a position (*sthāna*) specified by the genitive. In rules such as "nābhi nabhaṃ ca," the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. As for *viśravaṇa*, *ravaṇa*, and so forth, these are entirely distinct words belonging to the domain of suffixes (*pratyaya*). However, no suffix is added to the word *viśravas* due to the lack of traditional usage (*anabhidhāna*).

By this, the Bhāṣya on the rule regarding the technical term *vṛddhi*—which states that "substitutes occur in the place of that which is designated by the genitive"—is explained exactly as it was heard [by Patañjali]. Kaiyaṭa, however, has explained it with the intent that "only that which is capable of expressing the meaning of the original element (*sthānin*) is a substitute. His intention is as follows:

In the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, it is stated that in the rule *sthānivat*, the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has been removed. Nor does there arise the contingency of the general rule (*utsarga*) applying even where an exception (*apavāda*) exists; for, by the addition of the marker *ś* in *śyan* and other such exceptions (such as *śap*), it is made known that the general rule does not apply. Otherwise, the refutation (*pratyākhyāna*) of the sūtra *sanādyantā* would be untenable. This is likewise the case in this present sūtra.

Now, let there be the designation *śit* for the purpose of excluding *pit*. But surely that [exclusion] is already established by the designation *nit* alone? Indeed, that [designation *nit*] is for the sake of making the initial syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). However, if it were *pit*, then by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the *vikaraṇa* would also be so; consequently, by the rule "the *sārvadhātuka* substitutes for *l* are *anudātta* when following a root ending in *tās*, *an*, *udātta-less*, or *ṅit*" (P. 6.1.186), the *sārvadhātuka* suffix would be *anudātta*. Thus, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the acute accent would belong to the root itself. Therefore, [the designation *śit* is necessary].

Since there is no root (dhātu) with more than one vowel in the *divādi* class, it would be impossible to state that the *niṭ* designation is for the purpose of making [the word] have the udātta accent on the first syllable—given that the udātta accent on the final syllable would otherwise apply by the rule of the root-accent (*dhātusvara*). Nor can the root *vāvṛtu* in the sense of "turning" (*varttane*) be considered multivocalic; for in that case, the word *vā* functions as an optional marker for the *śyan* suffix and is therefore not included within the root itself.
Consequently: "Then, while turning away, she gazed at Rāma’s hall."

Thus, as in the usage of Bhaṭṭi, by relying on the word *vā* in the sense of *iva*, the meaning is "desiring as it were. Nor is that [meaning] established merely from its inclusion in the *bhūv-ādi* group; for its inclusion there is also justified as being for the sake of internal-group operations (*antargaṇakārya*), such as those prescribed by the rule "after roots beginning with *vṛt*, before *syas* and *san*" (*vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ*). This is not so. For the marker *niṭ* (the *n* in *kāmayamāna*) serves a purpose: it ensures that the base (*prakṛti*) is udātta-accented when the suffix *cānaś* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and so forth. Since the suffix *cānaś* is not a substitute for a *l*-suffix (*lādeśa*), the general rule for unaccented endings (*anudātta*) does not apply; consequently, by the accent rule for *cit* suffixes (*citsvara*), the final syllable would otherwise result in being udātta. By making the base udātta, the *niṭ* marker prevents this.

Nor is it the case that, even though *śyan* is marked with *ni*, the accent of the *cit* suffix would be unavoidable; for the accent of the *ni*-marker (*nitsvara*) is subsequently prescribed (*satiśiṣṭa*). Nor does the exclusion rule (*paryudāsa*) "except for [suffixes] having a *vikaraṇa*" apply here. This is because, according to the principle "locative cases [referring to suffixes] belong to those ending in them," this accent belongs to that which ends in a *vikaraṇa*, and not to the *vikaraṇa* itself; thus, that rule does not operate. But if this is so, does it not contradict the Bhāṣya on the *ghu*-designation rule, which states: "This [term *dā*] alone is *ghu*, but *daib* is not"?

[Objection: One might argue that because *dāyamāna* would be *śāpy-antodātta* (having the acute accent on the final syllable of the suffix) whereas [the form] with the *śyan* suffix would be *ādyudātta* (having the acute accent on the first syllable), there would be a difference in their phonological results; therefore, it is difficult to maintain its inclusion in the *divādi* class. [Response: Not so. Because such forms are not attested (*anabhidhānāt*), and in this context, the *cānaś* suffix alone does not exist.

Alternatively, initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) itself is desired, because of the accepted principle that "the authority of the sages increases in descending order. Or, according to the view that the particle *vā* is included within the verbal root due to the usage cited above, its purpose is clearly fulfilled by its being the subject of the rule for initial acute accent; for initial acute accent is not obtained in the case of the suffix *cānaś*. This is established in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the sūtra "ātmamāne khaś ca," which holds that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) refers only to the accent caused by the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). Furthermore, even in the case of the suffix *cānaś*, final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is difficult to obtain in the case of a word ending in *khaś*.

As for what was stated here by Kaiyaṭa—namely, that the *nittva* (the marker *n*) in the case of *dāyamāna*, derived from the suffix *cānaś*, is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta—that is merely an incidental argument (*abhyuccaya*). Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: since the *śittva* (the marker *ś*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), intended to prevent the application of the *pittva* (the marker *p*), how can it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply when there is an exception (*apavāda*)?

On this point, Kaiyaṭa says: "In accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*), the *śittva* is relied upon solely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with respect to the general rule, and not for the purpose of restriction. Alternatively, the *kittva* (the marker *k*) of the suffix *ṭak*, which is an exception to *kā*, serves as the authority (*pramāṇa*) for the aforementioned meaning.

What is the purpose of the phrase *analvidau*? It is so that [the rule] may not apply in a prescription concerning *ta*, *tena*, *tasmāt*, *tasya*, or *tasmin*. In a prescription concerning *al* (a letter), as in *mahoraskena*: by virtue of the status of being a *sthānin* (original element), the *visarjanīya* would undergo *ṇatva* (nasalization) because it was taught in the *aṭ* group in the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi*. In a prescription concerning what follows *al*, as in *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*: since *aut*, *āt*, and *akāra* would occupy the place of a *hal* (consonant), there would be elision of the *su* suffix according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. In a prescription concerning *al* itself, as in *dyukāmaḥ*: there would be elision according to the rule *diva ud*.

Nor does the mention of *vidhi* (prescription) serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is because [the rule] has already fulfilled its purpose in cases where there is no *hal* following, such as in the expression *ahar vimaladyuḥ*. If the prescription were applied when *al* follows, then for example in *ka iṣṭaḥ*, the substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca* would occur, since the *s* of *su* would be followed by a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) that is a *haś* sound. Furthermore, in the case of *saḥ*, the elision of *su* would occur because the *a* [of *as*] would be treated as a substitute and thus followed by a *hal*. Moreover, the term *vidhi* is included in order to obtain the various types of compounds mentioned above.

It should not be argued that one should simply say "na anal" for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), even when the nominative case is employed, because the meaning of that [nominative] is not intended to be expressed. Or else, one might suggest saying "alaḥ. This cannot be maintained, because since it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is no connection with a "place" (*sthāna*); and since the genitive case signifies a general relationship (*sambandha-sāmānya*), it would already succeed in encompassing the meaning of the aforementioned case endings. [To this we reply: The word "vidhi" (rule) is included in the sūtra precisely to prohibit the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) when *al* is resorted to as a subordinate element.

In examples such as *tena pradīvyati*, even though *al* is resorted to as a qualifier of the meaning of the term *ārddhadhātukam* (in the rule *valādeḥ*), there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). Otherwise, since that prohibition [of *sthānivadbhāva*] applies only where *al* is mentioned as the primary element—as in the rule *haśi ca*—it would not apply here. However, when the word *vidhi* (rule) is included, the analysis is *al-vidhiḥ* (a rule concerning *al*), based on the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). Thus, the operation of the prohibition occurs whenever *al* is resorted to, whether as the qualificand or the qualifier. The word *āśraya* means "that which is resorted to," derived from the root *śri* with the suffix *ac*.

The Bhāṣya statement, however, “*alam āśrayate*,” is for the purpose of illustrating the meaning, as there would otherwise be the undesirable application of the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. Kaiyaṭa maintains that because the word *āśraya* refers to the *al* (the phoneme) which is the substratum, its meaning is already conveyed; thus, it is simply not used, and its elision (*lopa*) occurs. If it is objected: "In that case, since there would be a prohibition even of operations concerning the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) of the substituend (*sthānin*), then *kit*-ness could not be obtained in forms such as *pradīvyati*," we say: not so. This is because, under the view that the indicatory letters are non-exclusive (*anekāntatva*), those [indicatory letters] do not possess the status of being *al* belonging to the substituend. Even under the view that they are exclusive (*ekāntatva*), they are elided prior [to the operation]. Furthermore, this is supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *na lyapi*. Other points have been stated previously.

It might be argued that, according to the principle that "what has taken the place of something inherits its properties," this sutra is unnecessary because its purpose is already established; for this very reason, the ritual properties of rice, such as threshing and so forth, apply to wild rice (*nīvāra*). This is not so.

In cases such as "one threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the words "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote that which accomplishes the *apūrva* (the transcendental result). Therefore, although the rule applies to *nīvāra* grass and the like because they also accomplish that *apūrva*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed by the rule "after *āṅ*, [the roots] *yam* and *han*" cannot apply to the substitute *vadha* for *han*. This is because [the rule] is governed by the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) "the form itself of the word [is what is meant]" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the rule applying even in cases such as *ātṛṇeḍhi*.

It might be argued as follows: let the meaning of the sūtra be understood from an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) alone. In the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*, the mention of *anādeśe* (except when there is a substitute) can serve to indicate the principle that "a substitute is like the original" (*sthānivadbhavati*). Furthermore, in the rule *ado jagdhir lyapi kiti*, since the result is already established by the word *kiti* alone, the mention of *lyapi* serves to indicate the portion of the rule stating "not when a rule is taught concerning an *al*" (*analvidhau*). For this very reason, even when an *al* is relied upon as a qualifier, the principle that "it is not like the original" (*na sthānivadbhavati*) is also established. This is true.

In the subsequent sūtra, the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ* must necessarily be stated; therefore, its formulation is begun by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), as this is more concise than resorting to *arthāpatti* (presumption). The phrase *analvidhau* is also for the sake of clarity, and to ensure the recurrence of the term *dvitīya-vidhi-grahaṇa* in the following sūtra, since the result [of that recurrence] will be explained there itself. It might be argued: the types of *atideśa* (extended application) would be those consisting of cause (*nimitta*), scripture (*śāstra*), designation (*vyapadeśa*), identity (*tādātmya*), and effect (*kārya*). These correspond respectively to the examples: *pūrvavat*, *karmavat*, *ādivat*, *tṛjvat*, *parāṅgavat*, and *ṇidvat*. Among these, "the *san*-affix is like what precedes" (*pūrvavatsanaḥ*) is an *atideśa* of cause (*nimitta*).

Although it is impossible to extend (*atideśa*) the status of being a Brāhmaṇa—which serves as the cause for being the first to eat—to a Kṣatriya or others, nevertheless, in the case of the rule "as before" (*pūrvavat*), it is not the *ṅit*-ness residing in the base that is extended to the *san*-affix; rather, it is simply the fact that the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) which resides in the base itself operates even when there is an intervention by the *san*-affix. It is on this basis alone that the technical term "extension of the cause" (*nimittātideśa*) is used. Nor should it be said that this is merely an "extension of the effect" (*kāryātideśa*), for if it were so, the augment *iṭ* would undesirably apply in forms such as *cikraṃsate* and *pracikraṃsate*.

In the case of the extension of a cause (*nimittātideśa*), however, *krami* itself—even though separated by the suffix *san*—is the cause for the application of the ātmanepada; thus, by the rule "after *snu* and *kram*, [there is no *iṭ*] when there is no cause for the ātmanepada," *iṭ* is not inserted, because in that context only a cause that is qualified by its result (*phalopahita*) is to be understood. The extension of a grammatical operation (*śāstrātideśa*) is optional in the rule "like the object [is the agent] when [the action is] through an object. The extension of a designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*) is expressed as "like the beginning and the end"; for when a usage characterized by being the beginning or the end is extended to a single entity, the required grammatical effect is accomplished by those very rules themselves.

And so say the ancients: designation [of one thing] as being like another occurs through (1) cause, as in *pūrvavat sanaḥ*; (2) transfer of form, as in *tṛjvat*, because the word *kroṣṭṛ* is prescribed in place of the word *kroṣṭu*; (3) transfer of identity, as in *subāmantrite parāṅgavat svare*, because in the phrase *yatte divo duhitarmartabhojanam*, the enclitic accent (*nighāta*) applies to the entire compound *divoduhitar*; and (4) transfer of operation, as in *goto ṇit*.

Thus, regarding this sixfold extension (*atideśa*), what is the determining factor that this particular one is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*)? It is not so. According to the reasoning of the *Vārttika*, "But [the rule] is established because of the prohibition of *iṭ* when it occurs in the same word as the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) ending," this [extension] "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is also an extension of the operation. For the application of the aforementioned rule—that [the suffixes] must reside in the same word—occurs in the case of both the root *kram-* and the middle voice ending.

However, although there is a distinction—wherein the *ātmanepada* suffix is applied in examples such as *pracakramse* by the rule *propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām*, and in examples such as *pracikraṃsate* by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ*—the application of the aforementioned restriction [that the operation applies to the whole] still occurs because the quality of being situated within a single word (*ekapadasthatva*) is equal in both cases. The principle *ādyantavat* (as if it were the beginning or the end) is also like that, according to the natural intention of Haradatta and others. This is because in forms such as *kurute* and *kurve*, even though there is a designation of "beginning" and "end," the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound—"that whose beginning is the final vowel"—is absent; consequently, since the designation *ṭi* does not apply, the substitution of *e* (in *kurve*) would otherwise be untenable.
For in cases such as *kurvāt*, the desired result is established precisely through the extension (*atideśa*) of the grammatical operation known as "the substitution of *e* for *ṭi*.

Even the extension of a rule (*śāstra-atideśa*) is only optional. As for the extension of identity (*tādātmya-atideśa*), it is sublated because the original element (*sthānin*) is removed by the substitute (*ādeśa*); this is because the application of that [extension] occurs at the very same time as the counter-correlates of the identity. However, in the case of the extension of form (*rūpa-atideśa*), the injunction for the substitute would be rendered useless, since an option is impossible according to the reasoning stated previously. Therefore, it is established that this is primarily an extension of the grammatical operation itself.

The author of the *Nyāsa*, however, maintains that the extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*) results in the same conclusion as the view based on technical names (*saṃjñāpakṣa*). He states that this [extension] does not occur simply by the force of the suffix *-vat*. Regarding this, Haradatta says:

"Under the view based on technical names, the *ātmanepada* affix would apply only to *vadhi*, but not to *han*, because it is a technical name of a word; thus, the rule 'one's own form' (*svaṃ rūpam*) does not apply. Consequently, there would be two faults: in forms such as *kena* and *kasmāt*, the operations pertaining to the *aṅga* (stem) and so forth would not take place. But under the view of the extension of designation, the term *han* is included by the rule 'one's own form,' and through the extension of that designation, it applies to *vadhi* as well.

"In this way, because the designations such as 'root' (dhātu) and 'stem' (aṅga), which reside in the substituend, are extended (atideśa) to the substitute beginning with *k*, the resulting grammatical operations are accomplished; therefore, due to this disparity, it is not the case that [the rule applies] in that manner. Here are the Vārttikas:

Its defects are as follows: there is the prohibition of both [the substitution of] *traya* and [the application of] *ādeśa*. In the case of a generic designation (*jāti*), there is the prohibition of the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the substitution of the word-form. In the inclusion of *ṅī* and *āp*, there is the prohibition of the long vowel. There is the prohibition of *īṭ* for the roots *āh* and *bhū*. In the case of the substitute *vadh*, there is the prohibition of *vṛddhi* and *tattva*, as well as the rule for *iṭ*. For stems ending in long *ā*, there is the prohibition of *nuk* and *ṣuk*. Regarding the substitutes for the imperative (*loṭ*), there is the prohibition of the absence of *śap*, the absence of *jab*, the state of being *dhita*, and the elision of *hi*. In the case of the substitute *traya*, there is the prohibition of that which ends in *s*. And in the rule for *ām*, there is the prohibition regarding accent (*svara*) in the case of the substitute *vasu*.

The [substitution of] *go* occurs before suffixes beginning with *pū*, *tvaṇ*, *ṇit*, and those affecting accent (*ātva-svara*). There is a prohibition regarding the roots *kṛ* and *pā*. This refers to the rule: "A substitute is like its original (*sthānivat*). Regarding that, whatever needs to be said concerning the first *vārttika* has already been stated under the *sūtra* on the *sarvādi* group. The second [vārttika] is also useless. Nor does there arise the contingency of *guṇa* by the rule "gher ṅiti" in the case of *vrīhibhyaḥ*, because the plural number is prescribed in place of the singular; for even if the substitute were *sthānivat*, only the transfer of meaning (*arthātideśa*) is stated there [in that context].

The meaning of the third [alternative] is as follows: in the cases *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *atikhaṭvaḥ*, the elision of the case-ending *su* would apply by virtue of the inclusion of the terms ending in *ṅī* and *āp*; therefore, this must be prohibited. Consequently, one should reject the view that [the rule applies to] "long vowels" (*dīrgha*) by reading [the sūtra] as *ṅī-ī-ā-āp*. Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even in cases such as *atikhaṭvena*, because in the mention of *āp*, the vowel *ā* is read in (praśleṣa) everywhere. Nor should it be argued that, even so, there would still be the undesired application of the augment *yāṭ* in *atikhaṭvāyai*, since both the *ātva* inherent in the base itself and the *āptva* resulting from *sthānivadbhāva* would be present.

This is because the rule is explained as "the *yāṭ* [augment] follows that which comes after a stem ending in long *ā*. Furthermore, when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), only that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed is included; this is due to the existence of the "rule of beginning-with-that" (*tad-ādi-niyama*) regarding feminine suffixes used as secondary members (*upasarjana*). Since the aggregate word *atikhaṭvā* does not end in long *ā*, and since the word *khaṭvā* alone lacks the status of being a stem (*aṅga*) in that context—because the case-ending (*sub*) arises only from the word *atikhaṭvā* itself—it is established that there is no fault, as there is no coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the status of being a stem and the status of ending in long *ā*.

For this very reason, there is no *samprasāraṇa* in forms such as *atikārīṣagandhyāputra*. However, in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), if one adopts the view that the term "prescribed" (*vihita*) qualifies the preceding element, there would be an under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases like *seti*, and an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases like *yaḥ saḥ*; thus, the purpose of the *praśleṣa* (the doubling of the vowel) is not redundant. Even according to the Vārttika school, the *praśleṣa* of the long *ā* in rules such as *yāḍāpaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.113) is necessary; otherwise, even if one were to resolve the issue in cases like *atikhaṭvāyai* by appealing to the fact that the suffix follows an *aṅga* ending in *ā*, the fault would remain unavoidable in cases such as *jarasā* and *nase pṛte*. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*) in forms such as *sutīḥ* (from *sutām icchan*).
Alternatively, it should be understood that by also eliding the letter *ā*, its power serves to exclude [the application of the rule] to that which has attained shortness in the middle.

The fourth *vārttika* is also redundant. Nor should it be argued that in *āha*, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the substitute for *brū*, the augment *īṭ* would apply via the rule "bruva īṭ," and in *abhūt*, the augment *īṭ* would apply to the substitute for *asti* (i.e., *bhū*) via the rule "astisico'pṛkte. This is because the rule "āhasthaḥ" provides a *jñāpaka*, indicating that the substitution of *tha* occurs only when a *jhal*-beginning suffix follows. Nor should it be argued that even if *īṭ* were applied, the substitution of *tha* would still occur by considering the original form (*bhūtapūrvagati*) as beginning with a *jhal*. For this would result in the prescription of the substitution of *tha* alone, which is more parsimonious (*lāghava*).

Because the substitutes beginning with *th*—and even those beginning with *ṇal*—are considered to have been preceded by a *jhal*-beginning [suffix] based on their former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), the substitution of *th* would be unavoidable there as well. Furthermore, the second fault is also avoided because, in the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*, the mention of the form with two *s*s (*dvisakāraka*) indicates that the augment *īṭ* is prescribed only for an *apṛkta* sārvadhātuka suffix following a root ending in *s*, such as *asteḥ*.

It might be argued as follows: if the letter *s* were elided immediately after *as*, then because it would no longer be a verbal root (*dhātu*), the suffix *tiP* would not apply; thus, the flaw mentioned by Mādhava would arise. Furthermore, since the *s* occurring within the root cannot be construed with the *sic* suffix, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *īṭ*, which is triggered by *sic*. Nor can it be said that the qualification "ending in *s*" is redundant for *asteḥ* (the form of the root *as*); for even so, the flaw remains in the case of the independent root *bhū*. By this [argument], the view that *sic* and *as* form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*)—with the ablative ending of *sicas* elided according to a Vedic rule (*saunaḥ*)—is also refuted.

Because [the word] *bhūtvā* ends in a *kutva*-derived form, there is no *kutva*. Furthermore, the compound is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "that which exists (*vidyamāna*) and is *sic*. Therefore, the interpretation that the rule applies after the root *as*, from which the *sic* has been elided and replaced by *bhū*, is refuted; for even if the form were established, it would fail to account for what is stated in the *Bhāṣya*. For this very reason, although *sic* ought to have been placed first—since it has fewer syllables and is more venerable due to its wider scope—the author did not do so; rather, through the use of *tantra* and other devices, he intended to convey the meaning "of the existing *sic*," as is also evident from the natural sense of the usage of the suffix *tip*.

Otherwise, one would have simply said "sicasbhyām. Nor is there an over-extension [of the rule] to the roots *as* and *tyaj*, because—as Mādhava has stated—it is impossible for an apṛkta sārvadhātuka suffix to follow those two when they are separated by a vikaraṇa; thus, his argument is also refuted.

Regarding this, they say: the analysis is *asti-sicaḥ*. [The rule applies] after the root *as* ending in *s*, but not after *sic* after which the change to *bhū* has already occurred; that is to say, it applies when *sic* is actually heard. Nor does this lead to an inconsistency with the *saṃhitā* reading "sico 'pṛkte," because under the view that "the end of a word which is a *saṃyoga*" is meant, the [loss of the final *t*] occurs due to the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga*; and even if that view is absent, it is easily established under the view that "the end of a *saṃyoga* which is at the end of a word" is meant. Furthermore, that [view] is well-established in the original treatises (*ākaras*). Nor does the fact that [the elision] is considered *asiddha* prevent the occurrence of *ru*-substitution for *r*.

This is because the rule "there is elision of the final member of a conjunct when *ru* undergoes vocalization" (*saṃyogāntalopo rorutve*) is read in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*, and this very citation serves as the basis for the meaning of that Vārttika. Alternatively, let there be no elision of the final member of the conjunct; once *ru*-vocalization has been applied to both *s* sounds, by the rule "after *at*, [there is elision] of *ru*" (*ato roḥ*), only a single *u* is produced for both. This is because, as in the case of the singular number in "for the sake of cattle" (*paśvekatva*), the singularity of the attribute to be enjoined is intended to be significant. Nor should it be argued that even if there were two *u*s, one should explain that after the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality), the *ādguṇa* (guṇa substitute for *a* + *u*) would subsequently apply.

Because it is *antaraṅga* (internal) by virtue of depending on a single word (*ekapadāśrayatva*), the rule *sica u* (Pāṇini 6.1.59) would necessarily apply, overriding the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution of homogeneous vowels), since only the *guṇa* [of the root] is involved. Nor should it be argued that there should be only one *ru*-substitution for both *s* sounds; for in the rule prescribing that [substitution], the term *pada* is understood to follow, and thus the condition of being at the end of a single word (*ekapadāntatva*) is not met, as the second *s* belongs to a separate word. Furthermore, one should not argue that because the vowel *a* is not posterior to the preceding *ru*, nor anterior to the second [ru], the substitution of *u* (*utva*) would not occur for either; this is because the term *ruḥ* is accepted as a reference to the genus (*jāti*).

And because in that case, only the previously stated rule (*nirddeśa*) serves as the authority; nor does the substitution of *ū* for the preceding sound by the rule *haśi ca* arise due to its being subsequent [to the rule for *ru*], since the status of *ru* as established (*siddha*) is lacking due to its being considered unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor can this be justified on the grounds of its dependence [on the original form], because even if such dependence exists regarding the element of the substituend (*sthānin*), it does not exist regarding the causal factor (*nimitta*). This is because there is no impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), since a *haś* (a consonant other than *r*) distinct from the letter *t* is also possible.

In this regard, the following must be stated: Is the second *sakāra* (the *s* in *asti-sicaḥ*) in the nominative case, in the ablative case, or devoid of any case-ending? It cannot be the first [option], because it would be impossible for it to function as an ablative qualifier of *sicaḥ*. Nor can it be the second, because that would result in the rule being treated as Vedic (*chāndasa*). Nor can it be the last, because in the absence of *padatva* (being a word), the substitution of *ru* (the *r* in *asti-r-ṅ*) would be impossible. By this, the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is also refuted. Thus, even the qualification of *sicaḥ* by its ending in *sakāra* is redundant. The reference "astisico'pṛkte" contains two *sakāras*.

This is because the authors of the Bhāṣya have stated that the word "of *as*" (*asteḥ*)—ending in the letter *s*—is indeed a qualifier of *as* itself; furthermore, in the Vārttika as well, the possibility of the augment *īṭ* and its prohibition are stated only with respect to the substitute for *bhū*. The intention of the Bhāṣya is precisely that there is a *praśleṣa* (elision/merging) of the letter *s* before the *śtip* affix, since this is justified by the fact that the *śtip* is a Vedic (Sautra) usage. Nor does it follow that the augment *īṭ* would apply by relying on the suffix being subsequent to *sic*.

This is because, by carrying over the term *bahulam* from the sūtra *gāti-sthā-*, and by relying on its having the same meaning as the particle *eva*, the commentary explains that "only the elision (*luk*) of *sic* occurs," thereby establishing the validity of the prohibition against the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). By this, the attempt to interpret the Bhāṣya—by adopting the aforementioned method of taking *sicaḥ* as a collective compound and then splitting it as *si ca* [meaning "the letter *s*" and *ca*]—and thus regarding the passage as intended to justify the rejection of the mention of *asti*, is also refuted.

Furthermore, it is cumbersome to assume that both the substitution of *bha-tva* and the elision (*lopa*) of the fifth vowel [in the word *ru*] are Vedic anomalies (*chāndasa*). By this, the claim that this very [rule] is the authority for the mention of the genus (*jāti*) is refuted, because there is no evidence for such a mention. Moreover, the principle that "when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned, the genus (*jāti*) is understood" does not apply here, because the term *roḥ* relies upon the composite whole. Furthermore, the substitution of *u* for both [phonemes] is untenable, because the substitution of *r* (*rutva*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor can it be established by virtue of its basis (*āśraya-siddhatva*), because that principle finds its application only where there is a single *r*.

Because the rule for *ut* would be rendered purposeless (*vaiyarthyāpatti*) without the status of being established (*siddhatva*), one must assume that status by way of restating it; furthermore, there is no evidence to sublate its non-established status (*asiddhatva*) regarding the second portion.

Alternatively, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that the Sūtra should be recited without the *śtip* affix. In that case, the word *assi* in the rule *assi co'pṛkte* should be explained as containing an additional *s*. As for the Bhāṣya statement "from the root *as*, ending in *s*," it is intended as an explanation of the portion *as*. This is because the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *asatya* has been refuted according to the method stated by Mādhava. If, however, the Bhāṣya is taken merely as an illustration of the solution, then *as* is a form with an elided ablative (*luptapañcamīka*), and *sti* is a qualifier of the *apṛkta* [affix].

The augment *īṭ* shall be applied to a single-consonant (*apṛkta*) *sārvadhātuka* suffix that follows either the root *as-* or a suffix ending in *s* or *t*. Because there is a restriction regarding the form of the single-consonant *sārvadhātuka* suffix following these two—namely, that it must consist of the sounds *s* or *t*—the mention of the specific forms [in the rule] serves to ensure "priority" (*paratva*) with respect to those instances delimited by that very form, since no other qualification is applicable. Consequently, this excludes the application of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original); such is the direction of the argument.

The meaning of the fifth [sūtra] is as follows: By the vārttika “*hano ṇbul bahulaṃ taṇi*,” the substitute *vadh* occurs for the root *han* in the domains of technical terminology (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic meter (*chandas*). Because that [substitute *vadh*] ends in a consonant, there would be the rule for vṛddhi by “*ata upadhāyāḥ*” and the substitution of *t* by “*hanasto’ciṇṇaloḥ*”; the status of these two as *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) must be prohibited. Furthermore, in the form *āvadhiṣīṣṭa*, because of the status of *sthānivadbhāva*, the element would be treated as an *aṅga* (stem), and consequently, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule “*ekāca upadeśe’nudāttāt*” would apply;
therefore, it must be stated that in this case, the designation of *aṅga* does not occur through *sthānivadbhāva*.

This point has also been rejected in the Bhāṣya: in the case of *avadhīt*, because the substitution of *vadha* is accepted as ending in a short vowel (*adanta*), there would otherwise be the undesirable application of the rule "ato halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.7), which prescribes vṛddhi. However, in the word *vadhaka*, the suffix *kvun* is applied by the Uṇādi rule "hano vadhaśca. Consequently, there is no occasion for either vṛddhi or the substitution of *tatva* (t for th), because the suffix lacks the marker *ṇit*. Furthermore, there is no prohibition of the augment *iṭ*; for, by the force of the specific accentuation of the substitute *vadha* as having an initial udātta, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) does not apply.

Nor should it be argued that in the form *vadhiṣīṣṭa*, because of the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *nipātair yadyadi...* (Pāṇini 8.1.30), the desired accent of the suffix would not occur; for [if that were so], there would be the undesirable consequence (*bādhā*) of its being sublated by the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) which is taught later. This is because the rules pertaining to *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes apply generally; thus, the substitution of *vadh* occurs even before the suffix arises, and since the suffix arises after that, its accent alone is what remains subsequently established (*satiśiṣṭa*).

In this regard, the following should be noted: according to the *Vārttika*, although the term "ārddhadhātuke" functions as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), the terms "liṅi" and so forth are accepted as locatives of sequence (*parasaptamī*). Consequently, in the rule concerning *sya* and *sic*, it is stated that "the *ciṇvadbhāva* [application] occurs before the *sīyuṭ* [suffix] by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)," because both are dependent on a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*).

According to the Bhāṣya’s view, however, since the substitution of *vadh* for *han* occurs even before the suffix arises, it lacks a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*). Consequently, because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), while the *ciṇvad-bhāva* (the treatment as if ending in *ciṇ*) is *bahiraṅga* (external) due to having a subsequent cause, there can be no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the *antaraṅga* and *bahiraṅga*. Thus, in response to the doubt as to how the *ciṇvad-bhāva* could apply, Kaiyaṭa states that the *ciṇvad-bhāva* applies because it is a *pratipada-vidhi* (a rule prescribed for a specific word-form).

It might be argued as follows: Does "being prescribed by a specific rule" (*pratipadavidhitva*) mean having no other occasion (*anavakāśatva*), or does it mean being directly mentioned (*sākṣādupāttatva*)? It cannot be the first, because the mention of *han* in the rule *syasicsīyuṭ...* finds its scope in forms such as *ghāniṣyate*, and the mention of *sīyuṭ* finds its scope in forms such as *kāriṣīṣṭa*. Nor can it be the second, because since the four suffixes beginning with *syat* are connected respectively with the four [roots] beginning with those ending in vowels, and because there is an absence of svarita accent, the principle of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) does not apply; rather, each of the suffixes beginning with *syat* is connected individually, and thus the application of the *ciṇvat* treatment is prescribed for the root *han* when followed by *sīyuṭ*.

That [objection] is without foundation. It should not be argued that because the substitution of *vadha* occurs first due to its being *antaraṅga*, and because it is subsequently included under the term *han* by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, the form would necessarily be *vadhiṣīṣṭa*—even when the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is applied to the *sīyuṭ* suffix—since the elision of the *a* (by the rule "ṇyallopau") would apply via the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* principle. This is incorrect, because there is no evidence that the connection of *hana* with the *sīyuṭ* suffix occurs only after the *antaraṅga* substitution of *vadha* has already taken effect. Nor is the latter [position] tenable; for the direct mention of *hana* in the rule "hano vadha liṅi" remains unchanged even when the substitute *vadha* is in place, and furthermore, the status of being *antaraṅga* applies more extensively [to the substitute].

On this point, they say: By the inclusion of the particle *ca* ("and") in the rule *ciṇvadiṭ ca*, the application of the *ciṇvad-bhāva* to the root *han* when the suffix *sīyuṭ* follows is established; thus, its status as a *pratipadavidhi* (a rule applying to a specific word-form) is indeed purposeful. Nor is there a lack of evidence for the view that the particle *ca* serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. For the venerable Bhāṣyakāra himself stated: "But he [Pāṇini] did it for that very purpose. Alternatively, *liṅi* is the general term and *sīyuṭi* is the specific one; *hanter* is common to both.
Thus, because it is an exception (*apavāda*), since the *ciṇvad-iṭ* would otherwise be impossible, even the particle *ca* could not have served to enjoin it.

Alternatively—since it will be stated that the rule "the internal is stronger" (*antaraṅgaṃ balavat*) is to be rejected by the principle "that which is unestablished is external" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*), and since that [rejection] is known to be non-permanent (*anitya*) due to the inclusion of the *kṛt* suffixes and the augment *tuK*, its abandonment here in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*) makes the conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*) appropriate. Or rather, let the word *liṅi* be taken as a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*). Then the augment *iṭ* would apply by virtue of being subsequent (*paratvāt*). Let there be no specific prescription of the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttanipātana*). Nor is there a lack of the augment *iṭ* in forms such as *vadhiṣīṣṭa*, as there is in *karttā* and so on.

[The root *han*] does not [fall under the scope of the rule] because, although it is taught as having one vowel (*ekāc*), it is taught as having many vowels (*anekāc*) in the case of the root *vadh*. For it is stated in the Bhāṣya itself that there are two teachings for the root *vadh*. Furthermore, the qualification "one" (*eka*) is intended to exclude those roots that are taught with many vowels. Nor should it be argued that if "vowel" (*ac*) were mentioned, it would apply only to that which ends in a vowel; for if that were so, the purpose of teaching the roots beginning with *pac* as unaccented (*anudātta*) would become redundant. Since the meaning of "having one vowel" is obtained by the mere mention of "vowel" (*aca*) through the intention to express singularity and the indication of the sense of "possessing" (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), the inclusion of the word "one" (*eka*) serves to emphasize the aforementioned meaning.

Even by taking [the rule] as having the stated meaning, the application of the *paribhāṣā*—"where there is the mention of 'one vowel' (*ekāj*)"—is established. Nor is there an impossibility of [the rule] "śtipā śāpā" etc. being an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that *paribhāṣā*, given that the aforementioned method renders the single word meaningful; for the very mention of the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) in rules prescribing *guṇa*, *yuṭ*, and so forth, in the case of roots such as *śīṅ* and *dīṅ*, is itself the indicator of that [paribhāṣā]. Therefore, *iṭ* is established after the root *vye*. For this very reason, Vyāghrabhūti made an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of roots ending in short *a* in his *aniṭ-kārikās*.
As for the fact that the form *ghāniṣīṣṭa* is produced by the substitution [of *han* for *vad*], and not *vadhiṣīṣṭa* as well, it has been stated in the Bhāṣya:

"Now, once the *ciṇvat*-substitution has been applied, why does the substitution of *han* not occur again by virtue of the principle of 'reapplication' (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*)? [The answer is: 'When a conflict occurs regarding what applies only once (*sakṛdgatau*), that which is sublated remains sublated; and there is a prohibition against the substitution of *han* and *niṅ*.'"

That is not so; for while there is no obstacle to the application of the substitute *vadh* when the *ciṇvat* treatment does not apply, there is no obstacle to its application when that treatment does apply. As for the prohibition regarding the substitutes *han*, *ṇiṅ*, and so on, it refers to what is obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of *ciṇvat* in the *syādi* (future) suffixes, because that [prohibition] takes precedence. Furthermore, since what is obtained in the *liṅ* (optative) does not fall within the scope of that [extension], the *Mahābhāṣya* rejects [the need for a separate rule] by relying on the extension of only those operations pertaining to the *aṅga* (stem). This was likewise stated first by the author of the *Prakriyākaumudī*.

For this very reason, the form *vadhiṣīṣṭa* is cited as an example in the Bhāṣya itself under the rule *ekācaḥ*. Furthermore, the five Vārttikas beginning with *ākārāntāt* are also unnecessary. To explain: in forms such as *vilāpayati* and *bhāpayati*, the augment *nuṭ* and the augment *śuk* do not occur simply because of the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *i* in the roots *lī-i* and *bhī-i*.

In the cases of *śiṣṭāt*, *hatāt*, *bhintāt*, *kurutāt*, and *stāt*, once *tātaṅ* is applied by virtue of its higher status, the following [operations] would appear to be applicable by way of *sthānivadbhāva*: the substitution of *ś* for *śā* (by *śāhau*), the substitution of *j* for *han* (by *hanterjaḥ*), the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* after *hu*, *hal*, and *bha* (by *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ*), the elision of *hi* after an affix ending in *u* that is not preceded by a conjunct consonant (by *utaśca pratyayādasaṃyogapūrvāt*), and the substitution of *e* for the root-final vowel in *dhv* and *as* before *dhau* (by *ghvasoreddhau*). However, these do not occur due to the maxim *sakṛdgatau vipratiṣedhe yad bādhitaṃ tad bādhitameva* ("when two rules conflict and one has been applied once, it is as if the other were never there"). By this same reasoning, the non-application of the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ śānaj* in the case of *puṣṇītāt* is also explained.

When the substitution of *tisṛ* has been made, the replacement by *trayaḥ* [from the rule *trestrayaḥ*] also does not apply, according to the aforementioned reasoning. By this, the case of *catasraḥ tiṣṭhanti* is also explained: once the substitution of *catasṛ* has been made, the augment *ām* [from the rule *caturanaḍuhoḥ*] does not apply. In the example *viduṣaḥ paśya*, because the substitute *vas* is included within the term *śatṛ* [in the rule *śatṛśānacoḥ pratiṣedhaḥ*], the rule *śaturanumo nadyajādī*—which depends on the condition that a following case-ending is high-pitched (*udātta*) after a stem ending in a high-pitched vowel—does not cause the case-ending to be high-pitched.

In the word *anuma*, one relies on the *um-pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term) starting from the letter *u* in the rule *tanādikṛñbhya uḥ* and extending up to the letter *m* in *num*. This is because the commentary explains [the rule] as referring to that which is devoid of this [pratyāhāra]. Furthermore, since the suffix *vasu* is included therein, one should not object that [the rule] would likewise fail to apply in forms such as *lunatā* and *punatā*, on the grounds that the *śnā* suffix is also included within that [pratyāhāra]. This is because the mention of *anu* is taken as a qualifier of the *śatṛ* suffix (*an*), and not as a qualifier of that which ends in it.

Even though the *śnā* augment does not apply when the suffix *śatṛ* follows, it lacks the nature of being the base (*prakṛti*) for that *śatṛ*. Furthermore, even if the term *num* is understood as referring to an augment, it serves as a qualifier specifically for the *śatṛ* suffix in its absence. If it were a qualifier for that which ends in *num*, then a prohibition would undesirably apply even in cases such as *muñcati*, because the form ending in *num* is possessed of the *num* augment by the rule "śe mucādīnām. However, the meaning of the Vārttika on *apatya* is this: in the case of *citragvagram*, the rule "sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ" would otherwise cause the formation of a single preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*).

Since the reading *nāntaḥ pādam* is established in the Bhāṣya, it is appropriate that the rule *sarvatra* also prescribes the formation of the single preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*). Kaiyaṭa, however, states that by this [rule] *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) is prescribed, not the *pūrvarūpa*. Therefore, he says that the meaning of the Bhāṣya is that the *pūrvarūpa* prescribed by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* would otherwise apply. His intention is that the reading is *prakṛtyāntaḥ pādam*, because the Bhāṣya on the Śākala-sūtra shows that the word *prakṛtyā* is drawn over from there by the particle *ca* in the phrase *hrasvaśca*. Furthermore, the Bhāṣya statement *eṅ iti tatra vartate* (the term *eṅ* is present there) is also consistent with this view.

The view of the earlier [authorities], however, should be understood here as being intended to apply everywhere through its continued recurrence. Nor should it be argued that there is no status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitutional equivalence) because of the non-occurrence of the term *eṅ* [in the rule]; for even so, [the fault] would be unavoidable in the case of *he citrago agram*, since the substitute itself is inherently *eṅ*-ending and thus does not depend on the elision of an *al* (vowel). Similarly, in *citraguḥ*, there would be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) due to the *ṇit* designation by the rule *goto ṇit*; and in *citragūn*, there would be *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) due to the reading of the *ṣāṣṭha-vārttika*: *ā goto'mśasoḥ*.

In this context, the mention of the *ṇit*-designation is redundant, because those two [suffixes] do not apply by virtue of the rule regarding the *ta*-paratva (the addition of *t* as an indicatory letter). This is because the reading "auto'mśasoḥ" remains established. Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *acinavam*, since by association with *śas*, only the *ām* of the case-endings (*sup*) is understood here. Otherwise, in *bahugumān*, the prohibition "na gośvantsāvavarṇa" would block the acute accent prescribed by "hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup. Therefore, the Vārttika "goḥ pūrvasvarayoḥ" is established.

Regarding the passage beginning with *bahuguṇāḥ*, the statement in the *Vṛtti* that there is a prohibition by the rule *na gośvan* against what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *antodāttād uttarapadād anyatarasyām* is questionable, as it contradicts the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities. Furthermore, the twelfth *Vārttika* is also unnecessary. Nor does the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) result in the occurrence of *guṇa* for the light penultimate vowel in forms such as *kurupibā*; for since the letter *a* in the root *kṛ* is one-mora (*mātrika*) due to its reference to the *tapara* [vowel *ṛ*], the substitution of *u* alone is correct. Thus, the *tapara* designation serves to exclude the two-mora duration obtained from another grammatical system; and because the root *pā* ends in a long vowel (*ādanta*), the rule applies. P. 1.1.56: *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*. (When a substitute is ordained in place of a vowel, it is treated like the original with respect to a preceding operation.)

This substitute (*ādeśa*) caused by another cause (*paranimittaka*) shall be treated like the original (*sthānivat*), provided that it is prescribed by something seen as preceding it, or by a cause seen [prior to the substitution]. This rule is for the purpose of avoiding operations concerning vowels (*alvidhi*). In the case of *vavraśca*, because the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratva*) would be treated as *sthānivat*, there would be a prohibition of the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the *v* according to the rule "not after a *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*na saṃprasāraṇe*). This is because the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* falls within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the "stem" (*aṅga*), and thus that substitution is prescribed when a suffix (*pratyaya*)—which is implied by the term "stem"—follows. Nor should it be argued that the governing heading of the "stem" applies only prior to the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsavikāra*).

This is because it has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that [the operation] applies up to the end of the seventh chapter. Furthermore, in the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoh*, the term *luk* (elision) was not included; therefore, when the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *v*—which is seen as preceding the vowel *ṛ* that serves as the *sthānin* (original element)—is to be performed, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) applies. Likewise, in the cases of *acitīkaḥ*, *sucitīkaḥ*, and *bahucitīkaḥ*, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *citeḥ kapi*. Thus, the accent (*svara*) dependent on the *sthānin* vowel is established by the rule *hrasvānte’ntyātpūrvam*.

In the rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment of a substitute as being like the original) applies only to substitutes that involve elision (*lopa*). Therefore, in examples such as *akhaṭvakaḥ* and *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*, the aforementioned accent does not apply due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the short vowel [resulting from] the rule *āpo 'nyatarasyām*; rather, one should note that by the rule *kapi pūrvam*, the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is simply acute (*udātta*). Consequently, in the case of a grammatical operation (*vidhi*), it is as follows: *tanvanti* and *tanvate*. Due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *yaṇ*-substitute, the augment *iṭ* does not occur.

Otherwise, because the vowel *u* would be treated as an *ardhadhātuka*, once the *yaṇ* substitution had taken place, the suffix *sa* would apply due to its being preceded by a *val*. That [suffix] is constant there as a cause, and it occurs before the *u*. Why does the rule specify "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider *viśnaḥ*, *dyūtvā*, and *syūtvā*; in the first two, the letter *cha* becomes *śa*. Since that [change of *cha* to *śa*] is dependent on a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*), if it were to undergo the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *tuk* augment prescribed by the rule "che ca" would not occur. But surely, because it is an *antaraṅga* operation, the *tuk* ought to apply even earlier?

Regarding the rule *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* ("an internal [āṅga] operation is stronger than a phonetic [vārṇa] one"), its application occurs only when two operations apply simultaneously (*yugapatprāptika*) and share the same locus (*samānāśraya*). In the case of the root *kṛ*, when followed by the suffix *ṇal*, the form *kṛ a* is established. Here, the rule *aco ñṇiti* (P. 7.2.115), which prescribes *vṛddhi*, prevails over the *yaṇ* substitution that would otherwise apply due to its being an *antaraṅga* operation. This is because *vṛddhi* finds its scope of application in examples such as *gaura*. However, in the case of *praśna*, there is a disparity in the timing of their application: the substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs after the production of the suffix, whereas the *tuk* augment occurs prior to it. Furthermore, the *ś* substitution is conditioned by the suffix *naṅ*, while the *tuk* is conditioned by the suffix *cha*; thus, they do not share the same locus (*samānāśrayatvābhāva*). Therefore, the rule *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* does not apply here.

In this regard, the intention of the Easterners (prācām) is as follows: it is clear from the final portion of the first Āhnika in the sixth [Adhyāya] of the Bhāṣya that the mention of *asavarṇa* ("non-homogeneous") in the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [principle].

For instance, the purpose [of the rule] is not to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *īyatuḥ* and *ūṣatuḥ*, because that is already accounted for by the principle that an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) is stronger. This is because the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) depends only on its constituent parts, whereas the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* depend on both the designation of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-saṃjñā*) and the designation of the stem (*aṅga-saṅjñā*). Furthermore, *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are not exceptions (*apavāda*) to that [homogeneous long vowel rule]; rather, according to the maxim "that which applies when another does not," they are exceptions specifically to the *yaṇ*-substitution.

Now, one might object: in the case of *iṣ* and *eti* with the suffix *ṇal*, when the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply to form *iṣ-a-i-a*, the doubling of the vowel *i* occurs by means of the formal extension (*rūpātideśa*) provided by the rule *dvirvacane'ci*. Since this [rule *aco ñṇiti*] is initiated even though the substitution of a long vowel by homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) would otherwise have applied, its status as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [long-vowel substitution] is unavoidable. This is because, in accordance with forms such as *ninyatuḥ*, it is impossible to maintain a restriction that a grammatical operation which has already taken effect must persist after the application of doubling.

Otherwise, because *iyaṅ* would have already applied first, the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by the rule *eranekācaḥ* would not occur after the doubling [of the vowel]. This is not so; for even if the mention of "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*) were made, that [rule *eranekācaḥ*] would result in having no scope [for application]. Nor can it be argued that, by the force of that [mention of *asavarṇa*], the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions apply again, overriding the *savarṇa-dīrgha* (long-vowel) substitution; for [the mention of *asavarṇa*] finds its utility in cases such as *iyarti*. Nor can it be argued that, even in the absence of the mention of *asavarṇa*, since the *yaṇ* substitution would be established as overriding [the *dīrgha*] in *iyarti* by the principle of "that which was not applicable [before] being overridden" (*yenanāprāptinyāya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of not including that [mention of *asavarṇa*].

Because if one accepts the application of *guṇa* and other operations in forms such as *iyeṣa* by virtue of [the rule’s] inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), the futility of including the mention of "non-homogeneous vowels" (*asavarṇa*) remains unchanged. One could simply formulate the sūtra as "artteśca," and by carrying over the term "yvoḥ" from the previous rule, when *iyaṅ* is prescribed for the *ikāra* of the root *ṛt*, the forms *iyeṣa* and others would be established even by the force of the statement "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*). Nor is there any failure to establish the form *ariyarti* in the *yaṅluk* formation of *ṛ* (from *ṛt*) if the reading were "artteḥ," because the term "uḥ" alone should have been stated; for by association with *iṇ*, the reference to the verbal root (*dhātu*) is already established.

Alternatively, it is because the vowel *ṛ* is qualified by its own *aṅga* (the entire stem). Consequently, there is no fault in cases such as *attragniḥ*. Nor does it follow that *iyaṅ* would apply in forms like *īṣatuḥ*—as it does in *īyeṣa*—because the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution) is *antaraṅga* (more internal). In *īyeṣa*, however, the long vowel does not apply due to the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the rule that what is about to be produced is considered already accomplished), since the occurrence of *guṇa* is anticipated. By this same reasoning, the non-application of *iyaṅ* and other such substitutions in forms like *ninyatuḥ* is also explained.

And the evidence for this is the inclusion of the term *samartha* in the sūtra “*samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*”. For that [term] is intended to prevent the undesired form *sāvutthitiḥ*, *vāyīkṣamāṇiḥ*—which would otherwise result because the internal *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel coalescence) would fail to apply due to the destruction of its cause by the future initial *vṛddhi* in forms such as *sa-utthitiḥ* and *vāy-u-kṣamāṇiḥ*. In that context, the meaning of the word *samartha* is "finality," which consists in having undergone the operations of *sandhi*.

The meaning of that technical definition is that, having perceived a sign (nimitta) tending toward destruction, they do not perform the action prompted by it. However, if the point to be understood were that they also cause what has already been performed to cease, then one should recognize an excess of complexity (gaurava), even though the result might otherwise be the same.

Therefore, in cases such as *iy-eṣa*, once the *guṇa* has been applied, the *yaṇ* substitution would otherwise apply because there is no scope for the *savarṇadīrgha* rule; thus, *iyaṅ* becomes an exception (*apavāda*) to that very *yaṇ*. Consequently, the inclusion of the term *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous) would appear redundant. To justify the non-application of *guṇa* in this context, the principle that "an operation concerning a letter (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning a suffix (*āṅga*)" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), thereby establishing the purposefulness of the *asavarṇa* mention. Nor should it be argued: "Since *guṇa* is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the condition 'when not followed by a homogeneous vowel' (*asavarṇe*) remains unimpaired; how then can the maxim *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the non-application of a rule when its cause is subsequently destroyed) take effect? This objection is invalid.

This is because the rule *na padānta* prohibits that [substitution] in the context of rules concerning homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). However, in the view where the mention of "homogeneous sounds" and so forth in that [rule] is rejected, it will be stated later that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* applies only to a rule for what precedes, and not to a rule for a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) where it itself is preceded by something; thus, one should understand that there is a sublation of the cause for a long vowel by a homogeneous sound (*savarṇadīrgha*). Therefore, since both [rules] apply simultaneously when they share the same basis (*samānāśraya*), the aforementioned Paribhāṣā is made known, and it is accepted that [the Paribhāṣā] pertains even to such specific cases, in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*).

It might be argued as follows: In the rule *samānāśraya*, what is intended is the identity of the two *kāryin* (the elements undergoing the operation), or else the identity of the two *nimitta* (the causes of the operation). The first alternative is not tenable. This is because it contradicts the works of Kaiyaṭa and others, who state that in the case of *syona*—where the sequence *si + ū + na* is established—the rule does not apply due to the absence of *samānāśrayatva* (having a common substratum). This is since both the *guṇa* and *yaṇ* substitutions would apply to the vowel *i* alone, and thus [according to your view] *samānāśrayatva* would actually exist there. Furthermore, it contradicts their statement regarding *āhva*—where the sequence *āh + u + ā* is established—that the rule does not apply because the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) and the substitution of *pūrva* (*pūrvatva*) have different substrata (*vyāśrayatva*), as both have the vowel *ā* as their designated object (*uddeśya*).

The second [alternative] is not tenable; for in the case of *i i atus*, the long vowel resulting from *savarṇadīrgha* (P. 6.1.101) has the *ik* vowel as its cause, whereas the *yaṇ* substitution (P. 6.1.77) has the *ā* of the suffix as its cause. Thus, because they do not share a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*), the application of the rule is untenable. Furthermore, when the word *śvan* is treated as a *bha*-stem and undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*, in the form *śu-an-as*, the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) would be caused by the *bha*-designation, while the *pūrva-vidhi* (the preceding operation) would lack that cause. To illustrate: from the root *siv*, with the addition of the *uṇādi* suffix *nap* according to the rule *bāhulakāt*, both *guṇa* and *ūṭh* would apply after the elision of *v*. In that situation, since *ūṭh* is an exception (*apavāda*), it prevails and subverts the elision of *v*.

Nor, even in this case, is there a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamakābhāva*) regarding the sublation of the *guṇa* [substitution], because the *guṇa*—which depends on the stem (*aṅga*) connected to the suffix, the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhā*), and the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix—is *bahiraṅga*. On the other hand, *ūṭh*—which depends on the stem ending in *v* and the suffix beginning with a nasal—is *antaraṅga*. When the form *si-ū-na* has been established, both *guṇa* (of the light penultimate) and *yaṇ* (vocalization) are applicable; however, because it depends on fewer phonemes (*varṇa*), *yaṇ* is *antaraṅga* and thus takes precedence.

Then, by the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ū*; thus, the form *syonā* is established. Similarly, having stated in the rule *kavidhau sarvatra saṃprasāraṇibhyo ḍaḥ* that the suffix *ḍa* is applied after roots marked with *saṃprasāraṇa*, and having cited *āhvaḥ* and *prahvaḥ* as examples, one might suspect that the form is established by the suffix *ka*. However, if the suffix *ka* were applied, and the *uvaṅ* substitution were made for the *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel, the result would be *āhuvā*. Nor can it be argued that the *uvaṅ* does not apply because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) of the elision (*ālopa*), since that elision is subject to the operation of *pūrvatva* (substitution of the preceding element), which would cause the *uvaṅ* to apply.

Having stated that because [the rule for] *paratva* (subsequent application) prevails, there would be only the elision of the vowel *ā*, one might object that because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), the substitution of *pūrva* (the preceding element) should occur. In response, it is said that according to the principle "an *āṅga* operation is stronger than a *vārṇa* operation," there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. If this is so, then the following must be considered here: should the elision of *ā* be performed, or the *saṃprasāraṇa*? Having raised this, it is concluded that because of *paratva*, the elision of *āt* occurs first. Then, when *saṃprasāraṇa* takes place and the *yaṇ*-substitution follows, forms such as *āhvaḥ* and *prahvaḥ* are established. Thus says the Bhāṣya.

In the introduction to the Bhāṣya passage beginning with *evaṃ tarhi*, Kaiyaṭa states: "Since it is accepted that 'an internal operation (*āṅga*) is stronger than one based on phonemes (*vārṇa*)' applies only when the locus (*āśraya*) is the same, and since the [loci] of elision (*alopa*) and the state of being preceded by /p/ (*pūrvatva*) are different, that rule does not apply. Immediately following that, in his commentary on the Bhāṣya's explanation that "the state of being preceded [by something] (*pūrvatva*) is internal (*antaraṅga*)," he says: "It has been stated that the rule 'an internal operation is stronger than one based on phonemes' concerns only cases where the locus is the same."

Thus, regarding the form *a-a-atus* derived from the root *ācārakvi-banta* (formed by adding *kvip* to the verbal base *ācār*) after the prefix *a-*—in this case, because the elision of the *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) depends on multiple factors (*vyāśrayatvāt*), the rule "ato guṇe" applies, resulting in a single substitute (*pararūpa*). This contradicts the *Manoramā* and other works. To explain: in the commentary on the sūtra "upeyivān," it is stated that after reduplication of the root *iṇ* and the lengthening of the abhyāsa syllable, the substitution of *iy* is prescribed as a *nipātana*. An objection is raised that, since the lengthening rule "dīrgha iṇaḥ" would supersede [the substitution], the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule might not apply. In response, it is argued that the lengthening itself does not block the single-substitute; rather, it is the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by "iṇo yaṇ" that would do so.

And that [substitution] is an obstacle only to its own application; however, since there is no possibility of *yaṇ* substitution here, it is simply a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)—so it is stated in the Bhāṣya. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa raises the objection that in the case of *īyatuḥ*, when the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-dīrghatva*) applies, if *yaṇ* were applied before the single-substitute according to the rule "the *āṅga* operation prevails over the *vārṇa* operation," then the single-substitute would apply again by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva*. Anticipating this, he states that because the *sthānivadbhāva* does not extend the form itself, the single-substitute—which depends on that form—is absent in the letter *yakāra*.

It has been explained that because the rule *vārṇādāṅgam* (an internal operation takes precedence over an external one) subordinates the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) by means of the *yaṇ*-substitution, there is no possibility [of the single-substitute applying] once the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) has been established. The meaning is this: in the state *i i atus*, just as the *yaṇ*-substitution for *iṇ* subordinates the single-substitute, so too does it do so even after the status of *sthānivadbhāva* has occurred, provided the single-substitute would otherwise apply.

Similarly, regarding the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* and the Vārttika *aṭo vṛddheriyaṅ*, in the commentary on the Bhāṣya passage concerning *adhyaiyātām*—which states that "the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) [vṛddhi] [takes precedence]"—there is a contradiction with Kaiyaṭa, who asserts that this was stated without relying on the principle *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* ("an operation affecting a vowel is stronger than one affecting a consonant").

Thus, regarding the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*, in the view that the substitution of *āy* results in the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel (*alo’ntyasya*), the forms such as *glānīya* are established. In the course of explaining this, consider the case of *glai* with the suffix *atus*: after the substitution of *āy*, we have *glā ā atus*. Here, both the substitution of *ekādeśa* (the single substitute *ā*) and the elision of the initial *ā* (*ātolopaḥ*) would apply. Since the *ekādeśa* depends on two phonemes (*varṇāśrayatva*), it is *antaraṅga* (internal) even so; nevertheless, by the maxim *vārṇādāṅgam* ("an *āṅga* operation [which depends on a single phoneme] takes precedence over one that depends on two phonemes"), the elision of the initial *ā* occurs first.

Having raised the objection that, because [the substitute] is not established due to its being *abhīya* (to be applied later) and because of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, the elision of the preceding *at* would not occur, Kaiyaṭa’s statement—that this was said without relying on the principle "that which pertains to a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is weaker than that which pertains to a suffix (*āṅga*)"—would also be inconsistent.

It might be argued as follows: that [condition] consists in having two types of predication (vidheyatā) relative to a single object of designation (uddeśyatā) residing in a single phoneme, which in turn is defined by a causality (kāraṇatā) residing in a single cause, as in examples such as *kṛ*. And this has been stated in the *Kauṣṭubha*: "For where, taking one and the same thing as the cause, there is a simultaneous application of both a phonemic operation (*vārṇa*) and a morphological operation (*āṅga*), only there does the rule 'the morphological is stronger than the phonemic' (*vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*) apply. In the case of *vicchinnaḥ*, because the difference between the causes—the letter *ch* and the letter *n*—is evident, there is no fault in cases such as *syonaḥ*.

In this regard, the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is the cause for the substitution of a *guṇa*, whereas for the substitution of a *yaṇ*, the cause is the presence of a vowel (*aj*) other than *i*; thus, there is a difference in the causes. Even in cases such as *āhva*, although the elision (*lopa*) and the state of being preceded by [the elided vowel] have the same objective (*uddeśya*), the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is the cause for the elision, but not for the state of being preceded [by it]; therefore, because there is no identity of cause, there is no fault. There is likewise no fault in the case of *śunaḥ*, because the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) is caused by the technical designation *bha*. Furthermore, there is no obstacle to the state of being preceded by the *saṃprasāraṇa* also being caused by the *bha*-designation, since what is intended to be expressed as the "cause" (*nimitta*) is precisely that which is common to both the direct motivator (*prayojaka*) and the indirect condition.

In reality, however, in the case of *śunaḥ*, only the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) is intended, based on the authority of the commentaries on the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra. This is because it will be demonstrated there that if the elision of *al* (*allopa*) were applied first, it would result in the occurrence of the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*. Furthermore, the statements of Kaiyaṭa and others regarding the *asiddhavat* rule in relation to the elision of *al* are merely displays of rhetorical skill (*prauḍhimātra*). Consequently, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) even in the case of *dyavatī*, since although the *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitutions share a single objective, they differ in their causes (*nimitta*), namely the vowel *ū* and the *sārvadhātuka* suffix respectively. [Objection: Do not say so.

In the case of *īyatuḥ*, [the substitution] does not occur here because of the absence of that [condition]. This is because there is a difference in the operands (*kāryin*): in the case of *savarṇadīrgha*, the first *i* is the operand, whereas in the case of *yaṇ*, it is the second. Nor should it be argued that, by the rule "one [substitute] for both the preceding and the following," the second *i* is also the operand in *savarṇadīrgha*; even so, there is a distinction, for in the case of *yaṇ*, the vowel of *atus* is the cause (*nimitta*), while in the case of *savarṇadīrgha*, it is the *i* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). [Objection: But surely, under the view that the doubling occurs in place of the original (*sthāne-dvirvacana*), the vowel of *atus* is also a cause for doubling.

If you argue that in the case of *cakratuḥ*, the status of being a cause for doubling (*dvitvanimittatva*) must be accepted only for that which is the actual instigator of doubling—whether directly or by virtue of being a constituent of the whole—in order to apply the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original) to the *yaṇ* [substitution], and that there is no obstacle to adopting such a principle here as well in accordance with the observed forms; and furthermore, that since the vowel *a* is the instigator of the second *i*, it also possesses the status of being a cause for the *savarṇadīrgha* (long-vowel substitution), while its status as a cause for *yaṇ* is indeed clear—then do not say so. For in the word *syona*, the vowel *ū* is the cause of the *yaṇ* substitution, yet because the *guṇa* [substitution] is also an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, that [suffix] too would be a cause for it.

In the case of *āhva*, the *samprasāraṇa* is the cause for the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*), and since the *kit*-status [of the suffix] is also a cause therein, it would follow that [the *samprasāraṇa*] shares the same locus (*samānāśrayatva*) with respect to the elision of the vowel (*ātolopa*) caused by the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix ending in *kit*. Nor can it be argued that the phrase "having a single cause" means "having a cause residing in that which is delimited by a single property," because in the case of *īyatur*, the *ikāra* and *akāra*—which are the causes respectively of the *savarṇadīrgha* and the *yaṇ*-substitution—are both delimited by the single property of being a vowel (*actva*).

In the case of the word *viśnaḥ*, even though the *n* and *c* sounds are caused respectively by the substitution of *śatva* and the addition of *tuka*, they are nonetheless subsumed under the single property of being *it*.

Furthermore, according to the previously mentioned method of establishing identity of place (*sthānaikya*) for both *yaṇ* and *savarṇadīrgha*, in the rule *ijādeśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.36), in the case of *ṛ ṛ atus*, both *savarṇadīrgha* and *yaṇ* would apply.
