Since *savarṇadīrgha* is subsequent, it takes precedence; thus, when we have *ṛ atus*, and by the principle that a single substitute is treated as the final part of the preceding and the initial part of the following (*ekādeśasyāntādivadbhāvaḥ*), the *ṛ*-vowel is included under the term "root" (*dhātu*). Consequently, by the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11), *guṇa* is applied, followed by *rapara* (substitution of *r*); thus, we obtain *aratus*. However, if [the first *ṛ*] were taken as the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), then by the rule *urat* (Pāṇini 7.4.66), *a* is substituted, followed by *rapara*, *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60), and *ata ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70).

In the Bhāṣyakāra’s apprehension that the form would be *āt-atus* when there is elision (*lopa*) of the long vowel *ā*, he raises the objection that in the stage *ṛ-ṛ-atus*, because [the *ṛ*] is part of the stem (*aṅga*), the substitution of *urat* (i.e., *u*) should indeed occur; anticipating this, Kaiyaṭa states that the rule *vārṇādāṅgam* ("an operation concerning vowels [or phonemes] takes precedence over one concerning suffixes") applies to cases where the locus (*āśraya*) is the same, whereas the substitution of *savarṇadīrgha* (homogeneous long vowel) depends on two phonemes and thus has a different locus (*bhinna-āśrayatva*). This constitutes a contradiction with Kaiyaṭa.

Furthermore, in the view that the doubling of the first [element] by the rule *ekāco dve* and the doubling of the second by the rule *ajādeḥ* are combined because there is no contradiction between them, the doubling of the second would be purposeless. To illustrate: when *aṭ* is followed by the suffix *san* with the augment *iṭ*, resulting in *aṭ-i-s*, the first element (*aṭ*) undergoes doubling. Then, after the doubling of *aṭ*—that is, *aṭ-aṭ*—the *ṭ* is eliminated by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, and the second element (*aṭ*) undergoes doubling, followed by *halādiśeṣaḥ*.

Regarding the forms *a-a-aṭ* or *a-a-aṭ*, there is no difference in the resulting form (*pararūpa*) whether three instances of the vowel *a* or two instances of the vowel *a* are involved. In this regard, anticipating the objection that the second doubling might occur even before the application of *halādiśeṣa*, Kaiyaṭa stated:

Because it is permanent (*nitya*), the *hal-ādi-śeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant) applies first; this is because it applies both when [the conditions for doubling] have been fulfilled and when they have not. However, the second doubling is impermanent (*anitya*) because it applies upon the occurrence of a different word-form (*śabdāntara-prāpti*). For that [second doubling] would apply to the augment *aṭ* once the *hal-ādi-śeṣa* has been performed, but to the syllable *ṭ* itself if it has not yet been performed. Furthermore, by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), the *pararūpa* substitution prescribed by "ato guṇe" (P. 6.1.97) overrides the *it* substitution prescribed by "sanyataḥ" (P. 7.4.79). Indeed, the *it* substitution of "sanyataḥ" is *bahiraṅga* (external) as it depends upon both the suffix *san* and the reduplication (*abhyāsa*).
According to the view that "the section on the stem (*aṅga-adhikāra*) precedes the modifications of the reduplication," the *it* substitution does not belong to the stem (*āṅga*).

Nor does the rule "an internal (aṅga) operation is stronger than a phonetic (vārṇa) one" apply here; for even if that were the case, since the substitution of *i* (itva) is not based on the *aṅga* itself, the paribhāṣā concerning *aṅga* and *vārṇa* operations does not present itself in this context. Furthermore, according to the reasoning already stated, since the suffix *san* is the cause for doubling (*dvitva*), it serves as the cause for the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) of the preceding *ā* and the following *ā* by way of producing the second *ā*. Thus, the substitution of *i* and the *pararūpa* would share a single cause. This is the general direction of the argument.

To this it is replied: here, what is intended by "having a common locus" (*samānāśrayatva*) is precisely "being prompted by a common cause. This is because Kaiyaṭa has stated that since the substitution of the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *san* and the reduplicated base (*abhyāsa*), as well as the substitution of the single substitute for *it* and the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), depend solely upon the phonemes themselves, they have different loci (*bhinnāśrayatva*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the specific passage beginning with "In the case of *īyatuḥ*, the long vowel *ī* following the reduplicated base would have a common locus with the *yaṇ*-substitution by virtue of being its substituend" would be inconsistent.

Likewise, because the substitution of *satya* itself for the form *pararūpa* would result in the same locus (*samānaśrayatva*) due to its status as the substituendum (*sthānitva*), it might be asked: "How is the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the aforementioned case avoided? It should not be so stated, because that which is intended [by the definition] exists there. To explain: [the definition is] the state of having an objecthood (*uddeśyatā*) for a phonemic operation (*vārṇakārya*) that is not pervaded (*aparyāpta*) by that which is the locus of being the cause (*nimittatva*) for a phonemic operation, while being a locus of objecthood (*uddeśyatva*) relative to an operation pertaining to an *aṅga*.

That [definition] consists in having as its cause either of two conditions: (1) the state of being co-located with a single substratum (*ekadharmiparyāptatva*) while the locus of the full distribution (*paryāptyadhikaraṇa*) of the property of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) remains one; or (2) the state of having as its cause that which possesses either of these two. There is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of those examples cited as having different substrata (*vyāśraya*), because the locus of the intended objecthood for an *aṅga*-operation is not the locus of the causality for a phoneme-operation (*vārṇakārya*). However, in the case of *vicchinnaḥ*, there is an over-extension, because the letter *cha*—which is the intended object of the *aṅga*-operation of *śatva*—is the cause of the phoneme-operation *tuk*. Therefore, the definition is refined by specifying that the intended objecthood of the phoneme-operation must not be fully distributed (*aparyāpta*) [over the same substratum].

In the case of *i i atu*, in order to avoid the deficiency (avyāpti) arising from the fact that the second *ikāra*—which is not the intended object (*uddeśya*) for the operation on the *aṅga*—serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for the phonological operation (*vārṇakārya*) of *savarṇadīrgha* and is itself the intended object, the definition must abandon "repetition" (*āvṛttitva*) and instead incorporate "non-pervasion" (*aparyāptatva*). Since this [second *ikāra*] is pervaded by both the preceding and following elements, there is no fault.

Since the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between being the objective (*uddeśyatva*) of a phoneme-based operation (*vārṇakārya*) and being the cause (*nimittatva*) of an auxiliary operation (*āṅgakārya*) does not exist in the cited examples—because they do not share a common substratum (*samānāśrayatva*)—the definition of co-referentiality has been formulated as "being the objective of a phoneme-based operation" and "being the cause of an auxiliary operation" in order to exclude the possibility of non-occurrence (*asambhava*). Although it might be argued that if one says, "The state of having an objective for a phoneme-based operation that is not pervaded (*aparyāpta*) by that which is the substratum of the objective relative to the auxiliary operation," there would still be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *si ū naḥ pṛcchati*.

Although the status of being the *uddeśya* (the subject of a rule) is fully present in the *ik* vowels and the *ūk* vowel when they are intended as the locus of a grammatical operation (*guṇa*), there would still be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *ṛtṛ-atus* and *aṭiṭiṣati*. This is because, in these instances, the *ṛ*-vowel of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) and the vowel *-a-* [of the root] are both locuses where the status of being the *uddeśya* for two types of operations resides—namely, the substitution of *ur* by *uratvam* and the substitution of *it* by *sanyataḥ*—yet they lack the status of being locuses where the status of being the *uddeśya* for a phonological operation (*vārṇakārya*) in the form of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) is fully present. Therefore, the phrase "locus of the cause of a phonological operation" (*varṇakāryanimittatvādhikaraṇa*) was stated [in the definition].

However, those two [the first two *sthānas*] do not possess the status of being the cause for a phonemic operation (*vārṇakārya*), because that status belongs only to the second two. Thus, since there is no established instance of that which is both the locus of the cause for a phonemic operation and co-locative with being the objective of an anga-operation, there is no fault in that regard. This is because the second two are not objectives of an anga-operation, and the first two are not causes with respect to a phonemic operation. If it were stated that "being the locus of the cause for a phonemic operation" means "having an objective for a phonemic operation that is not pervasively distributed (*aparyāpta*)," then over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would occur precisely in that case.

This is because, in the case of the two [rules *iko yaṇ aci* and *eṅi pararūpam*], they possess the status of being the locus for the complete satisfaction (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatva*) of the objecthood (*uddeśyatva*) of the *savarṇadīrgha* [substitution], and because they are the cause (*nimitta*) thereof. Likewise, in examples such as *pṛcchati*, the letter *cha*—which is the cause of the *tuk* augment—does not possess the objecthood of the *tuk* itself; rather, it is the short vowel (*hrasva*) alone that possesses such status. Therefore, it is stated that [the cause] must be "that which is the locus for the objecthood relative to an internal (*āṅga*) operation. In the aforementioned instances, however, there is no fault, because those [letters] do not possess the objecthood toward the internal operation. Furthermore, the phrase "complete satisfaction of objecthood" (*uddeśyatvaparyāpti*) and so forth is used to avoid the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of *kṛ-a*.

In this regard, there is no over-extension [of the definition], because the property of being the object of both *yaṇ-adeśa* and *vṛddhi* subsists completely (*paryāptyā*) in the letter *ṛ* alone, and the property of being the cause of both subsists completely in the letter *ā* alone; such is the general direction of the argument.

On this point, they say: Is the restriction of the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* to cases where the locus (*āśraya*) is identical assumed in accordance with the authoritative sources (*ākaras*), or on the strength of the very means of proof that establishes the rule (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*)? It cannot be the first, because in the *pūrvapakṣa* of the sūtra *ajādeḥ*, Kaiyaṭa, for the sake of the form *iyatiṣati*, relies upon the general principle "that which pertains to a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than that which pertains to a stem (*āṅga*)," rather than restricting it only to cases where the *aṅga* and the *vārṇa* share the same locus; he states that by this [general principle], the substitution of *it* alone takes effect, and not the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule. Nor can it be the second.

Because the purpose of the mention of "non-homogeneous vowels" (*asavarṇagrahaṇa*) cannot otherwise be justified, that [mention] is exhausted merely by making known the principle that "an *aṅga* operation is stronger than a vowel-based (*vārṇa*) operation"; it lacks the capacity to extend to the scope of having a common substratum (*sāmānāśraya*) alone. Furthermore, since the scope of that [principle] consists only in the two things to be prescribed (*vidheya*) having a common substratum in the form of a single object of reference (*uddeśya*), the aforementioned commonality of substratum is not established.

Furthermore, in cases such as *sautthitiḥ*, since [the rule] has been made known to apply when there is a common locus (*samānāśraya*), the maxim regarding the non-application of a rule once its conditions have been fulfilled (*akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*) would also operate only in that domain. This is not an acceptable conclusion, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of that maxim not applying in forms such as *seduṣīm*. Nor can it be argued that there is no common locus in those instances; for Kaiyaṭa has stated that, due to the common locus, the rule "that which pertains to the base is stronger than that which pertains to the phoneme" (*vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*) would result in the occurrence of *vṛddhi*.

By this, the view that this [vṛddhi] has as its object only those instances where there is simultaneous application is also refuted; for since vṛddhi is conditioned by a suffix, there is no prior application [of it].

Furthermore, regarding the term *viśvavāh*, the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is a *bahiraṅga* operation; according to the principle that a *bahiraṅga* operation is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when an *antaraṅga* operation is to be applied, the *asiddhatva* would apply only to that which has an *antaraṅga* operation subsequently applicable. Consequently, in forms such as *akṣadyūḥ*, since the *yaṇ* substitution would not even be applicable to the *bahiraṅga* *ūṭh*, the *asiddhatva* would not arise. Thus, the prohibition of this [application of the *asiddha* rule] by the author of the Bhāṣya in the maxim "nājānantarye" would be rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, in the case of *adhītya* and *pretya*, since there is no possibility for the insertion of *tuk*—which would be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) to the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) for the external single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)—the rule *asiddhaparibhāṣā* does not apply. Consequently, it would be untenable for the mention of *tuk* in the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* to serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the existence of the maxim *nājānantarye*. Nor should it be argued that this leads to the collapse of the *yathoddeśapakṣa* (the view that rules are effective at the time they are taught), because that maxim is not established here; its scope is restricted to cases where the location of the indicator is logically untenable, which is not the case here.

This is because that [distinction] is postulated in accordance with the requirements of the specific grammatical illustrations (*lakṣya*). Otherwise, if there were a rule restricting the operation to the same location as the indicator (*jñāpaka*), even for you, the position of the "time of the effect" (*kāryakālapakṣa*) would be undermined. Furthermore, Sīradeva and others have stated that the fact that *naṅ* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign in the rule "yajayāca... is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this [principle] operates even when the bases belong to different locations (*vyāśraya*). Otherwise, since the *tuk* augment would apply first due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the penultimate syllable would no longer be light; consequently, there would be no possibility of *guṇa* substitution, and thus the *ṅ*-sign added to prevent such *guṇa* would be rendered purposeless.

This is because the author of the *Nyāsa* states that in forms such as *cyavante* and *plavante*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule applies once the *guṇa* substitution has been performed; and because Kaiyaṭa states in the case of *sunaḥ* that there is elision of the *a* (*allopa*). It should not be argued that in those cases there is indeed a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*), since the vowel *a*—which is the objective (*uddeśya*) in the *āṅga* operation of elision—is itself the cause (*nimitta*) for the prior-form (*pūrvarūpa*) substitution under the rule "after a semivowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*)," which is explained as: "when a vowel follows a semivowel, a single substitute in the form of the prior vowel shall occur. This is because [in the case of *sunu*] there exists the quality of having an objective that is not exhausted by that [prior-form substitution].

In this context, the objective (uddeśyatā) must also be qualified by the property of not being delimited by the delimiting condition of the cause (nimittatāvacchedakadharma). This is because, in the previously mentioned form [of the rule], *actva* alone serves as the delimiting condition for both the causality and the objectivity; otherwise, the statement regarding the difference in substratum (*vyāśrayatva*) between the elision of *ā* and the state of being preceded by *pūrva* in examples such as *āhva* would result in logical inconsistency.

If it is argued that, in this way, since the substitution of *ś* (for *s*) would be established even in a case of different bases (*vyāśraya*) as in *viśraḥ*, the aforementioned defects regarding cases of different bases would still apply—this is true. However, because the rule *vārṇād āṅgam* ("an internal operation [āṅga] prevails over an external one [vārṇa]") is not universal, it does not apply there. And the proof for this is the mention of the *t* in the rule *ch-voḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.73). Nor should it be said that the word *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") is included in that rule merely to prohibit the *tuk* augment by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle; for the word *acaḥ* is necessary for other purposes. Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for this.

This is because the *ṣaṣṭhabhāṣya* itself is of that very nature; otherwise, since *tuk* would not apply once *śatva* (the substitution of *ś* for *s*) has been effected due to [the suffix] being an *aṅga*, the [commentary] would result in inconsistency. Therefore, there is no fault regarding the previously mentioned cases where different bases (*vyāśraya*) are involved. Nor should it be argued that the mention of *tuk* with the *n* (i.e., *satuk*) is intended merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the present paribhāṣā applies only to cases where the bases are identical (*samānāśraya*); for such a restriction to a specific domain would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and the aforementioned condition of having identical bases is itself cumbersome.

Now, one might argue that there is no possibility of *tuk* here at all, according to the maxim *akṛtavyūha* (the non-application of a grammatical operation when its cause subsequently disappears). This is not so; for even if that maxim is not universally valid, the specific mention of *satuk* (with *tuk*) serves as evidence for it. Thus, the *ṅit*-designation of *naṅ* is solely for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*. The statement of Sīradeva and others, however, intends the meaning exactly as it is heard [in the rule]. By this, it is explained that the *ṅit*-designation of *naṅ* itself is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the *akṛtavyūha* paribhāṣā. Furthermore, the rule *samarthānām* need not exist; this is also explained by the natural sense of the Bhāṣya: "The *samartha* sūtra should be formulated, and it is indeed formulated as 'of those that are semantically connected, the first [case-ending] optionally'."

Furthermore, in the rule *rāllopaḥ* as well, since there would be the undesirable consequence of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of [the suffix] *satuk* (with the augment *tuk*), the elision of the *ch* in forms such as *hūḥ*, *hurau*, and so forth—which lack the *tuk*—would not occur. Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the recurrence, only the pure *śakāra* (the letter *ś*) is intended there, because it is certain that the *chakāra* following a *repha* (the letter *r*) lacks the *tuk*. For it is possible that only the *vakāra* (the letter *v*) recurs, and there is no evidence for the recurrence of the *chakāra* itself.

On this point, they say: both *satukkavitukkau* are indicated here. Nor should it be argued that if this were a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*), a singular ending would result, whereas if it were a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*), a plural ending would follow; for the explanation is that one forms a collective compound of the two *cha*-sounds and then forms a copulative compound with the *va*-sound. Furthermore, in the case of the substitute (*ādeśa*), there is also an elision (*praśleṣa*) of a second *śa*.

Alternatively, because of the rule *na dhyākhyā*, which prohibits the substitution of *n* for the final letter of the root *murch* when followed by a *niṣṭhā* suffix, this serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that the letter *ch* in the rule *rāllopa* refers to the pure letter *ch*. This is because, in the absence of the elision of *ch*, there would be no possibility of the substitution of *n* since the condition of being preceded by a *repha* (the letter *r*) would not be met; such is the direction of the argument.

Let us return to the subject at hand. The counter-example for the rule *acaḥ* (P. 1.1.57) is *dyūtvā* and *syūtveti*. Otherwise, due to the status of *ūṭh* as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur. Nor should it be argued that because extensions (*atideśa*) do not preclude their own inherent properties, the property of being a vowel (*actva*) will still apply here on its own account; for by the force of the inclusion of the term *vidhi* (in P. 1.1.56), there is a preclusion of one's own inherent properties, and furthermore, it will be stated later that through the use of the suffix *-vat*, even an absence can be extended.

[Objection: But surely, while the *ūṭh* (the substitute) is the locus for the pervasion (*paryāpti*) of being an *ādeśa*, neither the *yaṇ*-triggering [original] nor the *ū* sound is the locus for the pervasion of being an *ādeśa*, because that [status of being an *ādeśa*] is pervasive over the entire aggregate. [Reply: This is not so. Because *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are non-exclusive (*anekānta*). Even if they were exclusive (*ekānta*), because the *ū* sound perishes immediately prior [to the operation], it alone is the locus for the pervasion of being an *ādeśa*. Likewise, in the case of *abhigatyā*, since the elision of the *m* is caused by what follows (*paranimittaka*), if it were to undergo the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the *tuk* augment prescribed by the rule "hrasvasya piti kṛti" would not apply.

One might ask: "Why was *akrāṣṭām* not cited as a counter-example? For in that case, since the elision of *sic* is conditioned by what follows (*paranimittaka*), the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* (by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ ka si*) would apply through the status of the elided element as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*). If you say this, it is not so; for there is a prohibition precisely by the rule: "In a matter dependent on what precedes (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*), [an operation] is not like the original (*na sthānivat*). What is the purpose of the word "in what follows" (*parasmin*)? Consider the example *yuvajāniḥ*. Here, the substitute *niṅ* for *jāyā* is an *ākāra*-substitution. When the elision of the preceding *yakāra* is to be performed (by the rule *lopo vyoḥ*), let there be no *sthānivadbhāva* [of the *ākāra*].

One who has feet like those of a tiger is a *vyāghrapāt*. In the rule "pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ," the elision (*lopa*) of the word *pāda* is not conditioned by anything subsequent (*aparanimittaka*). From that, the suffix *yañ* is applied because [the name] belongs to the *garga*-class, resulting in *vaiyāghrapadyaḥ*. Regarding the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* (as in the rule "pādaḥ pad"), the elision of the vowel *a* does not function as a *sthānivat* (as if the original element were still present) when the operation is to be applied. Nor can this be justified by the force of the specific rule itself; for if it were so, the same result would undesirably follow in cases such as *pādena*, due to the treatment of the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) as being like the initial element. Furthermore, the purpose of the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* is already fulfilled in forms such as *dvipadikā*.

In that context, by the rule *pādaśatasya saṃkhyādervīpsāyāṃ vun lopaśca*, the suffix *vun* is applied and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a*. Furthermore, the status of being "as if the original were present" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply here. Even though the elision is already established by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the force of the explicit mention of "elision" (*lopa*) again implies that this elision is not dependent on a subsequent cause (*paranimittakatva*). However, the rule *pādasya lopaḥ* has no such force [to prevent *sthānivadbhāva*], because it finds its scope of application in cases like *vyāghrapād*, where the designation *bha* is absent. But when the condition "in the presence of a subsequent element" (*parasmin*) is stated, then in forms such as *pādena*, the substitution of *pad* does not occur.

In forms such as *vaiyāghrapadya*, the substitution of *pad* (P. 6.4.130) has its own scope; however, there, because of the status of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), and because when a letter is mentioned the entire class is understood, that substitution would apply even to non-vowel substitutes. For this very reason, in cases such as *śrāyasau*, *gaumatau*, *cāturau*, and *ānuḍuhau*, where the single-substitute would otherwise behave as the initial element, the augment *num* and the feminine suffix *ām* do not occur. Likewise, if the word "in the subsequent" (*parasmin*) were not stated [in P. 1.1.57], then in *audavāhau*, because the single-substitute would behave as the initial element, the designation *bha* would apply, and consequently the substitution of *ūṭh* for *vāh* (P. 6.4.132) would take place.

"Udavāhaḥ" means "one who carries water"; [this is formed] with the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. [In the word "udavāhaḥ,"] the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* occurs when it is a name (*saṃjñāyām*). [In the word "audavāhiḥ,"] the suffix *iñ* is applied because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. In the forms *ādīdhye* and *āvevye*, the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* (the final vowel) of the root *ik* is caused by what follows; however, because that [substitution] would be considered as having the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the elision [of the *y*] prescribed by the rule *yīvarṇayordīdhīvevyoḥ* would occur. [The sūtra states] "for a preceding operation" (*pūrvavidhau*)—why? Consider the example *naidheyaḥ*. From the root *dhā* preceded by *ni*, the suffix *ki* is applied; there is the elision of the long *ā* (*āto lopaḥ*). Then, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rules *dvyacaḥ* and *itaścāniñaḥ*.

Because the elision (*āllopa*) would be treated as *sthānivat*, and because [the word] consists of three syllables (*tryac*), the aforementioned rule might fail to apply; for operations prescribed for words of two syllables (*dvyackārya*) do not apply to words of three syllables. Nor is the inclusion of the term "rule" (*vidhi*) redundant even if the reading were *pūrvasya* alone, since the meaning "when an operation is to be performed" can be inferred from that. This is because the purpose is to obtain both compounds: *pūrvasya* (genitive) and *pūrvasmāt* (ablative). An example of the ablative compound, however, has already been stated previously in the discussion of the form *tanvanti*.

Is it not the case that this [principle] is already covered by the rule *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*? Nor is there a prohibition by the rule *nājānantarye*, because according to Kaiyaṭa’s established doctrine, that [prohibition] applies only where there is immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of vowels (*ac*) within the *antaraṅga* operation; whereas here, since the *yaṇ* substitution—which is *bahiraṅga*—requires the immediate sequence of vowels. Not so. For Haradatta accepts that the prohibition [of *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*] operates in cases where, between an *antaraṅga* and a *bahiraṅga* operation, there is immediate sequence of vowels in either one of them.

On this point, they object as follows: Kaiyaṭa’s view alone is correct—that the paribhāṣā "that which is extraneous (bahiraṅga) is unestablished" does not apply where there is a dependence on a subsequent operation that occurs later—rather than Haradatta’s view that it applies when either of two operations occurs between them. Otherwise, there would result an inconsistency with the statement made by the Bhāṣya and Haradatta and others regarding *pacāvedam*, where they raise the objection concerning the non-application of "eta ai" by arguing that the guṇa substitution is unestablished due to its being extraneous (*bahiraṅga*).

For if a *guṇa* substitution had already taken effect, the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] would apply because there is no immediate sequence (*ajānantarya*) with the vowel *a*. However, according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, since the substitution of *ai* occurs after the *guṇa*, it does not depend on the immediate sequence of *a*; thus, the prohibition does not apply, and its invalidity (*asiddhatva*) as a "foreign" (*bahiraṅga*) operation is established. Furthermore, this is not in conflict with the Bhāṣya on the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke*, where the author provides a solution for the form *preddha* by relying on its invalidity as a "foreign" operation.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with Haradatta’s statement regarding the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58). Taking the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the example *daddhyatra*, he asserts that the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* does not apply because of the force of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*. However, according to his own logic, since the condition of immediate sequence with a vowel (*ajānantarya*) exists in the case of the *bahiraṅga* *yaṇ*-substitution, the non-application of that rule would be established by the very prohibition *nājānantarye* (Pāṇini 1.1.59); thus, his pursuit of the "force of the prohibition" (*sāmarthya*) is redundant.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya and Vārttika passages which reject [the rule] "saṃyogāntalope yaṇaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ" on the grounds of the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*. This is because, since the *yaṇ* and the *ac* are in immediate succession (*ajānantarya*), the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* would fail to apply due to the presence of that very condition. Therefore, the opinion of Haradatta should be disregarded, as it contradicts his own earlier and later statements and conflicts with the Bhāṣya.

In this regard, the following must be considered: where, in the formulation of a rule (*kāryavidhi*), there is a reliance on vowels (*ac*) by means of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), there the Paribhāṣā [stating that a rule does not apply across a hiatus] is not present due to the prohibition, as in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*. For in that instance, there is a reliance on vowels based on the statement "iko yaṇ aci. However, in this prohibitive sūtra (*na dhātulopa...*), there is no reliance on vowels; such is the text of Kaiyaṭa regarding the sūtra *na dhātulopa...*. In that context, is the dual number in "acoḥ" intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*) or not? It cannot be the first alternative, because it would contradict the authority that establishes the nature of the subject (*dharmigrāhakamānavirodhāt*).

In the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*, the requirement for the immediate sequence of two vowels (*aj-dvayānantarya*) is not expected, because the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed for a *yaṇ* following an *iṇ* vowel, and the insertion of *tug* is prescribed after a short vowel. Nor is the second alternative [the view that the rule applies to all operations] tenable; for even in the case of *dadhya atra*, since the doubling of a *yar* following a vowel is prescribed, the condition of immediate sequence with a vowel (*aj-anantarya*) exists. Consequently, the aforementioned prohibition [of the *sthānivadbhāva*] would apply, and thus it is necessary to follow the force of the prohibition against *sthānivadbhāva*.

Nor should it be argued that the prohibition "nājānantarye" applies only where a subsequent vowel (*ac*) serves as the cause—as in *akṣadyūḥ* and the like—whereas in *dadhyatra*, since the preceding vowel alone is the cause, that prohibition does not apply; for this would contradict the very nature of the subject (*dharmigrāhakavirodha*). This is because it is impossible to maintain that a maxim (*paribhāṣā*), which is taught in a context involving the non-proximity of vowels (*acorānantarya*) in an external operation (*bahiraṅga*), should apply only where such non-proximity of vowels occurs in an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).
Therefore, this is Haradatta’s intended meaning here:

The doubling [of the consonant] in *acori* is indeed intended to be expressed. Furthermore, there is no insistence on whether that [doubling] relies upon an internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*) operation. This is because, regarding the indicator (*jñāpaka*), even when there is a requirement for the non-intervening sequence of vowels (*ac-ānantarya*), that restriction is not included within the Paribhāṣā, as it must follow the specific requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*). For this very reason, the authors of the Bhāṣya stated: "In *dhinvanti* and *kṛṣvanti*, once the *yaṇ* substitution has taken place, the augment *iṭ*—conditioned by a consonant beginning with *v* (*valādi*)—would apply; however, it does not apply due to the status of the original element being preserved (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Otherwise, if the prohibition "there is no [application of the rule] when there is non-intervening sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*) were operative, the matter would already be resolved by the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* itself, rendering the aforementioned statement redundant.

Furthermore, regarding the question "What is the purpose of [the doubling] in *kartr-artha*?", one might suspect that the mention of *aṇ* in the subsequent rule (*uraṇ rapara*) should be for the sake of hearing two *r*s. However, the Bhāṣya itself states that even when the substitution of *r* has been applied, because the elision by the rule "ro ri" is mandatory once the *rapara* status is established, there is no hearing of two *r*s. For if the *asiddha-paribhāṣā* were to apply there, the elision would be impossible, and thus the claim that the purpose is to hear two *r*s would become untenable.

This is because the *bhāṣya* is consistent only if the prohibition "there is no [application of a rule] when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*) applies precisely at the stage of the substitution of *yaṇ*, since there is indeed an absence of vowel-adjacency (*ajānantarya*) due to its having occurred previously. However, once the elision (*lopa*) has taken effect at a later time, not even a single vowel remains to be expected; therefore, it is impossible to apply the aforementioned prohibition.

By this demonstration of the contradiction with the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated therein, the refutation of Haradatta’s view is also set aside; for the contradiction with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) should be raised against Kaiyaṭa’s view alone. Furthermore, the passage in the commentary on the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58) proceeds on the understanding that there is no inconsistency there even without the *nājānantarya-paribhāṣā*.

Even in Kaiyaṭa’s view, there is a contradiction because the term *ac* (vowel) is intended to be non-restrictive regarding doubling; thus, in forms such as *vṛtrahabhyām*, this prohibition would apply, resulting in the occurrence of the augment *tuk* by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*. Furthermore, this contradicts the statement in the Bhāṣya that "the elision of *n* is not established," as well as Kaiyaṭa’s own remark that this is due either to the rule *nalopaḥ supsvara-* or to the principle *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*. Moreover, the mention of its non-eternality (*anityatva*) applies equally even in Haradatta’s view regarding the rule *eta ai*.

As for the argument that there is no fault because, although [the substitute] *eta* arises in place of the vowel *ai*, there is an absence of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) with respect to the vowel (*ac*), that is incorrect. For immediate sequence consists either in an uninterrupted prior-posterior relationship between the cause and the effect, or else in one of the two being a vowel (*ac*). It cannot be the first, because the term *ac* would terminate its application only when duality is intended. Nor can it be the second, because [the condition] exists even in the case of *pacāvedam*.

The rejection of the Vārttika "yaṇaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ" (a prohibition regarding *yaṇ*) is intended to support the rule "jhalo lopāt" (the elision of a *jhal* [consonant] occurs), or alternatively, it is intended to show that this prohibition is not universally valid (*anitya*). This is because, even if the Paribhāṣā of "asiddha" (the non-established status of a rule) follows the principle of "kāryakālatva" (the time of operation coinciding with the effect), this present Paribhāṣā follows the principle of "yathoddeśa" (the time of enunciation). Such is the direction of the argument. Herein lies the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): the Paribhāṣā "an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) is stronger" is without exception; however, the Paribhāṣā "an external operation (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent" is an exception to what has been stated.

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedha-sūtra*) that the preceding *paribhāṣā* has already been explained, Bhagavṛtti, Kaiyaṭa, the author of the *Laghuvivaraṇa*, and others maintain that this is merely a supplementary argument (*abhyuccayamātra*).

However, the authors of the *Bṛhadvivaraṇa* say: "Let the *paribhāṣā* 'nājānantarye' not exist; for by its indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is precisely the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *asiddha-paribhāṣā* that is being indicated. Dīkṣita maintains that even the *Bhāṣya* passage "nājānantarye" should be interpreted solely as referring to the non-eternality of the *asiddha-paribhāṣā*.

In reality, however, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that the *ajānantarya* paribhāṣā is not strictly necessary to establish the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of [the rule] as delimited by specific objects. For this very reason, the Vṛttikāra and Sīradeva have stated: "In the rule *nalopaḥ supsvara*, the mention of *kṛti-tuk* indicates the non-eternality of the *asiddha* paribhāṣā. By means of this, in the case of *ām*, the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *utva* is established because the external operation (*bahiraṅga*) of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*)."

In the example *papuṣaḥ paśya*, because the external *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the rule), the augment *iṭ* prescribed by the rule *vasvekājād ghasām* does not occur. For this very reason, Haradatta maintains that since the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* is not universal (*anitya*), in the case of *yā sā*, the external change of *tyadādi* [to *ya-*] is not *asiddha* with respect to the internal formation of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

However, some say that the mention of *tuṅ* (the augment *t*) is indeed meaningful, because under the view that rules apply at the time of their enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), the paribhāṣā regarding what is "unestablished" (*asiddha*) does not operate there; and under the view that rules apply at the time of their operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), there is the prohibition "not when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*). [They argue] that by the very indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "not for *yā* and *ās*" (*na yāsayoḥ*), the paribhāṣā regarding what is "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*) does not operate in that case; but let this matter rest for now.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Now, since the genitive case in the word *pūrvasya* already establishes the inclusion of both types of relationship—namely, being the object of an operation (*kāryitva*) and being the cause (*nimittatva*)—the explicit mention of the term *vidhi* (operation) might seem unnecessary. For even there, it could be explained as meaning "in an operation [based] on what has been previously relied upon as a cause. Otherwise, in the case of *he gaur*, when an operation follows the letter *ga*, the substitution would be treated as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), and consequently, the elision of the vocative suffix prescribed by the rule *eṅhrasvāt* would undesirably apply. True. That term is intended for the purpose of splitting the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*). By this, [the meaning is]: "In an operation concerning what precedes, [the substitute] is indeed like the original (*sthānivat*), but not with respect to its own inherent properties (*svāśraya*)."

Alternatively—by the force of the mention of the word *vidhi* (rule), the status of being a *sthānin* applies to every rule (*vidhi*), whether scriptural (*śāstrīya*) or non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*). Therefore, in cases such as *paṭayati*, since the cause for the augment *vṛddhi* (via the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*) is absent at the very moment the *ṭi*-lopa has not yet occurred, it does not apply even after the *ṭi*-lopa has been performed; this is because the absence of *vṛddhi*, though non-scriptural, is extended by the present rule. [Objection: But surely the desired result is achieved simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *vidhi* from the preceding sūtra. [Response: Alternatively, by the power of the suffix *-vat* in the term *sthānivat*, even an absence is extended, just as in the expression "there are barley-grains in the Madra country, like in Uśīnara. As it has been said:

"If you say, 'Let it be extended as much as desired; for here there is no burden regarding what is existent or non-existent,' that is true. Nevertheless, the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) applies only to a rule concerning the preceding element, and not to a rule concerning both the preceding and the following elements, because [the rule] is intended as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*). By this, *īyatuḥ* is established. Otherwise, in the case of *iṇ* with the suffix *atus*, when the *yaṇ* substitute occurs, the rule *dvirvacane'ci* would cause the form of the original (*sthānin*) to be extended [to the reduplicated syllable]; thus, when the vowel *i* is doubled, at that time the *yaṇ* would be removed, and by virtue of its being *antaraṅga* (internal), a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) would result. This is because the rule *vārṇādāṅgam* (an *āṅga* operation takes precedence over a *vārṇa* operation) does not apply here, as they depend on different bases."

Furthermore, after the substitution of a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*, the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply because there is no sublater [of the former], and because the cause [for the latter] is on the verge of being destroyed. Even if *yaṇ* were applied, there would be no destruction of the cause due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). When *i-atus* is established, since it is included by the mention of "abhyāsa" (reduplication) in the rule "antādivacca," the shortening of the reduplication applies; then, by the rule "dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti," the vowel becomes long. By the force of that [rule], *yaṇ* is not applied, and the form would be *ī-atur*.

However, according to the aforementioned reasoning, since the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel coalescence) rule is a vidhi pertaining to both the preceding and the following elements (*pūrvaparobhayavidhi*), the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if it were the original substitute) to the *yaṇ* substitution is untenable. Consequently, this would result in the destruction of the cause (*nimittavighāta*) for the *savarṇadīrgha*. Thus, by the *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a grammatical operation does not apply if its cause is subsequently destroyed), the *savarṇadīrgha* does not take effect. Then, when the *yaṇ* substitution is applied to the second *ikāra* and the *dīrgha* is applied to the preceding one, the desired form is established. Here, although proximity (*sannidhi*) is equal [for both], "precedence" (*pūrvatva*) is understood only in relation to the *sthānin* (the original element), and not in relation to the substitute (*ādeśa*) or the cause (*nimitta*).

Therefore, in the case of *sauvaśvaḥ* (the son of a good horse), the grammarians do not apply the substitutes *āy* and *āv*—as prescribed by the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*—by relying on the status of the *yaṇ*-substitute as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is because these substitutes would apply after the *yaṇ*-substitution has taken place, and thus the condition of being "prior to an undesignated vowel" (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) is absent. As it has been said:
"The [application of] *ai* and *au* is established through the recognition of their being prior to a vowel.

Nor can it be argued that since the original element (*sthānin*) has been superseded by the substitute (*ādeśa*), how can one refer to its priority; for in the context of "priority," the original element serves merely as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Now, in this way, the substitution of *jagdhi* would occur in the case of *nirādyeti*, and the substitution of *vadha* would occur in the case of *ghātyāditi*. For in those instances, by the rule "ṇyallopau," the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) occurs first through a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), and subsequently, by the principle of "characteristic of the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the *vṛddhi* vowel is applied. Thus, there is no "precedence" (*pūrvatva*) for the two rules "anādiṣṭādacaḥ" and "ṇica ikārād ād ghāt" [relative to the original form]. If it is argued that, according to the maxim of "modification of a part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), these forms are included by the terms *adi* and *hang* [in the sūtras], we say no; because even in those cases, by way of their substituends (*sthānin*), they possess precedence over the undesignated vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*).

Nor should it be argued that since the meaning [of the substitute] is already established in the original element (*sthānin*), and because it lacks the status of being a scriptural operation (*śāstrīya*), it is ineligible for extension (*atideśa*); therefore, how could the substitute obtain the state of being prior to an unextended vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrva*)? This is because the extension itself in the rule *acaḥ parasmin* constitutes a scriptural operation, and it is precisely that which can be extended by the *sthānivadādeśa* rule. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* in the rule *na padānta...* serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) here;

otherwise, since the *anusvāra*—which occurs immediately after the elision of *a* (*allopa*)—would not be prior to an unextended vowel in its own form, the possibility of applying the *sthānivadbhāva* would not arise, rendering the prohibition in that rule purposeless.

But in that case, the form *kaṇḍūtiḥ* (the itching of a Brahmin) would not be established. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *kaṇḍūyati*, with the suffix *ktic*, there is the elision of the *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of the *y* (*yalopa*). Because of the status of the elided *a* as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), the substitution of *uvaṅ* would apply. Since this [substitution] is prior to the original vowel by way of its locus (*sthānin*), the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (P. 1.1.57) causes it to be treated as *sthānivadbhāva*. Consequently, because of the intervention of the letter *a*, the substitution of *ūṭh* does not occur; nor does the elision of the semivowel (*valopa*) occur by the rule *lopo vyoḥ* (P. 6.1.66). For if the rule *hali ca* (P. 8.2.77) applied, the undesirable form *kaṇḍūvitiḥ* would result.

Nor should it be argued that, although the *uvaṅ* substitute is prior to the vowel (*ac*) that has not yet undergone grammatical operation (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatve*), no operation applies to it here—rather, it applies only to the letter *v*—and since that *v* is not the locus for the property of being a complete substitute (*ādeśatvaparyāptyāśraya*), it too lacks the status of being prior to the vowel that has not yet undergone operation by way of its original base (*sthānidvāraka*). This is because, according to the maxim "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words," *kaṇḍū* is the substitute for *kaṇḍuv*. When the operation of *kaṇḍū* is to be applied, it is easy to establish the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) for the elision of *al* (*allopa*).

On this point, they say: the status of being prior to a non-specified vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) by way of its locus (*sthānidvāraka*) is non-eternal (*anitya*). This is because of the force of the example given in the *Bhāṣya*, namely *kaṇḍūtiḥ*, and because of Haradatta’s statement in his work: *titāpayati* (he causes the sieve to speak). Otherwise, in the case of *titāpayati*—where *ṇi* is added and *ṭilopa* occurs—the substitution of the long *ā* for the short *a* of the penultimate syllable would occur by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*. Even though there would be no *vṛddhi* by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, that substitution would still be considered as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) by virtue of its locus. Consequently, since the *u* would be preceded by that [substituted] element, the elision of the *u* (*ukāralopa*) would be impossible due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāvāt*), and thus the addition of the augment *puK* would be difficult to obtain.

Nor should it be argued that, because *puk* is a part of a whole ending in *ā*, and because the mere vowel *ā* alone precedes [the suffix], the *ukāra*-elision does not undergo *sthānivadbhāva* in the application of the rule for *puk*; for by the aforementioned reasoning, even the whole ending in *ā* is what precedes.

As for the argument that when *titau* + *ṇic* is established, since both the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) and the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix marker) are obligatory, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" takes effect due to its higher status; and subsequently, because the *ṭilopa* leaves the stem ending in *ā*, which is inherently prior to any non-specified vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*), the application of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) is unavoidable, making the *puṅ* augment impossible. Therefore, after the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* of *ṇic*, and the subsequent *vṛddhi*, the form is correctly *titāyati* after the replacement by *āy*. Nor can it be argued that when *titau* + *ṇic* is established, the *guṇa* of the initial vowels (*ādguṇaḥ*) applies first due to its being an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation, followed by *śap* and the replacement by *ay*, resulting in the undesired form *titayati*.

Because the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* prevents the application of *āṭ-ṭguṇa* (the *guṇa* substitution for *āṭ* and the following vowel) at an earlier stage; because the destruction of its cause (*nimitta*) would be brought about by the subsequent *vṛddhi*; and because the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*. Nor should it be argued that when *śap* is applied, the cause for *āṭ-ṭguṇa* is not destroyed due to the status of the preceding element as *sthānivadbhūta* by the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*; for there is no *sthānivadbhāva* in a rule concerning both the preceding and the following elements.

In the *Laghu-śabdendu-śekhara*, however, when the sequence *titā-ṇic-caṅ-tip* is established, according to the *vyutpatti-pakṣa* (the view that words are derived from roots), the rule *tanoterḍauḥ sanvacca* applies. Therein, by the prohibition of reduplication (*dvitva*) via the rule *anabhyāsasya*, the elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the suffix] by the rule *caṅparanirhrāse* does not undergo the status of being *sthānivat*. Consequently, because the short vowel [required for reduplication] is absent, and because the elision of the *ṇic* is either *sthānivat* or considered *asiddha*, the elision of the *at* [portion of the root] does not occur. Furthermore, since the status of being *sthānivat* is prohibited in the application of a long-vowel rule (*dīrghavidhi*), a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) is applied, resulting in the form *atitāt* alone, and not *atitāpat*.

That [objection] is to be considered. Because the elision of *ṭi* is obligatory (*nitya*), even though an increase (*vṛddhi*) might be obtained through the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) by the rule "acaḥ parasmin," [the elision remains] non-obligatory (*anitya*) because of the principle: "that which is obtained by another rule is non-obligatory. However, the authority for the claim that "even though it is non-obligatory, being prior to an *ac* that has not yet been subject to an operation (*anādiṣṭa*) is not desired here" must be considered.

In reality, however, there is no evidence for the claim that "being prior to an unspecified vowel" (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) is determined by way of the substituend (*sthānidvāraka*). This is because, being non-grammatical (*aśāstrīya*), it is unfit to be extended by rule (*atideśānarhatvāt*). For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* raises the objection regarding the form *āhva*: having raised the doubt that the form *āhva* is established through the substitution of *yaṇ* caused by the elision of *ā* (via *āto lopaḥ*), which would then be treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) following the semivowel change (*saṃprasāraṇa*), the *Bhāṣya* states that the elision of *ā* does not undergo *sthānivadbhāva* because the vowel *u* lacks the quality of being "prior to an unspecified vowel. This has been explained by Kaiyaṭa as follows:

[Objection: But surely, since the substitute *v* is [defined as] preceding a vowel that has not been specifically prescribed (*anādiṣṭāt*), the substitute for it will also possess the status of being "preceding a vowel that has not been specifically prescribed" by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). [Response: This is not so; the *sthānivadbhāva* is prescribed for the sake of accomplishing grammatical operations (*śāstrīya-kārya*), but not for the sake of a worldly property such as being "preceding a vowel that has not been specifically prescribed."

As for the claim that the extension (*atideśa*) itself—such as in the rule *acaḥ parasmin*—is a scripturally sanctioned operation (*śāstrīyaṃ kāryam*), that is incorrect. For the objection regarding the lack of scriptural sanction (*śāstrīyatva*) in the case of extension has not been resolved; and because being scripturally sanctioned in relation to the extension is irrelevant. What is required is precisely the status of being scripturally sanctioned in relation to that specific form (*rūpa*) for which an extension is sought when the primary instruction (*upadeśa*) fails to apply due to a deficiency in that form. Otherwise, even the imitation of ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*) would result in being considered ungrammatical.

If one were to proceed toward the prohibition of the use of incorrect forms by relying on their incorrectness, then that incorrectness itself would necessarily become subject to the authority of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), because it is required [for the prohibition]. For in that case, there is the extended rule (*atideśa-śāstra*) stating, "An imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*). The prohibition—"A Brahmin should not speak incorrectly"—is what is to be extended; and the incorrectness is a constituent part of that [prohibition]. In the present case as well, there is the extended rule stating, "A substitute is like the original" (*sthānivadādeśaḥ*). The status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is what is to be extended by the rule, "In the presence of a subsequent [element], [the substitute is] like the original vowel" (*acaḥ parasmin*)."

This is because both [the *ūṭh* substitute and the *yaṇ* substitute] share the common property of being situated before a vowel that has not yet been subject to grammatical operation (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), for it would contradict the Bhāṣya and other works by both ourselves and others located in the commentary on the *ṛlṛk* sūtra. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated that in the example *adyūtvā*, the objection raised in the Bhāṣya concerns only the impossibility of the *yaṇ* substitution, and not the possibility of the elision of the *yakāra* via the rule "lopo vyoḥ," since the condition of being situated before a vowel that has not yet been subject to operation is absent in the case of *ūṭh*.

In the sūtra *khyatyāt* as well, when the doubt arises that the elision (*alopa*) in *sakhīyateḥ* with the suffix *kvip* would not be subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* because it precedes the designated vowel (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*), it is stated there that the elision (*lup*) before *kvip* is not like its original (*na sthānivat*). Furthermore, in the sūtra *lopo vyoḥ*, having raised the objection that in the word *kaṇḍūḥ* the substitution *uvaṅ* might occur due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of the long *ā* (*ātolopa*), it was stated [as a solution].

In that very context, *ūṭh* will be applied based on the *kvip* suffix; and when *ūṭh* is to be applied, there is no status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, because [the substitute] precedes the original vowel (*ac*) from which it is prescribed. For this very reason, in forms such as *kaṇḍuvau* and *kaṇḍuvaḥ*, *ūṭh* occurs; and when *avaṅ* is to be applied, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision (*allop*). However, if one were to accept that [the substitute] precedes the original vowel even by way of its locus (*sthānidvāraka*), then many treatises would be contradicted, as that [rule regarding *sthānivadbhāva*] would have to be treated as non-eternal (*anitya*).

Regarding the point that Kaiyaṭa made in the commentary on *sthavīyān*—namely, raising the objection that since the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel and the elision (*lopa*) occur simultaneously, how can the *guṇa* be considered "prior" to the "unprescribed" (*anādiṣṭa*) vowel—and then resolving it by stating that because the original element (*sthānin*) is prior to the unprescribed vowel, the *guṇa* will also be so by virtue of that; and further asserting that once the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is established, the substitution of *ava* would not apply due to the intervention of the letter *a*—that is merely a concession (*abhyupetyavāda*). This is because of the reasoning already stated, and because [the rule] was written after first introducing the position that even for a substitute consisting of a vowel or a consonant (*ajjhalādeśa*), the property of the original element applies.

In examples such as *iyeṣa*, the purposefulness of the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) in the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* was stated by the author himself in order to demonstrate that the *guṇa* substitution destroys the conditions for the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*; furthermore, that [rule] is subject to rejection (*pratyākhyeya*). Moreover, in cases such as *nirādyeta*, the resolution is achieved through the *asiddhaparibhāṣā*. Finally, under the view that *sthānivadbhāva* applies only when the original form (*prakṛti*) is actually being resorted to, since the substitute *jagdhi* is not resorted to as the cause for the application of *ṇi*, the impossibility of *sthānivadbhāva* must be resolved in the manner already described.

And in this context, *vidhi* means "that which is prescribed"; the suffix *kip* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The genitive case in *pūrvasya* is a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), and it does not denote a substitute relationship (*sthāniyoga*), because a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). By this, the forms *āyan*, *āsyan*, and *āsann* are explained; for otherwise, by the rules "iṇo yaṇ" and "śrasorallopaḥ," the augment *āṭ* would apply due to the status of being a vowel-initial (*ajādi*) through the treatment as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is because the principle of being treated as a substitute applies even to the prescription of augments and the like, since the meaning is "in the prescription of something preceding [the substitute], whether it be a part of that [substitute] or a modification thereof."

In the rule *acaḥ*, however, the genitive case (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) is used because of its co-occurrence with the word *ādeśa* (substitute); here too, it is because the term *sthāne* (in place of) is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over). In the Bhāṣya, two further positions are mentioned: that "priority" (*pūrvatva*) may be either in relation to the cause (*nimitta*) or in relation to the substitute (*ādeśa*). However, in cases such as *vaiyākaraṇa*, there is no fault, because the diphthongs *ai* and *au* (*aic*) are not established (*asiddha*) [at the time the suffix is applied]. Furthermore, the paribhāṣā regarding immediate sequence (*nājānantarya*) is non-eternal (*anitya*). One might object: "Under the position that priority is in relation to the cause, how could there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases like *vaiyākaraṇa*, since only the *y* and *v* are the causes, while the diphthongs *ai* and *au* are what are to be prescribed? To this, the author of the Nyāsa replies: "Because those [diphthongs] are also parts (*avayava*) of those [causes]."

In this context, the term *vidhi* (rule) is derived with the suffix *ki* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). It should also be understood that the genitive case in *pūrvasya* (of the preceding) denotes the object (*karmaṇi*). Now, an objection may be raised: if "precedence" is determined relative to the cause (*nimitta*), then in examples such as *dvābhyām*, the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* etc. would be subject to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). Consequently, the rule *supi ca* would not apply to produce the long vowel, nor would the rule *īdyati* apply to produce the short *ī*. Furthermore, in forms like *lavanam* and *lāvakaḥ*, the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would be subject to *sthānivadbhāva*, and thus the substitutions of *ava* and *āva* would not occur. To this, the *Bhāṣya* replies: "These operations will take place by virtue of their own inherent basis (*svāśrayāḥ*). This means that these grammatical operations are triggered by the specific conditions of the elements themselves, rather than being obstructed by the presence of a substitute. Thus, the operations proceed based on the original form (*svāśraya*) of the elements involved.

Although the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that, by virtue of the mention of the *vidhi* (rule), there is a cessation of its own substratum (*svāśrayanivṛtti*) in this case of extended application (*atideśa*), Kaiyaṭa maintains that the result is nonetheless established through specific indications such as "the suffix *ḍatarac* [is used] when one of two," "that which is to be given (*deya*) in the sense of a debt," and "in the case of *kira* when meaning 'cutting'."

And the quality of being "prior" (pūrvatva) is common to both [directly preceding and separated by intervening elements], as seen in examples such as "Pāṭaliputra is prior to Mathurā. Because the word "of the prior" (pūrvasya) is explicitly mentioned, the rule "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe" ("when that which is specified is in the locative case") does not apply. Furthermore, in this way, the prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) in rules concerning vowels also becomes consistent. This is because in the word *cikīrṣaka*, the vowel *ī* is separated from the nasal *ṇ* of the suffix *san* by the *repha* (*r*) and the *ṣakāra*.

Even though the rule *svaravidhau vyañjanam avidyamānavat* ("in rules concerning accents, a consonant is as if non-existent") applies here, it does not apply in the case of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original substitute). For this very reason, an additional prohibition (*niṣedhopasaṃkhyāna*) will be stated regarding the shortening of the vowel following *caṅ*. Consequently, there is *sthānivadbhāva* in forms such as *paṭayati* and *avadhīt*, because according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the substitute *vadh* ends in a long vowel (*ādanta*), and because the term *ārddhadhātuke* refers to the "occasion" (*viṣayasaptamī*) [of the application of the rule], as previously explained.

It should not be argued that in the case of *paṭayati*, since a *ṇic* suffix is added to a word ending in a *sup* (case-ending), the status of being a *pada* arises due to the intervening case-ending, which would lead to the application of *jaśtva* (the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stops *j, g, d, d, b* for *c, ch, t, th, p, ph*); for in the rule prescribing that substitution, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited. This is because the *ṇic* is added directly to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that conveys the object, rather than to the word ending in a *sup*. Even in the view that it is added to a *subanta*, the designation of *pada* is set aside by the designation of *bha* extended [to the base] by the rule "in the presence of *ṇi*, as in the case of *iṣṭhan*" (*ṇāviṣṭhavad*). By this, the Bhāṣya—which states that *paṭvyā* and *mṛdvyā* are the most prominent examples of the sūtra—is explained, as these are mentioned in all commentaries.

For instance, when *paṭu ī ā* is present, once the substitution of *yaṇ* for the subsequent vowel (*parayaṇādeśa*) has been applied, if "being prior to the cause" (*nimittātpūrvatva*) were understood [in the sense of immediate contiguity], then the *u* would not be immediately prior to the cause of the *yaṇ*-substitution—the *ā*—because it is separated by the vowel *ī*. Consequently, when the *yaṇ*-substitution is to be applied to that [final *ā*], the *yaṇ* would lack the status of being a substitute for its original locus (*sthānitva*). Therefore, the desired result is established by resorting to the notion of "prior-ness" even for what is separated [by other sounds]. Nor should it be argued that the *yaṇ*-substitution for the preceding vowel (*pūrvayaṇādeśa*) should occur first; for the substitution of *yaṇ* for the subsequent vowel (*parayaṇādeśa*) is obligatory (*nitya*).

Nor should it be argued that, given the existence of *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution of the preceding *yaṇ* is also necessarily permanent because it applies whether [the subsequent rule] has been performed or not; for even so, by the "subsequent word" (*śabdapara*) version of the *vipratiṣedha* rule, the substitution of the subsequent *yaṇ* possesses greater force. This is because the two rules are distinct due to the difference in their respective domains (the preceding and the following), and because one and the same grammatical feature cannot simultaneously be both the subject of an operation and its cause; therefore, the determination is made on the basis of priority.

[Objection: But in this way, the accent would not occur in the form *kartryā*. For when the state *kartṛ ī ā* has been reached, if the substitution of *yaṇ* for the subsequent vowel were to take place by virtue of its being obligatory (*nitya*), then—due to the status of that [substitution] as "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*)—the vowel *ā* following the *udātta-yaṇ* (the *ṛ* of *kartṛ*) would not be present; thus, the *udātta* accent would not apply because the vowel *ī* is *anudātta*. However, if, on the other hand, the substitution of the preceding *yaṇ* occurs first because it is *antaraṅga*, then the *udātta* accent belongs to the *ṅīp* suffix, and since that too undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution, the same [accentuation] applies to the vowel *ā*; thus [the desired result] is established. [Response: Not so.

Since the udātta accent of the case-ending is established by relying precisely on the *pūrva-yaṇ* substitute as the locus for the udātta, there is no intervention by the subsequent *para-yaṇ* substitute; for in the application of accentual rules, a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, say: during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), the sequence of the cognition of the word's own meaning, substance, gender, number, and case-role is necessary. For instance—according to the maxim that "the qualifier is not apprehended without [apprehending] the qualified"—first the general property (*sāmānya*) is denoted. Then its substratum, the substance (*dravya*), is denoted, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) as the locus of gender and number. After that, gender is denoted; and number, such as duality and so on, is denoted last, because it is more external (*bahiraṅga*) due to its dependence on another entity. This is also true for singularity, since it serves to exclude duality and the rest.

Next is number (*saṃkhyā*). Because the powers of the case-role factors (*kāraka-śakti*) such as the object (*karman*) depend upon an action that is of a different genus from the substance (*dravya*), they are extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is [the substance] that is the factor (*kāraka*). Thus, grammatical operations (*kārya*) apply to the word-form precisely according to the sequence of the comprehension of meaning. Consequently, when there is a conflict between a substitution of *yaṇ* caused by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) and a substitution of *yaṇ* caused by the vowel *ī*, the substitution of *yaṇ* caused by the vowel *ī* is stronger. By this, the "subsequent conflict" (*para-vipratiṣedha*) regarding words is also refuted; for that which is extrinsic is weak due to its being considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*). Therefore, this is not a valid example [for that rule].
Furthermore, the maxim regarding the non-application of a completed configuration (*akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*) is non-eternal (*anitya*).

This might be the case: is the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original place) applicable where the substituend (*sthānin*) is relied upon as a cause (*nimitta*) for an operation, or even when it is not so relied upon? Not the latter; for in examples such as *śleṣmaghna*, *pittaghna*, *dadhy-aśva*, and *madhv-aśva*, if the *sthānivadbhāva* applied to the elision of the vowel (*al-lopa*) and the substitution of *yaṇ* (*yaṇ-ādeśa*), the designation of a "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) would be absent. Consequently, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) based on "heaviness" (*gurutva*) would be untenable. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the rules concerning reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the suffix *-vara-* (*vare-ya*), and elision (*lopa*) would have to be included in the subsequent sūtra.

Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule *anaci*, only a consonant (*hal*) similar to that [which follows] is resorted to there, and not a vowel (*ac*); thus, in the first position, since the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply, there is brevity due to the abandonment of that [vowel]. Objection: Even if a vowel is not resorted to in the case of the elision of *varey* (in *varey-lopa*), the original base (*prakṛti*) is indeed resorted to in the rule for the elision of *ā* (in *ākāra-lopa*) by the rule *aci ṅiti*. So how can the word *vareḥ* be cited in the Bhāṣya? Reply: Not so; because the *ā* which is a constituent of the *yaṅ* suffix is not itself a suffix (*pratyaya*). This is because the elision of *ā* is prescribed only when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows.

Regarding the form *adugdha*: if there were elision (*alopa*) of the *kṣ* by the rule *alo’ntyasya*, then because that [elided element] would be treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the elision of the suffix *sic* by the rule *jhalo jhali* would not occur; thus, an explicit rule for elision (*lugvidhi*) would have to be prescribed. Furthermore, regarding the form *ghnantī*: because of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of the *a*, the substitution of *k* for *h* (*kutva*) would not occur due to the absence of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). The first [objection] is not valid. For in the case of *nirādyā*, there would be the undesired application of the substitute *jagdhi*. In that instance, since the *ṇi* [of *ṇilopa*] is not relied upon, the status of being a *sthānivat* is untenable.

In the case of *akurvyāśām*, there is the possibility of the elision of the vowel *u* by the rule *ye ca*; in *alunthyāśām*, the substitution of *ī* by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ*; in *ajajñyāśām*, the optional substitution of *ā* by the rule *ye vibhāṣā*—either through the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix applied anomalously (*vyatyayena*) to the root *jan* in the sense of "producing," or through the reduplication (*ślau*) applied Vedicly (*chāndasatvāt*) to the root *jan* in the sense of "manifesting"; and in *rāyyāśām*, the substitution of *ā* by the rule *rāyo hali*. This would apply in all these cases because the original substituend (*sthānin*) is not being relied upon. However, this fault does not arise in the second view (*pakṣa*), because the status of being as if the original were present (*stānivadbhāva*) applies even when the preceding operation is separated [by the substitute].

On this point, the commentary states: The position that [the rule applies] without distinction (*aviśeṣeṇa*) is indeed logical. Since it has already been stated that the cessation of the operation [of a grammatical element] occurs when its own substratum ceases, there is no possibility for the elision of the vowel *u* and so forth. Furthermore, because the designation of a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is a rule dependent on both the preceding and following elements, there is no possibility of it being treated as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). Moreover, since other prohibitions have already been established within the very sūtra, that itself serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the phrase "without distinction. However, the explicit mention of the term *luk* in the rule "lugvāduha" (Pāṇini 6.4.76) is necessary; for in the form *aduh*, the letter *v* is not a consonant (*ajhal*).

In the case of *ghnanti*, however, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) produced by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is relied upon; whereas the intervention caused by the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not constitute an obstacle, because the operation applies there by virtue of the power of the specific rule. For this very reason, it will be stated in the seventh [chapter] that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *hananam*.

It might be argued as follows: let there be no compound with the ablative case (*pañcamī-samāsa*) in the rule *pūrva-vidhau*; for the three examples cited in the Bhāṣya—*bebhiditā*, *māthitikaḥ*, and *apīpacan*—can be accounted for otherwise. To explain: from the word *bebhidya*, the suffix *tṛc* is added. Because this is obligatory, the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) and the elision of *y* (*yal-lopa*) occur. Consequently, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ekāca-upadeśe-'nunāsikaḥ* would apply. This is because the term *upadeśe* functions as a qualifier for both [the conditions] *ekāci* and *anudātte*. Furthermore, reduplication consists of a double employment [of the root].

[Objection: "But since the *allop* [the elision of the suffix] would be treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the aforementioned prohibition does not apply because of the intervention [of the *ikādeśa*]. [Reply: That is not so, because we rely on the qualification that the suffix must be "prescribed" (*vihita*). Furthermore, since the suffix *tṛc* arises only after a reduplicated stem (*yaṅanta*), it is not produced from that which is "single-vowel" (*ekāc*) in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*). In the case of *māthitikaḥ* (meaning "one whose merchandise is *mathita*"), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "tadasya paṇyam. Then, the substitution of *ik* occurs. By the rule "yasyeti ca," there is the elision (*allop*) of the *i*. Because the stem ends in *t*, the substitution of *kā* for *t* also does not apply.

In the rule *ṭhasyeka*, since the vowel *a* in both the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) serves merely for the sake of pronunciation, the *sthānin* is a mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*). Consequently, because this is not a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme), the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *analvidhau* applies to the substitution of *i*. Even if the entire cluster were considered the *sthānin*, the matter is resolved by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. Furthermore, since the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is conditioned by the designation *bha* based on its being preceded by a vowel (*ajādi*), the substitution of *k*—which would destroy that status of being preceded by a vowel—does not apply when the state of ending in *t* is established by that very elision. Nor is *apīpacan* a valid example [for the necessity of the rule].

Objection: Since the *ik* of *jhi* is elided by the rule "itaśca," the single-substitute principle (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) ensures that the form *jhi* remains *jhi*; thus, when the substitution of *anta* for *jhi* occurs via the rule "jho'ntaḥ," the *caṅ* (the letter *c*) would, through its *a*, undergo the *pararūpa* substitution with the *a* of *anta*. Because this [resultant *ja*] would then behave like the initial element (*ādibadbhāva*) with respect to what follows, it would be included by the term *jhi*, and consequently, the substitution of *jus* would apply by the rule "sijabhyasta. However, if one argues that this does not happen because the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) is obstructed by the elision of the *ṇi* or the *pararūpa* substitution, we say: no.

Since the suffix *jhi* occurs only after the *laṅ* [tense] immediately following a verbal root, by virtue of its association with that, the rule prescribes the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* only when it is a substitute for *laṅ*, even in the case of what is termed "repeated" (*abhyasta*).

Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of association with *sic*, the *jhi* of the *luṅ* substitute alone takes *at*; for the association with what follows (*parasāhacarya*) is stronger, according to the maxim: "In case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]. For this very reason, Mādhava maintains that from the *yaṅ*-luṅ form of the root *bhū*, the *luṅ* [ending] becomes *abobhūvan*.
