Nor does this necessitate the requirement of a compound with the fifth case (*pañcamīsamāsa*) solely to prevent the application of the rule "adabhyastāt"; because when the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) is applied, there is no longer a *jh* [element]. Furthermore, since the substitution of an *al* (phoneme) is not possible under the principle of *antādivadbhāva* (treating the preceding as the end and the following as the beginning), and because when the substitution of *at* for the letter *jh* is to be performed, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) is impossible due to it being a rule concerning an *al*.

On this point, they say: here, the Blessed One does not intend concomitance (*sāhacarya*) as the restrictive factor, because of the example *apīpacan*. This is because the mention of the term "kṛtvas" in the rule *dvitricatur* indicates that [the rule] is not universal (*anitya*). Therefore, *abobhūvuḥ* alone is correct. For Mādhava and others have stated that the restriction *ātaḥ* applies only to those cases where the *jus* would otherwise be obtained by virtue of being followed by *sic*. Consequently, the *jus* based on the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) is unavoidable.

Since that restriction is simpler when it pertains to the general case, let there be the alternative form *abobhūvat* through the substitution of *at* by the rule *adabhyastāt*; for, due to its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), the *vuk* augment would override the *guṇa* substitution. However, the form *abobhūvan* is indeed questionable, because the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*) is difficult to justify.

On this point, they say: from the root *math* with the suffix *kvip*, after the elision of the *ṭi*-portion and the elision of the *ṇi*, and further by the elision [of the *u*] according to the rule "vare-pṛktasya," we have *mathit*. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is added in the sense of "one who moves by means of that. For the purpose of establishing the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) in that case, a compound with the fifth case (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is necessary. And for such a construction, the authority is precisely the example from the Bhāṣya: *māthitikaḥ*. [Objection: But if this were so, the form *vigaṇayya* would not be possible; because when the substitution of *ay* (by *ayādeśa*) is to be applied, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) would be treated as *sthānivat* (as if it were still present).

[The opponent argues: "Because [the rule] *anugamayya* and so forth has already fulfilled its purpose (*caritārthatā*) regarding those [roots] designated as having the marker *iṭ*, there is a lack of the capacity for its initial application (*ārambha-sāmarthya*). [The author replies: "Not so; because the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in a rule based on what precedes (*pūrvasmād vidhau*) is non-eternal (*anitya*). And thus Haradatta stated in the eighth [chapter]: "The status of being a substitute in a rule based on what precedes is non-eternal, because of the mention of *seṭ* in the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*. For instance, that [mention of *seṭ*] is not intended to exclude roots lacking the marker *iṭ* (*aniṭ*), because such a [substitute with *iṭ*] is impossible after a root ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of *saṃjñapta-paśu* (the animal consecrated by sacrifice), there is a prohibition [of the substitution of *iṭ*] by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, because [the root *śam*] is optionally subject to *iṭ* by the rule *sanīvanta*. This is because, in that context, the term *ekācaḥ* ("having a single vowel") is understood as a governing factor (*anuvṛtti*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a prohibition of *iṭ* even for the root *daridrā*. Furthermore, if the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) were mandatory after a preceding operation, then the prohibition would not apply at all, because of the intervention of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Therefore, it must be understood that this [status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*] is non-mandatory.

Kaiyaṭa also stated under the rule *vasvekāj* that the principle *pūrvasmād api vidhau* (even in a rule regarding what precedes) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Mādhava, having resolved the issue by setting aside the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix in the example *paridraḍhayya* on the grounds of its being based on different substrata (*vyāśrayatvāt*), raises the objection that there might be *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) due to the rule *pūrvasmāt*. He concludes, however, that this is not the case, citing the authority of the examples provided in the Bhāṣya: *prabebhidayya* and *prastanayya*.

Alternatively, the Dīkṣitas maintain that since the word "color" (*varṇa*) in the rule *laghupūrvāt* refers to a distinct object in the form of a phoneme, and since the mention of a "phoneme" implies the inclusion of the entire class (*jāti*), there is no fault even when there is an intervention [of other elements].

Pāṇini 1.1.58: *na padāntadvirvacanavareyalopasvarasavarṇānusvāradīrghajaścarvidhiṣu*. When a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) is conditioned by a subsequent cause, it is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original) in the following operations: at the end of a word (*padānta*), in the rules for doubling (*dvirvacana*), the substitution of *vara-e*, elision (*lopa*), accentuation (*svara*), homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), nasalization (*anusvāra*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the substitution of *jaś* and *car* sounds. Examples: *kāni santi* ("which are there? and *kau staḥ* ("who two are there?"). In these cases, regarding the two operations—the *yaṇ* substitution and the substitution of *āv*—the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) according to the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* is not *sthānivadbhūta*. One should not argue that this is already established because the elided *a* is not prior to the preceding vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatva-abhāvāt*). This is because, according to the view that words are extracted from sentences and then refined (*saṃskriyante*), such a state of being prior does indeed exist.

For instance, in rules such as *yuṣmadyupapade*, we observe the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a word even when it depends upon another word. Precisely for this reason, Kaiyaṭa stated in the rule defining the technical term *aṅga* that, in the case of *strī iyatī* under the view that word-refinement is independent of other words, the substitution of *idam* and its subsequent elision do not possess the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the property of acting like the original), because the vowel *i* of the word *strī* does not precede an undesignated vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*). This is because, by mentioning the alternative view (*pakṣāntara*), he indicates that the view under discussion is also his own preference.

Haradatta, however, maintains that although grammar teaches only words (*pada*) and not sentences (*vākya*), nevertheless, when a word such as *staḥ* occurring within a sentence is being taught, the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of a word like *kāu* is not contradictory even if it lacks the status of a formal cause (*nimitta*); thus, he says that [the *au*] precedes a vowel (*ac*) that has not been formally prescribed.

Some, however, say that in cases such as *goco gocaḥ*, there is a prohibition of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of *ac* (*al-lopa*) by the rule "of *ac*" (*acaḥ*) when the substitution of *avaṅ* is prescribed by the rule "avaṅ for Sphoṭāyana" (*avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya*); this is because the *au*-vowel (*aukārasya*) precedes a vowel that has not been formally prescribed.

Herein lies the essential point: the word *vidhi* (rule) is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*). The compound [in the sūtra] is formed with the genitive case of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), namely *padāntasya*. The word *anta* refers to the final constituent part (*caramāvayava*). Thus, where the status of being a prescribed element (*vidheyatva*) resides in the final constituent part of a word, there is a prohibition of the treatment as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). In the examples *kāni santi* and *kau staḥ*, if the *y* and *v* sounds were actually present, they would indeed be final constituents of the words; thus, there is the possibility of them being subject to a rule concerning word-final elements (*padāntavidhi*). This has been stated: "That *y* or *v* which is at the end of a word and is heard at the end."
And Kaiyaṭa has explained: "Since the letters *y* and *v* become word-final (*padānta*) precisely at the time they are being prescribed, there is indeed a prescription of their status as word-final.

However, in some cases, this occurs through the prescription of the technical designation *pada*, as in the case of *vetasvān* and others that will be mentioned below. As stated by the authors of the *Vivaraṇa*: "Even though the letter *s* remains in its own form, it is only when qualified as word-final that it is to be prescribed. But in the case of *ṣaḍika*, since both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) are already established beforehand, there is no prescription of something qualified by word-finality; thus, the aforementioned prohibition does not apply, as we shall explain.

In this regard, there is no requirement for the extension (*atideśa*) of the property of being the final member of a word (*padāntatva*) as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of what is to be prescribed (*vidheya*) within prescriptive rules (*vidhi-vākya*). For if that were required, it would lead to the consequence of inconsistency in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, because [the property of being the final member of a word] is not mentioned either as the delimiting factor of the substituendum (*sthānitā-avacchedaka*) or as the delimiting factor of the substitute (*ādeśatā-avacchedaka*).

If, however, the word *vidhi* is taken as referring to that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) through a verbal derivation (*karmavyutpatti*)—meaning "that which is enjoined"—and the genitive in *padāntasya* is interpreted as a residual genitive (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*) signifying the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*), then the rule would be explained as follows: "Wherever there is the status of being enjoined (*vidheyatva*) as determined by a status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) residing in the final element of a word, there the treatment as a substitute (*sthānivattva*) does not apply. If this were the case, the form *ṣaḍikaḥ* would not be established. To explain: *ṣaḍikaḥ* refers to one who is pitied, namely *ṣaḍaṅgulidattaḥ* (one given six fingers). The suffix *ṭhac* is applied here according to the rule *bahuco manuṣyanāmnaḥ*.

By the rule *ṭhājādāvūrdhvam*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the word *aṅguli*; by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. In that case, the designation of *pada* (word) which would be applied to the form *ṣaṭ*—based on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of an affix)—would be sublated by the designation of *bha*, because they share the same scope. And consequently, the change to *ḍ* by virtue of the *jaś* rule would not occur.

Nor should it be argued that because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elision (*al-lopa*) in the word *yasya*, there would be no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) due to the difference in their scopes—since the designation *bha* applies to what ends in *a*, while the designation *pada* applies to what ends in *ṣ*. This is because the designation *bha* also rests solely upon what ends in *ṣ*, owing to the application of the prohibition in the rule *na padānta...*. Nor can it be said that the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* here follows simply from the fact that this is a rule for *jaś*-substitution; for that [prohibition] operates only in the context of *jaś*-rules.

But here, since the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stop) has already been accomplished previously, it is only the attainment of the form *ṣakāra* that is to be prescribed here. Nor does the rule "that which is not established in what precedes is not like its original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*) apply; for the reason has already been stated. Such is the commentary following the *Ākara*.

On this point, some argue: "Even under the view that the word *vidhi* in the rule [P. 1.1.56] has *karman* (the object) as its means of derivation, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies only when a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) is to be performed in place of the final element of a word (*padānta*). However, the designation *bha* does not have the final element of a word as its locus; therefore, how can the prohibition take effect? Nor should it be said that the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies even toward a rule that contradicts a rule whose locus is the final element of a word—for instance, since *jaśtva* (the substitution of voiced stops) has the final element of a word as its locus, and the rule for the *bha* designation contradicts it, because *jaśtva* depends upon the designation *pada*."

There is no evidence for such a purpose [of the rule]. This is because the requirement is satisfied merely by the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* in a rule where the substitute is at the end of a word; furthermore, since this is already established in cases such as *kāni santi*, there is no further purpose in assuming a broader scope. By this, the following argument is refuted: "This *sthānivadbhāva* is the establisher of the designation *bha* residing in bases ending in *a*, which is necessary for the application of *jaś*-substitution (*kāni*). If that were absent, the *bha*-designation would reside in bases ending in *ṣakāra*; consequently, the *pada*-designation would be sublated by it, and thus *jaś*-substitution would be impossible."

Because the status of being the cause for the *jaś*-substitution is not adopted [as a condition], and because the preceding portion of the vowel *a* is established as a *pada* by virtue of the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) existing within it; for this very reason, the two prohibitions—"not before *jaś*" (*na jaśi*) and "it is not like the original when the *ādeśa* is not established" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*)—do not apply.

The meaning is that when *jaś* is to be applied, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply; for, by taking only that which is related to *jaś*, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies specifically to that which has a relationship with either the state of being sublated (*bādhyatva*) or the state of being the producer of what is to be produced (*niṣpādakatva*). Furthermore, even in the view where the suffix *-bhāva* denotes the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*), the form *ṣaḍikaḥ* is established, because the *jaś*-state to be enjoined possesses the quality of being at the end of a word (*padāntatva*).

Nor should it be argued that because the state of being a *jaś* (the substitution of voiced stops) has already been accomplished, there is no longer anything to be prescribed for the final of the word (*padānta*). This is because the designation *bha* is also possible; furthermore, due to the maxim regarding the non-application of rules when their conditions have already been met (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*), and by the principle that "an external operation (*bahiraṅga*) subverts even internal operations (*antaraṅga*) [if its conditions are already present]," that [substitution] does not apply. Moreover, even in the view where the term is derived as a passive noun (*karmasādhana*), there is an absence of anything to be prescribed that occupies the position of the final of the word. Nor should it be argued that since the status of being a *bha* is established by virtue of being the final of a word, the attainment of the form *ṣa* is what must be prescribed.
For, by association with [operations such as] reduplication (*dvirvacana*), only that which is prescribed by a formal rule (*śāstrīya*) is taken as the object of prescription.

That [interpretation] is utterly incorrect. The meaning of the sentence is: when a grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for the place (*sthāna*) of a final element of a word that is observed to precede an unspecified vowel (*anādiṣṭāt-acaḥ*), an *ādeśa* (substitute) for a vowel (*aj-ādeśaḥ*) conditioned by what follows (*para-nimittaḥ*) is not *sthānivadbhūta*. If this were so, there would be a contradiction with Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule regarding *dadhy atra*, where he states: "In the event of the contingency of the elision of a consonant cluster at the end of a word (*saṃyogāntalopa-prasaṅge*), this prohibition—namely 'not [applicable] with respect to an operation concerning the end of a word (*padānta-vidhim prati na*)'—does not apply; for while that prohibition applies when something is to be prescribed at the end of a word (*padānte vidheye*), the elision (*lopaḥ*) is not [at the end of a word] because it is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvātmakatvāt*)."

In this way, regarding the form *vṛkṣav*, since the elision of *v* (the element to be enjoined) lacks the status of being a constituent part (*avayava*), the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *na padānta* would not apply; thus, there is a contradiction with the texts of the *Kaustubha* and *Manoramā*. According to your view, because the *v* (the counter-correlate of the elision) possesses the status of being at the end of a word (*padāntatva*), the application of that prohibition would be unavoidable. Similarly, regarding the form *vetasvān*, there is a contradiction with the intent of the *Bhāṣya*, which states that no fault arises in the case where the suffix *-matup* is derived from the object (*karman*) rather than from the quality (*dharma*).

In the sense of "it exists in this," the suffix *ḍmatup* is applied after the words *kumuda*, *naḍa*, and *vetasa*. Due to the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. By the rule "tasau matvarthe," the technical designation *bha* is assigned, which prevents the substitution of *ru* (for the final *s*). Nor should it be argued that because this suffix belongs to the group of four meanings (*cāturarthika*), the same fault would apply even when it has the meaning of "produced from" (*nirvṛtta*) and so on; for it has been stated with the intention that such usage is not attested (*anabhidhāna*) in those cases. Furthermore, if the designation *bha* were applied to a form ending in *s*, then due to the status of the elided *a* as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the form would no longer end in *s*, and thus the designation *bha* would not apply.

Nor does the prohibition "not at the end of a word" (na padānta) apply here, because the designation *bha* does not occupy the position of the end of a word. Consequently, one must necessarily maintain that when there is a rule whose object is the substitution for the end of a word, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply even to a rule that is incompatible with it. Now, there exists a rule for the substitution of *ru* (the visarga) which occupies the position of the end of a word; the rule for the *bha* designation is incompatible with it. Since the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of *al* (*al-lopa*) is thus prohibited with respect to that [rule for *ru*], the *bha* designation for it is established.

Thus, the statement that there is no evidence for [the rule] having a further purpose (*adhikārtha*) is entirely incoherent. For this very reason, it is clear from both the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa that, in the case of a rule where the status of being a word-final (*padāntatva*) is already established even without the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*, the prohibition "not at the end of a word" (*na padānta*) applies under the interpretation of the word *vidhi* as a passive (*karmasādhana*). Indeed, in the example *vetasvān*, the *s* is not established as being word-final without the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*.

Because, when the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) exists, the designation of a word (pada-saṃjñā) rests solely upon that which ends in the vowel 'a'. In the case of *kāni santi*, even without the prohibition "not at the end of a word" (*na padānta*), the letter 'i' possesses the status of being at the end of a word; thus, when the substitution of *yaṇ* is to be applied, the prohibition of the status of being a substitute for the elision of 'a' (*allopa*) is easily obtained. That this is established even under the view where the suffix denotes the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*) is another matter.

Similarly, in the case of *ṣaḍika*, without the operation of the prohibition "not at the end of a word," the letter 'ṣ' would not be established as being at the end of a word; therefore, the application of that prohibition there is indeed difficult to obtain.

Nor should it be argued that its status as a "word-final" (*padānta*) is already established by the case-ending situated within [the compound]; for it has been stated that in the absence of a prohibition against *sthanivadbhāva*, that [status] would be sublated by the designation of *bha* (which shares the same scope). Furthermore, this very prohibition must be relied upon for the designation of that word (*pada*), as there is no distinction [in the result] between [the forms] *vetasvān* and so forth.

As for the claim that the justification for the prohibition [of *sthānivadbhāva*] applies only to the case of "which ones exist" (*kāni santi*), that is not correct. It must necessarily be stated that the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies to a rule where the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, or the relationship between the producer and the produced, pertains to a substitute (*ādeśa*) standing at the end of a word. This is because there is no difference from the rule regarding the substitution of *jaś*. Is the relationship of producer and produced intended to belong to the substitute or to the original element (*sthānin*)? Not the first, because the elision of *al* (*al-lopa*) does not exist in relation to the *yaṇ*-substitution. Nor the second.

In the case of *ṣaḍika*, even the vowel *a* is subject to the prohibition [of the application of the rule], because it is conducive to a rule that prescribes a substitution at the end of a word—namely, the *jaśtva* rule—by means of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "bh" residing within its own domain. If it is argued that "direct conduciveness" should be required [for the prohibition to apply], we say no; for there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in introducing the concept of "directness. Furthermore, what exactly constitutes this "directness"? Does it mean independence from any technical designation whatsoever, or independence from a designation occurring in something other than itself, or independence from a designation occurring in itself alone?

Not the first [alternative], because the letter *a* (akāra), by virtue of its form as a vowel (*actva*), is already suitable for the application of the *yaṇ* rule. Not the second, because the property of being a vowel (*actva*) also resides in things other than the letter *a*. Not the last, because it is unestablished. If it is argued that the meaning is: "in whichever individual instance the status of being a cause is finalized, there is no dependence on any designation other than those whose denotations are co-extensive with that [instance]," [we reply: even the designation *aṇ* and so forth is co-extensive with the letter *a*, and thus there remains a dependence on the designation *ac*, which is distinct from it.

Now, one might argue that while a technical name (*sañjñā*) that serves as a counter-correlate to a difference must also be stated as a cause for the operation at hand, names such as *aṇ* and so forth are not like that. This is not so; for even then, according to the *yathoddeśa* view, when an operation is observed to occur when a vowel (*ac*) follows, that same operation occurs even when there is a substitute (*ādeśa*). Thus, by means of the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), even though the [vowel] has been elided, the substitution of *yaṇ* and so forth would still apply by the rule "when something follows a vowel" (*acaḥ parasmin*), and consequently, the letter *a* could never function as a causal condition (*nimitta*).

And if it is argued that, under the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that the rule applies at the time the operation occurs), because there is no distinction in their being based on the scripture (*śāstrīyatva*), the designation *ac* residing in the vowel *a* alone is extended after the elision (*lopa*), while the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule "ikoyaṇaci" itself—even so, this is not correct, because the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) cannot be attributed to the vowel *a*. For even if the designation *ac* is extended after its elision, the status of being a cause rests solely upon the resulting effect.

Is such a conclusion [that there is] the production of a result, or is it merely a possibility? Not the first, because of the prohibition; in the present case, there is no production of a result. Not the second, because by virtue of being *act* (a vowel), the *ik*-sounds (*i*, etc. would likewise possess that status. Here, the non-production of a result occurs through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original), whereas in the case of *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, there is the exception (*apavāda*)—this is the distinction. Nor should it be argued that in the example *kāni santi*, there is no possibility of the *ik*-sound (*i*) being a cause [for the elision], since even when the *akāra* is elided, that [possibility] is absent.

Because even when there is elision (*lopa*), that [result] does not occur in the case of the vowel *a*. If it is argued that what is intended is the possibility resulting from the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), then it has already been stated that such a possibility exists only for the elision itself in both cases, and not for the vowel *a*.

Is it not the case that what is intended is the independence from any property other than those residing in that individual where the possibility of being the cause (nimittatva) defined by a rule concerning a word-final position is conceivable—provided that such an individual is delimited by whatever property has been determined as the delimitor of the cause (*nimittatāvacchedaka*) in the present context? In the present case, the property determined as the delimitor of the cause is *actva* (the state of being an *ac* vowel); so, regarding the specific instance of elision (*lopa*) delimited by that [property], which [properties] are there?

If it is argued that when the substitution of *yaṇ* is to be applied, the operation of such an elision (*lopa*)—which is the cause for the possibility of the *yaṇ*-substitution—is indeed independent of any property other than *actva* (the status of being a vowel), then this is true. However, it is because *actva* alone does not bring about the *yaṇ*-substitution; rather, it is only *actva* as qualified by another grammatical operation that brings it about. For one cannot formulate the following hypothetical application: "If there were a vowel (*ac*) here after [this], then the *yaṇ*-substitution would occur."

Even if the preceding [element] lacks *ik*-hood or possesses *pragṛhya* status, that [substitution] does not arise; therefore, "conduciveness" (*anuguṇatva*) must be stated as being the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of the absence of that which causes the absence of that [substitution]. Just as there is such a state for the vowel *a* in *kāni santi*, so too is there such a state for the vowel *a* in *ṣaḍika*. For in its absence, the designation *bha* would apply to the word ending in *ṣa* alone, and since this would cause the absence of *jaś*-ness, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* would be unavoidable; such is the direction [of the argument].

In the Siddhānta (the established conclusion), however, there is a prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) only where a rule is prescribed for that which stands at the end of a word (*padānta*). In the case of *ṣaḍika*, since the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) is already established as "previously proven" (*pūrvasiddha*), the prohibition does not apply; thus, when the *sthānivadbhāva* exists, the designations of *bha* and *pada* have different scopes, and consequently the designation of *pada* is successfully established for that which ends in *ṣ*. Therefore, there is no occurrence of the letter *ṣ* resulting from the absence of the *pada* designation. Nor does the prohibition apply by taking the prescription of the form *ṣ* itself as the basis, because that [form *ṣ*] is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of *jaś*-substitution. However, in the case of *anukampito vāgāśīrdatto vācikaḥ*, the elision of the entire final member is accepted on the basis of the rule: "The elision of the final member should be stated for those compounds whose prior members consist of a single syllable."

As for the claim that, by the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* or the *antaraṅgān api vidhīn bahiraṅgo lug bādhate* rule, the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stop) does not first occur in *ṣaḍika*, that is not correct. Regarding the first [alternative], it is not so, because according to the reasoning already stated, the cause [of the subsequent operation] is not yet facing destruction. Moreover, mere apprehension [of such destruction] is not a sufficient condition [for the application of the paribhāṣā]. Regarding the second [alternative], it is also not so; for although the technical designation (*sañjñā*) of "word" (*pada*)—which occurs via the rule *svādiṣu*—is difficult to obtain when a suffix elision (*luk*) has taken place because it rests solely on the status of being a "base" (*aṅga*), this is not the case for the designation based on being a "suffixed form" (*subanta*). Therefore, even when there is *luk*, that designation remains easily available through the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

Otherwise, in cases such as *pañca* and *sapta*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur; the same would apply in cases like *rājapuruṣa*, since even there only the elision of the case-ending (*luk*) is accepted, for otherwise the elision of *al* (*allopa*) would result. Furthermore, in cases such as *gomatpriya*, the augment *num* and so forth would result. Moreover, Kaiyaṭa’s statement that "the designation *pada* [is applied] because of the presence of a final *ṣakāra* by relying on the internal case-ending" indicates that, although the word ending in a *sup*-affix receives the designation *pada*, the ultimate result is still a word ending in *ṣakāra*, since the case-ending is not actually heard.

Now, in the view where [the suffix] is a *bhāvasādhana* (denoting the action), in the word *brahmabandhūḥ*, the substitution of *jaś* for the letter *dh* would occur; this is because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for [the *dh*] together with the suffix *ūṅ* is included by the mention of *ūṅ* itself due to its status as being like the latter member (*parādivadbhāva*). Consequently, when that [suffix] follows, the technical designation *pada*—by the rule *svādiṣu*—would apply to the word ending in *dh*. Nor can this be barred by the designation *bha*; for in that case, due to the operation of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, that [designation *bha*] would rest only upon a word ending in the vowel *ū*.

Similarly, in the word *vetasvān*, there would be the undesirable consequence of *ru*-substitution for the letter *s*, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies to what is prescribed at the end of a *pada*, and thus the designation *pada* remains firmly established for the word ending in *s*.

Regarding this, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "In the phrase *pade antaḥ*, *padāntaḥ* means 'at the end of a word' when a word follows. In the prescription of such [an ending], there is no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). However, in the case of *ḍmatup*, since it is not a word (*pada*), when the substitution of *r* for *s* (*rutva*) is to be performed, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* indeed applies; for even the designation *bha* is prescribed only for that which ends in *s*. Thus, because there is no difference in the limit (*avadhi*), the designation *pada* is sublated by the designation *bha*. Alternatively, just as other word-operations (*padakārya*) such as *rutva* and *jaśtva* apply, so too will this word-operation apply. What is it? It is the designation *bha*.

The meaning of this is as follows: in the context of the technical term *bha*, the word *pada* (word) is understood from the previous rule; thus, the sense is that "a word becomes designated as *bha*. Since the status of being a word (*padatva*) exists, there might otherwise be the substitution of *r* (ru-tva) conditioned by that status. To prevent this, even though the *bha*-designation pertains to the domain of words, it is still a rule concerning the end of a word (*padānta-vidhi*). Consequently, because the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*) is prohibited, the *bha*-designation applies only to that which ends in *s*. Thus, due to the sublation of the status of being a word by the *bha*-designation, the substitution of *r* does not occur. It is another matter that previously the designation of a word (*pada-sañjñā*) was the very basis upon which the *bha*-designation depended, whereas subsequently the *bha*-designation sublated that [word-status].

Let us return to the subject at hand. In the case of *suddhyupāsyaḥ* following reduplication (*dvirvacana*), when reduplication is to be applied by the rule "anaci ca," the substitution of *yaṇ* is not treated as *sthānivat*. Nor is there any persistence of the impossibility of reduplication on the grounds that "what is external (*bahiraṅga*) is considered unestablished" (*asiddham*); for according to Haradatta's view, this prohibition applies due to the restriction "not when there is immediate sequence with a vowel" (*nājānantarye*), and also because of the very force of the prohibition against *sthānivadbhāva* in this context.

Due to the specific rule (*nipātana*) "vare," there is no elision (*luk*) of the case-ending. Consequently, the substitution of *aj* (a vowel) caused by that [elision] is not treated as *sthānivat*. Thus, we have *yāyāvaraḥ*. From the root *yā* with the suffix *yaṅ*, the suffix *varac* is applied by the rule "yaśca yaṅaḥ. There is then the elision of the *a* [of the suffix *varac*]. When the elision of the *ā* [of the root *yā*] is to be effected by the rule "ātolopa iṭi ca," that [elision of *a*] is not treated as *sthānivat*. It might be argued: "The elision of the *a* does not even possess a subsequent cause (*paranimittakatva*), because according to the locative case used in the sense of 'scope' (*viṣayasaptamī*) in the rule 'ārddhadhātuke,' the elision of the *a* occurs only prior to the production of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix."

For this very reason, it will be stated in the *Vṛtti* on the rule *aco yat*: "What is the purpose of including the term *ac*? Since you will state that the suffix *ṇyat* follows bases ending in consonants (*hal*), [the inclusion of *ac*] is so that it may also apply to those that were previously vowel-ending, as in *ditsya-* and *dhitsya-*.

Regarding this, Haradatta and others argue: "By the force of the inclusion of the word *vara-* [in the rule *var-aca*], there is also the possibility of interpreting it as a locative case (indicating a condition). For this very reason, the word *ādi-* is included in the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*. If that were not present, it would be understood as 'from a base ending in a consonant' (*halantāt*). Consequently, in forms such as *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ*, the suffix *yuc* would not be applicable."

Furthermore, if this were a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*), then even before the production of the suffix, once the *at* has been elided, the suffix *yuc* would be established there simply because it ends in a consonant (*halanta*); thus, the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) would be redundant.

In the same way, from the root *yā* with the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*), when the suffix *ktic* is added, after the elision of *at*, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies to the rule for the elision of *y*, when *y* is elided, due to its status as a *sthānivadbhūta*, the *ā* is elided, and then the *y* is elided again, resulting in the form *yāti*.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that when both the *ākāra* and *yakāra* are elided, there would result the undesirable consequence of hearing only the suffix (*pratyaya*). This is because the elision (*lopa*) is either subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) or is *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent operations) due to being *ābhīya* (belonging to the subsequent rules). Nor should it be asked how something can be *asiddha* with respect to itself; for such a possibility exists by virtue of the logic of the *ciṇo luṅ* rule. As the Vārttika will state:
"The mention of *ta* [in Pāṇini 1.1.62] is useless in the case of the elision of *ciṇ*, because the entire complex is not a suffix and because the elision of *ta* is *asiddha*."

The meaning of this is as follows: In the rule prescribing the elision (*luk*) of *ciṇ*, the mention of *ta* (in *tāsi-tas-tā-...* etc. would be redundant for the purpose of preventing the elision of *tarap* and other suffixes in forms such as *akāritarām*, because the combination of *ta* and *tarap* does not constitute a single *pratyaya*. Nor can it be argued that after the elision of *takāra*, there would be the undesired elision of *tarap*; for the elision of *ta* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of the subsequent operation. Nor is it incorrect to maintain this distinction, since different grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*) are applied based on the difference in their respective domains (*viṣaya*).
However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the example given for the elision of *ya* is *kaṇḍūtiḥ* from the root *kaṇḍūyati* with the suffix *ktic*.

In the *Vṛtti*, however, it is stated that the suffix *ktin* [is used]. Although the suffix *ktin* is difficult to obtain there—since it would be superseded by the suffix *ap*, and because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya* that "one must have *kaṇḍūya* [with *ap*]"—nevertheless, the suffix *ktin* applies by the rule "*ktin āb-ādibhyaḥ*" (A 3.3.94). Haradatta maintains that the reading "*ktic-ī*" [instead of "*ktin-ī*"] is more appropriate. [Then follow: the elision of *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of *ya* (*yalopa*). Nor should it be argued that the elision of *a* (*allopasya*) would cause the undesirable application of *uvaṅ* due to its being treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies specifically with respect to the elision of *ya* (*yalopaṃ prati*). This is because such an outcome is actually desired (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Because the substitution *ūṭh* is possible for that [root] by the rule "chvoḥ". Nor does there arise the contingency of the substitute *uvaṅ* being treated as *sthānivat* with respect to that [substitution of *ūṭh*], because it precedes the vowel that has been substituted (*ādiṣṭāt*). For this very reason, Haradatta and others maintain that there is no further substitution of *uvaṅ* for the *ūṭh*.

Thus, from the root *sthā* with the suffix *ktic*, after the elision of *a* (allopa) and the elision of *ya* (yalopa), because the elision of *a* is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were still present), *iyaṅ* is applied; then, by the rule "lopo vyoḥ," there is the elision of *ya*, resulting in the form *teṣṭhiti*. From the root *pā* (in the form *pepīyati*), however, by the rule "eranekācaḥ," *yaṇ* is applied, and after the elision of *ya*, the form is *pepti*. From the root *śo* (meaning "to sharpen/thin") in its *yaṅ*-inflected form (*śośūyate*), when *ktic* and other suffixes are added, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies by the rule "pūrvatrāsiddhe na—" (the preceding is not considered *siddha* for the following), the change of *ś* to *ṣ* occurs, and subsequently *ṣṭu* is applied, resulting in the specific form *śāṣṭi*.

[The word] *ākarṣikaḥ* [is derived as follows]: in the sense of "one who moves," the suffix *ṣṭhal* is applied by the rule *ākarṣāt*. When the acute accent (*udātta*) is to be applied to the vowel *a* following the *k* by the rule *liti*, the elision of the *a* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Nor can the force of the specific wording [of the rule *yasyeti ca*] be taken as the reason [for this non-application], because that rule has already served its purpose in cases such as *kārakaḥ*. Furthermore, since consonants are considered as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) for the application of accent rules, it is impossible for the *repha* (the *r*) and other [consonants] to act as an intervention; for when immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is possible, one does not resort to those that are separated by an interval.

Kaiyaṭa states that the vowel-sandhi (*svara*) is not established by the presence of the *akāra* due to the force of the *liṭ*-suffix marker, because otherwise the long *ākāra* would also result in being acute (*udātta*) in certain cases.

Others, however, say that this is incorrect; they maintain that only immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) as perceived in actual pronunciation (*śruti*) is relied upon by the force of the *liṭ*-marker, just as in the case of the *ku*-substitution in forms like *ghnantī*.

In this context, the example to be understood is *cikīrṣaka*, where the elision of the *akāra* (*ato lopaḥ*) is not treated as a *sthānivadbhāva* when the acute accent is to be applied to the *īkāra*. Similarly, in *śiṇḍhi*, when the homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) or the anusvāra is to be applied, the elision of the *akāra* of *śna* and *as* (*śnasorallopaḥ*) is not treated as a *sthānivadbhāva*.

Now, one might object: "Once the elision (*alopa*) of *śna* and *as* has been performed, the substitution of *anusvāra* takes effect; since the *anusvāra* is not prior to a preceding vowel (*aj*), there is no possibility of it being treated as a *sthānin* (original element) at all. Nor can it be argued that priority to a preceding vowel is established through the medium of the *sthānin*, because such a property, being non-grammatical (*aśāstrīya*), is unfit for extension (*atideśa*)."

As for what Haradatta and others have stated—that when an extension (*atideśa*) based on being prior to an unspecified vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatva*) is to be applied via the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, the extension *sthānivad ādeśaḥ* operates—that is not correct, because it was refuted in the preceding sūtra. To explain: either the state of being prior to an unspecified vowel is extended by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, or the extension itself [is extended]. It cannot be the first, because that would be non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*). Nor can it be the latter.

Because the extended application (*atideśa*) expressed by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* does not apply even in the present case to the original element (*sthānin*), it is impossible to extend it to its substitute (*ādeśa*). Furthermore, what is not observed in the original element cannot be subject to extension. And this [point] is necessary for Haradatta; otherwise, his established conclusion—that the rule *na dhātulopa-ārdhadhātuke* was formulated to prevent the occurrence of *guṇa* (based on a light penultimate vowel) after *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* have been applied in forms such as *loluva*—would be untenable.

Since the substitution of *al* (the elision of *i*) could have been prevented from undergoing *guṇa* simply by treating it as *sthānivadbhāva*—by relying on its being "prior" to the non-specified vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) through the medium of its original locus (*sthānidvāraka*)—it was possible to block that [undesirable] result there.

Nor should it be said that, because of the rejection of that rule (*sūtra*), the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya* (Patañjali) that "priority to an *ac* which has not been prescribed [by a rule] is also mediated by the substituend (*sthānin*)" is necessarily implied. This is because there is no such intent on the part of the *Bhāṣya*-author regarding the rejection of that rule; furthermore, as has already been shown, this would contradict the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*. Nor should it be said that the *Bhāṣya* and other such texts intend to show that priority to an *ac* which has not been prescribed is merely non-permanent (*anitya*) when mediated by the substituend.

Since the status of being "prior" to an unspecified vowel (anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam) by way of its locus (sthānidvāraka) contradicts both logic and the treatise, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "for that [substitute] is prior to the specified vowel (sa hy ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvaḥ)" is indeed more authoritative.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāmatī* and other works that, in comparison with the statement, "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed imperishable," the Vedic text—"Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"—is more powerful, being supported by the inference of perishability based on the mark of having been produced (*kṛtakatva*). For this same reason, regarding the word *kaṇḍūti*, it was stated that the substitution of *uvaṅ* does not occur because [the *u*] precedes the prescribed vowel (*acaḥ pūrvatvāt*). This is true.

In both of these two positions—that "being prior" (pūrvatva) is either relative to the substitute (ādeśa) or relative to the cause (nimitta)—the prohibition is justified because the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) would otherwise apply. By this very reasoning, the view that the mention of "being prior to a vowel not yet prescribed" (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvasya*) refers to a priority mediated through the substitute is refuted, precisely because of the aforementioned prohibition.

However, some say that in the word *harit*—derived from the verbal root *lū* with the causative suffix *ṇic* and the suffix *vic*—in the form *harillunāti*, the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is for the purpose of prohibiting the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) for either the elision of the vowel *a* or the elision of the *ṇic* suffix, when the substitution of *l* for *t* is to be applied by the rule *tor li*. They argue that this cannot be established merely by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat* ("that which is not *sthānivadbhāva* applies when what precedes is asiddha"), because that very rule is restricted by the exception: *tasya doṣaḥ saṃyogādilopalatvaṇatveṣu* ("there is a defect in that [rule] regarding the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga*, the substitution of *l* for *t*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*").

Others, however, maintain that only the *latva* (substitution of *l*) explicitly prescribed in the rule itself is accepted there, and not that which results from the rule for *parasavarṇa* (the homogeneous following sound), because the latter involves a mediated cognition.

Others, however, argue that because the *lakāra* (the optative suffix) following the *repha* (*r*) is elided, the substitution of *l* for *t* in the rule *tor li* is also directly stated (*pratipadokta*), since there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in the continued application of the *parasavarṇa* rule.

In reality, however, by relying on the principle that "that which is not established in what precedes is not like its original substrate" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīye na sthānivat*), the mention of *savarṇa* (homogeneous sounds) can be rejected even in the final system (*siddhānta*); thus, this objection does not hold—this is how it should be understood.

Although the mention of *anusvāra* separately would be redundant—since the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* in the rule for *parasavarṇa* necessarily implies its prohibition in the rule for *anusvāra* as well (because the latter is impossible without the former)—nevertheless, that mention is intended to dispel the doubt that in cases where *parasavarṇa* does not apply, such as in *śiṃṣanti*, the *anusvāra* might not occur.

In the word *pratidīvnā*, when the lengthening required by the rule *hali ca* is to be applied, the elision of *al* (the final *a*) caused by the designation *bha* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. [This is because] after the prefix *prati*, the root *div* takes the suffix *kanin* according to the rule *kanin yuvṛṣitakṣirājidhanvidyupratidivaḥ*.

However, in the *Vṛtti*, it is stated that the lengthening occurs by the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca*; this was written down through the negligence of scribes, because the *v* of the root *div* is not a *upadhā* (penultimate vowel).
Haradatta and others maintain that since the *Vṛtti* itself explicitly states that in the word *pratidīvnā* the lengthening is by the rule *hali ca* with respect to the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca*.

As for those who have been initiated (*dīkṣitāḥ*), it should be understood that [the form] is derived from the root *ācar* with the suffix *kvip*. In that case, *pratidivan* ends in *n*; it is precisely that which receives the designation of a verbal root (*dhātu-saṃjñā*), and by virtue of that, the possibility arises for the *v* to be a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of lengthening the *a* before the elision (*alopa*) of the *v*—according to the rule "the penultimate nasal is lengthened before *kvip* and *jhal*"—because, by the maxim of "not applying what has not yet been formed" (*akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*), one considers the future elision of *v* and thus the internal operation of lengthening does not take effect.

Furthermore, they say that even in the absence of *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no impossibility of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) due to the rule "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent" (*asiddham bahiraṅgam*), because the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is considered non-existent; for it is known from the mention of *tuṅ* in the rule *kṛti-tuṅ* that this paribhāṣā is not universal (*anitya*). Moreover, under the *yathoddeśa* view, that paribhāṣā does not apply there. This must be stated according to both views.

In the phrases *sagdhiśca me* and *babdhāṃ te harī*, the root *ad* takes the suffix *ktin*; by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, it undergoes the substitution of *ghasl*. By the rule *ghasibhasorhali ca*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*). Then, by the rule *jhalo jhali*, there is elision of the *s*. This is because the author of the Bhāṣya does not accept the rule that there is elision of *sic* when *dhi* follows.

According to the Vārttika school, however, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that the *s* is elided because it is archaic (*chāndasa*). By the rule *jhaṣas tathoḥ*, the *t* of the suffix undergoes the change to *dh*. With respect to that [substitution], the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) does not behave as if it were in its original state (*na sthānivattva*) when applying the preceding rule, because that [elision] is non-permanent (*anitya*). When the change of *gh* to *g* is to be effected by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the elision of the penultimate vowel does not behave as if it were in its original state.

*Samānā gdhiḥ sagdhiḥ*: by the rule *samānasya chandasyamūrddhaprabhṛtyudarkeṣu*, there is the substitution of *sā-* for *samāna-*. In the second [form], from the root *ghas* (to eat), there is the *loṭ* suffix; *tas* becomes *tām*; the *śap* is elided (*ślu*). Because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), reduplication occurs first, followed by the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable. Then, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) and so forth proceed as before. Thus, *jakṣatuḥ*. From the root *ghas*, there is the *liṭ* suffix *atus*. By the rule *gamahana*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel. When the change of *gh* to *k* is to be applied by the rule *kharica*, that [elision] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were still present). Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:

"In the cases of vowel lengthening (*svaradīrgha*) and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as *sthānivat*; however, a substitute in the form of a positive presence (*bhāvarūpa*) is indeed *sthānivat*. By this [rule], in *pañcāratnyaḥ* and *daśāratnyaḥ*, when there is no *guṇa* due to the rule *chandasi vā vacanaṃ prāṅ ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* regarding the suffixes beginning with *jas*, the *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs. Because of its *sthānivadbhāva*, the *pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara* applies by the rule *igantakālakapāla-* etc.; such is the *Bhāṣya*."

Nor should it be said that this is already established by the *asiddhaparibhāṣā* (the rule that what is not yet accomplished is as if non-existent), because by the *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* (the rule that a grammatical operation does not take place if its cause is subsequently destroyed), the *yaṇ* substitution has not yet occurred at the earlier stage. In the case of *bahukhaṭvaka*, due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) does not apply to the vowel *a* before the *kh* according to the rule "before a short vowel, the penultimate [syllable] is acute," but rather only by the rule "before the suffix *kap*, the preceding [syllable is acute]. However, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that in the case of *prācitīka*, the rule "before a short vowel" does indeed apply.

In *kiyoḥ* and *giyoḥ*, although a long vowel would have been required by the rule "also before a consonant (*hali ca*)" under the view that these words are derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*), it does not occur due to the status of the substitute for the *yaṇ*.

Under the governing heading *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.56), the suffix *i* is applied by the rules *bhujeḥ kicca* and *kṝgṝśṝdṝkuṭibhidicchidibhyaśca*; furthermore, this suffix is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*). Regarding the statement introduced by Haradatta and the author of the Nyāsa, *kṝgro rica*, the Dīkṣitas remark that it should be sought in some version of the Uṇādi-vṛtti.

Others say that here, in the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca*, forms such as *kiryoḥ* and so forth are established even by resorting to the view of non-derivation (*avyutpattipakṣa*), according to the method stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*. As for the elision of the *v* in *vāyvoḥ* by the rule *lopo vyoḥ*, it can be prevented by the *asiddhaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding what is not yet established). Therefore, they maintain that in the aforementioned *Vārttika*, the word *svara* alone is necessary. [The *Vārttika* states: "An addition must be made for the cases of *kvip*-suffix, elision (*luk*), the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), the *aṅ* suffix, and the reduction of the following element (*paranirhrāsa*). And [the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara* states]: "In the case of what is previously unestablished (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*), there is a fault [if one applies this] regarding the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*)."

The meaning is this: with respect to an operation prescribed for *kvip*, [the substitute] is not like the original (na sthānivat). From the root *lū* (to cut), *lauḥ* is derived by applying the suffix *kvip*. Here, there is the elision of the *ṇic* affix and the elision of the *ṇi* affix; both of these are not like the original (*sthānivat*) with respect to the *ūṭh* substitution caused by *kvip*. Thus, by the rule "vṛddhi occurs before *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭh*," the *vṛddhi* replacement takes place. However, for those who read the rule as "that which is elided in *kvip* is not like the original," this result would not be obtained.

Similarly, in the case of *pipaṭhiṣati* (desiring to read) with the suffix *kvip*, when the elision of the vowel *a* (*ato lopa*) has occurred, there arises a prohibition against treating that elision as *sthānivat* when the augment *num*—conditioned by a *jhal* consonant or a *lac* vowel—is to be applied in the neuter plural. This is because [the elision] was performed when *kvip* followed, which would otherwise lead to the undesirable application of *num*. However, according to the view that "an operation conditioned by *kvip* does not apply," since *num* is not caused by *kvip*, the status of being *sthānivat* indeed holds.

Even in the previous case, although the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elision of *ṇi* caused by *kvin* is prohibited, there remains the contingency of *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of *ṭi* caused by *ṇi*; consequently, the substitution of *ūṭh* would be untenable. This is clear from the work of Haradatta. Kaiyaṭa also stated that the established meaning is "with respect to an operation prescribed after *kvin*" (*kvau vidhiṃ prati*), and not "that which is elided after *kvin*" (*kvau luptam*). However, his point is that in some instances, even the principle "that which is elided after *kvin*" (*kvau luptam*) is indeed resorted to.

For this very reason, regarding the sūtra *khyatyātparasya*, the Bhāṣya states: *sakhīyateḥ sakhīḥ, lūnīyateḥ lūnīḥ*. [The objection is as follows: When the suffix *kvip* is applied to roots such as *sakhīya*, after the elision of the *a* (by *ato lopaḥ*) and the subsequent elision of the *y* (by *lopo vyor vali*), the *ikāra* should undergo *yaṇ*-substitution because the elision of *a* (*āllopa*) is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Then, when the *y* is elided (*yalopa*), one might suspect that the elision of *y* would occur either because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies, or because it is not possible for it to be *sthānivadbhūta* since it precedes the original vowel (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*). Anticipating this, Kaiyaṭa provides the solution: "That which is elided by *kvip* is not *sthānivadbhūta*."

In this context, relying on the position that "an elision (*lopa*) substitute is not like its original (*sthānivat*)," it was stated that [the rule] applies to a vowel that has been substituted for the first [vowel]. Haradatta, however, maintains that *dayūḥ* from the root *devayati* is established in both ways.

[Objection: One might argue that even under the view that "a rule applies before *kvi*," the substitution of *ūṭh* is established; nevertheless, because *ūṭh* would be prior to the vowel by way of its substituendum (*sthānin*), and because the elision of *ṇi* would be treated as if it were present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule "vṛddhi occurs before affixes beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ*" would apply, resulting in a *vṛddhi* [vowel]. Therefore, one must necessarily rely on the principle that "what is elided before *kvi* does not cause *vṛddhi*. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated: "But this is an example of what is elided before *kvi*: from the root *devayati*, we get *dayūḥ*. How then can it be said that "it is so in both ways"? [Response: This is not so, because it has already been stated that there is no evidence for [the *ūṭh*] being prior by way of its substituendum.

Nor should it be argued that in either of the two views, the *vṛddhi* substitution is unavoidable in the case of *dyūḥ* by virtue of the definition of a *pratyaya*. This is because the *ūṭh* is *asiddha* with respect to the *vṛddhi*, being an external (*bahiraṅga*) operation. Thus, even though there is the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no harm. Nor can it be claimed that the rule "diva auT" would apply [to *dyūḥ*] on the basis of the maxim regarding partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). For the resolution of this will be stated in the Bhāṣya: either by the paribhāṣā concerning [roots] without an indicatory letter (*niranubandha*) or by the continued application of the term "non-root" (*adhātu*) from a previous context.

And all this [is said] under the view that "in an *ardhadhātuka*" (*ardhadhātuke*) is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). However, it should be understood that if it were a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), there would be no possibility of the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, because the elision (*lopa*) resulting from this [rule] would not have a subsequent element as its cause (*paranimittakatva*). This has been clearly indicated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* while stating the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the elision of *y* and the elision of *k* in the rule "lopo vyoḥ," and it has been explained by Kaiyaṭa; thus it is clear to those who know the original sources (*ākaravid*).

When a suffix is elided (*luk*), it does not behave as if it were present (*na sthānivat*). For example: *āmalakyāḥ phalam āmalakam* ("the fruit of the *āmalaka* tree"). Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ*. Then, by the rule *phale luk*, the suffix is elided; subsequently, by the rule *luktaddhitaluki*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is also elided. The elision of the vowel *i* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*) is conditioned by what follows (*paranimittaka*), and thus it does not behave as if it were present. Otherwise, due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the vowel *ī* would still be considered subsequent to the *a*, and consequently, the elision of the *a* would occur.

In the view that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix, however, *pañcapaṭu* means "bought for five clever ones," and *pañcendra* or *pañcāgni* mean "one whose deities are five Indras" or "five Agnis. In the first case, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "ārhāt. Its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule "adyardhapūrva. Although, by the maxim "even internal [rules] are superseded," the application of *luk* would occur prior to the *yaṇ*-substitution, there remains the possibility of *yaṇ* due to the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

If one assumes that, according to the logic of the *aviravika* rule, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied there only after the word *paṭu* and not after *paṭvī*, this results in an excessive burden on the understanding (*pratipattigaurava*). Furthermore, the transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "in the case of a *bha*-stem before a non-initial *taddhita*" does not apply here; for that rule is prescribed only when the *bha*-status is about to occur, whereas in this case, due to the elision (*luk*), that status does not exist. Moreover, even the rule "before *ṭhak* and *chaś*" is difficult to apply because, when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, there is no "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). In the second case, the example is clear because of the absence of the masculine transformation. [The suffix] *aṇ* is added by the rule "that which is its deity."

By the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*, there is elision (*luk*). Consequently, there would be elision of both the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*. By virtue of that elision, the long vowel *ai* (as in *aikāra*) and the augment *ānuk* would also be heard [in the phonetic form]. Nor can their removal be established by the principle of simultaneous prescription (*sanniyogaśiṣṭanyāya*). This is because, since the elision of the feminine suffix is prescribed when a *taddhita* suffix is elided, the removal of *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* is caused by that very elision; thus, when the removal of the long vowel *ai* and the augment *ānuk*—which precede them—is to take place, the rule *acaḥ parasmin* applies, resulting in the status of the preceding element as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*).

However, some explain that because of the *praśleṣa* (splitting) of *vara* as *vara ī* in the rule *vare*, the operation before the vowel *ī* is not subject to the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original); they thus claim that the mention of *luk* (elision) in the present Vārttika is unnecessary. This is clearly stated in the *Padamañjarī*. Others, however, argue that if this were the case, in a form such as *pañcagārgyaḥ*—meaning "one whose deities are five Gārgyāyaṇīs"—the elision of the *ṣpha* suffix would not be established after the elision of the *ṅīṣ* suffix, because due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elided *ṅīṣ*, the condition of being followed by a *taddhita*-elision (*taddhitalukaḥ*) would be absent.

For you accept the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment of a substitute as the original) only in cases where a grammatical operation is prescribed when the vowel *ī* follows; however, this [substitution of *ai* for *e*] does not fall under such a case. Consequently, in the example *pañcaśvaśuraḥ* ("bought with five mothers-in-law"), there would be the elision of both the *a* and the *u* vowels. Furthermore, in examples such as *aineyaḥ* ("descendant of Enī") and *śyaineyaḥ* ("descendant of Śyenī"), when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there would also be the removal of the *n*. This is because the *n* has already been established prior to that point and thus lacks the status of being a grammatical effect (*kārya*), which means the rule *sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau* ("a substitute is like the original, except in the case of an operation concerning an *al*") does not apply.

This is because an effect consisting of the mere absence of an operation is not sanctioned by the grammatical treatise (*aśāstrīya*). Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned prohibition does not apply because the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the augment *nakāra* are prescribed together, such that there would be no subsequent rule for the substitution of *īkāra*; for if *ānug* and *īkāra* were prescribed together with *ṅīṣ* and *ṅīp*, forms such as *pañcendra* would remain unestablished—so they say. That is not correct, because the elision (*luk*) of *ṅīṣ* occurs precisely along with the suffix *ṣpha*. For in that context, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the rule "for the Easterners, *ṣpha* is a secondary suffix" (*prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ*) indicates that femininity is the meaning of the suffix *ṣpha* itself, while *ṅīṣ* occurs by virtue of the indicatory letter *ṣ* (*ṣittva*).

When the status of being an *upadhā* (penultimate syllable) is to be established, [an operation] is not like the original (*sthānivat*). For example, in the case of *pārikhīyaḥ*: otherwise, if the suffix *aṇ* were applied to the word *parikhā* according to the rule for the four types of meanings (*cāturarthika*), then because of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision (*ālopa*) caused by that suffix, the syllable preceding the *kh* would lack the status of being an *upadhā*. Consequently, the suffix *cha* would not apply by the rule "after a word ending in *vṛddhi*, beginning with *aka*, *eka*, or *anta*, and having *kh* as its *upadhā*" (*vṛddhādakekāntakhopadhāt*). This is because the designation (*saṃjñā*) of *upadhā* is a rule dependent on what precedes it (*pūrvavidhi*).

Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *paṭayati*, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies to the elision of *ṭi*, the vowel *a* of the letter *p* would acquire the designation *upadhā*, thereby resulting in the undesired application of the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) which would cause Vṛddhi. This is because the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the aforementioned prohibition operates only in the prescription of suffixes conditioned by the designation *upadhā*. Furthermore, one should not ask how the statement in the Bhāṣya—that the example *saurī balākā* (a crane belonging to Sūrya) is explained otherwise simply by the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the elision of *y* (*yalopa*)—is justified under such a view. [This is because the Bhāṣya refers to a different context.]

Because it is merely a statement lacking firm foundation. For in that case, [the form *saurī*] is derived from [the base *saura-*] ending in the suffix *aṇ* by the addition of *ṅīp* according to the rule "tenaikadik. There, the first [element] is caused by the suffix *aṇ*, and the elision (*lopa*) of the second vowel *ā* is caused by the suffix *ṅīp*. Regarding the elision of both of these [suffixes], there is a prohibition of their being treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if they were the original element). However, because the second elision is *ābhīya* (belonging to the subsequent operation) and shares the same locus (*samānāśraya*), it is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the preceding operation); thus, the designation *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) applies to the *yakāra*, and its elision is established. Consequently, it has been stated that the status of being an *upadhā* pertains only to the elision of *yakāra*, and not to the prescription of a suffix. It is clear that *saurī* is the very example for the elision of *yakāra*.

The rule *caṅ-para-nirhrāsaś-caṅ-nimittako hrasvaḥ* (the shortening [of a vowel] occurs when followed by *caṅ*, caused by *caṅ*) applies as follows: [In the example] *avīvadad vīṇāṃ parivādakena* ("he caused the lute-player to play the lute"), if the elision (*lopa*) of the first *ṇic* were treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), the vowel *ā* would not be a *upadhā* (penultimate vowel), and thus the shortening prescribed by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyāḥ* would not take place. This is because the second *ṇic* which follows *caṅ* does not have the vowel *ā* as its *upadhā* within its own *aṅga* (stem); and although the vowel *ā* remains part of the *aṅga* of the first *ṇic*, that first *ṇic* itself is not followed by *caṅ*.

Thus, from the word *vāri* and from the causative form *tatkaroti* (with the suffix *ṇi*), the *caṅ* [causative-intransitive] form is *avīvarat*. Here, the elision of the *ik* vowel is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were present). Nor does the prohibition "not when there is elision of *a*" (*nāglopi*) apply. This is because it is accepted that the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) occurs after the *vṛddhi* has already taken place due to its higher priority. For this very reason, the forms *hal* and *kala* will be established as having final *a* by means of a *nipātana* (irregularity). Even regarding the substitution of *ku* for *c*, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. The word *arka* is derived from the root *arc* with the *uṇādi* suffix *kap*; *pākti* is derived from *pāc* with the suffix *ktic*. In the rule "the *c* is replaced by *k*" (*coḥ kuḥ*), the elision of the *ṇi* suffix is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the substitution of *ku*.

The substitution of *k* (kutva) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative instance). Therefore, it should be understood that forms such as *leḍhi* from *lehayati*, *dogdhi* from *dohayati*, *yāṣṭi* from *yājayati*, and *veṣṭi* from *veśayati* are established. This is because the inclusion of the *kutva* rule is based on the principle that "in the case of what is not established by a preceding rule, [the original form] does not remain as it was. That [principle] is also established by logic (*nyāya*): since a rule belonging to the third book (*traipādika*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to an extension (*atideśa*) such as "for a vowel, when a subsequent [element follows]" (*acaḥ parasmin*), that extension does not apply during the formulation of that [third-book] rule. Nor would the visarga fail to appear in forms such as *rāmaḥ*.

It should not be argued that because the *sthānivadbhāva* rule would likewise fail to apply by parity of reasoning, *padatva* (the status of being a word) could not be established due to the absence of *subantatva* (the status of ending in a case-suffix). This is because the application of that rule is guaranteed by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "a suffix" (*pratyaya*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the operations of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), anusvāra, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the *jaś* and *car* substitutions should also not be included in the rule; for such an outcome is desired. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "Reduplication and the rest [are included] except for *vareya*, elision (*lopa*), accent (*svara*)," and so forth.

It might be argued as follows: If the mention of *dīrgha* (long vowel) were omitted, then in another rule prescribing a long vowel (*dīrghavidhi*), by virtue of the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle, the examples cited by all authorities—namely *aśaṃśāmi* and *aśāmi* derived from a *yaṅ*-stem or a *ṇij*-stem followed by *ciṇ*—would not be established under the rule *ciṇṇamuloḥ*. Nor can it be argued that this is due to the force of the mention of *dīrgha*; for that mention is intended for the sake of forms like *ahīḍi*, and also for the purpose of excluding forms like *aheḍi*. To explain: the root *heḍṛ* meaning "disregard" belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group and is short; thus, one says *hiḍayati*.

In this context, if the option for a short vowel were prescribed when the suffixes *ciṇ* and *ṇamul* are applied, the forms would be *ahiḍi* and *aheḍi*; however, with a long vowel, the forms are *ahiḍi* and *ahīḍi*, as is clear from Kaiyaṭa and other sources.

On this point, they say: by apprehending the unity of the *ṇit*-class (*ṇitvajāti*), the form *aśāmī* is established from the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive without *yaṅ*) as well as *aśaṃśāmī*; for whether there is *yaṅ* or its elision (*luk*), there is no difference in meaning or accent. As for forms such as *grāhitam*, even though there is an intervention by *ṇic* due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the rule regarding the preceding [element], the long vowel prescribed by the rule "graho 'liṭi" does not apply. Nor is the long vowel unavoidable in the view of the Sūtra-author, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies specifically to the prescription of a long vowel; for one resorts to the qualification that the [substitute] must be "prescribed" (*vihita*). By this, the form *jarīgṛhitā* is also explained.
Mādhavācārya, however, states that after the *yaṅ*-lopped form (*yaṅluk*) of the root *grah*, there is lengthening of the vowel before suffixes such as *tṛc* (e.g., *jāgrahītṛ*).

Regarding this, [the author] says: according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "doubling is the second utterance" (*dvirvacanam*), the rule for *grah* is prescribed; furthermore, because the *yaṅluk* is not occasioned by a specific cause (*anaimitikatayā*), because it is a substitute for the *aj*-portion (*ajñalādeśatayā*), and because the elision (*luk*) has been effected, there is no application of the rule of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is his intention.

This, moreover, contradicts both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa. For in his commentary on the Bhāṣya under the rule *ekāco dve*, regarding the phrase *graheraṅgāt*, Kaiyaṭa states: "In *jarīgṛhītā*, there is no lengthening because of the qualification 'prescribed [affix]'; for the *ārddhadhātuka* affix prescribed after the root *grah* is the qualifier. The *tṛc* suffix makes *jarīgṛh* the *aṅga*, not *grah*; indeed, by the force of the qualification, one must rely upon the form exactly as it is heard [in the sūtra]. Although this was stated in the context of *yaṅ*, its intention is that there is no lengthening even in *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*), because it is the same as other cases.

On this point, the following must be said: since the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) lacks any specific cause [for its occurrence], there is no obstacle to the production of an affix after it; thus, by resorting to the form as it is heard in the rule, the fact that [the suffix] is prescribed after the root *grah* remains intact. Furthermore, it is not the case that the production of the *ārddhadhātuka* affix occurs only immediately after the application of reduplication and so forth. Rather, because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal), the *ārddhadhātuka* affix itself arises first. In the case of the *yaṅ*-ending, however, the *ārddhadhātuka* affix arises only after the word *grahya*, resulting in a deviation from the form as it is heard in the rule; such is the difference.

Nor does this contradict Kaiyaṭa’s statement that "jarīgṛh" is not an *aṅga* (base), for his intent was merely to exclude the pure root *grah* from being an *aṅga*. This is because, according to the literal reading, the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅ-lopa*) would be subject to a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*), which would lead to a contradiction; furthermore, it has already been stated by Kaiyaṭa himself that the suffix *tṛc* follows the word *jarīgrahya* prior to that [elision]. Alternatively, Mādhava’s intention may be as follows: since the *yaṅ* is actually heard there, reduplication and other operations caused by it occur first; however, in the case of *luk*-elision, reduplication and so forth—which depend on the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)—occur only later.

Regarding the rule *graho'liṭi*, although Haradatta has carried forward the mention of *ekāj* (a single vowel), he has explained therein how long-vowel substitution (*dīrgha*) nevertheless occurs in the case of the *yaṅ*-lopa formation; such is the general direction. "The fault of that [prohibition] lies in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*). This refers to the aforementioned prohibition. By this, even though the preceding operation is not established (*asiddha*) in these three instances, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) still applies. Consequently, in the forms *kākyartham* and *vāsyartham*, there is no elision of the *k* and *s*—which are the initial members of the conjunct at the end of the word—by the rule *skoḥ*.

If it is argued that there is no such over-extension because the word *it* is supplied from the rule *skoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), and since that [supply] is redundant as it does not prevent deviation in the rule *skoḥ*, or because even when the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is subordinate, the meaning is that the *s* and *k* at the beginning of a conjunction ending in a *jhal* consonant are elided—thus, by being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), the *yaṇ* substitution is considered as if non-existent and this over-extension does not occur—that is not so. For it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the form *kūḥ*, cited by Mādhava and others as derived from the root *kusmī* (in the *kvip* suffix), would be untenable.
