If the phrase "beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogādi*) were not included [in P. 1.1.58], then in the case of the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix would result. This is because Kaiyaṭa’s statement in his commentary on the Bhāṣya regarding *dadhy atra*—"The rule 'not like the original' (*na sthānivat*) does not apply when a preceding operation is *asiddha*, because the word 'beginning with a conjunct' (*saṃyogādi*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any elision characterized by a conjunct"—is intended merely to describe the position of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*). Furthermore, in the supplementary section of the *napadānta* sūtra, that same author [Kaiyaṭa] stated: "From *skand* comes *skan*; from *takṣ* comes *tag*. Thus, [the inclusion of *saṃyogādi* is necessary].

As for what was stated by him in his commentary on the *vārttika* "ścutvakatve" in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*—namely, that while one expects the form *madhug* from the root *ścut* preceded by *madhu*, when it is followed by a *kvip* suffix and then a *ṇic* suffix and another *kvip* suffix, the form *madhuḍ* would result—the intended meaning there is that, due to the force of the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the letter *s*, there is no elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*). Nor should it be argued that [the rule] has its utility elsewhere, such as in the case of *sañ ścotati*, because of the non-application of the rule "śi tuk"; for that can be resolved by the principle "what is elided before *kvip* is not treated as a *sthānivadbhūta*."

However, in the case of *kusmayate*, because of the absence of capacity [for the rule to apply], only the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would take effect; furthermore, from the causative forms of the roots *takṣ* and *rakṣ* with the suffix *kvip*, the forms *tak* and *rak* etc. would not be established, since the conjunct there ends in a *jhal* sound. But when the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) is to be applied, although the elision of the *ṇi* would be treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), that does not prevent the application of the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*)—because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies here—and thus the stated forms are established.

Nor should it be said that this usage does not exist because of the *bhāṣya* statement, "there is no such thing as 'kāṣṭhaśak'"; for that was stated with reference to the possibility of the elision of the letter *k*—which is preceded by a *jhal* consonant and begins a *saṃyoga*—in the form *kāṣṭhaśak-sthātā*, since the principle of non-occurrence (*anabhidhāna*) was only asserted where there was the contingency of eliding the initial member of a *saṃyoga*. However, in the present case, such a contingency does not arise because the elision of the *ṇi* suffix is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*). For this very reason, commentators maintain that the *kvip* suffix does not occur after roots ending in *k*.

Regarding the substitution of *l* for *r* (*latva*), as in *nigāryate* and *nigālyate*: because of the status of the elision of the suffix *ṇi* as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is an option for the substitution of *l* by the rule *aci vibhāṣā*. Alternatively, the substitution of *l* occurs simply by means of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Nor is this dependent on the phoneme (*varṇāśrayatva*), because this operation is understood to apply to the suffix when the root is grasped in its own form. This will be made known by the specific mention (*nipātana*) of the letter *t* in the word *bhrūṇahatya*. Or, if it is argued that the substitution of *l* occurs first—prior even to the elision of *ṇi*—on account of its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), let it not be so.

This is because it will be stated in the Bhāṣya that "the *Pratyayalakṣaṇasūtra* has as its sole result the exclusion of other [conditions], whereas the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) is established by the *Sthānivatsūtra* itself. Furthermore, in the case of *latva* (the substitution of *l* for *ṛ*) conditioned by an affix beginning with *a*, since the vowel (*al*) is relied upon as a qualifier, the prohibition "in the case of an operation not concerning an *al*" (*analvidhau*) applies. Nor is there success through the principle of *antarangatva* (internal operation), due to the contradiction with the maxim regarding the non-application of a rule when its requirements are already fulfilled (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*).

Furthermore, regarding the rule *upasargasyāyatau*, there are two positions: whether the condition of being followed by *ayati* qualifies the prefix (*upasarga*) or the letter *r*. In the first case, for the sake of the substitution of *l* in *plāyata*, the application of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original) is necessary; otherwise, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been effected, there would be an absence of the distinctness (*vyapavarga*) consisting of priority and posteriority. This is because the meaning of the rule is "of that prefix which possesses priority relative to what is established as posteriority in *ayati*. Moreover, when a grammatical operation depends on both sides [of a single substitute], the principle of *antādivadbhāva* (behaving like the end or the beginning) is prohibited.

In the second alternative (*dvitīya*), because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as if it were the subsequent element (*parādittvena*), although the form *plāyate* is established—since the root *ayati* follows the *repha*—the substitution of *l* for *y* would not occur in *palyayate*, because there is an intervention by the *yakāra*. Nor can the [rule] be justified by the force of the statement (*vacanasāmarthya*), for it has its scope elsewhere in *plāyate*. Nor can it be argued that even there, due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is an intervention by the *akāra*; for that is prohibited by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe*. However, if one allows the application of *sthānivadbhāva* specifically for the prescription of *latva*, then the substitution of *l* is established in both cases by the principle of "non-intervention by that which is inseparable" (*yenāvyavadhāna-nyāya*). This is the general direction of the argument.

The *Bhāṣya* states: "There is no *ṇatva* in *māṣavapanī*. Kaiyaṭa explains that although the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* (the final letter of the compound) is prescribed by the rule *prātipadikānta-*, it would apply before the suffix *ṅīp* arises because the formation of the compound precedes its production; this is due to the prohibition of treating the elision (*allop*) as *sthānivadbhūta*.

Here they raise an objection: because the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is external (*bahiraṅga*), it is considered as not having taken effect (*asiddha*), and thus the *n* does not qualify as being at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, in forms such as *prahiṇoti* and *pramīṇāti*, the rule *hinu-mīnā-* applies precisely by means of the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). Nor can this [rule] be intended for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ṇ* in *priyāṣṭan-*, since under the view that the time of application is determined by the effect itself (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the desired result is already established by the very fact of its being external. By this, the passage from the *Padamañjarī* which advocates the acceptance of *ṇ* in *priyāṣṭṇ-* is refuted. That is incorrect; for in that case, the substitution of *ṇ* has already been demonstrated previously.

As for the rule *aniterantaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.19), in order to justify the substitution of *ṇ* in *he prāṇ*, the prohibition by the rule *padāntasya* (8.4.37) is set aside by dividing the rule into two parts (*yogavibhāga*)—namely, *antaḥ*—thereby prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *ani* when it is at the end of a word. Alternatively, by taking the word *antaḥ* in the sense of "proximity," the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *ani* (or for a similar *n*) that stands in proximity to the cause [of the change] is established even without the division of the rule.

In the first case, such as *prāṇiti*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by virtue of the rule's application despite the intervention of a single vowel (*ā*). In the second case, however, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the initial element, the condition of being immediately preceded by *r* is possible for the root *an*, and thus the result is established. Regarding *paryaniti*, it was explained in the eighth [chapter] that the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur because there is an intervention of either two or one vowel. If the term "substitution of *ṇ*" (*ṇatva*) were applied here [to the rule *pra-para-mṛṣa...*], then just as in *paryaniti*, it would not occur in *prāṇiti* either, due to the intervention of two or one phoneme.

Nor does the rule possess sufficient force [to justify the specific formulation], because its purpose is fulfilled by the forms *niraṇiti* and *duraṇiti*. Nor should it be argued that one could simply have said "after *ni-* and *dur-*, when followed by *aṇiti*" (*nirduroraniteḥ*). For even though *ni-* would not be a prefix (*upasarga*) with respect to the root *an*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would undesirably apply in the case of *nirānayati*, since *ni-* there functions as a specifier of the meaning of the suffix *ṇi*.

Furthermore, since the word *niḥ* is derived from the root *ni* with the suffix *viṅ*, when it is compounded with the word *śabda* according to the rule "compounds beginning with *nis* [occur] in the sense of 'gone beyond' (*krāntādi*)", the designation *bha* applies; consequently, in the case of *al-lopa* (elision of *a*), there would be the substitution of *ṇ* in *nir-na*. To prevent this *ṇ*-substitution in cases such as *he prāṇi*, and for the sake of brevity of syllables, it is more appropriate to include the term *antaḥ* itself [in the rule]. Therefore, upon examining the Bhāṣya on the eighth book and other sources, the inclusion of the mention of *ṇatva* here should not be made. That too is incorrect.

If [the rule] were intended to apply only to that specific case, then the very rule "rādaniteḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.17) would be rendered superfluous; for it is possible to explain that rule as meaning "there is ṇatva for the 'ni' following an upasarga ending in 'r'. Furthermore, since there is no other purpose for the mention of "aniteḥ," and since an exception to the prohibition "padāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.39) is possible, this is the general direction [of the argument]. Although it might be easy to establish the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) in three instances by relying on the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *asiddhatva* (treatment as not having taken effect) based on a split of the yoga-rule in "na mu ne" (Pāṇini 8.2.3), nevertheless, because such a specific distinction is difficult to grasp, the composition of a Vārttika itself is preferable.
[The sūtra: "dvirvacane'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59).

An *aj*-substitute made in reliance upon a cause for reduplication (*dvitva*) should be treated as *sthānivadbhūta* when reduplication is to be performed. Since the rule "acaḥ parasmin" (P. 1.1.57) applies only to an operation concerning what precedes an *ac* that has not been directly prescribed (*anādiṣṭa*), the status of being *sthānivadbhūta*—which would otherwise not apply when reduplication itself is to be performed—is here expressly enjoined. Kaiyaṭa states that even in the view that the rule concerns an operation preceding [the substitute] with respect to its cause, the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* is prohibited regarding the operation of reduplication. This is an extension (*atideśa*) of form. [Examples: *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*.

When *kṛ* + *atus* becomes *kṛ us*, following the rule for *yaṇ* substitution, the doubling (*dvitva*) of the element *kṛ* occurs by means of the subsequent extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "liṭi dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.8). However, if one accepts the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), then once the *yaṇ* substitution has taken place, the base (*prakṛti*) would no longer consist of a single vowel (*anacka*); consequently, the doubling prescribed for a monosyllabic root would not apply. Thus, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), this very sūtra would result in the doubling of the entire form including the *yaṇ*. The evidence for the view that there is an extension of the form itself (*rūpātideśa*) will be stated later.

In this regard, five possible interpretations arise. To explain: (1) The term *aci* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the substitute; *dvirvacane* is a specification of the domain (*viṣayanirdeśa*). Thus, the first view is: "Whatever substitute occurs for a vowel (*ac*) when there is doubling (*dvitva*), that is like the original (*sthānivat*). (2) *Dvirvacana* is a specification of the domain; [the meaning is] "when that [doubling] is to be performed, it is as if the original were present, provided a vowel follows. (3) The word *dvirvacana* ends in the suffix *aṅ* (as in *arśa-ādi-gaṇa*) or is formed with the locative suffix *lyuṭ*.

And the mention of *aj* (vowel), qualified by being the cause of reduplication (*dvitva*), serves as an indicator for the substitute (*ādeśa*). This is the third [interpretation]: "That which is a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) when there is a vowel (*aci*) that is the cause of reduplication is like the original (*sthānivat*). The fourth [interpretation] is: the mention of *aj* in the aforementioned manner qualifies the state of being a substitute; thus: "A substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānivat*) when a vowel (*aci*) follows that is the cause of reduplication. In this case, the term *dvirvacana* (reduplication) is repeated. By the first [occurrence], the vowel (*aj*) is qualified; by the second, the state of being a substitute (*sthānibhāva*) is qualified; and by the latter [part of the rule], the scope (*viṣaya*) is specified.

The fifth [alternative] states: "When a doubling (*dvitva*) is to be performed, a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) is treated as the original (*sthānivat*), provided that a vowel which is the cause of the doubling follows. Here, the first [alternative] is not tenable. For there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a vowel-substitute made on the basis of a vowel lacking the status of being a cause of doubling would be treated as the original; this is because vowels are not specifically qualified as being the causes of doubling. Consequently, in the case of *acikīrtat*—where the suffix *ṇic* follows—the vowel-substitute *i*, which takes the place of *ṛ* by the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca," would also be treated as the original. Thus, when the root *kṝ* undergoes doubling by the rule "caṅi," and the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule "uraṇ raparaḥ," the result would be *acakīrtat*.

In *dudyūṣati*, having recourse to *ūṭh* and applying the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* to that which has undergone the substitution of *yaṇ*, there would result *didyūṣati* upon the doubling of the word *div*. In the case of *bubhavanīyiṣati*—derived from the desiderative (*san*) of the denominative (*kyac*) form *bhavanī* (meaning "desiring existence")—and subsequently the application of *lyuṭ*, there would result [the same] upon applying *sthānivadbhāva* to the two substitutions of *guṇa* and *av*.

The second [alternative] is not tenable; for the two defects, such as in *dudyūṣati*, would remain as they were. However, in *acikīrtat*, there is no defect because the short *i* (*itva*) is separated from the *t* by the letter *k*. For when an *ādeśa* (substitute) is subject to the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), at the time of prescribing its status as being like the original, it must exist as being like the original when an *ac* vowel immediately follows; for it is precisely when an *ac* follows that the application of that rule is accomplished.

In the case of *papau*, when the substitution of *au* for the *ṇal* suffix occurs according to the rule "āta au ṇalaḥ," the vowel *au* would not be considered a substitute by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original), because there is no longer any *aj* (vowel) following the substitute at that stage. Furthermore, in forms such as *jagmuḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) prescribed by the rule "gamahana—" would not occur because the operation would be separated [from the cause].

Nor is the third alternative tenable; for in the absence of a fixed temporal limit, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the original form persisting even after the doubling (*dvitva*) has taken place.
Nor is the fourth alternative valid; for the same defects would apply to cases such as *papau*, and moreover, there is no fixed determination of time.

The fifth [alternative] is not tenable, because [the rule for] *jagmuḥ* and so forth would be untenable; for, in relation to what is subject to elision (*lopapratiyogin*), there is no immediate posteriority (*avyavahitaparatva*) for *atus* and the rest. Therefore, the previously explained interpretation alone is correct. To explain: by qualifying the vowel (*ac*) as being the cause of reduplication (*dvirvacana-nimitta*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *acikīrtat*, since the *ṇic* suffix and the reduplication are the causes of the *ittva* (substitution of *i*) and the *caṅ* suffix [respectively]. Furthermore, because the substitute (*ādeśa*) is indicated [as the cause], there is no non-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *papau*, since the acquisition of the temporal determination through the re-mention of reduplication ensures that the state of the substitute persists after the reduplication has occurred.

Furthermore, the status of being a *sthānivadbhūta* (acting as the original), which is prescribed when an *ac* vowel follows as the cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*), would not apply in cases such as *cakratuḥ*. This is because, although the suffix *atus* is the cause of reduplication, the mere vowel *a* that constitutes a part of it lacks the status of being the cause. Nor can one argue that the rule must be formulated for its own sake (*ārambhasāmarthya*), because in examples such as *cakāra* and *cakre*, the causes of reduplication—the *yaṇ*-substitutes—are satisfied by residing in a single mora (*ekamātra*).

If, however, one were to supply the word *parasmin* (in the subsequent) and explain the qualification *tatrāci* as "when there is a rule regarding that which begins with a vowel (*ajādau*) in the subsequent [element]," and if it is assumed that in forms such as *cakre*, the status of beginning with a vowel (*ajāditva*) is established through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a designation as if it were the thing designated), even so, this does not provide a solution. For although the vowel-beginning [element] is the cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it is still the vowel itself (*ac*) that is the cause for the *yaṇ*-substitution.

In reality, according to the maxim "a technical rule applies to a positive injunction (vidhi), not to a restatement (anuvāda)," the application of the technical rule *yasmin vidhiḥ* is itself difficult to establish here; for the rule *aco 'ntyādi ṭi* is a restatement (*anuvāda*). In that context, since the substitute (*ādeśa*) is the object of the restatement, the term *aci* serves as its qualifier; consequently, the technical rule regarding the inclusion of what begins with that [term] (*tadādigrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*) does not apply. To this it is replied: the fact that reduplication is observed when a vowel (*ac*) follows is sufficient for the vowel to be the cause (*nimitta*) of the reduplication here. As they say:

"In this context, the status of being a cause consists merely in the fact that [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists. Thus, what is intended is simply the utility for duality, whether directly or by way of being a constituent of the aggregate.

As for the point that the suffix (*pratyaya*), implied by the term "reduplication" (*dvirvacana*), is qualified here by the word "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādī*); the word "in the presence of another" (*parasmin*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*). Just as when it is said, "Bring the one after Devadatta among these," a person of the same class who is immediately followed [by Devadatta] is brought, so too here, that which is immediately followed by another suffix is taken. Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is: when there is a suffix beginning with a vowel caused by reduplication, provided it is not separated by another suffix, any substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) is treated like the original (*sthānivat*).

By the force of the forthcoming *jñāpaka*, even though [the rule] applies when there is intervention by a *ṇic* suffix, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *didavanīyiṣati*, because of the intervention of multiple affixes. In *apīpyat*, however, the rule applies despite the intervention of phonemes (*varṇa*), because there is no other intervening affix. Furthermore, even when a *paribhāṣā* does not apply during a restatement (*anuvāda*), the intended meaning is established through the *paribhāṣā* concerning "that which is specifically mentioned" (*nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā*). For this very reason, the author of the *Nyāsa* states that the word "in the following" (*parasmin*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here.

This is precisely the intention even of Kaiyaṭa, who, by means of the repetition [of the word], asserts the implication of a suffix and the non-application of the indicator (jñāpaka) when there is an intervention by a suffix other than the causative marker (ṇic).

That is not correct; for the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "yasmin vidhiḥ" (P. 1.1.72) is difficult to establish here, and the meaning of that rule cannot be justified without its application. To explain: in the case of *amīṣām* ("of these"), since "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) serves as the delimiting property of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) in the context of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), the object of that [selection] is also understood to be humanity. Furthermore, because the word *para* signifies that which is immediately following, such a meaning is obtained.

And in the present case, there is no absence of intervention (avyavadhāna) relative to that which lacks a means of apprehending its status as a suffix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, for the sake of the form *ūrṇunaviṣati*, one must necessarily resort to the principle of "occurrence when [the cause] is present" (*tadbhāvabhāvitāmātra*). To illustrate: after the root *ūrṇu* with the desiderative suffix (*san*) and the augment *iṭ* have been applied by the rule "sanivant—" (*Pāṇ. 1.2.8*), resulting in *ūrṇu-is*, the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitution apply due to the absence of the marker *ṅit* by the rule "vibhāṣorṇoḥ" (*Pāṇ. 1.2.3*).

Regarding the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*: although the doubling (*dvitva*) is prescribed for a stem ending in *san*, because *san* is the cause of that doubling, the elements [of the root] undergo doubling by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to it. Consequently, when the syllable *nu* is doubled, the vowel *u* is heard in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). For in this case, if the augment *iṭ* were absent, the *san* would acquire the status of having a *kit* suffix according to the rule *iko jhal*, which would result in the absence of *guṇa*. Thus, the augment *iṭ*—by destroying the condition of the *san* being followed by a *jhal*-beginning suffix—is the cause of the *guṇa*; this is even more evident in the case of the *avādeśa* (the substitution of *ava*). However, the actual cause of the doubling is *san* itself, since no other qualifying factor is mentioned there.

And thus, even though [the substitute] has not entered into the limit of the cause (*nimitta*), its status as a cause is based solely on its existence therein; it is precisely by relying on this that the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth [of the substitute] possess the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

But in that case, *aririṣati* would not be possible. For when the suffix *san* is added to the root *ṛ*, after the augment *iṭ* has been applied by the rule *smipūṅrañjaśāṃ sani* and the subsequent *guṇa* substitution, the *is* sound (the result of *ṛ* + *iṭ*) would—by virtue of its being the cause of the *sthānivadbhāva*—be subject to reduplication according to the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya*. This would lead to the undesirable form *ariṣati*. If you argue that reduplication of the sequence *ris* is intended there, we say: not so. Because the sequence *is* is itself the object of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*), it cannot serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for reduplication; indeed, that which is the recipient of an operation is not taken as its own cause. This is known from the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the form *śayitari*.

Otherwise, because the root *śīṅ* is marked with the *ṅit* indicatory letter (*ṅ*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of *guṇa*. Nor should it be argued that, on this view, forms such as *ūrṇunaviṣati* would also not be possible; for although the rule for reduplication applies equally to a desiderative (*sannanta*) stem, it is impossible for the element *is* to serve as the cause of reduplication even there. This is because the prohibition of being a cause applies only to that which is endowed with a grammatical operation by means of the possessive suffix *ini*; and in the case of the root *ūrṇu*, since only the sound *nu* undergoes the operation [of reduplication], the *san* suffix itself is not superadded [as a cause].

However, in the case of *aririṣati*, there is a disparity because the syllable *ri* undergoes reduplication, whereas the suffix *san* is the cause of that reduplication. One might object: "If this is so, then even in forms such as *jeghrīyate* and *dedhmīyate*, since the elements *ghrīy* and *dhmīy* undergo reduplication, the suffix *yaṅ* would not be the cause of reduplication; thus, since there is no over-extension [of the rule] in those cases, how can the statements in the Bhāṣya, the Vṛtti, and other texts—which state that the word *ac* (a vowel) is mentioned in order to exclude them—be consistent? This is not a valid objection.

This is because, immediately following the statement in the *Prātiśākhya* that "the *anusvāra* and the consonant are limbs (*aṅga*) of the syllable," there is the rule: "Between vowels, the consonants belong to the subsequent [vowel]. Therefore, according to the intention of that [rule], in the aggregate form *ghrīya*, since the *yakāra* is a subsequent constituent part, the doubling applies only to *ghrī* and so forth.

However, if one follows the view of the *Bhāṣya* on the sixty-sixth *Vārttika*, adopting the principle that "the consonants [of the reduplicated syllable] are like those of a *naṭa*-wife," and thus assumes reduplication for what begins with a second *ekāc* (monophthongic) vowel, then the purpose of the mention of *aj* in the rule *adhijage* must be understood as a counter-example (*vyāvartya*). This is because the *Bhāṣya* states that, based on the dual-notation *gāṅ liṭi*, the substitution of *gāṅ* is prescribed specifically in the state of the suffix *la*.

If it is argued that this [substitution] is not even a purpose [of the rule], because according to the Vārttika school the words "liṭi" and so on are accepted as locatives of cause (*parasaptamī*), and thus although the substitute *gāṅ* has a subsequent cause, the Bhāṣyakāra accepts them as locatives of occasion (*viṣayasaptamī*);
then the example *jagle* and others [would serve as the purpose]. This is because the substitution of *ā* is prescribed when a suffix beginning with *ś* follows.

If, however, one adopts the method to be explained later—that the substitution of *ā* is non-causal (*anaimittika*) while there is a prohibition in the case of a *śit* suffix—then the word "aci" need not be mentioned at all.

Now, if it is argued that when *bhas* takes the suffix *kvas*, after the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) by the rule "ghasibhasor hali ca," the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment as the original) is necessary for that elision—regarding this, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others state: "In that case, whether *sthānivadbhāva* applies or not, there is no difference, because the form remains the same as *pṣvān*. Nor should it be said that when doubling occurs, there would be two *p*s; for the established conclusion is that 'in the Veda, one follows what is actually observed. Furthermore, the suffix *kvasu* is indeed rare in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), and the elision of the penultimate vowel is exclusively Vedic."

The term *aci* (before a vowel) is the very authority for the transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*). However, if it were a transfer of function (*kāryātideśa*), then only *ghrī*, *gā*, and *glā* would be subject to reduplication; in that case, the purpose of *aci*—which is to prohibit the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule—would be rendered redundant. But if the transfer of form is accepted, then when *ghrā*, *iṅ*, and *glai* undergo reduplication, the desired forms are not achieved. Therefore, the term *aci* is meaningful insofar as it serves to prevent the operation of *sthānivadbhāva* in those instances.
As it has been said: "The mention of *ac* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the transfer of form (*rūpasthānivadbhāva*)."

However, in the view that rejects the inclusion of the term *aj* (vowel), one must assume—on the basis of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the word *sthānivat*—that the word *sthānivat* in the rule *sthānivat* (P. 1.1.56), which has been determined to concern the extension of an operation (*kāryātideśa*), here functions as an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*) in accordance with the specific linguistic examples (*lakṣya*). Having carried over the genitive ending *acaḥ* from the preceding rule, the substitute (*ādeśa*) is to be qualified by it.

If it is asked, "Why is *aca* (a vowel) specified as a qualifier for the substitute? the answer is: not so. For if, in the case of *śuśāva*, the *samprasāraṇa* were also subject to *sthānivadbhāva*—just as the *vṛddhi* and *āv* substitutes are—the doubling of the root *śvi* would result in the undesired form *śiśāva*. Nor should one argue that because of the rule "the *samprasāraṇa* and the operation dependent upon it are stronger," the substitution occurs only at the stage of the suffix *la*, and thus there is no commonality of cause (*ekanimittakatva*) with the doubling; for in that case, the fault would be unavoidable in forms such as *vyatiśuśuvāte*.

Even if the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ* were to apply at the stage of the suffix *la*, there would still be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of its application in forms such as *ījāte* and *ījāthe*; for the status of being *kit* (which triggers the substitution) must apply immediately after the rule for the substitute has taken effect. Nor can it be argued that the rule for that [substitution] should also apply only at the stage of *la*, because it is superseded by the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitutes. Furthermore, due to the prohibition "there is no vowel-substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) when a vowel-substitution has already occurred," the vowel-substitution in *svāpeścaṅi* would be treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), resulting in the impossibility of the long *u* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in the form *aśūṣupat*.
However, when the condition "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*) is stated, the desired result is achieved through the doubling of *sup* itself.

By the statement "when reduplication is to be performed," it follows that only the form of the substitute remains thereafter; otherwise, there would be *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form). However, in cases such as *ninyatuḥ*, even though *iyaṅ* had applied previously, the *yaṇ* substitute—acting as an exception (*apavāda*) to it by the rule "eranekācaḥ"—occurs after reduplication. Alternatively, it should be understood that by the maxim "having first determined the scope of the exception, the general rule then applies," *iyaṅ* does not apply at all beforehand. Or else, because *iyaṅ* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being an *ābhīya* (intermediate) operation, *yaṇ* takes effect.

It might be argued as follows: Let us set aside the mention of *sthānivat* and, carrying forward the negative particle (*nañ*) from the rule *na padānta...*, let the prohibition of *ajādeśa* (substitution of vowels) be explained for the cases mentioned, since this is equally supported by the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, this is more parsimonious because it does not rely on the status of *sthānivat* as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), and it accords with its placement immediately following the rule *na padānta...*. Do not say so. For here too, the svarita accent of the letter *n* must be assumed, whereas that [svarita] is already established for the word *sthānivat*.

This is because it is necessary to assume a connection with the preceding rule for the purpose of carrying forward (*anuvṛtti*) the terms *ac* and *pada*, and because there is the further complication of assuming a connection with the rule "na padānta... [Pāṇini 1.1.58]. It might be argued as follows: If the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) were prescribed only for that substitute of an *ac* vowel which has been applied by depending on an *ac* vowel that is the cause of doubling, then in forms such as *cukṣāvayiṣati*, the doubling would not result in the hearing of the vowel *u* in the reduplicated syllable. This is because the substitution of *vṛddhi* (the vowel *au*) and other changes caused by the suffix *ṇi* would be impossible under that view, and consequently, only the vowel *a* would be expected to appear. The same applies to *uḍuḍāvayiṣati*. [In this case], from the root *uḍu-* (meaning "star"), one derives *uḍavati* (meaning "he acts like a star") via the denominative suffix *ṇic*; then, the desiderative suffix *san* is added to that.

If it is argued that in forms such as *caṅi auḍūḍavat*, *nunāvayiṣati*, *anūnavat*, *ūrṇunāvayiṣati*, *aurṇūnavat*, *pusphārayiṣati*, and *apusphurat*, the substitution of *ā* (by the rule *cisphurorṇau*) occurs [in the causative], then there is a Vārttika on this point:
"The statement regarding *oḥ puyaṇjiṣu* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇau*).

The meaning of this is as follows: By the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*, the substitution of *it* (i.e., *i*) is prescribed for the vowel *u* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) when followed by the letters of the *pa*-class, *yaṇ*, or *ja*, provided that a vowel (*avarṇa*) follows them.

In this regard, although in forms such as *pipaviṣate* and *yiyaviṣati*, the augment *iṭ* and the substitution of *guṇa* apply to the roots *pūṅ* and *yu* respectively before the suffix *san*—by virtue of the rules "smipūṅrañjaśām—" and "sanīvante"—and since the rule "dvirvacane'ci" applies when reduplication (*dvitva*) is to be performed, an *u*-sound can occur in the reduplicated syllable; thus, by prescribing *it* for that [u], the portions consisting of *p* and *y* are indeed meaningful. Nevertheless, the inclusion of the letters *ṇ*, *v*, and *j* in the *vargapratyāhāra* indicates that a substitute (*ādeśa*) applied before the causative suffix *ṇic* possesses the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivattva*).

Because it is not established that the *u*-vowel occurs in the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) when doubling [the root] only for those [roots] specifically characterized by the substitution [of *au* for *av*], and because the *it*-substitution (shortening) of the vowel *a* in the reduplication is established by the rule *sanyataḥ*; furthermore, apart from that, it is difficult to find instances of the *pa*-class consonants (*pavarga*), *yaṇ*, or *j* followed by an *a*-vowel; and because the augment *iṭ* is difficult to obtain for these [roots] in the desiderative (*san*). Examples include: *abībhavat*, *amīmavat*, *alīlavat*, *arīravat*, *bibhāvayiṣati*, and so forth.

And thus, since the substitution of an *aj*-vowel caused by *ṇic* is established as being *sthānivadbhāva* even when there is an intervention by *ṇic* from the vowel that is the cause of reduplication, forms such as *cukṣāvayiṣati* are free from objection. By the principle of "intervention by that which does not intervene" (*yenāvyavadhāna-nyāya*), it is accepted that the intervention of the vowel that is the cause of reduplication is only by *ṇic*, and not by suffixes such as *lyuṭ*, *kyac*, and so on—as in *ninavanīyiṣati*; therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For this very reason, they read the rule as: "That which is done in *ṇic* is *sthānivat*. But [one might object]: even if this were so, in *acikīrtat*, the quality of *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) made in *ṇic* would also have to be *sthānivat*.

Not so; for the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) applies only when a consonant (*hal*) follows a vowel other than *a* (*avarṇa*). Thus says the Bhāṣya: "This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding that which is of the same class. And what is of the same class? Those of the same nature as *pu*, *yaṇ*, *ja*, and *ya*. And of what nature are these? They follow a vowel other than *a*. However, the author of the Vārttika rejected this rule. For it is stated at the end of the section on doubling (*dvitva*) in the sixth book:

"Doubling takes precedence by way of prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over the substitutions of *yaṇ*, *āy*, *āv*, and *āva*, as well as elision (*lopa*), the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*), the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*), and the substitution of *u* in the case of *kikin*."

The meaning of this is as follows: in examples such as *dadhyatra*, the *yaṇ* substitution has scope; in *cayanaṃ*, *cāyakaḥ*, *lavanaṃ*, *lāvakaḥ*, and so forth, there are the four rules beginning with the *āy* replacement; in *godaḥ*, *kambaladaḥ*, and so forth, there is the elision of *ā*; in *śleṣmaghnaḥ* and so forth, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*); in *kāraṇā*, *hāraṇā*, and so forth, there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix; and in *nipūrtāḥ* and so forth, there is the change to *u*. The rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100), which prescribes the change to *it* in *kirati* and so forth, is also implied by this [general principle]. By means of this, forms such as *taturiḥ* will also be successfully established.

However, the rule for *dvitva* (doubling) finds its scope in cases such as *bibhidatuḥ*. Thus, when there is a conflict between both [rules], *dvitva* prevails over them due to the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the priority of the preceding rule). By this, forms such as *cakratuḥ*, *vivāya*, *lulāva*, *vivayitha*, *lulavitha*, *papatuḥ*, *jaghnuḥ*, *jagmatuḥ*, *āṭiṭat*, and *taturiḥ* are established. Nor should it be argued that, because *iyaṅ* is not mentioned here, *ninyatuḥ* would not be formed; [for it is established by other means].

Because it has been stated that, according to the maxim *prakalpya ca*, the substitution *iyaṅ* does not apply first after considering the future occurrence of *yaṇ*, this statement need not have been commenced. However, the authors of the Bhāṣya say:

"This conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is improper; since the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) and so forth are obligatory (*nitya*), while reduplication (*dvitva*) is non-obligatory (*anitya*), they do not possess equal strength. Furthermore, if this were a new conflict based on a specific rule (*vācanika*), that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Moreover, if by a specific rule there were an annulment even of internal operations (*antaraṅga*) just as there is for obligatory ones, then in forms such as *ninavanīyiṣati*, the vowel *u* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable."

Now, if the stated rule were a restrictive injunction (*vāraka*) applying only to *nitya* operations and not even to *antaraṅga* ones, then in forms such as *cukṣāvayiṣati*, since the *vṛddhi* and other operations would be *antaraṅga*, they would apply first; subsequently, after reduplication and the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsahrasva*), the substitution of *i* by the rule *sanyataḥ* would result in the hearing of the vowel *i*. Consequently, to prevent that, one would have to postulate a subsequent rule—following *utparasyātaḥ* and *ti ca*—namely, *odaudādeśasya cuṭutuśarādeḥ*, with the word *abhyāsasya* understood from the previous context.

The meaning of this is as follows: in that stem (*aṅga*) where *au* is substituted for *ā*, there is an *abhyāsa* (reduplicated syllable) beginning with *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, *śa*, or *ra*; of the vowel *a* belonging to that *abhyāsa*, *ut* shall be substituted. Thus: *cukṣāvayiṣati*, *uḍuḍāvayiṣati*, *nunāvayiṣati*, *ūrṇunāvayiṣati*, *śuśāvayiṣati*, *pusphārayiṣati*. Although in the last case, after the rule "the *khay* [consonants] preceded by *śar*" has applied and the *pa* remains, the status of being *śar-ādi* no longer exists, nevertheless, it should be understood that this status existed at the time the designation *abhyāsa* was first applied.

What is the purpose of the condition "of that which has *o* as its substitute"? [Consider: *cāyṛ* in the sense of "worship": *cicāyayiṣati*; *khada* in the sense of "firmness": *cikhādayiṣati*. What is the purpose of the condition "beginning with *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, or *śa*"? [Consider: *bibhāvayiṣati*. Why [is there] the condition "from *at*" (*ataḥ*)? [Consider: *ṛju*, *ṛṇa*, *ṛtu*, *aṃśu*, or *vā*; having narrated these, one says: *ārjijat*, *ārṇiṇat*, *ārtitat*, *āṃśiśat*. Here, because the rule for *vṛddhi* is subsequent, once *ṭilopa* has occurred, let there not be reduplication of the *saṇic* (the suffix *san* with *ṇi*). If the word "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) were not stated, then the phrase "beginning with *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, or *śa*" would qualify either the *aṅga* (the stem) or the *at* (the vowel).

And likewise, in the case of *śītalūḥ* (the sun) from *śītaṃ lunāti*, one wishes to express this as *śiśītalayiṣati*; here, the substitution of *u* for the vowel following the letter *t* would occur. Therefore, both rules must be recited by the author of the Vārttika. The same applies to the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*: it is intended so that the substitution of *i* occurs in forms such as *pipaviṣate*, *yiyaviṣati*, and *jijāvayiṣati*.

In the case of the roots *pū* and *yu* with the suffix *san*, since the augment *iṭ* follows, the substitution of *guṇa* would apply by virtue of its higher status; however, according to that [author's] view, reduplication occurs prior to the substitution of *av* by means of a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior counter-exception). The root *judh* mentioned in the rule *jucaṅkramya-* is a Vedic (*sautra*) root. From that, the desiderative suffix *san* is added after the causative (*ṇic*). In that context, although the substitution of *u* [for the penultimate vowel] would be required by the rule *cuṭutuśarādeḥ*, the substitution of *i* must be stated in order to set aside that [substitution of *u*]. Nor should it be argued that in the rule *cuṭutuśarādeḥ*, one should simply read the letter *ca* in place of the word *cu*; for if that were so, there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in this case.

Regarding the sounds *guṅ* and *ghuṅ*: because [the rules] would not apply in the case of the causative (*ṇic*) with the reduplication (*caṅ*), nor in the case of the desiderative (*san*), forms such as *ajūgavat*, *ajūghavat*, *jugāvayiṣati*, and *jughāvayiṣati* would be unestablished. Likewise, in the case of *didavanīyiṣati*, another rule must be initiated to prevent the substitution of *ut* (for *ava*), since it begins with the *tavarga* class.

Alternatively, one may interpret the rule by carrying over the mention of *san* from the rule *sanyataḥ* via the "frog-leap" method (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and explain that the substitution of *ut* does not occur when there is an intervention by something other than the causative suffix (*ṇic*), according to the principle of non-intervention (*yenanāvyavadhāna*).

[Objection: Even so, if the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of causation (*hetumaṇṇic*) to the root *tan*, which has the *kvip* suffix in the sense of habitual action (*ācārakvibanta*), then whether or not [the *ṇic*] is present, the substitution of *ut* would occur in forms such as *titanāvayiṣati* and *titanaviṣati*.

[Reply: Not so. The meaning of the Vārttika is that the substitution of *ut* applies to that vowel *a* which is either a constituent part (*avayava*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), or—wherever possible—a constituent part or a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the initial *o* or *au* of the original root. In *cukṣāvayiṣati*, it is a constituent part; in *pusphārayiṣati*, it is a substitute. However, in *titanāvayiṣati*, since neither of these two conditions applies, there is no fault. And thus, the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70) is also rendered meaningful.

Otherwise, in forms such as *āṭiṭat* (from *ā-ṭi-ṇic-aṅ-luṅ*), where there is a *caṅ* following a *ṇi*-affix, the rule prescribing *sanvadbhāva* would apply because the light syllable belongs to a portion of that which is the *aṅga*. Consequently, since this would lead to the undesired application (*prasaṅga*) even in cases like *ārjijat*, that [Vārttika] would be rendered useless. Thus, according to the Vārttika view, there is great complexity compared to the [Pāṇinian] Sūtra. One might argue: let both the present Sūtra and the Vārttika be omitted; let "oḥ puyaṇjyapare" alone serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). This indicates that reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs, overriding both what is *antaraṅga* and what is *nitya*. Subsequently, after reduplication, the application of *yaṇ*-substitution and other operations proceeds as far as possible.

On this point, Kaiyaṭa says: "Is the indicator (jñāpaka) based on a general rule or based on a specific one? Not the first, because in forms such as *acikīrtat*, if reduplication were to apply first—overriding the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel—one would end up hearing the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable. Nor the second, because forms such as *cakratuḥ* would remain unestablished. Therefore, the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.1] is necessary. Furthermore, regarding its scope, one must rely on an indicator according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya in order to achieve the desired results; such is the direction."

Regarding this, Upadeva established the following in his *Kāvyakāmadhenu*: some accept the form *āñcakad* on the grounds that, when the suffix *caṅ* is applied to the root *aṅk*, the elision of the *a* (following the rule for the substitution of *ṇic*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), resulting in the reduplication of the syllable *ka*. However, this contradicts the three great sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali). To explain: does the status of being a *sthānivat* follow from the rule "when a vowel follows, there is reduplication" (*dvirvacane'ci*), or by means of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*)? It cannot be the first, because the suffix *ṇic* is not the cause of the reduplication.

This is because it is stated in both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika that the status of an *ādeśa* beginning with a vowel as being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies only to that which has already been performed by relying on a non-vowel (*ac*) that serves as the cause for doubling (*dvitva*), due to the repetition of the word. It is not the latter [view], because it has been established in the Bhāṣya itself—by relying on the fact that an indicator (*jñāpaka*) pertains only to its own class—that the status of being "as if the original" occurs only when a consonant (*hal*) follows a vowel (*avarṇa*). This is obtained precisely from the authority of the Bhāṣya which refutes the Vārttika concerning the "prior contradiction" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

If the vowel *a* were indeed intended by the Bhāṣya in examples such as *āñcakāt*, then the author of the Vārttika would have had to formulate a separate effort for that purpose as well, which would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Since such an effort is absent, it is understood that the vowel *i* alone is what the Bhāṣya intends in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); thus, the status of the elision (*allopa*) as being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is not intended. Therefore, it is established that only the substitution of *u* is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, because it is only there—specifically in the case of a consonant followed by a vowel—that [the condition] following the reduplicated syllable with a subsequent *a*-vowel can possibly occur.

As for what is stated in the *Kāśikā* under the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*: having cited *aujaḍhat* as an example from the word *ūḍha* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the reduplication suffix (*caṅ*), it is further stated that for a form ending in *ktin*, the form is *aujiḍhat*. The author of the *Nyāsa* explained this by stating that the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) applied in the causative stage (*ṇau*) is treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). Furthermore, the author of the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa* formulated the rule as *ṇicyanit*. All of this is without foundation, as it contradicts the *Mahābhāṣya*.

In this very manner, it has been demonstrated by Durgagupta in his *Durgavṛtti*, by Trilocanadāsa in his *Kātantrapañjikā*, by Vardhamānamisra in his *Kātantravistara*, and by Hemasūri in his *Haimavyākaraṇa*. Furthermore, it has been shown that this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) to be understood as follows: the vowel *a* (avarṇa) alone [is substituted] when followed by the suffix *apavarga* (the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*). And Abhinavaśākaṭāyana, in his *Śabdānuśāsana*, has demonstrated that even when caused by the suffix *ṇi*, the doubling occurs before the vowel *a* (avarṇa), provided that [the *ṇi*] is followed by such a vowel.
Therefore, *āñcikat* and *aujiḍhat* are indeed more correct. Likewise, Nandikeśvara, Kṣīrasvāmī, and others have illustrated this in their *Dhātupārāyaṇas*:
"The forms *śuṣkikā*, *śuṣkajaṅghā*, *kṣāmimān*, and likewise *aujiḍhat*.

Furthermore, in the *Vaiyāghrapadyavārttika*, the reading with the vowel *i* (*aujiḍhat*) alone is the traditional one. However, Vedic scholars (*śrotriyas*) read *ja* in place of *ji* due to negligence. This has also been stated quite clearly by Kṣemendra in his *Jainendranyāsa*. Moreover, the *Vaiyāghrapadyavārttika* is intended to state the purpose of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*.

For instance, in the word *śuṣkikā*, the optional substitution of *i* for *ā* prescribed by the rule "udīcām ātaḥ sthāne yakapūrvāyāḥ" does not apply; because the substitution of *k* for the root *śuṣ* (as in *śuṣka*) is considered *asiddha*, the letter *k* is not preceded by the vowel *ā*. Similarly, in the word *śuṣkajaṅghā*, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "na kopadhāyāḥ" does not take effect.

In the word *kṣāmimān*, the substitution of *v* [for *m*] does not occur by the rule *mādupadhāyāśca*, because the substitution of *m* [for *y*] by the rule *kṣāyo maḥ* is considered *asiddha* (not yet established); consequently, the *m* is not in the penultimate position (*anupadhā*). In the word *aujiḍhat*, because the substitution of *ḍh* [for *j*] is *asiddha*, there is reduplication of the sequence *hti*.
Regarding this, they say:
"The elephant of the quarter Vāmana has been seized by the great crocodile Vopadeva."
By the very occasion of Kīrti’s fame, he was liberated by Mādhava.

To explain: is there a contradiction with the Bhāṣya, which is intent upon refuting the Vārttika regarding Vāmana’s statement, or is there a contradiction with the Bhāṣya, which describes the indicator (jñāpaka) as having a scope restricted to its own class? It is not the first.

Since the two objections—"the impossibility of the contradiction between the permanent and the impermanent," and "the non-establishment of forms such as *didavanīyiṣati*"—are not explicitly stated in the Bhāṣya, it is established that the Bhāṣya is intended as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of other objections. Consequently, since another objection must also be addressed following the Vārttika—namely, that in the case of the reduplication in *aujaḍhat*, the short vowel *a* would have to be specifically prescribed in order to ensure its hearing—the Vārttika should be formulated as follows: "*[The substitution of] u, o, or au for [the radical vowel] occurs when the reduplicated syllable begins with c, ṭ, t, or ś, provided there is the augment utsN.*" Then, "[This applies] even when the root has the elision of *a* (allop) due to the causative suffix (*ṇic*).*" Thus, the Vārttika should be composed in this manner.

The augment *at* would apply to the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsa*) of a root ending in *al* (a vowel) when followed by *ṇic*, as in *aujaḍhat* and *āñcakat*. It is not the second alternative [of the objection]. The established meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is that where there is reduplication, the first vowel of the subsequent portion of the reduplicated stem is treated as if it were the original (*sthānivat*). And in the case of the reduplication of the word *ha*, during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), there exists a vowel (*avarṇa*) in the subsequent portion. Nor should it be argued that because it is subsequently removed by the elision of the suffix *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*), it does not participate in the actual usage (*prayoga-samavāya*); for such participation in usage is not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*.

And thus, in cases such as *nunāvayiṣati*, although there is no *a*-vowel at the time the doubling (*dvitva*) occurs, the substitution (*sthānivadbhāva*) takes place by relying on that vowel which appears later; likewise, even though the word *hata* lacks it later on. To explain: is the state of being followed by an *a*-vowel intended at the time the doubling occurs, or in the final, completed form? Not the first, because it is absent in forms such as *cukṣāvayiṣati*. Nor the second, because it is absent in forms such as *āñcakat*.

Therefore, one must necessarily accept that this [rule] applies only during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). By this, the works composed by Vopadeva are also explained, because in his system the intention is to have the status of being followed by an *a*-vowel (*avarṇa-paratva*) intended only during the stage of derivation; furthermore, there is no contradiction with what Vāmana stated. However, in the case of *adyajīgapat*, when the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) applies, the suffix *ṇic* itself undergoes reduplication because it begins with *a* (*ajādi*); thus, since the condition of being followed by an *a*-vowel is absent in both instances, *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply, as it does not in forms such as *acikīrtat*. This being the case, the stubborn insistence that the *sthānivadbhāva* applies only to a substitute in place of an *u*-vowel is entirely baseless.

For this very reason, the commentary on the rule *lopaḥ pibaterīccābhyāsasya*—which states that in the form *apīpyat*, after the causative suffix *ṇic* has been added to the root *pibati*, followed by *yuk*, and then the *caṅ* suffix, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), and because of the status of that [elided portion] as *sthānivadbhāva*, the reduplication applies to the word *pāy-*—is consistent.

Here, however, it must be said: the intention of the Bhāṣya is that an substitute (*ādeśa*) is *sthānivat* only where there exists a consonant (*hal*) followed by a vowel (*avarṇa*) at the time the *sthānivadbhāva* operates; it is not as you have stated, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and lacks any authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).

By this, the objection that the commencement of the rule *allopo 'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134) is intended as a refutation of the Bhāṣya—on the grounds that the Bhāṣya is merely an illustration of a refutation—is also rejected. This is because there is no evidence that the Vārttika, which functions as a statement of a formal contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) between two explicit rules, intends the Bhāṣya to be a mere illustration of a refutation. Furthermore, the objection that a contradiction between what is permanent (*nitya*) and what is non-permanent (*anitya*) is untenable, pertains solely to the domain of well-known contradictions.

As for the argument that the Bhāṣya’s concern regarding the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the form *acikīrtat*—if the substitute *u* were treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*)—would be inconsistent [with the view that the Bhāṣya is a refutation], [that too is rejected].

That is hollow. For that [rule] operates precisely at the stage of understanding the literal meaning of the rule "that which is substituted for a *ṇi*-affix becomes like the original" (*sthānivadbhavati*). Otherwise, if one were to state that the objection is irrelevant because it contradicts the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it would follow that all objections whatsoever would be abolished. Furthermore, the irrelevance of that objection is unavoidable even for you who maintain that the condition of being followed by an *a*-vowel applies to either [the original or the substitute] in one case or the other; this is because, in that instance, there is an absence of being followed by an *a*-vowel even during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*).
By this, the claim that "being present in actual usage" (*prayogasamavāyitva*) is not a qualification mentioned in the Bhāṣya is refuted.

Even in cases such as *ūrṇunāvayiṣati*, at the stage when the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule is to take effect, the *avarṇa* is subsequent to the consonant (*hal*). This is also supported by the statement in the Bhāṣya: "Of what nature are these [instances] where an *avarṇa* follows?"

And this is logical. For the prescription of the substitution of *i* for the vowel *u* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), which is enjoined when a labial (*pavarga*), a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*), or the letter *j* follows an *a*-vowel (*avarṇa*), indeed makes known the existence of the status of being as if occupying the original position (*sthānivadbhāva*); this is established by both [the author of the *Vārttika* and the author of the *Bhāṣya*]. Furthermore, at the time when the application of the status of being as if occupying the original position occurs here, the labials and the others are indeed followed by an *a*-vowel; thus, the stated meaning is obtained. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states: "It is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for that which belongs to the same class."

Since, by implication, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the place of the original) applies to that which is of the same class [as the original], it is explicitly stated at the time of its application that there is a following *a*-vowel; therefore, there is no evidence for the view that—setting aside the *sthānivadbhāva* which presents itself first—the meaning intended is that "the first vowel of the second half of the reduplicated stem is the initial *a*-vowel. Consequently, even the proposal of the rule "there is *at* [substitution] for a *ṇic* that possesses *al*-elision" is cast far away.

Because the existence of the vowel *a* in the *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is not established by any authoritative means (*pramāṇa*), an undertaking of a rule for that purpose would be fruitless; furthermore, during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), the condition "having an *a*-vowel as its subsequent element" is not accepted in the *Nyāsa* and other such works.

For this very reason, regarding the rule *stautiṇyoḥ*, the author of the Nyāsa stated that in the form *siṣecayiṣati*—where *sic* is followed by the causal *ṇic*, then *guṇa*, then the desiderative suffix *san*, and then *iṭ*, after which *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa* have been applied—the doubling of the word *sic* occurs because the *guṇa* is treated as *sthānivat*. However, since there is no vowel *a* in the latter portion [of the reduplicated stem], it is impossible to explain the passage from that work (*Nyāsa*) concerning *aujaḍhat* according to the method you have proposed.

By this, the view that the *Nyāsa*’s statement "there is doubling of the *sic*" should be disregarded due to its contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* is refuted. For even in the case of *aujaḍhat*, since the status of the *al-lopa* as *sthānivat* is contrary to the *Bhāṣya*, [the author of the *Nyāsa*] himself, while in the process of analysis (*prakriyā-daśā*), had to assume the intention was to have a vowel (*avarṇa*) following [the *ḍh*], and thus [the rule] could not be applied as stated. Precisely for this reason, after stating a general indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the sake of establishing forms such as *aujaḍhat*, Sīradeva accepted its non-eternality (*anityatva*) in accordance with forms such as *acikīrtat*.
Therefore, the intention of Vāmana, the author of the *Pariśiṣṭapradīpa*, and others is simply that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon a general rule (*sāmānya*), and not as you have stated.
However, because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*—which states that "the indicator depends upon a specific rule (*viśeṣa*)"—their view is unacceptable; this is the secret [of the matter].

For this very reason, the reading of the vowel *i* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) as in *auṇinat* is consistent with the *Mādhavīyadhātuvṛtti* regarding the root *ūn* among the roots ending in *-ad*, as well as with the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī* on the rule "not in *nayati* and *dhvanati*."

By this, the claim that all of that is merely due to a scribal error—on the grounds that it contradicts the *Vāmana-mādhava* treatise found in another location—is also refuted. This is because the reading with the vowel *i* (ikāra), which accords with the meaning accepted by the *Bhāṣya*, must necessarily be the intended subject of Vāmana and others; thus, the situation is quite the opposite. If it is objected: "In that case, the fact that [the root] ends in the vowel *a* would be useless," we say no. For, by virtue of that [ending in *a*], when *vṛddhi* occurs, forms such as *ahkāpayati* and *āñcīkapat* are admitted.

If, however, one insists that here too [the rule] must be exactly like the established fact that in forms such as *citi* (from *cit*), the presence of the causative marker *ṇic* indicates an optionality of the augment *iṭ*, even then there is no harm. For in the alternative where *ṇic* is absent, the suffix *ām* applies because the root has more than two syllables (*anekāc*); furthermore, its meaningfulness is maintained by the fact that in forms such as *aṅkyāt*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*)—which would otherwise occur by the rule "aniditām"—does not take effect.

As for the claim that the final vowel *a* is meaningful for the purpose of hearing the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), that is questionable, since it has been established that the vowel *i* alone occurs there.

Now, if it is argued that even according to the view of all [grammarians], the hearing of the sound *ja* is untenable during reduplication because, by the rule "that which is not established in the preceding is not [treated as] established for reduplication," the sound *ḍha* alone is established—this is not so. Since that rule is non-eternal (*anitya*), its application occurs only in the case of the word *hrati*; let this matter rest without further elaboration.
Thus ends the eighth lesson in the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
"Non-appearance is elision" (1.1.60).

The non-appearance (*adarśana*) of that which is applicable [in its place] shall be designated as *lopa* (elision). This is because the term "in place of" (*sthāne*) is understood by way of anuvṛtti. It should not be argued that this designation (*saṃjñā*) applies only to the word *adarśana* itself, such that in rules like "lopo vyoḥ," that very word would result as the substitute (*ādeśa*). This is because, by the force of the designation being a *mahāsaṃjñā* (a major technical term), the thing to be designated (*saṃjñin*) is the meaning itself. Nor should it be argued that the meaning of the word *lopa* as used in common parlance will be understood directly from the specific rules (*pradeśasūtras*), just as in cases such as "animal" (*paśu*) or "offspring" (*apatya*), and therefore the rule establishing the designation (*saṃjñāsūtra*) need not be commenced. This is because [the designation is required to ensure the correct application of the term across various contexts].

The phrase "of that which is applicable" (*prasaktasya*) is employed in order to obtain a specific counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); otherwise, in cases such as *dadhi* and *madhu*, since the suffix *kvip* would naturally not be observed [after the elision], its designation as "elision" (*lopa*) would trigger the application of the rule for "suffix-characteristics" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), resulting in the insertion of the augment *tuk*. Accordingly, the Vārttika states:
"But [the desired result] is established because the non-observation of that which was applicable is designated as 'elision'."

[Objection: "Granted that this may be so according to the view of the *Vārttika*, since that rule is intended as an injunction (*vidhi*); however, according to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, it will be stated that the application of grammatical operations occurs by means of the rule *sthānivat* itself for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Furthermore, there is no possibility of the *tuk* augment applying here by that [rule], because the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is continued [from the previous rule] there. For this very reason, in cases such as *grāmaṇīḥ*, although *kvip* is prescribed when *aṇ* would otherwise apply—both on account of the meaning and the proximity of the root with its object—the *vṛddhi* substitute and other such changes do not occur. Therefore, if you say that this rule is purposeless (*nirarthaka*)," [Response: This is not so. For the *Bhāṣya* intends this to be a restrictive rule (*niyama*), and it is precisely for the sake of that restriction that the *sthānivat* rule is applied. Moreover, the *tuk* augment is not applicable here because the genitive case is continued from the previous rule. Consequently, in *grāmaṇīḥ* and similar forms, even though *kvip* is prescribed when *aṇ* would otherwise apply due to the presence of the meaning and the root along with its object, *vṛddhi* and the like do not take place. Thus, this rule is not purposeless.

Not so; for in the two rules—"The restriction is that there is indeed an elision of *ca*, *ha*, etc. (*cāhalopa eva*) and "Optionally [the first word is unaccented] when *ca* and others are elided" (*cādilope vibhāṣā*)—the term "elision" (*lopa*) refers precisely to the non-employment of *ca* and the rest. Since there is no rule prescribing elision by means of a genitive reference (which would be required for the technical designation *lopa*), the designation *lopa* is untenable. Consequently, the prohibition of the accentuation of finite verbs (*tiṅanta-nighāta*) in cases such as "Let this one go to the forest" (*ayamevāraṇyaṃ gacchatu*) and "Let this one go to the village" (*ayameva grāmaṃ gacchatu*), as well as the optionality of the prohibition of accentuation in cases such as "The rice-grains are white" (*śuklā vrīhayo bhavanti*) and "They milk the white cows for clarified butter" (*śvetā gā ājyā duhanti*), would both be untenable.
However, at the commencement of the Sūtra, there is no fault, because that [application] does not arise there either from the perspective of the treatise (*śāstra*) or from common usage (*loka*).

Nor should it be argued that, according to the view of the *Vārttika*, there would be *vṛddhi* in the word *grāmaṇīḥ*; for the possibility of the suffix *aṇ* is removed by *kvip*. This is because a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) operates only where a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) does not apply. In the domain of *kvip* prescribed by the rule "satsūdviṣa... (Pāṇini 3.2.61), there is simply no possibility for the application of "karmaṇyaṇ" (Pāṇini 3.2.1).
[The rule regarding elision is: "The suffixes *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* [are applied]. (Pāṇini 1.1.60).

These technical terms (*saṃjñā*) apply to those [suffixes] that have been designated as such through the method of *tantrāvṛtti* (repetition of the rule) and so forth, due to the capacity of the formulation of multiple terms. The non-appearance of a suffix effected by these words—*luk*, *ślu*, and *lup*—shall respectively bear those names. It should not be argued that, in this way, there would arise a mutual dependency (*itaretarāśraya*) in the sections prescribing rules, because even though the non-appearance is eternal, the designation of it as *luk* and so forth is brought about by the application of the term; thus, the previous objection regarding its impossibility is avoided. This is because the terms are understood as "prospective designations" (*bhāvisaṃjñā*).

And the specific rules include "luk taddhite," "juhotyādibhyaḥ śluḥ," "janapade lup," and so forth. Nor does the designation *lopa* (elision) undergo sublation by these [specific rules], because of the governing rule regarding the non-coexistence of designations (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*). This is because elsewhere we observe the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of designations. For this very reason, the prohibition "na lumatāṅgasya" is logically consistent; otherwise, since the rule "pratyayalope" would have no scope of application in cases involving *luk* and other such elisions, that prohibition would be meaningless.

This might be asked: for what purpose is the word *pratyayasya* ("of the suffix") used? It cannot be for the sake of excluding non-suffixes (*apratyaya*), because in all rules prescribing elision (*luk*) and so forth, it is only the suffix that possesses the status of being a *sthānin* (original element), and thus [non-suffixes] are not established as such. Furthermore, in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), only that which has already undergone such a transformation is understood.

But surely, in the rule *luk taddhitaluki*, since the term *gostriyoḥ* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of elision (*luk*) for the word *go* as well. This is because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). First, [the rule] is *gor upasarjanasya*; then, *striyāḥ*. In the rule *luk taddhitaluki*, the term *striyāḥ* is understood, while *goḥ* is excluded. Otherwise, even if the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) were made, there would be elision of the suffix *ḍoṣ* after the root *gam*.

In the rule *kaṃsīyaparaśavyayoḥ*, a *luk* elision is also prescribed for what follows the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*. Since the governing rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* is in force, this elision applies to the suffix following the stem; therefore, there is no elision of the radical portion (*prakṛti*). Otherwise, in the derivations *kaṃsaḥ* (from *kam-isa*) and *paraśuḥ* (from *parān śṛṇāti*), there would result the undesired elision of the phonemes *u* and *s*. Nor can it be argued that [the mention of the stems] is for the purpose of specifying the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) in rules such as *atribhṛgukutsa...*, because in those cases, the word *gotra* is understood by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *yaskādibhyo gotre*, and thus the elision is prescribed for that suffix which is ordained after the *gotra* [descendants] of Atri and others.

In the rule *janapade lup*, because of the governing context of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) and the recurrence of the term *pratyaya* (suffix), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix belonging to the fourfold sense (*cāturarthika*) prescribed for a country (*janapada*).

In the rule *lavaṇālluk* as well, it is only the suffix *ṭhak* that is elided, because it is the one under discussion; furthermore, by the principle *tasmādityuttarasya*, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is interpreted as having a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) sense, thereby referring to the suffix itself.

Now, one might object: in rules such as *yañañośca* and *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, since the affix that is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the elision (*lopa*) consists of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the rule *alo'ntyasya* would apply; and in rules such as *lavaṇālluk*, the rule *ādeḥ parasya* would apply. Thus, to ensure that the elision applies to the whole (as a universal substitute) rather than merely to the initial portion, the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) is included [in the definition of a substitute].

Not so. Even though elision (*lopa*) is the subject under discussion, the statement of elision in the rule *lugvā duha* (Pāṇini 6.4.90) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on general considerations, thereby establishing that all [substitutes] marked by *lu*, *mu*, or *nu* are replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Nor should it be argued that elision alone is the replacement for the whole, while *luk* and the others would instead follow the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) and thus replace only the final letter; for since elision is established as replacing the final letter due to its lack of conflict with other rules at the time of application, it is precisely *luk* and the others that are conceived as replacements for the whole.

Not so. In the rule *āgastyakauṇḍinyayoragastikuṇḍinac*, does the mention of *luk* from the preceding rule *lugaṇiñoḥ* carry over or not? It cannot be the first case. For there are two substituends (*sthānin*), while there are three substitutes (the two *agasti-* and *kuṇḍina-* suffixes along with *luk*). Since there would be a lack of correspondence in number (*yathāsaṃkhyaviraha*), it would follow that each single substituend would take all three substitutes. Consequently, the descendants of Agastya would be called *kuṇḍinas*, and the descendants of Kuṇḍina would be called *āgastayas*. Furthermore, because *luk* is a technical indicator (*jñāpaka*), it would be a total elision (*sarvādeśa*); thus, in both cases, only the case-ending (*vibhakti*) would be heard. Nor can it be the second case [that the mention of *luk* does not carry over].

Even though the present topic (*prakṛti*) has already been established, if one intends to apply a *prāgdīvyatīya* suffix beginning with a vowel (such as *añ*), as in "the pupils of the Agastis" (*āgastīyāḥ*), the substitution of *agasti-* would occur because there is no prohibition; consequently, since the base would not be *vṛddha*, the suffix *cha* would be inapplicable. However, when the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is included [in the rule], the portions of the suffixes in *āgastya-* and *kauṇḍinya-* undergo elision (*luk*), and the remaining parts are respectively replaced by *agasti-* and *kuṇḍina-*, thereby correctly deriving both *āgastayaḥ* and *kauṇḍināḥ*.

However, when the *prāgdīvyatīya* (relating to what comes before *divya*) sense is intended, the prohibition of elision (*luk*) by the rule *gotre ’lug acī* prevents the elision; consequently, the substitution of *agasti-* [for *agastya-*, which is taught in grammatical conjunction with that elision] is also withdrawn. Since *āgastya-* is then a *vṛddha* [stem], the suffix *cha* applies, and by the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastya-*, there is the elision of *ya*. Thus, the form *āgastīyāḥ* is established. As for *kauṇḍinya-*, there is no difference between the two cases, as will be explained in that very place. Therefore, since the word *luk* must necessarily be supplied there [from the previous rule], the mention of *pratyaya* (suffix) here is indispensable in order to avoid the aforementioned fault.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, states that the mention of the second [word, *pratyaya*] in the rule *pratyayalope* is for the sake of providing a qualification, while its inclusion for a second time is for the sake of subsequent rules. Consequently, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) occurs only when the entire suffix is elided, and not when only a portion of it is elided. Otherwise, in forms such as *āghnīya* and *saṃrāyaspoṣeṇa mīya*, because the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) would apply later, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) would occur again due to the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*). Haradatta, on the other hand, says that this [second mention] is also for the purpose of making the elision a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), since a general indication is a resort only when no other way is possible; such is the direction of the argument. *Pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (P. 1.1.62).

Even when an affix (*pratyaya*) has been elided, the grammatical operation conditioned by it should still take place. Therefore, in the form *atṛṇeṭ*, although the *tip* affix is elided, the augment *im* is applied by taking as its condition the *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*), according to the rule "tṛṇaha im. Nor is this point already covered by the rule "sthānivat" (the substitute is like the original). This is because even when an elided element is treated as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the prohibition "not in the case of a rule concerning an *al*" (*analvidhau*) is not accepted to apply here.

However, this is not the scope of the rule "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* when there is recourse to a phoneme" (*varṇāśraye pratyayalakṣaṇaṃ nāsti*), because that rule operates solely when the phoneme is predominant. For instance, regarding the present sūtra, one might simply say "when a suffix is elided, there is the characteristic of that [suffix]" (*pratyayalope tallakṣaṇam*); or rather, the second part [of the sūtra] need not exist at all, since the result is established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *sthānivat*.
