And by virtue of that capacity for taking up [the suffix], only that effect for which the property residing solely in the suffix serves as the delimiting condition of the cause (nimittatāvacchedaka) occurs when there is elision of the suffix; however, in cases such as *gohitam* ("beneficial to a cow"), the substitution of *ava* does not take place, because the property of being a vowel (*actva*), which serves as the delimiting condition of the cause there, is common to both suffixes and non-suffixes.

Even if there were a prohibition here by the rule *na lumatā*, nevertheless, in the case of *suyaśāḥ*, the substitution of *s* by the rule *vā śari* would be unavoidable due to the status of the original as a *sthānivadbhūta*; likewise, in the case of *suvṛṭ*, the change to a *cariṭ* sound (*cartva*) by the rule *khari ca* would be difficult to prevent. However, in the rule prescribing the augment *im*, since the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), its property of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*) subsumes the property of being a *sārvadhātuka*, and thus there is no obstacle to its application. This is because, in that context, the vowel is relied upon solely as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the condition "beginning with a consonant" (*halādau*).

This very point has been established in the statement "there is no [application] when depending on a *varṇa*. For this very reason, in the case of the *vic*-suffix after the roots *dhinv* and *kṛṇv*, when the *val* (consonant) is elided by the rule "lopo vyoḥ," that [elision] is not a cause [for the application of a grammatical operation]. Although the status of being a cause actually resides in the suffix (*pratyaya*), the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule "na dhātulope" does not apply; for the status of being an *ārddhadhātuka* is not the delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) for its causality in that instance, and the property of being a *val* lacks the quality of being non-pervasive (*avyāpyatva*) with respect to being a suffix.

By this, forms such as *sudhe*, *sudhenau*, *sudhenaḥ*, *sukaḥ*, *sukarṇau*, and *suvarṇa* are established. Following the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ*, there is elision of the suffix *su*; then, because the word has attained the status of a *pada*, the *n* is elided by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*.
By this [method], Rāma is [likened to] nectar (*sudhā*) for the gods due to the slaying of their enemies, and he is like a good cause (*sukāraṇa*) because of his lightness (*lāghava*).
He who would state here two qualifications of the original author is indeed a follower of Kaiyaṭa.
Thus it has been explained.

Since the desired result is already established by the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that in which there is the elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*)," the mention of the term *ārdhadhātuka* serves to ensure that its status as such is obtained as the cause [for the application of the rule]. Nor can it be argued that the mention is purposeful for the sake of excluding forms such as *totorti*, because the *yaṅ-luk* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) is Vedic (*cāndasa*). Even if it were within the scope of the common language (*bhāṣā*), it should be understood that the force of the second [mention of] *ārdhadhātuka* arises through repetition (*āvṛtti*). Furthermore, this is because the statement in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṅkiti ca" — namely, "the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* in the preceding rule is without scope"—is based on a lack of finality (*anāsthā*).

This, however, must be considered: by the mention of *ārddhadhātuka*, it is intended merely that the elision (*lopa*) and the *guṇa* substitution share the same individual as their cause (*ekavyaktinimittakatva*), and not that the effect-ness (*kāryatva*) is defined by a causality delimited by the property of being an *ārddhadhātuka*. Otherwise, the prohibition of *guṇa* in forms such as *loluva* would be untenable; for although the suffix *ac* is in fact an *ārddhadhātuka* when its elision occurs by the rule "yaṅo'ci ca," the property of being an *ārddhadhātuka* is not the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of its causality.

Therefore, there is a desire to specify a state of being an effect (kāryatva) as determined by a causality (nimittatva) that is delimited by a property (dharma) subsumed under the category of *ārddhadhātuka*. And this state of being subsumed (*vyāpyatva*) is common to both difference and non-difference, because what is intended in the property is precisely its occurrence in nothing other than the *ārddhadhātuka*. In the present case, however, since the property of *val*-ness occurs outside the *ārddhadhātuka*, the application of the prohibition does not take place; thus, the position is well-established.

According to the natural sense of the aforementioned commentary (*bhāṣya*), the *vikaraṇa* suffix *śnu* does not occur here. However, when the *kvip* suffix is applied and *ūṭh* is substituted, one obtains forms such as *dhinūḥ*, *dhinvau*, *dhinvaḥ*, *kṛṇūḥ*, *kṛṇvau*, *kṛṇvaḥ*, and so forth. They say that forms such as *sudhī*, *sudhinau*, *sudhinaḥ*, *sukīḥ*, *sukṛṇau*, *sukṛṇaḥ*, and so on, do not occur. Dīkṣita, however, maintains: "Since the *yaṅluk* (the elision of *yaṅ*) pertains to the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), the mention of 'ārddhadhātuka' [in Pāṇini 6.4.65] finds its scope of application in cases such as *atotori*; furthermore, there is no evidence for a double application [of the rule]. Therefore, even when the prohibition of *guṇa* applies, forms such as *sudhī*, *sudhinau*, *sudhinaḥ*, *sukīḥ*, *sukīrṇau*, and *sukīrṇaḥ* also occur."

[Objection: But in the case of *parivīḥ*, since the substitution of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) occurs by this very rule after the elision (*lopa*) of the *kvip* suffix—thereby sharing a single governing condition (*ekalakṣaṇatva*)—a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) would be impossible; consequently, due to its posteriority, the lengthening should not take place. [Response: Not so. For this is an extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*). Thus, the designation such as "a *kṛt* suffix" is extended to the elided element, whereas the actual grammatical operation (*kārya*) based on that designation occurs only through the respective rules (*śāstra*). Therefore, a conflict is established. As it has been said:
"But in the case of *sindhu*, the name of the original locus (*sthānin*) applies because of the extension of another state (*ānyabhāvya*)."

The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). The meaning is that this rule provides for the designation of the substitute by the name of the original element (*sthānin*). Therefore, according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, this [rule] is for the purpose of a prescription regarding the letter *al*. However, the Bhāṣyakāra says: this is not for the sake of forms such as *atṛṇeṭ*; for in that case, the condition *halī* (after a consonant) is removed. Nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms such as *tṛṇahāni*, because the phrase *na aci* is understood from the preceding rule *nābhyastasyāci*. Nor is it for the sake of *āśīḥ* in the application of *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, since that is already established by the specific mention (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *āśās-* in the context of the *kvip* suffix; for that [mention] is necessary even for you.

In that regard, [the rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so that [the substitution] does not occur in cases such as *āśāste* when only the root *śās* is mentioned; however, if *śās* were understood in the rule for the substitution of *it* by virtue of its association (*sāhacarya*) only with that *śās* which is a base (*prakṛti*) ending in an *aṅ* affix—as in *āśāste* and the like—then since it would not apply even in the case of *kvip*, the rule would instead be for the sake of an injunction (*vidhyartha*). Therefore, this [rule, P. 1.1.62] is for the sake of restriction: when there is the elision of an affix, only an operation conditioned by the affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) takes place, and not an operation whose causality is defined by a property common to both affixes and non-affixes.

In the case of *sudṛṣatprāsāda* ("a palace with beautiful stones"), the rule *sormanasī alomoṣasī*—which prescribes that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first syllable of a final member ending in *-man* or *-as* (provided they do not mean "hair" or "dawn") becomes udātta after the word *su*—does not apply. Instead, the rule *nañsubhyām* applies, resulting in the final syllable being udātta. Otherwise, when the suffix *jas* is elided by *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, the status of the final member as ending in *-as* would not be lost due to the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original).

However, according to the manner stated above, let there be no fault, because this [suffix] does not occur apart from the suffix (*pratyaya*); for in the rules concerning *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man*, the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavad-grahaṇa*) does not apply. Likewise, it should be noted that the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by the rule "atvasantasya" also does not occur. In the view of the Vārttika, however, there is the disadvantage of having to undertake a further effort in order to avoid the aforementioned faults.

It might be argued as follows: The result of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is indeed the exclusion of other alternatives. For in cases such as "One threshes the rice," since threshing is already established as a means for the purpose of removing the husk (the separation of the grain from the chaff) even by other means like pounding, there is a possibility of its performance being optional. When the injunction aims at establishing that [threshing] as the common means of attainment, the result is the cessation of other alternative means which were the counter-correlates of its occasional occurrence. Nor is this alone the fruit of restriction; for if there were no restriction in the form of prescribing what was previously unestablished (*aprāptāṃśaprapaṇa*), such a cessation would be untenable.

If it is argued that since its existence [as a substitute] follows from the very fact of its being established by the sense of the rule, and that in the absence of the present injunction (*vidhi*), there would be no possibility of the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), the following is said in response: Even here, *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is treated by the term "restriction" (*niyama*). This is because the statement "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten" is recorded in the *Bhāṣya* as being of the nature of a restriction (*niyama*). And although this [specification] possesses three defects—namely, the abandonment of the literal meaning, the assumption of a further meaning such as "those other than the five are not to be eaten," and the sublation of the eating of other five-nailed animals which was already established—it is nevertheless accepted.

Nevertheless, even if the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) intends to apply to cases where there is elision of an affix (*pratyaya-lopa*), an absolute annulment (*atyanta-bādha*) of what is established by that rule is impossible. Consequently, even for an operation whose cause is delimited by a property subsumed under "affixhood" (*pratyayatva-vyāpya-dharma*), there would necessarily be an option (*vikalpa*) due to the authority of both rules. However, eating more than five [fruits] is annulled because the passion (*rāga*) that serves as the source of its application is weak; thus, there is a difference in status. Therefore, it must necessarily be assumed that the general rule has a scope distinct from the aforementioned operations.

Therefore, there is no fault consisting of the sublation of what has been obtained (*prāptabādha*). Consequently, since the purport of the rule for suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is that it applies when [the original element] is different from that [substitute], and the purport of "it becomes" (*bhavati*) is that it does not become [the original] when it is other than that, the meaning is that [the substitute] does not become [the original] apart from the rule for suffixes. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the rule "as the original" (*sthānivat*) being restricted by this [present rule]; for that would result in the rule [of *sthānivat*] becoming useless.

Regarding the two statements, "Having divided that cake into four parts, he places the *puroḍāśa* upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)" and "He divides the *āgneya* [cake] into four," there is a difference because they are mutually restrictive (*upasaṃhāra*). The term *āgneya* excludes other oblations, while the term *puroḍāśa* excludes *puroḍāśas* dedicated to other deities. However, in the case of the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*, because there are differences among the intermediate speakers, a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) does not become redundant.

For this very reason, in cases such as "One should not clean one's teeth with a finger, nor with the index finger," where the statement is from a single speaker, there is no mutual restriction; rather, it is simply the postulation of an additional fault (*doṣa-adhikya-kalpanā*). This is the general direction.

Now, even so, what is the status of such passages as "pañca" (where *padatva* [the status of being a word] arises by the rule for suffixes), "samāsatvāt prātipadikatvam" (where *prātipadikatva* [the status of being a nominal stem] arises because it is a compound), "snukramoḥ" (where the augment *iṭ* is applied), and "ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi" (where the genitive case is used in the sense of the object when both [agent and object] are possible)? If it is argued that these are justified because the intention is to exclude other possibilities, and thus the general rule itself serves as the authority for those prescriptions—here they say:

The remaining [interpretation]—"the genitive [case ending] is [intended] when both [agent and object] are present," and so forth—should be explained in this way, and not as "prescribed. For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* stated that the rule in question is indeed a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)—namely, "when both are present, [the genitive is used] for the object"—and not a prescription (*vidhi*), by stating: "there is no prohibition when *aka*-type suffixes are employed.

Alternatively, since the absence of intent toward a specific case in a general rule must be inferred in both ways, let [the rule] beginning with *pratyayalakṣaṇa* remain exactly as it is heard in the text. And when there is a need for its purpose, the exclusion of operations other than those characterized by a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is established as its result.

For example, in the case of the injunction, "With the mantra 'They have grasped this rein of the Truth,' he takes up the horse's halter," this is a direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*). Because it operates prior to an injunction that would otherwise be inferred from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the words, it is indeed an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). Since the mere act [of taking up the halter] is already established by the injunction based on indicative power alone, its redundancy would otherwise follow; therefore, the exclusion of the donkey’s halter is postulated as its purpose.
As it has been said:
"Therefore, this is determined to be an original injunction of the mantra."
But when one investigates what the purpose of this injunction might be:
There is no fruit other than the turning back [of the donkey] from the tethering-rope called "donkey.

Nor should it be argued that, because the *sthānivadbhāva* rule is necessary here for the sake of another object, the *pratyayalopa* rule does not apply first in comparison to it, since both are equally direct (*pratyakṣatva*).

Nevertheless, although one may trace the various substitutes (ādeśas) through their respective original bases (sthānins) by virtue of their being sthānins and ādeśas, they are in reality distinct entities. Consequently, while the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*)—namely, *pratyayalopa* [P. 1.1.62]—remains present as long as the elision of the suffix is operative, the specific rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* [P. 1.1.62] generates a cognition characterized by a specific property (the status of being an ādeśa). Thus, there is no obstacle to its application first.

The only difference is this: in that case, the assumption of an inferential rule (*laiṅgika-vidhi*) is what is obstructed; but in the present case, it is merely the fact that the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) has as its scope the elision of an affix (*pratyaya-lopa*). Under this view, however, the previously mentioned texts are to be applied exactly as they are heard. By this, the two positions—that restrictive rules (*niyama-sūtra*) function either by way of prohibition (*niṣedha-mukhena*) or by way of injunction (*vidhi-mukhena*)—have been explained.
[Pāṇini 1.1.63: *na lumatāṅgasya*.

When the non-appearance of an affix (*pratyayādarśana*) is effected by any one of the terms *lu*, *mat*, *luk*, *ślu*, or *lup*, the grammatical operation dependent on that [affix] as its cause (*tannimitta-aṅgakārya*) shall not take place. For example: *gargāḥ* (the descendants of Garga), *mṛṣṭaḥ* (polished), *juhutaḥ* (they two sacrifice). Because of the elision (*lopa*) of the *yañ* and *śap* affixes by means of *lumat*, the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions dependent on them do not occur. Why specify "by *lumat*"? Consider *kāryate* and *hāryate*. Here, although the *ṇi* affix is elided by the rule "ṇer aniṭi," there remains a dependence on the *ṇi*; thus, in *amārṭ*, even though the elision of the consonant and following vowels (*hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*) occurs due to its obligatory nature, the *vṛddhi* of the root *mṛj* still takes place. Why specify "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*)? Consider *pañca* (five) and *sapta* (seven). In these cases, the elision of the case-ending is not caused by a suffix, so the prohibition does not apply.

In this context, by means of the definition of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the designation "word" (*pada*) should apply because [the element] ends in a *sup* suffix. Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika maintains that because the word *aṅga* is marked with the *svarita* accent, only that operation which is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*) is prohibited.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: if this were the case, then in *utkramasva* (imperative), the substitution of *hi* by *luṅ* according to *ato heḥ* would not occur; in *jigamiṣa*, the augment *iṭ* according to *gameriṭ parasmaipadeṣu* would not occur; and in *vivṛtsa*, the prohibition of *iṭ* according to *na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ* would not occur. This is because these [rules] fall under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the "stem" (*aṅga*). Therefore, this prohibition applies to whatever operation actually pertains to the stem, whether it falls within the governing heading of the stem or outside of it.

Nor does the aforementioned defect persist even when there is a prohibition of only that which is an *aṅga* (stem) operation; for the designation *aṅga* as defined by the *parasmaipada* suffix—which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the elision—resides solely in that which ends in the suffix *krama-iti*, and the long vowel [of *krīṇāti*], which possesses *aṅga*-status relative to the suffix *śap*, is prescribed specifically by the root *kram*. The same applies to the two subsequent cases as well.

Thus, the resulting meaning is this: based on the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being like the original) of that suffix with respect to which a certain element has *aṅga*-status, the operation caused by that suffix does not take place for that [element].

Furthermore, in both views, the accents prescribed by the rules *ñnityādir nityam*, *kitaḥ*, and *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne* would be unavoidable even when *luk* elision has taken place. Thus, for example: *gargāḥ* and *vidāḥ*, where there is *luk* of *yañ* and *añ*. Also, *uṣṭragrīvā*, where there is *lup* of the suffix *kan* (by the rule *ive pratikṛtau*) after the base *devapatha* etc. (by the rule *devapathādibhyaśca*). In that case, the initial syllable would be udātta by the rule *ñniti*. And this applies provided it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*).

Regarding the term *saṃjñā*, Kaiyaṭa states that [the rule] "in the case of a name (*saṃjñāyām*)," etc., is intended to have an acute accent on the first syllable. [In this context,] the descendants of Atri are called *Ātreyas*. By the rule "after a stem ending in *it*, [the suffix] *ḍhak* [is applied], except when *iñ* follows," the suffix *ḍhak* is used. Its elision occurs by the rule "the elision of *ḍhak* after Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa," etc. In that case, there would be an acute accent on the final syllable by the rule "an affix marked with *k* has an acute accent on its final syllable. This is because, according to the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix, the rule applies to the word ending in that suffix. Nor can it be argued that the acute accent on the final syllable is unavoidable due to the *phiṭ*-accent.

The two forms *atri* and *atrī* are established by the *uṇādi* sūtra "rāśadibhyāṃ trip" and "adestriniśca. In that regard, because the suffix is marked with *p*, it is *anudātta*; consequently, by the rule of "the remainder is unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*), the form *atri* ending in *i* has its first syllable as *udātta*. It is accepted that the form ending in *n* (i.e., *atrī*) has its final syllable as *udātta* due to the accentuation of the *nit* suffix. This is also supported by the usage of the first-syllable-accented form in "atreriva śṛṇutam" and by the usage of the first-syllable-accented form even when the suffix is elided in "atrīṇāṃ stomam adrivaḥ. One for whom the path is dear is *pathipriyaḥ*.

In the case of *supodhātu*, there would also be the acute accent on the first syllable by the rule *pathimathoḥ* and so forth; for these [rules] do not fall under the heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), and in reality, they do not constitute operations of a stem. This is because, unlike the technical term "word" (*pada*) defined as "that which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ*," the aforementioned accents are not operations of that which ends in an affix. Furthermore, the status of being a "stem" (*aṅgatva*) applies solely to the portion preceding the limit of the final affix.

One might object: "Let it be that the operation [of *kita*] does not apply to the *aṅga*; however, as for the other two [operations], since they are indicated by a locative (*saptamī*) case, they must indeed be operations of the *aṅga* in reality. Thus, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, how could there be any possibility of their application? If this is asked, the answer is no. This is because we accept that locatives referring to *saubvara* (phonological) matters are locatives of the final element (*tadanta-saptamī*). Consequently, the meaning of [Pāṇini’s rule] *ñnityādinityam* is "the first syllable of that which ends in *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *ti* is acute. In this regard, the evidence is the inclusion of the word *pūrva* ("preceding") in the rule *bhīhrībhṛhumadajanadhanaharidrājāgarāṃ pratyayātpūrvaṃ piti*. This indicates that the locative is indeed a locative of the final element.

Otherwise, since the status of being an antecedent operation (*pūrvakāryatva*) would be established for that which is prescribed when *pit* follows, such [prescription] would be redundant. For this very reason, in the rule "upottamaṃ riti," the acute accent (*udātta*) applies only to the vowel *ī* of the suffix following a stem ending in *ri*, as in the word *āhavanīya*, and not to the vowels *i* or *ā* of the penultimate portion of the base (*prakṛti*).

Likewise, the rule *caṅyanyatarasyām* also applies to that which ends in *caṅ*; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) prescribed by the rule *caturaḥ śasi* would apply only to a stem ending in the suffix *śas*, and that this would contradict the reading with a middle acute accent (*madhyodātta*) in the passage *ṣaṭtriṃśāṃśca caturaḥ kalpayantaḥ*. For, by the force of the explicit mention of *śas* [in the rule], there is a sublation (*bādha*) of [the application of the accent] to that which ends in it. Otherwise, the word *catur* would have been mentioned in the very rule *ūḍidampadādi*.

In that case, because the term *asarvanāmasthāna* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), there is no over-extension [of the accent]. Nor does that fault apply in forms such as *ābhyām*, for even according to the final established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the acute accent on the initial consonant is desired by the rule "ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ. Nor does it follow that in the rule for the *svarita* accent, a genitive case-nirdeśa would be required, since in cases like *ritaḥ* there is an excess of half a mora; this being the position reached, the Vārttika states:

"In the sense of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there is an extension of the rule for that which consists of a single vowel; with the exception of all vocatives (*āmantrita*), the *sij*-affix, and accentuation (*svara*). The purpose [of this extension] is for the elision (*luk*) and accentuation of *ñni*, *ti*, and *kit* suffixes, and for the elision of *pathin* and *mathin* before a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (*sarvanāmasthāna*)."

The meaning is this: although the accent of a single word (*ekapadasvara*) would apply by virtue of the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), it does not take place. The purpose of beginning the rule "except for the accent of the vocative (*sarvāmantrita*) and the elision of *sij*" (*sarvāmantritasijluk-svaravarjam*) is precisely this. However, that which depends on two words (*padadvayāśraya*) certainly does occur; for example, in the case of *dadhi tiṣṭhati*, the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*—which falls under the governing rules (*adhikāra*) of *padasya* and *padāt*—does indeed apply. This is because the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) must be relied upon for the term *dadhi* to receive the designation of a "word" (*pada*). The same should be understood for examples such as *iha tiṣṭha*.

What is the purpose of excluding *sarva* from the beginning [of the list]? It is so that the following rules may apply: in the case of *sarvastomo 'tirātraḥ*, the rule *sarvasya supi* (P. 6.1.193) ensures the acute accent on the first syllable; in *sarpir āgaccha* and *sapta āgacchata*, the rule *āmantritasya ca* (P. 6.1.198) ensures the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative; and in *mā hi dātām*, the rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* (P. 6.1.187) ensures the acute accent on the first syllable of the aorist marker *sica*.

Nor should it be argued that [the desired accentuation] is already established by the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* (P. 6.2.1) alone—on account of the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām adantānām* (P. 6.2.173)—because the word *sarva-* is udātta on its first syllable. This is because the application of *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* is dependent upon the non-application of *sarvasya supi* (P. 6.1.193). Furthermore, in the case of the word *sarpiḥ*, whether one adopts the view that words are derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*) or the view that they are underived (*avyutpattipakṣa*), it is udātta on its final syllable: by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) in the former case, and by the *phiṭ*-accent (*phiṭsvara*) in the latter. Consequently, the rule *nabviṣayasya* (P. 6.2.172), which prescribes an initial udātta, does not apply here.

Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed by the term *aniṣantasya*; Kaiyaṭa states that "it has an udātta accent on the final syllable due to its inclusion in the list beginning with *ghṛta*," but that [view] is intended from the perspective of the theory of non-etymological derivation (*avyutpattipakṣa*).

If it is argued that the word *sapta* is acute on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kanin* according to the rule *sapyaśūbhyāṃ tuṭ ca*, or even under the view that it is not etymologically derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), where it is so by the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ*, we say no; for it is acute on the final syllable due to its inclusion in the *ghṛtādi* group, and because of its usage in such passages as *sapta yuñjanti rathamekacakram*. Therefore, the purpose [of the rule] is the prevention of these three types of accentuation. In the rule *gātisthā*, the mention of the *sic* suffix by force of its inclusion ensures the establishment of the accent when that suffix is elided (*luk*).

Otherwise, he would have prescribed *luk* (elision) for *cleḥ* itself in order to establish forms such as *abhūt* and *apāt*; for even in the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*, there is the possibility of abandoning the inclusion of another *s* (*sakārāntarapraśleṣa*) in this very same manner.

Nor should it be argued that the rule *ātaḥ* would thus become solely prescriptive (*vidhi*) rather than restrictive (*niyama*), and that this would lead to the opposite inconvenience of having to state *clilukī* (with elision of *cli*) in order to exclude the present tense (*laṭ*), resulting in greater complexity. This is because the exclusion of *laṭ* is achieved simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ṅitaḥ*. Therefore, in the case of the elision of *sic* (*sijluk*) and its accentuation, as stated above, there is no need to include [the condition] as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the distinction. However, in the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭha-adhyāya*), this was resolved by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Thus, there is a Vārttika on the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam*:

"The statement that the initial [vowel] of *upamāna* (the standard of comparison) is udātta is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule regarding accentuation based on suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is prohibited in the case of an accent characterized by an *anubandha*. Otherwise, [in examples such as] *cañcā* (a mat) like *cañcu*, or *vardhrikā* (a small shovel) like *vardhrikā*, the suffix *kan* used for names undergoes elision by the rule *lum manuṣye*. In that case, since the desired result would already be established by the *nit*-accent itself through the application of the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the explicit mention of the initial udātta serves solely as an indicator for the aforementioned meaning. Furthermore, the prohibition "not when [a suffix] marked with *lu* is present, [affecting] the stem" (*na lumatāṅgasya*) does not apply here, because it falls outside the governing heading concerning stems (*aṅgādhikāra*). This is because the meaning is "of the beginning of that which ends in a *nit*," and because, in reality, this is not an operation pertaining to a stem (*aṅgakārya*).

The statement prohibiting accentuation in the rule *pathimathoḥ* must indeed be made; for since that [prohibition] does not possess the character of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), it cannot be avoided by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). Nor can it be assumed that the indicator applies only to the domain of accentuation, as this would result in the non-establishment of the accentuation for the vocative (*āmantrita*) and the elision of *sij*. Nor can it be argued that the indicator teaches a prohibition of the application of suffix-characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) regarding an accentuation specified in the locative case, because this would lead to the impossibility of the initial acute accent in forms such as *sarvastomaḥ*.

Alternatively, it is indicated that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the status of being a suffix) does not apply to a vowel specified in the locative case (*saptamī*). Thus, in the rule *sarvasya supi*, one should remove the locative *supi* and read it as *supaḥ*, ending in the genitive.

Regarding this, they say: An indicator (*jñāpaka*) is of two kinds—dependent on a general rule and dependent on a specific rule. If, in the case of the word *bhahrī*, there were a difference in result between the interpretation that takes the locative sense (*saptamyartha*) and the interpretation that takes the inclusion of the suffix (*tadantagrahaṇa*), then only in such a case would it be indicated by the principle: "Locatives belonging to Pāṇini himself [indicate] locatives that include their suffixes. For in that instance, in the absence of the mention of *pūrva* (the preceding), the acute accent (*udātta*) would apply only to the suffix itself; however, when the locative is relied upon, the acute accent applies to *bhī* and the others, excluding *pit*. Thus, there is a difference in the result.

In this same manner, it should be understood in rules such as *upottamaṃ riti* and *caṅyanyatarasyām*. However, in cases such as *ñnityādir nityam* and *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne*, there is no difference whatsoever, as the acute accent (*udātta*) applies to the beginning of the base (*prakṛti*) in both ways. Therefore, the locative case here does not denote "that which ends in [the element]" (*tadanta-saptamī*). Consequently, since the operation actually pertains to the *aṅga* (the entire stem), the prohibition in *na lumatāṅgasya* applies, and thus there is no occurrence of the *cit-svara* (the acute accent on the *cit* suffix).

The underlying intent of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the present Sūtra is also thus; as for those works in the sixth [Adhyāya], they are intended as indicators (jñāpaka) with respect to general principles—this is the direction of the argument.

Even in the case of *atrayaḥ*, there is no occurrence of the aforementioned accentuation, because the rule prescribing the final acute (*antodātta*) applies specifically to the *kit* suffix itself; and here, that suffix has been elided. This is because, when a suffix is elided, the rule of "suffix-characteristics" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) prescribes only those operations belonging to other elements [not the suffix itself]. An operation belonging to the suffix itself cannot take place when that suffix is elided, since it is impossible for both the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) and the status of being an effect (*kāryitva*)—as defined by a single element—to reside in one and the same thing. Nor can it be argued that even such an operation belongs only to what ends in a suffix.

For the rule *tadantasya* (P. 1.1.72) is not an independent statement regarding the inclusion of the affix; rather, its basis lies in the fact that the designation [of "bahuvrīhi"] applies to that which ends in such an affix. Furthermore, since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), the affix is not accepted as the qualifier in this context. Moreover, because elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence, it sublates both the finality (*anta*) and the udātta accent of that [affix]; consequently, even the rule on "substitution" (*sthānivat-sūtra*, P. 1.1.56) does not apply. Thus, in examples such as *rājapuruṣa*, the elision of *n* does not occur.

In reality, because of the explanation that [the term *ahan*] is an *aṅga* (base), because of the prohibition of the designation *bha*, and because of the elision of the nasal *n* by virtue of the designation *pada*—which applies because the word ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*)—the substitution of the letter *r* is also established in the example "ahardadāti. This is because the prohibition "not when *sup* follows" does not apply here, since the elision of the case-suffix (*subluk*) occurs due to the fact that [the operation] is actually an *aṅga*-operation. Nor is the fault unavoidable in the view of the Vārttika-author; for the rule "in the prescription of *r* for *ahan*" was specifically formulated. Furthermore, one should not argue that, by the force of the statement "not when *sup* follows," there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the principle that a grammatical operation applies as if a suffix were present).

Otherwise, even after the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* etc., there would arise the contingency of the letter *r* in the case of *dīrghāhā nidāghaḥ*. By this [argument], the view that the term "not before a *sup*" (*asupi*) is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion) is refuted; for in the case of *ahardadāti*, since there exists an element other than a *sub* following the root *dā*, the letter *r* would [erroneously] apply. Nor can it be argued that because the substitution of *ru* and *ra* are *asiddha* (unestablished), they are weaker and thus the *na*-elision (*nalopa*) occurs first, resulting in the contingency of *ru* and *ra* applying to the vowel *a* itself. This is because the very capacity to initiate both those substitutions prevents the *na*-elision in their specific domain; furthermore, there is no difference between the vowel *a* having the letter *r* or the substitute *ru*.

Nor should it be argued that the commencement of that [rule] is already fulfilled in cases such as *ahargaccha* and *he dīrghāho nidādha*, because there the prohibition of *na*-lopa applies; for even so, the substitution of *ru* in the rule *rūparātri* would be rendered purposeless. Nor can this [purposelessness] be avoided by claiming that the form is meaningful in the vocative case; for the commentary explains that the word *ahan* is repeated: by the first occurrence, the absence of *na*-lopa is established, and by the second, the substitution of *ru* is prescribed.

It might be argued as follows: in the cases of *paramavācā*, *paramagoduhā*, *paramalihā*, *paramadaṇḍinā*, *paramadivā*, and *paramakumāryā*, since the designation *pada* would apply to the final member (*uttarapada*) on account of the case-endings contained within the compound, the following rules would apply: *coḥ kuḥ* (P. 8.2.30), *dāderdhātordhaḥ* (P. 8.2.32), *ho ḍhaḥ* (P. 8.2.31), *na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (P. 8.2.7), *diva ut* (P. 6.1.131), and *iko’savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca* (P. 6.1.127). Nor can this be refuted by the designation *bha*, because their scopes (*avadhi*) are different.

The designation *bha* applies to the entire word-form (*samastapada*), whereas the designation *pada* applies only to the final member (*uttarapada*). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "In the context of the *bha* designation, the term 'ending in a case-suffix' (*subanta*) must be understood as carrying over [from a previous rule]. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when a suffix other than a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows—as in the case of *yajñā-* and so on—the preceding aggregate from which that suffix is prescribed is designated *bha*; and if there exists a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) within that aggregate, then that too becomes designated *bha*.

Furthermore, the designation *bha*—which is taught as being primary—does indeed apply even in cases such as *rājñaḥ*, where there is no constituent element ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), just as in examples like *haṃsāyate* according to the rule "after the root *kṛ*, [the suffix] *kyaṅ* [is added], and there is the elision of *s*."

Even so, the fault regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna* (case endings) remains unavoidable, because there the prohibition of *pada*-status applies via the rule "not before a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Furthermore, due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "ending in a *sup*" (*subanta*) and by the force of that very prohibition, the principle "a rule applies only to what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya vidhir vā*) does not operate here. Its meaning is as follows: when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows, neither the preceding aggregate nor its constituent part ending in a *sup* is designated as a *pada*.

Since the designation *pada* is obtained for the whole by the rule *svādiṣu* and for the part by the rule *subantaṃ padam*, its prohibition results in the establishment of forms such as *paramavācau*. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, [grammatical operations] such as the substitution of *k* for *g* (*kutva*) or the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur in cases like *suvāk* and *surājā*, because the designation *pada* is prohibited for both the whole and the part according to the aforementioned reasoning. This is not so.

In the rule *asarvanāmasthāne*, the term *yaci* is drawn over from the preceding sūtra *yaci bham*. This prohibits the designation *pada* for a word ending in an *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). Consequently, since the designation *pada* does exist when the nominative singular suffix *su* follows, there is no such prohibition. Nor does this imply that the preceding element would acquire the *pada* designation even while *su* is still audible; rather, this is precisely what is intended. Therefore, it is established that the final member of a compound never receives the *pada* designation when followed by a *sup* suffix beginning with a vowel.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be no elision (*aluk*) in cases such as *dūrānmuktaḥ*, nor would there be the substitution of *anaṅ* in cases such as *hotāpotārau*, because those rules are prescribed only when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). This is not so, because the term *uttarapada* is a technical term (*rūḍha*) for the final constituent of a compound, and thus does not depend upon the technical designation *pada*. Nor should it be argued that even so, in cases such as *dadhisecau*, the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would fail to apply. This is not so, because the analysis of the rule is *padād ādiḥ padādiḥ* ("the beginning of a *pada* is called *padādi*").

The meaning is that [the rule applies] when it is the beginning of another word (*śabdāntara*) while being at the end of a word (*padottaratva*). Nor does this lead to an undesired prohibition in cases such as *rāmeṣu*, because the aforementioned prohibition does not apply by taking into account the designation of "word" (*pada*) provided by the rule "in *su* and so on" (*svādiṣu*). And in that regard, the very inclusion of the term *ati* in the rule is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this]. And this is logical; for if one were to explain it as "the beginning of a word," then in cases such as *dadhisecau*, the substitution of *ṣ* would be unavoidable.

This is because it will be stated [later] that "there is a rule for the compounding of *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada* with *kṛt*-suffixes prior to the arising of case-endings (*sub*). Nor should it be argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in forms such as *bahusecau*, since the element *bahu-* is a suffix (*pratyaya*) and thus not a word (*apada*). For a specific rule must be formulated stating "not after *bahu-*" (*bahucaḥ parasya na*). Otherwise, one would simply have to say "from a word" (*padāt*), which would mean that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* would not occur for a *s* following a word.

And in place of the word *ādi*, the term *bahu* should be inserted [in the rule], so that there is no *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) after a *bahuc* suffix. However, the author of the Vārttika began with the term *bahuc* itself in order to establish forms such as *paramavāc*. He states this as follows:
"And when it is the final member of a compound (*uttarapadatve*), the rule regarding what is not the beginning of a word (*apadādividhau*) applies."

By the word "uttara" (subsequent), the subsequent member [of a compound] is understood. The phrase "tasya padatve" (when there is the status of being a *pada* for that) refers to a compound (*samāsa*). When the designation *pada* is to be applied to the final constituent of a compound, the rule of "pratyayalakṣaṇa" (treating as if the suffix were present) does not apply when the suffix has been elided by *lumat*. The phrase "in rules other than those concerning the beginning of a *pada*" (*apadādividhau*) is included in order to prevent the prohibition of the *pada*-designation even in cases such as "dadhisecau. The meaning is that the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* certainly applies when a rule concerning the beginning of a *pada* (*padādividhi*) is to be applied. Consequently, in this context, a compound prior to the arising of the nominal suffix (*sup*) is not what is intended to be expressed; for the sake of establishing forms such as "dhanakrītā," the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of that [prohibition] must be accepted.

Kaiyaṭa, however, states that this is not a *upapada-samāsa*, but rather a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) such as *dadhnaḥ secī*; and because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), the suffix *vic* does not apply after a word with an *upapada*. Therefore, he says there is no undesired consequence (*āpatti*) such as *dadhiṣecau*. Even so, the rule "and [the substitution] of that which is preceded by *bahu*" must indeed be formulated; for once *bahu* is added, the resulting complex becomes meaningful and thus a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), whereby the case-ending (*sup*) is elided. Since it will be explained later that a case-ending is subsequently produced after the complex, one might rely on the designation "word" (*pada*) based on the intervening case-ending and thus have the substitution of *k* for *s* (*kutva*) occur. To prevent this, the rule is necessary.

On this point, they say: "In the very sūtra *pratyayalopa*, one should read [the two rules] as *uttarapadatve ca padādividhau* and *bahucpūrvasya*. These two statements are for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies only when there is an operation concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*), and not when there is an operation concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*). Thus, by abandoning the negative particle (*nañ*), there is brevity (*lāghava*). Furthermore, [the objection] that even *sā* would be a word (*pada*) does not arise, because the previously mentioned method is not being adopted. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt...* says:"

"Now, that [suffix] also becomes a *pada*; thus, even so, the rope is caught on both sides. In the word *abhūvan*, the *jus* substitution does not occur, because the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Nor should it be argued that in the example *devadattaṃ yājayāñcakāra*, the *luk* elision would set aside the *tiṅ* suffixes by virtue of being subsequent, and once those [suffixes] have been elided by the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), the final syllable of the form ending in *ām* would be unaccented due to its status as a *tiṅ*-ending (by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*), which would consequently result in the prohibition of the accent for what follows it. For, according to the maxim *yenanāprāpti*, the *luk* elision operates precisely at the stage of the *l* (the *liṭ* suffix), thereby setting aside the *tiṅ* suffixes. As it has been said:
"One would [otherwise] elide [the *s*] due to the *ām*, and there would be no elision of that [genitive ending]; therefore, there is elision.

Nor should it be argued that in examples such as *devadatto yuṣmatputraḥ* ("Devadatta, your son"), the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would apply to the word ending in the genitive case. For by the inclusion of the term *sthā* ("standing/remaining"), those substitutions are prescribed only when the case-ending is actually heard (*śrūyamāṇāyām*). This is because in phrases such as *samaye tiṣṭha sugrīva* ("Wait at the appointed time, Sugrīva!"), the meaning understood is "do not abandon the time," since the root *sthā* functions here in the sense of "not abandoning. Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of *sthā* is intended to mean that forms like *vas* and *nas* apply only to the stems as qualified by a case-ending, and not to the stem portion alone.

This is established even by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyānām* (Pāṇini 2.3.62). Now, one might object: if the suffix *tal* is elided by the rule *ciṇo luk*, then in forms such as *avadhi bhavatā dasyuḥ*, *agāyi bhavatā grāmaḥ*, and *adhyagāyi bhavatā anuvākaḥ*, the substitutes for the roots *han*, *iṇ*, and *iṅ*—namely *vadha*, *gā*, and *iṅ* respectively—would not occur under the rules *hano vadha liṅi* and *luṅi ca*, *iṇo gā luṅi*, and *iṅaśca*, as well as *vibhāṣā luṅ-lṛṅoḥ*. If this objection is raised, we say no. For those substitutes are prescribed specifically for that context of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix which occurs in the *luṅ* tense; therefore, they apply precisely before the substitution of the *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*). Thus, the desired forms are correctly produced.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, in reality, the operation does not apply to the member itself.

*aco'ntyādi ṭi* (Pāṇini 1.1.64). The genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇe*). The singular number is used for the sake of denoting a class (*jātāvekavacanam*). Among vowels (*acām*), that which is the final vowel, along with what precedes it, is designated by the technical term *ṭi*. The rules (*pradeśāḥ*) where this is applied include such as "*ṭita ātmanepadānām*" (3.4.79) and others. The compound *antyādi* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that of which the beginning is the end. Because it is necessarily dependent [on another word], the compound is valid. However, where the final element is a consonant (*halanta*), the designation applies to that entire form characterized by it. Consequently, in forms such as *kurute*, the *ṭi*-designation applies to the letter *a*; and in forms such as *kurvāte*, it applies to both the letter *ā* and the letter *a*, resulting in the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*).

"A letter preceding the final consonant is called *upadhā* (Pāṇini 1.1.65). A sound preceding the final consonant (*al*) is designated as *upadhā*. By the rule 'pugantalaghūpadhasya ca,' there is *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *i*. [Objection: But since the term 'preceding' (*pūrva*) is used without specifying a limit, in the case of the root *śās*, the designation *upadhā* would apply to the entire collection consisting of the letter *ś* and the vowel *ā*. This is because, when a whole and its parts are in proximity, according to the maxim regarding the doubling of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*), the whole itself is the locus of the grammatical operation. Consequently, by the rule 'śāsa idaṅ-haloḥ,' the substitution of *i* would apply to the whole [the syllable *śā*]. [Response: This is not so."

Because, as a general rule, the preceding member refers to that which is immediately prior; and because even when a designation applies to a whole collection, there is no over-extension due to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of the final [element] of the [base] ending in *al*.

Now, one might object that there would be a prohibition based on the rule: "The rule concerning the final letter does not apply to what is meaningless, except in the case of modifications of a reduplicated syllable. Since the repetition of a word is a repetition of the form and not of the meaning, the reduplicated portion is meaningless; thus, rules such as "the root *bhṛ* becomes *i*" would result in a total replacement (sarvādeśa). To prevent this, the term "except in the case of modifications of a reduplicated syllable" (*anabhyāsa-vikāre*) was stated. Furthermore, a "modification" (*vikāra*) must consist of a change in state; therefore, in the case of *dehi*, the elision of the reduplicated syllable is indeed a total replacement. This is not so.

In the sūtra *tasya lopaḥ*, the inclusion of the word *tasya* (of that) for the purpose of effecting the total elision (*sarvalopa*) of the affixes *ñi*, *ṭu*, and *ḍu* indicates that this [total elision] is not intended by the author of the sūtra. This is because the author of the Bhāṣya has established those purposes in another way. For instance, in the case of *avyaktānukaraṇasya*, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) does not apply to the final syllable; this is due to the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā*. Otherwise, he would have simply said *āmreḍitasya vā*.

Even in the rule "ghvasoreddhau," although the mention of *lopa* (elision) is carried over from a previous context, the repetition of the term *lopa* here serves as an indicator (*sāmarthya*) that this is a total substitution (*sarvādeśa*). Thus, the formulation of the sūtra is: "ghorabhyāsasya lopohau. This has been explained. The meaning of "aseścait" is that for both *asti* and *ghu*, the substitution of *et* occurs when *hi* follows.

Alternatively, there is a word-break as *lopaś* (lopa-ś). Since there is no purpose for the indicatory letter *ś* in a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it functions as a substitute for the entire technical name (*saṃjñin*). As the Bhāṣya states: "The instruction contains two *ś*s. In that context, *lopa* is a separate word. Because the word *lopa*, being a primary derivative (*kṛdanta*), possesses meaning through its connection with the object of the technical name, the case-ending is applied, and the letter *ś* is used as a marker (*pratinirddiśyate*). Consequently, since the indicatory letter (*itsaṃjñā*) is assigned at the very time of its enunciation (*upadeśa*), *lopa* becomes a substitute for the whole.

Nor should it be argued that since the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) occurs before a *jhal* sound, and because it begins with the *s* of *su*, the rule is satisfied by reading the word with only one *śakāra* (the single *ś* in *śi*) for the purpose of eliding the *su* when followed by a *jhal*; for [the *ś*] has been retained for the sake of clarity, as there is no intention to elide it. This is precisely why the elision of *al* (*allopa*) was not applied in rules such as "ana upadhālopinaḥ."

Alternatively, just as in the rule *jhalo jhali*, the application of *skoḥ* occurs only when the cause (*nimitta*) and the object of the operation (*kāryin*) reside within the same word (*ekapadastha*). Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *ābhyām*, the rule *hali lopaḥ* would result in the elision of the final letter being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the elision of the *id* of *idam* (which is prescribed by *ido 'y puṃsi*), because that [elision] is conditioned by a following consonant (*hal*).

From the rule *anāpyakaḥ*, by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *an* and by interpreting the locative case *halī* as a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) within *an*, the elision is prescribed for *ana* itself. Consequently, by the maxim *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*, there is elision of the letter *na* alone, and through the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe*, the form *ābhyām* is established. Nor does this leave the problem of the elision being an "end-substitution" (*antyādeśa*) in the rule *atra lopo ’bhyāsasya* as it was before; for the explanation here is that the elision applies to the whole *abhyāsa* (reduplicated syllable) as its substratum, and not to a single part thereof.

If it is argued that the mention of *atra* (here) is for the sake of obtaining specific restrictions—namely, the mention of *san* to exclude forms such as *dadau* and *dadhau*; the qualification of *san* as *sādau* (beginning with a suffix) to exclude forms such as *jijñapayiṣati*; the mention of specific verbal roots such as *mīmā* to exclude forms such as *yiyakṣati*; and the mention of a specific object (*viṣaya*) to exclude forms such as *mumukṣati gām* according to the rule "the root *muc* takes *guṇa* optionally when intransitive"—this is not so, because these [restrictions] are established by mere *anuvṛtti* (carrying over from a previous rule).

Nor should it be argued that, even so, the *okāra* (the substitution of *o*) prescribed by the Vārttika—"vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavadaghavatām occāvasya"—would apply only to the letter *va*; for by the force of the specific mention of *avasya* instead of *vasya*, its status as a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatva*) is established. Therefore, there is no fault even if the designation applies to the entire aggregate. Furthermore, linguistic usages such as "having a conjunct as its penultimate" (*saṃyogopadhatva*) are also consistent with this view. In the alternative position, however, one should understand that the property of a part is superimposed upon the whole.

Alternatively, *alaḥ* is in the nominative plural (*jas*). Nor is there an impossibility of coreferentiality with *pūrvah*, which ends in the singular; for one may simply read *pūrve* as being in the nominative plural (*jas*). The attainment of the status of being an *al* for the final [phoneme] follows from the sense of the rule. Alternatively, *alaḥ* is a genitive used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*); the singular number is used for the class (*jātāvekavacanam*). The meaning is: "the *al* preceding the final among the *al*s."

"In that which is specified [tasmin], [the operation applies] to the preceding [pūrvasya]" (P. 1.1.66). When there is a specification by means of the locative case, the grammatical operation must apply to the preceding element; and that [preceding element] is "specified" when it is uttered without intervention. This is because the word *niḥ* conveys non-interruption (*nairantarya*) and the word *diśi* conveys utterance (*uccāraṇa*). Furthermore, this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), because it serves as the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) to that anticipated absence which would otherwise cause rules such as "a semi-vowel is replaced by a vowel before a vowel" (*iko yaṇ aci*) to apply indeterminately.

If this statement were not present, then, due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamakābhāvāt*), the substitution of *yaṇ* for *ik* would apply to [an *ik*] that is either prior or subsequent, proximate or non-proximate, immediate or non-immediate. However, when this [statement] exists, the operation rests upon the prior [element] alone. For in the rule "iko yaṇaci," the locative case is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*bhāvalakṣaṇā*). The meaning is: "when an *ac* is present. And being present is common to both the prior and the subsequent. The same applies to proximity (*upaśleṣa*) as well.

Furthermore, since the status of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an operation and the status of being the cause (*nimittatva*) cannot coexist simultaneously in a single locus, in examples such as *dudhyudakam*, the *yaṇ* substitution would occur alternately for both [the preceding and the following sounds]. Therefore, it is restricted by the rule "of the preceding alone" (*pūrvasyaiva*). Consequently, although [the condition] would apply even to a non-immediate predecessor in a case like *agnicit*, it is restricted to the immediate one. As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* that the *paribhāṣā* "in that [locus]" (*tasmin*) does not apply when there is a locative of existence (*sat-saptamī*), that is merely the bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*) of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

Objection: The word *tasmin* (in that) should apply only where [a grammatical element] is specifically indicated by it, as in "In that *aṇ*, and in *yuṣmākāsmākau*"; for in cases such as *gavityayamāha* ("He says 'go'"), the word *iti* conveys only the phonetic form of the word itself. Nor is there a lack of purpose [for this rule] in such cases, because in examples like "O *yauṣmākīṇa*, give to us" (*he yauṣmākīṇa asmabhyaṃ dehi*) and "O *āsmāka*, I give to you" (*he āsmāka yuṣmabhyaṃ dadāmi*), the result is the exclusion of the substitutes [yuṣmad- and asmad-] following the suffixes *khañ* and *aṇ*. Reply: This is not so.

In common usage, a word is understood to refer to its meaning; thus, by the particle *iti*, one assumes it refers to the word itself. In grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), however, because the focus is on the word-form, the particle *iti* establishes that the word refers to the meaning. This is because the particle *iti* causes a reversal of the word-meaning, and because it would result in the utterance of the preceding word [as a whole] in that very context. Furthermore, this is more parsimonious than assuming the commencement of a new rule. Therefore, in the expression *tasminn iti*, it is indeed the locative case-ending that is being cited. This is because the pronoun *tat* includes specific instances such as *aci* and *halī*, just as in the rule *tasyāpatyam*.

"Therefore, [the rule applies] to the subsequent [element]" (67). When there is a mention in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), the grammatical operation (*kārya*) must belong to the subsequent element alone, and that [operation] must apply to what is immediately contiguous (*avyavahita*). Consequently, the *nighāta* (elision of accent) prescribed by the rule "tiṅ-ṅatiṅaḥ" occurs only in the case of *agnim īḷe*, and not in the case of *īḷe agnim* either. Furthermore, this [ablative mention] is characterized by its connection with a direction (*dig-yoga-lakṣaṇā*), because a case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is impossible here. Moreover, since it would follow that the word *pūrva* ("prior") must also be supplied just as the word *uttara* ("subsequent") is, and because there would be the undesirable consequence of the operation applying to a subsequent element even when it is separated [by another word], this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Therefore, in the case of *utthānam*, the application of the rule "udaḥ sthā-stambhoḥ" does not occur.
As the Vārttika states:

"The statement 'from that [word] to that [word]' is for the sake of restriction, because there is no distinction between the preceding and following applications; it is like [the examples] 'that water' or 'he cooks rice'.

Here too, "tasmāt" is an imitation of words ending in the fifth case (ablative), and not intended to bring this rule into effect wherever the word "tasmāt" actually occurs, according to the reasoning stated previously.

Surely, in this case, doubt does not even arise because of the absence of any purpose. For [in the rule] *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*, since a base (*aṅga*) preceding a long vowel *ā*—as in *ata ādeḥ*—is impossible; and in the case of *tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi* as well, [the objection that] in forms like *vṛkṣān*, the *ṣ* preceding the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* would undergo *natva* (substitution by *n*), is prevented by the interpretation that the *natva* applies to the *śas* specifically indicated by the genitive case.

On this point, they say: the purpose [of the rule] is that [the substitution occurs] for what is being uttered (*uccarataḥ*) and not for what is not perceived (*anupalabhataḥ*). This is because there is the possibility of such an argument: lest the substitution of *n* for the *śas* ending—which has the word *uccaran* as its base—occur after the preceding vowel *ā* which has become long.

Similarly, in the rule "tasmānnuḍaci," one should apply the principle so that the augment *nuṭ* does not occur before the negative particle *nañ* (in forms such as *anaśva*) when its *n* has been elided.

In these two sūtras, the view that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed [by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*] is also mentioned in the Bhāṣya. It is as follows: by the recurrence of the word "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) from the sūtra *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*, even when there is a specification of meaning, the genitive refers to the immediately preceding element; and when there is a specification of the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*), the genitive would refer to such a subsequent element. Since the genitive occurs in examples such as *ikaḥ*, by restating that genitive, it is understood that this [genitive] refers only to what precedes—not to what follows, nor even to what precedes if it is separated [by other elements].

In cases such as *ānemuk*, however, even the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is postulated; the rest is as before. And that [genitive] is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) because its connection is not fixed. It is established by implication that the rule regarding the grammatical operation applies only to that which follows a genitive of location. However, where both [the element to be replaced and the replacement] are explicitly mentioned, neither possesses the status of a postulator (i.e., neither functions as the locus for the operation), because it is impossible for both the state of being the object of the operation (*kāryitva*) and the state of being the cause (*nimittatva*) to coexist simultaneously in a single entity. This is also indicated by the rule: "One [substitute] takes the place of both the preceding and the following."

Otherwise, in rules such as *ād guṇaḥ*, since the fifth case (*ād*) and the seventh case (*aci*) would have to be interpreted as a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), both [the preceding and following sounds] would be established as undergoing the *guṇa* substitute, rendering those two rules redundant. Thus, Kaiyaṭa says on that point: "Because of the authority of the two sūtras, there would be two [interpretations] based on assumption;
therefore, the status of being a sixth case here is relied upon for the purpose of providing a technical indication (*jñāpana*)."

There are two instances of the fifth and seventh case-forms (*pañcamī* and *saptamī*) functioning as substitutes for the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning of "of the sixth" is "of the mutual subsequent sixth. However, just as in the case of the rule-based interpretation (*niyamapakṣa*), even in this interpretation involving the assumption of a sixth case, the determination of the application is made on the basis of priority (*paratva*) and lack of scope (*anavakāśatva*). To illustrate: in the rule *āne muk*, the seventh case (*saptamī*) has no other scope; therefore, it supersedes the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in *ato yeyaḥ*, which has already found its application in preceding rules, and instead assumes a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [i.e., interpreting *ataḥ* as *ataḥ*].

Thus, in the case of *īdāsaḥ*, the ablative (*pañcamī*) *āsaḥ* has no scope [to apply], because the locative (*saptamī*) *āne* has scope in the preceding rule. Furthermore, in the rule *tāsyanudātenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudātamahnyanyatarasyām*, the locative *sārvadhātuke* has scope in the subsequent portion for the sake of the rules concerning the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) and the suffix *sij*; therefore, the ablative *tāseḥ* and so forth alone effect the transformation into a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), resulting in the meaning: "the *lasārvadhātuka* following *syat*, *tāsi*, and so forth, is optionally unaccented. Nor should it be argued that there is no locative there because of the reading of *lasārvadhātuka* as a nominative (*prathamānta*).

This is because it will be stated [later] that, since the initial syllables of those [roots] are *anudātta*, the mention of the locative case (*saptamī*) is for the sake of [distinguishing them from] the *abhyasta* roots and the suffix *sij*. Similarly, in the rule "there is elision of *bahu*" (*bahorlopaḥ*), the ablative *bahoh*—having no other scope—indicates a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in place of the locative *iṣṭhemeyassu*; the meaning is that there should be elision of these [suffixes] when they follow *bahu*. For this very reason, there is a genitive mention in the rule "and *bhū* [replaces the final vowel] of *bahu*" (*bhūca bahoḥ*). In the rule "after *gati*, [the suffix] is marked with *ṇit*," the ablative indicates a genitive in place of the locative *sarvanāmasthāne*.

Furthermore, there is no purpose for the *ṇit*-designation of the word *go*. Nor can it be argued that the result [of this designation] is the *vṛddhi* of the preceding vowel in the example "tiṣṭhati gauḥ," because the root *sthā* is not a subordinate element (*aṅga*) with respect to the word *go*. In the rule "āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ" as well, the ablative case [in *sarvanāmnaḥ*], being without scope, causes the sixth case to be understood in place of the locative *āmī*, which has scope in the subsequent rules. It should not be argued that the ablative [in *sarvanāmnaḥ*] is already fulfilled by its coreferentiality with the [implied] ablative *āditaḥ* (from the rule *āditaśca*), resulting in the meaning "from a *sarvanāman* ending in *a*."

Nevertheless, according to the position that [the sūtras] follow the order of their enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), because of its posteriority, the rule "therefore, for the subsequent" (*tasmādityuttarasya*) applies. As it has been said:
"When there is a mention of both [the preceding and the subsequent], the mention of the ablative (fifth case) prevails due to the conflict."

This has been stated as an admission [of the opponent's position]. To exclude cases such as *varṇāśrametarāṇām*, the rule specifies that the suffix *ām* is prescribed after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Furthermore, for the sake of forms such as *yeṣām*, it is explained that [the suffix applies] when it follows an *a*-vowel. However, if one were to explain it as "after a pronoun ending in an *a*-vowel," then it would not apply in cases like *yeṣām*. In the rule regarding the long vowel (*dīrghāt*), however, the ablative case is used in place of the genitive due to Vedic irregularity (*chāndasavyatyaya*). Consequently, the augment *tuk* applies only to the long vowel and not to the suffix *cha*; this is also indicated by the evidence of the rule: *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyā*.

Otherwise, after the letter *cha*, when the substitution of *tu* would apply, the substitution of *ścu* would occur; then, by the rule "before a *khar* [consonant], there is *car*," the substitution of *ca* would result, leading to two *ca* letters.

But surely, even in the rule for the prescription of suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*), such as "from *gup*, *tij*, and *kit*," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would effect the conversion of the nominative "san" into a genitive; and one should not say that this is an acceptable consequence because there is no other substitute for it, and thus no fault arises when "san" itself is the substitute for "san. For in this case, the original element (*sthānin*) alone is specified, and since there is no formal instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding a substitute, the designation of an *it* (indicatory letter) is untenable. Furthermore, since the original element is understood at the very moment of its production as being already inclined toward cessation, the designation of an *it* cannot apply to it.
On this point, they say:

Since the ablative case [in the rule *sārvadhātuke yaṅ*] has its function exhausted by producing the suffix *san* as qualified by "priority" (*paratva*), it lacks the capacity to serve as a *prakalpaka* (a factor that determines the application of a grammatical operation). Indeed, the genitive case is an *anuvāda-vibhakti* (a restatement case), and such a case applies only to that which is already established. Furthermore, in the context of prescribing an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*), there is no possibility of a restatement because that [prior state] has not yet been established. Moreover, a *paribhāṣā* (technical maxim) which functions to restrict what is otherwise unrestricted cannot properly apply when there is no possibility of non-restriction arising. Therefore, in the prescription of an affix, ablative cases do not function as *prakalpaka*s.
"A word's own form [is its name], except for a technical term [in grammar]. (Pāṇini 1.1.68).
Dīkṣita explains that in the science of grammar, a word's own form is the named entity (*saṃjñin*), provided it is not itself a technical term (*saṃjñā*).

The modern grammarians (*navya*), however, maintain that since forms ending in the nominative case are seen to provide the name (*saṃjñā*) in rules such as *aṇuditsavarṇasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), while forms ending in the genitive case are seen to provide the named entity (*saṃjñin*), the meaning of this rule is: "A word's own form shall be its name."
And likewise, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule concerning the elision of suffixes (*pratyayalopa*), it is stated:

"If it is the case that 'the word's own form (*svarūpa*) is its technical name (*saṃjñā*),' then the form *han* will also be the name for the root *han*; [but] here too, the form is the name of the word. Haradatta, however, explained: "The word 'to be grasped' (*grāhya*) is to be supplied. In the phrase 'of the word' (*śabdasya*), the genitive case is used according to the rule 'the agent of verbal nouns ending in kṛtya-affixes is optionally expressed by the genitive. Thus, the meaning is that the word causes its own form to be grasped. Furthermore, the word 'form' (*rūpa*) refers to the genus (*jāti*) residing in words such as 'fire' (*agni*). And the connection with grammatical operations occurs through the individual instances (*vyakti*)."
Therefore, by the rule *agner ḍhak*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied only after the word *agni* and not after the word *vahni*.

Why [is the word] *aśabda* used? It is so that in rules such as *upasarge ghoḥ*, the actual form of the word *ghu* is not understood; rather, only those verbal roots (*dhātu*) whose forms are *dā* and so forth are to be grasped. Consequently, the suffix *kip* is not applied to the root *ghu* because its meaning is "sound. Furthermore, the term *svapada* refers to whatever specific word is employed in a given context. The compound *śabde śāstre saṃjñā* is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*). This is because, in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the word-form being grasped even when technical names refer to meanings such as "object" (*karman*) and so forth.

But surely, even without the apprehension of its meaning, that very word itself should be grasped by its own name; for it is independent of instruction regarding its cognition, it is unique (asādhāraṇa), it is internal (antaraṅga), and its presence is invariably established. On the other hand, the object of meaning depends on the apprehension of the word's power (śakti) for its cognition; it is common (sādhāraṇa) because it can be understood through synonyms, it is external (bahiraṅga) because it is the object of knowledge produced by the cognition of the word, and its presence is not invariably established because it is not understood during the state of imitation (anukaraṇa).

On this point, they say: even in this context, the mention of *rūpa* (form) is intended to indicate that [the term *arthavat*] is meant to be understood here as well. By this, the principle "when there is the mention of something meaningful (*arthavat*), that which is meaningless (*anarthaka*) is not included" is established. Since meaning belongs to the object by virtue of the indicator (*jñāpaka*), and form belongs to the word because of the expression "form, form" (*rūpaṃ rūpam*), the inclusion of *arthavat* is established. Consequently, in cases such as *kāśe*, the status of being a *pragṛhya* (as indicated by the rule for *śe*) does not apply, and so forth. However, where a word is not relied upon in its meaningful form, this principle does not apply.
For example, in the case of the mention of phonemes (*varṇa*), such as the substitution of *etva* for *ṭi*; by that, the substitution of *etva* occurs even for that which is meaningless.

On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya says: This [objection] need not be undertaken. For in common usage, a word conveys its meaning through a relationship characterized by semantic fitness (*yogyatā*). Even in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), in cases such as *paśuḥ*, *apatyam*, *devatā*, *prāñcaḥ*, and *udañco bharatāḥ*, it is the meaning itself that is understood. However, in rules such as *agner ḍhak*, since it is impossible for an affix (*pratyaya*) to exist in temporal sequence with a meaning, it is the word-form itself that is understood; this is also because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) *ṅy-āp-prātipadikāt*.

Nor is this [sūtra] commenced for the purpose of [excluding] that which lacks the designation *aśabda*; for, precisely because the designation *ghu* is being introduced, there is no inclusion of the verbal root *ghu*, since it has been stated that "the restriction is for the sake of linguistic usage. By this, the analysis of *kumārīgha* as having the short vowel by the rule "gharūpa" [Pāṇini 6.3.43], where [the *ghu*] is the counter-positive of the absence, is explained. However, in the rule "ī halyaghoḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.113], the word *ghu* is not included simply because it does not end in the vowel *a*. This is because, in the absence of a negative exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the very possibility of its inclusion would entail its exclusion.

Nor is it for the purpose of making known the *paribhāṣā* "the mention [of a word] includes that which possesses the meaning," because that is established by logic (*nyāya*). For it is a general rule that an object is presented as qualified by its word; since an operation (*kārya*) applied to a qualified entity (*viśeṣya*) would be obstructed, it must be stated that the operation applies to the word functioning as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, rather than requiring the abandonment of the meaning, it is more appropriate that the word, as a qualifier, serves as the regulator of the operation.

And by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), that very word is grasped, and not its synonym, because the latter is not present (*anupasthitatvāt*). For this very reason, in cases such as *āgneyam*, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) arises through the word "Agni" itself when it is employed, and not through another synonym; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the section titled "The Word of the Injunction Being the Mantra" (*vidhiśabdasya mantratve*). By this, the maxim "Those whose word-meanings are manifested... and the distinction between the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhya*) are also explained. This is because the secondary meaning is not initially present.

Nor is there a need for the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *svaṃ rūpam* in the subsequent four sūtras, since they can be accounted for even without it. For in the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*, the inclusion of the [phoneme] itself is established because it is homogeneous with itself; otherwise, in forms such as *avāttām*, the elision prescribed by *jhalo jhali* would be untenable, as the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti-bheda*) is easily available here as well. The same applies to the rule concerning the *tapara* [phonemes]. In the case of *ādirantyena*, the matter is settled by the recurrence of the word *ādi*; the evidence for this is the prohibition in *nādici*.

Otherwise, in the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *akaḥ*, there would be no inclusion of the vowel *a*; consequently, since that [substitution] would not even arise, the prohibition [in the following rule] would be redundant. Furthermore, in the rule *yena vidhiḥ—*, the phrase *tasya ca* must be stated by the author of the Vārttika himself. Therefore, this sūtra has been rejected.

"For the sake of [denoting] specific types of trees and so forth. The term *sit* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
