Therefore, suffixes other than those marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* following *gāṅ* and the roots beginning with *kuṭ* should be treated as if they were *ṅit*. Here, the status of being a *kuṭādi* root consists in being uttered immediately after the utterance of *kuṭ*. And that [status] exists only among the *kuṭādi* roots themselves. Nevertheless, by means of a possessive *bahuvrīhi* compound based on that quality (*tadguṇa-bahuvrīhi*), there is also the cognition of *kuṭ* itself through its form as "being a *kuṭ*."

Nor should it be argued that there can be a cognition of the *kuṭa* (the "axe" or "wooden block") and the word-initial (*tad-*) etc., by way of a form common to both, such as being the object of a single cognition; for in the case of an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (non-co-referential) compound, the cognition must be understood as occurring precisely through a form excluded from the meanings of the constituent members of the *bahuvrīhi*. To ensure that [the meaning] is common to both [types of compounds], one must likewise assume this here as well, since in both cases the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is perceived in a single uniform manner. This is because the two-fold nature of the *bahuvrīhi* is based solely on whether the meaning of the constituent members serves as a mere qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The predecessors, however, state that there is a distinction: in an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (non-qualificative) [bahuvrīhi], the cognition occurs through a property (*dharma*) residing solely in the indicated object (*lakṣya*), whereas in an *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (qualificative) [bahuvrīhi], it occurs through a property common to both. Therefore, in the case of an *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*, they maintain that the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is indeed a property common to both the primary denotation (*śakya*) and the indicated object (*lakṣya*). For this very reason, in the context of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), Miśra and others have explained that in the expression "sound and so forth" (*śabdādi*), there is a comprehensive inclusion of all things by means of existence (*sattva*) which is co-located with the final term's difference from sound (*caramaśabdabhinnatva*) and excludes the non-real (*alīka*). Furthermore, the suffix *ṅit* is an extended application (*atideśa*). As it has been said:

"A word used in another sense conveys that meaning even without the suffix *vati*. Thus he studied [the rule]: "The substitution of *ī* occurs for the roots *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *hā* (jahāti), and *tiṣ* before a *hal*-beginning *ārdhadhātuka* affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. This refers to the substitution of the vowel *ī* caused by a *hal*-beginning *ārdhadhātuka* affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Regarding the root *kuṭ* in the sense of "crookedness": *cukuṭitha* (perfect) and *kuṭitā* (future). By the rule "before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*," there is a prohibition of *guṇa*. The roots ending with *kuṅ* in the sense of "sound" are included among the *kuṭādi* group.

Now, how is it that Amara says, "The wretched man, out of embarrassment, began to write something," and Subandhu says, "He could not be depicted even by a painting, as he was shrinking his entire body"? This is because the root *likh* is not included among the *kuṭādi* roots. For this very reason, Śrīharṣa writes, "to depict [her] in the scripts of Bhīma’s daughter.
On this point, they say: this is simply a mistake, or it may be resolved by the fact that a rule based on a specific technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Some, however, explain *kuṭādi* as a *tatpuruṣa* compound by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of two identical terms), asserting that the root *likh* is also included under the present sūtra.

This is not correct; for forms such as *lekhitā* have been cited as examples by the author of the Vṛtti, Haradatta, and others, and because such an interpretation would contradict the usage of the root form *ālekhane* found within the sūtra itself.

In this regard, three preliminary objections (*pūrvapakṣa*) have been refuted in the Bhāṣya. To explain: if the meaning were that suffixes following *gāṅ* and others should be marked with the marker *ṅ*, there would be a contradiction; for the suffix following such [roots] lacks the letter *ṅ* used as an *it*-marker. Alternatively, even if it did exist, this rule would be redundant because it would already be established by another statement. Nor can it be argued that this rule prescribes the marker only for *caṅ* and so on, because the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not being *ṇ* or *ṅ*" (*añṇit*) would otherwise be purposeless. As it has been said: "In the case of the mention of *ṅit* and *kit*, there would be no application [of the rule] due to the absence of those two. The mention of *kit* is intended to refer to what follows.

Let it be, then, that the second view is that there is a rule prescribing *hit* and *kit* by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to suffixes other than those whose original stems (*prakṛti*) are *gaṅ* and so forth. The meaning is that the letter *ṅ* of the aforementioned suffix is designated as an *it*. Because [the suffix] is prescribed as being characterized by the property of *it*, there is no requirement for a specific position—whether at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. Furthermore, the property of being an *it* serves to specify the particular grammatical operation even for those [suffixes] whose *it*-designation is not explicitly heard. Not so.

Because the properties of being *ṭit*, *kit*, and *mitt* are absent, and because a *bahuvrīhi* compound cannot convey the sense of "immediately following," the term *ṅit* must be understood as a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Consequently, by the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), there would be the undesirable consequence of substituting the letter *ṅ* for the initial sound of the subsequent element. Nor can it be argued that *caṅ* and the other suffixes, which are well-known to possess *ṅittva* in forms such as *kuṭitā*, should simply be prescribed here; for they lack the capacity to express that specific meaning. Furthermore, suffixes such as *tṛṅ* do not possess established usage (*prasiddhi*) in this context.

If one were to accept these as original injunctions (*apūrva-vidhi*) based on this very statement, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the final substitution (*antādeśatva*) by the rule *ṅicca*. Nor should it be argued that since markers (*anubandha*) effect grammatical operations while being non-existent, how can they be substitutes (*ādeśa*), given that a substitute is a positive entity and thus other [grammatical] consequences might arise; for, just as in the case of elision (*lopa*), it is possible for the letter *ṅ* bearing the *it*-designation to function as a substitute by virtue of the power of the specific rule. Furthermore, the disappearance of the letter *ṅ* is possible after the disappearance of the original element (*sthānin*). Nor is there an absence of a genitive indication (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*), because it is logical to interpret the ablative (*pañcamī*) or the nominative (*prathamā*) as having the force of a genitive. This has been stated as follows:
"If it is argued that [the rule] 'there is a prohibition of the ādeśa (substitution) when [the affix] follows,' then let the third alternative be:

'let that which follows gāṅ and the others be designated as ṅit, provided it is not ñit or ṇit. Not so! Because of the difference between the terms *kiti* and *ṅiti* derived from the word *kṅiti*, there would result a failure to recognize the bearers of the designation (*saṃjñin*). This is because a designation applies only to those things whose extent is precisely delimited; for one does not observe the nature of a designation in the utterance of a term that is either too narrow or too broad."

The designation *kit* for [the affix] after the root *vyac* is justified as being for the purpose of *saṃprasāraṇa*, because its status as belonging to the *kuṭādi* group has not been stated; and the designation *kit* for the *liṭ* [affixes] is also justified as being for the purpose of *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule "vacisvapi... etc. However, the designation *kit* for that which follows roots beginning with *māṅ* and the *kuṭādi* group would be entirely useless on account of logical necessity (*nyāya*), since in rules such as "kṅiti ca," only the etymological (*yaugika*) sense can be accepted. Furthermore, in cases such as "kiti ṅiti," only these two [technical designations] would be understood due to their being artificial (*kṛtrima*). Nor is the *ṅit*-designation of *caṅ* and other such affixes redundant.

Where there is no perception of the actual form of the technical name (*saṃjñā*), there—in those instances where *k* and *ṅit* are mentioned—the term is intended for the purpose of inclusion. As it has been said:
"In the formulation of a technical name, when *k* and *ṅit* are mentioned, there is no cognition [of the name itself] because of the difference between the words.
Therefore, it remains established that this is indeed an extension (*atideśa*).

[Objection: But in cases such as *sisṛkṣati* and *didṛkṣate*, even though the *san* suffix is prescribed as having the *kit* designation by the rule "halantācca," the augment *am* would still apply by the rule "sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti. As it has been said: "In the case of an extended application (*atideśa*), there is the contingency of the prescription of [an operation] that is prohibited by *kit*. This is because extended applications do not cause the cessation of operations dependent on their own original basis. [Reply: Not so. For the interpretation is that [the *kit* designation] does not apply when a *kit* suffix follows. As it has been said: "But it is established through the prohibition of what is otherwise applicable (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)."

Now, in cases such as *cukuṭiṣati*, there would follow the application of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because the suffix *san* is marked with the *ṅit* indicator; but this is not so, because the rule is explained as "from that which is marked with *ṅit* in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)."

In the Bhāṣya, however, by relying on the use of the suffix -vat in the sense of the locative case—as in "as if it were ṅit" (*ṅidvat*)—it is explained that the operation [of the suffix] is extended to the preceding element as if it were ṅit; therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not based on the fact that the suffix itself ends in a ṅit letter. This is supported by the Vārttika: "But it is established through the extension of the operation of the preceding element. Although the suffix -vat is not explicitly mentioned here, since an extension does not apply to every possible operation, it is understood through interpretation that the extension is intended for a specific operation.

Kaiyaṭa states that because the rule regarding the acceptance and following of instruction applies to the aforementioned case, the ātmanepada ending does not occur; thus, by implication, the sense is that this is an extension (atideśa) of the operation of the preceding [rule]. [The sūtra:
*vija iṭ* (2).

The suffix beginning with *iṭ* after the root *vij* is treated as if it were *ṅit*. By the recurrence of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) from the rule defining the technical term *vṛddhi*, the meaning "beginning with *iṭ*" is obtained. Since there is no purpose for the initial *iṭ* itself to be *ṅit*, the suffix beginning with it is what is understood. For this very reason, although the inclusion of the *iṭ* of the third-person singular ending would have been expected by the principles of "mentioning that which has meaning" (*arthavad-grahaṇa*) and "the mention of a suffix includes the suffix and not what precedes it" (*pratyayāpratyaya-paribhāṣā*), it does not occur; as the author of the Nyāsa states, this is because [the *iṭ*] lacks the status of being an initial constituent (*ādyavayava*).

Others, however, argue that since the mention of *āgama* (augment) is mandatory, and since it cannot be the cause for the designation *ṅit* (as augments do not possess properties), the mention of *ṅit* would otherwise be redundant; therefore, by means of a *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of possession), the term refers to a suffix (*pratyaya*) that possesses *iṭ*. And since *iṭ* is necessarily at the beginning of a suffix, the resultant meaning is "a suffix beginning with *iṭ*" (*iḍādipratyaya*). Consequently, they say that the continued reference to the word "beginning" (*ādi*) is superfluous.

The root *vijir* in the sense of "separation" (*pṛthagbhāve*) is not intended here, according to the commentary; however, Haradatta says this is because the augment *iṭ* is impossible [in that case]. Some, however, say that in the form *vivejitha*, the augment *iṭ* is indeed possible by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī* (Pāṇ. 7.2.13), because the status of being *kit*—which applies by the rule "after a non-conjunct, the *liṭ* suffixes are *kit*" (Pāṇ. 1.2.5)—does not apply here due to its being marked with *p*. [The root is] *ovijī* in the sense of "fear" and "trembling. This is generally preceded by the prefix *ud*. [Examples: *udvijitā*, *udvijiṣyate*. [Pāṇini 1.2.3 states: "Optionally [the *liṭ* suffixes are *kit*] after the root *ūrṇu*. 3.

The root *ūrṇ* (in the sense of "covering") belongs to the *adādi* class. An affix beginning with *iṭ* following this root may optionally be treated as having the marker *ṅ*. Thus we have *ūrṇunuvitha* or *ūrṇunavitha*, and *ūrṇuvitā* or *ūrṇavitā*. *Sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4): A *sārvadhātuka* affix that begins with a vowel (*apit*) is treated as having the marker *ṅ*. Therefore, in *tudati*, because the affix *śa* is treated as *ṅit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate short vowel. Regarding the application of a grammatical designation (*atideśa*), the suffix *vat* is prescribed only after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*), and not after words ending in the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or seventh (*saptamī*) cases. This is because the term expressing similarity (*sādṛśya-anuyogin*) is heard in the nominative case; otherwise, it would result in the possibility of using either the sixth or seventh case. Thus say the Dīkṣitas.

[Objection: "But surely, since the suffix *vat* is absent in the sūtra and is employed only in the explanatory (*vivaraṇa*) statement, it is not proper to force the words in the sūtra to have the endings of the seventh case (*saptamī*) and so forth in accordance with that [explanatory statement]. On the other hand, if one forces those endings in the explanatory statement itself, it would merely result in proving what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*). This is because the extension (*atideśa*) is obtained in the sūtra simply by the force of using two words with identical case-endings, and because there would be a contradiction with that which is being depended upon (*upajīvya*). [Response: Do not say so. Since the suffix *vat* is based precisely on a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), even in the explanatory statement, the case-ending found in the sūtra is possible; therefore, there is no evidence for postulating a different case-ending there as well. Kaiyaṭa’s own intention also lies precisely in this.

Now, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* [in the rule *pāṇini 1.2.4*] would be redundant. For even though the fact that *ṅvanip* is marked with *p* does not itself serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the status of *ṅit*, the fact that *caṅ* and others are marked with *ṅ* indicates the absence of the *ṅit* status for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Nor should it be argued that, by this same logic, the *ṅit* status of *tātaṅ* would indicate the absence of the *ṅit* status for *sārvadhātuka* suffixes as well; because the *p* status of *tip* serves the purpose of providing what was previously unobtained [i.e., the absence of *ṅit*]. Furthermore, an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon its own kind (*sajātīya*); therefore, there is no possibility of indicating the absence of *ṅit* status for *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.

Not so. If [the term *sajātīya*] were taken to mean "having the same object," then the suffixes *yaṅ* and *aṅ* would be indicators (*jñāpaka*) for those [suffixes] having a *luk*-elision; *nañjiṅ* for those pertaining to the present tense; *ṅvanip* for those pertaining to the past tense; *athaṅ* for those belonging to the *uṇādi* class; and *naṅ* for those having the sense of *ghañ*. Consequently, other *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes would incur the status of being *ṅit*. Nor can it be argued that "homogeneity" (*sājātya*) should be intended by means of a property not subsumed under the general category of "being a suffix" (*pratyayatva*), rather than by the aforementioned properties, because there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) [to support such a restriction].

It might be argued as follows: Is *apit* a paryudāsa (an exclusion) or a pratiṣedha (a prohibition)? Not the first; for in forms such as *cyavante* and *plavante*, after the substitution of *śap* and the replacement of the final letter by *ant* (the augment *num*), the rule *ato guṇe* applies to produce a single substitute (*pararūpa*). Since this single substitute is treated as the initial element of the following member (*ādivadbhāva*) according to the present rule, there exists a suffix that is not *pit*. Consequently, by virtue of being *ṅit*, the prohibition of *guṇa* would undesirably apply. Nor can it be said that the *guṇa* occurs prior to the *pararūpa* substitution, because the *pararūpa* is both obligatory (*nitya*) and more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the *guṇa*.

Although the single-substitute (ekādeśa) [of *i* and *a*] is a portion of the sārvadhātuka suffix, nevertheless, because it is treated as if it were the beginning (*ādivat*) with respect to what follows, the word *anta* (end) also refers to the sārvadhātuka; thus, there arises the contingency of the suffix being marked with *ṅ*. However, in the case of the third-person singular form *cyave*, since the entire sārvadhātuka suffix is replaced by a single substitute, the contingency of the suffix being marked with *ṅ* is easily established. As it has been said:
"If [the rule] 'an apit suffix is marked with ṅ' is applied, then there must be a prohibition regarding single-substitutes."

Not the second [alternative]. [In the forms] *tudāni* and *likhāni*, the augment *āṭ* is applied by the rule *āḍuttamasya picca*. Since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the *pi* (the *āṭ*) and the *apit* (the suffix) would behave like the initial element (*ādivadbhāvāt*), the prohibition of the *ṅit*-status based on the term *pit* would result. As it has been said:
"If it is argued that 'a suffix marked with *p* is not *ṅit*', then there would be a prohibition regarding the single-substitute in the first person.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "There is no fault in either case; because the single-substitute is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhavati*) for the sake of preceding operations, there is an intervention [which prevents the application of the *ṅit*-prohibition]."

Although the solution "the internal element (āṅga) prevails over that which depends on phonemes (vārṇāt)" is easily available here in the case of *cyavante*, Kaiyaṭa states that this was not relied upon because he wished to present a resolution common to both cases.
[Pāṇini 1.2.5: "The *liṭ* [affix] following a root ending in a non-conjunct consonant is *kit*."

The *liṭ* suffix following a root that does not end in a conjunct consonant shall be treated as *kit*. In *cakratuḥ*, although *guṇa* substitution would have applied by the rule "sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ," it is prohibited by the rule "kṅiti ca. Regarding forms such as *bibhidatuḥ* and *vibhiduḥ*, the *kit*-treatment of *liṭ* is obligatory, whereas *guṇa* is non-obligatory. In cases such as *vavṛte* and *vavṛdhe*, both [the *kit*-treatment and the *guṇa*] are non-obligatory.

Once *kit*-status has been established, just as with the *guṇa* [substitution], once the *guṇa* has been applied, the *kit*-status would also not apply because it follows after a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) due to the replacement of the vowel by *ra*. Consequently, by virtue of its higher status, the *guṇa* alone would occur; thus, this rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is initiated. Nor should it be argued that, just as the *guṇa* is blocked for the *ksa* suffix by the force of its *kit*-status, so too here it is blocked by the force of the extended application (*atideśa*); for in the case of making *ksa* a *kit*, there is no purpose [for the *kit*-status], as it would be without scope (*anavakāśa*).

But here, since the purpose is already accomplished by means of *samprasāraṇa*, and because the prohibition of *guṇa*—which would apply only through a weak extended application (*atideśa*)—is itself weak, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) with *guṇa* is untenable. The case of *tātaṅ* should also be considered here. Therefore, relying on the word *para* as denoting that which is desired, the author of the *Vārttika* undertakes this composition in order to clarify the very meaning already encompassed by the *Sūtra*.

It might be argued: "The *ṅit*-ness of a suffix having *gāṅ* etc. as its base, and the *kit*-ness [of a suffix] in rules such as *asaṃyogāt* etc., are extended [by analogy]. What is the reason for this disparity, since it would be more appropriate to extend only one or the other in both cases? By this, even the original instruction (*upadeśa*) is explained. To this, the Vārttika states: "The purpose of having separate indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) is: (1) the absence of vocalization (*asamprasāraṇa*) for roots such as *vac*, *svap*, and *yaj*; (2) the prescription of *guṇa* for the root *jāgr* before *sārvadhātuka* affixes and in forms such as *caṅ*; (3) the prohibition of *iṭ* for roots of the *kuṭādi* class; and (4) the prohibition of *kit*-ness for the suffix *ktvā*."

Just as in *supta* and so forth, there would be *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) in cases such as *svapita*. Furthermore, regarding *caṅ* and other suffixes, the *Bhāṣya* states: "*caṅ-aṅ-najiṅ-ṅvanip-thaṅ-naṅaḥ*". Just as in *śūna* and so forth, [the suffix] would apply in *aśiśviyat* and *aśvad*; and just as in *supta* and so forth, it would also apply in *svapna*. Just as in *iṣṭavān*, it would also apply in *yajvā*. Just as in *uṣita*, it would also apply in *āvasatha*; for after the rule "after *rud* and *vid*, the suffix is *ṅit*" (*rudividibhyāṃ ṅit*), the suffix *ṅit* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule "after *vas* with a prefix, the suffix *athap*" (*upasarge vaseḥ*).

Just as in the case of *iṣṭam*, so too would it apply to *yajña*; for by the rule "yajayāca—" [Pāṇini 3.3.90], the suffix *naṅ* would be applied. Just as in the case of *jāgṛta*, so too in *jāgarita* and similar forms, there would be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the condition "when not followed by an *aṅ*" (*aṅiti*). If, in the rule prescribing *guṇa* (guṇavidhi), one were to abandon the elision of the vowel *a* (*akārapraśleṣa*), then the explanation would have to be reversed, resulting in a discrepancy between the example and the subject of the illustration. Just as in *lūtvā* and *pūtvā*, so too in *nuvitvā* and similar forms, there would be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "śryukaḥ kiti" [Pāṇini 7.2.11].

Although it has been established that the *atideśa* (extended application) applies only to the operation of the former [root], and the prohibition of *iṭ* applies only to the latter, Kaiyaṭa states that this was said merely on the grounds that, because of the mention of the locative case in *kiti* (Pāṇini 1.2.5), there would also be an *atideśa* of the prohibition of *iṭ*. Consequently, just as in *devitvā* and *sevitvā*, there would also be a prohibition of *kittva* (the status of being a *kit*) by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* in cases such as *kuṭitvā* and *puṭitvā*; for since there is no distinction between them, the *kittva* resulting from *atideśa* can be sublated just like that which is original (*aupadeśika*).

Furthermore, since being directly taught (*aupadeśikatva*) is the first to present itself, the prohibition—which finds its fulfillment by subverting that—how could it possibly subvert the *kit*-status that is extended by rule (*ātideśika*)? Therefore, one should not argue that the scriptural injunction "one should not harm any living beings," which finds its fulfillment by prohibiting violence prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*), does not apply to the violence enjoined in such passages as "one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma. This is because the extension [of the rule] applies only to what has not yet been obtained; the intended meaning here is that the extension of the *kit*-status would simply not occur in the case of the suffix *ktvā*.

If the particle *ca* were taken in its literal sense, its meaning would be a conjunction with the prohibition of *iṭ*. Consequently, just as in *lūtvā* and *pūtvā*, there would also be a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* in forms such as *nuvitvā* and *dhuvitvā* (from the roots *ṇū* "to praise" and *dhū* "to shake"). It is for this very reason that the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* uses the expression *pariṇūtākhilodayaḥ*.

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), however, says: this is not the purpose [of the rule]. Even if there were an extension (*atideśa*) of the *ṅit*-status, since the original (*aupadeśika*) *kit*-status still exists, the prohibition would apply, resulting in the correct forms being only *dhūtvā* and *nūtvā*. This is because there is no contradiction, and the *kit*-status inherent to the root itself is not removed. Nor does it follow that the *kit*-status is sublated by the *ṅit*-status according to the principle of "that which applies where the other does not" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), for in cases such as *kuṭitā*, the extension of the *ṅit*-status is not initiated when the *kit*-status is absent. [This is stated] in the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.6).

The roots *indhī* in the sense of "shining" and *bhū* in the sense of "existence": after these, the *liṭ* suffix shall be marked with the *k* indicator (*kit*). The inclusion of *indhī* is for the sake of [avoiding] the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) restriction, while that of *bhavati* is for the sake of [avoiding] the *pit* restriction.

But is it not the case that the mention of *babhūva* in the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.5] is for the purpose of prescribing *kit*-ness? For, since the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115) has a specifically indicated locus (*nirdiṣṭasthānikatā*), the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] by "kṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5) does not apply there. Nor should it be argued that, by the force of *kit*-ness, there would be a prohibition even of *vṛddhi* not characterized by *iṅ*; for [the prescription of *kit*-ness] serves its purpose by prohibiting *guṇa* in the case of *thali* as in *babhūvitha*, and in the case of the first person singular *ṇal* as in *ahaṃ babhūva*, when *ṇit*-ness is absent.
On this point, there is a Vārttika:

"Because *indh-* is restricted to the Vedic domain (*chandas*), and because the *vuk* augment after *bhū-* is obligatory, the rule prescribing the *kit* status for the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix would be rendered useless.

This is a refutation of the aforementioned sūtra. For indeed, there is no *liṭ* immediately following *indh-* at all, due to the intervention of *ām* by the rule "ijādeśca gurumataḥ. However, in the Veda, because of the exclusion "not in a mantra" (*amantre*), even in the absence of *ām*, as in the case of *samīdhe*, the *liṭ* is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* by the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*). Consequently, by the rule "a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is not marked with *P* is *ṅit*," the *n* is elided. Furthermore, because it is a *sārvadhātuka*, there is an absence of the *śnam* augment. And thus says the mantra: [Mantra follows]

Kaiaṭa and others maintain that the intent [of the rule] is that there is no possibility of the *liṭ* occurring immediately preceded by *indh* in the colloquial (*bhāṣā*) language— as seen in the examples, "O Agni, the seer Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, kindled thee" and "one should kindle him, the greatest slayer of enemies"— but not that the root *indh* is generally unused in the colloquial language. By this,

the attempt to justify the correctness of the aforementioned usage in the colloquial language even in the absence of *ām* (the periphrastic marker) on the grounds of the force of the mention of *indh* is refuted, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika.

When *bhū* is established, the suffix *vuK* applies because it is obligatory (*nitya*). Nor is *vuK* non-obligatory due to the application of another rule (*śabdāntaraprāpti*), because that which is modified in one part remains essentially the same (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*). Furthermore, its obligatoriness is not lost because it applies both when [the condition for the other rule] has been applied and when it has not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*). This is because the term *or* from the rule "oḥ supi" does not recur here; moreover, once *vuK* is applied, there is no possibility for *guṇa* to apply.
[The roots] *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, and *vas* take the suffix *ktvā*. (Pāṇini 1.2.7)

It would be *kitsyāt*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition of the *kit* designation which will be stated later in the rule *na ktvā seṭ*. [The roots are: *mṛḍa* (to comfort), *mṛda* (to crush), *gudha* (to envelop) and *gudha* (to be angry), *kuṣa* (to extract), *kliśa* (to afflict) and *kliśū* (to afflict)—both the *divādi* and *krayādi* groups are included here. *vada* (to speak clearly), *vasa* (to dwell). *uṣitvā*: [the augment] *iṭ* is added after *vas* and *kṣu*; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajādi* group.

On this point, the commentary states: "The rule *na ktvā seṭ* need not be formulated. Let this rule serve as a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) to the effect that the suffix *ktvā* following roots such as *mṛḍ* and others alone is *kit*, and not after any other roots. Nor does there arise the contingency of a contrary restriction—that the *ktvā* following *mṛḍ* and others is *kit* while the *niṣṭhā* suffixes and others are not—because grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is rooted in actual usage, and thus an undesired restriction cannot be established."

Nor should it be argued that there would be an impossibility of *kittva* even in cases such as *lūtvā* and *pūtvā*, because the restriction would apply to *ktvā* in general, and since the letter *k* serves a purpose as a qualifier in the rule "kttvātosunkasunaḥ," [the restriction must be limited]. This is because the restriction begins only for *ktvā* that is followed by a *seṭ* (augmented with *iṭ*). Nor should it be argued that, according to the view of the rule "kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ," since the root *kliś* is *aniṭ*, the prescription of *kittva* for the *ktvā* following it would be for the purpose of excluding the non-*kit* status of *aniṭ* *ktvā*.

In the case of *gudha*, *kuṣa*, and *kliś*, because the optionality of *kittva* [prescribed by Pāṇini 1.2.5, "alo vyupadhād... is for the purpose of establishing obligatory *kittva*, it is impossible for that rule to serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). [Therefore, the *kittva* applies here.
Furthermore, [the suffix *ktvā*] follows *rud*, *vid*, *muṣ*, *grah*, *svap*, and *pracch* when preceded by the suffix *saṃ*. (Pāṇini 1.2.8)

By the word *ca* ("and"), the inclusion of the suffix *ktvā* is intended. [The roots included are: *rudir* (to shed tears), *vid* (to know), *muṣ* (to steal), *grah* (to seize), *ñiṣvap* (to sleep), and *pracch* (to ask). Examples: *rurudiṣati* (he wishes to weep) and *ruditvā* (having wept). Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The inclusion of *svapi* and *pracchi* is for the sake of the desiderative (*san*), for *ktvā* is indeed only [a suffix] marked with *k*. This is because the prohibition "not [a root] having *seṭ* after *ktvā*" does not apply to *suptvā* and *pṛṣṭvā*, since these roots are *aniṭ* (lacking an *iṭ* augment). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa maintains that this rule is not for the purpose of establishing the obligatory *kit*-status of *aniṭ* *ktvā*. [Now follows: *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9).

A *san* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant following a stem ending in a short vowel shall be treated as *kit*. The mention of *ktvā* has ceased to apply here; for a *san* that does not take *iṭ* is itself inherently *jhal*-initial. Thus, we have *bubhūṣati* and *didīṣate*. By virtue of being *kit*, there is a prohibition of *guṇa*. For this very reason, because it is no longer the domain of *ej* (a long vowel), the substitution of *ā* for *dīṅ* by the rule "for *mī*, *min*, and *dīṅ*" (*mīnātiminotidīṅām*) does not occur.

Nor should it be argued that the meaning of *san* is "ending in a *jhal* [consonant]," and consequently, *kittva* (the status of being *kit*) would apply only in cases like *cicīṣitā*—where there is elision of the vowel *a*—but not in cases like *cicīṣati*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the letters *s* and *a* in *san* would, by virtue of the rule regarding the "end-like nature" (*antavadbhāva*) relative to the preceding element, be considered as ending in a *jhal*. This objection is invalid, because the interpretation follows from the continued application of the mention of the word "beginning" (*ādi*). Furthermore, the root *ig* in the sense of "remembering" (*smaraṇa*) is not what is intended here; for this is known from the fact that the word *jigīṣu* is listed among the *garga*-type words in the *gaṇa*-list.

The author of the Nyāsa states that [the *s* of] *san* following *jan* would otherwise result in the impossibility of its being treated as *kit*, due to its association with the pratyāhāra *jhal*, and because a *hal* (consonant) cannot occur immediately after it, which would lead to the rule *halantācca* being inapplicable.

Regarding this, the Vārttika says: "The *ikaḥ* [rule] is *kit* so that there may be no *guṇa*; once [the *guṇa*] has been applied, [the lengthening] occurs by virtue of the introduction of the long vowel."
But [the use of] the short vowel is meaningless; rather, it would entail the application of long vowels.
For, by implication, the reduplication that is to be performed must depend upon a long vowel;
since the elision of the *ṇi* suffix cannot occur unless a long vowel has been produced, [the purpose of the rule is] the elision of *ṇi*.

The meaning of this is as follows: the intention of the objection is, "Let there be only one rule, *iko jhal halantācca*; what is the purpose of dividing the rules? To this, he states the answer according to the literal reading: "Lest there be *guṇa*. This means [lest there be *guṇa*] by the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*. Now, one might object: "In this case, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* will, by the maxim of 'that which applies where another does not' (*yenanāprāptinyāya*), serve as an exception to *guṇa*"; to this he replies: "Because of the formulation of the lengthening [rule]."

He states the answer—"it would occur when [the suffix] is applied"—in order to refute the objection that lengthening (*dīrgha*) follows from the application of the *guṇa* rule. The sense is that even though there is no difference in form, it is precisely the repeated application of the grammatical rule itself—like the recitation of a mantra—that serves as the means for attaining the result. An objection is raised: "In this case, the rule prescribing lengthening would be useless, because it is only an application preceded by the knowledge of the grammatical rule that constitutes the cause of merit (*dharma*), and not the mere operation of the rule. To this he replies: "But it is not purposeless."

He states the answer: "For the sake of the short vowels. The sense is that, although there would be no *guṇa* substitution for short vowels due to the force of the rule prescribing long vowels, there would be *guṇa* for those ending in long vowels because the rule for long vowels would not apply due to a lack of purpose; therefore, the *kit* designation is intended to prohibit that. As for the phrase "but for the long ones," the rule for lengthening indeed operates even in the case of long vowels to prohibit *guṇa*. This is because the maxim of "burning what is not yet burnt" is rooted in the absence of a [further] result; and the result in the case of short vowels is the attainment of a different form.

However, in the case of long vowels (*dīrgha*), there is no occurrence of a different form (*rūpāntara*); this is another matter. For this very reason, there is the rule for the substitution of *m* for *m* in the case of the suffix *kvip*: "mo rāji samaḥ kvau. This has been stated: "Indeed, by virtue of the [grammatical] capacity, it must be applied again. Now, one might object: "By the rule prescribing the long vowel, there would be an exclusion (*bādha*) of the *ikāra* (the short *i*) just as there is of the *guṇa*, as in *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*. For the long vowel is prescribed by the rule 'añjane' (*añj-ah ghuṭi*), while the substitution of *it* (short *i*) is intended there by the rule 'ṛta iddhātoḥ'. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The state of having *ṛt*," and so forth.

The meaning is that there is no sublation (*bādha*) of the substitution of *i* for *e* (and so on), because it possesses the property of being the counter-positive of an absence that is itself occasioned by the absence of length (*dīrghatva*). For it has been said: "That rule for which the instruction [of another] is rendered purposeless is sublated; however, that for which [the other rule] is merely the cause is not sublated. Now, one might object: even if short vowels do not undergo the substitution of *i* due to the absence of length, long vowels certainly do undergo the substitution of *i* precisely because of their absence of length. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For long vowels, [the substitution does not apply] as long as the length has not been effected."

In that case as well, the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*) must necessarily be applied in order to override the *guṇa* substitution; otherwise, because of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *guṇa* by the rule "by means of *it* and *ut*, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [are replaced] through conflict. Thus, when the futility of the *kit* designation has been established, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "But there is the elision of *ṇi*" (*ṇilopastu*). When *jñapi* + *sa* + *ti* is situated, three operations apply: *guṇa* of the *ṇi*, its elision (*lopa*), and lengthening (*dīrghatva*).

In that case, if the *kittva* (the property of having a *k* as an it-marker) were absent, then even the elision (*lopa*)—just like the *guṇa* substitution—would be sublated by the long vowel (*dīrgha*), because [the elision] would have no scope and there would be no distinction [between them]. This is because in forms such as *pāktiḥ* from *pācayati*, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix also has its own scope. According to the maxim, "Exceptions stated earlier sublate only the immediately following rules, not those that follow later," it would be the elision itself that is sublated, while the *guṇa* would certainly still occur. However, when the *kittva* is prescribed, since there is no possibility of *guṇa* in cases such as *cicīṣati*, the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) finds its scope there; consequently, by virtue of being subsequent, it sublates the elision of the *ṇi*-affix. Thus, the point is established.

It might be argued as follows: even if the *kit* designation were absent, by the principle of "that which was not applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would be the sublater of the *guṇa* substitution alone, but not of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*). Since the long vowel has its own scope through the sublation of the *guṇa*, it would simply be sublated by the subsequent *ṇilopa*; thus, the *kit* designation would be unnecessary. To this, they reply: although that may be the case when considering the sublation of specific rules, when considering sublation in general, one must accept the sublation of everything that applies within its own domain.

This might be the case: even if the *kittva* (the status of having a *k*-marker) were absent, in forms such as *animitsati* and *pramitsati*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would override the *guṇa* substitution because it is of non-occurrence (*niravakāśatva*) regarding the roots *mīnāti* and *minoti* when followed by the suffix *san*. Consequently, since *minoti* is also included under the term *mī*, the *guṇa* substitution is blocked by the fact that [the long vowel] is prescribed specifically (*pratipadavidhāna*). Subsequently, by the rule "and after a root ending in a consonant" (*halantācca*), the *kittva* blocks the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate syllable (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).

And likewise, in the case of "sanīmī," since the mention of "mī" is for the purpose of including the general form, once the rule for lengthening has achieved its purpose, then in "jñīpsati," the elision of the *ṇi* suffix will—by virtue of being subsequent—override the lengthening; thus, there is no need for the *kittva* designation.

Not so; for, according to the reasoning stated, since the long vowel (*dīrgha*) has its own scope, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the long vowel being sublated by both *guṇa* and *lopa*, and thus the introduction of the *kittva* designation is necessary. Nor should it be argued that the long vowel has no scope in roots ending in *ku*, because in the case of *cukūṣati*, the prohibition of *guṇa* is established simply by the root belonging to the *kuṭādi* class which entails *ṅittva*. For Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that, in accordance with the aforementioned *bhāṣya*, the root is determined to end in a long vowel.

Nor should it be argued that there is no scope for the roots *gup* (in the sense of "evacuating excrement") and *dhu* (in the sense of "motion and steadiness") being present participles (*sannanta*); for if that were the case, since the reading would necessarily have to be *uhanagamām* alone, the inclusion of the pratyāhāra *aj* would become redundant. Thus, the intention of the author of the Nyāsa is that even if the root *kuṅ* ends in a short vowel, there is no obstacle [to its application].
[This concludes the section on] "and after a consonant-ending [root]" (Pāṇini 6.4.10).

If the word *anta* were taken in its etymological sense of "part," there would be a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*), because an *ik* vowel cannot be a part of a consonant (*hal*). If one were to formulate the rule as "after a consonant ending in an *ik* vowel" (*igvato halantāt*), the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) would be the occurrence of *saṃprasāraṇa* in the form *pipakṣati*. If one were to formulate it as "after a consonant ending in an *ik* vowel which has a penultimate *ik*" (*igupadhāddhalantāt*), there would be over-extension (*avyāpti*) to the root *dambh*, and the rule would suffer from the fault of being split (*sūtrabheda*). Nevertheless, the word *anta* here signifies "proximity. Thus, a *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant following a consonant proximate to an *ik* vowel shall be treated as *kit*. For example: from the root *guhū* (to conceal), *jughukṣati*; from *bhidir* (to split), *vibhitsati*.

Now, in the case of *dambh* with the suffix *san*, as in *dhīpsati*, there would be no elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) because the *nakāra* is not followed by *san*, and the *bhakāra* is not in proximity to an *ik*-vowel, which would result in the absence of *kittva*.

It is said: [The status of *hal* is established] by relying on the identity of both [individual instances and the universal] of the *hal*-class (*hal-tvajāti*), because there is no loss of proximity to the vowel *i* (in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*). This has been stated: "The [term *hal*] is established because the mention of *hal* in the root *dambh* denotes the class (*jāti*). And this is indicated by the mention of the word "single" (*eka*) in the rule *nipāta ekāj*. Furthermore, the existence of the *hal*-class is established because a single cognition is produced regarding the letter *ha* and others. Even in the view that the class is nothing other than the individuals themselves with their differences set aside, the desired result is achieved by setting aside difference and relying on non-difference; so says Kaiyaṭa.

Although there is no evidence for a *jāti* (universal) distinct from the class of *hal*-ness according to the logic stated in the *Vṛddhi* sūtra, nevertheless, in the case of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the word *hal*, what is intended here is precisely that [the universal] is not delimited by any *jāti* directly pervaded by "phoneme-ness" (*varṇatva*) that exceeds those universals which function as qualifiers (*prakāratva*) for each individual [consonant] such as the letter *ha*.
[This is established by the rule: *liṅ-sicāv ātmanepadeṣu* (3.1.44).

The affixes *liṅ* (optative) beginning with a *jhal* consonant and *sic* (aorist marker), when followed by *ātmanepada* endings, are *kit* after a root ending in a *hal* (consonant). Thus: *klṛpsīṣṭa*, *klṛpsīyāstām*, *klṛpsīran*; *aklṛpta*, *aklṛpsātām*, *aklṛpsata*. Because the root is marked with *ūdit*, the augment *iṭ* is optional. Why "beginning with a *jhal*"? To ensure that in the case where *iṭ* is applied, forms such as *kalpiṣīṣṭa* and *akalpiṣṭa* do not result in *kit*-status.

It might be argued as follows: In the rule *ātmanepadeṣu*, is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇa-saptamī*) or in the sense of "in relation to" (*parasaptamī*)? Not the first, because selection pertains to members of the same class (*sajātīya-viṣayatā*), which would result in *liṅ* alone being the object of qualification; for by the term *liṅ*, there is the inclusion of its substitutes (*tad-ādeśa*). Nor the second, because even if it were a qualifier of *sic*, it would be inappropriate for *liṅ*; furthermore, if the referent of the word *liṅ* were that which is characterized by the suffix *sīyuṭ*, then it would be impossible for it to be subsequent to *liṅ* in relation to itself. Nor does it intend both meanings simultaneously, because the word is heard only once. Nor can there be an elliptical remainder (*ekaśeṣa*).

Because there is no difference in meaning and because there is no intention to express them simultaneously, the Bhāṣya on this point states: "In either case, there is no fault. To explain: the meaning is that the *liṅ* and *sic* suffixes [belong to] the *ātmanepada*. Nor is it incorrect for *sic* to be called *ātmanepada* simply because it is distinct from both [the *liṅ* and the *luṅ*], since the term *ātmanepada* is applied to *sic* figuratively by virtue of its being directed toward that [same category]. This is because one resorts to a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) based solely on the formal similarity between the primary and secondary senses of the word *ātmanepada*. There is likewise no fault in the second interpretation, either; for the sequence belonging to the parts is superimposed upon the whole, or else both meanings are obtained through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application).

However, it is only the *sij* [augment] that is qualified by the term "ātmanepada" due to the principles of possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), but not the *liṅ* [optative suffix]. This is because, among the *parasmaipada* suffixes, the *liṅ* lacks the initial *jhal* [consonant], and since the application of the term "ātmanepada" would thus be established for it even without the explicit mention, the qualification "ātmanepada" would be redundant.

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is *sic* also specified as a qualifier of *ātmanepada*? [Is it not sufficient to say *ikaḥ*? Because in forms such as *ayākṣīt*, there is exclusion by the word *ikaḥ* alone; in forms such as *acaṣīt*, the same result follows simply because there is no vowel (*ac*) following the root; and in forms such as *akoṣīt*, once the augment *iṭ* has been applied, there is an absence of the condition of beginning with a *jhal* consonant. Furthermore, in forms such as *abhaitsīt*, since the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by the rule "vadavraja" (Pāṇini 7.2.3) does not have the *ik* as its defining characteristic, the prohibition by the rule "viṅati ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5) does not apply; thus, even though there is *kittva*, there is no harm. Do not say so. For in forms such as *asrākṣīt* and *adrākṣīt*, there would follow the impossibility of the augment *ām*, which is characterized by the rule "sṛjidṛśoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.58).

12. *u* and [the suffixes] previously mentioned are treated as having the *kit* designation when they follow a root ending in *ṛ* and begin with a *jhal* consonant. [Examples: *bhṛṣīṣṭa*, *bhṛṣīyāstām*, *bhṛṣīran*; *abhṛta*, *abhṛṣātām*, *abhṛṣata*. 13. The [suffix *liṅ*] after the root *gam* is optionally [treated as *kit*].

The two previously mentioned [roots] *gam* and *han*, when followed by suffixes beginning with a *jhal* consonant, are optionally treated as having the *kit* designation. Thus: *saṅgasīṣṭa* (with *kit*), *saṃgaṃsīṣṭa* (without *kit*); *samagata* (with *kit*), *samagaṃsta* (without *kit*). In the case of the *kit* alternative, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopaḥ*). *Sic* follows *han*: 14. The suffix *sic* following the root *han* is treated as *kit* when an *ātmanepada* suffix follows. Thus: *āhata*, *āhasātām*, *āhasata*. The repetition of the term *sic* is for the purpose of indicating the maxim: "Those elements specified in a single grammatical rule either apply together or cease together. Consequently, in the two preceding rules, the full rule "the *liṅ* and *sic* [are *kit*] in the *ātmanepada*" is understood to carry over.

The suffix *sic* may optionally be applied after the root *yam* when used with the sense of "hinting" (*gandhana*). Hinting is the disclosure of another's faults. Example: *udāyata*. Why [is it] "when used with the sense of hinting"? Example: *udāyaṃsta pādān*. The meaning is "he dragged. Rule 16: Optionally so when used with *upayama* (marriage).

As before: Rāma obtained Sītā; he acquired the great weapons (*mahāstra*). [Pāṇini 1.2.17] *sthā* and *dhvṛ* take the augment *i*, and the suffix *sic* is *kit*; furthermore, there is the substitution of *i* for the final vowel and the following consonant. *samasthita*, *samasthiṣātām*, *sāmasthiṣata*; *adita*, *ādiṣātām*, *adiṣata*.

Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "If [the vowel] *i* were [meant to be included], why would there be the substitution of *t* for *k*, when even without it the long vowel [would apply]? Furthermore, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel should not occur in the immediate [context], yet the protracted is prescribed in its specific domain."

Furthermore, since there is no employment of a word expressing a cause (*hetu*) here, the rule "ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge" (Pāṇini 2.3.26) does not apply; consequently, there is no occasion for the third case ending (*hetutṛtīyā*) to arise in the phrase "of what? (*kasya*). This is because, in this context, [the relationship] is intended to be expressed solely as a general relation (*sambandhitva*). Just as in the expression "my sons" (*madīyāḥ putrāḥ*), the suffix *cha* arises in the sense of a general relation, because there is no intention to express the specific mode of being an offspring (*apatyatva-prakāraka-vivakṣā*). In the rule "takārettvam," the suffix *tva* follows a *karmadhāraya* compound. [The commentary states: "Let there not be a long vowel."

Because of the closest similarity (*āntaratamya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the substitute] would be that very same [vowel]. The rebuttal—"A vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)"—has not been stated; for the reason that in forms such as *amūbhyām*, even the vowel *ū* being taught is seen to be inclusive, and because there exists another solution. Regarding the phrase "even without it": since the substitution of *ī* is already established by rules such as *ghumāsthā*, the long vowel will not occur simply by the force of the prescription of the short *i*; thus, the *kittva* (the property of having the marker *k*) must indeed be prescribed.

Otherwise, even the rule *ghumāsthā* would not apply. He states another purpose: "So that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not occur in the immediate [subsequent] position. And that principle will be made known by the mention of the suffix *cha* in the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of *cha* after *bilvaka*, etc. Alternatively, once the *it*-designation of the vowel *ā* has been applied, the *vṛddhi* and *ay* substitutions take place; for even though the *vṛddhi* is blocked by the augment *yuk*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the *ik* vowel remains possible. Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *jagmivān* and *jaghnivān*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) would not occur; for this is established by the fact that the *kittva* (the status of having a *k* as an indicatory letter) is extended [to the *kvasu* suffix] by analogy. Kaiyaṭa, however, says: "In this case, once the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) has been applied, and after reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the single-substitute rule (*ekādeśa*), the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *vasvekājāddhasām*. For there, because of the prohibition of *kittva* (the *kit* designation), the *nalopa* is prevented; then, when *nuṭ* is applied due to the presence of two consonants (*dvihaltva*), the status of being a single vowel (*ekāctva*) is lost, which causes the *iṭ* to be withdrawn. Since it follows that the mention of *ktvā* should not be made, he says: "The mention of *gṛh*" [is for this purpose]. [Examples are] *nigṛhītiḥ*, *upasnihitiḥ*, and *nikucitiḥ*. Now, he rejects the mention of *ktvā*: "And *ktvā*," because of the "separation" (*vigrahāt*), that is, the division of the *yoga*—namely, "from the root *pū*."

After the root *pūṅ*, the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not *kit* when followed by a *seṭ* augment. Consequently, [the rule] "and *ktvā*" applies; the term "*pūṅ*" is no longer in force here. The meaning is that the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not *kit* when it is *seṭ*. [The rule] "The *niṣṭhā* [suffix is not *kit* after] *śīṅ*, *svidi*, *midi*, *kṣvidi*, and *dhṛṣ*" [applies]; the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not *kit* when *seṭ*. Examples: *śayitaḥ*. [In this case], the *iṭ* is optional according to the rule "Optionally [after roots ending in long *ī*] in the sense of state (*bhāva*) and beginning action (*ādikarman*)... Thus we have *prasveditaścaitraḥ* (Caitra has sweated) and *prasvinnaḥ* (sweated), etc. Why specify "*seṭ*" [in the rule]? [Consider: *prasvinnaṃ tena* (he has sweated). In the sense of state (*bhāva*), there is only *kit*-ness [of the suffix].

The *niṣṭhā* suffix, when it takes the augment *iṭ*, is not *kit* after a root having *u* as its penultimate letter, provided it denotes either a state (*bhāva*) or the beginning of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*). Thus, one says *dyotitam* or *dyutitam* by him; likewise, *pradyotitaḥ* or *pradyutitaḥ* [the sun]. The *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) and the sense of the state (*bhāve*) according to the rule "the *kta* suffix is used in the sense of the agent and in the sense of the beginning of an action. This [prohibition of *kit*] is desired only for roots that take the *śap* verbal class marker (*śabvikaraṇa*); here [it does not apply], so we have *gudhitam*. Furthermore, the *ktvā* suffix and the *niṣṭhā* suffix are not *kit* after the root *pūṅ*. (Pāṇini 1.2.22) The *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* suffixes are not *kit*.

But surely, by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rules *seṭ* and *anyatarasyām*, there would be an optional *kit* status only for those *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* suffixes that are marked with *iṭ*. Consequently, forms such as *puvitvā* and *puvita* would occur as alternative options, because of the optionality of *iṭ* prescribed by the rule *pūṅaḥ śca*.
Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "Or rather not [is there an issue], because the property of being *seṭ* depends on the absence of *kit*; or, when *iṭ* is absent, there is *kit* status."

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the rule for *iṭ*, the sūtra "pūṅśca" need not be commenced. By that [sūtra], this optional *kit* status applies only to the *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* suffixes when they are *aniṭ*. In the case where they have *kit* status, due to the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "śryukaḥ kiti," the forms *pūtvā* and *pūtaḥ* are established; in the absence of that [prohibition], however, with the application of *iṭ* and *guṇa*, the forms *pavitvā* and *pavitaḥ* are established.

The followers of Bhāradvāja, however, read: "There is always non-ṅit-ness for [roots] beginning with *iḍ* and others; the mention of *ktvā* is for the sake of what follows. Disregarding brevity (*lāghava*), the author of the Sūtras read "and *pū*" in the rule prescribing *iṭ*. Here, it is established that there is no recurrence of the option (*vikalpa*) because of the mention of *vā* in the subsequent rule; thus the desired result is achieved. This is merely an exposition of the intention of the Sūtras. Kātyāyana, however, rejected that Sūtra on the grounds of brevity according to the aforementioned method.

[The rule] "after a root ending in *ra* or *la*, having *u* or *i* as its penultimate letter, and beginning with a consonant, there is optionally *sa*" (Pāṇini 1.2.26).

Is this [the rule] an injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) regarding the *kit* designation? Not the first, because the mention of *ktvā* would be redundant; for in that case, the *kit* designation is already established. Nor the second, because the mention of *saṅ* (the suffix *san*) would be redundant; for it is itself not a *kit*. Do not say so; since the prohibition of *kit* status by the rule "na tkvā seṭ" applies here, it is more appropriate that this be an injunction.

The suffixes *san* (desiderative) and *ktvā* (gerundive), when followed by the augment *iṭ*, are optionally *kit* after a root ending in a consonant that has either *u* or *i* as its penultimate letter (upadha). Examples: *didyutiṣate* (he wishes to shine), *dyotiṣate*; *dyutitvā* (having shone), *dyotitvā*. Why "ending in a consonant" (*ralaḥ*)? Consider *dideviṣati* (he wishes to play), *devitvā*. Why "having *u* or *i* as its penultimate letter" (*vyupadhāt*)? Consider *vartitvā* (having turned), *vivartiṣate*. Why "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? Consider *eṣitvā* (having sought), *eṣiṣiṣati*.

In this system, even though doubling (*dvitva*) is a permanent [rule], it is superseded by a *guṇa* substitution; for by the marking of the root *oṇ* as having an *ṛdit* vowel, it is indicated that the operation concerning the penultimate vowel (*upadhākārya*) generally possesses greater force than doubling. Why include *seṭ*? [Answer: As in *bhuktvā* and *bubhukṣate*. The inclusion of the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) is for the sake of clarity, since a root ending in a consonant never fails to have a penultimate vowel. 27. A vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *ū*, *u*, or *u3* (long, protracted, or prolated) is respectively termed short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), or prolated (*pluta*).

The term *ūkāla* should be explained as "that which has the duration of *ū*," just like the expression *tatkāla*. Vowels (*ac*) consisting of one, two, or three morae (*mātrā*) are designated respectively as short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*). Although this is a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the masculine gender is used according to Pāṇinian convention. Nor is there a lack of authority for specifying three distinct designations; for these three terms serve as the indicators (*liṅga*) for the designations themselves. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the designations "short," "long," and "protracted" constitute a single unified designation; for subsequent usage employs the words "short" and so on individually, and thus the whole lacks the status of a single technical name (*saṃjñā*).

This might be argued: "In the stated sequence for the designation of technical names (*saṃjñā*), there is no restrictive rule. Nor can it be said that the *pluta* vowel is designated first; for without its designation at the end as having three morae (*trimātra*), it would lack the name *pluta*, and the status of *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) would be cast far away. By this, the claim that the short vowel (*hrasva*) is designated prior to the name *ghisaṃjñā* is also refuted, since the name *hrasva* itself depends upon being designated earlier."

Not so; for there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ*, which prescribes a protracted vowel (*pluta*) for a one-moraic (*mātrika*) vowel. For if [the term *heḥ*] were specified at the end of the duration of a mora, then by the application of the technical term *pluta* to that very [one-moraic vowel], the prescription of a one-moraic vowel for a one-moraic vowel would be redundant. Nor is it for the purpose of prescribing a dissimilar substitute (*visadṛśādeśa*), because it is impossible to set aside the directly perceived maxim of closest similarity (*antaratamaparibhāṣā*). Furthermore, the specification of the one-moraic vowel at the end is itself ambiguous.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, the short vowel would still be specified in the middle; for there is an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rules "ato dīrgho yañi" and "supi ca," which ordain lengthening. For if the one-measure (*mātrika*) vowel were specified in the middle, it would be as redundant as before.

Nor should it be argued that the two-measure (*dvimātra*) vowel would be specified at the end; for by the rule "om abhyādāne," the *pluta* (three-measure) is ordained for the two-measure vowel. Since redundancy would result as before, the short vowel is excluded by these two indicators—the final and the middle—and thus, by elimination, its specification at the beginning is established. This constitutes the settled determination of the technical names (*saṃjñin*).

It might be argued as follows: since a short vowel (*hrasva*) is *aṇ*, it would follow that the designation "short" (*hrasva-sañjñā*) would apply even to vowels of two or three morae (*mātrā*) because they are included among those homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds; however, since those [long and protracted vowels] are not *aṇ*, there is no fault of the designation "long" (*dīrgha*) or "protracted" (*pluta*) applying to a short vowel.

On this point, the Vārttika states: "But it is established by the mention of the *tapara* [term]. One should read the rule as *udūkālaḥ*. And because of the *tapara* suffix, [the long and protracted vowels] do not possess the status of being denoters (*grāhaka*).

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that when the *tapara* marker is used for the quick (*druta*) pronunciation, it would necessitate a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the medium (*madhya*) and slow (*vilambita*) pronunciations; for this has already been resolved in the *tapara-sūtra* by the statement: "The phonemes (*varṇa*) remain established as they are, but their modes (*vṛtti*) are distinguished by the speaker’s utterance being either long or short."

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), however, says: "There is no fault because of the mention of 'time' (kāla). Even when it is stated that *u* is *ac*, since there is no deviation in qualifying the letter *u* and others by their status as *ac*, they would become redundant; therefore, by implication, the vowels (*ac*) are qualified by *u* and the others themselves. Although the inclusion of a vowel similar to those [like *u*] is thus established through its being of the same duration (*kālatva*), the explicit mention of 'time' is for this purpose: that the qualification of time should apply only to the actually heard letter *u*, and not also to the other homogeneous letters (*savarṇa*) included by that [mention of *u*]."

Since a vowel of six measures (*mātra*) is impossible and because three technical designations (*saṃjñā*) are established, the word *kāla* (time/measure) is connected even with the single-measure vowel *u*. Alternatively, in the *grahaṇaka-śāstra*, the phrase "not a designation of a word" (*na śabda-saṃjñā*) should be understood as carrying over; thus, when a designation of a word is to be prescribed, an *aṇ* does not include its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), and so there is no fault. Furthermore, since qualities do not effect differentiation, vowels of one measure (*mātrika*) that possess accents such as acute (*udātta*) and so forth also receive the designation of "short" (*hrasva*).

However, since the mention of *at* has ceased in the definitions of *udātta* and so forth, the designation [of *svara*] is established for long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels as well. Nor does this result in the same designation applying to consonants (*hal*), because they are unsuitable [for such a designation]. Furthermore, rules such as "iko yaṇ aci" are not injunctions establishing designations; rather, they are restatements (*anuvāda*) of designations prescribed by the rule "ādirantyena. Thus, there is no fault.

Alternatively, by virtue of the power of the rule prescribing the designation "short" (*hrasva*), the designation "short" does not apply to long (*dīrgha*) or protracted (*pluta*) vowels. For if all three were designated as "short," then in the various rules concerning short vowels, all three would be present; consequently, when a substitute is prescribed according to the principle of closest similarity (*antarataama*), the designation "short" would be rendered useless. Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the specific statement, even a non-closest similar vowel might serve as the substitute; for in that case, one would have to state simply "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*) instead, since there would be no specific result achieved by the designation "short."

If it is argued: "Surely, if the designation *hrasva* (short) did not exist, then in those instances where a short vowel is prescribed for an *ec* vowel, one would have to state the rule as *eca ig* in each individual application; but since the designation exists, one can simply say once and for all, *eca ig hrasvādeśe*, which is more concise"—this is not so. For in that case, there would be four words: one for the designation and three for the other [rules], whereas in the formulation *eca ig hrasvādeśe*, there would be eight words (four for the designation and four for the rule). However, if one were to state *eca ig* in the three locations where it applies, there would be only six words. Thus, the argument fails because it results in the opposite of brevity.

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that there are ten words? For, regarding the root *heḍ* in the sense of 'to surround' (*veṣṭane*), the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.92] must be stated to account for the form *hiḍayati*; and regarding the sense of 'having agreed' (*paramanumanya*), the rule *khityanavyayasya* [Pāṇini 6.3.66] must be stated to account for the form *heḍaḥ*, since the rule *eca ig* [Pāṇini 1.1.48] would otherwise apply. Thus, even if one counts *āṅ* separately in the rule *hrasvādeśe* [Pāṇini 6.3.43], there is no relief from this. Even if the result were nine words, it is more parsimonious than ten. [This objection is raised.]

On this point, Kaiyaṭa says: "The Bhāṣya is intended to indicate brevity [of expression]. For even though there is verbal prolixity in employing the rule *'eCa iK'* five times, there is no loss of brevity in comprehension. Thus it is established that since the desired result is achieved through the more concise formulation, the prescription of the short vowel (*hrasva*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the designation *hrasva* does not apply to vowels of two or three morae (*mātrā*).
*Acaśca* || 28 ||

Where there is an injunction by means of the terms *hrasva*, *dīrgha*, or *pluta*, the word *acaḥ* (genitive singular of *ac*) stands as a governing element (*upatiṣṭhate*). Both the view that it is a "supplementary rule" (*taccheṣapakṣa*) and the view that it is an "exception" (*tadapavādapakṣa*) have been rejected here in the Bhāṣya. To explain: if there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) such that "rules apply to the final [element], and short, long, and protracted vowels belong to the final [vowel]," then it is the supplementary rule view. However, if there is syntactic division (*bhinnavākyatva*), such that "short and other vowels may belong to either the final or the non-final [vowel]," then it is the exception view.

Regarding the first fault, the *Vārttika* states: "If it is argued that by the rule *alo'ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], the substitution of short vowels and so forth applies only to the final letter, then there must be an explicit mention of the vowel (*ac*) in the cases of *vac*, *pracch*, *śam* and others, as well as in *han*, *gam*, and the long vowels. For example: *vāk*, *prāṭ*, *śāmyati*, *klāmyati*, *jighāṃsati*, and *jigāṃsati*. Since the vowel is not the final element [in these forms], the lengthening would not occur; therefore, in each such instance, the word "vowel" (*ac*) would have to be explicitly stated. Regarding the second fault as well: "If it is argued that [the rule] applies to the vowel (*ac*), then there must be a prohibition against [applying it to] non-final vowels in the case of neuter short vowels, *kṛt* suffixes, *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, and the long vowels of *nām*."

Otherwise, the family [of grammarians] would be divided by [the objection] regarding the six [roots], and the aforementioned rules would also apply here. In the explanation that "when there is a root beginning with *y*, [the vowel] which is a part of that [root] is the *ac*," the statement regarding the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *bhidyate* is made; for if the root were qualified by its parts such as *y*, that [over-extension] would not occur. Kaiyaṭa says that the same applies elsewhere. However, if the restriction regarding *nām* applied only to what follows a penultimate vowel (*nopadhāyāḥ*), then in cases like *anyate* and *tanyate*, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* would occur.

If [the rule] were simply "not before *nām*" (i.e., not before a case ending beginning with *nām*), then in the word *ṣaṇṇām*, the long vowel would occur by the rule "before *nām*" (*nāmi*). If, on the other hand, there are two restrictive rules (*niyamadvaya*), even so, the distinction remains; furthermore, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *suvāk* is indeed difficult to avoid.

Therefore, the position that [the word] presents its own form (*padopasthitipakṣa*) alone is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). To explain: in the specific rules (*pradeśeṣu*), when there is the presentation of "ac" as ending in the genitive case—as in the rules concerning *vac*, *pracch*, *śam* and so forth, as well as *han*, *gam*, and the long vowels—the words *vac* and others are the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and "ac" is the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Thus, the meaning is "the long vowel of those [roots] which have 'ac' [as their penultimate]. However, in rules such as "hrasvo napuṃsaka," the term "ac" is a qualifier for "of the neuter" and so forth; thus, by the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*), the meaning becomes "of the neuter [stem] ending in 'ac'," and so on. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
[Objection: But would not the term *it* also be present here in the rules "diva aut," "pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt," and "tyadādīnām aḥ"?

[Reply: Not so. Since the terms *hrasva*, *dīrgha*, and *pluta* denote their own forms (*svarūpa*) as the referents (*padārtha*), they function as qualifiers for that which is being prescribed; thus, the meaning is achieved as "of the vowel (*ac*) prescribed by the words *hrasva* and so on. Nor is there any utility for those [terms] to bring about the presence of the vowels (*ac*) as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), because those are already brought into presence by the word *ac* itself through its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). [Objection: If this is the case, then the mention of *ac* should be made right here [in these rules], and not in the preceding rule.
Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states:

"The mention of *ac* is for the purpose of excluding a collection of consonants (*saṃyoga*). Otherwise, in forms such as *prarakṣya* and *pratakṣya*, the short vowel *ṛ*—which is part of a *saṃyoga*—would also receive the designation of "short," and consequently, the augment *tuk* would apply. Furthermore, in the case of *titaucchatram*, because the collection of vowels (*acsamudāya*) consists of two morae (*mātrā*), it would receive the designation of "long," resulting in the optional application of *tuk* by the rules "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) and "optionally after a word-final [vowel]" (*padāntādvā*). Nor should it be argued that, by relying on a single vowel (*ac*), the *tuk* prescribed for a short vowel will also optionally occur in those cases.

Because it is subsequent, the rule characterized by length (dīrgha) sublates that [short vowel]; once it has applied, it does not apply again according to the principle *sakṛdgatau* ("when [an operation] has occurred once"). Nor is there the principle *punaḥprasaṅgavijñāna* ("the recognition of recurrence"), because there is a contradiction between a permanent option (*nityavikalpa*) and an injunction (*vidhi*), which would result in the sublation of the subsequent by the former. It is only in cases where the preceding injunction does not sublate the subsequent that one occasionally resorts to that [principle]. Furthermore, when parts are in the proximity of a whole, they do not independently initiate separate operations due to their dependence on the whole.

It should not be argued that even when the term *ac* is employed, because it denotes the genus (*jāti*), the designation of "long" (*dīrgha*) for a collection of vowels (*acsamudāya*) remains unavoidable; for Kaiyaṭa states that due to the qualification *ūkāla*, only the individual instance (*vyakti*) is taken up, since a genus lacks dimension and is therefore resorted to only by way of its instances. Furthermore, because a genus is manifested by each individual letter, it cannot be manifested by a collection [of letters]. *Uccair udāttaḥ* || 29 || [A vowel pronounced] with a high pitch is *udātta* (acute).
The grave accent (anudātta) is low-pitched. || 30 ||

Now, one might object: since "high" and "low" are relative and unstable, how can they function as defining characteristics? Nor should it be argued that the causes of "high" [pitch] are the stretching (*āyāma*) of the limbs in the form of contraction, harshness (*dāruṇya*) in the form of roughness, and the narrowness (*aṇutva*) of the sound due to the closure of the throat; while the causes of "low" [pitch] are relaxation (*anvavasarga*) in the form of looseness of the limbs, softness (*mṛdutva*) in the form of smoothness of tone, and the largeness of the throat resulting in the greatness of the sound.

For a person possessing great breath (mahāprāṇa), even when pronouncing with a low voice, pervades a large area; whereas one with little breath (alpaprāṇa), even when pronouncing loudly, pervades only a small area—thus the defect remains as it was.
On this point, there is a Vārttika:

"Let it be established [as such] because of the statement regarding the common mode of progression (*samānaprakrama*). *Prakrama* means "place" (*sthāna*), in the sense that the phonemes (*varṇa*) proceed (*prakramante*) therein. This is the meaning: the places of articulation, such as the palate and so forth, are divided into two parts by way of upper and lower. That which is articulated by the upper part is the acute (*udātta*); however, that which is articulated by the lower part is the grave (*anudātta*). This particular accent is to be understood through practice (*abhyāsa*). "Like the *ṣaḍja* note. These qualities belong only to vowels (*ac*), not to consonants (*hal*). Nevertheless, due to the coloring (*uparāga*) by a vowel, they are perceived as such even in the case of consonants.

This is as in examples such as *iṣetvorjetvā*. Nor can the reverse be the case; for in examples such as *āpyāyadhvam*, even though the vowel *ā* is udātta and the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is subject to *nighāta* (elision of accent), the *ā* remains udātta even without being followed by a consonant (*hal*). Therefore, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) that vowels alone follow the accents of the consonants. The *Bhāṣya* states: "They shine by themselves, hence they are called *svara*s (vowels); the consonant follows after them—thus the name is etymologically significant.
Although there is no actual similarity [between the two], this etymology exists merely by way of traditional convention (*sampradāya*).

Alternatively, Kaiyaṭa maintains that since the root *añj* has the sense of "going," the intended meaning of the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is "it goes in two ways due to conjunction" (*ajuparāgāt*).
The *svarita* accent is a combination (*samāhāra*). || 31 ||

Even though there is no *samāhāra* (aggregation) of vowels in cases such as *kāryam*, *kva*, or *kanyā*, because such an aggregation—whether direct or mediated through the substituend (*sthānin*)—is impossible there; yet in examples like *ṛhalorṇyat* and *kimo't*, the vowel is *svarita* due to the *tittva* (the *t*-marker). However, in cases such as *gāṅge'nūpaḥ*, since the word *gāṅga* ends in the suffix *aṇ*, it is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable); and since the word *anūpa* begins with an unaccented vowel according to the rule "anorapradhānakanīyasi," the resulting single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is *svarita* by the rule "svarito vānudātte padādau. This is because it is a different phoneme (*varṇāntara*).

Nor should it be maintained that the collection (*samāhāra*) of the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) tones alone is to be understood here, because the subject under discussion is the vowel (*ac*). Nevertheless, since a collection of the two substrates (*guṇin*) is impossible, one must resort to a collection of the two qualities (*guṇa*) which reside in them.

Nor should it be argued that a collection cannot function as the thing to be designated (*saṃjñin*), because the designation "circumflex" (*svarita*) appropriately implies that the vowel itself is the thing to be designated. This is because, by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), the vowel—which possesses the collection—is itself the thing to be designated.
