Nor does this contradict the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), such as "we study with the three accents" (*traisvaryeṇa*) and so forth; for that statement means that some [syllables] have the quality of acute (*udātta*), some have the quality of grave (*anudātta*), and some have both qualities. It does not intend to assert that there are exactly three types of accent.
Regarding that [first vowel]: "The first half of a short [vowel] is acute. (Pāṇini 1.2.32)
This undertaking is for the purpose of demonstrating the division [of accents] within the aggregate of the two qualities [grave and acute] while they remain [in combination].

Now, one might object that because of the mention of the *hrasva* (short vowel), this division would not apply to the *dīrgha* (long) and *pluta* (protracted) *svarita* vowels. For example, in *kanyā*, *śaktike3 śaktike*, there is an internal *svarita* according to the rule "kanyārājamanuṣyāṇām"; and in "svaritamāmreḍite'sūyā," there is a protracted *svarita*.

Not so. The word *arddhahrasva* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as a measure (*pramāṇa*). The mention of *hrasva* (short vowel) is for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). By this [term], however, half a *mātrā* is denoted; therefore, the suffix *mātra* is applied to the object of measurement (*prameya*). According to the rule *pramāṇe laḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Consequently, since it is possible through the intellect to divide even short, long, and protracted vowels into halves of a *mātrā*, there is no fault; thus it is settled in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa*.

For this very reason, the authors of the *Bṛhad-vivaraṇa* have stated regarding the rule "yenavidhiḥ": "Having accepted that the word 'short' (*hrasva*)—which [ordinarily] denotes a duration of half a mora (*mātrārdha*)—functions here in a non-literal sense (*amukhyayā vṛttyā*), the division into acute (*udātta*) accents is made for long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels as well."

On this point, the initiates [the Dīkṣitas] maintain: the mention of the "short" vowel is merely a reiterative reference by way of partial extraction (*avayutyānuvāda*). What is intended is simply "half" (*ardham*). Therefore, even for long and protracted vowels, the first half is udātta. And that [first half] does not consist of equal parts, but rather consists of a mere fragment (*leśa*). In this regard, according to specific Prātiśākhyas, there is a distinction: in some recensional branches (*śākhā*) it is an equal part, while in others it is only half a mora (*mātrā*). This is because the determination of features such as monotone (*ekaśruti*) is seen to depend precisely upon the Prātiśākhyas.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for the fact that a long vowel and a circumflex (*svarita*) [vowel] are half-accented (*ardhoddātta*). This is because, in the *pada-pāṭha* of the Ṛgvedic reciters, the *ekāra* in *ye'rāḥ* and the *ūdīta* vowels in *tanūnapācchacīpatim* are recited as being half-accented. Furthermore, regarding the words *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpati*, since both members of the compounds are initial-accented according to the rule "In the case of *vanaspati* and others, both [members are initial-accented]," the remaining syllables are unaccented (*śeṣanighāta*). And concerning the final syllable of the first members, *tanū* and *śacī*, their optional circumflex (*svarita*) accentuation is stated in the *Prātiśākhya*: [The Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya 3.5.2 states: "In the case of *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpati*, the final of the first member optionally becomes *svarita*. Thus, there is indeed authoritative evidence for the half-accentuation of long vowels and circumflex vowels.

"Or like the *jātya*, or likewise for the last two [svaritas], [the rule] 'tanū śacī' applies to the first two. Regarding the acute (*udātta*) nature of the half of a circumflex (*svarita*), the *Prātiśākhya* also states: "When there is a combination of monosyllables, the circumflex vowel of the first two [syllables] is more acutely accented than an acute, by half a mora or even by a quarter mora."
"The remaining [vowel] that follows is unaccented (anudātta),
provided that it is not heard as accented (udātta) because a subsequent syllable is either accented (udātta) or circumflex (svarita)."

The definition of the *svarita* [accent] extends up to the word "svara. This is because the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) possesses both *udātta* and *anudātta* pitches. It should be understood that the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) of that *svarita* is more elevated (*udāttatara*) than an independent (*svatantra*) *udātta*. The phrase "half-mora" refers to cases such as "kva3vo'śvāḥ. Nor does this imply that the half-mora which is more elevated than an independent *udātta* would consequently become *anudātta* due to its low position; for in that context, only an extremely low position is what is being designated as *anudātta*.

The word "or" (*vā*) refers to the intention of [the vowel] being long. The particle *eva* is used to indicate that this alone is to be accepted, because by this very [definition], all three [types of svarita] are subsumed; for, in comparison to a half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), a portion of equal measure is more abundant and thus serves as its constituent part. This is also supported by its placement at the end [of the list]. Furthermore, since the designation *Prātiśākhya* establishes that the text pertains to that specific Vedic recension (*śākhā*), and because in that recension the svarita is read as having an equal [portion] of the udātta. The phrase "anudātta," etc., is a restatement of a meaning established through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). That remainder possesses the auditory quality of the udātta.
Is this without distinction? No, he says—“and not,” etc. This means: excluding that which is followed by an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel.
Śākalya also says:
“But that circumflex (*svāra*) which is non-natural (*aprākṛta*), preceded by a circumflex or an acute.”
Then, having taken half of this, they strike the remainder while it is trembling.

They say that *udādāya* means "having made [the vowel] acute. Regarding this, they argue: this is not correct, because it contradicts the texts of the aforementioned grammarians (*ākara*). Even if such a reading exists in a particular recension (*śākhā*), it cannot be restricted to that alone, as this rule is common to all recensions and must be construed as a single syntactical unit with them. Furthermore, in ordinary usage, since there is no specific statement to the contrary, the intended meaning is simply that the acute accent consists of half a mora (*mātrā*). Moreover, the aforementioned *Prātiśākhya* is not a supporting authority for this position.

Regarding the two positions—"half a mora" (*arddhamātrā*) or "only half" (*arddhameva*)—these are established according to the intentions of Pāṇini and Śākalya, based on the distinction between general and specific definitions. The particle *eva* (only) serves to restate the exclusion of the general definition by means of the specific definition. The word *vā* (or) signifies an option restricted by context (*vyavasthitavikalpa*). Furthermore, if "equal parts" (*samāṃśa*) were understood, the mention of "half" (*arddha*) would be redundant, as the principle "it should be equal, because nothing [else] is heard" (*samaṃ syādaśrutatvāt*) would already establish it.

Nor is that [the term *arddha-hrasva*] for the sake of obtaining even half a *mātrā*, because there is no form common to both [the short vowel and the half-mātrā], because there is no single entity called "fractionality" (*leśatva*), and because even if one were to assume the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* compound, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). By this, the works of Haradatta and others—which claim that the word *arddha-hrasva* indicates (*lakṣayati*) half a *mātrā*—are refuted; they must somehow be interpreted as referring to a different view, since the meaning of the present sūtra is precisely what Haradatta has stated. As for the objection that it is improper because the word *arddha-hrasva* is said to be a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) for half a *mātrā* in the *Ākara* (the Mahābhāṣya), and because indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is impossible due to the absence of a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the whole [compound]: [this is incorrect].

That is not so; for even if [the term *svarita*] is conventionally established as referring to the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), the substratum delimited by that [half-mora] is obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, according to the method stated by Kaiyaṭa. This is because comprehension arises even in those who do not know the elision of the suffix *-mātra*. Furthermore, the rule governing that [suffix] functions merely to indicate the intended meaning of the secondary indication, much like the rule "from words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanebhyaḥ*). Let this suffice; let us return to the subject at hand. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "The rule 'of the svarita following an udātta or svarita which has an udātta of half a short vowel' is for the sake of establishing the operation 'after a svarita' [which applies] to an anudātta following an udātta that is higher than the preceding."

The meaning of this is as follows: the word *ā* is a truncation (*cheda*) of the rule *ā arddhahasvodāttāt*. These nine sūtras are to be recited in the eighth [chapter], following the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ*. Consequently, in the passage *imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati*, the words *gaṅgā* and so forth—which follow the word *me* (which is *svarita*) and are *anudātta* due to the *āmantrita-nighāta*—attain *ekaśruti* (monotone) by virtue of the rule *svaritātsaṃhitāyāmanudāttānām*.

Otherwise, because the *svarita* accent prescribed by the rule *udāttādanudāttasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.66)—which belongs to the third *pāda*—would be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of the rule *svaritāt* (8.4.65), the following *anudātta* syllables would not be situated after a *svarita*, and thus the *ekaśruti* (monotone) would not apply. Nor should one suspect that [the former] is established by virtue of its being the basis (*āśrayasiddhatva*), because that principle has its scope in cases such as *kāryam*, where the *svarita* of the sixth *pāda* is applicable.
Furthermore, [the rule *svaritāt*] is intended for the sake of the *svarita* and the *udātta*.

For instance: in *subrahmaṇyā*, the suffix *yat* [in *subrahmaṇya-*] is svarita because it is marked with *t*; the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is anudātta because it is marked with *p*; and the single substitute (ekādeśa) is svarita by virtue of being the closest phonetic match (*āntaratamya*). This is because a portion of the anudātta remains there. *Om* is udātta. By the rule "omāṅośca," the single substitute for an udātta and a svarita is itself svarita, due to the closest phonetic match among the constituent parts. Furthermore, the word *indra* is anudātta because it is a vocative (*āmantrita*).

In the case of *subrahmaṇyom indra āgaccha*, the rule "na subrahmaṇyāyāṃ svaritasya tūdāttaḥ" (P. 1.2.37), which prescribes that the circumflex (*svarita*) vowel *o* becomes acute (*udātta*), would have its scope; thus, the acute [prescribed by P. 8.4.66] for a circumflex vowel occurring within the domain of the third book (*traipādika*) would not apply. For example, in "indra āgaccha": according to "svaritodāttācca svaritārtham" (P. 1.2.39), in "indra āgaccha, hariva āgaccha," the word *ā* is acute (*udātta*). By the principle of the "remaining accent" (*śeṣanighāta*), *gaccha* is grave (*anudātta*). Consequently, by the rule "udāttādanudāttasya" (P. 8.4.66), the syllable following the acute becomes circumflex (*svarita*). Because that [circumflex] is considered "not yet established" (*asiddha*) [by P. 8.2.1], the aforementioned rule [P. 1.2.37] would not effect its change to acute.

"And for the sake of [making] the following *sannatara* (more depressed) when followed by a *svarita*: *māṇavakajaṭilakādhyāpaka nyaṅ*. By the rule "when preceded by *ni*, *adhi*, or *aca*," there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. Consequently, by the rule "the *yaṇ* substitute for an *udātta* or *svarita* [becomes *svarita*]," the vowel *a* becomes *svarita*. Because that [substitution] is not yet established (*asiddha*), the preceding [vowel] would not become *anudāttatara* (more depressed) according to the rule "that which follows an *udātta* or *svarita* is *sannatara*. Nor can its establishment be based on the fact that [the substitution] is dependent [on the preceding rule], because this would find scope in cases such as *māṇavakajaṭilakābhirūpaṃ kva*. Since the rule "that which has *ti* [as an affix] is *svarita*" is established, it is proven that the nine rules [of the *svarita* section] should be recited at the end of the treatise.

And this has been made known by the author of the Sūtras himself. As it is said: "The prescription of the anudātta accent for *deva* and *brāhmaṇa* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the established status (*siddhatva*) of [the preceding vowel] by the rule *svaritāt*. Otherwise, since the svarita would be asiddha, the anudātta quality would already exist [by default], and thus the prescription of the anudātta would be purposeless. For it is established in the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika that the established status of the svarita is not indicated by this [rule], because if it were, the following anudātta after the udātta portion of the svarita would result in becoming svarita itself.

On this point, the initiates [of this school] state: "The rule *svaritasya tūdāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.31) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the displacement of the current context. Nor can it be argued that, according to the method of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa, there is no scope for that rule in the case of *subrahmaṇyom*, because the application of the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5) is mandatory there. Furthermore, one should not say that the rule does not apply to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of an acute (*udātta*) and a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel because the Vṛttikāra stated that the word *anudāttasya* is understood (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding sūtra; for there is no evidence for such an understanding."

In the case of the phrase *kvāvaram*, the Bahvṛcas read it with an udātta accent [on the first syllable], because the word *kva* is svarita. Furthermore, among the Taittirīyas as well, in the passage "yājyayaivainametayā''pyāyayati," the second syllable is udātta due to the elision (praśleṣa) of the prefix *ā*.
For this very reason, the Bahvṛca-Prātiśākhya states: "When there is a merging with that which possesses an udātta, the resulting junction-syllable (*sandhya*) is udātta."

Regarding the verse: "But when followed by an *anudātta*, [the preceding vowel becomes] *svarita* if the following [vowel] is *svarita*" (*svaritopadhe*), the word *anudātta* is employed only in the second half of the verse; the word *punaḥ* ("again") is used to prevent the misconception that it connects with the first half. Furthermore, in the *Śaunakīya-svarāṣṭaka*, it is stated: "In a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) [with an *udātta*], one should lead each [substitute] to that very same accent. They say this is because the *anudātta* is not mentioned as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitvena*) in the case of a single substitute.

That is not so; for since such a reading in a specific recensional branch (*śākhā*) is already established by the rules of the *Prātiśākhya* itself, it is impossible to override the explanations of commentators such as Bhartṛhari, who observed all linguistic traditions, in accordance with that [rule].
[Pāṇini 1.2.33: "The single accent (*ekaśruti*) is used in addressing from a distance."

In addressing from a distance, a sentence shall be in the *ekaśruti* (monotone). For example: "āgaccha māṇavaka" ("Come, young boy"). Optionally, the final syllable of the word *māṇavaka* may be protracted (*pluta*) and acute (*udātta*). Addressing from a distance is indicated by the combination of *ekaśruti* and *pluta*, distinguished by their respective positions within the sentence. A word of address (*sambuddhi-pada*) refers specifically to the act of addressing; otherwise, there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "devo brāhmaṇāḥ" ("The gods are Brahmins"), where the word ends in the nominative singular. As it has been said: "In this science, both interpretations apply."

The meaning is that in some cases, even that which is unartificial (*akṛtrima*) is included. This is because the qualification "from afar" (*dūrāt*) would be inapplicable to the singular number (*ekavacana*), whereas for the vocative (*sambodhana*), such a possibility exists since it is of the nature of an action and can function as an ablative (*apādāna*). Furthermore, the single accent (*ekaśruti*) is not acute (*udātta*), because the acute is prescribed by the rule: "The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed higher [in pitch]. Otherwise, since it would already be established by the rule "In sacrificial ritual (*yajñakarmaṇi*)," the single accent alone would suffice. Nor is it grave (*anudātta*), because the grave is prescribed by the rule: "That which follows an acute or a circumflex (*svarita*) is grave, provided it is not followed by another [acute or circumflex]."

If [the single tone] were established merely by the persistence of the *ekaśruti*, then the prescription of the *anudātta* would be purposeless. Therefore, the meaning established is that *ekaśruti* is the concealment of the distinction between the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) tones, like milk and water. It is precisely here that the Vedic practitioners employ the term *pracaya*. However, in the case of the circumflex (*svarita*), both are perceived with their distinctions intact. Others, however, explain: in both cases, the mention of "both" (*ubhayatra*) is a *tantra* (a governing principle).

In the passage "somasyāgner vīhi vauṣaṭ," the rule for *ekaśruti* (monotone) is prescribed for the sacrificial ritual; in relation to that, the rule for the word *vauṣaṭ* being more acutely accented (*udāttatara*) is enjoined. And that [more acute accentuation] is untenable without the influence of an acute accent (*udātta*) upon the *ekaśruti*. This is because superiority (*utkarṣa*) is necessarily correlative. The same applies to the term "sannatara" (lower).

And thus there are seven accents: the acute (udātta), the more acute (udāttatara), the grave (anudātta), the more grave (anudāttatara), the circumflex (svarita), the acute-circumflex (svaritodātta), and the single-intonation (ekaśruti), which is the circumflex itself when colored by a following grave accent. However, since for some circumflex accents the acute portion is not colored by a following grave accent, it is established that the circumflex is specified separately. [This applies] in sacrificial rites, except for muttered prayers (japa), the *nyūṅkha* interjections, and the *sāman* chants. 34.

In the performance of sacrificial rites (*yajña-karman*), a mantra should be recited with a single tone (*eka-śruti*), with the exception of *japa* and similar practices. For example: "agnirmūrddhā divaḥ" (Agni is the head of heaven). Why specify "in sacrificial rites"? Because during the time of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), the threefold accentuation (*traisvarya*) alone should apply. Why specify "with the exception of *japa*"? For example: "mamāgne varco vihaveṣvastu" (May there be splendor for me, O Agni, in the invocations). *Japa* refers to a whispered application, such as that of one submerged in water. As for the *nyūṅkha*, they consist of sixteen *okāra*s. Among these, the first, seventh, and thirteenth are three *udātta* accents each of three morae (*trimātra*); the remaining thirteen are *anudātta* accents, each being half an *okāra*.

Thus it has been stated and cited by Āśvalāyana, according to the author of the *Prasāda*. The *Jaimini-sūtra* states: "The designation 'Sāman' applies to songs. Due to the exclusion of the *ajapa* [recitation], this single-intonation (* aikaśrutya*) applies to mantras similar to that. For this very reason, it is explained in the *Paspaśā* section: "When the word *indraśatru* is being modified (*ūhya*), this [rule] does not apply. Or, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is at a higher pitch (35).

In the performance of a sacrifice (*yajña-karman*), the word *vauṣaṭ* may be pronounced either more loudly or with a single accent (*ekaśruti*). For example: "O Agni, partake of the Soma—*vauṣaṭ*! The inclusion of the word *vaṣaṭ* is for the sake of variety, because according to tradition, it is the word *vauṣaṭ* itself that is intended [to be modified]. From this very indication, even in the absence of a specific mention of a phoneme, the suffix *kāra* is applied; by this, forms such as *svāhākāraḥ* and *hantakāraḥ* are established. 36. Optionally so in the Vedic texts (*chandas*).

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there is optionally the single accent (*ekaśruti*). And this option is determined by specific rules (*vyavasthayā*); for example, in the *Saṃhitā* of the Ṛgvedins there is the threefold accent (*traisvaryam*), whereas in the *Brāhmaṇa* there is the single accent, and so forth. Although the option was already under discussion, the term *vibhāṣā* is mentioned again to indicate the cessation of the rule "in sacrificial ritual" (*yajñakarmaṇi*).

One might object: "Since the mandatory and optional single-enunciation (*ekaśruti*) are mutually contradictory within the context of sacrificial ritual (*yajñakarman*), and because they cannot both be prescribed, the very capacity [of the rule] implies that 'in sacrificial ritual' must be excluded; therefore, the repeated mention of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is redundant. If this is argued, we say no. Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the phrase "except for the *ajapa*" and so forth, there is the possibility of establishing a distinction: that the mandatory single-enunciation applies to the domain of mantras (*mantra-viṣayaka*), whereas the optional one pertains to the Brāhmaṇa portion. Thus, the rule remains necessary.

Even on the side of the prohibition, it is possible that the single, constant recitation (*nityaikaśruti*) alone pertains to the subject matter of modification (*ūha*) and so forth, whereas the optional recitation (*vaikalpikī*) pertains to the subject matter of Vedic meters (*chandas*); thus, [the rule] is purposeful as a means to exclude that [optional recitation].

Regarding this, they explain as follows: by means of *tantra* (economy of expression) or *āvṛtti* (repetition), the negative particle (*nañ*) is elided from the rule *acchandasi*, so that there is an optional choice even in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*). In the rule concerning the *dāṇḍināyana*-group, it is stated: "The separate citation [of *aikṣvāka*] is for the sake of distinguishing its accent. Then, the *Bhāṣya* says: "It is established by the indication through single-enunciation (*ekaśruti*). For single-enunciation is a pronoun for accents, just as the neuter is a pronoun for genders. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, the composition of *śleṣa* (paronomastic) poetry by the learned is justified, because two compounds with conflicting accents are subsumed under a single accent (*ekaśruti*). For this same reason, the occurrence of a fault in the word *indraśatru* due to its *bahuvrīhi* accent is mentioned in the *Paspaśā* [section of the Mahābhāṣya], as well as the commentary at its end: "The white one runs, the rider of the Alambusas. However, the intention behind the statement in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, "In common usage, as in the Veda, accent is not a cause for determining a specific meaning," is that it refers to recitation in *ekaśruti*.

Nor is the rule "vibhāṣā bhāṣāyām" (optionally [the penultimate syllable is acute] in the spoken language) redundant, having begun with "jhalyupottamam" (when followed by a consonant, the penultimate [syllable is acute]). This is because, since the procedure was initiated with respect to the threefold accent (*traisvarya*), its purpose is to obtain the optional non-acute (*anudātta*) accent. Furthermore, although "vā" (or) is already understood, the author of the Sūtras employs the term "vibhāṣā" because the authors of the Tantras and other works do not favor such elliptical usage. Moreover, there is no governing heading for the Veda (*chandas*) in rules concerning accents. Let this suffice; for the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, however, the circumflex (*svarita*) becomes acute (*udātta*). 37.

In the *nigada* known as the *subrahmaṇyā*, the single accent (*ekaśruti*) obtained by the preceding rule does not apply; rather, by another injunction, the circumflex (*svarita*) becomes acute (*udātta*). Thus: "subrahmaṇyom," "indra āgaccha. The acuteness of the syllable *oṃ* has already been explained. However, there is no protracted acute (*plutodātta*) for the *oṃ* according to the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*), because that [rule] pertains to matters other than sacrificial rites (*ayajñakarman*). The word *indra* is acute on its first syllable as it is a vocative (*āmantrita*); the vowel *ā* is grave (*anudātta*) due to the rule of the suppression of the remainder (*śeṣanighāta*).

By the rule *udāttādanudāttasya*, that [letter] becomes svarita; by this [present rule], it becomes udātta. By the rule *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*, the vowel *ā* is udātta. For the word *gaccha*, there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. By the rule *udāttāt*, the vowel following the letter *ga* becomes svarita. That [svarita] also becomes udātta. Thus, the first four letters, excluding the letter *cha*, are udātta. Nor does the rule *udāttāt* result in the letter *cha* also becoming udātta;
for it has been stated previously that because this section is recited after that [rule], the svarita-udātta is not established [for the purpose of the preceding rule].

In the phrase *hariva āgaccha*, the first syllable of the vocative is udātta (acute), while the remaining syllables undergo *śeṣanighāta* (subsequent suppression). Of that [first syllable], there is a *svarita* (circumflex), and of that [svarita], there is the quality of being udātta; thus, in the word *hariva*, there are two udāttas and the final syllable is anudātta (grave). In *āgaccha*, it is likewise as before.
In the phrase *āgaccha maghavan*, the word *maghavan* is anudātta according to the rule "of the vocative."

Regarding the vocative form *medhātithi* (from the genitive *medhātitheḥ*), because it functions as the final member of a compound (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), the syllable *me*—which is part of the word *medhātithi*—is acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accent of the vocative. By the aforementioned rule, the syllable *dhā* becomes acute due to this [preceding acute], while [the remaining] *ti* is circumflex (*svarita*). Thus, *medhā* consists of two acute syllables; the rest is grave (*anudātta*). In the same manner, the application of *parāṅgavadbhāva* and so forth should be understood in cases such as *vṛṣaṇaśvasya mene kauravaskandin ahalyāyai jāra*.

Regarding the phrase *kauśika-brāhmaṇa-gotama-bruvāṇa*, here too there are two successive acute (*udātta*) accents, while the others are grave (*anudātta*). It should not be argued that the third [syllable] would also become acute by this rule because it follows an acute and is grave—according to the rule *udāttādanudāttasya*—and thus the same would apply to all subsequent ones; for if it were intended for all of them to be acute, [the author] would have omitted the word *na* and simply stated, "In the *subrahmaṇyā*, [the syllables] are acute. Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of both [terms], not all [syllables] are acute.

"O Maghavan, come to the *sutyā* tomorrow. The word *śvas* is acutely accented on its first syllable due to the accentuation rule for indeclinables (*nipātasvara*). Regarding the word *sutyā*: by the rule "In the sense of a name, [the suffix] *kyap* is added after the roots *samaj*, *niṣad*, *nipat*, *man*, *vid*, *asuñ*, *śīṅ*, *bhṛñ*, and *iṇ*," the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *sunoti*. Since the acute accent (*udātta*) continues to apply there, the word is acutely accented on the final syllable; by the rule of "the rest being unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*), the syllable *su* is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the rule "of that which follows an acute or circumflex [syllable]," it becomes doubly unaccented (*anudāttatara*). In the word *āgaccha*, the two initial syllables are acute and the following one is unaccented, as before. In the expressions "in two days' time to the *sutyā*" (*dvyahe sutyām*) and "in three days' time to the *sutyā*" (*tryahe sutyām*), the word *dvyahe* is acutely accented on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ṭac*.

And so says the Sāma-Brāhmaṇa: "Therefore, standing on the *utkara* heap, the Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā formula: 'Subrahmaṇyo3m, Subrahmaṇyo3m, Subrahmaṇyo3m. He says it three times like a woman, for the gods are true to the triad (*triṣatyā*). When he says, 'Indra, come!'—this 'Indra, come! is indeed his secret name; by that very name he calls him three times."

"O Hari, come!"—the two bay horses (*hari*) of Indra are the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, for by means of these he carries away all this. "The ram of Medhātithi"—it was indeed a ram that, having become so, carried off Medhātithi Kāṇvāyani. "The two wives of Vṛṣaṇaśva"—Vṛṣaṇaśva had a daughter named Menakā, whom Indra desired. "O Gaurāvaskandin"—having become a white deer (*gaura-mṛga*), he leaps down from the forest and drinks [the Soma] from the king. "The lover of Ahalyā."

Ahalyā Maitreyī had a lover, a Brāhmaṇa called Kauśika. A Brāhmaṇa would approach him, saying, "He is called Gautama. The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle; between them Gautama was traveling. Indra went to him and said, "May your honor wander as a spy here for us. He replied, "I am not able. Then [Indra] said, "Then I shall wander in your form. [Gautama] said, "As you think best."

As for the fact that Gotama moved about without speaking, it was either in the form of Gotama or he said this very thing: "He was Gotama. When he says, "O Ahi, come to the Soma-pressing, O Maghavan," it is as if one were to say to a worthy person, "I shall cook for you; therefore, come!"—in this very way he announces the pressing to the gods. Regarding the phrase "the gods are the Brāhmaṇas": the gods are indeed the gods, and those who are Brāhmaṇas—learned in sacred lore and well-versed in the Vedas—are the human gods.

"These oblations are for the gods; sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are for the human-gods. Indeed, one gratifies the gods with oblations and the human-gods with sacrificial gifts; one gratifies those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in them. "The word *asau* (that one) is the end [of the name]. This is based on a specific scriptural statement (*vācanika*). The final syllable of a word ending in the nominative case is acute-accented (*udātta*). For example: *gārgyo yajate*, *vātsyo yajate*. Because of the suffix *ñit*, the initial syllable would have been expected to be acute-accented.

And likewise, the *Drāhyāyaṇasūtra* states: "The definition of meaning (*arthanirvacana*) is uttered. "The definition of meaning" means that by which the meaning is defined—that is, explained or primarily set forth. This refers to the *pada*. However, it was not stated simply as "*pada*" [in the sūtra]; the commentators explain this so that in a compound, the preceding members do not become *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable). In the case of the elided form *yajate*, there is an *udātta* accent due to the rule "after an *udātta* [there is a *svarita*]" (*udāttād*). "Of this one" (*amuṣya*) [indicates] the end. This is an indication for the genitive case-ending. For example: "The father of Dākṣi sacrifices" (*dākṣeḥ pitā yajate*). It is to be understood as before.

"syāntasyopottamaṃ ca": for a word ending in *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) that ends in *a*, both the penultimate (*upāntya*) and—due to the word *ca*—"the final (*anta*)" syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). For example: *gārgyasya pitā yajate*, *vātsyasya pitā yajate*. [The rule] "vā nāmadheyasya" [applies as well].

In this name, either the penultimate syllable would be acute (udātta), while the final syllable would certainly remain grave (anudātta). In the phrase *devadattasya pitā yajate*, in the word *janiṣyamāṇānām*, the word *sya* is acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), whereas the suffix *śānac* is grave by the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* (*tāsyanudātteṭ*); thus, the following syllable becomes circumflex (*svarita*) by the rule "after an acute. By this present rule, that [circumflex] becomes acute; thus both *syam* are acute. The rest is grave by the principle of the remaining unaccented (*śeṣanighāta*).

However, in the case of *pitāpitāmaha*, since the word-final syllables of *pitāmaha* and *prapitāmaha* are udātta by the rule "asau," they become svarita by the rule "udāttāt"; consequently, by the present sūtra, only the syllables *pi-* and *pra-* are udātta, and not those following them as well.
[Pāṇini 6.2.39: "In *deva* and *brahman*, [the final syllable] is anudātta."

Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "Some [hold that] there is anudātta [accentuation] for *deva* and *brahman*. For example: *devā brahmāṇa āgacchata*. The meaning is as follows: in the view where the two words *devāḥ* and *brahmāṇaḥ* are in grammatical apposition (vaiyadhikaraṇya), because the preceding vocative (*āmantrita*) is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), both words receive the udātta accent on their first syllable. Once the subsequent *śeṣanighāta* (the anudātta accent for all remaining syllables) and the *svarita* accent have been applied, the rule prescribing the anudātta becomes meaningful.

If, however, there were coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) between those two, then—since the option "the plural is used optionally when a specific term is present" (*vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane bahuvacanam*) would apply—the rule "of the vocative" (*āmantritasya*) would suffice by means of the *nighāta* (elision of accent), and thus there would be no need [for the present rule]. [Now follows: 39. *svaritātsaṃhitāyāmanudāttānām* ("In the *saṃhitā*, [the substitution of] *anudātta* for [multiple] *anudātta* syllables occurs after a *svarita*... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with the number 39, indicating the beginning of a new sūtra.*

In *saṃhitā*, there shall be *ekaśruti* (monotone) for the *anudātta* (unaccented) vowels that follow a *svarita* (circumflex) vowel. For example: *imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati*. The word *imam* is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable); *me* is *anudātta* because of the governing rule "everything [following a vocative] is *anudātta*. By the rule "of an *anudātta* following an *udātta*," this [first syllable of *me*] becomes *svarita*. Consequently, there is *ekaśruti* for the subsequent words beginning with *gaṅge*. Why "in *saṃhitā*"? [To show that] in the *padapāṭha*, they should remain merely *anudātta* due to the suppression (*nighāta*) of the vocative accent.

This might be the case: is the plurality in the rule *anudāttānām* intended to be significant, or not? Not the first [option], because there would be no application [of the rule] in cases of duality or singularity, such as *āgniveśyaḥ* and *pacati*. For the word *āgniveśyaḥ*, being derived from the *gargādi* group with the suffix *yañ*, is udātta on its first syllable. By the principle of *śeṣanighāta*, the second syllable is *svarita* according to the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ*. The two syllables *veśya* are *anudātta*. In *pacati*, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is udātta; the suffixes *śap* and *tip* are *anudātta* because they are marked with *p*; the letter *ś* is *svarita*; and the following vowel is *anudātta*. Thus, the single-intonation (*ekaśruti*) would not apply here.

Not the latter [alternative]. For in the passage "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati," because the word *me* has a svarita accent, only the single word immediately following it would undergo *ekaśruti*, but not "yamune" and the others, because they are separated [from the svarita], according to the rule "tasmādityuttarasya.
Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "This is an *ekaśeṣa* of unaccented words ending in the three genders."

This [rule] applies under the view that the *sarūpa-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.2.64) is to be commenced. However, under the view of the "genus" (*jāti*), there is the plural form in the rule "jātyākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.58). Consequently, since a genus is perceived immediately following a circumflex (*svarita*) accent in the singular, dual, or plural, the attainment of the single tone (* aikaśrutya *) is established for all of them. If it is objected: "In the first case, the operation would apply only to six or more, because the rule for 'single remainder' (*ekaśeṣa*) is prescribed when there is a desire to express [the items] together, and thus the application of the grammatical operation belongs only to the collection as a whole," we say no. Even when there is a desire to express them together in the specific instruction, the operation applies to each individual item, just as in the expression: "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra—let them be fed."
40. That which follows an acute (udātta) or a circumflex (svarita) accent is more depressed (sannatara).
That anudātta which has an udātta or a svarita preceding it becomes anudāttatara. Examples: *sarasvati śutudri* and *vyacakṣayatsvaḥ*. Thus say the authors of the Vṛtti and others.

However, some maintain that the meaning is simply that the monotone (ekaśruti) accent becomes anudāttatara; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *ekaśruti dūrāt*.

Furthermore, because this [rule] is unestablished, the single-enunciation (*ekaśruti*) would also apply to the vowel *i* which is a constituent part of the word *sarasvatī* by means of the preceding rule.
Nor is this [present rule] an exception to that [preceding rule], since it finds its scope of application in cases such as *agnim* and *kanyā*.

Nor can one maintain—following the view of Haradatta and others—that there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*) in the rule *na mu ne* due to a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) of the word *na*; for such a split of the yoga is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya or other authoritative sources. Otherwise, even the assumption of a reading at the end of the treatise would be rendered useless. Furthermore, since the substitution of the circumflex accent (*svarita*) could be justified as an annulment by virtue of its posteriority—just like the single accent (*ekaśruti*)—the rule *nodāttasvaritodayam* would be redundant; so they say. 41. *apṛkta ekālpratyayaḥ*: A suffix consisting of a single phoneme (*al*) is termed *apṛkta*. Examples of its application include: *sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* and others.

It might be argued: one should simply say *ekahal* (a single consonant), because in the rule *apṛktam hal*, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in omitting the word *hal*. However, if *al* were used instead, it would be necessary to include it in order to prevent the elision of *ṇal* in forms such as *bibheda*; therefore, [the objection holds]. Not so. For in the rule *yūni lugaṇiñoḥ*, there is prolixity (*gaurava*) due to the utterance of two words. If, however, *hal* were used, one would have to state only *apṛktasya* in that context.

Nor can it be argued that, in this way, the offspring of Phāṇṭāhṛti would be called *Phāṇṭāhṛtaḥ*—resulting in the undesirable consequence of the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṇa* as prescribed by the rule "phāṇṭāhṛtimimatābhyām"—because that [undesirable result] is prevented by the fact that the suffix *aṇ* alone would suffice for the elision, making the prescription of *ṇa* redundant. Furthermore, its purpose cannot be to override the suffix *phak* prescribed by the rule "yañiñośca," since *phak* could have been avoided simply by including [the name] in the *Pailādi* list.

Not so. For even according to the alternative arrangement, there are three mentions of *hal*—namely, the mention of *hal* in the definition of the term *apṛkta*, the second mention of *hal* in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (P. 6.1.68), and the mention of *apṛkta* in the rule *aṇiñoḥ* (P. 4.1.78)—and likewise, according to the stated method, there are exactly three word-mentions: the mention of *hal* in the definition of the term *apṛkta*, and the mention of the two words *aṇ* and *iñ* in the rule *aṇiñoḥ*. Thus, there is no economy of expression.

And thus, even so, let there not be the mention of "one" (eka). Nor is there the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *darviḥ* and *jāgṛviḥ*, because of the interpretation that the suffix must be preceded by *al* alone. Otherwise, the word *al* would be redundant; for if the meaning were "of that which ends in *al*," then since a single [suffix] is treated as both beginning and ending [by the rule *ādyantavad ekasmin*], such a status would already be established, and there would be nothing left to exclude.

And it should not be argued that this is the same even in the case of the mention of *hal* (consonants), because [the mention of *hal*] would serve its purpose by excluding vowels (*ajanta*) through the application of the rule for "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The mention of 'one' (*eka*) is for the purpose of indicating that when a letter (*varṇa*) is mentioned, the genus (*jāti*) is understood. Kaiyaṭa says that although this was already indicated in the rule *nipāta ekāj*, it is restated here for the benefit of those of dull intellect.
A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is a *karmadhāraya*. 42.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is twofold: verbal and objective. The first is exemplified by the two words "blue lotus," because they possess identical case-endings. The second also occurs in that same instance, due to the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṹṣya-bhāva*) between their respective objects through non-difference. The distinction is this: the first is common to both [valid and invalid] cases, as seen in expressions such as "the barren woman is pregnant" (*matā vandhyā*); the second, however, occurs only where there is no contradiction. Since this is a treatise on the instruction of grammar, only the former is included here, as evidenced by the usage of learned authorities such as "possessing a fire made of gold" (*kāñcanamaya-vahnimān*).
A *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of two members that have the same case-ending shall be designated as a *karmadhāraya*.

This rule is introduced outside the general section on *tatpuruṣas* so that the designation *karmadhāraya* does not subvert the designation *tatpuruṣa*; for within that [general] section, there is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding a single designation. For example: *nīlaṃ ca tad utpalaṃ ca* (it is both blue and a lotus) becomes *nīlotpalam*. The term "tatpuruṣa" is used to exclude compounds such as *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows"), which is a *bahuvrīhi*, because it also possesses co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The term "co-referential" (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*) is used to exclude compounds such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's servant"), where the members do not share the same referent.

Nor should it be argued that because the *tatpuruṣa* compound is a single unit, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is untenable, since such a relationship is restricted to distinct entities. This is because the term "tatpuruṣa" here functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) for the individual words that constitute it. [Objection: But even in the case of a primary *tatpuruṣa*, coreferentiality is possible—as in "the king’s servant is handsome" (*rājapuruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ*). Since [coreferentiality] is already established there, why resort to indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? On this point, Kaiyaṭa states: "Coreferentiality of a *tatpuruṣa* with another word is external (*bahiraṅga*), whereas for the constituent members (*vartipada*) themselves, it is internal (*antaraṅga*)."

Nor does it follow that each individual word would thus incur the designation of *kramadhāraya*, because—according to the maxim of reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana*)—the designation is prescribed for the collection of words as a whole.
"In a compound, that which is indicated by the nominative case is the *upasarjana*. (Pāṇini 1.2.43)

In the rule for forming compounds (*samāsavidhi*), a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) is designated by the aforementioned technical term (*ukta-saṃjñaka*). For example, *kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ* becomes *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ*. Although words such as *kṛṣṇa* do not themselves end in the nominative case in examples like *dvitīyā-śrita*, they are so designated because the words in the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others that convey them—such as *śrita*—do end in the nominative. Thus, it follows that the term "compound" (*samāsa-pada*) refers to the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) that prescribes its formation. This is because, in comparison to the individual words constituting the compound, it is more logical for the term to refer to the rule itself, as the rule for forming the compound is simpler.

It might be argued as follows: since the compound depends upon the specific grammatical instruction, that which is designated by the nominative case in one instance would receive the designation *upasarjana* (subordinate member) in all instances. As it has been said: "In the case of a rule where something is designated by the nominative, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that same thing receiving the designation *upasarjana* elsewhere. Consequently, in the compound *rājakumārīśritaḥ* ("resorted to by the princess"), within the *śritādi*-type compound, because the word *kumārī* is designated by the nominative, the aforementioned designation would apply; this would result in both the shortening of the vowel caused by its status as an *upasarjana* and its placement at the beginning of the compound—even though it is the second member in a genitive *tatpuruṣa*. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:
"It is established by the statement: 'With respect to that which is [specified] in the rule for composition'.

This means that for a word such as *śrita* (gone to) and the like, when it is indicated in the nominative case (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*) in a rule prescribing a compound, the designation of *upasarjana* (subordinate member) applies specifically with respect to that [other word]. This is because the designation *upasarjana* is an etymological one (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), and thus it is understood that the designation belongs to that which stands in a relationship of non-predominance (*aprādhānya*) toward its correlative.

[Objection: But if this were so, in cases such as *ardhapippalī* (half-a-pear) and *puruṣavyāghra* (tiger-like man), where the meaning of the first member is predominant, the aforementioned designation would not apply to words such as *ardha*.

Not so; for names that are literal (*anvartha-saṃjñā*) function only when there is an actual referent, depending upon a basis for their application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*). In other cases, however, they function without depending on such a basis, by virtue of the force of the specific rule (*vidhāna-sāmarthya*). It is for this very reason that it will be stated later that the case endings beginning with *su* (the nominative) receive the designation *karmapravacanīya*.
By this, examples such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣasya*) are also explained.

In the Bhāṣya, however, another solution has also been stated. In the section concerning the rule for initial placement (*pūrvanipāta*), after rejecting the requirement for initial placement by saying, "Or rather, not so, because we observe undesirable results," it was stated: "In a compound of two words ending in the genitive case, because there is no difference in meaning, the principal member does not necessarily occupy the first position. This is because one must maintain the identity of meaning between the sentence and the compound; therefore, in the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, it is the king alone who takes the initial position, and not the man, otherwise a difference in meaning would result.

Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence of shortening the penultimate vowel in the compound *rājñaḥ kumārī* (the king’s daughter), because the desired form is achieved through the subsequent application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. For it will be stated [in Pāṇini 2.4.26]: "The gender of the latter [member of a compound prevails]," and [in 1.2.51]: "The word and its meaning. Although this point should have been refuted right there, the intent here is specifically regarding technical names (*saṃjñā*) based on their etymological meaning (*anvartha*). 44. And that which has a single case-ending [is a *samānādhikaraṇa*], except when it occurs as the first member [of a compound].

In a compound, that which possesses a fixed case-ending is also designated as *ukta* (expressed), yet it does not undergo prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). This is because, within each specific instance of usage, every word has only one case-ending; therefore, by implication, this designation applies only to that which does not possess all case-endings even alternatively. For instance, in the expression *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, the word *kauśāmbī* ends specifically in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) due to its connection with the power of the ablative (*apādāna-kāraka*) in relation to the action of departing; it does not admit other powers in relation to other actions.

It might be argued as follows: in a compound such as *śritakṛṣṇa* (one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa), this rule would also prohibit the prior placement of words like *kṛṣṇa*, which end in the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so on; for the preceding rule [P. 2.2.30] finds its scope in compounds of apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as *nīlotpala*. This is not so. Because here an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is adopted, the matter is already established by the preceding rule in that case.

Or rather, the prohibition applies only to that prior placement which is based on the technical designation *upasarjana* (secondary member) prescribed by the rule "ekavibhakti... [P. 1.2.44]. This is according to the maxim: "A rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately antecedent."

The rule "there is no mention of that which has a single case-ending when it is not ending in the sixth [genitive] case" should not apply here in the case of *ardhapippalī* (half a long pepper). This prohibition concerns only the *ekadeśin-samāsa* (part-whole compound); therefore, in cases such as *pañcakumāri* (an aggregate of five girls), there is indeed the status of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), as explained in detail in the second [book].
The purpose [of this discussion] is for the sake of [compounds] beginning with *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alaṃpūrva*, and those preceded by prefixes (*upasarga*) or *krānta*.

The examples in order are as follows: *pañcabhir gobhiḥ krītaḥ* (bought for five cows) becomes *pañcaguḥ*; *prāptā jīvikām* (attained a livelihood) becomes *prāptajīvikaḥ*; *āpannā jīvikām* (fallen into a livelihood) becomes *āpannajīvikaḥ*; *alaṃ kumāryai* (sufficient for a young girl) becomes *alaṅkumāriḥ*; *niṣkrāntaḥ kauśāmbyāḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī) becomes *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*.
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the second Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the Siddhāntasudhānidhi.

45. *Arthavadadhāturapratyayaḥ prātipadikam*: A meaningful linguistic form (*śabdarūpa*) that is distinct from both roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) shall receive the technical designation *prātipadika*. The use of this major technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the sake of conforming to the scriptural usage [of the Veda] which asks, "What is a root? What is a suffix? What is a *prātipadika*? The word "meaningful" (*arthavat*) refers to that which possesses a denotable object (*abhidheya*). This [definition] is intended to specify the particular entities to be designated. As it has been said: "The designation 'meaningful' should not apply to individual phonemes (*varṇa*). Nor is it the case that, by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of roots and so forth, only those things distinct from them that are meaningful are obtained [as *prātipadikas*].

Because that which possesses similarity through connection with another property (*dharmāntara*) is what must be excluded. Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to individual phonemes (*varṇa*). In the reading "and let it not be so for phonemes" (*varṇānāṃ ca mā bhūd*), the particle *ca* serves to include the collection of meaningless words such as "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*).

It might be argued: "Let phonemes be [the referents of] technical names (*saṃjñā*). Nor does the application of the suffixes *svādi* (beginning with *su*) follow; for those suffixes are prescribed by a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) to express number, object (*karman*), and so forth."

Not so; for [the suffixes] *su* and the rest would arise without distinction. Consequently, whether one posits a restriction on the meaning based on the context, or a restriction on the suffixes themselves, the occurrence of *sup*-suffixes after indeclinables (*avyaya*) and the like would be unavoidable. Furthermore, in cases such as *dhanaṃ* and *vanaṃ*, if the entire aggregate were designated as a distinct nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then because the [final *n*] would be included therein, the elision of the case-suffix (*vibhakti-lopa*) would entail the undesired elision of the *n* (*nalopa*). Nor can it be argued that this is barred by the prohibition "not being a verbal root" (*na cādhātuḥ*); for the elision of the suffix would apply to each individual [constituent], and in that state, there is an absence of the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*).

This is because the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful items pertains to cases where a specific form is explicitly mentioned, as in the rule *prādūhoḍha* and others. As for what was stated—that "due to the composite having a single meaning, there is an absence of case-endings [after the individual letters] because they are mere phonemes"—that holds true under the view that phonemes possess meaning, since by means of a single case-ending applied through the principle of *tantra*, the singular number residing in the meaning of both the whole and its parts is established. However, in the case of a name (*saṃjñā*) consisting of meaningless elements, since there is no object to be expressed, the suffix would apply even after each individual phoneme. This has been discussed elsewhere in the *Paspaśā*.

[Objection: But surely, because the word *dhātu* (verbal root) is mentioned separately in the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, it will be indicated that a verbal root lacks the designation *prātipadika*. Otherwise, since the elision (*luk*) would be established by the *prātipadika* status itself in cases such as *putrīyati*, the mention of *adhātu* (non-root) in the rule for *ahan vṛtram* and so forth would be useless, as the elision of *n* would not apply there.
[Response: Not so. Because in that case, the designation *prātipadika* is prohibited by the rule *apratyaya* (not a suffix), the mention of *dhātu* is justified for the purpose of that prohibition.

Nor is there a prohibition of the technical designation "non-suffix" (*apratyaya*) by virtue of the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). This is because it has been indicated that when an operation such as elision (*lopa*) is to be performed by the rule *na ṅi-sambuddhyoḥ*, the aforementioned exclusion (*paryudāsa*) does not apply, even if one relies on the definition of a suffix. Why say "non-suffix"? [Consider] *kāṇḍe*, *kuḍye*. If these were designated as "non-suffix," the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* ("the stem [ending in] a short vowel becomes [short] in the neuter") would not apply to the word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*).

In this commentary, although the mention of *kṛt* suffixes serves its purpose by providing the designation of *prātipadika* for forms such as *chid* and *bhid*—due to the prohibition [by Pāṇini 1.2.45] stating "not a verbal root"—the mention of *taddhita* suffixes will function as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the designation applies only to those word-forms ending in suffixes that are *taddhita*.

It might be argued as follows: even if each individual word (*pada*) ends in a suffix, the entire sentence (*vākya*) would still receive the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Nor can this be resolved by the exclusion of that which ends in a suffix; for according to the rule "when a suffix is mentioned, it includes what begins with that [suffix] and what ends with it," the term refers specifically to the aggregate of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix. But surely, its exclusion is achieved simply because it lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*); for it is only the words themselves that possess meaning through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), whereas the meaning of the sentence is obtained through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors.

Not so. A sentence, which is always manifested by *dhvani*, is the denoter of the specific sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) consisting of the relation between word-meanings. Otherwise, the sentence-meaning would not be verbal (*aśābdatva*). Thus, the sentence alone is the primary word (*mukhyaḥ śabdaḥ*), and the sentence-meaning alone is the primary word-meaning (*mukhyaḥ śabdārthaḥ*). The establishment of individual words and their meanings, however, is a conceptual construction based on assumed presence (*anvaya*) and absence (*vyatireka*) through similarity, for the sake of brevity; this is because of the established doctrine that it is impossible to acquire linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) with respect to every individual sentence. On this point, the *Vārttika* states: "The mention of compounds among meaningful aggregates is for the purpose of restriction."

But surely, in this way, there would be no designation (*saṃjñā*) for words such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*, *uccakaiḥ*, and *nīcakaiḥ* as well; for the suffix and the base are meaningful through the meanings [respectively] expressed and denoted by them, and thus they are delimited by the property that serves as the delimiting condition of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*), namely the state of being a collection of meaningful elements (*arthavat-samudāyatva*). Nor should it be argued that, just as the production of case-endings (*svādi*) does not occur in the absence of a designation, so too the elision of previously produced case-endings will not occur, and thus the desired result is established by that very [lack of designation]. This cannot be maintained, because it would lead to errors regarding accent (*svara*).

For instance, regarding the rule *citaḥ saprakṛter bahvakajartham* in the *Cita-sūtra*, the accent of the *cit* [element] is prescribed by including its base (*prakṛti*). Consequently, in the case of *paṭavaḥ* (nominative plural), since the base is related to the suffix *bahu-c* (the plural marker), the vowel *ja* (of *jas*) would become udātta. However, when the previously arisen *sup* suffix is elided, the newly arisen case-ending is not included within the base; thus, the vowel *ṭā* (of *ṭāp*) becomes udātta, whereby the desired result is established.

Even in cases such as *uccakaiḥ*, since there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*) following the entire form including the suffix *akac*, it would not be a word (*pada*), and consequently, in examples like *uccakaiḥ paṭhati*, the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would be untenable, because that rule is governed by the heading *padāt*. This [objection] arises from not resorting to the maxim of "that which falls in the middle of two" (*tanmadhyapatitanyāya*). Therefore, the term *apratyayaḥ* must be stated in order to indicate that the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) indeed applies to the aggregate of base and suffix. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of excluding forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*, because the prohibition applies only to that which ends in a suffix.

Nor can it be argued that "in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends in it"; for that prohibition applies only where a technical name is being prescribed, whereas here it is a prohibition of the technical name itself—thus there is a difference. Furthermore, one should not say that *bahupaṭavaḥ*, ending in *jas*, is also indeed "ending in a suffix" (*pratyayānta*); because the suffix *jas* arises from the word *paṭu* alone, the entire aggregate does not possess the status of "ending in that [suffix]."

Nor should it be argued that by means of a *bahuvrīhi* analysis—namely, "that in which no suffix (*pratyaya*) is found"—there would also be a prohibition of forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ* (where *paṭu-ādi-* [beginning with a suffix] is present). This is because a *tatpuruṣa* compound is more immediate (*antaraṅga*) due to the predominance of the meaning of the constituent members (*vartipadārtha*).
Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The restriction is made only for those of the same class, since the prescription of compounds applies only to those ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*)."

Nor should it be argued that in examples such as *aśvakrītī*, there exists a compound of a word ending in a *sup*-suffix with one not ending in a *sup*-suffix, based on the rule: "The statement regarding the compounding of prefixes, verbal roots, and secondary words (*upapada*) with *kṛt*-derivatives occurs prior to the arising of *sup*-suffixes. Kaiyaṭa states that this is because [the rule] applies to those things characterized by meaningfulness through the mediation of either difference (*bheda*) or relation (*saṃsarga*). Thus, the result is that the aforementioned restriction excludes a collection that has not entered into the relationship of base and suffix, provided that collection is distinct from a compound.

For this reason, out of fear of the aforementioned fault and by virtue of the prohibition of [the designation] for that which ends in an affix, the *Nyāsa* commentary explains the passage as being intended according to its literal meaning: "The designation indeed applies to the entire aggregate of the base and the affix."

However, some [hold that] the exclusion applies to that compound where the prior portion is a *pada* (word) but the subsequent portion is not an affix (*pratyaya*). In the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, there is no fault because the prior portion lacks the status of a *pada*. In cases such as *janmavān*, however, the subsequent portion is indeed an affix. Nor can the mention of the term *taddhita* (secondary derivative) serve as a restrictive indicator [for this interpretation], because its purpose is already fulfilled in examples like *aupagavaḥ*, where the prior portion receives the designation *bha*. Furthermore, the designation *pada* cannot be based upon an internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) [contained within the compound].

This is because that [designation] is sublated by the designation "bha," which has the same limit. Nor should it be argued that there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the entire aggregate—such as *ayam iyān*—receiving the designation [of "bha"], since even though the preceding portion is a word (*pada*), the subsequent portion is an affix (*pratyaya*), and thus, by the aforementioned rule, the designation does not apply there. For they say that "being prescribed by that" is also a qualifier of the affix; and since the absence of the qualified [condition]—which is conditioned by the absence of being prescribed by that—is still present there as well, [the designation applies].

Nor does the designation [of *kṛt*] apply to a collection of nominal and verbal suffixes (*sup-tiṅ-samudāya*), because the rule "the [suffix] *jah* expresses the agent frequently in connection with its object" (*jahikarmaṇā bahulamābhīkṣṇye kartāram cābhidadhāti*) is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Although the designation of a compound (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of [triggering] the final acute accent of the compound, Kaiyaṭa states that this was said in order to demonstrate that it belongs to the same class, since the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) follows simply from being a compound.

Nor does the undesirable consequence (āpatti) apply to a collection of finite verbs (tiṅ-samudāya) such as “paśya dhāvati” (see, he runs), because the rule “ākhyātamākhyātena kriyāsātatye” (a finite verb may be compounded with another finite verb to express continuity of action) is intended as a restrictive rule (niyamārtha). Therefore, it is established that by the mention of the term “compound” (samāsa), there is an exclusion of all similar types of sentences through restriction. On this point, they say: In the view of the Naiyāyikas, since a compound lacks both expressive power (śakti) and indication (lakṣaṇā), it possesses no meaningfulness (arthavattva); consequently, if [the rule] were intended to prescribe a designation for that which has not otherwise obtained its status, then forms such as “bahupaṭavaḥ” (many cloths) would be unestablished, because they would lack the status of a compound due to the absence of being a derivative ending in a secondary suffix (taddhita).

Nor should it be said that the mention of *taddhita* suffixes refers to those [suffixes] as qualified by that [meaning], because this would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *pacatakī*. That is not correct; for since the two word-meanings are construed respectively as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*prakāra*), those [grammarians] admit that only such a composite [form] which acquires a qualified meaning is devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*). However, in the case of the suffix *bahuc*, since it is a suffix with its own inherent meaning (*svārthika*), the word *paṭu* itself possesses that [qualified] meaning.

And thus, this is the distinction: for the Grammarians, since even sentences and compounds possess meaningfulness—just like "bahupaṭavaḥ" (those who are very clever)—the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, there arises the contingency of excluding such cases as "bahupaṭavaḥ" from the application of the technical term [“noun”], just as it excludes a sentence; therefore, the designation of a sentence is prevented by relying on that specific form which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) of the restriction, thereby excluding it.

For the Naiyāyikas, however, the technical designation [of *prātipadika*] applies to a compound because of specific rules governing compounds, but not to a sentence, due to the absence of such specific rules and because the general rule does not apply in the absence of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*). As for forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*, the designation of *prātipadika* follows from meaningfulness alone, according to both systems.

As for what was also stated—that if the mention of *samāsa* (compound) were not for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the whole [word] being included in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, because when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included; whereas in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the restriction established by the mention of *samāsa* excludes that [whole word] due to its superior status—thus, in the rule *kṛttaddhita*, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of *kṛt* does not apply at all, because there is no result [to be achieved].

That too is incorrect; for when a restrictive rule (niyama) operates by way of affirmation, a prohibition is necessarily implied, and thus a contradiction with perceptible injunctions is impossible. This is because the perceptual [injunction] is stronger than that which is merely implied, and because it must necessarily be assumed that a prohibition applies not only to a compound but also to a form ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*).

Even in the view that [the rule] functions by way of prohibition (*niṣedhamukhena*), once the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) has been established for that which is preceded by a *kāraka* by means of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*-affixes, there could be no exclusion even by a subsequent restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is because there is no scope elsewhere for the injunction establishing the designation of a nominal stem for that which is preceded by a *kāraka*; and since a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between a rule with scope and one without scope is untenable.

Nor does its non-application follow from the requirement of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is because there is no basis for a restrictive rule in the assumption that the rule pertains to elements other than *kṛt*-affixes, or in the contraction of the technical maxim regarding the mention of *kṛt* (*kṛdgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*). Furthermore, this would lead to a circular argument: if the maxim does not apply, the rule would be common to all *kṛt*-affixes; but once that is established, the maxim would not apply. On the contrary, since the maxim presents itself first, it is more logical that the rule pertains to elements other than those [governed by the maxim] once the designation is established for what is preceded by a *kāraka*.

Furthermore, in the rule *kṛttaddhita*, when the governing maxim (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes applies, there would be elision (*luk*) of the third case-ending even in the alternative where no compound is formed in the example *mūlakenopadaṃśam*. Nor is the rule prescribing the optionality of the compound redundant; for its utility is established by the need to apply the *śākala* substitution and the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) in the case of *dadhi-upadaṃśam*.

Otherwise, because the rule *amaivāvyayena* would result in an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), the prohibition of the *śākala-prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) would apply according to the statement: "The prohibition [of *prakṛtibhāva*] must be stated for *si* and obligatory compounds. This was stated by Kaiyaṭa in the fourth [chapter]. Furthermore, Sīradeva stated that such a [separate mention of *kṛt*] is justified in order to prevent the accentuation of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvara*) which would otherwise be triggered by the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*. However, he first stated that this is not the case, because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [of *kṛt*] is not sublated by the subsequent restrictive rule (*niyama*), and because the maxim regarding the mention of *kṛt* (*kṛdgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) simply does not apply here.

For instance, in cases such as *praṣṭhī*, one might suspect that the suffixes *ṅī* and others would apply even prior to the formation of the compound, by virtue of rules such as *puṃyogāt*. Anticipating this, it is stated that because the aggregate *praṣṭha-* and so on lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the feminine suffix is untenable. Then, suspecting that the designation [of nominal stem] might still apply to the aggregate because it ends in a *kṛt*-suffix—by virtue of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*—it is further argued that although the designation of nominal stem does not apply to what ends in a suffix due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*), the designation does apply to what ends in a *kṛt* by means of the mention of *kṛt*; however, [this is not the case].

It has been stated that [the suffix] applies even to that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. Therefore, the meaning of that text is as follows: once the compound has been formed, because of the designation of *prātipadika* based on that [compound], there is a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Consequently, both [authors] have stated that the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] does not apply there.
Therefore, it should be resolved in this way:

In the rule *kṛttaddhita* (Pāṇini 1.2.46), although there is no application of the principle of "extension to that which ends with [the element mentioned]" (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned in a technical definition (*saṃjñāvidhi*), it is clear from the Bhāṣya and other sources that—by virtue of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *arthavat* ("meaning-bearing")—one relies upon the meaningfulness attributed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Thus, the designation *prātipadika* applies to a collection that conveys a meaning, provided that such a collection conveys a meaning when the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are combined.

Consequently, even in the view of the Naiyāyikas, because the term *arthavat* (meaning-bearing) is understood to carry over [from Pāṇini 1.2.45], the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies only to the aggregate of base and suffix due to the force of the rule's formulation, and not even to that which is preceded by a *kāraka*. This is because there is no evidence for including more than that; and by virtue of that, the *paribhāṣā* itself does not apply.

In reality, there is no scope for that technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) here, because it will be made known under the rule *gati-r-anantara* (P. 6.2.49), the meaning of which is that only a prefix (*upasarga*) immediately preceding [the verbal root] is to be understood; for both types of prefixes are not taken simultaneously, and because we see the same in examples such as *avatatena-kula-sthitam* and *udake-viśīrṇam*. Now, one might object: this sūtra is redundant, since even in the view that words are derived (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*), the desired forms are established everywhere simply by virtue of being *kṛdanta* (ending in a primary suffix). This is not so, because [the sūtra] serves a purpose in the view that words are underived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*). In that case, the ancients maintain that this very sūtra is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of the existence of that view].

It is also stated in the *Nirukta*: "Śākaṭāyana holds that nouns are derived from verbs, as is the convention of the etymologists (*nairukta*); but Gārgya and some grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) hold that this is not the case for all [words].

Even regarding the position that [words] are derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), Haradatta’s claim that [this applies] to particles (*nipāta*) and onomatopoeias (*anukaraṇa*) is questionable, because even in those cases, it is possible to postulate a root-form (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

In reality, however, even according to the view that [the suffix] is derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*), the rule is for the sake of forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*. Nor should it be argued that the rule should simply have been formulated as "preceded by *bahu*," because this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases like *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, since these end in *kṛt*-suffixes; furthermore, without the *arthavat-sūtra*, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) could not function as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). So say the Dīkṣitas.

That is incorrect, because when differentiation is intended (*bhedavivakṣā*), there is no evidence for the optional application of the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth to onomatopoeias (*anukaraṇa*).

However, this is the distinction: in the view where difference (*bheda*) is intended to be expressed, the designation of *prātipadika* applies because of its meaningfulness through the original object (*anukārya*), as in the case of rules such as *bhuvo vuk*. But when non-difference (*abheda*) is intended, it does not apply, as in the case of *gavityayamāha*. Furthermore, since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding words like *mūlaka* has already been refuted, [the rule] *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca* (P. 1.2.46) [is established].

Words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, words ending in *taddhita* suffixes, and compounds receive the designation of *prātipadika*. Since the prohibition regarding those ending in suffixes was stated previously, this [present rule], being its exception, applies only to those ending in suffixes; thus the author of the *Nyāsa* maintains that the rule "in the formulation of a technical designation" (*saṃjñāvidhau*) does not apply here. In cases such as *liṭ* and *dhuk*, the exclusion "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*) applies, and in cases such as *kartā*, the exclusion "ending in a suffix" (*pratyayāntam*) applies; therefore, this [present rule] is commenced. Furthermore, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) has been explained as being for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).

Objection: Since a compound (*samāsa*) ends in a suffix, this rule would be one that applies where [the condition] has not otherwise been reached (*aprāpta-vidhi*). Reply: Not so; for when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇe*), the reference is only to that which begins with the element from which that suffix was prescribed. Nor should it be argued that, because of the rule "and in the case of a feminine suffix, provided it is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*)," there is no restriction regarding the initial element (*tadādi-niyama*) in the case of a non-secondary feminine suffix, and thus the rule would apply to forms such as *rājakumārī*.

Even though the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* etc. is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, it does not apply in the domain of nominal stems (*liṅgaviṣaya*), because the formation of a compound occurs only when the case-ending (*sup*) is actually heard, according to the maxim: "Having set aside the domain of an exception. In that context, since the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applies to the compound sentence by virtue of not ending in a suffix, it remains easily available even after the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktiluk*) by the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). For this very reason, in examples such as *gomatpriyaḥ*, the augment *num* and others do not occur; for once there is elision by means of *luk*, there is no application of the rule regarding the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

[Objection: Even so, [the rule] would still be for the purpose of prescribing [the technical name] in the case of an *asamartha-samāsa* (an unconnected compound). [Response: Not so; because the term *arthavat* ("meaningful") is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), and that [unconnected compound] is devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*).
