Nor does this result in the non-attainment of the technical name in that case; for its establishment is secured by the very evidence that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). For, by the rule "after *asūrya* and *lalāṭa*," the suffix *khaś* is applied when the word *asūrya* is an attendant word (*upapada*). And since it is impossible for something to be an attendant word unless it is a word-form consisting of a case-inflected item (*vibhaktyanta*) uttered prior to the main word, [the technical name must apply].

It might be argued as follows: this is an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) regarding the meaning of compounds such as "hare’s horn" (*śaśaviṣāṇa*), because those [individual words] are devoid of meaning. But one might object: the word "hare" refers to that which lacks a connection with a hare; its connection with "horn" occurs through identity (*abheda*). Thus, it should be said that the phrase means "a horn identical with that which lacks a connection with a hare," and so it is indeed meaningful. However, this cannot be maintained, for it would result in the sentence "there is no hare’s horn" being semantically impossible (*ayogya*). For this very reason, the learned authorities maintain that when there is a certainty regarding the absence of a connection between a hare and a horn, no verbal cognition arises from the sentence "an archer’s bow is fashioned from a hare’s horn. For this very reason—
Here goes the son of a barren woman, wearing a crest made of sky-flowers,
having bathed in the waters of a mirage, and bearing a bow made of a rabbit's horn.

Kṣīrasvāmin and others have stated that such [expressions as] "it is useless" (*ityāderapārthakatvam*) are meaningless. For this very reason, it was said in the *Bauddhādhikāradīdhiti*: "Because the apprehension of a conventional relation (*saṅgatigrahaṇa*) is absent, words such as 'hare's horn' lack denotative power. This is not so. According to the Patañjali Sūtra—"Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows verbal cognition and is devoid of an objective reality"—even an unreal thing like a hare's horn is cognizable by means of a word. Furthermore, the function (*vṛtti*) of a word is accepted in that case as being: "the unreal is denoted by this word. For this very reason, it was stated in the *Līlāvatī*: "Even a sky-lotus is apprehended through a verbal appearance (*śabdābhāsa*)."
For it has been stated by the author of the *Khaṇḍana* that "a word indeed produces a cognition even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent.

In reality, however, the word *śaśa* (hare) possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward that which is the counter-positive of the absolute absence residing in the hare. Consequently, because it possesses meaning through its referent, it receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The cognition "a horn characterized by a specific relation to a hare," however, arises solely from error. By this, the expression "there is no hare’s horn" is also explained; for in that case as well, it is the specific relation to the hare itself that serves as the delimiting factor of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatā*), and thus it is the object of error.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Dīdhiti*: "Because for one who has mastered the individual word-meanings such as 'hare' and so on, there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition of that [non-existent] object from words like 'hare's horn'"; this is said with the intention that the compound as a whole lacks semantic value (*arthavattva*).

However, this is the distinction: a compound such as 'hare's horn', which possesses the capacity for such a specific meaning, may sometimes convey a different understanding due to an error regarding its expressive power (*śakti*).
The ancients, however, maintain that words such as 'sky-flower' and 'hare's horn' possess semantic value because they denote non-existence (*abhāva*).

For instance: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "there is no flower in the sky" (*khe puṣpaṃ nāsti*), the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is included within the compound. The statement "it does not exist" (*nāsti*) in the analysis is for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the compound; however, the series of words beginning with "it does not exist" following the compound is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). This is clear from the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* and other works, so they say; this is the direction [of the argument]. [Pāṇini 1.2.47: "The short vowel replaces the final of a nominal stem in the neuter."

In the neuter gender, there is shortening of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *a*. By the mention of "short" (*hrasva*), the term "vowel" (*ac*) is brought to mind, and thus the rule of "ending-in" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. If one were to construe it as "of a vowel belonging to the nominal stem," there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and there would also be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *suvāk kulam* (the family with good speech). Nor is the inclusion of the word "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) redundant, since it might otherwise be inferred from the word "nominal stem" alone; its purpose is to exclude cases such as *kāṇḍe*, *kuḍye*, or *ramate brāhmaṇakulam* (the neuter noun used as a locative or verb). Furthermore, just as number is taken as a property of the substratum of the action, gender (*liṅga*) can likewise be taken as a property of the nominal stem itself.

It should not be argued that, by the logic already stated, in examples such as *doṣā brāhmaṇakulam* ("the Brāhmaṇa family [is] at night"), even though the word *doṣā* is metaphorical due to its association with the time of night, the indeclinable would still incur the fault of becoming short because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For the two words *doṣā* and *divā* signify "night" and "day" respectively, qualified by the sense of the locative case. When the time—being the locus of actions performed by the Brāhmaṇa family—becomes the locus for the family itself, one says: *doṣā dṛśyate*, *carati*, or *adhīte* ("he is seen," "he moves about," or "he studies at night").

Because the locus (adhikaraṇa) serves as the substratum for the action through the mediation of that which is to be contained (ādheya), it follows that the indeclinable (avyaya) is exclusively a locus and not itself a neuter noun.

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as *kāṇḍībhūtaṃ brāhmaṇakulam* ("the Brahmin family has become divided into sections"), since there is an intention to express non-difference between the base (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*), the word ending in the suffix *cvi* would also be neuter, resulting in over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Nor can it be argued that once the shortening (*hrasva*) has occurred, the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by the rule *cvau ca* will apply; for while the lengthening is internal (*antaraṅga*), the shortening is external (*bahiraṅga*), and thus the shortening is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the lengthening is to take effect. Similarly, one might argue that in *ramate*, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* (prescribed by *ṭeḥ*) does not occur after the shortening has taken place. [Response: This is not so.

Because an indeclinable (*avyaya*) does not denote a sentient being (*asattvavācin*), it lacks neuter gender. By this, verbal suffixes (*tibanta*) are also explained; for even a verb, which expresses number residing in the substance that is the substratum of power (*śaktyāśrayadravya*), lacks the capacity to express its [the substance's] gender, due to the inherent nature of linguistic power (*śabdaśakti*). Even in the case of "the two stalks stand" (*kāṇḍe tiṣṭhataḥ*), there is an absence of neuter gender because number is predominant.

If, however, the designation of neuter gender were applied to the aggregate (*samudāya*) which possesses the properties of its parts (*avayava*), then in cases such as *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*, [the rule] would apply; for since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the case ending (*vibhakti*) is included by the mention of "nominal stem," one would have to formulate the rule as: "The short vowel occurs in place of that [final phoneme] which is in the neuter. The meaning of this is that the shortening occurs when the neuter gender belongs directly to that [aggregate] itself, but not when it belongs to it through its parts.

Alternatively, the meaning is "of that very [aggregate] in which distinction has not yet arisen"; and since that which ends in a case suffix has distinction already arisen, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The intention of the author of the Sūtras, however, is this: here, only a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that functions as a neuter in its primary sense is taken. Because the status of being a nominal stem is extended [to these forms] through the application of the rule for "behaving like the end" (*antavadbhāva*), it is not primary. Therefore, in examples such as *yugavaratrāya*, *yugavaratrārtham*, and *yugavaratrebhyaḥ*, the short vowel does not occur; for the long vowels and so forth are considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) due to their being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). In the same way, it should be explained that in examples such as *atikhaṭvāyai*, the short vowel also does not occur by virtue of the subsequent rule. *go-striyor upasarjanasya* (1.2.48).

Regarding the term *upasarjana* [in the rule] *gostriyoḥ*: these two (*go* and *strī*) are qualifiers of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, there is an application of the rule regarding what ends in that [stem]. This is because the prohibition—"by means of a nominal stem that involves [the mention of] a suffix"—is restricted solely to the domain of rules prescribing suffixes. Thus, when *go* or *strī* function as an *upasarjana*, the short vowel [substitution] shall apply to the nominal stem ending in them. [This follows from the rule] *alo’ntyasya*. Examples: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *atikhaṭvaḥ*. Their status as *upasarjana* is established by the rule *ekavibhakti ca*. Example: *citraguḥ* (one who has brindled cows), because [the word *go*] is specified in the nominative case.
It might be argued that in cases such as *atiśrīḥ* and *atilakṣmīḥ*, there would be shortening [of the final vowel]. Not so;
for on this point there is a Vārttika: "The mention of *go* and *tāṅ* is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] kṛt suffixes."

The meaning is: "of all feminine bases," including those ending in *dhātu* (verbal roots). The term *ṭāṅ* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) beginning with *ṭāp* and ending with the *ṅ* of *ṣyaṅ*. Thus, there is no fault regarding feminine bases derived from *kṛt* suffixes, as they fall outside this range. However, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* state: "By relying on the *svarita* accent, only those suffixes prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) 'in the feminine' (*striyām*) are to be understood. This is because the principle that "by relying on the *svarita* accent" means that wherever the *svarita* occurs, the governing rule is to be supplied there, will also be explained later.

[Objection: But in this case, in examples such as *atikrānto rājakumārīm* ("one who has surpassed the princess") or *atirājakumāriḥ*, the short vowel [substitution] should not occur; for when there is a mention of an affix (*pratyaya-grahaṇe*), only that which begins with the element from which the affix is prescribed and ends with it is understood. Since the word *kumāra* is the base for the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, it is the word *kumārī* alone—and not the compound *rājakumārī*—that ends in a feminine suffix. [Reply: This is not so, because there is no restriction regarding the initiality of the base (*tadādiniyama*) when a feminine suffix is involved. For this very reason, the rule "vocalization of the semivowel in *ṣyaṅ*" (*ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*) applies in the example *paramakārīṣagandhīputraḥ*.

Is it not the case that when a feminine suffix occurs as an *upasarjana* (secondary member), the rule of "starting from that" (*tadādiniyama*) certainly applies; otherwise, in a form such as *atikārīṣagandhyāputraḥ*, the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) would undesirably occur? On this point, Kaiyaṭa states: "In some instances, even when a feminine suffix occurs as an *upasarjana*, the rule of 'starting from that' does not apply, because of the inclusion of the term 'long vowel' (*dīrgha*) in the sūtra *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [Pāṇini 6.1.68]. Otherwise, in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *atikhaṭvaḥ*, since these are *upasarjanas*, there would be no occurrence of a stem ending in *ṅī* or *ā*; consequently, the elision of the nominative suffix (*su*) would not be required, which would render that [mention of 'long vowel'] purposeless."

[Objection: But if this were so, since the suffix *ḍhak* would also arise after the word *kumbhakārī* (by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*), the form *kaumbhakāreya* would be established; consequently, its establishment in the rule *anupasarjanāt* would not occur, which would contradict the *Bhāṣya*. [Response: This is not so. For the intention there is that, in the absence of the restriction regarding the initial element of the compound (*tadādiniyama*), the suffix might sometimes apply even after the word *kārī*.

As for the author of the *Nyāsa*, he says: "This *paribhāṣā* is obtained through a split of the *yoga* in the rule defining the technical term *aṅga*. In that context, one must explain that its application does not occur here by relying on the recurrence of the word *vā* in the rule *vā'ami*, which serves to indicate an unrestricted option (*avyavasthitavibhāṣā*)."

Alternatively, one might argue that the particle *ca* (and) from the rule *kṛttaddhita* [Pāṇini 1.2.46] should be understood as continuing here for the purpose of including cases not explicitly mentioned.

To this, it may be replied: there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *gokula*. Furthermore, although the word *kumārī* in *kumārīputra* is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because it ends in a suffix, the word *rājakumārī* is a nominal stem by virtue of being a compound; consequently, there would likewise be an over-extension in the case of *rājakumārīputra*. However, no such suspicion arises regarding forms like *khaṭvāyāda* or *mālāyāda*, because the application of the rules of "end-like" (*antavadbhāva*) or "beginning-like" (*ādivadbhāva*) is prohibited when a single element depends on both sides of a boundary.

For here, both the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) are relied upon—namely, "that nominal stem which ends in a feminine suffix. Now, if the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) possesses the status of being the end of the nominal stem, then it does not possess the status of being the end of the feminine suffix; conversely, if it possesses the status of being the beginning of the feminine suffix, then it does not possess the status of being a nominal stem.

This is not so, because in examples such as *gokula*, that status of being the end [of the stem] is absent, and furthermore, because the application of the designation [of a property] to what is not identical with it (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) is prohibited in the case of a nominal stem.

Objection: Since the author of the *Vārttika* stated in the rule *yena vidhis* ("by which [a rule] is prescribed") that "the suffix *am* follows *roṇī*" (*roṇyā am*) and "and of that" (*tasya ca*), it follows that the term *svaṃ rūpam* ("its own form") is understood as being carried over [from the previous rule]. Consequently, even in the absence of the suffix *-anta*, a short vowel would occur in examples such as *gokula* simply because the actual form of the word *go* exists there. Reply: Not so. Because *svaṃ rūpam* is not carried over. This is because the *Vārttika* on the rule *ādyantavat* states: "The purpose [of the rule] is that when a grammatical operation is prescribed by means of something, that [something] includes what ends with it. Thus, the suffix *-anta* is required for the application of the rule.
Even so, there is no possibility of a short vowel in the word *gokulam* based solely on the Vārttika "and of that," because that Vārttika is supplementary to the [preceding] rule concerning *akṣa*.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable. For by the statement "of that which has as its final member a secondary element (*upasarjana*) consisting of a feminine suffix," one obtains precisely that finality which is relative to that very thing in relation to which there is the status of being a secondary element. Now, although the word *rājakumārī* possesses the status of being a secondary element relative to the compound with the word *putra* (i.e., *rājakumāryāḥ putraḥ*), it lacks finality relative to that same [compound]. Otherwise, even if the Vārttika "the prohibition of the preceding member" (*pūrvapadapratiṣedhaḥ*) were commenced, the [intended result] could not be established.

In the three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound *pañca-kumāryaḥ-priyaḥ* ("one whose beloveds are five maidens"), the first two members would undergo the formation of a *dvigu* compound according to the rule *taddhitārthottarapada*. Consequently, because the word *kumārī* would no longer occupy the position of a prior member (*pūrvapada*), its final vowel would undergo shortening (*hrasva*). This occurs because both the status of being a final member (*anta*) and the status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) apply to it with respect to different correlates. By this same reasoning, the form *agoputraḥ* is also explained.

Even so, the prohibition of the *dvandva* compound must still be stated. In the case of *kukkuṭamayūryau* ("the cock and the peahen"), because the meaning of the constituent parts is subordinate (*upasarjana*) to the meaning of the whole compound, and because the word *mayūrī* is subordinate due to its being designated in the nominative case under the governing rule "anekam," and because it occupies the final position in that very compound.

Not so; for since it will be stated later that "the gender [of a compound] is that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgam*) and "the word and its meaning [are both designated]" (*śabdaśabdārthau*), we accept the extension (*atideśa*) of both the gender and the suffix that convey that meaning. Thus, even though the word *mayūrī* has been shortened according to the aforementioned rule, the suffix *ṅīp* is justified after the *dvandva* compound because the two constituent meanings, being in close proximity to one another, constitute the meaning of the *dvandva*; consequently, due to their predominance, they do not possess the status of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

This might be the case: "A prohibition regarding *kap* must be stated," as in *bahukumārīkaḥ*. This [reference to *kap*] is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Because *kap* is internal (*antaraṅga*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the application of the short vowel rule even before *kap* has occurred. Nor can there be a prohibition by the rule "not in *kap*" (*na kapi*), because that [rule] prohibits only what is obtained by the rule "before *ka*, [the final vowel of a stem ending in] *aṇ*" (*ke'ṇaḥ*). This follows from the maxim "of what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya*). Otherwise, there would result the prohibition of forms such as *priyagrāmaṇikaḥ* (one for whom a dear village-headman exists), since the word *grāmaṇi* is neuter when it functions as a qualifier of *kula* and the like.

Not so; for since the suffix *kap* is a constituent part of the compound-ending (*samāsānta*), once *kap* has been applied, the feminine-stem ending [in *yavāgū*] lacks the status of being a nominal base (*prātipadika*) of the compound. Furthermore, in examples such as *bahuyavāgūkaḥ* and *atimālaḥ*, because both rules have their scope, *kap* alone prevails due to its higher priority (*paratva*). Nor should it be argued that shortening (*hrasvatva*) is "internal" (*antaranga*) because it depends merely on a nominal base ending in a feminine suffix that is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), whereas *kap* is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on a specific type of compound—a *bahuvrīhi* where the subsequent member is a river-name (*nadī*). This is because [the application of *kap*] is not dependent on the specific nature of the compound, but rather on the presence of the feminine suffix itself.

According to the view that *samāsānta* suffixes are those which follow the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) for the sake of the compound’s meaning, the suffix *kap* is internal (*antaraṅga*) relative to all other operations of the compound, because *kap* depends on a constituent part (*avayava*), whereas the short vowel (*hrasva*) depends on the whole (*samudāya*).

Therefore, the *vārttika* "The statement of masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies to a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *īyas*" must indeed be commenced. [Example: *bahuśreyasī* ("one who has many excellent things"), where there is a prohibition of *kap* by the rule "and after *īyas*" (*īyasaśca*). Why "of a *bahuvrīhi*"? Consider *atiśreyasiḥ* ("one who has surpassed the excellent"), a *tatpuruṣa* compound, so that the short vowel may apply there.
[Rule 49: *luk taddhitaluki* (When a *taddhita* suffix is elided, [the feminine suffix is also elided]).

There is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix. Since elision (*luk*), being of the nature of non-existence, cannot be posterior [to anything], [the rule applies]. For example: *pañcendraḥ*, meaning "that which has five Indrāṇīs as its deities. First, there is a compound by the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51). Then, the suffix *aṇ* is added by the rule "sā'sya devatā" (Pāṇini 4.2.24). That *aṇ* is elided by the rule "dvigorluganapatye" (Pāṇini 4.1.88). By this [present rule], there is elision of the *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule "indravaruṇa... (Pāṇini 4.1.49). By the principle of "being taught in conjunction" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭanyāya*), the augment *ānuk* is also withdrawn.

"Purchased for five *śaṣkulī*s" is *pañcaśaṣkulaḥ*. By the rule "that which is purchased by that" (*tena krītam*), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; this is elided by the rule "after *adhyardha* and [numerals] preceded by them... (*adhyardhapūrva-*). The fruit of the *āmalakī* is *āmalakam*. By the rule "always after *vṛddha* [stems] and *śara* etc. (*nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied; there is elision of the suffix when referring to the fruit (*phale luk*). In the same way, *badaram* and *kuvalam*. *Śaṣkulī* and the others end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaurādi* group. Their status as secondary members (*upasarjana*) is based on common usage (*laukika*), because both types are included here by the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*). What is the purpose of the mention of elision (*luki*)? [Consider: *gārgīkulam*.
From the word *gārgya*, by the rule "yañaśca," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; then, by the rule "yasyeti ca," the vowel *a* is elided, and finally, by the rule "halastaddhitasya," the *y* is elided.

This might be argued: the female descendant (gotra) of Avanti is *Avantī*. By the rule "vṛddhet-kosalājādāt," the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied. *Kuntī* is formed in the same way. The female descendant of Kuru is *Kurūḥ*. By the rule "kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ," the suffix *ṇya* is applied; then by the rule "striyām-avantikuntikurubhyaś-ca," there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. For the first two [Avantī and Kuntī], the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "ito manuṣyajāteḥ"; for the last [Kurūḥ], the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rule "ūṅutaḥ. In these cases, since the feminine suffixes of Avantī and the others are present as upasarjanas (subordinate members of a compound), and since the elision of the taddhita suffix has already been effected, there would have to be an elision of the feminine suffix itself.

Not so; for this elision (*luk*) operates only where there is an elision of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) following a feminine suffix. And in this case, the feminine suffix arises after the elision has already taken place. As it has been said: "Because [the suffix] is not followed by one that does not undergo elision" (*aluk-paratvāt*). This is the meaning. However, the author of the Vārttika stated this by relying on a conceptual priority (*paratva*) of the elision, which is mentally constructed.

For the author of the Bhāṣya, however, there is no fault precisely because of the absence of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). This is because the feminine suffix is qualified by a subordinate element, and since a technical (*śāstrīya*) subordinate element is impossible here, he relies on the status of being a subordinate element in the sense of being non-principal (*apradhāna*). Furthermore, in cases such as *avantī*, since the genus characterized by offspring (*apatya*) is expressed as the principal meaning, and because it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), there is no shortening of the vowel.

In cases such as *āmalaka*, however, because it ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); since it is introduced as being already qualified by gender, the technical rule regarding gender-qualified forms (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) does not apply. In *kurūḥ* as well, because the prohibition of the treatment as if it were the final element (*antavadbhāva*) applies when relying on both sides [of a grammatical operation], [the rule does not apply].

**Pāṇini 1.2.50**: *idgoṇyāḥ*. When a secondary derivative suffix is elided (*taddhitaluki*), the vowel *i* shall be substituted for the final vowel of the word *goṇī* in the aforementioned context. For example: *pañcagoṇiḥ*, meaning "purchased for five *goṇīs*. In this case, the compound is formed according to the rule "taddhitārtha—" (Pāṇini 2.1.51), and the suffix *ṭhak* is added in the sense of "purchased. As before, that suffix is elided. Since the elision would have resulted in a long vowel, the rule introducing the short vowel is established. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:
"It should be stated that [the rule] does not apply to *idgoṇī*, for shortness (*hrasvatā*) is indeed prescribed there;
or rather, if such a statement were made, it would serve only that specific purpose."

"By means of the feminine suffix *goṇī*, the substitution of *it* [for the final vowel] is established through the context, or else for the sake of [the forms] *sūcī* and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows: Now, one might object: "In the case of *goṇī*, it would be sufficient to simply prohibit the elision (*luk*) [of the feminine suffix], rather than prescribing the substitution of *it*; for the desired form is already established by the shortening rule [Pāṇini 1.2.48], *gostriyoḥ*. This is not so. For if one were to say *na* (prohibition) or if one were to say *it* (substitution), there would be no difference in the result. When this is merely *goṇī*—that is, when the suffix *mātra* is elided such that it becomes *goṇiḥ*—then, once the elision (*luk*) is prohibited, the shortening is successfully established.

Therefore, the purpose of including the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) in the rule for the first case ending is so that the first case may occur even where words denoting measure refer to the object measured, even in the absence of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). And thus, since [the word *goṇī*] is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*) and, by the metaphorical attribution of identity (*abhedopacāra*), it functions as the object of measurement, the shortening [of the vowel] does not apply; hence, the rule for *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) is prescribed. But if this were so, would *ittva* not apply everywhere to the word *goṇī*?

In that case, the term *upasarjanasya* (of the subordinate element) indeed continues to apply, but not the phrase *taddhitaluki* (when there is elision of a secondary suffix). Therefore, this rule for *it*-lengthening is prescribed where another meaning is conveyed by means of a word whose own primary meaning is subordinate; for in such a case, the desired form cannot be established by the short vowel [rule], because that rule does not apply since the word is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvena*). He rejects [the objection] by another method: "The *it*-lengthening of *goṇī* [is unnecessary]. The words "need not be taught" (*aśiṣyam*) are to be supplied as the remainder. [He says] "because of the context. The rule should simply have been formulated as *goṇyāḥ*. Nor does the proximity [of the previous rule] entail the undesirable consequence of the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the elision (*luk*).

Because it would result in redundancy; for [the desired form] is already established by that very [rule]. Thus, when the term *hrasva* (short vowel) is carried over, shortness is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to elision (*luk*), and the desired result is established. He states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In the case of *sūci*, etc. Although [the forms] such as *goṇi* are established even by the elision of the mere measure (*mātra-lopa*), nevertheless, this [mention of *hrasva*] is for the sake of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as *id*. By this, forms such as *pañcasūci* are established. Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence [of applying this to other cases], because its purpose is solely to establish what is intended. The inclusion of the *ta*-marker (*taparatva*), however, is for the purpose of excluding long vowels.

Nor is the prescription of the long vowel (dīrgha) redundant; for it is justified as having the purpose of subverting the short vowel (*hrasva*) and the elision (*luk*). Nor does the elision of the long vowel follow merely from its being a subject of grammatical derivation (*bhāvyamānatva*); because the elision (*luk*) has as its sole result the establishment of the word's own form by subverting the short vowel, it lacks the status of an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*).
[Pāṇini 1.2.51: "In the case of *lup*, the gender and number are like those of the thing expressed (*yuktavat*)."

When *lup* occurs, the gender and number remain as those of the base (*prakṛti*). By this rule, the gender and number associated with the meaning of the base are extended (*atidiśyete*) to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), because the word *yukta* refers to the base. This is because, although the meanings of the base and the suffix are mutually connected, it would be redundant to extend the properties of the suffix to the meaning of the suffix itself. The country that is the dwelling place of the Pañcālas is called *pañcālāḥ*. Similarly: *kuravaḥ*, *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ*, *kaliṅgāḥ*. [In these cases,] *lup* applies by the rule "there is *lup* when denoting a country" (*janapade lup*).

The suffix *ṇya* is applied after the word *kuru*, whereas elsewhere the suffix *aṇ* is applied; this is the distinction. This is the statement of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*), as it will be rejected later on. What is the purpose of the phrase "when denoting an individual" (*vyaktivacane*)? [Consider: *śirīṣāḥ*, meaning a village not far from *śirīṣa* trees. Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "and that which is not far from" (*adūrabhavaśca*), and its elision (*lup*) occurs by the rule "and after *varaṇa* and others" (*varaṇādibhyaśca*).

In the expression *teṣāṃ vanaṃ śirīṣavanam*, let there not be the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva); otherwise, since the status of being a *vanaspati* (tree) would be extended [to the compound] just as the individual and the number are, the rule "vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ" would require the substitution of *ṇ*. However, when that rule does not apply, there is no *ṇ* because the word refers to a village (*grāma*). This is because the distinction made in the rule for *ṇatva*—namely, "a *vanaspati* should be known as one that bears fruit"—is not invoked here. Similarly, a village situated near *kaṭubadarī* is called *kaṭubadarī*, and so forth.

It might be argued as follows: Even though the distinction (*vyatireka*) relative to the village belongs to the base form (*prakṛti*), it would still be extended [to the derivative] by means of *atideśa*, and thus the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would also occur; for the word *vacana* denotes suffixes such as the singular (*ekavacana*) and so on. This is because at the time of prescribing the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "singular," the word *vacana*—which arises as a corollary—is not deprived of its technical status. Furthermore, the genitive is observed in actual usage (*vākya*). Nor should it be said that only the number (*saṃkhyā*) itself is extended by the word *vacana*; for if the extension were to result in the extension of the word denoting that [number], then the genitive would also result in expressing the number, which leads to the aforementioned undesirable consequence.

Not so; for when the *lup* elision is applied, the specific relationship between the *śirīṣa* trees and the village that appears in the sentence is included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), just as in the case of *māsajāta* ("born in a month") and similar forms.

On this point, the Bhāṣya states: "Even prior to the formation of the compound, [the relation] is appropriate; and even once the compound is formed, it remains appropriate to whatever extent it was appropriate."
"And for the speaker, there is freedom of usage regarding gender and number prior to the occurrence of the grammatical operation."

The meaning of this is as follows: even prior to the formation of a compound (vṛtti), while in the state of the constituent sentence, the thing expressed by the base (prakṛti) is connected with the meaning of the suffix; after the formation of the compound, it remains exactly the same, because there is no difference in the meaning in either case. Regarding the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and of the speaker" (vaktuśca), its position is displaced; thus it should be construed as "prior to the formation of the compound. Because of the word "and," there is freedom of choice in extending the gender and number that existed prior to the formation of the compound to those of the compound as well.

And thus, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the gender and number belonging to the prior base (*vṛtti*); rather, by virtue of proximity, there is an extension only of the gender and number belonging to that which has undergone composition (*vṛtta*). Consequently, just as in examples such as *tāvakīnaḥ* and *māmakīnaḥ*, the understanding of a specific number for the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) occurs through the force of the substitute (*ādeśa*), or just as the understanding of that [number] occurs in the present tense (*laṭ*) because the substitute is seen to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the nominative case, so too here, since the number extended to the meaning of the suffix is understood, that same [number] is understood for the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*) as well.

In that regard, since the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) denotes the meaning of the principal member (*pradhāna*) within a compound, there is no distinction [between them]; therefore, because the purpose is merely the cognition of number, the nominative case alone occurs when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is intended as such. However, in cases such as *śirīṣāṇāṃ manuṣyāḥ* ("men belonging to the Śirīṣas"), the genitive case occurs due to the expectation of a distinction produced by the [subordinate] "men" and so forth; for the very relationship between the Śirīṣa trees and the village is already subsumed within the compound. Alternatively, those gender and number which existed prior to the formation of the compound are extended [to the compound]. Why, then, does the genitive case not occur?

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "In the extension of the general, there is no extension of the particular," there is an alternative reading. In that context, during the stage of the sentence (*vākya-avasthā*), those gender and number which belong to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*) are extended. However, the genitive case is based on distinction (*vyatireka*). Now, here there is no distinction of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*). Nor is number extended along with distinction; the meaning is that when only number is extended, there is no extension of number accompanied by a relation (*sambandha*). Thus says Kaiyaṭa.

Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "In a compound, there is the elision (*lup*) of the plural number of the final member. This [rule] is for the sake of a *dvandva* (copulative) compound consisting precisely of those word-meanings that require mutual expectancy. The transfer (*atideśa*) of the plural number applies only where the plural of the final member has been elided, and not to the initial member as well. Thus, one says *mathurā-pañcālāḥ*, but not *pañcāla-mathurāḥ*. Similarly, *mathurā-godāḥ*, but not *mathurā-godau*. Kaiyaṭa explains that even in a *dvandva*, the meaning of "Godā" does not exceed duality. Furthermore, [Pāṇini 1.2.52 states]: "And [the singular is used] for qualifiers, provided they do not denote a genus (*ajātiḥ*)."

The gender and number of the qualifiers of a *lu* (secondary derivative) stem are likewise those of the stem itself, and not those of the *jāti* (genus). For example: *pañcālā ramaṇīyāḥ* ("the Pañcālas are pleasant") and *godau ramaṇīyau* ("the two Godaus are pleasant"). Here, "Godau" refers to two specific lakes. Although this is established by the fact that qualifiers share the same grammatical status (*yogakṣema*) as the qualified, this rule is commenced for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] the *jāti*. For instance: *pañcālā janapadaḥ* ("the Pañcāla country") and *godau grāmaḥ* ("the Godau village"). The words *janapada* (country) and *grāma* (village) denote a *jāti*. Similarly, when they are qualifiers, one says: *godau grāmo ramaṇīyo bahvannaḥ* ("the Godau village is pleasant and has much food"), and so forth.

For here, when there is a connection through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the rule "the gender and number [of the compound] are like those of the qualified object" (*yuktavad-vyaktivacane*) applies to qualifiers that are distinct from the genus (*jāti*), but not to a qualifier whose form is the genus itself. However, when there is a connection through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), it does not apply to those qualifiers of the genus. This is an *asamartha-samāsa* (compound of unequal semantic power) due to the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the verb *bhavati*. In the first case, "Pañcālā janapadaḥ" (The country of Pañcāla) is established. But [if it were coreferential], then for its qualifiers such as "subhikṣaḥ" (well-supplied with food), "saṃpannapānīyaḥ" (abounding in water), and "bahumālyaphalaḥ" (having many garlands and fruits), there would have to be the use of the plural ending.

In the latter case, the opposite should be applied. Therefore, in the Sūtra, one should read *ājāteḥ* with *praśleṣa* (elision of the final vowel of the preceding word and the initial of the following), thus [the rule applies] as long as there is birth (*jāti*). Their designations possess fixed gender and number, just like *āpaḥ*, *dārāḥ*, *varṣāḥ*, *sikatāḥ*, and so forth; for even when referring to a single individual delimited by a particular genus, these terms function only in the plural.
[Pāṇini 1.2.54: *lubyogāprakhyānāt*.

Nor can it be enjoined as a yoga [compound], because its etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) is not manifest; that is to say, it is not apprehended. This is because from words such as *pañcālāḥ*, there arises only an understanding of a specific region characterized by the property of being "Pañcāla" (*pañcālatva*), since there is no established experience of an understanding based on a connection with a specific Kṣatriya.

Objection: Is it not the case that even for words that are technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*), there is indeed a derivation, as in the rules “*hastājjātau*” and “*kambalācca saṃjñāyām*,” since from words such as *hastī* there arises a cognition characterized specifically by a particular genus? Response: True. However, in those cases, there is a difference in form due to the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Here, on the other hand, because the elision (*lup*) is necessary, that [derivative] is absent; thus says the author of the Nyāsa. Furthermore, if the application of the rule were based solely on the etymological connection (*yogapramāṇa*), then [the word] would be observed only in the absence of that [elision]. (55)

The word *ca* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). "The authority for the etymological derivation" (*yogapramāṇa*) means that which causes the cognition of an etymological meaning; that is to say, it indicates the primary derivative sense. For if words such as *pañcāla* were to apply to a country and so forth only after denoting the connection with a Kṣatriya and the like—which serves as the ground for their application—then in the absence of that [connection], i.e., in the absence of the etymological derivation, there would be no perception or usage of the word *pañcāla*. This is because the word *daṇḍin* is not applied to a person when there is no connection with a staff. Nor is this a desired consequence, as it contradicts actual usage. [This is stated in the verse: "The statement regarding the meaning of the principal derivative suffix is [not absolute], because the meaning [of the whole] has another authority. (Pāṇini 1.2.56)

The word "statement" (*vacanam*) is followed by the ellipsis "not to be taught" (*aśiṣyam*). "That in which the meaning of the suffix is primary" means that where the meaning of the suffix is to be understood as primary, in the form of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) characterized by a mode (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). That is to say, it is a statement of the nature: "the meaning of the suffix is primary. It is "not to be taught" (*aśiṣyam*), meaning it need not be formally commenced [as a rule], because the relationship between qualifier and qualificand is established by other means, being rooted in worldly experience. For, by that [worldly experience], is primacy understood as delimited by the status of being the meaning of the suffix, or merely through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it?

Not the first [alternative], because in cases such as "ghaṭam" (the pot), although the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth, the number and other meanings denoted by the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) are qualifiers of the meaning of the nominal stem. Nor the second, because even the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is sometimes primary, and thus a statement regarding it [as being subordinate] even when it occurs in the meaning of a suffix would be useless. Thus, the intent of the two reasons is respectively: "because they convey a meaning contrary to worldly usage" and "because they convey a meaning established in the world.
This is the same for the case of time (*kāla*) and secondary elements (*upasarjana*). 57.

The present day consists of the latter half of the past night together with the first half of the coming night; this is the statement of the ancient teachers (pūrvācāryas), namely that "the qualification is the addition [of time]. In that regard as well, the lack of need for an explicit rule (*aśiṣyatva*) is the same, because it is established by common worldly usage (*lokasiddhatvāt*). Alternatively, the reason known as "being established by worldly usage" is equal [in both cases]. Thus, it should be understood that the lack of need for an explicit rule is thereby established.
[Pāṇini 1.2.58: "In denoting a genus (*jāti*), the plural may optionally be used for a single entity."

The meaning is clear. Although, under the view that the universal (*jāti*) is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) while the individual (*vyakti*) is the primary referent (*padārtha*), it would be more appropriate to have the singular number used for many [individuals], because of the commentary stating, "in the naming of the universal as a secondary indicator"; nevertheless, this [rule] applies when the universal is the primary referent. As it has been said: "In the naming of a genus (*jāti*), there is a unity of reference because of the denotation of the commonality."

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is also stated: "That which is Gārgya-ness in Gārgya is one. Kaiyaṭa explains that this is because the *gotra* (clan) is accepted as a technical *jāti* (universal), since Gārgya-ness exists as a single entity across many individuals belonging to the Garga lineage. Here, "universal" (*jāti*) is understood specifically as that which resides in multiple individuals existing at the same time, and not as that which resides in multiple individuals across different times, such as "Dittha-ness" (*ḍitthatva*). This is because, even though all words would technically be *jāti*-words under the theory that the word-referent is the universal, the specific mention of the rule "in the case of an expression denoting a universal" (*jātyākhyāyām*) serves as an indicator (*sāmarthyāt*) [of this restricted meaning].

Now, in this view, in the case of *vrīhibhya āgataḥ* ("come from the rice-grains"), would there not be *guṇa* substitution by the rule *ṛd-ṛd-it-i*, because the substitute *ṅi* (in *bhyas*) would be treated as having the property of being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅittva*) through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*? Not so. For by this [rule], only plurality (*bahutva*) is extended to a single referent (*ekasminnarthe*), and thus there is an absence of the relationship between original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*).
As it has been said: "It is established through the extension of meaning (*arthātideśāt*).
In the same way, in the case of *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ*, it should be understood that duality and plurality are expressed by the words "dual" and "plural" respectively.

"A prohibition must be stated regarding the employment of a numeral. This prohibition is initiated because the extension of plurality to a single entity would otherwise apply even when the word *eka* (one) is employed. For example: "A single grain of rice, when ripened, brings about an abundance of food. What is the purpose of this option? It is so that the form *vrīhiḥ* (rice) may also occur [without the singular suffix]. In such cases as "the ripened rice," although it refers to distinct individuals (*vyakti*), some maintain that the singularity relates only to the genus (*jāti*) of rice, since they accept that in certain instances there is a coreferential relation (*anvaya*) even between the word-meaning and the delimitor of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka*).

Others, however, maintain that since rice-ness (*vrīhitva*) and the like are presented in their own form as the delimiters of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of words such as "rice," they are not presented in the form of "rice-ness-ness" (*vrīhitvatva*), which is the delimiter of the relation to the other term (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). Consequently, because the connection with another word-meaning would otherwise be untenable, the number one is construed with the rice itself—the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—through the relation of "possessing that which is the delimiter of the base-meaning's referent" (*svāśrayaprakṛtyarthatāvacchedakavattva*).

The moderns, however, maintain that this is not correct. For singularity alone is not the meaning of the singular number, because it would be redundant—since it is already obtained as something meaningful by virtue of being common to all things—and because it serves no further purpose. Rather, [the meaning] is singularity qualified by the absence of another of the same class (*sajātīya*). And that [singularity] consists in a unity that is a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference residing in those of the same class. Furthermore, "being of the same class" is defined by the nature of the referent of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), as qualified by its relation to the object denoted by the word uttered in grammatical coordination (*samabhivyāhṛta*).

Therefore, in cases such as "the jar exists here," although there is no established instance of a unity residing in a jar that is not a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference residing in another jar—and likewise for a unity residing in some other object that is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in this jar—there is no fault. This is because the status of being a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in a jar qualified by its existence in this particular place is well-established in the very unity residing in that specific jar.

In that case, if one intends to express the existence of another jar, that [other jar] would simply not be established. For this very reason, in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), because singularity is intended to be expressed, there is an exclusion of other animals from that specific sacrificial act. As for the usage "a jar exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*) when many jars are present, it must be justified on the basis of intending the genus (*jāti*).

As for the claim that—just as in the case of the verb expressing existence (*bhāvākhyāta*)—singularity here too is not intended to be expressed, since its purpose is merely grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*); that is not correct. They say that while there might be no other recourse in that case, here there is none. Let us return to the subject at hand.
Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "Or rather, it need not be taught, because plurality is expressed through distinctness.

The meaning is that since the singular number is established when one intends to emphasize the genus (*jāti*), whereas the plural number is established when one intends to emphasize the individual substance (*dravya*), the rule need not be commenced. Furthermore, it must be stated: "In the case of the word *asmad* (the first-person pronoun), [the plural does not apply] when it is used with a qualifier."

[The rule] certainly applies in cases such as: "Devadatta Gārgyāyaṇa says, 'I am learned,' or 'I say so'; you are the king, and we too are elevated by the pride of wisdom gained from serving our teachers. Haradatta and others maintain that this is because the prohibition [of the plural] pertains to the qualifier of the subject being restated (*anuvādya*).

59. *asmado dvayośca*: When singularity or duality is intended, the plural may optionally be used for the word *asmad* ("we"). For example: *vayaṃ brūmaḥ* ("we say"), or alternatively, *ahaṃ bravīmi* ("I say") or *āvāṃ brūvaḥ* ("the two of us say").

This point has also been refuted in the *Bhāṣya*. For in common usage, both expressions are observed: "this eye of mine sees well" and "with this eye I see well. In the former case, the verb refers to the operation of conjunction and so forth; in the latter, it refers to the state of being the locus [of that operation]. Likewise, in such expressions as "we see," the word "we" denotes the sense organs, and because the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arises there just as it does with respect to the body.

Because the agency (*kartṛtva*) intended here is that of being the director through the indifference of the other senses when a single sense organ is active; however, when dependence (*pāratantrya*) is intended, the singular form "I" (*aham*) is used. Furthermore, in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the dual form is used because the word *asmad* alone expresses two meanings.
And [the rule] "of *phalgunī* and *proṣṭhapada*, not in the sense of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)" [applies].

In the sense of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), there may be an operation conditioned by duality or plurality: "the two Pūrva-phalgunīs have risen" or "the two Proṣṭhapadas have risen"; or "the Pūrva-phalgunīs have risen" or "the Proṣṭhapadas have risen. Why "in the sense of a lunar mansion"? [Consider: "the two Phalgunī girls."

This too has been refuted. That [objection] is incorrect, because multiplicity is possible by taking the moon [to be plural], as in the expression "those with umbrellas are going" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*) and so forth. Furthermore, even on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), there is a conjunction of the lunar mansions with the moon that has entered the solar disc. However, in the case of the single *uttarā-phalgunī*, the word *phalgunī* is repeated, so there is no singular number, as in the case of "the two sun-and-moon" (*puṣpavantau*). And because the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is the regulating factor, there is no over-extension.
Moreover, in Vedic usage (*chandasi*), there is the singular for the two *punarvasū* (61), and for the two *viśākhā* (62).

The singular may optionally be used for the dual: *punarvasu* or *viśākhā* as a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). In the alternative case, one says *punarvasū* or *viśākhe*. These two [options] are also rejected; for thus says the Vārttika:
"The forms *punarvasu* and *viśākhā* are established by the rules *supām suluk*, *pūrvasavarṇa*, etc."

In a dual compound consisting of the two lunar mansions Tiṣya and Punarvasu, the plural ending is invariably replaced by the dual ending (Pāṇini 1.2.63). Thus, plurality is treated as if it were duality. For example: *tiṣyaśca punarvasū ca* becomes *tiṣyapunarvasū*. Why is "Tiṣya" mentioned? [To exclude cases where it is not a lunar mansion. For instance, *kṛttikārohiṇyaḥ* (Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī) does not undergo this change. Why is "lunar mansion" (*nakṣatra*) mentioned? [To exclude cases where the words do not refer to actual stars. For instance, *tiṣyaśca punarvasū ca māṇavakāḥ* (the boys named Tiṣya and Punarvasu) becomes *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ*. One should not argue that the exclusion [of non-mansions] occurs simply because of their figurative nature (*gauṇatva*). This is because the word *tiṣyapunarvasu* is used in its primary sense (*mukhyatva*) when applied to boys who are born during the time associated with the conjunction of the Tiṣya and Punarvasu asterisms.

Nor should it be said that the word *nakṣatra* is obtained from the preceding sūtra alone; for that would exclude the words *tiṣya* and *punarvasu* when they signify time—as in: "Many *tiṣya-punarvasus* have passed; by which *tiṣya* did he pass? Alternatively, it is for the purpose of ensuring that even a grammatical operation (*kārya*) situated in another context applies only when these two denote a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Consequently, the term *nakṣatra* need not be explicitly mentioned in the rule: "In *tiṣya-punarvasvoḥ*, there is elision of *y* [when followed by] *nakṣatrāṇi*."

If it is argued that there is no difference whether that [term] is included there or here, then the form *siddhapunarvasū* is established for the purpose of including the *paryāya* (synonym) as well. What is the purpose of the rule "dvandve" (in a Dvandva compound)? Consider: *tiṣya* is the same as *punarvasū*; those who are deluded [about this] are called *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ*. What is the purpose of the term "bahv" (many)? It is so that [the singular] does not occur in a collective (*samāhāra*) sense, as in *uditam tiṣyapunarvasu*. Nor is it the case that the singular number prescribed by the class (*jāti*) is impossible because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "na cāprāṇinām" (not for non-living beings).

This is because it is indicated by the rule *sarvo dvandvo vibhāṣaikavadbhavati* ("every dvandva compound may optionally be singular"). By this, forms such as *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanaṃ* (singular) and *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanāḥ* (plural) are established. For it will be stated later that there is a distinction of scope: in a dvandva of non-living species, the singular form is mandatory; whereas in a dvandva of living beings, it is optional. This is because the section on singular dvandvas is intended to restrict the scope to cases where the dvandva is a collective (*samāhāra*) of body parts and the like.

And thus, since it is established by logic that for those words not included within a specific section, the *itaretarayoga* (separate) *dvandva* takes dual and plural endings according to the rule "cārthe dvandvaḥ," while the *samāhāra* (collective) *dvandva* undergoes singularization (*ekavadbhāva*), the inclusion of the plural marker [in the sūtra] serves as further evidence. Furthermore, since the *dvandva* of parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and so forth occurs only in the sense of a collective (*samāhāre*), the purpose of this [sūtra] is to prevent the reverse restriction; such is the intended meaning.
Thus ends the second lesson of the second chapter of the first book in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
Now begins the third lesson.

*Sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau* (Pāṇini 1.2.64). Among those words which possess similarity of form (*sārūpya*) by virtue of having any one of the case-endings beginning with *su* as their suffix, only one remains. For example: *vṛkṣau*, *vṛkṣāḥ*. Although the term *samānānām* (of similar things) would have been more concise—since the word *samāna* is conventional and understood to mean "equal"—and thus easier to comprehend, the term *sarūpāṇām* (of identical forms) involves a heavier process of understanding because it requires first grasping the meanings of two words (*sa-* and *-rūpa*) before reaching the meaning of the compound. Nevertheless, due to the intended application of the rule based on both the form of the word and its meaning, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would apply only in cases such as *vṛkṣāḥ* and the like, and not otherwise.

In cases such as *tvākṣāḥ* and *pādāḥ*, there is a difference in meaning; furthermore, by the inclusion of the word *rūpa* (form) in the rule *svaṃ rūpam*, it is indicated that even the acceptance of meaning is recognized in grammar. However, when *rūpa* is included, only the similarity residing in the phonetic form of the word itself is grasped, and thus there is no fault.

But surely, the mention of "one" (*eka*) is redundant. For, under the view that the word *śeṣa* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), the status of being a remnant (*śeṣatva*) is established for only one [element] due to its primacy. Even if it functions as an object noun (*karmasādhana*)—meaning "that which remains is the remnant" (*śiṣyate iti śeṣaḥ*)—the status of being a remnant is still established for only one, since singularity is intended to be significant. This is not so. In the first case, by the logic of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that even multiple [elements] could be remnants. In the second case as well, just as in the injunction "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the number of the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is not intended to be significant.

[Objection: Then the mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder) is redundant; for by supplying the elliptical remainder of the rule—"of those that are similar in form, one is correct"—it is possible to arrive at a single substitute that is the most similar (*antarataama*). [Response: Not so; because it would follow that there is no possibility of a single substitute. This is due to the restrictive rule: "The genitive case [in a grammatical rule] denotes the element in place of which [the substitute occurs]. Consequently, in the case of *aśvaś ca aśvaś ca* → *aśvau*, since both instances of the word *aśva* that constitute the compound have an acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable and an grave accent (*anudātta*) on the last, it would follow that the resulting word *aśva* would either be entirely acute-accented or entirely grave-accented.
Because, in place of a composite [stem] possessing two acute (*udātta*) or two grave (*anudātta*) accents, the substitute that possesses one of those [accents] is the most similar (*antaratama*).

Now, what is the purpose of the rule *ekavibhaktau* ("when there is a single case-ending")? It should not be argued that it is for the sake of preventing *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) in cases such as *payaḥ payo jarayati*, *vāso vāsaḥ chādayati*, or *brāhmaṇābhyāṃ ca kṛtaṃ brāhmaṇābhyāṃ ca dehi*; for the phrase *sahavivakṣāyām* ("when there is a desire to express them together") is necessarily required [in the definition of *ekaśeṣa*]. For this very reason, the absence of *ekaśeṣa* in the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* is logically consistent, since that [application of *ekaśeṣa*] is possible only when the elements have not entered into a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, however, because there exists a relationship of qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*) among the meanings of the constituent words, the author of the *Vārttika* will indeed state: "Or rather, it is not so, because of the contradiction in meaning; there is no simultaneous expression. Simultaneous expression means simultaneous intention to speak (*sahavivakṣā*). For *ekaśeṣa* occurs only where the remaining word is capable of expressing the meaning of the elided word(s). Furthermore, agency, objecthood, recipient-hood (*sampradānatva*), and so forth, cannot be conveyed simultaneously by a single [word], because two case-endings cannot arise simultaneously from one [stem].

The meaning is that when "brāhmaṇebhyaḥ" (to the Brahmins) is stated with the dative ending (*caturthyanta*), the sense of agency (*kartṛtva*) is not understood; and when "brāhmaṇaiḥ" (by the Brahmins) is stated with the instrumental ending (*tṛtīyānta*), the sense of recipient (*sampradānatva*) is not understood. This is because meanings presented by a single word—whether distinct or otherwise—must relate to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) in an identical manner.
Not so; for it will be explained later that this [similarity] is intended as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of similarity of form (*sārūpya*).

It might be argued as follows: since the employment of multiple words would result when one intends to convey multiple individuals, this rule is commenced for the purpose of precluding that. Consequently, just as the formation of *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (retention of a single form) was initiated because we observe the use of dissimilar multiple words in cases such as *dhava-khadirau*, so too, because we observe *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* in cases such as *vṛkṣāḥ*, one should instead initiate the rule "retention of a single [form] from among dissimilar [words]" (*virūpāṇāmanekaśeṣaḥ*). This is because the mere presence of examples and the absence of a logical reason are equal in both cases. However, if one is to follow actual usage, then something must indeed be commenced.

Even on the view that [the word] denotes an individual (*vyaktipakṣa*), it is possible for a single word to convey multiple meanings; otherwise, even if the rule for "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) were initiated, the system would remain unworkable. This is because the power of a word is not rooted in its explicit verbal statement. Furthermore, there is complexity (*gaurava*) in the case of *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (single remainder of similar forms): in the case of two [words], one remains; when three remain as one, then two [others] cease; and when four or more remain as one, then three or more cease while one persists. Thus, since the objects characterized by persistence and cessation differ, there arises a burden upon the intellect (*buddhigaurava*).

Since the word *śeṣa* (remainder) denotes a state qualified by exclusion (*nivṛtti*), when one undertakes a *virūpānekaśeṣa* (heterogeneous multiple remainder), the cognition regarding the domain of application is uniform; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). It is replied: because in rules such as *vṛddho yūnā* ("an elder [is designated] over a youth"), the *ekaśeṣa* (single remainder) alone is what is to be prescribed, whereas here, if a heterogeneous multiple remainder were prescribed, two distinct methods would result; therefore, for the sake of parsimony, the *ekaśeṣa* alone is appropriate.

However, this must be noted: since a single word, according to the method previously stated, signifies the absence of any other similar entity, it is precisely the exclusion of other words that is enjoined, while the remaining [of the word itself] is restated because it is already established. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated, "because of the difference in the objects characterized as engagement and withdrawal. At first glance, in cases such as "one offers with curd," there is the appearance that even the remaining [of the word] is something to be enjoined. Furthermore, the qualification of the exclusion by the remaining consists in its being of the nature of the non-existence of the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word that is being excluded.

And the establishment of the counter-correlative (pratiyogi) is easily obtained only in cases where there is another word co-occurring with the heard *tat* (that) word, or in an extraordinary syntactical construction (*alaukikaprakriyāvākya*).

This might be so. Here, six possible positions arise. To explain: *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is prescribed when a single case-ending follows a collective compound (*samudāya*), because the word *eka* is well-known as denoting number. Now, an objection: in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, a *dvandva* compound is formed only from items ending in the singular number, since it is a general rule that the meaning of the constituent members of a compound is understood as singular everywhere. In forms such as *yauṣmākīnaḥ* ("belonging to you all"), the plural endings (*svādi*) arise by the force of substitutes (*ādeśa*) and so forth from the plurality [of the referents], but not from the collective compound itself.

However, in rules such as *karturīpsitatamam* (Pāṇini 1.4.49), since we observe that the designation of "object" (*karman*) applies to one among two or many things desired by the agent, there is no intention to specify number (*saṃkhyāvivakṣā*) due to the requirement of the observed examples (*lakṣyānurodhāt*). Thus, there is a disparity [between this rule and the previous one]. Consequently, because a single case-ending (*vibhakti*) cannot follow from a collective whole (*samudāya*), the application [of the rule] is simply impossible. As it has been said: "If it is argued that [the rule applies] when there is a single case-ending, we say no, because of the absence of a case-ending [in the case of a collective]."

Not so. For when there is mutual dependence between the two members as they take up their own respective meanings—as is the case with the parts themselves—the meaning of the whole is experienced as something distinct from the meanings of the parts. Taking that [meaning of the whole] into account, the entire aggregate constitutes a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the application of case-endings is justified. Nor should it be argued that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule *arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ...* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) regarding meaningful aggregates; because that restriction pertains only to its own class (*sajātīya*), it serves only to exclude those [aggregates] which end in case-suffixes (*subanta*).

In compounds such as *rājadarśī* (one who sees the king), even though they are upapada and other types of compounds, the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is treated as ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) in order to permit operations on the word-form, such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*). Consequently, according to the maxim regarding the reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*), the formation of duals and other suffixes occurs from the entire compound as a whole. This is because the requirement for the meaning of the individual members to be assisted through their connection with number is fulfilled by that very [compound]. Nor should it be argued that in the derivation *rājan-rājan-au*, since the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-dīrgha*) would apply first—due to its higher status in the rule-order (*paratva*) and its obligatory nature (*nityatva*)—the single-remainder operation (*ekaśeṣa*) could not take place due to the resulting dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) between the two forms. This objection is invalid, because the possibility of *ekaśeṣa* exists even for words that are dissimilar in form provided they have the same meaning, as stated in the rule: *virūpāṇām api samānārthānām*.

Alternatively, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) applies because it is internal (*antaraṅga*). This is because the formation of the long vowel—which depends upon a specific case-ending that is a *sarvanāmasthāna* distinct from the vocative, as well as upon the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)—is external (*bahiraṅga*). Nor should it be argued that even in a *dvandva* compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of a case-ending arising from the entire aggregate even without a *dvandva*; for in the rule prescribing that [compound], the phrase "multiple inflected words" (*anekaṃ subantam*) is understood, which precludes the aforementioned logic. Thus, one position is that once the form *vṛkṣa vṛkṣa au* has been established, the operation of *ekaśeṣa* takes place.

Alternatively, *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) occurs when distinct case-endings (*vibhakti*) follow. Now, an objection might be raised: when the form *vṛkṣaḥ vṛkṣaḥ* is established, since the *ekaśeṣa* of similar forms depends upon the case-ending as its cause, the base (*prakṛti*) would be elided; consequently, the case-ending alone following it would have to be used. Nor can it be argued that there is a prohibition against using a base and a suffix in isolation from each other.

If these two [the *saṃyogādilopa* and *saṃyogāntalopa*] were intended to serve as mutual prerequisites for their application, then we would observe their usage even in the absence of one another, as in examples such as *agnicit* and *iyatī*. Furthermore, other instances of the letter *s* cannot be saved by the rule of *saṃyogāntalopa*, because that rule prescribes the elision of the final element of a word (*pada*) that ends in a *saṃyoga*. This is because, when the form *vṛkṣass* is established, there is no word that ends in a *saṃyoga*—since "vṛkṣam" is one [word], "s" is the second, and "s" is the third. By this, the possibility of *saṃyogādilopa* (elision of the initial of a *saṃyoga*) is also refuted.

Not so. The *bhāṣya* statement "there is elision of the final of a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntalopa*) should be explained as follows: the "end" (*anta*) of the "conjunct" (*saṃyoga*) is the letter *s*, and there is its elision; and that [elision] occurs by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). This is the second [interpretation]. Alternatively, let there be *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) when a single case-ending follows a compound. Since the word "in a *dvandva*" (*dvandve*) is understood from the first sūtra (Pāṇini 1.2.32), in the *dvandva* "tree and tree" (*vṛkṣaśca vṛkṣaśca*), we have *vṛkṣavṛkṣau*; here, *ekaśeṣa* applies. Consequently, because the following case-ending is elided by the rule *sapo dhātu-pratipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), there is no risk of its being heard [in pronunciation]. This is the third [interpretation].

Alternatively, there is the fourth [interpretation]: a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of all the words ending in case-suffixes individually, based on the reliance upon the *Nyāsa* commentary which states "of those having the same case-suffix. For if there were a reference to the locative case (*saptamī*), then upon the disappearance of the base alone, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the suffix; however, according to the aforementioned method, since it is precisely the words ending in case-suffixes that disappear, this does not occur. Thus is the fourth [view].

Alternatively, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) applies to the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) themselves. For instance, the rule "in the case of a single inflection" (*ekavibhaktau*) need not be formulated. By carrying forward the term "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) from the sūtra "the short vowel in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake*), the *ekaśeṣa* of similar nominal stems is prescribed precisely while the inflection has not yet been produced. This is possible even in the case of verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*, such as *pac-l pac-l*, because once they have assumed the designation of "nominal stem" by virtue of being *kṛt*-derived forms, the application of the rule is established. Consequently, there is no undesirable consequence of hearing an inflection whose original base (*prakṛti*) has been elided.

Nor does the mere desire to express similarity at the level of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) entail the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *ekaśeṣa* even for two words "mother" (*mātṛ*)—one denoting a biological mother and the other a female guardian—since this would apply equally under the view that *ekaśeṣa* occurs only between words ending in case-suffixes (*vibhaktyanta*), as there is similarity in some cases of inflection. Furthermore, it does not follow that *ekaśeṣa* must occur everywhere simply because similarity exists at the stage of the nominal stem, as that similarity is constant [and thus would over-extend].

Regarding the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for words that are identical in form (*sarūpa*) when they end in case-terminations (*vibhaktyanta*), it must be stated that *ekaśeṣa* occurs only in that particular case-ending where the forms are identical, and not in others. This is because, due to the contradiction in meaning (*arthavipratiṣedha*), *ekaśeṣa* would not even apply here [in the case of "mother"]. For if there were an *ekaśeṣa* of two instances of the word *mātṛ*, then when the subsequent word *tābhiḥ* is used, the masculine meaning is not understood; and when *taiḥ* is used, the feminine meaning is not understood. This is the fifth [point].

Alternatively, there is *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for words ending in dual or plural suffixes. When simultaneous reference to multiple substrates (*sahavivakṣā*) is intended, each individual word conveys two meanings; thus, the formation of dual and plural endings in forms such as *vṛkṣau* is established. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of subverting the sentence *vṛkṣaśca vṛkṣaśca* by means of the obligatory *ekaśeṣa*, because in that case there is an absence of simultaneous reference and the meanings are distinct, so there is no subversion of the sentence by the operation of *ekaśeṣa*.

This point is obtained from the interpretation that the word "in a *dvandva*" is carried over [from the previous rule], meaning "when a *dvandva* would otherwise have occurred"—this is the sixth [point].

In this regard—the first [alternative] is not tenable. For the derivation of *bhaikṣam* as "a collection of alms" (*bhikṣāṇāṃ samūhaḥ*) and so forth would be unestablished. To explain: when the form *bhikṣā bhikṣā bhikṣā ām* is established, since the rule for elision (*luk*) is stronger than all other rules, the elision of *ām* would occur; once that elision is performed, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) could not take place because there would be no subsequent case-ending (*vibhakti*). Nor can the presence of the suffix be assumed through the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, because that is prohibited by the rule "na lumatāṅgasya. Similarly, in the case of *rāma rāma au*, the *ekaśeṣa* would not occur due to the absence of a reason for applying the *vṛddhi* vowel replacement, which takes precedence.

Nor should it be argued that the suffix [of the compound] follows what is divided by the status of being "the end" (*anta*) and so forth; for that is prohibited when there is a dependence on both sides.

Nor is the second alternative [tenable], because it would necessitate the commencement of another rule for the sake of the dual and plural numbers, as well as for the prohibition of *dvandva* compounds. Furthermore, *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) cannot be a sublater of *dvandva* simply because it lacks scope, since *ekaśeṣa* does have scope in the case of verbal endings (*tiṅanta*). This is because, due to the difference in the factors of action (*kāraka*), there arises a difference in the actions, which leads to the contingency of multiple verbal endings. Consequently, by virtue of its higher status, the *dvandva* would apply. And there can be no subsequent *ekaśeṣa*, according to the maxim: "When an operation has already taken effect once... (*sakṛdgatau*).

Furthermore, even if one were to accept the cognition of recurrence (*prasaṅga*), a fault would arise regarding the elision of the final consonant (*m-ās-anta*) according to the method to be explained hereafter. In the case of *vṛkṣas vṛkṣas*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the optional elision of the preceding word *vṛkṣas* as well, resulting in the erroneous form *s-vṛkṣau*. This is because there is no restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) for the elision of only the subsequent [word]. The same logic should be applied to the plural number as well. Nor can the desired form be established through the elision of the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) and so forth, because the *hal* (consonant) at the beginning of that [cluster] is not related to a single word; for both *s* and *s* are individually considered *pada*s.

Furthermore, this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), because even in the case of the exclusion of others (*paranivṛtti*), the previously mentioned elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (Pāṇini 6.1.68) would be untenable; for since the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si* imply their respective bases (*prakṛti*), the rule prescribes the elision of *svādi* suffixes only when they follow a base ending in a consonant (*halanta*). Likewise, in cases such as *godau*, *dārāḥ*, and *sikatāḥ*, which have fixed numbers of referents (*niyatavacana*), where a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs, it is impossible even to suspect the application of the elision of *hal* and *ṅī*.

By this, it should be understood that a solution cannot be achieved even by resorting to the alternative view that "the final consonant of a word [is dropped] when preceded by a conjunct. Furthermore, it must be noted that there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the case-ending following the remaining nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Nor is the third alternative tenable; as it has been said: "If it is argued that 'it is a compound,' then there is a fault regarding accent and the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*)."
