For instance, in the *dvandva* compound *aśvaśvāśvaḥ*, when the final member of the compound is accented (*samāsāntodāttatva*) and the remainder is unaccented (*śeṣanighāta*), if the single-remainder rule (*ekaśeṣa*) applies first, then the entire compound would result in being unaccented; if, however, the single-remainder rule applies last, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being accented on the final syllable, because the application of the accentuation of the final member of the compound takes precedence over the single-remainder rule due to its being a subsequent operation. Nor should it be argued that, by the principle of "that which does not apply [otherwise] when something else has already applied" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), the single-remainder rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of the final member of the compound; for even after that [application of the accent], the application of the single-remainder rule is still possible, and there is no contradiction between them.

Thus, in the case of *ṛc ṛc a iti*, because the intermediate case-ending has been elided by *luk* and because the prohibition of the application of grammatical operations based on a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies, there is an absence of a subsequent case-ending; therefore, for the sake of *ekaśeṣa*, another case-ending must be produced from the entire aggregate. And in that [newly produced] ending, there is no similarity (*sārūpya*). For one word is *ṛc* and the other is *ṛcaḥ*. Nor should it be argued that a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is a member of the compound itself and not a part of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

Because the case endings (*vibhakti*) would not follow immediately after [the base] due to the intervention of the *samāsānta* suffixes, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) would not apply. Nor should it be argued that this very fault should be stated rather than the lack of similarity (*asārūpya*), for such was said by relying on the view that the *samāsānta* suffix is an integral part (*avayava*) of the final member (*uttarapada*) which constitutes the meaning of the compound. Likewise, in the case of *svasā ca svasārau ca*, once the *guṇa* and *dīrgha* substitutions have taken effect by virtue of their higher priority, there would be no *ekaśeṣa* due to the absence of similarity. Similarly, in cases such as *nauśca nāvau ca*, it should be understood that even when the substitution of *āv* occurs—which is an operation not pertaining to the stem (*anaṅgakārya*)—the same principle applies.

For instance, if—even when an internal case-ending has been elided by *luk*—the designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is resorted to by virtue of the power of the explicit statement, then there is a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) here. Alternatively, if "having a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktiparatva*) is understood as being dependent on the case-ending of the compound itself, even so the discrepancy remains as it was. Similarly, in the section concerning "verb with verb" (*ākhyātam ākhyātena*), one must assume the application of the rule *dvandvaś ca sarūpāṇām*; otherwise, the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) would not be possible.

Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable; for even if those elements being elided were to cease together with the suffix, it would follow that the remaining base and suffix would still be heard, which would necessitate the formulation of rules for their elision, the prescription of dual and plural endings, and the prohibition of *dvandva* compounds.

Nor is the fifth [alternative] tenable, because the term *bhaikṣam* would remain unestablished. For when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to a feminine stem ending in *ā*—according to the rule that *taddhita* suffixes are added to a meaningful nominal stem (*ṅyāpprātipadika*)—the initial *vṛddhi* (guṇa) takes effect due to its higher priority; consequently, because of the resulting difference in form (*vairūpya*), the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* compound would be impossible. This is because the forms differ: the feminine of *harita* is *hariṇī*, and likewise the feminine of *hariṇa* is also *hariṇī*; thus, in the case of *hariṇī ca hariṇī ca*, a *hariṇyau* formed by *ekaśeṣa* would not occur, as there is a difference in form at the stage of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The same applies to *śyenyaḥ* and *rohiṇyaḥ*.

Although the form *haritī* would result from the suffix *ṅīṣ* after the word *harita-* when denoting a female through connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), Kaiyaṭa maintains that the feminine form of the word *harita-* is *hariṇī*, and thus the word *harita-* here refers to one ending in a feminine suffix. Furthermore, because the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has been interrupted, and because nominal stems are not used independently in common usage, similarity is understood only by including it within another word. As it has been said: "Or rather, [there is no fault], because there is no usage of a word in isolation from its meaning."

Nor is the sixth [alternative] tenable. For in the case of a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound, both words would be devoid of meaning, which makes it impossible for each individual word to denote multiple meanings. Even in the view that the compound functions as *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning), it is improper to discard the singular number (*ekavacana*) that was applied first; otherwise, it would be impossible to form a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* or similar compounds, because even in those cases, the first member would have merged into the meaning of the second member, making the use of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or other such cases untenable.

And thus the Bhāṣya says: "This simultaneous expression of multiple substrates is both difficult and hard to justify. We shall elaborate upon this second point later. Therefore, when it has been established that all six positions are indeed flawed, the author of the Bhāṣya states the final conclusion:

"And [the formation of] *ekaśeṣa* for nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is established. For instance: in *ekaśeṣa*, the presence of a single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*) is not the cause; rather, it is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for homogeneity (*sārūpya*). *Ekaśeṣa* applies to those items seen as homogeneous in common usage within a single case-ending. And because it is not dependent on a specific cause, it does not require a case-ending; thus, due to its being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), it operates even prior to the production of the case-suffix (*sub*). Furthermore, the mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) in the *Bhāṣya* is itself an indicator; by this, the rule is established even for words such as *hariṇī*.

Based on the rule, "Of those [words] that differ in accent, that which follows remains," there is the retention (*śeṣa*) of the word *hariṇī*, which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. However, some maintain that when there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the words *harita* and *hariṇa* themselves, even though both denote both genders, one of them denotes color; thus they claim the feminine suffix is applied. Kaiyaṭa states that in their view, there would be the undesirable consequence of a difference in accent. In cases such as *bhaikṣyam*, because it is not dependent on any external cause (*anaimittikatvena*), the single-remainder occurs first due to its being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), and only then does the vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) take place.
Alternatively, since the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occurs only after the single-remainder, there is no fault.

Therefore, this is the meaning here: the term "inflected word" (*vibhaktipada*) refers here merely to [words] beginning with *su* (i.e., nominal endings). Even though there is a difference in action due to a difference in substratum, that [action] which has its differences ceased is what is understood by means of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). Furthermore, [qualities] such as excellence and repetition are caused by the repetition and so forth of their own substratum. And duals and other [number-endings] in forms such as *pacataḥ* express numbers residing in the agent and so forth. Nor should it be argued that for the *l*-suffixes prescribed for the agent and the object, a distinction is indeed appropriate because of the distinction between those [agents and objects].

This is because such an objection is accepted [as a desired conclusion]. In the rule *lasya*, by resorting to the universal *latva* (the property of being a *l*-suffix), the dual and plural suffixes apply in place of even multiple *l*-suffixes due to semantic proximity (*arthata āntarya*). Furthermore, a single word that has a common meaning must have meanings belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*). This commonality of class (*sājātya*) is not defined by being a case-ending (*vibhaktitva*), for [if it were], the term "word" (*pada*) alone would suffice, making the inclusion of the word "single" (*eka*) redundant; moreover, since phonological identity (*sārūpya*) is impossible when delimited by the property of being a case-ending, it cannot be intended as the defining characteristic here.

Since mere grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and similarity (*sārūpya*) are already obtained simply by the employment of the word "similar" (*sarūpa*), [the term *sarūpa* here] refers rather to [similarity] by means of *sutva* (the property of being a *su*-affix) and so forth, which are subsumed under the category of being a case-ending (*vibhaktitva*), but not by means of being a nominative (*prathamātva*) and so forth; for even in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣau*, and *vṛkṣāḥ*, there is an absence of similarity [if one were to rely on those broader categories]. Furthermore, by virtue of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the full extent (*yāvatva*) of the properties such as *sutva*—which serve as the delimiters of the referent of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*)—is understood. This is because similarity based on the delimitation of any such property whatsoever is established precisely through its exclusion from others.

And "being delimited" (*avacchinnatvam*) is the meaning of the locative case. Thus, the meaning is: "homogeneity" (*sārūpya*) exists in as many individual instances of suffixes (*pratyaya-vyakty-*) as there are properties, such as *sutva* (the property of being a *su*-suffix), which are subsumed under the class of suffixhood (*vibhaktitva*); that is, in each instance delimited by those respective properties. The term "each" (*pratyekam*) is stated because it is impossible for there to be a single suffix-instance delimited by all properties such as *sutva* and so on. The term "as many as" (*yāvat*) is stated to exclude homogeneity from any arbitrary instance delimited by *sutva* and so on.

Therefore, there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for the two words *mātṛ*, which denote "mother" and "measurer," because from the case-ending *au* up to *śas*, there is an absence of homogeneity (*sārūpya*). By this, the view that the meaning "only those that are homogeneous" is obtained through the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the word *eva* from the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 1.2.64] is refuted; for that meaning is obtained precisely by the method already stated. [Objection: If this were so, there would be no *ekaśeṣa* for words with fixed gender, such as *dārāś ca dārāś ca* ("wives and wives"). [Reply: Not so. For homogeneity is intended here as delimited by as many individual instances of suffixes as are possible from a given base. This is the general direction [of the argument].

It might be argued as follows: the form *gārgāḥ* would not be established. For when there is a plurality of descendants (*apatya*), many instances of the suffix *yañ* must be produced, since words are applied according to their respective referents; otherwise, the rule of "single-remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) would be rendered useless. Nor should it be said that for the second and subsequent *yañ*s, there would be no occurrence after the base (*prakṛti*). This is because the class-form (*ākṛti*) of *yañ* is one, and thus there is no intervention [between the base and the suffixes]. When the state *garga ya ya ya* is reached, the single-remainder rule would not apply to the first *yañ*, because of the dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) caused by its immediate connection with the base.

Thus, even in the view that the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is the cause of formation, it should be understood that because the entire aggregate ends in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), it receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and subsequently, a single case-ending arises. Furthermore, in the view that "when there is a desire to express [multiple items] together, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs among those ending in case-endings," the same applies when the form *gargā ya as ya as* is established. Nor can it be argued that the single remainder arises because the *ya*-sounds are identical in form once the base portions have been discarded.

Since the case-ending arises from the very aggregate qualified by its base (*prakṛti*), it is improper for that which is characterized by such similarity to undergo *ekaśeṣa* while being excluded from the case-ending; furthermore, the suffix *yañ* does not denote an aggregate independent of the meaning of its base. Nor should it be argued that because each individual meaning of the suffix is connected with the meaning of the base, and because it is logical for a subordinate element (*guṇa*) to repeat according to the repetition of the principal (*pradhāna*), there should be *ekaśeṣa* of the words *gārgya* themselves due to the plurality of the word *garga*.

This is because the elision of *y* (in the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu*) would otherwise be untenable; for that rule prescribes the suffix *yañ* and others only when they denote a plurality. Furthermore, in the case of that suffix, it is only through the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from several identical words) that the remaining *yañ* can properly signify plurality. However, according to the aforementioned reasoning, it is the word ending in *yañ* itself that possesses the plural sense.

Not so; for even the rule *tatkṛte bahutve* (P. 2.4.63) is explained as meaning "when plurality is caused by that which ends in *tad*" (i.e., the suffix *añ*). Nor should it be argued: "When the suffix *añ* is applied to a single descendant of Kaśyapa, the suffix *kan* is added according to P. 5.3.96 (*ive pratikṛtau*), and then, by P. 5.3.99 (*jīvikārthe cāpaṇye*), there is elision (*luk*) of that *kan*. Consequently, when one intends to express plurality of images (*pratikṛti*), the elision would also apply in the case of *kāśyapāḥ*, because the stem ending in *añ* here denotes plurality. This argument is invalid, because the rule for elision (*lopavidhāna*) applies specifically to that which expresses plurality of descendants, whereas this [stem *kāśyapa*] expresses plurality of images.

Alternatively, since all [the suffixes] following the single word *garga* denote the offspring qualified by the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), even though there is a difference in form caused by the combination with the base (*prakṛtisannipātakṛtavairūpya*), the rule "of those that are dissimilar but have the same meaning" (*virūpāṇām api samānārthānām*) applies, and thus the retention of one (*ekaśeṣa*) is established. If this sūtra did not exist, then after the production of case-endings for each individual, a copulative compound (*dvandva*) would result; however, when [this sūtra] exists, because there is no longer a plurality of *subanta* words, that possibility does not arise. By this, it is explained that *ekaśeṣa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *dvandva*.

If it is objected that, according to the view that a *dvandva* compound occurs when there is a difference in the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the referents (*padārtha*), there would be no possibility of a *dvandva* such as "the pot and the pot" (*ghaṭaśca ghaṭaśca*), we say no. This is because a *dvandva* is possible under the view that it occurs when there is a difference in the referents themselves; furthermore, in the case of "two waters" (*payasī*), there exists a difference in the delimiters of the referents, namely the properties of being water (*jalatva*) and being milk (*dugdhatva*). It might be argued: let there be a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) compound such as "one and one" (*ekaśca ekaśca*) or "two and two" (*dvau ca dvau ca*).

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "The *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) does not apply because the meaning of the number is not understood [as such], and because it is the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). *Ekaśeṣa* occurs only where a single word is capable of denoting multiple meanings, because grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) applies only to words already in usage. Furthermore, when "one" (*eka*) is uttered, since no meaning such as "companion" is perceived, there is no perception of duality. As for the phrase "and because it is the meaning of another word," the meaning is that its sense is conveyed by another unambiguous word, such as "two" (*dvau*).

By this [reasoning], even a *dvandva* (copulative compound) does not occur there, because it is not prescribed [by grammar]. Now, one might object: in the case of *gārgyau*, since a *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (retention of a single form for two similar words)—namely, "the Gārgya and the Gārgya"—is also possible, a doubt arises; and even though the meaning is not immediately understood, a *ekaśeṣa* is observed because the doubt is subsequently removed by context and other factors. Nor should it be argued that in that case (*gārgyau*), the rule "the elder [is retained] with the younger" (*vṛddho yūnā*) applies by virtue of its specific formulation, whereas here [in the case of *akṣau*] it does not because a non-doubtful domain exists. For if that were so, the rule would fail to apply even in cases such as *akṣāḥ*. [Reply: Do not say so.

Because when the meaning is not understood, [the compound] functions as a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound) since it has another word as its referent; this is because the qualified [referent] serves as the logical reason (*hetu*). Herein lies the intended meaning (*tātparya*): the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of two words occurs when that which is delimited by the delimitor of the word-meanness (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) is the locus of the complete inherence (*paryāpti*) of duality and so forth. However, that which is delimited by singularity (*ekatva*) is not the locus of the complete inherence of duality and so forth. [Objection: But surely, even that which is delimited by pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth is not such [a locus] individually, yet when combined, even that which is delimited by singularity is such; thus the cases are equal.

Nor should it be argued that in those cases the delimitor of the referent (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so on, is identical in both instances, whereas "oneness" (*ekatva*) differs with each individual instance; for even in examples such as *payasī* ("two waters"), there is an absence of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the delimiters of the referents, namely "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and "milk-ness" (*dugdhatva*). This is not so.

The *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder formation) applies between two words when the delimitor of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) does not serve as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatā*) residing in the number denoted by the suffix, which in turn is the delimitor of the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) of the difference [from the object denoted by the other word]. However, in the cognition "one is different from that which possesses duality," oneness (*ekatva*) is indeed the delimitor of the qualificandumness. The phrase "denoted by the suffix" (*pratyayārtha*) was stated in order to ensure that the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*) is obtained as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity.

Because the expression “two pots” (*ghaṭau*) is never used for a single pot, it is a matter of grammatical convention (*vyutpatti*) that the duality and other numbers expressed by case-endings (*vibhakti*) must be construed through the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*). However, in the case of “one is possessed of duality,” duality is a qualifier merely by way of being its locus (*āśrayatva*), and not through pervasion; thus there is no fault. Likewise, in the case of “the pot is different from that which possesses duality,” it is precisely the singularity (*ekatva*) that serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the aforementioned mode of difference, and not pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*); for the expression “two pots” is never used [in reference to a single pot].

For this very reason, in the case of "Caitra and Maitra go," although singularity is construed with each [individual] separately, the cognition of the duality denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is construed only by taking Caitra-ness and Maitra-ness as the delimiters of the property-possessor (dharmitāvacchedaka), and not singularity as well; thus there is no fault. This should be applied similarly to the word "two" and so forth.

Let us return to the subject at hand: it must be stated that there is a single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) even for words of different forms that have the same meaning. For example, *vakradaṇḍaśca kuṭiladaṇḍaśca* results in *vakradaṇḍau* or *kuṭiladaṇḍau*. This is because by the rule "for those of identical form" (*sarūpāṇām*), identity of meaning is also included. It must be stated that "among words differentiated by accent, there is a single-remainder for that [word] for which the subsequent accentual rule applies. That is to say, among words differentiated by accent—meaning those with different accents—for instance, *akṣaśca akṣaśca* results in *akṣau*.

The word *akṣa* in the first instance is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *aṇ* (from the rule *aśer devane*). The second, however, is ādyudātta because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*; thus, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of these two. [The term] *mīmāṃsakau*: one word *mīmāṃsaka* is madhyodātta because it ends in the suffix *vuñ* (from the rule *mīmāṃsā-saha-akṣa-hali-kalāt vuñ*). The other, however, is ādyudātta according to the rule *kramādibhyo vun* (meaning "one who studies the Mīmāṃsā"); thus, there is a *ekaśeṣa* of these two.

This also should be noted: in expressions such as *ghaṭau* ("two jars"), duality is cognized through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the delimiters of the referents (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). Even in cases such as *akṣau* ("two dice"), although there is no mutual co-referentiality between the two delimiters of the referents—namely, *bibhītakatva* (being a vibhītaka nut) and *devanatva* (being a die)—their co-referentiality with duality remains unimpeded, because duality is construed with each of the two substrata [of those delimiters] individually. This is the case regarding the delimiters of the referents.

This is because there is no established experience of a cognition of mutual coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because there is no purpose [for such a rule], and because it is impossible in cases such as *ghaṭau* (two pots). Furthermore, in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of one term), it is the word *akṣa* itself that generates a cognition qualified by the property of having the delimitor of the meaning of one word as its qualifier and the delimitor of the meaning of the other word as its qualifier; this is in accordance with experience. Thus, the *ekaśeṣa* rule need not even be commenced, since the comprehension of such a meaning is accomplished by a single word alone; otherwise, even if it were commenced, the difficulty would not be overcome.

Indeed, a power (*śakti*) that does not exist inherently cannot be created by a teacher, because the power of a word is to be inferred solely from worldly usage. Nor does it follow that, in cases such as *agnicit* or *somasut*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *kvip* suffix and so forth would likewise be rendered useless; for the purpose of those [elisions] is served by the rule of "characteristics based on suffixes" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) has no utility within the actual process of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Nor should it be asked how a single word can denote multiple meanings; for the situation is the same, since the objects to be understood are delimited by the specific property that serves as the delimitor of the scope of the derivative function (*vṛtti*).

This is because there is no distinction in the fact that the referents of one, two, or many objects—such as *ghaṭaḥ*, *godau*, and *dārāḥ*—are the objects of the application of their respective words. Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as *plakṣanyagrodhau*, where there is a desire to express [the items] together (*sahavivakṣā*), a second usage would be unnecessary because both referents are understood by a single word due to the emergence of a collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*). For when one says *plakṣau*, the association with another *plakṣa* tree is indeed perceived. Furthermore, we observe that in some instances, two referents are expressed even by a form that occurs twice; for example, *dyāvākṣāmā*.

Regarding the phrase *dyāvā cid asmai pṛthivī namete*: here, by the word *dyauḥ*, both heaven (*dyāvā*) and earth (*pṛthivī*) are denoted. The substitution of the vowel *ā* for the dual ending *au* is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). The form *pṛthivī* ends in the dual number. The long vowel resulting from the prior homogeneous sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*) is applied here by the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106). Thus, by the word *pṛthivī*, both heaven and earth are expressed.

Consequently, since in certain cases—by virtue of context and other factors—the specific meaning is determined even when there is a difference in the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*), and since it is observed that a word of different forms can denote multiple meanings, it is all the more appropriate in the case of a word with identical forms.

By this, the view that the initiation of the *ekaśeṣa* rule is necessitated by the requirement for multiple meanings is refuted; for, according to the reasoning stated above, a cognition characterized by two delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) can indeed be produced by a single word alone. Nor is this rule initiated for the purpose of excluding *dvandva* compounds, since that is already established simply because such a formation is not prescribed.
Thus, the rule has been rejected under both interpretations.

For this very reason, although the author of the *Bhāṣya* will later reject the two rules "sarūpāṇām" and "jātyākhyāyām," it is stated in the *Kaustubha* on the *Paspaśā* section that the adherence to the two interpretations is based solely on the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*).

However, with reference to a case where the delimiters of the word-meanings (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) are identical, the author of the *Vārttika* states: "Vājapyāyana [holds that] there is oneness [of meaning] in the case of an inflection because of the denotation of the form (*ākṛti*). Another *Vārttika*, "Vyāḍi [holds that] there is the denotation of the substance (*dravya*)," is intended merely to describe the intention of the Sūtra. We shall examine the relative gradation regarding both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) as the word-meaning in the section on the rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedhasūtra*).

He states the proof for the existence of the universal (*jāti*) as: "Because there is no difference in manifestation" (*prakhyāviśeṣāt*). This is because there is no distinction in manifestation—that is, cognition (*buddhi*)—due to its uniform nature. For even in the case of two cognitions having the form "beautiful," though they have distinct individuals as their objects, one experiences them as having the same qualifier (*samānaprakāraka*). Thus, the oneness of the universal is also established by the mental cognition that apprehends its locus (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). Furthermore, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is postulated as eternal; therefore, it cannot be destroyed by the destruction of its substratum. Nor should it be asked how a single universal can reside simultaneously in multiple individuals, for that too is established by the very cognition that apprehends its locus.

As for the Bhāṣya statement, “Indra, though invoked at one hundred sacrifices, is present everywhere simultaneously,” that is merely a poetic exaggeration (*abhūtaguṇotkarṣamātra*), since it has been established in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* that this is possible through the emanation of multiple bodies (*kāyavyūha*). Furthermore, in the view that the deity is insentient (*acetana*), proximity itself is not admitted.

Now, it might be argued that the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) must necessarily be denoted [by the word]; otherwise, when a particular cow (*go-piṇḍa*) is produced, there would be no cognition of it [as a cow]. As it has been said by the outsiders (Buddhists):
"It does not go there, nor was it there before; it exists later, yet it is not part-possessing."
Alas, a continuous succession of calamities first abandons its very support!
Consequently, there would also be a cognition of the universal "cowness" (gotva) with respect to a jar and other such objects.
As it has been said:
"If, because of its non-difference from the individual, that [universal] were all-pervading through one individual, [then it would be perceived everywhere]."

"It would follow that the universal (*jāti*) would be perceived everywhere"—this is not so. For it is accepted that the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), which is a specific type of relation, exists only with respect to the individual cows (*govyakti*). In this case, the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing acts as the regulator. For this very reason, even though souls (*jīva*) are all-pervading, the relation called "delimitation" (*avacchedakatva*) is accepted only with respect to a particular body; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that everyone would simultaneously experience the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of pleasure and so forth through the delimitation of every body.

As for the Buddhists’ claim that *apoha* alone—consisting in the exclusion of what is not that (*atad-vyāvṛtti*)—is the universal (*jāti*), because the exclusion of what is different from a cow exists in every horse and there is no evidence for a "cowness" (*gotva*) distinct from that, that is incorrect. In the expression "different from a cow," is the difference introduced as having some particular cow as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), or as having a counter-correlate delimited by cowness? Not the first, because even a cow is different from some other particular cow; since that [particular] difference also occurs in a jar, it would follow that the cognition "this is a cow" would arise with respect to a jar as well. Nor the second, because that would establish a distinct cowness. As they say:
Furthermore, an established [entity] would be sublated, and that [negation] consists in the negation of "cow";
therefore, it must be stated that it is precisely the cow which is being negated by the negative particle (*nañ*). Thus it is said.

Even action-words denote only a genus (*jāti*). Although there exists an internal distinction among individual instances of cooking, such as those of molasses or rice, the existence of "cooking-ness" (*pākatva*) is established by the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Just as the property called "ḍittha-word-ness" residing in various distinct words like "ḍittha" is the cause for the application of a non-different cognition to them, so too—in view of the identification of word and object through the judgment "this is that"—the [genus] superimposed upon the names (such as "ḍittha") serves as the cause for the application of a non-different cognition and designation, due to its connection with those named objects.

And thus, in the case of [words like] *ḍittha*, the property of being the word *ḍittha* (*ḍitthaśabdatva*), which resides in the individual (*vyakti*) by virtue of the relation of being denotable by its own substrate (*svāśrayavācyatva*), serves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) toward those objects. The intention is that this is just as, in cases such as "possessing fire" (*vahnimān*), the property of being fire (*vahnitva*) is the ground for application by virtue of the relation of conjunction with that which is inherent in itself (*svasamavāyisaṃyoga*). Furthermore, in cases such as "those two," the grounds for application are properties such as being remote (*parokṣatva*) or being perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*). Even in the case of "the four absences," one must likewise rely upon a universal (*sāmānya*) called "ineffability" (*nirupākhyatva*). As for the statement "cowness and horseness are universals," universals themselves possess a further universal, namely, the status of being the cause of a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*) with respect to excluded particulars (*vyāvṛtta*).

Alternatively, the view of the logicians—that universals are devoid of further universals—is not necessarily to be accepted by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). For their categories are inferred from their effects; thus, Kaiyaṭa maintains that even in universals there exists a universal. Nor should it be argued that such an acceptance of universals within universals leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because a genus (*jāti*) is not admitted therein due to the presence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), namely, the fact of having only a single individual instance (*ekavyaktitva*). As for the objection that [the universal] "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) itself possesses multiple instances, [that does not apply here].

That is not so; for there is no purpose in postulating a further common genus (*jāti*) distinct from that [genus of being], since the recurring cognition in those cases is sufficiently accounted for by the genus of generality (*sāmānyatva*) itself—this is the direction of the argument. Now, an objection: if the category (*padārtha*) is the universal (*jāti*), how can duality and so forth be construed with it, given that the universal is unitary? Do not say so. When there is an intention to express the connection with a single substratum, the singular number is used for the form (*ākṛti*); as in, "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). But when there is an intention to express the connection with multiple substrata, the dual and plural numbers are used. For the proponent of the universal as the word-meaning does not accept that the individual (*vyakti*) is non-denotable; rather, he accepts only its subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*).

In that regard, although action (*kriyā*) is predominant in forms such as *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, and *pacanti*, there is a difference in number (*vacanabheda*) caused by the number of the means (*sādhana*); likewise, even when the generic form (*ākṛti*) is predominant, [the difference in number] is caused by the number of the substance (*dravya*), and so forth—thus there is no fault. [Objection: Even so, there would be no difference in gender (*liṅgabhedo na syāt*) in cases such as *brāhmaṇī* and *brāhmaṇa*. For it has been stated under the rule "and of qualifiers, except for a genus" (*viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ*) that "a genus possesses an inherent gender" (*āviṣṭaliṅgā jātiḥ*). The meaning is that [the word] always adopts the very same gender residing in its substratum. [Reply: It is not so.

This is because worldly gender, such as femininity—which consists of the connection with breasts, hair, and so forth—is not adopted here as the grammatical gender (*liṅga*), for if that were the case, it would be impossible for it to be connected with other genders. Rather, the Grammarians (*śābdika*) rely upon the systematic framework of their own school. To explain: the states of increase, decrease, and equilibrium of sound and the other qualities—which are transformations of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—and which are accessible solely through verbal cognition, are accepted as the grammatical genders.

The increase of qualities is masculinity (*puṃstva*), their decrease is femininity (*strītva*), and their mere persistence is neuter-ness (*napuṃsakatva*). For this very reason, even though excellence and deficiency exist, the grammatical rule "the neuter is used for the general" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*) is consistent when one intends to express only the state of persistence, without intending to convey those [qualities]. We shall elaborate upon this under the rule *striyām*. 65. When an elder [is mentioned] with a youth, [the former alone remains], provided that the distinction between them consists solely in the characteristics [of age].

According to the technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) of the ancient teachers that "the term *vṛddha* refers to one whose offspring has disappeared," the word *vṛddha* here denotes a *gotra* [lineage], due to its association with the technical term *yuvan*. When there is a co-utterance (*sahokti*) with a word ending in a *yuvan* suffix, a word ending in a *gotra* suffix remains, provided that the entire difference between the two is caused solely by the suffixes mentioned. For example: *gārgyaś ca gārgyāyaṇaś ca gārgyau* ("Gārgya and Gārgyāyaṇa are both Gārgyas"). Why say "vṛddha" (an elder/lineage)? Consider: *gargaś ca gārgyāyaṇaś ca gargagārgyāyaṇau* ("Garga and Gārgyāyaṇa are Gargas and Gārgyāyaṇas"). Why say "yuvan" (a youth)? Consider: *gargaś ca gārgyaś ca gargagārgyau* ("Garga and Gārgya are Gargas and Gārgyas").

What is meant by "having many characteristics" (*tallakṣaṇa*)? For example: *gārgyaś ca vātsyāyanaś ca gārgyavātsyāyanau* (Gārgya and Vātsyāyana are Gārgya-Vātsyāyanas). What is meant by "entirely" (*kṛtsna*)? For example: *bhāgavittibhāgavittikau*. From the word *bhāgavitta*, the suffix *iñ* is applied to denote a descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) by the rule "*ata iñ*". From that [base ending in *iñ*], the suffix *ṭhak* is applied to denote a descendant in the younger generation (*yūnyapatya*) among the Sauvīras by the rule "*vṛddhāṭṭhak sauvīreṣu bahulam*". Here, the difference in form is caused not only by the suffixes but also by the factors of contempt and the status of being a Sauvīra lineage. This is because the word "contempt" (*kutsane*) is understood as a carry-over from the rule "*gotrastriyāḥ kutsane san*" (Pāṇini 4.1.137). What is meant by "entirely"? For example: *gārgyaś ca vātsyāyanaś ca gārgyavātsyāyanau*.

**66. Strī-puṃvac-ca.** When a female and [a male] are mentioned together with a youth (*yuvan*), the female is retained, and its meaning is treated like the masculine. This rule is commenced because the [desired] result would not otherwise be obtained due to the excessive irregularity caused by feminine gender. *Gārgī* and *Gārgyāyaṇau* become *gargāḥ*. Under the continued application of the rule "not in the feminine," there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "of *yañ* and *añ*"; thus, *Dākṣī* and *Dākṣāyaṇaḥ* become *dākṣī*.

In this context, regarding the term *strī* (feminine), when it is marked with the *svarita* accent, there are three possibilities upon the employment of a suffix under that governing rule (*adhikāra*): either an extension of non-existence (*abhāvātideśa*) according to the rule "the feminine suffix is like the masculine," or, in the absence of the *svarita* accent, the inclusion of the word-form (*śabdagrāhaṇa*), or the inclusion of the meaning (*arthagrāhaṇa*). The first [alternative] is not tenable. Because in the aforementioned instance, in the case of *gargāḥ*, there would result the hearing of the suffix *yañ*. This is because its elision is prohibited by the rule "not when [denoting] a non-feminine" (*astriyām*). Furthermore, this fault applies specifically to the interpretation as a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

In the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), however, because there exists an entity similar to the feminine, the remaining [term] denotes the meaning of that which is being excluded. Not the second [alternative], because since femininity has not ceased, the substitution of *na* in the rule "tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi" would be untenable in an expression such as *gargān paśya*. Therefore, the third [alternative] is correct; for when the masculine meaning is extended [by *pumvat*], the grammatical operations occasioned by it take effect. This should be understood in other cases as well. *Pumān striyā* (67).

When there is a co-utterance (*sahokti*) of words of identical form (*sarūpa*), the masculine is retained; and that [retained word] remains as if it were masculine (*puṃvat*), provided the distinction (*viśeṣa*) is characterized by that very [masculine gender]. *Haṃsaśca haṃsī ca* (the male swan and the female swan) becomes *haṃsau*. Since the retained [word] expresses the meaning of the elided [word], the feminine gender is also present, which would result in the application of the suffix *ṭāp*; however, because of the continued application of the rule "as if masculine," it does not occur. This single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs even when the specific characteristic is understood from another word. For example, Kaiyaṭa states: "This is a cow and this is a cow—these two are 'cows' (*gāvau*) as they move about."

The intention here is [the definition of] qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) as the absence of a specific property produced by something other than that [qualifier]. And the Dīkṣitas maintain that this [qualified absence] exists here too because of the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The author of the Nyāsa (Jinendrabuddhi) maintains that, due to the separation of the *yoga* (Pāṇini 1.2.67), there is a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) even in the absence of a specific property, and because the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*) serves as the regulator, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Because the genus *haṃsatva* is equally the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), even though the difference between the words [is merely] a mark of femininity alone, there is no single-remainder formation in cases such as *haṃsaś ca varaṭā ca*.
This is because, through the recurrence of "having the same form" (*sarūpa*), the identity of the base (*prakṛti*) is obtained.
[And: "The words *bhrātṛ* and *putra* [form a single remainder with] *svasṛ* and *duhitṛ* respectively. (Pāṇini 1.2.68)

*bhrātā* (brother) and *svasā* (sister) form *bhrātarau*; *putraḥ* (son) and *duhitā* (daughter) form *putrau*. This very rule serves as the authority for the recurrence of the term *sarūpa* (having the same form) from the preceding sūtra; otherwise, that [previous] rule alone would apply here as well. However, in the case of the rule *tyadādīni sarvaiḥ*, there is no recurrence of that [term], because it has been superseded. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: in the case of *gārgyaśca gārgyāṇaśca* ("Gārgya and the Gārgyas"), since the single commonality consisting of being a descendant of Garga—which belongs both to the elder and the younger—is intended to be expressed, the form *gārgyau* is established.

Regarding the inclusion here of both "old" (*vṛddha*) and "young" (*yuvan*), or whether it refers only to the "old," this is for the purpose of determining the specific distinction. Even in the view that initiates the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), since context and other factors must still be relied upon, the determination of the specific meaning is possible through those very means even when the general term is employed.

Nor is the initiation of *ekaśeṣa* intended to prevent the formation of a *dvandva* (copulative compound); for that is excluded simply by the fact that such a form is not conventionally expressed (*anabhidhāna*). Furthermore, in the case of a female and a male, forms such as *brāhmaṇau* are established when there is a desire to express only the genus (*jāti*), just as in the case of *mṛgakṣīra* ("deer-milk") and similar examples.

It might be argued as follows: In the case of *brāhmaṇavatsā* (the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa) and *brāhmaṇīvatsaḥ* (the son of a Brāhmaṇī), there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member of a pair) according to the rule *pumān striyā* ("the masculine [remains] after the feminine"). This is because such a situation exists where there is a single base for the suffix (*pratyaya-prakṛti*), while there is otherwise a difference in form (*vairūpya*). Nor should it be said that the application of *ekaśeṣa* is restricted by the continued validity (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition "when followed by a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*), such that *ekaśeṣa* occurs only when a distinction based on gender arises immediately before a case-ending that serves as the cause for *ekaśeṣa*; whereas here, since the distinction based on gender exists even in the case-ending of the preceding word (*pūrvapada*), the rule does not apply.

Furthermore, the formation of the dual *kārakau* from *kārakaḥ* and *kārikā* would not be possible through the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), because the substitution of *it* (the shortening of the vowel) here is a distinction caused by femininity (*strītvakṛta*), and this [distinction] lacks the quality of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) in relation to the case-ending that serves as the cause for *ekaśeṣa*. Nor should it be argued that although the substitution of *it* takes the form of a distinction created by a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), it does not take the form of a distinction created by the meaning of femininity itself; for if that were so, the form *gomantau* (from *gomān* and *gomatī*) would remain unestablished, since no other distinction is introduced here by the feminine suffix.

However, because the specific feature consisting of the suffix itself is already expressed by the meaning "femininity," and because a distinction—whether introduced by the meaning in some cases or by the feminine suffix in others—must necessarily be apprehended; nor should it be argued that in both views, *ekaśeṣa* would fail to apply in examples such as *paṭuś ca paṭvī ca paṭū*, since neither femininity nor the feminine suffix serves as the cause for the *yaṇ* substitution, as that *yaṇ* is prescribed solely on the basis of the form being a vowel (*aj*).

[Objection: Since the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is the cause for the *yaṇ* substitution merely by its presence (*tadbhāvabhāvitā*), and since femininity (*strītva*) is indirectly the cause as well, the same applies to the substitution of *it*; thus, in cases such as *brāhmaṇīvatsā ca*, the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) would be unavoidable. [Reply: Not so. Because that word (*tatpada*) is understood through syntactic connection (*anuvṛtti*), only the primary female and male [referents] are grasped. Furthermore, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* is prescribed when there is a desire to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*), and that [desire] pertains only to the primary [referents]. Therefore, *ekaśeṣa* occurs where the distinction is caused by the primary female and male; however, in the present case, a distinction caused even by non-primary females and males exists. Thus, [the objection does not hold].

69. When a neuter [word] is mentioned together with a non-neuter [word], the neuter remains, and it may optionally be treated as singular, provided that the distinction between them consists solely in their gender. When a white blanket (*śuklaḥ kaṃbalaḥ*) and a white cloth (*śuklaṃ vastram*) are mentioned together, the neuter form remains: *tad idaṃ śuklam* (this is white), or *te ime śukle* (these two are white). When a white blanket (*śuklaḥ kaṃbalaḥ*), a white cloak (*śuklā bṛhatikā*), and a white cloth (*śuklaṃ vastram*) are mentioned together, the neuter form remains: *tad idaṃ śuklam* (this is white), or *tānīmāni śuklāni* (these are white).

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states that when there is an intention to express mere coexistence (sthitimātra), the neuter gender is established as the general rule (autsargika). Nor is the sūtra intended for the sake of optional singular concord (ekavadbhāva), since the desired result is already established by intending the primacy of the genus (jāti-prādhānya).
[Pitā mātrā 70]

This is clear. The word "or" (vā) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. "Father and mother" (pitā ca mātā ca) form the compound *pitarau* or *mātāpitarau*. Regarding the explanation that "in the absence of a daughter, both parents are the heirs to the wealth": although, because a *dvandva* compound is prescribed for simultaneous expression of two substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), and since the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation is an exception to that, the sequence of the parents is not perceived in the taking of the wealth; nevertheless, due to the rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), and because of the word "mother" appearing first in the case where *ekaśeṣa* does not apply—namely, *mātāpitarau*—[the sequence is established].

Vijñāneśvara maintains that because the sequence of meaning is understood from the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), even when there is a connection to wealth, if a sequence is required, one must follow the very order already perceived; thus it is understood that first the mother is the heir to the wealth, and in her absence, the father.
By this, the verse "I bow to the two parents of the world" is also explained, as its determination ultimately rests upon other means of valid cognition such as suitability (*yogyatā*).

By this, another application of the rule is also explained: "May you and your beloved attain union with Śiva and Śivā. For there is no evidence for a restriction that the feminine noun must necessarily precede in a *vigraha* (analytic) sentence; as seen in the Bhāṣya: "Why does [the rule] not apply in cases such as 'the female camel and the young male camel,' or 'the swan and the female swan'?
[And likewise: "The father-in-law [is mentioned] with the mother-in-law. (Pāṇini 1.2.71)

This is clear. Regarding the pair "śvaśurau" (parents-in-law), meaning both mother-in-law and father-in-law, the commentary on the three relevant sūtras states as follows: In the domain of *vṛtti* (compound or derivative formation), it must be admitted that words such as *bhrātṛ* (brother) and others denote [their female counterparts] such as *svasṛ* (sister), even when the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) is initiated; this is because of the established principle (*siddhānta*) that the single member retained expresses the meaning of the members that are elided. However, it is better to accept that such a denotation occurs only when there is a desire to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*), without resorting to *ekaśeṣa*, since the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. Furthermore, due to the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), the dual compound (*dvandva*) of the words *bhrātṛ-svasṛ* (brother and sister) does not occur.

Furthermore, since you yourself accept that in the case of *mātāpitarau* (mother and father) and *śvaśrūśvaśurau* (mother-in-law and father-in-law), the disjunctive particle *vā* is understood within the *dvandva* compound; and because it must be stated that context and other factors serve as the determinants for deciding whether this is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of two similar forms or of two dissimilar forms. As for the passage in the *Bhāgavata*, "The brother-in-law [śyālaḥ] then took his sister-in-law [svāsroḥ]," the word *svasṛpada* is used figuratively to denote both the sister and her husband, based on the presence of the feminine gender, just as in the rule "He places the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks."

Nor can it be argued that because both [the two groups] are equal, the status of being "fewer" (alpatva) is untenable; for in that context, the mantra containing the word *prāṇa* is considered fewer in relation to the mantras devoid of it—so says Śrīdhara. This is because what is intended there is merely the absence of a plurality among the primary meanings (*śakya*) relative to the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*).

*Tyadādīni sarvair nityam* (Pāṇini 1.2.72): When used in conjunction with all other words except itself, pronouns beginning with *tyad* (such as *sa*, *eṣa*, etc. are always retained [as the sole survivors]. For example: *sa ca devadattaśca tau* ("He and Devadatta, those two").
"It should be stated: 'When there is a remainder from among the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, the gender and number [of the compound] follow those of the masculine or neuter.

Thus: *sā ca devadattaś ca tau* (she and Devadatta—those two); *sā ca kuṇḍe ca tāni* (she and the pots—those). Since the gender of the pronoun *tyad* and so on would have applied because it is the one remaining, this rule is commenced. However, when there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of both masculine and neuter, the neuter remainder prevails due to the subsequent application of the rule regarding words. Thus: *tac ca devadattaś ca te* (that and Devadatta—those). "And it should be stated: 'Not for dvandvas, tatpuruṣas, or qualifiers.'"

That cock and that peahen are "those two" (kukkuṭamayūryau). That [cock] and she [peahen] are "those two" (te), as in "those two half-pippalīs" (ardhapippalyau). This is established by logic (*nyāyasiddham*). Kaiyaṭa states that because the rule "the gender of a *dvandva* or *tatpuruṣa* compound follows that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgam dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*) transfers the gender to the meaning of the compound, it is thereby established that the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) which qualifies it takes that same gender. Since pronouns such as *tyad* and others function as *sarvanāmans* and thus refer to things in their most general sense, when they are used in conjunction with another word, it is logically established that the pronoun alone remains; therefore, this [rule] need not have been commenced.

It should not be argued that this sūtra is intended for the purpose of the rule "that which follows [the remaining] remains (*yatparaṃ tacchiṣyate*)," because without it, one would not obtain the prohibition regarding the subsequent word (*śabdapara-vipratiṣedha*). This is because the retention of the preceding element is also desired in cases such as *sa ca yaśca tāvān*, *ayaṃ ca yaśca yāvān*; and under the view that the sūtra is actually formulated, that [retention] would not be established. Nor is it for the purpose of excluding the usage *tad devadattau*, since the statement "there is no *dvandva* compound between a general term and a specific term" is necessarily required.

Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, such expressions as *śūdrābhīram*, *gobalīvardam*, and *tṛṇolapam* would be untenable; for the Ābhīras constitute a distinct caste. As it is said: "From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Ābhīra;
from a King (Kṣatriya) and the wives of Vaiśyas and Śūdras are born the Māhiṣya and the Ugra respectively."

Because of memory; for the word *go* denotes only a female cow, and thus a separate power (*śakti*) must be admitted for its application to a bull. Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) because the cognition of a specific meaning is established by a general term; for we observe usage such as "bring that Brāhmaṇa, Gārgya," where the general term, in proximity to a specific term, refers to a specific other than that [general], just as in the case of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, as seen in examples such as "the Brāhmaṇas have arrived" and "Vasiṣṭha has also arrived."

Therefore, since the use of the dvandva compound for both the general and the particular is necessary, and since [the desired form] is established from that very [rule], this sūtra need not be commenced; such is the intent of the Bhāṣya.
[The rule] "In the case of herds of domestic animals that are not young, the feminine [form is used]" (73).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67). Among these [animals], when there is a desire to express them together, the feminine form remains. Examples: *imā gāvaḥ* (these cows), *imā ajāḥ* (these goats). Why say "domestic" (*grāmya*)? Consider: *ime nyaṅkavaḥ* (these antelopes), *ime sūkarāḥ* (these pigs). Why say "livestock" (*paśu*)? Consider: *ime brāhmaṇāḥ* (these Brahmins). Why say "herd" (*saṅgha*)? Consider: *etau gāvau* (these two cows). Since it is impossible for a "quality" (*guṇa*) to exist in a mere pair, what is intended here must reside in the members constituting that group; for even though a group consisting of only two parts is possible, the inclusion of the word "herd" (*saṅgha*) by its very force implies that only a group composed of multiple members is intended. Why say "not young" (*ataruṇa*)? Consider: [the following example: *ime taruṇā gāvaḥ* (these young cows). In this case, because they are young, the feminine form does not remain. (Note: The text provided ends with "ataruṇeti kim", implying a question regarding the necessity of the term "not young," which is answered by the example of young animals.)

"These are young ones; these are rams. Since the properties of youth and its absence cannot logically apply to the *saṃgha* (the collective) as a whole, they are understood by implication to refer to the individual animals that constitute the *saṃgha*. [The rule] should be stated as: "among those with uncloven hoofs. This does not apply here: "these are horses," or "these are camels. According to the author of the *Nyāsa*, this is because the term is restricted by the continued application of the option (*vikalpa*).

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "This [sūtra] need not be commenced. In the case of herds, because female cows alone predominate, the designation of the feminine gender is established by its preponderance, as in the case of 'Mallagrāma' and similar names. However, among non-village animals, males alone are predominant; and since camels are wild (*āraṇyaka*), even if the sūtra were commenced, there would be no application of the feminine gender. Furthermore, in cases such as *brāhmaṇāḥ*, males alone are predominant. In cases such as *etau*, since the specific gender is already known, the masculine alone remains as the remainder. And in cases such as *ime vatsāḥ*, males alone are predominant."
Thus ends the third daily lesson (āhnika) in the second [chapter] of the first [part] of the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi; and this quarter (pāda) is also completed.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter.
"The roots beginning with *bhū* and *vā* are called *dhātu*s. (Pāṇini 1.3.1)

Verbal roots (dhātu) beginning with *bhū* that denote action shall be designated as "roots. [Examples: *bhavati*. Because they possess the designation of "root," the suffixes such as *laṭ* (present indicative) and others are applied. In expressions such as *yāḥ paśyasi* ("those which you see"), the term "denoting action" (*kriyāvacana*) is included to prevent the elision of the long vowel *ā* in the word *yāḥ* from occurring when the designation of "root" would otherwise apply. The inclusion of the phrase "beginning with *bhū*" (*bhvādayaḥ*)—which signifies those listed in the specific grammatical list (*gaṇa*)—is intended to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to particles (*nipāta*) such as *hiruk* meaning "excluding," and to finite verb forms ending in *tiṅ* (tense suffixes) such as *śiśye* ("he lay down"). One should not argue that the word *yāḥ* is excluded from the list simply because it is "derived" (*lākṣaṇika*, i.e., formed by a grammatical rule rather than being a primitive item). This is because even derived forms can be included in the list if they denote action.

Because in another place, the status of being explicitly stated (*pratipadoktatva*) is required there. Nor can it be argued that since the internal (*antaraṅga*) elision (*lopa*) is conditioned by meaning, the external (*bahiraṅga*) *ṭāp* suffix would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*). For gender is perceived prior to the case-role (*kāraka*), and thus the elision conditioned by affixes beginning with *aj* is itself the external factor. Some maintain that this is precluded by the rule "not when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*). Furthermore, the mention of the meaning is not a restrictive factor, because it was composed by other scholars and is therefore not the work of Pāṇini;
each meaning was demonstrated merely to describe the expressive power of the verbal root.
They should be followed according to their usage, for roots have multiple meanings.
This is also because there is no intention (tātparya) to exclude other meanings.

For this very reason, the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in "the roots *kurda*, *khurda*, *gurda*, and *guda* are used only in the sense of playing (*krīḍā*)" is appropriate; likewise, [the rule] "the root *śliṣ* is used in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*)" and so forth is consistent. Nor is there any inconsistency in the fact that the augment *it* [is applied] to "the root *ṭuvam* in the sense of vomiting (*udgiraṇa*") due to its being a nipātana (irregular formation), for others have stated that it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group precisely out of dissatisfaction with this [explanation].

The addition of the letter *va* [in the term *bhūv-ādayaḥ*] occurs by virtue of a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). Nor is this incorrect, for it is well-established within the community of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇanikāya*). Furthermore, it is not the case that the status of denoting action (*kriyāvacanatva*) is not obtained from the Sūtra; for the meaning is that "those which denote *bhū*, i.e., existence—the general category of action—are *bhūv-ādayaḥ*. Some maintain that although the suffix *iñ* is prescribed after the roots *vasi*, *vapi*, *yaj*, *rāj*, *vraj*, *sah*, *han*, *nī*, *vās*, *vādi*, and *vāri* in the rule "after *vasi*, *vapi*, *yaj*, *rāj*, *vraj*, *sah*, *han*, *nī*, *vās*, *vādi*, and *vāri*, [the suffix] *iñ* [is applied]," it is possible for it to apply to *vad* as well due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

Others maintain that here the suffix *iñ* is applied only to the root *vad*, because there is no difference in meaning due to the cessation of the causal (*preṣaṇa*) sense; furthermore, the Bhāṣya’s statement "they speak" (*vadanti*) is intended merely as an explanation of the meaning. Nor is it difficult to find these roots listed in the *gaṇa*s, since by the introduction of the rule "roots ending in *san* and others are verbal roots" (*sānādyantā dhātavaḥ*), it is inferred that only those already listed receive this designation. As for the roots *stambhū* and so on mentioned in the Sūtras, their status as roots is established by the addition of the marker *u* (*udit*) and by the prescription of operations falling under the governing heading of "verbal roots. And as for *culump* and others, they belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class-based group) beginning with *bhū*. This is because the marker *vṛt* is used to indicate the completion of the *yajādi* class.
By this [explanation], the inclusion of the *vṛt* (root) at the end of the *divādi* class is for the purpose of concluding the *puṣādi* group; by that, forms such as *mṛgyati* are also explained.

In reality, however, all is established by the *gaṇasūtra* at the end of the *curādi* class, which states: "This illustration is manifold (*bahulam*). Furthermore, the *ṇic* suffix may be added even to roots of the *bhvādi* class in the sense of the root itself (*svārthe*).

Alternatively, the recitation of the ten classes (*daśagaṇī*) is merely illustrative (*diṅmātram*); for the authors of the treatises have provided two-fold explanations: that other roots should also be understood from the usage of students.

Alternatively, *bhū* and *vā* form a *dvandva* compound. The two words *ādi*, which denote a mode of arrangement, undergo *ekaśeṣa*. Then, by means of a *bahuvrīhi*—namely, "those for which *bhū* and *vā* are the first"—the two aforementioned qualifications are obtained, and similarity is established by virtue of their being denoters of action (*kriyāvācitva*). Nor does this result in the non-attainment of *dhātutva* (verbal status) for the root *vāti*; for similarity that is not constituted by difference exists therein.

Alternatively, in the expression *vādaya*, there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) formation of both the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa*. According to the rule, "among those distinguished by accent, that which follows remains," the *bahuvrīhi* is what remains. *Bhuvo vādayaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and the meaning of the genitive case here is the relationship between the signified and the signifier.

Alternatively, both meanings are obtained through the methods of *tantra*, repetition (*āvṛtti*), and so forth, as in the case of the rule *dvirvacane'ci*. In this context, the essential point is simply that the words beginning with *bhū* are similar to the word *vās*.
By this—
"This letter *va* is employed at the beginning of the *bhūvādi* [group] for the sake of auspiciousness;
or, because they express the meaning of *bhuva* (to be), the *vādayaḥ* are traditionally known as *bhvarthāḥ*.
Thus the *vārttika* has been explained.

In reality, however, for the learned, *dhātutva* (the state of being a verbal root) consists precisely in possessing the status of a *dhātu*-word by virtue of its connection with specific technical designations (*paribhāṣā*). And the aforementioned sūtra is the indicator of that. It is not, however, "being one or another among *bhū*, etc.," because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the various forms in imitation words (*anukaraṇa*). Furthermore, it is difficult to state in any other way the property that constitutes "being one or another" among *bhū* and so forth, as distinct from those [designated roots]. For this very reason, there is inclusion of those mentioned in the sūtras as well as *culump* and others.
And for this very reason, the proclamation of the experts (*tāntrika*) that "the state of being a verbal root (*dhātvarthatva*) is the state of being an action (*kriyātva*)" is consistent.

Now, what is this so-called "action" (*kriyā*)? It is that which they describe as a specific operation existing at the time immediately preceding the fruit. As for [the actions of] placing on the stove and so forth, their status as action is merely figurative.
Thus it has been said:
"They know that to be action from which the fruit is produced immediately thereafter."

"Because it is the primary factor for the sake of that [result], the others are designated by its name. Nor is there any deviation [in this definition] due to the operation of wood and so forth, because what must be stated is "not being conducive to another producer. Nor does the consequence follow that one would say *pakṣyati* ("will cook") even at the start of cooking, because of the action's future state; for we accept the following rule: the term *apākṣīt* ("cooked") is used when the entire collection of actions—both primary and secondary—is past; *pakṣyati* when there is prior non-existence (of the result); and *pacati* ("is cooking") when some part exists. This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the *yaṅ-luk* rule.
That is not so; for when a primary sense is possible, it is improper to resort to a secondary one.

Now, if "the state of being a cooker" (*pacitva*) is a universal (*jāti*), based on the consistent usage of the term "he cooks" (*pacati*), then that itself is the action (*kriyā*). Nor does this lead to the consequence of its being unachievable (*asādhyatva*); for it is only the individual instances (*vyakti*) that serve as its substrata which possess that nature [of being achievable].
As it has been said:
"Others say that the universal (jāti) is a single action residing in multiple individuals;
though it is unachievable in its own form, it appears as if it were achievable through the form of the individual. Thus [it is said].

That is not correct. Since the operation of the stick and so forth is also conducive to the result, if the stick—which is the locus of that operation—were considered the agent (*kartṛ*), it would follow that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) must denote it. Consequently, in the sentence *daṇḍena devadattaḥ pacati* ("Devadatta cooks with a stick"), the nominative case would erroneously apply to the stick as well. Nor can it be argued that this third case ending has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), because instrumentality is incompatible with agency, given the rule: "Up to the limit of *kaḍāra*, there is only one designation. Furthermore, one cannot claim that there is no fault because the operation of the stick is not intended to be expressed as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) at that time;
for even then, there is no evidence that the cognition of the action's state of being accomplished (*sādhyatva*) could have a different object [than the action itself].
Now, action (*kriyā*) is that specific operation which is denoted as being in the state of being accomplished (*sādhyatva*). As it has been said:

"Whether already established or not yet established, that which is denoted as being in the state of being accomplished, because its nature consists of a sequential process, is called 'action'. Thus it is stated.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for [the status of] being denoted as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). For in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), *pākaḥ* ("cooking"), *karoti* ("he does"), and *kṛtiḥ* ("action"), although there is no difference in the cognition of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), we observe the presence or absence of an expectancy for another action. Thus, "being to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) is defined as that which delimits the non-arising of an expectancy for another action. This very state is what constitutes "non-substantiality" (*asattvabhūtatva*). Even on the view that the suffix denotes the action, this must necessarily be so, because it is observed in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and *pākabhavanam* ("the becoming of cooking").

That is not so; for a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the object is characterized by the mode of being something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) contradicts universal experience. Furthermore, it would contradict the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that in expressions such as "in order to eat" (*bhoktum*), an action that is not yet existent (*asattvabhūtā kriyā*) appears. If you argue that this is because the expectancy for another action (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣā*) exists there, as will be explained in the third [chapter], [we reply: no.

To this it is replied: action (*kriyā*) is indeed the collection of operations conducive to a result. As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "This thing called action is entirely imperceptible; having parts occurring in a temporal sequence (*pūrvāparībhūta*), it cannot be demonstrated as a solidified whole. The meaning is that because the constituent parts of the collection of operations are not delimited by a single moment, they cannot be perceived [simultaneously].
Thus, it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"A collection of things born in succession consists of subordinate parts..."
That which is non-different from cognition and not constructed by it is designated as "action" (kriyā).

The reason for the non-simultaneous existence of those things produced in succession is as follows: by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), specifically through a cognition that apprehends a collection of objects (*samūhālambana-jñāna*), there is a conceptualized non-difference (*abheda*) [among them]. Thus, just as in a collection of multiple phonemes (*varṇa*) there is the conventional usage "one word" (*ekaṃ padam*) because they are delimited by a single cognition, so too is it said in the aforementioned case regarding action (*kriyā*). Regarding the term *piṇḍībhūta* ("become a mass"): Kaiyaṭa states that just as atoms (*paramāṇu*) are perceived when they have become a mass and not in isolation, so too action is not perceptible because of its state of being a mass.
This has also been stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:

The object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is of the nature of an action (*kriyā*) whose constituent parts (*avayava*) are characterized by a temporal sequence of before and after. Its commentators also explain it thus: that which is to be accomplished is intended as something yet to be achieved; it is that verbal meaning, such as "cooking" (*pāka*), whose constituent parts—such as placing [the pot on the fire] (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth—are perceived as having a sequential order and are included within a cumulative whole (*pracaya*). Since there is no attainment of sequence for that which is non-sequential, and because the cumulative whole does not exist as something distinct from its respective individual parts, the notion that "cooking" occurs sequentially as each individual operation is considered a mere illusion.
For this very reason, it has been stated: "because it assumes a sequential form."

Alternatively, even the acts of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth are of the nature of action, qualified by their respective substrata; and although there is no sequence because the action and its qualificandum (the object) are one, a figurative attribution of sequence occurs due to the sequence of the substrata which serve as qualifiers. Others, however, say that the meaning of verbal roots such as *pac* ("to cook") is an action qualified by the cooking-pot, fuel, rice, and so forth; and the parts of that [action], while delimiting the power residing in themselves, have as their substrata the pot and other factors. They further maintain that the *ci* suffix is used because there is no real temporal priority or posteriority among those [parts].

Nor should it be argued that when the operations beginning with placing [the pot] on the hearth and ending with its removal occur simultaneously across various cooking acts by different agents, there would have to be a perception of the cooking act [as a single entity]. This is because those individual instances lack mutual cooperation.

One might object: "Cooking-ness (*pākatva*) resides in each individual operation; it does not, like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), subsist collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), for it is impossible for a single property to reside collectively in things existing at different times, and because such is understood from other cited texts."

It is also stated in the *Śabdakaṇṭakoddhāra*: "In the entire complex of operations beginning with lighting the stove and ending with taking [the vessel] down, the nature of cooking (*pākatva*), the nature of productive activity (*bhāvanātva*), or the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) resides in its entirety in each individual part—just as the nature of 'pot-ness' (*ghaṭatva*) does—because that which constitutes its meaning is the collection of operations delimited by the result.

And it is said in the *Bhāṣya*: "The action denoted by 'he cooks' (*pacati*) is manifold yet has a single purpose; it consists of placing the pot on the fire, pouring water, putting in the rice, stirring, heating the fire, moving the ladle, and taking [the food] down. If it is argued that, in this case, there would necessarily be a perception of the cooking [as a whole], we say no.

Even though the state of being a "cooked" thing (*pākatva*) exists as a real entity (*vastu*), it is only the collection (*samūha*) of those [atoms] that constitutes the object of the linguistic usage of "action. Furthermore, that [collection] is incapable of being perceived (*pratyakṣa*). For this very reason, it is stated in the third book [of the *Mahābhāṣya*] that in expressions such as "Look, the deer is running," only a single part [of the action], which is present, serves as the object of seeing. As Harivṛṣabha has said:
"The natures of those [atoms], whether existent or non-existent in succession, do not belong to a collection;
they do not enter into a relationship with the eyes and other senses, whose objects are real entities (*sad-vastu*)."

The logical consequence is that they do not go [to the object]. Since an action (*kriyā*) is a collection of successive operations (*vyāpāra*), it is impossible for such a collection to be present at a single moment; therefore, it cannot be grasped by the eyes and other senses. However, it is entirely reasonable that an operation which constitutes a part of that [action] and exists in the present should be perceptible to the eye. Thus, it is established that action is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

Now, what is the proof that the action of the aforementioned form constitutes the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*)? It cannot be the *Nirukta* statement, "The verb (*ākhyāta*) has the state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning," because the word *ākhyāta* does not denote a verbal root. [Objection: But surely, since the author of the *Nirukta* states, "Every noun (*nāman*) is born from a verb," it follows that [the word *ākhyāta*] denotes a verbal root; for the status of being a noun is possible through being produced by an affix (*pratyaya*). This is also supported by the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "And the *Nirukta*, as well as the *Śakaṭa-toka* in grammar, says that a noun is born from a verbal root.
Kaiyaṭa explains that "the offspring (*toka*) of Śakaṭa"—meaning the descendant—is Śākaṭāyana. Thus, [the term *nāman* refers to a specific type of word].

If it is argued that this is stated in the *Nirukta*: "In this regard, Śākaṭāyana and the tradition of the etymologists (*nairukta*) hold that nouns are derived from verbs," such is not the case. For there is no use of the term "verb" (*ākhyāta*) with respect to a verbal root ending in a *kṛt* suffix; rather, its application there is possible only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For this very reason, even in Jaimini’s Sūtra—"But those whose usage is not found in their own sense at the time of their origin are verbs"—the word "verbs" refers to verbal roots only by way of secondary indication. The phrase "at the time of their origin" means at the time of utterance; "their usage is not found in their own sense" means that they do not exist for the accomplishment of their own meaning [independently].

However, this is the distinction: in the Jaimini-sūtra, only a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in a finite verb suffix (*tiṅanta*) is intended; whereas in the Nirukta, by way of an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), the mere form of the root itself is meant.
