[Objection: Surely, from one's own sentence, there can be no understanding of its own syntactic connection, because of the absence of a real expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), which consists in the non-existence of a cognition having the same form as the intended understanding of the relevant connection.
[Reply: Not so. For in that context, it is precisely the cognition qualified by the absence of such a desire [to know] that is posited.

And so it has been stated in the *Śabdāloka*: "Just as there may be a desire to infer even when something is already known through perception, the desire 'May I know [this] through verbal testimony' is easily available; therefore, since the presence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) exists, it is difficult to maintain that there is an absence of other means of knowledge. For this very reason, in the second commentary (*Ṭīkā*), it was established as a tenet (*siddhānta*) that the word spoken by oneself conveys meaning to oneself.

However, if one accepts that the connection (*anvaya*) of one [word] occurs even in the absence of the other, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using the expression "Devadatta-Yajñadattau gacchati" (Devadatta and Yajñadatta go), just as one says "Devadatta and Yajñadatta go. Consequently, since it is necessary to maintain the ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) of the *dvandva* compound in such cases, it must be asserted that the speaker’s intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*) concerns only the cognition of the two acting together.

That too is incorrect. Since it has been established that [the two] are understood simultaneously, and because there is a rule that verbal roots and nouns must terminate in the same number, the aforementioned objection does not apply. Even if a dual ending is required for grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*), it is absent for the sake of cognition (*bodha*). This much is the distinction: in the active construction (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*), there is agreement in number with the word denoting the agent (*kartṛ-pada*), whereas in the passive construction (*karma-ākhyāta*), it is with the word expressing the object (*karma-vācaka-pada*). Therefore, the aforementioned *dvandva* compound is faultless.

But let us state our position after having conceded [the opponent's point]: let *hal* and *l* be treated as entirely separate. Nor should it be argued that the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is untenable here, on the grounds that a single word cannot possess the status of being "ending in a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntatva*), and because a collection of words is not included by the term "word" (*pada*). This objection is invalid; for if "being at the end of a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntatva*) and "being at the end of a word" (*padāntatva*) are taken as qualifiers of the letter *l*, then the rule is established. Since "consonant" (*saṃyoga*) is a qualifier of the "word," the elision is already accomplished by the rule of "that which ends in [it]" (*tadanta-vidhi*); however, the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the purpose of connecting it with the qualified noun, the "word" (*pada*), as well.

This is because of the explanation that the word *saṃyoga* [in the rule] has its genitive case-ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). Furthermore, according to the view that "the single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs after all [words] have been separately declined," the elision of a consonant at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is presented in the Bhāṣya itself for the form *vṛkṣas*. Nor does this contradict Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, which states that the Bhāṣya intends the elision of vowels and *hal* sounds (*halṅyādilopa*), for that [commentary] proceeds on the basis of another opinion, having introduced it with the words "here they explain. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine stated by Kaiyaṭa, namely, that "the base (*prakṛti*) is implied by the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si*."

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "asti-sico 'pṛkte" that the indication contains two *s*-sounds (*dvisakāraka*), this is because the *Kaustubha* itself explains it by analyzing [the word] as *sicaḥ* (genitive singular), whereby the final consonant of the cluster is elided.

As for the claim that this is merely an explanatory restatement (*anvākhyāna*) of a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) achieved through elision—that is untenable, because such a figurative indication cannot be established without knowledge of its primary meaning (*śakya*), which would result in a circular dependency (*parasparāśraya*).

That too is incorrect, because here we do not resort to a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) based on a relationship with the referent of the word *hal*. Rather, it is postulated that the aggregate *hal* refers to the aggregate *hall*; and this is not by way of secondary signification, but through the recollection of the letter *l*, since those who lack the knowledge of its elision would otherwise lack knowledge of the aforementioned aggregate. Secondary signification is accepted only in cases where such a meaning is understood even by those lacking knowledge of the elision, as in "the blue cloth" (*nīlaḥ paṭaḥ*) and so forth.
This is because the author of the *Maṇi* and others have stated that in forms such as *vyatise*, it is the very root (*dhātu*) which has been elided that conveys that meaning.

As for the argument that at the time the *it*-designation applies to the letter *l*, the sentence "something denoted by the word *hal* becomes *it*-designated" would result in the *it*-designation applying to all letters (*akṣu*), and furthermore, that even if [the rule] were applied according to the literal text for one who grasps it literally, it is proper to restrict the meaning of the scripture according to the maxim "there is no universal without particulars," and thus the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *l* is redundant once the matter is determined by another method—[this is refuted as follows:]...

That too is incorrect; for even the cognition that "there is something denoted by the word *hal*" has as its object only the *hal* itself. The difference between these two is this: the cognition [of it] as a denotable object (*vācyatva*) is determinate (*saprakāraka*) with respect to the unique property residing in *ha*, *la*, and so on, whereas the cognition [of it] as a *hal* is indeterminate (*niṣprakāraka*). As for the maxim "the universal is not without particulars," its meaning is that even a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is a universal has a particular as its substantive (*viśeṣyaka*), but it does not mean that it must have as its substantive a particular qualified by that [universal].

Even if the specific [referents] denoted by the word *hal* were not ascertained initially, they are ascertained subsequently; therefore, it is impossible for there to be no possibility of the application of that rule (*taddharma*) on that account. Nor should it be argued that the cognition "there exists something denoted by the word *hal*" is not useful for the operation of the rule, because it does not effect the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the linguistic items (*lakṣya*). This is because such existence [of the referent] is present indirectly (*paramparayā*). If one does not accept such a cognition, then even for you, the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the entire rule would not occur, since the apprehension of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is required therein. For it has been stated that when the intended meaning is present, there is repetition.

As for what was also said—that there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya because, by means of the Bhāṣya passage which establishes the absence of a name for a non-existent named object, one could likewise establish its absence even for an undetermined named object due to the equality of the underlying logic—this too is incorrect. For it is possible to determine that [named object] in accordance with conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). And thus Kaiyaṭa says on that point: "Whether the named object exists or does not exist, once it has been made the object of the intellect and previously indicated by the word, the name functions; let the elaboration suffice."

It might be argued: "Even so, the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is untenable in both cases, because a prohibition against *yaṇ*-substitution has been initiated there, and because the rule for the elision of a final *saṃyoga* ending in a *jhal* sound is established by drawing down the term *jhal* [from the previous rule]. This is not so. For the third alternative—that it is due to being characterized as *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic)—is what makes its occurrence possible.
As for what was also said: "When the *saṃyogāntalopa* is to be applied, which is *antaraṅga* (intrinsic), the elision of the *su* suffix, being *bahiraṅga*, is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)."

That too is incorrect, because [the rule] applies equally to the view that *jhal* is elided in cases such as *pacan*. Nor can it be argued that this is due to the force of the specific statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), for that statement has already served its purpose in cases such as *prāṅbhyām*. Furthermore, the view that [the rule] is merely a designation (*uddeśa-pakṣa*) can be easily maintained here as well. Nor should it be said that, in this way, the mention of "because of being a bahiraṅga characteristic" (*bahiraṅga-lakṣaṇatvāt*) would be untenable; for it must be stated that wherever there is the possibility of the elision of *yaṇ*, the rule operates by resorting to the *kāryakāla-pakṣa* (the view that rules apply at the time the operation is to take effect).

Nor is there a contradiction regarding the application and non-application of a single *paribhāṣā* within a single rule (*lakṣaṇa*), because this is possible by relying on the distinction between rules based on the distinction between the objects to be characterized (*lakṣya*). In reality, however, compared to the elision of *hal-ṅy-ādi* [sounds], the elision of the final of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) alone possesses the status of being "external" (*bahiraṅga*), because it is composed of two distinct technical designations (*saṃjñā*). It should not be argued that this [elision of the final of a conjunct] is equal [to the elision of *hal-ṅy-ādi*] because it too is composed of the designation "single-consonant" (*apṛkta-saṃjñā*), for that [designation] is also composed of a suffix (*pratyaya*). This is because the designation "conjunct" (*saṃyoga-saṃjñā*) is likewise composed of two designations; furthermore, the consonants (*hal*) are introduced therein as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), while the vowels (*ac*) are introduced as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of their absence.

A word (*pada*) consists of that which ends in a *su*-affix or a *tiṅ*-affix; for therein enters the twofold designation of *pada* by the rule "svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne. Furthermore, because [the rules] "rātsasya" and "skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ" function only upon consideration of their respective exceptions, whereas the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (etc. is without exception, and thus in its operation there is no need to avoid the scope of those exceptions. For this very reason, it is questioned in the Bhāṣya and other works that if the term *hal* were not included there, the elision of the *n* in forms such as *pacān* and *nityān* would be untenable.

Otherwise, even the elision [of a consonant] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* would remain as good as non-existent due to its being *asiddha*, because the fact that it applies to a specific grammatical feature (*lakṣaṇaviśeṣa*) does not render it irrelevant. Nor can it be argued that, in this way, the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not *antaraṅga* with respect to the *yaṇ*-substitution; for the prescription of the *yā*-substitute involves three technical names (*saṃjñā*), whereas the rule for the elision of a final conjunct is, according to the aforementioned reasoning, more cumbersome (*guru*). This is not so.

The intention of the Blessed One (Patañjali) is as follows: because there is a greater number of rules concerning *yaṇ* substitutes, and because the rule for *yaṇ* substitution—which functions with the requirement of considering its own domain—is not deprived of its status as "external" (*bahiraṅga*); and because that [rule] effects the refinement of the linguistic object (*lakṣya*) only when it has been refined by the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā*; and because the non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*) therein consists of being composed of phonemes that possess a difference relative to its own counter-correlate; whereas the constituent element of the technical term *saṃyoga* consists of *ac*-phonemes alone; and because the property of "selfhood" (*svatva*) is not uniform (*ananugata*). This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, in the *hal-sūtra* and in the *halantyam* sūtra, there is a mention of the *ḷ*-vowel alone as a subordinate element, as in the word *tavalkāra*. Nor can it be argued that the *ḷ*-vowel cannot thus receive the technical designation *it* because the designation *ac* is not yet established at this point—since the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) would be equal in both cases. This is true; however, Kaiyaṭa maintains that its status as an *it* can be made known by the rule *lṛditaḥ*.

Alternatively, the fact that *ṇal* is marked with the *l* letter serves to indicate that the *l* letter itself bears the technical designation *it*, because that [designation] is for the purpose of the accentuation of a *lit* suffix. It is not for the purpose of being heard [in pronunciation], because in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), a second mention of *hal* was made specifically to exclude *ṇal*. Otherwise, since *ṇal* would lack the status of being an *apṛkta* (uncombined) suffix, that rule would not apply to it anyway. Nor should it be argued that the second mention of *hal* is intended to prevent the substitution of *ḍā* in forms such as *bhavitā*.

Because the elision (*lopa*) of the case-endings beginning with *su* is prescribed after a base ending in a consonant (*halanta*) by way of implication from the rules for the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si*, and because a base ending in *t* or *s* lacks the status of being a base (*prakṛti*) in relation to the substitute *ḍā*; [one might argue that] this would not result in the elision of *su* in forms such as *yā sā*. Nor should it be said that, by the maxim of "modification of one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), there is indeed the status of being after a base ending in a consonant, since the modified portion is included as part of the preceding whole; for this would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *yaḥ saḥ*.

At the time of the application of elision (*lopapravṛttikāla*), there is an absence of the status of being *halanta* (ending in a consonant) in both cases; furthermore, since the elision depends on what follows an *ā*-stem, it is difficult to justify [the application of the rule] because the prohibition of the *antādivadbhāva* (treating the end as the beginning) applies when there is a dependence on both sides. Nor should it be argued that this prohibition is non-eternal (*anitya*) based on the indicative mark (*nirdeśa*) in the rule "tadasyāṃ praharaṇam," for even that cannot establish the force of that [prohibition] at a time when the meaning of the term *hal* has not yet been understood. And if it is argued that the rule "liti" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), that is not so, because it finds its scope of application in forms such as those ending in *lyuṭ*.

True. Even so, by that much, the knowledge of the *itsaṃjñā* (the designation "it") has already arisen, being common to the *ṇvul* suffix and others. And because that [knowledge] is subsequently ascertained to be consistent with the cognition produced by the rule "halantyam," it possesses validity; such is the intention of the Bhāṣya. It might be argued: "How can there be elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) prior to the designation of 'consonants' (*hal-saṃjñā*), since the designation of a 'consonant cluster' (*saṃyoga-saṃjñā*) contains the designation of 'consonants' within it? Or how can there be the compound *ha-l* [in the rule *halantyam*], since the designation of a nominal stem (*sup-saṃjñā*) has not yet been established?
By this, the [possibility of] a *dvandva*, a locative *tatpuruṣa*, and a *bahuvrīhi* are likewise explained. If this is said:

True. Even the understanding of the meaning of a grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), which is useful for the cognition of correctness (*sādhutva*), is not useful for the words denoted by that treatise to convey their own meanings; otherwise, the comprehension of meaning would be impossible anywhere. However, in the present case, even the knowledge of the referent of the word *hal* is a constituent of the causal complex for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning of "the last [letter] among the *hal*s" (*halantyam*). Therefore, there is a difference [between the two cases], as in this context there is a requirement for the knowledge of technical names (*saṃjñā*) for the sake of comprehending the meaning of the sentence "the first [letter] with the last [letter] as its indicator" (*ādirantyena sahetā*).

It might be argued as follows: even if *la* were designated by the technical term *it*, the comprehension of the meaning of this sentence would still not be possible. This is because the knowledge of the meaning of the exception (*apavāda*)—namely, "but [the designation *it* does not apply] to *su* and *am* in a case-ending"—is required beforehand. This is in accordance with the maxim: "For exceptions take effect first, and general rules (*utsarga*) afterwards."

And because there is a requirement for knowledge of the meaning of case-endings (*vibhakti*) therein, and knowledge of the meaning of *sup* and *tiṅ* endings therein, and knowledge of the meaning of the rule "the first [is designated by] the last" (*ādirantyena*) therein, and because knowledge of technical designations (*saṃjñā*) therein is dependent upon knowledge of the meaning of the sentence "the final consonant [is an *it*]" (*halantyam*), and because even the knowledge of the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is dependent upon knowledge of the meaning of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra*, and that [knowledge of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra*] depends on the portion beginning with "udīcām" (*udītyaṃśe*).

If it is argued that this is because [the application of] the technical name *it* depends upon knowledge, and because in the rule "an *anunāsika* is called *it*," the knowledge of the meaning of the word *uc* depends upon [prior] knowledge, such that there is an equivalence of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) according to the sequence stated; ... [the response follows: ...[this is not so], because the knowledge of the meaning of the word *uc* is established by the very fact that the *anunāsika* vowel following it is designated as *it*. Furthermore, since the designation of the *anunāsika* as *it* is based on the presence of the *it*-designation for the preceding *a*, there is no circularity. Moreover, the technical name *it* is applied to the *anunāsika* by virtue of its being taught in proximity to the *a* which has already been designated as *it*; thus, the process is sequential rather than simultaneous, and the objection of mutual dependence does not apply.

Not so. For it is not the case that the general rule (*utsarga-vākya*) fails to produce cognition prior to the operation of an exception (*apavāda*); for a prohibition cannot arise in the absence of a possibility of application (*prasakti*). Thus, once the cognition of the *it*-designation is established by taking "being a consonant" (*hal-tva*) as the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatā-avacchedaka*), there is no obstacle to the cognition of the meaning of words such as *sup* (case-endings) and *tiṅ* (verbal endings). Consequently, the sentence-meaning "not before a case-ending" (*na vibhaktau*) is understood; from this, the *it*-designation applies to what is delimited by "consonant-ness. Therefore, one must postulate the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of the initial cognition regarding the portions consisting of the *tavarga*, *s*, and *m* sounds situated within the case-endings. From that...

The delimiting condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) for the designation [of *it*] is established through the syntactic unity of both [rules] as being of the nature of a consonant (*hal*), provided it is distinct from the letters *t*, *th*, *s*, and *m*. Since this condition exists even in the case of *p* and other such sounds, the validity of the cognition of *sup* and other suffixes that arose previously remains uncontradicted.

As for the fact that the cognition of the designation *it* has arisen even for the letter *t* situated in a suffix, that is entirely irrelevant because it is rooted in a misconception regarding its scope; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Regarding the statement in the sūtra *na saṃprasāraṇe*: there is no prohibition of that which has already been produced (*niṣpanna*). Having raised the doubt as to how that which is not yet produced (*aniṣpanna*) can function as a cause (*nimitta*), it is argued that this prohibition applies specifically to the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* caused by *saṃprasāraṇa*. Alternatively, the two views—that the prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the preceding element occurs only when a *yaṇ* follows—have both been stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya; however, these are merely supplementary arguments.

In reality, since the inclusion of the term *samānāṅga* (belonging to the same base) is necessary there, we shall explain that the second view alone is correct, based on the fact that the word *saṃprasāraṇa* must be understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to its substitute.

Others, however, say that the rule *halantyam* itself must be repeated, meaning that in the rule *hal*, the final [letter] shall be an *it*. Then, once the designation *hal* is established, the designation *it* is applied to the letter *ca* and others by the rule *halantyam*, whereby the designations *ac* and so forth are established.

Others, however, hold that by the rule *hal* itself, the designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed with reference to the entire collection ending in *śaṣasaḥ*. Since the letter *l* is included therein, the designation *it* is applied by the rule *halantyam*, and thus the formation of the pratyāhāra *valādi* is established. It should not be argued that the designation *it* cannot apply because the collection ending in *r* lacks the nature of an *upadeśa* (instruction), defined as making known what was previously unknown. For, by the force of the composition of multiple rules, both forms [of instruction] are achieved through repetition (*āvṛtti*) and so forth; otherwise, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

This is established by the very force of the rule prescribing the designation "hal" (consonant), as it is only thus that [the application of the term] is possible; furthermore, because there is an actual instruction regarding the specific aspect of the sequence (*ānupūrvī*), whereas regarding the aspect of the phonetic form (*svarūpa*), it would be difficult for you even to state how it could be understood. Nor is there a lack of proximity (*āsatti*) due to the designator (*saṃjñā*) and the designated (*saṃjñin*) not being presented in a single sentence, since a single sentential unity (*ekavākyatā*) can be assumed through the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Moreover, because the meaning of the rule *halantyam* cannot otherwise be understood, that [single sentential unity] must be accepted as the apprehender (*grāhaka*) therein; otherwise, even the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the rule would be untenable.

For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the rule *tasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.9) is that the mention of *tasya* ("of that") is for the purpose of effecting the elision of all [elements]. Nor should it be argued that there is no justification for the non-continuation (*ananuvṛtti*) of rules such as *aiuṇ* while allowing the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of *haL* even when separated by others; for the non-continuation of those ending in *c* is established through a careful consideration of rules such as *nājjhalau*. Furthermore, if they were continued, it would result in the technical designation *al* having a scope neither less nor greater than its intended range, which would render those two technical designations (*saṃjñā*) redundant.

For, in the case of the repetition of the *hal-antyam* sūtra, there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *hal* within the sūtra that is non-different from that very word; even though it is obtained through the mere citation of that word, there is no cognition of it as being a sūtra non-different from that [original] word. Nor can it be argued that this [first occurrence] alone is to be grasped because it is the first to present itself, for at the time of the presentation of the sūtra "hal-antyam," there is no rule determining that this [first one] must be presented first.

This is because the term *hal* occurs even in these [rules]: *halo'nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ*, *nājjhalau*, and *ralo vyupadhāddhalādeḥ saṃśca*. If it is argued that the term *hal* refers to the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its occurrence in such sūtras, then the aforementioned visarga and others would necessarily receive that designation. If it is further argued that "primacy" (*prāthamya*) must be intended as starting precisely from the sūtra *aiuṇ*, even so, since the postulation of a cognition regarding that [starting point] is necessary anyway, there is no additional complexity in postulating the entire aggregate ending with *śaṣasar* as the subject (*uddeśya*).

Likewise, regarding the rule *hal*, if it is explained as "that which is final while being included within the rule *hal*," then it would be difficult to exclude the two occurrences of the letter *ha* that exist elsewhere [in the rule]. Therefore, "finality" must be intended to apply to that very rule. This results in the cognitive burden of taking the delimiting condition of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) to be "the state of being the object of an utterance immediately following the utterance of *ha*, while being included within the rule *hal*," as well as the necessity of postulating a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) based on the locative case. Furthermore, this [split] is not already established elsewhere, because the need to postulate such an intention (*tātparya*) for this specific context remains unavoidable.

By this, they say that even the rule *sup-supā* is explained. As for what they say— that if one intends to apply [the term] to a single part [of a word], the rule should have been formulated simply as *harantyam*, because the meaning you have stated would be obtained by that much alone, since the proximity (*samīpatva*) of the preceding element is not lost, and because the word *hari* could be used in place of the word *hal* everywhere— this is not correct.

Because there is no parsimony [in this case], the objection (*āpatti*) is not established; for if one intended to repeat the entire sūtra [to include *hal* as well], it would be impossible to avoid stating simply "beginning with a consonant" (*hal-ādi*), since the pratyāhāra *har* would be established by that alone.

Nor should one suspect that such an approach involves the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) due to postulating a separate sūtra like "the final [element] of a consonant-group is [itself an *it*]" (*hal-antyam*) for the sake of designations such as *aj-ādi*.

By carrying over the word *na* from the subsequent sūtra, the meaning—that a consonant (*hal*) distinct from the initial [of a root] shall receive the designation *it*—is established. Nor does this entail the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*), because there is actually economy (*lāghava*) due to the abandonment of the term *ādi* in the sūtra "The initial [consonants] ñ, ṭ, ṭh, and p [are *it*]" (*ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ*). Furthermore, the non-carrying over of the negative particle (*nañ*) in that context is agreed upon by both parties. Nor does it follow that the intermediate consonants would also incur the designation *it*.

For, when one perceives "firstness" (āditva) with respect to that which is final relative to a particular delimited entity (upādhi), there is no absence of the difference whose counter-positive (pratiyogin) is delimited by that same entity even in the middle [element]; thus, the attainment of a *dvandva* compound from that [middle element] would be untenable. Furthermore, due to the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "ḍhralope" following the elision by "rori," the form "hārantyam" would result, leading to an unwarranted complexity (gaurava). Nor can this be resolved by the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), because the rule "rori" is stronger and its application would be unavoidable.

Nor should it be said that "there is no conflict [of rules] regarding what is not established in the preceding [section]," because even so, the rule *rori* is stronger due to its being *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned).

Likewise, the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is difficult to obtain even by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) *rātsasya*. As for the view that the application of restrictive rules (*niyamasūtra*) occurs in the form of a prohibition—the meaning of which sentence is that there would be no elision of a final conjunct consonant other than *s* following *r*—in that case, since the letter *r* is heard as the cause (*nimitta*), a sound other than *s* must be understood as something distinct from *r*, according to the maxim of Māṭhara and others.

That is not so; for that position is unworthy of acceptance because it is burdened by unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because forms such as *ajarghāḥ* would remain unestablished. Furthermore, even in the view that does not accept the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-dīrgha*) in the root *kurd*, Mādhava has stated that when there is *yaṅ*-luk and the *laṅ* suffix with *sip*, the form is *acokūḥ*. [In this case,] *ru*-hood (*rutva*) applies by the rule "daśca. According to your own method, however, only the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would apply, and since the elision by the rule "rori" would not take effect, there would be a contradiction.
Some, however, say that in the rule "halantyam," the letter *l* should be understood as being joined immediately after the letter *m*.

Others, however, argue: "In the *Upadeśa*, [the rule] should be formulated as 'an *it* is that which is final, a vowel (*ac*), and exclusively nasal (*anunāsika*)'. The third sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): if something is a vowel and becomes an *it*, then it must be exclusively nasal; therefore, there is no over-extension (*āpatti*) to forms such as *bhū*. Nor can it be argued that this leads to an unintended restriction (*viparītaniyama*). This is because there is evidence (*liṅga*) in rules such as 'midaco'ntyāt' [P. 1.1.47]. Furthermore, one should not say that since the restriction has its purpose fulfilled by excluding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) obtained from the immediately preceding sūtra, the *it*-designation would be unavoidable in cases like *bhū*."

Others maintain that this [interpretation] is not tenable because it involves a heavy burden of cognition (*pratipatti-gaurava*), requiring the postulation of three distinct sentence-meanings, the postulation of a prohibitive nature within the restrictive injunction (*niyama-vākya*), and the further postulation of additional indicators (*jñāpaka*) to exclude the possibility of a contrary restriction and so forth.

They say that by the force of the *yogavibhāga* (division of rules), the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) obtained from the two preceding sūtras are excluded; for even if the designation *it* were prescribed for a non-final nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) in a single compound rule such as *ajanunāsikaḥ*, the resulting meaning would be the same—that the designation applies to the nasal vowel even if it is final—since it is difficult to maintain the inconsistency of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the final portion and a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) regarding the non-final portion. Even if one were to tolerate such a discrepancy out of necessity in some cases, it is improper to assume a formal presentation (*nyāsa*) tainted by that defect; for if one tolerates it, there is no harm in assuming two separate rules (*yogadvaya*) according to the method already stated.

Others, however, say that only the word "antyaṃ" (the final) should be repeated; then, once the designation *it* has been established by the rule "halantyam," there arises an understanding of the meaning of that sentence. They argue that the rule "halantyam" serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "If a *hal* consonant is to be an *it*, then it must be the final one. Thus, they claim there is no fault in the case of roots such as *bhū*.

In reality, the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra—who maintains that the letter *ḷ* is included—is as follows: having divided the rule *ac* into two separate rules (*a* and *ac*), one should carry forward the term *vādayaḥ* from the rule *bhūvādayaḥ*. By forming an *avyayībhāva* compound with the prefix *ā* in the sense of limit-inclusive (*abhividhi*) and the vowel *au*, and then applying the shortening of the neuter gender, the form *u* is obtained. Those whose beginning is the vowel *a* are called *ādayaḥ*; thus, through a *karmadhāraya* compound, we have "those beginning with *a* which are non-different from *u*" (*ukārābhinnā ādayaḥ*). The substitution of *yaṇ* then takes place. The meaning of the sentence is: those vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *au* bear the technical designation *ac*.

Therefore, according to the method previously stated, once the meaning of the term *hal* has been established, the rule *halantyam* (P. 1.3.3) applies; subsequently, the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *aṇ* and others are established. Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

By this, the view of certain scholars—which will be mentioned in the third [chapter]—is also refuted, namely that for the sake of brevity the sūtra *bhūvādayaśca* should be formulated after *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*.
This is because, in the present context, the recitation [of the list of roots] serves the purpose of reiterating what has already been stated.
By this very reasoning, the formulation of the rule "upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ" after the application of "halantyam" is also refuted; for the designation *ac* is established by the method already stated.

Alternatively, since the designation *hal* itself is established even without the operation of the rule "the first [element] with the last," a further effort must be made. One should divide the term as *hal* and then carry forward (*anuvarttanīyam*) the word *anu*. When the vowel *a* forms an *avyayībhāva* compound with the prefix *ā*, the form is *a*; however, for the diphthong *au*, the form is *u* according to the method already stated. Then, there is a *dvandva* compound of these two: *aṃ ca u ca*. When the *guṇa* substitution is applied and the neuter shortening occurs, the resulting form is simply *u*. Finally, through a negative (*nañ*) compound, the form *anu* is established.

The meaning is that "syllable-composite" (*samāhāra*) refers to a syllable distinct from those beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *au*. By the maxim of the particle *nañ* (negation) and the word *iva* (as if), there is obtained the status of being the locus of difference (*bhedānuyogitva*) for a syllable that possesses the property of being a syllable (*akṣaratva*), which resides in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that difference and whose nature as a counter-correlate is not delimited by the difference itself.

Alternatively, the designation *ac* may be established according to the method previously stated. As for the rule *nājjhalau*, since it has been rejected by the Bhāṣyakāra on the grounds of a difference in effort (*prayatna*), it should be explained as being intended for the prescription of the designation *hal*. This is because such a method is well-known in the works of Kaiyaṭa, the Kaustubha, and others regarding the rule *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ*. In the *saṃhitā* reading of the rule *nājjhalāv īdūded dvivacanam pragṛhyam*, the division is *nājjhalāp*.

A vowel (*ac*) does not acquire the designation *hal* when it is non-different from [the preceding]; that is to say, it does not possess the designation *hal* by virtue of being followed by a *hal*. In the view that accepts the literal reading [of the rule], there is no suspicion of redundancy because the purpose has already been fulfilled; for compared to the alternative of employing a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa-nirdeśa*), there is no burden of comprehension.

Alternatively, there is the *saṃhitā* reading: *nājjhalau*, *īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*. [The term] *hal* would be with the word *hal*. And "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) consists of the relationship of being denoted. It is precisely from the words of the commentators, which are rooted in an uninterrupted traditional lineage (*sampradāya*), that students gain knowledge of the referents of terms such as *hal*. Its authority, however, is established by the aforementioned method as being based solely on the Śāstra; this is the essential point. [Pāṇini 1.3.4: *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*.

The groups of consonants (*varga*), *s*, and *m* occurring in a case-ending (*vibhakti*) are not [included] here [in the definition of *it*]. Examples: *rāmān*, *paceyuḥ*; *brāhmaṇāḥ*, *pacataḥ*; *rāmam*, *adrākṣam*. Why specify "in a case-ending"? [Consider: *aco yat* (P. 3.1.97); *ūrṇāyā yus* (P. 5.2.123). Nor does this lead to an undesired prohibition in cases such as *na ca kimo't* (P. 5.4.11), because this rule does not apply when the term "case-ending" is used as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (P. 1.1.28). And the proof for this is the addition of the vowel *u* in *idamasthamuḥ* (P. 5.3.24), which serves to protect the *m* from being designated as an *it*.

And there is no possibility of the *mit* designation applying to the suffix *dānīm* in the word *tadānīm*, because that [suffix] ends in a *ya*-class letter (*yānta*). Since the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the technical designation *it*, it lacks the status of ending in a *m*.

Alternatively, it may be understood that this merely indicates the non-constancy of the prohibition [of *mit*]. Furthermore, in rules such as *aut* and *iṭo't*, the vowel *au* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the accentuation of a *tit* suffix. Moreover, in examples such as *urau vā yo* and *bhakṣīya tava rādhasaḥ*, we observe final acute accent (*antodāttatā*) due to the accent of the suffix. This is also confirmed by the fact that the *Bhāṣya* itself states that *laviṣīya* has a final acute accent. [The rule] *ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ* [is next].

These [roots] should be [considered] as having [the indicatory letter *ñ*] at the beginning in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). The word “beginning” (*ādi*) is a singular form used in the sūtra. From the root *indhī* (with *ñ*), we have *iddhaḥ*; since the rule “after a root ending in *ñ*” (*ñitaḥ*) is in force, the suffix *kta* is applied. From *vepṛ* (with *ṭu*), we have *vepathuḥ*; [this is formed by] the rule “*athuc* after a root ending in *ṭu*. From *ḍuvap*, we have *uptrimam*; [this is formed by] the suffix *ktri* according to the rule “after a root ending in *ḍu*. Why say “in the original instruction”? [Consider: *ñikārīyati*. From *ṅuṅ* (meaning ‘sound’), we have *ṅavaṃ*; [this is formed by] the rule “*ap* after roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*. [Then,] from the desiderative of the causative of that [root], one forms *ñiṅavayiṣati* (desiring to cause the sound to be made). One should also cite as a counter-example the case where the suffix *san* follows a causative (*ṇic*) of the form “he performs that” (*tatkaroti*). Why say “beginning”? [Consider: *paṭūyati*.

Because the word *paṭu* is taught among [the words] beginning with *pṛthu*, here—in this context of technical designation (*itsaṃjñā*)—the indicative mark (*liṅga*), which has not yet fulfilled its purpose regarding the individual member (*avayava*), serves as a qualifier for the whole (*samudāya*). Thus, the suffix *-athuc* would apply. **Sūtra 6:** *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* (The *ṣ* of an affix). The initial *ṣ* of an affix is designated by the technical term *it*. Example: *nartakī* (female dancer). [The suffix] *ṣvun* is used in the sense of a craftsman (*śilpin*). Because of the presence of *ṣit*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. [Question: Why "of an affix"? [Answer: [Consider] *ṣoḍaśa* (sixteen). Here, the word *ṣaṣ* is the original form (*upadeśa*) in the rule *ṣaṣa utvam* (the substitution of *u* for *ṣaṣ*). [Question: Why "initial" (*ādi*)? [Answer: [Consider] *aviṣaḥ* (goat-poison) and *mahiṣaḥ* (buffalo). [These are formed] by adding *ṭiṣac* after the roots *avi* and *mavi*.

[Objection: But surely, because there is no purpose [for it], the designation *it* does not apply here; for the desired result is already established simply by the fact that the suffix *ī* is marked with *ṭ*. Nor should it be argued that the *ṣ* in *ṣit* is intended for the sake of *ṅīṣ*—since if *ṅīp* were used, the suffix would be *anudātta*, whereas if *ṅīṣ* were used, it would be *udātta*, and thus the *ṣ* would ensure the latter case—because even the *ṅīp* following a *cit* suffix becomes *udātta* by the rule of the "accent of the cessation of the acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). [Reply: This is not so. Since there is no determining factor (*vinigamikābhāva*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of hearing the letter *ṭ* as well in some instances. [This is addressed by the rule: *cuṭū* (Pāṇini 1.3.7).

The letters *cu* and *ṭu* are designated as *it*. It will be stated that for the second and fourth letters of each varga—namely *cha*, *jha*, *ṭha*, and *ḍha*—the substitutes *īya*, *anta*, *ika*, and *eya* are applied respectively. [The suffix] *cphañ* is added after [words beginning with] *kuñja* etc. when forming a *gotra* (patronymic). *Kauñjāyanyaḥ*. [In the nominative plural: *jas*: *brāhmaṇāḥ*. The suffix *añya* is added after [words beginning with] *śaṇḍika* etc. [Example: His ancestral origin (*abhijana*) is *śaṇḍika*; thus, *śāṇḍikyaḥ*. The suffix *ṭa* is added after [the root] *car*. *Kurucarī*. The suffix *ḍa* is added after the root *jan*. *Upasarajaḥ*. The suffix *ṇa* is added after [words beginning with] *prajña* etc. *Prājñaḥ*.

And this [suffix] is *anitya* (non-obligatory), because of the force of the separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) which states that the suffix *cuṭuṣ* should be applied [only] after a *pratyaya*. Consequently, in forms such as *keśacuñcu*, the letter *c* does not receive the designation *it*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the word being oxytone (*antodātta*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the marker *p* would then serve only for the sake of providing an alternative form (*paryāyārtha*). In the case of *avaṭīṭaḥ*, the suffix is *ṭīṭac* according to the rule *nate nāsikāyāḥ*. Alternatively, the Bhāṣya states that in these instances, the letter *y* has been elided and indicated [by its absence] according to the rule *lopo vyoḥ*. Due to the authority of the Bhāṣyakāra’s statement, or because the group beginning with *rājadanta-* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the member representing the prior time is placed last. *L-ś-k-taddhite* (Pāṇini 1.3.8).

In an affix other than a *taddhita*, the letters beginning with *a*, *ś*, *k*, and *v* shall be designated as *it*. Examples: *bhavanam*, *bhavati*, *bhūtaḥ*, *priyaṃvadaḥ*, *jiṣṇuḥ*, *bhaṅguraḥ*, *haraye*. The designation *it* applies respectively to the letters *l* and others belonging to the affixes *lyuṭ*, *śap*, *kta*, *khaś*, *gsnu*, *ghurac*, and *ṅe*. Why "other than a *taddhita*"? Consider *caṇḍālaḥ* (where the suffix *lac* is applied by the rule "prāṇisthādātaḥ"). Consider *lomaśaḥ* (where the suffix *śa* is applied by the rule "lomādi-"). Consider *karṇikā* (where the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule "karṇalalāṭād").
In this case, there would otherwise be *vṛddhi* [of the vowel] by the rule "kitica".

[The Vārttika] states: "There must be an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *ir*. In the rule *irito vā*, the term *ir* is an imitation of the whole [compound] *ir-ita*. This rule is formulated because [the condition] would otherwise not apply, as it consists of a combination of vowels and consonants (*aj-jhal-samudāya*). When the whole is designated by a technical name (*saṃjñā*), its parts receive the designation *it* due to their dependence on the whole. This is because the explanation is that the designation *it* applies specifically to the two parts [of the compound] in the sense of "that which has *ir* and *it* as its components. [Objection: But in this case, there would be the undesirable application of the augment *num*. [Response: One should not say that *num* applies only to that where the mere vowel *i* (in *ir*) is designated as *it*, according to the maxim of the "pot and grain" (*kumbhīdhānya-nyāya*). For if that were so, there would be under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *nandati*.

[Objection: Since the *ṭu* (the letter *ṛ*) is also designated as an *it* (indicatory marker) in that context, [your argument] is not correct. [Response: This is not so, because those [roots] are based on having *ṛ* as their final element. Once the substitution of *it* (*i*) for the root-final *ṛ* has been applied by the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100), and the subsequent substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* has been made, there are the grammatical usages such as *bhidir*. Even though *anaṅ* is not a part of the root, it receives the designation *it* by way of a specific technical prescription (*nipātana*). In the case of *bhid ṛ*, first the *ṛ* is designated as *it*, and then the substitutions of *it* and *ra* for *ṛ* take place. Similarly, in the rule "irito vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.57), this [root] is called *irit* because its *ṛ* is designated as *it* through a technical prescription, following the substitutions of *it* and *ra* for *ṛ*.

Alternatively, the reading of the letter *n* in roots such as *skandi* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule that the augment *num* occurs only after those roots ending in an *it*. Nor is the teaching of the letter *n* intended to prevent the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), because such elision would not apply here simply due to the presence of the *it* marker.

Or else, the prohibition of the *k* suffix in the rule "not after the root *dṛś*" (*na dṛśaḥ*) is the indicator; for if *num* were present, the *k* suffix would not occur anyway, since the condition of having a penultimate *ik* vowel (*igupadha*) would be absent.

Alternatively, by carrying forward the mention of "at the end" (*anta*) from the sūtra "of *go* at the end of a line" (*goḥ pādānte*), one should explain that *num* occurs only after those roots ending in an *it*; thus, there is no *num* for the root *cakṣiṅ*.

9. *Tasya lopaḥ*: There shall be elision (*lopa*) of that [which has been designated by the term *it*]. The mention of *tasya* (of that) is for the purpose of ensuring the elision of the whole [term]. Otherwise, since elision—which is of the nature of non-existence—requires a positive correlate, it would follow from the context that only that which possesses the designation *it* would be understood [as the object of elision]. Consequently, there is no elision of the final letter of the affixes *ñi*, *ṭu*, and *ḍu*. Nor is this established by the rule *nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ* (P. 1.1.53), because that [rule] was rejected in the commentary on *alontyāt pūrvaḥ* (P. 1.1.64). 10. *Yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*: A subsequent enumeration of equal number [of elements] corresponds to the preceding ones respectively.

The correlation of equal numbers [of items] occurs according to their respective order (*yathākramam*). This applies to both the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), as in: "From *nandi*, *grahi*, *paci*, and so forth, [the suffixes] *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* [are added]" (*Pāṇini 3.1.134*), resulting in *nandanaḥ*, *grāhī*, and *pacaḥ*. An example where it applies only to the subjects is: "In the case of *samūla*, *akṛta*, and *jīva*, [the roots] *han*, *kṛñ*, and *grah* [take the suffix *ṇamul*]" (*Pāṇini 3.4.36*). Here, although the predicate (*vidheya*), namely the suffix *ṇamul*, is singular, the correspondence by number applies only to the two subjects—the verbal root and the prefix (*upapada*).

In rules such as *parasmaipadānāṃ ṇalatu-*, the determination [of the application] is not according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), because all [the parasmaipada suffixes] are simultaneously proximate (*pratyāsatti*) to the term *parasmaipada*. In common usage, when there is a compound designation such as *ajāvidhanau devadattayajñadattau* (Devadatta and Yajñadatta, the goat-shearer and the sheep-shearer), there is no restriction of order. This is because in a *dvandva* compound, a single word expresses a collective whole (*samudāya*) consisting of multiple members; thus, the present rule is commenced. [Objection: But would there not be an application according to numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) in cases such as *vidibhidicchideḥ kurac*, where three meanings—such as "one who habitually performs that"—are associated with the three roots? Similarly, would this not also apply in cases such as *khyatyāt ṅasiṅasoḥ*? [Response: [This is not so. In the case of *vidibhidicchideḥ kurac*, since the suffix *kurac* is introduced after each of the three roots, the number of items to be connected is equal on both sides, and thus there is no room for an objection regarding numerical correspondence. However, in the case of *khyatyāt ṅasiṅasoḥ*, the term *khyatyāt* is a single item, whereas *ṅasiṅasoḥ* consists of two items. Since the numbers are unequal, the objection regarding numerical correspondence does not arise. Furthermore, in the case of *parasmaipadānāṃ ṇalatu-*, although the term *parasmaipada* is a single item, it denotes many [suffixes] through its inherent capacity (*śakti*). Therefore, because the number of items to be connected is equal, the objection regarding numerical correspondence is not applicable here either. Thus, the commencement of the rule is justified.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: the term *svaritena* (by means of the circumflex accent) is drawn back [from the previous rule]; therefore, because of the absence of the circumflex accent, there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṅkhya*). For the followers of Pāṇini, the circumflex accent is merely conventional (*pratijñāsvarita*). For this very reason, in the rule *kartṛkarmaṇośca bhūkṛñoḥ*, there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration. Consequently, since the root *bhū* is intransitive, the suffix *khal* occurs only when a word denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) is the attendant noun (*upapada*); however, for the root *kṛ*, it occurs even when a word denoting the object (*karman*) is the attendant noun. Some, however, say that in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*), the suffix *khal* occurs after both roots even when either of the two types of attendant nouns is present. But in the case of the rule *nāḍīmuṣṭyośca*, it certainly does occur.

It might be argued as follows: In the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, there would be no correspondence according to numerical order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). This is because the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* each have eighteen varieties, while *lṛ* has twelve; thus, the *ik* vowels total sixty-six. Furthermore, there are only seven *yaṇ* consonants. Moreover, even though they are being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), the grammatical qualities (*guṇa*) do not serve to differentiate, and therefore the nasalized *y*, *v*, and *l* are also included. Nor can this be resolved by the maxim of the closest correspondence (*antaratama-paribhāṣā*) alone. Regarding the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*, [the question is asked: "What is the example?"

This is because it contradicts the Bhāṣya, which states: "The substitution of *yaṇ* for *iK* before a vowel (*aci*)—as in *dadhy atra*—is established even by the principle of corresponding enumeration (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*)."

On this point, they say: the meaning of the Sūtra is that those [sounds] delimited by the universals (jāti) such as *it*—which are understood by the word *ik*—become those delimited by the four universals such as *yat*, which are understood by the word *yaṇ*. Thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*), as even conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) need not be admitted. Nor should it be argued that since the adoption of the Paribhāṣā on "the most similar" (*antaratama*) is necessary to prevent the occurrence of nasalized *y*-sounds and so forth for non-nasalized [substitutes], this [Sūtra] has already been applied; for regarding that portion, the Paribhāṣā on "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṅkhya*) lacks any obstruction.

Even when the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the most similar substitute) is applicable, it operates according to the principle of "correspondence" (*yathāsaṅkhya*) alone with respect to the substituend (*sthānin*), because of its superior status [in the order of rules]. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa states that there is a formal correspondence (*sāmya*) in the recitation of the *pratyāhāra* [table].

By this, the view that—when each of the thirty vowels is presented individually by means of both *ṛ* and *lṛ*—the substitute for *ṛ* would be *lṛ* and the substitute for *lṛ* would be *r*, is also refuted.

For this same reason, it is stated in the *Śabdakaustubha* that if one were to propose the formulation *harayavaḍi* in place of *iyavaraṭ*, correspondence alone would prevail due to the superior status [of the rule of correspondence].

11. *Svaritenādhikāraḥ* (The governing authority is indicated by the circumflex accent). The instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*). "Authority" (*adhikāra*) means application (*viniyoga*). The state of being circumflex (*svaritatva*) is for the purpose of indicating the governing authority, and is not inherent in the actual usage. A word-form endowed with the circumflex accent should be understood as being under the governing authority. For example, [the term] "affix" (*pratyaya*) and so forth recur in subsequent sections; sometimes they also recur in preceding sections. As it has been said: "The term *atiṅ* is a remainder for both. However, regarding the specific limits [of the governing authority], the commentary is the authority.

The governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the verbal roots (*dhātu*) extends up to the end of the third chapter, but not merely prior to the substitutes for *l*-affixes (*lādeśa*). This is because we observe that the governing authority of the stem (*aṅga*) continues until the conclusion of the seventh chapter, and not merely prior to the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), and so forth.

Alternatively, the meaning is that when a circumflex accent (*svarita*) occurs, there is no further governing authority; by this, the preceding governing authority is suspended. Accordingly, since the circumflex accent is observed in the rule "viṃśatikātkhaḥ," the suspension of the rule "dvitripūrvād" is inferred.

Nor can it be argued that there is no possibility of resolving the doubt—namely, that one *svarita* accent serves for the purpose of governing (*adhikāra*) while the other serves for the purpose of terminating that governance—because such a resolution is possible through interpretation (*vyākhyāna*).

Nor should it be said: "In that case, let interpretation alone be the regulator of whether a rule continues (*anuvṛtti*) or ceases (*ananuvṛtti*), so what is the use of this present sūtra? For [the sūtra] is intended to include other meanings as well.

For instance: the meaning consisting of a governing rule (*adhikāra*) is to be understood by means of the *svarita* accent. Therefore, because the word *strī* in the rule *go-striyoḥ* is declared to have the *svarita* accent, the suffix prescribed under the governing rule *striyām* is what is taken [as the referent]; thus, the Vārttika stating "the mention of *go* and *strī* is for the purpose of excluding *kṛt*-suffixes" becomes redundant.

Furthermore, there is the additional scope of *kāryakādhikāra* (the governing authority of the operation). The meaning is that even gravity (*gaurava*) is taken into account. Therefore, where the principle of primary and secondary application (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) is not desired, there the circumflex accent (*svarita*) should be recited, as in the case of the ablative (*apādāna*) and locative (*adhikaraṇa*) case endings. Consequently, the rejection [of the rule] based on a mentally constructed departure (*apāya*) in rules such as "bhītrārthānām" becomes consistent. Because the term "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) is an authoritative word, its application extends even to the Veda in the form of the *ārṣa* (sage-authored) texts, which are considered secondary.

For this very reason, its correctness (*sādhutva*) due to being Vedic (*ārṣatva*) has been proclaimed here and there. In expressions such as *gaṅgāyāṃ gāvaḥ* ("cows in the Ganges"), although the word *gaṅgā* refers to the river, the locative case is used because the status of a substratum (*ādhāratva*) is secondary (*gauṇa*) due to proximity. However, when the word *gaṅgā* intends the bank (*tīra*), then the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) resides in the base noun itself, while the case ending retains its primary meaning; this is the distinction.

Furthermore, this subsequent rule (*adhikaḥ kāraḥ*)—namely, the present *kṛti* [sūtra]—supersedes even the preceding one due to its connection with the *svarita* accent. Consequently, there is a compendium of all cases of "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Moreover, the purpose of those Vārttikas is for the sake of such discrimination: that a subsequent rule of the same class is superseded by a preceding one, but not one characterized by "perpetual" (*nitya*) status and so forth; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus ends the first Āhnika of the third Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*. [Now begins: *Anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* (1.3.12). The suffix *ātmanepada* occurs after a verbal root that has an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the indicatory letter *ṅ*. [Commentary: The term *anudātta* here refers to the indicatory vowel (*it*), not the actual pitch of the vowel itself. This is because the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (1.1.55) applies to the whole of the element marked by the *it*, and since the *it* is a single phoneme, it cannot be considered "multisyllabic" (*anekāl*). Furthermore, if the actual pitch were intended, it would lead to an undesirable result: in the case of roots like *tud* (which has an *anudātta* vowel), the *ātmanepada* would apply even when a prefix is present, whereas it should not. Therefore, the *anudātta* is understood as an *it*. As for the *ṅit*: the *ṅ* is an *it* used for the purpose of marking the beginning of the affix. Thus, the *ātmanepada* suffixes are those that have *ṅ* as their initial marker. For example, in *pacate*, the suffix *te* is *ṅit* because it is included among those whose initial marker is *ṅ*. Regarding the mention of both *anudātta* and *ṅit*: the former serves to exclude the *parasmaipada* suffixes, while the latter serves to exclude the *ubhayapada* suffixes. For instance, in the case of the root *div* (which is *anudātta*), the *ātmanepada* is applied to exclude the *parasmaipada*; however, since *div* is also listed among the *ubhayapada* roots, the mention of *ṅit* is necessary to exclude the *ubhayapada* application in favor of the *ātmanepada* alone. Thus, the *ātmanepada* is employed after roots marked by an *anudātta* vowel or an *it* letter *ṅ*. [End of First Āhnika] [Second Āhnika begins: *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* 12. The suffix *ātmanepada* occurs after a verbal root that has an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the indicatory letter *ṅ*. [Commentary: The term *anudātta* here refers to the indicatory vowel (*it*), not the actual pitch of the vowel itself. This is because the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (1.1.55) applies to the whole of the element marked by the *it*, and since the *it* is a single phoneme, it cannot be considered "multisyllabic" (*anekāl*). Furthermore, if the actual pitch were intended, it would lead to an undesirable result: in the case of roots like *tud* (which has an *anudātta* vowel), the *ātmanepada* would apply even when a prefix is present, whereas it should not. Therefore, the *anudātta* is understood as an *it*. As for the *ṅit*: the *ṅ* is an *it* used for the purpose of marking the beginning of the affix. Thus, the *ātmanepada* suffixes are those that have *ṅ* as their initial marker. For example, in *pacate*, the suffix *te* is *ṅit* because it is included among those whose initial marker is *ṅ*. Regarding the mention of both *anudātta* and *ṅit*: the former serves to exclude the *parasmaipada* suffixes, while the latter serves to exclude the *ubhayapada* suffixes. For instance, in the case of the root *div* (which is *anudātta*), the *ātmanepada* is applied to exclude the *parasmaipada*; however, since *div* is also listed among the *ubhayapada* roots, the mention of *ṅit* is necessary to exclude the *ubhayapada* application in favor of the *ātmanepada* alone. Thus, the *ātmanepada* is employed after roots marked by an *anudātta* vowel or an *it* letter *ṅ*. [End of First Āhnika] [Second Āhnika begins: *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* 12. The suffix *ātmanepada* occurs after a verbal root that has an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the indicatory letter *ṅ*. [Commentary: The term *anudātta* here refers to the indicatory vowel (*it*), not the actual pitch of the vowel itself. This is because the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (1.1.55) applies to the whole of the element marked by the *it*, and since the *it* is a single phoneme, it cannot be considered "multisyllabic" (*anekāl*). Furthermore, if the actual pitch were intended, it would lead to an undesirable result: in the case of roots like *tud* (which has an *anudātta* vowel), the *ātmanepada* would apply even when a prefix is present, whereas it should not. Therefore, the *anudātta* is understood as an *it*. As for the *ṅit*: the *ṅ* is an *it* used for the purpose of marking the beginning of the affix. Thus, the *ātmanepada* suffixes are those that have *ṅ* as their initial marker. For example, in *pacate*, the suffix *te* is *ṅit* because it is included among those whose initial marker is *ṅ*. Regarding the mention of both *anudātta* and *ṅit*: the former serves to exclude the *parasmaipada* suffixes, while the latter serves to exclude the *ubhayapada* suffixes. For instance, in the case of the root *div* (which is *anudātta*), the *ātmanepada* is applied to exclude the *parasmaipada*; however, since *div* is also listed among the *ubhayapada* roots, the mention of *ṅit* is necessary to exclude the *ubhayapada* application in favor of the *ātmanepada* alone. Thus, the *ātmanepada* is employed after roots marked by an *anudātta* vowel or an *it* letter *ṅ*. [End of First Āhnika] [Second Āhnika begins: *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* 12. The suffix *ātmanepada* occurs after a verbal root that has an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the indicatory letter *ṅ*. [Commentary: The term *anudātta* here refers to the indicatory vowel (*it*), not the actual pitch of the vowel itself. This is because the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (1.1.55) applies to the whole of the element marked by the *it*, and since the *it* is a single phoneme, it cannot be considered "multisyllabic" (*anekāl*). Furthermore, if the actual pitch were intended, it would lead to an undesirable result: in the case of roots like *tud* (which has an *anudātta* vowel), the *ātmanepada* would apply even when a prefix is present, whereas it should not. Therefore, the *anudātta* is understood as an *it*. As for the *ṅit*: the *ṅ* is an *it* used for the purpose of marking the beginning of the affix. Thus, the *ātmanepada* suffixes are those that have *ṅ* as their initial marker. For example, in *pacate*, the suffix *te* is *ṅit* because it is included among those whose initial marker is *

The term *dhātavaḥ* (verbal roots), which is carried over from the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*, is transformed into the ablative case (*dhātubhyaḥ*). Kaiyaṭa maintains that this usage of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is based merely on similarity, since in reality another suitable word is actually present. According to the Kaustubha, the verbal root and the *lakāra* (tense/mood marker) are both implied by the term *ātmanepada* itself, just as the verbal root is implied by the term *san* in the rule *iko jhal*. Because the suffix *ṅit* qualifies the verbal root, the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) applies to that which ends in such a suffix.

The word *it*, which is heard at the end of a *dvandva* compound, is connected with both members. This is because there is no purpose for applying the rule of "having that as its final element" (*tadantavidhi*) in the case of the term *anudātta*. The term *upadeśe* (in the original enunciation) is understood [from the previous sūtra]. Thus, the *ātmanepada* suffixes alone shall occur in place of *la* after a verbal root that is *ṅit*—meaning either one whose original enunciation (*upadeśa*) has an *anudātta* vowel, or one that ends in such a *ṅit*—as well as after a root ending in such a *ṅit*. Examples: *edhate*, *spardhate*, *bobhūyate*, *ṛtīyate*. As for the root *śīṅ*, however, it possesses the status of ending in a *ṅit* by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which is designated" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

In examples such as *vidhīyate*, the suffix *ṅ* (in *vidhi-ṅ*), which has no other function within its own constituent parts, renders the form ending in *kyaṅ* as *ṅit*; consequently, by the principle of "designation as possessing the property" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the entire form is considered to end in a *ṅit*. Why specify "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*)? Consider *cukuṭiṣati*: here, the *ṅittva* of the suffix *san* is due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "after *gāṅ* and the roots beginning with *kuṭ*" (*gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ*). Why specify "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*)? It is so that [the *ṅittva*] does not apply to the suffixes *caṅ* and *aṅ*. For example: *adudruvat* and *acyutat*.

By this, forms such as *cinutaḥ* and *sunutaḥ* are also explained, because the *ṅittva* in those cases is also merely an extended application according to the rule "all *sārvadhātuka* suffixes except *apit* are *ṅit*" (*sārvadhātukam apit*).

[Objection: But surely the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the words "upadeśa" and "dātuḥ" is useless, because the principle that "a restriction (*niyama*) is stronger than [the application of] *vikaraṇa*s" will be made known in the rule "vṛddhyaḥ syasanoḥ," since the restriction regarding the *ātmanepada* would apply from the very beginning.
[Response: To this they say:

Even by means of a *ṅit* suffix that is yet to arise (*upasañjaniṣyamāṇena*), there would be a sublation (*bādha*) of the *parasmaipada*, even though its cause has already arisen (*upasañjātanimittasya*). This is because it is possible to make known that the restriction applies even when there is an intervention by a *vikaraṇa*, and because the strength of the restriction is only optional (*pākṣikatvāt*).

Haradatta, however, explained [the rule] simply as "of that which has the marker ṅ" (*ṅitaḥ*), because there is no purpose for the continued application of the term "root" (*dhātu*). Furthermore, due to the superior force of the restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is no fault regarding forms such as *caṅ*.
Nor is there sublation by a future ṅ-marker, because the Parasmaipada suffixes take precedence.

For this very reason, the author of the *Prasāda* stated: "In the case of *caṅ* and *aṅ*, although they possess the ṅ-marker, the taṅ-suffixes do not apply, because they apply only after the Parasmaipada suffixes have already taken effect."

However, some, suspecting that the *ṅ* in *yaṅ* and *īyaṅ* has its purpose fulfilled by the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, propose the following: they join an unaccented (*anudātta*) *a* before *yaṅ*, and thus the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings follow simply because [the root] ends in an unaccented vowel. Nor does there arise the contingency of the suffix *yuc* after a *yaṅ*-stem according to the rule "anudāttetaśca halādeḥ," because its absence is indicated by the rule "jucaṃkramyadandramya.

They further imagine that one should join an unaccented *i* or *ī* before *īyaṅ*; in the first case, since it does not end in an unaccented vowel, there is no *num*; in the second case, because of the continued application of the rule "ekāc," the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "śvīdito niṣṭhāyām" applies. Thus they have reasoned.

But surely there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *yaṅ-luk* (the elision of *yaṅ*), because by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, the suffix would still be considered as ending in a *ṅit* letter.

On this point, the ancients say: the prescription of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *tij-* after its *yaṅ-luk* form—as seen in the example *bobhūtetikte*—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the middle voice does not apply to a *yaṅ-luk* form by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule. For this very reason, they state that the explanation of the phrase "and *carkarītam*" in the *adādi* class—whereby the addition of the letter *ca* indicates that it takes the parasmaipada—is intended to clarify the meaning established by that indicator.

Alternatively, since the property of being *ṅit* applies both to suffixes and non-suffixes alike, the *ātmanepada* ending does not occur here by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule. For this very reason, there is no absence of the application of *ātmanepada* caused by that [suffix]. For this same reason, [the rules for] *ava* and so on do not apply in cases such as *gohitam*. Furthermore, in the case of *sudṛṣat* (that which has beautiful stones), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that neither the accent prescribed by the rule "sormanasī" nor the lengthening prescribed by the rule "atvasantasya" occurs.

Now, in the case of *pāsparddhi*, the ātmanepada ending would occur because the root *spardh* is anudātta; for, according to the established doctrine that "doubling is the second mention [of the root]," there is no difference in the underlying base (*prakṛti*).

Not so; for there is a prohibition [against such an application] by the rule *stipā śapā’nubandhena*. Indeed, the mention of an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is twofold: specifically and generally. The first occurs in rules such as *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ*; the second occurs in rules such as *anudāttetaḥ*. In rules like *āṅoyamahanaḥ*, only the *anubandha* of the prefix (*upasarga*) is mentioned, not the *anubandha* of the verbal root (*prakṛti*); therefore, [the rule applies] even when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*). This is because the aforementioned prohibition serves as an exception to the principle that when a verbal root is mentioned, it includes its *yaṅluk* form.
For this very reason, in forms such as *cetitaḥ* and *marīmṛṣṭaḥ*, the prohibition [of guṇa] by the rule *kṅiti ca* takes effect.

The *ātmanepada* characterized by the *anudātta* accent is not mandatory, as evidenced by the addition of the *ṅit* marker to the root *cakṣiṅ*. This is because in forms such as *vicakṣaṇaḥ* and *prathayan*, the suffix *yuc* must be applied according to the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), which necessitates determining that the root is indeed *anudātta*. For this very reason, Murāri writes: *sphāyannirmokasaṃdhipracaladavigalatsaṃmadasvedapūraḥ*. However, in the phrase *sa evāyaṃ nāgaḥ sahate kalabhebhyaḥ paribhavam*, the form *sahate* is derived from the root *sah* with the optional causative suffix (*ṇic*) prescribed by the rule *ādhṛṣād vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.25).

And this section is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because [the suffixes] *tiP* and so forth have been prescribed for *la*, as well as *śatṛ* and *śānac* for *laṬ*, *kānac* optionally for *liṬ*, *Kvasu* and *Kasu* [for *liṬ*], and *sadvat* optionally for *lṛṬ*, thereby establishing the distinction between the Ātmanepada and Parasmaipada terminations.

This might be the case: there would be scope for the *vikaraṇas* (conjugational suffixes) in the case of *ānaś* and others that are distinct from the substitutes for *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*). As for the restriction [that they apply only to non-ārdhadhātuka suffixes], it applies to the *āśīr-liṅ* (precative) and the *liṭ* (perfect), because their substitutes are *ārdhadhātuka*; thus, the *vikaraṇas* have no scope there. Furthermore, this applies to *luk*, *ślu*, and *śnam*. In the first two cases (*luk* and *ślu*), the *vikaraṇas* are absent; and in the last case (*śnam*), there is no intervention because it falls between [the root and the suffix]. In examples such as *spardhate*, where both [the *vikaraṇa* and the restriction] would apply, the restriction would not operate because the *vikaraṇas* arise first—due to their being subsequent [in the order of rules] and being obligatory—and thus create an intervention.

Therefore, let it be that the injunction belongs to a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). For indeed, by means of the two indicative marks—the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* endings—this section applies to the rule for the substitution of *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*). In that case, since the suffixes are prescribed by the "Great Sentence" (*mahāvākya*), the *vikaraṇas* (conjugational markers) are applied subsequently by relying on the *sārvadhātuka* status; thus there is no fault. If it is argued: "Even so, because *sy-* and the other suffixes are prescribed while still in the state of *la*, the fault remains as before due to their intervention," [the response follows].

No; because the substitutes for *la* (lādeśas) depend only on the general category of *la*, they are internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas *syat* and the others depend on specific *lakāras* and are thus external (*bahiraṅga*). Therefore, the substitutes for *la* apply first. It is only after the substitutes for *la* have occurred that *syat* and the others apply; otherwise, the rule stating that the accent of the *vikaraṇa* does not sublate the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*—as seen in the injunction that the *sārvadhātuka* following *tās* is unaccented—would be impossible to justify as an explanatory indicator (*jñāpaka*), as will be explained in the third [chapter].

Furthermore, this is established either by the principle of "that which applies when another is already applicable" (*yenāprāpte nyāya*), whereby [the *lādeśas*] sublate *śap* and the rest, or because [the *lādeśas*] are continued in the rules prescribing *śap* and the others.

[Objection: But surely there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the designation (*saṃjñā*) is established by means of the rule of prescription, and the designation is for those [elements] already prescribed. If it is argued that under the view of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), since the rules for *l*-substitutes have not yet occurred previously, it is impossible to prescribe the designations *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* by way of restating what has been prescribed.

Not so; for by omitting the enumeration of the *parasmaipada* [voices], there is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) in that case. Nor does this lead to the undesired consequence [of *ātmanepada*] even for roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*, because their connection with the *ātmanepada* is understood, which subverts their connection with the *parasmaipada*. Furthermore, the enumeration of those [roots] is not strictly necessary for the purpose of prohibiting the *ātmanepada* in the rule "after *anu* and *parā*, [the root] *kṛ* [takes the *parasmaipada*]" (*anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ*). This is because the rule "after [a root] marked with a svarita or an indicatory *ṅ*, [the *ātmanepada* is used] when [the agent is] the subject" (*svaritañitaḥ*) should be followed immediately by the sūtra "after *anu* and *parā*, *kṛ* does not [take the *ātmanepada*]" (*kartary anuparābhyāṃ kṛño na*). Moreover, regarding the *ātmanepada* endings, the designation is understood as referring to the future state.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "The rule *'puṣādidyutādyḷditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu'* and *'ātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām'* etc., indicates that 'the restriction (*niyama*) is stronger than the suffixes (*vikaraṇa*),' because it is only those [roots] which remain established without confusion due to the application of the restriction that can properly serve as the cause [for the suffix]. Therefore, there is no fault.
If it is argued that even prior to the restriction, something may serve as a cause by mere possibility, then the rule *'anupasargādvibhāṣā'* serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).
But one might object: "This too could be for the sake of the *liṅ* and *liṅ* (optative) moods—as in *cakrame*, *cakrāma*, *kramyāt*, and *kraṃsīṣṭa*."

On this point, Kaiyaṭa and others state: "The rule *vṛddhyaḥ syasanoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.92), which prescribes an option for the suffix *sya*, is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Otherwise, if the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) were applied first, the restriction would not apply because [the root] would be separated by that [suffix], and thus both forms would be established even without the optional rule; so what purpose would the optional rule serve? Therefore, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) alone is appropriate. Furthermore, there is the disadvantage of complexity (*gaurava*) in assuming a designation for something yet to come (*bhāvisaṃjñā*)."

This might be the case: is this a restriction on the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*), such that the *ātmanepada* occurs only after a root marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*; or is it a restriction on the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthaniyama*), such that the *ātmanepada* occurs only for the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), and the *ātmanepada* alone occurs for these two? Nor should it be argued that, because of the preceding restriction, the rule "for the action and the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*) serves merely as an injunction (*vidhi*).
