For the intention is that the entire section on the *ātmanepada* constitutes a single syntactical unit (*vākya*); otherwise, the *parasmaipada* would undesirably follow even after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or *ṅ*.

Even if, by the stated restriction (*niyama*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is excluded from roots with anudātta indicatory letters (*anudāttaṅit*) and others, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) would still be unavoidable after such roots. To prevent this, one would have to initiate the restriction "from the rest [roots], when denoting the agent" (*śeṣātkartari*), which involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, if the active voice were optionally applied by the rule "optionally for *kyaṣ*," then since the middle voice is restricted to roots with anudātta indicatory letters in your view, only the *lakāra* suffixes would be heard, and not the personal endings. The second alternative is also untenable, because it would result in the non-occurrence of the *tṛc* and other affixes after roots with anudātta indicatory letters. The same applies even if the restriction is interpreted as meaning that the middle voice occurs only in the sense of the passive and impersonal (*bhāva-karman*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) here is as follows: because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "the *parasmaipada* [suffixes] occur only after the remaining [roots]," there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the first position. Nor is there any complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the formulation of that rule, for it is authoritative (*prāmāṇika*). Nor should it be argued: "Since it is stated 'in the sense of the agent' (*kartari*), let the *parasmaipada* occur only for the agent; however, in the case of the passive and middle voices (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), as in examples such as *jāgaryate* and *adyate*, the *parasmaipada* would [undesirably] occur. This is not to be said, because there is a restrictive rule that in those cases the *ātmanepada* occurs exclusively. Furthermore, the objection beginning with "moreover" (*kiñca*) and so forth is also invalid.

Once the substitutes [for *ti*] have been applied, the restriction (*niyama*) operates because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed as an option. Since the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is established by the very rule regarding "the remainder" (*śeṣa*), one must ask: what kind of restriction is intended there? Is it "the active voice occurs after the remainder when the agent is expressed," or "it occurs only after the remainder when the agent is expressed"? The first alternative is not tenable; for even if that [active voice] were excluded from non-remainder roots when the agent is expressed, it would still be unavoidable in the case of the impersonal (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*) voices, whether from a remainder or a non-remainder root.

Not the latter; for even if that [suffix] is excluded from the "remainder" (śeṣa) when it applies to the states of being (bhāva) and the object (karman), it remains unavoidable when applied to the agent (kartṛ) from what is not the "remainder."

Not so; for by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule), two restrictions (*niyama*) are adopted: "the *parasmaipada* suffixes occur only after the *śeṣa* [roots] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed," and "only the *parasmaipada* occurs [in that case]. Thus, there is no fault even regarding the restriction concerning the *kṛtya* suffixes. This is because suffixes such as *-tṛc* would have no scope [otherwise]; for even there, the scope [of the *parasmaipada*] would be precluded by the restriction "only *parasmaipada*. Furthermore, the rule for *tavyat* and other suffixes in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*)—namely, *tayoreva*—"only in those two"—would also have no scope; likewise, the *ciṇ* suffix would have no scope, since in reality, the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes have the abstract action and the object as their meaning.

Nor should it be argued that even so, the *ghañ* suffix would not occur; for although the rule "not when denoting the agent" (*akartari*) has its scope in cases such as the ablative (*apādāna*), the rule prescribed for the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) remains without scope [otherwise]. Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurring in forms such as *atti* (he eats), because of the restrictive rule: "the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs after the remainder. Nor should it be argued that, even if that rule excludes the middle voice only when the agent is expressed, it would still be difficult to prevent the active voice from occurring in the sense of the action or object after the "remainder," since there is a restrictive rule stating that "in those cases, only the middle voice occurs.
Therefore, both restrictive rules remain established.

In this regard, the following should be noted: it is more logical that there be a restriction on the *prakṛti* (the verbal root). To explain: instead of stating "after the remainder, [the suffixes] when the agent is denoted" (*śeṣāt kartari*), the rule should simply be formulated as "the *parasmaipada*" (*parasmaipadam*). In cases where both *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* would otherwise apply, the *parasmaipada* alone would occur. However, under the view that the restriction applies to the *pratyaya* (the suffix), one would have to state both "after the remainder" (*śeṣāt*) and "when the agent is denoted" (*kartari*). Furthermore, the rule would have to be split, resulting in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Moreover, there would be a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*) with the rule concerning *tiP* and other suffixes.

Furthermore, the three defects resulting from the application of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) are common to both types of restriction (*niyama*). If these are not tolerated, then because this section forms a single syntactical unit with the rule "lasya tibādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.78), this section must indeed be prescriptive; likewise, the rule "śeṣāt kartari" (Pāṇini 3.1.68) must also be applied. To avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), a future designation (*bhāvisaṃjñā*) should be understood. In this way, there is no defect regarding the *vikaraṇas* (verbal suffixes), since they apply after the substitutes for *la* have been established, by relying on the term *sārvadhātuka*. Nor is there a defect regarding the *syādi* (conjugational) suffixes.

The author of the *Kaustubha* maintains that once the internal *tiP* and other suffixes have been applied by virtue of their dependence on the mere verbal root (*dhātu*), the external *syas* and other substitutes (*ādeśas*) apply by virtue of their dependence on specific *lakāras*.

Regarding *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13): the *ātmanepada* shall occur for the *laṭ* prescribed [in the preceding rule]. As for whether this is an injunction (*vidhi*) through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) or a restriction (*niyama*) through syntactic disjunction (*bhinnavākyatā*), the former view holds. That [restriction] is also twofold: a restriction regarding the affix (*pratyayaniyama*) and a restriction regarding the meaning (*arthaniyama*). However, under the latter view, there would be no establishment of the *ghañ* suffix in the example "What gain have you obtained? (*ko bhavatā lābho labdhaḥ*), because [the restriction] would exclude only its own classmate, the *parasmaipada*.

But surely, in the case of *bhidyate kuśūlaḥ svayameva* ("the granary bursts open by itself"), the *parasmaipada* ending would apply because it is a case of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartṛ*). For there is an extension (*atideśa*) of either the grammatical rule or the designation [of the object] by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*. And thus, by that respective rule, the corresponding grammatical operation must be performed. [One might argue: "The scope for *ātmanepada* in the sense of 'the object' is when it is a pure object; the scope for *parasmaipada* in the sense of 'the agent' is when it is a pure agent; and when both [rules] apply simultaneously in the case of a *karmakartṛ*, the *parasmaipada* prevails due to its higher priority."

Not so; that is merely an extension of the *kārya* (grammatical operation) based on its predominance, because all extensions (*atideśa*) serve the purpose of an operation. In the alternative view, however, having carried over the term "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) from the rule "when there is a reciprocal action between agents" (*kartari karmavyatihāre*) to the rule "after the remaining [roots], in the sense of the agent" (*śeṣātkartari*), the meaning is: the *parasmaipada* suffix occurs when the agent is indeed an agent [and not an object]. That is to say, it is a case where there is no scope for another designation. In that situation, while the agency is inherent (*svāśraya*), the objecthood is adventitious (*ātideśika*); therefore, the *parasmaipada* does not apply. [Pāṇini 1.3.14: *kartari karmavyatihāre*.]

The *ātmanepada* affix shall occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting an action that has become the object of a reciprocal exchange (*vinimaya*), when used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Example: *vyatilunīte*. If it is asked: "But since actions possess only the nature of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), how can there be a reciprocal exchange?"—on this point they say: Reciprocal exchange of actions (*kriyā-vyatihāra*) is the transposition of two actions whose relationship as goal (*sādhya*) and means (*sādhana*) has been established by virtue of their mutual fitness, such that one thinks, "This action of mine is to be accomplished by him," and "This [action] of his is the means for me. For example: *saṃpraharante rājānaḥ* ("the kings strike at one another"). Here, a single action appears as if it were moving from one to the other. The mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule.

[The rule] "not after [roots] meaning motion or injury" (Pāṇini 1.4.24) means that what was obtained by the preceding [rule] would not occur. Examples: *vyatigacchanti* ("they go against each other"), *vyatighnanti* ("they strike against each other").
[Vārttika: "An addition should be made for *has* and so on in the prohibition."
They laugh together (*vyatihasanti*). The word *ādi* (and so forth) has the sense of "type" (*prakāra*), by which words and meanings are included. They converse together (*vyatijalpanti*).

[The rule] "there is no prohibition for the root *hṛ*" applies: kings plunder together (*sampaharante*). By the force of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*), the prohibition applies only to those roots that function in the senses of "motion" or "injury" independently of any other word. However, since the root *hṛ* functions in the sense of injury only through its connection with a prefix, they say that this [prohibition] does not apply here.

Regarding the statement, "Then, seeing Karṇa and Dhanañjaya about to strike each other," Kaiyaṭa maintains that the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) is not intended here. [The prohibition of *ātmanepada*] does not apply to the root *vah*, because its meaning is "to cause to reach" (*prāpaṇa*), since motion is understood through implication. For example: *saṃvivahante gargāḥ*.
And [the *ātmanepada* suffix is used] after the roots preceded by the mutual or reciprocal words *itaretara* and *anyonya* (Pāṇini 1.3.16).

The *ātmanepada* ending would not occur [in the case of *vyatilunanti*]. Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the *ātmanepada* occurs] when preceded by the word *paraspara*," [the example is] *itaretaraṃ vyatilunanti*. Since there is no regard for brevity of expression in common worldly usage, words such as *itaretara* and prefixes (*upasarga*) are employed to indicate the reciprocity of action; likewise, one might expect the *ātmanepada* ending here as well. Therefore, this prohibition is commenced. In the verse, "By the exchange of their fortunes, both bestowed the two worlds," the reciprocity of the action is not intended to be expressed. 17. *ner viśaḥ*: The *ātmanepada* ending shall occur after the root *viś* when preceded by the prefix *ni*. Example: *niviśate*. Why "preceded by *ni*"? Example: *praviśati*.

Now, as for the forms *nyaviśata* and *nyavikṣata*, it cannot be resolved by the principle that "one's own member (*svāṅga*) does not constitute an intervention," because although the augment *aṭ*—which is a portion of the verbal base (*aṅgabhakta*)—is a constituent part relative to the suffix, it is not a constituent part relative to the root (*dhātu*).

On this point, they say: the augment *aṭ* occurs precisely in the state of the *L* suffix (*lāvasthāyām*). This is because it will be stated in the Bhāṣya that in the rule "luṅ-laṅ—" there is a mention of two *L*s (*dvilakāraka-nirdeśaḥ*). Furthermore, since the augment *aṭ* depends upon a specific *L* suffix, it is superseded by the internal operations (*antaraṅga*) such as *tiP* and others, which depend only on the general *L*. This is because the restriction (*niyama*) applies once those internal operations have taken effect, according to the established principle (*siddhānta*) that "the restriction is stronger than the verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). Even if it were argued that, by means of that very indicator (*jñāpaka*), the restriction is understood to apply even when there is an intervention by a suffix, there would still be no fault.

Because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), when the *ti*-suffixes and so forth are present, between the two non-eternal elements—the augment *aṭ* and the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*)—the *aṭ* applies first due to its being subsequent (*para*). Nor should it be argued that the suffix is obtained from another word-form (*śabdāntara*) but not for another word-form; for this is not a formal rule (*vācanika*), but rather a logical principle (*nyāya*). And thus, just as an element is non-eternal when it applies to one word-form, it is likewise non-eternal when it applies from another word-form.

Because the attainment [of a grammatical operation] by virtue of its connection with a particular individual was previously established, it remains equal even when attained again by virtue of that same connection with that individual. For this very reason, some maintain that the Vārttika—"An addition should be made for the case of non-intervening vowels (*aḍ-vyavāya*) when there is a restriction regarding what is preceded by a prefix"—was rejected by the Blessed One (Patañjali) under the rule *śadeḥ śitaḥ*; such is the direction of their argument.

However, some maintain that because the augment *aṭ* occurs earlier than the verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) due to its higher status, it does not act as an intervention, since it is an integral part of the verbal root (*dhātubhakta*). Furthermore, even if the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the suffixes were stronger, the augment *aṭ* lacks such strength; therefore, the restrictive rule "after *nis*, [the prefix *pra* is used] with *viś*" cannot apply before the augment *aṭ*, as it is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*).

It should not be argued that the intended meaning here is that the restriction (niyama) applies only before the suffixal element (*vikaraṇa*) and not even before the augment *aṭ*; for if the augment *aṭ* were applied first due to its priority, it would—being part of the verbal root (*dhātubhakta*)—not act as an intervention, and thus the restriction would apply. This is because, although the restriction is stronger than the suffixal element, it has not been stated that a constant suffixal element which follows the augment *aṭ* is weaker; therefore, the application [of the restriction] prior to the augment *aṭ* cannot be prevented.

Furthermore, the utility of that paribhāṣā is established in cases where the augment *aṭ* is absent. The claim that "even when there is intervention by a *vikaraṇa*" and so forth is also incorrect, because there is no evidence for the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of a *vikaraṇa*. This is because the author of the Bhāṣya uses the term "non-eternality" only in reference to something else that would otherwise apply. Moreover, the logical principle underlying the statement "a rule that applies to a different word-form is non-eternal" is not well-established. Finally, although the author of the Bhāṣya states the eternality of *aṭ*, he does not state the non-eternality of *vikaraṇas*.

Based on the principle that a rule is considered eternal (*nitya*) merely by virtue of its application to both what has already occurred and what has not yet occurred, [the author] rejects the sūtra *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca*—arguing that since the suffix *vuK* is eternal for the root *bhū*, and since the root *indh* belongs only to the Vedic domain, the prescription of the *kit* designation for the *liṭ* affix after those two roots is redundant. Relying on the statement—"A rule that applies to something else, as indicated by the inclusion of the word *bhavati* as a part of that sūtra, is non-eternal"—and relying on the logical eternality of the augment *aṬ* and the verbal class marker (*vikaraṇa*), [the author maintains that] because of its superior status (*paratva*), the augment *aṬ* occurs prior [to the class marker].

Alternatively, having accepted the occurrence [of the prefix], they say that since the Vārttika was rejected by relying on the fact that *neḥ* is in the genitive case, the works of Vṛttikāra and Sīradeva are also thereby refuted.
[Pāṇini 1.3.18: *parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ*.

The ātmanepada ending shall occur after the root *krī* (to buy) when preceded by these [prefixes]. In the word *kriya*, because the imitation follows the original form (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), it is treated as a verbal root (*dhātu*), and thus the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs. This rule is commenced for the purpose of expressing that the action does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). Examples: *parikrīṇīte*, *vikrīṇīte*, *avakrīṇīte*. Only those prefixes beginning with *pari* are understood here because they are mentioned in conjunction; therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *ve krīṇāsi*. Since a form modified by the alteration of one part is not considered different from the original, the application [of the rule] would otherwise follow.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because Kaiyaṭa will state that this modification belongs to the word *vi* as qualified by its case-ending, and not to the stem *vi* alone; for the case-ending is elided, and thus the modification occurs only to the portion that constitutes the base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, they say [there is no fault] because Kaiyaṭa will also state that, while a word *vi* denoting a bird is possible, the term "preposition" (*upasarga*) is understood here due to association (*sāhacarya*).

In reality, because of its higher status and its being eternal (*nitya*), the substitution of *guṇa* occurs first, and only afterwards is there the elision of *su*. Otherwise, the mention of *eṅ* in that rule would be purposeless. Furthermore, in that case, one should understand that *vis* undergoes the modification *ves*, and thus the word *vi* undergoes the modification *ve*.
[Pāṇini 1.3.19: *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*.

He conquers; he is defeated. Here, both senses—conquest (*jaya*) and overcoming (*abhibhūti*)—are included. However, in the case of "he conquers the forest which has many birds" (*bahuvijayati vanam*), [the suffix] does not occur; for in the *jahatsvārthā* mode of derivation (*vṛtti*), the constituent members are devoid of meaning, and even in the *ajahatsvārthā* mode, that meaning is subordinate (*upasarjana*). As for the vocative, it has been explained previously.

Nor should it be argued that in the word *vijayate*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the final element of the preceding portion, there exists a root *ji* followed by the suffix *parasmaipada* (here *śap*, which is replaced by *śyan*); for the treatment as the final element (*antavadbhāva*) applies only when an operation is to be performed upon the preceding element. [In the sentence] *parā jayati senā*, the meaning is "the army is superior. Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the extended rule (*atideśa*) stating "as if it were the original base" (*prakṛtivat*), there is an absence of the *iyaṅ* substitution in the form *jer*.
[The sūtra] *āṅo do’nāsyaviharaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.3.20).

The *ātmanepada* ending shall be used after the root *dā* (to give) preceded by the prefix *ā*, when it has the sense of opening the mouth or a different meaning [from its usual sense]. Kaiyaṭa states that other forms of the root *dā* are not included here because they lack the sense of functioning with respect to the mouth (*āsya*). Examples: *vidyām ādatte* (He acquires knowledge). The mention of *āsya* (mouth) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for specific instances. *mukhaṃ vyādadāti* (He opens his mouth). *vipādikāṃ vyādadāti* (He opens a sore on the foot). *nadīkūlaṃ vyādadāti* (The riverbank gives way/splits open). Regarding the rule "not when the object is something other than the mouth," the prohibition is not desired in cases where the action involves a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), according to the Vārttika: "And also when the object is a limb of one's own body. Thus: *parasya mukhaṃ vyādadāti* (He opens another's mouth). *parasya pādaṃ vyādadāti* (He opens another's foot). *parasya vipādikāṃ vyādadāti* (He opens another's sore on the foot). *parasya nadīkūlaṃ vyādadāti* (The riverbank of another [i.e., a public place] gives way).

In this context, "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*) refers to a limb that is not fluid even when embodied; such is the technical definition. Ants open the mouth of a moth. Because of the inclusion of the *ṅit* marker [in the rule], this does not apply here: "he begs for alms" (*bhikṣām ādadāti*). They say that this letter *ā* is traditionally taught [as having this specific function]. This rule is commenced for the purpose of [denoting] an action not intended for the agent. However, when the action is intended for the agent, it certainly occurs even with the mouth as the object: "the king of birds opens his own mouth. Regarding the expression "he sleeps having opened his mouth," Vācaspatimiśra states that its meaning is reversed: "having slept, he opens his mouth."

Pāṇini 1.3.21: *krīḍo’nusaṃparibhyaśca* (The suffix *ātmanepada* is applied after the root *krīḍ* [meaning] "to play," following the prefixes *anu*, *sam*, and *pari*; and by the word *ca* [in the sūtra], also after *ā*. Examples include *anukrīḍate* and so forth. Because of its association with verbal prefixes (*upasarga*), the prefix *anu* here is not a *karmapravacanīya*. Example: *māṇavakamanukrīḍati* ("He plays along with the boy"). The meaning is "with him. Here, *anu* is a *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*).
[The rule continues: *samo’kūjane* ("After *sam*, when it does not mean 'making a sound'...").
Śrīharṣa uses the form *saṃkrīḍati* in the phrase *cakricakre saṃkrīḍati*. However, the reading *krīḍate nāgarājaḥ* is an error.
[The root] *ā-gam-i* [is used] in the sense of "endurance.
Thus, *āgamayasva tāvat* means "endure for some time; do not hasten. Śrīharṣa uses the form *āgamayate* in the verse *yāvadāgamayate'tha narendrān*.

Regarding the rule *śikṣer jijñāsāyām*: "He applies himself to the sciences. Here, the root *śak* is understood as being followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*). This [sūtra] is for the purpose of prescribing [the Ātmanepada ending]. Furthermore, the root *śak* is employed with reference to an action, as seen in examples such as *bhoktuṃ śaknoti* ("he is able to eat"). In this context, however, *śak* is taken as having *jijñāsā* (the desire to know) as its object. The meaning is: "He strives to desire to know the science. And there is no possibility of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurring here; for some maintain that the desiderative sense is understood through the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) itself.

Others, however, say that the inclusion [of the root *śikṣ*] is for the purpose of restriction, based on the rule "the root *śikṣ* is used in the sense of acquiring knowledge. Nor should it be argued that it is inconsistent to say that *jijñāsā* (desire to know) means "an intention whose object is knowledge," since in the first case [the desire] has as its object a power qualified by knowledge; for even though knowledge is a qualifier, its status as an object is not lost. The suffix *san* expresses the desire, while the power is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); furthermore, the fact that the desire has knowledge as its object is indicated by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). [The Vārttika states: "An addition should be made [to the rule] regarding the root *kṛ* (kirati) in the senses of joy, livelihood, and making a nest."

The root *kṛ* has the sense of "scattering," while joy (*harṣa*) and the like are presented as its objects. It is precisely with respect to these meanings that the suffix *suṭ* is prescribed by the rule "apāccatuṣpād-. Thus, one says *apaskirate* (he scatters) when a bull is joyful, a cock is seeking food, or a dog is seeking shelter. Why [is it not used] in cases such as joy? For example: *apakirati kusumam* (he scatters a flower). Although in the prescription of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) the fact of being performed by a four-footed animal or a bird is not taken as a condition, nevertheless, this *taṅ* (the middle voice ending) shares the same scope as *suṭ*. Therefore, they say that in the case of a person, one simply says *gajo 'pakirati* (the elephant scatters).
[Also: *harater-gatatācchīlye* (after the root *hṛ*, the middle voice is used when expressing habitual movement).

The sense of *gata* (gone) [is implied]. Horses imitate their father; cows imitate their mother. The meaning is that they constantly practice the behavior (*prakāra*) gone by [the father] and so forth. Kaiyaṭa states that in the Bhāṣya on the rule concerning the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), in the phrase "he imitates his mother," mere similarity (*sādṛśya*) is intended. Regarding the statement "an addition [should be made] for the roots *ṇu* and *pracch* with the prefix *ā-*": *ānute*. The meaning is that he makes a sound preceded by longing. The root *ṇu* means "to praise"; it belongs to the second class (*adādi*). *Āpṛcchate guruṃ* ("he takes leave of the teacher").

"nāthaḥ in the sense of benediction (āśis). This is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha). Nor is the fact that [the root] is marked with an indicatory udātta vowel (anudāttettva) redundant, because the form *nāthana* is intended to include the suffix *yuc*. In *sarpiṣo nāthate*, the meaning is "he desires that clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) may be mine. In the rule "nāthaḥ in the sense of benediction," the genitive case is used for the object (*karman*). Regarding the example *dīnaṃ tvāmanunāthate kucayugaṃ patrāvṛtaṃ mā kṛthāḥ* ("She entreats you, the wretched one: 'Do not cover your pair of breasts with leaves'"), they say that the form *nādhase* is used here. "The root *śap* is used in the sense of reproaching (*upālambhana*)."

The root *śap* (to curse/revile) is marked with the svarita accent. This rule is commenced for the sake of cases where the fruit [of the action] does not accrue to the agent (*akartṛgaphala*). *devadattāya śapate*—the meaning is that he makes an oath, saying, "I touch your feet; this was not done by me. The designation *sampradāna* (recipient) applies here by the rule: "In the case of the roots *ślāgh*, *hnuṅ*, *sthā*, and *śap*, the one being made aware [of the matter] is the recipient. According to some, the one being made aware is the person to whom it is told; according to others, it is the person to whom it is addressed. However, in the sentence *sakhyaḥ śapāmi yadi kiṃ cid api smarāmi* ("O friends, I swear that I do not remember anything at all"), there is merely the intention to express one's own internal state. [Next is the rule: *sam-ava-pra-vibhyaḥ sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.22).

Regarding the passage beginning with *saṃtiṣṭhate*: there is an extension [of the rule] for the prefix *ā-* when expressing a formal proposition (*pratijñā*). One establishes the *sakāra* of the root *as*; one establishes the augmentations (*āgama*) of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. The meaning of this is as follows: Āpiśali reads only the *sakāra* in the rule "√as, to be. He prescribes the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ* in forms such as *asti* and *āsīt*. And [there is the rule]: "In the senses of manifesting and being established. (Pāṇini 1.3.23)

The gopī stands before Kṛṣṇa; she reveals her own intention. *Stheya* means one who decides a point of dispute. By virtue of the rule of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *yat* is applied here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Śrī Harṣa says: "Stand for the sake of truth, right here in your own mouth. The meaning is: "Resort to me for the purpose of determining the truth. [Pāṇini 1.3.24: "The root *sthā* takes the prefix *ud-* except when the action is directed upwards."

The [substitution of *ī* for *uti*] after the root *sthā* preceded by *ud-* is as previously stated, because it excludes an action whose result is upward conjunction (*ūrdhvasaṃyoga*). The Vārttika "uda īhāyām" is intended to state the purpose of employing the word "action" (*karma*). That is to say, it refers to physical effort (*ceṣṭā*) consisting of bodily movement. Otherwise, he would have simply said "anūrdhve" (except when not upward). Since it is a rule that a verbal root denotes action, that [meaning] is already obtained [from the root itself]. But the other [case], "uttiṣṭhamānaḥ" (one who is rising), is different. Why "anūrdhve"? [Example: *javena pīṭhād udatiṣṭhad acyutaḥ* (Acyuta rose quickly from his seat). Why "īhāyām" (in the sense of effort)? [Example: *uttiṣṭhati senā* (the army rises); the meaning here is "it is being produced. [Next: *upa* [is used] before a root when the instrument is a mantra. 25.

The suffix *ātmanepada* is applied after the root *sthā* preceded by *upa*, when it has the sense of performing an action with a mantra, as previously stated. Example: *aindryā gārhapatyam upatiṣṭhate* ("He worships the Gārhapatya fire with a verse addressed to Indra"). Why specify "with a mantra"? Consider: *bhartāram upatiṣṭhati yauvanena* ("She attends upon her husband with her youth").
It should be stated that [the rule] applies to the sense of worshiping a deity, joining, making friends, and paths: *upād devapūjā-saṅgatikaraṇa-mitrakaraṇa-pathiṣu iti vaktavyam*.
This is for the purpose of excluding the sense of performing an action with a mantra. Example: *ādityam upatiṣṭhate* ("He worships the Sun").
Even among many who lack consciousness, there is one who possesses consciousness;
behold how, in this army of monkeys, there is one who attends upon the sun.
Do not think thus: "This one possesses a mind, for he is just like us";
O monkey, even that which you do as a monkey—namely, that you wait upon the sun—is indeed a monkeyish act.

Thus says the Bhāṣya. Kaiyaṭa explains that, considering it to be worship of a deity, the Ātmanepada occurs in the first instance; however, in the latter case, since this is mere fawning and not true worship, the Ātmanepada is absent. Sarasvatī worshipped [the king] with meaningful hymns of praise (*upatasthe*). This is because she superimposes upon him the status of a deity. He waits upon the chariot-drivers (*rathikān upatiṣṭhate*). The meaning is that he attaches himself to them (*upaśliṣyati*). He waits upon the horse-riders (*aśvārohān upatiṣṭhate*). Even though he is not physically attached to them, there is a connection through friendship. This path leads to Srughna (*srughnam upatiṣṭhate*). The meaning is that it reaches it (*prāpnoti*).
"It should be stated that the [Ātmanepada] applies optionally when there is a desire for gain (*lipsā*)."

A beggar *upatiṣṭhate* or *upatiṣṭhati* a Brahmin; the meaning is that he approaches him out of a desire [to obtain something]. From an intransitive verb [the suffix *ātmanepada* is used] (Pāṇini 1.3.26).
At the time of eating, he *upatiṣṭhate*; the meaning is that he remains present.

The root *tap* [takes the ātmanepada endings] after the prefixes *ud* and *vi*. (Pāṇini 1.3.27) It applies only when the verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Examples: *uttapate*; "the lord of rays (*tviṣām patiḥ*) warms," as Murāri says; the meaning is "shines.
Also [it takes the ātmanepada endings] after [a prefix] when its own body part (*svāṅga*) is the object (*karmaka*). (Pāṇini 1.3.28)

*Uttapate vitapate pāṇim*: "He heats his hand. Here, Devadatta does not heat Yajñadatta’s hand; the meaning is that he causes it to suffer pain (*santāpayati*). *Suvarṇam uttapati*: "He heats gold," meaning he causes it to suffer pain or he melts it (*vilāpayati*). Why [is the rule] restricted to the prefixes *ud-* and *vi-*? [Consider: *niṣṭapati*. In this case, the substitution of *ṣ* for *t* occurs by the rule "nisastapatau" (Pāṇini 8.3.102).

Objection: Since the rule "after *ud* and *vi*, *tap* takes the Ātmanepada" already exists, this present statement must be intended to exclude the *yak* and *ciṇ* affixes. Thus, *niṣṭapate* should be cited as an example. For the root *tap* is indeed intransitive when meaning "to shine," but it becomes transitive when functioning with an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) in the sense of "causing heat. Furthermore, when there is a desire to express the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), the Ātmanepada is established by the rule that the agent behaves like the object (*kartuḥ karmavadbhāva*).

Not so; for even in the absence of the status of being like an object (*karmavadbhāva*), we observe that transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*) can function as intransitives (*akarmaka*) when there is a difference in meaning, as seen in such usages as *nadī vahati* ("the river flows") and *bhāraṃ vahati* ("he carries a load"). Therefore, the rule is intended solely for prescriptive purposes. [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.28:
*āṅo yamahanaḥ*.

The *ātmanepada* suffix shall be used after the roots *yam* and *han* when preceded by the prefix *ā*, provided they are either intransitive or have their own body parts (*svāṅga*) as objects. Examples: *āyacchate* (he draws back), *āhate* (he strikes himself). *āyacchate pāṇim* (he draws back his hand); *āhate śiraḥ* (he strikes his head). By this rule, the usage in Bhāravi’s poem—*etena mohād āhadhvaṃ māraṇyuttamam* ("Therefore, out of delusion, strike the best of the Māras")—is explained. This is because the *ātmanepada* is firmly established here, as there is an absence of an external object (*parāṅkarmabhāva*). Why say "intransitive"? Consider: *āyacchati rajjuṃ kūpāt* ("He draws a rope from a well"); *āhanti vṛṣalaṃ pādena* ("He strikes a low-born man with his foot"). Why say "one's own body part"? Consider: *paraśira āhanti* ("He strikes another's head").

The wielder of the *gāṇḍīva* struck the chest of the three-eyed Lord with his two arms, which resembled a slab of gold; however, some maintain that this usage by Bhāravi is erroneous. Nor should one suspect that the word *āja* is to be split [as *ā-aja*] and interpreted as the dative singular (*caturthī-ekavacana*) of the root *han* (to kill) in the sense of "for the purpose of killing" (*ghne = hananāya*), formed with the suffix *kvip*; for the form *vivāya* is accepted on the basis of the substitution of *vī* for *aj*.
According to some, having approached Śiva, he struck his own chest according to the tradition of wrestlers (*malla-saṃpradāya*).

Alternatively, the word "Gāṇḍīvī" (the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow) is to be supplied as the subject, meaning he stood facing [the enemy] with speed like a leaping crocodile in the celestial river (Gaṅgā), having come toward the river of arrows. The verb "ājaghne" (was struck) is in the passive voice (*karmaṇi lakāraḥ*). The word "tena" (by him) is to be supplied. Alternatively, "Gāṇḍīvī" refers to one who desires the Gāṇḍīva for himself; this is formed by adding *kvip* after the denominative suffix *kyac*. Regarding "kanakaśīla": this is formed by adding *kvip* in the sense of an agent (*kartari*) after the nominalizing suffix *kvip* used in the sense of habitual action (*ācāre*), followed by the instrumental case. The two words form a *karmadhāraya* compound. The phrase "nitarāṃ bhā yatra" (where there is intense luster) is an adjective qualifying the chest. In the phrase "unmajjanmakara," the locative case is used because it follows a *karmadhāraya* compound. The verbal suffix (*lakāraḥ*) remains in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*).

29. *sama* [is used] with *gam* and *ṛcchi*. After these two roots preceded by *sam*, when they are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *śyan* is applied as before. Examples: *saṅgacchate*, *samṛcchate*. Why "when they are intransitive"? Example: *khagaḥ saṅgacchati yaddinādhipam* ("The bird goes toward the lord of the day"). As for the phrase *taccaikyaṃ samagacchata*, it is Vedic (*ārṣa*). Furthermore, the augment *aṭ* does not occur before the substitution of the *l*-suffixes due to its being subsequent [in the order of rules]; for the substitution of the *l*-suffixes is obligatory by virtue of applying whether [the augment] has been applied or not, since even when *aṭ* has been applied, the root is still included by the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) and thus there is no intervention. The augment *aṭ*, however, is non-obligatory.

After the substitution of the *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*), the *vikaraṇa* suffixes [such as *śap*] necessarily precede them because they are prohibited [by them]; and after the *vikaraṇa*, [the augment *aṭ* applies] because it would apply to a different word-form (*śabdāntara*). Although once the *l*-substitution has been made, the designation of *luṅ* and so forth persists by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), and thus even when the cause for *aṭ* exists, *aṭ* is set aside by the *vikaraṇa* due to its obligatory nature—nevertheless, that whose cause is destroyed by another rule is not considered non-eternal (*anitya*). Since both [the *vikaraṇa* and *aṭ*] are eternal, *aṭ* prevails due to its posteriority.

Even so, it should not be argued that because the augment *aṭ* is a part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), it does not act as an intervention, and thus the ātmanepada suffix is established. The intention of the Vārttika is that since the *vikaraṇa* (conjugational sign) arises before the restriction [of the *ātmanepada*] due to its being obligatory, the *aṭ*-augment becomes an integral part of the ending of the *vikaraṇa*; consequently, because it intervenes between the root and the suffixes *viśi*, etc., these suffixes do not occur immediately after roots such as *nyā*. Therefore, the ātmanepada would not be applicable.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, maintain that the substitutes for *l* (the *lādeśas*) are *antaraṅga* because they depend only on the general category of *l*, whereas the augment *aṭ* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on a specific instance of *l*. Now, there is no comparison to be made between the *lādeśas* and the [augment]; rather, the comparison is with the restrictive rule (*niyama*). For after the substitution of *l*, three things present themselves: the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), the augment *aṭ*, and the restrictive rule. In that case, if the restrictive rule were stronger than everything else, then the desired result would be achieved even without the Vārttika. Nor can it be maintained that the restrictive rule is stronger than the verbal suffixes.

Even if [the rule] were stated as "even when a vikaraṇa has been applied, it does not cause intervention," the indication of that fact would still be established otherwise. Furthermore, such a restriction is not necessarily permanent. For in cases such as *nivekṣyate* and *niviśate*, where a bare vikaraṇa causes intervention, the restriction would indeed apply; however, once the vikaraṇa has been applied, the augment *aṭ* occurs, and because *aṭ* then causes intervention, the restriction does not apply. Indeed, it is impossible to apply *aṭ* prior to the vikaraṇa, since the vikaraṇas are prescribed to precede the *aṅga*.

Otherwise, forms such as *tarataḥ* and *taranti* would not be possible; for, in the absence of the *śap* suffix, there would be no *guṇa* substitution, since the suffixes beginning with *tas* are marked with the *ṅit* indicator. Consequently, the *it*-augment (*ittvam*) itself would have to apply first. Furthermore, even in the case of the *aṭ* and *āṭ* augments, another *aṅga* (stem) must be desired to precede them. Otherwise, in the form *upārcchat*, if the *āṭ* augment were applied first, it would result in the substitution of *ṛcchi* applying only to that which is qualified by it [the augmented stem]. This is because, since the rule for *ṛcchi* depends solely on a specific phoneme (*varṇamātra*), it would be superseded, and the *vṛddhi* substitution alone would apply first. Nor is it the case that an *aṅga* operation is stronger than one conditioned by a suffix (*vārṇāt*); for both share the same locus of application (*samānāśrayatvāt*).

If it is argued that because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the beginning of the preceding element, when the substitution of *ṛcchi* occurs, the form would be *ṛcchat* and not *ārcchat*; and that since the augment *āṭ* has not yet been applied to this different word-form, it will occur again; and that the substitution of *ṛcchi* and the augment *āṭ* will occur repeatedly, leading to the undesirable consequence of instability (*avyavasthā*); therefore, the Vārttika is necessary— [The response follows: This is not so. For the substitution of *ṛcchi* applies only to the specific form *ṛccha*, and once that form has been replaced by the single substitute, the condition for the application of *ṛcchi* no longer exists. Furthermore, the augment *āṭ* is prescribed specifically for the root *ṛccha* when followed by the suffix *liṅ* or *luṅ* with the augment *m* (*māṅ*), and it does not apply to the entire word-form resulting from the single substitute. Thus, there is no room for the recurrence of either the substitution or the augment, and the objection regarding instability is unfounded. Consequently, the Vārttika is not required.

No; for in the case of *tarati*, since the substitution of *i* (the *it*-augment) is non-permanent while the *vikaraṇa* suffix is permanent, that [suffix] alone operates. In cases such as *tarati*, because the *guṇa* substitution is also permanent, that [suffix] alone applies due to its higher priority. In *upārcchat* as well, by the aforementioned reasoning, there is again the augment *āṭ*. Nor does there arise a recurrence of the state of being *ṛcchi*; for a fixed rule can be established according to the desired outcome (*iṣṭataḥ*). This has been stated on the basis of concession. In reality, however, the state of being *ṛcchi* occurs first, and only afterwards does *āṭ* apply due to its higher priority. Therefore, once the substitutes for the *l*-suffixes have been applied, the augment *aṭ* follows by virtue of its higher priority.

Furthermore, the augment *aṭ* is not obligatory (*nitya*). This is because it is logical that [an operation] is non-obligatory even when it applies from one word-form to another, just as it is when it applies to a different word-form altogether; for the criterion of "applying whether [the other rule] has been performed or not" (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*) is common to both cases. Alternatively, since the augment *aṭ* is based on the universal property (*jāti*) of being a "stem" (*aṅga*), there is no absence of application to a different word-form. Or rather, the term *neḥ* is indeed a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and not an ablative (*pañcamī*); for a connection is possible because that which is separated [by intervening elements] can still function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) through its meaning.

Alternatively, the meaning of the rule *nerviśaḥ* is that the word *viśati*, ending in an ātmanepada suffix, becomes grammatically correct after the word *ni*; they say that even though the augment *aṭ* occurs, there is no fault because [the prefix] *ni* must immediately precede [the root]. [The rule] *mriyater luṅliṅoś ca* [is as follows]: 61.

The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs only after the root *mṛ* when it is in its original form (*prakṛtibhūta*) and is followed by a *śit* affix (i.e., one marked with *ś*), as well as in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* tenses; it does not occur after it in any other context. The status of being a *śit*-originated form (*śitprakṛtitva*) should be understood through suitability even prior to the actual production of the *śit* affix; however, in the case of *luṅ* and *liṅ*, this applies only once they have actually arisen—this is the distinction. Examples: *mriyate*, *mriyate*, *mriyatām*, *amriyata*, *amṛta*, *mṛṣīṣṭa*. What is the purpose of this restrictive rule (*niyama*)? [To exclude forms such as: *mamāra*, *martāsi*, *mariṣyati*, *amariṣyat*. Furthermore, the *ṅit* designation for the root *mṛ* is for the sake of accentuation (*svarārtha*).

In the case of *mā hi mṛta*, the rule *lasārvadhātukam* [1.1.40] applies after the instruction of the marker *ṅit* so that the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) may occur. Nor is the elision of *sij* considered non-existent (*asiddha*), because of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the *ṅit* marker. Furthermore, there is no *nighāta* here due to the prohibition by the rule *hic ca* [8.1.34].
[The next rule is: *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [1.3.62].

The meaning is that whatever cause for the *ātmanepada* exists after a simple [root] in the *śuddha* (pure) state, that same cause brings about the *ātmanepada* even after that root when it is followed by the suffix *saN*. It is precisely because of this much that this is designated as an "extension of the cause" (*nimittātideśa*). The expression "equal to the preceding" (*pūrveṇa tulyam*) is derived from a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) with the suffix *vati*; it is not derived from a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), as there is no such rule for its application. However, the sense "as if from the preceding" (*pūrvasmādiva*) is what is intended, just as in the example: "He studies from a Vaiśya in a manner equal to [studying] from a Brāhmaṇa. In that instance, the word "Brāhmaṇa" refers to the study whose source is the Brāhmaṇa. Examples: *āsisiṣate*, *śiśayiṣyate*, *nivivikṣate*.

Regarding the examples *mumukṣate* and so forth: here [in *śiśatsati*] there is no [desire for] cutting. *Mumūrṣati*. Indeed, this form ending in *śad* and *mri* is not a base (*prakṛti*) that ends in a *śit* affix; therefore, it is not a cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). However, when the desiderative suffix (*san*) is applied, the base of the desiderative itself becomes the one ending in a *śit* affix. But in cases such as *śiśayiṣyate*, since the *ṅit*-ness of the original base (*prakṛti*) does not depart, its status as a cause is extended by analogy (*atideśa*); thus there is a disparity. Nor should it be argued that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *anucikīrṣati*, because it would result in the extension of the *ñit*-ness—which is a cause for the middle voice—to the meanings of "hinting" (*gandhana*) and so forth.

This is because, upon considering the rule *anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ*, it is established that the suffix *ātmanepada* is triggered only by that [root] which is characterized by the absence of the prefix *anu*.

Alternatively, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the grammatical effect itself: namely, that from those roots which take *ātmanepada* prior to the addition of *san*, it occurs even when they are followed by *san*. This is because all extensions serve the purpose of bringing about a grammatical effect, and thus the extension of the effect holds primacy. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the roots *śad* and *mṛ*; for in both rules—*śadeḥ śitaḥ* and *mriyater luṅliṅoś ca*—the word "not" (*na*) from the previous context is carried forward (*anuvartate*), and the rules are explained through a division of sentences (*vākyabheda*).

In examples such as *jugupsate*, however, because the root is invariably followed by the suffix *san* (desiderative), the Ātmanepada ending is not observed prior to that *san*; therefore, this extended application (*atideśa*) does not operate. Nevertheless, it will be stated that the Ātmanepada occurs there by virtue of the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* [Pāṇini 1.3.12], precisely because of the attachment of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*). This is according to the maxim: "That which has no purpose in its constituent part [is applied to the whole]. Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms like *jugupsayati*, since the requirement is satisfied by qualifying the element up to and including *san*; there is no evidence for applying the qualification beyond that.

Nor should it be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *gopayati*, because [the rule] should be qualified by "only when preceded by *sa*" (*san-eva*), and not by "when preceded by *ṇic*," for there is no basis for such a restriction. This is because, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), those roots such as *gup* which take the *san* affix in senses such as censure (*nindā*) etc. are themselves marked with the low-pitched indicatory letter (*anudāttet*); whereas in other senses, the roots *gup* and others remain in the *curādi* class without any such indicatory marks.
[The next rule is: "The *kṛñ* used in subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) is treated like the *ām* affix. (Pāṇini 1.3.63)

The *ātmanepada* affix is applied after the root *kṛ*, even when it is used following a root that has taken the *ām* prefix, just as it would be after that same root in its original form (*prakṛti*). The term "that from which the *ām* affix arises" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the quality of the *ām* itself is not intended. This rule is for the purpose of cases where the result does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). For example: *īhām cakre*. Nor does this lead to an over-extension in cases such as *indām cakāra*, because of the continued application of the word "as before" (*pūrvavat*). Furthermore, since the explanation is made through a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) for the sake of restriction—meaning that the *ātmanepada* occurs only as it did previously and not otherwise—the rule is restricted accordingly. Why mention *kṛ*? To prevent the rule from applying to the roots *bhū* and *as*. For example: *babhūva*, *āsīt*.

Due to the force of the inclusion of *kṛñ*, there is no reference here to the *kṛn* pratyāhāra. For this very reason, the inclusion of the *kṛn* pratyāhāra will be mentioned later in the rule for subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). Regarding *propābhyāṃ yujeḥ ayajñapātreṣu* (Pāṇini 1.3.64):

the rule applies to the root *yujir* meaning "to join," which belongs to the *rudhādi* class and is marked with a svarita accent, specifically for the purpose of an action not intended for the agent. It does not refer to *yuj* meaning "to concentrate" from the *divādi* class, because that root is marked with an anudātta accent and because the context of sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*) is impossible in that case.
"It should be stated: 'preceded by a vowel or [an upasarga] ending in a vowel.

The meaning is that, setting aside the rule *propābhyām*, one should read it as: "preceded by that upasarga which has a vowel at its beginning or end. By this, upasargas other than those ending in a consonant are included. Examples: *udyuṅkte* ("he exerts himself"), *niyuṅkte* ("he employs"). Why say "except for *yajña*"? [Example: *dvandvaṃ nyañci pātrāṇi prayunakti* ("he arranges the vessels in pairs, facing downward"). *samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ* (6.1.135).

The reading *samogamyṛcchibhyām* is separated from the preceding rule in order to prescribe [the ātmanepada] even after a transitive root. For example: *saṃkṣṇute śastram* ("he sharpens the weapon"). Murāri says: *vakṣaḥpīṭhe ghanāstravraṇakiṇakaṭhine saṅkṣṇuvānaḥ pṛṣatkān* ("sharpening his arrows upon the surface of his chest, which is hardened by the calluses of wounds from thick weapons").
[The rule *bhujo'navane* (1.3.66) follows.]

The root *bhuj* is defined as "protection and eating. Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the sense of "non-protection," the rule for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed specifically for the sense of "eating. Consequently, this does not include the root *bhuj* meaning "crookedness. This is because, just as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), separation (*viprayoga*) is also a cause for determining a specific meaning. For this very reason, just as in the phrase "Hari with the conch and discus," the word "Hari" refers to Nārāyaṇa even in the phrase "Hari without the conch and discus. As it has been said, beginning with the discussion of conjunction and separation: "These are the causes for the recollection of specific [meanings]."

And that has been explained in detail elsewhere. [The rule applies when] *bhunakti* means "to eat," as in *odanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats rice"). Why [is the condition] "not in the sense of protecting" (*anavane*) stated? Consider *mahīṃ bhunakti* ("he protects the earth") or *bubhuje pṛthivīpālaḥ* ("the protector of the earth enjoyed [it]"); in such cases, the meaning is "enjoyment" or "making one's own. It does not apply here in *vibhujati pāṇim* ("he stretches out his hand"). Therefore, the Vārttika "in the sense of protecting and crookedness" (*anavanakauṭilyayoḥ*) is for the sake of clarity. [Now the sūtra: *ṇer aṇau yatkarma ṇau cet sa kartānādhyāne* (1.3.67). When there is a causative suffix (*ṇic*), that which was the object (*karma*) of the root in its non-causative form (*aṇau*) becomes the agent (*kartā*) in the causative form (*ṇau*), provided the action is not one of remembering (*anādhyāne*).

The *ātmanepada* suffix shall occur after a root ending in the causative marker *ṇic*, except in the sense of "remembering with longing" (*anādhyāne*). The second sentence is: "If that which is the object in the *aṇ* [non-causative] state is also the object in the *ṇic* [causative] state. By the word "that" (*yat*), the word "that" (*tat*) is implied, because of the constant connection between "that which" (*yad*) and "that" (*tad*). Since no other property is specified, it is the status of being an object (*karmatva*) itself that is referred back by virtue of its proximity. And by this reference—"if that which is the object in the *aṇ* state is that same object in the *ṇic* state"—the exclusion of any other object is effected. However, what is being established is not the existence of the object-status of the object in the *aṇ* state within the *ṇic* state.

Because his status as the agent is established by another sentence stating "he is the agent" (*sa kartā*), since it is contradictory for one and the same entity to simultaneously possess both the status of object and agent with respect to a single action. Since the remainder of the rule may be supplied as desired, the exclusion of any other object is obtained by supplying the word "only" (*eva*)—that is, "if that which was the object in the *aṇ* [causal] stage is indeed the object in the *ṇi* [causal] stage. Consequently, the third sentence, "he is the agent," has the purpose of establishing that what was the object in the *aṇ* stage becomes the agent in the *ṇi* stage.

When these [rules] form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), they constitute a "great sentence" (*mahāvākya*) which effects the refinement (*saṃskāraka*) of the object to be characterized. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the example given in the *Bhāṣya*, "The king shows his servants," because there exists another object, namely the servants, distinct from the king who is the object in the non-causative state (*aṇau*). For the exclusion applies only to an object other than those which are the agent and the object in the non-causative state; as in the case: "The elephant, being mounted, causes the men to mount the ground."

In this case, however, since the status of being the object (*karman*) in the *ṇic*-formation belongs only to those agents (*kartṛ*) who were [already] objects in the non-*ṇic* state—namely, the servants—the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) indeed occurs. For this very reason, the counter-example "The thicket of forest bushes causes him to remember by itself" (*smarayatyenaṃ vanagulmaḥ svayameva*) is consistent; such is the meaning following Kaiyaṭa. And it should not be argued: "Since the word 'yat' (in the rule) mentions only the object and not the agent as well, how can there be an exclusion of an object distinct from both the agent and the object? [This is because the rule intends to exclude an object other than that which was the agent in the non-*ṇic* state.]

From the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*, the term *kartari* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and transformed into the nominative case; then, by forming a *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena* compound with *yac ca* and *yaś ca*, and applying the rules for *ekaśeṣa* and *ekavadbhāva*, the explanation is established. In this way, even the initial usage *kareṇurārohayate niṣādinam* (“the female elephant causes the rider to mount”) becomes logically consistent.

In this regard, the following should be noted: when there is no other agent for that which is the object (*karman*) in a causative construction (*ṇyanta*), the *ātmanepada* ending is established precisely because of its status as both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*). For instance: "Devadatta cuts the field" (*lunāti kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*) becomes "the field cuts itself" (*lūyate kedāraḥ svayameva*). Just as the field is the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*) in the former, so it is also in the causative form: "the field causes itself to be cut" (*lāvayate kedāraḥ svayameva*). For the root *lū-* (to cut) functions with respect to the act of causing to become divided, having the state of being divided as its subordinate aspect.

This is because it is necessary for transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*) to denote an operation delimited by a result. In the sentence "Devadatta cuts the field" (*lunāti kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*), the meaning is that he causes the field—which is becoming divided—to become divided. When there is an intention to express an excellence of facility, the mere act of becoming divided is its meaning, since verbal roots possess multiple meanings.

In reality, there is a distinction between verbal roots (*dhātu*) based on a difference in meaning; however, due to their similarity in form, they are determined to be identical. In that context, regarding the field (*kedāra*) as the agent in the process of being split in two, the application *kedāraḥ svayameva lūyate* ("the field is being cut by itself") occurs because the operations of the object are extended [to the agent] by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*. The mention of the word *svayam* ("itself") is for the purpose of excluding any other agent. If, however, the sense were simply "by itself" (*ātmanā*), then the status of the object would indeed exist in relation to that [agent], and the result would have been established solely by the suffix *lakāra* in the passive voice.

Alternatively, while the root *lū* (to cut) primarily denotes the mere act of becoming divided, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to express the operation of an instigator such as Devadatta, the meanings of "Devadatta cuts the field" (*lunāti kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*) and "Devadatta causes the field to be cut" (*lāvayati kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*) are identical. Furthermore, when there is a desire to emphasize an excess of ease (*saukaryātiśaya*), and the operation of Devadatta is not intended to be expressed, the meaning of the root *lāv* (the causative form of *lū*) is merely the act of being divided.

In this regard, the meaning of "the field causes itself to be reaped" (*lāvayate kedāraḥ svayameva*) is identical to that of "the field is being reaped by itself" (*lūyate kedāraḥ svayameva*). Nor does the cessation of the relationship between the instigator and the instigated entail the cessation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), because the cessation of the means (*upāya*) does not imply the cessation of the end (*upeya*). This is because one accepts the division into base and suffix for the sake of deriving established words, as well as the adoption and abandonment of their respective meanings. For this very reason, in expressions such as "the crested one (*śikhī*) has perished," the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) does not cease even when the statement refers solely to the destruction of the attribute.
As it has been said:
"It is said that when the causal suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to a root from which the act of instigation has ceased, it expresses the original (primitive) meaning.

Thus, in this view where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*), there are four stages; the distinction is that among them, the first and third, as well as the second and fourth, have identical meanings. Now, for the view where the instigation is superimposed (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇapakṣa*): Devadatta cuts the field; because of an excess of facility, the field prompts Devadatta who is cutting. Thus, the *ṇic* is applied to the operation of the field: "The field causes Devadatta to cut" (*lāvayati kedāro devadattena*). The meaning is: one who possesses an operation conducive to that operation of Devadatta which is itself conducive to the act of cutting.

And that operation (*vyāpāra*)—such as the ripening of rice and so forth—is the cause of the ease of reaping. Furthermore, when there is no intention to express the relationship between the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*), and both instances of instigation (*preṣaṇa*) expressed by the verbal root and the causative suffix (*ṇic*) are simultaneously abandoned, one has the form *lāvayate kedāraḥ svayam eva* ("the field causes itself to be reaped"). Thus, there are three stages (*kakṣā*). In this case, the meaning is identical to that of the "withdrawn instigation" (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*), which is equivalent to the "superimposed instigation" (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*). This being the case, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established for the action of withdrawn instigation by the rule *karmavatkarmaṇā*.

In the sentence "Devadatta causes the field to be harvested" (*lāvayati kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*), the very same action that constitutes the state of being split into two parts—which is the object-state (*karmāvasthā*) of the field in the causative sense—is present in that same verbal root in its agent-state (*kartṛvasthā*). Therefore, the rule *aṇau cet sa kartā* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) need not have been formulated.

It should not be argued that, under the view of superimposed agency (*adhyāropitapakṣa*), because the elephant lacks the status of an object (*karman*) in the case of the verb *ārohayati*, there would be no status as an object within the same verbal root (*samānadhātu*); and consequently, the treatment as an object (*karmavadbhāva*)—as in "Devadatta cooks rice" versus "the rice cooks itself"—would not apply. Nor should it be argued that this would not hold even if one were to abandon the view of superimposed instigation (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇapakṣa*). For even upon abandoning the view of superimposed instigation, there is no loss; since all desired results are established simply by the cessation of the act of instigation (*preṣaṇakriyā*).

Nor should it be argued that this [sūtra] is intended for the purpose of excluding *yak* and *ciṇ*, on the grounds that it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) meaning: "If that which was the object in the *aṇ* [denominative base] becomes the agent in the *ṇi* [causative], then only the *ātmanepada* suffixes are used after the *ṇi*, and not others. This is because the Vārttika—"In the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there must be an addition for the causative *ṇi* of roots meaning 'to impel' (*hetu*), *śri*, and *brū*"—is indispensable, and the desired result is established by that alone.

But surely, in the case of *udapupucchata* ("he raised his tail"), the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.67] prohibiting the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes after a root ending in *ṇic* would apply to the reflexive sense; and since the word *puccha* denotes a substance (*dravya*), there is no object (*karman*) at all in its state prior to the addition of *ṇic*, so that prohibition would be unavoidable even by the present rule, because the word *puccha* occurs in reference to the act of raising which has the tail as its object. Therefore, the suffix *ṇiṅ* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*).

If it is argued that when the wagging tail, by virtue of its residual momentum (*saṃskāra*), is intended to be expressed as acting independently in the act of whirling—just like a wheel—it is then a restrictive rule that the *ātmanepada* ending alone should apply, as in *udapupucchata*, following the suffix *ṇiṅ*; [we reply: no, for here the Vārttika is recited by the Bhāṣyakāra and others even after omitting the word *hetumat*. Otherwise, [the form] *gaṇayati gaṇaṃ gopālakaḥ* would not be accounted for.

In the case of *gaṇaḥ svayam eva gaṇayati*, another rule would have to be initiated for the purpose of prohibiting the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes; for since the group (*gaṇa*) itself is the object of the action when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes would be unavoidable there by virtue of the present restrictive rule.

But surely, in this case, the very status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) is difficult to establish. To explain: the status of being "like the object" applies to verbs whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the object and those whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the object. Furthermore, the conventional distinction between "action" and "state" arises because they are accomplished by means (*sādhana*) characterized respectively by motion (*parispanda*) and its absence. If it is argued that "counting" (*gaṇana*)—which consists of a specific cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*) characterized by delimitation based on number—resides in the agent (*kartṛ*) and not in the object (*karman*), we say no. For the verb *gaṇayati* ("he counts") also functions in the sense of arranging [things] part by part.

The cowherd causes the herd, which is standing in parts, to stand as a whole. In that case, because the herd is the primary factor (anukūlatva), when there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the herd itself, there arises the possibility of the application of *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment of the subject like the object) due to its having a state residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvakatva*).

Regarding this, the authors of the *Vivaraṇa* maintain that although the word "tail" (*puccha*) is the object under the rule for the non-causal base (*aṇau*), this sūtra does not apply there; however, they admit that this is merely a concession (*abhyupagamyavāda*), because in reality the word "tail" does not function in the action whose object it is, which contradicts experience.

For this very reason, even though the term *ṇeḥ* (of *ṇi*) is used as a general designation, it does not include the *ṇiṅ* affixes such as those in *puccha-* and *bhāṇḍa-*, because, as Haradatta has also stated, "the status of being an object (*karman*) is impossible for [an action] in the non-causative (*aṇau*) stage. If it is argued that this rule exists so that the Ātmanepada may occur when what was an object in the non-causative stage becomes an object in the causative stage (*ṇau*), but it should not occur when what was an object in the non-causative stage becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative stage—this is not correct. For here too, the Ātmanepada is desired. Furthermore, since the causative suffix *ṇic* is compulsory (*nitya*) and there is no usage of roots like *cur* etc. alone without it, it would follow that an object in the non-causative stage is impossible; therefore, the causative *ṇic* due to an incentive (*hetumaṇṇic*) is what is intended by the term *ṇi*.

The prohibition "in the case of *aṇ*" is also logically applicable to that very [root] due to proximity; thus, since the group [of objects] is the object (*karman*) in the case of the non-causative (*aṇic*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) in the case of the causative (*ṇic*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be unavoidable even by the present sūtra.

Now, since it is impossible to enjoin a prohibition whose scope has not been specified, the entire sūtra is commenced for the purpose of prohibiting [the ātmanepada] in cases other than "causing to remember" (*anādhyāne*). If it is argued that the ātmanepada should not occur in the example, "The cuckoo remembers the forest thicket; the forest thicket itself causes him to remember," because here the state [of remembering] resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*), and thus there is no possibility for the application of the *karmavadbhāva* rule—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Although [the rule] is established by the application of *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment of the agent as the object) according to the method stated for those roots where the state resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*), this sūtra is intended to prescribe the *ātmanepada* endings for those roots where the state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*). To explain: the author of the Bhāṣya will state under the rule *yaddhituparaṃ chandasi* that the root *ruh* denotes a specific kind of motion. Nor should it be argued that even here the result, consisting of the act of bending down (*nyagbhāva*), resides in the object; for that [bending] does not constitute the primary result (*phala*) [of the action]. As it is said in the Vākyapadīya: "Where there is the perception of a specific change, there the action is established."

"But for others, the determination of the action is established solely by means of words. Therefore, the location of the action (tātsthya) is determined either by observing a specific change produced by the action or by following the meaning of the word. Thus, for verbal roots such as *paci* ("to cook"), the action resides in the object (*karmastha*), because rice and the like are perceived as possessing states such as softening (*viklitti*). Wherever a change produced by the action is perceived in the object even after the action has ceased, there alone does the action reside in the object. However, it is quite clear that this is not the case in instances such as *jānāti* ("he knows").

In the case of the verb *ārohati* ("ascends"), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is simply the activity conducive to going upwards, and not the subduing of an elephant or other object. For the instruction is "I should go upwards," and not "let there be the subduing of the elephant. Precisely for this reason, when one bends down a branch while standing on the ground, the expression *ārohati* is not used. Therefore, since verbs such as *ārohati* do not have a state residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvakatva*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed for them by this rule.

For instance, elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the meaning is that they cause it to bend down. Then, when the activity of the elephant-keepers ceases, the elephant mounts [the rider]; the meaning is that it bends down.
As it was said by Bhartṛhari:
"When the instigation has ceased, the object remains situated in its own constituent action."
"When the status of being an object (*karmatva*) ceases, it remains in the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*).

Thus, "one whose prompting has ceased" (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*) refers to that which is not intended [to be expressed] as the locus of the result produced by the agent's operation. Rather, it is intended to be expressed independently as residing within its own sphere, as a constituent of the action consisting of the result, by virtue of delimiting a specific action. In such a co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), since the result itself constitutes the action, the locus of that result possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*). However, because the qualified operation (*viśiṣṭavyāpāra*) is not considered the action here, the locus of that [operation] does not possess the status of an agent.

The meaning is that when the *para* (the object) is distinguished [as the primary], since the operation (*vyāpāra*) itself constitutes the action (*kriyā*), that which is the locus of the result (*phala*) is precisely the object (*karman*). Consequently, when the causative suffix *ṇic* has its causal force withdrawn (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*), one says: "The elephant-keepers cause the elephant to mount" (*ārohayanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*), which means "they cause [him] to mount. Then, upon further abandoning the meaning of the causative, one says: "The elephant mounts" (*ārohayate hastī*), which means "it becomes lowered" (*nyagbhavati*). As it has been said:
"In the case of the root *ruh* in its pure form, both the causing of lowering (*nyagbhāvana*) and the act of lowering itself (*nyagbhavana*) are understood."
The meanings "making subordinate" (*nyagbhāvanam*) and "becoming subordinate" (*nyagbhavanam*) are understood even when the suffix *ṇic* is present.
He describes the fifth state: the causative (*ṇyanta*) occurs when that same object acts as the agent;
the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is said to be applied to the root in its original sense once the instigation has ceased.

Although in the first stage (*kakṣā*) subordination (*nyagbhavana*) is indeed perceived through the cognition of the operation delimited by the result, nevertheless, the meaning is that subordination itself possesses the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). Therefore, in the second stage, when the aspect of the operation alone is set aside, only subordination is perceived; this is the second stage.

Then, in the causative (*ṇyanta*) form, subordination (*nyagbhāvana*) is understood just as in the first stage; this is the third stage. However, this is the distinction: in the simple verb (*śuddha*), both [subordination and the act of subordination] are the meaning of the root *ruh*; but in the causative, the meaning of the root *ruh* is subordination, while the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*). Then, when there is the intention to express the operation that is the meaning of the causative suffix, the fourth stage is exactly like the second stage. Here, the distinction is that in the simple causative, subordination is cognized through the primary power (*śakti*), whereas the act of subordinating is cognized through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Regarding the phrase "in the primary sense" (*prākṛte 'rthe*), some maintain that it means "belonging to the base (*prakṛti*) in a sense common to both the denoted and the indicated.

However, the authors of the *Vivaraṇa* explain it as "in the primary [sense], that is, in what is expressed by the base," referring to that which denotes the prompted agent alone when the instigation has ceased.

Their position is as follows: if one accepts that the expressive power (*śakti*) of a verbal root resides in an operation delimited by a result, then the cognition of the result alone occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because it is accepted that when words denoting a qualified entity are used with reference to the qualifier alone, the process is necessarily one of indication. However, if one accepts a partial expressive power for both the result and the operation, then—due to the absence of speaker-intent (*tātparya*) regarding the operation—the cognition of the result occurs through primary expressive power (*śakti*) itself, while the operation remains uncognized.

If, however, it is maintained that because the partial power (*khaṇḍaśakti*) is denotative only by being included within a single utterance, its cognition in each individual form is strictly through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and for this very reason the established doctrine is that from words such as *puṣpavant* the cognition of either "moon-ness" or "sun-ness" alone occurs only through indication—then, if one adopts this modern approach, it should be understood that the cognition of subordination (*nyagbhavana*) occurs only through indication.
It might be argued: since only four stages have been mentioned, how can there be a fifth state?

On this point, some say: "According to the aforementioned method, when the fourfold cognition has arisen, the *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed by the present sūtra; thus, with respect to the sequence of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti-krama*), there is a fifth stage, yet for the sake of actual usage (*prayoga-arha*), there are only four stages.

The authors of the *Kaustubha*, however, maintain that since the two pure forms (*śuddha-ṇyantau*)—which denote the qualified [agent]—have two denotable portions (*vācya-aṃśau*) due to the difference in their denoters (*vācaka-bheda*), these are counted as two; thus, they state that the four states are intended to be situated in the third stage, while the fifth state is intended for the fourth stage.

Thus, the root *dṛś* (to see) has as its purpose the bringing about of the status of being an object, with the attainment of that status being subordinate. "The devotees see Bhava" means they make him an object of the eye. When the activity of the devotees is set aside, [the sentence] becomes "Bhava sees," meaning he becomes an object of the eye. However, this is the distinction: in the second stage of roots such as *lū* (to cut), when the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, there occurs the application of the rule for "acting like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*), because the action consists of a state residing in the object; but this is not the case here in both instances.

And thus the commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "The root *ruh* has an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*); the root *dṛś* has a state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāva*). This has already been explained previously. Therefore, in the causative form (*ṇic*), as in *darśayanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ* ("the devotees cause Bhava to see"), the meaning is the same as in the first stage (the primitive form). Then, when the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is not intended to be expressed, one says *darśayate bhavaḥ* ("Bhava sees"); this is the meaning corresponding to the second stage. By the present rule, however, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed; such is the direction.

On this point, the initiates [into the tradition] state as follows: For Kaiyaṭa and others who describe it in this manner, there is a contradiction with the text of the *sūtra*, the *bhāṣya*, and the *vārttika* under discussion. For, in the first section, when the objection of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) was raised regarding the example "the elephant being mounted causes the men to mount the ground," it was established that [the rule does not apply] because of the existence of another object (*karman*), namely "the men.
