In the second section, when the objection was raised that "it is established by virtue of being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*"), it was established that [the rule applies] "for the purpose of excluding *yak* and *ciṇ*. In the third section, it was established that [the rule applies] "for the sake of cases where the state [of the action] resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāva*)."

Among these, the first is contradictory, because humans are agents (*kartṛ*) with respect to the atom (*aṇu*). Since, in this context, the agent and the object of the human state are themselves the objects [of the action], there is no additional object; consequently, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be unavoidable. The second [position] is also contradictory, because according to the reasoning stated therein, the status of being "like an object" (*karmavadbhāva*) is simply absent. For the Vārttika states: "Those that are intransitive are like [those that have] an object. For this very reason, the third [position] is also not tenable. Thus, it results in a mere forgetting of the subject matter; this is a great oversight, even for the great.

Furthermore, a statement intended for the exclusion of other actions would be entirely fruitless, because such an example is difficult to find. For it is not possible for there to exist two objects (*karman*) distinct from those which are the agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) in the case of a root with the suffix *ṇic* (*aṇau*), such that this [rule] could exclude them. Regarding this, some say: although Haradatta and others have stated in the first section that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the object "men" (*manuṣyān*) exists, Kaiyaṭa has not so stated; for his intention was simply that there is no over-extension because the object in its physical form (*sthalarūpa*) exists.

Having refuted the view that the rule serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*) as intended by the author of the *Vārttika*, Kaiyaṭa follows the *Bhāṣya* which establishes the rule as having an injunctive purpose (*vidhyarthatva*). Consequently, his contradiction with the second section of the *Vārttika* is of no consequence. Furthermore, you yourself must accept the injunctive nature of the rule even in cases where the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakriya*). Nor is the third alternative [tenable], because Kaiyaṭa has described the meaning exactly in accordance with the *Bhāṣya* of the third section; thus, by speaking in this way, you have forgotten your own objective.

Thus, the conclusion is this: the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is simply that the commencement of the sūtra is for the sake of actions residing in the agent (*kartṛstha-kriyā*), and not that the application of this sūtra is restricted only to those instances where the object becomes the agent and the verbal root denotes an action residing in the agent; for there is no evidence for such a restriction. However, in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, the example "the king causes his servants to see [himself]" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*) serves as an indicator of the intended meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the example must be one where the action is intransitive (*akarmaka*) because of the doubt that [the reflexive] is established by virtue of being both object and agent; for that [rule] applies solely to the specific case of "the field causes itself to be harvested" (*lāvayate kedāraḥ*). Otherwise, the counter-example "the thicket of forest causes him to remember all by itself" (*smarayatyenaṃ vanagulmaḥ svayameva*) would be inconsistent.

As for what Kaiyaṭa and others have stated—that here the object (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed—since the word "him" (*enam*) exists as an object here, there is no possibility of the treatment of the verb as having an object (*karmavadbhāva*) by virtue of the rule *karmavad akarmakāṇām*. However, this does not preclude the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by that very sūtra, because another object [the self] is present. Therefore, it should be demonstrated as: "The thicket of forest bushes causes itself to be remembered" (*smarayati vanagulmaḥ svayam eva*). The root *smṛ* belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group; the meaning is that it becomes the object of a recollection preceded by longing (*utkaṇṭhā*).

And as for what was explained regarding the example "there is a herd [of cows] on the deep river" (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), where—even after the cognition of the non-difference between the referents of the words "deep" and "river" has occurred, and even when there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank—the meaningfulness of the word "deep" is established by taking into account the initial cognition; so too here, in the view that the causal operation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, in the second stage when the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has been construed with the object, and subsequently even the object is abandoned, the meaningfulness of the causative suffix and the word denoting the object is somehow established by taking into account the initial cognition, through the relation of that which is to be made known (*svajñāpyasaṃbandha*).

This is because it is accepted as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and because that which is to be made known here consists of the meaning of a qualified sentence. This indeed is the way in which praise is indicated through *arthavāda*s. This is the method for explaining established [words]. However, since the employment of words is under one's own control, it would be more appropriate to employ them entirely free from [the category of] objects (*karman*). Or, having accepted that [usage], it is stated merely as a formal discussion (*vādamātra*) because it follows the opinion of the Vārttika; for Kaiyaṭa has himself demonstrated in the remainder of the Sūtra, according to the aforementioned method, that there is an intention to express the object (*karma-vivakṣā*).

By this, the following is refuted: the claim that the primary examples concern the *karmakartṛ* (the agent as object), while the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply because the action and its state reside in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakriyatva*), as established in the core of the Siddhānta according to the conclusions of the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other works. This is because it has already been stated that there is no evidence for restricting [the rule] to only those roots that are intransitive (*akarmaka*); furthermore, there is no obstacle to its application even to such transitive roots, just as it applies to cases where the state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāva*) when they are outside the scope of *karmavadbhāva*.

By this, the argument beginning with "in the case of *gabhīrāyām*" and so forth is also refuted; for there is a disparity between that sentence, where the word *gabhīra* has already produced a cognitive connection (*anvayabodha*), and the present sentence, where—according to your own view—the object (*karman*) does not contribute to the production of a cognitive connection.

As for your claim that in the second stage (*kakṣā*) of the position involving the superimposition of the instigating act (*preṣaṇādhyāropa*), there is a connection with the object—that too is incorrect.

That is incorrect; for even if there is connection with other sentences, there would be a lack of purposefulness in that specific sentence itself unless it were connected within it. As for the causative suffix (*ṇic*), however, since its application is justified as being merely expressive of its own meaning (*svārthika*), it does not incur the fault of redundancy; thus there is a disparity between the two cases. Furthermore, because all sentences would be connected within other sentences, it would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of having to include words that are not actually connected within a particular sentence.

In the case of an *arthavāda*, such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," since the literal meaning is not sublated, the excellence consisting of praise is indicated through the very relationship with the sentence-meaning—namely, that Vāyu, possessing the quality of swiftness (*kṣepiṣṭhatva*) which is the object of the verbal cognition produced by the knowledge of the literal sense, bestows the fruit arising from the ritual for which he is the presiding deity most rapidly.

In cases such as "The sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle)," however, because the literal meaning is sublated, there first arises a verbal cognition (*śābda*) through secondary indication (*gauṇī*) that the *prastara* performs a function similar to the function performed by the sacrificer. Subsequently, based on the relationship with the sentence-meaning consisting of its own performance of that function, excellence (*prāśastya*) is indicated (*lakṣyate*). It is not the case that this [excellence] belongs to the sentence-meaning itself while the meanings of the words being heard remain unconnected; therefore, this objection is of no consequence.

It might be argued: "If this were so, then even in the second stage of the view where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, the ātmanepada suffix would necessarily occur; consequently, the use of the parasmaipada suffix in the phrase *lāvayati kedāro devadattena* as employed by Kaiyaṭa himself would be inconsistent.
To this they reply: "The reading is such only due to the error of a scribe."

As for what was stated by the authors of the *Vivaraṇa*—"The mention of *ṇau* (causative) is for the sake of [indicating] a common action; and since the causative (*ṇyanta*) does not have a common action with the non-causative (*aṇyant*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not applied"—that should be disregarded because it is motivated solely by a dullness of faith in the passage of Haradatta which is yet to be cited. We shall explain this further below. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is nothing to be excluded by the sentence intended to preclude other objects (*karmāntara-nivṛtti*), [we respond as follows].

That is incorrect; for the authors of both the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya have stated that the very purpose of the rule "ārohayamāṇo hastī sthalamārohayati manuṣyān" (the elephant, being mounted, causes men to mount the dry land) is precisely to exclude such cases. Therefore, to assert its absence is nothing but mere rashness.

However, this is the distinction: the author of the Vārttika, taking the meaning of the sūtra exactly as it was heard, began the statement: "In the prescription of the ātmanepada for the causative (*ṇi*), there is the perception of the object of that which ends in *am*; otherwise, there would be over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*). Its meaning is this: when that which is the object of the causative ending in *am* becomes the very same object when the verb is in its non-causative form (*aṇyanta*), then the ātmanepada occurs.

However, the Commentator (Patañjali), relying on the method stated by Kaiyaṭa in his previous citation, has avoided the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case by means of the very words of the Sūtra itself, by resorting to a distinction between intermediate sentences (*avāntaravākyabheda*). If it is argued: "Since Kaiyaṭa has stated that the intention [of the Sūtra] is to exclude a *karman* other than those which are the *kartṛ* and *karman* in the causative (*ṇic*), and since in the example 'men are making the platform ascend' (*ārohanti sthalaṃ manuṣyāḥ*), both the men and the platform—which are the *kartṛ* and *karman* respectively in the non-causative (*aṇic*)—become the *karman* in the causative (*ṇyant*), the Ātmanepada should indeed occur here," we say: No.

In the sentence "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant," there exists another object—namely "the ground"—distinct from the agent (the elephant-keepers) and the object (the elephant) associated with the root *aṇ* (in its non-causative sense). Nor should it be argued that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by taking the state of the root in its non-causative form, as in "Men mount the ground," because in that state, what constitutes the object (the ground) lacks the status of being an agent in the aforementioned causative state; thus, the objection is already precluded by the very meaning of the third rule.

Since it is impossible to establish an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by taking the agent and object present in the non-causal (*aṇyanta*) state and the absence of any object other than those, it follows that the intended meaning is the exclusion of any object other than those very agents and objects which, in that same non-causal state, become the agent and object respectively in the causal (*ṇyanta*) state. Thus, in the case of *ārohayamāṇo hastī* ("the elephant being made to mount"), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) indeed occurs.

In the third stage of the position where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, there is no fault whatsoever; for since the qualificand itself is absent, there is necessarily an absence of an object distinct from it. However, in the second stage of the sentence *darśyate bhṛtyai rājā* ("The king is caused to be seen by the servants"), which corresponds to the non-causative (*aṇyantā*) state—namely, *paśyanti bhṛtyā rājānam* ("The servants see the king")—the servants, who are the agents (*kartṛ*), themselves become the objects (*karman*). Thus, because there is no agent-object distinct [from the object], the specific absence [required by the definition] does not occur. Therefore, there is no defect.

By this, the separation from Bhāravi is also explained: "Free from pride, he constantly shows his kin as if they were under his own sovereignty. For this very reason, in the commentary on the *vārttika*—"An addition regarding *abhivādi* and *dṛśi* when the *ātmanepada* is used"—under the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām*, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have explained that in the examples "the servants see the king," "the king shows himself to the servants," and "the king shows himself by means of the servants," the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by virtue of the rule *ṇeraṇau*.

Nor should it be said that this *bhāṣya* intends only the exclusion of the notion of "object" (*karmasañjñā*). For there is no evidence (*māna*) for such a restriction. By this, the meaning of the second sentence is already understood through proximity (*pratyāsatti*). When it is stated, "The *ātmanepada* suffix shall occur after a *ṇi*-caused root, provided that what was the object in the non-*ṇi* form (*aṇau*) becomes the agent in the *ṇi*-caused form (*ṇau*)," it is understood through proximity as follows: by whichever *ṇic* the *ātmanepada* is intended to be prescribed after a *ṇi*-caused root, if that very same thing which was the object in its original non-*ṇi* base (*prakṛti*) is the agent in that very same *ṇi*-caused form. However, in cases where this condition is fulfilled, the *ātmanepada* is indeed applied, as in the example *ārohayamāṇaḥ*.

Regarding the statement that "in *sthalam ārohayati*, because the object *sthala* lacks the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative (*ṇi*), this condition (*upādhi*) simply does not exist, and thus there is no occasion for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)," that too is incorrect. For in the sentence *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("the elephant-keepers are mounting the elephant"), just as there is an absence of the causative suffix (*ṇi*) within the base of the present participle suffix (*śānac*), there is likewise an absence of the causative suffix within the base of the finite verb ending (*tiṅ*). Consequently, since the agenthood of the object *hastin* exists in the causative form *sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān* ("he causes the men to mount the platform"), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the rule is unavoidable.

If it is argued that in the case of *manuṣyāḥ sthalam ārohanti* ("people are making [themselves] ascend the dry land"), since the ground (*sthala*) is the object of the causative (*aṇ*), it cannot be the agent there—[we ask]: does the proponent of proximity (*pratyāsatti-vādin*) maintain that for as many things as there are objects in the *aṇ*-stem, there must be that many agents in the causative (*ṇi*-stem)? If you say "yes," it is not so; for in the third stage involving superimposed instigation (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇa*), such as *ārohayamāṇo hastī* ("the elephant is being made to mount [riders]"), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

In the case of "men ascend the ground" (*manuṣyāḥ sthalam ārohanti*), because the ground (*sthala*), which is the object in the state without the causative suffix (*aṇyantāvasthā*), lacks the status of an agent in the third stage [of the causative process], [there is no over-extension]. By this, the objection that there would be an over-extension in the aforementioned example—on the grounds that by taking the identity based on the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇitva*), the elephant (*hastin*) itself, which is the object in the absence of the *ṇi* contained within the base of the present middle participle (*śānac*), becomes the agent in the meaning of the causative base of the finite verb (*tiṅ*)—is also refuted.

Some hold that since the absence of the *ṇi* contained within the base of the finite verb is also present there, the over-extension is established by the aforementioned method alone; thus, there is no purpose in intending to express identity based on the presence of the causative suffix.

It might be argued: "The meaning of the term 'proximity' (*pratyāsatti*) is that when a *ṇic* suffix is intended such that the *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed for the *ṇi*-derived form, then the *ātmanepada* occurs after such a *ṇi*-derived form where—upon the absence of that *ṇic*—those two [the agent and the object] possess the status of object and agent respectively. This is not correct, because there is no coverage (*avyāpti*) for the third stage involving superimposed instigation (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*) and the fourth stage involving ceased instigation (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*), since in those cases the object is not established.

Now, if it is argued that, according to the circumstances, the agent of the *ṇic*-formed verb becomes the object of the non-*ṇic* (*aṇ*) verb, and the object of the *ṇic*-formed verb becomes the agent of the non-*ṇic* verb—this is not so. For the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains as it was in the aforementioned case; because in the third stage of the process where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*), the object of the *ṇic*-formed verb (the humans) exists as the agent of the non-*ṇic* verb. Furthermore, there is an over-extension even in the second stage, such as in "The elephant mounts [him]," where the object of the *ṇic*-formed verb (the elephant) exists as the agent of the non-*ṇic* verb.

It might be argued as follows: Let it be that for which the *ātmanepada* affix is intended after a *ṇic*-derived root, when that *ṇic* is absent, there is a certain result that delimits the meaning of the verbal root; then, from that *ṇic*-derived root where that very same result delimits the meaning of the root, or where that result constitutes the meaning of the root itself, the *ātmanepada* affix occurs.

In the case of *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("the elephant-keepers mount the elephant"), the factor that delimits the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is "descending" (*nyagbhavana*). However, in the case of *sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān* ("he causes the men to mount the platform"), the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the operation conducive to "descending," as well as the operation conducive to that [operation] which resides in the men. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The platform is descending; the elephant possesses the operation conducive to that [descent]."

In that context, the state of being subordinated (*nyagbhāvanā*) is precisely the delimitor of the delimitor of the meaning of the causative root (*ṇyantadhātu*), and not the delimitor of the root-meaning itself, nor the root-meaning. Since it is only the two operations (*vyāpāra*) that possess such a status in succession, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It was stated, "or the root-meaning," because in the final stage (*caramakakṣā*), since the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the delimitor of the root-meaning is unestablished.

Furthermore, the statement "the king does not show [himself] to the servants" would not be a case of *saṃgraha* (inclusion), because the [action of] making [them] reach the state of being an object lacks the property of delimiting the meaning of the verbal root. For in the sentence "the servants see the king," the meaning of the root *dṛś* (to see) is indeed the bringing about of the state of being an object, where the state of being an object is subordinate. However, when another instigation (*preṣaṇā*) is superimposed, the resulting cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya-bodha*) is as follows: the king is the locus of that operation which is conducive to the visual contact and so forth residing in the servants—which is itself conducive to the operation that brings about the state of being an object; and this [latter] operation consists in staying in a location favorable to the visual contact and so forth.

It must be stated that when [the action] results in the attainment of objecthood (*viṣayatvāpatti*), the fact that it resides in the king is understood by implication; and in that case, it is precisely the contact of the eye (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyoga*) and so forth that serves as the delimitor of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyat*), rather than the attainment of objecthood itself.

Because, in the state where the suffix *ṇic* is absent, the term "delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*) is intended to refer to that which is the locus of the result [of the action], provided that it is not understood as residing in anything other than the locus of that result; and because it is intended to refer to that which is the locus of the result delimiting the meaning of the verbal root, provided that it is not understood as residing in anything other than the locus of that result, while being merely a qualifier (*prakāratva*) of the meaning of the verbal root, whether directly or through a causal chain (*sākṣāt-paramparā-sādhāraṇa*).

And here, because there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since the state of not being perceived as having an occurrence other than the king—which is the attainment of the status of being an object—is present; for in the case of "the elephant-keepers mount the elephant," although the act of subordination (*nyagbhavana*) is perceived in the sentence "he makes the men mount the elephant onto a spot" as having an occurrence on a spot other than the elephant (which is the substratum of the subordination that delimits the meaning of the verbal root), there is no over-extension. If this is argued, we say: No.

For, by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), that which ends in *ṇic*—wherein the absence of its counter-positive (*pratiyogika-abhāva*) serves as the indicator of the object (*karma*) and the state of ending in *ṇic* serves as the qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*)—is to be understood as that single specific instance of *ṇic*. Once this much is established, the meaning of the rule is as follows: "In a case where, during the state of being *ṇic*-inflected, the substratum of the result delimited by the root-meaning is the same as the substratum of the operation denoted by *ṇic*, there shall be *ātmanepada* after the *ṇic*-inflected form. Thus, even in the aforementioned instance, the desired result is achieved once the contingency has arisen.

However, since it is not understood as extending up to the point where it is not perceived to reside in anything other than what has been stated, it is necessary to resort to the meaning of the second sentence in the manner described in order to obtain such a sense; thus, the intended meaning is established from that very source, according to the intention of the Blessed One. Therefore, it is a rash claim to say that whatever meaning is intended by the force of the second sentence's meaning is obtained through proximity even when there is unity of the sentence.

Thus, this is the essential conclusion of the Bhāṣya: when a root is in the *ṇic* (causative) form, those two which are indeed the substrata of the result and the operation in the non-causative form—wherever those exist in the causative form, there is an absence of any other object; that [original] object becomes the agent (*kartṛ*), and from such a verbal root, the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs, provided the meaning is not that of "meditation" (*anādhyāna*). This path penetrates the knots of the intention found in the principal texts of the Vārttika, the Bhāṣya, and Kaiyaṭa.

According to the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti*, however, the meaning is as follows: the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after a root with the causative marker (*ṇic*), provided it does not denote "thinking" (*adhyāna*). The purpose of the rule *aṇau yatkarma* ("that which is the object in the non-causative") is to exclude other objects. The explanation follows exactly the method stated by Kaiyaṭa. The only difference is this: in that [other view], the exclusion of other objects is obtained by the phrase ending with *ṇau cet*; here, however, it is obtained by the phrase *aṇau yatkarma* alone. Because of the force of the context and because of the proximity of the word *ṇeḥ* ("of the causative"), it is established that the status of being the agent in the causative state is prescribed for that which was the object in the non-causative state.

Because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) in the *aṇ* [causal] stage is already established by the force of the restatement (*anuvāda*) "that which is an object in the *aṇ*," it is useless to enjoin that very same thing there again. Thus, the word "object" (*karman*) refers only to the object itself, and not to both the agent and the object.

The third sentence is "if [it is] in the *ṇ*" (*ṇau cet*). By the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of "that which in the *aṇ*," the meaning is: if that very thing which was expressed in the *aṇ* is also to be expressed in the *ṇ*, [then this rule applies]. This is because the natural sense of the commentary (*vṛtti*) is that the mention of "if in the *ṇ*" is for the purpose of ensuring the identity of the action (*samānakriyārtha*).

"He is the agent"—this is the fourth [rule]. Its meaning is: "If that which was the object (*karman*) in the *aṇ* [root] becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇi* [causative], [then the *ātmanepada* affix is used]. Furthermore, under the view that the prohibition is a general negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), "except when there is reflection" (*anādhyāne*) is the fifth sentence. Examples: *Ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* (The elephant-keepers mount the elephant). *Ārohayate hastī svayameva* (The elephant mounts himself). *Siñcanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* (The elephant-keepers sprinkle the elephant). *Secayate hastī svayameva* (The elephant sprinkles himself). *Paśyanti bhṛtyā rājānam* (The servants see the king). *Darśayate rājā svayameva* (The king sees himself). Why is it said "after the *ṇi*" (*ṇeḥ*)? [To exclude cases where the *ṇi* is not present.]

The elephant-keepers mount the elephant; as he is being mounted, the elephant mounts well. Why [is it said] "in the case of a non-anu"? [Consider: *gaṇayati gaṇaṃ gopālaḥ* ("the cowherd counts the herd"), *gaṇayati gaṇaḥ svayameva* ("the herd counts itself"). The root *gaṇ* in the sense of counting belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in a long vowel (*a*). Due to the status of the elision of that *a* as being *sthānivadbhūta*, there is no *vṛddhi* [strengthening]. When the herd being counted attains favorability toward the act of counting, then, because the causative suffix *ṇic* functions solely with respect to that [herd's] activity, [the form arises]. Furthermore, this is the counter-example in the state where the instigation has ceased.

In the case of the causative suffix *ṇic*, the group (*gaṇa*) is the object and the agent is the same as there; therefore, the *ātmanepada* ending does not apply. Nor does it apply by virtue of the "treatment like an object" (*karmavadbhāva*), because the action resides in the agent. This is because counting—which consists of a specific cognition caused by number—occurs only in the agent. Why is the mention of "object" (*karman*) necessary? [Consider: *lunāti dātreṇa* ("he cuts with a sickle") and *lāvayati dātraṃ svayameva* ("the sickle causes itself to cut"). In the non-causative state (*aṇyantāvasthā*), the sickle functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*). The mention of "*ṇau*" (in the causative) is for the purpose of ensuring the action is identical. [Example: *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("the elephant-keepers mount the elephant").

An elephant being mounted sprinkles those who are afraid with its urine. Even though there is a difference in action characterized by the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the one being instigated (*prayojya*), let there not be the *ṇic* affix; rather, it should apply only when the action is already expressed by the verbal root itself—this is the intended meaning. Although the reflexive middle (*ātmanepada*) is indeed prevented by this rule even when there is a difference in action due to the relationship between the instigator and the instigated, nevertheless, the different verbal root *secayati* is cited as a counter-example in order to demonstrate an absolute difference [in the actions]. Furthermore, in this context, those who are afraid are the object (*karman*) of the verb *ā-ruh*, not of the verb *siñc*.

In the word *ārohayamāṇa*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule *ṇicaśca*; alternatively, it may be formed with the suffix *cānaś*. For those who are being made to mount [the elephant] out of fear urinate out of that very fear, and by that the elephant is sprinkled. Since the object is not intended to be expressed, the root *sic* (to sprinkle) is treated as intransitive (*akarmaka*). The inclusion of the term *yat* is for the purpose of excluding other objects; for it is said:

"When the connection is already established through the reference and the subsequent mention, the repeated use of *tat* serves to exclude other objects by means of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)."

Therefore, elephant-keepers mount the elephant. In the case of the sentence "the mounting elephant causes men to mount onto dry land," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur, because there exists another object consisting of the men.

Although the *ātmanepada* is already established for the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), this rule must nevertheless apply only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the same [as the object in the causal construction]; the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is stated for the purpose that it should apply only when that very agent who was the object in the non-causal (*aṇi*) stage becomes the agent in the causal (*ṇi*) stage, and not when there is a different agent. Therefore, in the example *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("the elephant-keepers mount the elephant"), the rule does not apply to *tān ārohayati mahāmātraḥ* ("the chief keeper makes them mount"). Since the root *ruh* signifies motion (*gatyartha*), the elephant-keepers receive the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*). If this is so, then the rule will simply not apply here because of the presence of another object.

This is not so. For here, even when there is no *ṇic* suffix, the elephant (*hastin*) is construed as the object (*karman*) both in the absence of the causative and in its presence. Furthermore, unless there is a rule prescribing [the agenthood of the original agent], the exclusion of other objects cannot be obtained. Alternatively, because the focus is on the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), this serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for those cases where the elephant-keepers (*hastipaka*) are not intended to be expressed as the object. [Question: What is the purpose of the restriction "except in the sense of remembering" (*anādhyāne*)? [Answer: *smarati vanagulmaṃ kokilaḥ* ("The cuckoo remembers the forest thicket"). *smarayaty enaṃ kokilaṃ vanagulmaḥ* ("The forest thicket causes the cuckoo to remember it").

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the genitive case in *vanagulmasya* is intended as an indication of the status of being an object (*karma*). When there is a desire to express the agency (*prayojakatva*) for the purpose of demonstrating the beauty of the forest thicket, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied. As for the word *enam*, because its referent is present in the mind, the cuckoo receives the designation of "object" (*karman*). This too is merely an illustration, since the [application of the rule] would not otherwise occur due to the existence of another object. Therefore, the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) should be understood as occurring when the status of being an object is not intended to be expressed; such is the meaning according to Haradatta. We shall explain this further below.

The authors of the *Kaustubha*, however, have explained [the sūtra] as follows: *ṇeḥ* is one sentence; its meaning is as before. *aṇau yatkarma ṇau cet* is the second [sentence]; its meaning is that if the very action which was the object (*karman*) in the non-causative (*aṇ*) is expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇi*), [then the agent of the non-causative becomes the object of the causative]. This is because, as in the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*, the word *karman* is understood here to refer to the action (*kriyā*). *sa kartā* is the third [sentence]; by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase beginning with *aṇau*, the meaning is that the factor which was the object (*karmakāraka*) with respect to the meaning of the base of the causative suffix (*ṇic-prakṛti*) is itself the agent (*kartā*) when the causative suffix is present.

Because, by relying on the governing authority of the term *śabda*, the word *karman* (object) is here explained as referring to a specific *kāraka* (participant in an action). Furthermore, in both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, the word *karman* occurring in the second sentence must also be explained as referring to the action (*kriyā*) itself. The purpose of the second sentence, however, is to ensure that [the definition] does not apply in the second stage (*kakṣā*) under the view that the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed; for in that case, due to the addition of the instigation, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). The purpose of the third sentence, moreover, is to ensure that [the definition] does not apply in the third stage under the view that the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*).

In that case, since there is only the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and not the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) in the atom (*aṇu*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Furthermore, in the view where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*), because the meaning of the third sentence is connected with the first stage and the meaning of the second sentence is connected with the second stage at the fourth stage, there is no over-extension.

In this regard, the following must be said: since the author of the Bhāṣya accepts the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) even in the second stage where the causative force (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, the exclusion [of such cases] is untenable. Likewise, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the third stage as well; for in the case of *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("the elephant-keepers mount the elephant"), one perceives an activity qualified by the act of subduing (*nyagbhavana*), whereas in *ārohayate hastī* ("the elephant causes itself to be mounted"), one perceives merely the act of subduing. Thus, because the actions are not identical, the definition fails to apply.

As for the claim that only the excess of the action is excluded, and not its deficiency as well—that is incorrect. For if the very same action denoted by the root were also expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), then only the exclusion of both deficiency and excess would be perceived. This is because, taking "being the action denoted by the root" as the delimiting property of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*), there is a perception not only of the exclusion of being denoted by the causative suffix in anything other than what is delimited by that [root-action], but also of the fact that it is denoted by the causative suffix in that which is so delimited.

This is because of the rule that the cognition of the property serving as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) denoted by the particle *eva*—which has the property to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*) as its qualifier—manifests both as a qualifier and as the delimiting factor of the objective determination (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatayā*). Therefore, in such cases as "Pārtha alone is the archer," the exclusion of being an archer from anyone other than Pārtha and the possession of archery by Pārtha are both understood.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the doubt, "Is Pārtha an archer or not? would not be removed by the comprehension of the meaning of that sentence; such is the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*).

It might be argued as follows: In the sentence *ārohati hastī* ("the elephant mounts"), in the second stage where the causal suffix has ceased its operation (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*), since "merely becoming submissive" (*nyagbhavanamātra*) is the action denoted by the verbal root, there is indeed the cognition that this is expressed by the causative (*ṇic*) simply through its coreferentiality with the delimitor of the qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*). Thus, even though [the condition for the *ātmanepada*] is not met in the final stage because of the impossibility of the equality of all actions delimited by the aforementioned delimitor of the qualificandumhood, the *ātmanepada* suffix remains easily obtainable. This is not so.

In the view where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be unavoidable even in the second stage [of derivation]. This is because, in the case of *ārohati* as well, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) can be included within the root meaning; thus, the cognition produced by the sentence *ārohati hastipakān hastī*—namely, "the elephant possesses an activity conducive to an activity residing in the elephant-driver which is conducive to its own subordination"—is identical to the cognition produced by the sentence *ārohayati hastipakān hastī*. Consequently, there would be an equality between the causative (*ṇyanta*) and non-causative (*aṇyanta*) forms in terms of their having the same action (*samānakriyatva*).

Even in the third stage (*kakṣā*) involving superimposed instigation (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇa*), the statement regarding the equality of action is made by taking recourse to the second stage where instigation has ceased (*nivṛtta-preṣaṇa*). There is no status as agent for that which was the object in the *aṇ* [root] in the *ṇic* [derivative], because in that case, the very elephant—which was the object in the first stage—is the object there; since the elephant-drivers alone are the agents in both instances, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and thus there is a disparity. If it is argued that this stage was not mentioned by the authors of the treatises, we say no, because when the underlying logic (*nyāya*) is the same, such an omission is irrelevant.

If the mere fact of having the same meaning as a causative (*ṇyanta*) were the sole basis for [the action] being external, then even the first and second positions regarding the "withdrawal of the instigation" (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*) would be subject to annihilation. Furthermore, it is unproven that the authors of the treatises did not state this, for it is explained by many commentators even in the case of the simple root (*śuddha*), by including the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij*) within it. Moreover, in the *Vākyapadīya*, it is stated directly that the fifth stage belongs to the action in the sentence "the elephant makes itself mount" (*ārohayate hastī*): "He states the fifth stage: 'The causative [form] occurs when the object becomes the agent'. This is because the previously mentioned forced interpretation (*kusṛṣṭi*) is unacceptable. Likewise—
"In the case of the root *ruh* in its pure form, both 'causing to descend' (*nyagbhāvana*) and 'descending' (*nyagbhavana*) are understood.

Here, by the term "causing to descend" (*nyagbhāvanapada*), two levels are intended, comprising both the operation conducive to descending and the operation conducive to that operation conducive to descending, as explained for both the simple and the causative forms of the word "causing to descend. Thus, in the sentence "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant," the first level of meaning is: "They possess the operation conducive to that descending which resides in the elephant."

Then, when the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is internalized, "the elephant mounts the elephant-drivers" (*ārohati hastipakān hastī*) occurs; the meaning is that [the elephant] possesses an activity conducive to the activity residing in the elephant-drivers which is itself conducive to the state of being mounted (*nyagbhavana*). Thus, the accusative case is used. Then, when even these two activities are not intended to be expressed, forms such as "the elephant mounts" (*ārohati hastī*) occur as before. Therefore, the fifth stage—wherein the form *ārohayate hastī* is appropriate for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—is reached. This is because, in the second stage itself, the cessation of the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is not the determining factor.

But surely, there is no over-extension [of the rule] here precisely because the one who is not an *aṇ* [agent] lacks the status of being an agent when [the root] is followed by *ṇi*. This is because [the condition] exists in both cases: "The elephant mounts the mahouts" (*ārohati hastipakān*) and "The elephant causes the mahouts to mount" (*ārohayati hastipakān*). Nor should it be argued that the intention is to refer to the status of being an agent in the *ṇi*-causative for that very object which, having assumed a certain state, constitutes the equality of action; for this would result in non-application in the third stage of the "superimposed instigation" (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇa*) model, since the equality of action there is based on the second stage, and in that case, the status of being an object is unestablished.

However, in the third stage where the causal operation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, although there is equality of action when taking the first stage into account, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because the previously stated meaning of the third sentence does not connect [with it]. This is clear from the difference [between the two cases]. This is precisely the intention of the author of the *Vṛtti* as well; for he explained [the definition] by means of the exclusion of another object (*karmāntara-nivṛtti*) in order to exclude such instances as "the elephant being mounted mounts the men onto the platform" (*ārohayamāṇo hastī sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān*).

Otherwise, in view of the example "elephant-drivers mount the elephant," since there is no equality of action due to the perception of a different action [of mounting] in that case, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would be impossible. This is because even in that [opponent's] view, it is accepted that the mention of *ṇau* (in the causative) is for the sake of [indicating] the same action.

However, this is the distinction: in your view, the attainment of "same action" is through the rule *aṇau yatkarma ṇau cet*; in his view, however, it is through *ṇau cet* together with the preceding [contextual] reference.
By this, the claim that the word *karma* (object) refers to "action" (*kriyā*) in any authoritative text is refuted.

However, according to the aforementioned method, since the operation conducive to subordination (*nyagbhāva*) exists in "the elephant mounts the mahouts" (*ārohati hastipakān hastī*) just as it does in "he causes the men to mount the ground" (*sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the equality of the action (*kriyāsāmya*). This [over-extension] can be avoided by the rule that excludes another object (*karmāntaranivṛtti-vākya*). But in the absence of another object such as "the ground," the subordination is understood by the very force of the meaning (*arthāt*) as residing in the elephant itself.

By this [argument], the passage in the *Vivaraṇa*—which states that because there is an absence of identical action (*samānakriyatva*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur in the second stage (*kakṣā*) where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed (*adhyāropita*)—is also to be reconsidered. By this same reasoning, Haradatta’s explanation—that the rule should not apply in cases such as "the elephant-drivers mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*) and "the elephant makes them mount" (*tān ārohayati hastī*)—is also explained away; for even in the second stage of the view where instigation is superimposed, the identity of action exists by taking the second stage of the view where instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*) as the basis for comparison, exactly as previously explained.

By this, the statement of Haradatta—that because in the *nivṛttapreṣaṇa* (cessation of instigation) view the first two stages lack the causative suffix (*ṇic*), while in the third stage the elephant lacks the status of agent, and in the fourth stage there is connection with the object; and because in the *adhyāropitapreṣaṇa* (superimposed instigation) view there is an absence of identical action in the second stage, an absence of the causative suffix in the first stage, and an absence of connection with the object in the third stage—[and thus his position] is swallowed by the possibility of what was not stated, is refuted by the *Kaustubha*.

Therefore, it is established that even when there is no intention to express the identity of the action (*samānakriyatva*), the *ātmanepada* ending is unavoidable in the second stage (*dvitīyakakṣā*) where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has been superimposed.

However, some maintain that if the meaning [of the *ṇeraṇau* rule] were intended by the author of the *Sūtras*, he would have placed the *sūtra* "ṇeraṇāvanādhyāne" immediately after "karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ. This is because, by explaining it as "in the absence of meditation (*anādhyāne*), when the root remains the same (*samānadhātāu*), the agent of the causative (*ṇyantasya*) whose action is equal to that of the object (*karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*) is treated like the object (*karmavat*"), the intended meaning would be obtained. Furthermore, according to your view, since the result would be established simply by resorting to the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), there would be no need for the laborious effort of implying a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) which you favor.

This is because the justification for the commencement of the sūtra—to signify actions whose state (bhāva) resides in the agent—is identical [in both cases]; furthermore, since the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* must be prohibited by a specific rule even for actions whose state resides in the agent, just as they are for those whose state resides in the object (*karman*).

Furthermore, in the third stage (*kakṣā*) where the causative sense has ceased—as in "the elephant causes [the riders] to mount the mountain"—the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would still apply because there is equality of action (*kriyāsāmya*) when taking the first stage into account; for in the sentence "the mahouts mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*), the elephant is the object (*karman*) in the non-causative form (*aṇi*), and it possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative. Moreover, you do not accept a statement that excludes other objects (*karmāntara-nivṛtti-vākya*).

Nor should it be said that, taking whichever stage (*kakṣā*) results in the equality of action (*kriyāsāmya*), it is intended that the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) for that very same object (*karman*) in that stage applies when [the root] is followed by *ṇi*. For this would lead to an impossibility; because, under the view of the "withdrawal of the instigation" (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*), the commentary itself explains that the equality of action is established by taking the second stage, while the status of being an agent for the object in the first stage is explained by taking the second stage—and specifically, the status of being an agent for the object in the second stage is explained by the commentary itself.

In the second alternative, the very status of "object" (*karman*) is unestablished. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the views of the author of the *Bhāṣya* and others. This is because it is established that the purport of the sentence regarding the exclusion of other objects is to exclude any object other than those two—the agent and the object—which exist in that very state where the non-causative (*aṇ*) stage becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative (*ṇyanta*) stage. Furthermore, both the *Vṛtti* and the *Kaustubha* accept only intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*) as examples [for this rule]. Thus they say.

It might be argued as follows: In the case of the sentence *ārohayanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("the elephant-keepers cause the elephant to mount"), which has the same meaning as *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("the elephant-keepers mount the elephant"), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would also occur under the view that the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased. This is because, in the sentence *ārohati hastī hastipakān* ("the elephant mounts the elephant-keepers"), the elephant-keepers—who were the object (*karman*) of the root *ṇi* (in *ārohayanti*)—become the agent (*kartṛ*) of the root *ṇic*. Furthermore, since there is no object other than those who are the agent and the object [of the causative], it would be difficult to specify a particular second stage involving superimposed instigation (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*). If this is the objection:

No; for even according to the view of the Bhāṣya, equality of action (*kriyāsāmya*) is intended to be expressed. Furthermore, in the stage where the causative suffix has been elided and the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, there is an absence of that [equality] because the action is deficient. However, in the second stage where the instigation is superimposed (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*), the ātmanepada is justified because the equality of action qualified by the aforementioned condition (*upādhi*) exists. In both views, in the final stage—taking the state of "the elephant ascends" (*ārohati hastī*) as the basis—the ātmanepada is established because the equality of action exists, accompanied by the absence of the previously mentioned qualification.

And the equality of action (*kriyāsāmya*) should be explained precisely according to the method stated by Haradatta; Kaiyaṭa’s intention also lies in this very point, as the author of the Kaustubha accepts that "the state of having the same action" (*samānakriyatva*) is the consensus of both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa.

However, this is the distinction: in that [other] system, it was stated in such a manner to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the second stage (*kakṣā*) where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed; whereas for us, it is in the third stage where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*) as previously described. For this very reason, the authors of the *Vivaraṇa* have introduced there the mention of the causative suffix (*ṇau*) for the purpose of understanding the identity of the action (*samānakriyā*). By this, the claim that their commentary is motivated merely by a dullness of faith in the *Padamañjarī* is also refuted.

The secret is this: because it is in accordance with the Bhāṣya and other authorities according to the method stated above, the point requiring reflection in the Vivaraṇa concerns only the fact that, in the second stage involving superimposed instigation (preṣaṇa), there is no equality with the action denoted by the root in its non-causative (aṇyant) form.

For this very reason, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, there is no contingency of having to begin this sūtra immediately after "karmavat karmaṇā," following the manner previously stated; for [otherwise] there would arise the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of the ātmanepada in the second stage where the instigation (preṣaṇa) is superimposed. However, in the view of the Kaustubha, since that [stage] is not considered a subject of the rule (alakṣya), the fault mentioned by some does not apply—such is the difference. It is precisely for the purpose of establishing such an intention of the Bhāṣya that the author of the Vṛtti has explained the fourth sentence-meaning in the example "the king causes his servants to see [himself]" (*darśayate rājā bhṛtyān*).

Furthermore, because the unity of opinion between the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vṛtti* is determined by that very statement using the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the example "the king shows himself to his servants" (*darśayate rājā bhṛtyān svayameva*) is a target of application even in the view of the *Bhāṣya* at the fourth stage; thus, it is not established that this [example] is not a target of application for the *Vṛtti* at the second stage, where the transfer of the instigation (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*) is assumed.

Is it not the case that the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "in the case of the object-agent" (*karmakartari*) follows the view of the *Vārttika*, whereas the passage beginning with "for the sake of an action residing in the agent" (*kartṛsthakriyārtham*)—like the *Bhāṣya*—expresses the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*), and not the exclusion of connection with something else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), because the underlying logic is the same? Furthermore, the passage "the group itself counts" (*gaṇayati gaṇaḥ svayameva*) also follows the view of the *Vārttika* alone, because the authors of the *Bhāṣya* understand the mention of the causative suffix *ṇic* as referring only to the causative used in the sense of instigation (*hetumaṇṇic*), and because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is cited as an example therein.

For this very reason, Helārāja stated that regarding the example *gaṇaḥ svayameva gaṇayati* ("the group counts itself"), the *vārttikakāra* established the rule *ṇeraṇau* as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*) in order to exclude the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). As for the counter-example—*ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*, *ārohayamāṇo hastī bhītān secayati mūtreṇa* ("the elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the mounting elephant causes the frightened ones to be sprinkled with urine")—its meaning is as follows: "The frightened ones sprinkle the elephant with urine" is the first stage.

The meaning of the word *siñcati* (he sprinkles) is an operation conducive to an action residing in a liquid substance that is conducive to conjunction. The sense is: those who possess an operation conducive to that action in a liquid substance in the form of urine, which resides in the elephant and is conducive to conjunction [with the ground]. Consequently, when the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is included, "the elephant sprinkles with urine out of fear" means: one who possesses an operation conducive to the operation that is conducive to an action in a liquid substance that is conducive to conjunction.

In a secondary stage where the causative sense is superimposed upon this same meaning—namely, "the elephant is made to be sprinkled with urine by those who are afraid"—the ātmanepada suffix indeed occurs. Because the rule governing roots such as *gati*, *buddhi*, and so forth finds no scope here, the frightened ones do not possess the status of an object (*karman*); thus, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent (*kartṛ*).

68. *Bhī* and *smi* take the *ātmanepada* when used with the sense of fear caused by a cause (*hetubhaya*). The term "fear" (*bhaya*) here also indicates "forgetting" (*vismaraṇa*). With these two roots in their causative forms (*ṇyant*), the *ātmanepada* occurs only when the agent of the causative is the actual producer of that [fear or forgetting]. *Muṇḍo bhīṣayate* ("The shaven-headed one causes fear"). [In this case,] the augment *ṣuk* is applied by the rule "bhiyo hetubhaye. In the alternative view where the vowel *ā* is optional (as in *bibhataḥ*), one would have *bhāpayate*. However, because the vowel *ī* is elided [before the augment *ṣuk*] in the rule prescribing *ṣuk*, there is no such *ā* here. *Jaṭilo vismāpayate* ("The matted-haired one causes astonishment"). What does "caused by a cause" mean? For example: *kuñcikayā bhāyayati* ("He causes fear by means of a key") and *rūpeṇa vismāyayati* ("He causes astonishment by means of his form"). Here, since the key or the form is not the direct cause of the internal state of fear or astonishment, the *ātmanepada* does not apply.

In this context, the substitution of *ā* (in *smāyayati*) does not occur by the rule "nityaṃ smayateḥ," because the phrase "having the meaning already expressed" (*uktārthaka*) and "caused by fear" (*bhaya-hetu*) are understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) from that rule. Although the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed for the operation of a cause, even so, by the force of the qualification, the meaning is that the very form of the verbal root itself—being independent of anything else—is the prompter (*prayojaka*) of the verbal action.

By this, the statement "astonishing Manu’s lineage-banner with human speech" is explained. The reading *vismāpayan* is erroneous. Alternatively, it may be justified by understanding that, in the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the word *vācā* functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) or, alternatively, refers to the indirect agent (*prayojyakartṛ*). [Pāṇini 1.3.69 states: "The roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* [take the ātmanepada] in the sense of deceiving."

The ātmanepada is used after these two roots ending in *ṇic* when they mean "to deceive": *māṇavakaṃ gardhayate* or *vañcayate* ("he deceives the boy"). Why [is it] "in the sense of deceiving"? [Consider: *śvānaṃ gardhayati* ("he makes the dog greedy"); the meaning here is that he produces a desire for something in him. [Or: *ahiṃ vañcayati* ("he avoids the snake"); the meaning is that he shuns it. [And also] after the root *lī* (in the sense of deceiving), as well as in the senses of honoring and causing shame: 70.

By the inclusion of the word *ca* ("and"), the root *līṅ* (in the sense of "embracing") is understood. *Līṅ* belongs to the *divādi* class; *lī* (without the *ṅ*) belongs to the *krayādi* class. Both are included here. This is because the rule regarding "the maxim of the suffix without an indicatory letter" (*niranubandhakaparibhāṣā*)—as evidenced by the addition of the indicatory *ṅ* in the rule "from *vāmadeva*, the suffixes *ḍyaṅ* and *ḍyauc*"—is restricted to the domain of suffixes. Examples: 1. *jaṭābhir ālāpayate*: "He causes [himself] to be addressed with matted locks. The meaning is that he receives honor. 2. *śyeno vartikām ullāpayate*: "The hawk makes the quail cry out. The meaning is that he treats her with contempt. 3. *bālam ullāpayate*: "He makes the child cry out. The meaning is that he deceives him.

In this context, the substitution of *ā* for *lī* (in *līyate*) is obligatory because it is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Nor should it be argued that because the term "līyateḥ" is specified with the *śyan* affix, the substitution of *ā* would not apply to the root *līnāti*; for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that this specification includes both roots. Why [is the condition] "in the sense of honoring and so forth" (*saṃmānanādiṣu*) stated? [Consider: *bālam ullāpayati*. This means "he causes the child to embrace. 71. [The suffix *ṇic* is applied] after the root *kṛñ* when preceded by the word *mithyā*, in the sense of repetition.

The *ātmanepada* suffix shall be used after the root *kṛ* when it is in its causative form (*ṇyanta*) with *mithyā* as its prefix, provided there is repetition (*paunaḥpunya*). Example: *padaṃ mithyā kārayate*. The meaning is: "He repeatedly utters a word incorrectly," that is, with faulty accents and so forth, due to some lapse. Here, the root *kṛ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*) in the sense of "uttering. However, in its causative form (*ṇyanta*), it is transitive (*sakarmaka*) in the sense of "causing to utter. Why say *mithyā*? [Counter-example: *padaṃ suṣṭhu kārayati* ("He causes the word to be uttered well"). Why say *kṛñaḥ*? [Counter-example: *padaṃ mithyā vācayati* ("He causes the word to be spoken falsely"). Why say *avyāse* (not in the case of repetition)? [Counter-example: *sakṛt padaṃ mithyā kārayati* ("He causes the word to be uttered falsely once"). [Now, the rule for the *ātmanepada*] when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*) applies to roots marked with a svarita accent or the letter *ñ*. (Pāṇini 1.3.72)

The *ātmanepada* suffix shall be used after a root that has a circumflex (*svarita*) accent on its indicatory letter (*ñit*), provided that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. Here, "fruit of the action" refers to that objective for the sake of which the action is undertaken; it does not refer to an intermediate result. As it has been said: "That purpose for the accomplishment of which roots such as *pac* (to cook) and others are commenced is their primary fruit; [mere] gain and the like are not the [intended] purpose."

Therefore, by taking *dakṣiṇā*, *vetana*, and so forth as examples, the *ātmanepada* [suffix] is not applied. Here, if there is an intention to express that the fruit of the action goes to someone other than [the agent], the *ātmanepada* is incorrect; however, this is not the case when there is no intention to express that it goes to the agent. For this very reason, [the commentary] explains: "What is the purpose of [specifying] *kartrabhiprāye*? It is so that [the suffix] does not apply when [the fruit] goes to someone other than the agent," and not that there is an absence of the fruit going to the agent. Consequently, the statement in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*—"In the verse *kāmam kuraṅgekṣaṇā kurute bhallīnām iva pānakarma* (at will, the deer-eyed woman performs the act of drinking [killing] with arrows), the *ātmanepada* is redundant"—is consistent.

Otherwise, [the *saṃskāra*] would be included within the category of *cyuta-saṃskṛta* (transferred impressions), so say the author of the *Pradīpa* and others. According to the rule that whatever fruit one performs an action with the desire for attains belongs to that very person, a *śrāddha* performed at Gayā produces heaven for the father, and the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice produces heaven and purity for the son. Furthermore, sacrifices such as the *Puṣkaraṇī-yāga*, performed with the desire for the heaven of one's mother, father, and so forth, produce heaven for the mother, father, and others; for in cases such as "one desiring heaven," heaven—whether common to oneself or others—is conceived as the fruit.

The author of the *Maṇi* (Rucidatta) maintains that the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is correct simply by virtue of the fruit of the action being intended by the agent, even if that fruit does not reside in the agent. The *Miśras*, however, argue that when a specific rite is prescribed for a particular person to obtain a specific result, if that rite were performed with the desire for the fruit to reside in that person, yet it were to produce the fruit in another person, this would be permissible; thus, rites such as the *jāteṣṭi* could even be performed for the sake of the purification of another's son. In this view, the desire for the fruit is the motivator only insofar as the fruit is taught by the scripture to reside in that very person.

In the scriptural injunction "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice]," since ownership (*svatva*) is the default rule, there would be a contradiction in performing sacrifices such as the *puṣkaraṇī* for the sake of the heaven of one's mother, father, and so forth. Furthermore, in passages such as "one should offer the *śrāddha* daily for the ancestors every month," there would arise the contingency of obtaining the results for the ancestors of others. Moreover, the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix is grammatically correct only when the fruit of the action resides in the agent; for it is explained that the suffix is used when the agent "intends" or "connects" the fruit of the action to himself.

For this very reason, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the agent's intention and the fruit of the action is consistent with the Sūtra; for it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to assume that the word "intention" (*abhiprāya*) indicates its object [the fruit]. For this same reason, "the priests sacrifice" (*yajanti yājakāḥ*) serves as a counter-example. It is not the case that their intention is directed solely toward the fee (*vetana*); rather, since the fee is received only when the fruit together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) is realized, there exists an intention toward the fruit itself, even though it is colored by the fee.

Therefore, they say that because the learned perform acts such as the construction of lotus ponds, sacrifices, and great gifts for the sake of others without contradiction, one who desires heaven and other rewards common to both oneself and others should perform such acts as the construction of lotus ponds; thus, a specific Vedic injunction is inferred.

However, some maintain that, in view of that [general rule], since the injunction for direct perception (*pratyakṣavidhi*) itself is determined to have a general sense by the force of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), it is logical that its inherent tendency toward its own literal meaning (*svaparatā*) should be set aside as a general rule (*autsargika*). As for [the case of] "to the fathers" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*) and so on, the author of the *Maṇi* has rightly stated that, because it forms a single syntactical unit with other statements such as "to one's own fathers" (*svapitṛbhyaḥ*), and because of the conduct of the learned, it refers to one's own fathers by virtue of their being the relevant relatives; thus, its inherent tendency toward "one's own fathers" is indeed appropriate. Furthermore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs only when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent.

By means of the locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*), when the fruit of the action pertains to the object and is intended for the agent, the meaning [of "self-interest"] is obtained through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of *karma* as "that which is intended" (*abhipreyate*). For this very reason, even when the sacrificer’s heaven and so forth are desired through the mediation of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the like, the authors have stated: "The officiating priests sacrifice" (*yajante yājakāḥ*). However, if only the sacrificial fee and such were intended in that way, they would have stated simply: "The officiating priests sacrifice" (*yajanti yājakāḥ*). Words do not forfeit their capacity regarding sentence-meanings. For do logs, when they burn, fail to produce cooking? *Note: The term *viṣayasaptamī* refers to a locative case used to indicate the object of an action; here it signifies that the result of the action is directed toward the agent.*

Thus they say: because the Ātmanepada has been employed by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita and others even when the agent’s intention is not intended [to be expressed]. Some, however, maintain that this Ātmanepada occurs in the sense of "arranging" (*saṃvidhāna*). For example, *pacate* means "he causes to cook" (*pācayati*). Likewise for *yajate* and so forth. Since roots have multiple meanings, when the root itself functions in the sense of arranging, then the Ātmanepada suffix serves as its indicator (*dyotaka*). But when the arrangement is not already established by the root, then the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is produced to express it, as in *pācayati*.

But when the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after a root ending in *ṇic* by the rule "ṇicaśca," then the operation of the causative (*ṇyanta*) applies to the second type of arrangement (*saṃvidhāna*). For example: *rājā pācayate* ("the king causes [the cook] to cook for himself"). By the rule "when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*), it is precisely the specific kind of action consisting of such an arrangement that is indicated. As it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:

"In the initiation of an action, some declare that the distinction between being for one’s own sake or for the sake of another—whether it actually exists or does not exist—is based solely on the speaker’s intention."
For some [roots], the ātmanepada ending is optionally used along with the causative suffix (ṇic) when the action is intended for the agent;
for others, the base form itself has that same meaning.
One buys, cooks, maintains, gathers, and even sifts;
in these cases, the causative sense is expressed through the usage of trustworthy authorities.

By the phrase "asatīva," those [grammarians] who hold that the ātmanepada suffix expresses the meaning of the causative (*ṇyartha*)—such as those who argue that it signifies "those who perform the opening of the lotus grove"—are supported; for even in that case, the intention to express the primary sense (*svārthatā*) is possible. By the verse beginning with "keṣāñcit," the two views are summarized: one holding that the ātmanepada is the denoter (*vācaka*) of the causative meaning, and the other holding that it is the indicator (*dyotaka*). They say that the sequence of meanings is as follows: *cinoti* (he gathers), *cinute* (he gathers for himself), *cinoti* (he causes to gather), and *cāyayati* (he causes to gather for another).

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: even according to the view that the *ātmanepada* occurs in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*), because of the inherent nature of the verbal root's power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*), only those roots marked with a svarita accent or the letter *ṇ* (svaritañit) function in that way, and no other roots do; thus, the mention of "those marked with svarita or ṇ" (*svaritañidgrahaṇa*) has been rejected in the Bhāṣya.

Some say that when an action is begun for one's own benefit, the *ātmanepada* is used, whereas when an action is begun for the benefit of another, the *parasmaipada* is used. Furthermore, they maintain that this distinction between acting for oneself or for another is based on the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) and applies only to cases involving roots marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*) or the marker *ṅ*, such as *dīp* and *jīv*, and not to cases like *yāti*. In their view as well, the mention of roots with a circumflex accent or *ṅ* is considered redundant. This position is stated in the verse beginning with "kriyāpravṛttau."

In the example *pañcabhir halaiḥ kṛṣati* ("he ploughs with five ploughs"), there is optionally no middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because of the rule *vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne*. In *svāmidāsau pacataḥ* ("the master and the servant cook"), the parasmaipada is used when there is an intention to express the action alone. Kaiyaṭa maintains, however, that if the property residing in the master is superimposed upon the servant, the middle voice does indeed occur. 73. *apād vadaḥ*: In the aforementioned context, the middle voice occurs after the root *vad* preceded by the prefix *apa*. Example: *nyāyam apavadate* ("he refutes the legal principle"). Why [specify] "when the result accrues to the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye*)? [Counter-example: *apavadati* ("he speaks ill of").

74. *ṇicaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74). In the aforementioned scope, the Ātmanepada suffix follows a root ending in the causative marker *ṇic*. Example: *kaṭaṃ kārayate* ("he causes the mat to be made"). The *parasmaipada* suffix shall be used after a causative (*ṇic*) verb derived from a root that is intransitive when not preceded by another causative, provided its agent possesses consciousness (*cittavat*). In case of conflict, the subsequent rule takes effect.

When there is a conflict between two rules of equal strength, the subsequent rule shall take effect. [The term] *sedha* is derived from the root *sidh* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of "action," and the meaning "conflict" is obtained through the force of the prefix (*upasarga*). *Vipratiṣedha* means mutual opposition. It refers to the possibility of the co-occurrence of two grammatical rules—which have found scope by mutually excluding one another in different domains—within a single instance. The word *kāryam* (should be done) is a gerundive (*kṛtya*) used in the sense of fitness; thus, it signifies that which is fit to be performed. Since they are of equal strength, they are both fit for application; therefore, there is the suspension of the constant (*nitya*), the internal (*antaranga*), and the exception (*apavāda*) rules.

In this regard, that which is obligatory prevails due to its necessity; that which is internal (antaraṅga) prevails due to its parsimony (lāghava); and an exception (apavāda) prevails due to the authority of the specific rule. However, what differs from these concerns the subject matter of the present *bhū* section. As it has been said: "Among the obligatory, the internal, and the exceptional, each subsequent one is stronger than the preceding.
Here, both the perspective of the universal class (*jāti*) and the perspective of the individual instance (*vyakti*) are possible.

For instance, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" resides in the genus (*jāti*) alone. For this very reason, there is a Vārttika on the *Sarūpa-sūtra* stating: "Because the form [the genus] is denoted, there is oneness; so says Vājapyāyana regarding the case-ending. Vājapyāyana was a particular teacher. Thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) when the genus is the denoted meaning, because it is impossible to grasp the denotative power with respect to individuals due to their infinity. Furthermore, if one were to postulate the denotative power in that which is qualified by the genus—such as "that which possesses cowness"—then, according to the maxim that "a qualifier cannot be grasped unless it is itself grasped," it would be more appropriate to postulate the denotative power in the genus (*gotva*) itself.

Furthermore, if one were to accept that the cognition of another individual arises through the apprehension of the word's power (śakti) as residing in one particular individual, there would be the fault of deviation (vyabhicāra). Nor does this lead to an inconsistency in cases such as *vāhayati* (he causes to carry) or *dogdhi* (he milks), because the action is connected with the individual indicated by the class-term. Thus, the Jaimini Sūtra states: "There is no distinction [between the individual and the class] because the usage is for the sake of that [class]. This sūtra indeed aims to refute the objection that, under the theory of the class (jāti-pakṣa), injunctions such as "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) or "if the consecrated animal should escape, one should sacrifice another of the same color and age" would be untenable.

However, since the performance of acts such as threshing is possible by taking the individual (vyakti) indicated by the universal (jāti), there is no lack of connection [between the word and its meaning].

To explain: where it is impossible for the universal *vrīhitva* (rice-ness) to be the locus of a result—such as the removal of husks produced by the act of threshing—it is through the connection of the status of being an object (*karmatva*) with the individual indicated by that universal that the universal itself connects with the action. But where, as in "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), there is an explicit hearing of the instrumental case (*karaṇatva*), there the universal itself can function as the instrument by means of its operation of delimiting the substance; thus, in such cases, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In passages such as "another of that color" (*anyaṃ tadvarṇam*), the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) must also be explained as having as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) the individual (*vyakti*) indicated by the word "animal" (*paśu*).

Although, according to the Guru’s school, the established doctrine is that "the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in what is connected to an action (*kāryānvita*)," and since a universal (*jāti*) cannot be connected to an action, [the meaning] must nevertheless be justified by accepting that the connection to an action occurs precisely through the individual delimited by that [universal]. This is because the presentation of that very view is seen in the *Śabdamaṇi*.

By this, the claim that "the capacity [of a word] resides in the individual qualified by the universal (*jāti*)"—a view accepted by the Guru (Prabhākara)—is refuted; otherwise, their doctrine that the capacity of words resides in that which is connected to the action (*kāryānvita*) would not be established. However, the Neo-Naiyāyikas (*navya*) argue as follows: there is no reason for preference (*vinigamanāviraha*) between taking "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as the delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) such that the cause-determiner (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) is the state of being a certainty regarding the possession of a pot through the relation of capacity, or taking "the word 'pot'" (*ghaṭapadatva*) as the delimiting property of the subject such that the cause-determiner is the state of being a certainty regarding the possession of a pot through the relation of capacity. Consequently, [if one accepts the former], there is complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the capacity residing in the individual.

On the view that the word’s denotative power resides in the universal (jāti), however, the word "pot" is [the object of] the cognition "it possesses potness by way of the relation of denotative power"; thus, it is precisely the nature of a certainty regarding the possession of potness, where the delimiting property of the subject is "word-ness" and the relation is "denotative power," that serves as such [a cause].
