Pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) cannot function as the subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of its relation to "denotability" (*śakyatva*), because it would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) if "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*)—defined as being inherent (*samaveta*) while not being the delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the mutual absence residing in pots (given that it does not reside in non-pots)—were taken as the delimiting factor of the subjecthood (*dharmitāvacchedaka*). However, when pot-ness is the qualifier (*prakāra*), "pot-ness-ness" need not enter into the definition, since it is accepted that a universal (*jāti*) can function as a qualifier in its own right (*svarūpataḥ*).

Furthermore, they say that in the definition of inference as "that which is delimited by inherence" (*samavāyāvacchinna*), the phrase from the *Dīdhiti*—"being other than experience" (*anubhavatvānyatva*)—is explained as follows: since the portion "provided it is not inherent in anything other than experience" (which contains the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the difference) would be redundant, the nature of experience (*anubhavatvatva*) must be defined simply as "inherence in all experiences. Consequently, because the property of being other than what is inherent in all experiences does not exist in [the universal] "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) and so forth, these are excluded even without [explicitly] mentioning "experience-ness" as the qualifier intended to exclude cognition-ness and the like. Thus they explain it.

As for the claim that individuals possess ultimacy (āntyatva), that is not correct; for it is possible for a universal (*jāti*)—even one that is itself incapable of being denoted—to serve as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*).

Nor is there a rule that something which is not the substrate of the property it delimits cannot be its delimitor, since we accept that even a non-pervasive entity can be the delimitor of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatāvacchedakatva*). By this, the charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is also refuted.

And it has been stated in the *Pratyakṣadīdhiti*: "Since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would result from something non-pervasive being an object of inference can be avoided simply by its being a delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*), so too the over-extension that would result from something incapable of being denoted being an object of verbal cognition can be avoided simply by its being a delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Even if the primary power (*śakti*) resides in the delimitor of denotability, that power is not required for the cognition of that [delimitor]; for just as there is the possibility of cognizing a delimitor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) without a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), so too there is the possibility of cognizing that [delimitor of denotability] even without the primary power."

As for the claim that there are two distinct causalities due to a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), that is not correct. For even in the case of the "qualifier-ness" (*prakāratā*) [in the cognition "this is a pot"], the property of being potness (*ghaṭatvatva*) is no different from potness itself in its status as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*). This is because logicians accept that in the case of a universal (*jāti*), there is an undelimited qualifier-ness (*niravacchinnaprakāratā*) with respect to the universal-part, based solely on inherence (*samavāya*) and identity (*tādātmya*) with its own substratum. Furthermore, in the expression "other than experience-ness" (*anubhavatvānya*), such a view is not accepted by anyone. For this very reason, some have explained that experience-ness enters [the definition] precisely as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "experience."

Or, even if being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), there is still a lack of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*), because being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) by its own nature is also possible.

For it has been stated by certain commentators on the *Miśra* [work] in the *Śabdakhaṇḍa*: "Because being a qualifier by its own nature is possible, just as being a qualificand by its own nature is also possible. This is the direction of the argument. In this way, if the universal (*jāti*) were the denotable meaning (*śakyatva*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a verbal cognition having that [universal] as its qualificand, since words generate a cognition whose qualificand is their own denotable meaning. And this contradicts experience in cases such as "a jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*).

Furthermore, the property of being a verbal cognition (śābdatva) having "potness" as its qualifier and "pot" as its qualificand is not the delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka) for the knowledge of the power of potness; otherwise, that [property] would undesirably follow even in the case of the cognition "potness exists. Let this elaboration suffice. We now return to the subject at hand. At the stage of grammatical analysis (prakriyā), two positions are adopted in accordance with the specific linguistic examples (lakṣya).

For, in the view that [the suffix] denotes the universal (*jāti*), since a direct realization of that [universal] is impossible, one must admit that its application occurs only to a specific individual delimited by that [universal]. By this much alone, the purpose of the rule enjoining the universal is fulfilled. Consequently, because the rule *supi ca* has its scope in examples such as *rāmābhyām*, and the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* has its scope in examples such as *rāmeṣu*, there would be no application of either rule in the case of *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, where both rules apply simultaneously due to the absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamakābhāva*).

As it has been said: "Or there is non-application [of both] because they possess equal strength. In that regard, the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra serves to establish a priority: "the subsequent [rule] takes effect. Once that [subsequent rule] has been applied, if the cause for the preceding [rule] still exists, then that too certainly occurs. For example, in the case of *abhinat hi*, although *akac* is superseded by *hibhāva* due to its posteriority, *akac* nevertheless occurs once *hibhāva* has been applied. As it has been stated: "It is established through the recognition of repeated application (*punaḥprasaṅga*)."

In the view that [the word] denotes the individual (*vyaktipakṣa*), however, every individual would be the object of reference by virtue of its own specific individuality; yet, even when the rule applies to one individual, it cannot achieve its purpose without also applying to that other individual. Consequently, due to the conflict between two rules and the lack of any other way out, there must be an option (*vikalpa*). Thus, when both [rules] are applicable alternatively, the commenced sūtra on conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), meaning that the subsequent [rule] alone takes effect, and not the preceding one.

In the case of *juhutāt tvam*, once *juhu hi* has been established, the substitution of *dhi* is superseded by the subsequent application of *tāt* (the substitute for *hi*). Since the status of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply here, the substitution of *dhi* does not recur.
As it has been said: "When a conflict occurs and a rule has been applied once, that which was superseded remains superseded."

Nor does it follow that another scripture would likewise lack authority because it would fail to apply to that same individual, since its subject matter is that very individual. This is because the intent of the scripture intended to be excluded is restricted precisely to those individuals who are not the objects of the application of the other scripture; thus, in effect, it results in the conclusion that there is no intent regarding those individuals who are the objects of the application of the other scripture. Therefore, both positions are established in accordance with the requirements of the specific cases (lakṣya).

That which is *nitya* (obligatory) is always stronger than even that which follows it. Therefore, in the case of the root *radh* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *num* augment—by the rule "radhijabhoḥ"—supersedes even the subsequent vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) prescribed by "ata upadhāyāḥ. Although that [lengthening] is technically *anitya* because it applies when a different word-form arises, it is nevertheless accepted as *nitya* on the grounds of its being independent of whether [the *num*] has been applied or not. Consequently, the form *randhayati* is established. In examples such as *adudruvat*, the substitution *uvaṅ* occurs because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), thereby superseding even the subsequent *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.

In the case of *śunaḥ*, even though the elision (*al-lopa*) [of the final vowel] follows later in the order of rules, it is superseded by the rule "after a *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel, the preceding [vowel] takes its place" (*saṃprasāraṇācca*). For if the elision were applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* would occur due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, in the case of *bahuśvā nagarī*, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply according to the rule "for a word ending in *an* that undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel. Nor should it be argued that the *ṅīp* prescribed by the *gaurādi* group would also apply here; for that is not the case because the word is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). As for the fact that the *Bhāṣya* on this sūtra mentions *bahuthunī*, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this was formulated under the assumption of the elision of the final vowel (*al-lopa*), and thus does not represent the final established position (*siddhānta*).

One should not ask: "Why was it not stated that in forms such as *śunī*, the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the elision of the final vowel) would apply? This is because there is a prohibition by the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇa-* ("not after *go*, *śvan*, or *sāvavarṇa*"). Furthermore, it is made known that the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* does not apply to this [word] *śvan* because it is listed among the *gaurādi* group. In the case of *śunī*, since the *ṅīp* suffix would become acute by the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*, it would be impossible to justify the prescription of *ṅīṣ* for the sake of making the word end-acute. In the case of *sausthitiḥ*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) prevails over the accent because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

When *su-utthitaḥ* is established, if the first *u* were to be udātta, then by the rule "or [it becomes] svarita when [the preceding vowel is] anudātta at the beginning of a word," it would optionally become svarita. However, when the single-substitute (ekādeśa) occurs first, there is invariably initial udātta. In the case of *vṛddhi*, [we have] *it* and *ut* vowels: *stairṇiḥ*, *paurṇiḥ*. When *stṛta-i* is established, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the *it*-vowel change occurs first, and then the *vṛddhi*. But regarding the accent (*svara*), there is no difference. If, in the case of *āpo-pūryate*, the doubling (*dvirvacana*) which is obtained due to its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is set aside by the *it* and *ut* changes because they are more internal (*antaraṅga*).

In the case of *iṅ* and *śī*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs because it is antaranga (internal) compared to the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*). When *ayaja indram* is established, *guṇa* applies by virtue of being antaranga, overriding the *savarṇadīrgha* which would otherwise apply due to its higher status [in the order of rules]. Examples for *ṅi* and *śī* are *vṛkṣe indram* and *ye indram*.

Although the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) is an exception (*apavāda*)—since it does not apply in cases such as *daṇḍāgram* because the *guṇa* substitution would otherwise apply, nor in cases such as *kumārī īhate* because the *yaṇ* replacement would apply—it nevertheless follows that the long vowel for homogeneous vowels has its own scope (*sāvakāśatva*) by way of subverting other rules that share the same cause (*ekanimitta*). Therefore, it is improper to subvert an internal rule (*antaraṅga*). The established principle is that even an exception is subverted by an original general rule (*utsarga*), provided that the exception has already found its application elsewhere.

However, when there is another rule that leaves no room for application (*niravakāśa*), it overrides even an internal (*antaraṅga*) rule that does have room for application (*sāvakāśa*). For example, in the case of *gotre'lugacī* (Pāṇini 4.1.89), the non-elision (*aluk*) overrides the elision (*luk*). Similarly, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *ūṅ* and *āp* overrides both the substitution of *īt* and the elision (*lopa*).

In the case of *khaṭvīyati*, when the form *khaṭva-ā-ya-ti* is established, the substitution of *ī* (by P. 7.1.2) would apply by virtue of its being a subsequent rule (*paratva*), but this is set aside by the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). Otherwise, if the *ī*-substitution were applied first, a *guṇa* would result. Furthermore, the elision of *y* (by P. 6.4.148) is not possible here, because by the principle "that which precedes a rule is treated as non-existent for the application of a subsequent rule" (*pūrvavidhau*), this [the *ī*-substitution] would be considered as having the status of a *sthānivadbhāva*. In the cases of *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ* and *bhādravāheyaḥ*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs by virtue of its being an internal operation, even setting aside the elision of the suffix *ḍha* (by P. 6.4.149, *ḍhe lopo 'kadr̥̄k*), which is a subsequent rule.

Nor should it be argued that the reading *lopetau* (in the rule *lopetau ca*) is more appropriate because the long vowel *ī* cannot occur after the suffix *ūṅ*; for that reading serves the purpose of preventing the application of the rule of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). Nor should it be asked how this can serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), since the rule *ajādyadantam* is likewise appropriate; for in grammatical rules, this [rule of correspondence] is generally disregarded. Consequently, in the case of *vauḍiḥ*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would first prevent the elision of *ā* (*ālopa*); then, if the *ā* were elided first, the substitute would be treated as the original (*stānivadbhāva*) and, being considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*), the elision of *ā* would not occur, and thus the *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *u* and *ā*] would take place.
[This is because: "The substitution of *āt*, the shortening of neuter secondary members (*upasarjana*), and the rules for *ay*, *av*, *aikāra*, and *tuṅ* [take precedence over other operations]."

In the case of *glāchatram*, when analyzed and explained as *glai chatram*, if the augment *tuk* were applied, then because it would no longer end in *ej* (the vowels *e* and *o*), the substitution of *ā* would not occur, as it does not in forms such as *ḍhaukita*. This statement was made without regard for the inclusion of the term "original instruction" (*upadeśa*). Similarly, in cases such as *atiryatra* and *atinvatra*, when *ati rai atra* and *ati nau atra* are situated, once the substitutions *āy* and so forth have taken place, the word would not end in *ej*, and thus the shortening [of the vowel] would not occur.

If *ārāśastrī* were established as *ārāśastrī-idam*, then after the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has first taken place, the short vowel (*hrasva*) would apply due to the status of that substitute being "like the final" (*antavadbhāva*), resulting in the incorrect form *ārāśastrīdam*. Furthermore, if the word-group were analyzed through successive grammatical operations (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*), then in the case of *agnic-atra*, after the *yaṇ* substitution has first occurred, the *tuk* augment would not apply; for even though there is an intervention by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) in the masculine, the *yaṇ* would result in the neuter.

The *tuk* is feared [to be blocked] by the following rules: the *yaṇ* substitution, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), the *guṇa*, the *vṛddhi*, the *aut* (dative singular), the long vowel (*dīrgha*), the *it* (the *it* augment), the *um* (genitive plural), the *et* (locative singular), and the rule for *īt* (feminine suffix).

The *iyaṅ* substitution takes precedence over these [other rules] because it is *antaraṅga*. This has been explained by way of the *yaṇ* replacement. [Examples follow: *agnicit* here [is an exception] due to the *ekādeśa*; in *agnicitaḥ*, etc., due to *guṇa*; in *prārcchakaḥ*, etc., due to *vṛddhi*; in *agnicitī*, etc., due to *autva*; in *jagadbhyām*, *jaganvadbhyām*, etc., due to lengthening (*dīrghatva*); in *jagatyati* (from the *kyac* suffix), due to *ītva*; in *agnicinmanyaḥ*, etc., due to the insertion of *mum*; in *jagadbhyaḥ*, etc., due to *etva*; and in *sukṛtyati*, etc., due to *rītva* in the *kyac* suffix. The *iyaṅ* replacement [thus prevails] over *guṇa*.

The root *dhā* (in the sense of "holding") takes the suffix *tip*. Since *tip* is a sārvadhātuka suffix, the rule for *guṇa* substitution would apply by virtue of its higher status; however, because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal), *ad* replaces the root vowel before the *iṭ* augment. Similarly, in forms such as *prādudruvat*, *uvaṅ* is applied.

In *śuśuvatuḥ* and similar forms, although the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by the rule *eranekācaḥ* would apply by virtue of its higher status, *uvaṅ* is applied instead because it is *antaraṅga*, thereby overriding the *yaṇ*. Regarding the root *śvi*, the *pūrvatva* (precedence) of the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs prior to the *yaṇ* replacement. In *śuśuvatuḥ* etc., *uvaṅ* applies because it is *antaraṅga*, overriding the *yaṇ* that would otherwise be obtained due to its higher status.
Why is it that [the vowel] preceding [the elided *ākāra*] becomes long? Because of the elision of the *ākāra*.

In the case of *juhuvatuḥ*, when *hvā* and *atum* remain, the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) occurs by the rules "hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam" and "abhyastasya ca. Once this *saṃprasāraṇa* has been applied, the elision of *ā* (*ālopa*)—which would otherwise apply due to its being a subsequent rule—is set aside, and the single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) takes effect because it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation. If the elision of *ā* were to occur first, then either due to the status of that [elided] element as a *sthānivadbhāva* or because it is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) as an *ābhīya* (belonging to the *ārdhadhātuka* section), the *uvaṅ* substitution would not take place. This is because the accentuation depends on the presence of the vowel. In the word *aupagavī*, once the suffix *aṇ* and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* have been applied, if the elision [of the final vowel of the base] were to occur first—whether due to the suffix having an acute accent (*udātta*) or being unaccented (*anudātta*)—then the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the disappearance of the acute) would not apply to the vowel *ī*.
The rule for suffixes (pratyaya) takes precedence over both the substitution of a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) and the substitution of *yaṇ*.

In examples such as *agni-indram*, *vāyu-udakam*, and so forth, the production of the suffix occurs even by overriding the subsequent rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). Although there is no usage of the base form (*prakṛti*) alone, this analysis is nevertheless carried out during the analytical exposition (*anvākhyāna*) of the sentence. Even though the suffix is obligatory (*nitya*), the resolution is made on the basis of its being an "internal" (*antaraṅga*) operation. Similarly, one may cite *agnir atra* as an example. The substitution of *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*) takes precedence over the rule for phonemes (*varṇavidhi*).

In examples such as *pacatvatra*, if the *yaṇ* substitution occurred first, then because it would not be a rule concerning an *al* (an *alvidhi*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would be absent, and consequently, the replacement by *u* (*utva*) would not take place.
Furthermore, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) of the *tatpuruṣa* compound results from the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the prior member.

In the case of the three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound *pūrvā-śālā-priyaḥ*, once it has been formed, a two-word *tatpuruṣa* compound occurs between the first two members according to the rule *taddhitārtha-*. In that situation, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member—which would be triggered by the three-word *bahuvrīhi*—does not apply because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Instead, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of the word *śālā*, which is based on the *tatpuruṣa* compound, prevails. As for the accent of the first member, it is acute on the initial syllable (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule *svāṅga-śiṭām-adantānām*.

In this regard, the following should be noted: Kaiyaṭa maintains that the *paribhāṣā* "between the internal (*antaraṅga*) and the external (*bahiraṅga*), the internal is stronger" is based on the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). However, the maxim "the external is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) when the internal is to be applied" is made known by the rule "ūṭh for *vāh*" (*vāha ūṭh*). When the form *dityavāh-am* is established, only the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *vāh* should be performed; once that has been preceded by the substitution [of *ū*], and the *guṇa* [substitution] occasioned by the suffix *ṇvi* has taken place, the [desired] form *dityauhaḥ* is established through the application of the rule "vṛddhi for *eC*" (*vṛddhireci*). Thus, the result is achieved.

Nor can it be argued that where there is no upapada ending in -ā, how is the rule maintained? For, based on the authority of the Bhāṣya which demonstrates its indicatory nature (jñāpakatva), one must assume that the suffix *ṇvi* does not occur there. However, since it is observed in certain Vedic instances, it is possible for it to occur with the *kvip* suffix after the root *ūh*. Thus, the prescription of *ūṭh* serves as an indicator (jñāpaka) of the aforementioned paribhāṣā. For if that paribhāṣā were present, the internal (*antaraṅga*) *guṇa* substitution would not take place because the external (*bahiraṅga*) *saṃprasāraṇa* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*); therefore, the employment of *ūṭh* is purposeful.

Therefore, in examples such as *pacāveda*, the substitution of *aitva* (of *ai* for *e*) does not occur. Furthermore, by the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*, the *paribhāṣā* "there is no assumption of externality (*bahiṣṭva-praklṛpti*) when there is immediate sequence of vowels (*nājānantarye*)" is indicated as an exception to that [rule]. For in cases such as *ko'siñcad adhītya*, since the external *ekādeśa* is already treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the prohibition of *ṣatva* and the application of *tuṭ* would otherwise be rendered purposeless by that very statement of non-existence (*asiddhavacana*).

As for the commentary on this point, which states that the *paribhāṣā* "that which is internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger" is not commenced because its purpose is already served by the *asiddha-paribhāṣā*, that is contradictory, because [the former] is established by logical reasoning (*nyāya*) and because the *asiddha-paribhāṣā* possesses exceptions (*sāpavāda*).

However, if—according to the method stated in the *Vivaraṇa*—"by the rule *ṣatvatukoḥ* (P. 6.1.86), the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *asiddha-paribhāṣā* alone is indicated, and not the *paribhāṣā* 'there is no [application of a rule] when there is immediate sequence of vowels' (*nājānantarye*), due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*)," then this very *bhāṣya* is indeed appropriate. This has been explained in detail previously.

Surely, if the internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger, then in the case of *pūrva-iṣukāmaśamaḥ* and *apara-iṣukāmaśamaḥ*, when the form *pūrva iṣukāmaśamī a* is established, the *guṇa* substitution would apply due to its being internal; consequently, because there would be no separation (*vyapavarga*) between the two members of the compound, and because the rule prohibiting the treatment as "end-like" or "beginning-like" (*antādivadbhāva*) applies to that which depends on both sides, the *vṛddhi* of the subsequent member prescribed by the rules *diśo madrāṇām* and *prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām* would not occur.

If [it were argued]: "In the case of *uttarapadavṛddhi*, because of the word *ca* in the rule *sarvaṃ ca*, the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member (*pūrvapadāntodāttatva*) prescribed for directional words would not apply; for in an example such as *pūrvakārṣṇamṛttika*, both rules would have their scope. Furthermore, in examples such as *guḍodakam*, the rule *udake kevale* (P. 6.2.96) prescribing the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member would not apply, since in examples such as *udaśvit udakam*, that rule already has its scope"—[the answer is: No.

By the prohibition "not [the vowel] of *indra* or the subsequent [element]," it is indicated that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is set aside and the operation pertaining to the preceding and following words takes effect; otherwise, since both vowels would be removed by the elision (*lopa*) according to "and [the *i* or *u*] of that which has *y* or *v*" (*yasyeti ca*), a vowel accent would not apply there at all. In another grammar, however, there is the rule stating that when *vṛddhi* would apply to *y* or *v*, *iy* and *uv* occur respectively. Thus, for example, in the other system, one finds *sauvaśvaḥ*.

Regarding this, one might raise the objection that because the substitution of *yaṇ* is internal (*antaraṅga*), it would apply first, and consequently the substitutions of *iy* and *uv* would not occur. Anticipating this, the Bhāṣya states: "They will occur because they are without scope (*anavakāśa*). It should not be argued that these two [substitutions] have scope in instances devoid of *yaṇ*, for they are prescribed only when a vowel (*ac*) follows. Otherwise, although the elision by "lopo vyoḥ" might be possible in forms such as *aitikāyanaḥ* and *aupagavaḥ*, it would be impossible in cases such as *praiyamedhaḥ* and *praiyaṅgavaḥ*.

Otherwise, even in this case, the derivation of *paceyuḥ* and so forth would not be established. When the form *pac-a-yām-us* is reached, after the elision of *s*, the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) would apply because it is antaranga; consequently, due to the absence of distinct separation (*vyapavarga*), the substitution of *iy* would not occur. This is because, even if the single substitute were treated as the final element (*antavadbhāva*), the form would still remain unestablished.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "In the rule *ato yeyaḥ*, the meaning is not that the word *yā* undergoes the substitution of *iy*; rather, it is the word *yās* itself that undergoes *iy*. This is because the *saṃhitā* reading is based on a Sūtra convention. Thus, the substitution of *iy* is an exception to the elision of *s*, and since the elision of *s* has not occurred, there is no occasion for the application of the rule *usyapadāntāt*."

The elision (*luk*) takes precedence over *lopa*, *ayaṇ*, *ayav*, and *aikādeśa*. Therefore, in examples such as *gomatpriyaḥ*, the elision is by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (P. 2.4.71), and not by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (P. 6.1.68); for if the latter were applied, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the appearance of *num* and other suffixal markers due to the presence of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). *grāmaṇyaḥ kulam* becomes *grāmaṇikulam*. If the elision were applied after the substitution of *yaṇ* had taken place, the form would not be established. The same applies to examples such as *gohitam*, *raikulam*, and *naukulam*. In *vṛkādbhayam* becoming *vṛkabhayam*, if the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) were applied first, the form would fail to be established because of the status of the substitute as being like the initial (*ādivadbhāva*), which would trigger the elision of the case-ending.
Furthermore, this is established because the fact that an external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules is indicated by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*.
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the fourth Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
**Yū stryākhyau nadī || 3 ||** The two vowels *ī* and *ū*, when they denote a feminine, are called *nadī*.

Vowels ending in *i* and *u* that are invariably feminine are designated as *nadī*. This designation applies to those ending in long vowels; it was stated previously that for those ending in short vowels, this designation is superseded by the *ghi* designation. Consequently, in forms such as *dhene*, the shortening prescribed by the rule *ambārthanadyor-hrasvaḥ* does not occur. Furthermore, the term *yū* is not intended to exclude words ending in long *ā*.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *khaṭvābandhu*, the rule *nadībandhuni* would result in an udātta accent on the final syllable of the first member, and in cases such as *bahukhaṭvaka*, the suffix *kap* would necessarily apply by the rule *nadyṛtaśca*. This is because there is an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *ṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ*, which mentions *āp* separately [from *nadi*]. Thus, since the word *khaṭvā* is udātta on its first syllable by the accent of the *tit* suffix, the initial udātta is established in *khaṭvābandhu* and similar forms by the rule regarding the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). Nevertheless, [one might object] that in cases such as *mātre* and *mātari*, the augment *āṭ* would still apply.

Nor can that [the term *mātṛ*] be excluded by the mention of the word "name" (*ākhyā*), because the word denoting a biological mother is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), whereas the word denoting a male relative (a "definer") is different from that. Nor does the separate mention of the vowel *ṛ* in the rule *nady-ṛtaś-ca* indicate the absence of the designation "nadī" for words ending in *ṛ*, since that is for the sake of forms such as *bahupitṛka*.

The *Bhāṣya* states: "The [term] *yū* is a designation for only the two long vowels (*dīrgha*). In that case, the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) occurs due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*). Nor is there an impossibility of connection in the rule *ṅiti hrasvaśca*; for, since a connection as identity between short and long vowels is impossible, it is explained as: 'the short vowel which is a homologue (*savarṇa*) of *y* and *v*. [Question: What is the purpose of the phrase 'designating feminine' (*stryākhyau*)? [Example: *vātapramye*. [Objection: But if the analysis is *striyam ācakṣāte*, then it should be *stryākhyāyau*. For in cases such as *suglaḥ*, the suffix *ka* (prescribed by *ātaścopasarge*) would be superseded by the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by *karmaṇyaṇ*). [Response: Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* says: 'This is Vedic (*chāndasam etat*')."
Therefore,
there is the following usage: "He who, upon the birth of a son, gave ten thousand cows to the Brahmins who brought the pleasant news, he now lives by gleaning."

Alternatively, "stryākhyau" means those two which are designated as feminine or prescribed for the feminine gender. The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the suffix *ghañ*. This forms a locative tatpuruṣa compound (*saptamī-tatpuruṣa*). If this were the case, one might object: "In that case, words such as *tantrī*, *lakṣmī*, *śrī*, and *bhū* would not receive the designation of *nadī* (feminine declensional markers), because their long *ī* and *ū* vowels are not prescribed for the feminine gender in the same way that the suffixes *ṅī* and *ūṅ* are. By this argument, one might further reject the analysis of the term as a bahuvrīhi compound—where "ākhyā" means "designation" (derived from the root *khyā* with the prefix *ā* and the suffix *aṅ* according to Pāṇini 3.3.106: *ātaścopasarge*)—and interpret it as "those two whose designation is feminine. [The author continues: This objection is refuted by the following...

True; because the suffix *vic* is possible [by P. 3.2.75], and since it is not identical in form (*asarūpa*), it is not barred by the suffix *aṇ*. Furthermore, because the property of the whole is superimposed upon the part, even a *kṛt*-formed feminine word receives this designation under this view. Alternatively, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for words such as *mūlavibhuja* (P. 3.2.5). The question in the Bhāṣya—"What is the purpose of including the word *ākhyā*?"—is taken literally in the case of the *vic* alternative. However, in the case of the *ka*-suffix alternative, it serves as a specification of the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Since the status of being feminine is already obtained through the rule "feminine stems ending in long vowels" (*yū stryām*, P. 4.1.3), the inclusion of the word *ākhyā* has the force of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

The meaning is that they designate only the feminine gender, and not any other gender mark (*liṅga*). Consequently, in the case of *grāmaṇye* and *senānye*, the designation *nadī* (feminine) does not apply; because these are action-words (*kriyāśabda*) meaning "one who leads a village" or "one who leads an army," they are common to all three genders, and thus the *nadī* designation is absent even when [the word] refers to a female.

[Objection: In that case, for words such as *iṣvaśanī* which possess both genders, and for quality-words (*guṇavacana*) such as *paṭu* which have all genders, the designation *nadī* (as prescribed by P. 1.4.3) would not apply even when they function in the feminine, because they lack the feminine object [of application]. [Response: Not so; for in those cases, having set aside the mention of "name" (*ākhyā*), there is the continued application (*anuvartana*) of the word "feminine" (*strī*) alone.

In this matter, the truth is as follows: Kaiyaṭa maintains that "being eternally feminine" (nityastrītvam) consists in not denoting another gender. Haradatta, however, holds that it is the state of existing in the feminine without the co-occurrence of another word. Nor is this meaning unobtainable from the very syllables of the sūtra; for from the root *cakṣ* with the prefix *ā-* (meaning "to see all around"), both the non-denotation of another gender and this [quality of being independent] are obtained. This is because the sense of "all-around-ness" (*samantādbhāva*) can be understood not only as referring to that alone, but also as referring to independence (*nairapekṣya*).

As for the objection that there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *śriye* and *brāhmaṇī*—derived from the root *śrī* with the *kvip* suffix in the sense of the agent (kartṛ)—it is not the case that the meaning "denoting a female" is obtained by virtue of the creation of this technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*). For if that were so, the portion "necessarily" (*nityām*) would also be obtained [from the designation itself], which would render the expression *stryākhyau* ("denoting a female") redundant. Furthermore, even though the meaning "Brāhmaṇa" has already been expressed [by the suffix], the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is also expressed; thus, the fact that [the word] "subsists in a female" (*striyāṃ varttamānatva*) is not lost. Nor should it be argued that this gender (*liṅga*) does not reside in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

[The opponent argues: "Because the word that expresses the agent of cognition (*bodhaka*) is not mentioned in the sūtra. [The author replies: That is not correct. Since the accusative case in the phrase *striyam ācakṣāte* ("they call her a woman") signifies the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), that meaning is obtained from the sūtra itself. This is because it is already established that in examples such as *ghaṭaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the jar"), the accusative case signifies the state of being the qualificand. Furthermore, if one were to grant an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) based merely on the expression of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), then even in Kaiyaṭa’s view, that [over-extension] would be unavoidable in the present case, since the existence of the non-expression of another gender (*liṅgāntarānabhidhāyakatva*) is present there.

Furthermore, in the opinion of Haradatta, there is no risk of the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) applying even in cases such as *grāmaṇye*, because the words *grāmaṇī*, *khalapū*, and *kaṭaprū* exist in their primary sense only in the masculine, due to their inherent capacity (*śaktatva*) and lack of fear [of gender conflict]. Moreover, since the departure from Kauśāmbī and so forth are common to both women and men, there is no instance of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Furthermore, in Kaiyaṭa’s view, there would be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya regarding the form *ādhyai brāhmaṇyai*, because the status of being the agent of meditation (*ādhyāna*) is common to all three genders; thus, like the word *grāmaṇī*, the designation *nadī* would be untenable.

One might object: "In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *āsapantāddhīḥ*, the final member (*uttarapada*) is a *nadī* [term] because it is invariably feminine; for it will be stated later that 'the gender of the first [member] is to be taken'—just as in the case of *atilakṣmyai brāhmaṇāya*. This is not correct, because the substitution of *yaṇ* would then be impossible. In the rule "only that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is intended," the mention of a *kāraka*-preceded word is understood to refer to an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), due to its association with the *gati* [in the same rule]. Furthermore, only a *samāsa* explicitly prescribed as a *gati-samāsa* is accepted here.

Therefore, in examples such as *durdhiyaḥ* and *nirbhiyāḥ*, because the compound is not obligatory (*anityasamāsa*), the substitution *yaṇ* does not apply by the rule *eranekācaḥ*; this is how Puruṣottama and others have explained it.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the mantra *mā naḥ samasya dṛḍhyaḥ* under the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*, explains [the word] as *durdhiyaḥ*. This is an explanation of the meaning by way of proximity; however, in the mantra to be explained, the analysis is *duṣṭaṃ dhyāyati*, which is indeed a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*). From that, the *yaṇ*-substitution occurs. Then, by the Vārttika on the *pṛṣodarādi* rule—namely, "there is the substitution of *u* for *dur* before the roots *naś*, *dāś*, *dabh*, and *dhyai*, and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the initial of the following word"—the substitutions of *u* and *ṣṭu* take place.

As for the statement in the commentary on that *Vārttika*, "He meditates on what is evil" (*duṣṭaṃ dhyāti*), where Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others claim that the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge*: that is to be reconsidered. For, in accordance with the *svarita* accent on the final syllable and in accordance with the sense, it must be explained as a mere imitation of the form *khyāti* etc., after the *yaṇ*-substitution has already taken place. Its connection is with the third quarter [of the verse]: "May the destruction (*aṃhati*)—the affliction—of every evil-minded person not slay us."

Regarding the word *aṃhati*, the *Amara-kośa* states that it means "removal" (*apavarjana*). However, the Dīkṣitas maintain that since the word *aṃhati* is conventionally established in the sense of "gift," what is to be understood here is specifically that which is employed for malevolent purposes, such as sorcery (*ābhicārika*), and so forth. In reality, while that may be the case for the mantra under discussion, it is more appropriate to include the form ending in the suffix *kap* (i.e., *aṃhika*) in the Vārttika, because both meanings can coexist through the application of *tantra* (the principle of simultaneous reference). For this very reason, the intention of the elders is that the Atharvaṇa mantra—"By whom you were sent to perform a rite, O evil-minded one, with the intent to kill us"—is thus rendered consistent.

The interpretation that *ādhyāna* (the act of meditating) is [the same as] *ādhī* (anxiety), based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of quality and the possessor of the quality, should be accepted as the correct explanation of the Bhāṣya; however, this [alternative view] must be disregarded because there is no evidence for such a metaphorical usage. Therefore, in Kaiyaṭa’s opinion, the contradiction with the Bhāṣya regarding the form *ādhyai* remains established.
On this point, the Vārttika states: "And the inclusion of the primary gender; the purpose is for the sake of *kvip*, *lup*, and compounds."

The meaning is as follows: when a word first denotes an object qualified by femininity, but subsequently—by another mode of expression—refers to a different substance qualified by a different gender, the designation *nadī* (feminine noun), which would otherwise not apply because the word is no longer called "feminine" at that time, is prescribed by this rule. For example: from *kumārīm icchati* ("he desires a girl") comes *kumārīyati*; or from *kumārīvācarati* ("he acts like a girl") comes *kumārayati*. From these, the suffix *kvip* is applied; then the elision of *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) occur. By the rule "that which is elided before *kvip* is not treated as having its original position" (*kvau luptaṃ na sthānivat*), the feminine marker *yam* (the long *ī*) does not remain. Thus we have *kumārī brāhmaṇaḥ* ("a Brahmin who is a girl"). Because it ends in a *ṅit* suffix, there is elision of the case-ending *su*. Then *kumāryai brāhmaṇāya* ("to the Brahmin who is a girl"); here, by the rule *āṇ nadyāḥ*, the augment *āṭ* is added.

If it is argued that, according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, even a word ending in *ṅīp* which serves as the base for *kyac* and *kvip* does not possess obligatory femininity—since the word *kumārī*, derived from the root *kumāra* via *kyac* and *kvip*, shares its form with the three genders—this is not so; for we rely on the principle that words differ according to their difference in meaning.

This is the distinction: *kumāryau*, *kumāryaḥ*. By the rule *eranekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.82], *yaṇ* is substituted; thus, in the *am* and *śas* cases, we have *kumāryam*, *kumāryaḥ*, just like *prathyam*, *prathyaḥ*. Nor does the prohibition "only for that which is preceded by a gati or a kāraka" apply here, because the meaning is "not when preceded by anything other than those"; for the absence of a qualifier exists even in the simple form, as in the feminine gender in *kumāryai* and so on. Thus: *he kumāri brāhmaṇa* and so forth. However, for the word *kumārī* derived from the word *kumāra*, the plural is *kumārīḥ*; because it ends in a *ṅit* suffix (*aṅ*), there is no elision of the *su* (nominative singular).

Because it does not end in the suffix *an*, there is no shortening in the vocative, as in the case of *vātapramī*. However, from the word *patnī*, forms such as *patniyau* and *patniyaḥ* occur due to the substitution of *iyaṅ*. In the case of *kumārīḥ* (referring to a Brāhmaṇī woman who desires a son for herself), according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, the form follows the masculine (*pūṃvad-rūpa*), whereas according to Haradatta’s view, it is like *lakṣmī*. The distinction lies in the fact that *yaṇ* is substituted in the accusative singular (*am*) and nominative plural (*śas*). Thus, the *kvip* suffix has been explained.

In the example *kharakuṭyai brāhmaṇāya*, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "like" (*iva*) to form *kharakuṭī-iva*. This suffix is then elided by the rule *lum manuṣye*. Although here, by the rule *lupi yuktavad vyaktivacanau*, the feminine gender is also present, nevertheless, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that the technical designation *nadī* (long vowel) does not apply; for the masculine gender inherent in the base itself is not set aside, and thus [the word] does not function solely as a feminine. Therefore, the *nadī* designation is not triggered.

The initiates (Dīkṣitas), however, say: "In this way, in cases such as *cañcāḥ paśya*, there would result the substitution of *n* for the *śas* ending. Therefore, the truth is that by words such as *kharakuṭī* and *cañcā*, which have the suffix *lup*, a worldly male qualified by femininity is denoted. And thus, even the mention of *lup* as having a purpose [for the formation of the feminine] should be considered doubtful."

In reality, it should be understood that there is no absence of *natva* (the substitution of *n*) due to the force of the statement regarding the treatment of words as if they were *yuktavat* (possessing a suffix). *Atitantryai brāhmaṇāya*: This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "one who has transcended the lute" (*tantrīmatikrāntaḥ*). *Bahuśreyasī*: This means "one who possesses many excellent [qualities]" (*bahvyaḥ śreyasyo 'sya*). There is a prohibition of the feminine suffix *kap*—both by the rule *īyaso bahuvrīher na* (which prohibits *kap* after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *īyas*) and by the rule *īyasaś ca* (which prohibits *kap* after a word ending in *īyas*). In the vocative case, these forms undergo shortening; in the *ṅit* cases, the addition of the augment *āṭ* and so forth—the grammatical operations pertaining to a *nadī* (feminine) stem—are established because they pertain to the feminine nature of the constituent part (*avayava*).

The meaning is that since the designation *nadī* (feminine river) had already applied here previously due to its being called "feminine" (*stryākhyatva*), it does not cease even when a later, extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) connection with another gender arises; thus, since the result is established by the femininity of the constituent part alone, the previous Vārttika need not have been composed. In the view where the designation refers to the phoneme (*varṇa*), the grammatical operation is accomplished because the entire aggregate ends in a *nadī*.

If the option for the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) applies to that which ends in [the suffix] *tad*, then—by the rule stating "in the context of a stem (*aṅga*), it refers to both that [stem] and its subsequent member"—in the case of *atitantrabandhu*, the preceding member is also qualified by the *nadī* [designation]; consequently, there would be udātta accent on the final syllable of the preceding member. This same explanation should be applied to the elision (*luk*) of *kvip* as well.
Regarding this, there is a critical Vārttika:

"In the prohibition of the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, there follows the undesirable consequence of prohibiting the application of *iyan* and *uvaṅ* even to those [stems] that stand in the place of *iy* and *uv*, because the constituent part (*avayava*) stands in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*."

Just as the designation *nadī* applies to a whole because its parts refer to feminine entities, so too, because the parts [of the word *adhi*] possess the status of being bases for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, the whole would also possess the status of being a base for *yaṇ*; consequently, the subsequent rule would result in the prohibition of the *nadī* designation [for the whole]. For example, in *ādhyai brāhmaṇyai*, the part *adhi* has *iyaṅ* (in *dhiye*), whereas the whole undergoes *yaṇ* by the rule *eranekācaḥ*. Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "It is established, however, because of the mention of the form of the stem (*aṅga*); since the prohibition applies to that stem which possesses *iy* and *uv*."

The meaning of this is as follows: In the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām*, the term "stem" (*aṅga*) is implied by the operations *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, because these fall under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem. Consequently, the designation *nadī* is prohibited for that stem in which *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are produced. In the case of *ādhyai*, the constituent part does not possess the designation "stem," and the whole does not possess the status of being the locus (*sthāna*) for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*—since that status is precluded by the application of *yaṇ* substitution—and thus there is no fault. It is precisely for this purpose that the word "locus" (*sthāna*) is included there [in the rule], so that the prohibition may apply when *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are actually present, but not when they are superseded by an exception (*apavāda*).

"Also when there is non-application [of the *yaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutes] in the feminine gender," is another rule. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the statement "it is established by the inclusion of the constituent parts. When there is the application—that is, the transition to another meaning—of those [stems] that stand in place of *yaṅ* and *uvaṅ* in the feminine gender, the technical name [of *yaṅ-uv-asthāna*] applies only to the feminine gender, not to the expression of other genders. By the word "also" (*ca*), the meaning is "and when there is non-application. Examples: *śakaṭyai* (dative) or *atiśakaṭaye* (dative) *brāhmaṇāya*; *śriyai* (dative) or *atiśriye* (dative) *brāhmaṇāya*.

In this case, however, there must indeed be two forms: *atiśriye* or *atiśriyai*, as well as *brāhmaṇyai*; this is the statement of the Bhāṣya. Nor should it be said that femininity (*strītva*) is absent here, for according to Haradatta’s view, it does exist. Even in Kaiyaṭa’s view, it has been stated that the term *ākhyā* (name/designation) does not carry over into the rule *ṅiti hrasvaśca*. Thus, in the words *sudhī*, *svayambhū*, *atilakṣmī*, and *aticamū*, two forms each should be understood. However, in the case of *niṣkauśāmbiḥ pumān*, even if the designation *nadī* (river/feminine) were applied, there would be no difference [in the resulting form].

Because the *nadī* [designation] is removed by the substitution of the short vowel (*hrasvādeśa*), the shortening before the vocative case ending (*sambuddhi-hrasva*) does not apply, since the *varṇa* (the phoneme itself) possesses the status of *nadī*. However, its designation as feminine (*stryākhyatva*) exists merely by virtue of being the locus of the expressive power (*śakti*), as the requirement of being the substratum of the relation of pervasion (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatva*) is not intended here. Even under the view that the *nadī* designation applies to that which ends in such [a word], it is a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) according to the maxim "all substitutions are substitutes for the whole word. Nor can there be the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), because it has been stated that the prohibition applies even when an *al* (vowel) is relied upon as a qualifier. As for the optional rule "before a *ṅit* [suffix], there is also the short vowel," it certainly does apply; thus says the Kaustubha. "Those [words] which are the loci of *neyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions, provided they are not feminine. (Pāṇini 1.4.4)

Where the presence of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occurs, those [stems] are not designated as *nadī*, except for the word *strī*. "Presence" means the absence of an exception (*nirapavādā prasaktiḥ*). Examples: *he śrīḥ*, *he bhrūḥ*. Why say "except for *strī*"? [Because in] *he stri*, due to its being a *nadī*, there is the shortening in the vocative. Now, how is it that Kālidāsa says, "O fair-browed one (*subhru*), whence this disrespect in your father’s house? and Bhaṭṭi says, "Alas, father! Where are you? O fair-browed one (*he subhru*)! thus he lamented profusely? And Bhavabhūti says, "And it makes my eyes close; alas, O fair-browed one (*subhru*), this distress is total"? [Note: The technical point here is that the designation *nadī* applies to feminine stems ending in long *ī* or *ū* when they do not undergo the substitutions *iyaṅ* or *uvaṅ*. Since *strī* undergoes these substitutions, it is excluded from the *nadī* designation. Consequently, in the vocative singular, the rule for shortening the vowel of a *nadī* stem does not apply to *he stri*. However, in the examples provided by the commentators, the forms *subhru* and *he subhru* are treated as if they were *nadī* stems, which is explained by the fact that the designation *nadī* is traditionally extended to words like *subhru* when they appear in specific grammatical contexts, such as the vocative.]
"Śrī Harṣa [is] *babhru* (tawny-browed) together with the one whose bow is made of flower-arrows (the God of Love), for their eyebrows originate from the same lineage"—thus it is said.
Regarding this, Haradatta and others state that it is simply an error.

However, the author of the *Durghaṭavṛtti* says: after the word *bhrū*, by the rule *aprāṇijāteḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.63), the suffix *ūṅ* is applied; then, in the compound, because of its status as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), by the rule *ūṅutaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.60), the *ūṅ* becomes part of the entire composite form, and thus the position of *uvaṅ* substitution does not apply.

But the initiated [teachers] say: "This is not correct, because there is no evidence for the suffix being part of the base (*bhakta*). Since the status of the substitute as being 'like the end' (*antavadbhāva*) does not remove its status as a constituent of the word *subhrū*, and since it is undisputed that the mention of 'that which follows' (*taduttarapada*) in the context of the governing rule on bases (*aṅgādhikāra*) applies even when the suffix belongs to the entire complex, the suffix *ūṅ* functions [there]. Furthermore, forms such as *subhruvau* are accepted by all. Some say that the neuter gender is used in a general sense;
others say it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) according to the possibility of the case.
Or [the suffix] ām. || 5 ||

Or, they may be understood as having the names "nadī" (feminine) as previously stated. [Examples: *śrīṇām* (of the Śrīs), *bhrūṇām* (of the eyebrows). Only when it is not a feminine (*astrī*) [is the rule applied]; [otherwise, for example: *strīṇām*. However, the accusative singular ending is not included here, because there is no distinction [in its application].
[The rule] *ṅiti hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.6) [also applies].

The short *i* and *u* vowels (*yū*) that stand in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are optionally termed *nadī* when followed by a *ṅit* case-ending in the feminine. [Examples: *śriyai* or *śriye*, *bhruvai* or *bhruve*, *kṛtyai* or *kṛtaye*, *dhenvai* or *dhenave*. In the alternative where the *nadī* designation applies, there is the augment *āṭ* by the rule "āṇ nadyāḥ," and by the rule "āṭaśca," there is vṛddhi. [This applies] only when it is not feminine (*astrī*). [Example: *striyai*. Why say "feminine gender" (*strīliṅgau*)? [Counter-example: *agnaye*, *vāyave*. Here, because the mention of "the original gender" (*prathamaliṅga*) is absent, it is stated that [compounds like] *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *harivat* [do not take the *nadī* designation]. However, there is a distinction in the case of *atistriḥ*. In forms such as *atistriyau*, the substitution *iyaṅ* occurs by the rule "striyāḥ," and that occurs even when [the word] is secondary (*gauṇatve*). But—

It should be understood that, due to its posteriority, the substitution *iy* for the word *strī* is superseded by the addition of the suffix *puṃs*, as well as by the absence of qualities (*guṇa*), the lengthening (*vṛddhi*), and the augment *nuṭ* when [the word] is in the masculine; and it is also superseded by the augment *num* when [the word] is in the neuter.

The suffix *jas* [is replaced by] *īn*; *atistrayaḥ*. [In the case of the feminine stem *atistri*,] *auṭ* and *śas* [are replaced by] *atistriyam*, *atistriyaḥ*, and *atistrīḥ*. For *auṭ* and *śas*, there is *riyaṅ*. [By the rule] *āṅo nā'striyām*, [we have] *atistriṇā*. [By the rule] *gher ṅiti*, [we have] *atistraye*, and so forth. In *osi*, [we have] *atistriyoḥ*. By the rule *hasva-*, there is *nuṭ*: *atistrīṇām*. [In the locative singular,] *atistrau*. "The substitution of *iy* occurs invariably for the vowel *au* in *os*, but optionally for *am* and *śas*; however, the substitution of *iy* occurs before a vowel-ending (*ac*) and not otherwise when the feminine form *strī* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in the masculine"—so says the *Kaustubha*.

In the neuter, the augment *num* is applied; thus, *atistriṇī* and so forth, like *vāri*. In the feminine, however, there is an option regarding the technical designation (*sañjñā*) by the rule "ṅiti hrasvaśca" (Pāṇini 1.4.6). Nor does the prohibition "na cāstrī" (Pāṇini 1.4.5) apply here, because that [prohibition] qualifies only those [stems] that are the bases for the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions, as it is connected to that [previous rule]. Furthermore, the prohibition cannot qualify the [suffix] *ṅi*, for there is no evidence for such a qualification. Consequently, we have *atistriyai* and *atistraye* (where the latter form arises because the substitution of *au* is superseded by the subsequent rule "idudbhyām" [Pāṇini 7.3.118], which prescribes *ām* for the locative singular *ṅi*). In the locative, we have *atistriyām*; alternatively, in the other case, *atistrau*.

In this context, the rule should have been formulated simply as *vāci hrasvaśca* ("and [the vowel] becomes short before *vāc*"); it should not be two rules, namely *vām iṅiti* and *hrasvaśca*, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, these two rules serve to indicate (*jñāpana*) the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. For if the status of being the beginning of a vowel-group (*ajāditva*) were the cause for the designation *nadī*, then the designation *nadī* itself—being the cause—would prevent the application of the augment *nuṭ*; thus, in the case of *bhrūṇām*, there would be the undesirable consequence of violating the status of *āma* as the beginning of a vowel-group. This is stated in the *Kaustubha*. *Śeṣo ghy asakhi* || 7 || [The remaining [stems ending in long vowels], excluding *sakhi*, are designated *ghi*.]

Those short vowels *i* and *u*, at the end of a word which is not a feminine noun (*anadī-saṃjñaka*) and is other than *sakhi*, shall be designated as *ghis*. [Examples: *haraye*, *bhānave*. Why "short"? [Counter-example: *grāmaṇye*, *khalapve*. Why "vowels" (*yū*)? [Counter-example: *mātre*. Why "not *sakhi*"? [Counter-example: *sakhye*. Why "not a feminine noun" (*anadī-saṃjñaka*)? [Counter-example: *matyai*. In cases such as *susakheḥ*, the designation does indeed apply, because the entire compound is distinct from the word *sakhi*. Furthermore, there is no rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*), because there is no connection with a qualified object (*viśeṣya*).

[Objection: But in this way, in the case of *sakhī* ending in *ṅīṣ*, the explanation of the elision of the *ikāra* by the rule *yasyeti ca* would be useless, since there is no defect even if a long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) were applied. Nor is it possible for the purpose stated in the *Vṛtti*—namely that in the case of *atisakher āgacchati*, the prohibition of the designation *ghi* would apply because the long vowel resulting from *savarṇadīrgha* would, by the principle of "behaving like the final element" (*antavadbhāva*) with respect to the preceding portion, be considered the end of the word—to hold true; for even if *antavadbhāva* were present, the prohibition would remain as it is, since the entire form does not cease to be different from the word *sakhi*. [Reply: Not so.

In forms such as *sakhī*, *sakhyau*, and *sakhyaḥ*, the elision (*lopa*) is necessary in order to prevent the application of *anaṅ* and the feminine marker *ṅīp*. Nor can it be argued that the fault remains even with the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the inclusion of the gender-distinctive form), because when a case-ending follows, a form qualified by gender is not included [in the application of grammatical operations].
*patiḥ samāsa eva* || 8 || [The word *pati* is subject to this rule only when it occurs in a compound.]

The word *pati* is designated as *ghit* only when it occurs in a compound. For example: *bhūpataye*. It is not so here: *patyā*, *patye*. The particle *eva* (only) is used to preclude the reverse restriction—that the designation *ghit* applies to the word *pati* alone [and nothing else in a compound]. By this, forms such as *dṛḍhamuṣṭinā* are established.

In the rule *iha patigṛhe*, a separate sūtra is provided for the purpose of establishing a fixed order of precedence (*pūrvanipātaniyama*) because of its designation as a *ghi* term; otherwise, he would have formulated the rule as *śeṣo dhyasakhipati*. However, the designation *ghi* applies to a compound preceded by *bahuc* just as it does to *susakhi*. Examples such as *sākhinā vānarendreṇa*, *klībe ca patite patau*, *sītāyāḥ pataye namaḥ*, and *kṛṣṇasya sakhirarjunaḥ* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). According to others, since the suffix *i* is added to the object of a verb derived from a denominative (*ākhyāna-ṇyantāt*) by the rule *aca iḥ*, and because this is based on a technical definition (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*), it is not included in the exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

In such instances as *vaco vācaspater api*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending does not occur due to the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*. By this same principle, the word *naiṣadham* in the phrase *rasāt divaspater ādaradarśinā* is explained. Likewise, *vāstoṣpatiḥ* is also explained; here, the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyāḥ pati-*, etc. Some maintain that the augment *suṭ* is applied here because of the requirement of forms such as *śriyaḥ patiḥ*, and that the word *chandasī* (in Vedic usage) is understood to carry over from that context. Others hold that it is due to the class beginning with *pāraskara*.

In the compound *dyāvāpṛthivīśunāsīramarutvadagnīṣomavāstoṣpatigṛhamedhāccha*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending does not occur because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that depends on the general rule. The change to *s* occurs by virtue of belonging to the *kaska-* group; however, others maintain that the change to *ṣ* occurs because it follows the root *iṇ*.
In Vedic usage, as seen in examples such as *vācaspatiṃ viśvakarmāṇamūtaye* and *vāstoṣpate prati*, these are read as separate words.
In the Vedic language, [the word] joined with a genitive case-ending is optionally [retained].

The word *pati* is designated as *ghisaṃjña*. [In the verse] "kṣetrasya patinā vayam," there is a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) for the term *ca*. The term *chandasī* (in Vedic) is understood to follow. Therefore, the meaning is that all grammatical rules are optional in the Veda. Expressions such as *bahulaṃ chandasi* (frequently in the Veda) are for the sake of detailed exposition.
A short vowel is *laghu* (light). || 10 ||

And [the root] *cit* is used in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñāna*). There is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Furthermore, even in the rules concerning short vowels (*hrasva*), the term "light" (*laghu*) is not employed as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). For if it were, in forms such as *sarpiṣṭvam*, there would result an absence of the *ṣatva* (the change of *t* to *ṣ*) by the rule *hrasvāttādau taddhite*. This is because the designation "heavy" (*guru*) would subvert the designation "light. Therefore, since the section on "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*) has not yet commenced, the introduction of the designation "short" (*hrasva*) occurs precisely prior to that.

As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya regarding that [sūtra], where—having raised the objection concerning the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the designation *hrasva* with the designations *dīrgha* and *pluta*—it was said, "This rule will be formulated under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'one designation' (*ekasaṃjñā*)," the intention there is that by means of the particle *ca* and so forth, the coexistence of the designation *hrasva* with [the designations] *guru* and *laghu* will be effected. Alternatively, it should be understood that for this very reason, another alternative view (*pakṣāntara*) is presented therein.
A syllable with a conjunct consonant is heavy. || 11 ||

A short vowel is designated as "heavy" (guru) when followed by a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga), as in *śikṣā* and *bhikṣā*. [The suffix] *ap* is applied after a heavy syllable ending in a consonant according to the rule *gurośca halaḥ*.
And [a long vowel is also heavy]. 12.
It should have the designation "heavy" (guru). He desired [to act]. [The suffix] ām [is applied] by the rule: "And after a root beginning with a vowel that has a heavy syllable."
Since there is an injunction regarding an affix, that which begins with it is the base (aṅga) when an affix follows. 13.

That which begins with the element after which a suffix (*pratyaya*) is prescribed shall be designated as a *aṅga* (base) when that suffix follows. For example: *rāmeṇa*. Why specify "after a suffix"? Consider *strī iyatī*. Here, from the word *idam*, there is the substitution of *gh* for the *v* of *vatup*, the change of the base to *ī*, and the elision of the *ya* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Since there is a prescription for the suffix *su* and the elision of *t* following the word *strī*, both the designation *aṅga* and the designation *bha* would apply; consequently, the elision of *ya* by the rule *yasyeti ca* would occur due to the influence of both designations.

Nor does the elision of the substitute (*ādeśalopa*) become non-existent due to its being *asiddha* (provisionally unreal) by virtue of being *ābhīya* (belonging to the subsequent rule), such that the condition of "being followed by an affix" (*pratyayaparatva*) would be absent; for some accept that *asiddhatva* applies only prior to the operation of the rule in question. Nor can there be the status of being "as if the original were present" (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is because, under the view that word-formation (*padasaṃskāra*) occurs independently of other words, the vowel *e* in the word *strī* is not preceded by an undesignated vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*). That same purpose also applies to the word "rule" (*vidhi*); for if that were absent, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to supply the word "subsequent" (*para*) as well.

As for the counter-example *dadhi adhunā* cited in the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa states that this is because it is impossible under two alternative views: first, the view that the suffix *adhunā* is introduced as a nipātana (irregular formation) with the elision of *idam*; and second, the view that the substitution of *aś* for *idam* occurs along with the suffix *dhunā*. Furthermore, even if the term "vidhi" (prescription) were included [in the definition of *aṅga*], the defect would not remain, because by means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), one relies on the principle that a stem is designated as *aṅga* only when that very suffix which was prescribed after it follows.

Therefore, in the expression *strī am paśyati*, the substitution *iyaṅ* does not apply. Although the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from *ami pūrvaḥ* is treated as the beginning of the following element (*parādivadbhāva*) and thus possesses the status of an affix (*pratyayatva*), the *am* is not prescribed after the word *strī*. Similarly, in the case of the suffix *at* added to the root *at* (with the elision of the *ṭi*-portion), even though the word *a* itself possesses the status of an affix, there is no fault; for the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed after the root *at* specifically, and thus it does not have *strī* as its base (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that the designation *aṅga* applies to as much of the preceding portion as exists in relation to the suffix (*pratyaya*), and not merely to that much of it which possesses the status of a base (*prakṛti*) at the moment the suffix arises. Consequently, in forms such as *vadāmi* and *vadiṣyāmi*, since the entire form ending in the suffix *śap* (vikaraṇa) receives the designation *aṅga*, the rule "there is lengthening before a suffix beginning with *yañ*" (*ato dīrgho yañi*) applies to produce the long vowel. Nor is the [separate] formulation of this rule purposeless, for it finds its utility in cases like *pāpāmi* and *pāpāvaḥ*—derived from the root *pā* (in the sense of "going") with *yaṅ* elision and the subsequent elision of *y* and *v* by the rule "elision of *y* and *v*" (*lopo vyor vali*)—where the preceding portion ending in the suffix *śap* must be treated as an *aṅga*. [Example: *kuṇḍāni*.

When *num* is treated as subsequent (*parādi*), then by the rule *supi ca*, there is lengthening [of the vowel]; however, in forms such as *dadhīni*, it does not occur because the word lacks an *ā*-ending. Under the view that *num* is a prior element (*pūrvānta*), this is established just as in the case of *sāmāni* and so on. But when the view that it is not an integral part of the suffix (*abhakta*) is held, then this is the purpose of including the term "beginning" (*ādi*). Since the view of it being a prior element has been established, this [purpose] is unnecessary. Why [specify] "before a suffix"? So that [the lengthening] does not occur for something qualified by a suffix, or for something even more extensive than that.

If that were the case, then in the form *vavraśca*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.19) would not obtain its status as having a subsequent cause (*paranimittatva*). Consequently, because the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) would not apply, there would be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *v*. This is because it is impossible to justify the application of the rule "the substitute is like the original" (*sthānivād ādeśaḥ*) when the operation is based on a phoneme (*alvidhi*).

As for the claim that "it would be more appropriate to state simply that 'the base (prakṛti) and so forth are members of the suffix (pratyaya)' for the sake of brevity, while the status of the base alone [as an *aṅga*] is established through the principle of 'designation as if possessing the property' (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) in cases such as 'the agent of the base alone' or 'the factor of action' (*kāraka*)," that is to be considered. For it is difficult to define a "base" other than an "aṅga," which would lead to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Indeed, being immediately prior to a suffix cannot be the definition of being a "base," because it would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to forms such as *strī* and *iyatī*, and under-apply (*avyāpti*) to forms such as *bahuguḍa*. This is clearly explained in the *Bhūṣaṇa*; let this suffice.

In this context, there is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as follows: "Since there is an injunction regarding an affix (*pratyaya*), that which begins with it [is the base] when an affix follows. This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical metarule). Because the rules (*sūtra*) possess an implicit supplement (*sopaskāra*) through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the phrase "when an affix is being mentioned," by this means—in rules such as *ñ-nity-ādir nityam*, where an affix is indicated in the locative case—the term "that which begins with it" is understood. Consequently, in examples such as *devadatto gārgyaḥ*, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) does not apply to the entire compound, but rather to the word *gārgya* alone. Furthermore, in the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the restriction to "that which begins with it" is established by this same principle.

The rule regarding the suffixation of *kyac* applies to the object (*karman*) or to that which begins with it when it is a qualifier; by this, in examples such as *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"), *kyac* does not arise from the entire compound. This is because the entire compound is not a word ending in a case-suffix (*asubanta*), and because the constituent part is dependent [on another], resulting in a lack of syntactic independence (*asāmarthya*). In the case of *devadattaś cikīrṣati*, the composite whole does not receive the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātu*). In *devadatto gārgyaḥ*, the composite whole does not receive the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*). However, in *devadatto gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises from the composite whole.

Otherwise, the accent of increase (*vṛddhi*) would apply to the entire complex (*saṃghāta*), and there would be the elision (*luk*) of the preceding case-ending (*sup*). Therefore, it is established that the metarule (*paribhāṣā*)—"when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with what [the suffix] follows and ends with that [suffix]"—is based on explicit scriptural authority (*vācanikī*). Where the preceding element is relied upon as the locus of the operation (*kāryitvena*), the operation applies to that which begins with it; but where the entire complex ending in a suffix is relied upon, the meaning is that there is the inclusion of that which begins with it and ends with the suffix.

However, some say that if this were obtainable through the aforementioned split of the *yoga* (yogavibhāga), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the portion "of that which ends in that" (*tadantasya*) in this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) would be rootless, because the word "ending in that" (*tadanta*) is not explicitly mentioned here. That is not correct; for by means of the acceptance of one part, the inclusion of the other part stated by the ancient masters is established. There is no reason why such a thing should apply only in the case of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), since the purpose of achieving the desired result is the same in the case of a split of the *yoga* as it is in the case of an indicator.

If it is objected that, in this case, there would be no compound for instances such as *avatataptenakulasthitam* ("staying like a scorched mongoose") and *udakeviśīrṇam* ("dissolved in water"), because [the rule] does not apply when there is something additional to the *gati* or *kāraka*, we say: no. This is established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included.
The purpose [of this rule] concerns compounds, secondary derivative suffixes (*taddhita*), prescriptions, and accents.

In examples such as *sāṃkūṭinam* and *vyāvakrośī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *aṇinuṇaḥ* after a word with a prefix (*upasarga*). However, if the suffix *aṇ* were applied directly to the root *kūṭin*, then the vṛddhi would occur only for that initial syllable. In the example *dūrādāgataḥ*: the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense (*karman*) to form *āgataḥ*, meaning "that which has been come. By the accent rule for *gati*-words, the word *āgata* is udātta on its first syllable. Then, the compound *dūrādāgataḥ* is formed according to the rule *stokāntika-*. The elision of the fifth case ending (*pañcamyāḥ*) does not occur due to the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*. Here, the final syllable is udātta by the rule for the accent of words beginning with *tha* (the *thāthādi-svara*). This result is not achieved by the general accent rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*).

"An immediately preceding *gati* [prefix] is a *prakṛti-svara* (base-accented) when followed by a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix; this is because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for initial accentuation (*ādyudātta*). Consequently, the word *dūrādāgataḥ* would otherwise be middle-accented (*madhyodātta*). However, if this *paribhāṣā* is accepted, then—having set aside the *kṛt-svara* which is an exception to the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*—one applies the *kṛt-svara* which is an exception to the rule *thāthaghañktājavitrakāṇām*. This is because the latter rule includes the inclusion of words preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*."

Nor should it be said that the *gati*-accent is an exception (*apavāda*) even to the accent of the suffixes *tha*, *thā*, and so forth; for that [exception] applies only to the case where the following word ending in *kta* is inherently oxytone (*antodātta*). This is because of the established rule (*siddhānta*) that when a word follows a *kāraka* (agentive or objective factor), the accent of the *tha-thādi* suffixes alone prevails.

If it is argued: "Even though the word *āgata* is acutely accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*), when it is compounded with the word *dūra*, the compound will necessarily be oxytone (*samāsāntodātta*) because it is the subsequently prescribed accent (*atiśiṣṭa*)," [the reply is as follows:]

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that the intended meaning is as follows: when the word *āgata* is obtained with an acute accent on the first syllable by the *kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara* rule—since it is formed with a prefix (*sa*) for another purpose—the *thāthādi-svara* applies by overriding even the *gati-svara*, which would otherwise have been the sublater because *sa-gati* also ends in a *kta*-suffix and thus its accent would have shifted elsewhere. It is not, however, intended that the accent itself constitutes an example that cannot be established otherwise. And in this regard, the mention of the word "immediate" (*anantara*) in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Indeed, in the example *taddhi abhyuddhṛtam*, this [rule] is for the purpose that the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the word *abhi* should not occur. If this rule did not exist, then because the word *uddhṛta* would not end in a *kta* suffix, the accent prescribed for when a *gati* element precedes an immediately following word ending in *kta* would not apply at all; thus, [the rule regarding *gatis*] would be rendered useless.
A word (*pada*) consists of that which ends in a sup (nominal) or tiṅ (verbal) affix. (Pāṇini 1.4.14)

That which ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) and that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) shall be designated as a *pada*. [Examples: *brāhmaṇāḥ*, *ūcuḥ*. Although this is established by the principle that when a suffix is mentioned, that which ends in it is understood, nevertheless, the mention of "end" (*anta*) is for the purpose of indicating the rule: "In the formulation of a technical designation (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, that which ends in it is not included. By this, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of "she who is both a girl and more white," the form *kumāra-gauritarā* is established.

If the designation *gha* were applied to the suffix *tarap*, then in the case of the word *kumārī*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would be superseded by the subsequent rule, and only the short vowel [of the first syllable] would occur according to the rule *gharūpa-*.
