Furthermore, in the case of the word *gaurī*, the short vowel would not occur when *tarap* follows.

But if this were so, there would be the burden of having to include the word *anta* (end) in the rule *sanādyantāḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.32]; otherwise, if only *san* and the rest were designated as verbal roots (*dhātu*), then only that which begins with them would be the *aṅga*, and consequently, the augment *aṭ* would have to precede it. Furthermore, the designation *saṃjñā* (verbal root) would apply, and thus [the forms] *bhid*, *chid*, and so on, would not be established. Nor can the result be achieved by the rule *arthavat* [Pāṇini 1.2.45], because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *adhātuḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.46]. Nor can it be achieved by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of a rule conditioned by an affix), because that principle operates only where some operation is prescribed for something else on account of an affix.

Because the function that belongs specifically to the suffix (*pratyaya*) is difficult to achieve through that [suffix alone], since it is impossible for that which is non-existent (*asat*) to possess the status of being an effect (i.e., having a meaning) even by means of a hundred statements. If it is argued that, in the case of *aupagavaḥ*, if the suffix (*taddhita*) alone were designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then the sixth case-suffix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not be elided because it would not be included within the nominal stem, [the answer is as follows]: Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "In the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (P. 3.1.32), the mention of the word *anta-* (ending) has already been made; however, in the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāś ca* (P. 1.2.46), the term *arthavat* (meaningful) is understood to carry over. Thus, it is the whole ending in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix that is meaningful, and not the *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffixes alone."

It might be argued as follows: if meaningfulness (*arthavattā*) were ultimate (*pāramārthikī*), it would not exist even for that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix, because such status belongs only to the word (*pada*) or the sentence (*vākya*). If, on the other hand, it is argued that at the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), meaningfulness is attributed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and thus exists for *kṛt* and *taddhita* formations as well—on this point they say: by the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*), that meaning which is perceived in elements ending in suffixes—which is closely related to worldly meaning and more clearly manifest—is what is resorted to. That is to say, it is the capacity to convey a meaning belonging to the base and the suffix combined. *naḥ kye* || 15 ||

In the *kyaṅ* and *kyac* suffixes, only that which ends in *n* receives the designation *pada*. This is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because it will be stated later that those suffixes are produced after words ending in *sup* (inflected nouns). Thus, *rājāyate* ("he acts like a king"): the *n* is elided by the rule "the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is dropped. However, according to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, a form ending in *kyaṣ* is not an example here, because the *Bhāṣya* states, "This [suffix] is not prescribed after a word ending in *n*," and because it is prescribed only after roots such as *lohita* and those ending in *ḍāc*. Why say "only that which ends in *n*"? Consider *vācyati* and *srucyati*; since they lack the status of a *pada*, there is no substitution of *ku*-sounds (*kutva*) and so forth.

Nor does this entail the fallacy of an inverted restriction (viparītaniyama), because of the *jñāpaka* [indicative evidence] provided by the rules "naṅi saṃbuddhyoḥ" and "nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya. Otherwise, [the author] would have simply stated "nalopaḥ kye. And also in the case of a *sit* suffix. (P. 8.2.16)

When a *siti* suffix follows, the preceding element is designated as a *pada*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation of *bha*. In *bhavataṣṭhak-chasau* [P. 4.2.115], we have *bhavadīyam*. Because it is a *pada*, *jaś*-substitution applies. In *ṛtu-prāpto'sya ṛtviyaḥ* [P. 5.1.105], there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution by the rule *orguṇaḥ* [P. 6.4.146]. [The rule continues: *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* [P. 1.4.17]...

When suffixes beginning with *sva* (i.e., the case-endings) follow—provided they are not *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes and end in the *kap* affix—the preceding element receives the designation *pada*. For example: *rājabhyām*. However, when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix follows, as in *rājānau*, and so forth, the preceding element is not designated as *pada*.

[Objection: But in this way, the elision of *n* would not occur in the word *rājā*, because by the rule of "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there is the status of being followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* [affix], and thus, due to the aforementioned prohibition, the designation *pada* would be difficult to obtain. [Response: This is not so, because the term "not a *sarvanāmasthāna*" (*asarvanāmasthāne*) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Thus, there is no sublation of the designation *pada* obtained by the rule "that which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ* is a *pada*. Alternatively, even if it were a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there is no fault, because the prohibition applies only to what is reached by this specific sūtra, according to the maxim "of that which is immediately preceding" (*anantarasyeti nyāyaḥ*).

Nor does this [rule] sublate the rule *su-p-tiṅ-antam* on account of its posteriority, because this [latter rule] is prohibited. As it has been said: "Being prohibited, it is not able to sublate. For regarding the application of *svādiṣu*, should it be the sublater of the prior application, or rather the object of sublation by the prohibition?

In this regard, since what has already been superseded cannot be applied again, and since inference regarding non-application constitutes a sublation (*bādha*), a general rule (*utsarga*) operates by excluding the domain of its exception (*apavāda*). Consequently, because the rule *svādiṣu* does not apply to the portion concerning *sarvanāmasthāna*, it is impossible for that [rule] to sublate the rule *suptiṅantam padam*. For this very reason, in the case of *vṛkṣāḥ*, when the long vowel of the same class as the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) fails to apply within the scope of the prohibition *nādici*, the rule *vṛddhireci* takes effect.

Alternatively, the rule *svādiṣu* is divided into two separate rules: "In the case of suffixes beginning with *su*, the preceding element is designated as a *pada*"; and another rule: "In the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix that does not begin with *ac*. In this second rule, the negative particle (*nañ*) heard in the phrase *asarvanāmasthāne* is connected with the term *yacī*. Since there is no *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix beginning with the letter *ya*, the mention of *yakāra* is for the sake of the subsequent rule. Thus, the designation *pada* is prohibited for a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), but not for one beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādi*); consequently, the designation *pada* is established for the word *rājā*.

Therefore, in the designation *bha*, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected only with the term *sarvanāmasthāna*. The meaning is that when it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*—that is, when it begins with the letter *ya* or with a vowel beginning with *a*—the preceding element receives the designation *bha*.

Now, one might object: even in this analysis of the word, in the case of "bhadraṃ karoṣi gauḥ," there would be the undesirable application of the rule "pūrvasyārddhasyāduttarasyatedutau. This is because the restriction to "the end of a word" (padānta) would not prevent it there. Do not say so. For that rule is prescribed for the final *ec* vowel of both a sentence (*vākya*) and a word (*pada*); however, here the final sound of the sentence is the *visarjanīya*, and not the vowel *au*. [Furthermore,] there is an extension of the rule to the two cases of *bhuvadvadbhyaḥ* and *dhārayadvadbhyaḥ*.

When the designation *bha* would otherwise apply by the rule *tasau matvarthe*, the designation *pada* is prescribed [instead]. In the case of the suffix *śatṛ*, there is a substitution (*vyatyaya*) whereby the *śap* of the root *bhū* is elided, followed by *uvaṅ*; then comes the suffix *matup*.
By the rule *yaci bham*, [this becomes *bha*].

The syllable beginning with *yakāra* (the letter *y*)—that is, the portion starting from the suffix *ya*—is designated as *bha* when it follows any of the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) that are not *sarvanāmasthāna*, up to and including the suffix *kap*. This is an exception to the designation *pada*. Examples: *gārgyaḥ* [from *gārgī-ya*, where the *ya* is *bha*]; *rājñaḥ* [from *rājan-as*, where the *an* is *bha*]. Regarding the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), there is elision [of the *ī* in *gārgī*]. Regarding the rule *allopo'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134), there is elision of the *a* in *rājan*.
When the designation *bha* applies, there is a prohibition of the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) in the word *ṣaṣ*.

The word *ṣaḍaṅgulidatta* (given by one with six fingers) becomes *ṣaḍika*. [Derivation: By the rule *bahvaco manuṣyanāmnaḥ* (P. 5.3.83), the suffix *ṭhac* is added in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*). By the rule *ṭhājādāvūrdhvam* (Vārttika on P. 6.4.142), there is elision of the word *aṅguli*. Then, by the rule *yasyeti ca* (P. 6.4.148), the vowel *a* is elided. In this case, since the designation *padam* (word) would apply—because the word ends in a *sup* (case-ending) due to the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix) and the simultaneous application of the *bha-saṃjñā* (designation as *bha*) which has the same scope—the quality of being a *jaś* (voiced unaspirated stop) would not occur. Therefore, this [rule] is commenced. [But the result is already] established by the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the vowel *ac*.

When the designation *bha* is being prescribed, because of the status of the elision of the vowel *a* as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*), this [form] ending in *a* is understood as having the designation *bha*. Thus, because they have different points of reference (*bhinnāvadhitva*), there is no relationship of sublation between the designations *bha* and *pada*. Nor does the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* in the rule "not at the end of a word" (*na padānta*) apply here; for that [prohibition] operates when the end of a word is the object of a grammatical operation (*vidheya*). This is seen in examples such as *kāni santi* and *kau staḥ*, where the ends of the words are indeed the objects of the operation. However, in the present case, the substitution of the *jaś*-sounds has already taken effect previously.

[Objection: But if this is so, then in the case of *vāgāśīrdatto bācikaḥ* as well, there would be the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *bācikaḥ* instead of *vācikaḥ*). [Response: Not so. This is established because of the rule stating that for words whose prior member consists of a single syllable, the subsequent member is elided. And since that [elision] is a substitute (*ādeśa*) beginning with a consonant (*hal*), there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle; thus, by the technical designation *bha*, which has the same scope [as the condition for *ku*-substitution], the [undesired] result is blocked. Furthermore, because of the specific mention of "the sixth [case-ending] beginning with a vowel" (*ṣaṣaṣṭhājādi*), the letter *a* is elided separately, so there is no fault. Regarding the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] for *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* when the suffix *vat* follows": [the forms are] *nabhasvat*, *aṅgirasvat*, and *manusvat*. However, if these were treated as *pada*s, there would be the substitution of *ru* (visarga), not *satva* (the substitution of *s*). This is because of the rule "of that which is not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*).

In the case of *vṛṣaṇvasvaśvayoḥ*, *vṛṣaṇvasuḥ*, and *vṛṣaṇaśvasya yacchiraḥ*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] would not occur because of the prohibition regarding the end of a word (*padānta*), and furthermore, there would be the elision of *n*. Nor can it be argued that the elision of *n* does not apply because [the stem] has the designation of *bha*; for the designation of *aṅga* (stem) is absent, since that [designation of *bha*] falls under the governing rule of *aṅga*. Kātyāyana states that these supplementary rules (*upasaṃkhyāna*) pertain specifically to the domain of Vedic literature (*chandas*). [The sūtra:
*tasau matvarthe* || 18 || [is stated].

The suffixes *tānta* and *sānta* are designated as *bha* when followed by a suffix expressing possession (*matvartha*). For example: *taḍitvān* (possessing lightning) and *yaśasvī* (possessing fame). It should not be argued that [the designation] would not apply in the case of *yaśasvān*, because the possessive suffix *matup* also functions to express possession. For instance, when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas be brought to Devadatta’s house," since the property of being a Brāhmaṇa resides in Devadatta, Devadatta himself is also included in the operation [of the command], because he is delimited by the very form that serves as the delimitor of the object of the injunction (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). However, when it is said, "Let Devadatta’s house be cleaned," this is not the case, because the property of being a house (*śālātva*) does not reside in Devadatta.

It is for this very reason that after stating the rule regarding the sense of the suffix *cvy-* (becoming something else), the prohibition *acvau* ("not when there is no *cvy-") is logically consistent.
In the Vedic language, [the suffixes] -āyasa and so forth [are used for the genitive]. 19.

Because of the governing rule over two designations (*saṃjñā*), this [designation] prescribes the correctness of these [words] through both doors as far as possible, according to the *Vārttika*: "Even those having both designations. Having raised the objection—"Since it is stated that 'the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*) after these two,' how can there be *mayaṭ* in Vedic (*chandas*)?"—the author of the *Nyāsa* replies: "Precisely because of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Others say: "[The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs] after a word of two syllables in Vedic. Here, due to the designation of *bha*, there is an absence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*). Because of the designation of *pada*, there would be *kutva* (the substitution of *k*), but due to the designation of *bha*, there is an absence of *jaśtva* (the substitution of *g*). This is because the status of being a *pada*, which is part of the same syntactic unit as the rule for *kutva*, is sublated by the status of being a *bha*. In many [instances], there is the plural number. 20.

This [usage] would occur in cases of plurality, such as *vṛkṣāḥ* (trees) or *dārāḥ* (wife/wives), where there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of plurality residing in the parts onto the whole (*avayavin*). This is because the requirement that [the number] reside in the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is fulfilled by that much alone. Regarding the usage *āpaḥ* (waters) even for a water-atom (*jalaparamāṇu*), Vardhamāna and others hold that this is due to taking its qualities [into account]. Nor does the undesirable consequence follow that one could say *ghaṭāḥ* (pots) even for a single jar; for in that case, there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a superimposition. However, in the case of *dārāḥ* and so on, the restriction is governed by factors such as lexicons and the linguistic usage of elders which establish the rule of obligatorily using the plural ending. "Two endings, the dual and the singular, are used for the numbers two and one respectively. (Pāṇini 1.4.22)

"vṛkṣau" and "vṛkṣaḥ" [are examples]. The words *dvi* and *eka* are primarily expressive of the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*), for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of plural number. In the preceding rule as well, the term *bahu* refers to plurality (*bahutva*). The plural number is used because plurality residing in the substratum (*dharmī*) is superimposed upon the property (*dharma*). This is so that the plurality in the form of a number pervading multiple individuals may be grasped; and this is for the purpose of excluding the inclusion of the word *bahu* when it signifies "abundance" (*vaipulya*). Therefore, it does not apply in cases such as *bahuḥ sūpaḥ* ("much soup"). Regarding this, the *Ślokavārttika* states:
"The meanings of case-endings (*sup*) include the object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as number (*saṃkhyā*); and likewise for verbal endings (*tiṅ*)."
In that case, there is either a well-known restriction (*prasiddho niyamaḥ*) or a restriction regarding the primary elements (*niyamaḥ prakṛteṣu*).

In rules such as "the second case-affix is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), the prescriptive power arises through the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the science of number (*saṃkhyāśāstra*) with the *svādi*-sūtra. When there is a relationship between the quality (*guṇa*) and the qualified (*guṇin*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—such as "in the case of a single object"—number, object, and so forth, become the meanings of the nominal suffixes (*sup*). The science of number also possesses syntactic unity with the sentences concerning *ti*-affixes and the like; it is for this very reason that "and number" (*saṃkhyā caiva*) is mentioned separately. The restriction regarding meaning (*arthaniyama*) is stated by the third quarter [of the verse].

By the fourth [sūtra], the restriction of suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*) with reference to the subject matter at hand is stated. Because of the exclusion of those of the same class by means of this restriction, the production of *svādi* suffixes from indeclinables (*avyaya*) occurs; for by the restriction "the singular number is used only in the sense of oneness," the exclusion applies specifically to duality and so forth. Or, let there be a general restriction regarding suffixes; nevertheless, the *Bhāṣya* states that the establishment of *svādi* suffixes from indeclinables follows from the rule for elision, "after an indeclinable, *āp* and *sup* are elided" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*), and thus, due to their status as words (*padatva*), the occurrence of *ru*-substitution and so forth is justified.
Thus ends the third lesson in the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
In the case of a kāraka (grammatical participant). || 22 ||

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). The locative case here has the sense of the nominative. Since there is no established usage [of the locative in this sense] and because it is not prescribed elsewhere, the employment of the locative is untenable; for it is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) itself that must be enjoined as the thing to be predicated.

[Objection: But if this were so, because of the governing rule of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there would be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the designations such as *apādāna* and the rest.

On this point, they say: By means of the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra *dhruvam apāye*, the technical designation of a *kāraka* is prescribed for that which is fixed (*dhruva*). Consequently, the term *kāraka* from the rule *apādānam* is carried over (*anuvartate*), as is the phrase *dhruvam apāye*. The meaning is: "That which is a *kāraka* receives the designation of *apādāna*. Even though an option (*paryāya*) would have been obtained by the force of the statement alone even without the carry-over, the fact that the carry-over is employed establishes their coexistence (*samāveśa*). This should be explained in the same way for the *saṃpradāna* and other designations. In cases such as *stamberama*, the locative case (*saptamī*) occurs because of its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

The author of the commentary [the *Kāśikā*] states: "In the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*, it is established that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member [of the compound] applies; for in the rule concerning *thā-tha*-suffixes and so on, only the suffix *erac* is included by virtue of its association with *apa*. Nor is that [accent] established merely by virtue of being an *upapada*, because that which is qualified by being in the locative case does not itself constitute what is 'indicated as being in the locative' (*saptamīnirdiṣṭa*)."

On this point, the Naiyāyikas state: A *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is that which, being connected to the action through the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), serves as the cause of the action. In the sentence "The king’s man goes" (*rājñaḥ puruṣo gacchati*), the term "connected to the action" is used to exclude the king, who is the prompter of the going only through his servant. Direct connection with the action does not belong to the village (*grāma*) and so forth. Nor does it belong to the king, since he is connected only through one who is himself connected [to the action]. Therefore, the phrase "through the meaning of a case-ending" is employed. However, the relation itself has no connection with the action, because the cause of a cognition whose qualifier is a relation is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a noun.

For this very reason, relatives [of the action] do not possess the status of *kāraka*. Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the *apādāna* and *sampradāna*, because those two lack the status of being causes of the action; for giving (*dāna*) is a specific kind of relinquishment (*tyāga*) whose result is the ownership of another, and since the recipient (*sampradāna*) is a cause of the factor of "other-ownership" which qualifies that act, they possess the status of *kāraka*. Furthermore, since acceptance (*svīkāra*) is the cause of ownership, [the recipient is a *kāraka*]. Likewise, falling (*patana*) is an action whose result is disjunction (*vibhāga*) while having contact with a lower point as its result; in that case, since the source (*apādāna*) is the cause of the factor of disjunction, it possesses the status of *kāraka*.
For example, they say that a village is the cause of "going," which consists of an action whose result is conjunction, by virtue of being the cause of the subsequent conjunction [with that village].

The grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas), however, maintain that the nature of a *kāraka* is either the state of being one of the [six] factors such as the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth, or the word "kāraka" itself through the relation of a specific technical convention (*saṅketa*).
As it has been said:

"Universals are denoted by them, or rather, *sattā* (Being) as qualified by them; or else, the very form of the nominal stem (*saṃjñāśabda*) is [denoted] by suffixes such as *tva*, *tal*, and so on. Thus it is said. However, its being the "agent" (*kāraka*) of that action must be understood through the relation of "being the object of comprehension" (*bodhyatva*) in place of a specific convention (*saṅketaviśeṣa*), such as "being one of the various types of that action," because there is no convention regarding the agent of that action. Nor should it be asked how, in the case of an intransitive action, there can be "being one of the various types" when it involves an object (*karman*); for it is precisely that which is devoid of an object that is the denotable meaning.
This designation is etymologically significant: that which "does" (karoti) is a "kāraka. Therefore, the designation does not apply to that which is not connected with an action. [Objection:

But in the sentence *brāhmaṇasya putraṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* ("He asks the son of the Brahmin for the way"), how can even the son be a *kāraka*, since although the questioner is the agent of the act of asking, the son cannot be the producer (*janaka*) of that [act]? [Reply: True. For a question is a sentence whose object is the domain of a desire to know (*jijñāsā*). And a desire to know is a desire directed toward knowledge. Since the son is the producer of that knowledge—which is one part of the [sentence as a whole]—he is a *kāraka*, just like the ablative (*apādāna*) and other grammatical relations.

[Objection: But how can there be the status of a *kāraka* (participant in an action) in cases such as "the sprout arises" (*aṅkuro jāyate*), since [the sprout] does not exist prior [to its arising]? [Reply: This is not so, because we accept that an object established by cognition possesses the status of being an action or a *kāraka*. However, some say that in such cases, the word "sprout" (*aṅkura*) has a conventional secondary meaning (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇika*) referring to its material cause (*upādāna*). Thus, they claim the resulting cognition is: "The constituent part of the sprout possesses the activity conducive to its production. [Objection: This might be so; however, in the case of "the leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*), the tree would incur the status of a *kāraka*, because the status of a *kāraka* is already established in the expression "it falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt patati*).

Now, if it is argued that in this case the tree is intended [as the referent] solely by virtue of its relationship [to the leaf], and for this very reason the expression "the leaf of the tree falls" is not used when the leaf on the branch has fallen even though it has not left the tree—nevertheless, in the sentence "he asks the Brāhmaṇa's son the way," the Brāhmaṇa would incur the designation of *karman* (object).
This is not so. For the technical term (*saṃjñā*) *kāraka* is based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), namely "that which acts" (*karoti iti kārakam*).

Objection: If this were the case, since the word *kāraka* would have the same meaning as the word *kartṛ* (agent), expressions such as "the instrument is the *kāraka*" or "the locus is the *kāraka*" would be untenable; because instruments and the other factors are subordinate to the agent.

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "But it is established that for roots such as *pac* (to cook), because there is a distinction in action (*kriyābheda*) according to each factor (*kāraka*), the status of being an agent (*kartṛbhāva*) belongs to both the instrument (*kāraṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

The meaning of this is as follows: since all [factors] possess independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to their own respective operations (*vyāpāra*), and since they contribute to the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*) by means of performing those [individual] operations, the status of being a factor (*kārakatva*) does not cease even when [the factor] is in proximity to the agent; nor does it cease even when it is in a state of dependence (*pāratantrya*). Thus, the status of being a factor persists.

For instance, the actions of placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, adding fuel, and removing [the food] are the operations of the primary agent (*kartṛ*). When there is an intention to express the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), Devadatta is the agent, and thus one says, "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*). Holding and supporting are the operations of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); when that is prioritized, one says, "The pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*). Flaming until the rice is softened is the operation of the wood; in that case, one says, "The pieces of wood cook" (*kāṣṭhāni pacanti*). This should be applied similarly to cases such as "Devadatta cuts" (*devadattaś chinatti*).

If it is argued that, in this way, since there is no usage such as *grāme grāmam āgacchati* (he comes from village to village) regarding the ablative (*apādāna*), agency does not exist there—[we reply that] this is not so, because we observe such usages as *balāhakād vidyotate* (it flashes from the cloud), *balāhake vidyotate* (it flashes in the cloud), and *balāhako vidyotate* (the cloud flashes). This is because the intended meaning is the non-difference between the lightning and the cloud. As it has been said: "The agency of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is sufficient to illustrate the agency of the ablative (*apādāna*) and the others."

The meaning is this: since there is no utility in the primary action without the performance of its own specific operation, the [operation] exists in the ablative (*apādāna*) and other cases as well, according to the principle of the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, the expression "the village comes" (*grāma āyāti*) is not used, because another meaning is understood and the operation of the ablative is not determined. Similarly, in the sense of "he gives to the Brahmin," the expression "the Brahmin gives" (*brāhmaṇo dadāti*) is not used. Furthermore, due to the inherent nature of the power of words, the verbal root does not denote the operation of the ablative or the dative (*sampradāna*).

In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: although all things possess autonomy (*svātantrya*) in their own respective operations, nevertheless, when there is an intention to express manifest autonomy, one says "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*). However, when there is an intention to express manifest dependence (*pāratantrya*), then—even though autonomy exists—it does not produce its own effect because it has been suppressed (*nyagbhāva*), just as ministers do not undertake activities irrelevant to the king in his presence.

Although all factors are equal insofar as the production of an action arises from the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*), nevertheless, because the instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors function in dependence upon the agent (*kartṛ*), and because that agent acquires its capacity prior to them from another source—as seen in cases such as "he sits" (*āste*) or "he lies down" (*śete*) where the agent alone is observed even in the absence of instruments and so forth—and because instruments and the like are never observed in the absence of an agent, the agent possesses primacy. Therefore, while all factors are common to the action in their status as objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*), they all possess the nature of agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the action.

However, when there is a desire to express a specific intermediate state, they possess the status of instrument and so forth. For example, in the production of offspring, the mother and father have the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) when there is no intention to distinguish [their roles]; but when there is a desire to distinguish them, such that one says "this [father] begets this [child] from her" or "she begets this [child] from him," they possess the status of locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) and ablative (*apādānatva*). Yet, in their state as instrument and so forth, they do not receive the designation of agent (*kartṛsaṃjñā*).

In the rule "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), since independence is already obtained simply by virtue of being a *kāraka*, the explicit mention of "independent" (*svatantra*) serves as a restrictive definition (*niyama*). Its purpose is to ensure that the designation "agent" applies only to that which possesses independence by its own nature, and not to that which possesses both dependence and independence. However, the designation "kāraka" proceeds on the basis of the independence that exists according to the actual state of affairs (*vastusthiti*), even if it is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), because of the capacity of the rules for enjoining instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth.

Where there is a simultaneous desire to express the relationship between cause and effect among various capacities (*śakti*), there a conflict of technical designations (*saṃjñā-vipratiṣedha*) is stated. For example, in the case of *dhanuṣā vidhyati* ("he pierces with a bow"): since the bow lacks the status of being the "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) without the intention to express it as the point of departure (*apāya*), both designations would apply; however, due to its subsequent position [in the rule], it receives the designation of instrument (*karaṇa*). In the case of *asiś chinatti* ("the sword cuts"), although the status of being the most effective means is indeed present, because independence (*svātantrya*) is intended to be expressed, the subsequent designation of agent (*kartṛ*) applies. Sharpness and other such qualities constitute the instrumentality.

However, when there is a desire to express their agency (*kartṛtva*), the self (*ātman*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is because, depending on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), qualities such as sharpness are established as either agent or instrument. Therefore, it is established that agency and so forth are determined by intention.
As it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"In reality, that [agency] cannot be designated; for a thing is not fixed [in its status]."

"Because this intention is observed [in such expressions] as 'it is cooked in a pot' (stālyā pacyate). Thus: "That which is fixed in relation to a departure is the *apādāna* (ablative case). (Pāṇini 1.4.24)

Separation (*viśleṣa*) is *apāya*; when that [separation] is to be accomplished, that which is fixed (*dhruva*) with respect to the external object (*adhibhūta*) receives the technical name *apādāna*. The root *dhru* means "to move" and "to be steady"; it belongs to the *kuṭādi* group. From this root, the suffix *ac* is added according to the *pacādi* class. However, if the reading is *dhru* in the sense of "steadiness," then the suffix *ka* is applied because it has a short vowel as its penultimate element (*igupadha*). Thus, its meaning is the state of not being the substratum of action (*kriyānāśrayatva*).

And thus, the nature of being the *apādāna* (ablative source) with respect to a particular action is that state of being the substratum of the disjunction produced by that action and the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) residing in that [substratum], as intended by the speaker. The word "that" (*yat*) refers to the meaning denoted by the word [in the ablative case]. Consequently, in the expression *vṛkṣādvṛkṣe patati* ("it falls from the tree onto the tree"), the meaning of the locative-ending word is not the *apādāna*, because it is qualified by being the denotation of a word ending in the seventh case-suffix. In the expression *vṛkṣātparṇaṃ patati* ("the leaf falls from the tree"), the meaning of the fifth case-suffix (*pañcamī*) is the state of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of both the disjunction and the mutual absence; the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is the locus (*āśraya*).

The action of falling (*patana-kriyā*) is construed as the locus (*vṛtti-tvena*) of that [falling]. And the two meanings of the ablative case (*pañcamī-artha*) are construed respectively through the relations of being a producer (*janakatva*) and essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

According to the method of the Naiyāyikas, however, since the meaning of the ablative is "being a producer of disjunction" (*vibhāga-janakatva*), even that is construed through essential identity alone. The leaf is construed with its locus by way of non-difference (*abheda*), while the tree is construed with disjunction (*vibhāga*) and mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) as their locus (*vṛtti-tvena*).

The verbal cognition is: "Falling, which resides in the locus of the color of the leaf, is the generator of a disjunction residing in the tree and is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) residing in the tree. The specific feature of the Logicians (Tārkikas) is the cognition having the leaf as its qualificandum (viśeṣya), namely: "The leaf is the locus of the aforementioned falling.

However, some [hold] that the meaning of the ablative case (pañcamī) is both "disjunction" and "inherence in another" (parasamavetatva). Thus, the cognition is: "The leaf is the locus of that falling which generates a disjunction residing in the tree and which inheres in something other than the tree."

Now, in this context, regarding the difference that delimits the meaning of the ablative suffix (*pañcamyarthatāvacchedakabheda*), does the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), such as "tree," connect merely as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitāmātreṇa*), or as a counter-correlative delimited by the delimitor of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedakāvacchinnapratiyogitayā*), or as a counter-correlative of some particular locus of the delimitor of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedakāśrayayatkiñcitpratiyogitayā*)?

It cannot be the first [option], because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that "a leaf falls from a leaf" (*parṇāt parṇaṃ patati*). This is because even in relation to itself, there exists a difference delimited by duality (*dvitvāvacchinnapratiyogitayā*) with respect to its own self.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it would result in the absurdity that [the leaf] falls from a substance (*dravya*). This is because a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by substantiality (*dravyatva*) does not exist in a leaf and the like; for only a property residing in the locus of the difference (*anuyogin*) can serve as the delimiter of the counter-correlativity of that difference. The third [alternative] is also not tenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that one could say "the leaf falls from the tree" and "the leaf falls from the leaf. For falling does not produce a disjunction (*vibhāga*) residing in that very leaf, and because [the leaf] resides in a leaf that possesses a falling which has as its counter-correlate a specific individual leaf other than the one that is the substratum of the property "leaf-ness"—which is the delimiter of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*). If this is argued:

This is true; they say that because the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) undergoes a relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*) with [the object] which follows as a distinct entity, it is related by way of having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by that very individuality (*tadvyaktitva*).

As for the claim that "the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative source), and so forth, is indeed an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) property," that is not correct, because there is no cognition [of it] in that form, and because indivisible adjuncts (*upādhi*) are not admitted. Let us return to the subject at hand.

In expressions such as "the horse falls while running" (*dhāvato’śvaḥ patati*), although the horse possesses action (*kriyāvattva*), there is indeed the nature of that action which is the substratum of the relation with the separation (*vibhāga*) denoted by the ablative case of the base (*prakṛti*). This is likewise the case in "two rams move away from each other" (*parasparān meṣāv apasarataḥ*).
As it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"That which is indifferent (*udāsīna*) regarding the departure (*apāya*), whether it be moving or stationary..."
It is certainly called the "point of departure" (apādāna) precisely because there is no penetration into it.
Since the horse is certainly falling from the wall, and since the wall is what the horse falls upon,
the wall and so forth are likewise said to be certain in that horse's fall.
Although both rams are unstable when the disjunction is produced by the actions of both, the two actions remain distinct and established separately therein.
The status of being a limit (avadhitva) for each of the two rams is distinct, depending respectively on the action of the other ram;
and their status as agents (kartṛtva) is also distinct, depending on their own respective actions.

To exclude cases such as "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ syandate*), where the leaf is the locus of the disjunction produced by the motion, the term "action" (*kriyā*) is used to refer specifically to the action denoted by a transitive verbal root. Likewise, by qualifying the disjunction as not being delimited by the meaning of the verbal root itself, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "he abandons the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ tyajati*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because the action qualified by disjunction constitutes the meaning of the root *tyaj*, and thus disjunction lacks the property of being produced by an action qualified by disjunction; [we reply:]...

No, for since "falling" (patati) means an action delimited by conjunction with a lower point, expressions such as *vṛkṣāt patati* ("he falls from the tree") would also be unestablished; this is because the property of being produced by an operation characterized by that [conjunction] is the same in both cases regarding the disjunction (*vibhāga*). Therefore, in cases such as *vṛkṣād vibhajate* ("he separates from the tree"), the meaning of the ablative case is "limit-hood" (*avadhitva*) in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*). The sense is that in the case of departure—that is, in disjunction—the "fixed" (*dhruva*) is that which serves as the limit. The resulting cognition is: "The leaf is the locus of a disjunction whose limit-ness is not instantiated in the tree."

Nor does the undesirable consequence follow that [a thing] is not distinct from itself; for the logicians maintain that just as conjunction qualified by having itself as its counter-correlative does not reside in itself, so too division qualified by having itself as its limit does not reside in itself.
And this [division] is of three kinds. As it has been said:
"Some have a specified object, and likewise some have an implied object."
And that which has an implied action; thus the apādāna is said to be threefold.

The first [type of ablative] is that where the motion (*gati*) is expressed directly by the verbal root (*dhātu*), as in "he falls from a horse" (*aśvāt patati*) and so forth. The second is that where the action expresses its own meaning as qualified by the meaning of another root, as in "it flashes from a cloud" (*balāhakād vidyotate*). Here, the meaning of the root *dyut* (to shine) is "shining characterized by emerging"; the sense is "having emerged from the cloud, it shines.
By this, examples such as "he cooks from the granary" (*kusūlāt pacati*) are explained, because the meaning is "having taken [grain] from the granary, he cooks."

Regarding the third [example], however, Kaiyaṭa and my venerable father maintain that it is "non-going" (*agamanam*) established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddham*). Thus, when one asks, "From where have you come? and the other replies, "From Pāṭaliputra," this is the illustration for the third [case]. For in that instance, the word denoting the limit of the action (*kriyāvadhipadam*) is not explicitly heard, but is merely implied.

Although here the ablative case is used according to the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42) because the basis of selection (*nirddhāraṇāśraya*) possesses a distinct division, the Bhāṣya states: "He who has attained equality with them uses this expression."

The meaning of this is as follows: since those from Sāṃkāśya and those from Pāṭaliputra possess equal qualities, one who perceives their equality employs a sentence by setting them apart again through recourse to excellence (*prakarṣa*). Thus they say that [the usage] is established by the rule *dhruvam apāye* alone.

Their intention is as follows: there is no evidence for a difference between the sentences "He falls from the granary" (*kusūlāt patati*) and "Whence have you come? (*kuto bhavān*). Furthermore, the employment of a verb is possible in both cases, as in "Having taken [grain] from the granary, he cooks" (*kusūlād ādāya pacati*) and "Whence have you come? (*kuto bhavān āgataḥ*). For in those instances, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not cooking qualified by taking; rather, taking is understood through implication (*ākṣepa*), while cooking is merely implied.
Therefore, it is correct to say that where there is an absence of the use of a verbal form for an action that is required, yet the action is nevertheless understood, that is the case in question.

This might be the case: how can there be the status of *apādāna* (ablative) in the expression "he is deserted from the caravan" (*sārthād dhīyate*), given that by the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 1.4.29], the caravan would result in being designated as the *kartṛ* (agent)? As it has been said: "The subsequent rules [supersede] the *apādāna*. Otherwise, that which is being abandoned would not receive the designation of *karman* (object), because it lacks the quality of being pervaded by the activity of the agent. Consequently, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) and the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object—such as in *hīyate* and *hīnaḥ*—would not be possible. Nor can this suffix be used in the sense of a "reflexive object" (*karmakartṛ*), because the action of the root *jahāti* resides in the agent.

On this point, they say: this [term] refers only to the *karmakartṛ* (the object-as-agent), because the root *jahāti* has the sense of "departing. And that [departure] consists in Devadatta’s performing actions conducive to it by means of suppressing hunger and so forth. But when [hunger] departs by itself through the suppression of hunger and so forth, then there is the status of being a *karmakartṛ*. [Objection: Is not the mention of the word *dhruva* (fixed/immovable) here redundant? Nor can it be said that it is for the purpose of excluding the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in the case of "he comes from the village by means of a cart" (*grāmād āgacchati śakaṭena*).

Even if the term *dhruva* (the fixed point) were included [in the definition], just as the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) would still apply by virtue of its higher status in the case of "he pierces with a bow," so too would it apply even if [the term *dhruva*] were not included. Nor is it for the purpose of excluding the vessel in the example "coming from the village, he eats rice from a bronze dish with his hand," because that [designation] is already barred by the designation of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*).

Although the bronze vessel (*kaṃsapātrī*) is not the means for the act of coming, while the two arms are the means, and it was stated in the rule *ākaḍārāt* that the term "location" (*adhikaraṇa*) applies there because of its fixed nature (*dhruva*), nevertheless, according to the actual state of affairs, the coming is primary here and eating is its subordinate member. From the words, however, there arises a contrary cognition of the status of the subordinate and the primary.
As it has been said:
"While walking, study; while muttering prayers, perform the walking."

"Even though the fact of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is not different [in both cases], a distinction is perceived from the word. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa explains that the meaning of the *bhāṣya*’s refutation is as follows: since the act of eating (*bhuj*) is the means, the act of going (*gaman*) is also a means by way of that [eating]; thus, the objection is established. However, by taking the verbal primacy (*śābdam prādhānyam*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is applied precisely because of that [verbal primacy]. Here, the *bhāṣya* states: "In the case of 'the leaf of the tree falls' (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*), it is for the sake of excluding the tree [as the agent]."

Now, one might object that here there is no status of being a *kāraka* because there is no "departure" (*apāya*), since it has been stated that "there is departure only when a limit (*avadhi*) exists. For it is accepted that without a limit, there is no departure even if there is motion. Regarding this, some say: "This point was not stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* because it is easily understood and because it was already mentioned in the previous rule. Others, however, maintain that Kaiyaṭa holds that if the term *dhruva* ("fixed") were included here, a specific kind of departure would be obtained; but if it were absent, then since in common usage mere falling is known as "departure," the counter-example would be given without regard for the governing heading on *kārakas*.
"An addition [to the rule] should be made for the meanings of the roots *jugups* (to loathe), *viram* (to desist), and *pramād* (to neglect):

'He loathes unrighteousness' (*adharmāj jugupsate*). The fifth case (*pañcamī*) denotes the object-domain (*viṣayatva*), and the meaning of the verbal root is 'censure' (*nindā*). The sense is: 'He censures unrighteousness. 'He desists from unrighteousness' (*adharmād viramati*). The fifth case denotes the object-domain. The meaning of the verbal root is the non-performance [of an action] for as long as one lives, following the performance [of that action]. The relation of the object-domain (*viṣayatva*) is construed with both the performance and the non-performance. The sense is: 'One who possesses an absence of the performance directed toward unrighteousness, which pervades his life and is delimited by the time subsequent to a performance directed toward unrighteousness.'"

They say that from the word "as long as life lasts" (yāvajjīva), the stated application [of the rule] does not apply to unrighteous acts performed during states such as dreaming; furthermore, they maintain that where one desists for some time and subsequently commits an unrighteous act again, the stated application there is merely figurative.

Others, however, hold that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists of an action (*kṛti*), its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), their co-temporality (*samānakālatva*), and the absence (*abhāva*). Among these, the destruction is related to the action by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); that [destruction] is related to the co-temporality; and that [co-temporality] is related to the absence. Furthermore, that action is a qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to the destruction by virtue of a specific expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). A single individual instance of destruction appears as such due to the force of preceding and subsequent expectancies. The resulting cognition is: "The destruction of an action—which is co-located with itself and occurs at the same time as an action directed toward unrighteousness—is resident in the locus [of the agent]."

In this context, co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) must be stated as subsistence by means of inherence (samavāya) delimited by a body of the same class as the body that does not cut off its own production. And "being of the same class" (sājātya) is [determined] by the universal such as Devadatta-hood, which is presented by the word uttered in immediate proximity.

Therefore, it is refuted [by the following argument]: since the destruction of this [present] effort shares the same locus and occurs at the same time as the effort that produces demerit (adharma) with respect to the delimitation of a future body, how could there be the usage "Devadatta desists from demerit" by taking that [future effort] into account? Furthermore, even while one is performing demerit with respect to a youthful body, how could there be the usage "he desists" by taking into account a final effort produced with respect to a childhood body? This is because the future production of demerit lacks the aforementioned co-locus (svasāmānādhikaraṇya) [with the present effort].

Furthermore, because an action delimited by a young body is co-located with the destruction of an action delimited by a child's body. Nor does it follow that, by taking this very destruction of an action, one would incur the undesirable consequence that Caitra—though performing unrighteousness (adharma) delimited by a future body—would cease from unrighteousness even while delimited by that future body; for co-location is a constituent of the definition [of cessation] only when it involves inherence in a body denotable by the word co-occurring [in the sentence]. This is because, when a qualified self is denoted by a term such as "Caitra," the body is also denoted.

However, they say that in cases such as "the self desists" (*ātmā viramati*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) appears by way of pure inherence (*śuddhasamavāya*); thus, there is no deficiency even in the absence of a word denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) that signifies the body.

In reality, however, both effort (*kṛti*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) are the meanings of the verbal root. And [the meaning of the root] is construed with destruction by way of two relations: first, a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the effort itself, related to that effort through both the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relation of time (*kālika*); and second, counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) itself. Thus, the cognition arises as follows: "one who possesses that destruction of an effort directed toward unrighteousness which is distinct from that which possesses effort related [to it] by way of both co-location and temporal qualification."

The term *bhinna* (distinct) is included to exclude such a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) that coexists with the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of another action whose object is unrighteousness (*adharma*). Even in that case, because an action residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa-kṛti*) exists in relation to the destruction of that action by way of temporal relation (*kālika*), the term *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (co-occurrence in the same locus) is used. Furthermore, since co-occurrence in the same locus with a past action exists even in the destruction of such an action, the term *kālika* (temporal) is understood [to specify the relation]. In the expression *dharmāt pramādyati* ("he neglects dharma"), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) denotes the object (*viṣayatva*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes non-attention (*anavadhāna*), and the suffix (*tiṅ*) denotes the substratum (*āśrayatva*). Thus, the meaning is "the substratum of the absence of attention directed toward dharma as its object."

On this point, the commentary states: "In this context, terms such as *jugupsā* (disgust) refer to desisting preceded by disgust; therefore, the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative), though constructed by the intellect, certainly exists. This is because desisting occurs after reaching the intellect through the cognition that [the object] is a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatājñāna*). Furthermore, since 'attainment'—defined as possessing cognition through the relation of being the qualificandum as determined by the mode of being a means to an undesirable end—is present in the case of [objects like] poison and the like, there is no non-application of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) to secondary (*gauṇa*) meanings. This is because, within the section on *kārakas*, even secondary meanings are included, and because the terms such as *apāya* (separation) are marked with the *svarita* accent, thereby precluding the application of the maxim regarding primary and secondary meanings.
July 1–Continuation.
In the case of roots meaning "fear" or "protection," the cause of fear [is the agent]. || 24 ||

In connection with words meaning "fear" (*bhaya*) and "protection" (*trāṇa*), the cause of fear is the *apādāna* [ablative case]. Examples include: *corād bibheti* ("he fears the thief"), *udvijate* ("he is agitated by it"), *trāyate* ("he protects"), *rakṣati* ("he guards"), and so forth. The meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is "being produced from" (*janyatva*). The cognition is: "the locus of fear produced from the thief. Protection (*trāṇa*) is the absence of fear, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The activity (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*). Thus, the sense is: "one who possesses an activity conducive to the absence of fear produced from an enemy. Since this is already established by the rule for the ablative of cause (*hetu-pañcamī*), this present rule is for the sake of elaboration. The inclusion of the term "cause of fear" (*bhayahetu*) is for the sake of clarity, because in cases such as Caitra, the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) would otherwise apply due to its higher priority.

"Of whom, when his wrath is aroused, do even the gods fear in battle?"—in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the construction is "of whom in battle. [This refers to] the root √parā-jṛ (to conquer), with the suffix *asaḥ* (the genitive singular of the present participle). || 25 ||

He is defeated by his studies (*adhyayanāt parājayate*). Here, the root *ji* (to conquer) possesses the sense of "not enduring" (*asahiṣṇutva*). And that [non-endurance] is either a specific kind of aversion or the cognition of the impossibility of being overcome; this is because the commentary explains it as "he does not endure the study. The meaning is: one who possesses the cognition of the impossibility of being overcome with respect to the study. In the case of "he defeats the enemy" (*śatrūn parājayate*), the designation of "object" (*karman*) applies because of its higher priority [in the rule]. The meaning is "he overcomes. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *asoḍha* ("not endured") is for the sake of clarity. [The next rule: "In the case of roots having the sense of 'warding off' (*vāraṇa*), that which is not desired (*anīpsita*) [is called the object]. (Pāṇini 1.4.27)

When verbs meaning "to ward off" (vāraṇārtha) are employed, that object which is intended to be reached by the action shall be designated as the *apādāna* (ablative). For example: *kūpād andhaṃ vārayati* ("He wards off the blind man from the well"). If it is asked: "Since the well is desired by neither the one being warded off nor the one warding off, how can it receive the designation of *apādāna*? [The answer follows: [It is so designated because it is the point of departure for the action of warding off.]

On this point, they say: In the view that "prevention" (*vāraṇa*) is the obstruction of activity (*pravṛtti-vidhāta*), even though only the blind person and others are the "most desired" (*īpsita*) because they possess the result expressed by the root in question—which is produced by an operation residing in the preventer—nevertheless, since there is no evidence for such a restriction and since activity itself is included within the denotation of the word "prevention," the well and other such things are also "most desired" because they possess the result consisting of contact, which is produced by the operation of going residing in the one being prevented. On the alternative view, however, that prevention is an operation conducive to separation (*vibhāga-anukūla-vyāpāra*), since separation resides in both [parties], it is clear that both the one being warded off and the warder-off are "most desired" because they possess that [separation].

That is to be considered: in the case of warding off [someone] from a well, since the conjunction with the blind person never arises at all, it is impossible to say that he possesses it [i.e., the result]. By this, disjunction (*vibhāga*) is also explained. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the expression "he wards off the blind man from the well" would also apply [as a result].
As for the claim that, because conjunction itself is absent, the status of being a result consists merely in the preservation of an already established disjunction—that is incorrect.

That too is not correct; for in the absence of conjunction, even disjunction—which consists of a specific quality—cannot arise. Furthermore, if it is argued that a previously established other disjunction is the result, then the aforementioned usage would fail to apply in a case where, prior to that particular instance, no disjunction from the well had even occurred. Nor should disjunction be intended here as merely the absolute non-existence of conjunction, since the aforementioned usage is observed even when one has fallen into a well.

Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because conjunction, being non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), exists alongside its absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*); for no one performs an action conducive to warding off [an object] with the aim of establishing the absolute absence of a conjunction that is co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇa*). This is because such an absence exists by its very nature. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of using the expression "he wards off the blind man from the well" even when the person is engaged in an action conducive to the blind man's conjunction with the well. This is the general direction of the argument.

Therefore, because the act of warding off is preceded by the desire "May the blind man not have contact with the bottom of the well," and because that desire has as its object the absence of contact between the blind man and the region below the well, the state of being "desired" (*īpsitatva*) must be understood as consisting in having a qualifier-role (*prakāratā*) delimited by a relation of "substratum-ness" (*anuyogitva*), which itself is delimited by a relation of "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*) residing in the contact, and this counter-correlativity is in turn qualified by a qualifier-role residing in the contact and determined by a qualificand-role (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in one's own absence. Consequently, even if the contact between the blind man and the well is unestablished (i.e., non-existent), there is no logical flaw.

This is because the speaker’s intention (*ukticchā*) is well-established even in that case. Here, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) denotes falling as an action conducive to contact with what is below (*adhaḥ-saṃyoga*). The second case (*dvitīyā*) denotes falling as conjoined with the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is the meaning of the verbal root. The meaning of the verbal root is an operation contrary to [the aforementioned falling]. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses an effort (*kṛti*) directed toward an operation contrary to the action conducive to contact with what is below, which resides in the well (*kūpa*) situated on the bank (*andha-vṛtti*). Some maintain that where falling into a well is not commonly known, the aforementioned usage is simply ungrammatical (*asādhū*).

Others, however, hold that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is an operation conducive to an absence; the meaning of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*); and the meaning of the accusative (*dvitīyā*) is either counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) or sub-stratumness (*anuyogītva*), as qualified by the absence that delimits the meaning of the verbal root. Furthermore, this absence is related—by virtue of its co-occurrence with words such as "well" (*kūpa*)—to the conjunction with the lower region produced by falling and so forth. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "one who possesses an effort directed toward an operation conducive to an absence whose counter-positive is located in the well."

Thus, regarding the statement "He prevents his friend from eating poisoned food" and similar cases, they say that where the friend's eating of poisoned food is not well-known, and where the absence of a friend—who is characterized by the act of eating poisoned food—through its connection with the act of eating is likewise not well-known, there arises the cognition: "One who possesses an effort directed toward an operation conducive to the absence of a friend (as the counter-correlate) characterized by the act of eating poisoned food, through its connection with the act of eating."

However, some maintain that in this context, "prevention" (*vāraṇa*) is an activity conducive to the absence of falling, preceded by a desire whose qualifier is the absence of falling. The meaning of the ablative case is "objectness" (*karmatva*), and the meaning of the accusative case is "agency" (*kartṛtva*); these both connect with the desire through the relation of being the qualifier as determined by the qualificandum-ness of falling. Even though falling into a well is not established in certain cases, there is no fault, because such a desire exists [in general].

The meaning of the sentence is: "one who possesses an effort directed toward that operation which, preceded by a desire for the absence of falling, is conducive to the absence of falling, [and is undertaken] with the well as its object and with the agent being Andhaka. Similarly, in cases such as "from poisoned food," "prevention" (*vāraṇa*) is defined as an operation preceded by a desire for the absence of eating, which is conducive to the absence of eating. They say that the rest is as explained previously.

Others, however, state that in both cases, the meaning [of the root] is falling in the first instance and eating in the second; and the meaning is an activity conducive to the absence in both instances. The meaning of the ablative case is delimitedness in the first instance and the status of being an object (*karmatva*) in the second, while in both instances, duality is also the meaning. The meaning of the accusative case is agency (*kartṛtva*). The substratumhood of the falling, etc., which is the meaning of the verbal root, connects with the absence that delimits the meaning of the verbal root. Duality, as delimited by the meaning of the ablative case, connects with the absence that delimits the meaning of the ablative case.

Due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), there is also an occurrence of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) with respect to the absence of both the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*), as delimited by duality (*dvitva*). Thus, in the first case, the cognition is: "one who possesses an effort directed toward an operation conducive to that absence of the pair consisting of [the action's] being delimited by a well and [its] having a thief as its agent, with respect to falling in general"; and in the second case, it is: "one who possesses an effort directed toward an operation conducive to that absence of the pair consisting of [the action's] having poisoned food as its object and [its] having a friend as its agent, with respect to eating in general."

In sentences such as "The pot does not see space" (*ākāśaṃ na paśyati ghaṭaḥ*) or "Caitra [does not see space]," by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the accusative case-ending conveys (1) the state of being an object (*viṣayitva*), (2) its occurrence in the pot and so forth, and (3) duality. The verbal root denotes perception (*pratyakṣa*) as delimited by ordinary objectivity (*laukika-viṣayitva*). Thus, the meaning is: the pot is that which characterizes the absence—occurring in the general class of ordinary perceptions—of both the property of having space as its object and the property of occurring in the pot.

They say that even in the case of a perceptual presentation (upanītabhāna) regarding space as its object, there indeed exists the absence of both the property of having space as its object and the property of residing in Caitra, as delimited by ordinary objectivity (laukikaviṣayitva). This is likewise the case in other instances where [the counter-positive] is unestablished.
By means of the *antardhāyī* [mantra], one desires invisibility. || 27 ||

The absence of being an object of perception inherent in [the agent] which is intended for the self is the *apādāna* [ablative case]. In the example, "The student hides from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād antardhatte śiṣyaḥ*), the meaning of the verbal root consists of an activity conducive to the absence of contact that is favorable to that [absence], preceded by a desire for the absence of one's own perception. The meaning of the fifth case [suffix] is "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*). Its connection is with the absence of one's own perception. The cognition is as follows: "An activity subsisting in the student, which is preceded by a desire for that absence of one's own perception which subsists in the teacher, and which is conducive to the absence of contact favorable to perception. Because of the inclusion of "desire," there is no fault even when visual perception exists.
The ablative case is used after a verb denoting "informing" when it concerns formal instruction.

*Upayoga* (acquisition) is study preceded by a formal rule (*niyama*). In that context, the speaker is the *apādāna* (ablative). For example: *upādhyāyād adhīte* ("He studies from the teacher"). Study is the mental coordination (*anusandhāna*) with the word as it is being uttered by another. The meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) here is "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*). Thus, [the meaning is]: "The coordination with the word produced by the utterance subsisting in the teacher.

This [interpretation] has also been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*, because the desired result is already established by the rule *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (P. 1.4.24). As it has been said: "If [the student] departs, why does he not depart forever? Because [the learning] is continuous. Or rather, cognitions are like lights."

And Kaiyaṭa has explained [the phrase] "because of continuity" as follows: the meaning is that the sounds (*dhvani*) which manifest the word, though distinct from one another as they are produced by the teacher, are determined by the listener—as if they were identical—due to their similarity; these sounds, repeatedly entering the path of the listener's hearing, manifest the word either in the form of the individual *sphoṭa* (*vyakti-sphoṭa*) or in the form of the universal *sphoṭa* (*jāti-sphoṭa*). Alternatively... [he says].

Just as a flame, appearing in the form of light, arising without interruption and being determined as identical due to its similarity, is perceived as continuous (*santata*), in the same way, the distinct cognitions of a teacher, undergoing transformation into the form of sound, are said to be continuous. Here, the view of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) is that cognition undergoes the attainment of the form of sound.
And so it has been said:
"The attainment of the state of sound is held to belong to air, atoms, and cognition."
"For the difference in views among various doctrines is indeed unsettled.
[Pāṇini 1.4.30: "The source (prakṛti) of that which is the agent of birth (janikartṛ). 29.

The cause (*hetu*) of that which is being born (*jāyamāna*) is designated as the *apādāna*. "Joy arises from the son" (*putrāt pramodo jāyate*). "Beings are born from Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ prajāḥ prajāyante*). The term "birth" (*janī*) is used here to include the general sense of arising. "You arise from limb after limb" (*aṅgādaṅgāt sambhavasi*). [The suffix] *iñ* is applied after the root *jan*; or [the suffix] *iṇ* is applied after *jan* and *ghas*, according to the rule *janighasibhyām iṇ vā*. In the word *jani*, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *jānivadhyośca*; it is a compound with a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Alternatively, the very fact that this is taught serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] stated in the rule *kartari ca*.

This too has been refuted. A scorpion is born from cow dung; durva grass is born from the hair of cows and sheep. In these cases, "coming forth" (apakramaṇa) is figurative. For in common worldly usage, when something is produced from something else, it is said that it "comes forth" from it. However, according to the Vaiśeṣika school, the effect—being inherent in its causes such as atoms—is produced in a location not distinct from those causes; thus, there is no "coming forth. Likewise, in the Sāṃkhya system, because they accept transformation in the form of birth and destruction characterized by manifestation and concealment, [the notion of coming forth] does not apply.

The *Bhāṣya* states: "Because they form a continuous series (*saṃtata*), they do not depart entirely. The meaning is "due to non-interruption" (*avicchedāt*). Kaiyaṭa explains that just as a serpent with a long body, even while emerging from a hole, is still perceived there because its body is unbroken, so too are the [roots] of the *dūrvā* grass.

On this point, the authors of the *Advaitacandrikā* state: In the case of departure (*apakramaṇa*) consisting of separation (*vibhāga*), there is no cognition of the [object] at its very limit (*avadhi*). However, here, the departure in the form of being "impelled" (*prayuktatva*) is indeed accepted as being cognized at its limit; for such is the experience. If it is asked, "How is 'being impelled' the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*)?"—the answer is: No. Just as in cases such as "he falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt patati*), where separation delimited by the tree is cognized, so too in cases such as "the jar from the potsherd" (*kapālād ghaṭaḥ*), there is a cognition of being impelled delimited by the potsherd. Therefore, that which is impelled can also be expressed by the word "departure" (*apāya*).

And thus, this is the intended meaning of the commentary: here, the meaning of the word *apāya* (separation) is also the relation with the immediately succeeding moment. This is because, within that single part—namely, the state of being immediately subsequent—the limiting factor (*avadhi*) in its aspect as a relatum is denoted by the word *dhruva*. Furthermore, although the entire causal complex (*kāraṇasamūha*) constitutes that limit, it is possible to apply it even to a single instrument, due to the metaphorical identification of the whole with its parts.

Although even that which is otherwise established (anyathāsiddha) possesses the status of being a limit (avadhi) as stated, nevertheless, because "not being otherwise established" (ananyathāsiddhatva) must also be included [in the definition], there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) such as "the jar arises from the color of the staff" (daṇḍarūpāt). In cases such as "the jar is produced from the staff," the jar possesses the production (utpatti) which is non-different from its relation to the moment immediately following the collection (samūha) consisting of the staff—which is not otherwise established with respect to the jar.

In cases such as "the jar [arises] from the stick" (*daṇḍād ghaṭaḥ*), since the supplementation of a verb such as "is born" (*jāyate*) is necessary, the meaning of the ablative case is simply "immediately following that" (*tādṛśāvyavahitottaratvam*). In this way, through its connection with the moment included within the meaning of the verbal root, the desired sense is obtained. In reality, however, the meaning of the ablative is simply "being employed" (*prayuktatvam*), because that alone can be expressed by the word *apāya* (departure/separation) and the word *dhruva* (fixed/constant).

Furthermore, just as in the case of a jar and the like, there is also the state of being prompted by a staff and so forth even in its production; thus, the statements "the jar is produced from the staff" and "from the staff the jar [is produced]" possess validity, since even in its production, the jar is prompted by the staff and so forth. As for the statement of Kaiyaṭa, however, it intends another solution: the phrase "long coil" (*dīrghabhoga*) is used to indicate the time of the production of the action that precedes the disjunction and extends over a gross duration, specifically the time delimited by the production of the action conducive to the disjunction.

And thus there is the production of division; for just as in the case of a snake previously in a hole, the movement—whether it be the act of being urged forward or the actual stepping out—is perceived in the hair and so forth only at a later time, not at the very moment of production. This is because of the lack of contact with the eyes and other sense organs. As for the cognition that the grass and such exist in the hair at the moment of production, that must be explained away according to the manner previously stated.

As for the claim that Kaiyaṭa’s meaning of the sentence is as follows—even though there is an exit in the form of a disjunction from the hole delimited by the tip of the snake's body, just as it is perceived in the hole due to its [continued] conjunction with the hole delimited by its base—likewise, in the case of a blade of durvā grass and the like, although it is perceived as connected to a portion of its own transformed hair and so forth, there is an exit in the form of an absence of connection with the hair and so forth delimited by another portion of the hair and so forth—that is not correct.

They say that because expressions such as "it moves from the tree" are not employed even when leaves and the like move while the tree remains stationary, the absence of conjunction with the tree and so forth—specifically that which does not exist at the same time as the conjunction with the tree—is what constitutes the referent of the term *apāya* (separation); whereas the absence of conjunction with a hole or similar location is not the referent of the term *apāya*.
He is the source of the world. 30.

The origin (*prabhava*) of the agent of the action of becoming (*bhū*) is as previously explained. "The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat" (*himavataḥ gaṅgā prabhavati*). Here, "becoming" (*bhavana*) refers to conjunction with the exterior (*bahiḥ-saṃyoga*). The referent of the word "exterior" (*bahiḥ*) is the ground of Jambūdvīpa that is distinct from the Himavat. The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is the state of being simultaneous with the destruction of that conjunction. This [meaning] relates to the conjunction with the exterior through the relation of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) that pervades the nature of conjunction with the exterior. The meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is substratum-ness (*āśrayatva*). Thus, the cognition is: "The Gaṅgā is the substratum of a conjunction with the ground of Jambūdvīpa—which is distinct from the Himavat—occurring at the time of the destruction of the conjunction with the Himavat."

In the statement "The Gaṅgā originates from Prayāga," because of the absence of such usage [elsewhere], a relation that pervades the state of being a conjunction with something external [to its source] is posited. The state of being a conjunction of the Gaṅgā with the land of Būdvīpa, which is distinct from Prayāga, exists even at the beginning of a Kalpa in the land of Gaṅgādvāra and other places; however, since it does not possess the property of being simultaneous with the destruction of the conjunction of the Gaṅgā with Prayāga, that [over-extension] is excluded.
