On the other hand, with respect to the delimitation of the state of being a conjunction of the Gaṅgā with anything distinct from the Himavat mountains, the property of being simultaneous with the destruction of the conjunction of the Gaṅgā with the Himavat mountains indeed exists; thus, there is no fault.

Others, however, in order to exclude the aforementioned application [of the rule], state that the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is "the first conjunction with the exterior. The referent of the word "exterior" (*bahiḥ*) is a portion of the earth. "Firstness" (*prāthamya*) consists in occurring at the moment immediately following the destruction of the conjunction. They say that the resulting cognition is: "The Gaṅgā is the substratum of a conjunction with the earth that occurs at the moment immediately following the time of the destruction of the conjunction with the Himālaya. This too has been rejected, because of the Lord’s statement: "Other [Gaṅgās] appear again and again. By this, the usage of Śrī Harṣa—*lūnair... anyānyaśayyāracanāya* ("with [lotuses] plucked for the making of various other beds," etc.)—is also explained.

Regarding this, some argue that even if the stated applications are somehow justified, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would still apply by virtue of the primary meaning [of the agent], as in the example *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he hears from the actor"). This is because there is no distinction between the actor and the teacher in terms of the activity conducive to the action. However, a rejection based on the "Brahma-weapon" of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*) is not satisfying; furthermore, it contradicts the *Mahābhāṣya* on the relevant *sūtra*. Likewise, the *vārttika* concerning *jugupsā* is also necessary. Thus, the mention of the technical designations (*saṃjñin*), such as "the fixed cause of fear which is not endured," is also purposeful.

Even though those respective technical designations (*saṃjñā*) apply due to their higher status, when there is an intention to express "remainder-ness" (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case is desired—as in "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇāmaśnīyāt*)—and therefore [the rule] serves to exclude the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) in that context. Consequently, there is a contradiction with the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* here; for it is impossible to assert that "the genitive is not desired in the case of the teacher (*upādhyāya*), yet it is desired in the case of the causes of fear (*bhayahetu*) and so forth. This point should be investigated by the learned.

With this in mind, our venerable father has stated: "The *apādāna* is that which possesses the status of a limit (*avadhi*). And the status of being a limit consists in having the cessation of a relation with either the agent or the object, as occasioned by the meaning of the verbal root in question. In the example "Devadatta falls from the horse," the meaning of the root in question is falling; the cessation of the conjunction (with the horse) belonging to the agent, Devadatta, is occasioned by that [falling]; since the horse possesses that [cessation], the horse is the *apādāna*.

In the case of "the two rams move away from each other," there too, the cessation of the conjunction between the two rams is brought about by their movement away. In "he fears the wolf," the cessation of Devadatta’s connection with the wolf is caused by the wolf. In "he protects Devadatta from the thieves," the cessation of the connection with Devadatta—who is designated as the object—is caused by the act of protection directed toward the thieves. In "he studies under the teacher" as well, the cessation of the sound—which is the nature of the verbal action—resides in the teacher.

The rule [of *apādāna*] mentioned by Kaiyaṭa should be understood here as follows: Kaiyaṭa’s intention is that the sound (*dhvani*) produced [by a speaker] ceases because it is non-eternal (*anityatva*). In the example "He wards off the cow from the beans" (*māṣebhyo gāṃ vārayati*), there is a cessation of the connection of the cows—which are the objects (*karman*)—with the beans, brought about by the act of warding off. In cases such as "A scorpion is born from cow dung" (*gomayād vṛściko jāyate*), there is likewise a cessation of the connection consisting of the identity of the scorpion—the agent—with the cow dung and so forth.

Even in such cases as "The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," there is a cessation of the connection between the Himavat and the water of the Gaṅgā—which is the agent of the action of originating—because some waters emerge from the Himavat while others remain there. In the expression "The ocean is a water-jar," the status of being an ocean is attributed to the water-jar because of its abundance of water; or, conversely, the status of being a water-jar is attributed to the ocean because of its clarity, even though this is unreal. Thus, the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative source) exists everywhere, common to both the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*). This is the general direction [of the argument].
That person whom one intends through an action is the recipient (saṃpradāna). || 32 ||

That person whom the agent of an action intends by means of the object that has become an instrument (karaṇa) of that action receives the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient). In other words, the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) consists in being intended as one who is to partake in the fruit produced by the object functioning as the instrument. For example: "He gives a cow to the teacher" (*upādhyāyāya gāṃ dadāti*). In the sentence "He goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the term "functioning as an instrument" is included to exclude Caitra or others who are intended as the goal because they possess happiness and so forth produced by the village—the object of the act of going. For the village is not an instrument in the act of going; whereas wealth is indeed an instrument in the act of giving.

This is because [the cow] is the cause of ownership that constitutes the act of giving, which consists specifically in the renunciation of one's own ownership for the sake of another's ownership. In the case of gifting a cow to a Brāhmaṇa with the aim of securing heaven for one's father, the father is intended as the recipient of the fruit produced by the act of giving, and not as the possessor of the fruit produced by the cow; thus, there is no deviation (in the rule). Nor should it be argued that even the fruit such as heaven is produced by the cow through the medium of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), since the intention is expressed as "the cow, once given, will produce heaven for the father."

Because the fruit [of the action] is qualified by its not having the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as its means, or by its being the delimitor of the root-meaning; in the aforementioned instance, the state of having the Brahmin’s ownership as its objective—consisting in the form of being produced by his desire—is connected with the act of giving (*dāna*) via the dative case, whereas the meaning of the accusative is ownership (*svatva*). The resulting cognition is: "He possesses an effort conducive to a gift that generates in the recipient an ownership whose objective is the ownership of the Brahmin."

And thus, since it is not accepted that the status of being a recipient (*sampradāna*) is determined solely by the act of giving, even in cases such as "he sprinkles water for the tree" (*vṛkṣāyodakaṃ siñcati*), the tree possesses the status of a recipient because it is the intended object (*uddeśya*) as the locus of the fruit produced by the water. The cognition [involved] is: "one who possesses an effort directed toward the act of sprinkling with the tree’s leaves, etc., as the intended object. Nor should it be argued that one would instead say "he sprinkles water on the tree" (*vṛkṣam udakaṃ siñcati*), just as one says "he leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati*), because the tree could potentially be the object (*karman*) by virtue of its possession of conjunction, and the water could be so by virtue of its possession of the action of a liquid substance.
This is not the case, because [such usage] is not expressed (*anabhidhānāt*).

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, understand the term *saṃpradāna* (recipient) according to its etymological meaning as follows: it is that which possesses acceptance (*svīkāra*) while being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) of the substance being relinquished. Acceptance is the formal taking (*pratigraha*) that brings about the fitness for use as one pleases. Being the intended object means being the content of the cognition produced by the utterance of a word ending in the dative case.
One should give with perfect faith, having pronounced the name and lineage, and having mentioned the place, time, and so forth, saying, "I give this unto you."
One should even proclaim the cessation of the sense of "mine" regarding one's own possessions;
thus endowed with faith, one should perform acts such as giving and fire-offerings.

This is according to the statement of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha. The substantive [in the definition] is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a deity. The state of being a deity consists in being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) of the substance being abandoned; this exists in the entity such as Indra. It consists in being expressed by a word ending in the dative case at the time of abandonment; this exists in the word. The status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is denoted by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), as established by the usage of the learned (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*). For this very reason, when the status of being a deity is obtained through a secondary derivative suffix, the dative case is weaker. This is because the status of being a deity—defined as being the intended object of the substance being abandoned—is obtained from the dative case itself by means of the exclusion of the aspect of "acceptance" (*svīkāra*). As it has been stated by the Bhaṭṭas:

The connection with a deity occurs either through a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita), or by the dative case, or again by the indicative mark of a mantra; among these, each subsequent means is weaker than the preceding one.

In that context, acts such as giving are obtainable from other sources; the meaning of the dative case is merely "being the intended recipient. And in examples such as "he gives a garment to the washerman," there is figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). This is precisely the intention of the author of the Vṛtti as well.

Kaiyaṭa and others, however, state: "Because of the observation [in the scripture], 'One should not give instruction to a Śūdra,' and because of the example cited by the author of the Bhāṣya, 'He gives a slap to Khaṇḍikāputra,' giving consists in the cessation of one's own ownership up to the point of transferring it to the ownership of another. Furthermore, the designation of the recipient (*sampradāna*) applies only to the domain of the verb *dadāti* (to give). Therefore, they say that both [the definition and] the Vārttika stating 'The mention of the action must be made' are incorrect."

If it is argued that, according to this view, the dative case would not be weaker than the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), we say: not so. This is because the mere presence of that [dative] does not establish weakness. To explain: in the section concerning qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), it was established that regarding the scriptural text, "He pours curds into hot milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* is for the Vājins," the sentence concerning the *vājina* is [intended] as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the preceding sacrifice.

Is it an injunction for either the substance or the deity, or is it an injunction for a separate ritual act? Since the substance and deity mentioned within its own sentence are presented first in comparison to the substance and deity mentioned in another sentence, the sacrifice—already occupied by them—is rendered devoid of expectancy; thus, there is no room for the inclusion of the substance and deity mentioned in the other sentence. Furthermore, the *yaji* (sacrifice) found in the sentence concerning the whey (*vājina*) requires the context known as "qualification" (*adhikāra*), and therefore it serves to indicate the previously established sacrifice. However, the *yaji* found in the sentence concerning the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) does so without requiring that context at all.

Because of the proximity [of the word *āmikṣā*] in its syntactic connection with the word for the deity within the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), there is the cognition of the relationship between the substance and the deity—which is the basis for inferring the act of sacrifice—through the single-word expression *vaiśvadevī* in the case of the *āmikṣā*. However, in the case of the *vājina*, because it is expressed by a separate word (*vājibhyaḥ*), there is remoteness. This is because, in the term *vaiśvadevī*, according to the grammatical rule "that which has this as its deity" (*sāsya devatā*), the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is a specific substance qualified by a deity; furthermore, if the substance were not denoted [by the derivative], its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *āmikṣā* would be untenable.

Nor can there be a cognition of that [deity] by way of the principle of individual instances (*vyakti*), because that would entail the grammatical rule "the *taddhita* suffix is used for the deity" (Pāṇini 4.2.24), rather than the rule "the dative case is used in the sense of giving" (Pāṇini 2.3.13). Nor should it be argued that the referent of the *taddhita* suffix is merely the substance (*dravya*) while deityhood (*devatātva*) is a relational property (*saṃsarga*); for in a grammatical instruction concerning word-meanings (*padārtha*), a relation is unfit to be taught as such. Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that even "sonship" (*apatyatva*) would not be the meaning of the suffix in expressions such as "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*). Nor does the word *āmikṣā* become redundant if the *taddhita* suffix denotes a specific substance.

Because a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) expressing a general category does not bring to mind a specific form such as *āmikṣā*-ness in the absence of the co-occurrence of another word, it serves a purpose by acting as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Even if a doubt regarding a specific substance arises upon hearing only the word ending in a secondary derivative—since the substance is presented in its general form by that derivative—nevertheless, even when the specific [substance] is supplied by the word *āmikṣā*, the fact that the connection between an unascertained specific substance and a deity is based solely on the direct statement of the words (*padaśruti*) remains intact.

The dative case in "vājibhyaḥ" is indeed ambiguous in its own form, because it is common to both the fourth and fifth cases. Even the dative case, while expressing only the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), would denote the status of a deity only through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by abandoning the aspect of being a recipient; it would not, however, express a connection with the substance. Furthermore, even if the deity were to imply the substance through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) as its counter-correlative, that [connection] would not have scriptural authority (*śābdatva*). Nor is such an implication even possible, because it is necessary only in the absence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And here, because the word *vājina* exists, even though the word *vājibhyaḥ* requires a substance (*dravya*), the connection with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*)—being understood from another word—is more remote than the connection with the whey (*vājina*). Nor can there be an insertion [of the number] by bringing about a substance as in the case of a number; for when the nature of the ritual act is delimited by oneness, it is upon that repeated act that the number eleven is inserted, since numbers such as duality and so forth are necessarily co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the oneness previously established.

Since the whey (*vājina*) cannot be included by way of being co-referential with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), and since it is impossible for even the repeated action to find a place [in the original rite] because it remains obstructed by the *āmikṣā*, therefore a distinct sacrifice—characterized by the connection between a substance and a deity and having the *sānnāyya* as its archetype—is enjoined as a subordinate part of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice alone, for the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the whey produced from the *āmikṣā*. Consequently, the accessory (*guṇa*), which does not fit into the previous ritual action, is a differentiator (*bhedaka*).

And there is no application [of the rule] in the present case due to proximity, remoteness, and so forth, according to the principles already stated; or, in some instances, because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), as has been established elsewhere.

Furthermore, since the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is understood here through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), even in the absence of a formal seed-reason (*bīja*), the weakness of the dative case is established by the aforementioned alternative principle.

Let us return to the subject at hand. The term "action" (*kriyā*) must be included [in the definition]. In the example *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband"), the husband receives the designation of *saṃpradāna* because he is desired through the action of lying down. However, the authors of the Bhāṣya maintain that since an action is also sought after by means of seeing, resolving, praying, and so forth, it is also an artificial object (*kṛtrima-karman*). Thus, the point is established by the rule itself; for even though the actions of seeing and so forth are not explicitly expressed, the husband is intended as the goal by the action of lying down, which serves as their object.

For the sequence is as follows: first there is the cognition of the act of lying down, then the desire, and then the exertion. Furthermore, it is clear that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to the act of lying down and so forth, as it is defined by the action such as cognition. This is because the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is observed to depend upon an action that is actually perceived, as seen in examples such as *praviśa piṇḍīm* ("enter, [eat] the cake"). This is also supported by the natural sense of the rule *kriyārthopapadasya...* (Pāṇini 3.3.10). [Objection: But if this were the case, then in instances such as *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat"), there would also be the undesired consequence (*āpatti*) of the mat being considered a recipient (*sampradāna*).

On this point, they say: when [actions] such as "seeing" (*saṃdarśana*) and so forth are intended to be expressed as distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then the designation *saṃpradāna* applies. And that intention is restricted to specific objects based on the observation of actual usage; therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is because, in those cases, the distinction is not intended to be expressed. For this very reason, the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* will be rejected. And it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"And when there is an intention to express the distinction with respect to each preceding action..."
Since the other member [of the compound] functions as the object (*karman*), the term "action" (*kriyā*) was not included [in the definition].
But when unity is intended for the collection of actions, then the object,
by virtue of its connection with those actions, is figuratively designated by its own name [as "action"].
The intention to express either difference or non-difference is established by its own inherent nature;
therefore, no deviation is observed regarding the status of being the object of a verb meaning "to go."
If both these notions were everywhere to exist solely through conceptual construction,
then the rejection of the undertaking of yoga would be equivalent [to rejecting the world].

That which is well-spoken [the teaching] is figuratively designated—that is, treated—as the *karman* (object) by virtue of its nature as the desired action (*kriyopsitatva*), and not by the designation of *sampradāna* (recipient). However, in the case of the object of a verb meaning "to go," both distinction and non-distinction are intended to be expressed alternately; thus, two case-endings are established due to the two designations. The rest is clear.

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that this [definition] is not tenable because there is necessarily no cognition of [the object] as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth. For this very reason, they state that in the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi*, the Vārttika—"the mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) is also enjoined therein"—has been adopted by the author of the Bhāṣya as a mandatory injunction; we shall clarify this point in that very context. And this [object] is of three kinds: "That which is desired by the agent through the action, provided it is not excluded by him, is the object (*karman*). [Pāṇini 1.4.49] It is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for the agent’s relinquishment [of effort].
And by means of instigation and consent, one attains the status of a recipient (saṃpradāna).

Thus, from the *Vākyapadīya*: "He gives an *arghya* offering to the Sun; he gives a cow to a Brahmin; he gives a cow to a preceptor. These are the examples in their respective order. Helārāja states that this sūtra is not redundant because it would already be established by the fourth case (*caturthī*) expressing "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*). Since the act of giving is primary due to its connection with the fruit [of the gift], it is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) that is "for the sake of" the gift, and not the act of giving that is "for the sake of" the recipient; therefore, [the application of the fourth case by *tādarthya*] does not arise here. For this very reason, it is stated that [the recipient] is "the object desired through the action" (*karmaṇepsita*) as a subordinate part of the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*).

When the object of the action (*saṃpradāna*) is intended to be expressed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the object (*karman*), [the following applies]: *paśunā rudraṃ yajate* (he worships Rudra with an animal). The meaning is "he gives the animal to Rudra. This, however, is established through Vedic irregularity (*chāndasavyatyaya*). In common usage (*loka*), however, since the root *yaj* has the sense of "worship," the animal functions as the instrument.
[Now begins the section on roots] having the sense of "pleasing" (*rucyarthānāṃ*): the one who is being pleased [is the recipient]. (Pāṇini 1.4.33)

It should be designated by the aforementioned technical term (*saṃjñā*). For example: *devadattāya rocate* or *svadate modakaḥ pathi* ("The sweetmeat is pleasing or tastes good to Devadatta on the road"). Why is the word *pathi* included [in the rule] when it is already understood that the one who is pleased (*prīyamāṇa*) is the recipient? It is so that the designation does not apply to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in *ādityo rocate* ("The sun shines"), where the sense is "shining" (*dīpti*) and thus the designation does not occur.
Regarding this, the *Vākyapadīya* states:
"Whether it functions as a cause (*hetu*), is designated as an object (*karman*), or remains as a residual factor (*śeṣa*), it is still a *kāraka*."
In the case of verbs meaning "to please" and others, that [object] is designated as the recipient (saṃpradāna) by the grammatical treatise.

The meaning of this [sūtra] is as follows: the sense of the root *ruc* (to please/delight) is "desire residing in another," because it is understood that [the object] becomes the object of desire. Devadatta employs such a sweetmeat (*modaka*). Since he acts in accordance with it out of greed, Devadatta receives the designation of *hetu* (cause). However, when the root *ruc* has the sense of "pleasing" (*prīṇati*), Devadatta receives the designation of *karman* (object). When the sense is "it becomes the object of Devadatta's desire," the designation of *śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive of relation) would otherwise apply; therefore, the designation of *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is initiated. [The rule continues:
"In the case of the roots *ślāgh* (to praise), *hnuṅ* (to deny), *sthā* (to stand), and *śap* (to curse), the one being made aware [of the matter] [is the recipient]. (Pāṇini 1.4.34)

In the employment of these [verbs], the one intended to be informed is the *sampradāna*. "He praises for Devadatta" (*devadattāya ślāghate*); the meaning is that he lauds him. For it is in this way that Devadatta can be made aware: some say it means he tells Devadatta about something praiseworthy, whether concerning himself or another.
"Praising [his own prowess] before the wives of others, the lord of the Rākṣasas went there."

Thus, according to the usage of Bhaṭṭi, the meaning is "praising himself as superior to other women. Since the first alternative results in [the object being] a *karman* (direct object), and the second results in the application of the genitive case for the *śeṣa* (remainder), this rule is commenced. Verbs such as *hnu* ("to deny") are transitive because they signify the making known of something qualified by their own specific meaning. Consequently, the term "one being made to know" (*jñīpsyamāna*) is a qualifier of the technical designation (*saṃjñin*). For example, in *devadattāya hnuve*, the sense is that while denying Devadatta—i.e., concealing him—one makes Devadatta aware of that concealment; the meaning is that one denies him even though he is present, thereby deceiving the creditor or others.
Alternatively, the meaning is that Devadatta is being made aware of what ought to be concealed. Devadatta is made aware by such a manner of standing as [the speaker] says, "I am like this.
Who would stand before him who is fond of his retinue?
Who [could stand] before the Destroyer of Jambha, whose pillar-like arms blaze with the circle of light from flaming thunderbolts?

Thus says Murāri: "He swears an oath against Devadatta. The meaning is that he makes something known by means of an oath. Because of the statement [in the rule] "when being made to know" (*jñīpsyamāne*), this designation does not apply here: "O Devadatta! In examples such as "Devadatta praises by means of his Gārgika-kinship" (*ślāghate gārgikayā*) or "he praises on the road" (*ślāghate pathi*), the designation does not apply when the agent and so forth are involved.
"The creditor in the case of *dhārayati* (to owe) [is called *saṃpradāna*]. (Pāṇini 1.4.35)

*Uttamarṇaḥ* means the owner of wealth. It is derived from the root *ṛ* (to go) with the suffix *kta*; the prefix *ut* is added because it signifies an excellent object (*utkṛṣṭārtha*), and the superlative suffix *tamap* is applied due to the excellence of the substance. Regarding the rule "the *ṇatva* [nasalization] occurs in the sense of creditor and debtor," since only the act of exchange is intended there, the *ṇatva* does not apply to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). Precisely because of this irregular formation (*nipātana*), even when the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) ends the compound, it is placed at the end in a *bahuvrīhi*. Example: *devadattāya śataṃ dhārayati* ("He owes a hundred to Devadatta"). "Owing" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to the taking of an object after having promised to give it back. This rule is commenced because the genitive case would otherwise have been required. Why say "creditor" (*uttamarṇa*)? [To exclude cases where the debtor is meant].

In the usage "grāme" (in the village) and so forth within the aforementioned sentences, let there not be [the designation of *hetu*]. Nor is its establishment achieved merely by priority [of rule], because the designation of *hetu* would then undesirably apply even to a creditor (*uttamarṇa*). [Now begins:
"The desired object of the verb *spṛh* [is called *saṃpradāna*]. (Pāṇini 1.4.36)

The root *spṛh* (meaning "desire") belongs to the *curādigaṇa* and ends in the vowel *a*. When used with this root, that which is desired (*īpsita*) shall receive the technical designation [of *saṃpradāna*]. Example: *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati* ("he desires flowers"). However, when there is the sense of being the most desired (*īpsitatama*), the designation of *karman* (object) applies by virtue of its higher priority. Example: *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati* ("he desires flowers"). When one intends to express the remaining relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case alone is used. Example:
*kumārya iva kāntasya trasyanti spṛhayanti ca* ("like young maidens, they tremble at and desire their beloved").

Thus say Haradatta and others. Helārāja maintains that this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) supersedes both the designation of "object" (*karman*) and the genitive of the "remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). According to this view, in the aforementioned usage, the form *kāntāya* results from a change of case-ending. In the phrase "mutually possessing desirable beauty," one should assume that the suffix *-anīya-* denotes the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), just as in the expression "a Brahmin to be given [something]."
In the case of verbs meaning "to be angry," "to hate," "to envy," "to be jealous," or "to find fault," [the fourth case ending is used] for that person toward whom the anger is directed. || 37 ||

When roots meaning anger and the like are employed, that *kāraka* (participant) toward whom the anger is directed receives the aforementioned designation (*saṃjñā*). Examples include "he is angry with Devadatta" (*devadattāya krudhyati*), and so forth. Anger (*krodha*) is wrath; malice (*droha*) is doing harm; envy (*īrṣyā*) is intolerance of another’s virtues; and spite (*asūyā*) is the disparagement of another’s virtues. Although these are indeed defects of the mind, it would have been more appropriate to say "of roots meaning defects of the mind" (*vittadoṣārthānām*); nevertheless, in cases such as "he hates us" (*yo 'smān dveṣṭi*), since the root *dviṣ* does not mean "not rejoicing" [in the sense of the mental defect] but rather expresses mere aversion, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the rule to that case.

"He hates the medicine" (*auṣadhaṃ dveṣṭi*): the verb *dviṣ* (to hate) is used here even though there is no actual taking pleasure in [the medicine]. Why say "towards whom" (*yaṃ prati*)? [Consider: "He is jealous of his wife" (*bhāryām īrṣyati*). The meaning is that he cannot bear her being seen by others. Since *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice) are intransitive, when they are used with an object, the genitive case of the "remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply; however, since the other two (*īrṣy* and *dviṣ*) are transitive, the accusative case would have applied. Therefore, this rule is commenced. **Pāṇini 1.4.38:** When *krudh* and *druh* are preceded by a prefix, the object is [marked by the sixth case]. (Note: This sūtra is provided as part of the grammatical context for the preceding commentary.)

When these two roots are accompanied by prepositions (*upasarga*), the previously mentioned designation of "object" (*karman*) applies; this is an exception to the preceding rule. Examples: *devadattam abhikrudhyati* (he is angry with Devadatta), *abhidruhyati* (he bears malice toward Devadatta).
[In the case of] *rādh* and *īkṣ*, that person whose inquiry is made is [the object]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.39)

The *kāraka* associated with these two roots in connection with various questions is designated as *sampradāna*. For example: *kṛṣṇāya rādhyati* or *īkṣate*. The meaning is that Garga, being questioned, deliberates upon what is auspicious or inauspicious. Since the objects consisting of the auspicious and inauspicious are included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the roots are considered intransitive (*akarmaka*). This statement is made because the genitive case would otherwise apply. In the form *rādhyati*, the suffix *śyan* is used because it is intransitive; thus, there is a rule within the *divādi* sub-group: "After the root *rādh*, when it is intransitive, [the suffix *śyan* is applied] only in the sense of 'increasing' (*vṛddhi*)."

The suffix *śyan* is applied to *rādh* only when it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), because the particle *eva* (only) is placed out of its logical position (*bhinnakrama*). This is as in the rule *bṛddhau*. For this very reason, the commentary on the sūtra *karmavat karmaṇā* states, "the rice ripens" (*rādhyaty odanaḥ*), since it has the sense of "is accomplished" (*sidhyati*). By this, the claim that for these two [roots] the object (*karmakāraka*) is the recipient (*sampradāna*) is refuted. Some say that the word *yasya* is redundant, because the desired result is established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "towards whom" (*yaṃ prati*). That is not correct.

Since the word *pratītya* signifies "having that as its object," upon reflection, only the auspicious (*śubha*) and the inauspicious (*aśubha*) can be its objects; yet, the auspicious and the inauspicious themselves lack an [external] object. Furthermore, to assume a different meaning by relying on the governing rule for the prefix *pra-* would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
[The sūtra states: "With the prefixes *prati* and *āṅ*, the agent of the preceding action [is the karmapravacanīya]. (Pāṇini 1.4.90)

The roots *śru* preceded by *prati* and *āṅ* have the sense of "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*). Its prior operation is the act of instigation (*pravartana-kriyā*), and the agent of that [act] is the recipient (*sampradāna*). For example: *viprāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti* or *āśṛṇoti*. The meaning is that, having been prompted by the Brahmin with the words, "Give me a cow," he promises. Since the designation of "cause" (*hetu-saṃjñā*) would otherwise apply, this rule is stated to prevent such usage as *vipreṇa pratiśṛṇoti*. Some maintain that, depending on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā-bheda*), one may say *devadatto gāṃ pratiśrāvayati*.

In this way, one might even say, "Devadatta approves of the sweetmeat" (*rocayati modakam*). This is not an unintended consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the texts of both our own and other schools on that point. Others hold that since the sublation of the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) applies equally to the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the present case as well.
And [the rule applies] to *anu-prati-gṛṇa* as well (Pāṇini 1.4.40).

The grammatical factor (kāraka) preceding either *anu* or *prati* is likewise employed [as a governing word] with the root *gṛṇāti*. The form *gṛṇā* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root ending in the *śnā* affix. There is a compound (*samāsa*) of *anu*, *prati*, and *gṛṇā*; the vowel *ā* is elided according to the rule *āto dhātoḥ*. However, some say that *anu-prati* is a separate word, and because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is the elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*) by the rule *prakṛtivat*.

The meaning of that [term] is the encouragement of the reciter. The first action is the recitation (*śaṃsana*). One "responds to" (*anugṛṇāti*) or "replies to" (*pratigṛṇāti*) the *hotṛ*. The sense is that the *adhvaryu* encourages the *hotṛ*, who recites first, with words such as "O gods, may we eat. That which is the most effective instrument is the *karaṇa* (instrument). || 42 ||

A *kāraka* that is the most effective instrument (*prakṛṣṭopakāraka*) in an action is designated as the *karaṇa*. It should not be argued that since the status of being an "accomplisher" (*sādhakatva*) is already obtained through the governing rule (*adhikāra*) on *kārakas*, the purpose of excellence is already established by the mere repetition of the term, making the suffix *-tamap* redundant. This is because it is taught that, by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), excellence is not understood in this context [of the governing rule]. By this, examples such as *gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ* ("the hamlet on the Ganges") are established; for the quality of distance residing in the bank is metaphorically attributed (*upacāra*) to the current. However, if the word *gaṅgā* were taken as directly denoting the bank (*tīralakṣaka*), this would not serve as a purpose [for the rule]. [Another example: *rāmeṇa bāṇena hato vālī* ("Vālī was killed by Rāma with an arrow").

On this point, the ancient teachers [define] instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) as being the cause of an action while not having its purpose fulfilled by another factor (*kāraka*). The purpose of the qualification "not having its purpose fulfilled by another factor" is to exclude being a cause of an action through the mediation of an operation residing in another factor. There is no deviation [in the definition] regarding the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), because they are causes of the action through the mediation of an operation residing in the instrument. The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) likewise possesses that status through the mediation of the operation of either the agent or the object.

In such cases as "Caitra cooks rice in a pot in the house," the house is useful by way of the agent's activity, and the pot is useful by way of the object's activity. Likewise, the recipient (sampradāna) is so by way of manifesting consent or by way of generating the agent's desire; and the point of departure (apādāna) is so by way of the disjunction that destroys the contact which prevents falling. Nor is there a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the contact with an axe and the like, since these are already accounted for within the activities of the agent and the object; for it is only the final cause (*caramakāraṇa*) that is the subject of the definition. For this very reason, they say: "An instrument (*karaṇa*) is a cause delimited by the non-connection with the result."

Others, however, define the instrument (*karaṇa*) as being that which possesses activity (*vyāpāravattva*) while also being a cause (*kāraṇatva*). Nor does it follow that the self (*ātman*) would incur the status of an instrument because *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) and mental contact (*manoyoga*) act as its activities with respect to all effects, such as cognition; for [the definition] specifies "activity" [as something distinct from the agent]. For this very reason, there are usages such as "you know the self by means of the self. Even though a single entity may possess both natures—agency and instrumentality—there is no fault, as these are merely distinctions based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In the case of auditory perception, the activity is the contact between the ear and the mind, not the sound itself; for [if it were the sound], there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the perception of the absolute non-existence of sound.

They say that in the case of visual perception and the like, the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the eye and so forth is their conjunction [with the object]; and in inference, the operation of the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection).

Others, however, define instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) as being the object of the agent’s operation. And that consists in possessing an operation residing in the agent that is conducive to the result. For, in the case of an axe and the like, there exists the possession of a conjunction and so forth residing in the agent, which is conducive to the act of cutting. Nor is there an inconsistency [in this definition] regarding the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), since it too is the object of the operation residing in the agent; for its status as an instrument is accepted, as seen in such usage as "he cooks the rice in a pot. As it has been said:
When the accomplishment of an action is intended to be described as occurring immediately after the operation of a particular factor,
that factor is then remembered as the instrument (karaṇa).
In reality, that [agenthood] is indefinable, for no entity is fixed [in its role];
since we observe the intended meaning in such expressions as "the pot cooks."

By this, [the rule] "he accomplishes the gift with a cow" (*gavā dānam sādhayati*) and "he accomplishes it with a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇena sādhayati*), and so forth, is explained. Since expressions such as "Caitra cooks by himself" (*caitra ātmanā pacati*) or "Caitra cooks by means of Caitra" (*caitreṇa pacati*) are not used, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—which possesses an activity (*vyāpāravān*) and is distinct from that which possesses the effort (*kṛtimat*) by virtue of being its delimiting factor (*avacchedakatayā*)—must be a final constituent (*antyāvayavin*). By the inclusion of the term "final constituent," cases such as "he cooks with his hand" (*hastena pacati*) are subsumed. Furthermore, this status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is not common to inference (*anumāna*) and the like; therefore, in those cases, it is indeed distinct. And they say that the word *karaṇa* has multiple meanings. Pāṇini 1.4.43: *divaḥ karma ca* ("And [the agent of] *div* is also the object").

That which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for the action denoted by the root *div* (to gamble) receives the designation of *karman* (object); and by the word "and" (*ca*), it also receives the designation of *karaṇa* (instrument). The conjunction "and" (*ca*) serves to effect a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both designations, because the term *karaṇa* is carried over [from the previous rule] or because the alternative option (*anyatarasyām*) to be mentioned later is drawn in. The result of this is explained in the rule *ākaḍārāt*. P4.4.44: In the case of hiring for wages (*parikrayaṇe*), the [person hired] is optionally designated as *sampradāna* (recipient).

*Parikrayaṇa* (purchase) is the act of acquiring [something] by means of wages or the like, under the restriction of a specific agreement; that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in that act is optionally designated as the *sampradāna*. [Examples: *śatāya parikrītaḥ* or *śatena parikrītaḥ* ("purchased for a hundred").
The locus (*ādhāra*) is the *apādāna* (ablative). (Pāṇini 1.4.45)

That by which an action (*kriyā*) is supported is called a locus (*ādhāra*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the rule "adhyāyanyāya... and so forth. The status of being a locus for an action belongs to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), because they support [the action]. This is because the direct substrata of the action—the agent and the object—are sublated by the subsequent technical designations of "agent" and "object. A factor of action (*kāraka*) that is the substratum of the action through the mediation of either the agent or the object is designated as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Thus Hari says: "That which supports an action indirectly, mediated by the agent and the object..."
In the accomplishment of the action that provides assistance, the locus (adhikaraṇa) is traditionally taught in the grammatical treatise.

"He sits on a mat," "He cooks in a pot. But surely, in that case, such usages as "he cooks in fire" would be untenable, because [the fire] lacks the possession of action through either the agent or the object. Nor can it be assumed that such a usage does not exist at all;
for it is prescribed that the oblation is to be offered in that very fire in which one cooks the food.

This is because such usage is observed in Smṛti texts. Furthermore, the hypothesis of certain scholars—that the word *agni* (fire) and others function through *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) to refer to the cooking-pot (*sthālī*) and so forth, thereby making the aforementioned indirectness possible—is not tenable. For if that were the case, the word *yat* would also have to refer to that [the pot], resulting in the undesirable consequence that the injunction "the oblation is offered in it" would become syntactically disconnected. To this we reply: True; however, this is justifiable on account of its being Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Now, it cannot be said that being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) consists in being related to its own property (*svadharma*), for since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like reside in both [relata], it would follow that a jujube fruit (*badara*) and so forth would be the locus as defined by a bowl (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth. Nor can it be argued that it is a relation to a property of itself, because the bowl and so forth are not properties of the jujube fruit; for if "being a property" were defined as the state of being the superstratum (*ādheyatā*), and that [superstratum-ness] were defined as being the specifier (*nirūpaka*) of a locus-ness residing in itself, there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

It should not be argued that the substratum (adhikaraṇa) for origination, subsistence, and cognition does not require anything else—such as the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) for a jar and the like; the earth and so forth for a universal (jāti) and the like; and that which is related by its own nature (svarūpasambandhin) for inherence (samavāya) and the like—serving as examples in their respective order. For if the word "requiring" (apekṣaṇīya) were taken to mean "cause," there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to non-inherent causes (asamavāyin) and others. Furthermore, it is untenable for the cognition of "jar-ness" and so forth to have the jar and such as its inherent cause.

Regarding this, the ancients say: "The state of being a substratum (adhikaraṇatva) consists in being corporeal while possessing a conjunction that prevents its falling, provided it is distinct from that [object]. The term "corporeal" is used to exclude God, who is the locus of the conjunction that supports the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). As for universals, qualities, and so forth, their being a substratum consists simply in their inherence (samavāya) in that [object]. Since inherence and other relations possess a relation of identity (svarūpa-sambandha) with that [object], they too possess the status of a substratum; thus, they assert that the nature of being a substratum is manifold.

The Navyas, however, maintain that because such a definition lacks universal applicability (*ananugama*) and because it would result in the locative case (*saptamī*) having multiple meanings, locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatva*) is indeed an additional property. Nor should it be argued that the additional property is simply "the state of being contained" (*ādheyatva*), while "the state of being a locus" (*ādhāratva*) is the state of being its determiner (*tannirūpakatva*); for there is no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) [to prefer one over the other]. Therefore, they say that both are additional properties.

On this point, those who follow the ancients say: "The nature of being a locus (ādhāratā) is simply that specific conjunction, inherence, or other relation [between the locus and the located]. And the property of being a locus (ādhāratātva) is something over and above [the relation] that is common to all such cases; therefore, there is no lack of uniformity (ananugama). When one says 'the locus of the staff,' although the relation is grasped as the property of being a locus, it is not grasped specifically as a conjunction; hence, a doubt may arise as to whether or not [the person] possesses a conjunction with the staff. This is because only a cognition in which the qualifierhood (prakāratā) is delimited by the property of conjunction (saṃyogatva) and so forth stands in opposition to such a doubt."

In the expression "the pot on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭaḥ*), the locative case (*saptamī*) signifies the state of being a locus (*ādhāratva*). This [locus] is construed with the pot through the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*). The resulting cognition is: "the pot is the determiner of the substratum-ness residing in the ground. The ancient logicians (*tārkika-prāñcaḥ*) maintain that "residing-in-ness" (*niṣṭhatva*) and "determiner-ness" (*nirūpakatva*) are the two relations [involved].

The moderns (navyāḥ), however, say that in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale na ghaṭaḥ*), there would be no cognition [of the absence], because since the relation of *nirūpakatva* (the state of being a determiner) is not a restrictor of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), it cannot be the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence; thus, the meaning of the locative case is *ādheyatva* (the state of being located). In that context, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed with [the locative meaning] through the relation of *nirūpitatva* (being determined by), and the meaning of the locative case is construed with the jar and so forth through the relation of *āśrayatva* (substratum-ness). Thus, they maintain that the resulting cognition is: "the jar is the locus of the state of being located as determined by the ground. [And: "The object of the roots *adhi-śī*, *adhi-sthā*, and *adhi-ās* is the locus. (Pāṇini 1.4.46)
The substratum (ādhāra) of these verbs preceded by *adhi* shall be designated as the object (*karma*). For example: *hariḥ vaikuṇṭham adhiśete*, *adhitiṣṭhati*, or *adhyāste*.
And [the substratum] of *abhiniviś* [is also so designated]. (Pāṇini 1.4.47)

The substratum (*ādhāra*) for this preceding [verb] *viśati* (enters) is as before. One "enters into" (*abhiniviśate*) a village. "Adherence" (*abhiniveśa*) means insistence; because it takes that as its support, this verb is intransitive in its own sense. In that case, this is a rule prescribing the designation "object" (*karman*) for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This is because, in the sense of "entering," that [designation of locus] is already established. Since the optionality (*vikalpa*) is carried over from the sūtra "In the case of hiring (*parikrayaṇa*), [the agent is] the recipient (*sampradāna*") by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and because it is accepted as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the locative case is used in examples such as "he is intent upon sin" (*pāpe 'bhiniviśate*).

For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samartha-sūtra* states: "of those intent upon these meanings. Furthermore, this usage of the two prefixes follows the aforementioned sequence, as indicated by the fact that *ni-* is placed last. Therefore, it does not apply here: *yadi śūkaśikhā pade niviśate* ("if the tip of a grain awn enters into the foot"). However, when the status of the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used even in that instance.
[Pāṇini 1.4.48: *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ*.

One fasts, dwells along with, dwells upon, or dwells in a village or an army. A prohibition must be stated for the root *vas* when it has the sense of *aś* (eating). The word *artha* here signifies "cessation. The two genitives are in different cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: "of that *vas* which expresses the cessation of eating, i.e., the sense of *aś*. Alternatively, *śyartha* means "the sense of *śī*" (to lie down); *na śyarthaḥ* is *aśyarthaḥ*, meaning "not having the sense of lying down. This is because in examples such as *jalāśayaḥ* ("water-reservoir"), the root *śī* is seen to have the sense of staying or abiding. Example: *grāme upavasati* ("he fasts in the village").

In the sense of "he stays in the village," one says "he dwells near the village" (*grāmam upavasati*). In the expression "having fasted for one night" (*ekām rajanīm upoṣya*), the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.5]. In the expression "one should not eat on the eleventh day" (*ekādaśyāṃ na bhuñjīta*), the locative case is used because it denotes a temporal locus (*kālika-adhikaraṇatva*), since the kāraka-case endings possess greater force. "The object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent. (Pāṇini 1.4.49)

The *kāraka* which is the object of an absolute desire for attainment residing in the agent is designated as the *karman*. It is understood from the context that it is "desired to be attained by that very [agent] whose agency is caused by its possession of activity. By this, the state of possessing the fruit produced by the action is obtained. Since the desire for the fruit, acting as a desire for a means, generates the desire for the action, the fruit itself is the most desired (*īpsitatama*). Nor does there arise the unwanted consequence that Caitra, who possesses the conjunction [with the village], would also be the *karman* in sentences such as "Caitra goes to the village," because the action is qualified by the condition of being inherent in another (*parasamavetatva*).

Regarding this, the author of the *Khaṇḍana* [Śrīharṣa] states: there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of the ablative (*apādāna*) in examples such as "the leaf falls from the tree," because the leaf possesses the fruit in the form of a disjunction produced by the action of falling inherent in itself. Nor is this an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for it would result in the leaf being used with the accusative case-ending. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "the jar is made" (*ghaṭaḥ kriyate*), because in the usage "he makes the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), that very same action is expressed with the accusative case-ending in another instance of usage.

Nor should it be said that when there is the intention to express [an object] as an object (*karman*), the application of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is caused by that intention rather than by the state of being an object (*karmatva*) alone, because one cannot intend multiple grammatical factors (*kārakas*) simultaneously. For when the state of being an object exists, the intention to express it is unavoidable. Nor should it be said that the consensus of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasaṃpradāya*) is the regulator [of the rule], because then the definition would absurdly apply to "whatever is merely an entity" (*vastumātraṃ karma*). Furthermore, such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is easily avoided by the very method already stated. Nor is "being other than the source (*apādāna*)" a qualifying attribute [for the object].

In cases such as "the river increases" (*nadī vardhate*), where the result of the action is conjunction and disjunction with a portion of the bank that was previously unattained—since this increase consists of the accumulation of parts—the definition would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to the bank itself, which possesses those results. Furthermore, one might argue that there is no such over-extension because an increase destroys only non-conjunction, whereas a village or similar object possesses a conjunction that serves as the cause for destroying the motion inherent in the traveler. However, this must be rejected, because since the conjunction resulting from an increase does indeed destroy the action, the over-extension to the bank remains as it was. Likewise, there is under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "he knows himself" (*ātmānaṃ jānāti*).

On this point, they say: the fruit of an action is expressed by some verbal roots as residing in someone other than the agent, while by others it is not so expressed; or rather, it is expressed by some verbal roots as residing in the agent, while by others it is not. Alternatively, there is an intention (*tātparya*) in certain verbal roots to convey the fruit as residing in someone other than the agent, whereas in others there is no such intention; or rather, there is an intention to convey the fruit as residing in the agent.

In this context, an object (*karman*) is that which possesses a result conveyed by a verbal root (*dhātu*), based on a locus distinct from the substratum of the action (*kriyāśraya*). Neither the tree nor the bank possesses such a status. This is because, in the case of a specific utterance [of *patati*], the result consisting of separation is not the meaning of the root *pat*; rather, its meaning is conjunction with a lower location (*adhaḥ-saṃyoga*). Furthermore, by the root *vardhati*, nothing is denoted as residing in a locus other than the agent (*kartṛ*). Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of "he knows himself" (*ātmānaṃ jānāti*).

This is because what is intended is the state of being the locus of a result of that same class as the result which resides in something other than the substratum of the action, by virtue of possessing a result of an action inherent in another. For [in this view], verbal usage and the like, which reside in jars and so forth and belong to the same class as such usage, are also possible in the case of the Self. Alternatively, even if the Self lacks "otherness" (paratva) and is not the locus of the result, there is no fault, because the result—by virtue of residing in something other than the substratum of the action—is not expressed by the verbal root.

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that [the object of an action] is that which possesses the fruit delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The meaning of *gam* (to go) is an action delimited by conjunction (*saṃyoga*); that of *tyaj* (to abandon) is [an action] delimited by disjunction (*vibhāga*); and that of *pat* (to fall) is [an action] delimited by downward conjunction. For if the mere vibration (*spanda*) were their meaning, it would follow that they are synonyms. Consequently, if one were to take the disjunction produced by going or falling as occurring in the prior location, or the conjunction as occurring in the subsequent location, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the prior or subsequent location would not be the "object" (*karman*) of the action of abandoning.

Furthermore, since the verbal root *spand* (to vibrate) denotes mere activity (*vyāpāra*) alone, the property of being the delimitor of the meaning of the root (*dhātvarthatāvacchedakatva*) is absent in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); therefore, there is no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the preceding and succeeding locations or the riverbank would possess that status [as the primary object]. It is precisely because they express an activity delimited by a result (*phala*) that verbal roots possess their primary transitivity (*sakarmakatva*). In the case of roots such as *jñā* (to know), however, that [transitivity] is secondary (*gauṇa*), consisting in the expression of a meaning that is connected with the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), namely a "cognitive object" (*viṣayatva*) distinct from the "status of being intended" (*uddeśyatva*) which is connected with the meaning of a noun (*nāmārtha*).

From expressions such as "he knows the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), there arises the understanding that [the agent] is the substratum of a cognition characterized by having the jar as its object (*viṣayatā*). Accusative suffixes occur only in connection with transitive roots (*sakarmaka-dhātu*) common to both [the agent and the object]. For this very reason, the root *pat* ("to fall") is not transitive, because the sense of being an intended goal (*uddeśyatva*), which is the meaning of the dative case, is construed only with what is connected to the meaning of a noun (the object). This is evident from the usage "even though he does not eat, he strives for eating" (*abhuñjāne 'pi bhojanāya yatate*). Furthermore, the property of "being produced by an action inhering in another" (*parasamavetakriyājanyatva*) must also be included in the definition of the result (*phala*).

Because of the usage "the bird goes to the ground" (*bhūmiṃ prayāti vihagaḥ*) and "it abandons the tree" (*vijahāti mahīruham*), [the action] does not [apply] to itself; for [in these cases], conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) constitute the result that delimits the meaning of the verbal root as stated. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the agent] being its own object (*karman*) due to possessing those [results]. Nor does it follow that in cases such as "one wrestler goes toward another wrestler" (*mallo mallaṃ gacchati*), where the conjunction is produced by the action of both, there would be the linguistic application of being the object of an action whose agent is oneself with respect to oneself.
This is because we accept that something is the object of a specific action when it possesses a result produced by an action inherent in another (*parasamaveta*).

And thus, for the accusative case and others, the meaning is "residing in another" (parasamavetatva) as connected with the action. Furthermore, "otherness" (paratva) is conveyed by the nominal suffix (sup) in relation to its own base-meaning (prakṛtyartha). However, the distinction is that in the case of an object-verb (karmākhyāta), it is conveyed in relation to that which is connected with the fruit of its own meaning. Thus, from such expressions as "he goes to the earth" (bhūmiṃ prayāti), there arises the cognition: "one who possesses an effort conducive to that movement which produces a conjunction residing in the earth and residing in something other than the earth."

Therefore, since the effort conducive to that movement—which resides in another wrestler, inheres in something distinct from oneself, and produces a conjunction residing in oneself—is absent in oneself, there is no such usage as "the wrestler goes to himself," and so forth. And here, the village and other objects are construed with "remoteness" (*paratva*) by way of a relation whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the individuality (*vyaktitva*) of that very individual in which the result (the fruit of the action) denoted by the accusative case and so on is construed.

They say that in expressions such as "the earth moves" (*tena pṛthivī prayāti*), there is no fault even though the absence of difference—whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*)—does not exist in the act of moving; nor is there the undesirable consequence of using such an expression as "it moves itself" (*svaṃ prayāti*), because the difference from itself does indeed exist within its own self.

Others, however, say that words such as "earth" are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to refer to each individual instance of earth, in accordance with the grammatical rule that the counter-correlativity must be delimited by the property that serves as the delimitor of the relation's occurrence (*anvayitāvacchedaka*).

However, some say that the meaning of the accusative case is the property of being a delimitant of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedakatva) of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) as qualified by action, and not "residing in another" (parasamavetatva). Consequently, the cognition [arising from the sentence "He goes to the earth"] is: "He possesses an effort conducive to that movement which is both produced by a conjunction residing in the earth and is a delimitant of the counter-correlativity of the mutual absence residing in the earth. They argue that since an action residing in oneself lacks the property of being a delimitant of the counter-correlativity of a mutual absence residing in oneself, there is no undesirable consequence (āpatti) such as "He goes to himself."

This being the case, for a wrestler who has not gone against another wrestler, there would have to be the grammatical usage "the wrestler goes against the wrestler" (*mallo mallam gacchati*), because the action of that wrestler—which is delimited by the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) residing in the other wrestler—produces a conjunction occurring on the ground occupied by that [other] wrestler. However, if it is argued that the relation of difference (*bheda*) is construed with the individual wrestler who is the locus of the result (*phala*), then there would be an infinite number of powers (*śakti*), since the universal "that-individualness" (*tadvyaktitva*) and so forth would have to serve as the qualifiers (*prakāra*).

Others, however, maintain that rather than postulating "relationalness" (saṃsargatva), it is simply "inherence in another" (parasamavetatva) that is correct; for even if mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), there is no impairment [to the definition]. Now, if it is argued that since "falling" (patati) means a motion delimited by contact with the downward direction, then the ground and so forth—which possess such contact—would incur the status of being the object (karman), resulting in the undesirable usage "the leaf falls from the tree to the ground" (vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ bhūtalaṃ patati); we say no, because such a usage is intended when one wishes to express it in that way. For this very reason, the rule prescribing a compound with a word ending in the second case (dvitīyā) in connection with "fallen" (patita)—as in the sūtra *āśritātītapatitādi*—is consistent.

Others, however, say that the distinction between transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*) verbs does not depend on the nature of the operation (*vyāpāra*), but rather on specific words (*śabda-viśeṣa*) by taking into account specific delimiting results (*avacchedaka-phala*). To explain: when a result is denoted by a verbal root as the delimitant of the operation, and there arises an expectancy for its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), it is the meaning of the word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā-anta*)—being proximate—that is construed as such. Thus, in the sentence "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), the sentence-meaning is an operation that produces a conjunction having the village as its counter-correlate. And in the case of the conjunction that delimits the meaning of the root *pat* (to fall), a tree is not construed as its counter-correlate because of inappropriateness (*ayogyatva*).

The ground (bhūtala) is not [the object], because the verbal root—which denotes an operation delimited by conjunction with the locus below—presents the result as being specifically qualified by its counter-positive; thus, since the requirement for that counter-positive is satisfied, there is no designation by the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*). This should be understood similarly in cases such as *vardhate* ("it grows").

Consequently, in instances like *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat"), the mat and so forth possess primary objecthood (*mukhya-karmatva*) precisely because they partake in the result in the form of origination, which delimits the meaning of the root *kṛ*.

However, some say that [roots] such as *pat* (to fall) are intransitive because they bring about a result consisting of contact with a lower level (*adhaḥ-saṃyoga*) that resides solely in the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas roots such as *gam* (to go) are transitive because they bring about that same result residing in the village (*grāma*).

According to this view, one must accept a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the operation delimited by contact, and thereby justify the rule for the formation of accusative compounds (*dvitīyā-samāsa*).

Some, however, maintain that *pati* (to fall) is exclusively transitive, but its meaning is simply an action of a distinct class produced by gravity (*gurutva*). The accusative case coreferential with it, on the other hand, signifies "objecthood" (*karmatva*) characterized as contact with a lower location (*adhaḥ-saṃyoga*). Similarly, for verbs such as *tyaji* (to abandon) and *gami* (to go), the meaning is merely the operation (*vyāpāra*), and not the operation as delimited by a result, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). The accusative and other cases, however, by virtue of being indicators of the intended meaning through their co-occurrence, refer to [the results] such as separation (*vibhāga*) or contact (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, there is no synonymy between the two expressions "he abandons the village" (*grāmaṃ tyajati*) and "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*).

This is because it is accepted that the delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka) for the verb *tyaj* is the state of being a verbal cognition whose object is a motion delimited by disjunction (*vibhāga*), and for the verb *gam*, it is the state of being a verbal cognition whose object is a motion delimited by conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Consequently, even in the case of the expressions "going" (*gamana*) and "leaving" (*tyāga*), there would be the impossibility of a verbal cognition having disjunction as the qualificandum with a specific motion as its qualifier; furthermore, there would be the impossibility of a verbal cognition that apprehends the mutual qualification of both disjunction and conjunction along with the motion, precisely because what is intended [as the delimitor of the effect] is nothing other than the state of being a verbal cognition that apprehends the mutual qualification of both disjunction and conjunction along with the motion.

This is because both [the properties]—having a specific motion as its qualificandum with separation and so forth as its qualifier, and having separation and so forth as its qualificandum with a specific motion as its qualifier—are included. Furthermore, the conventional usage of the term "transitive" (sakarmaka) is based on various non-uniform causes. They maintain that the objecthood (*karmatva*) of a particular verbal root's meaning consists in being the locus of a result that is connected to that same verbal root's meaning and which inheres in something other [than the agent]. Consequently, they argue that the prior location and so forth do not possess objecthood in relation to the verb *gam* ("to go") and the like.

Others say that this is not so; for it is impossible for an object (*karman*) or an ablative (*apādāna*) to function as a *kāraka* without being the cause of an action. The meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is the act of throwing [an oblation] into fire with a specific deity in mind. And that [act] is an effort such as pushing or striking, residing in the ghee and so forth, which is conducive to an action that is itself conducive to conjunction with fire. Nor is there a lack of expectancy when the meaning of the locative case in expressions such as *agnau juhoti* (he sacrifices in the fire) is construed [with the verb], because the meaning of the verbal root consists precisely in an effort conducive to an action that is conducive to conjunction.

Therefore, since action (*kriyā*) is that which delimits the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), only the ghee (*ghṛta*) and such, which possess that action, have the status of the object (*karman*), and not the fire (*agni*), which possesses conjunction (*saṃyoga*). This is because conjunction is that which delimits the delimiter of the meaning of the verbal root, and thus is not itself the delimiter of the meaning of the verbal root. For only that which is directly a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the verbal root is the delimiter of the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, the cognition [arising] is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to an operation conducive to an action delimited by the conjunction of fire residing in the ghee."

Giving (*dāna*) is the act of relinquishment that, without the receipt of a price, results in the destruction of one’s own ownership and the production of another’s ownership. Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the act of relinquishment whose fruit is the destruction of one’s own ownership with reference to a deity. Sale (*vikraya*) is the act of relinquishment prompted by the receipt of a price, which results in the destruction of one’s own ownership and the production of another’s ownership. Purchase (*kraya*) is the act of acceptance prompted by the receipt of a price, which results in the destruction of one’s own ownership and the production of ownership [in the seller]. Acceptance (*pratigraha*) is the act of acceptance that produces ownership over the object already given.

And thus, in cases such as "he gives a cow to a Brahmin," "he worships Viṣṇu," "he sells a cow," "he buys [a cow]," or "he accepts [a gift]," [the agent] is: one who possesses an effort conducive to a renunciation that, without receiving a price, causes the destruction of his own ownership and the production of another's ownership regarding a cow intended for a Brahmin; one who possesses an effort conducive to a renunciation that causes the destruction of his own ownership regarding [an offering] intended for Viṣṇu; and one who possesses an effort conducive to an acceptance that is favorable to his own ownership, prompted by the giving of a price for a cow.

The cognition is: "He possesses an effort conducive to an acceptance that generates ownership over the object given by the cow-protector. According to the ancients, Viṣṇu has the status of an object (*karmatva*) because he possesses a result consisting in the destruction of his own ownership, through the relation of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatā*).

The Navyas, however, argue that since giving (*dāna*) generates ownership in another, the act of selling and the like would be excluded by that very fact; thus, the mention of "receiving payment" (*mūlyagrahaṇa*) is redundant. If, on the other hand, it is held that acceptance (*pratigraha*), being of the nature of a specific kind of appropriation, is itself what generates ownership—since in cases of ownership arising from acquisition (*aupādānika-svatva*), appropriation is already established as the cause of that ownership—then [the inclusion of payment] would otherwise render acceptance useless. Furthermore, this would contradict the Smṛti text: "A Brāhmaṇa shall acquire wealth through sacrifice, teaching, and acceptance."

Giving (*dāna*) is said to be that which produces merely the destruction of one's own ownership (*svasvatva-dhvaṃsa*) without bringing about another's ownership (*parasvatva*). Even so, the flaw of futility (*vaiyarthyatā*) remains, as well as the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of indifference (*upekṣā*), because that too brings about another's ownership by way of the destruction of one's own ownership. Furthermore, there would be ownership for a person who, having accepted a substance that was previously ownerless—having been relinquished with a distant recipient in mind—accepts it without that recipient being the intended object. If it is argued that a renunciation directed toward another is opposed to [the arising of] such ownership, that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

The same state of futility remains; furthermore, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of indifference (*upekṣā*), since that too, by way of destroying one's own ownership, serves as a cause for the ownership of another. Moreover, ownership would arise for a person who accepts a thing that was previously ownerless—having been relinquished with reference to a distant vessel—simply because of his acceptance, even though he was not the intended recipient. And it should not be argued that a relinquishment directed toward another is merely a semblance of a gift (*dānābhāsa*) because it contradicts [the true nature of] giving, given that the recipient is a cause of the gift only by way of manifesting consent.
If wealth intended for a sacred site is given elsewhere,
the donor obtains its fruit, while the recipient incurs no fault.
Having mentally designated a worthy recipient, one should pour water upon the ground;
the end of the ocean may be found, but the end of giving is not found.
If one is intent on giving while the recipient is out of sight,
one should meditate upon that recipient as the embodiment of majesty, and upon the object given as having the Sun-god as its deity.
If the gift is prepared in the absence of the recipient, how can it be accomplished when no worthy recipient is present?
In such a case, one should give it to members of one's own lineage; in their absence, to one's own kinsmen.

This is because such a view would result in contradiction with the *Nāradīya-Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* and other Smṛtis, among others. Likewise, the phrase "that which produces the destruction of one's own ownership" (*svasvatvadhvaṃsajanaka*) is also redundant, as it fails to serve as a distinguishing characteristic (*avyāvartakatvāt*). The claim that "Homa is the casting into fire" (*agniprakṣepo homaḥ*) is also incorrect. For Vācaspati Miśra has stated: "Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) intended for a deity that produces the destruction of one's own ownership; that very same act, when delimited by casting [into fire], is Homa. And Viveka states: "Homa is simply Sacrifice itself, as qualified by casting into a specific location. Furthermore, through the relinquishment performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there occurs the destruction of the sacrificer’s ownership. This is like the destruction of one's status as an owner resulting from a specific act of relinquishment by a slave who has been permitted [to do so].

In reality, the specific universals (jāti) such as "giving" (dānatva), "sacrifice" (yāgatva), and "offering" (homatva) are apprehended through mental perception. Nor is there any confusion (saṃkara) in that regard due to the distinction made—that the Śrāddha is a sacrifice with respect to the ancestors and a gift with respect to the Brāhmaṇas—because the Śrāddha possesses both of those forms in a secondary (gauṇa) sense.

In such expressions as "one sacrifices to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajate*), the meaning of the accusative case is *uddeśyatva* (the state of being the intended recipient), which consists in being the object of a cognition of superimposition (*āropa*) in the form "this belongs to him. According to the view that deities possess consciousness, since the deity accepts ownership, sacrifice (*yāga*) is a sub-class of giving (*dāna*), and oblation (*homa*) is a sub-class of that [sacrifice]. Thus, the worship of gods and similar acts are indeed sacrifices. For this very reason, in cases of joint ownership (*saṃsṛṣṭi*), where a common ownership arises following the destruction of the unique individual ownership, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of giving; for the genus of "giving-ness" (*dānatva-jāti*) is not admitted in such cases.

Some maintain that this is not the case because [the action] is qualified by being conducive to one's own ownership (*svatva*) for another. Others hold that while the prior ownership remains intact, there is merely the production of another's ownership therein; and they argue that there is no contradiction in the production of another's ownership in what already possesses ownership, because the [agent's] desire acts as an excitatory factor (*uttejaka*). Still others say that the [objection] is refuted by qualifying [the action] as producing *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit).

However, the definition of sacrifice (*yāga*) as the renunciation of a substance intended for a deity (*devatoddeśyaka-dravyatyāga*) is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) with respect to giving (*dāna*) to a deity.
