Nevertheless, in the act of giving, what is intended is the ownership of the deity, whereas in a sacrifice, this is not the case. For this very reason, learned people (*śiṣṭas*) throughout all lands utilize substances such as perfumes and flowers—which are the materials for a sacrifice in the form of worship—but they do not say that these have been "given" to the deity [in the sense of a gift], nor do they use them for purposes such as decorating their own homes.

However, it is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) who effects the extraction [of ownership]. In the absence of that [recipient], how could there be giving? And without that, how could there be ownership? Otherwise, it would follow that ownership arises even in the case of a sacrifice (*yāga*). Nor can ownership, while as yet unproduced, serve as a differentiator merely by being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*); for there is no evidence for its being the intended object in that sense. Nor is the use of the verb *dadāti* (to give) proof, since the expression "one should give a *śrāddha*" is frequently used even in the context of the *śrāddha* rite. Furthermore, the *śrāddha* itself is not a gift, because that would contradict the consensus of all tradition.

The common usage regarding the property of a deity is based merely on the status of being the intended object. Thus, there is no utility in [defining] the decoration of the house and so forth [as the recipient].
He who has the form of Hari in his heart, His name in his mouth, the food offering in his stomach,
and the water from His feet and the floral remains upon his head— he is indeed Acyuta himself.

Nor is there a contradiction with the Lord's statement: "One should not even offer the light of a lamp to Me. This is because that statement is established as referring to inanimate objects unique to Him, or to food obtained through attachment. Alternatively, the meaning is: "What has been offered to another, one should not employ for oneself, nor should one offer it [to the Lord]."

"Whoever offers to Viṣṇu what remains as leavings from the ancestors or other deities"—on account of such censure [in the scriptures], and because there is an absence of mantras in the case of giving (*dāna*), there is no mantra in offerings to the gods (*devaddha*) and so forth; that alone is the sacrifice (*yāga*), not anything else. For this very reason, acceptance is the cause for giving when there is a priest (*ṛtvij*), but not when there is no priest. Therefore, it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya* regarding renunciation (*utsarga*): "And this sevenfold [sacrifice] is thus described:
'That which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*)—thus it is considered threefold.'"
That is the most excellent action; the other is considered to be fourfold.
That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent,
that which is not designated by other names, and that which has never belonged to another.
Thus, the definition of the first three types [of objects] has also been stated:
"That whose material cause (prakṛti), whether existing or non-existing, does not undergo transformation (pariṇāmin),
is declared to be 'nirvartya' (that which is produced by being brought into existence)."
However, when there is an intention to speak of the material cause (*prakṛti*), some [grammarians] describe the object differently;
thus, in the grammatical treatise, the object is shown to be both that which is produced (*nirvartya*) and that which is modified (*vikārya*).

That which is non-existent and comes into being, or that which exists and is manifested through birth—having excluded these, action is established as twofold: the transformative (nirvartya) and the modifiable (vikārya).
It is said that this [object] is to be attained either through perception or through inference, like the modification of gold and the like resulting from the production of some other quality.

This is the meaning: in the expression "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), although the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the jar exists, it is not intended to be expressed as undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*); thus, it is a *nirvartya* (that which is to be produced). In the expression "he makes ashes" (*bhasma karoti*), likewise, when the material cause in the form of wood and so forth—which does exist—is not intended to be expressed, yet that aforementioned material cause is intended to be expressed as undergoing transformation, some maintain that it is indeed a *vikārya* (that which is to be modified). However, the Sāṃkhyas and others hold that it is *sat* (existent). As it has been stated in that very same work:
"The existence prior to production is based on its state in the intellect (*buddhi*)."
He becomes indistinguishable from another existing agent of birth.
When the cause abides in the state of the effect, then,
having acquired the designation "effect," it arises in the form of the effect.
Just as a serpent assumes the state of being coiled, or as scattered parts attain completeness,
so too do some declare that existent things possess the nature of being produced.

The first verse is intended to resolve the doubt as to how objects such as jars can possess agency (kartṛtva) in their production according to the theory that the effect does not pre-exist (asatkāryavāda). Agency is applicable for the purpose of linguistic usage by taking into account an existence conceived through the intellect (*buddhi*). In that context, the requirement of existing at a time immediately preceding the effect is unnecessary; moreover, a thing is simply not admitted to be its own cause in a way that would entail such a dependence. Even regarding origination, it is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar itself that serves as the efficient cause (*nimitta*).

Even in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) as accepted by the Vedāntins and others, since the effect is non-existent prior to its arising in the form in which it subsequently originates, the mere existence [of the cause] in the form of the material cause (*kāraṇarūpa*) is not a sufficient ground [for asserting the pre-existence of the effect]; this is explained in detail in the *Tarkakautūhala* during the commentary on the passage: "This, indeed, was then unmanifested" (*tad idaṃ tarhy avyākṛtam āsīt*).

The final two [theories], however, intend the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). When a jar undergoes destruction, there is the cognition: "The bracelet itself has become a crown," and so forth; because of this experience of identity between the prior state and the subsequent state, there is non-difference between the prior and subsequent states. Even though they belong to different times, since the experience is the same, it is possible for there to be identity characterized by the relation of counter-correlativity and coreferentiality (*pratiyogitvānuyogitva*). This very [identity] is designated by the Vedāntins with the term *saṃskāra* (transformation). However, the distinction from the Sāṃkhya view lies in its being illusory (*mithyātva*).

We now follow the subject at hand. The object to be modified (*vikārya*) is twofold: that which is produced by the will of the self as its material cause (*prakṛti*), as in "he turns wood into ash"; and that which is produced through the emergence of a different quality (*guṇāntara*), as in "he makes gold into an earring. The distinction is that in the state of ash, there is no cognition of "wood-ness," whereas in the state of an earring, there is a cognition of "gold-ness. It should also be understood here that this depends on whether one intends to express the transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) of the wood or the gold.

Nor should it be asked how wood—which is not the locus of a fruit produced by an action—can possess the status of an object (*karmatva*). This is because such status arises through the intention to express non-difference between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti*) based on established usage; or else, because the meaning is "transforming the wood, he makes ash," just as in the expression "moistening the rice grains, he produces boiled rice. And this has been explained in the case of the verb "to see" (*paśyati*): although the removal of an obstruction or the state of being an object—which constitutes a specific change produced by the action—is accessible to the perceiver, it is nevertheless inaccessible apart from that [act of seeing].

While walking through a village with indifference, he touches grass. He eats poison unintentionally. That which is not designated by other technical names is called *akathita* (unspoken); for example, "he milks the cow for milk. That which has another [kāraka] preceding it when another designation would otherwise apply is subject to the designation of *karman*; as in "he becomes angry at the cruel one," and so forth.

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that the "object to be modified" (*vikārya*) is that which possesses the fruit of an action such as conjunction and so forth, and which, having already attained its own existence, undergoes a change of state—just as was previously illustrated. For in that case, the word "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) refers to its constituent parts; since those [parts], while already existing, attain another state consisting in their becoming ashes and so forth. Nor should it be said that an object is "modified" when an action produces a fruit that causes the destruction of that very object; for if that were so, one would have to say "he cuts the wood" (*kāṣṭhaṃ lunāti*) in the case of [the wood being destroyed].

In that case, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is a part of the wood that functions as the object (*karman*), because the action [of cutting] does not possess the capacity to destroy the wood itself. For in this context, the word "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) refers to its part, and the root *lunāti* (to cut) signifies an effort conducive to an action which is the cause of a disjunction that opposes the productive conjunction (*ārambhaka-saṃyoga*). Thus, from the verbal cognition—namely, "one who possesses an effort conducive to an effort that is conducive to an action which is the cause of such a disjunction residing in a part of the wood"—it follows that the part of the wood is indeed the "attained object" (*prāpyakarman*).

Because there is no attainment of a different state [in the case of the rice], in the expression "he cooks the rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the word "rice" (*taṇḍula*) indicates its constituent parts. The meaning of the root *pac* is contact with fire delimited by the transformation of color and other qualities. Consequently, because it possesses a result produced by the action and because it attains a different state, it possesses both types of objecthood (*karmatva*). In expressions such as "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the object is of the "to-be-produced" (*nirvartya*) type. Here, since the root *kṛ* signifies an operation delimited by a result, the objecthood is figurative (*gauṇa*).

Because it lacks the status of being the cause of an action (*kriyānimitta*), it does not possess primary *kāraka*-hood; rather, its status is secondary, consisting in being the object of an effort (*kṛti*) termed "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). The meaning of the accusative case and so forth when used in co-utterance with the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is precisely this aforementioned object-hood (*viṣayatā*). For this very reason, the expression "he makes the potsherd" (*kapālaṃ karoti*) is not employed by virtue of [primary] power (*śakti*), because in that instance there exists only the object-hood termed "material cause" (*upādānatva*).

The predecessors, however, maintain that the word "jar" (ghaṭa) is used figuratively with respect to the potsherd (kapāla). Therefore, because it possesses the result consisting of a jar produced by the action, its status as an object (karmatva) and so forth is indeed primary. They say that the expression "he makes the potsherd" (kapālaṃ karoti) does not occur through primary power (śakti), because the word "jar" and others occurring in conjunction with the root *kṛ* (to make) have a conventional (nirūḍha) figurative meaning with respect to its parts.

As for the claim that the meaning of the case-terminations denoting agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), object (*karman*), and locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is simply the substratum (*āśraya*): the object is the substratum of the result, the agent is the substratum of the operation, and the locus is the substratum of either the agent or the object. In this view, since the result and so forth are obtainable from other sources, the meaning [of these suffixes] is merely the substratum. The delimitor (*avacchedaka*) is precisely that [substratum-ness] itself, in the form of an impartite power (*akhaṇḍaśakti*). Nor does it follow that in cases such as "Caitra goes to the village" (*caitro grāmaṃ gacchati*), the second case-ending would apply to Caitra and others as well, on the grounds that they too are objects.

This [objection] is to be reconsidered; for it is only the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "object" (*karman*), as distinguished by the absence of any other designation, that serves as the motivator for the application of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*). Since the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*)—being subsequent—sublates the designation of "object," and since coexistence is impossible due to the rule that only one designation applies at a time, [the objection stands]. However, if the mere substratum (*āśrayamātra*) were the expressed meaning, then the designation of "agent" could not be established, and consequently, it would be impossible for it to sublate the designation of "object."

Nor should it be argued that when one intends to express the substratum of the result as a qualifier of the [action], it receives the designation *karman* (object), whereas when the operation (*vyāpāra*) is so intended, it receives the designation *kartṛ* (agent). For although the state of being the substratum of the result and so forth may be the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), in the case of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the state of being the substratum of either the agent or the object is not the object of verbal cognition; thus, there is no restrictive rule for that case.
*Tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam* || 50 || (And that which is not desired [to be attained] is likewise [treated as an object]).

That which is connected with an action, even if it is not intended [by the agent], is designated as the *karman* (object), just like that which is most desired. For example: "He sees the thieves" (*caurān paśyati*). Even though the thieves are not intended [to be seen], they become objects of vision by virtue of the contact of the eyes.
And: "That which is unexpressed" (*akathitaṃ ca*) [is also called *karman*]. Pāṇini 1.4.51.

A *kāraka* that is not intended to be specified by particular [case-roles] such as the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth is designated as the object (*karman*). An enumeration [of these cases] must be made in order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as "he hears from the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*). Thus says the Bhāṣya: "In the case of the roots *duh* (to milk), *yāc* (to beg), *rudh* (to obstruct), *pracch* (to ask), *bhikṣ* (to beg), and *ci* (to gather)—when the result is not already established [by another rule]—as well as for the purpose of utility (*upayoga*), and that which is connected with the quality (*guṇa*) of the roots *brū* (to speak) and *śās* (to instruct): that is what the Sage has treated as the 'unspoken' (*akīrtita*)."
It is the settled conclusion that among roots with two objects, *nī* (to lead), *vah* (to carry), *hṛ* (to take), and likewise those whose meaning is "motion," they must be included [in this rule].

In the case of *prachitya*, there is the absence of the *tuṅ* augment according to the rule *anityam āgamaśāsanam*. This is similar to the absence of *nuṭ* and other such augments in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci* and *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*. The term *upayoga* (utility) refers to the primary object (*mukhyaṃ karma*), such as milk or fruit; the cow and so forth are the instrumental causes (*nimitta*) for that utility. In the sentence *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("He milks the cow for milk"), the cow is not the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) because it is merely being utilized, whereas the milk is. Nor can its status as an object be established by the rule *tathāyuktam ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.50), because it lacks the quality of being "so connected" (*tathāyuktatva*).

That which is connected with or associated with the action (karman) by way of its quality (guṇa)—since the action is primary because it is that which is to be accomplished (sādhya), while the factors of action (kārakas) are subordinate—the root *ṣac* (to be attached to) is marked with the svarita accent. In the view that reads this as a parasmaipada root, it is the form of *ṣaca* (to serve), which is anudātta; this is due to the fact that roots have multiple meanings. By "the poet" (*kavi*), meaning one who has transcendent vision, a wise teacher—that is what is intended. "Unstated" (*akīrtita*) means "unmentioned"; the sense is that it is so treated according to established usage.

He says "in the case of an original injunction" (*apūrvavidhau*) because this [rule] applies when there is no intention to express [the relations of] *apādāna* and so forth. The meaning is that it applies to cases outside the scope of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *apādāna* mentioned previously. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the scope of the designations *hetu* and *kartṛ* which will be mentioned later; for "previously" (*pūrva*) is used as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of anything other than those. Furthermore, the subsequent sublation of the state of being a completed object (*bhūtatva*) by the rule "that which is not otherwise mentioned" (*akathita*) does not apply here, because that [state] is not intended to be expressed. For this very reason, according to the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*), even that which is about to be defeated (*parājiṣyamāṇa*) possesses the status of an *apādāna* in expressions such as *parājer asoḍhaḥ*.

The modern grammarians (navyāḥ) maintain that this [designation] is superseded by the designations of "cause" (hetu) and "agent" (kartṛ) due to their higher status, because of the governing rule regarding a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*).

The phrase "of those having the sense of motion" (*gatyarthānām*) is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those roots included in the *gatibuddhi* sūtra and others. Kaiyaṭa states that the word "and" (*ca*) includes roots such as *jayati*. These have been stated by Mādhava:
Of *jayati*, *karṣati*, *manthi*, *muṣi*, *daṇḍayati*, and *paci*;
The taking up [of the breath] is by means of *tāra* (OM), its release by *grāha*, its retention by *mocya*, and its collection by *dīpa*.

And because the word "ca" (and) is used in the *kārikā*, the separate mention of "bhikṣi" (to beg) would be redundant. This is because the instruction regarding "duh" and the others is intended to convey their specific meanings, and [the meaning of "bhikṣi"] is already included by the mention of "yāci" (to ask). Nor is there a lack of evidence for this intentionality toward the meaning; for in the Bhāṣya on that *rājasūya* sūtra, it is stated: "I too consider this not to be a valid objection. Furthermore, since "cud" is a synonym for "pṛch" (to ask), it is possible for it to have two objects. For this very reason—

"Even a mountain peak spoke loudly to that very king with affection"—such usages by Kālidāsa and others are thus consistent. If it is argued that for this very reason *tyaj* (to abandon) is also included because its meaning is identical to *duh* (to milk), they reply: here, *yāci* (to beg/solicit) has the sense of conciliation (*anunaya*), as is evident from the expression "he conciliates the ill-behaved for the sake of discipline. Nor should it be said, "In that case, let there be the inclusion of *yāci* alone"; for since words differ according to their meanings, the *yāci* used here does not convey the sense of mere petitioning (*prārthanā*). However, in the alternative view, the mention of *bhikṣi* (to beg) is for the sake of clarity.

Examples: *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (he milks milk from the cow); *pauravaṃ gāṃ yācate* (he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru); *avinītaṃ vinayaṃ yācate* (he begs discipline from the ill-behaved); *anvavaruṇaddhi gāṃ vrajam* (he shuts the cow in the pen); *māmavakaṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* (he asks me the way to Avaka); *pauravaṃ gāṃ bhikṣate* (he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru); *vṛkṣamavacinoti phalāni* (he gathers fruits from the tree); *putraṃ brūte dharmaṃ, anuśāsti vā* (he tells or instructs his son in dharma); *ajāṃ nayati grāmam* (he leads the goat to the village); *vahati bhāraṃ grāmam, harati vā* (he carries the load to the village, or brings it); *rāmayati devadattaṃ grāmam* (he causes Devadatta to go to the village), and so forth; *śataṃ jayati devadattam* (he wins a hundred [pieces] from Devadatta).

"He drags the branch to the village"; "he fines him a hundred [pieces]"; "he cooks rice into porridge"; "he causes the monkeys to cross the ocean"; "he causes the boy to grasp the Veda"; "he causes Devadatta to abandon his anger"; "he causes the students to illuminate the meaning of the scripture. It should not be said that the status of being an object (*karman*) depends solely on the act of grasping (*grahaṇa-kriyā*), which is not explicitly used, based on the sense that "having taken the goat, he leads it to the village."

In the sentence *ajā nīyate grāmam* ("The goat is led to the village"), there would be the undesirable consequence that the goat, as the object of the act of grasping (*grahaṇakarma*), would not be expressed by the suffix attached to the subsequent verb *nayati*. This is because the *Mahābhāṣya* states: "If one were to say it is 'another object,' then there would be no application of the *l*-suffixes [to denote the agent]. In this context, the view that the root *grah* is inherently transitive (*dikarmaka*) is not accepted by many, since its status as such is possible in the aforementioned instance simply because it has the sense of "understanding" (*budhyarthatva*). For this very reason, it is not accepted by many—since in the stated case it is possible precisely because it has the sense of understanding—it is said:
*ajigrahattaṃ janako dhanustat* ("Janaka made him grasp that bow").
Thus, by this [citation], it is made known that the burning of Tripura was performed by the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) through the employment of the word *bhaṭṭi*.

And by citing the usage of Kālidāsa—“The Mountain (*adri*) was not able to make the God of Gods (*devadeva*) accept his daughter when she was not asked for”—it is made known as an example of marriage (*udvāha*).
First, [the author] [discusses] the meaning of the family sciences (*kulavidyā*), he who is the best among those who know the meaning.
Afterwards, his father caused him to take the hands of the daughters of kings.

Thus, they explained that construction by changing the case ending of *tena* (by him) to *tasya* (of it) in the second half of the verse. For this very reason, Śrīharṣa wrote: "He caused Nala to take the spittoon" (*patadgrahaṃ grāhitavān nalena saḥ*).

Furthermore, the fact that the root *pac* takes two objects has been clearly demonstrated by Kaiyaṭa in his commentary on the Vārttika included in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, which states: "In the case of the roots *duh* and *pac*, which are transitive, [the object] is frequently treated as the agent. Mādhava also concurs with this view.

But surely this contradicts the Bhāṣya on the sūtra defining the term *karman*, where it is stated that the root *pac* has two meanings; for there, the two fruits—softening (*viklitti*) and production (*utpatti*)—as well as the operation (*vyāpāra*), constitute the meaning of *pac*. Thus, rice grains possess the status of *karman* by virtue of possessing softening, while boiled rice possesses it by virtue of being produced. Consequently, the meaning is: "the operation residing in Devadatta which is conducive to the production of the rice grains. However, in the case of *taṇḍulān pacati* ("he cooks the rice"), the meaning is rather "he causes [the rice] to soften."

Because, when *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is included as a *dhātu* (verbal root), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with *viklitti* (the softening of the grain) as the object (*karman*) in its form as that which is being cooked; thus, [the action] is described by "he cooks the rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*). However, if [the verb] were to have two objects (*dvikarmaka*), the aforementioned effort would be futile. This is not so, because [the definition] intends to refer to different philosophical views. By this, if the word *akathita* (unmentioned) were taken to mean "that which is non-primary," then in the sentence "he milks milk into a bronze vessel with his hand" (*pāṇinā kāṃsyapātryāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), the hand and the vessel would also receive the designation of "object" (*karman*).

Nor is there a lack of scope for those two [rules], because they find scope in roots such as *paci* (to cook); nor does that same contingency apply even there, because of the specific enumeration of roots beginning with *duhi* (to milk), as explained in Haradatta’s commentary. As for the objection that if *grāhi* were transitive, the form *jāyāpratigrāhitagandhamālyām* would not be established—since in the analysis *jāyayā gandhamālyaṃ pratigrāhitaṃ yayā* ("she by whom the perfume and garland were caused to be received by her husband"), a *bahuvrīhi* compound would be difficult to obtain, given that the *bhāṣya* will state that the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) applies to the three [factors]—nor can the analysis be *gandhamālye pratigrāhite yayām*.

Because it is the causative object (*prayojyakarman*) in the form of the cow itself that is expressed by the *kta* suffix—since it will be stated later that "in a causative construction, the agent [of the causative] is treated as the object"—it is for this very reason that [the following example is valid]:
"The kings were made to bestow wealth upon the Brahmins, though they were free from desire."

Such is the application [of the rule]. However, there is no inconsistency in analyzing the compound as "by whom the perfume and garlands were caused to be accepted" (*pratigrāhite gandhamālye yayā*), just as in the case of *uḍharatha* and similar forms. Nor should it be argued that the status of being a "two-object verb" (*dvikarmaka*) applies only when the [grammatical relations of] ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth are not intended to be expressed, whereas when they are intended to be expressed, the aforementioned analysis will apply. This is because, although verbs such as *jayati* (which are conjoined by the particle *ca* in the rule *harateśca*) fall under the scope of the *akathita* sūtra, the same principle applies to those conjoined by *tathaiva ca*: namely, that what is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causal (*ṇic*) form becomes the object (*karman*) in the non-causal (*aṇ*) form. This is established through their association with verbs meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*).

For this very reason, *tārya* and others are included separately; for if the agency of the one who causes the grasping (*grahaṇakartṛ*) is not intended to be expressed, then since the prompter (*prayojaka*) would lack the status of a causal agent (*hetu*), the suffix *ṇic* would be impossible. Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of *dīpi* is redundant, because its status as an intransitive verb is already established by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇāmaṇikartā sa ṇau*. This is to be considered doubtful, because its purpose is fulfilled when it occurs after a root ending in *ṇic* followed by another *ṇic*. Thus: "There, having utterly defeated the Gandharvas in battle, Bharata caused them to grasp only their musical instruments and made them completely abandon their weapons."

Accepting that the word *pratigrāhita* has the meaning of "caused to understand," the formation is possible through the application of the suffix (*pratyaya*) to either of the two actions according to one's own will, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *yāṃ jāyayā bodhite gandhamālye*. Alternatively, in the word *pratigrāhita*, the suffix *kta* denotes the state (*bhāva*). Then, *jāyāyāḥ* forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). By the rule beginning with *arśa-ādi*, the suffix *ac* is applied. Thus, it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*): "she whose [gifts] are characterized by that activity which is the instigator of the cow’s act of acceptance, directed toward the wife. This "characterization" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) consists in being the object of the desire, "May this belong to the cow. By this [explanation], [the objection is answered].

The phrase "unnidracandra" (the wide-awake moon) is explained as "the wide-awake moon which was the object of the intense request made by a child who was captivated by the delusion that it was his own play-swans. This means: she is one for whom the wide-awake moon became the object of a longing request residing in a child. By this, the objection—that because the secondary object (*apradhānakarman*) is expressed by the past passive participle (*kta*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as "she by whom the wide-awake moon was requested by a child" would be difficult to justify (as in the example "having approached [him] while he was wearing a side-lock of hair, she requested him")—is refuted.

The following point should be noted here: the meaning of the root *duh* (to milk) is an operation conducive to an action that is conducive to separation (*vibhāga*), and the meaning of *nī* (to lead) is an operation conducive to an action that is conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*). In this context, the word "cow" (*gām*) is construed with the [action of] separation, and the word "milk" (*payaḥ*) is construed with the [action of] motion. There arises the cognition of an operation—such as the squeezing of the udder—which is conducive to an action residing in the milk and which is itself conducive to a separation residing in the cow; and there arises the cognition of an operation which is conducive to an action residing in the goat and which is itself conducive to a conjunction residing in the village.

The status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to the milk and the goat, which possess the aforementioned action that delimits the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*). However, because the cow and the village lack connection with the results—namely, separation (*vibhāga*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—which respectively delimit the delimitation of the meaning of the verbal root, the technical designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) is prescribed for them by this rule. For this very reason, the *Mahābhāṣya* explains that the root *pac* has two objects: rice grains, by virtue of their connection with the result consisting of softening (*viklitti*), and boiled rice (*odana*), by virtue of its connection with the result consisting of production (*utpatti*). Thus, its status as a transitive verb with two objects (*dvikarmaka*) is established.

For this very reason, the inclusion of the root *pac* (to cook) by means of the particle *ca* (and) is accepted by him [Patañjali]. By this, the suspicion of contradiction with that Bhāṣya regarding the two-object nature (*dvikarmakatva*) of *pac* is dispelled. However, when the cow's status as the point of separation (*avadhi*) is intended to be expressed, then the cow possesses the status of an ablative (*apādāna*), as in "he milks milk from the cow" (*goḥ payo dogdhi*). This is because the cognition arises in the form: "an action residing in the milk which is conducive to a separation having the cow as its limit. But when the relation to the milk is intended to be expressed, the genitive alone is used, because the cognition arises in the form: "the operation conducive to an action which is conducive to a separation residing in that milk which is related to the cow.
And that separation is understood, through the force of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), as having the cow specifically as its limit.

This also should be noted: regarding the suffixes *la*, *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khal*, the author of the Bhāṣya states the following rule concerning their application to the primary or secondary object when used with verbs that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*):

"For roots that take two objects, the suffixes beginning with *la* (i.e., verbal terminations) are said to denote the principal object (*pradhāna-karman*) when it is to be expressed; for roots such as *duh* (milk), they denote the non-principal object (*apradhāna*). Furthermore, in the case of causative forms (*ṇyanta*), they denote the object which was the agent (*kartṛ*) of the simple verb."

In this context, by the phrase "dvikarmapadena" (by the term 'two objects'), three roots—*nī*, *vah*, and *hṛ*—are understood as being conjoined by the word *ca*; furthermore, *kṛṣ* is also included. By the phrase "duhādipadena" (by the term 'the group beginning with *duh*'), those roots mentioned in the *Kārikā* that are conjoined by *ca* and are non-causative (*ahetumaṇṇyantāḥ*)—such as *ji*, *daṇḍ*, and others—are included. By the term "ṇyantapadena" (by the causative term), those roots mentioned in the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* and conjoined by the word *ca*—such as *tāry* and others—are included. The meaning is that in these cases, the agent (*kartā*) of the non-causative (*aṇau*) becomes the object (*karma*) in the causative (*ṇau*), and the *l*-affixes (*lādayaḥ*) are used to express that [object]. Even therein, regarding roots whose meanings involve cognition (*buddhi*) or consumption (*pratyavasāna*) and those that have two objects (*śabdakarmakeṣu*), there is another view according to which the secondary object (*guṇakarmaṇi*) is expressed; this is what the *Bhāṣya* states.

Remember these words of the one of no small intelligence: when [an action] has been stated or expressed, the rule for *la* and other suffixes applies to a quality-action (*guṇakarma*); furthermore, the rule for *sa* and other suffixes applies to that which is constant (*dhruva*) in the context of effort (*ceṣṭita*), even when it is not a quality.

Here, the first quarter-verse is intended to refute the opinion of certain grammarians who maintain that when the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) is expressed by *l*-suffixes and the like, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be used for the secondary object (*guṇakarman*). That [opinion] was indeed stated previously: "If *l*-suffixes and the like are employed when [the object] has already been mentioned, one should then use the genitive for the secondary object, provided one recognizes it as a *kāraka*; whichever [case] one deems appropriate, that shall be used."

"‘The cow yields milk’ (*duhyate gauḥ payaḥ*) and ‘He begs a blanket from the Paurava’ (*yācyate pauravāt kambalaḥ*) are examples for the first half [of the rule]. However, when there is a desire to express the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action), the respective case-endings apply: ‘Milk is yielded from the cow’ (*duhyate goḥ payaḥ*) and ‘A blanket is begged from the Paurava’ (*yācyate pauravāt kambalaḥ*). Thus, the term ‘the expressed’ (*kathita*) refers to the primary object (*pradhānakarman*). When that [primary object] is expressed, however, this [secondary object] requires a second case-ending; the prescription of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies to it as something distinct. This is the opinion of a certain teacher-like person (*ācāryadeśīya*), but not that of the Teacher [Pāṇini] himself. The meaning is that the second case is observed to occur with the non-primary object."

He states the correct position: "In the case of a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*). In the rule *sapare*, the word *para* refers to the sūtras concerning motion (*gati*) and so forth. When [the object] associated with that [motion] is a subordinate action, the *l*-affixes and others apply to the root *duh* and the like. Because the activity of milking and so forth is for the sake of the milk and other such [products], the cow and other [objects] are not primary. As for the production of the suffix in that context, it is because one who desires the milk and so forth first engages with the cow and the like. Thus it has been said: "The prescription of the *l*-affixes and others occurs first in relation to the subordinate action, because of its prior connection with the subordinate action;
since the one desiring the primary object first exerts effort toward the substance."
Therefore, for the root *duh* (to milk) in its pure form, there is a connection with "cow" (*gavā*) even prior [to the addition of the suffix].

"Because milk is the primary object [of the action] prior to that [causative suffix], the *l*-class suffixes (*laḍ*, etc. occur in reference to it. For example: *gaur duhyate payaḥ* (the cow is milked for milk), *dogdhavyā* (is to be milked), *dugdhā* (was milked), *sudohā* (easy to milk), and so forth. In the causative (*ṇyanta*), however, the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) possesses formal primacy (*śābda-prādhānya*), because it functions as the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) and thus assumes the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The operation of the one being prompted (*prayojya-vyāpāra*), on the other hand, is implicit (*ārtha*), since it exists for the sake of the instigator's operation; therefore, the same applies to their respective objects (*karman*). Consequently, the verbal suffix occurs alternatively in both cases: *bodhyate māṇavakaṃ dharmaḥ* (the boy is made to understand the Dharma) or *māṇavako dharmaṃ* (the boy understands the Dharma).

Roots associated with *dhruva* (the fixed point) are intransitive (*akarmaka*) according to the convention of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). Roots associated with *ceṣṭita* (volitional movement) have the sense of "going" (*gatyartha*). In these cases, when the object (*karman*) is not a quality (*aguṇa*), the suffixes *la* and others [denoting the passive] are applied. For example: *devadatto grāmaṃ gamyate*, *gamayitavyaḥ*, *gamitaḥ*, *sugamaḥ*, and so forth. This is the view of the teacher of vast intelligence; it was set forth in the second and third quarters [of the verse]. The statement "remember! is an expression intended to ensure the non-interruption of the tradition (*āgama*) and to refute the notion that this is his own invention.

Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of the application of *l*-affixes (*la-ādi*) to the secondary object (*guṇakarma*) alone in the case of roots meaning cognition (*buddhi*), returning (*pratyavasāna*), objects of speech (*śabda*), and action (*karma*), because the rule *ṇyante kartuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) would, by virtue of its higher status, sublate the rule *saparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.49). For it is generally understood through the phrase "another says" (*apara āha*) that an alternative is established even in those cases, as this indicates a different opinion.
Thus, the summary is as follows:

In the case of the primary object (*mukhye karmaṇi*), [the *l*-affixes apply] to the roots *hrī*, *vah*, and *kṛṣ*; in the case of the secondary object (*guṇe karmaṇi*), they apply to the group beginning with *duh*; and for roots meaning speech (*śabda-karmaka*), cognition (*sabuddhi*), and eating (*aśana-artha*), [they apply] optionally (*vā*).
Indeed, the affixes *la*, *kta*, *khalartha*, and *kṛtya* convey the notion of the "instigator" (*prayojya*) when applied to the object of a verb ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*.

Now, if one asks: "In the case of a verb with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), when used with a *kṛt* suffix, which of the two objects takes the genitive case?"—the *Bhāṣya* on this point states: "According to both views, [it is so] according to Goṇikāputra. For example: *netā aśvasya srughnam* or *srughnasya*. Here, since it is impossible for a single word to denote two objects that differ in status—one subordinate and the other primary—it is logical that the primary object is denoted.

The sixth case (genitive), however, is prescribed separately from both the subordinate and the principal [actions], just like the second case; thus, by way of exclusion (*avaroṣāt*), it is obtained for both. According to the authority of the *Bhāṣya*, it is obligatory when the principal action is concerned, but optional when the subordinate action is concerned. For it is said: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are designated as the object (*karman*) of intransitive verbs."

It should be stated that "the word denoting location (*deśa*) [is used] with intransitive verbs (*akarmakāṇām*). Examples: *gantavyo'dhvā* (a path to be traveled), *adhvagantavyaḥ* (a traveler's path). The subsequent placement of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) [before the qualified] occurs by way of an irregular grammatical derivation (*nipātana*). Nor is the word *gantavya* redundant; for its purpose is to restrict the scope to those distances well-known in the world as having fixed measures, such as a *krośa* or a *yojana*. Examples: *māsam āste* (he sits for a month); *godoham āste* (he sits for the duration of a cow-milking, meaning he remains seated throughout that time); *krośam āste* (he sits for a *krośa*); *kurūn svapiti* (he sleeps throughout the Kuru country). Nor is the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) redundant, since the accusative case would already be established by the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasamyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5).

Even though the cow-pen (*godāha*) and the like serve as qualifiers of time (*kālopādhi*), they are not established as "time" (*kāla*) per se. Furthermore, in the case of "time" (*kāla*) and "distance" (*adhvan*), [the suffixes] *la* and so forth are prescribed for the sake of expressing the action. Thus: "A month is sat through," "it is to be sat through," "it was sat through," or "it is being sat through. Likewise: "A *krośa* is slept through," and so on. The term "place" (*deśa*) refers to specific aggregates of villages such as Kuru, Pañcāla, and others, based on the force of the examples given in the *Bhāṣya*. Therefore, Kaiyaṭa maintains that rules such as *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsām* (Pāṇini 1.4.46) are not redundant.

If, however, roots such as *ās* (to sit) and others denote sitting and so forth as qualified by the meaning of another transitive root, then it is already established by the preceding rule (*apūrveṇaiva*), because the sense is "he pervades the month by means of sitting. As he will state later in the second [chapter] in detail: "This is indeed an inherent object (*prākṛta-karman*), just as in 'he makes a mat' (*kaṭaṃ karoti*).

*Gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇi kartā sa ṇau* || 52 || [In the case of roots] having the sense of motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), or eating (*pratyavasāna*), those having sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), and those that are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the agent (*kartā*) of the action when expressed by a non-causative suffix (*aṇi*) becomes the object (*karman*) when expressed by a causative suffix (*ṇau*).

In the case of verbal roots meaning motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), eating (*bhakṣaṇa*), those that have sound as their object (*śabdakarmaka*), and those that are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *aṇ* (non-causative) stage shall become the object (*karma*) in the *ṇic* (causative) stage. Although the designation "object" for the activity of the prompted agent is already established—since the activity of the prompted agent is indeed the most desired (*īpsitatama*) by the activity of the prompter—nevertheless, this rule is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It means: if the status of being an object applies to that which is being reached by the meaning of the *ṇic*, then it applies only to roots meaning motion and so forth, and not to others. Therefore, in the example *pācayati devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook"), since the primary designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) which was previously active remains established for the prompted agent who performs the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used. As it has been said: [The rule] "The agent of the root in the *aṇ* [stage] becomes the object in the *ṇic*" is for the purpose of restriction; it restricts the application to roots meaning motion and so forth. Thus, in *pācayati devadatto yajñadattena*, the third case is employed because the original designation of "agent" persists for Yajñadatta, the performer of the subordinate action.
Having attained the status of an object (*karman*) through the act of commanding due to its independence regarding the action of a quality,
it is expressed by its own grammatical function because of the restrictive rule concerning the technical designation "object."

By its own nature (*svadharmeṇa*), that is to say, by the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) which expresses the agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*). For example: *devadattaṃ grāmaṃ gamayati* ("He causes Devadatta to go to the village"). In the state where the root is not followed by the causative suffix (*aṇ-antāvasthā*), namely *devadatto grāmaṃ gacchati* ("Devadatta goes to the village"), Devadatta possesses the status of the agent (*kartṛtva*). There is a prohibition regarding the roots *nī* (to lead) and *vah* (to carry). Since these have the sense of "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇārthatayā*), there is a perception of motion (*gati*) due to their being qualifiers; thus, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [of "object"] would otherwise apply. Therefore, one says: *nāyayati vāhayati vā bhāraṃ devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to lead/carries the load by means of Devadatta"). The prohibition applies only to the root *vah* when it does not have a controller (*aniyantṛka*). As in: *vahanti vāhāḥ* ("The draft animals carry [the load]").

A charioteer (*sūta*) causes the horses (*vāhān*) to carry the chariot-rider (*rathinam*). The term *niyantṛ* (driver) refers merely to one who impels animals; therefore, in expressions such as "he causes the oxen to carry the crop" (*vāhayati balīvardān sasyam*) or "he passes the time" (*kālaṃ yāpayati*), the status of being an object (*karmatvam*) is established by this very rule. This is because in the root *yā* meaning "to go," the act of going itself constitutes the meaning of "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*). Regarding the rule *budhyartha* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), only those roots expressing general cognition (*jñāna-sāmānya*) are included, and not those with specific meanings such as *smṛ* (to remember), since the inclusion of *śru* (to hear) and *dṛś* (to see) will be stated as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) later on. Example: "He teaches the dharma to the boy" (*bodhayati māṇavakaṃ dharmam*).

He causes the young student to eat or feed him rice; he causes the food to be eaten or chewed by the boy. There is a prohibition [of the *ṇic* suffix] for the root *bhakṣ* when it means "not killing. Nor is it the case that [the application of this rule] is unestablished because [the root *bhakṣ*] belongs to the *cur*-class (*curādi*) and ends in *ṇic*, for since the rule is prescribed for the causative *ṇic* (the *hetu-ṇic*), and because of its proximity, it is precisely that which is prohibited even in the context of "in the absence of *ṇic*" (*aṇau*). This is because it applies here as well, in the sense of "in the state of being devoid of the causative *ṇic*. He causes the food to be eaten by the boy. Why "not killing"? [Example: The oxen eat the grain.

"He causes the oxen to eat the barley standing in the field," because one accepts that the barley has consciousness; for when they eat the barley, there is injury to its owner. This is because the root *bhakṣ* ("to eat") is accepted as functioning with respect to eating, which is a constituent part of injury (*hiṃsā*). Those [roots] for which the word "object" (*karman*) is the grammatical factor are "those having an object consisting of sound" (*śabdakarmakāḥ*). However, the word "object" (*karman*) here does not refer to the action itself. For, since such a meaning is already obtained from the very reading of the rule "the meaning of the word *pratyavasāna* [is eating]," the force of the separate mention of the word "object" (*karman*) is to indicate something distinct from that. "Devadatta causes his son to study" or "causes him to recite."

There is also an addition [to the rule] for the root *dṛś* (to see): *darśayati hariṃ bhaktān* ("he shows Hari to the devotees"). Although this is established by the fact that [the root] refers to cognition (*buddhi*) because it pertains to the visual faculty (*cākṣuṣa*), this addition is made to indicate that in that context only those roots expressing general cognition are included, and not those expressing specific types of it. As for the example *śrāvayati ślokaṃ devadattam* ("he causes Devadatta to hear the verse"), however, this is due to the addition of *śru* as well, in the sense of "those whose action consists of sound" (*śabdakriyāṇām*). Otherwise, it would be established simply because [the object] is the object of a verbal action involving sound (*śabdakarmakatvāt*).

In the first case, a prohibition must be stated for the usage *hvāyayati* or *krandayati devadattena*. In both cases, a prohibition must also be stated for the root *śabdāyati*, because its intransitivity (*akarmakatva*) would otherwise lead to its application [as a transitive]. This is because the object, "sound" (*śabda*), is included within the meaning of the verbal root itself. Thus, one says *śabdāyayati devadattena*. The term "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) here refers to those roots that lack any other object such as time (*kāla*) and so forth. By this, forms such as *māsam āsayati caitram* (he causes Caitra to sit for a month) are established. Furthermore, in examples such as *devadattena pācayati* (he causes Devadatta to cook), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) does not apply [to Devadatta].
In the case of the roots *hṛ* (to take) and *kṛ* (to do), [the agent] may optionally [be designated as the object]. || 53 ||

"He causes the servant to carry" (*hārayati*) or "he causes the servant to make" (*kārayati*), or [he causes it to be done] by the servant (*bhṛtyena*). Regarding the rule *naveti vibhāṣā* ("the option is not [applicable]"), there is a Vārttika stating that this option applies in both cases. For instance, in the examples *abhyavahārayati māṇavakam odanam* ("he causes the boy to eat the rice") or *māṇavakena* ("by means of the boy"), the rule would already apply because the action involves consumption (*pratyavasāna*). However, in the case of *vikurvate chātrāḥ* ("the students change/distort themselves") or *vikārayati chātrān* ("he causes the students to change") or *chātraiḥ* ("by means of the students"), since the rule would not otherwise apply, this [Vārttika] is commenced.
It should be stated: "The [option] applies after the roots *abhivad* ('to greet') and *dṛś* ('to see') when the Ātmanepada voice is used."

Regarding the verb *abhivādayati*: since [the action] of saluting (*abhivādayati*) does not apply [to the object], but the action of seeing (*dṛś*) does apply because it has the sense of cognition (*buddhy-artha*), or because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*). *Abhivadati guruṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta salutes the teacher). *Abhivādayate guruṃ devadattaṃ devadattena vā* (He causes Devadatta to salute the teacher, or he salutes the teacher by means of Devadatta). *Darśayate rājānaṃ bhṛtyān bhṛtyair vā* (The king shows himself to his servants, or he shows the servants to himself). However, in the case of the *parasmaipada* endings, when there is no designation as the "object" (*karman*), the *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *ṇeraṇau*. But in that other case [where the object designation applies], it is by the rule *ṇicaśca*. "The independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*). (Pāṇini 1.4.54)

The meaning intended as being independent (*svātantrya*) with respect to the action shall be designated as the agent (*kartṛ*). And independence consists in being the substratum of the operation expressed by the verbal root. As it was stated by Hari:
"When the action has been expressed by the verbal root, the status of being an agent is always desired for the *kāraka*."

The term "operation" (*vyāpāra*) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to actions whose locus is a result derived from the [material] constituents (*dhātūpāttaphalāśraya*). In examples such as *caitro maitreṇa pācayati* ("Caitra causes Maitra to cook"), since both the act of cooking and the operation denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) have their operations derived from the verbal root (*dhātūpāttavyāpāratva*), both possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*). However, the distinction is that because the agency residing in Caitra alone is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the number (*saṃkhyā*) is construed with that [agency] alone. In the case of *caitro maitraṃ gamayati* ("Caitra causes Maitra to go"), although Maitra possesses the status of agent, the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not apply, because it is precluded by the technical designation of "object" (*karman*).

In expressions such as "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*), the pot possesses agency because the activity residing in the pot is precisely what is denoted by the verbal root. Consequently, in cases such as "Caitra does not cause [the pot] to cook" (*caitro na pacayati*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding Caitra and others, because the activity denoted by the root is absent in them. This is because, although that activity is the counter-positive of the absence [denoted by the negative particle], its status as the meaning of the root is not lost; furthermore, the property of appearing as subsisting in Caitra is included within the definition [of agency].

As for the objection that there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "the pot is not a cloth," because the pot—which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)—lacks the substratumhood (*āśrayatva*) required by the meaning of the verbal root; and as for the claim that this is not a problem because the verb "is" (*bhavati*), which is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*), indicates the process of becoming identical with both (*ubhayatādātmyabhavana*), and since such a process of becoming is the counter-correlate of the non-existence, the understanding of mutual non-existence arises from the verbal cognition itself, and since that process of becoming exists in both by virtue of their identity, it is possible for both to function as the agent (*kartṛ*). This cannot be maintained, because it would entail that the number (*saṃkhyā*) denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) applies to both [the pot and the cloth], resulting in the impossibility of the usage "the pot is not two cloths" (*ghaṭo na paṭau*).

By this, the following view is refuted: that in the expression "the pot is not a cloth," the word *nañ* indicates that which possesses the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) having the pot as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and thus serves as a marker of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*); and therefore, just as in the cases of "white pot" and "non-pot cloth," both [the pot and the cloth] are construed with the supplied verb (*adhyāhṛta-kriyā*) through a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*), by taking recourse to a contingent relation of non-difference (*pākṣika-abheda-sambandha*). This is because, in instances such as "the pot perishes" (*ghaṭo naśyati*), agency (*kartṛtva*) is in no way possible [if *nañ* were taken in the sense of mutual absence].

That is incorrect, because the counter-positive of mutual non-existence lacks agency. For you yourself have admitted that when the nominative case—which is the indicator of grammatical correctness—is to be employed, the absence of any reason for bypassing that nominative case is itself the governing factor.

Furthermore, that which is the locus of an object presented by a word that does not connect with the gender (liṅga) delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) possesses the status of being its agent (*kartṛ*). This is because in examples such as *caitreṇa pacyate* ("It is cooked by Caitra") and *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), Caitra and others are the loci of the effort (*kṛti*) delimited by the meaning of the root; and because even when the suffix of the passive (*lākāra*) expresses the effort, [the effort] is expressed [as being delimited by the root-meaning]. In cases such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("The pot comes into being"), the suffix of the verb (*ākhyāta*) indicates the locus, and [the relation of] counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) is indicated [by the negative particle], while "delimitation" (*avacchinnatva*) is a specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*), and not something like causality (*janakatva*).

Therefore, there is no deficiency even if effort (*prayatna*) and the like do not produce destruction and so forth. In expressions such as *caitraḥ pācakaḥ* (Caitra is a cook) and *paktā* (the cooker), since the *kṛt* suffix expresses an effort conducive to cooking that does not connect with gender, there is no fault. In forms ending in *ghañ*, such as *caitrasya pākaḥ* (Caitra’s cooking), although the meaning of the *ghañ* suffix connects with gender, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), because the operation delimited by cooking—which is indicated (*lakṣya*) by the verbal root—does not connect with gender. Alternatively, the *ghañ* suffix expresses both the effort through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the cooking through primary denotation (*śakti*). Since Caitra connects with the effort, agency (*kartṛtva*) is established;
or, because the genitive is used in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*), there is no deficiency even in the absence of agency, and so forth.

That too is incorrect; for there is no evidence that the gender [of the suffix] does not connect with the action (*kṛti*), since we observe such instances as "Caitra is the agent of cooking" (*caitraḥ paktā*) and "Mitrā is the female agent of cooking" (*mitrā paktrī*). Nor should it be argued that the gender resides only in the substratum (*āśraya*) and not in the action itself, because the cognition of femininity and so forth arises from the suffixes attached to words like *kṛt* (agent) and *kṛti* (action). Even so, if the action were distinct from the meaning of the *ghañ*-suffix, it would be difficult to maintain that the gender does not connect with the action.

Furthermore, because the view that "cooking" (pāka) means "that which is to be accomplished by an effort conducive to cooking," where the meaning of the suffix *ghañ* and others is a state that has attained the condition of being already established (*siddha*), contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Moreover, the genitive case of the residual type (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) in expressions such as "Caitra’s cooking" (*caitrapāka*) is defective precisely because it would result in an incorrect accentuation of the base of the subsequent member of a *kṛt*-derived compound; we shall elaborate on this in the second [chapter].

Furthermore, in the case of "the pot is not the cloth," the verb *bhavati* (is), which is supplied by ellipsis, indicates both the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) and the substratum-ness (*āśrayatva*). The resulting cognition is that the counter-correlativity and the substratum-ness reside, respectively, in the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) existing between the pot and the cloth, in relation to their connection. Moreover, the rule that the number expressed by the verb refers only to the number residing in the locus (*anuyogin*) and not also to the number residing in the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) must be postulated in accordance with empirical experience.

Alternatively, there is the superimposition (adhyāhāra) of two verbs: "the jar does not exist" and "the two cloths do not exist. The word *na* is an indicator (*dyotaka*). The cognition is that the state of being the locus of existence residing in one jar is the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) whose counter-positive is the state of being the locus of existence residing in the two cloths. The connection between the two verbal forms occurs through the relation of possessing a mutual absence whose counter-positive is itself, as in the case of "Look, the deer is running. Furthermore, the experience of the difference between the jar and the cloth is mental (*mānasa*).

That too is incorrect, because it would lead to the absurd conclusion that "a pot is not a pot. If it is argued that the relation of the pot to its counter-positiveness is simply its being delimited by potness (*ghaṭatvāvācchinnatva*), we say no; for even by taking the pot's counter-positiveness with respect to the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) residing in what is other than a cloth, and the cloth's being the locus of a mutual absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a property other than potness, the aforementioned cognition could still be accounted for.

Even under the conceptualization that "the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) is understood as residing in that very thing which serves as its locus," there would be no cessation of verbal doubt such as "Is this a jar or a cloth? and so forth; furthermore, this would contradict the experience of [the sentence] being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*).

By this, the alternative view beginning with "or rather" (*yadvā*) is also refuted, because the experience of the difference between the jar and the cloth is verbal (*śābda*). Let this matter rest for now.

Most logicians, however, say that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the instigator of another factor (*kāraka*), while not being instigated by other factors. They hold that the phrase "while not being instigated" excludes tools such as axes, because these are instigated [by the agent] since they are not qualified by operations such as conjunction produced by the person [the agent]. This view is to be considered; for it would result in the non-attainment of agency for individual souls (*jīva*) who are instigated by God. Furthermore, it would lead to the over-extension (*avyāpti*) [of the definition] to potters and others, because the stick and so forth are instigated by them [the potters] due to their being qualified by conjunctions produced by the stick.

The moderns (*navya*), however, maintain that being the agent of an action consists in possessing an effort (*kṛti*) conducive to that action. This is because the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is not applied to firewood even when one perceives it as possessing an activity conducive to cooking. Furthermore, according to the method stated by the Teacher (*ācārya*)—namely, "by means of the distinction between what has been done and what has not been done"—the word "agent," which is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *tṛc*, conveys the locus of effort (*yatna*). Since its application to insentient things is figurative (*gauṇa*), and since there is an absence of the conventional usage of "being the agent of that action" when an action such as lifting a very heavy load fails to be accomplished despite the presence of an effort directed toward it, the property of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatva*) is adopted instead of "having [that] as its object" (*viṣayakatva*).

If, however, agency does not belong to one even by taking into account an effort directed toward a different object that is conducive to that [action], then for this very reason, when there is the linguistic usage "I have eaten the flour, but it was not done by me," Caitra would not be the agent in the case of eating sugar and so forth—even though his effort was an indispensable means—unless the property of having that as its object is also included. And that [objecthood] must be specified as being in the form of "being what is to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*). Consequently, although heaven and the like exist as objects of the effort toward sacrifice and so forth by way of the objecthood known as "intendedness" (*uddeśyatva*), the performer of the sacrifice and so forth does not possess agency with respect to heaven and the like.

"It is indeed accepted that 'the Lord cooks' [is a valid expression]. Otherwise, however, they say that one must include a unique suitability (anukūlatva) characterized by a producedness (janyatā) not delimited by being an effect (kāryatva).
And the cause (hetu) is that which prompts it. (55)

The instigator (prayojaka) of that agent is designated as a *hetu* (cause), and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is also designated as an agent (*kartṛ*). [Example: *hariḥ kārayati* ("Hari causes [the servant] to act"). Because of the designation as a *hetu*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26) to express the operation of the cause. Since [the servant] possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is used in the active voice (*kartari*). Nor should it be argued: "How can there be agency for the one being prompted, since he lacks independence? For even when in the presence of an instigator, his independence with respect to his own action is not lost. Precisely for this reason, it is stated clearly in the Bhāṣya that even while the one being prompted is performing the action, there is the designation "he causes [him] to do."
Thus ends the third Āhnika of the first [section] in the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi.
Now begins the second Adhyāya: "A rule concerning words applies when they are semantically connected (samartha). (Pāṇini 2.1.1)

A rule (*vidhi*) concerning word-connection (*pada-sambandhin*) should be understood as being dependent on semantic capacity (*samartha*). This is because the term "semantically capable" (*samartha-pada*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to refer to that which depends upon such capacity. The word *vidhi* is derived as a passive noun (*karma-sādhana*). In the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*, the suffix *ki* is applied; however, when the suffix *i* is added to the root *vidh* (in the sense of "arranging") by means of an Uṇādi suffix, the word *vidhi* is acutely accented (*udātta*) on its first syllable. The distinction here is that this [other] word *vidhi* is acutely accented on its final syllable (*anta-udātta*). Regarding this, one position is that semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists in "becoming a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), while the second position is that semantic capacity consists in "mutual expectancy" (*vyapekṣā*).

The third position is that capacity (*sāmarthya*) is twofold and constitutes the governing condition (*adhikāra*). Thus, including the case where it is a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), there are six positions. Among these, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that capacity consists in semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) and is a technical rule; the others are prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is settled in the original treatise (*ākara*). A "word-rule" (*padavidhi*) is that which operates when either one or both members are nominal stems ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that "being a rule for words" (*padavidhitva*) is precisely that which is common to all factors that cause something to be a word (*padatva*). Therefore, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice or with barley," there is no simultaneous application (*samuccaya*) of both rice and barley. This is because, if they were mutually expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), they would lack syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*), and consequently, the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) would be untenable. They argue that since the designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) occurs only when the case-ending has been produced, the rule for the instrumental ending is also a "rule for words" by virtue of being a factor that causes the designation "word"; thus, it falls under the scope of the maxim regarding "competency" (*samartha-paribhāṣā*).

That is incorrect; for there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) precisely when there is a requirement for connection with another word. Otherwise, even in the absence of a conjunction (*samuccaya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-occurrence of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*) because of the expectancy for actions such as threshing (*avaghāta*). Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-occurrence of the case-ending in examples such as *nīlaṃ ghaṭam* (the blue pot), because of the lack of semantic competency due to the expectancy for "blue," just as in the case of *ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s prosperous servant). In my view, however, there is a difference: since it is not a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*), the technical paribhāṣā does not apply.

For this very reason, in the *Mahābhāṣya*, regarding the view that the objecthood (*karmatva*) belongs to the meaning of the verbal root as qualified by the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*), it is stated that even though the root requires the prefix, the suffix *san* is still applied to the root. This is because, since it is not a rule dependent on a word (*padavidhi*), the technical paribhāṣā concerning semantic competency (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) does not apply. However, in the case of "he desires a great son" (*mahāntaṃ putram icchati*), there is no such fault; for since the suffix *kyac* is prescribed after a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is a rule dependent on a word (*padavidhi*), as explained in the *Bhāṣya*. According to your position, however, when a finite verb (*tiṅ*) is produced from a form ending in the suffix *san*, that [form] would indeed possess the designation of a "word" (*pada*). Consequently, since it would be a rule dependent on a word (*padavidhi*), the application of the *samartha-paribhāṣā* would be unavoidable, leading to an insurmountable contradiction.

By this, the following objection is also refuted: that since a qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatva*) is impossible without the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyāvṛtti*), if there were dependence on another substance, even qualifierhood would be untenable, and thus the semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) characterized as *sāmarthya* (syntactic expectancy) would be impossible. For if one accepts qualifierhood only upon the exclusion of connection with another, then expressions such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*) would be untenable. However, if one intends merely the exclusion of non-connection with itself (*svāyogavyāvṛtti*), there is no fault even in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, in the case of intending merely the exclusion of non-connection with itself, there is no defect even in the case of conjunction.

For this very reason, in the passage—"If the Soma sacrifice has the Rathantara-sāman, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the Bṛhat-sāman, those beginning with the Sukra; if it has the Jagat-sāman, those beginning with the Āgrayaṇa"—the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even though the *pṛṣṭha* chants accomplished by the Bṛhat and Rathantara are optional (*vikalpa*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, they can function as qualifiers by excluding their own non-connection [with the sacrifice]. Thus, because the capacity characterized by "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*) is not lost, the qualified sacrifice serves as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the precedence (*āgratā*).

In cases such as "with rice" (*vrīhibhiḥ*), however, since the injunction makes known merely the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between being produced from rice and being a sacrifice, even when the coreferentiality with being produced from barley is understood through another scriptural text, it is postulated that in both instances the delimitor of the state of being produced (*janyatāvacchedaka*) is simply the nature of a distinct type of sacrifice (*vijātīyayāgatva*), according to the maxim of the grass, the fire-drill wood, and the gem (*tṛṇāraṇimaṇinyāya*).

Furthermore, semantic competency (*sāmārthya*) does not consist in the capacity to convey meanings that are mutually related, for this would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as "the king’s wife" (*rājño bhāryā*) and "Devadatta’s man" (*puruṣo devadattasya*). Rather, it consists in being the intended object (*tātparyaviṣayatva*) by virtue of conveying a meaning connected with the meaning of that [other word]. In those cases, however, the intention is toward a cognition of connection between the king and the referent of the word "wife" alone, and not with the "man"; thus, there is no fault.

Furthermore, this [definition] applies neither to a sentence (*vākya*) nor to semantic expectancy (*vyapekṣā-sāmarthya*), because under the view that there is a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), one must accept that the composite whole alone possesses the power for a specific meaning; such a capacity [of individual words] is therefore absent. Regarding this, they state the following justification: in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man"), if the two words were directed toward their own respective primary meanings, then even in a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), there would be a connection with qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), just as in a sentence. The same should be understood for cases such as *putrīyati* ("he treats like a son"), *kumbhakāra* ("pot-maker"), and *aupagava* ("descendant of Upagu").

Nor does it follow from the statement that "there is no occurrence [of a compound] with qualifiers, nor is there a connection of qualifiers with that which has already occurred" that such a consequence arises; for if one were to prevent that by means of such a statement, it would result in unnecessary complexity (gaurava). Rather, according to the reasoning stated above, since the whole possesses the power to denote a qualified meaning, it is established that the connection of a qualifier is impossible within its constituent part—the referent of the word *rājan*—and thus the aforementioned statement is accepted merely as a restatement of what is already established by logic, thereby achieving parsimony (lāghava).

In the case of the mental presentation (upasthiti) generated by the word *śvaśura* ("father-in-law"), when the wife is presented as a qualifier of the father-in-law, qualifiers such as "well-behaved" (*suśīlā*) cannot be construed with her. Likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the particle *ca* even in a compound, as in the case of *dhavaśca khadiraśca* ("the dhava tree and the khadira tree"). Nor should it be argued that this consequence does not arise because I also accept a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) for such a meaning; for it is more appropriate to accept a primary denotative power (*śakti*) itself rather than a metaphorical indication.

Furthermore, in compounds such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), there would be the undesirable consequence of the use of a nominal suffix (*yat*); and in expressions such as *prāptodako grāmaḥ* ("a village reached by water"), since the agent is the primary meaning of the suffix in the word *prāpta* (which ends in an agentive suffix), it would follow that the agent is predominant, making the meaning "a village which is the object of an arrival whose agent is water" impossible.

Others, however, say: in the expression "rājapuruṣa" (king’s man), because the word *rāja* (king) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of one related to the king, the king becomes a part of the referent of the compound; therefore, it is impossible to bring about the connection of an attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) even with that [part]. In reality, the reason for the lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) when that which is presented as an attribute does not connect with other word-meanings is this very point.

Furthermore, just as in cases such as "raktaḥ paṭo bhavati" (the cloth becomes red), when there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words like "ṛddhasya" (of the prosperous one), a syntactic connection is possible through an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) that is raised; therefore, the rule "saviśeṣaṇānām" (of those accompanied by qualifiers) is necessary to indicate that [such usage] is ungrammatical (*asādhutva*). Consequently, there is no fault even in instances involving a compound where elision (*aluk*) has not occurred.

As for the argument that in cases such as "the grandson is handsome" (*naptā sundaraḥ*) or "the pot is eternal" (*ghaṭo nityaḥ*), one must generally determine that a sentence is ungrammatical when there is a connection with only a part of the word-meaning—without resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (indication)—in order to prevent the grammaticality of such sentences from being established by taking the connection of "handsome" (*sundara*) with the grandson and "eternal" (*nitya*) with the nature of a pot (*ghaṭatva*). Furthermore, since such usage is observed, the existence of *śakti* (denotative power) must be accepted; this is incorrect. For then even sentences like "Caitra’s grandson" (*caitrasya naptā*) would result in being ungrammatical. Moreover, since understanding can occur even through error, the acceptance of *śakti* does not make the aforementioned fault unavoidable. [The meaning of a word] is constrained by the distinctions of the relations between the qualified and the qualifier and by the distinctions of limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
Even in the absence of that correctness, the understanding [of meaning] is not precluded here.

This is because such is our accepted position. Nor should it be argued that sentences such as "the jar is eternal" would possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) even without *lakṣaṇā* (indication), since the property of eternality would be understood as residing in the jar-ness; for this is not undesirable (*iṣṭāpatti*). This is because such a cognition does not arise precisely due to a lack of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For, in the case of a cognition where a word-meaning is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and another is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of the former, produced by the word, in its capacity as a qualificand.

In some cases, however, by the force of natural expectancy (*svārasikānubhāva*), even for the sake of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the delimitor of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), it is postulated that the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the word—even as a delimitor—is a cause. For this very reason, there is no linguistic usage of "incorrectness" (*asādhutva*) in expressions such as *ghaṭaḥ karmatvam* ("the pot is the object-ness").
