As for what was stated in the *Śabdakaustubha* under the rule *dhruvam apāye* (Pāṇini 1.4.24)—that because of the connection with the act of bringing (*ānayana*) on the part of the jar, and because of the connection with the suffix *kṛt* on the part of the word *ānayana*, there arises the contingency of the genitive case used with a *kṛt*-suffix (the so-called *kṛdyoga-ṣaṣṭhī*), this sentence [“ghaṭasyānayanam”] is indeed ungrammatical—that is incorrect. For here, the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between the jar and the act of bringing is not intended; rather, it is the relation of the jar as the object (*karman*) that must be predicated of its connection to the act of bringing. Furthermore, the objection regarding the necessity of employing the particle *ca* (‘and’) is unworthy of consideration, since the meaning is established simply through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the jar as qualified by the conjunction.

Because it is more appropriate to accept *lakṣaṇā* (indication) than to postulate an additional power (*atiriktaśakti*), there is no contingency of employing the word [“cow”] itself [in the compound]. Even though such [employment] occurs in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), in the compound (*samāsa*) the word “cow” indicates the owner of the brindled cows; thus, since the primacy of the owner is established, there is no purpose for employing that word in the compound.

In the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*), since the cows alone function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) for the understanding of the meaning of the compound, how could the analytical statement convey that meaning? It is precisely for the sake of establishing the status of the master—the referent of the word *yat*—as the qualificand by means of the word *tat*, that the two words *yat* and *tat* are employed in the manner of subject and predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*). If it is objected: "If the word *go* (cow) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to the owner of the cow, there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the word *citrā* (variegated), because [the owner] is merely a part of the meaning of the word *go*. Nor can the word *citrā* have a secondary signification referring to the owner of the variegated [cows], because there would be no syntactic connection with the meaning of the word *go*. [The response follows:]...

On this point, the teachers Vaṭeśopādhyāya [hold as follows]: Metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs only in the sentence, and not in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) itself—namely, "one for whom there is a brindled cow" (*citrā gauryasya*). In that case, the referent of the word *yat* (which has been elided and then remembered) is what connects with actions such as bringing; for it is through the relation of being connected to a brindled cow that the referent is presented, and thus its connection with the status of being an object (*karmatva*) would otherwise be untenable. Nor is the word *yat* in the analytical statement devoid of case-endings, because that would result in the analytical sentence failing to convey the syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Furthermore, the meaning of the sentence is not "bring him for whom there is a brindled cow," because such is not experienced.

And they say that there is no presentation of the word *tat* (that) due to the obligatory connection between *yat* (which) and *tat*, because that would entail the fault of supplying an unstated word (*adhyāhāra*). For this very reason, in sentences such as "a hamlet on the deep river," the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) resides in the sentence itself. After the mutual relation between the "deep" and the "river" has been understood, the bank—which in reality is connected to the deep river—is indicated there in its form as a mere "bank."

Without the cognition of mutual connection, it would be impossible to understand the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—which consists in a relation to what is signified by the words themselves—as residing in the "bank," because there would be no quality of being made known by the sentence in a qualified sense. For this very reason, the Vedāntins maintain that in the sentence "Brahman is Truth, Consciousness, Bliss," the pure Brahman, which in reality is related to the qualified sentence-meaning, is indicated. Similarly, in sentences such as those consisting of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the metaphorical indications such as praise are clear in other systems [of Mīmāṃsā].

Likewise here as well, following the cognition of the non-difference between the variegated [cow] and the cow (*gav-abheda-anvaya-bodha*), there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of being the owner of the variegated cow (*citragosvāmitva-rūpeṇa*)—which is related to the cow denoted by itself (*svajñāpya-gosambandhin*)—but not in the sense of mere ownership (*svāmitva*) or in the sense of Devadatta. This is because it conforms to the specific experience (*viśiṣṭānubhava*) and because that [specific identity] is obtained through the word "Devadatta" and so forth itself; this is how it should be understood. As for the author of the *Maṇi* (Raghunātha Śiromaṇi), he says: "In the phrase 'in the deep river,' indication occurs either in the initial part (*gabhīrāyām*) or in the final part (*nadyām*). It is not the first case, because since that [initial part] is not the base form (*aprakṛti*), the meaning of the nominal suffix (*sub-artha*) cannot be construed with its own meaning. Nor is it the second case, for the very same reason, and because the meaning of a nominal suffix cannot be construed with the meaning of another nominal suffix. Thus they say.

Others, however, argue that because the aggregate (samudāya) possesses the status of a noun (*nāman*) by virtue of its denoted meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), the first fault does not apply. Even if there is no syntactic connection between the individual meanings of the suffixes and the base, there is no second fault either, since the meaning of the sentence as a whole is not of that nature. Nor should it be argued that, because the sentence here lacks a nominal ending (*asubanta*), it is impossible for it to convey the denoted meaning; for although it is a noun by virtue of having a meaning, the meaning in the form of the "bank" cannot connect with the action through identity due to incompatibility, nor can it connect through difference because such a construction is unestablished (*avyutpanna*).

By accepting figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) only in the case of the word functioning as the riverbank, the sentence can possess a form ending in the accusative case; thus, the syntactic relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) with the verb is possible. Even in cases such as "Trees were produced by a deep river" (*gabhīrayā nadyā vṛkṣā janitāḥ*), where the ending in the accusative is otherwise untenable, there is neither ungrammaticality nor a lack of semantic connection, because figurative indication is accepted precisely at the end of the word "river" (*nadī*). This same method should be understood to apply to explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as well, which possess indicatory power. For even there, as in other instances, the excellence (*prāśastya*)—consisting in the fact that [an action] is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence—is first construed with the verbal action itself, and only subsequently with the meaning of the verbal root, so they say.

In this regard, the following must be considered: nevertheless, it is untenable for the aggregate (samudāya) to be a suffix (*pratyaya*), because that which has been prescribed as a suffix is itself the base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, even if the aggregate possesses a referential meaning (*lakṣyārthavattva*), it is untenable for it to be a noun (*nāman*), because the word *nadī* is excluded by the rule "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) due to its ending in a suffix.

Nor should it be argued that, by the paribhāṣā rule stating that when a term denoting a suffix (pratyaya) is mentioned, there is a reference to that suffix itself, as well as to what precedes it and what ends with it, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by that [rule] applies only to the word *nadī* and not to the technical designation (*lakṣaṇā*), because the designation resides in two words and thus lacks the status of a meaningful aggregate (*arthavat-samudāyatva*) since only a single aggregate possesses meaning—even so, the meaningfulness of the two [words] together is not lost.

Otherwise, on the view that the sentence-meaning is what is indicated (*lakṣaka*), the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) would unavoidably apply to the sentence as a whole, since the qualified meaning is conveyed by the aggregate [of word and suffix]. For this very reason, the doubt raised in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts—that the prohibition of the designation [of nominal stem] would follow for the base and suffix due to their being meaningful through the meanings expressed and suggested by them—is consistent [only with our view]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the case-ending in *gabhīrāyām*, because it would be a part of the nominal stem.

By this, the example "gabhīrayā nadyā" (by a deep river) and others are also refuted; for that very reason, the second [position] is also discarded. For in the case of "nadyām" as well, there would be the further consequence of the elision of the case-ending (*vibhakti-lopa*), since the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) would apply there too due to the presence of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*). Moreover, you yourself accept its status as a noun (*nāman*) by accepting its having an accusative ending (*dvitīyāntatva*) as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Let this digression suffice. Others, however, say: "Let there be a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in both words of the *bahuvrīhi* compound due to the lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*); nevertheless, there is no assumption of a primary denotative power (*śakti*), because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*)."

The moderns (navya), however, maintain that there is indeed a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) for a qualified object within the word *go* itself. For this very reason, in cases such as *ardhapippalī* (half-a-pple) and *upakumbham* (near the jar)—which are respectively genitive-tatpuruṣas and avyayībhāvas where the meaning of the prior member is predominant—it is accepted that the secondary signification belongs only to the subsequent member (*pippalī* and *kumbha*) in the sense of "half of a pippalī" and so forth; the prior member, meanwhile, serves merely to indicate the intended meaning (tātparya-grāhaka). Furthermore, because the meaning of the prior member functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the object signified by the subsequent member, the established linguistic usage is thereby maintained.

By this, the objection that if the word *go* (cow) were to indicate the owner of the cow (*gosvāmin*), there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the variegated cow (*gavicitra*) with one part [of the indicated meaning] is refuted. Nor is there a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) by resorting to a qualified indication (*viśiṣṭalakṣaṇā*) for the word *citra* (variegated); for since that word denotes a quality (*guṇa*), its indication would consist of a mediated relation (*paramparāsambandha*), and as such, it is more cumbersome (*guru*). By this, the objection that even in the case of words like *prāpta* occurring within a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the genitive sense is absent, there is no deciding factor because they denote the agent (*kartṛ*) etc., thereby possessing a direct relation, is also refuted.

Nevertheless, these words denote a substance in a general form, whereas words such as "water" (udaka) and the like denote it in a specific form. Although there is a rule that words such as "hero" (śūra) denote a substance qualified by a quality, in the present case, words such as "variegated" (citra) are not distinct from them in this regard; furthermore, in cases such as "a brave man" (śūraga), the decisive evidence is well-established. This is because the mere absence of denoting a quality alone is irrelevant, and because when there is secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) in the subsequent word, the proximity of the suffix is obtained.

Nor should it be argued that since the rule for the *bahuvrīhi* compound is prescribed when multiple inflected words (*subanta*) refer to another word as their external referent (*anyapadārtha*), it would be untenable for a single word alone to have another word as its external referent; for the authors of the *Maṇi* and others have stated that such usage is functional through its role in conveying the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Otherwise, because a compound lacks multiple words, the contradiction regarding its expressive power would remain as it was for you as well.

As for the objection that, since even in words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) a division into stem and suffix is possible, one could assume that the suffixal portion has a secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to a specific genus and so forth, which would result in the collapse of the word’s collective power (*samudāya-śakti*): that is not so. For is it the case that the collapse of the collective power is being urged regarding the etymological meaning (*yaugika-artha*), or regarding the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi-artha*)? It cannot be the first, because that is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor can it be the second, because in that case there is no connection with the meanings of the constituent parts.

Even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, only if Devadatta-ness and the like were the delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) would it be equivalent to [the denotation of] "pot," "cloth," and so forth; however, this is not the case, because the difference between the two types of cognition is universally accepted. Nor should it be argued that Devadatta-ness as qualified by the state of being the owner of the "variegated cow" is itself the delimitor of denotability, while the word "Devadatta" merely serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). For such an argument would entail the fault of polysemy (*nānārthatva*), and it would contradict the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) stating that the referent of a *bahuvrīhi* is the "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*).

Furthermore, it would follow that the entire meaning of words such as *devadatta* is expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself, with [the compound] merely serving to indicate the intended sense (*tātparya*). For this very reason, both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa state that the subsequent employment of the word (*anuprayoga*) is untenable once the word-meaning has already been expressed, because it has already been denoted. Just as the particle *ca* is not employed in a *dvandva* compound because its meaning is already expressed by the rule "in the sense of 'and' there is a *dvandva*," so too, since the meaning of the word *devadatta* is already expressed by the compound, the employment of the word *devadatta* and so forth would not occur.

Having thus raised the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, that because [the specific meaning] is not expressed, words such as "Devadatta" would not be employed—the final position (*siddhānta*) was established by the statement "not so, because it is not expressed": even though the general meaning is expressed by the compound, the specific [meaning] is not expressed; therefore, for the sake of understanding the specific, words such as "Devadatta" are employed. And thus, the nature of the cognition of the owner of brindled cows (*citragosvāmitva*) as its mode is precisely the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the knowledge of the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) of the term "brindled cow-possessor" (*citragu*).

And thus, there is this distinction regarding the logicians' (*tārkika*) lack of knowledge concerning the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "cow's foot" (*gopada*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Mīmāṃsāvārttika*:
"If a horse's ears were somehow to belong to a tree, who would ever postulate an unestablished power (*śakti*) for the whole [compound]?"

Thus it has been stated. Furthermore, because the theory of non-etymological derivation (avyutpatti-pakṣa) must necessarily be accepted in accordance with the sūtra beginning with "arthavat" (Pāṇini 1.2.45), it would be improper for the collective power (samudāya-śakti) to be lost. Moreover, when the question arises as to which word is etymologically unformed (avyutpanna), the criterion is clear: it is that word for which the resulting cognition cannot be accounted for by taking the meaning of its constituent parts. This is because, in cases such as *ghaṭate* and *ghaṭaḥ*, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the basic stem portion (*prakṛti*) and the suffix portion (*pratyaya*).

This is because [the word "pot"] does not produce a cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualifier and the pot as its qualificand. By this, the counter-example of the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus") is refuted; for in that case, the acceptance of a conventional power (*śakti*) for the whole form is solely for the sake of producing a cognition having "lotus-ness" as its qualifier.

As for the objection that, even so, there would still be no connection with the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakty-artha*) therein—on the grounds that the established linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) is that suffixes convey their own meanings as connected to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and that because no suffix is prescribed after the final member of a compound, the meaning of that compound cannot be considered the "meaning of the base"—that is trivial. For "being a base" (*prakṛtitva*) is simply "being a subordinate element" (*aṅgatva*). This is because of the rule stating: "That which serves as the limit for a suffix is the subordinate element (*aṅga*) for all suffixes beginning with that [limit]. And thus, since the case-ending is prescribed after the compound.

Even though there is a disparity in that one [word] functions as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) while the other functions as the indicator (*lakṣaka*), the status of being the meaning of the base form (*prakṛtyarthatva*) is not lost for the indicated sense. By this, the objection that "there would be no case-ending after a compound" is also refuted.

Even granting [the opponent's position], we say: the designation of *prātipadika* follows precisely from the mention of the "compound" (*samāsa*). [Objection: If that were so, since it would lack the status of being a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), the sūtra *kṛttaddhita-samāsāś ca* would result in the designation of *prātipadika* for the entire aggregate in the case of *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, because the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes includes even those preceded by *gati*s and *kāraka*s. [Reply: Not so. For what is actually brought about by this [sūtra]? Is it the introduction of a case-ending after the aggregate, or the elision of the case-ending after the aggregate? It cannot be the first, because that is our desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).

The first [option] is not tenable because elision (*lopa*) is easily obtained through its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Nor is the second; for it would result in the redundancy of the mention of "the third case" (*tṛtīyā*) in the rule *tṛtīyā-prabhṛti-ny-ānyatarasyām*. This is because the rule *upadaṃśas-tṛtīyāyām* pertains exclusively to the suffix *ṇamul*, and thus the compound is already established by the rule *amaivāvyayena*. That [mention of the third case] is indeed intended for the purpose of hearing the third case ending in the alternative view. Even there, if elision were to occur, what would be the use of an optional rule?

In reality, however, when there is the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix, there is the inclusion of both that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*, as well as that which is alone (*kevala*). Otherwise, in examples such as *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*, the compound under the rule "the second case with *śrita*" would not occur. Consequently, the prescription of the technical name *prātipadika* for a *kṛdanta* form—whether alone or preceded by a *kāraka*—would be rendered useless. Thus, the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* does not apply here, as has been explained in detail in that very [work]; let this suffice for now.

By this [principle], the objection that—in the case of the injunction "one sacrifices to Sviṣṭakṛt with three limbs" (tryaṅgaiḥ sviṣṭakṛtaṃ yajati)—an injunction of the number three is impossible as a secondary reference to the limbs (*aṅga-anuvāda*) because it would entail the violation of the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratā-bhaṅga*) in a compound; for it is proper that a single word be either the subject or the predicate, but not both a subject and a predicate simultaneously, which would contradict established doctrine—has been refuted. This is because, when there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the final member [of the compound], the status of being a single word-meaning is easily maintained.

In the case of a *vasta-bahuvrīhi*, there is indeed a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the final member; however, in expressions such as *upakumbham* (near the jar) and *ardhapippalī* (half a pepper), the connection of the meaning of the prior member—namely, "proximity to the jar" and "half of a pepper"—with the meaning of the case-suffix and with the meaning of another nominal stem is not untenable.

In such a cognition, there is a distinct requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the immediate sequence of the two words—the compound and the other word—and for the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the two words, namely the compound and the other word with the same case-ending, in order to produce a cognition of the non-difference (*abheda*) of their respective referents as denoted by the nominal stems. This is a novel path [of interpretation], because the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as an injunction (*vidhi*), making the subsequent case-ending easily available. Nor should it be argued that in that case, the understanding would occur through the relation of subject and predicate (*uddeśya-vidheyabhāva*).

This is because, in verbal cognition (*śābda*), the requirement is that the presentation (*upastiti*) produced by two words not contained within a compound must be the cause [of the cognition] through a subject-predicate relationship (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*). By this, the objection—that in cases such as "The king’s man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣaḥ sundaraḥ*) or "If the Soma sacrifice were characterized by the Rathantara-sāman, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu" (*yadi rathantarasāmā somaḥ syādaindravāyavāgrān grahān gṛhṇīyāt*)—there would be no such syntactic connection—is refuted; for what is intended is that both the subject and the predicate must be outside of a compound.

By this, the suspicion of sublation (*bādha*) regarding such passages as "the first draught belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer" is dispelled; for there is universal agreement on the rule that in verbal expression, that which is mentioned first is the subject (*uddeśya*) and that which is mentioned last is the predicate (*vidheya*). This has also been demonstrated in the *Vṛddhi* sūtra; let the elaboration suffice. Therefore, this is the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya here.

In the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the king [is related] to the meaning of the genitive case, which is the relation [of possession]; and since that [relation] is a qualifier of the man by way of being its locus (*āśrayatva*), the cognition is: "the man who is the locus of the relation with the king. Here, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), the king, connects with the meaning of the genitive case through the relation of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*). Thus, there is a distinction: while the relations of being the counter-correlative and being the locus function as the mode of connection (*saṃsargatva*), the other [constituents] constitute the word-meanings (*padārthatva*).

Furthermore, this cognition cannot be accounted for through the compound by accepting a cognition that has "man" as its qualificandum (viśeṣyaka), where the relation is non-difference (abheda) and the mode (prakāra) is "connected with the king" via the secondary function (lakṣaṇā) of "connected with the king."

And thus, it is postulated that the property of being a cognition possessing a qualificandum-ness residing in the person—which is itself determined by a relational objectivity residing in the substratum, which in turn is determined by a qualificandum-ness residing in the relation, which is itself determined by a relational objectivity residing in the counter-correlativity, which is determined by a qualificandum-ness residing in the king—is the delimitor of the effect-ness of the knowledge of the word-potential (*śakti*) for the term *rājapuruṣa*. Nor should it be argued that such a meaning is established through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the whole [compound] alone.

Since both [the primary and secondary meanings] possess equal status as conveyors of meaning and their usage has been identical since beginningless time, the insistence that the function [of the word] must necessarily be *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) results in nothing more than a mere stubborn prejudice.

Nor should it be argued that, since no one accepts a cognition identical in form to the analytical statement (*vigraha*) in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *prāptodaka*, there could be no expressive power (*śakti*) in that [compound] either. For even so, there is no obstacle to postulating that same [expressive power] there as well, since it has already been established in one instance. Nor should it be argued that because number also appears as a qualifier of the king and so forth in the sentence, how can there be identity of form? For it is improper to abandon even those parts for which the occurrence is possible.

Nor should it be argued that the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) should be postulated as "the substratum of the relation with the king qualified by oneness" and so forth; for there is no such experience. This is because of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that in the *vṛtti* (the integrated expression), only the number of non-different oneness (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) appears. The number of non-different oneness is the state of particular numbers existing without distinction. As it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"Just as all the juices of medicinal herbs, when placed in honey, exist without distinction, they know that number to be of such a kind."

Alternatively, Kaiyaṭa states that the general category of number (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*), which is devoid of specific distinctions, is the number of non-differentiated unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*). As it has been said: "Or, through the abandonment of particularities, that number is of such a kind;
by means of the operation of the class-component, it functions through the exclusion of differences."
Just as one is perceived as "possessing color" by means of a color whose specific qualities have not been grasped,
yet the distinctions between colors such as white and so forth are not cognized.

This is merely an illustration of different opinions, as there is no evidence for [the existence of] number in general. It should be understood that this was also implied by Kaiyaṭa when he refuted the connection of indeclinables with gender in general. In cases such as *dviputra* ("having two sons"), a specific number is understood because of the employment of a specific word. In cases such as *tāvakīnaḥ* ("your") and *māmakīnaḥ* ("my"), it is due to a specific substitute (*ādeśa*). In the case of *śaurpikam*, it is because the measure itself is presented as qualified by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In cases such as *māsajātaḥ* ("born after a month"), it is because the intention is to convey a specific time.

In this manner, other cases should also be understood accordingly. Nor should it be argued that—on the basis of its being the first to appear and by the logic of the *kapiñjala* (the rule regarding the three partridges)—there should be a cognition of singularity for the king and others in expressions such as "the king’s servant" (*rājapuruṣa*). This is because, unlike that case, there is here no word expressive of number. Furthermore, it should not be argued that in such a case even the generality of number would not be cognized; for what is intended is that the referent of the word "king" and so forth appears precisely as unqualified by any particular number.

By this, the view that a general cognition of "number-ness" (saṃkhyātva) must be postulated for [compounds] such as *rājñaḥ* or *rājñoḥ* in accordance with the desire to know [the specific number] is refuted; for that [desire] is satisfied by the very cognition of "number-ness" through mental perception (*mānasa*) and so forth. Furthermore, there is no evidence that this [general cognition] serves as the cause for doubt regarding number. Therefore, the rules concerning the elision of case-endings (*vibhakti-lopa*) and so on are merely procedural formalism (*prakriyāmātra*). The word *rājapuruṣa* and the like are indeed indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). The recognition of the word as being the same [as its constituent parts] is an error based on similarity—this is the conclusion.

It might be argued as follows: In the case of *karmadhāraya* compounds such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*), the view of other philosophical systems is that the word "blue" (*nīla*) is construed with the referent of the word "lotus" through the relation of identity (*abheda*). The Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*) maintain that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). This being the case, in the injunction "one should cause a Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice," if it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the primary meaning in the first member; however, in a *karmadhāraya*, the relation is simply identity. Therefore, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is a *karmadhāraya* alone [that is accepted].

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the burden resulting from the postulation of a novel cognition (*apūrvavidyā*) is justified because it pertains to the result (*phalamukha*). This would not be the case in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), since they accept a specific expressive power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) even in the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and thus there is no burden resulting from the assumption of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). On this point, they say: "The consideration of whether [the apprehension of power] is internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*) applies to the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) which exists at a moment immediately preceding the final verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*)."

This is the meaning: in the compound *niṣādasthapati*, according to the view that the word has multiple powers (*aneka-śakti*), it could mean "a carpenter who is a Niṣāda," "the carpenter of the Niṣādas," or "another person whose master is a Niṣāda. Because it possesses all these powers, it is multivalent. In that case, since the specific meaning is understood through the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), one assumes that the intention lies specifically in the sense of "a carpenter who is a Niṣāda," due to the parsimony of factors such as mental presence (*upasthiti*).

This is the meaning: the term *niṣādasthapati*—under the view that it possesses the power of compound expression—is multivalent because it has the capacity to denote a chief who is himself a Niṣāda, a chief of the Niṣādas, or another person whose master is a Niṣāda. In that case, since the specific meaning is understood through the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), it is postulated that the intention lies solely in the sense of a chief who is himself a Niṣāda, on account of the parsimony of factors such as mental presence (*upasthiti*).

It might be argued: "Is the aforementioned simplicity intended for the analytical statement (*vigraha*) or for the compound (*samāsa*)? It cannot be the first, because in that case, since non-difference (*abheda*) is the meaning of the case-ending of the qualifier, there is no simplicity compared to the analytical statement of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Nor should it be said that even in the sentence, non-difference is the relation (*saṃsarga*); for in that context, since the correctness of the meaning is more important than the mere grammatical correctness of the usage of the case-ending, it is more logical that the case-ending has non-difference as its very meaning."

For this very reason, having raised the objection—given that non-difference (*abheda*) appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in a sentence, whereas it appears as a relation (*saṃsarga*) in a compound (*samāsa*), how can these two have the same meaning?—it is clearly stated in the *Śabdāloka* and other works that they have the same meaning merely by virtue of having the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*), and not even by the identity of their qualifiers. And thus, since non-difference in the form of the absence of difference appears as a qualifier in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), the analytical statement of the *karmadhāraya* would be more cumbersome, leading to the opposite conclusion. Not the second [alternative].

This is because, in accordance with the requirement that the compound have the same meaning as its constituent analysis (*vigraha*), it must be stated that even a *karmadhāraya* possesses the capacity to generate a cognition having "sthapati" as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and a specific relation of qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatā-viśeṣa*) characterized by non-difference (*abheda*) as its mode (*prakāra*). Furthermore, in this case, there is no complexity (*gaurava*) compared to the *tatpuruṣa* compound, which generates a cognition having "sthapati" as its qualificandum and a relation of non-difference characterized by the connection to a *niṣāda* as its mode.

To this it is replied: Even by those who maintain that there is no difference between the meanings of case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*) in a sentence, it is stated that in a compound (*samāsa*), non-difference (*abheda*) is indeed nothing but relation (*saṃsarga*). For it has been said by the Miśras: "Nor should it be thought that in a *karmadhāraya* compound as well, there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding non-difference as the meaning of the case-ending; for that would contradict the section concerning the *niṣādasthapati* (the 'chief of the Niṣādas'), since it is accepted that in a *karmadhāraya*, non-difference appears through the very nature of relation."

Likewise, here too, it is accepted that the *karmadhāraya* compound generates a cognition having "stha-pati" as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and a relation of non-difference (*abheda-saṃsarga*) with the qualifier (*prakāra*) "niṣāda. Thus, since in a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) the relation of non-difference enters as the relation (*saṃsarga*) for the qualifier residing in the meaning of the first member, and in a *karmadhāraya* the same non-difference enters as the relation for the qualifier residing in the meaning of the first member, the resulting complexity—due to the inclusion of an additional related element within the scope of the *śakyatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of denotability)—is unavoidable.

For this very reason, it was determined in the section concerning designations (*tadvyapadeśādhikaraṇa*) that even though there is no difference between types of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), indirect indication based on figurative usage (*gauṇī*) is weaker than indication based on possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). And thus: "When a compound is capable of expressing a qualified meaning through the application of primary denotation (*śakti*), and when such a possibility exists, one should prefer the simpler property [of interpretation]. (Verse 1)
Let this detailed discussion suffice for now.

Now, if it is asked how [compounds such as] *devadattasya gurukulam* (Devadatta’s teacher’s family) and so forth are formed, the answer is: in cases involving relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*), a compound (*vṛtti*) indeed occurs even when there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*).
As it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Every word denoting a relative is always dependent and is compounded;
for that mutual expectancy which exists in a sentence is not lost even in a compound."

Thus: "Therefore, in the case of compounds, verbal suffixes, primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and qualifiers, there is no connection with a specific [word]; however, this [connection] would occur when [the word] is dependent."

Alternatively, the relation denoted by the genitive case is something distinct [from the individuals themselves], related to them through the relation of "being connected with that which has itself as its locus. As it has been said:
"For those things whose connection is with a whole, such as a teacher or a family, they are joined with that [whole] by first touching their own parts. (1)

Thus [it is said]. In cases such as *caitrasya naptā* ("Caitra’s grandson"), the meaning of the genitive case also connects with the substantive (*dharmin*) through the relation of being produced by its own locus; this is stated in the *Śabdāloka*. However, in some instances, even when there is dependence on another word, the compound occurs—even in cases where the related term is distinct—on the authority of the *Mahābhāṣya*. For example: *kimodanaḥ śālīnām* means "of which rice-grains? (i.e., what kind of rice?), since rice is of two types, red and white. Similarly, *saktvāḍhakam āpaṇīyānām* means "an *āḍhaka* measure of flour belonging to those found in the market" (i.e., flour associated with the marketplace).

"Whence do you come? From Pāṭaliputra. [The form] *pāṭaliputrakaḥ* means "come from Pāṭaliputra. [The suffix] *vun* is applied by the rule *ropadhetoḥ prācām*. There are two [meanings for] *pāṭaliputra*: [it can mean either the city itself or one who has come] from Pāṭaliputra; thus the meaning is "whence have you come, from which Pāṭaliputra? However, it is established that compounds such as *akiñcikurvāṇa* ("doing nothing") are non-compositional (*asamartha*) and therefore incorrect. Thus, it is proven that compounds and the like occur when there is the capacity for a unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Furthermore, in the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) to be stated hereafter, this capacity (*sāmarthya*) is a qualifier, but it does not apply to the compound itself.

This is according to the maxim: "A quality [is compounded] when its own refinement has been accomplished. Thus, the meaning of the sentence in various contexts is that what has become unified with a single referent through option (*vikalpa*) is then compounded; however, the sense that compounding occurs by way of option regarding one and the same object is impossible. That is to say: where there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), there is only the sentence (*vākya*); but where there is unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), there is only the compound (*samāsa*).

Although there is no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) in the ungrammatical analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) because it does not generate verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), nevertheless, just as one postulates that capacity for the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) based on observing the absence of the relation between qualifiers and the qualified in the final form (*pariniṣṭhita*), and based on observing the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the accusative case and so forth in forms such as *śatṛ*, likewise, since the word *citragu* refers to the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), its reference to that same meaning is postulated even in the ungrammatical stage. They say that this is established by the very fact that the Sūtra’s mention of "the meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*) and so forth implies that the deity possesses a physical body (*vigraha*).
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the illustrious Siddhāntasudhānidhi.
When addressed as *subāmantrita*, it is treated like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavat*) with respect to accentuation.

When followed by a vocative (*āmantrita*), that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*) shall be treated like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavat*) for the purpose of accentuation (*svara*). This is an extension (*atideśa*) based on identity. "The mention of its cause (*tannimittagrahaṇa*) must be made. The meaning is: that which is the cause of the object denoted by that vocative word—namely, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself ending in a case-suffix—is to be treated like a subsequent member, but not anything other than that. [For example: *yatte divoduhitar marta-bhojanam*. Because of the treatment as a subsequent member of the word *divaḥ*, there is the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) prescribed in the eighth chapter [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*]. Now, one might object: "In this rule, the mention of 'ending in a case-suffix' (*sub-grahaṇa*) is redundant."

Since the status of being a "subordinate element" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) prescribed when an *āmantrita* (vocative) functions as a word (*pada*) is a rule dependent on words (*padavidhi*), the *samartha-paribhāṣā* (the maxim concerning semantic connection) applies; consequently, it is possible to exclude a form ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). This is because such a [verbal] form is in fact semantically unconnected (*asamartha*) when it has a different grammatical subject (*vyadhikaraṇa*), whereas for a form with the same subject (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there exists an explicit statement of connection in the form of the rule *samānādhikaraṇasamartham*. Furthermore, since that very rule is necessary to prevent the over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the statement "the vocative is a kāraka expressed by the genitive case," it is precisely from that [rule] that forms ending in a verbal suffix are excluded.

On the contrary, if "sub" were taken [as the referent], then in the example *sīvyann* (from *sīvyan*), the status of being like the subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) would not apply to the entire collection ending in a *sup*-suffix, because according to the maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it would lack the status of ending in a *sup*-suffix. If this is argued:

True; for there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) such as [the application of the rule] to "pīḍye," "pīḍyamāna," and "karoṣyaṭan. Indeed, there is semantic expectancy (sāmarthya) here, because it will be stated that a vocative word is connected with the verb. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault in the case of "karoṣyaṭan" because, in order to prevent the substitution of *ṣ* in "sarpiḥ kālakam" and similar forms under the rule "isusoḥ sāmarthye," it was stated that the term must be in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) and possess semantic expectancy. For, in order to establish the substitution of *ṣ* in "sarpiḥ pīyate" and similar forms, it was also stated that the word must not be expressed by a verbal root (adhātvabhihita).

Nor should it be argued that, according to the view that "everything is born from a verbal root" (*dhātujam*), the same [application of the rule] would follow even for words like *kālakā* (a type of bird); for the exclusion applies only when there is the cognition of an action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, in light of the rule *ṣaṣṭhyāmantrite* ("when a vocative follows a word ending in the genitive"), it is more appropriate to take that very [genitive] as the cause [for the application of the rule]. Otherwise, the status of being a "subordinate member" (*paraṅgavadbhāva*) in the example *goṣu svāmin* ("O master of the cows") would be inexplicable. For *goṣu* does not end in the genitive; nor is the master the "agent" (*kāraka*) of the action denoted by the verbal root in the vocative, since the locative case is prescribed in the remaining scope [of the rule] by the statement *svāmīśvarādhipatī*.

However, the status of being a *nimitta* (condition) certainly exists in the case of ownership (*svāmitva*), because ownership depends upon a substance (*dravya*) and cows serve as its determiner (*nirūpaka*). Consequently, in the examples "O Agni, with that *kṣatra*, take possession of long life" (*tena kṣatreṇāgne svāyuḥ serabhasva*) and "O Agni, strive for the acquisition of friends with a friend" (*mitreṇāgne mitradheye yatasva*), there is the application of the rule regarding the treatment as if they were subordinate members of a compound (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). Likewise, it should be noted that this applies to the word *ṛtena* in the passage "O Mitra and Varuṇa, through Truth, you who increase Truth and touch Truth, you have attained great wisdom" (*ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāvṛtāvṛdhā vṛtaspṛśā, kratuṃ bṛhantamāśāthe*), and to the word *ayam* in the passage "This one, O Agni, knowing... (*ayamagne jānatā*).

It might be argued as follows: even for the compound *mitrāvaruṇau*, there would be no application of the rule *parāṅgavadbhāva* (the treatment of a preceding element as if it were the final member of a compound). This is because the etymological derivation of *ṛtāvṛdhau*—meaning "the two who increase the Ṛta"—is derived from the root *vṛdh* with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, followed by the suffix *kvip*, and then applying the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* to lengthen the vowel. In that case, since Mitra and Varuṇa do not function as the cause (*nimitta*) [of the action denoted by the root], the rule should not apply. Nor is this a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would result in the lack of *nighāta* (elision of the accent) for *ṛtāvṛdhau*. This is because, being at the beginning of the second quarter of a verse, the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam apādādau* (everything is unaccented except when at the beginning of a quarter-verse) would apply by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

For this very reason, in the mantra *imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri stomam*, although the preceding vocatives (*gaṅge*, etc. are treated as if they were non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applied by virtue of their following the word *me* occurs only for the triad beginning with *gaṅge*, and not for *śutudri* as well; such is the established rule. Consequently, even though *ṛtena* stands at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pādādau*), its initial syllable would be udātta by the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19), because it is treated like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāvāt*) of the preceding vocative.

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) for [the word] *mitrāvaruṇau*? Because of the rule *āmantritaṃ pūrvam avidyamānavat*, it would be as if non-existent. For, by the force of the mention of the "preceding word" (*pūrvapada*), the status of being as if non-existent is extended only to the effect of the subsequent word; therefore, it is inapplicable to its own effect, which is the status of being like a subordinate member. For this very reason, in examples such as *agne naya*, even though the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* does not occur, the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative (*āmantritādyudāttatva*) still takes effect.

Alternatively, there is no fault because of the rule stating that "when addressed in apposition, a general term [is not treated as a separate word]. The term *mitrāvaruṇau* is a general term, and the meaning is that its specific qualifier *ṛtāvṛdhau* does not behave like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavat*). Thus, just as in the case of *ṛtena*, it is difficult for *mitrāvaruṇau* to undergo the status of being a subsequent member.

In this context, [works] such as the Vedabhāṣya and the Śabdakaustubha [are relevant]. The mention of "that cause" (tannimitta) need not be made. For indeed, here "capacity" (sāmarthya) should be understood as characterized by mutual expectancy in the form of syntactic connection. It is for this very reason that the commencement of this [rule] is appropriate here.

And likewise, in the passage "ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāvṛtāvṛdhau" (by Truth, O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who increase Truth), since the *kārakas* (grammatical factors) are construed only with the action, the term "ṛtena" is construed with the verb "āśāthe" (you two have attained) found in the second half-verse—"kratūṃ bṛhantamāśāthe"—and not with "mitrāvaruṇau. Thus, due to the absence of semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) with Mitra and Varuṇa, the rule of "acting like a subordinate member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) does not apply. However, although "mitrāvaruṇau" and "ṛtāvṛdhau" are semantically connected to the action through verbal expression, they possess semantic connection through a mutual reciprocal relation of mutual exclusion (*pārṣṇika-parasparāvacchedana-abheda-anvaya*); therefore, the application of the rule of "acting like a subordinate member" is established.

As for the rule that "a word in grammatical apposition is incapable [of forming a compound]," it has already been stated that this refers specifically to cases where the meaning is not expressed by a verbal root. Furthermore, one should not argue that, by the same logic, the word *śutudrī* would also undergo *nighāta* (anudātta accentuation) because the word *sarasvatī*, through its status as a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), would not be at the beginning of a *pāda*. Nor should one argue: "If that were so, how could words restricted to singular number be construed with a verb ending in the plural? Thus, in the absence of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), even *nighāta* would be impossible. This is not a valid objection, because although each individual word may have such a restriction, the application of plurality is possible when they are taken together.
For example: *ahaṃ ca tvaṃ ca vṛtrahan saṃyujyāvasanibhya ā*.
"The teacher and the teacher’s wife greeted them with affection," they say,
based on the observation of such usage in Vedic literature.

In this regard, the following must be said: By the statement "the two increasers of Truth (*ṛta*)," it is clearly established that Mitra and Varuṇa possess the status of being the cause for the increase of Truth; therefore, it is incorrect to claim that they do not have that status as its cause. This is because what is intended to be expressed is also the possession of a property that delimits the causality which is the counter-correlate of an effect delimited by that [specific] property. Otherwise, there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "O daughter of Heaven" (*divo duhitṛ*), and also an over-narrow application in cases such as "O master of the cows" (*goṣu svāmin*).

Nor should it be said that, according to the aforementioned method, that [operation] need not be performed even without the apprehension of its cause; for the established doctrine is that "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) and "governing context" (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, since the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* have determined that there is no fault when [the rule applies] by virtue of the treatment as if it were a member of another (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), because the capacity based on mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā-sāmarthya*) cannot be accepted here. Why [is the word] *aṅga* used? So that two [words] might not both have the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) separately. Why [is the word] *vat* used? So that [the operation] may also occur by its own inherent basis (*svāśraya*).

"Ām kuṇḍanāṭa. Here, because "ām" is an *ekāntara* (separated by one syllable) vocative, it receives the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent. Why specify "in a word" (*svara*)? [To prevent the following: In examples such as *kūpe siñcan* and *carma namnan*, let there not be the treatment of the preceding element as if it were part of the subsequent word (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) with respect to the rules for *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*. For if that treatment were present, then due to the lack of a single word (*aikapadya*), the initial *s* would not be at the beginning of a word; consequently, the prohibition of *ṣatva* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would not apply, and furthermore, *ṇatva* would occur because the elements would reside within the same word.

Regarding this, the commentary states: By means of extended application (*atideśa*), the status of being the beginning of a word (*padāditva*) residing in its own locus is not negated, as there is no contradiction. Furthermore, due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only after a preceding member when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*)," the substitution of *ṇ* does not take place. This is because, although the term *pūrvapada* is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) to mean the first constituent of a compound, by the logic of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the etymological (*yaugika*) sense of "the preceding member" is also included. Alternatively, because of the mention of the "vocative word" (*āmantrita-pada*), the treatment of being "like a subsequent member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) applies only with respect to an operation conditioned by the status of being a vocative.

An addition must be made for [the case of] a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), because it follows immediately [after the previous rule]. For example: *tīkṣṇayā sūcyā sīvyan* ("sewing with a sharp needle") and *tīkṣṇena paraśunā vṛścan* ("cutting with a sharp axe"). This rule is commenced because, by the application of the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "when 'in that' (*tasmin*) is specified, [the operation applies] to what precedes," the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*)—which is prescribed when a vocative (*āmantrita*) follows—does not apply across an intervening element. Nor should it be argued that once the status of being like a subordinate member has been established for the subsequent member, it will also apply to the preceding one.

By the restrictive term *svara* (accent), when the status of being a subordinate element (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) is to be applied, that status is otherwise difficult to obtain. [Therefore, it is stated: "In the Veda, even what follows may be treated as a subordinate element of what precedes. For example: *ā te pitarmarūtāṃ sumnametu*, *prati tvā duhitardivaḥ*, *vṛṇīṣva duhitardivaḥ*. Here, *pitaḥ* is unaccented due to the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the non-accentuation of a vocative); consequently, the following word *marūtām* is also unaccented. Furthermore, there is a prohibition regarding indeclinables (*avyaya*): *uccairadhīyāna*, *nīcairadhīyāna*.

"It should be stated that this does not apply to *avyayībhāva* compounds. For example: *upāgnim adhīyānaḥ*. Although it was previously stated that the purposes [of this rule] are the absence of the *luṅ* augment, the accent on the first member (*mukhasvara*), and the application of honorific treatment (*upacāra*), nevertheless, this has been stated here for the sake of clarity.
From here until before *kaḍāra*, the topic is *samāsa* (compound)."

The rule "compound" (samāsa) is governed from this point until before the rule "kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye. By repetition, first the designation "compound" is applied, and then the designations "avyayībhāva" and so forth; thus, the status of being a pervader of other designations is established. Otherwise, the two designations would apply alternatively, just as the designations "upasarga" and "karmapravacanīya" do.

It might be argued as follows: "The co-occurrence [of the two rules] will take place precisely because the designation *samāsa* (compound) has no other scope. Nor should it be said that its scope is found in examples such as *vispaṣṭapaṭuḥ*, for by the rule *vispaṣṭādīni guṇavacaneṣu*, which prescribes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, it is indicated that the compound is established here according to the maxim of 'the old maiden’s husband' (*vṛddhakumārīvara-nyāya*); thus, the application of the rule *saha supā* is unnecessary in this case."

In that case, because clarity (*vispaṣṭatva*) is construed through the force of linguistic convention with the proficiency (*pāṭava*) that delimits the meaning of the second member, there is no possibility of it being a *karmadhāraya* compound; this is because the delimiter of the meaning of the first member and the delimiter of the meaning of the second member do not refer to a single substratum (*ekadharmī*).
For this very reason, they recite: "When asked 'What kind of compound is this? in reference to the scope of 'clear-proficient' (*vispaṣṭapaṭu*)."
Those who speak merely of "equality" are indeed clearly of poor discernment.

Nor is there any room for [the application of] the *kākatālīya* or *ajākūpāṇīya* rules here; for even in this case, since the compound is established simply by the force of the rule "after a compound ending in *taddhita*, when it refers to that [base], the suffix *cha* is applied" (Pāṇini 5.3.106)—which is an extension of the rule governing compounds used in the sense of *iva*—the requirement of the rule *saha supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) is redundant. Nor should it be argued that this is merely a *bahuvrīhi* because the meaning of the word *iva* is predominant in *kākatālam*; for a *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed only in the sense of possessive (*matvartha*).

In reality, because the word expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) itself functions as the object of comparison (*upameya*), there is no predominance of the sense of "like" (*iva*). Since the words *kāka* (crow) and *tāla* (palmyra tree) refer to the actions inherent in them, the compound is formed in one sense upon a single meaning expressed by *iva*: "Caitra’s arrival is like the crow’s coming; the bandits’ sudden appearance is like the falling of the palmyra tree. In the second sense, the suffix *cha* is applied: "Just as the crow was killed by the falling palmyra tree, so was Caitra killed by the bandits. Thus it is said: "The meeting of the bandits with him, and the killing of him by them—that this occurred suddenly is 'crow-and-palmyra-like' (*kākatalīya*)."

Furthermore, one should not argue that in the example *na ca punārājaḥ punargavaḥ*, the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) has its own scope even without the designation of a *tatpuruṣa*—on the grounds that the form is established by splitting the rule *nañ* (Pāṇini 2.2.6) into separate rules (*yogavibhāga*). For in the case of *punargavī*, the suffix *ṭac* is required for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; since the *tatpuruṣa* designation is necessarily required there, it must be stated either by the rule *avyayaṃ pravṛddhādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.30), or by including it in the *mayūra-vyaṃsaka*-group, or simply by explicitly stating that it is indeed a *tatpuruṣa*.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) for *punarādheya* is superfluous because no specific grammatical effect is observed therein; for it must be stated that the designation of a *gati* is necessary for the sake of accentuation according to the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*. Since the *gati* designation is required for the sake of accentuation by the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*, it must be stated that it applies specifically to a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*. This is because, by the rule *anāvaḥ*, the word *dheya* is acute-accented on its first syllable; consequently, in the word *punarādheya*, the vowel *e* is acute. Otherwise, there would be the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound.

Furthermore, a mended garment should not be given; there is scope for the expression "a repaired chariot" (*punarniḥkṛto rathaḥ*). It should not be argued that when the word *punaḥ* is designated as a *gati*, its final syllable is udātta by the rule *thāthādisvara*; for if that designation were absent, the accent would instead be determined by the rule for compound accents (*samāsasvara*), and thus there would be no distinction. However, because of the inclusion of the term "immediate" (*anantara*) in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* regarding the *gati* designation, the accent of the word *ud-* (in *ut-syūtam*) remains its original pitch (*prakṛtisvara*), thereby overriding the *thāthādi* accent.

However, because there is a specific rule, the *anudātta* (low-pitched) accent of the particle *punaḥ*—which would otherwise result from the rule *śeṣanighātaḥ* (the non-accentuation of the remainder)—is superseded by the rule *gatir gatāv* (a *gati* [particle] is unaccented when followed by another *gati*), due to its higher status in the order of rules. Nor can it be argued that this is established by the rule *punaścanasau chandasi* (the two particles *punaḥ* and *canaḥ* are unaccented in the Veda), for in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), the designation of *gati* is necessary for the establishment of the correct accent. Furthermore, one should not say that in the *Kāṭhaka* recension the word *punarutsyūta* is read with an acute accent on the final syllable; for that is established either by the occurrence of an irregularity (*vyatyaya*) or because the group beginning with *pravṛddha* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

If it is argued that, therefore, let the rule "in a compound" (*samāse*) alone be made the governing heading, that is true; for under the governing heading of a single technical term (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the occurrence of mutual exclusion (*paryāya*) is necessary. Although the Bhāṣya will state that a compound whose definition has not been previously prescribed is prescribed by this rule *saha supā*, nevertheless Kaiyaṭa maintains that the designation "compound" (*samāsasaṃjñā*) applies to all cases because of its unconditioned recitation in the text, whereas the demonstration of its lack of scope [under the previous rules] is merely for the purpose of establishing the underlying logic (*nyāya*).
*saha supā* || 4 ||

The rule *saha* is analyzed [into two parts]. From the previous rule *subāmantrite*, the term *sub* is carried over by anuvṛtti. A word ending in a *sub*-suffix is compounded with a word that is "capable" (*samartha*) of being connected with it. For example: *yo jāta eva paryabhūṣat* ("He who, as soon as born, overpowered"), *yaḥ śambaram anvavindat* ("He who found Śambara"), *anuvyacalat* ("He moved along after"), and *anuprāviśat* ("He entered after"). Because this is prescribed again by the rule *sup supā* and is restricted solely to a few instances of finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), there is no over-extension [of the rule]. Since the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of achieving desired results, it does not apply here: *samprayaccha vṛṣṇyā indrāya bhāgam* ("Give the portion of virility to Indra").

In this case, the number is intended to be significant. Therefore, the compound with *vi-* occurs first, and subsequently the compound with *anu-*. Because of the prohibition of Śākala’s rule regarding compounds, the *yaṇ* substitution takes place. However, the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound does not occur; some maintain that this is because it is superseded by the *nighāta* (elision) rule, *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.

Others, however, argue that if it were so, then in the word *nigātaḥ* (from *ni-gataḥ*), where the rule *gati-gaty-ōḥ* applies, the prefix *ni-* would be acute (*udātta*). Consequently, according to the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito 'nudāttasya*, the resulting *yaṇ*-substitute would be circumflex (*svarita*). This being the case, the example from the Bhāṣya, *anuprāviśat*, would be rendered useless [as its accentuation would not match]. Therefore, because it is taught later (*sati śiṣṭatvāt*), the final member of the compound must indeed be acute. Nor does this entail the production of a case-ending (*sub*); for they say that the singular number has already been expressed by the finite verb (*tiṅ*).

Others, however, maintain that by virtue of the inclusion of the word "vacana" (number), the nominative case (*prathamā*) indeed occurs even for those [numbers] already mentioned, such as singularity (*ekatva*), and so on. Nor does this result in their being heard [in the utterance], because the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* is possible. For this very reason, they say that in the phrase *ekapadyādāmanupraviśa devadatta*, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent—based on the rule *āmantritasya ca* which states that an *āmantrita* is separated from its preceding word by one interval—is the purpose of designating a compound (*samāsa*); thus, they argue, the designation of a compound serves to prevent the application of the *tiṅ-antavighāta* rule.

In this regard, Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta, who have merely written down the nature of the opinion [of others], have not determined whether the *nighāta* (elision of accent) applies due to its being subsequent (*paratva*), or whether the final acute accent of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) applies because it is more established (*satiśiṣṭatva*). Furthermore, it is worth investigating whether the original accent of the final member (*uttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*) occurs according to the rule "after a prefix, a kāraka, or an upapada," since the mention of the term *kṛt* has been rejected by the author of the Vārttika. Moreover, let it be as it is in cases such as *anuvyacalat*.

However, in cases such as *yo jāta*, because of the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *yadvṛttānnityam*, the final acute accent (*samāsāntodāttatva*) of the compound is unavoidable. Furthermore, according to the view that the final acute of the compound prevails due to its being "later taught" (*sati śiṣṭatva*), the reading of the acute accent on *āṅ* in the verse *atyāyāhi śaśvato vayaṃ te* would be inconsistent. Moreover, there is an inconsistency that is difficult to justify: in *niriṇāmi*, there is a *nighāta* on the word *ni*, whereas in *vitanvate*, there is a *nighāta* on the word *vi*; yet, under the rule for the final acute of a compound, there is no such accent on *riṇāti*, while there is one on *tanvate*. Therefore, the truth of the matter here is as follows: [The subsequent text provides the technical solution regarding the application of accents.]

According to the view of the Vārttikakāra, the first position alone is correct. This is because the explicit mention of *kṛt*-suffixes [in the rule for compounds] is rejected; furthermore, since the formation of a *gati* compound is accepted as being a *tatpuruṣa* by prescribing a *tiṅ* compound under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *tatpuruṣa* through the rule stating that "a *tiṅ* ending with an udātta vowel or containing a *gati* word must be stated [as forming a compound]. In the case of *vitanvataḥ*, the final udātta accent is to be understood as resulting from its inclusion in the *tricakra* group. However, in the case of *atyāyāhi*, there is a compound with *āṅ* following the elision of the accent of the subsequent *tiṅ* (by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅ*).

Because the final member of the compound lacks an udātta accent, there is no *gati*-accent; thus, by the rule regarding the original accent of the first member when it is an indeclinable (*avyaya-pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*), the word is udātta on its initial syllable (*aṅ-udātta*). Then, when the compound is formed with the word *ati*, since the inclusion of the term "kṛt" [in the definition of a compound] has been rejected, the desired result is established by the original accent of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*). In the case of *niriṇāti*, however, because the prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of accent) applies due to its connection with the word *yat*, the desired result is established exactly as before.

According to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, because the formation of the compound is stated through a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) in the rule *saha supā*, it lacks the designation of *tatpuruṣa*. Consequently, in the absence of the accent of a *gati* and the accent of the original form of the first member (*avyaya*) being an indeclinable, the form *vitanvate* is established by means of the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*). As for the original accent of the final member in forms such as *anvavindat* and *niriṇāti*, they say that this is to be accounted for by the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

However, this must be stated here: if the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is rejected, then two types of suffixes are prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), namely *tiṅ* and *kṛt*. In that case, compounding occurs with the *kṛt* suffixes, but not with the *tiṅ* suffixes. From the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya, "In that regard, even without the mention of *kṛt*, it will apply only to the *kṛt* [compounds]," it is understood that the accent rule "after a prefix (*gati*), a kāraka, or a subordinate word (*upapada*) [compounded with a *kṛt*-derived word]" does not apply to a *tiṅ* compound.

Since a finite verb (*tiṅ*) exists as a formal entity, the absence [of another finite verb] must be expressed as being characterized by the absence of the aforementioned accent; for this very reason, the objection that the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] results in an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in the case of *prapacatitarām* was raised. Otherwise, such an objection would have arisen in the case of *prapacati* itself. Furthermore, in the commentary on the Vārttika which states, "A compound with a finite verb (*tiṅ*) that possesses an acute accent (*udātta*) and is accompanied by a word denoting motion (*gatimat*) should be prescribed," the example given for that which possesses an acute accent is *yatpariyanti*.

In the case of *nipātaiyadyadīti*, because the prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies, the word *yanti* is udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Therefore, the word *pari* forms a compound with *yanti*. Regarding *anuvyacalat*: since the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28] applies later due to its higher status, it receives the *nighāta* accent; consequently, because it lacks an udātta accent, it is stated separately as "possessing motion" (*gatimat*). In that case, the three words [forming the compound] receive the udātta accent on their final syllable by virtue of being a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*).

In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its original accent] when it has the sense of 'equal to' (*tulyārtha*), or is a third-case, seventh-case, or indeclinable word, or an upamāna, or a second-case word, or a *kṛtya*-suffix" does not apply here. This is because the particle *anu* is unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule "a *gati* [particle] before another *gati*," and because in that context, the mention of "acute" (*udātta*) and "circumflex" (*svarita*) accents continues to apply. Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa himself has explained that this is because the word *vi-* lacks the status of being the first member (*pūrvapada*). Thus, it is clearly stated that the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) indeed occurs.

This also should be noted: the compound of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ-samāsa*) is exclusively Vedic. Otherwise, although one might manage cases such as *paryabhūṣat* by means of the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*), and cases such as *yat karoti* by accepting neuter gender, there would still result the undesirable consequences of shortening in *yat prakurute* and the elision of the *n* in *hrasvasya prakurvīran*. Since the elision of the *u* must be stated as being Vedic, the established conclusion is that in poetry and other [secular] literature, a prefix is indeed a separate word.

"It should be stated that there is a compound with *iva*, the non-elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktyalopa*), and the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. By means of the two rules already mentioned, the compound is established; here, by way of restating that established compound, the non-elision of the case-ending and the accent are prescribed. Furthermore, this [rule] is not obligatory (*anitya*), as seen from examples such as *udbāhuriva vāmanaḥ* and the fact that in the Taittirīya recension of *jīmūtasyeva bhavati pratīkam*, the words are read as separate *pada*s. By this, the claim that compounds with *iva* are Vedic (*chāndasa*) is also refuted, since rhetoricians have cited the compound *śrautī upamā* (verbal simile) as occurring within such compounds."
I experience non-duality as if it were a bilva fruit held in the palm of my hand, and I behold the body as if it were a mere husk.

Dīkṣita maintains that all such constructions are indeed consistent with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *anyapadārthe*, which states: "For [the compound] does not exist with [a word] ending in the nominative case alone," and so forth, regarding the various meanings of the *anyapadārtha*. [Now begins] the section on *avyayībhāva* (5).

This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). Although it is the traditional usage of the ancients that an *avyayībhāva* compound has the meaning of the first member as its predominant sense, a *tatpuruṣa* has the meaning of the second member as its predominant sense, a *bahuvrīhi* has the meaning of a word other than those two members as its predominant sense, and a *dvandva* has the meanings of both members as its predominant sense—nevertheless, even here, because of the creation of these major technical designations (*mahāsaṃjñā*), that usage is accepted only as a general rule (*prāyika*).

Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that [the compound] *unmattagaṅgam* is an *avyayībhāva* because the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant; *ardhapippalī* is a *tatpuruṣa* because the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant; and *dvitrāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* because the meanings of both members (*ubhayapadārtha*) are predominant. Furthermore, in a *samāhāra-dvandva*, the predominance of the meanings of both members is not observed, and under the theory of "single-meaning-ness" (*ekārthībhāva*), even both words are devoid of independent meaning.

An indeclinable (avyaya) remains unchanged when used in the senses of case-relation (vibhakti), proximity (samīpa), prosperity (samṛddhi), decline (vyṛddhi), absence (arthābhāva), passing away (atyaya), inappropriateness (asamprati), manifestation (śabdaprādurbhāva), posteriority (paścāt), according to order (yathānupūrvya), simultaneity (ayaugapadya), similarity (sādṛśya), attainment (saṃpatti), totality (sākalya), and limit (anta). || 6 ||

In this context, by dividing the rule into two separate *yogas*, the term *apadiśam* is to be established [as a neuter noun]. "The neuter *antara* is called *apadiśa*; the intermediate direction between two cardinal directions is *vidiś* (feminine)."

Some say that [the word] *ittham* is an *amara* (an indeclinable); but that is to be questioned, because it is not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works. It is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*). The suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *avyayībhāve śaratprabhṛtibhyaḥ*. Kṣīrasvāmin has explained there that its neuter gender follows from the rule *avyayībhāvaśca*; furthermore, he has shown the analysis of the compound as "this which belongs to the two directions" (*diśoḥ idam*). Moreover, since a relationship is understood according to the requirements of the meaning, it is specifically the intermediate form (*madhyarūpa*) that is grasped here. Now, one might object: in this context, the word *vibhakti* refers merely to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

It should not be argued that such a [technical] designation (*vikṣakti*) is unnecessary because the general term [for case-ending] would be rendered redundant, since it would follow that only the word *adhikaraṇa* (locative) would be understood as a remainder. For if that were so, there would be an excess of one *mātrā*. This is not correct. If the intention were merely to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), then for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), it would follow that the term *ṅi* alone should have been used in place of the term *vibhakti*. Nor does it follow that only one [case-ending] would be obtained; for if that were the case, it would follow that only *su* should be mentioned, since it is the first to present itself [in the sequence].

Therefore, by the natural force of employing the term "case-ending" (*vibhakti*), it is intended that even indeclinables (*avyaya*) which function with meanings exceeding [the mere absence of] a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) are to be included; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Consequently, since an indeclinable functioning as a power (*śakti*) in the form of agent, object, instrument, recipient, or point of departure is not well-known, it is established that here an indeclinable is understood as one whose primary referent is both the substratum and the relation.

Regarding the statement that "in cases such as *nārada ity abodhi* ('[it was understood] thus, 'Nārada''), because it is well-known that the word *iti* denotes the object (*karman*), the compound *nāradam* is indeed an avyayībhāva due to the inherent force of the case-ending," so some have said.

That is to be considered. For that [cognition] occurs only with respect to the state of being an object (*karmatva*). To explain: the difference between the cognition produced by "Nārada was cognized" (*nāradaṃ abodhi*) and the cognition produced by "he was cognized as Nārada" (*nārada ity abodhi*) is established by experience. In the former case, it is invariably understood that the knowledge to be delineated has Nārada as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*); however, having Nārada-ness as its qualifier (*prakāra*) is merely the default rule (*autsargika*), because even a cognition that has another property as its qualifier can have Nārada as its qualificand and still be delineated by that [term].

In the second case, however, the state of having "Nārada-ness" as the qualifier (*prakārakatva*) is necessarily understood, whereas the state of having Nārada as the qualificand (*viśeṣyakatva*) is not so. This is because such usage is observed even when there is a cognition that has Nārada-ness as its qualifier but a different object as its qualificand. Thus, in connection with verbal roots whose meaning is "cognition" and the like, the meaning of the accusative case is "objecthood" in the sense of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). The word *iti*, on the other hand, has "the state of being a qualifier" (*prakāratva*) as its meaning, since the state of having the delimitor of the referent of the word co-occurring with it as its qualifier necessarily appears in the cognition.
