However, the state of having as its qualificandum the meaning of the word co-uttered with itself is obtained in the case of valid cognition (*pramā*), but not in the case of error (*bhrama*); we shall explain this under the *anabhihita* sūtra. Furthermore, if an *avyayībhāva* compound were accepted there, then because such a compound is obligatory (*nityasamāsa*), the usage "it was understood that Nārada [was the speaker]" (*nārada ity abodhi*) would result in being grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*); this is the general direction of the argument. The term "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) refers to the power of the factor (*kārakaśakti*) which takes the form of its own meaning, specifically the nature of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth. The word "number" (*vacana*) refers to the meaning through a verbal derivation (*vyutpatti*) from the root *vac* (to speak). The connection of those meanings [the factors and numbers] occurs non-differently (*abheda*) with the case-endings and the rest.

An indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), when occurring in senses such as those of the locative (*adhikaraṇa*), is compounded with a compatible word (*samartha*). Nor is this established by the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), because its re-enunciation here indicates that the former rule is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). For this very reason, since the application of the governing term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) does not preclude the compulsory nature of what was previously taught, the analysis *pūrvaṃ bhūtaḥ* is stated for the compound *bhūtapūrvaḥ* in the commentary (*vṛtti*). It should be understood that the same applies in cases such as *vāpyaśvaḥ* ("a horse from a pond") and so forth, even according to Kaiyaṭa regarding that compound.

If the rule *sup-sup-eti* were also mandatory (*nitya*)—just as the rule *saṃjñāyām-iti-vat* is—then the inclusion of the word "mandatory" (*nitya*) in the Vārttika, "In the case of a mandatory compound and a mandatory suffix, there is a prohibition of the Śākala [substitution]," would be purposeless. This is because the Bhāṣya passage—"There is no need for the mention of 'mandatory'; by this [mention], the following is also established: *vāpy-aśvaḥ*, *vāpy-aśvaḥ*"—would otherwise be untenable. For even according to the Vārttika as it stands (without the word *nitya*), that very prohibition is established. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus") would also lack an analytical etymology (*avigrahatva*) because they are mandatory compounds; for [in their case, the status of being a compound is not absolute].

The Dīkṣitas [hold that] even when the analysis (*vigraha*) is shown by prioritizing the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*), the collective meaning—namely, "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*)—is in fact established as such because it is cognizable solely through the compound. In the case of *vibhaktau harau* (in the locative case, in Hari), the ungrammatical sentence (*alaukika-vākya*) is *hari ṅi adhi*. According to the rule *antaraṅgān api...* (P. 1.4.2), the elision of the genitive suffix (*ṅerluk*) occurs, and not the substitution of *au* (the *aut* augment) due to its being subsequent; for if the *au* were applied first, the form as stated would not be established when the *gher* (the *ghi*-class stem) undergoes the substitution of the short vowel *a*. Due to proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), only the case-ending belonging to the members of the compound itself is to be understood.

And that meaning is indicated by the word *adhi*. Nor does this result in the impossibility of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) when the meaning is already expressed by the particle (*nipāta*); for its occurrence is due to the force of the rule prescribing composition with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). For this very reason, the usage of even an expressed meaning will be explained in examples such as *dvijārthaḥ sūpaḥ* ("soup for the sake of the twice-born"). Only an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that functions solely to express the meaning of a case-ending is intended here; this is because the mention of the word "number" (*vacana*) has the force of connecting [the term *avyaya*] individually with each [member of the compound], otherwise it would be redundant.

In cases such as *gṛhasyopari* (above the house) or *grāmasya puraḥ* (before the village), although these words have the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), no compound is formed because they function with reference to direction, place, or time as something additional (*adhika*). However, some maintain two views: that this compound is formed with a word ending in the nominative case because the meaning is already expressed by the particle (*nipāta*), or that it is formed with a word ending in the genitive case; since both views are stated in the *Parishṣṭa*, they have accepted them. But this is questionable, because unless the compounded word ends in the locative case, it is illogical to employ the word *adhi*—which signifies a locus—within a compound.

The predecessors, however, state that the analysis (vigraha) is "having Hari as the object" (*harim adhikṛtya*). In this case, even though it is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), its status as having an analysis with non-co-referential members (*asvapadavigraha*) remains intact, because the gerund ending (*lyap*) is introduced as something distinct from the constituents of the compound. Nor should it be argued that it is improper for something that does not convey even a trace of the meaning of the compound to be included within its analysis; for if being excluded from the analysis were based on conveying a meaning distinct from the compound's meaning, then even the expression *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker," analyzed as *kumbhaṃ karoti*) would not be possible.

Because in the case of *aṇ* (the nominal suffix), there is no cognition of the number [of the object] as being present, and because the capacity to convey the meaning of a compound is equal in both cases according to the maxim that "that which has entered further is superior. Furthermore, if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the analytical statement (*vigraha*), since there is nowhere a case where the analytical statement conveys a meaning neither less nor more than the compound; for instance, in the case of *citraguḥ*, the number residing in the cow is not conveyed by the compound, whereas it is conveyed in the analytical statement. This is the general direction of the argument.

*Upakṛṣṇam* means "in the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa. Since this is a term whose meaning is consistent with its etymology (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), it primarily emphasizes proximity (*sāmīpya*). However, when the emphasis is on that which is situated nearby, the *bahuvrīhi* compound *upadaśa* will be discussed [later]. Therefore, in the present case, the connection is through the distinction (*bheda*) of proximity; whereas in that other case, the connection is through the non-distinction (*abheda*) of that which is situated nearby—this is the difference. Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, or *ārāt*, because those refer to proximity qualified by its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), as is understood from the cognition "in the vicinity of the village" (*grāmasya samīpe*).

In expressions such as *upakumbham* ("near the jar"), proximity is understood as residing in the jar and so forth; thus, in that case, proximity [resides] in another location, and its occurrence therein is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the jar and so forth. However, in *upakumbham* and similar cases, the distinction is that the jar itself is the relatum of the proximity and the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

As for the claim that there is no compound in such cases because of the force of the rules prescribing the second and fifth case endings, that is not correct. For the rule prescribing those endings finds its purpose in non-compound forms where there is a lack of semantic integration (*asāmarthya*), such as *caitrasya grāmaṃ gaccha* ("Go to Caitra's village"). Nor can it be argued that because a compound is obligatory, a word that has entered into a compound cannot be connected with a qualifier—thus avoiding the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of forms like *caitrasya* [being used with a qualifier]—since the rule *saviśeṣaṇānām na* (Pāṇini 2.1.1) also exists. Furthermore, one should not say that this rule refers to non-obligatory compounds, for there is no evidence for such a restriction; moreover, when those [words] are employed, a compound would not even be applicable due to the absence of the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

Nor does the undesirable consequence follow that one would say *sthūlasya kumbhasya kāraḥ* ("the maker of the large pot"), because an *aṇ* suffix cannot occur without a verbal connection (*karmayoga*), and because the compound *sthūlaṃ kumbhakāraḥ* lacks semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states that expressions such as *mahāntaṃ putrīyati* ("he desires a great son") are non-expressive. This is because its meaning is that when there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), there is only a sentence (*vākya*), whereas when there is unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), there is only a derivative formation (*vṛtti*). Regarding prosperity (*samṛddhi*), *sumadram* ("prosperous Madras") is formed by the *su* suffix after the word *madra*. However, if *madra* is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, it forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound: *samṛddhā madrāḥ sumadrāḥ* ("the prosperous Madras").

In the case of *vyṛddhi* (failure), the compound is *duryavana*. However, in the case of the absence of a thing (*arthābhāva*), the compound is formed with the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of that absence. Here, the distinction is that it is the prosperity (*ṛddhi*) which is the counter-positive of the absence, and not the Yavanas themselves. In the case of the absence of a thing, we have examples such as *nirmakṣika* (absence of flies) and *avighna* (absence of obstacles). This type of compound occurs in the case of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*), because that [non-existence] stands in opposition to the meaning of the word being compounded. This is not the case for difference (*bheda*), however, because difference stands in opposition only to the delimiting property of the referent (*padārthatāvacchedaka*).

As for the claim that in the expression "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭo na*), there is no cognition of the absence of the jar because an *avyayībhāva* compound is necessarily a fixed compound (*nityasamāsa*), that is not correct; for the rule for *avyayībhāva* applies only when the absence (*abhāva*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). According to the Maithila tradition, when the intended meaning is a cognition where the jar is the qualificand, relatedness (*pratiyogitva*) is the relation, and the absence is the qualifier—namely, "the jar is the counter-correlate of an absence residing on the ground"—then the term "on the ground" (*bhūtale*) functions as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the case of *atyaya* (passing away), *himasyātyayaḥ* means "the passing away of snow," which signifies its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Nor is the separate mention [of *atyaya*] redundant when [destruction] is already established by the term "non-existence" (*arthābhāva*), because in that context only absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is intended, and here the very use of the word *atyaya* serves as the authority. Therefore, the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) does not apply in the sense of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

As for the claim that the nature of destruction (*dhvaṃsatva*) is an indivisible property pervaded by non-existence, and thus its separate mention is for the sake of excluding "non-existence" (*abhāva*), that is incorrect; for even if the nature of destruction is not constituted by non-existence, destruction does not forfeit its status as a non-existence (*abhāvatva*).
The indeclinable *samprati* primarily denotes the locative force (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*).
Regarding the statement from the *Amara-kośa*, "etarhi," "saṃprati," "idānīm," "adhunā," and "sāṃpratam" all mean "now" (*tathā*).

The verb "to be fit" (*yuj*), which is implied by the locative case as the locus of action, is negated by the particle *nañ*. *Atinidram*: the meaning is that sleep is not appropriate at this time. The commentary states: "*atisaisṛkam ācchādanam*" (a garment made of *tisṛka* wool). Regarding the formation of *tisṛkā*, there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the suffix *kan* when it forms a proper name; thus, *tisṛkā* is the name of a village. A garment produced there is called *taisṛka*. Such a garment is suitable for use during extremely cold weather. The meaning here is that the *taisṛka* garment is not fit for use now.
They say that although *sṛkapada* requires the word *ācchādana*, it forms a compound because it is expressive (*gamaka*).
However, the ancients say that *asaṃprati* means the absence of *saṃprati*; by this, the negation is made of that very present time which belongs to the object of enjoyment.

Objection: Is it not the case that the connection of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) with respect to the negation is contradictory? For in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground," the ground does not appear as the counter-positive of the absence. Response: This is not so. In reality, the locus is not the counter-positive of the absence. Nor is it the case for that which is perceived as the locus in the cognition produced by that [negation]. It cannot be the first [alternative], because since the locus is a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*), it would follow that even a jar or similar object would possess that status [of being a locus]. Nor can it be the second [alternative].

By one who asserts that time (*kāla*) is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of negation, its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—as experienced in common usage—is not admitted. Nor should it be argued that in an absence (*abhāva*), that which has the power of being a locus as its primary sense cannot be construed as the counter-correlate, as is the case with "the ground" (*bhūtala*). For even in the case of the word *divā* (day), although it possesses the predominance of the power of being a locus, in the expression *divā manye* ("I think during the day"), that predominance of the locus-power is set aside, and by the very nature of its grammatical function (*vṛtti*), it is accepted as having the status of an object (*karman*). Thus, the meaning of *atinidram* is "the absence of a time suitable for sleep."

In the expression *śabdaprādurbhāve*, [the compound] is *itihari*. The meaning is "the manifestation of the word *hari*. Here, the word *hari* refers to the phonetic form of the word itself; it is compounded with the word *iti*, which has the sense of "manifestation. In the phrase *anuratham*, the meaning is "behind the chariots" (*rathānāṃ paścāt*). In this case, the failure to place the word *vyṛddhi* first—which would otherwise have been required because it has fewer syllables—is for the purpose of indicating that this is not a regular compound (*samāsa*). Consequently, some maintain that even the sentence form is grammatically correct. Because of its association with words such as *samīpa* ("near") that do not end in a *taddhita* suffix, only such a word [ending in a *taddhita* suffix] is understood here.
Others maintain that [the word "para" in the rule] *acaḥ parasmin* means "after that," and [the word "para" in the rule] *anekam anyapadārthe* means "at the very end," according to the Bhāṣya.

The meanings of *yathā* are fitness (*yogyatā*), repetition (*vīpsā*), non-exceeding the word-meaning (*padārthānativṛtti*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*). In the sense of fitness: "fitness for form" (*rūpasya yogyaṃ rūpānurūpam*). In the sense of repetition: "with respect to each object" (*arthaṃ arthaṃ prati* → *pratyartham*). According to the authority of the Bhāṣya, even the sentence [form] is correct. Alternatively, because the word *prati* here functions as a *karmapravacanīya*, it delimits the relationship; however, the repetition is indicated by the double mention [of the word]. Therefore, Haradatta and others maintain that there is no compound because the indeclinable does not occur in the sense of repetition.

However, some say that by the force of the rule prescribing the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the word *prati* when used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), a sentence containing it [as a compound] is also [permissible]. Nor should it be argued that the prescription of the second case ending in "grāmasya vṛkṣaṃ prati" finds its scope precisely there because a compound would otherwise not apply; for if a compound were mandatory, the qualifier itself could not be syntactically connected [to the verb]. The similarity to Hari is *sahari*. The state of being preceded (*anu-pūrva*) is *ānūpūrvyam*; [the suffix] *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class, and because it has the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, resulting in *ānupūrvī*. "Anujyeṣṭham" means "in the order of the eldest."
In the case of simultaneity, [the compound] is *sacakram*. The word *saha* undergoes compounding; in an *avyayībhāva*, by the rule *cākāle*, there is the substitution of *sa-* for *saha*.

*Sasakhi* means "similar to a friend"; the commentary (*vṛtti*) states it is "one who has a friend. A female jackal (*mṛgālī*) of diminished size is called *kikhī*. The distinction here is that in the former case similarity is predominant, whereas in this case the possessor of that quality (*tadvat*) is predominant. Otherwise, as in the example *sumadrāḥ* ("prosperous Madras"), if the predominance of the meaning of the indeclinable were absent, the compound would not occur. Regarding the *naiṣadhacarita* verse, *sapallavaṃ vyāsaparāśarābhyām*: in the sense of the hand, it means "resembling a sprout. *Saṃpatti* (accomplishment) is a corresponding state of being.
The state of being a Brahmin is appropriate for those belonging to the class of Brahmins.

When there is totality (*sākalya*), one consumes even grass; he does not reject anything, yet his intent is not on the consumption of grass. In the expression "he studies as far as the *agni*," the word *agni* refers to the texts containing that [name]. The meaning is that he studies up to that point. Nor is there establishment through totality alone; for when a certain extent of territory has been accepted as the scope of study, the word "end" (*anta*) denotes completion relative to that, while the word "totality" (*sākalya*) expresses completion with respect to the whole. The analysis of the compound is "together with the *agni*" (*sāgni*).

Some maintain that "being the end" (*antatva*) is what is being illuminated [by the suffix], [explaining] *agniḥ anto 'sya* ("fire is its end"). Others hold that the analysis of the compound is *agneḥ antatvam* ("the state of fire being the end").

As for the objection that this [interpretation] is not tenable because the word *saha* does not denote "end" (*anta*), and thus "end-ness" (*antatva*) is even more difficult to obtain, and furthermore, it would lack syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the act of study (*adhyayana*), that is incorrect. For there is no obstacle to expressing the meaning by means of a word that merely indicates (*dyotya*) it when the analysis (*vigraha*) is not within its own constituent parts (*asvapadavigraha*). Precisely for this reason, "end-ness" is also easily obtained. Indeed, if the word were to denote "end" as its primary meaning (*prādhānyena*), the aforementioned doubt might arise; however, even though "end-ness" is indicated rather than denoted in the analysis ending in the third case (*tṛtīyāntavigraha*), the connection with the act of study remains equal [in both cases]. Moreover, the mere fact that it delimits the object of study (*adhyetavyaparicchedakatva*) is exactly the same here as well. This is the general direction [of the argument].
The suffix *yathā* is used in the sense of "not being like" (asādṛśya). || 7 ||

This is for the purpose of excluding that which is obtained either by way of its actual meaning or by way of similarity. The word *yathā* is compounded with a word denoting an object different from similarity. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of: *hathā haristathā haraḥ* ("Hara is like Hari"). Nor should it be argued that the word *hara* must necessarily be compounded with the word *tathā*; for such a rule is prescribed only with respect to a word that is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of similarity. This is because it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that the meaning of the word *yathā*, namely similarity, is construed through the relation of being a counter-correlate.

However, because there is a difference [in grammatical function], the meaning of the word *tathā* connects [with the preceding] solely through the relation of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*). Nor should it be argued that a compound would be impossible for the word *yathā* ending in the suffix *thāl*, which expresses a manner of similarity as in *yathāśakti* ("according to one's power") or *yathābalaṃ* ("according to one's strength"), since such a compound does not exist; for its formation is possible with an uninflected indeclinable (*avyutpanna*).
[The rule: *yāvat* is used in the sense of limitation (*avadhāraṇe*). (Pāṇini 2.1.8)

The indeclinable *yāvat*, which functions to delimit a specific quantity (*iyattā*), is compounded with a case-inflected word (*sup*). The analysis (*vigraha*) of *yāvat* is not within its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*), as it ends in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). For example: *yāvadamatraṃ brāhmaṇān āmantrayasva* ("Invite as many Brahmins as there are vessels"). Here, the Brahmins are delimited by the vessels (*amatra*). The meaning is "Brahmins equal in number to the vessels. Although the Brahmins are delimited by the number of vessels, nevertheless, because a mere number cannot function as a delimiter and because they conform to the vessels, it is stated that the vessels are their delimiters.
What is the purpose of the restriction [to the ablative]? "As much as was given, so much was eaten. The meaning is: "I do not determine how much it was.
[The rule] *suppratinā mātrārthe* (Pāṇini 1.4.90) [applies].

A word ending in a case-suffix (subanta) is compounded with *prati* when *prati* has the sense of "a small portion" (*alpārtha*). Examples: *śākaprati* ("a bit of vegetable"), *rūpaprati* ("a bit of form"). The re-mention of the term *sup* (ending in a case-suffix) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the governing rule for indeclinables (*avyaya*) no longer applies here. Otherwise, since words such as *svarādi* (beginning with *svara*) are observed to have substantive predominance (*sattvapradhānatā*) in their usage—for instance in *doṣāmanyam ahaḥ* ("a day considered as night") and *divāmanyā rātriḥ* ("a night considered as day")—compounding with *prati* would apply only to such indeclinables. What is the purpose of [specifying] the sense of "measure" (*mātrārtha*)? It is so that [compounding] does not occur in cases such as *vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati* ("he waters toward the tree").

Nor should it be argued that there is no compound formation because of the force of the rule prescribing the designation *karmapravacanīya* for that [word]; for that [designation] is justified as being for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ṣ*.
The numbers of dice and stalks are the *pariṇas*. 10.

In the case of a number, there is the apprehension of a specific [count]; in the case of a die (*akṣa*) or a counter (*śalākā*), it is the apprehension of their own form. The words *akṣa* and *śalākā* end in the singular. The numbers ending up to four—these are all in the third case. When defeat is understood in the context of a gambler’s practice, in the sense that "the roll was unfavorable," they are compounded with *parā* (as in *parā-pañca*). Their status as being in the third case is established by the fact that they are the agents of the action currently taking place; otherwise, it would have to be stated explicitly. A game called *pañcikā* is played with five dice or five counters.

In that case, when all [the dice or sticks] are face-up or face-down, there is victory for the thrower; in the event of inequality, there is defeat. A roll contrary to the die is *akṣapari*; a roll contrary to the stick is *śalākāpari*. Likewise, a roll with one [of a kind] is *ekapari*; similarly, *dvipari*, *tripari*, and *catuṣpari*. However, it should be noted that since victory is certain when the five are of a single form, the term *pañcapari* does not occur at all.
[The suffix *pari* is used] optionally (*vibhāṣā*). 11.
This is a governing rule (adhikāra); for this very reason, those mentioned previously are considered obligatory compounds (nityasamāsa).
[Pāṇini 2.1.12] "The words apa, pari, bahiḥ, and añcu [form compounds] with a word ending in the fifth case."

These [words] are optionally compounded with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: *apahareḥ saṃsāraḥ* (the cycle of existence is away from Hari), or *apahareḥ*. Likewise for *pari*: *bahirgrāmam* (outside the village) or *bahirgrāmāt*; *prāggrāmam* (east of the village) or *prāggrāmāt*. Because they are used in mutual association (*parasparasāhacarya*), *apa* and *pari* are *karmapravacanīya*s in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). When used in conjunction with these, the fifth case is employed by the rule *pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ*. *Añcati* is also indeed an indeclinable (*avyaya*); because of its association with them, the *Bhāṣya* states that in those cases as well, the fifth case is used according to the rule *añcūttarapada*.

The mention of the fifth case (pañcamī), however, is for the purpose of indicating that the fifth case occurs even in connection with the sense of "outside" (bahis) where the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) would otherwise be expected; therefore, the supplementary rule stating that there is an addition [of the fifth case] in connection with "outside" need not be commenced.
The prefix *āṅ* is used in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*).

"Saṃsāra" [is used] from *āmukti* or *ā mukteḥ*; "devotion to Hari" (*haribhakti*) [is used] from *ābāla* or *ā bālebhyaḥ*. In this case, the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) could have been omitted, since the designation of *karmapravacanīya* and the rule for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) are prescribed only for these two meanings. However, the reading "*āparamāṇorā ca bhūgolaṃ*" is a scribal error; the reading "*bhūgolakāt*" alone is appropriate. They say that because of the separation of the compound by the particle *ca*, the ablative case is necessary even when there is no compound.
**Pāṇini 1.4.90:** *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye* || 14 || [The words *abhi* and *prati* are designated as *karmapravacanīya* when expressing direction toward a mark.]

The prefixes *abhi* and *prati* are optionally compounded with a word expressing a "sign" (*cihna*) when they signify "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*). Because *abhi* is a *karmapravacanīya* when used in the senses of "marking" (*lakṣaṇa*) or "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhūta*), it governs the second case. For example: *abhyagni śalabhāḥ patanti* ("Moths fly toward the fire"). In this case, both the relationship between the mark and the marked (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) and the sense of "facing toward" are expressed by *abhi* and *prati*. Why [is the condition] "when it is a mark"? Consider: *srughnaṃ prati gataḥ* ("He has gone toward Srughna"). This means he has come from Srughna and has gone back toward that very place.

Therefore, *srughna* has the status of an object (*karman*), not that of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). This is not the case in the example "he went by the fire facing [it]," because there is no mention of "facing" (*abhi*) or "toward" (*prati*). What is the purpose of including the mention of *abhi* and *prati*? Consider the examples *abhyaṅkā gāvaḥ* ("cows with marks toward [the sun]") and *pratyaṅkāḥ* ("cows with marks facing [the sun]"); these mean those cows which have new marks on them. One should not argue that there is no possibility of this being an *avyayībhāva* compound here simply because the general rule of the predominance of the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is absent; for its purpose is to indicate that an *avyayībhāva* compound occurs even in the domain of a *bahuvrīhi*. By this, forms such as *dvimuni vyākaraṇam* ("Grammar [studied during] two Munis") are established.
*anuryatsamayā* || 15 || (The word *anu* [forms an *avyayībhāva*] when it means "near to" or "along with").

The word *yat* is neuter because it denotes a general category. It refers to that object which is the correlate of proximity (*samayā*); that is to say, the object by means of which [proximity] is characterized. This [word *anu*] is compounded with such a word as a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Example: *anuvanaṃ aśanir gataḥ* ("the thunderbolt struck following the forest"). [In this case,] *vanasya anu* ("after the forest") indicates the vicinity of the forest and serves as a pointer to the location where the movement of the thunderbolt occurred. Why is the word *samayā* mentioned? Consider: *vṛkṣam anu vidyotate vidyut* ("the lightning flashes near the tree"). Here, the tree is merely a characteristic mark; it does not indicate proximity. Since the rule would have been established by the previous sūtra *avyayaṃ vibhakti...* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), this present sūtra is for the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). **[Sūtra 2.1.16: *yasya cāyāmaḥ*** (And [the word *anu* is compounded] with that whose length [is measured by another]). 16.

The term *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. That by which the extension (*āyāma*) is indicated by the prefix *anu*—by that indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), the object is measured along. For example: *anugaṅgaṃ hāstinapuram* (Hāstinapura [extends] along the Gaṅgā); *anugaṅgaṃ vārāṇasī* (Vārāṇasī [extends] along the Gaṅgā). When the extension is the indicator and is to be expressed by *anu*, the connection of Vārāṇasī with length (*dairghya*) occurs through the relation of being characterized (*upalakṣitatā*). Thus, when the extension—which is the meaning of the prefix *anu*—is construed as a qualifier, it is stated that "being an indicator" (*lakṣaṇatva*) is indeed the relation (*saṃsarga*) [of that qualifier], because the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) can be construed with the meaning of the noun (*nāman*) even through the relation of difference (*bheda*).

If, however, "being characterized" (upalakṣitatva) is also part of its meaning, then when "dairghya" (length) is connected with the other sense of the prefix *anu* in the expression "upalakṣitā," it is construed non-differently (*abhedena*) with Vārāṇasī; thus, the resultant meaning is "extending northwards. And [this applies to] the group beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*. (Pāṇini 2.1.17)

These [compounds] are formed by elision (*nipātana*). "The time for milking is *tiṣṭhadgu*," meaning that at which the cows stand. The particle *ca* has the sense of *eva*; its purpose is to exclude the entry of other grammatical operations (*vṛtti*). Now, if it is asked: "In the usage of Bhaṭṭi, 'Then, reciting while the cows were standing, he performed the evening twilight ritual (*paścimām āyatīgavam*),' although the first [instance, *tiṣṭhadgu*] is resolved through the elision of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-lopa*) and the status of being separate words (*pṛthak-padatva*), how is the second [instance, *āyatīgavam*] resolved? To this they reply: Only a compound of a different type (*vijātīya-vṛtti*) is prohibited; however, an *avyayībhāva* compound certainly does occur here.

Others maintain that the reading is *āyatīgava* and so forth; in this view, words such as *khaleyava* are nominative singular forms. The meaning is that they are not used except in the sense of the mere nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). *Tiṣṭhadgu* and *vahadgu*: the substitution of the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) occurs by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and the shortening of the vowel follows from the rule *go-striyoḥ*. *Āyatīgavam*: this involves the substitution of *śatṛ*, the prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), and the addition of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). *Khaleyavam* and *khalebusam*: here there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending. *Lunayavam*, *lūyamānayavam*, *pūyamānabusam*, *saṃhriyamāṇayavam*, and *saṃhriyamāṇabusam* [are formed similarly].

These [compounds] have time (*kāla*) as their meaning and are *samābhūmi* (level ground) and *samapadāti* (level foot). In the term *bhūmeḥ samatvam*, the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant. When both members end in the suffix *-m* (as in *saṃ-bhūmi*), the augment *mum* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) to the prior member. In readings such as *sambhūmi*, there is elision of the final vowel. Alternatively, the particle *sam* may be used in the aforementioned sense. Examples are *suṣamam*, *viṣamam*, *duḥpamam*, *niḥsamam*, and *apasamam*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: the excellence, absence, defectiveness, departure, or removal of "evenness" (*sama*).

*Āyatīsamam* (equal to the future), *āyatīsamaṃ* (the same as the future); the prohibition of the substitution of *śnā*, the elision of the augment (*puvattva*), and the forms *pāpasamaṃ* (equal to sin) and *puṇyasamaṃ* (equal to merit); *samāsaṃ* (a year); *prāhṇam*, *pramṛgam*, *praratham*, *pradakṣiṇam*—the analysis (*vigraha*) of these is "that which has gone forward from the day" and so forth. *Samprati* (now/at this time) is the state of having come together with that which is present. *Asamprati* (unfit/unseasonable) is the opposite. When there is a mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*), [the suffix] *ic* is applied, as in *daṇḍādaṇḍi* (stick-for-stick). Since this rule is also prescribed for *dvidaṇḍyādi* and similar forms, that too is an *avyayībhāva*. [The words] *pāre* (on the far side) and *madhye* (in the middle) [form compounds] optionally with a word in the genitive case. 18. *pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā* || 18 || (Pāṇini 2.1.18) (Note: The provided text contains a mix of commentary and examples related to Pāṇini’s rules on *avyayībhāva* compounds.)

The words *pāra* and *madhya*, when ending in the genitive case, are optionally compounded with another word [ending in the genitive]. Due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), they take the form ending in *-a*. Although this is established by the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case, it would not account for forms such as *madhyegaṅgād ānaya* (bring from the middle of the Gaṅgā). Here, according to the alternative view of the option, the purpose of the genitive-tatpuruṣa compound is achieved through the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*) even in the absence of the avyayībhāva and tatpuruṣa rules; for there is a rule that when one of two mutually exclusive options does not apply, the other must necessarily apply. However, if another option exists, the tatpuruṣa is established by the force of the context (*sāmarthya*).

For this very reason, elsewhere in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, regarding the optionality of a general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*), it is stated that the general rule applies when the exception has been set aside. Consequently, in the case where there is no formation of a *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound) in the expression "pūrvakāyasya," there is only a syntactic construction (*vākya*) and not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Furthermore, in the derivation of "Dākṣi" from "the offspring of Dakṣa," the suffix *iñ* is set aside, resulting in the absence of the suffix *aṇ*. It is for this same reason that the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) beginning with "udaśvito 'nyatarasyām" is introduced.
[Pāṇini 2.1.19: "A numeral [is compounded] with a word denoting a lineage (*vaṃśya*)."

*Vaṃśya* means "one born in a lineage" (*vaṃśe bhavaḥ*). This is twofold: by learning and by birth. A numeral is optionally compounded with a word having that meaning. For example: *dvau munī pāṇinikātyāyanau* (the two sages Pāṇini and Kātyāyana) = *dvimuni* [grammar]; *trimuni* [grammar]. As for [lineage] by birth: *ekaviṃśati bharadvājam*. Here, the analysis (*anvaya*) is as follows: the meaning of the first member qualifies the meaning of the second member, and both qualify the referent of the compound, namely the descendant in the lineage. However, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states that in the case of *dvimuni vyākaraṇam* (grammar is the two sages), it is due to the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of those who possess the quality with the quality itself, namely through learning.

Regarding the term *lakṣaṇa*, Dīkṣita maintains that because the word *abhimukhya* (facing toward) is included in the sūtra, it is an *avyayībhāva* compound even when the primary meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is not predominant.
[Pāṇini 2.1.20: *nadībhiśca*.

A numeral is compounded with words denoting rivers. It should not be argued that in the case of *dvirāvatīka* (the land having two Āvatī rivers), there would also have to be an *avyayībhāva* compound, because the rule for compounding is established by the mention of the preceding and following members without specifying a particular meaning, and thus there would be no distinction [between this case and others]. This is because of the Vārttika stating: "There is a prohibition when another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*) is intended. Since there is an absence of predominance of the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*), an *avyayībhāva* is untenable in the case of *dvirāvatīka*. Nor is it the case that the same [prohibition] applies to *saptagaṅgam* (the land having seven Gaṅgās).

It must be stated that when the term *samāhāra* (aggregation) is derived through an abstract suffix (*bhāvavyutpanna*), it denotes a collection as its external referent (*anyapadārtha*). Since this [compound] ends in a kṛt-suffix denoting an object (*karman*), it refers to the things being aggregated; thus, the meaning of the latter member, as qualified by the meaning of the former member, is predominant. This is because, while the meaning of the word *dvi* (two) is introduced, there arises an expectancy for a specific substratum (*dharmī*), and upon the word *yamunā* being uttered, the meaning of the former member functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the latter member.

Alternatively, since words such as *dviprabhṛti* (beginning with two) refer to duality and so forth within the scope of their function (*vṛtti*), the expression "the duality of the two Yamunās" constitutes the meaning of the compound; thus, the status of the prior member's referent (*pūrvapadārtha*) is maintained. Nor should it be argued that because the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is understood through the whole [compound], the predominance of the prior member's referent exists precisely because that [referent] is designated by both the prior and posterior members. This is because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that those two [members] denote only the number and the specific river respectively; and this [predominance] is desired in the case of collective compounds (*samāhāra*). For example: *saptagaṅgam* (the seven Gaṅgās), *dviyamunam* (the two Yamunās).

Neither the word *svarūpa* nor the technical term *nadī* is intended here [to be included], due to the force of the plural number. In the example *sarvamekanadītaraḥ*, it is not a *avyayībhāva* compound because there is no collective aggregation (*samāhāra*). Otherwise, by the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇībhyaḥ*, the suffix *ṭac* would have applied. It should not be argued that since the rule is formulated through a split of the yoga (*na vācyatra*), it would be unavoidable in the case of *godāvaryāśca nadyāśca*; for, based on observed usage, that rule does not apply when there is "crossing over a single river" (*ekānadītara*).
And [the *tatpuruṣa* applies] when the meaning is another word (*anyapadārtha*) and it is a name (*saṃjñā*). (21)

A nominal stem ending in a case-suffix, when it functions as a word meaning other than its own constituents, is always compounded when it forms a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *unmattagaṅga* (the region named "Mad-Ganges"), *lohitāgaṅgam* ("Red-Ganges"), *śanairgaṅgam* ("Slow-Ganges"). Why "other" (*anya*)? [To exclude cases like] *kṛṣṇaveṇī*. Why "when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? [To exclude cases like] *śīghragaṅga* (the region "Fast-Ganges"). Although this occurs under the heading of the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*), it is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), because the intended name is not understood through the analytical sentence (*vākya*).
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. (Pāṇini 2.1.22)
This is a governing rule (adhikāra) prior to [the section on] the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
And the *dvigu* [is also included]. 23.

A *dvigu* compound is also designated as a *tatpuruṣa*. It has been stated that this [rule] is redundant because the coexistence of the designations is established by the reading of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ* (P. 2.1.52). When a *dvigu* is a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffixes *ṭac* and *ḍac* serve as its purpose. For example: *pañcarājam*. By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (P. 5.4.91), the suffix *ṭac* is applied. Since it is an integral part of the whole compound, the final member does not end in the vowel *a*; therefore, there is no feminine gender. However, according to the view that "suffixes added at the end of the final member for the sake of the compound" (*samāsānta*) apply here, it would belong to the *pātra*-class (which prevents the feminine suffix). Thus, the form *pañcarājī* is without foundation. An example with *ḍac* is *dvyahaḥ*.

In *ahnaṣṭakhoreva*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *ṭi*. In *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*, [the word] *ahan* becomes masculine. *Pañcāham*: [formed with] *ṭac* by the rule *goranaddhitalukī*; it does not take the feminine gender as before. *Dvyaṅgulam*: [formed with] *ac* by the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*. [The following is taught:
"A word ending in the second case is compounded with *śrita*, *atīta*, *patita*, *gata*, *tyasta*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna*. (Pāṇini 2.1.24)

A word ending in the second case (accusative) is compounded with these words ending in case-terminations; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, as should be understood from here on. Examples: *kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ* → *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa"); *duḥkhātītaḥ* ("gone beyond suffering"); *kūpapatitaḥ* ("fallen into a well"). As for the rule *tanipatyośca* (Pāṇini 7.1.64), which allows for the optional *iṭ* augment, one might object that by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), the *iṭ* would be prohibited in the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix. However, the *iṭ* augment does occur here precisely because of this specific irregularity (*nipātana*). Some, however, maintain that the inclusion of roots like *kṛtī* among those whose *iṭ* is optionally applied by rules such as *se sic* (Pāṇini 7.2.50) is intended to indicate that the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* is not merely optional but rather establishes a permanent prohibition (*nityatva*) in those cases where the *iṭ* is otherwise optional.

They say that by this [rule], forms such as *ebharājādhiya* (having mounted the king of elephants) are also established. Examples: *grāmagataḥ* (gone to the village), *tuhinātyastaḥ* (set behind the snow), *sukhaprāptaḥ* (attained happiness), *sukhāpannaḥ* (fallen into happiness).

There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for roots such as *gam* (to go) and *gam-i* (future participle): *grāmaṃ gamī* (going to the village), *grāmagamī*. The suffix *-in-* here is derived from the Uṇādi rule *gameḥ-iniḥ*; however, according to the rule *āṅi ca ṇiḥ*, the suffix *-ṇi-* occurs even after the simple root due to its general applicability (*bāhulaka*). Since the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* applies to the future sense, the mention of the accusative case in the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* is intended to provide for cases where an exception would otherwise apply; thus, the accusative is used even in connection with a *kṛt* suffix.

According to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, since the sūtra regarding the sense of motion (Pāṇini 2.3.12) has been rejected, the genitive case is desired in connection with a *kṛt* suffix; thus, in that school's position, the prohibition of the genitive by the rule "akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.70) applies.

Thus says Śrī Harṣa. Vāmana, however, maintains that [the form] *madhupipāsu* and others are established by the rule governing *gami-gamya* and so forth. [Objection: "The cluster of buds (*mukulajāla*) of the creepers (*vīrudhām*), frequented by honey-bees (*madhuvrata*) who are thirsty for honey (*madhupipāsu*), has blossomed. Surely, since the formation is already established through a *bahuvrīhi* compound with words such as *śrita* (as in Pāṇini 2.2.35), the rule prescribing a *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* compound (Pāṇini 2.1.30) is redundant; for there is no difference in meaning. Nor is there a difference in accent, because even in a *tatpuruṣa* compound like *ahīna-dvitīya*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is not specifically prescribed [to override the general rule]. [Response: This is not so. For the *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* is necessary to establish the specific sense of "one who desires honey" (*madhu-kāma*) as a subordinate element, whereas the *bahuvrīhi* would imply a different nuance. Furthermore, there is indeed a difference in accent: in a *tatpuruṣa* such as *ahīna-dvitīya*, the accent of the first member is indeed maintained, but this does not apply universally to all such compounds. Thus, the specific rule for the *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* is not superfluous.

However, with words such as *atīta*, *atyasta*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna*, a *tatpuruṣa* compound must indeed be prescribed for the sake of the correct accent (*svarārtha*). This is because, by the rule *atītātyastayor ahīne* and by the exclusion [of these words] under the rule *anupasarge*, the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is not desired there; rather, the accent of the *tatpuruṣa* is necessary to establish the final acute (*antodātta*) via the rule *thāthādisvareṇa*. Nor can it be argued that this is already established in a *bahuvrīhi* by the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyo ’nācchādanāt ktaḥ akṛtamitapratipannāḥ*, which prescribes the final acute for a *kta*-suffix following words denoting genus, time, or happiness, provided they do not denote clothing.

There would be a fault regarding the accent when words such as *śrita* follow words like *jāti*; for if a *tatpuruṣa* compound were commenced, there would be a dual accentuation: the final acute (*antodātta*) of the *bahuvrīhi*, and the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) of the *tatpuruṣa* according to the rule *ahīna*. However, it must be stated that if a *tatpuruṣa* is not resorted to, there is only the final acute. This is because in the case of *vājātaḥ*, even within a *bahuvrīhi*, both accents can be easily established by including *śrita* and the others under the rule *jāta-śrita-patita-gata*.

Nor should it be argued that there is no difference when *śrita* and other such words enter into either a case-compound (*samāsa*) or a possessive compound (*mamāsa*), because of the parsimony [of the rule] "the second member in an *ahīna*," which would not need to be formulated. Furthermore, there is no distinction regarding the dual accentuation whether one adopts both types of compounds or adopts the *bahuvrīhi* alone. Nor should it be argued that this [rule] is intended to indicate that where both *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* are applicable, only the *tatpuruṣa* occurs—thereby establishing that in the case of *rājasakha*, only the *tatpuruṣa* is used and not the *bahuvrīhi* such as *rājā sakho 'sya*.

"May there be well-being! O friend of Soma, come back; O friend of the cows," [is used] because both [Soma and the cows] are desired; [this is an example] of [the compound] with a word ending in the suffix *kta*.
(Pāṇini 2.1.25)

The word *svayam*, being a *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix) derived from a base ending in the suffix *kta*, is compounded with that which ends in a *sup* (case-suffix). However, it has no connection here with the second case (*dvitīyā*), because its meaning is that of the agent (*kartṛ*). Through the formation of the single word *svayaṃkṛtam*, it enters into other types of compounds. There is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule *āma ekāntaram*. Furthermore, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *svāyaṃkṛtiḥ*—meaning "the offspring of one who has made himself"—is also formed.
The word *khaṭvā* [is used] in the sense of throwing. || 26 ||

The word *khaṭvā*, ending in the accusative case, is compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta* that also ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), when expressing censure. For example: *khaṭvārūḍho jālmaḥ*. According to Amarasimha, a *jālma* is one who acts without reflection. Although the act of ascending a bed (*khaṭvārohaṇa*) is prescribed after the return home from studentship (*samāvartana*), the performance of that act prior to that time constitutes a censured behavior; this prohibited conduct is the basis for the application of the term, while the literal meaning of the individual components is not intended. As it is said: "By which action a man becomes 'ascended to the bed' (*khaṭvārūḍha*), he is one who lies upon the bed in a state of remorse."
One who desires the welfare of one's own self should not perform that from the very beginning.
In such cases, since no censure is understood from the sentence, the compound is obligatory even though the section on "optionality" (vibhāṣā) is in force.
[Pāṇini 2.1.27] *sāmi*.

This [word] ending in a case-suffix is optionally compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*. Regarding the term *sāmi*, Amara states: "The word *sāmi* means 'half' or 'despised'. Because it does not denote a substance (*asattvārthatvāt*), it does not take the second case-ending. Examples include *sāmikṛtam* ("half-done") and Śrīharṣa’s verse: "Was it perhaps the Mandākinī that was previously fashioned half-finished by the son of Gādhi? [Now, the section on] Time-words (*kālāḥ*).

Words denoting time ending in the second case are compounded with a word ending in *kta*. This rule is stated for the purpose of excluding cases of absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Example: *māsaṃ pramitaḥ* (measured for a month) = *māsapramitaḥ*, referring to the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipaccandra*). [Note: The root] *māṅ* is used in the sense of measuring; the suffix *kta* is applied here in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarma*). The meaning is: "he has begun to measure [the moon's growth] for a month. There is no absolute connection between the moon of the first day and the month, because the specific quality of being the first day is absent in the moon of other lunar days. And [this applies] in the case of absolute connection as well. (Pāṇini 2.1.29)

The word *kālāḥ* (time-periods) alone [is meant]. This undertaking is for the purpose of including words ending in *akta*. *Muhūrtamukham* means "the face for a moment"; the meaning is that it pervades that [moment]. The accusative case is used here because of the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5), which prescribes the accusative for time and distance when there is continuous connection. [Now follows: "The third case [is used] with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) when the [state] is produced by that. (Pāṇini 2.1.30).

A word ending in the third case is compounded with a quality-expressing term (*guṇavacana*) that denotes "that which is produced by the counter-correlative of the capacity to produce [an effect] residing in its own meaning," as well as with the word *artha*. The expression *tatkṛta* (produced by that) is used separately; the elision of the third case-ending here is Vedic. The word *tat* refers to the meaning of the third-case ending. The state of being produced by that (*tatkṛtatva*) also applies to the quality-term through its own meaning. For example: *śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* becomes *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ* ("broken by a wedge"); *kiriṇā kāṇaḥ* becomes *kirikāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye from a boar"). [The roots] *khaḍi* means "to split" and *kaṇ* means "to blink."

The words *kāṇa* and *khaṇḍa*, ending in the suffix *ghañ*, although they denote substances qualified by a quality through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) or through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*, nevertheless function as denoters of the quality itself through metaphorical usage or the elision of *matup*. This is because the intention here is not to express the mere denotation of that [quality] alone. Furthermore, by the force of the inclusion of the word "word" (*vacana*), those that denote a quality in isolation are not included. For example: *ghṛtena pāṭavam* ("skill with clarified butter"). *Dhānyārthaḥ* ("need for grain"): [this is formed] with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the abstract state (*bhāva*).

*Prayojana* means desire; its object is *tadartha*. [The compound] is formed with the third case-ending (*hetu-tṛtīyā*) in composition. Why say "caused by that" (*tatkṛta*)? [To prevent the application of the rule] in cases such as *dadhnā paṭuḥ* ("clever because of yogurt"), where the status of yogurt as an instrument (*karaṇa*) depends upon the act of eating (*bhuṅkte*). However, when even yogurt—which has not been processed with a specific substance—produces proficiency, and the relationship of action and factor (*kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*) is intended to be expressed, then the compound certainly occurs. Therefore, even in cases where the action is not perceived in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the compound still takes place on the basis of being caused by that.

The mention of "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*) is included so that there may not be [the application of the rule] when the capacity [to produce the state] is mediated by eating and so forth. In this way, there is also a compound in cases such as *kuṅkumena lohitaṃ mukham* ("a face red with saffron"). What is the purpose of the word "quality" (*guṇa*)? Consider *gobhir vapāvān* ("fatty because of cows"). Here, the fatness results from eating cow-products such as curd, so there is indeed the state of being produced by that; however, this word (*vapāvat*) is not a "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*). It should not be argued that it is indeed a quality-word, for only that which primarily denotes a quality and only occasionally denotes a substance qualified by that quality is considered a "quality-word. The word *vapāvat* denotes the substance alone. Furthermore, a "quality" will be defined as that which "enters into an existent entity and departs from it."
[The suffix *vat* is used] with the words *pūrva*, *sadṛśa*, *samasama*, *artha*, *kalaha*, *nipuṇa*, *miśra*, and *ślakṣṇa*. || 31 ||

Together with these [words], the third case ending is applied up to the end of the *tṛtīyā* [sūtra], as before. By the very fact of the rule for compound formation (*samāsavidhāna*), the third case is understood to occur in connection with words such as *pūrva*. Examples: *māsapūrvaḥ* (one who is earlier by a month); *mātrāsadṛśaḥ* or *samaḥ* (equal to his mother); *mātṛsadṛśaḥ* or *mātṛsamaḥ* (like his mother). The third case is used here because of the rule "with words having the sense of *tulya*" (*tulyārthaiḥ*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the word *sadṛśa* [in that rule] was rejected by the authors of the *Bhāṣya* on the grounds that the sixth case would apply to the words *sadṛśa* and *pratirūpa* when expressing similarity (*sādṛśya*).

For instance: since there is also a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī*) with the meaning "having the same object," its formation is established by that very [rule]. Nor should it be argued that this [sūtra] is for the sake of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member in a *tatpuruṣa*—whereby the third case would have the sense of "equality"—because in a genitive compound, the final syllable would instead result in being accented (*antodātta*). This is because the desired form is already established by the rule *sadṛśapratirūpayoḥ sādṛśye*. Nor should it be argued that the mention of *sadṛśa* (similarity) alone should suffice in that very rule; for it is necessary [here] to prevent the final accentuation that would otherwise occur in the alternative of a genitive compound.

Nor should it be argued that the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) should simply not exist because it is not explicitly taught; for the *Bhāṣya* cites "dāsyāḥ sadṛśaḥ" (resembling a female slave) as an example of a compound where the genitive case-ending is not elided by the rule "ākrośe" (in the sense of abuse). Nor should it be argued that the word "sadṛśa" is mentioned here for the purpose of forming a compound with an instrumental ending denoting cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*); for the desired result is already established by the very fact of being produced by that [cause]. Nor should it be argued that since the word "sadṛśa" does not exclusively denote a quality (*guṇa*), this compound would not be possible—unlike the case of the word "vapāvac"—because the formation is indeed possible through a genitive compound alone.

Since the word *artha* was already explained [in the sense of composition] by the previous sūtra, the mention of *artha* here is connected with *ūna*, and not with *pūrva* and the others. This is because the word *sama* is mentioned separately. Examples: *māṣeṇonaṃ māṣonaṃ kārṣāpaṇam* (a kārṣāpaṇa deficient by one māṣa); *māṣavikalam*. *vācakalahaḥ* (a verbal quarrel) [is *vācaḥ kalahaḥ*]. *ācāraniṣṇaḥ* (skilled in conduct). *guḍamiśrāḥ* (mixed with molasses). *ācāraślakṣṇaḥ*. When the word *miśra* is included, that which has a prefix is also included. This is also established by the inclusion of the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) in the rule *miśraṃ cānupasargamasandhau*. An addition should be made for the word *avara*: *māsāvaraḥ* (lacking by a month).
A word ending in a *kṛt* suffix that denotes the agent or the instrument is frequently compounded with another word ending in a *kṛt* suffix.

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*), when it signifies either [the instrument] or [the agent], is frequently compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Examples: *hariṇā trātaḥ* (saved by Hari) becomes *haritrātaḥ*; *nakhair bhinnaḥ* (split by claws) becomes *nakhabhinnaḥ*. When a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, it includes that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. Example: *nakhanirbhinnaḥ* (pierced by the nails). Why is the word "meaning" (*artha*) included? [To exclude cases where the third case does not signify the instrument or agent, such as: *bhikṣābhir uṣitaḥ* (dwelt because of alms). This third case is used here in the sense of cause (*hetu*); due to the inclusion of the word "frequently" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*), it is not compounded with forms such as the present participles in *-śatṛ* and *-śānac*, or the past participles in *-ktavatu*, etc., as in *hastena kurvan* (doing with the hand), and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that one should simply say "by a *kta*-affix" (*ktena*); for in cases such as *nakhanirbhedaḥ*, a compound would be untenable with words ending in *ghañ* and other affixes. Therefore, "variously" (*bahulam*) alone is correct, in order to avoid both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Indeed, because of the inclusion of the term "variously," there is a compound even with the fifth case (*pañcamī*) denoting the *apādāna* (ablative), as in *pādābhyāṃ hārakaḥ* ("one who steals by means of the feet"), where the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Similarly, in *galecopakaḥ* ("one who seizes by the throat"), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) after the causative form of the root *cup* (meaning "to move") which ends in *ṇic*; here, the elision of the *ṭi*-portion does not occur according to the rule *amūrdhamastakāt svāṅgāt*. Why specify "after a *kṛt*-affix"? [So that the rule does not apply] in cases like *kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatitarām* ("he cooks very well with wood").
The suffix *kṛtya* is used to express an additional purpose (*adhikārtha*).

A statement of additional meaning (*adhikārthavacana*), which has as its purport either praise or censure and lacks a purport for its own literal sense, is compounded with gerundives (*kṛtya*) when the third case ending occurs there in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). For example, *kākapeyā nadī* ("the river drinkable by crows") expresses praise, in that because the river is full, it can be drunk even by crows standing on the bank; or it expresses censure, in that because there is so little water, it could be drunk even by crows. Some maintain that since the mention of the action has as its purport praise or censure, the agent and instrument are secondary (*gauṇa*), and thus this rule prescribes a compounding that would otherwise not have been obtained.

Others, however, maintain that first there is the connection between the action and its agent, and only thereafter is there the comprehension of praise or censure, according to the logic of the *Arthavāda* section [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras]. Therefore, they say this [mention of the agent] is for the sake of elaboration; for this very reason, a compound is seen even when a word with an unformed suffix (*akṛtya*) expresses an additional meaning, as in the example "the river drunk by crows" (*kākapītā nadī*). [The rule: "Sauce with rice. (34)

A word ending in the third case that denotes a *saṃskāraka* (an agent of refinement) is compounded with the word denoting the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*), as previously stated. For example: *dadhnā upasikta odano dadhyodanaḥ* ("rice sprinkled with curd" = "curd-rice"). Here, although there is no mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) between the two *kārakas* [the curd and the rice], their capacity for composition is achieved through the act of sprinkling (*upaseka-kriyā*) which is included within the compound. This is because, without the act of sprinkling, the perceived relationship of refiner and refined between the two would be untenable. Nor can it be argued that the compound occurs despite the lack of capacity by virtue of the explicit statement of the rule; for if that were so, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of forming a compound even in cases such as *dadhnā odano bhujyatām* ("Let rice be eaten with curd"). [The next rule follows: "With a word denoting food, [it is compounded] with a word denoting a mixing ingredient. (Pāṇini 2.1.35).

*Guḍamiśrā dhānāḥ* (parched grains mixed with molasses) is *guḍadhānāḥ*. In this compound, the act of mixing (*miśraṇa*) is included within the formation. That which is to be eaten is *kṣya*; it is *svaram* (hard) and *viśadam* (distinctly separated). One should not ask how [the term] *abbhakṣyam* (water to be drunk) and so forth are formed; for since the root *bhakṣ* ending in the suffix *ṇiC* already expresses that meaning, it is established there either through its figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) or by treating it as a derivative of the root *bhaj* ending in *aṇ*. Pāṇini 2.1.36: "The fourth case is compounded with words meaning 'for the sake of' (*tadartha*), 'meaning' (*artha*), 'offering' (*bali*), 'beneficial' (*hita*), 'pleasant' (*sukha*), and 'protected' (*rakṣita*)."

A word ending in the dative case is compounded with words such as *artha* (meaning) and others that denote the object intended by that which is expressed by the dative-ending word, provided the relationship is one of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*). In this context, a compound is desired only when there is a relationship of material cause and its product (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*). This is because of the force of the inclusion of the term *vilīna-rakṣita* [in the commentary]; otherwise, since even the *vali* (the skin-folds) belong to Kubera, the compound would have occurred by the rule *tadartha* itself. Examples include: *yūpāya dāru* → *yūpa-dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post") and *kuṇḍalāya hiraṇyam* → *kuṇḍala-hiraṇyam* ("gold for an earring"). But not here: *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking").

The *Bhāṣya* states that *aśvaghāsa* and similar compounds are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds. In cases such as *yūpadāru* (sacrificial post-wood), the cognition is one in which the object denoted by the second member (*uttarapada*) is characterized by being intended for the object denoted by the first member (*pūrvapada*). However, in *aśvaghāsa* and the like, the distinction is that [the cognition] is characterized by the relation of belonging to the horse and so forth. It should be stated that there is an obligatory compound with the word *artha*, and that it takes the gender of the qualified noun (*viśeṣyaliṅgatā*). For example: *dvijārthaḥ sūpaḥ* (soup for a Brahmin), *dvijārthā yāvagūḥ* (barley-gruel for a Brahmin), *dvijārthapayaḥ* (milk for a Brahmin).

In this case, since the sense of "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya) is already expressed by the dative case itself, it is established by logic that the separate employment of the word *artha* is impossible; thus its necessity is proven. However, in the case of a compound, by the force of the specific rule, the word *artha* is employed even though its meaning has already been stated. This constitutes the difference [between the two cases]. Therefore, in order to set aside the rule regarding the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅga*), one must simply state that the gender of the compound follows that of the substantive (*viśeṣyaliṅgatva*).

But surely, for that purpose, in the rule *vikṛteḥ prakṛtau* (Pāṇini 4.3.130), one should formulate the sūtra as *tadarthe sarthap*. By this, the dative case ending would be implied through its sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*). Alternatively, there is the continuation from the rule *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5); or, when the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tadarthe*) is to be expressed, the suffix *sarthap* should occur after a word ending in the dative case. In the *saṃhitā* reading of *ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ* and *ṣaḥ pratyayasya*, two *ṣ*-sounds are indicated; therein, by the rule of *ṣṭu* substitution, the *s*-sound is included, and thus the *s*-sound receives the technical designation *it*. By the rule *siti ca*, it acquires the status of a word (*padatva*).

In examples such as *rājārtha* and *bhavadartha*, there is the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) and the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*). The letter *p* is for the sake of the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*). Consequently, the original accentuation of the base (*prakṛti*) is established as it was before; therefore, the rule prescribing the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) for the word *artha* need not be commenced. Furthermore, because it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), there is no possibility of its separate usage. And because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it takes the gender of the object denoted (*abhidheya-liṅgatā*). If one asks, "What is the purpose of this [suffix]?"—it is not so, because if it were merely a suffix (*pratyaya*) [and not a *taddhita*], then in forms like *śvaryartha* and *śvārtha*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would undesirably apply.

Furthermore, there is no evidence for the elision of the letter *sa* (in *brāhmaṇārtha*). Moreover, if the suffix *sap* were applied according to the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi-sūtra*, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *tṛṇasāya*. Now, one might argue: let there be a *bahuvrīhi* compound, *vrāhmaṇārtha*, meaning "that whose purpose is a Brāhmaṇa," because an object intended for a Brāhmaṇa is employed for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa. Nor should it be said that in examples such as *advijārthaṃ payaḥ* ("milk not for a twice-born"), since the milk is already established [prior to the relationship], the Brāhmaṇa cannot be the motivator (*prayojaka*) therein; for such a relationship is possible through the mediation of an action (*kriyādvārā*). And thus, there is no absence of analysis (*vigraha*) with a word ending in the dative case.

If it is argued that both the taking on the gender of the qualified noun (*viśeṣyaliṅgatva*) and the preservation of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*) are established solely by virtue of being a *bahuvrīhi* compound, this is not so; for in the case of the word *mahadartha*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the application of the augment *āt* and the suffix *kap*.

It might be argued as follows: let the word *artha* be substituted for the subsequent member that has that meaning (*tadartha*). In this way, the absence of a formal analytical compound (*vigraha*) and the capacity for all genders (*sarvaliṅgatā*) are established. Nor is there any impossibility in the usage of words such as *paya-* (milk), because the use of the substitute is justified by its need to manifest a specific meaning through its commonality with other words. Thus, there is a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as *tadartha-artha*. The meaning is that the word *artha* is optionally substituted for the subsequent member that has that meaning.

Consequently, the word *artha* would also be a substitute for *bali* and *rakṣita*. For example, *kuverārthaḥ baliḥ* (the offering intended for Kubera) would become *kuverabaliḥ*. Since this is already established by the preceding rule, this [present rule] is for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). It indicates that the substitution of *artha* is obligatory in cases other than those involving the relationship between a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*). Thus, one says only *randhanārthā sthālī* (a pot for cooking), and not *randhanasthālī*. If it is argued that both forms—*yūpārthaṃ dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post) and *yūpadāru* (sacrificial-post wood)—are correct, this is not so.

Because in the case of *udakārtho vīvadhaḥ* (a carrying-pole for water), if the word *vīvadha* were to undergo the substitution of *artha*, it would follow that the word *udaka* would undergo the substitution of *uda-* by the rule beginning with *manthaudana-*, and so forth. Therefore, the original formulation alone is elegant.
The fifth [is used] out of fear. || 37 ||

A word ending in the fifth case (ablative) is compounded with a nominal stem ending in a case-affix that expresses the cause of fear, as previously stated. Examples: *caurabhayam* (fear of a thief). It should be stated that [the compound is formed] with words meaning "fear," "one who has become afraid," "fearfulness," and "fear. Examples: *vṛkabhītaḥ* (afraid of a wolf). Here, however, there is no fear from wolves [as a general state]. This is an elaboration of the aforementioned rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). By this, compounds such as *grāmanirgataḥ* (departed from the village) and *adharmajugupsuḥ* (disgusted by unrighteousness) are also formed.
The words *apeta*, *apoḍha*, *mukta*, *patita*, and *apatrasta* are optionally used with the third case ending when they signify a small degree [of separation]. (38)

When these [words] are compounded with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) that signifies "little" (*alpa*), it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Even though there is a rule stating that in the context of "many or few" (*vahvalpārtha*) one must specify whether it refers to something auspicious (*maṅgala*) or inauspicious (*amaṅgala*), the elision of the case-ending (*acch*) occurs here by virtue of this very nipātana (irregular formation). Examples: *sukhāpetaḥ* (devoid of happiness), *kalpanāpoḍhaḥ* (free from conceptual construction), *cakrapatitaḥ* (fallen from the wheel), *svargapatitaḥ* (fallen from heaven), *taraṅgāpatrastaḥ* (scared away by a wave). Because the word *alpa* is stated [in the rule] to mean "not pertaining to all" (*asārvatrikatva*), it does not apply here in cases such as *prāsādātpatitaḥ* (fallen from the palace). This is merely an elaboration of the principle of *bāhulaka* (diversity/irregularity).
The words *stoka*, *antika*, *dūra*, *artha*, *kṛcchra*, and *ākiṃcana* [govern the accusative case when used adverbially]. || 39 ||

The previously mentioned qualifiers are: *stokānmuktaḥ* (freed from a little), *alpānmuktaḥ* (freed from a small amount), *antikādāgataḥ* (come from near), *abhyāśādāgataḥ* (come from close by), *dūrādāgataḥ* (come from afar), and *kṛchrānmuktaḥ* (freed from difficulty). [In these cases], there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending due to the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*. [Now begins: "The locative [case-ending is compounded] with *śoṇḍa* and others. (Pāṇini 2.1.40)

The plural number [in the rule] indicates that the term *śauṇḍa* and others are intended; for, as in the expression "the umbrella-bearers are going," the word *śauṇḍa*—by means of a definition (*lakṣaṇā*) that does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*)—refers to a group consisting of rogues and the like who possess that quality. Thus, one is called *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* ("addicted to dice"). Since the action in the form of "addiction" (*prasakti*) is included within the compound, the locative case is applied there to express its sense. Regarding the word *antaḥ*, which is listed here [as a governing preposition], when it is connected with a whole (*avayavin*), the locative case is used to indicate its status as a substratum (*ādhāra*), just as in the example "the branch in the tree" (*vṛkṣe śākhā*). For instance: *vane'ntar* or *vanāntaḥ* ("within the forest").

Because this [compound] is optional, there is an *avyayībhāva* in one alternative: *antarvaṇam*. Haradatta maintains that the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *pra-nir-antaḥ-pareṣu saṃjñā-āmredita-yoś-ca*. However, the Bhaṭṭojidīkṣitas hold that since it is impossible for the mere case-ending (*vibhakti*) alone to be employed when one intends to explain the meaning of the word *antaḥ*, the word *madhya* is used merely for the sake of grammatical correctness; thus, because this [word *madhya*], which denotes a location qualified by a container, does not function solely in the sense of a case-ending, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur in that way.

In reality, even when "in the middle" (*madhye*) is expressed, there is no meaning for the word *antar* other than its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), because it would be cumbersome to postulate another word that functions solely as a locus. Nor should it be argued that this is untenable because of the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound itself as "within the forest" (*vane'ntar*), since in such a case the formation of an *avyayībhāva* compound—rather than a *tatpuruṣa*—would follow, and because that [avyayībhāva] is obligatory, it would preclude the sentence. For in the analysis, one must state that the locative case in "in the forest" (*vane*) has a meaning beyond that of mere locus.

The word *adhi* is also recited here. When the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is predominant, it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound; however, when the located (*ādheya*) is predominant, it forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound by this rule. Because *adhi* is the final member, the suffix *kha* is applied [to form *īna*]. Thus, *brāhmaṇādhīnaḥ* (dependent on Brāhmaṇas). The analysis (*vigraha*) is *brāhmaṇeṣvadhi*. In the group beginning with *śauṇḍa*—namely *śauṇḍa*, *dhūrta*, *kitava*, *vyāḍa*, *prakīrṇa*, *saṃvīta*, *antara*, *adhi*—this [compound] has the locus as its predominant element. [The list continues: *paṭu*, *paṇḍita*, *kuśala*, *capala*, *nipuṇa*, *vṛt*. The meaning of "completed" (*vṛtta*) is that the *śauṇḍādi* group has ended. And [the suffix *kha* is applied] with *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, and *bandha*: || 41 ||

The word *saptamī* (locative case) is compounded with these [words]: *saṃkāśyasiddhaḥ*, *kāmpillyasiddhaḥ*. A forest is called *sākāśya* or *kāmpilya* because it was established by Saṃkāśa or Kampaḷi; the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the rule *saṃkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*. The meaning is "one who has attained perfection (*siddha*) there through asceticism. [Examples: *ātapaśuṣkaḥ* (dried by the sun), *sthālīpakvaḥ* (cooked in a pot), *cakravandhaḥ* or *cakrebandhaḥ* (bound in a circle). In the latter, the elision of the case-ending is optional according to the rule *bandhe ca vibhāṣā*. [The locative is compounded] with *dhvāṅkṣa* when expressing censure (*kṣepa*). (Pāṇini 2.1.42)

A word ending in the locative case is compounded with a word denoting a crow (*dhvāṅkṣa*) when contempt is expressed. For example: *tīrthadhvāṅkṣaḥ* (a "crow at a sacred bathing place") or *tīrthakākaḥ* (a "crow at a sacred bathing place"). Just as a crow does not remain long at a sacred bathing place, so too another person whose conduct is unstable due to fickleness in his duties is described in this way. The sense of "like" (*iva*) is included within the compound formation. Why [is it] "when contempt is expressed"? [Answer: "The crow stays at the sacred bathing place.
[Now,] with words denoting debt (*ṛṇa*), [compounding occurs] with gerundives (*kṛtya*). (Pāṇini 2.1.43)

The term *ṛṇa-pada* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all obligatory (*avaśyaka*) [compounds]. By the word "kṛtya," the suffix *yat* is also understood based on the commentary. The plural number, however, is intended to refer to the variety of base forms (*prakṛti*). Examples: *māse deyam ṛṇam* (a debt due in a month); *pūrvāhṇe geyaṃ sāma* (a Sāman to be sung in the forenoon). In a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛtya* suffix, there is no elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending]. [This applies] when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). 44.

A word ending in the seventh case (locative) is compounded with a *sup*-ending word when it forms a conventional name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *araṇyetilakāḥ* ("wild sesame plants"), *araṇyemāṣāḥ* ("wild beans"), *vane-kaserukāḥ* ("wild kaseruka plants"). Because of the rule *haladantāt saptamyāḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.9), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. Since the conventional name cannot be understood through the analytical sentence (*vākya*), this is an obligatory compound (*nitya-samāsa*). [The following rule applies: "Parts of days and nights are compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*. (Pāṇini 2.1.45)

The members of *dina* (day) and *rātri* (night), ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), are compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*. Examples: *pūrvāhṇakṛtam* (done in the forenoon), *aparāhṇakṛtam* (done in the afternoon), *pūrvarātrakṛtam* (done in the first part of the night), *apararātrakṛtam* (done in the latter part of the night).
