Why "members" (*avayava*)? [To exclude cases like] *ahni dṛṣṭam* (seen during the day). Some say that because of the use of the term "frequently" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*), there is compounding even in cases such as *rātrivṛttamanuyoktumudyataḥ* (ready to question about what occurred at night). Alternatively, when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) may be formed. Regarding that: || 46 ||

In this context, a word ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) is compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*. Examples are *tatrabhuktam* (eaten there) and *tatra kṛtam* (done there). Although the nominative case alone would be appropriate after the word *tatra*, since the sense of the locus has already been expressed [by the compound], the author of the Vṛtti maintains that because forms such as *tatrabhavān* are observed even with other case-endings, the word *tatra* still requires the locative case for the purpose of conveying the locus. However, Dīkṣita argues that although the locative case is prescribed here, it is overridden by the requirements of the meaning.

They say that the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is established precisely because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); furthermore, since the elision of the locative case-ending (*saptamī-lopa*) is treated as a single substitute (*ekadeśa*), its status as common to other case-endings remains unchanged.
In the case of censure. || 47 ||

A word ending in the seventh case is compounded with a word ending in *kta* when censure is intended. For example: *avataptanakulasthitam* ("like a mongoose standing in a heated place"). Just as a mongoose does not remain for long in a heated spot, so too one who begins tasks but abandons them midway is described in this way. Because the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix includes that which follows a prefix (*gati*) or a case-factor (*kāraka*), there is a compound with the word *nakulasthita*. *udakeviśīrṇam* ("dissolved in water"), *pravāhemūtritam* ("urinated in a stream"), *bhasmanihutam* ("offered into ashes")—the meaning is "fruitless. In these cases, the elision of the *kṛt*-suffix is not applied due to the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*. Furthermore, the group beginning with *pātresamitāḥ* (those who meet at the dining table) is also included.

These are listed as *nipātas* (irregular forms) used in the sense of censure (*nindā*). Since the status of these words ending in the *kta* suffix is already established by the preceding rule, their inclusion here—despite being included in the group beginning with *yuktyārohī*—is for the purpose of ensuring that the first syllable of the preceding member bears the acute accent (*ādyudātta*), according to the internal sub-rule (*antargaṇasūtra*) beginning with *pātresamitādayaśca*. Examples: *pātresamitāḥ*: those who have come together only at the time of eating, and not for any other business. *pātrebahulāḥ*: those who are numerous only at the time of eating. *udumbaramaśakaḥ*: a gnat [satisfied] with a fig tree; one who, out of meager contentment, thinks there is nothing else. *udumbarakṛmiḥ*: a worm in a fig tree. *kūpakacchapaḥ*: a tortoise in a well. *kūpamaṇḍūkaḥ*: a frog in a well. *kumbhamaṇḍūkaḥ*: a frog in a jar. *udapānamaṇḍūkaḥ*: a frog in a water-pool.

The city-crow; the city-raven; a man toward his mother, a hero toward his father—this is due to a lack of prowess elsewhere, as in the case of the gnat among *udumbara* figs and so forth, which is an implied comparison (*upamākṣepa*). "A man toward his mother" refers to serving a neighbor. Regarding "a hero in a crowd" (*piṇḍīśūra*) and so forth, the meaning is due to a lack of exertion. A hero in a crowd; a hero in the house (*geheśūra*); one who roars in the house (*gehenardī*); one who bellows in the house (*gehekṣveḍī*); one who urinates in the house (*gehemehī*); one who conquers in the house (*gehevijitī*); a tiger in the house (*gehevyāḍaḥ*); one who is arrogant in the house (*gehevṛptaḥ*); one who is impudent in the house (*geheghṛṣṭaḥ*); one who is satisfied in the house (*gehetṛptaḥ*); a crow that digs in the ground (*ākhanikavakaḥ*).

An *ākhanika* is one who digs a water-channel; the meaning is that just as one who has dug there eats whatever he obtains, so does another. [Examples include: *goṣṭheśūraḥ*, *goṣṭhevijitī*, *goṣṭhekṣveḍī*, *goṣṭhepaṭuḥ*, *goṣṭhepaṇḍitaḥ*, *goṣṭhepragalbhaḥ*, *karṇeṭiriṭirā*, and *karṇecurucurā*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). The particle *ca* is for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). By this, [the compound] is only *paramāḥ pātresamitāḥ* and not any other compound. However, Kaiyaṭa states that if the reading were *paramapātresamitāḥ*, then, like *vispaṣṭapaṭu*, the application of a compound suffix (*samāsānta*) would follow.
The words *pūrva*, *kāla*, *eka*, *sarva*, *jara*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* [form a compound] with a word in grammatical apposition. (Pāṇini 2.1.49)

The seven [categories] ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) are compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix that has the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*). This is a specification of the nature of some [compounds], while for others it indicates their meaning as "that which occurs at a prior time" (*pūrvakāla*). Because of their relational nature, a compound is formed between a prior time and a subsequent time. Although this would be established by the rule "it is a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇam*), this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restricting the position of the first member. However, in the case of the word *eka*, it is indeed a new rule (*apūrvavidhi*), because by the restriction "direction and number [are compounded] when they form a name" (*dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām*), that [prior-position] does not otherwise apply.

By this, the claim made by some—that the rule *dik-saṃkhye* (Pāṇini 2.1.50) is non-eternal because of the specific mention of *ekādhikaraṇe* (being in the same substratum)—is refuted. *Snātānuliptaḥ*: "one who has first bathed and afterwards been anointed. Here, the meaning of the compound pertains to both the prior and subsequent times; the sense is "one who is the locus of anointing occurring immediately after bathing," which conveys the priority of the bathing. Examples include: *ekaśāṭī* ("one who wears a single garment"), *sarvayājñikāḥ* ("all ritualists"), *jarattārkikāḥ* ("old logicians"), *purāṇamīmāṃsakāḥ* ("ancient Mīmāṃsakas"), *navapāṭhakāḥ* ("new students"), and *kevalavaiyākaraṇāḥ* ("mere grammarians").

What is the purpose of the requirement that [the first member] be in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)? [Consider: "the whiteness of one" (*ekasyāḥ śauklyam*). By the rule *pūraṇaguṇa* (P. 2.2.11), even a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is prohibited here.
[Next: *dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (P. 2.1.50).

The term "with a word in apposition" (samānādhikaraṇena) continues [as a governing rule] until the end of the chapter. Only when forming a technical name (saṃjñā) is there a compound of a directional word and a numeral with a word in apposition, and not otherwise. *Pūrveṣukāmaśamī*: here, the word *pūrva* ("eastern") is compounded with the word *iṣukāmaśamī*; this is the name of a specific village. *Pañcāmrāḥ* ("five mangoes") and *saptarṣayaḥ* ("seven seers"). Not so in cases such as *uttarā vṛkṣāḥ* ("northern trees") or *pañca brāhmaṇāḥ* ("five Brahmins"). Words such as *trivalī* ("three folds") are formed by the elision of the middle member (*madhyamapadalopa*). In expressions like *pūrvasūtram* ("the eastern aphorism"), the compound occurs because the meaning is that of direction (*dig-artha*), not because it is a technical name.
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the first Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the Śrī Siddhāntasudhānidhi. Śrī.
The compound occurs when there is the sense of a secondary derivative (taddhita), or when it is the final member of a compound, or in the case of a collective aggregate (samāhāra). Pāṇini 2.1.51.

When a *taddhita* suffix is intended, when a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) follows, and when a collective compound (*samāhāra*) is to be expressed, the directional term (*dik*) and the numeral (*saṃkhyā*) are compounded with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Thus, due to the difference in the scope [of application], a difference in the meaning of the locative case should be understood. For example: "born in the eastern hall" (*pūrvasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*) results in *paurvaśālaḥ*. When the intention is to apply a *taddhita* suffix, the compounding of the words *pūrva* and *śālā* occurs precisely before that suffix arises. Subsequently, by the rule *dikpūrvapadādasaṃjñāyām ñaḥ*, the suffix *ñ* is applied, resulting in *āparaśālaḥ*.

Thus, in the case of the subsequent member [in *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ*], because both [members] are explicitly taught [by rule], there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the rule *asarvanāmnaḥ*. First, there is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; by the accentual rule for the final vowel of a compound (*samāsāntodātta*), the vowel *ā* of the word *la* (i.e., *śālā*) becomes udātta. If, however, the *tatpuruṣa* were not present in the prior part, then by the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), the beginning of the prior member would be udātta. There is no collective formation (*samāhāra*) regarding directions, because such a usage is not expressed [by the language]. There are exactly two examples of directional words.

Three examples in sequence for [the suffixes following] a numeral are as follows: the offspring of six mothers is *ṣāṇmāturaḥ*; *pāñcanāpitiḥ*—here there is no elision (*luk*) because of the exclusion [of the case ending] by the rule *anapatya* ("not offspring"); that which is prepared in five potsherds is *pañcakapālaḥ* *puroḍāśaḥ* (sacrificial cake)—here the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*, and it is elided by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*; he whose wealth consists of five cows is *pañcagavadhanaḥ*—this is a compound formed as before, with the suffix *ṭac* added by the rule *gor ataddhitaluki*.

Nor should it be argued that because the *tatpuruṣa* compound is optional according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there would occasionally be the form *pañcagodhana*; for the *Vārttika* begins with the statement: "The rule regarding obligatory composition applies when the final member follows a *dvandva* or a *tatpuruṣa*. Precisely for this reason, in the case of *vākatvacapriyaḥ* ("one who loves bark-garments")—where it is a three-word *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one for whom bark-garments (*vāk* and *tvak*) are dear"—the obligatory suffix is applied by the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in *udaṣah*," resulting in *chatropānahapriyaḥ*.

And this [rule] is established by logic regarding the *tatpuruṣa* portion, because when the two preceding *yat* suffixes are included within the *bahuvrīhi* due to the existence of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning), the formation of the *tatpuruṣa* is unavoidable; for when the *mahāvibhāṣā* (great option) applies, the unification of meaning makes the compound unavoidable, since it is contradictory that the unification of meaning should exist for the whole aggregate while being absent in its constituent parts. Thus, some maintain that the works of the ancient grammarians—which state that the rule is prescribed as obligatory (*nitya*) when an option (*vikalpa*) would otherwise have applied—are indeed inconsistent.

That [interpretation] is to be considered doubtful; for when the three [words] are compounded, since they shift toward the meaning of another word (anyapadārtha), there is an absence of mutual relationship, and thus neither a *dvandva* nor a *tatpuruṣa* would apply—making the statement [of the rule] itself inconsistent.

Regarding the statement that "the *bahuvrīhi* occurs by virtue of the capacity for *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning)," what is the intended meaning when it is said that there is *ekārthībhāva* even for the two constituent parts, namely the two words *pūrva-śālā*? Is it the integration of the two words [into a single meaning], or is it the integration of all two words [of the compound] [into a single meaning]? It cannot be the first, because there is no dispute regarding the integration of three words into a single meaning with respect to the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), and because, in that case, it would be impossible for the two preceding words to form a *tatpuruṣa* compound, as such a compound is obligatory [only between two words]. Nor can it be the latter.

Because the argument that "there is an absence of mutual connection" is untenable; for since the formation of a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is optional, it is impossible to avoid the occasional occurrence of a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the application of the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the rule allowing optionality) occurs only where a sentence is used in the absence of a compound formation? Here, however, since the use of two constituent words of a *bahuvrīhi* within a three-word compound would be untenable, the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the designation *tatpuruṣa* is established by implication. Therefore, because the designation is not understood through a sentence, one accepts the obligatoriness of the compound—even though it falls under the scope of the *vibhāṣā* section—prescribed by rules such as "in the case of a designation" (*saṃjñāyām*). [Response: If you argue thus...

This being true, let your honor first explain this: does this compound occur where there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) or where there is no semantic capacity? It cannot be the former, because that would contradict your own statement that "there is an absence of mutual relationship. Nor can it be the latter, because in cases such as *susūkṣmajaṭakeśe na* ("not in one with very fine matted hair"), a Bahuvrīhi consisting of multiple words would entail the application of the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*; yet the avoidance of that [application] through the use of the term *bahulam* ("optionally") is well-established in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa’s* commentary on the *Samartha-sūtra*.

Because, in the absence of semantic necessity (*sāmarthya*), it would be impossible even to suspect the application of a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (adjective compound). Likewise, in the case of *adhika-ṣaṣṭi-varṣa*, since it has been suspected that the *bahuvrīhi*—by the rule *saṃkhyayāvyaya-*—would apply there by virtue of its higher status, thereby overriding the *tatpuruṣa* [prescribed] by the rule *taddhitārtha-*;

for although the *tatpuruṣa* of *taddhitārtha-* operates when a subsequent word follows due to the force of the specific grammatical statement, there is no basis for the operation of a *bahuvrīhi* such as *saṃkhyeya-utpādi-*, since that [former rule] finds its scope of application in cases like *dvi-trāḥ*.

But what is the meaning of the phrase "where there is no compound" (*vṛttyabhāve*)? Does it mean where there is no three-membered *bahuvrīhi*, or where there is no *tatpuruṣa* in the prior member? Not the first, because the sentence "one for whom the eastern hall is dear" (*pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ*) is accepted [as a valid example]. Nor the second, because "eastern hall" (*pūrvaśālā*) is also accepted [as a valid example]. If you argue that it means "where there is the separate usage of the two members that are included within a compound," that is not so, because such a case is unestablished.

This is because that [distinction] is absent even in cases such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), since there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) anywhere between the compound (*vṛtti*) and its specific components when they are separate sentences; furthermore, in those instances, the components are used independently. In examples such as *rājapuruṣam ānaya* ("bring the king's man"), although there is a difference in the intermediate meanings (*avāntarārtha*) between the compound and the sentence, there is no difference in the principal meaning (*pradhānārtha*). It is precisely for the purpose of ensuring that the understanding from a sentence does not occur through a compound that the rule concerning the "Great Option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*) is established. The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the distinction between a compound and a sentence is determined by their very nature (*svabhāva*).

And thus says the Bhāṣya: "In this case, there are two alternatives: occurrence (*vṛtti*) and non-occurrence (*avṛtti*), and that occurs by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). Since both the sentence (*vākya*) and the compound (*vṛtti*) are present, and since a permanent suffix would [otherwise] apply to the domain where occurrence is natural, what else could possibly be connected by the mention of the option (*vā-vacana*) other than the technical name (*saṃjñā*)? And neither the existence nor the non-existence of a technical name is intended here," and so forth. Because occurrence is necessary when there is the state of having a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), it is impossible to prescribe an option regarding that occurrence; therefore, there can only be an option regarding the technical name.

And thus, the meaning is that there would result the contingency of conceptualizing an effect based on that [compound]. However, if in this case it were a *tatpuruṣa* compound by the force of the statement alone, even without [inherent] capacity (*sāmarthya*), then since such a conceptualization could be established, there would be no occasion for introducing this commentary (*bhāṣya*) in the present context.

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, having raised a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the tenth book (*daśamika-adhikaraṇa*)—specifically regarding the injunction "the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] should have two *sāmans*, like the *ekāha*"—based on the Vārttika which states that in the passage "the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) should be performed with the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* *sāmans*," there is a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva* in its prior member; they then conclude that because the Vārttika applies only to cases where a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is required for the first member, this is merely a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*. Therefore, every day, between the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, some *sāman* must be used, but not both.

They established the conclusion that there are two [sets of six days]. Regarding this, Dīkṣita says: "That is not so, because there is no reason for insisting on a specific distinction in accent up to the end of the compound. Nor should it be argued that this results in the occurrence of two separate compounds; for it has already been stated in the *pūrvapakṣa* itself that, since the conjunction is understood through the very exhaustion of the six-day period, those [two sets] do not occur every day.

In reality, however, since only three examples involving the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) are cited in the Bhāṣya, and since Kaiyaṭa also states that the *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds therein function precisely as non-counter-examples to the absence of the application of compound-final suffixes, it is proper to conclude that [the rule] pertains exclusively to those cases. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa states: "And here, the *dvandva* is governed by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*."

However, it has been stated that in the case of *itaretarayoga-dvandva*, the distinction [from *samāhāra*] arises precisely through the resulting meaning (*kārya*); otherwise, even in *itaretarayoga*, there would necessarily be a difference in accent, which would lead to the conclusion that the aforementioned text is inconsistent. This should be carefully considered. In the case of *samāhāra*, examples are *pañcamūlī* and *pañcakumārī*; the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is "the collection (*samāhāra*) of five roots" and "the collection of five young women. It is not, however, "five roots collected," because the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant.

Nor should it be argued that even when resorting to the collective application of the *karma* (object) and the *sādhana* (means), that [term] would still be correct; for in the case of *pañcakumārī*, the shortening of the *upasarjana* would not apply. This is because, in the rule governing compounds (*samāsa-śāstra*), it is not prescribed as the first member (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*); and since it lacks a fixed case-ending due to its connection with various case-endings, the designation of *upasarjana* cannot be established even by the rule "that which has a single case-ending" (*ekavibhakti*).

Nor can the matter be settled by [assuming] the neuter short vowel [for *kumāri*], because even so, the form *pañcakhaṭvī* would remain unestablished. For this form occurs under the view that it is feminine according to the rule "optionally when ending in *ṭāP*" (*vā ṭāvantaḥ*). In that case, in the absence of the short vowel, the suffix *ṅīp* would not apply by the rule "after a *dvigu* compound ending in a short vowel" (*dvigor ataḥ*). However, in the final Siddhānta, since the connection with various case-endings resides in the collective sense of the compound, the word *kumārī* is invariably in the genitive case; thus, its status as an *upasarjana* (secondary member) is established by the rule "that which has only one case-ending" (*ekavibhaktiś ca*).

Nor should it be argued that because it will be stated later that "the singular number does not apply when there is a single case-ending [other than the genitive]," its application is precluded here—as in the case of *arthapippalī* and similar compounds—since that rule is intended only for *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compounds). For in this context, the authority is precisely the Bhāṣya which establishes the term *samāhāra* as denoting an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*). Furthermore, there is greater complexity [in the alternative view] due to the introduction of the rule "the singular number for a *dvigu*. However, if the term refers to the abstract state (*bhāva*), since the collection (*samāhāra*) is inherently one, that rule is unnecessary; thus, there is simplicity.

Nor does this lead to an impossibility of connecting the substance with actions such as "bring" in cases like *pañcamūlīm ānaya* ("bring the five-roots [compound]"), because that connection is possible through implication (*ākṣepa*), just as in *gām ānaya* ("bring the cow") under the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning. As for the rule *dvigurekavacanam* ("the dvigu compound takes the singular ending"), it should be understood that its formulation was intended for the upcoming statement *sa napuṃsakam* ("it is neuter"). It might be argued: since the words *samāhāra* ("aggregate") and *samūha* ("collection") have the same meaning, and since the aggregate is also the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the mention of *samāhāra* would be redundant because the desired result is already established by the rule *taddhitārtha-* itself. Furthermore, there is no risk of hearing the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) pronounced, because the elision (*luk*) is possible by the rule *dvigor lug* ("elision after a dvigu").

One might object: "In this case, for the word *pañcamūlī*, the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—by the rule *aparimāṇavistācitakambalyebhyo na taddhitaluki*—would apply, just as in *pañcāśvā* (‘bought with five horses’) and similar forms; furthermore, in *pañcagavam*, the suffix *ṭac* would not occur, because of the exclusion [of such cases] by the rule *gorataddhitalukī*. This objection should not be raised, because in both instances, one can avoid the phrase *na taddhitaluki* (‘when there is no elision of a taddhita suffix’) and instead read the sūtra as *samāhāre* (‘in the sense of a collective compound’), and by relying on its restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*), all cases are successfully accounted for.

The feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the compound-ending suffixes occur only when there is a collective sense (*samāhāra*) following the elision of a secondary derivative (*taddhita-luk*), and not otherwise. Therefore, "a collection of five horses" is *pañcāśvī*, and "a collection of five cows" is *pañcagavam*; however, it is not the case that *pañcāśvā* refers to [the horses] or that *pañcaguḥ* means "bought for five cows. This very point was stated by the author of the Vārttika: "Since there is no distinction between a collection (*samāhāra*) and an aggregate (*samūha*), the mention of 'collection' is redundant because it is already established by the meaning of the secondary derivative. Because there is no distinction—that is, no difference in meaning—the rule of single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) does not apply, as the focus is on the phonetic form of the words themselves.

Regarding this, the commentary states: if this were the case, then in the example *pañcakumāri*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix by the rule *luk-taddhita-luki*. Therefore, because of the separate mention of "aggregation" (*samāhāra*), it is explained that for the compound alone the meaning of aggregation is expressed, and not for the secondary derivative (*taddhita*); thus, there is no occurrence of the secondary derivative. For this very reason, in the rule *taddhitārthe*, the locative case is explained as a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Consequently, in examples such as *pāñcanāpitī*, the production of the secondary derivative occurs. However, if the meaning of the secondary derivative were already expressed by the compound itself, that derivative would not arise due to the principle of "the expression of what has already been stated" (*uktārthatvāt*).

And likewise, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *dvigor-luk* would also be inconsistent; for if one were to explain the production of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) on the strength of that very [elision], it would involve excessive complexity—so enough of this prolixity.

The rule for forming a *dvigu* compound is stated by means of the word "uttarapadena" (with a final member) and "parimāṇinā" (with a measure-possessor). Examples are *dvimāsajātaḥ* ("born two months ago") and *trimāsajātaḥ* ("born three months ago"). For in this case, since time-periods are [treated as] measure-possessors (*parimāṇin*), a three-word compound is desired; however, it would not be obtained under the rule *sup supā* because of the intended expression of singular number. Therefore, this *vārttika* is commenced. In that regard, the intention of expressing singular number is the very mark [of its necessity]. Once the word *jāta* has been placed as the final member (*uttarapada*), a *dvigu* compound is formed between the words *dvi-* and *māsa-* based on the final member, according to the rule *taddhitārtha-utpattya-vīpsāsu* etc.

At the end of the word *kāla*, when a *dvigu* compound is formed, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member shall apply; and in the case of *dvyahnajāta*, there is also the application of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*).

Nor should it be said that *dvimāsam* (two months) is a *samāhāra-dvigu* compound which, by virtue of being included in the *pātrādi* group, does not take the feminine gender, and that this [term] forms a *taddhita* compound with *tajjātasya* ("born of that"). For if that were the case, the vowel *ā* of the suffix *-as* would be udātta, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the vowel *ā* of the word *dvimāsa-* would also be udātta. It must rather be stated that the prohibition applies everywhere in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). For in the analysis (*vigraha*) "she has five beds" (*pañca khaṭvā asyā vidyante*), there would only be a *tatpuruṣa* compound under the rule *taddhitārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), and not a *bahuvrīhi*; because the *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed specifically for the sense of possession, and that sense of possession is precisely what constitutes the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix.

Nor can the capacity of the rule prescribing *bahuvrīhi* compounds be invoked as a justification; for that rule finds its scope in examples such as *citraguḥ* (one who has brindled cows), where it is indeed applicable. Nor can one accept this as a desired outcome (*iṣṭāpatti*), because [if it were so], the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule "after a *dvigu* ending in *ā*, [there is] *ṅīp*" (*āvantatvena dvigoḥ*), and in the alternative case where that suffix is absent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of neuter gender. Similarly, in the case of *pañcaguḥ*, the suffix *ṭac* would have to occur. Nor can this be resolved by the rule "elision of the *matup* after a *dvigu*" (*dvigor lug*); for the governing heading is "before *prāgdīvyataḥ*" (*prāgdīvyateḥ*), and the *matup* falls outside that domain. Thus, the fault remains: the statement must be commenced for the purpose of eliding the *matup*.

Since the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the compound-final suffixes is established by the very rule *ataddhitaluki*, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, because it will be stated that the remainder [of the rules] follows from the triplet [of suffixes], the *bahuvrīhi* applies by virtue of its subsequent position; such is the direction.
"A *dvigu* is a compound preceded by a numeral. (Pāṇini 2.1.52)

A *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by a numeral, prescribed in the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51), shall be designated as a *dvigu*. By this [designation], the elision (*luk*) of the suffix taught in the rule "dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.88) is explained in the case of *pañcakapāla*. In *pañcanāvapriya*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule "nāvo dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.99). In *pañcamūlī*, where there is a collective sense, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.21); because only the immediately preceding sūtra is understood [in that context], there is an absence of that [suffix] in *ekabhikṣā*.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of *ekaśāṭī*, the suffix *ṅīp* would not apply by virtue of the rule for *dvigu* compounds; for in that instance, the compound is formed with the word *śāṭī* itself ending in *ṅīp*. In the case of *śāṭakā*, however, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for generic names (*jāti*) from the stem *śāṭa*, which serves as the base for the suffix *kap*. Nor should it be argued that *ekāpūpī* would not be possible; for its formation is established precisely by the rule concerning collective compounds (*samāhāra*).

Because a single [act] can also constitute a *samāhāra* (aggregation) due to the greatness of a gift or an undertaking involving multiple objects, or due to an excess of faith, or due to the excellence of the task, since that very [single act] possesses the nature of an aggregate. Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as *pañcahotāraḥ* and *daśahotāraḥ*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*)—prescribed by the rule *igante dvigau*—would not occur; for that is possible because of the Vedic extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of words such as *divodāsa* within the section concerning initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*).

For this very reason, in the compound *saptarṣayaḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member does not occur; rather, there is only the udātta accent on the final syllable. This is because of the observation [in the Vedic texts] that "the seven seers who sat down for austerity" (*saptarṣayas tapase ye niṣeduḥ*).
*Kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.53): [A word denoting something contemptible is compounded with words expressing the grounds of that contempt.]

In the *gatyādi-sūtra*, because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *kuts* (to despise) in the present tense. Due to the use of the plural number, the view that the rule refers merely to the phonetic form of the word is rejected. Words denoting objects of contempt are compounded with words expressing that contempt. This [compounding] occurs only when the contempt pertains to the cause for the application of the word (*pravṛttinimitta*). Furthermore, this [sūtra] is intended to ensure that the qualifier (*viśeṣya*) is placed first; thus we have *vaiyākaraṇakhasūci*. [The term *khasūci* is derived from] the root *mūc* with the addition of the suffix *i* according to the rule *mūcayateḥ ic ca*.

When one who is questioned by an opponent, in order to avoid being drawn into that line of inquiry, says something such as "Oh, how cloudless is the sky! or gazes at the sky, he is described in this way; the intent is his incapacity for investigation. It is not here a censure of the study of grammar, but rather of a lack of intellectual brilliance (*pratibhāna*). Nor should it be said that such [lack of brilliance] is not the cause for the application of the term [to him], because the censure of the study is justified precisely on the grounds that it does not produce a particular kind of intellectual brilliance.

A *yājñikakitava* (a sacrificial gambler) is generally a gambler who, out of a desire for wealth, asks "What do you have?"—this being the meaning of the word *kitava*, as seen in the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) from the imitation of the sound "kiṃ tava asti" ("What do you have?"). For this very reason, the *Śruti* states: "The gambler goes to the assembly hall asking [for stakes]. Thus, even a ritualist (*yājñika*) who, being intent solely on the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), officiates at a sacrifice for one who is unworthy to be sacrificed for (*ayājya*), is called a *yājñikakitava*. Regarding the term *mīmāṃsakadurdurūṭha*: the root *dul* means "to throw up. The suffix *kūṭa* is an *auṇādika* formation added to the prefix *dur-*, which here conveys the sense of "difficult to fill" or "excessive. Thus, it refers to a stubborn or perverse Mīmāṃsaka.

The elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs frequently even in other instances. Regarding the identity of *ra* and *la*: "If some fault has been attributed to me by certain people in a particular dialect—such as 'the grammarian is poor'—it is not the study [of grammar] that is censured here, but rather the person who possesses the quality [of poverty]; and poverty and so forth are caused by that [fault]. [This is expressed by the rule: *pāpāṇake kutsitaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.54).

These are compounded with words denoting contempt; this is for the purpose of reversing the rule regarding the prior placement [of the first member]. Examples: *pāpanāpitaḥ* (a bad barber), *aṇakakulālaḥ* (a wretched potter); the meaning is "contemptible. [The next rule is:
"Words expressing a standard of comparison are compounded with words expressing a common property. (Pāṇini 2.1.55)

Words denoting the object of comparison (*sādṛśyapratiyogin*) are compounded with a word expressing a quality (*dharmavācin*) that serves as the cause for the similarity between the two. For example: *ghana iva śyāmo ghanaśyāmaḥ* ("dark like a cloud," i.e., "cloud-dark"). In this instance, although "darkness" (*śyāmatva*) is presented as an attribute of the object of comparison (*upameya*), the darkness of the cloud is nonetheless understood through the sense of the meaning (*arthagamyam*). For this very reason, the word *vacana* is included [in the rule] to ensure the inclusion of a term denoting a substance (*dravya*) qualified by a quality. Here, the word *ghana* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean something similar to a cloud.

However, on account of past usage, it possesses the status of a standard of comparison; for this very reason, they say that in the expression *mṛgīva capalā* ("fickle like a doe"), the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) is triggered by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) according to the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*.

In reality, even in the case of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), if the masculine form were applied by virtue of the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) induced by that [indication], then in the example *śāstrīśyāmā*, the same [masculine form] would occur; for the prohibition [of the masculine form] by the rule *jāteśca* is equal in both cases. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated that the application of the masculine form is otherwise established simply by not intending to express the feminine gender, as in the case of *mṛgakṣīra* ("deer's milk") and similar expressions. In the expression *aravindasundaraṃ mukham* ("a face beautiful like a lotus"), there is *lakṣaṇā* on the part of the word *aravinda*, which indicates the cause of the similarity relative to the lotus.

According to some, there is a connection (*anvaya*) with beauty—which is a single part of the object "beautiful"—through the relation of non-difference (*abheda-saṃsarga*). Thus, the cognition arises: "The face is non-different from that which possesses the beauty that is the cause of the similarity as determined by the lotus. Others hold that the word "lotus" itself has all the meanings through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), while the word "beautiful" serves merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Still others maintain that the entire compound refers to such a qualified object.

In all these cases, however, the status of being an "elliptical simile within a compound" (*samāsagata-vācakaluptopamāna*), as established in the tenets of the Alaṅkāra school, would not be maintained; this has been explained by us in the *Alaṅkāra-kaustubha*.
A word denoting comparison is compounded with words such as *vyāghra* (tiger) and the like when used without the addition of a common property (*sāmānya*). Pāṇini 2.1.56.

The object of comparison (*upameya*) is compounded with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such as "tiger" (*vyāghra*) and so forth, provided that the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) which serves as the basis for the similarity is not explicitly used. This is a rule intended to ensure that the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is placed first in the compound. For example: *puruṣo vyāghra iva* (a man like a tiger) becomes *puruṣavyāghraḥ*. The meaning is: a man who possesses a similarity whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a tiger. Precisely for this reason, according to the tradition of the Alaṅkārikas, in a *upamita-samāsa* (comparison compound), the meaning of the prior member is predominant, whereas in a *rūpaka-samāsa* (metaphorical identification compound), such as *mukhaṃ candraḥ* (the face is the moon), the meaning of the subsequent member is predominant. Why is the word "common attribute" (*sāmānya*) used? [Consider: *puruṣo 'yaṃ vyāghra iva śūraḥ* (this man is a tiger-like hero). Here, because the word "hero" (*śūra*) is used, the compound does not form.

Now, one might ask: "How is it that the ocean of the Bhāṣya is 'extremely deep'? And one should not say that this is merely a *mayūravyaṃsaka*-type compound; for if that were so, it would result in the abandonment of the primary status of the Bhāṣya under discussion. To this, they reply: "In this case, the similarity based on depth is not intended; rather, it is precisely the similarity based on being difficult to fathom due to its vast extent and so forth. Since that [similarity] is not explicitly stated [in the compound], the formation of the compound is easily achieved. Nor should it be said that the rule for forming such compounds applies only when there is an absence of a common property (*sāmānyadharma*).

The meaning of the sūtra is that there is no non-employment of that property which is intended to bring about similarity (*sāmya*); for it is precisely by the employment of such a property that [the similarity] is established. Nor should it be said that there is a lack of evidence here, because since the non-employment of a mere generality (*sāmānya*) is contradicted [by the very fact of similarity], the final sense of the sūtra concludes as: "there is non-employment of that property which is intended [to express similarity]. *Viśeṣaṇam viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (2.1.57). [This sūtra provides the rule: An adjective is frequently compounded with the noun it qualifies.

A qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is compounded with a coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For example, *nīlam utpalam* (a blue lotus) becomes *nīlotpalam*. Furthermore, there is no insistence that a qualifier must be exclusively a differentiator (*vyāvartaka*), but rather it is simply a mode (*prakāra*); this is because of such usages as *prameyavahnih* (a fire that is an object of knowledge). For this very reason, this compound occurs when either the qualifier or the delimitor of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) deviates from the other, but there is no rule requiring mutual deviation. Although such deviation exists in cases like *nīlotpalam*, it is absent in the aforementioned instances.
Likewise, there is no rule that this compound occurs only when the delimitor of the qualifier (viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka) deviates from the delimitor of the qualificand (viśeṣyatāvacchedaka).

For this very reason, Murāri [uses] "the moon-sprout that is the ornament of the matted locks on the slopes of Mount Kailāsa"; Śrīharṣa [uses] "the mountain that is the moon, O beautiful one, according to its own will"; Vardhamāna [uses] "the thousand-rayed sun to the lotus-flower of the system of logic (tarka-tantra)"; and Haradatta [uses] "the mango tree of the science of grammar (śabda-śāstra). Regarding these, Kaiyaṭa maintains that since the status of being the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) are inherently relational, even though either one might be understood through implication (*ākṣepa*), the mention of both is for the sake of clarity.

Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of the term "viśeṣya" (the qualified) is necessary for the sake of establishing the designation *upasarjana* by virtue of being mentioned first, and for the sake of the rule regarding the obligatory prior placement of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because that [designation] is already established simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *sub*. And this is the distinction: where both terms are quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), or action-words (*kriyāśabda*), or both quality and action-words, there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*) regarding the status of qualifier and qualified; this [rule] concerns that domain.

However, with respect to words denoting qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*), a word denoting a substance (*dravyaśabda*) possesses only the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). This is because by employing the term "qualificand," one obtains conformity with established usage. Consequently, in cases such as *khañjakāṇaḥ* / *kāṇakhañjaḥ*, *pāṭhakapācakaḥ* / *pācakakapāṭhakaḥ*, and *khañjapāṭhakaḥ* / *pāṭhakakāṇaḥ*, there is optional prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) in both ways. But in cases such as *kṛṣṇatilāḥ*, *nīlotpalam*, and *pācakabrāhmaṇaḥ*, the rule is that the substance alone is the qualificand.

This is because a quality, by means of delimiting the substance, participates in the action; thus, with respect to that [quality], the substance holds primacy within the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

For this very reason, regarding the injunction "one should immolate a white goat," when a [goat] qualified by both [whiteness and goat-hood] is not available, one immolates a goat that is delimited by another quality (such as redness), but not some other substance delimited by whiteness; so say the authors of the Bhāṣya. Likewise, the claim that "the blue lotus" (*utpala-nīlam*) is indeed grammatically valid is refuted and should be disregarded because it is rootless. This is because, even though the speaker's intention alone is the regulator of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that such a compound is ungrammatical (*asādhutva*), and because the author of the Nyāsa and others have explicitly stated the same. The commentators on the *Līlāvatyupāya* also hold this very view; such is the direction of the argument.

What is the purpose of including the word *bahula* ("mostly")? It is so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *takṣakaḥ sarpaḥ* ("Takṣaka the serpent"), *rāmo jāmadagnyaḥ* ("Rāma the son of Jamadagni"), or *arjunaḥ kārtavīryaḥ* ("Arjuna Kārtavīrya"). Furthermore, it ensures that the compound occurs invariably in cases such as *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ* ("black snake") and *lohitaśālir* ("red rice"), whereas in cases like *kārtavīryārjunaḥ*, the compound indeed occurs because it is observed in usage. Thus, in instances involving the relation between a general term and a particular term, the established rule is that the general term functions as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and the particular term functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
This is because, according to the principle that "a general term without a particular is no general term at all," there is necessarily a requirement for a particular.
And [the terms] pūrva, apara, prathama, carama, jaghanya, sama, anu, madhya, madhyama, and vīra [are also used as ordinal numbers]. || 57 ||

These words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) are compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix that has the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*). This rule is intended to establish the fixed position of *pūrva* and other such words even when they are compounded with words denoting qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*). Examples include *pūrvavaiyākaraṇaḥ* (a former grammarian) and *aparādhyāpakaḥ* (a latter teacher), and so forth. Although in the case of *dṛptaḥ sarājanyakamekavīraḥ* ("the proud one, the sole hero among the assembly of kings"), the application of this very rule would be correct—since it applies later and thus overrides the rule *pūrvakālaika-* (P. 2.1.49)—resulting in *vīraikaḥ*; nevertheless, some maintain that a "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) should be understood here. Others say that this is due to "diversity of usage" (*bāhulaka*).
Guilds and the like [are formed] by those who have completed their apprenticeship and so forth. || 59 ||

The statement regarding the sense of the suffix *cv-* should be applied to words such as *śreṇi* (guild). For example: "those who were not guilds (*aśreṇayaḥ*) have been made into guilds (*śreṇayaḥ*)" is expressed as *śreṇīkṛtāḥ*. Because a word ending in *cv-* functions as a *gati*, it forms an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, resulting in the form *śreṇīkṛtāḥ*. A *śreṇi* is a group of those who subsist by a single craft or trade. There is no compounding of *śreṇi* when it refers to established groups; however, when there is the imposition of a new quality—specifically, when those who were previously separate are brought together into a guild—then compounding occurs. As Māgha says: "where on the merchant's highway there are groups formed [into guilds]."

*Śreṇī*, *eka*, *pūga*, *kunda-rāśi*, *viśiṣṭa*, *nicaya*, *nidhana*, *indradeva*, *muṇḍa*, *bhūta*, *śravaṇa*, *vadānya*, *adhyāpaka*, *abhirūpaka*, *brāhmaṇa*, *kṣatriya*, *paṭu*, *paṇḍita*, *kuśala*, *capala*, *nipuṇa*, and *kapaṇa*—these constitute the group beginning with *śreṇī*. The group beginning with *kṛta* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). [Pāṇini 2.1.60: A word ending in a *kta*-suffix, when not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, forms a compound with another word ending in a *kta*-suffix that is not itself preceded by *nañ*.

A word ending in *ktā* (past passive participle suffix) that is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ* is compounded with another word ending in *ktā* that is joined with *nañ*, provided that the former exceeds the latter in syllables (*mātrā*). For example: *kṛtaṃ ca tad akṛtaṃ ca = kṛtākṛtam* ("done and not done"). This expresses the state of being both done and not done with respect to a single object, delimited by a single part. Examples include *pītāpītam* ("drunk and not drunk") and *uditānuditam* ("risen and not risen"), and so forth. Here, in the rule "not preceded by *nañ*," the term *anañ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. When there is a requirement for a qualifier, the word ending in *ktā* which is presented by a word in the instrumental case is connected as a nominative due to its status as a qualifier.

Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "If the restriction is expressed by the negative particle *nañ*, it should not be assumed to be qualified by the augment *nuṭ* or the augment *iṭ*. And: "But if there is an intention to express something additional, the operation applies to that which has the same root. The meaning of this is as follows: the word *viśiṣṭa* (qualified) refers, when there is an intention to express a comparative determination (*sampradhāraṇa*) between two things, to an excess qualified by the restriction; however, when there is an intention merely to describe the essential nature (*svarūpa*), it refers to mere excess alone.

When it is said, "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are wealthy and handsome, but Devadatta is superior to Yajñadatta in his Vedic study (*svādhyāya*)," there is indeed a superiority based solely on Vedic study. However, from experience, one perceives either the equality of other qualities at some times, or merely the superiority in Vedic study at others; for it is understood that other qualities are not intended to be expressed [in the latter case].

And here, regarding the phrase "qualified by *nañ*," if the intention is to express merely the addition of *nañ*, then just as [the rule] does not apply to other verbal bases—as in the case of *siddhaṃ cābhuktaṃ ca*—so too it would not apply when qualified by *nuṭ* or *iṭ*, as in *kliṣṭākliśitam* or *uditānuditam*, and so forth. Alternatively, if the meaning is merely the addition [of the augment] and not the exclusion of other specific features, then just as it applies when there is the addition of *nuṭ* or *iṭ*, it would likewise apply to other verbal bases, such as in *siddhaṃ cābhuktaṃ ca*.

Therefore, it should be stated that [the rule applies] when the *prakṛti* (base) is the same. Consequently, it does indeed apply when there is an increase in modifications (*vikāra*) that do not result in a different meaning; however, it does not apply when there is a different *prakṛti* at the beginning. For example: *chātāṃchāvam*. Here, the substitution of *ā* by "śāchor anyatarasyām" occurs. But in cases such as *trāṇātrātam*, because the [substitution of *na* for *ṇa*] is treated as *asiddha* (not yet established), there is no differentiation caused by the change to *na*. An addition should be made for compounds such as *kṛtapratikṛta*: *kṛtāpakṛtam*, *muktavimuktam*, *pītavipītam*, *gatapratyāgatam*. In these, the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*).

The term *gatapratyāgatam* is formed by the association of a journey with a return occurring shortly thereafter; likewise for *yātānuyātam*. The term *krayākrayikā* ends in the suffix *ka* in the sense of "smallness" (*alpārtha*) and is feminine by its very nature (*svabhāvāt*). The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *anyeṣām api* (Pāṇini 6.3.137). Because the second member [of the compound] signifies "small," the first member, *kraya*, implies by implication a "large purchase. Similarly: *puṭāpuṭikā*, *phalāphalikā*, and *mānonmānikā*. To establish forms such as *śākapārthiva* and others, the elision of the middle member (*uttarapadalopa*) must be added to the list [as a supplement]. Thus, one who is fond of vegetables (*śākapriyaḥ*) and is a king (*pārthivaḥ*) is called *śākapārthivaḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its form).
The words *san*, *mahat*, *parama*, *uttama*, and *utkṛṣṭa* are compounded with those that are being honored. (61)

These [words] are compounded with words that are praiseworthy (*praśasya*). This rule is commenced to establish the fixed position of words such as *sat* at the beginning of a compound when joined with words expressing qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*). Examples: *satpāṭhakaḥ* (an excellent reader), *mahārājaḥ* (a great king). As for the case of *puruṣottamaḥ*, some—relying on the *Upāya-grantha*—argue that since the word *uttama* would logically take the first position in a compound because it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), they justify the placement of the word *puruṣa* first by appealing to "optional usage" (*kāmacārāt*). That view should be disregarded, as it contradicts this very rule. [The question is: Why is the word *pūjā* (worship) mentioned? [To provide a counter-example:]...

"An excellent ox" (*utkṛṣṭo gauḥ*) means "one raised from the mud. In compounds such as *mahodadhiḥ* ("great ocean"), the term *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier) applies. However, in cases like *mahāpāpam* ("great sin"), this [type of compound] applies precisely because of being honored; for the purpose of praise consists in an excellence that is co-locatable with the delimitor of what is expressed by the final member of the compound. And that [excellence] should be understood as simply the production of greater suffering in comparison to other sins.
[The rule] "That which is being honored is compounded with *vṛndāraka*, *nāga*, and *kuñjara*" (Pāṇini 2.1.62).

Some say that since [the term] belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by its form) beginning with *vyāghra*, the rule is established; this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction, meaning "only when being honored. Others say it is for the purpose of an injunction even in the case of general usage. In reality, that [usage] occurs when similarity (*sādṛśya*) is to be understood; however, this [present rule applies] only when excellence (*prāśastya*) alone is to be understood. This is because from expressions such as *govṛndāraka* ("an excellent bull"), there arises a cognition characterized by excellence, and not a cognition whose qualificand is the referent of the first member and whose qualifier is a similarity having the referent of the second member as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). The meaning of "being honored" (*pūjyamāna*) is that the compound occurs when honor is to be understood. *Katara-katamau jātiparipraśne* (2.1.63): [The terms] *katara* and *katama* [form a compound when used] in an inquiry regarding a genus (*jāti*).

These two [words] are compounded with a capable [word]: *katarakaṭhaḥ* (which Kaṭha?), *katamakalāpaḥ* (which Kalāpa?). According to the technical definition, "a lineage (*gotra*) together with its branches (*caraṇa*) constitutes a genus (*jāti*)," [the suffix] *-tama* is applied. Although it is established that the word *katama*, being derived by the rule "optionally, when there is an inquiry regarding a genus among many, the suffix *-tamaj* [is used]," refers exclusively to that [genus], and thus by association (*sāhacarya*), the inclusion of the word *katara*—which likewise refers to that [genus]—is also achieved; nevertheless, the explicit mention of "inquiry regarding a genus" in the case of the word *katama* is for the purpose of making known its correctness even in other instances.
For this very reason, they offer the counter-examples: "Which Devadatta among you, or of yours, is he?
[The particle] *kim* is used in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). 64.

"What kind of king? [means] "one who does not protect. There is a prohibition of the *samāsānta* suffix [in this case] by the rule *kimaḥ kṣepe*. What is the purpose of the mention of *kṣepa*? "What king?"—this is a question.

[The following compounds are formed with the first member being a genus (*jāti*) and the second member being one of the following: *poṭā*, *yuvati*, *stoka*, *katipaya*, *gṛṣṭi*, *dhenu*, *vaśā*, *vehat*, *baṣkayiṇī*, *pravaktṛ*, *śrotriya*, *adhyāpaka*, and *dhūrta*. (65)

*Poṭā* is defined by Amara as "one possessing the characteristics of both female and male. Some maintain that its primary denotation (*śakti*) is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*), while the commentators on Amara state it refers to a woman endowed with breasts and a beard. *Gṛṣṭi* is a cow that has calved once; *dhenu* is one recently calved; *vaśā* is a barren cow; *vehad* is one that destroys the fetus; *vaṣkayiṇī* is one whose calf dies; *ibhapoṭā* is a young female elephant; *agni-stoka* is a small spark; *udaśvit* is buttermilk; and *gogṛṣṭi* and so forth. Śrīharṣa writes: "The milk of a mare, a female donkey, a *vaṣkayiṇī*, and a *dūṣkayiṇī*... (Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya).

"Kaṭhapravaktā" and so forth. Nor is the meaning of "kaṭhadhūrta" already covered by the rule *kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.53), because that rule applies only when there is a censure of the *pravṛttinimitta* (the primary ground for the application of the word). Here, however, it is the substratum (*dharmin*) itself that is being censured. They say that [the reading] "dhūrtabakobālamatsyānām" is an error. As for the usage in the *Kusumāñjali*, "If it be argued that even the ascetics learned in the three Vedas are merely *dhūrtabakas*," one should understand that the compound involves the word *baka* used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean those similar to a *baka*, combined with a locative of specification (*nirdhāraṇasaptamī*).
And [there is a compound] with words denoting praise (*praśaṃsāvacana*). 66.

The inclusion of the term *vacana* (word) is for the purpose of including words that are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) solely in the sense of praise, by excluding: (1) derivative words such as *praśasta* and others which denote specific qualities and are used in senses other than their own primary meaning; and (2) words such as *vyāghra* (tiger) and others which indicate praise through metaphorical usage when applied to something other than their own primary meaning. As Amara states: "The words *matallikā*, *macarcikā*, *prakāṇḍa*, *udgha*, and *tallaja* are denoters of what is excellent (*praśasta*). Furthermore, these [words] are restricted to specific genders.

"Arir madhuraikṣata gomatallikām" (The enemy looked at the excellent cow)—thus says Māgha. Similarly, there are forms such as *gomacarcikā* and so forth; the meaning is "an excellent cow. This is because the author of the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi* states: "The words *matallikā*, *praśastā*, *prakāṇḍa*, *sthalamitta*, and others [denote excellence]. Regarding the phrase "the temples (*kapolabhittī*) of that single elephant," the commentators on the *Raghuvamśa* maintain that the word *bhitti* is used here in the sense of praise. Some suggest that since the two rules—"words of praise" (*praśaṃsāvacana*) and "prostitute, young woman" (*poṭā-yuvatī*)—could have been combined into a single rule, the result of having formulated them as two separate rules should be considered. [And: "A young man [is compounded] with a bald man, one with grey hair, one with wrinkles, and an old woman. (67)

"jaradbhiḥ" is an alternative reading. Regarding the first reading, since the word *yuva-* has a different gender, it cannot stand in grammatical apposition with the feminine word *jaratī-*. Consequently, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" is made known as the means of establishing that the word *yuvati-* ends in the feminine gender. Nor should it be argued: "Even so, because there is a difference in meaning, let that [inclusion] occur even earlier, through the mere imposition of apposition. This is because [the rule] must be stated precisely for that purpose.

This is because it is appropriate to establish a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) everywhere based on the impropriety [of the alternative] and in accordance with the requirements of the *lakṣya* (the forms to be explained). Furthermore, since many feminine forms such as *śramaṇī* and others are listed [in the *gaṇapāṭha*], the rule "with *śramaṇa* and others" (*kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ*) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Nor should it be argued that there is no distinction here because an objection (*ākṣepa*) is possible in that case; for in the rule prescribing the suffix *phañ* after words like *aśva*, the fact that the *gaṇasūtra* specifies "when masculine" (*puṃsi jātaḥ*) can itself serve as the indicator.

Otherwise, if the word *jāta* were specified in the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*), its mention would be useless because it would be impossible to include that which is qualified by a different gender; for in reality, since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is grasped as the end of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavat*), the term *puṃsi* (in the masculine) serves the purpose of excluding [other genders], and thus they say that the previously stated view alone is correct. *kṛtyatulyākhyā ajātyā* || 68 || [Words] called *kṛtya* and those expressing similarity [are compounded] with words not denoting a genus (*ajāti*). || 68 ||

Words ending in kṛtya suffixes that have the same meaning as [words expressing] "equal" (tulya) are compounded with words not denoting a genus (ajāti). Examples: *bhojyoṣṇam* (food that is hot), *bhojyalavaṇam* (food that is salty), *tulyaśvetaḥ* (equally white), *sadṛśaśvetaḥ* (similarly white). Why say "not denoting a genus"? Consider *bhojya odanaḥ* (rice that is fit to be eaten); here there is no compound because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*), due to the force of the prohibition. Regarding the usage by Bhāravi, *tasya satkṛtyaśālinaḥ*, they say that although this [rule] would apply after *sanmahat-* (P. 2.1.61), it is instead a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. 69. A word denoting color is compounded with another word denoting color.

A word denoting a specific color is compounded with such [a word denoting another color]. For example: *kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ* (black-spotted). Even though the term "variegated" (*citra*) could apply to a mixture of black and other colors, the word "black" is used because, according to the view that "variegated" is a collection of various colors existing non-pervasively (*avyāpyavṛtti*), black is also present therein. However, according to the view that "variegated" is a distinct entity, since the cognition of it can be accounted for by the blackness residing in its parts alone, there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding that [whole].

[Objection: But surely this is already established by that very rule. Likewise, the rule "the first member retains its original accent (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) when [a word] ending in *varṇa* is compounded with [another] word ending in *varṇa*" need not be prescribed either, since it is already established by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, when the third member has the sense of *tulyārtha* (having the same meaning as 'equal to,' etc.)". [Reply: Not so. Because in cases such as *śukababhruḥ* ("tawny like a parrot") and *kṛṣṇaśuklaḥ* ("blackish-white"), that [result] does not occur. For this very reason, the rule concerning accent must be stated by both [rules]. In the case of *kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ* ("black-spotted"), it is for the purpose of preventing the first member from retaining its original accent by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, when the third member has the sense of *tulyārtha*."

And likewise, in the Svarasūtra, let it simply be "varṇo 'netaḥ. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the rule "tatkṛtena" (Pāṇini 2.3.21)—wherein there is a compound ending in an instrumental case—would also apply where there is a compound with "varṇa" as the first member; for [the rule] refers only to a compound of "varṇa" that is explicitly stated in the text.

However, some maintain that this sūtra need not exist because it is justified by a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) alone; they say that the *sva*-sūtra should remain exactly as it is heard [in the original text]. It should be stated: "When there is a desire to form a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), a *karmadhāraya* compound is not formed. By this, forms such as *vīrapuruṣavān grāmaḥ* ("a village possessing heroic men") would not occur. Rather, when the relation [of possession] is intended from the very beginning, the *bahuvrīhi* compound *vīrapuruṣaḥ* itself is used. And this is obtained through logical necessity (*nyāyalabhya*), according to the Bhāṣya.

For when a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied after a *karmadhāraya* compound, one must first rely on the predominance of the meanings of the constituent members (*vartipada*) to establish the *karmadhāraya*, and then rely on those same member-meanings being subordinate elsewhere to establish the possessive suffix; thus, there is a burden of conceptualization (*pratipatti-gaurava*). Kaiyaṭa, however, maintains that when the meaning of an external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is intended from the very beginning, the subordinate status of the constituent member-meanings is adopted right from the start; therefore, because it relies on the predominance of its own [compound] word-meaning, there is simplicity (*lāghava*).

However, some say that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the cognition of the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) arises from the two compounded words alone, whereas in a *karmadhāraya*, it arises only with the requirement of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*); thus, there is brevity (*lāghava*) in the expression. Furthermore, the separate usage of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is equal in both cases. Nor does this lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *vṛkṣavanasya*; for they maintain that since such usage is observed, the aforementioned brevity is disregarded only within the specific scope of the present topic.

It should not be argued that, if this were so, expressions such as *kṛṣṇasarpa-vān valmīkaḥ* ("an anthill possessing a black snake") or *lāhitaśāli-mān grāmaḥ* ("a village possessing red rice") would be impossible; for a specific class [of possessive suffixes] is understood only through a *karmadhāraya* compound. However, the formation of a *karmadhāraya* with words ending in *sarva-* and words ending in vowels (other than *a*) is desired. Therefore, it must be stated that here the suffix *ṭhan* is set aside and only *ini* occurs: *sarvadhanī*, *sarvabījī*, *sarvakeśī*. [The rule continues: "A *kumāra* [is compounded] with *śramaṇa* and so forth. (Pāṇini 2.1.70)

In this context, the word *kumārī* (young girl) forms a compound with words such as *śramaṇā* (ascetic), which are listed with feminine endings; however, it forms a compound in both ways [as feminine and masculine] with words such as *adhyāpaka* (teacher), which have masculine endings. This is because when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that stem is understood to include its specific gender forms as well. Thus: *kumārī-śramaṇā* (a young female ascetic) and *kumāra-śramaṇā* (a young male ascetic). The feminine forms are: *śramaṇā*, *pravrajitā* (renunciant), *kulaṭā* (unfaithful woman), *garbhiṇī* (pregnant woman), *tāpasī* (female ascetic), *dāsī* (female slave), and *bandhakī* (prostitute). The masculine forms are: *adhyāpaka*, *abhirūpaka* (handsome man), *paṇḍita* (scholar), *paṭu* (clever), *kuśala* (skilled), *capala* (fickle), and *nipuṇa* (expert). Furthermore, the aforementioned technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

In the supplementary rule regarding *śakti* and *lāṅgala*, the word *ghaṭī* is mentioned separately from *ghaṭa*; by virtue of this separate mention, in the case of *mahatī-priya*, the substitution of *ā* (as prescribed by the rule *ānmahataḥ*) does not occur, and in the case of *dviṣatī-tāpa*, the suffix *khac* (prescribed by the rule *dviṣatparayostāpeḥ*) also does not occur. Similarly, it should be noted that in *madrarājñī*, the suffix *ṭac* also does not occur.
[Pāṇini 4.1.64: "The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a bahuvrīhi compound ending in *catuṣpād* when it means 'pregnant' (*garbhiṇī*)."

Some maintain that the term *jāti* (genus) is carried over [from the previous rule] by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Others hold that [the terms denoting genus] are understood because they are capable of conveying their meaning through internal fitness (*antaraṅgatva*) even without being mentioned alongside other words; however, terms such as *kālakṣepa* ("wasting time") are not included, because these etymological (*yaugika*) terms convey their meaning only through the proximity of other words. A word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) denoting a genus consisting of four parts is compounded with the word *garbhiṇī*. Thus, Bhavabhūti [uses the example]: "He who carries a fresh bundle of grass dear to the pregnant cow. (*gogarbhiṇīpriyanavolapamālabhārin*)

"In this place, there is the easy commission of the sin of killing the fetus of a pregnant doe by stumbling upon stone slabs scattered by the horns of buffaloes"—thus says Murāri. What is the purpose of the word *jāti* (genus/species)? [Consider: "a pregnant *kālākṣī* cow. Since the word *kālākṣī* denotes "pregnant" only through a modern convention (*ādhunika-saṃketa*), [the rule does not apply]. Why the requirement of "four-footed" (*catuṣpād*)? [Consider: "a pregnant Brāhmaṇī woman.
And [the compound] *mayūravyaṃsakādayaḥ* is also included. (Pāṇini 2.1.72)
These are derived as irregular compounds (*nipātana*). *Mayūra-vyaṃsaka* means "a peacock and a rogue"; here *vyaṃsaka* means a cheat. Some say this applies to all terms ending with *muṇḍa*.

Others, however, say that this is a compound that serves as an exception to the *upamita-samāsa* (metaphorical compounds), such as *mayūra iva vyaṃsakaḥ* ("a deceiver like a peacock"), *chātra iva vyaṃsakaḥ* ("a deceiver like a student"), and *kāmboja iva muṇḍāḥ* ("shaven-headed ones like Kāmbojas"). Nor is it redundant, because its purpose is to supersede the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) prescribed by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthā-tṛtīyā-iti*. This is because, in that context, only a compound containing a word for an object of comparison (*upamāna*) explicitly mentioned in the sūtra itself is intended to be included. [Examples from the Veda are: *chandasi pādagṛhya*, *hastagṛhya*, *laṅgūlagṛhya*, *punardāya*; and *yat prākṣiṇaḥ pitaraṃ pādagṛhyaḥ*.

Agni, the Hotṛ-priest, led [her] away by taking her hand. The third [example], *udāhāryam*, should be cited: "having given back the wife of the Brahmin. As for the designation of *gati* (prepositional prefix) in the phrase *punar canasauchandasī*, it is stated in a Vārttika.

In the case of *ehi-ḍā* and others, when they form a compound with another word as the referent (*anyapadārtha*), such as *ehi-ḍa*, it refers to that action in which [one says] "come, ḍa"; thus, *ehi-yava*. *Ehi-vāṇijā* is that action in which one says "come, merchant" (*ehi vāṇija*); likewise, *apohi-vāṇijā*. *Prehi-vāṇijā* is similar. *Ehi-svāgatā* is that action in which one says "come, welcome" (*ehi svāgata*). *Proha-karaṭā* is that action in which one says "push aside, Karaṭa" (*proha karaṭa*); likewise, *proha-kaṭā* and *proha-kardamā*. The use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Uddhara-cūḍā* is that action in which one says "pull up, crest-lock" (*uddhara cūḍā*). *Āhara-bālā* is that action in which one says "bring, child" (*āhara bāla*). *Āhara-vasanā* is that action in which one says "bring, garment" (*āhara vasana*). *Āhara-vanitā* is that action in which one says "bring, woman" (*āhara vanitā*).

*Kṛntavicakṣaṇā* refers to that action in which there is "cutting" (*kṛnta*) and "looking about" (*vicakṣaṇa*). *Kṛndhivicakṣaṇā* is an alternative reading. *Uddharotsṛjā* refers to that action in which there is "taking up from the vessel" (*uddhara*), "setting aside" (*utsṛja*), and "giving" (*dehi*); the mention [of these actions] is for the sake of indicating non-continuity (*asātatyārtha*). *Uddhamavidhamā*, *utpacanipacā*, and *utpatanipatā* [are formed similarly]. Since the action, which is the referent of the other member of the compound, possesses femininity, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied. *Uccāvacam* means "upward and downward. *Uccanīcam* means "high and low. *Ācopacam* (or *ācapracam*) means "heaped up and gathered together" (*ācitaṃ copacitaṃ ca*). *Ācapracam*.

*niścatam* (ascertained) and *pracitam* (accumulated) form *niścapracam*. One who possesses nothing is *akiñcanaḥ*; [the negative particle] *na* becomes *a-* before *kiñcana*, hence *yatkiñcanaḥ*. *Akālakaḥ* (one who has bathed): the final member of the compound is udātta by rule, and the absence of the suffix *lyap* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is understood in relation to an action contained within the compound, as is evident from the meaning "he has become [so]. *Asthirakaḥ* (one who has become steady) after drinking; *asuhitaḥ* (one who has become well-satisfied) after eating; *pāpīyān* (one who has become worse) after departing. Bhaṭṭi says: "O King, abandon that wretched man who, having departed, has become even more evil. *Apākalā* (one who has become unripe) after rising.

That which becomes pale after leaping up is *hastijvara*, also called *pākala*; its specific variety is *kūṭapākala*. Bhavabhūti says, "The *kūṭapākala* is as if harsh toward the young elephant (*kalabha*). According to the commentators on the *Gajaśāstra*: "The wind-natured *kūṭapākala* would indeed kill the elephant. [There are also the fevers] *nipatyarohiṇī*, *nipadyaśyāmā*, and *apehipraṇasā*.

The word *jahī*—the second person singular imperative of the root *han*—is frequently compounded with the object (*karman*) when repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is intended, provided that the agent (*kartṛ*) is also expressed. The form *jahī* is the ending of the second person singular of the *loṭ* (imperative) mood. When repetition is to be understood, it is optionally compounded with the object; by means of this compound, the agent is also implied. For example, *jahijoḍaḥ*: one who says "kill, o fool" repeatedly is called *jahijoḍaḥ*. Similarly, *jahistambaḥ* and *ujjahistambaḥ*.

When one verbal action is joined with another to express continuity of action, it is called *ākhyātamākhyātena*. For example, *āśrītapibatā* (eating and drinking), where it is said that [the action] is performed constantly; as Bhaṭṭi says: "She was intent on the work of love, eating and drinking. Other examples include *pacatabhṛjjatā* (cooking and roasting), *khyādatamodatā* (eating and rejoicing), *āharanivapā* (bringing and sowing), *āharaniḥkaṣā* (bringing and scraping out), *utpacanipacā* (cooking up and cooking down), and *bhindhilavaṇā* (break and salt) or *pacalavaṇā* (cook and salt)—that in which such [actions] occur is so named. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); other instances should also be understood from the usage of learned authorities.

One who has no fear from any source is *akutobhaya*. One who asks, "In which direction shall I go? is *kāndiśīka*; the suffix *īkaṇ* is applied by virtue of the rule for *pāṭhasāmarthya*, and there is no elision (*aluk*) of the second case ending. Amara states: "A *kāndiśīka* is one who has fled in fear. "Aho puruṣa" means one who possesses egoism (*ahaṃkāra*); the state of such a person is *āhopuruṣikā*. Kaiyaṭa notes that the suffix *vuñ* is applied here because the word belongs to the *manojñādi* group. Śrīharṣa says: "The sun’s vow of being an *āhopuruṣa* consists in his attentiveness to the lotus and the kuśa grass."

*Ahama-hamikā* is that state in which one thinks, "I am capable, I am capable. *Yadṛcchā* means "by chance" or "accidental. *Ehireyāhirā* is that [state] in which one says, "Come here! Go away! [The long vowel *ā* at the end is due to the rule of *pāṭhāt ātvam*. *Unmṛjā'vamṛjā* is that state in which one says, "Wipe it up! Wipe it down! In these two cases (*eireyāhirā* and *unmṛjā'vamṛjā*), the suffix *ā* is grammatically correct. *Avaśyakāryam* means "that which must necessarily be done. *Vanāntaram* means "another forest"; the word *antara* has the sense of "different. Here, it qualifies "forest" by way of non-identity. Furthermore, the opposition (*pratiyogitva*) is perceived as belonging specifically to the referent of the first member of the compound when there is a difference.

In expressions such as *vanāntaraṃ gacchati* ("he goes to another forest"), there arises the cognition that "he goes to a forest distinct from this forest. Furthermore, this is observed in cases such as *vanāntarādupāvṛttaiḥ* ("having returned from another forest"). Therefore, the word *antara* has the meaning of "distinct" (*bhinna*). Alternatively, the word *vana* (forest) is construed twice. It functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the difference (*bheda*), through a relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by the property of being that specific individual (*tadvyaktitva*). Moreover, it should be noted that it possesses the status of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*), which is determined by the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) of the difference as delimited by its own qualification (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchinna*).

Thus, "the meaning of the nominal stem itself" (prātipadikārtha eva) means merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārthamātra*). In the case of *mukhacandraḥ* ("moon-face"), where there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*), the grammarians hold that the compound is formed according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsaka*-type compounds. Regarding this, some maintain that the cognition is "the moon as non-different from the face" (*mukhapratiyogikābheda-vān candraḥ*). Others hold that it is "the moon as the counter-correlative of the non-difference residing in the face" (*mukhaniṣṭhābhedapratiyogī candraḥ*). This detailed analysis is clearly explained in the *Alaṅkāra-kaustubha*.
Thus ends the third section (*ahnika*) of the first quarter (*pāda*) of the second chapter in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*, and the quarter is completed.
Now the second quarter: "The words *pūrva*, *apara*, *adhara*, and *uttara* [are compounded] with a word denoting a single whole when expressing a part thereof. (Pāṇini 2.2.1)

The words "pūrva" (front) and others are compounded with a whole (*avayavin*) qualified by the number one. For example, *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* becomes *pūrvakāyaḥ* (the front part of the body). It should be stated that the substitution of *paśca* for *apara* occurs [in this context]. As Kālidāsa says: "He entered with the hind part of his body, for the most part, out of fear of the falling arrow. This rule is intended to exclude the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For the word *pūrvakāya* is established even by the descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), according to the maxim that words functioning to denote a whole may also apply to its parts. Thus they say.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *diś* (direction) is seen [in the compound], the term *dik-śabda* refers to a word denoting direction, and thus when joined with the word *pūrva*—which also denotes a direction—the fifth case (*pañcamī*) alone would be appropriate by the rule *anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte*, rather than the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This is because the indicator (*liṅga*) in the rule *tasya param āmreḍitam* shows that the sixth case is intended precisely when there is a connection with a constituent part (*avayava-yoga*).
