As for the claim that the word *ekadeśin* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) for a constituent part, and for this very reason they say it possesses a suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*), that is not correct.

The rule "not from a *karmadhāraya*" (Pāṇini 4.1.54) is set aside by the very fact that it is a *sautra* (Vedic-style) formulation, just like [the rule] "after *eka-gopūrvāt*" (Pāṇini 4.2.104), which takes the suffix *ṭhañ*. As for the expression "the followers of one part of the Nyāya" (*nyāyaikadeśinaḥ*) and so forth, it is figurative in both cases. However, if the word *ekadeśin* is ungrammatical when referring to the owner of a part, then it must be assumed that this is a *nipāta* (irregular formation) specifically denoting the relationship between a part and the whole. Why say "by the *ekadeśin*"? Consider the example: *pūrvaṃ nābheḥ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body from the navel"). Here, the ablative case in *nābheḥ* is used in the sense of direction (*digyoge*). The meaning is: the anterior portion of the body in relation to the navel.

In this context, [the compound] *pūrva-pratinābhi* is not a compound because "prior" (*pūrva*) lacks the status of being a whole (*avayavin*) with respect to the limit (*avadhi*) which is the navel; however, it does indeed form a compound when combined with "body" (*kāya*), as in *pūrva-kāyo nābheḥ* ("the front part of the body from the navel"). This is because the word "prior" is invariably dependent on a correlative. Why is the requirement "having a single substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇa*) stated? Consider: *pūrvaṃ chātrāṇām āmantrayasva* ("First, address the students"). Here, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the collective group. Because the distinction between its parts is prominent, there is plurality; and because it is not delimited by unity, no compound is formed.

Regarding this, the commentators state that by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *saṃkhyā-visāya-pūrvasya*, the substitute *ahna* is applied to every word denoting a part of the day, such as *madhyāhnaḥ* (midday) and *sāyāhnaḥ* (evening), because otherwise the status of being preceded by *sāya-* would be untenable. Furthermore, since that *jñāpaka* refers to the general case, it is indicated that any word expressing a part [of time] is compounded with a word for time. By this, forms such as *madhyarātraḥ* (midnight) and *uparatāḥ paścimarātragocarāt* (ceased from the sphere of the latter part of the night) are established.

They say that because the rules *ahaḥ sarvaikadeśa-* etc. and *āhna āhnika-* etc. apply only to *ekadeśi-samāsa* (partitive compounds), they cannot account for both cases through a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (attributive compound); furthermore, by the maxim "that which is established by a *jñāpaka* [indicative rule] does not apply everywhere," forms such as *dinamadhya* (midday) are established.
The neuter [gender] is half. || 2 ||

The word *ardha* (half), being invariably neuter (*nityaklība*), is compounded with a whole (*avayavin*) that is delimited by oneness (*ekatvāvacchinna*). For example: *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* becomes *ardhapippalī*. Furthermore, the rule regarding the neuter gender means that the compound occurs only in that sense where the word is necessarily neuter. This is not established merely by the mention of the form *ardham* [in the rule], because that is intended to indicate that gender and number are non-essential (*atantra*) in this sūtra. Consequently, in expressions such as *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that"), the application of the rule occurs even when all three genders are present.

According to Amarasimha: "The word *bhitta* means a fragment or a piece; the word *ardha*, when denoting an equal portion, is masculine or neuter. The meaning is that the word *ardha*, when expressing an equal division, functions as a neuter gender only.

Regarding this, they say: the term *vā puṃsi* (or masculine) applies to both [the remaining two cases]. Among those, because of the neuter indication for the first two, and because a grammatical alternative between masculinity and femininity is untenable, the meaning is "not feminine" (*astriyām*). This is because it is established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that there is no copulative compound (*dvandva*) of words with different genders, and thus a neuter gender is impossible for the word *khaṇḍa*. Furthermore, in the case of the word *śakala*, the absence of femininity is certain precisely from its stated indication. However, in the case of the word *ardha*, since masculinity is understood from its indication, the phrase *vā puṃsi* applies without distinction to both the feminine and the neuter.

Furthermore, [the opponent argues] that the word *ardha* is feminine; however, this is incorrect. Since the status of [the word *ardha*] as not being feminine (*astriyām*) has already been established previously, it is logical that its meaning remains the same in subsequent instances as well. Moreover, the governing rule concerning words (*śabdādhikāra*) is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). In cases such as "the deities (*daivatāni*) are optionally masculine," "or [the word] *padma* is masculine," or "or *haricandana* is masculine," since the optional masculine alternative is obtained only along with the neuter, the mention of the neuter gender would result in an unintended optionality with respect to the feminine as well.

It should not be argued that, whereas in those [other cases] the prescription of both masculinity and its absence leads to the acceptance of the gender specified in the case of its absence, here—because the masculinity already established by the specific mention and the rule is unfit for further prescription, and because there is no distinction in the prescription of its absence—the other two genders are established, since there is no reason to accept only one of them. This is because the state of being neuter exists in both the preceding and the following [cases], and because elsewhere, in the case of its absence, only one [gender] is prescribed.

Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that [the word] must be stated as being in all three genders (*triṣu*). If femininity is intended, let it be so on the basis of other authorities; however, the *Amarakośa* intends [the word] to be of both genders (*dviliṅga*) alone. Kaiyaṭa states that when denoting a part, it takes all genders according to the nature of what is expressed (*abhidheya-vaśāt*). Kṣīrasvāmin also, having stated "in the masculine by usage" (*nirdeśāt puṃsi*), explained: "some say it follows the gender of the object expressed (*vācyaliṅga*). The commentary on the *Yaṭṭīkā* says: "'It follows the gender of the object expressed' refers to its application to the individual parts. This is the general direction.

Furthermore, in a *vigraha* (analytic) sentence, because the word *pippalī* has a fixed case-ending, it does not incur the shortening of its vowel by virtue of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). This is due to the prohibition: "When there is a single case-ending, [the rule applies] only to those words that are not in the genitive case. What is the purpose of the condition "having the same substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇe*)? Consider: *ardhaṃ pippalīnām* ("half of the *pippalī*s"). However, the form *ardhapippalyaḥ* occurs through the application of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of similar forms) after the compound has been formed. The difference in meaning, however, is clear. Why is the condition "with a part-possessor" (*ekadeśinā*) stated? Consider: *ardhaṃ paśor Devadattasya* ("half of Devadatta's animal"). Here, Devadatta possesses ownership (*svāmitva*) with respect to the animal;

however, the compound is indeed formed with the animal as before. Why is the neuter gender specified? Consider: *grāmārdhaḥ*, *nagarārdhaḥ* ("half of a village," "half of a city"). These are masculine.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, have rejected this [view]. They argue that by accepting the application of words whose function resides in a whole (samudāya) to its parts (avayava), forms such as *ardhapippalī* are established precisely as *karmadhāraya* compounds. Otherwise, in cases such as *ardhākāraḥ*, *ardhajaratīyam*, *ardhoktam*, and *ardhavilokitam*, the formation would be untenable due to the absence of an equal division (*samavibhāga*). Nor is it for the purpose of subverting the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), since that too is desired; as Kālidāsa says: "By love, she who takes half of Śiva’s body... By this, [the following is also explained]: "Their faces were proud from chewing betel-leaves bought for half a *paṇa*."
These pilgrims, whose saliva drips from lack of practice [in walking], proceed on their way. || 1 ||
This and so forth has been explained.
[The forms] *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, and *turya* may optionally [be used]. 3.1.24.

These [words] are compounded with a whole (avayavin) when there is identity of substance (dravyaikye). The second example is *bhikṣāyā dvitīyam* (the second of the alms), which becomes *bhikṣā-dvitīyam*. The same applies to other cases. The rule is also accepted for the fourth case (*turīya*). Why "with a whole"? [Consider: *dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāyā bhikṣukasya* (the second alms of the beggar). Here, let there not be a compound with the owner, the beggar. Why "when there is identity of substance"? [Consider: *dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāṇām* (the second of the alms). And in this case as well, this rule is not redundant, because—as in the previous instance—it would otherwise be covered by the *karmadhāraya* or the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

This is because the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is prohibited by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa* (Pāṇini 2.2.11). Nor is that same fault present even when the sūtra is introduced; for, by the force of the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally"), the prohibition does not apply. Nor can it be argued that this [term *vibhāṣā*] serves to establish an alternative syntactic meaning, since that is already established by the *mahāvibhāṣā* itself. Furthermore, one cannot assume that the prohibition of the genitive compound does not apply here by forming the word *tīya* with the suffix *an* in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to the rule *pūraṇādbhāge tīyād an*, on the grounds that derivative suffixes (*svārthika*) possess meaning through the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*), and thus the suffix *an* also conveys the sense of "filling" (*pūraṇa*).

This follows from the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Nor does the status of being for the purpose of filling consist solely in being prescribed by the rule governing filling (*pūraṇa-adhikāra*); for in that context, only the general state of being for that purpose is taken as the criterion. Furthermore, there is no inconsistency in forms such as *kumbhapūraṇabhavaḥ paṭuruccaiḥ*, because even though the words *pūraṇa* and so on would not themselves become udātta [by that specific rule], the term "filling" (*pūraṇa*) and others in the grammatical indications (such as *pādapūraṇam*) refer specifically to suffixes (*pratyaya*).

And it is not the case that, because the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "after the sixth and eighth, *añ*" (Pāṇini 5.2.127) would also be subject to the prohibition due to its being a pūraṇa-saṃjñaka, the usage of Kālidāsa—“*tānyuñchaṣaṣṭhāṅkitasaikatāni*” (those sandy banks marked by the sixth [gathering] of gleanings)—would be untenable. Some say this is because that usage is erroneous. Others say that from the word *ṣaṣṭha*, by adding the causative suffix *ṇic* according to the rule "that which one does, one describes" (Pāṇini 3.1.26), and then the suffix *ac* because it belongs to the *pacādi* class, [the form *ṣaṣṭha* is derived]. Still others say it means "the sixth among the gleanings" or "the sixth consisting of gleanings," according to the maxim that words function with respect to the whole (*samudāyavṛtti*).
And [the suffix *kta* is used] after [words meaning] "attained" (*prāpta*) and "arrived" (*panna*) when combined with the second case. (4)

*Prāptajīvikaḥ* means "one who has obtained a livelihood. Similarly, *āpannajīvikaḥ*. In these cases, the compound is formed by the rule *dvitīyā-śrita-* (Pāṇini 2.1.24). Thus, we have *jīvikāprāptaḥ* and *jīvikāpannaḥ*. Nor is the meaning already expressed by a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for otherwise, the final accentuation of the compound would not be established. Furthermore, in examples such as *prāptasukham*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the past participle being placed at the end according to the rule *jāti-kāla-sukhādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.59). By the maxim regarding words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa-paribhāṣā*), *prāptajīvikā* refers to a woman who has obtained a livelihood.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *jīvikā* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) by virtue of the rule *ekavibhakti ca*, its vowel would be shortened, and thus the substitution [of *ā*] would not occur in the word *prāptā*. This is because the *Bhāṣya* states that the vowel *a* is elided (*praśleṣa*) so as to prescribe the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the preceding member. Nor does the elision of *a* after the dual ending result in the application of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), according to the ancients, on the grounds that this is a Vedic-style (*sautra*) usage. Alternatively, it is a collective *dvandva* compound; the requirement for the substitution of *ā* depends on the context, meaning that the substitution of *ā* occurs for the words *prāpta* and *āpanna*.

Nor does it follow that the designation *upasarjana* would fail to apply to those two because they lack the status of being "first-mentioned" (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*), for that designation is established for those two alone either by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *su*, by proximity (*sannidhāna*), or by the inherent force of the formulation of the rule itself. Kaiyaṭa maintains that if the designation were established for what ends in the second case (*dvitīyānta*), then the purpose of the rule would already be served by the previous rule, *dvitīyāśrita-* etc. Dīkṣita, however, holds that there is a phonetic combination (*praśleṣa*) at the end of the sūtra. *Kālāḥ parimāṇinā* || 5 || [Time-denoting words [are compounded] with a word denoting the object measured. || 5 ||

Time-words are compounded with a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix that expresses the object to be delimited. For example, one for whom a month has passed since birth is called *māsajātaḥ* ("month-born"). It should not be argued that even in a compound there would be no hearing of the genitive case in the word *jāta*; for the relationship, being expressed by the compound, is included therein, and according to the principle that "what has already been expressed [by a compound] is not used [again in a separate word]," the genitive does not appear. However, in expressions such as *māsajātasya vastram* ("the cloth of the month-born"), the genitive occurs because it denotes the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). This is because the relationship of delimiting and delimited (*paricchedyaparicchedakabhāva*) alone is included within the compound formation (*vṛtti*).

For this very reason, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound and its analytical expansion (*vigraha*), the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is reversed; this is due to the inherent nature of linguistic power (*śabdaśakti*). Consequently, in expressions such as "let one born after a month be seen" (*māsajāto dṛśyatām*), it is only the one who is born that connects with the action, and not the month, even though the month is the primary element in the analytical expansion. Furthermore, singularity is understood here in reference to the month, again due to the inherent nature of the word, since numbers such as duality and so forth are relative. For this same reason, it was stated by Hari:

"In the case of *śaurpika* (a measure of grain) and 'born after a month' (*māsaja*), the measure [of time] functions according to its own nature, having recourse to limiting conditions (*upādhi*) through various distinctions of number."

Devadatta’s state of being delimited [by a month] is mediated by birth; the meaning is that he is the locus of that birth which is delimited by the month. And thus, the resultant meaning is that "being delimited" is a relation (*saṃsarga*). This [relation] consists in the property of occurring at a time that is not the locus of the prior absences (*prāgabhāva*) of the days constituting that month. It does not, however, consist in the property of ending at a time that is not the locus of the prior absences of the moments constituting that month, because the term "born in the month" (*māsajāta*) is applied even to one who was born at midday on the first day of that month.

In view of the requirement for the application of that suffix (*tacchabda*), the month is established by the force of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of applying the suffix even to something produced after that month, because the pastness (*atītatva*) of the meaning of the suffix is also manifested in the act of production (*janana*). Thus, the meaning is: "that which is the substratum of a past production occurring at a time that is not a locus for the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the days constituting that month. Expressions such as *dvyahnajāta* ("born two days ago") have been explained previously.

If this is the case, then while it is established that a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of three words occurs only when there is a measure (*parimāṇin*), whereas elsewhere it consists of only two words, how then are [the following] to be explained: Kālidāsa’s “*trilokanāthena satā makhadviḥ*” (by him, being the lord of the three worlds, who was twice a sacrificer) and the *Kāvyaprakāśa*’s “*navarasarucirām*” (delightful with its nine sentiments)? Nor should it be argued that one first forms a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (descriptive compound) of the first two words and then forms a two-word *tatpuruṣa* from that result; for such a rule is prescribed only for the names of directions and numbers (*dik-saṃkhyayoḥ saṃjñāyām*). Furthermore, in the case of a collective *dvigu* compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

Because it is impossible to assume that [the word *trilokī*] belongs to the *pātra*-class based on the observation of such forms as "yadi trilokī gaṇanāparā syāt" (if the triple world were intent on counting), they say here: the triple world (*triloka*) consists of three parts (*tryavayava*). It belongs to the *śākapārthiva*-class, because the word *loka* refers to the aggregate [of the three worlds]. And this is clear in the Bhāṣya.
[The suffix *nañ* follows. 6.

This negative particle (*nañ*) is compounded with a noun. Examples include *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (non-Brahmin) and *avṛṣalaḥ* (non-Śūdra). Regarding this, they say: the state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is indicated by the negative particle; and that [state] resides in the delimitor of the referent of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārthatāvacchedaka*). Thus, the compound is denotative (*śakta*) of that which is qualified by the superimposed Brahminhood. The relation between the qualifier and the qualificand is indeed the superimposition itself. However, the cognition of one who is different from a Brahmin is the result of the implied meaning (*ārtha*). For this very reason, since [the term] is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*), the functions of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*)—such as those prescribed for "not that" (*atasmin*) and so forth—are successfully established.

In this regard, the following must be said: since superimposition (*āropa*) is necessarily untenable, how can there be a cognition whose relation is that [superimposition]? This is because the superimposition residing in the speaker is sublated by the non-perception of what is fit for perception (*yogyānupalabdhi*), and because a superimposition residing in another [person] is beset by a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*). Indeed, it is impossible for a cognition whose relation is superimposition to arise from the word "Brāhmaṇa," since the relation [of the word's meaning] is precisely the inherence (*samavāya*) that serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the effectness of the knowledge of its own expressive power (*śakti*).

Because the term "brāhmaṇa" is not applied to one who possesses *brāhmaṇatva* (the property of being a Brahmin) by means of temporal relation (*kālika*) and so forth, and because Miśra and others maintain that a cognition whose qualifier-part regarding the universal (*jāti*) is unconditioned (*niravacchinna-prakāratā*) occurs only when inherence (*samavāya*) or identity with its own locus (*svāśrayatādātmya*) function as the relational content (*saṃsargatā*), it is impossible for a cognition that does not have something else as its qualifier regarding the portion of *brāhmaṇatva* to serve as the relational content of a superimposition (*āropa*). Nor should it be argued that here the relational content of the superimposition is simply that which is qualified by the relation of inherence or identity with its own locus.

Nevertheless, it is not tenable for "superimposition" (*āropitatva*) to be expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*), because we do not accept that a relation (*saṃsarga*) can be expressed [by a particle]. Furthermore, if superimposition were the relation, there would be no possibility of subsequently cognizing a difference (*bheda*) as being real. Nor should it be argued that superimposition appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) over "Brahminhood," and that a cognition of difference arises implicitly because superimposition is not accepted in its own locus; for if that were so, the statement that superimposition is the relation would become redundant.

Furthermore, because "brahminhood" is not present as itself [in the cognition], it is impossible for its status as being superimposed upon that [substratum] to appear as a qualifier; moreover, this contradicts the experience of [the cognition] as being non-qualificative with respect to the aspect of brahminhood.

Furthermore, is "being superimposed" (*āropitatva*) a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)? It cannot be the first, because there is no evidence for such a superimposition at that time. Nor can it be the second, because since that which is superimposed [as "non-Brahmin"] exists in a Kṣatriya and others as well as in a Brahmin, the resulting cognition of difference from them would not be established even in a figurative sense. Therefore, in the expression "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), it is correct that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—namely, difference—is construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) delimited by Brahminhood, while the difference itself is construed as a qualifier in its locus. For this very reason, the term is not applied to an actual Brahmin.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*) would not be established; for the Naiyāyikas maintain that this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), just as in the case of *ardhapippalī* and similar compounds. By this, the view that "mere superimposition (*āropa*) is what is indicated, and the relation is the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*)" is also refuted. If it is objected: "In this case, in forms such as *asaḥ* and *asarvasmai*, the substitution of *satva* (the replacement of *s* by *r*) and the replacement of *su* by *smāy* would not occur, because the internal class-properties (*antargaṇakārya*) of the group of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) are not admitted for subordinate members (*upasarjana*)," we reply as follows: In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), even you must accept that the rule *etattadoḥ sulopaḥ* means "there is elision of the *su*-case ending which expresses oneness residing in the referent of *etad* or *tad*. Thus, the elision of *su* is established even in these cases.

And thus, in examples such as *aneṣo dadāti* ("this one gives") and *aso dadāti* ("that one gives"), since the meaning of the suffix is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), the number "singularity" cannot be construed with it; consequently, the elision (*lopa*) [of the case-ending] would not otherwise apply. Therefore, this is intended to indicate that in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāman*) apply even to the subordinate member. Nor should it be argued that in the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.106), the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) need not be required, as there is no evidence for it. For, by the inclusion of the qualifier *akoḥ* (meaning "not having the augment *akac*"), which serves to exclude forms accompanied by *akac*, the rule specifically refers only to those two [forms, *etad* and *adas*], when they are indeed pronouns.

In the phrase "savyate'nekayā sannatāpāṅgayā," however, the singular number is used because the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is singular. For this very reason, in examples such as "etānyaneke jaladherivormayaḥ" ("these many waves, like those of the ocean"), plurality arises from the cognition of the substantive. By this, the rule "anekamanyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24) is explained; for even there, the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*)—referring to the genus (*jāti*)—is the substantive. Thus, the plural form "aneka" is used because the things superimposed with unity constitute the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and not because of an intention to refer to a plurality of actual bases.

Alternatively, one should not even resort to the view that this is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) compound consisting of "many" and "not many. Let this detailed discussion suffice. As for the opinion that this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant—taking the predominance of the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its basis, meaning "that in which Brāhmaṇahood does not exist"—and that in cases such as *unmattagaṅga*, since the *avyayībhāva* here subordinates the *tatpuruṣa* to the *bahuvrīhi*, the result is the absence of the suffix *kap* by the rule *nadyṛtaśca*; that too has been refuted in the *Bhāṣya*.

Because [the rule] beginning with "atasmin" (Pāṇini 1.4.10) is not established; because in the case of "avarṣā hemantaḥ," there would result a singular ending even for a specific [instance] occurring in winter; and because in cases such as "adhano brāhmaṇaḥ," there would result the adoption of the gender of the subsequent word. However, according to another view, the definition of a Brāhmaṇa is: austerity, sacred learning, and birth.

Because of the statement: "He who is devoid of austerity (tapas) and sacred learning (śruta) is merely a Brāhmaṇa by birth. Words such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth are capable of denoting both the collection of his qualities and his birth; thus, the meaning of the compound *abrāhmaṇa* is "an incomplete Brāhmaṇa. That too is incorrect, because it would result in the application of the word *abrāhmaṇa* even to one who is a Brāhmaṇa by birth.
[As it is said: "One is known as a Brāhmaṇa by birth; he is called twice-born (dvija) through sacramental rites (saṃskāra)."

Furthermore, in accordance with such statements, austerity (*tapas*) and sacred learning (*śruta*) merely bestow excellence and thus lack the status of being the primary grounds for the application of the term *brāhmaṇa*. For this very reason, based on the authority of Kumārila’s statement—"The prohibition against drinking liquor, however, rests upon the caste (*jāti*)—this is the settled rule"—the established doctrine is that in injunctions such as "A *brāhmaṇa* shall not drink liquor" and "One shall not kill a *brāhmaṇa*," the reference is solely to the caste.

Therefore, it is stated in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* that even though Jābāla was devoid of [Vedic] purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and the like, Gautama’s engagement in performing those rites for him arose from his ascertainment of his Brahminhood, as expressed in the passage beginning with "A non-Brahmin does not deserve to speak thus. This is also clear in the *Vedānta Sūtra*: "And [the rites are performed] when there is an ascertainment of the absence of that [non-Brahminhood]. Let us return to the subject at hand. As for the statement:
"Resemblance to that, its absence, its difference from that, its smallness..."

"Non-praise and opposition are proclaimed as the six meanings of the negative particle (*nañ*). Among these, the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). The others, however, are understood through the force of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), intended meaning (*tātparya*), and so forth. In the case of "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), when there is the cognition "one distinct from a Brahmin," it is understood that the non-existence [of the distinction] possesses a substrate-ness (*anuyogitā*) delimited by a property that is the direct pervader of the delimitor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*) residing in the counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*) of the distinction. This is because the term "non-Brahmin" is not applied to things such as jars.

For this very reason, in the case of the rule *ajapa-nyūṅkha-sāmasu*, since the single-tone (*ekaśruti*) is prescribed for that which is distinct from *japa* and the like—specifically for that which is delimited by the property of being a mantra (*mantratva*), which is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the functions such as *japa*—it is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that this [single-tone] is absent in the modified (*ūhita*) word *indraśatru*. Thus, the meaning is that the similarity of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) with respect to the property of the substratum (*anuyogin*), such as "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*), exists in reality (*vastugatyā*); however, there is no manifestation (*bhāna*) of similarity itself therein.

The "smallness" [of the water] in such cases as "there is no water in the pond" arises because the word *jala* (water) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for abundant water. By this, the expression "the girl has a slender waist" (*anudarā kanyā*) is explained. In the case of "you cook poorly, you scoundrel" (*apacasi tvaṃ jālma*), there is no elision of the negative particle (*nañ*) according to the rule *tiṅi kṣepe*. This is understood either through the figurative application of the root *pac* to excellent cooking, whereby the connection is with the absence of that [excellence], or through the root *pac* itself having the sense of poor cooking, whereby the connection is with the absence of that [poor cooking]; in both cases, the negative particle functions merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). The same should be applied to expressions such as "he has no knowledge of this."

In such cases as "contradiction is non-dharma" (*virodho 'dharmaḥ*), since a distinction from dharma exists even in actions such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) which produce that [dharma], the contradiction understood here is defined as the state of not producing dharma. This is perceived in acts such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmavadha*). Therefore, these meanings appear either by way of being specific counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) or otherwise; this is the general direction [of the argument].

However, this must be noted: even in the case of *avighnam*, a *tatpuruṣa* compound would apply here because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Since the *avyayībhāva* has its scope in examples such as *nirmakṣikam*, this objection being raised, it is said in reply: the coexistence of both types of compounds is indicated by the usage in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*, namely in the statements "the purposes [of grammar] are the avoidance of [grammatical] errors, the preservation [of Vedic texts], ease, and lack of ambiguity," "now, for the sake of non-phonetic combination (*asaṃhitāya*)," and "in the non-rapid [recitation], there is no phonetic combination (*asaṃhitā*). Thus, both are understood to apply.

This should be noted: if one intended to express the simultaneous connection of both the negation (*nañ*) and the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) with the word *brāhmaṇa*—as in "the state of not being a Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇatva*)—then, given that the formation of the compound and the addition of the suffix would both apply, the suffix would occur first because it is of higher priority. Furthermore, by the principle of "repeated application" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the compound would follow later. In that case, according to the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-tṛtīyā-...*, the word *abrāhmaṇatva* would have its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) due to the original accent of the first member of the compound. However, what is desired is that it should have its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix.

Therefore, the compound itself must come first; for since the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is dependent [on another], it lacks the required semantic independence (*asāmarthya*), and thus the suffix cannot arise. However, the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) does indeed occur because its principal member is independent; this constitutes the difference. Consequently, because it is taught later (*sati-śiṣṭatva*), the accent of the suffix prevails. Furthermore, they say that the acute accent on the preceding syllable is established by the rule *tal-ti-kit-su ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.169).
Slightly unmade. || 7 ||

Regarding this, there is a *vārttika*: "By the term 'denoting a slight quality' (*īṣadguṇavacanena*). The meaning is that, having removed [the word] *akṛta*, one should state instead simply "by that which denotes a quality" (*guṇavacanena*). By this, forms such as *īṣatpiṅgalaḥ* ("slightly tawny"), *īṣadraktam* ("slightly red"), and *īṣadunnatam* ("slightly raised") are established. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *īṣadgārgyaḥ* ("a slightly [inferior] Gārgya"), because although excellence and deficiency do not exist in the status of being a descendant of Garga, they are possible for the actions and qualities that function within that same referent; thus, in examples like *gārgyakalpaḥ* ("one who is almost a Gārgya") and *gārgyapāśaḥ* ("a wretched Gārgya"), qualities co-referential with that very referent are connected to its meaning. [The rule for] the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) follows. 8.

A word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is compounded with a compatible word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). For example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man) becomes *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king-man). Here, even for those who do not recognize the elision of the sixth case-ending, the understanding of the meaning occurs; thus, one alternative view holds that the word *rājan* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote "one related to the king," and its relation to the "man" is by way of identity (*abheda*). However, according to the Grammarians (*Śābdika*), since they accept a primary denotative power (*śakti*) within the compound itself, the cognition is such that the "man" is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), and the relation is the substratum-ness (*āśrayatva*) characterized by the connection to the king—this was stated previously. Furthermore, it should be stated that the sixth case ending resulting from a connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is also subject to compounding.

*idhmapravraścanaḥ* (wood-cutter), *palāśaśātanaḥ* (leaf-shatterer). This is a preliminary statement for what will be taught [later]: "The sixth case ending is not compounded when prescribed by its own specific rule. Other things shall be stated further on.
And [compounding occurs] with *yājaka* and so forth. 9.

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is compounded with these [words]. This is an exception (*pratiprasava*) to the rule "with *tṛc* and *aka*, when denoting the agent" (*tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari*). Examples: *brāhmaṇayājakaḥ* (one who sacrifices for Brahmins). [The following words are included: *yājaka*, *pūjaka*, *paricāraka*, *pariveṣaka*, *snātaka*, *adhyāpaka*, *utsādaka*, *udvartaka*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhartṛ*, *rathagaṇaka*, *pattigaṇaka*, and *vṛta*.

"It should be stated that 'there is a compound with a word ending in *tarap*, and there is the elision of *tarap*,' provided that the word *sarva* denotes excellence (*guṇakārtsnye*). This was recited in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra [Pāṇini 2.1.49]. A compound occurs between a word ending in *tarap* and a word expressing a quality (*guṇavācin*), and there is the elision of *tarap*. Examples are: *sarveṣāṃ śvetataraḥ* (the whitest of all), *sarveṣāṃ mahattaraḥ* (the greatest of all), and *sarvamahān* (the greatest of all). The Bhāṣya states that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 2.1.67] beginning with *pūraṇaguṇa*. The Vṛtti [on the sūtra *na nirdhāraṇe*] states that this applies to the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* [Pāṇini 2.2.10]. Its intention is that the prohibition of compounding for a quality (*guṇa*) applies only when the quality is compounded with its own substratum (*svāśraya*). *Na nirdhāraṇe* || 10 || [The compound is not formed when there is selection from a group. [Note: The term *guṇakārtsnye* refers to the state where a quality is intended to be taken in its entirety or in its highest degree; thus, the compound is permitted when the word expresses a superlative degree of a quality.]

The genitive case used in the sense of specification (*nirddhāraṇa*) does not form a compound. For example, in *nṛṇāṃ dvijaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* ("among men, the twice-born is the best"), because specification depends upon a reference to the class from which one is being distinguished, a compound would otherwise have been required. Now, how is it that *puruṣottamaḥ* ("the best among men") is formed? Regarding this, some say: specification occurs when both the object of specification and its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) are delimited by a single common attribute.

In the example "Among cows, the black one gives much milk," since the property of being a cow (*gotva*) exists in both [the subject and the object], there is a restriction (*nirdhāraṇa*). However, in this case, because the genus of selfhood (*ātmatva-jāti*), which is established as the delimiting factor for the inherent causality of pleasure, does not subsist in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is neither a restriction nor a negation. They say that if the delimiting factor for the denotation of the word "self" were established, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as all-pervading space or salt. This is not correct; for by the aforementioned reasoning, selfhood itself is established as the delimiting factor for the denotation of the word "self," and thus its establishment exists even in the water-atoms (*jalaparamāṇu*).
For this very reason, the use of the scriptural term "self" with respect to the Lord (*īśvara*) is consistent.

Others, however, say that the prohibition of the compound applies when both the object of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-viṣaya*) and its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), as well as the property serving as the basis for that selection (*nimitta-dharma*), are expressed by words. In the case of "the Supreme Self from among living selves" (*jīvātmabhyaḥ paramātmā*), since the possession of eternal knowledge and so forth is the basis for the selection, the compound occurs because that [basis] is not explicitly employed [as a word]. This is also the apparent intent of Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *dvivacana-vibhajya-upapade* (Pāṇini 5.3.94). In the *Līlāvatyupāya*, however, the compound with the ablative is formed through the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the fifth case (*pañcamī*).
"As I transcend the perishable (*kṣara*) and am superior even to the imperishable (*akṣara*), therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama."
Thus it has been stated, as spoken in the Bhagavadgītā:
"There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable."

The commentators on that [text] maintain that because it is stated there in this way, the meaning [of the compound] is thereby obtained. However, in the *Kusumāñjalī-upāya*, the compound is formed with a locative of specification (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*). Nor is the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) rendered useless; for it is stated that there is a difference between them: in that case (the genitive), the accent is on the final syllable, whereas in a locative compound, being a *tatpuruṣa* under the rule "tulyārtha" etc., the original accent of the first member is preserved. As for the objection that, since the compound [by the rule] "saṃjñāyām" is obligatory, a dissolution in its own words (*svapada-vigraha*) is improper—that is of no consequence.

In the rule *saptamī-śauṇḍaiḥ*, the compound is prescribed through the separation (*yogavibhāga*) of the term *saptamī*. For this very reason, the usage *nara-śūraḥ* ("a hero among men") is also established; the details regarding this have been explained elsewhere. Furthermore, it must be stated that a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not compounded. For example: *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"). Here, the genitive is prescribed by the rule *jño 'vidarthasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.51). Excluding the genitive prescribed by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50), every other genitive is one prescribed by a specific rule. Nor is the prohibition *na nirdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.2.10) redundant.

Since the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41) prescribes only the locative case, the particle *ca* was included so that the general sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which would otherwise be applicable, might not be superseded by the specifically prescribed locative; yet even with this allowance, it is the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50) alone that actually prescribes that [sixth case]. Thus, in cases such as *svāmī-īśvara-* and so forth, forms like *gṛhasvāmī* ("master of the house") and *sarveśvaraḥ* ("lord of all") are established.

In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: in the fourteen rules beginning with *jño 'vidarthasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.51) and the six rules beginning with *tadarthasya* (Pāṇini 2.1.36), the term *śeṣa* (the "remainder") is understood to carry over [from Pāṇini 2.3.50]. Since that [sixth case] is already established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50) alone, its prescription here is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). The sixth case occurs only where it is heard [in the rule]; for the absolute exclusion of non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) regarding the occurrence of the sixth case is established precisely by the mention of *śeṣa*. Even when connected with a verb, the particle *eva* has the sense of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

Furthermore, because there is an established linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) in certain instances such as "knowledge grasps the object" (*jñānam arthaṃ gṛhṇāti*), where the nominative case occurs; or alternatively, since there is no other case-ending (*vibhakti*) previously applicable that would need to be excluded by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only the genitive occurs," it is the elision (*lopa*) itself that must be excluded. Thus, the resulting meaning is that a compound (*samāsa*) is precisely what causes the elision of the genitive, and therefore does not occur here. Since a compound cannot possibly be excluded in the case of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)—as it never applies there—the purpose [of the rule] is to ensure the absence of genitive elision in examples such as "the remembering of the mother" (*mātuḥ smaraṇam*).

The authoritative scholars maintain that the example "mātuḥ smarati" (he remembers his mother) cited by the author of the Vṛtti and others is merely an illustration of forms ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Nor does this lead to the untenability of forms such as "harismaraṇam" (the remembering of Hari), for such forms are possible through composition with a genitive of object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). Nor is there a lack of distinction [between the two cases], because there is a difference: in the former case, the accent falls on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*), whereas in a compound with a genitive of object, the accent is that of the original form of the final member which ends in a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) due to its being governed by a grammatical factor (*kāraka*). This has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "When an action is expressed by *kārakas* and is further heard [as a verbal root], the 'word-for-word' genitive (*pratipada-ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed to prevent composition."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the expression *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("remembered by the mother"), because the prohibition of the genitive case for the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) applies by the rule *na lokāvyaya-niṣṭhā-khal-artha-tṛṇām*, and because a compound cannot occur with the remaining genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) according to the method already stated, the sentence alone is grammatically correct. As it has been said: "When a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is involved, the genitive case referring to the object is prohibited; a compound with that genitive, characterized as 'residual' (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*), is not desired there."

And thus, the prohibition [stated as] *pratipadavidhāna* (prescribed by specific rule) would be redundant; likewise, its exception (*apavāda*) stated as *kṛdyogācca* (also [prohibition] when joined with a *kṛt*-suffix) would also be redundant. However, in the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, because the word *śeṣa* (remainder) has been removed, this [rule] prescribes the genitive case even where it was not previously applicable; therefore, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) certainly occurs in connection with that. This is the general direction. [Now follows:

"With a word expressing a fraction (*pūraṇa*), a quality (*guṇa*), a word having the sense of *suhita*, a past participle (*sat*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a gerundive (*tavya*), or a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). (2.2.11)

The genitive case is not compounded with words meaning "ordinal" (pūraṇa) and with words such as "existent" (sat). For example: *satāṃ ṣaṣṭhaḥ* ("the sixth among the virtuous"). It was stated previously that only suffixes having the sense of "ordinal" are understood here. Regarding the term *guṇa*, those [words] which denote a quality alone (*kevala-guṇa*) as well as a substance qualified by a quality (*guṇaviśiṣṭa-dravya*) are included. For in examples such as *candanasya gandhaḥ* ("the fragrance of sandalwood"), there is indeed a difference in grammatical register (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). There is never a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as *candanaṃ gandhaḥ*. However, in the case of words like "white" (*śukla*), both constructions—*paṭasya śuklaḥ* ("the white of the cloth") and *śuklaḥ paṭaḥ* ("a white cloth")—are established.

Although grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) may occur through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* or by means of a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the substratum—this being the case even in expressions such as "sandalwood possessing fragrance" (*gandhavaccandana*) where the cognition of the substratum is equally restricted—nevertheless, the distinction is precisely this: [coreferentiality] does not exist without the possessive suffix *matup*. Furthermore, there is no established conventional usage (*nirūḍhatva*) of figurative indication for those specific words, and modern figurative indication is expressly prohibited. If it is objected that, according to the doctrine of non-difference-in-difference (*bhedābheda*), since the non-difference of qualities is admitted in the substance itself, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this principle to words such as "color" (*rūpa*) and so forth—the answer is: no.

For those [grammarians] also do not accept the usage or the cognition of "the form of the pot" (*ghaṭasya rūpam*); rather, they maintain that only those properties subsumed under *rūpatva* (the generic property of being color/form) can serve as the delimiters of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) for non-difference. Therefore, this prohibition applies only to those words delimited by a single sequence (*ānupūrvī*) which denote both a quality and the substance qualified by it; thus, in cases such as "the fragrance of sandalwood" (*candanagandhaḥ*) or "the form of the cloth" (*paṭarūpam*), the compound is indeed valid.

Nor should it be argued that there would be no negation in the case of "the whiteness of the cloth" because [the quality and the substrate] are always in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*); for even by one who maintains that a word expressing a quality to be conveyed brings about a cognitive connection through either grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), a compound is prohibited with such a word as well.

Furthermore, there exists in the word *śauklya*—which has as its base a word denoting a substance qualified by a quality (the suffix *-tva* expressing the abstract state that delimits the meaning of the base) and which denotes the white quality (*śuklaguṇa*)—the property of being expressible by it; and this is because the word *śukla*, which expresses that [quality], is expressive in both ways [as a quality-word and as a substance-word]. Nor should it be argued that, by taking the word *śukla* as expressing the quality expressed by the word *rūpa*, the same prohibition would apply to that [word *rūpa*] as well; for it was stated that the status of being expressive is determined by having the same mode of presentation (*samānaprakārakatva*).

It should not be asked: "How is such a distinction obtained? For there is authority for the *vārttika* rule, "and [the quality] is compounded with those qualities residing in that [substantive]. This is because the meaning of that rule is the capacity to convey a relation through distinction (*bheda*) with the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*). And since that capacity is common to all qualities, it follows that the capacity to convey a relation through mere distinction is obtained. Nor should it be argued: "The example 'the Brahmin's white' is not valid, because [the word 'white'] has expectancy only with respect to teeth and so forth. For when the substantive is determined by context or other means, it is capable of being connected even with the quality 'white.'

However, there is no prohibition regarding *śaikṣya* (the state of being under training). Furthermore, the addition of "one hundred thousand" to "niṣka," as well as "one hundred *krośas*" and "one hundred *yojanas*," is established because the statement of the Three Sages—"he gives even one hundred *khārīs*"—serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Moreover, this prohibition of the genitive compound with a quality word (*guṇa*) is not absolute, as evidenced by the usage of the Sages such as "subordination of the meaning of the second member" (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*). Consequently, compounds such as *yatnagaurava* ("great effort") are established. Words having the sense of *suhita* mean "satisfied. For example, "satisfied with fruits" (*phalānāṃ suhitāḥ*). When there is a desire to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case is used; for the prohibition in the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛṇām* applies specifically to the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix.
But surely, in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence [of forming a compound] with the third-case instrumental, as in "satisfied by fruits" (*phala-tṛpta*) and so forth:

"Satisfied by various kinds of fruits and by sweet, cool waters, they asked that radiant lady, 'To whom does this city belong? *phalair nānāvidhaiś citraiḥ svāduśītaiś ca vāribhiḥ | tṛptās tāṃ bhrājathumatīṃ papracchuḥ kasya pūr iyam ||*

This is because, by the application of the rule *itibhaṭṭi*, it is impossible to state a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that in connection with words having the sense of "satiated" (*suhita*), there must be a desire to express only the residual relationship (*śeṣatva*). Nor can one accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), for that would render the prohibition useless. If this is argued, we say no; for if the genitive were used, there would be an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) in the compound. However, when the instrumental is used, there is a distinction: the accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applies according to the rule *tṛtīyā-karmaṇi*, which is an exception to the *thā-thādi* accent rules.

Because the root *tṛp* (to satisfy) is transitive even when used with the construction "he satisfied the ancestors" (*pitṝn atārpsīt*), the suffix *kta* can occur in the sense of the object; thus, in the compound *phala-tarpaṇam*, the accent of the final member of the *kṛt*-derivative applies due to its position after the *kāraka* [the object]. For this very reason, Haradatta has expressed dissatisfaction with the view that when a word meaning "satisfied" (*suhita*) is joined [with another], the instrument (*karaṇa*) must be intended as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). This is what they say.

In *sat dvijasya kurvan* and *dvijasya kurvāṇaḥ*, the genitive is used as a residual case (*śeṣeṣaṣṭhī*). In *corasya dviṣan*, the genitive is used for the object according to the alternative rule stating that the genitive may optionally apply to the object of the present participle *dviṣat*. However, there is no such application in *brāhmaṇasya paśyan*, because the use of the genitive is prohibited when a substitute for *la* (the verbal suffix) is employed, and because [the participle] lacks semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) with the word *odana* (rice) etc., which it requires as its object. In *avyayaṃ brāhmaṇasya kṛtvā*, the genitive is used to express the residual relationship of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*). The meaning is: "having performed an action pertaining to the Brāhmaṇa."

In this way, the fire should be established before the rising of the sun, as will be explained later. Regarding the phrase *atra vṛkṣasyopari*, Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta maintain that because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is a prohibition against its compounding. Rakṣita and others, however, hold that based on the association with what precedes and follows, the prohibition applies only to indeclinables ending in a *kṛt* suffix. For this very reason, Mādhava stated that by the term "indeclinable," those *kṛt* suffixes ending in *m* (i.e., *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun*) are understood. Thus: *tena yatkṛte 'rīn nigṛhṇīmaḥ*.

The established usage "tat-pāṇi-m-ātma-upari-pātukaṃ" (and so forth), as well as the Bhāṣya citation "sarva-paścāt," serves as authority for this point. Because the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.96] mentions *tavya* without an *anubandha*, the compound is indeed formed with *tavyat*. According to the rule "gatikārakopapadāt kṛt" (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the accent of the final member of the *kṛdanta* compound remains its original pitch (*prakṛtisvara*). Since *tavyat* ends in *ti*, it retains its final accent; however, since *tavya* is udātta on its first syllable, it would result in a middle udātta—this is the distinction.

The *Bhāṣya* states: "With a word in apposition, as in *śuklasya māṇavakasya* (of the fair boy), *rājñaḥ pāṭaliputrakasya* (of the king from Pāṭaliputra), and *pāṇineḥ sūtrakārasya* (of Pāṇini, the author of the Sūtras). Regarding *mārāvikaḥ*: he says, "Let the sound *mā* be made. *Mārāvī* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *ru* (to cry) preceded by the particle *mā*, ending in the suffix *iṇ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "there is an addition for words beginning with *mā*" (*māśabdādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*). In the reading *mārāvidasya*, the meaning is the same: one who gives the aforementioned word. In this way, *takṣakasya sarpasya* (of the serpent Takṣaka) should also be cited as an example. We shall explain other matters further on.
**Pāṇini 2.1.49:** *ktena ca pūjāyām* (And [the sixth case is used] with a past passive participle when honor is expressed).

A word ending in the suffix *kta* prescribed after the roots *man*, *budh*, and *i* (in the sense of "to honor") does not form a compound with a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Because these rules are formulated for words meaning "to honor" (*pūjā*) and for words beginning with *mati* (meaning "thought"), the suffix *kta* prescribed by that specific sūtra is indicated [here]. Consequently, there is also a prohibition for a word ending in *kta* whose root has the sense of "motion" (*gati*) and so forth. For example: *rājñāṃ mato buddhaḥ pūjito vā* ("respected, understood, or honored by kings"). Here, the genitive is used according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. However, in cases such as *kalahaṃsarāmamahitaḥ kṛtavān*, since the agent (*kartṛ*) is treated as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the genitive is applied, followed by the compound. When a genitive in the sense of a "remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) forms a compound, it is oxytone (the final syllable bears the udātta accent).

Some say that there is no prohibition [of the compound] because the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaraḥ* (P. 6.2.139) specifically prescribes that the accent of the final member remains as it was in its original form when the suffix denotes "being intent upon" (*paratva*) in a sense other than that of the action itself. Others, however, maintain that the third case ending occurs after a word ending in the past passive participle (*ktānta*) when it denotes the agent, as seen in the example *pūjito yaḥ surāsuraiḥ* ("he who is honored by gods and demons"). They argue that the compound is formed by P. 2.1.32, *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. This is because, under the governing heading *tena*, the specific mention of *uṣita-jñāta-* (in P. 2.1.35) indicates that the usage of the past participle is intended to apply generally, in accordance with the present context. And [there is also a compound] with a word denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇavācinā*). 13.

The genitive case is not compounded with a word ending in *kta*. For example: *idam eṣām āsitam*, *gatam*, or *bhuktam* ("this is the place where they sat, went, or ate"). Regarding the rule *kto'dhikaraṇe ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.76), when the suffix *kta* denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the genitive is used for the agent (*kartṛ*). The inclusion of the term *vāci* ("denoting") is for the sake of clarity. In examples such as *kiṃvṛttam* or *yadvṛttam*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Alternatively, some say that in these cases the suffix *kta* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), and thus it is a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). And [the genitive is not compounded] with a word denoting the object (*karman*) when the suffix *kta* follows a verbal root meaning "to eat" (*ad*) or "to drink" (*pā*) (Pāṇini 2.2.14). For example: *idam eṣām bhuktam* ("this is what was eaten by them") or *pītam* ("drunk"). Here, the suffix *kta* denotes the object (*karman*), and the genitive is used for the agent (*kartṛ*). This is also for the sake of non-compounding. However, in cases like *idam eṣām bhuktam odanasya* ("this is the rice eaten by them"), where the object is explicitly stated, the genitive is indeed compounded because the suffix *kta* here denotes the action (*bhāva*). Similarly, in *idam eṣām pītam payasaḥ* ("this is the milk drunk by them"), the genitive is compounded. But in *idam eṣām pītam payasā* ("this is the drinking of milk by them"), where the suffix *kta* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), the genitive is not compounded. Thus, the prohibition applies specifically when the suffix *kta* denotes the object (*karman*). The mention of *ca* ("and") implies that the prohibition also applies to words ending in *kta* derived from roots meaning "to eat" or "to drink," even when the suffix denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). For example: *idam eṣām bhuktam* or *pītam* (where the agent is implied). In this case, since the suffix *kta* denotes the agent, the genitive is not compounded. The mention of *karmani* ("in the sense of the object") is for the purpose of excluding cases where the suffix *kta* denotes the agent. Therefore, the prohibition does not apply to examples such as *idam eṣām bhuktam odanasya* or *pītam payasaḥ*, where the suffix *kta* denotes the action (*bhāva*). In these instances, the genitive is indeed compounded. The mention of *ca* ("and") serves to include the prohibition of compounding for words ending in *kta* when they denote the agent (*kartṛ*), provided they follow roots meaning "to eat" or "to drink.
