The word *cakāra* (and) has the sense of the particle *iti*. The term *karmaṇi* is an imitation of a word ending in the locative case. A genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) prescribed after pronouncing that word [namely *karmaṇi*] is not compounded; that is to say, it is the genitive prescribed by the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*. For example: *citraṃ gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("the wonderful milking of cows by one who is no cowherd"). Here, the genitive in *goḥ* is due to the restriction [of the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*]. However, in the expression *atha śabdānuśāsanam* ("now, the instruction of words"), the genitive is indeed [governed] by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ*. This is because there is no intention to exclude the specific agent when the meaning is "the instruction of words, and not of meanings."

Therefore, they say that this is not a prohibition. With this very intention, it was stated in the *Kalpataru* regarding the [sūtra] *athāto brahmajijñāsā*: "In the present case, however, only the status of Brahman as the object (*karman*) is taken up, and not an excellence belonging to the agent (*kartṛmata*). Since there is no possibility of both [agent and object] being obtained simultaneously, the genitive case is used according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*. Thus, the compound *brahmajijñāsā* is justified."

However, some maintain that because the prohibition of the feminine suffixes *ā* and *kā* applies there, the genitive case in *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) takes precedence over *ubhayaprāptau* (Pāṇini 2.3.66); thus, they say that a compound is formed [with the genitive]. Their intention is that what is required is merely the possibility (*prasakti*) of both [the agent and the object], not their explicit mention (*śābdam upādāna*) in the rule. For this very reason, the view that the compound is formed with the "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) has also been stated by Kaiyaṭa and others. Others, however, say that since the alternative of "optionally without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa vibhāṣā*) will be mentioned there, this [formation] occurs under the view where the restrictive rule (*niyama*) does not apply. *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (Pāṇini 2.2.15).

There is no compound with a word ending in the sixth case (genitive) when it is joined with a word ending in *tṛ*, *aka*, or *ṇvul* that has the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*). This is because the suffix *tṛc* never fails to denote an agent. The term "agent" (*kartari*) is a qualification for *aka* alone; thus, examples such as *apāṃ sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters") and *vajrasya bhartā* ("the wielder of the thunderbolt") are valid. Nor should one suspect a compound here on the grounds that *bhartṛ* belongs to the *yājakādi* group; for in that list, only the sense of "husband" (*pati*) is intended. [Counter-example: What is the purpose of specifying "when denoting the agent"? Consider *ikṣūṇāṃ bhakṣaṇam* ("the eating of sugarcane"), which forms *ikṣubhakṣikā*. The suffix *ṇvuc* is used after roots meaning "turn," "deserve," "debt," and "origin. Alternatively, the suffix *ṇvul* is used when there is a specification of the root's meaning.

Now, how can there be a quarrel between the creator of jars and the architect of the three worlds? [The verse continues: "To awaken the knowledge that he has descended as one's own eye," and so forth. Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāsa* says: "This is a compound with a word ending in the suffix *tṛn*. There is no prohibition of the genitive case here by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*. For the non-universality (*anityatva*) of that rule is established by the mention of the *anubandha* [the letter *ṇ*] in the present sūtra. Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that it is a compound with a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Others, however, say that because of such indications as "the source of the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*) and "the prompter of that is the cause" (*tatprayojako hetuśca*), this prohibition is non-universal. And [the rule] *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16).

There shall be no compound of a genitive of the agent with an *aka*-suffix. For example: *bhavataḥ śāyikā* ("your lying down"). [This is formed by] the suffix *ṇvuc* according to Pāṇini 3.3.57 (*paryāyārharṇotpattiṣu ṇvuc*). Since the agent is already expressed by the suffix *tṛc*, a genitive of the agent is untenable; therefore, there is no recurrence of the suffix *tṛc* here.
[The rule] "always [forms a compound] with words ending in *ṇvul* and *kvun* when meaning 'sport' or 'livelihood'" (Pāṇini 2.2.17) applies.

The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is always compounded when it expresses two meanings [the object and the agent]. It should not be argued that here the word "always" (*nityam*) applies only to the prohibition (*niṣedha*), because of its proximity; for that prohibition is already permanent by the very force of the commencement of the rule prohibiting [compounding] otherwise. Moreover, since the positive injunction (*vidhi*) is optional, the statement is purposeful only if "always" applies to that [injunction]. *Udṛlikapuṣpabhāñjikā*: The suffix *ṇvul* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the rule *saṃjñāyām*. This is a name for a particular game; thus, the genitive is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). *Dantalekhakaḥ*: When referring to one's livelihood (*jīvikāyām*), the genitive is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

In the rule *krīḍāyāṃ vikalpaḥ*, *jīvikāyāṃ tṛjakābhyām* (Pāṇini 2.2.17), the term *kartari* ("in the sense of the agent") is a qualifier for the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and not for the two suffixes (*tṛc* and *aka*). Nor is the mention of that [term] redundant because the genitive of the agent (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī*) is impossible in connection with *tṛc*, which already denotes the agent; for that mention serves the purpose of the subsequent rule. Indeed, in the sūtra *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16), the mention of "agent" (*kartṛ*) is a qualifier for *tṛc* and *aka*, meaning: "The genitive [of the agent] is not compounded with *tṛc* and *aka* when they denote the agent. This is the resulting meaning even according to this view.

It is exactly the same as the meaning previously stated; however, the distinction is that there is a difference in the meaning between the two sūtras. In the sūtra *nityaṃ krīḍā-*, the example is identical in that it consists solely of the suffix *aka*.

Vāmana, however, states that even for the sense of "livelihood" (*jīvikā*), the suffix *tṛc* forms a compound, as seen in his commentary on the rule *ake jīvikārthe*. Having asked "Why [is] *aka*? in the rule *ake jīvikārthe*, he provides a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for it. Since there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sense of "play" (*krīḍā*), the suffix *tṛc* does not apply there; yet, since the suffix *ṇvul* is easily available in the sense of livelihood by the rule *ṇvultṛcau*, the suffix *tṛc* is also readily applicable. For this very reason, it is explained that the mention of *tṛc* is for the sake of what follows. Otherwise, if the connection were severed at the rule *karmaṇi ca*, it would follow that *tṛc* could not be carried forward here either—so they say. *kugati-prādayaḥ* || 18 ||

The words *ku* and its synonyms, as well as *pra* and the other particles (*prādayaḥ*), are always compounded with a semantically compatible word (*samarthena*). Here, the word *ku* is understood in the sense of "evil" (*pāpa*) and not in the sense of "earth" (*pṛthivī*), because of its association with indeclinables (*avyaya*). This is because, according to the Vārttika statement "of the negative particle (*nañ*), *ku*, and particles (*nipāta*) [the substitution of *kā* occurs]," it too is an indeclinable. Thus, *kupuruṣaḥ* means "an evil man" (*kutsitaḥ puruṣaḥ*). Furthermore, due to the rule prescribing the substitution of *kā* for *ku* in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*), there is also a compound in that case, as in *ūrīkṛtya*. The inclusion of the term *prādi* ("pra and others") is intended to exclude the word *gati*.

Regarding this, the classification of the objects [of these prefixes] has been stated by the Vārttikas: *ati* is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). As in *subhujā* ("one with beautiful arms") and *atirājā* ("one who is a great king"). Regarding *atirājā*, there is a prohibition of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) by the rule *na-pūjanāt*. Kaiyaṭa states that *ati* is also compounded in the sense of transgression (*atikramaṇa*), as in *atisiktam eva bhavati* ("it is indeed over-sprinkled"). Because *ati* is a *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of transgression, there is no change to *ṣ* (by Pāṇini 8.3.65). In *suṣṭhu vamiti*, however, there is a change to *ṣ* because it functions as a preverb (*upasarga*). *Dus* is used in the sense of censure (*nindā*). As in *durgavaḥ* ("a bad ox"); here the compound-ending suffix *ṭac* is applied. *Āṅ* is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*). As in *ākaḍāraḥ* ("slightly tawny"). But when used in connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*), it is a *gati* and thus forms a compound.

However, in the case of the verse "Come, O Indra, with the mild, peacock-haired bay horses," although there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), no compound is formed because [the word *mayūraroma*] does not relate to Indra and because it lacks even a slight connection to him.

The words beginning with *pra* (prādayaḥ) form a compound with a word in the first case (*prathamayā*) when they convey meanings such as "gone" (*gatādi*). For example: *pragata ācāryaḥ* = *prācāryaḥ* ("a teacher who has departed"); *prāntevāsī* ("a student who has gone away"); *prapitāmahaḥ* ("a great-grandfather"). Although the prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) do not possess the status of a *gati* when they function within a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), a compound is still formed by the force of the rule's inclusion of the term *prādi*. Words beginning with *ati* (atyādayaḥ) form a compound with a word in the second case (*dvitīyayā*) when they convey meanings such as "transcended" (*krāntādi*). For example: *atikrānto mālām* = *atimālaḥ* ("one who has surpassed a garland"). Words beginning with *ava* (avādayaḥ) form a compound with a word in the third case (*tṛtīyayā*) when they convey meanings such as "drawn down" (*kṛṣṭādi*). For example: *avakṛṣṭaḥ kokilayā* = *avakokilaḥ* ("one drawn down by a cuckoo"). Words beginning with *pari* (paryādayaḥ) form a compound with a word in the fourth case (*caturthyā*) when they convey meanings such as "worn out" (*glānādi*). For example: *pariglāno'dhyayanāya* = *paryadhyayanaḥ* ("one weary of study").

*pariglāna* means "exhausted by study" (*paryadhyayana*). *alaṃkumāryai* means "sufficient for a maiden" (*alaṃkumāri*). Because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) according to the rule *ekavibhakti ca*, there is shortening [of the final vowel]. Even though this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), a sentence may optionally occur due to the force of the prescription of the dative case. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on that sūtra states: *alaṃkumāryai* and *alaṃkumāriḥ*.

However, this is not the scope of the rule *dīkṣita* (Pāṇini 2.1.40), because the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the *prādi*-compound class, and furthermore, the word *alaṃ* lacks the status of being a *prādi*. Rather, it is said that a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by *alaṃ*—which is made known by the rule *dviguprāptāpannālaṃpūrva-* (Pāṇini 2.1.29)—is treated as a separate category in this sūtra due to its specific mention. Consequently, even when combined with a word ending in the suffix *paryāpti*, such a compound occurs with a word in the dative case alone, in accordance with the requirements of expression (*abhidhāna*). Moreover, they maintain that its non-obligatory nature (*anityatva*) remains entirely unimpeded.

Words beginning with *nis* and others [such as *pra*, *pari*, etc. are compounded with a word in the fifth case when they convey the sense of "departing from" (*krānta*) and so forth. For example: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has departed from Kauśāmbī"). Now, one might object: since the mention of *prādi* (words beginning with *pra*) includes those that have no meaning of their own (*anarthaka*), it would follow that *karmapravacanīyas* (prepositions) could also form compounds. This objection is refuted by the specific rule stating: "The prohibition must be stated for *karmapravacanīyas*. An example of a *karmapravacanīya* is: *vṛkṣe prati vidyotate vidyut* ("the lightning flashes toward the tree"). If it is asked, "How then is [the compound] *adhītya* formed?", some say: it is because *adhi* and *pari* are *karmapravacanīyas* when they are meaningless (*anarthaka*). To this, others reply: [it is not so].

They say that because of the mention [in the rule] "by deceitful teachers" (*adhyāpakadhūrtaiḥ*), the prohibition is not universal (*anitya*). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa and others have stated that compounds such as *sustuta* and *matistuta* are formed even in the absence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). The truth of the matter is that in examples like *adhītya snātvā*, the compound is justified by the authority of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra concerning the "throwing away of the bed" (*khaṭvākṣepa*). It should be stated that an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is compounded with words such as *pravṛddha* and others; thus we have *punar pravṛddham*, *punargavam*, and *punaḥ sukham*. Furthermore, there is the rule "with *iva*, the case-ending is not elided," and so forth.

"One should state that an indeclinable is compounded with an indeclinable [when used] in the sense of 'having caused the master of the sacrifice to reach. An indeclinable is compounded with a finite verb (tiṅ) that possesses an acute accent (udātta) and expresses motion. Examples: *anuvyacalat* ("he went after"), *yatpariyanti* ("that which they go around"). This principle was stated in the rule *saha supā*.
"An upapada [is compounded] with a word that is not a finite verb (atiṅ). 19.

An *upapada* ending in a case-suffix is always compounded with a word that is semantically connected to it; furthermore, this compound must not end in a finite verb (*atiṅ*). For example: *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker"). Why "not ending in a finite verb" (*atiṅ*)? Consider: *mā bhavān bhūt*. Otherwise, because of the rule *māṅiluṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.175), which prescribes the *luṅ* suffix when the particle *māṅ* is present, there would be a compound between *māṅ* as the *upapada* and the form ending in *luṅ*. Although it is not explicitly stated in the Bhāṣya, it is clear that in this sūtra the term *atiṅ* is not a qualifier of the *upapada*, but rather a qualifier of the compound itself.

Nevertheless, it is established as follows: having stated that the mention of *kiṃvṛtta* (words derived from interrogative pronouns) in the rule *anavaklṛptyām* is redundant because *kiṃvṛtta* is not within the scope [of the governing rule], one might suspect that it is for the purpose of providing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "upapada. However, since that designation is rendered useless by the prohibition of compounding in the rule *atiṅ*, this conclusion is reached. Furthermore, in the preceding rule as well, the term *gati* should be separated and *atiṅ* applied separately. Consequently, there is no compounding in examples such as *prapatati*. Nor should it be argued that the exclusion of forms ending in *tiṅ* is already secured by the governing rule *sup supā*.

This is because the phrase *sup-supā* is intended to indicate the cessation [of its application]; however, the word *sub*, ending in the nominative case, continues to apply. Otherwise, in forms such as *rājadarśin*, the elision of the *n* (nalopa) would not occur because the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) would not end in a *sub*. Furthermore, in *nirgataḥ*, the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṛt* (ṛtvam) would not take place, nor would there be the optional substitution of the *tipara-savarṇa* in *saṃyyante*. Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya that "the phrase *sup-supā* has ceased," Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that its intent refers only to the cessation of one part [of the rule].

One might argue: "In the example *kārako gataḥ*, since the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* when the word *gata* is an attendant word (*upapada*) meaning 'gone' for the purpose of performing an action, the mention of *atiṅ* (a non-finite verb) in the rule must serve to prevent compounding. Otherwise, the form would be *gatakāraka*. However, if *akriyā* (non-action) were mentioned instead, then because the suffix [denoted by *ṇvul*] arises based on the action expressed by the base, it would denote an action; thus, there would be no compounding. If this is argued, we say: No.

The term *atiṅ* serves as a qualifier for that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*); since a word ending in a case-suffix denotes a substance (*dravya*), it lacks the capacity to signify an action (*kriyā*). In the case of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, the action denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) functions as a qualifier for the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix. For this very reason, there is no possibility of compounding with the word *gata*, because only a verbal root (*dhātu*) can serve as a subordinate member (*upapada*), and a root denotes an action from which the suffixes based upon it arise. Nor should it be argued that, in such a case, the compounding would apply to the root alone.

Because it is impossible to extract a compound that is already merged with the meaning of a suffix, and because [the extracted element] would lack the status of being a *subanta* (an inflected nominal stem). Nor should it be argued that the mention of *atiṅ* (not ending in a verbal suffix) in the rule *gati-kāraka-pada-...* is intended to prohibit compounding with that which ends in a suffix expressing an action (*bhāvapratyaya*), since that suffix denotes an action that has attained the state of a substantive (*sattva*), whereas an action in its form as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is understood by the verbal root alone; for a *subanta* does not denote an action.

Furthermore, because that which expresses an action (kriyāvācin) lacks the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (subanta), and according to the maxim that "an action expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix appears like a substance," it follows that [the verbal root] assumes the properties of a substance, such as gender and number. This is the meaning. We shall explain this further below. Therefore, the very purpose [of the rule] is the removal of the requirement for the suffix *sup*.

By this [rule], the technical rule (paribhāṣā) that "there is an instruction regarding the compounding of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s with *kṛt*-suffixes prior to the occurrence of *abū* [in Pāṇini 2.2.19]" is indicated. This is because it is possible to indicate an entire technical rule through the acceptance of one part of it, in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*). For example, regarding *gati*s: *vyājighrati* becomes *vyāghrī*. [This is derived] by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.3]. Nor does there arise the contingency of the suffix *śa* by the rule *pāghrā...* [Pāṇini 3.1.137], because a prohibition has been initiated for the root *jighra-* when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

The compound *viāiti* is formed with the two prefixes (*vi-* and *ā-*) directly from the word *ghra*, precisely because no case-ending (*sup*) arises [from them]; otherwise, if one were to rely on the grammatical process (*prakriyā*) wherein suffixes are added sequentially for their own meaning, substance, gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*), then—since the requirement for gender would necessarily arise first—the suffix conditioned by that [gender] would have to be *ṭāp* alone, as there is no other rule [to apply]. This is because the mere word *ghra* does not denote a genus (*jāti*), and furthermore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* has its scope in cases such as *sūkarī*.

In the compound *paścād-rati*, although the word *vyāghrī* denotes a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply because it lacks the final vowel *a*. However, if the compound is formed prior to the application of case-endings (*sub-utpatti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ*—characterized by denoting a genus—is established for the word *vyāghra* as it is already present. Nor does there arise the contingency of applying the general suffix *ṭāp* in that case; because the compound itself applies first due to its being an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation, and subsequently, *ṅīṣ* alone supersedes it.

Thus, regarding the term *abhraliptī*, it is a compound formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), meaning "the agent or the instrument [is compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Following that, since the phrase *karaṇapūrvāt* is still in force, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ktādalpākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.50). If this were to occur after the case-ending (*sup*) had been produced, then because the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply once the *ṭāp* suffix had already been produced previously—due to the governing context of the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.4)—the desired form would not be obtained. Nor can the force of the specific statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*) be invoked as a justification; for if it were so, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would undesirably apply even in the stage of the analytical sentence (*vākya-avasthā*), such as *abhrair viliptā dyauḥ*. Furthermore, the word *pūrva* here signifies "priority" in terms of grammatical operation (*vyavasthā-vacanatva*).

This is because one must assume either that the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from this" (*ataḥ*) or the governing rule "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) is being annulled; for otherwise, [the forms] such as *tasya dhanakrītā* would be untenable. If it is objected: "Even according to your view, the aforementioned usage remains untenable; furthermore, in cases such as *dadhisecau*, the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would not apply."

On this point, they say: since a compound of a *kāraka* occurs even when a case-ending (*sup*) has been produced, the intent of the rule is simply the removal of the requirement that the case-ending must precede the compound; it does not mean that the compound must occur before the case-ending is produced. Thus, in accordance with the specific grammatical operation required, the compound occurs sometimes when the case-ending has been produced and sometimes when it has not. As for the example *dadhisecau*, it was previously stated that it is established by forming a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) after the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *sic* without an upapada.

Regarding the examples of *upapadas*: as in *kacchapī*, which means "she who drinks with her throat" (*kacchena pibati*). Kaiyaṭa states that the suffix *ka* is applied here because of the rule *supi* following a *yogavibhāga*, and because of the rule *ātonupasarge ka*, the suffix *ka* is added; furthermore, since the meaning of the individual parts is necessarily set aside by the fact that [the word] is based on a genus (*jāti*), it should be explained like *vyāghrī*. As for the claim that the term *atiṅ* is a qualifier of the *upapada*, and that therefore [the suffix does not apply] in *vrajati* because it is the principal [verb], that is incorrect; for it would follow that the mention of the nominative case (*prathamāntam*) would also be removed. [The sūtra continues: *amaivāvyayena* || 20 ||

This is the restrictive rule (*niyama*): that which is designated as an *upapada* by the sūtra prescribing *ām-mātra* (the suffix *ām* alone) is compounded with an indeclinable (*avyaya*). This is established because the word *āmaiva* is repeated, whereby the state of being determined solely by *ām* (*āmanirūpitatva*) becomes the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*). Since this qualifies the *upapada*, the final sense obtained is: "That whose status as an *upapada* is determined solely by *ām* is compounded with an indeclinable. And since that much [of the condition] is already established by the preceding rule, the fact that "only that" is compounded follows from the inherent nature of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*). Thus, the intended meaning is established.

And thus, one need not supply the phrase "the rule is the same" (*tulyavidhānam*). [Examples: *svāduṃkāram*, *saṃpannaṃkāram*, *lavaṇaṃkāram*. This is because the mention of *svādu* in the rule *syādumi ṇamul* is intended to convey its meaning [generally]. Due to a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), the final syllable of the first member ends in *-m*. Since there is no rule for another suffix here, the word *svādu* possesses the status of an *upapada* (governing word) only with respect to the suffix *am*. For this very reason, since it lacks the status of an *upapada* with respect to other indeclinables, the compound is formed only with *am*. [Examples: *agrebhojam*, *agrebhuktvā*.

In this case, however, because the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are prescribed by the rule *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrvoṣu*, that [designation of upapada] is not determined solely by them; therefore, there is no compound. This is because there is no evidence for a difference in the designation of *upapada* as being determined by both [the preceding and the following elements]. The purpose of the restriction [in Pāṇini 3.4.26] is that the suffix *tumun* applies after [words meaning] *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā*; thus, in examples such as *kālo bhoktum* ("it is time to eat"), the application of *tumun* should not be precluded. Why [is the word] "with an indeclinable" (*avyayena*) specified? It is so that in cases such as *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker"), the formation of a compound with *kumbha* and so on is not excluded.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the rule being restricted to the effect that only that which functions as an *upapada* (governing word) with respect to the suffix *am* is compounded as an *upapada*. Nor should it be argued that, because the preceding sūtra (*pūrvasūtra*) has no other scope, the restriction will apply to [compounds] ending in an indeclinable (*avyaya*). For that would result in a restriction meaning: "That *upapada* compound which occurs with a form ending in *am* is [only] that which is prescribed by a rule identical to the rule for *am*. This is because, even though there is no compound in cases such as *agrebhojam*, it would be unavoidable in cases such as *agrebhuktvā kāle bhoktum*. *Tṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām* || 21 || [Pāṇini 2.1.27] "Words beginning with those governed by the third case-ending may optionally [be compounded]."

In rules such as *upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām* ("the word *upadaṃśa* [is compounded] with a third-case word"), those words which serve as *upapadas* (governing adjuncts) are optionally compounded with an indeclinable (*avyaya*). This is an optionality that applies in both cases (*ubhayatra vibhāṣā*). In the examples *mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* and *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*, the compounding is already established by the rule *avyaye 'yathābhipretākhyāne kṛñaḥ ktvāṇamulau* (Pāṇini 3.4.59), which prescribes both suffixes (*ktvā* and *ṇamul*) after the verb *kṛ* when expressing an action contrary to one's intention. However, in the example *uccaiḥkāram ācaṣṭe*, the compounding is not otherwise established; therefore, this rule provides for it. In this compound, the accent is determined by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), which prescribes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member when it ends in a *kṛt* suffix.

In the absence of compounding, however, *uccaiḥ* has its final syllable udātta. According to the rule *ādir ṇamuli anyatarasyām*, the *kāra* in *uccaiḥkāram* has its initial syllable udātta. *Amā* means "together with. "He is not capable of eating here. [The suffix] *tumun* is used after words expressing capability, as well as *ktvā*. (Pāṇini 3.4.22)

Words beginning with the third case (instrumental) are compounded either with a word ending in the suffix *ktvā* or with another word; in the case of compounding, the suffix *lyap* is substituted [for *ktvā*]. Examples: *uccaiḥ kṛtya*, *uccaiḥ kṛtvā*. The suffix *ktvā* is also applied after an indeclinable when it denotes something contrary to one's intention. Why "beginning with the third case"? Consider examples such as *alaṃ kṛtvā* and so forth.
The remainder [of compounds not covered by the previous rules] is the *bahuvrīhi*. 23.

Is this a governing rule (*adhikāra*) or a remainder (*śeṣa*)? It is a remainder. For those words for which no other technical name has been stated in a particular sense, the compound formed in that sense is a *bahuvrīhi*. One should not argue that because of the rule "from *akaḍāra* onwards, there is only one technical name" (*eka-saṃjñā*), the names such as *avyayībhāva* will apply due to their having no other occasion (*niravakāśatvāt*). For if the reading were "prior to *kaḍāra*, the subsequent operation [applies]," then by virtue of its being subsequent (*paratvāt*), the designation *bahuvrīhi* would result [even where it is not intended]. However, within the governing rule of "one technical name," the *śeṣa* (remainder) is explained in the *Bhāṣya* as being threefold. To illustrate:

Beginning with the rule *dvitīyāśrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.24), the formation of six groups of three [case endings] beginning with the second case has been explained. Consequently, since the first case is treated as the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), it is established by implication that a *bahuvrīhi* compound consists of words ending in the first case, even when they are not in grammatical apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). In examples such as *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("He whose throat is black"), however, the *bahuvrīhi* is established by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule prescribing the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of the seventh case. Thus ends the first Āhnika of the second Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*. Śrī. The second Āhnika of the second Pāda. 2.2.2.2.106–115. (Continued) [The following rules concern the formation of *tatpuruṣa* compounds: 2.1.27. *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* | In a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the gender of the final member shall prevail. 2.1.28. *pūrvavad aśvavaḍavau* | The compound *aśvavaḍavau* ("horse and mare") takes the gender of the first member. 2.1.29. *hemantaśiśirāv ahorātre ca cchandasi* | In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the compounds *hemantaśiśirau* ("winter and cool season") and *ahorātre* ("day and night") take the gender of the first member. 2.1.30. *rātrāṅgāhāḥ puṃsi* | Compounds ending in *rātra*, *aṅga*, and *aha* are masculine. 2.1.31. *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* | The compound *apatha* ("not a path") is neuter. 2.1.32. *ardharcāḥ puṃsi ca* | Words such as *ardharca* ("half-verse") may be masculine as well as neuter. 2.1.33. *paravat* | [This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) for subsequent rules. 2.1.34. *upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyām* | A *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with *upajñā* or *upakrama* takes the gender of its final member when there is a desire to express that these were the first [of their kind]. 2.1.35. *chāyā bāhulye* | The word *chāyā* takes the gender of its final member in a *tatpuruṣa* when it signifies abundance. 2.1.36. *sabhā rājāmanuṣyapūrvā* | The word *sabhā* takes the gender of its final member in a *tatpuruṣa* when preceded by a word denoting a king or something other than a human being. 2.1.37. *aśālā ca* | And [the word *sabhā*] also [takes the gender of its final member] when it does not mean a house (*śālā*). 2.1.38. *vibhāṣā senāsurāchāyāśālāniśānām* | In the case of *senā*, *surā*, *chāyā*, *śālā*, and *niśā*, the gender of the final member is optional in a *tatpuruṣa*. 2.1.39. *paraval liṅgaṃ dvandvasya* | For a When multiple [words] are used [in the plural], it denotes something other than the meaning of the individual words. || 24 ||

A plurality of words ending in case-suffixes, when functioning in the sense of another word, may be compounded; that is *bahuvrīhi*. The term "another word" (*anyapada*) refers to something distinct from the two words being compounded. Furthermore, the two words being compounded must end in the nominative case (*prathamā*), because the remaining [case-roles] are already expressed by the threefold [inflectional endings]. That "other word" ends in the accusative or other cases, and its meaning—such as the object (*karman*) and so forth—is understood as a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). For this very reason, they recite: "And this [compound occurs] in the sense of a case-ending other than the nominative."

Thus, the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* compound is indeed qualified by the meanings of the second case and so forth. For example: "the village which has reached water" is *prāptodaka*; "the manless one by whom a chariot was carried" is *ūḍharatha*; "Rudra to whom a beast was offered" is *upahṛtapasu*; "the pot from which rice has been removed" is *uddhṛtādana*; "Devadatta to whom variegated cows belong" is *citragu*; and "the village in which there are heroic men" is *vīrapuruṣa*.

In all these cases, there is the apprehension of the village and so forth as qualified by [grammatical] relations such as being the object (*karmatva*): namely, the object of the attainment whose agent is water; the agent of the carrying whose object is the chariot; the intended recipient of the bringing whose object is the cattle; the locus of the extraction whose object is the rice; the owner of the brindled cows; and the locus of the person who is non-different from the hero—such is the understanding that arises.

Therefore, in expressions such as *vṛṣṭe deve gataḥ* ("the rain having fallen, he went"), although the two words ending in the locative case used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) intend to convey—as the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*)—an action of going by way of delimiting time, there is no *bahuvrīhi* compound. This is because, upon hearing the expression, one perceives only that the act of going occurred at a time subsequent to the cessation of the rain, and there is no cognition of [the rain] being the object (*karman*) or any other grammatical relation. By this same reasoning, in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) *citragavo yasya* ("one whose cows are brindled"), the cows are the primary element (*pradhāna*). However, in the compound, there would be a difference in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) between the derivative sentence (*vṛtti-vākya*) and the original analytical statement (*vākya*), [since the owner would be the qualificand in the compound].

Therefore, the Mīmāṃsaka claim that the analysis (vigraha) of *citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam* and so forth is the correct one is refuted; for without the two words being compounded in the nominative case, a *bahuvrīhi* is simply impossible. Furthermore, this contradicts the statement of Kātyāyana that "a *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*"), since the suffix *matup* is prescribed after a word ending in the nominative to express the sense of "that which belongs to it. Moreover, the difference in the grammatical subject between the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and its analytical sentence (*vākya*) is not a cause for invalidating the compound.
Thus, having begun by stating that in some cases the relative prominence of meanings is not intended to be expressed, it was said by Hari:
It has been stated that verbal and nominal derivatives (taddhita) indicate to some extent the relationship between the subordinate and the principal;
however, in that regard, a reversal is observed.

One who plays with dice is *ākṣikaḥ*; one who studies grammar is *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*; one who cooks is *pācakaḥ*. Although the agent (*kartṛ*) is subordinate to the action (*kriyā*) in the analytical sentence (*vigraha*), it emerges as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the compound (*vṛtti*) because of the suffix. Furthermore, the difference is that for them (the Pāṇinīyas), the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), whereas for us (the Naiyāyikas), it is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The distinction regarding the difference in the qualificands between the compound and the analytical sentence in the case of *māsajaḥ* has already been explained. For this very reason, in all systems of thought, the analysis is shown as "one whose cows are brindled" (*citrā gāvo yasya*); such is the direction [of the argument].
The inclusion of the term "aneka" (more than one) is for the purpose of establishing compounds involving many [words]. Thus, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *Samartha-sūtra*:

"By means of one who has very fine matted hair, one who is well-clad in deerskin, and one whose hundred apertures are well-restrained—if these were applied as a dual compound, it would not be established."

This is a four-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound. In the rule *ḍhyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasor* [Pāṇini 6.3.63], due to the mention of "variously" (*bahulavacanāt*), the short vowel occurs in the word *jaṭā*. Alternatively, having first formed a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*, one subsequently forms a *bahuvrīhi* with the word *keśa*. In this way, it should be explained as: "that in which the garment is well-bent. The analysis of *samantrāṇi śitīni randhrāṇi yasya* is: "he whose apertures are accompanied by mantras and are cool."

Now, one might object: in a three-word *bahuvrīhi* such as *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ* ("one who likes the eastern hall") or *pañcagavadhanaḥ* ("one whose wealth consists of five cows"), although the acute accent (*udāttatva*) on the word *śālā* and the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) are established by the designation *tatpuruṣa* caused by the subsequent member, nevertheless, in the case of *khādiretaraśamyam* ("one for whom the other peg is made of *khadira* wood"), the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the word *khādirī* would not occur, because the subsequent member does not follow immediately after it. [Response: This is not so.

In this case, by forming a *karmadhāraya* compound from "that" (*itarā*) and "peg" (*śamyā*), the meaning is expressed by a two-membered *bahuvrīhi*: "one whose other peg is made of *khadira* wood. Since the word *khādirī* ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) indicating a modification, the prohibition [of the *vṛddhi* substitute] by the rule "of that which is caused by a *vṛddhi*" does not apply.

Now, in examples such as *pūrvaśālāpriya*, the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound would be unavoidable because it is an exception (*apavāda*). Nor can it be argued that there is no conflict due to a difference in scope; for since the [other] rule depends on a constituent part, it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*), and thus the *bahuvrīhi* accent itself would prevail. Nor can the matter be resolved by taking both rules as simultaneously applicable, because two accents cannot coexist within the two words governed by the rule *anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam*. Furthermore, one should not argue that being "internal" is not the reason for the strength of an accent, since even an "external" (*bahiraṅga*) accent can sublate another when it is "later-enjoined" (*satiśiṣṭa*).

Nevertheless, since the accent of the *naimittika* (the result) is stronger than the accent of the *nimitta* (the cause), in a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the accent depends on its own final member, the accent of the *tatpuruṣa* is appropriate—having set aside the *bahuvrīhi* accent because the two preceding members function as the cause for that [subsequent *tatpuruṣa*]. Nor is there a lack of evidence for the strength of the *naimittika* accent; for there is proof in the inclusion of the word *ekaśitipād* among the *yuktārohī* group. Otherwise, the word *eka* would be treated as ending in the suffix *kan*.

Alternatively, because of the rule *yadvā svāṅgaśiṭām* [which prescribes] an udātta accent for the first syllable, in a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *ekaḥ śitiḥ pādo yasya*, the accentuation of that [first syllable] would prevail over the accentuation of the two [members] in the subsequent *tatpuruṣa* formed by the rule *taddhitārtha-*; thus, since the initial udātta of the first member in the *bahuvrīhi* is established by the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*, the reading of that [specific] word in the sūtra would be redundant.

[Objection: One might argue that in the case of *ekaśitipāt*—where the first member (*pūrva-pada*) contains a *karmadhāraya* within a *bahuvrīhi*, and it ends in the suffix *-añ* (as in *dvigu*)—the acute accent on the first syllable of the first member is established by the rule *dvigau* (Pāṇini 6.2.29). Alternatively, in the analysis "those whose feet have one white [mark] are *ekaśitayaḥ*; he whose [feet] are such is *ekaśitipāt*," where the first member contains a *bahuvrīhi* within a *bahuvrīhi*, the desired result is established by the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam* (Pāṇini 6.2.1). Thus, since the reading of the word *ekaśitipāt* in the list of *aṣva* (horse-names) could be justified by these logical derivations, how can it serve as an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence)? [Response: True.

Nevertheless, it must be accepted that this is based on an explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*) to the effect that "the accent of the substantive (*nimitti-svara*) is stronger than the accent of the indicator (*nimitta-svara*). Nor should it be argued that in a three-word *bahuvrīhi* such as *susūkṣmajaṭakeśena*, the two preceding words would incur an *antodātta* (final acute) accent due to their designation as *tatpuruṣa*. For here, what is being enjoined is not the *tatpuruṣa* status of the constituent parts of the *bahuvrīhi*; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those words for which the *tatpuruṣa* designation has already been established by another rule.

However, there is an asymmetry in the rule for designating a *tatpuruṣa* compound in the case of "direction" (*dik*) and "number" (*saṃkhyā*), which states: "When the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or when a subsequent member [is present], [the compound is a *tatpuruṣa*]. Nor can it be argued that the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" applies there as well; for it is established by the use of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) that a distinct designation for a constituent member does not apply within a complex formation (*vṛtti*) unless there is a specific statement to that effect. Otherwise, since the form "apūrvaśālāpriyaḥ" would also be established by another rule, the formulation of the *tatpuruṣa* rule when a subsequent member follows would be redundant.

[Objection: But even so, in the case of *adhikaṣāṣṭhivarṣa*, where there is a three-word *bahuvrīhi*, because the word *adhika* is designated as a number (*saṃkhyā*) due to the inclusion of the term *adhika* [in Pāṇini’s rule], there would result an oxytone accent for the two-word *tatpuruṣa* compound formed by the rule *taddhitārthottarapada* (Pāṇ. 2.1.51). [Response: Not so; the acute accent on the first syllable of the prior member is established by the rule *igante dvigau* (Pāṇ. 6.2.29).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the defect remains as it was in the example *adhikaśata-varṣa*? Furthermore, even in the case of *adhika-ṣaṣṭhi*, there would be the undesirable application of the suffix *ḍac* according to the rule *tatpuruṣe saṃkhyāyā upasaṃkhyānam* in the section on *ḍac*. Moreover, since the rule *taddhitārthottarapada...* prescribes a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would set aside the *bahuvrīhi*; however, if a *bahuvrīhi* were formed by the rule *saṃkhyayāvyayāsannādūrādhikasaṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye*, there would again be the undesirable application of *ḍac* by the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍaj*. [Reply: This is not so. The supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is intended to apply only to indeclinables (*avyaya*) and the like, in order to account for forms such as *go-triṃśat*. Thus, the objection does not hold.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "one whose [age] consists of more than sixty years," because the word *ṣaṣṭhi* (sixty) refers to a number (*saṃkhyā*), it does not refer to the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*). Nor should it be argued that, since the years are the things numbered, the rule for a *bahuvrīhi* compound where multiple words serve as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) would apply; nor should it be argued that because it resides in the things numbered, the suffix *ḍac* would also apply when denoting one who has reached a certain age (*vayasvin*); nor should it be argued that there would be the contingency of a *bahuvrīhi* within a *bahuvrīhi*.

In the domain of grammatical function (*vṛtti*), because the rule beginning with "of two or one" (*dvyekayoḥ*) and so forth indicates that even numbers such as ten and the rest refer merely to the number itself, and because the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) constitutes the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the compound, the *bahuvrīhi* in which a number is the final member has been rejected [by Pāṇini]. Furthermore, following the analogy of *avya-vika*, it is accepted that a phrase such as "more than sixty years" (*adhikā ṣaṣṭhir varṣāṇām*) remains a mere syntactical construction (*vākya*). Nor should it be argued that, even so, in the case of "more than a hundred years" (*adhika-śata-varṣa*), the acute accent (*udātta*) would apply only to the vowel *a* of the suffix *-ta*, and not to the initial syllable of the word *adhika*; for that [accentuation] is to be understood from the list of *yuktārohī* and others.

It might be argued: "The mention of 'several' (*aneka*) must be for the purpose of assigning the designation *upasarjana* even to the final member [of the compound] in cases such as *citraguḥ*. This is not so; for [the desired result] is already established by the rule *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipātaḥ*. In examples such as *citragumānaya*, even when the meaning of the compound is connected with a different case-ending, there is a restriction that the two words being compounded in the analytical statement (*vigraha*)—namely, "whose cows are brindled" (*citrā gāvo yasya*)—must both end in the nominative case.

Nor should it be argued that there is an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because the word *kumārī* also has a fixed case-ending, as seen in examples such as "the king's daughter" (*rājñaḥ kumārī*) or "look at her" (*tāṃ paśya*). For in those cases, the analysis (*vigraha*) is accepted even with the word *kumārī* ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) and so forth. This is because, in every specific instance of usage, all words possess the same case-ending; thus, the meaning results in: "that which has a single case-ending, insofar as it is the analysis (*vigraha*) of a Tatpuruṣa or other compound defined by a property pervaded by the status of being a compound."

Therefore, the position that the analysis (vigraha) is by means of a word ending in the nominative case alone is the correct one. Otherwise, since the status of being an object (karmatva) and so forth would already be expressed by the compound itself, the second case-ending and others would not occur in expressions such as *rājakumārīṃ paśya* ("see the king's daughter"). Consequently, when there is a desire to express merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), the first case is applied; thereafter, when there is a desire to express a relation such as "see" and so forth, the occurrence of the second case and others is untenable. Furthermore, how could the aforementioned case-ending—which is external to the compound—be included within the analysis?

Thus, in the *Pūraṇaguṇa* sūtra, the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is also redundant. To explain: in the case of *takṣakasya sarpasya* ("of the serpent Takṣaka"), the genitive is dependent on an external compound-meaning such as "poison" (*viṣa*). Likewise, in the alternative view where both the mat (*kaṭa*) and the qualities (*bhīṣma*, etc. are objects (*karman*), there is a mutual delimitation (*parasparāvaccheda*) between the two nominal stem meanings (*prātipadikārtha*) after the genitive has been applied to both. Consequently, it is clear that there is a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) between the two words ending in the genitive.

Furthermore, since only two words ending in the nominative case would result in a compound, it was previously stated that this does not occur due to the rule of *bahulam* (diversity). Likewise, the concern that in the phrase *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ* there would be no fixed rule for the prior placement of either of the two genitive-terminating words is also weak; for in the word *kumārī*, being in the nominative case is necessary. Therefore, when it is argued that analysis (*vigraha*) must be performed with only a nominative-ending word, the following is said in reply:

In the case of a compound consisting of more than two members (*samāsottara*), even for a second member and subsequent ones, there is entry into the analysis (*vigraha*) after the second word, because it is present [in the mind] and there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*). Otherwise, since the case endings would be fixed in the analysis, the term *upasarjana* would apply, resulting in the undesirable shortening (*hrasva*) of the vowel in words such as *kumārī*. Furthermore, this is because [the presence of the second member] serves as a means of proof (*sādhakatva*). For this very reason, in the analysis of a second member derived from a *bahuvrīhi*, there is no usage of the word following the constituent member (*vartipada*), because it would possess a contradictory meaning by not conveying the objecthood (*karmatva*) residing in the possessor (*svāmin*).

For this very reason, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth is not denoted by a compound. If [the case-role] were denotable merely by its entry [into the meaning of the base], then in forms such as *pacanti* (they cook) and *pācakāḥ* (cooks), even plurality would result in being part of the meaning of the *kṛt*-suffix. Furthermore, since compounds such as genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) and appositional compounds (*karmadhāraya*) are common to all case-terminations, it is impossible to include the meanings of specific terminations within the respective scope of those [compounds]. Therefore, it is more appropriate to postulate that the denoter of the meaning is something common to all cases.

Furthermore, because [the objecthood] of the various [kārakas] such as the object (karman) is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of their respective case-endings; for this very reason, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the meaning is that of the second case (accusative), since the objecthood and so forth are already perceived as qualifiers of the substantive through the meaning of the constituent member (*varti-pada*), there is a rule that the second case ending and others are not used to convey the objecthood etc. as determined by the action denoted by that [first] member, but rather only to convey the objecthood etc. as determined by another action.

Thus, even in a case such as *nīlotpalasya* ("of the blue lotus"), where there is an analysis using the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the relation (*saṃbandha*) does not enter into the compound, because that element lacks the quality of being a semantic explication (*vivaraṇatva*). For this very reason, the prohibition [against the application of *para-aṅgavadbhāva*] is meaningful, since the mutual restriction (*parasparāvaccheda*) remains effective even after the subsequent [semantic integration], as the capacity (*sāmarthya*) has not been lost. Furthermore, in the case of *mitrāvaruṇāvṛtāvṛdhā* ("Mitra and Varuṇa, who increase the truth"), although the two first connect with the verb, it was previously established that *para-aṅgavadbhāva* applies by virtue of their capacity based on a subsequent non-difference (*abheda*).

In reality, because there is a rule that only case-inflections denoting *kārakas* (grammatical participants) can be construed with the action, even the mat (*kaṭa*) is first construed with the action according to the principle that "only those ending in such [kāraka] inflections are objects," and only subsequently does the mutual delimitation occur. However, since the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) lacks the status of a *kāraka*-inflection, its meaning is construed with the nominal stem-meaning right from the beginning; for the position that "the case-inflection [is determined] by virtue of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [nominal stem]" is firmly established.

For this very reason, since the genitive case connects with the action (*kriyā*) even before it connects with the meaning of the noun, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in examples such as *aśvābhidhānīm* ("the horse's halter"), despite the fact that a qualified object is being designated. For this same reason, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that "a term in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is [otherwise] incapable [of forming a compound]" is a rule based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). It is for this reason that the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have cited *sarpiṣaḥ pīyamānasya* ("of the clarified butter being drunk") as an example of the prohibition against a genitive compound of terms in apposition. Their intention is that this is because of an explicit scriptural restoration of capacity (*sāmarthya*) through the rule *adhātvabhihitam*.

And thus, on the view that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors, just as case-endings such as the accusative are employed after the nominal stem merely as indicators (*dyotaka*), so too is it in cases such as *rājakumārīm*. Therefore, even the difficulty [of explaining the formation] need not be resorted to. Likewise, in the non-ordinary analytical statement (*alaukika-vigraha*), the case-ending is exactly as in the ordinary analytical statement (*laukika-vigraha*). Consequently, the position that the analysis is performed with a fully formed case-ending is also faultless; let this detailed discussion rest.

What is the purpose of including the term *anya* ("other")? It is so that the *tatpuruṣa* compound—which finds its scope when the meaning of the constituent members (*vartipadārtha*) is predominant—may be superseded by the *bahuvrīhi* when the meaning of a word other than the constituents is intended, because the *bahuvrīhi* is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Otherwise, in co-referential cases such as *nīlotpalaṃ saraḥ* ("a lake with blue lotuses"), there would result the unwanted consequence of the *bahuvrīhi* alone superseding [the *tatpuruṣa*]. This is because in non-co-referential cases such as *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("one who has Kāla on his neck"), the *bahuvrīhi* already finds its scope. Why is the word *pada* ("word") included? So that [the rule] does not apply to the meaning of a sentence, as in *grāhavatī nadī* ("a river possessing crocodiles").

For the intended meaning of the sentence is "Do not bathe in this," which is understood through the overall purport (*tātparya*). Why is the word *artha* (meaning) included [in the definition]? It is so that it may apply to the entire referent of the word (*padārtha*). Otherwise, the "meaning" would consist merely of the relation expressed by the genitive case; and in that case, coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *devadatta* and so on would not be possible, because a difference in gender and number between the meanings of two nouns prevents their syntactic connection (*bhedānvaya*). Since the remainder (*śeṣa*) has already been mentioned in the three preceding rules, the *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs only among words that are coreferential. Not here: *pañcabhir bhuktam asya* ("five have eaten for him").

In the case of *pañcabhuktavantaḥ* ("those by whom five have been eaten"), [the suffix] also does not occur because it has not been so prescribed. Regarding indeclinables (*avyaya*), it must be stated [as an exception]: *uccairmukhaḥ* ("high-faced"). Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this statement is necessary because, since the word *uccais* primarily denotes the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and thus the rule would otherwise not apply. Others, however, argue that since the mere state of ending in the nominative (*prathamāntatva*) exists here as well, this [exception] need not be made at all. For this very reason, when a three-word *bahuvrīhi* is formed such as *vākca dṛkca priyā yasya*, an intermediate *dvandva* is accepted [between *vāk* and *dṛk*].

A *bahuvrīhi* compound consisting of words beginning with *pra* and others followed by a verbal derivative (*dhātuj*) should be stated as either retaining the suffix or having the final member elided; for example, *prapatitaparṇaḥ* (one from whom leaves have fallen) becomes *praparṇaḥ*.

A *bahuvrīhi* compound consisting of the negative particle *nañ* followed by words expressing existence (*astyartha*) may optionally have the final member elided; for example, "that place where a pot does not exist" is *aghaṭaṃ bhūtalam* or *avidyamānaghaṭam*.

The inclusion of words such as *astikṣīra* (having milk) is established because they are not formed with case endings (*asubanta*) and are indeclinables (*avyaya*). Since they are not formed with verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*), the rule [for indeclinable compounds] would not otherwise apply; thus, this statement is made. However, there is a refutation based on the view that these are indeclinables that are "counterparts" (*pratirūpaka*) of verbal forms. Even though in the case of *kiṃsabrahmacārī* ("with what fellow-student?"), one might analyze it as a compound meaning "one whose fellow-students are 'who' (*ke*)," the subsequent word *kaṭha* would be untenable. This is because if the question were in the plural, a singular form in the answer would be inappropriate. Furthermore, even if it were analyzed as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "of whom [are the fellow-students]? (*keṣām*), the same fault remains, and there would also be the impossibility of the initial vowel being accented acute (*ādyudāttatva*).

By this, the view that "kaḥ sabrahmacārī" (who is the fellow-student) is a *sāmānādhikaraṇa* compound according to the rule *sup-supā* is refuted. Even if the formation of the compound "kaḥ sabrahmacārī yasya sa ka-sabrahmacārī tvam" (you, whose fellow-student is who? were possible in terms of number and accent, the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "I" in the expression "ahaṃ kaṭhaḥ" (I am a Kaṭha) would be untenable, because the subject of the question would be someone other than that [the speaker]. Nevertheless, the *bahuvrīhi* interpretation mentioned first is indeed correct; for by stating that he himself is a Kaṭha, it implies that they too are Kaṭhas, otherwise their status as fellow-students (*sabrahmacārin*) would be impossible.

Therefore, in response to the plural form "the Kaṭhas," there is never an absence [of the plural]. Because the meanings of the constituent members (*vartipada*) are subordinate, while the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) indicated by them is primary, they are not denoted by the compound *ṛk-sabrahmacārī*. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that when the question is expressed by a sentence, the plural indeed occurs in the answer as well. For example, two *droṇas* and one half-*droṇa* are called "three and a half *droṇas*" (*ardhatṛtīyā droṇāḥ*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those of which a third is a half."

Nor should it be argued that a *bahuvrīhi* compound is impossible here because there is a rule that the referent of a compound (*anyapadārtha*) must be distinct from the referents of its constituent members (*vartipadārtha*), since in this case the constituent members themselves are included within the compound due to the necessity of accounting for the plurality [of the referent]. The meaning of the compound is the aggregate (*samudāya*) consisting of the "half" and the "two. Its parts may sometimes be intended as distinct and sometimes as non-distinct. For example, in the expressions "an assembly of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ saṃghaḥ*) and "the Brahmins are forming an assembly" (*saṃghībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ*).

Consequently, since the meaning of the compound is a collection whose constituent parts are differentiated, the plural number is used. There is no fault [in this], because the word *droṇa* functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to two *droṇas* and half a *droṇa*, thereby establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that in expressions such as "he followed the Pāṇḍava with no second" (*asidvitīyo'nusasāra pāṇḍavam*) or "may the strength of Kṛṣṇa increase, who has Saṃkarṣaṇa as his second" (*saṃkarṣaṇadvitīyasya kṛṣṇasya balam vardhatām*), the dual number would apply—since the "second" which completes the pair is a member of a dyadic aggregate, and that aggregate is the meaning of the compound. This is because in those instances, the word *dvitīya* is used in its unanalyzed (avyutpanna) sense of "companion."

This *bahuvrīhi* compound is of two kinds: *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the qualities of the members are understood) and *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the qualities of the members are not understood). The former is that in which the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is connected with the action; for example, in "Bring the long-eared one" (*lambakarṇam ānaya*). In the absence of such connection, it is the second kind; for example, in "Bring the owner of brindled cows" (*citragum ānaya*). Thus, the distinction between *tadguṇa* and *atadguṇa* is based on whether the qualifier functions as a defining characteristic (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

As for Kaiyaṭa’s statement that there is *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* when the relationship is characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), whereas in a *bahuvrīhi* with relationships such as that of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), there is *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*—this is merely a brief description of possible cases. This is precisely why he said "in brief" (*saṃkṣepeṇa*). For instance, in the rule *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*, the designation *sarvanāman* would be untenable because the word *sarva* as a whole lacks both of the aforementioned types of relationship.

Furthermore, in the aphorism "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]," it is untenable for "birth" alone to be the definition of Brahman. The distinction between qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the like has been explained in the *Kalpataru*: "For that which differentiates by being connected with the effect is a qualifier, as whiteness is to a lotus; whereas those which differentiate without such connection are established as adventitious attributes (*upādhi*) and defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). That which persists as long as the effect exists is an adventitious attribute;
that which causes the cognition of difference only occasionally is a defining characteristic."

And the state of being an *upalakṣaṇa* (secondary indicator) consists in the intellect’s being co-locative with that [object] while not delimiting the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the object to be conveyed; whereas the state of being a *viśeṣaṇa* (primary qualifier) consists in its delimiting that [exclusion], and so forth, as is clear elsewhere. In the present context, however, this is to be understood precisely through the connection or non-connection with the effect (*kārya*). Among these, the first—the *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*—is the default case because of the primacy of the state of being a *viśeṣaṇa*. But when there is a means of cognition [for the contrary], the second [type of *upalakṣaṇa*] applies.

In passages such as "the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha," the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa are understood through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with other scriptural statements. For this very reason, the view that a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing two words is necessarily a *tadguṇa-saṃvijñāna* (one where the quality itself is understood) is refuted; for there is a deviation [from this rule] in cases such as "the six beginning with *jakṣati*" (*jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ*), as stated in the *Advaitacandrikā*. [The sūtra:
Numbers, indeclinables, words meaning "near," "not far," "more than," and numerals [are compounded] with a word denoting the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*). (Pāṇini 2.2.25)

Indeclinables and other words are compounded with a numeral that has the sense of a countable object (*saṃkhyeya*). Those which are near ten are *upadaśāḥ* (near-ten). In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the suffix] *ḍac* is added by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* denoting a countable object. By the rule "after *tri* and *viṃśati*, [the suffix] *ḍiti*," there is the elision of *ti*. Murāri says: "This hero conquered the earth twenty-one times" (*vārān upaviṃśam ajayat*). It was stated previously that when proximity (*sāmīpya*) is the primary sense, it is an *avyayībhāva*. Similarly, Murāri says: "He who has nearly destroyed the sprouts of the various kṣatriya lineages" (*āsannaviṃśān viśasita-viṣama-kṣatra-jāti-prarohaḥ*). [Examples include: *adūratriṃśāḥ* (not far from thirty) and *adhikacatvāriṃśāḥ* (more than forty).

"Dvitrāḥ" means two or three. Although this could have been established by the previous rule even with the analysis "dvau trayo yeṣām unmugdhānām" (those among the deluded who are two or three), because a *bahuvrīhi* compound does not function to denote a specific number, the application of the suffix [ḍac] would be difficult to obtain. Furthermore, if the analysis were "dvau vā trayo vā," there would be the undesirable consequence of using the dual number in some instances. Nevertheless, when the number is unspecified, the plural must be employed, as seen in the usage "How many sons do you have? (*kati bhavataḥ putrāḥ*).

Some say that this [number] is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*); others, however, maintain that because the word "or" (*vā*) here indicates doubt, and because doubt involves a consideration of indefinite numbers, and because there exists a multiplicity of objects for such doubt, this number is established by logical necessity (*nyāyasiddha*).

Alternatively, even if the connection with the action resides in only one of the two [the agent or the object], all five [factors] are objects of cognition; thus it is said: "This speech is presided over by the five. Regarding the term *dvidaśāḥ*, the analysis is not *dvau daśa* (two tens), because the number ten is singular. Nor is it the case that the word *dvi-* refers to a number residing in the repetition of the state of being ten, for the word *dvi-* ending in the suffix *suC* (*dvi-daśa*) is a distinct word from the numeral *dvi-*, and thus lacks the meaning of a number. Nevertheless, the analysis is indeed with the word ending in *suC*, because it is accepted that the analysis may be non-co-referential (*asvapada-vigraha*).

Due to the inherent nature of the power of words, the meaning of the suffix *su*—which characterizes the repetition of an action—is expressed by the compound itself; therefore, that suffix is not employed there. However, in a sentence (*vākya*), because that meaning is not understood without the suffix *su*, it is employed; this is the distinction. And thus, by parity of reasoning, "two tens" (*dvau daśatau*) is also a valid analysis (*vigraha*). As it has been said:
"Although specific distinctions are heard in sentences due to the difference in words, this derivative term (*vṛtti-śabda*) is indeed different, being based on a different meaning."

The meaning of the *kārikā* is as follows: even when specific suffixes such as *suc* are employed in a sentence, the word "two" (*dvi*) and so forth, being contained within the compound, conveys the meaning of *suc* and the others because it is distinct from them. Nor should it be argued that in examples such as *dvitrāḥ* ("two or three") and *dvidaśāḥ* ("twelve"), the rule is already established by the preceding one (*pūrveṇaiva*) due to the predominance of the meanings of *vā* ("or") and *suc*; for those two meanings do not possess predominance, and furthermore, this is intended to prevent the application of the suffix *kap*.
[Pāṇini 2.2.26: *diṅnāmānyantarāle* ("Names of directions [are compounded] when expressing an intermediate direction").

The names of the directions are compounded when the intermediate space between them is to be expressed. The intermediate space between the southern and eastern directions is "southeast" (*dakṣiṇapūrvā*). According to the *Bhāṣya*, there is masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) when a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) occurs from a pronoun. The word "name" (*nāma*) is used for the purpose of including conventional designations; therefore, compounds such as *aindrīkauverī* (between the directions of Indra and Kubera) do not occur when the intermediate space is the primary meaning. Since it has been stated that this applies to meanings other than the first case-ending, and because of the difference in grammatical coreference (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), this rule is prescribed because it would otherwise not be established by the preceding one.

In the rule *vibhāṣā diksamāse* (Pāṇini 1.1.28), which allows for the optional designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*), this very [term *idam*] is included; furthermore, this is intended to ensure its status as a *pratipadokta* (explicitly mentioned) form, and also to prevent the suffix *kap*.
Regarding that, the rule *tatreṇedam iti sarūpe* (Pāṇini 2.4.21) applies.

When two similar words (*sarūpa-pada*) are present—one ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) regarding the object of seizing (*grahaṇa*), and the other ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) regarding the object of striking (*praharaṇa*)—they may be compounded in the sense that "this battle has commenced" when there is a mutual exchange of actions (*karmavyatīhāra*). By the word *iti*, which refers to common worldly usage (*laukika-vivakṣā*), the objects of seizing, striking, mutual exchange of action, and battle are obtained. Even so, the distinction is that while "battle" (*yuddha*) is the contextual subject (*viṣaya*), the others are the expressed meanings (*vācya*). In the words *grahaṇa* and *praharaṇa*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied respectively in the locative (*adhikaraṇe*) and instrumental (*karaṇe*) senses.

Having seized each other by the hair, this battle proceeded as a *keśākeśi* (hair-to-hair); *muṣṭīmuṣṭi* (fist-to-fist); and having struck with staffs against staffs, it was a *daṇḍādaṇḍi* (staff-against-staff). The suffix *ic* is applied here according to the rule *ic karmavyatīhāre*. Its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is due to its inclusion among the *tiṣṭhadgu-prabhṛti* group within the category of *avyayībhāva* compounds. The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *anyeṣām api*.

Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) should be prescribed by prefixing the letter *ā* to the word *idam* itself, since there would be no purpose for it given the necessity of the elision (*lopa*) of the final syllable when followed by another word (*uttarapada*). This is because the *Bhāṣya* has shown that an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would occur in forms such as *asyasi*, based on the principle that "if, by rule, its lengthening were to occur only through this [substitution]. Consequently, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that the form *muṣṭāmuṣṭi* is merely an error (*prāmādika*). [Question: Why is the condition *sarūpa* ("having the same form") stated? [Example: *halaiśca musalaiścedaṃ yuddhaṃ pravṛttam* ("This battle has commenced with clubs and maces").

This sūtra is intended for the purpose of expressing non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), for the purpose of overriding the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) regarding the meaning of the first case-ending (*prathamāvibhakti*), and for the purpose of preventing the suffix *kap*. Otherwise, because they are intended to be expressed together (*sahavivakṣitatva*), possess the same form (*sarūpatva*), and belong to the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktitva*), there would be *ekaśeṣa*. However, since this technical designation of *bahuvrīhi* refers to a collective whole (*samūha*)—which would otherwise be untenable—and because its formulation possesses sufficient force to override that [rule of *ekaśeṣa*], it does so. Nor can it be argued that the rule of *ekaśeṣa* is overridden by the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*) due to its higher status (*paratva*); for in comparison with the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), that [preceding rule] is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

This is because the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member) is stronger even than that which is more internal (*antaraṅga*). Nor can it be argued that the suffix *ka* is absent due to being superseded by the suffix *ic*, which is specifically prescribed; for the suffix *ic* has its own scope of application in the alternative case where *ka* is absent, according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. To explain: in that context, the word *śeṣa* (remainder) refers to both meanings through the principles of *tantra* (simultaneous application), *āvṛtti* (repetition), and so forth. First, "remainder" means that which is other than what has been employed [in the formation]; that is to say, it refers to a compound that has not yet received a *samāsānta* suffix. Second, "remainder" refers to the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the section. By the first sense, there is an absence of *ka* in examples such as *priyamadhuka*; by the second sense, there is an absence of *ka* in examples such as *dakṣiṇapūrva*.

In the rule *diṅnāmāni* (P. 1.1.34) and others, because the term *śeṣa* (remainder) is not carried over [from the previous rule], it is understood as referring specifically to the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the remainder" (*śeṣādhikāra*), and not merely as "that which is other than what has been employed. Regarding Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *Phakkikā*, however, they say that by connecting the particle *eva* with the verb, the meaning is that the governing heading of "the remainder" is indeed included, but it is not restricted to being "only that which is other than what has been employed"; thus, the intent is to exclude the interpretation of taking it as referring solely to something unused. The word *saha* (with), when expressing equality of connection (*tulyayoga*), is optionally compounded with a word ending in the third case. For example: *putreṇa saha saputra āgataḥ* (he has come with his son) or *sahaputraḥ*. The substitution of *sa-* for *saha* occurs by the rule *vopasarjanasya*. This statement is made even though the father (*pitṛ*)—who is the referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*)—is predominant, in order to ensure grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and to prevent the suffix *ka* from being added after a word ending in the first case. Why specify "expressing equality of connection"? Consider: *sahaiva daśabhiḥ putrair bhāraṃ vahati gardabhī* (the she-ass carries the load together with her ten sons). Here, there is no compounding because the sense of equality of connection is absent.

The meaning is: "while those [others] exist. For this very reason, in the mantra *agnā i patīvat sajūr devena tvaṣṭrā somaṃ piba svāhā*, since the connection with a single action is possible even without the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that Tvaṣṭṛ does not possess the status of a deity (*devatātva*). The mention of "equal connection" (*tulyayogavacana*) is merely common (*prāyika*), as evidenced by rules such as *vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe* and *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya*. By this, forms such as *sakarmaka* are established.
(Pāṇini 2.2.29) "A *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*)."

A compound consisting of multiple *subanta* (inflected) words previously mentioned, occurring in the sense of *ca* ("and"), may be compounded; that is *dvandva*. The meanings of *ca* are: conjunction (*samuccaya*), sequential mention (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the connection of mutually independent [words] with a single [action]. For example: "Day after day, leading away the cow, the horse, the man, and the beast, Vaivasvata is not satiated, like a wicked person with liquor. Here, the connection with "leading away" applies to the cows and the others. Because the meaning is already understood, the word *ca* is not employed.

*Anvācaya* (conjunction of sequence) is the connection with different actions based on their being either primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*anuṣaṅgika*) objectives. For example: "Go for alms and bring the cow. Here, the going for alms is mandatory, while the bringing of the cow is optional depending on whether it has been done or not. Although in a case such as "Cut the *dhava* tree and also the *khadira*," there is equality of action when one intends to express the necessity of either one, it is still *anvācaya*. In cases like "Bring the jar and the cloth," where both are intended to be equally primary, it is simply *samuccaya* (conjunction). Nevertheless, Kaiyaṭa maintains that unity or diversity of action are not the determining factors; rather, it is solely the intention to express a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*).

The *anvaya* (connection) of things joined together is *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction); the collection [of them] is *samāhāra* (aggregation). Among these, there is no compound for the first two types because of a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). However, for the latter two, we have examples such as *dhavakhadirau* (the *dhava* and *khadira* trees) and *vāgdṛṣadam* (speech and stone). Nor does it follow that the *dvandva* compound would become an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it is prescribed in the sense of *ca* ("and"), since it is not recited within that specific section [of the rules governing indeclinables]. Why is the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) included? [It is so that the rule does not apply] in cases such as *yājñikaścāyaṃ vaiyākaraṇaścāyaṃ yājñikavaiyākaraṇaḥ* (this sacrificer and this grammarian), *kaṭhabahvṛcaḥ* (the Kaṭhas and the Bahvṛcas), or *nīlotpalam* (a blue lotus).

In the case of [the rule] beginning with *viśeṣaṇam*, there is an absence of being a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) because it has already been employed [in another function]. Otherwise, since the meaning exists through the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of multiple attributes within a single substratum (*dharmin*), the technical designation of a *dvandva* would apply; consequently, due to its greater importance (*abhyarhitatva*), the term "grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and so forth would have to be placed first. However, in the case of a *tatpuruṣa*, the non-fixed placement of the prior member is established, as in the example *kāmakhañja* ("lame from desire").
