This holds true under the view that "this is the subsequent operation" (*paraṃkārya*). But under the heading "one technical designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the designation of *tatpuruṣa* is established precisely because it is prescribed as a specific exception. Furthermore, this is not the case under the alternative view that accepts the mention of the word "remainder" (*śeṣagrahaṇa*). [Example: "He silently approached the great lake of the Gaṅgā, which was thick with moss."
And if one were unable to go against Droṇa, one would have to die after having performed or left undone what was required.

In this regard, one might argue that a *dvandva* compound would not apply here because the rule for forming such compounds—“with a word ending in a *kta*-suffix, provided it is not qualified by a negative particle (*nañ*)”—is intended to be exhaustive. However, this must be refuted, because in the case of *kṛtākṛta*, two distinct actions are indeed intended. Furthermore, the application of the rule “with a word ending in a *kta*-suffix,” etc., occurs only when there is an intention to express the state of being both done and undone with respect to a single object delimited by a single part. On this point, some maintain that a *dvandva* occurs when there is a difference between the referents (*padārtha*) themselves; others, however, hold that a *dvandva* occurs when there is a difference in the delimiters of the referents (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). They further argue that the phrase "in the sense of *ca*" (*cārthe*) does not mean "when a difference is understood."

In the expression *dhava-khadirau* ("the dhava and khadira trees"), because there is no presentation of the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), one cannot function as a qualifier of the other; consequently, it is impossible for difference (*bheda*) to appear as a relation (*saṃsarga*). For this very reason, [difference] cannot appear either as a qualifier or as a specific attribute (*prakāra*), because it is not the meaning of a word (*apadārthatva*) and because it would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the verb "cut" (*chindhi*). Therefore, only an actual, ontological difference must be intended. Furthermore, since there is no restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) here, that difference must have a word-meaning as its counter-correlative (*padārtha-pratiyogika*).

Therefore, although there is identity of meaning in cases such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and "the property of the subject qualified by pervasion" (*vyāptiviśiṣṭapakṣadharma*), it is possible [to apply the definition] because there is a difference between the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the meanings being compounded, namely "pervasion-qualified" and "subject-property."

Nor is the grammatical rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) redundant; for in the case of "payasī" (two waters), when it refers to both water and milk, that rule serves its purpose due to the difference between the property-delimiters (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), namely "water-ness" and "milk-ness. It should not be argued that in the expression "nīlaghaṭayoḥ" (of the blue and the pot), there is no application of duality because it is sublated in the referent (*padārtha*), since the delimiter [of the compound] is a part [of the whole] and, being distinct from the substance, is unfit for the application of duality. This is because [the rule] serves merely to ensure grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*). Nor should it be argued that in the expression "nīlaghaṭayorabhedaḥ" (non-difference of the blue and the pot), let it simply be a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Nor should it be argued that the use of the dual number is untenable, on the grounds that there is no grammatical rule prescribing a dual suffix after a *dvandva* compound, just as there is none for a *karmadhāraya* when it refers to a single substratum (*ekadharmī*). For, if the jar were presented through the *karmadhāraya* itself as non-different from "blue," it would lack expectancy for non-difference (*abhedānākāṅkṣatva*), resulting in a failure of syntactic connection (*ananvayāpatti*). They say that even though non-difference appears there as a relation (*saṃsargatayā*), it lacks expectancy because of the requirements of the result (*phalānurodhena*).

In cases where there is a difference between the objects denoted by the words, a *dvandva* compound is formed; therefore, there is no inconsistency in either case. This is because in the instance of *ekaśeṣa* (the "one-remainder" rule), there is a difference between two jars, whereas here there is a difference between the quality of blueness and the nature of being a jar. Nor should it be argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of calling a single jar "jars" (*ghaṭāḥ*)—as in "jar and jar are jars"—on the grounds that the objects denoted by those terms (the individual jar, the universal jar-ness, and their inherence) are distinct. For what is intended is the difference between all the individuals denoted by one of the two compounded words, as distinguished from the individuals denoted by the other word.

Alternatively, it is because what is intended for the other word (*anyapada*) is the state of having a result delimited by a relation of objectivity (*viṣayitā-sambandha*) that is distinct from that which delimits the result of the first word (*ekapada*) through the same relation; however, in this case, they say that for both words, the delimitor of the result is precisely this jar as qualified by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Let us return to the subject at hand. What is the purpose of including the term "multiple" (*aneka*)? [Consider the example: *hotṛ-potṛ-neṣṭod-gātāraḥ*. Nor should it be argued that this is a *dvandva* compound of only two [words], for then the suffix *ānaṅ* would undesirably apply even to *hotṛ* and *potṛ*.

It might be argued as follows: if there were no mutual connection (*ananvaya*) between *dhava* and *khadira*, there would be no compound because of a lack of semantic capacity (*sāmarthyābhāva*). Nor can this be resolved according to the method stated by Kaiyaṭa—that semantic capacity consists simply in the connection with a single action—because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the form *kṛtaḥ sarvamṛttikaḥ* could be used in the sense of "made entirely of clay. This is because both the referents of the words *sarva* and *mṛttikā* would be connected to the action through their respective roles as instrument (*karaṇatva*) and object (*karmatva*).

Nor should it be argued that a compound occurs by the force of the statement even when there is no semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), or that semantic capacity consists in the capacity for connection in a single form such as being the object (*karmatva*); for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases of conjunction (*anvācaya*), such as *aharahar* ("day after day"), and because the dual number and so forth following the second member would be untenable, since its referent is singular. Therefore, the word *dhava* refers to both the *dhava* and the *khadira*, and likewise the word *khadira*.

And thus, while there is a semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*) between the meanings of the two words consisting of their mutual non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*), such compatibility is clearly absent in the sentence as a whole. Furthermore, the employment of a different word [in the compound] is for the sake of conveying the meaning of the second member; since only two distinct meanings are to be understood from the two words, there is no occasion for the use of the plural number. For this very reason, the dual ending of the word *pṛthivī* in the phrase "both heaven and earth bow down to him" (*dyāvā cid asmai pṛthivī namete*) is consistent. [The form *dyāvā* is derived by applying] the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106), which effects the substitution of the preceding vowel.

Otherwise, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the dual-ended word *anyathāsaṃnamete*, nor would there be the use of the particle *iti* after the word *pṛthivī* at the time of reciting the *padapāṭha*, nor would there be the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) based on the designation of a *pragṛhya*. Having considered all of this, the author of the *Vārttika* stated: "A *dvandva* [compound] occurs when there is a simultaneous expression of two substrates (*adhikaraṇa*). The term "substrate" refers to the meanings of the words being compounded; "simultaneous expression" means that both words convey the meanings of both words.

Regarding this, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* state: "This simultaneous denotation of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*) is difficult and hard to establish. It is "difficult" because it contradicts experience; for the word *dhava* lacks the capacity to convey the *khadira*. Furthermore, there is a distinction here from the cognition produced by the sentence "the *dhava* and the *khadira*" (*dhavakhadirau*), and because a verbal cognition is untenable when the delimitor of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) are identical, as in the case of "a pot is a pot."

Furthermore, if one were to accept the cognition of non-difference between the primary meaning of one word and the primary meaning of the other word, there would be a lack of semantic competency (*yogyatā*). Moreover, even if they have the same meaning, if such a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is possible, the effort in postulating that both words convey two distinct meanings is futile. Furthermore, in the case of the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*), the dual number can be justified in place of the singular through Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa-vyatyaya*). Or, since a copulative compound (*dvandva*) denotes a collection, the dual number and so forth are justified. Nor does it follow that the singular number should apply because the collection is a single entity.

Because a collection whose constituent parts are manifested is the meaning of a compound (*samāsa*). Furthermore, by virtue of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*), that which is indicated by the particle *ca* is a *dvandva*. However, in cases such as *gām aśvam* ("a cow and a horse"), since a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is understood even in the absence of the use of *ca*, it is not the case that [the compound] is indicated solely by *ca*; rather, the "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is exactly as previously stated. Otherwise, one would fail to reach a conclusion even according to the manner described above; for in the case of *kṛtaḥ sarvamṛttikaḥ* ("all made of clay"), there is no occurrence of a compound due to the absence of an injunction (*vidhi*).

This is because it has been established that [the formation] occurs simultaneously with the action. Furthermore, since the occurrence of a compound could easily be assumed merely by observing a case of incapacity (asāmarthya) in some instances, the undesired consequence would follow that the expression *sarvamṛttikaḥ*—which is not a compound—would have to be treated as one simply because of the presence of the word *asūryampaśyā*, which is a compound; this [undesirable result] cannot be avoided even by that [proposed rule]. This argument is trivial, as the principle of "the authority of the specific statement" (*vacanaprāmāṇya*) applies equally to both cases.

When it is said, "Let the *nyagrodha* tree be seen, and the *plakṣa* tree," the denotative function (*arthavṛttitva*) does not reside in the word *nyagrodha*, but rather in the word *plakṣa* alone. Therefore, because a multi-word expression lacks a denotative function [in such a context], no compound is formed.

As for what they say—that the difficulty of expressing simultaneous reference to multiple substrata (*yugapadadhikaraṇavācitā*) applies to the analytical statement (*vigraha*) and not to the compound itself: that is incorrect, because simultaneous reference to multiple substrata is indeed observed in the preceding analytical statement; this is evident from examples such as *dhavau ca khadirau ca*, which is logically consistent with that very principle. Furthermore, it is improper to abandon the singular number that was first employed during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Nor should it be argued that if both meanings belong to each individual word in the compound, the same must hold true for the analytical statement as well.

In examples such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("king's man"), since the word *rājan* would have to be taken as indicating its relation (*sambandha*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the analytical statement (*vigraha*) would also result in the form "he is both a king and a man. This is not an acceptable consequence, because it would contradict rules such as *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (Pāṇini 6.3.21), which prescribes the non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending, as well as the rules governing its accentuation. Thus [it is argued].

That is incorrect. For even in the compound *tad-viṣayam* (in the previous text), simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatva*) has been demonstrated; thus, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that the refutation applies precisely because of this commonality. Otherwise, it would be impossible to justify the grammatical rule (*nyāsa*) "cārthe dvandvaḥ" (a copulative compound occurs when there is the sense of 'and'). Furthermore, it would be impossible to exclude [the application of the rule] in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), since the very nature of that rule is to apply to that which conveys the meaning of a compound. Nor does this result in the abolition of genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) and the like, for in those cases, the relation denoted by the genitive can still be expressed.

If it is argued that the relationship has not yet been stated even then, what of it? For only the mere property (*dharma*) has been stated; and because, in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), it is impossible even for Brahmā to bring about identity in all respects. Furthermore, in the analysis "the *dhava* trees," it is impossible to convey the meaning of the accusative case of the word *dhava* which is contained within the compound.

For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the rule for *aluk* (non-elision) and others. For this same reason, regarding the passage "of the two objects of the cognitions of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*," the ancient masters of the Upaniṣads have stated that—anticipating the objection that the analysis (*vigraha*) in the compound must consist of the dual-ended forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in order to conform to the requirement of simultaneous denotation of the substrates (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatva*)—there is an absence of such [dual endings] in both cases, in accordance with the aforementioned *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa*.

[Objection: But in that case, from *āṅgaś ca vāṅgaś ca kāliṅgaś ca*, the form *aṅgavaṅgakaliṅgāḥ* would not be possible; for by the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.62), when plurality caused by the offspring is intended, there is prescribed the elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting the offspring. Furthermore, without simultaneous coreferentiality (*yugapad-adhikaraṇatā*), the plurality cannot be construed with the meaning of the *tadrāja* suffix. And if the meaning were that "there is elision when plurality is expressed by that [suffix] which follows a *tadrāja*," then the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would apply even in the case of *priyavāṅgāḥ*. [Response: This is not so.

This is because you yourself must admit that, by taking the sense of "occurring in many," the plurality currently perceived belongs to the substratum which was previously denoted by the *tadrāja* suffix; furthermore, my distinction is that this [plurality] follows the *sup* (case-ending) after the compound. For the authors of the Bhāṣya have themselves stated that even under the view that the word expresses the substratum simultaneously [with its parts], the plural number indeed occurs after each individual member, so there is no fault.

In the analysis of non-worldly (alaukika) compounds, under the view that the constituent members (*varti-pada*) denote their referents simultaneously (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatva*), the fact that these members end in the singular number would contradict that intended meaning. However, in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), as in "play the hands-and-feet" (*pāṇipādaṃ vādaya*), the objecthood (*karmatva*) relates to a portion of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*), whereas oneness (*ekatva*) relates to the collective itself, due to the unique nature of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti-vaicitrya*).

As for the claim that the designation "aggregate" (*samāhāra*)—like *nadī*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth—is merely technical (*pāribhāṣikī*) and does not constitute the actual meaning of the word, and that singularity is simply unconnected [to the referent], and that there is no consequence of applying the dual number and so on because such usage would be ungrammatical (*asādhutva*): that is not correct. Why? Because it contradicts the section concerning the sound of a chariot (*rathaghoṣādhikaraṇa*). In the passage, "With the sound of a chariot he consecrates the *māhendra* cup," it was stated therein that, compared to a *samāhāra-dvandva* where both members are figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) in which only the first member is figurative is more figurative. This is the general direction of the argument.

Regarding the expression *ekaviṃśati* ("twenty-one") and others, the Bhāṣya states that this is a *samāhāra-dvandva* (an aggregative copulative compound). Nor does there arise the contingency of it being neuter, because gender is dependent upon worldly usage (*lokāśrayatvāt*). Consequently, in the case of a *dvandva* consisting of many *rājanya*s—such as *andhakavṛṣṇiṣu saṃkhyā*—the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is established. This is done to exclude [the application of] genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) in cases such as *śatasahasram*; for that [rule regarding the accent of the first member] applies specifically to the domain of *dvandva*s. However, if one were to apply the elision of the word "adhika" (as in *śākapārthiva* and similar compounds) to derive *ekādhikā viṃśatiḥ*, then the final syllable of the compound would be udātta.
**Upasarjanam pūrvam** || 30 || [The subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is placed first. || 30 ||

In a compound, the *upasarjana* (subordinate member) should be placed first. For example: *adhihari*. Now, one might object that in the expression *rājñaḥ pūruṣasya* ("the king's man"), since both members are in the genitive case, the rule for compounds would cause them to be designated as *upasarjana* because they are indicated in the nominative in the sūtra; consequently, there would be the undesirable contingency of either being placed first by turn. This is not so, because this technical name (*saṃjñā*) is defined etymologically (*anvartha*) and applies only to that which is non-principal (*apradhāna*). Here, because the "man" (*puruṣa*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it alone possesses primacy. [The sūtra continues: "In the group beginning with *rājadanta*, the [subordinate] comes last. (Pāṇini 2.2.31)

In these [compounds], the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) should stand first. *Rājadantaḥ* ("king of teeth" = the front tooth): king among teeth. *Agrevaṇam* ("forest at the front"): at the front of the forest. [The absence of *samāsānta* suffix] is due to a specific rule (*nipātana*) regarding the class (*gaṇa*). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Regarding words such as *dharma*, no fixed rule is desired. *Arthadharmau* ("wealth and duty") or *dharmārthau* ("duty and wealth"). *Jampatī*, *dampatī*, *jāyāpatī* ("husband and wife"). Due to the reading in the *gaṇa*-list, the substitution of *daṃ* or *jaṃ* for *jāyā* occurs. **Pāṇini 2.2.32:** In a *dvandva* compound, that which ends in a *ghī*-vowel (i.e., short *i* or *u*) stands first.

Hari and Hara. When there is the possibility of multiple [names] being applied, the restriction to one is the "aniyama" (non-restriction); for the remainder, Hari, Hara, and Guru [are used]. That which begins with 'a' and ends with a short vowel is placed first. (33)

In a *dvandva* compound, that which begins with a vowel other than *a* (or *ā*) and ends with a short *a* shall stand first. When there are many members, there is no fixed rule. Examples: *aśvarathendrāḥ* or *indrāśvarathāḥ*. In case of conflict, a word ending in *dhi* (long *ī*) and a word beginning with a vowel other than *a* (or *ā*) and ending in a short *a* take precedence over one another. Example: *indrāgnī*. A word with fewer syllables shall stand first. (Pāṇini 2.2.34)

In a *dvandva* compound, that which has fewer syllables should stand first. It should not be argued that this rule would not apply when many items are present, because the suffix *tarap* (forming the comparative) cannot arise due to the absence of a dual-number word as a qualifier; for it is accepted that *tarap* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*) by means of a *nipātana* (an irregularity), and that the changes of *t* to *k* and *c* to *ch* do not take place. Examples include: *dhavakhadirau* (the *dhava* and *khadira* trees); *prāsāde dhanapatirāmakeśavānām* (in the palace [of] Dhanapati, Rāma, and Keśava); and *mṛdaṅgaśaṅkhatūṇavāḥ pṛthag vadanti saṃsadi* (the drum, the conch, and the flute speak separately in the assembly). In such cases, one forms a separate *dvandva* for each pair first, and then forms another *dvandva* with the preceding rule.

Nor does the rule for "treatment as a single unit" (*ekavadbhāva*) apply on the grounds that the genus (*jāti*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because [the compound] refers to specific substances; nor on the grounds of being a component of musical instruments (*tūryāṅga*), because the conch shell (*śaṅkha*) is not one of them. Alternatively, it is because only those who subsist by the craft of music are included as components of musical instruments. By the rule of contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*), that which has fewer syllables takes precedence over the two preceding ones: *vāgagnī*, *vāgindrau*. This section is non-eternal (*anitya*), as seen from such indications as *lakṣamahetvoḥ* and *samudrābhrāddhaḥ*.

By this, Jaimini’s sūtra—"there is no [application of the term] *śat* to *barhis* and *ājya* when there is no consecration (*saṃskāra*)"—as well as [the maxim] "through study, understanding, practice, and propagation," etc., have been explained.

When the names of seasons and constellations consist of an equal number of syllables, their precedence should be stated according to their traditional order: *śiśira-vasantau* (winter and spring), *kṛttikā-rohiṇyau* (the constellations Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī). Regarding those who come together (*sametika*), as in *grīṣma-vasantau* (summer and spring), that which is more venerable (*abhyarhita*) comes first. For example, *mātā-pitarau* (mother and father); these are to be honored, and among them, the mother is superior, so says Yājñavalkya. That which has fewer syllables (*laghu-akṣara*) comes first, as in *kuśa-kāśam* (Kuśa grass and Kāśa grass). It should be stated that that which is more venerable comes first even before that which has fewer syllables, as in *bhrātuḥ jyāyasaḥ* (of the elder brother); for example, *yudhiṣṭhira-arjunau* (Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna).

When the number to be counted is fewer than eleven: eleven, twelve; this [formation] occurs even outside of a *dvandva* compound, as in *dvitrāḥ*. This is established by the rule *dveyekayoḥ* being found in the *sūtra* (Pāṇini 5.3.94).
In a Bahuvrīhi compound, when a word ending in the seventh case is used as a qualifier, [the feminine suffix ṅīp is optionally applied]. 35.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) should be placed first. For example: *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("He who has Kāla on his neck"). When it is known in a general sense that "something is on the neck" and then it is specified as "Kāla," then because the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is the thing qualified (*viśeṣya*), the seventh case is used separately. Otherwise, its status as a qualifier is established by default. For example: *citraguḥ* ("He who has brindled cows").

[The Vārttika] states: "An addition must be made for all pronouns (sarvanāman) and numerals. Examples: *viśvadevaḥ* ("the All-gods")—this also applies when the word *viśva-* functions as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). *divaśuklaḥ* ("white as the sky"). [Objection: Since two [words, *dvi-* and *putra-*,] function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), there would be the contingency of irregularity. [Response: Forms such as *dviputraḥ* ("having two sons") are established even from their status as qualifiers. [Regarding the term *tapara*: That which has *t* as its subsequent element is *tapara*. [Regarding *jahatsvārthā*: That which abandons its own [meaning] is *jahatsvaḥ*. As for the statement that "a compound in which the constituent members abandon their own meanings is *jahatsvārthā*," they say this is established either through the usage in the Sūtra and Bhāṣya or by virtue of belonging to the *rājadantādi* group.

This is stated because, when both [conditions] coincide, one must resort to the *vipratiṣedha* (the rule of the later) regarding the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*). For this very reason, it was not said that [the rule applies] to "number and pronoun" (*saṃkhyā-sarvanāmnor*). Examples: *dvyanyāya*, *tryanyāya*.

Or [the compound] *priyaguḍaḥ* (one who loves molasses) and *guḍapriyaḥ* (molasses is dear). It should be stated that the locative case [is used] after words such as *gaḍu*: *gaḍukaṇṭhaḥ* (one with a goitre on the neck), *gaḍuśirāḥ* (one with a goitre on the head). In some cases it is not so: *vahegaḍuḥ* (one with a goitre on the shoulder). Here, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the locative case refers to the general rule; by this, forms such as *manuṣyajanmāpi surāsurān guṇaiḥ* (even though born a human, he [excelled] gods and demons by his virtues) are established. And thus Vāmana says: "A *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *janman* and similar words is not to be avoided. Furthermore, because the usage of the learned serves as a restrictive authority, there is no over-extension of the rule.

As for the statement in the *Śābarabhāṣya* regarding the final position (*siddhānta*) on the passage "he performs the *agnihotra*" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is an oblation (*hotra*) for Agni," and as Someśvara has stated that it is a genitive *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that of which Agni is the *hotra*": although this involves a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and contradicts the final acute accent (*antodātta*) found in the Taittirīya recension, nevertheless—since the reading with all-acute accents (*sarvodātta-svara*) in the Vājasaneyaka cannot be accounted for even by a *tatpuruṣa* compound—it is necessary to assume that one or the other [interpretation] is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The intention is that there is no great fault [in this view], because even a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound with members in different grammatical cases) is sometimes resorted to.

However, the Neo-Mīmāṃsakas maintain that, following the rule "the *uṇ*-suffixes etc. are manifold" (*uṇādayo bahulam*), the suffix *traṇ* is applied to the root *hu* (to sacrifice) in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, it is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the sacrifice (*hotra*) belonging to Agni. Since the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is understood from scriptural authorities such as "that which is for Agni," the specific relation to the substance is the meaning of the genitive case by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, having Agni as its deity is the ground for the application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) of the term. Nor should it be argued that this is not the case because the status of having Agni as its deity is absent in the morning performance.

They say that even when a single *homa* is performed repeatedly in the evening and morning—as in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—there is no difference in the ritual action (*karma-bheda*). Since the homogeneity of the class of *homa* exists precisely through its subsistence in a common substratum, its [repetition] is thus justified. (For it is not the case that the very same [action] is delimited by that [time]). Likewise, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *Vaiśvadeva*," although the connection with the Viśvedevas resides in only a single sacrifice, they accept that this is the name for a group of eight sacrifices.

As for the statement that the word *hotra* is derived in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and is thus a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, one should reflect thereon that in the cognition "the locus of the oblation related to Agni," the status of being a locus does not actually belong to Agni; this is the general direction [of the argument]. [End of section on] the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). 36.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix (a past passive participle) should stand first. For example, *kṛtakṛtyaḥ*. This is because the term *niṣṭhā* refers only to those participles prescribed by the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.26], and thus does not include the *kta* suffix used in the sense of an abstract action (*napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*), as in the example *cārusmitam*. It should be stated that a *niṣṭhā* suffix following words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), or happiness (*sukha*) and so forth, must stand at the end of the compound. Examples include *sāraṅgajagdhī* ("eaten by a deer"), *palāṇḍubhakṣitī* ("eaten by an onion"), *māsajātā* ("born after a month"), *sukhajātā* ("born in happiness"), and *duḥkhajātā* ("born in suffering"). This is established by the very fact that the rule prescribing the acute accent on the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapadāntodātta*) for these cases serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). If the *niṣṭhā* were not required to stand last, there would be no occasion for such an accentuation. Thus, the rule is proven.

The phrase "those who have not performed the act" (*akṛtamita-pratipannāḥ*) refers to those whose negation is intended; for it is their posterior position (*paranipāta*) that must be stated [by the rule]. However, in reality, since a negation presupposes the possibility of the final syllable of the subsequent member being udātta, and since that [udātta-ness] would be impossible without posterior position, their formation is established by the very fact of this negation serving as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In some cases, however, it is not so: e.g., *kṛtakaṭaḥ* (one who has made a mat) and *pītodakaḥ* (one who has drunk water).
[This applies] in the case of *vāhitāgni* and similar compounds. (Pāṇini 2.2.37)

*Āhitāgniḥ* (one who has established the sacred fires) and *agnyāhitaḥ* (one to whom the fires have been established). The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) and the locative case (*saptamī*) follow words such as *praharaṇa* (weapon) and others: *asyudyataḥ* (with a raised sword), *susalodyataḥ* (with a raised club), *asipāṇiḥ* (sword-in-hand), *daṇḍapāṇiḥ* (staff-in-hand). In some cases, this does not occur: *vivṛtāsiḥ* (with a drawn sword).
Kaḍāra (tawny) and other such words [may optionally precede] in a *karmadhāraya* compound. (38)

The meaning is "beginning with *kaḍāra*," as in the rule "he places the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks. [The list is: *kaḍāra*, *gaḍula*, *karaṇa*, *khañja*, *kuṇṭha*, *khoḍa*, *khalati*, *gaura*, *vṛddha*, *bhikṣuka*, *piṅgala*, *tantu*, *jaraṭha*, *vṛd*. Examples: *kaḍārajaiminiḥ* (Jaimini who is tawny) and *jaiminikaḍāraḥ* (the tawny Jaimini); *gaḍulaśāṇḍilyaḥ* (Śāṇḍilya who is goitre-affected) and *śāṇḍilyagaḍulaḥ* (the goitre-affected Śāṇḍilya). Why "in a *karmadhāraya*"? So that it does not apply in a *bahuvrīhi*: *kaḍārapuruṣako grāmaḥ* (a village whose men are tawny).
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the second Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the *Siddhāntasudhānidhi*.
And the chapter is completed.
Now begins the third chapter, the first section.
When [the action] is not already expressed [by another word]. || 39 ||

This is a restrictive rule (*avadhikāra*). The meaning is that the second and subsequent case-endings (*vibhakti*) occur when the object (*karman*) and so forth have not already been expressed. "Expression" (*abhidhāna*) means communication. For example: *aśvābhidhānīm ādatte* ("He takes up the horse's halter"). In the verse regarding "expression," since the roots *hi* (in the sense of binding or uttering) and *nī* (in the sense of movement or increase) are not applicable to the present context, they are not considered here. *Caitraḥ taṇḍulam pacati* ("Caitra cooks rice") and *caitreṇa taṇḍulaḥ pacyate* ("Rice is cooked by Caitra"). In the first sentence, because the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) arises in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), both the agent and the object are expressed; therefore, due to this expression, the third case does not occur for the agent. In the second [sentence], it is due to non-expression [of the agent].

Furthermore, because the object (*karman*) has already been expressed [by the suffix] and the agent (*kartṛ*) has not yet been expressed, both would require the second case (*dvitīyā*); however, they are deprived of it by the third case (*tṛtīyā*).

Expression [of grammatical relations] occurs generally through verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*). For example: *devadattaḥ pācakaḥ* ("Devadatta is a cooker")—here the suffix *ṇvul* expresses the agent. *devadatena pakvaḥ taṇḍulaḥ* ("The rice was cooked by Devadatta")—here the suffix *kta* expresses the object. *aurapagavaḥ* ("the son of Urvaśī") and *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows")—because the relationship of producer and produced, as well as the relationship of owned and owner, have been expressed by the secondary derivative and the compound respectively, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply. In some cases, expression also occurs through particles (*nipāta*): "Even a poisonous tree, having been nurtured, is not fit to be cut down by oneself."

The meaning is that [the former usage] is not tenable. Now, how is it that Murāri says: "Having remembered the arms of Vālin, those monkeys ought not now to be disregarded"? It is said in reply: in that case, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is determined by the act of disregard (*avajñāna*). For this very reason, both "having cooked, rice is eaten" (*paktvaudanaṃ bhujyate*) and "rice, having been cooked, is eaten" (*paktvaudano bhujyate*) are authoritative.
As in: "He was recognized as Nārada in due order."

To explain: "This is Nārada" [is the meaning]. The knowledge associated with Śrī Kṛṣṇa is expressed by the word *iti*, and the word *iti* refers to that specific form [of knowledge]. The meaning of the accusative case following the pronoun *adaḥ* (this) is the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). Thus, the meaning is: "Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the locus of a knowledge whose qualificand is the aforementioned individual and whose mode (*prakāra*) is 'Nārada-ness'. This is because, through the word *iti* which refers to the form of the knowledge, one obtains—in that very knowledge being referred to—the property of having as its mode the cognition produced by the words immediately preceding it. This alone constitutes the expression of the object (*karman*).

However, there is this distinction: when used in conjunction with a verbal root meaning "to know," the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). This is because expressions such as *ghaṭaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the cloth as a pot") are not employed when there is knowledge of a cloth under the aspect of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). On the other hand, the word *iti* indicates the aforementioned mode [of cognition], as seen in the usage *paṭaṃ ghaṭa iti jānāti* ("he knows the cloth as 'pot'").

Consequently, while the accusative case generally conveys that the cognition has the meaning of the base as its object—characterized by having as its qualifier a property other than that which delimits the meaning of the base—the particle *iti* specifically conveys that the cognition has as its qualifier a property other than that which delimits the meaning of the word preceding it. Furthermore, there is no rule that the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) must necessarily be the meaning of the preceding word; it may be something else. For this very reason, the accusative case is used in "amum" (in the expression *amum iti*), because the status of being the qualificand is not expressed by the particle *iti*.

In the case of "he knows the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), however, because the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) are expressed by a single word, there is no contingency for the accusative case on the word *ghaṭa* with respect to *ghaṭatva*. This [previous] example is not appropriate here; nevertheless, even though such a thing occurs in cases where the qualifier has a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa-prakāraka*), in the present instance it is so because the cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The intention is that the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) in Nārada is also what is to be understood by that [cognition].

Nor should it be argued that, by this same logic, the accusative case would not occur in the expression "amum" (this one) either; for in the cognition "This is Nārada," the fact that Nārada is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is not necessarily manifested. This is because the objective content delimited by "thisness" (*idantva*) is distinct from the objective content delimited by "Nāradata-ness" (*nāradatva*). Such is the direction of the argument.

It might be argued as follows: Since the rule "that which has already expressed its meaning need not be employed" (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*) applies when objects such as the *karman* (object) are denoted by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like, there would be no possibility for the occurrence of case-endings such as the second (*dvitīyā*), and thus this governing rule (*adhikāra*) would be redundant. Nor can one point to exceptions such as *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, and so forth; for in those cases, it is accepted that there is a distinction between the two numbers belonging to the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). For instance, in the word *śatam* ("a hundred"), the number "hundred" which serves as the ground for the application of the suffix (*pravṛttinimitta*) resides in the substance and so on, whereas the number "one" residing in the hundred—which constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—is distinct from the number that is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*).

Likewise, here too, it is possible that the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) and the singularity expressed by the case-ending (*vibhaktivācya*) are distinct. As stated by Hari: "In the phrase 'the cause is one,' the singularity is not denoted by the case-ending; rather, the case-ending applies to that which possesses that [cause] and is singular."

On this point, they say: what is to be conveyed is that the mat (*kaṭa*) qualified by the attributes [such as *bhīṣma*] is the object (*karman*). Since, without the production of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*), there would be no cognition of the mat being qualified by those [attributes], the mat itself would not be the object either; therefore, by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the second case is applied to *bhīṣma* and the others. Nor should it be argued that the nominative (*prathamā*) alone should occur, because the second case is the one presented immediately after the word denoting the substantive (*viśeṣya*). This is because the presentation of the nominative—dependent on the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)—is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*) compared to this [immediate syntactic requirement].

Alternatively, when there is a desire to enjoin a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), since mere substratum (*dharmimātra*) does not suffice for satisfaction and because the properties (*dharma*) are the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), they too possess the status of an object (*karman*). Furthermore, that [object-hood] is not denoted by the accusative case-ending following a word expressing something else. However, in cases such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is made"), because the *kta*-suffix follows the verbal root, it does not denote merely the object-hood residing in the specific meaning of the nominal stem; rather, it denotes that [object-hood] residing in both the property and the substratum without distinction. Thus, all [words] take the nominative ending—this is the difference.

For this very reason, in cases such as "aruṇayā ekahāyanyā" (with a red, one-year-old [cow]), the connection of the case-endings denoting *kārakas* with the action is verbal (*śābda*). However, the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified is subsequent (*pārṣṭhika*), because even though a quality cannot be a direct means of accomplishing the action, its status as a means to the action is established precisely by its delimiting the substance—the cow—which is the actual means to that action; so say the Mīmāṃsakas. In cases such as "nīlaṃ ghaṭam" (the blue pot), non-difference (*abheda*) is the relation.

The Naiyāyikas maintain that since the cause of the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the suffix is only a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a noun (*nāmārtha*) characterized by either difference (*bheda*) or relation (*saṃsarga*), the case-ending of the qualifier is for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Likewise, "being other than an indeclinable" (*avyayātiriktatva*) is also a qualifier of the noun. This is because in examples such as *candra iva mukham* ("the face is like the moon") and *ghaṭo na* ("not a jar"), the moon and the jar are construed with the similarity and the absence—both meanings of the indeclinables—as the relata (*pratiyogin*), while the face and [the absence] are construed as the correlates (*anuyogin*) with the similarity and so on. Thus, the case-ending of the qualifier has non-difference (*abheda*) as its meaning.

Therefore, the term "involving difference and connection" (bhedasaṃsargaka) need not be included in the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) of the effect. Regarding expressions such as "like the moon" (candra iva), the proponents of that particular school [of thought] maintain that the meaning of the case-ending following the word "moon" is counter-positiveness (pratiyogitva), while the meaning of the case-ending following the word "like" (iva) is sub-positiveness (anuyogitva).

It might be argued as follows: In the view that the Sūtra is to be formulated, the term *anabhihite* (when not expressed) would mean either a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) or a *paryudāsa* (relative exclusion). It cannot be the first, because that would result in the faults of an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) and a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). For instance, in the case of *prāsāde āste* ("he sits in the palace"), since the palace is the locus distinct from the action, and since that [locus] is already expressed by the suffix *-ghañ* itself which has *sad-* as its base, there would follow the undesirable consequence of prohibiting the locative case based on that very expression. By this, the second alternative (*paryudāsa*) is also refuted, because that which is already expressed cannot be different from what is expressed.

Nor should it be argued that even when the locus-power (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) defined by the act of sitting (*āsikriyā*) is not expressed, the locative case (*saptamī*) still applies despite the non-expression of the locus-power defined by the act of sitting; for this would fail to account for instances such as *āmane āste* ("he sits on a mat") and *śayane śete* ("he lies on a bed"). Since there is no evidence for a factor of action (*kāraka*) distinct from the substance (*dravya*), it is necessary to posit both [the substance and its power] as distinct factors of action. Furthermore, power is not apprehended through perception apart from the nature of the substance, and inference, which is preceded by perception, likewise does not apply to it.

If it is argued that [the probans] is unestablished because the effect merely follows the presence and absence of the substance, and because it is not the counter-positive of an absence that serves as the cause for the non-existence of the effect;

It is said: if the means [of action] were merely a substance (*dravyamātra*), then, because that substance possesses a single nature and is the object of an uncontradicted recognition based upon it, there would be no differentiation of designations based on the performance of various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*). Yet such differentiation is observed: when asked, "Where is Devadatta?", the answer "He is at the tree" presents the tree as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); whereas when asked, "In which [tree]? regarding the specific tree, the answer "The one who stands there" presents it in the form of an agent (*kartṛ*).

Indeed, it is impossible to deny the distinction between the two cognitions—one as the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) and the other as the agent (*kartṛtā*). And this distinction is dependent upon a difference in objects; for if [the self] were of the nature of cognition alone, one would fall into the position of the Buddhist school (*saugata-mata*). Therefore, in order to account for this, the six powers (*śakti*) in the form of agent and so forth must necessarily be admitted. It is through their presence that various distinct designations apply to what is in fact a single entity. Otherwise, there would be no systematic distinction between object, instrument, and the rest.

This has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "The six powers of others are eternal. And these [powers] are indeed differentiated by the distinctions among actions; otherwise, such statements as "this one is the agent of going, but not of cooking" would be untenable. However, their distinction does not arise from the difference in individual substances (*dravyavyakti*), for there is a lack of evidence [for such a claim]. Furthermore, it must be accepted that agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth are the unifying factors (*anugamaka*) and the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of those [powers]; otherwise, even the uniform linguistic usage regarding that portion [of meaning] would not occur.

If it is asked how [the phrase] "then he sits upon the seat" and so forth is to be understood, they say here: by words such as *āsana* (seat), *śayana* (bed), *karaṇa* (instrument), *apādāna* (ablative), and *saṃpradāna* (dative), the mere substance suitable for the action of sitting and so forth is denoted, with its power (*śakti*) not yet manifested. In that regard, a case-ending must necessarily be produced in order to demonstrate the manifestation of that power. Therefore, the intent of the Bhāṣya statement "the instrument of sitting" (*asisādhana*) is to exclude other instruments; the meaning is that the action of sitting is mentioned here solely for the sake of the etymological derivation of the word.

And this very [cognition] is the "emergence" (*udbhava*), which consists in the cognition [of the locus] as qualified by a specifier such as a particular time that is to be superposed (*ādheya*). This is because, in the case of the word *āsana* ("seating"), there is no comprehension of either a particular time or a particular thing to be superposed; and because the mere use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is unfit for employment; and because when another verbal root is employed, one obtains only a superposed entity and so forth that is specified by a different action and does not specify a locus, leaving the aforementioned deficiency intact—namely, the failure to comprehend a superposed entity that specifies a locus specified by the act of sitting (*āsikriyā*).

Furthermore, even when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is denoted by a suffix (*pratyaya*), the pure nature of the power (*śaktisvarūpa*), uninvested with any other capacity, is not conveyed. This is because, in cases such as *āsanena* ("by means of sitting"), one experiences the connection with [other] factors like the object (*karman*), and thus it is the case-endings themselves that convey the pure power of the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). As the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda has stated: "By means of a *kṛt*-suffix, indeed, a factor qualified by a substance (*dravya*) is expressed; but by a case-ending alone, the isolated power is not [expressed]. And so, [if that were the case], one would have to say 'the factor by the factor' (*kārakaṃ kārakeṇa*). Thus, the apprehension of the isolated form itself is what constitutes "emergence" (*udbhava*); this is the general direction.

[Objection: Even so, the expression "having cooked, rice is eaten" (*paktvaudano bhujyate*) would not be possible; for no one accepts that the *ktvā* suffix denotes the object (*karman*). Even if the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expresses the object-power as determined by the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*), since it does not express the object-power as determined by the action of cooking (*pacikriyā*), a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would result. [Reply: Not so. Because grammatical operations based on whether something is expressed or not are governed solely by the power determined by the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*). Thus, the expression or non-expression [of a power] proceeds only in accordance with that which is determined by the principal action.

The argument that "by this Caitra, having eaten, he comes"—which occurs precisely because of the extension (*atideśa*)—is refuted on the grounds that even when an operation prompted by the mention of the principal element is extended, there is no prohibition of operations prompted by its own status (*svaniṣṭha*) or not prompted by it; for such is the established usage regarding extension. Furthermore, this is rejected because grammatical operations pertaining to subordinate elements proceed solely in accordance with the principal element, which contradicts Kaiyaṭa and others, and because it is established by the *Bhāṣya* and other texts on the rule *karmavat* (Pāṇini 3.1.87) that only that which is contrary to the extension proceeds as an inherent property of the element itself.
As Harivṛṣabha has stated:
Where there are two distinct powers of a substance belonging to a primary and a secondary action,
and these powers are based on qualities, there the primary action is followed.
When the power whose primary object is the principal element is expressed by a suffix, then,
even if it is not explicitly stated, it is understood in the same manner when [that power] resides in a subordinate element.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: in the sense of a sentence, the action expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) alone is the primary element. As for the other [words], their placement after the word ending in *ajādi* (feminine suffixes) or *ac* (consonant) is for the sake of obtaining their status as correlates (*pratiyogin*) to that primary element. The word *pṛthak* ("separate") is also included because the powers (*śakti*) [of the kārakas] differ according to the difference in actions. He explains "is followed" (*anurudhyate*) with the word "primary" (*pradhāna*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "when it is denoted. Even though [the power] is not explicitly stated by the verb (*ākhyāta*), this is because only the power as determined by the action of its own base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is denoted.

Because it is impossible to express a capacity that is determined by the action denoted by the suffix *ktvā* (the gerundive). As stated previously: since subordinate elements (*guṇa*) depend upon the principal element (*pradhāna*), when there is a cognition of the grammatical operation (*kārya*) induced by the expression of the principal capacity within a single word, it is illogical for that same word to induce an operation contrary to it that would be occasioned by its own non-expression. The meaning is that the relationship of subordinate and principal between the two capacities of those [elements] is mediated by the action. Furthermore, the principle of "conflict between the primary and the subordinate" (*aṅguṇavirodhanyāya*) should also be considered here.

As for what has been stated by the Mīmāṃsakas: "If this were so, then such usages as 'odanaṃ bhuktvā śāstraṃ paṭhyate' (having eaten rice, the scripture is studied) and 'śrutvāpyarthaṃ nānumatastenaso'rthaḥ kubuddhinā' (even having heard the meaning, its purpose is not approved by one of evil intellect) would be untenable; therefore, that which is the state of being the cause of the application of the nominative case is the fact of being conveyed by a word through its own function (*vṛtti*) as expressing the action connected with itself. This is 'abhihitatva' (the state of being expressed), and the connection is the primary one."

In the case of "The sacrificial post is made of udumbara wood; one desiring heaven should sacrifice," even when there is a lakṣaṇā (indication) of the post as the object (*karman*)—as in the thought "one should bring about the post"—the first case ending (*prathamā*) is justified because agency (*kartṛtva*) is stated in the cognition produced by the word's primary power (*śakti*). However, where the initial cognition produced by lakṣaṇā arises due to the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*), the first case ending is indeed ungrammatical. For example, in "Agni strives for cooking" or "Caitra strives for cooking," since the word *yatate* does not denote the instrument (*karaṇatva*) of Agni, the use of the first case ending would be incorrect.

And in cases such as "rice is eaten after being cooked," the word *odana* (rice) does not syntactically connect with the act of cooking; rather, there is simply the ellipsis of a second-case form of the word *odana*.

That is incorrect. For in that case, there is no obstacle to the commencement of an action based on whether it is expressed or unexpressed, depending on the distinction between the substratum (dharmin) and its subordinate or primary powers (guṇa-pradhāna-śakti). Furthermore, when a suffix expresses the power residing in a factor (kāraka) presented by a particular word, that very power—residing in the same factor presented by that word—is incapable of initiating a contradictory action. In the second case, there is no such objection because the words are distinct. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of using the expression "caitreṇa bhuktvā caitro gacchati" (Having eaten, Caitra goes, by Caitra).

Because there is no deviation regarding the requirement of a common agent, and because a word denoting a separate agent is never employed for a subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), the expression "Caitra, having become, goes" (*caitro bhūtvā caitro gacchati*) is not used. Furthermore, since identity of object is not strictly necessary, the object may sometimes be mentioned separately; a detailed discussion on this point occurs in the *Tarkakautūhala* during the commentary on the sentence: "Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva*), let me manifest names and forms."

Let us return to the subject at hand. As for what has been stated by the Neo-Mīmāṃsakas: since the verb *pacati* (he cooks) prompts the question "In what manner?", the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), refer to the agent and so forth in order to provide the knowledge of the substratum (*dharmin*) that establishes that [action]. Therefore, it is precisely such a denotation [of the agent] that governs the distribution of case-endings (*vibhakti*). Nor should it be argued that there is an impossibility of a common denotation for both [the suffixes], because the kṛt-suffix denotes [the agent] through primary power (*śakti*) while the tiṅ-suffix denotes it through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [This is not a problem, as] the denotation itself remains common to both.

The claim that "because [the suffix] is to be explained by its function (vṛtti), it has that as its purpose" is incorrect; for this being the case, it is more appropriate to postulate the power of the agent and so forth—which is established by grammatical instruction—with respect to both [the root and the suffix].

Even where, according to the principle stated for the sixth [case], there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends a plurality of substrata—as in the case of a husband and wife—there is no indication of the substratum by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in injunctional sentences such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), because it would result in the non-connection of singularity [with the action]. Furthermore, there is no evidence for indicating duality [of the substratum]. Therefore, in that case, what is indicated by the verbal suffix is the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), specifically the agency consisting in the performance of the action as defined by the delimitor of the indicated; the substratum itself is not indicated, since the understanding of it arises from the context alone.

For even in such cases as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), the word functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote merely that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*). However, the reason for employing the nominative case everywhere is simply the mention of agency (*kartṛtva*). And there is a distinction: where agency is indicated with respect to the agent (*kartṛ*), the cognition has agency as its qualifier; where agency is indicated with respect to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), the cognition has agency as its qualificand.

Alternatively, since agency and so forth are construed with the act (kriyā) through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the agent and so forth appear by virtue of being constituents of that [act] precisely through the operation of the relation itself. It is with reference to this very fact that the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) is formulated. Consequently, in the definition of "being expressed" (*abhihitatva*), the term "by means of a function" (*vṛttyā*) need not be included; rather, it is simply the state of being conveyed by way of verbal cognition (*śābdavidhayā*), common to both [the case of] objective content residing in a relation (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*).

That too is incorrect, because it contradicts grammatical injunctions such as *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), and because relation (*saṃsarga*) is not the intended object of the treatise. Furthermore, regarding the refutation of the position that in cases such as *vaiśvadevī* (discussed in the *Guṇādhikaraṇa*), the status of being a deity is understood through the force of the relation between the meanings of the base and the suffix, [the author] himself stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-kaustubha*: "Since the grammatical treatise functions to instruct upon word-meanings, it is untenable for [the treatise] to operate with respect to that which appears merely as a relation."

In the case of the expression *kartari kṛt*, since the meaning "when [the agent] is to be expressed" (*vācye*) is accepted, the interpretation "in some way to be conveyed" (*pratipādye*) for subsequent cases is untenable. Furthermore, the governing rule regarding words (*śabdādhikāra*) is not particularly favored here, because the specific cognition produced by that word alone constitutes the "denoted word-meaning" (*abhihitapadārtha*). Even though non-difference (*abheda*) functions as a relation (*saṃsarga*) in expressions such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer"), there is no conventional usage of treating that non-difference as the denotation of the word *daṇḍin*. In expressions such as *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), however, even when the agency—which serves as the delimitor of the word-meaning—is construed [with the action], there is no harm to the number [of the agent].

Regarding this, they say: the status of being a deity and the status of being an agent belong only to those who are mutually dependent, as in the case of Agni and Soma. And because there is unity in the form of the agent, the number conveyed by the verbal suffix is not contradictory even when used together—as in the expression "Agni-Soma are the deities. Thus it is said.

The Naiyāyikas, however, hold that the phrase "anabhihita-saṃkhyāke" (when number is not expressed) serves as a governing rule (*adhikāra*). This is because in the sentence "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), the number of the agent is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), whereas in "The rice is cooked" (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*), it is the number of the object that is expressed. Nor does it follow that both numbers would be expressed when the agent and the object have the same grammatical number; for their connection occurs only when there is a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*). As the Teacher has said: "When the object of numbering is obtainable through implication (*ākṣepa*), there is no assumption of its being directly denoted (*abhidhāna*). Even when the mere object of numbering is obtained, the determination [of which number applies] is established based on that which possesses the expectancy."

Nor can it be argued that because the notion of singularity is obtained from the *sup* [nominal] suffix itself, the *tiṅ* [verbal] suffix does not have that as its meaning; for in the case of "Caitra and Maitra go" (*caitraśca maitraśca gacchataḥ*), the cognition of duality is accomplished by the *tiṅ* suffix alone. Nor can it be said that there is merely a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of duality in the *sup* suffix; for if one were to accept secondary signification in a nominal case-ending, it would contradict the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) regarding the transposition of suffixes (*vyatyaya*). Nor should it be asserted that while there is no secondary signification of the meaning of another case-ending in the *sup*, duality is nevertheless the meaning of that very case-ending.

Nevertheless, because it would follow that only Caitra and the other [individual] would be understood, the cognition of duality residing in both would be untenable; for the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) there is that the suffix denotes a number residing solely in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Nor can duality be construed with what is presented as singular, since that singularity is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣitatvāt*). Even when singularity is cognized in each of the two individually, the cognition "the two possess an effort conducive to going" is still logically possible.

Furthermore, in the case of the sentence "brāhmaṇāḥ paṭhanti" (the Brahmins read), there is no undesirable consequence of understanding that "many Brahmins" or "two possess the volitional effort conducive to reading. This is because the cognition of the sentence "brāhmaṇāḥ paṭhanti" acts as an obstacle to the cognition of duality produced by the verbal suffix. Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the verbal singular number having the meaning of singularity as its denotation;

for while the singular forms of the second case and others may have the denotation of singularity in accordance with examples such as "taṇḍulaṃ pacati" (he cooks rice), there is no decisive reason [to restrict this] regarding the singularity denoted by the first-case singular.

Thus, in a cognition where the number is the qualifier (prakāra) of the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), the cause is the mental presence (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case, related to it through the relation of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) as determined by the mode of the productive operation (bhāvanā). And the qualificandum of the productive operation is that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case, provided it is not itself a qualifier of anything else. This is because the productive operation requires a substratum (āśraya), and the person (puruṣa) likewise requires an action (kriyā).

This has been stated by the Teachers: "Indeed, expectancy for one [of the two] is not the cause of syntactic connection; rather, it is expectancy for both. For the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not having obtained connection with a result, requires a connection with an action (*kriyā*). The productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as well, being itself an activity, requires an agent (*vyāpārin*); thus, there is expectancy for both. Therefore, the distinction is established by whether number is expressed or unexpressed in the case of *tiṅ*-suffixes, whereas in the case of *kṛt*-affixes, it is by whether the agent or the object is expressed or unexpressed.

The meaning of the term *anabhihite* (when not already expressed) is that the number of the agent or object, or the agent and object themselves, have not been expressed. By this, [objections] such as "there is complexity regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) due to the property of being a single agent" and so forth are refuted.

The modern [grammarians], however, argue that in the case of "the rice is cooked" (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*), if the meaning of the verbal root were the action delimited by the result, and the meaning of the agent-suffix were the substratum-ness of the action, then the resulting cognition—"the rice possesses a result produced by an operation residing in Maitra"—would not occur. This is because it would entail a reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship between the capacity (the result) and the substratum (the rice). Therefore, the operation is the meaning of the verbal root, the result is the meaning of the middle voice suffix (*ātmanepada*), and the relation of being produced is the semantic connection (*saṃsarga*). Thus, the cognition is: "the rice possesses a result produced by an operation produced by an effort (*kṛti*) residing in Maitra."

And thus, in the case of *pacati* ("he cooks"), there is the expression of the *kṛti* (volitional effort), whereas in *pacyate* ("it is cooked"), there is the expression of the result (*phala*); this distinction is established by what is expressed and what is not. In instances such as *ghaṭo jñāyate* ("the pot is known"), there is the figurative (*bhākta*) status of "object-ness" (*viṣayatā*) for the pot, and in *ghaṭo naśyati* ("the pot perishes"), there is likewise the figurative status of "agent-ness" (*kartṛtva*) for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*). In all these cases, there is the expression of that which is common to both. Furthermore, in the case of *kṛt*-suffixes, even if they denote a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) in order to maintain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), since the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also expressed, it is possible to maintain uniformity across all instances.

They say that it is not correct to claim that the suffix *kṛt* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which is qualified by effort (*kṛti*), because even when the suffix *kṛt* occurs, there is never an understanding of mere effort alone. [Pāṇini 2.3.2 states:
"The second case ending is used for the object (*karman*). 40.

The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) shall occur when the object (*karman*) is not already expressed by another word. Examples include *grāmaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to the village") and *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), and so forth. The terms "second" (*dvitīyā*) and so on refer to the triplets of *sup*-suffixes according to the usage of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). Thus, being possessed of the word-forms "second" and so on, through a specific conventional relationship (*saṅketaviśeṣasaṃbandha*), constitutes "second-ness" (*dvitīyātva*) and so forth; otherwise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasakti*). Furthermore, [defining it as] "having the sense of object" (*karmārthatva*) would result in mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), and there would be deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of verbal endings (*ākhyāta*) and the like. Here, the rule is either an injunction (*vidhi*) as part of a single syntactic unit with the *svādi-sūtra*, or a restriction (*niyama*) by means of a distinct syntactic split.

Whether it be a restriction on the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*)—such as "the second case is used for the object" and so forth—with reference to the meaning of the base (*prakṛta*), or a restriction on the meaning (*arthaniyama*)—such as "the second case is used only for the object"—all such positions are established in the text:
"The meanings of the nominal suffixes (*sup*) are the object and so forth, as well as number; likewise for the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).
In that regard, there is a well-known restriction, or the restriction applies to those [meanings] already introduced by the base. (Verse 1)

This is because of the statement in the Bhāṣya. Here, by the natural force of the word *tiṅām* (of verbal suffixes), the same applies to nominal suffixes (*sup*) as well: the expressed meaning is the object (*karman*) and so forth themselves, not the property of being an object (*karmatva*). If the verbal suffixes were to express the property of being an object, then—given that the words "of those two" (*tayoreva*) are carried over from the rule *tayoreva*—the same would apply to primary derivatives (*kṛt*), leading to the undesirable consequence that in expressions such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), there could be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the noun and the derivative. Furthermore, in rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* ("the [suffix] *la* [denotes] the object") and *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case suffix [is used] for the object"), one would fail to obtain the sense of the property (*dharma*) [being the denotation].

In the case of "ghaṭam" (the pot-accusative), it is not tenable to claim that the "pot-ness" (karmatva) and so forth appear as both a qualifier (*prakāratva*) and a relation (*saṃsargatva*), based on the cognition of non-difference—namely, "the pot is the object"—and the subsequent connection of the pot and so forth with actions such as bringing via the relation of "object-ness. This is because it contradicts experience.

Nor should it be argued that both [theories] are authoritative because of such linguistic usages as "the pot is the object of bringing" (*ghaṭa ānayanakarma*) or "the bringing of the pot" (*ghaṭīyamānayanam*); for by the usage "the mountain possesses fire-connection" (*parvato vahnisaṃyogī*) or "the fire belonging to the mountain" (*parvatīyo vahniriti*), it would follow that in cases such as "the mountain has fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), there is either an identity between the mountain and the fire-possessor, or else fire itself is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to the mountain by way of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). This is not an acceptable consequence, because the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)—"I infer the fire-possessor"—does not arise.

Because the non-difference from that which is in contact with fire lacks the status of being a relation that delimits pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), its status as an object of inference is untenable; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is because the same logic applies to the claim that the description of the form of the inference does not intend to convey that [non-difference], but merely states the actual state of affairs (*vastugatikatva*).

Nor should it be argued that this is inconsistent because, in the case of fire, even though it is conjoined [with smoke], it is apprehended by another inferential mark or by perception; whereas here, since there is no connection of the pot with "bringing" anywhere through the relation of being the object (*karmatva*), how can that [relation] exist in reality? For even in the absence of verbal cognition, the relation is established in reality by the existence of the pot as the object in the act of bringing. Thus, the two cases are comparable once one takes into account a subsequent similar cognition.

Because there is no restrictive rule stating that if a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) with a certain qualifier, a certain relation, and a certain qualificand does not arise, then a different kind of cognition (*jñāna*) with those same features also cannot arise; for even when a verbal cognition of a person as being in contact with a staff does not occur, such visual perceptions (*cākṣuṣa*) and other types of cognitions are universally established. It is for this very reason that the objection—that in cases such as "the rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), there would be the unwanted consequence of the rice being construed with the act of cooking through the relation of objecthood (*karmatva*)—is logically consistent.

Furthermore, since there would be no expectancy for the cloth (*paṭa*) and so forth to connect with the object (*karman*) as a non-distinct entity, it would be impossible for them to connect with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through the relation of being an object; moreover, there is an absence of such cognitions as "bringing has the jar as its object" or "bringing is like the jar. Let this suffice. The locus (*ādhāra*) or the located (*ādheya*) is the meaning of the accusative case. In the sentence "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), because there is a cognition of the softening (*viklitti*) qualified by that which is the locus in the form of rice, the relation is "locatedness" (*ādheyatva*). Alternatively, the meaning is the softening as located in the rice. This is because the meaning of the suffix, in the form of the located, stands as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*).

Another alternative position is that "being the locus" (*ādheyatva*) itself is the relation. Even in that case, the status of "being the locus" as a relation must consist either in its being the non-predicative objectness (*aviśeṣyatā*) of the meaning of the suffix—qualified by the predicative objectness (*prakāratā*) of the meaning of the base—or in its being the predicative objectness of the meaning of the verbal root—qualified by the predicative objectness of the meaning of the suffix. It cannot be the first [option], because it is logically untenable for something to be its own relation with respect to its own resident objectness. Nor can it be the second, because that [relation] is likewise incompatible even with respect to its own resident predicative objectness.

Therefore, it is logical that the meaning of the sentence is: "The operation performed by Maitra as its agent, which produces that softening (viklitti) which is non-different from that [softening] possessing the 'being-located-in' (ādheyatva) characterized by the 'locus-hood' (adhikaraṇatva) residing in the rice (odana)," because the rice is connected—via the relation of being the qualifier—to the 'being-located-in' which is a part of the meaning of the second case, and that [rice] is further connected via identity to the verbal root-meaning, softening. Alternatively, according to the method of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, another view holds that the meaning [of the locative] is either locus-hood (*ādhāratva*) or being-located-ness (*ādheyatva*).

In reality, according to both views, in the sentence "he cooks the rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the second case suffix is the state of being the locus of inherence (*ādheyatva*), while in the sentence "the rice is cooked by Maitra" (*maitreṇa pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*), the meaning of the verbal suffix is the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consisting of the nature of a substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*). Thus, the resulting cognition is as before: "that which is the disintegration residing in the rice," and so forth.

In the second view, however, the grain (*taṇḍula*) is construed with the locus of the verbal root-meaning (*tiṅartha-ādhāra*) either as its occurrence (*vṛttitva*)—in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*)—or simply as its locus (*ādhāratva*). The locus is construed as an occurrence, and the state of being a locus (*ādhāratva*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), namely softening (*viklitti*), by means of the relation that defines it (*svanirūpaka-sambandha*). The intended meaning of the cognition is: "the operation (*vyāpāra*) which produces that softening which occurs in the locus that is rice," or "that softening which resides in the grain and possesses the property of being located (*ādheyatva*) as defined by the state of being a locus residing in the grain."

Therefore, in the sentence "The rice is cooked by Caitra," the meaning of the instrumental case is *vyāpāra* (effort/activity); the meaning of the verbal root is the result (*phala*); and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the meaning of the suffix *tiṅ*. The connection of the result with the effort denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix occurs through the relation of being produced (*janyatva*). Consequently, the meaning is: "The rice is the locus of the softening (*viklitti*) produced by the effort residing in Caitra. This is what has been proposed by others in the *Tattvabodhinī* commentary on the *Kārikāvalī*, as should be understood.

According to another view, however, these case-endings (*vibhakti*) are merely relational (*saṃsarga*), while the intention (*tātparya*) is grasped solely by them. Furthermore, this is because, under the position that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is distinct from the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), there is no utility for regarding even a *kāraka* as a relation (*saṃsarga*), since it is itself the meaning of the noun. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding the rule: "The operation [of the accusative] applies with *ubha* and *sarvatas*, with the three beginning with *adhika* and *upari*, and with reduplicated words; it is also seen elsewhere than those."

The suffix *tasi* is connected to both [words]. When the two words *ubha* and *sarva* ending in *tasi* are used in conjunction, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is employed; however, the form *ubhe* is stated because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*). This is because the permanence (*nityatva*) of this [Vedic usage] was stated previously. The word *dhik* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*); the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound (*jaśbhāva*) is an archaic (*ārṣa*) feature. Some, however, say that it is due to the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case, by virtue of the extended application (*atideśa*) "as in the base form" (*prakṛtivat*); otherwise, just as the elision of *v* does not apply here in the example *gavityayamāha*, the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound would likewise not apply. They further argue that if [the word] ended in *g* alone, the universally accepted form *dhigiti* could not be accounted for, since the rule *kasyacid* would not apply.
