Because of the inclusion of the word "generally" (*prāya*), there is an absence of the nominative and accusative cases of the pronoun; the other cases are used according to what is observed. Some say that the mention of synonyms (*paryāya*) is for the purpose of excluding others. Others say it is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*) because it serves as an illustration. Examples include: "He dwells for the reason of food" (*annena hetunā vasati*), etc. "The fifth case ending is used for debt (*ṛṇa*) when it is not the agent. (Pāṇini 2.3.24)

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used for that debt which is distinct from the agent and serves as the cause; this is an exception to the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Example: *śatād baddhaḥ* ("bound because of a hundred [debt]"). Why "not the agent"? Example: *śatena bandhitaḥ* ("caused to be bound by a hundred"). The status of being a debt is well-known in the case of the hundred. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *tatprayojako hetuś ca*, it is also designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*). This is because there is no obstacle to including the general, technical sense of "cause" (*hetu*) from the preceding sūtra; for in that context, the third case would have been established by the rule *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* due to its superior force.
25. *vibhāṣā guṇe 'striyām* ("Optionally [the fifth case is used] when a quality [is the cause], provided it is not feminine").

When a non-feminine *guṇa* (quality) serves as the cause (*hetu*), the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) may optionally be used. For example: *jāḍyāj jāḍyena vā baddhaḥ* ("bound because of dullness") or *pāṇḍityāt pāṇḍityena vā muktaḥ* ("released because of learning"). Why "guṇa" (quality)? [Counter-example: *dhanena kulam* ("the family [is distinguished] by wealth"). Why "not feminine" (*āstriyām*)? [Counter-example: *buddhyā muktaḥ* ("released through intelligence"). The term *guṇa* here refers exclusively to that which is dependent on something else (*paratantra*), as in the rule: "The application of a word occurs due to the presence of a quality (*guṇa*). According to some, this allows for the fifth case in examples such as *vahnimān dhūmāt* ("there is fire because of smoke").

In cases such as "there is no jar because it is not perceived," however, [the genitive is established] by the application of the Vārttika: "The base form [is used] optionally due to frequent usage and the rarity of its observation. Others, however, say that it is established in both cases through the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*). *Ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.26): "The sixth case ending [is used] when a word expressing a cause (*hetu*) is employed."

When the word *hetu* (cause/reason) is employed and the state of being a cause is to be indicated, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. When a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is used [in this sense], the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is also used. (Pāṇini 2.3.27) Example: *annasya hetor vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of food"). [And with a pronoun: *kena hetunā vasati* / *kasya hetor vasati* ("For what reason does he dwell?").
In the sense of "cause" (pūrvaviṣaya), the third and sixth case endings are used: *kena hetunā vasati* or *kasya hetoḥ*. In the sense of "ablative" (apādāna), the fifth case ending is used: || 28 ||

"He comes from the village. [The rule] "An addition [should be made] regarding the object and the locus when there is an elision of a *lyap*-affix" [is stated]. "He looks out from the palace, from his seat. The meaning is: "having ascended the palace, having sat upon the seat. Some say that this applies even in the case of the use of a form ending in *lyap*, provided that the sense of that [action] is understood. This is an exception to the second and seventh case endings.

In the case of questions and narratives, [the rule asks] "From where do you come? [The answer is] "From Pāṭaliputra. This is a statement of an accomplished fact based on the action of going (*gamyamāna-kriyā*). Regarding the rule: "When there is a delimitation (*nirmāṇa*) of distance or time, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used; furthermore, the first (*prathamā*) and seventh (*saptamī*) cases are prescribed for the distance associated with that, and the seventh case is also prescribed for the time. Here, *nirmāṇa* means delimitation. The connection with that [delimitation] occurs through the meaning [of the action]. Examples: "Sāṃkāśya is four *yojanas* from Gavīdhuma," or "in four *yojanas*. "From the full moon of Kārtika to the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇa" [is one month].

In both cases—spatial and temporal priority—the meanings of the nominative and locative cases respectively, as well as the locative case alone, are as follows: there, the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) is a qualifier by means of the relation of being delimited (*avacchinnatva*). Its connection with Sāṃkāśya and Āgrahāyaṇī occurs through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva*). [Specifically,] it is that which has Sāṃkāśya as its substratum by means of the relation of being four *yojanas* delimited from Gavīdhuma, and it is that which has Āgrahāyaṇī as its substratum by means of the relation of being a month delimited from Kārttikī. Such is the resulting cognition (*anvayadhī*).

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "When four *yojanas* have been traversed after departing from Gavīdhumat, then one reaches Sāṅkāśya; or rather, when four *yojanas* have been gone, then from there is Sāṅkāśya. Thus, since the rule is established by taking the action of "being traversed" (*gamyamāna-kriyā*), the Vārttika need not be commenced. From the usage in the Bhāṣya, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in connection with *prabhṛti*. Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on that, explains that because the word "meaning" (*artha*) is included [in the rule], it means "starting from there" (*tata ārabhya*).
By this, forms such as "he described her from the hair down to the nails" (*iti sa cikurādārabhyaināṃ nakhāgraṃ varṇayan*) are established.
When joined with a feminine word ending in the suffix *ā* that has a following member [in a compound]. || 29 ||

The ablative case (*pañcamī*) should occur after these [words]. The word *anya* (other) is intended to convey the general sense; the inclusion of the word *itara* is for the sake of elaboration, since the usage with words meaning "inferior" is already established by the rule *pañcamī vibhakte*. Examples include *ghaṭād anyaḥ* or *bhinnaḥ* ("different from the jar"). Here, the meaning of the ablative is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*). Its connection is with the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), which is a part of the referent of the word. Now, one might object that this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ghaṭaḥ paṭo na* ("the jar is not the cloth").

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because [the negative particle] conveys mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), since the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is prescribed when joined with a word denoting the locus of that [non-existence]; for this is not established in cases such as *bhinnaḥ* ("different"). To this, they say: there is no fault because the negative particle (*nañ*) is merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

Others, however, argue that even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of a jar," where the non-existence has a counter-correlate delimited by identity (*tādātmya*). Therefore, they say that from words such as *anyonyābhāva*, the understanding arises as the absence of identity—which is the denotation of the word *anya*—and not as mere difference (*bheda*). For the negative particle (*nañ*) as well, the delimitor of its denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is simply "non-existence" (*abhāvatva*), which is common to both [mutual non-existence and absolute non-existence]; thus, there is no fault. Nor is the use of the genitive case unavoidable when joined with *nañ*; for some indeclinables have restricted usage, and this is supported by the usage in the *Bhāṣya*: "this is not optional" (*neyaṃ vibhāṣā*), and so forth.

That is not so; for the authors of the Dīdhiti and others have stated that the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *nañ* (the negative particle) is precisely the state of being mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) and the state of being absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvatva*). Otherwise, the cessation of doubts regarding various specific modes [of negation] would be untenable. Therefore, the ablative case occurs only in connection with words denoting "otherness" (*anya*) that have the sense of existence (*sattva*). It should be understood that in this context, the word "other" (*itara*) serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

In the *Guṇarahasya*, however, it is stated: "But others [hold that] even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as 'the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of a jar,' where it is an absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Therefore, words such as 'mutual non-existence' convey [their meaning] as the absence of identity, which is denoted by the word 'other' (*anya*), and not as 'difference' (*bheda*). For the negative particle (*nañ*) also has as its delimitor of denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) only 'absence-ness' (*abhāvatva*), which is common to both; thus, there is no fault."

They say: "Even when joined with the negative particle *nañ*, the genitive case is unavoidable; for some indeclinables have restricted usage, and this is not an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*), as evidenced by such usages in the *Bhāṣya*. This is not correct. For even the term *anyonyābhāva* (mutual absence) conveys its meaning precisely as a type of difference (*bheda*), just like the word *bheda* itself. Indeed, a cognition [of an absence] as the absence of identity must either apprehend identity as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) or apprehend it as the delimiting factor of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). It cannot be the first, because we experience only the jar and so forth as the counter-positive. Nor can it be the latter.

If difference (*bheda*) were defined as the state of being an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) whose counter-correlativity is delimited by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like; for conjunction is of the nature of identity with that which possesses conjunction. Furthermore, the Neo-Naiyāyikas do not accept that the counter-correlativity of difference is delimited by a relation, and they maintain instead that it consists of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

For the authors of the *Dīdhiti* and others have stated that the property of being absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvatva*) and the property of being mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) are each independently the delimiters of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *nañ*. Otherwise, it would be impossible to account for the cessation of doubts regarding those respective modes of apprehension. Therefore, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs only in connection with a word expressing existence (*sattva*) that denotes something other [than the subject], and in that case, the inclusion of the word *itara* serves as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*); hence, there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) when *nañ* is employed.

Others, however, maintain that where the co-referential connection (*anvaya*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) with mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) is not grammatically established, there is a requirement for either the genitive or the ablative case following the word denoting the counter-correlate; as in examples such as "the absence of a jar" (*ghaṭasyābhāvaḥ*) or "different from a jar" (*ghaṭād anyaḥ*). They argue that because a difference in meaning between the referents of two nouns—provided they are other than particles (*nipāta*)—cannot be construed, there is no requirement for either the genitive or the ablative when the referent is the negative particle (*nañ*), since the connection of cloth and so forth with the meaning of *nañ* through the relation of counter-correlativity is well-established in usage.

*Ārāt* is used in the senses of "far" and "near. In the example *ārād devadattāt*, the rule *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyantarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.34) would have required the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), but [the fifth case is used instead]. Regarding *ṛte*, it was previously stated that the second case (*dvitīyā*) may also be employed. In *srag ṛte pārijātasya na śālām*, [the word *ṛte* expresses exclusion]. A "direction-word" (*dik-śabda*) is a word observed to denote a direction. When used in conjunction with such a word, even if it does not itself denote a direction, it means "whenever it refers to a direction. In *grāmāt pūrvo deśaḥ* ("the region east of the village") and *caitrāt pūrvaḥ phālgunaḥ* ("the month of Phālguna preceding Caitra"), the sixth case alone is used when there is a connection with a whole (*avayavin*).

It was stated previously that [the word] *pūrva* is used with reference to the body (*kāya*). Although the word *añcu* has a directional meaning (*dik-śabda*) when it forms the final member of a compound, it is mentioned separately in order to override the rule "by means of a genitive case ending or an affix having the sense of *atas*. Nor should it be said that this [separate mention] serves to provide the ablative sense in examples such as *sadhryaṅ*; for, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), only a directional word (*dik-śabda*) having *añcu* as its final member is understood. Thus: *prāk grāmāt* (east of the village), *pratyak grāmāt* (west of the village); *dakṣiṇā grāmāt* (to the south of the village); *dakṣiṇād āc* (from the south) or *dakṣiṇāhi*, *uttarāhi* (from the north) from the village; *āhi* is used after *uttara* when denoting distance, as in *uttarācca*. [This concludes the section on] "by means of a genitive case ending or an affix having the sense of *atas*. (30)

"To the south or to the north of the village. [This is formed by] adding *atasuc* after *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*. Similarly, there are *puras*, *purastāt*, *upari*, and *upariṣṭāt*. Regarding the statement, "Kṛṣṇa and others are not accepted by any learned men as being to the south of the Vindhya," some say that this is because the usage in the *Bhāṣya*—namely, "it will fall away from there"—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on a general rule.

Others, however, say that this is merely an error, because the indicator [the word *enap*] subsequently has as its scope only the suffix *yogamātra*. Furthermore, it is the suffix *atasuc* itself that is the cause here, not the one that has been elided; for in examples such as *prāk grāmāt*, Kaiyaṭa has established that when a suffix is elided, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur.
*Enapā dvitīyā* || 31 || [The second case ending is used after a word ending in *enap*.]

By means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule), the genitive case is also [prescribed]. Thus we have: *dakṣiṇena grāmam* or *grāmasya*; likewise *uttareṇa*. However, some maintain that the reading "our house is to the north (*uttareṇa*) of the house of the Lord of Wealth" is an error; they argue that *uttareṇa* ends in the third-case singular. Others hold that in the phrase "the target is seen from afar by means of the beautiful archway which is like the bow of the Lord of the Gods," the word ending in the third case is connected through identity (*abhedānvaya*). Still others maintain that *gṛhān* ends in the second case. Pṛthak, vinā, and nānā optionally take the third case. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.32)

The term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Following the "frog-leap" method (*maṇḍūkapluti*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is carried over. When used in conjunction with these [words], both the third and fifth cases occur. Examples: *ghaṭāt pṛthak* or *ghaṭena pṛthak*. According to Amara, *hiruk* and *nānā* mean "excluding" (*varjana*). Kṣīrasvāmin says: "The worldly course of a woman is fruitless, being *nānā* [different from] a woman. According to the *Vṛtti*, because of a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the second case also occurs: *nānā viṣṇum mokṣadaḥ*, meaning "no other god than Viṣṇu is the giver of liberation.
And [the third case is used] for the instrumental (*karaṇe*) when expressing *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya*, provided they do not denote a substance (*asattvavacana*). (33)

In the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*), the third and fifth case endings are used after these [words] when they do not denote a substance (*adravyārtha*). For example: *stokena* or *stokāt muktaḥ* ("released with little effort"). Why say "when not denoting a substance"? Consider: *stokena viṣeṇa hataḥ* ("killed by a small amount of poison").
With words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the sixth case ending is optionally used. (Pāṇini 2.3.34)
There is an option with the fifth [case]. [Examples: *dūram antike grāmasya* (far/near from the village) or *grāmāt*. [The rule:
"The second case is also used after words meaning 'far' or 'near'. (Pāṇini 2.3.35)

By virtue of the word "ca" (and), the fifth and third case endings [are also included]. This rule applies to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), and not to any specific meaning of a case ending here. For example: *grāmasya dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*. The same applies to *antikam* (near). Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "The prohibition of the fifth case ending after that which is connected with it is either not [necessary], because it is observed even there. That is to say, the fifth case ending should not occur in relation to that from which distance is measured; or rather, since it is observed even there, the prohibition is unnecessary. As it is said: "One should urinate far from a village, and wash one's feet far [from it]."

"One should stay far from bandits and far from an angry teacher. In this instance, when the word *dūra* (far) refers merely to the quality (*dharma*), the rule "expressing non-existence" (*asattvavacana*) applies by way of ellipsis (*anuvṛtti*). However, when it refers to the substratum (*dharmin*), then, due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it must share the same case-ending as its substantive. For example: *dūraḥ panthāḥ* ("the path is far"), and as Murāri says: *adavīyānayaṃ panthāḥ svarlokamupatiṣṭhate* ("this path, not far [from here], leads to the world of the gods").
And [the locative case is used] for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*): *saptamyadhikaraṇe ca*. (Pāṇini 2.3.36)

The letter *ca* (in the rule) has the sense of a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*) of "distance" (*dūra*) and "nearness" (*antika*). Examples: *kaṭe āste* ("he sits on a mat"), *dūre grāmāt* ("far from the village"). Because this locative case prescribed by the present rule is conjoined with the three previously mentioned cases, four cases are established for words expressing distance and nearness. Regarding the statement, "There is an addition [to the rule] for the object of that which ends in *in*, when it denotes seeking": the meaning is "that which ends in *in*. Example: *adhīti vyākaraṇe* ("he is a student of grammar"). Here, the word *adhīta* ends in the past passive participle suffix *kta*, meaning "studied by him. From this word *adhīta*, the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of the agent according to the rule *iṣṭādibhyaś-ca*. Thus, *adhītī* means "one who has studied. The locative case is used here because the suffix *ini* denotes seeking (*anveṣaṇa*).

The rule prescribing the second case (dvitīyā) for the object (*karman*) would apply here—as in the example *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*—and this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. Even though the seventh case (*saptamī*) is established when there is an intention to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the second case remains unavoidable when there is an intention to express the object (*karman*). For instance, in *māsam adhītī vyākaraṇe*, the seventh case does not occur after *māsa*. This is because time is an external object (*bahir-aṅga-karman*). Nor can it be argued that since the object is already expressed by the suffix *-kta*, how could there be the possibility of the second case?

Because there is no connection with a word ending in *kta* that has already entered into a state of semantic unity (*ekārthībhāva*) with the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [the rule does not apply]. Furthermore, since it is possible for the object to be connected even with a subordinate action, as in "he studied grammar together [with someone]," and so forth—this will be explained in detail later. Regarding the rule "also when used in the sense of 'proper' (*sādhu*) or 'improper' (*asādhu*)," [the examples are]: "Kṛṣṇa is proper toward his mother" and "he is improper toward his maternal uncle. This statement is made because the locative case would otherwise not apply to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) due to the absence of an action.

Some, however, say that even though [the locative case] is established by virtue of being a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) related to an object, this rule is for the purpose of prohibiting the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Although [the locative] is already established by the rule *sādhunipuṇābhyāmarcāyām* (P. 2.3.43), the mention of *sādhu* here is for the sake of cases other than "reverence" (*arcā*). Consequently, the locative occurs in connection with *sādhu* even when expressing the true nature of something. In that context, the word *arcā* is a qualifier only for *nipuṇa*. According to the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*), in the example *sādhurbhṛtyo rājñaḥ* ("the servant is good toward the king"), the genitive is used in relation to the servant (*bhṛtya*), and not in relation to the quality of being good (*sādhu*).
Others also say that the word *sādhu* is included in the sūtra so that the sūtra does not become redundant due to the Vārttika.

"In the case of those worthy [of agency] acting as agents and those unworthy [of agency] not acting as agents, and the reverse thereof. When the wealthy are eating, the poor sit [idle]. While the Brahmins are crossing over, the *vṛṣalas* sit [idle]. The wealthy and others possess the worthiness for eating. When the fools are sitting, the wealthy eat. While the *vṛṣalas* are sitting, the Brahmins cross over. The fools lack the worthiness for eating and so forth. The non-agency of those worthy of agency, and the agency of those worthy of non-agency, is "reversal" (*viparyāsa*). When the wealthy are sitting, the fools eat.

"Vṛṣalas lie down while the Brāhmaṇas are seated"—this [example] is for the purpose of prescribing the locative case (*saptamī*) when there is no intention to express the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣya*) and the indicated (*lakṣaṇa*). Otherwise, [the rule] would be established by the subsequent sūtra; so say Kaiyaṭa and others.

However, some maintain that by the word "are seated" (*āsate*), the absence of eating is indicated, and by words such as "prosperous" (*ṛddha*) or "poor" (*daridra*), the fitness or unfitness for action is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Thus, propriety (*aucitya*) and impropriety (*anaucitya*) constitute the suggested sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). They argue that since such a relationship between indicator and indicated is excluded from the scope of the subsequent sūtra, the Vārttika is not redundant. [Nyāsa on Pāṇini 2.3.36: "In connection with an object (*karman*) following a cause (*nimitta*)."

The word *nimitta* (cause/motive) refers to the result (*phala*), by virtue of being the object of the knowledge that serves as the cause for the activity [of the agent]. This is an exception to the rule regarding the instrumental case (*hetutṛtīyā*). The actual connection (*yoga*) with the action is either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*); however, there is no restriction that it must be the object of verbal expression (*śābdaviṣayatva*). The meaning of the Vārttika is that the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the result which possesses a relationship with the object of the action. "He kills the leopard for its skin; he kills the elephant for its two tusks; he kills the yak for its hair; the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland."

*Puṣkalaka* means a stake (*śaṅku*). Some say it refers to something driven into the ground for the purpose of marking a boundary (*sīmā*). Others say *puṣkalaka* means a musk deer (*gandhamṛga*), and *sīmā* means the scrotum; they say it refers to one killed for that purpose. In the case of *carmaṇi*, there is a collection (*samavāya*) of both leather and a tiger; it is a conjunction of three [entities], because teeth, hair, and so forth do not constitute parts of the body [in this context]. Even when it means the musk deer, the distinction remains that it is a "collection. What is the point of [specifying] "connection with an action" (*karmayoge*)? [Example: He reaps grain for wages (*vetana*).

On this point, the Naiyāyikas [state]: here, the meaning of the locative case is either "being a producer" (*janakatva*) or "being produced" (*janyatva*). The word "skin" (*carma*) refers to its disposal according to one's will (*yatheṣṭaviniyoga*). [The sentence thus means: one who possesses an effort conducive to the killing of a leopard that produces the disposal of the skin according to one's will. Alternatively, it is "causality" (*nimittatva*), which is the state of being the object of a desire by virtue of being the object of disposal according to one's will.

The state of being the object of such a desire, which is the meaning of the locative case, is construed with "killing" (*hanana*) by way of the relation of being produced (*janyatva*). Furthermore, what is intended here is the connection of a verbal root (*dhātu*) that generates a cognition having some object as its qualifier (*prakāra*). This quality of being a generator [of such a cognition] exists in a transitive root through its connection with a word denoting an object, as in the case of *carmaṇi* and so forth; however, in the case of an intransitive root, it exists through the power (*śakti*) of its own meaning as qualified by an object, as seen in the expression: "That which rises when the night of ignorance has perished," which means "it ascends the peak of the mountain of sunrise."

Although the end of night is not produced by the rising of the sun, it is nonetheless the *nimitta* (efficient cause) because it serves as the objective for the cognition [of that end]. This is like the expression, "The musk-deer was killed at the boundary. Therefore, the meaning is: "He rises so that people may have the cognition of the end of night. Some, however, say: Night is the time characterized by the absence of contact with all the solar rays present in this continent; the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) qualifies the absence of contact. They argue that when those rays arise and their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is destroyed, the destruction of the characterized time follows, making it easy to establish that the rising of the sun is the cause of the end of night.
And [the locative case is used] when there is the indication of an action by means of another action. (Pāṇini 2.3.37)

The locative case should be used for that action by which another action is delimited, because an action whose time is not known is delimited by an action whose time is already known. For example: *goṣu duhyamānāsv āgataḥ* ("He arrived while the cows were being milked"). Here, *duhyamānāsu* is an adjective qualifying the cows, as is evident from experience. The meaning of the locative case is temporal coreferentiality (*kālika-sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Its connection with the action of arriving is as follows: it is the substratum of that arrival which occurred at the time residing in the locus (the cows) qualified by the state of being milked.

Furthermore, since cows distinguished by the act of milking no longer possess that qualification at a later time due to its having ceased, the [implication] of the arrival results in being simultaneous with the milking; therefore, the status of [the compound] as a *bhāvalakṣaṇa* (denoting a temporal marker) remains unimpaired. In the case of "The cows have arrived after they were milked" (*dugdhāsvāgataḥ*), because the simultaneity with the past time of milking is contradicted in relation to the arrival, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding that which is qualified by the cessation of the milking.

And thus, the meaning is: "in cows which are the objects of milking that have a presently existing destruction as its counter-positive. The contemporaneity with the destruction—which is a qualifier of the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitva) itself, which in turn is a qualifier of the milking—is manifested in the arrival. Consequently, [the sentence means]: "the arrival is a locus of time that is the substratum of a presently existing destruction whose counter-positive is the milking having the cow as its object," and so forth.

In the case of *dhokṣyamāṇāsu* as well, the construction should be applied as: "the substratum of that prior absence of milking which has destruction existing [at that time]," and so forth. This is because of the usage by the learned: *guṇakarmānyatve sati sattvāt* ("because of existence, while being distinct from quality and action"). The meaning of the rule (*sūtra*) is that where one property is presented through another property by way of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there the genitive is used. Therefore, the logicians (*tārkikāḥ*) maintain that there is no fault even when the presentation of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so on occurs through a spatial coreferentiality composed of both qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
And the genitive is also used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*). (Pāṇini 2.3.38)

When the sense of disregard (*anādara*) is predominant as a characteristic of the state (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*), both the sixth and seventh case endings may be used. For example: *sudati rudato vā prāvrājīt* ("He went forth [into homelessness] while [his wife] was weeping"). The meaning is that he renounced the world regardless of her weeping, such as that of a son or others. Here, because the son and others—who are not the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the passion that caused his departure—were unfavorable to his renunciation, there is disregard for them. This is because such disregard is not perceived in other contexts. [The genitive is also used] with the words *svāmī*, *īśvara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, *sākṣin*, *pratibhū*, and *prasūta*. (39)

With these seven [words], the sixth (genitive) and seventh (locative) cases occur. This statement is for the sake of the optional seventh case; the sixth case is merely permitted. *Gavāṃ goṣu vā svāmī* ("the owner of cows"). *Dāyaṃ bhāgam ādatte dāyādaḥ* ("he who takes a share of the inheritance is an heir"). By irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *ka* is added even after a word with a prefix. The meaning of the word "cow" connects with "inheritance" without distinction. The sense is: "one who takes a portion consisting of cows. *Gavāṃ prasūtaḥ* ("born of cows"). The sense is: "born to experience cows themselves. Pāṇini 2.3.40: *Āyuktakuśalābhyāṃ cāsevāyām* ("Also with *āyukta* and *kuśala*, when there is habitual practice").

*Āsevā* means being devoted exclusively to that. For this purpose, the sixth and seventh case endings are used with these two [words]. [Examples: *haribhajanasya āyuktaḥ* or *haribhajane āyuktaḥ*, meaning "engaged in" or "skilled in the worship of Hari. Why say *āsevā*? [Counter-example: *āyukto gauḥ śakaṭe* ("the ox is yoked to the cart"); the meaning here is "slightly yoked.
And [the sixth case ending is used] after that [word] from which a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is made. (Pāṇini 2.3.41)

Selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is the separation of one part from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*saṃjñā*); the genitive and locative cases are used after that [whole] from which such selection occurs. Examples: *nṛṇāṃ* or *nṛṣu dvijaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* (among men, the twice-born is the best); *gavāṃ* or *goṣu kṛṣṇā bahukṣīrā* (among cows, the black one yields much milk); *gacchatāṃ* or *gacchatsu dhāvan śīghraḥ* (among those walking, the running one is the fastest); *chātrāṇāṃ* or *chātreṣu maitraḥ paṭuḥ* (among the students, Maitra is clever). In these instances, the meaning of the case ending is mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) and absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), as well as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

In the case of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between "cow" (*go*)—which is non-different from "black" (*kṛṣṇa*)—and [the word "among"] through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), by means of a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by cowness (*gotva*) as qualified by blackness (*kṛṣṇatva*). That [absence] is connected to the referent of the word "cow" (*gopadārtha*) by way of being its substratum (*anuyogitā*); that [cow] is connected to the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) by way of being its locus (*vṛttitva*); that [absence] is connected to its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*); that [counter-correlate] is connected to the quality (*guṇa*) such as "abundant milk-ness" (*bahukṣīratva*), which serves as the basis for selection (*nirdhāraṇanimitta*), by way of non-difference (*abheda*); and that [quality] is connected to the cow that is non-different from the black one. Consequently, [the meaning of the sentence is: "non-different from that which possesses abundant milk-ness, which is the counter-correlate of the absolute absence residing in a cow that is non-different from a black cow."

The cognition of the syntactic connection is "the black cow. And thus, when the property of having much milk and so forth is perceived as the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence in relation to the correlate of the selection (nirdhāraṇapratiyogin), its status as the ground for the selection is also logically consistent.

As for the claim that difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*) are the meanings of the nominal suffixes, such that the meaning of the word "cow" (*go*) is construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) with respect to the objects denoted by "Kṛṣṇa" and "milk," and as the locus (*āśraya*); and that in the case of non-difference, the meaning of the word "cow" is construed as the counter-correlate with respect to the object denoted by "Kṛṣṇa," and [the latter] as the locus; and that consequently, the cognitions arise as "The cow, which is different from Kṛṣṇa, is not the most abundant in milk" and "Kṛṣṇa, who is non-different from the cow, is the most abundant in milk"—that is incorrect. Why? Because it contradicts the experience of a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatva*), and because it involves a double construal of the meanings of the words "Kṛṣṇa" and "cow" in a manner that reverses their status as qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*).

Furthermore, the meaning of the case endings is as before: when there is a difference from the referent "Kṛṣṇa," [the relation] is that of being its locus in the cow; when there is a difference from that [cow], it is that of being its counter-correlative in the one possessing the most abundant milk; when there is a difference from that [one possessing the most abundant milk], it is that of being its locus in Kṛṣṇa. Therein, the [relation] of non-difference with the one possessing the most abundant milk is the connection. Thus, the cognition is: "The Kṛṣṇa, who is non-different from the cow, is non-different from the one possessing the most abundant milk, who is non-different from the cow, who is non-different from Kṛṣṇa."

Or, one might argue that the cognition has "the black cow" as its qualified object (viśeṣya), such that it is understood as: "The most excellent in milk, which is non-different from a cow that is non-different from a black [cow]," or "The most excellent in milk, which is non-different from a cow that is non-different from a black [cow]. This too is incorrect, because it would result in an excessive number of syntactic relations (anvaya). Furthermore, it would be impossible to eliminate the doubt: "Is the black cow the most excellent in milk, or is it non-different [from it]? Moreover, it would involve the unnecessary complexity (gaurava) of having the very thing denoted by "black" serve as the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) in the relation of difference.

However, some maintain that non-difference (*abheda*) is the meaning of the case-ending. In that view, "cow" (*goḥ*) is construed as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*). Non-difference with the cow is then construed with both the black cow and the one possessing the most abundant milk. Furthermore, through the relation of non-difference, non-difference with the cow possessing the most abundant milk is construed with the black cow who is non-different from the cow. Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "The black cow, who is non-different from the cow, is non-different from the cow possessing the most abundant milk. Nor is there a failure to account for the cognition of the absence of the state of possessing the most abundant milk in other cows.

They say [that this is so] because the relation of non-difference is qualified by pervasion (*vyāpakatva*). That too must be considered. For there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) if the non-difference from a cow were construed with a black cow that possesses the highest degree of milk; furthermore, it would be impossible for such a construction to remove the doubt regarding the possession of the highest degree of milk in a cow that is non-different from the black one.
[Pāṇini 2.3.42: "The fifth case-affix is used in the sense of 'distinct' (*vibhakta*)."

The ablative case (pañcamī) shall be used for the correlate of a selection (*nirdhāraṇa-pratiyogin*) when the property that delimits the correlatehood (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*) does not exist in the object of the selection. For example: *māthurāḥ pāṭaliputrakebhya āḍhyatarāḥ* ("The people of Mathurā are wealthier than the people of Pāṭaliputra"). The people of Mathurā possess that state of being wealthier which is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in the people of Pāṭaliputra. Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the meaning of the ablative.

In this context, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) [the people of Pāṭaliputra] occurs as the locus (*vṛttitva*) within the absolute non-existence, and that [non-existence] occurs by way of its counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) in the state of being wealthier, which serves as the basis for the selection.
The seventh case ending is used after the words *sādhu* and *nipuṇa* when expressing worship, provided they are not preceded by *prati*.

When these two [words *pra* and *ati*] are used with the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā-tātparya*), the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall occur; however, not when there is the employment of *prati*. Examples: *sādhur mātari* (good toward his mother) or *nipuṇo mātari* (skilled toward his mother). Why "in the sense of praise"? Example: *sādhur bhṛtyo rājñaḥ* (the servant is good toward the king)—here the intention is merely to state the essential nature (*svarūpa-kathana*). It was stated previously that when used with the word *sādhu*, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) occurs even when it is not in the sense of praise. It should be stated: "not with *prati* and others. Examples: *sādhur nipuṇo vā mātaraṃ prati pary anu vā* (good or skilled toward his mother).
With the words *prasita* and *utsuka*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) also [occurs]. (Pāṇini 2.3.44). Because of the word "also" (*ca*), the seventh case ending also [occurs].
"According to Amara: *tatpara* means *prasita*, *āsakta*, *viṣṭa*, *arthārthodyukta*, or *utsuka*.

Therefore, in the sense of 'excellently white' (*prakarṣeṇa sitaḥ śuklaḥ*), this [the suffix *ka*] is absent. Thus, *prasita* or *utsuka* may take either the second or the seventh case ending when used with *hari*: *harimā harau vā* (eager for Hari). In the phrase *svaprāṇeśvaranarmaharmyakaṭakātithyagrahāyotsukam* ('eager to receive the hospitality of the pleasure-palace of her own lord of life'), the fourth case ending is used according to the rule *tumarthācca* (Pāṇini 2.3.15). In the *Ratnāvalī*: *paryutsuko nijamahotsavadarśanāya* ('eager to see his own great festival').
And [the suffix *ka* is also absent] when the word *nakṣatra* is elided. (45)

When the sense of the suffix whose elision is prescribed by the technical term *lup* is present, the third and seventh case endings occur after a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) which functions as the base (*prakṛti*), provided it denotes time as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: *mūlenāvāhayed devīm śravaṇena visarjayet* ("One should invoke the Goddess under Mūla; one should dismiss her under Śravaṇa"), or alternatively, *mūle* and *śravaṇe*. [Similarly: *puṣye pāyasamaśnīyāt* ("One should eat milk-rice under Puṣya") and *maghābhiḥ palalaudanam* ("[One should eat] rice with sesame under Maghā"). [In these cases,] the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*, and its elision occurs by the rule *lup aviśeṣe*.

Because no specific distinction is perceived as to whether it is a conjunction with the root [asterism] delimited by night or delimited by day. What is the example for the locative case? "Saturn is in Puṣya" (puṣye śaniḥ) and "Today is Puṣya" (adya puṣyaḥ).
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the third Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi.
Now begins the third Āhnika of the third Pāda.
The first case ending is used in the sense of the mere nominal stem-meaning, gender, measure, and number. || 46 ||

The word *mātra* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and because it is heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, it connects with each member. In the phrase *prātipadikasya*, the genitive case-meaning of "being produced by" (*janyatva*) connects with "cognition" (*jñāna*), which is one part of the referent of the word *artha*. The meaning of the suffix *-tva* is "the state of being the qualificandum" (*viśeṣyatva*). The nominative case should occur when there is merely the qualificandum of the cognition produced by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), whether it be gender alone, measure alone, dimension alone, or number alone; for the word *vacana* refers to number.

The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is that which is intended when it is not the locus of the *prakāratā* (qualifierhood) as determined by the *viśeṣyatā* (subjecthood) residing in the referent of the verbal cognition that follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [stem]. Therefore, there is no defect even though number such as singularity is experienced [as part of the stem-meaning]. And "suffix" (*pratyaya*) refers to that which has its own base (*prakṛti*); thus, there is no fault even when it is connected to the agent, which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). [This is because] it is connected to the meaning of the suffix.

And thus, even in cases such as "the face is like the moon," where similarity and so forth are construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the defect remains as it was under the view that the nominative case-ending (*tara-vibhakti*) signifies non-difference (*abheda*). This is because one must resort to the principle that the case-ending [indicates the relation] due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), or because this [coreferentiality] serves as the regulator only for the independent nominative; and because the claim that the case-ending has the counter-correlate and so forth as its meaning is accepted only by certain partial theorists (*ekadeśin*).

By this [argument], having raised the objection that in expressions such as *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the brave man") there is an absence of the status of being the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), it is shown that because the relation (*saṃsarga*) constitutes the sentence-meaning and is thus extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), it is impossible for it to subvert the grammatical operation (*saṃskāra*) of the word *vapuḥ*, which occurs first and is conditioned solely by its own primary meaning. Otherwise, if the nominative case were to apply everywhere prior [to other cases], the section on the second case (*dvitīyā*) and subsequent cases would be rendered purposeless. Since the syntactic connection of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) is universal in the absence of [specific] objects such as the accusative, the nominative is applied by the force of the explicit rule.

This difficulty is refuted because even in cases such as "the jar" (*ghaṭa*), the supply of a verb like "exists" (*asti*) is necessary; because by the introduction of the rule "in the case of *mātra* and in address" (*mātragrahaṇe sambodhane ca*), the predominance of the meaning expressed by the case-ending is excluded; and because even in cases such as "the head of Rāhu" (*rāhoḥ śiraḥ*), the genitive occurs due to a distinction based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*), so that non-difference cannot be the meaning of the genitive. Furthermore, this is because the nominative case has its own scope within indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Nor should it be argued that since this [rule] operates in syntactic unity with the treatise on number (the *Saṃkhyāśāstra*), how can it apply there; for although it is stated that "the first case ending occurs in the sense of the meaning," when the expectancy arises as to "in whose sense," it is possible to supply "of that from which [the suffix] is prescribed" by means of the rule "from a nominal stem (*ṅy-āp-prātipadika*") which presents the base. Furthermore, because the mention of the term *prātipadika* is superfluous [if the rule were restricted to numbered nouns], the fact that the first case ending occurs even in the sense of an indeclinable devoid of number is established by the original source (*ākara*). This is also evident from the fact that examples such as *uccaiḥ* and *nīcaiḥ* have been recorded [by the author] as illustrations of this very point.

Even though the status of being a *pada* (word) is established by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone, the first case (*prathamā*) is required for the application of the rule "optionally [the substitution of *su~*] occurs after a first case ending preceded by something" (*sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā*) in examples such as *grāma uccaistava svam* and *grāma uccaiste svam*. Nor should it be argued that this [rule] is equally without scope (*niravakāśa*) because non-difference (*abheda*) is present in the relation between the village and so forth even there; for its scope is not lost in cases like *vijayate*, where it applies to prefixes (*upasarga*) which are merely indicators (*dyotaka*).

Nor is there a lack of purpose for its initial production [as a suffix], because in instances such as *ā te pitar marutāṃ sumnametu* and *pratitvā duhitardivaḥ*, the substitutes (*ādeśa*) for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* prescribed after a word (*pada*), as well as the suppression (*nighāta*) of the finite verb (*tiṅ*) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*, occur precisely because of that [suffix]. This is according to the Vārttika: "A meaningless particle receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," or else because it possesses meaning solely through the sense it illuminates (*dyotya*). Furthermore, although words such as *jayati* refer to preeminent victory (*prakṛṣṭajaya*), there is still a positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) with the prefix *pra* regarding that preeminence.

Furthermore, in cases such as *svaḥ paśya* ("Look at heaven!"), since it must necessarily be accepted that the nominative alone follows the indeclinable (*avyaya*), one must state either that the word beginning with *svar* (i.e., *svaḥ*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root through the relation of objecthood (*karmatva-saṃsarga*), or that the nominative case-ending has the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) of objecthood. And thus, even in that instance, the availability of the rule for the nominative is easily established. Moreover, its scope is precisely in examples such as *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"). Nor should it be argued that this is not the case because [the agent] is construed with the agent denoted by the *tiṅ*-suffix through the relation of identity (*abheda*).

This is because the Naiyāyikas accept that the connection (*anvaya*) in that case belongs to the action (*kṛti*) alone; furthermore, it is possible to assume—on the basis of this—that the author of the Sūtras intended a cognition in which the subject is primarily qualified by the nominative ending; and also because in examples such as *dhānyena dhanī* ("wealthy by means of grain"), non-difference (*abheda*) is indeed the meaning of the case-ending, since it is difficult to deny that non-difference is the meaning of the genitive when it is used in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Because, in cases such as [the relation] with time (*kāla*), since all things possess a relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) with respect to everything, this would exist in every word-meaning (*padārtha*) as being delimited by the status of being a relation that delimits what is expressed by the genitive case; consequently, it would be impossible to exclude [the relation] from being something additional to what is expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). By this, the Vārttika—"Or rather [it is not so], because it is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*)"—is explained. As for the argument regarding the rule *prātipadikārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.3.46), whether there is an application of the maxim concerning gender-qualified bases (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) or not: it cannot be the first alternative, because if the meaning were restricted to "from whatever [stem] the case-endings (*svādi*) are prescribed," then the mention of the term *prātipadika* would be redundant.

Not the latter [alternative], because in cases such as *mṛḍānī* and *himānī*, the occurrence of the nominative case (*prathamā*) would be improper. However, if one adopts the formulation "the first case occurs when there is a meaning" (*arthe prathamā*), then by obtaining the principle "from that which the suffixes beginning with *sva* (i.e., the nominal suffixes) are prescribed," and since the suffixes beginning with *sva* are prescribed after a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) and after that which is qualified by a suffix expressing gender, the status of being a feminine (*strītva*)—as in *nayati upasthitaḥ*—is understood as the meaning of those suffixes; likewise, since the connection with a male (*puṃyoga*) or greatness (*mahattva*) and so on are also of that nature, the desired result is established.

That is trivial. For when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "it includes that which is qualified by gender" has as its sole purport only those operations prescribed with reference to the nominal stem itself; this is because it is established as such by the very authority that establishes the subject matter. And here, the prescription of the nominative case is not made with reference to the nominal stem, but rather [it is prescribed] when the meaning of the nominal stem is to be expressed.

Because it is universally accepted that the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* itself prescribes the case-endings *sva*-etc. with reference to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the application of the Paribhāṣā [that "the meaning of the stem is included in the meaning of the affix"] is valid there; nor is the aforementioned defect applicable, since that [exclusion] is established by the inclusion of the word *liṅga* (gender). Nor should it be argued that this is not so because meanings such as "connection with a male" (*puṃyoga*) are understood as additional meanings; for what is to be excluded is only that which exceeds the meaning of the suffix signifying gender. Furthermore, connection with a male, greatness, and so forth, are understood through the suffixes *ṅī* etc. themselves. By this, words such as *mṛṇālī* are explained. As Amarasimha states: "The word *strī* may refer to something like a lotus-stalk (*mṛṇālī*) when there is a desire to express diminution."

As for the argument that the rule is justified by the placement [of the word] "in the sense" (*arthe*), that is not correct. This is because, in comparison with the specific expectancy (*viśeṣākāṅkṣā*) "of what?", the expectancy "in which sense? is more internal (*antaraṅga*) as it pertains to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the object. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the first case ending could apply even to the senses of "object" (*karman*) and so forth. Since "object" and the rest are proximate and have been presented previously, the term "sense" (*arthatva*) is intended merely to subsume the delimiters of capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) such as "objectness" (*karmatva*) and "instrumentality" (*karaṇatva*); thus, it is established that "objectness" and the like are indeed obtained through verbal cognition (*śābda*).

This is because, just as [the property of] being present in the intellect (*buddhisthatva*) and so forth, the identity of the delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) among pronouns also brings about the identity of their denotative power (*śakti*). Consequently, since there would be no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) such as "of what?", it would be impossible for the *pratiyogitva* (counter-correlativity) to be obtained by the nominal stems (*pratipadika*) ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*; this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of a total collapse of the system. Furthermore, since the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others are prescribed when the object (*karman*) and so forth are not already expressed (*anabhihita*), while the first case (*prathamā*) applies commonly whether [the object] is expressed or unexpressed, it is possible for the first case to co-occur optionally with the second case and others in instances where [the object] is unexpressed.

By this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*)—namely, the mention of *sambodhana* (the vocative)—even the rejection of the inclusion of the term *mātra* (only) is refuted; for, according to the method already stated, that [rejection] would result in the rule being a purely original prescription (*apūrva-vidhi*). However, when the word *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is included, there is a disparity: because it is *antaraṅga* (internally dependent), the expectancy is satisfied by its connection with the *sambandhin* (the related element) alone, and thus the case-role (*karman*, etc. cannot be connected. Consequently, in your view, the rule itself would become redundant, since the nominative case is already prescribed by rules such as *sv-au-jas-am-auṭ*.

Under the view that the rule is one of restriction regarding the meaning—namely, "the second case ending is used only for the object" (karmaṇi dvitīyaiva)—the purpose of the sūtra is intended to establish two restrictions: first, to exclude the second case endings from being used for the mere meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārthamātra), and second, to exclude the nominative case from being used for the object and other such meanings. However, this would be cast far away [as a valid purpose], because it would entail the prescription of the nominative case only for the object and other such meanings.

[Objection: "But surely, under the view that [the rule] is a restriction (*niyamapakṣa*), since the first case-ending (*prathamā*) would apply to the object (*karman*) and so forth by its own force, one would not assume the purport (*tātparya*) of the Sūtra to be the prescription of the first case-ending for the object and so forth—out of fear of the Sūtra being redundant—but rather that its purport lies precisely in the rule *ṅy-āpprātipadikārthe*. [Reply: This is not so, because a restriction must be postulated only in accordance with the purport of the science (*śāstra*). For if the prescription of the first case-ending for the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) itself were untenable, then the aforementioned restriction would be as non-existent as a hare's horn."

For it would follow that the intent of grammatical rules such as "the second case [is used] for the object" (*dvitīyā karmaṇi*) would be solely to exclude one another regarding mutually distinct meanings; because by means of rules such as "the second case is used only for the object" and "the third case is used only for the agent and the instrument," they would themselves take the form of restrictive rules (*niyama*). Furthermore, it is possible that the exclusion of the third case and so forth is the result of those rules. However, since the nominative case (*prathamā*) is prescribed only for the object and other such roles, its exclusion [from those roles] would be impossible.

Furthermore, once the application of the nominative case (*prathamā*) is established as occurring merely upon the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the restriction on the suffix must serve the purpose of excluding [the application of] other cases; and once that is established, the rule for the nominative applies to the mere meaning of the nominal stem—thus, the fault remains unavoidable. Otherwise, if one were to propose the formulation "the nominative occurs in the sense," it has already been stated that this would lead to the impossibility of the nominal stem’s connection with that sense by way of being its counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*). Let this matter rest for now.

In this way, the inclusion of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is also necessary. For the cognition that arises when the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is related non-differently to the measure denoted by the first case (*prathamā*), and that measure is related to the rice (*vrīhi*) through the relation of being delimited (*paricchinnatva*), would otherwise remain unestablished. Nor should it be argued that such a cognition is indeed unestablished, because one might claim that the mention of "measure" merely restates a meaning already established by logical necessity (*nyāyaprāpta*) due to its association with gender (*liṅga*) and so forth, and thus one need not postulate that measure is the expressed meaning (*vācya*). [This is because] even if gender and the like are mentioned together with measure, the mention of measure serves as a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) for the specific measure intended, just as the mention of gender restricts the understanding to a specific gender. Therefore, since the mention of measure is not redundant, it must be accepted that measure is indeed the expressed meaning of the nominal suffix. Furthermore, the cognition of a specific measure—such as "one *droṇa* of rice"—cannot be accounted for unless the measure is admitted to be the expressed meaning of the suffix. Thus, the inclusion of "measure" is indispensable. Finally, the mention of "measure" is also required to exclude the possibility that the meaning of the base is related to the meaning of the suffix through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence that a cognition such as "rice is a *droṇa*" would be possible. Hence, the mention of "measure" is necessary. This concludes the discussion on the meaning of the first case. Now, the meaning of the second case is discussed. The second case denotes the "object" (*karman*). As stated in the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā*: "The second case ending is used in the sense of the object. Here, "object" refers to the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) designated as "object," and not the mere physical object (*vastumātra*). This is because the suffixes expressing the *kārakas* are taught to denote *kārakas* specifically. Moreover, the term "object" here does not refer to the grammatical participant called "object" as defined in Pāṇini’s rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* ("that which is most desired by the agent is the object"), but rather to the "object" as defined in the rule *tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam* ("and that which is connected in the same way [as the primary object] but is not desired"). This is because the former definition applies only to the primary object (*mukhyakarma*), whereas the latter applies to both the primary and secondary objects (*gauṇakarma*). Since the suffixes expressing the *kārakas* denote all types of *kārakas*, the term "object" here must be understood according to the latter rule. Consequently, the second case ending is employed to express the "object" as defined by the rule *tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam*. This is illustrated by examples such as *grāmaṃ gacchan tṛṇaṃ spṛśati* ("while going to the village, he touches grass") and *edhodakaṃ harati* ("he carries firewood and water"). In these cases, although the grass and the water are not what is primarily intended by the agent, they are nonetheless expressed by the second case ending because they are connected to the action in the same manner as the primary object. However, this does not apply to instances such as *payasā odanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats rice with milk"), where the milk is an instrument (*karaṇa*) and not an object. In such cases, the milk is not expressed by the second case ending. Therefore, the term "object" in this context must be understood as referring to the "object" as defined by the rule *tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam*. This concludes the discussion on the meaning of the second case. Now, the meaning of the third case is discussed. The third case ending is used to express the "instrument" (*karaṇa*). As stated in the rule *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*: "The third case ending is used in the sense of the agent and the instrument. Here, "agent" (*kartṛ*) refers to the *kāraka* designated as "agent," and "instrument" (*karaṇa*) refers to the *kāraka* designated as "instrument. The suffixes expressing the *kārakas* denote the *kārakas* themselves; therefore, the third case ending is used to express the "instrument" as defined by the rule *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* ("that which is most effective in accomplishing the action is the instrument"). This is illustrated by examples such as *dātreṇa lunāti* ("he cuts with a sickle") and *ghaṭaṃ cakreṇa karoti* ("he makes a pot with a wheel"). In these cases, the sickle and the wheel are expressed by the third case ending because they are the instruments. However, this does not apply to instances such as *rāmeṇa bāṇena hato vālī* ("Vālī was killed by Rāma with an arrow"), where the arrow is an object (*karman*) and not an instrument. In such cases, the arrow is not expressed by the third case ending. Therefore, the term "instrument" in this context must be understood as referring to the "instrument" as defined by the rule *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*. This concludes the discussion on the meaning of the third case. Now, the meaning of the fourth case is discussed. The fourth case ending is used to express the "recipient" (*sampradāna*). As stated in the rule *caturthī sampradāne*: "The fourth case ending is used in the sense of the recipient. Here, "recipient" refers to the *kāraka* designated as "recipient," and not the mere physical recipient (*vastumātra*). This is because the suffixes expressing the *kārakas* are taught to denote *kārakas* specifically. Moreover, the term "recipient" here does not refer to the *kāraka* called "recipient" as defined in Pāṇini’s rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti sa sampradānam* ("that which one intends to reach with the object is the recipient"), but rather to the "recipient" as defined in the rule *dānasya yaḥ svāmī tadvyatirikto yaḥ sa sampradānam* ("that which is other than the owner of the gift is the recipient"). This is because the former definition applies only to the primary recipient (*mukhyasampradāna*), whereas the latter applies to both the primary and secondary recipients (*gauṇasampradāna*). Since the suffixes expressing the *kārakas* denote all types of *kārakas*, the term "recipient" here must be understood according to the latter rule. Consequently, the fourth case ending is employed to express the "recipient" as defined by the rule *dānasya yaḥ svāmī tadvyatirikto yaḥ sa sampradānam*. This is illustrated by examples such as *viprāya gāṃ dadāti* ("he gives a cow to the Brahmin") and *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband"). In these cases, although the Brahmin and the husband are not the owners of the gift or the act of lying down, they are nonetheless expressed by the fourth case ending because they are the recipients. However, this does not apply to instances such as *maitrāya kupyati* ("he is angry with Maitra"), where Maitra is the object of anger (*kopa*) and not a recipient. In such cases, Maitra is not expressed by the fourth case ending. Therefore, the term "recipient" in this context must be understood as referring to the "recipient" as defined by the rule *dānasya yaḥ svāmī tadvyatirikto yaḥ sa sampradānam*. This concludes the discussion on the meaning of the fourth case. Now, the meaning of the fifth case is discussed. The fifth case ending is used to express the "ablative" (*apādāna*). As stated in the rule *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam*: "That which is fixed (*dhruva*) in separation (*apāya*) is the ablative. Here, "separation" means the movement away from a fixed point. That fixed point from which the movement occurs is the "ablative. This is illustrated by examples such as *vṛk

In cases such as "ananta-sthale" (in endless instances), it is more appropriate to assume that the nominative case itself denotes the meaning of words like "droṇa," with reference to its characteristic of being limited by that measure. Nor should it be argued that because a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is necessary in examples such as "bring a *droṇa* of rice" (*droṇaṃ vrīhim ānaya*), the same must apply to nominative instances as well; for even so, the inclusion of the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is necessary to ensure that the metaphorical indication is established as a conventional usage (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*), just as in the rule "the elision of *matup* is desired after words expressing qualities" (*guṇavacanebhyo matupo lugiṣṭa*).

The inclusion of the word "vacana" (number), however, is so that [the rule] may apply even to those [numbers] such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth that have already been expressed—as in "one," "two," or "many. Otherwise, because of the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not [already] expressed"), and because this section [of the grammar] forms a single syntactic unit with rules such as "the plural is used for the plural," and because the enumeration [of specific cases] has been rejected, singularity and the rest would be considered expressed by the base (*prakṛti*) itself. Even if the governing heading *anabhihite* were rejected, the nominative case (*prathamā*) would still not occur simply because the meaning has already been expressed.

As for the argument that the first case ending (*prathamā*) will necessarily arise after words such as *eka* simply because of the rule stating that "the base alone is not to be used, nor is the suffix alone," otherwise there would be no other alternative in cases such as *ekaṃ paśya* ("see one") or *ekena kṛtam* ("done by one"), that is not correct. For in those instances, since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth has not been expressed, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) and others are possible. Nor is it equivalent to say that the first case arises because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) has not been expressed; for that [meaning] has already been expressed by the nominal stem itself.

Nor does this result in the impossibility of a subject for the rule prescribing the nominative case; for even if the nominative is applied there by the force of the specific statement, it is unavoidable that a shift in number (vacanavyatyaya) must occur in instances such as "eka" (one).

As for the argument that, although duals and other suffixes are excluded by restrictive rules of meaning—such as "the singular suffix occurs when there is oneness"—the principle *uktārthānām aprayogaḥ* (that which has already been expressed need not be used) does not apply here, because there is no rule prescribing the singular suffix and so forth specifically for oneness and the like. Even under the view that the restriction applies to the suffix itself—namely, "the singular suffix occurs when there is oneness"—while duals and others are excluded from other numbers by virtue of being restricted to their own kind (*sajātīya*), the singular suffixes are not excluded from that which is devoid of number.

Regarding the statement beginning with "eka" (one), there is no restrictive rule [in the system] that the cognition of singularity and so forth arises only from the case-ending (*sup*) and not from the base (*prakṛti*), nor is there any evidence for the total abandonment of meanings that have already been presented. Furthermore, such a restriction would only apply when another number is possible; moreover, dual endings and the like are simply impossible in the case of the word "eka" and others, as the case may be. This too is to be considered carefully: if the meanings are not within the intended scope of the grammatical treatise, there is no harm even if they are abandoned, because mere presentation [of a meaning] is not a sufficient condition [for its application].

By this, the argument that "the use of a mere restatement (anuvāda) is more logical than the use of a non-connexive expression" is refuted; for if [the nominative] were to apply first, the occurrence of the singular number in the case of "dvau" (two) and "bahavaḥ" (many) would be unavoidable. Furthermore, as for the claim that the mention of "mātra" (mere) is redundant because the rule *sambodhane ca* indicates that the nominative does not apply when there is a superaddition of the accusative and other cases: [this too is incorrect].

Regarding this, they say: "Since that [rule] would otherwise result in the application of the sixth case (genitive) in all remaining instances, the present sūtra is necessary to block that; how then can it be considered merely restrictive (niyamārtha)? [The opponent replies: "If that were so, then rules such as 'the second case (accusative) is used for the object' (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) would also not be restrictive. [The proponent answers: "Therefore, let the entire section consisting of both general rules and exceptions be the very thing that effects the refinement of the linguistic forms (*lakṣya-saṃskāraka*). And thus, in the absence of the rule 'the second case is used for the object,' the rule 'the sixth case is used for the remainder' (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*) would also be absent; since the second case would then be applicable [everywhere], it is indeed appropriate that the former rule be considered restrictive."

In this regard, the following must be said: the author of the Vārttika states, "the nominative occurs when [the meaning] is expressed. This means that when the agent and so forth are expressed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like, the nominative case ending occurs. Examples such as *vṛkṣaḥ* ("the tree") are provided because the verb "is" (*asti*) is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Thus, the intention is that even in cases such as *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the hero man"), where there is an additional relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), the nominative is established because [the agent] has been expressed [by the suffix].

And this has been refuted by the principle that "the first case ending (*prathamā*) occurs when [the locus] is not already expressed (*anabhihite*). The meaning of this is as follows: in the sentence *prāsāde āste* ("he sits in the palace"), the locus called "palace" is not specified by two distinct actions; rather, it is expressed by the *ghañ*-affix (in *prāsāda-*) which has *sad-* as its base, and it is not expressed by the *laṭ*-suffix (in *āste*) of the verb *ās-*. Since one power (*śakti*) [of expression] is already occupied, the first case ending—which is dependent on that [power]—would arise, overriding the seventh case ending due to its higher priority. Now, it must be stated that the first case ending occurs when there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

In the cases mentioned, however, because they reside in different substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the nominative case does not occur. For grammatical coreferentiality (*tiṅ-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in the relationship between that which is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and that which expresses it. And this exists in examples such as *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), because Caitra is expressed both by the verbal suffix in its form as "agent" (*kartṛtva*) and by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in its own specific form. But in the case of *prāsāde āste* ("he sits in the palace"), since there is an absence of expressing a specific agent already denoted by the verbal suffix, the nominative case does not occur after the word *prāsāda*. If this is argued:

Not so; for it would result in the non-occurrence of *tiṅ* suffixes in the *laṭ* [present tense]. To explain: when the situation "devadatta pac laṭ" arises, since there is no coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a *tiṅ* prior to the production of that *tiṅ*, the restrictive rule that "only the nominative case applies" does not hold. Consequently, all case endings beginning with the nominative (*su*), which are prescribed without distinction, would indeed be possible after the word "devadatta. Thus, because there would be coreferentiality with non-nominative cases, only the present participles *śatṛ* and *śānac* would apply. But this is not an acceptable consequence, as it would lead to the disappearance of the sentence "devadattaḥ pacati" (Devadatta cooks).

Nor should it be argued that because one relies on the restrictive rule regarding case endings—such as "the second case [is used] only for the object" (*karmaṇy eva dvitīyā*)—therefore the second case and so forth will not occur [in these instances]. For under the view that the restriction pertains to meaning—that "the second case is used only when there is an object"—that consequence would indeed follow. Furthermore, the sixth case (genitive) is possible here by virtue of its being a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). Nor should it be argued that the third person endings (*tiṅ*) and so forth will occur due to the force of the rule prescribing them; for the prescription of *tiṅ* endings has its scope in the *laṅ* and other tenses. For this very reason, the prescription of the nominative (*prathamā*) also lacks such force, since its scope lies only in cases where the suffix is other than *laṭ*.

Nor should it be argued that, by relying on the interpretation of *na cāprathamāsāmānādhikaraṇe* as a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the application of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* is precluded when there is coreferentiality with a nominative (*prathamāsāmānādhikaraṇya*), and since such coreferentiality exists here, the occurrence of *śatṛ* and *śānac* does not arise; for this would involve the unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) of resorting to an *asamartha-samāsa* (compound with non-coordinated members) and a syntactic split (*vākya-bheda*).

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that even under the view of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there is no fault regarding the restriction of case-endings (*vibhakti-niyama*). Dīkṣita maintains that this [Bhāṣya statement] is to be considered [with caution]. For, even if the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others do not arise due to a restriction such as "the second case is used only for the object" (*dvitīyā karmaṇyeva*), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) remains unavoidable; this is because the rule "the genitive is used only for the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe eva*) is restrictive. Since "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers precisely to those cases where the restriction of other case-endings has not taken effect, and since there exists coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a case-ending different from the nominative (*prathamā*), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would be unavoidable.
And [the same applies] in the case of address (*sambodhana*). (Pāṇini 3.2.125) 47.

The first case (prathamā) occurs [in the following example]: *caitra maitra āgacchati* ("O Caitra, Maitra is coming"). This is an address (*sabodhana*), and it consists of the desire: "May this person become a possessor of the understanding of the meaning of this sentence. In that context, by distinguishing between what is intended and what is not, the desire is the meaning of the first case. The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—namely, the person Caitra—is connected to the desire through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*). Furthermore, that desire is connected to the action (*kriyā*) through a relation consisting of the subjectness (*viṣayitā*) as determined by the subjectness residing in the desire itself, which is in turn delimited by the subjectness residing in the cognition (*bodha*) that possesses a modehood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the subjectness residing in the desire. Thus, the action is connected to the desire via the relation of subjectness as determined by the subjectness residing in the cognition that has a modehood delimited by the subjectness residing in the desire.

This is because such a desire—namely, "May there arise in him the cognition of the act of going having Maitra as its agent"—is possible in exactly that way. In that desire which has Caitra as its object, the cognition (bodha) which serves as the qualifier by way of being the object (viṣayatva) is that in which the act of going having Maitra as its agent occurs as a qualifier (prakāratā) through the relation of objectness (viṣayitā). By this, the case of vocative address (sambodhana) is also explained, since the aforementioned desire is possible there as well. Consequently, by virtue of forming a single syntactic unit (ekavākyatā), the low-pitched accent (nighāta) applies in cases such as *vrajāni devadatta*. This was stated by Hari: "The word used for vocative address is a qualifier of the action."
In the phrase "vrajāni devadatta," there is a *nighāta* (tonal suppression) here because of that being so.
It is addressed. || 48 ||

That which ends in a first case (prathamā) as stated [in the previous rule] shall be designated as *āmantrita* (vocative). Due to the force of employing this major technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*), there is the inclusion of that which ends in it [the first case]. The applications of this designation (*saṃjñāpradeśa*) are such as "the preceding *āmantrita* is treated as non-existent," and so forth. Why is the word *sā* ("that") used?
