[It is used] so that in forms such as *he pacan* and *he pacamāna*, even though the suffixes *śatṛ* and others are prescribed only for the purpose of addressing (*sambodhana*), the designation previously mentioned by the former rule should still apply to the first case, because those suffixes are included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) itself.

But when even the *luṅ* suffix and others, when devoid of reduplication, denote the agent just like the *loṭ* suffix, then the nominative case applies by the rule "also in the vocative" (*saṃbodhane ca*). Since the application of that very designation [of "nominative"] occurs by the principle that "a rule applies to what is immediately preceding," the term *set* (the marker *s*) need not be prescribed for the sake of establishing the form.
[The rule is: "The singular number is the vocative" (*ekavacanaṃ saṃbuddhiḥ*).

The singular number of the vocative case shall bear the technical name *sambuddhi*. The applications of this term are found in rules such as "after *eṅ* or a short vowel, [the *s* of] *sambuddhi* [is elided]" (*eṅ-hasvāt-sambuddheḥ*). Although it would have been sufficient to say "the *su* [suffix] is *sambuddhi*," the inclusion of the word "singular" (*ekavacanam*) ensures that the name applies to the suffix alone and not to the word ending in that suffix, following the established method.
6.1.68: *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (The sixth [case] is used for the remainder).

The word *śeṣa* (remainder) means "other. In this context, when the previously mentioned factors such as the object (*karman*) and so forth are construed as correlates (*pratiyogin*), those meanings other than the case-factors (*kāraka*) such as the object are called *śeṣa*. Although a real relationship between action and its factors exists everywhere—for instance, in the expression "the king's man," there is a relationship of agent and recipient based on the underlying cognition that "the king gives [something] to the man"—[it is still designated as *śeṣa*].

According to common worldly usage, [the genitive] "of the tree" (*vṛkṣasya*) refers to the tree itself as in "the branch of the tree" (*vṛkṣasya śākhā*); however, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, the locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatva*) belongs to the branch. Furthermore, because the means of acquiring ownership—purchase, seizure, begging, and barter—are essentially actions (*kriyātmakatva*). Although seizure is not declared by the scriptures to be a cause of ownership, it nonetheless functions as a means through its nature of permitting disposal at will (*yatheṣṭaviniyoga*). Nevertheless, when there is an intention to express merely the relationship of owner and owned, the relation of action and factor (*kriyākārakasambandha*), though existing in reality, is simply disregarded. As it has been said: "The relationship [of possession], which is distinct from the factors of action, is preceded by the relation between action and factor."
"He is designated [as the *śeṣa*] whether the action is expressed or unexpressed.

In the case of an unexpressed action, as in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and so on; in the case of an expressed action, as in "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*) and so on—the meaning being that the remembrance is related to the mother. Here, according to the view that restricts the application of suffixes, the mention of *śeṣa* (remainder) is for the purpose of restriction, namely, that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs only in the case of the *śeṣa*.

But if the position is that the meaning is restricted [to the genitive], then it should simply be stated as "the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For when both the sixth case and another [case] would apply, [the rule] says "only the sixth case. Now, one might argue: let the mention of *śeṣa* (remainder) be for the purpose of excluding the sixth case from the correlative (*pratisambandhin*), since the sixth case would apply to that as well because a relation resides in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*). Nor should it be said that the nominative (*prathamā*) applies because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) when there is only the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), since the sixth case applies to the relation; if this is argued, we say no, because it has already been stated that the relation, being an additional element, is cognized later as part of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

When the word *puruṣa* (man) is uttered, there is the cognition of the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Even when only the word *rājñaḥ* (of the king) is spoken, there is the cognition of ownership (*svāmitva*) that is not yet delimited by a specific correlate (*pratiyogin*). Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the application of the genitive case is justified by the established relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇa-pradhāna-bhāva*) between the king and the man. As it has been said: "Although this [relationship] resides in both, because it exists for the sake of another, it is distinguished among the subordinate elements; however, when being expressed, it is employed with respect to the principal elements."

The meaning is that since a relation, which resides in both relata, is already conveyed by the genitive case expressing the subordinate element (guṇa), the genitive is not used for the principal relatum (pradhāna), which is the counter-correlate.

For instance, the capacities of the *kārakas* are postulated with respect to actions within the meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). When there is a desire to express the penetration of action into the meaning of the nominal stem, and thus an excess of meaning characterized by capacity arises, then those capacities do not attain the status of being the meaning of the nominal stem itself. In that case, the usage is simply "he cuts with a sickle" (*dātreṇa lunāti*), and not "the sickle is the instrument" (*dātraṃ karaṇam*). When the connection with action is intended to be expressed, the capacities are not conveyed by words such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*), but rather by case-endings (*vibhakti*) alone; for the denotation of an abstracted capacity is accomplished solely by that [case-ending]. And this has been analyzed previously.

But when there is an intention to express mere fitness (*yogyatā*), then [the rule applies] as "the sickle is the instrument" (*dātraṃ karaṇam*). And in that case, when the case-ending arises, the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) do not serve as the cause [for the application of the ending]. As it has been said:
"But when [a thing] is denoted by its own word, that property [of being an instrument, etc. is not denoted;
rather, this functional assistance (*upakāra*) is understood through the case-endings and so forth alone."

Thus: the term *vibhakti* (case-ending) refers to both *sup* (nominal suffixes) and *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes). The term *ādi* (and so forth) refers to *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes that have the sense of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant). Accordingly, when there is a desire to express a specific relation with its own [related] object, we have *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's servant"). But when the intention is merely the state of being an owner, the sense is *rājā svāmī* ("the king is the owner"). However, when the king's ownership as defined by the property residing in the servant is intended to be expressed, then we have *puruṣasya rājā* ("the king of the servant"). In the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam* ("the wealth of the king's servant"), however, since the relation between the servant and the wealth is not already expressed by the sixth case ending following the word *rājan*, the sixth case is understood to be employed for the purpose of expressing that [specific relation].
The sixth case-affix is used for the instrument of a verb meaning "to know" when it is used in the sense of "not knowing."

The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the instrument (*karaṇa*) when it is intended as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) in relation to the verb *jñā* (to know), which is here intended to have a meaning distinct from [mere] cognition. For example: *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"). In reality, the activity related to that ghee which has become the instrument is expressed; the word *jñāna* refers to activity through the relationship of being preceded by [the perception of] ghee. It was explained previously that this section is for the purpose of excluding compound formation (*samāsa*). As for the examples with verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) found in the treatises, authoritative scholars maintain that these are merely illustrative of those roots ending in *kṛt* suffixes.
[Now follows: *Adhigarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.52). [This sūtra prescribes the sixth case for the object of verbs meaning 'to find' (*adhigati*), 'to pity' (*day*), and the root *īś*.]

The genitive case is used when [the object] is intended as a *śeṣa* (remainder). [In the rule for] *iṅ* (to remember), the letter *k* is included here solely for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). The inclusion of the prefix (*sopasarga*) is, however, for the sake of indicating—by means of assenting to a partial application—that "the roots *iṅ* and *ik* do not deviate from being preceded by a prefix. For this very reason, it was not stated as *smṛtyartha* (having the meaning of 'remembering'). Nevertheless, in the rule *iṇvadikaḥ*, this is necessary to exclude the root *āya* (as in *kaṭī-āya*) which is elided, and because of the certainty of its *kit* status. Examples include: *mātuḥ adhyayā* (learning from the mother) and *pituḥ smaraṇam* (remembering the father), and so forth. *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* || 53 || (The genitive is used after the root *kṛ* when there is a sense of improvement or restoration.)

*Pratiyatna* is the bestowing of a quality; for example, *edho dakasyopaskaraṇam* ("the preparation of fuel for water"). [The rule "a collection of non-living things" applies here, resulting in a singular compound.
[The sixth case ending is used] after verbs meaning "to cause pain," provided they denote a state (*bhāva*) and do not take *jvar* as their object. (Pāṇini 2.3.54)

It should be stated that "ajvara-santāpyoḥ" [is the rule]. The meaning is that *santāpi* (causing fever) should also be included within the category of the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the distinction. For those verbs denoting illness (*rujārtha*) whose agents are abstract states (*bhāva*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the object when it is not intended as the primary factor (*śeṣe*). For example: *caurasya rogasya rujā* ("the affliction of the thief's disease"). In the word *vacana*, because the suffix *lyuṭ* is employed merely for grammatical correctness and its specific meaning is not intended, while the agent—the meaning of the suffix—is indeed intended, the sense of "having an abstract state as its agent" (*bhāvakartṛka*) is established.

However, some say that those for whom the word denotes the state (*bhāva*) are "words denoting the state" (*bhāvavacanāḥ*); that is to say, those whose utterance or expression is directed toward the agent in the sense of the state, meaning their designation serves to convey the meaning of a verbal root where the agent is the state itself. Why [is the rule] stated as *ajvarī-* etc.? It is so that in examples such as *rogasya corajvaraḥ* or *corasaṃtāpaḥ*, there may be only the genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), whereby the formation of the compound is established and there is a distinction in accent (*svara*), as previously stated. In the Vedic language (chandas), the genitive case is frequently used for the instrument; for example, *ghṛtasya* or *ghṛtena yajate*.
When used with words expressing frequency or purpose (*kṛtvas-artha*), it denotes time as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

On this point, the ancient commentators [state]: the term *śeṣa* (remainder) is understood to carry over into the subsequent sūtra because of the mention of *karman* (object). Otherwise, he would have said "and in the case of the agent" (*kartari ca*). It is precisely for the purpose of ensuring that the mention of *karman* connected with *śeṣa* does not carry over that *karman* is separately mentioned there.

Others, however, state that since the mention of *karman* (object) can serve to exclude only the immediately preceding governing rule (*adhikāra*) contained in the current sūtra, this very fact is the proof for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *śeṣe* (remainder). Examples: *pañcakṛtvo 'hno bhojanam* (eating five times a day); *dvirahno bhojanam* (eating twice a day). Why "in the remainder"? [To show: *dvirahany adhīte* (he studies twice a day)—lest there be a sublation of the locative case by the genitive [as required by the following rule]. 65. *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (P. 2.3.65): [The sixth case-affix is used] for the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows.

The word "śeṣa" (remainder) is excluded. When used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be employed for both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). Example: *bhavataḥ śāyikā* (your lying down); *apāṃ sraṣṭā* (the creator of waters). Why specify "agent and object"? [Consider: *śāstreṇa bhettā* (one who breaks by means of a treatise).

But is it not redundant to say "after a *kṛt*"? For two types of suffixes are prescribed after a verbal root: *tiṅ*s and *kṛt*s. Among these, since the use of the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* when there is a *tiṅ*-suffix, the application of the genitive is easily established only in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. Furthermore, the prohibition of the genitive that will be stated for the use of indeclinables (*avyaya*) applies only to those agents and objects belonging to an indeclinable that ends in a *kṛt*-suffix; it should not apply to cases like *uccaiḥ kaṭānāṃ sraṣṭā*, where the indeclinable does not end in a *kṛt*-suffix. Therefore, [the word *kṛtī*] is stated for that purpose.

This must be stated: because [the word] *sraṣṭā* (creator) is a *kṛdanta* (a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix), its agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*)—namely, "of the mats" (*kaṭānām*) and "situated in a high place" (*uccaiḥ-sthāna-sthitānām*)—are indeed [the agents and objects] of that which expresses an action, and not of the word *uccaiḥ*, which does not express an action. This is because the inclusion of the term *kṛt* is obtained there by implication alone. Furthermore, in the rule to be stated later, *ubhayaprāptau kṛti* ("when both [agent and object] are possible in connection with a *kṛt*"), since the word *kṛti* denotes the substantive (*viśeṣya*), it is established that *ubhayaprāptau* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Otherwise, due to its being more internal (*antaraṅga*), it would be a *tatpuruṣa*.

Furthermore, since two [factors] are intended to be expressed, let there be no prohibition of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) therein; for it should be stated as "this is a wonderful event: the cooking of rice and the appearance of Brahmins. Nevertheless, even in that case, there is no purpose in including those [two]; moreover, in that instance as well, the determination of the *bahuvrīhi* compound is possible through grammatical interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). If this is argued:

Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya states that the mention of *kṛt* [in Pāṇini 2.3.65] is intended so that [the genitive] does not apply to the agent or object of a *taddhita* suffix. For example: *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat") and *bhuktapūrvī odanam* ("one who has previously eaten rice"). In these cases, the compound *kṛtaṃ pūrvamanena* ("this person has previously made") is formed by the rule *sup-supā*. Then, by the rule *sapūrvācca*, the suffix *ini* is added. Since the agent is already expressed here by the *taddhita* suffix, the genitive would not have applied to him; however, the mention of *kṛt* ensures that the genitive does not occur for the object, "mat" (*kaṭa*).

It might be argued as follows: In the analysis (*vigraha*) "the mat was made by him previously" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ pūrvamanenānena*), because the object (*karman*) is already expressed by the *kta* suffix, the accusative case should not occur; all the more so, the genitive, which is an exception to it, should not occur here either, since the governing rule [Pāṇini 2.3.1] "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*) applies. Furthermore, since the word *kṛta* is thus dependent on *kaṭa*, both the compound (*samāsa*) and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would be untenable. To this, they reply: Even when [the action of] making is divested of its connection with a specific object such as a mat, another word *kṛta* occurs that is independent of any such specific [object].
When the verbal suffix -kta denotes the abstract state (bhāva) while the root remains intransitive,
then there occurs a connection between that [state] and the objects as agents possessing action.
Just as an action that is formless and resides in [the past] states such as "gone" is connected with objects such as villages through verbal suffixes,
so too is it connected in cases such as *kṛtapūrvī* (one who has previously done).

The meaning of this is as follows: in the sentence "the mat was made by him" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭo 'nena*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between *kṛta* and *kaṭa*; however, in this specific sense, such a relation cannot possibly exist through the operation of *vṛtti* (compound formation), because that [operation] has only a general scope. For instance, when the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of a general object or a state (*bhāva*), the word *kṛta*—without yet having entered into a connection with a specific object in the form of a "mat"—is compounded with the word *pūrva*.

Nor should it be argued that, under the view that [the suffix] expresses the general action (*karmasāmānya*), the denotation of the mat (*kaṭa*) is unavoidable and that it could be expressed just as in the case of "it is possible to destroy hunger" (*kṣud upahantuṃ śakyam*) and so forth; for in a secondary derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*), the meaning of the word *kṛta*—having become a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhūta*)—cannot be separately connected with the mat. This is the meaning of the first verse.

[Objection: "In that case, since the word *kaṭa* (mat) would also lack connection with an action (*kriyā*), the accusative case ending would not apply. [Response: This is not so; for in examples such as *grāmaṃ kṛtavān* ("he has made a village"), we observe that the factors of action (*kāraka*) are connected even with an action that is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Thus they say: "It is not restricted to being expressed by a finite verb" (*avigraha*). The meaning is: "even when it is not grasped as the primary element. In the case of *kṛtapūrvī*—which is derived from the sense "one who previously made"—since the meaning "he previously made" is established, its status as the object (*karman*) in relation to the action of *karoti* (to do/make) is not lost. Thus [it is explained].

On this point, the Neo-Mīmāṃsakas argue as follows: If this were so, then even in the case of the word *rāja-* (king), when it is compounded with the word *puruṣa-* (man) independently of the word *ṛddha-* (prosperous), there would subsequently follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of its connection with *ṛddha-*. Furthermore, there would also be the undesirable consequence of a second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) in such instances as *odanaḥ pacyatetamām* ("the rice is cooked most thoroughly") and *gururdharitrī kriyatetarām tvayā* ("you must make the teacher the earth"). This is because, according to the stated reasoning, if one asserts that the connection of the rice and other objects is with the object (karman) which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) and has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), then the same undesirable consequence would apply to the meaning of the *kta*-suffix as well.

Just as in the case of the factors of action (*kāraka*) [which require a verb], power (*śakti*) also possesses an expectancy toward its possessor (*śaktimat*), because there is no reason for a discrepancy [in their relationship]. Furthermore, in the impersonal construction "rice is cooked" (*odanaṃ pacyate*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the accusative case ending. Therefore, the object does not connect with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). In the Mīmāṃsā school's view, the connection of the *kārakas* is not with the meaning of the verbal root, but rather with the meaning of the nominal suffix (*taddhita*) itself.

In this context, since agency (*kartṛtva*) is the meaning of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), whether as a qualifier—as in *pācaka* ("cook")—or by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or even independently, the action (*kṛti*) is also the meaning of the suffix. When that [action] is construed with gender and is presented by the word expressing the substantive (*viśeṣya-vācaka-pada*), there is no dissolution of the compound, just as in the case of "the cooker of rice" (*odanasya pācakaḥ*). Furthermore, because the word expressing that [action] does not denote the objecthood (*karmatva*), there is no occurrence of the nominative case. However, in expressions such as *pacyatetamām* ("it is cooked most excellently"), only the excellence (*atiśaya*) is the meaning of the suffix, and thus the action is not denoted.

In that case, just as with the meaning of the suffix *la* (the verbal suffix), because the objecthood (*karmatva*) is already expressed by that very [suffix] through its connection with it, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not occur. This is because we accept that the suffix *tarap* functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*), and since the form *tarām* is devoid of independent meaning, there is a grammatical convention (*vyutpatti*) for it to connect even with that which requires a qualifier. The same principle should be applied to examples such as "the best cooker of rice" (*odanasya pācakatamaḥ*). Furthermore, in the expression "he is wise in grammar" (*vyākaraṇaṃ prājñaḥ*), one should observe that the connection with the object occurs there because the primary derivative suffix (*svārthika-taddhita*) also conveys the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix.

It should not be argued that, in such cases as "the cooker of rice" (*odanasya pācakaḥ*) or "the doer of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya kṛtī*), there would be no connection with the *kāraka* (grammatical participant), because you do not admit [the presence] of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) there, and because the meaning of the suffix *ghañ* is what possesses the gender (*liṅga*) connection; for even if such a connection were admitted, it would follow that this would also apply to the referent of the word "entity" (*vastu*). To this we reply: even in those cases, just as in the case of "the cooker" (*paktṛ*), there is the denotation of the cooking qualified by the effort (*kṛti*), or else there is the separate denotation of the effort and the cooking through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the effort; thus, the connection of the *kāraka* with the effort is logically established. This is because the connection is possible in the form: "the cooking is that which is to be accomplished by an effort conducive to cooking."

Alternatively, there is simply a genitive of residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) there; even that has an indirect connection with the supplied verbal action such as "is" (*asti*), and thus the rule prescribing the genitive in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is not rendered redundant. This is because that rule is justified merely by the presence of suffixes like *-tṛc* which denote the agent and so forth. Thus it is established that the genitive for the agent and the object occurs only in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, and not in connection with a meaningful secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or a secondary derivative expressing a case-role (*kāraka*). To this effect, the mention of "*kṛt*" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that case-roles [denoted by *taddhitas*] are construed with a *kṛt*-suffix.

In this regard, the following must be said: the avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is easily achieved simply by following the actual usage (*prayoga*). Otherwise, how could there be an over-extension even in cases such as *pāṭaliputraka*, since the formation of an "ungrammatical compound" (*asamartha-samāsa*) is established by the *Bhāṣya* and is thus universally accepted? Furthermore, in this case, does the suffix [in *kṛta*] denote the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*)? It cannot be the first, because that would entail the absence of any evidence for the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) having the sense of a primary derivative (*kṛt*). Otherwise, the same would apply to forms such as *śayyate*. Nor can it be the latter.

Is this [agent] a general (sāmānya) or a specific (viśeṣa) form? Not the first, because it would entail the defects you have mentioned. Not the latter, because either "lack of syntactic connection" (ananvitatva) or "the denotation of the mat" (kaṭābhidhāna) would be unavoidable. Furthermore, since the secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix in the word *pūrva* is connected with gender, how could there be a connection with a case-role (kāraka) in its meaning? If it is argued that the agent alone is what is connected with gender in that instance—

No; for since the meaning of the suffix *ghañ* is not distinct from the act (*kṛti*), it is impossible to determine that the act does not possess a connection with gender. Furthermore, it has already been stated that "cooking" (*pāka*) is that which is to be accomplished by an act conducive to cooking. Moreover, this contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that suffixes such as *ghañ* convey a state (*bhāva*) that has attained the status of an accomplished entity (*siddha*). Nor can the purposefulness of the rule be restricted solely to the domain of suffixes such as *tṛc*.

In compounds such as *hari-smaraṇam*, if the genitive were a "genitive of object" (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), then because the compound would be preceded by a kāraka, the rule *kṛd-uttara-prakṛti-svaraḥ* (the accent of the final member of a kṛd-derivative) would apply; this would result in the failure of that compound, which is accepted by all authorities. Furthermore, forms such as *mātuḥ-smṛtam* would be unestablished. For you must maintain that since the genitive connected with a kṛt-affix does not apply there, it is only the "residual genitive" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) that is prohibited in the context of a past participle by the rule *na-loka-*. Let this suffice for the details.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Here, they raise an objection: "Let there be some way of applying [the term] by abandoning its primary meaning, since we observe the abandonment of both the application and the sentence in cases such as *māsajāta* (born after a month). Even so, the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is redundant; for by the rule *na lokā-*, the prohibition of the genitive case is established when used in conjunction with a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). This is because that prohibition applies when there is a connection with an action conveyed by a verbal root ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix. Furthermore, in examples such as *grāmaṃ gatavān* ('he has gone to the village'), the case-factors (*kāraka*) are connected directly with the action itself."

Nor should it be argued that the prohibition exists for the sake of preventing the genitive case from arising for the instigator (prayojya)—who is the agent of the action denoted by the base of the causative suffix (ṇic)—in examples such as *caitro maitreṇa pācayati* ("Caitra causes Maitra to cook"). For the prohibition is established simply by the rule "not in connection with a *la*-suffix" (*layoge na*). Furthermore, one should not argue that the prohibition applies only when there is a connection with the action presented by the causative stem (*ṇijanta*), and not with an action presented by a *la*-suffix ending, because the causative suffix (*ṇic*) itself is a type of *la*-suffix. This is because the meaning of the rule—"not [the genitive] in connection with whatever action is conveyed by the base of a *la*-suffix or by a word ending in a *la*-suffix"—is common to both primary actions (*guṇakriyā*) and subordinate ones.

Because the maxim regarding the primary and secondary senses does not apply when following the requirements of the specific grammatical context; otherwise, even the third case-ending would not occur there. This is because the use of the genitive case is desired in both instances: *bhedikā devadattasya* (the divider of Devadatta) and *yajñadattasya kāṣṭhānām* (of Yajñadatta's wood).

Regarding this, the traditionalists (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*) say that the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is for the purpose of excluding those [compounds] where there is an excess of a *taddhita* suffix, as in the case of "grammar" (*vyākaraṇam*) and "wise" (*prājñaḥ*), where the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to the rule *prajñādibhyaśca*. Thus, the intention of the authors of the treatises is that in an expression such as *odanasya pācakatamaḥ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur. Furthermore, the mention of *kṛt* serves as an exclusion even for cases like *kartavyapūrvī kaṭam*, so that [the genitive] does not occur when joined with a *tavya* suffix; thus, the purpose of the exclusion is indeed possible. Since the *Bhāṣya* remains neutral on this point, Dīkṣita maintains that one or the other must be determined based on the observation of usage by learned authorities (*abhiyukta*).

The secret [of the matter] is that, according to the maxim *yathālakṣaṇam aprayukte*, it is more appropriate to say *kartavyapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who previously made a mat"). On this point, Pakṣadharamiśra explains: in the case of *devadatta odanam*, if the word *pacati* ("cooks") is not supplied, there would be the fault that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would apply because the agent is not expressed; yet this fault remains even if that word is supplied, because in the view of the followers of the Nyāya school, the agent is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). If it is argued that "the number of the agent is expressed," then the same undesirable consequence of the third case ending would follow in the expression *devadattasya pākaḥ* ("Devadatta’s cooking"), because the number is not expressed by the *kṛt*-suffix. Thus they have explained the passage from the *Maṇikāra*.

[Objection: "But surely, in this case, when there is a connection with a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone serves as the exception; otherwise, since the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) would be applicable, the formulation of that rule [Pāṇini 2.3.65] would be untenable. [Response: Not so. Even when connected with a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive does not convey the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) as its specific mode (*prakāra*), but rather as a mere relation (*sambandha*). That the relation is indeed agenthood is another matter. Thus, the meaning is: if the number of the agent is not expressed, then for the sake of a cognition of connection where agenthood is the mode, the restriction of the instrumental would apply even in the present case.

But if this were so, the Sūtra would be redundant; for the [intended] understanding characterized by the mode "being a relation" is already established simply from the statement of the *śeṣa* (remainder). Furthermore, in cases such as *caitrasya gataḥ* ("Caitra's going"), the application of the genitive of the *śeṣa* would be untenable, because according to this view, the prohibition of the genitive of the *śeṣa* by the rule *na loke* (Pāṇini 2.3.69) would have to be stated [as a necessary exception]. Moreover, in compounds such as *harismaraṇam* ("remembrance of Hari"), if the genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) were used, the accentuation of the final member as the base-accent (*kṛd-uttara-prakṛti-svara*) would be impossible.

Finally, since the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and others generate an understanding characterized by the mode "agency" (*kartṛtva*), it is appropriate that the genitive, which is its exception, should likewise function in that same way.

It is said: the *ṭīkākṛt* (the author of the commentary) maintains that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which conveys agency (*kartṛtva*) or objecthood (*karmatva*) as a form of relation, is not correct when used in conjunction with a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*); however, by the intended meaning of the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*, it is precisely correct when it conveys a different kind of relation. Nor is this [position] incorrect, because even the "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) conveys nothing other than agency and so forth, insofar as they take the form of a general relation (*sambandhatva*).

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa has stated two views regarding the sūtra *adhīgartha...* (Pāṇini 2.3.52): either the relationship between "mother" (*mātṛ*) and "remembering" (*smaraṇa*) is caused by the action of "standing" (*sthāna*) and so forth; or else, because it takes the form of the action of remembering itself, it is produced by another action—namely, addressing (*saṃbodhana*)—just as the adhesion between lac and wood is caused by the lac, while the lac's [adhesion] is caused by itself and not by another lac. Otherwise, since the genitive of the "remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would also function as a relation, if only the object were understood, the doubt [regarding the need for a specific rule] would not be resolved, as in the case of "he remembers his mother" (*mātaraṃ smarati*).
Furthermore, being a relation is simply the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), as even Miśra’s statement refers to the genitive used in connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛd-yoga-ṣaṣṭhī*).

In reality, however, let there be in both cases a cognition where the qualificandum is agency (*kartṛtva*) and the mode (*prakāra*) is the property of being a relation (*sambandhatva*). Nevertheless, the rule is not redundant. This is because it serves a purpose by providing the basis for the application of the genitive case mentioned in this very rule, which functions as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the prohibition stated in the *na-loka-ādi* rule. By this, the accentuation is also explained. Nor should it be argued that since the genitive case would already apply even in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix by virtue of the general rule for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the present rule must be commenced solely to prevent the formation of compounds—just as in the case of the group of eight rules beginning with *jño 'vidarthasya*. [This is not so,] because...

Otherwise, the rule prohibiting compound formation when [the sixth case ending] follows a word in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ca*) would be redundant; for that rule serves merely to exclude the application of the sixth case prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). Furthermore, the rule *ubhayaprāptau* (Pāṇini 2.3.66) is intended solely to establish a restriction regarding the sixth case understood through this very context. Moreover, rules such as *adhīgartha...* (Pāṇini 2.3.52), which prescribe the residual sixth case (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) for the object, would become useless, since it has been established as a settled doctrine (*siddhānta*) that those rules apply exclusively to verbal derivatives ending in *kṛt* suffixes. In that case, according to your own view, the prevention of compounding would be accomplished by this very rule alone.

And this has been stated according to the actual state of affairs (*vastugati*), because it is sufficient [to explain the rule] as being intended merely to indicate the incorrectness of the third and second case endings when used in conjunction with a *kṛt* suffix. Furthermore, in examples such as *caitreṇa hataḥ* ("killed by Caitra"), the prohibition of the genitive case when used in conjunction with a *niṣṭhā* suffix will be stated later.
[Pāṇini 2.3.66: "When both [the agent and the object] are eligible [for the sixth case], [the sixth case ending is used] for the object."

Where there is the possibility of the application of the genitive case to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), the genitive should apply to the object alone when a *kṛt* suffix is used. This is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Example: *āścaryaṃ gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("It is wonderful, the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd"). It should be stated that "the prohibition does not apply in the case of the use of [suffixes] ending in *a* or *ā*. The meaning is that the aforementioned restriction does not operate. Examples: *bhedikā devadattasya kāṣṭhānām* ("Devadatta's cutter of wood") and *cikīrṣā viṣṇumitrasya kaṭasya* ("Viṣṇumitra's desire to make a mat"). In both cases, the genitive is used.

And it should not be argued that the rule *na ca ktinā bādhā na bhavati* (and there is no sublation by the suffix *ktin*) is inconsistent with the commentary stating "there is no sublation of *sīyuṭ* by *suṭ*," because the vowel *a* alone is understood first by the rule *apratyayāt*, and because the vowel *a* is not mentioned in the present context of the rule *gurośca halaḥ*. Some say this; others say it is due to the intention to express instrumentality (*karaṇatva*). It should be stated as an explanatory supplement (*vaktavya*) that "the option applies in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*). Some say this refers exclusively to the domain of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). Indeed, the composition of Pāṇini’s sūtras is diverse, or rather, it was composed by Pāṇini himself.

Others, however, say that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs merely in relation to what is distinct from both [the agent and the object], because the maxim regarding the application of the negative particle (*nañ*) is not universal. "The instruction of words" is performed by the Teacher (*ācārya*) or for the Teacher.
[This concludes the section on] the suffix *kta* when denoting the present time. 67.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition that will be stated hereafter. When used in conjunction with a *kta* suffix having a present sense, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed. For example: *rājñāṃ mataḥ*, *buddhaḥ*, or *pūjitaḥ* ("respected," "known," or "honored by kings"). There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the neuter gender when expressing an abstract state (*bhāva*). For example: *chātrasya hasitam* ("the laughing of the student"). Alternatively, this is established by the rule regarding the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). When the agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended to be expressed, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used: *chātreṇa hasitam*.
And [the sixth case is also used] after words expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). (Pāṇini 2.3.68)

The genitive case is used in connection with a word ending in *kta*. For example: *idameṣāṃ śayitam* ("this is their lying down"). However, in the case of intransitive verbs, [the genitive] is used for both [the agent and the object]. For example: *idameṣāṃ bhuktam odanasya* ("this is the eating of rice by them"). And the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (A 2.3.66) does not apply here, because that rule is intended solely for the purpose of [prescribing the genitive] for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows. Thus, there is a fourfold usage with roots meaning "to go": 1. *ihāhinā sṛptam* ("here is the crawling by a snake")—this is in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). 2. *ihāhiḥ sṛptaḥ*, *idamahisṛptam* ("here the snake has crawled")—this is in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). 3. *ihāheḥ sṛptaṃ grāmasya pārśve* ("here, near the village, is the place where the snake crawled").
The use of the word *pārśve* indicates that this is not a *kta*-suffix in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*), but rather in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*).
The sixth case-affix is not used after words ending in *loka*, *avyaya*, *niṣṭhā*, *khalartha*, or *tṛn* suffixes when they are in construction with a word ending in the sixth case. || 69 ||

Regarding the word *tṛṇām* [in Pāṇini 8.4.39], some hold that the substitution of *ṇ* was not applied because the specific form of the suffix was obscured; others, following Kaiyaṭa, maintain it is due to its being a *sautra* (Vedic/Pāṇinian) usage. In connection with these [suffixes], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur; this is an exception to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*. [Examples of] substitutes for *la* (the verbal suffix): *odanaṃ pacan*, *pacamānaḥ*, *pecānaḥ*, *pacivān*. [Commentary: "The mention of *sat* and *liṭ* in the context of the substitute for *la* is for the purpose of excluding *kikin*. One should state "with *sat* and *liṭ*" instead of removing the mention of *la*. Here, *sat* refers to the inclusion of both *śatṛ* and *śānac*.

By the word *liṭ*, the designation *liṭ* is prescribed for the suffixes *kānac* and *kvasu*, as well as for *kikin*. However, according to the alternative arrangement [of the sūtra], since *kikin* would not be a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *la*, the prohibition [against the application of the augment *iṭ*] would not apply in cases such as *papiḥ somam* and *dadir gāḥ*.

In the Bhāṣya, however, the statement "the *kikin* suffixes are like the *liṭ*" is an extension (*atideśa*) of the operations of *liṭ*, not the designation (*saṃjñā*) of *liṭ*. And when a specific operation is extended, the general property is also extended, because there is no deviation [from that rule]. Therefore, it is stated that the prohibition of the genitive case (in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi...*) is based on the mere fact of being a *l*-suffix. For example: *uḥ kaṭaṃ cikīrṣuḥ* ("one desiring to make a mat for his father") and *kanyām alaṅkariṣṇuḥ* ("one desiring to adorn a maiden"). This is because the meaning is "when used with a word ending in *u*"; furthermore, by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the prohibition is easily obtained even with a single [word] alone.

Having formed a *dvandva* compound with *uka*, there is subsequently a compound with *la*. However, if it were a *dvandva* with that [the *la*] alone, the substitutions *yu* and *ṇa* would occur. Examples of *uka*: *kāśīm āgāmukaḥ* (one who goes to Kāśī). There is no prohibition for *kamu* in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*): *lakṣmyāḥ kāmukaḥ* (one who desires Lakṣmī). An indeclinable: *kaṭaṃ kṛtvā* (having made a mat). There is no prohibition for *tosun* and *kasun*: *purā sūryasyodetoḥ ādheyaḥ* (it should be established before the rising of the sun); *purā krūrasya visṛpaḥ virapśin* (O Virapśin, before the gliding of Krūra). The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*): *devadattena kṛtam* (done by Devadatta); *odanaṃ bhuktavān* (he has eaten rice). The suffixes having the sense of *khal*: *tvayā sukaram* (easy for you to do).

"In a matter difficult for the Ikṣvākus to achieve"—this is the sense of the genitive case used as a *śeṣa*. Alternatively, it may be construed with "successes" (*siddhayaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "even Deśānana was easily conquered by him," the term *surāriḥ* (enemy of the gods) is used. The rule *śānaś ca ānaś śatṛṇām upasaṃkhyānam* (an addition concerning *śānac*, *ānaś*, and *śatṛ*) refers to a *pratyāhāra* formed by the letter *ṇ* in *tṛn*, starting from the rule *tṛn* and continuing through *śatṛ-śānacau*. By this means, *śānac* and the others are also included. Examples include: *somaṃ pavamānaḥ* (purifying the Soma), where *śānac* is used after the roots *pū* and *yaj*; *naḍam āghrāṇaḥ* (smelling the reed), where *ānaś* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and so forth; and *adhīyan pārāyaṇam* (studying the Pārāyaṇa).

In *indhāna* and *ārya*, there is the suffix *śatṛ*. [The suffix] *tṛn* [is also used]. "Indra is the drinker of the pressed Soma; he is the giver of all property; like a blade of grass, he conquers the lord of the gods"—thus says Subandhu. "It should be stated that [the prohibition applies] optionally after the root *dviṣ* when followed by *śatṛ*. This is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the rule] when a specific suffix is mentioned (*pratyayagrahaṇa*). The distinction is that when a *pratyāhāra* (a collective term) is mentioned, it is for the purpose of prescribing [the application of the rule].
"Akṛt suffixes and the suffix *u* do not denote the future or debt-relationship. (Pāṇini 2.3.70)

The *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is for the purpose of preventing [the application of the suffix] in numerical order. It will apply to the word *aka*. [In the rule] *ina ādhamarṇye ca*, by the word *ca* (and), there is the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "in the future tense" (*bhaviṣyati*). [Otherwise], the genitive case would not occur. Example: *edhānāhārako vrajati* ("He goes to fetch fuel"). *vrajaṃ gāmī* ("He is going to the cow-pen"). In the sense of debt (*ādhamarṇye*): *śataṃ dāyī* ("A debtor of a hundred"). Because the term *bhaviṣyat* (future) is marked with a *svarita* accent, the followers of Pāṇini accept that certain words are *svarita* by convention (*pratijñāsvaritāḥ*). Consequently, only that *aka* prescribed under the heading of the future tense (*bhaviṣyad-adhikāra*) is understood here; thus, it does not apply in the example *varṣaśatasya pūrakaḥ* ("Completer of a hundred years"). This suffix is prescribed generally by the rule *ṇvultṛcau*, and it is not situated within the section on the future tense.
The sixth case ending is optionally used for the agent of verbal nouns formed with *kṛt* suffixes.

Or rather, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may occur: *idaṃ kṛṣṇasya kṛtyam* (this is to be done by Kṛṣṇa) or *kṛṣṇena* (by Kṛṣṇa). It should not be argued that the mention of the agent (*kartṛ-grahaṇa*) is redundant because *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed only for the expression of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), and since the object must necessarily be expressed there, the genitive has no occasion to apply. For [the genitive] is possible in cases such as *geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* (the boy is to sing the Sāmans), because the suffix is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule *bhavyageya...* etc., and thus the object is not expressed. Nor should it be said that the mention of the agent is for the sake of avoiding a fault in examples such as *ākraṣṭavyā grāmaṃ śākhā* (the branch is to be dragged to the village).

It should not be argued that because the verb *kṛṣ* (to plow) takes two objects, the primary object (*śākhā*, the branch) is expressed by the *kṛtya* suffix, while the secondary object (*grāma*, the village) is not expressed [and thus requires the genitive]. This is because such a contingency is prevented precisely by the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). The phrase "not so when both [objects] are applicable" (*ubhayaprāptau na*) from the previous rule (*Pāṇini 2.3.68*) is understood here; therefore, even when the agent is expressed, the genitive does not occur, but rather only the instrumental. *netavyā vrajaṃ gāvaḥ kṛṣṇena* ("The cows are to be led to the cow-pen by Kṛṣṇa"). Or, when the agent is expressed: *kartari vā*. [In this case], everything [the restriction on the genitive] is withdrawn. The meaning is as before.

**Pāṇini 2.3.72:** *tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyānyatarasyām* ("With words having the sense of 'equal', except for *atula* and *upama*, the third case ending is optionally used [for the standard of comparison]").

When there is a connection with that which has the same meaning [as the agent], the third case ending may optionally be used; in the alternative, when it is treated as a residual relation (*śeṣa*), the sixth case ending is used. For example: *kṛṣṇena* or *kṛṣṇasya tulyaḥ*, *samaḥ* (equal or similar to Kṛṣṇa). Why "not with *tulā*" (*atuleti*)? Because in cases such as *kṛṣṇasya tulopamā vā nāsti* ("there is no equal or likeness to Kṛṣṇa"), the word *tulā* is not used in this sense. However, how is one to explain such instances as *tulāṃ yadārohati dantavāsasā* ("when he ascends the scale with Dantavakra") or *sphuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā* ("clearly comparable to Śiva, white with ashes")? [In these cases, the word *tulā* refers to the actual weighing scale.]

On this point, some say: *tolanam* (weighing) is *tulā*; here, by the rule of *nipātana*, there is the elision of both the suffix *aṅ* and the suffix *ṇi*. *Upamiti* (comparison) is *upamā* because it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root; therefore, the third case is used [with the word expressing that which is compared], as in the example "dark like a *tamāla* tree" (*tamālanīlam*). However, since the present sūtra is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive of the residual category (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the rule prescribing the third case does not apply here. Others, however, say that the third case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*saha-yoga*), as in the example: "Those who desire a comparison (*tulā*) for their own mass of hair with the hair on the heads of yaks (*camaryyaḥ*). They argue that the only distinction is that the sense of "together with" (*saha-artha*) is merely implied (*gamyamāna*) here.

The truth is this: since the words functioning as the correlates (*anuyogin*) of the difference serve to present the substratum (*dharmin*), the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of the difference belongs to those very same words *tulā* and *upamā*. This is because in the expression "there is no equal or likeness (*tulopamā*) of Kṛṣṇa," it is accepted that the words *tulā* and *upamā* refer to that which possesses such [equality]. However, in cases such as "that which ascends the scale" (*tulām ārohati*), since these words refer merely to similarity (*sādṛśya*), this third case ending does not apply. For this very reason, there is no possibility of the third case when *iva* and other such particles are employed; furthermore, in those instances, even the genitive of the remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) is not applicable.

Even though "veti" (or "vā") is understood from the preceding rule, the inclusion of "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is for the purpose of carrying forward its own status by means of the word "ca" (and) in the subsequent rule; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of carrying forward only the third case (*tṛtīyā*) which is in immediate proximity.

And the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used [in the sense of the dative] with words expressing a blessing (*āśis*), such as *āyuṣya*, *madra*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *sukha*, *artha*, and *hita*. (Pāṇini 2.3.73)

When these [words] are used in conjunction with [another word], the fourth (caturthī) and sixth (ṣaṣṭhī) case endings occur when a blessing (āśis) is intended. Having formed a dvandva compound of the words ending in *sukha*, a bahuvrīhi compound is made with the word *artha*. Some say that either *madra* or *bhadra* need not be recited. Others hold that the word *artha* is also a separate cause [for the application of the rule]; however, according to the commentary, all the words here have *artha* as their referent.

May there be long life (*āyuṣya*) or longevity for Caitra or for Caitrī. Likewise: *madram*, *bhadram*, *kuśalam*, *nirāmayam*, *sukham*, *arthaḥ*, *prayojanam*, *hitam*, *pathyam*, and so forth. Since the dative case has its scope when used with the word *hitam* in a non-benedictive sense, there is an option [to use the genitive] here in the benedictive sense. Why "in the benedictive sense"? [Answer: *caitrasyāyuṣyam asti* ("Caitra possesses longevity"). This is a statement of fact. Thus ends the third lesson of the second chapter in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*. And this chapter is completed. Now begins the fourth chapter.
A *dvigu* compound takes the singular number. || 1 ||

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of its frequent application (*bāhulaka*). It is neuter because it denotes a general concept (*sāmānya*). A *dvigu* compound that expresses a single object should denote a collective (*samāhāra*). It is established in the rule *taddhitārtha-* that the word *samāhāra* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*); thus, singularity is logically established. This was stated by the author of the Vārttika: "Or rather, [the neuter gender] does not apply because the collective is singular. Therefore, this sūtra is intended to dispel the misconception that [the term] functions as a concrete noun (*karmasādhana*), and to ensure the application of the rule *sa napuṃsakam*.

It should not be argued that this is for the purpose of prescribing singular number in a *dvigu* compound where the final member (*uttarapada*) is the cause [of the formation]. For even though the status of being a nominal stem (*pratipadikatva*) exists because the meaning of that [first member] is subordinate to the meaning of the final member, no case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises. Furthermore, even in a *dvigu* compound whose meaning is a *taddhita* derivative, if one were to first apply the suffix indicating "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*) to the word *pañcakapāla* and then perform the *ekaśeṣa*, the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) would not apply—even if such a rule existed—because the collection of meanings belonging to the *dvigu* lacks the nature of being the meaning of a *dvigu* itself, and because the singular treatment has already fulfilled its function in the inner (*antaraṅga*) *dvigu* which was established first, while the outer (*bahiraṅga*) [operation] is still pending; thus it is all the more established by logic (*nyāya*).

But when, as in the case of *pañcasukapāleṣu saṃskṛtāḥ*, the meanings intended are already delimited by plurality from the very outset, then there is no fault, because the nature of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) does not exist at all.
And [the rule] "A copulative compound (*dvandva*) is formed of parts of living beings, musical instruments, and armies" [applies]. Pāṇini 2.4.2.

The word *aṅga* (limb/part) is connected with each member [of the compound]. When all the words forming a *dvandva* (copulative compound) denote limbs that are any one of the three types mentioned above, there is *ekavadbhāva* (singular collective form). Examples: *pāṇipādam* (hands and feet), *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* (the drummers and the pan-plyers), *rathikāśvāroham* (the charioteers and the horsemen). But not here: *mārdaṅgikāśvārohāḥ*. One should understand that "limbs" refers to the parts of living beings (*prāṇin*), "accessories" refers to musical instruments (*tūrya*), and "components" refers to the objects of a specific relative cognition regarding an army (*senā*). Since the rule *pāṇipādam* etc. would already be established by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*, this statement is for the purpose of excluding cases of confusion (i.e., ensuring the restriction applies only to the specified categories).

In passages such as *rathavājipattikariṇīsamākula*, one should explain the formation by first creating a *dvandva* compound of the words denoting the components of the army (*senāṅga*), excluding the final member, and then applying *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) with the final member. In cases such as *pātitai rathanāgāśvaiḥ*, the construction may also be resolved by forming a *dvandva* and then applying *ekaśeṣa* (retention of only one of the identical members). By this same principle, the verse from Māgha, *itthaṃ ratāśvebhaniṣādināṃ prage*, is also explained.

Although the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) is established by logic even in a collective *dvandva* (through the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ*), this [sūtra] is nevertheless for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It means that a *dvandva* of these [words] occurs only as a collective (*samāhāra*) and not as a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). It should not be argued that there might instead be a reverse restriction—that a *dvandva* of these [words] occurs only as a collective—because in the sūtra *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ*, the use of the plural number excludes the singular collective form in such cases as *tiṣyapunarvasvidam*; thus, that [plural marker] serves that specific purpose.
[The rule applies] to the names of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*) in the context of a restatement (*anuvāda*). (3)

The word *caraṇa* refers to [Vedic] schools such as the Kaṭhas and Kalāpas. While words like "Kaṭha" are used primarily for the specific Vedic recensions (*śākhā-bheda*), they are used figuratively for those who study them. This is clear from the section concerning other recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, according to the rule "the lineage is together with the schools," these are designated as "classes" (*jāti*). In that regard, since the rule "for non-living beings" already establishes the singular collective form for words denoting different recensions, this present rule is commenced for the purpose of establishing the singular collective form for distinct individuals. Examples: "The Kaṭhas and Kalāpas have risen"; "The Kaṭhas and Kauthumas have stood firm"; "The Kaumodas and Paippalādas have risen."

When the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas have risen or are established, one should go there; thus, having forgotten what was previously stated, the statement "it is a restatement regarding one who is seated" applies. It should be stated: "after the roots *sthā* and *i*, [the suffix *ktvā* is used] when the past tense (*adyatanī*) follows. Here: "May the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas rejoice! May the Kaṭhas and Kauthumas prosper! Why "in the past tense"? [Example: "The Kaṭhas and Kālāpas are rising. [Now,] "The sacrifice of the Adhvaryu is not neuter. (Pāṇini 2.4.4).

"The Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ priests are, respectively, experts in the Yajus, Sāman, and Ṛc. (Amara-kośa). Here, the word *adhvaryu* refers to the *Yajurveda*. According to this rule, a *dvandva* compound consisting of non-neuter nouns that denote sacrifices arising from or prescribed by those [Vedas] is treated as a singular. Examples: *arkāśvamedham* (the Arka and Aśvamedha sacrifices); *sāhnātirātram* (the Sāhna and Atirātra sacrifices). Why include the word *adhvaryu*? [Counter-example: *iṣuvajrau* (the arrow and the thunderbolt); *udbhidbalabhidau* (the Udbhid and Balabhid sacrifices). The Vṛtti states that because the word *kratu* is conventionally restricted (*rūḍhi*) to Soma sacrifices, it does not apply in cases such as *darśapaurṇamāsau* (the New and Full Moon sacrifices).

Why is it not neuter, as in *rājasūya-vājapeye*? It serves as a counter-example in the case of its being neuter, due to its inclusion in the *ardharca* group. [The rule applies to] those whose names are not separated by study. 5.1.130.

The dvandva compound of those whose names are not remote—that is, proximate—on account of their study is treated as a singular. For example: *padaka-kramakam* (the one who knows the *pada-pāṭha* and the *krama-pāṭha*), *kramaka-vārtikam* (the one who knows the *krama-pāṭha* and the *vārtika*). [In the case of] "one who studies the *pada* or the *krama*," the suffix *vun* is applied after *krama* and other such words. One who studies the *vṛtti* or the *saṃhitā* is called a *vārtika*.

Because [the words] begin with *ukthya*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; the sequence of "first the study of the *pada-pāṭha*, and subsequently the study of the *krama-pāṭha*" constitutes proximity (*sannidhi*). However, in the latter case, it should be understood that the study of the *krama-pāṭha* is precisely the counter-positive of the absence conditioned by the absence of the study of the *saṃhitā-pāṭha*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "study"? [Example: "father and son. Why [specify] "not separated"? [Example: "the ritualist and the grammarian.
"The genus (*jāti*) of non-living beings [is compounded]. (Pāṇini 2.4.6)

A *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting species (*jāti*) whose life-activities (*vṛtti*) differ from those of living beings (*prāṇin*) is treated as a singular (*ekavat*). Example: *ārāśastri* (the flint and the striker). Why "species"? [Consider] *nandakapāñcajanyau* (the sword Nandaka and the conch Pāñcajanya); these do not possess the status of "species" because they each consist of only a single individual (*ekavyaktikatva*). Why "not living beings"? [Consider] *brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviṭśūdrāḥ* (Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras). By the maxim of "negation and connection with 'iva'," only a species that resides in a substance (*dravyavṛttijāti*) is understood here. Therefore, it does not apply here in cases such as *rūparasau* (color and taste) or *gamanākuñcane* (going and contracting). However, in expressions such as *pṛthivyaptejovāyūnām* (of earth, water, fire, and air), the primacy of the substance (*dravyaprādhānya*) is intended, as this is desired in examples like *badarāmalakāni* (jujube and myrobalan fruits). In phrases such as *rañjitā nu vividhāstaruśailāḥ* (various trees and mountains appear as if painted), there is an elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa*).
Rivers and regions that possess specific genders [are neuter], except for those containing villages.

The term *agrāmāḥ* (non-villages) in the sūtra is in the plural. A *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting rivers or regions that differ in gender and are distinct from villages is singular. For example: *udayā ca irāvatī ca* becomes *udayairāvatī*; *kuravaś ca surukṣetraṃ ca* becomes *kurukurukṣetram*. Why "differing in gender"? [Consider: *gaṅgāyamune* (the Ganges and the Yamunā); *madrakekayāḥ* (the Madras and the Kekayas). Why "rivers or regions"? [Consider: ...

Regarding the rule for *kukkuṭamayūryau* ("the cock and the peahen"), the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] applies to cities (*nagara*) in this context. However, because in examples such as *abhakṣyo grāmakukkuṭaḥ* ("the village cock is not to be eaten"), the word *grāma* includes cities as well, this [specific rule] was formulated. The meaning is that this is not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of cities. Examples: *mathurāpāṭaliputram*. "The prohibition for villages (*grāma*) applies on both sides. This means that in a *dvandva* compound of both a village and a city, the prohibition conditioned by the village alone takes effect. Example: *śauryaṃ nagaram*, *ketavatā grāmaḥ* → *śauryaketavate*.

What are non-villages? The city of Jāmbava; the village of Śālūkinī; both Jāmbava and Śālūkinī. Here, "region" (deśa) refers to a district (janapada); therefore, Kailāsa and Gandhamādana are not [included among villages] because they are mountainous.
Small creatures (kṣudrajantu): || 8 ||
The copulative compound (dvandva) of these [small creatures] is treated as a singular. For example: *yūkālikṣam* ("lice and nits").
A small creature may be one that has no bones, or it may simply be small;
some say they are those whose weight is a hundred [grains] in a handful, or even down to the size of a mouse.
The author of the treatise maintains that the very position presented last should be accepted because it is all-pervasive;
furthermore, for those [opponents] whose contradiction is eternal. (9)

"Enmity" (*virodha*) means hostility (*vaira*), and not such things as "incompatible coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "the counter-positive and its absence. "Permanent" (*śāśvatika*) means occurring at all times. By virtue of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the substitution of *ikā* [for *śāśvatika*]. Furthermore, "essential nature" (*tatva*) here refers to the absence of being joined for a single purpose. Examples are *govyāghram* (cow and tiger) and *gajasiṃham* (elephant and lion). Why "permanent"? [Consider: "The gods and asuras churned the ocean for the nectar. By this, it is refuted that their enmity is not permanent, since it was absent at the time they were engaged in the churning.

If one intends to express enmity as being unconditioned by time, there would be non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "the cow and the dog" (*govyāgram*), because that enmity is necessarily interrupted during states such as sleep or when moving toward another object. Here, the option for the singular or dual number in a *dvandva* compound of animals and birds finds its scope in examples such as *mahājorabhram* (a large goat and a ram) or *mahājorabhrāḥ* (large goats and rams); *haṃsacakravākam* (a swan and a ruddy goose) or *haṃsacakravākāḥ* (swans and ruddy geese). Under the rule *yeṣāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.9), we have *śramaṇabrāhmaṇam* (an ascetic and a Brahmin), *mārjāramūṣakam* (a cat and a mouse), and *aśvamahiṣam* (a horse and a buffalo).

In the case of *kākolūkam*, because it is subsequent, the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) would have applied; however, since the particle *ca* has the purpose of specifying a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), that optionality is set aside, and singular number alone applies. Consequently, regarding the dual compound of animals and birds (*paśuśakunidvandva*), there is no need to formulate a "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) for those who are in conflict.
[This applies to] Śūdras who are not excluded from the community (*aniravasita*). 10.

When Śūdras who have been excluded from the community are mentioned together in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), it is treated as a singular unit: *takṣāyaskāram* (the carpenter and the blacksmith), *rajakatantuvāyam* (the washerman and the weaver). "Exclusion" (*bahiṣkāra*) means being cast out; and that [excluded region] is the Āryāvarta, which is defined as extending east of the Ādarśa mountain, west of the Kālakavana forest, south of the Himālayas, and north of the Pāriyātra mountains—so says the Bhāṣya. Kaiyaṭa states that the Ādarśa and others are specific mountains. However, if this were the case, forms such as *kiṣkindhagāndhikam* (the Kiṣkindha and the Gāndhika) or *śakayavanam* (the Śaka and the Yavana), and *śauryakrauñcamati*, would not be established.

Furthermore, if the intention were to express existence outside of villages, hamlets, cities, and so forth, there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "Caṇḍālas and Mṛtapās. Also, if it were expressed as being outside of a sacrifice or a ritual act, it would not apply to cases like "the carpenter and the blacksmith" (*takṣāyaskāram*). Therefore, the meaning is simply "those who have been excluded from the sacrificial vessel (*pātra*).
And [the rule applies to] "cows, horses, and so forth" (*gavāśvaprabhṛtīni*). (Pāṇini 2.4.11)

These are established as *nipātas* (irregular formations) having been treated as singular compounds (*ekavadbhāva*). *gavāśvam*, *gavāvikam*, *gavaiḍakam*, *ajāvikam*, *ajaiḍakam*: for these, the optional application of the rule for animal *dvandvas* was already applicable. *kubjavāmanam*, *kubjakairātam*, *putrapautram*, *śvacaṇḍālam*, *strīkumāram*, *dāsīmāṇavakam*, *uṣṭrakharam*, *śāṭīpracchadam*. The recitation [of these examples] serves to prescribe the formation for those denoting classes of living beings (*prāṇijāti*), and to ensure the formation for non-living things (*aprāṇijāti*) that do not consist of many constituent parts. Examples: *uṣṭraśaśam*, *mūtraśakṛta*, *mūtrapurīṣam*.

Liver and fat; flesh and blood; *darbha* and *pūtīka*; *arjuna* tree and *puruṣa* tree; grass and *ulapa* reed; female slave and male slave—here there is no application of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule for "male and female" (*pumān strī*). Hut and hut; *bhāgavatī* (female devotee of the Lord) and *bhāgavata* (male devotee). Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "In the case of *gavāśva* and similar compounds, the dual form occurs according to how it was uttered; the meaning is that the singular form applies only when it is uttered with a specific form [as prescribed]. Therefore, it does not apply in the alternative where the *avaṅ* substitution is absent: 'Others than cows and horses are indeed non-animals; cows and horses are animals.'"

[The feminine suffix *ī* is applied] after the words *vibhāṣā*, *vṛkṣa*, *mṛga*, *tṛṇa*, *dhānya*, *vyañjana*, *paśu*, *śakuni*, *aśva*, *vaḍavā*, as well as after [words ending in] *pūrva*, *apara*, *adhara*, and *uttara*. (Pāṇini 4.1.44)

The *dvandva* compound ending in *śakuni* (birds) is subject to the rule that it may optionally be treated as singular (*ekavadbhāva*). The other three *dvandva*s mentioned explicitly [in the rule] are also subject to this. Regarding trees and the like, there is a specific restriction. Because a single word cannot form a *dvandva*, there is a remaindering of two words (*padadvayaikaśeṣa*). Furthermore, because of the remaindering of synonyms even when they are dissimilar in form (*virūpa*), provided they have the same meaning, and because the prohibition of a *dvandva* between a general term and a particular term is expressly stated by rule, and because the mention of "the Easterners and the Bharatas" indicates that the rule is not universal—nevertheless, in the present case, the prohibition alone applies. Thus, we have *plakṣanyagrodham* (singular) and *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ* (plural).

rurupṛṣatam | rurupṛṣatāḥ | kuśakāśam | kuśakāśāḥ | vrīhiyavam | vrīhiyavāḥ | dadhidhṛtam, dadhidhṛte | gomahiṣam | gomahiṣāḥ | tittirikapiñjalam | tittirikapiñjalāḥ | aśvavaḍavam, aśvavaḍavau | pūrvāparam, pūrvāpare | adharottaram, adharottare.

The *Aṭrāvārttika* states: "There is a single substitute for many bases in the case of fruit-bearing trees, forest trees, wild animals, birds, small creatures, grains, and grasses. The meaning is that the *dvandva* compound of these words becomes a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*) only when the constituent members are in the plural; it does not occur otherwise. By this, the singular substitution prescribed by the general rule is restricted to specific domains, rather than being limited solely to what is ordained by this particular sūtra. Otherwise, in the case of *plakṣanyagrodhau*, there would result an obligatory singular substitution according to the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*.

Regarding the form *vadarāmlakam*: the Bhāṣya states *badarāmalakāni*. On this point, Kaiyaṭa explains that although the form *vadarāmalakāni* would have been expected, there is obligatory singularization (*ekavadbhāva*) by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6). Some, however, say that since obligatory singularization would have applied, an option is established by this [sūtra].

Others, however, say that this is not correct; for since this [sūtra] is intended as a rule for optional singularization when many items are the source [of the compound], it would result in obligatory singularization in other cases, which contradicts the Bhāṣya statement: *badarāmalake tiṣṭhataḥ*.

Here, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: when a *dvandva* compound of fruits and so forth becomes singular by this rule or by another characteristic, it consists of many original bases (*prakṛti*). Therefore, in cases such as *plakṣanyagrodhau*, *vrīhiyavau*, and *kuśakāśau*, neither the optional application of the present rule nor the prohibition "of non-living beings belonging to a genus" (*jātir aprāṇinām*) applies. However, the specific distribution of the scope for those items included in this sūtra is now demonstrated.

Regarding non-living things (*aprāṇin*), when [the application of a compound] is established, an option (*vikalpa*) is prescribed; this refers to those classes (*jāti*) that are pervaded by a single class—meaning, those classes that are directly pervaded by a class which is itself pervaded by a property (*upādhi*) that distinguishes categories (*padārtha-vibhājaka*). However, for heterogeneous classes (*vijātīya*), the rule applies as it is established. In the example *vrīhikuśaplakṣam*, because it is a class of non-living things, the word *plakṣa* is always placed first. In the example *plakṣaśabdasparśāḥ ṣaṭ*, both [orders] are possible, because the sense is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Since sound-ness (*śabdatva*) and the like are classes that do not reside in substances (*adravyavṛtti-jāti*), the rule "for non-living things" (*jātir aprāṇinām*) does not apply.

Since elephants, horses, and so forth constitute parts of an army, an option (*vikalpa*) is always applicable [regarding their being expressed as a singular collective]. However, regarding the section on wild animals (*mṛga*) and birds (*śakuni*), the dual compound (*dvandva*) with a singular number that was optionally applicable (*vibhāṣā*) is restricted to specific types of wild animals together with *tairava* birds, and not with others. With other [animals], however, the result is that there is only a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*). This is the established meaning.

By this, the cases of "prior and posterior" (pūrvāpara) and "lower and upper" (adharottara) have been explained. The specific mention of "horse and mare" (aśvavaḍavau), although already established by virtue of being a pair of animals, is for the purpose of prescribing it as a *pratipadavidhi* (an original rule). Consequently, in the alternative where there is a singular form (*ekavadbhāva*), the rule *sanapuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17) applies, overriding the previous rule *aśvavaḍavau* (Pāṇini 2.4.12). This is because the pronoun *tat* (in the rule *sanapuṃsakam*) refers back to that which is characterized by the singular formation. However, the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*) applies to the alternative where the singular formation does not occur.
And [the rule] is contradicted when it refers to words that do not denote a substratum. 13.

This is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). A *dvandva* compound that is characterized by singular number (*ekavadbhāva*) and is optionally prescribed—provided it consists of words with contradictory meanings—if it occurs, then it applies only to those [words] that do not denote substances (*adravyavācin*). Consequently, in the case of words denoting contradictory substances, there is only mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). For example: "Cold and heat exist in the water" (*śītoṣṇe udake staḥ*).

In this context, "contradictoriness" (*viruddhatva*) is the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of mutual absolute non-existence. Indirectly, the contradictoriness of water is the co-occurrence of mutual absolute non-existence; indirectly, the heat of water is the contradiction between two waters qualified by those two qualities through that medium. What is "mutually opposed" (*vipratiṣiddha*)? "The Nandaka sword and the Pāñcajanya conch. This is an optional collective *dvandva* compound. "Lust and anger" (*kāmakrodhau*) is cited as a counter-example in the *Vṛtti*.

Regarding this, they say: Just as in the case of "cold and heat" (*śītoṣṇam*) or "pleasure and pain" (*sukhaduḥkham*), an optional singular collective formation (*ekavadbhāva*) is unavoidable, because the present sūtra serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*). Nor is its intended meaning that if a singular formation occurs for words not denoting substances (*adravyavācin*), it occurs only for those that are contradictory (*vipratiṣiddha*); for the example "cold and hot water" (*śītoṣṇe udake*) is given in that very same context as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the rule concerning non-locative expressions, since by the aforementioned reasoning, an optional singular formation would likewise apply there.
"Not [in the case of] *dadhi* (curd), *payas* (milk), etc. (Pāṇini 2.4.14).

These are not to be eaten on the same day: curd and milk; honey and ghee; and ghee and honey. Otherwise, because they would be mere condiments, there would be an option [to eat them together]. Brahmā and Prajāpati; Śiva and Vaiśravaṇa; Skanda and Viśākha.
Both Skanda and Viśākha were born as his two sons.

Thus [are the examples from] the *Bhārata*: *parivrāṭ-kauśikau* (the wandering mendicant and Kauśika), *pravargyopasadau* (the Pravargya and Upasad rites), *śuklavṛkṣe* (two white trees), *idhmābarhiṣī* (the sacrificial fuel and the grass). [In these cases,] the substitution of *ā* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). [Other examples include: *dīkṣātapasī* (initiation and austerity), *śraddhāmedhe* (faith and intelligence), *medhātapasī* (intelligence and austerity), *adhyayanatapasī* (study and austerity), *ulūkhalamusale* (mortar and pestle) [and] *udūkhalamusale* (mortar and pestle), *ādyavasāne* (beginning and end), *śraddhāmedhe* (faith and intelligence), *ṛksāme* (the Ṛg-veda and Sāma-veda), and *vāṅmanase* (speech and mind). One should not suspect that in cases such as *dadhipayasī* (curds and milk), even though the prohibition of optionality based on their being consonants applies, there exists an obligatory singular collective expression (*ekavadbhāva*) characterized by their being a genus (*jāti*).

There is no prohibition [of the singular] because that which has not been taken up as a material cause is the counter-correlative for the attainment of specific characteristics. Thus, since there is a prohibition of *dvandva* in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) by that [rule] and in the case of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*) by the present sūtra, it must be said that a *dvandva* would not occur at all for these [words]. This is because, according to the view that restrictive rules (*niyamavākya*) function in a positive manner, this [present rule] prohibits the singleness (*ekadbhāva*) enjoined by rules such as "the singleness of non-living beings" (*jātir aprāṇinām*).
And [the rule applies] when the extent of the subject matter is defined. || 15 ||

This [objection] would not apply if there were a cognition of a number (*saṃkhyā*) regarding the substances (*dravya*). [For example: "ten teeth-and-lips" (*daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ*). And this prohibition—that a *dvandva* compound of limbs of living beings is only a collective (*samāhāra*)—does not apply to a collective *dvandva*. This is because it would be redundant; for the number ten would necessarily attach itself to the collective itself, which is the predominant element, just as in the case of "ten or five bundles" (*daśapañcapūlya-*). Thus, when there is an intention to convey a specific number of the meanings of the constituent members (*vartipada*), an *itaretarayoga* (coordinative) relation follows by logical necessity.

By this, [the formation of] *pañcasvihāsyāṃghrikareṣvabhiṣyābhikṣādhunā mādhukarī sadṛkṣā* and so forth is established. Nor is there an inconsistency in cases such as *daśabrāhmaṇakṣatriyāḥ*; for that is excluded by the very logic already stated. However, the truth is that exclusion by the aforementioned logic is not easily accomplished, because—according to the method to be explained in the subsequent sūtra—it is possible for the number to apply to the parts themselves. In the example, however, there is a disparity, since the things being combined (*samāhārin*) are already restricted by their own respective numbers.
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies when [the word] is in proximity (*samīpa*).

There may be a restrictive rule (*niyama*) such that when the substance is qualified by a number delimited by proximity to the number expressed by the word, it must be a collective compound (*samāhāra*); for example, *upadaśam pāṇipādam* (nearly ten hands and feet) or *upadaśāḥ pāṇipādāḥ* (nearly ten hands and feet), which means nine or eleven.
