In that context, *upadaśam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) when proximity is predominant; it has been stated that when proximity is predominant, it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). Thus, the usage of the indeclinable compound occurs in the case of singular concord (*ekavadbhāva*), while otherwise the possessive compound is used.

This is because it conforms to the understanding of an equal number. Although an *avyayībhāva* compound is devoid of number, the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*) holds that it intends the number "one" in the sense of non-differentiation. There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between proximity and that which is proximate. Furthermore, since the connection of number is possible only with the aggregate (*samāhāra*), it is untenable for the members of a *dvandva* compound to be delimited by it; this is because there too, identity is metaphorically attributed to the aggregate and its constituents. In the alternative view where singular number does not apply, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, owing to its having a common case-ending.

Because the plural number is untenable in an *avyayībhāva* compound; and even if it were possible, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *am*. Furthermore, even under the view that there is singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*), if a *bahuvrīhi* were subsequently applied, then in the genitive case one would have to say *ṣaṣṭhyām upadaśasya pāṇipādasya*; however, the accepted form from the source is *upadaśaṃ pāṇipādasya*. [The rule continues: "That [compound] is neuter. (Pāṇini 2.4.17)

In a collective compound (*samāhāra*), both *dvigu* and *dvandva* shall be neuter; this is an exception to the rule that the gender of a compound follows the gender of its final member (*paravalliṅga*). Examples: *pañcagavam* (a collection of five cows) and *dantoṣṭham* (teeth and lips). Although the term "collective" (*sa-*) could have been understood from the context as the subject to be qualified, its explicit inclusion is for the purpose of including even those collective *dvandva*s that fall outside the scope of this particular section. For this very reason, they state that in rules such as *yuvoranākau*, there would otherwise be the neuter gender in a collective *dvandva*. By this [principle], the commentary of Śaṅkara on the aphorism *janmādyasya yataḥ*—which reads *janmasthitibhaṅgam*—is explained as being in accordance with the neuter gender used in the aphorism itself (*sautranapuṃsakatva*).

A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the vowel *a* is desired to be feminine. For example: *pañcapūlī*. The rule for the suffix *ṅīp* after a *dvigu*—occurring under the governing heading *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.4)—is the indicator (*liṅga*) that this [femininity] applies here as well. "A word ending in *ā*": a *dvigu* ending in *ā* is optionally feminine. For example: *pañcakhaṭvam* or *pañcakaṭvī*. Regarding the alternative of femininity, it was explained previously that the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs when there is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

"Furthermore, there is the elision of *n*, and optionally so when it is a *dvigu* compound in the feminine. Examples: *pañcatakṣam* (five carpenters) or *pañcatakṣī* (feminine). It should not be argued that the elision of *n* is established because the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is a word (*pada*) due to the case-ending contained within it; for the rule "when it is the final member of a compound (*uttarapadatve*), the designation of suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) is prohibited in rules concerning what is not the beginning of a word (*apadādi-vidhau*)" applies here. There is a prohibition [of this elision] when the word ends in *pātra* and others. Examples: *pañcapātram* (five vessels), *tribhuvanam* (the three worlds), *caturyugam* (the four ages), *dvimāsam* (two months). The group beginning with *pātra* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). And so too is the *avyayībhāva* compound. (18)

It would be neuter. In *adhistri unmattagaṅgam*, since there is an absence of gender when the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant, and since the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyaliṅga*) would otherwise apply when the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, this rule is commenced. By the word "and" (*ca*), [the forms] *puṇyāham* and *sudināham* are included. [This is based on the rule: "After *puṇya* and *sudina*, the word *ahnaḥ* becomes neuter. In a *karmadhāraya* compound, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*. This is an exception to the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*. The word *sudina* has the sense of "excellent"; as seen in the passage: "In excellent assemblies, one should especially investigate this matter oneself."

The rule *pathaḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.74] applies. For example, the path of three is *tripatham*; a deformed path is *vipatham*. Because of the association with the word *patha* when preceded by a number or an indeclinable (which invariably requires a compound-ending suffix), this rule applies only to those forms where the compound-ending suffix has already been added. Thus, it does not apply here: *atipanthāḥ* and *supanthāḥ*, because the prohibition of the compound-ending suffix is established by the rule *na pūjanāt* [Pāṇini 5.4.69]. Furthermore, due to the specific enumeration (*parigaṇana*) in the rule *svatībhyāmeva* [Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.4.74], the form *satpathaḥ* is established in the sense of "honored" or "well-trodden. Regarding the synonyms *vyadhvaḥ*, *duradhvaḥ*, *vipathaḥ*, *kadadhvā*, and *kāpathaḥ*, Kṣīrasvāmī and others maintain that the correct readings in this context are *vipatham* and *kāpatham* (with the neuter suffix).

However, some maintain that *vāra*, *patha*, and *mārga* are synonyms according to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*. From the root *path* (meaning "to go"), by adding the suffix *ac*, the word *patha*—ending in the vowel *a*—is derived in the sense of "that which extends. It should not be argued that, although forms such as *vipatha* are thus established, the form *kāpatha* would be untenable because the substitution of the element *ka-* is prescribed only before the word *pathin*. For they say that when *ka-* is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*), it effectively results in the sense of "contempt" (*kutsā*).

Others, however, argue that if this were the case, the rule *patho vibhāṣā* would be redundant; for *apatham* would already be established by the rule *apathaṃ napuṃsakam*, and *apanthāḥ* would be established by the rule *pathaḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*. Still others maintain that because the mention of the completed compound-ending (*samāsānta*) in the rule *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* has the force of an indicator, it results in the permanent sublation of the prohibition of compound-endings (*samāsānta-niṣedha*)—which otherwise applies to the word *pathin* by the rule *nañastatpuruṣāt* and finds its scope in examples such as *asakha*—and thus the rule *patho vibhāṣā* is necessary to establish the form *apanthāḥ*.

That is to be considered [as follows]: since the word *apatha* is established by the aforementioned method through the word *patha*, there is no harm even if that [specific rule] is set aside. Furthermore, there is no basis for the insistence that in the form *apatham*, the word *patha* is being referred to as having already taken the samāsānta suffix. This is because the determination that the word *pathin* is being referred to is possible precisely through the connection of the genitive-ending qualifier in the rule *pathaḥ saṃkhyā-vyadhy-avyayādeḥ*. Moreover, the forms *apathaḥ*, *vipathaḥ*, and *kāpathaḥ* would otherwise remain unestablished, which we accept as the desired result.

By this, the argument that—in accordance with the sequence [of rules] where the *vārttika* "pathaḥ saṃkhyā" is recited immediately after the rule "rātrāhvāhāḥ" in the rule "apathaṃ napuṃsakam"—it is proper that only a form with the *samāsānta* suffix applied should be used, is refuted; for in the absence of a specific purpose, mere association (*sāhacarya*) is of no consequence.

As for Kaiyaṭa’s statement—that since the Vārttika is necessary, the Sūtra would be redundant because the word *apatha* is established by that very Vārttika alone, and thus he offers "because of the priority [of the Sūtra]" as the reason—it is entirely pointless to cite that [priority], for nothing at all is untenable without the form *patha* ending in -m. On the contrary, if the word *patha* exists, the Sūtra can be explained as having that very word *patha* (containing the -m) as its object; therefore, because their scopes are distinct, the doubt regarding the Sūtra being rendered superfluous by the Vārttika does not even arise.

To claim that this would not be the case is merely trivial, as it contradicts Kaiyaṭa’s own commentary (*phakkikā*) on your very statement. Furthermore, this prescription of the neuter gender is an exception specifically to the rule of "taking the gender of the final member" (*paravalliṅgatā*). Consequently, in the example *vipathā nagarī*, where there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has surpassed the path," and a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "that which has gone beyond the path" (*atipatha*), the neuter gender does not apply. This is because, in the word *atipatha*, the prohibition against taking the gender of the final member applies by the rule: "In *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alam-pūrva*, and compounds with a *gati* [prefix], [the final gender is] not [retained]. Thus, the neuter gender is established.

Nor does this contradict Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, which explains that *asutpatham* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound with *ku* as the first member; for in that case, since the analysis is "an excellent path" (*utkṛṣṭaḥ panthā*), and not "gone out from the path" (*patha udgataḥ*), it lacks the status of a *gati* compound, and thus the gender of the final member would necessarily prevail. Therefore, it is established that this prescription of the neuter gender applies when the meaning of the second member is predominant.
A Tatpuruṣa compound that is not a negative (anañ) is a Karmadhāraya. || 19 ||

The term *karmadhāraya* refers here to a *samānādhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa*. Thus, according to the view that [the compound] possesses a partial denotative power (*khaṇḍaśakti*), since the *tatpuruṣa* is the object of a separate denotative power, there is a syntactic connection with the word *nañ* as well. Consequently, the meaning is: a *tatpuruṣa* that is distinct from a *nañ-tatpuruṣa* and distinct from a *samānādhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa*. Some, however, say that "wherein the state of being a *nañ-karmadhāraya* does not exist," because of the predominance of the abstract state (*bhāvapradhānya*). This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

Is it not the case that this [rule] has no utility in the subsequent sūtra *saṃjñāyām*? For, regarding a name (*saṃjñā*), there is no possibility of a compound ending in *kathā*—whether it be an *īśvarādi*-type *tatpuruṣa* or a different type such as a *karmadhāraya*—other than a *tatpuruṣa*. This is because in that context only an eternal name (*anādisaṃjñā*) is intended, and a contemporary name is not included. Nor does it serve a purpose in the sūtra *upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyām*, since without a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, the abundance of the meaning of the prior member would not be understood.

If it is argued that the word *sabhā* here does not mean "assembly" because of the rule *na śālāyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.24), and since the word *sabhā* is understood here only in its sense of a "gathering," and because a gathering is impossible apart from those who gather, it follows that only a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound is possible—this is true, for that [meaning] is applicable in the rule *vibhāṣā senā-* (Pāṇini 2.4.25). However, in that context, due to the force of the meaning, it is impossible for it to result in a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. What is a *tatpuruṣa*? For example: *dṛḍhaseno rājā* ("the king with a firm army"). Why "not preceded by a negative particle" (*anañ*)? As in: *asenā* ("no army"). Why "not a *karmadhāraya*"? As in: *paramasenā* ("supreme army").
They say that the inclusion of this term in the governing heading (*adhikāra*) is for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect.
In the sense of "name," [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *uśīnara*, when it refers to the people of Kaṇṭha. || 20 ||

The Tatpuruṣa compound ending in *kanthā* is neuter, provided it is a name for a blanket produced in the land of the Uśīnaras. For example: the descendants of Suśama are the *Sauśamayāḥ*; their blanket is *sauśamikantham*. Why "if it is a name"? [Consider] *vīrakanyā*. Why "in the land of the Uśīnaras"? [Consider] *dākṣikanthā*.
[The Tatpuruṣa compound] beginning with *upajñā* or *upakrama* is neuter when there is a desire to express that these two are the first of their kind. (Pāṇini 2.4.21)

That which is first known is called *upajñā*. By the rule *ātaścopasarge*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). That which is first undertaken is called *upakrama*; here the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object. By the rule *nodāttopadeśasya*, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution. A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *upajñā* or *upakrama* shall be neuter when there is a desire to express the priority of the meaning of the aforementioned verbal roots. For example: *pāṇinerupajñā* (the first knowledge of Pāṇini) results in *pāṇinyupajñaṃ granthaḥ* (a work first known by Pāṇini); *nandopakramaṃ droṇaḥ* (the first undertaking by Nanda). Because of the inclusion of the term "desire to explain" (*ācikhyāsā*), when one merely intends to express a general relationship, as in *devadattopajño rathaḥ* (a chariot first made by Devadatta), the neuter gender does not apply.
The word *chāyā* [is used] in the sense of abundance. || 22 ||

When there is an abundance of the meaning of the first member of the compound, a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *chāyā* shall be neuter. For example: *ikṣucchāyam* (the shade of sugarcane). This is because a single stalk of sugarcane is not a sufficient cause for a shade that serves as a means of subsistence. However, in the expression *ikṣucchāyāniṣādinyaḥ* ("those sitting in the shade of sugarcane"), some hold that the singular number refers to the genus (*jāti*), while others hold it refers to those sitting all around.
A *sabhā* (assembly/hall) preceded by a word denoting a king or something other than a human being [is feminine]. (Pāṇini 2.4.23)

The word *sabhā* (assembly), when preceded by *rāja* (king) or *manuṣya* (human), is neuter. Examples: *inasabham*, *īśvarasabham*. This is intended only as a restrictive rule (*paryudāsa*). As was stated previously, this is obtained through the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a* following the word *sabhā*. It does not apply here: *rājasabhā*, *candraguptasabhā*. This is because the specific term [here] has a denotation that is not delimited by the quality of being a king; thus, it lacks similarity to a king. Some, however, maintain that in the phrase "he went to the *nṛpatisabhā* trembling," the word *nṛpati* signifies a particular type of king, just like *gajapati*.

In the word *nṛpati-sabham*, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; with the word *sabhā*, there is a *karmadhāraya*. According to the rule "not a *nañ*-compound or a *karmadhāraya*," others maintain that there is no neuter gender. The word *amanuṣya* (non-human) is used by convention (*rūḍhi*) to refer to *rakṣas* (demons), *piśāca* (goblins), and so forth. Thus, *rakṣaḥ-sabham* [is valid], but here *kāṣṭha-sabhā* [is not].
And [it is neuter] when it does not mean a hall (*a-śālā*). 24.

The word *sabhā* denotes both a dwelling (*śālā*) and an assembly (*saṃghāta*). When preceded by a word denoting a king or a non-human being, the neuter gender of the preceding member was stated by the previous rule; this present rule is commenced for the sake of including other meanings. *Strī-sabham*: the meaning is "an assembly of women. Why say "not a dwelling" (*a-śālā*)? Consider *anātha-sabhā*; the meaning here is "a hut for the destitute. [Now follows: *Vibhāṣā senā-surā-cchāyā-śālā-niśānām* (2.4.25).
[This rule states that the words *senā*, *surā*, *chāyā*, *śālā*, and *niśā* may optionally be neuter when compounded with a word denoting a king or a non-human being.]

This Tatpuruṣa compound may optionally be neuter: *brāhmaṇasenam* / *brāhmaṇasenā*; *yavasuram* / *yavasurā*; *kuḍyacchāyam* / *kuḍyacchāyā*. Here, the word *chāyā* is used in the sense of "beauty" as well: "Where even a tiny fragment of its shade is found on a sprout. *gośālam* / *gośālā*; *śvaniśam* / *śvaniśā*. [The form] *kṛṣṇacaturdaśī* is mentioned [as an example]. [The neuter gender is used] because even animals have a desire for fruit, as stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya: "We see that dogs fast on the fourteenth day. **Pāṇini 2.4.26:** *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* || (The gender of a Dvandva and a Tatpuruṣa is like that of the final member.)

The gender of these two [compounds] shall be like the gender of the final member. For example: *kukkuṭamayūryau ime* (these two are a cock and a peahen), *mayūrīkukkuṭau imau* (these two are a peahen and a cock); *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* = *ardhapippalī* (half of a long pepper). Since the gender of a *dvandva* compound whose meaning is primarily that of the final member is already established by itself, there arises—due to its being primarily the meaning of both members—the possibility of both genders occurring alternately; therefore, this rule is for the purpose of restriction in the case of a *tatpuruṣa*, and for the purpose of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*).

"A prohibition must be stated for *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alam* (with its derivatives), and compounds where the first member is a governing word (*gati*) [regarding the application of gender]. Examples: *pañcakapālaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* (a sacrificial cake made of five vessels); *prāptajīvikaḥ* (one who has obtained a livelihood); *āpannajīvikaḥ* (one who has fallen into a livelihood); *alaṃjīvikaḥ* (sufficient for a livelihood); *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī). Here, this should be noted: if one holds the view that there is no whole distinct from its parts, then the locative ending in *dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* [is understood]. The meaning of the rule is: "In a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa*, the gender is like that of the subsequent member."*

And thus, because there is no mention of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*) [itself], and because the word *para* is inherently relational, it follows that the operation would apply only to the preceding member implied by that [word *para*]. Consequently, in the case of *mayūrīkukkuṭau*, since the preceding member is masculine, there would be the transfer of masculinity and the removal of the feminine suffix; whereas in the case of *kukkuṭamayūryau*, the feminine suffix would indeed occur.

If, however, one were to assume that the genitive case-ending indicates a distinct collective whole (*samudāya*) and, based on this, were to extend the gender from the subsequent member—meaning that a gender different from the gender of the subsequent member is prescribed for the meaning of the compound—then, in the case of *aśvavaḍavau*, since the rule *paravalliṅgam* (the gender of the final member prevails) would apply, a gender similar to that of the first member would be prescribed for the meaning of the compound rather than that of the subsequent member. Consequently, because the feminine nature would not be removed, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *āp* would have to be specifically stated when its presence is otherwise required. This has been said:

"If it is argued that [the word *aśvavaḍavau*] is something other than a compound, [we reply: there is the statement regarding the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix (*ṅīp*) in the case of *aśvavaḍavau*, because even though the meaning of the compound is masculine, the femininity of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is not lost. Nor can one find a solution by means of the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*), because in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), although all members are designated as the first-mentioned (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*), they lack the technical designation of "subordinate" (*upasarjana*). This is because in a *dvandva*, the meaning of every member is primary (*sarvapadārtha-pradhānatva*), and the designation *upasarjana* is based on its etymological sense (meaning "one who goes near" or "secondary"). For this very reason, it was stated previously that there is shortening in the case of *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ*. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the subordinate status (*upasarjanatva*) arises because the meaning of the individual member is secondary (*guṇabhāva*) within the meaning of the whole aggregate.

Even when the meaning of a dvandva compound is accepted as a collective form distinct [from its parts], the individual meanings of the members possess primacy in effect, because they are connected with the action.

Nevertheless, we speak having accepted [the opponent's position]. Even so, the defect remains as it was in the case of *kukkuṭamayūryau* ("the cock and the peahen"). Now, if it is argued that in that case it is established by the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), it has been stated [in the Mahābhāṣya]: "By the rule *paravalliṅgam*, since both word and meaning [are referred to], a suffix denoting gender is not possible through the *tantra* method and so forth; therefore, in that instance, there is only the extension (*atideśa*) of the meaning. However, in cases such as *mayūrīkukkuṭau* ("the peahen and the cock"), where there is a connection with both [words], the form is *kukkuṭamayūryau* and so on.

Thus, it is established that for a word derived by direct rule (*aupadeśika*) there is shortening (*hrasva*), while for one derived by extended application (*ātideśika*) there is the hearing of the long vowel; and there is no further occurrence of shortening. This is because the final member [of the compound] is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*) and is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*). Nor should it be argued that even so, in cases such as *dattā-gārgyāyaṇyau* and *dattā-kārīṣagandhye*, once shortening has been applied, the suffixes *ṣpha*, *ṣyaṅ*, or *ṅīṣ* would arise again from the compound. For, by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.149), the possibility exists for the removal of those previously produced suffixes, and thus the desired result is achieved.

It cannot be so, for in the case of *dattā ca yuvatī ca*, there would result the undesirable consequence of hearing two suffixes (*pratyaya*), and because the designation *bha* is absent there, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would be untenable. Therefore, it is established that the shortening of the *upasarjana* (in the rule *gostriyoḥ...*) indeed results in a fault. Such is the conclusion reached.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "If it is argued that [the compound] would take the gender of another [word], this is established by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*), as in the case of the rule regarding the elision of *ṭāp* in *aśvavaḍavau*. The intention is that in the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga...* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), the elision of *ṭāp* in the form *aśvavaḍavau* is established by the specific pronunciation of the short vowel (*hrasva*). Furthermore, the *vārttika* *dviguprāpta-* is also rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. To explain: the *vārttika* *paravalligaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* is likewise rejected in the *Bhāṣya*; for it should simply be stated as *paravalligaṃ dvandvasya*.

Nor is there a failure to establish forms such as *pūrvakāyaḥ* ("the front part of the body") or *ardhapippalī* ("half a long pepper"), because the *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound) and the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.2.2) are rejected by resorting to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Nor is that [rule] intended for the purpose of precluding the *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* (genitive compound), since the possibility of such a compound has already been stated previously. Furthermore, in the case of *pūrvāpara*, the preclusion of the *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* is possible simply because it is not mentioned [by the rule].
As before, the term *aśvavaḍavau* ("horse and mare") is a dual *dvandva*. (27)

The dual number is not intended as restrictive; this is an extension of the meaning. It is an exception to the rule that the gender of a compound follows the gender of the final member. Examples include: *aśvavaḍavau* (a horse and a mare), *aśvavaḍavān* (horses and mares), and *aśvavaḍavair javanaiḥ* (with swift horses and mares), and so forth.
In the Vedic language, the words *hemanta* and *śiśira* optionally [take the dual ending] for the two [consecutive] days and nights.

As before: "I gratify the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira. Hemanta and Śiśira are "Hemanta-Śiśirau. Some maintain that one should not read "Hemanta-Śiśirau" because the word *śiśira* is of both genders according to the rule *hemantaḥ śiśiro 'striyām*. However, in reality, even though the neuter word *śiśira* occurs as the final member of a compound, this [form] is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding the Vedic usage of "Hemanta-Śiśirau. May day and night be auspicious; the dual number is not intended as a restrictive rule (*atantra*), since it is an extended application of meaning (*arthātideśa*) and not a formal irregularity (*nipātana*).

Therefore, [the text] states: "The subsequent sections are the fillings (purīṣa) for those based on the preceding sections; the days and nights are the bricks. This is not established merely by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) within a collective *dvandva* compound, because even in that case, the masculine gender would have to be stated [separately]. In common usage, however, [the terms] *hemanta* and *śiśira* are used for the two cold seasons (*duḥkha*), while *ahorātrau* is used for the two auspicious [periods];
and [the rule] "rātri, ahan, and āha are masculine" applies. (29)

These two types of compounds—the *dvandva* and the *tatpuruṣa*—ending in [the word] *rātri*, are masculine only. The first part of the night is *pūrvarātraḥ*. This is an *ekadeśisamāsa* (compound denoting a part of a whole). By the rule "after *ahan*, [the suffix] *ac* is added when expressing the whole or a part," the suffix *ac* is applied, resulting in *pūrvāhṇaḥ*. By the rule "after *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*, [the suffix] *ṭac* is added," the suffix *ṭac* is applied. Then, by the rule "for *ahan*, [the substitute] *ahna-* occurs after these [words]," the substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan* takes place. Finally, by the rule "the *ṇatva* [nasalization] occurs after *ahan* ending in a vowel," the *ṇatva* is applied. Thus we have *dvyahaḥ*. In the case of *dvyahaḥ*, there is a prohibition of the *ahna-* substitution by the rule "there is no *ahna-* substitution after a numeral" when forming a collective (*samāhāra*). Furthermore, by the rule "*ahnaḥ* [the final vowel is elided] only before *ṭa* and *khara*," the *ṭi*-portion (*an*) is elided. This is an exception to the general rule "the gender of a compound is like that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgam*), because of its proximity [to that rule].

However, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], it subverts the neuter gender in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*). Thus, we have *ahorātraḥ* (a day-and-night). It should not be argued that this rule prescribes the masculine gender only for those compounds where *rātri* and so on appear as the final members of the compound; whereas for those ending in such words, the masculine gender is already established by the rule *paravat* (which states that a compound takes the gender of its final member). For if that were the case, the neuter gender would result for the collective compound, since the present rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to that *paravat* rule. Nor can one accept this as a desired outcome (*iṣṭāpatti*), for it would follow that "by a month there would be a day-and-night" (*māsena syād ahorātraḥ*).

However, that [masculinity] is contradicted by such rules as "thirty days and nights" (*triṃśadahorātra*). As for compounds like *dvirātra* (two nights) and *trirātra* (three nights), since the *Liṅgānuśāsana* prescribes specific masculinity for the term *rātri* when preceded by a numeral, the masculinity stated in the *Vṛtti* and other works should be considered doubtful. One should state: "Words such as *anuvāka* are masculine. Examples: *anuvāka*, *śaṃyuvāka*, *sūktavāka*. This rule is begun because these words would otherwise be neuter due to their meaning being specific types of speech (*vākya-viśeṣa*).
The word *apatha* (pathless) is neuter. (30)

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the word *pathin* is masculine]; however, in other cases, it is *apatha* (neuter) when referring to a city. This restriction does not apply here because of the specific prohibition regarding the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*): *apanthāḥ*.
[The words] beginning with *ardharca* are both masculine and [neuter]. 31.

The letter *ca* serves to include the neuter (*klība*) words; the plural number is used for the sake of including the "and so forth" (*ādi*). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Those [words] have been collected in the *Gaṇaratna*, and they are here recorded by us according to the order of their syllables:
*ardharca-kūrca-kavaca-kraka-cāḥ*, *varcas-ka-paṅka-valīkāḥ*;
*niṣka-anīka-pināka-aḍhaka-modaka-kaṭa-kaṭaṅka-piṇyākāḥ*. (1)
Mañcaka, pañcaka, daṇḍaka, taṇḍaka, ṣaṣṭika, caṣaka, saraka, śoka;
śāka, aśoka, śulka, mastaka, varaka, viṭaṅka, piṭaka, and śūka. || 2 ||
Phalaka, napuṃsaka, mūlaka, pātaka, nakha, puṅkha, śaṅkha, śṛṅga, viḍaṅga, taḍāga, udyoga, nidādha, dhvaja, vraja, and ambhoja. (3)
Grove, horse, cock, crown, peak, mountain-top, hamlet, gate;
river-bank, cart, armor, cloth, basket, monastery, thorn, and staff. (4)
Nests, eggs, fragments of shells, grass, stumps, bamboos, dust, and reeds resounded;
while the archways, golden ornaments, coins, elephants, and the feet [of those walking] rang out.
May there be [the attainment of] ten thousand ambrosias of springtime, characterized by the practice of harsh roars, wherein the hands are covered by the dust of wounds from arrows,
and which are sustained by the fat of aged Drona.
The remaining words are both masculine and neuter: ūrdhva, piṇyāka, kaṇṭaka, modaka, taṇḍaka, ṭaṅka, śāṭaka, kharvaṭa, and arbuda. || 7 ||
Ghātaka, udyoga, caraka, tamāla, āmalaka, naḍa, kuṣṭha, muṇḍa, sīdhu, pustaka, kṣvoḍita, kṣema, and kuṭṭima. || 8 ||
Saṃgama, Śatamāna, Arbha, Śambala, Avyaya, Tāṇḍava, Kaviya, Kandakārpāsa, Pārāvāra, and Yugandhara. || 9 ||
The words *pṛya*, *patrīva*, *pātrīva*, *yūṣa*, *camasa*, and *cikkasa* [are masculine];
in Vedic usage, the masculine gender and other qualities of words such as *ghṛta* are certain when they appear at the beginning of a half-verse (*ardharca*) and so forth. || 10 ||
That has not been mentioned here; even if it exists in this world, let it be as a "remainder" (*śeṣavat*).

*Piṇyāka* is oil-cake or sesame dregs. *Taṇḍula* is rice. *Parisvāra* is a specific section of the *Chandoga* texts. *Daṇḍaka* is a cutting or a staff. *Kharvaṭa* is a collection of four hundred villages. *Arbuda* refers both to a type of eye disease and a numerical unit. *Pātaka* refers to sins such as cow-slaughter. *Caraka* is a specific type of physician. *Naḍa* is a hollow reed. *Pusta* is a meat-cake. Two *kṛṣṇalas* make one silver *māṣa*; sixteen of those make a *dharaṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, and likewise, ten *dharaṇas* make one *pala*.

Thus says the Smṛti. *Arbha* means eye-pain; *śaṃvala* means expenditure on the road; *kaviya* means a horse's halter; *pāram* and *avāram* mean the two banks of a river; *pūya* means putrid blood; *pragrīva* means a window; *pātrīva* means a sacrificial implement; *viṣkasam* means a barley-back (a type of vessel). Following the occasion of the application of the rule of extension (*atideśa*) that "the gender [of a compound] is like that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgam*), the sūtras of Pāṇini’s *Liṅgānuśāsana* are now being explained.

The gender is feminine. These [terms] are mentioned in the rule concerning eligibility (*adhikāra-sūtra*). The first [category] is pervasive; the second extends up to the word *puṃsi* ("in the masculine"). The words ending in *ṛ*—namely *mātṛ*, *duhitṛ*, *svasṛ*, *yātṛ*, *nanāndṛ*, and *pitṛ*—[are included]. For other words ending in *ṛ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed. Among the seven beginning with *svasṛ*, the two *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are excluded because the substitutes for *tri* and *catur* do not end in *ṛ*. Thus, these five alone are feminine. A verbal root ending in the suffix *an* [is feminine], such as *avanī* (earth) etc., which ends in the suffix *an*. A verbal root ending in the suffix *ū* [is feminine], such as *camū* (army) etc., which ends in the suffix *ū*. Why mention "suffix" (*pratyaya*)? [Consider] *dayūḥ* (heaven), derived from the root *div* with the suffix *kvip*. It is [feminine] only when it functions as a substantive (*viśeṣya-nighna*).

The words *aśani*, *bharaṇī*, and *araṇi* are masculine. Since they would otherwise have attained permanent femininity by virtue of their final *ī*, this rule is commenced to establish their optional masculinity, as in "this is a thunderbolt" (*iyam ayaṃ vā aśaniḥ*). Words ending in *min* and *nip* are feminine. For example: *bhūmiḥ* (earth) and *glāniḥ* (exhaustion). [Objection: In cases such as *bhavāmi* and *bhavānī*, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because these are not abstract states (*asattvabhūta*).
[Response: The words *vahni*, *vṛṣṭi*, and *agni* are masculine; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.

The words *śreṇi*, *yoni*, and *ūrmi* are feminine; so too are those ending in the suffix *ktin*, such as *kṛti* and others, as well as those ending in long *ī*, such as *lakṣmī* and others. *Śroṇi* is also feminine. *Ipamaya* is neuter. *Pums* is masculine. *Śreṇi* ends in *ktin*. *Kṛti* and so forth [end in *ktin*];
*lakṣmī* and so forth end in long *ī*.

Feminine nouns ending in *ūṅ* and *āp* are [declined like *kurūḥ*]. A monosyllabic word beginning with *y* or *v* [is declined like *strī*]. A word ending in *ī* or *ū* is treated as before; e.g., *śrīḥ*, *bhūḥ*. Why "monosyllabic"? [Consider] *vātapramīḥ*. Numbers from twenty (*viṃśati*) up to ninety (*navati*) [are feminine]. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities of the members are understood (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). The prefix *āṅ* denotes pervasion (*abhivyāpti*); e.g., "this is the twentieth. [The others are: thirty (*triṃśat*), forty (*catvāriṃśat*), fifty (*pañcāśat*), sixty (*ṣaṣṭhiḥ*), seventy (*saptatiḥ*), eighty (*aśītiḥ*), ninety (*navatiḥ*).

Regarding the drum-beaters: it was indeed by Dundubhi that this was done when Draupadī was lost [in the dice game] because he had fallen [into the trap]. What does "akṣa" mean here? By whom was this drum struck, which resounded in harmony with our own lion-roars?
The navel belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ; this is the navel.

Both [words] are used elsewhere than in the masculine; however, *dundubhi* and *nābhi* are stated to be in the masculine when used in this sense. *Nābhi* refers to a Kṣatriya. From the usage of Bhāravi—"with navels as delicate as the centers of blooming lotuses, reaching up to the waist"—masculinity is also established, because gender depends upon worldly usage. *Nābhi* is masculine when meaning a preeminent king, the center of a wheel, or a Kṣatriya.

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *kastūrikāmade* may refer to two things that serve as signs of living beings, and it is feminine. Words ending in the suffix *-tala* are feminine; for example: *śuklatā* (the state of being white), *brāhmaṇatā* (the duty or nature of a Brahmin), and *grāmatā* (a collection of villages). *Devatā* means simply "deity" (*deva*). The following are synonyms for earth, lightning, river, creeper, and woman: *bhūḥ* and *bhūmiḥ* (earth); *vidyut* and *saudāmanī* (lightning); *sarit* and *nimnagā* (river); *latā* and *vallī* (creeper); *vanitā* and *yoṣit* (woman). The word *yādas* is neuter; the term *yādas*, though meaning "river," is also used in the neuter gender.

*bhās*, *sruk*, *sraj*, *diś*, *uṣṇih*, and *upānah* [are feminine]. This refers to *bhās* and so forth. *Sthūṇā* and *ūrṇā* are [feminine] and also neuter. They may be feminine or neuter: *sthūṇā* / *sthūṇam*; *ūrṇā* / *ūrṇam*. *Sthūṇā* means a pillar; *ūrṇā* means the wool of sheep and similar animals.

The words *gṛha* and *śaśa* [form neuter nouns] when compounded with [the word *sthūṇa*]. This is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). Examples: *gṛhasthūṇam* (a house-pillar), *śaśorṇam* (hare-hair). Amara states: "The word *śaśorṇa* means the hair of a hare. The words *prāvṛṭ*, *vipruṭ*, *ruṭ*, *tṛṭ*, *viṭ*, and *tviṣ* are feminine. Vācaspatimiśra states: "The word *vipruṣaḥ* refers to drops of water perceptible by mere touch. The words *darvī*, *vidi*, *vedi*, *khani*, *śāṇī*, *śrī*, *veśī*, *kṛṣi*, *oṣadhi*, *kaṭī*, and *aṅguli* optionally take the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Thus, one has *darvī* or *darvi*, and so forth.

*Tithi*, *nāḍi*, *ruci*, *vīci*, *nāli*, *dhūli* (and *kikiḥkeṃli*, *cavi*, *rātri*, *jyā* etc.); "this is the lunar day" (*iyaṃ tithiḥ*) and so forth. According to Amara, *tithi* refers to both [the lunar day and its duration]. Śrī Harṣa says: "all the nights and full-moon lunar days. *Śaṣkulī*, *rājikā*, *kuṭī*, *aśani*, *vartman*, *bhrukuṭi*, *truṭi*, and *valipakti*—these also may be feminine. *Pratipad*, *āpad*, *vipad*, *saṃpad*, *śarat*, *saṃsat*, *pariṣad*, *uṣas*, *saṃvit*, *kṣut*, *pūṣan*, *samidh*. Regarding "this is the first lunar day" (*iyaṃ pratipad*) and so forth: *Uṣas* is the deity of the dawn; Bhavabhūti says, "like the goddess Uṣas, who is to be worshipped at dawn, the Blessed One in the Veda."

*Āśis*, *dhur*, *pūr*, and *gī* are [names for] doors (*dvāra*). "This is a blessing" (*iyam āśīḥ*), and so forth. For the words *ap*, *sumanas*, *sikatā*, and *varṣā*, there is a plurality [of forms]. Here, the word *sumanas* has the meaning of "flower. And their plurality is merely conventional; for the *Bhāṣya* states: "A single grain of sand (*sikatā*) is incapable of yielding oil. The *Sūtra* says: "She gives birth year after year" (*samām samām vijāyate*). In the *Mṛcchakaṭikā*: "A courtesan is to be avoided like a flower from a cemetery" (*veśyā śmaśānasumanā iva varjanīyā*).
*Sraj*, *tvac*, *jyok*, *vāk*, *yavāgū*, *nau*, and *sphic* are clear [in their usage].
The suffixes *tṛṭ* and *sīmā* are to be connected [to the preceding]. This is clear. *Culliveṇī* and *khārī* are also [feminine]. This is clear.

*Tārā*, *dhārā*, *jyotsnā*, and so forth, as well. The word *śalākā* is always feminine. The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) is for the purpose of indicating that there may be occasional deviation in other cases.

Thus ends the section on feminine endings; this is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). It extends until the end of another governing heading. It ends in the suffix *ghañ*. Examples: *pākaḥ* (cooking), *tyāgaḥ* (giving up), *karaḥ* (hand), *garaḥ* (poison). This [section] refers exclusively to the abstract sense (*bhāvārtha*). This is because the neuter gender is restricted to the abstract sense by the suffixes *kta* and *lyuṭ*, whereas the feminine gender is restricted by *ktin* and others, leaving [the masculine] as the remainder. However, in the case of the object (*karman*) and other kārakas, even words ending in *ghañ* and so forth may take the gender of the substantive they qualify, according to the usage in the Bhāṣya: "The relationship will follow the gender of the related term."

Those ending in *ghañ* are also [neuter]. The detailed scope is as follows: *caya*, *jaya*, and the words *bhaya*, *liṅga*, and *bhaga* are neuter when they denote a state (*pada*). This is clear. Those ending in *naṅ* are: *yajña*, *yatna*.
[This rule applies] to feminine nouns. It is an exception to the preceding [rule].

A verbal root ending in the *ky* suffix is designated as *ghu*. A root ending in the *kip* suffix is designated as *ghu* when it denotes a masculine. Examples: *ādhiḥ*, *nidhiḥ*, *udadhiḥ*. Why "ending in *ky*"? Consider *dānam*. Why "is *ghu*"? Consider *jajñiḥ vījam* (the seed that has produced). *Iṣudhiḥ* is also feminine. This is an exception to the preceding [rule].

The following words are masculine: *deva* (god), *asura* (demon), *ātman* (self/soul), *svarga* (heaven), *giri* (mountain), *samudra* (ocean), *nakha* (nail), *keśa* (hair), *danta* (tooth), *stana* (breast), *bhuja* (arm), *kaṇṭha* (neck), *khaḍga* (sword), *śara* (arrow), and *paṅka* (mud). Examples include: *devāḥ*, *amarāḥ*; *asurāḥ*, *daityāḥ*; *ātmā*, *kṣetrajñaḥ*; *svargaḥ*, *nākaḥ*; *giriḥ*, *parvataḥ*; *samudraḥ*, *akūpāraḥ*; *nakhaḥ*, *kararuhaḥ*; *keśaḥ*, *kacaḥ*; *dantaḥ*, *daśanaḥ*; *stanaḥ*, *kucaḥ*; *bhujaḥ*, *doḥ*; *kaṇṭhaḥ*, *galaḥ*; *khaḍgaḥ*, *karavālaḥ*; *śaraḥ*, *mārgaṇaḥ*; *paṅkaḥ*, *kardamaḥ*, and so forth.

In the case of *triviṣṭapa* and *tribhuvana*, the neuter gender is established; however, because these are synonyms for heaven (*svarga*), there is an exception that prescribes the masculine gender. *Dyauḥ* is feminine. The terms *dyo* and *div* are mentioned together in the rule (*tantra*).
*Iṣu* and *bāhu* are also feminine; by the word "and" (*ca*), they are also masculine.
The words *bāṇa* and *kāṇḍa* are neuter, as before. [Words ending in] *-n* [take the suffix *suṅ*]: *rājā*, *takṣā*. An exception will be stated [below].

Words denoting seasons, persons, temples, shrubs, and sacrifices [are masculine]: *ṛtuḥ*, *yajñaḥ*, etc. *Abhra* is neuter; this is an exception to the masculinity that would otherwise apply by virtue of its being a name for a cloud.
[Words] ending in *-u*: *prabhuḥ*, *ikṣuḥ*. This [rule applies] provided there is no word expressing a specific [gender].
The words *dhenū* (cow), *rajju* (rope), *kuhū* (the new moon), *sarayu* (a river), *tanu* (body), *kareṇu* (elephant), and *priyaṅgu* (a type of grain) are feminine.

In a compound, however, *rajju* may also be masculine, as in *karkaṭarajjvā* (with a crab-rope) and *karkaṭarajjunā* (by a crab-rope). The words *śmaśru* (beard), *jānu* (knee), *vasu*, *svādu* (sweet), *aśru* (tear), *jatū* (leather), *trapu* (tin), and *tālu* (palate) are neuter. The word *vasu* here signifies "wealth" (*arthavācin*). Consequently, in cases such as *vasurmaya-khāgni-dhanādhipeṣu* ("in rays, fire, wealth, and lords"), it retains its masculine gender.
*madgu*, *madhu*, *śīdhu*, *sānu*, and *kaparda* are neuter; however, they are masculine when ending in *rut*. Examples: *meruḥ*, *setuḥ*.
*Dāru*, *kaśeru*, *vastu*, and *mastu* are neuter; this is an exception to the preceding rule.

Before the word *raśmi*, words ending in *a* are [masculine]; from the point where "denoting rays or days" begins, the rule regarding those ending in *a* applies. This concludes the section on those beginning with *a*.
Words ending in *dha* [are masculine], except for *kopadhaḥ* (words with *ka* as the penultimate letter), *stabakaḥ*, and *kalkaḥ*.

The words *cibuka*, *śālūka*, *prātipadika*, *aṃśu*, and *kolmuka* are neuter; this is an exception to the preceding rule. The words *kaṇṭaka*, *anīka*, *sarakam*, *modaka*, *caṣaka*, *mastaka*, *pustaka*, *taṭāka*, *niṣka*, *śuṣka*, *varcaska*, *pināka*, *bhāṇḍaka*, and *pulāka* are neuter; this is also an exception to the preceding rule. Words ending in *ṭa* [are masculine] provided they end in the vowel *a*; for example, *ghaṭaḥ* and *paṭaḥ*. The words *kirīṭa*, *mukuṭa*, *lalāṭa*, *vaṭa*, *vīṭa*, *śṛṅgāṭa*, *karāṭa*, and *loṣṭa* are neuter. The words *kuṭa*, *kūṭa*, *kavāṭa*, *karpaṭa*, *taṭa*, *nikaṭa*, *kīṭa*, and *kaṭa* are neuter; however, by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), they may also be masculine.

A word ending in *ṇ* with a penultimate *ṇ* is neuter; [e.g.,] *guṇaḥ*, *pāṣāṇaḥ*. The words *ṛṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *parṇa*, *toraṇa*, *raṇa*, and *uṣṇa* are neuter; this is an exception to the preceding rule. The words *kārṣāpaṇa*, *svarṇa*, *suvarṇa*, *vraṇa*, *caraṇa*, *vṛṣaṇa*, *viṣāṇa*, *cūrṇa*, and *tṛṇa* are neuter and [masculine]. A word ending in *th* with a penultimate *th* is masculine; [e.g.,] *rathaḥ*. The words *kāṣṭhapṛṣṭha*, *riktha*, and *uktha* are neuter.

The word *kāṣṭhā* is feminine when it means a direction or a limit; as in *imāḥ kāṣṭhāḥ*. The words *tīrtha*, *prātha*, *yūtha*, and *gātha* are neuter as well. Words with *n* as their penultimate letter (*nopadha*) ending in *i* are neuter: *phenaḥ*. The following words—*jaghana*, *ajina*, *tuhiṇa*, *kānana*, *vṛjina*, *vipina*, *vetana*, *śamana*, *mithuna*, *śmaśāna*, *ratna*, *nimna*, and *cihna*—are neuter. This is an exception to the preceding rule. The words *māna*, *yāna*, *abhidhāna*, *nalina*, *udyāna*, *śayana*, *āsana*, *sthāna*, *candana*, *ālāna*, *saṃmāna*, *vasana*, *bhāvana*, *saṃbhāvana*, *vibhāvana*, and *vimāna* are neuter as well.

*popadhaḥ* (words ending in *p*): *yūpaḥ*, *dīpaḥ*. *Pāparūpoḍupa-talpa-śilpa-puṣpa-śaṣpa-samīpāntarīpāṇi napuṃsake* (the words *pāpa*, *rūpa*, *uḍupa*, *talpa*, *śilpa*, *puṣpa*, *śaṣpa*, *samīpa*, and *antarīpa* are neuter). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the previous rule. *Śurpa-kutapa-kuṇapa-dvīpa-viṭapāni napuṃsake ca* (the words *śūrpa*, *kutapa*, *kuṇapa*, *dvīpa*, and *viṭapa* are also neuter). Examples: *śūrpaḥ*, *idaṃ śūrpam*, etc.
*bhopadhaḥ* (words ending in *bh*): *stambhaḥ*, *kumbhaḥ*.
*talabha* is neuter. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.

*jṛmbha* is also neuter. [The following words] have *m* as their penultimate letter (*mopadha*). *soma*, *bhīma*, *rukma*, *sidhma*, *yugma*, *idhma*, *gulma*, *adhyātma*, and *kuṅkuma* are neuter. This is an exception to the preceding rule.
The words *saṃgrāma*, *dāḍima*, *kusuma*, *āśrama*, *kṣema*, *toma*, and *homa* are neuter; likewise, those ending in *y* (yopadha) such as *samaya* and *haya*.

The words *kisalaya*, *hṛdaya*, and *uttarīya* are neuter. The words *gomaya*, *kaṣāya*, *malaya*, *anvaya*, and *avyaya* are neuter as well as [masculine]. Those ending in *r* (ropadha) include *kṣura* and *aṅkura*.

The following words ending in the suffix *tra* are neuter: *dvāra* (door), *agra* (front), *sphāra* (expansive), *takra* (buttermilk), *cakra* (wheel), *vaprakṣipta* (thrown into a rampart), *kṣudra* (small), *ccidra* (hole), *nāra* (man), *tīra* (bank), *dūra* (far), *kṛcchra* (difficulty), *randhra* (aperture), *āśra* (slope), *śvabhra* (chasm), *gambhīra* (deep), *timira* (darkness), *krūra* (cruel), *vicitra* (variegated), *keyūra* (armlet), *kedāra* (field), *udara* (belly), *śarīra* (body), *kandara* (cave), *mandāra* (celestial tree), *pañjara* (cage), *jaṭhara* (womb), *ajira* (courtyard), *avaira* (enmity-less), *cāmara* (yak-tail fan), *puṣkara* (lotus), *gahvara* (abyss), *kuhara* (cavity), *kuṭī* (hut), *karūlī* (a type of vessel), *catvara* (crossroads), *kāśmīra* (saffron), *nīra* (water), *ambara* (garment), *śiśira* (cool), *tantra* (system), *mantra* (incantation), *kṣetra* (field), *mitra* (friend), *kalatra* (wife), *citrasūtra* (painting thread), *vaktra* (mouth), *netra* (eye), *gotra* (lineage), *aṅgulitra* (finger-guard), *bhalatra* (shield), *astra* (missile), *śāstra* (treatise), *vastra* (cloth), *patra* (leaf), and *pātra* (vessel). This is an exception to the previous rule [regarding masculine endings].

The word *śukra* is neuter when it refers to a deity; otherwise, this *śukra* means semen. The following words are neuter: *cakravajra*, *andhakāra*, *sāra*, *vārapāra*, *kṣīra*, *tomara*, *śṛṅgāra*, *bhṛṅgāra*, *mandāra*, *uśīra*, *timira*, *asi*, and *śiras*. The words *sopadha*, *vatsa*, *vāyasa*, and *mahānasa* are also neuter. The words *panasa*, *bisa*, *busa*, and *sāhasa* are neuter. The words *camasa*, *aṃsa*, *rasa*, *niryāsa*, *upavāsa*, *kārpāsa*, *vāsa*, *māsa*, *kāṃsa*, and *māṃsa* are neuter. Furthermore, *kaṃsa* is neuter when not referring to a living being; *kaṃsa* (masculine) is a drinking vessel, but as a living being, *kaṃsa* refers to a king.
The section on words ending in *a* is completed.
[Now follow] the names for rays and days; these are masculine. *Raśmi*, *mayūkha*, *divasa*, *ghasra*.
*Dīdhiti* is feminine [and is an exception to the preceding rule].
The words *dina* and *ahar* are neuter; likewise are terms denoting measures of capacity. *Kuḍava*, *prastha*, and *droṇa-āḍhaka* are also neuter; for example:
*idaṃ droṇam* (this is a droṇa) and *ayaṃ droṇaḥ* (this is a droṇa).

The words *khārī* and *mānikā* are feminine: this is a *khārī*, this is a *mānikā*. The words *dāra*, *akṣata*, *lāja*, and *asū* take the plural number: these are we; these are the wives (*dārāḥ*). Words meaning "wound" (*vraṇa*) and "limb" (*aṅga*), when preceded by the word *nāḍī*, [are neuter]: this is a sinus ulcer (*nāḍīvraṇaḥ*); a side-glance (*apāṅgaḥ*); a country (*janapadaḥ*). This sūtra is stated for the purpose of removing the neuter gender in the aforementioned instances.
*Marud*, *garut*, *uttara*, and *ṛtvij* [are masculine]; this refers to the group beginning with *marut*.

The sages (*ṛṣi*), blessings (*āśis*), seasons (*ṛtu*), grammarians (*granthika*), worms (*krimi*), sounds (*dhvani*), offerings (*bali*), the Kaula school (*kauli*), crowns (*mauli*), sun (*ravi*), poet (*kavi*), monkey (*kapin*), and sages (*muni*); as well as flag (*dhvaja*), elephant (*gaja*), *muñja* grass, and clusters (*puñja*);

hand (*hasta*), spear (*kunta*), multitude (*vrāta*), wind (*vāta*), messenger (*dūta*), rogue (*dhūrta*), spy (*sūca*), *tūta*, and hour (*muhūrta*). Regarding "hour" (*muhūrta*), Amara states: "The word *muhūrta* is not feminine."

The words *khaṇḍa*, *maṇḍa*, *karaṇḍa*, *varaṇḍa*, *tuṇḍa*, *gaṇḍa*, *muṇḍa*, *pākhaṇḍa*, and *sikhaṇḍa*; the word *vaṃśāṃśa* and *puroḍāśa*—the latter being called *puroḍāśa* because it is offered (*puro dāśyate*), with the substitution of *ḍa* by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The words *hrada*, *kanda*, *kunda*, and *budbuda*; the words *argha*, *pathin*, *mathin*, *ṛbhukṣin*, *stamba*, *nitamba*, and *pūga*; the words *pallava*, *palvaka*, *kapha*, *repha*, *kaṭāha*, *nirvyūha*, *maṭha*, *maṇi*, *taraṅga*, *turaṅga*, *gandha*, *skandha*, *mṛdaṅga*, *saṅga*, *samudra*, *puṃs*, and *ravas*.

*Sāra*, *ṛcī*, *tithi*, *kukṣi*, *vasti*, *pāṇi*, and *añjali*—thus ends the section on masculine nouns. Now begins the section on neuter nouns (*napuṃsaka*). This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). [The suffix] *lyuṭ* occurs after a verbal root to denote the action itself (*bhāva*). Example: *hasanam* (the act of laughing). Why "denoting the action"? [Counter-example: *idhmavraścanaḥ* (an axe for cutting fuel-wood); here it denotes the instrument. (Note: The text provided contains a fragment of Pāṇinian grammar, specifically from the *Liṅgānuśāsana*. The term *sāra* refers to the heartwood; *ṛcī* refers to a verse of the Ṛgveda; *tithi* refers to a lunar day; *kukṣi* refers to the belly; *vasti* refers to the bladder; *pāṇi* refers to the hand; and *añjali* refers to the hollowed palms joined together.)

The term *niṣṭhā* and *bhāva* are understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Examples: *hasitam* (the act of laughing), *gītam* (the act of singing). The suffixes *tva* and *yañ* are secondary (*taddhita*) affixes. Examples: *śuklatvam* (whiteness), *śauklyam* (whiteness). By virtue of the marker *ṣ*, there is optionally femininity: *cāturyam* (cleverness) and *cāturī* (cleverness); *sāmagryam* (completeness) and *sāmagrī* (completeness). After words denoting the action of a Brahmin and other such qualities, the suffix *yañ* is applied: the action of a Brahmin is *brāhmaṇyam*.
The suffixes *yaṅ*, *yak*, *yañ*, *aṇ*, *vuñ*, and *cha* [are applied] when the meanings of "state" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*) are to be expressed.
After the word *stena*, the suffix *yat* is applied: *steyam*. After the word *sakhi*, the suffix *ya* is applied: *sakhyam*.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *kapi* and *jñāti*: *kāpeyaṃ* and *jñāteyam*.
The suffix *yak* is applied after words ending in *pati* and after *purohita* and others: *ādhipatyam*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after words denoting a genus of living beings, words expressing age, and *udgātṛ* and others: *auṣṭram*.
The office of the Udgātṛ priest (*audgātra*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words beginning with *yuva*; e.g., *dvaihāyana*.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after dvandva compounds and words beginning with *manojña*; e.g., *paitāputraka*, *mānojñaka*.
The *acchāvākīya* [suffix] is applied after words such as *hautra*.
This is an *avyayībhāva* compound: *ādhistri*. There is singular number for a *dvandva* compound: *pāṇipādam*.

In non-Vedic usage, *hemanta-śiśirau* and *ahorātrau* [are singular]. A *tatpuruṣa* compound that is not a *nañ*-compound or a *karmadhāraya* is [governed by this rule]. This is a heading (*adikāra*).
*Chāyā* [is feminine] when it means "not small" or "autumnal shade";
*sabhā* [is feminine] when preceded by *rājan* or *amanuṣya*, as in *inasabham* and so forth;
and *chāyā-śālā-niśā* are feminine when preceded by *surā-saṃjñā*.

The remaining [tatpuruṣa compounds] follow the gender of the subsequent member. Any other tatpuruṣa compound shall take the gender of the subsequent member. Words ending in *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine. The words *apatha* and *puṇyāha* are neuter.
A word for "night" (*rātri*) preceded by a numeral is [neuter]. Why "preceded by a numeral"? [Consider: *sarvarātraḥ*.
A *dvigu* compound ending in a feminine noun; e.g., *pañcamūlī*, *tribhuvanam*. Words ending in *is* and *us*; e.g., *haviḥ*, *dhanuḥ*. The word *arciḥ* is also feminine; e.g., this or that *arciḥ*.

*Chadiḥ* and *paṭalam* are exclusively feminine; however, Amara states that *chadiḥ* is [also] neuter. The commentators on Amara’s lexicon maintain it is neuter due to its association [with other neuter terms]. Terms for the mouth, eyes, iron, forest, flesh, blood, bow, hole, plough, and cloud are not restricted [to a single gender]. For example: *mukham*, *ānanam*; *nayanam*, *locanam*, and so forth.
The words *sīra*, *artha*, and *odana* are masculine; whereas *vaktra*, *netra*, *araṇya*, and *gāṇḍīva* are also neuter. The word *aṭavī* is feminine.
Those ending in the suffix -up- are neuter: *kula*, *kūla*, *sthala*.

The following are masculine: *tūla*, *upalatāla*, *kusūla*, *tarala*, *kavala*, *deva*, *lava*, *vṛṣala*—this *tūla* being an example. Furthermore, the following are both masculine and neuter: *śālibhūla*, *maṅgala*, *sāmala*, *kamala*, *tala*, *musala*, *kuṇḍala*, *palala*, *mṛṇāla*, *vāla*, *nibala*, *palagala*, *aviḍāla*, *akhila*, and *śūla*.

Numerals beginning with "hundred" [are neuter]: *śatam* (a hundred), *sahasram* (a thousand). Why say "beginning with hundred"? [To exclude: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ* (one, two, many). The word "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*) is used for the purpose of excluding compounds where the first member is a non-numeral, such as *śataśṛṅgaḥ* (the mountain named Hundred-Peaked). The words *śata*, *ayuta*, and *prayuta* are masculine; *lakṣā* and *koṭī* are feminine. How much is five thousand? How much is a *lakṣā*, a *koṭi*, or even more? According to Amara’s lexicon, which states "or *lakṣā* and *niyutam* are neuter," *lakṣam* is also neuter.
*Śaṅkuḥ* (a peg) is masculine; *sahasraḥ* (a thousand) is [masculine] in some cases.

A word ending in *man* with two syllables is neuter when not denoting an agent (*akartari*). A word ending in *man* with two syllables is neuter, but not when it denotes an agent. Examples: *carma* (hide), *varma* (armor). Why "with two syllables"? [Counter-examples: *aṇimā* (minuteness), *mahimā* (greatness). Why "not when denoting an agent"? [Counter-example: *dāmā* (one who gives). *Brahman* is masculine and [neuter]. *Nāman* (name) and *loman* (hair) are neuter. This is for the sake of elaboration. A word ending in *as* with two syllables [is neuter]: *yaśaḥ* (fame), *manaḥ* (mind), *tapaḥ* (asceticism). Why "with two syllables"? [Counter-example: *candramāḥ* (the moon).
*Apsarāḥ* is used in the feminine. [Examples of] words ending in *tra*: *patram*, *chatram*.

The words *yātrā*, *mātrā*, *bhastrā*, *daṃṣṭrā*, and *varatrā* are feminine only. The words *bhṛtrā*, *amitra*, *chātra*, *putra*, *mantra*, *vṛtra*, *meḍhra*, and *uṣṭra* are masculine; for instance, Māgha says: "His enemies (*amitrāḥ*) are those who are not his friends (*na mitrāṇi*). The words *patra*, *pātra*, *pavitra*, *sūtra*, and *chatra* are both masculine and neuter. Words denoting strength, flowers, battles, cities, and forests are likewise [masculine and neuter]. The words *padma*, *kamala*, and *utpala* are both masculine and neuter; Amara states that *padma* is not in the masculine. Śrī Harṣa says: "The lotuses (*padmāḥ*), the days, the rainy season, and the khañjarīṭa birds..."
The words *āhava* and *saṃgrāma* are masculine; *āji* is exclusively feminine. Regarding the class of fruits: a word denoting a fruit is neuter, as in *āmalakam* and *āmram*.
The genus *vṛkṣa* (tree) is used only in the feminine; this [usage] occurs only in certain instances, such as *harītakī*.

*Viyat*, *jagat*, *śakaṭa*, *kṛṣat*, *pṛṣat*, *śakṛt*, *yakṛt*, *udaśvit*, *navanīta*, *avatāna*, *ṛta*, *nimitta*, *vitta*, *pitta*, *vrata*, *rajata*, *vṛtta*, *palita*; *śrāddha*, *kuliśa*, *daiva*, *pīṭha*, *kuṇḍa*, *aṅgada*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, *ājya*, *asya*, *dākāśa*, *kaṇva*, *bīja*; *daiva*, *puṃs* (in the masculine); *dhānya*, *ājya*, *sasya*, *rūpya*, *kupya*, *paṇya*, *adhiṣṇya*, *havya*, *kavya*, *kāvya*, *mati*, *apatya*, *mūlya*, *śikya*, *kuḍya*, *harmya*, *tūrya*, *sainya*;
*dvandva*, *barhas*, *duḥkha*, *baḍiśa*, *piccha*, *bimba*, *kuṭumba*, *śara*, *vṛndāraka*; *akṣa* (in the sense of a sense organ). Thus ends the section on neuter nouns.

[The following words are used] for both feminine and masculine: *gomat*, *maṇi*, *yaṣṭi*, *muṣṭi*, *pāṭali*, *śālmali*, *tṛṣṭi*, *maṣi*, *marīci*; *manyu*, *sindhu*, *karkandhu*, *kiṣku*, *kaṇḍu*, *reṇu*; and words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) ending in the vowel *a*. The practical meaning is that these are of three genders. For example: *paṭu* (neuter), *paṭuḥ* (masculine), *paṭvī* (feminine). [In the case of] secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) denoting offspring: *aupagavaḥ* (masculine), *aupagavī* (feminine).
Thus ends the section on women and men.

In the masculine and neuter genders: *ghṛta*, *bhūta*, *mustaka*, *kṣvelita*, *airāvata*, *pustaka*, *busta*, *lohita*; *śṛṅga*, *ardhanidāgha*, *udyama*, *śalla*, *dṛḍha*; *vraja*, *kuñja*, *kutha*, *kūrca*, *puccha*, *darpa*, *arman*, *īrman*, *darbha*, *puccha*; *kabandha*, *auṣadha*, *āyudha*, *andha*. *Daṇḍa*, *maṇḍa*, *khaṇḍa*, *śava*, *saindhava*, *pārśva*, *ākāśa*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *aṅkuśa*, *kuliśa*. Regarding *kuśā*, it refers to a small stick (*śalākā*) or a tool made of iron (*ayovikāra*).
Also: *gṛha*, *meha*, *deha*, *paṭṭa*, *paṭaha*, *aṣṭāpada*, *ambuda*, *kakuda*.
Thus ends the section on masculine and neuter genders. [Now follows] the section on words whose gender is not specifically distinguished.

[The following are indeclinables: *avyaya*. [The words] *kati*, *yuṣmad*, and *asmad* [are indeclinables]. Numerals ending in *ṣ* or *n* [are feminine]. The remaining [numerals] follow the gender of the word they qualify (*paravat*). A numeral ending in *ṣ* or *n*, when not followed by *ī*, takes the gender of the noun it qualifies (*viśeṣyaliṅga*).
And "deception regarding qualities" means a sign of one who possesses dharma.

And [the suffix] *kṛtya*. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). "The words beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns (*sarvanāman*). These three sūtras are for the sake of clarity. Thus ends the Pāṇinian instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*).
In the first section of the fourth chapter (we now return to the subject at hand):
*idamaḥ anvādeśe 'ś anudāttaḥ tṛtīyādau* || 32 || [The substitute *aś* for *idam* is anudātta when used in a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) before the third case-ending and those that follow.]

In the case of the word *idam* when it is the subject of an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference), there shall be the substitution of *as-* for it in the third case and subsequent cases, provided it is unaccented. *Anvādeśa* is the non-repetition of that which was already employed as the object of prescription (*uddeśya*) in one rule, even though it is not explicitly mentioned in another rule. If it were merely a matter of subsequent mention, then the substitution *enad-* would undesirably apply in such an instance as: "Feed Devadatta, and [feed] this Yajñadatta," where the speaker is referring back to someone previously mentioned.

In this context, the Bhāṣya states that "anvādeśa" (subsequent reference) is simply the restatement of what has already been said, using the word "tathā" (so it is), for the purpose of dispelling the delusion [that it is something new]. Therefore, there is no insistence that it must be expressed by a different word or by the pronoun "idam" (this). For this very reason, the Vṛtti explains: "Anvādeśa is the second presentation of a single referent that was previously presented by a preceding word. And the status of being the "subject" (uddeśyatva) is common to all that falls within that category.

In the verse "His skin was not spread by a wild elephant; then Adreṣṭā’s daughter lamented for him," the word *asya* (of him) functions as both the subject (*uddeśya*) and an attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*). Now, regarding the question: "How is it that [in the verse] 'This one is timid; therefore, O Rādhā, you yourself lead him home,' [the pronoun] is used?

On this point, some say that the reading should instead be *tadamum* ("him there"), so that the word *adaḥ* (that) is employed. Others, however, maintain that "this one is timid" is not an injunction (*vidhi*), but rather a restatement (*anuvāda*).

This is not so; for in the case of "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), just as with fire, it is a specific type of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) alone that constitutes the meaning of the positive particle (*vidhi*) here, since the nature of being a positive injunction—consisting in causing the cognition of what was previously unknown—is not intended. In the case of "this person is timid" (*ayaṃ bhīruḥ*), by virtue of its word-order, it is necessary that timidity be the predicate (*vidheya*) with respect to this [subject] as the subject-mention (*uddeśya*). What is the meaning of the phrase "in order to inform one who has not previously known"? Does it mean "to inform the person being addressed," or "to inform anyone at all"? It cannot be the first, because that is unestablished in a sentence devoid of an addressive vocative.

Therefore, [the first alternative is untenable] because of the non-establishment of such claims as "this [world] transgresses the command of the Creator" and so forth. Nor is the latter [alternative tenable], because that [transgression] exists even in the case at hand.

Therefore, anvādeśa occurs only when two sentences are mutually independent. Here too, because there is no perception of *bhīrutva* (timidity) as the cause through the word *tat*, there is no single-sentence unity (*ekavākyatva*), and thus it is not so [an anvādeśa]. Some maintain that although the fact that "his skin was torn off by a wild elephant" is a cause for lamentation, there is no fault because that [cause] is not expressed by the word *tasya*. By this, the examples "this staff is to be taken by him" (*ayaṃ daṇḍo harānena*) and "one should know this to be afflicted" (*etaṃ ātaṅkitaṃ vidyāt*) are also explained; for these form a single sentence with the phrase "and in the sense of limit or inclusion" (*maryādābhividhau ca yaḥ*).

This has been stated by the authors of the *Vṛtti*: "An *anvādeśa* is that where, having enjoined something by one sentence, another thing is subsequently taught by a further sentence; however, in this case, after merely indicating the subject matter, there is only a single injunction. By this, the argument that it lacks the status of an *anvādeśa* because it is independent is refuted, since the absence of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) is clearly perceived, given that an *anu-ādeśa* is an injunction (*vidhi*) made subsequent to [the first].

As for the objection that this contradicts the statement, "Nevertheless, decree for him who has transgressed your command that he become a guest in the abode of the Destroyer (Yama)," it is not so; for the status of being an *anvādeśa* depends upon a specific sentence, and the status of *anvādeśa* exists only when the mere meaning of that sentence serves as the reason for the subsequent sentence. Furthermore, in the phrase "tadenam" (him, therefore), there is the causality of multiple sentence-meanings; such is the direction of the argument.
"O Rohiṇī, you are blessed among women of virtuous character.
O friend, restrain this ill-behaved husband."
"He has entered my dwelling through the lattice;

he touches the slope of my hips—is this his family custom?"—in this case, the construction should be reversed as "he touches the slope of my hips; ward him off. Regarding the phrase "the delivery of a bite to the lip by a venomous serpent shall not be counted again by you as a misfortune," the status of being an object of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) is not intended here. As for the phrase "there was a king, a friend of the gods," they say that the rule regarding the non-recent past tense (*anadyatana*) does not apply.

[Objection: But surely, the substitution for *ṭā* and *ām* will be taught as a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), and all other case-endings (*vibhakti*) beginning with a consonant are already established by the elision of the form *tad-*; therefore, one might argue that only its low-pitched accent (*anudāttatva*) needs to be prescribed. [Response: No, because the introduction of the substitute is for the sake of including the suffix *sak* (the *ka* of *imaka*). For in that case, the elision of the form *tad-* cannot be obtained, due to the prohibition by the rule *akaḥ*. [Example: "The two students, *imakābhyām*, studied at night, and furthermore, they studied during the day. However, the inclusion of the marker *ś* is for the sake of making it a replacement for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*); otherwise, it would apply only to the final phoneme (*alontyasya*).

Nor should it be argued that this [suffix *ka*] is excluded from the final substitute because there is no purpose for it, since the vowel *ā* already exists there by virtue of the substitution of *tyad* etc. with *at*. This is because its utility is possible as a prohibition against other substitutes, just as in the case of rules such as *mo rāji samaḥ kvau*. Alternatively, this substitute consists of two vowels (*a* and *ā*); since it has more than one *al* (phoneme), it will apply to the whole word, and thus the status of being marked with *ś* (*śit*) need not be prescribed. Or rather, only the property of being unaccented (*anudātta*) should be prescribed. For the formations of *taddhita* suffixes are diverse; thus, in the case of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), *akac* does not arise.

This is because one understands that the *vibhāṣā* (alternative views) are established according to the scope of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. Furthermore, there is no comprehension of an unknown meaning without the particle *akac*. This remains the case even under the view that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*), as the reasoning is identical. If its application were established through context and so forth, then it would be possible even without *akac*; thus, parsimony (*lāghava*) is achieved.

In this regard, the following should be noted: in the case of *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference), *ābhyām* is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*), because the case-ending is also unaccented by the rule for the accentuation of nominal suffixes (*sup-svara*). However, in the absence of *anvādeśa*, it is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*), because the case-ending is accented by the rule *ūḍidampadādyapprumraidyubhyaḥ*. Now, one might object: even in the case of *anvādeśa*, the case-ending would be accented by the aforementioned rule; and this is not a desirable conclusion, since such accentuation is not observed in instances such as *prate babhru vicakṣaṇa śaṃsāmi* and *ābhyāṃ gā anu*. This is not so.

Because of the continued application of the rule regarding "acute on the final syllable" (*antodātta*), an acute accent is prescribed for the case-ending that follows *idam* and others which have an acute on the final syllable; furthermore, the suffix *śas* is itself anudātta (unaccented). One might argue: even so, the rule *sāvekācastṛtīyādivibhaktiḥ* would still make it unavoidable for the third-case ending and those following to be acute, since the term *sāu* refers to the nominative plural.

As for what Haradatta says: "Because of the force of the continued application of the rule *ūḍidamparaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.171) as an acute accent (*udātta*), the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168) does not apply here. This is because there is no difference whether the acute accent is applied by that [former] rule or by this one. And it should not be argued: "In the case of *yadīmenā uśataḥ*, that [rule *sāvekācaḥ*] serves its purpose by excluding the *śas* ending; for in that instance, *sāvekācaḥ* does not apply."

Even though [the word] *kakṣa* is bound to the neck (*grīvāyām*), this is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule] to forms such as *matsyam nadīna udamiṅkṣiyantam*; for since the term *ekācaḥ* (of a monosyllabic [root]) must necessarily be carried over [from a previous rule], the desired result is established by that very [restriction]. Furthermore, because only those [words] ending in an udātta accent, such as *āsanni*, etc., are recited in the section prescribing the substitutes. Alternatively, the term *sāu* should be understood as the nominative singular case-ending itself. Nor is there an over-extension of the rule to the form *tvayā*, because of the prohibition [stated in the rule]: *nagośvantsāvavarṇa*. Moreover, according to the view that "the elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*) is the same as the elision of the *ṭi*," there is an absence of the condition of being a monosyllable (*ekāctva*) when the case-ending is present. And since there is no purpose in expressing the specific form [in cases like *ebhiḥ*], there is no possibility of the rule applying to *ebhiḥ* and similar forms at all.

That is questionable; for the continued application of the rule regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is exhausted by the very exclusion [of the case] by the word *ābhyām*. Indeed, the rule *sāvekācaḥ* does not apply there. In the locative plural form *eṣu*, the form is *e-iti*, which is absent in *ābhyām*. Consequently, in instances such as *ebhir agne sunvanti somān pibasi tvam eṣām*, since the form *e-iti* exists, the undesired consequence would be that the case-ending would be acutely accented. Others, however, cite *aś* as an example in the context of *anvādeśa*.

According to Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, the objection that "in the case of the seventh-case plural [forms] ending in *eṣu*, there is a single vowel (*ekāc*) due to the substitution of *aś*, whereas in the nominative singular this is not a single vowel, and thus the accentuation rule would not apply," is accepted as the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the Vedic recitation. Furthermore, the second solution is also incorrect; for if the specific form were not intended to be significant, there would arise a contradiction regarding the middle-udātta accent in Taittirīya passages such as *doṣābhyāṃ svāhā* (where the word would have to be treated as a single vowel in the nominative singular), and there would also be the impossibility of the final udātta accent in the passage *indro jāto vasitasya rājā*.

Because the form *yād* does not exist in the genitive case; however, if the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*) is understood, then since the base form ending in *t*, namely *yād*, exists even in the genitive, the udātta accent of the case-ending is established. On this point, the Dīkṣitas state: "In the rule *sāvekācaḥ*, the term 'ending in an udātta vowel' (*antodātta*) must also be carried over [as an anuvṛtti]. Therefore, there is no possibility of the udātta accent occurring in cases of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), such as *ābhyām* and *ebhiḥ*. Even though the author of the Vṛtti and others did not mention it, there is no obstacle to carrying that term over for the sake of the desired result. The forms *etad-as* and *tratas-au* are also anudātta. (33)

The substitute *aś* shall take the place of *etad* when it is the subject of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), and it is unaccented (*anudātta*). Furthermore, when *tratas* follows, both *tā* and *tasi* are also unaccented. For example: "We live happily in this village; therefore we study here, and for that reason we will not go. The rule for the unaccented status is introduced so that the accentuation of *tratas* as a suffix (by the rule of the accent of suffixes) does not occur.

If it is argued that once *trata* and *sau* have been applied, the base will become acute by the accent of the *lit* suffix (*litsvara*), while the two [suffixes] themselves will become grave by the rule of "the remainder" (*śeṣanighāta*), and thus the portion of the rule stating "trata and sau are grave" (*tratasaścānudāttau*) need not be formulated—this is not so. For although the *litsvara* is subsequent, it is nevertheless obligatory (*nitya*). The *litsvara*, however, does not apply once the [following] grave accent has been established, due to the very force of the prescription for that grave accent. Consequently, in the absence of the preceding [base] which would otherwise have become acute, the rule ensures that the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*) prevails as it naturally occurs for *trata* and *sau*.

Because the general rule (*utsarga*) operates only when there is an absence of an exception (*apavāda*). For this very reason, in the case of *goḥ padapraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ*, since the suffix *ṇamul* and the elision of the vowel *ū* are prescribed together by the rule *varṣapramāṇe lo paś cāsya antatarasyām*, the initial accentuation of the suffix (*pratyayādyudāttatva*)—which would otherwise result from the absence of the *lit-svara*—is overridden; thus, by the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*, the word is established as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Therefore, the status of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) must necessarily be commenced [as an exception]. 2.4.34: *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ* (The substitution of *ena* for the word *idam* occurs after the second case ending, the sixth case ending, and the seventh case ending in the plural).

In the case of the second [demonstrative pronoun], when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is present and the case endings *osi* and *os* follow, the substitutes *enad* and *etad* shall respectively take the form *ena-* within the scope of anvādeśa (subsequent reference). For example: *imaṃ chātraṃ chando 'dhyāpaya, enaṃ vyākaraṇam adhyāpaya* ("Teach this student the Veda, and teach him grammar," etc.); or *etaṃ chātraṃ chando 'dhyāpaya, atho enaṃ vyākaraṇam adhyāpaya* ("Teach this student the Veda, and then teach him grammar," etc.).

Although the word *idam* does not carry over (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding sūtra, nevertheless, since no specific substitute is mentioned here, that [word] must necessarily be implied. Thus, by means of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) characterized by mutual requirement, the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) for *idam* and *etad* as introduced in the previous sūtra is established. However, in cases such as "one should know this [form] as having a ṅit ātmanepada affix" or "this staff, take it with this," the explanation follows the actual occurrence of the substitute (*yathādeśa*).

And thus, since this word "etad" refers back to the four previously mentioned meanings, it cannot possibly refer back to that which is the subject (*uddeśya*) in the rule prescribing the *ṅit* designation. This is because the meaning "the *ṅit* status applies to that which is distinct from both [the masculine and neuter]" is already established by following the fourth quarter of the verse. In the case of the expression "this staff" (*ayaṃ daṇḍaḥ*) as well, "this" (*idam*) is the subject, and "staff" (*daṇḍa*) alone is the predicate (*vidheya*).

And thus, since the staff was not introduced as the object of reference (*uddēśya*) in the preceding rule (*pūrvavidhi*), it does not possess the status of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*). For this very reason, it is stated [in the commentary] that "of that which was introduced as the object of reference in the preceding rule. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this; for the very usage cited in the *Bhāṣya* and other sources is precisely such an instance.

Now, how [is this to be explained] regarding the verse: "Behold his crimson foot, the abode of beauty; Sarasvatī herself is ever intent upon serving him. O fortunate one, worship him, the lord of the world! For who would not worship him, he whose mind rests in the lotus? Nor should it be said that, by taking the subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the second instance lacks the status of an *anvādeśa*, because the definition of *anvādeśa* is common to both, and there is no evidence for such a distinction. Nor should it be said that this applies only to a sentence containing a word ending in an affix with injunctive meaning (*vidhi*), for there is no evidence for that.
Furthermore, it would contradict usages such as "he enlightened him" (*enaṃ pratyabodhayat*).

It is said in reply: because the word *idam* (this) lacks the capacity to refer back to that which has been previously indicated, and because it has already been designated by the word *tat* (that). Nor is it redundant, for such redundancy would not occur in the case of a conjunction (*saṃbheda*). For this very reason [it is said]: "O Lord, he who perceives this entire circle of objects as conceptual construction sees Your entire body."

Regarding the statement, "When the world is filled with those belonging to his own side, how can there be fear for him who is eternally happy?"—the fact that the word *idam* (this) here has the same meaning as the word *tat* (that) is indeed accepted in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other such works. Similarly: "That fierce and most formidable kṣatriya splendor which belonged to this king, while he was playing with dice, was surely lost by him then. "He who, assisted by his sword and his formidable arms, was the sole matchless wrestler of Vijaya-Arjuna in battle..."
