It has also been stated that in such instances as "If he were appointed by the king to that task, then what would have been done would indeed be done," even the pronouns *tad* and *adas*, occurring immediately after the relative pronoun *yat*, serve to present only the subject (*uddeśya*). By this, the expression "you yourself him" (*tvameva tamim*) is also explained; for it cannot be construed as a single compound word. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*), because priority alone serves that purpose: the meaning is that "some resort to this well-known Varuṇa, who was previously enjoyed [by others]."

By this, the usage of Kumārila—“O you whose preparation was remembered by cruel gods before it was completed; fashion this very left foot for me, who am devoid of passion”—is explained, as is the *Kusumāñjali* passage: “This very [Self] by means of sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma. For this very reason, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* passage, “They desire to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas,” is consistent.

This has been stated in the aphorisms beginning with "One should meditate upon that as the Self" and ending with "It is the bridge, the support," and because it has been explained as "this witness of the intellect. Regarding the form *enat*, it should be stated that it occurs in the neuter singular; otherwise, by the rule "āt-om-am-bhāvaḥ," the form would incorrectly become *enam*, as in: "Bring the pot, wash it, turn it over, [and] turn it back."

If it is argued that this very same [principle] should be stated everywhere, since the substitution of *yat* for *tyad*-class stems would be established in the masculine as *enam* (by virtue of its commonality with the neuter), and forms such as *enaḥ*, *enau*, *enān*, and *enāni* would likewise be established—[we reply: no, because the form *enācchritakaḥ* is desired. For, according to the principle "an external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules," the elision (*luk*) takes effect by subverting the *tyadādyatva* substitution; and once the elision has occurred, the *tyadādyatva* substitution does not apply due to the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of a rule based on the presence of a suffix).

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "In the case of 'yathālakṣaṇam aprayukte'," when usage is not perceived, grammatical refinement proceeds according to the rules (*lakṣaṇa*). In that context, concerning the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, if there were a reference to the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), then in the prescription of this substitute which falls outside that [heading], because it would possess the character of being conditioned by an affix (*pratyayalaksanatva*), the form would have to be *enach-chhitakaḥ* in the Bhāṣya. However, the experts of the tradition maintain that the prohibition of the character of being conditioned by an affix applies to all operations related to the stem (*aṅga*), and does not involve the grasping of the fact that [the operation] was prescribed under the heading of "stem"; therefore, the form should be *etac-chritakaḥ* in the Bhāṣya.

However, some maintain that this [substitution] occurs only after *eta*, because it is precluded by the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending prescribed by the rule *supo dhātv-ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), or else by the substitution of *enad*. This is because, although the substitution of *enad* would apply when the internal *luk* of *su* and *am* has occurred—given the power of the pronunciation of the letter *t* in *enad* and its status as depending on a single word—it does not apply when the external *luk* of the compound occurs.
[The section on] *ārddhadhātuka* [suffixes]. (35)

This [rule] applies up to "ṇyakṣatriya" (Pāṇini 2.4.58). Now, since the individual instances (*vyakti*) are specifically the intended objects of the treatise when the word-meaning is an individual instance, the term *ārddhadhātuka* would have to be interpreted as a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). Consequently, the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes would first arise, and only then would the substitutions (*ādeśa*) mentioned later take place; otherwise, there would be no basis (*nimitta*) for them. While there is no fault in this regard concerning specific *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes such as those in *jagdhī* and so on, there is nevertheless a problem with those based on general categories, such as *aster bhūḥ*, *ajervī*, and *cakṣiṅa*.

In the case of *khyā* and other roots, the fault is unavoidable; for instance, one would not expect forms such as *bhavyam*, *praveyam*, or *ākhyeyam*. This is because after the suffix *ṇyat*, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the substitute [of *ya*] instead of *i*; furthermore, since the root ends in a consonant (*hal*) prior to that, the suffix *yat* is difficult to obtain. Nor should it be argued that, by resorting to the view of "genus" (*jāti*), the general category of *ārddhadhātuka* is what is depended upon rather than the specific instance, because a universal devoid of particulars does not exist. [Otherwise,] in cases such as *lavyam* and *pavyam*, the substitution of *guṇa* and *avādeśa* would apply to the general category of *ārddhadhātuka*.

Furthermore, once [the suffix] *ṇyat* has been applied, the characteristic of having a penultimate *ḍhal* (ḍh, l) would be unavoidable. Also, in forms such as *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*, since the *at*-elision occurs in the general category of *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the application of *ṇyat*. Nor should it be argued that, after prescribing *jha*, *dhi*, and so on without distinction, the prohibition "by a *sārvadhātuka*" will be established, whereas the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the case of an *ārddhadhātuka*" will not apply; for that would entail the fault of splitting the sūtra (*sūtrabheda*).

It is said that the *jāti*-view (the view that a word denotes a universal) alone must be adopted, and there is no fault of "desiring what is not intended" (*aditsyamitidoṣa*). This is because it will be stated later that the mention of *ac* in the rule *aco yad* is for the sake of including even those [bases] which were formerly *aj*-ending; nor is it impossible for a universal (*jāti*) to be posterior [to its instances]. Precisely for this reason, by resorting to the locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), when there is a desire to express an *ārthadhātuka* suffix, the substitutes (*ādeśa*) and so forth apply first, and subsequently the specific suffixes are established according to their respective causes (*nimitta*). Furthermore, the state of being present in the intellect (*buddhisthatva*) occurs once the specific suffix has been manifested.

It should be understood that [the term] *ārdhadhātuka* refers precisely to the object of a cognition characterized by the form [of the word] *ārdhadhātuka*. However, according to the view that [words denote] individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), one should read [the rule as] *ārdhadhātuṣu*; since the suffix *ac* occurs by virtue of belonging to the *arśa-ādi* group, the locative case [is used], meaning: "when the collections of words beginning with *asti* are being derived as having *ārdhadhātuka* [suffixes] following them, then *bhū* and the others are the substitutes."

[Objection: "But surely, since the rules for *jagdhi* and so forth are prescribed within the domain of the *ārddhadhātuka*, this governing rule (*adhikāra*) may be abandoned once that section is reached. [Response: Not so; for in forms such as *jakṣatuḥ*, *adhijage*, *adhyagīṣṭa*, *vabhūva*, and *vivyatuḥ*, the respective substitutes would be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) by virtue of being *ābhīya* (belonging to the subsequent rule), which would result in the absence of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), the elision of *at* (*at-lopa*), *vuk*, and *yaṇ*. [Objection: "In that case, let those [substitutes] also be prescribed right here [in the *ārdhadhātuka* section]. [Response: That cannot be said either; for in forms such as *gataḥ* and *gatavān*, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) would be *siddha* (already established), which would lead to the undesired elision of the *at* (*at-lopa*).

If one explains that "at the time of the instruction of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, it [the root] ends in the vowel *a*," then, upon the rejection of the rule *asiddhavat*, let there be only a single governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *ārdhadhātuka*. This is because, by the force of the *jñāpaka*, it is possible for this governing heading of the *aṅga* to function in both ways—as a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*) and as a locative of sequence (*para-saptamī*). *ado jagdhiḥ lyap-ti-kit-i* // 36 //

The substitution of *jagdhi* for *ada* (the root "to eat") occurs when followed by a suffix beginning with *t*, provided that suffix is marked with the *k* or *ṅ* indicatory letters (*kit*), as well as when followed by the suffix *lyap*. Thus: *prajagdhyam*, *jagdhaḥ*, *jagdhīḥ*. [Question: Why is it not so in the case of *annim*? [Answer: The *Vṛtti* states that this is due to the specific irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the word *annam*. [Objection: One might argue that since the suffix *ktvā* precedes the substitution of *lyap*, one should simply rely on the *ktvā* suffix itself for the form *jagdhi*; what is the purpose of mentioning *lyap* separately? Furthermore, by the rule of priority (*paratva*), shouldn't *lyap* apply first? [Response: No, because the substitution of the base (*prakṛti-ādeśa*) is *antaraṅga* (internal), depending only on a suffix beginning with *t*, whereas the substitution of *lyap* is *bahiraṅga* (external), depending upon the preceding member of a compound (*pūrvapada*). Thus, the former takes precedence. If this is your objection:

Not so; for this is intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that an external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules. Consequently, in forms such as *pradhāya* and *prasthāya*, the substitution of *lyap* occurs by subverting both the *hi*-substitution of the root *dhā* and the *i*-substitution of the root *sthā*. Otherwise, since those two [substitutions] would apply due to their being internal, one would have to resort to the statement: "The rule regarding *upadeśiva*d is for the sake of what has not yet been prescribed, because it is characterized as external."

Therefore, in *pradāya*, there is no substitution of *da* for *dā*; in *prakhanya*, there is an absence of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) by the rule *janasana-*; and in *yevibhāṣā*, there is an optionality. In *prakramya*, there is an absence of lengthening by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*; and in *āpṛccha* and *pradīvya*, it should be understood that the rule *naśca dhātvoḥ* applies. For this very reason, Vyāghrabhūti said: "The rule regarding *jagdhi* [the substitute for *ad*] exists as something established by chance in the case of *lyap*, because it is prescribed [only] before a suffix marked with *k*. But know that in the case of *hi* and so forth, *lyap* is always *bahiraṅga*."
When the *jagdhi* substitution is established, the rule "lyap is used when *ti* and *kit* follow" (*tikitīti*) is stated because it is *antaraṅga*.
This indicates that there is an annulment (*bādhana*) of *antaraṅga* operations by means of *lyap*.
[The suffix] *gharuḷ* is applied after the roots *luṅ* and *san*. (Pāṇini 3.1.43)

In the *luṅ* (aorist) and *san* (desiderative), there is the substitution of *ad* for *ghas*. Because it is marked with the *ḷ*-sign (*lṛdit*), the suffix *aṅ* is applied; thus, *aghāsat*. To eat, he desires: *jighatsati*. By the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*, there is reduplication. By *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, all but the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable are elided. By *sanyataḥ*, the vowel *a* is changed to *i*. By *kuhoścuḥ*, the letter *j* is substituted for the initial *g* in the reduplicated syllable. There is an inclusion (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the root *ac*. One who eats excessively is called *praghasaḥ* (from *pra-aś* with the suffix *ghañ*). And [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] after roots ending in *ap*. (Pāṇini 6.4.98).
From these two roots [ghas and ad], [the forms] *ghaslṛ*, *ghāsaḥ*, and *praghasaḥ* [are derived]. By the rule *upasarge 'daḥ*, the suffix *ap* is applied;
furthermore, in Vedic usage (*chandasi*), this occurs diversely (*bahulam*).

*Ghastām nūnam*: The inclusion of the term *bahulam* (variously) is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) in the mantra form *ghasa*. *Āttāmattam adhyato meda uddhṛtam*: The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (the augment is optional in Vedic). *Sagdhiś ca me*: This has already been explained.
*Liṭy anyatarasyām* || 40 || [The substitution of *kvasu* for the *liṭ* suffix is optional].

In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, this substitute (*ada*) may optionally occur. Thus, *jaghāsa* (from *ghas*) and *āda* (from *ad*). It should not be argued that since *ghaslṛ* (meaning "to eat") is listed independently among the *bhvādi* roots, the form *jaghāsa* is established from that root, and since the form *āda* is established from the root *ad*, what is the purpose of this rule? This is because the rule serves to indicate that the status of being *liṭ-lit* (having *liṭ* as its indicator) for *ghas* is not universal. Consequently, it is used only where there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) or an explicit statement (*vacana*), and not elsewhere. For instance, its recitation in the *bhvādi* list with the *śap* suffix and in the *parasmaipada* is the indicative mark; hence: *ghasati*, *ghasatu*, *aghasat*, *ghaset*. Its designation as *lṛdit* is for the sake of the *aṅ* suffix [in the imperfect].

"aghasad" and so forth. In the *aniṭ-kārikās*, the reading [of the root] is for the purpose of [deriving] forms such as *ghas* and *ārthadhātuka*. Thus: *ghastā*, *ghatsyati*, etc. Because of the specific mention of *sṛdhasyadaḥ* in the rule for the suffix *kmarac*, we have *ghasmaraḥ*; otherwise, there is no designation [of this form]. For the root *veñ*, there is *vañiḥ*. (41)

The substitution of *vayi* for the root *veñ* is optional before the *liṭ* suffix; [the forms are] *ūyatuḥ*, *ūyuḥ*. By the rule "in *liṭ*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* for *vay*" (*liṭi vayoya*), there is a prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the letter *y*. [The forms] *vavau*, *vavatuḥ*, *vavuḥ*, etc., are the forms when the substitution does not occur.
[In the case of the root *han*,] *vadha* [is substituted] in the *liṅ* [optative]. (Pāṇini 2.4.42)
And also in the case of a scriptural injunction. || 43 ||

In this context, the substitute *vadha* is applied. Thus we have *vadh-y-āt* (in the optative) and *avadh-īt* (in the aorist). However, it does not apply in the prescriptive optative (*vidhiliṅ*) because [the suffix] lacks the status of an *ārthadhātuka*. Thus, we have *hanyāt*. If the vowel *a* were merely for the sake of pronunciation, then in the aorist (*luṅ*), the rule *ato halāder laghoḥ* would cause the vṛddhi substitution conditioned by a stem ending in a consonant. [Furthermore,] from the root *han*, the word *vadhakaḥ* is formed with the suffix *ṇvul*; here the substitute *vadha* is introduced by a supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*). In that case, the vṛddhi substitution prescribed by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* would apply; although it is prohibited by the rule *janivadhyoś ca*, even so, due to the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *t* in *hana-st-a* would become a final substitute (*antādeśa*).

In forms such as *avadhīt*, there would also be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt*. This being the case, the Vārttika states: "There is a prohibition of [the application of] *vṛddhi* and *tva* in the substitute, and the prescription of *iṭ*. Thus, according to the intention of the Vārttika, the over-extension [of the rules] is resolved by this stated statement.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says: this [root] is indeed one that ends in a vowel (*adanta*). Therefore, because of the status of the elision of *a* as being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), it does not possess the quality of ending in a consonant (*halantatva*); thus, there is no occasion for the application of Vṛddhi. Furthermore, even that [Vṛddhi] which is prescribed for the final letter of the base (*alontyasya*) does not occur here, because the letter *a* has been elided. This is because there is an absence of the status of being like the original (*sthānivattva*) in the case of rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*). Nor does it apply to the letter *dh*, because by virtue of the elision of *a* being like the original, the letter *dh* lacks the status of being the final letter. Moreover, because it is taught with its own [original] form and consists of more than two syllables (*anekāc*), the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* does not apply. Other points have been determined in the Sthānivatsūtra. [Now begins: "In the case of the Ātmanepada endings, optionally" (Pāṇini 7.2.44).

The substitution of *vadh* for *han* occurs when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix follows that which is a *luṅ* (aorist) in the *ātmanepada*. [Examples: *āvadhiṣṭa*, *āvadhiṣātām*, *āvadhiṣata*; *āhata*, *āhasātām*, *āhasata*. The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ*. The *kit* designation is applied to the *sic* suffix after *han* by the rule *hanaḥ sic*. The elision of the nasal (*n*) occurs by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...*. Due to the force of the word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) in the preceding sūtra, this rule does not apply to the *liṅ* (optative) in the *ātmanepada*.
*iṇo gā luṅi* || 45 || [In the *luṅ* (aorist), *gā* is substituted for *iṇ*.]

In the *luṅ* tense, the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go") undergoes the substitution *gā*. By the rule *gāti-sthā-*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*. Thus: *agāt*. It should be stated that [the rules] apply as for *iṇ* even when the prefix *adhi-* is present. Thus: *adhyagāt*; *adhyaguḥ* (where *jus* is substituted for *jhi* by the rule *ātaḥ*).
In the causative (*ṇic*), the root *gam* is used except in the sense of "understanding. (Pāṇini 2.4.46)

The root *gam* shall take the place of *iṇ* before the suffix *ṇic*, except when meaning "to cause to understand. Thus, *gamayati*. But when meaning "to cause to understand," it is *pratyāyayati*. It should be stated that [the rule] applies as if to *iṇ*: *adhigamayati*. The root *ik* means "to remember. Regarding this, some say: there is an extension (*atideśa*) of grammatical operations even for those not included within the *ārdhadhātuka* domain; therefore, by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*, *ik* also undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution. Thus: *adhiyanti*, *adhītya*. They further state that by the rule *eti-stu-śāsv-...* the suffix *kyap* is applied. Others, however, say that there is only the extension of operations belonging to the *ārdhadhātuka* domain, and thus only *iyaṅ* occurs: *adhīyanti*. For this very reason, Bhāravi says in the *Kirātārjunīya*: "studying the two Rāghavas together with Sītā" (*sasītayorāghavayoradhīyan*).
And before the suffix *san*. (Pāṇini 6.1.47)

The root *gam* may replace *iṇ* [in the sense of motion], but not in the sense of "understanding. [Example: *jigamiṣati* ("he wishes to go"). However, in the sense of understanding, [the form is] *pratīṣiṣati*. Here, once the suffix *san* has been applied, by the rule "of that which begins with a vowel, the second [syllable]," there is reduplication of the suffix *san* itself. By the rule "in *san*, [the vowel] *a* becomes *i*," the vowel substitution occurs. By the rule "for [the *s* of] an affix following a substitute," the retroflexion (*ṣatva*) occurs. The meaning is: "he wishes to understand. Due to the extended application (*atideśa*), the initial [augment] also applies: *adhijigamiṣati*. In the passive voice, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used. By the rule "lengthening of the vowel of roots ending in *aj*, *han*, or *gam* before *san*," there is lengthening when *san* begins with a *jhal* consonant. Because of the statement "the augment *iṭ* follows *gam* in the *parasmaipada*," it is absent in the *ātmanepada*. [Example: *jigāṃsyate*.
*adhijigāṃsyate*. Because the rule for lengthening applies only to the substitute *gami* (from *iṇ*), there is no lengthening in the original form *gam*. [Examples: *jigaṃsyate*, *sañjigaṃsate*.
Also from *iṅ*: Pāṇini 6.1.48.
The root √i, meaning "to study," becomes √gā when followed by the desiderative suffix (saN). *Adhijigāṃsate* means "he desires to perform the act of studying.
Rule 49: *gāṅ liṭi* ("the substitute *gāṅ* occurs before the perfect tense marker *liṬ*").

When the *liṭ* [perfect] affix follows, the substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ* (the root meaning "to study") may optionally take place. Thus, we have *adhijage*. Nor is the *ṅ*-marking (*ṅittva*) redundant once the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (treating the substitute as the original). This is because the purpose of the *ṅ*-mark is to ensure that the substitute *gāṅ* is not included in the rule *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.1]. Otherwise, in a form such as *agāsātāṃ grāmau devadattena*, the *ṅ*-marking would cause the substitution of *ī* [for the final vowel] to apply. Nor can one argue that only the root *gāṅ gatāv* ("to go") is intended there; for while the *ṅ*-mark of that specific root serves its purpose by triggering the middle voice, the *ṅ*-marking of the substitute is more powerful, as it serves no other purpose.

Now, when a word with an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is uttered with a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the substitution occurs even before the *itsaṃjñā* (the designation "it") has been applied; or, once the *itsaṃjñā* has been applied, the operations dependent upon it do not take effect. It is for the purpose of indicating this that the letter *ṅ* is specified [in the rule]. As it has been said: "The mention of a substitute with an *anubandha* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is an absence of *it*-operations. Consequently, in the case of the substitute *khyāñ* for the root *cakṣiṅ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur invariably, but rather only optionally, because of the presence of the *ñ*.

In the example *pacamānau yajamānaḥ*, the substitution of *aitva* (the replacement of the penultimate vowel with *e*) does not occur because of the rule *ṭitaḥ*. In the example *nandanāḥ kārakāḥ*, once the substitutions *an* and *aka* have been applied by the rule *yuvoranākau*, neither the suffix *ṅīp* nor the augment *num* occurs, according to the rules *ugitaśca* and *ugidacām*. This is because the statement in Amara’s lexicon that "the suffix *lyu* denotes the agent" (*lyuḥ kartari*) is merely general; for this very reason, Śrīharṣa specifically refers to her as *sā bhīmanarendranandanā*.

[Objection: But if this is so, then in the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ*, since *mi* is specified with its *anubandha*, the designation *pit* would be impossible for the substitute *am*. Consequently, because of the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* [which treats substitutes ending in *ap* as having the *ṅit* property], there would be no *ṅit*-ness; thus, in forms such as *acinavam* and *akaravam*, there would be no guna by the prohibition *ṅkiti ca*. Furthermore, in *mā hi sma cinavam*, there would be no anudātta accent. Similarly, in *veda* and *vettha*, there would be no guna in the substitutes for *ti* and *sip*. [Reply: This is not so, because one should read the rule simply as *tasthasthāmnām*, having removed the letter *p*.

Furthermore, in the rule for the substitution of *ṇal* and *thal*, the forms *tiP* and *sip* are not mentioned as being qualified by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "Since the optional application of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings is established by the very force of the inclusion of the indicatory *ṅ* [in *ṇal*], because the status of being *ātmanepada* is prescribed only for those [endings] that are actually mentioned in rules such as *tiP-tasi-*, etc. This is established because it will be stated later that 'the status of being *uG* is due to the nasalization of *yu* and *vu*. Consequently, since the status of being *uG* does not exist in the original substituends (*sthānin*), its existence in their substitutes is far removed. Therefore, it is settled that the indicatory *ṅ* is solely for the purpose of qualification. [The rule: *vibhāṣā luṅ-lṛṅoḥ* || 50 || [The ātmanepada endings are optionally used after the roots *dīp*, *jīp*, *pīp*, *rīp*, *vīp*, *śvit*, and *mīp* in the *luṅ* and *lṛṅ* tenses.]
And [the substitution of *guṇa* for *vṛddhi*] does not occur before the affix *ṇau*, nor before the *saṅ* (i.e., *san*) or *caṅ* (i.e., *aṅ* of the reduplication). || 51 ||

The root *iṅ* may optionally become *gāṅ* when followed by a causative suffix (*ṇi*) that is itself followed by a desiderative suffix (*san*) or an aorist suffix (*caṅ*). Thus: *adhijigāpayiṣati* (he desires to cause [the pupil] to study) and *adhyāpipayiṣati* (he desires to cause [the pupil] to study). By the rule "for *krī*, *iṅ*, and *jī* before a causative suffix," there is the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel; hence: *adhyajīgapat* (he caused [the pupil] to study) and *adhyāpipat* (he caused [the pupil] to study).
Asterbhūḥ. || 52 ||

The substitution of *bhū* for *as* occurs before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. The rule is formulated there specifically to prevent the application of *as* in such contexts. Examples include *bhavitā* (he will be) and *bhavitum* (to be). In forms such as *indāmāsa*, the substitution of *bhū* occurs by virtue of the specific injunction regarding the auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*). Otherwise, having recited the rule *abhūtatadbhāve 'sti-kṛ-bhū-yoge* (Pāṇini 5.4.50), one would have placed *as* outside the pratyāhāra (the group of roots beginning with *as*). In the established system, according to the rule *maya u yaṇ* (Pāṇini 6.1.78), if both the *bhakāra* and *vakāra* were doubled, it would result in the redundancy of half-mātrās. Alternatively, one might simply state that *kr* is used as the auxiliary.

In such examples as *prādurāsan bahulakṣapācchavayaḥ*, the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which is a substitute for a verbal form (*tiṅanta-pratirūpaka*) is indeed indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). By this, the expression *prādurāsur atha kāmakelayaḥ* is also explained. Vāmana maintains that the form *āsa* is derived from the root *as*. [The root] *as* is used in the senses of "going," "shining," and "taking. Because it is indicated with a *luk* elision, there is no substitution of *bhū* for it.
The word *brū* denotes speech. || 53 ||

The root *būñ* means "in distinct speech. In the context of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, this [root] is replaced by *vac*. From the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking," the *luṅ* (aorist) tense is formed; with the augment *um*, it becomes *avocat*.
For the root *cakṣiṅ*, [the substitute] *khyāñ* [is applied].
And [the augment] liṭ.

On this point, the Bhāṣya states: This substitution is *kh-śāñ*. Within the governing rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, it should be stated as an optional (*vibhāṣā*) insertion that the change of *ś* to *y* occurs immediately after the section on *ṇatva*. Consequently, because that [substitution of *y*] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the grammatical operation caused by it does not take place; rather, only the operation caused by the letter *ś* occurs. As for the change to *c* (*cartva*), since it is subsequent, when it is to be applied, the substitution of *y* is already established as valid; thus, the change to *c* does not proceed, and forms such as *khyāta* are established. In the alternative case where the substitution of *y* does not occur, when the change to *c* is applied to the letter *kh*, forms such as *kśāta* are established.

And so says the Vārttika: "The statement that *śa* is applied to *asiddha* is optional (*vibhāṣā*). By this, from *suṣṭhu pracaṣṭe*, we derive *suprakhyaḥ*. According to the rule *ātaścopasarge*, the suffix *ka* is applied. From *suprakhyasya bhāvaḥ*, we derive *sauprakhyam*. In the sense of "belonging to one who is well-known" (*sauprakhyīyaḥ*), the suffix *vuñ* is applied by virtue of the word ending in *ya* (i.e., *prakhya*). In the absence of *vuñ* under the rule *dhanvayopadhāt*, the suffix *cha* is applied after a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel. In the case of *ākhyāta*, there is no substitution of *ṇatva* for the final *t* because of the rule *saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ*. In *pukhyānam*, there is no substitution of *ru* for the *m* of *pum* because of the rule *pumaḥ khayyampare*.

In the word *paryākhyānam*, because of the intervention of the letter *śa*, there is an absence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ*. Similarly, for the root *khyā* in the sense of "speaking," [there is no ṇatva] due to the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) in the form *lubayogāprakhyānāt*. In the expression *namaḥ khyātre*, since there is an absence of homogeneity (*sasthānatva*), only the rule *śarpare* applies. This is the technical name used by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*) for the *jihvāmūlīya* sound. Therefore, it is established that *kh* is the substitute for *ś*. The prohibition must be stated in the case of exclusion (*varjana*). For example: *avasaṃcakṣyāḥ*, *parisaṃcakṣyāḥ*, meaning "those who are to be excluded."

There is also a prohibition regarding the two forms *asanayoḥ*. In the Veda, it is *nṛcakṣārakṣa*, whereas in common usage (*loke*), it is *nṛcakṣorakṣa*; [the latter] is derived from *vicakṣaṇaḥ* by the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), which prescribes the suffix *yuc*. The statement "frequently" (*bahulam*) is for the sake of including *taṇi*, *anna*, *vadha-ka*, *gātra*, *vicakṣaṇa*, *ajira*, and so forth. This introduction serves as a general supplement to the entire section. The technical term *taṇi* is a convention established by ancient teachers for the Vedic language (*chandas*). *Anna*: here there is no substitution of *jagdhi*. *Vadhaka*: this is formed with the suffix *ṇvul*; in that case, the substitution of *vadh* is prescribed. *Gātra*: from the root *iṇ*, with the suffix *ṣṭran* (an *uṇādi* suffix), there is the substitution of *gā*.

In the word *vicakṣaṇaḥ*, there is an absence of the substitution of *khyāñ*; in *ajirā*, the meaning is the absence of the substitution of *vī*. Here, this should be noted: some maintain that the root *khyā* is also listed in the *ad*-class (the second class) with the sense of "speaking" (*praka-thana*). This applies exclusively to the domain of sārvadhātuka suffixes; otherwise, in the expression *tasmān namo khyātre*, the substitution of the jihvāmūlīya [ḫ] would be unavoidable, and consequently, the Vārttika *namaḥ khyātre*—which prescribes the replacement by the sibilant of similar place of articulation (*sasthānatva*)—would become inapplicable. Thus say some.

That is questionable; for even on that basis, it is more appropriate to assume that such a usage does not occur in a co-occurrence where the *jihvāmūlīya* (the guttural fricative) would otherwise be required. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the rule *na dhyākhyā* becoming inapplicable; for the prohibition applies only to the root *khyā* in the sense of "speaking," as it is specifically mentioned by its own form (*pratipadokta*), and not to the substitute *kh* for *śā*, according to Kaiyaṭa’s statement that the substitution of *yatva* (the palatal *y*) in that case is based on a derivative definition (*lākṣaṇika*). Moreover, this contradicts Kaiyaṭa’s own commentary on the sūtra *lubyogāprakhyānāt*, where he establishes that the absence of *ṇatva* (nasalization) occurs due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*).

By this, the argument that the inclusion of *khyā* in the rule *na-dhy-ākhyā-* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) is unnecessary is refuted; for neither the author of the Bhāṣya nor the author of the Vārttika has stated it so. By this same reasoning, the works of Haradatta, Mādhava, and others—which claim that the root *khyā* also belongs to the *khśādi* class and that the rule for the substitution of *ya* applies to both [roots *khyā* and *cakṣiṅ*]—are also rejected. This is because that rule is prescribed specifically starting with the root *cakṣiṅ*, and because if it were as they claim, the use of forms from the *khśādi* class would undesirably result even in the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. Even if one were to accept such a consequence, it would contradict the authors' own and others' established texts.

By this, the analysis of *gosaṃkhya* as "one who enumerates cows" (*gāḥ sañcaṣṭe*) is also refuted. For this very reason, the author of the *Nyāsa* states that there is no usage of the root *khyā* preceded by the prefix *sam*. For this same reason, it was stated by that very same author in the rule *dṛśe vikhye ca* that the suffix *ka* is also applied to *khyā*. As for the usage *saṃkhya*, his intention is that it is the substitute [for *khyā*] that takes the suffix *ka* in the rule.

By this, the statement of the ancient authors—"some [say] not in the verbal root *khyā*"—is explained. This is because in the case of the form *puṃkhyānam*, the meaning is "it does not exist at all" for the sake of uniformity in the result; furthermore, since the suffix *vuñ*, the *ru*-sound, and the *jihvāmūlīya* are accepted in those very treatises, there is no obstacle to both forms. Nor is it impossible for [the rule] to be an indicator (*jñāpaka*), since the application of the substitute [in *aprakhyānāt*] is justified even by other means, and because of the prohibition of *as* and *san*. Moreover, there is no evidence for the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Such is the direction [of the argument]. [The rule applies] optionally in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. (55)

The previously mentioned [substitution] may optionally occur before the *liṭ* suffix: *cakhyau*, *cakśau*, *cacakṣe*. According to the rule "the second consonants [of the reduplicated syllable] remain when followed by a sibilant (*śar*), according to Pauṣkarasādi," there is no substitution of *kh* for the *k* here.
[Next: *ajervyaghañapoḥ* || 56 || [The substitute *vi* is applied in place of the root *aj* (to go) except before the suffixes *ghañ* and *ap*.]

The root *aja* (meaning "to go" and "to throw") optionally undergoes the substitution of *vī* when followed by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, with the exception of the suffixes *ghañ* and *apa*. [Examples: *vivāya*, *vivyatuḥ*, *vivyuḥ*. Regarding the prohibition of the change to *vī*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *kyac*: [example] *samajyā*. It should not be argued that this is already established by taking the letter *pa* as the starting point of the pratyāhāra for *kyap*, beginning from the *akāra* of *apo*. For in the case of *saṃvītiḥ*, the change to *vī* would otherwise be untenable. In fact, the rule should be explained by carrying over the word "optionally" (*vā*) and interpreting it as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

By that [rule], there is the substitution of *vī* for *vyā* in the forms *pravetā*, *pravetu*, *pravītorathaḥ*, and *saṃvītiḥ*. However, in *samājaḥ*, *udājaḥ*, *samajanam*, and *samajyā*, there is an absence of that substitution. Consequently, there is an option regarding the substitution of *vī* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant having a marker *ṅ* (valādi), such as the suffix *lyuṭ*; thus, the form *prājitā* is also established. As Amara states: "The driver (*niyantā*), the charioteer (*prājitā*), the controller (*yantā*), and the groom (*sūta*). [The forms] *prājanam* and *pravayaṇam* are likewise established. Nor is the rule for *vāyau* redundant; for it does not serve the purpose of providing that option.

Furthermore, the word *yajimani* is formed with the suffix *uCi* by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *vī* for *aj*. Thus, the *Bhāṣya* states that by this, *vāyuḥ* is established. In the same way, forms such as *ājitha* and others should be understood in the case of the suffix *thal* and so on. Since the suffix begins with a consonant (*hal*) even before the production of the *yaṅ* affix, the *yaṅ* occurs [in *vevīyate*]. However, there is no *yaṅ-luk* (elision of *yaṅ*), because the scope is removed by the elision (*luk*), and thus there is an absence of the manifestation of the specific form of the *ārdhadhātuka* [suffix]. This summary is stated in the *Kaustubha*: "The substitution of *vī* for *aj* is not accepted in the case of the *ghañ*, *ap*, or *kyap* suffixes.
It is optional after suffixes beginning with a *val* sound or *y*, but elsewhere it is mandatory; such is the settled conclusion."
The section on *ārdhadhātuka* affixes is completed. [Now follows:

"After a patronymic derived from a word ending in the suffix *ṇya*, or from a *kṣatriya* name, or from a *ṛṣi* name, when the suffix *añ* is added, there is elision (*luk*) of both *aṇ* and *iñ* in the sense of a younger descendant. (Pāṇini 2.4.58)

The term *kṣatriya-pada* refers to the [specific] lineage (*gotra*) of that [class]. *Ārṣa* means "the offspring of a seer" (*ṛṣi*). In the case of [the word *ārṣeya*], because it follows the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied; however, in cases such as *ārṣeyaṃ vṛṇīte*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it belongs to the *śubhra* group. There is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*—which follow [respectively] a word ending in the suffix *ṇya* denoting a *kṣatriya* lineage, and a word ending in a lineage suffix (*gotra-pratyaya*) denoting a seer (*ṛṣi*), provided they denote a younger descendant (*yuvan*). [Example: From the root *kuru*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied: *kauryaḥ* (the father). From that, the suffix *iñ* is applied for the younger descendant; there is its elision (*luk*). Thus: *kauravyaḥ* (the son).

As for the word *kauravya* occurring in [the list] beginning with *tikādi*, since it is prescribed by the rule *kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ* as denoting a *kṣatriya* lineage (*gotra*), the form *kauravyāyaṇiḥ* takes the suffix *phiñ*. However, this [present case] is a *brāhmaṇa* lineage; [here] the suffix is *ṇyaḥ*. By the rule *ṛṣyandhaketi aṇ*, [we have] *iñ*; its elision (*luk*) occurs. *Śvāphalkaḥ* is the father; *Śvāphalkaḥ* is the son. [This is] a *kṣatriya* [lineage]. By the rule *vasiṣṭhādṛṣyaṇ*, [we have] *aṇ*; from that, *iñ*; its elision occurs. *Vāsiṣṭhaḥ* is the father; *Vāsiṣṭhaḥ* is the son. [This is] an *ārṣa* [lineage]. By the rule *vidādyañ*, [we have] *yañ*; in the *yuvan* [generation], *iñ*; its elision occurs. *Baidaḥ* is the father; *Baidaḥ* is the son. [The suffix is] *ñit*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [patronymics] such as *taika* and others; then *phiñ*; then, for a descendant in the younger generation, *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "from here up to *prāgdīvyataḥ*"; then there is its elision (*luk*). Thus: *taikāyaniḥ* is the father; *taikāyaniḥ* is the son.
Regarding the sense of contempt (*kutsā*), the lineage of the Sauviras is excluded; otherwise, because of the rule "there, *phic* or *cha*," the suffix *cha* would apply.

"Yamunda and Suyāma take the suffix *phiñ* after [the patronymic] Vārṣyāyaṇi"—thus the elders say, because this enumeration is based on the authority of the sages (*ārṣa*). What is the purpose of this? [The rule] "from *śiva* and others, the suffix *aṇ*" applies. Then, for a young descendant (*yuvan*), the suffix *iñ* is applied, which is subsequently elided (*luk*). Thus: *kauhaḍaḥ* is the father; *kauhaḍiḥ* is the son (the young descendant). Why "for a young descendant"? [Consider: "the pupils of Vāmarathya" = *vāmarathāḥ*. Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) by the rule "from *kurv* and others, the suffix *aṇya*; from *kaṇva* and others, [the suffix *aṇ*] in the sense of lineage. Since everything regarding Vāmarathya follows the pattern of *kaṇva* and others due to his inclusion among the *kurv*-group, there is no elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. Why "of *aṇ* and *iñ*"? [Consider: the young descendant of Dākṣi is *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*. Here, the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule "after [patronymics ending in] *yañ* and *iñ*, [the suffix *phak*]."

An addition [to the rule] regarding the elision (*luk*) of the *yu* suffixes [such as *iñ* and *phiñ*] after [patronymics] consisting merely of non-Brāhmaṇa lineages (*gotra*). The word "merely" (*mātra*) signifies "entirety. The meaning is that even in the absence of the Kṣatriya or other castes, by the mere fact of being a non-Brāhmaṇa, there is elision of the suffix following that [base], even if it is different from *aṇ* or *iñ*. For example: Baudhi is the father; Baudhi is the son. Jābāli is the father; Jābāli is the son. Audumbari is the father; Audumbari is the son. Bhaṇḍijaṅgha and Karṇakhara were two Vaiśyas; from them, the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ*. From a base ending in that [suffix], there is elision of the *phañ* suffix. Thus, Bhāṇijaṅghi is both the father and the son. Kārṇakharaki is likewise.
And [there is elision] after the group beginning with Paila (Pailādi). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.59)

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan* suffix after [the patronymic] *pīlāya*, following the rule for the *aṇ* suffix. Then, by the rule "after a word ending in *aṇ* having two syllables," there is the *phiñ* suffix; its elision results in *pailaḥ* for both father and son. Other names such as *paila* and so forth end in *iñ*. Although the elision of *iñ* is established by the rule "of the *iñ* suffix after [names of] the Easterners," this recitation is for the purpose of including those not belonging to the Easterners. The list includes: *paila*, *śālaṅki*, *sātyaki*, *sātyaṃkāmi*, *audavraji*, *audameyi*, *audañci*, *audamañji*, *daivasthāni*, *paiṅgali*, *audayini*, *bhauliṅgi*, *vāṇi*, *saumani*, *audamāni*, *auñjihmayani*, *auñjihāni*, *audaśuddhi*; this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).

The rule "tadrājāccaṇaḥ" is an internal sub-rule (antargaṇasūtra). It prescribes the elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan* suffix after a *tadrāja* [patronymic] ending in *aṇ*. [In this case: from the word *Aṅga*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "dvyañmagadha... [Pāṇini 4.1.170]. From that *aṇ*-ending, the suffix *phiñ* is applied by the rule "aṇo dvyacaḥ" [Pāṇini 4.1.156]. There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix], resulting in *āṅgaḥ pitā putraśca* ("the father and son are both Āṅgas").
In the opinion of the Easterners, [the augment *iṭ* is added] after the root *iṇ*.

The suffix *iñ* is elided after a patronymic (*gotra*) ending in *ya*, provided that the patronymic belongs to the Easterners (*prācām*). The mention of "the Easterners" is not intended to provide an option; this is because it is so explained by authoritative commentators. *Pannāgāra*: one by whom a house (*gāra*) has been reached (*panna*) is *pannāgāra*. From that, the suffix *iñ* is applied. Then, by the rule *yañiñoś ca*, the suffix *iphak* is added. That [suffix] is elided. Thus, *pānnāgāriḥ* applies to both the father and the son. Why "of the Easterners"? Consider *dākṣiḥ*: the father is *dākṣāyaṇiḥ* and the son is *dākṣiḥ*.
Not after [patronymics ending in] -taulvali. || 61 ||

The elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan*-suffix following [names] beginning with *taulvali* does not occur by virtue of the preceding rule. *Taulvaliḥ* is the father, being the offspring of *Tulvala*; [the suffix] *phak* [is applied]. *Taulvalāyanaḥ* is the son. [The names] *taulvali*, *tailvali*, *dhāraṇi*, and *pārāṇiṣa* are derived from the roots *dhṛ* and *pṛ* respectively with the suffix *lyu* (as per the *nandigrahipacādibhyaḥ lyuṇinyacaḥ* rule), followed by the suffix *iñ*. [The names] *dailīpi*, *daivāli*, *daivamitri*, and *daivayajñi* are formed similarly; *daivamitri* means "one whose friend is the gods" (*devā mitram asya*), and *daivayajñi* means "one whose sacrifice is for the gods" (*devebhyo yajño 'sya*).

Prāṇehati, cāpaṭaki, ānuharati, śvāphalki, ānumati, āhisi, āsuri, āyudhi, naimiṣi, āsibandhaki, baili, pauṣki, pauṣkarasādi, ānuhārati. He who sits at Puṣkara—a specific sacred site—is Puṣkarasat. "Anuharati" means he follows or imitates; the suffix *iñ* is applied because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. There is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts of the compound because it belongs to the *anuśatika-ādi* group. Pauṣyi, vairīka, vaihati. Vaikarṇiḥ refers to one whose ears are deformed (*vilakṣaṇau karṇau asya*). Kāmali.

"Upakośala Hāvai Kāmalāyana," thus [says] the Chandogya Upaniṣad. "Kāreṇupāli": one who protects an elephant (*kareṇu*) is a *kareṇupāla*. Glory! Thus ends the first daily lesson (*āhnika*) in the fourth quarter of the second book in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
The second section of the fourth chapter.
In the case of a descendant of a king, [the suffix] is applied by the word "bahusuta" itself, provided it does not refer to a female.

The suffix *rājanya* (denoting a descendant of a king) shall undergo elision (*luk*) when expressing only the plural number of its own base meaning, but not in the feminine. Thus: *aikṣvākaḥ*, *aikṣvākau*. From a word denoting a country, the suffix *añ* is applied when it signifies a Kṣatriya; this suffix is elided in the plural: *ikṣvākavaḥ*. As Kālidāsa says: "In a matter difficult for the Ikṣvākus to achieve... (*ikṣvākūṇāṃ durāpe 'rthe*).

"How then [should one explain] Murāri’s statement: 'May our blessings bear fruit today among the Ikṣvākus and the Maithilas'? Regarding this, they say: [The word *aikṣvāka*] means "born in the country (*janapada*) of the Ikṣvākus. By the rule *kopadhādaṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; because this [country] is not a *tadrāja* (a name of a king), there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix. [Similarly,] *kaukhyāḥ paśavaḥ* ("cattle born in that same [place]"); and in such cases as *teṣām eva raghoḥ pāṇḍyāḥ* ("the Pāṇḍyas of that very Raghu"), it should be explained as "those who are fit (*sādhavaḥ*) for Kaukha and for Pāṇḍya. "I shall describe the lineage of the Raghus; you are those Raghus of renowned luster, by whom even the Lord of the Gods..."

Regarding the verse beginning with "nirudhyamānā yadubhiḥ kathañcit," the author of the commentary [the Granthakṛt] maintains that although the elision of the patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*) is untenable because the status of being a king (*rājatva*) is absent in them, the term is used there figuratively to denote their offspring. Lineage (*vaṃśatva*) consists in being either the progenitor or the progeny, as no other definition can be easily stated. Thus, he says: "I shall describe the progeny of Raghu—both those who were born from him and those who were his progenitors. Here, the quality of being a progenitor (*janakatva*) is common to both direct and indirect descent. By virtue of being a progenitor, all ancestors up to Raghu are included; by virtue of being progeny (*janyatva*), Daśaratha and the others are included.
Since they too are the offspring of Aghora, there is no fault in including Aja as well by virtue of being their progenitor.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Here, there arises a doubt as to whether the term *bahupada* refers to the plural number (*bahuvacana*) or to the sense of plurality (*bahvartha*), since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) exists for both. To explain: the statement "by that very [rule]" (*tenaiva*) serves as the indicative mark in the first case; for it is intended to prevent the elision (*luk*) in the formation of *priyavāṅgāḥ*, meaning "those to whom pleasant speech is dear. However, that [elision] is not possible [in that context], because when the Taddhita suffix denoting a royal descendant (*tadrāja*) occurs in the plural, there is no application of the compound (*vṛtti*), and thus the elision does not even arise; consequently, there would be no need to employ a means to prevent it. But if [the term] refers to the plural number, then the elision would indeed arise there.

And thus, the inclusion of the phrase "by that very [rule]" implies that the rule *bahuṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.21) is intended to convey the sense of the plural number, by virtue of its causing the contingency of that which is the counter-positive of the negation occasioned by itself; this is the resultant meaning.

The second [view], however, holds that "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is a *liṅga* (indicatory mark). For that [mark] is intended to prevent the application of elision (*luk*) in the rule *āṅgyaḥ striyām*. But there is no possibility of such elision there according to the aforementioned method, because the plural number is separated by a feminine suffix and thus does not follow immediately after a *tadrāja* [patronymic] stem. However, when there is multiplicity of referents, since the women denoted by the word *āṅgī* are many, [the term *striyām*] serves to indicate that the meaning of the prior member [of the compound] is predominant. Among these, the first position—that there is elision when a plural case-ending follows—is incorrect.

Otherwise, there would be the cumbersome requirement of formulating a prohibition stating "not when [the suffix] is feminine" (*astriyām*). However, according to this system, since that [prohibition] does not apply precisely because of the intervention of a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), such a prohibition is unnecessary. One might argue: "In the case of *ambaṣṭhyaḥ*—meaning many female descendants of an *ambaṣṭhi* woman—the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied by the rule *vṛddhet-kosala-ajādāt*. Then, by the rule *yaṅaś-cāp*, the suffix *cāp* is added. This results in a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*. Since this [long vowel] is treated as if it were the final element (*antavadbhāva*), it does not constitute an intervention; thus, the [suffix] would be subject to elision (*luk*) even under the opponent's view, and therefore the restriction 'not when feminine' (*astriyām*) is essential. This objection is invalid. Because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, the elision (*luk*) does not apply.

Nor should it be argued that even in the Siddhānta there is parsimony (lāghava) because the word "tenaiva" (by that very [suffix]) is not employed; for in the case of *priyavāṅga*, where the meaning of the compound is plural, the elision (*luk*) would not apply simply because the suffix ending in *tadrāja* does not denote a plurality. Even so, in cases such as *gārgyaś ca vātsyaś ca vājyaś ca* → *gargavatsavājāḥ*, the elision would not occur because the patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*), which is the counter-correlate of the elision, was produced with reference to only a single referent (*artha*), and thus lacks plurality.

The meaning is that, since it has been stated that "there is an elision [of the case-ending] when there are many in a *dvandva*," another rule would have to be commenced for the sake of that elision (*luk*). Nor should it be argued that even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the elision is prescribed when a plural suffix follows, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when this is specified, it refers to what precedes" applies; thus, since the plural suffix following the compound as a whole does not follow each individual member, the elision would not occur—because the plural suffix produced from the compound follows only the final member. For the elision of the final member alone is already established.

Furthermore, the descendants of Bida are many, hence *baidāḥ*. By the rule *bidādi-tvād-añ*, the suffix *añ* is applied. The young descendant (*yuvāpatyam*) of the Bidas is *baidaḥ* (dual: *baidau*). Here, by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañato luk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix. In this case, the patronymic suffix, which was originally produced in the sense of a plural number of descendants, has shifted to another meaning—specifically to a meaning characterized by duality or singularity—when there is a desire to express a young descendant. Since that suffix was produced in the plural, its elision would have been required; therefore, the statement of non-elision (*aluk-vacanam*) must be undertaken. However, according to the view that [the suffix] remains as a suffix (*pratyaya-pakṣe*), there is no elision precisely because there is no subsequent plural number (*bahuvacana-paratva-abhāvāt*).

As it has been said: "When a *gotra* [patronymic] stem ending in the plural, which otherwise undergoes elision (*lopin*), is applied to denote many, there is elision (*luk*) when two or one are meant. The mention of "two or one" here is an indication that the primary focus is on the state (*bhāva*) [of duality or singularity]. Nor should it be argued that the desired result is already established by the rule *gotre'lugacī* (Pāṇini 4.1.89), which prohibits elision (*luk*) before an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group; for in this case, there is no subsequent affix beginning with a vowel. Furthermore, the rule regarding the non-application of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* applies specifically when the operation depends upon a phoneme (*varṇa*). Thus, the offspring of one *Baida*, or of two *Baidas*, being many young students (*māṇavaka*), are called *Bidāḥ*.

In this case as well, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *yañañośca* would not occur, because the suffix *añ* does not have multiple bases (*bahuprakṛti*). Nor should it be argued that the elision is established because, when a suffix is mentioned, there is an inclusion of that which ends in it (*tadantagrahaṇa*), and thus the plural number serves as a qualifier specifically for that which ends in *añ*; for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *kāśyapāḥ*, meaning "images of Kāśyapa. *Kāśyapa* means the descendant of Kaśyapa in the lineage (*gotra-apatya*); the suffix *añ* is applied here because [Kaśyapa] belongs to the *bidādi* group. The suffix *kan* is then added in the sense of "an image thereof" (*tatprakṛti*) according to the rule *ive pratikṛtau*, or alternatively, according to the rule *jīvikārthe cāpaṇye*.

Alternatively, the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] may occur because of the reading "in images, worship, purpose, paintings, and banners. However, since there is the possibility of elision for this suffix ending in *añ* when it occurs in a plural sense, one must state in that context simply: "after *añ*, in the plural. This is because the technical designations such as *luk* are prescribed for the non-appearance of suffixes themselves; and since suffixes alone are the bearers of grammatical operations, they alone are to be qualified by plurality. Consequently, in the case of *bidāḥ*, since the suffix *añ* has been produced from only a single [base], there would be no elision; therefore, the rule for elision must be formulated.
As it has been said: "When a singular form is applied to many [objects], there is elision of the dual ending for the sake of the youth (yuvan). This has already been explained.

Now, it might be argued: since the *dvandva* compound is defined as expressing multiple substrates simultaneously (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacana*), in the case of *gargavatsavājāḥ*, each of the two constituent members expresses three referents; thus, the plural suffixes of the *tadrāja* secondary endings indeed possess a plural sense for each member individually. Consequently, the previously mentioned rule regarding the elision (*luk*) when there are not many [referents] in a *dvandva* would simply not have been formulated at all. If that is so, then the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) also accepts the elision when a plural suffix follows; therefore, since the plural suffix exists even after each individual member, there is no room for that defect, and the situation is the same for both sides.

Nor should it be asked how [the grammatical operation] occurs when *luk* (elision) has been applied; for the matter is resolved by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating as if a suffix were present). Nor should one fear the prohibition stated in *nalumatāṅgasya*; for its explanation is that when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, any operation prescribed under the heading of *aṅga* (stem)—whether internal to the stem or external to it—does not take place. Since *luk* is an operation pertaining specifically to the suffix and not to the entire stem, the application of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* is easily established.

By this [principle], in the case of *atyaṅga*—derived from *ati-aṅga* with the suffix *jas*—once the *luk* elision has first been applied according to the maxim "even internal [rules] are superseded," the elision of the *ra* in *tadrāja* would not occur because the condition of being followed by a plural ending (*bahuvacana*) is absent.

But surely, in this way, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *pañcagārgyaḥ* ("a cloth bought for five Gārgīs") or *daśagārgyaḥ*. Here, the suffix *ṭhak*—which expresses the sense of "bought" (*krīta*) and is added by the rule *arhīya*—is elided by the rule *adhyardha-*. Then, by the rule *luk-taddhita-luki*, the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is elided. In that case, since the elision of *yañ* (by *yañañośca*) is not an operation on the base (*aṅgakārya*), one might rely on the application of the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (P. 1.1.62) according to the method stated above; consequently, the elision of *yañ* by the rule *yañañośca* would apply, resulting in the undesirable form *pañcagargaḥ* or *daśagargaḥ*. Nor can this be resolved by the condition *na cāstriyām* ("not when [the base] is feminine").

The objection that—in the case of *gargamayam*, where the meaning of the base-word (*varti-padartha*) is shifted to another sense—the suffix would not take the *luṅ* augment because it is not followed by a plural number (since the suffix is produced from the nominal stem itself even when the analytical vigraha is expressed with a *subanta*), is also refuted. This is because of the governing rule *samarthānāṃ prathamād vā*; since there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) only with a *subanta*, and because it is the second [element] which must be a *subanta* that is connected [to the first]. Furthermore, the governing rule regarding the nominal stem (*prātipadika-adhikāra*) serves only to qualify [the base] as being "old" (*vṛddha*) and so forth.

Indeed, the objection raised against the Siddhāntin—that in cases such as *bidānām apatyam* ("the offspring of the Bidas") and *baidau* (dual), there would be elision (*luk*)—is inconsistent. This is because, according to the reasoning already stated, the Pūrvapakṣin must also maintain that there is no elision due to the presence of a plural suffix. If, however, the prohibition is indeed by the rule *aci* (Pāṇini 7.3.119), then the prohibition based on the principle *varṇāśraye* (Pāṇini 1.1.56) does not apply here. This is because the prohibition *varṇāśraye* serves to prohibit operations conditioned by the specific form of a phoneme (*varṇa*), whereas the present case concerns a situation where the cause for the operation is the specific form of the affix itself, which is not merely a phoneme. Thus, the prohibition *varṇāśraye* does not have scope over this instance.

Therefore, in examples such as *go-hitam*, the substitution of *ava* and so forth does not occur, because the property of being a vowel (*actva*) depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśrayatva*) common to both suffixes and non-suffixes. However, in the case of *atṛṇeḍ*, the augment *iṭ* occurs even though the suffix *tip* has been elided, by virtue of the "suffix-characteristic" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because that [augment] depends on a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*halādi*). This is because the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* is subsumed under the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatvavyāpyatva*). If it is argued that the same applies to elision (*luk*)—namely, that because it depends on a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādipratyaya*), it lacks the status of depending on a phoneme—that argument is equally applicable [to the previous point].

Alternatively, one might argue that the suffix *aluk* should be prescribed without qualification, and then the prohibition "not after *halin*" should be stated. By this, there would be no fault in forms such as *gargarūpyam*. Nor should it be said that, in this case, *aluk* would also apply to a form like *bidānām apatyāni bahavo māṇavakāḥ* ("many boys who are the offspring of the Bidas"). This is because, outside the governing context of "offspring" (*apatya*), the term "lineage" (*gotra*) refers only to the worldly sense of offspring; thus, the elision (*luk*) by the rule *yañañośca* is possible only when there is a plurality of *yuvan* (descendants). And it should not be argued that even in that case, the application of *aluk* would still occur.

This is because of the interpretation of the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamād vā* (Pāṇini 4.1.83) as "among those [suffixes] that are applicable, the elision of *luk* does not occur for the first *gotra*-suffix. In examples such as *gārgiyāḥ*, the "firstness" belongs to that suffix which denotes the primary meaning of the *gotra*. However, in the present case, once the *yuva*-suffix has undergone *luk*, the word *baida*—which ends in a *gotra*-suffix—has shifted to a second meaning characterized by the *yuvan* (descendant), and thus lacks "firstness"; consequently, the rule for *aluk* does not apply again.

And this must necessarily be accepted: *atribharadvājikā*, *vasiṣṭhakaśyapikā*, *bhṛgvaṅgirasikā*, *kutsakuśikikā*. [The forms] "the offspring of Atri" (*atrerapatyāni*) take the suffix *ḍhak* by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*. "The offspring of Bharadvāja" takes the suffix *añ* because it belongs to the *bidādi* group. From both [Atri and Bharadvāja], when expressing the plural of the younger generation, the suffix *iñ* is applied; that [suffix] is elided by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣa...*. For "Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa," etc., there is the elision of *ḍhak*. By the rule *yañañośca*, there is the elision of *añ*. [The form] "the sexual union of the Atris and Bharadvājas" takes the suffix *vuñ* after a *dvandva* compound by the rule *vairamaithunikayoḥ*. From Kaśyapa and Kutsa, the suffix *añ* is applied. From Vasiṣṭha and the others, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied.

If the *aluk* (non-elision) were to apply even when [the suffix] has transitioned to the second meaning (*artha*), or if—in the case of the literal formulation *gargabhācī*—the *aluk* were unavoidable; or alternatively, if the mention of *gargabhārgavikā* were for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): namely, that after *garga* and others there is *yañ*, which is elided; after the word *bhṛgu* there is *ṛṣyaṇ*; after that [suffix] there is *yūnyañ*, which is elided; and then *vun* is added in the sense of "the sexual union of the Gargas and Bhṛgus"—in this case, the elision [of *vun*] which would have been required by the rule *atribhṛgukutsa-* etc., is prohibited by its inclusion in the *gopavana-* group.

If the *aluk* (non-elision) were to apply even when [the suffix] has transitioned to a second meaning, then the reading of *gargabhārgavikā* in the *Gopavana* group would be useless. Therefore, it is inferred that the rule for *aluk* does not operate when [the suffix] has transitioned to a second meaning; thus, no fault arises. This [objection] is likewise equal. As for what was said—that in the case of "the offspring of Baida" (*baida*) or "many Māmakas who are Bidās," since the *añ* suffix does not have multiple bases, there would be no elision (*luk*)—[that too is refuted].

"And there is no fault in the case of *kāśyapāḥ* [meaning] 'images of Kāśyapa,' because the suffix *-añ-* ending [word] is understood there only when it denotes a plurality of offspring; since the word *kāśyapāḥ* ending in *-añ-* here functions to denote a plurality of images, the elision (*luk*) does not apply. Furthermore, because the meaning already stated is obtained through the desire to express a commonality (*sājātya*) by treating the object of the elision as the meaning of the suffix—given that there is a commonality between the lineage-descendant (*gotra*) and the younger descendant (*yuvan*) insofar as they are both offspring, whereas that [commonality] is absent in the case of an image—therefore, even in the final position (*siddhānta*), there is no complexity. If this is argued, it is true;
nevertheless, since the fault has not been pointed out even in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the objection stands]. Thus, it being established:

The author of the Bhāṣya states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): If it were stated that "elision (*luk*) occurs when a plural suffix (*bahuvacana*) follows," there would be a fault in the case of *atrayaḥ*. To explain: from the word *atri*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*; since this suffix is marked with *k*, it has an acute accent on its final syllable. If elision (*luk*) were then applied to the suffix *jas* (the nominative plural ending), the *jas* would acquire an acute accent by the rule *anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ* (which prescribes an acute accent for a vowel where an acute-accented vowel has been elided). Thus, the desired result would not be achieved.

In the case of the *arthapakṣa* (the view that the suffix is meaningful), however, because there is no subsequent cause (*paranimittatva*) for the elision (*luk*), that contingency does not arise; thus, there is simply the low-pitched (*anudātta*) accentuation by the rule *jaso 'nudāttau suppitau*. As for the inclusion of the phrase *astriyām* (not in the feminine), it has indeed been made precisely to exclude forms such as *āṅgyaḥ striyaḥ*; such is the direction of the argument.

Now, if [the rule] "not in the feminine" (*athāstriyām*) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), or if it is a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*): in the first case, in a *dvandva* compound such as *gārgī ca vātsyaś ca vājyaś ca*, there would be elision (*luk*) of all [members], because each individual word-form denotes a collective consisting of both female and male. In the second case, however, [the objection] that "it is clearly not so" is indeed valid; yet regarding this point as well, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The gods (*devāḥ*) ought to know. That is to say, "the gods" refers to those with divine vision, i.e., scholars (*paṇḍita*). On this matter, Kaiyaṭa has provided a twofold explanation.

Some say that because it forms a single syntactical unit with the exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it is more logical due to its parsimony (*lāghava*). Others, however, say that since the word *gārgī* denotes meanings associated with femininity, the suffix *yañ* should not be elided; whereas for others, it should indeed be elided.

Now, where there is a compound of both those that undergo elision (*lopabhāj*) and those that do not, the question arises: does the elision apply because the word ending in the suffix that is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*) of the elision has a plural meaning, or does it apply by virtue of the rule itself? If it is argued that plurality is caused by the absence of proximity [to the eliding factor] and thus is not caused by that [suffix] alone, [the answer is: here too, the *Bhāṣya* states "in both ways," because of the existence of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). This is seen from the usage in *bhṛguvatsāgrāyaṇeṣu* and *agārgyagālavānām*; for in the first case, two [names] undergo elision.

As for *āgrāyaṇa*, because it ends in *phak* after *naḍa* and others, it does not receive the designation of *tadrāja*; thus, the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is applied, and the suffix is elided when two [ancestors] are indicated. However, according to the latter view, both [suffixes] undergo elision. Gālava, however, holds that it ends in *ṛṣyaṇ* and, as before, does not elide the *y*. Nor is there an elision of the elided portion; thus, the sense is that both views are valid due to the existence of these two indicators (*jñāpaka*). [Pāṇini 2.4.63: *yaskādibhyo gotre*.

There shall be elision (*luk*) of a subsequent gotra-suffix when plurality is caused by that [gotra], but not in the feminine. Since the section on gotra-suffixes begins with "In the sense of gotra, after *kuñja* and others, the suffixes *añ* and *phañ*," the term "gotra" here refers to the secular (laukika) gotra in cases other than that. Within the governing context of *apatya* (descendant), the mention of "gotra" specifically intends the technical (pāribhāṣika) gotra. Examples: *yāskāḥ*, *lāhyāḥ*. Why "in the plural"? [Counter-example: *yāskaḥ*, *lāhyaḥ*. But in the feminine: *yāskyaḥ striyaḥ*. Why "gotra"? [Counter-example: *yāskāḥ chātrāḥ* ("the students who are Yāskas").

From *yaska*, *lahya*, *druhya*, *ayasthūṇa*, and *tṛṇakarṇa*—these five—the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "śiva" (*śivādibhyaṣṭhak*). From *sadāmatta*, *kambalabhāra*, *ahiroga*, *karṇāṭaka*, *piṇḍījaṅgha*, and *bakasaktha*—these six—the suffix *iñ* is applied. From *viśri*, *kadrū*, *ajabasti*, and *mitrayu*—these four—the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by virtue of their inclusion in the *śubhrādi* group.

The suffix *iñ* is applied after these twelve: Rakṣomukha, Jaṅkhāratha, Manthaka, Utkāṃsa, Kaṭuka, Puṣkarasat, Veṣapura, Piramekhala, Koṣṭumāya, Kroṣṭumāna, Kroṣṭupāda, and Śīrṣamāya. Although the elision (*luk*) of *iñ*—which would otherwise apply by the rule "for those from the East" (*iñaḥ prācām*)—is prohibited for names such as Taulvalya, there is no dispute regarding the eastern origin of Puṣkarasat; thus, its elision is established by the rule "the elision of *iñ* after polysyllabic [names] among the Easterners and the Bharatas" (*bahvaca iñaḥ prācyabharateṣu*).

Nevertheless, his inclusion among the descendants of Yaska and others is for the purpose of precluding the prohibition [of the *gopa-van* group] and so forth; for in that context, the rule beginning with "taulvaly-ādayaḥ" is recited by some. Even by those who do not recite it there, the inclusion of *tulvala* and other bases within the *gopa-van* group must be inferred from this very indicator (*jñāpaka*). From *kharapa*, the suffix *phak* is applied because it belongs to the *naḍādi* group. From *padaka* and *paryaṅka*, the suffix *iñ* is applied after the elision of *at*. From *bhalandana*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it belongs to the *śivādi* group.
From these four—*bhaṇḍila*, *bhaṇḍiva*, and *bhaṇḍita*—the suffix *phañ* is applied because they belong to the *aśvādi* group. [The rule] *yañañośca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64) [follows].

When there is a suffix *yañ* or *añ* in a *gotra* (patronymic) name, there is elision (*luk*) of both these suffixes when they produce a plural number, provided it is not feminine. Examples: *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*. Here, by the rule *gargādibhyo yañaḥ luk*, there is elision of *yañ*. Examples: *vidāḥ*, *ūrvāḥ*. Here, by the rule *vidādibhyo 'ñ luk*, there is elision of *añ*. Why say "produced by them" (*tatkṛta*)? Consider *priyagārgyāḥ*. Here, the plurality is produced by the meaning of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*). Why say "not feminine" (*astriyām*)? Consider *gārgyaḥ striyaḥ* ("the Gārgya women"). Why say "in a *gotra*" (*gotre*)? Consider *dvaipyāḥ*. [This is formed] by the rule *dvīpāt anusamudraṃ yañ*. Consider *autsāḥ*. [This is formed] by the rule *utsādibhyo 'ñ*. Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to what is well-known from the *Pravarādhyāya*. It does not apply here in cases such as: [e.g., *dvaipyāḥ*].
The terms *pautra* and *dauhitra*. This initial [rule] is commenced for the purpose of [defining] the secondary suffixes (*guṇa*) for those that lack the designation of *tadrāja*.

An addition [to the rule] is that when there is a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of one or two members beginning with *yañ*, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [ending] is elided. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), those suffixes to be mentioned later which undergo elision when plural are also included; this is because the word "etc. is used here in its restrictive sense (*vyavasthā*). For example: *gārgyasya* or *gārgyayoḥ kulaṃ* becomes *gārgyakulaṃ* or *gārgakulaṃ*. *Baidasya* or *baidayoḥ kulaṃ* becomes *baidakulaṃ* or *bidakulaṃ*. Why "beginning with *yañ*" (*yañādīnām*)? To prevent it from applying to cases such as *āṅgakulam*. Why is the specific number [one or two] mentioned? [To show that it does not apply when more than two are involved: *gargāṇāṃ kulaṃ* remains *gargakulam*.

Let there be no option because [the word] occurs later. Why say "tatpuruṣa"? [Counter-example: *upagārgyam*, meaning "near Gārgya. Why say "of the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*)? [Counter-example: *śobhanagārgyaḥ*, meaning "an excellent Gārgya. Let it not apply in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound.
[Also excluded are compounds ending in] Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, Vasiṣṭha, Gotama, and Aṅgiras. (65)

When there is plurality, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the *gotra* suffix. Examples: Atrayas, Bhṛgavas, Kutsās, Vasiṣṭhās, Gotamās, Aṅgirasaḥ. As the Atharvaṇa Śruti says: "Just as the ancient Aṅgirases, Bhṛgus, Atris, and Vasiṣṭhas dwelt [there], so may you drive them away from here. By that very rule, [we have] Priyātreyas. The restriction "provided it is not feminine" (*āstriyam*) applies: feminine forms are Ātreyyaḥ (women).
Regarding the Bahvṛcas, there is elision of the suffix *iñ* among the Easterners and the Bharatas. (Pāṇini 2.4.66)

The suffix *iñ* is elided after a patronymic derived from a base belonging to the *Bahvṛca* class, provided it belongs to the Eastern (Prācya) or Bharata lineages and occurs in the plural. Examples: *pannāgārāḥ*, *mantharaiṣaṇāḥ*, *yudhiṣṭhirāḥ*, *arjunāḥ*, *babhravaḥ*. Why [is the condition] "descendant" (*apatya*) stated? [Consider: *caikayāḥ*, *pauṣayāḥ*. Why [the condition] "Eastern or Bharata" (*prācyabharateṣu*)? [Consider: *bālākayāḥ*, *hāstidāsayaḥ*. In this case, the mention of "Eastern" (*prācya*) within the *karmadhāraya* compound is redundant, because there is nothing to be excluded. However, in the case of a *dvandva* compound, since there are no Bharatas other than those who are Eastern, the desired result is established by the mention of "Eastern" alone.

Although there is a scriptural prohibition against forming a *dvandva* compound of general terms (*sāmānya*) with specific terms (*viśeṣa*), nevertheless, such a formation is possible precisely because it is prescribed by Pāṇini (the *sūtrakāra*). Furthermore, the separate mention of the Bharatas is for the purpose of indicating that when "Easterners" (*prācya*) are mentioned elsewhere, the Bharatas are not included. Consequently, in the rule *ineñaḥ prācām* (A 4.1.101), there is no inclusion of the Bharata gotras. For example: Auḍālaki is the father; Auḍālakāyana is the son.
[The rule] *na gopavanādibhyaḥ* (A 2.4.67) [prohibits the plural suffix *cha*].

There is no elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix when it is conditioned by *gotra*. Examples: *gaupavanāḥ*, *śaigravāḥ*. The group beginning with *gopavana* is an internal sub-group (*antargaṇa*) within the *bidādi* group; this is because there is no insertion of the marker *vṛt* in the middle [of that sub-group] to mark its conclusion. Since it would follow that the suffix is included up to the end of the entire *gaṇa*, it must be stated that there is a prohibition for the *gopavanādi* group prior to the *haritādi* group. Consequently, in the case of *hāritāḥ*, there is indeed no elision (*aluk*).
In a copulative compound (dvandva), [the first member retains its original accent] when preceded by *tiki*, *kitava*, and so forth.

In these cases, the *luk* (elision) of the *gotra* suffix occurs when there is a *dvandva* compound of many members. For example: *taikāyanayaś ca kaitavāyanayaś ca* becomes *tikakitavāḥ*. Here, the *phiñ* suffix [from Pāṇini 4.1.156] is elided by the rule *tikādibhyaḥ phiño luk*. One should not argue that since only those forms appearing as *dvandvas* are listed in the *gaṇa*, one could simply say "after *tika* etc. (*tikādibhyaḥ*). This is because the purpose is to remove the doubt that the *luk* elision applies only to the suffixes of the preceding members of the *dvandva* and not to those of the subsequent members. For example: *vāṅkharayaś ca bhāṇḍīrathayaś ca* becomes *vaṅkharabhaṇḍīrathāḥ*; here, the *iñ* suffix [from Pāṇini 4.1.95] is elided.

From *aupakāyana* and *lāmakāyana*, [the suffix] *upakalamaka* is formed; here the *luk* elision applies to the *pha*-suffix beginning with *naḍa*. From *māḍhakaya* and *nārakaya*, *maḍhakanaraka* is formed; here there is *luk* elision of the *iñ* suffix. From *vākanakhaya* and *svāgurapariṇadvaya*, *vakanakhaśvagurapariṇaddha* is formed. From *aubjaya* and *kākubha*, *ubjakakubha* is formed; here there is *luk* elision of the *iñ* suffix and the *aṇ* suffix derived from the *śivādi* group, respectively. From *lāṅkaya* and *śāntamukhaya*, *laṅkaśāntamukha* is formed; here there is *luk* elision of the *iñ* suffix. From *auragaya* and *śālaṅya*, *uragaśalaṅkaya* is formed.

The suffixes *phiñ*, *ataiñ*, and *añ* are elided (*luk*), as are the names Kārṣṇājinaya and Kārṣṇasundaraya; thus we have Kṛṣṇājina and Kṛṣṇasundara. The suffix *ataiñ* is elided: Āgniveśya and Dāśeraka become Agniveśa and Dāśeraka. The suffix *yañ* from the *garga*-class and the suffix *ataiñ* are elided: Bhrāṣṭraka and Kāpiṣṭhala become Bhrāṣṭraka and Kapiṣṭhala; here the suffix *ataiñ* is elided.
After the words *upaka* and others, the suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is optionally applied when they do not form a *dvandva* compound.

In these [lists], there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the *gotra* suffix when there is a plurality, whether in a *dvandva* compound or not. This is because the mention of "not a *dvandva*" (*advandve*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the term "*dvandva*" does not necessarily carry over [into this rule]. Regarding these, the *Vṛtti* states that three of them—*tika*, *kitava*, and so on—are recited in the *tikakitavādi* group. Kaiyaṭa, however, says that the reading of the *dvandva* "bhrāṣṭraki-kāpiṣṭhali" in the *tikakitavādi* group is un-Vedic (*anārṣa*), because the Mahābhāṣya provides the examples "bhrāṣṭrakakapiṣṭhalāḥ" and "bhrāṣṭrakikāpiṣṭhalayaḥ."

Therefore, for *kṛṣṇājina*, *kṛṣṇasundara*, and [the others], there is obligatory elision (*luk*) of the suffix when these appear as a *dvandva* compound; when not in a *dvandva*, the elision is optional. Examples: *upakāḥ* and *aupakāyanāḥ*; *lamakāḥ* and *lāmakāyanāḥ*; *kṛṣṇājināḥ* and *kārṣṇājinayaḥ*; *kṛṣṇasundarāḥ* and *kārṣṇasundarayaḥ*. For others, however, the elision is optional both in a *dvandva* and when it is absent: *bhrāṣṭrakāḥ* and *bhrāṣṭrakayaḥ*; *kāpiṣṭhalāḥ* and *kāpiṣṭhalayaḥ*.

Vaḍāraka, Aḍāraka, Bhraṭuka, Akandhaka, Piṅgalaka, Piṣṭha, Suṣiṣṭa, Mayūrakarṇa, Kharijaṅgha, Śavāṣama, Patañjala, Kāveriṇi, Gaḍu, Uṣitaka, Kuśa, Kutsa, Nidāgha, Kalaśīlakaṇṭha, Kānkaṇṭha, Kṛṣṇapiṅgalakarṇa, Parṇaka, Jaṭilaka, Badhiraka, Jantuka, Anuloma, Pratiloma, Avidagdha, and Pratāna-anabhihita.
In place of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*, [the forms] *āgasti* and *kauṇḍini* are used.

In the case of the plural, there is elision (*luk*) of the *yañ* suffix which is a *gotra* suffix; furthermore, the substitutes for the stem portion shall apply respectively.
