[One might ask: "Why not simply prescribe the two specific substitutes for the two specific [stems] respectively, rather than first prescribing the elision of the suffix and then applying the substitutes to the stem portion? [The answer is: No, because that would result in the failure to establish forms such as *āgastīyāḥ*. From *agastya*, with the *ṛṣyaṇ* suffix, we derive *āgastyaḥ*.

In the case of *agastīnāṃ chātrāḥ* ("the pupils of the Agastis"), although the suffix *añ* (as in *ādi*) belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is intended, the substitution of *agasti-* would apply; consequently, because the condition of being *vṛddha* (containing a long vowel in the first syllable) would be absent, the suffix *cha* would not occur. However, if one applies the elision (*luk*) and then prescribes the substitution *agasti-*, then—because of the prohibition of elision by the rule *gotre 'lug acī*—"the elision does not take place in the case of a *gotra* [name] when followed by a vowel"—the substitution, which is taught as being co-occurrent (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*) with that elision, also does not occur. Thus, due to the presence of the *vṛddha* quality, the suffix *cha* is applied, and after the elision of *ya* by the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyeti yalopaḥ*, the form *āgastīyāḥ* is established. In the case of *kauṇḍinya*, however, there is no difference between the two methods.

From the word *kauṇḍinya*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* and the *ya* of the patronymic is elided by the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite'nāti*, the form *kauṇḍināḥ* (the students) is established. The inclusion of the letter *c* [in the rule] is for the sake of the accent; for the word *kuṇḍinī*, when the suffix *ini* is added, has the middle vowel as its udātta. By the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*, [from *kauṇḍinya*] one would obtain *kauṇḍya*. However, if the rule *bhasyāḍhe* were applied to effect the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), the *ṭi* would be elided by the rule *na-staddhite*, resulting in *kauṇḍya*. It is precisely because of this specific irregularity (*nipātana*) that the masculine-like treatment does not occur. Then, the *i* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*. In reality, however, only the non-elision of the *ṭi* is what is irregularly prescribed. [The next rule is: *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (7.1.39).

There is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) belonging to these two [members]. He desires a son for himself: *putrīyati*. Since the designation "root" (*dhātu*) applies to that which is qualified by an affix such as *san* (P. 3.1.32), the second case ending following the word *putra* is elided. From a form ending in a case-ending, the affix *kyac* is applied: a king’s man is *rājapuruṣaḥ*.
The suffix *śap* is elided after verbal roots beginning with *ad*.

From these [roots], there is the elision (luk) of the *śap* suffix. In forms such as *atti* and "those who worship another god" (*anyadevam upāsate*), the form is derived from the root *ās* in the sense of "taking. In "the night-stalkers would trust" (*āśvaseyuḥ niśācarāḥ*) and "one should not trust the untrustworthy" (*na viśvased aviśvaste*), there is no elision because the operation of the *gaṇa* is non-obligatory (*anitya*). Some maintain that this is indicated by the addition of the marker *ṣ* in the rule *kṣamūṣ*, even though the result would have been established simply by the rule *ghaṭādayaḥ ṣitaḥ*. Others hold that the form is derived from a denominative (*ācārakvib*) based on a word ending in the *pacādyac* suffix.

By this, the *Meghadūta* verse "the wives of travelers trust again" (*pathikavanitāḥ pratyayād āśvasanti*) and the usage of Bhānudatta, "sheaving deeply for the words of the Goddess" (*devīgirām dīrghataram śvasantī*), are explained.
The moon is full on the fourteenth day. || 73 ||
The elision of *śap* occurs frequently. In *vṛhaṃ hanati*, it becomes *vṛhā*; in *ahiḥ śayate*. Because it is stated "frequently," it also occurs elsewhere: *trādhvaṃ no devāḥ*.
The substitution of *yaṇ* for *iK* occurs before a vowel (*ac*) and also at the end of a word.

There is elision (*luk*) of *yaṅ* when an *ac*-affix follows. Examples: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*. [The suffix] *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). This very rule indicates that all verbal roots (*dhātu*) are included within the group beginning with *pac*. Due to the word "also" (*ca*), this occurs diversely (*bahulam*) even elsewhere. Examples: *vebhidīti*, *cecchidīti*. Here, the distinction is that the elision caused by the *ac*-affix is dependent on a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*), whereas the elision obtained through the force of the word "also" (*cakāra*) is independent of any cause (*anaimittika*). In this matter, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, there is the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "in the Veda" (*chandasi*), but not according to the view of the Vṛtti.

In the rule *huśruvoḥ*, because of the mention of the term *sārvadhātuka*, the author of the Bhāṣya also accepts the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) even in some instances of the common language (*bhāṣā*), since the regulation of usage is possible solely on the basis of preceding usage.

If it is argued that here "aj" should simply be understood as a *pratyāhāra* (a technical abbreviation for vowels), the [commentators] say: if that were the case, he would have said simply "aṇi," because no vowel other than one ending in *yaṅ* is possible [in this context]. Nor is its occurrence possible in the form *pāpacyai*, because of the intervention of the *śap* suffix; and because of the status of the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, since the substitution of *eś* for the *ta* and *jha* of the *liṭ* is necessary, and because of the rule "not in a mantra" (*amantra*), even if its occurrence were somehow possible in a mantra, [the term "aj"] must refer to the suffix *yaṅ* due to its association with that suffix.
The *ślu* [elision of the suffix] occurs after the roots beginning with *hu* (to sacrifice).

The suffix *śap* is carried over by "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and not even the immediately preceding *yaṅ*, because of the force of the rule prescribing reduplication in *ślau*; otherwise, it would have been established by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* alone.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *o* for *as*] occurs frequently.

The suffix *śap* shall be elided (*ślau*). Furthermore, it is not [elided] after the roots beginning with *hu* in certain cases. May Indra, the bounteous Maghavan, bestow well-being upon the gods; he grants what is dear. [This applies] even from other [roots]: he fashions the full [oblation]; he proclaims the births.
The augment *iṭ* is not applied after the root *gam*, nor after roots ending in long *ā*, nor after *stha*, *ghu*, *upa*, *āp*, and *bhū*, when followed by the suffix *sic* in the *parasmaipada*.

After these [roots], there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic* in the *parasmaipada*. Only *luk* is understood here, not *ślu*, because of the explanation [of the commentators]. Furthermore, the substitute *gā* is taken here as the one taught with the suffix *śtip* (in *gāti*), due to the mention of the elision of *śap* (*śabluk*); the substitute *gā* taught in [Pāṇini 2.4.45] is not intended here. For this very reason, the rule "there is no distinction in the mention of *gam*, *āda*, and others" does not apply, because the substitute *gā* is mentioned specifically to exclude other forms. Even though the substitute *gā* pertains only to the *luṅ* tense, the elision of *śap* applies even in the case of its citation [as a root], by virtue of the extension [of rules] stating that "the citation form behaves like the original. Examples: *agāt*, *asthāt*, *adāt*, *adhāt*.

The root *pā* (to drink) alone is intended here, and not *pā* (to protect), because when there is a choice between a root with a *lu*-suffix (*luk-vikaraṇa*) and one without (*aluk-vikaraṇa*), only the one without the suffix is taken. Thus, we have *apāt* and *abhūt*. This form also belongs to the substitute for *as* (the verb "to be"), because the rule regarding *lu*-suffixes does not apply to that [substitute], as it lacks a connection with the elision of *śap* (*śap-luk*) which occurs only in the domain of *ārdhadhātuka* affixes. As for the root *gai* (to sing), we have *agāsīt*; in the sense of protecting (*pā rakṣaṇe*), we have *apāsīt*, with the augment *iṭ* added by the rule *yamaramanamātām iṭ*. The root *pai* (to dry, *pai śoṣaṇe*) is also not included here, because its inclusion would be merely figurative (*lākṣaṇikatva*). Why specify "in the Parasmaipada"? Consider: *agāsātāṃ grāmau devadattena* ("Devadatta caused the two villages to sing").

The form *mā bheḥ* is derived from the root *bhī* with the suffix *ṅasā*. By the rule *eranekācaḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs; thus, the interpretation that "the form *mā bheḥ* is established by the fact that there is no Rāhu in the wine equal to the moon" is unacceptable. This is because it contradicts Bhartṛhari’s statement: *mā syād bhaiṣīs tvam* and so forth. As for *mā bher māṃsaṃ vikthāḥ*, that is Vedic (*chāndasa*). They say that *mā bheḥ* [in the secular sense] is merely due to a scribal error (*prāmādika*). Alternatively, the absence of the augment *iṭ* may be justified on the grounds that the teaching regarding augments is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
The suffix *san* is optionally applied after the roots *ghr̥*, *dheṭ*, *śā*, *chā*, and *sā*.

Or there is elision (*luk*) in the case of a preceding object. Regarding the root *dhā* (to suck), there is an option: by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 3.1.56], the substitution of *āt* is obtained; by the other rule [Pāṇini 3.1.44], the substitution of *a* is obtained. Thus: *aghrāt*, *adhāt*, *aśāt*, *acchāt*, *asāt*. [The roots] *śo* (to sharpen) and *cho* (to cut) mean "making thin," while *ṣo* (to destroy) means "ending. In the alternative case, one says *aghrāsīt*, and so forth. [Question: Why "in the parasmaipada"? [Answer: *aghrāsata sumanasaḥ devadattena* ("the flowers were smelled by Devadatta"). Here, *taṅ* (the ātmanepada endings) occurs because of the object. [Now follows the rule: *tanādibhyastathāsoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.79). "After the group of roots beginning with *tan* (the *tanādi* class), the suffixes *ta* and *thas* [take the augment *siC*]."

The suffix *sic* is elided when followed by *tathāsoḥ*. Because it occurs in association with *thās* and *as*, only the singular form is understood here. Examples: *atata*, *atathāḥ*, *ataniṣṭa*, *ataniṣṭhāḥ*, *asāta*, *asāthāḥ*. [In these cases,] there is the substitution of *ā* according to the rule *janasanakhanām...*. Optionally: *asaniṣṭa*, *asaniṣṭhāḥ*. There is no elision (*luk*) in the case of *yūyam ataniṣṭa*, because the plural number is not mentioned here. [In the Vedic Mantras, the suffix *liṭ* (perfect tense) is replaced by *luṅ* (aorist) after the following roots: *ghas*, *hvar*, *ṇaś*, *vṛ*, *daha*, *ad*, *vṛc*, *kṛ*, *gam*, *ji*, and *ni*. (Pāṇini 2.4.80)

The suffix *leṭ* is elided (*luk*) after these [roots] in mantras: 1. *akṣan pitaro'mīmadanta pitaraḥ*: After the substitution of *ghas*, by the rule *gamahana...* there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). By the rule *śāsivasighasīnām ca*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*. In the absence of the augment *aṭ*, [the example is] *mā tvā vṛkāso aśivāsa ukṣan*. Here, there is a reference to the root *hvr̥* (meaning "crookedness") as characterized by its *guṇa*-strengthened form; the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). [The example is] *mā hr̥d matryasya dhūrter naśiṣṭa*. By the rule *naśervā*, there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *ṣ*). The term *vṛ* includes the inclusion of both *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*. [The example is] *suruco vena āvaḥ*. [In] *mā no adhak*, there is the inclusion of the root ending in long *ā*. 2. *dāt*: This is the inclusion of roots ending in long *ā*.

He has filled the earth and the sky, and the intermediate space. In the straight path for the avoidance [of evil], in this great contest, they have reached the further shore; as they reached the further shore, the performers of the rite, the makers of the rite, have come. The mention of the *mantrapada* is also an indication for the *brāhmaṇa*. Or rather, "his teeth fell out"—this is Varuṇa’s speech to Hariścandra in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*.
The inclusion of the term *liṭ* (the perfect tense) is for the purpose of preventing the application of the accentuation rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām*.

"Otherwise, it would have followed *sica* itself," so say Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others. Nor does this result in the elision (*lopa*) of the *liṅ* and *laṭ* [moods] as well; for the interpretation is that "the *liṅ* which is the substituend (*sthānin*) of *sic*. However, some maintain that the word *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is understood here, on account of examples such as *na tā agṛbhṇan* and *ajāniṣṭa hiṣaḥ*. According to them, even the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of *sic* and so forth is fruitless. Furthermore, there is no possibility of the elision (*luk*) of *liṅ* and *laṭ*, because in Vedic usage (*chandas*), other forms are not to be produced [by such rules]. [Pāṇini 3.4.90: *āmaḥ* || 81 ||

This will be explained by the rule beginning with *ijādeśca*. Following that, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix. This [suffix] applies precisely at the stage of the root (*lāvasthāyām*), because it is an exception to the substitutes such as *tiP* and others. Consequently, in examples such as *cakṣuḥ kāmaṃ yājayāṃcakāra*, the suffix *ām* is not unaccented (*anighāta*) because it does not end in a verbal suffix (*atiṅantatvāt*). Furthermore, the verb being subsequently employed (*anuprayujyamāna*) is accented. Since the form ending in *ām* ends in a case-suffix (*subantatvāt*), it possesses the status of a word (*padatva*). Due to the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*, the case-suffix is elided because it is an indeclinable (*avyayatvāt*), since in the rule *kṛdatiṅ*, the designation *kṛt* is prohibited for a *lakāra* that is about to become a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

Nor should it be argued that, in the case of *yat-prakāra-yācakāra*, when the suffixes such as *tiP* are elided, the *pra* would not undergo *nighāta* (the loss of accent) by the rule *gatir gatau tiṅi codāttavati*, because the form ending in *ām* (*-ācakāra*) is not a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). For when *pra* is compounded with *kārayām*, the rule for the accent of a compound (*samāsa-svara*) would result in an oxytone (*antodātta*), while the rule for the original accent of the first member of an indeclinable (*avyaya-pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) would result in an acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Once the accent of the root *kṛ* (*kṛt-svara*) is applied to override those, the *anudātta* (unaccented) status of *pra* is established precisely by the subsequent rule of *śeṣa-nighāta*.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *nakārayāṃcakāra*, there would be the occurrence of a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) due to the presence of a word ending in a case-suffix, which would consequently result in the elision of the letter *n*; for there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the suffixless negative particle (*nam*) and that which ends in a case-suffix, since its meaning is not fully manifested.

There is an extension [of the rule] for the elision of *ām* in the *luṅ* and *loṭ* tenses: "They have known her, O Vaijavāpīs"; "May you know this, sirs. Kaiyaṭa states that since the mention of the suffix (*li*) continues [from the previous rule], the elision would not apply elsewhere, and thus this rule is commenced. However, the Bhāṣya maintains that because the force of the expression "subsequent application" (*anuprayoga*) implies that only the elision of the suffix is intended, the continuation of that [mention of the suffix] does not occur here. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa says that the elision (*luk*) is also established by means of a nipātana (irregularity). Since the meaning of the form ending in *ām* is not clearly expressed, the non-occurrence of suffixes such as *tarap* is natural; it is merely explained through the door of elision (*luk*).
After an indeclinable (avyaya), the case endings (sup) and the feminine suffix āp are elided.

There is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *sup* and of the feminine suffix *āp* prescribed after an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Regarding that [elision], there is this Vārttika: "The statement of the elision of *āp* after an indeclinable is purposeless, because of the absence of gender. Nor can it be argued that this [elision] would follow because of coreferentiality with a feminine word; for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *bhūtam iyaṃ brāhmaṇī* ("this Brāhmaṇī woman is a ghost"). Even though, under a unified rule such as "the suffix *su* occurs when there is singularity" (*ekatve suḥ*), the production of case-endings (*sub*) would not apply to indeclinables because they lack number, nevertheless, since the production of *svādi* endings applies without distinction, rules such as "in the dual and singular" (*dvyekayoḥ*) function as restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*).

Alternatively, the derivation of the case-ending (sup) occurs from this very indicator (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, by the rule of "treatment as a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the status of being a word (*padatva*) is established, which in turn accounts for the substitution of *r* and other such changes. For this very reason, the tradition of the logicians (*tārkika-sampradāya*) maintains that in cases such as *ghaṭo na* ("the pot is not") and *śaṅkhaḥ pāṇḍuraḥ* ("the conch is white"), the case-endings following the particles (*nipāta*) have their denotation (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) and so forth.
The suffix *am* does not occur after an avyayībhāva compound ending in *a*, except when it is the fifth case (ablative). Pāṇini 2.4.83.

Here, there is a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). [First: *Lopa* (elision) does not occur for the case-endings (*sup*) after an indeclinable (*avyayībhāva*) compound ending in 'a'. [Second: For that [compound], the substitution of *am* occurs for [case-endings] other than the ablative (*pañcamī*). It follows that the non-elision (*aluk*) applies to all case-endings equally, whereas the substitution of *am* applies only to those other than the ablative. Otherwise, since the substitution of *am* occurs in the ablative, it would follow that non-elision (*aluk*) would also apply there. Alternatively, the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Thus, even if taken as a single syntactical unit—meaning "only *am* [is substituted] for [case-endings] other than the ablative, but for that [ablative], elision (*luk*) occurs"—the intended meaning is established. An example is *apadiśam*, meaning "between the two directions."

In the prohibition regarding the fifth case (pañcamī), the fifth case of the *apādāna* (ablative) is what is intended. Here, in the sentence "It rained as far as Pāṭaliputra" (*āpāṭaliputraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ*), the fifth case is used in connection with a *karmapravacanīya* particle. Alternatively, this is a prohibition of the substitution of *am* for the fifth case prescribed after an *avyayībhāva* compound; however, in this instance, that fifth case is prescribed after the final member of the compound. Since that [final member] is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), when the elision (*luk*) has occurred and the suffix *su* is produced from the compound, its substitution by *am* takes place. But when the fifth case is prescribed after the entire compound, it is indeed heard [as such]: *āupakumbhāt*. [Here,] *ā upakumbham* is an *avyayībhāva* meaning "near the jar"; then, in connection with the particle *āṅ*, the fifth case is applied.
In the case of the third and seventh cases, [the substitution] occurs diversely.

The state [of the suffix] would be *ambhāva*. Examples: *upadiśam*, *upadiśena*, *upadiśe*. By this, the *Naiṣadha* commentary explains: "In the vicinity of the marketplace, there is a water-mill (*gharaṭṭa*) and so forth. It should be stated that [the suffix *aṇ*] is obligatory after a word denoting prosperity (*ṛddhi*), a river compound (*nadīsamāsa*), and a numeral expressing a part (*saṃkhyāvayava*). This is a statement of the meaning already established by the mention of the term *bahula* (diversely). Prosperity (*ṛddhi*): *sumadram*, *sumagadham*. River compound (*nadīsamāsa*): *unmattagaṅgam*, *lohitāgaṅgam*. Numeral (*saṃkhyā*): *ekaviṃśatibhāradvājam*, *tripañcāśadgautamam*. [Meaning: twenty-one Bhāradvājas; fifty-three Gautamas. [Note: *ekaviṃśati-* is used here as a numeral.]

"Tripañcāśad-gautamavaṃśyāḥ" (those belonging to fifty-three Gautama lineages) is a compound formed with the word "vaṃśya" (belonging to a lineage). Kaiyaṭa maintains that because the constituent members (*vartipada*) denote a different meaning qualified by their own respective meanings, the words *gautama* and *bhārgava* undergo a transition (*saṃkrama*) into a single meaning qualified by singularity; consequently, there is no elision (*luk*) according to the rule *tadrājasya*. Dīkṣita, however, argues that since elision would have applied—just as in the case of "the family of the Gargas" (*gargakulam*)—prior even to the formation of the compound, the absence of the nasal (*n*) is due solely to the usage found in the Bhāṣya. Following this, the locative case [is applied]. The substitution of *ambh* is obligatory. [This concludes the section on] the forms *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* for the first person of the periphrastic future (*luṭ*).

These substitutions shall take the place of the first-person endings of the *luṅ* substitute. Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) would occur in the *ātmanepada* endings due to their subsequent position; for by the principle of "repeated application" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the aforementioned substitutions operate precisely after those [other operations] have taken effect, just as in the case of reduplication (*dvitva*) after *saṃprasāraṇa* has occurred in forms such as *ījatuḥ*.

If it is objected: "There are six bases (*sthānin*) but only three substitutes (*ādeśa*); therefore, how can the correspondence be established by number (*yathāsaṃkhyam*)?"—it is not so, because the arrangement is possible through semantic proximity (*arthata āntaryeṇa*). Alternatively, by resorting to a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) in the form "ḍā-rau-ras-śca ḍā-rau-ras-śca," then, in a *dvandva* compound of those items that have already undergone *ekaśeṣa*, the substitute *ḍā* would apply to the singular and dual [endings], *rau* to the plural and singular, and *ras* to the dual and plural. However, if *ekaśeṣa* is applied after the *dvandva* has been formed, then *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* apply respectively to *ti*, *tas*, and *jhi*.
Regarding the forms *ta*, *ātām*, and *aṅ*, the desired result is achieved through the substitution of *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. This is the meaning stated in the Bhāṣya:
"Just as when *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* have been substituted, the *ṭe* [elision] and the doubling or *prasāraṇa* occur;
there is no need for an equal number [of substitutes], for it is established that [the substitute] takes the place [of the original] by virtue of its meaning."

"The arrangement is based on proximity; thus, for all [substitutes], there are only these three [possibilities]. And since the substitution of *ṛ* for *e* occurs because it is subsequent, let these [three] remain even when that [substitution] has been performed.

It might be argued as follows: "The substitute beginning with *ḍ* (ḍādi) would apply only to the final letter by the *alontyaparibhāṣā* (the rule concerning the final letter). Nor can this be resolved by the presence of the indicatory letter *ś* (*śit*), because that would result in the [substitute] being treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. Consequently, in the case of *śvaḥ kartā*, the rule *tāsyanudāttet*—which prescribes that a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following *tās* is unaccented—would wrongly apply to the *tās*. Furthermore, the prohibition *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (which prevents the accentuation of a finite verb following another finite verb) would not apply here, because of the specific prohibition *na luṭi* (this prohibition does not apply to the *luṭ* future). [Response: This is not so. The *alontyaparibhāṣā* is set aside by the *śitparibhāṣā* (the rule governing substitutes marked with *ś*). Moreover, the *śitparibhāṣā* applies only to those cases where the original element (*sthānin*) consists of more than one letter. Since the original element here (*ṛ*) is a single letter, the *śitparibhāṣā* does not apply. Therefore, the *alontyaparibhāṣā* remains in force, and the substitute would indeed affect only the final letter. However, this is not the case, because the *alontyaparibhāṣā* is superseded by the *ādeḥ parasya* rule (P. 1.1.54), which dictates that a substitute replaces the initial portion of the original element. Thus, the entire original element is replaced. Consequently, the objection regarding the accentuation of the *tās* in *śvaḥ kartā* does not arise, as the substitute is not considered a *sārvadhātuka* suffix in this context. As for the objection regarding the prohibition *na luṭi*, that too is resolved by the fact that the *śitparibhāṣā* overrides the *alontyaparibhāṣā* in this instance. Therefore, the substitute affects the whole of the original element. Thus, the three possibilities established by proximity hold true for all cases.

No; for even with the substitution of the final letter, the desired form is established by the elision of the *ṭi* (the first vowel), since the entire element *ās*—including the *t* of the verbal suffix—is replaced. Nor should it be argued that when the final letter is replaced by *ḍ*, the *t*-ending portion would not be an *aṅga* (stem), because the *t* is a part of the suffix, and the designation *aṅga* is prescribed only for that preceding portion which stands prior to the suffix. This objection is invalid, because by the force of the *ḍit* marker, the designation *bha* applies even without the designation *aṅga*. Nor should it be argued that in this way, the term *tiṅ* would fail to include [the forms], as their form would have changed;
for, as in the case of *pacanti* and *pacantu*, that which has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original.

Alternatively, since these—namely, the designation *sarvādeśa* (substitution for the whole), the designation *it*, and elision (*lopa*)—are mutually dependent upon one another in their preceding order, the result is established precisely because [the substitute] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). For if it were a substitution for the final sound (*antādeśa*), it would be merely a part of the suffix and not the suffix itself; this is because only the entire aggregate possesses that status. In the absence of that, there would be no designation as *it*; and in the absence of that, there would be no elision. Therefore, by virtue of having more than one phoneme, it is first a substitution for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), and subsequently it receives the designation *it*; thus, there is no fault. Or rather, this is a composite instruction (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*) consisting of "a" and "a"; therefore, according to the Bhāṣya, it is a substitution for the whole due to having more than one phoneme.

It might be argued as follows: "The low-pitched (anudātta) nature of *tiP* and other suffixes would apply by virtue of their higher status [in the order of rules], because the substitution of those suffixes is non-permanent due to the fact that they are replaced by other sounds. Consequently, they would not possess the high-pitched (udātta) accent. If this is said, we reply: No, because the substitutions themselves must apply first, owing to their being *antaraṅga* (internal).

Nor should it be argued that even so, when there arises the consideration whether the anudātta (low-pitched) accent should be applied to those [suffixes] or whether they should be elided, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) must occur because it is subsequent; and then, by the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the anudātta accent of the *ḍa*-suffixes and others would indeed follow. For, immediately after the *ṭi*-elision, based on the conflict of accents (*svaravipratiṣedha*), the accent of the "cessation of the acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*)—as prescribed by the rule *tāsyanudātenṅidadupadeśālla-sārvadhātukamanudāttam*—prevails, thereby overriding the anudātta accent.

But this is not so; for when the substitution of *ḍā* in place of the singular *ātmanepada* ending *ti* occurs, since *ṭilopa* applies by virtue of its higher priority (*paratva*), the rule "where there is elision of an acute vowel" (*anudāttasya ca yatro dāttalopaḥ*) does not apply, because that rule only operates after the substitution has been made and the resulting form is characterized by that substitution—namely, where there is an elision of an acute vowel conditioned by that specific [substituted] element. Since the substitute *ḍā* for *ti* is unaccented (*anudātta*) due to *ti* being marked with *p*, it remains unaccented by the principle of "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*); thus, in that case, the accentuation would indeed occur through the "acute of the disappearance of an acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*).

If it is argued that when the substitute *ḍa* takes the place of *takāra*, there can be no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) because the accent prescribed by *anudāttasya ca* would have no scope at all without the application of *tāsyanudātteṭ*—to this the authors of the Bhāṣya reply: The lack of acute accent (*anudāttatva*) for the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffix is indeed an exception (*apavāda*) to the general accent rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). And exceptions do not apply to the domain of their own sublation; thus, even though the *ṭi*-elision (*ṭilopa*) occurs later, the accent prescribed by *anudāttasya ca* still operates. This is because the word "acute" (*udātta*) in that context [of *tāsyanudātteṭ*] is intended to signify merely the absence of an acute accent.

This being the case, even though the technical *anudātta* (unaccented) status is absent, since the accent of the suffix does not apply to the substitute *ḍa*, the *anudātta* status—defined as the absence of the acute (*udātta*)—is present; therefore, the *udāttanivṛttisvara* (the accent that occurs when an acute is removed) operates without any obstacle. Nor should it be argued: "How can there be an elision of an acute (*udāttalopa*) at all, given that the *ṭi*-elision (*ṭilopa*) applies even before the acute of *tās* has occurred?"

Because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), the suffix *tās* (the augment of the periphrastic future) operates as qualified by the acute accent (*udātta*); however, in the case of the substitution of *ḍā*, since the application of the exception (*apavāda*) is imminent, the accent of the suffix does not apply previously. Thus, there is a disparity. Therefore, the accent is established in both words; all is auspicious. Thus ends the second Āhnika of the fourth Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*. This Pāda and this Adhyāya are completed.
[Salutations to] him who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the Vedas, honored by the feet and speech of the virtuous and learned.

In this *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi* composed by Viśveśvara—who attained the birth of awakening through Lakṣmīdhara—let the wise study chapter after chapter; now, let the intellect be applied here for the sake of purifying the subject matter through repeated reflection. 1.
Now begins the third chapter.
The condition. || 1 ||

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending up to the end of the fifth book (*pañcamasamāpti*). The technical designation *pratyaya* (suffix) applies to those elements prescribed herein; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth. Now, even with this, one might argue that over-extension is unavoidable in the case of augmentations (*vikārāgama*), such as in the rules *hanasta ca* ("and *ta* replaces *t* of *han*") and *trapujatunoḥ ṣuk* ("*ṣuk* is added after *trapu* and *jatun*"), because they are not suffixes. Nor should it be said that these will not receive the designation because they lack "subsequent-ness" (*paratva*); for the status of being a suffix is accepted for *śram*, *bahu*, *jak*, and *k* even without subsequent-ness. If this is argued:

Regarding this, they say: "Because there is no purpose [for it], they do not have that designation (*saṃjñā*). To explain: their designation as such is not for the sake of the subsequent rule (*paravidhi*), because the relationship to the locus (*sthāna*) or the relationship to a constituent part (*avayava*) is already established by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) itself. Nor is it for the sake of the acute accent (*udāttatva*), because for augments (*āgama*), a specific rule for the non-acute accent (*anudātta-svara*) is prescribed; for substitutes (*vikāra*) that lack vowels (*niracka*), there is simply an absence of accent; and for those with vowels (*sāckaka*), the accent of the original element (*sthānin*) applies at the very time of its occurrence due to its being more internal (*antaraṅga*). Furthermore, there is an absence of any mention in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*).

Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of that [genitive], priority (*paratva*) would arise solely by the force of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "suffix" (*pratyaya*); for when a specific relation is already expressed within its own rule by the genitive case itself, it is impossible for the priority mentioned in another rule to apply, due to the contradiction involved.

But if this were so, then even in cases such as *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8), where a suffix is produced through the understanding of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denoting immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), there would be no rule for the suffix in instances involving substitutes (*vikāra*) or augments (*āgama*). This is because in those instances, that which is to be substituted (*anuvādya*) is indicated by the genitive; and since there is no mention of the ablative (*pañcamī*), the relationship between the two heard elements—the original (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), or the augment (*āgamin*) and the base to which it is added (*āgama*)—could not be established. For the syntactical connection (*vākya*) would be required to convey that relationship, and there is no other sentence available to specify that particular relationship.

Nor should it be argued that in the rule *hanaḥ taC* (Pāṇini 3.1.108), by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *dhātoḥ* from the preceding rule, and in the rule *trapujatunoḥ ṣuk* (Pāṇini 4.3.139), by the continued application of the word *prātipadikāt* ending in the ablative case, the suffix is prescribed by that [ablative]; and that the relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*) as well as the relationship of augment and augmented (*āgamāgamibhāva*) is established by the actually heard genitive-ending [word]. This cannot be maintained, because the root *han* would be irrelevant in a rule prescribing a substitute, and because of the difference in case endings. Consequently, since the root could be qualified [by the ablative], there would arise the unintended meaning of the sentence: "the substitute *t* applies to *han*, and the suffix *kyap* applies after every root."

Alternatively, [the rule] "after *han*" means that the suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *han*; why "after *han*"? Because by a division of the sentence, the root *han* serves as a qualifier for the verbal root (*dhātu*). Alternatively, the creation of this technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the purpose of establishing its etymological significance (*anvarthatva*). Consequently, suffixes that are meaningless modifications (*vikāra*) or augments (*āgama*) do not receive the designation of "suffix" (*pratyaya*). And the meaninglessness of modifications and augments is beyond dispute, because their purpose belongs solely to the base (*prakṛti*), as determined by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and because—unlike [suffixes such as] *-tarap* and the like—they lack the capacity to indicate a distinct meaning.

Nor should it be argued that once the designation of "suffix" (pratyaya-saṃjñā) is established, its meaningfulness (arthavattva) is secured by the meaning of the base (prakṛti) alone; for if it were stated that suffixhood itself does not exist due to a lack of meaningfulness, the aforementioned reasoning would fail to emerge, as it would be seized by the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).

Now, is the word *pratyaya* derived as an agent-noun (*kartṛ-sādhana*) meaning "that which causes comprehension," or as an object-noun (*karma-sādhana*) meaning "that which is comprehended"? It cannot be the first, because it would lack application (*avyāpti*) in the case of suffixes that convey their own meaning (*svārthika*). This is because such suffixes do not produce a cognition whose object is a meaning distinct from that of the base (*prakṛti*). Nor can it be the second, because according to its definition, a suffix would have to be one "whose meaning is comprehended by the base" (i.e., *pratyāyyamānārtha*), and this would fail to include the *san* suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika-san*). Even if the *svārthika-san* were included, there would still be a lack of application in the case of *san* and others used in the sense of desire (*icchārthaka-san*), since these convey meanings understood through the base. If you argue that this is not so [because they do indeed convey such meanings], [we reply:]...

It is said: because a single word, through its connection with multiple powers (*śakti*), is authorized as delimited by two grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to both cases according to the possibility. Due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) of the form ending in *ṇic*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *ṇi* before a vowel suffix. Nor should it be argued that this would also apply to an augment (*āgama*); for while a suffix is used even apart from an augment, an augment does not exist apart from it. Thus, by the method of presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the status of having meaning (*arthavattva*) is established for the suffix alone.

The author of the *Anunyāsa*, however, states that the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), as in "that by which one understands the meaning. Alternatively, he says that the suffix *gha* is applied in the masculine to form a technical name (*saṃjñā*). One should not object: "How can these two suffixes [ac and gha] apply to the word *karṇa*, since they are superseded by the suffix *lyuṭ*? For there is no application of the rule of non-identity of forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) in the case of the suffixes *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tun*, *khal*, and *artha*. This is because, in that specific context, the suffix *lyuṭ* is not included under the heading "in the sense of instrument and locus" (*karaṇādhikaraṇayoḥ*). The details are found elsewhere.

Thus it is established that this term *pratyaya* is etymological (*yaugika*), and there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to roots (*prakṛti*) and the like; for being prescribed by a specific governing rule (*adhikāra*) is merely a condition of usage (*prayogopādhi*). Since there is an absence of cognition having that [condition] as its qualifier, it is impossible to state that the aforementioned property serves as a delimiter of conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Nyāyacintāmaṇi*: "In the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word 'cow,' cowness (*gotva*) is not the limiting condition (*upādhi*), because the resulting cognition has that [cowness] as its qualifier.
The Naiyāyikas, however, hold: "That which possesses a function (*vṛttimat*), other than a root in the sense of such-and-such and other than an indeclinable (*nipāta*)," [is a suffix].
In such a sense, that word would be a cognition; and that [cognition] is of four kinds.

The phrase "of such a meaning" (*yādṛśārtha*) also connects with the term "function" (*vṛtti*) in this definition. "Function" (*vṛtti*) here means either primary denotation (*śakti*) or conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), because the suffix *matup* is prescribed in the sense of excellence (*prāśastye*). Thus, a word which—while being distinct from a stem or a particle—is possessed of one of the aforementioned functions with respect to a certain meaning, is a suffix having that meaning as its object. The term "distinct from a stem" (*prakṛtibhinna*) is included to prevent over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) to words like *śukla-stha* (white-standing), which, through one of the aforementioned functions, convey the relationship between a quality and its possessor (*guṇa-guṇin*) or between staying and the place of staying (*sthiti-prasthāna*).

To exclude cases such as the particle *ca* and others which indicate conjunction (*samuccaya*), the term "distinct from a particle" (*nipātabhinna*) is included. However, words such as *svara* (accent) and the like are *prakṛtis* (bases) only when they refer to themselves, and not in the sense of singularity and so forth. Even though there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of objecthood (*karmatva*) and the like in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and others, this is not a conventionalized (*nirūḍha*) usage because such usage is generally absent. In expressions such as *paśunā rudraṃ yajate* ("He worships Rudra with an animal"), however, it is based on grammatical prescription (*ānuśāsanika*). The meaning of a purely derivative suffix (*svārthikapratyaya*) is its own form. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms such as the denominative (*san*) in *jugupsate devatām* ("He feels aversion toward the deity").

The same explanation applies to abstract nouns (*bhāva*) ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes, because the word "abstract" (*bhāva*) refers to the essential nature of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*). Otherwise, in expressions such as "see the cooking" (*pākaṃ paśya*), the verbal root's meaning could not be construed as the object (*karman*), since it is a matter of established linguistic convention (*avyutpatti*) that the meaning of a verbal root cannot be construed with the meaning of a nominal suffix (*sub-artha*). Alternatively, a suffix (*pratyaya*) is defined as follows:

"That which, being other than a particle (*nibha*) and so forth, is incapable of conveying its own meaning when that meaning is not delimited by another meaning, is called a suffix. (This excludes particles like *iti*, which can convey their own meaning even when not delimited by others.)

A word is a suffix (pratyaya) with respect to a particular meaning if, by virtue of not being qualified by another word, it is inherently capable (*svarūpayogya*) of producing a cognitive relation (*anvayabodha*) in which the meaning of a verbal suffix (*tiṅartha*) is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and that specific meaning is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In examples such as "Caitra exists" (*caitro 'sti*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because the capacity to produce a cognitive relation where the meaning of a verbal suffix is connected to the nominal stem's own meaning—unrestricted by the meanings of other words—is precisely what is intended; for the agenthood (*kṛt*) is connected to Caitra himself, who is qualified by the property of being Caitra (*caitratva*), since he constitutes the single referent of the nominal stem.

The meaning is: that which, having the meaning of another word as its *dharmitāvacchedaka* (delimitor of the subject-property), simply does not result in a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of that [other] word. By the phrase "another word" (*padāntara*), one should understand a word other than that which, through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*), becomes the locus of a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning intended by the suffix.

Otherwise, since the difference from a *tiṅ* suffix exists even in the word "Caitra," there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because a cognition arises where Caitra-ness is the *dharmitāvacchedaka*, Caitra is the qualificand, and the action denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix is the qualifier.

In cases such as *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice") and *sthīyate* ("it is stayed"), the meaning of the suffix *tiṅ* (such as the present tense) conveys its own meaning—presentness and so on—only with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) as delimited by the suffixes *kyac* and others (in *putrīyati*, etc.), or by *kṛt* suffixes (in *pācakaḥ asti*, etc.), or by *taddhita* suffixes (in *kāśyapiḥ*, etc.). It does not convey it with respect to that [base meaning] as delimited by those suffixes themselves; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in these cases. They say that since words such as *nibha*, *anīkāśa*, and others—which occur only in compounds—are inherently incapable of conveying the connection of the meaning of a *tiṅ* suffix to their own such meaning, the condition "being other than *nibha*-type words" (*nibhādyanyatvam*) must also be included [in the definition] to exclude them.
And the subsequent [syllable]. || 2 ||

The meaning is self-evident. If it is objected: "But since the status of being 'subsequent' (paratva) is established by supplying the word 'following' (*para*) through the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), and by relying on immediate succession (*ānantarya*) in the case of the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*) in rules such as *gāpoḥ*, this [mention of the word *pūrva*] is redundant," we say: No. For it is possible for the limit (*avadhi*) required by the ablative case to be supplied by the word *pūrva* as well; furthermore, since immediate succession can also be maintained by way of being "prior" (*pūrvatvena*), the rule operates as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the rules for *bahuc* and *akac* are intended as restrictive (niyamārtha)—meaning that *bahuc* alone occurs before [the stem] and *akac* alone occurs in the middle—other suffixes will, by implication, necessarily occur after [the stem] due to the exclusion of those positions. This is not so, because since the "middle" is not specifically defined, even if that rule were to restrict the specific middle position as being "before the final vowel" (*ṭeḥ prāk*), it would still be impossible to exclude other intermediate positions. Furthermore, since *bahuc* and *akac* are the items to be prescribed (*vidheya*), *bahuc* must occur only before [the stem], and *akac* must occur only before the final vowel (*prāk-ṭeḥ*).

Furthermore, since the rule *prāk kṛteḥ evākac* is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), it is impossible to exclude the occurrence of different suffixes in other instances. Nor can this difficulty be resolved by the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya*; for that rule applies only to an operation that pertains to what follows [the specified antecedent], and it serves no purpose in prescribing that the *dharmī* (the base) itself should follow [the suffix]. Moreover, a restrictive rule does not apply when a previously non-existent injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) is being established.

Now, on the view that words are eternal (*nitya-śabda-pakṣa*), the mere correctness of subsequent elements such as suffixes (*sanādi*) is established by their very nature; even on the view that words are produced (*kārya-śabda-pakṣa*), there is no purpose for the mention of "the subsequent" (*para*). This is because the term *tasmāt*, indicated by its ablative case-ending (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), results in two possible meanings when it occurs in the various rules (*pradeśa*): either it refers to that which is already existent being taken as the recipient of an operation (*kāryin*), in which case the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses dependence on the operation, meaning "the operation of the subsequent takes place"; or it refers to the cause of production. Therefore, the mention of "the subsequent" is unnecessary.

Since it is taught that when there is the prescription of something previously non-existent, the subsequent element comes into being, the genitive case (kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī) is used in relation to that "coming into being" (*bhāva*). Nor should it be argued that the use of the nominative case in expressions such as *san* is redundant; for its purpose is merely to provide a formal indication, since the genitive case is subsequently understood in the sense that "the subsequent *san* comes into being."

Alternatively, even if the production of *san* and other suffixes occurs in an indefinite location, the grammatical operations prescribed by rules concerning technical designations such as *kṛt*, *kṛtya*, and so forth, apply only to that [suffix] and not to one in another location. Since usage will occur only for that which possesses the grammatical operation pertaining to its own location, there is no fault. Furthermore, in the case of modifications (*vikāra*) and augments (*āgama*), the previously mentioned method should be followed. In rules such as *gā-po-ṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8), because of the governing context of *dhātoḥ* ("after a root"), it should be explained as: "the suffix *ṭak* comes after a root, and *ṣṭak* comes immediately after the roots *gā* and *pā*."

Nor should it be argued that, because *kvi* and other such suffixes—which are not inherent in the application (*prayoga*) and are always the counter-correlates of elision—do not trigger the rule "from that [which precedes], the subsequent [is affected]," their elision would occur at an indefinite location; and that, therefore, the purpose [of the present rule] is to ensure that elision occurs only for those [suffixes] that follow [the base]. This is because it is determined by the mark of the attachment of indicatory letters (*anubandha*) that their elision occurs only when they are subsequent. It is determined by the mark of the attachment of indicatory letters that their elision occurs only when they are subsequent.

This is because an operation conditioned by an *anubandha*—such as those prescribed by rules like *kiti*—depends upon a suffix (*pratyaya*) that stands subsequent [to the stem]. This follows from the rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya*, which states that when a specific element is mentioned [in a rule], the operation applies to what precedes it. Nor should it be argued that even under the view that the position [of the *anubandha*] is indefinite, the operation could still depend on an optional posteriority (since the rule *tasminniti...* allows for such a possibility), and that once this optional posteriority is accepted, the attachment of the *anubandha* achieves its purpose; consequently, how can one establish its posteriority as a necessity? For even so, the resulting occasional redundancy (*pākṣika-vaiyarthyam*) remains difficult to avoid.

In cases such as *spṛśo 'nudake*, where a single ablative case (*pañcamī*) is heard, its validity is established by supplying either the word "prior" (*pūrva*) or "subsequent" (*para*). When the word "prior" itself is supplied, since the meaninglessness of the *anubandha* (the marker *k*) would otherwise be unavoidable, and since there is no obstacle to its being an indicator (*liṅga*) for the elision of what follows, this [interpretation] is initially reached.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "Or rather, it is for the purpose of restricting the usage. The word *vā* (or) has a disjunctive sense, because according to the view of the *Vārttika*, the alternative position—that the rule is for the sake of *kvip* and other suffixes—is already settled. However, according to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, since [the rule] is otherwise established by the method already stated, the word *tarhi* (then/in that case) signifies: "In that case, the usage of [suffixes] only when they follow [the base] is intended, and not when they do not follow. This [rule] is for the purpose of restriction. Nor should it be argued that this is not so because no contrary usage is observed.

One must understand that a restriction is being taught: "A base alone should not be used, nor should an affix alone. This is because one observes the non-usage of forms such as *babhru*, *maṇḍu*, and *lamaka* when one ought to have used *sadevadatto bābhravyo māṇḍavyo lāmakāyanaḥ*, and the non-usage of *kimasya* when one ought to have said *kiṃmasyadvayasam*. Nor should it be argued that these are incorrect due to the metaphorical treatment of identity—as in the case of "The moon is the face"—for [the grammatical rules] do not permit such usage here.

Since we observe the metaphorical application of identity even in the case of servants and others, and because the meaning of "offspring" is not invariably understood [from the word *apatyam*], it has been stated by Hari: "If words such as *babhru* were used without a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) due to the relation 'this is that' (*so'yam*), there would be no restriction regarding offspring."

Therefore, when there is a desire to express the offspring (apatya), this statement is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) so that, apart from the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), there may not be the use of singular-ended words such as *babhru* and others in the same way as plural-ended forms like *gargāḥ*. By this, the traditional commentary (*sāṃpradāyikagrantha*) which states that in cases such as *raghūṇām* there is a "characteristic of non-difference" (*abhedalakṣaṇā*) is explained; for it is precisely by means of the metaphorical treatment of non-difference that the prohibition of usage [in other cases] is established. For this very reason, the word *gavaya* used for a cow through a delusion regarding its primary denotation (*śaktibhrama*) is incorrect (*asādhu*), whereas its use through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of similarity (*sādṛśya*) is indeed correct—this is the accepted position.

This is a restriction of both [the preceding and the following]. Since the rule "from that" (*tasmāt*) and "of the subsequent" (*uttarasya*) already establish that the application must occur only after the base (*prakṛti*) and not before it—lest it should ever remain unapplied—it might be argued: "In the case of the mention of 'optionally' (*vā*), the suffix occurs optionally when characterized by posteriority, but in the other alternative it does not arise at all; therefore, let the mention of 'subsequent' (*para*) be for the sake of ensuring the non-arising of the suffix in that alternative. This is not so, because since the application of posteriority is fixed, there can be no intention regarding its cessation.

If it is argued that otherwise, by the phrase "or by the recurrence of the condition" (*vāvacanena*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the suffix itself rather than its application—this is not so; because in the case where the suffix *san* is applied, it is obligatory (*nityatvāt*), and in the case where it is not applied—as in "he wishes to do" (*kartum icchati*)—it does not arise at all, thus the mention of the option (*vāvacana*) is rejected. Therefore, it is established that [the rule] is solely for the purpose of regulating usage (*prayoga-niyamārtha*).
And it has the acute accent on the first syllable.

If it is argued that since the pronunciation of a vowel without a specific accent is impossible, and because the properties of being *cit* (marked with *c*), *pit* (marked with *p*), or *tit* (marked with *t*) are restricted to specific suffixes by those very markers—such as the final acute (*antodātta*) for *cit*, the low (*adhaa*) for *pit*, and the circumflex (*svarita*) for *tit*—then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it follows that other suffixes must necessarily have their initial syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). This is not so. For when suffixes such as *cit* and others would otherwise receive an unrestricted accent, the rule "the suffix *cit* is specifically final-acute" serves as a restriction; it does not mean that only *cit* is final-acute. Otherwise, there would be no justification for excluding other accents from that suffix.
Thus, this [rule] is intended as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*) regarding suffixes lacking such markers, which would otherwise receive an unrestricted accent.

It might be argued as follows: "The rules *ñ-n-ity-ādir nityam* and *pratyayasya ca ad-upadeśāl lasārvadhātukam anudāttam sup-pitau ca* would prescribe the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) accents only when other accents are present; therefore, there is no need for the technical designation 'affix' (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*) in conjunction with those prescriptions. Thus, there is economy (*lāghava*) in mentioning the acute and grave accents only once. This is not so.

If that were the case, when the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is included [in the rule], then by the *paribhāṣā* "that which is proximate [is designated] as well as what begins with it and ends with it," the beginning of the entire aggregate of base and suffix would become acute (*udātta*) and the end grave (*anudātta*). However, there is no such fault, because the rule *ādyudāttaśca* applies at every occurrence: thus, only that which is characterized by initial acuteness arises as *tavya*-type suffixes, while that which is characterized by gravity arises as *ati*-type suffixes and so forth. This is because the grammatical operations such as being designated as "beginning with it" apply only to a suffix that has already arisen, and not to one that is currently arising.

It might be argued as follows: because of the very commencement of the rule *ñ-n-ity-ādir nityam*, the mention of "that-beginning" (*tad-ādi*) is not intended here. Otherwise, since the result would already be established by the rule *pratyayaś ca* alone, its inclusion would be redundant. Similarly, by virtue of the prescription of the final acute accent (*antodātta*) for verbal roots (*dhātu*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*), there is no mention of "ending in that" (*tad-anta*) in the rule *suptiṅoś ca*; for the prescription of their final acute accent is purposeful only in cases where they are followed by an unaccented suffix (*anudātta-pratyaya*). This is evident from the audible presence of the suffix in forms such as *yāti* and *kṛṣṇatara*, where the suffix is marked with the *pit* designation.

In examples such as *yāta*, this is because the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), being subsequently prescribed (*satiśiṣṭa*), sublates that [original accent]. Nor should it be argued that in cases like *āste* or *śete*, where the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented by the rule *tāsyanudāttet*, there might be scope for the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*); for by the same logic, the principle of "taking that as the beginning" (*tadādigrahaṇa*) would apply there as well. Furthermore, in the case of the standard formulation, in forms such as *lavitavyam*, since the suffix *tavya* is unaccented on its initial syllable by virtue of being prescribed at the time of its production (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), the augment *iṭ* which follows it becomes unaccented by the rule of "the remainder is unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*).

However, according to the method stated above, it must be said that after the suffix *tavya* has arisen, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is superseded by the augment *iṭ* because the latter is subsequent; yet, when the initial acute accent applies again due to the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), it would rest upon the augment *iṭ* itself. This is because the fact that augments are necessarily unaccented (*anudātta*) must be postulated, and thus the matter is already settled by that rule alone.

To explain: from the root *lū* in the sense of "cutting," after adding the suffix *luṭ*, there is *tip*, which becomes *tāsi* with the augment *iṭ*. If the *iṭ* here were not *anudātta* (unaccented), then, being a part of *tāsi*, it would be *udātta* (accented); and by the rule of *śeṣanighāta*, the vowel of *tāsi* would be *anudātta*. Once the *ṭi*-lopa is performed, since that [elision] does not constitute the elision of an *udātta* vowel, the vowel *ā* remains *udātta*, and thus the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent resulting from the disappearance of an *udātta*) is established. For in this case, both the initial *udātta* [of the stem] and the *iṭ* would apply; however, by the principle of *paratva* (subsequent application), the *iṭ* takes precedence. This is because both are *nitya* (obligatory) due to their applicability regardless of whether the other has been applied or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*). Furthermore, once the *iṭ* has been applied, the same status is maintained because no change in the word-form (*śabdāntara*) occurs.
Because the accent of the suffix [as taught] in the *āgama* [rules] is the cause for the distinction between words, and because the difference in pitch (*śrutibheda*) is equal in both cases.

Alternatively, due to its being *antaraṅga*, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) alone operates first; for it is enjoined in connection with the very production [of the suffix]. Once the suffix has been produced, the augment *iṭ* for the stem (*aṅga*)—which depends upon both the stem and the suffix—is *bahiraṅga*. Nor should it be argued that by the maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), when the suffix is resorted to, the stem is also necessarily resorted to; for it was stated immediately after this that in the rule prescribing the accent of a suffix, there is no extension to the beginning of that [suffix].

If it is argued: "In that case, since the augment *iṭ* occurring immediately after an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) will itself become unaccented by the rule of 'the rest being unaccented' (*śeṣanighāta*), why is the unaccented nature of the augments (*āgama*) being prescribed? [The answer is: No. Even so, in the form *laviṣīya* (the potential mood, *liṅ*, of the root *lu*), because the suffix *sīyuṭ* is specifically prescribed [for the potential], it would apply first; subsequently, when the replacement of the *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*) takes place, the initial acute accent applying there would belong to *sīyuṭ* alone.

However, some maintain that if the rule for the low-pitched (anudātta) accentuation of suffixes (*āgama*) were applied, then once the low-pitched accent of *sīyuṭ* had been established, the high-pitched (udātta) accent of the substitute vowel *ā* in place of *iṭ* would be automatically accomplished; thus, that rule must necessarily be initiated. Consequently, the intention of the Bhāṣya is understood to be that once a suffix (*āgama*) is added, it is only that which is qualified by the suffix that possesses the status of a suffix (*pratyayatva*), and not the [original] suffix alone. Otherwise, even when *sīyuṭ* is added, since the high-pitched accent of *iṭ* would already be established by its being a suffix, there would be no need for the [separate] rule.

Others, however, maintain that because an augment (*āgama*) is sometimes a suffix (*pratyaya*) in its own right—whether it is a specific suffix or a suffix alone—the vowel *ī* of the suffix *sīyuṭ* might occasionally be acute (*udātta*). To exclude this possibility, the statement that augments are "as if non-existent" (*avidyamānavat*) is indeed necessary. For this very reason, the interpretation that "the substitute *jh* applies to the beginning of a suffix" is faultless. Regarding the form *śayāntaiḥ*, they explain that even when the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ* have been applied, the status of the letter *ḍh* as the beginning of a suffix (*pratyayāditva*) is not lost.

As for the claim that because of the specific rule stating "augments (āgama) are unaccented" (*anudātta*), once the *sīyuṭ* augment has become unaccented, the [rule for] acute accent (*udāttatva*) does not apply there—that is incorrect. For the authors of the Bhāṣya have presented the aforementioned difficulty precisely in the view that such a rule was not commenced. Indeed, it is out of fear of the stated fault that the rule regarding the unaccented nature of augments was resorted to, and that [fact] is obtainable through the force of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because, by the statement that "the *yāsuṭ* in parasmaipada endings is acute and marked with *ṅ*" (*yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅicca*), one infers that other augments are unaccented.

It should not be argued that in examples such as *na cācinuyāt*, since the augment *yāsuṭ* is a portion of the *pit* [element], it would follow that it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and therefore that rule exists for the purpose of prescribing an acute accent (*udātta*). For even by prescribing *apit*-ness for the *liṅ* in connection with *yāsuṭ*—namely, by the rule *apiccaliṅ*—the same result is achieved. Indeed, according to the other formulation (the *yathānyāsa*), there would be nine morae (*mātrā`), whereas in the stated formulation there are only six; thus, the possibility of parsimony (*lāghava*) exists. Consequently, the indication—that augments are unaccented—is established without obstruction by the force of adopting this more cumbersome formulation.

Even if, by means of the *āgama*s, the initial status of what follows them is negated, how can there be an acute (*udātta*) accent on the first syllable? For if one applies the rule that *āgama*s are to be treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), then the substitution of *ava* and so forth would not occur. If it is argued that non-existence applies only for the purpose of prescribing accents, then in the case of *lavitā*, the circumflex (*svarita*) accent prescribed by the rule "after an acute, an unaccented [syllable] becomes circumflex" would not occur; for this word is acute on the first syllable because it ends in a *tṛn* suffix, and the other two syllables are unaccented due to the rule of residual depression (*śeṣanighāta*). In that case, by virtue of being treated as non-existent, the circumflex nature of the augment *iṭ* would be untenable.

Nor should it be said that this extension [of accentuation] applies only to the rule concerning the accent of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-svara-vidhi*); for if that were so, the accent prescribed by the rule *niṣṭhā ca dy-aj-anāt* would undesirably apply to the word *cintitaḥ*. Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the extension is stated in the rule concerning the accent of suffixes (*pratyaya-svara-vidhi*). Furthermore, that extension is established by an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark).

If, when the acute accent (*udātta*) on the beginning of a suffix is to be applied, the augment (*āgama*) were to cause the loss of its status as the "beginning" (*āditva*) of the suffix, then in forms such as *ācinuyātām*, the acute accent would already be established because the *yāsuṭ* augment is part of the beginning of the suffix; consequently, the explicit rule for the acuteness of *yāsuṭ* would be redundant. Therefore, this [redundancy] indicates that when the operation of accenting the beginning of a suffix is to take effect, augments are to be treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavadbhāva*). Thus, there is no logical inconsistency. Consequently, even on account of the requirement for the augments to remain unaccented, the rule for the initial acuteness [of the suffix] should not be formulated in conjunction with the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "suffix."

Now, in cases such as *sraughnī* and *māthurī*, when analyzed and derived [from *sraughna-ī*], once the form *sraughna-ī* is established, the rule *yasyetica* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) would—by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*)—substitute the elision of the vowel *a*, thereby overriding the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*). Consequently, because there would be no "cessation of an acute" (*udāttanivṛtti*), the accent known as *udāttanivṛttisvara* (Pāṇini 6.1.161) would not apply. If it is argued that, since the initial acute accent is prescribed in conjunction with the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayasaṃjñā-saṃniyoga*), the accentuation occurs before the elision of the *aṇ* suffix takes effect, and thus when the unaccented (*anudātta*) feminine suffix *ṅīp* follows, the aforementioned accent fails due to the subsequent elision of that suffix—this too is incorrect.

According to the principle that "cognitions of *svārtha* and so forth occur in sequence," the suffix conditioned by femininity is *bahiraṅga*; consequently, the elision (*lopa*) conditioned by it is likewise *bahiraṅga*. Thus, since the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*), which is *antaraṅga*, applies first, the desired accentuation is established. Furthermore, the *bahiraṅga* nature of the elision should be understood from the fact that it depends upon both [the condition of] being an *aṅga* and being a *bha*.

Otherwise, even in the case of *autsī*, *kaṃsikī*, and *ātreyī*, there would arise the undesirable consequence that the accentuation of the *ñit*, *nit*, and *kit* suffixes would subvert the accents of the vowels [of the stem] by means of elision (*lopa*), and thus the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the vowel whose preceding portion has lost its accent) would not occur. Even though the accents of *ñit* and so forth are stronger precisely because they are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of suffixes—as in *kaṃsikī* (feminine of *kaṃsika*), derived from *kaṃsena krītā*—where, by the force of the inclusion of the *c*-marker in the rule *kaṃsāṭ ṭiṭhan*, the substitution of *ikā* occurs first; then follows the acute accent (*udātta*) of the suffix-initial, then the acute accent of the initial [of the stem], and finally the elision of the final [vowel]—there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) here.

Nevertheless, regarding the form *ātreyī*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*. According to the principle that "the instruction [of the base] should be treated as if it were original (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) for the sake of the accentuation of the *āyan* and other suffixes," the substitution of *ey* occurs first; subsequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. In this context, without the application of the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*, the *anudāttanivṛtti-svara* (the acute accent replacing the grave) would not occur. Therefore, the objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the explicit statement of the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) in connection with the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyaya-saṃjñā-sanniyoga*) is redundant.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that in the aforementioned arrangement (*nyāsa*), the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would supersede the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) due to its posteriority; whereas in the alternative arrangement, the accent of the verbal root supersedes the accent of the suffix due to its posteriority. In this very context, it is more appropriate to prescribe the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*), because the weight of authoritative tradition (*prāmāṇika-gaurava*) is justifiable.

For instance, there is an occasion for an affix to be udātta by virtue of a specific rule (pratyayādyudātta), as in the case of *samatvam*, where the base (*prakṛti*) is anudātta. However, where the verbal root accent (*dhātusvara*) applies—such as in *pacati* and so on, or in *gopāyati* and *dhūpāyati* where the affix is anudātta—the rule *anta* [Pāṇini 6.1.220] prevails over it by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). For in that case, the word ending in *gup* is first udātta at the end, and subsequently, it remains udātta at the end.

Likewise, in examples such as *apacati* and *kāryam*, where the *anudātta* (low-pitched) and *svarita* (circumflex) accents based on the markers *p* and *t* respectively have their scope, consider the case of *kāryā*. Here, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs first. Because that substitute behaves like the final element with respect to what precedes it, the *titsvara* (the accent of the marker *t*) would apply; however, because it behaves like the initial element with respect to what follows it, the *pitsvara* (the accent of the marker *p*) would also apply. By the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the *titsvara* prevails. Furthermore, the *citsvara* (the accent of the marker *c*) prevails over the *pitsvara* by conflict. The scope of the *pitsvara* has been stated previously.

The term "calana" (moving) and "kampana" (trembling) are formed with the suffix *yuc*. In the case of *āmbaṣṭhyā* and *sauvaryā*, when the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix is also applied, both [rules] would apply; however, the *cit-svara* (acute accent on the *cit* element) prevails due to its higher status [in the order of rules].

In reality, however, this contradiction is not tenable. Since the suffix *āya* is taught as being conditioned by its association (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*), even when the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) has been applied, the subsequent application of the term "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*)—which results in an enclitic accent (*antodātta*)—remains unimpeded according to the principle that "the accent of what is subsequently established is stronger. Furthermore, although the accent of a *pit* suffix and the accent of a *tit* suffix are both non-eternal because they apply to different words (*śabdāntara-prāpti*), once the circumflex (*svarita*) has first taken effect due to its priority, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation occurs; and since the circumflex and the grave (*anudātta*) are most similar to one another, the resulting accent of the single substitute is the circumflex (*svarita*).

Because even in a *svarita* accent, there exists a portion that is *anudātta*. Furthermore, in the case of *āmbaṣṭhyā*, the final acute (*antodātta*) is established by the force of the application of the marker *c* [in the rule *āmbaṣṭhyā-sauvīryābhyāṃ ca*]. Nor should it be argued that the particle *ca* is for the purpose of preventing a general rule [and thus its presence does not indicate the force of the *c*]; for if it were intended for that purpose alone, it would follow that the prescription [of the acute] should have occurred in the very section on the suffix *ṭāp*. Therefore, it is established that the prescription of the initial acute (*ādyaudātta*) for suffixes in conjunction with technical names (*saṃjñā*) is meaningful. "Sup and pit are *anudātta*. (Pāṇini 3.1.4)

This is an exception to what precedes it: suffixes that are *suP* (nominal endings) and those that are *pit* (marked with *p*) are *anudātta* (unaccented). In the rule, the doubling [of the term] occurs by following from both the status of being *suP* and the status of being *pit*. Examples: *dṛṣat*, *dṛṣadau*, *dṛṣadaḥ*; *pacati*, *paṭhati*. [Now, the rule: *san* is added after the roots *gup*, *titikṣ*, and *kita*. (Pāṇini 3.1.5)

The root *gup* means "to hide"; *tij* means "to sharpen"; and *kit* [is used] in the sense of "dwelling" and "removing disease. These are indicated as having anudātta (low-pitched) accents, according to the Bhāṣya, which states that they will be explained in a subsequent sūtra. On the basis of this very implication (*svarasa*), Vardhamāna maintains that in the commentary on the *Khaṇḍana*, the form *cikitsatu* is appropriate, as in the phrase "let someone treat his own [disease]. Kaiyaṭa, however, explained that *kit* is listed here merely to show its sequence in the Dhātupāṭha and is not itself anudātta.

It should be understood that these roots take the *ātmanepada* endings only with respect to the meanings to be mentioned hereafter; in other meanings, they are simply *cur*-class (*curādi*) roots, as they lack an indicatory marker (*anubandha*). Although this specific restriction of meaning was not stated by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali), it has been set forth by the authors of the commentaries (*vṛttikāra*) and others in accordance with usage, because the rule for the suffix *san*—which includes the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*)—is applied in these two rules as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) specifically on the basis of these particular meanings.

Therefore, because these [roots] are distinct verbal roots (*dhātu*) for these specific meanings, they always take the suffix *saN*; since the characteristic of having an unaccented vowel form (*anudātta-rūpa-liṅga*) has its purpose fulfilled in the individual parts, it serves as a specifier for the whole. Consequently, when the suffix *saN* is added, they trigger the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). This is the distinction: *gup* takes *saN* in the sense of "censure"; *tij* in the sense of "endurance"; *kit* in the sense of "remedy for disease," "restraint," "removal," "destruction," and "doubt"; *mān* in the sense of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*); *badh* in the sense of "mental agitation"; *dān* in the sense of "straightforwardness"; and *śān* in the sense of "sharpening."

By the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, [the forms ending in *san* etc. possess the status of verbal roots (*dhātutva*). By the rule *taṅ-sanyaṅoḥ*, there is reduplication. Since the designation "root" (*dhātu*) has not been revoked, they do not have the status of "semi-vocalic suffixes" (*ārdhadhātuka*). Consequently, the augment *iṭ* and *guṇa* substitution do not apply. Although the absence of *guṇa* is easily established by the fact that *san* is *kit* according to the rule *halantācca*, nevertheless, since the application of that rule is precluded by the aforementioned reasoning, what is the point of following it? Thus we have: *jugupsate*, *titikṣate*, *cikitsati*. Because they end in a suffix, the augment *ām* is applied, as in *jugupsāṃ cakre*, and so forth. [Now, regarding the rule: *mān-badha-dān-śānbhyo dīrghaśca-abhyāsasya* || 6 || [The suffix *san* is applied] after the roots *mān*, *badh*, *dān*, and *śān*; furthermore, there is lengthening of the vowel in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).]

The suffix *saN* may be added after these [roots], and there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). [Roots: *māna* (in the sense of honoring), *vadha* (in the sense of binding). Here, *dāna* and *śāna* are *svarita*-accented; the first two (*māna* and *vadha*) are *anudātta*-accented. Examples: *mīmāṃsate*, *bībhatsate* (where *bhaṣ*-substitution occurs before a *c* sound). *dīdāṃsati*, *dīdāṃsate*; *śīśāṃsati*, *śīśāṃsate*. [Objection: But surely, lengthening of the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable would apply here. Since a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) overrides a general rule (*sāmānyabādhaka*), the substitution of *i* by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79) would be impossible. Furthermore, even when the word "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) is used, there is no evidence that it requires the application of the *i*-substitution. [Response: This is not so.
