The word "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) is intended to indicate the sequence of operations. Even though the reduplicated syllable is expected, there is no lack of authority for the requirement of the *i*-substitution. Thus, the rule *sanyataḥ* is indeed applicable. Therefore, the form *dīdāṃsati* is established. The same applies to *śīśāṃsati*. As for *mīmāṃsate*, the *i*-substitution is obtained by the rule *sanyataḥ*. The *bhaṣ*-substitution in *bībhatsate* occurs because the root *badh* is *bhaṣ*-ending. The *svarita*-accentuation of *dāna* and *śāna* is for the purpose of the rule *svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* (Pāṇini 1.3.72). It is said: the rule should be formulated as *īccābhyāsasya* ("the substitute *ī* [is applied] to the reduplicated syllable"). Nor does this result in the sublation of the *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* rule (P. 7.4.60), because it must be stated as *īcca* ("and *ī*"). Since, without the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, the reduplicated syllable would not end in a vowel (*ajanta*), that [substitution of *ī*] would not be sublated. Alternatively, the rule should be formulated as *dīrghaścetobhyāsasya* ("and the long vowel *ī* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable"). Thus, by the force of the restatement (*anuvāda*), the lengthening occurs after the substitution of *i* has taken effect. Or else, there is a word-break (*cheda*) as *ābhyāsasya*; *ābhyāsa* means a modification (*vikāra*) of the reduplicated syllable, and that modification is, by implication, the substitution of *i*.

Because elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence, it is impossible to prescribe a substitute for it; for "being a *sthānin*" (the original element) consists precisely in being the counter-positive of the cessation brought about by that [elision]. Furthermore, if a long vowel were prescribed for a short *ā*-vowel, the mention of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) would be redundant; and if a long vowel were prescribed for a long vowel, there would be no distinction [between the original and the substitute]. Alternatively, [the rule] refers only to a modification caused by a proximate cause.

In reality, however, there is no fault; for exceptions (apavāda) do not subvert general rules (utsarga) when they concern modifications resulting from repeated application (abhyāsa-vikāra). This is because it will be made known by the inclusion of the term *aki* in the rule *dīrghokitaḥ* that the lengthening occurs immediately after the *it* (the *i* of *kit*). In the *Bhāmatī*, however, the word *mīmāṃsā* is derived from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "to measure" (*māne*). Nor does its failure to appear in the [original] *sūtra* imply that the suffix *san* is unestablished; for by the very form *mān*, the ending *n* is treated as a *nipātana* (irregular formation), thereby making the inclusion of the stated root possible.

In the *Muṇḍamiśra* and other sūtras, it is stated—both by the words and the intended meaning—that *hal* and *kala* are treated as ending in *a*, just like [the roots] ending in *a*. Nor does there arise the contingency of the substitution of *is* for *san* by the rule *sanimīmeti*; for Dīkṣita maintains that this rule is prescribed only for the *san* of desire (*icchā*) due to its association with *ghu* and others. And thus, it is not proper to include the nipātana (irregularity) regarding the ending in *n* within one's own conjecture, because Vācaspati Miśra has himself already stated this. Furthermore, the conjecture regarding the intended meaning of Miśra—that the commentary text *māna pūjāyām* must be explained by splitting [the compound]—is also improper.

For this reason as well, because the suffix *san* is written only in combination [with other elements]; therefore, in the word *mīmāṃsā*, derived from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring," its meaning is "revered inquiry" by virtue of established usage (*prasiddhi*), whereas [the form] derived from *māna* in the sense of "honoring" is according to the traditional grammatical rule (*smṛti*) alone—this is what was stated there by the author of the *Kalpataru*. This is the direction [of the argument].
[Pāṇini 3.1.7: "After a verbal root denoting an action, when the agent is the same, the suffix *saN* is optionally used in the sense of desire."

In this context, the objecthood (*karmatva*) and the identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) are determined by the desire (*iccha*) itself through its semantic role (*arthadvāraka*), as they are in close proximity [to that desire]. Thus, when there is a desire whose object is the meaning of a verbal root, the suffix *san* is added to that root; both the meaning of the root and the desire must have the same agent. That is to say, the desire must have an agent identical to the agent of the root-meaning. For this very reason, in expressions such as *jijñāsā* ("desire to know"), there is the cognition of a desire for knowledge that resides in the same locus (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) as the self. For example: "Caitra desires to cook" (*paktum icchati pipakṣati caitraḥ*).

The meaning of the desiderative suffix *san* (desire) is construed as the object (*viṣayatva*) of the meaning of the verbal root itself. Thus, the resulting cognition has the desire as its primary qualificand: "the desire whose agent is non-different from Caitra and whose object is cooking. This is because, since the desiderative form functions as a verbal root, the desire is the principal element. However, according to the Nyāya school, the suffix of the verb following a root that denotes a transitive action (one with an object) indicates the locus (*āśraya*). Consequently, the desire is construed as non-different from Caitra, who is the locus of that desire. The resulting cognition has the cooking as its qualificand: "Caitra is non-different from the locus of the desire for cooking."

According to the view of Maṇika, however, the desire itself is construed with Caitra through the relation of substratum (āśrayatva). Since it has been stated that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) serves merely for the grammatical correctness of the root, the resulting cognition is "Caitra is the substratum of the desire. In the case of *odanaṃ bubhukṣate* ("he desires to eat rice"), because one experiences the rice as the object of the desire by virtue of its being the qualificandum of the eating, the suffix *san* expresses a desire whose qualifier is denoted by the root. They say that even in *pākaṃ cikīrṣati* ("he desires to cook"), the cooking is experienced primarily as the object of the desire, and not the act of doing (*kṛti*).

However, some maintain that even in the case of transitive roots, when the object is not intended to be expressed—as in "he remains in the house" (*gṛhe tiṣṭhāsan*) and similar instances—there is indeed an experience of a desire directed toward the meaning of the verbal root itself. Therefore, with the intention of expressing a desire whose qualifier is "staying" and whose substantive is "the house," the expression "he desires to stay in the house" (*gṛhaṃ tiṣṭhāsan*) is not used. Nor should it be argued that if "substantive-ness" (*viśeṣyatva*) were not the meaning of the accusative case—as in "he wishes to eat rice" (*odanaṃ bubhukṣate*)—then one would also have to say "he desires to cook" (*pākatvaṃ cikīrṣati*) or "he desires the enemy's wealth" (*śatrudhanaṃ cikīrṣati*) when there is a desire for the destruction of the enemy's wealth. [This objection is invalid because]...

They say that when used in conjunction with the root *kṛ*, the meaning of the second case is either of the two objects of action known as "the state of being accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) or "the state of being intended" (*uddeśyatva*). One might ask: what is the purpose of the word "dhātoḥ" (of the verbal root)? It cannot be said that it is for the sake of excluding [the application of the suffix] after a prefix (*upasarga*), because otherwise, reduplication and the augment *āṭ* would belong to the prefix alone. This is not so, because the [conditions of] "objecthood" (*karmatva*) and "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) are mentioned, and these two are defined solely by reference to the action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, since the action is expressed by the verbal root alone, and the prefix is merely an indicator (*dyotaka*), it is possible for those [suffixes] to arise from the verbal root itself.

Even in the view that [the prefix] is expressive (*vācakatva*), the objecthood belongs to the qualificand alone, while the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is triggered by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the qualifier; for in this view, the meaning of the prefix is not a separate object. Even in the view where both the mat (*kaṭa*) and the qualities such as "terrible" (*bhīṣma*) are objects, the entire complex is not an object, and therefore the suffix would not arise. Otherwise, even if it were stated that [the suffix applies] "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), the difficulty would not be resolved. For if the objecthood of the complex were accepted as being mediated by its meaning, then because the individual component is not an object, the *san* suffix would not occur.

This is because of the specification of the ablative case in the word *karmaṇaḥ*. Nor should it be argued that one should rely on the genitive case in *karmaṇaḥ*, interpreting the meaning as "the suffix *san* occurs after a root that is a part of a verbal root"; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its non-occurrence after a simple root alone. Therefore: "Because they are conceived as distinct entities for the sake of establishing the rules for [augments] such as *aṭ* and others, it is determined that between a root and a prefix, the root is that which expresses the action."

Nor is it for the purpose of preventing the occurrence of *san* after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because in that context, *kyac* and other suffixes prescribed as specific exceptions (*viśeṣavihita*) act as sublaters (*bādhaka*) by way of being counter-exceptions (*apavāda*). Nor should it be argued that since *san* is optional, *kyac* and the others find their scope of application in the alternative where *san* is absent; for when both the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) are optional, the general rule does not apply once the exception has been set aside, and thus only the sentence itself (the syntactic construction) proceeds.

Furthermore, since the suffix *san* is produced after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is easy to prevent its application even by means of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*), due to the failure of desire (*icchā*) to be understood [from a base that lacks a case-ending]. Nor is it for the purpose of preventing the production of *san* from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because the rule explicitly states "by the object" (*karmaṇā*), and when there is the status of being an object, the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix is necessarily required. This is precisely what the author of the Vārttika says: "Due to the mention of 'object,' the mention of 'verbal root' (*dhātu*) in the rule prescribing *san* is redundant. If it is argued that "the object is [the verbal root] along with its prefix," [then the answer follows].

Since a prefix (*upasarga*) serves to qualify the object (*karman*), the [action] without a prefix is the object, whereas that with a prefix is not; for even though the context concerns verbal roots (*dhātu*), the suffix *san* is not prescribed there because [the action with a prefix] lacks the status of being an object (*akarmatva*). This being the position reached—

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: First, as for what was stated—that [the suffix *san*] does not apply because it is not so prescribed—that is merely a resort to a desperate position (*agatikagati*). For it is logical to establish the scope of a rule by resorting to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since, in the absence of any other alternative, the determination of the rule's application in cases such as *pacanti* is made in accordance with the intended meaning (*lakṣya*). Furthermore, as for the claim that [the suffix *san*] is barred by the exceptions (*apavāda*) such as *kyac* and others—that too is incorrect. This is because the suffix *kyac* and others are prescribed only when there is a desire for something expressed by a *sub*-ending word to belong to oneself (*ātmīyatvena*); whereas in cases such as *rājñaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires the king’s son"), where the desire concerns something belonging to another (*parakīyatvena*), the suffix *san* is unavoidable.

Now, in this context, there is no fault precisely because of the requirement that the agents be identical (*samānakartṛkatva*). This is because identity of agent with a word ending in a *sup*-suffix (a nominal) is impossible; for words such as "son" (*putra*) denote an already existent entity (*sattvabhūta-artha*), whereas only that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is capable of being related to a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Nor should it be argued: "In examples such as 'he makes a mat' (*kaṭaṃ karoti*), since the mat and other objects also denote existent entities, how can there be an expectancy for a means? For in those cases, the status of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is understood solely through the proximity of another word. As Harivṛṣabha stated:

"The locus of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana-āśraya*)—whether it be something to be produced (*nirvartya*), something to be modified (*vikārya*), or something to be reached (*prāpya*) [is the object]."
Since it is actions alone that are to be accomplished, that which is of an established nature is designated [as the object].

Therefore, it is said that the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is not for this purpose; nevertheless, in cases such as *āsitum icchati* ("he wishes to sit") and *śayitum icchati* ("he wishes to lie down"), because the suffix *tumun* expresses a state yet to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*), there is the possibility of its connection with an agent, and thus the suffix *san* would be unavoidable there. This is because the prohibition against [the application of *san*] after words ending in *-m* or indeclinables will be stated later under the rule for *kyac*. Now, one might object: "In these examples, since the desire is already expressed by the word *icchati*, which is the cause of the *tumun* suffix, *san* should not occur, according to the principle that what has already been expressed need not be used again (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*)."

If it is argued that, since the suffix *tumun* requires a verbal root as its cause (*nimitta*) and cannot occur in the absence thereof, the application of the rule for the desiderative suffix *san* would be difficult to justify because it would subvert the usage of the verb *icchati*.

True; nevertheless, because the suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed solely for the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), it lacks the condition of having a word meaning "desire" as its complement. Consequently, the application of *saN* (the desiderative suffix) is unavoidable. Nor should it be argued that here too there can be no connection with a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) because the state denoted by *lyuṭ* is of the nature of a real entity (*sattva*). For, since the action expressed by the verbal root is of a non-substantial nature (*asattvabhūta*), a common agency with respect to it is logically possible. Furthermore, the sentence must have the same meaning as the derivative form (*vṛtti*).

The sentence *āsitum icchati* ("he wishes to sit") has the same meaning as *āsisiṣate*; this is because the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is understood in both cases. However, in the case of *āsanam icchati* ("he desires sitting"), there is ambiguity as to whether the desire belongs to oneself or another; thus, since there is no rule ensuring the perception of a common agent, the suffix *san* will not occur. This is because it is impossible to include the identity of the agent within the scope of that *san* suffix. Otherwise, even when the term "root" (*dhātu*) is mentioned [in the rule], the suffix *san* would be unavoidable in a construction such as *devadatta icchati yajñadattena saṃgatim* ("Devadatta desires a meeting with Yajñadatta").

Since a verbal root is never used in isolation here, the suffix *ktvā* is employed because the suffix *san* is likewise to be applied to the root; for when one wishes to express a common agent, as in "the calf desires to go" (*saṃjigantsate vatsaḥ mātaram*), the suffix *san* is desired.

In this way, the inclusion of the condition "having the same agent as the action" (*karmasamānakartṛka*) is also redundant. For the commencement of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is for the purpose of distinguishing between correct and incorrect usage when observing mixed applications. This is because we do not observe such usages as *jigamiṣati* or *bubhukṣate* in the sense of "he desires Devadatta's going" or "he desires Devadatta's eating. Since the formation of the desiderative suffix (*san*) is already justified by the rule for expressing desire, and since the object of desire necessarily exists, one must—by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*)—accept that the objecthood belongs solely to the meaning of the base verb itself.

If it is argued that the requirement of having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) can also be established through proximity alone, we say no; for it is necessary to mention either the "root" (*dhātu*) or the "action" (*karma*) in order to determine the extent of the *aṅga* (the base to which suffixes are added). This is because the property of having the same agent is more cumbersome (*gurutvāt*). Furthermore, if it were stated as "in the sense of desire" (*icchāyām vā*), then even though the root would be implied by its status as the antecedent of the suffix, in forms such as *prācikīrṣat*, the prefix (*upasarga*) along with the root would have to be considered the *aṅga*. However, when there is a direct specification of the particular root, the nature of the *aṅga* is easily understood.

And although this [designation] could be established even by the mention of "one or the other" (*anyatara*), nevertheless, the mention of "dhātu" (root) alone is necessary. Since the designation *ārdhadhātuka* for *san* is established because it is prescribed after explicitly uttering the word "dhātu," [the rules for] *guṇa* and *iṭ* are thereby established in forms such as *śiśāyiṣate*. However, it has already been stated that the *san* which is prescribed by the two preceding rules does not possess the status of *ārdhadhātuka*.

It cannot be argued that the prescription of *kit*-hood for the suffix *san* in the rule *nacekojhaliti* is intended to prohibit *guṇa*, and that by being the cause (*prasaṃjaka*) of the very prohibition it itself triggers (*ākṣepsyati*), it implies the status of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix for *san*. For if this were a general indicator (*jñāpaka*), that [status] would apply everywhere; whereas if it were restricted to a specific case, it would not imply that [status] for any other root ending in a semivowel (*iganta*).

As for what was also stated—that that which is accompanied by a prefix is not an object (*karman*)—that too is incorrect. Because the specific action is initiated by the compound as a whole, the status of being an object, which is mediated by meaning, comes to rest in the aggregate itself; for it is only a qualified action that can be brought about by its means (*sādhana*).

For the meaning here is not a mere collocation [of two things], as in the case of a "blue pot," because the qualifier and the qualified are each produced by their own respective causes. In that case, since blueness and potness are delimited as effects relative to distinct causes, the qualified object is established through its parts; but here, no other cause for the excellence (*prakarṣa*) is postulated. Nor should it be argued that, because a prefix (*upasarga*) is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), the meaning is simply the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) as qualified [by it].

Nevertheless, since such a specific quality is not conveyed by the word here, it is the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) itself that possesses the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which serves as the cause for the cognition of the qualified [object]; therefore, the suffix *san* would necessarily follow from that very [aggregate].

As for what was stated in the rule *yasmātpadādupasargastasmādeva dhātostasya prayogaḥ* (P. 1.4.81)—namely, that "the instrument (*sādhana*) brings about the action, while the prefix (*upasarga*) qualifies it"—that too is based precisely on the production of a qualified action; thus, there is no contradiction. Even in the view that "the verbal root (*dhātu*) is first joined with the instrument," since it is intended here to convey the status of being an object (*karman*) specifically for the qualified action, and because the possibility of the suffix *san* arises from the root together with its prefix, [the rule applies].

As for the claim that the suffix *san* would not occur after a qualified [base], that too is incorrect; for there is the interpretation: "after a verbal root which is a member (*avayava*) of the action. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence [of *san*] occurring after a simple [root] alone; because by the principle of "designation as the principal" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), even a simple [root] is its own member. This is because when rules such as *anudāttaṅitaḥ* require the interpretation "ending in a *ṅit* [element]," the status of being "ending in a *ṅit*" must be stated in exactly the same way for roots like *śīṅ*. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the suffix *kyac* would also occur in examples such as *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"), and so forth.

Because the suffix *kyac* is not prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is a rule dependent on words (*padavidhi*); thus, by the application of the maxim regarding semantic competency (*samarthaparibhāṣā*), there is a lack of competency due to the presence of an external expectancy. However, in the prescription of the suffix *san*, since it is not a rule dependent on words, the suffix *san* occurs even when there is an external expectancy.

Alternatively, since the verbal root itself denotes the qualified action and the prefix is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), there is no requirement for mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*). Furthermore, the mention of the word *vā* (or) is redundant; for the formation of a compound (*vṛtti*) pertains to the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), whereas a sentence (*vākya*) pertains to mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). Since a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) cannot logically exist between two distinct domains, the status of the sentence remains secure. On the contrary, by the inclusion of the word *vā*, it would be impossible to prescribe the absence of suffixal designation (*pratyayasaṃjñā*) in the case of unified meaning; thus, the very absence of that designation would have to be prescribed, leading to its own redundancy. Moreover, this would result in the undesirable contingency of optional application (*vikalpa*) regarding the grammatical operations based upon that designation.

The *atravārtika* states: "Or rather, [the suffix] *san* may follow a word ending in *tumun*, with the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. This is the meaning: the rule should be formulated as "after a word ending in *tumun*, there is *san*," because it is more concise (*lāghava*) since it does not mention the requirement of having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*) or the object of the verbal root (*dhātukarma*). Furthermore, by the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), the *san* suffix occurs optionally in its own sense, overriding the hearing of the *upapada*. The mention of "desire" (*icchā*) must necessarily be made for the purpose of specifying the meaning of the suffix; and the elision of the *tumun* suffix must also be stated.

If it is argued that, in this way, because a form ending in *tumun* is a word (*pada*), once the *tumun* suffix has been elided (*luk*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision of *n* (e.g., in *jighāṃsati*) and so forth—on this point they say: "There is no fault, because by the principle that 'what is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what is internal (*antaraṅga*),' the elision (*luk*) is as if non-existent. Alternatively, according to this arrangement of the rule, the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix must be inferred for the sake of achieving the desired result, based on the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *iko jhal*. [The Vārttika states: "It should be stated that after the first person plural of the optative (*liṅ-uttama*), the desiderative suffix (*san*) may occur, and there is the elision of the first person plural ending. Thus: *cikīrṣati* ("he desires to do") from *kuryām* ("may I do").

In this context, it should be noted that in the example *caitraś cikīrṣati* ("Caitra wishes to act"), this [suffix] is prescribed for the meaning of the root *iṣ* (to wish), which is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) that serves as the base for the desiderative suffix (*san*), and not for the roots ending in the *āś* or *śyan* conjugational markers. Regarding the rule "there is an extension [of the application] to inanimate things in the sense of apprehension," we have: *śvā mumūrṣati* ("the dog wishes to die") and *kūlaṃ pipatiṣati* ("the bank wishes to fall"). Although the dog is indeed sentient, this was stated because, since death is undesirable, a desire for death cannot logically exist there [in the case of a dog] as a cause for the absence of suffering; the point is that the mention of "inanimate things" need not have been made.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, infers the desire [of the agent] from such signs as physical movement, just as one uses expressions like "he wishes to make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ cikīrṣati*). Thus, even in the case mentioned, the suffix *san* occurs because of an inference of desire based on signs such as the loosening of limbs or the falling of a clod of earth. In reality, there is no harm even if desire does not actually exist in the bank (*kūla*) and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the falling of a clod of earth and the like cannot be the effect of desire; for delusion and inference are accounted for precisely through superimposition (*āropa*). As for the statement "or established through analogy" (*upamānādvā siddham*), it has been rejected.

"There is no simile with a verbal form ending in *tiṅ*. Regarding this, they explain: there is no simile by means of the meaning of a *tiṅ*-ending [verb]. This is because action (*kriyā*) has exclusively the nature of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because it lacks a completed form, and because there is an absence of the reflective apprehension "this is that. Furthermore, the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) has as its domain real entities that are the objects of such a reflective apprehension.

For instance, in expressions such as "Devadatta goes," Devadatta and the like are referred to by the word "Devadatta" and so forth; and in expressions such as "He goes" or "This one cooks," they are referred to by words such as "he" or "this. However, there is no such reference for the action (*kriyā*). This is because in expressions such as "this [action]," it is only the action that has attained a completed state (*siddharūpa*) that is denoted. What more need be said? Even by words such as "action" (*kriyā*), there is no production of a cognition identical in form to that produced by "he cooks" and the like. For this very reason, it has been stated by the Mīmāṃsakas: "Just as the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), so too is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
That [meaning] is never expressed by other words in that very same form."

Nor should it be argued that even so, there is no inconsistency regarding the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*). This is because comparison (*upamā*) is based upon a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and an action (*kriyā*) that is not yet established cannot serve as a substratum for such properties. For if one were to accept that it does serve as a substratum, it would follow that the action becomes an already established entity (*siddharūpa*), which entails the loss of its essential nature as an action—a point that will be stated in the fifth chapter. Nor should it be argued that this [objection] is incorrect, on the grounds that even in the case of an unestablished jar or similar object, properties such as being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva-pratiyogitva*) do exist.

Although that may be the case there due to the force of common perception and because it cannot otherwise be explained, in the present instance there is a lack of evidence. For this very reason, logicians maintain that "pot-ness" does not exist in a pot that has passed away. Furthermore, the act of comparison—such as of a face with a full moon—is entirely completed within its own substratum, since it is devoid of both superiority and inferiority. As it has been said:
"For the very same reason that a swan is called 'flying,' because that [action] is complete in itself, the purpose of comparison does not exist."

In this case, the meaning of the word "completion" (*samāpti*) is simply the equality of the downward motion inherent in both [the object and the subject], caused by their conjunction with the lower surface. Furthermore, there can be no similarity between actions belonging to different classes (*bhinnajātīya*), because only a property common to both determines a simile (*upamā*), whereas the mere fact of being an action (*kriyātva*) is irrelevant. With this in mind, after citing the example from the *Kāvyādarśa*: "The darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium," the teacher Daṇḍin stated:
"A delusion regarding a simile arises here for some due to the hearing of the word 'iva';
they disregard the authoritative statement that a simile cannot be formed with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)."

This is the meaning: what here serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)? It cannot be the agent (*kartṛ*), because that agent, being a qualifier of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is the meaning of the verbal root, cannot function as a "manner" (*prakāra*) in the sense of *iva* (as if). For it is impossible for a qualifier of one thing to be construed with another. As it has been said:
"If the agent were the standard of comparison, he would be subordinated within the verbal expression [of the action];
being preoccupied with accomplishing his own action, he is not capable of looking toward another."

The means (*sādhana*) is construed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) within the action whose own [subject] is the qualificand (*svaviśeṣya*). In that case, [the subject] is "engrossed" (*vyagra*), meaning it is devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*) regarding its connection with that [means]. It is incapable of expecting something else—that is, distinct from the action—or of becoming the qualificand in a cognitive apprehension where its own property is the qualifier. Nor is it the case that, as in examples such as "odor is only in earth" (*pṛthivyāmeva gandhaḥ*), there is a simultaneous connection in both places—namely, of the earth and so forth, which are qualifiers of the locative sense, with the meaning of the particle *eva* (i.e., mutual absence)—due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

Alternatively, it may be postulated that the particle *eva* conveys the state of being other than what is delimited by the delimitor of the referent of the word uttered in its proximity. In that case, the agent would have an equal syntactic connection both with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) and with the similarity. Or else, it must be said that the word *iva* has as its primary meaning the similarity of the agent. Even so, because the verbal root-meaning functions as a qualifier of the agent, the cognition "he is similar to the agent of smearing" would be impossible; furthermore, it would result in the subversion of the primacy of the action.

Nor should it be argued that there should be an understanding that "the action of smearing has a agent similar to the agent of smearing," because this cannot withstand scrutiny. Does the similarity of the agent expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) connect with the action, or does the meaning of the particle *iva* consist precisely of the agent as qualified [by similarity]? It is not the first case, because that [similarity] connects only with the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha). Nor is it the second, for that would require the meaning of the root—smearing—to connect with both [the agent and the similarity], or else the meaning of *iva* would have to be the similarity to the agent of smearing. It is not the first, because it is impossible for that [similarity] to function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Nor is it the second.

This is because a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is necessarily excluded from the meaning of words such as *iva*; because the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is presented as not being delimited by the form that serves as the delimitor of the state of being the object of comparison (*upameyatāvacchedaka*); because the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśya*) requires [the presentation of] the agent of the metaphorical transfer (*lepa*); because if one intends to express similarity precisely through the agency of the metaphorical transfer, it would result in the identity of the property (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison; because a similarity based on the agency of the metaphorical transfer through another property would be useless for the context at hand; and because in cases where the similarity is not well-known, it is necessary to explicitly mention the property that serves as its cause.

In cases such as "Her face is like the moon," although one may accept both the omission and the mention of a quality because the cognition of qualities such as "delightfulness" arises through the force of conventional renown, this is not the case in instances such as "That heaven indeed acts like Bhārata," where, in the absence of a phrase like "adorned by gods residing within," the failure of similarity to manifest is established by the experience of the learned; thus, the details are explained elsewhere. Nor is the act of smearing itself the standard of comparison, because there is no common property shared between the act of smearing and darkness.

Because it is impossible for that [property] to belong to the ointment itself; because the relationship between property and property-possessor (dharma-dharmin-bhāva) is based on difference; and because even those who maintain the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (bhedābheda-vādins) accept a distinction in the forms that delimit the status of property and property-possessor. It is their established tenet that there is no tautology by resorting to difference, while there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) by resorting to non-difference. For this very reason, even in cases such as cause and effect, difference and non-difference are accepted in a different manner. As it is said in the *Bhāmatī*: "There is multiplicity in the form of the effect, and non-difference in the nature of the cause;
there is difference in the nature of gold and so forth, and difference in the nature of the earring and so forth."
This has been stated:
"If the act of smearing itself is what is intended, who else could there be called 'the smearer'?
No one but a madman would say that the property (dharma) and the possessor of the property (dharmī) are one and the same."

It might be argued: "In the sūtra *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced*, the status of the action as the object of comparison (*upameya*) is established by the sūtra, the vārttika, and the bhāṣya; however, according to the reasoning stated above, that would not be possible. For even if an action is the object of comparison, if one intends to express its dependence on a common property (*sāmānyadharma*), it would follow that it possesses the nature of a substance (*sattvarūpatva*), and thus its distinction from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—which is an action—could not be defined."

It is said: the authors' intention is precisely that action cannot function as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). As for the consequence of [action] being of the nature of a substance (*sattvarūpatva*), that is merely an illustration of another logical argument. To explain: in the case of "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*), is the intended meaning the ellipsis of the word *iva* (as in "the bank is like one wishing to fall"), or is it a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the impossibility of any other [explanation]? It is not the first. For is the desire to fall the counter-correlate of the similarity, or is it the bank? Not the first, because it is accepted that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is subordinate within the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

Furthermore, this is because of the traditional grammatical rule (Nirukta) stating that "the verb (ākhyāta) has the action (bhāva) as its primary meaning. Nor should it be argued that being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) or having that [action] as its meaning depends solely on the expectation of the meaning of the noun (*sattvārtha*). For this is not a matter of explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), such that it could be established by the aforementioned method; rather, it is established by experience assisted by the logic of parsimony (*lāghava*). Consequently, in other cases, there would necessarily be the requirement of postulating a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for its connection. Moreover, since the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, which are the meanings of the verb, do not themselves possess gender or number, they too would consequently result in being qualifiers of that [action].

Furthermore, this is because the fruit (*phala*) is likewise [subordinate]. Nor is the intention [of the grammar] that primacy belongs solely in relation to the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); for if that were so, it would follow that the word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) would be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, the primacy of a verb ending in a *tiṅ*-suffix is relative to another action. For this very reason, in examples such as "he cooks and [it] comes to be" (*pacati bhavati*) or "look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), the actions of cooking and running are connected to the actions of coming-to-be and seeing by way of their being the agent and the object, respectively.

Moreover, in cases such as "he cooks in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pacati*), the connection of the meaning of the base of the infinitive suffix (*tumun*) with the action denoted by the *tiṅ*-suffix by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established by the Sūtra; this will be explained in detail later.

Furthermore, there can be no connection of similarity of action with the bank (*kūla*), because neither the bank nor a similar bank is present [in the cognition]. Nor is the second alternative [possible], because similarity with the bank is absent in the desire to fall (*pipatiṣā*). By this, it is shown that there is no escape even by treating the particle *iva* as an indicator (*dyotaka*). Nor is the second alternative [valid] regarding indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because it is impossible even to suspect indication for something similar to the desire to fall. This is because action (*kriyā*) consists precisely of a collection of successive operations; therefore, a verbal root (*dhātu*) lacks the capacity—even through indication—to convey any part exceeding that.

For this very reason, since that which is similar to what is produced by desire (*icchājanya*) possesses the meaning of "being" (*sat*), and since that [similarity] is connected with the falling, one should not even suspect the cognition: "the falling has the bank as its agent and is similar to what is produced by desire. This is because it is an established principle that the cause for a cognition having the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) as its qualifier is the semantic presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the suffix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, since being produced by desire is common to other objects, there would be no determination of the specific object of comparison; and finally, even if it were intended to mean such a falling, it would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

In expressions such as *brāhmaṇavad adhīte* ("he studies like a Brāhmaṇa"), although the word *brāhmaṇa* refers to the study from which that [Brāhmaṇa] is the source (*apādāna*), the study is not presented by the finite verb ending (*tiṅanta*). Therefore, the study is construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) in similarity, which is the meaning of the suffix *-vat*. And since that [similarity] is related to the action of studying denoted by the finite verb, there is no fault. In cases such as *rodītīva gāyati* ("he sings as if he were weeping"), however, one action is construed with another action through the relation of similarity, because the word *iva* functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). For this very reason, its status as a non-substantial entity (*asattvarūpa*) is maintained.

Because [the object] has not attained the status of a qualifier with respect to the meaning of another word; and because it has been stated that even the states of being an object (*karmatva*) and an agent (*kartṛtva*) possess the status of a relation (*saṃsargatā*) alone. Nor should it be argued that there is the consequence of the action of the object of comparison (*upameya*) becoming its locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), for the primary sense of "locus" is only that which is delimited by a relation that governs the application of a term (*vṛttiniyāmaka-saṃbandha*), and such a locus is not understood here. If mere possession of a specific property (*vaiśiṣṭhya*) were taken as such, there would be a deviation in cases such as "the fire on the mountain" (*parvatīyo vahnir*).

Therefore, according to the view of Bhaṭṭa, since the identity (*tādātmya*) between the ground and its absence is accepted, the use of the locative case in expressions such as "the absence of a jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭābhāvaḥ*) is for the purpose of establishing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and not for the purpose of conveying the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*); this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

And thus, because it is not denoted by the base word (*prakṛtipada*) that possesses the case-ending of a *kāraka*, it is of a non-substantial nature (*asattvabhūtatva*). Furthermore, its lack of connection with gender (*liṅga*) is quite evident. As for number (*saṃkhyā*), although it is perceived—on the strength of Bhāṣya usages such as *uṣṭrāsikā āsyante* ("camel-sittings are being sat") and *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante* ("dead-man-lying postures are being laid")—nevertheless, its connection is only with the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) expressed by the suffix *ṇvul*, and not with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). This is because the verbal root, being already satisfied in its requirement for number, cannot logically admit that connection.

Otherwise, in cases such as *caitreṇa sthīyate* ("it is stayed by Caitra"), there would be the unwanted consequence of the number one also being construed [with the verb]. By this, the view that even in the case of the construction of the number of a *kāraka*, [the agent] is of the nature of a non-substance (*asattva*) precisely because it is unfit for reference by a pronoun, is refuted; for there is no evidence for such a restriction, as will be explained in detail later.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Alternatively, *icchā* (desire) itself may be [the meaning of the desiderative suffix], because the word *icchā* denotes a state of being (*sattvabhūta-artha*), and therefore its referent serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Consequently, the rule for the desiderative suffix (*san*) applies even to an activity (*vyāpāra*) that resembles desire. And that activity consists of vibration (*spanda*) and so forth residing in the parts of the bank, by virtue of causing the loosening of those parts. In accordance with the observed usage (*lakṣyānurodha*), the principle of "primary versus secondary" (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*) does not apply here; thus, the suffix occurs in both cases. As for the other solution provided in the Bhāṣya—that everything possesses consciousness (*acetanavatva*)—[that is intended to show that] even insentient things can possess volition.

When it is said, "O Āskandaka and Kapilaka," [the former] leaps upon the grass; when it is said, "The iron moves toward the magnet"; and from the indicative mark (liṅga) in the mantra, "Listen, O stones.

Furthermore, as for the explanation that this applies to the doctrine of the non-duality of the Self (ātmādvaitadarśana), and that because all objects are perceived in their diversity, one should not raise the objection of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) everywhere—that is merely a bold assertion (prauḍhivāda). For the Vedāntins accept that in such passages as "Brahman alone is all this," grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) exists either through sublation (bādhā) or superimposition (adhyāsa), but not through identity (abheda). Therefore it has been said:
"Existence, manifestation, loveliness, form, and name—these are the five aspects (aṃśapañcaka)."
The first three are of the nature of Brahman; thereafter, the two are of the nature of the world.

"In the elements of air, fire, water, and earth, and among gods, animals, humans, and so forth, existence, consciousness, and bliss are undivided; it is only form and name that differ. Thus [it is said].

This is because even the Sāṃkhyas admit that [the world] is a transformation of insentient *prakṛti*; such is the direction of the argument. In the expression "he wishes to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gantum icchati*), if both the village and the going were objects of the desire (*iṣi*), then the dative case in "he wishes to go to the village" (*grāmāya gantum icchati*) would not occur according to the rule for the object of a verb meaning "to go" (*gaty-arthakarmaṇi*). This is because [in that analysis] the village would lack the status of being the object of the act of going. Furthermore, if it were argued that the village is the object of "going" (*gam*) while the going itself is the object of "desiring" (*iṣ*), then in the expression "the village is desired to be gone to" (*iṣyate grāmo gantum*), the village would not be expressed by the passive suffix (*karmapratyaya*), because it would lack the status of being the object of the desire.

Because the mode of being the means for accomplishing the object inherent in the root itself is what is expressed by the suffix; therefore, the established conclusion is that for the root *gam* (to go), the village is the object (*karman*), whereas for the root *iṣ* (to desire), the village is the object and going is the action. In the expression *iṣyate grāmo gantum* ("the village is desired to be gone to"), since going has the village as its purpose, it is subordinate; and because two objects belonging to different levels cannot be denoted by a single [suffix], the operation applies to the primary element, and thus only the village is denoted.

Since the action of going (*iṣikriyā*) is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātānta*) and is therefore primary, it is denoted by the primary power [of the suffix]. Consequently, because the action of going (*gamikriyā*) is subordinate, the second or fourth case endings are inappropriate with respect to it; for it has been stated previously that a subordinate element does not initiate an operation contrary to the primary.

A secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) formed from a word ending in a possessive suffix (*matubarthīya*), or a possessive suffix formed from such a secondary derivative, is not desired if it is of the same form (*sarūpa*). A desiderative suffix (*san*) is not applied after another desiderative.

Although it cannot be said that the suffix *san* is not used again because it already expresses desire (*icchā*), for even if it expresses the desire for cooking (*pākēcchā*), the desire directed toward that desire for cooking has not yet been expressed. Otherwise, in the form *pratīṣiṣati*, there would be no *san* after the root *iṣ*. Nevertheless, this prohibition is merely based on a specific scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). This applies to the *san* following a desiderative (*icchā-san*) as well; for instance, in forms such as *jigupsiṣate* and *mīmāṃsiṣate*, the *san* is desired after a desiderative that itself ends in *san* in its own sense (*svārtha-san*).

Examples for the rule beginning with *śaiṣikāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.92) are as follows: from *śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ* ("located in the hall"), we have *śālīyaḥ ghaṭaḥ* ("a pot located in the hall"); however, from *tatra bhavam udakam* ("water located there"), the suffix *cha* does not apply again. But a different form (*virūpa*) certainly occurs: from *ahicchatre bhavaḥ*, we have *āhicchatraḥ*; from *tatra bhavaḥ*, we have *āhicchatrīyaḥ*. From *daṇḍo 'syāsti* ("he has a staff"), we have *daṇḍikaḥ*; but from *sosyāsti* ("it belongs to him"), the suffix *naṭhan* does not apply. Yet a different form certainly occurs: *daṇḍimatī senā* ("an army possessing staves"). Likewise, the logicalian's usage *vahnimadvān* ("possessing that which possesses fire") is based on a mistake, because the designation *bha* applies by the rule *tasau matvarthe* (Pāṇini 1.4.19), making the word-level operation of *jaśtva* difficult to obtain.
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya in the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi.
Now begins the second Āhnika.
[Pāṇini 3.1.8] *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (The suffix *kyac* is added after a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix, when the object is related to the agent himself).

The suffix *kyac* is optionally applied after a *subanta* (inflected nominal) that denotes an object of desire related to its own locus (*svāśraya*). The word *sva* here refers to "desire. "Being the locus of one's own" means being the inherent substrate (*samavāyitva*). Due to its being a part of the verbal root, the case ending (*sup*) is elided. By the rule *kyāc ca*, the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final vowel of the stem]. Thus, from *putram ātmana icchati* ("he desires a son for himself"), we derive *putrīyati*. In the cognition of the desire whose object is the son, the son's "belongingness to oneself" (*svīyatva*) exists only as a factual state (*svarūpasat*) and serves as the regulator of usage; for there is no contradiction with the experience of it appearing as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the verbal cognition (*śābda*).

Although the letter *c* in *kyac* is not for the purpose of making it *udātta* at the end, since this is already established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) due to its being a single-syllable (*ekāc*) suffix—given that the order exists such that the suffix-accent applies first and the root-accent (*dhātusvara*), which is *satiśiṣṭa*, applies afterwards—it is also not for the sake of qualifying [the rule] "in *kyac* and *ic*" (*kyaci cecca*). This is because the exclusion of *kyaṣ* is already achieved by the principle: "when there is a mention of a specific marker (*anubandhaka*), that which does not possess that marker is not included. For the meaning of that principle is: "having set aside that which possesses only those markers, there is no inclusion of that which possesses both [markers] in addition to them."

Nor is the inclusion of *na* in the rule *naḥ kye* intended to prevent the application of the general term [kyac]; otherwise, following the aforementioned reasoning, there would be no inclusion of *kyap* therein. [Objection: But surely in the word *icchati*, the suffix is one denoting the abstract state (*bhāva*), while in *ātmanaḥ*, the genitive case denotes the agent (*kartari*). This is because the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) is more internal (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, even in the case of *rājñaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires the king's son"), *kyac* should occur. [Reply: Not so. For the qualifier *ātmanaḥ* would then be redundant; it would connect only with the inflected word (*subanta*) itself, disregarding the aforementioned relationship.

This is because it is the very relationship of desire belonging to the self (ātman) as mediated by that [object] which must be expressed. Thus, it follows that the suffix *kyac* occurs when the well-known relationship between the substratum of desire (*icchā-samavāyin*) and the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the state of being desired (*iṣyamāṇatā*). Otherwise, since the quality of "being produced by the owner who is the desirer" exists even in the king’s son, the same fault would persist. However, in cases such as *mā tvāvṛkā aghāyavo vidan*, the suffix *kyac* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), because a desire for one's own connection with misfortune (*vyasana*) is logically impossible. And here, the prescription of the long vowel *ā* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) intended to prevent the substitution of *it*.

Now, for what purpose is the term *sup* [used]? It is not, first of all, for the purpose of excluding the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because there is no difference whether the suffix *kyac* is added to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) or to a nominal stem. Nor is the designation "word" (*pada*) itself the distinction; for if the production of the suffix occurs after a word ending in a case-suffix, the rule *naḥ kye* must necessarily be taken as restrictive, whereas if its production occurs after a nominal stem, it can be taken as prescriptive. Nor is it for the purpose of excluding verbal roots (*dhātu*), because the suffix *san*, being specifically prescribed, would supersede [the application of *kyac*], and furthermore, because *san* does not occur when expressing the desire of another.

It is said that although "he desires a great son" (*mahāputram icchati*) is intended by the term *mahāputrīyati*, the mention of the *su*-suffix is for the purpose that [the suffix] should not apply to the sentence "he desires a great son" (*mahāntaṃ putram icchati*).

If it is argued that even so there is no escape because each [member] ends in a *sub*-affix, we say: no. Is the application [of the suffix] from the whole (*samudāya*) or from the parts (*avayava*)? Not the first, because when a suffix is mentioned, only that which begins with the element from which it is prescribed is understood; furthermore, it is impossible to grasp two distinct wholes consisting of base and suffix. Nor the second, because of the lack of expressive power (*asāmarthya*); for example, the expression *mahāntaṃ putrīyati* ("he desires a great son") would not convey meaning. This is like [the expressions] *ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man who is wealthy"), *ṛddhasyopagorapatyam* ("the offspring of Upagu who is wealthy"), or *ṛddhasyaupagavaḥ* ("the descendant of Upagu who is wealthy"). As it has been said:

"In all cases, there is no occurrence [of the operation] among words in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) because of the non-connection with one [of them]. This means that among words in apposition, there is neither the exclusion of one nor the inclusion of another within the scope of the operation; for it is only the son who possesses qualities (saguṇa) that constitutes the object of the desire (*icchā*). Nor does this lead to an over-extension (prasaṅga) in the case of *rājñaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires the king's son"), because the rule "there is no occurrence among words in apposition because of the non-connection with one" must be understood as applying only to those [words] accompanied by qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the meaning of the nominal stem *putra* lacks the status of being the object of desire (*icchā-karmatva*), the use of the accusative case and so forth would be unjustified; for the entire compound is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatva*), and thus [the case ending] could arise from that as well. This is because the suffix arises from the subordinate members (*guṇa*) merely through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the suffix [kyac] appearing after the subordinate member itself, due to the prohibition "not after those with qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇānām*). Furthermore, the expression *mahāntaṃ putrīyati* ("he desires a great son") would be non-expressive [of its intended meaning]. This is because a qualifier that has already attained oneness of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) with the meaning of *kyac* cannot logically enter into a relation of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). For it is impossible for both oneness of meaning and mutual expectancy to coexist simultaneously.

If it is argued that [the compound] *muṇḍayati māṇavakam* ("he shaves the boy") is impossible due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), we say no; for in this case, the boy is not the object of the action of "making" (*karoti*), but rather the state of being shaven (*muṇḍatva*) itself is so. Where both possess such a status, the compound formation indeed occurs, as in *balīvardaṃ karoti muṇḍam* ("he makes the ox shaven"). Furthermore, because the root *muṇḍi-* denotes a specific action, the accusative case is applied to the boy in relation to that action. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of forming a *kyac*-derivative in the sentence *māṇavakaṃ muṇḍamicchati* ("he desires the boy to be shaven").

It should be stated that only the state of being shaven (*muṇḍatva*) is intended [by the word *māṇavaka*], while the word *māṇavaka* itself serves to convey the specific substratum (*āśraya*) of that quality; for both are desired, since the boy (*māṇavaka*) is to be refined by the quality of being shaven. Alternatively, because the word *muṇḍa* denotes a quality (*guṇavacana*), it forms a compound even when it is dependent on another term. As for the suffix *kyac*, its scope is elsewhere, as in examples such as *putrīyati*; thus there is a difference between the two cases.

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as *muṇḍayati ayaṃ nāpitaḥ* ("this barber shaves [him]"), since there is no desire to express proficiency regarding the state of being shaven (*muṇḍatva*), a specific substance is not required, and thus the suffix *ṇic* also finds its scope there. For although the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*) already accounts for such cases, the re-enactment of the rule for words like *muṇḍa* is intended for the sake of that specific prescription, even if it involves dependence on other factors. Alternatively, the verbal roots mentioned in the Sūtra take *ṇic* in their own sense (*svārthe*), just like those belonging to the *curādi* class; and although no distinction is explicitly stated for them, their determination is possible simply through observation of usage.

Alternatively, in the expression "he milks the cow for milk" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), the root *duh* (to milk) first connects with the word "cow" (*go*) alone; subsequently, it connects with the "milk" (*payas*) through the act of milking. Similarly, [in the case of *muṇḍayati māṇavakaṃ śikhayā*], the root first connects with "shaving" (*mauṇḍya*), and that [root] as qualified by shaving then connects with the boy (*māṇavaka*). Thus, there is no fault. Alternatively, when a specific object is required, a full sentence (*vākya*) is used; when a general object is required, a nominalized form (*vṛtti*) is used. In that context, words such as "boy" (*māṇavaka*) are employed for the purpose of conveying the specific object. Nor does this entail the occurrence of the suffix *kyac*, because [the meaning] would not be understood [thereby].

Regarding the doubt as to whether the suffix *kyac* should be applied in the sense of "the undesired son is desired" (*atheṣṭaḥ putra iṣyate*), as in the expression *putra iṣyate*, some say: since the rule for *kyac* prescribes it in the sense of "desiring," just as in the analysis *icchati* (which contains a suffix denoting the agent), it occurs even when the analysis is made with two suffixes denoting the object as stated.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: because the word *iṣṭa* (desired) is in grammatical apposition with the son (*putra*), and because the connection with the specific object "son" has already been experienced [in the primary sense], there is no verbal activity (*vṛtti*) at all in that state—just as in the case of expressions such as "a mat was made by him previously. This is because when one intends to express the predominance of the fruit of the action, such as the son, one employs only sentences like "the son is desired" (*putra iṣṭaḥ*). Since a verb ending in *kyac* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), no suffix denoting the object can arise; therefore, it is impossible to demonstrate a form ending in the accusative suffix (*kta*) for such a meaning derived from a *kyac*-stem.

And in a sentence, once either an agentive suffix or an objective suffix has arisen, because the verb subsequently becomes intransitive, no further objective suffix can arise with respect to the object.

"An exception [is made] for that which ends in *m* and for indeclinables (*avyaya*) before the suffix *kyac*. For example: *idamicchati* ("he desires this"), *kimicchati* ("he desires what?"), *uccairicchati* ("he desires loudly"), *nīcairicchati* ("he desires softly"). "Some say [the suffix applies] after words ending in *gautama*, those not ending in a vowel, and those ending in *n*. This means that they compose the *Nyāsa* commentary stating that the suffix *kyac* is added after these. Thus: *gavyati*, *ghaṭīyati*, *madhūyati*, *dadhīyati*, *kartrīyati*, *rājīyati*, *takṣayiti*. However, in this case, forms such as *vācyati* would be unestablished. The learned authorities maintain that the author of the *Bhāṣya* introduced this [discussion] merely to demonstrate the existence of different opinions.
In the words *aśanāya*, *udanya*, and *dhanāya*, [the suffix -ya] denotes hunger, thirst, and greed, respectively. || 9 ||

Three words ending in the suffix *kyac* are treated as irregular formations (*nipātana*): *aśanāyati*, *udanyati*, and *dhanāyati*. Their meaning is a desire for food, water, or other wealth for the purpose of immediate enjoyment; thus, they signify hunger and so forth. However, when food is intended for use at a later time, water for the purpose of bathing, or when there is a lack of wealth and a desire for it, one uses forms such as *udakīyati*. In this way, hunger and the others serve as the conditions for the application [of these terms].

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of *aśanāyati* and similar forms is simply hunger and so forth, because the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is not intended [to be expressed]. They further state that *udanyā* means thirst (*pipāsā*) or *tṛṭ*, according to the lexicon (*kośa*), and that it also means "wealth" (*dhana*) based on the usage of Bhāravi: "What wealth is there to be acquired? (*kimudhanaṃ dhanayitum*). For this very reason, Mayūra says: "The stream of rain became a desire for wealth" (*dhārārāyo dhanāyāyadīti*).
The suffixes *kyac* and *kāmyac* are applied after the words *aśva*, *kṣīra*, *vṛṣa*, and *lavaṇa* when expressing one's own pleasure (*ātmaprītau*).

The suffix *kāmyac* shall occur in the sense previously mentioned. For example: *putram ātmana icchati* (he desires a son for himself) becomes *putrakāmyati*. The inclusion of the letter *c* is for the purpose of making the word end-acute (*antodātta*), since this would already be established by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). Nor is it for the purpose of preventing the designation of the letter *k* as an *it* (indicatory marker), because that would result in the *k* having to be placed at the beginning [of the suffix]. Nevertheless, since this suffix is designated as *cid*, and because the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.3]—"an *it* is designated as such only when it is not designated by another [suffix]"—is restrictive in nature, the protection of the letter *k* from being an *it* is thereby established.

The *Aṭavārttika* states: "If [the suffix] *kāmyac* were [to include] the letter *k*, it would be purposeless, because there is no object for it. This is the meaning: precisely because there is no purpose, the letter *k* does not receive the designation *it*. Alternatively, in the absence of a specific grammatical operation (*kāryaviśeṣa*), the mere elision (*lopa*) cannot be established as the fruit of the instruction of phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*). Furthermore, in the *saṃhitā* reading, that [letter *k*] remains even with the two *c*s in the form *kāmyacc*. Nor is the prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate vowel in *saghū* (as in *agnicitkāmyati*) a result [of including *k*].

Because [the suffix] *kāmyac* is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), it lacks the status of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, the possibility of *guṇa* substitution is virtually non-existent. Nor is there *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) in the case of *upayaṭkāmyati*, according to the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kitī* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). This is because that rule applies only when a suffix marked with *k* follows roots such as *yaj* and others, whereas this suffix is prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Furthermore, since the suffix *vic* is prescribed only in Vedic usage (*chandas*), no instance of *saṃprasāraṇa* is observed there either.

Thus, in the case of *vāk-kāmyati*, the status of being *kit* would be for the purpose of *saṃprasāraṇa*; therefore, it is more appropriate that [the *kit* designation] be a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇatva*). Alternatively, since when a verbal root is mentioned by its own form, the operation is understood to apply to a suffix attached to it, there is no fault. Consequently, it is established that the *cit* designation is redundant.

The suffix *kyac* is added after a word ending in a case-ending that functions as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) when expressing the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*). For example: *putrīyati chātram* (he behaves toward the pupil as if toward a son). It should be stated that this also applies after a word denoting a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: *kuṭīyati prāsāde* (he behaves in the palace as if in a hut); the meaning is that he acts as though he were in a hut. [Example: That king, skilled in various deeds, treats the citizens on the battlefield as if they were his own womenfolk.
Beholding his exploits on the field of battle, the enemy army acts like a woman, with sword in hand.

Thus, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, regarding the simile (*upamā*) where the denotative word (*vācaka*) is elided, three instances have been illustrated: the suffix *kyac* used with the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the suffix *kyac* used with the agent (*kartṛ*).

Regarding this, they explain as follows: If affixes such as *kyac* and others denote mere conduct (*ācāra*) alone, then when that conduct is associated with [an object] such as "one's son" (*suta*), there can be no connection with an object such as "the townspeople" (*paura*). Nor can there be a connection with the townspeople through a conduct that is not itself associated with the son; for a meaning of an affix cannot be understood if it is not connected to the meaning of its base (*prakṛti*). Otherwise, at a time when one has the subverting cognition "Caitra does not cook," the sentence "Caitra cooks" would lead to the erroneous understanding "Caitra possesses an effort" (*kṛtimān*). Furthermore, rather than postulating an unuttered word such as *iva*, it is more reasonable to postulate the expressive power (*śakti*) of the affix *kyac* and so forth.

Nor is there any complexity [in this view], for otherwise even in the case of the suffix *saN* and others, there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of their power to denote desire; since in those cases as well, it is possible to supply words such as "he desires" (*icchati*). If it is argued that in those cases the expressive power (*śakti*) exists because of the authority of grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) and because understanding occurs even without supplying [the verb], then the same applies to *kyac* and other suffixes. Therefore, the meaning of *kyac* is the practice of a particular kind of conduct and the distinction [between that conduct and the object]. For this very reason, forms such as *sutam sutīyati* ("he treats the son like a son") do not occur.

Thus, the meaning of such expressions as *pauraṃ sutīyati* ("the citizen acts like a son") is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to that conduct which belongs to the class of conduct similar to that of a son, and which resides in a citizen distinct from a son. And so, because there is a cognition in which similarity is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) regarding the son, the citizen, and so forth, this is a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*) based on direct expression (*śrautī*), and not one where the expressive word is elided (*vācakaluptā*).

In this regard, the following must be said: it cannot be established by grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) that the suffix *kyac* possesses the power to denote difference and so forth, just as the suffix *san* denotes desire. Furthermore, forms such as *sutam sutīyati* are excluded precisely because they are incapable of syntactic connection with a word for "difference" (*bhedādi*) that has been supplied (*adhyāhṛta*). As for the claim that [the meaning of the suffix] is "connected with the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthānvita*), etc., that is incorrect; for while a mutual connection between the meanings of the base and the suffix is necessary, it is not the case that the connection of the suffix's meaning must occur prior to the connection of the base's meaning.

For by that much alone, the cognition "Caitra possesses an effort" is prevented at the time of the aforementioned understanding. Thus, having established the very attainment of the aforementioned linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*), the cognition of non-difference between the time immediately preceding [the action] and the word "today" in expressions such as "having stood today" (*adya sthitvā*) has been supported by Upakṣadhara Miśra, Jalada, Ṭhakku, and others in their *Dravyopāyavivṛti*.

Therefore, in cases such as "the jar was seen by Devadatta," one accepts the understanding that the object (viṣaya), which is the meaning of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*), is connected first with the meaning of the third case (instrumental)—namely, the action—and only thereafter with the meaning of the base (the seeing). Thus, the cognition arises: "The object of the seeing whose agent is Devadatta's action. Consequently, the meaning of the supplied word *iva* itself is both "occurring in something other than that" (*tadbhinnavṛttitva*) and "not occurring in that" (*tadavṛttitva*). Accordingly, the resulting cognition is: "One who possesses an effort conducive to conduct directed toward Paurava, which occurs in someone other than a son and also occurs in a son."

[Objection: If this is so, it follows that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), such as "daughter" (*sutādi*), is construed with the sense of difference (*bhedādi*) [in *iva*], and the sense of *iva* is construed with the sense of the suffix *kyac*, namely "behaving" (*ācāra*). But this is not tenable; for the meaning of the base cannot be construed elsewhere if it is not already construed with the meaning of the suffix, and because there is an absence of construction for anything distinct from the meaning of the base within the meaning of the suffix. [Reply: This is not so. Even though "daughter" and the like are not directly construed with the meaning of the suffix in the form of "behaving," they do indeed possess a construction with it once they have attained the status of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) for "difference" and the rest.

For this very reason, the Miśras have demonstrated that the grammatical competency (*vyutpatti*) for the connection of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) with [the suffix] is maintained through some kind of relation whatsoever. Furthermore, they themselves have written that when there is a difference in the meaning of the *kyac* suffix, its connection with the object (*paura*) occurs precisely through the mediation of the meaning of the suffix, which consists in the act of behaving like that (*ācāra*). For this same reason, the authors of the *Dīdhiti* and others accept that in the sentence "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *Atirātra* sacrifice," the cognition produced is that the non-taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* is a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*), and so forth.

Furthermore, because it is not accepted that the meaning of the verbal root is connected with the present tense when it functions as the meaning of a verb, there is no second rule [to prevent such a connection]. Moreover, Vācaspatimiśra, the author of the *Dīdhiti*, and others, while explaining the *Nyāyasūtra* passage "because of non-appearance without having destroyed," interpret it as "because of the absence of appearance without having destroyed," thereby establishing a connection between the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the act of appearing, and further accepting the connection of the ablative case-meaning (cause) with that [negated term].

This is because even in the sūtra, "Of these, delusion is the worst, for the others do not arise in one who is undeluded," there is an admission of the understanding that the other [faults] do not arise; and because the Prābhākara school accepts the syntactic cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) as being "the task (kārya) whose object is the non-existence of eating *kalañja*. The details are found elsewhere.

Although Caṇḍīdāsa and others have stated that in the case of *nārīyate*, there is no loss of the expressive word (*vācakalopa*), because the suffixes such as *kyaṅ* are prescribed for that very purpose and are thus capable of expressing its object; yet, since the suffix cannot function independently in that way, this applies equally to forms such as those ending in *vat*. In both philosophical views—that the entire word is the expressive unit, or that the base and the suffix express their respective meanings—the case of *vat* and the like is identical to that of *kyaṅ* and the like. This is because there is no evidence to support the claim that the meaning of *kyaṅ* and other such suffixes is "conduct similar [to that of the standard]."

"Even if there is a loss of the common property (*dharma*) here in this simile—on the grounds that a property consisting of conduct (*ācāra*), like 'being a thing' (*vastutva*) and so on, does not serve to establish the simile"—that too is incorrect. For by the word *upamānāt* ("from the object of comparison"), the specific properties [of the object] are understood as being included under the category of "object of comparison," and likewise by the word *ācāraḥ* ("conduct"), the specific properties are understood as being included under the category of "conduct. This is because we perceive qualities such as "overflowing with affection" in cases like *sutīyati*, and qualities such as "timidity" in cases like *nārīyati*. Furthermore, the writing of authoritative scholars serves as witness in this matter; the details are found in the *Alaṅkāra-kaustubha-vivaraṇa*. [Now the rule: *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11).
"The suffix *kyaṅ* is added after a verbal root denoting the agent, and there is the elision of the *s* [of the root *as*]. 13.

From a word ending in a case-suffix that serves as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is added in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*). When that [suffix] ends in *s*, there is also elision of the *s*. This is because the particle *ca* functions as a conjunction of accumulation (*anvācaya*) and the acceptance of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). One behaves like Kṛṣṇa; thus, *kṛṣṇāyate*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṅ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed. In the rule regarding the elision of *s*, the term "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*) is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); since it qualifies the *s*, the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies. Thus, the meaning is "elision of the *s* at the end of the agent. Consequently, there is no fault in forms such as *haṃsāyate*. It should be stated: "The elision of *s* is optional. Thus, one obtains both *payāyate* and *payasyate*.

The word *ojas* [ending in the nominative] is always to be used [with the suffix *am*]. For example: "He who slew Ahi while he was exerting his strength" (*ojāyamāne*). [In the form] *apasarāyate*, it is derived from *apasara*. Similarly, the word *ojaḥpada* follows that [same rule]. Murāri [uses] the word *ojas* as a qualifier with the sense of a general property (sāmānyadharma): "This very sky, being filled within by those [clouds] covering the earth, becomes *ojāyate*" (i.e., acts with vigor).

Another says: [the form] is simply *apsarasaḥ* with the elision of the *s*. As for *ojāyamānām*, it is established by virtue of being Vedic (*chāndasatvāt*). Kaiyaṭa states that this presentation is for the purpose of showing a difference of opinion and not an established position (*sthitaḥ pakṣaḥ*). By this, the verse from the *Naiṣadha*—“*payāyatāmabhyudayastvadīyaḥ*” (let there be prosperity for you)—is also explained.

After the words *ācora*, *avagalbha*, *klība*, and *hoḍa*, the suffix *kvip* is optionally applied: *klībāyate*, *hoḍate*, *hoḍāyate*. Since these very verbal roots possess multiple meanings, their capacity to express an action characterized by "behaving like" (*ācāra-lakṣaṇa*) is also established. Furthermore, in forms such as *avahoḍa*, the absence of a suffix is established even by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103). Nevertheless, the rule is commenced for the sake of forms such as *avagalbhāñcakre*, because [without this rule] they would end in a suffix.

Another says: the suffix *kvip* should be stated after all nominal bases (*prātipadika*) [to form denominatives], as in *aśvati* ("he acts like a horse") and *gardabhati* ("he acts like a donkey"). Because the term "nominal base" (*prātipadika*) is explicitly mentioned here, there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "sup" (i.e., nominal endings).
