Consequently, by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the *guṇa* substitution of the vowel of the root with the vowel *a* of the suffix *śap* results in a single substitute (*pararūpa*). This is because there is an absence of *pada*-status [for the root-final vowel]. Nor is the previous Vārttika thus rendered useless; for its purpose is to provide for the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings by means of an anudātta indicatory letter (*it*), since *kvip* is what is being restated there. From this, forms such as *galbhati* and so on are to be understood. Similarly, from *a* (the sound 'a') one forms *ati* ("he acts like 'a'"), and *anti* ("they act like 'a'").

Regarding the statement that "in place of [the rule for] *pratyayagrahaṇa*, there is the mention of *anekāc*," [the forms] *atuḥ* and *uḥ* are derived as follows: by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the *pararūpa* (single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel) applies, overriding the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) due to its being *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned). Nor does the elision of *at* occur by the maxim *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (a rule concerning vowels is stronger than one concerning consonants), because the two rules depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatva*). Nor does the lengthening [of the vowel] apply first by virtue of its being subsequent (*paratva*) and obligatory (*nityatva*), because it is rendered *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being *bahiraṅga*. Nor does it apply by way of being an exception (*apavāda*), because it has already served its purpose in cases such as *ānarda*. For it is accepted that even an exception, having already found its scope elsewhere, is overridden by an *antaraṅga* rule.

Since the form of the subsequent element is included by the mention of the "stem" (*aṅga*), this would result in the elision of the *at* [by *ato lopaḥ*]. However, setting aside that [elision], because it is subsequent, the long vowel [is applied] by *ata āder iti dīrghaḥ*, and the substitution of *au* occurs by *āta au ṇalaḥ*. Regarding forms such as *atus*, they say that the elision of the *āt* [occurs] by *āto lopaḥ*.

In reality, even when the substrata are different, the application of the *paribhāṣā* is established in the *Kaustubha* on the sūtra *acaḥ parasmin*; furthermore, because the second *ā* is the common locus for both the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) and the elision (*lopa*), there is a shared substratum in that respect; and since the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* governs the *pararūpa*, both *ā*s are its substituends. Moreover, the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) would be unavoidable as it would override the long vowel (*dīrgha*) prescribed by *ṇyallopau*. Therefore, the matter must be determined by the learned after examining the specific instances of usage (*lakṣya*).

The word *mālāti* means "she acts like a garland" (*mālā ivācarati*). By the rule regarding the inclusion of forms distinguished by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as part of the preceding base (*pūrvāntatvena*); thus, it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and the suffix *kvip* is applied. Because it ends in a suffix, the suffix *ām* is added: *mālāñcakāra*. [In the aorist: *amālāt*. Because of its association with the feminine suffix *ṅī*, the elision of *āp* occurs only before the suffix *su* (the nominative singular), as prescribed by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [Pāṇini 6.1.68]. Regarding the aorist, the suffixes *iṭ* and *suk* are added by the rule *yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca*: *amālāsīt*. Like a poet (*kavi*), she acts like a poet: *kavayati*. In the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), it is *kavīyāt*. Kaiyaṭa and others hold that there is no *vṛddhi* substitution for a denominative root (*nāmadhātu*); thus, they give the form *akavayīt*. Dīkṣita states that Mādhava gives the form *akavāyīt*.

In both views, however, the truth is that there is only *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening); this has been examined by us in our commentary on the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*. Consequently, forms such as *abhavīt* and *adravīt* from the roots *bhū* and *drū* are also incorrect. Since only the root *bhū* found in the Dhātupāṭha is taken [as the base], the operations of the elision of *sic*, the addition of *vuk*, and the substitution of *at* for the reduplicated syllable do not apply. Thus, we have *bubhāva*, *bubhuvatuḥ*, and so forth.

The Easterners (Prāñcas), however, cite *ām* as an example [of the suffix] because it is a suffix ending in *ām*, as in *svāmāsa* and *svāṃcakāra*. Nor should it be argued that this is incorrect because the mention of "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*) in the rule for *kāsi* is for the sake of forms like *culumpa*, since the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) will be rejected there and thus the condition of having more than one vowel is absent; for if that were so, it would result in the untenability of examples from the Bhāṣya such as *klībāṃcakre*. Nor should it be argued that *ām* applies by force of the statement even to what was previously [a form] having more than one vowel.

For it is established in the Bhāṣya that its purpose is fulfilled by the non-attachment of a suffixal element (*anubandha*). For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated, "so that the suffix *ām* may occur after the suffix *kāspratyaya*. If the status of being caused by the suffix *ām* were not delimited by the property of being "ending in a suffix" (*pratyayāntatva*), then it would be improper to formulate the rule by taking that form as the delimiting factor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). This is because it would result in the necessity of stating only "after *kāsi* which has more than one vowel (*ane-kāj*)" for the suffix *ām*.

Haradatta [says] that from the word *ka* [the suffix *kvip* is added], resulting in *cakā*. Mādhava [says] that because of the rule "elision of the *ṇi* and elision of the *al*" (*ṇyallopau*), the elision of the *at* (the *a* of *bhū*) subverts the *vṛddhi*, and thus [the form] is *cakā*. From the word *div*, Mādhava says [the form is] *devatī*. [In this case,] by the rule for *ūṭh*, there is *yaṇ*. Nor is it the case that the *ūṭh* is treated as "not established" (*asiddha*) with respect to the operation of *yaṇ* because it is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), due to the prohibition [in Pāṇini 6.4.22]: "there is no [application of the rule for *asiddha*] when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*). Nor is it the case that the *guṇa* occurs first according to the rule "an internal element (*āṅga*) takes precedence over an external one" (*vārṇād āṅgam*), because the two depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*). Therefore, the Dīkṣitas say [the form is] *dyavatī*. [The suffix *kvip* is added] after words such as *bhṛśa* etc., when the root *bhū* follows, provided *acvi* is not present; and there is the elision of the consonant [of the prefix]. (Pāṇini 3.1.14)

The phrase "the assumption of a state not previously existing" (*abhūtatadbhāvagrahaṇam*) must be supplied [to the rule]. After words such as *bhṛśa* ("intense") which have as their object the assumption of a state not previously existing, the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs in the sense of "becoming," and there is elision (*lopa*) of these [words] when they end in a consonant. The particle *ca* serves to indicate a conjunction (*anvācaya*), whereby there is a division of the sentence as before. One who was not intense becomes intense: *bhṛśāyate*. Why say "not previously existing"? Consider: *kva divā bhṛśā bhavanti*? This is an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) meaning: "Where do those stars and other things that are intense at night become during the day? In this way, the prohibition *na cvau* need not be stated.

For instance: since the suffix *ḍāc* is prescribed for non-existent (*abhūta*) objects, the suffix *kyaṣ* will not apply after it, because words whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed [again]. Nor should it be argued that in the case of *paṭapaṭāyate*, *kyaṣ* would not occur even after *ḍāc*, because *ḍāc* is also prescribed for that same purpose. This is not so, because in the rule *lohitādi-ḍājbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.13), the specific mention of *ḍāc* after the group beginning with *lohita* possesses sufficient force [to indicate the exception]. For while *ḍāc* is prescribed by the authority of the statement when there is a desire to express the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*) even though the verb *bhū* itself is not used, *kyaṣ* is subsequently prescribed in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavaty-arthe*). Thus says the Vārttika.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, say: "Since the suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) for that which is not *cvi*—that is, for cases resembling *cvi* involving the transformation of one state into another (*abhūtatadbhāva*)—the Vārttika need not have been commenced at all. In this regard, the bases *abhimanas*, *sumanas*, *unmanas*, and *durmanas* are listed as having consonants as their final sounds (*halanta*). There, an inquiry arises as to whether the prefixes (*upasarga*) function as qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix or of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

If the word *manaḥ* is not compounded with *sudurudabhayaḥ*, then it is the first alternative; and in that case, the word *manaḥ* refers to the possessor of the quality (*tadvat*) in relation to the state (*vṛtti*). According to some, the formation of the sense is achieved through the suffix *kyaṅ* in the meanings "he becomes well-minded," "he arises," "he becomes weak," and "he becomes present."

Others, however, maintain that in this context the root *bhū* is understood in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*). Consequently, they say that the word *manas* refers to that which possesses [the quality], by means of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus, the meaning is "one who attains a beautiful mind," and so forth. But when there is a reference to fire and the other deities through the word *manas* forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then [the word] functions as a qualifier of the primary meaning (*prakṛtyartha*); this is the second position.

In that regard, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), in examples such as *abhimanāyate*, because the suffix *kyaṅ* follows the word *manas*, there is the form *manāyate*. Since this is a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) following a non-verbal form (*atiṅanta*) such as *sva*, the rule *tiṅ-ṅatiṅaḥ* would require the suppression of accent (*nighāta*). However, if [the *kyaṅ*] is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), then in the case of *sumanāyate*, the entire complex is a single verbal form; thus, there is no subsequent non-verbal form distinct from it, and consequently, there is no suppression of accent.

However, there would be a fault regarding the *aṭ* augment and reduplication in those cases. Since a prefix (*upasarga*) is included within the very form of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the *aṭ* augment would have to precede it. Consequently, due to the absence of a compound (*samāsa*), the suffix *lyap* would not occur. Furthermore, when the desiderative suffix *san* is added to a verb ending in *kyaṅ*, the reduplication would apply to the entire form including the prefix. Thus, forms such as *svamanāyata*, *sumanāyya*, and *abhimimanāyiṣata* would not be possible. Not so; for the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.29] which prescribes the status of a root for *saṃgrāmayati* must necessarily apply even when it is accompanied by a prefix, so that forms such as *asasaṃgrāmata śūraḥ* may occur.

Nor should it be argued that *saṃgrāma* is taught as an indivisible unit and not as a form with a prefix; for otherwise, the optional substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) by the rule *vā padāntasya* would be untenable. Furthermore, that [mention of *saṃgrāma*] is for the purpose of restriction: namely, that this applies only after a prefix such as *sam*, and not after anything else. Thus, it is indicated that when a suffix conditioned by the verbal root designation (*dhātusaṃjñā*) is to be applied, the preceding member—which has the same form as a prefix—must be treated separately. Otherwise, he would have recited *grāma* alone as having an anudātta accent, since the presence of the word *sam* could have been understood by implication.

In roots such as *ik* (meaning "to remember"), there is an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) like *dh* and so forth; furthermore, there is a second vowel *a* there because of the adoption of the *pararūpa* (substitution by the following form). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of shortening the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) by the rule *ṇau caṅi*. Because of the inclusion of the word "preceding" (*pūrva*), the separation [of the prefix] occurs only where there is a compound, but not in cases such as *āndolayitvā* or *preṅkholayitvā*. Examples are: *āndudolat* and *apipreṅkholat*. Regarding *avadhīrat*, the designation of the causative (*ṇyantasaṃjñā*) applies according to the rule "in the sense of contempt. Thus: *āvavadhīrat*. So says Bopadeva.

Disregarding this [objection], the usages in poetry such as *dhīra* should be justified by inferring a different verbal root (*dhātu*). And thus, there is no fault even regarding the rules for accents (*svaravidhi*), because in that case the prefix (*upasarga*) is included within the verbal root. The view that the suffix denotes its own meaning (*pratyayārthapakṣa*) is likewise more sound. Nor should it be argued that, since the *kyaṅ* suffix is prescribed there in the sense of a prefix, its usage would not occur; for among the meanings of *kāka*, *rā*, and so forth, since no specific meaning is understood, a particular prefix is employed to convey that specific sense. This is also the case in forms such as *utpucchayate*.

Because a specific distinction is necessary due to the existence of many [other] *yogavāhins*, [the following are included]: *bhṛśa*, *śīghra*, *capala*, *paṇḍita*, *utsuka*, *unmanas*, *abhimanas*, *durmanas*, *rodas*, *śaśvat*, *pramada*, *vehat*, *raśvita*, *tṛpata*, *śucivarcas*, *ojas*, and *sujarat*.
[The suffix] *kyaṣ* is added after words beginning with *lohita* and after those ending in primary suffixes (*ḍāj*). (Pāṇini 3.1.13)

In the previously mentioned context, there is an option for the *parasmaipada* ending by the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ*. Thus: *lohitāyati* or *lohitāyate*; *paṭapaṭāyati* or *paṭapaṭāyate*. When the suffix *ḍāc* is intended after an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*), doubling occurs according to the rule *ḍāci bahulaṃ dve*. Thereafter, the *ḍāc* suffix causes the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). Regarding the *takāra* which is the final constituent of the preceding word *paṭat*, it is included within the *pakāra* due to the formation of a single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule *nityam āmreḍite* [Pāṇini 8.1.2]. In this regard, the *kakāra* and *ṣakāra* have been rejected in the Bhāṣya.

In the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ*, [the mention of *ky*] is established even by the word *vāyāt* (from P. 7.2.36). Since the context is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatva*), there is no fault in cases such as *pāśyā*. Furthermore, in the rule *kyāc chandasi*, in order to include forms such as *bhuraṇyu*, it must be stated that it is simply *yāt*. By this, the letter *k* is also explained. Nor is it for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*, because that [prohibition] does not even apply due to the absence of the status of being an *ārddhadhātuka*. Nor is it for the purpose of including the general term in the rule *yasya halaḥ kyasya vibhāṣā* (P. 6.4.49), because this [suffix] is not prescribed after a stem ending in a consonant.

By this, our view that [the rule] *kye* has this specific purpose is also refuted. Nor is there a need for [the rule] *lohitāyati* to provide for the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*; for in that case, the mention of *kiṅat* does not recur. Nor is there the contingency of lengthening in *uruyā*, where the third-case ending is replaced by *yā* according to *supāṃ suluk*; for that is Vedic usage, and because, as in the example *upagāyantu māṃ patnayo garbhiṇayo yuvatayaḥ*, a short vowel can occur again.

The *Atravārtika* states: "The rule for *kyaṣ* after words beginning with *lohita* and those ending in *ḍāc* [should apply]; the others [should be] among the *bhṛśādi* group. Thus, *kyaṣ* should be prescribed after the word *lohita* and after words ending in *ḍāc*. The word "beginning with" (*ādi*) is redundant, because the other words are accounted for by their inclusion in the *bhṛśādi* list, and because the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is not desired here. Therefore: *Lohita*, *śyāma*, *duḥkha*, and *harṣa*, *garva*, *sukha*;
*Mūrchā*, *nidrā*, *kṛpā*, *dhūma*, *karuṇā*, and *nitya-carmaṇī*.
Thus, the citation of these two words as examples is without foundation.
[The rule] "kaṣṭāya kramaṇe" (Pāṇini 2.1.39).

The dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*). From a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) meaning "difficulty" (*kaṣṭa*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied when the sense is "stepping" (*kramaṇa*), due to the inherent nature of the expression. What is obtained is a specific kind of stepping, namely crookedness (*anārjava*). This is precisely the meaning explained by the author of the Vārttika in the rule: "After *satra*, *kakṣa*, *kaṣṭa*, *kṛcchra*, and *gahana*, [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] in the sense of a desire to commit evil. In this context, words such as *satra* and the others are synonyms for "evil" (*pāpa*) within the scope of their grammatical function (*vṛtti-viṣaye*). Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the word "evil" (*pāpa*) itself, because the optionality is understood to be restricted (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Thus: *kaṣṭāyate* (he acts with difficulty) and *satrāyate* (he acts with treachery); the meaning is that he proceeds to commit an evil deed.
The suffix *cha* (forming *varticara*) is applied after the words *romantha* and *tapas* when they denote the action of one who subsists by means of them. 17.

The suffix *kyaṅ* is added after the verbal roots *romantha-* and *tapa-* in the sense of "performing" (*vartanā*) or "practicing" (*caraṇa*), and in the sense of "exertion" (*utsāha*). *Romantham vartayati* becomes *romanthāyate*. *Tapaś carati* [becomes *tapasyati*]; however, because of the rule *tapasaḥ parasmaipadaṃ ca*, one says *tapasyate lokajigīṣur agneḥ* (the one desiring to conquer the world exerts himself in penance before the fire), as this is Vedic usage. According to the *Bhāṣya*, *romantha* is the chewing of what has been regurgitated (*udgīrṇa*) or swallowed (*avagīrṇa*). Kaiyaṭa explains that *udgīrṇatva* is the state of being drawn back from the region of the mouth, while *avagīrṇatva* is the state of having emerged from the region of the anus.

It should be stated as *hanucalana* (movement of the jaw). By this, it indicates the chewing of what has been masticated, preceded by drawing it from the region of the mouth, accompanied by the movement of the jaw. Not here: *kīṭo romanthaṃ vartayati* ("the insect performs rumination"). Kaiyaṭa says the meaning is "it eats that which has emerged from the place of excrement. The author of the Nyāsa and others say it means "it makes it round. The Bhāṣya states that [the suffix] does not apply here because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). Regarding the form *vartī*, although *yuC* would be expected due to the presence of the causative marker (*ṇi*), many hold that it is formed with *kvip* due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*).

In reality, this [word] ends in the vowel *i*. There is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding its meaning, because it has been explained as such by those who possess the knowledge [of grammar] in passages such as "he worships the unreal" (*yad upāsti-masad avratet*). The form *caroḥ* is derived from the root *car* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
[The rule applies] after *bāṣpa* and *ūṣman* when there is the act of vomiting (*udvamana*). || 18 ||
One emits vapor or steam, or "becomes tearful" (bāṣpyāyate) or "becomes steaming" (ūṣmāyate). Regarding this, it should be stated: "and [the suffix *kyac* occurs] after the word *phena*";
as Murāri says: "Like a churning-stick, the ocean of darkness suddenly began to foam (*phenāyate*) with its froth."
The suffix *karaṇa* is added after the words *śabda*, *vaira*, *kalaha*, *abhra*, *kaṇva*, and *megha* when they denote the instrument (*karaṇa*). || 19 ||

"He makes a sound" (*śabdaṃ karoti*) and "he sounds" (*śabdāyate*), and so forth. "The hollow bamboos (*kīcakāḥ*), being filled by the winds, sound sweetly," as stated in the *Meghadūta*. "Who would wage war (*vairāyat*) against that first among the proud, the great hero?"—thus says Murāri. In the *Harṣacarita*, Durvāsas, quarreling with the second sage named Upamanyu, became blinded by anger while singing a *sāman* chant and produced a discordant note (*visvaram akarot*). According to the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is also desired in the sense of "he does that," as in *śabdayati* and so forth.

"The forms *aṭā*, *aṭṭā*, *aśīkā*, *akoṭā*, *apoṭā*, *soṭā*, *pruṣṭā*, and *sruṣṭā* [are derived from roots] with the suffix *ghañ*; the apprehension of [the meanings] 'fair day,' 'ill day,' and 'mist' must be made.
[Examples: *aṭāyate*, *aṭṭāyate*, and so forth.
[The rule applies] "after [words] such as *sukha* (pleasure), etc., when the agent experiences the sensation" (Pāṇini 3.1.18).

The term *kartṛ* (agent) has its genitive case ending elided; it is a qualifier of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. This is because such a qualifier would be redundant unless there were an agent of the feeling (*vedana*), for [feeling] is otherwise untenable. Thus, the meaning is: "in the feeling of the agent of the feeling, which is pleasure and so forth. In short, the word *kartṛ* serves to indicate the intended sense that the word *vedanā* refers to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). This is because, since the qualities of others are inaccessible to them, one's own pleasure alone is the object of one's own perception. [Thus one says: "one feels pleasure" (*sukhāyate*), "one feels pain" (*duḥkhāyate*).

The meaning is as follows: "The king’s attendant does not experience happiness here [directly], but infers it from signs such as the serenity of his face," and so forth. Pāṇini 3.1.18: *sukha-duḥkha-tṛpra-āprā-pra-alīka-karuṇa-kṛpaṇa-soḍha-pratīpa-namovarivaś-citraṅaḥ kyac* || [The suffix] *kyac* is applied after these words: *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *tṛpra*, *āpra*, *āprā*, *alīka*, *karuṇa*, *kṛpaṇa*, *soḍha*, *pratīpa*, *namaḥ*, *varivaḥ*, and *citraṅ*.

In the case of *kriyāviśeṣe* (specific action), [it occurs] in worship (*pūjā*), service (*paricaryā*), and wonder (*āścarya*). Since the term *karaṇe* (in the sense of instrument) is understood as a recurring element, it is to be understood as having a specific application according to the requirements of the examples; this should be understood in the same way for *puccha* and so on. Nor does the mention of *vedanā* (feeling/sensation) exclude the sense of *karaṇa*, because the connection is possible as "in the sense of feeling which is an instrument. Thus, *namasyati devān* (he pays homage to the gods) and *varivasyati gurūn* (he serves his teachers); the meaning is *cittrīyate*, i.e., he is amazed. The letter *ṅ* is an indicatory suffix (*anubandha*) attached to the *kyac*-derived stem; since there is no purpose for an indicatory suffix on a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), by that [suffix], the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied after the *kyac*-derived form.

Some, however, say that its meaning is "the production of wonder residing in another," based on the usage by Bhartṛhari: *tataścitrīyamāṇosau* ("then he was filled with wonder"). Now, as for the question: "In the expression *namasyati devān*, how is the accusative used when the dative would be expected?"—this is not so. Even if one assumes another internal component similar to the word *namaḥ* for the sake of deriving the verbal root *namasyati*, it remains a distinct base (*prakṛti*). This is because the rule prescribing the dative applies specifically to the indeclinable (*nipāta*) *namaḥ* when it possesses its own meaning. Alternatively, it is established that a case-ending denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is stronger than a case-ending arising from a secondary adjunct (*upapada-vibhakti*). [Pāṇini 3.1.20] *pucchabhāṇḍacīvarāṇṇiṅ*. (The suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied after these words to form denominative verbs.)

He raises his tail: *utpucchayate*. "With ears pricked up, tossing their tails in joy, eager for the cow-pen" (*harṣotpucchayamānakarṇakaravotkarṇaṃ vrajāyotsukāḥ*). He wags his tail: *vipucchayate*; he tosses it about: *paripucchayate*. "Tossing" (*vyasanam*) means lifting up in various or contrary ways; "tossing around" (*paryasanam*) means tossing all over. [In these forms,] the suffix *ṭi* is elided because the suffix is treated as if it were *ṇiṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix). He gathers the goods together: he makes them into a heap. A monk gathers his robes: *saṃbhāṇḍayate*, *saṃcīvarayate*; that is, he collects them or puts them on. *udapupucchata*; *samababhāṇḍata*.

The letter *ca* [in *cacīra*] is for the purpose of indicating the *ātmanepada* (middle voice); the letter *ṇa* is for the purpose of including the general rule "before an affix beginning with *ṇ* that lacks an indicatory *i*" (*ṇer aniṭi*).
The causative suffix *ṇic* is applied after the verbal roots *muṇḍ*, *miśra*, *ślakṣṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *vrata*, *vastra*, *hala*, *kala*, *kṛta*, and *tūsta*.

[The suffix] *ṇic* is used in the sense of the action denoted by the root (*kṛñarthe*). Furthermore, since this [formation] is already established by the rule "from a nominal stem, in the sense of the meaning of a root" (*prātipadikāddhātvarthe*), its mention here is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañcārtham*). This is because even in examples such as *atyararājat* ("he surpassed the king"), we observe that the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*) or "he describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*) is not intended to be a restrictive rule limiting the meaning to the root-meaning alone. It was stated previously that *ṇic* is also applied after [words] that require a complement (*sāpekṣebhyaḥ*). Examples include *muṇḍaṃ karoti* → *muṇḍayati* ("he makes [him] bald"), and so forth. The word *vrata* [is used] in the sense of fasting (*abhojana*) and the cessation thereof (*tan-nivṛtti*). [Examples are: *payaḥ vratayati* ("he observes a milk-vow") or *śūdrānnaṃ vratayati* ("he abstains from the food of a Śūdra"). [The suffix is used] after *vastra* in the sense of covering completely (*samācchādana*).

He causes to clothe. [The suffix *ṇic* is applied] after words such as *halī* and others in the sense of "grasping. The fact that they end in *a* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). One grasps the plough (*hala*) or the measure (*kala*); thus, *halayati* and *kalayati*. *Hali* means a large plough. Because the rule for Vṛddhi (P. 7.2.115) is subsequent, Vṛddhi occurs first, and subsequently there is the elision of *ṭi*. Due to the status of being treated like the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*), it lacks the elision of *at*; therefore, the rules for *sanvadbhāva* and lengthening do not apply. Thus: *ajahalat*, *acakalat*. This has been stated: "The irregular derivation of *halī* and *kalī* as ending in *a* is for the purpose of prohibiting the application of *sanvadbhāva*. Nor does the elision of *at* constitute an *aglopa* merely because of the elision of the vowel *i*.

Because [the substitution] is subsequent, when the *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs, the elision of the vowel *ai* does not take place due to its absence [at that stage]. One causes the *kṛta* [coins] to be accepted: *kṛtayati*. One causes the *tūsta* [hair] to be removed: *tūstayati*. Nor is the elision necessarily permanent (*nitya*) on the grounds that it applies both before and after the application of the rule; for the *vṛddhi* substitution is likewise [not permanently fixed]. Nor is it non-permanent on the grounds that it results in the acquisition of a different form; for the *vṛddhi* substitution is likewise [not permanently fixed]. Even if, in the absence of the elision, the *vṛddhi* were to apply to the final *i* by the rule "of a vowel, when followed by a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ" (*aco ñṇiti*), [the elision still prevails].

If, however, there were the possibility of elision (*lopa*), then by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*, the *vṛddhi* substitution—which is prescribed by a single rule and has a single substitute (*ekāsthānika*) for the *ā* following the *ha*—would not be obtained from another word-form (*śabdāntara*). Nevertheless, the author of the Bhāṣya spoke thus by relying on the non-difference between the two on the basis of their being denotable by the term *vṛddhi*.

[Objection: But surely, because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the elision of *ṭi*, the rule "vṛddhi of a penultimate vowel" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*) would not apply. [Response: On this point, they say: "When [the condition for the rule] is met, the status of the substitute acts as an obstruction; for that status is prescribed for the sake of a preceding operation (*pūrvavidhi*). However, when [the condition] is not met, since there is no preceding operation, the status of the substitute would not exist at all. In reality, once the elision has been performed, since the *vṛddhi* does not apply, its permanence (*nityatva*) must be stated. It was stated otherwise, however, for the purpose of demonstrating the underlying logic. *Sūtra 22:* *dhāto-rekāco hal-ādeḥ kriyā-samabhihāre yaṅ* (The suffix *yaṅ* is added to a root consisting of a single vowel, beginning with a consonant, when there is repetition of the action).

The suffix *yaṅ* shall occur after a monosyllabic root beginning with a consonant when there is an excellence of action. For example: *pāpacyate*, meaning "he cooks repeatedly" or "he cooks excessively. There is reduplication by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*, and lengthening of the reduplicated syllable. Although "repeated performance" (*samabhihāra*) is a property of multiple material entities occurring at the same time, and a single verbal root cannot simultaneously express multiple actions—since it denotes only one action whose distinctions have ceased due to its nature as a single thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and since there is no simultaneity among the constituent parts such as placing the pot on the fire and so forth, which form the aggregate—nevertheless:
A collection of parts that arise in succession,
whose non-difference is mentally constructed by the intellect through their subordinate status as parts, is designated as "action.
Such a collection exists in each of the constituent members of the aggregate.
Therefore, when there is a distinction [between them], the possibility of a difference in time arises.

In this manner, since an aggregate of operations belonging to the prior, posterior, and simultaneous stages—having become the object of a particular mental cognition—is what constitutes "action" (*kriyā*), one must here resort to a figurative sense of "intensity" (*samabhihāra*) residing either in the intermediate subordinate operations that are its parts, or in the principal action itself when it is performed repeatedly. Alternatively, actions such as placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) are considered "actions" because they serve that purpose. However, the primary sense belongs only to that operation immediately following which the result arises. As it has been said: "They know that to be an action after which the result is conceived."

Because it is the primary element, the name of that [action] is applied to the others for the sake of its purpose; therefore, its status as a constituent part (*avayavatva*) and its commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) have been stated. The mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is to be explained like the word "root" (*dhātu*) in the rule concerning *san* (Pāṇini 3.1.7). Why [is the restriction] "having a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ*)? [Consider] *jāgarti*. Why "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? [So that the suffix does not apply] in cases such as *īkṣate bhṛśam*, etc. However, in cases such as *bhṛśaṃ śobhate* or *rocate*, it does not apply because of non-occurrence (*anabhidhāna*). But they say that it certainly applies when there is repetition (*paunaḥpunya*). There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the roots *sūci*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭhi*, *arti*, *aśi*, and *ūrṇoti*. This statement is made because [the suffix] would otherwise not apply due to having more than one vowel (*anekāctva*) or beginning with a vowel (*ajāditva*). [Examples: *sosūcyate*, *sosūtryate*, *aṭāṭhyate*.
*arārthyate*, *aśāśyate*. The substitution of *ūrṇu* for *ūrṇu* [in the form *ūrṇunāvati*] is prescribed; its purpose is the establishment of the *yaṅ* [intensive] formation.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of prohibiting the *ām* suffix, provided that the root consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*) and is marked with an *udātta* accent (*upagraha*).

Due to the extension (*atideśa*) of the state of having a penultimate *u* (*nuvadbhāva*), there is the absence of *yaṅ* and *iṭ* which would otherwise be occasioned by the root having a single vowel (*ekāctva*). Furthermore, because the condition of beginning with *ij* is absent, there is the absence of *ām*. Examples include: *ūrṇonūyate*, *ūrṇunāva*, *ūrṇutaḥ*, *ūrṇutavān*, and so forth. Thus, since the purpose is already served by this necessary extension, the intention is that an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the application of *yaṅ* to the root *ūrṇoti* need not be formulated. Regarding the frequent repetition of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix is prescribed by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*) to *yaṅ*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *yaṅ* consists of cases such as *lolūyate*, where there is no connection with a verbal root (*adhātusaṃbandha*).

But the *loṭ* [suffix], when it consists of multiple syllables, begins with a consonant (*ahalādi*), is connected to a verbal root (*dhātusaṃbandha*), and functions in the sense of repetitive action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). For example: "May your honor wake up! He wakes up thus repeatedly" (*sa bhavān jāgṛhīty evāyaṃ jāgarti*); "May he strive! He strives thus repeatedly" (*īhasva īhasvety evāyam īhate*); "He obtains both thus repeatedly" (*ihobhayam prāpnoti*); "May your honor cut! He cuts thus repeatedly" (*sa bhavān lunīhi lunīhīty evāyaṃ lunāti*). In these cases, the *loṭ* suffix prevails by virtue of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedhena*).

Since the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix alone does not manifest the sense of "intensive repetition" (*samabhihāra*), reduplication applies to that which ends in it. However, when another intensive repetition is intended to be expressed by means of a form ending in *yaṅ*, then because there is no contradiction, it certainly occurs; for example: *lolūyasva lolūyasva*—thus he *lolūyate*. Alternatively, it is not so, because the rule for the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed for the agent and the object due to their having different meanings; whereas *yaṅ* occurs in its own sense (*svārtha*) with respect to a specific action.

The *loṭ* suffix is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on the agent and so forth, as well as on the connection with a verbal root; whereas the *yaṅ* suffix, prescribed for the sake of its own meaning in the sense of repetition (*samabhihāra*), is "internal" (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, there is no need to initiate a rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Alternatively, since the *san* suffix is prescribed [after a root], and by the attraction of the mention of that [root] to the *yaṅ*, the latter is optional; thus, in the alternative where it is absent, the *loṭ* has its scope. Likewise, since the repetition is already indicated by the *yaṅ* itself, there is an absence of reduplication under the rule "in the sense of constant action and pervasion" (*nityavīpsayoḥ*) or "in the case of repeated action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre dve bhavataḥ*).
However, when there is a desire to express intensity (*bhṛśārtha*) or frequency (*paunaḥpunya*), it certainly occurs as *pāpacyate pāpacyate*.
The root *ni* always [means] crookedness and going. || 23 ||

The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after a one-vowel root beginning with a consonant that signifies motion (*gatyartha*), specifically when there is a repetition characterized by crookedness (*kauṭilya*). This is because the inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*). For example: *caṅkramyate*, which means "he moves crookedly. The inclusion of the word "always" has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. This is because the meaning conveyed by the word *caṅkramyate* cannot be conveyed by the sentence "he moves crookedly" (*kuṭilaṃ krāmati*); thus, the sentence does not apply to express that specific meaning. However, when one merely intends to convey the sense of crookedness, the use of the sentence is desired. Pāṇini 3.1.24:

*lupasadasacara-japa-jabha-daha-daśa-gṛbhyo bhāvagarhāyām* (The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after the roots *lup*, *sad*, *car*, *jap*, *jabh*, *dah*, *daś*, and *gṛ* when there is censure regarding the action).

The suffix *yaṅ* occurs after these roots only when there is censure (*garhā*) of the root meaning. For example: *lolupyate* ("he steals despicably"). Because there is no possibility of obtaining that which is censured, or because the object of comparison is unfit for being "lost," there is a censure regarding the loss of its opposite. Examples include: *sāsadyate*, *cañcūryate*, *jañjapyate*, *jañjabhyate*, *daṃdahyate*, *daṃdaśyate*. [In *jeglyate*,] by the rule *japajabhadahadaśaitinuk*, there is the insertion of *nuk*; and in *groyaṅīti*, there is the substitution of *l* for the *r*. According to the maxim of *takrakauṇḍinya* (the curdled milk for Kauṇḍinya), since the *yaṅ* has been accepted as setting aside the repetition of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) in favor of censure regarding the absence of crookedness (*kauṭilyabhāva*), there is no *yaṅ* in that specific sense [of mere repetition].

The affix *ṇic* is applied after the verbal roots *satya*, *apapāśa*, *rūpa*, *vīṇā*, *tūla*, *śloka*, *senā*, *loman*, *tvaca*, *varman*, *varṇa*, and *cūrṇa*, as well as after those beginning with *cur*. (Pāṇini 3.1.25)

Since the meaning of the verbal root is already established by the rule on verbal roots (dhātu-sūtra) stating "from a nominal stem [is derived the sense of the root]," the inclusion of items other than *jūr* and so forth is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). One makes true: *satyāpayati*.

"It should be stated that [the suffix] *āp* occurs after the words *artha*, *veda*, and *satya*. Thus: *arthāpayati*, *vedāpayati*. Regarding this, many alternative views (*pakṣa*) have been presented in the Bhāṣya to demonstrate the differences of opinion among the teachers. Having raised the objection that if *āp*, *puK*, or *āk* were applied first, and subsequently the causative suffix *ṇiC* were introduced as qualified by those [suffixes], then the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) would occur by the rule of extended application (*atideśa*), "as in the case of *iṣṭhan*" (*ṇāviṣṭhavad iti*), it is concluded that [the suffix] must indeed be applied immediately after the root. Once the *vṛddhi* substitution has taken place by the rule "of vowels before *ṇiC*" (*aco ñṇiti*), the suffix *puK* is introduced because the word ends in *ā*.

In this case as well, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) would result; nor can the force of the rule itself prevent it, since its purpose could be fulfilled by merely subverting the *vṛddhi* [substitution]. For that [result] is established even without the addition of the augment *āgama*. Therefore, the suffix *āpuk* must be prescribed; because it is a part of the causative (*ṇic*), when the *ṭi*-elision of the stem-vowel *ā* occurs, one forms *āpayati*. Alternatively, either *puk* or *āk* should be prescribed. By the force of the specific rule, there is no *ṭi*-elision.
The science of causes. || 26 ||

The term *hetu* (cause) here refers to the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the causal agent (*hetu*) in its technical sense; the object of that [instigator's] operation is the category of the *hetumat* (the one possessing the cause). This is threefold: impelling (*preṣaṇa*), requesting (*adhyeṣaṇa*), and performing what is conducive to it (*tatsamarthācaraṇa*). Although the designation of the instigator as the "cause" depends upon the cooking or other results to be accomplished by all the factors of action (*kāraka*), it does not depend upon intermediate operations such as impelling for the sake of those results. This is because we observe that fuel (*kāṣṭha*) possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to cooking, yet possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to burning.

Furthermore, since the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is defined by the act of cooking (*pāka*), it is that [act] alone for which the designation "having a cause" (*hetumat*) is appropriate, and not instigation (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth, because those do not define it. This is because it is established as a rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) that a relational term denotes its correlate (*pratiyogin*) as that which defines itself. Nevertheless, since the primary action is already manifested by the verbal root (*prakṛti*) itself, the suffix *ṇic* is not employed to denote that [action]; therefore, that [action] does not constitute the meaning of the word *hetumat*.

Nor can it be the activity of the prompted (prayojya), for that is a substance and thus established in form, whereas the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—whether by its own nature or because it falls under the heading of instruments—is intended to denote action. Therefore, by the principle of elimination, only that activity is grasped which has cooking as its purpose and is characterized as a prompting (preṣaṇa) and so forth, and which is to be accomplished by the prompter (*prayojaka*), being indicated by the fact that it serves as the cause for designating the prompter as a cause in relation to the cooking and other such acts. When "he cooks" (*pacati*) is said here, only the activity to be accomplished by the prompted is understood, not the activity to be accomplished by the prompter.

Therefore, because the instrumental suffix (*karaṇa*) has the sense of an instrument and is qualified by the term "having a cause" (*hetumat*), when the suffix-meaning is taken as the qualifier, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) consists of instigation (*preṣaṇādi*). Alternatively, since verbal roots have multiple meanings, or because of its purposefulness, even the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*)—like the act of placing [fuel] on the fire—is the meaning of the root, as seen in the expression "he plows with five ploughs. However, in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), there is no such perception because of the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), which would otherwise indicate it. This is the position that the root-meaning is the qualifier. Thus concludes the investigation into both views.

One might object: "In the case where [the term *hetumat*] qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), there ought to be a mention of the ablative case as 'from that which possesses a cause' (*hetumataḥ*). However, since there is a mention of the locative case as 'in that which possesses a cause' (*hetumati*), it must be concluded that it qualifies the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) alone; so how can there be any doubt? To this it must be replied: Because we observe even locatives of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) in rules such as *pramāṇe striyām* ("when [the word] refers to a measure or a female"), where the sense is "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurring when a measure or a female is to be expressed. Similarly, in the present context, it is possible that the meaning is either "the suffix *ṇic* occurs when 'that which possesses a cause' is to be denoted" (*hetumaty abhidheye*), or "the suffix occurs from a verbal root (*dhātu*) occurring in the sense of 'that which possesses a cause'" (*hetumati vartamānāt*). Thus, the possibility remains.

In this regard, it is more logical that [the meaning of] the suffix (*pratyaya*) serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). This is because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the expressive agent (*vācaka*). Furthermore, postulating it to be merely indicative (*dyotaka*) involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because the term *pratyaya* is etymologically significant (meaning "that which follows"). For this very reason, in cases such as *tanūkaraṇe takṣaḥ* ("the root *takṣ* [is used] in the sense of making thin"), making thin and so forth are not the meanings of the base; rather, the agent and other factors are the meanings of the verbal suffixes (*sārvadhātuka*). Moreover, if the meaning belonged to the base, the causative suffix would have to appear in expressions such as *uktaḥ karoti* ("he does what was told") and *preṣitaḥ karoti* ("he does what he was sent to do").

Even if the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is stated by the verbal root itself, its inclusion [in the meaning of the suffix] would be unavoidable, even when it is expressed by words such as *preṣita* ("sent") mentioned above; for the meaning of the root *kṛ* has as its object that which possesses a cause (*hetumat*). However, if the suffix were to express that [operation], then because its meaning would already have been expressed, the causative suffix *ṇic* would not occur. Furthermore, in the sentence *pācayaty odanaṃ devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook the rice"), since both the one being prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*) would be agents (*kartṛ*), there would be the undesirable consequence of them both being denoted by the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-lakāra*), resulting in the form *pācayato devadattayajñadattau*.

This is because of the equality [of the two cases] regarding being the substratum for the operation inherent in the verbal root (*dhātūpāttavyāpārāśrayatva*). However, if [the *ṇic* suffix] were to denote the meaning of the suffix (i.e., causation), then since the operation expressed by the root would be a qualifier of the operation expressed by the suffix, the agent of the meaning of the *ṇic* itself would be primary; consequently, it would be that agent which is denoted, and not the agent of the base (the root). In that case, since the agent is not denoted, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would apply. Furthermore, in a construction such as *gamito grāmaṃ devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta was caused to go to the village by Yajñadatta"), since both operations would constitute the meaning of the root *gam*, the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* would require the *kta* suffix to denote the agent (*kartari*). Yet, this is not desired; rather, because the prompted agent (*prayojya*) is treated as the object (*karman*), the suffix should denote the object. As it has been said:

Regarding the rule "In the case of *duh* and other roots when used with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the agent [of the causative] is treated as the object [of the base]," in the expression *vyatibhedayante*, since the specific meaning of the verbal root is what constitutes the action, the prohibition of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by the rule "not after roots meaning 'motion' or 'injury'" would apply. However, if the meaning of the suffix is taken as primary, then the reciprocal exchange (*vyatīhāra*) pertains to the activity of the instigator—the meaning of the *ṇic*—and not to the activity of the one being instigated, which is the meaning of the base root; thus, the middle voice suffix (*taṅ*) occurs because the reciprocal exchange is the cause based on the meaning of the suffix.

Now, on the view that the meaning of the suffix is primary, the designation *karman* (object) would apply to the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*), because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is predominant, and by means of that [suffix], the agent is the most desired-to-be-reached (*īpsitatama*). Consequently, in expressions such as *grāmaṃ gamayati* ("he causes [him] to go to the village") and *grāmāya gamayati*, the two case-endings prescribed for the object of a verb meaning "to go" (*gaty-artha-karman*) would not occur; for, relative to the meaning of the causative suffix itself, both the village and the prompted agent would be objects, and thus the village would lack the status of being the object of the act of going. Furthermore, in the expression *bhedikā devadattasya yajñadattasya kāṣṭhānām* ("the cutter of Devadatta's wood by Yajñadatta"), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not occur for the prompted agent.

In examples such as *abhiṣāvayati*, since the prefix (*upasarga*) merely specifies the meaning of the root, it is not a prefix with respect to the root *sunoti*; therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* should not occur. [Reply: This is not so. The rule *gati-buddhi-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that only those [roots] mentioned therein—such as roots denoting motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), etc.—have their agent in the non-causative (*aṇyantā*) state designated as the "object" (*karman*) in the causative (*vyantā*) state, but not others. Consequently, there is no fault in cases such as *pācayati*. Furthermore, one should not argue that in those cases, since the prompted agent (*prayojya*) also possesses the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) in view of its own operation (*svavyāpāra*), the rule *gati-buddhi-ādi-sūtra* exists solely for the purpose of prescribing the designation "object" (*karman*) by overriding that [designation of "agent"] due to its posteriority (*paratva*). Because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is primary, the status of the "object" (*karman*) is established for the prompted agent (*prayojya*) who is most desired by that [primary action]; for when both primary and secondary operations are present, only the grammatical operation caused by the primary one takes effect. However, by virtue of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), when the operation caused by the primary is excluded, the status of being an "agent" (*kartṛtva*) is established due to the existence of the operation caused by the secondary one. As it has been said: "Having attained the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the causative command (*preṣaṇa*) because of its independence in the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), it is expressed according to its own characteristic (*svadharmeṇa*) due to the restriction of the technical designation 'object' (*karmasaṃjñā*)."

Even in the case of *grāmaṃ gamayati* ("he causes [the servant] to go to the village"), the village is the object (*karman*) of the meaning of the verbal root itself, and not of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*); for it is understood that the servant reaches the act of going which has the village as its object. Similarly, in *edhodakasyopaskuruṣva* ("prepare fuel and water"), the command (*preṣaṇa*) is directed toward the action itself as qualified by its means; thus, even in *edhodakasyopaskārayati* ("he causes [someone] to prepare fuel and water"), the fuel and water are the object only in relation to the meaning of the verbal root.

Even in the case of *bhedikā* (a cutter), because the mention of a *kṛt*-affix [in Pāṇini 2.3.65] serves the purpose of including even those who were previously agents, there is the possibility of a genitive based on agency with respect to its own action. Since the prefix *abhi-* signifies only the orientation toward the activity of the prompted agent (*prayojya*), and since that [orientation] qualifies the meaning of the root *su-*, the substitution of *ṣ* in *abhiṣāvayati* is established. However, if it were to qualify the meaning of the causative affix (*ṇi*), the absence of *ṣ* is desired. Thus, the Bhāṣyakāra has supported only the view that the meaning [of the prefix] belongs to the affix.

Kaiyaṭa, however, maintains that the view [taking] the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) as the referent is also entirely correct, because the objections can be easily avoided. Since the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), which has the operation of the prompted (*prayojya*) as its subordinate element, constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), and since it is precisely this [meaning] that is manifested by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *l*-suffixes arise only with respect to the primary agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, there is no expression of two agents; thus, it is logically consistent for the prompted agent to be expressed by the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Furthermore, by the causative suffix acting as a manifestor (*dyotaka*), the status of being a "motion" (*gati*) belonging to the primary [agent] is set aside.

Because the primary meaning [of the root *gam*] consists of an action conducive to going, a *kta*-suffix cannot arise from a *vyant* root in the sense of the causal agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). Even in the case of *vyatibhedayante*, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is specifically an action conducive to injury (*hiṃsā*), injury itself is not the primary referent; therefore, he states that there is no prohibition of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

Now, if it is argued that in the case of "atha pṛcchatu mā bhavān" (then may you ask), since the questioner is the one being prompted (*prayojya*) and the speaker of this sentence is the prompter (*prayojaka*), the suffix *ṇic* would necessarily apply to that activity; and thus, because they share the same object, *ṇic* and the imperative (*loṭ*) would be interchangeable—[we reply: no, because here what is to be enjoined is the very agency (*kartṛtva*) of the act of questioning, as in "Be [you] the king, fight! (*rājā bhava yudhyasva*). For once the engagement in the act of questioning is established, there is no longer any status as a prompter (*prayojakatva*) therein, and thus *ṇic* does not apply.

If it is argued that [the objection] is exactly the same even in cases such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), because incitement (*preraṇā*) is unnecessary when one acts of one's own accord, we reply: True. For a question is a sentence concerning an object of inquiry. Furthermore, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is threefold as previously stated: (1) commanding (*preṣaṇa*), which is an order; (2) entreating (*adhyeṣaṇa*), which is a request; and (3) capable conduct, which consists of consent (*anumati*), instruction (*upadeśa*), and favor (*anugraha*). Consent is the desire for the absence of obstruction; instruction is the statement of a means to one who desires that [result].

In such cases as "one desiring to remove fever should drink a decoction of the ten roots," there is assistance; and in the case of one who, by some means, obstructs another fleeing while intending to kill them, there is assistance by way of removing the absence of the cause [of death]. In the expression "the fire of dried cow-dung teaches," the fire is an assistant by way of removing the coldness that is unfavorable to study. Thus, the separate mention of "consent" (anumati) follows the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (gobalīvardanyāya); for when the desire of the person being favored is contrary [to the agent's intention], the consent of the agent constitutes assistance by virtue of the absence of that [desire], since it does not oppose the agent's own activity.

Likewise, it is also incorrect to claim that "instigating" (*pravartanātva*) is the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). This is because such [instigation] is merely the operation of a conscious word, and thus it is logically impossible for fire and the like to be the instigators of activities such as Vedic study. Furthermore, there is no evidence for an "instigation" distinct from that [operation of the word].

Even in the case of the statement, "The blessed Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness," the Blessed One acts as a benefactor by facilitating instruction that serves to remove the ignorance (*avidyā*) which obstructs the direct realization of Brahman; and according to the Vedāntins, that removal occurs through instruction alone, whereas the logicians (*tārkikas*) maintain it occurs through a succession [of stages] beginning with meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*).

This being the case, the speaker of this sentence has no utility regarding the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), because that [desire] is produced by a cognition of the fact that the object of knowledge is a means to a desired end. Nor does the speaker have utility regarding the sentence uttered, because that [desire] arises precisely through a cognition—resident in the hearer—that the sentence is a means for producing a cognition whose qualificandum is a specific object and whose qualifier is the state of being the object of one's own desire to know.

However, by this [statement], he merely demonstrates his own capacity to provide explanations for the matters to be asked, as in such passages as: "Venerable Brahmins, let whoever among you desires it question me, or let all of you question me. And that [capacity] is not useful for the nature of the question itself, because even if the cessation of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not established by the questioning of the ignorant, the nature of the question is still carried out.

Thus, it is established that whatever operation is useful—by one of the aforementioned modes—for the accomplishment of the nature of the action which is the object of the agent's activity, that alone is the instigator (*prayojaka*).
By this—
When there is an injunction regarding the mere substance (dravyamātra), the imperative suffix (loṭ) is prescribed for words such as *pṛccha* (ask);
however, when it is used with an action (sakriya), that is the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Thus, the statement of Hari has been explained; for since the word *praiṣa* (command) clearly denotes an instigation that has already set in motion, it culminates precisely in the meaning as stated. By this, it is refuted [by others] who claim that the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is "instigation" (*prayukti*) as qualified by the activity of the one being impelled, whereas the meaning of the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is mere instigation alone. Or else, they claim that "instigation" as a property of the instigator is the meaning of the imperative, while the causative suffix signifies an instigation whose agent is not fixed. [In their view,] in "cook! (*paceti*), the speaker alone is the instigator, whereas in "he causes to cook" (*pācayati*), the instigator may be someone other than the speaker. Our position, however, is that the mere mention of such non-scriptural dissimilarities is rejected.

Even in the absence of activity on the part of the person being prompted (*prayojya*), the linguistic usage such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook") occurs; and although the employment of a word may depend upon a particular speaker, instigation (*preraṇā*) is a single property [common to all]. Such is the direction [of the argument]. On this point, the author of the Vārttika states that there is no non-occurrence [of the suffix] in cases such as plowing (*kṛṣi*). For we observe the usage *pañcabhir halaiḥ kṛṣati* ("he plows with five ploughs") even when [the agent] is devoid of activity; in that case, it is understood from others that he is "causing [them] to plow" (*karṣayati*). Since the root *kṛṣ* has the meaning of "tilling," the application of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would follow, and thus its prohibition must be stated. Alternatively, there is a reversal in the case of sacrifices (*yajyādi*) and so forth: *puṣpamitraḥ yajate* ("Puṣpamitra sacrifices"), while the officiating priests cause him to sacrifice (*yājakā yājayanti*).

For here, since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) has the specific meaning of "offering into the fire," the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the actual agents (*kartṛ*) therein, while the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). Consequently, one would expect the forms *puṣpamitra yājayate* ("Puṣpamitra causes [others] to sacrifice") and *yājakā yajanti* ("the officiating priests sacrifice"). In that case, it must be explained why the causative suffix *ṇic* does not appear in the expression for Puṣpamitra’s own activity.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, maintain that here "kṛṣ" does not mean the act of plowing or scratching the soil, but rather refers to the activity characterized by effective performance consisting of the provision [of resources] such as food, seed, and oxen; for verbal roots have multiple meanings. For this very reason, even when there is no actual plowing at the time when the aforementioned arrangement is being made, the aforementioned usage is consistent. Consequently, because that meaning is already expressed by the verbal root itself through its connection with the upapada, the causative suffix (ṇic) is not applied. Furthermore, due to the rule "bibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne," the ātmanepada ending is absent.

But if the meaning is "plowing," then in the expression "he plows with five ploughs" (pañcabhir halaiḥ karṣayati), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is indeed required. Furthermore, the meaning of "sacrificing" (*yaj*) is not merely a preparatory act (*prekṣepa*), but rather a specific kind of relinquishment (*tyāga*); and since that [relinquishment] can only be accomplished by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it is established that those who cause him to do so are the instigators (*prayojaka*). Thus they say, "The desired [result] is proven."

The addition *tatkaroti* (he does that) is for the purpose of including examples such as *sūtrayati* (he formulates a sūtra). In the sense of "he formulates a sūtra of grammar," the causative suffix *ṇic* must be stated even when the meaning is simply "he does. Alternatively, since the word *vyākaraṇa* (grammar) refers to the aggregate of both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the genitive case is used; however, if it refers only to the characteristic, the genitive is used by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

In this context, even though the word *sūtra* (meaning "benefit for beings") has a single unified meaning with the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it lacks expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for a connection with the word *vyākaraṇa* (grammar). Therefore, after the word *vyākaraṇa*, the genitive case is not used; rather, because of its semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) with that [word *sūtra*], the accusative alone is used due to its dependence on the sense of the root *kṛ* ("to do"). This [accusative usage] is for the sake of analyzing the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Kaiyaṭa maintains that the verbal root *sūtri* expresses a specific action (*viśiṣṭakriyā*).

Regarding the rule *ākhyānāt kṛtaḥ tadācaṣṭe iti kṛl-luk prakṛti-pratyāpattiḥ prakṛtivat ca kārakam*: "ākhyānam" (narrative) is derived from the root *khyā* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of "that which is told. From that, in the sense of "he tells that," the suffix *ṇic* is added. There follows the elision (*luk*) of the *kṛt* suffix contained within the narrative, the restoration of the base form (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*), and the retention of the case-role (*kāraka*) as it was in the base. The statement explains that just as the acts such as the "slaying of Kaṃsa" (*kaṃsavadha*) possess the status of an object (*karman*) in relation to the act of narrating, so too does Kaṃsa himself—even though he lacks the status of an object relative to that [act of slaying]—possess it in relation to the act of telling. This is because the base form remains in its own nature (*svarūpeṇāvasthāna*) after the removal of the *kṛt* suffix, and since it is the base (*prakṛti*) in relation to the *ṇic*, the case-role is maintained by taking the "slaying of Kaṃsa" and so forth as the object for the purpose of the narrative action. Thus it is said that even for Kaṃsa and others, who do not possess the status of an object in relation to the act of killing, they do possess it in relation to the act of narration.

Furthermore, the teaching regarding "behaving like the base" (*prakṛtivadbhāva*) and so forth is as follows: since [the object] such as Kaṃsa is external with respect to the verbal base (*ṇic-prakṛti*), it lacks the designation of an "aṅga" (inflectional base), and therefore no augment such as *aṭ* occurs after it. However, by means of the suffix *-vat*, there is the application of even operations pertaining to its own locus; thus, in cases such as *puṣyayogaṃ jānāti* and *puṣyeṇa yojayati*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is employed. Alternatively, one must accept that—due to the reliance on two types of extended application (*atideśa*), namely "it behaves in the same way as the base" (*prakṛtyā tulyaṃ vartate*) or "like the base" (*prakṛter iva vā prakṛtivat*)—and in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*), the application of this or that rule varies according to the specific instance.

Furthermore, by the restoration of the original form (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*), there is also the cessation of the elision of *n* (as in *nalopa*) and so forth; thus, the formation of such expressions as "he causes the king to come" (*rājānam āgamayati*) is justified. For this very reason, it is not explained that [the object] is like that which is a *kāraka* with respect to the meaning of the base of the *kṛt*-suffix being elided; for here, since the king's status as an agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to his own coming is not established as an object (*karman*), [the rule would otherwise apply]. Therefore, what is to be understood here is the narration of an action (*kriyākhyāna*), and not merely the narration of a name (*saṃjñābhūtākhyāna*). [For example: "He narrates the killing of Kaṃsa" (*kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe*) means "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*).

One forms *baliṃ bandhayati* because, in the rule governing *kṛt*-suffixes, there is the inclusion of even those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*; thus, words such as *kaṃsavadha* possess the nature of being *kṛdanta*. When the activity [of the speaker] has the sense of "seeing," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is prescribed. This is similar to the previous cases in rules such as *kṛtaṃ tad ācaṣṭe*. The same applies hereafter. In *mṛgān ramayati*: when one who is staying in the forest describes to someone who is already enjoying themselves that "in this very place there are such deer," then, because the activity is for the purpose of seeing the object to be conveyed, the causative is used. But when one staying in a village describes the sporting of deer, since the deer are not present, the activity does not have the sense of "seeing"; therefore, in that case, only the verbal phrase (*vākya*) is used.

The elision of *āṅ* occurs when there is a connection with an extreme duration of time (*kālātyantasaṃyoga*) or when it denotes a limit (*maryādā*). For example, *ārātrivivāsam ācaṣṭe* means "he tells [the story] until the end of the night" (*rātriṃ vivāsayati*). Here, the elision of *āṅ* is additional; the meaning is that he tells stories until the cessation of the night.

When expressing wonder (*citrīkaraṇa*), the suffix *ṇic* should be stated in the sense of reaching (*prāpyartha*). When a cause for astonishment is to be understood, in the sense of "he reaches that," *ṇic* is prescribed. For example: *ujjayinyāḥ prasthito māhiṣmatyāṃ sūryam udgamayati*. This means "having set out from Ujjayinī, he causes the sun to rise at Māhiṣmatī"; the meaning is that he reaches the sunrise there. It is a marvel because he arrives there in a single day.

In the sense of "knowing" when combined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), one says *puṣyayogaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the conjunction with Puṣya") or *puṣyeṇa yojayati* ("he joins [the moon] with Puṣya"), or *maghābhir yojayati*. Since Puṣya is the agent of the act of conjunction (*yogakriyākartṛ*)—for it is he who connects the moon—the third case compound is used in the absence of the sixth case, according to the rule: "When both [agent and object] are present, [the sixth case is used] for the object.

In examples such as *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("he causes Kaṃsa to be killed"), although the substitute *vadh* is withdrawn due to the absence of the *kṛt* suffix by the principle of "being taught in connection with" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*), here, because the substitution of *ku* (in *ghātayati*) is not "taught in connection with" the suffix, the statement regarding the "return to the original form" (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*) is made in order to prevent that substitution.
In reality, however, in all cases it is simply "possessing a cause" (hetumat) that applies, even to that which functions in dependence on others. All things proceed from their respective causes;
even the conformity to another's intention is for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose.

This is because, according to the method stated in the *Vākyapadīya*, the [causative suffix] ultimately results in denoting its own primary meaning through a traditional sequence. For, the attainment of fruits pertaining to this world and the next through the execution of the commands of a teacher and others depends upon the state of being "instigated" (*prayojyatva*), which in turn is contingent upon following the intention of the instigator (*prayojaka*). This is illustrated by the fact that the Sun fulfills the intention—"May I reach Māhiṣmatī quickly"—by means of his own rising. Nor should it be argued that the *vārttika* is indispensable because, in cases such as *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("he causes Kaṃsa to be killed"), there can be no connection with the present tense when the action has long since passed.

Because actors who imitate Kaṃsa and others are designated by the term *śaubhika* due to their performance [of those roles], the word *kaṃsa* refers to the actor as the qualificand of a specific cognition whose mode is the reality (*sattva*) residing in the spectator. Furthermore, because in paintings one observes [the representation of] raised and fallen blows, and because even in storytellers there is the designation of "present" by virtue of being objects of the intellect. As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "Those [objects] whose forms are imparted by words, having become objects of the intellect..."
One regards things such as hair, which are not actually perceived, as being the means of accomplishment.

"Therefore, through the perception of that [object] and so forth, there is the observation of attachment, aversion, and the like, as well as their effects, directed toward that object as appropriate"—this is the Bhāṣya.
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
Now begins the third Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya. || 3 ||
The suffix *yak* is applied after verbal roots listed in the *kaṇḍvādi* group.

The suffix *yak* is added to these roots in their own sense (*svārthe*). These are of two kinds: verbal roots (*dhātu*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*). For if they were exclusively verbal roots, then the long-vowel readings of some would be redundant, since the lengthening would already be established by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ*. Conversely, if they were merely nominal stems, the *kit* status of *yak* would be purposeless, because there would be no possibility of *guṇa* substitution due to the absence of *ārdhadhātuka* status. Furthermore, in forms such as *kaṇḍūyamānaḥ* and *mantūyamānaḥ*, the use of the suffix *ya* would not occur, because *yak* is obligatory [in those cases].

Now, it might be argued that the desired form is established simply by adding *kvip* to a stem ending in *yag*; nor can it be said that the substitution of *uvaṅ* would result because of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) following the elision of *al*, since that status is prohibited in the cases of *kvi*-elision, the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), the *caṅ* augment, the subsequent elision (*paranighnasa*), and the substitution of *kutva*. Furthermore, one should not say that *sthānivadbhāva* would indeed apply here because the rule "that which is elided by *kvip*" is only occasional (*kvācitka*) and because *uvaṅ* is not caused by *kvip*, for even when *uvaṅ* has been applied, the substitution of *ūṭh* is still possible for the letter *v*.

If it is argued that because the *vakāra* (the *v* of *uvaṅ*) precedes the initial vowel [of the suffix], when that [suffix] is to be applied, the elision of *al* (*allopa*) lacks the status of being "as if *stānivat*" (*stānivadbhāva*), and thus due to the presence of a *kit* suffix, the *uvaṅ* substitution does not apply again—this is not correct. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of forms such as *kaṇḍuvau* and *kaṇḍuva*. This is because the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by the rule *oḥ supi* would follow a non-conjunct consonant (*asaṃyoga-pūrva*). Furthermore, in the case of *kaṇḍūvā*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of the acute accent on the case-ending (*vibhaktyudātta*) by the rule *noṅ-dhātvoh*. Additionally, there would be the undesirable consequence of long vowels in cases such as *valgur mantuh*.

This is because [the elision of *y*] is *antaraṅga* (internal) with respect to the elision of [the *k* of *kvip*], and because the elision of *y* would not otherwise apply due to the absence of a suffix beginning with *val*. Nor does the elision of *y* occur prior to the elision of [the *k* of] *kvip*; for the elision of *kvip* is stronger due to its being both subsequent (*para*) and obligatory (*nitya*). Furthermore, by the rule *vali*, there is an absence of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of suffix rules) when the condition depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*). This has been stated without relying on the view that the elision of [the *k* of] *kvip* occurs before the elision of the *val*-beginning [suffix]. If that view were respected, this fault should be addressed externally. [Objection: But in that case, the word "optionally" (*vā*) will be employed; thus, in the alternative where *yaṅ* is absent, the formation of all [forms] will be established.

It should not be argued that even with the addition of *kvip* after the *yaṅ*-intensive stem, this same defect remains; for in the case of *kaṇḍūḥ*, since no agentive meaning is understood, *kvip* does not arise after these *yaṅ*-intensive stems. This is not so, because *kvip* is unavoidable in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) due to their inclusion in the *saṃpadādi* group. For this very reason, the usage *kaṇḍūyati* (he itches) is appropriate when referring to the action, while *kaṇḍūḥ* (itching) is appropriate when referring merely to the sensation. As it has been said:

"By virtue of being within the context of verbal roots (*dhātu-prakaraṇāt*), and because [the suffix] *ka* is not attached to anything else, he [Pāṇini] has taught this long vowel; I consider the root to be optionally designated as such."
This has been largely explained.

As for what the ancients say—that after the rule for *yak* from the *kaṇḍvādi* group (which applies in its own sense or in the sense of the root *kṛ*), namely "he performs itching" (*kaṇḍūyati*), they state that because this [current] rule begins immediately after the prescription of *yak*, the *yak* is prescribed for the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself; therefore, the prescription from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the continuation of the word "in the sense of an instrument" (*karaṇe*) do not conform to that view. Furthermore, there is no dispute regarding the connection of the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) with the preceding and following rules in the context of *hetumatī* (causative), such as in *gupū-dhūp-*.

Furthermore, because the result consisting of the designation *ārdhadhātuka*—namely, the application of suffixes such as *yaṅ* and so on—is clearly evident even in the domain of [the root] *sukh* and others; and because the elision of the vowel *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) in forms such as *sukhyati* would otherwise be inexplicable. By this, the interpretation that the *kit* status of the suffix *yak* implies its *ārdhadhātuka* nature—on the grounds of necessity and parsimony (*lāghava*), and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply—is refuted. For if one were to assume an *ārdhadhātuka* nature that is irrelevant to the context and abandon the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the base root (*prakṛta-dhātu*), the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) would be the exact opposite [of parsimony].
Moreover, it would lead to the absurdity of their own established twofold classification of the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class becoming untenable.

Nor can it be argued that while those ending in *yak* are verbal roots (*dhātu*), the simple forms are nominal stems (*prātipadika*); or that the term "verbal root" is applied figuratively to those parts of the *yak*-ending root because of the difference in their states according to whether a suffix is present or absent, resulting in this twofold division. This must be rejected because the statement that "the *kaṇḍvādi* group consists of those characterized by *yak*" is contradicted by the fact that *yak* is not an augment (*āgama*). Furthermore, even if the expression "*kaṇḍvādayaḥ*" refers to a collection qualified by *yak*, it is clear that such a collection lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Some maintain that such a twofold distinction cannot be specifically mentioned because it is common to all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that serve as the bases for suffixes such as *kyac*.

However, this must be stated here: regarding the doubt as to whether the *kaṇḍv-ādi* items are merely nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and whether the suffix *yak* is optional when they serve as their base, the solution is indeed established in the Bhāṣya. Both [the stem and the suffix] must be assumed to possess the status of an *ārdhadhātuka*, because they both occasion the guna-strengthening that is prohibited by the *kit* designation. The difference, however, lies in whether the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) is attributed to the base through the mediation of the suffix or directly. Nor can the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* be inferred in the manner described above, since the occurrence of guna is accounted for even by that much.

It must be stated that if one were to imply that *prakṛti* is a verbal root (*dhātu*), only the status of being an *ārddhadhātuka* would be established, because the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* is sublated.
