This is because the absence of *sārvadhātuka* status is determined by two factors: the absence of *tiṅ*-ness and *āśit*-ness, as well as the absence of being prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Furthermore, rather than requiring the sublation of these two factors, it is more logical to assume the status of *ārddhadhātuka* based on the knowledge of the absence of being prescribed after a verbal root; this is also supported by the requirement for the elision of the vowel *a* in forms such as *sukhyat*.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Sanskrit-sūtra* is that [the suffix] applies to the action (*karman*) through the knowledge of the measure of the members (*aṅga-parimāṇa-jñāna*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction even in the statement "the *kaṇḍvādi* group consists of roots ending in *ya*" (Pāṇini 3.1.27), because such usage is intended with reference to the augment (*āgama*), and not with reference to the base form (*prakṛti*). This is because, in this case as well, a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) has been stated regarding the components of the root ending in *ya*. In the statement "the *kaṇḍvādi* group is twofold," what is intended is the mere verbal form of words such as *kaṇḍū*, which is common to both [types];
and the meaning of the text concerning the twofold nature is that in some cases it constitutes a part of the root, while in others it does not.

By this, the objection that the rule *kaṇḍv-ādibhyaḥ* refers to a collection qualified by the *ya*-affix, and thus such a collection lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), is refuted; for it is impossible for a person of refined intellect to even suspect that the very property which serves as a differentiator (the *vibhājaka-upādhi*) could itself be the thing to be differentiated (*vibhājya-upādhi*). By this same reasoning, the argument that since he [Pāṇini] has stated the two-fold division [of verbal roots], the suffix *ya* would arise from a nominal stem, and thus forms like *kaṇḍūvatī* could not be derived from a simple root, is also discarded. For when the text is explained with the intention of referring merely to the status of being a nominal stem, the aforementioned fault constitutes a "reproach against one who is beyond reproach" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*).

*kaṇḍ* is used in the sense of rubbing the body; *muntur* in the sense of offense and anger; *valgu* in the sense of praise and sweetness; *asūñ* in the sense of affliction—another reading is *manaso’patāpe* (affliction of the mind). Dīkṣita maintains that the word *manas* is included within the indication of the meaning [of the root], while others hold that it is a separate root altogether. Some say *asū* and *as*. One forms *asyati* and *asūyati*. *leṭ* and *loṭ* are used in the sense of wickedness, prior state, and sleep—some maintain that *pūrva* itself is also a root. One forms *leṭyati* and *loṭyati*. *lelā* is used in the sense of shining.

Regarding the Vedic text, "He meditates as it were, he flickers as it were," the Vedāntins maintain that [the Self] merely appears to move. The roots *iras*, *irañ*, and *iraj* mean envy (*īrṣyā*). From these, one forms *irasyati*. By the rule *halica* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), there is lengthening of the vowel, resulting in *īryati* and *īryate*. *Uṣas* means the state of dawn. *Veda* means stealing and sleep. *Medhā* means quick apprehension. *Kuṣubha* means casting away or abuse. *Magadha* means surrounding; or, alternatively, servile speech. *Tantas*, *tampas*, and *dampas* mean suffering (*duḥkha*). *Sukha* and *duḥkha* mean the action of experiencing those [feelings]. One forms *sukhyati* and *duḥkhyati*; the meaning is that one experiences them. *Sapara* means worship (*pūjā*).

*Saparyati* means to serve. *Arara* is used in the sense of non-action (*arakarma*). *Bhiṣaja* is used in the sense of medical treatment (*cikitsā*). *Bhiṣṇaj* is used in the sense of attendance or service (*upasevā*). *Iṣudha* is used in the sense of holding arrows. *Caraṇa* is used in the sense of movement (*gati*). *Khuraṇa* is used in the sense of steadfastness or plowing (*dhaurya*). *Turaṇa* is used in the sense of haste (*tvarā*). *Bhuraṇa* is used in the senses of supporting and nourishing (*dhāraṇapoṣaṇa*). May those seeking wealth prosper; may the panegyrists sing praises; may the sacrificers be intent on their rites; and Rāma wanders through the forest.

In this context, [the root *gam*] has the meaning of "going. *Gadgad* is used in the sense of faltering speech. *Elā*, *kelā*, and *khelā* are used in the sense of play; others say *ile*. *Lekhā* is used in the sense of faltering, and in the view that it ends in *-a*, it takes the form *lekhyati*. *Liṭ* is used in the sense of smallness and contempt; it forms *liṭyati*. *Lāṭ* is used in the sense of living. *Hṛṇīñ* is used in the sense of anger and shame. *Mahīṅ* is used in the sense of worship; in the world of heaven, one "is honored" (*mahīyate*), which means one becomes worthy of worship. *Rekhā* is used in the sense of praise and attainment. *Dravas* is used in the sense of distress and service. *Tiras* is used in the sense of disappearance. *Agada* is used in the sense of being free from disease. *Uras* has the meaning of strength.

*Taraṇa* means "to go"; *payas* means "to flow"; *saṃbhūya* means "to come into being in abundance"; *ambara* and *saṃvara* mean "to fill" or "to cover. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).
The suffix *āya* is applied after the roots *gūp*, *dhūp*, *vicch*, *paṇi*, and *pani*.

The suffix *āya* is added to these roots: *gup* (to protect), *dhūp* (to fumigate/emit smoke), *vicch* (to go), *paṇ* (to bargain and to praise), and *pan* (to praise). Examples include *gopāyati*, *dhūpāyati*, and so forth; *paṇāyati*; and *panāyati*. Since the property of being *anudātta* (low-pitched) serves its purpose only when the root is used alone [without the *āya* suffix], the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings do not apply here. Therefore, Kṣīrasvāmin—who cites *panāyate* as an example of the ātmanepada—is to be considered questionable. Nor should it be argued that the root *pan* also possesses two distinct meanings; for Jayāditya, Sīradeva, Dīkṣita, and others maintain that the separate mention [of *pan* alongside *paṇ*] would otherwise be redundant.

However, some maintain that according to that [opponent's] view, because the indication of the root-meanings is admitted to be a modern innovation, it is improper to rely on semantic concomitance (*sāhacarya*). Furthermore, since the two meanings of the root *paṇ* are listed together, it is impossible to determine the meaning [of one] through its concomitance with *pani*; for there is no simultaneous recitation of these two in the sense of "praise. Nor does this entail a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ*, where, by virtue of concomitance, only the sense of "exclusion" (*varjana*) is understood for *pari*.

They say that because the rule *apaparī varjane* (Pāṇini 1.4.88) lists these two [words] together, their association is observed in the sense of "exclusion"; thus, by relying on this distinction in meaning, their determination is possible. And Bhaṭṭi [says]: *na copalebhe vaṇijāṃ paṇāyām*.
The suffix *īyaṅ* is substituted for the root *ṛt*.

In its own sense: *ṛtīyate*. The verbal root *ṛte* ending in *-ta* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "disgust" (*jugupsā*) and "compassion" (*kṛpā*). This is because of Bhaṭṭamalla’s statement: "The form *ṛtīyate* occurs in the sense of the two [i.e., disgust and compassion]. Furthermore, according to the lexicon: "Disgust (*jugupsā*), pity (*karuṇā*), and compassion (*ghṛṇā*) [are synonyms]. And Amara states: "*Artanam*, *ṛtīyā*, and *ṛṇīyā* have the meaning of compassion.
Some maintain that its ending in *-ta* is established by the rule *vañciluñcyṛtaśca*.

Others, however, say that the pronunciation of the long vowel *ī* in the word *īyaṅ* is an indicator (*liṅga*) for that [rule]; for if it were simply *id*, one would have applied *iyaṅ* alone, since the desired result would be established by the general rule for the lengthening of *sarvaṇa* vowels. This is not correct, because [if it were *id*], the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply due to the rule *eranekācaḥ*.

It should not be argued that the form would be established by *yaṅ* alone even with the long vowel *ā* in *akṛtsarva*; for some say this is because it would result in reduplication (*dvitva*) according to the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*. That is not correct, because by association with *san*, only that *yaṅ* which denotes a specific meaning can be understood there. Nor is it the case that only the *yaṅ* added to a desiderative (*san*)—which is *svārthika* (having its own meaning)—can be understood there; for even though *san* is also included there as a *svārthika*, the fault remains as before, since the result of the marker *ṅ* (namely, the middle voice *ātmanepada*) could still occur through the *ṅit* status of the initial [root].

Because [the desired form] is established by the prescription of the suffix *ṅīp*, since the property of ending in a *ṅit* [suffix] is easily available for the entire complex [of the root and suffix]; otherwise, it would be impossible to explain such things as the fact that the vowel *ṛ* of the root *bhrāj* could have been recited even earlier [in the Dhātupāṭha].
The affix *niṅ* occurs after a verbal root denoting a desire. || 30 ||

The root *kam* is used in its own sense (intransitive), meaning "to desire" (*kāntau*). It forms *kāmayate*. Now, the letter *ṇ* here is redundant; for it cannot serve the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) because that is prohibited by the rule *kiṅati ca*. Nor can the *vṛddhi* be justified on the strength of the letter *ṇ*, since its capacity is exhausted by its role in the general inclusion [of all roots] in the rule *ṇer aniṭi*. Furthermore, the letter *ṅ* is not rendered purposeful there [in *kāmayate*] by being intended to prevent the general inclusion [of the root *kamu*] in that very rule, because such a prevention could be achieved even by another *anubandha* (indicatory letter). Moreover, the letter *ṅ* serves its purpose in providing for the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) endings.
And thus, since both [statements] have scope, it is the prohibition of *vṛddhi* alone [that prevails], because prohibitions are stronger as they constitute exceptions to injunctions.

It might be argued as follows: because of the prohibition of *mittva* (the status of being a *mit* vowel) by the rule *na kamy-amicamām*, there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi* for the root *kam*. Otherwise, since the prohibition of *vṛddhi* would already remain in force simply due to its *ṅit* nature, the prohibition of *mittva* would be redundant. If it is then argued that the rule does have purpose in the sense of preventing the shortening (*hrasvatva*) of the *vṛddhi* caused by the *ṇic* suffix—specifically when one employs [the agent] who desires (*kāmayamānam prayuṅkte*), which involves a *ṇic* following a *ṇiṅ* suffix—then this is not correct. For it cannot be said that the shortening of the *vṛddhi* caused by the *ṇic* does not apply at all because of the intervention of the *ṇiṅ*; for once the *ṇiṅ* is elided by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, that intervention ceases to exist.

Nor should it be argued that this is due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*); for even so, the rule has its purpose fulfilled by the fact that it ensures the shortening caused by the suffix *ṇaṅ* does not apply to the vowel increase (*vṛddhi*) caused by the causative suffix *ṇic*.

If it is argued that, in that case, shortening (*hrasvatva*) itself would not even apply—because when the internal (*antaraṅga*) shortening is to be performed, the external (*bahiraṅga*) *vṛddhi* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)—nevertheless, since the *vṛddhi* caused by the suffixes *ṇic* and *kan* is separated from the end of the stem by the suffix *ṇiṅ*, there is no possibility of its application at the end; and even if the elision (*lopa*) has occurred, [the *vṛddhi* remains] due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor should one suspect a prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding operations concerning the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), as per the rule *kvilugupadhā...* (P. 1.1.5), because that rule applies only to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*).

Therefore, in forms such as *paṭayati*, there is no vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate syllable due to the status of the *ṭi*-elision as being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Consequently, since there is no possibility for the vowel lengthening caused by the *ṇic* suffix to apply to a form ending in *ṇiṅ*, the prohibition of the *mit* designation would not be meaningful for the purpose of preventing that lengthening; if this is argued, we say no.

Nevertheless, one might argue that the prohibition of *mittva* (the designation as having an indicatory *m*) is unnecessary; for the purpose of this prohibition is to ensure that the rule "the long vowel is optionally applied after *ciṇ*, *ṇamul*, etc. (*ciṇṇamulodīrgho’nyatarasyām*) does not apply when the suffix *ṇiṅ* is added to the root *kam*. It could be argued that instead of prohibiting *mittva*, one should simply prescribe an option for the short vowel there. This is because, in forms such as *aśami* and *aśāmī*, the short vowel is easily obtained when it is applied, while its absence results in the natural retention of the *vṛddhi* vowel. Thus, it may be contended that the prohibition of *mittva* serves no purpose. [Response: This is not so. Even if the option for the short vowel were prescribed, the prohibition of *mittva* would still be required for the sake of forms like *kāmayitvā*. For if *mittva* were not prohibited, the rule "after a root designated with *m*, the penultimate vowel is short" (*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*) would apply, resulting in the undesirable form *kāmatvā*. Therefore, the prohibition of *mittva* is indeed necessary. Furthermore, the option for the short vowel cannot be prescribed in the case of the suffix *ktvā*, because the rule "the short vowel is optionally applied after *ciṇ*, *ṇamul*, etc. already provides for the short vowel in that context. Consequently, since the short vowel is already available through that rule, there is no need to prescribe an option for it specifically in the case of *ṇiṅ*. Thus, the prohibition of *mittva* remains necessary.

When a *ṇic* affix is added to a root ending in a *ṇic*, if the preceding *ṇilopa* occurs, then due to the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is an intervention by the *ṇic*; consequently, the short vowel [of the penultimate] becomes difficult to obtain. However, if a long vowel is prescribed, its attainment is possible because the rule *na padānta...* prohibits the application of *sthānivadbhāva* when a long vowel is being prescribed; thus, there is a discrepancy between the two cases.

Furthermore, since the *āya*-substitutes and others are optional before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, when a *ṇic* is applied to a root ending in *ṇiṅ* (such as *kameḥ*), the prohibition of the *mit* designation remains meaningful [only in that specific case], yet the [resulting] *vṛddhi* and its prohibition would still be unavoidable.

Regarding this, the Vārttika states: "Because of the context of the suffixes *ika* and *kya*. This prohibition (*ṅkiti ca*) applies only to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* that are characterized by an *it* vowel. However, the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel in *ata upadhāyāḥ* is not characterized by an *it*. This is because the rule *ataḥ* specifies the original element (*sthānin*) as *at*. Thus, when the suffix *phañ* is applied after bases such as *naḍa*, forming *nāḍāyana*, the *vṛddhi* also occurs by virtue of the rule *ṅkiti ca*. This is the meaning.
The affixes *āya* and the others are optionally applied before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

In this case, regarding the status of the seventh case (locative) as "para" (subsequent), two alternatives are possible. When the rules for *āya* and the other affixes are prescribed by independent injunctions that do not depend on this specific sentence and which themselves do not require a subsequent cause, then—by this [present rule]—their optional elimination is effected when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows those *āya*-affixes. Even though words are eternal (*nitya*), their elimination occurs through processes such as elision (*lopa*) during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*).

In some cases, it is taught that by means of an exception (*apavāda*), the non-arising of a general rule (*utsarga*) within its own scope is indicated; thus, the position of "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) is also tenable. Alternatively, if their application occurs as a single syntactical unit with those three rules as subordinate elements (*śeṣa*), then the position is that *āya* and the others arise optionally before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix when it follows a verbal root ending in *āya* and so forth. And in this way, there is no difficulty in obtaining *āya* and the others even before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

In the rule *gupū-dhūp-eti* (Pāṇini 3.1.28), although it could have been stated simply as *ardhadhātuke vā* ("optionally before an affix beginning with an *ardhadhātuka* suffix"), the fact that it is recited separately indicates that one understands that the *āy*-class suffixes (*āy-ādi*) occur even before *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. Consequently, in the first case, one would derive *gopāyāṃcakāra*, but *gopāyati* would not be possible; for the word *gopāya* would end in a suffix, and the suffix *ktin* would be barred by the presence of the vowel *a*. Furthermore, in the form *gupta*—where the suffix *kta* follows—the optional disappearance of *āy* would result in the undesirable application of *guṇa* (vocalization) due to the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha-guṇa*), by virtue of the "suffix-characteristic" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the word "elision" (*lopa*) does not explicitly mention elision in this sūtra, the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an element as if it were present despite its elision) does not apply here. This is because in the *pratyayalopa* sūtra and the *tadbhāvita* sūtra, the inclusion of the term "that which is brought about by it" (*tadbhāvita*) is not required. However, in the second case, there would be the failure of the form *gopāyāñcakāra*, because the suffix *-ām* is difficult to obtain without the presence of a suffix [to trigger its application]. Furthermore, if the *ām* suffix were not produced, the *āya* suffix would not arise due to the absence of its cause.

Now, when there is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix such as *liṭ* following roots that take *āy* and so forth, since the optional application of *āy* and the rest occurs before that suffix, and because these [augmentations] fall within the scope of the *vikaraṇas*, this [form] is established. Nevertheless, the form *gopāya* would not be possible; for, due to the absence of being "ending in a suffix" (*pratyayānta*), the rule *apratyayāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.51) does not apply.

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "But [the forms] are established by the rule for the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes due to the mention of 'always' (*nitya*). Having prescribed the *āy*-class suffixes and others without distinction, the statement 'always in the *sārvadhātuka*' was formulated. [Objection: But in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *syat*-class suffixes (the *liṅ*) subverting the *āy*-class suffixes; for in forms such as *kariṣyati* and *gopāyati*, both sets have their scope, as they exclude one another. Consequently, in a form like *gopāyiṣyati*, the *syat*-class suffixes would apply because they are subsequent [to the *āy*-class], and in *gopāyati*, since there is no purpose for the *śap* suffix, it would not arise. [Reply: This is not so.

Even in that case, because the suffix *śap* is mandatory in the rule "gopāyati" (Pāṇini 3.1.69) for the sake of the meaning "to protect," and because the conditions [for its application] are present; and because in the case of "kāmayate," the desired result is established even without *śap*; thus, by being without any other scope (*niravakāśatva*), the *āya*-suffixes and others are established there. If it is argued that even so, the sublation of the *si*-suffixes (*syādi*) by the *āya*-suffixes (*āyādi*) would be unavoidable, then the rule should simply be formulated as "śapi nityam" (the suffix *śap* is always applied). Nor should it be said that even with this, there would be no inclusion of the root *vicch* because it belongs to the *tudadi* group; for the rule could instead be formulated as "śiti nityam" (the suffix *śap* is always applied before a *śit* suffix).

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, maintain that the term *ārdhadhātuke* [in Pāṇini’s rule] is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Consequently, they argue that even when optional affixes such as *āya* and others are applied to roots like *gup* and so on with the intention of forming an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the subsequent suffixes will occur according to their respective rules; thus, there is no need to resort to splitting the sūtra.
Verbal roots include those ending in *san* and other affixes.

The twelve suffixes beginning with *san*—namely *kāmyac*, *kyaṅ*, *kyaṣ*, *kvip*, *ṇic*, *ṇiṅ*, *yaṅ*, *yac*, *āya*, and *īyaṅ*—as well as those ending in these, shall have the designation "root" (*dhātu*). The inclusion of the word "ending in" (*anta*) is for the purpose of indicating that the designation applies to the entire complex ending in these suffixes; for when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical designation, there is no inclusion of what ends with that suffix. If it is argued that the designation "root" is already established for those ending in *san* and so forth because they denote action—as explained by the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* ("*bhū* and so forth are roots")—we say no. This is because that rule defines roots based on their meaning (denoting action), whereas the present rule establishes the designation based on formal grammatical structure (the presence of specific suffixes). Thus, the two rules serve different purposes.

The terms *bhū* and so forth are designated as verbal roots (*dhātu*) because they are listed in the [Dhātu-]gaṇa while possessing the status of being expressive of action, based on the meaning that they are "like a dwelling" (*vāsa-sadṛśa*). Otherwise, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *hiruk*. If it is objected: "In that case, this designation would not apply to substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *bhū*, *vac*, and *khyāñ*; for although *bhū*, *vac*, *khyā*, and so forth are recited within the midst of the verbal roots, the substitutes are distinct from them, and furthermore, forms such as *jagdhi* are not recited even in their own original form (*svarūpa*)," [We reply: No, because that is established through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Regarding this, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "The meanings of *iṣ* and so forth are indicated [by the term] 'ādi' (and so on) in the context of *san* and the others. Since *iṣ* and the others are included within the recited list (*pāṭha*), their status as verbal roots (*dhātu*) is established by virtue of their being substitutes (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor should it be argued that because the word 'substitute' (*ādeśa*) is a conventional term (*rūḍha*), the status of being a substitute belongs only to that which causes the cessation of the original element (*sthānin*); for in the case of the application of *iṣ* and the others, there is no formal injunction (*vidhāna*) of *san* and the rest. This is because the term 'substitute' (*ādeśa*) is based on the action [of indicating], as in the etymology: 'they are indicated (*ādiśyante*) [therefore they are] substitutes (*ādeśāḥ*'). Furthermore, it should not be argued that 'a substitute for that which is designated by the genitive case is like the original element.'"

It should not be argued that because the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is excluded there, the general rule (*utsarga*) would apply even to exceptions (*apavāda*), leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that those exceptions themselves would undergo substitution by virtue of being treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. This is because the addition of the marker *ś* in forms such as *śyan*, which serve as exceptions to forms like *śap*, makes it known that [the general rule] does not apply to them.

Here they raise an objection: If the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) were prescribed for *san* and the others by virtue of their being "as if in the place" (*sthānivadbhāva*) [of the original root], then—since in the prescription of a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no application of the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*)—it would follow that the suffixes themselves, and not the roots, would undergo the operations of verbal roots such as the augment *aṭ*. This is because those suffixes alone are prescribed for the sake of meanings such as the desiderative (*iṣya*). Furthermore, since the suffix *yaṅ* expresses the action qualified by repetition (*samabhihāra*), and the suffixes *āya* and so on are prescribed for the bare sense of the root's own meaning (*svārtha*), there is no cessation of any substitute (*sthānin*) for them; consequently, because the status of being "as if in the place" is untenable, the designation *dhātu* is likewise untenable.

On this point, Kaiyaṭa states: "In the sense of 'desiring to do' (*kartum icchati*), which involves the factor of the instrument (*karaṇāṅga*), the word *cikīrṣa* ending in the suffix *san* is substituted for the root *iṣ* as it occurs; thus, by the maxim that 'all [substitutes] are substitutes for the entire word,' the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is established for that which ends in it. Similarly, the word *lolūya* is substituted in place of the root *lū* when it signifies the act of cutting characterized by repetition (*samabhihāra*), and the word *gopāya* is substituted in place of the root *gup*; such is the intention of the venerable author of the Bhāṣya."

[Objection: One might argue that although the exact number of suffixes such as *san* cannot be determined in the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.1) when considering the placement of *sanādyantāśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), nevertheless, the rule *bhūvādayaśca* should be formulated immediately after *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*. This would result in greater brevity (*lāghava*) by employing the term *dhātu* only once. Some maintain that this is indeed correct. However, this is questionable, because the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *dhātu* from the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* (Pāṇini 1.3.12) is well-established according to Kaiyaṭa and others; furthermore, if that [term *dhātu*] were introduced only here [in the proposed sequence], its application there [in 1.3.12] would be difficult to obtain. *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* || 33 || [Pāṇini 3.1.33]

The term *lṛ* is a general designation for both *lṛṅ* and *lṛṭ*. Accordingly, the suffixes *syatāsī* are added to *lṛ* and *luṭ* respectively. [Examples: *bhaviṣyati*, *bhavitā*. By the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*, the augment *iṭ* is applied.

But surely, what exception (*apavāda*) is there for the general rule (*utsarga*) regarding the *vikaraṇas*? It cannot be said that the *yaṅ* suffix is the exception, because it is prescribed for all *sārvadhātuka* affixes by virtue of the continued application of the mention of "bhāva" (state) and "karman" (object). Nor can it be said that the *śa*-class and *syādi*-class affixes are its exceptions because they are prescribed as specific rules; for in forms such as *pacati* and *pacataḥ*, since the exceptions—the *śa*-class and *syādi*-affixes—already have their scope, [the *yaṅ* would still apply]. Consequently, in *pakṣyati*, the *śa*-class affix etc. would occur by virtue of being subsequent (*paratva*). Furthermore, since the *yaṅ* is prescribed specifically for the states of "bhāva" and "karman," there is no relationship of general rule and exception between them.

This is because they do not share the same object of application (*samānaviṣayakatva*). Nor should it be argued that *śap* is the general rule (*utsarga*) while *śyan* and the others are the exceptions (*apavāda*); for in cases such as *dīvyati* and *pakṣyati*, where both rules find scope, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that in forms like *deviṣyati*, the suffixes beginning with *sy-* (the future tense markers) would be superseded by *śyan* and the others due to their higher status (*paratva*). It is not so. *Śyan* and the others are substitutes for *śap*; thus, *śap* is superseded by *sy*-suffixes and the like. Consequently, in the domain of *sy*-suffixes following roots of the *div*-class and others, since *śap* itself does not even apply, its substitutes—*śyan* and the others—cannot possibly apply either.

This is because the word *śap*, which is carried over from the rule *kartari śap* (Pāṇini 3.1.68), is transformed into a genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) by means of the ablative *divādibhyaḥ* (3.1.69) through the principle *tasmād ity uttarasya* ("from that [ablative], the following [is affected]"). Alternatively, [the suffixes] *yak*, *syatāsīlaluṭoḥ*, *cliluṅi*, and *cleḥ sic* follow immediately after *kartari śap*; likewise, *śyan* follows immediately after *divādibhyaḥ*. The same should be understood in other cases as well.

Alternatively, [the suffixes] *sy* and so on would apply at the very stage of the *l*-suffix (*lā-sthāyām*), and thus they are internal (*antaraṅga*); whereas *śyan* and so on, which apply when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, are external (*bahiraṅga*). [Objection: But surely, because they are subsequent, only *l*-suffixes such as *laṭ* and so on should occur; moreover, these [suffixes like *sy*] are not non-eternal (*anitya*). Even if *sy* and the others were applied, since the rule for the third case ending has been reached, and even though there is the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "root" (*dhātu*), the substitutes for *l* would still result by resorting to the qualification that the *l* must be prescribed after a root. [Reply: Not so. For even though they occur subsequent to the substitutes for *l*, the status of *sy* and the others as internal (*antaraṅga*) is not lost.

In the case of that [rule prescribing *śap*], there is no requirement for the properties of an affix such as being *sārvadhātuka*, nor for specific meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*), and so forth. However, in the rule prescribing *śyan* and other such affixes, those [properties] are necessarily relied upon; therefore, they are *bahiraṅga* (external).

Furthermore, the application of the rules for *syat* and other such suffixes must necessarily be accepted as occurring immediately after the substitution of the *l*-suffixes; otherwise, the rule prescribing the acute accent (*udātta*) for the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tās* would not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that "the accent of the *vikaraṇa* does not override the accent of the verbal root."

Since the lack of acute accent (*anudāttatva*) for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix following the root *ās-* (in the form *tāsi*) after a *l*-substitute has not yet been established, that rule would necessarily be a new prescription (*apūrva-vidhi*). However, if *tāsi* were to apply only after the *l*-substitution has occurred, then because the acute accent of *tāsi* itself would be the "later remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*), the subsequent *sārvadhātuka* suffix would already be established as unaccented by the general rule of *śeṣanighāta*. Consequently, the prescription of the unaccented nature would be redundant; therefore, the fact that this unaccented status is prescribed serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned principle.

By this, Kaiyaṭa refutes the argument that "because the rule for the substitution of *l*-suffixes forms a single syntactical unit with the rules for number, the *ātmanepada*, and the *parasmaipada*, and because the *l*-substitutions are *bahiraṅga* while the *syādi* suffixes are *antaraṅga* at the stage of the *l*-stem and are prescribed by specific rules (*pratipadavidhāna*), the *syādi* suffixes occur [before the *l*-substitutions]. This is because the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) is untenable.
*Sib bahulaṃ leṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.34): "The suffix *siP* is diversely applied in the *leṭ*."

The *leṭ* [suffix] will be discussed in the section on Vedic usage (*chandasi*). The general rule for the *sip* [suffix] must be stated as an option (*vācya*) for formations beginning with *san* and so forth in the Veda. Without depending on a preceding cause (such as an augment), the *sip* should be prescribed after a verbal root within the group of formations beginning with *san*. Once that which ends in this [suffix] receives the designation of a "verbal root" (*dhātu*), forms such as *indreṇa vastena neṣatu* are established. [Objection: This can be established from the root *nī* by applying *guṇa* before the *sip*, and then treating it as *loṭ*; furthermore, since *neṣ* is a separate root in the list beginning with *geṣṛ*, *neṣṛ*, *bhreṣṛ*, and *heṣṛ* meaning "to go," it would be established even there. [Response: Even so, in the case of *avayāsisīṣṭha*, the prohibition of the *iṭ* augment—which is conditioned by the fact that the root has only one vowel (*ekāj*)—must not apply. Therefore, the *sip* suffix must be explicitly stated.

From the root *yā* preceded by *ava*, there is the suffix *liṅ*. [In this context,] *suṭ* and *sīyuṭ* are added. Because the stem (*aṅga*) ending in that [suffix] has more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the augment *iṭ* is applied. Nor should it be argued that the multi-vowel nature belongs to *sip* alone; for since *sip* would otherwise be audible [in the form], its purpose must necessarily be stated as being merely for the sake of pronunciation. Consequently, because the root ending in that [suffix] would then consist of only one vowel, there would result the undesired application of the prohibition of *iṭ*.

Now, if it is argued: "The *yā* [of *yās*] is unaccented (*anudātta*) in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), and therefore no *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows it, because it is separated by the *sip* [suffix]. Furthermore, although the *ārdhadhātuka* follows that which ends in *sip*, this [element after *sip*] is not unaccented in its original enunciation"—this is not so. For, according to the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, the meaning is that those whose parts (*avayava*) are *san* and so forth receive the designation *dhātu*. Consequently, since *sip* has *yā* as one of its constituent parts, it would be included under the term *yāti* (by the principle of inclusion), and thus there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the prohibition of *iṭ* applying. Moreover, even in the view where that rule is rejected on the grounds of the *sthānivadbhāva* [analogy], there would still be the undesirable consequence of the form ending in *sip* being unaccented by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva*.

Alternatively, this commentary refers to the reading according to the traditional recension (*yathānyāsa-pāṭha*). Even though, because of the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the elision of the *a* is necessary, the letter *s* would not be heard anywhere [in the actual form], and consequently, its *anubandha*, the letter *p*, would be useless; for there is no hearing of an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel [in that position]. Nevertheless, when only the letter *s* is applied, by the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), the *liṅ* [optative] in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*)— [The text continues: ...is treated as if it were both [present and non-present]. Thus, the *liṅ* ending *yāt* becomes *syāt*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *anubandha* *p* is indeed purposeful, because it serves to distinguish this [suffix] from others. For otherwise, the suffix *tās* [of the periphrastic future] would also be subject to the same rule, since it too ends in *s*. Therefore, the *anubandha* *p* is necessary to exclude that. Moreover, the *anubandha* *p* is used to indicate that the augment *īṭ* does not apply after this [suffix]; for if it were not so indicated, *īṭ* would have to be added here as well, because the suffix *tās* is also included under the category of *liṅ*. Consequently, the *anubandha* *p* is indeed meaningful. As for the mention of *liṅ* in the commentary, it is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), and should be understood to include other suffixes such as *luṅ* [aorist] and *lṛṅ* [conditional] as well. Thus, the meaning is established. End of section. [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]

Since it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix following a root taught with an initial vowel (*adupadeśa*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix would be unaccented; consequently, by the accent of the affix, the vowel *ā* of the word *sa-* would be acute. When the augment *iṭ* follows that [acute vowel], the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48) would cause the acute accent of the *iṭ*—by the rule regarding the disappearance of the acute accent (*udāttanivṛttisvara*)—to apply to the [remaining] syllable. However, because of the explicit pronunciation of the letter *p*, the vowel *ā* of the word *sa-* does not become acute by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), due to the force of that [pronunciation of *p*].

Alternatively, because of the reading in this specific section, the *dhātu-svara* (accent of the verbal root) belongs to the word *yā* itself; thus, there is elision (*lopa*) of the non-udātta vowel *ā* of the word *sa*, but not of the udātta one, and consequently, there is an absence of the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*. The elision (*nighāta*) prescribed by *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* is prohibited by the rule *nipātairyadyadi*. The word *ava* undergoes elision (*nighāta*) by the rule *tiṅicodāttavati*. It should be stated that in the Veda, the suffix *sip* is frequently *ṇit*. [Examples: *savitā dharmasāviṣat*; *pra ṇa āyūṃṣi tāriṣat*. From the root *sū* in the sense of "impelling" and from the root *tṛ*, the suffix *leṭ* is applied. Due to its being *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi*. [The rule] *kās-pratyayādām amantre liṭi* [3.1.35] applies.

The suffix *ām* shall be applied after the root *kās* when followed by a suffix ending in a *pratyaya* (affix) that occurs in the *liṭ* (perfect tense), but not in a *mantra*. Therefore, in the *Brāhmaṇa* literature, it occurs exactly as follows: *taṃ ha kaśyapo yājayāṃcakāra* ("Kaśyapa caused him to sacrifice," etc.). Regarding the mention of *kās*, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the root *cakās*: *cakāsāmāsa*. Nor is the desired form established merely by the mention of *kās* [in the rule], because the mention of *kās* here would otherwise be purposeless. Alternatively, the mention of *kās* along with "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*) is for the sake of including *culump*. Having removed the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*), it should be stated instead as "after a monosyllabic root" (*akāca*). Thus: *culumpāṃcakāra*. Bopadeva states that *culump* means "to swallow."

"Those who scoop up water from the ocean with their palms, as if it were coconut juice," so says Bhavabhūti. The formation of the *vṛt* section is for the purpose of concluding the list beginning with *yaji*. This is because the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) holds that the *bhvādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Examples such as *daridrāsi*, *cikīrṣābabhūva*, and others ending in *īṅ* should be cited accordingly.
And after a root beginning with a vowel (ij-ādi) that contains a heavy syllable (gurumat), [the suffix -aC is added], except for the root ṛcch.

After a verbal root beginning with a vowel (ijādi) that possesses a heavy syllable (gurumat), the suffix *ām* shall be applied when the *liṭ* affixes follow, provided the root is other than *ṛcchati*. Examples: *indāmāsa*, *edhāñcakre*. Regarding the prescription of *ām* for roots possessing a heavy syllable, there is a prohibition when the root is caused by a *liṅ* affix; this is so that it does not occur in cases such as *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa*. Although in the case of *uvoṣa*, *ām* should optionally apply according to the rule *uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām*, nevertheless, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited this example by not relying on the principle that a specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) is stronger [than a general one], because the root possesses a heavy syllable due to the absence of *guṇa* in the dual and plural forms.

The point is that even in cases such as *īṣatuḥ* and *īṣuḥ*, because of the presence of a heavy syllable (*gurumatva*) following the formation of the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel by homogeneous combination), the suffix *ām* would be applicable everywhere after roots beginning with a consonant (*ijādi*) due to that heaviness. However, the inclusion of the term "having a heavy syllable" (*gurumad-grahaṇam*) must be for the purpose of excluding forms such as *iyajitha tvam*, *iyajāham*, and *upavāham*.

Alternatively, it should be explained as "gurumataḥ" [meaning "having a heavy syllable"] in the context of the *upadeśa* (the original formative stage). Thus, the aforementioned Vārttika [P. 1.4.2 Vārt. 1] becomes unnecessary. Nor should it be argued that there is an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in the case of *vyucchāñcakāra*, because the status of being "heavy" (*gurutva*) applies only after the addition of the *tug* augment, at which point the syllable is already heavy due to the conjunction of consonants (*saṃyoga*). This is because the exclusion of the form *ṛccha-* [in P. 1.4.2] indicates that the status of being "gurumad" based on the *tug* augment is not excluded by the inclusion of the term *upadeśa*. Furthermore, the mention of *tug* is merely an illustration for any augment in general.

By this [rule], the formation of *tenokhāṃcakāra* is established even though it possesses the heaviness (*gurutva*) that is the cause for the introduction of the augment *num*. For this very reason, the rule is intended solely as an informative statement (*jñāpaka*)—and not for the purpose of a prohibition—since it is possible to inform us of the absence of *ām* after the root *ṛcchati* in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense by means of the prescription of *guṇa* in the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām*. Nor should it be argued that even if *ām* were prescribed, that prescription would be for the sake of *guṇa*; for it is simpler (*laghu*) to assume an informative statement regarding the absence of *ām* than to assume a subversion of the *paribhāṣā* rule "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (when a specific element is mentioned, the operation applies to what precedes it).

Nor can it be argued that the rule *ṛ gatau prāpaṇe* exists for the purpose of prescribing the *guṇa* [substitution]; for although that substitution is prescribed specifically for the *śit* [affixes], it is absent in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], making it impossible for the rule to refer to that [specific form]. However, it is possible for it to refer to the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself as its basis. This is because in examples such as *tiṣṭhateḥ* or *jighrateḥ*, even though the substitutes *tiṣṭha* and *jighra* do not occur when followed by *caṅ*, the roots *sthā* and *ghrā* are still mentioned; likewise here, it can be said that the mention of the root is made by means of the *śtip* affix in the form *ṛcchati*.

Nor is the injunction of the *guṇa* substitution there purposeless; for once the doubling (*dvirvacana*) and the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* have been applied, since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included under the term "root" (*dhātu*), it would end in *ṛ*, and after applying *guṇa* and substituting *ra* for *ṛ*, the forms would be *aratuḥ* and *aruḥ*. This is because doubling occurs before the *yaṇ* substitution due to its higher priority; furthermore, even after the *yaṇ* substitution, doubling still applies by virtue of the status of the original as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), as both rules are obligatory (*nitya*). Alternatively, in the case of *ninyatuḥ*, one should consider the future *yaṇ* substitution and understand that the *iṅ* substitution does not apply as before.

If one argues that once doubling (*dvitva*) has been applied, the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) applies first so that *yaṇ* does not occur; whereas if *yaṇ* were applied first, doubling would follow by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule—[we reply: the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) prevails over the *yaṇ* replacement because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. However, if the root is included within the term "abhyāsa" (reduplication), then the following operations apply: substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, substitution of *ra* as the final element (*raparatva*), the elision of all consonants except the first (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*), lengthening of the initial *ā* according to the rule *āta āder dīrghaḥ*, and the elision of the *ā* according to *ato lopaḥ*. Thus, the forms *āratuḥ* and *ārur* are established. If this is argued, [the answer follows].

Because the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uradatva*) applies later than the long vowel by *samprasāraṇa* (*savarṇadīrgha*). Nor should it be argued that since the long vowel by *samprasāraṇa* depends solely on the phonemes (*varṇamātra*), while the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* is *bahiraṅga*—being dependent on the heading of *aṅga* and thus having a further cause—the long vowel by *samprasāraṇa* should occur first; for the heading of *aṅga* is not resorted to until after the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsavikāra*). Furthermore, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* is also *antaraṅga*. Consequently, by virtue of being both subsequent (*paratva*) and *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* takes place first. Then follows the substitution of *ṛ* for *r* (*raparatva*), the retention of the initial consonant (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*), and finally the lengthening of the vowel according to the rule *ata āder dīrghaḥ*.

If you argue that the designation *aṅga* (stem) applies up until the end of the seventh chapter because of the use of the plural number [in Pāṇini’s rules], otherwise forms such as *vavraśca* would not be established; for if the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* were not caused by what follows (*paranimitta*), then by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (1.1.57), there would be no status as a *sthānin*, and consequently, the prohibition in the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108) would not apply, leading to the undesirable result of the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the letter *v*. [Response: This is not so. The designation *aṅga* applies only to the extent necessary for its own purpose, just as the term *pratyaya* (suffix) applies only where required. Otherwise, even in the case of *vavraśca*, the *ṛ* of *vṛ* would be subject to the substitution of *u* by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (1.1.51), and since this substitution is caused by what follows, the status of *sthānin* would indeed exist. Consequently, the prohibition in *saṃprasāraṇācca* would apply, and the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* for *v* would be prevented. Thus, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the plural number used in the rule *paraśca* (3.1.2) is merely for the sake of clarity (*vyakti*), as the singular form *param* is also understood through the principle of *ekatva-saṃkhyā-vivakṣā*. Therefore, the designation *aṅga* does not extend beyond the sixth chapter. Consequently, the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* is not caused by what follows, and the status of *sthānin* does not arise; thus, the prohibition in *saṃprasāraṇācca* does not apply, and the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* for *v* occurs as desired. Hence, the objection is refuted.

Nevertheless, because in the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11), the term *ṝtām* is read as a *praśleṣa* (split compound) to specifically prescribe *guṇa* for the root *ṛ*, it is impossible to include that [root] by means of the word *ṛcchati*. Nor should it be argued that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *cakratuḥ* when the letter *ṛ* is specified, because in the case of the mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), the inclusion of what ends with it (*tadantagrahaṇa*) applies. This is because the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.10) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Therefore, even without the explicit mention of *guṇa* for *ṛ*, forms such as *āratuḥ* are established; likewise, the *guṇa* of *ṛ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is achieved even without the mention of the root *ṛcchi*. Thus, it is settled that either the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) *anṛcchaḥ* or the rule *ṛccherāmb* (Pāṇini 7.4.12) must necessarily be present.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, maintains that neither [of these two] need be stated. This is because the rule *gurumata upadeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.69) is not relied upon here. Nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *eyāteṣu*; for this is resolved by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. It is impossible for the *guṇa* produced by the conjunction with *liṭ* to serve as a cause for the *ām* which is the cause for the elision of *liṭ*, because if *ām* were present, the elision of *hi* would necessarily follow. As for the root *ūrṇu*, there is no issue, because the addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the state of having *nu* has been prescribed. Alternatively, it is because of the reading in *saṃhitā* as *ṛcchordayāyāsaśca*; since the prohibition applies to vowels following an *ṛcch* ending in *u*, [the rule does not apply].
Furthermore, this is a reference where the case-ending is elided: *dayāyāsaśca* (3.1.37).

The root *day* is used in the senses of giving, moving, protecting, and striking; *ay* in the sense of moving; and *ās* in the sense of sitting. After these roots, the suffix *ām* is optionally added in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). Examples: *dayāṃcakre*, *ayāṃcakre*, *āsāṃcakre*. [Pāṇini 3.1.38] states:
"After the roots *uṣ*, *vid*, and *jāgṛ*, [the suffix *ām* is optionally added]."

He caused to burn: *oṣāṃcakāra*, *uvoṣa*. He knew: *vidāmāsa*, *viveda*. He became awake: *jāgarāṃbabhūva*, *jajāgāra*. It should be stated that [the root] *vid* takes the augment *k* [before the suffix *ām*]; by this, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Alternatively, in the rule prescribing *ām*, the form *videt* (ending in *a*) is combined; therefore, because it lacks a light vowel as the penultimate (*laghūpadha*), there is no *guṇa*. Because it is specified "in the prescription of *ām*," the form *vetti* is established. However, if it were stated "by connection with the *liṭ* [suffix]," then even *viveda* would not occur. Thus, the followers of Bhāradvāja recite: "The *ām* after *vid* is *kit*, or else there is an absence of *guṇa* due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). And: "As in the case of *bhī*, *hrī*, *bhṛ*, *hu*, and *vas* [with *liṭ*], so also [with *vid*]. (Pāṇini 1.2.6).

The roots *ñijī* (to fear), *hrī* (to feel shame), *ḍubhṛñ* (to support and nourish), and *hu* (to give and eat)—after these, the suffix *ām* is optionally used in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). When *ām* is present, the operations of *ślau* (the reduplication rules) apply. Regarding the purpose of this extended application (*atideśa*) as being like *ślau*: by the extension [of the *ślau* rule], *guṇa* substitution occurs during reduplication. This is because the prohibition stated in *na lumatāṅgasya* pertains to the scope of application of the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*. Examples: *bibhayāṃ cakāra*, *jihrayāmāsa*, *vibharāṃ babhūva*, *juhavāmāsa*. Furthermore, the root *kṛ* is invariably employed after these verbs when the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) follows. (Pāṇini 3.1.40)

The roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are employed as subsequent suffixes (*anuprayujyante*) after forms ending in the affix *ām*. An example has been stated. Now, one might object: even without an explicit rule, the employment of the subsequent suffix is established. For indeed, from a form ending in *ām*, only a specific time is understood, but not the grammatical means (*sādhana*), number, and so forth. Therefore, for the purpose of manifesting those [factors], the employment of another verbal root (*prakṛti*) is necessary. In that case, the subsequent suffix cannot be the very same root; for example: *oṣāmuvoṣa*.

It is precisely by means of the subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*) that all meanings are understood, for otherwise the suffix *ām* would be rendered useless; nor can it be the case that verbs such as *pacati* (he cooks) are used [after *ām*], because they do not convey the means (*sādhana*) and other factors connected with the original base (*prakṛti*). However, the verb *kṛñ* (to do/make) is employed [after *ām*] because it expresses a general action (*sāmānya-vacana*). This is because, as in the case of "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*," there is a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) between the general and the particular, and thus it is capable of conveying the meaning of the former. Nor is the rule intended to exclude the use of *bhū* (to be) and *as* (to exist), since their employment after *ām* is desired. Furthermore, this is not something that cannot be obtained from the rule itself.

In the rule *kṛbhvastiyoga*, the word *kṛ* refers to the root *kṛñ* by means of the inclusion of the entire class through the letter *ñ*. Furthermore, the mention of *sampadā ca* excludes *sampad* because, although it falls within that same class, its meaning is not compatible [with the context]. Nor is this for the purpose of prescribing the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Since the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) is already established, the restatement is for the sake of ensuring the employment of a form that is strictly concordant. Therefore, after a verbal base ending in *ām* that takes the middle voice, only a form of *karoti* ending in the middle voice is employed as the subsequent verb. Thus, it should not be said that the rule *pratyayavat* is unnecessary.

Since the agentive meaning is understood even through the *parasmaipada* [ending], the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of that [root] would be unavoidable—contrary to the rule "like the suffix *ām*"—unless one were to exclude it. Nor can it be for the purpose of preventing the subsequent employment of the present tense (*laṭ*), because there is no possibility of such employment; the present tense conveys a time that contradicts the time inherent in the meaning of the *ām* suffix. This is because the subsequent employment serves to manifest the meaning of the *ām* suffix, and when the immediate present is possible, the use of the present tense with reference to a former past state is untenable.

Nor is it for the purpose of prohibiting the subsequent employment of another [verb] ending in *niṣṭhā* (the past participial suffixes -ta/-tavant), because that would entail the impossibility of perceiving the specific distinctions of person (*puruṣa*) and voice (*upagraha*), which would thereby prohibit its subsequent employment. Nor is it for the purpose of prohibiting [the subsequent employment of] one ending in *luṅ* (the aorist suffix), because that is precluded by the fact that it conveys the non-recent past time (*anadyatana-kāla*). Nor is it for the purpose of prohibiting [the subsequent employment of] one ending in *laṅ* (the imperfect suffix), because that is absent precisely due to the fact that it conveys the non-recent past and the remote past (*parokṣa*). Nor is it for the purpose of prohibiting the subsequent employment of one ending in *laṅ* after the roots *iṇ* and *haś*, since the rule "after *iṇ* and *haś*, *laṅ* optionally" prescribes *laṅ* specifically for the non-recent past when it is remote.

In the employment of the *liṭ* (perfect tense), it is logical that only those [roots] ending in it should be used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), because such is observed in both worldly usage and the Veda. Furthermore, among optional means such as the *khadira* or *palāśa* wood, the conclusion must be performed by the very same means with which one began; for if the commenced action is abandoned, one must employ its substitute and not another means altogether, since a difference in the means results in a different action, thereby failing to complete the action originally commenced.

In common worldly usage as well, when one begins with the genitive case to express the relationship between owner and owned—as in "the owner of cows" (gavām svāmī)—then the genitive alone is employed even in the phrase "and of horses" (aśvānām ca). For if one were to say "in horses" (aśveṣu), there would arise the unwanted implication that he stands in the horses and so forth.

As for the objection that, because doubt arises in every case, there would be the undesirable consequence of eliminating the use of the locative ending (*saptamyanta*), and that such usage would result even where the conditions for removing doubt are present—leading to a contradiction with the Bhāṣya since there is no doubt in the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) because no doubt regarding another meaning exists after an *ām*-ending form followed by the use of a *laṅ*-ending verb—that is not correct. For there is no evidence that doubt occurs universally; moreover, when a sentence begins with a locative ending, the use of a locative ending is indeed possible.

Therefore, whatever meaning is commenced to be communicated by a particular verbal form, that very meaning must be brought to completion by it, for the sake of cognitive economy (*pratipatti-lāghava*). Otherwise, there would result the cumbersome requirement of cognizing the expressive power (*śakti*) directed toward another word, the contraction of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) to something other than that, and the necessity of reflecting upon the fact that the word is intent upon the subject matter already under discussion. This being the position reached—

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "For the purpose of removing error and for the purpose of removing intervention. Since the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) is already established, this statement is for the sake of a restriction (*niyama*). It means that the subsequent employment must occur immediately after [the form ending in] *ām*, neither before nor with an intervening element. How then are examples such as "He first caused him to fall, and afterwards he fell himself" (*taṃ pātayāṃ prathamamāsa papāta paścāt*) or "At one spot of the ocean, the pot-born sage (Agastya) even made him a mere handful" (*sindhoḥ so'pyekadeśe tamapi culukayāṃ cakāra kumbhayoniḥ*) possible? Some say that these are simply errors.

Others explain that *pātayāḥ* means "he goes to fall" (*pātaṃ yāti*), and so forth; however, even so, the phrase "he joined [them] according to rule, together with his assembled kinsmen" (*saṃyojayāṃ vidhivadāsa sametabandhuḥ*) remains untenable. If it is argued that this is because the suffix *ghañ* would result in the form *saṃyoga*, we say no, for the suffix *kap* is to be understood as having the same meaning as *ghañ*. Let us return to our subject matter. Since the two verbs *bhū* and *as* used in conjunction with the suffix *ām* are transitive by virtue of following that suffix, the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is employed in the sense of the object (*karmani*), because the action expressed by the suffix *ām* is primary.
Even during the summer season, those who were heaps of fat shone throughout the nights.

This is because of such observations as these. Regarding the root *as* (to be) when the *liṭ* suffix is applied in the sense of either the action itself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), there is a disagreement concerning the forms *eś* and *iṭ*. Some maintain that in both cases the substitute *ha* occurs according to Pāṇini 7.4.52 (*ha eti*), resulting in the forms *edhāmahe* and *īkṣāmahe*. Others hold that by virtue of its association with *tās* (the *liṭ* augment), the substitution of *ha* applies only when *iṭ* is present, since the substitution of *eś* for *tās* is impossible here. Still others argue that precisely because of that association, the substitution of *ha* occurs only before an *sārvadhātuka* suffix—and not in this case, because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; therefore, in the two aforementioned instances, the forms are simply *edhāmāse* and *īkṣāmāse*. Pāṇini 3.1.41 states: "In the case of *vidāṃkurvantu*, [the substitution of *ku* for *āṃ*] is optional."

The form *vidām* is a substitute for the imperative (*loṭ*), and the subsequent employment of the root *kṛ* ending in the imperative is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the imperative suffix belonging to the root *vid*. In the rule *āmaḥ*, since the term *leḥ* (the suffix *liṭ*) is understood by way of anuvṛtti, the elision of the imperative suffix follows from that very source. This should be understood to apply similarly to the aorist (*luṅ*) and the optative (*liṅ*) in the subsequent sūtra. As for person and number, they are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). Because the word *iti* is used here in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), similarity is to be understood as the employment of an imperative form of *kṛ* after *vidām*; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Example: *vidāṃkurvantu mahatastalaṃ vidviṣadambhasaḥ* ("May they pierce through the depths of the great ocean of enemies"—Māgha).
"What need have we of that? Let the Blessed One, the beloved of the fresh lotus, know [it] for us.
Thus ends the section on *murā* and so forth.
Similarly, "know this" (*vidāṃ kuru*) and so on. In the case of the *ām* suffix, one has *vettu*, *vittāt*, *vittām*, *vidantu*, and so forth.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the following forms occur: *abhyutsādayām*, *prajanayām*, *cikayām*, *ramayāmakar*, *pāvayām*, *kriyā*, and *dvidāmaktra*. (Pāṇini 3.1.42)

The form *akarat* is prescribed as a substitute for the root *kṛ* followed by the suffix *luṅ*, along with the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the verb *kṛ*; this is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) applied to the first four [roots]. Even therein, in the case of *cikayām* [from *ci*], there is the substitution of *ām* for the pure root *ci*, reduplication, and the change of *c* to *k* (*kutva*). The distinction is that for the other three roots, which are *ṇic*-derived, there is merely the addition of *ām*. In *akarat*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs before the *tip* ending; then the elision of the *ti* (by *halṅyādi-lopa*), and the elision of *sic* (by *mantre ghasah*). [Examples are: *abhyudasādayāmakaḥ*, *prajanayāmakaḥ*, *cikayāmakaḥ*, *ramayāmakaḥ*; [and in the past tense: *abhyudasīṣadat*, *prājījanat*, *acaṣīt*.

In common usage, [the form] is *arīramat*; however, in the Veda (*chandas*), this [form *aramṇāt*] also occurs due to the following of the optional rule (*vikalpasyānuvartanāt*). [The form] *pāvayāṃ kriyāt* is derived from the root *pū* (to purify) or *pav* (to flow), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the benedictive mood (*āśīrliṅ*) with the suffix *ām*. Only such a form [ending in *ām*] is followed by the auxiliary verb *kṛ* (*anuprayoga*). [The form] *vidāmakran* is from the root *vid* (to know) in the aorist (*luṅ*) with *ām*; there is the addition of the auxiliary *kṛ* after the aorist ending, and the elision of *sic*. There is the elision of the final *i* of the suffix *jha* (which becomes *an*) by the rule *itaśca*. There is also the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). The meaning is "they have known. Thus ends the third Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
The fourth Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya.
In the *Cilupa* [Tantra], verse 43:

The *cli* suffix shall occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. Although it never actually appears in usage because its scope is preempted by substitutes such as *sij* and others, nor does it perform any operation like *kvip* and other suffixes, nevertheless, the prescription of *cli* is for the purpose of providing a general term (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*) via the word *li* in the rule *mantre ghasahvaraṇaśavṛdadvṛc-kṛgamijanibhyo liṭ*, where *liṭ* is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*) to the elision (*lopa*) that is to be prescribed. Otherwise, one would have to explicitly mention *caṅ*, *aṅ*, and *sic*.

The distinction is as follows: because the root *dhā* ends in the vowel *ā*, the substitution of *ghas* for it is intended for the purpose of the *caṅ* affix; and because the roots *gam* and *jan* are marked with the indicator *ḷ*, the substitution of *sica* for them is intended for the purpose of the *aṅ* affix and for the sake of other roots. However, regarding the *ciṇ* affix prescribed after *jan*, if its elision (*luk*) is observed in the Vedic mantras, then that fourth [instance of *ciṇ*] must also be included; with this intention, it was stated in the Bhāṣya: "In that regard, at least three are to be understood."

"In the rule prescribing *k* [as a substitute for *s*], the mention of *aniṭ* is for the purpose of indicating the *cli* [affix] when it is separated [from the root]. This is the meaning: in the rule *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*, the prescription of *cli* by the term *aniṭ* is for the purpose of qualifying the *cli*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of it qualifying the verbal root (*dhātu*). If it is asked, "What is the fault in that? [the answer follows].

For in that case, one would have to rely on the property of being *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) residing in another suffix; because elsewhere there is no introduction of the augment *iṭ* for the root from which [the suffix arises], the substitutes of *luṅ* are treated as *sārvadhātuka*, and thus they lack the possibility of having *iṭ*. Consequently, it is impossible to state that the property of being *aniṭ* resides in them, and therefore the suffix *kso* would not apply after roots such as *guh* and others, since they possess *iṭ* elsewhere by virtue of its optional application. However, if their status as *aniṭ* were asserted based on the absence of *iṭ* in one alternative case, then *kso* would necessarily apply.

But when the *cli* suffix is the qualificand, because it is an *ardhadhātuka*, for that [suffix] which has roots such as *guh* as its base, since the root contains the marker *u*, when there is an absence of *iṭ*, then by the substitution of *ksa*, the form *aghukṣat* is established; but when there is *iṭ*, then by the substitution of *sic*, the form *agūhīt* is established.

There is another Vārttika: "Or [the substitution of] *ghaslṛ* occurs in the state of the verbal root (*dhātu-bhāve*). For instance, in the case of the *luṅ* suffix, when there is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the substitution of *ghaslṛ* for the root must be prescribed therein. In that context, once the substitution of *ghaslṛ* has occurred before the *clu* suffix, the replacement by *aṅ* is established because the root is marked with the *ḷ*-indicator (*ḷ-dit*). Otherwise, the substitution of *ghaslṛ* would occur only before the *sic* suffix, resulting in the undesirable consequence of hearing the *sic* suffix (i.e., its presence in the form). This is because even a general rule (*utsarga*) that has already begun to apply cannot be sublated by an exception (*apavāda*), since the very non-application of the general rule constitutes the function of the exception.

Thus, in the rule *mantredhaseti* (*mantredhasa*), which prescribes the elision (*lug*) of the suffix *sic*, the accentuation would be governed by the rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām*. This is because even when that [suffix] is elided by a marker containing *lu*, its accentuation is desired by means of the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). However, the inclusion of the marker *it* in the rule *mantredhaseti* as well as in the rule *āmaḥ* is for the purpose of including the general term *liṭ*. Consequently, there is an elision of both *cli* and *liṭ* as far as possible. The particle *ca* is for the sake of not obstructing that [inclusion]; otherwise, the mention of *liṭ* would not occur.

However, in the rule *cleḥ siC*, there is no fault even if *luṅ* is explicitly mentioned; for by the mere continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of *luṅ*, there is no over-extension (*anatiprasaṅga*) to the *liṅ* and *liṭ* [tenses], since it is impossible for those two to follow *luṅ*. Furthermore, this is resolved by the *tadanubandhakagrahaṇaparibhāṣā* (the metarule concerning the inclusion of that which possesses such an indicatory letter).

On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya [states]: according to the alternative arrangement, there would be three mentions of *cli*—namely, in *acliluṅi*, *cleḥ sic*, and *ler*. Since this depends on those, even though there is a mention of all three (*caṅ*, *aṅ*, and *sic*) in the rule *ghasetaḥ* (P. 2.4.37), there is no lack of brevity; for one could simply state *sijluṅoḥ*. Nor should it be argued that, according to the alternative arrangement, in the rule *gātisthā...* (P. 2.4.77), one should read *ler* alone, discarding *sicaḥ*; and that since *ler* would then carry over from that very rule into the rule *ghasetaḥ*, there is no loss of brevity by abandoning *ler* there. This is because [the former argument fails].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the form] *agheṭat*. Furthermore, in the rule *vibhāṣā ghrā-dheṭ-śāc-chā-sā-hnā-vy-ā-yā-vā-pā-ghrā-dhmā-sthā-mnā-dāṇ-dṛśy-arti-sarti-śada-sado vā* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), because the term *liṭ* is understood as a governing word (*anuvṛtti*), once the substitutes for *liṭ* have been applied, the status of being a "substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*) would cause it to be included by the mention of *liṭ*; consequently, when the elision (*luk*) occurs, the reduplication conditioned by *caṅ* would apply, leading to the undesirable result that *adadhāt* could also occur. Only the three forms *adadhat*, *adhāt*, and *adhāsīt* are desired.

Nor should it be argued that because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elision of the *caṅ* suffix, the rule *āto lopaḥ* applies, resulting in the form *adadhat* alone; for the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies to what is elided by *luK*, and furthermore, due to the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of rules based on a suffix) by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, the elision of the vowel *ā* is difficult to achieve. If you say that when there is *luK* of the *caṅ* suffix, there is no reduplication because of the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, even so, since the form *adhāt* would result in the plural, the fourfold set of forms remains unavoidable.

When there is an option regarding the elision of *s* after *caṅ*, only the three forms *adadhuḥ*, *adhuḥ*, and *adhāsiṣuḥ* are desired. It should not be argued that, by relying on the injunctive force of *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110)—which is otherwise intended as a restrictive rule—the form would be *adadhuḥ* even when *caṅ* is elided due to the application of *jus*. This is because, in that case, the elision of *caṅ* would preclude the substitution of *jus* since the mention of *s* (in the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*) continues to apply. Furthermore, if the continuation of *s* were not admitted, then *jus* would undesirably apply even in *abhūvan* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle.

Now, if it is argued that *luk* will be prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to *sic*, so that *luk* occurs for *liṭ* itself before the substitutes have been applied—thereby ensuring that *jus* does not occur in *abhūvan* by the rule *ātaḥ*, and that forms such as *adhur* and *adurayuḥ* are established as being due to a previously non-existent rule (*apūrvavidhi*)—it is not so.

For in the case of *mā hi dātām*, the accentuation would be untenable according to the rule *sico'nyatarasyām*. Furthermore, if one were to adopt the formulation *leranyatarasyām*, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to *caṅ* and other affixes.

Therefore, one must necessarily state that the elision (*luk*) occurs immediately after the substitution of *cl* for *liṭ*, in accordance with the requirements of the accent (*svarānurodhena*). Consequently, since the recurrence of the term *sij* in the rule *ātaḥ* is required to prevent the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) seen in forms such as *abhūvan*, and because the substitute *jus* would be impossible under the alternative view of the elision of *caṅ*, the fourth form *adhān* would be unavoidable. Thus, in accordance with that requirement, the mention of *sij* itself should be made in the rule *gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*.

And thus, in the rule *mantre ghasah*, the word *liṭ* must necessarily be included; consequently, the three occurrences of the mention of *cli* are unavoidable. Furthermore, since the inclusion of *caṅ*, *aṅ*, and *sic* in that rule results in greater complexity than the *nyāsa* (alternative) view, it is more appropriate to formulate the rule for *cli* in accordance with that [simpler] position.

As for what was said—that "in the rule prescribing *kṣ*, the mention of 'without *iṭ*' (*aniṭ*) is for the purpose of indicating the *cli* affix"—that too is incorrect. For in that context, it is the root itself that must be qualified by the term "without *iṭ*" (*aniṭ*). It should not be argued that because *iṭ* is a part of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the designation "without *iṭ*" (*aniṭ*) applies only to that [suffix] due to its absence, and not to the root; for a negation is preceded by the possibility of its counter-positive. Nor should it be argued that the basis for that designation is simply a specific absolute non-existence determined by convention.

The genitive *ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvrīhi* compound is justified because there exists a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) between the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the augment *iṭ*; for in the present context, the relationship of part and whole (*avayava-avayavi-bhāva*) cannot serve as the delimiting relation (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha*). Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyartha*), owing to the force of the qualifier.

Now, even so, if the meaning were "not taking the augment *iṭ* before any *ārdhadhātuka* suffix," then *ksa* would not apply to roots such as *guh* and others, because they optionally take *iṭ* due to being marked with *ū*. On the other hand, if the meaning were "not taking *iṭ* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes," then *ksa* would necessarily apply even to *guh* and others. Nor is this a desired consequence, for it is intended that there be an option regarding them. Furthermore, since many roots ending in *śal* and having *ik* as their penultimate vowel—such as *iṣ*, *riṣ*, *śriṣ*, *pruṣ*, and others—which optionally take *iṭ* before *ktvā*, do not take *iṭ* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes, *ksa* would undesirably apply to them as well.

If [the rule] were intended to mean "in the case of a root that is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) in the *liṭ* [perfect]," then [the suffix *ksa*] would never apply at all. For even roots such as *guh*, which end in *śal* and have *ik* as their penultimate vowel (*igupadha*), are *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*) in that context due to the restrictive rule of the *krādi* group. Nor can it be argued that one must rely on the *aniṭ* status [of the root] in relation to the *kṣa* suffix, because the meaning is "that which is *aniṭ* when the *kṣa* suffix follows. This is not so, because the explanation is: "it is *aniṭ* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *bal*. This is because there is a distinction between roots like *guh* for which the *iṭ* is optional, depending on whether the *iṭ* is absent or present. Thus, the desired result is achieved: the suffix *sic* applies after those [roots] characterized by the presence of *iṭ*, while the suffix *kṣa* applies after those devoid of it.

As for what was also said—"or [the substitution of] *ghaslṛ* occurs"—that too is incorrect. For it is explained that the rules pertaining to *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes apply generally by resorting to a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). They say that the substitution of *ghaslṛ* proceeds by resorting to the general property of being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix inherent in the *aṅ* augment.

[Objection: But if *cli* is thus rejected, then in the case of the elision of *sic* by the rule "in a mantra, [there is elision] of *ghas*" (Pāṇini 6.4.101), the acute accent on the initial syllable prescribed by the rule "the initial of *sic*" (Pāṇini 6.1.187) would occur.

Regarding this, they say: in Vedic (chandas), there are instances where the augment *aṭ* or *āṭ* should be acute, and instances where it should be unaccented (*nihata*). However, in cases where *aṭ* or *āṭ* exists and the prohibition of the accent on the finite verb (*tiṅ-nighāta*) applies while the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) is desired, such [a distinction] does not exist in the Veda. This is understood from the fact that the author of the Bhāṣya rejected (*pratyākhyāna*) the rule for the suffix *cli*. As for examples such as *mā hi lāvīḥ*, since the suffix *sic* itself is marked with the indicatory letter *c* (*cit*), its own accent will override the unaccented nature of the augment (*āgama-anudāttatva*), which serves no other purpose; therefore, the suffix *cli* need not be introduced for the sake of attaching an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). *cleḥ sic* || 44 ||

The *cli* [affix] shall be replaced by *sij*. However, its status as a *cit* marker is not for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the rule "vṛddhi occurs before *su*" (P. 7.3.109) does not over-apply to forms such as *agniḥ* or *vāyuḥ*, because these belong to the *parasmaipada*. Since they are mentioned separately, there is no possibility of suspecting a conjunction (*samuccaya*) through the determination of the relationship between the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*). Nor is it for the sake of accent (*svara*), because it does not consist of vowels (*anactkatvāt*). And it cannot be argued that in forms like *mā hi kārṣṭām*, the *cit* marker serves to provide an acute accent (*udātta*) to the root via the principle of "that which has a *cit* marker is treated like its original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Because of the optional application of the acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule *ādi-sico 'nyatarasyām*, [the suffix] does not fall within the scope of the *cit* accent. Nor is the purpose of [marking] that [suffix] as *cit* for the sake of making the augment *iṭ* acute; for that is already established by the accent of the affix (*pratyaya-svara*). Nevertheless, since the rule "augments are unaccented" (*āgamā anudāttāḥ*) would apply, the purpose of the rule prescribing the acute accent is to override that.
