[Objection: But surely the status of being *cit* is established through the principle of "acting like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*); thus it has been said: "The marking of *sic* as *cit* is useless because of *sthānivadbhāva*. If this is argued:

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "The purposeful inclusion of the marker *c* [in the rule for the suffix *iṭ*] establishes that *iṭ* is acute by virtue of its own capacity. This is the meaning: the acuteness of *iṭ* is not established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original). According to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, the lack of acuteness (*anudāttatva*) of an augment (*āgama*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of a suffix; therefore, it would follow that even the acuteness obtained through *sthānivadbhāva* would be set aside, resulting in the undesired consequence of *iṭ* being unaccented. However, by the force of the inclusion of the marker *c*, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) prevails.

On this point, some [object]: there are two exceptions to the accentuation of a suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The fact that an augument is unaccented (*anudātta*)—as indicated in the rule *yāsuṭ*—and the accent of a *cit* element which occupies the same position as that [augument], namely the sixty-first [rule], are both exceptions. Since these two exceptions are in conflict, the accent of the *cit* element alone will prevail. Therefore, the *cit* designation for the suffix *sic* is redundant.

On this point, Kaiyaṭa says: The unaccented nature of the augment (*āgama*) and the *cit*-accent are not exceptions to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). This is because there is no application of that [suffix-accent] to bases, augments such as *ānu* and others, or to *cit*-marked elements like *kuṇḍina*, since they do not fall under the category of suffixes. Furthermore, the rule "as if it were the original" (*sthānivat*) is an extension of the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*), not an extension of the form (*rūpātideśa*). Moreover, the *cit*-accent does not possess priority [over other rules]. Since the unaccented nature of the augment applies without distinction, it should be understood as subverting all other accents. Therefore, it is established that the *cit* designation of the *sic* suffix is for the purpose of overriding those [other accents].

The designation *idit* (having the marker *it*) is not, however, for the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal (*na*-lopa) in forms such as *ahasta*, because it has already been made known that the elision of the nasal does not occur after a stem ending in *sic* by virtue of the rule prescribing the *kit* status of *sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14). Otherwise, since the prohibition of nasal elision would follow simply from its being *idit*, the prescription of *kit* status would be useless for the purpose of preventing the elision of the letter *n*.

Objection: Is it not the case that this [rule] is intended so that the elision (*lopa*) occurs precisely by taking the *sic* as the cause, and not by taking as the cause that *sārvadhātuka* suffix which follows it? For if that were so, then by the rule *ato lopaḥ*, the elision of the vowel *a* would occur by depending on the *sic*. And if the vowel *a* were elided by depending on the *sic*, then because they share the same basis (*samānāśrayatva*), the elision of the vowel *a* would be "as if unestablished" (*asiddhavad atrābhāt*) according to the rule *asiddhavad atrābhāt*; thus, the rule *ato lopaḥ* would not apply. [Response: No, that is not so.

Because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)—which pertains to the external suffixes of the *sārvadhātuka*—is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*), its non-application is secured by the rule "that which is external is as if unestablished with respect to that which is internal" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*). Furthermore, because the elision is prescribed for that which ends in *a* at the time of the instruction of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes; otherwise, there would be no resolution in cases such as *hataḥ*. As they say: "For those [roots] where an element is elided, there is no elision of the *at* (the *a* of the root). Therefore, the inclusion of the *it* marker is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*); thus, the status of being *it* is redundant.

It should be stated that the suffix *sic* is applied after the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp*. This rule is intended to provide an optional application of *sic* for three of these roots—where *ksa* would otherwise apply—and for two others—where *aṅ* would apply due to their inclusion in the *puṣādi* group. Examples: *aspṛkṣat* / *asprākṣīt* (from *spṛś*) *amṛkṣat* / *amrākṣīt* (from *mṛś*) *akṛkṣat* / *akrākṣīt* (from *kṛṣ*) *atṛpat* / *ātraptsīt* (from *tṛp*) *adrāpsīt* (from *dṛp*)

Furthermore, because the inclusion of the letter *c* in the term *cli* has been rejected and because there is no purpose for it, the substitute *li* is not prescribed; rather, *cli* itself is prescribed in the absence of the *it*-designation for the letter *k*. Consequently, due to the status of being *clādi*, the augment *am* applies by the rule "of an unaccented [root] ending in a single consonant preceded by *u*" (*anudāttasya cardupadhasya*). Since the cause for the substitution of *ksa* would otherwise be absent, *sic* is applied. In the alternative where *am* is not present, the desired form *ksa* is established. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the suffixes beginning with *sic* would apply to the final letter, resulting in the audible *k*; for since *sic* begins with *y*, it is multi-consonantal (*anekāl*) and can therefore be a substitute for the whole. Moreover, the elision occurs by the rule "there is elision of *y* and *v*" (*yasya ca lopo vyor*), and thus the rule "of the first of the following" (*ādeḥ parasya*) does not apply.

Moreover, even so, there is no impossibility of *caṅ* and *aṅ* being substitutes for the whole [stem], because those two—*caṅ* and *aṅ*—are also explained as having multiple phonemes (*anekāl*). In the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* as well, the letter *c* does not have the designation *it*, and thus its status as a substitute for the whole is established. For if it were merely a final part (*antāvayava*), it would not receive the designation of an affix (*pratyaya*); consequently, it would not have the designation *it*, and thus there would be no elision (*lopa*). This is clear from the rule *luṭaḥ prathamasya*.

Because there is no requirement for the mention of a verbal root (*dhātu*) here, the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54) finds no scope of application. However, in cases such as *dīpajana-*, even though the scope of that rule would otherwise apply, it must be explained that the *ciṇ* affix is prescribed after the *cli* augment following roots like *dīp*. If it is argued that this *vārttika* is therefore redundant, we say: No.

Because the *it*-designation for the letter *c* [in the rule *cakṣiṅ vyaktāyāṃ vāci*] has not been explicitly stated as having the purpose of preventing the application of the general [rule], and because the letter *l* lacks the quality of being a *jhal*, there would be no insertion of the augment *am*; consequently, only the suffix *ksa* would apply. Thus, the *vārttika* is necessary for the sake of the suffix *sic*. Accordingly, when *ksa* is applied, one obtains *aspṛkṣat*; when *sic* is applied with the optional *am* augment, one obtains *aspṛkṣīt*; and in the absence of that [augment], with the [regular] *vṛddhi* increase, one obtains *aspārkṣīt*. In this way, the three forms are established.
The suffix *ksa* is applied after a verbal root beginning with *śal* that has a penultimate *i*, provided it does not take the augment *iṭ*.

Regarding the rule *śalanto ya igupadhas tasmād aniṭaś cleḥ ksādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.45): [the substitute] *ksa* is applied to the *cli* affix after a root ending in *ś*, having a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, which does not take *iṭ*. For example: *aghukṣat*. Objection: Since the *guṇa* substitution caused by the *cli* affix occurs first, the condition of having a penultimate *i* (*igupadhatvam*) never exists at that stage. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that the presence of the letter *k* in *ksa* is justified as a qualifier for the rule *pūrvaksasyācī* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), based on the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the *kit* designation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of eliding the *s* in forms like *vatsāḥ* as well. Moreover, both the reliance on a "formerly existing state" (*bhūtapūrvagati*) and the reliance on a "qualifier of what is prescribed" (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*) are well-established. Reply: Not so. The *guṇa* substitution takes place only after the *ksa* replacement has already occurred. This is because the *ksa* replacement is specifically prescribed for roots ending in *ś* and having a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*. Therefore, the condition of having a penultimate *i* remains intact even after the *guṇa* has been applied. As for the objection regarding the letter *k*, its purpose is indeed to serve as a qualifier for the rule *pūrvaksasyācī*, as in the case of *vatsāḥ*; however, this is established through the principle of "formerly existing state," which is widely accepted in grammar. Thus, there is no fault.

[The opponent argues: "It is well-established [that the term *s*] relies on a former state (*bhūtapūrvagati*) and relies on a specified qualifier (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). [The author replies: "Not so. If it relied on a former state, the *kittva* (the *k*-mark) would be redundant. Even if it were stated as *sasyāci*, since this very *s* possesses the status of an affix (*pratyayatva*) and is meaningful (*arthavattva*), its inclusion is possible. Furthermore, because the *uṇādi* derivatives are considered underived (*avyutpanna*), there is no fault in cases such as *vatsāḥ*. Moreover, since a form qualified by an *anubandha* has no other scope of application, the substitution of *aksā* must take effect precisely before the *guṇa*."

[Objection: But surely, since a *sic* suffix must necessarily follow [a root ending in a consonant], its own form—characterized by the absence of the augment *iṭ*—does not exist anywhere; thus, the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished. [Response: Not so. Because the *ksa* replacement has not yet applied prior to the *sic* suffix, thinking "this is the domain of *ksa*. For a general rule (*utsarga*) applies only after excluding the domain of an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, even for *ksa*, there is no application yet, because the qualification "after a root that does not take *iṭ*" (*aniṭ*) has not been determined. Therefore, since the *liṅ* suffix itself possesses the status of a *valādi* ārdhadhātuka, when there is the contingency of *iṭ*, the absence of *iṭ* (*anitva*) exists, and thus the *ksa* replacement occurs. However, in the absence of the prohibition of *iṭ*, only *sic* occurs, as in *akoṣīt*.
The root *śliṣ* is used in the sense of embracing. || 46 ||

In this context, "śliṣ" constitutes one rule (yoga). The substitute *ksa* shall take the place of the *cli* affix following the root *śliṣ*. This is intended to set aside the *aṅ* augment that would otherwise apply because [the root] belongs to the *puṣādi* class. Then, "in the sense of embracing" (*āliṅgane*) is another rule. Although the previous rule already established this, the present one is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*): the *vasu* suffix occurs only in the sense of embracing, and not merely when there is proximity. Example: *samāślikṣat kanyāṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta embraced the maiden"). Here, however, it does not apply: *samāśliṣaj jatu kāṣṭham* ("The lacquer adhered to the wood"). Furthermore, even in the case of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), *ksa* alone should apply, overriding *ciṇ*.

And therefore, it should not be argued that the rule "the girl was embraced by Devadatta" would not be established; for when considering the specific things to be sublated (*bādhyaviśeṣacintā*), there is no sublation of that [rule] according to the maxim: "Exceptions [applied] in the middle sublate preceding rules, not those following. However, when considering the general things to be sublated (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), it will be stated later that the mention of *ciṇ* is for the purpose that it should apply only as *ciṇ*, and that whatever else might otherwise apply, that should not occur.

[Objection: But surely, if *śliṣ* were not included among the roots beginning with *āṅ-yam*, then by the rule *śaligupadhā-kṣaḥ*, the suffix *kṣa* would apply [in the past passive participle]. Consequently, even though there is no difference between the suffixes *ātām* and *vas* regarding the elision of *kṣa* before a vowel (by the rule *ksasyāci*), the form *āśliṣṭhāḥ* would be impossible without the suffix *sic*, as in the example "they licked the lac with wood" (*samāślikṣata jatūni kāṣṭhaiḥ*). If you argue that this would lead to the undesired form *āślikṣataḥ*, we say: not so.

By the force of the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule), the suffix *kṣa* is also excluded by the restriction [of Pāṇini 1.2.19], *śala igupadhāt...*. For if the *kṣa* obtained by the rule *śliṣaḥ* were excluded by that very restriction, the [splitting of the rule] would be purposeless; for such a meaning is established even by a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) in the case of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, it is established that in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*), other than where *ciṇ* applies, there is only *sij*, and not *kṣa*.
[The rule] *na dṛśaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.48) [is explained as follows].
The suffix *kso* would not occur; rather, by the rule *iritovā*, the suffixes *aṅ* and *sic* are applied. Thus: *adarśat* or *adrākṣīt*.
The suffix *caṅ* is applied after the roots *ni*, *śri*, *dru*, and *su* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.

The *caṅ* substitute is prescribed for the *cli* suffix following roots ending in *ṇic*, as well as for the pure roots *śri* and others. [This triggers] reduplication and so forth, resulting in forms such as *acīkarat*. Examples include *aśiśriyat*, *adudruvat*, and *asusruvat*. Because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *uvaṅ* takes place; as it has been said: "Because that which ends in *śap* and *caṅ* is characterized by being an internal operation. Regarding the rule "there is an addition for the root *kam*": since the *ṇiṅ* affix is optionally prescribed before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, this statement is made because the *sic* suffix would otherwise apply in the absence of that option. However, in the case where *ṇiṅ* is applied, the form is established simply by virtue of the root ending in *ṇic*.

In that context, because it ends in a consonant (*vyantatvāt*), the rules for *san*-like behavior (*sanvadbhāva*) and lengthening (*dīrgha*) apply. Regarding *acīkamata*: although it should have been stated as "the *san*-like behavior occurs when there is a light syllable in the *caṅ*," the inclusion of the term *para* (following) by force of its presence indicates that the referent of the compound is the *ṇic* suffix. This is because no other [light syllable] is possible. The meaning is: when a *ṇic* follows a *caṅ*, whatever light syllable follows that [root], the operation of the *san* should take place upon the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in relation to that light syllable. However, in the alternative view where the *ṇiṅ* suffix is absent, the form is *acakamata*. "They go to heaven, desiring happiness, on well-yoked mares-drawn chariots; but those who speak of what they did not desire (*acīkamata*) go on foot."

The meaning of this is as follows: In response to the question "What is the form [of the verb] in the *luṅ* [aorist] tense? those by whom it was said "he desired" (*acakamata*) go to the celestial realm (*nāka*), which is the desired happiness, because they have remembered the aforementioned definition. However, those by whom it was said "he did not desire" (*acīkamata*) go only on foot. Kaiyaṭa states that even though the general definition has been remembered, this is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for the sake of remembering the specific definition, and thus serves to show respect for the recollection of the definition.

However, those who maintain that the form *akamiṣṭa* occurs [as a result of the suffix] are themselves referred to by the word *akamiṣṭa* through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Because the non-difference between the original object (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is intended to be expressed, no case ending is applied. Even while walking on level ground, they do not find ease because of their incorrect pronunciation. On the other hand, those who say *acīkamata* explain that even as foot soldiers, they proceed with ease.

An addition should be made [to the rule] regarding the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*): *acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayam eva* (the mat made itself), *udaśiśriyata kaṭaḥ svayam eva* (the mat raised itself). Since the status of being an agent exists even in the case of the agent who is also the object, and since there is no subverting factor, this is established by the sūtra itself. Nor is *ciṇ* the subverting factor there; for there is a prohibition [of *ciṇ*] by the rule: "In the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, an addition must be made for the causative suffix *ṇic*, and for the roots *śri*, *brū*, and *as*."

Surely, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*) even when there is no actual causal agent, as in "the cow raised its tail" (*udapupucchat gaur*). Thus, "the cow raises its tail" is expressed as *utpucchayate gauḥ*. However, when the cow is the object because the causative sense is internalized (*antarbhāvita-ṇyarthatva*), then one says *utpucchayate gām*; the meaning here is "one who possesses an activity conducive to the activity residing in the cow that is favorable toward raising the tail. If it is argued that, when one intends to express the cow itself as the agent due to an excess of ease (*saukaryātiśaya*), and when referring to the past tense (*bhūtakāla*), the *luṅ* suffix is used—[we reply: no.

This is because the prohibition is initiated solely with respect to the *ṇic* suffix, having set aside [the rule] due to its being based on a specific cause (*hetumat*). Thus, the followers of Bhāradvāja recite: "In the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there should be an addition [to the rule] for roots ending in *ṇi*, for *śranth*, *granth*, *brū*, and for those that are intransitive when in the *ātmanepada*.
49. *vibhāṣā dheṭ-śvyoḥ* (The augment *iṭ* is optional after the roots *dheṭ* and *śvi*).

After these two roots, the *cli* of the subsequent [tense] optionally becomes *caṅ*. [Examples: *adadhat*. In the case of the *sic* suffix, there is optionally elision (*luk*) by the rule "optionally after *ghrā*, *dhmā*, and *heḍ*" [Pāṇini 2.4.80]. [Examples: *adhāt*; *adhāsīt*. The root *ṭuośvi* (meaning "to move" and "to grow") [forms: *aśiśviyat*. Here, the *aṅ* augment is also optional. [Examples: *aśvat*; *aśvayīt*. The restriction "in the active voice" (*kartari*) applies here as well: *aśviṣātām gāvau vatsena* ("the two cows grew with the calf").
The suffix *gu* is applied after the root *gup* in the Vedic language.

Or there is the substitution of *caṅ*. [Examples are: *imān mā mitrāvaruṇā gṛhān ajūgupatam* (you two have protected these houses of mine), *agopiṣṭam*, or *agoṣāyiṣṭam*. However, in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*), the forms ending in *caṅ* are excluded.
[The suffix *na* is applied] after the roots *nī*, *dhā*, *el*, and *ard*. || 51 ||

The suffix *caṅ* is not used after the roots *ūn* (to diminish), *dhvan* (sound), *il* (to impel), and *ard* (to afflict or beg) in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). *Mā tvāyato jarituḥ kāmamūnayīḥ*: "Do not diminish the desire of the singer who seeks you. The meaning is: "Do not make the wish of the praising devotee who desires you deficient. *Mā tvāgnirdhvanayīddhūmagandhiḥ*: "May the smoke-scented fire not cause you to sound [be disturbed]. *Vāmamelayīt*: "He has impelled what is desirable. *Mainamardayīt*: "May it not afflict him. In the common language (*bhāṣā*), however, the forms are *auninat*, *ādidhvanat*, *elayit*, and *ārdidat*.
The suffix *aṅ* is applied after the roots *as*, *ti-vac*, and *khyāti*.

An exception to *sij* (the *aorist marker*). [The forms] *paryāsthata*, *avocat*, and *akhyata* are explained as follows: the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by the rule "after a prefix, the roots *das*, *ūh*, etc. [Pāṇini 1.3.20]. In *āsthata*, the *thuk* augment is applied by the rule "after the root *as*" [Pāṇini 6.4.70]. In *avocat*, the *um* augment is applied. In *akhyata*, the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule "elision of *ā*" [Pāṇini 6.4.64]. The inclusion of the root *as* [in the rule for *thuk*] is for the sake of the *ātmanepada* endings; for in the *parasmaipada*, the desired form is already established by its belonging to the *puṣādi* group [which takes *aṅ* in the aorist]. The placement of the *vṛt* marker (*vṛt*) in the middle [of the list] is for the purpose of indicating the end of the *radhādi* group, according to the established doctrine that the *puṣādi* roots extend up to the end of the *gaṇa*.

In this case as well, since no specific grammatical operation (kārya) pertaining to the object is prescribed by way of extension (atideśa), and there being no sublater (bādhaka), the operation belonging to its own locus (svāśraya) indeed proceeds toward the agent who is also the object. Thus, [the action] remains in the earrings themselves. Therefore, a supplementary rule (upasaṃkhyāna) need not be commenced.
And [the word] *lipiśīrṣa*. || 53 ||

After the roots *lip* (to smear), *sic* (to pour), and *vheñ* (in the sense of rivalry and sound), the substitute *aṅ* shall take the place of *cli*. [Examples: *alipat*, *asicat*, *ahvat*. In the last case (*vheñ*), there is elision of the final *ā*.
In the case of the ātmanepada endings, [the substitution] is optional.

After these [roots], *cleri* may optionally become *aṅ* in the Ātmanepada. Because the first two have a svarita accent and the last has the marker *ñ*, the Ātmanepada occurs when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. *alipata*, *asicata*, *ahvata*. In the alternative (*pakṣe*), *sic* is used: *alipta*, *asikta*. By the rule *jhalo jhali*, there is the elision of *sic*. *ahvāsta*.
[The rule] *puṣādidyutādyḷditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (3.1.55) [applies].

The suffix *aṅ* shall replace *cli* following a root that has the *śyan* affix, roots beginning with *puṣ*, roots beginning with *dyut*, and those marked with *ḷt*, when followed by a *parasmaipada* ending. The roots beginning with *puṣ* (in the sense of nourishing) from the *divādi* class up to *gṛdh* (in the sense of longing) are the *puṣādi* group. Example: *apuṣat*.

It might be argued: "Since the root *puṣ* (in the sense of nourishing) is listed in the *bhvādi*, *kryādi*, and *curādi* [classes], what is the reason for taking only those *puṣ*-roots belonging to the *divādi* class? This is true; however, because the *dyutādi* roots are mentioned separately, the *bhvādi* roots are not included. Furthermore, since they are read immediately after *puṣ* in the other classes, their inclusion is already established by their status as *puṣādi* roots. Moreover, even in the *kryādi* class, there are only four roots following *puṣ*, and their inclusion is justified simply by the fact that they are marked with the *lṛt* indicatory letter (*lṛdita*).

Nor is there any complexity in the non-assignment of multiple indicatory markers (*anubandhas*), because the three [roots] lack such markers. Furthermore, in the case of the root *grah*, the status of having a circumflex accent (*svaritettva*) is established even by the presence of the marker *ḷ*. Moreover, since the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed for roots beginning with *cur*, the suffix *cli* cannot follow immediately after it. Therefore, only the *puṣādi* group belonging to the *divādi* class is to be adopted.

If it is argued that the *puṣ* group and the *dyut* group should be recited as having the marker *ḷ* (i.e., as *ḷdita*), we say no; for the opposite would be the case regarding the redundancy of including the letter *ḷ* in so many roots. Nor should it be said that there is no redundancy because the letter *ḷ* is recited in place of the original indicatory markers (*anubandhas*); for in those lists, there exist markers such as *ādi*, *īdi*, and *ūdī*. Consequently, specific grammatical operations prescribed for those with *ñiṣvidā*, *midī*, *śamu*, *sūti*, *sūyati*, *dhūñ*, and others marked with *ūdi* could not be properly accomplished.

Beginning with *dyuta* (to shine) and ending with *kṛp* (to be able), the roots starting with *dyut* belong to the *bhvādi* class. From these *dyut*-roots, there is an option for the *parasmaipada* (active voice) in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; the distinction is that *aṅ* is used for the *parasmaipada*, while *sic* is used for the *ātmanepada*. Examples include: *adyutat* (he shone) and *adyotiṣṭa* (he shone); *aśvitat* (he was white) and *aśvetiṣṭa* (he was white), and so forth. As for those marked with *ḷ* (indicating an irregularity), such as *gamlṛ* (to go): *agamat* (he went); *ghaslṛ* (to eat): *aghavat* (he ate); *śaklṛ* (to be able): *aśakīt* (he was able), and so forth. [Pāṇini 1.3.90]: "And after the roots *sṛ* (to go), *śās* (to teach), and *ṛ* (to go)."

After these [roots], *cleri* (the imperfect suffix) takes the form *aṅ*. Because of its association with *śāsi*, which has its *śap* elided, only the roots *sarti* and *atyati* from the *juhoty-ādi* class are understood by the rule *ṛsṛgātām*. Examples: *asarat*, *aśiṣat*. By the rule *śāsaidaṅhaloḥ*, there is *itva* (substitution of *ī* for *ai*). By the rule *śāsivasighasīnām ca*, there is *ṣatva* (substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). Example: *ārat*.
According to *irito vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.57), the augment *iṭ* is optional after a root ending in *ṛ*.
The suffix *aṅ* optionally replaces *cli* following the root *ścyut* (meaning "to drip"). From *ścyut*, [we have] *aścyutat*; in the alternative case, *aścyotīt*.
And [the suffix *kan*] is applied after the roots *jṝ*, *stambhū*, *mru*, *luc*, *gruc*, *gluc*, *gluñc*, and *śvi*.

The root *jṝ* (meaning "to grow old") belongs to the *divādi* class; *stambh* is a *sautra* root; *mruca*, *mluca* (meaning "to go"); *gruca*, *gluca* (meaning "to steal"); *gluñca* (meaning "to go"); and *śvi* as previously mentioned—from these, *aṅ* is optionally substituted for *cl*. Examples: *ajarat* (from *jṝ*); here, by the rule *ṛdṛśo’ṅi*, there is *guṇa* substitution. *astabhat* (from *stambh*); because the affix is *kit*, there is elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) and an absence of *guṇa*. *amrūcat*, *amrocīt*, etc. (from *mruca*). In the case of *śvi* with *aṅ*, by the rule *śvayater aḥ*, the vowel *a* is substituted [for the *i*], resulting in the form *aśvat*.

In this context, either *gluci* or *gluñci* should not be accepted [as the root]. If *gluci* were accepted, there would be two forms for it: *nyaglucat* and *nyaglīcīt*; for *gluñci*, however, there would be two forms: *nyaglucat* and *nyagluñcīt*. But if *gluci* is accepted, there is the form *nyaglocīt*. Thus, by accepting either one, all three forms are established. Furthermore, there is no difference in meaning, because roots have multiple meanings; such is the Bhāṣya. And so, the assumption that there is no elision of *n* in *aglucat* by virtue of the force of accepting both roots is baseless.
(Pāṇini 6.1.59: *kṛmṛdṛruhibhyaśchandasi*).

Or there is the substitution of *cleraṅ*. Examples: *akarat*, *atho 'marat*, *adaradarthān*, *antarikṣād divam āruham*. Why "in Vedic" (*chandasi*)? [Because in non-Vedic usage we have] *akārṣīt* and so forth.
[The rule] *ciṇ te padaḥ* [is now applied].

The root *pad* means "to go. [In the rule] *ātmanepada*, the word *at* is to be understood as the singular suffix *ta*. When the suffix *ta* follows, the *sic* of the root *pad* is optionally replaced by *ciṇ*. By the rule *ciṇo luk*, there is the elision of the suffix *ta*. Thus, *pratyapādi*; the meaning is "he accepted" (*pratipannavān*). [The rule continues:
After the roots *dīp*, *jan*, *budh*, *pūr*, *tāy*, and *pyāy*, [the substitution of *ciṇ* for *sij* occurs] optionally. (Pāṇini 3.1.61)

*dīp* [is used] in the sense of shining; *janī* in the sense of manifestation; *budha* in the sense of understanding, belonging to the *divādi* class. Because of its association with the preceding and following roots which are invariably *ātmanepada*, the root *budh* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class—meaning "to wake"—is not included here. Nevertheless, it does indeed occur when it is transitive, as seen in examples such as *kramādamuṃ nārada ity abodhi saḥ*. *Pūrī* is in the sense of filling; *tāyṛ* in the senses of continuity and protection; *opyāyī* in the sense of increasing. When the suffix *ta* follows in the singular number, *ciṇ* optionally replaces *cl* after these roots; in the alternative case, *sic* is used. Examples: *adīpi* (it shone) or *adīpiṣṭa* (it shone).
In *ajani* (from the root *jan*), there is no *vṛddhi* substitution because it is as if the suffix were *jhi*. [Examples include: *ajanista*, *abodhi*, *abuddha*, and so forth.
[The affix] *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) and the passive (*karman*). (Pāṇini 3.1.61)

The affix *ciṇ* is substituted for *cli* when it follows a verbal root expressing either a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*). Examples: *aśāpi devadattena* (it was caused to be eaten by Devadatta); *apāci taṇḍulaścaitreṇa* (the rice was caused to be cooked by Caitra). The repetition of the word *ciṇ* is for the purpose of making the rule obligatory; or rather, it is so that whatever else might otherwise apply [by default] shall not take effect.
When a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows, the affix *yak* is applied.

The phrase "in the sense of the state [of being] (bhāva) and the object (karman)" is understood to carry over. *sthīyate caitreṇa* ("it is stayed by Caitra"); *pacyate taṇḍulas tena* ("the rice is cooked by him"). The suffix *lakāra* is prescribed by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*. Here, in the sense of the state (*bhāva*), there is only the singular number; however, in the sense of the object (*karman*), there are three numbers according to that [object]. This is the distinction. Now, because action, having the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is conveyed by the verbal root as devoid of any internal differentiation, it has been said:
"In the verb (*ākhyāta*), every action is expressed as entirely devoid of differentiation."
The conceptualization of distinctions among things that cannot be distinguished by scripture.

And thus, even in the case of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) expressing the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), the dual and plural numbers occur due to the difference in the number of the means (*sādhana*). Likewise, those [numbers] should also occur in the case of the verbal suffix expressing the abstract action (*bhāva*). If it is argued that in that case [the *bhāva*], the dual and so on do not occur because they express the number residing in the agent or object which are the meanings of the suffix, whereas here [in the *bhāva*], it is not so because the means—the agent and so forth—is not expressed by the *tiṅ*-ending; [we reply: this is not correct, because then the dual and so on would also fail to occur in cases such as *pākaḥ* (cooking) and *pākau* (two cookings), since the non-expression of the agent and so forth is equal in both instances. To this we say: not so.

It has been stated previously that *śakti* (capacity) is the *kāraka*. And the substance (*dravya*) which is its substratum is manifold. It should not be argued that in an expression such as *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"), since the capacity itself is denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) expressing the object (*karman*), there would be an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the rice and so forth, which are its substrata. This is because such coreferentiality is possible through the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of the identity between the capacity and its possessor. This being the case, although even the number one is unfit for connection with an action (*bhāva*)—since it is not a substantial entity (*asatvabhūta*)—nevertheless, the singular number is used by taking "oneness" in the sense of the absence of difference.

Alternatively, in the formulation "the singular [is used] for one" and "the dual and plural [are used] for two and many," the justification for the singular number lies simply in the absence of duality and plurality. However, since action (*bhāva*) in its form as a substance (*sattva*) is denoted by suffixes such as *ghañ*, the distinction in number is based on the distinction in the substance and the distinction in its number—just as there is a distinction in the cooking based on the difference in the substrates, such as molasses, sesame, or boiled rice.

Nor does the *bhāva* (action/state) expressed by a verbal suffix possess a difference of substratum; thus, there is no contingency of a change in verbal expression, since such variation is accepted in certain cases. For example: *uṣṭrāsikā āsyante* ("the camel-sitting postures are being sat") and *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante* ("the dead-man-lying postures are being lain"). Indeed, the acts of sitting and lying are distinct when they are endowed with various modes based on the difference of substrata such as camels and so forth. For the sitting postures of camels are inherently diverse, and the dead lie in many ways—face up, face down, with hair disheveled, and unclothed.

And thus, the meaning is that Devadatta and others perform actions such as mounting and lying down in exactly the same manner as those performed by camels and horses; for that meaning is understood even without the word *iva*. However, in the expression "you are being sat upon" (*bhavadbhir āsyate*), although there is a distinction between the states (the act of sitting), it is not intended to be expressed because there is no purpose for it—the distinction between the states is understood solely from the distinction between their substrata (*āśraya*). This is like [the expression] "a redness arose among the *palāśa* leaves. Furthermore, the cognition of a distinction between the dependent [action] based on a distinction between its substrata does not occur in all cases;
for in examples such as "he cooks the pots," one understands the act of cooking itself as being non-distinct.

In reality, by virtue of the authority of the Bhāṣya, the plural number here alone is correct. Some, however, say that this *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), because the state (*bhāva*) consisting of the "camel-sitting" (*uṣṭrāsikā*) functions as the object, just as in the expression "the milking of cows is desired" (*godohaḥ sūyate*). Others, however, maintain that *uṣṭrāsikāḥ* is a feminine plural accusative; since it is a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), and because the perception of femininity and plurality precludes the application of neuter gender and singularity. Thus, the meaning is: "seats similar to those [camel-sittings] are being made. Nor does this contradict the statement that [the action] is not a substance (*asattva*); for the intent is merely the absence of connection with gender, action, substratum, or case-role (*kāraka*).

That is questionable: does the plurality in the expression *uṣṭrāsikāḥ* arise from the plurality of what is denoted by the verbal root, or does the plurality arise from that [plurality] in the sense of "they sit" (*āsante*)? It cannot be the first, because there is no evidence for it; for there is no difference in cognition regarding the aspect of not apprehending number between the cases of *āsate* ("they sit") and *tiṣṭhanti* ("they stand"). Furthermore, according to your view, the accusative case would apply to a modifier of the action due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Yet, in this instance, the term *uṣṭrāsikāḥ* does not connect with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), namely "sitting," through identity, because that would contradict the meaning of the word as "such other types of sitting."

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because there is a lack of evidence; for it is possible for that which ends in a plural suffix to be construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), since there is no contradiction in the number [of the plurality] being present in the meaning of the root. Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of "The moon is the face," the construction with the meaning of the root occurs through non-difference (*abheda*) alone—as in "the seats of the camel-riders" (*uṣṭrāsikānām*)—and that the statement "they are similar" is merely an expression of the resultant meaning. For in that case, there is the presence of the presentation (*upasthiti*) of both [referents] as delimited by distinct properties, and because the cognition "the seats are non-different from the camel-riders" is free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*).

This is because, in a case of non-difference (abhedānvaya), the requirement is that the presentation [of the objects] be delimited by distinct properties; for we do not accept a verbal cognition such as "the one with a red staff" (raktadaṇḍavān) as being identical to "the one with a staff" (daṇḍavān), since the former does not apprehend an additional property within the aspect that delimits the qualificand (viśeṣyatāvacchedaka).

Thus, Kaiyaṭa’s intention is precisely that the connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) for *uṣṭrāsikāḥ* occurs through the relation of similarity (*sādṛśya*). In that case, the fact that [the word] ends in the accusative case is simply irrelevant. Therefore, the employment of the verbal root in the form *āsyante* is for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) alone, as in examples such as *dadhnā juhoti*. There is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *uṣṭra* in the sense of something similar to its sitting; its connection with the "sittings" (*āsikā*) occurs by way of identity (*abheda*). This has the same meaning as the expression *uṣṭrāsikāḥ kriyante*.

However, plurality (*bahutva*) is construed with that which has attained the nature of a substance (*sattva*), as presented by the suffix *ṇvul*. Nor does this lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) elsewhere, because the postulation of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth is made solely in accordance with the usage of authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*). Otherwise, such [an application] would result even in other modes [of expression].

Therefore, there is a distinction between the action expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and that expressed by a primary suffix (*kṛt*); for instance, in the case of *pākāḥ*, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the *kṛt*-derived forms, but not of the verbal forms. This is because a single verbal form cannot convey actions occurring at multiple times, since verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) that denote different times cannot coexist simultaneously within a single utterance. Furthermore, an action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix manifests like a substance (*dravya*), owing to its connection with gender, number, and grammatical relations (*kāraka*).

Although the nature of being a substance (*dravyatva*), which consists in being eligible for reference by a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), is equal in both cases, nevertheless, the relationship of example and exemplified (*dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika-bhāva*) exists due to their respective familiarity and unfamiliarity. Here, the connection with number (*saṃkhyā-yogitva*) has arrived incidentally (*saṃpātāyāta*), because it has already been established by the preceding sentence alone.

For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states: "A substance attains the status of a means (*sādhana*) in the accomplishment of an action; and likewise, when it is denoted by a *kṛt*-suffix, as in 'the cooking is occurring' (*pāko vartate*), it does not [itself] possess action. Here, only the connection with a *kāraka* (participant in action) is illustrated. Thus, the interpretation of the meaning as "producing a cognition whose qualificandum is a substance" is appropriate. This is because a substance is capable of connecting with a *kāraka*, and because a cognition having that [substance] as its qualificandum is evident in cases such as *pākaḥ*; furthermore, the cooking (*pāka*) presented by that [term] is capable of connecting with a *kāraka*.

Nor should it be argued that this meaning is possible when the suffix is a *kṛt*-suffix, but not when it denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*); for even there, the status of being a generator (*janakatva*) by way of being an object (*viṣayatayā*) is possible. Even if the object itself is not a cause in verbal cognition (*śābda*), the status of being a generator—in the form of being the object of the presentation (*upasthiti*) which is the cause of the verbal cognition—is possible. Therefore, the objection that [this view] is groundless and contrary to the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) is to be disregarded, as it stems from a failure to grasp the intended meaning.

It should not be argued that in expressions such as *odanasya pākaḥ* ("the cooking of rice"), there would be the fault of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and others being unable to connect [with the action], because factors of action (*kāraka*) can only connect with an action. For in forms like *pākaḥ*, the action is denoted by the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) portion as something non-existent (*asat*), and by the suffix (*pratyaya*) portion as something existent (*sat*). As Haribhadra has stated:

"In a verbal form (*ākhyāta*), the status of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is distributed between the two parts according to the grammatical treatise; the same sequence applies even in the case of [nominal stems ending in] *ghañ* and other suffixes."
"In that context, action as something to be accomplished is based on the form of the verbal root;
however, its state as a substantive entity is based on suffixes such as *ghañ*."

Therefore, when [the word *stoka*] functions as a qualifier of the *kṛdanta* (the nominalized form), we have "stokaḥ pākaḥ" (a small cooking); but when it functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the accepted usage is "stokaṃ pākaḥ" (a small cooking). Here, this should be noted: the intention is not to convey two distinct actions by means of the two words; rather, sometimes the purport lies solely in the verbal root regarding the act of cooking, and sometimes in the entire complex. As for the fact that in the *Rūpa-prantha*, the author of the *Dīdhiti* refuted the view that the complex ending in *ghañ* denotes a thing qualified by the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or disjunction (*vibhāga*), and instead established that words such as *saṃyoga* are merely technical designations (*naimittika-saṃjñā*), the logicians (*tārkikāḥ*) maintain that this was merely a display of rhetorical boldness (*prauḍhimātra*).

In the verse from the *Kusumāñjali*, "yattvamṛtarasaprasyandamādhvīkabhūḥ," [Udayana] explains that "the essence of nectar" (*amṛtasya rasaḥ*) means "the nectar being tasted" (*rasyamānamamṛtam*). He then cites the rule *kṛdabhihito bhāvo dravyavat* (Pāṇini 1.2.56). The underlying intention here is as follows: the suffix in *rasaḥ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve kṛt*). In the phrase *amṛtasya*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*). To resolve the doubt—namely, how a grammatical relation (*kāraka*) can be construed with something expressed by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) since such a suffix denotes an action that has attained the status of a substance (*sattvarūpatva*)—he invokes the rule *kṛdabhihita...* and so forth. The core point is that the construction occurs with the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

Alternatively, regarding the objection that if [the word *amṛtam*] signifies only the state (*bhāva*), then since a state is not a substantial entity (*asattvabhūta*), how can case-endings (*sub*) and so forth arise there—the rule "when expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix" (*kṛdabhihita*) and others serves as its support. However, it should be noted that the resolution of the aforementioned objection remains exactly as previously stated. Thus, the cognition is "the tasting whose object is nectar" (*amṛtakarmakaṃ rasanam*). In this regard, the term "flowing" (*prasrāva*) is employed for the sake of connecting with the meaning of the word; "being tasted" (*rasyamāna*) is used for the purpose of establishing the predominance of the nectar.

By this, the fallacious objection—that because of the contradiction with the commentary stating "the nectar being tasted," the suffix *kṛt* in *rasana* cannot have the sense of the action (*bhāvārtha*)—is refuted; for the sentence in question is intended as an explanation of two words and does not intend to convey the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix alone. By this same reasoning, the commentator's statement—"for [it provides] appropriate instruction"—in accordance with the principle stated in the verse of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, "suitable for instruction through its similarity to a beloved woman" (*kāntāsammitatayopadeśayuje*), is also explained. Let this suffice.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Now, it might be argued that even one action can indeed function as a *kāraka* (participant in an action) with respect to another action, as seen in such examples as *pacati bhavati* ("he is cooking") and *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("see, the deer is running"). Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa says that what is intended [by the definition] is that [an action] does not enter into a relation [with another action] by way of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) or any other *kāraka*. However, this is merely a concessive argument (*abhyupagamyavāda*), because the status of agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) is admitted to be manifested only through the relation of inherence (*saṃsarga*). Furthermore, the phrase "absence of *kārakatva*" is intended to mean the absence of being the base (*prakṛti*) for a *kāraka*-case ending.

Nor should it be asked how the action that is the object of accomplishment (*sādhyakriyā*) can simultaneously possess the status of both agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*); for due to a difference in perspective (*viṣayabheda*), it is possible for a single entity to stand in the relationship of both the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*). As Harivṛṣabha (Bhartṛhari) has said:
"In that regard, the action is [regarded as] unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that [entity] toward which it is the goal (*sādhya*);
but it is established (*siddhā*) with respect to that very same entity toward which it is [then regarded as] the goal."
"Just as one says, 'The deer runs, look!'"— in this way, the relationship between the object to be established and the means of establishment is established through the distinction of objects.

Thus [ends the citation]. The meaning of this is as follows: the collection of actions (*kriyā-samūha*) does not possess the status of being the object (*karman*) of perception, because the parts (*avayava*) are sequential and thus cannot be apprehended by ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*). Rather, it is only those parts that are already established (*siddha*) which [are so apprehended]. Consequently, while the state of being an "accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) is present in the aggregate for the purpose of connecting with the factors of action (*kāraka*), the state of being "established" (*siddhatva*)—which is useful for perception—is also present in the individual parts. This is because the agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) of the "being" (*bhāva*) denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) are contradictory; for its agency depends solely upon the action of "becoming" (*bhavati*).

Since every entity exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), agency (*kartṛtva*) is logically established in the act of existing (*bhavane*). This is because agency is observed everywhere in that which is being produced and is as yet unestablished; thus, even when its status as an object (*sādhyatva*) is present, the connection with agency in the act of existing is appropriate. Furthermore, since the action is predominant even with respect to the result in the form of the object, it possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) as well. However, instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and the other kārakas do not apply here, because they are absolutely incompatible with predominance, as they cannot exist without the subordinate nature of all their aspects.

As for the claim that in the theory of "supplying meaning from context" (arthādhyāhāra), agency and so forth are merely modes [of the action], that is not correct. For it would follow that even sentences such as "he sees the jar" (ghaṭaṃ paśyati) would be grammatically correct [without a verb]. This is because the power of a *kāraka* cannot be extracted and expressed by a word other than its case-ending (*vibhakti*). Furthermore, the meaning belonging to the base alone or the suffix alone cannot be obtained even through the supplying of meaning from context, since in cases such as "the door" (dvāram), what is observed is precisely a meaning qualified by [an action] such as closing.

This also should be noted: "pacati bhavati" (he cooks, he exists) is not a single sentence, just as "pacati vrajati" (he cooks, he goes) is not. This is because, according to the Grammarians (*śābdika*), action (*kriyā*) is the primary element in the meaning of a sentence; furthermore, the act of cooking cannot logically be construed with "goes. Even in the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*), in a cognition where the meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyātārtha*)—namely, effort (*kṛti*)—is the qualifier, the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a word ending in the nominative case; since that [effort] cannot be construed with "going," [the two verbs do not form a single sentence].

Observe that even in the case of "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" (see, the deer runs), the connection of the running performed by the deer as the object of the act of seeing is indeed appropriate; thus, the resulting cognition has the act of seeing as its objective domain. For the Naiyāyikas, however, "mṛgo dhāvati" (the deer runs) is a distinct sentence. In the word "paśya," the meaning of the entire sentence serves as the object, and consequently, there is no accusative case-ending following it, because a sentence lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). By this, the objection that one should instead say "dhāvati mṛgaṃ paśya" (see the running deer) is refuted, because an action (*bhāvanā*) cannot logically enter into a relation with what is presented by a word ending in the accusative case.

Furthermore, if the qualified deer (*mṛga*) were the object (*karman*), then expressions such as "see the running deer" (*dhāvantaṃ mṛgaṃ paśya*) would be impossible, because the use of the present participles *śatṛ* and *śānac* would be unavoidable. As for the argument that even if the qualified entity is the object, since it is not distinct from its parts, the status of being an object must belong to both the qualifier and the qualified—this is incorrect. For the meaning of the word "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) is precisely the objective state (*viṣayatā*) residing in both [the qualifier and the qualified] by way of the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*). Otherwise, since each part is already well-known, there would be the undesirable consequence that instances where a qualified entity is not established would be rare. Thus, because individuality (*pratyekatva*) is the locus of the pervasion of objecthood, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not apply to it; moreover, such [objecthood] is impossible in the case of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*).
And since that which is qualified lacks the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is no fault.

By this, the following is refuted: "It should not be said that the nominative case is merely based on a formal rule (*vācanika*); for such a statement does not exist in Pāṇini’s grammar; rather, it is inferred from the experience of a cognition whose primary object is the action (*kriyāviśeṣyaka*). This is because the rule "the nominative is used for the mere meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātre prathamā*) indeed exists. Otherwise, even in the view where the action is the primary object, one would not escape the difficulty. By this, the sentence "The deer is seen running" (*darśanaṃ mṛgo dhāvati*) is also refuted, as it has never been cited by any authoritative scholar (*abhiyukta*).

By this, the objection that there would be no distinction between the two sentences "The deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*) and "See that [deer]" (*taṃ paśya*) is refuted; for the distinction is clear: in the one case it is the running of the deer, and in the other it is the deer itself as the object (*karman*). Furthermore, in the former sentence, the property of being a deer (*mṛgatva*) appears as the delimiting factor of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*), and even in the sentence "See that deer which is running," the deer qualified by the action of running is indeed the object.

For this very reason, although it is necessary for the sentence "The deer runs, look at it" to be a cause of cognition, the sentence "Look, the deer runs" does not possess the status of being such a cause, because of its complexity (*gaurava*). As for the claim that the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) or complexity (*gaurava*) cannot apply here due to the absence of identity of object (*ekaviṣayatva*), that is incorrect; for it is precisely when postulating a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) that the identity of the object is required. For this same reason, the authors of the *Dīdhiti* and others maintain that "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) is not the delimiting factor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*), whereas "the state of being the prior absence of smoke" (*dhūmaprāgabhāvatva*) is the delimiting factor, because the former subsists in what is not the locus of smokeness.

In the present context, however, since there is no appearance of evidence for postulating that the cognition produced by the two stated sentences is of a different nature, and since there is no obstacle to postulating that they are causes only for a single uniform cognition, the following argument is refuted: "In cases such as *apākṣīd devadatto 'vehi*, there is no possibility at all for the suffix *śatṛ* and so on, because [the suffix] *laṭ* alone is prescribed for that. For, in the case of *paśya mṛgo dhāvati*, since there is the possibility of *śatṛ* and so on, the meaningfulness of the rule "the accusative is not used after [words denoting] a deer and so on" has been presented.

The meaning of the verse from the *Vākyapadīya* cited previously is as follows: In a verb such as *dhāvati* ("he runs"), there are two components. By means of the first component, which is the verbal root itself—as seen in its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words like *paśya* ("see")—there is the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*), as well as either the connection of other factors of action (*kāraka*) within itself, or its own connection to another [action] by way of being a factor of action. In the sentence *mṛgo dhāvati* ("the deer runs"), there is the state of being a means-of-accomplishment (*sādhanatva*), as well as the connection to another action through the relation of being an object (*karmatva*). This is because, when it occurs in co-occurrence with *paśya*, that [deer] has a requirement for an object; thus, the very action of running (*gamana*) that is presented [in the mind] is connected [to "see"] precisely in that capacity [of being the object].

By this, through these two verbal forms—*paśya* and *dhāvati*—one perceives that the action expressed by *paśya* is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), while *dhāvati* functions as the means (*sādhana*) by way of being a *kāraka*, thereby connecting with another action. And it is not the case that "the state of being, which is not yet a substance (*asattvabhūta*), is denoted by verbal endings (*tiṅ*)."

Thus, the claim from the *Vākyapadīya* that it must be explained how the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) becomes the object (*karman*) and yet is the meaning of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)—on the grounds that its being the meaning [of the suffix] consists in its being construed with another [word] as an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth—is refuted. This is because it would result in a discrepancy between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*), since in the former there are two verbal suffixes, whereas in the latter there is a root and a suffix; furthermore, it remains unproven that a single entity can possess both the nature of the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*).

According to my view, since the relationship of primary and subordinate status depends on the co-occurrence or non-occurrence of another word, it is impossible for both [the primary and subordinate status] to belong to either one [of the two words]. Therefore, even the citation of the *Vākyapadīya*’s own commentary—which states that in the phrase "The deer runs, look! there exists the nature of the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*)—is not to be accepted as authoritative. This is because the intention of that passage is that when "The deer runs" is uttered, the deer possesses only the status of being the goal, whereas upon the co-occurrence of "look!", it also possesses the status of being the means.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of obtaining a reversed relationship of goal and means through the rule of corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). Let this matter rest for now.

In this way, even in the case of *ghañ* and other such suffixes, the verbal base (*prakṛti*) denotes an action that has attained the status of a non-substance (*asattva*). It is because of this [denotation] that, in expressions such as *odanasya pākaḥ* ("the cooking of rice"), the sixth case endings expressing the agent or the object occur; and in expressions such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking in order to eat"), the suffixes like *tumun* are employed based on their connection with the action. By this, the doubt that "only the residual sixth case (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would occur there" is refuted; for otherwise, the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) would become redundant.

However, through its co-occurrence with the portion consisting of the *pratyaya* (suffix), that very [action] attains the state of being a substance (*sattva-rūpatva*). This is because it then enters into a grammatical relation (*anvaya*) as a means (*sādhana*) for another action. For this very reason, it is clearly stated in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the fifth book (*Pañcamādhyāya*) and elsewhere that in expressions such as "the cooking of ghee is equal to the cooking of oil" (*tailapākena tulyo ghṛtapākaḥ*), the third case endings (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth are based upon that [state of being a substance]. Thus, the sense is that there would be a failure to accomplish both types of grammatical effects: the state of being a substance caused by co-occurrence with suffixes like *ghañ*, and the state of being a non-substance (*asattva-rūpatva*) based on the inherent nature of the verbal root (*dhātu-svarūpa*).

And this is logical: since it is necessary to postulate that the knowledge of the root's denotative power (*dhātu-śakti-jñāna*) is the cause for the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose object is an action (*kriyā*), it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate causal status for *ghañ* suffixes and the like. Nor should it be argued that it is contradictory for a single action to possess both forms (of being an object and an instrument), because such a contradiction does not exist when there is a difference in the relata (*nirūpaka-bheda*). Otherwise, one could not resolve the difficulty even in the case of the illustrative example; for in that case, the coexistence of the two forms is indispensable, and there is no difference in the expressive words (*vācaka-bheda*). Otherwise, there would be the connection of *kārakas* (case-factors) with the act of going (*gamana-kriyā*).

Therefore, both expressions "stokaṃ pākaḥ" (a slight cooking) and "stokaḥ pākaḥ" (a slight cooking) are logically consistent as qualifiers. However, if it were held that a single action is understood through both the base and the suffix, there would be a contradiction with empirical experience. Consequently, there is no escape by means of a relation of non-difference (*abheda*) with the object; for the presentation of an entity as delimited by a single form is incompatible with a relation of non-difference.

For this very reason, the suffix *kta* in the expression “it shines like a substance” (*dravyavat prakāśate*) found in the *Bhāṣya* is consistent; for it indicates a distinction from words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), which denote objects consisting solely of the quality of existence (*sattva*). Otherwise, since the state denoted by the suffix *ghañ* would consist solely of existence, the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) would be untenable. Thus, Kaiyaṭa’s position—that jars and the like possess the status of a standard of comparison by virtue of common usage—should be explained merely as a statement made while provisionally accepting [the opponent's view].

This is because the meaning of "expressed by a *kṛt*" necessarily implies "expressed by a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix," whereas there is no dispute regarding this point in the case of "expressed by a *tiṅ*. Furthermore, since the rule of "including that which ends in [the term mentioned]" (*tadantagrahaṇa*) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned is well-established, there is no complexity involved. Moreover, this very meaning is made explicit in the subsequent verse, "In that system, action is that which is yet to be accomplished" (*sādhyatvena kriyā tatra*), because the "action" (*kriyā*)—which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*)—is what is taken up in the second half of that verse.

Therefore, in cases such as "If one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, one would attain happiness," when there is co-utterance with words like "if" (cet), the connection of one action with another action occurs through the relation of cause and effect, by virtue of the expectancy that has arisen. Otherwise, this would undesirably apply even to sentences such as "One should bow to Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, in cases such as "Having cooked, he eats," the distinction is that the expectancy for another action belongs specifically to the suffix of the verbal root, based on factors such as having a common agent.

Therefore, the state of being an object (*sādhyatva*) is not the possession of a property that does not give rise to an expectation for another action. This is because it would contradict the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that even in expressions such as *paktvā* ("having cooked"), an action that has not yet reached the state of being accomplished (*asattvabhūta-kriyā*) is perceived.

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "If the word is construed with the fruit (*phala*) which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then words like *stoka-* (e.g., *stokam pacati*) would require the accusative case and neuter gender; whereas if it is construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) which is the meaning of the root—as in *jyotiṣṭomena bhaktipūrvaṃ yajeta*—then the nominative case would apply and the neuter gender would apply to the general category. However, when construed with the meaning of the suffix *ghañ* (the completed action), the nominative case applies and the masculine gender applies. Thus, the necessity of postulating a separate denotative power (*śaktyantara*) for the sake of such a distinction is rejected. By this, [the objection]— [...is also refuted].
The state of completion and the state of being to be accomplished are proclaimed of action.
They maintain that substance exists in the state of completion; it is precisely there that they apply the rule for the *ghañ* suffix.

Thus, the *Vākyapadīya* is also explained. The meaning is that the rule for the suffix *ghañ* is intended to establish the status of being a means (*sādhana*) even in the case of an action (*kriyā*) that is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is because it is impossible to say that the suffix *ghañ* and others are for the sake of producing a cognition whose mode is "already established" (*siddhatva*). Since the states of being "to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) and "established" (*siddhatva*) cannot be modes of the cognition produced by the verbal root (*dhātu*), the intent is actually this: that the state of being "to be accomplished" and so forth occurs there according to the circumstances. The same applies to the statement "it is denoted as being to be accomplished. Thus: "The nature of the action (*bhāva*) in the verb ending (*ākhyāta*) is exactly the same as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)."

"It is not described by those very same words, but sometimes by other words"—thus the verse of Bhaṭṭa has been explained. Furthermore, it is precisely a specific type of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) that determines whether there is a requirement for another action or no such requirement.

In expressions such as *pacati* ("he cooks") or *pākam utpādayati* ("he produces cooking"), the state of being produced (*utpādyatva*) alone is the delimitor of the relation with the factors of action (*kāraka*). For this very reason, when *pacati* is uttered, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—"from what? for what? where? in what manner?"—and the connection of the factors of action that fulfill that expectancy, is logically consistent only with that [state of being produced]. This is because only that which is presented as possessing the property of arising (*utpattimat*) has expectancy for the factors of action. Furthermore, since that [action] is understood to be itself something to be produced and is therefore not yet established (*asiddha*), its connection—as stated in the Bhāṣya—with other actions as their means (*sādhana*) is appropriate, because only that which is already established can serve as a means for an action.

That is to be considered. Even if there were an association with "being produced" (*utpādyatva*) in cases such as *kriyājanyā* ("produced by action"), there would still be no association with the *kārakas* (factors of action). Furthermore, in cases such as *apākṣīt* ("he cooked [in the past]") and *papāca* ("he cooked repeatedly"), there would be no association with the *kārakas*. This is because, based on the cognition "he brought about an activity conducive to cooking," that activity is already established (*siddha*), and thus there arises a lack of expectancy (*anākāṅkṣā*) for it. This is due to the rule that what has had its origination in the past is necessarily established. If, however, one were to claim that the mere state of being the counter-positive of origination (*utpatti-pratiyogitva*) is the regulator of that expectancy, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of associating *kārakas* even with things like a jar (*ghaṭa*). This is the direction of the argument. *Śap* [is the affix] after the verbal root when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. (Pāṇini 3.1.68)

When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, the affix *śap* is added to the root in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Now, one might object: let the meanings of the agent, the passive (*bhāva*), and the object (*karman*) belong exclusively to the affixes *yak*, *śa*, and so forth; for these are absent whenever a *sārvadhātuka* suffix is present. Yet, even in the absence of those [affixes], we find the cognition of the agent and others in examples such as "go to the village" (*gaccha grāmam*), "it was slept by you" (*aśāyi bhavatā*), and "the mat was made" (*akāri kaṭaḥ*), because the suffixes there denote the agent and so on. Furthermore, in cases like "he eats" (*atti*), the cognition of the agent occurs despite the absence of an affix. Finally, in cases like "you have not woken up" (*ajāgarbhavān*), the meaning is understood even when both [the *sārvadhātuka* and the affixes] are absent.

Furthermore, [if] the singular number and so forth were the meaning of those [suffixes] when they function as *sārvadhātuka*, it would contradict the rule that "the singular number is used when there is oneness," because by that [rule], the agent (*kartṛ*) and other factors distinct from oneness are also understood. For this very reason, the author of the *Khaṇḍana* stated, while refuting the definition that "a word ending in an inflection is a meaningful unit (*pada*)," that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of the verb *bhavati*. If it is argued that this is because the *śap* suffix is prescribed for the agent; and if [it is further argued] that such is the explanation of its commentators—

Not so; for there is no contradiction, since the rule that "in the case of singularity, only the singular suffix is used" must be stated [as a restrictive rule]. Even if the rule were "only in the case of singularity," it would merely exclude duality and the rest. Furthermore, in cases such as *dhāraya*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*); for since suffixes do not arise after any *kṛt* affix, one would necessarily have to state that *kṛt* affixes alone express the agent. Moreover, by the statement "the *la*-suffixes [denote] the object and so forth," it is necessary that the agent and other roles be the meanings of the *lakāra* suffixes.

One might object: "Should it not be explained that *la* follows a *vikaraṇa* occurring before the root (in the context of *karma* etc.)? And it should not be argued that this is untenable because the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* resides in *tiṅ* suffixes and the like, and thus the *vikaraṇa* would not exist prior to them, making the causal condition impossible. This is not so, for by relying on the locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) in the rule *sārvadhātuke*, the explanation is that when the *vikaraṇa* applies first, the *la* suffix following a *vikaraṇa* that expresses the sense of the action, the object, or the agent becomes valid.

Not so; for since the *liṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes are *ārdhadhātuka*, no *vikaraṇa* (conjugational sign) would arise there, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the substitutes for *l* (the verbal endings) would be grammatically incorrect. If it is argued that they are correct by virtue of their being specifically prescribed, then there would be the undesirable consequence that the meanings of "becoming" (*bhāva*) and so forth could not be understood. If you then argue: "Just as in the case of the action of going (*gamikriyā*), there are two factors—the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*)—wherein the *lakāra* occurs for the agent and the accusative case-ending for the object in examples such as 'he goes to the village' (*grāmaṃ gacchati*); likewise, when *la* denotes the passive or the impersonal state (*bhāva-karman*), then the *vikaraṇa* occurs for the agent, and when *la* denotes the agent, then it occurs for the passive or impersonal state"—this is not tenable.

In that case, although a distinction in grammatical operations (*kāryabheda*) might arise because the agent and the object are expressed by separate words, it is impossible for the *vikaraṇa* and the *sārvadhātuka* suffix—which have contradictory meanings—to mutually assist one another in conveying a qualified meaning when they reside within a single word. Furthermore, if the object were the meaning of the *vikaraṇa* in *pacati*, it would follow that the accusative case could not occur after words such as *taṇḍula*. This is because the specific enumeration [of such cases] has been rejected.

Therefore, the agent and other grammatical roles (kartṛ-ādi) have as their sole purpose the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. For this very reason, it was stated by the author of the Maṇi: "Because of the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding even those [suffixes] such as *iṭ*, *num*, and others, which are themselves devoid of meaning, as well as the modifications of phonemes such as *ṣ* and *ṇ*, and the *vikaraṇas* such as *śyaP* and *śyan*. By this, the claim made in the Mīmāṃsā-kaustubha—that in forms like *gaccha*, the *vikaraṇa* alone expresses the activity (*vyāpāra*), because cognition arises even when the *tiṅ* and other suffixes are absent—is refuted.
The affix *śyan* is applied after verbal roots beginning with *div*.

He plays (dīvyati). The affixes *śyan* and others are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *śap*. By the rule "that which has *ñ* or *ṇ* as its marker is always [udātta at its beginning]," the initial syllable of *śyan* becomes udātta; since the following *sārvadhātuka* affix is anudātta, the forms in the four types of *lakāra* are udātta on the first syllable. This same status applies in the *laṅ* and *liṭ* by virtue of their accentual rules. [The roots] *vā*, *bhrāś*, *bhlāś*, *bhramu*, *kramu*, *klamu*, *tras*, *truṭ*, and *laṣ* [take *śyan* optionally]. (Pāṇini 3.1.70)

The affix *śyan* is optionally applied after these roots. This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) applicable in both cases: because it is prescribed where the affix would otherwise be obligatory—namely for *bhrami* (in the sense of "wandering") and *klamitri*, since they belong to the *divādi* class—and where it would otherwise not be applied—namely for the other roots. *bhrāśṛ* and *bhlāśṛ* (meaning "to shine") are *anudātta* (unaccented) roots. Bopadeva states that they end in dental consonants (*dantya*). *Bhramu* (meaning "to move") belongs to the *bhvādi*, *jvalādi*, and *phaṇādi* classes. *Bhramu* (meaning "to wander") belongs to the *divādi*, *puṣādi*, and *śamādi* classes. From the *bhvādi* class, the form is *bhramyati*; from the *śamādi* class, however, the long vowel is substituted, resulting in *bhrāmyati*.

In the absence of the suffix *śyan*, both [roots] cause the suffix *kyaṅ* to be applied; thus there is a threefold form. The root *kramu* means "to step"; *klamu* means "to be weary"; *trasī* means "to tremble with fear"; *truṭa* means "to cut"; *laṣa* means "to desire";
and *yas* [takes the suffix] when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). (71)

Or, due to the rule concerning verbal roots with prefixes, the suffix *śyan* is applied after the root *yasu* [meaning] "to strive": *yasyati*, *yasati*. Why "without a prefix"? [Observe: *āyasyati*, *prayasyati*. Because it belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix is applied invariably.
And also after the root *saṃ-yas*. (Pāṇini 3.1.72)

He exerts himself (*saṃyasyati*); he restrains himself (*saṃyasati*). In the previous sūtra, the condition "when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) was rejected in the Bhāṣya, because this [present rule] serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatvāt*). If there were an option for *yasa-* when preceded by a prefix, then it would apply only when preceded by *sam-*. After roots beginning with *su-*, the suffix *śnu* is applied. (Pāṇini 3.1.73)

The root *suñ* means "to press. According to the Cāndras, "pressing" (*abhiṣava*) also means "bathing. Murāri says: "They spend three days pressing [Soma] and maintain their bodily existence with forest products. In examples such as *somam abhiṣuṇoti* ("he presses Soma"), it has the sense of "purification" (*saṃskāra*). In the section on liquor (*surā*), Amara states: "Pressing (*abhiṣava*) would be the mixing (*saṃdhāna*). The letter *ś* serves to designate the suffix as *sārvadhātuka*; thus, by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, the suffix *su* (the *vikaraṇa*) is treated as having the marker *ṅ*, and consequently there is no *guṇa* substitution caused by that *vikaraṇa*. However, for that which ends in it, there is *guṇa* caused by the *tiṅ* suffix. The same applies in subsequent cases. In forms such as *sunutaḥ*, there is no *guṇa* because that suffix is not marked with *ṅ*.
The word *śruvaḥ* becomes *śṛca*. 74.

The root *śru* (in the sense of "hearing") takes the suffix *śnu*, and by the very application of that suffix, there is the substitution of *śṛ* for the root. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*. In forms such as *śṛṇoti* and *aśrauṣīt*, this [suffix] does not apply because *śap* is not applicable there.
The word *akṣa* [takes the suffix *kan*] optionally.
The root *akṣū* means "to pervade. With the suffix *śnu*, it becomes *akṣṇoti*; with [the suffix] *ti*, it becomes *akṣati*.
The word *takṣ* [is used] in the sense of making thin. || 76 ||
Or [the suffix] Śnu is used in the sense of *śapa* (cursing). As in *takṣṇoti* or *takṣati*. *Takṣaṇa* means the separation of parts. But not here: *vāgbhiḥ saṃtakṣati*; the meaning is "he reviles."
The suffix *śa* is applied after [roots] beginning with *tud*.

The suffix *śit* is for the purpose of subverting the *guṇa* substitution caused by the light penultimate vowel. Due to the absence of the property of being *pit*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffix subverts the final acute accent of the root, because it is "later taught" (*sati śiṣṭatva*). Consequently, according to the rule that a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following a root with an *adupadeśa* (a root taught with an initial vowel) is unaccented, the resulting forms have the middle syllable as acute. However, in the case of *tudanti*, when the final syllable becomes unaccented, the single-substitute accent (*ekādeśasvara*) results in the initial syllable being acute.
The suffix *śnam* is applied after the roots beginning with *rudh*.

[The augment] follows after the final vowel of the root. An augment also possesses the status of an affix (*pratyayatva*), because there is no contradiction [in doing so]. Consequently, by virtue of being the beginning of an affix, *ś* receives the designation *it*. Now, its status as *śit* is not for the purpose of preventing *guṇa*, because the suffix *śnam* is prescribed after the word *bhi* itself; and because the portion of that [suffix] which is the word *bhi* lacks the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*). Furthermore, since there is no root in the *rudhādi* class that ends in an *ik* vowel, this cannot be for the purpose of avoiding the status of an *ārddhadhātuka*. Indeed, because of the absence of the stem designation, the application of the augment *iṭ* is not even possible.

Furthermore, in the case of *pṛṇati*, where the *śnam* affix is applied to the roots *pṛ* and *mṛ* belonging to the *kryādi* class by means of a Vedic anomaly (*vyatyaya*), the mention of "roots beginning with *pra*" [in Pāṇini 6.1.15] is for the purpose of shortening the vowel before a *śit* affix.
