This is because these roots are listed in the *tudādi* class as *pṛṣu* and *praṇi*. By this, the form *śrṛṇati* is also explained.

Nor is [the substitution of *śna*] for that purpose in the case of *pṛṇase*, because it is established there by the shortening of *śnu*. For the shortening of *śnu* is necessary in Vedic usage for the sake of forms such as *pratyaya*. Nor should it be argued that *śna* alone must be stated for the sake of making the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following an *adupadeśa* (a verbal root with an initial vowel) unaccented; for if *śna* were used, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision (*allopa*) of both *śna* and *śnu*. Furthermore, if the term "penultimate" (*upadhā*) were to carry over [from the previous rule], there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms like *añjate* and *añjati*. Nor is it for the sake of providing a qualifier in the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* ("there is elision of the *n* after *śna*").

It should not be argued that otherwise there would be the undesirable elision of *n* (*nalopa*) even in cases such as *yajñānām*; for [one might say] that the lengthening occurs first. This is not correct, because the elision of *n* would still apply due to its higher status (*paratva*). Nor should it be argued that even if the lengthening by the rule *nāmī* does not apply, the lengthening by the rule *supi ca* will take effect; for that [latter rule] does not apply on account of the *sannipāta-nyāya*. Nor should it be argued that even with the presence of the marker *ś*, the application of that [elision] is unavoidable in cases like *viśnānām*; for that is prevented by the maxim regarding "that which is taught by a specific rule versus that which is taught by a general rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktanyāya*). [The suffix] *u* is applied after the roots of the *tanādi* class and *kṛñ*. (79)

He extends [the root]. By the rule *sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.3.84), there is *guṇa* substitution. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "Since *kṛñ* belongs to the *tan*-class, the form is established; and even when the *sic* suffix is elided, there is no fault.
There might be a fault here in the case of *ciṇvadbhāva*, but that too is optionally applicable."

The meaning of this is as follows: since the root *kṛ* is already established [as belonging to the *tan*-class] by virtue of being included in the *tanādi* group itself, its separate mention is redundant. Nor can it be argued that this is for the purpose of indicating that the operations pertaining to the *tanādi* group—specifically the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) according to the rule *anudāttopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām*—should not apply to *kṛ*. For such an elision is not even applicable here simply because the root lacks a nasal. Nor can it be argued that it is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the suffix *s* (in forms like *akārṣīt*) according to the rule *tanādibhyastathāsor*. For if that were required by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*, there would be no difference [in the result].

Nor should it be argued that because the elision of *sij* is "not established" (*asiddha*) by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, the substitution of *ciṇvadbhāva* cannot take place when that elision occurs; for although *ciṇvadbhāva* would not apply when there is an elision of *sij* by the rule *tanādibhyaḥ*, it is nonetheless established in the alternative case where such elision does not occur, since the elision [of the final *i*] by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt* then applies. Nor should it be argued that, according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, the elision of *sij* by *tanādibhyaḥ* necessarily sublates the elision by *hrasvādaṅgāt*, and thus how could this be so; for sublation is impossible in the alternative case where the former rule does not apply.
[Roots] *dhinv* and *kṛṇv* take the augment *ak* [before *liṭ*]. (Pāṇini 6.4.80)

The roots *dhiv* (to please) and *kṛv* (to injure) take the augment *num* because they are marked with the indicator *it*. The mention of the letter *i* [in the sūtra] serves to indicate these two. In place of the final vowel of these two roots, there shall be the substitution of the vowel *a*, and the suffix *up* shall also be applied when the suffix *śap* is in scope. First, the vowel *va* is replaced by the vowel *a*; then, the vowel *u* is drawn forward [from the previous rule]. There is elision of the *a* (by *ato lopaḥ*). Because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel does not occur. Thus, we have *dhinoti*. In forms such as *dhinutaḥ*, there is no *guṇa* because the suffixes are marked with the indicator *ṅ*. For this very reason, the elision of the vowel *va* was not prescribed.

Because the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would apply. Nor can one argue that the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* applies there as well; for since the letter *u* is taught as being conditioned by its association with the letter *ṛ*, it cannot logically serve as the cause for the elision of the *val* (consonant). Furthermore, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] is established only in cases where the elision is caused by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, and since [the elision here] is not caused by an *ārdhadhātuka*, [the prohibition does not apply]. Moreover, that rule (*na dhātulopa...*) has been rejected [by the author of the Mahābhāṣya]. The mention of the form [ending] in *num* (as in *sunoti*), however, is intended so that the substitute *a* may occur immediately after the *num*. Otherwise, the *num* would follow the letter *ā*; because [in that case], the *num* would be the final phoneme (*antyāctva*) of the stem.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that *num* occurs first because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Nor should it be argued that *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) is *antaraṅga* because it is taught as being co-occurrent with the production of the suffix (*pratyaya*), whereas the augment *num* is *bahiraṅga* since it depends upon both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix; for if that were so, *ātva* would indeed occur first, because *num* is based on the *aṅga*. This is because it will be stated later that the mention of "as if taught" (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) in the rule for *num* is for the sake of the rule prescribing the suffix. Otherwise, in forms such as *kuṇḍā*, the suffix *ap* prescribed by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* would be impossible. Thus it has been explained.

In this regard, the following should be understood: the root *kṛ* in the sense of "injury" belongs to the *svādi* (second) class. The forms of both *kṛṇvi* and *kṛṇoti* are identical, such as *kṛṇoti* and so forth; however, in the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) voice, they are *kṛṇute* and so forth. In the *liṭ* (perfect tense) and other such moods, they follow the pattern of *karoti*, such as *cakāra* and so forth; whereas for these two [specific roots], the forms are *cakṛṇva* and so forth.

However, some read these two roots (*kṛ* and *hi*) in the *svādi* class. Nor does the occurrence of the *ūṭh* augment follow from the force of their inclusion in the *svādi* class when the *śnu* affix is applied; for the prescription of the substitutes [for *ṛ* and *hi*] is intended only for the domain of *śnu*. Otherwise, if they were read in the *bhvādi* class, the *śap* affix would also be unavoidable. This is also because it accords with the natural sense of the *Vṛtti* that they belong to the *svādi* class. There is no evidence for explaining them as belonging to the *kryādi* class by virtue of following *kṛṇoti*. [Pāṇini 3.1.81: *kryādibhyaḥ śnā*.
The suffix *śnu* is applied after the roots *stabhu*, *tumbhu*, *skambhu*, *skumbhu*, and *skuñbhu*, and it also takes the form *krīṇāti*.

The four roots beginning with *stambh* are from the *sūtra* (Dhātupāṭha), ending in *śnā*, and according to some, they mean "to obstruct" (*rodhana*) when the vowel *a* is not the penultimate letter (*an-akaropadhā*). Mādhava states that the first and third have the meaning "to prop up" (*stambha*), the second means "to shake off" (*niṣkopaṇa*), and the fourth means "to be uncertain" (*anavadhāraṇa*). [The root] *skuñ* means "to flow away" (*āpravaṇe*). Examples include *stabhnāti*, *stabhnāti*, and so on; [also] *skunoti*, *skṛnute*.
[The rule] *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* [Pāṇini 3.1.83 applies].

The substitute *śānac* takes the place of *śan* when a consonant (*hal*) precedes it and the suffix *hi* follows. The specific mention of *śna* [in the rule] is for the purpose of establishing that this is a substitute; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a separate, independent suffix. Some say that one should not take *śānac* from the sūtras, citing examples such as *stabhnīhi*. However, Mādhava and others maintain that it is indeed *stabhāna*, because there is no evidence for such a restriction. For that very reason, Vedic usages such as *uddivaṃ stabhāna* ("support the sky with your splendor") and *divam uttabhāna* ("uphold the sky") are possible.

By this, my usage in the *Rukmiṇīpariṇaya*, "stabhāna" (be firm), which contains the nasal *m* and is situated within the tears of the eyes, is explained. The letter *ś* [in the suffix *śānac*] is for the sake of making it a *sārvadhātuka*. Consequently, there is no *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *kuṣāṇa*. This is established by the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* due to its being *śit*. However, this is not for the purpose of indicating that the indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) of substitutes for *sārvadhātuka* suffixes do not become *sthānivadbhūta*. Therefore, the letter *ṅ* need not be attached as an indicatory letter to the substitute *tātaṅ*; rather, the status of being *ṅit* is established through extension (*atideśa*) from the original [suffix].

If it is argued that, in the same way, for *taptanaptanathanāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.45), the status of being *ṅit*—which is triggered by the substitution of *tā* being an *apit* sārvadhātuka replacement—does not apply; and therefore, in examples such as *śrṇota grāvāṇaḥ* and *āsmin havyā juhotana*, there is no *guṇa* substitution, [we reply: no, because in cases like *acinavam*, the *ām* replacement would be *apit*, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of prohibiting *guṇa*. The same logic should be applied to *veda* and *vettha* etc. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *vasu* replacement for the *śatṛ* in *videḥ śatur vasuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.36) being *aśit*. Moreover, since the *ṅit*-ness and so forth of *tātaṅ* and the others have already been established, there is no redundancy (*gaurava*). This is the general direction of the argument.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffix śāyac is also applied.

It should be stated that this applies "everywhere"; that is to say, even when [the suffix] *hi* is present. In the phrase *jātavedaḥ pratihavyā gṛbhāya jihvayā madhu*, the meaning is "grasp" (*gṛhāṇa*). In the phrase *yo askabhāyad uttaraṃ sadhastham*, [the sense is] "he lifted up" (*udagṛbhāyat*) or "he propped up" (*unmathāyata*). *Skambhu* is a Vedic root; in the *laṅ* tense, there is the insertion of *śna*, followed by *śāyac*, and the augment *aṭ*. The particle *api* is for the purpose of precluding the *śānac* suffix. [In the phrase] *badhāna vatsam*, there is a frequent transposition of grammatical elements (*vyatyayo bahulam*).

The term *chandasi* (in the Vedic language) is understood to carry over. By means of a formal division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), there is also a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). For example: *āṇḍā śuṣmasya bhedati*. This occurs where *bhinatti* (he splits) would otherwise be expected; and *na marati mriyate*, where *mriyate* (he dies) would otherwise be expected. Also: *yo añjasānuśāsati*, where *śāsti* (he instructs) would otherwise be expected. Following that, there is a transposition of all grammatical rules. For example, regarding nouns (*sup*): *yuktānāsīddhuri dakṣiṇāyāḥ*. This occurs where *dakṣiṇasyām* (in the southern one) would otherwise be expected. Regarding finite verbs (*tiṅ*): *caṣālaṃ ye aśvayūpāya takṣati*. This occurs where *takṣanti* (they carve) would otherwise be expected. (This is repeated for emphasis.)

Regarding gender (*varṇa*), as in *triṣṭubhaujaḥ śubhitam ugravīram* (where *śubhitam* is used when *śudhitam* was expected). Regarding grammatical number (*liṅga*), as in *madhostṛptā ivāsate* (where *madhoḥ* is used when *madhunaḥ* was expected). Regarding time (*kāla*), as in *śvo'gnīnādhāsyamānena* and *śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena* (where *ādhātā* and *yaṣṭā* were expected). Regarding person (*puruṣa*), as in *adhāsva vīrairdaśabhīrviyūyāḥ* (where *viyūyāt* was expected). Regarding voice (*upagraha*), as in *brahmavāriṇamicchate* (where *icchati* was expected), and *pratīmamanya ūrbhiryudhyati* (where *yudhyate* was expected).

The author of the grammatical treatise intends a transposition (vyatyaya) of these: case endings (sup), verbal suffixes (tiṅ), voice (upagraha), gender (liṅga), number (nara), tense (kāla), the suffix *hal*, vowels (svara), the agent (kartṛ), and the *yaṅ* affix; and that [transposition] is established by way of abundance (*bāhulyena*).
The suffix *yaṅ* occurs after a verbal root ending in *liṅ* when it expresses a benediction.

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *aṅ* occurs in the optative (*āśīr-liṅ*) as an exception to *śap*. Its purpose is seen in the forms *sthā*, *gā*, *ami*, *vīc*, and *viday*. One should worship the bull who is dear to those [who seek him]. One should sing of the truth directly. May I attain a firm foundation through sacrifice. May we go to the houses of those who know. May we speak the mantra to Agni. [The root] *vac* becomes *um*. May I obtain this foundation in speech. It should be stated that [the suffix *aṅ*] follows *śak* and *ruh* as well. May we be able to kindle you. May we ascend the flowing waters for our well-being.

The suffix *ag* should be stated [as an alternative] for the root *dṛś* (to see). For if *aṅ* were applied, there would be *guṇa* (vowel strengthening). [Thus we get] *pitaraṃ ca dṛśeyam mātaraṃ ca* ("May I see my father and mother"). It should also be stated that *āṭ* is applied [before the optative suffix]. In the case of the root *sthā*, when the optative (*liṅ*) suffix *mas* follows, there is *yāsuṭ*, *aṅ*, elision of *ā*, and elision of *s*. By the rule *ato yeya*, *iy* is substituted [for the *yās* of *yāsuṭ*]. Then *āṭ* is added to *mas*. Otherwise, due to the elision of *y*, one might also get the form *upasthemā*. However, the author of the Bhāṣya says that because it is a *sārvadhātuka* (present-stem) suffix, there is elision of *s*, and because it is an *ārddhadhātuka* (non-present-stem) suffix, there is the substitution of *e*. He further states that in Vedic usage, both designations (*sārvadhātuka* and *ārddhadhātuka*) apply simultaneously.
Thus ends the fourth Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya in the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi.
That which has an action similar to that of the object is treated like the object. (Pāṇini 3.1.87)

The word *karmaṇā* (by the object) refers here to the action residing in that [object]; likewise, the word *karman* (object), by virtue of its underlying power (*śakti*), refers to the object such as rice (*taṇḍula*). Since the word *kartṛ* (agent) is understood from the rule *kartari śap*, it follows as a nominative form; thus, the construction is with that [word] ending in the first case. Consequently, an agent whose action is equivalent to the action residing in the object shall be treated like the object (*karmavat*). In this context, verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook) denote both the result, such as softening (*viklitti*), and the activity conducive to that result. Among these, when Devadatta and others possess agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the activity...

And in cases such as "he cooks rice," it is intended that the rice and so forth are the substrata of the fruit produced by that [action]. Thus, there are usages such as "Devadatta cooks rice. However, when [the roots] denote merely the softening and so forth, setting aside the aspect of the operation (*vyāpāra*), then the rice and so forth themselves possess the status of agent (*kartṛ*). As stated by Bhartṛhari: "When the instigation has ceased, the object remains within its own action; as its status as an object ceases, it persists in its own status as an agent."

And thus, the action residing in the object (*karmasthā kriyā*) consists of the state of being softened (*viklitti*), because even the fruit (the result) is an action as it constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). When the rice and so forth are the agent with respect to that [action], the agent becomes one whose action is equal to that of the object (*karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ kartā*). If it is objected: "Since the two substrata (the rice as object and the rice as agent) are identical, their action must also be one and the same; how then can there be a 'sameness' based on a distinction? We reply: No, for what is intended is precisely this: that the action delimited by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of 'objecthood' is the very same action as that delimited by the limiting adjunct of 'agenthood'. For this very reason, the conventional designation "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*) is used here. As it was said by Durgasiṃha:
But that action which, while being performed,
succeeds by itself through its own easily managed constituent parts, they know as "karmakartṛ" (the agent-patient).

The purpose of the rule beginning with *karmasthakriyayā* is that the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) should apply only to those actions whose locus is the object (*karmasthakriyā*), and not to those whose locus is the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*). This is because both [the agent and the object] serve as the substratum for action. The distinction between these two is explained in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Where there is the perception of a specific change, there action is established."
"But for others, the determination of action is merely constructed by means of words.
Indeed, softening in the form of the loosening of constituent parts is observed in cooked grains of rice.

Furthermore, when wood is split, there is a division of its constituent parts; and when Soma is pressed, there is fluidity and so forth—thus, these possess the quality of having their action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*). Although in the case of [verbs like] *gam* (to go) and others, there exists a result such as conjunction produced by the act of going with respect to the village and so on—since there is a rule that transitive verbs denote a result residing in the object (*sakarmakāṇāṃ karmasthaphalābhidhāyitvaniyamāt*)—nevertheless, that [result] does not reside in the object [in this context]. This is because only that result which can be known merely by observing the object falls within the scope of such a technical definition.

Merely by seeing a village, it cannot be understood that "this village has been gone to by someone. The meaning of the second half of the verse is that for verbal roots (*dhātu*) with such meanings, the action resides in the agent (*kartṛstha-kriyatva*). By this, verbs such as *jñā* (to know) and others are explained. As it has been said: "The status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) is desired in the case of both the produced (*nirvartya*) and the modified (*vikārya*) objects, but not in the case of the reached (*prāpya*) object; this established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is settled thus."

And thus the king sees for himself, or the elephant mounts by itself—such is the form [of the expressions]. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that those who demonstrate the application of the *karmakartṛ* (object-as-agent) rule in the case of "the elephant is mounted" (*āruhyate hastī*) should be disregarded, as it contradicts the logic of the Bhāṣya.

If it is argued that this contradicts the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*, which state that there is a prohibition for transitive verbs in cases such as "they embrace each other" (*anyonyam āśliṣyataḥ*), and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, which asserts that the result in the form of conjunction resides in the object (*karman*) and thus the rule would apply—this is not so. For it is accepted that the examples provided are merely illustrative (*diṅmātra*) and not definitive ones. In this regard, the following should be noted: in the state where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, the result itself is the action; since the object (*karman*) is the locus of that [result], it possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "The roots *pac* and others [denote] either a single part or the collection of operations."
They proceed by their own nature, relying upon an identical form.

The plural number in "of the operations" (*vyāpārāṇām*) is intended to signify the plurality of results, as in the expression "those with umbrellas are going. Regarding its explanation, Helārāja stated: "In cases such as 'the rice cooks by itself,' the result itself is the action because it is the meaning of the verbal root; and because the rice and so forth are the substrata of that [result], they possess the status of agent (*kartṛ*)."

It might be argued as follows: even in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the rice and so forth would possess the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) because they are the substratum of the result (*phala*). This would follow by virtue of the subsequent rule [defining the agent]. Nor should it be said that the designation of "object" (*karman*) is without scope while the designation of "agent" has scope in Devadatta and others who are not the substratum of the result; for even so, the status of object would still undesirably accrue to Devadatta and others who are the substratum of the conjunction [with the village] in cases such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*). Furthermore, the nature of action (*kriyātva*) consists precisely in being the object of a cognition produced by a verbal root, qualified by not being a qualifier of anything other than the meaning of the suffix.

In that case, however, because the result (phala) serves as a qualifier for the specific activity denoted by the verbal root (dhātvartha), it does not possess the nature of an action (*kriyātva*) in the manner described. It must be stated that in expressions such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), the phrase "other than the meaning of the suffix" (*pratyayārthānya*) was included in order to preserve the status of the root-meaning activity—which is itself qualified by the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij*)—as being an action. [Otherwise], there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), since in cases such as *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("see, the deer runs") and *pacati bhavati* ("it is cooking"), the activities of running and cooking are qualifiers of the activities of seeing and becoming, which are the meanings of the suffixes.

Regarding this, some say: "Action-ness (*kriyātva*) consists precisely in being the object of a cognition produced by that verbal root, as qualified by not being a qualifier of the meaning of that verbal root."

In this regard, the following must be considered: under the view that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), because the meaning of the verbal root—consisting of the operation of the prompted agent—is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root consisting of the operation of the prompter. This is because it is [already] accepted that in the case of *pacyate odanaḥ svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), the cognition is that "there is a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) conducive to cooking, having a substratum non-different from the rice itself. Furthermore, if the operation were not the meaning of the verbal root, its status as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) would be untenable; therefore, in this context, the verbal root denotes only the result (*phala*). It is taught: "The operation is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*); that very thing is production (*utpādanā*), and that very thing is action (*kriyā*)."

Because of this admission, since the rule for *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment of an agent like an object) is prescribed when one intends to express that the substratum of the result itself is the substratum of the operation (*vyāpāra*), the meaning is: "the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) which has a substratum non-different from the rice and is conducive to the cooking of the rice. Why is the suffix *-vat* used? So that the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) may also occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), as in "it is split by the granary" (*bhidyate kūṣūlena*). Otherwise, if only the agent were assigned the technical designation "object," there would be no occurrence of the verbal suffix in the sense of the abstract action, because the designation "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) would be absent.

Why does the rule specify "by means of an action" (*karmaṇā*)? It is so that the designation of *kartṛ* (agent) may not apply to an agent whose action is identical to that of the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: *sādhvasiś chinatti* ("the sword cuts well") and *sādhu sthālī pacati* ("the pot cooks well"). In these cases, the action consisting of conjunction, holding, and so forth, resides in the sword and the pot respectively. Now, one might object: in expressions such as *asinā chinatti* ("he cuts with a sword") and *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("he cooks in a pot"), the operation of the instrument and the locus is not denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*). However, when that operation is intended to be expressed by the root, then those two [the sword and the pot] possess the status of *kartṛ* (agent) alone.

And thus, since at the time of the intended expression [of the action] through the states of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), the operation of that [agent] is not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and because in the state of being an agent there is likewise an absence of an action equal to that [action of the object], there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in those cases. Consequently, since only an action inherent in the agent or the object is denoted by the verbal root, the definition "an agent who has an action equal to the action residing in the agent" is untenable; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), one obtains equality with an action residing in the object, and thus the word "object" (*karman*) [in the sūtra] would be redundant. If this is argued, we say: no.

This is because the action, which serves as the counter-correlate for similarity, is not specifically qualified by being denoted by the verbal root; furthermore, in reality, the status of being the meaning of the verbal root exists even in the case of the operation of the instrument and other factors.

Furthermore, the phrase "having a similar action" (*tulyakriya*) is redundant; for it is possible to explain the word "by" (*karmaṇā*) as a third case ending through the ellipsis of a word meaning "similarity. Moreover, in the example "one who runs similarly by means of an action" (*karmaṇā tulyaḥ sarta*), the similarity is understood precisely through the action itself.

Not so; for even in the sense of "together with" (*sahārtha*), the instrumental case is possible, which would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "Devadatta cooks rice," where an agent is presented together with an object (*karmaṇā saha yaḥ kartā*). However, the word "object" (*karman*) is appropriate as being intended to exclude intransitive verbs such as "he sits" (*āste*). Furthermore, by stating "having the same action" (*tulyakriya*), the meaning is obtained that "in whatever [grammatical relation] the action is observed to be the same as when it was an object, even though it has become the agent"; thus, the stated purpose is established.

Here, by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "dhātoḥ" (of the verbal root) and through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the meaning obtained is: "If the agent possesses an action equal to the action residing in that very object which belongs to a certain verbal root, then [the agent] shall be like the object (*karmavat*) with respect to that same verbal root. By this, the rules "intransitives have the status of being like the object" (*akarmakāṇāṃ karmavadbhāvaḥ*) and "within the same verbal root" (*samānadhātāv*) are established. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as: *bhidyamānaḥ kusūlaḥ pātrāṇi bhinatti* ("The granary, while being split, splits the vessels"), or *pacatyodanaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks the rice"), or *rādhyatyodanaḥ svayameva* ("The rice ripens by itself").

In the case of *odana* being the object (*karman*), the action characterized by softening (*viklitti*) is exactly the same as when it is the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because the root *rādh* expresses the sense of softening. Although these two types of sentences are not used simultaneously in common worldly usage, the phrase "he cooks the rice" (*pacaty odanam*) is employed here in order to demonstrate the identity of the action. Otherwise, such [analogical] application would be untenable even in cases such as "Devadatta mows the field" (*lunāti kedāram*) and "the field mows itself" (*lāvayate kedāraḥ svayam eva*).

[Objection: Since there is a difference between *lunāti* (he cuts) and *lāvayati* (he causes to cut), the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*), which is prescribed for a root within its own verbal class (*samānadhātu*), should not apply—just as it does not in cases such as *āhara kumbham* (bring the jar) or *karoti kaṭam* (he makes a mat), where the suffix *ṇic* is added. [Reply: This is not so. Some maintain that even with the addition of the *ṇic* suffix, because the two are recognized as the same, there is no difference between *lunāti* and *lāvayati*. Others hold that in the case of *lāvayati* itself, the field possesses both the status of being the object and the status of being the agent. By this, the Vārttika—"the status of being like the object applies to an intransitive [root] when it belongs to the same verbal class"—is explained.

This point must also be examined here: does the extension [of the rule] result in the cessation of the operation on its own locus or not? However, since it has been stated that the suffix *vat* is for the sake of the operation on its own locus, this doubt itself is untenable. Not so; for that statement is justified in order to raise another objection. It cannot be the first case, because in the example *acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayameva*, even though there is a prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there would follow the non-application of *caṅ* and *śap*, which are operations on their own locus. Similarly, in the case of *bhiduram*, the suffix *kurac* would not occur.

Although it will be stated later that "the agent of a root ending in *l* is treated like the object" (*karmavat*), this is nevertheless stated here for the sake of immediate clarity. It cannot be the second alternative, because both the prescription of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the prohibition of *śap* and so forth would have to be explicitly stated; otherwise, the occurrence of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) and *śap*—which reside in the same locus [as the root]—would be unavoidable.

It is not so; for it has been explained that "the *parasmaipada* suffixes occur there when the agent itself is the agent. Furthermore, because of the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) in the rule *kartari śap*, the *śap* and other affixes are sublated by the *yaṅ*. Alternatively, this is a case of the extension (*atideśa*) of an operation: due to the mutual contradiction between the *parasmaipada* and the *śap* etc., the latter ceases to apply, since only that which is not in conflict with the extension proceeds by virtue of its own basis.

It might be argued as follows: even in the case of affixes denoting the gerundive (*kṛtya*), the past passive participle (*kta*), and those having the sense of the suffix *khala*, there would be the treatment of the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*) as being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*). Consequently, because they would be transitive, these affixes would apply only to the object; for example, one would have forms such as *bhettavyaḥ kusūlaḥ* (the granary is to be split), *bhinnaḥ kusūlaḥ* (the granary was split), and *īṣadbhedaḥ kusūlaḥ* (the granary is slightly split).

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "The mention of *liṅ* [as] *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* contains two *lakāra*s. This is the meaning: according to the rule *vyatyayo bahulaṃ liṅyāśiṣi*, in the *saṃhitā* reading, the second *lakāra* is elided after the *makāra* through *parasavarṇa* and the subsequent loss of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*). However, in the view that a word ending in a *saṃyoga* [is subject to elision], the elision occurs by the rule *halo yamām yami*. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "The agent of that which ends in a consonant behaves like the object."

The author of the Vārttika expresses this as follows: "In that context, there is an extension of the rules for the object to that which ends in a *l* affix. Here, "in that context" (*tatra*) refers to the state of being denoted (*vācyatva*), which is the meaning of the genitive case. Consequently, the status of being treated like the object (*karmavadbhāva*), which is prescribed for the agent denoted by an affix ending in *l*, results—by virtue of the sense of the word—in an operation pertaining specifically to that which ends in *l*. Therefore, since this extended rule does not apply to the *kṛtya* suffixes and the like, those [suffixes] arise in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) because they are intransitive; thus, the agent is not expressed. Consequently, when used with a *kṛd*-suffix, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occur [respectively] according to the rule regarding connection with a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛdyoga*). For example: *kusūlasya bhettavyam* (the granary is to be split) and *kusūlena bhettavyam* (it is to be split by means of the granary).

And in the case of "the granary splits" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ*), the accusative case is not used because the agent is expressed as the object (*karmakartṛ*). In the expression "the granary has split by itself" (*bhinnaḥ kusūlaḥ svayameva*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent because the verb is intransitive; this is according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* [Pāṇini 3.4.72]. This is because, under the rule *sinotergrāsakarmakartṛkasya*, the counter-example will be given as "the morsel has been chewed by itself" (*sino grāsaḥ svayameva*). It might be argued: let this very sūtra be omitted, for cases such as "he kills himself" (*hantyātmānam*) or "he is killed by himself" (*ātmanā hanyate*) can be explained through a distinction based on limiting conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*). For this reason, expressions such as "you know yourself by yourself" (*ātmānamātmanā vetsi*) are consistent. As it has been said:
When a distinction is imagined for a single entity through its various cognitive states,
the status of object, instrument, and agent arises.

And thus, in cases such as "the rice is cooked" (*odanaḥ pacyate*), even in the absence of the cessation of the instigation (*nivṛttapreṣaṇatva*), let the suffix denote the primary object itself; for the word *svayam* is explained as referring to the agent in the sense of "by itself. Even in cases such as "the rice cooks itself" (*odanena pacyate*), by supplying the word *ātman* (itself), there is no defect even if the *lakāra* suffix is not produced in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Nor should it be argued that in expressions like "the granary is to be split" (*bhettavyaṃ kusūlena*) or "slightly split" (*bhinnaṃ īṣadbhedam*), the *kṛtya* suffixes and others would not occur in the sense of the abstract action; nor should it be argued that if they were admitted in the sense of the object, there would be the consequence of masculine gender due to the requirement of the qualifier *ātman*. [Note: This passage addresses grammatical nuances regarding the passive construction and the application of suffixes when the agent is implied as acting upon itself.]

This is because the neuter gender is possible when referring to a general category, and because it is possible to supply a neuter substantive such as "nature" (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, even under the view that the sūtra was intentionally composed, the usage "the self is to be broken by the granary" (*ātmā kusūlena bhettavyaḥ*) would be unavoidable according to the aforementioned intended meaning.

This has been stated by the author of the *Vārttika*: "But it is established because it is an inherent object (*prākṛtakarma*). The meaning is that since [the status of being an object] is already established by virtue of being an object directly taught (*aupadeśika*), there is no dependence on that [status] when it is transferred (*ātideśika*). Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa and others argue: "For if this were so, the prohibition in the rule *na-duha-snu-namām* would apply only to pure objects (*śuddhakarma*); because a transferred object-status (*ātideśika-karmatva*) is not well-known [in such cases]. Consequently, one would have only *gaur gopālena dugdhe* (the cow is milked by the cowherd), and not *duhyate* (is milked). Nor should it be said that the rule *na duha* is simply unnecessary."

This is because [the rule] *namate daṇḍaḥ* and so forth would remain unestablished; for the *taṅ* (middle voice) suffixes would be difficult to obtain in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *yak* suffix in the sense of the object (*karman*). Furthermore, the optional application of *ciṇ* by the rule *acaḥ karmakartari* would be rendered without scope (*niravakāśa*), since the "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*) would be unestablished. Moreover, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ātmanā ātmā ajñāyi*. Nor can it be argued that in the case where the action of instigation has ceased, the status of being an object exists by way of its prior state while the status of being an agent exists by way of its present state, and thus the rule applies precisely there.

Because [if this were not the case], there would be the non-occurrence of *śap* and other affixes in the *laṭ* and other tenses, and the undesired application of *yaK* and other affixes. Furthermore, the purpose of the word "himself" (*svayam*) is to establish that the field (*kedāra*) alone is the agent, by means of excluding any other agent; otherwise, the field would incur the status of being the object (*karma*).

[This is because] it has been stated: "A prohibition must be stated for transitive verbs. For although in the example "you know yourself by yourself" (*ātmānam ātmanā vetsi*), the rule regarding the object-like behavior (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply because the state [of the action] resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*), in the example "you create yourself by yourself" (*sṛjasy ātmānam ātmanā*), that [object-like behavior] is unavoidable because the state [of the action] resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvakatva*).

It might be argued as follows: The status of the self (*ātman*) as the object (*karman*) is derived from the act of production consisting in its connection with the body and the senses; whereas the agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to God by virtue of an effort in the form of a will conducive to that [production], while for the individual soul (*jīva*), it is derived from an effort in the form of such things as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). And thus, where there is identity of action delimited by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of agency, there is no application of the "object-like behavior" (*karmavadbhāva*) prescribed [for the agent]. Similarly, in the case of the expression "they embrace each other," there is the understanding that they are not the substrata of the efforts conducive to mutual conjunction.

"Taking conjunction as the action (*karman*) and taking the act of moving (*gamanādi-kriyā*) as the agency (*kartṛtva*), there is no identity of action. To this they reply: "In the case of *'ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati'* (he leads the goat to the village), even when the goat's agency is intended to be expressed, the verb remains transitive because of the object in the form of the village; therefore, the aforementioned Vārttika was stated to exclude that [undesired application]. For in the cognition arising from *'ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati'*—namely, 'the possessor of an effort conducive to an effort residing in the goat which is conducive to conjunction with the village'—the goat has the status of an object by virtue of being the substratum of the action consisting of the effort conducive to conjunction with the village, and it has the status of agent in the aforementioned instance precisely because it is the substratum of that [effort]."

On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya states: "This Vārttika need not be commenced. For, by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) in the rule *tapaḥ-tapaḥ-karma-kasyaiva*, it is explained as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that only the agent of the root *tap* when it is transitive becomes like the object."

This might be so: if austerity (*tapas*) in the form of fasting and the like were the agent, then the root *tap* would have the sense of "suffering," based on the understanding that "the austerity torments the ascetic" (*tapas tāpasaṃ tapati*), meaning it causes him pain. But if the ascetic is the agent, knowledge is likewise [the object], based on the cognition that "the ascetic performs austerity" (*tapyate tapas tāpasaḥ*), which means he knows the austerity. And thus, since the agent does not possess an action identical to the action residing in the object, the status of being treated like the object (*karmavadbhāvaḥ*) would not apply; therefore, the Vṛttikāra maintains that this rule is for the purpose of an original injunction (*vidhyartha*). How then can it be for the purpose of a restriction (*niyamārtha*)?

On this point Kaiyaṭa says: "The action characterized by bodily suffering is the same in both states; for the activity of the ascetic consists precisely in that acquisition characterized by bodily suffering. Thus, the agent of another transitive root does not behave like the object (*karmavat*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the intransitive root *tap* (to suffer) also behaving like the object, because its exclusion is ensured by another restrictive rule: that it applies only to *tap* when it has [bodily] suffering as its object.

"It should be stated that [the rule] *duhi-pacyoḥ bahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ* applies extensively. Examples: *gauḥ payo dugdhe* (The cow yields milk); *udumbaraḥ phalaṃ pacyate* (The udumbara tree bears fruit). Regarding *gaur dugdhe*, the understanding is "milk" (*payaḥ*). Since *duh* is transitive, even though the action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) and thus the condition for [the passive marker] is not met because it is transitive, the rule is commenced here because it would otherwise not apply when one intends to express the tree as the agent in the case of *pacyate*. In the case of *pacyate*, since there is no prior application [of the rule] when the tree is intended as the agent, this is the commencement [of the rule].

However, some maintain that *pac* (to cook) is a two-object verb (*dvikarmaka*) because the ripening of fruit is impossible without the ripening of the tree; thus, the tree is the "non-stated object" (*akathita-karman*). When one intends to express that very tree as the agent, then this [verb] undergoes the status of being like a transitive verb (*karmavad-bhāva*). But they say that in cases such as *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), it does not apply because [the tree] is not denoted [as the agent]. Thus, in the expression *udumbaraḥ phalaṃ pacati* ("the udumbara tree cooks the fruit"), during its state as a two-object verb, the understanding is: "that which possesses an activity residing in the udumbara tree conducive to the ripening of the fruit, which in turn is conducive to the ripening of the fruit. In its state as an object, the action characterized by the ripening of the udumbara tree [is understood].

That very [action] exists in the state of the agent, because there is the cognition that "the udumbara tree possesses an activity conducive to the ripening of fruit residing in the udumbara," and because that [activity] has the nature of ripening.

The rule *sṛjīyajyoḥ śyaṃstu* means that for these two [roots] which are transitive (*sakarmaka*), the agent (*kartṛ*) frequently behaves like the object (*karmavat*), and the suffix *śyan* is to be prescribed as an exception to *yaṅ*. Regarding *sṛj*, it should be stated that [the *śyan* suffix applies] only when the agent is motivated by faith (*śraddhā*). Example: *sṛjyate srajaṃ bhaktaḥ*. The meaning is: "The devotee produces a garland out of faith for the sake of the gods, etc. Why specify "motivated by faith"? Consider: *srajaṃ sṛjantyā tadaśādhi sādhu*. Here, the creation of the garland is solely for the purpose of enjoyment. Furthermore, by the presence of *śyan*, only *yaṅ* is superseded, but not *ciṇ*.

This is because the Bhāṣya states that [the rule] is for the sake of the *ciṇ* affix and the *ātmanepada* endings. For example: *asarji mālām* ("He was caused to create a garland") and *yujyate brahmacārī yogam* ("The religious student is joined to yoga"). In the latter case, the statement "yoga joins the religious student" (*yogo brahmacāriṇaṃ yunakti*) has the sense of "it connects him. Therefore, this [application of the rule] occurs when one intends to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the religious student.

"It should be stated that 'an agent whose action is similar to that of the instrument often behaves like the object' (*karaṇena tulyakriyaḥ kartā bahulaṃ karmavad iti vaktavyam*). In the examples *kaṇṭakā vṛkṣaṃ parivārayante* (the thorns surround the tree) and *kaṇṭakaiḥ parivārayati vṛkṣam* (he surrounds the tree with thorns), 'surrounding' (*vāraṇa*) means the prevention of contact with a harmful substance. The operation of the thorns is their complete contact [with the tree]. When the thorns are the agents, however, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is simply contact itself; the sense is that they cause [the tree] to possess a contact delimited on all sides. Because of the inclusion of the word 'often' (*bahula*), there is no fault in cases such as *sādhvasiś chinatti* (the sword cuts)."

"A prohibition must be stated for [roots] such as *sravati*. Water flows from a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*). Water flows from anthills (*valmīka*). Since the water is emerging, there is an application [of the rule] because the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is the same [as that of causing to emerge]. However, the author of the Bhāṣya says that in the case of "water flows from anthills," the meaning understood is "they emit" (*visṛjanti*); furthermore, in common usage, the word *visarga* is seen to have the sense of "giving. They say that precisely because the actions are different, there is no application of the *karmavat-bhāva* (the status of being treated like the object) here.

The meaning is that for the roots *bhūṣ* (to adorn), *kṛ* (in the sense of scattering), *kirādi* (roots beginning with *kṛ* such as *vṛt*), and *san* (the desiderative suffix), the affixes *yak* and *ciṇ*, as well as the augment *ciṇvad-iṭ*, do not occur except when the ātmanepada endings are used; rather, only the ātmanepada endings apply. Since the fruit of the action—namely, beauty—is observed in the object, these are actions residing in the object (*karmasthakriya*). The inclusion of the term *bhūṣā* (adornment) is for the sake of [excluding] those roots which lack the causative marker *ṇic*. Examples: *alaṅkurute kanyā svayam eva* (the maiden adorns herself); *alamakṛta* (she adorned herself). However, in the case of the causative form (*ṇyantatva*), the prohibition of those [affixes] is established by the Vārttika to be mentioned later. Example: *avakirate hastī svayam eva* (the elephant scatters [musth] upon himself); *avākīrṣṭa* (he scattered upon himself).

Someone scatters dust and the like upon an elephant; in that case, when the ease [of the action] is intended to be expressed, the elephant is the agent. The mat desires to be made by itself (*kaṭaḥ svayaṃ cikīrṣate*). It desired to be made (*acikīrṣiṣṭa*).

[Objection: Since the meaning of the suffix is [the object], in the case of a desiderative (*sannanta*), primacy belongs to the desire (*icchā*) alone; and since that [desire] resides only in the agent (*kartṛstha*), the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply here. [Response: To this they say: with respect to the action of *karoti* (to do), there is here the state of having an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*); and the primacy of *karoti* is based on the sense (*ārtha*), because the desire has that [action] as its purpose. The root *kṝ* and others belong to the sub-group *tudādi*. *girate* (he swallows). *agīrṣṭa* (he swallowed). *ādriyate*, *ādṛta*. The meaning is: "he becomes an object of respect. *Tap* (to heat) [is used] only when it has *tapas* (penance) as its object. (Pāṇini 1.3.26) 88. *tapas-tapaḥ-karma-kasya-eva* || 88 || [The rule applies only to *tap* when penance is its object.]

The *vṛtti* states: "In the case of the root *tap-* [meaning] 'to perform penance,' the agent of *tap-* shall be like the object because of the difference in the action; this is an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*). The *bhāṣya* says it is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). That has already been explained previously. [Thus: "The ascetic performs penance" (*tapyate tapas tāpasaḥ*). Since the agent undergoes the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*), it is also expressed [in the same way as the object]; therefore, in both cases, the nominative case ending is used.

It might be argued as follows: The word *tapaḥ* is derived from the Uṇādi suffix *-asun*, denoting the abstract action (*bhāva*). In the case of the sentence *tāpasena tapastapyate* ("The ascetic performs penance"), when the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the object (*karman*), we observe that the very action expressed by the root becomes the meaning of the object-suffix. Now, between an action and its object, there must be a distinction based on their relationship as the "accomplisher" (*sādhana*) and the "thing to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). However, in this instance, because no such distinction exists, it is untenable for the root and the suffix to have separate meanings. Furthermore, since it is stated that "penance is the object of someone," it would be contradictory to maintain that the objecthood belongs solely to the meaning of the root.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "The heating of a part is the action of heating. The meaning of this is that a specific kind of austerity consisting of knowledge is the action (*karman*), because the word "part" (*avayava*) is explained here as signifying "specific" (*viśeṣa*). Why [is it said] "the action of heating"? [Consider: "The goldsmith heats the gold."
The affixes *cak* and *ciṇ* occur after the roots *duh*, *snus*, and *nam*. || 89 ||

For these [roots], the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes do not occur when they function as both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*). Their application would otherwise follow from the extension of the rule regarding "behaving like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*). Examples include Bhāravi’s “*svayaṃ pradugdhe 'sya guṇair upasnutā*” (she yields herself through his virtues) and Māgha’s “*svayaṃ praṇamate 'lpe 'pi*” (she bows down herself even at a slight [insult]). This prohibition applies to the *yak* suffix after the root *duh* as well; however, for the *ciṇ* suffix, there is an option provided by another rule. Thus: *dugdhé gáuḥ svayám eva* (the cow milks herself); *adugdha gáuḥ svayám eva* (the cow milked herself). Regarding the form *adohi*, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the *ksa* suffix in the case of *ciṇ*. For the root *snū*: *prasnuté gáuḥ svayám eva* (the cow flows forth herself); *prāsnoṣṭa* or *prāsnāviṣṭa* (she flowed forth herself).

[Objection: But surely this prohibition applies to the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment just as it does to the *ciṇ* suffix itself, because in the rule *ciṇvat*, the suffix *vat* is understood to follow a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Since the prohibition of *ciṇ* is also an operation belonging to *ciṇ*, [the prohibition of *ciṇvadiṭ* follows]. [Reply: Not so. For in that context, the suffix *vat* is explained as following a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*). It is only the operation that occurs when *ciṇ* follows which is extended [by the *ciṇvat* rule]; the prohibition of *ciṇ* cannot possibly prohibit the extension of that [operation].

As for the argument that because the prohibition of *ciṇ* is not prescribed when *ciṇ* follows [the root], there is no extended application (*atideśa*) regarding its performance—on this point they say: it would be inappropriate to state that "the prohibition is not extended" when one ought to have said that "the extended application is not contradicted. In reality, however, regarding the statement "there is no extended application when that prohibition of *ciṇ* is to be performed or enjoined," what is intended by the relation that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is simply counter-correlativity itself. Thus, the prohibition of *ciṇ* does not, by way of being the counter-correlate, take the *ciṇvad-bhāva* as its object; that is to say, it does not have the *ciṇvad-bhāva* as its counter-correlate.

"In the prohibition [of the *ātmanepada*] for roots ending in *yak* and *ci*, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to include causative *ṇic*, *śri*, and *brū*. However, the followers of Bhāradvāja read: "The causative *ṇic*, *śranth*, *granth*, and *brū* when used in the *ātmanepada* and as intransitives [are included]. *Kārayate* (he causes to do). *Acīkarata* (he caused to cause to do). *Ucchrayate daṇḍaḥ* (the staff rises up). *Udaśiśriyata* (the staff was raised up). Because the fruit of the act of speaking is the manifestation of sound, it resides in the object (*karmastha*). *Śrathnāti granthaṃ Devadattaḥ* (Devadatta unties the knot). *Śrathnīte granthaḥ svayam eva* (the knot unties itself). *Aśranthiṣṭa granthaḥ* (the knot was untied). *Grathnāti ślokaṃ Devadattaḥ* (Devadatta composes a verse).

The verse strings itself together (*grathnīte ślokaḥ svayameva*). The verse was strung together (*agranthiṣṭa ślokaḥ*). Here, both *śranth* and *granth* from the *curādigaṇa* are included. Nor is the meaning already established by the mention of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), because it serves a purpose in the alternative where the suffix is absent due to its belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* group. [Examples: *granthate*; *śranthate*. In the *luṅ* (aorist), it is as before. [Example: *brūte kathā svayameva* (the story tells itself); *avocata kathā svayameva* (the story told itself).

Those verbal roots which are specified as being intransitive (*akarmaka*) when prescribed for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—when they possess an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) and thus enter a transitive state (*sakarmaka-daśā*), the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* would otherwise apply due to the rule of "acting like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*). These are therefore prohibited. For example: *vikurvate saindhavāḥ*. The meaning is "the horses gallop. When someone else causes them to gallop, they then possess the status of an object (*karman*). However, when one wishes to express an excellence of facility (*saukarya*), one says: *vikurvate saindhavāḥ svayam eva* ("the horses gallop by themselves"). [In the past tense: *vyakṛṣata*. [Another example: *utpucchayate gauḥ* ("the cow wags its tail").

Because the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is included within the root itself, there arises the application of the *karmavat-bhāva* (the treatment of the root as if it were in the passive), which results in the occurrence of the object (*karman*). For example: *puccham udasyati* (he tosses his tail) becomes *utpucchayate gauḥ* (the cow tosses her tail). Because the causative sense is included within the root, there is the application of *karmavat-bhāva*, resulting in the occurrence of the object; thus, when the causative sense is included, we have *utpucchayate gām*. When, however, the agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended to be expressed again, the form is as previously stated: *udapupucchata*. Due to the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, the suffixes *śap* and *caṅ* are applied.
Regarding the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*, according to the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*), the suffix *śyan* is used along with the Parasmaipada endings. (Pāṇini 3.1.90)

The roots *kuṣ* (in the sense of "pulling out") and *rañj* (in the sense of "coloring") take the suffix *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings when used in the reflexive (*karmakartṛ*) voice; the suffix *yak* and the *ātmanepada* endings do not apply here, as they are respectively set aside by this rule. Thus: *kuṣyati* or *kuṣyate pādaḥ* ("the foot pulls itself out"), *rajyati* or *rajyate vastram* ("the cloth colors itself"). The prescription of *śyan* is for the sake of ensuring the presence of the *num* augment and for the sake of the accent. Consequently, in the form *kuṣyantī jaṅghā*, the *num* is applied because of the rule *śap-śyanor nityam*. Furthermore, the initial syllable is acute-accented (*udātta*) according to the rule *ñ-nity-ādiḥ*.

However, if the *anudātta* (unaccented) quality of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix were applied, there would be the hearing of the *udātta* (accented) quality of the *yak*. And this [rule] operates only in the domain of *yag*, because a prohibition must be preceded by its application. Therefore, it does not apply in the domain of *syat* and other affixes belonging to the *liṅ* (optative) and *āśīr-liṅ* (precative).
[Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.162: *dhātoḥ* (after a root).

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending up to the end of the third chapter. Otherwise, there would be a fault regarding the substitutes for *la* (the verbal suffixes). For instance, since the word "dhātoḥ" (of the root) is present there, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "tasmād ity uttarasya" (that which follows from that), the meaning would be that *ti* and other suffixes occur immediately after a root. Consequently, there would be a failure to establish *ti* and other suffixes when they are separated by an affix (*vikaraṇa*), because *si* and other suffixes apply only while the element is still in the state of *la*. This is also the case for *śa* and other suffixes under the view that "sārvadhātuke" is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that the substitution of *l* (the *l*-affixes) must apply prior to the *vikaraṇas* because of its higher status; for the *vikaraṇas* are considered *nitya* (obligatory) due to their application regardless of whether [the *l*-substitution] has already occurred or not. Nor is there a lack of scope (*niravakāśatva*) for the *l*-substitutions, since they find scope in cases where there is *luk* or *ślu* elision of the *vikaraṇa*, as well as in the *liṅ* and *liṭ* tenses where the *vikaraṇa* does not arise at all. Likewise, if the substitution of *e* were prescribed for that which follows a verbal root, then by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("of the first of what follows"), there would be the undesirable consequence of replacing only the *t* with *e*; thus, to ensure a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*), one would have to assign the *śit* designation to it, resulting in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

In the view that [the rule] applies even before the Lādeśas (the substitutes for *loṭ*), since the aforementioned Paribhāṣā does not apply, its establishment occurs even without the status of being a *śit* (having *ś* as an indicatory letter), due to the force of the specific injunction (*vidhāna-sāmarthya*). Nor does there arise the contingency of it being a substitute for the final letter by the *al-ontya-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning the final letter), because there is no purpose in prescribing the substitution of *e* for *e*. In the same way, one should understand the following rules: *loṭo laṅvat*, *eruḥ*, *serhyapicca*, *anityaṃ ṅitaḥ*, *itaśca*, *tasthasthamipāṃ tāṃ taṃ tāmaḥ*, *liṅaḥ sīyuṭ*, and *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣu*. This is because, by virtue of being subsequent to the verbal root (*dhātu*), they would qualify that [root], and thus they do not apply when there is an intervention by a *vikaraṇa* (conjugational suffix).

It is said [in response]: likewise, because the mention of the term *dhātu* (root) is necessary in the definition of the technical name *ardhadhātuka*, otherwise there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *vṛkṣatvam*. Furthermore, in the rule *parasmaipadānām*, if the substitution of *a* were applied in place of the *tha* of the second person, it would result in the necessity of applying the property of being marked with *ś* (*śitva*). However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), by explaining the rule as "of the *tha* following a root," when the substitution of *a* is applied to the *tha* alone, the desired form is established through the application of *ato guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) for the resulting single substitute.

Nor, even in that case, can the status of being a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśatva) be established by the force of the maxim "the substitute is for the final" (alontyaparibhāṣā), because the prescription of the substitution of *a* for *a* would otherwise be purposeless; for [the rule] has its utility fulfilled by establishing a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) with *ṇal* and the other suffixes.

Nor does there arise the undesirable contingency of the augment *iṭ*; for the substitution of *a* is obligatory (*nitya*) because it applies both when [the condition] has occurred and when it has not. Once that [substitution] has taken place, the augment *iṭ* cannot apply because the condition of being followed by a consonant-group beginning with a semivowel (*valāditva*) no longer exists. Nor can it be argued that the substitution of *a* is non-obligatory due to the occurrence of a different word-form, on the grounds that once *iṭ* is applied, the substitution would affect the vowel *i*, whereas if *iṭ* is not applied, it would affect the letter *ṇ*. This objection is invalid because such cases are merely incidental; furthermore, the aforementioned defects do not arise, since rules such as those concerning *śap* are prescribed only when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows.

Even in cases such as *syāt*, [the rule applies] by resorting to the qualification that the suffix must be prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), as per the rule *lasya*. Now, one might object: would there not be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of [the substitution of] *ṇal* and other suffixes even in forms like *vindati*, because of the interpretation that [the rule applies] to a suffix prescribed after a verbal root that immediately precedes the root *vid*? Furthermore, in forms such as *ajakṣiṣyan* and *ajapāriṣyan*, would there not be the undesirable consequence of *jus* replacing *jhi* after the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*), because of the interpretation that [the rule applies] to a suffix prescribed after a reduplicated stem that immediately follows a verbal root? However, in the case of the rule *ātaḥ*, it should be interpreted as applying to a suffix prescribed after the vowel *ā* that immediately follows a verbal root.

Even if one were to explain it as "prescribed after a [stem] ending in the letter *ā*," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *apiban*. Therefore, it is established that the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*) extends through the third chapter.

The purposes [of this rule] are: (1) the non-occurrence of suffixes such as *tavya* from nominal stems (*prātipadika*); (2) the designation of "base" (*aṅga*); and (3) the designation of "verbal complement" (*upapada*). Among these, the first is not [the case]. This is because the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed by the rule *tayoreva* (Pāṇini 3.4.70) specifically for the meanings of "action" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*), whereas *kṛt* suffixes are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, and *tiṅ* suffixes are prescribed for the action, the object, and the agent. Since the instrumental means (*sādhana*) consisting of the agent and others are absent in nominal stems, those suffixes do not arise from them. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others, which are prescribed for the object and so forth, would likewise not arise from nominal stems.

By the force of the statement, that [term] functions only with respect to a factor (sādhana) dependent on an action expressed by another word; however, in the present case, since it is possible for the root to depend on a factor relative to an internal action expressed by itself, one does not resort to factors relative to an external action expressed by another word.

The second [alternative] is not [tenable], because the mention of "root" (dhātu) continues [in the rule] from the prescription of the *yaṅ* affix. Therefore, in forms such as *prāsthita*, even though the root together with its prefix has the meaning of "going," the designation of *aṅga* applies to the root alone and not to the aggregate of root and prefix. By this, the distinction regarding the augment *āṭ* and others is maintained; otherwise, if that [mention of "root"] did not continue in rules such as those for the *sya*-affixes, the designation of *aṅga* would not apply in cases like *kariṣyati*. Nor does it follow that the *ṇic* affix would apply to every root merely by virtue of the rule *cūrṇa-curādibhyo ṇic* and *dhātoḥ*, because the rule *hetumati ca* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its absence [in other cases].

This is because [the suffix *ṇic*] is prescribed for the sense of "making otherwise" (*anyathākaraṇa*) even when there is a causal agent (*hetumat*), since its application as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is already established. Now, one might argue that the mention of the *cur*-class (*curādi*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). However, this is not the case, as the rule is otherwise established by the purpose of [the rule] *prātipadikāddhātvarthe* (P. 3.1.27), which applies to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in the sense of verbal action (*dhātvartha*). Furthermore, there is no possibility of applying the suffix *ya* to mere roots in the case of the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyaḥ* (P. 3.1.27), for that would result in the redundancy of mentioning the *kaṇḍu*-class. This is because it was previously stated that their status as roots is established by the fact that the suffix *yak* is marked with the *k*-indicator (*kitva*). Moreover, since the desired result could be achieved from the rule *dhātoḥ* (P. 3.1.91) alone, and since it is more appropriate to interpret the connection in *kaṇḍvādibhyaḥ* as a coreferential construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—meaning "from the roots *kaṇḍu* etc."—rather than as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The third [alternative] is not tenable, because it is appropriate that only the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛt* and *upapada* constitute the governing rule (*adhikāra*), as it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to assume merely the status of being *svarita* in those cases. Nor can it be argued that this governing rule for "root" (*dhātu*) is intended for the purpose of the designation *ārdhadhātuka*; for if one were to explain it as "that which is prescribed after a root," there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *jugupsate* and *lūbhyām*. This objection should not be raised, because the desired result is established by relying on the restriction of the prescription itself—namely, that the term "prescribed after a root" applies only to that which follows the root as it is continued from the rule prescribing the *yaṅ* affix.

If there is such insistence that the operation of the word [the suffix] cannot be obtained without the mention of a second verb, then the mention of "the second verb" must be carried over from the rule *śamityaṣṭābhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.14). In this context, the term *upapada* refers to that which stands in the locative case. (Pāṇini 3.1.92)

In this section concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), that which is indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*) in a rule prescribing an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*) receives the technical designation "co-occurring word" (*upapada*). For example, in rules such as *karmaṇy-aṇ* ("the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a root when there is an object"), the term *karmaṇi* ("when there is an object") [is so designated]. Consequently, in examples like *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker"), words such as *kumbha* receive the designation of *upapada*. This is because they are specifically included by the word *karman* (object) [in the rule], and because it is impossible for a word's own form (*svarūpa*) to be grasped [by a rule] unless it is explicitly a technical term (*saṃjñā*). Nor should it be argued that the mention of the word *stha* (standing/located) is redundant, on the grounds that the requirement of being "indicated by the locative" would already be established by the word *saptamī* itself. [This is not the case, as the word *stha* serves to restrict the application to the specific sense of being located within the domain of the rule.]

In the case of examples such as *stambe ramaḥ* and *karṇejapaḥ*, where the locative case is heard, there would arise the undesirable consequence that only that which is explicitly indicated by the word "locative" (*saptamī*)—according to the rule *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ*—would receive the designation [of *upapada*]. Consequently, the designation would apply to the locative case ending alone, and not to the word ending in it; for this is a rule prescribing a designation (*saṃjñā-vidhi*). However, the compound is established only for that which follows it, by virtue of the maxim regarding semantic competency (*samartha-paribhāṣā*), since the locative ending alone lacks semantic competency. By the mention of the word *sthā* (in the rule *supi sthaḥ*), the designation is prescribed for what is indicated by the locative case; thus, the formation of *kumbhakāra* and similar forms is also accomplished.

In this context, the mention of "therein" (*tatra*) is for the purpose of indicating the domain (*viṣaya*). That is to say, "therein, within this governing rule" (*dhātvadhikāre*). Otherwise, there would be the disadvantage of having to rely on a governing rule for every individual sūtra, which would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*). In examples such as *āhara kumbham* ("bring the jar") and *karoti kaṭam* ("he makes a mat"), the word *kumbha* does not receive the designation of *upapada*, because it lacks semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) with the verb. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a large jar"), because the formation *mahākumbhakāraḥ* ("a maker of large jars") is indeed intended. Nor does it follow that one could form *mahāntaṃ kumbhakāraḥ*.

This is because the technical designation *upapada* is etymological; that is, a word uttered near [another] (*upa-uccarita*) is called an *upapada*. Furthermore, since this is a rule concerning words (*pada-vidhi*), the governing maxim regarding semantic compatibility (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) applies. Consequently, it is impossible for the pot (*kumbha*), which depends on the referent of the word "great" (*mahat*), to form a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) with an element ending in the suffix *-aṇ*.
A *kṛt* suffix [is called a *pratyaya*,] except for *atiṅ*. Pāṇini 3.1.93.

In this context, an affix other than *tiṅ* is designated as *kṛt*. Thus, the definition is: being an affix other than *tiṅ*, while falling under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for verbal roots (*dhātu*). Why say "other than *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*)? [Consider the example: *karoti*. This is to prevent the designation from applying to *tiṅ* affixes such as *tip*. It should not be argued that, even if the *kṛt* designation were prescribed for affixes following a root according to the view that the *dhātu-adhikāra* (the governing rule for roots) applies prior to the substitution of *l*-substitutes (*lādeśa*), there would still be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to *tiṅ* affixes because they are separated by *vikaraṇa* affixes. For even so, there would still be over-extension in cases such as those involving *luk*-elision of *vikaraṇas*.

Furthermore, because the *vikaraṇas* arise before an *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the *lakāra* would acquire the designation *kṛt*; consequently, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), there would be a fault regarding the *tiṅ* suffixes. Nor is the fault unavoidable even if one adopts the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *atiṅ* (non-*tiṅ*). This is because, by the force of that exclusion, the *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply; for it is only the *lakāra* that is to become a *tiṅ* which is introduced as the counter-correlative of the difference. For this very reason, in forms such as *kārayāṃcakāra*, the designation *kṛt* applies to the element ending in *ām*, since the *lakāra* itself has been elided there and thus lacks the status of being about to become a *tiṅ*.

Let it be granted that *tiṅ*-affixes have the designation *kṛt*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the designation *prātipadika* applying to them by the rule *kṛttaddhita-*, which would then trigger the addition of case-endings (*svādi*) starting with *su*; for since number (such as singularity) is already expressed by the *tiṅ* itself, those endings do not apply. Nor does this lead to the application of suffixes such as *aṇ* and others, because there is no connection with meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*). Furthermore, this is supported by the force of the separate mention of *tiṅ* in the rules *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* and *tiṅaśca*. Nor should it be argued that in forms like *pacati*, the suffix *tuK* would undesirably apply by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*; for in that rule, the word *dhātoḥ* ("of a verbal root") is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*), and what ends in *śa* (the *śatṛ* suffix) is not a verbal root. Thus, [the objection] cannot be maintained.

Even there, there is an intervention by the *śap* [suffix]; for even when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, the intervention still exists due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the preceding rule. True; the reality is that this is because [the condition] "not being a *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*) is simply not to be adopted.
Thus ends the fifth Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*.
*vā'sarūpo'striyām* || 94 || [Pāṇini 3.1.94] "In the case of feminine forms, a non-homogeneous suffix may optionally take the place of another."

In this context, a suffix that is dissimilar in form (*asarūpa*) to the general rule (*utsarga*) may serve as an exception (*apavāda*) and thus subvert the general rule, with the exception of those rules stated under the heading of "feminine" (*stryadhikāra*), where there is always subversion. The status of "feminine" is obtained because the word *strī* is marked with the *svarita* accent. However, if the meaning were simply "when the feminine is to be expressed," then in forms such as *labhyā*, the suffix *tavyat* would not occur in *lavitavya* because it has already been subverted [by the feminine suffix]. Since the general rule would be subject to constant subversion by the exception, this sūtra is commenced to ensure the optional application of the general rule. As it has been said:
"The statement regarding 'dissimilarity in form' is for the purpose of allowing the general rule to apply in cases where it would otherwise be subverted by an exception."

This might be the case: first of all, forms such as *tavya* are not examples [of this rule]. For verbal roots (*dhātu*) are of only two kinds: those ending in vowels (*ajanta*) and those ending in consonants (*halanta*). Among these, the suffix *yat* is prescribed after vowels and *ṇyat* after consonants. Since all possible cases are already covered by these two, the very fact that *tavya* and the others are prescribed [separately] establishes their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) through the force of their initial formulation. Nor can they apply in the domain of the *pacādyac* suffixes; for since the suffix *ac* is prescribed after all roots, the application of *ṇvul* and *tṛc* is also established by the force of that very rule.

It is said: [This rule] applies to the domain of [Pāṇini 3.1.135] *ig-upadha-* etc., for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both the suffix *ṇvul* and the suffix *tṛc*. Why does it say "asimilar" (*asarūpa*)? It is so that [the suffix] *ka*, prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.2.3] *ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ*, may always override the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the object [of the action]. Similarity is not determined by the presence of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Thus, one should understand that similarity exists between the two specific forms of the suffixes when they are divested of their indicatory letters. Why does it say "not feminine" (*astriyām*)? It is so that the suffix *ap*, prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.3.104], may always override the suffix *ktin* in the feminine.

Regarding this, those who follow the *Vṛtti* maintain that this prohibition applies only when both the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) pertain to women. Dīkṣita and others, however, hold that it applies even when only the exception pertains to women.
[Now for the section on] *kṛtya* suffixes. (95)

"It should be stated that [the rule] precedes *ṇvul*. The suffixes to be mentioned prior to the rule *ṇvultṛcau* (Pāṇini 3.1.133) are designated as *kṛtya*. This designation is subordinate to the designation *kṛt*. Why is it said 'prior to'? So that the designation *kṛtya* does not apply to *ṇvul*. Otherwise, by the rule *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.70), it would follow that *ṇvul* applies only in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the passive state (*bhāva*). But since the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) applies, *ṇvul* would apply only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). In reality, however, the very mention of *tṛc* in the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.169) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the jurisdiction of *kṛtya* begins precisely before *ṇvul*."

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the *tṛc* suffix would be included by the term "kṛtya" itself. Consequently, the *ṇvul* suffix would not attain the designation "kṛtya," as stated by the author of the Vṛtti:
