"The suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* [are kṛtyas]. (Pāṇini 3.1.96)

These suffixes shall occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*). The *t* in *kit* is for the purpose of causing the acute accent on the circumflexed vowel (*svarita*). The *r* in *rit* is for the purpose of making the penultimate syllable acutely accented when followed by *rit*; thus, the penultimate syllable of a stem ending in *rit* is acutely accented. For example: *karaṇīyam*. The long *ī* is acutely accented. According to the established doctrine that "the locative cases [of the suffixes] taught by Pāṇini refer to those ending in them," there is an addition of the rule: "The suffix *kelimara* should also be included. Examples: *pacelimā māṣāḥ* (these beans are fit to be cooked), *bhidelimāḥ saralāḥ* (these pine trees are fit to be split). The meaning is "to be cooked" (*paktavyāḥ*) and "to be split" (*bhettavyāḥ*). The letter *k* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitution; the letter *r* is for the purpose of the accent.

The interpretation that this [suffix] occurs in the sense of the agent as the object (*karmakartṛ*) is incorrect, because it is stated in the Bhāṣya that it occurs only in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the rule *vaseḥ stavyaḥ kartari ṇicca*: due to the *ṇit* designation, there is *vṛddhi*. Thus, from the root *vas*, we derive *vāstavyaḥ* in the sense of "one who dwells" (*vasati*). Alternatively, *vāstavyaḥ* means "that which exists on a site" (*vāstu*). According to the Bhāṣya, the suffix *yat* is applied here because the word belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. This is because a derivation can be explained in some way or another. As it has been said:
"They describe those means as things to be abandoned even after they have been adopted; for there is no fixed restriction regarding the means."

Nor is there a difference in accent. If the suffix is *tavya*, then by the rule *kṛtyokeṣṇuc*, there is udātta on the final syllable. But if it is *ya*, then by the rule *yayatoścātadarthe*, [the accent is the same], since there is no distinction.
[The rule] *aco yat* || 97 || applies.

The suffix *yat* shall occur after a verbal root ending in a vowel. Examples: *ceyam*, *jeyam*. By the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, there is *guṇa* substitution. Since it will be stated later that *ṇyat* occurs after roots ending in a consonant, this [rule for *yat*] applies when the root ends in a vowel; nevertheless, why is the mention of "ending in a vowel" (*ajanta*) made? It is so that [the suffix] may occur even after what was previously a root ending in a vowel. For example: *ditsyam*, *dhitsyam*. This is so that even though the root does not end in a vowel at the time the suffix is produced—because the elision of the *ā* (by *āto lopaḥ*) occurs precisely when one intends to express an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix—the suffix should still apply. And this has been explained in the commentary on the sūtra *na padānta...*.

Therefore, the author of the Nyāsa states that the mention of *aj* in the rule regarding the locative case of the subsequent element (*parasaptamī*) is for the sake of clarity alone. His intention is that, in forms such as *gaṇayati*, because the elision of the vowel *at* is conditioned by a subsequent factor, it is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), and thus there is no vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāvṛddhiḥ*).

"The addition of *taki*, *śasi*, *cati*, *yati*, and *janī* [to the list of roots taking the suffix *yat*] is prescribed. This rule is initiated to override [the application of] the suffix *ṇyat*. The reading *śaṃsīti* with an anusvāra is to be rejected, because it contradicts the rule *īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ*. [Examples are: *takyam*, *śasyam*, *catyam*, *yatyam*, *janyam*. Nor is this addition redundant on the grounds that the form *janyam* is identical to that derived from the root *jan* with *ṇyat*—where, by the rule *janivadhyośca*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies—because its purpose is specifically for the meaning 'a boat' (*nāv*) as in the rule *yato nāvaḥ*."

"Or rather, that which is to be stated is *hantervā*. [The word] *vadhyaḥ* means "to be killed" (*ghātyaḥ*). It is established by the suffix *yat* according to the rule *daṇḍādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.66), in the sense of "one who deserves killing" (*vadham arhati*). One should not say: "There would be the impossibility of forms such as *asivadhyaḥ* because there is no rule prescribing a compound," for that [compound] is established for the sake of words like *pādahāraka*. Do not say so; for it would result in a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). Since the suffix *yat* is treated as having an indicatory *t* (*tit*), it would follow that the acute accent (*svarita*) would fall on the final syllable of the word *asivadhya* (according to Pāṇini 6.1.185).

In a compound with a *kṛt*-derived word, however, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member applies; thus, the word *vadhya* is established as having its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). In reality, however, it is difficult to justify the suffix *yaṅ* after the word *asivadhya*, because the word *vadha* alone is listed in the *daṇḍādi* group, and because the extension of a rule to include what ends in a particular suffix (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited when that suffix is prescribed by a specific rule (*pratyayavidhi*).
After a consonant, [the augment *it* is added] following a reduplicated syllable. || 98 ||

The suffix *yat* is applied after a verbal root that ends in a labial (*pa-varga*) and has a short vowel as its penultimate (*a-du-padha*). This is an exception to the suffix *ṇyat*. Examples are *śapyam* and *labhyam*. It should not be argued that *ṇyat* might also apply here by the rule of "non-identical forms" (*vā-sarūpa-nyāya*), because the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) holds that "non-identity of form is not caused by the presence of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*)."
And [the substitution] of śakār and hakāra. || 99 ||
It is possible; it is endurable.
The roots *gada*, *mada*, *cara*, and *yama* take the affix *aṅ* when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes them.

The locative case is used in the sense of the ablative. The suffix *yat* is applied after these [roots] when they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). Alternatively, it may be said that *yat* occurs after these [roots] provided there is no connection with a prefix. Examples: *gadyam*, *madyam*, *caryam*. Regarding the root *car*, it should be stated that [the suffix *yat* is applied] even when preceded by *āṅ*, except in the case of "heavy" (*aguru*) [words]. Example: *ācaryodeśaḥ* (the instruction of a teacher). Why "except in the case of heavy"? Because in the word *ācārya*, the suffix *ṇyat* alone would apply. Nor should it be argued that this is already established by the rule *poradupadhāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.98); for the present rule is restrictive (*niyamārtha*), intended to prevent the application [of *yat*] after [roots] with prefixes. Consequently, in *prayāmyam*, the suffix *ṇyat* alone applies. Nor does this imply that [the term] *aniyamyasya* is illogical; otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in such expressions as *tvayā niyamyā nanu divyacakṣuṣā* ("Surely you, O divine-eyed one, are to be restrained").

Because of the usage in the *Vārttika*, "Therefore, there should be no restraint therein," it follows from inference that [the suffix] *yat* occurs even after the prefix *ni*. As for the word *niyama*, it is correct when the suffix *yat* is optional according to the rule "after *yama* with *sam* and *upa*" (*Pāṇini* 3.3.63); whereas the word *niyamya* is to be derived with the suffix *yat* [in the sense of the gerundive]. Nor should it be argued that, if the genitive of the agent were required due to its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, the instrumental third case in "by him" (*tena*) and "by you" (*tvayā*) would be difficult to obtain; for since the term *kṛtya* does not apply here, the rule "the *kṛtya* suffixes denote the agent" (*Pāṇini* 3.4.71) does not operate. Rather, the instrumental case is justified as expressing the instrument.

Alternatively, one should understand that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by relying on the opinion that the root *yam* is included in the list beginning with "niyamayan" (as in the rule *yamo'pariveṣaṇe mit*), even though it has already reached its conclusion [in the preceding rule]. Or rather, let there simply be the suffix *ṇyat*; however, because it is preceded by a technical term (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution]—but this is questionable, as it is a strained interpretation. Furthermore, if "by you" (*tvayā*) is taken as the instrument (*karaṇa*), it would entail the necessity of supplying an agent (*kartṛ*). This would require assuming that the sense of the *ṇic* causative suffix is not intended, and that the principle "because it is preceded by a technical term" is being invoked as a last resort when no other way out exists. [The words] *avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* [are derived from the roots] *vad*, *paṇ*, and *vṛ* respectively, in the senses of "blameworthy," "to be sold," and "prohibition. (Pāṇini 3.1.101)

These [terms] are formed as nipātanas (irregularly prescribed forms) for three specific meanings in their respective order. When the prefix *nañ* is present with the root *vad*, both suffixes *yat* and *kyap* are applicable by rule (*supīti yat-kyapoḥ*). This nipātana is for the purpose of two restrictive rules: that *yat* alone is used, and that it is used only in the sense of censure (*garhā*). Thus, *avadyam* means "sinful" or "blameworthy. Why specify "censure"? Consider *anudyam* (not to be mentioned), which refers to the names of one's elders. Here, only *kyap* is used. Even though there is no censure involved, it is because the name is unfit to be uttered; for the Smṛti states, "One's own name and the name of one's elder [should not be pronounced]. *Paṇyā gauḥ* ("the cow for sale") means "to be traded. *Pāṇyam* is something else; it means "fit for praise."

Nor should it be argued that because the word *paṇitavya* is common to both meanings, how can that which has the sense of praise be excluded; for its meaning is restricted by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). It is said: "The formation of nouns (*nipātana*) serves to secure the attainment of verbal roots, suffixes, and tenses, as well as restriction, and for the sake of conventional usage regarding secondary suffixes (*anubandha*) and modifications."

Because of this statement: "A maiden is *varyā* (to be chosen) by a hundred [suitors]," since there is no restriction regarding those who seek her hand. The suffix *yat* is applied to the root *vṛṅ*, because the sense of non-restraint (*anirodha*) is more appropriate when expressing the meaning of suitability (*saṃbhakti*); such is the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*). As for the root *vṛ* (to choose), it will be stated that the form is *vṛtyā*. Here, at the end of the word *varyā*, the reference is without a case-ending; it is not a *dvandva* compound. Therefore, the irregular form (*nipāta*) *varyā* is used only in the feminine. In the masculine, however, the suffix *ṇyat* is used: *vāryā ṛtvijaḥ* ("the priests are to be chosen"), as stated in the *Vṛtti*. Some, however, maintain that it is indeed a *dvandva* compound, citing the usage of Bhaṭṭi: *sugrīvo mama varyo'sau* ("this Sugrīva is my choice"). *Vahyam* refers to the instrument. 102.

By means of this, one carries; thus, *vahyam* refers to a cart (*śakaṭa*). In the sense of the object (*karman*), however, it is *vāhyam*. Because it ends in the letter *h*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied. The meaning is "that which is to be carried.
[The word] *aryaḥ* [is used] for a master and a Vaiśya. (103)

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat* which would otherwise apply because the word ends in *ṛ*. It should be stated that in the word *svāmin*, the final syllable is udātta. Why [is the example] *svāmī*? [Consider] *āryo brāhmaṇaḥ*; the meaning is "one who is to be attained.
Regarding the rule *upasaryā kālyā prajane* (Pāṇini 5.2.93): [the word *upasaryā* means] "fit for breeding" (*kālyā*).

In the context of *prajana*, meaning "conception" or "the taking of a fetus," the word *kālyā* means "having reached the proper time. This is based on the rule *tad asya prāptam* (Pāṇini 5.1.12), which remains in force, followed by the suffix *yat* after a word denoting time (*kāla*). Thus, *upasaryā gauḥ* ("a cow fit for breeding") means a cow fit to be approached by a bull for the purpose of impregnation. Why mention *prajana* and so forth? Consider *upasāryā kāśī*: it means "fit to be reached.
*Ajaryaṃ saṃgatam* ("an undecaying union"). 105.

When the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *jṛ* preceded by the negative particle *nañ* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), it functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the word with which it is connected (*saṃgata*). Therefore, the usage of that connected word must also be expected [in the same construction]. For this reason, Bhaṭṭi [uses] "Make the noble Rāma’s old age (*āryeṇa rāmārmajaryaṃ*) pass quickly" (*saṅgataprayoga*). However, in Kālidāsa’s usage—"Old age (*jarasā*) taught what is not to be aged (*ajarya*) by deer"—that [connected word] must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). Some, however, say that in the case of the word *ajarya*, where the absence of aging is the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) in connection [with the deer], there is a non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*). That is not correct.

For from the meaning of the Sūtra, there is obtained the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) of a specific cognition produced by non-synonymous words joined together; otherwise, the application of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional) would be unavoidable. Nor does the occurrence of redundancy in the usage of Bhartṛhari constitute a sublation [of this view], since in that case it is possible for the word to function as a mere qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
[Pāṇini 3.1.106: "After the root *vad*, when a *sup*-ending word follows, [the suffix] *kyap* is also applied."

The term *anupasarge* (in the absence of a prefix) carries over [from the previous rule]. From the subsequent sūtra, the word *bhāve* (in the sense of an abstract action) is drawn down [to this point]. After the root *vad*, the suffix *kyap* shall occur in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), and it shall also occur after roots beginning with *cha*. When a nominal stem (*sup*) other than a prefix (*upasarga*) is the attendant word (*upapada*). Examples: *brahmodyam* (the recitation of the Veda). Due to the *kit* designation, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). In the case of *yat*, we have *brahmavadyam*. The meaning is "the speaking of the *brahman*, i.e., the Veda. Others hold that this suffix occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*). However, according to the natural sense of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the subsequent sūtra, the mention of *bhāva* is for the sake of the following rules. But when a prefix is present, we have *anuvādyam* and *apavādyam*. The usage of *kyap* in forms such as *anūdyā* is occasional and incorrect. *bhuvo bhāve* || 107 || (After the root *bhū*, the suffix *kyap* occurs in the sense of an abstract action.)

What could [the suffix] *kyap* be? "The state of Brahman" (*brahmabhūyam*). The word "state" (*bhāva*) is for the sake of what follows; for since the root *bhū* is intransitive, there is nothing from which it could be excluded—this is the Bhāṣya. Kaiyaṭa says that although the root meaning "to reach" (*prāpti*) is transitive, it is not present first [in the mind], and furthermore, because [the rule] does not apply to the object of time and so forth.
*hanas-tac* || 108 ||

The suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *eti*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*, provided they are followed by a case-ending (*sup*) other than an upasarga, and there is the substitution of *t* for the final letter [of the root]. It should be stated that [the feminine suffix] *cit* is added; because it is marked with *cit*, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable. The killing of a Brahmin is *brahmahatyā*. The femininity [of the word] is due to the fact that gender is based on worldly usage (*lokāśrayatvāt*). However, regarding the Vedic usage cited in the Bhāṣya as *dasyuhatyāya*, Kaiyaṭa states that its neuter gender is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
[Roots ending in] *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, or *ṝ*, as well as *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*, take the suffix *kyap*. (Pāṇini 3.1.109)

*ityaḥ*, *stutyaḥ*, and *vṛtyaḥ*. [In the rule for the suffix] *ṇyat*, there is the inclusion of the root *vṛ* (meaning "to choose"), but not *vṛṅ* (meaning "to choose as a bride"). This is because, due to its association with *īḍ* and *vand*, only *vṛṅ* is taken [in the rule *īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ*], as both *īḍ* and *vand* are *ātmanepada* roots. However, from *vṛ* [the form is] *vāryā ṛtvijaḥ* ("the priests are to be chosen"). [The form] *ādṛśyaḥ* [is derived from] the root *dṛś* preceded by *ā*; this is because the root *dṛś* is used only when preceded by *ā*. In all these cases, the augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*. [The forms are] *śiṣyaḥ* and *juṣyaḥ*. In *śiṣyaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ī* by the rule *śāsaidaṅhaloḥ*, and the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*. *Juṣyaḥ*.

The repetition of the term *kyap* here, even though it was already mentioned previously, is for the purpose of indicating its distinction from the former rule. By this, it is established that the former [rule] applies to the feminine gender even in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the suffix *ṇyat* in the word *avaśyastutya* by virtue of the rule *orāvaśyake*; for the suffix *kyap* is established there by means of a statement regarding "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). However, if the sole purpose of the repeated mention of *kyap* were indeed this [establishment of the feminine], then one should understand that the property of being marked with *c* (*cittva*) is based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*).

"There is an addition [to the rule] for the word *ājya* when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), derived from the root *añj* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. The root *añj* means 'to manifest' and so forth. By virtue of the principle of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). There is elision of the nasal according to the rule *aniditām...*. Thus, that by which one anoints (*añjati*) is called *ājya*. Nor is there any impossibility regarding the lengthening of the vowel, because of the presence of the prefix *āṅ*. If the suffix *ṇyat* were used instead, there would be no elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*). Nor does the status of being a word (*padatva*) following *āṅ* entail the occurrence of an avagraha (separation in recitation); for the makers of the word-lists (*padakāra*) are not to be followed by the grammatical rules, as it is accepted that the grammatical rules must follow the word-lists. Indeed, the *saṃhitā* (the continuous text) alone is of non-human origin (*apauruṣeyī*)."

The division of words (*padaccheda*), however, is a human [convention]. For this very reason, where there is no certainty regarding the meaning, there is no *avagraha* (separation). As it has been said: "haridruranavagṛhya" (the word *haridru* is not separated), because of the doubt as to whether it is the word *hari* or the word *harit*.
[This is also the case for] a word ending in *ṛ* in the penultimate syllable, except for the roots *kṛp* and *cṛt*. (Pāṇini 6.4.110)

The suffix *kyap* is applied after verbal roots ending in short *ṛ*, provided they are distinct from *kḷp* and *cṛt*, and have a short vowel (*ṛ*) as their penultimate letter (*upadhā*). Examples: *vṛtyam*, *vṛdhyam*. Because the suffix is marked with *k* (*kit*), Guṇa substitution does not occur. Why "distinct from *kḷp*" (*aklṛpi*)? [Counter-examples: *kalpyam*, *cartyam*. In these cases, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied and Guṇa occurs. Why "short" (*tapara*)? [Counter-example: *kīrtyam*. In the alternative view where the causative suffix *ṇic* is absent, *ṇyat* is applied; however, when *ṇic* is present, *acoyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97) applies. The suffix *kyap* is also applied after the root *khana* preceded by *ī*. (111)

And *tkpap*: *kheyam*. Here is the commentary: the short vowel *i* alone should be prescribed [as the substitute]. For there is no difference in the resulting form, as it would be established by the rule *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87). Nor is there a risk of the application of *tuk*—as in *adhītya* and similar forms—on the grounds that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of *i* for *i-i*] is "not yet established" (*asiddha*) by the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.86); because that rule declares that only a single substitute occurring between the end of a word and the beginning of a word is "not yet established. Otherwise, in *vṛkṣecchatram*, there would result the obligatory application of *tuk* based on the short vowel [by Pāṇini 6.1.71], since the optional application [of *tuk*] by the rule *dīrghātpadāntādvā* (Pāṇini 6.1.75) is what is actually desired.

However, some maintain that by means of a *praśleṣa* (conjoined) reading, the second *ikāra* is prescribed to block the application of the *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) under the rule *ye vibhāṣā*, which would otherwise apply because it is subsequent. They argue that the scope of *ātvam* under *ye vibhāṣā* is when [the suffix] *khak* is present; the scope of *itvam* is in the absence of *ātvam*; but in the case where *ātvam* applies, since both would result, *ātvam* alone would prevail due to its posteriority. This is not correct, because *itvam* is *antaraṅga* (internal) as it is taught in conjunction with *kyap*, whereas *ātvam*, being prescribed when a suffix beginning with *yakāra* follows, is *bahiraṅga* (external).

Furthermore, there can be no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between an internal (*antaraṅga*) and an external (*bahiraṅga*) rule. Nor should it be argued that because the locative case in *ye* is taken as a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), the substitution of *āt* lacks a subsequent cause (*paranimitta*) and is therefore internal; for Kaiyaṭa maintains that in this instance, the locative is properly understood as a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*).
[Pāṇini 3.1.68: *bhṛño’saṃjñāyām*.

*Bhṛtyāḥ* means servants; that is, those who are to be supported. Regarding the rule *samaśca bahulam*, we have *saṃbhṛtyāḥ*; in the alternative case, *sambhāryāḥ*. Now, because of the proximity of the prohibition *na ca saṃjñāyām*, this [prohibition] would apply only to the scope of the present sūtra; consequently, in the case of a name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *kyap* would be unavoidable by the rule *samajanipada...*. Thus, the word *bhāryā* would not be established. Therefore, it must be stated that by the force of this very prohibition, the prohibition of *kyap* applies even to that which would otherwise be obtained through another rule.

This is because it is logically consistent as a prohibition against the designation "woman. The term *bhāryā* refers to a Kṣatriya; for, by way of etymological derivation (*karmavyutpatti*), a proper noun (*saṃjñāpada*) refers to the bearer of that name (*saṃjñin*).

Objection: Should it not be taught that immediately after the rule *samaja-samudra-* (Pāṇini 3.3.69), the rule *na striyām* (3.3.70) should follow? For, according to that, since the governing heading *striyām* (3.3.94) applies to the positive injunction, the suffix *kyap* would be used in *bhṛtyā* because it refers to a technical (śāstrīya) feminine; whereas in the prohibition, since *stanakeśavatī* (a woman possessing breasts and hair) refers to a worldly (laukika) feminine, the prohibition of *kyap* would apply, and thus the suffix *ṇyat* would result in the form *bhāryā*. Reply: Not so, for that would result in a split of the sūtras (*sūtrabheda*). It is said: in the sūtra *saṃjñāyām*, there is the carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "state" (*bhāva*) from the preceding rule *vrajayajorbhāve kyap* (3.3.98).
Since the word *bhāryā* is derived as an object (*karman*), there is no occasion for the application of *kyap* there.

Alternatively, in the rules prescribing [the suffix], the word *saṃjñā* is not a *karmasādhana* (an action-noun denoting the object), but rather a *bhāvasādhana* (an action-noun denoting the state). Therefore, if a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is understood from that which ends in the suffix, then the suffix is applied. And since the word *bhṛtyā* does not denote a housewife, the suffix *kyap* is not used. Thus says the Vārttika: "Because it is seen to be masculine in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the form *bhāryā* is not established by those [rules]; since the scope for the suffix denoting a state (*bhāva*) exists in the feminine, *bhāryā* is thus established."

Alternatively, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). As it has been said: "Or rather, it is recorded in the tradition that the kṛtya suffixes are applied diversely when forming technical names."

Just as "bhitti" is [derived] from the root *bhid* ending in a short vowel (*ajantāt*), so too [is it derived] from a root ending in a consonant (*halantāt*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulakāt*). Alternatively, in the sense of "wall," the suffix *ktin* is applied in place of *aṅ*. Some, however, say that the suffix *kyap* is applied after the long-voweled root *bhṝ* (from which *bibharti* is formed), while *kyap* is applied only to *bhṛ* belonging to the Tudādi class; for they maintain that when a specific marker (*anubandha*) is mentioned, it does not include a root with a different marker. *Mṛjor vibhāṣā* || 113 || [The suffix *kyap* is optionally applied after the root *mṛj*.]

The word *mṛjaya* is formed with the suffix *kyap*. In the alternative case, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, resulting in *mārgya*. There is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) for the root *mṛj*, and by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for the final consonant.

The words *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *mṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kupya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, and *avyathya* are [formed as] *nipātana*s (irregularly formed words). 114. *rājasūya-sūrya-mṛṣodya-rucya-kupya-kṛṣṭapacya-avyathyāḥ* || 114 ||

These [words] are derived as irregular forms (nipātana). [The term *rājasūya* means] that which is to be pressed (*sotavya*)—that is, to be produced by means of pressing—by the king. Because we see such usages as "he buys the king" (*rājānaṃ krīṇāti*), *soma* refers to the plant itself; it is called *sūya* because the soma-plant is pressed or crushed therein, thus forming a locative *kyap* suffix. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Although the *Rājasūya* consists of sixteen principal rites, including animal sacrifices, *iṣṭis*, and *soma* sacrifices, even a connection with only one part [of the whole] serves as the basis for the application of the name.

In such cases as "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," it is observed that the word *vaiśvadeva* refers to eight sacrifices, even though the term *viśvadeva* (all-gods) applies only to one part [of them]. *Sūrya* is derived from the root *sṛ* in the sense of "to move" (*sarati*), meaning "the mover"; the change to *ū* is by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Alternatively, it is derived from *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*), belonging to the *tudādi* class; it impels (*suvati*) the worlds toward their tasks. The suffix *kyap* and the augment *ruṭ* are by way of irregular derivation. From the prefix *mṛṣā* alone, the root *vad* takes the suffix *kyap* necessarily in the sense of the object; therefore, the suffix *yat* does not apply here. This word follows the gender of the noun it qualifies (*viśeṣyaliṅga*).
Regarding *kṣīra* and *payas*, although they both denote milk, let there be today a "false speech" (*mṛṣodya*) concerning this multiplicity of meanings within a single subject.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "the statement that it expresses two meanings should be called a false utterance (*mṛṣodya*). The qualities of height and beauty are false utterances (*mṛṣodyāḥ*). Regarding *rucya*: it is pleasing (*rocate*), thus *rucya*. Amara states: "that which is beautiful is *rucya*. Regarding *kupya*: it is used when forming a specific name (*saṃjñāyām*). Anything other than gold and silver is *kupya*. There is the substitution of *ku* for the initial [of the root] *gup*. Regarding *kṛṣṭapacya*, there is an udātta accent on the final syllable when it functions as both object and agent (*karmakartari*). Those that ripen by themselves in a plowed field are *kṛṣṭapacyāḥ*. [As in: "May my crops be both those that ripen in plowed fields and those that ripen in unplowed fields. When the agent is pure [not functioning as object], they are *kṛṣṭapākyāḥ*. *Avyathya* means that which does not suffer distress (*na vyathate*).
The roots *bhid* and *vyadh* take the suffix *naṅ* when meaning "to flow."

The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *bhid* and *ujjh*, and there is also the substitution of *dh* for the root-final *j* in *ujjh*. Thus, that which breaks the bank is *bhidyaḥ*; that which abandons the water is *udhyaḥ*. Because the rule "that which begins with *a* and ends in *a*" is not universal (*anitya*), the word *bhidyapada* (as a compound) takes the prior position [in the copulative compound]. Why is it said "in the sense of a river" (*nade*)? [Observe: *bhettā* (the breaker) and *ujjhitāḥ* (those who have abandoned).
Under the asterisms Puṣya and Siddha. || 116 ||
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *puṣ* and *sidh* when used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, that in which objects flourish or succeed is called *pūṣpaḥ* or *sidhyaḥ*.
The suffix *kvi* is applied after the roots *vipūya*, *vinī*, and *jī* when followed by the words *muñja*, *kalka*, and *hali* respectively. || 117 ||

The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *pūj*, *nij*, and *ji*. *Vipūya* refers to *muñja* grass; it is that which must be purified for the purpose of making ropes and the like. *Vinīya* refers to a medicinal paste (*kalka*), or specifically a ground medicinal substance. Regarding the word *kalka*, the *Mahābhārata* begins by stating, "Sin is not *kalka*; study is not *kalka*," and concludes, "those very things when corrupted by one's disposition (*bhāva*) are *kalka*. Furthermore, the lexicon (*koṣa*) states, "*Kalka* means sin in the sense of a sinful intent. *Jitya* refers to a *hāli* (a plowshare); it is that which is to be dragged by force. It is a wooden wedge used for leveling the furrows. In these cases, what [is the meaning]? Elsewhere, it is simply that which is to be done. For example: *vipavyam*, *vineyam*, and *jeyam*.
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the root *grah* when preceded by the prefixes *prati* and *api*.

It should be stated that [the suffix *ya*] occurs in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). [The forms] *mattasya na pratigṛhyam*, *anyatra pratigrāhyam*, and *apigrāhyam* [are examples]. And [the suffix *ya* occurs] after the word *pada* when it means "not one's own master," "an outsider," or "one belonging to an opposing faction. (Pāṇini 3.1.119)
The word *pada* (foot/step) can be *avagṛhya* (separable) or *pragṛhya* (unseparable). The word *gṛhya* means one who is not independent (*asvairī*), that is, one who is dependent on another.
Birds and deer that are attached to their nests or dwellings are called *chekāḥ*, and they are also *gṛhyakāḥ*.

Thus says Amara. *Grāmagṛhya* means "outside the village," as it is held outside of it; because the term is specified in the feminine gender, it does not apply to the masculine or neuter. *Pakṣya* means "belonging to a side" (*pakṣa*); the suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. *Āryagṛhya* means "one who is held by the Āryas," that is, one who has taken refuge in their faction. Regarding such a person, Kālidāsa wrote: *tam āryagṛhyaṃ nigṛhītadhenuḥ*. [The rule] *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ* [is now introduced].
*kṛtya* (to be done), *vṛṣya* (to be rained); in the alternative [sense], *ṇyat*: *kārya* (to be made), *varṣya* (to be rained).
And a vehicle on a leaf. || 121 ||

The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *yuj* to form *patra* and *vāhana*, with the change of *j* to *g*. This rule is intended to exclude the application of the suffix *ṇyat*; for the forms could have been established by the *taddhita* suffix [ṭhak] prescribed in the rule "tadvahati rathayuga... (Pāṇini 4.4.76).
On the new moon day, [the sacrifice] may optionally [be performed]. 122.

Now, what is elided here? Is it the optional *vṛddhi* when the suffix *yat* is applied, or the optional shortening when the suffix *vyat* is applied; or is it the two composite wholes [the word-forms] in which the distinction between base and suffix has vanished? Not the first, because in the rule *amāvāsyāyā vā*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the word *amāvāsyā* not being mentioned [as the base]; for by the mention of a derivative form (*vikṛti*), the original base (*prakṛti*) is not included. Furthermore, because of the statement *yatonāvaḥ*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the second member of the compound, whereas it is precisely the circumflex (*svarita*) on the final syllable that is desired. Not the second [alternative].

Even if the accentuation and the secondary suffix (taddhita) were established by this rule, it would not apply here because it contradicts the governing context. Nor is the latter alternative [the case], because the svarita accent is untenable when a suffix beginning with *ti* is included in the technical term *pratyaya*. Do not say so; for the short vowel is prescribed as an optional substitution (*nipātana*) in the case of the suffix *ṇyat*. Furthermore, by the maxim of "modification of one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the word *āmāvāsyā* is also considered a modification [of *amāvāsyā*]. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that this word should have been read only in the section on the suffix *ṇyat*.

The words *chandasin*, *niṣṭarkya*, *devahūya*, *praṇī*, *unnī*, *ucchiṣya*, *marya*, *tartṛ*, *adhvaryu*, *khanya*, *khānya*, *devayajyā*, *pṛcchya*, *pratiṣīvya*, *brahmavādya*, *bhāvya*, *stāvya*, *upacāyya*, and *pṛḍa* [are formed with the suffix -ya]. || 123 ||

These [words] are treated as irregular formations (*nipāta*). The meaning is that in the case of *niṣṭarkya*, there is a reversal of the initial and final [elements] of the root *kṛ*; that is, in the formation of the word *kṛt* (as in *tarku* and so forth), the letter *k* becomes the final element and the letter *t* becomes the initial element. The suffix *ku* in *kṛti* is an *uṇādi* suffix. Regarding this, there is a verse from the *Ślokavārttika*:
"One should know that in *niṣṭarkya* there is a transposition; the substitution of *ṣ* for *nis* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
In *upacāyya*, the two [elements], namely the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *āy* for *ai*, are treated as irregular formations."
The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after one [root], and the suffix *kyap* occurs after four; the suffix *yat* is prescribed after four [roots].
The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after one [root], the word *yaś* occurs after two, the suffix *kyap* occurs after two, and the rule for *ṇyat* applies to four.

From the root *kṛt* preceded by *ni*, although *kyap* would have been expected, *ṇyat* is applied; there is a transposition of the letters *ka* and *ta*, and the *s* of the prefix becomes *ṣ*. Thus: "One desiring cattle piles the *niṣṭarkya*. In the group of four beginning with *devahūya*, *kyap* is added to the four roots; because of the *kit* suffix, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Due to the difference in prefixes, there is a distinction in the forms of the root *nī*. In the group of four beginning with *maryādā*, *yat* is applied; by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the first syllable is udātta-accented. In *khānya*, *ṇyat* is applied. In *devayajyā*, the suffix is *yak*. In the pair beginning with *āpṛcchyā*, *kyap* is applied; due to the *kit* suffix, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the absence of *guṇa*.

In the group of four beginning with *brahmavādya*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied. The word "four" (*catur*) here ends in the suffix *suj*; the meaning is that which is prescribed four times. *Upacāyya* is a nipātana (irregular formation) when the word *pṛḍa* follows as the second member. Regarding the statement "it should be stated [that this applies] to *hiraṇya*," [the form] *upaceyapṛḍam* is different; [the root] *mṛḍ* means "to be gracious," and from *pṛḍa* (meaning "to crush"), since it has an *ig-upadha* (a light vowel in the penultimate), the suffix *ka* is applied.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or *hal*.

The sixth case ending is used in the sense of the fifth case ending. The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* and those ending in a consonant (*hal*). It should not be argued that only the root *ṛ* (meaning "to go") is intended here; for the term *hal* is included to indicate the inclusion of phonemes in general, as evidenced by the rule stating "the subsequent operation" (*paraṃ kāryam*), and by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in rules such as *īḍavanda-*. Otherwise, the application of *ṇyat* after the root *vṛdh* would be unestablished. Examples: *kāryam*, *varṣyam*.

Regarding the rule *pāṇau sṛjer ṇyad vācyaḥ*: this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kyap* which would otherwise apply by virtue of the rule *ṛdupadhāt*. Thus, *pāṇibhyāṃ sṛjyate* yields *pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ* (a rope released by the hands). From the rule *samavapūrvācca*, we have *samavasargyā*. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after the roots *lap* and *dambh* as well; this is an exception to the suffix *yat* prescribed by the rule *por adupadhāt*. Examples include *apalāpyam* and *apadābhyam*. The root *dambh* acquires the status of a verbal root (*dhātubhāva*) by the force of a Vārttika. An example is *viṣṇur gopā adābhyaḥ* ("Viṣṇu is the protector, unassailable"), based on such usages as *na mā naśanti na dabhāti taskaraḥ* ("They do not destroy me, nor does the thief deceive me").

The author of the Vṛtti, however, having read "larpi" after "rapi" in the sūtra beginning with "āsuyi," states that the inclusion of "dabh" is effected by the letter "ca"; this contradicts what has been stated in the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika.
Or [it is used] in the sense of "necessity" (avaśyaka). || 125 ||

*Āvaśyakam* means "inevitability" (*avaśyaṃbhāva*). The suffix *vuñ* is applied because the word belongs to the *manojñādi* group. For indeclinables, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) when any *bha*-suffix follows. When this meaning is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇyat* is added after a verbal root ending in a nasal (*upadhmanīya*/*anusvāra*). This is an exception to the rule *aco yad*. Examples: *lāvyam*, *pāṇyam*. There is *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *aco ñṇiti*; then the substitution of *av* for *au* occurs by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*. In some cases, the word *avaśya-* is also employed for the sake of clarity: *avaśyalāvyam*. By the rule *lumpedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye*, the letter *m* is elided. A compound is formed because the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.

Nor does this result in the undesirable consequence of the final vowel being udātta by virtue of the rule on compound endings; for the desired result is established through the specific grammatical prescription (nipātana) that the original accent of the second member is retained in the list beginning with "mayūravyaṃsaka."
And [the roots] *āsu*, *yu*, *pi*, *ra*, *pitṛ*, *pā*, and *cam* [have the augment *iṭ* in the perfect tense]. 126.

From the root *su* preceded by *ā*, meaning "to press," we derive *āsāvya*. From *yu* meaning "to mix," we derive *yāvya*. However, the root *yuñ* meaning "to bind" is not included here because it possesses an *anubandha*. The inclusion of these four roots beginning with *upa* is for the purpose of superseding the application of the suffix *yat* prescribed by the rule *poradupadhāt*. Examples: *vāpyam*, *rāpyam*, *trāpyam*, *cāmyam*.
[The suffix *yat* is applied] after *ā-nī* when the object is not permanent: *ānāyya*. (Pāṇini 3.1.127)
Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:
"If it is argued that the *ānāyya* fire is non-eternal because it is established in the *dakṣiṇāgni*, one should know that it exists in a single source; otherwise, it would be merely *āneya*."
If the term "falling" (*nipātana*) were stated merely as "impermanent," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to objects such as a jar;

therefore, it must be specified as "in the *dakṣiṇāgni*. Even in that case, it should be stated as "having a single source" (*ekayoni*). That *dakṣiṇāgni* which is brought from the *gārhapatya* fire together with the *āhavanīya* is the one with a single source. Its impermanence is due to its not being continuously kindled. However, in the case of that [fire] which is brought from the house of a Vaiśya or elsewhere, this "falling" does not apply; such is the meaning. For it is heard in scripture that there is an option regarding the sources of the *dakṣiṇāgni*: "from the house of a wealthy Vaiśya, from a frying pan (*bhrāṣṭra*), or from the *gārhapatya*. Thus, when the *dakṣiṇāgni* is carried forth after being taken from the *gārhapatya*, [it is subject to this rule].
"Having brought him there," according to Amara.
*Praṇāyyaḥ* is used in the sense of "not approved. || 128 ||

*Saṃmati* means being an object of affection. *Praṇāyya* refers to a thief, because he is unworthy of affection. *Saṃmati* also means the desire for enjoyment; *praṇāyya* refers to a pupil, meaning one who is dispassionate. *Praṇeya* has another meaning.

[The suffix -yaṅ occurs] after the roots *pā*, *sāṃ-ṇī*, *ni-kā*, *dhā*, and *mā* when followed by the words *āna*, *havis*, *nivāsa*, and *sāmidhenī* respectively: *pāyya*, *sāṃnāyya*, *nikāyya*, *dhāyyā*, and *māyya*. (Pāṇini 3.1.129)

That by which something is measured is *pāyya*, meaning a measure; the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), *m* becomes *p*, and *ā* is replaced by *yuk*. That which is properly led toward the fire for the sake of an oblation is *sānnāyya*, the sacrificial offering; in the *darśa* sacrifice, specifically the *agniṣomīya* rite, the suffix *ṇyat* and the replacement of *ā* occur, along with the lengthening of the vowel in *sam*. That in which grain and such are gathered is *nikāyya*, a dwelling; here too the suffix *ṇyat* and the replacement of *ā* occur, while the initial *dh* of the root changes to *k*. That by which fuel is placed is *dhāyyā*, a verse; in the original ritual formula, fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses are prescribed.

Because the rule of seventeen [verses] pertains specifically to modified forms (*vikṛti*) such as the *Mitravindā* sacrifice; when, in specific modifications such as "one should recite twenty-one," an increase in the *sāmidhenī* verses is heard, there arises a doubt as to where the verses being introduced should be placed. Regarding this, it is said: "This [verse] is indeed the *samidhyamānavatī*, and that is the *samiddhavatī*; that which is between them is the *dhāyyā*. Since the *dhāyyā*s are praised as being the intermediate space (*ākāśa*) between the two verses—the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī*—which are conceived as Heaven and Earth, they must be inserted after the former [verses].

Because the *āgantu* (interpolated) verses are designated as *dhāyyā*s due to their being "placed" (*dhīyamāna*) [into the ritual], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they should be inserted in the midst of them. However, being "placed" is not the cause for the application of the term *dhāyyā*, because the term is not applied to those verses placed for the sake of praise or recitation (*stotra-śastra*) during the injunctions for *stobha* and so forth. Rather, Vedic usage such as "the two *pṛthupājavatī*s are *dhāyyā*s" indicates that the term *samidhenī*—which refers to the specific type of verses denoted by the word *dhāyyā*—should be understood here as referring to that particular class. What about [the terms] *mānya*, etc.? They are to be measured elsewhere; they are to be fixed, carried together, or placed.
In the *kratu* [sacrifice], there are the *kuṇḍapāyya* and *saṃcāyya*.

In this sacrifice, Soma is drunk from a *kuṇḍa* (vessel); thus it is called the *kuṇḍapāyya* rite. Here the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*), and not *vyat*. [This is because] if *vyat* were used, it would result in an initial accent due to the rule *nitsvara*. However, by the rule *yatonāvaḥ*, the word *pāyya* has its first syllable acute. In a compound, the original accent of the final member (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) applies. Thus says the Vārttika: "The rule for *yat* applies in *kuṇḍapāyya*. It is collected; thus it is *saṃcāyya*. The suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*), and there is the substitution of *āy* [for *ya*]. Why "in the sense of a rite" (*kratau*)? [Counter-example: *kuṇḍapānaṃ saṃceyaḥ* (the collection of the drinking-vessel). *Agno-paricāyyopacāyyasamūhyāḥ* || 131 || [The words *paricāyya*, *upacāyya*, and *samūhya* are formed with the suffix *ṇyat* in the sense of the locus.]

By the word *agni*, a site constructed with bricks for the purpose of supporting that [fire] is to be understood, as seen in such passages as "one piles the fire-altar with bricks" (*iṣṭakābhir agniṃ cinute*). From the root *ci* preceded by *pari-upa*, the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *āy* occur; from the root *vah* preceded by *sam*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and lengthening. However, in the Bhāṣya, since the form is established simply by adding the suffix *ṇyat* to the root *ūh*, the term *samūhya* need not be [derived from *vah*]; for, due to its polysemy, *ūh* has the meaning of *vah*. This is stated because of the usage in the Brāhmaṇa: "One desiring cattle should pile the *samūhya* altar; cattle indeed are men; thus he piles up cattle for him."
And [the rules regarding] the building of a fire-altar and the piling of the fire-altar [apply here as well]. 132.

The word *agni* follows [from the previous rule]. And that is a qualifier of the first [term] alone, not of the second, because as it denotes an abstract state (*bhāva*), it cannot denote the fire itself. That which is piled up is the *citya* fire; [the suffix] *kyap* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). In the case of *agnicityā*, it is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*)—the piling of the fire. Both of these [words] are oxytone (accented on the final syllable).
The section on primary suffixes (*kṛtya*) is completed. [Now follows: The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc*. (Pāṇini 3.1.133)

These two suffixes, *kartṛ* and *kāraka*, occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). However, their inclusion of the letter *t* is not for the sake of accentuation, because there is no difference between those ending in an initial udātta vowel and those ending in a final udātta vowel when they are singular. Nor is it for the purpose of qualifying [the suffixes] in the rule *aptṛn-tṛc-...*, for it should not be argued that if only *tṛ* were mentioned, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms such as *mātarau*. This is because the mention of *naptṛ* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*): according to the view that these are derived (*byutpatti-pakṣa*), among those words ending in the *uṇādi* suffix *tṛ*, lengthening occurs only for the word *naptṛ* and not for others.

However, in the Vedic rule *tuśchandasi*, the particle *tu* is intended for the purpose of including the general category [of suffixes] in the rule *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*; otherwise, because that [suffix *tu*] lacks an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), only this very suffix would be included there, and not *tṛn* and the others.

The suffixes *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* are applied respectively after the roots *nandi*, *grahi*, and *paci*. For example: *nandanaḥ* (from *nand*), *grāhī* (from *grah*), and *pacaḥ* (from *pac*). It should be stated that the suffix *ac* is also applied after all roots. The beginning of the *pacādi* group, however, is for the purpose of attaching specific indicatory letters (*anubandhas*). [Examples: *nadaṭ* → *nadī*; *coraṭ* → *corī*. Furthermore, these are intended to set aside the suffix *aṇ* in the case of the words *jārabhara* and *capaca*. However, the suffix *aṇ* also occurs as an alternative, because the word *śvapāka* is listed in the *nyaṅkuvādi* group.
The suffix *ka* is applied after roots ending in a short vowel (*ik*), those with a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* (*igupadha*), and after the roots *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṝ*.

Who among these [could be]? *kṣipaḥ*, *budhaḥ*, *jñaḥ*, *priyaḥ*, *kiraḥ*. By the rule of *vāsarūpa* (optionality of forms), there are the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc*: *kṣepakaḥ*, *kṣeptā*, and so forth. [The rule] *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136) applies.
The suffix *ṇa* is an exception to [the suffix] *ṇya*. Examples: *suglaḥ*, *prajñaḥ*.
The suffix *śa* is applied after the roots *pā* (to drink), *ghrā* (to smell), *dhmā* (to blow), *dheṭ* (to suck), and *dṛś* (to see).

Because [the root *pā*] is marked with the *śit* designation, there is the substitution of *piba* and so forth. Because [the suffix] is marked with *ṅit* by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening for *piba*. Thus we have *pibaḥ*, *jighraḥ*, *dhamaḥ*, *ghayaḥ*, and *dhayā kanyā*. Since the root *dheṭ* is marked with *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply here as well—yielding *stanandhayī*—but Haradatta and others maintain that *ṅīp* is not desired after the suffix *khaś* except in specific cases. We have *paśyaḥ*; however, this is not used when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), as evidenced by the usage in the rule *vyāghrādibhiḥ*. Furthermore, this prohibition applies to the suffix *śa* and not to the absence of *jighra*, because without the suffix *kap*, the elision of the vowel *ā* (in *jighra*) would be difficult to justify.

The inclusion of the term *upasarga* (prefix) does not carry over here [to this rule]. This is because of the usage by Bhaṭṭi, Śrīharṣa, and others, such as *dhayairāmopiba stave*, and also because of Vedic usage such as *yadā paśyaḥ paśyati rukmavarṇam*. [The suffix *ac* is applied] after the roots *limpa*, *vinda*, *dhāri*, *pāri*, *vedi*, *udeji*, *ceti*, *sāti*, and *sāhi*, when they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasargāt*). (Pāṇini 3.1.138)

The suffix *śa* occurs after these roots when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes them. Because of its *śit* designation, it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. After roots beginning with *tud*, the suffix *śa* is applied. By the rule *śe mucādīnām*, the augment *num* is inserted. Thus: *limpaḥ*, *vindaḥ*. Only the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining" is taken here, because of the indication by the inclusion of *num*. Since there is an absence of the status of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix for causative (*ṇyanta*) forms, there is no elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*). The suffix *śap* is applied, followed by *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa*. Thus: *dhārayaḥ*. The root *dhṛñ* means "to hold"; *dhṛṅ* means "to stand. Both are included here because they are causative forms. In the expression *namasyam atra uttara-dhārayasya te*, there is a compound with the sixth case ending in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus: *pārayaḥ*.

At the completion of the *pāra-karman* (the action of crossing over): *vedayaḥ*. The root *vid* is used in the senses of perceiving, narrating, and so forth; it is either one of those roots meaning "to know" etc., or it is the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of a root meaning "to cause to know. *Udejayaḥ*: from *ejṛ*, meaning "to tremble," preceded by the prefix *ud*. *Cetayaḥ*: from *citī*, meaning "to perceive," in its causative form (*ṇyanta*). *Sātayaḥ*: *sāti* has the sense of happiness; it is a Vedic (*sautra*) root in its causative form (*ṇyanta*). *Sāhayaḥ*: from *ṣaha*, meaning "to endure"; it belongs to the *curādi* class or is the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of a root meaning "to cause to endure. Why [is it said] "when not preceded by a prefix"? [Consider] *pralipaḥ*; here, because the root ends in a short vowel followed by a semivowel (*igupadha*), the suffix *ka* is applied. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix *ka* is applied] after *lip* when preceded by *ni*": *nilimpāḥ* refers to the gods.

After the root *vid*, when preceded by *go* etc., [the suffix *ka* is applied] in the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñā*): *govindaḥ*, *aravindam*. This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the object of the action (*karmaṇyaṇ*).
The suffix *kvin* is optionally applied after the roots *dā* (to give) and *dhā* (to place).

[The suffix] *śa* should occur [after the roots *dā* and *dhā*]. Optionally, because they end in long *ā*, the suffix *ṇa* will be taught [later]; thus we have *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ*. However, when preceded by a prefix (*sopasarga*), we have *pradaḥ* and *pradhaḥ*. Objection: But since *dā* means "to give" (*dāne*) and *dhā* means "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*), the forms *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ* are established by adding the suffix *yac* to these two; likewise, *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ* are established by adding *ṇa* to *dāñ* and *dhāñ*. Response: It is said that this rule is for the sake of establishing the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable as the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) in the cases of *adadaḥ* and *adadhaḥ*. For if [the suffix] *ac* were applied—according to the rule *ackāvaśaktāv antodāttaḥ*—there would be the undesirable consequence of the word ending in an udātta accent.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after verbal roots ending in *jvaliti*, *kāś*, and *ante*.

The word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth. After roots beginning with *jval* and ending with *kas*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), there shall be the suffix *ṇa*; optionally, the suffix *ac* may also apply. Thus: *jvālaḥ* (from *jval*) and *jvalaḥ*; *cālaḥ* (from *cal*) and *calaḥ*. However, when preceded by a prefix, as in *ujjvalaḥ*, the suffix *ac* applies. There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the root *tan*: "An addition for *tan*. Here, the optionality regarding the absence of a prefix does not apply, because the *Bhāṣya* provides the example *avatānaḥ*.

And [the roots] śyaiṅ (to coagulate), vyadh (to pierce), as (to throw), ruvati (from ru, to cry out), iṇ (to go), vas (to dwell), avahṛ (to carry away), lih (to lick), śliṣ (to embrace), and śvas (to breathe) [are also used with the ātmanepada endings]. || 141 ||

The suffix *ṇa* shall always occur after these roots. Since the mention of "not being preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarga*) is repeated in the subsequent rules, its connection with the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) mentioned here is also withdrawn. The analysis of the rule is: *śyaiṅ*, "roots ending in long *ā*," and so forth. Here, there is no inclusion of *śīṅ* (after its *yaṇ*-substitution), nor of *ata* (meaning "to go"), nor of roots ending in *ac* such as *pat* and others, nor of roots ending in short *a*; this is due to the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). Nor is it necessary to list *śyaiṅ* and *avas* separately since they would already be covered by the category of roots ending in long *ā*; [nevertheless, they are listed for clarity]: *pratiśyāyaḥ* (catarrh), *dāyaḥ*.

The suffix *ghañ* [is applied after roots] preceded by *āṅ* and *sam* when meaning "wearing" (*sraj*) or "flowing" (*sruti*). Examples include *āsrāvaḥ* and *saṃsrāvaḥ*. Some, having read the root as *śru* with a palatal *ś*, cite *āśrāvaḥ* and *saṃśrāvaḥ*. Other examples are *atyāyaḥ*, *avasāyaḥ*, *avahāraḥ*, *lehaḥ*, *śleṣaḥ*, and *śvāsaḥ*.
The [augment] *iṭ* is not applied after the root *du*, when there is no prefix (*upasarga*).

[The suffix] *na* would [be applied]. Due to association with that which possesses an *anubandha*, there is the inclusion of only the root *ṭudu* (meaning "to afflict"). From *dunoti*, we derive *dāvaḥ*. However, from the root *du* (in the sense of "going"), the suffix *pacādyac* is applied. With the prefix *upa*, as in *dupati*, we have *upadavaḥ*; but with the prefix *pra*, as in *pradavati*, we have *pradavaḥ*. [Likewise], *praṇayaḥ*.
The term *graha* is used in the sense of "option" (*vibhāṣā*). || 143 ||

According to the established option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), *grāha* refers to a crocodile when it denotes a water-dweller, and *graha* refers to a planet when it denotes a celestial body. In the case of the word *bhāva*, [the suffix] *ac* is applied to the root *bhāv-* (to conceive) to form *bhāvāḥ* (entities/meanings), whereas in the case of *bhava* (existence), it is applied to the root *bhū-* (to exist). However, the *vṛtti* states: "And there is an addition [of the suffix *ac*] to the root *bhū-*. "
Who is in the house? || 143 ||

The word *geha* is not an *upapada* (an accompanying noun), but rather an indication of the agent (*kartṛ*) which is the meaning of the suffix. This is because of such usages as *gṛhapatinā saṃyukte ca*. When *geha* is the agent, the suffix *ka* should be applied after the root *grah*. Due to its *kit* nature, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). That which holds (*gṛhṇāti*) grain and so forth is a *gṛha* (house). Because they reside therein, the word *gṛha* refers to wives (*dārāḥ*). However, some say that since the word *gṛha* is established by adding the suffix *ka* to the root *graha* (meaning "to seize")—which belongs to the *bhvādi* class and has an *ik* vowel in its penultimate position—this rule is redundant.
The suffix *ṣvun* is applied after [verbal roots] meaning "craftsmanship. || 145 ||

The suffix *ṣvun* occurs after roots signifying skill in an action when the agent is the subject. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after the roots *nṛt* (to dance), *khan* (to dig), and *rañj* (to color). Thus: *nartakaḥ* (dancer), *khanakaḥ* (digger), *rajakaḥ* (dyer). Regarding the form *rajaka*, the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) from the root *rañj* is established by an enumerative rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Because the suffix is marked with *ṣ*, feminine forms such as *nartakī* and others are derived. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is stated that the suffix *kvun* will be applied after the root *rañj*.
The guest-house. || 146 ||

The suffix *thakan* occurs after the root *gai* in the aforementioned sense; this is because of the maxim that "in the case of rules concerning the inclusion of *gā*, there is no distinction between the roots *gai* 'to sing' and *gā* 'to go'. However, it does not apply to the root *gāṅ* 'to move,' according to tradition, because the word *gāthaka* is conventionally restricted to one whose craft is singing.
And the suffix *ṇyuṭ* [is applied]. 147.
Gāyanaḥ; because it has the marker *ṭi*, [the feminine form is] gāyanī.
And [the substitution of] *ha* occurs for [the vowel *a*] in the words *vrīhi* and *kāla*. (148)

The root *hāṅ* (to abandon) is used with the suffix *korṇyuṭ* (*ana*) to denote either rice (*vrīhi*) or time (*kāla*). A rice plant is called *hāyana* because it "abandons water" (*jahāty udakam*). This abandonment of water occurs through upward growth after having been sown for the purpose of sprouting. Alternatively, it is called *hāyana* because it "abandons" (*jahāti*) or "transcends" (*jihīte*) preceding and succeeding states; thus, it refers to the year (*vatsara*).
The suffix *vun* is applied after the word *prusrulva* to express repetition (*samabhihāra*).

"In the sense of repeated action (*samabhihāra*), it should be stated that [the suffix *vuñ*] applies to one who performs the action well. Or rather, this should be understood as being directed toward that very term "repeated action" (*samabhihāra*). This is so that the suffix may apply even when someone performs the action well only once; it should not apply to one who performs it poorly even many times. Examples: *pravakaḥ*, *sarakaḥ*, *lavakaḥ*.
And [the suffix *vuñ* is applied] in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). (Pāṇini 3.2.150)

*Bhāṣya*: *Āśis* (blessing) is the wishing for the welfare of another. From a verbal root (*dhātu*) whose activity is directed toward that [welfare] as its object, the suffix *vun* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. For example, from the root *jīv* (to live), we have *jīvakaḥ* ("one who wishes 'may he live'"), and from *nand* (to rejoice), *nandakaḥ* ("one who wishes 'may he rejoice'"). The meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) consists in being the locus (*āśrayatva*) of the life of the father and so forth, and the wishing for that. When there is the state of being the locus of his life, that [locus-ness] is construed with the wish (*icchā*), which is one part of the object of the wish. The fact that the wish resides in the speaker (*prayoktṛvṛttitva*) appears by implication. Thus, the resulting cognition (*bodha*) is: "The son and so forth is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) of a wish whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is the state of being the locus of a long-lasting life."
Thus ends the sixth lesson in the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi*. This quarter is now concluded.
Now begins the second quarter:
"The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root when an object [is to be expressed]. (Pāṇini 3.2.1)

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root when there is an *upapada* that is an object (*karman*). For example, "one who makes a pot" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*) is a *kumbhakāraḥ*. The nature of the object has already been determined previously. This [suffix] does not apply in cases such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*) or "he sees the sun" (*ādityaṃ paśyati*), because they are not designated as such. When *aṇ* is applied, some maintain that in the non-grammatical analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*)—namely, "of the pot" (*kumbhasya*) and "maker" (*kartari*)—the word *kumbha* ending in the sixth case due to its connection with a *kṛt* suffix is compounded with the following word by the rule *upapadam atiṅ*.

That is questionable. Since the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.1] cannot arise in the absence of an object (*karman*) as a subordinate element (*upapada*), there can be no connection with a *kṛt*-suffix prior to its production; thus, the occurrence of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is necessary. There is no evidence for its abandonment, and it is more appropriate that it enters even into the non-standard analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*) of the compound. Otherwise, since the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply even when connected with a *kṛt*-suffix, and since the rule "the sixth case ending occurs when connected with a *kṛt*" would then apply, a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) would result. Furthermore, if one considers only the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that conveys the object, it is difficult to avoid the inclusion of the sixth case ending within the analysis (*vigraha*).

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding semantic capacity (*samartha*) would fail to apply. For this very reason, in the example sentence "a great potter" (*mahāntaṃ kumbhakāraḥ*), which is cited as a counter-example in the *Bhāṣya* and other works, the accusative case is indeed seen to be used for the qualifier. This is because if the word "pot" (*kumbha*) within the compound were in the genitive case, then the same [accusative] would necessarily follow for its qualifier, the word "great" (*mahat*). For this same reason, it was previously stated by [the author] himself that even under the view that a *dvandva* compound expresses multiple substrates simultaneously (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacana*), it is precisely the singular number that, having already applied first, enters into the non-linguistic (*alaukika*) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).

In examples such as "the maker of the jar" (*kumbhasya kartā*), since the connection with the object (*karma-yoga*) is not presupposed, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arises after the case-suffixes for the agent (*kartṛ*) and so on have been produced; subsequently, when that [object] is connected, the sixth case occurs by way of an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others—this is the point of disparity, and such is the direction of the argument.

"An affix with a karmopapada [i.e., a word denoting the object] takes precedence over one without such an upapada, by way of conflict (vipratiṣedha). Although, under the view that the suffix *ac* is added after all verbal roots (*sarvadhātubhyaḥ*), the suffix *aṇ*—which applies when there is an object—finds no scope because it is already superseded by *ac*, and thus there would be no conflict according to the maxim *yenanāprāpte* (since *aṇ* is not applicable where *ac* is already applicable); for an exception (*apavāda*) and its general rule (*utsarga*) do not possess equal strength; nevertheless, a conflict between *kāṇ* and *aṇ* should be understood in the case of *kāṣṭhabheda*. This is because, due to the conflict between those two—which are both exceptions to *ac*—the suffix *aṇ* does not apply. As for the statement in the Bhāṣya, "odanapāka," it should be understood as referring to the suffix *ac* applied to roots listed in the *gaṇa* lists.

Regarding the rule "The suffix *ṇa* is added after [roots ending in] *śīl*, *kāmin*, *bhakṣ*, and *ācari*, and there is the accentuation of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-svaratva*)": it should be stated that this also applies after the roots *īkṣ* and *kṣam*. Thus: *māṃsa-śīlā*, *māṃsa-kāmā*, *māṃsa-bhakṣā*, and *kalyāṇācārā*. Because it ends in a suffix, the word *māṃsa* has its acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). The word *kalyāṇa* has the acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*), according to the rule "when the penultimate syllable is light, or when there are two light syllables, the heavy syllable [among them] is acute" (Pāṇini 6.2.173). In these cases, the introduction of the accentuation of the preceding member is intended to override the natural accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound (*kṛd-uttara-prakṛti-svara*).

But is it not the case that [the suffix] *ac* is not prescribed after the root *bhakṣ*? Since this rule—“*ac* is added to roots ending in *a* and to those that do not take *ṇic*” (*eraj-aj-ṇyantānām*)—was not stated by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali), the desired accentuation is established simply by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, namely, “that which has a month-long meal” (*māsaṃ bhakṣo 'sya*). Nor should it be argued that the necessity of the aforementioned Vārttika is proven because, in the case of “one who has many meals” (*bahavo bhakṣā asya*), the rule “*nañ* functions like the negative particle when followed by a word denoting abundance” (*baho-rnañ-vad-uttara-pada-bhūmnī*) would otherwise result in an oxytone accent.

Having derived the word *bhakṣa* in the sense of "eating," when one forms a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of "one for whom there is eating" (*bhakṣo 'syeti*), that [suffix] does not apply because the word lacks the status of being a final member (*uttarapada*). Consequently, only the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*) applies. Nor is this [rule] indicated by the Vārttika stating that "when the meanings are identical, a *bahuvrīhi* is not formed"—that is, when the meanings of the *bahuvrīhi* and the object-suffix (*karmopapada*) are identical—because the formation of *bahuvrīhi* compounds such as *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* ("one who cuts stalks") and *māṃsasakāmaḥ* ("one who desires meat") is also desired.

Regarding the form *ambhobhiga*, because it is not prescribed [by the rule], and because there is an absence of both a bahuvrīhi compound and a word used as a subordinate object (*karmopapada*), the form *ambhobhigāmī* alone is desired. True; however, this [rule] was indeed commenced for the purpose of preventing the application of the suffix *aṇ*.
And [the word] *hvāva* [is also used]. || 2 ||

The roots *mā* (to measure) and *mī* (to destroy) are not included here, because they are intransitive (*akarmaka*). [Examples: *svargahvāyaḥ* (one who calls out for heaven), *tantuvāyaḥ* (a weaver), *dhānyamāyaḥ* (a measurer of grain). Since this would have been established by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), this new rule is commenced to provide exceptions (*apavāda*) to what will be stated later. By this, a suffix prescribed after a root ending in long *ā* is also established as being valid after a root ending in *e*. Thus Kaiyaṭa says:
"By the statement *hvā-vā-mā-ś-ca*, every suffix that would otherwise be caused by the presence of long *ā* is now made known to apply even to roots ending in *e*."
The suffix *ka* is applied after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*).

The suffix *ka* shall be applied after a root ending in long *ā*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), when a word denoting the object (*karman*) is present as an upapada. This is an exception to the rule for *aṇ*. "Those who possess sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇāvant*) in heaven, those who give horses, they shine with the sun; the givers of gold partake in immortality (*amṛtatva*); the givers of clothing prolong their lifespan through Soma. However, when a prefix is present, the suffix *aṇ* is used: *gosandāyaḥ* ("one who gives cows"). In the context of the rule for *ka*, "after roots that undergo *saṃprasāraṇa*, [the suffix] *ḍa* is used everywhere. Thus: *brahmajyaḥ* ("one who harms the Veda/Brahman"). Because of the mention of "everywhere," this applies even to cases governed by the rule *ātaścopasarge* ("after a root ending in long *ā*, when a prefix is present"). For example: *āhaḥ* ("one who speaks") and *prahvaḥ* ("one who is bent down").

The *Atravārtika* states: "The substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* for *hv-* is permanent; because a rule concerning phonemes (*vārṇa*) takes precedence over a rule concerning grammatical operations (*āṅga*), there is no [application of] *pūrvatva* (the substitution of the preceding element). For that which precedes an unaltered vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*) is indeed subject to the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original) regarding its grammatical effect. The venerable Kātyāyana has declared this, and therefore the *yaṇ* substitution is not established. According to the rule *ātaḥ kauliṇaiṅaḥ pūrvaḥ*, when [the *yaṇ*] is thus established, the form *āhvastathā* is obtained."

The meaning of this is as follows: by the suffix *kap* alone, forms such as *āhva* are established. In the case of *āhvāḍa*, since the process is easily accomplished through *saṃprasāraṇa*, elision of the vowel (*ātolopa*), and the substitution of *yaṇ*, there is no occasion for the application of *uvaṅ*. This is because the elision of the vowel (*ātolopa*) is treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). Nor does the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*) apply by superseding even the subsequent elision of the vowel, due to its being an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation; for an *āṅga* (vowel-based) operation is stronger than a *vārṇa* (consonant-based) one. However, if that [rule of relative strength] is accepted only when the locus (*āśraya*) is identical, then at the stage *hvā-a*, the elision of the vowel (*ātolopa*) would supersede the *saṃprasāraṇa*, after which the *saṃprasāraṇa* would take place.

Because of the status of the substitute as the original (sthānivadbhāva), there is no substitution of *uvaṅ*. Nor can it be argued that the *saṃprasāraṇa* is obligatory because it applies both when [the elision] has been performed and when it has not; for the elision of the *āt* vowel is likewise [obligatory]. Nor should it be said that once the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) have been effected, there is no occasion for the elision of the *āt*, and thus how could it be considered obligatory? For it is accepted that a rule is not "non-obligatory" (i.e., not *anitya*) merely because its cause is obstructed by another rule. This is because, although the cause for the elision is removed by the preceding form, that cause is not removed by the *saṃprasāraṇa*.

[Objection: Even so, since the letter *a* (of *sthā*) does not precede the non-specified vowel (*ac*), how can there be the application of *sthānivadbhāva* when *uvaṅ* is to be applied? Nor can it be argued that this [application] is mediated through the *sthānin*, because the *v* which is the *sthānin* for the *u* is already present prior to the elision (*lopa*) of the *ā*. This is because that argument has been refuted under the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (P. 1.1.57). Therefore, *uvaṅ* remains unavoidable. [Reply: No; for by the principle *asiddhavadatrābhāt* (P. 6.4.22), the elision of the *ā* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), thereby preventing [the application of *uvaṅ*]. This is because in both cases, the suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādipratyaya*) serves as the cause (*nimitta*), and thus they share the same basis (*samānāśrayatva*).

But surely, in this way, there would be the failure of forms such as *juhuvatuḥ*; for in that case, under the view that the rule *aśiti* is a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), since the substitution of *āt* would apply by virtue of its higher status, overriding [the *pūrvarūpa*], there would be no possibility of the *pūrvarūpa* at that time, and thus [one might argue] that the *lopa* of the *āt* applies. This is true.

In the rule *eṅaḥ padāntāt*, by dividing it as *eṅaḥ* and continuing the word *saṃprasāraṇāt* from the previous sūtra, the interpretation is that "the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) shall occur for an *eṅ* following a *saṃprasāraṇa*. Consequently, by the prescription of "precedence" (*pūrvatva*), the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) is barred. Nor does this undesirable consequence apply to the present case [of *liṭ*], because when the condition of ending in an *ā* vowel (*ādantatva*) is being examined, the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) is what must be relied upon [as a prerequisite]. Furthermore, there is a disparity between the two cases, because *liṭ* is prescribed after any verbal root (*dhātu*) whatsoever, whereas [the substitution of *ā*] is not.
In the [first] person dual, [the ending is] *sthaḥ*.

The term *sup* is analyzed [as follows]: after a word ending in *ā*, when a *sup*-ending word is an upapada, the suffix *ka* is applied. One who drinks with the neck is a *kacchapa* (tortoise); one who drinks with two arms is a *dvipa* (elephant).

However, some say that in the case of *kaccham pibati*, the suffix should indeed be applied as one conditioned by an object (*karman*) as an accompanying word (*upapada*), because there is no harm even when the meaning of the constituent parts does not connect, due to the word being a conventional term (*rūḍhi*). It is improper to provide a grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) for conventional terms even when possible, by resorting to non-existent meanings of their parts. But in cases such as *tailapāyikā*, one must resort to non-existent meanings because there is no other way, so says Kaiyaṭa. In the rule for *stha*, the word *supi* is understood from the previous rule. Since the agent (*kartṛ*) is already established by the preceding rule, this [suffix] is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), according to the maxim "those whose meaning is not specifically prescribed [denote the action itself]."

It should not be argued that [the distinction between] "one situated in equilibrium" (*samastha*) and "one situated in disequilibrium" (*viṣamastha*), and so forth, would not be established due to the consequence of contradiction; for even though the term "existence" (*bhāva*) is the ultimate conclusion, the word "existence" itself is not explicitly employed [in the definition].

Some, however, claim that the suffix *ka* is established for the root *sthā* by the very Vārttika rule "the prescription of *ka* in the sense of *ghañ*. This is not correct; for here the suffix *ka* is prescribed after an *upapada* (in accordance with the rule *upapadam atiṅ*), which serves the purpose of making the compound obligatory (*nityasamāsa*). In that Vārttika, the mention of the word *sthā* is already fulfilled by its application to non-agentive (*akartṛ*) factors. Examples include: *ākhūtthaḥ* ("an emergence of mice"), *śyenotthaḥ* ("an emergence of hawks"), and *śalabhotthaḥ* ("an emergence of locusts"). However, the neuter examples contradict the *Ākara* (the source commentary), because Amara states that the suffix *ka* is masculine when used in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*)—as in "the suffix *ka* [is masculine] after roots ending in *ghu*, and [neuter] otherwise, provided it begins with *pra*"—thereby declaring the *ka*-formed word denoting "state" to be masculine.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the verbal roots √tund and √śuc when they mean "to wipe away" (*parimṛjā*) and "to dispel" (*apanuda*), respectively. || 5 ||

In order, what [is the meaning]? It should be stated: "in the sense of laziness and the bringing of happiness. *Tundaparimṛjaḥ* means lazy; *śokāpanudaḥ* means a bringer of happiness. In other cases, it is *tundaparimārjaḥ* and *śokāpanodaḥ*. The meaning is: one who effects the cessation of grief by manifesting the impermanence of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). "In the section on the suffix *ka*, there is an addition for words such as *mūlavibhuja* and others": *mūlavibhujaḥ* (a chariot), *mahīdhraḥ* (the earth-bearer, i.e., a mountain), *kudhraḥ* (a mountain), *saroruham* (a lotus).
Before the one who bestows knowledge. || 6 ||

The suffix *ka* shall be applied after the verbal root *jñā*, when it is preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*) and begins with the letter *dā*, provided that a word denoting the object (*karman*) is present as an *upapada*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *sarvapradaḥ* (one who bestows everything) and *pathiprajñaḥ* (one who knows the way). However, this does not apply when joined with other prefixes (*upasargāntara*), because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "not when there is no prefix" (*anupasarge*). Even though the aforementioned rule would have applied to the mere prefix *pra*, it is superseded here; yet, since there is no supersession in other cases, [the suffix applies]. Examples: *gosampradāyaḥ* (the tradition of the cows) and *samīkṣyaḥ* (to be examined).

The Nyāsakāra maintains that there is no usage of the root *khyā* preceded by the prefix *sam-* in the sense of "counting," as in the expression *gosaṃkhyaḥ* ("one who counts cows"). However, the claim that the root *khyā* is restricted solely to the domain of sārvadhātuka suffixes has already been refuted.
