The suffix *ka* is applied after the verbal roots *gā* (to sing) and *puṣ* (to nourish). || 8 ||

The suffix *ṭak* is applied after the roots *gai* (to sing) and *pā* (to drink), when they are used without prefixes (*anupasarga*) and have an object as an *upapada*. Here, only the root *gai* is intended, and not *gā-gāni*, because the latter is not attested in usage. Thus: *sāmagaḥ* (one who sings Sāman hymns), *sāmagī* (a female singer of Sāman). Regarding the root *pā* (to drink): since there is a choice between taking the form with a *luk*-elided marker (*luk-vikaraṇa*) or one without (*aluk-vikaraṇa*), only the one without the elided marker is taken here. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] to the root *pibati* when *surā* (liquor) or *sīdhu* (spirit) are the objects: *surāpī* (a woman who drinks liquor), *sīdhupī* (a woman who drinks spirits). However, the word *surāpā* refers to one who guards or protects liquor; it does not apply here because of the restriction regarding the *upapada*. Thus, *kṣīrapā* (one who drinks milk) is formed from *kṣīraṃ pibati*. [The suffix is applied] diversely (*bahulam*) in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*) or in Vedic literature (*chandas*). For example: "She becomes a Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks liquor; the gods do not lead her to the world of her husband"—here the term *surāpā* is used. Or: *surāpā vā* (or a drinker of liquor).
The affix *ac* is applied after the root *hṛ* when it does not take the prefix *anu*.

*Aṃśaharaḥ* (an heir). Here, the root *hṛ* (to take) has the sense of "taking" (*grahaṇa*). But when it means "lifting up," we have *bhārahāraḥ* (a bearer of a load). In the section on *ac*-suffixes, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the roots *śakti*, *lāṅgala*, *aṅkuśa*, *yaṣṭi*, *tomara*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭī*, and *dhanus* when used with the root *grah*. Examples include *śaktigrahaḥ* (seizing a spear), *lāṅgalagrahaḥ* (seizing a plough), and so forth. The inclusion of the word *ghaṭī* is intended to indicate that the rule regarding the inclusion of forms distinguished by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*). Furthermore, in the case of the word *sūtra* when it refers to its literal meaning (the string), we have *sūtragrahaḥ* (holding a thread). However, where one merely collects the aphorisms (*sūtra*) but does not actually hold them [as a physical string], the form is simply *sūtragrāhaḥ* (one who collects the aphorisms).
And [the same applies] regarding age. || 10 ||

*Vayaḥ* (age) is a specific state of the body characterized by time; when this is to be expressed, the suffix *ac* is added to the root *hṛ*. Thus, *kavacaharaḥ kumāraḥ* ("a boy who takes up armor"). The term *udyamana* refers to the undertaking for the purpose of lifting [the armor]. Whether there is an actual lifting of the armor or not, what is understood is merely the specific stage of life. The meaning is "one fit for taking up armor," because even when the result is not yet present, the fitness remains unimpaired.
The suffix *āṅ* is used [after a verb] in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

When a word denoting an object (*karman*) follows as an upapada, the suffix *ac* is added to the root *hṛ* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* to express habitual action (*tācchīlya*). One who habitually gathers flowers is called *puṣpāharaḥ*. Habitual action refers to a natural or constant inclination; otherwise, one is called a *bhārāhāraḥ* (a carrier of burdens).
The Arhat. || 12 ||
When *karman* is the upapada, the suffix *ac* is applied after the root *arh*, as an exception to [the suffix] *aṇ*. Example: *pūjārha brāhmaṇī* (a Brāhmaṇī worthy of honor).
In the case of *stamba* and *karṇa*, when they are not denoting fire and the ear respectively. || 13 ||

"It should be stated: 'in the case of *hastin* and *sūcaka*. [This refers to] the non-elision (*aluk*) of the suffix prescribed by the rule *haladantāt*. Thus, *stamberamaḥ* means "an elephant," and *karṇejapaḥ* means "a slanderer. In other cases, one finds *stambe rantā* ("one who delights in a tree-stump") and *karṇejapitā* ("one who whispers into the ear").
The suffix *śam* is applied after the verbal root *dhā* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed. || 14 ||

"When *śam* is the upapada, the suffix *ac* is applied after the verbal root alone, provided it is a name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *śambhavaḥ*, *śaṃvadaḥ*. The mention of "the verbal root" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of prohibiting [the suffix] in cases such as the cause (*hetu*) for the root *kṛ*. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *ac* has been stated; the scope of *ṭa* is, for example, *śraddhakaraḥ*. A female wandering ascetic named Śaṅkarā is one whose nature is that [of performing auspicious acts]; in that case, because *ṭa* is subsequent [to *ac*], it would apply. However, by the force of the mention of "the verbal root," only *ac* applies. But Kuṇaravāḍava says: having derived the word *śaṅgara* from the root *gṛ* (to sound), the letter *ga* becomes *ka* by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, thus the word *śaṅkarā* is established. And so, according to this, the mention of "the verbal root" is unnecessary—this is the Bhāṣya.
The suffix *kha* is applied after the root *śī* when it occurs in the sense of "lying down" with respect to a location (*adhikaraṇa*).

One who sleeps in the sky is *khaśayaḥ*. There is an extension [of the rule] to include *pārśva* and others: one who sleeps on his sides is *pārśvaśayaḥ*; likewise *pṛṣṭhaśayaḥ* (one who sleeps on his back) and *udaraśayaḥ* (one who sleeps on his belly). It should be stated that [the suffix applies] when preceded by *digdha* and *saha*: the word *upapada* here refers to the compound *digdhasaha*, not to each word individually. One who sleeps with the poisoned [arrow] is *digdhasahaśayaḥ*. Kaiyaṭa says that this is a compound because it belongs to the *mayūra-vyaṃsaka* group. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] when the agents (*kartṛ*) are *uttāna* and others: one who sleeps supine is *uttānaśayaḥ*. *Avamūrdhaśayaḥ* means one whose head is bent down; that is to say, one who sleeps face-downward.

"It should be stated that *ḍa* occurs after *giri* in Vedic usage. Thus, *giriśaḥ* means "he who sleeps on the mountain. Alternatively, the suffix *śa* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *loman*-class; or else, the suffix *śas* is applied according to the rule "after a word ending in *sekhya* in the singular. This is because even for words that are conventional (*rūḍha*), some kind of etymological derivation must be provided.
Vairava, Vāsiṣṭha, Giriśa, Sthaikāgārika,
and others have been described by some in various ways through a confusion of causes and limits.

By this, it is explained that "the fair-haired one (Sukeśī) attended upon Giriśa every day. As for Kaiyaṭa’s statement that the word *giriśa* is ungrammatical in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*) because of the rule *chandasī* ("in Vedic [usage]"), the expression "they say" (*āhuḥ*) therein indicates a lack of finality (*asvarasa*). The reason for this is that its grammatical correctness has been established through another method, and thus it is not incorrect.
He is desired by those who practice care. || 16 ||

When a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the accompanying word (*upapada*), [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]. For example: *kurucaraḥ* (one who moves in the Kurus), *kurucarī* (a woman who moves in the Kurus). Why "when a locus"? [Consider] *kurūṃścaratīti*; here only *aṇ* is applied. One for whom the Kurus themselves are merely to be reached is a *kurucāraḥ* (a traveler to the Kurus); whereas one who wanders about within the Kurus is a *kurucaraḥ*. In this case, the word *kuru* refers to a part of that [whole region].
And in [the case of] alms-food, armies, and vehicles. || 17 ||

A *bhikṣācara* is one who wanders for alms; here, the meaning of the root *car-* is "to acquire," with "wandering" being subordinate. The sense is that he acquires alms by means of wandering. In *senācara*, the meaning is "entry. *Ādāya* is an imitation of a form ending in the suffix *lyap*; although it requires an object, the compound is formed by specific rule. *Ādāyacara* means one who resorts to wandering after the time of taking [something]. However, forms such as *sahacara* arise from the inclusion of *caraḍ* in the list of *pacādi* roots. The prescription of the suffix *ṭa* (which results in *cara*) is for the purpose of ensuring an obligatory compound.
The word *puraḥ* is derived from the root *sṛ* (to move) when used in the senses of "before," "in front of," or "ahead. || 18 ||

*Puraḥsaraḥ* means "one who goes before. *Agrataḥsaraḥ* means "one who goes at the front. [The term] *agresaraḥ* means one who moves (*sarati*) at the head (*agram*), by the head (*agreṇa*), or ahead (*agre*). The change to *e* [from *a*] occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Haradatta states that the word *agrasara* belongs to the *bāhuka* group.
In the preceding [sūtra], the agent [is the referent]. || 19 ||

*pūrvasaraḥ* means "one who goes forward" (*pūrvaḥ sarati*). Why [is it] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*)? [Because otherwise it would mean: *pūrvasāraḥ*, meaning "one who goes to the eastern region" (*pūrvaṃ deśaṃ sarati*).
The suffix *kṛt* is applied after the root *kṛ* (to do) in the senses of cause, habitual action, and compliance.

The word *hetu* means a certain cause. *Yaśaskarī* means knowledge that brings fame; hence, by the rule *kṛ-kami-*, there is the substitution of *satva* (the semivowel). The meaning is "that which excludes non-fame. *Śrāddhakaraḥ* refers to one who performs ancestral rites. *Ānulomyam* means favorableness. *Vacanakaraḥ* refers to one who carries out instructions; here, favorableness is what is indicated.

[The suffix *ka* is applied] after the words *divā*, *vibhā*, *niśā*, *prabhā*, *bhāskara*, *anta*, *ananta*, *ādi*, *bahula*, *nāndī*, *kiṃlipi*, *libi*, *bili*, *bali*, *bhakti*, *kartṛ*, *citra*, *kṣetra*, *saṃkhyā*, *jaṅghā*, *bāhu*, *ahaḥ*, *yatta*, *dhanus*, and *arus*. (21)

The present undertaking concerns the meaning of *ahetu* and so forth; in these cases, the suffix *kṛt* (the *kṛt* affix) should be applied. Examples include *divākara*, and so on, as well as *bhāskara*. In *bhāskara*, the *s* occurs because the word belongs to the *kaska*-group (*kaskādi*). The word *bahu* signifies abundance, since it is mentioned separately from "number" (*saṃkhyā*). The words *lipi* and *libi* are synonyms. Examples are *ekakara*, *dvikara*, and *ahaskara*; the latter belongs to the *kaska*-group. In *dhanuṣkara*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule: "In a compound, when not standing at the end of a final member, [the *s* of] *dhanus* [is replaced by *ṣ*]."

Regarding the rule for the suffix *kvip* after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *kim*, *yat*, *tat*, or *bahu*: Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that this is a *vārttika*; Mādhava and others consider it a mere wish (*iṣṭi*). Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others hold that because the suffix *ac* (in *kiṃkara*) sublates the *ṭāp* ending, the form *kiṃkarī* is ungrammatical. However, Śrīharṣa [uses the form] in the verse: "O you who abandon! Abandon me! I am your servant (*kiṃkarī*)."

The proponents of the *nayāsa* (the *Nyāsa*), however, [hold that] it is precisely by the previous sūtra [Pāṇini 3.2.120] regarding "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth. Therefore, he states that [the suffix] *kiṃkara* is thus established. This is his intention: it is universally accepted that the sūtra beginning with "divā" (Pāṇini 3.2.21) has the meaning of "cause. That very same domain belongs to the Vārttika "kiṃyad" (Pāṇini 3.2.26), which is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. By this, the claim that the qualification "in the absence of cause and so forth" was not provided by the three sages (Patañjali, Kātyāyana, and Pāṇini) in the rule for the suffix *ac* is refuted. Thus, when there is the intention to express a cause, the suffix *ṭa* is indeed properly applied.

By this, the objection that "the prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) lacks a basis" is refuted, for it operates precisely according to the stated intention. For this very reason, the ancients read [the text] as "it is indeed the *Vārttika*. Nor is there the contingency of the suffix *aṇ* [by P. 3.2.1] applying to the word *pakṣa*, because in the absence of the suffix *ac*, only that [suffix *aṇ*] applies by virtue of the rule *divāvibhāniśā...* (P. 3.2.21). Nor should it be asked, "How can this be, since Haradatta and others have stated that the mention of *kim* etc. should be removed from the *sūtra*? For as long as the aforementioned purpose remains possible, the removal of that [mention] cannot be definitively established.

Others, however, suggest that the mention of "kim-ādi" (beginning with *kim*) should be removed from this rule and that the reading should be simply "*kiṃyattadbahuṣu kṛña*" within the *pacādi* group itself; this is also the intention of the Vārttika. Thus, since the Vārttika has its purpose fulfilled by overriding the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the object (*karman*), they say that when there is an intention to express [the agent as] a cause (*hetu*) and so forth, the suffix *ṭa* (forming *kartrī*) overrides it due to its higher status; consequently, even without a connection to a male (*puṃyoga*), forms such as *kiṃkarī* would indeed be valid.
In the sense of wages for work, [the genitive case is used]. || 22 ||

When the word *karman* is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ* when "wages" (*bhṛti*) is understood; thus, *karmakaraḥ* means "one who works for wages. Nor does this result in the adoption of the meaning [of the rule] based on the distinction between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), because of the force of the repeated mention of the word *karman*. Elsewhere, it is *karmakāraḥ*.
Nor [should one apply it] to sounds, verses, quarrels, songs, enmity, flattery, aphorisms, or mantra-words. || 23 ||
This is a prohibition of the suffix *ṭa* which would otherwise apply after words such as *hetu*; for example, in the case of "śabdakāra" and so forth.
The suffix *rin* is applied after the words *stamba* and *śakṛt*.
"It should be stated as 'in the case of rice and a calf'. "The stalk-forming nature [of rice] does not depend on the merit of the sower.
Thus [it is said in] the *Mudrārākṣasa*. A calf is a producer of dung (*śakṛtkari*); elsewhere it is a producer of stalks (*stambakāraḥ*). [Elsewhere] it is a producer of dung (*śakṛtkāraḥ*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *hṛ* and *nī* when followed by the word *dṛti*, provided that the referent is an animal. || 25 ||

When these two words are used as upapadas with the verb *hṛ*, the suffix *in* is applied to form the agentive noun *hari* when the agent is an animal: *dṛtihariḥ* (a leather-bag-stealer) and *nāthahariḥ* (a nose-string-stealer), both referring to an animal. A *dṛti* is a leather pouch; a *nātha* is a nose-rope.
Phalegrahi and ātmambhari [are used as nouns]. || 26 ||

In the first case, the suffix *in* is applied, and the final vowel of the upapada is replaced by *e*. For example: *phalāni gṛṇhāti* (he seizes fruits) becomes *phalegrahiḥ*. In the second case, the augment *mum* is added and the suffix *in* is applied. For example: *ātmambhariḥ*. By the addition of *ca*, *kukṣimbhariḥ* and *udarambhariḥ* are also formed. This is because of the reading in the Cāndra-vyākaraṇa: "after the words *ātman*, *udara*, and *kukṣi*. Śrīharṣa says: "He who fills his belly with heaps of straw whose forms are like very soft hands. In Vedic usage, the suffix *van* is applied after the roots *van*, *san*, *rakṣ*, and *math*. (Pāṇini 3.2.27)

The suffix *in* is added after these [roots] when a verbal noun (*karmopapada*) follows: *brahmavani*, *kṣatravani*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one who desires the Brahman," "one who desires the Kṣatra. [Examples: *vājasani* ("winning booty"), *rayimasme suvīram* ("wealth with good heroes for us"). [Also: *pathirakṣayaḥ* ("protectors of the paths") and *haviḥmathīnām abhi* ("towards those who churn the oblation").
After the root *ej*, the suffix *khaś* is added. (28)

The mention [of the root] is in its causative form (*ṇyanta*), not in its simple form, as is clear from the commentary. Because it has the marker *ś*, the suffixes *śa* and so forth are applied; by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*, the augment *mum* is added. Thus, one who causes the enemy to tremble is called *janamejaya*. As for what is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "Since he conquered his enemies by means of his exceedingly pure birth, and because the root *ej* signifies trembling, he is remembered as *janmejaya*."

Thus it has been stated. In that regard, even though there is no prefix *ud*, the suffix *śa* is applied according to the rule *anupasargāllimpavindati-ādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.138), despite the absence of the word *ud*. This should be understood as being due either to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*) or through etymological derivation (*nairuktavyutpatti*).

"In this same section (*khap prakaraṇe*), there is an addition [to the rule] regarding the words *vāta*, *śunī*, *tila*, and *śardha* after the roots *aja*, *dheṭ*, *tud*, and *jahāti*: *vātamajā* (deer born of the wind), *śunindhayaḥ* (suckling from a female dog). By the rule *khityanavyayasya*, there is shortening [of the final vowel]. *Tilaṃtudaḥ* (one who crushes sesame). *Śardhaṃjahā māṣāḥ* (beans that abandon the *śardha*). *Śardha* is the sound of flatulence; Mādhava and others hold that it means "those which abandon it," with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) not being internalized. However, the reading *garddha* contradicts the Bhāṣya, the Vṛtti, and other authorities. In all these cases, the augment *mum* is applied by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*. [The rule continues:
"After *nāsikā* and *stana*, [the suffix *kha* is added] after the roots *dharm* and *dheṭ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.29)

In this regard, there is a Vārttika intended to set aside the rule of "respective order" (yathāsaṃkhya): "It should be stated that [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the root *dheṭ* when *stana-* is the object, and after the root *dhmā* when *nāsikā-* is the object. Thus, *stanandhayaḥ* ("an infant who sucks at the breast"). Because the *ṭi*-designation of the root *dheṭ* does not serve its purpose in relation to a part (*avayava*), the suffix *ṅīp* is added [to form the feminine]: *stanandhatī*. However, Vardhamāna, Kṣīrasvāmī, Haradatta, and others maintain that the suffix *ṅīp* is not desired after other suffixes; therefore, according to the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*), when the suffix *śa* or *kap* is applied, only the suffix *ṭāp* is used. Examples: *nāsikaṃdhamaḥ* ("one who blows through the nose") and *nāsikaṃdhayaḥ* ("one who drinks through the nose"). There is also an addition [to the rule] regarding *ghaṭī*, *khārī*, and *kharī*: *ghaṭindhamaḥ* ("one who blows a jar"), *ghaṭindhayaḥ* ("one who drinks from a jar"), and so forth. And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi*. (Pāṇini 3.2.30)

The rule *dhmādheṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.41) continues [into this sūtra]. According to the Bhāṣya, the Vṛtti, and other authorities, there is a correspondence between the two terms [in the order they appear]. They state that the reversal of the order of the first two terms in both cases serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) does not apply here. As for the Bhāṣya statement under the *yathāsaṃkhya* sūtra (*nāḍīmuṣṭyośca*), it refers merely to the possibility of such a construction. Examples: *nārḍidhamaḥ*, *nārḍidhayaḥ*. [Now begins] 3.2.31: *udi kūle rujivahoḥ*. (When the prefix *ut* is present, the suffix *kha* is applied after the roots *ruj* and *vah* when *kūla* is the object.)

The suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *ruj* (to break) and *vah* (to carry) when preceded by the prefix *ud*, provided that *kūla* (bank) is the object (*karman*) in composition. *Ruj* means "breaking" and *vah* means "carrying. Thus: *kūlamudrujaḥ* (one who breaks the bank) and *kūlamudvahaḥ* (one who carries away the bank). Kaiyaṭa maintains that the locative case in *udi* (*ud-iti*) functions in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*), and the genitive case in *vahoḥ* (*vahoḥ-iti*) functions in the sense of the ablative; therefore, there is no correspondence between the order of the words and their respective meanings (*na yathāsaṃkhyam*). Dīkṣita adds that this is because it is impossible for the word *ucchabda*—which denotes a non-substance (*asattvavācin*)—to be construed with the term *karmani* (object).

Consequently, the *vārttika* "upasarjana-saṃnipāte" in the rule *prāg-dhātoḥ* refers only to the perspective of a person who mistakenly believes both [the prefix and the root] to be subordinate adjuncts (*upapada*), as is clear from Kaiyaṭa himself.
The suffix *lih* is applied after the word *vaha* when followed by *abhra*. || 32 ||

In examples such as *skandhaliho gauḥ* ("a bull that licks its hump"), *abhraṃliho vāyuḥ* ("the cloud-licking wind"), and *abhraṃlihāḥ parvatāḥ* ("cloud-licking mountains"), the meaning of the root *lih* (to lick) is "contact. Because the suffix *khaś* is marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
[The next rule is: *parimāṇe pacaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.33).
The words *prasthapaca* and *khārīpaca* [form a compound] when referring to a cooking pot (*sthālī*) and a large cauldron (*kaṭāha*), respectively;
and so too when [the agent] has trimmed nails (*mitanakhā*). Pāṇini 2.1.51.

"Regarding *kadarya*, [the following are synonyms]: *kṛpaṇa*, *kṣudra*, *kiṃpacana*, and *mitaṃpaca*. *Nakhaṃpacā* refers to gruel (*yavāgū*). Here, the root *pac* has the sense of "causing distress. As Māgha says: 'The burden of her breasts does not cause distress even to her beloved (*na nakhaṃpacaḥ priyasya*).
[The rule] *vidhvaruṣostudaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.35) applies."

*Vidhutudaḥ*, *aruntudaḥ*. In the case of *mumikṛte*, there is the elision of *s* according to the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*. Amara states: "An *aruntuda* is one who touches the vital points (*marmaspṛk*). [The compound] *arustuda* means "one who pierces a wound" (*aruḥ* = a wound; *tudati* = pierces). This is because the piercing of a wound is the cause of extreme pain. Amara states: "*Arus* (masculine and neuter) is a wound; *marman* is a vital point. [The sūtra] *asūryalalāṭayordṛśitapoḥ* || 36 || [is applied].

"Those who do not see the sun" are the *asūryampaśyāḥ* (those who do not look upon the sun), namely the wives of kings. Although there is no semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) between the word "sun" (*sūrya*) and the negative particle "not" (*nañ*) due to their lack of mutual relation, the compound is formed by the force of the grammatical rule itself. Here, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) refers to a specific condition of concealment, rather than the mere absence of seeing the sun or the seeing of something other than the sun. Regarding that [latter sense], they say that the suffix *khaś* does not apply because of a lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). That is not correct. For Śrīharṣa has employed the term in the phrase, "Listen, listen! She is indeed not an *asūryampaśyā*," and Vidyanatha has used it in the phrase, "The *asūryampaśyāḥ* are the western rocks of the boundary mountain. Thus, the objection is refuted.
The Ugras, Paśus, Yamas, Madras, Pāṇis, and Dhamas. || 37 ||

These are irregularly formed (nipātita). One who sees "fierce" (ugram) as it truly is is called *ugraṃpaśyaḥ*. That which intoxicates or blazes with *ira*—that is, water—is *irammadaḥ*, meaning the light of the clouds (*meghajyotiḥ*). Because of this irregular formation, the suffix *śyan* is not applied. A path covered by darkness from which hands are blown (*pāṇayo dhmāyante*) is called *pāṇindhamaḥ*; for there, out of fear of snakes and the like, one makes sounds with the hands to dispel them. The intended meaning refers merely to the difficulty of passage. Murāri says: "By the very clash of weapon against weapon, the forest paths, filled with the noise of the blowing of hands, narrow in the sky; the barren [paths] do not give birth to warriors."
The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *vad* when preceded by *priya* or *vaśa*.

"Priyaṃvadaḥ" (one who speaks kindly) and "aniṣṭhuroktiḥ" (one who uses non-cruel speech). From the root *vad* with the sense of steadiness, *vaśavadaḥ* should be understood; its etymological derivation is "one who speaks or acts under control. Although the suffix *khaś* suffices for the formation of the word, another suffix is used for the sake of what follows. Even there, the purpose will be stated later. Here, however, the mention of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating that the suffix *khac* occurs even from other roots. That very point has been stated in the Vārttika:

An addition [to Pāṇini’s rules] should be made: *gameḥ supi upasaṃkhyānam* (an addition regarding the root *gam* before a nominal suffix). This cannot be established by the rule *gamaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.47), because that rule applies only when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed. Thus, we have *mitaṃgamā hastinī* (a female elephant that travels measuredly). Regarding the word *vihāyasa*, it should be stated that *vihaḥ* is substituted for it, and the suffix *khac* is optionally treated as having the marker *ḍit*. Thus, *vihaṃgamaḥ* (a bird). In the case where the suffix is *ḍit*, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion. However, if the suffix were *khaś*, this would not occur because the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix would be impossible; furthermore, due to its being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the *śap* augment would apply. [The following rule applies: *dviṣatparayos tāpeḥ* (3.2.39).

One who torments an enemy is called *dviṣantapaḥ*; likewise, *paraṃtapaḥ*. However, this does not apply in the case of *dviṣatītāpaḥ*, because the rule regarding the inclusion of gender-specific forms (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory.
[Pāṇini 3.2.40: The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *yam* when preceded by *vāc*, provided it refers to a religious observance (*vrata*).

When the word *vāk* is used as an upapada (governing word) with the root *yam*, the suffix *khac* is applied provided that a religious observance (*vrata*) is understood. Thus, *vācaṃyamaḥ* refers to one who observes the vow of silence. However, when the vow of silence is undertaken due to incapacity or similar reasons rather than as a formal observance, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the object; thus, *vāgyāmaḥ*.
The word *pūḥ* [is used as a feminine noun] after the roots *dṛ*, *sarva*, *yā*, *dāri*, and *sah*. (41)

Regarding *puraṃdara*: [the rule] "vācaṃyamapuraṃdarau ca" [Pāṇini 3.2.40] prescribes the absence of the suffix *matup*. Regarding *sarvaṃsahaḥ*, Haradatta [states]: "The portion 'puridāra' in the rule [3.2.41] is redundant; for the suffix *khac* is already possible by the rule 'vācaṃyamapuraṃdarau ca' itself, and the fact that it applies specifically to the domain of religious observances (*vrata*) is obtained precisely through the force of the irregularity (*nipātana*). Therefore, in this case, the rule 'sarve saha' [3.2.44] alone would be more appropriate."

The root *dṝ* is understood here only in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*), and not in the senses of "fearing" (*bhaye*) or "respecting" (*ādare*); such is the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*). The inclusion of the prefix *sa-* is for the purpose of excluding technical names (*asaṃjñārtham*), because [the formation of] technical names will be explained later.
Pāṇini 3.2.42: *sarvakūlābhrakarīṣeṣu kaṣaḥ* (The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *kaṣ* when preceded by the words *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*).

The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *kaṣ* when preceded by *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, *karīṣa*, *doḥsaṃdoha*, and *vaśīkṛtatribhuvanaśrīgarva*. Examples: *sarvaṃkaṣaḥ khalaḥ* (a wicked person who scrapes away everything), *kūlaṃkaṣā nadī* (a river that erodes its banks), *abhraṃkaṣo vāyuḥ* (wind that scrapes the clouds), *karīṣaṃkaṣā vātyā* (a whirlwind that scrapes up dried cow-dung). Thus says Murāri: "He who scrapes away the pride of the Fortune of the Three Worlds, which had been brought under his control by the mass of his arms.
The suffix *khaś* is also applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *megha*, *ṛti*, and *bhaya*. (43)

Medhaṃkaraḥ, kṣatiṃkaraḥ, bhayaṃkaraḥ; by the rule of elision of the final element (tadantavidhi), [we have] abhayaṃkaraḥ. Also, after [the words] kṣema, priya, and madra, the suffix aṇ is applied [to form a compound]. (Pāṇini 3.2.44)

[The suffix *kha* occurs after the root *kṣai*] in the sense of "one who makes secure," as in *kṣemakaraḥ*, *kṣemakāraḥ*, and so forth. Alternatively, having omitted *va*, the inclusion of *aṇ* is for the purpose of preventing the suffix *ṭa* in cases such as the instrumental (*hetv-ādi*). [The suffix *kha* occurs] after roots beginning with *alpārambha-* in the sense of "one who makes secure," when there is a desire to express the object (*karman*) as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*).
[The suffix *kha* occurs] after the root *bhū* following the word *aśita* in the senses of "doing" (*kāraṇa*) and "state of being" (*bhāva*). (45)

That by which one becomes satiated is *āśitambhava*; it refers to rice (*odana*) sufficient for the feeding of guests and others. The term *āśitambhava* means "the becoming-satiated of one who has eaten. By the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), the suffix *lyuṭ* may also be applied, resulting in *āśitabhavana* (masculine) or *āśitabhavanam* (neuter). However, the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others maintain that the suffix *ghañ* is superseded here because it is of the same form (*sarūpa*). As for the objection that the application of *lyuṭ* is improper because the rule of optional forms does not apply to the suffixes *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and those with the sense of *khala*, that is not correct.

This is because [the rule] refers only to those instances where *ktā* and other suffixes would otherwise apply by virtue of being superseded by *ghañ* and others. However, in this case, *khac* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *lyuṭ*; it is not the case that *lyuṭ* is an exception to *khac*, for the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) would otherwise be unavoidable. The Dīkṣitas conclude that the principle of "non-identity of form" does not apply in cases where one suffix is a superseder (*bādhaka*) of another, but it certainly does apply in cases where one is the superseded (*bādhyatva*).
In the sense of "name," [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the roots *bhṛ*, *vṛj*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam*. (46)

*Viśvaṃbharā* means the earth (*bhūḥ*). *Rathaṃtara* is that which crosses over with a chariot (*ratha-tara*). This word is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as a name for a *sāman*. However, its etymological fruit (*utpattiphala*)—namely, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) and the *avagraha* pause—is seen in cases such as *vasiṣṭho rathaṃtarājabhāvāḥ*, because of the original accent of the second member of the compound according to the rule for *kṛt* suffixes. If it were not a compound (but a single word), there would be the undesirable consequence of it being acutely accented on the first syllable and lacking an *avagraha*, by the rules *nabviṣayasya* and others. *Patimvarā* refers to a maiden who chooses her own husband. *Śatruñjayaḥ* refers to an elephant. *Yugandharaḥ* is a specific mountain. Regarding the *Bhārata* passage, "one should consume curds at Yugandhara," [the word is used in its conventional sense].

*Śatrusahaḥ*, *śatruṃtapaḥ*, and *ariṃdamaḥ*: these are transitive because their meaning involves the act of pacifying (*śamana*), or because the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is inherent within them.
And there is also the word *gama*. 47.
Sutaṅgama.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the words *anta*, *atyanta*, *adhva*, *dūra*, *pāra*, *sarva*, and *ananta*.

The word *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name) is no longer [applicable]. [The suffix *ḍa* applies when] it means "he goes to the end," as in *antagaḥ*, and so forth. There is an addition [to the rule] regarding *sarvatra* and *panna*: *sarvatragaḥ* (one who goes everywhere); *pannagaḥ* (a snake), because it goes on its feet (*padbhyāṃ gacchati*). There is also elision of *uras* [with the suffix *ḍa*]: *uragaḥ* (a snake). [The suffix *ḍa* applies] after *su* and *dur* in the sense of a location (*adhikaraṇe*): it is gone easily here, thus *sugaḥ*; with difficulty, thus *durgaḥ*. After *nis* in the sense of a location: that from which one does not go out is *nirgaḥ*. However, in reality, it should be stated that [the suffix *ḍa*] is seen after other words as well: *grāmagaḥ* (one who goes to a village), *gurutalpagaḥ* (one who goes to the teacher’s bed), and so forth.
The root *han* takes the augment *āś* when used in the sense of a benediction. || 49 ||

The suffix *ḍa* shall occur [after the root *han*]. *Śatruhaḥ* means "one who would kill an enemy" (*śatruṃ vadhyāt*). The meaning is: one whose specific desire has as its objective the act of killing an enemy. Why is the condition "in the sense of a benediction" (*āśiṣi*) stated? [Otherwise: *śatrughātaḥ*, meaning "one who kills an enemy" (*śatruṃ hanti*). Regarding the rule *dārāvāhano’ṇantasya ca ṭaḥ saṃjñāyām*: *dārvāghāṭaḥ* is the name for a type of woodpecker (*vanaspatīnām*). It should be stated that [the suffix *ḍa* occurs] after the root *han* when preceded by *cāru*. Thus: *cārvāghāṭaḥ* (variant: *cārvāghātaḥ*). By the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*: *varṇasaṃghāṭaḥ* (variant: *varṇasaṃghātaḥ*), meaning "one who strikes together the letters"; likewise *padasaṃghāṭaḥ* (variant: *padasaṃghātaḥ*), meaning "a collection of words.
[The suffix *ḍa* occurs after the root *han*] with the preposition *apa*, when [the object is] *kleśa* or *tamas*. (Pāṇini 3.2.50)

The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *han* (to kill) when preceded by the prefix *apa*, provided that *kumāra* or *śīrṣa* are the attendant words (*upapada*). This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding cases involving benediction (*āśis*). Examples: *kleśāpahaḥ putraḥ* (a son who removes affliction); *tamopahaḥ sūryādiḥ* (the sun and others which dispel darkness).
The suffix *ṇini* is applied [after the root *han*] when *kumāra* or *śīrṣa* are the attendant words. (51)
*kumāraghātī* (one who kills a youth). The form *śīrṣa-* for *śiras-* occurs due to irregular substitution (*nipātana*). *śīrṣaghātī* (one who strikes the head).
The suffix *ṭak* is applied after *jāyā* and *patnī* when they denote a characteristic mark. (Pāṇini 3.2.52)

The term *lakṣaṇa* is an adjective qualifying the agent (*kartṛ*). When the agent possesses such a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇavat*), the suffix *ṭak* is applied to the root *han* with these two upapadas. Thus, *jāyāghna* means "a man" and *patighnī* means "a woman"; the meaning is one who is the locus of a characteristic mark indicating that [the killing].
And [the same applies] when the agent is non-human. || 53 ||

*jāyāghna* means *tilaka* (a mark on the forehead); *patighnī* means a line on the hand; the meaning here is that which indicates such [a fate]. *pittaghnam* means *ghṛtam* (clarified butter). Why "not a human" (*amanuṣya*)? [In the case of] *ākhudhātaḥ śūdraḥ* (a Śūdra who kills a mouse), it is not so. Words such as *pralambadhna*, *śatrukṛtaghna*, and others are formed according to the rule for words beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. Words such as *coradhāta* (mouse-killer) and *nagaraghāta* (city-destroyer) [referring to] an elephant are formed by virtue of the rule regarding diversity (*bāhulaka*). [The suffix *kha* is applied] after *hasta* and *kapāṭa* when [the sense is] capability (*śakti*). (54)

The suffix *iṣṭak* is applied after the root *han* when "capacity" (*śakti*) is to be expressed. This rule is commenced for the purpose of referring to an agent who is a human being. Examples: *hastighnaḥ* (an elephant-killer) as a man; *kapāṭaghnaḥ* (a door-breaker) as a thief. Regarding the reading *kavāṭa*, Svāmī states that the substitution of *v* for *y* occurs because it belongs to the *yavādi* group. Haradatta, however, says that *kavāṭa* is derived from the root *aṭ* with the suffix *ac* (forming *aṭa*), preceded by *kava*; the substitution of *ka* for *ka* occurs due to a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *kavaṃ coṣṇe*. The meaning of the word "capacity" (*śakti*) here is the ability to kill by means of one's own strength. The suffixes *gha* and *tāc* are applied after the roots *han* and *tāḍ* respectively when the agent is a craftsman (*śilpin*). (Pāṇini 3.2.54) Examples: *pāṇighaḥ* (a drummer) and *tāḍaghaḥ* (a striker). The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pāṇi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pāṇi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking with the hand. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pāda-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pāda-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking with the foot. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *ajha-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *ajha-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking with the chin. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *tal-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *tal-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking with the palm. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *muṣṭi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *muṣṭi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking with the fist. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *prahara-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *prahara-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking with a blow. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *niṣpra-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *niṣpra-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking with a downward blow. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pari-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pari-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking around. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *upari-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *upari-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking from above. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *ava-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *ava-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking downwards. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *vi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *vi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking apart. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *sam-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *sam-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking together. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *abhi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *abhi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking towards. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pra-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pra-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking forward. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pari-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pari-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking around. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *upa-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *upa-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking near. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *ni-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *ni-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking down. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *vi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *vi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking apart. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *sam-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *sam-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking together. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *abhi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *abhi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking towards. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pra-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pra-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking forward. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pari-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pari-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking around. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *upa-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *upa-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking near. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *ni-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *ni-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking down. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *vi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *vi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking apart. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *sam-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *sam-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking together. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *abhi-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *abhi-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking towards. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pra-*; the suffix *tāc* is applied after the root *tāḍ* with the prefix *pra-*. Both denote a person whose profession is striking forward. The suffix *gha* is applied after the root *han* with the prefix *pari-*; the suffix *tāc* is

In the word *hanta*, the elision of the suffix *iṣṭhan* and the substitution of *ghatva* are prescribed by way of irregularity (*nipātana*). What is the purpose of the mention of *śilpin* (artisan)? [To show that it does not apply] in cases such as *pāṇighāta*. There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the word *rājadha*. He was a destroyer of kings (*rājadha*) because of his royal consecration (*nīrājanā*).

The suffix *khyun* is applied after the root *kṛ* when expressing an instrument (*karaṇa*), provided it refers to things dear to the blind, and provided the suffix *ac* is not present. (Pāṇini 3.2.56)

The suffix *khyun* is applied after the root *kṛ*, when words such as *āḍhya* and others—provided they do not end in *cu*—are used as upapadas (governing words) in the sense of the instrument (*cvyartha*). For example: *āḍhyakaraṇaṃ* ("that by which one makes someone wealthy"). Why "not ending in *cu*"? Consider *āḍhyīkaraṇaṃ*; here, only the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied.

Objection: Since there is no fault in both cases (the *cv*-suffix and the *khyun*-suffix), the mention of *cvi* is redundant. This is because there is no difference between them in terms of form or accent; for the suffix *khyun* is also prescribed by the rule "ṅīp, pañcan, añ, snañ, īkak, khyun, taruṇa, and taluna," and because, just as with the *upapada-samāsa* in the case of *khyun*, the *gati-samāsa* is also obligatory in the case of *lyuṭ*. Furthermore, the accent is identical—either by the *lit-svara* or the *nit-svara*—since both result in an udātta on the first syllable of the root *kṛ*. Finally, the prohibition "except for indeclinables" (*anavyayasya*) applies to the short vowel *mum* [in the case of *lyuṭ*], whereas a word ending in *cvi* is itself an indeclinable.

The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this states: "That [the mention of *kṛt*] is for the sake of what follows. Thus, since it has been determined by the authority of the *bhāṣya* and the *vārttika* that [the mention of *kṛt*] serves solely the purpose of what follows, the suffix *lyuṭ* certainly occurs after the *cvī* [suffix]. However, the authors of the *vṛtti* say that because the mention [of *kṛt*] would otherwise apply only to what follows, the force of the mention here—according to the maxim "when something is mentioned in a specific place, it applies to that place"—prevents *lyuṭ* from occurring here as well. That view is to be considered. [Now begins: *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau* (Pāṇini 3.2.57). "After the root *bhū*, the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are used in the sense of the agent."

In the previous section concerning the agent (*kartṛ*), these two suffixes—*iṣṇu* and *uc*—follow the root *bhū*. Examples: *āḍhyambhāvukaḥ* (one who is about to become wealthy) and *āḍhyambhaviṣṇuḥ* (one who will become wealthy). The venerable Maitreya Rishi says: "The arrows of Nārāca were [like] those which were about to cause tears to the beloved wife of Kṛtavīrya’s son. The traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) holds that the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is for the purpose of dispelling the confusion that the suffix *uc* might carry over from the previous rule regarding the "instrument" (*karaṇa*), and also for the sake of the subsequent rules. Nor is it the case that non-carrying over is established merely by the lack of an indicatory vowel (*asvaritatva*), because that would be an improper resort when a better solution exists. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "The suffix *iṣṇuc* follows the root *bhū* with the initial vowel of the suffix being udātta, and this is done for metrical reasons."
However, for the sake of establishing the correct accentuation of the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is held to begin with the vowel *i*.

The meaning of this is as follows: Since the root *bhu* takes the augment *iṭ*, the suffix *iṣṇu* is already established by the rule for *iṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35) following a consonant; thus, only *kṛṇu* should be prescribed, not *iṣṇu*. Nor does the objection arise that once the substitution of *kh* for *k* is made, there would be uncertainty as to whether *katva* or *śatva* applies in the form *kṣṇu*—for such a specific determination is obtained from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). This is the objection. The resolution is that in the negative compound *anāḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇu*, the suffix *iṣṇu* is intended for the sake of making the final syllable udātta, according to the rule *kṛtyokaiṣa-aṇ-uccārvādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.160).

Otherwise, there would be the inclusion of only that *iṣṇuc* which is explicitly taught (*pratipadokta*) by the rule beginning with *alaṃkṛñ*, as it is superseded [by other rules] therein; furthermore, because the rules for *ṣatva* and *ṇatva* are not established when the suffix *snu* is present, the form *ṣṇu* would not exist. Now, one might object: "This is already established merely by the presence of the indicatory letter *c* (in *caṅ*). Nor can its necessity be set aside on the grounds of being for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*), since the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is established by the accent of the suffix itself. For it has been stated that in the matter of the accent of a suffix, augments (*āgama*) are treated as non-existent."

As for Haradatta’s claim that the inclusion of this [root *spṛś*] is due to the force (*sāmarthya*) of the rules regarding the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṇ*, that is incorrect; for when a suffix accompanied by those [substitutions] is prescribed in preference to a suffix lacking them, the force of the argument is exhausted by the resulting economy of grammatical procedure (*prakriyālāghava*). Consequently, the vowel *i* would be entirely useless. Do not say so. For, by the paribhāṣā "the mention of a term with a specific *anubandha* [excludes others]," there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *kvin* not being included there. However, the force of the pronunciation of the vowel *i* overrides that [paribhāṣā]. Nor can the force be attributed to the letter *k*, as there is no deciding factor (*vinigamaka*) between them. [The rule continues: *spṛśo'nudake kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58).

When *udaka* or *bhinnena* is the upapada, the suffix *kin* is applied after the root *spṛś* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Examples: *dhṛtaspṛk*. The mention of "object" (*karman*) has ceased [to apply]. Although it might seem appropriate for "object" to follow because *spṛś* is transitive, nevertheless, since the mention of "agent" (*kartṛ*) in the previous rule was for this very purpose, in order to avoid its redundancy, there is one [application] when the object is the upapada and another when the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth are the upapadas; thus, for the sake of the agent-suffix, it applies in both cases.

Success! Regarding the rule *supyupapade* [Pāṇini 3.2.4], the ancients say that [the suffix *kvip*] is established by [the subsequent rule] *paryudāsāt*. However, the Dīkṣitas maintain that it is already established by the suffix *kvip* itself in the word *mantraspṛk*. They argue that because the substitution of *kutva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*) is prescribed elsewhere as well by resorting to the meaning "that after which the suffix *kvin* occurs," [the rule *supyupapade* is unnecessary]. Here, the letter *n* is not for the sake of the *nitsvara* accent, because there is no distinction since this prescription applies only to monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*). Furthermore, in the case of *dadhṛk*, the word will be taught as having the udātta accent on the final syllable. This is because the desired result is already established simply by reading *kvipratyayasya* instead of *kvinpratyayasya* in the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.62].

The term "explanation" (*nirdeśa*) refers to either a single instance or two instances, because doubt is removed by such an exposition; furthermore, the suffix *kvip* is not explicitly mentioned due to the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning that which follows it.
[This applies to the forms] *ṛtvij*, *dadhṛk*, *srak*, *dhruk*, *guṣṇik*, *añcu*, *yuj*, and *kṛ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.59)

The first five [roots] are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) with the suffix *kvin* ending in a short *i*. The suffix *kvin* is prescribed after three roots. Certain operations, even though not part of the standard grammatical rules (*alākṣaṇika*), are obtainable through these irregular formations. *Yaj* (to sacrifice) takes *kvin* when *ṛtu* is the upapada. After *dhṛṣ*, there is reduplication and the udātta accent on the final syllable. After *sṛj* (to emit), *kvin* is added in the sense of the object (*karman*). There is also the augment *ram*. After *diś* (to point out), [the suffix *kvin* is added] in the sense of the object. After *snih* preceded by *ut*, *kvin* is added; there is the elision of the *t* of the prefix and the change to *ṣ*. After *añc* (to bend), *kvin* is added when a *sup*-ending word is the upapada. So too for *yuj* (to join). After *kruñc* (to bend), there is the absence of the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).
After *dṛś* (to see), when it does not mean "perceiving" (*anālocane*), *kañ* is added when *tyad* and other pronouns are the upapadas. (Pāṇini 3.2.60)

The suffix *kvun* [is added after a nominal stem ending in *ā*]. Examples include *tādṛśaḥ* and *tādṛk*; the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) occurs because the word begins with a pronominal base (*sarvanāman*). Similarly, there are forms such as *yādṛśaḥ*. The letter *ñ* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta. Although the desired result could have been achieved by using *n*, the letter *ñ* is employed here to serve as a qualifier in the rule *kañ-kvarapau* (Pāṇini 5.2.139). For if *kan* were used there, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the suffixes *kan* and *kan* prescribed by the rule *apamityayācitābhyāṃ kakvanau* (Pāṇini 4.4.21).

The addition of *samāna* and *anya* [to the rule] provides for the substitution of *dṛś* with *dṛk*. Thus, *sadṛśaḥ* becomes *sadṛk*. Now, one might object that this suffix (*kvip*) should apply to the agent (*kartṛ*), yet it occurs here in the sense of the object (*karman*). This is because the agency is intended to be expressed due to the ease of the action; the meaning is: "People see him as if he were that [other person]," or "Being seen as that very person, he sees himself as if he were that. This has been stated merely to accord with the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi-artha*), for in reality, there is only the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśya*). [Now, the following rule: After the roots *sad*, *sū*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *vid*, *bhid*, *chid*, *jin*, and *rāj*, the suffix *kvip* is applied even when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present. (Pāṇini 3.2.61)

The suffix *kvip* is applied after these [roots] when *sup* (a nominal ending) follows as an *upapada*, whether an *upasarga* (prefix) is present or not. Although the term *sup* is understood from the previous rule, the explicit mention of *upasarga* is for the purpose of indicating that the mention of *upasarga* does not apply elsewhere where *sup* is mentioned. Consequently, the inclusion of "not when an *upasarga*" in the rule *vadaḥ supi* is unnecessary. However, in the case of *dusad*, this is because of the continued application of the restriction "not in the Veda" (*na chandasi*). As for *diviṣadaḥ*, Mādhava and others maintain that the change to *ṣ* occurs by virtue of its belonging to the *suṣāmādi* group.

Even though some roots beginning with *sad* (to sit) are transitive (*sakarmaka*), the word "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) does not apply there; rather, it applies to the root *sad* alone. In the phrase *hotā vediṣad atithir duroṇasat*: one who sits on the altar (*vedi*) is called *vediṣat*. The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt*. One who sits in the house (*duroṇa*) is called *duroṇasat*. The word *upaniṣat* is derived from the root *sad* preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni*, in the sense of "perishing" (*viśaraṇa*), with the suffix *kvip*. It is explained as follows: having brought near (*upanīya*) the non-dual Brahman, it destroys ignorance along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā-avidyā*); thus, it refers to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

Because they are the causes of that [knowledge], the Vedāntas are included through their association with the roots *ad* (to eat), *dviṣ* (to hate), and so on. However, this does not include the roots *sū* (in the forms *sū* and *sūyati*) or *div* (in the forms *div* and *divyati*). The root *dviṣ* means "enmity"; *duh* means "desire to harm"; *duh* means "to fill"; and *yuj* means "concentration. Both forms of *yuj*—meaning "union" and "joining"—are taken here. Because the root *vid* with the indicatory vowel *a* (*vid*) is intended, the roots *vid* in the sense of "knowing," *vid* in the sense of "investigation," and *vid* in the sense of "existence" are included; however, *vidlṛ* is not. *Bhidlṛ* means "cleaving"; *chidṛ* means "cutting into two"; *ṇīj* means "leading"; and *rājṛ* means "shining."

The suffix *sū* is added after *aṇḍa* and *prasū*, and so forth. After the roots *nī* (to lead) following the words *agra* and *grāma*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* should be stated; this is because of the specific grammatical usage (*nirdeśa*) "sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ" (he is their village-leader). This rule applies specifically to the scope of suffixes that result in total elision (*sarvalopī*), as established by the authoritative means of cognition (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*) that apprehends the nature of the rule. Therefore, it does not apply in cases such as *grāmanāya*. The suffix *ṇvi* is added after the root *bhaj* (to share/partake). 62.
[A suffix] beginning with *aṃśa* is applied [to the root *bhaj*]. [The suffix] *prabhāk* [is applied to the root *bhās*]. Due to the presence of the marker *ṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* [of the vowel].
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the suffix] *sahaḥ* [is applied to the root *sah*]. 63.
The suffix *ṇva* occurs [after a verbal root] to form a masculine noun denoting an agent: *duścayavanaḥ*, *pṛtanāṣāṭ*, *ayudhyaḥ*, *sahitraḥ*, and *abhivāhaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.138)
*dityavāt* and *dityauhī* belong to me; the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows.
The suffixes *puṃ*, *iṣ*, *purīṣ*, and *īṣan* are applied after the verbal root *kṛ* (to do/make).
Kavyavāhana, Purīṣavāhana, Purīṣyavāhana;
[the word] ananta [is used] in the sense of "infinite" when referring to the sacrificial oblation (havya). || 66 ||

When the word *havya* is an upapada, the suffix *ñyuc* is applied to the root *vah* in the Vedic language when it occurs at the end of a metrical foot (*pādānte*). This is because the rule *anantaḥ pādam* (Pāṇini 6.2.183) states that the entire form ending in the suffix must not be a constituent part of the latter half of a verse-quarter. Example: *agniś ca havyavāhanaḥ*. Why "at the end of a foot"? Counter-example: *kavyavāḍ agnir ajaraḥ pitā naḥ*.
[The suffix] *viṭ* is applied to the roots *jan*, *san*, *khan*, *kram*, and *gam*. (Pāṇini 3.2.67)

The root *jan* is used in the sense of "begetting" (*janane*), *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*), *ṣaṇ* in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*), and *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "sharing" (*sambhaktau*). According to tradition, both [roots] are to be understood here. By the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*, the nasal vowel becomes *ā*. Thus: *abjāḥ*, *gojāḥ*, and *goṣā indro asi*. In *sanoter anaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. [Examples: *iyam śuṣmebhir visakhā ivārujat*, *ādidhikrāḥ*, *śavase pañca kṛṣṭīḥ*, *vāyur agregā yajñaprīḥ*, and *ado 'nnane*. (68)

The phrase "in Vedic usage" (*chandasi*) is no longer applicable. When the word *anna* is the accompanying word (*upapada*), the suffix *viṭ* is applied to the root *ad*. [Examples: *grāmād annam*, *sasyād annam*. Why say "not food" (*ananne*)? [Counter-example: *annādaḥ*.
Also [when the word *kravya* is the accompanying word]: *kravye ca* || 69 ||

*Kravyād* means "one who eats raw meat. This rule is commenced to set aside the suffix *aṇ* established by the preceding [rule]. However, the form *kravyāda* is derived from the word *pakvamāṃsa* (cooked meat) with the suffix *aṇ*; the substitution of *kravya-* for the upapada [i.e., *pakva-*, "cooked"] occurs because the word belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. As for the statement that the suffix *aṇ* does not apply to *kravyāda*, the meaning of the original source (*ākara*) is that this applies when the intended sense is "one who eats raw meat" (*āmamāṃsabhakṣaka*).
[The suffix] *kap* [is added] after the root *duh*, and *gha* is also [substituted for the final consonant]. (Pāṇini 3.2.70)
Milk out desire at will from the wish-fulfilling cow; know me as that gracious wish-fulfilling cow—O Lord of Mantras, O White Steed, O Reciter of Hymns, O Oblation-Eater, O Soma-Presser! 71.

When *śveta* and other words are used as upapadas (governing words), the suffix *ṇvin* is applied after roots such as *vah*. This is a nipātana (irregular formation) for the sake of producing non-technical (alākṣaṇika) effects. Thus, "those very white ones carry [him]," and so Indra is called *śvetavāh*. When the word *śveta* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix is applied to the object (*karman*) of the root *vah*. One who recites the *ukthas* is called an *ukthaśās*, namely the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). In the sense of the ritual action (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the *uktha*, the suffix is added to the root *śaṃs* with the elision of the nasal (*n*). That which they offer (*dāśanti*) before (*puras*) is a *puroḍāś*. In the word *puras*, the suffix is applied to the root *dāśṛ* (to give/offer) in the sense of the object (*karman*), and there is the substitution of *ḍa* for *da*.

"It should be stated that [the rule applies] to words such as *śvetavāh* where there is the status of being a *pada* (a word-form) ending in a *ḍa* suffix. This means that where there is the status of a *pada* for that which ends in a *ḍa*, the suffix *ḍas* occurs; elsewhere, however, only *ṇvi* occurs. Furthermore, this is an exception (*apavāda*) even to the *ṇvi* prescribed by the rule *ave yajaḥ*. Examples: *śvetavā indraḥ*, *śvetavobhyām*, *śvetavobhiḥ*. [Objection: Why specify "of a *pada*" (*padasya*)? [Counter-example: *śvetavāhau*, *śvetavāhaḥ*. [Reply: It should not be argued that the specific rule of nipātana (irregular formation) for *avayāḥ* and *śvetavāh* is redundant because the lengthening of the vowel would be established by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* alone. This is because [without the present rule], the *ḍas* suffix would not apply to form the nominative singular *śvetavāḥ*. Thus, the mention of *padasya* is necessary.

The form *he śvetavāḥ* is for the sake of the vocative case; nor is the substitution of *ḍas* redundant, as it serves the purpose of forms such as *śvetavobhyām*. Nor should it be argued that the rule for the substitution of *ru* applies only to the domain of nominal stems (*pada*), for if *utva* (the substitution of *u*) did not occur after the vowel *ā*, the desired form would remain unestablished. Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that the substitution of *ru* must be prescribed for the vocative form *ukśaśāḥ*, provided there is evidence for it in the Vedic mantras.
[Pāṇini 6.4.141: *ave yajaḥ*.

When the word *ava* is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied to the root *yaj* in the context of a mantra. [Example: *tvaṃ yajñe varuṇasyāvayā asi*. [Derivation: He sacrifices away (avayajate) is *avayāḥ*; dual *avayājau*; plural *avayājaḥ*; dual instrumental *avayobhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *vij upe chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.73). When *upa* is an upapada, the suffix *vi* is applied to the root *yaj* in the Vedic language. [Example: *upayajati*. [Derivation: He sacrifices near (upayajati) is *upayāj*. Dual *upayājau*; plural *upayājaḥ*; dual instrumental *upayāgbhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *chandasy ṛdabhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.74). In the Vedic language, the suffix *vi* is applied after roots ending in short *ṛ*. [Example: *praṣṭhavāh*. [Derivation: He carries forward (prakarṣeṇa vahati) is *praṣṭhavāṭ*. Dual *praṣṭhavāhau*; plural *praṣṭhavāhaḥ*; dual instrumental *praṣṭhavāḍbhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *anyeṣv api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.75). The suffix *vi* is seen to be applied even after other roots. [Example: *sūyavasa*. [Derivation: Good pasture (suṣṭhu yavasam) is *sūyavasaḥ*. Dual *sūyavaso*; plural *sūyavasaḥ*; dual instrumental *sūyavobhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *karmaṇi sami ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76). When *sam* is an upapada, the suffix *vi* is applied to the root *yaj* in the sense of an object (*karman*). [Example: *saṃyājam*. [Derivation: He sacrifices together (saṃyajati) is *saṃyājaḥ*. Dual *saṃyājau*; plural *saṃyājaḥ*; dual instrumental *saṃyāgbhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *upāsane gṛhapateḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.77). When *gṛhapati* is an upapada, the suffix *vi* is applied to the root *yaj* in the sense of "worship" (*upāsana*). [Example: *gṛhapatīnāṃ saṃyājaḥ*. [Derivation: The joint sacrifice of the householders (*gṛhapatīnām upāsanam*) is *gṛhapatīnāṃ saṃyājaḥ*. Dual *saṃyājau*; plural *saṃyājaḥ*; dual instrumental *saṃyāgbhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *some suñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.78). When *soma* is an upapada, the suffix *vi* is applied to the root *su* (*sunoti*) in the Vedic language. [Example: *somasut*. [Derivation: He presses Soma (somaṃ sunoti) is *somasut*. Dual *somasutau*; plural *somasutaḥ*; dual instrumental *somasudbhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *rājani yudhikṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.79). When *rājan* is an upapada, the suffix *vi* is applied to the roots *yudh* and *kṛ* in the Vedic language. [Examples: *rājayudhvā*, *rājakṛtvā*. [Derivations: He fights with kings (rājñā yudhyate) is *rājayudh*; he acts for kings (rājñaḥ karoti) is *rājakṛt*. Dual *rājayudhvānau*; plural *rājayudhvānaḥ*; dual instrumental *rājayudhvabhyām*, and so forth. Dual *rājakṛtvānau*; plural *rājakṛtvānaḥ*; dual instrumental *rājakṛtvabhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *sahe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.80). When *saha* is an upapada, the suffix *vi* is applied to the roots *yudh* and *kṛ* in the Vedic language. [Examples: *sahayudhvā*, *sahakṛtvā*. [Derivations: He fights with (saha yudhyate) is *sahayudh*; he acts together with (saha karoti) is *sahakṛt*. Dual *sahayudhvānau*; plural *sahayudhvānaḥ*; dual instrumental *sahayudhvabhyām*, and so forth. Dual *sahakṛtvānau*; plural *sahakṛtvānaḥ*; dual instrumental *sahakṛtvabhyām*, and so forth. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *kṣemapriyamadre ’ṇ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.81). When *kṣema*, *priya*, or *madra* are upapadas, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and also the suffix *vi*, to the root *kṛ*. [Examples: *kṣemakāraḥ*, *kṣemakāraḥ*; *priyakāraḥ*, *priyakāraḥ*; *madrakāraḥ*, *madrakāraḥ*. [Derivations: He performs what is secure (kṣemaṃ karoti) is *kṣemakāraḥ*; he performs what is dear (priyaṃ karoti) is *priyakāraḥ*; he performs what is pleasant (madraṃ karoti) is *madrakāraḥ*. Dual *kṣemakārāu*; plural *kṣemakārāḥ*; dual instrumental *kṣemakārābhyām*, and so forth. Dual *kṣemakṛtvānau*; plural *kṣemakṛtvānaḥ*; dual instrumental *kṣemakṛtvabhyām*, and so forth. The same applies to *priyakāraḥ* and *madrakāraḥ*. The mention of both suffixes (*aṇ* and *vi*) is because they are not mutually exclusive. The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. [Next rule: *ākrośe ’vanyor grahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.82). When *ava* or *ni* are upapadas, the suffix *vi* is applied to the root *grah* in the sense of reviling (*ākrośa*). [Example: *avagrāhaḥ*, *nigrāhaḥ*. [Derivations: He seizes (ava gṛhṇāti) is *avagrāhaḥ*;

The suffix *ḍap* is applied after the root *yaj* when the word *upa* is the preceding member (*upapada*), according to Vedic usage. Thus we have *upayaṭ*, as in *upayajau* and *upayajaḥ*. The reason for the term *upayaṭ* being used for these offerings is that they are performed with the formula *upayajanti ūrdhvam*. Its formation is established by the rule *na cānyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* ("it is also seen after other roots"). This is because the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.108] is intended as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*)—namely, that *upayajaḥ* occurs only in the Veda. The inclusion of the indicatory letter *c* (in *ḍap*) is for the purpose of preventing the general application of the rule *ver apṛktasya* (which would otherwise cause the elision of the suffix).
The suffixes *manin*, *kvanip*, and *vanip* are added after verbal roots ending in *ā*.

When a preposition (*upasarga*) is present as an attendant word (*upapada*), these three suffixes—*man*, *van*, and *vin*—occur after a verbal root ending in long *ā* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Furthermore, the suffix *vic* also occurs. Examples: *sudāmā*, *sudhīvā*, *supīvā*, *bhūridāvā*; *ghṛtam*, *ghṛtapāvānaḥ*; *kīlālaye somapṛṣṭhāya vedhase*; *aśva iva tiṣṭhatyaśvatthāmā*. They are also seen after other roots. (Pāṇini 3.2.75)

The phrase "in the Vedic language" (*chandasi*) is no longer applicable. Four suffixes may also occur after other verbal roots. From *śru* (to hear): *suśarmā* (one who hears well); the augment *iṭ* is not applied because of the rule *neḍ vaśi*. From *i* (to go): *prātaritvā* (one who goes early in the morning); *tuk* is added because of the suffix having the marker *p*. From *jan* (to be born): *vijāvā* (one who gives birth); the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *viṅvanor ātvaṃ*. From *oṇṛ* (to remove): *avāvā*; here, the substitution of *ā* for the nasal and the replacement by *ava* take place. From *ru*, *reṭ*, and *sugaṇ*: [the suffix *kvip* is applied]. The inclusion of the term *dṛśi* is for the sake of following actual usage. And the suffix *kvip* [is also applied]. (76)

This [sūtra] is also like the previous one; it is an elaboration of *satsūdviṣa-* etc. By the recurrence of the word *api* (also), the meaning is that [the suffix *kvip*] occurs after all roots in both Vedic (*chandas*) and common usage (*bhāṣā*). *Ukhāyāḥ sraṃsate* (it falls from the pot) becomes *ukhāsrat*. *Parṇād dhvaṃsate* (it falls from the leaf) becomes *parṇadhvat*. The substitution of *d* for *t* is by the rule *vasusraṃsu-*. *Vāhāt bhraśyati* (it falls from the shoulder) becomes *vāhabhraṭ*. The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is by the rule *vraśca-*. The commentary (*vṛtti*) reads *vahābhraṭ*; *vahaḥ* means "shoulder. Haradatta states that by the rule *anyeṣām api*, there is lengthening of the final vowel of the upapada. *Sthaḥ ka ca* (7.4.44): [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *sthā*, and the letter *k* is substituted for its final.]

[The suffix] *kvip* [is added]. Since the forms *śasthaḥ* and *śaṃsthāḥ* are established by the previously mentioned *kvip* and by the rule *supi sthaḥ*, this [new rule] is commenced for the purpose of overriding (*bādhārtham*) the vowel *a* of the root *śam*. Kaiyaṭa says that because of the statement "the substitution of *ī* occurs before a suffix beginning with *v* or *y*" (Pāṇini 6.4.64), or because the form *śam* does not occur as a verbal base (*bhāṣya*), there is an absence of the substitution of *ī* by virtue of the rule on "the appearance of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). This is according to the view that the rule on the appearance of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇasūtra*) is intended to provide a grammatical operation (*alvidhyartham*) when the suffix is predominant. However, according to the view that it is a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*), Dīkṣita maintains that there is no status as a substitute (*sthānivattvam*) due to the prohibition in the rule *nalvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56).

[Objection: Why not formulate the rule simply as *sthaḥ kaC* immediately after *śami dhātoḥ*, with the letter *ca* serving to include the vowel *ac*? Thus, by the rule for lengthening a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*), the form *saṃsthā* would be established. In this way, there would be the economy of having the general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*) occupy the same location, and the possibility of the *ītvam* (substitution of *ī*) would not arise. [Reply: To this they say: If that were the case, in the word *asaṃsthā*, the final syllable of the compound would be udātta according to the rule *ackāvaśaktāv* (P. 6.2.172), because the word *saṃsthā* ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) by virtue of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*-affixes. However, when there is a *nañ*-compound with a *kvip*-derived form, the initial syllable is udātta due to the original accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which serves as the prior member.
The suffix *ṇini* is added after a verbal root ending in *su*, when not denoting a genus (*ajāti*), provided the sense is that of habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*).

When a word ending in a *sup* suffix (a nominal case-ending) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṇini* shall be applied to express habitual action (*tācchīlya*), provided the sense of "birth" (*ajāti*) is not intended. Although the term *sup* was already understood from the previous rule, its explicit mention here is for the purpose of excluding the restriction "not when preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarge*); thus, it applies even when there is merely a *sup* suffix. Examples are *udāsariṇyaḥ* and *pratyāsariṇyaḥ*. This is the statement of the Bhāṣya. As for the claim that the mention of *sup* is for the purpose of excluding prefixes—cited by Jayāditya, Haradatta, Mādhava, and others, who say "there is an extension [of the rule] for *sṛ* after *ut* and *prati* when followed by *māṅ*"—that is clearly contrary to the Bhāṣya.

Therefore, there are such usages as *liṅgaśeṣavidhir vyāpī* ("the rule for the remainder of gender is pervasive") and *sa babhūvopajīvinām* ("he became the sustainer of those who live off him"). [Question: Why [is the word] *ajātau* ("not denoting a genus") used? [Answer: As in *brāhmaṇānām āmantrayitā* ("one who invites Brāhmaṇas"). [The suffix] *tṛn* indicates habitual action (*tācchīlya*). [Question: Why "habitual action"? [Answer: As in *kadācid uṣṇaṃ bhuṅkte* ("sometimes he eats hot food"). Regarding the statement "the suffix *u* is taught for one who performs an action well": *sādhukārī* ("one who does well"), *sādhudāyī* ("one who gives well"). Regarding *brahmaṇi vadaḥ*: *brahmavādinaḥ vadanti* ("the exponents of Brahman speak"). This is the distinction between the follower of the Buddha (*saugata*) and the exponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*). Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that these two rules are intended to express that habitual action.

If it is objected that, in this case, the Bhaṭṭa-vārtika’s explanation of the word *brahmavādin*—as referring to one who has that as their habit (*tacchīla*), that as their duty (*taddharma*), or one who performs it well (*sādhukārī*)—would be inconsistent, they reply as follows: By the rule *supyajātāv* (Pāṇini 3.2.78), with the addition of the explanatory supplement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), the suffix *ṇini* applies in the sense of one who performs [an action] well (*sādhukārī*). Furthermore, by the rule *āvaśyakādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.170), the *ṇini* suffix ultimately results in the sense of "one whose nature it is" (*taddharma*). Thus, according to the aforementioned vārtika, even if there were no supplementary rule for the *ṇini* suffix in the absence of habitual action and so forth, it would still be easily available in the senses of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so on. The assumption that there exists a vārtika prescribing the *ṇini* suffix under the governing heading *ākveḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.57) is entirely baseless.
The suffix *kṛt* is applied when the object of comparison (*upamāna*) functions as the agent (*kartṛ*).

The sūtra is intended to convey the meanings of non-observance of conduct (*atācchīlya*), genus (*jāti*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*). In this context, the meaning of the secondary word (*upapada*) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix. Examples include *uṣṭrakrośī* ("one who cries out like a camel") and *dhvāṃkṣarāvī* ("one who screeches like a crow"). Although the cognition [produced] there is that "one who is the locus of crying out similar to a camel," one should not suspect that the meaning of the secondary word is connected to the meaning of the suffix as its locus—just as similarity is—because such a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meaning of the secondary word and the meaning of the suffix is not observed elsewhere. Nevertheless, similarity is indeed the meaning of the suffix *-in*.

In that context, the meaning of the *upapada* (the word "uṣṭra") is construed as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). And similarity (*sādṛśya*) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) by way of being its motivator (*prayojaka*), and with the other meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*)—namely, the locus (*āśraya*)—by way of its own nature (*svarūpasambandha*). [Finally], it is construed non-differently (*abheda*) with Devadatta and so forth. Thus, the cognition is: "Devadatta is non-different from the locus of the braying which is the motivator of the similarity to a camel. This is because it is a well-established rule of grammar (*vyutpanna*) that the construction of another word with the meaning of the suffix occurs even before the construction of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Why is the term "agent" (*kartari*) specified? [Consider: *apūpān iva bhakṣayati māṣān* ("He eats beans as if they were cakes"). Why is the term "standard of comparison" (*upamāne*) specified? [Consider: *uṣṭraḥ krośati* ("The camel brays").
In the case of a vow. || 80 ||

The suffix *ṇini* may be applied [in this sense]. For example: *sthaṇḍilaśāyī*. Regarding this, Amarasimha states: "He who sleeps on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍila*) by virtue of a religious vow is called *sthaṇḍilaśāyī*."

He is one who eats what is unasked for (*ayācitāśī*) and does not eat at a *śrāddha* (*aśrāddhabhojī*). Although the word *śrāddhabhojī* here does not refer to a religious vow (*vrata*), its formation as a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with the *ṇini*-derived form in the non-conventional analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*)—namely, "not a *śrāddha*-eater"—is nonetheless established. This is because, otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the word being *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable), whereas by the rule *kṛd-uttara-pada-prakṛti-svara*, the final syllable is desired to be *antodātta*. Nor can the initial accent of the preceding member be established by the rule *ṇin-i*; for if one were to follow the interpretation that the term *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name) is understood in that context, a logical flaw would arise. In this case, the analysis is not "one who eats a *śrāddha*" (*na śrāddhasya bhojī*).

Since the form *bhojī* is not grammatically correct when preceded by a subordinate term (*upapada*) other than *su*, one must instead form the sentence "he eats the *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhaṃ bhuṅkte*), and then, having formed an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) of the negative particle *nañ* with *śrāddha*, the suffix *ṇini* is to be applied when the word *aśrāddha* serves as the subordinate term. Now, an objection might be raised: since eating both what belongs to a *śrāddha* and what is different from it occurs through natural inclination (*rāga*), the purpose of the injunction is merely the prohibition of eating the *śrāddha* food, and not the prescription of eating non-*śrāddha* food as well—just as in the rule "five-clawed animals are to be eaten" (*pañca pañcanakhā bhakṣyāḥ*).

If it is asked how the Bhāṣya—"In that case, when one who has resolved not to eat at a *śrāddha* does not eat on a day when there is no *śrāddha*, would there not be a violation of his vow (*vratalopa*)?"—is consistent, Kaiyaṭa explains this as follows: "For one who has made the resolve, 'I must certainly eat [only] non-*śrāddha* food,' if he fails to eat on a particular day when there is no *śrāddha* while hunger is present, there would indeed be a violation of his vow.
[Pāṇini 3.2.81: *bahulam ābhīkṣṇye*.
