The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a word ending in a sup-case when the sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) is to be expressed. For example: *kṣīrapāyiṇa uśīnarāḥ* (the Uśīnaras are habitual drinkers of milk) and *kaṣāyapāyino gāndhārāḥ* (the Gāndhāras are habitual drinkers of decoctions). Because of their capacity or desire, or because there is no other [kind of] drinking, they drink decoctions; it is not due to habituality (*tācchīlya*). [Next, the rule for] *manas*: 82.

In the rule *manijñāne*, the root belonging to the *divādi* class is intended, and not the root *manu* in the sense of "understanding," because otherwise the suffix *khaś* in the subsequent sūtra would result in the impossibility of the *śyan* affix. When a word ending in a *sup* suffix follows, the suffix *ṇini* is added to the root *man*. Example: *darśanīyamānī* (one who considers himself beautiful).
Furthermore, when expressing self-regard (*ātmamāna*), the suffix *khaś* is also applied. (Pāṇini 3.2.83)

When the suffix *khaś* has the meaning of "to consider" (*man*) and takes an object, the suffix *khaś* is replaced by *aṇ*, provided it is not preceded by *iṇ*. Nor should it be said that this is already established by the rule of *vāsarūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.94); for in rules such as *karaṇe yajaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.85), the mention of both [suffixes] together is intended to delimit the scope of *ṇin* so that it may continue to apply there. One who considers oneself learned is called *paṇḍitamanyaḥ* or *paṇḍitamānī*. [In the latter], *māna* is a noun formed with the suffix *ghañ*. There is a compound with the word *ātmanaḥ* ending in the genitive case used as an object. Here, the word *mati* is used figuratively to refer to an error having the self (*ātman*) as its qualificandum. The word *paṇḍita* refers to that which has the non-difference from a learned person (*paṇḍita*) as its qualifier.

Through the relation of non-difference (*abhedasaṃsarga*), there is the connection with the error (*bhrama*). The locus (*āśraya*) is the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix. Thus, the meaning is: "the locus of an error whose qualificandum is the self and whose qualifier is the non-difference from a scholar.
[In the case of] the past tense (*bhūte*). || 84 ||

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). It extends as far as the rule *vartamāne laṭ*. Furthermore, this [term *bhūte*] qualifies the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because of the governing rule *dhātoḥ*. Nor is it the case that the suffix *kta* is to be prescribed after the verb *bhū* when it has the sense of a past action; for if that were so, the word *bhūta* would acquire the status of referring to a past action. Thus, there would be a circularity: the suffix *niṣṭhā* would depend on the governing rule, and the governing rule would depend on the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
In reality, however, there is no fault, because the understanding of the meaning of the word *bhūta* does not depend upon the comprehension of the rule prescribing the suffix *niṣṭhā* and so forth.

Now, the purposes [of the rule]: by the rule *kumāra-śīrṣayor ṇiniḥ*, the suffix *ṇini* is prescribed for the future and the present, overriding the *ṇini* [prescribed] for the past according to the maxim of Takra-Koṇḍinya. If the heading *bhūta* (past) did not exist, the prescription would apply to both [future and past] equally as a general rule; or rather, the re-presentation [of the rule] could be justified as being for the purpose of excluding the *asarūpa* (non-homogeneous) suffixes. Similarly, by the restriction that *kvip* follows *han* in the sense of the past only when preceded by "Brahman" and so forth, *kvip* is excluded from *han* when used with other words in the sense of the past.

In cases such as *tevākhuhā*, [the suffix] indeed occurs at another time (*kālāntara*). Since the suffixes *śatṛ* and *ṅvanip*—prescribed for the present and the past respectively by the word *eva*—do not stand in a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) due to their distinct domains (*viṣayabheda*), [there is no conflict]. However, if the rule were not commenced under the governing headings of both the past and the present, then the suffix *śatṛ*, being prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) in connection with sacrifice (*yajñasaṃyoga*), would sublate *ṅvanip* even in all three times. Consequently, in the past tense in connection with sacrifice, the form *sutvā* would not be possible. Nor can *ṅvanip* be established by the rule regarding "different forms" (*vāsarūpanyāya*).

In the case of the rule *śrutvā śrutvā* (having heard, having heard), there would be no restriction regarding the difference in time [between the two actions]. Likewise, for the root *svap* (to sleep), the suffix *liṭ* is prescribed for the past tense (*bhūta*), while *nañjiṅ* is prescribed for the present tense (*vartamāna*). If there were no governing authority for both [tenses], then *liṭ* would be sublated by *nañjiṅ*, which is specifically prescribed for *svap*. Similarly, in the case of *aneha* (not here), the suffix *asi* [in the form *ehac*] in the rule *nañyāhana ehaṅ* would certainly sublate [the general suffix] only in the present tense; if this [dual authority] did not exist, it would sublate it even at other times. Thus, *kānac* in the past tense and *ānaś* in the present tense—[the latter] does not become a sublater of *kānac*.

Although there is no difference [between the two suffixes] because the rule *ādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.71) applies only to *sārvadhātuka* substitutes for *la*-suffixes—and thus does not apply to *cānaś* either—nevertheless, since *kānac* is marked with the *ātmanepada* designation, it occurs only when the action benefits the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), whereas *cānaś* occurs without such restriction; this distinction should be understood.
The root *yaj* [takes the suffix *kyap*] when used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). || 85 ||

When a word denoting an instrument (karaṇa) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṇini* shall be applied after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) in the sense of the agent (kartṛ). For example: *agniṣṭomayājī*, meaning "one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma. Vṛttikāra, Nāgōjibhaṭṭa, Haradatta, and others explain this as: "one who has brought about heaven by means of the Agniṣṭoma as the instrument. Their underlying intention is that [the suffix applies] to the general operation consisting of the production of heaven.

In the operation of the qualified object (viśeṣya), namely the sacrifice known as the Agniṣṭoma, although the sacrifice is itself unestablished and thus—being unfit to function as a means—is a *karman* (object) because it is being performed, nevertheless its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is also established due to a distinction in its capacities (*śakti*). This is seen in the expression "the cuckoo is intoxicated by the honey being drunk," where the honey, despite being the object of the act of drinking, functions as the instrument in the act of intoxication. In the case of *yajati* and similar roots, there are two forms: the general property of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) and the specific property such as being the root *yaji* (*yajitva*).

In that context, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of another factor—presented in the form of "sacrificing-ness" (*yajitva*) and so forth—with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is included within the verbal root as the "giver-ness" (*dātṛtva*). For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsaka position that the productive activity is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-artha*) is to be disregarded.

However, this must be stated here: let it be as it may in the case of an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*); but this is a reiterative sentence (*anuvāda-vākya*). And in this case, there is no expectancy for the three factors (*aṃśatraya*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), because the factor of the result is not experienced in its general form as "heaven" and so forth. Therefore, here it is the very nature of the sacrifice that is presented by the root *yaj*, while the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) merely reiterates the status of being an instrument already obtained from the injunctive sentence—just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on level ground. In both an injunction and a reiteration, the sacrifice is intended to be the instrument;
when an instrumental ending occurs in proximity to it, it does not relinquish its denotation of that [instrumentality].

Because of this statement by the author of the Vārttika, the meaning is that what is understood through implication (*ākṣepa*) as the "thing-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) in an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*) is not what is restated in the restatement sentences (*anuvāda-vākya*); rather, it is the "instrumentality" (*karaṇatva*) understood therein that is restated. Therefore, even according to the Grammarians’ view, the cognition is appropriately expressed as: "the substratum of the destruction of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) which has as its instrument the sacrifice non-different from the Jyotiṣṭoma. However, in the Mīmāṃsakas’ view, since the productive urge is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and because there is no evidence for such an implication here, [the cognition] is simply: "the substratum of the destruction of the sacrifice named Jyotiṣṭoma. This is the general direction [of the argument]. [Now follows: *karmaṇi hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.72).

The governing rule (*adhikāra*) "after a verbal root" (*karmaṇi*) extends up to the word *saha* [in Pāṇini 3.2.98]. "One who has killed his paternal uncle" is *pitṛvyaghātī*. Here is the commentary: "The mention of 'the contemptible' (*kutsita*) must be supplied. It does not apply here in the case of "one who has killed a thief" (*coraṃ hatavān*). This [supply] is obtained by bringing down (*apakarṣa*) the mention of "the contemptible" which will be stated later in the rule *karmaṇīniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.95). The author of the Nyāsa says: "It occurs when the agent is censured for performing an action that is already established as such—namely, the killing of a paternal uncle and so forth—and not otherwise.

Others, however, say that this is also obtainable from the power of the word itself, even though it is supported by the Bhāṣya. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied after the roots *brahmán*, *bhrūṇá*, and *vṛtra*. (Pāṇini 3.2.87)

Regarding the rule *hano bhūte kaṅkiṣ* (Pāṇini 3.2.105): "The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *han* in the sense of the past (*bhūta*). This sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). The commentary (*vṛtti*) states that this applies to all four: the root (*dhātu*), the prefix (*upapada*), the time (*kāla*), and the suffix (*pratyaya*). However, the *Bhāṣya* states that it applies only to the root and the time. In this regard, the intention of the *vṛtti* is as follows: the formulation of the sentence would be *yatraivopapadeṣu hanter bhūte kvip*. And thus, the formulation of the sentence would be *yatraivopapadeṣu hanter bhūte kvip*.

And thus, according to the maxim that "where there is the particle *eva*, restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) applies to what is other than that," the restriction "only in the case of *brahmā* and so forth" follows immediately [from the rule], resulting in a restriction of the verbal root whose fruit is the exclusion of connection with any upapada other than *brahmā* and the rest; this restriction pertains to the object of killing. Furthermore, because the word *bhūte* ("in the past") is employed here, the suffix *kkip* indeed occurs even after another upapada at a different time [than the present]. For example: *puruṣahā* ("one who has killed, will kill, or kills a man").

In the rule *brahmādiṣu hanter bhūte* (Pāṇini 3.2.87), although there is equality in terms of immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), the restriction is placed on the *upapada* (governing word) because of its priority. Here too, by virtue of relying on the term *bhūte* ("in the past"), the suffix occurs even after another root at a different time; for example, *vṛtraṃ jayati* or *jeṣyati* results in *vṛtrājit*. In the rule *brahmādiṣu hanter bhūte eva kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.86), although there is equality regarding the proximity of both base and suffix, the restriction is placed on the suffix because of its predominance. Here, by virtue of relying on the phrase *brahmādiṣu*, forms such as *puruṣahā* are established as before.

The restriction regarding time—that the *kvip* suffix occurs after the root *han* when preceded by *brahmā* and others only in the sense of the past—is established here as well. Even in this case, when there is another governing word (*upapada*), another suffix will certainly occur even in the past tense, as in *pitṛvyaghātī*. Since this restriction applies only to cases where there is a governing word, and because of the maxim that "an exception [applies] in the middle," the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix indeed occurs in the sense of "he killed Vṛtra. Therefore, it is established that due to the absence of a definitive deciding factor, the restriction here is fourfold.

This [interpretation] is to be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya. There is a restriction on the verbal root (*dhātuniyama*): the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *han* only when *brahmā* and others are the upapadas, and not with any other upapada. Therefore, in the case of "he killed a person" (*puruṣaṃ hatavān*), there is no *kvip*. There is also a restriction on time (*kālaniyama*): after the root *han*, when *brahmā* and others are the upapadas, only *kvip* occurs in the sense of the past tense, and no other suffix. Thus, by means of *kvip*, the past tense is restricted. Consequently, when *brahmā* and others are the upapadas, the suffix *ṇini*—as in the rule *hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.86) for the past passive participle—is not applied.

For this very reason, the subsequent sūtra is consistent with the requirement to establish *kvip* even when another word (*upapada*) is present in the past tense. Thus, Kaiyaṭa maintains that both—the restriction regarding the word (*upapada-niyama*), namely that *kvip* occurs after the root *han* only when *brahman* and others are the words; and the restriction regarding the suffix (*pratyaya-niyama*), namely that *kvip* occurs after *han* only in the past tense—are not supported by the Bhāṣya and should therefore be disregarded. Consequently, *kvip* occurs after *han* in the past tense even when other words are the *upapadas*, and it certainly occurs even after *han* when preceded by words such as *brahman* at other times [not in the past]. For example: *puruṣaṃ hatavān* (he has killed a man) → *puruṣahā*.

It should be understood that "brahmakṛt" means "one who performs the Brahman-rite. Furthermore, when resorting to the restriction of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and tenses (*kāla*), the very basis is compliance with the observed usage (*lakṣya*). By this, the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamakābhāva*) is refuted, since the establishment of the system of observed usage is achieved solely in accordance with the *Bhāṣya*. As for the reason stated here—that because the verbal root and tense are presented by a secondary means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arising from the context (*prakaraṇa*), whereas the *upapada* (governing word) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are presented by direct statement (*śruti*), it is therefore more logical that the restriction applies only to the subject matter presented by the context—that is not correct.

Because the accomplishment of the meaning of a sentence occurs equally through all four—case-role (dhātu), time (kāla), grammatical concord (anvaya), and syntactic exclusion (vyatireka)—the presence [of a word] by way of context (prakaraṇa) is weak precisely when it contradicts direct statement (śruti). For here, there is no sublation of that [contextual presence] by direct statement, as there is no contradiction; rather, it should be understood that [the sublation occurs] by means of another sentence that must be inferred.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution] occurs frequently.
The suffix *kvip* is diversely applied after the root *han* even when preceded by other upapadas: e.g., *mātṛhā*, *pitṛhā* (matricide, patricide); [also] *mātṛghātaḥ*.
After the root *kṛ*, it is applied when *sukṛta*, *karmakṛt*, *pāpakṛt*, *mantrakṛt*, and *puṇyakṛt* are the upapadas. || 89 ||

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the words *su*, *karma*, and so forth. Although the word *karmani* (in the sense of "object") is understood from the previous rule, it does not connect with the word *su*, because as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it cannot logically function as an object. The *Vṛtti* states that there are three types of restrictive rules (*niyama*) concerning time, upapadas, and affixes. The author of the *Nyāsa* maintains that this [restriction] is obtained through the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously"). Thus we have examples such as *sukṛt* and *karmakṛt*. Because of the restriction that [the suffix applies] only in the past tense (*bhūte eva*), when one intends to express "he performs a mantra" or "he will perform a mantra," the suffix *kvip* is not applied.

Due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that [the suffix *kvip*] occurs after the root *kṛ* only when followed by words beginning with *sva*, there is no *kvip* in the case of *mantrādhyāḥ* (one who has studied the mantra), as it is derived from *adhi-i*. Due to the restrictive rule that [the suffix *aṇ*] occurs after the root *kṛ* only when followed by words beginning with *sva*, there is no *aṇ* in the case of *karmakṛtaḥ* (one who has performed the action). Because there is no such restriction that [the suffixes occur] only after words beginning with *sva* and only after the root *kṛ*, the suffix *kvip* occurs even with other upapadas, as in *śāstrakṛt* (author of a treatise) and *bhāṣyakṛt* (author of a commentary). [The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *suñ* when *soma* is the upapada: [Pāṇini 3.2.90].
The Soma-presser has pressed the Soma;
[he offers it] into the fire. || 91 ||
The one who has piled the fire is called *agnicit*. The commentary states that the fourfold restriction applies in both cases [the agent and the object].
[Pāṇini 3.2.91] "In the case of an action, when it is designated by the word 'fire' (*agni*). (92)

When the object (*karman*) is the upapada and refers to that very same *kāraka*, the suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *ci* (to pile). This occurs when naming a specific site for the installation of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*). For example, *śyenacit*: the meaning is "that which has been produced in the shape of a hawk (*śyena*) by means of piling bricks.
Regarding the suffix *in*, [the rule is] "after a verbal root ending in a vowel, provided the object is present" (*karmaṇīniḥ vikriyaḥ*). 93.

The suffix *ini* shall occur after the root *krī* (to buy) preceded by the prefix *vi*, when a word denoting the object (*karman*) is used as an upapada. "The term 'contemptible' (*kutsita*) must be supplied. This [requirement] is further obtainable from the repetition of the word 'object' (*karman*). Examples: *somavikrayī* (a seller of Soma), *ghṛtavikrayī* (a seller of clarified butter). Because that [act] generates demerit (*pratyavāya*), the agent of it is considered contemptible. Why "when contemptible"? Example: *dhānyavikrāyaḥ* (a seller of grain). [Now follows: *dṛśeḥ kvanip* (94). [The suffix *kvanip* occurs after the root *dṛś* (to see) when a word denoting the object is used as an upapada.]

Since [the suffix] is established by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*, this [rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). By this, the suffixes *manin* and others, as well as *aṇ*, are excluded; however, the *niṣṭhā* (past participle suffixes) remains. For example: *pāraṃ dṛṣṭavān* ("one who has seen the further shore"). Thus, one who has seen or sees the further shore is called *paradṛśvā*. Although the commentators and others have stated that this is for the purpose of excluding other suffixes, they have not stated that it is for the purpose of excluding other times (tenses). [Now begins: *rājani yudhikṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.95).

The suffix *kvanip* shall occur [after a verb ending in *a*]. The root *yudh* has the sense of the causative (*ṇic*) inherent within it. One who has caused the king to fight is called *rājayudhvā*; likewise, *rājakṛtvā*.
[The suffix *kvanip* occurs] also after the root *sah*. (Pāṇini 3.2.96)

The term "karmaṇi" (in the sense of the object) is excluded here because the word *saha* has the meaning of a non-substantive (*asattvārtha*). Śrīharṣa says: "He describes the exhaustion [caused] by the night, by the darkness, and by the battle. Murāri says: "The ten-headed one [Rāvaṇa], acting as a companion to the victory of Sutrāman [Indra].
[The suffix] *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan* when the locative case is used. (97)

*Sarasijam* (a lotus): [formed from *sara* + *sija*, with the elision of *s*]. *Sphuradurasijabhārabhaṅgurāṅgī*: [formed from *sphuradura* + *asija* + *bhāra* + *bhaṅgura* + *aṅgī*, with the elision of *s*]. *Haladantādityaluk*: [the elision of the final letter of the preceding member when followed by a consonant or a vowel beginning with *i*, as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.108]. *Mandurajaḥ* (born in a stable): [formed from *mandurāyām* + *jātaḥ*, with the shortening of the final vowel according to Pāṇini 6.4.149, *ṅyāporbahuvrīhau*.
This occurs in the sense of "born" (*jāta*) following a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), provided it does not denote a genus (*ajātau*). 98.

When a word denoting a genus (jāti), other than a verbal root, ending in the fifth case (pañcamī) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ḍa* is added to the root *jan* (to be born). Examples: *saṃskārajaḥ* (born of refinement), *adṛṣṭajaḥ* (born of unseen merit/demerit). The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that "refinement-ness" (*saṃskāratva*) and "unseen-ness" (*adṛṣṭatva*) are not genera because there is no means of defining them. [Furthermore, the suffix *ḍa* is applied] after *jan* when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), provided it forms a technical name (*saṃjñā*). (Pāṇini 3.2.99)

That which is born is *prajā* (offspring). The word *prajā* occurs in the sense of progeny or people when a technical name is intended through the combination of a verbal root, a prefix, and a suffix;
[here it is formed] with the suffix *an* in the sense of the object (*karman*). 100.

The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan* (to be born) when preceded by *anu-pūrva-* (in sequence), provided that a word in the accusative case (*karman*) is used as an upapada. For example: *pumanujā* ("born following a male") and *stry-anujaḥ* ("born following a female"). The meaning of the root *jan* here is "birth" qualified by "following. The status of being the object (*karmatva*) is attributed with respect to the "following" which is one part of that [qualified] birth.
This [suffix] is also seen after other roots. (Pāṇini 3.2.101)

The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan* even when there is another word as an *upapada*. For example: *ajaḥ* (unborn) and *brāhmaṇajaḥ* (born of a Brahmin). Since the rule specifies the locative case (*saptamī*), only another word as an *upapada* is obtained [as the condition for application]. Therefore, in order to obtain other verbal roots as well, it must be stated that "it is also seen after others. By this, it occurs even with other *kārakas* and even from other roots. For instance: *parikhā* (a moat), which is "dug all around" (*paritaḥ khātā*). As for the Vārttika on the rule *antātyantā-*, which states "it is also seen elsewhere," that is intended for cases where the meaning is not restricted to the specific time of birth (*bhūtakāla*).

In reality, however, since the word *api* in the present sūtra signifies deviation from all conditions (*sarvopādhivyabhicārārthatva*), even those two Vārttikas beginning with "and this" (*tadetacca*) need not have been commenced; for according to the natural sense of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *iko guṇavṛddhi*, it must be stated that this suffix *ḍa* applies to the root *gam* as well. *Niṣṭhā* || 102 ||

The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) that expresses an actual state of being (*bhūtārtha*). The distinction is this: the former (*kta*) occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), while the latter (*ktavatu*) occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Now, one might object: "In this very context, the technical name 'niṣṭhā' should be applied to *kta* and *ktavatu*. [The rule should read: 'Those two, *kta* and *ktavatu*, when occurring in the past tense, are designated as *niṣṭhā*. By the force of this specific restatement (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*), their prescription for the past tense can be inferred. Otherwise, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): first the technical name is applied to those already prescribed, and then the prescription is made by means of that technical name. And it is not correct to say that the objection is resolved by the principle "but it is established because words are eternal" (*siddhaṃ tu nityaśabdatvāt*).

For, by the rule "there is vṛddhi for √mṛj" and so forth, the grammatical correctness of the phonemes /ā/ and others as they occur in actual usage is explained; this is because the technical designation (saṃjñā) [of "niṣṭhā"] cannot apply to the meanings of the suffixes -kta and -ktavat. Nor is there a circular dependency (anyonyāśraya), because when the term "niṣṭhā" is uttered, the technical definition (saṃjñā-vākya) is recalled, and its application is established through that capacity.

"It should be stated that the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] are used in the sense of the initial action (*ādikarma*). Here, the word "action" (*karman*) refers to the activity (*kriyā*). This rule is introduced because the suffix would not otherwise apply by the general sūtra, since the collective action as a whole has not yet reached the state of being past (*bhūtatva*), even though some individual instances of the constituent activities have passed. The meaning of the Vārttika is that the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs when there is the pastness of some portion of the initial action. Furthermore, it will be stated that this applies to the agent (*kartṛ*) as well. Nor can the application of the *niṣṭhā* suffix to the initial action be established merely by the force of that subsequent reference (*anuvāda*), for that could also be explained as referring to a *niṣṭhā* suffix whose primary sense is the present time.

The commentators, however, say: "That [action] whose operation has passed away from the individual instance is established by the very rule through the intention to express it. For this very reason, just as the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta is making a mat) and *prakaroti kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta makes a mat), the use of the aorist (*luṅ*)—as in *prākarot kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta made a mat)—is also desired. And because that [aorist usage] cannot be easily accounted for except by the intention to express the first operation. As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "That aggregate, being of such a nature, is completed in each of its constituent parts;
therefore, the distinction of time is possible within the differences [of those parts]."
However, with reference to the collective whole (samudāya), the desired form *kaṭaṃ prakaroti* is established.
[The suffix] *vanip* follows the root *suyaj*. 103.
Having heard [it] repeatedly; *yajvā* means one who has sacrificed according to the rule;
*jīrṇaḥ* [is formed] from the root *jṝ* with the suffix *atṛn*.
*jaran* and *jarantau*. By the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), [we have] *jīrṇaḥ* and *jīrṇavān*. [The suffix] *liṭ* [is used] in the Veda (*chandasi*). 105.
In the sense of a general past tense (*bhūtasāmānye*): "I saw the sun on both sides"; "I stretched out heaven and earth.
[The suffix] *kānac* may optionally be used instead of the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix. 106.
The suffixes *cakrāṇa* and *vṛṣṭi*, as well as *kvasu*, [are used after verbal roots]. 107.

"O Agni, [the one] who is not giving, the malevolent one... [In *ararivān*: because of the final vowel *ā*, [the suffix] *kvasu* is applied by the rule *vasvekājādvasām*. In a *nañ*-compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. By the rule *dīrghādaṭi*, the *n* is replaced by *ru*. By the rule *āto ṭi nityam*, the *ru* becomes an *anunāsika*. Now, is the mention of the option (*vāvacana*) not redundant? Nor can it be for the sake of hearing the *liṭ* substitute optionally, since in the case of substitutes for *la* (tenses/moods), there is no application of the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*asarūpa-vidhi*). This is because it is already established by the rule *chandasi luṅ liṭau*. Do not say so; it is for the sake of what follows. Furthermore, what is the purpose of making both [suffixes] *kit*?

[Objection: Since the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (P. 1.2.5) already establishes [the status of the affix], there is no need for this. Furthermore, in the case of *vadhradhāna*—derived from the root *badh* (in the sense of "binding") with the suffix *kānac*—that [rule] is intended to effect the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) by virtue of its being *kit*, because the *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (P. 7.4.60) does not apply due to its being a *saṃyoga*. This is because the condition *asaṃyogāt* (not preceded by a conjunct consonant) would otherwise have no scope [due to the presence of the *saṃyoga*]. [Reply: Do not say so. It must be stated that it is also for the sake of the elision of the *n* in *ājivān*, derived from the root *añj* with the suffix *kvasu*. [Objection: But that is unnecessary, because by the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (P. 3.4.117), the suffix is treated as *sārvadhātuka*; and since it is *sārvadhātuka*, the elision of the *n* is established by the *ṅit*-ness itself via *sārvadhātukam apit* (P. 1.2.4). [Reply: True.

The purpose [of the *kit* designation] is to prohibit the *guṇa* substitution for roots ending in *ṛ*; otherwise, in forms such as *teratuḥ* and *titirāṇaḥ*, the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām* would result in *guṇa*. This cannot be prevented merely by the *ṅit* nature [of the suffix], because that [rule *ṅiti ca*] is prescribed specifically for the domain of prohibitions. However, due to the force of the *kit* designation, that [prohibition] is overridden. By this, the assumption that these two [roots] are correct even in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*) on the strength of the *kit* designation is refuted.
[Pāṇini 3.2.108: *sadavasaśruvaḥ* (in the colloquial language).

In these cases, the *liṭ* [perfect] occurs in the sense of the general past (*bhūtasāmānya*), and for that, *kvasu* is invariably substituted. For it is stated in a Vārttika: "In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), the *liṭ* is optionally [used] after *sad* and other roots. Otherwise, by the force of prescribing this substitution, the *liṭ* inferred from roots such as *sad* would subvert the *luṅ* [aorist]. Indeed, there are three exceptions to the *luṅ*: the *liṭ* inferred from this sūtra; the *laṅ* in the sense of non-today's time (*anadyatana*); and the *liṭ* in the sense of the remote past (*parokṣa*). Where, due to a conflict between exceptions (*apavāda*), only the *laṅ* and *liṭ* would apply, [the *liṭ* prevails] because the general past provides its scope. Since the rule "the *liṭ* in the remote past" is not under discussion here, it does not have the nature of a rule prescribing the substitution of *kvasu*.

"And the *liṭ* [perfect] should optionally be prescribed for both the non-recent (*anadyatana*) and the non-evident (*parokṣa*). Thus: *upasedivān kautsaḥ* (Kautsa has approached), *upāsadat*, *upāsīdat*, or *upasasāda*. Regarding the rule "for him, the *kvasu* suffix is used as if it were not non-evident" (*tasya kvasuraparokṣeva*), this means that even in the case of the non-recent past, when the *liṭ* is not applied by virtue of the Vārttika, the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes occur. However, in the case of the rule "the *liṭ* for the non-evident" (*parokṣe liṭ*), the substitutes for verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-ādeśāḥ*) arise because of the presence of the *kvasu* suffix.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, say: here the word *vā* (or), which is carried over [from the previous rule], is connected with *liṭ* (the periphrastic perfect suffix), not with *kvasu*. In the alternative case where *liṭ* does not occur, there is *luṅ* (the aorist). Consequently, by the recurrence of this very sūtra in the rules prescribing *laṅ* and *liṭ*, it is established that after roots such as *sad*, the *liṭ* optionally occurs even for non-recent (*anadyatana*) and non-evident (*parokṣa*) times. [The words] *upeyivān*, *anāśvān*, and *anūcāna* [are formed by this rule]. (Pāṇini 3.2.109)

These are irregularly formed (nipātita). The prefix *upa* is not restricted [to its usual sense]. *upeyivān*, *īyivān*, *samīyivān*: here the *liṭ* (perfect) and the suffix *kvasu* are used in the general sense of the past (*bhūtasāmānye*), as previously stated. "She who has reached the state of being a forest (*aṭavī*) by wandering loudly. From *aśrauṣīt* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, there is the suffix *kvasu* and the absence of *iṭ*. From *vac* preceded by *anu*, the suffix *kānac* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*):
*anucānaḥ*, meaning one who has studied the *pravacana* along with its auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*) under a teacher.

In the form *īyivān*, the suffix *kvasu* follows the root *iṇ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Because it is a permanent (*nitya*) rule, the substitution of long *ī* for *iṇ* (by Pāṇini 7.2.77, *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti*) applies prior to the augment *iṭ*. Consequently, there is no single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) replacement [of the *ī* and *iṭ*]. Nor is there any scope for the long vowel in forms such as *iyatuḥ*, because even there, by the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitution of *yaṇ* would entail the occurrence of a single-substitute. This is because both types of rules—those concerning the preceding element and those concerning both—are considered "rules concerning the preceding" (*pūrvavidhi*).

Furthermore, when the suffix *iṭ*—characterized by the rule for *valādi*—is prohibited by the rule "there is no *iṭ* after *vaś* and *kṛt*" (*neḍ vaśi kṛtī*), it would then be subject to the restriction "after *krādi* roots, etc. (*krādiniyamāt*). By the restrictive rule "the *iṭ* of *vasu* [is added] only after these [roots], being single-vowel (*ekāc*) and ending in a consonant (*hasānta*)" (*vasvekājāddhasām*), the *iṭ* is prohibited for others. Since, according to the aforementioned method, there is an absence of being a single-vowel root (*ekāctvābhāvāt*), if one accepts that the *iṭ* is introduced here as an irregularity (*nipātyate*) only in the former case (of *vaś*), then because no specific distinction is mentioned, the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *iṭ* would arise even in the case of vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

Therefore, this is merely a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to what was prohibited by the rule *vasvekājādghasām*; thus, the augment *iṭ* occurs only before *val* and the like, and not before *aj* and the like—so there is no fault. Consequently, after reduplication and the lengthening of the abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable), there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of the preceding and following vowels]. The substitution of *iy* for that [single substitute] is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). If the substitution of *iy* were not prescribed as an irregularity, forms such as *īyivān* would not be possible. Nor does the lengthening [of the abhyāsa] subvert the single-substitute; for it is only the rule *iṇo yaṇ* that is so subverted. And in this case, since the conditions for that [subversion] are absent, the single-substitute remains secure.

Nor can it be argued that, after the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-dīrgha*), the substitution of *yaṇ* for *ha* would apply—overriding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) by the maxim "an internal operation (*āṅga*) prevails over an external one" (*vārṇād āṅgam*)—because it has already been stated that the single-substitute would then apply again due to the status of the preceding element as a *sthānivadbhāva*. Furthermore, it cannot be asked how this [lengthening] can override the single-substitute, because the single-substitute whose form is based on the nature of the letter *i* (the *ikāra*) does not apply to the letter *y*, since its form is not extended [to the substitute]. Moreover, even if the single-substitute were treated as a *sthānivadbhāva*, it would remain overridden; and finally, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* when an operation concerns both the preceding and the following elements.

Alternatively, when the lengthening by repetition (*abhyāsa*) has been performed, the *yaṇ* substitution for the following *i* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātita*) before a consonant-initial suffix, even though it would otherwise not apply; subsequently, the augment *iṭ* occurs by the rule *vasvekājādghasām*. Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms beginning with vowels such as *aj*. Another says:

*upeyivān* need not be treated as an irregularity (*nipātita*), because the augment *iṭ* occurs due to its higher priority [in the *paratva* principle]. They say that for other one-syllable (*ekāc*) roots, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is obligatory.
Furthermore, for this [root], the augment *iṭ* is obligatory and its reduplication is not obstructed;
however, because it consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*), reduplication occurs first, and therefore the *iṭ* augments the reduplication.

The meaning of this is as follows: in the secular language (*bhāṣā*), when expressing past time in general, the *liṭ* suffix alone is optionally prescribed for the root *iṇ*. And for that [root], the substitution of *kvasu* is mandatory. This is because, despite the rule for reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the [substitution of] *iṭ* applies first due to its higher priority. Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *bibhidvān* or *cicchidvān*, because that reduplication is mandatory; consequently, since the root has more than one vowel (*anekāc*) after reduplication, there is no obstruction to the application of *iṭ*. Thus, since *iṭ* is established by virtue of its higher priority and mandatory nature, nothing needs to be specifically prescribed [as a nipātana]. [Now begins the section on] *luṅ*. 110.

The *luṅ* [suffix] is used after a verbal root when there is a general reference to past time (*bhūtasāmānya*). For example: *apākṣīt* (he cooked). The distinction is this: when there is a desire to express the general past, *luṅ* is used; when there is a desire to express a specific past, *laṅ* and *liṭ* are prescribed. It should be stated: "After the root *vas*, *luṅ* is used when it refers to the remainder of the night, provided that the waking has been continuous throughout the period not belonging to the current day. When one has stayed awake for the first three watches of the night and uses the expression "I stayed there in the fourth watch," then—since the stay during the three watches of the night that have passed does not belong to the current day—the *laṅ* suffix would otherwise be applicable; therefore, *luṅ* is prescribed. Why say "provided that the waking has been continuous"? [Example: [If there was an interruption in the waking, *luṅ* is not used.]

When one has remained awake for even a short time within the interval of three watches (prahara) and employs [a verb] during the fourth watch, the *laṅ* suffix alone should be used to express "I slept there," according to the rule:
*anadyatane laṅ* (Pāṇini 3.2.111).

The *laṅ* suffix occurs after a verbal root denoting an action that took place in the past (bhūta) but not within the current day (*anadyatana*). According to the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*), the "current day" (*adyatana*) consists of the entire day together with the last watch of the preceding night and the first watch of the following night; that which is different from this is the "non-current day" (*anadyatana*). Furthermore, the "day" to be understood here is the locus of the actual utterance of the word, and not the locus of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). For if it were the latter, then even a past action—such as one occurring on a day prior to the utterance—would be considered "non-current" in relation to a verbal cognition concerning a future day, which would result in the improper application of *laṅ*. Example: *apacat* ("he cooked").

That in which the present day does not exist is "non-present" (*anadyatana*). Therefore, in the domain of two days [past], only the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is used: *adya hyaścābhuñjmahi* ("we ate today and yesterday"). It should not be argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using the *laṅ* (imperfect) even for the present day due to the absence of the present day, because the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is based on difference. This is because it is logically consistent to maintain that while the whole is the present day, its parts—the individual days—are non-present, by resorting to the distinction between the whole and its parts. Thus Haribhadra said: "Ordinary people indeed point to another time within a [given] time."

Nor is exclusion established by mere mention alone, because due to the multiplicity of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the present time, the occurrence of one [action] in another [time] is indeed possible. However, it does not occur in a single form, because there is no cognition such as "now, now"; yet it certainly occurs in distinct forms. "The *laṅ* suffix should be prescribed for that which is past, known, and beyond the range of the speaker's perception. For example: *aruṇad yavano sāketam* ("The Yavana besieged Sāketa"). This means that the *laṅ* is used when the object, although beyond the speaker's perception, is known by the speaker as being simultaneous with his own time [of speaking]. Why "beyond the speaker's perception"? [To exclude cases like: *ajayaj jayantaḥ pāṭaliputram* ("Jayanta conquered Pāṭaliputra"), where the action is within the speaker's perception.
The sun has risen; it is known. What did Devadatta do? He made a mat. Regarding what was within the range of sight: Vāsudeva indeed slew Kaṃsa.
When there is a statement of something already known, the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix is used. 112.

Regarding the term *abhijñā* (recollection): as for any brick that one might recognize as being mentioned in a Brāhmaṇa text, it should be placed in the middle layer (*madhyamā citi*), according to the statement, "They [the bricks] should be in the middle layer, as they are declared in the direct Brāhmaṇa. The Mīmāṃsakas have stated that this root *jñā*, preceded by the prefix *abhi*, functions in the sense of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, that is merely a common usage (*prāyika*). Furthermore, its denotation of "recollection" (*smṛti*) does not consist in having "being recollection" (*smṛtitva*) as its restricted denotable property (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), but rather in being employed with the intention (*tātparya*) of recollection. By this, terms such as *buddhi* (understanding) and others synonymous with knowledge (*jñāna*) are also included.

When a word expressing remembrance (*smṛti*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *luṭ* (future) is employed after a verbal root in the sense of the past not belonging to the current day; this is an exception to *laṅ*. Example: *abhijānāsi kāśmīreṣu vatsyāmaḥ* ("Do you remember that we shall dwell in Kaśmīra?").
[This rule does not apply] when *na* is used. (Pāṇini 3.2.113)
It was not stated in the context of *yoga*; do you remember, Devadatta, that we lived among the Kaśmīras? [The rule] *vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe* (Pāṇini 3.2.114) applies.

Because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) possesses a mutual expectancy through the relationship of the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*), the *lṛṭ* (future tense suffix) is used in the aforementioned context; or rather, it should be stated that "it applies everywhere. This means it applies both when there is a connection with *yad* and when there is not. By the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *yadi*, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. "Devadatta, do you remember how we were going to Kaśmīra? That we would eat rice there. "Devadatta, do you remember [the time] when we were going to Kaśmīra and [the time] when we would eat rice there? In both cases, one may also say: "We went" or "we ate. Here, the act of going is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), because it is employed for the sake of another, being well-known [as the cause].
The food is the object, because it is being brought to mind.
The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix is used for that which is out of sight (*parokṣa*).

The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) whose action refers to a past time that is not of today and is beyond the range of direct perception (*parokṣa*). Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "In the case of the *liṭ* used for a past action that is beyond the range of direct perception, the substitution of *para-* for *akṣa-* is observed.
The substitution of *u* for the vowel of *pāda-* following *para-* may be considered established either by rule or by technical designation (*nipātana*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: the word *parokṣa* serves as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for the rule contained in the sūtra *parokṣe liṭ*. [The derivation is: *para* (beyond) + *akṣi* (eye); *parokṣam* [is formed] by the rule *mayūravyaṃsakādayaśca* (Pāṇini 2.1.72), which prescribes a compound. Here, *akṣi* refers solely to the external sense organs (*bāhyendriya*). For this very reason, some maintain that the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule *akṣṇo’darśanāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.76). Alternatively, it is formed by the rule *ac-pratyanvava-* (Pāṇini 5.4.75); here, the final member of the compound takes the suffix *ac* either through a separate grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) or by means of a specific irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Or else, the suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule *prati-parasamanubhyo’kṣṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.82).

Even though the rule for *avyayībhāva* compounds applies to it, since it is impossible for the word *para* to form such a compound with the word *akṣa*, another type of compound (*tatpuruṣa*) occurs. Furthermore, "remoteness" (*paratva*) consists in not being the object of a cognition produced by that [perception]. Otherwise, since that [object] is also capable of being directly perceived (*sākṣātkāra*), its being remote would be untenable. And "direct perception" (*sākṣātkāra*) should be understood as residing in the agent of the action. Thus, there is the usage: "He cooked yesterday" (*hyo papāca*).

As for the alternatives stated in the Bhāṣya—such as "that which occurred a hundred years ago," "that which occurred a thousand years ago," "that which is hidden behind a wall or a mat," or "that which occurred two or three days ago"—these are intended merely as illustrations. Even so, since an action consists of a series of non-simultaneous operations and its constituent potencies are always inferable (and thus necessarily imperceptible), this qualification would appear redundant. Nevertheless, what is intended here is the imperceptibility of the substance (*dravya*) that possesses those potencies.

This is because one falsely imagines that the action is either perceptible or imperceptible based on whether its substrate is perceptible or imperceptible. Nor should it be argued that the expression "he cooked thus" would not be possible because Devadatta, who possesses the capacity [to cook], is perceptible; for it must be admitted that the action, when manifested through its specific operation, is indeed imperceptible.

However, some maintain that here it is the action (*kriyā*) itself whose "remoteness" (*parokṣatva*) must be explained. For even if the aggregate is remote, each individual constituent is not remote; this is because of the natural sense of the *Bhāṣya*: "When [the actions] are massed together, they cannot be pointed out. They argue that when the word *dhātu* refers to action, the relation is "being denoted by itself" (*svavācyatva*), whereas when it refers to the means (*sādhana*), the relation is "being the means for its own object" (*svārthasādhanatva*); thus, the simplicity of the delimiting condition of the thing to be defined (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka-sambandha-lāghava*) alone serves as the differentiator. This is because, even though action-ness (*kriyātva*) does not belong to each individual [action], the status of being the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvarthatva*) is not lost.

That is to be considered. For even in a case where [the action] is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), the suffix *liṭ* would undesirably apply to every individual operation that constitutes the whole, since the "remoteness" (*parokṣatā*) of the whole remains intact there as well. Thus, the qualification "remote" (*parokṣa*) itself would become purposeless. If it is argued that here the remoteness intended refers only to the parts (*avayava*), then does it refer to some parts or to all parts? Not the latter, because the aforementioned pointlessness (*vaiyarthyatā*) remains unchanged. Nor the former, because it would contradict your own established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*).

For even when there is direct perception of only a portion of the activity (*vyāpāra*), the use of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) suffix is undesirable; otherwise, it would contradict the *Bhāṣya*, which states that when one sees rice and water in a pot, the form *apācīt* occurs precisely because the means (*sādhana*) are imperceptible or the activity is imperceptible—since it is specifically the imperceptibility of the entire activity that is mentioned there. Furthermore, even when the agent and the means as qualified by the action are perceptible, the qualification "not being qualified by the action" (*kriyānāviṣṭatva*) would be redundant, given the existence of other means that are imperceptible.

In this way, "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) would also be a qualifier of the action-part (*avayava*) alone. This is because, when the action-part is the delimitor of the connection with the past tense suffix (*parokṣā*), it is that very part which must be the delimitor of the connection with "pastness. Consequently, in the usage "he cooked yesterday" (*hyaḥ papāca*), there would be an impossibility of understanding the connection with "pastness" as delimited by the nature of the operation conducive to the cooking in question; such is the direction of the argument.

"It should be stated that [the rule applies] to one who is asleep or intoxicated. While asleep, I indeed prattled; while intoxicated, I indeed spoke much in his presence. And this is merely an illustration of a cause for mental distraction. This is also the scope of the logical principle, because it is possible for one not to reconnect with one's own actions due to preoccupation and the like.

"It should be stated: 'In the case of absolute negation (*atyantāpahnava*). For example: 'He did not go to Khaṇḍika, nor did he go to Kaliṅga. When it is said, 'You have lived for a long time in forbidden regions,' there is a negation of going to those regions for the purpose of negating the long residence. [Examples include: 'He did not cook,' 'He did not drink,' 'He did not accept the gift of a cow,' or 'What man would strike me to kill me? The property of being a negation (*apahnavatva*) is the restrictive factor as something existing in its own right (*svarūpasat*), and not as an object of verbal cognition (*śābdadhīviṣaya*), because that would result in a contradiction with the nature of negation."

By saying, "Having become the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), I did not drink the Soma," one who has become the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) himself denies his status as a priest by failing to perform the sacrifice for which he was appointed; thus, his very priesthood is repudiated. *Dādhā* refers to a specific region; by saying, "I was not born there," one completely denies being born in that place, and consequently, the denial of having accepted a gift becomes even more absolute, since accepting gifts from such a person is prohibited. The meaning is: "What man would strike me by falsely attributing [faults] to me? It should be understood that when there is an intention to deny the pervaded (*vyāpya*), the denial of its pervader (*vyāpaka*) constitutes an absolute repudiation (*atyantāpahnava*).

Now, how is it that Udayana "spread forth" (*vyātene*) the *Kiraṇāvalī*? As for the claim that the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is used here according to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*, on the grounds that the meaning is "he desires to do," that is not correct; for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that in that case, only the aorist (*luṅ*) is extended by analogy. As for what they say: "Although the prescription of the three substitutes for the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*) is fulfilled by establishing a correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhya*), nevertheless, due to the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *ṇaluttamo vā*, the perfect tense is valid even when there is no immediate past (*aparokṣa*),"—that is not correct, because that rule has its application in cases such as sleep (*supta*). And as for the claim that "even here, there is a distraction of mind due to the haste of composing the work"—that is not correct.

In a work consisting of verbal compositions that produce a determination of the meaning of the treatise—which is to be accomplished through extensive mental application—it is impossible for the temporal categories of "non-recent" (*anadyatana*) and "past" (*atīta*) to apply to the act of expansion. This is true. Some say it is a particle (*nipāta*) that imitates a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). Others say this [work] is intended for the world of students (*śiṣyaloka*). And this is clear from Vardhamāna’s commentary and other such works.
*haśaśvator laṅ ca* || 116 ||

In the case of the conjunction of these two [particles], the *laṅ* suffix is optionally used in place of the *liṭ* suffix; thus, one says *hākarot* or *śaśvadakarot*, as well as *cakāra*. Also, when a question concerns recent time, the same applies. (Pāṇini 3.2.117)

When the time is near and the matter is being questioned, it is as before: within five years is "near," and beyond that is "not near"—this is the traditional rule. [Examples: "Did he go? "He went. But when it is not near, one asks: "Did he kill Kaṃsa?"
The suffix *laṭ* is used after a word containing *sma*.

When used in conjunction with the word *sma*, the suffix *laṭ* (present tense marker) is employed; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *liṭ* (perfect tense). For example: *dharmeṇa sma kuravo yudhyante* ("The Kurus used to fight according to dharma"). It should be stated: "In the case of *sma* and *purā*, [the suffixes apply] only when there is a mere past (*bhūtamātra*), not when there is a recent past (*adyatana*). By the words *sma* and *purā*, the group of five sūtras is understood through the imitation of their initial and final forms. Among these, the suffixes apply only to the mere past. The meaning of the two Vārttikas is that the suffixes indicated by the three sūtras beginning with *sma* and *purā* do not apply to the recent past.

And thus, by the three sūtras "laṭ sme," "aparokṣe ca puriluṅ cāsme," and "nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane," a suffix denoting the immediate past (anadyatana-bhūta) is established; and by the rule "nanvor vibhāṣā," it is concluded that this applies to the general past tense.

Regarding this, the commentary states: "If the rule for *sma* and *purā* were applied without distinction, what would be achieved by Kātyāyana here when he says 'not with *sma*, *purā*, or the non-recent past (*anadyatana*)'? There would be no recurrence of the term 'non-recent past' in the rule *laṭ sma* (Pāṇini 3.2.117), and thus the function of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be lost. [Furthermore,] in the case of *na-nau* (the prohibitive particles *na* and *mā*), there would be an option regarding the non-recent past and the non-evident (*aparokṣa*), and the rule for *caṅ* (the reduplication substitute) would be excluded. [Consequently,] the sentence would become *na purānadyatane* (instead of *na sma purānadyatane*), and even there, the mention of the *luṅ* (aorist) would be required. Listen further: if [the rule] were stated without distinction as *sma-purā-hetū* (with *sma*, *purā*, or a causal particle), then too [the aforementioned faults would follow]."

The phrase "in the non-proximate" (*aparokṣe ca*) was intended to apply prior to the word *puri*; since that [restriction] has ceased, when [the rule] applies everywhere to the non-proximate past, what is the purpose here of the negative particle (*nañ*)? [Objection: It might be argued that this is possible even for the non-proximate past, as in the case of *smādau* (before *sma* and so on), where it is possible to exclude [the application of the rule] by means of the expression *parokṣe* in the rule *laṭ sme*. [Response: Such a thought might occur to you; however, even though it is established in this very way by the definition of *sma*, the rule *laṭ sme* would not serve its purpose. Therefore, it must be stated for the sake of another [purpose].

The meaning is this: since the [desired] result is already established in the three aforementioned *sūtras* by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "non-recent past" (*anadyatana*), the second *vārttika* need not be composed. Furthermore, the two *sūtras* beginning with *nanau* (Pāṇini 3.3.175–176) achieve their operation through the absence of that continued application. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would be no continued application of that term in the rule *puriluṅ cāsme* (Pāṇini 3.2.122); for it must be stated that [the term "non-recent past"] is required there to ensure the rule pertains to the general past (*bhūtasāmānya*). This is because the very mention of the *luṅ* suffix in that rule allows one to infer the continued application of the term "non-recent past."

If this [rule] were intended to apply only to non-real generalities (*abhūtasāmānya*), then since the *laṭ* would already be established optionally by the recurrence of the *vibhāṣā* rule through its alternative application, the mention of *luṅ* would be unnecessary. However, if the recurrence of "not of today" (*anadyatana*) is not assumed, then without the inclusion of *luṅ*, it would be difficult to obtain; for if an option were prescribed, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *laṅ* alone occurring in the absence of *laṭ*. Thus, the specific inclusion of that [term] is purposeful.
And [the rule applies] when there is no immediate perception (*aparokṣe*). 119.
The present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the past not of today when used with *sma*: "Thus the father says."
The particle *nanau* is used in response to a question. || 120 ||

Both [the conditions] "not pertaining to the current day" (*anadyatana*) and "out of sight" (*parokṣa*) are excluded. [Objection: In the case of *nanu*, the present tense (*laṭ*) occurs for the past time in the subsequent sentence. And since a reply must be preceded by a question, the word for the question (*praśnapada*) is redundant. [Response: This is not so, because the intention toward a contradictory statement and the seeds of that intention must also be expressed. For example: "Did you cook?"—"Indeed, I am cooking, sir. [Objection: According to the rule *nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane* ("when *nanu* is used in a reply to what was asked," A 3.2.120), this should not be taught [as a case requiring the present tense]. [Response: Because there is an intention to express the completion of the action. This is the meaning of the rule.

Even when the action of cooking and so forth has ceased, because its result—such as fatigue—persists, the use of the present tense suffix *laṭ* is established by the very rule "in the present tense, *laṭ*" (*vartamāne laṭ*), provided there is an intention to express that the action is not yet fully concluded. If such a sense of the present were not included, then in cases such as "look, I am indeed doing it" (*nanu māṃ kurvantaṃ paśya*) or "look, I am indeed doing it" (*nanu māṃ kurvāṇaṃ paśya*), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, which are substitutes for *laṭ*, would fail to apply. Regarding the rule *nanvor vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.3.46): in connection with these two particles (*nanu* and *nu*), *laṭ* is optionally used; in the alternative case, *laṅ* is used in the aforementioned context. Examples: *apākṣīḥ* ("Did you cook?"); *kiṃ na pacāmi* ("Why do I not cook?"); *na apākṣam* ("I did not cook"); *ahaṃ nu pacāmi* ("Indeed, I am cooking"); *ahaṃ nvapākṣam* ("Indeed, I cooked").
And before the augment *luṅ*, [the substitution of *ātmanepada* endings does not take place]. || 122 ||

The term *anadyatana* (non-current day) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. When used with the word *purā* (formerly), in the sense of the past non-current day (*bhūtānadyatana*), there is optionally the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix, and not the *liṭ* (perfect); however, this is not the case when used with *sma*. In the alternative case, *liṭ* occurs. Examples: 1. *rathenāyaṃ purā yāti* (He goes by chariot formerly). 2. *rathenāyaṃ purāyāsīt* (He went by chariot formerly). 3. *āyāt* or *yayau* (He came or he went). But when used with *sma*: *sma* + *purā*: *yāti sma purā* (He used to go formerly). Regarding the conflict with *ha* and *śaśvat*: "In the presence of *ha* and *śaśvat*, that which indicates the past takes precedence by way of prohibition" (*vipratiṣedhena*). *rathena ha purā śaśvad yāti* (He always used to go by chariot formerly). *ayāsīt* etc. [is used instead]. As for *sma*, it takes precedence over all [other suffixes] by way of prohibition; the meaning is that it prevails through both subsequent and prior prohibitions.
Thus, the intention is that the mention of "us" (*asme*) need not be made. As it is said: "Agni always burns for us what has been cut down by the axe.
The suffix *laṭ* denotes the present tense. || 123 ||

The *laṭ* suffix is prescribed for a verbal root when it denotes time characterized by an action that has begun but not yet been completed. Examples: *pacati* (he cooks), *karoti* (he does). Regarding the statement, "In the case of an action that has commenced and not ceased, as well as in the case of constant activity, the [suffixes] should be taught because of the absence of the present state," the term *bhavantī* is the designation for *laṭ* according to the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*). Examples: *ihādhīmahe* (here we study); *tiṣṭhanti parvatāḥ* (the mountains stand); *sravanti nadyaḥ* (the rivers flow). [Objection: In the case of "here we study," there would be no application [of the rule] because of the intervention of actions such as eating in between. [Response: [This is so] because of the intervention of actions such as eating in the middle. [Examples of constant activity: *tiṣṭhanti parvatāḥ*; *sravanti nadyaḥ*.

Since location (*sthāna*) and the like are eternal, they lack the status of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); consequently, they lack the nature of action (*kriyātva*), and thus even the property of "presentness" (*vartamānatva*), which is a characteristic of action, is absent. This is the reason for the commencement of the discussion. The intention is as follows: because that which is produced necessarily possesses prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), and because "presentness" is the opposite of those two, there can be neither presentness nor the nature of action for that which is eternally active, since it lacks both pastness and futurity. Furthermore, the mention of "mountains and so forth" (*parvatādi*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for eternal things such as the self (*ātman*) and space (*ākāśa*), because the stability of [the former] is not eternal.

Here is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "But it is logical [that eating and so forth are included], because there is no cessation [of the action]. This is established by the very rule itself, because eating and other such acts occurring after the commencement of study and prior to its completion do not constitute an interruption due to their being incidental (*nāntarīyaka*), or because they are part of that [action]. Otherwise, even in cases such as "he eats" (*bhuṅkte*), there would result an interruption by drinking water and the like. As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "In a composite action, an act such as 'eating' appears as if interrupted and as if separated by the intervening activities."
Nor does that [action], even when its form appears interrupted, cease because of an interval;
for every action whatsoever is perceived as if intermingled with something else.
Or rather, every action of the parts, being observed within that interval,
is perceived as belonging to that [whole] because of its similarity, despite the existence of a difference.

In such cases as "the mountains stand," one must explain that the actions of past, future, and present kings—which are distinguished by their respective temporal divisions—serve as the differentiators of the standing of the mountains and so forth. As Hari says:
"Everything is differentiated by another, but the self is not conceptualized [as distinct].
Therefore, the standing of the mountains and so forth is differentiated by the form of the other."
Activities whose distinctions are well-known consist of actions of dissimilar parts;
those with similar parts are distinguished by their association [with other activities].
The meaning is that activities whose dimensions are well-known constitute time itself, because they serve as the delimiters of other activities, and because time is the cause of activity.

It might be argued as follows: since an accomplished object is already past and an unaccomplished one is yet to be, and there being no other mode of existence, the present time is difficult to define. Thus they say: "The wheel does not turn; the arrow is not shot; the rivers do not flow toward the ocean. The world stands motionless; there is no activity. He who sees it thus perceives your [false] creation.
This was thought by a young Mīmāṃsaka, esteemed for his intelligence.
The crow asks: "What is the characteristic of your falling?
Does the agent fall before the action has occurred, or after it has passed?
If you fall at the very moment [of the action], then the entire world falls simultaneously."
Even Himavat goes;
[he perceives] the three: the future, the past, and the present.

There is no movement anywhere; why then is it said that "it moves"? The meaning is this: since the action of revolving occurs over multiple moments (*kṣaṇa*) and these moments lack simultaneity, how can that action possess the status of being present? If one asserts its unity by taking a gross temporal adjunct (*upādhi*), then by taking an adjunct such as an eon (*yuga*) and so forth, there would result the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of treating even the counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) as present during the state of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) occurring within that [adjunct]. Nor should it be said that the very time delimited by which something exists is its present time.

Because everything would incur the consequence of having itself as its own locus by virtue of possessing a present form. Nor can existence (*sattva*) be merely a relation; for if being "related to that" were simply the state of being constituted by that relation, then the relation between [an object] and its own destruction or prior non-existence would be over-extended (*atiprasakta*). Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because, although the [destruction] has a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) residing in that [object], the intended [object] lacks a counter-correlativity residing in that [destruction].

This is because that relation itself exists at the time of the destruction and so forth, by virtue of its being the locus of a destruction whose counter-positive is that [relation]. Nor should it be argued that "the present time of a thing is that moment at which its absolute non-existence does not exist," for such a definition is unestablished; since even at a time when a jar is present as its locus, the absolute non-existence of the jar exists there.

Nor should the absence be qualified by being "non-resident in the locus of the counter-positive," because that absolute absence exists even at the time intended to be present, during both prior and subsequent times. Nor can it be argued that there is no absolute absence of the counter-positive in its locus—whether by means of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)—delimited by a prior time; for even then, the absence of a jar (whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a property or relation residing in a different locus) still exists in such things as the ground or the potsherd.

Furthermore, because the absolute absence of a jar—which resides in an entity existing at a time prior to the destruction or prior non-existence of that jar—is of the nature of its locus (adhikaraṇasvarūpa), such an absolute absence exists even where the jar is present.

Nor can it be defined as being distinct from the past and the future; for "past-ness" and so on are themselves definable by their distinction from the future and the present, respectively. To this, it is replied:
That which is the exertion for the sake of whatever cause prompts the commencement of an action...

Having investigated that [cause], one should employ it, proceeding without hesitation. The cause, the purpose, or the motive for going is the attainment of another location; it is for that sake, for the sake of the result, as is evident here from recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Since the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been established, Devadatta’s attainment of another location cannot be without a cause; therefore, the action of going itself is its cause. And based upon that, the uncontradicted cognition "he goes" arises; thus, existence (*sattva*) is at least provisionally established.

Furthermore, if action lacks the status of being present, it follows that the past and the future would also be non-existent; for it is within the present that the states of having been (pastness) and about to be (futurity) are realized. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa maintains that one employs expressions such as "he goes" by mentally synthesizing a continuous series of actions consisting of a collection of many momentary instants. This is the underlying idea: that which is the counter-positive of a presently existing prior absence is "future," and the time characterized by that [absence] is likewise so designated.

If the mere fact of being the counter-positive of destruction (dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva) and so forth constituted "pastness" and the like, it would follow that such a state would always be perceived. Now, one might object: "In cases such as 'the mountain stands,' this [definition] is untenable because at the time of that usage, the existence of the mountain and so forth is not past; for existence (sthiti) consists in a relation to a time not delimited by destruction or prior non-existence (prāgabhāva). This objection is true, as it applies all the more to passages such as "In the beginning there was darkness, hidden by darkness, enveloped by the void... In the beginning this was indeed the Self alone. However, [our position holds]: if one were to define existence merely as a relation to a time not delimited by destruction or prior non-existence, then even in the case of "the mountain stands," the existence of the mountain at that time would have to be considered "present" rather than "past," since its destruction has not yet occurred. Therefore, we must accept that existence is a specific kind of relation to time that is distinct from both destruction and prior non-existence. Thus, in the case of "the mountain stands," the existence of the mountain is indeed past, and our definition remains consistent. Furthermore, in the Vedic passages cited, the term "existence" (astitva) refers to the relation of the entity to a time delimited by its own destruction, which is why they are described as "past" despite the lack of a subsequent destruction. Consequently, there is no contradiction.

This is because the established doctrine (siddhānta) holds that "presentness" here consists solely in the existence of the substratum (dharmin). For the Vedāntins, however, in the expression "Brahman exists" (asti brahma), they accept that the use of the verb suffix (lakāra) is merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Indeed, it is impossible for Brahman to possess the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) characterized by independence with respect to the action of abiding (*sthitikriyā*), because of its eternity. Nor can there be the state of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*) in the sense of securing well-being (*kṣema*), as long as all other individual instances—which are either identical to or pervaded by itself—continue to exist.
The affixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* take the place of the present tense marker (*laṭ*), provided they do not share the same grammatical subject as a word standing in a case other than the nominative.

These two [suffixes] replace *laṭ* when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word ending in a nominative case-suffix that is not distinct [from the subject]. For example: *pacantaṃ* or *pacamānaṃ paśya* ("see him cooking"). The letter *ś* is for the purpose of designating these as *sārvadhātuka*. The letter *ṛ* is for the purpose of triggering operations associated with *ugit* stems. The letter *k* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta-accented, as in *kurvāṇaḥ* and so forth.

Although non-nominative coreferentiality (aprathamā-sāmānādhikaraṇya) in cases such as *pācakam devadattam paśya* ("see Devadatta, the cook") is caused by connection with another action—since a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix denotes its agent as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), and it is thus logically possible for that agent to function as the object (*karman*) in relation to the action of seeing and so forth—the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), however, although prescribed for the agent and the object, denotes an action where the agent or object is subordinate. This is because, in instances such as *pacaty odanam devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks rice") and *pacyate odano devadattena* ("Rice is cooked by Devadatta"), the primacy of the action is established.

Furthermore, because one action cannot be connected with another action, it is impossible for the power of the object (*karman*) and so forth to inhere [in the action]. Otherwise, constructions such as "he cooked the rice, look at Devadatta" would be unavoidable. It is difficult to maintain that the action expressed by the *laṭ* (present tense) suffix can be connected with another power, whereas that expressed by the *laṅ* (imperfect) and other suffixes cannot. Nevertheless, the power resides in the agent and so forth—which are subordinate to the action—for the *lakāra* that occurs as a *tiṅ* (finite verb); however, in the case of the domain of *śatṛ* and other [suffixes], the power resides in that which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the action.

In cases such as "See Devadatta cooking" (*pacantaṃ devadattaṃ paśya*), because we observe coreferentiality with another case-ending in the substitute (*ādeśa*), that same [coreferentiality] is inferred for the original element (*sthānin*) as well. Nor can it be argued that the general inference (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*) is sublated by the direct perception of the absence of coreferentiality with non-nominative cases—since the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) does not participate in the actual utterance—because that perception of its absence is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddhi*) by the fact that the *lakāra* itself is not employed in the sentence.

This is because the inference based on the otherwise inexplicable nature of the non-co-referentiality with a non-nominative case in the grammatical prescription (*ādeśa*) is more powerful [than the perception]. For this very reason, even when there is a perception of color at every momentary division in the case of the illusion of a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*), there occurs the error of not perceiving the touch that accompanies it. As Harisvāmin stated:
"Just as a continuous stream of touch is admitted when one revolves a wheel with the hand, it is not so in the case of the whirling firebrand, for that is touched only in disconnected [moments]."
Therefore, the established conclusion is that this same logic applies even to the cognition of a "flaming log" (*jvālaukya*).

Now, is this a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) or a *pratiṣedha* (negation)? It cannot be the first, because [the rule] is not established for suffixes or subsequent members of a compound. For instance, in *kaurvataḥ* ("the descendant of one who is doing"), since the present participle suffix *-śatṛ* depends upon Devadatta and others, there is a lack of semantic independence (*asāmarthya*), and thus a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) cannot arise. Furthermore, if there were independence from other words, there would be a lack of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and thus suffixes such as *-śatṛ* would be untenable. [In the case of] *kurvato bhaktiḥ* ("the devotion of one who is doing"), the former member [of the compound] would be required. Nor can it be the second [option], because forms such as *kurvatī cāsau bhaktiśca* ("she is both doing and devotion") would be untenable.

In this way, the formation of *kurvattara*, *kurvadrūpa*, *kurvatkalpa*, and so forth—where the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) function as words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the base—is also to be understood as untenable, because of their lack of apposition with other words such as "Devadatta. [Objection: But surely another rule, *pratyayottarapadayośca* ("and when a suffix or a subsequent word follows"), must be formulated. [For otherwise,] even though the separate mention of "subsequent word" (*uttarapada*) would allow the rule to apply after elision (*luk*) by the maxim *antaṅgānapīti*, the substitution of *śatṛ* (the present participle suffix) would not take effect there, because the prohibition of the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies once elision has occurred. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not exist.

Not so; for it has been said: "The status of being a cause [of grammatical operations] for the suffix and the subsequent member is unestablished," because the suffix and the substitute are mutually dependent causes.
