When a subsequent member exists, the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes occur; when those two have the designation *kṛt*, the production of the case-ending (*sub*) occurs; the compound (*samāsa*) is caused by the case-ending, and the subordinate word (*upapada*) is caused by that compound. Thus, the circularity (*itaretarāśraya*) is evident.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) here is: "Or rather, there is no [fault] because the *lakāra* is a *kṛt*. This is the meaning: by virtue of being a suffix distinct from those [already defined], the *lakāra* also receives the designation *kṛt*. Consequently, that which ends in it receives the designation *prātipadika*. Through the subsequent production of case-endings (*sup*) based on that, suffixes such as *aṇ*, *itarac*, and others arise. Since the rules for substituting *śatṛ* and other [suffixes] are prescribed when these [new suffixes] follow, there is no fault. Furthermore, even in cases involving a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*), case-endings arise by virtue of their higher status, thereby overriding the substitution of *tiṅ*-suffixes. Nor is there the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this rule to forms such as *pacati*.

Because the substitution of *tiṅ* [suffixes] is obligatory (*nitya*) in those cases due to the application of both the performed and the unperformed [forms], one might argue that the same would apply here as well. However, such a consequence does not arise in the present case; for since the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *tiṅ*, it is inappropriate for them to apply in the domain of those [exceptional forms]. Nor does this lead to the following faults: first, in forms such as *vaikṣyamāṇiḥ*, the suffix *iñ* would not occur because the word lacks the ending in *ā* (i.e., it is not *ā-kārānta*) in the absence of *śānac*. Second, in forms such as *pacatitarām* and *pacatirūpam*, the suffixes *śatṛ* and so on would result. This is because the rule *tiṅaśca* [Pāṇini 5.3.56] has its scope elsewhere, namely in the domain of *laṅ* and other [mood endings], as seen in examples like *apacattarām*.

In the same way, in cases such as *pacati* and *paṭhati*, since the *la*-affix is a *kṛt*, when the case-ending (*sup*) is produced, the substitution of *śatṛ* and so on—which is prescribed for an affix—would occur. This is because the *tiṅ*-affixes find their scope of application in the *liṭ* and other tenses. True. However, the desired restriction is established by the continuation of the term *vibhāṣā* from the rule *nanvoḥ* and by understanding this as a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). Nor should it be argued that rules such as *am-ādi* (Pāṇini 7.1.28) would then be redundant, since the two constant substitutions would be established by the very same fixed option. For the continuation of *vibhāṣā* applies to the single rule *śatṛśānacau* (Pāṇini 3.2.124).

The second rule, "not in coreferentiality with the nominative" (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*), is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This is because, due to the optionality being fixed by specific distribution (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), there would otherwise be a lack of clear comprehension. Thus, the scope of the option is coreferentiality with the nominative. Consequently, there is no undesired application (*āpatti*) to forms such as *pacan*, *pacamānaḥ*, or *pacati vā devadattaḥ*; nor is there an undesired application to *devadattaḥ pacati* or *devadattaṃ paśya*, because the second [rule] is an obligatory prescription (*vidhi*).

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "Since *laṭ* is already understood [from the previous rule], the explicit mention of *laṭ* in the rule for the present tense (*vartamāne*) is intended to provide for cases where there is coreferentiality with a nominative (*prathamā-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as well as cases where there is no coreferentiality with a nominative (*aprathamā-sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Consequently, forms such as *pacan* and others, as well as those with suffixes and subsequent words (*pratyayottarapadayośca*), are established as substitutes for that [present tense marker]. This is because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, and because there is no greater complexity (*gaurava*) in employing *laṭ* than in employing *śatṛ-śānacau* (the rule for the present participles) in relation to the rule *laṭaḥ*.
And [the rule applies] in the vocative (*saṃbodhane*). 125.

*he pacan*, *he pacamāna*. Since the meaning of a word ending in the vocative case lacks the entry of powers such as being the object (*karmatva*) as defined by another action, and since there is also an absence of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the nominative (*prathamā*) due to its connection with [its own] action, [the rule] is commenced because it was not otherwise obtained.
Pāṇini 3.2.126: *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (The present participle suffix *śatṛ* is used after a verbal root when the action is the indicator or the cause of another action).

These two [suffixes] occur after the present tense marker *laṭ* following a verbal root that expresses a cause which indicates another action. The word "cause" (*hetu*) refers to both the result and the instrument. "While standing, he urinates"; "while walking, he urinates. By means of the actions of standing and so forth, the action of urinating and so forth is indicated.

Here are the Vārttikas: "An addition [to the rule] regarding qualities (*guṇa*): When many people are urinating and one asks, "Which one is Devadatta?", the answer "the one who is urinating" indicates Devadatta; or rather, a quality such as impurity (*aśauca*) is understood. Since in that case only a substance (*dravya*) and a quality (*guṇa*) are indicated, this [rule] is commenced because it is not established by the [original] sūtra. "It should be stated that when the indicator of the agent (*kartṛlakṣaṇa*) occurs alternately with the verb *aci* (to eat), [the locative is used]: 'He who is eating is Devadatta,' or 'he who is sitting is studying.'"

In the preceding rule (*pūrvavākya*), since the word *guṇa* refers to a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), this present rule serves to provide synonyms for that very meaning. However, when the term *aśauca* (impurity) and others are included, it serves the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). What is the purpose of the mention of *aca* (a vowel)? [Consider: "He who sits and studies—that is Caitra. Due to the connection with the particle *ca*, [the rule] should not apply here. "And in the case of stating a natural state (*tattvākhyāna*). "The *dūrvā* grass grows while lying down. "The lotus-root grows while sitting. This is a description of their inherent nature; there is no relationship of indicator and indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) between the act of sitting and the growth. "Also after *sad* and *as*, in various instances (*bahulam*). "He is a Brāhmaṇa" (*san brāhmaṇaḥ*). "There is a Brāhmaṇa" (*asti brāhmaṇaḥ*).

Regarding the rule "iṅjuhotyor vā": one says *adhīte* (he studies) for *adhīyānaḥ* (the one studying), and *juhoti* (he offers) for *juhvānaḥ* (the one offering). However, in the Bhāṣya, it is stated that the action of standing (*tiṣṭhati*) is indeed the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the action of urinating (*mūtrayati*), and since this is already established by the very sūtra [Pāṇini 3.4.26], which states that the present participle suffix *śatṛ* occurs after roots meaning "to stand" when another action of the same agent is indicated, so too is it established in cases such as *yo 'dhīte* (whoever studies). This is because the mutual relationship of indicator (*lakṣya*) and indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) between the actions of studying and sitting is established through synonymy (*paryāya*).

Furthermore, when used in conjunction with *ca* (and), because two combined actions serve as the defining characteristic (*kartṛ-lakṣaṇa*) of the agent, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since the two actions lack a mutual relationship of the defined (*lakṣya*) and the definer (*lakṣaka*). It has been stated that in examples such as "the person is characterized by consciousness" (*caitanya-lakṣaṇaḥ puruṣaḥ*), even a statement of fact (*tattvākhyāna*) serves as a definition, and thus forms such as *śayānaḥ* (lying down) and so forth are established. It should be stated: "When *māṅ* [is used], [the affixes] *laṭ*, *liṭ*, and *luṅ* [are employed]. Examples: *mā pacan* (let him not cook), *mā pacamānaḥ* (let him not be cooking). By virtue of this authority, this [rule] sets aside the *luṅ* suffix. *Tau sat* (1.3.27): "The two [affixes *laṭ* and *liṭ*] are called *sat*."

Those two, *śatṛ* and *śānac*, are designated by the technical term *sat*. The use of the word "those two" (*tau*) is for the purpose of prescribing the designation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of prescribing [new] suffixes. Furthermore, because that pronoun (*tacchabda*) refers to the mere form of *śatṛ* and *śānac* and lacks reference to any specific substituendum (*sthānin*), the designation is established even for those [suffixes] that replace other *lakāra*s. Nor is there a failure [of the designation] due to the exclusion of the previously mentioned specific [condition], because it is necessary for the term "present time" (*vartamāna*) to be carried over into the subsequent [rules].

Therefore, this [term *vartamāna*] is the designation for the substitutes of *laṭ*, as well as for the substitutes of *lṛṭ* which have the sense of proximity to the present. Nor can its establishment be claimed on the basis of the mention [of *vartamāna*] in the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (P. 3.2.123) or the statement *lṛṭ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* (P. 3.2.124), because in the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* (P. 2.1.69), the word *sat* cannot logically include those two [substitutes]. Furthermore, in the rule *vartamānavat* (P. 3.3.131), since it occurs within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of suffixes, the designation is extended [to the substitutes]; and the same applies to the rule *lṛṭ* (P. 3.3.13).

Even though in the case of *piṣṭapiṇḍāḥ siṃhāḥ kriyantām* ("Let balls of flour be made into lions," etc.), there is the prescription of items that merely resemble those bearing the designation *sat*, once they are prescribed, the grammatical operations dependent upon that designation do not cease.

It might be argued as follows: since the word *tat* refers to what is proximate, it would be difficult to obtain the inclusion of the substitutes for the endings marked by the letter *L*. Nor should it be said that the rule *tāu* (Pāṇini 3.4.78) is redundant because the two previously mentioned [substitutes] are obtained through mere *anuvṛtti* (contextual carry-over), for a purpose must follow from the authority of the evidence [of the grammatical system]. This is not so.

Having analyzed the rule *tau* as "the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur after a verbal root alone" (*dhātumātrāt*), and having established that the technical name *sat* is assigned to *śatṛ* and *śānac* by the subsequent rule *sad*, [one might object]: since those two were treated as substitutes (*ādeśa*) in the preceding rule, they should likewise be so here; and thus, when there is a requirement for an original element (*sthānin*)—whether it be *tṛc* and the like, or the elision (*lopa*) of *kvip* and the like—the absence of such a substitute would result in the application of the rule by default (*pariśeṣāt*). Consequently, because the suffix [in question] would be an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule whose application is precluded by the presence of these specific substitutes...

If it is argued that the rule *tayor vidhānam* (Pāṇini 3.1.133) implies that the suffixes *ṇvul* and *yuca* should be replaced by *śatṛ* and *sānac*, resulting in the failure to derive forms such as *nandana* (from the root *nand*), because the rule *yuvoranākau* (Pāṇini 7.1.1) finds its scope in the domain of *taddhita* suffixes—this is not so. For the rule *lṛṭaḥ sadvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.14) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*): if a suffix follows immediately after a verbal root (*dhātu*), then it must be *lṛṭ* (the periphrastic future). Nor can it be claimed that this rule lacks the status of a restriction because it prescribes an option; for the rule *lṛṭaḥ sad* itself functions as a restriction.

By the word *tāu* (the two), there is a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*—which are specifically prescribed by rules such as *apratamāsamānādhikaraṇe*—by means of the rule *lṛṭaḥ sad*. However, by the word *ve* (or), those two are optionally prescribed even in cases where there is coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) and so forth, just like the suffix *laṭ*. Thus, it is not necessary to state that they are obligatory when not coreferential with the nominative; this constitutes parsimony (*lāghava*).
The suffix *śānan* is applied after the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj*.
Pavamāna is the sacrificer.
The suffix *cānaś* is used [after a verbal root] to express habit, age, or ability. (Pāṇini 3.2.129)

When these meanings are to be expressed: "enjoying a pleasure," "wearing armor," "slaying enemies. [Pāṇini 3.2.130: The suffix *śatṛ* is used after the roots *iṅ* (to study) and *dhṛ* (to hold) when there is no difficulty.

The suffix *śatṛ* occurs after these two [roots] when the sense of "effortless" (*anāyāsa*) residing in the agent (*kartṛniṣṭha*) is to be expressed. Examples: *adhīyan*, *dhārayan*. The meaning is "studying effortlessly. It does not apply here in the case of *kṛcchreṇādhīte* ("he studies with difficulty"). Now, this might be raised: Are these three suffixes independent, or are they substitutes for *la* (the verbal suffixes)? There is doubt because of the connection with both possibilities—whether the term *laṭ* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) or not. It cannot be the first [option]. For if they were independent, it would result in the undesirable consequence that forms such as *pacate*, *yajate*, and *adhīte* would have to be expressed [as having the same meaning], since there is no prohibition against them being substitutes for *la* in the case of the Atmanepada. Furthermore, it would follow that these suffixes could also occur in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*).

This is because these [affixes] are intended to apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, since they are *sārvadhātuka* by virtue of being substitutes for *l*-affixes, there would be the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the rule *tāsyanudāttet* applying in cases such as *pavamānaḥ*. Moreover, the marker *c* has its scope in cases such as *nighnānāḥ*, and otherwise, one would have to begin a prohibition of the designation *ātmanepada* specifically for the sake of forms like *nighnānāḥ*. Nor is the second alternative [correct], because in cases such as *somaṃ pavamānaḥ*, the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* would be untenable. This is not so; for the prohibition of the genitive in connection with these [affixes] is established precisely by the inclusion of the pratyāhāra *tṛn* in that rule.

Nor does that [prohibition] apply even when there is a connection with the root *dviṣ* (to hate). For the rule *dviṣaḥ śatru-vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.69) is justified as being prescriptive (*vidhy-artha*) when the term *tṛc* is understood as a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) intended for prohibition; however, it is prohibitive (*pratiṣedha-artha*) when *tṛ* is understood as the specific suffix.
[The rule is: *dviṣo 'mitre* (Pāṇini 3.2.131).

The suffix *śatṛ* occurs [after the root *dviṣ*]. *Dviṣan* means "enemy. The word *amitra* is masculine, according to the rule of the *Liṅgānuśāsana*: "After the negative particle *nañ*, [the suffixes] *añ*, *ara*, *ama*, and *ras* [are applied]."
The suffix *suÑ* is applied after [the word *soma*] when it is connected with a sacrifice (*yajña*). || 132 ||

The suffix *śatṛ* shall be used [after the root *su*]. Examples: *yaḥ sunvantam avati* ("he who protects the one who presses [the Soma]"); *sarve sunvantaḥ* ("all those who press"). Why "in a sacrifice"? To prevent it from applying in a case such as *surāṃ sunoti* ("he brews liquor"), where the sense of pressing does not pertain to a sacrifice. [Objection]: Even if it were stated simply that the suffix applies after *su* when there is a sacrifice (*yajña*), the same result could be achieved by explaining it as "when the meaning of the root *su* has the sacrifice as its object. Thus, the inclusion of the word *saṃyoga* (conjunction) would be redundant. [Response]: Here they say: It is for the purpose of making the primary agent understood, so that the suffix does not apply to anyone other than the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). In this way, even by the general rule, the suffix does not apply to a non-primary agent. *Sūtra 133*: The suffix *arha* is used in the sense of praise.
The suffix *arhat* is used in the sense of praise. [Example: *coro vadhārhati* ("the thief deserves death").
[The suffix] *ākvi* is used in the senses of "having that as one's habit," "possessing that quality," or "acting skillfully in that. (134)

The prefix *āṅ* signifies pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). It should be understood that the suffixes to be mentioned hereafter, extending up to and including *kvip*, apply when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*), and the like. The three occurrences of the word *tat* refer to the respective meanings of the verbal roots that serve as the bases (*prakṛti*) for *tṛn* and the other suffixes.

*Kartā kaṭān* ("The maker of mats"). It should be stated that [the suffix *tṛc* is applied] after roots meaning "to sacrifice" (*ṛtvij*) when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*). This rule is commenced for the sake of meanings other than habitual action (*atācchīlya*), etc. Examples: *hotā*, *potā*. Why "when there is no prefix"? Consider *praśāstā*, *pratihartā*; here, only the suffix *tṛ* is applied. Consequently, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound (as a *kṛduttarapada*) is maintained. If, however, the suffix *tṛn* were used, then by the rule *tādau ca niti kṛtyatāviti*, the initial syllable would be acute due to the original accent of the root (*gati*). It should be stated that the augment *ṣuk* is added after the root *nī* ("to lead"). Or rather, it is not necessary, because [in the case of *neṣati*] it is a different verbal root. As in *indro vastena neṣatu* ("May Indra lead you with wealth"), this is from the root *neṣati*.

Because it is a different root-form (*prakṛtyantara*). If the suffix *ṣuk* were applied, however, the *guṇa* substitution would not occur. It must be stated: "In the sense of a deity, the vowel *a* is substituted for the penultimate [vowel] of the root *tviṣ*, and it is also *aniṭ*. Thus, *tvaṣṭṛ*. The status of being *aniṭ* applies generally to both those roots already mentioned and those to be mentioned hereafter, because *tviṣ* is inherently *aniṭ*. By this, forms such as *praśāstṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *kṣattṛ* are established. It must be stated that the suffix *tṛn* is added to the root *kṣad* when the meaning is not appropriate [for the agent]. Thus, *kṣattṛ*. "In the Veda, the suffix *tṛc* should be stated [for *kṣad*]. As in: *namaḥ kṣatṛbhyaḥ saṃgṛhītṛbhyaḥ* ("Salutation to the charioteers and the gatherers"). Because it has the marker *c*, it is udātta-accented on the final syllable.
The suffix *iṣṇuc* is added after the following roots: *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *prajan*, *utpac*, *utpat*, *unmad*, *ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *sah*, and *car*. (Pāṇini 3.2.136)

The specific mention of the prefixes is for the purpose of excluding others. Here, *kṛñ* refers to the root *karoti* because it is well-known [in this context], and not in the sense of "harming. Although it would have been logical to list the words *pat*, *pac*, *mad*, and *muc* by way of a single *tantra* (a collective reading), they are each pronounced individually in order to exclude other prefixes. Therefore, according to tradition, there is no [application of the suffix] in forms such as *samutpatiṣṇu*. Bhaṭṭi [uses] *utpatiṣṇu* and *cariṣṇu*. Some, however, having read *pad* in place of that [list], say *utpatiṣṇu* and so on. Likewise, *rociṣṇu* and so forth. [The rule] *ṇecchandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.137) [applies].
The forms *vīrudhaḥ*, *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*, and *ayāman* [are examples]. In the case of the root *iṇ*, there is the substitution of *aya*; and so too for the root *bhū*. (Pāṇini 6.4.138)

The rule *chandasi* (in Vedic) applies here as well. *Bhuvuṣṇuḥ*, *prabhaviṣṇuḥ*, and *vaiṣṇavam* are erroneous readings, because *aprasahiṣṇuḥ* alone is well-established [by the rule *saherṣṇuc*]. According to the *Vṛtti*, the word *cakāra* (the suffix *ka*) implies *bhrājiṣṇuḥ*. Others say that *kṣayiṣṇuḥ* is also included, but that is without foundation. Pāṇini 3.2.139: *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ* (The suffix *ksnu* is added after the roots *glai*, *jyā*, and *sthā*).

*glāsnuḥ*, *jiṣṇuḥ*, *sthāsnuḥ*; and by the word "and" (*cakāra*), *bhūṣṇuḥ*. Now, is this [suffix] marked with *k* (*kid*) or marked with *g* (*gid*)? Not the first, because in the case of *sthāsnuḥ*, the substitution of *i* (by Pāṇini 6.4.66, *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām...* [sic]) would result. Nor the second, because in the case of *jiṣṇuḥ* there would be *guṇa*, and in the case of *bhūṣṇuḥ* there would be the insertion of *iṭ*. Not so; for the status of being *gid* alone is correct. Since in the rule *kṅiti* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the letter *g* is also included by means of the phonetic change (*cartva*) [of *k* to *g*], the prohibition of *guṇa* applies even when it is *gid*. Likewise, in the rule *kiti* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the letter *g* is also included by phonetic change [of *k* to *g*], and thus, due to the presence of *it*, that [prohibition of *guṇa*] does not occur [in *bhūṣṇuḥ*].
Or else, it is because of the indication [of the rules] without *saṃhitā* (i.e., as separate words). Thus says the Vārttika:
The vowel *ī* in *vas*, *nu*, and *git* [is substituted] by the rule "of *ṅit* and *it*" (*ṅitoritvam*).

The absence of *guṇa* in the three [cases] is for the sake of traditional recollection (*smārtha*). The substitution of *ī* in *śri*, *yu*, and *ku* occurs by the rule "after *ka* and *go*" (*kagoritaḥ*). There is an extension [of the application] of the root *daṃś* to the Vedic language (*chandasi*); [thus we have] *daṃṣṭrāḥ paśavaḥ*. [The suffix] *knu* is added after the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*: [Pāṇini 3.2.140].

*trasnuḥ* (timid); *neḍvaśi*—the suffix *iṭ* is not applied [to *vaś*]; *gṛdhnuḥ* (greedy); *dhṛṣṇuḥ* (bold). Śrīharṣa says: "He threw away this straight-winged arrow. The suffix *ghinuṇ* is added after eight roots beginning with *śam*. (141)

The word "iti" (thus) signifies the beginning of the topic. The suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied after the eight roots beginning with *śam*. Thus: *śamī*, *damī*, *śramī*, *bhramī*, *klamī*, *pramādī*. [In these cases], by the rule "not for a root taught with an initial udātta vowel," there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* for roots ending in *m*. In forms such as *śaminitarā* and *śaminītara*, there is an optional shortening (*hrasva*) by the rule "after a stem ending in an *ugit* vowel. Regarding the application of the *num* augment, the *Bhāṣya* states that because the mention of *jhal* is continued [in the rule], *num* does not apply in forms like *śaminau*. Consequently, the view of the *Vṛtti* author—that the letter *u* [in *ghinuṇ*] is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*)—is to be rejected. However, the *Bhāṣya* states that this suffix is not applied to transitive verbs due to non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).

By the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the form *unmādī* is also possible; for the prohibition [of the *ṇini* suffix] regarding words denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*) is only generally applicable. [The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the following roots:

*sam-pṛc*, *anu-rudh*, *aṅ-ayam*, *āṅ-ayas*, *pari-sṛ*, *sam-sṛj*, *pari-dev*, *sam-jvar*, *pari-kṣip*, *pari-raṭ*, *pari-vad*, *pari-dah*, *pari-muh*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *ā-krīḍ*, *vi-vic*, *tyaj*, *raj*, *bhaj*, *ati-car*, *apa-car*, *amuṣ*, and *abhi-ahan*. (Pāṇini 3.2.142)

The substitution of *ku* for *gh* occurs due to the presence of the suffix *kvip*. [Examples: *samapakvī*, *anurodhī*, *āyāmī*, *āyāsī*, *parisārī*, *saṃsargī*, *paridevī*. The root *div* (in the sense of "lamenting") belongs to the *bhvādi* class; the inclusion of the causative form *dīvyati* is not intended here because it is a derivative form (*lākṣaṇika*). [Further examples: *saṃjvārī*, *parikṣepī*, *parirāṭī*, *parivādī*, *paridāhī*, *parimohī*, *doṣī*, *dveṣī*, *drohī*, *dohī*, *yogī*, *ākīḍī*, *vivekī*, *tyāgī*. Regarding *rañjayati*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) by nipātana (irregular prescription). Thus, one who colors is called *rāgī*. [Other examples: *bhāgī*, *aticārī*, *apacārī*, *āmoṣī*, *avyāghātī*. [The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the roots *kaṣ*, *las*, *kattha*, and *srambh* when preceded by the prefix *vi-*: || 143 ||

*kaṣ* in the sense of harming; *las* in the sense of clinging and sporting; *kattha* in the sense of boasting; *srambh* in the sense of trusting. One who sports, one who boasts, and one who trusts [are formed from these roots]. And [the suffix *ṇini*] also follows *laṣ*. (144)
The root *laṣ* is used in the sense of longing (*kānti*). One who does not long is *apalaṣī*, as is *adviṣī*.
[The suffix *ini* is applied after the roots] *pra-lap*, *sṛ*, *dru*, *math*, *vad*, and *vas*. (145)

The suffix *vuñ* (i.e., *-aka*) is added after the following verbal roots to form nouns denoting the agent: *nind* (to blame), *hiṃs* (to injure), *kliś* (to afflict), *rav* (to sound), *vad* (to speak), *vināś* (to destroy), *parikṣip* (to throw around), *parivādi* (one who reviles), and *vyābhāṣ* (to address). [Examples: *pralāpī* (one who talks excessively), *prasārī* (one who stretches out), *pradrāvī* (one who runs away), *pramāthī* (one who crushes), *matha* (in the sense of churning or agitating), *pravādī* (one who speaks out), *pravāsī* (one who dwells abroad). 146.

The suffix *vuñ* shall be applied after these [words]. Regarding *naś*, there is a mention of the root *naś* ending in the causative (*ṇic*) with the elision of the *n* (as *naś*); the vowel *a*, however, is for the sake of pronunciation. Some read it simply as *vināśī*. It is like *parivādin*. [The word] *asūyati* belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* group. This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). [The form] *asūñ* is the singular ablative case. Thus, having explained [the compound] as a coordinate copulative compound (*itaretarayogadvandva*) ending in the plural nominative, the assumption of a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*) by the *Vṛtti* and other commentators is not to be accepted.

Nor does the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.106) apply to form a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) for the collective [compound], because it is simpler to maintain that there is no compound-ending suffix by relying on the fact that the rule for suffixes is non-mandatory (*anitya*) due to its dependence on irregularity (*vyatyaya*), or else by explaining it as forming a *dvandva* of words ending in *bhāṣā* and then adding *vuñ* after that. As for "reviler" (*nindaka*) and so forth: although the form is established by *ṇvul* alone for words like *nindā* because the forms are identical and because of the identity of the acute accent (*ādyudātta*), the suffix *vuñ* must nevertheless be prescribed specifically after the root *asūyati*.

By the accentuation rule for the *ṇvul* suffix (*litsvara*), the syllable preceding the suffix is acute; however, because there is a specific rule stating that for *vuñ* and others, the preceding syllable is acute, [one might wonder about the purpose]. Nevertheless, the prescription of *vuñ* is for the purpose of indicating that the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*) does not apply to suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*). This results in the exclusion of *tṛc* and other such suffixes, because the indicator (*jñāpaka*) refers to suffixes in general. [The rule continues: "And after the roots *du* and *kruś*, when a prefix is present. (Pāṇini 3.2.147)

The rule for *div* includes both the root *div* with the suffix *ṇic* (i.e., *dīvyati*) and the root *div* belonging to the *cur*-class. Examples: *ādevakaḥ* (one who plays/shouts) and *ākrośakaḥ* (one who reviles). Why "with a prefix"? Consider *kroṣṭā* (a jackal). [Sūtra 3.1.148:
The suffix *yuc* is applied after roots meaning "motion" or "sound" that are intransitive (*akarmaka*).

The term *artha* (meaning) is connected with both [the preceding and the following]. *Cālanaḥ*, *copanaḥ*, *kampanaḥ*, and *śabdanaḥ* [are derived] from the verbal root *śabda* belonging to the *curādi* class in the sense of "making manifest. Vyāḍi maintains that [the suffix *lyuṭ*] is applied after the nominal stem *śabda* when followed by the sense of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), or after the causative (*ṇijanta*) form of *śabda* as in the rule beginning with *śabda-vaira-kalaha-*. [Examples: *ravaṇaḥ*. Why say "after an intransitive verb" (*akarmakāt*)? [Counter-example: *paṭhitā vidyām* ("one who has studied the science").
And [the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied] after a root beginning with a consonant (*halādeḥ*) that is marked with an anudātta accent. (Pāṇini 3.3.149)

The rule applies only to roots that do not have an object (*akarmaka*). Thus, [forms such as] *vardhanaḥ* and *vartanaḥ* are excluded. If the mention of "beginning with" (*ādi*) were absent, then by implication [the rule would apply only] to those ending in a consonant (*halanta*), and consequently forms such as *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ* would not be possible, because they end in a vowel (*ajanta*). Therefore, the mention of "beginning with" is for that purpose. Nor is there an absence of the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*); for the low-pitched vowel belonging to a constituent part qualifies the entire complex ending in *san*, as stated in the Bhāṣya: "gup and the others are low-pitched."

If it is argued that, under the view that "in the domain of *ārdhadhātuka*" (*ārdhadhātuke*) is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), the status of these two roots as ending in *i* is easily established because the elision of *ut* would apply even before the suffix arises, [the author replies: True; however, this was stated specifically according to the view that it is a locative of co-occurrence (*parasaptamī*). [The suffix *ac* is applied] after the verbal roots *ju*, *caṅkramya*, *dandramya*, *sagṛdhri*, *jvala*, *śuca*, *laṣa*, *pata*, and *pada*. (Pāṇini 3.2.150)

The root *judhātu* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to go," which is to be supplied here by its very mention [in this list]. Others say it means "speed. Amara states: "one who is swift (*javana*) is one whose speed is excessive (*javādhika*). The roots *kram* and *dram* take the suffix *yaṅ*; thus we have *caṅkramaṇaḥ* and *dandramaṇaḥ*. Similarly, *saraṇaḥ*, *garddhanaḥ*, and so on. Their formation is established by the rule *anudāttetaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.149). Since the suffix *anaṭ* is not desired after transitive roots, this refutes the attempt to form such expressions as *caṅkramaṇo grāmasya* (one who wanders about the village). True; however, this is taught so that the suffix *ukañ* (from Pāṇini 3.2.154, *laṣapatapada...*) does not supersede the suffix *yuca*.

In the *Nindādi-sūtra*, it was indicated that the rule of non-identity of form (*asarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply between suffixes denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*) and those that do not; however, the distinction here is that it applies even with those denoting habitual action. Consequently, in the domain of *alaṅkṛñ* and *itīṣṇuc*, the suffix *tṛn* is employed. It should not be argued that, in this case, *tṛn* would not occur after the root *gam* because it is superseded by *ukañ*; for it will be stated later that the aforementioned indication is merely general (*prāyikatā*).
And [the suffix *tṛn* occurs] after roots meaning "to be angry" (*krudha*) and "to adorn" (*maṇḍa*). (Pāṇini 3.2.151)
The wrathful one is the ornament.
Nor is it that which [is not]. || 152 ||

The suffix *yuc* is not applied after roots ending in *yā*. For example: *knūyitā*, *kṣmāyitā*. The root *knūyī* means "to sound," and *kṣmāyī* means "to shake. This is not merely a rule for the application of a suffix after the root *nī* in the sense of "going," because that would already be established by the rule *anudāttetaśca*. Therefore, this is indeed a prohibition of the *yuc* suffix which would otherwise have been applicable.
[The suffix *yuc* is also prohibited] after the roots *sūd*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ*: *sūditā*, *dīpitā*, *dīkṣitā*. (Pāṇini 1.2.21–22)

The suffix *yuc* does not apply [after these roots]: *sūditā*, *madhusūdanaḥ*, *andyādiḥ*, *dīpitā*, *dīkṣitā*. Since the suffix *reṇi* (the suffix *an*) would have already barred *yuc* by the rule *namikampī-* (*Pāṇ. 3.2.167*), the explicit mention of *dīpi-* is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *gs* (the suffix *an*) alongside *yuc*. Therefore, according to the *Bhāṣya*, forms such as *kamrā yuvatiḥ* and *kamanā* are established. Furthermore, regarding this [rule], the intention is that the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhiḥ*) does not apply between suffixes denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*) and those [suffixes] themselves; however, this is merely a general principle (*prāyika*). It does not, however, restrict the co-occurrence to *rayuc* alone. Consequently, forms such as *gantā* and *vikatthanaḥ* are established. [The suffix] *ukañ* is applied after the roots *laṣ*, *pat*, *pad*, *sthā*, *bhū*, *vṛṣ*, *han*, *kam*, *gam*, and *śṝ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.154)
*Lāṣukaḥ*, *pātukaḥ*, and so forth.
[The suffix] *ṣākan* is added after the roots *jalp*, *bhikṣ*, *kuṭṭ*, *luṇṭ*, and *vṛṅ*. (155)
"Jalpāka," and so forth;
[the suffix] *ini* follows the root *praj* (Pāṇini 3.2.156).
*prajavī*, *prajavinau*, and so forth; [the suffix *vin*] also follows the roots *ji*, *dṛkṣi*, *viśrī*, *ṇvama*, *avyatha*, as well as *apari-bhū* and *pra-sū*. (157)

"Jayī, darī," and so forth. There is the inclusion of both roots *ji* (to conquer) and *kṣi* (to perish). [The root] *śri* (to serve) is preceded by *vi-*; *vyathi* is preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. By means of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), there is a compound of the negative particle with the verbal root, and after the elision of the *n*, the suffix is applied. [The root] *sū* (to impel) is used in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*) because of the forms *sūti* and *sūyati*, which possess indicatory letters (*sānubandhaka*). In this very context, one ought to abandon the previous rule by reading *pra-ju* and *ini* [here], for there is brevity (*lāghava*) in abandoning the separate case-endings and the word *ca*—so say the Dīkṣitas. Pāṇini 3.2.158: *spṛhi-gṛhi-pati-dayi-nidrā-tandrā-śraddhābhya āluc* || [The suffix] *āluc* is added after the roots *spṛh* (to desire), *gṛh* (to seize), *pat* (to fall), *day* (to pity), *nidrā* (to sleep), *tandrā* (to be weary), and *śraddhā* (to have faith).

The first three [roots] belong to the *curādi* class and are without a final vowel (*adanta*). By the rule *ayāmantāṇṇviṣṇucaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ay* for the suffix *ṇi*. Thus: *spṛhayāluḥ*, *guhuyāluḥ*, *patayāluḥ*. From the root *drā*, there is a compound with the word *ta*; furthermore, the form *tada* is prescribed as having a final *n*. Thus: *tandrāluḥ*. Now, one might object: let there simply be the suffix *lu*. Since it is marked with *ś*, it would be treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; consequently, in forms such as *spṛhayāluḥ*, the long vowel would be applied by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*. Moreover, because of the continued application of the term *sārvadhātuka* from the rule *turustuśamyamaḥ*, it would not be a *tiṅ* suffix. Nor would there be the undesirable consequence of the letter *l* being designated by the technical term *it*. This is because, through the inclusion of the preceding element (*praśleṣa*), the suffix begins with the letter *y*.

Or rather, [the rule] is unnecessary because there is no purpose [served]. Since the single substitute [for *li* and *lu*] is acute by the rule "a single substitute for an acute vowel is acute," the acute accent is present in both cases, and thus there is no distinction between the accent of the *lit* affix and that of the *lup* affix. Nor should it be argued that the word *śraddhālu* would not be established because the root *ludh* would undergo reduplication; for we rely on its non-universality (*anityatva*) due to its being based on a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*). Furthermore, since roots have multiple meanings, the form is possible from the root *heṭ*. Nor is there a prohibition of *ātva* by the rule *na cāśiti*; for that is established by the elision of the vowel *ā* in the form *ā-śraddhā*.

Furthermore, since the prohibition of that [suffix] will be stated later when the letter *ś* at the beginning is designated as having the technical marker *it*, this is true. However, its initial vowel is *ā* for the purpose of providing a rule for other cases, as in *śayāluḥ*. Thus, the mention of *śīṅ* is for the sake of clarity.
Pāṇini 3.2.159: *dādheṭsīśadasado ruḥ* (The suffix *ru* is added after the roots *dā*, *dhā*, *iṭ*, *sī*, *śad*, and *sad*).
They say that *dā* and *do* are included in the term *deṅ*. [The suffixes] *u*, *ru*, *śru*, and *dra* follow [the roots *dhā* and *sā*].
The suffix *kmarac* follows the roots *sṛ*, *ghas*, and *sad*. (160)
The suffix *ghurac* is applied after the roots *sṛ*, *mṛ*, *ghas*, *ad*, and *mid*. [Examples: *sṛmaraḥ*, *ghasmaraḥ*, *admaraḥ*. Pāṇini 3.2.161.

The traditional teaching is that the suffix *kurac* is applied only when the verb *bhañj* functions as a reflexive (karmakartṛ), due to the inherent nature of its denotation; thus we have *bhaṅghura*, *bhāsura*, and *medura*. [The suffix] *kurac* is also applied after the roots *vid*, *bhid*, and *chid*. (162)

Regarding "vidura" and so forth: the root *vid* is understood here in the sense of "knowing," not in the sense of "obtaining," because of the [grammatical] commentary. As for the form *chidura*, the *vṛtti* states that it is formed in the sense of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartari*); and it should not be argued that this is without foundation, for there are usages such as *gurumatsaracchidurayā*. Furthermore, forms such as *mṛṇālatantuchidurā satī sthitiḥ* are also observed. [Pāṇini 3.2.163: *iṇ-naś-ji-sarti-bhyaḥ kvarap*.

"He became *itvara*," so says the *Harṣacarita*. Amara states: "A woman who is unchaste is called *asatītvarī*. [The suffix *tvarap* is applied after verbal roots] such as *naś*, *ji*, *sṛ*, and *gam*: *naśvaraḥ*, *jitvaraḥ*, *sṛtvaraḥ*, and *gatvaraḥ*. (164)
There is also the irregular elision of the nasal (anunāsika) [in the case of the root *jāgṛ*]. [The example is: *jāgarūkaḥ*. 165.

In the word *jāguḥ*, when the distinction between the original form (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is intended, it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus ends in the ablative case. [The rule] states that the suffix *ūka* should be added after the root *jāgarti*. However, if it were treated as a fixed form (*nipāta*) such as *jāgarūka*, the recurrence of the suffix *ū* would not apply in subsequent rules. [The next rule is: "After the roots *yaj*, *jap*, and *dṛś*, following the intensive suffix *yaṅ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.166)

The suffix *uka* is applied after these roots ending in *yaṅ*. The form *daśokaḥ* is intended to illustrate the elision of the *in* suffix. *Yāyajūkaḥ* [is derived from √yaj]; *jañjapūkaḥ* is one who possesses a rosary (*akṣamālāvān*), according to Bhāravi. *Dandaśūkaḥ* is a hole-dweller (*bileśaya*). The word *vāvadūkaḥ* belongs to the *tūṣṇīkādi* group; others maintain that it is established by its inclusion in the *kurv-ādi* class.
The lamp of non-violence, which is free from attachment and aversion, shines forth. || 167 ||

*namraḥ* (bowed), *kampraḥ* (trembling), *smeraḥ* (smiling). With the negative particle (*nañ*) as a prefix, the root *jas* takes the suffix *u* in the sense of continuity: *ajasram* (incessantly). *kamraḥ* (desirous), *hrasvaḥ* (short), *dīpraḥ* (shining).
After the roots *nas*, *āśaṃs*, and *bhikṣ*, the suffix *u* is applied [to form the present participle]. (168)

The suffix *san* is not included here [in the rule for *cikīrṣu*] because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*). This is because the word *jigīṣu* is listed in the *gargādi* group, and it would be cumbersome to assume that it is an unanalyzed formation (*avyutpanna*) there. The prefix *āṅ* is used before *śaṃsu* in the sense of desire: *āśaṃsuḥ*, *bhikṣuḥ*, *vinduricchuḥ*. (169)

In this context, the substitution of *ś* for the root *iṣ* (to seek) is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). This nipātana does not apply to other roots meaning "to know" (*vid*) nor to the forms *iṣṇāti* and *iṣyati*, because they are not so designated [by grammatical authority].
[Pāṇini 3.2.170: *kyāc chandasi* (In the Vedic language, the suffix *kyac* is added after a word ending in *kyap*).

He goes toward the gods, desiring their favor. In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there is no substitution of *ī* for *ya* nor the absence of lengthening [of the vowel] in the case of *aputra*. Here, the term *kyac* does not refer to the entire suffix; rather, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both *ki* and *yac*. By this, the *yak* of the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class is also included. Thus, forms such as *turaṇyavaḥ* and *bhuraṇyuḥ* are accounted for. Furthermore, in the phrase *gṛṇhanti hyanasūyavaḥ*, the suffix is derived from the *mṛgayv-ādi* group. [The rule] *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.171] applies.

The suffixes *k* and *kin* occur after verbal roots ending in *ā*, those ending in *ṛ*, and after the roots *gam* and others, in the Vedic language (*chandas*); these two suffixes function like the *liṭ* (perfect) tense. The mention of *ā* includes the letter *d*. If *t* were used instead, then because of the rule regarding *ṛ* followed by *t* (Pāṇini 6.1.71), there would be no inclusion of roots ending in long *ṛ*. Examples: *dadir gāḥ* ("he gave cows"), *babhrir vajram* ("he bore the thunderbolt"), *taturiḥ*, *jaguriḥ*. The change to *u* occurs frequently in the Veda, as in: *śubhaṃ bhāvāno vidatheṣu jagmayaḥ* ("moving beautifully toward the sacrificial assemblies"). In *jaghniḥ vṛtram amitriyam* ("he slew the unfriendly Vṛtra") and *jajñiḥ*, the *kit* status of the suffix serves to prohibit *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11). In *taturiḥ* and similar forms, the *kit* status likewise prevents *guṇa*.

Nor should it be said that the designation *parasmaipada* would [otherwise] apply; for that designation belongs only to the substitutes (*ādeśas*). Furthermore, since the rule *kartari kṛt* prescribes the occurrence of *kṛt* suffixes such as *ki* and *kikin* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended, this undesirable consequence does not arise even for the case of the action itself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), because the meaning taught by a rule applied later (the extended application or *atideśa*) cannot be connected with the meaning taught at the time of the suffix's original production, provided there is no conflict with that original meaning. Nor is there an extended application of the past tense, because the context concerns the present tense. Furthermore, there is no possibility of the occurrence of *tiṅ* substitutes or the suffixes *kasu* and *kānac*, because that would result in the sublation of their own specific forms.

The *Aṭavārttika* states: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the suffix *kvip*] is seen after *sad* and others, as in *utsargaḥ*. Examples include *sedih*, *nomiḥ*, and so forth. By the rule *ata ekahal-madhye*, there is the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*). In the common language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after *dhā*, *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *gam*, *jan*, and *nam*: *dadhiḥ*, *cakriḥ*, *sasriḥ*, and so on. There is an addition to the list (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *sāsahi*, *vāvahi*, *cācali*, and *pāpati*. Because of the technical designation (*nipātana*), there is also the absence of the feminine suffix (*nīp*) in *pāti*. However, according to the authority of the *Bhāṣya*, this applies only to the view that begins with the statement "after *sah*, *vah*, *cal*, and *pat*, the suffix *yaṅ* [is applied].
[The suffix] *nañjiṅ* is applied after the roots *svap* and *tṛṣ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.172)
*svapnak*, *tṛṣṇak*; *svapnajau*, *tṛṣṇajau*, and so forth. From the rule "and from *dhṛṣ*" (Pāṇini 3.2.140), the form *dhṛṣṇak*.
From *śṝ* and *vand* comes *āru*: || 173 ||*
*Śarāruḥ* means one who is murderous or injurious; *vandāruḥ* means one who salutes or pays homage.
The two [names] Kruka and Lukana are [the names of] Arhats. || 174 ||
*bhīruḥ* (fearful), *bhīlukaḥ*; "the suffix *kruk* should also be mentioned": *bhīrukaḥ*.
[The suffix] *vra* is added after the roots *sthā*, *īś*, *bhās*, *pis*, and *kas*. (Pāṇini 3.2.175)
Sthāvara, īśvara, bhāsvara, yesvara, kasvara, and that which ends in yaṅ. 176.
The suffix *varac* is applied after the root *yā* when it ends in the *yaṅ* (intensive) affix;
thus, *yāyāvaraḥ*. This has been explained in the section on word-final forms (*padānta-sūtra*). The suffixes denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*) are concluded.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *bhraj*, *bhās*, *dhurv*, *vidyut*, *ūrj*, *pṝ*, *jugrā*, and *stuvaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.177)

*vibhrāṭ*, *bhāḥ*, *bhāsau*, *dhūḥ*, *vidyut*, *ūr̥k*, *pūḥ*, *jūḥ*, and *juvau* [are formed with the suffix *kvip*]. Due to irregularity (*nipātana*), there is a compound of the word *grāvan* with a verbal root; thus, *grāvastut* refers to a specific officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
[The suffix *kvip*] is also seen after other roots as well (Pāṇini 3.2.75).

The purpose of beginning [this rule] with the term *anupasarga* (without a prefix) is because, in the rule *kvip ca*, there is the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of both *supi* (after a nominal stem) and *upasarge* (after a prefix). [Examples: *bhid* (from *bhid*), *chid* (from *chid*). Nor is the prescription of *kvip* after the word *grāvan* (as an upapada) in the preceding rule redundant; for if the reading were *prāk kveḥ* (before *kvip*), then *kvip* would have to be prescribed in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and so forth. Furthermore, it is not the case that only what is prescribed by this present rule has the meaning of habitual action and so on; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *tṛn* subverting [the scope of *kvip*], since it has been stated that for suffixes denoting habitual action, the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply.

The inclusion of the term *dṛśi* (to see) is for the purpose of prescribing [the suffix *kvip*] even after roots that undergo long *saṃprasāraṇa*, its absence, or shortening; for we see the Vārttika stating: "It should be stated that *kvip* is added after *vac*, *pracchi*, *āyata*, *stu*, *kaṭapru*, *ju*, and *śrī*, with lengthening [of the vowel], and that there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* for *vac* and *svap*"; and "it should be stated that there is doubling [of the initial consonant] for *dyuti*, *gami*, and *juhoti*. Although [the forms] are established for some by the Uṇādi-sūtra beginning with *kvibvacī*, they are mentioned again so that they may not be superseded by the suffix *tṛn* when expressing "one who has that habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. *Vāk*: that by which one speaks (*vakti*). *Prāṭ*: one who asks (*pṛcchati*).

He is both he and a judge; thus, *prāḍvivākaḥ*. One who praises while stretching out [his voice] is *āyatastūḥ*. One who moves toward a mat is *kaṭaprūḥ*. *Jūḥ* has been mentioned previously. They hear her, thus *śrīḥ*. *Didyut* means the world (*jagat*). By the rule "in order for *dyuti* and *svāpi*" and "after *gam*, *kvip*," there is the substitution of semivowels for vowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and elision. That by which one sacrifices is *juhūḥ*. Nor does the fault of over-extension (*dīrghāpatti*) apply even to *dyuti* and the others.

At the time of the long-vowel compounding (*dīrghasamuccaya*), because *acaḥ* is present [in the rule], it results—by the principle of "specification of the final" (*tadantavidhi*)—in the sense of "ending in an *ac* vowel. Consequently, since this refers exclusively to the root *juhoti*, [the suffix applies] to *dīryati* and *darat*. In *dīryati*, there is a short vowel due to the rule for the root *dṝ* in the sense of fear (*bhaye*). In *dhīḥ*, it is derived from *dhyai*. Because of the inclusion of *dṛśi*, there is sometimes a deviation regarding the agent (*kartṛ*); this is either due to the metaphorical attribution of agency to the instrument (*karaṇa*), or because the suffix is prescribed as arising from the instrument itself in order to follow the meaning of the root's components.
**Pāṇini 3.2.179:** *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayoḥ* (The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *bhū* in the sense of a name or a different state).

A certain person who has the notion of being a friend; a *pratibhū* (surety) is one who establishes trust between a creditor and a debtor. This [suffix] is obtainable by the continued application of the rule for *dṛśi*. Nor is its establishment [possible] merely from its being a technical term (*saṃjñā*), because it is the object of usage occurring only at the time prior to the repayment [of a debt]; whereas a technical term persists as long as the substance [to which it refers] exists.
[The suffix] *ḍvas* is applied after *vipra* and *sambhu* when not forming a technical term. 180.

The form *ḍu* is an indeclinable citation. *Vibhuḥ*, *prabhuḥ*, and *saṃbhuḥ* [are derived from roots with the suffix *u*]. The causes for these meanings here are pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and the act of bringing forth (*janana*). However, when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), *vibhūḥ* refers to a certain person. There is an addition to the rule regarding words such as *mitadru*: "an addition [should be made] for words like *mitadru*. Thus, one who runs a measured distance is *mitadruḥ*. One who brings about well-being or causes prosperity is *śambhuḥ*. The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after the root *dhā* in the sense of the object (*karman*). (Pāṇini 3.2.182)

The roots *dhā* and *dheṭ* are included because they are specified by their own forms. [The suffix *kvip* occurs] after the roots *dhā*, *jan*, *mal*, *ka*, *vas*, and *matṛ* when expressing the sense of "nurse" (*dhātrī*), "mother" (*jananī*), "myrobalan tree" (*āmalakī*), "earth" (*vasumatī*), and "mother" (*upamātṛ*) respectively.

[The suffix *kvip* also occurs] after the roots *dam*, *niś*, *sā*, *yu*, *yuj*, *stu*, *tud*, *si*, *sic*, *mih*, *pat*, *daś*, *naha*, and *kṛ* when expressing the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). (182)

The suffix *ṣṭran* shall occur [after the roots mentioned]. *Dātram*: that by which one cuts; from the root *dā*, meaning "to cut. *Netram*, *śastram*, *yotram*, *yoktram*, *totram*, *sotram*—[the latter] they bind or fasten with it, hence *setram*; *sektram*. [In the rule for] *meḍhra*, *patra*, and *daśa*, the mention of *daśa* is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal (*n*) even when a suffix other than *kit* follows. By this, the form *daśanoti* is established. Nor is there an undesired application [of this rule] in the present case [of *netra*, etc.], because of the specific mention in the rule *śuno danta-daṃṣṭrā-...* and so forth.
[The suffix *ṣṭran* occurs after the root *pū*] when referring to a plow or a boar: *pūtraḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.183)

The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after the roots *pūṅ* and *pūñ* when they denote an instrument (*karaṇa*), provided that this instrument is a constituent part of a plow (*hala*) or a pig (*sūkara*). By this, the status of these two roots as upapadas (governing words) and their being expressed as such are excluded. *Potram*: meaning "the snout" (*toyamukha*). In all these cases, the prohibition of *iṇ* (the substitution of *ī*) applies by the rule *titutra-tatatha-sisusarakaseṣu ca*.
After the roots *ṛ*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *khan*, *saha*, and *cara*, the suffix *tra* is applied. (Pāṇini 3.2.184).
*aritra*, *lavitra*, *dhūti*. Because the suffix is marked with the indicator *ṅ*, guna is prohibited, and thus *uvaṅ* is applied: *dhavitra*, *savitra*, *khanitra*, *sahitra*, *caritra*.
[The suffix *itrac* is added after the root *pu* when it denotes a name. (Pāṇini 3.2.185)
The *pavitra* is a means for producing clarified butter (*ājya*), consisting of *darbha* grass, or it is a ring made of *darbha* worn around the ring finger.
[The suffix] *kṛt* is used when the agent is a seer (*ṛṣi*) or a deity (*devatā*). 186.

In the case where the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the deity (*devatā*) is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the Vedic mantra, [the term] *pavitra* is used; it is that by which one is purified (*pūyate*). "May Agni, the purifier (*pavitra*), purify us together.
[The suffix] *kta* is applied after the root *ñī*. (187)
In the sense of the present: *svinnaḥ* (sweated), *iddhaḥ* (kindled), *kṣviṇṇaḥ* (distressed). The meaning is that [the suffix] applies to the substratum of present perspiration and so forth.
And [it applies] after roots having the sense of "thought," "cognition," and "reverence" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.188).

*Matih* (the act of thinking) is distinct from *buddhih* (the state of being enlightened), because they are mentioned separately. In the expression "the king’s *mataḥ*" (thought of/respected by the king) or "*buddhaḥ*" (enlightened by the king), this [suffix] is used with an object because it is transitive (*sakarmaka*). By this rule, the restriction that a *kta*-suffix derived from roots such as *man* (to think) refers only to the past is set aside, according to the maxim of the curd and Kauṇḍinya (i.e., a specific rule overrides a general one). However, in the case of *jñātīn matya* (having known his kinsmen), even though it refers to the past, the suffix is used because of the application of the rule *upajñātam* under the governing heading *tena*. Otherwise, there would be the occurrence of the genitive case by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; thus says the Bhāṣya: "Also *śīlitaḥ*, *rakṣitaḥ*, *kṣāntaḥ*, *ākruṣṭaḥ*, and *juṣṭaḥ*."
Both "ruṣṭa" (angry) and "arucita" (displeased) are also used when [the person] has been addressed.
"Both [the worlds] are possessed by joy and likewise overcome; both are restrained and exerted.
'Suffering will come to pass,' so said the immortals, as they were born as before."
Thus ends the third Āhnika in the second Pāda of the third [Adhyāya] in the Śrīsiddhāntasudhānidhi;
and this Pāda is completed.
Now begins the first Āhnika of the third Pāda. 1.
The *uṇādi* suffixes are applied diversely.

Generally, because these words are conventional (*rūḍha*) and do not follow the meanings of their roots and suffixes, they are not explained in detail; rather, this [treatise] merely permits the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of those words already explained in other sciences. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "Abundance [of irregular forms] is not due to observation; for that which arises from Vedic usage and convention is perfectly correct. And Nirukta, Vyākaraṇa, and Śakaṭāyana declare that even a noun is a verbal root."

The meaning of this is as follows: One might object that the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) here is redundant, since the sanction of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is established by the rule itself, "uṇādayaḥ" (the uṇādi suffixes [are used in various ways]). Anticipating this objection, he says: "tanudṛṣṭeḥ" (because of the observation of their scarcity). In the word "prakṛteḥ," the singular number is used with reference to the class (*jāti*). The word *tanu* emphasizes the state of being; it refers to the observation of the small number of verbal roots (*prakṛti*). The meaning of the word *bahula* is the inclusion of many meanings. Thus, the uṇādi suffixes are prescribed even from those roots not listed therein. Consequently, the suffix *ulac* is applied after the root *hṛṣ*, and *śaṅkula* is also formed from the root *śaṅk*.

Thus, because of the use of the plural number, suffixes not specifically prescribed there [in the *Dhatupatha*] are also included; hence, from the root *ṛt*, we have *ṛpiḍa* and *ṛpiḍḍu*. The same applies to grammatical operations (*kārya*); for example, in the word *ṣaṇḍa*, there is an absence of the substitution of *s* (satva), or rather, the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*). Now, one might object: "In that case, all suffixes would apply to all roots. To this he replies: "Vedic" (*naigama*). That which occurs in the *nigama*, i.e., in the *Chandas* (Veda). The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *aṇṛgayanādibhyaḥ*. It is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), meaning established usage. The meaning is that since actual usage (*prayoga*) serves as the regulator, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Regarding the classification of *prakṛti* (bases) and so forth, as well as their derivation, he states the consensus of other teachers with the words "and [the opinion] of Nāma. The *Nirukta* has also been cited under the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*. The meaning is that Śākaṭāyana is the offspring (*toka*) or descendant of Śakaṭa.

"In technical names (*saṃjñā*), one should recognize the forms of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and the suffixes (*pratyaya*) following them; one should learn the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) from the grammatical operation (*kārya*). This is the rule regarding the *uṇādi* suffixes."
This has been explained.
[The suffixes] are also seen [to be used] with reference to the past. || 2 ||

Nor is the other two subsequent sūtras rendered superfluous merely by the exclusion of those entitled to perform the rite in the present time; for their meaning is that [the suffixes] generally apply to the present, while in certain cases they apply to another time.
"The future tense is used for 'gamyā' and so forth. (Pāṇini 3.3.3)

*grāmaṃ gamī* or *gāmī*: these [suffixes] have the general future (*bhaviṣyat-sāmānya*) as their scope. However, when a specific [future] is intended to be expressed, the suffix *luṭ* (the periphrastic future) applies by virtue of an exception (*apavāda*) and a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). Examples: *śvo grāmaṃ gantā* ("he will go to the village tomorrow"); also *lṛṭ* by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*): *gamiṣyati*, *bhaviṣyati*, etc. The governing heading (*adhikāra*) for the future exists so that the suffix *laṭ* (the present tense) may be used correctly only in the future when joined with the particles *yāvat* and *purā*, because the present tense is superseded by the future tense. Furthermore, if there were no specific rule regarding the time denoted by the word itself, those [particles] would not be employed. If this [heading] did not exist, the suffix *laṭ* would be correct even for the past. *Yāvat-purā-nipātayoḷ-laṭ* || 4 || (When the particles *yāvat* and *purā* are used, the suffix *laṭ* is employed.)

*yāvadbhuṅkte* (he eats as much as... and *purābhuṅkte* (before eating)—these two are indeclinables (*nipāta*) used in the sense of certainty. The meaning is: "he will eat immediately after. The mention of the term *nipāta* is for the purpose of making known that the technical rule concerning forms taught by definition (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory. In the case of *yāvadbhuṅkte*, either by the rule of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) or because *yāvat* and *purā* continue to apply up until that point, the suffix *luṭ* is employed.
[Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.5: *vibhāṣā kadākarhyoḥ* (the suffix *luṭ* is optionally used after the words *kadā* and *karhi*).

The suffix *laṭ* shall be used for the future tense; alternatively, *luṭ* may also be used. For example: *kadā* or *karhi* *bhuṅkte*, *bhokṣyate*, or *bhoktā*. Nor is it improper to use *laṭ* in connection with the word *karhi*, because although *karhi* refers to a non-present (future) time, the rule for *laṭ* is established as referring to the general future (*bhaviṣyatsāmānya*), and its application in connection with *karhi* is explained accordingly. Furthermore, there is no sublation of *laṭ*—which is prescribed for the general future—by *luṭ*, which is prescribed for specific cases within that same domain, because it has already been stated that the former continues to apply in that very context. [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.7] states: "When a word ending in *kim* is used, *laṭ* is used in the sense of desire (*lipsā*). (6)

The suffix *laṅ* may optionally be used [in the sense of the future]. For example: "Whom (*kam*, *kataram*, or *katamam*) do you feed, will you feed, or are you going to feed? Here, the speaker's desire is understood from the context. And [the suffix *liṅ* is also used] when there is the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained. (Pāṇini 3.3.156)

When the accomplishment of heaven and so forth is to be understood through food and the like that is intended to be eaten, the *laṭ* (present tense) may optionally be used even when there is no word beginning with *kim*. This is the commencement of the rule concerning what does not begin with *kim*. "He who gives you food goes to heaven; he who will give, or the giver, will go to heaven. Kaiyaṭa states that, however, because the term "beginning with *kim*" (*kiṃvṛtta*) was included in the previous sūtra, this [current] sūtra serves to exclude the *laṭ* in cases of inquiry (*lipsā*) where there is no word beginning with *kim*, even though the action is intended to be performed.
And [the *laṭ* is used] when there is an indication of the sense of the imperative (*loḍ-artha*). (Pāṇini 3.3.8)

The present tense (*laṭ*) may optionally be used for a verb denoting a future action when it follows another verb meaning "to send" (*preṣa*) and so forth, provided that the latter serves as an indicator of the former. For example: *kṛṣṇaśced bhuṅkte tvaṃ gāścāraya* (If Kṛṣṇa eats, you should tend the cows), where the future sense is expressed by either *bhokṣyate* or *bhoktā*.
And the optative suffix [is used] when [the action] occurs after more than a muhūrta. || 9 ||

By irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in the final member of the compound. When a verb denotes an action that will take place after a short interval (*muhūrta*), the suffixes *liṅ* and *laṭ* are used; optionally, *lṛṭ* and *luṭ* may also be used. For example: "If the teacher should come, or is coming, or will come, or is about to come after a moment, then you must study the Veda. The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when one action is performed for the sake of another action. (Pāṇini 3.3.10)

When an action is for the sake of another action, these two suffixes (tumun and ṇvul) are applied after a verbal root that denotes that [purpose], provided it occurs as an *upapada* (governing word) and refers to the future. For example: *kṛṣṇaṃ draṣṭuṃ yāti* ("He goes in order to see Kṛṣṇa") and *kṛṣṇaṃ darśako yāti* ("He goes as one who will see Kṛṣṇa"). Here, the act of going has the purpose of seeing; therefore, the suffix *tumun* is used after the root *dṛś*. [Objection: But surely the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed without distinction and is thus already established even in this specific case. Furthermore, the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70)—which prohibits the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by restating the future tense—is intended precisely for the purpose of such a prescription. [Response: This is not so. The prohibition of the sixth case ending applies only when a word ending in *akac* or *ṇvul* follows a word denoting the future or a debt (*ādhamarṇya*). However, in the present instance, the word *darśakaḥ* does not follow a word denoting the future; rather, it follows the word *kṛṣṇam*, which is in the accusative case. Therefore, since the condition for the prohibition is absent, the sixth case would indeed occur here, and its prevention is necessary. Thus, the specific prescription of *ṇvul* in this context is indeed required.

It is because that [prohibition] is logically consistent only when the general rule itself has a future sense. Nor can it be argued that the purpose of [specifying] "being prescribed under a future heading" is to obtain its status as the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that prohibition. For if only the future sense were so [the delimiting property], then in the case of *aṅga yajatāṃ lapsyante 'sya yājakāḥ* ("O worthy one, those who will sacrifice for him shall obtain [fees]"), since there is an explanation [of the genitive] as *ye enaṃ yājayiṣyanti* ("those who will cause him to sacrifice"), the prohibition of the genitive would undesirably apply even when a future sense is connected with an agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, it should not be said [that the specification is necessary].

This is because, through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *yājaka* (sacrificer), the suffix conveys future tense specifically regarding the actual state of affairs; for instance, in expressions such as "these are his sacrificers," the word *yājaka* refers to the past by the very nature of its linguistic power, since the designation occurs through the attribution of future sacrificer-status. Furthermore, the suffix *tumun* does not sublate the suffix *ṇvul* in order to provide a specific injunction, because *tumun* denotes the abstract action (*bhāva*) and thus does not obstruct the *ṇvul*, which is devoid of such an action.
Moreover, the suffix *ṇvul* is also justified by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*).

It is said that the prescription of the suffix *ṇvul* is for the purpose of setting aside [the application of] the suffixes *tṛc* and others; otherwise, by the rule of *vāsarūpa*, those [suffixes] would also apply. Therefore, according to the grammatical tradition (*ākara*), forms such as *kartum vrajati* (he goes in order to do) or *kartāvrajati* (he does not go while being an agent), and *vikṣipo vrajati* (he goes while scattering), are not employed. [Question: Why "for the sake of an action" (*kriyāyām*)? [Answer: So that it does not apply when a substance (*dravya*) is the attendant word (*upapada*). For example: *bhikṣiṣye ityasya jaṭāḥ* (his matted hair is such that he thinks "I shall beg"). However, in the case of *bhikṣitum jaṭāḥ* (matted hair for the purpose of begging), the verb *dhārayati* ("he wears") must be supplied. [Question: Why "for the sake of an action" (*kriyārthāyām*)? [Answer: [Consider the sentence: *dhāvataste patiṣyati daṇḍaḥ* (as you run, the staff will fall upon you).

Although the act of running is the cause of the falling of the staff, it does not have that [falling] as its purpose, because "having that as its purpose" applies only to that which is performed with a specific aim. In the expression *kṛṣṇam* (towards Kṛṣṇa), the meaning of the accusative case is "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*). This relates to the act of seeing; and through the relation of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*), the act of seeing connects with the act of going. The resulting cognition is: "The going, performed by Caitra, has as its intended object the seeing of Kṛṣṇa. Futureness, however, is not an object of verbal expression, since this is obtained simply from the inherent nature of desire, which takes as its object that which is not yet established.

In the case of the word *darśaka*, however, the substratum of the suffix *ṇvul* (agentive) is construed with the act of seeing (*darśana*) by way of the relation of possessing a desire for its own object. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The going has as its agent the substratum of a seeing whose object is Kṛṣṇa. When the seeing is construed with the agent of the going by way of the relation of possessing a desire for its own object, it follows by implication that the going has the seeing as its intended purpose.

As for the claim that the meaning in both cases is: "a journey whose purpose is to see a future [object] whose object is Kṛṣṇa, which has as its agent an agent who performs such a future seeing, and which has you as its intended recipient"—that is not correct. For it contradicts your own treatise, which states that "the identity of agent" is a contextual condition (*prayogopādhi*) obtained through the force of the expression; furthermore, it is untenable for a contextual condition to be the domain of the word itself, and because, according to the reasoning already stated, that [identity of agent] is obtainable from other sources.

By this [argument], since the syntactic awareness (*anvaya-bodha*) produced by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) pertains to the agent, there would be an impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) in the case of the word *yāti* ("goes"). As for the claim that the action of going (*yāna-kriyā*) is the producer of the seeing (*darśana-janikā*), that too is incorrect; for the aforementioned usage occurs even when the seeing is not immediately brought about (*darśanānupadhāne*). Even if one intends to express "intrinsic fitness" (*svarūpa-yogyatā*), the aforementioned usage would undesirably apply even in cases where the seeing is produced by something intended for another purpose. Furthermore, if one accepts that "being the intended object" (*uddeśyatva*) is a relation (*saṃsarga*), then there is no reason to postulate "being a producer" (*janakatva*) as such a relation. And [the rule] *bhāvavacanāś ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.11) applies.

The suffixes *ghañ* and others, which will be discussed in the section on *bhāva* (action/being), shall occur when a verbal root meaning "action" has another action as its object (*upapada*) and the sense is that of the future. This rule is for the purpose of a specific prescription (*pratipadavidhi*) regarding those words denoting *bhāva* that have been prescribed according to their respective rules. The word *yathā* is not compounded; alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi*: "those whose prescription is according to what has been prescribed" (*yathāvihitaṃ vidhānaṃ yeṣām*).

The meaning is as follows: since the suffix *tumun*, which is prescribed specifically for the sense of "purposeful action" (*kriyārtha-kriyā*), would necessarily exclude (*bādhaprasaṅga*) suffixes such as *ghañ* within its own domain, the word "object" (*padam*) is included in the rule to ensure that the same specific conditions under which *ghañ* and other suffixes are prescribed after particular verbal roots apply even in the aforementioned case. Otherwise, there would be an undesirable confusion (*avyatikara*). [Example: *yāgāya yāti* ("he goes for the sake of sacrifice"). By the rule *tum-arthācca* (Pāṇini 2.3.15), the fourth case ending is used; the meaning is "going directed toward the sacrifice. [Next rule: *aṇ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.12).

*Kāṇḍalāvaḥ vrajati* (The reed-cutter goes). This means going for the purpose of cutting reeds. Now, one might object: "Is it not true that the suffix *aṇ*, prescribed generally for the object (*karman*), is already established even in this specific case? True. However, the repetition [of the rule] is intended to prevent its removal from the scope of exceptions (*apavāda*). One might further object: "Since a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) is simpler than a new injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), this [repetition] should serve to secure the suffix even in the scope of general rules (*utsarga*); otherwise, because of the prescription of the suffix *ṇvul*, the suffix *aṇ* would be as difficult to obtain as *tṛc* and other such suffixes. How then is the establishment of *aṇ* for the object secured even in the scope of exceptions?

Not so; for that [suffix] is established in the sense of the object (*karman*) merely by the continued application of the term "word" (*vacana*). Since the repetition of the word "object" is intended to include the object alone, the suffix *aṇ* is established even in cases where it would otherwise be superseded [by another rule]. Thus, forms such as *kambaladāya* are established, because this [suffix] supersedes the suffix *kap* due to its higher status. [Objection: Even so, it might sometimes occur when the object is the upapada and sometimes when the action is the upapada. [Response: This is not a fault, because the statement has purpose insofar as it serves to supersede the exceptions [to the general rule], thereby ensuring its application in the future.

If, however, by means of the particle *ca* (and), there were an injunction for the inclusion of multiple *upapadas*, then because each [word] individually would lack the status of being an *upapada*, the *upapada-samāsa* with the word *kāṇḍa* would not occur. It is not so; for since they are specified separately by means of individual locative case-endings, the status of being an *upapada* rests upon each one individually.
And [the rule applies] when *lṛṭ* remains as the remainder: *lṛṭ-śeṣe ca* || 13 ||

The suffix *lṛṭ* occurs after a verbal root in the sense of the future, whether there exists another action for the sake of which the first action is performed, or not. [Example: "He will be. Now, one might object: since the rule is established even without the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "when there is an action for the sake of another action," what is the purpose of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*)? Do not say so. For in examples such as "he goes thinking 'I shall do'," the suffix *luṭ* would be untenable—just as it is with *tṛc* and other suffixes—because it would be superseded by *ṇvul*. However, because of the inclusion of the word "remainder," we infer the recurrence of that phrase, and thus *lṛṭ* is established in both cases. As it has been said: "The mention of *śeṣa* regarding *lṛṭ* is for the sake of a specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) concerning an action."

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the intended meaning here because the word *śeṣa* (remainder) must ultimately refer to an *upapada* distinct from a verb; for according to the view of the Vārttika, the suffix is prescribed here as well by virtue of the particle *ca*. However, the authors of the Bhāṣya state that since the form is established through the analysis of the rules—by the rule *lṛṭ* [Pāṇini 3.3.13] when a verb signifying an action is the *upapada*, and by the rule *śeṣe* [Pāṇini 3.3.16] when such an *upapada* is absent—the particle *ca* is redundant.
*lṛṭaḥ sadvā* || 14 || [The suffix *sa* optionally replaces *lṛṭ*.]

The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* take the place of *lṛṭ*. The mention of *lṛṭ* is for the purpose of specifying the original element (*sthānin*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of these being independent suffixes. It should be stated that "the rule for *sat* (present participles) is permanent when not co-referential with a word ending in the nominative case. This is also an illustration; it should be understood that [the rule applies] in cases of address (*saṃbodhana*), when indicating an action (*kriyālakṣaṇa*), when expressing a cause (*hetu*), when followed by another word (*uttarapada*), and when followed by a suffix (*pratyaya*). Examples: "See him who will sacrifice" (*yakṣyantam* / *yakṣyamāṇam paśya*); "O you who will do" (*he kariṣyan*); "He dwells intending to acquire or intending to study" (*arjayiṣyan* / *adhyeṣyamāṇo vasati*); "Devotion toward one who will act" (*kariṣyadbhaktiḥ*); "Form toward one who will sing" (*kīraṣyadrūpaḥ*).

In the case of the first [person], there is an option regarding coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). One says: "Devadatta will do" (*kari�ṣyati devadattaḥ*) or "he who is about to do" (*kariṣyamāṇaḥ*); or "the jar will be" (*ghaṭo bhaviṣyati*). Here, the suffix arises after the verbal root (*dhātu*). The meaning of the suffix is either being at a time that is the counter-positive of the present prior non-existence, or being at a time subsequent to the present. Its connection (*anvaya*) is with the meaning of the verbal root. In this context, the word *ādya* (beginning) implies that space and time also connect with "origination" (*utpatti*), but not with "being the counter-positive of the present prior non-existence. For if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one might say "it will happen today" regarding something that is to happen tomorrow.

It should not be argued that there is no such undesirable consequence because the word "today" (adya) and so forth are construed with both the counter-positive and the prior absence, since the cognition would be "the jar today is the counter-positive of the prior absence existing today. For [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence that one could say "Caitra will exist on the new moon day" regarding Caitra who is about to be born at the very first moment of the new moon day; this is because, although the new moon day is the locus of Caitra, it is not the locus of the prior absence of Caitra.

And thus, the understanding is that the jar is the substratum of that origination which occurs in this location and is the counter-positive of a present prior non-existence (*vartamāna-prāgabhāva*). In the view of the Grammarians (*śābdika*), the distinction is that it is such an origination of the jar [as denoted by the suffix].
[The suffix] *luṭ* is used for what is not of today (*anadyatana*). 15.

The *luṭ* suffix occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when referring to a future time not belonging to the current day (*anadyatana*). This is a compound (*bahuvrīhi*) designation, similar to the rule for *laṅ*. Therefore, in the case of "he will come today or tomorrow," only *lṛṭ* is used. Here, by the rule "in the non-current day" (*anadyatane*), two suffixes bearing the technical name *sat* are prescribed in place of *luṭ* when the non-current day is intended. For example: *śvonagnīnādhāsyamānena* ("by one who will establish the sacred fires tomorrow") and *śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena* ("by one who will sacrifice with Soma tomorrow"). By the mention of *luṭ*, the prescription of *luṭ* for the non-current day is established. Examples include *śvaḥ kartā* ("he will do tomorrow") and *śvo'dhyetā* ("he will study tomorrow"). The very prescription of these substitutes (*ādeśa*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *luṭ* applies to the non-current day.

Regarding lamentation (*paridevana*), it should be stated that the *śvastanī* [suffix] denotes a future sense. This is the prescription for the *luṭ* suffix in the general sense of the future. Lamentation means grieving. *Śvastanī* is the technical name for the *luṭ* suffix used by the ancient teachers. An example is: "When will she go, she who places her feet [here]? Or: "This one is a learner, though he is not yet diligent.
