[Objection: "The mention of the term 'kṛtya' is redundant, because as a general rule it is precisely these [suffixes] that are understood. [Reply: "It should be stated: 'The *kṛtya* and *uṭ* suffixes occur diversely (*bahulam*).'"

The term *kṛtya* should be removed and the term *kṛt* alone should be employed because it is more comprehensive; thus, the intended meaning is that even for *lyuṭ*, a separate mention is unnecessary. *Pādahārakaḥ* (one who carries with his feet); *galecopakaḥ* (one who is cheated by the neck). Here, the suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). "By one who will establish the sacred fires tomorrow" (*śvo 'gninādhāsyamānena*); "by one who will sacrifice with Soma tomorrow" (*śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena*). The suffix *lṛṭ* occurs even when referring to the non-today (*anadyatana*).
The suffix *kta* is used in the neuter gender in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). || 114 ||

The suffix *kta* occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when the sense is a state (*bhāva*) characterized by neuter gender. Examples include *isitam* (the act of smiling) and *śayitam* (the act of lying down), and so forth. It might be argued: "The status of *kta* as expressing a state is already established by the rule *tar-ot-kṛtya-ktakhalarthāḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.104], which prescribes the suffixes *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khala* after the roots *tṛ* and *ar*. This is not so. In that rule, only the suffix *kta* prescribed by the rule *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 3.2.102]—which falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the past tense (*bhūta*)—is intended to be included. This present rule, however, is an injunction for *kta* in the sense of a state (*bhāva*) regardless of specific time. For this very reason, because this rule is subsequent, it supersedes the suffixes *ghañ* and *ac* within its own scope; thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that those two (*ghañ* and *ac*) have masculine gender.

Now, one might argue that this [application of the rule] should also apply to the object (*karman*) because the phrase "and after intransitive verbs" (*bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*) is not present here. True; however, since forms such as *gataṃ tiraścīnam* ("the horizontal movement") are attested in usage, we accept the desired result. Nor should it be said that there would be an undesired occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) in connection with those [forms], because the genitive is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛṇām*. For, regarding the sūtra *ktasya ca vartamāne*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) has been made for the genitive after a neuter abstract noun ending in *kta*; and even in the view where that [addition] is rejected on the grounds of intending the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), we assume that in those specific cases the intention is indeed to express the "remainder," based on the authority of the Bhāṣya on that point.

Some say that [the mention of] "having wandered through many difficult and treacherous regions" is intended because a second [agent] is not seen in certain instances. Others, however, maintain that this [suffix -ta] occurs only after intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*). This is because the phrase *tayoreva* (only those two) is explained as a separate syntactical unit (*vākyabheda*) following the rule *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (and in the sense of the abstract state [bhāva], after intransitives). Thus, by restating the kṛtya suffixes and others prescribed by their respective rules, one sentence prescribes the meaning as being restricted to the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) alone. Consequently, the fact that the past participle suffix (*kta*), as prescribed by the rule *niṣṭhā*, has the abstract state as its meaning is established.

Regarding the rule *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*, they say that by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *kta* from the preceding rule *bhāve ca*, the domain of the suffix *kta* when used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) is restricted to "intransitive verbs" (*akarmakebhyaḥ*). Since both types of *kta* [past passive participle and gerundive] are mentioned there without distinction, this [rule] also pertains solely to those [suffixes] used in the sense of an abstract action for intransitive verbs alone. As for examples such as *gataṃ* (gone) and *bhuktaṃ* (eaten), they possess the status of being intransitive because the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita-karmatvena*).
And [the suffix] *lyuṭ*. (Pāṇini 3.3.115)

The suffix *lyuṭ* may also occur in the sense of a neuter abstract action (*bhāva*). [Examples: *śayanaṃ*, *hasanaṃ*. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of preventing the recurrence of *kta* in subsequent rules. And [the suffix *lyuṭ* is used] in the sense of the object (*karman*) when, through contact with it, pleasure arises in the body of the agent. (Pāṇini 3.3.116)

In the word *sparśa*, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the action (*bhāve*). The genitive case in *kartuḥ* is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). According to the rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable, [the sixth case ending is used] for the object," the third case ending is used for the agent in the word *yena*. Furthermore, the status of being an agent must be understood as that which is defined by the same action that defines another's status as an object. Thus, when the action of touching produces bodily pleasure for the agent who is being touched, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the neuter gender in the sense of the action (*bhāve*), with the object serving as the *upapada*. The rule regarding *upapada* is formulated to ensure the formation of a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*). An example is: *payaḥpānaṃ sukham* ("drinking milk is pleasant").

Although pleasure arises from eating alone, nevertheless, the word *sparśa* (touching) is merely indicative of that [eating] and others as well. [Question: Why is the locative case used? [Answer: "The rising from the mattress is pleasure. Here, because the pleasure belongs to the agent who is touched by the ablative (*apādāna*), and not to the object (*karman*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the previous rule itself. [Question: Why is the word *kartuḥ* (of the agent) used? [Answer: "Bathing the teacher is pleasure. Even though the teacher is the agent with respect to the pleasure, he is not the agent of the action of bathing; for in the action denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the student alone is the agent.

By the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha...* [Pāṇini 1.4.52], the teacher (*guru*) possesses the status of an object (*karman*). This is because the verb *snapayati* (he bathes) is intransitive in its state without the causative suffix (*aṇ-antadaśāyām*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "body" (*śarīra*) here is for the purpose of obtaining the sense that pleasure has as its instrumental cause the conjunction with a body. Consequently, this does not apply in cases such as *dhanasyāsādanaṃ sukham* (the acquisition of wealth is pleasure), because in that case, pleasure arises solely through the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*).
And [the term *karma* is also used] in the senses of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*) [by Pāṇini 3.3.117].

The suffixes *la* and *yuṭ* are applied in these two senses. It should not be argued that these two [suffixes] have only the status of being an *upapada* (governing word) and not the status of being the meaning of the suffix itself; for that is not the case, as evidenced by usages such as *karaṇa*. Examples are: *idhmavraścanaḥ* ("wood-cutter"), *palāśaśātanaḥ* ("leaf-shatterer"), and "one desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a *godohana* (milk-pail). This [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ghañ*, according to the maxim "that which applies where another does not already apply" (*yena nāprāptinyāya*). Furthermore, it subverts the feminine suffixes *ajā* and *ap* and other feminine suffixes because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], as he will state later: "after *aja* and *abhi*. In the masculine, when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *gha* generally applies. (Pāṇini 3.3.118)

In the sense of the instrument (karaṇa) and the locus (adhikaraṇa), the suffix *gha* generally occurs in the masculine when it denotes a technical name (*saṃjñā*). For example, *dantacchadaḥ*: "that by which the teeth are covered"; the shortening [of the vowel] occurs because of the rule "after the root *chad*, before *gha*". *Ākaraḥ*: "in which they act" (meaning, where they conduct their business). Why say "generally"? [Counter-example: *prasādhanaṃ*.
Also included are *gocara*, *saṃcara*, *vaha*, *vrajya*, *vraja*, *āpaṇa*, and *nigama*. (Pāṇini 3.3.119)

The suffix *ghañ* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) to the same two meanings as previously mentioned; it is an exception to [the rule] *halaśca*. *Gocaraḥ* means a place or region where cows graze (*gāvaścaranty atra*). *Saṃcarī* means a path, because they move along it (*saṃcarante 'nena*). *Bahaḥ* means a shoulder, because they carry [loads] by means of it (*vahantyanena*). *Vrajaḥ* means a cow-pen (*ghoṣa*), because they go there (*vrajanty atra*). *Vyajaḥ* means a palm-leaf fan; due to irregular derivation, the change to *vī* does not occur. The mention of *gocara* and so forth is for the sake of illustration, because the term "mostly" (*prāya*) is understood from the rule *halaśca*; Kaiyaṭa maintains that since the suffix *ghañ* is sometimes absent due to the recurrence of the word "mostly" in that rule, *ghañ* occurs here specifically. Otherwise, forms such as *nikaṣaḥ* (a touchstone) derived from the root *kaṣ* would remain unestablished.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots *ava*, *tṛ*, and *stṝ*.

*Avatāraḥ* refers to the descent into a well and the like; *avastāraḥ* refers to a curtain (*cavanikā*). Because of the inclusion of the term "generally" (*prāya*), the meaning is "in that which serves as the condition for causing descent. According to the *Vṛtti*, it is also used in some cases even when not a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*).
[Pāṇini 3.3.121: *halaśca*.

The suffix *dhak* (i.e., *an*) follows a stem ending in a consonant (*halantāt*). This is an exception to the suffix *gha*. *Apāmārgaḥ*: that by which disease is wiped away (*apamṛjyate*). *Vimārgaḥ*: that by which refuse is swept away (*vimañjyate*); it means a broom (*samūhanī*).
[The words] *adhyāya*, *nyāya*, *udyāva*, and *saṃhāra* [are also formed with this suffix]. (Pāṇini 3.3.122)

That in which one studies is *adhyāya*; that by which they restrain is *nyāya*; that by which they push upward, and so forth. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The addition of *avahāra*, *ādhāra*, and *āvāya* should be made," for these words have the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). However, the author of the *Vṛtti*, having inserted the words *ādhāra* and *āvāya* from the *Vārttika* into the *sūtra*, says that the word *avahāra* is included by means of the particle *ca*. This is clear in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others. [Pāṇini 3.3.123: *udaṅko 'nudake*.

When the word *udaka* is used as a distinct preceding term (*upapada*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *añc* preceded by the prefix *ut*. Although this is established by the rule *halaśca*, this specific rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding *udaka* from that general rule. In *ghṛtodaṅkaḥ*—meaning "a leather vessel" (*carmapātra*) in which clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is poured out (*udacyate*) or drawn up (*uddhriyate*)—the suffix *ghañ* is applied. Why is it said "not when *udaka* follows"? Consider *udakodanvacanaḥ*. Even though, since *ghañ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *gha*, it would be more logical for *gha* alone to apply in the absence of *ghañ*, nevertheless, due to the force of the prohibition of *ghañ*, there is also an absence of *gha*; this is because their forms are identical.

[The suffix *ghañ*] is [assigned] because of the similarity in being oxytone (antodātta) both by the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member when *gha* is added, and by the *thāthādi*-accent rule even when *ghañ* is used. "The mention of *an-udaka-* is useless because it is a statement of general practice (*prāya-vacana*). This means that since the suffix *gha* does not apply in the case of *udakodañcana-* precisely because it is a matter of general usage, the sūtra need not have been commenced.
*Jālam ānāyaḥ* || 124 ||

Since the word *jāla* is established by the rule "the suffix *ṇa* comes after roots ending in *jvaliti* and *kas*" when meaning "water" or "grain," it is specifically the word *ānāya* that is here treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). It is called *ānāya* because fish and other creatures are brought (*ānīyante*) by means of it. What is a net? It is an *ānaya*.
[The suffix] *ghañ* follows the root *khan*. (Pāṇini 3.3.125)

The suffix *cāddhañ* [is applied after the root *khan*]. Thus: *ākhanah* (a digger), *khanah* (a digger). Since there is no constituent part of these words that would require the substitution of a guttural (*kutva*) by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, the addition of the marker *ḍit* would otherwise be useless; however, by virtue of its presence, this suffix applies even after other roots. By this means, the form *bhagam* is established. It is stated: "After the root *khan*, the suffixes *ḍaḍ*, *ara*, *ika*, and *ikavaka* should be mentioned. Thus: *ākhaḥ*, *ākharaḥ*. Because of the marker *ḍit*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*). *Ākhanikaḥ*, *ākhanikavakaḥ*. These six—*ākha*, etc.—denote a digging tool.

On this point, the Vārttika states: "The suffixes *strī*, *khal*, and *ana* [supersede] *striyāḥ* by way of conflict; *khal* [supersedes] *striyāḥ*. In cases such as *cayaḥ*, *lavaḥ*, *kṛtiḥ*, and *dṛtiḥ*, where both [suffixes] have scope, *ktin* prevails due to its higher status in the order of rules (*paratvāt*) in instances like *citiḥ* and *śrutiḥ*. In the case of *idhmavraścana*, [the suffix *ana*] applies in the sense of "space for a cart" (*ana-avakāśa*), while in cases such as *palāśacayana*, it applies specifically to the cart itself (*ana eva*). Similarly, in the case of feminine suffixes such as in *kṛtiḥ*, the scope of the suffix *khal* is in instances such as *īṣadbheda*. In cases like *īṣadbhedā* or *durbhedā*, the suffix *khal* applies. Likewise, in examples such as *saktudhānī* or *tailapīḍanī*, one should understand that the suffix *ana* applies by overriding the feminine suffix.
*Sūtra 126:* The suffix *khal* is applied after verbal roots when preceded by the particles *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *su*, in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*) or ease (*akṛcchra*).

When these words—*duḥkha*, *sukha*, and *artha*—are used as upapadas (governing words), the suffix *khal* occurs in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Because of the rule stating "only in those two" (*tayoreva*), the application to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is excluded. Here, the distinction that *duḥ* has the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*) while the other two do not have the sense of difficulty is to be understood through contextual fitness (*yogyatā*). *Duṣkaraḥ kaṭo bhavatā* ("The mat is difficult for you to make"). *Īṣatkaraḥ* or *sukaraḥ* ("It is easy to make"). The suffix *yuc* is added after a verbal root ending in a vowel within the aforementioned scope; this is an exception to [the suffix] *khal*. Examples: *īṣatpānaḥ somaḥ bhavatā* ("Soma is easily drunk by you"), *duṣpānaḥ*, *supānaḥ*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), it is added after roots meaning "to go. (Pāṇini 3.3.129)
In the case of *khalaviṣaya*, the meaning is that the fire is "easily accessible," i.e., capable of being approached with ease.
[The suffix *aṇ*] is also seen after other words. (Pāṇini 5.2.130)

[The suffix] *yuc* should be stated after the roots *śās*, *yudh*, *dṛś*, *dhṛṣ*, and *mṛṣ* in the common language (*bhāṣā*). *Duḥśāsanaḥ*, *duryodhanaḥ*, *durdarśanaḥ*, *durdharṣaṇaḥ*, *durmarṣaṇaḥ*. When there is proximity to the present time, the verb may optionally be treated as if it were in the present tense.

Regarding the term *sāmīpya*, some hold that the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), while others maintain it denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*). Kaiyaṭa argues that there is no impossibility of forming the compound, because the relationship of proximity belongs not only to the meanings of the suffixes to be extended (*atideśya*) but also to the present tense itself; this is possible through a mediated connection (*paramparayā*). By this, the statement of the author of the Nyāsa—that a compound with the word "present" (*vartamāna*) would be impossible when the suffix denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*), since proximity is related to the proximate object rather than the present tense, and thus proximity is a quality of that [proximate object]—is refuted.

Some maintain that the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) applies only to *rūpa* and so forth; others hold that it is "non-eternal" (*anitya*). Still others argue that the prohibition applies only to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) as implied by the quality itself; furthermore, they claim that the present time near [the past or future] is not the possessor of the quality, but rather the past and future are. The use of the suffix *-vat* is for the sake of establishing the systematic arrangement beginning with the base (*prakṛti*); otherwise, since a particular suffix is prescribed after a specific verbal root in the sense of the present, that suffix—due to the lack of specification of a distinction—might arise even after a different verbal root by virtue of this extended application (*atideśa*).

Because of the understanding of the meaning that "those suffixes which are prescribed after certain bases by means of a certain condition—in the form of the base itself or as expressed by an accompanying word (upapada)—occur after those very same bases in that very same condition, even when referring to the recent past or the future," it follows that the *śānan* suffix prescribed after the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj* occurs after those two roots alone, even in proximity to the present, and not after any other. Similarly, the suffix *iṣṇu* prescribed by the rule *alaṃkṛñ* etc. for an agent characterized by habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth, occurs only when that same kind of agent is the condition, and not otherwise, and so on.

Otherwise, there would be no contradiction with the extended application (*atideśa*) "as in the case of the present," because this [rule] has as its purpose the exclusion of deviation regarding time alone. For example: "When did you come?"—"I am coming" or "I have come. "When will you go?"—"I am going" or "I shall go. The mention of past and future time in the interrogative sentence serves to clarify that [present time] in the illustrative sentence; the word "this" (*ayam*) and so forth indicates the proximity to the present of the act of coming and so on, because it refers to [the person] as characterized by perspiration, the tightening of the belt, and other such factors invariably concomitant with the acts of going and coming.

[Objection: But surely only the *laṭ* [present tense] is cited here; in that case, the rule *bālaṭ* alone would be appropriate. [Response: No, because it is for the sake of forms such as *eṣo’smi pacan* ("here I am, cooking") and *eṣo’smi pacamānaḥ* ("here I am, cooking"). One should understand that the suffix *śānan* applies after the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj*, the suffix *cānaś* applies when expressing habitual action (*tācchīlya*), age, or ability, and the suffix *śatṛ* applies after roots such as *iṅ* and *dhāry*. This is because in the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*, what is prescribed for the present tense (*vartamāna*) is taken up. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of those substitutes prescribed by rules such as *laṭ sme* also being substituted. This [objection] has been refuted by showing that it can be accounted for through the imposition (*āropa*) [of the present tense onto other times].
**Āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca || 132 ||** [The suffixes of the past tense are used] in the sense of "expectation" (*āśaṃsā*), and they function like those of the past.

*Āśaṃsā* (expectation) is the desire for a desired object. Although it exists in its own nature as a present state, it is described as such because its object is yet to come; it is also the domain of *atideśa* (extended application). The meaning is that when there is expectation regarding an object, suffixes belonging to the future tense (*bhaviṣyat*) are applied to the verbal root expressing the action expected, just as they would be in the past or the present. For example: "If the god had rained, or if he is raining now"—this is an extended application based on the commonality of the past tense, not because of a general extension of the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes, according to the maxim: "When there is an extended application of a general rule, there is no extended application of specific ones. [Pāṇini 3.3.132] [Next Sūtra: "The suffix *lṛṭ* is used after a word expressing 'speed'. (3.3.133)

The inclusion of the word *vacana* (utterance) is for the purpose of excluding the mere form [of the word]. In the previously mentioned scope, the suffix *lṛṭ* is used. For example: "When it rains, we shall sow quickly, soon, or swiftly" (*vṛṣṭiścotkṣipram āśu vā yāsyati śīghraṃ vapsyāmaḥ*). This rule is commenced to express a sense other than hope (*āśaṃsā*). By setting aside the prohibition, the mention of *lṛṭ* is intended to apply even in the scope of *luṭ*. For example: "Tomorrow we shall sow quickly" (*śvaḥ śīghraṃ vapsyāmaḥ*). When there is an utterance expressing hope, the suffix *liṅ* is used. (Pāṇini 3.3.134)

When a word expressing hope (*āśaṃsā*) is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*), the conditional (*liṅ*) is employed for the future tense. This is an exception to the rule "as if it were past" (*bhūtavacca*). For example: *guruśced upeyāt, āśaṃse 'dhīyīya* ("If the teacher should come, I hope that I might study"); *āśaṃse kṣipram adhīyīya* ("I hope that I might study quickly").

[However, this does not apply] when there is continuity of action (*kriyāprabandha*) or proximity (*sāmīpya*) to the present time; in those cases, the conditional is not treated as if it were referring to the immediate past (*anadyatanavat*). Pāṇini 3.3.135.

The *laṅ* (imperfect) and *luṭ* (periphrastic future) are not used for actions that are continuous (*sātatya*) or proximate (*sāmīpya*), because the prescription of those two [tenses] pertains to non-contemporary time (*anadyatana*), and thus the prohibition also applies specifically to that same domain. For example: "He gave food as long as he lived" (*yāvajjīvam annam adāt*) or "he will give" (*dāsyati*). Proximity (*sāmīpya*) means non-intervention by a similar [action]. For instance: "On this full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) which has passed, he established the sacred fires (*agnīn ādadhīta*)"; or "on this new moon (*amāvāsyā*) which is coming, he will establish the fires" (*ādhāsyate*) and "he will sacrifice with Soma" (*yakṣyate*).
Even if there is intervention by another lunar day, there is no fault, because there is no intervention by another full moon or another new moon.

It might be argued: "Let the rule be formulated simply as *anadyatanavat* and so forth, because it is more concise (*lāghava*) with respect to the prohibition. This is not so. For if that were the case, it would result in the rule being an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion (*saṃkara*) between the spheres (*viṣaya*) of the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* tenses. Nor can the force of the suffix *-vat* prevent this; for even if the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* were enjoined by employing the words "past" (*bhūta*) and "future" (*bhaviṣyat*), since the state of being "seen" (*dṛṣṭatva*) exists in the non-immediate past (*anadyatana*), the application of those suffixes to times other than their own proper time would be unavoidable based on that alone. Furthermore, the word *vat* can be justified as having the sense of "being seen" (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

In the alternative interpretation (*yathānyāsa*), however, the inclusion of the suffix *vat* is for the purpose of prohibiting even those [tenses] specifically prescribed for the non-immediate past (*anadyatana*), as there is no other purpose. This is because the rule would have been established by the phrase "not the non-immediate past" (*nānadyatane*) alone. Therefore, this is a prohibition of those [tenses] prescribed by the following rules: "the *liṭ* for the remote past," "the *laṅ* for *ha* and *śaśvat*," "the *laṭ* when *mā* is used with *purā*," and "the *luṅ* when *mā* is used with *asme*. By prohibiting the suffixes of the non-immediate past, the original prescriptive rules themselves—having set aside their own scope of exceptions—prescribe their respective suffixes; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. [The suffix *lṛṭ* is used] in the future tense when expressing a limit, provided that the limit is in the subsequent direction (*avarasmin*). (Pāṇini 3.3.136)

The term *ārambha* (commencement) signifies the non-continuity of an action and the sense of proximity; by the force of the statement, it excludes those two [past and future], and when a limit (*maryādā*) is expressed in the future tense, it functions like the *anadyatana* (non-current-day) past in its preceding portion. For example: "Of this path that is to be traveled from Pāṭaliputra, in that part which is prior to Kauśāmbī, we shall drink barley-gruel.
And in the division of time, provided it does not concern days and nights. (Pāṇini 3.3.137)

The recurrence of the preceding [rule] is for the sake of the subsequent [sūtra]; the *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule) is for the purpose of what follows. In the expression *an-ahorātrāṇām*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of a general relationship. Therefore, whether it is a division of days and nights by another time, or of something else by days and nights, or of days and nights by days and nights—in all such cases there is a prohibition; this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa*. "Of this coming year, that which is prior to the Āgrahāyaṇī festival, during that [period] we shall study, being engaged [in it]. Why "not of days and nights"? (This is asked to provide an example where the prohibition does not apply.)

"This month which is to come—during its latter fifteen nights we shall study. In this case, the division [of the month] is indeed by means of the delimitation through the first fifteen nights of the month.
"In the case of another [word], there is an option" (Pāṇini 2.3.138).

The two preceding sūtras are carried over (anuvṛtti), but not the word *na tv avare*. This is because of the inclusion of the qualified term (*viśeṣya*) "in the subsequent" (*parasmin*). This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) for that which has not [otherwise] been established. "In this coming year, during that which follows the Āgrahāyaṇī festival, we shall study," or "we will study. Now, one might object: "Would this rule not also apply when there is a division of space? No, it would not.

In the rule *bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane’varasmin*, although it could have been formulated as a single rule stating "in the future, when there is a statement of a limit, provided that [the period] is not less than a day and night," the fact that it is formulated as two separate rules indicates that the subsequent rule (*parasmin*) teaches a connection with the mere division of time. Consequently, in the sentence "On that part of the road which is beyond Kauśāmbī—[the road] that must be traversed as far as Pāṭaliputra—we shall drink barley-meal there," the suffix *luṭ* (future) is used. Now, regarding *liṅ nimittē lṛṅ kriyātipattau* (Pāṇini 3.3.139): "The conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used when the cause for the application of the optative (*liṅ*) exists, provided there is a failure of the action."

The cause (*nimitta*) of the conditional suffix (*liṅ*) consists of the relation between cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) and so forth, wherein the conditional (*lṛṅ*) occurs when the non-actualization of an action is implied. Here, the meaning of the conditional (*lṛṅ*) comprises futurity, the relation of cause and effect, and "over-extension" (*atipatti*). Over-extension refers to the attribution of an action to a place or time other than that in which it actually occurs. Among these, futurity connects with the effort (*kṛti*) in cases where the verbal suffix denotes effort, and with the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) in cases where the suffix denotes the locus (*āśrayatva*).

In the case of an action, the relation of cause and effect (hetu-hetumad-bhāva) is related as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), while the meaning of the nominative case ending is related as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatayā*). For instance, in the sentence "If I had lived for a thousand years, then I would have fathered a hundred sons," the meaning of the word *yadi* consists of an unspecified particular time connected with the action. Furthermore, the meaning of the accusative case is "absolute connection" (*atyanta-saṃyoga*), through a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*) based on its pervasiveness.

And thus, the cognition is as follows: "I am the qualificand of a particular probability whose mode is a life-span pervading a thousand future years, occurring at a specifically determined time; [and] I am the qualificand of a particular probability whose mode is an activity conducive to the production of a hundred future sons as its object at that time. In this context, some hold that when there is a state of contradiction regarding one's own living for a thousand years, that very possibility (*prasakti*) is what constitutes probability (*sambhāvanā*); whereas in the absence of such contradiction, it is merely doubt (*saṃśaya*).

Others, however, maintain that even when there is certainty regarding the fitness [of the conditions] in that case, the verbal cognition is "induced" (*āhārya*). The resulting awareness is: "I am one who possesses a life of a thousand years, which will occur at some unspecified time in the future and serves as the cause [for the following]; and I possess an activity conducive to the production of a hundred sons, which will be the effect at that same time. Alternatively, in such a situation, once the mere presentation of the word-meanings has occurred, by the force of that, upon the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, there arises a purely mental awareness consisting of doubt—just like the ancient view regarding whether sound is eternal or non-eternal.

However, they say that the intention of the sutra is that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is ungrammatical in such a case of transgression. Others, however, say: "My lack of producing a hundred sons is caused by my lack of living for a thousand years in the future."

Now, one might ask: if it is said, "If he had obtained meat, then he would have eaten," since the act of eating could still be accomplished by another means even when the means such as meat are absent, how can the *lṛṅ* (the conditional) be applied here? Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "Because there is a difference in actions due to the difference in instruments, when meat is absent, there is indeed the non-occurrence of the specific action of eating meat. By the natural force of this statement, the meaning of the word *cet* ("if") is the absence [of the condition]; in that context, its connection with the future tense and the meaning of the verbal root associated with *cet* serve as qualifiers.

And the absence [of eating meat] is construed with another action as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) within the absence related to the future time by way of the relation of being brought about (*prayuktatva*). This is because it is accepted that the state of being related to the future time—which is the meaning of the *lṛṅ* suffix—expressed by another verbal root is again construed with the positive entity (*bhāva*). Thus, the understanding is: "The act of eating meat is the counter-positive of an absence brought about by that absence of the act of eating meat which is related to the future time. The same should be inferred in other cases as well. [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.178: *bhītrā*... || 140 ||
The first sūtra applies universally. Examples will be given starting from "uta-āpyoḥ samarthayoḥ" up until the statement regarding optionality; prior to that, it is optional.
[Pāṇini 3.3.141] "votāpyoḥ" (or after *uta* and *āpi*).

The analysis of the compound is *ota-apyoḥ*. In that regard, there is a compound (*samāsa*) of *uta* and *api*, namely *utāpyoḥ*. By imitating the form ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*), it is compounded with *āṅ*; because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the case-suffix is elided (*luk*). It should be understood that the rule "after *uta* and *api*, when they are semantically connected, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is used instead of the optative (*liṅ*) when the cause for the optative has already occurred" applies prior to this point. Here, *āṅ* signifies a limit (*maryādā*); since the rule "the present tense (*laṭ*) is used after *api* and *jātu* when expressing reproach" prescribes the present tense, the cause for the optative is absent.

The rule for the optative (*liṅ*) beginning from *vibhāṣā kathaṃ* and extending up to, but not including, *utāpyoḥ samarthayoḥ*, results in the following practical meaning: in those cases, the optative is optional when referring to the past, but it is mandatory when referring to the future. [Pāṇini 3.3.142:
In the Gāthā meter, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used with *api* and *jātu*.

When used in conjunction with these two [words], the present tense (*laṭ*) is employed for all three times to express censure (*garhā*). This rule supersedes the rules for the aorist (*luṅ*) and other tenses because it is of higher priority. "Even though you abandon your wife, you take up a courtesan—this is censurable. The word "censurable" (*garhita*) is included for the sake of clarifying the intended meaning, according to Kaiyaṭa’s statement: "The sense of the verbal root is qualified by censure and so forth. Also: "Optionally [the present tense is used] after 'katham' and the optative (*liṅ*). (Pāṇini 3.3.143)

In the sense of reproach (*garhā*), the potential (*liṅ*) and the present indicative (*laṭ*) are used for all three times. For example: *kathaṃ dharmaṃ tyajeḥ* (How could you abandon dharma? or *tyajasi* (You [dare to] abandon it). Because the potential is optional, in its alternative form, the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) of all three times may be used: *kathaṃ nāmātrabhavān dharmam atyakṣyat* (How indeed could your honor have abandoned dharma?). Furthermore, after a word expressing a completed action (*vṛtta*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) and the future (*lṛṭ*) are used. (144)

The option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding censure (*garhā*) does not carry over [to this rule]. Who, which of two, or which of many would censure Hari? Or will censure him? The conditional (*lṛṅ*) is as before.
[The conditional is also used] even when no interrogative pronoun is present, in the sense of "impossibility" (*anaklṛpti*) and "impatience" (*amarṣa*). (Pāṇini 3.3.145)

The phrase "in the sense of censure" (*garhāyām*) is excluded [from this rule]. "Impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) means non-occurrence; "impatience" (*amārṣa*) means intolerance. These two [terms] follow [the previous rules] up until the point where "and in the sense of censure" (*garhāyāṃ ca*) occurs. One does not consider it possible, or one does not tolerate it, that "you should censure Hari," or "you will censure him. The forms *kaḥ* and *kataraḥ*, etc., are as explained previously. It should be understood that although this *lṛṭ* (the conditional suffix) is prescribed for all three times, because it is not prescribed by the specific marker *ī* (which denotes the future), the substitution of *s* for *lṛṭ* (as per Pāṇini 3.3.14) does not take place even when there is a connection with a future meaning. In the sense of "what indeed" (*kiṃ kila*) and in the sense of existence (*asti*), the *lṛṭ* [is used]. (146)

This is a collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*) having the sense of anger. The roots *as*, *bhū*, and *vid* have the sense of existence (*astyartha*). Both [the particle *kila* and the verbal forms] are optionally the attendant word (*upapada*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the optative (*liṅ*). [Examples: "I do not believe it" or "I cannot endure it": *kiṃ kila tvaṃ śūdrānnaṃ bhokṣyase?* ("How can you possibly eat the food of a Śūdra?"); *asti*, *bhavati*, or *vidyate śūdrīṃ gamiṣyasi?* ("Is it possible that you will go to a Śūdra woman?"). **Pāṇini 3.3.147:** *jātuyadorliṅ* (The optative suffix *liṅ* is used after the particles *jātu* and *yad* when expressing a possibility).

Regarding the rule "yadai yadyor upasaṃkhyānam" (an addition concerning *yadā* and *yadi*), it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *lṛṭ* suffix. [Examples: *jātu*, *yat*, *yadā*, or *padi*: "If one like you were to revile Hari, I would not tolerate it; I would not endure it."
And [the suffix *yat* is used] after the words *yad* and *tad*. || 148 ||
And whatever you might do, or wherever [you might do it], in such a manner, I do not believe it; I do not tolerate it. The division of the rule is for the sake of what follows:
"Also in the sense of reproach" (garhāyām). 149.

It should be stated that [the suffix *liṅ* is used] in the sense of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) and "impatience" (*amarṣa*). And when used with *yat* and *yatra*, only *liṅ* should occur: "That you, O Śūdra, should sacrifice for [someone], or that you should sacrifice for someone—this is improper.
Also [it is used] in the sense of "wonder" (*citrīkaraṇa*). (Pāṇini 3.3.150)

That you should officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra, or that you should do so anywhere—this is a marvel! [The suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verb expressing censure, with the augment *yaṭ* and the like. 151.

When *yat* or *ca* are used as upapadas (governing words), the *lṛṭ* (future tense suffix) is employed when wonder (*āścarya*) is to be understood. Example: *āścaryam andho nāma kṛṣṇaṃ drakṣyati* ("It is a wonder that a blind man should see Kṛṣṇa"). Why "not beginning with *yat*" (*ayadau*)? Consider: *āścaryaṃ yadi sa bhuñjīta*. Here, since the word *yadi* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvana*), the intention is understood as referring to possibility; thus, according to the Bhāṣya, the *liṅ* (optative suffix) is used by this very rule [Pāṇini 3.3.155]. When *uta* and *api* are synonymous (i.e., both expressing possibility), the *liṅ* is used. (Pāṇini 3.3.152)

The two [particles] *uta* and *api* have the same meaning in the sense of "certainly" (*bāḍham*). For example: *uta api vā hanyād aghaṃ hariḥ* ("Hari will certainly destroy sin"). Why [is this said] regarding these two capable [of expressing certainty]? [Counter-example: *uta daṇḍaḥ patiṣyati* ("Will the staff fall? and *apidhāsyati dvāram* ("Will he close the door?"). Here, the meanings are "question" and "covering," respectively. From this point onward, when there is a reason for the conditional (*liṅ*) and there is a non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*), the conditional suffix (*lṛṅ*) is used invariably even for the past tense.
[The rule continues: "In the expression of a wish, except when *akaccit* is used. (Pāṇini 3.3.153)

The optative (*liṅ*) is used after the word *kaccit* when one’s own desire (*svecchā*) is being expressed. For example: *kaccid bhavān bhuñjīta* ("I hope you will eat"). The meaning is: "Your act of eating is the object of my desire. Why say "after *kaccit*" (*akacciti*)? Consider: *kaccij jīvati* ("I wonder if he lives"). Here, the word *kaccit* signifies a question (*praśna*). Thus, the meaning is: "Living is the object of my desire and the object of my inquiry. *Sūtra 154*: When expressing possibility (*sambhāvanā*), if the word *alam* is used and the verb is not in the completed (past) form (*asiddha-prayoga*).

In this context, "alamartha" means proficiency or capability. When a probability (*sambhāvanā*) characterized by that [proficiency] is to be understood, the suffix *lṛṭ* (the future tense marker) is used after the word *alam*, provided that the word *alam* is not used in its established form (*siddhaprayoga*). This meaning is indicated by a change in case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*). That which is understood even in the absence of the use of [the word *alam*] is called *siddhaprayoga*. Example: *api giriṃ śirasā bhindyāt* ("He might even split a mountain with his head"). Why say "provided it is not used in its established form"? Consider: *alaṃ kṛṣṇo hastinaṃ haniṣyati* ("Kṛṣṇa is capable of killing the elephant"). *Vibhāṣā dhātau sambhāvanavacane 'yadi* (Pāṇini 3.3.155): [The suffix *lṛṭ* is optionally used] when expressing a probability (*sambhāvana*), provided the word *yadi* is not present, and when the verbal root itself expresses that probability.

The suffix *liṅ* is optionally used when a verbal root expressing "possibility" (*sambhāvana*) is the attendant word (*upapada*), but not when it is joined with *yat*. This rule is commenced for the sake of providing an alternative option. Example: *sambhāvayāmi bhuñjīta bhavān bhokṣyate vā* ("I think it possible that you might eat, or you will eat"). Why say "not when joined with *yat*"? Example: *sambhāvayāmi yad bhuñjīthās tvam* ("I think it possible that you would eat").
*Liṅ* is used [after a word] expressing cause and effect (*hetu-hetumat*). (Pāṇini 3.3.156)

There may be an alternative explanation (*vibhāṣā*): if one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, one would attain happiness; if one will bow to Kṛṣṇa, one will attain happiness. This [usage] is desired only for the future tense. It does not apply here: "He flees because he strikes. Here, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the substitution of *śatṛ* (the present participle suffix) by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ* does not occur. Accordingly, the Vārttika states:
"In the case of the rule *devatrāto garo grāhaḥ*, the prescription of *sat* (the present participle) does not optionally alternate with other forms; thus we have *gavākṣaḥ* and *śaṃsitavrataḥ*."

The meaning is that among these, the absence of *natva* and *latva*, the absence of the substitute *ṇa* for *sad*, and *avaṅ* with its subsequent *itva* always apply, because they are understood through the principle of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionality). Now, one might ask: since it is established in the Bhāṣya that an action expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) can only be construed as a means (*sādhana*) toward another action, how can there be a mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) between those two [the finite verb and the nominal] here?

On this point, some say: the intention of the Bhāṣya is that syntactic connection consists in the form of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), because a specific co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) serves as the regulator. And here, through the co-utterance with words such as *yat*, there arises an expectancy for another action on the part of the [first] action; however, this is not the case in expressions such as "one should bow to Kṛṣṇa," and therefore they claim there is no fault.

Regarding the mixed [type of injunction], in the passage "He who threatens a Brāhmaṇa should be punished with a hundred [blows]," it is understood—by virtue of the grammatical rule *liṅ* denoting cause and effect—that one who possesses the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the attempt to kill a Brāhmaṇa will possess the subsequent state of undergoing a hundred punishments. Here, "being a cause" (*hetutve*) means being a prior factor (*pūrvavartitve*), and "being the effect" (*hetumattve*) means being a subsequent factor (*uttaravartitve*), according to the rule for the *liṅ* suffix. Furthermore, they say that the restriction (consisting of conjunction and priority) is obtained through the force of the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*).

Others, however, say that there is no fault even regarding the restrictive portion (*niyamāṃśa*) when [the action] is capable [of occurring], because the essential purport of the root [sūtra] is that "a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority is understood. Thus, in this case as well, the action of obtaining happiness occurring subsequently—qualified by the action of bowing to Kṛṣṇa which occurs previously in a fixed manner through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—is construed precisely with the two actions qualified by the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) through coreferentiality, and not as a means (*sādhanatva*). Therefore, they maintain, there is no fault; such is the view following the essential purport of Kaiyaṭa.
*Liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used] after verbs having the sense of desire (*icchārtha*). (Pāṇini 3.3.157)
The kṛtya suffixes are also used in the senses of command (praiṣa), permission (atisarga), and the arrival of the proper time (prāptakāla). || 158 ||

*Praiṣa* (command) is the instigation toward an object already within reach; *atisarga* (permission) is the authorization for acting according to one's own will. However, in cases such as "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), because [the action] has not yet been reached, the suffix refers solely to the qualificand. [In examples like] "You must sacrifice" (*bhavatā yaṣṭavyam*) or "May you sacrifice" (*bhavān yajatām*), the particle *ca* serves to prevent the sublation of the *loṭ* (imperative) in the sense of "proper time," thereby ensuring its absence.
Furthermore, the *liṅ* (optative) occurs in the sense of "immediate futurity" (*ūrdhvamauhūrtika*). (Pāṇini 3.3.159)

When *praiṣa* (commands) and the like are to be understood, the optative (*liṅ*), the gerundive (*kṛtya*), and the periphrastic future (*ṇyad*) are used: *ūrdhvaṃ muhūrtād yajeta*, *yajatām*, *tvayā yaṣṭavyam*. [When the particle] *sma* [is used], the imperative (*loṭ*) is employed. (160)

When the word *sma* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*), the *loṭ* (imperative) is employed in the same scope as previously mentioned. For example: *ūrdhvam muhūrtād yajataṃ sma*. This is an exception to the rules for the *liṅ* (optative) and the *kṛtya* suffixes.
Furthermore, [the *loṭ* is used] in the sense of *adhīṣṭa* (requesting or honoring). 161.
In this context, when the sense is implied and *sma* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*), the imperative (*loṭ*) is employed: "You [should] teach, indeed" (*tvaṃ smādhyāpaya*).
[The suffixes] *tumun*, *ktvā*, and *ṇamul* are used after verbal roots to express time (*kāla*), occasion (*samaya*), and juncture (*velā*). (Pāṇini 3.3.167–168)
It is time to eat; it is the proper moment or the occasion—if [the word] *liṅ* is used. 163.

The suffix *liṅ* (optative) is used when the word *yat* or words such as *kāla* (time) etc. function as *upapadas* (governing words). For example: *kālo yadbhuñjīta bhavān* ("It is time that you eat"). Here, two types of *upapadas* should be understood: the word *yad* and any one of the group beginning with *kāla*. [Pāṇini 3.3.169] "The *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* are also used in the sense of fitness (*arha*)."

When that [suffix] is joined [to a root], and the agent is to be understood, the *liṅ* (optative), as well as the *kṛtya* suffixes and the *tṛc*, may occur. For example: *tvaṃ kanyāṃ vaheḥ* ("you should carry the maiden"). The meaning is "you are fit to carry. *Kreyaṃ* means "fit for purchase. *Stutimarhaḥ stotā* means "one who is worthy of praise is a praiser. The *kṛtya* and *tṛc* suffixes are prescribed so that there might not be sublation by the *liṅ*.
[The suffix] *ṇini* occurs in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) and debt (*adhamarṇya*). (Pāṇini 3.3.165)
"one who will go to the village" (grāmaṃ gamī); "one who owes a hundred" (śatam ṛṇaṃ dāyī). By the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*, the prohibition of the sixth case [genitive] applies.
And [the same applies to] kṛtya suffixes. (Pāṇini 2.3.70)
These [suffixes] would apply to the two meanings already stated. The separation of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows:
"The optative (liṅ) and [the suffixes mentioned above] also [occur] after the root √śak. (Pāṇini 3.3.172).

The *liṅ* and the *kṛtya* suffixes are used in the sense of capability (*śakti*). Example: *tvaṃ bhāraṃ vaheḥ*. The meaning is "you are capable of carrying the burden. [Examples of *kṛtyas* are: *voḍhuṃ śakyaḥ*, *voḍhavyaḥ*, *vahanīyaḥ*, or *vāhyaḥ*. The mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes here is so that the application of the *liṅ* might not be precluded. Nor can this be established by the rule of optional forms (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*), because it is taught that after the section on feminine endings (*stryadhikāra*), the rule of optional forms does not apply. Although that [rule] could have been made known even by the phrase *kṛtyāśca* in the sūtra *praiṣe ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.163), nevertheless, it can be made known here by the mere presence of the word *ca* ("and").

However, in that context, they say that because of the complexity [involved] in both the mention of *kṛtya* and the mention of *kṛtya-tṛc*, it is more appropriate for this very [sūtra] to serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The purposes of the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) are now stated. In the case of *chātrasya hasitam* or *hasanam*, the suffix *ghañ* is not used for the neuter gender in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), because that falls within the scope of the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. In the expression *icchati bhoktum*, the imperative (*loṭ*) is not used to express a wish (*āśis*), because the optative (*liṅ*) is specifically prescribed by the rule *liṅ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.161). In the case of *īṣatpāna*, the suffix *khal* is not used where *yuC* would otherwise apply; this is the summary. It should be stated [as a definition]: "In the expression of a desire" (*kāmapravedane*). This does not apply here in *icchan karoti*, which is the communication of one's own inclination (*svavṛttīcchāyā jñāpanam*). Here, however, the desire is the cause of the action (*kṛtihetu*), whereas in the other case it is the inclination of another.

And thus, the meaning is that the term *liṅ* refers to the intention (*tātparya*) of the word *icchā* (desire) when it is intended by the speaker who utters the *liṅ*. Now, an objection: if this were so, the rule *akaccit-kāmapravedane* would be redundant; for its purpose is to cover cases where the expression of desire is understood even through the context of the matter (*arthaprakaraṇa*) and so forth. Furthermore, even if this were the case, the rule would still not be redundant, because it serves as the meaning of the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix. The *liṅ* is mentioned here so that there might be no sublation (*bādha*) of the *liṅ* by the *loṭ*, which is prescribed for a specific [limited] scope. Nor can the point be settled by the rule *loṭ ca* alone; for if *liṅ* were merely drawn back (*anukarṣa*) by the particle *ca*, then the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) connected with it would also necessarily follow.

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that the meaningfulness of that sūtra according to the aforementioned method is devoid of logical justification. Therefore, they say that by this sūtra, the optative suffix (liṅ) is prescribed for the sense of "desire" itself, and not in connection with a verbal root meaning "desire. Consequently, in such cases as "If the Soma sacrifice were to have the Rathantara-sāman, one should take the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu," the meaning is "one should desire to take [them].
And [this applies to] the optative suffix (liṅ). || 168 ||

When verbs expressing desire (*icchārtha*) having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*) are used as *upapadas*, the suffix *liṅ* is employed. For example: *bhuñjīyetīcchati* ("he desires that he should eat"). Since the suffix *tumun* will be taught for [verbs] having the same agent, one might argue that just as *tumun* sets aside the *loṭ* obtained by the preceding rule, it would likewise set aside *liṅ*; therefore, this rule is commenced for the sake of *liṅ*. Furthermore, the principle of *vāsarūpa* does not apply here, because that principle is prohibited in the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and words having the sense of *khal*. [Now, regarding the next sūtra: "After roots meaning 'to desire,' there is optionally [the use of *liṅ*] when the present tense is intended. (Pāṇini 3.3.160).

In the sense of possibility (*pakṣe*), the *laṭ* [present tense] is used: *icchet* (he might wish) or *icchati* (he wishes); *kāmayeta* (he might desire) or *kāmayate* (he desires). By this, the verse from the *Naiṣadha*: "I desire the seizing of the hand of Damayantī, O moon of the earth" (*pāṇipīḍanam ahaṃ damayantyāḥ kāmaye mahimahīmihikāṃśo*) is explained. The *liṅ* [optative mood] is used in the senses of injunction, invitation, permission, request, inquiry, and entreaty. (Pāṇini 3.3.161)

In the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), [the form is] "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. In the case of an invitation (*nimantraṇa*), [it is] "May you eat here. That which prompts a grandson or others to perform a necessary rite such as a *śrāddha* meal is that [invitation]; and by its transgression, there is sin for the one who was invited. An entreaty (*āmantraṇa*) is permission to act according to one's own will; it is that in the non-performance of which there is no sin. It amounts to a desire that indicates the absence of any prohibition, as in "May you sit here. Its purport lies merely in the exclusion of what is not desired by oneself. A request (*adhīṣṭa*) is a desire directed toward a listener that indicates honor and respect.

"You should teach your son. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that although the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*) is already present within these [other categories], they are mentioned separately for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). Haradatta likewise states:

"Whether for the purpose of establishing the underlying logic (*nyāya*), or even for the sake of detailed exposition, the four beginning with the injunction (*vidhi*) have been set forth at the outset."
The nature of continuous progression is woven through all four as well.

In that very case, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) should be prescribed; what is the point of intending a distinction [between the meanings]? An inquiry that motivates expression is a "question" (*praśna*): "O sir, shall I study the Veda, or rather logic? A desire for gain is a "request" (*prārthanā*): "May I obtain food. In this regard, one view is that meanings such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth are to be indicated (*dyotya*). Otherwise, since the agent and other factors are not already established [by other means], if injunctions and the like were specified [as denoted meanings], there would be the consequence of their sublation. Furthermore, this would lead to the non-expression of the agent, and consequently, the impossibility of the dual and plural numbers, because duality and the rest [as the referents of those numbers] would only be connected with either the agent or the object, and not with both.
Furthermore, because [the denotation of] the agent and so forth would otherwise be untenable.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that these [agents and so forth] are indeed denotable, as there is no contradiction with the injunctive suffixes and the like. In the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), because the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is used for the sake of including all [tenses and moods], or because both [the agent and the object] are accommodated, the agent and others are not sublated. Thus, the use of dual and plural endings based on the duality and plurality residing in the agent and the object is justified. Moreover, since specific meanings such as "present time" and so forth exist in all instances of the *laṭ* suffix and others, it would follow that those [specific meanings] would sublate the meaning of the agent and so forth; consequently, the agent and others would have no scope at all. This is the path established by the authoritative sources (ākara).
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the third [chapter].
Thus ends the third quarter (pāda).
In the fourth quarter of the third chapter, the first daily lesson begins.
Now begins the fourth quarter.
Suffixes [are applied] when there is a relationship between verbal roots (dhātu). || 1 ||

Although singularity is the default rule regarding the occurrence [of a word] here, duality is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), because a relation is necessarily restricted by the difference between its relata. "Connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandha*) means a connection whose relatum is a verbal root. And the term "verbal root" refers to its meaning, since a relation characterized by the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) is possible therein. This is because the verbal root is utilized solely for the presentation of its own meaning, and thus does not connect with the sentence-meaning; furthermore, even in the view that the meaning is manifested as presented by the word, it is the root's own meaning alone that serves as the qualifier.

Because they cannot function as qualifiers for one another. Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of the suffix *san* (desiderative), there is a qualifier-relationship mediated by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*)—namely, through the objecthood (*karmatva*) and the common agenthood (*samānakartṛkatva*)—so too here there may be a relationship mediated by the meaning of the root. For, based on the logical necessity (*arthāpatti*) that suffixes occur when multiple roots are used whose meanings are mutually connected, forms such as *gomān āsīt* ("the cow-owner existed") would be unestablished; this is because the verb *as* ("to be") is not employed in the present tense here, and a relationship is untenable with respect to that which is not being employed.

And thus, this sūtra is intended to authorize the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of suffixes prescribed for one time even when used at another time, in relation to the connection between the meanings of two verbal roots (*dhātvartha*). The meaning of the sentence is: where suffixes are prescribed for a particular time in connection with the meaning of a root, they may also occur at a time different from that. The base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), and the governing word (*upapada*) remain exactly as they are; however, there is a discrepancy only regarding the time, and therefore no confusion arises. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*), because in rules such as *vartamānasāmīpye* ("in proximity to the present"), it is precisely the deviation of time that is to be expressed.

While residing, he saw a *laṭ* suffix [indicating the present tense] in the sense of "he will be. The meaning is: "He will be the son of one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice"; "will be" [indicates] the *ṇini* suffix. The sense is that the arising (birth) of the son—who is about to perform the Soma sacrifice—is the counter-positive of a present non-existence whose agent is that [son]. Even though the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is already understood from the previous rule, the explicit mention of the suffix here is for the purpose of including suffixes prescribed after other bases (*prakṛti*). Consequently, in examples such as *gomān āsīt* ("he was possessed of cows"), even though the time of the base-meaning associated with the referent of the *matup* suffix—which denotes a state qualified by present existence—is past or future, the form remains grammatically correct (*sādhutva*).

Now, since there would be the consequence of non-connection (*ananvaya*) due to the two actions—standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified—being obstructed by contradictory times, this [present discussion] is commenced for the sake of resolving that. And that [resolution] must be established through the reversal of time in one of the two. If it is asked: "Since it is also possible through the reversal of time in the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), what is the restrictive factor for the sublation of the time belonging to the nominal stem (*suvaṃta*)?"

On this point, they say: since the action expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the time associated with the meaning of the stem and suffix—which expresses a subordinate action—is sublated in view of that [primary] sublation. This is because it is improper for the principal to conform to the subordinate; according to the maxim, "In the case of a subordinate, an improper assumption is permissible. One might object: "How can this rule apply to the Naiyāyikas, who maintain that the cognition has the meaning of the nominative (*prathamānta*) as its primary qualificand, given that both actions are equally qualifiers? Do not say so.

Even though that [the son] is primary according to the verbal testimony, its status as the primary object is justified because the birth of a son qualified by the performance of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is what is enjoined. Nor should it be argued that because it is a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi), the qualifier itself must also be an enjoined object; for since the injunction regarding the qualifier is merely postulated through the necessity of otherwise accounting for the qualified injunction, the status of being the primary object belongs to the verb "bhavet" (should become) alone, as it is that which the other depends upon.

Now, one might object: "In verbal syntactic connection (*śābdānvaya*), it is the word itself that determines predominance; thus, because the connection between the meanings of two non-nominative terms is more 'internal' (*antaraṅga*), the connection of the word *bhavituḥ* (of the one who will be) would occur with the son qualified by having performed the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Consequently, rather than subverting the time [of the action] which is first presented, there would simply be a subversion of the time of *bhavituḥ*. If this is argued, we say: No.

For here, the temporal restriction [of the injunction] is due to the fact that the cognition—namely, that the son, who is qualified by an activity conducive to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, possesses an origination that is the counter-positive of a presently existing prior non-existence—is sublated. Indeed, the cognition that "this son has a past origination" or "he possesses a past enjoined activity" is sublated; whereas the cognition that "his son will exist as one possessing a future activity conducive to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice" is not sublated. This alone is the decisive factor (vinigamaka), and such is the general direction of the argument.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, maintain that the action which serves as the qualificand (viśeṣya) reaches its completion at its own time, whereas the action which serves as the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) is employed by way of a mere indicator (upalakṣaṇa). Thus, there is a designation of both future and past states. Consequently, at the stage of word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*), when the word *viji* has been derived by the suffix *ṇini* as "one who has conquered" (*bhūta*), it acquires the sense of another time (*kālāntara*) upon being uttered in proximity with the word *bhavitā* ("he will conquer"). Therefore, the cognition of another time is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). And since that [extrinsic cognition] is incapable of subverting the intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) formation of the word, this sūtra need not have been commenced.

Furthermore, it must necessarily be accepted that the rule for the conditional suffix (*pratyaya*) applies only at its own proper time. They say that in the expression *bhāvikṛtyamāsīt* ("the future action was [past]"), if the word *bhāvi* were to denote the past time, then because the words *bhāvi* and *āsīt* would be synonyms, their simultaneous usage would be untenable.

[The sūtra: "In the case of the repetition of an action, the imperative (*loṭ*) is used; for the imperative, the substitutes *hi* and *sva* are used optionally in place of *ta* and *dhvam*. (Pāṇini 3.4.2)

*Kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition) consists of frequency (*paunaḥpunya*) and intensity (*bhṛśārtha*). And this qualifies the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), not the *upapada*, because [if it were the latter] it would not apply to simple roots. Here, two alternatives are possible: that the substitutes *hi* and *sva* are substitutes for *tiṅ*-affixes, or that they are substitutes for *lakāra* (the general term for verbal suffixes). Now, since the mention of the original element (*sthānin*) in the rule *loṭaḥ* is explicit, the doubt regarding the first alternative might seem untenable; however, that is not so, because even as substitutes for *svādi* (the *ātmanepada* endings), that [the application of the rule] is possible. Regarding the first alternative, the justification is as follows:

Since *hi* and *sva* would also override the *tiṅ*s prescribed by general rules—just as *śatṛ* and *śānac* do—it must be understood here that the substitutes for *tiṅ* are indicated by virtue of their being the original bases (*sthānin*). This has been stated: "The mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* in the rules for *hi* and *sva* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] *lādeśa* [rules]. For if they were *lādeśas*, the designation *pada* would not apply, because they would lack the status of being *tiṅ*-final. However, if *la* is designated as a *kṛt* suffix, then by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), *hi* and *sva* would also possess the nature of a *kṛt*. Consequently, by virtue of ending in such a [suffix], they would receive the designation *prātipadika*, and through the subsequent production of case-endings (*sub*), they would indeed be designated as *pada* precisely because they are *sub*-final. Furthermore, there is no possibility of hearing [the suffix *la*] itself, because it is elided.

It is postulated that because these two *hi* suffixes resemble short vowels (*hrasva*) which bear the designation of case-endings (*vibhakti*), they function as indeclinables (*avyaya*), thereby allowing for the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*). Nevertheless, in such cases as *sa bhāvan lunīhi lunīhītyevaṃ pralunāti*, the rule of suppression (*nighāta*)—stated as *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*—would not apply. Furthermore, the restriction that *hi* occurs only after roots ending in *parasmaipada* (active voice) and *sva* only after roots ending in *ātmanepada* (middle voice) would also fail. This is because, if they were substitutes for *l* (*lādeśatva*), both would possess the designation of *parasmaipada* by the rule *laḥ parasmaipadam*, and consequently, both would necessarily follow only *parasmaipada* roots.

For this very reason, the supplementary statement "and [the substitutes] ta and dhvam" is consistent. For if the substitution of *hi* and *sva* were prescribed for the *lakāra* itself, then since the forms *ta* and *dhvam* do not occur as substitutes for the *loṭ* suffix, their mention as substituends would be untenable. This being the case—

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that *hi* and *sva* are indeed substitutes for *la*. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the substitute *hi* for *tip*, *sip*, and *mip* would, by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, be considered *pit* (bearing the *p*-marker), it would lack the status of *ṅit* (bearing the *ṅ*-marker). Consequently, in forms such as *lumīhi* and *lunīhi*, the substitution of *i* (the *it* augment) would not occur; and in *brūhi* and *brūhi*, the augment *iṭ* would [undesirably] apply. Furthermore, in *bhuṅkṣva* and *bhuṅkṣva*, since the rule *āḍuttamasya piñca* (Pāṇini 3.4.92) applies later, the augment *āṭ* would intervene; thus, due to the absence of the *ṅit* status, the elision of the vowel *a* prescribed by *śnasorallopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111) would not take place.

In the case of the second instance of the word *lunīhi*, although it is desired that its subsequent *amreḍita* (repeated) form be unaccented (*anudātta*) according to the rule "tasya paramāmreḍitam anudāttam ca," the first *hi* would also have to be unaccented because it is marked with the *p*-diacritic (*pit*). Furthermore, in the form *tṛṇḍhi*, there would have to be the substitution of *tṛṇaha*. Moreover, since the substitute is prescribed generally in place of a *tiṅ* suffix, and due to the absence of a specific restriction regarding the locus of the substitute, both [the *hi* and *sva*] would have to be substitutes for two words, resulting in two-word substitutions. However, this fault does not apply even in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because by this rule, the *hi* and *sva* are prescribed as being similar to those *hi* and *sva* which are actual substitutes for the imperative (*loṭ*) suffixes.

Therefore, *hi* is prescribed after roots that take the *parasmaipada* endings in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), while *sva* is prescribed after those that take the *ātmanepada* endings in the senses of the action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*). This distinction is established because the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) for the personal endings (*tiṅ*) is also logically consistent [only under this interpretation]. However, the technical designations "person" (*puruṣa*) and "number" (*vacana*) do not apply here, because the prescription of *hi* and *sva* would otherwise be rendered purposeless; for those two [designations] are already established by other rules. Nor does this contradict the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) "of *ta*, *dhvam*, etc.," as that refers to a different context.

This is because the locative case here denotes the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), as that [meaning] is established by it. For the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is indicated by the words *tad* and *dhvam* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in such a way that those two suffixes are possible with respect to that specific object. Since the word *loṭ* occurs at the beginning of the passage, it is not contradicted [by anything else]; therefore, it is more appropriate to assume secondary indication for the remainder of the sentence in relation to it.

This is the meaning: when the aforementioned sense is to be conveyed, the *loṭ* suffix is applied to the verbal root (*dhātu*). And for that [suffix], *hi* and *sva* occur in place of both person and number. The restriction regarding the meanings of the base and the suffix has already been stated. Examples are now given: *lunīhi lunīhītyevāyaṃ lunāti* ("He cuts repeatedly, as if saying 'cut, cut!'"). Or: *lunīhi* or *lunāmi*. In this same way, examples should be cited for other numbers and other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). As for the doubling [of the word], it occurs because of the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre* (in the case of the repetition of an action). Nor should it be argued that doubling is impossible because the action has already been expressed by the root alone—otherwise, it would also occur in the case of the *yaṅ* intensive suffix.

Because the *lakāra* suffix is prescribed here only for the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, and because it conveys that meaning only when accompanied by reduplication; whereas in the case of the *yaṅ*-affix, since the repetition of the pure action (*śuddhakriyāsamabhihāra*) is already indicated by the *yaṅ* itself, there is no such [requirement for reduplication]. However, as stated previously, when there is a desire to express the repetition of the action denoted by the *yaṅ*-affix, reduplication does indeed occur there as well.
[Pāṇini 8.1.44: "In the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), optionally. (3)
When the conjunction of multiple actions is to be indicated, the previously mentioned [suffixes] may optionally be used;
however, in the former case, there must be the subsequent employment of a verb according to the rule. (Pāṇini 3.4.3)

According to the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre*, where the imperative (*loṭ*) occurs, the verbal root that serves as its base must be employed in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). This has been illustrated accordingly. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "Since number, tense, person, and so forth are not manifested by the forms ending in *hi* or *sva*, their manifestation necessitates the mandatory employment of the subsequent application; thus, the employment of that specific root is established. Nor does this entail the possibility of employing other roots with the same meaning, because the subsequent rule establishes a restriction that the subsequent application must be of the same root used in the compound.

In the case of *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition), since the application of the subsequent verb is established by the rule itself (*yathāvidhi*), there is no possibility of applying a different verbal root in *kriyāsamabhihāra* due to a contrary restriction such as "only a word expressing a general action" [as required in *samuccaya*]. This is because, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*) and due to its immediate proximity (*upasthitatva*), the subsequent verb must be the very same base as the *loṭ* suffix; furthermore, the reversal or the intervention of other words in this context is not intended. [The rule] "in *samuccaya*, [the subsequent verb] is that which expresses a general action" [applies]. || 5 ||

According to the rule *samuccaye’nyatarasyām*, where there is the imperative (*loṭ*), there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a verbal root in its general sense. For example: *saktūn piba dhānāḥ khāda* (Drink the barley-meal, eat the parched grains)—he consumes [them]. *annaṃ bhukṣva dādhikasvādasva* (Eat the food, taste the curd-mixture)—he consumes [it]. In the case of the second person plural (*tad* and *dhvam*), one says: *pibata khādata* (Drink, eat)—you consume; *bhuṅgdhvaṃ svādayadhvam* (Eat, taste)—you consume. In these instances, the suffixes *hi* and *sva* are optionally used. Here, there is a syntactic connection (*abhedānvaya*) with the general meaning of the subsequent application, because the specific actions being conjoined are not distinct from that general sense.

Thus, the meaning is: "the act of consuming which is non-different from both drinking the barley-meal and eating the parched grain. By this, the verse—"He, the powerful one, having waged war against the enemy of Namuci, brought about such constant ill-health for heaven day and night: he stormed the city, he lopped the Nandana grove, he plundered its treasures, and he carried off the celestial nymphs"—is explained. For the meaning is: "the past act of ill-health which is non-different from the storming of the city and so forth."

This is because the two meanings of *liṭ*—the non-recent (*anadyatana*) and the remote (*parokṣa*)—are not accepted as objects of verbal cognition (*śābdaviṣaya*) by virtue of their very nature being the restrictive factors for usage; furthermore, there is no manifestation (*bhāna*) here of the condition of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), and since there is no difference between the general and the particular, there is no possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

This also should be noted here: when the second *loṭ* is prescribed for "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), the term "repetition of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) also carries over. For this very reason, Vācaspatimiśra, in his commentary on the *Nyāyavārttika*, explained the sentence "be born and die" (*jāyasva mriyasva ca*) as "he runs on," stating that "running on" (*saṃdhāvana*) means a "succession of operations" (*vyāpārapracaya*), such that one is born again and dies again, or having been born, one dies, and having died, one is born. Nor does there follow the consequence of having two *loṭ*-endings.

Since the *samuccaya* (conjunction) of even non-homogeneous actions—as well as homogeneous ones—is expressed by the *loṭ* suffix itself through repetition (*āvṛtti*), there is no contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* which demonstrates that [the rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). This is because the base ending in *loṭ* applies merely to the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*); whereas in the case of intensification of action qualified by conjunction, it applies to the general sense. Such is the direction [of the argument]. *Chandasi luṅ-liṭau* || 6 || [In the Vedic language, the *luṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes are used.]

When there is a connection with the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in a general sense of time (*kālasāmānya*): "The god has come with the gods" (*deva devebhir āgamat*). Here, the *luṅ* (aorist) is used in the sense of the *loṭ* (imperative). "I shall pay homage to them" (*ahaṃ tebhyaḥ karaṃ namaḥ*). Here, the *laṅ* (imperfect) is used in the sense of the *laṭ* (present). "This sacrificer has chosen Agni as the Hotṛ today" (*agnim adya hotāram avṛṇītāyaṃ yajamānaḥ*). Here, the *laṅ* is used in the sense of the *laṭ*. "He died today" (*adya mamāra*). In that same context, the *liṭ* (perfect) may also be used. The *leṭ* (subjunctive) is used in the sense of the *liṅ* (optative). || 7 ||

In the case of injunctions and so forth, as well as in the relationship of cause and effect and so forth, one performs the *samit* sacrifice; likewise in cases of mutual agreement and non-doubt. || 8 ||

*Upasaṃvādaḥ* is a formal agreement or contract: "If you do this for me, then I shall do this for you. "I alone am the lord of cattle" is the speech of Rudra when he was entreated by the gods for the sake of slaying the demon Pura. "Your cups shall be drawn before mine; your vessels shall be called *maddevatya* (dedicated to me)"—this is the statement of Aditya when addressed by Indra with the words, "Accept a share of the Brahman-slaughter. *Āśaṅkā* is the inference of an effect from its cause. "Lest, being crooked-minded, we fall into hell."

By means of crooked conduct (*jihyācaraṇa*), a fall into hell is possible; the meaning is "may it not happen. The particle *it* has the sense of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*). Nor is there an establishment [of the relationship] between the two by way of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), because in the case of a mutual agreement (*upasaṃvāda*), only the relationship of limit and that which is limited (*avadhy-avadhimadbhāva*) is perceived; and even in the case of apprehension, there is no certainty regarding the relationship of cause and effect.

[The following suffixes are used] in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*): *se*, *sen*, *ase*, *asen*, *ekase*, *ekasen*, *adhyai*, *adhyain*, *kadhyai*, *kadhyain*, *śadhyai*, *śadhyain*, *tavai*, *taven*, *tavenaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.9)

The *bhāva* (the action itself) has the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).
