If it were merely the agent (*kartṛ*), the rule would be established by *kartari kṛt* alone, making the mention of *tum-artha* redundant; furthermore, since the case-roles (*kārakas*) are not implied by the action, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the suffix *tumun* would apply only to the objects (*karman*) and so forth. *vakṣe rāyaḥ*: from the root *vac*, with the suffix *si*. *tāvāmeṣe*: from the root *iṇ*, with the suffix *sen*. In all these cases, there is a difference in accent (*svarabheda*) due to the presence of *ni* and *su*. *śarade*: from the root *jīv*, with the suffix *as*. *jīvasedhāḥ*: from the root *jīv*, with the suffix *ase*. In *ase*, there is a difference in accent due to the suffix *na*. *preṣe*: from the root *iṇ*, with the suffix *se*. *gavāmiva śriyase*: from the root *śri*, with the suffix *kasen*. *upācaradhyai*.

*Adhyai* and *adhyain* are identical; there is only a difference in accent. *Āhuvadhyai*. *Kadhya* and *kadhyai* are identical. [The form] *nādhasaḥ sahamādamadhyai*. From the root *mad* (to rejoice), [we have] *śadhyai*. [The form] *vāyave pibadhyai*. From the root *pā* (to drink), although *śadhyai* would result in a *sarvadhātuka* suffix due to its *śit* designation, which would lead to the application of *yak*, the *śap* is used by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). Haradatta states that the elision of *yak* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Similarly, some hold that in *mādayadhyai*, there is both the elision of *yak* and the presence of *śap*. [The forms] *śadhyai* and *sadhyai*.

[The suffix] *tavya* is used in the sense of "to drink" (*pibadhyai*) and "to exhilarate" (*mādayadhyai*). [In the word] *pātave*, [the suffix] *taven* is used in the sense of "to praise" (*stavai*). In *daśame māsi sūtave*, it should be understood that the initial vowel is acute by way of irregularity (*vyatyayena*). Because the suffix *tavoṅ* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
[Examples include: *prayai*, *rohiṣyai*, and *avyathiṣyai*. 10.

From the root *yā* preceded by the prefix *pra*, the suffix *ka* is applied; by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, there is elision of the long *ā*. From the root *ruh* with the suffix *iṣyaṇ* and from *vyath* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. The meaning is: "to go forth," "to ascend," and "not to suffer distress.
[The suffix *ka* is also applied] after the roots *dṛś* and *vi-khyā*. || 11 ||

The suffix *ke* is applied after the root *dṛś* (to see): *dṛśe viśvāya sūryam* ("for all to see the sun"). Regarding the root *khyā*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. The author of the Nyāsa states that the suffix *ke* is applied to either *cakṣiṅ* or *khyāti*. [Thus we have] *vikhye tvāharāmi* ("I bring you forth to see," meaning "to make known"). Dīkṣita notes that the utility of the separate rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be considered.
The suffixes *ṇamul* and *kamul* are applied after the root *śak* (to be able). (Pāṇini 3.4.12)

The suffixes *tosun* and *kasun* are employed when the word *īśvara* (capable) occurs as an upapada. For example: *vibhājaṃ nāśakat* (he was not able to divide), *apalupaṃ nāśakat* (he was not able to plunder); the meaning is "to divide" and "to plunder," respectively. Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.13: *īśvare tosun-kasunau*.

*Īśvaro viracitum*, *īśvaro vilikhitum*. The meaning is "capable of composing" and "capable of painting. Because the suffixes *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun* are indeclinables (*avyaya*), there is elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*). Consequently, since the condition for the prohibition of the substitution of *t* for *s* (by the rule *pratyayalopalakṣaṇam*) does not apply here, the lengthening of the vowel (by the rule *tvasantasya ca yatuḥ*) does not occur. [The suffix] *taveni* is used in the sense of the kṛtya suffixes. 14. The suffix *taveni* is used in the sense of the kṛtya suffixes.

These [suffixes] occur in the sense of the agent (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). This is because they are specifically prescribed for those two senses alone by the rule *tayoreva* (Pāṇini 3.4.70). Therefore, there is no fault even if the *kṛtya* suffixes are accepted in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in *bhavyādau kartari* ("in the sense of the agent, such as in *bhavya*" etc. and *snānayim* ("for bathing" etc.). [Examples: *brāhmaṇena mlecchati vai* ("the Brahmin indeed speaks barbarously"). [This means] "in the act of immersing. *didṛkṣeṇyaḥ* ("desirable to see"): the suffix *kenya* is applied after the root *dṛś* followed by the desiderative suffix *san*. Similarly, *śuśruṣeṇyaḥ* ("desirable to hear"). *Bhūyam* ("more") has a clearly expressed agent. *Karoti* ("he does") ends in *an*. The meaning is "that which is to be done" (*kṛtya*). Some say that the suffix *tva* is applied after the root *kṛ* when it ends in *vi*. Others say that in that case, the visarga would be unavoidable. And [the suffix *kenya* is applied] after *avacakṣe* ("to speak"). (15)

*Ripunānāvacakṣe* means "it should not be announced by the enemy. [The suffix] *eś* is applied to the root *cakṣiṅ*; because it is marked with *ś*, it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. Consequently, there is no substitution of *khyāñ*. [Now follows:

*bhāvalakṣaṇe stheṇ-kṛñ-vad-ci-hu-tami-janibhyas tosun* (Pāṇini 3.4.16). [Translation of the sūtra: The suffix *tosun* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *iṇ*, *kṛ*, *vad*, *ci*, *hu*, *tam*, and *jan*, when a characteristic of an action (*bhāva*) is to be indicated.

They sit until the end; that is to say, they sit until completion. The words "completion" and so forth function as temporal limits (*avadhi*) characterizing the action. One should establish the sacred fires before the rising of the sun. Before driving away the calves. He offers the oblation before the lowing [of the cows]. Before the ritual performance begins. It concludes before the offering is finished. He stands until the exhaustion [of the day]. "May we come together until the birth of a child"—this is the prayer for a boon by women, meaning "may we attain union with a man until the time of childbirth.
The suffix *kasun* occurs after the roots *sṛp* (to creep) and *tṛd* (to pierce). (Pāṇini 3.4.17)

[The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a verb denoting an action that serves as a characteristic mark (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*). "O Virapśin (mighty one), before you glide forth [to devour], before you pierce through the collarbones. Regarding this, some say the meaning is "before gliding forth" and "before piercing. [They argue this is so] because the root *sṛp-* is not listed among the roots ending in *n*, and because the term *bhāvalakṣaṇe* is understood to carry over from the previous rule. Dīkṣita, however, maintains that this is contrary to the Vedabhāṣya, which states: "It means 'before the flow of blood' (*rudhiraniḥsaraṇāt*). Pāṇini 3.4.18:
After the prohibitive particles *alam* and *khalu*, the suffix *ktvā* is used according to the Eastern grammarians.

These two [suffixes] have the status of an *upapada* when they convey the sense of prohibition. The phrase "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) is for the sake of honor; for forms such as *alaṃ rodanena* ("enough with weeping") are established by the rule of optional forms (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*) itself, since that rule is prohibited only when [the suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *lyuṭ*, whereas here it is that which is to be excepted. Furthermore, although the rule of optional forms is generally not applicable after the section on feminine stems (*stryadhikāra*), there is no obstacle to accepting it here. With the intention that such an obstacle does not exist, the *Vṛtti* states that "of the Easterners" indicates an option. [Examples include: *alaṃ vilanghya* ("enough of transgressing"), *priya vijñāya* ("having understood what is dear"), and *añcām* ("of those ending in -añc").

The word *khalu*, when used as a verbal prefix (*vācika*), forms a compound with the indeclinable *ama* according to the rule "with the indeclinable *ama*. This is not a *upapada* compound because of that specific restriction. What is the purpose of these two [rules]? [Example: *mākārṣīt*. Why "of the two prohibitions"? [Example: *alaṅkāraḥ*. [Now follows:
"In the dialect of the Northerners, the root √māṅ [forms a compound] when there is an exchange of action. (Pāṇini 6.1.140)

In the case of *meṅ* (the root *māṅ*) with the prefix *pra*, [the suffix *ktvā* is used] after *apamitya* when it means "having borrowed" or "having asked for. Although the agents of the two actions are the same (*samānakartṛkatva*), this rule is introduced to signify that the action of borrowing occurs at a time prior to the action of asking. If it is argued: "But since the action of asking also precedes [the action of borrowing], shouldn't the suffix *ktvā* apply there as well?"—it is not so. For the two actions would have to occur either simultaneously or successively. Not the first, because of the restrictive option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) provided by the rule "tatrodīcām" (Pāṇini 3.4.19). Nor the second, because the form "having asked, he borrows" (*yācitvāpamayate*) is indeed desired. Furthermore, this is not merely a reference to the root *māṅ* meaning "to measure," because that root lacks the sense of "exchange" (*vyatihāra*) required here.

Nor is it the case that the substitution of ātva is untenable due to the absence of the designation *ejanta* (ending in *e*); for it is taught that the status of not ending in *e* (*anejantatva*) is not affected by an *anubandha*. The result [of this teaching] is made clear in the sūtra defining the technical term *dhū*.
And [the rule applies] in the sense of connection between the prior and the posterior (*parāvarayoge*). 20.

Because these are relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*), the prior [term] is connected with the subsequent, and the subsequent with the prior. "The mountain is before the river" means that the mountain is proximate in relation to the Gaṅgā; that is, it is closer to the Gaṅgā than the southern region. "The river is beyond the mountain" means that the river is distant from that very same Vindhya range; that is, it is further away from the Vindhya than the southern region. Here, spatial priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) are being taken up. And for these two, there is a dependence on a third location, based on both the limit (*avadhi*) and the substratum (*āśraya*). Otherwise, even from the southern region, the Vindhya would be distant in relation to other rivers.

Even though there is equality in both cases regarding the proximity of the Vindhya mountain and the remoteness of the Gaṅgā river relative to the Himavat mountain, there is a distinction in the cognition: in the first case, the proximity to the Himavat is the qualifier in the Vindhya [relative to the Gaṅgā], while in the second case, the remoteness from the Vindhya is the qualifier in the Gaṅgā [relative to the Himavat].
[The suffix *ktvā* is used] after two verbal roots having the same agent, when the action denoted by the former occurs earlier in time. (Pāṇini 3.4.21)

Because the context concerns the *dhātu* (verbal root), the identity of agent applies to the two [actions] denoted by it. Nor is there an impossibility of that identity on the grounds that the capacity (*śakti*)—the means (*sādhana*)—of the actions of eating and walking is distinct; for the intended meaning is the non-difference between the capacity and that which possesses the capacity (*śaktimad*). This is because the unity of those two is established by the presence of the two agents' capacities within a single entity, such as Devadatta, who is the means of accomplishing both the actions of eating and walking. The genitive or locative case here is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

The suffix *ktvā* is applied to that verbal root-meaning which occurs at the earlier time between two actions performed by the same agent. For example: *bhuktvā vrajati* ("having eaten, he goes"). Here, *ktvā* is used because of the priority in time relative to the action of going performed by that same agent. However, the conclusion is that when there is a comparison with an action of eating performed by a different agent, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* will be applied as will be stated later under the rule beginning with *vibhāṣā*. Thus, forms such as *āsitvā bhoktum* do not occur due to lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*); rather, only forms such as *laṭ* (present tense) and others are used, as in *āsitvā bhuṅkte*.

Furthermore, duality is independent [of the sequence], as in "having bathed, drunk, and eaten, he goes," or "having bathed, eaten, and drunk," and so forth. Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of "bring all these first" (*sarveṣām pūrvam ānaya*), the suffix *ktvā* would apply only to that which is first relative to all others; for since the action expressed by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is primary, all other actions are construed with it alone, and thus there is no mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified among them. This is according to the maxim: "Since subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there can be no connection between them, as they are equal [in their dependence]."

The supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "he sleeps having opened [his mouth]" is stated because there is no prior time [for the action of opening]. This introduction is for the sake of the suffix *ktvā* when it occurs at a subsequent time. The *Bhāṣya* states that this is already established because the action of opening is indeed prior in time with respect to the act of sleeping which follows immediately after the opening. According to the *Vārttika* "the indeclinable *kṛt* suffixes denote the state" (*bhāve*), this [suffix] refers to the state when it has reached the condition of being yet to be accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*). Through the rule "of two actions having the same agent," the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) acquires the status of a relation (*saṃsargatā*). The term "prior time" (*pūrvakāla*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Since selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) has as its domain that which belongs to the same class (*sajātīya*), it follows that the action (*kriyātva*) is obtained as its object. Therefore, the preceding time is what is indicated (*dyotya*). Thus, by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the connection with both [actions], the action denoted by the base of the suffix *ktvā* is a qualifier of the action denoted by the verbal ending (*tiṅanta*). This is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusaṃbandhe*).

By this, the claim that the prior time (*pūrvakāla*) and the identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) are the expressed meanings [of the suffix] is refuted; for, as the meaning of the suffix, those two would result in being the qualificands (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, if the action were not predominant, there would be no doubling (*dvitva*) in cases of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*). If that [repetition] were expressed by means of an action that has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of doubling even in words such as *pācaka* ("cook"). Moreover, since in rules such as *yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ*, the phrase "connected with the verbal root" (*dhātusambaddha*) is established as referring to direct connection, that [indirect connection] would be contradicted. Finally, there is the absence of the expression of the prior time as *ktvā*.

If one were to accept that [the relation] is denotable merely by the mention of the seventh case (locative), there would be the over-extension [of the rule] to such instances as *kartṛsthe cāśarīre kartari* ("when the agent is bodiless and resides in the agent"); for the fact of being obtainable from another source is equal here as well, and no distinction from the *karmapravacanīya* [particles] would arise. Thus, according to the method of the Grammarians (*śābdika*), even in this case, the relation is accepted as appearing solely as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*).

Regarding this, they say: in the rule *avyayakṛto bhāve* ("the indeclinable kṛt-affixes denote the state"), the word *bhāva* (state), which expresses pervasion (*vyāpti*), has already expressed the immediate succession and so forth of the connection with another action; for the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is obtained from other sources alone. For this very reason, in the verbal cognition arising from such expressions as *bhuktvā vrajati* ("having eaten, he goes"), there is no doubt regarding its [the eating's] kāraka-factors. This is because, since the temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) functions as a relation (*saṃsarga*), there is an absence of a cognition having that [sequence] as its qualifier; thus, there is no obstacle to a doubt having that [sequence] as its qualifier.

Furthermore, if the locus (*āśraya*) were obtainable through other means, then in your view, the capacity of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*) would not be established; and if [the objecthood] and so forth were also merely relations (*saṃsarga*), then the second case endings and others would lose their respective capacities. This is because the resulting cognition having that as its qualifier (*tat-prakāraka-bodha*) is identical here as well. Nor should it be argued that there is a disparity [between our views], since the requirement that the linguistic presentation generated by an inflection (*vibhakti-janya-upasthiti*) must be a cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a noun-stem is necessary to prevent a cognition where objecthood is the relation in sentences such as "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*). For if this were stated in general terms, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the present case.

This is because even that which ends in the suffix *ktvā* is a noun (*nāman*), and because the requirement [of the rule] is satisfied simply by the fact that [the action] is illuminated by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). As for the non-occurrence of such usage as *pītvā tṛptaḥ* ("having drunk, he is satiated"), it is due to a lack of intended meaning (*tātparya*); otherwise, there would be no way to account for the temporal sequence being a relation (*saṃsarga*) [rather than a qualifier]. Furthermore, since the meaning of the rule is "from a verbal root denoting an action occurring at a prior time among two actions having the same agent," everything is logically consistent. Moreover, the prior time is a qualifier of the action; for it is accepted that even the meaning of the suffix, such as singularity and so on, serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*).

Regarding the view that the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* denotes immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), although that [sequence] is primary, the doubling [of the verb] is nonetheless justified by relying on the subordinate action (*guṇībhūtakriyā*). This is because there is no such usage [in the absence of subordination], which prevents over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and because of the Vārttika stating: "The sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) occurs with verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) and with *suk*, an affix ending in *kṛt*. Furthermore, in your own view as well, the action is subordinate; for being subordinate to the meaning of the suffix is not the determining factor. Moreover, it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to include "directness" (*sākṣāt*) in the rule *dhātusaṃbandhe...* [Pāṇini 3.4.1]. [Example: *alaṃ bhuktvā*. (Enough with eating.)

Furthermore, in the case of "a mountain not reaching a river" (*aprāpyanadīṃ parvataḥ*), even now [the suffix] is abandoned; and because there is a disparity, in that in the case of a *karmapravacanīya* the relation is the meaning of the case ending (*vibhaktyartha*), whereas here it is the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix (*kṛdartha*).

Furthermore, what fault is there in the absence of semantic disparity (*vaiṣamya*) regarding a *karmapravacanīya*? For mere identity of meaning does not constitute a fault. Otherwise, since the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and the second case (*dvitīyā*) would have the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) as their respective meanings, even finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) would likewise possess those meanings. Nor does it follow that the second case would apply [to the *karmapravacanīya*], because that rule is prescribed only when that specific technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is present. Otherwise, since the relation between the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) is the meaning of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), that same consequence would apply there as well.

In that case [of the *ṛk*], the word "anu" establishes, in a specific sense, a relationship that is understood only in a general way through the second [word]; however, here, there is no such thing as the relationship being the meaning of another word, so the disparity is quite clear.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "It should be stated that suffixes such as *ātum* and *unaḥ* occur when they are in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) [with the verb]," the meaning is this: in the absence of this rule, because of the general injunction *kartari kṛt* (P. 3.4.67), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *ṇamul* occurring in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, in the sentence *svādukāraṃ yavāgūrbhujyate devadattena*, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) would not occur, because the agent has already been expressed [by the suffix]. Nor can it be argued that the instrumental occurs because the agent is not expressed by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*.

It should be stated that this is because one relies on the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) interpretation of the rule *anabhihite*. For if it were not so, since the object (*karman*) would be unexpressed by the suffix *ṇamul*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would undesirably apply even to the word *yavāgū* [in the example *yavāgūṃ svāduṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte*]. Nor can one find a solution by starting the rule *avyayakṛto bhāve* (the suffixes added to indeclinables denote the action itself); for then the second case would still be unjustified in the example *svāduṃkāraṃ yavāgūṃ bhuṅkte*. The same logic should be applied to examples such as *paktvaudano bhujyate devadattena* ("The rice is eaten by Devadatta after having been cooked") and *bhoktumodanaḥ pacyate devadattena* ("The rice is being cooked by Devadatta in order to eat"). However, if the aforementioned rule is started, there is no fault, because the meaning of *ktvā* and other such suffixes is simply coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and not the agent (*kartṛ*) or other factors.

And this has been rejected. Because of the rule "the kṛt suffixes [ending in] *avyaya* are used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*)," and because of the continued application of the term "in the sense of *tumun*," the suffixes such as *ktya* are prescribed only for the abstract state; therefore, the meanings of agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth do not apply. If, however, the intention of the Bhāṣya regarding the rule "when there is a prior time" were that the suffix *ktvā* applies to an action occurring at a prior time, then both the aforementioned doubt and the threefold resolution stated would be untenable. This is because, according to your view, the status of expressing the abstract state (*bhāvārthakatā*) would not be obtained even from the word "prior time" itself. Furthermore, since the subsequent case is also established by the continued application of this very principle, [your objection is invalid].

This is because it is more appropriate for the word "prior time" (*pūrvakāla*) to be carried over [from the previous rule] as a proximate term, rather than carrying over the word "the sense of *tumun*" (*tumunartha*), which is separated [by intervening rules]. If, however, the meaning were simply the verbal root denoting a prior action, then the form would have to be *pūrvakālāt* (ablative), since the sentence-meaning would be that the suffix *ktvā* is applied to such a root. Therefore, the meaning of *tumun* must be stated as follows: "The suffix *ktvā* shall occur after a verbal root in the sense of a prior action. Since the prescription of *ktvā* after a root denoting a subsequent action is untenable, it follows by implication that *ktvā* is indeed valid only after a root denoting a prior action.

Thus, *pūrvakāla* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the time of the prior [action]," for brevity is accepted by all schools of thought over a *bahuvrīhi* compound in such cases. The meaning is: "at the time of that action which is prior among two actions having a single agent. The masculine gender substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs because of the rule "in all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), a pronoun [retains its gender]. Since the connection of a part [of a whole] with a related word is a well-established linguistic usage (*vyutpanna*), the term *sarvanāman* (pronoun) applies here. The inclusion of the phrase "between two" (*dvayoḥ*) is necessary, as otherwise the quality of being "prior" would apply universally to any action whatsoever.

And thus, Kaiyaṭa’s statement—that in the commentary on the Bhāṣya explaining how the suffix *ktvā* does not occur when the prior time is expressed by its own word (*svaśabda*), [the rule] prescribes *ktvā* and so forth for the state of being prior (*paurvakālya*) and not for the object (*viṣaya*)—is also consistent. This is because, if the word "prior time" (*pūrvakāla*) in the Sūtra were taken as referring to an action (*kriyā*), the doubt that it is not the object would be untenable.

If "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*) consists simply in being denotable by a word distinct from the verbal root (*dhātu*), then its negation is untenable; for since it is understood through the verbal root itself, objecthood would have to be what is denoted [by the suffix], and thus it would be stated by the very term [the suffix] itself as something already obtained by the verbal root. Furthermore, just as in the expression *brāhmaṇānāṃ pūrvam* ("among the Brāhmaṇas, the first"), the word *pūrva* alone conveys the sense of the locus of selection (*nirdhāraṇaviṣaya*), so too must it be here. Otherwise, there would arise a discrepancy between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). Moreover, this is precisely what is obtained from the works of Kaiyaṭa and others.

In that regard, the distinction is this: in the former case [the direction of space] is prior in terms of location (*daiśika*), whereas here it is prior in terms of time (*kālika*). What need is there for much? In the sense you have stated, the word "time" (*kāla*) would be redundant; for the term "prior ones" (*pūrve*) would be insufficient, since the meaning is successfully established by taking the word as referring to the substratum (*dharmī*) alone. Therefore, the intended meaning of the Sūtra, Vārttika, and Bhāṣya is that the primary denotation (*śakti*) of the word refers to the prior time. For if only "prior ones" were stated, the fact that time is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) would not be obtained.
Furthermore, if the word "prior" (*pūrva*) were intended merely to denote time in general, it would be meaningful because it connects with a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) that depends upon an action.

It might be argued as follows: the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* is simply "having the same agent. Even though both [the prior and the posterior actions] are necessarily present, the prior time is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*). This is because, even when one observes several actions by a single agent occurring simultaneously—as in "wearing the sacred thread, looking at the path, and studying while walking"—there is a rule that a single agent does not perform multiple primary actions at once; thus, the prior sequence is implied by that very rule.

Now, if "primacy" (*pradhānatva*) consists in the impossibility of [the two actions] occurring at the same time, then in the expression *adhītya gacchati* ("having studied, he goes"), there would be no cognition of priority (*pūrvatva*), because there is no implication [of such a sequence]. Nor should it be argued that primacy is "primary status as an objective" (*mukhyata uddeśyatva*) in the sense that "let this [action] occur or not, but let this [other action] necessarily occur," and that if the two aforementioned actions were thus [related], there would be a rule of priority; for even if studying and going were equally primary objectives, there is a deviation [from the rule] due to their possible simultaneous occurrence.

This is not so, because [the action] cannot be restricted by way of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*). For it is precisely the fact of being accomplished by efforts occurring at different times that constitutes primacy; for actions accomplished by efforts occurring at unequal times are necessarily pervaded by the property of having unequal timing. If being accomplished by different efforts were [the defining characteristic], then that would be absent in such cases as "the Lord, having created, destroys," and so forth.

However, they argue that when multiple actions are presented as being mixed—by way of predominance and by having a common agent—a single agent does not perform them simultaneously. In such cases, there is a restriction regarding their essential meaning (tātparya) solely in terms of their temporal sequence (pūrvāparībhāva), as in "Your body is dirty; you should bathe," and so forth. In the co-occurrence of an accomplished state and a state to be accomplished, the relationship of cause and effect is understood through linguistic convention (vyutpatti) by inferring that specific intention (tātparya). Similarly, since the prior state is understood through the very implication of the intended meaning regarding the sequence of actions presented with a common agent, there is no expressive power (śakti) for that [sequence] in the word itself. This is what they say.

Nor should it be argued that even so, since the action of going (*vrajana*) can be accounted for by the mere implication of its priority in time, there would not necessarily be a cognition of the priority of the action ending in the suffix *ktvā*; for one observes such forms as *vrajati bhuktvā* (he goes having eaten), and thus it is difficult to state that the "priority of presentation" (*pūrvopastiti*) is the restrictive factor. Indeed, there is no experience [of the world] that the actions of eating and going have a single agent;

for the rule that the meaning of *ktvā*—namely, "having the same agent"—must necessarily connect with the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*), makes it impossible for it to connect as a qualifier with the action of going as the qualificand.

Therefore, there is no such experience as that the two actions of eating and going have the same agent, or even that the action of going has the same agent as the action of eating. Rather, since the meaning expressed by the suffix *ktvā* is "having the same agent" in the sense of being produced by an effort (*kṛti*) that is co-located with itself but exists at a different time from it—and since the word *sva-* (self) refers here to the "going" mentioned in proximity—the [proposed] experience does not arise.

In the cognition "eating is produced by an agent who possesses an action of the same time and so forth as the action of going," since going is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and eating is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the relation of priority (*pūrvatva*) applies only to the former. It should not be argued that, because in that case only the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) are essential, there is no reason for the relation of priority to apply to the principal element alone even when the sequence of one or the other is determined. This is because, according to the Mīmāṃsaka school, even that which is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) is admitted to enter into the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

In reality, because the word *vrajati* ends in the suffix *laṭ*, which denotes the present tense, the act of going (*vrajana*) is presented as being connected with the present time; thus, since its priority [over another action] is contradicted, it is understood that the act of eating alone possesses that [priority]. By this, expressions such as *bhuktvā jagāma* ("having eaten, he went") are also explained. Nor is there any inconsistency in cases such as *bhuktvā apākṣīt* ("having eaten, he cooked"); for if such a grammatical convention exists in one instance, it must exist elsewhere as well, and furthermore, that which is presented as being connected with a prior time does not require [further specification of] time.

Nor should it be argued that in such cases as "having eaten at that time, he went," there could be no cognition of the priority [of the eating] because the eating is already occupied by the time denoted by the word *tadā* (at that time). This is because the syntactic connection between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is primary; however, since there is no other way for the meaning of the word *tadā*, it connects through identity with that [eating]. For when a connection is possible with an object presented as not being occupied by time, there is no reason to assume a connection with an object presented as already occupied by time.

It should not be argued that in such cases as "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*) or "having offered the oblation, one should give the sacrificial fee" (*hutiṃ hutvā dakṣiṇāṃ dadyāt*), there is no cognition of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). For it is an established tenet of the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) that these are resolved by supplying an intermediate action. Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* is indeed the state of having a common agent.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the cognition of necessary antecedence (*niyatapūrvatva*)—as asserted by you—is difficult to establish and remains unproven according to the reasoning already stated. This is because there is the possibility of a subsequent [cognition] occurring first; because, in the absence of such presentation, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) itself is difficult to grasp; and because the capacity (*yogyatā*) exists in both cases. Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that the status of being prior is implied by having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). For that [common agency] must be either (1) accomplishment through a single effort (*kṛti*), (2) accomplishment through efforts of the same kind, or (3) identity of the substratum of the effort. It cannot be the first, because the efforts conducive to eating and walking are distinct.

This is because even various forms occurring at the same time belong to a single genus. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because there is a deviation in cases such as the simultaneous cutting of various blades of grass accomplished by a single act. [This is so] due to the power of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) between the agent of eating and the agent of walking. Therefore, when the priority [of one action over another] is presented by the suffix *ktvā*, the rule of its connection [to the meaning of the base] is well-established by the very linguistic convention that a suffix conveys its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). This is because it is impossible for that [priority] to be the expressed meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). Since the agent is denoted by both the *ktvā* suffix and the verbal ending, the non-difference between them functions as a relation (*saṃsarga*).

Alternatively, even if those two [suffixes] denote merely the action (*kṛti*), their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone constitutes the sentence-meaning. Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in such cases as "he goes to eat" (*bhoktum vrajati*) or "he goes while seeing" (*paśyan vrajati*), because the suffix *tumun* and the present indicative (*laṭ*) do not express the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛtva*). Vācaspatimiśra maintains that in the case of "having slept, he opens his eyes" (*suptvā vyādatte*), the usage is reversed. In instances such as "the jar remains after having come into being" (*bhūtvā ghaṭastiṣṭhati*), although the times of origination and duration are distinct, there is no fault, because one intends to express the existence of the jar at a time prior to its remaining, in accordance with empirical experience. Therefore, it is established that priority (*pūrvatva*) is the meaning of the suffix *ktvā*.

However, in the case of mixed [actions], it is possible for that [sequence] to have non-intervention as its very core, because it conforms to common experience (*pratīti*). This is because one does not perceive [the sequence] between morning eating and evening going; rather, there is the cognition that "having eaten, he moved," which implies that he moved only when the eating was already completed. For this very reason, the apprehension of causality also arises from the suffix *-ktvā*. Otherwise, there would be an impossibility [of the suffix's application], since there is no movement in the moment immediately following the eating. This is because the meaning of "non-intervention" (*avyavadhāna*) consists in being uninterrupted by an action favorable to [the subsequent action]. Since an action favorable to that [subsequent action] does not itself constitute an intervention, otherwise, organs and the like would fail to be producers [of their effects] due to being intervened by an operation (*vyāpāra*).

In the phrase "having stood today" (*adya sthitvā*) and so forth, there is a syntactic relation of identity between the immediately preceding time denoted by the suffix *ktvā* and that which is expressed by the word "today" (*adya*). This is because, in comparison with a much longer duration, the day of "today" is indeed immediate. Otherwise, since the action presented as being connected to a prior time would lack expectancy, its connection with the word "today" would be untenable. Nor should it be argued: "How can there be a relation of identity with the mere preceding time denoted by *ktvā*, given that the word 'today' is already occupied by the sense of the locative case? [The answer is that] it is not so.

They say that this is because the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* must be restricted to the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*), otherwise its syntactic connection would be untenable; nor should it be argued that the meaning of a suffix cannot connect with the meaning of another word before it connects with the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*), for such a rule of grammar is not established, as evidenced by the cognition "the object of Devadatta’s act of seeing" from expressions such as *devadattena dṛṣṭaḥ*.

The meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of the principal action belonging to the agent of the *maṇi*-derived action; for the prior time, as the qualifier of that [succession], is cognized only secondarily. This is because from the expression "he goes after eating" (*bhojanānantaraṃ vrajati*), there arises a cognition in which the act of going is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the act of eating is the qualifier (*prakāraka*). If, however, [the suffix denoted] priority, there would be an experience in which the act of eating is the qualificand. Thus, this very fact is the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*). Nor does this lead to the violation of the rule that an affix denotes its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); for such a rule applies only to nominal suffixes (*sub-vibhakti*).

This is because it is accepted that the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is construed with the agent; and furthermore, even for the person to be fed (*bhojanīya*), [the action] is a qualifier of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). Now, is this immediacy capable of being defined in terms of effort (*kṛti*) or in terms of action (*kriyā*)? It cannot be the first, because if there were no connection of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) even as a counter-correlative, it would result in a violation of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Nor can immediacy be defined in terms of effort, because since effort is a part of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśa*), it would follow that it could not be construed with the action. Nor can it be the latter, because an action presented [in consciousness] without being connected to immediacy is devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), and thus it would follow that the effort could not be construed with it.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition is "one who possesses the effort to go to another meal, which is the object of his own effort," based on the connection with the first [effort] alone. For there is no established linguistic rule (*avyutpatti*) whereby a word, having first brought about the connection of its own primary meaning with another word-meaning, subsequently causes the connection of that qualified other primary meaning with yet another. This is not so, because the connection with the locus of that [effort] occurs through the first [effort] itself. Thus, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is: "The agent of eating possesses the effort to go to another meal. Nor is there the fault of the eating being connected to both [the effort and the going].

They say that in cases such as "by a jar" (*ghaṭena*), since the co-referential connection (*anvaya*) of the jar is accepted with both the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) presented by the instrumental case-ending and with singularity (*ekatva*), this is because one must resort to such a connection out of necessity. Nor should it be argued that even when simultaneous connection is possible, connection with both is observed to occur sequentially; for they say that by the maxim "the qualifier [is connected] to the qualificand, and another qualifier to that [qualifier]," simultaneous connection is accepted, and thus one does not accept a connection with something already unconnected (*ananvita*).

However, some say that the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is also pervasion (*vyāpti*), because one uses expressions such as "having opened [the mouth], he sleeps" (*vyādāya svapiti*) or "having studied, he remains" (*adhītya tiṣṭhati*), which occur only when the state of remaining (*sthiti*) is pervaded by the act of studying; and because one does not use expressions such as "having opened [the mouth], he sleeps," even when the sleeping occurs at a time subsequent to the opening of the mouth.

Others, however, say that there is no evidence for [the presence of] that [causality] in this case. This is because there is no pervasion of it by the property of being a state (*sthititva*) in general; for if it were intended to refer to its specific state, it would result in the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication). Furthermore, the use of this expression would not apply to the opening of the eyes following sleep, since there is likewise an absence of pervasion of that person's opening of the eyes by the property of being his specific state of sleep. By this, they also refute the view that pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) constitutes the relation (*saṃsarga*).

Others, however, say that there is a comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya-bodha*) by the principle of "the qualification of a qualified [subject]" (*viśiṣṭe vaiśiṣṭyam*), wherein the state of being the locus of sleep is [predicated] of the locus of yawning—which is obtainable through the general power (*sāmānya-śakti*) [of the word *mugdha*]. Through the force of intention (*tātparya*), the simultaneous occurrence of yawning, sleep, and so forth, which are the default meanings, is obtained. Alternatively, they say there is comprehension through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*), as in the expression "having slept, he yawns."

Others, however, say that [if the *samānakartṛka* rule applied] after the primary action of opening, then the expression "he sleeps having opened his mouth" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*) would be impossible; for the locus of the sleeping would already exist at the time of the opening. Furthermore, there would be no distinction between "he opens his mouth and sleeps" (*mukhaṃ vyādatte svapiti*) and "he sleeps having opened his mouth" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*), and there would be a contradiction regarding the single suffix (*ekāra*) required by the connection of verbal roots (*dhātusambandha*). Thus they argue.

Now, we shall state the intended meaning of the Mahābhāṣya: the understanding is that the action of going is qualified by an earlier time of eating. The earlier time is construed as a property residing in the act of eating, and that [time] is construed with the act of going through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). When the earlier time is construed with the action denoted by the base of the *ktvā* suffix, the immediate succession is obtained for the action denoted by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) by the very force of the meaning; for this is because the property of residing in a time that is the locus of the prior non-existence of the first operation constituting that specific action is obtained in the final operation constituting the act of eating.

Otherwise, if one were to eat while cooking something else, there would be the undesirable consequence of that [eating] being considered a "preparatory act" (*prayoga*). Furthermore, since the act of eating can serve as a qualifier for the act of walking, there is no restriction on the scope of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the connection between verbal roots (*dhātu-sambandha*). This is because, under the various views that the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the action itself (*kṛti*), the substratum (*āśraya*), or pervasion (*vyāpti*), such a consequence would be unavoidable. In cases such as *mukhaṃ vyādāya* ("having opened the mouth"), although there is no priority with respect to the entire collection of operations constituting sleep and so forth, priority must nevertheless be accepted with respect to some part thereof, on the strength of actual usage.

As for the claim that there is no evidence for the experience of suchness [tathātva]: furthermore, does "prior time" mean (1) being a time that is the locus of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), (2) being a time that is not the locus of its own destruction (*svadhvaṃsa*), or (3) being the state of not being the locus of its own destruction? It cannot be the first, because it is impossible if one does not accept prior non-existence. It cannot be the second, because it would lead to the absurdity that one could say "having cooked, he eats" even while he is currently cooking or eating. It cannot be the last, because it is more cumbersome than the notion of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), which consists in occurring at a time that is not the locus of its destruction. Thus.

That is incorrect, because only that experience which is consistent with the Bhāṣya and other authoritative texts possesses validity. If the word *tat* were taken to refer to any action whatsoever, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of applying it to such expressions as *pacamānaḥ* (the one who is cooking). However, if the final action is adopted, there is no such over-extension in my view, since I accept the connection of the final action of cooking with the property of occurring at a time that is not a locus for the destruction of the act of eating.

In examples such as *devadattaḥ paktvaudanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("Devadatta eats rice after having cooked it") and *paktvaudano bhujyate devadattena* ("Rice is eaten by Devadatta after having been cooked"), there is no contingency for the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*), because the agentive and objective capacities (*kartṛ-karma-śakti*) as defined by the act of cooking are not expressed [by the suffixes]. This is possible because the restriction is established by the non-expression of the primary capacity. Thus, this has been elaborated upon precisely in the rule *anabhihite*. When repetition (*paunaḥpunyam*) is to be expressed, the suffixes *ṇamul* and *ktvā* are used in the same scope as previously mentioned; however, these two are incapable of expressing frequency (*abhīkṣṇyam*) apart from reduplication, due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words. Therefore, by the rule "also in the sense of frequency," reduplication occurs: *smāraṃ-smāraṃ namati śivam* (bowing repeatedly, remembering again and again, he bows to Śiva).
[The suffixes *ṇamul* and *ktvā* are not used] when there is no mutual expectancy (*anākāṅkṣe*). (23)

When a sentence containing actions in prior and subsequent order does not require another [sentence] for its completion, that which was obtained by the suffix *yat* when the word *yat* is the subordinate term (*upapada*) would not occur. Consequently, there is a prohibition of both the *ṇamul* prescribed by the preceding rule and the *ktvā* prescribed by the rule even further back. It should not be argued that, according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately antecedent," the prohibition ought to apply only to what is obtained by the rule *ābhīkṣṇye* (Pāṇini 3.4.22) and not to what is prescribed by the same rule (*samāna-sūtra*). This is because the commencement of the prohibition regarding the prior action is made with reference to the entire section (*prakaraṇa*).

When he eats, then he recites. Why is there expectancy? [Because] "Having eaten, he goes; then he studies"—the sentence ending with "he goes" is expectant, since the two sentences formed by the words *yat* and *tat* manifest a single unified sentence.
[This is governed by the rule: *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu* (Pāṇini 3.4.24).

In the word *agre*, because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form ending in the locative case, it lacks the status of being an actual case-ending; therefore, unlike in examples such as *asyavāmīyam*, there is no elision of the case-ending. When these words are used as governing objects (*upapada*), the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are optionally employed within the scope of the same rule. Now, is this an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what is already established, or regarding what is not yet established? There is doubt based on whether the word *ābhīkṣṇye* (in the sense of repetition) is understood to carry over or not. It is not the first case; for if *ktvā* and *ṇamul* were already established in the sense of repetition, then by prescribing their absence in certain instances, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the *laṭ* and other suffixes could also occur in the sense of repetition. For it is precisely in the sense of repetition that *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are intended [by this rule].

[The opponent argues: "In *agre bhojaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* (he goes along eating repeatedly), [the suffix -am] occurs after each instance of *bhuj*. However, suffixes such as -laṭ and others are not desired; for example, one does not say *agre bhuṅkte bhuṅkte vrajati*. Thus, because the suffixes -ktvā and -ṇamul would be unestablished when there is no repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), and because forms such as *agre bhojaṃ vrajati* are intended [by the author], the second alternative is not tenable. If the mention of 'repetition' (*ābhīkṣṇya*) were removed, then since *agra-* and the others would serve as the cause for the production of the suffixes, they would acquire the designation of 'subordinate word' (*upapada*), and consequently, the formation of an 'upapada compound' (*upapadasamāsa*) would result. [The author replies: This fault does not apply if the mention of 'repetition' is removed, provided that for *agra-* and the others, the rule is treated as an optional application (*prāptavibhāṣā*). For if the mention of 'repetition' is removed, *agra-* and the others become the conditions for the arising of the suffixes; thus, they receive the technical name 'subordinate word' (*upapada*), which leads to the undesirable consequence of forming an upapada compound.

In the *Prāptavibhāṣā* (the view that the option applies when [the suffix] would otherwise necessarily apply), this fault does not arise; for since the suffixes are prescribed by the rule for frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) itself, the prohibition of suffixes after words such as *agra* serves only as a condition for that very prohibition. Do not say so. It is more appropriate to hold that it is an *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an option where [the suffix] would otherwise not apply). For, by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only with an indeclinable ending in *am*," there is no possibility of compounding [in the first place]. Furthermore, because [the suffix] is prescribed equally both with *am* and with others other than *am*, and because when [the suffix] is applicable in the sense of frequency, the two obligatory suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are desired by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) in cases other than frequency.

Nor should it be argued that since the suffix *ṇamul* is not otherwise obtained [by rule], whereas the suffix *ktvā* is obtained by the rule *samānādikarmakeṣu tumun* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) applies to both; for the mention of "optionally" would be useless in relation to the *ktvā* prescribed by that specific rule. Furthermore, the forms such as the present tense (*laṭ*) are established in their alternative cases simply by the principle of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*). Moreover, the mention of "optionally" in the rule prescribing *ktvā* along with *ṇamul* is for the purpose of indicating that when these two are prescribed together, the principle of non-identity of form does not apply. Consequently, in the case of repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*), the present tense and other suffixes do not occur after the prior action; such is the direction.

In this context, words such as *agra* (first) have as their object the priority of the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment), not the priority of the *kriyā* (the action); for, since that priority has already been expressed by those very [words], it is impossible for the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* to apply, as their purpose would already have been served. Nor can there be any force in the word *ārambha* (commencement), because words like *agra*, which have the priority of the *sādhana* as their object, have already fulfilled their function when they serve as upapadas. Furthermore, it has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* (Pāṇini 3.4.21) that if the priority of the action were expressed by the word *pūrva*, the suffix *ktvā* would not arise.

Regarding the rule for *rk* (the suffix *ktvā*), since the option (*vibhāṣā*) is already established by the determination [of the previous rule] concerning the inclusion of words such as *agra* when they refer to the priority of an action (*kriyāpaurvakālya*), a doubt about it is untenable. This is because, by the rule on frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are prescribed only when there is priority of action. Even if the mention of frequency were carried over by the words *agra* and so forth, it would still be a case of an unestablished option (*aprāptavibhāṣā*). Furthermore, those two suffixes do not arise merely for the sake of indicating frequency, because even they lack the necessary semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) without reduplication (*dvirvacana*).

Therefore, only those [words] such as *agra* (before) and so forth, which have as their object the priority of the means (*sādhana*), are employed here. Thus, the meaning of *agre bhojanam* is that "having eaten before other eaters, he departs. And since eating does not possess priority in relation to that [departure], it is understood here as being relative only to the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*) which is to be accomplished by it, because the linguistic usage of *kāraka* (grammatical participant) has action (*kriyā*) as its domain. Although in expressions such as *prabhor agre bhuṅkte* ("he eats in front of the master") the word *agra* signifies a particular place (*deśaviśeṣa*), in this context, due to its association with the words *prathama* (first) and *pūrva* (prior), it is taken as referring specifically to time (*samaya*).

This is the meaning: here, priority in time (*paurvakālatā*) is of two kinds—relative to the action of going (*vrajikriyā*) which has a single agent, and relative to the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*) which has different agents. The first is expressed by the suffix *ktvā*, while the second is expressed by words such as *agra* and others. Thus, when the meaning of the grammatical treatise (*ākara*) is established, the suffix *ktvā* possesses the denotative power of priority in time just like the words *agra* and so forth, because the word *viṣaya* (denoting the scope of application) is used in both cases. [Now follows the rule: "After the root *kṛ*, the suffix *khamuñ* is added in the sense of an object (*karman*) when it is not explicitly stated. (Pāṇini 3.4.25)

In this context, *karman* (object) is the upapada; *ākrośa* (insulting) is to be understood as the sense. Because the suffix ends in *t*, *mum* is substituted [for the final *r*]. In the expression *coraṃkāram ākrośati* ("he insults him by calling him 'thief'"), the verb *kṛ* has the sense of "uttering. This is because, in the insulting sentence "you are a thief," the utterance of the word "thief" serves to accomplish the insult, rather than to accomplish the state of being a thief. For that [state of being a thief] is a property of the thing itself and cannot be produced by speech. Therefore, the meaning is: "he insults him by saying 'you are a thief. Pāṇini 3.4.26: *svādumi ṇamul*. (The suffix *ṇamul* is used after a verb when the upapada is a word ending in the locative case expressing the sense of "being good" or "to one's liking.")

The inclusion of the word *svādu* is for the purpose of grasping its meaning [as a quality]; it is derived from the instruction of a teacher through an uninterrupted tradition. Its status as ending in *m* (i.e., *svādm*) is established by nipātana (irregular derivation). It should not be argued that one should simply employ the suffix *khamuñ* or *rkiṇamul* here; for if one says, "having made it sweet (*svādvīṃ*), he eats it," or "he eats with a sweet-making (*svādukāram*"), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would erroneously apply by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*. This is because the status of ending in *m* is intended to prevent the application of the suffix in the future case of the feminine. Furthermore, the status of ending in *m* is not established among the indeclinables (*avyaya*) by means of *khamuñ*, because that which ends in *cvī* is itself an indeclinable.

Nor should it be argued that only the status of ending in *m* (māntatva) should be treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*), while the suffix should simply be *khamuñ*. For if only the status of ending in *m* were irregularly prescribed, it would result in the word being exclusively an indeclinable (*avyaya*), which would lead to the undesirable application of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. However, in the case of the suffix *ṇamul*, since the status of ending in *m* has already been established by a previous rule, it is understood that its purpose is to prevent the appearance of the long vowel *ī* (īkāra), rather than for the sake of the letter *m* itself. Furthermore, the subsequent prescription of *ṇamul* is necessary; otherwise, there would be no distinction between using *ṇamul* here or elsewhere. Thus, one eats "having made [it] well-prepared" (*saṃpannakāram*) or "having made [it] salty" (*lavaṇakāram*). Alternatively, by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), one may also say "having made it sweet" (*svādu kṛtvā*) before eating.
If [it is argued that] *anyathā*, *evam*, *katham*, and *ittham* are established as uninflected forms (siddha-aprayoga). || 27 ||

In this manner, up to the word *ittham*, when these [words] ending in the locative case follow a *dvandva* compound, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *kṛ*. Provided that the root *kṛ* is "accomplished" (*siddha*), meaning that it is not actually employed (*aprayoga*). This means that whether the root *kṛ* is used or not used, there is an absence of any difference in the perception of the specific meaning. For example, *anyathākāraṃ bhukte*, *evaṃkāram*, *kathaṃkāram*, or *itthaṃkāram* have the same meaning as *anyathā bhukte*, *evaṃ bhukte*, and so forth, as well as *anyathākāraṃ bhukte*, and so forth. Why is the word *siddhe* (provided that it is accomplished) mentioned? [Consider the counter-example: *śiro 'nyathā kṛtvā bhukte* ("having turned his head otherwise, he eats"). In this case, the root *kṛ* is actually employed, and thus the suffix is not applied.

In the expression "having done this" (*atra kṛtvā*), the head (*śiras*) functions as the object (*karman*). This status is not perceived without the employment of the verb *kṛ*; for the status of being an object is perceived only in relation to the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*). Otherwise, that [objectivity] would be perceived as residing solely in the action of eating and not as residing in the head; therefore, the employment of that [verb] is necessary.

Regarding this, they say: it was stated that "the use of an established [form] is prohibited" because it lacks utility; however, one should not be deluded into thinking it is because it is entirely fruitless. For if there were an absence of anteriority (*paurvakālya*) based on a distinction [of action] and a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), the suffix *ṇamul* itself would be difficult to obtain. Furthermore, it would result in the subversion of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the connection of verbal roots (*dhātusaṃbandha*). Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ṇamul* and its usage occur by the force of the specific rule (*vacana-sāmarthya*); for in that case, the suffix *ktvā*, which is desired as an alternative by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), would become impossible to obtain.

Otherwise, how could there be a refutation by treating what was raised as one thing and resolving it as another, given the usage in the Bhāṣya such as "kathaṃ kṛtvā" (how having done)? By this, the claim of their being ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*) as stated by Bhaṭṭapāda is refuted; for, just as forms ending in *ṇamul* are established by the force of the Sūtra, so too forms ending in *katvā*, even if they are semantically redundant, are justified as correct by the force of the Bhāṣya.

In reality, however, by words such as *anyathā* and others, a mode belonging to the general category of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is conveyed; and thus, in a form ending in *ṇamul*, it serves as a qualifier with respect to an action qualified by a specific mode of the meaning of the root *gam* (to go), or an action qualified by a result presented by roots such as *bhuj* (to eat). This is because even a single action, when differentiated by the coloring of its qualifiers, can admit the relation of qualifier and qualified. Nor is the resolution of the *ktvā* suffix through this adventitious distinction untraditional, for no tradition more authoritative than that of the Bhāṣyakāra himself is known to exist. [This applies to the rule: "The suffixes *yathā* and *tathā* are used in response to expressions of envy. (Pāṇini 5.1.98)

As before: "I shall eat in such a manner; I shall eat in that manner. What is this to you? It is unfit to be asked: 'How will you eat? This is the answer given out of envy (*asūyā*). Why "out of envy"? [In the absence of envy: "Having done so, I shall eat; he will see it accordingly. This is a statement of truth (*tattvākhyānam*). [The rule] *karmaṇi dṛśividoḥ sā kalye* (Pāṇini 3.4.29) [applies]: when the object of the roots *dṛś* ("to see") and *vid* ("to know") is used, the genitive case is employed provided there is a desire for welfare (*kālya*).

The suffix *ṇamul* is applied when these two [roots] have a word denoting an object (*karman*) as their subordinate term (*upapada*). The abundance (*bāhulya*) qualifies the object. For example: *kanyādarśaṃ varayati* ("He chooses [all] girls for marriage"). The meaning is "all the girls. In the case of *brāhmaṇavedaṃ bhojayati* ("He feeds the Brahmins until they know"), only roots whose meanings involve the acquisition of knowledge, reflection, or begging are included, and not the root *vid* in the sense of existence, because that is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Here, the intended meaning is totality or excellence: "girls delimited by being objects of sight" and "Brahmins delimited by being objects of knowledge.
Regarding the rule *yāvativindajīvoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.30): [The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the roots *vid* and *jīv* when followed by *yāvat* as an object.]

"He eats as much as this [plate]. This means "as much as he might obtain. This [usage] is commenced for the sake of expressing non-completeness (*asākalya*). "He performs the *agnihotra* as long as he lives. Through this, the pervasion of the act of offering by the duration of life is obtained.
[The suffix *yap* occurs after a word denoting a measure of capacity] when it expresses the filling of a skin or a stomach. (Pāṇini 5.2.37)

This is a reference to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *pṛ* (to fill), because no other [form] is transitive. Examples: *carmapūraṃ stṛṇāti* (he spreads so as to cover the hide); *udarapūraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats until his belly is full). The meaning is that the act of eating is sufficient for the filling of the belly. Here, a connection with the preceding time is impossible and is not even perceived. The same should be understood accordingly in other cases as well. [Pāṇini 3.4.31]:
*varṣapramāṇa ūlopaścāsya anyatarasyām* (When the measure is a year, there is optionally the elision of *ū* in this [root]).

When a word expressing an object (*karman*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is added to the root *pṛ* (to fill), and there is optionally the elision of the vowel *u* of the root. When the measure of rain is to be understood through the combination of the base, the suffix, and the *upapada*, the form *goḥpadapram* is used, as in "the rain fell to the depth of a cow's footprint" (*goḥpadapraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ*). This refers to an act of raining characterized by the filling of a cow's footprint; only its smallness is intended to be conveyed. For example: "The moon shone with rays that were like drops falling from a water-jar."

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: The rule "ūlopaścānyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.4.146) need not have been formulated. This is because the form *goḥ-padapram* is established simply by adding the suffix *kap* to the root *prā-pūraṇe*. Since it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), it possesses the status of an object (*karman*) and is neuter; furthermore, the use of the singular number for the case-ending is desired in such expressions as *ekena goḥ-padapreṇa*. Thus ends the section on the formation of *goḥ-padapra*. However, forms such as *goḥ-padaprantaram* are not desired. This is understood from the force of the Bhāṣya, which is intent upon rejecting the elision (*lopa*) [of the final vowel].

One might argue: "Since [the form] *nanugopadapūra* and others would also not be established by means of the suffix *ghañ*, let the suffix *ṇamul* also be rejected. Do not say so. For if it were formed with a *ghañ*-ending word denoting an instrument (*karaṇa*) in a genitive compound, the rule *thāthādi* would result in an udātta accent on the final syllable; whereas if it were a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a *ghañ*-ending word denoting a state (*bhāva*), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) would apply. However, in the case of *ṇamul*, because of the accent of the *liṭ* affix, the vowel *ū* becomes udātta; thus, there is no difference in the case of *goḥ padapram*. This is because, in the case of the suffix *kap*, the rule *thāthādi* results in an udātta accent on the final syllable.

Because, when there is elision of the *ṇamul* suffix and the *u*, the preceding element lacks the status of being the bearer of the acute accent (*udātta*), it becomes oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the whole word (*kṛtsvara*). Kaiyaṭa states: "Because, when there is elision of the *ṇamul* suffix and the *u*, the preceding element lacks the status of being the bearer of the acute accent, it becomes oxytone by virtue of the accent of the whole word.
[Pāṇini 6.2.130: *cele knopeḥ*.

When words meaning "clothing" (*cela*) are used as upapadas for the roots *kṣip* and *pū*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied. The inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is based on the [commentarial] explanation. Examples: *celaknopaṃ* or *vasanaknopaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained so much that the clothes made a noise"). The meaning is: to such an extent that the clothes make a sound by being struck by that water. [The rule continues: After the root *kaṣ*, when the words *nimūla* and *samūla* are used as upapadas, [the suffix *ṇamul* is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.4.34)

[The suffix] *ṇamul* is used only when [the preceding word denotes] an object (*karman*). In this context, there is no connection with the prior time-period (*pūrvakāla*). That from which the root has gone out is *nimūla*; that together with the root is *samūla*. The application of the base form (*prakṛti*) and the subsequent use (*anuprayoga*) of the verb will be stated in the case of *ṇamul*. One says *samūlākāṣam* or *nimūlakāṣam akāṣat*: the meaning is "he scrapes it up together with the root" or "he scrapes it down to the root. They say that the meaning of the base form of *ṇamul*, as qualified by the meaning of the subordinate word (*upapada*), serves as the qualifier for the meaning of the subsequent use.
[The suffix *ṇamul* is used after the root] *piṣ* when [the objects] *śuṣka*, *cūrṇa*, and *rūkṣa* are involved. (Pāṇini 3.4.35)

He grinds it dry; he grinds it into powder; he grinds it coarse. [The suffix *kha* is applied] after the roots *han*, *kṛñ*, and *grah* when combined with the words *samūla*, *akṛta*, and *jīva*. (Pāṇini 3.4.36)

He strikes with a total destruction; he performs what has not been done; he seizes by the life—meaning while alive. [This applies] to the root *han* when used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). || 37 ||

*pādaghātam hanti* means "he strikes with the foot. This [rule] is for the purpose of allowing the subsequent application of the verb according to its original form (*yathāvidhi-anuprayoga*), for the sake of the suffix *san*, and for the sake of non-compounding (*asamāsa*). However, it should be understood that in the case of the rule *hiṃsārthānām*, there is a connection with other verbal roots (*dhātvaṃtara-sambandha*), and by the rule *tṛtīyā-prabhṛtīni anyatarasyām*, there is an option regarding compounding (*samāsa-vikalpa*).
[The next rule is: *snehane piṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.46).

When the word expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) by which something is made unctuous (*snehya*) is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇamul* is added to the root *piṣ*. In *udapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*, the substitution of *uda-* [for *udaka-*, meaning "water"] occurs according to the rule *peṣaṃ-vasityādi*. The meaning is "he grinds with water. For this very reason, the mention of "making unctuous" (*snehanagrahaṇa*) was not included in the rule *śuṣka-ādi-sūtra*, because in that context, only the object (*karman*) is carried over.
[The next rule is: *haste vartigrahoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.38).

The term *hasta* is used here to signify "taking" (*grahaṇa*), as established by the commentary. *Hastavartaṃ vartayati* means "he rolls with his hand," or *karavartaṃ vā*. The meaning is that he makes a pill with his hand. *Hastagrāhaṃ gṛṇhāti* means "he seizes with his hand"; the sense is simply "with the hand. [Sūtra 40:
*sve puṣaḥ* (the suffix *ṇamul* is added after the root *puṣ* when the object is one's own).

"In the sense of the instrument" (karaṇe) alone [is understood]. It was stated previously that "sva" includes synonyms for its own form as well as specific instances. One nourishes one's own prosperity (svapoṣaṃ puṣṇāti), or the prosperity of wealth (dhanapoṣaṃ), or the prosperity of cattle (gopoṣaṃ).
"In the sense of the locus, [the suffix is used] with the root *bandh*" (adhikaraṇe bandhaḥ) || 41 ||
The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *bandh* (to bind) when the object is a wheel (*cakra*). It means "he binds in a wheel-pattern. [This applies] when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). 42.

This undertaking is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *anadhikaraṇa* (non-receptacle). [Examples: *krauñcabandhaṃ baddhaḥ* (bound in the *krauñca* posture), *mayūrikābandham*, *aṭṭālikābandham*. These are technical names for specific types of bonds.
[The suffix *kta* is used] for the two agents (*kartṛ*), namely the living being (*jīva*) and the person (*puruṣa*), but not after the roots *śvi* and *hu*. (43)
*jīvanāśam* means "the destruction of life"; *jīvaḥ* is the meaning. *puruṣavāham* means "carrying a man"; *puruṣaḥ* is the meaning.
[The suffix *kha* occurs] after *śuṣi* and *pūra* when preceded by *ūrdhva*. (44)

When the agent is the meaning [of the action], and *ūrdhva* (upwards) is the accompanying word (*upapada*), [the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied]. For example: *ūrdhvaśoṣaṃ śuṣyati* ("it dries while standing upright"). The meaning is that a tree or similar object dries while remaining upright and without having fallen. *Ūrdhvapūraṃ pūryate* ("it is filled while standing upright"). The meaning is that a jar or similar object is filled with rainwater and so forth while its opening faces upwards.
[The suffix *lyuṭ* is also applied] when the object (*karman*) is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). (Pāṇini 3.4.45)

And [the suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). "In the battle, look at him who is like the sun in the heat of summer," so said others; yet that lord of the earth moves again, following the movements of Pārtha. Regarding this, the *bodha* has been examined by us in the *Alaṃkāra-kaustubha*:
"In the case of roots such as *kaṣ*, there is the subsequent employment of the root according to its original form (*yathāvidhi-anuprayoga*). (Pāṇini 3.4.46)

The verbal root itself, which is the base of the *ṇamul* suffix, must be employed as an auxiliary (*anuprayuj*) for the purpose of manifesting specific number, tense, and so forth; this is clear from the examples.
[Pāṇini 3.4.47: "When the third case ending is present, *upadaṃśa* [is used with *ṇamul*]."

From this point forward is the connection with the preceding section. Regarding the rule *tṛtīyā-prabhṛtīny anyatarasyām*, there is an option for compounding (*samāsa-vikalpa*). One eats with radish as a side-dish (*mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*), or *mūlakenopadaṃśam*. Since the radish functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of eating, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is applied. Nor is it the case that, because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) with the agent of the side-dish (*upadaṃśin*), the suffix and the compound would be untenable; for they are established by taking the objecthood (*karmatva*) to be based on the meaning (*ārtha*). This is due to the force of the inclusion of the word "third" (*tṛtīyā*); otherwise, the rule would have simply said "in the sense of the instrument" (*karaṇe*).
And [the same applies] to verbs meaning injury (*hiṃsārtha*) when they share the same object (*samānakarmaka*). (48)

When a word ending in the third case is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is added after roots meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsārtha*), provided there is identity of the object between that which is the base of the suffix and the root that is subsequently employed (*anuprayujyamāna*). Examples: *daṇḍopaghātaṃ gāḥ kalayati* (he drives the cows by striking them with a stick), *daṇḍenopaghātam*, *daṇḍatāḍam*, *daṇḍena tāḍam*. [The root] *taḍ* meaning "to strike" belongs to the *carādi* group. In both cases, the cow alone is the object. Why say "identity" (*samāna*)? Consider: *daṇḍena coramāhatya gāḥ kalayati* (having struck the thief with a stick, he drives the cows). Here, the difference in objects is clear. And when a word ending in the seventh case is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is added after the roots *pīḍ*, *rudh*, and *karṣ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.49)

In the case of *pīḍā* and so forth, when they form a collective dvandva compound, the term "beginning with *pīḍā*" (*pīḍādi*) is a compound in which the final member has been elided (*uttarapadalopin*). The masculine gender and the change in case-ending are due to the archaic nature of the Sūtra (*sautratvāt*). The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after verbs preceded by *upa*, provided that a word ending in either the seventh or third case is present as an upapada (governing word). Examples: *pārśvopapīḍaṃ śete* ("he lies down pressing against his sides"). This can be analyzed as *pārśvayor upapīḍam* ("pressing against the two sides") or *pārśvābhyām upapīḍam* ("pressing with the two sides"). *vrajoparodhaṃ gāḥ sthāpayati* ("he stops the cows by blocking the pen"). This can be analyzed as *vraje uparodham* ("blocking in the pen") or *vrajena uparodham* ("blocking with the pen"). *pāṇyupakarṣaṃ dhānāḥ saṃgṛhṇāti* ("he gathers the parched grains by pulling them with his hand"). This can be analyzed as *pāṇāv upakarṣam* ("pulling in the hand").

The mention of the root *karṣati* with the long vowel (*ā*) is intended to indicate the presence of the *guṇa* substitution [to form *karṣati*], and it serves to exclude roots such as *tud* (from the *tudādi* class). This is because, although that root (*tud*) shares the meaning of "smearing," it refers only to the act of scratching or ploughing a field, as evidenced by the usage *pañcabhir halaiḥ kṛṣati* ("he ploughs with five ploughs"). Therefore, the learned authorities maintain that from that [root *tud*] one cannot derive the form *upakṛṣya* after *kṣetre* or *hale* using the suffix *ktvā*, but rather [the suffix] *ṇamul*.
[This applies to the rule concerning] proximity (*samāsatti*). || 50 ||

When the previously mentioned words are used as upapadas (governing words), the suffix *ṇamul* is applied to a verbal root when "proximity" (*saṃnikarṣa*) is to be understood. For example: *keśagrāhaṃ yudhyante* ("they fight seizing by the hair"), meaning "having seized [them] by the hair. *Hastagrāham* ("seizing by the hand") means "having seized [them] by the hands. Here, the specific mention of "hair" (*keśa*) is not restrictive; the intended meaning is proximity in general. [The rule applies to] measurement (*pramāṇa*). (Pāṇini 3.4.51)

The word *upādām* is used in the sense of "previously. One cuts a piece (*khaṇḍikā*) with an elevation of two finger-breadths; that is, by measuring it with two finger-breadths. A short fragment is called a *khaṇḍikā*. [This occurs] in the sense of the ablative case when there is a desire for completeness (*parīpsā*). (Pāṇini 3.4.52)
