When the word *apādāna* (the point of departure) is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇamul* is added to a verbal root when haste is implied. [For example: "First, upon rising from her bed, that daughter of Vidarbha—either having risen from her bed or [while still on it]—[beheld him].
This applies also in the case of the second [verse]. (53)

"Tvārāyam" (in the phrase *tvārāyam*) is an example. They fight while grasping the sacrificial staff (*yaṣṭigrāham*); they fight while grasping clods of earth (*loṣṭagrāham*). Regarding the rule "a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]," the intended meaning here is that even in this case, the unaccented portion must be pronounced without delay.
[The next rule is: "In the case of a body part, if it is not fixed. (Pāṇini 6.2.177)

The same applies in the second case. *Dhruvatva* (steadfastness) is the state of being the counter-positive of the absence of life. He describes the movement of the eyebrows: "the movement of the eyebrows. Why [is it not used] in *adhruka*? One speaks while raising the head. And also when one is suffering. (55)

When a body part denoted by a word ending in the second case is being afflicted in its entirety, the suffix *ṇamul* is used. For example: *uraḥ pratipeṣaṃ yudhyante*, meaning "they fight while crushing the entire chest. Also: *urovidāre praticaskare nakhaiḥ* ("he scratched at the chest with his claws until it was torn"). This undertaking is for the sake of something unstable.
[The rule applies] when there is repeated practice (*māna*) or habitual action (*āsevyamāna*). (Pāṇini 3.4.56)

In the second [sūtra], *ṇamul* is prescribed after roots such as *viś* when the sense of being pervaded (*vyāpyamāna*) or being repeatedly performed (*āsevyamāna*) is to be understood. Examples: *gehānupraveśam āste* (he sits while entering the house), *gehaṃ-geham anupraveśam*, *geham-anupraveśam*, *anupraveśam-anupraveśam*. In the case of a compound, there is no reduplication, because by that very nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyena*), those two meanings are already expressed. However, in the non-compound form, there is optional reduplication of both the subordinate term (*upapada*) and the *ṇamul*-ending form. Although *ṇamul* was previously prescribed for the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), it is prescribed again here with the words "in the case of repeated performance" (*āsevāyām*) for the purpose of establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "subordinate term" (*upapada*).

Therefore, there is an option regarding the compound. Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the complete connection of the meanings of the subordinate words with the actions denoted by the base of the *ṇamul* suffix; this is because words such as "house" (*geha*) are intended to denote specific instances of those [actions]. Repetition of an action is "practice" (*āsevā*).
[The suffix *ṇamul* is used] after the roots *as* (to throw) and *tṛṣ* (to thirst) when another action occurs within [the time of] the [action of] time. (Pāṇini 3.4.57)

*kriyāntara* means that which intervenes between two actions. The suffix *ṇamul* is added after the roots *as* (to throw) and *tṛṣ* (to thirst), when they denote an action that intervenes between the action expressed by the immediately preceding verb and another action, provided that words denoting time ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) are used as attendant words (*upapada*). Examples: *dvyahātyāsaṃ gāḥ pāyayati* (he makes the cows drink [water] with an interval of two days); *dvyahenātyāsam*; *dvyahatarṣam*. The meaning is: having made them drink today, he makes them drink again after two days have passed. However, in this [verse]: *lihate rātrītarṣaṃ rathāṅgavihaṅgamā madhu nijavadhūvaktrāmbhoje’dhunādhara-nāmakam* (the cakravāka birds now lick the honey called "lower lip" on the lotus-faces of their own wives, with an interval of one night). [Note: The commentary explains that here the intervention is not by time, but by the action of licking itself.]
Thus ends the illustrious Harṣa;
[the suffix] nāmni follows the root ā-diś preceded by graha. (58)
The female cakravāka birds,
their tongues parched by separation and utterly distraught, call out repeatedly,
addressing their companion by name.
Thus says Śrī Harṣa.
In the sense of expressing something contrary to one's intention, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are used after the root *kṛ*. (59)

*Ayathābhipreta* is a qualifier of the act of telling; it means "in an undesired manner. [The sūtra] *uccaiḥkṛtya*, *uccaiḥkṛtvā*, or *uccaiḥkāram* refers to one who tells something unpleasant. Even though the telling itself may not be undesirable, it should be understood that the undesirability lies in the aspect of the manner, such as its loudness. [Next: *tiryacyapavarge* (Pāṇini 3.4.60).

When the word *tiryak* is used as an upapada, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied after the root *kṛ*, provided that completion (*samāpti*) is understood. Examples: *tiryakkṛtya* or *tiryakkāram āgataḥ*. The meaning is "having completed. Why [is it said] "not when there is displacement" (*apavarga*)? Example: *tiryakkṛtvā kāṣṭham gataḥ*. The meaning is: "having placed it sideways because it was not straight, [he has gone] having moved it from the front to the side. The *Bhāṣya* states that *tiryac* is a Vedic (sautra) form. Kaiyaṭa says: "The objection regarding the loss of the form being imitated is not a valid refutation, for the persistence of a specific purpose is not a criterion [for determining the correct form]. [The rule] *svāṅge tas-pratyaye kṛ-bhv-oḥ* || 61 || [is stated]. (This refers to the subsequent sūtra.)

When such a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows as a subsequent member, and when that which is one's own limb (*svāṅga*) is the subordinate word (*upapada*)—that is to say, when the entire complex consisting of that [limb] and the suffix is the subordinate word; for a mere limb cannot function as a subordinate word by itself. Examples: *mukhataḥ kṛtya*, *mukhataḥ kṛtvā*, or having gone after having made [it] "in front of the face" (*mukhataḥ kāram*); *mukhatobhūya*, *mukhato bhūtvā*, or having come to the state of being "in front of the face" (*mukhato bhāvam*). The suffix *tasi* occurs in the sense of the locative case due to the inclusion of the root *adi*. Why is the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) necessary? [Consider: *mukhatā* ("the state of being in the face"). Here, the suffix *kip* is applied to the root *tasu* (meaning "to perish") after the word *mukha*. The commentary states: *mukhataḥ kṛtvā*.

Some maintain that since the desired result is already established by the *paribhāṣā* "when a suffix is mentioned [it denotes something beginning with that suffix]," the explicit mention of the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is indeed redundant. Others hold that there is no authority for that *paribhāṣā*.
[The rule] "not before a suffix having the sense of *nañ*, nor before one having the sense of *cvī*" (6.3.76) [is stated].

The suffixes *arth* (in *dhārtha*), as well as *dhamuñ* and others, do not include the negative particle (*nañ*) or its derivatives (*nānā*, *vinā*). In that context, when a word meaning "becoming different" (*cvyartha*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied after the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. Examples: *nānākṛtya*, *nānākṛtvā*, *nānākāram*; *vinākṛtya*, *vinākṛtvā*, *vinākāram*; *nānābhūya*, *nānābhūtvā*, *nānābhāvam*. Similarly: *ekadhā bhūya*, and so forth. Why is there the mention of "not being a suffix" (*apratyayagrahaṇa*)? [Because] in cases such as *hiruk kṛtvā* and *pṛthak kṛtvā*, the mention of the "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*) serves a purpose even when a suffix is present, as seen in rules like *dvitryośca dhamuñ*.

By carrying forward the phrase *tadvidhaudha* (a collection of those), under the view that [the suffix] is a substitute for that, the result is established through the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule. Thus, one should cite as an example the suffix *ḍa*, prescribed by the rule *dhamuñantātsvārthe ḍaḥ* after words ending in *dhamuñ*. Kaiyaṭa states that the mention of the word *artha* is also for the purpose of including *añ*; otherwise, according to the *paribhāṣā* regarding suffixes without an indicatory letter (*aniranubandhaka*), only the first [of the two *añ* suffixes] would be included in the rule *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau*.
[The next rule is: *tuṣṇīmi bhuvaḥ* || 63 ||
*tūṣṇīṃbhūya*, *tūṣṇīṃbhūtvā*, and *tūṣṇīṃbhāvam*. The inclusion of the suffix *bhū* (in *bhūya* and *bhūtvā*) is for the purpose of excluding the root *kṛ*. [Next:
*anvacyā* is used in the sense of favorability (*anulomya*). 64.

Regarding the form *anūcī*, the *Bhāṣya* states that although *anūcī* would be expected, the Vedic (sautra) reading is *anvacī*. *Ānulomya* means favorability (*ānukūlya*). [The example is] *anvagbhūyāste*. This means "having become favorable" (*anvagbhūtvā*) or "having become favorable" (*anvagbhāvam*); that is, having become favorable from the front, the side, or the back, he remains. Since the word *anvak* refers merely to favorability, there is no restrictive factor for its application to a specific location. Dīkṣita maintains that if favorability is already obtained through some other means of knowledge, the suffix *ṇamul* does not apply to the word *anvak* because it does not convey that [favorability] [as a primary object]; rather, only the suffix *ktvā* applies.

The suffix *tumun* is used after the roots *śak* (to be able), *dhṛṣ* (to dare), *jñā* (to know), *glai* (to be weary), *ghaṭ* (to strive), *rabh* (to begin), *labh* (to obtain), *kram* (to step), and *sah* (to endure), when they have the sense of "being capable," "deserving," or "possessing. (Pāṇini 3.4.65)

The present section begins for the purpose of explaining the meaning of verbal roots that do not denote action (*akriyārtha*). [Examples: *bhoktum śaknoti* ("he is able to eat")—the meaning is "he endures" or "he knows. When the root *bhuj* (to eat) is construed as the object (*viṣaya*), proficiency therein is understood. In *glāyati* ("he is weary"), however, incapacity is meant. In *ghaṭate* and *arhati* ("he is fit/entitled"), capability is meant. In *ārabhate*, *utsahate*, and *prakramate* ("he undertakes/exerts himself"), effort (*prayatna*) is meant. In *labhate* ("he obtains"), the absence of refusal by another agent is meant. In *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyate* ("it exists/is"), mere possibility is meant; such is the distinction.
[This applies] to words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*) in the sense of "being able to" (*alam*). (66)

*Paryāpti* (sufficiency) is non-deficiency (*anyūnatvam*). Here, the meaning of *alam* is "capacity" (*sāmarthyam*), as established by the commentary. In the case of words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti-vacana*), being qualified by capacity is to be understood through the relation of denotative power (*bodhakatva*). Alternatively, the term *alam-artha* here refers to a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its meaning is "that which denotes sufficiency while possessing the capacity to denote [it]. Thus, the suffix *tumun* is used when the attendant word (*upapada*) denotes a capacity qualified by sufficiency, as in examples such as *paryāpto bhoktum pravīṇaḥ* ("capable/skilled enough to eat") or *kuśalaḥ*. Why say "in the case of sufficiency"? (To exclude cases like *alaṃ mallo mallāya*, where *alam* means "enough" in the sense of "stopping," not "sufficiency").

*Alam* [is used] with the gerund (*kta*) in the sense of "enough. *Alam bhuktvā* ("Enough of eating"). *Alam artheṣu kim?* ("What is the use of wealth?"). *Paryāptam bhuṅkte* ("He eats sufficiently"). Here, mere abundance is understood, not capability. However, the inclusion of the term *śaki* (capability) in the preceding rule was so that the suffix *tumun* might occur when there is ease or possibility. The kṛt suffixes [are introduced] when the agent is expressed. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.67)

A *kṛt* suffix shall occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Examples include *pācakaḥ* (cook) and *pakta* (one who cooks), and so forth. This is a general rule (*utsarga*). Now, one might object: this rule is not for the purpose of excluding the sense of "action" (*bhāva*), because the intended meaning is established by the very force of the context. For instance, let the rule simply be *ghan*; since it is taught with the sense of "action" (*bhāva*) indicated [by the previous rule], it would apply there. Following that, one should read the rule *pada-ruja-viśa-spṛśaḥ*. In this way, since the sense of action is already established, the explicit mention of "action" (*bhāva*) is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*): namely, that *ghan* alone occurs in the sense of action, and no other suffix does. Consequently, since the *kṛt* suffix is established in the sense of the agent, which is implied by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), [the agent is understood].

Nor can it be argued that [the suffix] is for the purpose of excluding the agent, since the agent is already implied by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*). This is because the rule *dhaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran* is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the suffix *ṣṭran* occurs only when the object is present, and not otherwise. Furthermore, even in the absence of such a restriction on the suffix, there is no possibility of its application to other *kārakas*, because there is no other rule prescribing it; or rather, because of another restrictive rule stating that *ṣṭran* occurs only when the object is present.

For even when other *kārakas* are intended, specific rules are prescribed for the desired suffixes: namely, that suffixes denoting the instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*) [apply to those meanings], while *dāśagha* and *oghan* apply to the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and *bhīma* and others apply to the point of departure (*apādāna*). Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), suffixes such as *ṇvul* occur only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended; this is because, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the application of this rule is not accepted when [the suffixes] are prescribed for other *kārakas*.

Nor should it be argued that there is a restriction regarding the agent [in the rule] *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukanau*, because of the rule *kartari carṣidevatayoḥ*; for in both cases, since the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) serves as an injunction [to include the agent], the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*) would have been excluded from both. This is not so. For although that [word "instrument"] is excluded by that restriction with respect to the external state (*bāhyabhāva*), it remains for the purpose of excluding the internal state (*ābhyantarabhāva*). This distinction has been demonstrated in the rule *sārvadhātuke yak*.

It might be argued as follows: even so, suffixes such as *khyun* would still apply in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Nor should it be said that these [suffixes] serve as exceptions (*apavāda*) because they have the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; for the two rules constitute distinct sentences (*nānāvākya*). It is only in a sentence uttered together—such as "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya"—that the buttermilk serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the curd. However, when the giving of curd is prescribed for the morning and the giving of buttermilk for the afternoon, such sublation does not occur.

It should not be argued that this contradicts the principle that when the *mika-paribhāṣā* and the *alontya-paribhāṣā* form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), they stand in the relation of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) to one another, whereas when they form separate syntactical units (*bhinnavākyatva*), they stand in the relation of "exception" (*apavāda*). This is because there is a disparity between the two cases. In the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the genitive in *aṅgasya* denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) in view of the *ik* vowels; thus, the meaning of the sentence is "of the *ik* which is a part of the *aṅga*. Since there is no evidence for a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) here, the *alontyasya* rule does not apply. Consequently, [the present rule] effectively functions as an exception to that [general rule].

In this case, however, because it is possible to prescribe suffixes such as *khyun* for the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth by means of the general term "action" (*bhāva*) and the specific term "object" (*karman*), both [the agent and the object] are possible alternatively even when the two meanings are not expressed simultaneously. For this very reason, the restrictive particle *eva* in the rule *tayoreva* (Pāṇini 3.4.70) is appropriate; otherwise, since the agent would already be sublated by the object and the action, there would be no purpose for that particle as a means of excluding [other roles]. Thus, by making known the co-occurrence [of the agent and the object] elsewhere, the mention of the word *vā* ("or") in the rule *bhavyageyādi* (Pāṇini 3.4.68) need not be made.

Even though they are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the passive and middle voices (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*) is logically possible. In the rule *kartari carṣidevatayoḥ*, the particle *ca* (and) serves to include the instrumental (*karaṇa*); it indicates that there is no such co-occurrence [between the agent and the instrument].

Although there is no evidence [for the application of the rule] because the suffix is prescribed when the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the deity (*devatā*) is the agent (*kartṛ*), thus precluding their simultaneous occurrence, nevertheless, the intention of the Vārttika is that the "correspondence in number" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) is not intended here. Furthermore, the particle *eva* in the phrase "of those two only" (*tayoreva*) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The meaning of the sentence is: "The kṛtya suffixes occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," and "the words beginning with *bhavya* occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Some say that the rule for *bhavya* and so on (*bhavyādi-sūtra*) need not be formulated at all. Others hold that the kṛtya suffixes and others will not occur in the sense of the agent due to non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). Such, then, is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) according to the Vārttika.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, say: since the sublation of a general rule (*utsarga*) by an exception (*apavāda*) is established by logic (*nyāya*), there is no need for an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, the indication provided by the particle *ca* is untenable according to the reasoning already stated. As for the argument that [the two rules] belong to different locations (*nānādeśatvāt*), that is incorrect; for we observe that even sentences belonging to different times within a treatise form a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatva*) by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). In the second case, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *gotre 'lug ac-i* is accepted as an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision [prescribed by *gotre 'lug ac-i*] itself when applied to the fourth and sixth cases before a following word (*uttarapada*). This was stated by Bhartṛhari: "Even when many [rules] are joined together, a sentence consists of the general rule and its exceptions."
Some maintain that it is indeed one, though it exists as if having diverse forms.
When that is the case, there is restriction, prohibition, and specification;
they know that which is called elision (luk) in the second [chapter] to be the remainder of that elision (alūka).

The particle *eva*, however, serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Its placement after the rule "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*) is for the sake of making known their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*). Furthermore, the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the rule concerning *bhavya* and other such terms need not be made. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of co-occurrence in cases such as "the *dāśagha* and *augha* affixes [denote] the recipient" (*saṃpradāne*), because by the rule "the *kta*-affix in the sense of the beginning of an action [denotes] the agent," the desired result is already established; the inclusion of the particle *ca* (in the subsequent rule) makes it known that from this point onward, there is no co-occurrence.

In this context, the discussion in the Bhāṣya is for the purpose of establishing the point that "the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. The first position is based on the acceptance of words as being products (*kārya*), while the second position is based on the acceptance of words as being eternally established (*siddha*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that suffixes such as *khyun* would acquire the technical designation *kṛt*. This is because there is an investigation into whether the designation *kṛt* applies to *khyun* and others—either on the grounds that "here too, *khyun* occurs in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*)" or that "whatever functions by its own nature is correct (*sādhutva*)". Consequently, since the designation *kṛt*, which is governed with respect to every suffix, would apply to *khyun* and others, the first position is not tenable.

Because a fault would arise in the case of the form *kāṣṭhabhidbrāhmaṇa*. To explain: even the suffix *aṇ* in *kāṣṭhabheda* denotes the agent only by virtue of a specific rule (*vacana*). Since there is no distinction between the various forms of the vowel *a*, the *a* of the word *brāhmaṇa* would also denote the agent by virtue of that same rule. Consequently, if it were designated as a *kṛt* suffix, the case endings (*svādi*) would be produced [after *brāhmaṇa*]. If it were designated as a *pratyaya* (suffix), then, based on the designation of the stem (*aṅga*) caused by that suffix, the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix would apply. Nor can it be argued that it lacks the status of an *ārddhadhātuka* because it is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), for in this instance the word *kāṣṭha* is the object complement (*upapada*).

The root is *bhid* (to split). Since the letter *a* follows it, there is no distinction from the word *kāṣṭhabheda* (wood-splitter); thus, it is difficult to establish that this [suffix] was prescribed for this particular root and not another, because the status of denoting the agent would be unavoidable even for that [other word]. This is because suffixes prescribed by one's own grammatical rule are restricted to specific meanings by this [rule]. Nor should it be argued that, since the *kvip* suffix has been elided, the root itself is employed there in the sense of the agent and not the letter *a*; for it is logical that the specific form as a whole—just like *yāvaka* and other such words—possesses that meaning.

[Objection: There is no fault in restricting the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [of *kṛt*]. For here, in common usage, the suffix *kta* does not have the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), but rather the sense of negation; thus, the designations of *kṛt* and *pratyaya* do not apply. [Reply: This is not so. In cases such as *vibhaktā bhrātaraḥ* ("the brothers divided") and *pītā gāvaḥ* ("the cows drank"), since the *kta* suffix—which by its very nature denotes the agent—is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "brothers" and "cows," it would follow that it is correct (*sādhutva*) when used in the sense of the agent. Furthermore, the occurrence of words denoting the agent through the relation of action and factor (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) in such cases is not intended.

If, however, the position is that the rule restricts the *pratyaya* (suffix), then there would be no fault; for according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka...* (Pāṇini 3.4.72), the suffix *kta* following those verbal roots enumerated therein is restricted to the agent (*kartṛ*), and since the roots *bhaj* and *pib* are not enumerated there, [the suffix] would apply to the agent. Do not say so. For even in the position that the rule restricts the *saṃjñā* (technical name), the operation of the sūtra *gatyarthākarmaka...* is indeed present. By accepting that the *kta* following those roots is by its very nature denotative of the agent and is designated as a *kṛt* suffix, the stated *kta* would fail to achieve correctness when applied to the agent.

Therefore, it is established that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of words existing in their respective meanings by virtue of their own nature is explained through the prescription of technical names (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*). As for the words *vibhakta* and *pīta*, they are correct only when derived as agent-nouns (*karma-vyutpanna*), because the class beginning with *arśas-ādi* is an open-ended group (*ākṛti-gaṇa*); thus, the correctness [of *vibhakta-uṣāḥ* and *pīta-uṣāḥ*] is based on the fact that "wealth is divided" and "water is drunk" by them. Alternatively, the state of being divided residing in the wealth is superimposed upon the brothers, and the state of being drunk residing in the water is superimposed upon the cows; such is the general direction. [The suffix *anīyar* is applied after verbal roots ending in vowels to form nouns denoting the object or the action itself, provided they are used in the sense of the future (*bhavya*), the singable (*geya*), the worthy of instruction (*pravacanīya*), the worthy of attendance (*upasthānīya*), the producible (*janya*), the washable (*āplāvya*), the fallible (*āpātya*), or the obtainable (*āvāpya*):
*bhavya-geya-pravacanīya-upasthānīya-janya-āplāvya-āpātya-āvāpyāḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.68)

These *kṛtya* suffixes ending in *-ya*, etc., are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) as if they were agentive (*kartari*). In some cases, however, they also apply to the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: *bhavyaḥ* means "he who is to become" (*bhavati*), or "that which is to be brought about by him" (*bhavyam anena*). *Geyaḥ māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* means "the boy who sings the Sāmans," or "the Sāmans that are to be sung by the boy. Vācaspatimiśra maintains that in forms such as *rajanīya*, *kopanīya*, and *mohanīya*, the *kṛtya* suffixes denote the agent because these are included in the list of *bhavya-geya-ādi*. Although this is not a class-based group (*ākṛtigaṇa*), since only specific items like *bhavya-geya-ādi* are enumerated in the rule (*sūtra*), it is not a general category.

Nevertheless, the reading [of *pravacanīya*] in that [sūtra] should be accepted because of its frequent usage by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Udayanācārya maintains that this is so because Pāṇini himself has demonstrated an exception (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the rule *karmapravacanīyāḥ*. Nor should it be argued that this is inconsistent because the word *pravacanīya* is read in the aforementioned sūtra; for in that case, the suffix is prescribed in the sense of the present tense (*vartamāna*), whereas in the rule *karmapravacanīyāḥ*, its application in the past tense (*bhūta*) is intended. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa and others have explained that in that instance, the suffix *anīyar* occurs in the sense of the past agent (*bhūte kartari*) due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). *Laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* || 69 ||

The particle *ca* (and) serves to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) from both preceding rules. Thus, after transitive roots (*sakarmaka*), the *lakāras* (tense-mood markers) express the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*); however, after intransitive roots (*akarmaka*), they express the state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). For example: *pacyate* (is cooked) and *pacati* (cooks); *bhūyate* (is/exists) and *bhavati* (becomes). Regarding this, some say that *iha* (here) refers to the nominative case (*prathamā*). Others hold that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in relation to the substitutes (*ādeśa*). The *lakāra* is twofold, distinguished as those that result in verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-bhāvin*) and those that do not (*atiṅ-bhāvin*). Among these, those that result in verbal suffixes—due to the absence of the technical designation *kṛt*—do not trigger the application of the rule *kartari kṛt* (P. 3.4.67), and thus they denote their own inherent meaning, which is the state (*bhāva*).
Since the rule "kṛt affixes [denote] the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67) would result in the suffix *atiṅ* being correct only when denoting the agent, this present sūtra is commenced.

It might be argued as follows: Since the *ātmanepada* endings are prescribed for the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), and the *parasmaipada* endings for the agent (*kartṛ*) when [the verb] is "otherwise" (*śeṣāt*), it is inferred that the meanings of the *l*-suffixes—or rather, of their substitutes which are present in actual usage—are the passive, the object, and the agent. This is because the *l*-suffix is not established independently of these two sets of terminations; even though the *l*-suffix exists as the basis for the *ām*-periphrastic construction, it is removed by elision (*luk*). Furthermore, in the absence of a restrictive rule, there would be no contingency of the *l*-suffix occurring in the sense of the passive even after transitive verbs—such as the undesirable consequence that one could say *pacyate yavāgūṃ devadattena* ("The gruel is being cooked by Devadatta")—because the rule *bhāvakarmaṇor akarmakāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.13) precludes such an occurrence.

Furthermore, the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) by implication refers to the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), because for intransitive verbs, an object is impossible. Thus, the meaning of "being" inferred for the *l*-suffix (the verbal suffix) pertains exclusively to the domain of intransitive verbs, and the desired result is established. Nor should it be argued that there is redundancy in mentioning "intransitive" there [in Pāṇini 1.3.26], since it is present here as well; nor should it be said that the mention of "intransitive" here is necessary solely for the sake of the rule *tayoreva* (Pāṇini 3.4.70), and that this very mention benefits the *l*-suffix as well.

Since only these two—*karmaṇi* and *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*—are to be recited here from those two [rules], you should read the word *laḥ* here, whereas I have read the word *akarmaka* in the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*. This is because there is an equality in the inclusion of two words; for the sake of a mere slight economy of syllables (*mātrālāghava*) was not intended here.

Nor should it be argued that because the suffix *śānac* bears the technical designation *ātmanepada*, it follows from the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" that it denotes only the passive and impersonal (bhāva) voices; consequently, in forms such as *śayānaḥ* ("lying down"), the suffix would not occur when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). For even under the view that [the rule] is newly introduced (*ārambhapakṣe*), the suffix *śānac* is established for the agent as well, since its occurrence is secured by rules such as "anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam," which prescribe the *ātmanepada* endings for the agent.

Alternatively, the scope of the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) is such as in *āsyate* ("is sat") or *pacyate* ("is cooked"), because in those cases, due to the absence of the designation *kṛt*, the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) does not apply. As for the suffix *āna*, while both rules (*kartari kṛt* and *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*) would otherwise apply, it arises only in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) because of its subsequent position in the order of rules. Nor does there arise the contingency of [the suffix *āna*] applying to the agent after roots of the *parasmaipada* class; for by the restrictive rule that the *ātmanepada* occurs only after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*, and not after any other, that contingency is excluded.

And it should not be argued that, if *anudāttaṅitaḥ* were thus a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) for the suffix *śānac* with respect to specific roots, then *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* endings) and *āna* would not occur, because there would be no rule (*vidhāyaka*) prescribing them for those roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*. This is because it is impossible for a single sentence to possess both the nature of a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*). For the sentence *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* serves as the restrictive rule, while the second sentence, which recurs from *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, serves as the prescriptive rule.

Indeed, if *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* (Pāṇini 1.3.12) were to form a single syntactic unit with *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13), the meaning of that single sentence would be: "The Ātmanepada suffixes occur after roots ending in an anudātta vowel or marked with Ṅ or Ṇ, when the sense is that of a passive or a state (bhāva). Consequently, forms such as *guruṇā āsyate* ("the teacher is being sat upon") and *gurur atiśayyate* ("the teacher is being surpassed") would be possible. However, because the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* would then serve as a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) for the independent application of the Ātmanepada, the suffix *śānac* would not occur after roots that are inherently Parasmaipada. Thus, in examples such as *bhūyate* ("it is being") and *gamyate* ("it is being gone"), the Ātmanepada would not occur, since those roots are distinct from those ending in an anudātta vowel or marked with Ṅ/Ṇ. Furthermore, in cases such as *āste* ("he sits") and *śete* ("he lies"), the Ātmanepada would not occur in the active sense (*kartari*), because there would be no provision for it.

It is not so; for the desired result is established through the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*). First, there is the rule: "The *ātmanepada* affixes follow roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*, in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Following that, there is another rule: "In the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), when the suffix *iC* follows. Here, the phrase "marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or *ṅ*" is carried over (*anuvṛtti*), while "in the sense of the abstract action or the object" is discontinued. Thereafter, "in the sense of the agent" is carried over. Both "in the sense of the abstract action or the object" and "marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or *ṅ*" are discontinued. Consequently, by the rule "in the sense of the agent when *iC* follows," the *ātmanepada* is prescribed after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or *ṅ* in the sense of the agent. Since the *ātmanepada* endings are prescribed for the agent in sentences such as "after the root *viś* preceded by *ni*," everything is logically consistent—this being the position reached.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because of the aforementioned contradiction, the suffix *ana* would necessarily apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because in examples such as *bhūyamānaṃ* and *gamyamānaṃ*, its application to the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) is untenable. If, however, the word *la* (referring to verbal suffixes) is included here, then in the case where [the suffix] is sixth-case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), there is no scope for it; rather, by the rule *tiṅ-kartari-kṛt*, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others take precedence due to their higher status. Thus, the meaning of *ana* is determined by this very rule, and its establishment is secured through a systematic distribution among the action, the object, and the agent. In the alternative view where [the suffix] is first-case-ending (*prathamānta*), its scope is the *tiṅ* suffixes expressing the action (*bhāva*) and the future tense (*lṛkara*).

Regarding the rule *kartari kṛt*, it has already been stated previously. However, since the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) has not yet appeared [at that point], the determination of its meaning is made by this very [rule] due to its subsequent position; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the *śatṛ* and *kvasu* suffixes would also apply to the passive and middle voices (*bhāva-karman*) because this [present rule] would apply by virtue of its subsequent position; for that is not the case, owing to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.

[Objection: But surely, on the view that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed [in Pāṇini’s rule], there would be no specification of the meaning for *la* (the verbal suffix) which is the subject of elision (*luk*) by the rule *ām*. [Reply: Not so. For even *luk* (elision) is established as having a meaning because it is a substitute (*ādeśa*). This is because, in the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, it has been shown that even an elision (*lopa*) functions like a substitute (*stānivadbhāva*) when it is a substitute beginning with *ij*. Nor is it impossible for an absence-form substitute to express a meaning; for, although it lacks connection with actual usage—just like *kvip* and other such suffixes—it is inferred to possess meaning through the author's formal declaration (*pratijñā*), and its meaning is manifested by means of the subsequent verb form (*anuprayoga*). Otherwise, the rule *kartari kṛt* (P. 3.4.67) would also fail to apply to *kvip* and the like.

As for the claim that there is a connection with the meaning only when [the suffix] is in the *jas*-form (i.e., plural), whereas in the case of the genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), there is the burden of supplying a substitute (*ādeśa*) and an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), that is incorrect. For those who maintain that the power of the substitute resides in the meanings inherent in actual usage—due to the proximity of the meaning—the aforementioned objection is not a fault, since they accept that the indication of the meaning occurs precisely through the substitute. Therefore, the meanings are the action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*).

For this very reason, the rule governing the distribution of case-endings based on whether these are expressed or not expressed has been elaborated upon in the *Anabhihita-sūtra*; such is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*).

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that effort (*kṛti*) alone is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). If the denotatum (*śakti*) were the substratum of effort, then effort would be the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and the property of being an effort (*kṛtitva*) would be the delimitor of that delimitor; this involves complexity (*gaurava*). But if effort itself is the denotatum, then the property of being an effort is simply the delimitor of denotability, which is simpler (*lāghava*). Furthermore, [the substratum] is obtained from the nominative word itself. This is because when effort is construed with Caitra and others through the relation of substratum-hood, the sentence-meaning is "Caitra is the substratum of effort," and thus the substratum of effort is cognized.

As for the objection that since the suffixes *śatṛ*, *śānac*, and others are also substitutes (*lādeśa*) for *la*, they would have to denote mere effort (*kṛti*) by virtue of their denotative power; and since the relation of difference between the meanings of two nouns is untenable, it would be impossible for the agent to appear as a relational qualifier, and thus you too would have to admit that these suffixes refer to the agent—[we reply: even so, in your view, since the substituendum (*sthānin*) itself is the expressive unit, how could that [substituendum] in a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*) refer to mere effort? This has been refuted in many ways in the *Paspaśā* [section of the Mahābhāṣya].

As for what was stated—that the non-difference between name and meaning (*nāmārtha*) constitutes their relation (*saṃsarga*), which serves as the basis for treating *kṛt* suffixes as denoters of the agent—that is equivalent to the position that *tiṅ* suffixes [denote the agent] as well, in accordance with examples such as *pacatikalpaḥ* and *pacatirūpam*. This is because a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, if one asserts that a *tiṅ* suffix is not a name (*nāman*), then no [suffix] would be a name at all. And if it is said that a name ends in the letter *a*, then by parity of reasoning, words ending in *kalpa* and so forth would likewise be names.

That is incorrect; for while being a *taddhita*-suffix ending is the determinant of being a noun (*nāmatva*), it is the denotability of that [ending] which is the determinant of being a noun. [If one were to argue that] "there would be no syntactic connection with a difference," in that case, the reference is to the locus (*āśraya*). However, in examples such as *pacatikalpam*, being a *taddhita*-suffix ending is the determinant of being a noun, yet the denotability of that [ending] does not belong to the action (*kṛti*), but rather belongs only to the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Thus, since there is an absence of being the meaning of a noun, there is no obstacle to the locus having the status of a relation (*saṃsargatā*).

If the meaning of a noun (*nāma*) were simply whatever word-meaning happens to be included within a collection that has attained the status of a name, then by accepting a "segmented power" (*khaṇḍaśakti*) for the verbal root (*dhātu*), the result (*phala*) would be a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*) through the relation of being its producer. In that case, how could your own established doctrine—that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) [qualifies the operation]—be maintained in examples such as *pacati kalpam* ("he cooks slightly")? This is because the locus of the result and the locus of the operation would both become the meaning of the noun, and thus they would be incapable of being construed with each other through a relation of mutual difference. And so it is said: "The verbal root is traditionally held to denote the result and the operation, while the verbal suffixes denote the locus."

"The operation (vyāpāra) is primary in the fruit (phala), while the meaning of the verbal suffix (tiṅ-artha) is a qualifier"—starting from such [principles], the establishment of our own correct view proceeds as follows: As for what was stated regarding the Grammarians' (Śābdika) position—that the meaning of the verbal suffix is the locus (āśraya) alone, since both the fruit and the operation are obtained from the verbal root itself; that in some cases the operation is construed [with the suffix] and in others the fruit; and that the locus-ness is an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) power-form (śakti-rūpa) which serves as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka), and thus there is no charge of excessive complexity (gaurava) due to the entry of the *kṛt* suffixes and so forth—[we respond as follows].

That too is incorrect; for it would result in the unintended consequence that the object is expressed in "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), and the agent is expressed in "Caitra is cooked" (*caitreṇa pacyate*). Nor can it be argued that the substratum (*āśraya*) functioning as a qualifier of the fruit-portion is the meaning of the term *karma* (object), while the substratum functioning as a qualifier of the activity-portion is the meaning of the agent-affix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*). For if the substratum qualified by both the fruit and the activity were the denotatum, it would follow that both the object and the agent are denoted. If, on the other hand, the fruit and the activity are taken merely as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), there would be no common indicator-determinant (*upalakṣyatāvacchedaka*) to unify them.

Now, if it is argued that the objective power (*karma-śakti*) is in reality distinct from the agentive power (*kartṛ-śakti*), and therefore, even though both are expressed by the term "substratum" (*āśraya*), the distinction is established solely by whether the substrata consisting of the objective and agentive powers are denoted or not denoted—this is not so. For if the mere power were the referent, then since Caitra and other such subjects (the possessors of those powers) could not logically enter into a relation of non-difference with that [power], the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) intended by you—as taught in rules such as *yuṣmadyupapade*—would result in collapse.

Furthermore, since the position that "capacity (*śakti*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*)" is presented in the foundational texts merely as the view of others and not as the author's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is justified. Otherwise, given the rule *kartari kṛt* ("kṛt suffixes denote the agent"), if suffixes such as *śānac* were to denote only capacity, coreferentiality would be untenable. Moreover, the *Vākyapadīya* states, "The six [categories] are eternal for others," thereby indicating that it is one of several alternative views. Finally, it is because the locus of the operation expressed by the verbal root is designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*), while the locus of the resulting fruit is designated as the "object" (*karman*).

If it is argued that [the existence of] a power (*śakti*) as an independent entity is unestablished, then the burden of complexity (*gaurava*)—namely, that the substratum (*āśraya*) denoted by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is an indivisible [entity]—is unavoidable. Furthermore, the view that "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) consists of an indivisible power is not established by the texts of the [Pāṇinian] tradition; for it is the power itself that is established as indivisible by the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities, and you yourself have now abandoned that very position.

If it is argued that this statement was made on the basis of the position that "being a substratum" (*āśrayatva*) consists merely in being a locus (*ādhāratva*), and not with the intention of referring to a power (*śakti*), we say no. This is because it would contradict your own statement that [the relation] is an indivisible power-form (*akhaṇḍa-śakti-rūpa*). Furthermore, if even the third and subsequent case-endings (*vibhakti*) had only "substratum" as their meaning, the conventional usage of them as denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth would be unestablished; moreover, it would contradict grammatical rules such as *kartṛ-karaṇayos tṛtīyā* ("the third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument").

Furthermore, since you yourself accept that the terms *kartṛ* (agent) and *karman* (object) refer merely to the substratum (*āśraya*)—namely, the substratum of the activity (*vyāpāra*) and the substratum of the result (*phala*) respectively—it is untenable for you to charge me with the fault of [my view] being limited to the mere effort (*kṛti*) in the case of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*). This is because partial reference (*ekadeśaparatā*) exists in both cases. Nor can you argue that partial reference applies to both [the agent and object] in my view, but only to one in yours; for when partial reference is present in both, it is more logical that it applies to only one. Thus, this is a clumsy exposure of your own vital weakness.

Furthermore, the position that "capacity" (*śakti*) is the *kāraka* is indeed the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the original treatises (*ākara*). This is because, in the rule *saptamī-pañcamyau*, the author of the Sūtras himself has stated that [the case endings] denote being "in the midst of *kārakas*"; because the author of the Bhāṣya has provided a solution based on that very position; because in great works such as the Vṛtti, Nyāsa, and Kaiyaṭa, [the rule] *samāna-kartṛka* and others have been explained precisely by means of the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the capacity and its possessor; and because the commentary on the *anabhihita* rule has been explained by relying solely on the position of capacity—this is perfectly clear to those who know the original treatises.

By this, the claim that the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth must be denoted [by the verb] in order to account for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also refuted. For if the capacity (*śakti*) were the factor of action (*kāraka*), then even in your own view, coreferentiality—in the form of denoting a single substratum through two distinct attributes—would be untenable. In my view, however, it is easily established that [the word] denotes attributes residing in a single locus. Furthermore, the objection that "if [the verb] denoted only the effort (*kṛti*), the agent would not be expressed, and thus the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would result" is merely the prattle of a child.

Even if [the position] were that [the verb expresses] the substratum alone, the objection would be equally applicable, since there is no difference between the two cases regarding the fact that the qualified [agent] is not expressed. If it is argued that "the non-expression of the substratum is precisely the non-expression of the agent," we reply that this is simply the non-expression of the action (kṛti), as it is equally subject to criticism.

By this, the view that the agent is the expressed meaning (vācya), based on the statement of the Vārttika beginning with "when [the agent] is expressed, the first case-suffix occurs" (abhihite prathamā), is also refuted; for what is intended there is precisely the non-expression of the capacity (śakti).

"Power (*śakti*) whose primary object is the [action] is denoted by the suffix," according to the writings of authoritative texts such as the *Vākyapadīya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. Therefore, in the sentence "The rice is cooked by Caitra," the meaning of the instrumental case is the operation (*vyāpāra*), the meaning of the verbal root is the effort (*kṛti*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the result (*phala*), and the relation is that of being produced (*janyatva*). The resulting cognition is: "The rice possesses a result produced by an effort residing in Caitra."

The Teachers (Ācāryas), however, maintain that when the number of the agent is not expressed, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used, and when the number of the object is not expressed, the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is used; specifically, when there is singularity of the object, the singular form of the second case is employed. This is because the section concerning "the unexpressed" (*anabhihita-adhikāra*) is meaningful only under the view that the number is the meaning of the case-ending. Under the view that the "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, this [interpretation] is established as being refuted in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, there is no lack of a restrictive rule regarding the statement that in "Caitra cooks the rice," it is only the number of Caitra that is expressed.

In cases such as *caitraḥ śākasūpau pacati* ("Caitra cooks vegetables and soup"), *śākasūpaudanān pacati* ("He cooks vegetables, soup, and rice"), *caitreṇa śākaḥ pacyate* ("Vegetables are cooked by Caitra"), and *śākasūpau pacyete* ("Vegetables and soup are being cooked"), one observes the exclusion of contradictory numbers; for it is observed that the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) applies respectively to the agent and the object, since it is determined that this application occurs even when both [the agent and the object] are expressed in the singular. This is according to the maxim: "A rule of grammar established in one instance applies elsewhere as well."

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that in cases such as "the sacrificial porridge (caru) consists of barley," the word *yava*—which is determined through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) to refer to long-bearded barley—is understood to refer to that same thing even in the absence of a sentence-remainder in passages such as "he sprinkles the sacrificial post with water mixed with *vaimatī* [barley-flour]. Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) denoting number, since the requirement is satisfied by the number's connection with the nominative case-meaning alone. For the nominative case would then result in not expressing number at all, serving merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), given that the delimitors of expressiveness (*vācakatāvacchedaka*)—namely, the status of being a singular suffix and so on—are identical.

The meanings of the nominal suffixes (*sup*) include the object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as number (*saṃkhyā*); likewise for the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). This is because there exists evidence for the apprehension of such capacities in the form of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*. Furthermore, in examples such as "Caitra and Maitra go," it would follow that the singularity and other numbers of the person being addressed could not be understood; for it is impossible for one who is not insane to maintain that the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) could be construed with that [person]. Since both [the nominal and verbal suffixes] are authoritatively established as denoters of number.

Otherwise, the rule *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) would be untenable in the subsequent sūtra. The meaning is that [the suffix *kta*] occurs after intransitive verbs in the sense of the action (*bhāva*), but after transitive verbs in the sense of the object (*karman*). Examples: *caitreṇa śayitavyam* ("it must be slept by Caitra") and *paktavya odanaḥ* ("the rice is to be cooked"). The word *eva* has been explained. *kta* [is used] in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*) and also in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). (Pāṇini 3.4.71)

In the *niṣṭhā* sūtra, the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] are stated to occur in the sense of the beginning of an action; they occur with the agent (*kartṛ*), as appropriate, and also in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). For example: *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta has begun making the mat); *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaścaitreṇa* (the mat has been begun by Caitra). *śayitaṃ devadattena* (it has been slept by Devadatta).
[The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are also used after roots] meaning "to go," after intransitive roots, and after the roots *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.72)

The suffix *kta* is as previously explained. Examples: *gaṅgāṃ gataḥ* (gone to the Ganges), *gaṅgāṃ prāptaḥ* (reached the Ganges); or, in the alternative sense, "the Ganges was reached by him. [As it is said: "Where one sleeps, one does not desire any object of desire. *lakṣmīm āśliṣṭo hariḥ* (Hari embraced Lakṣmī). But in the alternative sense, it is like one embraced by his beloved who, having lain down completely, perceives nothing external. Otherwise, since it would already be established by the very fact of being intransitive (*akarmaka*), this rule would be redundant. Other cases are similar. The words *dāśa* and *goghna* are used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). (Pāṇini 3.4.73)

The *dāśa* (servant) gives to him; the guest who kills a cow for him is called a *godhna*. For instance, when another [guest] arrives at a royal court, it is heard in the scripture: "He shall eat a bull or a barren cow.
The suffix *apādāne* (indicating the point of departure) is applied after the words *bhīma*, etc. (Pāṇini 3.4.74).

*Bhīma* means "one from whom others fear"; *bhīṣma* means "the cause of fear. *Praskandana* and *prarakṣa* mean "one who leaps forward" or "one who protects. *Camū* means "an army. *Khalati* means "bald.
Other words beginning with the suffix *uṇ* are derived from these two roots (*cam* and *khal*). 75.

The *uṇādi* suffixes may occur when there is a factor other than the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) or the source (*apādāna*). Thus, from the root *tan*, we have *tantuḥ* (thread); from *vṛt*, *vartma* (path); and from *car*, *carma* (skin). Furthermore, the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after roots whose meanings involve remaining stationary (*dhrauvya*), motion (*gati*), or consumption (*pratyavasāna*).

The suffix *kta* shall occur after these [roots] when they denote the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). In other cases, it occurs as prescribed by the general rules. The inclusion of "those whose action is fixed" (*dhruva*) refers to intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*). This is because in the rule *dhruvaceṣṭitayuktāḥ*, the term *dhruvayukti* includes the intransitives. Examples: *āsyate 'smin* → *āsitam* (the place where one sits); *gamyate 'tra* → *gatam* (the place where one goes); *bhujyate 'tra* → *bhuktam* (the place where one eats). In the alternative case: *āsito mukundaḥ* (Mukunda has sat), *tena āsitam* (he has sat), and so forth. [Now begins the section on] *la*. (77)

This is the specification of the substituends (*sthānin*) for the suffixes to be mentioned hereafter. Nor should it be argued that if the rule were applied to a mere phoneme (*varṇa*), the maxim *arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā* would find no scope, leading to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *lunāti* and *cūḍāla*; for the term *dhātoḥ* (from a verbal root) is understood by anuvṛtti. And that [term *dhātoḥ*] qualifies what is prescribed; therefore, there is no undesired application in the case of *agnicillabhate*. Nor is there over-extension in the case of the suffix *la* prescribed after the roots *śā*, *mā*, and *mlā* (as in *śālā*, *mālā*, *mālā*) by the rule *śāmāmalibhyo laḥ*; for we accept that these are non-etymological (*avyutpanna*) words. Nor is there a fault regarding the suffix *lyuṭ* in words like *candana*; for that is precluded by the assignment of the technical designation *it*.

When an elision (*lopa*) has occurred, the original element (*sthānin*) no longer exists; furthermore, since this is not a rule prescribing an *al*-element (*al-vidhi*), the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited. Nor does the designation of *it* (*itsaṃjñā*) apply here either, because there is no purpose for it. Nor is the accent of the *lit* affix (*litsvara*) itself the purpose, because by the *bahuvrīhi* compound *laidyasya*, an affix is prescribed whose *la* member is such that its parts are designated as *it*.

If it is argued: "Even though the designation *it* has been applied by resorting to various *karmadhāraya* compounds, because of the power of the rule prescribing *tiP* and other suffixes while restating *l*, there is no elision (*lopa*). Furthermore, since the term 'bhāva' and so forth continue to apply, it is impossible to prescribe substitutes for *la* in the sense of 'bhāva' and the like; therefore, let the substitutes *tiP* and others belong to those [forms of *l*] where elision has not yet occurred"—this is not correct. For even so, the designation *it* would be purposeless. Alternatively, the nasalized *l* is taken here as being *sthānin* (the original element). Or else, *laḥ* is a form with an elided genitive case (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). By the pronoun *asya* ("of this"), there is a reference to that which expresses the meaning of 'bhāva' and so forth.
tip, tas, jhi; sip, thas, tha; mip, vas, mas; tāt, tāṃ, jha; thās, āthām, dhvam; iṅ, vahi, mahiṅ. || 78 ||

These eighteen shall be substitutes for *la*. Here, there is either a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) or separate words. The letter *p* is for the sake of making [the substitute] unaccented (*anudātta*) and for the sake of preventing it from being treated as having the marker *ṅ*. The letter *ṭ* in *iṭaṣṭakāra* is for the purpose of qualifying [the substitute] in the rule *iṭo't*. If only the letter *i* were used, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *at* even for the *i* of *vah* and *mahiṅ*. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of forming the pratyāhāra *tiṅ*; it is an indicatory marker (*anubandha*) of the entire group, not of a single component, according to the traditional explanation.

Therefore, even though the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) *p* is a constituent part of the *sup* suffix, there is no harm in its being used for the purpose of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation). Consequently, in forms such as *saṃpapracchimahe* and *saṃvavraścimahe*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization). Furthermore, in the case of the root *iṣ* with the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative) in the sense of "desire," as in *eṣiṣīmahi*, the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *kṅiti ca* does not apply.
[Now follows: *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere* (Pāṇini 3.4.79).

The substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* of the *ātmanepada* substitutes of *la* [the verbal suffixes] shall take place. Thus, *edhate*, *edhete*, *edhante*, and so forth. Now, an objection might arise that the rule would apply excessively (*ativyāpti*) to forms such as *pavamāna*. However, there is no fault, because it has been indicated (*jñāpita*) by the fact that the substitute *gāṅ* for the root *iṅ* (to study) is marked with the *ṅit* indicator that operations dependent on the *it* indicator do not apply to a substitute when it is accompanied by an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*). This is because, in this context, the quality of being *ṭit* is employed as a qualifier of the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix), and not as a qualifier of the *ātmanepada*. Nor can the reading found in some manuscripts—"of the *ṭit* *ātmanepada* suffixes"—be used to resolve the difficulty.

In the case of *akurvi*, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the substitution of *et* even for the *iṭ* augment of the first person singular ending. However, if the *ṭ* is taken as a qualifier of the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix), then since it is a substitute for *laṅ*, there is no such fault. Objection: It should rather be stated that this [ending] is *ḍit* itself, and one should read the rule simply as *iṭo'd*. Otherwise, in forms such as *laviṣīṣṭa*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *iṭ* augment itself being replaced by *ad*. Reply: Not so. In the Vedic passage *iṣamūrjamahamita ādīta*, the *iṭ* of the first person singular *laṅ* is treated as *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*. Therefore, this [ending] is indeed *ṭit*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of it being merely an augment (*āgama*).

It should not be argued that the presence of *ṭ* is an indicator (*liṅga*) of an augment (*āgama*). For when the word *laḥ* is uttered once, if it were to convey the relationship between part and whole through the genitive case, it would result in favoring the augment *iṭ* alone; however, it is more logical to favor the majority [of elements]. This is because [the rule] conveys only the relationship of the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), and consequently, the augment *iṭ* is also understood as a substitute (*ādeśa*) in accordance with that. Nor is there a fault in the form *caliṣīṣṭa*, because the augment *iṭ*—which depends on the base (*aṅga*) being followed by a *val*-beginning ārdhadhātuka suffix—is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) and thus considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the substitution *iṭ* (for *si*) is to be applied based on its connection with the *liṅ* suffix.
Therefore, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) in forms such as *pavamānaḥ* is unavoidable.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *ti* and so forth here, the substitution of *ā* for the final phoneme (*ṭi*) is prescribed for those [suffixes] that take the form of *ātmanepada*. Alternatively, Kaiyaṭa maintains that it is because, by virtue of the context, only *ti* and so forth are referred to by the word "ātmanepada. By this, the doubt that one should instead read the rule as *ṭitaḥ taṅām* is explained away.
The *Atra-vārtika* states:
"But this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the substitution of *e* [in place of *ai*] in the case of *ṭit*, *taṅ*, *ām*, *śi*, and *sīr*."

Regarding the rule *ḍāraurasaḥ ṭitaḥ*: how can there be *tadguṇa* (the substitution of the original) here? Its meaning is this: if [the substitution] were for the element *etva* (the replacement of *ā* by *e*), then [the rule] *āne mug* would not apply; for that would result in the undesirable form *ānayi mug*. Therefore, it is made known that *etva* applies to those *taṅ* affixes which are substitutes for *ṭit*, but not to *āna* as well. Even so, one might ask why [the substitution of] *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* does not occur in forms such as *adhyetā*; to this he says: *iśi sīrica*. For the sake of brevity, the substitutes *iś*, *si*, and *iri* should be prescribed by the two rules *liṭas tajhayoreśirec* and *thāsaḥ se*; because *etva* is already established by the rule *ṭita* itself.

Therefore, the prescription of the substitute *ekāra* (e) for the *lādeśas* is for the purpose of making known the absence of *etva* (the substitution of *e*) for those [substitutes] that do not have *iṭ*. The solution to the problem regarding *akurvi* is as follows: in the case of *laṅ*, which is designated by *aṭ* (*aṭita*), the *ṭit* suffix *iṭ* does not undergo *etva*. This is because, in the present context, the prescription of *taṅ* applies only to those [suffixes] that are included within the *taṅ-pratyāhāra*, whereas *iṭ* is excluded from that *pratyāhāra*. The phrase "for the sake of *guṇa*" is for the purpose of the subsequent rule. Regarding the question: "In *pacāveda*, once *aguṇa* has been applied, why does *etva* (via *eta-ai*) not occur?", the answer must be stated in that very place. **Thāsaḥ se || 80 ||** [The substitute *se* is applied in place of *thās*.]
In place of *thās* following a suffix marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, *se* shall be substituted. As in: *edhase*. Why "following a *ṭi*-suffix"? Consider: *edhathāḥ*.
In place of *ta* and *jha* of the *liṭ* [perfect] suffixes, *eś* and *irec* are substituted respectively.

These two [suffixes] are respectively the substitutes for the two forms of the *liṭ* affix. *Cakre*, *cakrire*. The designation *śit* is for the purpose of making it a substitute for the whole [stem]. The letter *c* is for the purpose of [marking] the high-pitched accent (*udātta*) at the end.
For the *parasmaipada* [affixes], there are the following substitutes: *ṇal*, *atus*, *us*, *thal*, *a*, *tha*, *us*, *ṇal*, and *vam*. (Pāṇini 3.4.82)
These [forms] are, respectively, the substitutes for the nine *liṭ* suffixes beginning with *tiP*, such as *babhūva*, *babhūvatuḥ*, and so forth.

"The inclusion of the marker *ṇ* in *ṇal* is for the purpose of making it a substitute for the whole [stem]; otherwise, it would apply only to the final letter [of the stem]. Nor can its status as a substitute for the whole be established merely by virtue of having multiple letters (*anekāl*) due to the presence of the marker *ṇ*, because there is no determining factor [to restrict it otherwise], and because it is accepted that the property of having multiple letters is not produced by a marker (*anubandha*). And this applies under the view that the section on verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*) precedes the rules for substitutes (*l-ādeśa*). Otherwise, however, the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (P. 1.1.54) would have to be applied."

Although, if the letter *ś* were pronounced before the letter *ṇ*, then because it would not be at the beginning of an affix (*pratyaya*), the designation *it* would not apply to the *ṇ*; and if it were in the middle, it would not apply to the *ś*; and if it were at the end, it would not apply to the *l*. Nevertheless, *l* is what must be prescribed. The intention of the Vārttika is that one should read "laś" [instead of "ṇal"], or that an extension (*atideśa*) should be stated such that "ṇal is treated like śit. Nor is the status of being *ṇit* (having *ṇ* as an indicatory letter) necessary for the purpose of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*). This is established by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as: "after *go*, [the ending] is *ṇit*; *laś* and *laś* are treated as *ṇit*, and from that, the last [vowel] becomes long. Do not say so. For this is already established by the letter *l* itself, which is indispensable for the sake of the accent (*lit-svara*).

Now, one might object: since the suffix *pratyaya* is *anudātta* because it is marked with *pit*, and the verbal root (*dhātu*) is *antodātta*, then when the subsequent reduplication (*dvirvacana*) takes place, the result would be established by an *antodātta* substitute due to *āntaratamya* (phonetic proximity); thus, there would be no purpose for the accentuation of the *liṭ* suffix here. Nor should it be argued that, by the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as identical to its designation), since the quality of being *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) also exists [in the reduplicated form], that accent would consequently apply. This is because the rule "like the original" (*sthānivat*) is an extension of a grammatical operation (*śāstrātideśa*), and by the rule "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), only an *antodātta* is established; for there is no rule prescribing an *ādyudātta* for the verbal root.

Not so; for it is established that the rule *sthānivat* is a transfer (*atideśa*) of grammatical operations. Furthermore, since the *dvirvacana* (doubling) taught in the sixth book (*Aṣṭādhyāyī*) refers to the "original" (*sthānin*), there would result a final acute accent (*antodātta*) for both [the original and the substitute] due to the absence of doubling in the original. Therefore, the accent of the *liṭ* suffix must necessarily be taken into account. However, in the case of a multi-vocalic root (*anekāc*) that is acutely accented on the final syllable, once the *śeṣanighāta* (subsequent suppression of other accents) has occurred, there is no distinction between the first vowel being doubled and its resulting in a completely grave (*sarvānudātta*) tone. In the case of a mono-vocalic root (*ekāc*), the accent of the *liṭ* suffix should be understood [as applying]. As to how the *ā* of the substitute for the second-person plural ending attains the status of a complete replacement (*sarvādeśatva*), this has been explained in the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) beginning with *dhātoḥ*.
The suffix *laṭ* is optionally used after the root *vid*.

After the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing," the suffixes *ṇal* and so forth may optionally replace the present tense marker (*laṭ*). Thus: *veda*, *vidatuḥ*, *viduḥ*. Due to the rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*), there is no reduplication. In the alternative case: *vetti*, *vittaḥ*, *vidanti*, and so on. [Pāṇini 3.4.84] *bruvaḥ pañcānāmādita āho bruvaḥ*: For the five [suffixes beginning with *liṭ*], *āha* replaces *brū* (the root *brū* in the sense of "speaking").

The root *brūñ* means "in distinct speech. After this root, the five suffixes beginning with *tiP* (i.e., *tiP*, *tas*, *jhi*, *siP*, *thas*) are respectively replaced by the five substitutes beginning with *ṇal* (i.e., *ṇal*, *atus*, *us*, *thal*, *athus*). Furthermore, *bruvaḥ* (the root *brū*) is replaced by *āh*. [Examples: *āha*, *āhatuḥ*, *āhuḥ*; *āttha*, *āhathuḥ*. Vāmana, Gada, and others maintain that the usage of this root in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta-artha*) is based on error.
[Sūtra 1.4.85: "In place of the *loṭ* [suffixes], those of the *laṅ* [are substituted]."

In the example *loṭaḥ*, the genitive case is seen in the object of comparison (*upameya*); therefore, in *laṅa iva*, the suffix *vati* is applied based on the genitive compound. Consequently, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of whatever operation applies to the *laṅ* [tense], but not of that which is prescribed when *laṅ* follows. Thus, the two rules—"the augment *aṭ* is udātta in *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*" and "the augment *āṭ* is added to the beginning of vowel-initial [roots] after these"—do not apply to the *loṭ*. It might be argued: in forms such as *yāntu* and *pāntu*, the suffix *jus* would occur by the rule "for *laṅ*, according to Śākaṭāyana," and the substitution of *utva* (of *ā* to *o*) would not be an obstacle, because [the *jus*] is introduced by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

This is because [the rule] *vānto yi pratyaye* and others have been explained in that very same way by the Bhāṣya and other authorities; for, by reversing the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified and applying the *tadantavidhi*, one would have to explain it as "of that which ends in /s/ and has /ṅ/, /l/, or the first person ending," which results in the elision of /s/ via the *alontyaparibhāṣā*, and this is burdened by excessive complexity (*gaurava*).
Furthermore, from this [it follows]. (100)

In the case of the substitutes for *ṅit* [affixes] among the *parasmaipada* endings, there should be the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *i*. But if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the elision of the *i* in the substitute *yās* in forms such as *bhavet*. Nor should it be argued that because of the explanation regarding the substitute *iy*, there is no fault here due to its subsequent position (and thus the rule does not apply), since for that very reason, there would still be the contingency of elision even for the augment *īṭ* in forms like *abobhavīt*. This is not correct; for in forms such as *aruditām*, the fault remains unavoidable even then. Do not say so. For the word *itaḥ* is understood from a previous rule, and the meaning is that there is elision of an *i* that is of the form *it* (i.e., the phoneme *i*).

Furthermore, the absoluteness (*atyantatva*) of the qualifier [in the rule *parasmaipadeṣu*] is established because such [a qualifier] alone is prescribed for elision; otherwise, the qualifier would be redundant. This is because, in the alternative explanation—where one changes the locative ending of *parasmaipadeṣu* into a genitive singular (*parasmaipadasya*) and interprets it as "of that parasmaipada which ends in /i/"—there is the fault of violating both the case-ending portion and the number portion, resulting in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
*Tasthas-thamipāṃ tāmtamtāmaḥ* || 101 || [The substitutes *ta*, *tha*, and *tha* for *tas*, *thas*, and *tha*; and *mip* for *mi* are replaced by *tam*, *tam*, and *tām*, respectively.]
For the suffixes *tas* and so forth belonging to those [roots ending in *ṅit*], *tām* and so forth shall occur in their respective order: *abhavatām*, *abhavataṃ*, *abhavata*, *abhavam*.
The augment *sīyuṭ* is applied after the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

Because this [suffix *sīyuṭ*] is superseded by *yāsuṭ*, which is specifically prescribed for the *parasmaipada*, its application occurs in the *ātmanepada*. It should not be argued that just as *sīyuṭ* occurs after [the suffix] *suṭ* has been applied in forms such as *kṛṣīṣṭhāḥ*, so too would it occur even when *yāsuṭ* has been applied; for since *yāsuṭ* is a part of the *liṅ* [suffix], there is no conflict with *sīyuṭ*, which begins with that [same *liṅ*]. This is because, despite the absence of conflict, a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) supersedes a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*), as is established in the case of curd and buttermilk (*dadhitakra*). We shall explain the difference regarding *suṭ* later. The letter *ṭ* is for the sake of specifying the position [of the augment], and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation.
The affix *yāsuṭ* is acute-accented and marked with the *ṅit* indicatory letter when applied to *parasmaipada* endings.

The *yāsuṭ* augment added to the *parasmaipada* endings of the optative (*liṅ*) is acute (*udātta*) and marked with the *ṅit* designation. For example: *cinuyuḥ*, *sunuyuḥ*. It has been explained in detail under the rule *ādyudāttaśca* that the explicit mention of "acute" is for the purpose of indicating that the augments themselves are unaccented (*anudātta*).
[Pāṇini 3.4.104: *kidāśiṣi*. [In the case of the optative expressing a blessing (*āśis*), the affixes are marked with the *kit* designation.]

The augment *yāsuṭ* shall be *kit* in the case of the *liṅ* (optative) used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). [Examples: *bhūyāt*. Although the prohibition of *guṇa* is already established by the fact that [the *liṅ*] is *ṅit*, the *kit* designation is introduced for the sake of *saṃprasāraṇa* in forms such as *ijyāt* (from *yaj*), according to the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti*. Furthermore, in *jāgaryāt*, the *kit* designation is initiated for the sake of *guṇa*, according to the rule *jāgro 'vicirṇalṅitsu*.
[Rule 105: For *jha*, there is *ran*.

For the *jh* suffix of the optative (*liṅ*), *ran* shall be substituted. [As in: *yajeran*. This is an exception to the rule "for *jh*, *anta*" (Pāṇini 3.4.105). [Now,] for the *iṭ* augment, *at* shall be substituted. (106)

The augment *iṭ* in the third person singular of the optative (*liṅ*) shall be replaced by *ad*. [Thus we get] *labheya*. The prevention of the over-extension of the augment *iṭ* has been stated previously. Nor does there arise the contingency of the prohibition of the designation *it* for the letter *t* by the rule *na vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 1.3.4), because the letter *t* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation and is not a constituent part of the substitute (*ādeśa*).
[Next: *suṭ tithoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107).

The augment *suṭ* shall be applied to the *takāra* and *thakāra* of the *liṅ*. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. [Examples: *bhaviṣīṣṭa*. Nor does there arise an objection that this [rule] would subvert the application of *sīyuṭ* just as it does *yāsuṭ*, because their domains differ: *sīyuṭ* is prescribed for the *liṅ*, whereas *suṭ* is prescribed for *t* and *th*. For this very reason, the *liṅ* has not been explained as the qualified [head-word]. Otherwise, since *suṭ* would also result in being a constituent part (*avayava*) of the *liṅ*, there would arise the undesirable consequence that *sīyuṭ* would be subverted by *suṭ*. *jharjus* || 108 || [The substitute *jus* is applied in place of the *jhaḥ* [the six endings from *jas* to *sup*] when they follow a stem ending in a consonant.]
After the *liṅ* (optative) suffixes, *jhi* is replaced by *jum*. This is an exception to [the substitution of] *jha*. [Examples: *bhaveyuḥ*.
Also after the *sij* (aorist), the reduplicated (*abhyasta*), and *vidi*: [the same substitution applies]. (Pāṇini 3.4.109)

The commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of the non-causative (*aliṅ*) meaning. Here, the root *vid* (to know) is included; otherwise, because of the intervention of the *vikaraṇa* suffixes, it would be impossible for the *jhi* suffix to follow immediately. Furthermore, since the roots *vid* in the sense of "obtaining" and "existence" are *ātmanepada*, the *jhi* suffix itself is impossible there. The mention of the "reduplicated" (*abhyasta*) and "the two *vid*s" is for the sake of including the form *as* (to be). By the continued application of the term "having an indicatory *ṅ*" (*ṅitaḥ*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the present tense (*laṭ*) and other such forms. After the *sic* augment, after a reduplicated stem, and after the two *vid*s, the *jhi* suffix that is connected with an indicatory *ṅ* is replaced by *jum*. Examples: *acetiṣuḥ*, *ajuhavuḥ*, *aviduḥ*.
